He’s also developing a changeup, but needs to further refine the pitch as he hardly needed to throw it against prep hitters. Lange added 25 pounds of muscle prior to the Draft and entered the Padres system with a lofty ceiling. In order to reach that ceiling he’ll have to improve his secondary pitches and tighten up his inconsistent command. It’s an encouraging sign that he’s already shown the ability to improve the slider and considering he’ll be just 20-years-old for the bulk of the 2022 season, Lange has time to refine his game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lange put his name on the map with a big-time fastball that erupted in the early spring preceding the 2020 Draft. He routinely hit the upper 90s and touched 100 mph, vaulting into the supplemental first round, where he signed with the Padres for $2 million as the 34th overall selection. After he made a rocky 2021 pro debut in Rookie ball, San Diego traded him to the Yankees for Luke Voit in March. Lange's fastball sits in the mid-90s and can feature both run and sink. He has the makings of a second power pitch in a slider that could become a plus mid-80s weapon with bite. The pitch is inconsistent, however, and should be a focal point of Lange’s as he begins to face pro hitters. He will also incorporate a changeup, which he rarely threw against high-school opposition. A quick-twitch athlete, Lange added 25 pounds of muscle in the offseason prior to the Draft and had one of the best bodies in the 2020 high school pitching class. He has a huge ceiling but will need time to reach it, given his unrefined secondary pitches and shaky control and command. His slightly unorthodox low-arm-slot delivery also raises a few question marks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Guardians used their savings on No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana to invest heavily in high school pitching in the 2024 Draft, and one of their most exciting finds was Oakie, who signed for a well-over-slot $2 million in the third round. The Gatorade Iowa High School Player of the Year for 2024, Oakie displayed wobbly command to begin his pro career in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League but had an ascendant end to the season with Single-A Lynchburg, where he compiled a 2.22 ERA with 31 strikeouts in 24 1/3 frames. Oakie is armed with perhaps the best two-pitch mix of any starter in the Guardians' system. His mid-80s slider -- the righty's top knockout offering -- was one of the best in his Draft class and features two-plane depth and plenty of spin. His fastball sits 94-98 mph and actually improved in velocity over the year, which is impressive considering it declined over his final high school season. He's working on a sinker to differentiate from the four-seamer, and his low release point helps give his changeup ample arm-side movement, although he still needs to work on its playability after barely using it in his debut season. The main thing holding Oakie back to date is his strike-throwing, which adds relief risk. The Guardians believe that they'll be able to help sync up his delivery more as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame, but his control is currently below average, with his command a tick behind that. Given that he's a long, fluid multisport athlete (basketball) from a cold-weather state, there's plenty of reason to believe he has untapped potential to become a mid-rotation starter, although his two plus pitches can make him a devastating reliever if the command never comes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Oakie stood out the most in a deep 2023 Area Code Games, striking out five of the 12 batters he missed while reaching 96 mph and throwing some unhittable sliders. He also excelled at the 18-and-under World Cup that fall and while winning Gatorade Iowa high school player of the year accolades last spring. The state's highest-drafted prep pitcher since 2014 (Mitch Keller), he signed for a well-over-slot $2 million as a third-rounder. Oakie featured one of the best sliders in the 2024 Draft, a mid-80s weapon with two-plane depth and plenty of horizontal movement. It works well in tandem with his two-seam fastball, which sits at 92-94 mph and tops out at 97 with considerable armside run and sink. He has begun to work on a changeup with similar action, though it was too firm in high school and he barely used it in games. While Oakie doesn't have an ideal starter's delivery and needs to provide more consistent strikes, he does have a quick arm and works with little effort. He adds deception with a flat approach angle that could be conducive to throwing a four-seamer with more velocity and carry up in the zone. His competitiveness and work ethic contribute to his mid-rotation upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: TJ Pre-Season 2026
mlb_pipeline.text: Forret wasn’t a Draft pick or a sought-after recruit coming out of Providence HS in Charlotte, N.C., ultimately landing at State College of Florida’s Manatee-Sarasota campus. That put him close enough to Baltimore’s Spring Training/Minor League complex in Sarasota for the Orioles to get plenty of looks at him, and they liked what they saw enough to sign him for $450,000 as a 14th-round pick in the 2023 Draft. The right-hander’s velocity jumped in his professional debut, which he finished at High-A, then he was even more dominant while posting a 1.58 ERA with 91 strikeouts over 74 innings between High-A and Double-A last year. Always looking to add impact pitching to their system, the Rays landed Forret as part of their prospect haul for starter Shane Baz. Forret ranked second in the Minors last year (minimum 70 innings) in both ERA and WHIP (0.82), and his .157 average-against was the fifth-lowest mark in the Minors. But he’s not your typical overpowering starter. The 6-foot-3 right-hander beats hitters with deception, a deep arsenal and command. There’s some crossfire action in his delivery, making him tough on right-handed hitters. His changeup, his best secondary offering, more than compensated for whatever platoon advantage lefties might gain against his delivery. He has shown different variations of his fastball (with a mid-90s four-seamer and a two-seamer that runs), changeup (including a kick change) and slider (including a sweeper), but there’s still some work to do in building out his package of breaking balls. Forret’s delivery and unpredictability help his fastball play up, and he has done a good job getting ahead in counts by keeping the ball in the strike zone early in his career. A lower back issue limited him to 19 outings last year, so he has yet to pitch more than 100 innings in a season. That makes it difficult to determine his ceiling, as we haven’t seen if he can sustain his elite production over a full season. Regardless, he has the stuff and control of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Forret wasn’t hugely recruited coming out of the North Carolina prep ranks, but pitched collegiately right in the Orioles’ spring backyard at the State College of Florida, Manatee-Sarasota. That proximity gave Baltimore the inside-track at some early looks at the right-hander in 2023. They made him a 14th-round pick that year and spent over the $150,000 slot value for Day 3 picks to sign him for $450,000. Forret spent his pro debut making that look like a worthwhile investment, experiencing a velocity jump, posting a 28.8 percent strikeout rate as a 20-year-old and finishing at High-A Aberdeen. He built on that breakout with a 1.58 ERA and 91 strikeouts at High-A and Double-A in 2025, while working around lower back discomfort, and was traded to the Rays in the offseason in the Shane Baz move. Forret is a 6-foot-3 righty with a varied pitch mix and a lot of projection, but all his stuff is pointing in the right direction. He has two potentially plus fastballs -- a mid-90s four-seamer that touches 97 and a runny two-seamer. He has two sliders, with the sweeper the best of his secondary offerings. He also throws two changeups, including a kick change, and a splitter. It’s a deep pit of weapons, one that’s proven effective in this age of the pitch mix. Though Forret kept the ball in the strike zone relatively well during his debut, his control picked up even further in year two with a 7.4 percent walk rate. He’s still yet to throw more than 100 innings in a single Minor League season, clouding his ceiling somewhat. The depth of his pitch mix could make him a mid-rotation starter. It’ll at least give his new Rays coaches and coordinators plenty to work with in his new system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tornes was one of the youngest players in his class as the 2025 international signing period opened. The Cuban outfielder trained at former big leaguer Alex Sanchez’s academy in the Dominican Republic. Ranked No. 15 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list, he was the Braves’ top target, receiving just under $2.5 million to sign. He had a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, raising the excitement level for him to come stateside in 2026. Tornes is a switch-hitting center fielder who made his pro debut at age 16 and won’t turn 18 until July. He already stands out with his bat speed and ability to hit the ball very hard with his physical 6-foot-2 frame. There’s plenty of power for him to tap into, and his extra-base authority showed up from the left side especially during his pro debut. He’s shown a semblance of an approach with some on-base skills, giving more confidence he can be an accomplished all-around hitter. The teenager played center field during his debut and there is athleticism and decent speed that point to him at least getting a chance to stay there. He could eventually move to right field, where his strong arm and potential run-producing bat would profile really well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Alex Sánchez, a Cuban native who spent parts of five seasons in the big leagues, was done with his career, he eventually opened a training academy in the Dominican Republic. His star pupil for the 2025 international signing class was Tornes, also initially from Cuba. One of the youngest players in the class, the Braves made him their top acquisition when the signing period opened in January, giving the outfielder just shy of $2.5 million to sign. Though he’ll still be 16 when making his pro debut, Tornes stands out with his frame, physicality and impressive bat speed. He’s a switch-hitter with the ability to generate power, especially from the left side of the plate. He’s gotten some comps to Anthony Santander because of his offensive profile and could grow into being a middle-of-the-order run producer if it all clicks. With an above-average arm and that hitting potential, Tornes could fit into the prototypical right-fielder mold, an athletic one with above-average speed. The Braves haven’t had much to show for big position player expenditures on the international market lately, but Tornes has the chance to buck that trend and be an impact player on both sides of the ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davidson began his college career at Guilford Tech (N.C.) JC in 2021 before taking the next year off and resurfacing at Caldwell (N.C.) CC, where he batted .412/.508/.876 with 16 homers as a sophomore in 2023. Giants part-time scout Paul Faulk signed him for $50,000 as a nondrafted free agent that summer out of the Coastal Plains League, and he quickly blossomed into one of the system's best prospects. He earned all-star accolades in the High-A Northwest League last year and slashed .281/.376/.468 with 18 homers and 19 steals in 114 games between that level and Double-A. Davidson features plus raw power and improved his ability to tap into it in 2025, turning on more pitches and driving them in the air more often. His quick left-handed stroke and feel for hitting have enabled him to make an easy transition to handling pro pitching despite his limited amateur experience against quality competition. He consistently hits the ball hard, and while he misses in-zone fastballs more than he should, he doesn't strike out excessively. Davidson has one of the best power/speed combinations in the system but has yet to make the most of his above-average wheels on the bases and in center field. After playing mostly left field in his first two pro seasons, he spent all of 2025 in center, where he's an average defender who's still refining his instincts. He's more solid on the corners with arm strength to match.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2023, Giants part-time scout Paul Faulk signed two nondrafted free agents out of the summer Coastal Plains League who quickly blossomed into two of the organization's best prospects: Davidson for $50,000 and right-hander Trent Harris for $10,000. Davidson began his college career at Guilford Tech (N.C.) JC in 2021, took the next year off and then slashed .412/.508/.876 with 16 homers at Caldwell (N.C.) CC as a sophomore. A hamstring injury cost him the first half of his first full pro season but he recovered to post the best batting line in the Single-A California League (.328/.438/.608, 173 wRC+) before acquitting himself well in the Arizona Fall League. Davidson offers one of the best combinations of raw power and speed among Giants farmhands, grading as plus in both categories. He won't fully tap into his pop until he starts turning on more pitches and lifting them more frequently, but he has the bat speed and strength to hit 20 or more homers per season. He could be one of the best pure hitters in the system, as he has a sound left-handed swing and a fairly disciplined approach that allowed him to handle southpaws and all types of pitches in Single-A despite his inexperience. Davidson is still refining his instincts on the bases and in the field but has the quickness to become a 20-20 center fielder. Though he played mostly left field at San Jose last year in deference to speedster Jonah Cox, he's capable in center and will see more time there in 2025. His solid arm strength fits anywhere in the outfield and helped him record nine assists in 58 games last summer.

just_baseball.label: JB 2026 Preseason
just_baseball.text:
Height/Weight: 6’2″, 215 | Bat/Throw: L/R | UDFA: $50,000 – 2023 (SF) | ETA: 2027

A unique story, Davidson played at two different junior colleges with a year off in between before the Giants identified him in the Coastal Plains League.

Davidson offers an intriguing combination of above-average power and speed, breaking out in 2024 between the complex and Low-A, capped by a solid AFL showing. He followed that up by posting a 137 wRC+ between High-A and Double-A in 2025.

Starting slightly stacked towards his back side, with his hands relaxed in front of his back shoulder. It’s a simple pre-swing operation, with a moderate stride and a slight pull backwards with his hands.

There’s more cohesion to Davidson’s swing now, with his lower half and torso working more in tandem, aiding his timing while looking more under control against spin.

While Davidson has improved against spin, he still struggles to stay back at points. That may be why he starts stacked towards the back side, but he may need to find a move that helps him stay there longer.

Overall, 2025 has been a step in the right direction for the pop-up prospect. His bat speed is plenty evident when he is turning around velocity, punishing fastballs in the zone, which can also make him overly ambitious against heaters at the top.

He’s flashed plus power, with a 90th percentile exit velocity of 106 MPH and a max of 112.5 MPH with room for more. There’s a decent gap between his average exit velocities and the top 10%, meaning too much weak contact is still getting mixed in, predominantly against secondaries.

Even with the hit tool gains, it will be a power-over-hit profile, but there’s enough power to push towards 30 homers if it all works out.

A plus runner with a good arm, Davidson has the tools to stick in centerfield if his reads and navigation can continue to come along, but if he settles in a corner, he’d project as above average there.

There’s a chance that Davidson could slow down a tick if he continues to fill out, adding more likelihood that he pushes to a corner, the late-bloomer nature of his game, and improvements he has already made in center make it difficult to count him out.

Davidson swiped 19 bags on 25 tries in 2025 and should be a threat for around 20 bags per season as he continues to settle in as a base stealer.

If Davidson can stick in center, that would take some pressure off the bat, but he has the power and defensive ability to be an above-average regular in a corner. If things stall defensively, he should at least be able to get by in centerfield when needed.

There’s platoon risk as he has struggled some in left-on-left matchups, though his ability to potentially play all three outfield spots–even if centerfield is not his primary position–should help him stay in the lineup. There’s plus power and speed potential with a player whose late-blooming nature and projectable frame imply potential for more in the tank.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De León has steadily grown into one of the best pitching prospects in the Orioles’ system since signing out of the Dominican Republic for just $30,000 during the 2021 international period, long showing a tantalizing mix of stuff and upside. He took a big step forward in 2025, reaching Double-A down the stretch and then heading to the Arizona Fall League, where he was one of the circuit’s top pitchers. De León is a long, lean, left-handed ground-ball machine. His lynchpin is a 95-98 mph sinker with significant arm-side run that generates tons of weak contact, leading to a 1.92 GO/AO rate in 2025, and he also throws a four-seam fastball with more rise. He complements those heaters with a full array of secondary offerings: a sharp slider, an improving changeup and an emerging splitter. All can be plus pitches because De León throws everything with good arm speed and angle when his mechanics are clicking. These varied weapons make him extremely difficult for hitters to square up; he didn’t allow a home run in 87 1/3 innings of work in ‘25. De León has always had inconsistent command, and his control can unravel when his mechanics fall out of sync. But his stuff plays up when he’s repeating his delivery and staying on top of his release, and he’s shown improvement in the free-passes department, slicing his walk rate every season as he’s matured. If he can consistently throw all of his pitches for strikes and limit the walks, his weapons give him the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter, with the raw stuff to impact a big league bullpen even sooner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles signed the Dominican Republic native De León as an 18-year-old late in the 2020-21 international signing period for $30,000, which could turn into great value given the left-hander’s tantalizing combination of stuff and upside. His stock began rising at Single-A Delmarva, where De León racked up 72 strikeouts in 54 1/3 innings across 2023-24, but he wore down after a mid-season move to High-A last summer and struggled mightily down the stretch. Though he’s still a little raw and unpolished, teams tend to salivate over left-handers with De León's profile. He’s a long, lean, athletic 6-foot-3 with a legitimate three-pitch mix that is very difficult for hitters to square up when he’s commanding it well. The heavy-sinking fastball he slings generates tons of weak grounders and he can reach back and touch the upper 90s with it at times. His secondary offerings are a sharp slider with three-quarter break and a fading changeup. Both have a chance to be average pitches because De León throws everything with good arm speed and angle when his mechanics are clicking. When they aren’t, below-average control and inconsistent command undercut his effectiveness and things can spiral. The walk issues stem from De León’s need to find a consistent release point and better repeat his delivery, which should help him stay ahead of hitters, pitch in fewer defensive counts and limit damage. There is still time for him to do that, given that he'll be 22 for all of the 2025 season. If he can improve at throwing all three of his pitches for strikes, he has the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter, though his stuff is probably good enough to impact a bullpen sooner if something clicks mechanically.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the end of the 2020-21 international signing period, the Orioles had just enough bonus pool money remaining to ink De León in December, signing the Dominican left-hander for $30,000. It’s looking more and more like a big bargain after he pitched his way to full-season ball in 2023, raising his stock enough to be targeted by clubs in trade talks during the summer. He finished the year by striking out more than a batter per inning in 26⅓ frames at Single-A Delmarva. Long, lean and athletic at 6-foot-3, De León uses big arm speed to sling heavy mid-90s fastballs that hitters tend to pound into the ground. He’s revved that heater up to 98 mph and has a pair of secondary offerings that could be average or better in the future -- a changeup with good fade and a sharp slider with three-quarter break. There are some mechanical issues to clean up that should allow De León to improve his command and control, as walks can still be an issue. Though De León lacks full polish right now, he’ll only be 21 for the 2024 season and he’s athletic enough to make the adjustments necessary to command his arsenal long term. The stuff is plenty enough at this point to get excited about, with a legitimate three-pitch mix from the left side, giving De León a chance to stick as a starter. If he can continue throwing all three for strikes as he adds strength and gets more reps, there is a chance De León can develop into an impact arm -- and soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After reclassifying his senior season at Pittsburgh’s Mt. Lebanon HS (where he was the star quarterback, too), Shields was just 17 years old when the Royals selected him in the second round (No. 41 overall) in 2024. He started 2025 in the Arizona Complex League but jumped to Single-A Columbia after just one start. He pitched well there, with a 2.01 ERA across 18 starts, striking out 81 batters and issuing just 15 walks and allowing three homers in 71 2/3 innings. Shields helped the Fireflies to the Carolina League Championship Series, was named the league’s Pitcher of the Year and was the Royals’ Paul Splittorff Pitcher of the Year. Shields’ four-seam fastball averaged 90 mph in ‘25. He doesn’t blow hitters away and probably never will, but the Royals believe there’s more in the tank -- he has previously flashed in the mid 90s. It plays up because of its life and above-average command, along with some deception. Shields’ two breaking balls can blend some, but he was getting much more depth on his curveball in the spring of ‘26. They both project to be average pitches and can get swing-and-miss. Shields’ 83 mph changeup was a focus for him in ‘25, and it paid off; it’s a plus pitch on some nights with good deception out of his hand. Shields is strong with a mostly clean delivery. He’ll need to find some more velocity eventually, but he has the look, arsenal and advanced feel of a starter. That’s how the Royals will continue to develop him as one of their highest-upside prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shields reclassified his senior season at Mt. Lebanon (Penn.) HS and was still just 17 on Draft Day when the Royals selected him in the second round and signed him for a $2.3 million bonus to pass on his commitment to Miami. A multisport athlete as the starting quarterback and top starting pitcher in high school, Shields' decision to quit football and focus on baseball paid off. He pitched on the backfields and in instructional league after the Draft last summer, so his official pro debut will come in 2025. Shields was around 93-94 mph with his fastball at instructs in late ‘24, and the Royals expect some more power as he physically matures. The pitch has some deception to it, helped along by Shields’ good extension. His fringe-average breaking ball blends between a slider or curveball depending on who is assessing the pitch, but it typically sits in the low 80s and has the potential to be above average with consistency. Shields has flashed a circle changeup with good armside fade, but that will be a focus for him in his first full year. Shields already shows good command and is a great athlete with a projectable body and a clean and simple delivery. His makeup is strong, and he's already growing into a mature pro and competitor. He has upside as a starter, potentially even a No. 2 or 3, and the Royals will develop him as such. They’ll manage his innings like most of their prep pitchers out of the Draft, but he's been tremendous out of the gate at Single-A in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally an outfielder, the Royals signed Ramirez as a catcher during the 2023 international signing period for $57,500 out of Venezuela, and he stood out in the Dominican Summer League that year along with an impressive performance on the back fields during that fall’s instructional league. After a strong Arizona Complex League season in 2024, Ramirez headed to Single-A Columbia in '25, where he posted a .244/.339/.442 slash line with 11 home runs and 12 doubles across 70 games. He missed almost two months of Carolina League action with left hand inflammation in June and July, which seemed to zap his power upon returning. Evaluators often describe Ramirez as fearless at the plate, and he possesses impressive raw power with the ability to drive the ball to any part of the park, with some projecting him to be a 20-plus homer guy. He has a simple setup and efficient swing with a leg lift, and he’s been able to handle velocity well even at a young age because of his bat speed. Ramirez’s offense is what carries him, but he’s made strides defensively since joining the Royals organization. He has a plus arm and has always been able to throw. He’s improved with his receiving but still needs to work on that and his blocking. Officials believe he’ll be able to stick behind the plate. The Royals have lots of catchers at the big league level and in the system, so there’s no need to rush Ramirez. If he continues to improve his defense, he has a shot at becoming an everyday bat-first catcher in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals signed Ramirez, who grew up as an outfielder in Venezuela, as a catcher during the 2023 international signing period for just $57,500, but he almost immediately became well known via his performance in the Dominican Summer League that year. Ramirez got his first taste of stateside ball in 2024, slashing .265/.379/.459 with seven homers and 10 doubles over 49 games in the Arizona Complex League. Ramirez is an advanced hitter with impressive raw power for his age. With a simple setup, he has a natural feel for the barrel, a powerful but efficient swing and bat speed that enables him to handle velocity. His strikeout-to-walk ratio in ‘24 wasn’t quite what it was in the DSL, but he showed a solid approach with the ability to draw walks. A quieter hand pump has allowed him to find better rhythm and timing, and experience should help him even more with his plate discipline. Defensively, Ramirez is still new to catching and is learning the routines and demands of the position. He has a plus arm, but he’ll need to work on his receiving. Right now Ramirez is a bat-first catcher, with physicality that leads to some questions about whether he’ll remain at the position. But the Royals like how he has handled himself there so far, and he showed up in ‘25 looking leaner but more muscular. More advanced Single-A pitching will be a good test for Ramirez, both offensively and defensively. He’s still raw and has a ways to go in his development, but the tools are exciting and the upside is promising, especially if he’s able to improve at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez grew up as an outfielder in Venezuela, but the Royals signed him as a catcher in 2023 for just $57,500. He popped onto the radar almost immediately, slashing .344/.440/.615 with eight homers and more walks (21) than strikeouts (18) in 41 games in the Dominican Summer League. The Royals brought him to the States when the DSL ended, and Ramirez once again impressed in the instructional league. Ramirez is advanced in just about everything he does. His swing is powerful with a natural feel for the barrel with batted-ball data that excites evaluators the most, as he consistently hits the ball hard. Ramirez has a traditional setup and a smooth swing that can handle velocity instead of matching effort-for-effort like so many young hitters do. There’s a chance he grows into a player who hits for average and power. Ramirez needs more development with catching, but he has a plus arm and is athletic behind the plate -- that’s a good foundation to stick at catcher. Ramirez has a physical and mature frame and is a tick-below-average runner. With Ramirez’s emergence, the Royals’ catching core is as deep as it’s been in a long time. Playing behind the plate can tax young players over time, and it’s yet to be seen how Ramirez adjusts to non-Complex-level pitching over a larger sample. Those concerns aside, the power potential at a premium position is exciting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 45 | Cutter: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 Max Clark caught much of the attention from the Indiana high school ranks in 2023, but Letson -- the only prep pitcher taken from the Hoosier State that year -- has pushed his way into prominence as well. Signed for $482,600 as an 11th-round pick, the former Purdue commit got off to a solid start at Single-A in 2024 and looked set for a bigger breakout in his second full season, only to suffer a shoulder injury that knocked him out for three months and limited him to 41 1/3 total innings. He managed to get in one Double-A start five days before his 21st birthday. The Brewers have already developed one right-handed starter with elite extension in Jacob Misiorowski, and Letson, who stands 6-foot-4, can move down the mound for 7 1/2 feet -- a number that would rank among the best in the Majors. That helps his 91-95 mph four-seamer zip past bats despite closer to average velocity, and his sinker helps ground balls come in abundance. An 80-82 mph sweeper works against batters from both sides with the way it yanks to the glove side late and elicits a lot of chase. Letson has worked in an 88-91 mph cutter as a bridge pitch and barely uses his mid-80s changeup at this stage. Letson’s willingness to go right after hitters enabled his control to improve by a few ticks in 2025, but obviously the sample size was still small. He’s expected to be healthy and ready to go for his age-21 campaign, though with some innings limits, and the Brewers are hopeful he could squeeze out a little more velocity with more of an emphasis on his lower half. He has mid-rotation upside and may just need to stay healthy to realize it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Three Indiana high schoolers went in the 2023 Draft -- Max Clark being the most famous as the No. 3 overall pick -- but only one was a pitcher. That was Letson, who went to the Brewers in the 11th round but signed for closer to fourth- or fifth-round money with a $482,600 bonus. The former Purdue commit spent his entire first full season with Single-A Carolina and posted a 3.13 ERA with 57 strikeouts and a .195 average-against in 63 1/3 innings. The 6-foot-4 right-hander really gets down the hill with elite extension similar to fellow Brewer Jacob Misiorowski. Letson brings a pair of fastballs to the mound with a four-seamer and sinker -- the latter showing impressive horizontal movement -- and he’ll typically sit 92-94 mph and touch 95, already showing a bump from his amateur velo. His 79-83 mph slider gets whiffs with good sweep, giving him a second above-average pitch. His 82-85 mph changeup can get some chase out of the zone but sits behind the other two in effectiveness. Letson showed more willingness to go right after hitters the more pro experience he gained, and the additional confidence may only go with added experience in year two. The Hoosier State native has the individual ingredients (size, stuff, projectability) to be a potential mid-rotation starter in Milwaukee down the line, but a shoulder issue has held him back from a bigger breakout 2025 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Letson trended upward throughout his senior spring at Floyd Central (Ind.) HS and placed 179th on MLB Pipeline’s 2023 Draft rankings heading into the summer. A blister resulted in a bad outing in front of several scouts in May, and that performance may have scared some teams off as he continued to fall the first two days of the Draft. The Brewers moved to take the Purdue commit in the 11th round (the first without slot bonuses attached) and signed him for $482,600, close to fourth- or fifth-round money. The 6-foot-4 right-hander was up to 88-94 mph with his fastball in 2023, an upward trend that helped place him in Milwaukee’s Draft discussions. There’s an expectation that even more velocity could be coming as he fills out his lanky frame, and the pitch already plays well because of its solid ride. His low-80s tight slider could give him another above-average pitch with further development, while his sinking changeup in the same velo range has the workings of a decent third pitch. Adding to the optimism that the Crew picked up a Day 3 starter is that Letson has a repeatable and athletic delivery that could help him throw strikes in pro ball. The 2023 uptick certainly helped Letson’s trajectory, but it’s still mostly about projection with the young arm. Milwaukee believes proper professional pitching instruction could help Letson get to a future Major League rotation even if it takes a long road as is typical for cold-weather arms.

espn.label: ESPN 2026 Preseason
espn.text: Type : Lanky righty with massive extension and starter feel who has above average stuff that could be plus as he adds more strength Letson was a later-rising prospect in the 2023 draft from an Indiana high school; the Brewers landed him in the 11th round for just under $500,000. He was a projectable 6-foot-4 righty with some effort to his delivery tied to his giant extension, but he didn't have a long track record at national events like most high picks. Letson was good in 2024 but broke out in 2025, reaching Double-A as a 20-year-old after carving up High-A. He is within an inch or two of the best extension in all of pro baseball, which helps him get lower on the mound to improve his fastball shape. Letson's 92-96 mph fastball has average big league velocity but plays as above average because of the shape and command; if his velo jumps another tick or two, he'll shoot up this list. His sweeper is also an above-average-to-plus pitch and his lightly used cutter and changeup are both average to a bit above. The question here is health as Letson missed much of 2025 with a shoulder issue, making just 11 appearances. Letson has most of the markers I look for in projecting a breakthrough season, so front-line potential is still within reach and I'll take an aggressive stance here, presuming he'll be healthy in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: TJ Pre-Season 2026
mlb_pipeline.text: After taking college hitters with their first three picks in the 2024 Draft, the Twins dipped their toes in the high-end high school arm bucket by drafting Hill, a projectable left-hander from Texas, in the Competitive Balance Round B, signing him for an above-slot $2 million. While on a monitored workload, he dominated the Single-A Florida State League, posting a 2.77 ERA, .190 batting average against and 11.8 K/9 over 52 innings, earning a late promotion to High-A Cedar Rapids and capping things off with a Midwest League playoff win. The Twins were thrilled with how Hill acclimated to pro ball. His fastball touched 99 mph at times and averaged 95 during his debut season and it’s not tough to imagine hitting upper registers more consistently as he continues to add strength to his 6-foot-5 frame. His low-80s sweeper was his go-to secondary, producing a 41-percent miss rate according to Synergy and he also has a big upper-70s curve that missed bats at the same rate, though he throws it less frequently. His 84-mph changeup was key in neutralizing right-handed hitters. There isn’t a need to tinker too much with his arsenal, especially after he posted a strikeout rate over 30 percent in 2025, but something like a cutter or a harder slider could be useful for a different look from his two big breaking balls. Other than the need for more innings, Hill’s next order of business will be to attack the zone more, with those harder, shorter secondary offerings perhaps easier to land in the zone. The walk rate was high, but there’s confidence that will improve with time and the Twins are excited to see what he can do in year two, at age 20, after spending all offseason at the complex in Fort Myers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Twins aggressively went after advanced bats in the 2024 Draft, taking college hitters with seven of their first eight picks, they made one exception in Competitive Balance Round B. That’s when they took Hill, a super-projectable Texas high school left-hander. The best prep southpaw from the Lone Star State since Kyle Muller, Hill received an over-slot bonus of $2 million to sign him away from his Dallas Baptist commitment. He didn’t pitch last summer, instead focusing on building up and preparing for his first full season of pro ball. Following a growth spurt during his senior year, Hill now stands 6-foot-5 and saw his velocity increase thanks to his added size and strength. While pitching in live BP settings with the Twins, he was consistently 93-95 mph with his fastball, touching 96, in line with how he was dealing during his senior season. His low-80s sweeper is his best pitch, thrown with high spin rates and the ability to backfoot right-handed hitters. His upper-70s curve is a distinct breaking pitch with more depth and his changeup flashes average or more movement and should be a weapon, especially against right-handed hitters. The Twins will be conservative with Hill’s usage out of the gate as a high schooler who still could add a ton of strength to his long frame. They’ll want to see how his stuff plays against pro hitters before trying to change much in terms of pitch design, and it's more about getting innings under his belt while he refines his secondary offerings and focuses on repeating his delivery to land all of his stuff in the strike zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the biggest beneficiaries of the initial MLB Draft Combine in 2021, McDougal earned an over-slot $850,000 bonus in the fifth round following his strong performance. He made six brief appearances in Rookie ball that summer before blowing out his elbow, leading to Tommy John surgery that October and delaying his full-season debut until 2023. He took a huge step forward in 2025, compiling a 3.26 ERA with 136 strikeouts in 113 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. Few pitchers can match McDougal's ability to light up a radar gun and spin a breaking ball. His fastball sits in the upper 90s and peaks at 101, though it comes with more downhill plane than life and can get pounded if he doesn't command it well. His high-spin 78-82 mph curveball features so much downer movement that it's both extremely difficult to hit or land in the strike zone, so his upper-80s slider that also has tremendous depth is more effective. McDougal is similar to Grant Taylor in that he's a right-hander with overwhelming stuff and not much finesse. After control and command woes led to a demotion to Single-A in July 2024, he dedicated that offseason to getting in better shape and did a much better job of locating his pitches last year. He could be a mid-rotation starter, but he doesn't trust his upper-80s changeup with some fade and still needs to add more polish, so it's also possible that his best long-term fit is as a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McDougal overcame an inconsistent senior season as a Nevada high schooler with one of the better performances at the inaugural MLB Draft Combine in 2021. After he spun two shutout innings with impressive pitch metrics, the White Sox selected him in the fifth round and bought him out of an Oregon commitment with an over-slot $850,000. He blew out his elbow following a brief pro debut, had Tommy John surgery in October 2021 and returned to game action on tight pitch counts in Single-A last season. McDougal had a low-90s fastball with plenty of induced vertical break, and now he's operating at 94-96 mph and touches 98 -- albeit with a lesser movement profile that features downhill plane more than life or carry. He can spin both of his breaking balls in excess of 3,000 rpm, and Chicago had him focus on a solid upper-70s curveball for most of last season before bringing back an average low-80s slider toward the end. His upper-80s changeup will flash some promising fade but is too firm. In order to make it as a starter, McDougal will have to reduce the effort in his delivery and improve his control and command. He did a better job of finding the zone later in the season and could take another step forward as he puts his elbow reconstruction further behind him. A tough competitor, he has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few players helped themselves more at the inaugural MLB Draft Combine in 2021 than McDougal, who had an inconsistent senior season as a Nevada high schooler. The son of Mike McDougal, a right-hander who reached Triple-A in the Orioles system, he parlayed two shutout innings and impressive pitch metrics at the Combine into an over-slot $850,000 bonus as a fifth-rounder. After a brief pro debut, he blew out his elbow and had Tommy John surgery in October 2021. McDougal had a 90-96 mph fastball with quality induced vertical break and high spin rates before he got hurt, and he ran his four-seamer up to 97 during instructional league last fall. With his projectable 6-foot-5 frame and the track record of pitchers adding velocity after elbow reconstruction, his heater could sit in the mid-90s in the future. He also showed he had regained the feel for his upper-70s curveball and low-80s slider, both of which can exceed 3,000 rpm, though they can blend together. McDougal's changeup lags behind his other pitches but can show promising fade at times. He does pitch with effort and will need to smooth out his delivery to provide consistent strikes and reach his ceiling of a mid-rotation starter. The White Sox love his competitiveness and the way he attacked his rehab.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox have made a habit of giving over-slot bonuses to high school right-handers in recent Drafts, and they did so again by paying McDougal $850,000 in the fifth round. The son of Mike McDougal, a right-hander who reached Triple-A in the Orioles system, he had an inconsistent senior season as a Nevada high schooler but performed well in showcases and at the inaugural MLB Draft combine. After a brief pro debut in Rookie ball, he blew out his elbow and had Tommy John surgery last October, so his full-season debut will be on hold until 2023. McDougal featured some of the best pitch metrics among 2021 prepsters, including quality induced vertical break and high spin rates that give his 90-96 mph four-seam fastball promising carry up in the zone. Both his mid-70s curveball and upper-70s slider exceeded 3,000 rpm at the Combine, though they tend to blend together at times and could use more power. He's still figuring out his changeup, which has some fade but not enough velocity separation from his heater. McDougal still has lots of projection remaining in his lanky 6-foot-5 frame and there's a long track record of pitchers coming back from elbow reconstruction stronger than ever, so he should have added velocity in his future. His delivery features effort and he'll need to iron it out in order to provide more consistent strikes. He comes with both a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter as well as a good deal of reliever risk.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mayfield won Gatorade Oklahoma Player of the Year honors in 2023 and 2024 but took the summer off in between those years to preserve his health. A standout showing at the Super 60 Pro Showcase in February 2024 helped his Draft stock, and after he carried that momentum into spring, the Padres selected him 25th overall and signed him for $3,442,100. Mayfield posted a 2.97 ERA and struck out 88 over 60 2/3 innings with Single-A Lake Elsinore in his first full season; his 34.1 percent strikeout and 23.3 percent K-BB rates ranked second and third among 163 Single-A pitchers with at least 60 frames in 2025. The 6-foot-4 southpaw’s fastball velocity rose to where he was sitting 92-95 mph and touching 97 in his final amateur spring, but that fell closer to 90-92 (touching 95) in the California League. He lost some weight due to a spring sickness and was hampered by shoulder trouble in the first half, and both could have contributed. The fastball has some ride and run, although it can bleed into the dead zone, and if he gains some heat back in his age-21 season, that’ll be a boost to his profile. Mayfield’s low-80s changeup is the show stopper anyways – a true plus pitch he sells with arm speed, only to dive down and armside late. Mayfield’s upper-70s slider has slurvy characteristics, and he was more successful against righties as a result. Mayfield has repeatable and loose delivery, and while he walked 10.9 percent of batters in the California League, he should have enough control to start as he matures. Getting lefties to expand more against the slider could help him deliver strikes. Regaining the velocity, holding it and staying healthy will be key markers if Mayfield is to meet his mid-rotation ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 Mayfield was a two-time Gatorade Oklahoma Player of the Year in 2023 and '24 out of Elk City High School. He took the summer off between those two campaigns, eschewing the showcase circuit in order to preserve his health following a heavy workload in ’23, and the move seemed to pay off. He stood out in the Super 60 Pro Showcase in February and continued his momentum throughout the spring. Evaluators believed he could sneak into the back of the first round, and that’s just what he did when the Padres selected him 25th overall in July and signed him for slot at $3,442,100. The 6-foot-4 left-hander showed improved velocity in his final amateur spring, pushing his fastball to sit 92-95 mph and touch 97 with good carry and armside run. His low-80s changeup appears to be his best pitch -- something not often said about high-school arms -- with significant drop as it reaches the plate. It’s something hitters have to constantly worry about, and that helps the fastball play up too. Mayfield also locates a slurvy upper-70s breaking ball well, but it doesn’t have standout shape and could be sharper. The former Oklahoma State commit repeats his delivery well at this early stage of his development, and his command was advanced coming out of high school. His improved velocity as a senior calmed some concerns among scouts who didn’t get to see him in the summer, and even though he’s already 20 entering his first full season, he still has plenty of runway to become a potential mid-rotation arm in the Padres system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from the Dominican Republic, Soto landed the highest bonus in Boston's 2025 international class at $1.4 million. Scouts liked his offensive upside and makeup, and both attributes were obvious while he slashed .307/.362/.428 with 14 extra-base hits in 47 games in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. His successful pro debut was reminiscent of that of a former Red Sox big-bodied shortstop prospect: Xander Bogaerts. A switch-hitter, Soto generates electric bat speed and high exit velocities from both sides of the plate. While his long arms mean that his stroke can get long as well, he still exhibits good bat-to-ball skills and uses the entire field. He already displays the aptitude to drive balls in the air and could grow into considerable power. Because Soto projects as a fringy runner once he develops physically, there are some questions about his ability to stay at shortstop. He moves well for his size and makes plays, and the Red Sox wonder if he might develop more range as he gets stronger. If not, his quick, reliable hands and solid arm strength would work well at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The prize of Boston's 2025 international class, Soto signed for $1.4 million out of the Dominican Republic. His stock was rising as his January signing date approached, as he earned strong reviews for his offensive upside as well as his makeup. He's similar to fellow Dominican shortstop Yoeilin Cespedes, who has torn up two levels of Rookie ball since signing with Boston for the same bonus two years ago. A switch-hitter, Soto is equipped to hit for both average and power. While he does employ a big leg kick at the plate, he has a good sense of timing along with impressive bat speed and an advanced approach for his age. He already exhibits average raw power from both sides at age 17, and that should grow as he continues to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame. Soto has average speed and fine actions at shortstop, though he may slow down a bit and outgrow the position as he develops physically. He'll break into pro ball at short but projects more as a third baseman. His agility, quick hands and plus arm strength should fit nicely at the hot corner, and his bat would profile well there as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thomas established himself as one of the best Draft-eligible sophomores in the Class of 2024 by putting up a .349/.435/.635 line with 16 homers at the University of Texas and he hit well in his pro debut after the Rockies took him in the second round of that July’s Draft as icing on the cake. Hitting .330 with a .922 OPS over 73 games with High-A Spokane during his first full season certainly did nothing to dampen enthusiasm about his bat, though swing-and-miss concerns once he got to Double-A and then during a stint in the Arizona Fall League, did come up. At least part of the explanation for the spike in strikeouts might have been what turned out to be a broken left hamate, which he had surgery to fix after his AFL experience. When 100 percent, he’s very hitterish from the left side of the plate with a smooth swing that helps him typically barrel up baseballs consistently with sneaky power. When he got to Double-A, he did have more trouble recognizing spin, leading to high miss rates against breaking stuff. He’s dug into his swing decisions with the Rockies’ new hitting team to re-establish his approach. An above-average runner who swiped 33 bags in 2025, Thomas has enough defensive chops to play center field, though he might be best in a corner, and has seen more time in left field than anywhere else. A post-hamate injury Thomas who sticks to his gameplan at the plate could be mashing balls at Coors Field in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There’s an old adage that guys who know how to hit find their way into the lineup. Thomas, the Rockies’ second-round pick in 2024, looks like he might be just that type who hits his way to the big leagues after being one of the best pure hitters in his class as a Draft-eligible sophomore with the University of Texas. Exhibiting impressive bat-to-ball skills since back in his Texas high school days, Thomas slashed .349/.435/.635 with 16 homers in his final season with the Longhorns, then went 11-for-33 during his brief pro debut with Single-A Fresno for good measure. Even in his short time with the Rockies, Thomas showed off what a good feel he has for his left-handed swing. He has the chance to really hit at the next level, routinely finding the barrel and not trying to do too much. There’s some sneaky pop in there, and as he showed during his sophomore year, he can sacrifice a little contact for pop without completely selling out for it. Thomas is a pretty good athlete who runs better underway and has the ability to play multiple positions. He played more first than anywhere else with the Longhorns, but showed he could capably handle center field as a sophomore and the Rockies will likely work him at all three outfield spots during his first full year of pro ball. He’s already opened some eyes across the industry as the Rockies were getting calls about him from other teams.

mlb_pipeline.label: TJ Pre-Season 2026
mlb_pipeline.text: Stanifer has the potential to be a massive player development win, one of the best examples in the Toronto system of how valuable patience can be when the numbers don’t come right away. A 19th-round pick of the Blue Jays back in the 2022 Draft, when he signed for $125,000 to turn away from his commitment to Cincinnati, Stanifer put up a six-plus ERA in each of his first two seasons in the FCL and Single-A Dunedin. Then, it all came together in 2025. Stanifer went stride for stride with Trey Yesavage in the early months of 2025, often following Yesavage in games to manage his season-long workload. The end results were spectacular, with a 2.86 ERA and 161 strikeouts over 110 innings. While his control won’t be quite as big a battle as Johnny King’s in this system, it’s still a similar conversation. If Stanifer throws strikes, he’ll be a big leaguer. His breakout season featured a velocity bump up to the 94-96 mph range, which gets on hitters in a blink thanks to his quick arm action. As if that wasn’t enough, the heater has exceptional ride (17-20 inches of induced vertical break) and ample armside run that can give hitters fits. His 83-86 mph slider has a gyro shape and drops almost straight down; batters didn’t have a single hit off it in Single-A in 2025. The changeup still lags behind and will be crucial to his development, but if Stanifer can take even a small step forward with his control, he could position himself as a long-term option in Toronto’s rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Illinois' best prep prospect in 2021, Hess spurned offers from pro teams to attend Alabama, where he missed time in his first two seasons before staying healthy in his third. Though he posted a 5.80 ERA as junior, his 35 percent strikeout rate better testified to his stuff, and the Yankees signed him for $2,747,500 as a first-round pick. He made an impressive 2025 pro debut despite losing a month to a hip injury, logging a 3.22 ERA, .177 opponent average and 139 strikeouts in 103 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. Hess' fastball operates at 92-96 mph and tops out at 98, playing better than its radar-gun readings because of the extension and carry he creates with his big frame. His breaking balls don't stand out for their velocity either, but they both work as plus pitches. His mid-70s curveball has surprising depth coming out of a low arm slot, and the Yankees switched him from a tighter mid-80s slider to a sweepier version that sits around 80 mph with plenty of action. While his 83-85 mph change has nice fade at times, he has trouble landing it for strikes and doesn't trust it very much. Hess' 6-foot-5, 255-pound build and arsenal prompt comparisons to Lance Lynn, though he has yet to translate his big-bodied athleticism and clean delivery into consistent strikes like the two-time All-Star did. He could become a frontline starter if he can refine his control and show more durability. He developed a stress fracture in his back in high school, the sustained a freak offseason injury and a flexor strain in college.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Hess ranked as the best prep prospect in Illinois in 2021, he declined offers from pro teams because he wanted to attend Alabama. After missing time in both of his first two college seasons with injuries, he stayed healthy in 2024, posting a 5.80 ERA but also a 35 percent strikeout rate. The third first-rounder in Crimson Tide history, following Joe Vitiello and Taylor Tankersley, he signed for $2,747,500 as the No. 26 overall pick and will make his pro debut this year. Hess can overpower hitters with a four-seam fastball that parks at 92-96 mph and peaks at 99 with armside run, and the flat approach angle and extension in his delivery make it more difficult to barrel. While his curveball sits in the mid-70s, it gives him a second plus pitch with its ability to fool hitters thanks to its depth and sweep coming out of a low arm slot. His mid-80s slider can feature two-plane depth at times but lost some sharpness last year, and he no longer trusts a fading mid-80s changeup that once looked like a potential solid offering. At 6-foot-5 and 255 pounds, Hess draws some comparisons to Lance Lynn, and his strong frame and clean delivery should translate into strikes and durability. But his walk rate jumped from 5 percent in 2023 to 11 percent last spring, and his health issues have included a stress fracture in his back in high school and a flexor strain as an Alabama sophomore. The Yankees excel at developing pitchers and believe they can help him regain the slider and control he showed in the past, which could make him a No. 2 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brito was hardly a big-time prospect when the Astros signed him out of Venezuela in November 2023. He was considered old at age 19, and he came for a bargain at $10,000. But Brito broke onto the scene with a dominant stint in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, earning him a trip stateside that concluded with seven excellent Single-A outings. A stress reaction in his right shoulder limited him to 49 1/3 innings at High-A last season, but he erased any doubts about his health with a masterful performance in the Arizona Fall League, where he struck out 22 of the 47 batters he faced. The Rays saw him as a potential frontline arm when they got him and Jacob Melton from the Astros as part of a three-team deal involving the Pirates last December. Brito has an electric fastball, which sat around 98 mph and touched 100.1 in the Fall League. He gained about 5 mph during his first season of pro ball, and he’s likely to sit in the mid-to-upper 90s with good carry at the top of the zone. He throws a slider with big horizontal sweep, to the point that it could be broken up into two separate breaking balls to add variety to his arsenal, and he spins a curveball in the mid-80s with impressive depth. He’s also shown a changeup and a sinker, giving him a full starter’s arsenal, although the changeup is clearly behind the heater and breaking stuff. Brito is considered mature and polished for his age, and he does a good job repeating his simple delivery. But walks were an issue last year, and there will be concerns about his durability considering how hard he throws and his 5-foot-10 frame. He has the talent to be a mid-rotation starter or better, and his floor is that of a high-leverage reliever if he can’t handle a starter’s workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brito is yet another older pitcher (age 19) signed cheaply ($10,000 out of Venezuela in November 2023) by the Astros who could become a big league asset. He broke into pro ball by logging a 0.40 ERA with 40 strikeouts in 22 1/3 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, then came to the United States and made one scoreless start in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League before thriving in Single-A. His combined 39 percent strikeout rate ranked fifth among all Minor League pitchers (minimum: 50 innings). Brito dealt with a stress reaction in his right shoulder that limited him to 49 1/3 innings at High-A during the 2025 regular season, but he dominated a pitching-starved Arizona Fall League, fanning 22 of the 47 batters he faced. The Rays acquired him from the Astros as part of a three-team deal in December. Brito gained about 5 mph of fastball velocity in his first year as a pro, working in the mid-90s and touching 99 mph with good carry up in the zone. His low-80s slider has huge horizontal action and projects as a second plus offering, and he also can spin a mid-80s curveball with promising depth. He has some feel for an upper-80s changeup with some depth that still needs a lot of refinement. The athletic Brito repeats his simple delivery with ease and threw consistent strikes before tiring toward the end of his pro debut. Only slightly bigger than his listed 5-foot-10 and 155 pounds, he lacks physicality and will have to prove he can hold up and maintain his stuff over a full season's workload of starts. He has the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter and could become a high-leverage reliever if durability continues to be an issue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of both the 2021 Appalachian and 2022 MLB Draft Leagues, Nett had dropped out of college at St. Charles (Mo.) CC and was working jobs in construction and as a Home Depot employee when the Padres came calling, signing him as an undrafted free agent for $10,000 in August 2022. It did not take long for him to ascend through San Diego’s system. Bouncing back from an elbow issue in ‘23, Nett finished ‘24 at Double-A San Antonio and began the following season there, reaching a career high in innings pitched by the time he was traded to the A’s in the Mason Miller and JP Sears deal at the Trade Deadline. Nett finished ‘25 with Double-A Midland. Nett has had to work through some injuries -- shoulder issues in 2023, then his elbow in 2024. When healthy, he’s shown a blazing fastball that can touch up to 99 mph, as it did at times throughout last season. He sits around 94-97 mph and has been able to generate swing-and-miss up in the zone with it in the past. His low-90s cutter is a pitch he utilizes mostly against lefties and his upper-70s curveball has emerged as a strong secondary offering with good vertical drop. He also throws a tight 81-84 mph slider and 88 mph kick-change as another weapon against lefties that improved throughout last season. Nett is a great competitor on the mound with a no-nonsense attitude, but consistent strike-throwing has proven to be a challenge at times. That, along with past injury history, leads to some speculation about whether he’s a starter or reliever over the long-term. He certainly has the deep arsenal needed to make it as a starter, while his impressive velocity also makes it easy to envision him thriving out of the bullpen. For now, he will get a shot to continue in the rotation with his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nett participated in both the 2021 Appalachian and 2022 MLB Draft Leagues, and after showing a raw but promising arsenal in the latter, the St. Charles (Mo.) CC product signed with the Padres for $10,000 in August 2022. Shoulder issues limited his first full season to 40 1/3 innings between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Lake Elsinore, but he confirmed his spot on the radar with 21 strikeouts in 17 1/3 frames in the Arizona Fall League. Nett, who dealt with elbow tightness in the summer, expanded his workload slightly to 65 innings in '24 and made 19 of his 20 appearances with High-A Fort Wayne before a cup of Double-A coffee. He made up for the lost innings with a stellar turn (1.02 ERA, 23 strikeouts in five starts) in the Puerto Rican Winter League. He had already surpassed his career high in innings pitched in his first full season in the Texas League when he was part of the four-prospect package sent to the A’s in return for Mason Miller and JP Sears at the Trade Deadline. While working around the injuries, Nett has continued to show stellar velocity, touching as high as 99 mph in the Minor Leagues last season. He typically sits 95-97 mph and gets swing-and-miss up in the zone thanks to ample carry. He also throws a tight 81-84 mph slider that ran a 38 percent whiff rate in ’24 and a sharper 90-92 mph cutter that can catch hitters off guard. He’ll mix in an upper-70s curveball with more vertical drop and he’s scrapped a low-80s splitter in favor of a much more effective 88 mph kick-change that really neutralizes lefties. Nett has some effort in his delivery, and the 2025 season (pre-trade) was the first time he’d posted a walk rate below 13 percent at any Minor League stop. Combine that with the early injury concerns, and it’s easy to think he could be a reliever eventually. But his arsenal is deep enough, and his stuff is promising enough -- when combined with strides taken this season -- to keep landing him in a starting role in the upper Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nett is a testament to the possible stories collegiate summer leagues can provide. The St. Charles (Missouri) CC product pitched in the Appalachian and MLB Draft Leagues in 2021 and '22 respectively, and it was his raw showing in the latter that got the Padres interested. San Diego signed the right-hander in August 2022, only for his first full season to be slowed by shoulder issues. He eventually cracked Single-A Lake Elsinore in late August and made up for the lost time in the Arizona Fall League, where he posted a 4.67 ERA with 21 strikeouts and 10 walks in 17 1/3 innings. The 6-foot-3 hurler affirmed his standing as an interesting arm during that time in the desert, starting with his mid-90s fastball that showed ample carry. It added a few ticks from his time in the Draft League and looked explosive at times up in the zone. He plays off that with a high-spin slider with sharp action and a cutter. His low-90s changeup isn’t much of a weapon as of yet with little separation off the heater, and he wasn’t as effective against lefties in the AFL as a result. Nett’s control was certainly improved in the fall, but there’s still a good amount of effort in his delivery, pointing to long-term concerns. He has the stuff to be an eventual two-pitch Major League reliever, which would be a major developmental win for himself and the Padres considering his amateur background.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Panama's top prospect in the 2019 international class, Preciado set a bonus record for his nation when he signed with San Diego for $1.3 million (later broken when the Cubs signed catcher Adan Sanchez for $1.5 million in January 2022). He participated in two instructional leagues with the Padres but had yet to play in a pro game when they traded him, three other prospects and Zach Davies to Chicago for Yu Darvish and Victor Caratini in December 2020. Preciado debuted by batting .333/.383/.511 in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last summer. A switch-hitter, Preciado is still in the early stages of his offensive development but has a chance to hit for average and power. Though he's 6-foot-4, he has a relatively compact swing from both sides, with impressive hand-eye coordination and promising bat speed. His to-do list includes adding strength, improving his ability to recognize pitches, honing his strike-zone discipline and making less ground-ball contact. Though Preciado split his first pro season between shortstop and third base, the Cubs have a logjam of young shortstops and he fits better at the hot corner. He has good body control for such a tall youngster, but he's already a fringy runner who figures to slow down as he matures physically. He has the soft hands and strong arm to play at least an average third base, though he does need to shorten his throwing stroke.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trained by his father Victor, who played briefly in the Yankees system, Preciado emerged as Panama's top prospect in the 2019 international class. Signed for a Panamanian-record $1.3 million by the Padres, he participated in instructional league the last two falls but never made his pro debut before they traded him to the Cubs last December. He was the best of the four prospects Chicago received along with Zach Davies in exchange for Yu Darvish and Victor Caratini. Preciado will need time to develop but could hit for power and average from both sides of the plate. He has a relatively compact swing for a 6-foot-4 teenager and displays promising bat speed and plenty of projectable strength. His body and offensive potential have led to Corey Seager comparisons since his amateur days. Preciado presently has fringy speed and figures to lose some quickness as he matures physically. Though he has a good first step and better than expected actions at shortstop for a gangly youngster, most scouts project that he'll eventually move to third base. He has the athleticism, soft hands and strong arm to be a solid defender at third base and right field would be his worst-case scenario.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clifford looked like he was headed to Vanderbilt in 2022 until the Astros took him in the 11th round and signed him for $1,256,530, roughly second-round money. He was dealt to the Mets a year later along with Drew Gilbert in a swap for Justin Verlander, and New York wasn’t afraid to push Clifford aggressively past High-A Brooklyn in 2024 to get him out of pitcher-friendly Coney Island. After a decent (if strikeout-heavy) campaign in Binghamton, the lefty slugger repeated Double-A in 2025, posting a 148 wRC+ with 24 homers in 105 games and ending his age-21 campaign with 34 games in Triple-A. The North Carolina native has a strong lower half and utilizes it with a simple operation in the box from the left side -- open stance, limited front leg movement to close and fire. His combination of strength, bat speed and lift-and-pull angles helps his power play in games, and he’s knocking on the door of being a 30-homer hitter at the top level. That said, while his strikeout and in-zone contact rates improved in 2025, Clifford still struggled with breaking balls below the lower third. He’s less of a three-true-outcome player now than he was in 2024, but the concern remains. The Mets kept Clifford in constant rotation between first base and the outfield corners in 2025. He has enough footspeed to make it work on the grass, and his arm is certainly a fit in right. His future position may well come down to organizational need. New York has created lanes in both the outfield and first this offseason with the departures of Pete Alonso, Jeff McNeil and Brandon Nimmo, and it’s on Clifford to force the issue by closing some of the holes in his swing and keeping the bat as the carrying tool.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clifford ranked 92nd in the 2022 Draft class, but a lack of showcase-circuit success and a commitment to Vanderbilt caused him to fall to the Astros in the 11th round. Houston signed Clifford for roughly second-round money with a $1,256,130 bonus and saw him get off to a hot start in his first full season with 18 homers and a .919 OPS in 83 games between Single-A and High-A. He was promptly dealt alongside Drew Gilbert to the Mets at the Trade Deadline for Justin Verlander and slowed down at pitcher-friendly High-A Brooklyn. The Mets got Clifford out of Coney Island quickly in 2024, and the lefty slugger produced a .231/.359/.456 line with 18 homers in 98 games for Double-A Binghamton to close out his age-20 campaign. On one hand, Clifford was one of only five hitters aged 20 or younger to meet the qualifying standard at Double-A in 2024, and his 133 wRC+ only trailed Roman Anthony's 143 and Samuel Basallo's 134 in that group. He has plus power and gets to it well with an uphill bat path that helps him lift and pull. On the downside, while Clifford typically runs a healthy walk rate, he continues to have trouble making contact against softer stuff, leading to his status as a king of the three true outcomes. After struggling against righties in 2024, his splits have switched to more traditional ones in 2025 back in Binghamton. Clifford is also a below-average runner, and even though he has the arm strength for outfield corners, the majority of his starts continue to be at first base. His power would play there, but it’d be helpful if he can be more than a homer-walk-strikeout type. That said, Clifford is pushing for a Major League debut by his age-22 season of 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clifford was a well-decorated U.S. national team player and had one of the best all-around bats among 2022 high-schoolers, but a lack of showcase-circuit success and a commitment to Vanderbilt caused him to drop to the 11th round, where he would no longer be tied to a specific slot bonus. The Astros took him there and talked him away from the Commodores with a $1,256,130 bonus, roughly second-round money. Clifford quickly climbed from Single-A to High-A after 25 games in his first full season. The left-handed slugger dominated at hitter-friendly Asheville, slashing .271/.356/.547 with 16 homers in 58 games, and moved to the Mets in a Deadline deal that sent Justin Verlander the other way. His move to High-A Brooklyn was an uneasy one (.188/.307/.376 in 32 games), though rough hitting conditions in Coney Island likely played a factor. Regardless of where he played, Clifford ended 2023 with 24 homers, tied for second-most among Minor League teenagers. His uphill bat path helps him get the most of his significant raw pop, and it plays well to all fields. In fact, he may have gone oppo a little too much in ’23 and could increase the power by aiming for more pulled balls. It certainly helped him to get away from Coney Island with a first-half promotion to Double-A Binghamton this summer. He has high three-true-outcome potential with good walk rates but also his share of swing-and-miss issues. Clifford has just fringy speed, and while his arm strength could certainly play in a corner outfield spot, both the Astros and Mets gave him ample looks at first base where his lack of quickness is less of a concern. He still has some room to grow defensively there too, but his bat is so good that some evaluators preferred him over Drew Gilbert in the Verlander trade.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clifford first played for U.S. national teams at age 12 and won gold medals at international events with the 12-and-under squad in 2015 and the 15-and-under club in 2018. Though he was regarded as one of the better all-around hitters in the 2022 prep class, he didn't dominate the showcase circuit and he was committed to Vanderbilt, so he wound up sliding to the 11th round. Signed for $1,256,130, the equivalent of late-second-round money, he hit .247/.426/.390 with two homers in a 25-game pro debut split between Rookie ball and Single-A. He climbed quickly from Single-A to High-A in his first full season and had a .903 OPS at the higher level before being traded to the Mets for Justin Verlander at the Deadline. Clifford's approach is more mature than that of most players his age, as he works counts and focuses on making hard contact. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to develop 20-25 home run power, and he does a good job of letting his power come naturally. He has a pretty left-handed swing and an efficient bat path, though his 30 percent strikeout rate in his introduction to pro ball showed he'll need to do a better job of recognizing offspeed pitches. While Clifford possesses just fringy speed and could slow down as he gets stronger, he works hard to improve his quickness and defense. His reads and routes need to improve, but he has solid arm strength and could get the job done at an outfield corner. He has also gotten ample looks at first base as a pro, though his need to hit jumps if he lands there long-term with New York.

just_baseball.label: JB 2026 Preseason
just_baseball.text:
Height/Weight: 6’3″, 210 | Bat/Throw: L/R | 11th Round (343), 2022 (HOU) | ETA: 2026

Drafted in the 11th round by the Astros, Clifford signed for second-round money ($1.25 million) to forego his Vanderbilt commitment before being traded alongside Drew Gilbert for Justin Verlander at the 2023 deadline. Clifford made some mechanical adjustments during the 2025 season which helped him cut down swing and miss.

Clifford starts wide with his hands rested on his shoulder, before pushing his hands up and back to his slot with a pronounced coil as he loads. The emphasis on the coil is likely in an effort to mitigate his tendency to be heavy with his front foot, but during the 2025 season, he cut down his stride which in turn helped him hold his back side longer.

Now not pushing onto his frontside as early or heavily, Clifford’s barrel did not drag nearly as much, turning around velocity much more effectively. His contact rate on fastballs 93+ MPH jumped from 63% to 74% in 2025 with an OPS up roughly 200 points.

His improvements against velocity seemingly helped him control his at bats better as well. Now looking less rushed in the box, Clifford was much more effective against changeups as well, recognizing and staying back more easily.

Utilizing his lower half more effectively also translated into more consistently strong exit velocities. His hard hit rate jumped by 14% with a gaudy 90th percentile exit velocity of 108.5 MPH. His patience in the box can border on passivity at times, but Clifford’s swing decisions improved in 2025.

The contact rates are unlikely to be better than fringy at the highest level, though it is much easier to envision a quality power bat as he has rounded out some of the edges to his offensive profile while further tapping into his plus raw power in 2025.
