He showed plenty of bat speed from the right side before the shoulder injury, though it's becoming clear the bat will need longer to develop than the other aspects of his game. He had little issue putting the ball in the gaps in high-school showcases, and given his current size, he projects for potential plus power at his peak once he reins in his early whiff issues. He certainly follows in his father’s footsteps on the defensive side. Jones’ plus-plus speed is an obvious asset in center, and he has the instincts to track down balls most would miss. His well-above-average arm strength gives him another weapon from the grass and may aid his own future Gold Glove pursuits. He’s in a system with two other stellar outfield defenders in Alek Thomas and Corbin Carroll, though it’ll likely be years before the trio joins forces depending on how Jones’ bat takes to the pro game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers used their top pick (36th overall) in the 2023 Draft on the fastest player in the class, signing George for a below-slot $1,847,500. After an inconsistent first full pro season, he earned Midwest League All-Star honors in 2025 after leading the High-A circuit in on-base percentage (.409), runs (93), walks (84) and steals (100). He swiped 42 bases in his final 39 games to become the fourth Minor Leaguer to reach triple digits in the last two decades. If the scouting scale ranged wider than from 20-80, George might earn 100 grades for his speed. He went from the left side of the plate to first base in 3.4 seconds on a bunt in a PDP League game in 2022, and he routinely gets there in less than four seconds on normal balls in play, allowing him to register 40 hits on grounders to the left side of the infield last year. He creates havoc on the bases and covers a lot of ground in center field, though he still has room to improve his reads and jumps in both areas. His arm is below average but playable in center. Los Angeles unsuccessfully tried to help George add a bit of pop in 2024, leading to a 28 percent swing-and-miss rate, but he cut that to 19 percent last season by playing to his strengths. He focuses on getting on base by using a discerning eye and slashing at balls, posting the lowest pull rate (23 percent) and the 10th-highest groundball/flyball ratio (2.93) in the Minors in 2025. That approach yields almost no power and all three of his homers last year occurred from April 13-18, though one came off a 94 mph Chase Burns fastball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: George created havoc for Team USA at the 18-and-under World Cup in September 2022, reaching base 10 times in 18 plate appearances and stealing five bases. The fastest player in the 2023 Draft, the Texas high schooler went 36th overall to the Dodgers and signed for a below-slot $1,847,500. He continues to dazzle with his speed and stole 36 bases in 84 Single-A games last year, but there are questions about his bat and impact after he struck out at a 21 percent clip and slugged just .328. Some scouts have joked that George possesses 90 speed on the 20-80 scale, and he got from the left side of the plate to first base in 3.4 seconds on a bunt in a PDP League game in 2022. His quickness enables him to run wild on the bases and cover wide swaths of ground in center field, though he needs to refine his reads and jumps so he could become dominant in both regards. He's a potential big league basestealing champ and Gold Glover, though he comes with a below-average arm. George understands his strengths and weaknesses at the plate, recognizing that he lacks the physicality to be a slugger and should focus on getting on base. Los Angeles has helped him incorporate his legs more in his left-handed stroke and to learn how to pull and lift balls more frequently so pitchers will have to respect him, changes that have produced higher exit velocities but also more swing and miss. He still doesn't drive balls particularly hard and produces a lot of grounders to the left side of the infield, but he can turn those into infield hits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As fast as any player in last year's Draft, George starred for Team USA at the 18-and-under World Cup in September 2022, reaching base 10 times in 18 plate appearances and stealing five bases. The Dodgers selected him with their top pick (supplemental first round) out of a Texas high school last July and signed him for a below-slot $1,847,500. More advanced as a hitter than expected, he batted .362 in Rookie ball and .381 in Single-A during his pro debut. George raced from the left side of the plate to first base in 3.4 seconds on a bunt in a PDP League game in 2022 and regularly covers that distance in less than four on a normal swing, prompting some evaluators to joke that he's a 90 runner on the 20-80 scale. His raw speed alone allows him to wreak havoc on the bases and cover tremendous ground in center field. The next step will be to hone his reads and jumps so he can become a dominant basestealer and potential Gold Glove defender (albeit with a below-average arm). George repeats his compact left-handed stroke easily and makes consistent contact. He's not very physical and understands his strengths and weaknesses, focusing on making contact and getting on base rather than worrying about power. While he won't ever be a slugger, he did add 10 pounds as a high school senior and Los Angeles thinks he can unlock a bit more pop if he does a better job of incorporating his legs in his swing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lindsey missed most of the prime events on the 2023 high school showcase circuit because of a leg injury and football, but his stock shot up the following spring. He drew repeated Trea Turner comparisons while establishing himself as the fastest player in the 2024 Draft, where he went 23rd overall and signed for $3,297,500. He played just 32 games in his pro debut last year, with an impingement in his right (throwing) shoulder landing him on the injured list in mid-May and back issues shutting him down after he made four rehab appearances in July. Lindsey batted .280 in Single-A but also struck out at a 32 percent clip, taking too many early-count pitches and then coming up empty when he turned his right-handed stroke loose. The Dodgers believe it's more an approach issue than a swing issue, and his .431 average on balls in play alludes to the pressure his speed puts on a defense. He won't be a huge home run threat but is hitting the ball harder than he did as an amateur and could go deep 12-15 times per season. With his top-of-the-scale speed, Lindsey can get from home to first in 3.5 seconds on a bunt, beat out routine grounders for hits and contend for big league stolen base titles. There were questions about whether his average arm would allow him to remain at shortstop even before his injury, though he certainly has the actions and quickness to do so. If he has to move, he has the tools to become a quality defender in center field or at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lindsey wasn't highly touted entering 2024 after missing much of the summer showcase circuit with a leg injury, then skipping the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October because he was busy playing quarterback for Hardee HS (Wauchula, Fla.). But his stock rose quickly during the spring, when he gave off Trea Turner vibes as one of the fastest players and best shortstop prospects in the prep class. The Dodgers signed him for $3,297,500 as the 23rd overall pick, their biggest Draft bonus since 2010 and earliest selection since 2017. Lindsey clocked sub-6.3-second times in the 60-yard dash and has the top-of-the-scale speed to be a devastating basestealer and to cover plenty of ground in the field. Los Angeles had him focus on adding strength and tightening his right-handed swing rather than making his pro debut after he signed. While he won't be a slugger, he's barreling balls more consistently and hitting them harder, which could result in 12-15 home run pop. Turner had similar power projections at the same stage of his career, and like Lindsey, came with questions about whether his average arm would allow him to remain at shortstop. Lindsey has the actions, range and quick hands to play there, and the Dodgers believe they can help him improve his arm strength and release. If not, he has the tools to become a plus defender in center field or at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some baseball players are athletic compared to their peers, and others take it to another level. Overn fits the latter category. He was not just a high school baseball player, but also a football player and a track star, so gifted that he was recruited to USC to play outfield for their baseball team and wide receiver for their football squad. He left the gridiron after one season to focus on baseball, and he was drafted by the Orioles as a sophomore in 2024, signing for an above-slot bonus of $850,000. He played his way to Double-A in his first full season, then got dealt from the Orioles to the Rays in December as part of the Shane Baz trade. It should come as no surprise, given his background, that speed dominates Overn’s profile. Some scouts considered him an 80-grade runner in the Draft, and those wheels can make him a menace on the bases and an elite defender in center field. He stole 64 bases in 114 games while only being caught eight times last year, and he has earned high marks for his instincts, reads and routes in addition to his pure speed in the outfield. He’s a no-doubt center fielder, even with an arm that doesn’t grade out as well as the game’s best out there. The question is what Overn can do at the plate. Evaluators believe there’s some power in his 6-foot frame and left-handed swing, but he’s been more of a slasher who tries to be a tough out, find his way on base and let his speed do the rest. If he can make enough impact to turn his base hits into doubles and triples, with the occasional homer, he could be a more well-rounded player. (Perhaps he could simply repeat whatever he did for High-A Aberdeen against the Rays’ Bowling Green affiliate last summer, when he went 9-for-22 with four homers, a double and five steals in five games to earn an immediate promotion to Double-A.) He has the traits of a high-floor regular, but the Rays will give a player with his speed and defensive ability every chance to let the rest of his game catch up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Athletic enough to play four sports as a California prepster, Overn played wide receiver as a freshman at USC before giving up football to focus on baseball in 2023. He was one of the fastest players in his Draft class a year later, starring in the Cape Cod League before the Orioles took him in the third round and signed the Draft-eligible sophomore for an over-slot bonus of $850,000. He then enjoyed a fine debut, producing an .865 OPS and 16 steals over 21 games, finishing the year at High-A Aberdeen. He hit .249/.355/.399 with 13 homers and 64 steals in 114 games at High-A and Double-A in his first full season before being traded to the Rays in the offseason as part of the Shane Baz deal. Overn’s carrying tool is that speed, which some scouts hung an 80 grade on coming out of the Draft. Those wheels make him a legitimately disruptive threat on the bases and a double-plus defender in center field, where he uses good reads, instincts and body awareness to run down balls other defenders can’t. Overn’s athleticism allows him to make such an impact with his glove and feet it’ll likely keep him in center long-term despite what might be a tick-below-average arm. Overn’s potential impact at the plate is more of an open question. He’s a left-handed slasher type in the classic table-setter mold who needs to focus on putting the ball in play, getting on-base and making things happen. Though he can occasionally drop the barrel, his slug should come from turning singles into doubles and doubles into triples rather than trying to hit homers. His glove-first speedster profile is not unlike his former organizationmate Enrique Bradfield Jr.. Now with Tampa Bay -- an organization that values speed and defense highly -- the progress Overn makes offensively will determine whether he develops into a high-floor regular or more of a bench player in the Reggie Willits mold.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seattle’s recent track record on the international market -- from Julio Rodríguez to Noelvi Marte, Lazaro Montes and Felnin Celesten -- has earned the organization the benefit of the doubt when it invests heavily in young talent. And Bautista may be next in line. The Venezuelan outfielder, ranked No. 6 on the 2025 Top 50 International Prospects list, signed for $2.1 million and arrives with some of the loudest tools in the class. Nicknamed “La Bestia,” Bautista is a left-handed hitter and thrower whose raw power immediately stands out. His setup is unconventional -- he rests the bat on his back shoulder before striding -- but the results speak loudly. Evaluators consistently note the elite bat speed and double-plus raw pop. In batting practice and cage work, the ball carries farther and faster than most of his peers, and it showed up in games during his debut, with seven homers in the Dominican Summer League. Beyond the tools, it’s Bautista’s presence that resonates. In the Dominican Republic, he carried himself with a polish uncommon for his age -- mature in his routine, professional in his work habits and advanced in the way he controls the barrel. Defensively, his arm strength rivals his power, giving him a chance to profile in right field long term. But with plus speed and athleticism, he’ll get an opportunity to develop in center field. He’s young and still evolving, yet the combination of physicality, makeup and explosive tools makes him one of the most exciting recent additions to Seattle’s system, and he’s expected to play in the United States for the first time in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners are no strangers to landing big-time players on the international market, from Julio Rodríguez in 2017 to Noelvi Marte the year after that, not to mention Top 100 prospects Lazaro Montes (2022) and Felnin Celesten (2023). The Mariners are trying not to be too excited about Bautista, the No. 6 prospect on the 2025 Top 50 International Prospects list, the Venezuelan outfielder they signed for $2.1 million. Nicknamed \"La Bestia\" (The Beast), he has as loud of tools as just about anyone in the class. A left-handed hitter and thrower, Bautista utilizes an unusual swing and set up, resting his bat on his back shoulder until he strides forward. It's worked for him so far, with elite bat speed and double-plus raw power that he'll be able to continue to get to consistently as he gets more reps. Bautista's arm strength matches his power as one of the strongest in the class. He has the chance to be a plus defender, and he should get the chance to play center field with his plus speed as he gets his pro career underway this summer. He could end up in right field -- his arm and power bat certainly fit there, eventually, but they also said the same thing once about Rodríguez.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario reclassified to the 2020 Draft and was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 71 prospect in the class but went undrafted, in part because of his strong commitment to Miami. He never popped with the Hurricanes as expected, and the Rangers took him in the fifth round of the 2023 Draft as a build-back project. The right-hander took off in pro ball, posting a 2.24 ERA with 129 strikeouts and only 13 walks in 88 1/3 innings at Single-A and High-A; his 33.1 K-BB percentage was the best among Minor Leaguers with at least 80 frames in that 2024 season. Rosario injured his elbow getting ready for Spring Training in 2025, and Tommy John surgery was delayed until 2026. Before he officially underwent the procedure, the Nationals acquired him in January as part of the prospect return in the MacKenzie Gore deal. Rosario and the Nationals now must target a 2027 return to the mound, making him one of the biggest dart throws in prospectdom. He showed a 94-98 mph fastball that touched 100, and his move away from sinking movement and more toward riding action fueled his breakout. An 88-92 mph splitter became his best secondary pitch with tumble that A-ball hitters couldn’t handle. He also discarded a curveball and cutter from his Miami days and focused more on an 83-85 mph slider that flashed plus. The Rangers moved Rosario to the third-base side of the rubber and had him more focused on deception with a more closed delivery, and the improvements in control were astounding on the pro side. But by 2027 (his age-25 season), his early success will be a distant memory, and he’ll need to show his stuff and strike-throwing can return after a lengthy two-year layoff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario rated as a top-three-rounds talent after reclassifying into the 2020 Draft as a Florida high schooler, yet went undrafted because he was strongly committed to Miami. He got pounded for a 6.47 ERA in three years with the Hurricanes before the Rangers took him in 2023's fifth round and gave his mechanics and pitch mix a makeover. The results were dramatic during his pro debut last year as he posted a 2.24 ERA between two Class A stops while ranking first in the Minors in K-BB percentage (33.1 percent) and second in strikeout percentage (36.9 percent) and K/BB ratio (9.9) among pitchers with at least as many as his 88 1/3 innings. But then he injured his elbow getting ready for Spring Training in February and after other health issues, he still couldn't get his needed elbow surgery until 2026. Despite those, the Nationals acquired him as part of the mega-prospect return in January’s MacKenzie Gore trade. Rosario operated at 94-98 mph and reached 100 with his fastball in 2024, and he found more success blasting it by hitters at the letters in pro ball than he did sinking it down in the zone in college. His 88-92 mph splitter was a swing-and-miss pitch with devastating tumble and run at its best last year. He has scrapped the curveball and cutter he toyed with at Miami to focus on an 83-85 mph slider that shows flashes of giving him a third plus offering. After Rosario turned pro, the Rangers moved him to the third-base side of the rubber and had him keep his delivery closed longer to hide the ball better from hitters. He also creates some deception with his flat approach angle and his new mechanics have allowed him to pound the strike zone after he battled his control and command with the Hurricanes. Before he got hurt, he once again looked like the pitcher who intrigued scouts in high school and has the upside of a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his three years at San Diego State, Carrigg showed off electric tools while touching every position on the diamond at least once between his time with the Aztecs and playing in summer leagues. After the Rockies took him No. 65 overall in the 2023 Draft, he began seeing time behind the plate, at shortstop and in center field while flashing a power-speed combination at the plate. He had a solid first full season with High-A Spokane, but things unraveled a bit with a move to Double-A, even as he still occasionally showed off his pop and wheels. The conundrum with Carrigg has been how to allow him to keep the fire/aggression he plays with while helping learn to turn down the temperature just a little bit. A passive Carrigg won’t be successful, but high miss and chase rates led to a 27-percent strikeout rate in 2025 (vs. a just 8.4 percent walk rate). The switch-hitter has a flatter path and decent attack angle with his right-handed swing, but he doesn’t get that many at-bats from that side. He tends to tinker a lot with his left-handed swing and takes big hacks all the time. With an up-tempo style of play, the Rockies have worked with him on sticking with an approach and staying present pitch-to pitch. Carrigg’s speed certainly plays, with 99 steals over the last two years, and his defensive assignments have been simplified by having him play the outfield exclusively in 2025, while still having him work out on the dirt not in games, and his double-plus arm racked up 18 assists last year. He’s an above-average defender in center, at least, one who has big league regular tools if he can find a little balance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes you can have a Swiss Army knife and realize you don’t necessarily need to use every single thing it can do. That’s what the Rockies are learning about Carrigg after taking him in Competitive Balance Round B of the 2023 Draft. He had spent three years at San Diego State doing just about everything but selling hot dogs, showing flashes of all five tools while playing all over the diamond. He followed up a solid pro debut after signing by leading the High-A Northwest League in home runs (16) and finishing second in stolen bases (51) while whittling down his defensive homes. A super high-energy player who gets some “hair on fire” evaluations, Carrigg is a switch-hitter who makes a ton of contact from both sides of the plate. There was some concern about his aggressive nature and hit tool and how it would translate to this level, but the transition has gone well so far as Carrigg doesn’t strike out much and even drew a decent amount of walks. There’s more pop than many expected, with most of it coming from the left side of the plate to his pull side. He also can turn singles into extra-base hits and doubles into triples -- he led the league in three-baggers, too -- with his plus speed clearly an asset and giving him at least 20-30 potential. With one of the best arms in baseball, there were some who wanted to see if catching would work at this level, but that’s been shelved. He’ll keep getting some reps on the dirt at shortstop to maintain some versatility, but it should surprise no one if he shows up to Coors Field as an every day center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his three years at San Diego State, Carrigg did everything but play first base (including some relief appearances on the mound). His flashes of incredible tools excited scouts even more than his versatility, really jumping on the Draft prospect map when he hit .329 with 15 stolen bases in the Cape Cod League in 2022. That put him on the precipice of first-round conversations, but while he wasn’t bad during his junior year, he wasn’t quite as dynamic and ended up going to the Rockies in Competitive Balance Round B. He signed for $1.3 million and then opened some eyes with a .350/.408/.600 debut between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Fresno. A switch-hitter who can make a ton of contact from both sides of the plate, Carrigg can be a little overly aggressive at times. There were some questions about how his bat would transfer to the pro game, but so far they’ve been unfounded, as he’s been athletic in the box and shown good bat speed with the ability to drive the ball. He’s a plus runner who should continue to be a threat on the basepaths. Defensively, Carrigg has seen most of his time up the middle: at short, in center field and behind the plate. His double-plus arm is an asset in all three spots, as is his athleticism. His best position is center, with the Rockies cognizant that a plus arm is needed there in the vast expanse of Coors Field. He’s constantly on the attack on ground balls at short, and there’s confidence that would play if he got more reps there. He loves to catch, but it’s seen as the third-best option and the Rockies may not want to take his speed away by having him there full-time. Wherever he is, his hair-on-fire style of play should help him maximize his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best athletes in the 2022 prep class, Jordan went undrafted because he was a three-star wide receiver set on playing two sports at Mississippi State. He never stepped on the gridiron for the Bulldogs but performed well for two seasons before signing for a well-above-slot $1,997,500 in 2024's fourth round. He led the Single-A California League with 14 homers in his first full pro season despite missing the final month with an oblique strain, and he fell just one hit and one RBI short of the triple crown. Jordan has the quickest swing and the best all-around tools in the system. His right-handed stroke generates huge exit velocities and at least double-plus raw power that plays to any part of any ballpark. Though he still needs to tame a tendency to swing through in-zone fastballs and chase breaking balls, he did cut his strikeout rate from 27 percent with the Bulldogs to 23 percent last year. Jordan can get from home to first base in less than four seconds on a grounder, and he started translating that plus-plus speed into stolen-base and center-field prowess in 2025. He swiped 27 bags in 31 attempts (87 percent) after stealing just seven in two college seasons, and he looked very comfortable in center after playing only 13 games there at Mississippi State. He still needs to hone his defensive instincts but his 30/30 upside will work anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Jordan was one of the best high school athletes in the 2022 class, he went undrafted because he planned on playing baseball and football at Mississippi State. A three-star wide receiver recruit, he never took the gridiron for the Bulldogs but batted .336 with 30 homers in two seasons. After forfeiting their 2024 second- and third-rounders to sign free agents Matt Chapman and Blake Snell, the Giants were thrilled to find Jordan available in the fourth round and paid him a well over-slot $1,997,500. Jordan may have had the quickest swing in the 2024 Draft, and his bat speed and strength produce high-end exit velocities and plus-plus raw power to all fields. He'll need to tame his right-handed swing and approach to make the most of his pop, because he swings through fastballs in the zone and chases breaking balls off the plate. While he did improve his pitch recognition and plate discipline during two seasons in college, he still struck out at a 27 percent clip. Jordan has at least plus baseball speed and may have double-plus straight-line quickness, but he's still figuring out how to use it. He's not aggressive on the bases -- he swiped just seven bags in two years at Mississippi State -- and has shaky instincts in the outfield. He spent most of his time with the Bulldogs on the outfield corners while improving his arm strength from fringy to average.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas all-state wide receiver in high school, Cauley signed for an over-slot $1 million as a 2021 third-rounder. No one in the system offers a better combination of speed and defensive versatility, but his offensive game is still a work in progress entering his sixth pro season. His .253/.325/.448 batting line and 25 percent strikeout rate in Double-A last year represented the best numbers of his career. Cauley's small stature, big personality and ability to barrel balls with a high-effort right-handed stroke drew Dustin Pedroia comparisons in high school. His aggressiveness hasn't worked as well in pro ball, where he chases too many pitches and has some in-zone contact issues, even against fastballs. He does produce high exit velocities and elevates balls to his pull side, so he could provide 15-20 homers per season. Cauley uses his plus-plus speed well on the bases, where he's a prolific basestealer with a career 87 percent success rate. His quickness gives him good range at shortstop, where he displays solid arm strength but has had some issues with inconsistent accuracy with his throws. He played center field for the first time in 2025 and looked natural there, and he's also a quality defender at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas high schooler who signed for an over-slot $1 million as a 2021 third-rounder, Cauley drew some comps to a speedier Dustin Pedroia because he was a small middle infielder with a big personality and impressive hitting ability. While Cauley’s bat-to-ball skills haven’t translated to pro ball, he has shown promise in other phases of the game and with his nonstop energy. He slashed .235/.297/.411 with 35 extra-base hits and 27 steals in 93 games at High-A in 2024, missing a month early in the season with turf toe. After displaying a smooth right-handed stroke with plenty of bat speed and good feel for the barrel in high school, Cauley has had in-zone swing-and-miss issues as a pro. He gets overly pull-conscious and swings with so much effort, resulting in a 29 percent strikeout rate last year. He does hit the ball hard when he makes contact and could deliver 15-20 homers per season, but he may never provide much in the way of batting average or on-base percentage. A Texas all-state wide receiver in high school, Cauley has plus-plus speed and uses it aggressively on the bases, stealing 111 bags at an 89 percent success rate in 297 games during his first four seasons. His quickness also allows him to cover plenty of ground at shortstop, where he has solid arm strength but doesn’t always make accurate throws. He’s much more reliable at second base and has the tools to become a dynamic center fielder, though he hasn’t played there as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas high school product, Cauley reminded some area scouts of Dustin Pedroia as a small infielder with hitting ability and a ton of swagger. Since signing for an over-slot $1 million as a 2021 third-rounder, he hasn't displayed the same bat-to-ball skills he showed as an amateur but has delighted the Rangers with the rest of his game and constant energy. He slashed .245/.333/.411 with 12 homers, 36 steals and a 31.6 percent strikeout rate between two Class A stops last year, then had more issues making contact in the Arizona Fall League. Cauley showed a smooth right-handed stroke with plenty of bat speed and good feel for the barrel in high school, but he has gotten too aggressive as a pro. He swings with so much effort and gets overly pull-happy at times, throwing off his timing at the plate, though he hits the ball hard when he connects. He may never hit for a high average but he could provide 20 homers per season with plenty of walks. A former Texas all-state wide receiver, Cauley can create havoc with plus-plus speed that translated into 84 steals in 95 attempts (88.4 percent) in 201 games during his first three seasons. His quickness also gives him plus range at shortstop, where he has solid arm strength and some issues with throwing accuracy. He's a dynamic and more reliable defender at second base, and has similar upside in center field, where he has yet to play as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An all-state wide receiver before he gave up football as a Barbers Hill (Mont Belvieu) senior, Cauley led the Eagles to their first Texas 5-A state championship last spring. With his hitting ability and swagger packed in a frame generously listed at 5-foot-10, he reminded some area scouts of Dustin Pedroia. After signing for an over-slot $1 million in the third round last July, he batted .255 with 10 steals in 24 games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. Though Cauley's hand-eye coordination and smooth right-handed stroke should allow him to make consistent contact, he struck out at a 30 percent clip in his pro debut. It might simply have been a case of trying to do too much, as he got too pull-happy at times. He has enough bat speed and sneaky strength to produce 12-15 homers per season, though he'll need to launch balls more regularly to get there. A sparkplug built for the top of a batting order, Cauley has well-above-average speed and uses it to wreak havoc on the bases. He has the quickness, actions and instincts to remain at shortstop unless his merely average arm forces a move. He'd profile well athletically and offensively at second base or center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown homered 13 times in 26 games as a fifth-year senior at NCAA Division II Florida Southern in 2021, then signed for $7,500 as a money-saving 10th-rounder. He crushed Rookie-level pitching in his pro debut, a prelude to a spectacular first full season in 2022 during which he led the Minors in hitting (.346) and OPS (1.060), ranked second in slugging (.623) and sixth in OBP (.437) and totaled 23 homers and 44 steals in 103 games. A right knee injury limited him to two Double-A at-bats, required cleanup surgery that kept him out of the Arizona Fall League and the subsequent rehab cost him the first month of last season. He also battled hamstring injuries and played in just 59 games, slashing .221/.284/.421 in Double-A. Brown offers a stunning combination of physicality and tools, but he also enters 2024 at age 25 with precious few at-bats against advanced pitching. His massive strength and the bat speed in his right-handed stroke creates well above-average power, combining with his plus-plus speed and basestealing acumen (72-for-79 as a pro) to give him 30-30 upside. He has solid range in center field and is a plus defender on the corner, and his average arm plays fine at all three positions. Injuries cost Brown 500 at-bats in the upper Minors and the AFL in 2022-23, and he still has yet to prove he can handle high fastballs and stop chasing breaking balls against age-appropriate pitchers. Those issues and his pull-happy mentality resulted in 37.5 percent strikeout and 43 percent swing-and-miss rates in Double-A last year. He worked on reducing his leg kick and head movement last year and will have to make further adjustments to approach his lofty ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pandemic protocols limited NCAA Division II Florida Southern to 26 games in 2021 and cut down on Brown's exposure, but he homered 13 times as a fifth-year senior and Giants area scout Jim Gabella spearheaded the decision to take him in the 10th round. Signed for a mere $7,500, Brown tore up Rookie ball in '21 before leading the Minors in hitting (.346) and OPS (1.060) while ranking third in slugging (.623) and sixth in OBP (.437) during his first full pro season in 2022. He added 23 homers and 44 steals in 103 games while rising from Single-A to Double-A, though right knee discomfort limited his Double-A stint to two at-bats and led to cleanup surgery that kept him from playing in the Arizona Fall League. Brown will be 25 this season and has dominated significantly younger competition, but he's as physical as any player in the Minors and his tools are real. His massive bat speed and quick right-handed swing create well-above-average raw power and his plus-plus speed and base-stealing savvy contribute to his 30-30 potential. His quickness also translates to the outfield, where he's a plus defender on the corners and solid up the middle, and he possesses average arm strength. Despite his runaway success in his first two years as a pro, Brown will have to prove he can repeat it against more advanced and age-appropriate pitching. He struck out at 26 percent rate in 2022 and can get overly pull-conscious, though he did a better job of using the opposite field in High-A. He does have some holes in his swing, and some scouts wonder whether he can catch up to high fastballs and lay off breaking balls that veer out of the strike zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario was a tooled-up South Carolina high schooler when the Cubs selected him in the sixth round of the 2023 Draft and signed him for $325,600, and he's continued to flash major offensive potential since the Guardians traded Eli Morgan for him a little over a year later. The Dominican native has steadily climbed the rungs, making it to Double-A at age 21, and he tied for second in the Guardians' system in homers (21) and ranked ninth in OPS (.806). Big, strong and athletic like a linebacker, 6-foot-2 Rosario stands out for his power, with plenty of raw strength and bat speed. Getting to that power is the major question, as he ran a 33.1 percent strikeout rate with a simply unworkable 59 percent contact rate at Double-A. His approach could use work, as focusing on pull power maximizes his damage when he makes contact but has left him vulnerable to secondary offerings. Rosario is larger than most center fielders but will be given the opportunity to stick there because of his foot speed. There's a chance he'll continue to fill out his already-stout frame and slow down, which would push him to right field. The good news is he displayed the best arm strength of any player during a brief stint in the Arizona Fall League last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in the Dominican Republic, Rosario grew up in New Jersey before moving to South Carolina for his high school senior season in 2023. The younger brother of Padres infielder Eguy Rosario, he stood out with his physicality and raw tools on the showcase circuit, though he also was dogged by swing-and-miss issues and lasted until the Cubs took him in the sixth round. He finished fourth in the Single-A Carolina League in both homers (16) and strikeout rate (32 percent) in his first full pro season before Chicago traded him to the Guardians for Eli Morgan in November. Rosario is a study in extremes as a right-handed hitter. On the positive side, he has more bat speed and strength and generates more raw power and higher exit velocities than most 20-year-olds. But he's also overly aggressive, tries to launch every pitch he sees to his pull side and struggles to recognize or deal with non-fastballs. Rosario's big swing slows him down coming out of the batter's box, but he can flash well above-average speed once he gets going and he knows how to use it on the bases. His quickness gives him a chance to remain in center field if he can hone his defensive instincts. If not, his plus-plus arm strength is perfect for right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wolf opened eyes when he hit 97 mph in his first appearance as a senior at St. Thomas High (Houston) in 2019, and he parlayed a strong spring into an above-slot $2.15 million bonus from the Mets as a second-rounder. He dazzled during his abbreviated pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, where he struck out 12 of the 33 batters he faced, and again in instructional league following the canceled 2020 Minor League season. The Indians acquired him as part of a four-player package in the January trade that sent Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco to New York. Adding strength to his 6-foot-2 frame and lowering his arm slot has helped Wolf’s stuff take off. Those changes increased the velocity and movement on his fastball, which ranged from 90-97 mph with armside run during the spring and averaged 94 mph during his pro debut. He has a second future plus pitch in a curveball that registers in the low 80s with 12-to-6 break when he stays on top of it. Wolf's changeup isn't as effective as his other two pitches, though he can flash some solid ones with fade and tumble that point toward it becoming at least average. Wolf’s athleticism, quick arm and clean delivery enable him to pitch to both sides of the plate and all four quadrants of the strike zone, and he earns high marks for his aptitude with regards to making adjustments. He has plenty of room still to add strength to his projectable frame and should continue to get better with those physical gains as well as his development on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: How’s this for symmetry? Needing a reliable reliever in July 2025, the Rays traded the 37th overall pick in the Draft (a Competitive Balance Round A selection) to the Orioles for right-hander Bryan Baker. About five months later, the Orioles traded a haul of young talent -- including de Brun, who they took with that selection -- to get starter Shane Baz from … the Rays. Drawing comparisons to D-backs star Corbin Carroll, another undersized outfielder from the Pacific Northwest, the 5-foot-10 de Brun received an over-slot bonus of $4 million from Baltimore and didn’t play a professional game before he was dealt to Tampa Bay. Don’t let de Brun’s height fool you: He’s still a physical player. He earned attention with his performance on the summer showcase circuit in 2024, then showed up ahead of the Draft with more strength and an improved ability to drive the ball with his left-handed swing. But power isn’t necessarily going to be the key for de Brun. He has a pretty simple approach and stays behind the ball well, allowing him to put the ball in play and get on base, then use his plus speed to wreak havoc on the bases. He’s built well for that, as he has above-average bat-to-ball skills and an advanced eye at the plate for his age. de Brun’s speed also helps him in the outfield, where he has plus range and enough arm to let the rest of his skills carry him as a no-doubt center fielder. He has a big personality -- and a side gig as a musician/producer going by the name of “Lil Slayyy” -- and is highly regarded for his energetic attitude and work ethic. He’ll have to show what he can do on the field as he begins his pro career, but he has the makings of a table-setting offensive player and an impactful defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After logging an 0.89 ERA, .095 opponent average and 47/7 K/BB ratio as a Tennessee freshman reliever in 2023, Russell came down with shoulder soreness and forearm pain when he tried to start as a sophomore. He had internal brace surgery in June 2024 and was inconsistent in just 25 1/3 innings of work after returning last spring, but his unicorn fastball still intrigued scouts. The Rangers drafted him in the second round and signed him for an over-slot $2.6 million. Russell's heater parks at 93-96 mph and tops out at 98 with an unhittable combination of an exceptionally low release point, wide angle, significant armside run and carry. Hitters repeatedly chase his fastball out of the zone, miss it in the zone and rarely do damage when they do make contact. His low-80s slider features plenty of sweep and grades as a plus pitch when it's on, though it wasn't as reliable in 2025 as it had been previously. Despite using it only sparingly last spring, Russell made some progress with a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink, giving him a viable third pitch. His control hasn't been as sharp since his spectacular freshman year, but he throws enough strikes to succeed in the rotation. He has a ceiling of frontline starter but will have to prove he can hold up and maintain his stuff in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The switch-hitting Perez made big strides in 2021 to earn a promotion from the Arizona Complex League to Low-A Modesto for the final two weeks of the season, hitting a combined .308/.455/.378 (.832 OPS). This followed a strong impression he made in his age-17 season during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019. The Nicaragua native joined the Mariners’ organization the year prior for $175,000. Perez’s on-base numbers are among the best in Seattle’s system, thanks to an incredibly relaxed and confident approach at the plate and solid barrel control. His flatter-than-usual swing path leads to more quiet contact, which is why his power numbers aren’t off the charts, yet he makes up for it with his high average. For that reason, and given how young he is, the Mariners might opt to let that approach be for the time being. While his hitting profile doesn’t exactly stand out for a third baseman, he does have the chance to play there defensively with a huge arm and decent actions. Though some are worried about his range long-term, the Mariners are bullish on his potential to add more strength, grow into more power and fit the corner infield profile long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The switch-hitting Perez impressed in his professional debut during the Dominican Summer League in 2019, slashing .274/.381/.388 with four homers as a 17-year-old. Though he is so young, there is still plenty of room to grow athletically. He projects more as a third baseman, but he’ll need to show more pop at the plate to wind up there long term. His arm strength could even allow the Mariners to move him to the outfield if needed. Though he’s been more effective from the left side, the uber-confident Perez has shown elite bat-to-ball skills that have led to high line-drive and fly-ball rates, thanks to some quality bat speed. His power could be the determining factor in whether or not he remains at third, though the Mariners are bullish on his potential to rake, particularly after getting more looks at him at the fall developmental league in Arizona in 2020 -- his first reps stateside. Entering 2021, the “next step” phase for Perez will be simply playing. He was one of the many victims of the cancellation of the Minor League season, and the Mariners are excited about getting a clearer scope of how he projects by referring to a more tangible representation of his profile that can only be accumulated with playing time in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lalane received the highest bonus of any pitcher in the Yankees' 2020-21 international class, signing for $350,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He spent his first two pro seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before making his U.S. debut in 2023, when he was as impressive as any mound prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. He struck out 34 and walked just four in 21 2/3 innings. Lalane has the potential for three plus pitches, beginning with a fastball that parks at 93-95 mph and touches 97 with running action and good carry up in the strike zone. He has advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup that fades at the plate. His change is more consistent than his slider, though the latter still misses bats and sits around 80 mph. Despite being young and 6-foot-7, Lalane does a nice job of keeping his long limbs in sync and repeating his delivery to throw strikes. He shows the makings of solid command and features a low release point that belies his height and adds to his deception. While he'll need time to reach his ceiling, he has the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of the former St. Francis and European pro basketball forward of the same name, Lalane was born in the Bronx, moved back to his dad's native Dominican Republic as a youngster and played the outfield before taking up pitching at age 14. He signed for the largest bonus ($350,000) the Yankees gave to a pitcher in their 2020-21 international class, then opened eyes in his U.S. debut in 2023, when he was the best pitching prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. He looked great in two shutout innings against the Blue Jays during Spring Breakout last March, but shoulder issues restricted him to just 12 1/3 frames during the regular season. When healthy, Lalane demonstrates the potential for three plus pitches with possibly control to match. His fastball can sit at 93 mph and touch 97, though it could use more armside run and carry to keep it off barrels against more advanced hitters. He has advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks, while he's still learning to harness a sweeping 78-82 mph slider. The 6-foot-7 Lalane inherited size and athleticism from his father, and he does a fine job of keeping his long limbs in sync to repeat this delivery and pound the strike zone. His big frame offers some natural extension, and his low release height provides extra deception. While he has a huge ceiling, he also worked just 123 2/3 innings -- and just six above Rookie ball -- in his first four years as a pro and will be Rule 5 Draft-eligible after this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in the Bronx, Lalane is the son of former St. Francis and European professional basketball forward of the same name. He moved back to his dad's native Dominican Republic as a youth and played the outfield before moving to the mound at age 14. The recipient of the largest bonus ($350,000) of any pitcher in the Yankees' 2020-21 international class, he made his U.S. debut last year and stood out as the best pitching prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. He missed the first half of the 2024 season with shoulder issues. Lalane could have three plus pitches when he's a finished product, starting with a fastball that sits at 93-95 mph and reaches 97 with plus arm-side run and carry up in the zone. He already demonstrates advanced feel for a fading mid-80s changeup that's his more reliable secondary offering at this point. His 78-82 mph slider has a lot of lateral action, but he doesn't command it as well as his other two pitches. The 6-foot-7 Lalane has inherited his father's height and athleticism, and he has the body control to keep his long limbs in sync and repeat his delivery. He pounds the strike zone, shows the makings of solid command and works from a low release height that creates deception. He'll need time to develop but has a huge ceiling as a potential frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 70 | Arm: 50 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Still 17 on Draft Day in 2024, Payne was one of the youngest and fastest players in his class, and though he was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 53 prospect that year, he went 17th overall to the Brewers in July, signing for $3.44 million. He spent his entire first full season with Single-A Carolina, hitting .240/.354/.382 with eight homers and 31 steals in 77 games. Payne was one of only 11 players in their age-18 seasons or younger to get 300 or more plate appearances at Single-A in 2025, joining fellow Brewers Jesús Made, Luis Peña and José Anderson on that list. Payne’s plus-plus wheels continue to pop most on the diamond, and while he wasn’t always the most efficient attempted basestealer, his speed still gave opposing defenders plenty to consider. He glides well between the gaps in center field and could become a plus defender in the middle of the grass with more work there. The lefty hitter’s exit velocities have brought some intrigue to the offensive side of his game, and that added strength hasn’t come with the loss of any athleticism. Payne takes his walks by not expanding the zone, but after employing a leg kick, he can pull out of his swing quickly, leading him to be out of sync. His 30.1 percent strikeout rate in 2025 was no mirage with high whiff rates against all pitch types, and the choppiness of his swing led to a lot of ground balls. There could be more of a focus on waiting for pitches in the heart of the zone -- rather than generally swinging at most strikes -- that could help Payne build on his potential as a power-speed threat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered one of the fastest players in the 2024 class, Payne was also one of its youngest with his 18th birthday coming one month after the Draft itself. He was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 53 prospect in the group but became a Day 1 shock when he went 17th overall to Milwaukee. Payne signed for below slot at $3.44 million, allowing the organization to spread savings for later in the Draft, and he played briefly for Single-A Carolina, including two games in the Carolina League postseason. Payne’s plus-plus speed is a game-changer as he proved in that quick dip in the pros with four steals in five attempts. Batting from the left side, he can explode out of the box and often opens up early in his swing to give himself a head start on the way to first. That can often lead to ground balls -- some of which he’ll beat out with his legs -- and it’ll be important for him to add some more lift on his swings as he enters the pros over a larger sample. To his credit, he impressed some Brewers coaches with his physicality after reporting, and his exit velocities have been better than expected out of the gate, offsetting some strikeout concerns in 2025. Because of his speed, Payne can track down balls gap to gap in center field, and he should get plenty of looks there throughout his career. Once considered fringy, the former Houston commit should also have an average arm to help his defensive work. Payne’s speed should work well in the modern game and gives him a decent floor, and considering he’ll be 18 for much of his first full season, he’ll be given plenty of space to fill out the rest of his game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Winokur was a bit of a unicorn in the 2023 Draft class, a 6-foot-6 high school shortstop who showed flashes of all five tools at times. Concerns about his hit tool along with his signability deterred many teams, but the Twins took him in the third round of that July’s Draft and gave him second-round money ($1.5 million) to sign. In his first two full seasons of pro ball, Winokur has shown glimpses of putting those raw tools to use while also showing things he needs to work on to reach his considerable ceiling. While the numbers may not jump off the page in either of Winokur’s two seasons, there have been signs of an ability to put up numbers. The power-speed combination was on display with High-A Cedar Rapids, tying for the Midwest League lead with 17 homers while swiping 26 bags. The raw power is elite and it’s a question of him making swing changes so he can get to it. In the past, his swing path led to him not finding the barrel, leading to a lot of pull-side groundballs or flares the opposite way. Committing to adjustments to square up the ball more consistently will be key. Winokur is a freakish athlete whose agility has allowed him to play more shortstop than anyone thought possible when he was drafted. He’ll keep getting reps there and at third, where his plus arm plays very well and he’s an outstanding outfielder as well. There’s a lot of offensive development still needed, but Winokur will still be just 21 years old for all of the 2026 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Winokur, owner of some of the most impressive raw tools in the 2023 Draft class, wasn't taken on Day 1 of that summer's Draft, most thought he'd be heading to UCLA for college. The Twins were creative with their bonus pool and nabbed Winokur in the third round, giving him $1.5 million -- second-round money -- to sign. They were thrilled how much the tools showed up during his first full season in the largely pitching-friendly Florida State League, and while he has plenty to work on, he finished third in the league in OPS and in the top 10 in home runs (14) and wRC+ (116). Winokur is capable of flashing close to plus tools almost across the board on any given day. While there's definitely work to be done on his overall approach after a 115/34 K/BB ratio last year, he actually cut down on his K rate compared to his brief debut in the Florida Complex League. Because of the 6-foot-6 right-handed hitter's long levers, there's always going to be some swing-and-miss, and while he'll be focusing on his feel for contact and plate discipline moving forward, the Twins can live with some strikeouts if he reaches his considerable power potential. Perhaps the best overall athlete in the system, Winokur can really run, especially underway, and should continue to be a basestealing threat. His arm works very well from a number of positions, and while someone his size typically doesn't profile at shortstop, he was pretty solid at the premium position. He'll keep getting reps at third and also could end up being a good defender in center field or an elite one in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2023 Draft approached, there were teams who were no doubt interested in Winokur's size and the raw tools he showed, albeit inconsistently, the summer prior on the showcase circuit and then during his senior year at Edison High School in California. When the first day of the Draft came and went and Winokur's name had not been called, many expected he would head on to UCLA. The Twins had other ideas, going over slot ($1.5 million) in the third round to sign him, then sent him out for a brief debut in the Florida Complex League. During his 17 games in the FCL, the 6-foot-5 Winokur showed off some of his tools, namely his power, and also some of what he has to work on, striking out in more than 32 percent of his plate appearances. That's obviously a very small sample size, but there's long been concern about his swing-and-miss, as the right-handed hitter has long levers and employs a big leg kick, though he had shown at times as a prepster that he can be short to the ball. The raw power is legitimately at least plus and he's already done a lot of work since signing on making adjustments and his bat-to-ball skills so he can tap into it more consistently. Winokur is a tremendous athlete who runs very well, especially once he gets going. The Twins have been pleasantly surprised with how well he's moved on the dirt and they aren't ruling it out that he plays shortstop for longer than anyone anticipated. He'll get some reps at third and in the outfield, in center or perhaps a corner in deference to first-rounder Walker Jenkins.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dickerson had a senior year to remember in 2024, first helping Morris Knolls HS win a New Jersey state title in hockey in the winter and then tying Mike Trout’s single-season homer record in the state with 18 in the spring. The Nationals selected Dickerson 44th overall in that year’s Draft and coaxed him away from a Virginia commitment with a $3.8 million bonus, the largest handed out after the first round in the bonus pool era. After a brief stint in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League, Dickerson spent most of his age-19 season with Single-A Fredericksburg, hitting .204/.309/.319 with five homers and 21 steals in 83 games. Dickerson’s numbers are a good lesson in patience with prospects that have interesting raw tools. Despite his age and size at 5-foot-11, Dickerson topped out with an exit velocity around 112 mph in the Carolina League, a max that would fit in fine in the Majors already. His strength was something that interested scouts before the Draft, and more could be coming after he dealt with a wrist injury for at least part of ’25. Dickerson can look stoic at the plate, starting with hands held high and limited movement, until he began a leg kick, and while his swing decisions were decent, he still missed on a few fastballs and sliders. Dickerson will fly out of the box, putting pressure on the defense on even the most mundane ground balls, and if he could improve his angles off the bat (namely cut down on infield popups), he could test opponents even more with those wheels. He wasn’t exactly a sure-handed defender at shortstop with the FredNats, and with Eli Willits coming, the Nationals will move Dickerson around to second base and the outfield to make use of his athleticism.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 50 Dickerson was late to the baseball season in the spring of 2024 for a very good reason; he was helping Morris Knolls High School win a New Jersey state championship in hockey. When he did take the field, he created a bunch of helium and was being talked about as the top prep position player in the Northeast after tying Mike Trout’s single-season homer state record with 18. Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 49 prospect in the 2024 Draft class, Dickerson went 44th overall to the Nats in the second round and, in a sign of Washington’s enthusiasm for his trajectory, signed for $3.8 million – the largest bonus after the first round in the bonus pool era. There was plenty of intrigue on Dickerson’s bat headed into the Draft. Scouts believed in his feel for the barrel and were impressed by his ability to strike the ball to all fields. There’s ample strength in his short, right-handed swing that contributed to the power jump in his senior year, but some question whether he’ll have enough bat speed to handle pro pitching right away. Measured at 5-foot-11, Dickerson has a compact build and ample speed, flashing near top-of-the-scale wheels in 60-yard dash recordings. He has the right actions for shortstop at this early stage in his career, and the Nats have every incentive to give him plenty of looks there. His arm might be tested on throws deep in the hole, but his athleticism should help with a move to second base or center field, if it ever comes to that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets have had success with former two-way players recently, having drafted and developed Nolan McLean and Carson Benge, and Voit could be their next success story. Voit hit and pitched in his first two years at Michigan before internal brace surgery in July 2024 forced him to focus on being a position player in his Draft year. He hit .346/.471/.668 with 14 homers and a 34/40 K/BB ratio in 56 games as a Wolverines junior, and that performance pushed him to New York with the 38th overall pick. He signed for below slot at $1.75 million and got in 25 games with Single-A St. Lucie afterward. As can be the case when two-way types hone in their focus on one side, Voit saw improvements nearly across the board in his final collegiate season, particularly when it came to making better swing decisions. Despite relatively down performance in a small sample, he also showed wicked bat speed in the Florida State League, and if that holds up in his first full season, he could stand to be an above-average hitter when combined with the discipline. Voit projects for average power right now, though he could occasionally challenge for 20-plus homers. Voit has plus speed, and he isn’t afraid of using it to his advantage on the basepaths; he went 20-for-21 in steal attempts in the FSL. Between college and the pros, he got the bulk of his work in at second base, but he sprinkled in some shortstop with St. Lucie and impressed evaluators with how well his athleticism could translate to the more premium position. Voit’s plus arm strength from his pitching days will play anywhere on the dirt, and the Mets plan to keep rotating him to keep his avenues to Flushing wide open.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Asigen turned 16 years old in August 2025, making him one of the youngest players in this year’s international class, but he also entered the pro side with ample international experience, including a turn with the Dominican Republic’s squad at the 2024 WBSC U-15 Baseball World Cup in Colombia. (He walked 12 times in eight games in that tournament.) After being considered arguably the most advanced offensive player in this year’s international group, he signed with the Mets for $3.9 million at the opening of the window on Jan. 15. A left-handed hitter, Asigen already shows inspiring traits in the box. Despite his age, he’s already posted exit velocities above 110 mph, and using his quick hands, he shows an advanced feel for finding the barrel. He can create loft with his swing that could also help his loud contact translate nicely to the pro side. That said, Asigen did struggle to make contact on elevated fastballs on the outer third of the zone during his World Cup run a year ago, and his overall contact rate will deserve monitoring in the Dominican Summer League and beyond. A plus runner who can flash above that, Asigen has the quick-twitch movements that have enticed international scouts and made many believe he could stick at shortstop long-term. Those wheels could help elsewhere on the dirt if he were to ever move to second or third, but Asigen’s athleticism looks like it will be enough to hold off those chats for at least a few years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers grabbed the top Venezuelan prospect in three straight international classes: Diego Cartaya in 2018, Luis Rodriguez in 2019 and Diaz in 2020-21. Diaz commanded a $2,697,500 bonus with his potential for solid or better tools across the board. Beset by nagging injuries in his 2021 pro debut, he batted just .232/.308/.354 in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, and he has had swing-and-miss issues in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League this year. Scouts who saw Diaz as an amateur thought he had the upside of a .280 hitter with 20 homers per season. He has a quick right-handed stroke and some aptitude for driving the balls in the air, but he tries to launch nearly every pitch he sees and chases way too many of them out of the strike zone. He'll need to tone down his swing and improve his plate discipline and may have to repeat the ACL in 2023. Diaz has plus speed that presently translates more into range at shortstop than stolen bases. He's a gifted defender at short with smooth actions and plenty of range and arm strength. He'll need time to develop but still has one of the higher ceilings among Los Angeles' position prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers landed the top Venezuelan prospect in each of the last three international classes, including signing Diaz for $2,697,500 in January. He comes from the same training program (Alexis Quiroz's AQ Sport Agency) that also spawned Dodgers catching prospects Diego Cartaya and Yeiner Fernandez. He had one of the more advanced bats in the 2020 international crop and has the potential to develop solid or better tools across the board. With a quality right-handed swing and an advanced ability to recognize pitches, Diaz makes hard contact to all fields. He also has plenty of bat speed and loft in his stroke, and he could become a 20-homer threat as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame. His speed enhances his offensive profile, as he has been clocked at 6.4 seconds in the 60-yard dash and shows promise as a basestealer. Diaz has the athleticism, quickness and arm to play several positions, though there's no reason he should have to move off shortstop. He has smooth actions and covers plenty of ground, projecting as a possible plus defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peete was a two-way standout as a Georgia prepster but focused on hitting in his senior spring, when he showed as much bat speed as any other high-schooler in the country. The Mariners selected him 30th overall and signed him for $2.5 million. Peete showed tantalizing tools at Single-A (2024) and High-A (2025) in his two seasons in the Seattle system but struck out more than 30 percent of the time at both spots. Despite a career-high 19 homers with Everett last year, he registered just a 79 wRC+ in the Northwest League. The M’s traded him to the Cardinals as part of the prospect return in the Brendan Donovan trade. Several components make Peete a high-ceiling prospect and an interesting rebound candidate for the rebuilding Redbirds. He’s built like a wide receiver with a slender 6-foot-2 frame and packs a punch as well with plus raw power. He retains his plus arm strength from his pitching days, and after beginning his career on the dirt, he moved to center field in 2025 to strong reviews because his plus speed helps him gallop gap to gap to chase down balls. But so much comes down to Peete’s ability to make contact. Opposing pitchers have eaten him alive with non-fastballs. His left-handed swing can look pretty, but he’ll yank over the top of inside breakers and swing over changeups on the outer half with little hope for contact. Recognizing offspeed earlier out of the hand could certainly help, and to Peete’s credit, he did a better job of lifting and pulling when he did put bat on ball last year. It isn’t a hit tool that can be fixed overnight, but in its talent acquisition and development phase, St. Louis can take its time getting Peete to hit just enough for an everyday role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners took high school hitters in the first round for three Drafts in a row, ending with Colt Emerson in 2023. They also took three straight prep bats that year, following Emerson with Jonny Farmelo and then Peete, all taken in the Top 30 picks. Peete signed for a little under slot, $2.5 million, and the former Georgia two-way standout split his brief pro debut between the Arizona Complex League and full-season Modesto as he focused on hitting only. He spent his first full season back with Modesto and showed flashes of the tools that made him a top prospect, but also inconsistencies that need to be addressed. He still didn’t quite click offensively at High-A in 2025 and was traded to the Cardinals in the offseason as part of a three-team deal for Brendan Donovan. A premium athlete with a wide receiver's 6-foot-2 frame, Peete has a left-handed swing geared to do damage at the plate. He has immense raw power and showed flashes of it in 2024, with an approach that could let him crush balls to all fields. But he just as easily can get out of that approach when he tries to sell out for power, and while he does draw some walks, the 30.7 percent strikeout rate he registered in 2024 and 30.6 percent mark in ’25 aren’t going to work as he moves up the ladder. He doesn't have great rhythm and feel at the plate and could be an ambush power-over-hit type of offensive player. Peete uses his speed well on the basepaths, and he stole 70 bags over his first two full seasons in pro ball. He's seen time at shortstop, third base and in the outfield, and he might fit best long term in center, where he saw the bulk of his duties in the summer before his move to St. Louis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Touted as arguably the most athletic prep position player in the 2023 Draft, the Mariners were extremely bullish on Peete's potential, to the point where they took him in Competitive Balance Round A at No. 30 overall and signed him for $2.5 million, earmarking him to be a huge part of their offensive future along with many of his peers taken in that year's class. A two-way player in high school in Georgia, Peete dialed his velocity up to 95 mph off the mound but will transition exclusively to the hitting side in the pros. With a 6-foot-2, 193-pound frame, Peete has the look of a small forward or wide receiver and probably could've pursued a path in either sport. He has an electric left-handed swing that taps into tape-measure power, evidenced by grand slams in consecutive innings at Low-A Modesto last August, which were also the first two homers of his pro career. He also runs extremely well and has decent range, which keeps his options open at shortstop, third base and center field and makes him a potential premium player should he fully realize his potential. The knock on Peete in his incredibly early stages is that he can be susceptible to peaks and valleys at the plate. He rarely uses the opposite field and can get out of a solid approach when trying to pull balls. Those moments make him an easy target for quality pitchers, which he'll need to improve upon to continue climbing up the system. But the tools are all there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez was part of the Royals’ 2023 international signing class and joined the organization for $157,500. Two years later, he’s looking like one of the standouts of that group. The 6-foot-2 outfielder made his stateside debut in 2024 and his full-season debut in ‘25, when he logged 115 games and 415 at-bats for Single-A Columbia. Gonzalez slashed .239/.365/.289 with 12 doubles, three triples and one homer, along with a whopping 78 stolen bases. However, he was also caught stealing 26 times. The defense is the pull here with Gonzalez, a plus center fielder who can really run in the grass and on the bases. He’s efficient with his routes and has good instincts to go along with an above-average arm. There’s no doubt he can stick in center and play it at the Major League level, but getting there will be dependent on his bat. Gonzalez is very athletic at the plate and has a smooth swing, but it doesn’t translate into much power or quality contact with a lot of balls on the ground. He’s fast enough that he can beat out infield singles, though, and once he’s on base, he’s a true threat to steal. There’s an argument to be made that he’s the fastest runner in the system (some will say new international signing Angeibel Gomez, though). Gonzalez is young and still growing, so there could be some better contact in there as he adds strength. Gonzalez’s defense and speed will play as a Major Leaguer, but in order to fully make an impact, there will have to be more in the bat. The good news is that there’s still lots of development time for him, as he'll be only 20 years old for the entire 2026 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez signed with the Royals in the 2023 international signing class out of Venezuela for $157,500 and is beginning to look like a standout from that class. After earning midseason All-Star honors in the Dominican Summer League in 2023, Gonzalez made his stateside debut in ‘24, playing in 41 games in the Arizona Complex League with a .285/.398/.384 slash line, 11 doubles, 22 stolen bases and 110 wRC+. He jumped up to Double-A for four games at the end of the year. Another true center-field prospect in the Royals system, Gonzalez is a plus defender who looks like a natural in center already. He has average-to-a-tick-above-average arm strength that should improve as he grows. He’s 6-foot-2, 170 pounds right now and should be able to add more strength to his tall frame. That might help him find more pop in his bat. He’s more of a contact hitter with good exit velocities, an efficient mover despite his long arms and lankiness. His swing is more slashy with a lot of ground balls, but he does make quality contact -- having only struck out at a 20.3% clip in the ACL -- so there’s belief that the loft can come because of the foundation he has already. Gonzalez is a plus runner who has become more efficient on the basepaths with more reps. Gonzalez might have the highest ceiling of all of the Royals’ center fielders because of his foundation and projection, but he still has a ways to go in his development. He’d be a prototypical leadoff hitter who can be a weapon on the bases and a defensive asset if he puts it all together. He has strong makeup too and has transitioned to full-season ball at Single-A Columbia in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since Gil signed with the Braves in January 2023 out of the Dominican Republic for $110,000, he’s proven to be the best prospect from the class in the Braves' system. He hit well in his debut in the Dominican Summer League and has continued to hold his own in the United States, reaching full-season ball at age 18 in 2024, then turning in a solid overall season back with Single-A Augusta in '25. A 6-foot-1 right-handed hitter, Gil has some attributes -- from his speed to his defensive acumen -- that give him an intriguing combination of high floor and exciting tools. His nearly top-of-the-scale speed has allowed him to steal 94 bases over the past two seasons in the United States. At the plate, he already seems to understand that his job is to get on base, drawing walks at a good clip and limiting his strikeouts. That’s a good foundation to be a solid hitter with routinely competitive at-bats, even if he hasn’t shown much impact yet. Added strength should help him on both sides of the ball. He has a good chance to stick at shortstop, with that 70-grade speed helping with his range, and enough arm to play the left side of the infield. He’s played some third as well and could no-doubt handle second should that be needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gil was one of eight players the Braves handed out bonuses of six figures or more to at the start of the 2023 international signing period, starting with the $2.5 million Luis Guanipa received. Gil was at the bottom end of that group, getting $110,000 to join the organization, but his tools have stood out as much as anyone from the Braves class as he’s played his way from the Dominican Summer League in 2023 to the Florida Complex League and up to full-season Augusta during his United States debut in 2024 at the age of 18. In his brief time as a pro, Gil has already stood out for some loud tools, led by his close to top-of-the-scale speed. He’s at least a 70 runner, one who stole 40 bases in 48 attempts over 90 combined games in 2024. He’s shown a knack for contact and can really punish fastballs and he’s impressed with his overall approach, not chasing, drawing walks and getting on base (.376 on base percentage heading into 2025). He hasn’t shown much impact offensively yet, but there’s optimism that there is some juice to come in his right-handed swing as he gains strength. While Gil has seen time at both shortstop and third thus far, he has a real chance to stick at short long-term and the plan is to largely keep running him out primarily at the premium position, with a lot of range and enough arm to handle it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two productive years in Baton Rouge, Morgan was part of the loaded national title-winning LSU team in 2023, just before going to the Rays in the third round. He enjoyed a strong first full season with a .324/.408/.483 line, 10 homers and a 48/48 K/BB ratio over 100 games across Single-A, High-A and Double-A and was rewarded with trips to the All-Star Futures Game and Arizona Fall League. Morgan played all of 2025 with Triple-A Durham, finishing with a .274/.398/.412 line in 92 games after missing the start of the season with an elbow injury. After breezing through the lower levels in his age-21 season, Morgan met more of his match at the Minors’ top rung, though he showed promising signs late with a .339 average, .581 slugging percentage and as many extra-base hits (nine) as strikeouts in 16 games after September.
