His two-strike approach is one of the most pronounced in the game; he’ll choke up on his hockey-puck-knob bat and cut down on his leg kick to get quicker to the ball. But the Rays challenged him to not wait for two strikes as much, get off more competitive swings earlier in counts and give himself a better shot at tapping into his average raw power. Relying on pure contact ability will only get Morgan so far. On the other side, he’s one of the most gifted defensive first basemen of his prospect generation, thanks to soft hands and quick reactions. (His play on a squeeze bunt remains the stuff of College World Series legend.) Tampa Bay will still get him the occasional start in left field -- where he’s average -- because of the presences of Jonathan Aranda and Yandy Díaz in the Majors, but in either spot, he could use a more productive overall bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morgan was a three-year performer for LSU and a key piece of the Tigers’ 2023 national championship team. He was selected in the third round by the Rays that summer and didn’t disappoint in his first full season of pro ball, slashing .324/.408/.483 with 10 homers, 20 steals and an even 48/48 K/BB ratio over 100 games across three levels, including Double-A Montgomery. He was an All-Star Futures Game pick and finished out the year with a .338 average and an .891 OPS over 19 games in the Arizona Fall League. Using a puck knob bat and a choked-up grip, Morgan hits like a player anemic to the K. He stays balanced to cover plenty of the plate, and when he gets into a two-strike count, he spreads out wide and eliminates a leg kick to keep things as short to the ball as possible. His 11 percent strikeout rate was seventh-lowest among 628 Minor Leaguers with at least 400 plate appearances in 2024, but it's nearly doubled at Triple-A in 2025. By his own admission, his power comes more from the gaps than over-the-fence, but he’ll run into the occasional homer. From LSU to Tampa Bay, anyone who watches Morgan’s soft hands and quick reactions at the cold corner comes away thinking he could win multiple Gold Gloves there. As is their wont, the Rays got him some time in the outfield to expand his versatility, but he’s such a good fit defensively at first it might be best to leave him there. Rays officials say they aren’t worried about Morgan’s lack of power diminishing his value at first base and are willing to let him be himself given the plus tools in the rest of the profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: On the surface, Morgan profiles almost exactly as the opposite of Xavier Isaac, Tampa Bay’s Top 100 first-base prospect. Whereas Isaac is all power, Morgan came out of Louisiana State in 2023 highly regarded for his bat-to-ball skills and elite defense. Meanwhile, Morgan hit only 20 home runs during his entire three-year career as a starter for LSU. Nevertheless, the Rays selected the 2023 national champion in the third round of last year’s Draft and signed him for roughly slot value at $781,300. Why would the Rays be so aggressive on a first baseman who doesn’t seem like a prototypical slugger? For one, they view him as a truly elite defensive player at first, a rangy infielder with soft hands and thus a potential future Gold Glove Award winner. He proved it in college, even in the biggest moments, like when he made a game-saving play on a safety squeeze in the College World Series semifinals with the Tigers’ season on the line. He could play left field, as he did at LSU, but he’d be a fringy defender there with uninspiring arm strength. The Rays want to watch him play first, anyway. There might also be more at the plate than Morgan showed in college. Listed at 6-foot-1 and 215 pounds, he has the plate discipline to walk more than he struck out during his final spring at LSU and his professional debut. He rarely swung and missed at LSU, although that often resulted in weak contact. With his physicality and his selectivity, it wouldn’t be surprising if the Rays give Morgan the freedom to tinker with his setup and swing, thereby taking more chances on pitches he can hit hard in the air. Time will tell if he successfully implements those changes, but if he does, he’d be an all-around, everyday position player to watch in the Rays' system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport guy who played wide receiver and pitched for two years at Iowa, Brecht focused on the mound starting in 2023. A full-time member of the Hawkeyes rotation for two years, he showed first-round caliber stuff, but without the ability to command it, so he was on the board when the Rockies took him No. 38 overall in the ‘24 Draft. A back issue slowed him out of the gate, so he worked out of a piggyback system with Single-A Fresno in his first full season to get him innings in more of a rehab-like setting and continued to miss bats, and the plate, though he finished the year with a very strong seven-inning start in the California League playoffs. When Brecht is locked in, he can deliver an outing like that postseason one, giving some hope to his ability to start-long term. He’s touched triple digits in the past with his fastball and was sitting more in the 96-mph range with Fresno. The velocity is nice, but it can straighten out too much at times. The true out pitch is his slider, which he can crank up to 90 mph with horizontal and vertical action to it, a breaker that elicited a 58 percent miss rate last year, per Synergy. He added a curve at instructs, which immediately looked like a solid third pitch, while his splitter is a distant fourth. As athletic as Brecht is, his delivery has some timing inconsistencies, he can land too firm on his front side and he will change his arm slot at times. The lack of mound time because of his back didn’t help, but he’ll have to show he can find the zone more regularly after walking 5.2 per nine during his debut if he wants to stay in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brecht’s desire to play football and baseball at Iowa moved him away from being seriously considered in the 2021 Draft out of high school. After redshirting in football as a freshman and not getting that much playing time as a wide receiver for the Hawkeyes as a sophomore, he left the gridiron behind to focus on pitching as a junior. He shook off a slow start in 2024 after what evaluators felt was too much tinkering by the program with his mechanics and pitches, making his own adjustments and finishing very strongly. With stuff as electric as anyone in the class, his command issues likely pushed him out of the first round, but the Rockies leapt at the chance to take him No. 38 overall. Brecht’s fastball and slider combination are downright nasty when he’s locked in. His fastball sits in the 96-99 mph range and he touches triple digits. It can have good running action to it, though he struggles to locate it and it can straighten out. His slider is virtually unhittable, thrown up to 91 mph with a lot of horizontal and vertical action, eliciting a 56 percent miss rate last year. He doesn’t throw his low-90s splitter very often and he doesn’t have great feel for it. The biggest hurdle for Brecht to clear will be his command and control, as he left Iowa with a career 6.8 BB/9 mark. The cause for optimism on that front -- fueling the belief that he can develop into being a mid-rotation starter -- is that he’s a premium athlete and is committed to being more than just a pure thrower. There’s reliever risk for sure, but he could also take a huge step forward with more insightful instruction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez’s Draft stock wasn’t hurt without a high school season in 2020, with the Royals still selecting him in the second round and signing him for a $1.45 million bonus. He had already proven himself in ’19 at the inaugural Prospect Development Pipeline League when he worked six hitless innings over three outings. The Chicago native tossed 31 1/3 innings with a 4.31 ERA in Low-A Columbia last season before being shut down with fatigue. Hernandez did make it back to finish the season in the Arizona rookie league. Hernandez’s delivery features very little effort and is very repeatable, showcasing deceiving velocity with his 90-94 mph sinking fastball. But his changeup is his calling card, a devastating pitch that has tremendous fade and generates whiffs. Hernandez put an emphasis on improving his breaking ball last season, which also may have led to his 4.88 walks-per-nine ratio. But the mid-70s curveball did look improved, and it has the makings of being a plus pitch if he can throw it consistently with more power. He’s also learning how to manage his velocity and can see the ball elevate more than he wants, which also may have led to the 17 walks last season. Hernandez has great mound presence and the foundation to remain a starter with his athleticism and advanced feel for pitching. He needs to get a full season of work in for the Royals to see what they really have in him, but he has a high floor and the chance to move quickly if it begins to click.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez didn’t get a high school season in 2020 because of the pandemic, but that didn’t affect his Draft stock. He had proven enough for the Royals to take him in the second round and sign him for a $1.45 million bonus. Hernandez was the best pitcher at the inaugural Prospect Development Pipeline League in 2019, working six hitless innings over three outings while walking one and striking out seven. He also struck out the side in a perfect ninth inning at the Under Armour All-America Game. The Chicago-area native finally donned a Royals uniform at their instructional league in Arizona in the fall. Hernandez easily had the best changeup in the 2020 Draft. The pitch is devastating, and he showed in the fall that he can get swings and misses with it. It sits in the low 80s and has tremendous fade. His 90-95 mph fastball has some sink to it that plays up because of his command. His mid-70s curveball is his third offering and has the makings of being a plus pitch if he can throw it with better arm speed and power. Hernandez’s delivery features little effort, and he can repeat it very well. Hernandez has an advanced feel for pitching and the body and athleticism to remain as a starter. The Royals eased him into the season at Low-A Columbia because of his low innings count from last year, but he has a higher floor and the chance to move quicker than a typical prep pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carraway first piqued Dallas Baptist's interest as a center fielder and threw in the mid-80s as a Texas high school senior in 2017, so he wasn't a high-priority recruit and didn't attract interest from pro clubs. His velocity began to climb as a freshman but he was so raw that he made just two appearances and retired only one of the seven batters he faced. He made a huge leap forward as a sophomore, averaging 15.6 strikeouts per nine innings as the Patriots' closer and becoming the first player in school history to make the U.S. collegiate national team. The favorite to be the first reliever drafted in 2020, Carraway has a pair of overpowering pitches in his fastball and curveball. His heater sits at 93-96 mph and touches 98 with riding action, while his downer curve usually parks in the upper 70s. His pitches play up because they have high spin rates and he gets good extension in his delivery, and both can grade as well above average when at their best. As a 6-footer who lacks physicality and features a lot of effort in his high three-quarters delivery, Carraway is strictly a reliever. His control and command have improved in college but still need to get better if he's going to hold down a high-leverage role in the big leagues. He should be one of the first players from the 2020 Draft to reach the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tiger played three seasons at Butler County (Kan.) CC sandwiched around a one-year sabbatical, setting school records for career wins (21) and strikeouts (243) as well as single-season whiffs (121). The highest pick in Grizzlies history as a seventh-rounder in 2023, he starred in Spring Breakout the following March, missed the first two months of the season with elbow inflammation and then returned to pitch well and reach High-A before his elbow gave out in August. Internal brace surgery a month later cost him all of him 2025 but he's fully healthy for this season. Before he got hurt, Tiger's fastball sat at 94-97 mph and touched 100 with good carry but just modest life, and he held his velocity deep into games. He also could overpower hitters with an upper-80s slider that climbed to 92 mph and featured two-plane depth, though it was more of a chase pitch than something he could trust to land for strikes. The Rangers had him scrap his mid-80s changeup after he turned pro, replacing it with a promising upper-80s splitter. Tiger's athleticism and clean delivery translate into decent control, though his lack of fastball movement and overall deception means he can get hit hard when his command is off. Texas has discussed giving him a curveball to use as a non-power offering, but his elbow issues put that plan on hold. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter but is also 25 years old with just 50 innings of pro experience, so the Rangers could be tempted to expedite him as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 60 | Splitter: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Tiger spent the shortened 2020 season at Butler County (Kan.) CC, left school in 2021, then returned for the next two years. He set Grizzlies records for single-season (121) and career (243) strikeouts, as well as career wins (21) in 2023 and became the highest pick (seventh round) in school history. He dazzled during Spring Breakout last March, missed the first two months of the season with elbow inflammation, then compiled a 2.93 ERA with 59 strikeouts in 46 innings at three stops. But his elbow gave out in August, requiring internal brace surgery in September that will sideline him for all of 2025. A healthy Tiger can blow hitters away with a four-seam fastball that sits at 94-97 mph and tops out at 100 with quality carry but modest life, and he holds his velocity deep into games. His upper-80s slider hits 92 mph and misses bats with its two-plane depth, though it’s more of a chase pitch than one he can land regularly for strikes. After he turned pro, Texas had him dump a traditional mid-80s changeup and add a promising upper-80s splitter. Tiger’s athleticism and clean delivery give him decent control, though his lack of fastball life and overall deception means his stuff can get hit harder than it should if his location is off. The Rangers considered having him try a curveball to give him a non-power pitch, but his elbow issues scrapped that plan, at least for 2024. He has the upside of a No. 3 starter but he’ll also be 25 with just 50 innings of pro experience when he returns next year, so he could get expedited as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tiger began his junior college career at Butler County (Kan.) CC during the shortened 2020 season, was out of school in 2021 and then returned for the next two years. He set school records for single-season (121) and career (243) strikeouts as well as career wins (21) in 2023 and became a rare 22-year-old juco draftee when the Rangers made him the highest pick (seventh round) in Grizzlies history. He impressed in a brief pro debut that included six strikeouts in three hitless innings in the Single-A Carolina League playoffs. Tiger's four-seam fastball parks at 94-97 mph and tops out at 100 with carry but only modest life, and he maintains his velocity deep into games. His upper-80s slider touches 92 mph with two-plane depth, inducing a lot of empty swings, though he'll have to prove he can land it for strikes when hitters don't chase it. Texas had him scrap a traditional mid-80s changeup and install an upper-80s splitter with promising tumble. A quality athlete with a clean delivery, Tiger provides a decent amount of strikes. He does lack fastball movement and overall deception, so his stuff gets hit harder than it should at times. The Rangers will work with him to improve his pitch shapes and perhaps add a curveball to give him a softer option, seeing a potential No. 3 starter who also offers some intrigue as a relief option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Neighbors put himself on the map in a big way as a sophomore at Kansas State, emerging from relative nowhere to strike out 86 batters in 48 ⅔ innings in 2023. He endured some non-arm injuries the following year that muted his Draft stock a little, but he still went to the Padres in the fourth round and signed for around slot at $600,000. Neighbors then spent his first full pro season essentially replicating his eye-popping college numbers by pitching to a 1.53 ERA and compiling 83 strikeouts in 59 innings. The Orioles acquired him as part of the massive six-player package for Ryan O’Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the 2025 Trade Deadline and watched him finish the year with 12 dominant outings in his new organization. The 6-foot-2 Neighbors looks like a potentially electric closer who could move quickly. All three of his primary pitches could be plus offerings, including a four-seam fastball that he dialed up to 97 mph after the trade. The heater gets great induced vertical break because Neighbors throws it out of a high slot, and it’s most effective when he keeps it at the top or above the zone and lets it ride above the hitter’s barrel. His mid-80s slider is a potential wipeout pitch, and his curveball is a low-80s breaker with big depth. His strikeout rate was 36.4 percent in ‘25, including 31.6 percent at Double-A. Neighbors is energetic and fiery on the mound, having long grown comfortable pitching in high-leverage situations. He doesn't issue too many walks for a relief prospect and trusts his stuff enough to work it outside the zone, where it gets whiffs. He will be 23 in 2026 and could be pitching his way into big league consideration before long.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals were down $500,000 in their international spending pool for 2024 after signing Willson Contreras the previous offseason, but they still managed to bring in a pair of interesting talents that year in Top 100 prospect Rainiel Rodriguez and Padilla, who signed for $760,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He and Rodriguez were both Dominican Summer League midseason All-Stars that year with Padilla posting a .287 average and a .795 OPS in 35 games. He headed stateside for 2025 and slashed .283/.396/.367 with seven extra-base hits, 24 steals and a 21/18 K/BB ratio across 38 games. A switch-hitter, Padilla has spent significantly more time as a lefty hitter at this early stage in his career, and the experience shows in the results with better impact coming from the left side. His overall contact rate took a nice jump with his move to the Florida Complex League, but coincided with less swinging overall, including on drivable pitches over the plate. Balancing out those decisions should be a priority higher up the chain. Padilla will flash good exit velocities for his age, including a 102.1 90th-percentile EV in the FCL, but he needs to improve his angles by cutting down on ground balls and easy-out infield popups. With plus wheels, Padilla is always a threat to steal bases and his athleticism, which includes a plus arm, has kept him locked in at shortstop to this point. He still requires development to remain at the six, but if he fills out with more strength, he could slide over to third where he’d handle the throws well. Everything hasn’t quite clicked into gear for Padilla yet, and there’s a chance some of his skills could backslide in full-season ball. But he still has everyday upside at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals weren’t massive spenders at the opening of the January 2024 international window -- they were down $500,000 in pool money due to Willson Contreras’ signing the previous offseason -- but they still might have managed to sign a potential star in Padilla for $760,000 out of the Dominican Republic. The shortstop slashed .287/.391/.404 with one homer, four triples, five doubles and 22 steals in 35 games. He was named a Dominican Summer League midseason All-Star alongside fellow Top 30 talent Rainiel Rodriguez. A switch-hitter, Padilla saw a lot more time from the left side than the right, where he only got 24 plate appearances and went 2-for-18 (.111) with five walks. That’s a sample-size issue but something worth monitoring as he heads stateside. His overall contact rate was solid, and he’s already shown a willingness to take his walks against wild DSL arms. His power was limited to the gaps in ’24. Optimistic evaluators expect he’ll get to at least average in-game pop as he fills out his frame, while others are concerned he’s behind the curve when it comes to current raw power. Padilla can fly, though, and he can turn those balls to the gaps into doubles and triples with ease. He’s also a constant stolen-base threat, and he uses those wheels well with his promising range at shortstop. His plus arm strength gives him another defensive weapon, and while there’s always a chance he could slide to third, those concerns are quieter now than when he signed. The best farm systems are built around high-quality shortstops, and after graduating Masyn Winn in 2024, the Cardinals could have their next one at the six in Padilla.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knowing how difficult it can be to acquire prospects once they’ve put themselves on the radar, the Rays have no reservations about pushing to land them a year early rather than waiting for a breakout. That was the mentality with Johnson, whom they picked up alongside Santiago Suarez in a November 2022 trade with the Marlins for Xavier Edwards and JT Chargois. Johnson was a reliever at Duke in 2021, didn’t pitch well as a starter during his final season with the Blue Devils, went to Miami in the fourth round of the ’22 Draft and had a mostly forgettable professional debut. But in Johnson, the Rays saw a big, physical strike-thrower with the command to potentially be a big league starter. The 6-foot-6 right-hander mostly delivered on that promise in his full-season debut last year, posting a 3.74 ERA while walking only 3.9 percent of the hitters he faced for Single-A Charleston, a level where he was expected to succeed as a polished college pitcher. He has three average-or-better pitches, puts them all where he wants them with pinpoint control, knows what he’s trying to do and works quickly. His 82-85 mph slider is his best pitch, while his fastball has sat between 90-94 mph (with a tendency to flatten out when it’s on the lower end of that scale) and his changeup clocks in around the mid-80s. Johnson handled a starter’s workload last season, knocking down 130 innings over 26 outings. But there was some concern when he lost weight as the season went on, making his tall frame look even more wiry. He put on 10-15 pounds of muscle over the offseason, which enhanced the velocity (and carry) on his fastball at the outset of the spring; if that holds up, Johnson could take another step toward his potential as a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After serving as the top reliever at Duke in 2021, Johnson only spent one season in the Blue Devils’ rotation and didn’t perform well during his platform season, going 1-8 with a 5.61 ERA in 13 outings. But scouts were still intrigued by his size, physicality and starter traits, so the Marlins picked him in the fourth round of the ’22 Draft and signed him for $507,500. Although he posted mediocre-at-best results in his brief organizational debut for Miami, the Rays were pleased to land Johnson alongside righty Santiago Suarez in November 2022 as part of a trade for Xavier Edwards and JT Chargois. The lanky, 6-foot-6 righty has a three-pitch arsenal headlined by a high-spin slider that sits between 82-85 mph with two-plane depth. He’s also implemented a mid-80s changeup more often since moving into the rotation. The real question is about Johnson’s fastball, which sat between 90-94 mph last spring, down from his days as a reliever. It has some arm-side run and carry, but the pitch flattens out and can be barreled up when he’s not locating it well at the top of the strike zone. Johnson still has plenty of room to add strength to his tall frame, and he’s athletic enough to keep his long limbs in sync and repeat his clean delivery. He has a lot of traits that Tampa Bay likes -- specifically his size, stamina, strike-throwing and ability to spin the baseball -- so they can look past his stats and dream on what he’s occasionally shown he can be, like when he struck out 10 over five innings in his final start last season. He's been one of the Minors' best strike-throwers in 2023, and that ability to fill the zone helps those Tampa Bay dreams.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Once viewed as a potential top-five pick out of high school, Watson fell to the No. 16 pick in 2021 -- and was traded to the Guardians two years later -- in part due to makeup concerns. He's had a winding path through the Minors but has shown flashes of the talent that earned him a $4,540,790 bonus. Watson reached Triple-A for the first time at age 22 and put together his best campaign yet, with a .250/.346/.467 slash line, 16 homers and 17 steals. The North Carolina native is a dynamo athlete at 5-foot-9 and displays plus raw power from the left side with a quick, lofted swing that's geared for extra bases. That power comes with plenty of whiffs, though, especially against secondary pitches, and the team is working to improve his approach, especially as he gains more access to information on how teams attack him. He did make notable strides in being more selective and making better contact upon his promotion to Triple-A. Watson has also struggled against southpaws, which could point to a platoon role if his bat-to-ball skills don't continue to develop as hoped. After coming up as a shortstop and moving around the infield, Watson spent an entire season in the outfield for the first time in 2025 and looked like a viable center fielder. He made dramatic progress throughout the season and displayed great reads for someone with little experience. He has enough arm to play anywhere in the outfield, and his plus straight-line speed is an asset there -- he's also working to utilize his speed better on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A candidate to go No. 1 overall to the Pirates on a below-slot deal in the 2021 Draft, Watson instead dropped to the Marlins at No. 16 amid signability and makeup worries and landed an over-slot $4,540,790 bonus. His first full pro season was a struggle, as he hit .232/.296/.395 with a 35 percent strikeout rate and got demoted for a month after making a threatening gesture toward an umpire. He posted similar numbers in 2023, when the Guardians bought low on him in an August trade that sent Josh Bell to Miami. Watson still has the physical tools and the upside of a 25-25 shortstop that made him a first-round pick. He has a smooth left-handed swing, some of the best bat speed in the system and plus raw power. He also can flash well-above-average speed and show off plus arm strength at his best. The question is whether Watson can translate those tools into skills and approach his ceiling. He made some progress with his discipline in 2023 but still gets out of control at the plate, chasing pitches and not keeping his upper and lower halves in sync. He covers ground at shortstop but is erratic there, looks much more comfortable at second base and probably will get some time in center field this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A candidate to go No. 1 overall in the 2021 Draft on a below-slot deal to the Pirates, Watson instead slipped all the way to the Marlins at No. 16 amid signability and makeup concerns. Signed for $4,540,790, he batted .232/.296/.395 with a 35 percent strikeout rate in Single-A during his first full pro season and was demoted for a month after making a threatening gesture toward an umpire in July. He was posting similar numbers in High-A this year before Miami shipped him and Jean Segura to the Guardians for Josh Bell at the Trade Deadline. Watson still possesses the physical ability that enchanted the Marlins. He has a smooth left-handed swing, plenty of bat speed and sneaky strength that lead to at least solid raw power and well-above-average speed. But he won't come close to realizing his potential if he can't learn to make better swing decisions and stop getting himself out at the plate, and he also needs to do a better job of controlling his emotions. An explosive athlete, Watson has the quickness to be a dynamic basestealer and cover plenty of ground at shortstop. He has nice infield actions and plus arm strength but needs to develop more consistency after making 14 errors in 51 games at short last season. He was more reliable at second base and that also has been the case in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watson was a candidate to go No. 1 overall to the Pirates on a below-slot bonus as well as a consensus top-10-pick talent last July, but he dropped all the way to the Marlins at No. 16 when his signability became a factor due to the slide. Miami signed him for $4,540,790, the largest bonus it has ever given a high-school position player, but his first full pro season has gone poorly after a strong April. He has struck out in nearly 40 percent of his plate appearances, and the Marlins sat him down for three weeks for gesturing at an umpire. Listed at just 5-foot-9 and 178 pounds, Watson plays much bigger than that at the plate thanks to an abundance of bat speed and a take-no-prisoners left-handed stroke. But after he had a history of making consistent hard contact as an amateur despite his aggressive mentality, his approach has been exploited by Single-A pitchers and he has yet to show he can make adjustments. He has plus raw power that could produce 20 or more homers per season if he can improve his hittability and turn on more pitches. Watson is an explosive athlete who can use his well-above-average speed to wreak havoc on the bases. He has all the attributes needed to play a solid shortstop, including smooth actions, range to both sides, arm strength and keen instincts, and he just needs to develop consistency that should come with experience. He has the athleticism to play almost anywhere on the diamond and also has seen action at second base this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: By the time Castillo blossomed physically as a Venezuelan amateur, teams had committed most of their bonus pool money, allowing the Rangers to sign him for the relative bargain price of $647,500 in 2024. He slashed .377/.481/.415 in his pro debut between two Rookie levels and then held his own as an 18-year-old in Single-A at the end of 2025. He has one of the highest floors among the system's position players as well as a high ceiling, especially if his power develops. Even against significantly older competition, Castillo continued to display impressive bat-to-ball skills and an advanced approach. The right-handed hitter has begun to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame, which along with increased bat speed allows him to flash high-end exit velocities. Though he only went deep once in his first 123 pro games, his hitting ability and projectability portend at least future 15-homer power if not more. Castillos' solid speed, quick first step and instincts helped him steal 29 bases in 31 attempts (94 percent) during 88 games last season. His smooth actions, range to both sides, quick hands and solid arm strength leave no doubt that he'll stick at shortstop, and he also looked good at third base last summer. His high baseball IQ and strong work ethic allow him to get the most out of his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A late bloomer physically as a Venezuelan amateur, Castillo signed for $647,500 in January 2024. He would have commanded a higher bonus had teams not previously committed most of their bonus pool money, and he definitely would now after one of the best debuts in the 2024 international class. He batted .377/.481/.415 with nearly twice as many walks (27) as strikeouts (15) in 35 games between two Rookie leagues, hitting his way to the United States after just a month in the Dominican Summer League. With a contact-oriented right-handed stroke and a very mature approach for a teenager, Castillo has some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the system. Though he had just five extra-base hits (all doubles) in his introduction to pro ball, he has plenty of room to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame and could grow into 15-homer power once he does. His bat speed has increased as he has begun to mature physically and should continue to do so. Castillo has solid speed with a quick first step that should help him steal a few bases. He's a no-doubt shortstop with smooth actions, range to both sides, quick hands and solid arm strength. The Rangers love his makeup and high baseball IQ as much as they appreciate his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Listen to coaches, scouts and staff describe Pierce long enough, and you’ll realize that some of the commonly held beliefs about coach’s kids just might be true. Pierce’s father, Paul -- no, not the former NBA star, although LeBron James once made that mistake on social media -- was his coach at Mill Creek HS in Hoschton, Ga. Pierce was his dad’s best player and exactly what you’d expect, given his background: a sponge for knowledge, a tireless worker and someone who gets the most out of his ability. The Rays liked what they saw in terms of his physical ability and makeup, prying him away from a Georgia commitment with a $4,313,100 bonus as the 14th overall pick in 2025. Pierce is generally regarded as a well-rounded player, not your typical showcase star. He has a mature, all-fields, contact-oriented approach at the plate. The right-handed hitter controls the strike zone well and doesn’t necessarily sell out for power, although he should grow into more pop as he continues to grow and add strength. He put on some muscle in his first professional offseason, and the Rays saw encouragingly early leaps in his exit velocity readings heading into his debut season. If there is one standout tool at Pierce’s disposal, it’s his plus speed. He runs well enough to project as a future stolen-base threat, and he uses his natural athleticism at shortstop. He’s a confident, aggressive defender there with good hands, range, actions and arm strength. He still needs to improve his body control, but that’s to be expected of someone his age. Pierce draws rave reviews for his competitiveness, makeup and work ethic. He’s tried to model his game after Bobby Witt Jr., and while he may not reach that level of superstardom, he could develop into an all-around impact player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending his first two college seasons at East Carolina, Root transferred to Arkansas and became the ace of a team that finished third at the 2025 College World Series. He finished fifth in NCAA Division I with 126 strikeouts in 99 1/3 innings and offered one of the highest floors among college starters. The Dodgers chose him with their first pick at No. 40 overall and immediately followed with Razorbacks teammate Charles Davalan at No. 41. Root used a low-90s sinker to generate groundball contact in college, but Los Angeles is having him focus on a four-seamer with nasty ride up in the zone that topped out in the upper 90s during offseason workouts. His best weapon is a fading 83-85 mph changeup, though his low-80s curveball is close behind and he topped D-I with 51 strikeouts via his bender last spring. He also employs a mid-80s cutter/slider and mixes his pitches very well. Root creates a lot of deception with an unusual delivery that features a high leg kick and a deep arm swing leading up to a three-quarters arm slot that enables him to stay on top of his offerings. His mechanics don't hamper his strike-throwing ability, though he's not overpowering and sometimes catches too much of the plate. Signed for $2,197,500, he'll make his pro debut in 2026 and is a reasonable bet to become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from the Hudson Valley region of New York, Stafura was a high school infielder taken by the Reds in the second round of the 2023 Draft, getting an over-slot bonus of $2.5 million. The Reds sent him to the Arizona Complex League to begin his first full season, and Stafura hit so well there that he got moved to full-season Daytona after just 15 games. He was back in the Florida State League having a solid 2025 when he was sent to the Pirates in the Ke’Bryan Hayes deal at the Trade Deadline. He got pushed from Single-A Bradenton quickly up to High-A Greensboro for a playoff push, and the whirlwind of three teams in seven or so days was a bit overwhelming. While Stafura struggled a bit after the trade, the Pirates feel there are some underlying metrics that point to future impact. The right-handed hitter’s top-end exit velocities were still well above average, even during his rough stretch in Greensboro while playing at the level at age 20. He can try to muscle up too much and get rigid, and he needs to rely on his natural athleticism in the box more. There’s a bit too much swing-and-miss and chase, especially against spin and elite velocity up in the zone, but his strike zone knowledge has helped him offset that with a career walk rate close to 15 percent heading into the 2026 season. Stafura’s floor is raised because of his speed -- he’s stolen 30-plus bases in each of his two full seasons of pro ball -- and his defense. The Pirates have every confidence in his ability to stick at shortstop, already liking his outstanding range, actions and instincts at the premium position. They’ll get to help him find out what kind of offensive player he is, and that will determine his ultimate ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stafura became just the second high school infielder from New York to be taken in the top two rounds of the Draft, following Yankees 2010 first-rounder City Culver. Signing for an over-slot $2.5 million, Stafura struggled in his first brief taste of pro ball in the Arizona Complex League but clearly learned some lessons he brought with him into 2024, when he posted a 1.031 OPS in 15 games back in the ACL to earn a promotion to Single-A Daytona, where he continued to show impressive on-base skills and basestealing acumen. It was more of the same back in Daytona for the 2025 season when he was sent to the Pirates close to the Trade Deadline for Ke’Bryan Hayes. Staying more athletic in the box will continue to be key for Stafura, along with using the big parts of the field, rather than trying to muscle up too much. A bat wrap he used back in high school can show up at times, making it a little tougher for him to catch up to elite fastballs, but he’s shown that he can make adjustments and has a pretty good idea of the strike zone, so there’s confidence that more reps will help him address those things. He uses his speed very well, turning his .384 on-base percentage with Daytona over two years into 55 steals in 166 games. Stafura’s athleticism is an athlete on the dirt as well. He’s played shortstop almost exclusively thus far in his pro career and there are no plans to change that, and he has the range, hands, actions and arm to stick there long term. He’s gotten high marks for his passion for the game and his work ethic, with considerable ceiling to reach as he continues to learn about what it takes to manage a season-long workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s never clear how a high school player from a cold-weather state is going to transition to pro ball after signing. Stafura, who rose up Draft boards in 2023 while playing in New York, landed in the second round and got an over-slot bonus of $2.5 million to sign rather than head to Clemson. His debut in the Arizona Complex League was a very brief 12-game stint, but showed it might take a little time for the infielder to get acclimated. The Reds feel that during his senior season, Stafura got away from what made him a prospect in the first place. He was often too stiff, with strength over bat speed as he perhaps tried to tap into his natural raw power too much. The hope is that he can get back to the more athletic and complete hitter he was previously, staying through the middle of the field. There’s some work to be done in terms of consistency in his approach and repeating his swing mechanics will be key. While he struggled a bit offensively out of the gate, there were no such bumps with the other facets of his game. He’s an easily plus runner, and he showed off very impressive defensive skills in the ACL and instructional league play. A tireless worker with great passion for the game, there’s plenty of confidence he’ll start showing more consistent results once he gets more reps against premium stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $775,000 as the Rangers’ third-rounder in the shortened 2020 Draft, Roby has mixed promise with a checkered health history in the six years since. He has exceeded 100 innings in a Minor League season only once, in 2022 with then-High-A Hickory. Texas traded him to the Cardinals a year later as part of the Jordan Montgomery swap at the ’23 Deadline in Roby’s first of two seasons in which shoulder issues held him back. He looked on track to break through to the Majors perhaps in ’25 with 16 starts -- including six at Triple-A Memphis -- before he needed Tommy John surgery in late July, a procedure that will keep him out for much, if not all, of 2026. Roby’s four-seam fastball ran 94-97 mph and despite some ride and cut on the heater, Triple-A batters read it pretty well from his high release and average extension. A sinker at least generated more soft, ground-ball contact. The real star of the show remained his breaking pitches. An 80-83 mph curveball can confound lefties with 4 1/2 feet of drop and classic 12-to-6 shape. An upper-80s slider was his most whiff-heavy option against same-side bats, standing out more for its drop than its gloveside movement, and an 83-86 mph changeup could flash above-average with good separation (though it was crushed at Triple-A). Roby didn’t struggle for strikes at either Double-A or Triple-A before his elbow surgery, in part because he got batters to chase each of his pitch types at impressive rates. After running reverse splits in ’24, he evened those out nicely last year. But now in his second year on the 40-man roster, Roby still can’t shake the health concerns that could keep him from his mid-rotation promise.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roby signed with the Rangers for $775,000 as the 86th overall pick in the shortened 2020 Draft and has shown flashes of being at least a midrotation starter in his four Minor League seasons since. That said, he’s only topped 100 innings once (at High-A Hickory in 2022) and didn’t throw more than 60 during the regular season in either 2023 or 2024 due to shoulder issues. He was traded from Texas to St. Louis while on the Double-A IL in the 2023 Deadline deal for Jordan Montgomery and Chris Stratton but missed more than three months of what should have been his first full season as a Cardinal last year. The 6-foot-1 right-hander sat 94-97 mph in the Texas League before his latest stay on the shelf but was more in the 92-95 range over three Single-A rehab appearances late in the year. The heater can act like a plus pitch when the velo’s there due to a flat angle and good extension. His 80-83 mph curveball remains the best pitch in his arsenal, a real snapper that generated a ton of whiffs. He’d also show a harder slider and a low-80s changeup with tons of separation off the heat despite being a fourth pitch in terms of usage. Righties crushed Roby in 2024, especially the four-seamer if he didn’t locate it high enough in or above the zone. He’s at his best when he’s playing a north-south game with the heat and the deuce, but there’s also no grade for health. Roby threw 78 1/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A in 2025 -- his highest mark since 2022 -- but needed Tommy John surgery in late July, a procedure that will shut him down until the second half of 2026 at the earliest.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 144 in the 2020 Draft class by MLB Pipeline, Roby went 86th overall to the Rangers and was signed away from a Troy commitment with a $775,000 bonus. He showed promise on the mound during his time in the Texas system, particularly in 2022, but battled a sprained elbow in 2021 and a shoulder injury in the first half of 2023. The Cardinals picked up the Double-A arm at the Trade Deadline in the Jordan Montgomery deal, gave him four starts in Springfield and then got him innings in the Arizona Fall League. Roby touched as high as 99 mph in the Fall League as he re-established his health and was generally around 93-96 in the Texas League with a four-seamer that played up with good extension and flat angle. He spots the fastball well too, giving it another chance to be a plus pitch. His 80-83 mph curveball plays well off the heat, dropping nearly straight downward to get swings-and-misses. He added a low-80s slider with the Rangers, but it’s a tighter pitch that can be hammered when left up. His 81-83 mph changeup can generate whiffs but lacks consistency. The 6-foot-1 righty repeats his delivery and sidestepped free passes well in 2023 (6.3 percent walk rate). He could avoid the center of the zone better and might just need more experience to improve the command. Shoulder issues have continued to dog Roby in his first full season as a Cardinal, bringing greater questions about his ability to handle a starter's workload. The stuff remains undeniable, however.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After taking Evan Carter in the second round of the 2020 Draft, the Rangers used their third-round pick on another high schooler whom they valued more than the rest of the industry. They signed Roby away from a commitment to Troy for a slightly over-slot $775,000 and have been pleased by his development since. After getting shut down with a sprained elbow in 2021, he was fully healthy last year and held his own as one of the youngest starters (age 20) in the High-A South Atlantic League. Roby moved up to Double-A Frisco and was better than his traditional numbers in 2023, when he was moved to St. Louis in the Jordan Montgomery deal while he nursed a shoulder injury. Roby can attack in any direction with his four-pitch repertoire. He can work north and south by pairing a fastball that plays better than its 92-96 mph velocity thanks to its outstanding induced vertical break and the extension in his delivery with a high-spin upper-70s curveball with downer break. He can also operate east and west with a fading low-80s changeup moving in the opposite direction from a low-80s slider that he added last summer. Though Roby may not have a true plus pitch, he could have four solid offerings once he's fully developed. He has a loose arm and repeats his delivery well enough to provide strikes, though his command is a work in progress. He misses in the middle of the zone more than he should, leaving him vulnerable to homers, but he could become a mid-rotation starter if he locates his pitches more consistently as he gains experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers liked Roby more than the industry consensus in the 2020 Draft, and they took him in the third round and signed him away from a Troy commitment for a slightly over-slot $775,000. He flashed three plus pitches during instructional league that fall and again in his pro debut last spring. He posted a 2.45 ERA with 35 strikeouts in 22 innings as a 19-year-old in Low-A before getting shut down in mid-June with a sprained elbow. Roby's fastball sits at 90-94 mph and reaches 97, playing well above its velocity because of high spin rates and a flat approach angle that create plenty of carry up in the zone. His upper-70s curveball may be his best pitch, peaking at more than 3,000 rpm with big downer break, and he began utilizing a harder slider with similar promise late this summer. His low-80s changeup is an asset as well and continues to improve as he uses it more often. Though Roby stands just 6-foot-1, he has long limbs that create extension and angle that add to his deception. He has a loose arm and repeats his delivery well, allowing him to pound the strike zone. He'll have to prove he has the durability to take the ball every fifth day over a full season but if he does, he could fit in the front half of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roby made a name for himself on the showcase circuit in 2019 and was building off that momentum at his Florida Panhandle high school last spring when the season abruptly ended. The Rangers saw enough to draft him in the third round and sign him away from a Troy commitment for a slightly over-slot $775,000. He showed flashes of three plus pitches in instructional league, impressing enough to possibly earn an assignment to low Class A to begin his pro career. Roby has high spin rates on his four-seam fastball, which sat in the low 90s in high school, parked at 93-94 during shorter stints in instructs and tops out at 96 mph. His heater pairs well with his upper-70s curveball that features downer break. He also shows advanced feel for a low-80s changeup with fade that should improve as he uses it more often. Though Roby is just 6-foot-1, he has long limbs that create extension and angle, making life more difficult for hitters. His athleticism helps him repeat his loose delivery and provide strikes. He has plenty of starter traits and eventually could fit into the middle of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After growing up in Iowa, Gamble attended IMG Academy tennis and baseball camps in Florida during the summer. But his baseball talent stood out, and he was invited to come year-round for high school. Gamble evolved into a Draft prospect at IMG and played against premium competition before the Royals took him No. 23 overall in the 2025 Draft, signing him away from a Vanderbilt commitment with a $3,997,500 signing bonus. Gamble made his unofficial pro debut in 2025 playing in Bridge League games and then the instructional league at the club's complex in Arizona. The Royals drafted Gamble as an athletic, toolsy hitter, but he showed up in the spring already taller, leaner and with more strength than what he had in the fall. His left-handed swing is smooth and direct, with good bat speed and a knack for finding the barrel. He’s finding more and more power as he gains strength, and he has a good understanding of the strike zone. Gamble is a plus runner with the instincts to be a basestealing threat, and that speed will help him in center field. He’s probably more natural in the outfield, but he’ll likely get reps in the infield this season too. Gamble has an above-average arm that helps him wherever he plays. Evaluators rave about Gamble’s makeup as a competitor and leader. He should be headed for a full-season debut in 2026 at Single-A Columbia, and the Royals will take their time with his development. But they feel Gamble, as well as fellow top 2025 draftee Josh Hammond, are major reasons why the farm system has become more athletic recently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Frey won Louisiana 2-A state titles in his final two seasons at Rosepine HS in 2021 and '22, then two College World Series championships at Louisiana State in 2023 and '25. He got just 76 at-bats in his first two years with the Tigers, in part because of a torn labrum in his right shoulder that required surgery in the summer of 2024. He didn't become a full-time starter until midway through last spring yet finished with the best batting line (.331/.420/.641) in LSU's lineup and provided several clutch hits during the postseason. After signing for $997,500 as a third-rounder, he slashed .330/.434/.470 during a month in Single-A. Physically imposing at 6-foot-6 and 225 pounds, Frey generated the highest measured bat speed in the 2025 Draft as well as some of the best exit velocities. He's a disciplined hitter who waits for pitches he can drive, and he has shown the ability to handle lefties and righties and all types of pitches. The Astros hope he can create a steeper bat path so he can elevate the ball more consistently and realize his 30-homer potential. While he spent most of his college career as a DH, Frey is an underrated athlete who was a catcher and dual-threat quarterback in high school. A solid runner who's quicker once he gets going, he'll get the opportunity to play center field in pro ball. At worst, he projects as a right fielder with solid arm strength and perhaps more if he can lengthen his arm action.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the most physical shortstops in the 2026 international class, Fermin has a projectable 6-foot-3 frame reminiscent of fellow Samana, D.R., product Hanley Ramirez at the same stage of their careers. He received the highest bonus in Houston's crop this year, signing for $2,147,500. Besides his tools, scouts also like his makeup and how he plays the game with swagger. A switch-hitter who's more advanced from the left side because he has gotten more at-bats there, Fermin has advanced feel for contact. He already shows some ability to recognize pitches and control the strike zone, and he hits the ball harder than most 17-year-olds. Once he fills out and learns to elevate balls, he could develop plus raw power and provide 20 or more homers per season. Fermin's potential offensive impact overshadows his athleticism. He'll flash plus speed but likely will settle in as a solid runner once he's physically mature, and he has a strong arm that definitely works on the left side of the infield. His quick first step enhances his chances of remaining at shortstop, though it's possible that he outgrows the position and winds up at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays spent years scouting Valdez, who comes from the Dominican city of Baní, and their belief in him was evident in the $3.5 million signing bonus they awarded him in January 2026. It was the third-largest sum the Rays have given an international amateur, trailing only the bonuses given to Wander Franco ($3.85 million) and Brailer Guerrero ($3.7 million). It’s a big bet on a young player with a long way to go and extraordinary upside. Valdez has the traits of a middle-of-the-order hitter. He sprays line drives to all fields with a simple right-handed swing and a mature approach for his age. He has a good feel for the strike zone and doesn’t chase too much. He’s already producing 100-104 mph exit velocities in games, which speaks to his physicality and strength, and he has shown the ability to use his hips to pull the ball with authority. A move to third base seemed inevitable for Valdez at one point, and that would be a fine outcome given his offensive profile and his cannon of an arm that fires 92-94 mph throws across the infield. But the Rays are going to give him a shot to stick at shortstop, believing he showed enough leading up to his signing that he has earned the opportunity. He showed improvement in his first step, smooth actions and above-average body control. Wherever he lands in the infield, his bat gives him a chance to be special.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A bargain $10,000 signing from the Dominican Republic in 2019, Santos made some mechanical adjustments after getting rocked in High-A in 2023. He took off the following year, leading the system in wins (11) and strikeouts (138 in 110 1/3), appearing in the Futures Game, reaching Double-A and grabbing a spot on the Rangers' 40-man roster. He made just two starts in Double-A in 2025 before a stress reaction in his back sidelined him for four months, though he returned for the end of the season and the Arizona Fall League. Santos maintained a quality fastball during his rough 2025, sitting at 95-97 and touching 100 with impressive carry and armside run, though his secondary pitches regressed a bit. His tight mid-80s slider was merely an average offering rather than the plus weapon it was the season before. His slightly harder changeup tumbled at times but lacked consistency. Santos isn't very physical and has never pitched more than 110 1/3 innings in a season, so he still needs to prove he can hold up as a starter. His athleticism helps his cause, as does his ability to provide reliable strikes from a low release height. If he can refine his fastball command and hone his slider and changeup, he could be a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2019, Santos had his pro debut delayed until 2021 by the pandemic but progressed nicely until getting tuned up for a 6.29 ERA at High-A in 2023. He made some mechanical adjustments at the end of that season that paid off with a breakout last year between that level and Double-A. He led the system in wins (11) and strikeouts (138 in 110 1/3 innings), pitched in the Futures Game and claimed a spot on the the Rangers' 40-man roster. Santos' fastball added a couple of ticks of velocity in 2024, sitting at 94-96 mph and maxing out at 98 with natural cut and ride. He also tightened his mid-80s slider into a legitimate plus offering that he can throw by hitters in the zone or get them to chase. His mid-80s changeup isn't as reliable as his other two pitches, but it plummets at the plate when it's working right. Santos is just 6 feet tall and lacks physicality, but he's athletic and provides plenty of strikes from a flat approach angle. He surrendered eight homers in 10 Double-A starts, mostly on heaters that he didn't locate high enough in the zone. Once he refines his fastball command and changeup consistency, he could be a mid-rotation starter. After making just two starts for Double-A Frisco this season, Santos landed on the IL in June due to a stress reaction in his back and is expected to be out indefinitely.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $2.5 million out of the Bahamas in July 2017, Robinson vaulted to as high as No. 43 on MLB Pipeline's preseason Top 100 in the spring of 2020. That April, he was arrested and charged with assaulting a police officer after he was seen walking on a Phoenix-area highway. He later said the incident was the result of mental health struggles, but legal issues -- including those surrounding his visa -- kept him from playing in official Minor League games until the 2023 season. Robinson slashed .283/.382/.532 with 14 homers and 23 steals in 65 games across three levels following his return, reaching as high as Double-A. Added to the 40-man roster in 2021, he was designated for assignment last August but remained in the organization. Allowed to work out at the D-backs' facility and participate in extended spring training games during his absence, Robinson still had plenty of rust in his bat upon his return, as expected for someone with that much missed time. He struck out 31.6 percent of the time in 2023, a stat that increased with every stop. At Double-A in particular, Robinson often whiffed against quality softer stuff. That aside, he did show some pop out of a relaxed batting stance when he did make contact, and the hope for eventual plus all-fields power remains entering his age-23 season. Robinson moves well in his 6-foot-3 frame, and as he showed in 2023, he isn't afraid of pushing the envelope on the basepaths. He did move primarily from center field to the corners last season, and he could be an above-average defender in either spot with enough arm for right. Robinson will work back toward the 40-man with more at-bats in '24.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs tapped into the same Bahamian talent pipeline from which they signed Jazz Chisholm ($200,000) in 2015 to get Robinson, signing the toolsy outfielder for $2.5 million in July 2017. He made a strong impression on club officials in his pro debut the following year, finishing the season in the Rookie Pioneer League at age 17. Robinson garnered midseason All-Star honors in the Class A Short Season Northwest League in 2019 to earn a full-season promotion up to Class A Kane County, where he was more than three years younger than the Midwest League's average player. Robinson spent time at the D-backs' alternate training site and fall instructional program in 2020 and sat out all of 2021 as he worked his way through a legal issue, though he did get in some work at the D-backs' facility in the Dominican Republic. With Robinson's special combination of size and athleticism, it should come as no surprise that the young outfielder also possesses multiple impact tools. None is louder than the massive right-handed raw power that could one day make Robinson one of the sport's premier sluggers. He gets to it often, generating effortless pull-side power, as well as opposite-field pop that was much improved in 2020 after Robinson improved his diet and added nearly 25 pounds of muscle. Scouts who wonder whether he will ever hit enough to reach his power ceiling cite his swing-and-miss issues and ground-ball tendencies as reasons for concern. Others are more optimistic about Robinson's bat, viewing him as a natural hitter whose offensive development has been slowed by a lack of reps. Robinson's plus speed and long strides give him enough range to play center field for the time being, though it's widely expected he will outgrow the position and move to an outfield corner -- most likely right field, where his plus arm strength fits well. Robinson has been away from game action for two years, so it remains to be seen how much -- if anything -- has changed. While the two lost years hurt, Robinson is still young and will play the entire 2022 season as a 21-year-old. If he's able to get back into form quickly, he has the tools to be a quick riser through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs tapped into the same Bahamian talent pipeline from which they signed Jazz Chisholm in 2015 ($200,000) to get Robinson, signing the toolsy outfielder for $2.5 million in July 2017. He made a strong impression on club officials in his pro debut the following year, finishing the season in the Rookie Pioneer League at age 17. Robinson garnered midseason All-Star honors in the Class A Short Season Northwest League in 2019 to earn a full-season promotion up to Class A Kane County, where he was more than three years younger than the Midwest League's average player. Robinson spent time at the D-backs' alternate training site and fall instructional program in 2020. While Robinson has not played in any games in 2021 as he works through a pending legal issue, he has gotten in some work at the D-backs' facility in the Dominican Republic. With Robinson's special combination of size and athleticism, it should come as no surprise that the young outfielder also possesses multiple impact tools. None is louder than the massive right-handed raw power that could one day make Robinson one of the sport's premier sluggers. He gets to it often, generating effortless pull-side power, as well as opposite-field pop that was much improved in 2020 after Robinson improved his diet and added nearly 25 pounds of muscle. Scouts who wonder if Robinson will ever hit enough to reach his power ceiling cite his swing-and-miss issues and ground-ball tendencies as reasons for concern. Others are more optimistic about Robinson's bat, viewing him as a natural hitter whose offensive development has been slowed by a lack of reps. Robinson's plus speed and long strides give him enough range to play center field for the time being, though it's widely expected he will outgrow the position and move to an outfield corner -- most likely right field, where his plus arm strength fits well. Such a move down the defensive spectrum should have little impact on Robinson's development, and there are some who think it could even lead to his expedited arrival in Arizona.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Brooklyn native, Palmer attended Holy Cross High School in Flushing, New York, about three miles east of Citi Field. The Mets took the local kid in the 22nd round of the 2018 Draft and bet on his raw skills with a $200,000 signing bonus. After two years at Rookie levels, Palmer finally got to experience full-season ball in 2021 and hit .276/.378/.386 with two homers and 23 steals in 66 games for Low-A St. Lucie. He was promoted to High-A Brooklyn but floundered, hitting .189 with a 38.5 percent strikeout rate in 169 plate appearances. Palmer’s raw power is at least above-average, and he makes hard contact when he puts the bat on the ball. How much that happens remains up in the air. Palmer takes his walks, but his 13.9 percent walk rate in 2021 was also indicative of how much he sat back against certain pitches, rather than being aggressive on the pitches he could drive. His swing can get lengthy at times, too, and that leads to more misses. Seeing more pitching is often what helps players coming out of the Northeast develop the right approach, but it remains a question of whether Palmer will ever be a solid-to-average hitter. Defensively, the homegrown talent has bopped around short, third and second but was primarily an outfielder by the time he reached Brooklyn. His easy plus speed and good arm could make him a serviceable center fielder in time, though he needs more reps to get comfortable out there. There is still a considerable ceiling because of that power-speed combo and the ability to stay up the middle. Palmer just needs to start making contact more consistently to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets didn’t have to go far to find Palmer in the 2018 Draft. The infielder came out of Holy Cross High School in Flushing, New York, about three miles away from Citi Field. Palmer had shown an interesting mix of raw power and athleticism as an amateur in Queens, allowing New York to take him in the 22nd round and offer a $200,000 signing bonus. He held his own with above-average numbers in the Gulf Coast and Appalachian Leagues in 2018 and 2019 and continued to show promise in instructional league ball last fall. Palmer’s power is the standout tool here. It could be a legitimately plus skill in time with the amount of hard contact when he puts the bat on the ball appropriately. What holds him back is his contact rate. The right-handed slugger struck out 39.1 percent of the time in Kingsport in 2019. The Mets believe part of the issue was his getting too heavy on his front side in his batting stance. The organization worked on getting him to stay back more in hopes that he can improve the contact rate and allow the power to play more in games. Palmer is an above-average runner at 6-foot-3, and the Mets believe that athleticism – along with an above-average arm -- will help him play multiple spots since it’s likely he’ll outgrow shortstop in the long term. He played short and third base two years ago and saw some time in outfield corners last fall. The Mets are giving Palmer so many defensive looks because they believe that the bat will someday be valuable enough to get in a Major League lineup every day. The slugger will be 20 for much of the 2021 season, meaning there is plenty of development time remaining, but his first taste of full-season ball should provide some answers on just how far his contact rate can carry him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aponte was one of the best shortstops in the 2025 international class and the Reds had circled his name, signing the Venezuelan infielder -- he hails from Miranda, home of big leaguers like Miguel Rojas and Oswaldo Cabrera -- for $1.9 million. Known primarily for his defensive work, Aponte showed some unexpected life at the plate during his debut in the Dominican Summer League, leading his team with seven home runs. Conversation about Aponte, who will play all of the 2026 season at age 18, still starts with his glove. One of the best defenders in his class, he’s going to play shortstop for a long time, with plus agility, actions and the ability to make highlight-reel type plays. Like with a lot of young middle infielders, he can still improve on making the routine play, and while he has enough for the premium position, he should able to improve his arm strength as well. It surprised some that Aponte found as much power as he did right out of the gate because he has more of a handsy, “hitterish” approach at the plate. He makes a lot of contact and can use the whole field. The Reds want him to keep staying up the middle and making good swing decisions and not chase power. And even with the home run total, he needs to add strength before he’s ready to come stateside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aponte hails from Miranda, Venezuela, home to big leaguers like Miguel Rojas and Oswaldo Cabrera. He hopes to be the next to represent his hometown after the Reds made him their primary target at the start of the 2025 international signing period, bringing him into the organization for $1.9 million. Aponte leads with his glove, but added strength helped improve his stock, landing him at No. 18 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list at the start of the signing period. At the plate, Aponte has good contact skills from the right side of the plate, using a simple toe tap to time up pitchers. He’s content to use the middle of the field to spray line drives. He’s likely never going to be a huge power guy, but is good with bat control and the ability to bunt and move runners over while not striking out much. As intriguing as his bat might end up being, Aponte’s glove is what got him paid. He’s possibly the best defender in his signing class, with evaluators saying things like he has “magic in his hands.” He makes tough plays look easy with plenty of flash along the way. He’s a no-doubt shortstop with plenty of arm, range and actions, even if he has to learn some consistency on the mundane plays to be as well-rounded of a defender as he can be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays had high hopes for Goss when they selected the right-hander 36th overall out of Cypress (Texas) High School in the 2019 Draft and signed him for $2.05 million, the slot value for his Competitive Balance Round A pick, and you could argue he’s still only barely had a chance to show them what he’s capable of. He made nine appearances in his pro debut, sat out 2020 due to the canceled Minor League season then pitched only 10 1/3 innings in 2021 due to a shoulder injury. Goss didn’t require surgery on his shoulder despite tearing his labrum, and he handled a decent workload (101 1/3 innings) over 25 starts in his return last year. Remaining in Single-A all season, the starter posted a 4.00 ERA with 101 strikeouts and only 21 walks. It’s still unclear where Goss’ stuff will settle coming back from his injury -- shoulder rehab can be trickier than Tommy John rehab, in some ways -- and he pitched with lesser stuff last season than before his injury. But Tampa Bay saw the better version of Goss down the stretch and expects more of that after a normal offseason, which would give him a chance to reach his ceiling as a middle-of-the-rotation or back-end starter. Goss has an athletic 6-foot-3 frame that he harnesses well to repeat his delivery, consistently throwing strikes with good control. He throws a fastball in the low-to-mid 90s, touching 96, with backspin and riding life. He has a good feel for his changeup and throws a low-80s slider with late bite and two-plane depth. It’s a three-pitch mix that Goss commands well, but one that hasn’t yet been tested against upper-level competition -- even as his Rule 5 Draft eligibility looms at the end of 2023 -- due to the time he missed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The COVID-19 pandemic and a shoulder injury limited Goss to 27 1/3 innings during his first three professional seasons combined. The Rays selected Goss 36th overall out of Cypress (Texas) High School in the 2019 Draft and signed him for $2.05 million, which was the slot value for his Competitive Balance Round A pick. He made nine appearances in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, recording a 5.82 ERA with 16 strikeouts and only two walks in 17 innings, then had a 6.10 ERA with 12 strikeouts and no walks over four outings in complex-league ball last year. 2nd: The good news is that Goss did not require surgery on his shoulder despite tearing his labrum. He entered the 2022 season healthy, fully ready to go and has been fairly effective as a starter in Single-A. When healthy, Goss has his fastball sit in the low-to-mid 90s and touches 96 mph with backspin and riding life, and it’s reasonable to think he’ll add more velocity as he keeps growing into his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. He has a good feel for his changeup, but his slider is the most likely pitch to become a plus weapon. He throws that low-80s breaking ball with late bite and two-plane depth. Goss repeats his mechanics well and fills up the zone with control, command and understanding that were – when he entered the system -- considered to be advanced for his age and experience. He repeats his delivery well enough to command his arsenal, but he’ll have to prove it in game action after so little time on the mound as a pro. Perhaps his most valuable experience to this point came in the fall of 2020, after the Minor League season was canceled when he spent time pitching in front of the Rays’ staff during their instructional league camp. With Goss, Tampa Bay is betting on projection. It’s hard to reach those projections when you’re not pitching, but he has the arsenal, delivery and advanced feel to break out and reach his potential as a Major League starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Goss went nine picks ahead of his Cypress (Texas) High School teammate Matthew Thompson in the 2019 Draft, as the Rays selected Goss 36th overall and Thompson went to the White Sox shortly thereafter. Goss then signed with Tampa Bay for $2.05 million, which was the slot value for his Competitive Balance Round A pick, and made nine appearances in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, recording a 5.82 ERA with 16 strikeouts and only two walks in 17 innings. Shoulder issues kept him from pitching until the final month of the 2021 season. The right-hander was invited to the Rays’ instructional league camp last fall, giving him a chance to pitch in front of their staff despite losing what would have been his first full season to the pandemic. When healthy, Goss’ fastball sits in the low 90s and touches 95 mph with riding life, and it’s reasonable to think he’ll continue adding velocity as he grows into his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. He has a good feel for his changeup, but his slider is the most likely pitch to become a plus weapon. He throws that low-80s breaking ball with late bite and two-plane depth. Goss repeats his mechanics well and fills up the zone with control, command and understanding that are considered to be advanced for his age and experience. There’s still a long way to go considering his pro career only just began before the pandemic and this year's injury concerns, but he has the arsenal, delivery and advanced feel to break out and reach his potential as a Major League starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: German didn’t jump out on Draft boards after posting a 6.43 ERA at the University of Seattle, but the Orioles saw hidden potential and selected him in the 11th round of the 2023 Draft. The following year, German dominated hitters in the low Minors in what was the best pitching debut in the Orioles’ system that summer, though he was older than most of his competition. He built on that success in 2025 with a 3.93 ERA and a 10.4 SO/9 in 123 2/3 innings across three levels while reaching Triple-A. German learned how to miss bats during his junior year in college, and the Orioles have helped him build on that skill as he’s progressed through the system. The 6-foot-3 hurler is a pitchability righty with a four-pitch mix, above-average command and a unique over-the-top delivery. He works up-down with the ability to locate his low-to-mid-90s fastball at the top of the zone and spot his two breaking balls low or below the strike zone if necessary to generate whiffs. He relies on a slider and a curveball that are already above-average pitches as well as an effective splitter he uses against left-handed hitters, then added a cutter toward the end of last season that he’s still developing. German proved durability in ‘25 after missing time to injuries during his debut. His well-rounded arsenal and strike-throwing ability outshine any of his individual pitches, giving him the look of a No. 4 starter with a reliever floor as he pushes toward a big league debut in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles saw German as a diamond in the rough at the University of Seattle, where he pitched to an ERA over six but made a jump with his ability to miss bats during his junior year. After the Orioles drafted him in the 11th round in the 2023 Draft, German didn’t make his pro debut until '24.
