Of course, he has to prove himself in affiliated competition, and it’s a relatively low rate of success for international pitchers making it to the Majors. But Urbina looks like the top international amateur arm signed by the Rays in 2023, and there was a lot of buzz around him entering the year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As they’ve reemerged into the international market in recent years, the Orioles have proven more prone to sign position players to large bonuses than pitchers. As such, the $150,000 they used to sign Mejia out of the Dominican Republic in 2024 represents one of the biggest bonuses the current front office has bestowed upon a hurler. He racked up 97 strikeouts across his first 68 professional innings in the Dominican and Florida Complex Leagues in 2024 and '25, then flashed triple-digit radar readings in three starts with Single-A Delmarva. It might not be long until Mejia proves more than worthy of that initial investment. The 6-foot-3 righty features electric stuff, easily overpowering lower-level hitters with a fastball that cranks up to 102 mph with arm-side run. His best secondary offering is a hard, gyro-like slider he can snap in the low 90s, and he also throws a firm, developing changeup in the low 90s that is still a work in progress despite good action. Mejia throws from a low, three-quarters slot and is getting better at repeating his delivery, which should lead to improved command as he gains experience. Bettering that command could be critical -- he’s walked more than five per nine in his brief career -- in determining how high Mejia’s ceiling actually is. Just 19 for all of the 2026 season, he still offers plenty of projection, both in terms of size, strength and ability. But there is a ton to dream on here, given his tantalizing combination of age and eye-popping raw stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in the 2017-18 international signing class, García got $2.5 million to sign with the Phillies and almost immediately set out to prove he was worth it, making his pro debut stateside and winning the Gulf Coast League batting title in 2018. His move to full-season ball in 2019 was a disaster offensively and then he missed out on a year of at-bats due to the shutdown. He did use 2020 to add strength and that started showing when he repeated Low-A, putting up better numbers all around and earning a late bump up to High-A and a 40-man roster addition in the offseason. His offensive struggles returned in 2022, however, and the Tigers claimed him on waivers from the Phils in September. A switch-hitting shortstop, García really started to find his swing in 2021, especially in the power department, more than doubling his career total with 13 homers for the season. That added strength has led to better bat speed and increased exit velocities from both sides and his improved approach -- his walk rate increased significantly and his strikeout rate dropped compared to 2019 -- allowed him to get to his raw power more consistently. Even with the increased physicality, García still looks every bit like an everyday shortstop defensively. He’ll need to continue to watch his conditioning, but he has excellent actions and a plus arm from the premium position. He’s continued to get reps at second and with there being enough confidence in his future as a middle infielder, he still has time to turn himself into a bench option in the Detroit system. García only turns 22 in October.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Way began his college career at NCAA Division II Belmont Abbey (N.C.) in 2019, then excelled at Northwest Florida State JC in the shortened 2020 season. The Yankees saw enough of him there and in the Cape Cod League the previous summer to take him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft. Way was having a good start to 2022 and continued that after he was one of three pitchers traded to the Royals for Andrew Benintendi at the Trade Deadline. Way finished the season in High-A Quad Cities and posted a 3.79 ERA in 35 2/3 innings with a 30.7% strikeout rate but an 11.1% walk rate. Utilizing a four-seam fastball with ride and a two-seamer with sink, Way is a power pitcher with a three- to four-pitch mix. He sits around 95 mph with his fastball and the low-80s with his plus slider, which features sweeping action and could be labeled as the best slider in the Royals’ system. Way’s tumbling changeup is his third pitch that he’ll need to use more as he moves up levels, but it has potential. There is some effort in Way’s delivery, but his lack of control and command are his biggest issues. While his stuff misses bats, he often finds himself out of counts and out of the zone. The Royals will develop Way as a starter until he shows them he’d be better suited out of the bullpen. Evaluators do see relieving in his future, where he can let his fastball and slider go in shorter stints. But at 6-foot-4 with a durable frame along with a three-pitch mix, Way will continue to start and see if he can fix the command issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Way spent his first season in college at NCAA Division II Belmont Abbey (N.C) at 2019 before impressing scouts in the Cape Cod League that summer, prompting him to transfer to Northwest Florida State JC so he'd be eligible for the 2020 Draft. He ranked third nationally among juco pitchers in wins (five), fourth in strikeouts (58 in 40 innings) and eighth in ERA (0.67) during the shortened season, then gave up a Louisiana State commitment after the Yankees selected him in the fourth round. He showcased a live arm during his pro debut last year, exhibited improved control to begin 2022 and was traded to the Royals at the Deadline in a deal for Andrew Benintendi. Way utilizes both four-seam fastballs with ride and two-seamers with sink and both gained velocity over the course of last season, each sitting around 93-96 mph with his four-seamer topping out at 99 late in the year. He also added some power and sweeping action to his low-80s slider, which shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch. His mid-80s changeup with tumble has potential as well but lacks consistency. Though Way dominated as a starter in junior college, many scouts believe he's more of a reliever. His lack of control and command are the biggest issue, and New York kept him in extended spring training for most of May last year so he could work on locating his pitches. There's effort in his delivery and he may be more effective just airing out his fastball and slider in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Way pitched at NCAA Division II Belmont Abbey (N.C.) as a freshman in 2019 before impressing in the Cape Cod League that summer and transferring to Northwest Florida State JC, making him eligible for the 2020 Draft. One of the top two-year college prospects in last year's crop, he ranked third nationally among juco pitchers in wins (five), fourth in strikeouts (58 in 40 innings) and eighth in ERA (0.67). He passed up a Louisiana State commitment to sign with the Yankees in the fourth round for an above-slot $600,000. Way sits at 91-95 mph and touches 97 with riding action on his four-seam fastball, and he still has room to add strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which could bring more velocity. His mid-80s changeup tumbles at the plate and grades as a plus pitch at times. His low-80s slider lags behind his other two pitches in terms of consistency and missing bats. While Way starred as a starter in junior college, some scouts believe he's destined to become a reliever. He'll need to refine his slider, maintain the improved control he showed as a sophomore and upgrade his command. He features some effort in his delivery and struggled to throw strikes while coming out of the bullpen at Belmont Abbey and on the Cape.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies scouting department did fine work finding Rincon, who had moved to the Pittsburgh area from Venezuela for high school. The Phillies liked Rincon, who played his high school ball at Shaler Area High and committed to San Jacinto Junior College, and his defensive actions and upside enough to take him in the 14th round of the 2022 Draft, knowing he was eager to begin his pro career. He had a solid first full season in 2023 but has had trouble gaining traction since, missing much of 2024 with hamstring issues, then hitting the injured list again in 2025 with a broken hamate. Both times, he made up for lost at-bats by going to the Arizona Fall League, though he didn’t swing the bat well there. Thus far, all of Rincon’s value comes from his glove. He’s a no-doubt shortstop for a very long time, with plus actions, hands, footwork and more than enough arm for the premium position. Even though he’s not a burner, his defensive instincts give him plenty of range. He’s only played shortstop thus far, but he could easily slide over to other spots on the dirt if he ends up in a utility role. While his defense gives him a decent floor, what his ultimate role will be depends entirely on how much, if any, offensive impact he can find. There are some tools to build with for the switch-hitter. He swiped 40 bases thanks to excellent instincts on the basepaths, and he actually doesn’t swing-and-miss or chase all that much, doing damage when he swings. But his strikeout rate jumped to nearly 29 percent in 2025 because he got too passive and didn’t swing enough. If he can find any production in his age 22 season, he could rejuvenate his prospect luster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Venezuelan native headed to the Pittsburgh area for high school, the Phillies took Rincon, previously committed to San Jacinto Junior College, in the 14th round of the 2022 Draft. He jumped on the prospect map in 2023 with a performance that allowed him to reach High-A in his first full season. He wasn’t able to build off of that in 2024 as he missed three months with hamstring injuries, though he did return to action at the end of the regular season and made up for some lost reps by competing in the Arizona Fall League. While Rincon’s overall numbers as a pro don’t jump off the page (a career .711 OPS heading into 2025), he does bring some solid offensive traits to the table the Phillies are hoping he can get back to with a clean slate. The switch hitter makes a ton of contact with low miss and chase rates, and he draws a lot of walks. The hope is with continued added strength and healthy legs under him, he can provide enough contact and on-base skills to fit regularly into a big league lineup. What will get him to the big leagues -- and gives him a very high floor -- is his defensive ability at shortstop. He has excellent hands, footwork and plenty of arm for the premium position, and thanks to his instincts, he’ll have more than enough range, especially the further removed from those hamstring issues he gets. He may always be a glove-first guy, but he’s one who could do it as a starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rincon grew up in Venezuela but came to the Pittsburgh area to live with an uncle and play baseball for Shaler High School. He had committed to San Jacinto Junior College had the Draft not worked out, but the Phillies took a low-risk chance in Round 14 and signed him for Day 3 slot ($125,000). While his numbers from his first full season, in which he reached High-A, weren't amazing, he showed off a ton of skills that should continue to translate as he moves up the ladder. He shook off a very slow start this spring back in High-A and was performing better in May when a hamstring injury ended his 2024 season. Playing at age 20 for all of 2024, Rincon has a very high floor thanks to his defensive ability. His hands, range and footwork are excellent and play up because of his plus instincts. He has more than enough arm for the premium position, and even though he’s not a burner speed-wise, he should be able to play shortstop for a very long time. There’s optimism that Rincon’s offensive skills will continue to develop as well. He’s a switch-hitter with outstanding contact skills, rarely chasing and limiting strikeouts while drawing a good amount of walks. He’s continued to add strength and there could be more power to come in the future as well. The Phillies feel there could be some Bryson Stott in him in terms of him playing above his tools and becoming an everyday middle infielder in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: January of 2023 was an exciting month for the Salas family. First, Ethan Salas signed with the Padres as the top player in the amateur international class, then a few days later, older brother Jose was traded from the Marlins to the Twins as part of the deal for Luis Arraez. The older Salas grew up in Florida and moved to Venezuela to continue in the family business -- his grandfather, father and uncle all played professionally -- before signing with the Marlins for $2.8 million as one of the top prospects in the 2019-20 international class. He played across two levels of A ball as a teenager in 2022. The Twins are excited to have Salas and his offensive upside in their system. He’s a switch-hitter with a quick swing from both sides of the plate and a solid overall approach in terms of pitch recognition and discipline. The Twins have already been impressed with his feel for what he needs to work on as he’s focused on better swing decisions, especially from the left side, where he’s shown more pop to date. That should help him tap into the raw power he’s starting to develop as he gets stronger. A plus runner, Salas should be a base-stealing threat, another area in which his baseball IQ helps his tools play up. He’s gotten more reps at shortstop than anywhere else, but he saw considerable time at second and third last year. He’s fully bilingual and his leadership skills and maturity jump off the page, not only in the way he’s mentored his younger brother, but in how he jumped into getting up to speed in his new organization during the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Florida, Salas grew up in Orlando before moving as a teenager to Venezuela, where his grandfather, father and uncle all played professionally. The Marlins' primary target on the 2019 international market, he signed for $2.8 million and stood out with his strength and athleticism during their instructional league program in the fall of 2020. He boosted his stock further when he made his pro debut last summer, tearing up the Rookie-level Florida Complex League for a month before earning a promotion to Low-A at age 18. He became a Twin in January, when he was sent to Minnesota in the deal for Luis Arraez. A switch-hitter, Salas has a quick swing from both sides and recognizes pitches better than most hitters his age. He has gotten stronger since signing and could produce 20-25 homers per season once he adds some polish at the plate. He has a good understanding of the strike zone but can get aggressive and pull-conscious, and presently makes more ground-ball contact than is optimal. Salas combines physicality with twitchy athleticism, showing plus speed and solid arm strength. His proponents think his finely tuned internal clock will help him stick at shortstop, while other scouts believe he'll lose some quickness as he fills out and wind up at second base, third base or center field. His background has given him a high baseball IQ and made him fluent in both English and Spanish.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While his grandfather, father and uncle all played professionally in Venezuela, Salas was born in Florida and grew up in Orlando. After moving back to Venezuela, he became the Marlins' primary target in their 2019 international class and signed for $2.8 million. Ticketed to make his pro debut in the United States last summer until the coronavirus pandemic wiped out the Minor League season, he impressed with his strength and athleticism during instructional league last fall. A switch-hitter with a quick swing from both sides, Salas is more advanced than most hitters his age and already recognizes pitches well. He put on a show in batting practice at Marlins Park after he signed and has the upside of 20-25 homers per season in his prime. He currently has plus speed but could lose some quickness as he continues to add strength. Some international scouts wondered about Salas' long-term ability to remain at shortstop, but the Marlins believe he has the actions, twitchy athleticism, solid arm and good internal clock to make it happen. He has the tools to handle the defensive responsibilities and fit the offensive profile at second base or center field if he moves off short. Because of his background, he has a high baseball IQ and is fluent in both English and Spanish, both of which should expedite his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid Georgia high school prospect, Simmons struggled at the plate a bit during his senior year in 2018 to hurt his Draft stock. The Phillies liked the power potential and overall athlete enough to take him in the sixth round that June and go over-slot to sign him away from his Georgia Tech commitment for $750,000. It’s been a slow development process since, though he did lead the New York-Penn League in slugging percentage in 2019. He did show some glimpses of his offensive upside in his full-season debut in 2021, but injury, a pitch to the helmet and COVID-related shutdowns limited him to just 46 total games. Simmons has always had considerable raw power from the right side of the plate; the question since his high school days was if he’d hit enough to tap into it. He’s had flashes of bringing a solid approach to the plate, with a willingness to draw walks, but he does strike out a fair amount. When he does make contact, it’s loud with good exit velocity and the ability to hit the ball over the fence, especially to the pull side. The Phillies believe his bat is trending in the right direction. The high school shortstop has played three infield positions professionally, but as his body continues to get bigger and stronger, it doesn’t look like he’ll be able to play short long-term. He’s probably best suited for third, where his strong arm plays well, but will continue to get plenty of time at second base as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Céspedes played for Cuba at the 2017 World Baseball Classic at age 19 before defecting two years later while the national team was in the independent Canadian American Association. The younger brother of two-time All-Star Yoenis Céspedes, he was cleared to sign in March 2020 but wanted to join the White Sox and waited until they had more money available in the next international period. Signed for $2.05 million in January 2021, he finished third in total bases (200) and sixth in steals (33) in the Double-A Southern League last year. His formidable strength and bat speed create well-above-average raw pop that plays to all fields, but Céspedes undermines himself with a grip-it-and-rip-it approach. His right-handed swing gets too long, leaving him vulnerable to quality fastballs, and he hasn't met a breaking ball he won't chase. He had the fifth-worst strikeout minus walk percentage (24.4) in the Minors in 2022 and would do more damage if he would just let his pop come naturally. Céspedes aggressiveness extends to the bases, where he uses his solid speed to steal when he gets the opportunity. He covers ground in center field but plays too shallow at times, reducing his effectiveness. His arm earns double-plus grades from some evaluators and would fit nicely in right field if he moves to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of two-time All-Star Yoenis Céspedes, Yoelqui played for Cuba at the 2017 World Baseball Classic before defecting two years later while with his nation's team in the independent Canadian American Association of Professional Baseball. Cleared to sign in March 2020, he wanted to sign with the White Sox and had to wait until they had more money available in the 2020-21 international period, landing a $2.05 million bonus in January 2021. Visa issues delayed his U.S. debut until mid-June, after which he batted .285/.350/.463 with eight homers and 18 steals in 72 games between High-A and Double-A. Céspedes added 20 pounds to his 5-foot-9 frame while training with his brother in advance of signing with a big league club, and his impressive bat speed and strength give him well above-average raw pop from the right side of the plate. He hit better than most scouts expected after a two-year layoff from competition, though his long swing and extremely aggressive approach lead to swing-and-miss issues that restrict his power in games. He struck out at a 28 percent clip in his debut while walking just 5 percent of the time, and his impatience grew as he homered just once in 46 Double-A and Arizona Fall League contests. Céspedes posts plus straight-line speed in workouts but is more average out of the batter's box and solid once he gets going. He has a nose for stealing bases but may not have more than average range in center field. His arm, which earns plus to double-plus grades, easily would fit in right field should he have to shift to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Yoenis Cespedes, Yoelqui played for Cuba at the 2017 World Baseball Classic and defected two years later while playing on Cuba's team in the independent Canadian-American Association. He added about 20 pounds to his 5-foot-9 frame while training with his brother in advance of joining a big league club, boosting his raw power and his prospect stock. He became eligible to sign in March 2020 but elected to wait until the subsequent signing period, accepting a $2.05 million bonus from the White Sox in January 2021. Cespedes' bat speed and strength give him well above-average raw power, though some evaluators wonder how much he'll be able to tap into it against quality pitching. His right-handed swing has a tendency to get long and uphill and he's overly aggressive at the plate. A younger, less physical Cespedes batted just .287/.351/.415 in four seasons in Cuba's top league and just .253/.343/.316 in 27 games over two years of Can-Am play. Cespedes can demonstrate plus straight-line speed in workout settings but has shown mostly average quickness in his Minor League debut. That leaves his ability to remain in center field in doubt, though his plus-plus arm strength would make him an easy fit in right. He's similar to but more athletic than White Sox outfield prospect Micker Adolfo, who has been slowed by injuries since signing for $1.6 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2013.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vasquez was a relatively little-known prospect when he was signed as part of the Rays’ 2019 international class, then he exploded onto the scene after a strong Rookie-level stateside debut in '21 that ended with him being part of Single-A Charleston’s championship run as a teenager. Two uneven years later, the risk and uncertainty in his profile have caught up to the excitement he generated heading into 2022. Vasquez started striking out more and walking less as he got into the A-ball levels, and his batting average has plummeted each of the past two years as he slashed just .233/.310/.393 for High-A Bowling Green a year ago. The Rays believe there were a variety of issues, from the loss of someone close to him to mechanical issues to learning to handle the hype of being a young, highly regarded prospect. The 22-year-old is listed at 6-foot-2 and has plenty of speed and strength, with the latter creating an explosive right-handed swing. It’s just a matter of whether he can take the adjustments he made last season -- like adding a leg kick at the plate -- and make them quicker moving forward now that he’s learned to fail as a professional player. Vasquez has moved around the infield, spending most of his time at third base. He has the arm strength and lateral range to handle the hot corner, and he’ll likely see more time there with Carson Williams at shortstop and Tanner Murray likely at second base in his Double-A infield to begin this season. The tools haven’t backed up at all for Vasquez, and the Rays still believe he has another breakthrough in him. But if it doesn’t happen this year, and he takes another step back instead as the competition gets tougher, he could find himself out of the prospect spotlight.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vasquez burst onto the scene before the 2022 season, going from a relatively under-the-radar prospect signed as part of the 2019 international class to someone consistently ranked among the top 10 in a deep Rays system. Tampa Bay had marked him as someone to watch after his first instructional league, coming off a solid 17-year-old season in the Dominican Summer League, then he thrived in the Florida Complex League and earned a promotion to Single-A Charleston amid a championship run. Now, although there is still plenty of risk and uncertainty in his profile, Vasquez remains a prospect to watch. Vasquez is 6-foot-3 with a strong build, foot speed and bat speed. His explosive right-handed swing packs plenty of punch. He struggled out of the gate in 2022, although there’s some belief that could be ascribed to him trying too hard to prove he was indeed a top prospect. Because when Vasquez began to bounce back in June, he performed for Charleston like the player they expected, slashing .289/.355/.472 with all 10 of his homers and a more reasonable strikeout rate (22.4 percent) than his first two months. There are still some questions about his ability to adjust to higher-level pitching, which he’ll have to answer moving forward, but he’s still young (21) and has plenty of time to improve. When the Rays signed Vasquez, he was listed as a third baseman – and, scouts will tell you, international amateur prospects listed as third basemen are really outfielders. But Vasquez has seemingly found a home at the hot corner, spending most of his time there with a handful of games at shortstop and second base sprinkled in. He’s shown good speed, with 25 steals in 28 attempts in 2022, and a strong arm. Wherever he winds up, the key for Vasquez will be harnessing his talent and continuing to improve at the plate the way he did throughout his second half with Charleston.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vasquez wasn’t a high-profile player when the Rays signed him as part of their 2019 international class, but he quickly earned more attention. The Rays felt they’d landed an under-the-radar steal despite him being listed as a third baseman. (When an international amateur is listed as a third baseman, many scouts will tell you, he’s an outfielder.) Vasquez hit the ground running as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League, and the Rays marked him as someone to watch coming out of his first instructional league. Last year, he hit .288/.382/.411 with a 20-to-27 walk-to-strikeout ratio in 40 games in the Florida Complex League. That warranted a postseason promotion to Low-A Charleston, where he delivered a bases-clearing triple in Game 5 of the Low-A East championship series. As with any player of his age (20) and experience (three games in Low-A, the rest in Rookie-level complex leagues), there is risk and uncertainty in his profile. But Vasquez also possesses a tremendous amount of upside. He had been listed at 6-foot but has grown to 6-foot-3, and he’s gained noticeable strength and speed during his time in Tampa Bay’s system. That added physicality shows up in his quick right-handed swing, and some evaluators expect he’ll wind up being a power-over-contact hitter with the kind of encouraging plate discipline he’s already shown. He’ll have to prove himself at the plate against better pitching this year, answering questions about his ability to hit tougher breaking balls and adjust to more involved game planning, but he’s produced – with the underlying data to back it up -- at every level so far. Defensively, Vasquez has moved over to third base primarily in deference to first-rounder Carson Williams in Charleston this summer. He has above-average speed and agility that helps anywhere on the infield with enough arm to ease the transition. The 20-year-old struggled offensively early on in 2022 but has come on strong in the second half in the Carolina League, restoring faith that he’ll have enough bat to profile anywhere he lands on the dirt.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies were looking to fill a future outfield at the start of the 2024 Draft, taking those who patrol the grass with four of their first five picks. The first two were high schoolers, with Dante Nori in the first and Burkholder in the second, and both signed for the same $2.5 million bonus as the Phillies went well over slot to lure Burkholder away from the University of West Virginia. He hasn’t been able to get as many on-field reps as hoped, with a hamstring issue ending his summer debut after signing following just two plate appearances. He was limited to just 34 total games during his first full season. It’s hard to not like Burkholder’s physicality and athleticism, and even with the lost year, he’ll play nearly all of 2026 at age 20. He is capable of making very hard contact, registering high-end exit velocities when he’s been on the field, with at least plus raw power. He has made some swing adjustments and found better angles, but he struggled with his overall approach with too much swing-and-miss, particularly against breaking and offspeed stuff. Missed development time because of the injuries has not helped in this regard. Healthy again, Burkholder will hopefully be able to get back to using his speed well. He’ll turn in some 70-grade run times, but it doesn’t translate the same on the basepaths in terms of stolen bases. It’s also looking like he’s better suited for a corner outfield spot rather than center, and he’s gotten most of his time in right field to date.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Phillies were able to sign 2024 first-round pick Dante Nori under slot, they were able to use their savings to also bring Burkholder, their second-rounder, into the fold. The Virginia high school standout turned a strong summer showcase circuit and excellent senior season to rise up Draft boards, enabling him to land a $2.5 million bonus from the Phillies. He tripled in his first professional at-bat last summer with full-season Clearwater but got shut down after just one more plate appearance because of a hamstring issue. Big, physical and athletic, the Phillies have taken to calling Burkholder “Captain America” because he can do everything well. There’s a ton of raw power for him to tap into, but in high school he didn’t always find the barrel consistently. He’s shown off early aptitude by already making the most swing adjustments of anyone in the system, eliminating some length in his swing and fixing some angles, allowing him to barrel up the baseball much more frequently. Assuming the hamstring is fine, Burkholder has close to top of the scale speed that works on both sides of the ball. He has the skills to play center field long-term, and could trade off with Nori for the time being, with the Phillies very excited if they can form a dynamic duo in the big leagues with Nori in center and Burkholder in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the premier power hitters on the 2026 international market, Rosario signed for $2.5 million, the largest bonus in the Rangers' class. He hails from East Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic, which also has produced big league outfielders Bryan de la Cruz and Victor Robles. Rosario grew up playing shortstop but transitioned to the outfield as he got more physical. Already 6-foot-2 and 195 pounds at age 17, Rosario is built to hit for power. He has present and projectable strength, along with a quick right-handed stroke with loft, enabling him to generate impressive exit velocities and launch balls out of the park to all fields. He aggressively looks to do damage, so he does come with some swing-and-miss concerns. Rosario has average speed but could lose a step as he continues to mature physically. Though he has outgrown shortstop, some scouts believe he still moves well enough to play third base. His solid arm strength would work at the hot corner or in right field, his likely destination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Already 6-foot-5 and 200 pounds at 16, Solarte is a rare physical specimen and one of the best athletes his age. Ranked as the No. 16 overall prospect in the 2026 international class, he signed with the Marlins for $1 million and will head to the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League to begin his pro career. The Venezuela native immediately stands out for his physical strength with near-top-of-the-line exit velocities from the left side of the plate. The question as he matures, of course, is how much he'll be able to tap into it. Solarte is quite coordinated for his size, although his longer limbs will challenge his ability to make consistent contact. Still, he has plenty of bat speed from his closed-off stance and displays strong pitch recognition. Solarte is currently an above-average runner but figures to slow down as he adds weight. He uses his athleticism well on defense with clean actions and a strong arm. There are few big league shortstops his size, but he'll be given every chance to stick there, even if the Marlins may give him playing time at second and third, as they do with most infield prospects. He will have as much upside as anyone in the Marlins' system if he can tap into his tremendous tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davalillo has extensive baseball family ties with a grandfather (Vic) and great-uncle (Pompeyo) who played in the Majors, a father (David) who reached Double-A before becoming a manager and scout, and a younger brother (Gabriel), who signed with the Angels for $2 million in 2025. David also has a career 2.35 ERA in four pro seasons, led the Minors with a 1.88 mark in 2024 and was the Rangers' organization pitcher of the year in 2025. He originally signed with the Mets for $30,000 out of Venezuela in January 2021, had the deal voided two months later and landed with Texas for $10,000 until June 2022. Davalillo's best trait is his ability to kill spin on a low-80s splitter that plummets at the plate, limiting hitters to .077/.153/.092 line with a 54 percent swing-and-miss rate in 2025. He also can miss bats with a sweeping low-80s slider that has become a solid offering and an upper-70s curveball, though he has trouble landing the curve in the strike zone. He throws just enough fastballs to keep batters honest, but his two- and four-seamers range from 92-97 mph and are more notable for their command than its life. Besides his splitter, Davalillo also stands out with the best pitchability and competitive makeup of anyone in the system. He can get strikes with six different pitches -- he also toys with an upper-80s cutter -- and excels at mixing shapes, locations and sequences to get the most out of his arsenal. He'll have to keep proving that he can succeed with a below-average fastball but his formula already has worked through Double-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 45 | Slider: 50 | Splitter: 60 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Davalillo’s grandfather Vic and great-uncle Pompeyo both played in the Majors, while his father, David, reached Double-A before continuing in baseball as a manager and scout and David's younger brother, Gabriel, signed with the Angels for $2 million in January. Davalillo had a more humbling entry into pro ball, signing with the Mets for $30,000 in January 2021, having the deal voided two months later and hooking up with the Rangers for $10,000 in June 2022. He raised his profile significantly by leading the Minors with a 1.88 ERA between two Class A stops last season. Davalillo’s low-80s splitter generated a 58 percent swing-and-miss rate last year and is the lone pitch in his arsenal that grades as better than average. His fastball sits in the low 90s and maxes out at 96 mph, and he’ll ride four-seamers up at the letters and sink two-seamers down at the knees. He has some feel for spinning the ball with his sweeping 78-82 mph slider more effective than his mid-70s curveball, but both could use more power. Though Davalillo doesn’t have the smoothest delivery, he repeats it well. He throws strikes with his entire repertoire, commands his fastball well and sequences his pitches well. He has some of the system’s best feel for pitching, giving him a chance to succeed as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sullivan began his college career at Northwestern then moved on to Wake Forest, where he got a chance to move into the weekend rotation as a Draft-eligible sophomore. Since the Rockies took him in the second round of the 2023 Draft, the left-hander has defied typical expectations, reaching Double-A and pitching well despite stuff considered light by any measure. Sullivan never had a big fastball, but it took another hit in 2025 as he was coming back from hip labrum surgery. The Rockies had held him back until early May to let him build back up, but he never quite got there. Somewhat amazingly, he found success in Double-A with a fastball that averaged around 86-87 mph and scraped 90 mph, using a combination of deception, angle and up-slope movement to the pitch to get outs. His upper-70s changeup is probably his best offering and while his mid-to-upper 70s slider can be slurvy, he manipulates the velocity and shape of it and it missed a fair amount of bats last year. While the left-hander is never going to light up radar guns, there is hope that Sullivan can still find a few more ticks of velocity. For one thing, he had a normal offseason throwing program, rather than rehabbing his hip. For another, with the new pitching group in the fold, Sullivan might be able to get back to being more rotational like he was in college, and averaged 91-92 mph with his heater, as opposed to focusing on a deep hinge on his back side and getting a little stuck in his delivery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Can a starting pitcher succeed these days with a fastball that barely breaks 90 mph? The Rockies are hoping to find out soon enough after taking Sullivan in the second round of the 2023 Draft following his solid turn moving into Wake Forest’s weekend rotation that spring. His smoke-and-mirrors show worked very well during his first full season of pro ball, both with High-A Spokane and Double-A Hartford, as he led all Minor League pitchers with an 8.33 K/BB rate and topped the Rockies in a host of pitching categories. Sullivan uses a lower slot to come at hitters with a kind of upshoot fastball, getting huge carry up in the zone. Even though it only averaged around 88 mph in 2024, the lefty threw it a lot and got decent swing-and-miss on the pitch thanks to that life and his outstanding command of the pitch. There could be a little more velocity in the tank now that he’s had a hip labrum issue fixed, so he might be able to get to 93-94 mph more moving forward. His upper-70s changeup is his best pitch, one that has terrific movement and misses bats in and out of the zone. His sweeping slider can be effective, but he doesn’t locate it as well as his other two offerings. The Rockies will be sure to bring Sullivan along slowly and manage his workload as he’s coming back from the hip issue, but he’s already defied expectations thanks to confidence in his pitch usage, his unusual mechanics and his extreme strike-throwing ways. He’ll be at the upper levels continuing to show that his unusual profile just might work in a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For years, the Rockies would tend to draft pitchers who fit a certain mold, usually power guys with a sinker-slider combination. Sullivan, a left-hander who started his career at Northwestern and then transferred to Wake Forest, certainly does not belong in that bucket. Moved into the weekend rotation in 2023 when Teddy McGraw got hurt for the Demon Deacons, Sullivan showed that his combination of deception and feel for pitching could work just fine, helping him to land in the second round with the Rockies. Sullivan is an outlier in a number of ways, not just for being the antithesis of how the Rockies have drafted pitching. Even though his fastball averaged just a tick over 90 mph last year (though he could touch 95 mph), he threw it 75 percent of the time with Wake. Because of his lower slot and wide angle that leads to huge carry up in the zone, it doesn’t get hit even when hitters know it’s coming (36 percent miss rate on the pitch in 2023). Right now, Sullivan’s best secondary offering is his changeup, which can also miss bats and is an easy average pitch. He has a tendency to change the slot on his slider, hurting its consistency, but the Rockies think it could improve as he works on pitch design with pro instruction. Sullivan does an excellent job of filling up the strike zone despite his unusual mechanics, and he tunnels his mix well to make him even harder to hit. It remains to be seen if this will work in Colorado, but he’s the kind of pitcher you don’t try to change. Seeing how his stuff plays in his first full season of pro ball will be an interesting storyline in the Rockies' system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Eagen really struggled in his first two years at Presbyterian and dealt with elbow and shoulder issues in his sophomore year in 2023. He found regained health and success that summer in the Appalachian League and returned to the Blue Hose to win the 2024 Big South Pitcher of the Year with a school record 122 strikeouts in 77 2/3 innings. He became the first Presbyterian player drafted in 11 years when the D-backs selected him in the third round in ’24, and he added to his award closet as the 2025 Northwest League Pitcher of the Year after posting a 2.49 ERA with 132 strikeouts in 97 2/3 innings. After adding four Double-A starts, Eagen led all Arizona farmhands with 153 total K’s. Solidly built at 6-foot-4, Eagen added velocity late in his collegiate career and continued to run his four-seam fastball into the mid 90s during his first full pro season. His high arm slot helps him generate really good carry out of the hand with induced vertical break up to 20 inches. His 81-83 mph curveball complements that nicely with its sharp downward action that makes it effective against batters from both sides, and a mid-80s gyro slider can be equally good as a weapon versus righties. Eagen has folded in an 85-88 mph splitter too, and it shows flashes of being a future average MLB offering. Eagen doesn’t have the most effortful delivery with that high release, but he can finish with a flourish moving toward the first-base side. He relies on batters biting on the breaking stuff moving out of the zone, and when more disciplined hitters lay off those, he could settle into slightly below-average control if trends continue. He would still have enough of a mix to work as a backend starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Presbyterian last had a Major Leaguer in World War II hero Lou Brissie, who retired in 1953, but Eagen has a great shot at being the next. The right-hander struggled in his first two seasons with the Blue Hose and missed most of 2023 with elbow and shoulder concerns before making up for the lost time in the Appalachian League. He was rejuvenated upon his 2024 return, winning Big South Pitcher of the Year honors while setting a school record with 122 strikeouts in 77 2/3 innings. The D-backs took him in the third round and signed him for $650,000, ending an 11-year drought for Presbyterian Draft picks. The 6-foot-4 hurler's fastball velocity jumped roughly 5 mph in his final season on campus. It sat 93-94 mph and touched 96 with good carry out of his high arm slot. He played off it well with an 80-82 mph downer curveball that contrasted nicely with the high heat and sported a 53 percent whiff rate in his junior year. His mid-80s slider was a distinct third option (and rarely used against lefties) but got plenty of swing-and-miss. He didn’t use much of a changeup in school and will focus on developing one as a pro. Eagen’s velocity trajectory proved promising, especially since he didn’t add effort to his delivery to get there. Bolstering the mix with an armside offspeed pitch could be key to his starting chances in pro ball, even if he continues to pound the strike zone, but the fastball-curveball combo would at least get him MLB looks as a reliever if its quality is maintained.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox planned on giving an Oppor, a Wisconsin prepster who played for their Area Code Games team, an over-slot bonus in the 11th round of the 2022 Draft, but the Athletics took him seven picks in front of them. He didn't sign, allowing Chicago to land him a year later out of Gulf Coast State (Fla.) JC with a fifth-round choice and over-slot $550,000 bonus. After spending two seasons in Rookie ball and focusing on adding strength, he logged a 3.08 ERA, .199 opponent average and 116 strikeouts in 87 2/3 innings during his full-season debut between two Class A levels in 2025. Oppor could have three plus pitches once he's a finished product, starting with a fastball that sits at 93-97 mph and tops out at 100 with run and sink. His low-80s slider has so much sweep that it's hard to control and often misses the plate by two much to entice chases, but it can be unhittable when it's on. His changeup has similar velocity and more reliability, neutralizing right-handers with its tumble. The most athletic pitcher in the system, Oppor provides a lot of deception with an upright delivery, a low three-quarters arm slot, low release height and some crossfire. He's doing a better job of repeating his unorthodox mechanics as he has added muscle, though his walk rate jumped back up to 13 percent in High-A. He still needs time to develop but could be yet another frontline southpaw starter for Chicago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With an uptick in velocity and stuff during his senior season, Slawinski displayed an exciting combination of projectability and polish to become the best pitching prospect in Texas (and one of the best prep lefties in the 2025 class). He was projected to go in the top two rounds, but landed in Round 3 to the Angels, who went way over slot with a $2.5 million bonus -- around Competitive Balance Round A money -- to sign him away from his Texas A&M commitment. From the scouting department to player development, there is universal excitement about Slawinski’s upside and how he carries himself. The 6-foot-3 lefty finished his senior season with a fastball that sat in the 90-93 mph range and touched 95, and it plays up because of its ride and the extension in his delivery. He has two breaking pitches, with an upper-70s slider that has two-plane depth ahead of his mid-70s curve, which isn’t as consistent. He already has very good feel for his fading low-80s changeup. As a four-sport standout in high school, Slawinski uses his athleticism on the mound to his advantage. He gets down the mound with ease and has a very good feel to pitch, with the ability to land all his offerings for strikes. Continued added strength will only help his stuff tick up, and going from a tiny school to pro instruction could help him eventually develop three plus pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Southisene family in Nevada sure seems to know how to produce baseball players. Ty signed with the Cubs as a fourth-round pick in 2024 while his twin brother, Tee, headed to pitch at Southern Cal and is now at the College of Southern Nevada. Troy is a Class of 2026 grad committed to Oregon State. And in between came Tate, who landed as the Braves’ first-rounder in the 2025 Draft, with all Southisenes coming through the Basic HS program. Tate got a small taste of pro ball with a 15-game debut at Single-A Augusta after signing for a below-slot bonus of $2.62 million. Tate is a more physical version of his brother with the Cubs, and while he’s still a sub-six-footer, he has the chance to have real impact from the right side of the plate with legitimate bat speed. He can be very aggressive, and that hurt him during his brief debut, but he doesn’t get cheated in the box. He’ll have to tone that down as he gets going for real, but he’s shown excellent bat control and a feel for the barrel in the past to get to his power. Southisene has surprised the Braves a bit with his speed, at times recording 70-grade run times. He’ll settle in as a plus runner and his athleticism is a real asset on both sides of the ball. He has the actions and arm to stick at shortstop, and he saw time at second base during his summer debut, while some amateur scouts really liked him in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his three years at Texas A&M, Cortez spent more time relieving than starting. He really shined in his junior year as a multi-inning bullpen guy, especially during a dominant postseason run to help the Aggies finish as the runners-up in the 2024 Men's College World Series. That led to him being taken in the second round of that summer’s Draft and the Angels sent him to High-A Tri-City as a starter in 2025. There were a lot of things that went well for Cortez. His stuff largely held up over 26 starts and 113 2/3 innings, and he missed bats largely with his sinker-slider combination. It’s a power two-seamer, sitting in the upper 90s and touching triple digits. Hitters just can’t square it up, a big reason why he produced a 61.8 percent ground-ball rate in 2025. His upper-80s slider can feature horizontal and vertical action and serves as a true put-away pitch, missing a ton of bats. There have been rare sightings of a mid-to-upper 80s changeup. The biggest thing standing in Cortez’s way to being a starter, which he’ll keep developing as for the time being, is his command. He walked 6.7 per nine and that’s a number that must come down, even if he ends up back in a bullpen. He could have multi-inning or setup potential with a good combination of strikeouts and ground balls if that move occurs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s not typical that a college pitcher’s performance in the College World Series impacts his Draft stock that year, but it’s hard to imagine that Cortez’s run coming out of Texas A&M’s bullpen as the Aggies finished second in Omaha didn’t help him. Cortez had started and relieved over his three years, and he took off with a multi-inning bullpen role last year, dominating postseason play (1.18 ERA, 29 strikeouts in 15 2/3 inning) to cap off a very strong junior campaign. The Angels nabbed him in the second round of last year’s Draft and signed him for $1.6 million but didn’t send him out to pitch at all after his long year. Cortez enters pro ball with two plus pitches that really play. He actually threw his 86-92 mph power slider more than his fastball last year, and it’s easy to see why. It features horizontal and vertical action and elicited a 56-percent miss rate, according to Synergy. His fastball averaged a tick over 98 mph in 2024 and topped out at 101, thrown with power sink that’s extremely difficult to leverage. He has an upper-80s changeup, but it gathered a lot of dust on the pitching shelf. The 6-foot-1 right-hander generates those premium pitches without much effort, so there is some thought that he could be stretched out to start in pro ball. For that to work, he’s going to have to find the strike zone a lot more consistently (5.1 BB/9 last year was an improvement from 2023) and develop a third pitch. If he sticks in the bullpen and can be around the zone at all, he could zoom through a system in an organization that likes to get guys to the big leagues in a hurry.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the 2018-19 international signing period opened on July 2, 2018, the Angels had to wait until the end of August to sign Ramirez when he turned 16, getting the outfielder for $1 million. He immediately showed off his power, and the holes in his swing, during his Dominican Summer League debut in 2019. It was more of the same during his United States debut in 2021, though he did enough in the Arizona Complex League to get a late promotion to full-season Lake Elsinore shortly before he turned 19. Ramirez’s potential is tied to his raw power from the right side of the plate. He has as much raw pop as anyone in the organization, with high exit velocities and the ability to drive the ball to all fields. His swing gets long and he’s super-aggressive, a combination that has led to a 34.7 percent strikeout rate heading into 2022, leading some to wonder if he’s going to make enough contact to be productive. He does draw some walks, but needs to be better at recognizing and not chasing spin out of the zone. A solid athlete, Ramirez runs well enough to keep getting reps in center field, where he’s largely played since signing. As he physically matures, right field seems like a better long-term home, with the hope that more reps will help him refine his approach and provide the kind of run-producing bat the Angels need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez was one of the youngest players in the 2018-19 international amateur class, one who couldn’t sign until the end of August, when he turned 16. The Angels were more than willing to wait, inking the outfielder for $1 million on his birthday. He showed off his raw power with 17 extra-base hits in 39 games during his 2019 debut in the Dominican Summer League, but also struck out in more than 33 percent of his plate appearances, trends that continued during his United States debut in 2021. It is the 6-foot-2 Ramirez’s offensive profile that made him such an attractive prospect in the first place. His calling card is certainly his easily plus raw power from the right side of the plate. He drives the ball to all fields and had very high exit velocities during his brief professional career thanks to outstanding bat speed. There is some length to his swing which, in combination with an aggressive approach, has contributed to that high strikeout rate. More reps will help his pitch recognition, and there’s confidence in time he’ll refine his gameplan at the plate. With a big, strong and athletic frame, Ramirez showed he could handle playing center field during his debut with a tick-above-average speed. He’s likely destined to a corner, with an arm that should be strong enough for right field in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just because the Reds were limited in their international spending during the 2017-18 signing period does not mean they didn’t find any good players. Case in point is Cerda, a toolsy outfielder who signed for $100,000 in July 2017. After a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2018, Cerda struggled when he first came stateside, though he still hit for power in the rookie-level Appalachian League. He tapped into it with more consistency in his full-season debut in 2021, earning a late promotion up to High-A and getting added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. Though he’s still far away from the big leagues, the Reds thought Cerda’s tools were loud enough to warrant protection on the roster. He has tremendous raw power from the right side of the plate, but has yet to maximize it in games due to inconsistency in his approach. There’s plenty of bat speed, but he chases too much, leading to high strikeout rates, though he is willing to draw walks to help offset that a bit. While Cerda has above-average speed, he hasn’t been much of a basestealing threat. And while he’s largely been a center fielder in the early stages of his career, most think he’ll be best suited for right field, where he played after his promotion to High-A. He could be a more controlled version of former Reds outfield prospect Jose Siri at the plate, one who fits the corner outfield power profile well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds weren’t allowed to spend over $300,000 on any player on the international market during the 2017-18 signing period. They think they may have found a steal in Cerda, who signed for $100,000 at the start of the signing period and then posted a very respectable .841 OPS during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. Aggressively jumped to the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019, he couldn’t replicate that success, though his power was still on display. Big, athletic and projectable, Cerda’s raw power is his calling card on the offensive side. The raw pop is plus from the right side of the plate, but there are questions about his ability to make enough contact to get to it. He uses a narrow stance with a high leg lift and hasn’t always been on time, contributing to a 26.6 percent strikeout rate in his brief career. He does offset the swing-and-miss somewhat with a willingness to draw walks (11.9 BB rate). Cerda might have a tick above-average speed and combines that with good instincts to give him every chance to play center field for a long time. He’ll flash an above-average arm that might be plus in time, so he could profile as a power-hitting right fielder should he have to shift over to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cunningham thrived much more as a Cape Cod League starter than he did as a Vanderbilt swingman in his first two college seasons, then blossomed into the Commodores' top starter in 2024. He featured some of the best pitch metrics that spring before the Yankees floated him down to the second round and signed him for a well over-slot $2,297,500. He had a mixed pro debut in 2025, compiling a 1.93 ERA in his first eight outings in High-A before missing three months with shoulder inflammation, then getting rocked when he returned in August and in the Arizona Fall League. Cunningham's best pitch is clearly his upper-80s changeup with so much fade and sink that it's as difficult to control as it is to hit, so there are times when he doesn't trust it. His fastball lost a couple of ticks of velocity last year, sitting at 92-94 mph and peaking at 96, and it didn't have the same carry he showed as a Vanderbilt junior. His sweeping mid-80s slider serves as an average third pitch but was his most effective offering in the AFL. After improving his strength and athleticism in his final year in college, Cunningham began repeating his delivery more efficiently and providing more strikes. He looked like a mid-rotation starter in the first half of last season but wasn't the same following his shoulder issues. If he's fully healthy in 2026, he could move quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During his first two years in college, Cunningham had much more success as a Cape Cod League starter (two all-star game appearances, two championships with Bourne) than he did as a Vanderbilt swingman (6.33 ERA). He emerged as the Commodores' best starter in 2024, as his stuff and command improved and he displayed some of the best pitch metrics in college baseball. After New York floated him down to the 53rd overall pick and signed him for a well-over-slot $2,297,500 bonus, he'll make his pro debut in 2025. Cunningham works with a mid-90s fastball that tops out at 97 mph, and he learned last spring to more consistently avoid barrels by locating it up in the zone with quality carry. The shape of his heater plays extremely well with his hard upper-80s changeup that fades and sinks so much that it can be difficult to land for strikes. His sweeping mid-80s slider gives him an effective third pitch -- one that the Yankees specialize in refining. Cunningham improved his strength and athleticism as a Vanderbilt junior, which enabled him to repeat his clean delivery more easily. In turn, he provided a lot more strikes and maintained his stuff deeper into games. If New York can upgrade his slider, he could become the system's best pitching prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herring was a key part of Louisiana State’s bullpen for two years, helping the Tigers win the 2023 national championship and continued to dominate as a Draft-eligible sophomore reliever in 2024. The Yankees went well over slot to sign him in the sixth round of that year’s Draft, then sent him out as a starter in 2025. He threw very well across two levels of A ball before being sent to the Rockies in the Ryan McMahon Trade Deadline deal. He finished off with seven strong starts in High-A with his new organization, finishing second among all Minor Leaguers with his 1.89 combined ERA. One conversation with Herring would leave you thinking he was an analyst and not a pitcher, and his ability to integrate data into what he does on the mound should serve him well, especially with the Rockies’ new pitching group. There’s hope there might be a bit more in the tank with his fastball which currently sits around 90 mph but plays above that because of movement and command of the pitch. He throws his slider a lot, a sweeping mid-80s breaker that misses a ton of bats. His changeup took a very nice step forward during his first full season as a pro, and the Rockies think the mid-80s cambio could be a third at least above-average offering in time. Herring’s feel to pitch is a huge asset and while he has a longer arm action and not the smoothest delivery, he throws enough strikes, while showing he can find success down in the zone as well as up, keeping hitters off-balance by mixing his offerings well and pitching backwards. He has the ingredients to stay in a rotation, especially if he can find just a few more ticks on the fastball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the unsung heroes in Louisiana State's 2023 national championship run, Herring worked 4 2/3 innings of scoreless relief to beat Wake Forest in an elimination game at the Men's College World Series. The Tigers' best bullpen option as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2024, he logged a 1.79 ERA with a 67/13 K/BB ratio in 50 1/3 innings while scouts lamented that he was too valuable in that role to get an opportunity to start. The Yankees gave him that chance when he made his pro debut this year after signing for a well-over-slot $797,500 in the sixth round and he was running with it, pitching well across two levels of A-ball when he was dealt with Josh Grosz to the Rockies for Ryan McMahon near the Trade Deadline. Herring's best pitch is a sweeping mid-80s slider with horizontal and vertical action that confounds both lefties and righties. He can't overpower hitters with his fastball, which operates in the low 90s and tops out at 94 with some armside run, and he'll need to find more velocity or life against better competition. He threw only 11 changeups at LSU but emphasized the pitch more during three Cape Cod League starts last summer, showing some decent if firm mid-80s cambios with depth. Herring has a long arm action and a less-than-smooth delivery, though it throws batters' timing off and didn't stop him from pounding the strike zone as a sophomore. To succeed as a pro starter, he'll need to add more strength to his 6-foot-2 frame and improve his fastball and changeup. If he can't, he still could become a high-leverage reliever thanks to his slider and mound presence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have assembled a line of shortstop prospects in their system, but Montilla might be the least publicized of the bunch. Signed out of Venezuela for a $500,000 bonus in the 2022 international class, the speedy switch-hitter has been on a slow but steady climb up the organizational ladder. It’s not an indictment on his ability as much as a history of mastering a level with time. He was on his way to a strong campaign with the Flying Tigers and a potential summer promotion when a torn ACL ended his season in July. Montilla brings a lot of tools to his game, from athleticism and speed on the bases to a slashing bat, though he’s more effective hitting from the left side. He handles velocity well and produces strong hard-hit rates for a young player who has yet to hit for power at any level. More of his exit velocity comes from line drives than fly balls, and he showed an ability to use all fields well before his injury. His strikeout rate is a little high for someone with a reasonable swing rate, but he needs to make more consistent contact, particularly from the right side. He has the athleticism and skills to stick at shortstop with a little more consistency. The Tigers could find themselves with options at shortstop in a few years with any luck. Montilla could break out as a shortstop prospect and still find himself in competition with Bryce Rainer, who’s returning from injury as well. How Montilla matures at the plate could determine whether he’s a full-time player or more of a utility infield option. He’ll need some patience first as he adjusts back to the daily grind once he returns from his knee surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers haven’t been as active in the Venezuelan amateur market as in past years, but Montilla was a big get in the 2022 class, signing for a $500,000 bonus. He played two seasons in the Dominican Summer League, improving markedly at the plate with the extra time before advancing to the States. He got off to a hot start at the Rookie-level Florida Complex League before fading over the summer, and he still finished among the FCL’s top hitters before advancing to Single-A Lakeland in August. Though Montilla doesn’t have a big frame, his simple swing has a pull-heavy, fly-ball approach that produces extra-base hits for him. He has battled strikeouts at his various stops but has worked to become more selective with his swings and focus on pitches where he can do damage. His approach has the potential for more power as he physically matures, but opinions are mixed whether he’ll eventually be a noted power hitter. He has an aggressive approach on the basepaths but has yet to translate that into triples. Scouts are divided whether his defense will stick long term at shortstop, but he has enough arm to shift to third base. Like many infielders off the international market, how Montilla is valued depends a lot on whether he sticks at shortstop. The Tigers have several options there at the lower levels, but Montilla’s skill set and switch-hitting bat make him intriguing. He returned to the Florida State League for his age-20 season and played 67 games before suffering a torn ACL that will knock him out for a good bit of 2026 as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aloy’s rise from unheralded Hawaiian recruit to one of the most accomplished players in college baseball culminated in a dominant 2025 season at Arkansas, where he won both the Golden Spikes Award and SEC Player of the Year honors. After transferring from Sacramento State, he continued to build momentum as a sophomore and then took a significant step forward as a junior, playing his way into first-round consideration before the Orioles selected him No. 31 overall and signed him for full slot value ($3.04 million). He then enjoyed a productive pro debut at Single-A Delmarva, logging an .856 OPS in 20 games. Offensively, Aloy offers uncommon power for a middle infielder. He generates plus raw pop with a combination of bat speed and strength that produced 35 homers in two seasons at Arkansas and eight in only 21 games in the Cape Cod League in between his sophomore and junior seasons. The power plays to all fields and against quality pitching, though it's especially potent to his pull side. His hit tool is less advanced. His right-handed swing can get overly uphill and become susceptible to swing-and-miss, particularly against breaking balls outside the zone, but improved pitch selection could unlock more of his overall offensive profile. Despite fringy speed, Aloy should be able to stick at shortstop given his smooth actions, reliable hands and strong arm, and his range and instincts allow him to project as at least an average defender up the middle. If a move becomes necessary, his skill set would fit comfortably at second base or third, where his offensive upside would be an asset.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McKenzie was a Top 100 prospect as the 2025 Draft approached, one who reminded some of fellow North Carolina high school product MacKenzie Gore, especially in terms of his ability to spin a breaking ball. He didn’t have the same velocity jump as Gore did in his senior year, but some scouts did think McKenzie flashed first-round potential as the Draft approached. His commitment to LSU stood in the way, but the Braves took him in the fourth round, giving him a first-round caliber bonus of $3 million to walk away from the Tigers. The Braves have never shied away from a high school pitching prospect, and McKenzie is very much a ball of clay ready to be molded. His feel for spin is unquestionable, with a hammer 75-78 mph curveball that is already a plus pitch; it will only get better as he adds strength and power. He showed glimpses of excellent velocity (90-95 mph) out of the gate last spring, but isn’t yet able to maintain it deep into his starts. There’s some fade and sink in his low-80s changeup, something he’ll have to commit to throwing more as a pro to allow it to develop. McKenzie has shown an ability to throw strikes overall, but that also can improve if he can tighten up his delivery and long arm action. There’s room to add to his 6-foot-2 frame, though he has a narrow build. There’s a great variance in what he can become, but there are those who thought had he gone on to LSU, he might have emerged as the next Kade Anderson, who went No. 3 overall in the 2025 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a year at Western Kentucky and a very strong sophomore season following a transfer to Indiana, Sinnard looked like he could take a huge leap forward in 2024. But when he blew out his elbow in a 2023 regional start and needed Tommy John surgery, he missed all of what should have been his junior season. He threw bullpens for clubs and the Braves, in the third round, saw enough to take a chance on him coming back to full strength. The early returns -- 72 1/3 innings and getting to High-A Rome during the regular season before 15 2/3 more in the Arizona Fall League -- are making it look like it might have been a worthwhile gamble. Sinnard's stuff all seems to be trending in the right direction. His velocity continues to tick up, averaging 93 mph with his fastball during the regular season, then finding more in the AFL, with an average fastball around 95 and touching 98-99. His fastball has always played up with high spin rates and carry to miss bats, and he added a sinking 2-seamer late in the year. His upper-80s slider has cutter-like action; it's short and hard and it elicited close to a 35 percent miss rate at all stops last year. He has a distinct low-80s curve that he no longer uses very often, and his low-80s splitter gives him an effective offspeed offering that also misses bats. All of his stuff comes from Sinnard's 6-foot-8 frame and high three-quarters arm slot, making it hard for hitters to pick up the ball. He tends to be around the zone, and the next step in putting TJ behind him is refining his command so he can be a starter long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a freshman year at Western Kentucky where Sinnard pitched sparingly and poorly, he transferred to Indiana and had a huge sophomore season, with a Hoosiers record 114 strikeouts in 86 1/3 innings to put himself firmly on the early-rounds map for 2024. But he blew out his elbow in a 2023 regional start and missed all of 2024 following Tommy John surgery. He did throw bullpens for clubs leading up to the Draft and the Braves liked what they saw enough to take him in the third round. Coming from his 6-foot-8 frame and high three-quarters arm slot, Sinnard does not give hitters a comfortable at-bat. While his fastball sat 91-93 mph before he got hurt, topping out at 96 mph, the heater played up with high spin rates and carry to get a lot of swing-and-miss. He has two distinct breaking balls: His 78-82 downer curve missed a lot of bats and his mid-80s slider with cutter action got more chases. His low-80s changeup with depth was a distant fourth pitch he didn't use frequently. Sinnard did a nice job in 2023 in keeping his mechanics in sync despite his size and filled up the strike zone consistently. The 2025 season will be about seeing if he can get his stuff all the way back and eventually refine his command so he can reach his ceiling as dependable big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arronde signed with the Royals for $100,000 in 2021 out of Cuba, and ever since coming stateside in '24, he has skyrocketed onto the radar and turned into one of the Royals’ best pitching prospects. With High-A Quad Cities in 2025, Arronde posted a 2.80 ERA across 26 games (24 starts) and 128 2/3 innings, marking his second consecutive season of a sub-3.00 ERA and more than 110 innings. He held batters to a .210 average and struck them out at a 19.5 percent clip while posting an 8.1 percent walk rate, along with 0.63 HR/9 allowed. Arronde leaned heavily on his above-average 94-95 mph fastball in 2025, and the pitch can touch 97. He added good muscle to his projectable frame over the offseason, which helped with the velocity. He tightened up his slider, too, and the mid-80s pitch has more movement. Arronde is working on a curveball and he throws an 85 mph split-fingered changeup that has the potential to be a plus pitch, but he just didn’t use it as often as officials would have liked and needs to tighten it up; it does get whiffs when he goes to it. Arronde is athletic and pitches from a clean and easy delivery. The knock against Arronde is that he doesn’t strike batters out, but he fills up the zone to get quick and weak contact. There is still some development to go, and he’ll need to find the swing and miss part of his game, but Arronde’s control, delivery and arsenal give him a very good chance to start in the big leagues one day. The next challenge awaits at Double-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two months after turning 18, Arronde signed with the Royals for $100,000 out of Cuba in 2021. He spent two seasons in the Dominican Summer League but has taken off in the past two seasons stateside. Arronde particularly flew onto the radar in 2024 pitching in Single-A Columbia, where he posted a 2.94 ERA across 110 1/3 innings with a 1.02 WHIP, a 23.5% strikeout rate and a 7.3% walk rate. With some strength now in his 6-foot-3 frame, Arronde’s velocity has steadily increased and sits 93-94 mph. But he can lose velocity late in the year as he struggles to keep weight on, thus leading to more hard contact on the pitch. What makes Arronde so interesting is his low-to-mid-80s split-finger changeup, a plus pitch that disappears under bats at the last second. He can land it for strikes, generate weak contact and get swing-and-miss on it. Arronde is also working on a low 80s slider that has a chance to be average or above. His clean delivery from a high three-quarters slot lends itself to throwing strikes. Arronde gets high marks for his tenacity and competitiveness on and off the mound. He’s still young with more strength needed and more development to go, but the split gives him an interesting profile as someone to keep an eye on. If his third pitch improves, he has potential as a back-end starter, but the splitter would certainly play in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 118 Draft prospect in 2019, Mears showed off some late-blooming loud tools that helped him surge into the second round to the Padres that summer. After finally getting to move up to full-season ball in 2021 due to the lost pandemic season, he’s logged over 50-plus games at both Single-A and High-A, while striking out at least 39.2 percent of the time at both spots. His 14 homers and 121 wRC+ in 52 games at Fort Wayne last summer pushed him to Double-A, where he was young at 21, and it showed with a mind-numbing 47.9 percent K rate. When Mears does make contact, it’s incredibly loud with exit velocities routinely above 110 mph, and perhaps it came as no surprise that he finished 2022 with nearly as many homers (22) as singles (28). But unless a pitch is in his sweet spot in the zone, Mears fans far too often with a 43.9 percent K rate and 21.6 percent swinging-strike rate that ranked first and eighth among the 1,031 Minor Leaguers with at least 300 plate appearances in 2022. The Padres have worked with Mears on altering his swing to find any way to more contact, including a midseason trip back to Arizona last year, but nothing has caught yet. To his credit, Mears’ profile isn’t all wrapped up in his pop. He has more speed than many think, earning above-average runtimes from some scouts, and he can play a capable center field, where he made all 24 of his Double-A defensive starts. But perhaps more than anyone else in Minor League Baseball, he needs to increase his contact rates by at least 10 points to have any chance of meeting his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mears was a relatively unknown high school player from the Pacific Northwest until a late breakout landed him in San Diego with the 48th overall pick in the 2019 Draft. He put forth a strong display in Rookie ball in 2019, batting .253/.354/.440 with seven home runs and then continued to mash in his 2021 full-season debut, slashing .244/.368/.529 with 17 homers over 71 games for Low-A Lake Elsinore.
