He knows he's on the smaller side and is said to love to model himself after Marcus Stroman, though he's got a fundamentally different profile reliant on a big four-seamer alongside three high-quality secondary pitches that entered the organization with great pitch profiles, with the Twins feeling like there's not too much work needed on those. The fastball sat in the low 90s while he was in high school but was said to be up to 95-96 and touching 97 entering '22. Raya pitches with a chip on his shoulder and is said to have made big strides in his mental development toward the end of '21, and as is the case with many young pitchers, the Twins hope he'll simplify and attack the strike zone with his quality stuff, which he's done in the past. He has the ability to quickly build his stock with strong live outings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Raya was a bit of an under-the-radar high school right-hander from Texas when the 2020 Draft rolled around, one who didn’t quite make MLB Pipeline's Top 200 Draft prospects list and who many felt would go on to continue his amateur career at Texas Tech. Despite a shortened spring, the Twins' scouting staff had seen enough to take him in the fourth round last June and then saw him throw well during instructional league play last fall. While he's a bit undersized at 6-feet tall, Raya's combination of stuff, athleticism on the mound and feel for pitching give him the chance to start. He has a legitimate four-pitch mix, five if his two- and four-seam fastballs are separated out. In high school, he was up to 93 mph with his sinking two-seamer and was up to 96 mph with his four-seamer at instructs last year. The Twins liked that Raya entered pro ball with two distinct breaking balls, a tight curve that touches the upper-70s and a sweeping mid-80s slider. His changeup, another future average pitch, has good fade and sink. Raya's stuff plays up even more because of very high spin rates on his fastball and breaking stuff and he does a nice job of filling up the strike zone with all of his offerings. Super young for a high school draftee, he was still 17 at the time of the Draft, Raya has the Twins excited for what he can do as he physically matures and climbs the organizational ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kuroda-Grauer displayed a knack for hitting as a three-year starter at Rutgers by combining to hit .343 across three seasons, including a .428 batting average with a 1.082 OPS as a junior. That standout season led to the A’s selecting him in the third round of the 2024 MLB Draft, which saw them land Nick Kurtz, Tommy White and Gage Jump with their earlier picks. Joining the same system as college teammate Ryan Lasko, a second-rounder by the A’s in 2023, Kuroda-Grauer continued to perform as an impressive pure hitter last season between High-A Lansing and Double-A Midland. He also got some extra work in the Arizona Fall League, hitting .345 with a .898 OPS in 18 games for the Mesa Solar Sox. Kuroda-Grauer profiles as a Jacob Wilson-type hitter with his strong bat-to-ball skills that have led to remarkably low strikeout totals as a pro. The A’s would like to see him take a few more chances when he has count leverage by trying to backspin some balls to the pull side and drive them to the gap, something he has not really shown the ability to do. Doing so would help him take the next step as a hitter, providing another layer to what is already considered an advanced approach at the plate. Kuroda-Grauer has always provided strong defense at short, but upon the arrival of Leo De Vries to Double-A Midland last season, he saw more reps at third and surprised the A’s with how well he handled the hot corner. Speed is also an element of Kuroda-Grauer's game, as he stole 27 bases last season. It remains to be seen if he can ever generate more power than he’s shown, but all the other tools in his bag set him up with a decent chance to reach the big leagues with the floor of at least a versatile utility-type player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kuroda-Grauer was a three-year starter at Rutgers who shined as a hitter from the jump, combining to hit .343 across those three seasons. After receiving an invite from USA Baseball to train at their Collegiate National Team Training Camp, he went to the Cape Cod League and overcame some regular-season struggles by hitting .444 in the playoffs before returning to Rutgers for his junior season. That was by far his best, as he hit .428 with a 1.082 OPS. That performance led to the A’s selecting him in the third round of the 2024 Draft, marking the second straight year in which they took a Rutgers player (after drafting his teammate Ryan Lasko as a second-rounder in 2023). After 24 games between Single-A Stockton and High-A Lansing, the A’s rewarded him with four games at Triple-A Las Vegas to end the season. Across those 28 total games, he hit .324 and struck out just nine times in 126 plate appearances. Kuroda-Grauer’s athletic size and hard-working mentality remind some in the A’s organization of a young Marcus Semien. While he may never have Semien-type power, his high-level ability to frequently make contact and rarely strike out is reminiscent of another more high-profile touted top prospect in Jacob Wilson. His advanced approach at the plate allows him to work counts and make good decisions with his simple swing. The power remains below-average, though the A’s believe he could grow into some extra pop with 15-homer potential as a ceiling. There is a speed element to Kuroda-Grauer’s game, and while he may not be a burner, his 40 stolen bases in college show he can be a decent threat on the basepaths. Defensively, his arm is average, but his overall glovework and instincts give him the chance to stick as a shortstop with second base as a fallback. Between that and his excellent bat-to-ball skills, Kuroda-Grauer enters his first full professional season with a chance to quickly rise through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Santos joined the Mets system for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic just before the 2017-18 international period closed. He has been slowly working his way through the system, playing for one club per season in his last three campaigns. He spent 2022 entirely at High-A Brooklyn, throwing a career-high 116 2/3 innings for the Cyclones. Santos posted a 4.47 ERA with 105 strikeouts in 116 2/3 innings in the South Atlantic League and was left unprotected and unpicked in the offseason Rule 5 Draft. The lack of a stellar strikeout rate doesn’t tell the whole story because Santos was nearly elite at one thing -- keeping the ball on the ground. His 58.7 percent ground-ball rate was the third-highest in the Minors among the 311 pitchers with at least 100 innings in 2022. A 93-96 mph fastball is the main culprit because its impressive sink made it difficult for batters to square the ball up, enabling the pitch to play up to plus level. His low-80s slider shows some promise but still lacks the depth to be more than average, while an upper-80s changeup drops some but didn’t prevent Santos from getting lit up (.295 average-against) vs. lefty hitters. The 6-foot-7 right-hander has always been projectable, and the velocity and movement have certainly come, along with a little better control than many his size. There’s something to be said for a pitcher that elicits ground balls by the bucketful in an age when hitters prioritize lifting the ball in the air, but a lack of surefire secondary pitches -- and the ticking roster clock -- could make 2023 a make-or-break year for Santos.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets signed Santos for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of the 2017-18 international signing period, seeing the 6-foot-6 right-hander as a projectable arm. He ascended quickly stateside after only 11 Dominican Summer League outings as a 17-year-old in 2018 but took a step back at Rookie Advanced Kingsport (5.09 ERA, 36 strikeouts in 40 2/3 innings) the following year. Following the missed 2020 season, Santos saw full-season ball for the first time with Low-A St. Lucie and didn’t miss a ton of bats, striking out 79 in 96 innings. He finished with a 4.59 ERA. Heading into just his age-20 season, projection remains the name of the game for Santos. Previously sitting at 92-93, he added a little velocity to be in the 93-96 mph range with his fastball now. The pitch typically shows promising sink, so it’s not straight velo either. Everything else remains in development. A low-80s slider shows promising spin, but lacks the consistency to be more than an average pitch. An upper-80s changeup does little more than show separation from the heater and remains his third pitch by far. Santos got better at throwing strikes in the second half last season, and with an 8.9 percent walk rate, that remains less of a concern than it did entering '21. The Mets are still working with Santos on developing consistent mechanics to help him command the ball better in general, because as his low strikeout rate proved, he could be quite hittable inside the zone. His size, youth and fastball still give Santos some promise, and discussions about a move to the bullpen remain at least a year away.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets saw plenty to dream on when they signed Santos for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in September 2017. At 6-foot-8, Santos stood out in more ways than one in his first taste of pro ball in the Dominican Summer League, prompting a move stateside in the midst of his age-17 season. His results took a step back in 2019 at Rookie Advanced Kingsport – namely his 5.09 ERA, 1.75 WHIP and 25 walks in 40 2/3 innings – and he missed out on more chances to develop due to the pandemic and a broken toe suffered not long after leaving Spring Training. He was healed in time for instructional league in the Dominican Republic and salvaged some time throwing there. As is true of many tall pitchers, Santos’ fastball is the star of his arsenal. It usually sits around 92-93 and can touch 95 and earns extra points for the way he bears down on hitters with it thanks to his massive extension. There could be even another tick of velocity in the tank as he adds more strength to his frame. As he showed in the Appalachian League, control can be an issue at times because of his size, however, and that’s something Santos will have to find the more he throws. The breaking ball and changeups are works in progress. The former was a particular point of emphasis last spring before camp broke and can look the better of the two offerings because of its promising spin, though it’s not yet a plus pitch. Mechanics and secondary pitches will be what decides how much of a role Santos can play in the Majors. If he can only keep the fastball as a plus pitch, then he could head to the bullpen like fellow 6-foot-8 Met Dellin Betances. If he can develop a better breaking ball, then starting could be a real option. With an August birthday, he will still be a teenager for much of the 2021 season, an indication that time is very much on his side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilken set the ACC career record with 71 homers over his three years at Wake Forest, prompting the Brewers to take him with the 18th overall pick in 2023. It hasn’t been an ideal start to his career from a health standpoint. Wilken was hit in the face in his fifth game of in his first full season, and while he returned to Double-A Biloxi a month later and got some time in the Arizona Fall League, he admitted later he needed eye therapy to work on his depth perception the following offseason. He returned to the Southern League for 2025 and had a .392 OBP, .550 SLG and 18 homers in 65 games before suffering a dislocated left kneecap during a first-round division title celebration. He tried to return in August, but issues still lingered and he underwent knee surgery early in the offseason. The Demon Deacons legend would have broken through to Triple-A at last in the second half if not for the most recent injury, and the IL time has very much clouded his standing. From the positive side, he did an even better job of honing in on pitches in the zone at Double-A in ’25, and his ability to lift and pull the ball allowed him to post big slugging numbers when healthy. Among the negatives, his stiffness at the plate still makes him highly vulnerable to sliders down and away, and upper-level arms will pick up on that. With well-below-average speed, Wilken was never a stolen-base threat, and while he has the arm for the hot corner, his lack of quickness will hinder him from being an asset there. He’s yet to play first base in the pros entering 2026. Health will be paramount in his push to bring his pop to Milwaukee before becoming Rule 5-eligible next offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilken was a slugging force during his days at Wake Forest, winning the 2021 Cape Cod League MVP and setting the ACC career record with 71 homers (31 of which came in his junior year). Milwaukee selected the hulking infielder 18th overall in 2023, signed him for $3.15 million and got aggressive with him in his first full season with an opening assignment to Double-A Biloxi. He was hit in the face by a fastball on April 11 in just his fifth game of 2024, missed roughly a month and never quite recovered in terms of results, finishing with a .199/.312/.363 line and 17 homers in 108 games with the Shuckers. A move to the Arizona Fall League, where he batted .155 with 32 strikeouts in 100 plate appearances, didn’t do much to end the year on a high note. It's tough to balance the impact of the early-season HBP, as well as the move to the pitcher-friendly Southern League. Batting hunched over from the right side with a toe tap, the Demon Deacons legend is built to rip hard-hit balls in the air to the pullside, and he still has ample strength. His 17 homers were fourth-most in the SL, but he’s also proved to be extremely vulnerable to soft stuff low and away, and pitchers took advantage. To his credit, he'd done an impressive job of cutting down on his chase rate in a return to Biloxi in 2025 and looked to be pushing for a move to Triple-A before suffering a dislocated patella in his left knee. A well-below-average runner, Wilken has been third-base-only in pro ball, and while he has ample arm strength for the hot corner, he still might be a better fit at first base long-term, given his range and 6-foot-4 frame. His early 2025 trajectory provided hope that he could still be valuable at either corner-infield spot when healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Cape Cod League MVP in 2021, Wilken set multiple home run records at Wake Forest and finished as both the Demon Deacons’ and ACC’s all-time leader with 71 long balls over his three years on campus. Thirty-one of those came in his junior campaign, placing him second in Division I. That helped push him into the first round to the Brewers with the 18th overall pick and he signed for $3.15 million. Wilken reached Double-A Biloxi in his first taste of the pros and finished with a .285/.414/.473 line with five homers over 47 games across three levels. The right-handed slugger relies on the strength in his upper half to generate bat speed and loft that helps him send balls over fences in bunches. He can look almost hunched over the plate before ripping at the ball with a slight step as a lower load. Wilken’s swing decisions improved over his time at Wake, and while he’ll take his walks, the early strikeout concerns that emerged in college could return against more advanced pro arms, as they did in his small Double-A sample. Standing 6-foot-4, Wilken clocks in as a well-below-average runner. He can move around capably at the hot corner and has more than enough arm for the position, but his defense doesn’t figure to add much value to his overall profile. Given his size and speed, he might have to move across the diamond to first, where his power would still more than fit the bill.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After plucking Kasevich out of the second round in the 2022 Draft, he quietly built momentum in ‘23 and ‘24 as a favorite among many coaches and player development staff in the organization. In ‘24, Kasevich hit .296 with a .733 OPS over 128 games between Double-A and Triple-A. The ‘25 season was supposed to be a launch pad for Kasevich, but back and wrist injuries limited him to 42 total games and he was never able to gain much traction, including during a stint in the Arizona Fall League. Early in 2026, it feels like Kasevich has regained some of that momentum, though, and is driving the ball harder on top of his impressive contact skill, which is crucial if he’s going to raise his ceiling. The floor is still awfully attractive, though. You’ll hear “machine” and “robot” thrown around, which are high compliments. Kasevich is a natural leader by example, a young player who even more veteran Minor Leaguers have followed. He fits the Blue Jays’ idea of a model teammate, fully and completely. Defensively, the Blue Jays are much higher on Kasevich than many are externally, and it’s easy to see where their confidence comes from. He’s not flashy, but he won’t give you a reason to pick apart his defense, either. He’s steady and reliable with a chance to play games at shortstop in the big leagues, while also mixing in some second and third. If Kasevich can drive the ball harder and get it off the ground more consistently, he profiles as a big leaguer based on the all-around package he presents.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming off a successful NCAA career at Oregon and a good stint in the Northwoods League, the Blue Jays selected Kasevich in the second round of the 2022 Draft and signed him to a $1 million bonus. Along with third-rounder Alan Roden, that’s got a chance to be a fine Draft class for Toronto. Kasevich got his feet wet at Single-A that season, then jumped to High-A in ‘23 where he posted a .284/.363/.365 line. In ‘24, he opened at Double-A and eventually jumped to Triple-A with a combined line of .296/.348/.385. Kasevich is an organizational favorite, from coaches to the development staff. You’ll hear the word “machine” a lot, and some coaches have even noticed older players gravitating towards Kasevich, given how he handles his business. Prospects younger than Kasevich have tried to emulate him, too, which is one of the highest forms of praise. Another extremely intelligent young prospect, Kasevich is also one of the strongest defensive shortstops in the organization with tremendous body control while fielding. He’ll still see the odd game at third base, but the Blue Jays fully believe in Kasevich as a shortstop long-term, betting heavily on both his mental and physical games. At the dish, contact is Kasevich’s identity. His 10 home runs in 247 career Minor League games don’t paint much of a power hitter, but that’s not his game. If Kasevich can drive the ball more consistently, sneaking a few more balls through the infield while turning some singles into doubles, that should be enough to make his bat play at the MLB level. If that happens, Kasevich’s defense will help his case, and his intangibles could take him over the top. A stress reaction in his lower back has kept Kasevich from pushing through the Minors' top level in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays selected Kasevich in the second round of the 2022 Draft, fresh off a successful career at Oregon and a good run in the Northwoods League, and signed him to a $1 million bonus. His brief introduction to pro ball was a learning experience, batting .262 with little power (.336 slugging percentage) over 25 games with Single-A Dunedin, but strong internal reviews earned him a trip to High-A Vancouver in ‘23 and Kasevich did not disappoint. There, Kasevich hit .284 with a .728 OPS over 94 games, and while his four home runs don’t point to much power, there’s belief he could grow into 10-15 homers annually. Few players in this organization receive stronger reviews than Kasevich for his work ethic and approach to the game. He’s been lauded as a teammate for making those around him better and is one of the best defensive shortstops in the organization. Internally, the Blue Jays are very high on his defensive profile. Kasevich may not be the flashiest athlete at shortstop but is solid fundamentally and makes nearly every play he gets to. He’ll still see plenty of time at third base, but make no mistake, Kasevich will keep shortstop on his résumé right through to the higher levels. At the plate, Kasevich’s identity will need to be that of a contact hitter and he shines in that role. Strikeouts should never be an issue, and in an organization preaching “competitive at-bats,” Kasevich fits the bill, though he could be particularly prone to BABIP-related fluctuations if he doesn’t begin driving the ball more. If that suddenly happens, then Kasevich climbs to another tier, but his ability to put the ball in play and defend at short -- plus the intangibles -- will keep him ranked highly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kasevich showed some impressive contact skills over his final two seasons with the University of Oregon, hitting .324 and .310 respectively, and he carried that success into the Northwoods League, where he batted .374 over 40 games in 2021. The Blue Jays picked him up in the second round of the 2022 Draft and signed Kasevich for a $1 million bonus. Kasevich got a taste of pro ball in ’22, hitting .262 with a .681 OPS over 25 games for Single-A Dunedin. There, he walked 11 times while striking out only nine, showing the same plate discipline the Blue Jays liked in the Draft. Kasevich has a strong contact profile that he should show more of in the coming years, but power will be a separating factor for him. He’s worked to add more, focusing on keeping his bat path in the zone a bit longer. The Blue Jays believe Kasevich has the tools to stick long term at shortstop, where he’s fundamentally sound and moves well enough for the position. He’ll continue to see some time at third base too, and that positional versatility should only help as he climbs the ladder. At 22 with his NCAA experience, Kasevich could be a quick mover once he gets rolling through a full season, depending on how well the slugging ability translates to the pro game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: O’Donnell started his college career at Northwestern, but after a strong Cape Cod League performance following his sophomore year, he transferred to Virginia. As a junior, he posted a .354/.448/.587 line with 13 homers and 18 steals, helping him land in the sixth round with the Reds. For two summers in a row, he’s finished strongly, posting a .960 OPS during his debut and then battling through a shoulder issue for much of his first full season to put up a 1.076 OPS in August with High-A Dayton. That set the stage for a move to the upper levels. A left-handed hitter, O’Donnell is capable of making a ton of hard contact with an ability to drive the ball to all fields. It might be more gap-to-gap type thump for extra bases, but there is some ability to reach the seats, and some think that there’s more offensive upside here now that he’s not dealing with a bad shoulder. He can get a little too overly aggressive and will have to watch his tendency to chase out of the zone as he advances. An above-average runner who swiped 30 bags a year ago, O’Donnell has the skill set to play center field regularly, even though he saw most of his time with Dayton in the corners because of teammates on the roster. The Reds now know he’s an above-average defender in all three spots and could be the type of valuable fourth outfielder who can beat you in a number of ways.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at Northwestern, including a big sophomore season, O’Donnell turned in a solid performance in the Cape Cod League and transferred to Virginia for his junior season in 2023. Posting a 1.034 OPS with 13 homers and 18 steals for the ACC power certainly put him on the map, and he landed in the sixth round of that summer’s Draft, where he signed for a bit under slot. Despite playing through a shoulder issue for the first couple months of his first full year, he reached double digits in homers and swiped more than 30 bags with High-A Dayton, helping his numbers tremendously with a fully healthy August that led to an OPS over 1.000. O’Donnell has a knack for making a lot of hard contact from the left side of the plate. He has solid swing mechanics and he could end up being a better pure hitter than his numbers indicate with the shoulder issue in his rearview mirror. He may never be a huge power guy, but he can drive the ball to all fields with some sneaky over-the-fence pop, especially to his pull side. O’Donnell runs well and has shown he knows how to steal a base. He’s seen time in all three outfield spots, but his ability to play center field regularly gives him a very high floor. He might be a fourth outfielder when all is said and done, but he could develop into a big league regular up the middle if it all clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If not for Roki Sasaki (and his $6.5 million bonus), Peña would have been the talk of the 2025 international signing class after he joined the Mets organization for $5 million that January. (New York only had a bonus pool of $6,261,600.) He was closely watched in the Dominican Summer League, only to open 0-for-26 in his first nine games. Peña hit .342/.463/.618 with nine homers in 46 contests the rest of the way and had the DSL’s only two three-dinger games of the 2025 season. He was one of only two age-17 players with nine or more homers in the DSL, Detroit’s Cris Rodriguez being the other. When it was going right for Peña last season, he was the poster boy for the “elevate and celebrate” mentality, often turning on inside pitches and driving them in the air for extra-base hits. He wasn’t getting wild with his approach either in search of such contact, exhibiting good swing decisions, but more experienced pitchers might attack his uppercut swing differently. How his exit velocities hold up stateside after another year of physical maturation will deserve monitoring. Despite the high steal count last year, Peña doesn’t project to be a burner by the time he reaches the Majors, and his future position splits evaluators. Some believe he’ll have the actions to be a solid shortstop, noting that his above-average arm strength works from the left side of the infield, while others believe he’s headed elsewhere on the dirt down the line. It’ll likely be the bat that drives Peña’s value toward becoming an everyday player in Queens, and improved consistency in the box would go a long way in ’26 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Azua, Dominican Republic might sound familiar to anyone who has followed baseball in the last decade or so. Sure, established Major Leaguers like Yainer Diaz and Maikel Franco hail from there, but it also came up as the hometown of top 2024 international signing and current Top 100 prospect Leodalis De Vries. The city came up again this January when Peña signed for $5 million with the Mets, who only had a $6,261,600 bonus pool this year. Only Roki Sasaki ($6.5 million) signed for more under the 2025 international rules. Peña wowed evaluators as an amateur with his elite plate discipline, often refusing to expand the zone in showcase settings, much like De Vries did a year earlier. He has ample bat speed from the left side too, and he’s shown a capability of spraying the ball to all fields when he finds a pitch worthy of a swing. There could be even more power to come as he continues to mature and fill out his 5-foot-10 frame, but it already projects for at least average. Peña is a solid runner, though some scouts are concerned he’ll slow down as he ages. His footwork, hands, arm strength and overall actions certainly fit shortstop right now, and if he needs to move on the dirt to either second or third, he could be above-average defensively there too. Anything could happen on the long road of development – and a big bonus isn’t indicative of future success on its own – but Peña has all the pieces to become a prominent piece of the Mets’ current pipeline and future Major League club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A hamate bone injury caused Tresh to miss the start of his 2020 collegiate season, but he put himself back on the radar at North Carolina State in 2021, when he homered 15 times in 56 games and helped the Wolfpack finish third at the College World Series. The Royals selected him in the 17th round and gave him a high bonus – $423,000 – to sign him away from returning to school. Tresh posted an .828 OPS between High-A and Double-A in his first full pro season in 2022, with 14 homers and 54 RBI. Tresh is a strong hitter who generates impressive exit velocities with his raw power and bat speed. He made more contact in 2022 with a 24.3% strikeout rate between both levels. Tresh is still aggressive, and there are still improvements to be made in his approach, especially with pitches on the outer part of the plate, but he has a lot of power potential. Behind the plate, Tresh showed significant improvement with his receiving last year. He has a plus arm and should become at least an average defender. Tresh receives high marks for his ability to run a pitching staff, a quiet competitor who leads by example. How far he goes and what his ceiling ends up being depends on whether he can continue his improved approach and contact at the higher levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At North Carolina State, Tresh caught sparingly behind Patrick Bailey, the No. 13 pick in 2020, and Tresh missed the start of the 2020 season with a broken hamate bone in his left hand. He put himself back on the radar and filled Bailey’s void in ’21, homering 15 times in 56 games last spring and helping the Wolfpack finish third at the College World Series. It felt like a steal when the Royals selected him all the way down in the 17th round, but Tresh stuck to his signability and wasn’t afraid to go back to school if needed. The Royals were able to sign him for $423,000, roughly the slot of a fourth-round selection. Tresh posted a 1.143 OPS in six games in Rookie ball after he was drafted, earning him a quick promotion to Low-A Columbia, where he struggled more in 10 games. Tresh has obvious raw power and consistently high exit velocities thanks to massive strength and bat speed. He’s aggressive at the plate and will need to do a better job of consistent contact, but the Royals see room for improvement as he spends more time with the hitting development program. Behind the plate, Tresh is inexperienced for a college catcher, but he showed significant improvement as a receiver in the fall. He has a plus arm to keep the running game in check and should become at least an average defender if the Royals keep him at catcher. Tresh earns praise for his leadership, ability to run a pitching staff and his quiet competitiveness. He still has a lot of ceiling for a college player, which was appealing to the Royals in the Draft. How far he will go depends on his improvement with contact and time behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Santucci headed from Massachusetts to Duke and mixed a heavy dose of strikeouts (138 in 117 2/3 collegiate innings) with injuries (elbow surgery in 2023, rib issue in 2024) during his time in Durham. An elevated walk rate as a junior, along with the missed time, may have pushed him out of the first round in 2024, but the Mets gave him full slot to sign out of the second round with a $2,031,700 bonus. Santucci opened his first full season with a 8.14 ERA in his first six starts with High-A Brooklyn but sharply steadied the ship the rest of the way, finishing with a 3.06 ERA and 138 strikeouts in 117 2/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. The 6-foot-2 left-hander throws a 92-95 mph four-seamer (touching 97) from a high release angle that generates good carry toward the top of the zone. What the heater might do best, though, is set up Santucci’s 86-88 mph slider, a two-plane breaker that tunnels well off the fastball only to snap late enough that hitters can’t touch it. He used it against both righties and lefties with strong effect, and that’s important because he didn’t go to his low-80s curveball or upper-80s changeup much at all. Developing a cambio with more velocity separation has been a key goal heading into his second full campaign. Santucci’s walk rate improved impressively in his first taste of the pros, though he relies on batters expanding the zone when they bite on his best breaking balls. He could get to the Majors on the fastball-slider mix alone and deliver enough strikes to be a useful backend starter, but to fit in the middle of the rotation, he’ll likely need a quality third pitch to round out the arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Massachusetts native, Santucci joined Duke’s rotation early as a freshman and proved to be a strikeout fiend in all three years with the Blue Devils with a career 13.9 K/9 mark over 40 appearances. His time on campus was also marked by injury concerns, first with elbow surgery to remove bone chips as a sophomore in 2023 and then a rib injury as a junior in 2024. He managed a 3.41 ERA with 90 strikeouts and 36 walks in 58 innings, and the missed time and high walk rate likely pushed him out of the first round come July. The Mets swooped in to select him in the second round and signed him for full slot at $2,031,700. The 6-foot-2 southpaw’s 92-96 mph fastball comes in with a flat approach and impressive carry, and college hitters couldn’t much touch it. As if that wasn’t enough, Santucci also threw out an 82-85 mph slider with tough two-plane break that was a menace to batters from both sides; even right-handers whiffed on 56 percent of their swings against it in 2024. His upper-80s changeup may not have had much separation from the traditional heater, but it came with sufficient fade to keep hitters off-balance. The Blue Devils lefty wasn’t a consistent strike-thrower in school, but his athleticism as a former two-way player and overall mechanics point to a pitcher who could become average in the control department with more professional instruction. The southpaw has already reached Double-A in his first full season, relying on that fastball-slider combo to keep the strikeouts coming and keep his place as the top LHP in the Mets system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kent starred in both baseball and football as an Illinois high schooler before heading to the University of Arizona. He went from a redshirt freshman in 2022 to the Wildcats’ Friday night starter in '24, and that ascent, along with an impressive Cape Cod League run, pushed him to the Nationals in the fourth round. He posted a 4.61 ERA with 132 strikeouts over 123 innings between High-A and Double-A in his first full season, and his 18.5 K-BB percentage was best in the Washington system. The 6-foot-3 left-hander generates huge extension, allowing him to lower his release height and create a difficult angle for opposing batters. His fastball only sat 91-93 mph (touching 95) in 2025, but the ride on the pitch showed more promise than that. Early spring reports indicate that Kent could be set to add a little extra velo in his second full season. Maybe the best thing his current heater does, however, is set up his plus changeup, an 80-83 mph armside offering with just the right amount of velo separation and movement to keep righties swinging over it time and again. (The pitch had a 51 percent whiff rate in 2025.) Kent can also spin a mid-80s slider against lefties and flips in an upper-70s curveball, though the command of the latter can be all over. There is some effort in Kent’s delivery to get to his extension, and his walk rate did jump from 6.5 percent at High-A to 10.7 in a limited Double-A sample. But the southpaw commands the fastball well enough to deliver strikes, while setting up the changeup for chase. If the velo bump holds, he could be a backend rotation candidate in the Majors by the end of his age-23 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 45 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 After starring in both baseball and football back home in Illinois, Kent headed to the University of Arizona, where he redshirted in 2022 and worked as a reliever in 2023. He headed to the Cape Cod League that summer and put himself squarely on the radar with a 2.52 ERA and 27 strikeouts in six starts (25 innings). The Wildcats made Kent their Friday night starter, and he handled himself well with the elevated role, posting a 4.08 ERA with 89 strikeouts in 86 frames. The Nationals selected him in the fourth round and signed him to a $625,000 bonus. The 6-foot-3 southpaw has a full bevy of pitches that can leave hitters guessing. He bumped up his fastball velocity ahead of the Draft to sit 90-93 mph, and he touched as high as 96. The pitch can play better than the velo too with a flat approach from a lower angle in his delivery. Kent’s 82-84 mph changeup is his most effective offering – one that works well down and armside leading to whiffs and groundballs. He has two different breaking pitches in a low-80s slider and mid-70s curve. The former was slightly more effective at missing bats in school, but the latter can drop in for an easy strike too. Kent had some control issues on the Cape but was much better at sticking to the zone with the Wildcats in the spring. With only one year as a starter against quality competition under his belt, Kent could keep building on his 2024 gains, but even if he’s capped at being a hurler with a deep arsenal but no true plus pitch, that could still work in the back of future MLB rotations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Projected as the No. 1 overall pick in the Korea Baseball Organization's September 2023 draft, Jang announced a month in advance that he wanted to follow his dream of pitching in Major League Baseball. The Dodgers, who signed the first Korean big leaguer (Chan Ho Park) in 1994, traded righty pitching prospects Aldrin Batista and Maximo Martinez to the White Sox for $1 million in international bonus pool funds, then landed Jang for $900,000. He posted a 6.14 ERA in his pro debut but lowered that mark to 1.47 in his final seven starts between the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League and Single-A. Jang struck out 41 percent of the batters he faced in his first taste of pro ball while displaying some of the best stuff in the system. He works with a 94-96 mph fastball that reaches 99 with good carry up in the strike zone, and he might have more velocity in his strong but still projectable 6-foot-4 frame. His tight mid-80s slider gives him a second plus pitch and he emphasized it last summer over his upper-70s downer curveball. His upper-80s changeup has been better than anticipated, featuring deceptive tumble. After a history of throwing strikes as an amateur, Jang issued 27 walks in 36 2/3 innings last year with a delivery that includes some effort and head whack. The Dodgers believe his issues were related more to targeting than mechanics and think his athleticism will help him improve in the future. He's a potential No. 2 starter if he can refine his control and command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jang projected as the No. 1 overall pick in the Korea Baseball Organization's September 2023 draft until he announced a month beforehand that he would rather pursue his dream of pitching in Major League Baseball. The Dodgers, who signed the first Korean big leaguer (Chan Ho Park) in 1994, coveted Jang but had little cash remaining in their 2023 international allotment. They traded righty pitching prospects Aldrin Batista and Maximo Martinez to the White Sox for $1 million in bonus pool money, then signed Jang for $900,000. Jang's four-seam fastball parks at 94-96 mph and tops out at 99 with carry up in the strike zone, and he could add more velocity as he continues add strength to his 6-foot-4 frame. His advanced feel for spin results in a pair of plus breaking balls, a hard 84-87 mph slider and a 76-82 mph curveball with downer break. His changeup has been better than expected, arriving in the upper 80s before dropping at the plate. Though there's some effort in Jang's delivery, his arm works well and his mechanics aren't a concern. He has battled his control throughout his pro debut after having no trouble throwing strikes as an amateur, but Los Angeles believes in his athleticism and thinks his walks this summer are more of a targeting issue than anything. Because he helped Korea win the Asian Games last fall, he's exempt from the mandatory 18-21 months service required of his nation's males and will be able to come to the United States this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gill Hill has outpaced perhaps even the Rays’ initial expectations for his development, a testament to his maturity off the mound and ability on the field. He was 17 when the Rays selected him out of New York’s Westchester County in the sixth round of the 2022 Draft, and he was quite raw as a player who didn’t focus exclusively on pitching until his junior year of high school. That may have shown during his professional debut in 2023, but he took a massive step forward in his full-season debut for Single-A Charleston in ’24 and kept progressing through the system with a full season for High-A Bowling Green last year. Gill Hill’s numbers took a step back in 2025, but his arsenal is largely the same. He has a four-pitch mix of average or above-average offerings, headlined by a pair of 93-95 mph fastballs that can touch 97 and a cutter in the upper 80s. He also throws a bigger-sweeping slider and a changeup, with the former taking a step forward last year, and he does it all from an upper three-quarters delivery that creates depth on his offspeed stuff. He’s not a huge strikeout artist but he puts the ball on the ground a lot. The jump in his ERA last year was mostly a product of his increased home run output, as he gave up 17 in 25 starts after allowing only 12 during his first two Minor League seasons. The 21-year-old helps himself by limiting walks. He issued only two free passes per nine innings last year, and he has earned high praise for his competitive maturity at such a young age. He might need to develop a plus pitch to separate himself from his peers, but he has a deep enough arsenal and a good enough feel for it to stay on a starting track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When he was selected in the sixth round of the 2022 Draft, Gill Hill looked like he might be a long-term developmental project for the Rays. He had been hitting and pitching for his high school team in New York’s Westchester County, hardly a baseball hotbed, and focused exclusively on pitching during his junior year. He didn’t turn 18 until two months after the Rays picked him and signed him for $597,500. He was extremely raw, and it looked that way during his professional debut in 2023. But Gill Hill may have improved as much as any player in the organization last year, posting a 3.15 ERA in 108 2/3 innings over 22 outings for Single-A Charleston in his first full season. Last spring, Gill Hill put on more muscle on his 6-foot-2 frame and shifted his arm slot up to an upper three-quarters delivery, which led to improved velocity and more depth on his offspeed stuff. His primary pitch is a fastball in the 93-95 mph range, touching 96-97, although his velocity faded a bit toward the end of his first full season. He complements that with a low-80s slider, a cutter in the mid-to-upper 80s and the occasional changeup that helped him limit lefties to a .650 OPS last year. Especially for such a young player -- he turned 20 last September -- Gill Hill displayed impressive control, walking only 2.2 batters per nine innings. Arm slot consistency played a part in that, but he has also shown impressive maturity and intent despite his inexperience. The right-hander doesn’t have a true plus pitch at this point, but the depth of his arsenal and his feel for using it should keep him on a faster-than-anticipated track toward the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 60 | Field: 45 | Overall: 50 Dinges dealt with a frightening bout with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) as a sophomore at Tallahassee Community College, and for the 2024 season, he transferred to Florida State, where he wore No. 43 for the total days of his hospital stays. He was an impressive performer as a DH with the Seminoles and the Brewers took him in the fourth round. He moved back to catcher in his first taste of the pros but still stood out most for his bat, hitting .300/.416/.514 with 13 homers in 77 games between Single-A and High-A. He was limited by hamstring issues during the regular season and a brief trip to the Arizona Fall League. A right-handed slugger, Dinges displays big-time bat speed as he unleashes vicious cuts out of a straight-up stance. When he makes contact, it’s loud and generally in the air. The aggression in his hacks is always evident, and some evaluators have pause about the general length of his swing. Dinges struggled mightily against changeups, biting often against them while swinging over the top in his move to High-A, and more experienced pitchers could take advantage unless he finds a way to adjust. It’s more likely that Dinges’ ability to pound balls helps his average than his overall contact rate. There was some thought out of the Draft that the 5-foot-11 backstop should just head to left field and focus on mashing, but he’s made some steady gains as a catcher. His plus arm strength is an obvious asset, and his issues with receiving and blocking might get better as he works with pitchers with better command. Entering ’26, Dinges is more raw than a typical 22-year-old and could push toward MLB starting catcher status with more time at and behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Cappe defected from Cuba in late 2018, he didn't make his pro debut until mid-2021. By the time MLB declared him a free agent, teams had committed most of their bonus pool money for 2019-29, so he opted until the next international signing period opened in January 2021 before joining the Marlins for $3.5 million. He earned physical comparisons to Carlos Correa as an amateur but has struggled to add muscle to his 6-foot-3 frame since turning pro. Cappe's sound right-handed stroke and feel for the barrel give him some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the system. But while he does a good job of putting the ball in play for a youngster facing older competition, he chases and pulls too many pitches and is hapless against breaking balls. With his frame and bat speed, it's easy to project him developing 20-homer power if he can gain more strength. Cappe possesses solid speed but still is learning the nuances of basestealing. Primarily a shortstop in his first two pro seasons, he spent more time at second base in 2023 and projects as a solid defender there once he develops more consistency. He continues to baffle scouts with his throwing, as his arm strength flashes plus at time but plays below average at others.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cappe defected from Cuba in late 2018 and by the time MLB cleared him as a free agent, most teams already had committed their bonus pool cash for the 2019-20 signing period. One of top prospects in that class, he opted to wait until the 2020-21 period opened in January 2021 and landed a $3.5 million bonus from the Marlins. He slashed .290/.328/.438 with nine homers and 13 steals in his 67-game U.S. debut last season, split between Rookie ball and Single-A. Cappe has a sound right-handed swing and good feel for the barrel, giving him some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the system. Though he has had no problems making contact, his aggressive, pull-happy approach does cut into his walk totals and could be exploited at higher levels. As a 6-foot-3 shortstop, he garnered physical comparisons to Carlos Correa as an amateur, but he needs to add strength in order to make good on his power projection and deliver 20 or more homers per season. There's some question as to whether Cappe may outgrow shortstop and he has spent more time at second base in 2023. He has solid speed and nice actions at short, but he could lose a step if he eventually adds 40 pounds of muscle to his lean frame. His plus arm is an asset at any position, though the game sped up on him a bit when he played third base in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cappe left Cuba in late 2018 and became one of the top prospects in the 2019 international class, but most clubs already had committed their bonus pool money to other players. He decided to wait for a bigger bonus in the 2020 signing period, which the pandemic pushed back to January 2021. After signing for $3.5 million on the first day, he enjoyed a solid debut against lesser competition in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. As a 6-foot-3 shortstop with a ton of projection remaining, Cappe drew comparisons to Carlos Correa as an amateur. He has already begun to add strength and makes repeated hard contact while also showing the ability to launch balls in the air. He does a good job of keeping his right-handed swing under control and managing the strike zone, though he can get overly pull-conscious. Presently a solid runner, Cappe could lose some quickness as he fills out and may outgrow shortstop. That may be a moot point because the presence of Kahlil Watson and Jose Salas in the Marlins system may push Cappe to third base anyway. He does have quick actions and plus arm strength, though like a lot of young shortstops, he needs to improve his defensive consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After defecting from Cuba in late 2018, Cappe quickly became one of the top prospects in the 2019 international class. Because most teams had already committed the bulk of their bonus pools to other players, he opted to wait for more money in the 2020 signing period, which didn't open until January 2021 because of the coronavirus pandemic. He inked with the Marlins for $3.5 million on the first day. As a shortstop with an extremely projectable 6-foot-3 frame, Cappe draws repeated physical comparisons to Carlos Correa. He has a chance to hit for power and average once he's physically developed, as he already shows the ability to make hard contact to all fields. He'll need to watch the length of his naturally long right-handed swing but has a mature approach and understands the strike zone. Cappe presently has solid speed but could lose some quickness as he adds muscle, making it possible that he'll outgrow shortstop. He'll begin his pro career at short and may be able to remain there because he has quick actions and hands as well as a plus arm. Third base would be his fallback position and he has all the tools to fit that profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Doncon began his career with the Dodgers, signing in January 2021 for just under $500,000. He made it to full-season ball full-time in 2023 but struggled some there. Doncon then found himself on the move when the Twins acquired Manny Margot from the Dodgers, a deal that included a prospect swap of Doncon for Noah Miller. Playing at age 20, Doncon made strides in his offensive game that allowed him to go from Single-A Fort Myers to High-A Cedar Rapids in his first season with his new organization. The right-handed-hitting infielder’s biggest issue when he scuffled in 2023 was with his overall approach, with a 103/36 K/BB ratio. He controlled the zone much better in 2024, upping his walk rate even when he got to High-A. There’s plenty of raw power for him to tap into, and he’s gotten to it at times, especially to left, and he can get too pull-happy at times. His ability to continue to control the zone and add strength to consistently be an impact hitter is a key to him reaching his ceiling. Doncon played both third base, his natural position, and shortstop with the Twins in 2024, and the staff felt he played better up the middle than expected. He has plenty of arm for the left side of the infield, though he’s also played second in the past with the Dodgers, and he’ll at least see reps at short and the hot corner, especially with the influx of infield talent who will be at the same level. If the approach gains stick and he can get to his pop consistently, he could profile as an every day guy at third in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $497,500 out of the Dominican Republic, Doncon has been the top performer from the Dodgers' 2020-21 international class. He made an easy transition to pro ball in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2021, then came to the United States last year and showed increased strength and power. He finished last summer by homering three times in 11 Single-A games as an 18-year-old. He struggled with a full-time move to full-season ball in 2023, though his power showed up a bit, and then was sent to the Twins with Manny Margot in the late February deal that sent Noah Miller to the Dodgers. Doncon's combination of hitting ability, bat speed and projectable strength give him at least plus raw power that plays to all fields. He has an aggressive, pull-happy approach but has had a knack for putting the barrel on the ball with a right-handed swing that he repeats with ease, though his approach suffered in 2023. While he may have to make adjustments against more advanced pitchers, he has at least 25-homer potential. Doncon presently shows average speed and can steal an occasional base, but he projects as no more than a fringy runner once he's physically mature. The Dodgers liked his actions at shortstop, where he was more consistent in 2022 following an erratic debut, and he has the solid arm strength for the position. If he loses some quickness, second base may be his long-term home and he saw time at three infield spots in 2023.

The Dodgers like his actions at shortstop, where he was more consistent in 2022 following an erratic debut, and he has the solid arm strength for the position. If he loses some quickness, second base may be his long-term home.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Overshadowed by Wilman Diaz and Jesus Galiz in the Dodgers' 2020-21 international class, Doncon outperformed them both in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League during their debuts last summer. Signed for $497,500 out of the Dominican Republic, he batted .283/.387/.455 in the DSL and also showed well in instructional league. One of the most advanced young bats in the system, Doncon could be a plus hitter with 20 or more homers per season if he reaches his ceiling. He repeats his simple right-handed swing with ease, has a knack for barreling balls and possesses plenty of bat speed and projectable strength. He already shows the ability to drive balls in the air, though he can get overly pull-conscious. While the Dodgers believe Doncon has the actions and solid arm strength to possibly remain at shortstop, he's an average runner who might lose some quickness as he matures physically. He's still learning to play under control in the field and likely will wind up at second or third base, with more than enough offense to profile at either spot. Club officials praise his makeup as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed the Venezuela native on his 16th birthday in 2019, but Arias couldn't make his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League until '21 due to the pandemic. After finally jumping stateside in 2023, his breakout came in '24 when he posted a line of .283/.390/.443 over 87 games between Single-A Dunedin and High-A Vancouver. Those numbers took a slight step back in ‘25 between High-A and Double-A, but Arias remains one of the most exciting outfield prospects in a group that’s quickly growing deeper in Toronto. Arias’ upside as a left-handed hitter is a great starting point and he is one of the better young defensive outfielders in the organization. He’ll need to prove his offense can hold up against more advanced pitching at the upper levels, but he drives the ball loudly, thanks to a swing with a ton of intent, and could end up being a bat that produces 15-20 homers per year if it all comes together and he can learn to elevate more on contact. One of the first things you’ll hear from anyone when asked about Arias is that he’s a “bulldog,” playing with incredible intensity and grit. The Blue Jays had been waiting for one of their young outfielders to click, and from that crowded group, Arias will still have every opportunity to rise to the top. He did undergo a procedure on his non-throwing shoulder, so he’ll be late to start this season, but there’s still plenty of time and talent to work with here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed the Venezuela native on his 16th birthday in 2019, but Arias couldn't make his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League until 2021 due to the pandemic. He was a DSL repeater in '22 before finally jumping stateside in '23, but his breakout finally came in '24. Last season, Arias posted a line of .283/.390/.443 over 87 games between Single-A Dunedin and High-A Vancouver. Now just 21, he’s thrust himself onto this list and become one of the Blue Jays’ better development success stories in a hurry. There’s a ton of upside here. Arias posts impressive walk rates as a left-handed hitter and is one of the better young defensive outfielders in the organization, so that’s a fine place to start. He’ll need to prove his offense can hold up against more advanced pitching at the upper levels, but he drives the ball loudly, thanks to a swing with a ton of intent, and could end up being a 15-20 homer bat if it all comes together and he can learn to elevate more on contact. One of the first things you’ll hear from anyone when asked about Arias is that he’s a “bulldog,” playing with incredible intensity and grit. The Blue Jays had been waiting for one of their young outfielders to click, and Arias is now going on two consecutive years of impressive production at full-season levels. Having reached Double-A in his age-21 season, Arias could be an option for the Jays as early as 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tigers fans of a certain age can be forgiven for looking at the lefty Jacobs and his specs and thinking back to former Detroit starter Nate Robertson. Even the arsenals have some similarities. But Jacobs was very much a West Coast pitcher, from his prep days in Huntington Beach to his first college stop at UCLA. After five innings for the Bruins as a freshman, Jacobs transferred to Arizona State and blossomed into the Sun Devils’ Friday night starter. He entered his Draft season with first-round potential but fell to the third, where the Tigers made him part of their search for young pitching and signed him for $722,500. Jacobs doesn’t have a dominant pitch that he leans on so much as he succeeds with a good mix and a feel for hitters, from a 92-94 mph fastball that can touch 96 to a traditional low-80s slider and a changeup with good fade. While his strikeout rates were impressive at ASU, he has to show in the pros that he can get outs in the strike zone and put hitters in situations where they’re apt to chase. He repeats his delivery well, which should bode well for progress in strike throwing. Jacobs has a chance to advance quickly in the system, starting with full-season ball, if he can demonstrate an ability to get outs in the zone. He has the profile of a backend starter if he makes the adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McGraw’s professional journey has been defined by elite stuff tempered by injury setbacks. A Wake Forest product, he was drafted by Seattle in the third round in 2023 despite undergoing his second Tommy John surgery prior to the season. The Mariners have a track record of rehabilitating talented arms, and McGraw’s raw tools made him worth the gamble. Initial hopes of a breakthrough were stalled when he made only four appearances in August 2024 due to lingering elbow issues. He did manage to amass 28 1/3 innings in 2025. When healthy, McGraw’s arsenal is electric. His fastball can reach 97 mph with heavy sink, complemented by a sharp upper-80s slider that projects as a plus swing-and-miss pitch. He also mixes in a fading mid-80s changeup capable of keeping hitters off balance. In 2025, the sinker and slider stood out, showcasing why evaluators see him as one of the organization’s most intriguing pitchers. Command has been a work in progress, though, and his primary focus has been simply staying healthy. Now entering a season fully healthy in 2026, McGraw is transitioning to the bullpen, a move designed to maximize his effectiveness while managing workload. Scouts describe him as in a great spot physically, with velocity sitting in the low-to-mid 90s and his slider continuing to rank among the best in the system. The goal is incremental progression -- shorter, more controlled outings should allow him to rebuild stamina while still letting his stuff play. If McGraw stays healthy and adapts to a reliever’s routine, he has the potential to be a dynamic, high-leverage arm. With his combination of velocity, movement and polished secondary offerings, he’s quietly one of the most exciting pitching prospects in Seattle’s pipeline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There was hope that a full season of McGraw on the mound in 2024 would raise his profile tremendously and vault him up prospect lists such as this. The Mariners had taken the Wake Forest product in the third round of the 2023 Draft even though he had undergone his second Tommy John surgery prior to the start of the season. They liked his electric stuff and have not been afraid to bring injured pitchers into the system and rehab them, but hopes of another successful reclamation project were initially dashed when McGraw made just four appearances in August with more elbow trouble. When McGraw is healthy, which hasn’t happened often, he has a nasty power repertoire, especially his fastball and slider. He can throw his heater up to 97 mph and it features heavy sink. He backs it up with a slider that could be plus, a true out pitch with sharp break and his upper-80s fading changeup can be an excellent pitch as well. He used all three in his brief time on the mound last year, with the sinker and slider really standing out. As exciting as his stuff can be, he’s never fully harnessed all of his pitches at once, struggling with walk rates throughout his time at Wake Forest, though that’s secondary to trying to get him healthy for any length of time. He avoided surgery this time for his elbow and there’s cautious optimism about him getting his career going, this time with a move to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With first-round potential leading into the 2023 season, McGraw’s stock dropped after needing his second Tommy John surgery just prior to his junior campaign at Wake Forest. He underwent the previous one in 2019, which cost him his senior year of high school. Yet a Mariners organization that’s thrived drafting injured arms with upside snagged him in the third round and signed him well-below slot value, at $600,000. For those reasons, McGraw is maybe Seattle’s most intriguing prospect arm entering ‘24 -- along with Cole Phillips, who also hasn’t pitched since 2022. A healthy McGraw operated in the 93-96 mph range on his fastball, which generated more grounders than whiffs due to its sinking action. His upper-80s changeup has the fade and tumble to miss bats. But it’s the slider that’s his best offering -- with plus-plus potential -- and which he consistently lands in the zone. There’s much potential for each of his three pitches, though if there is a knock on McGraw, it’s that he has not harnessed them all at once on a consistent basis, evidenced by walking 5.8 batters per nine innings in his first two seasons at Wake Forest. Those are typically fixable issues, though, which makes him a potentially smart gamble within a pitching-driven organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Georgia high school standout, Johnson began his college career in his home state, with the University of Georgia. But after a freshman year that saw him pick up just 46 at-bats, he transferred to Chipola Junior College and went off. His 1.079 OPS in 2019 garnered plenty of attention, with the Reds able to nab him in the fourth round that June. He played his way from Low- to High-A in 2021, his first true full season, but because he missed a month on the injured list, he got more reps in the Arizona Fall League. Residual hand pain led to eventual hamate surgery this offseason. Johnson is a switch-hitter who can handle the bat from both sides of the plate. The left-handed swing is better, particularly in terms of power, though he did some damage right-handed as well in the AFL as he hit six homers total in 17 games. He can get overly aggressive and needs to refine his overall approach so he can do more damage in hitter’s counts. Johnson has played more shortstop than anticipated, but few think he’ll play there long-term. He’s better suited at second, with the chance he could end up showing enough thump to move to third. The hand surgery slowed him out of the gate a bit, but he was swinging the bat well when some shoulder inflammation landed him back on the injured list in August.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chipola Junior College has built a reputation as one of the best two-year baseball programs in the country, with alumni like Russell Martin and Jose Bautista. Johnson, taken from the Florida school by the Reds in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, hopes to be the first Chipola product to make it to the big leagues since 2012 draftee Andrew Toles. Johnson had a solid, if unspectacular, pro debut in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019, then opened a lot of eyes with strong instructional league play in 2020. A switch-hitting middle infielder, Johnson has the chance to really hit, with excellent bat speed from both sides of the plate. His swing might be a touch better from the left side, and his raw power has shown up more left-handed as well, particularly to his pull side. While he’s not a burner, Johnson uses what speed he does have smartly on the basepaths. Most thought Johnson was destined to be a second baseman as a pro, and that might still be the case as his range might be a bit light. But he’s surprised some with his abilities at short, making some body control plays at instructs that stood out. He’ll get a chance to play his way off of short, with his bat potentially profiling just fine at second, where he’s seen time, or even at third.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Almonte was on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 International Prospects List when the 2020-21 signing period opened in January 2021. He and fellow Dominican outfielder Marvin Valdez headed up the Reds’ class that period, both receiving seven-figure bonuses to join the organization. After Almonte signed for $1.85 million, he had a solid pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, and then followed up by showing off a similar skillset stateside in the Arizona Complex League in 2022. Just 19 years old for all of the 2023 season, Almonte has the chance to fit the corner-outfield profile well, with the kind of loud bat teams like for right field. He has the ability to drive the ball to all fields and should have plenty of power, with that pop already showing up in games, especially to his pull side. While his strikeout rate did balloon to 29.9 percent last year, the Reds feel that was more a case of him getting acclimated to new surroundings and better pitching, and they were still pleased with his willingness to draw walks and overall pitch recognition. Almonte has added a lot of strength to his frame, and while he’s likely to slow down as he continues to fill out, he’s athletic enough to cover ground in right field, where his strong arm plays as well. There’s always likely to be some swing-and-miss to his game, but the plate discipline and pop should offset it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top outfield prospects in the 2020-21 international signing class, Almonte got one of the two seven-figure bonuses the Reds handed out in that signing period, getting $1.85 million right as the period opened on Jan. 15. He went to the Dominican Summer League to get his pro career started and made a solid first impression with an OPS of .836 to go along with 15 steals. Almonte’s bat is what will carry him to the big leagues. He has the potential to hit with power to all fields and some of it is already showing up, mostly to his pull side and right-center field. The Reds were very pleased with his approach and strike zone awareness as he drew a lot of walks and didn’t chase often, even if DSL umpires were expanding the zone. He’s grown a substantial amount since signing, now standing at 6-foot-4 and around 215 pounds. While he’s a fringy runner, Almonte is athletic enough to play a solid right field, with good jumps and reads. His above-average arm works from the corner spot as well. He’s making his United States debut in 2022 as an 18-year old with the upside of being a run-producing corner outfielder, one who could eventually hit in the middle of a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2020-21 international signing period didn’t begin until Jan. 15, 2021 because of the pandemic. The Reds wasted no time once the period began by handing out eight bonuses of six figures or more, two of the seven-figure variety. Almonte, No. 26 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list for the class, got one of them, signing on Jan. 15 for $1.85 million. A left-handed hitter and thrower, Almonte has the makings of an exciting corner outfielder with the offensive profile to match. With an advanced approach at the plate, especially given his age, Almonte has a loose swing that generates good backspin. He can drive the ball to all fields, particularly to left-center, and has shown a knack for making consistent contact and limiting his swing-and-miss. While there’s work to be done in terms of reads and routes from the outfield corners, Almonte has the makings of a plus arm and should be a solid defender in the future. It’s the bat that will carry him up the ladder, with the chance for him to eventually be a run-producer in the middle of a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Conley was initially slated to head to Miami for college, but he decided to transfer to Texas Tech, sitting out the 2019 season as a result of the NCAA’s transfer rules. He made a strong first impression with the Red Raiders with an OPS over 1.000 in the shortened 2020 season, then backed it up by slashing .329/.393/.587 in 2021, enough to land him in the fourth round of that summer’s Draft. After a very slow start with Single-A Augusta to kick off his first full season of pro ball in 2022, Conley played his way to High-A and performed well in the Arizona Fall League. The son of former Minor Leaguer Brian Conley, Cal is the kind of player who is better than the sum of his parts. A switch-hitter, Conley has displayed a knack for contact, particularly from the left side of the plate. While the undersized infielder is a hit-over-power, gap-to-gap, use-all-fields type, there’s more extra-base pop than you might think, with the 16 homers he hit in 2022 not an aberration at all. While he’s not a burner, Conley does have solid speed and he maximizes it with excellent instincts and aggressiveness on the basepaths, not to mention a “gamer” mentality that has his engine going full throttle at all times. Those instincts help him play a capable shortstop, the spot he’s seen the most time at thus far, but some see a move to second base in his future, where he might have the best chance at being a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Brian Conley was a Minor League player for the Cubs and Reds in the 1990s and went on to coach in the Cincinnati organization. His son Cal starred at Texas Tech after transferring from Miami, and an uptick in power (15 homers) in 2021 helped land the steady middle infielder in the fourth round of last summer’s Draft, signing for $422,500 and making his pro debut with Low-A Augusta. Conley is a switch-hitter who has very good bat-to-ball skills, though the contact rate is better from the left side and right side features a bit more swing-and-miss. He is hit-over-power, though his added strength did translate into more pop in his last year at Texas Tech and he showed that it translates with a wood bat in his hands during his first full season with the Braves. With above-average speed and very good instincts, Conley is capable of playing a solid shortstop, though his arm might be a bit short for him to be an everyday player at the premium spot. He’s mostly played short as a pro, though he’s gotten times on the right side of second base, and second is the more likely spot where he could develop into a big league regular, with a more likely outcome of being a heady utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz wasn't drafted in 2017 after his senior year at George Washington High School in New York, but the Phillies took a flier on him and his raw power after seeing him playing for the New York Nine Scout Team that summer. Things started to click in 2022 when he got to Double-A and mashed 17 homers before hitting well in the Arizona Fall League. A full season spent with Reading in 2023 yielded 24 more long balls, but he was left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft this past offseason and went unselected. At 6-foot-8, there's no question about De La Cruz's raw power, and he started to learn how to make adjustments to better pitching in Double-A to get to it more. While there's always going to be swing-and-miss to his game, he actually cut his strikeout rate in 2023 and upped his walk rate, controlling the zone better and not chasing as much as the idea that more consistent contact will lead to more home runs sunk in. De La Cruz runs well, especially once underway, and has shown he can handle all three outfield spots. He saw more time in center field with Reading after Johan Rojas got called up and looked fine up the middle. He'll keep getting reps across the outfield and at first base to give the Phillies more options should they deem his power bat ready for Philadelphia.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It may seem impossible for a 6-foot-8 player to fly completely off the radar, but that’s exactly what happened with De La Cruz. A product of George Washington High School in New York, the alma mater of Manny Ramirez, De La Cruz went undrafted in 2017. The Phillies noticed when he put up gaudy numbers that summer for the New York Nine Scout Team and took a flier, signing him as an undrafted free agent. He was nothing more than a feel-good story until 2022, when he played his way to Double-A, hitting 17 homers in the process, then performed well in the Arizona Fall League. Especially given his size, De La Cruz has a solid feel to hit with a clean swing from the right side of the plate. There is work he needs to do in terms of his overall approach, with better pitch selection and discipline allowing him to tap into his considerable raw power, which could be plus with those adjustments. While he’s an average runner, he’s better once he gets underway. De La Cruz is a better overall athlete than you might imagine given his size, and he does post good sprint speed numbers once he gets going. That allows him to track balls well underway in the outfield, and he’s shown he can handle all three spots out there, playing a better-than-expected center field, while also providing a very big target at first base when needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estrada was a sleeper $175,000 signing out of Venezuela as part of the Orioles’ 2022 international haul, but he’s grown into one of the most exciting prospects from that class by performing at every level he’s been challenged at so far. Estrada put himself on the map with a big debut in the Dominican Summer League, climbed to High-A as a teenager and took another step forward in 2025, reaching Double-A as a 20-year-old and hitting .300/.355/.500 in his first 27 games at the level. Opposing clubs have frequently targeted Estrada in trade talks in recent years, and that shouldn’t change after he produced an .813 OPS and 34 steals across two levels last season. Estrada does a lot of little things well without wowing with any one individual tool. He’s an undersized but athletic switch-hitting infielder who knows what he's doing in the box, managing the strike zone well from both sides of the plate and making a ton of contact. There is a little pop in there from the left side, as he’s strong enough to opportunistically turn on mistakes, but it’s a hit-over-power profile. He’s a strong runner who is getting smarter on the basepaths, having improved his stolen base percentage significantly last season. Estrada played five defensive positions last year and has played everywhere except first base and catcher since turning pro. He’s best suited for second base long-term, but that versatility enhances his value, and his arm is solid enough to handle any position in a pinch.
