He’s a hard-nosed player with a blend of skills who could develop into a bat-first utility-type who can help a big league team in a variety of ways.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estrada was sort of under the radar when he signed with the Orioles for $175,000 as part of their 2022 international class, but he quickly made a name for himself with a big debut in the Dominican Summer League, ranking among the leaders in hitting (.368), on-base percentage (.483) and OPS (1.049). He wasn’t as dynamic in the Florida Complex League the following year, but looked more like the DSL version of himself during his full-season debut in 2024 as he slashed .286/.356/.416 with nine homers and 39 steals and earned a promotion to High-A Aberdeen at age 19. The quasi-breakout raised Estrada’s stock so that he became a frequent target in trades talks the Orioles had with other clubs. Though he’s undersized and lacks any big tools, there’s a lot to like about what Estrada brings to the table. He’s a switch-hitting infielder who makes a lot of contact and manages the zone well from both sides of the plate. He isn’t a slugger, but there is probably enough raw pop in there -- more from the left side -- for him to get to double-digit homers per year. He’s a strong, aggressive runner, which enhances what is a high-floor hit-over-power profile. Primarily a middle infielder, Estrada is athletic enough to move around and has already played six positions in his brief career. His average arm is good enough to not hurt him anywhere. Overall, he’s probably best suited long-term for second base, where he has a potential ceiling of an everyday player. If that doesn’t quite materialize, his blend of skills projects a helpful utility type who can do a little bit of everything.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Blanco didn’t attract much attention when he was just a 5-foot-6, switch-hitting shortstop hailing from Caracas, Venezuela’s capital city. But Rays scouts were nonetheless impressed every time they saw him even then, believing at times he was the best player on every field he took, even when he was physically outmatched by his peers. They offered him a $1 million bonus when others weren’t as interested, then saw him shoot up to 5-foot-11 and become a Top 50 prospect in the 2026 international class before they signed him. Now with much more physicality than he possessed before his growth spurt, Blanco is viewed as a complete player with tremendous makeup. He has above-average bat speed and contact skills thanks to his quick hands, and he could develop above-average power from both sides of the plate. Pitch selection will be an issue, and he’ll need to gain more experience as a right-handed hitter as he enters professional baseball. He’s a solid runner and not afraid to be aggressive on the basepaths, but he wasn’t a huge stolen-base threat as an amateur. Blanco has a strong arm and quick feet, so he should be able to stick at shortstop. He’ll have to compete for reps there with top international prospect Victor Valdez, among others, but he is highly regarded for the way he handles himself at a premium defensive position. If he continues to improve like he did before signing, he’ll become a prospect to watch no matter his size.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vukovich averaged 27.8 points and 13.1 rebounds per game as a senior and was a finalist for Wisconsin’s Mr. Basketball Award, but he was headed to Louisville to play baseball. The D-backs changed that route by signing him for $1.25 million as a 2020 fourth-rounder, and the Badger State native has meticulously climbed the ladder since, most recently completing a full season at Double-A Amarillo in '23. Vukovich slashed .263/.333/.485 with 24 homers and 20 steals over 115 games, making him one of Arizona’s two 20-20 Minor Leaguers last season alongside Jordan Lawlar. Vukovich rounded off ’23 with 20 more games in the Arizona Fall League, where he posted just a .663 OPS. The right-handed slugger has shown at least above-average raw power throughout his career, but it’s becoming a bigger question of how it will play in games. Of Vukovich’s 24 homers in 2023, 18 of them came in Amarillo’s hitter-friendly confines, and he slugged just .362 away from HODGETOWN, in part because he ran a 48.9 percent ground-ball rate. Getting more consistent elevation will be an issue as he heads into his 40-man roster decision season. On the positive side, Vukovich did a better job of easing his aggression in the box and posted a career-high 9.1 percent walk rate by spitting on his fair share of breaking stuff outside the zone. His troubles with high velo might dull the offensive ceiling, but at least the approach is trending upward. An average runner, Vukovich moved from third base to the outfield on a more full-time basis in ’23 and didn’t touch the dirt at all defensively in the AFL. The extra room to roam is a better fit for his athleticism, but he’s still likely limited to a corner with arm strength that can play in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vukovich was just as notable for playing hoops in high school when he was a finalist for Wisconsin’s Mr. Basketball award after averaging 27.8 points and 13.1 rebounds per game. Originally recruited to Louisville for baseball, he instead went in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft to the D-backs, who gave him a $1.25 million bonus – almost $800,000 above slot. After splitting 2021 at two A-ball levels, Vukovich hit .274/.308/.450 and tied for fifth in the Northwest League with 15 homers in 106 games for High-A Hillsboro last year. He spent 11 games with Double-A Amarillo late in the season. The right-handed slugger has at least plus raw power from the right side emanating from his 6-foot-5 frame, and he has enough loft in his swing to tap into it, even on a pitcher-friendly circuit like the Northwest League. What may keep Vukovich from putting up more eye-popping stat lines, however, is his aggression at the plate. He may cover the strike zone well enough when he swings, but he severely lacks patience. His 4 percent walk rate and 0.17 BB/K ratio were second-lowest among 137 High-A qualifiers. The Badger State native still has the athleticism he showed on the court in his basketball days, and that should serve him well as he continues getting looks in the outfield, where he made 32 starts in 2022. He's become more of a full-time outfielder in 2023, in part as he's bumped up against Deyvison De Los Santos and Ivan Melendez, and his athleticism might be a better fit out there anyways. His bat should certainly play in a corner outfield spot moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A finalist for Wisconsin's Mr. Basketball award, Vukovich was a two-sport athlete in high school who averaged 27.8 points and 13.1 rebounds per game. On the diamond, the D-backs liked his power and selected him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft, going well over slot with a $1.25 million bonus to sign him away from a commitment to Louisville. He made his professional debut with Low-A Visalia and got off to a slow start, but started to hit as the summer wore on and worked his way up to High-A Hillsboro in August. He finished his first full season with a .272/.320/.446 slash line and 13 homers over 92 games. Vukovich has long levers and a lot of projectable strength in his 6-foot-5 frame, which combines with the bat speed and loft in his right-handed stroke to produce the well-above-average raw power. He opened eyes in 2020, showing not only his power, but also a hit tool that was better than expected. Vukovich has a chance to develop into an impact bat at the highest level, but needs to refine his approach a bit and eliminate some of the swing-and-miss as he continues to climb the ladder. Drafted as an outfielder, the D-backs moved Vukovich to third base and it was a rough go initially. However, he’s made noticeably big gains over the past two years and it appears the game is starting to slow down for him. He’s shown enough growth that club officials believe he’ll be able to stick long term at the hot corner, where both his bat and strong arm profile well. If necessary, he has the tools and athleticism needed to play a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A finalist for Wisconsin's Mr. Basketball award, Vukovich was a two-sport athlete in high school. He averaged 27.8 points and 13.1 rebounds per game. On the diamond, the D-backs liked his power and selected him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft and went well over slot at $1.25 million to sign him away from a commitment to Louisville. He made his professional debut with Low-A Visalia and got off to a slow start, but started to hit as the summer wore on and worked his way up to High-A Hillsboro in August. Vukovich has long levers and a lot of projectable strength in his 6-foot-5 frame, which combine with the bat speed and loft in his right-handed stroke to produce the well above-average raw power that was on display as he slugged 10 homers over 62 games with Visalia before his promotion. Vukovich opened some eyes during Instructional League in 2020, flashing the big-time power, but also showing an excellent hit tool. The D-backs stuck him at third base for the first time and it was a rough go initially, but he made huge strides this season and is continually improving at the hot corner. It’s starting to look as if he can stick there long term, and both his bat and strong arm would profile well. If necessary, he has the tools and athleticism needed to play a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of an NFL lineman, Bateman had the size (he’s 6-foot-8) and skills (he throws left-handed) to get noticed coming out of the Southern California prep scene even if he didn’t have the ability. But he does. The Padres selected him in the second round of the 2024 Draft and signed him to an over-slot $2.5 million bonus. Bateman was working through a nice full-season debut in the Single-A California League when he was sent as part of the huge package of prospects to the Orioles in exchange for Ryan O’Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the 2025 Trade Deadline, and he finished the year at High-A Aberdeen. Bateman’s stuff befits the enormous high-makeup package it comes in. His fastball can live in the low-to-mid-90s and touched 98 mph during his debut, part of a four-pitch mix that features a pair of breaking balls. The best is a slider that flashes plus. While he needs more reps throwing his 1-to-7 curve and developing changeup, he is seen as having the aptitude to tackle his developmental needs and potentially add pitches to that mix with time. Bateman did a decent job throwing strikes before his walks spiked at Aberdeen at the very end of the year, though that can probably be attributed to fatigue more than anything. He still has work to do overall to get to average control, though if he gets there, he'll look like a mid-rotation starter given his ability and pitch mix. The heater and breaking ball alone give him a floor of a big dominant left-hander out of the ‘pen, which wouldn’t be a bad outcome either.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Of course, Bateman was going to make for a close follow everywhere he went as an amateur. For starters, he’s 6-foot-8. Secondly, he’s a left-handed pitcher. But he proved to have more than just those two attributes with quality appearances in the PDP League and Area Code Games heading into his senior year at Adolfo Camarillo (Calif.) High School -- the alma mater of 2003 No. 1 pick Delmon Young. Bateman joined the Padres as a second-round pick and signed for $2.5 million, roughly the slot of a selection 15 picks higher. He was more than holding his own during his full-season debut in the Single-A California League when he was sent as part of the huge package of prospects to the Orioles in return for Ryan O’Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the Trade Deadline. Scouts dreamed on Bateman’s size and praised his makeup as part of the evaluation process, but the stuff was plenty good too, and it’s shown up so far as a pro. He touched 97 mph with his fastball and generally sat 91-93 during summer showcases and has again been up to 97 mph during his debut season. He throws from a high three-quarter slot and has both a slider and more of a 1-to-7 curve, though he doesn’t really throw the latter breaking ball. He continues to work on developing his changeup, a pitch he didn’t need much in high school. Bateman improved his strike-throwing heading into the Draft, and while his history with walks isn’t perfect, his trendlines should get him to average control with advanced instruction, and he did a solid job of finding the zone in 2025. He’ll only be 19 for the duration of the 2025 Minor League season, and the upside is significant, especially if he carries his impressive work ethic into the pros. There’s always the fallback of being a big, dominant lefty out of the bullpen with that heater and breaking ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Izzi was teammates with White Sox left-hander Noah Schultz at Oswego East HS in Illinois before the big lefty was taken in the first round and the right-hander was selected by the Mariners in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft. A $1.1 million bonus was enough to get Izzi to sign away from his Wichita State commitment. After making only nine Arizona Complex League starts in 2023, he emerged more on the scene with a 2.85 ERA and 95 strikeouts in 110 2/3 innings with Single-A Modesto a year later. Izzi opened 2025 with an oblique injury and was slowly building back into his own with High-A Everett when the D-backs acquired him at the Deadline in a move for Josh Naylor. Standing 6-foot-3, Izzi gets good extension down the mound and shows average four-seam velocity around 94 mph, touching 97. He’ll also mix in a sinker for another fastball look, but he doesn’t miss many bats with his heater. He throws two forms of a breaking ball in a mid-80s gyro slider and low-80s sweeper, and he’ll go to the vertical break of the former against batters from both sides. That’s useful because his changeup still needs more consistency to become an MLB weapon. Izzi works exclusively out of the stretch and positions himself on the first-base side of the rubber. There aren’t too many moving pieces in his delivery, and as he got built up just before and after the trade, his control really took off down the stretch in the Northwest League with a 4.9 percent walk rate in his final eight starts. He should head to the upper Minors for the first time in his age-22 season aiming to develop a plus pitch that could turn him into a back-end Major League starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Oswego East High School in Illinois may not seem like a factory for high-end arms, but it was in 2022. That’s where Noah Schultz -- now the top left-handed pitching prospect in the game after the White Sox took him in the first round of that Draft -- and Izzi were teammates. Izzi showed enough for the Mariners to take him in the fourth round, going over slot with $1.1 million to sign him away from his Wichita State commitment. It was a slow rollout for the right-hander, not pitching after signing and throwing just 18 1/3 innings in the Arizona Complex League in 2023. But the gloves came off in 2024 and Izzi threw well, topping 100 IP for full-season Modesto. After opening 2025 with an oblique injury, he came into his own by midsummer and was then dealt to the Diamondbacks as part of the Deadline deal for Josh Naylor. Izzi is pitching at age 21 for the 2025 season, and the 6-foot-3 right-hander built a pretty good foundation to work from. His fastball typically sits at least 94 mph and can touch as high as 97 at times, and he does a very good job of separating his four-seamer up in the zone and his sinking two-seamer down. His low-80s sweeper has the chance to be a solid pitch that misses bats. He didn’t have a great feel for his changeup with Modesto. Whether that necessitates a move to the bullpen remains to be seen, although there is some thought that because of his excellent separation between his two fastballs, he might be able to stay in a rotation without a changeup. His splits were near-even before the trade, and his control had shown steady improvement, aiding the belief that he should still get rotation looks with Arizona.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Izzi wowed ahead of the 2022 Draft when area scouts attended one of his high school outings to see a teammate, which prompted the club to do more homework and eventually select the highly projectable righty in the fourth round for over-slot value at $1.1 million, enough to sign him away from his Wichita State commitment. It’s more upside than floor with the youngster, who didn’t throw competitively the rest of the year after being drafted -- a by-design, health-related effort with the rest of Seattle’s high school pitching selections. He was among the many invited to the club’s high-performance camp, with the goal of putting on more weight and strength. Beyond conditioning, it’s about throwing more strikes and being consistent, because he can already reach 97 mph with his four-seamer, while sitting in the low-90s with modest life. The heater gives him a far higher ceiling than most his age. His low-80s slider also has good depth and is a pitch he can build upon, though his higher arm slot might be more conducive to a curveball instead. The path to starting long term will require polishing those two pitches, but more so fortifying the changeup, which is still a bit off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from a Hagerty HS program in Florida that has produced big leaguers like Zach Eflin and Riley Greene, Baumann got an over-slot bonus of close to $750,000 in the fourth round to sign him away from his commitment to Central Florida in 2023. He's moved basically a rung at a time, posting solid numbers with Single-A Augusta in 2024 and then with High-A Rome last year, showing a combination of arm strength, strike-throwing and durability. At 6-foot-8, Baumann and fellow prospect Luke Sinnard could form a solid frontcourt. Still just 21 for nearly all of the 2026 season, Baumann really stands out with his fastball velocity and ability to command the heater. His velo ticked up in 2025, averaging 96.5 mph and flirting with triple digits. In college, he was very sinker heavy, and he uses his 2-seamer to get ground-ball outs, but he's gained more and more control over his 4-seamer up in the zone with some carry. The rest of Baumann's stuff is still a work in progress, though the splitter he uses as his change of pace has become a solid offering, thrown in the upper 80s. He's still figuring out his breaking ball, with a low-to-mid-80s sweepy slider getting too slurvy at times. He'll need to find a second pitch that can miss bats to accompany his heater to give him a chance to be a workhorse-like starter long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2023, the Braves kicked off their Draft with three straight college arms in the first 70 picks overall. They dipped into the prep pitcher market for the first time in Round 4 when they took Baumann out of Florida power Hagerty High School and going over slot to sign him away from Central Florida. He had a very successful first full season in pro ball, finishing with just under 100 innings pitched and touching High-A while spending most of the year at age 19. Baumann is a surprising strike-thrower given his enormous 6-foot-8 frame, with all of his stuff trending in the right direction. He landed his fastball, which averaged around 94 mph for the 2024 season and touched 98, for a strike 72 percent of the time and he did that while working on improving his fastball shape. Baumann entered pro ball relying on a sinker and early in 2024, he would sink the heater at times and have it have carry others, without rhyme or reason. By the end of the year, he has more control over the pitch's action, and in that last start with High-A Rome, he averaged 95.8 mph with the pitch. Both his fading changeup and sometimes slurvy slider took steps forward as well. The one knock about Baumann had been his inability to miss bats. But while he does lack a true out pitch, he did register a 30-percent strikeout rate from July 1 on, a harbinger of good things to come. The Braves are willing to bet on someone with his strike-throwing capabilities and think he's perhaps just starting to unlock his considerable potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hagerty High School in Florida has produced a fair amount of big leaguers over the past dozen years, from Zach Eflin on the mound to Ryan Mountcastle, Vaughn Grissom and Riley Greene at the plate. Baumann hopes to follow Eflin's path after putting his name on the map at MLB's PDP League and Perfect Game's All-American Classic on the summer showcase circuit, then performing well as his senior season wore on, landing him in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft, where the Braves gave him an over-slot deal of close to $750,000 to sign him away from Central Florida. The 6-foot-8 Baumann made just one appearance with full-season Augusta after signing, so the Braves will really get a sense of what they have on their hands in 2024. With his huge frame, it's easy to dream on more velocity as he tended to sit around 93 mph with his sinking fastball, though he could reach back for 96-97 mph at times. He has a changeup that flashes at least above-average, a mid-80s offspeed offering with fade that he sells well. He's worked to improve his slurvy breaking ball, a slider that has lacked out pitch bit at times, but there is some feel to spin he can work with if he can continue to firm it up. Not surprisingly for someone his size, Baumann's arm action can get long and he'll need to work hard to keep his delivery in sync so he can find the strike zone consistently. If he can do that, he has the ingredients to be a starter long-term, but it's going to take some time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Padres for $125,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019, Baez had to wait two years just to make his Dominican Summer League debut due to the pandemic. His full-season debut in the Minors didn’t come until 2023, when he posted a 3.84 ERA with 99 strikeouts across 98 1/3 innings between Single-A Lake Elsinore and High-A Fort Wayne. Last season, he joined the A’s organization as part of the return for Mason Miller and JP Sears at the Trade Deadline. Baez had a 1.96 ERA in 20 starts for Double-A San Antonio and was leading the Texas League in ERA, WHIP (1.00) and batting average against (.195) at the time he was traded, but after making three starts with Double-A Midland, he sustained a forearm injury that cut his season short. Baez made a full recovery this offseason and joined the A’s for big league Spring Training. Baez has increased his velocity over the years, running his fastball up to 99 mph last season and sitting around 94 for most of the year. The heater also carries good sinking action, leading to his high ground-ball rates. What was once a curveball has evolved into more of a slider that generates a decent amount of swing-and-miss. His upper-80s changeup provides good separation from his fastball, though it’s clearly less effective than the slider. He’s tinkered with a cutter that remains a distant fourth pitch at this point. Baez’s control has remained encouraging as the innings build up for him. That quality will likely keep him in a starting role for the time being, though the A’s might be intrigued to see what he looks like as a reliever at the Major League level with his arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baez signed with the Padres for $125,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019 but couldn’t debut in the Dominican Summer League until two years later due to the pandemic. He didn’t make a full-season debut until 2023 when he split the season between Single-A Lake Elsinore and High-A Fort Wayne, finishing with solid numbers (3.84 ERA, 99 strikeouts in 98 1/3 innings). He wasn’t added to the 40-man roster that offseason when Rule 5-eligible, however, because of his distance from the Majors. Baez enjoyed his big breakout last year, winning Padres Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors after posting a 2.99 ERA and a 1.09 WHIP with 109 strikeouts in 26 1/3 innings between Fort Wayne and Double-A San Antonio, and San Diego added him to the 40-man in November. His success continued with San Antonio in 2025 and he was leading the Texas League in ERA, WHIP and batting average against when he was included in the prospect package sent to the A’s in return for Mason Miller and JP Sears at the Trade Deadline. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has gained velocity steadily in his years as a pro and has touched as high as 99 mph this season. He typically sits around 94 mph, working north-south with the pitch while getting most of his whiffs up and to the armside. He played off that with a 76-79 mph curveball that could have more slurvish tendencies, but at its best, it snapped downward to fool batters sitting on the high heat and it had produced a 47 percent miss rate at the time of the trade. He also utilizes an 83-86 mph split-change to miss bats, but it stands out more for its separation than movement profile. Baez took a major jump in workload but didn’t let his control improvements suffer. That certainly helps his starting chances, as does his 50.1 percent ground-ball rate from 2024. He’s still only 22, but with his place on the roster now set, the A’s (never afraid to move guys quickly) could try to see what it looks like in the big leagues in a relief role to ease him in.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clarke had Tommy John surgery as a high school junior in Virginia and later developed thoracic issues before he could pitch for Alabama. He didn’t truly blossom in college until his second year at State College of Florida (Manatee-Sarasota), and he was considered the best JUCO prospect in the 2024 Draft after striking out 107 in 74 1/3 innings and showing out at the MLB Draft Combine. The Red Sox took him in the fifth round, signed him for below slot at $400,000 and saw him post a 4.03 ERA with 60 strikeouts and 27 walks in 38 innings at Single-A and High-A in a first full season that was limited by blister issues. Clarke was traded to the Cardinals in the offseason as part of the Sonny Gray deal. The 6-foot-4 southpaw has absolutely electric arm speed and elite extension that make him tantalizing as a prospect. He sits 95-98 mph with a pair of fastballs -- his four-seamer acts more like a cut-ride option and the sinker runs armside from his low three-quarters delivery. His slider has become one of the Minors’ best breakers -- an upper-80s offering with tight spin that he can land on both edges of the plate; batters missed on 63 percent of their swings against it last year. With two plus pitches, Clarke didn’t find a need for his upper-70s curveball or upper-80s changeup because he struggled to command both. Clarke certainly brings athleticism, as the extension shows, but he lacks polish with his control. The blister issues could have played a part in 2025, but that underlines another issue: his injury history. He underwent offseason surgery on his left shoulder to address a blood-flow issue that may have caused the blisters in the first place. Clarke could absolutely be a high-leverage reliever given the stuff but should get looks as a starter in St. Louis’ rebuild.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clarke bounced back from Tommy John surgery as a junior to become Virginia's best prep pitching prospect in 2021. He developed thoracic issues while coming back from his elbow reconstruction, so he redshirted at Alabama in 2022 and worked just 3 2/3 innings the following year at the State JC of Florida (Manatee-Sarasota). He became the best junior college prospect in the 2024 Draft, leading Florida juco pitchers with 107 strikeouts in 74 1/3 frames last spring and impressing at the MLB Draft Combine before signing with the Red Sox for a below-slot $400,000 as a fifth-rounder. After his first full season (in which he was limited to 38 innings by issues with blisters), he was traded to the Cardinals in November in a deal for Sonny Gray. Clarke throws harder than most lefty starters, sitting at 95-98 mph and reaching 100, though his fastball features more downhill plane than riding or running action. He has unveiled a devastating slider this season, with the pitch operating in the upper 80s and touching 91 mph with huge sweep as well as depth. He has relieved heavily on his heater and slide piece, rarely using an upper-70s curveball and an upper-80s changeup with some mild fade, both of which he struggles to land for strikes. Still very much a work in progress, Clarke stands out more with his athleticism and quick arm than his polish. He gets down the mound well, creating a low release height with plenty of extension, but he lacks a smooth delivery and currently doesn't repeat it easily enough to have more than fringy control. He comes with a high ceiling and a good deal of reliever risk, making him an intriguing development project in his second organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the top pure high school hitter in the 2022 Draft class, Johnson was ranked No. 4 on MLB Pipeline’s Draft Top 250 Prospects list and selected No. 4 overall by the Pirates. He hasn’t really lived up to the billing of being such a gifted hitter in many respects, with a career .250 average and a .779 OPS. At the same time, he spent all of 2025 at Double-A. He turned 21 in June and finished in the top 10 in batting average and on-base percentage in the Eastern League, with a 118 wRC+ to show for it. While Johnson’s impact was limited in 2025 -- he posted a .382 slugging percentage -- there were many underlying factors that point to him actually heading in the right direction. He’s always had plus strike zone knowledge with a career 16.4 percent walk rate, and last year, his strikeout rate came way down to below 19 percent. He still routinely hits the ball hard as one of the younger players at his level and it was encouraging that he wasn’t trying to sell out for power as much as he used to, understanding that Altoona’s home park is not friendly for left-handed hitters. For the first time, Johnson played second base exclusively in 2025 and that will be his long-time home. He still has work to do on things like turning double plays, but his overall defensive work improved last year. Perhaps the biggest encouraging sign this offseason is that Johnson bought more into the need for things like a nutrition routine and a physical plan, getting his body conditioned better than it has been since he joined the Pirates organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 4 pick in the 2022 Draft, and billed as one of the best pure high school hitters in recent memory, Johnson has gotten off to very slow starts in each of his first two full seasons. But in both years, he gained momentum down the stretch and earned a promotion up a level. So while a career .239 average heading into 2025 isn’t exactly what people projected, he did make it to Double-A at age 20 in his second full season before going on to the Arizona Fall League and Team USA in the Premier12 Tournament. Small, compact and strong, Johnson is a left-handed hitter with elite pitch recognition skills. His 186 combined walks in 2023 and 2024 are second among all Minor Leaguers and while he swung and missed more than expected out of the gate, he’s largely kept the strikeouts in check. Johnson has impressive bat speed and the chance to get to even more power, but he needs to trust his all-fields approach more. He’ll get too big at times with his leg kick and hand movement, trying to put the ball 20 rows deep to his pull side. At his best, he can send line drives to the left side. The more he can trust that his power will come naturally, the better all-around hitter he can become. While the consensus continues to be that Johnson is best suited for second base long-term, he’ll continue to get reps at shortstop to challenge him and keep him athletic. The Pirates are still bullish on his offensive upside given his age and those underlying traits, with the hope that more reps at the upper levels will help unlock all of that potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2022 Draft approached, Johnson emerged as not only one of the best pure hitters in the class, but was perceived to be one of the best high school hitters in recent memory. After hitting well on the summer showcase tour and continuing to impress during his senior season in Georgia, his name was mentioned as a possible No. 1 pick before he landed at No. 4 with the Pirates. Slowed out of the gate by a hamstring injury to kick off his first full season, Johnson struggled at first, but found his footing to homer 18 times, draw over 100 walks and earn a late bump up to High-A Greensboro. Known for his incredible hand-eye coordination, swing decisions and contact rates entering pro ball, it was concerning that Johnson was striking out at a high rate to kick off his 2023 campaign. But after he shook off the rust from the missed time early, his K rate plummeted, from a 35.2 percent rate through the end of May to 23.2 percent for the remainder of the season. He has big-time power potential with plus bat speed and consistently worked deep counts, which can lend itself to some strikeouts. A shortstop as an amateur, Johnson has settled in professionally at second base and should be just fine at the keystone with decent range, hands and enough arm. His bat will carry him to the big leagues and there’s excitement about what he can do, assuming health, to live up to his Draft billing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the past, high school players who profiled as second basemen weren't thought of as premium Draft prospects. But Johnson was very much the exception to that rule as he emerged as one of the best pure prep hitters scouts had seen in years. He teed off against good competition throughout the summer showcase circuit and kept impressing in his senior season, landing him in the conversation for the Draft's No. 1 pick before being taken No. 4 overall by the Pirates and given a slightly over-slot bonus of $7.2 million to sign. The left-handed hitter combines elite hand-eye coordination and swing decisions to help him post otherworldly contact rates. He turns around premium velocity and good breaking stuff alike with fast hands and a compact stroke. He can drive the ball to all fields, and despite his listed 5-foot-10 frame, he routinely barrels up the baseball and uses bat speed and strength to generate the kind of power that could lead to 25-plus homers annually. While Johnson was a shortstop in high school and got a little time there during his brief pro debut in 2022, he’s going to be a second baseman moving forward. His average arm and speed fit there better, although he leaned out his frame and worked with a speed and agility coach this offseason to improve his range. He does have good hands and footwork and should be a very capable defender at the keystone. But it’s his bat that could help him get to the big leagues faster than the typical high school player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rijo is an international prospect who quickly drew attention for his advanced offensive profile, who ranked No. 12 in the 2026 international class. He signed with the Mariners for $2.2 million at the start of the 2026 signing period, highlighting Seattle’s confidence in his upside. Listed at 6-foot-1, Rijo has added solid weight and tapped more into his raw power, giving evaluators a vibe similar to JoJo Parker (MLB No. 43), the No. 8 overall pick by Toronto in the ‘25 Draft. A left-handed hitter, Rijo has an advanced understanding of the strike zone and lets the ball travel, helping him spray hits to all fields. He has excelled at every stop in his amateur career, including strong showings in high-profile tournaments in the Dominican Republic, and his polished swing is built for loft and consistent contact. These traits, combined with his growing power, make the bat the clear carrying tool for his development. Defensively, Rijo is likely to settle into a corner outfield spot, though he still brings above-average instincts, decent range and a solid arm that keep him versatile. Seattle sees him as a player whose offensive ceiling outweighs defensive limitations, a prospect capable of impacting games consistently once he acclimates to professional pitching. With a combination of feel for the game, emerging power and a strong amateur track record, Rijo is one of the most intriguing signees in the Mariners’ 2026 international class.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 5-foot-8 Areinamo was not necessarily a big-time prospect, having signed with the Brewers for just $150,000 out of Venezuela in January 2021, but he quickly turned out to be a solid player for Milwaukee. The first hint that he might be more came in 2022, when he was an Arizona Complex League All-Star, and it became more apparent when he hit .306 in 103 games for Single-A Carolina in his age-19 season in ’23. He kept hitting for High-A Wisconsin in ’24, leading the Midwest League with a .301 average and 30 doubles in 110 games. He was sent back to Wisconsin for 94 games last year, but the Rays pushed him to Double-A after acquiring him for catcher Danny Jansen in July. Areinamo’s numbers weren’t great down the stretch, but he generated a fair amount of excitement within Tampa Bay’s organization with a skill-set full of mostly average tools that tend to play up whenever he’s on the field. And he created some more hype with an otherworldly winter ball performance in his native Venezuela, batting .364 with 13 homers in only 36 games. He initially gained some notoriety for having one of the more bizarre hitting setups in the Minors, as he took the bat off his shoulder during the pitcher’s delivery and whipped it around like a lasso. He has tightened that up a bit, creating the same circles with his hands but keeping it closer to his body, to improve his timing. He’s consistently made contact to all fields from the right side of the plate, with just a 12.2 percent strikeout rate in the Minors, and there’s enough power in his bat for 30 doubles and 10-15 homers. But he will expand his zone quite a bit, and he’s dependent upon his average to drive his profile because he doesn’t walk much. Areinamo doesn’t have blazing speed, but he stole 32 bases in 2024 and 21 in ’25. His most likely future is as a utility infielder, because Milwaukee moved him around the dirt a lot and Tampa Bay tends to love that profile. His best fit is second base, although he has enough arm to occasionally handle third and enough range to back up at shortstop. His standout tool defensively is his hands, arguably the quickest in the Rays system, which helps with his transfers and double-play turns at second. The Rays put him on their 40-man roster in November, so he could arrive in the Majors sooner than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed Areinamo for $150,000 out of Venezuela in January 2021, and he was a dependable producer over his five years in the system. He burst onto the radar as an Arizona Complex League All-Star in 2022 and even saw time at Single-A Carolina and High-A Wisconsin that same summer. He hit .306 with four homers in 103 games back in the Carolina League a year later and jumped to the Midwest League for 2024, when he was the circuit’s leader in average (.301) and doubles (30) over 110 games. Areinamo was back with Wisconsin for 94 games in 2025 when he was traded to the Rays in late July for Major League catcher Danny Jansen. The right-handed hitter has one of the most interesting hitting setups in baseball, taking the bat off his shoulder as the pitcher delivers and whipping it forward in the air almost like a lasso. It’s worked for him so far with solid contact rates, but his eagerness to expand the zone brings concern to his hitting profile. Some see a batter who can still spray the ball around the diamond. Others worry the chasing will catch up to Areinamo at the upper levels. He needs a solid average to bring value because he isn’t likely to get on base through walks, and his limited power lowers the ceiling more. The 5-foot-8 infielder is a fringy runner but doubled his career high in steals to 32 in 2024. He’s moved around the dirt plenty early in his career, in part because Milwaukee was so loaded with great defensive shortstops in the lower levels, but he’s proven to be a strong fit at second base with good reactions and lateral movement but just an average arm. Even with that glovework, Areinamo might be headed toward being a utility player in the Majors if he can’t hone in more on the zone as a hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $150,000 signing out of Venezuela in January 2021, Areinamo carved out a prominent role in the Brewers organization in 2022 when he was named an Arizona Complex League All-Star after hitting .323/.416/.472 with as many walks as strikeouts (19) in 34 games. Milwaukee gave him looks at Single-A Carolina and High-A Wisconsin that summer, but he remained at the former for the duration of his 2023 season, finishing with a .306/.333/.407 line, four homers and 16 steals in 103 games. Picture Gary Sheffield’s pre-swing bat movement. Now abbreviate it to one wiggle and make that one more pronounced, and you have Areinamo. It can look like he’s casting a spell by using his bat as a wand at times. That activity helps the right-handed hitter get his quick hands moving, and he does a nice job of making contact with an 8.3 percent swinging-strike rate that was eighth-best among Carolina League qualifiers. He can get overly aggressive in search of that contact however and lose out on chances for free passes; his 4.0 percent walk rate was fourth-worst among Single-A qualifiers. Standing 5-foot-8, Areinamo has mostly gap power at this stage. The 20-year-old is a fringy runner but gives pitchers and catchers something to think about with his smart baserunning decisions. That lack of speed has moved him away from shortstop -- Milwaukee has quality defenders there at the lower levels -- and while he’s spent some time at third base, he’s a better fit for second because of just average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Areinamo was not one of the most noteworthy players added by the Brewers on Jan. 15, 2021, when he signed for $150,000, but it hasn’t taken long for him to rise to some prominence. In his first move stateside, the Venezuela native was a 2022 Arizona Complex League post-season All-Star after hitting .323/.416/.472 with an even 19/19 K/BB ratio over 34 games. He moved to Single-A Carolina for 28 games in August and even got a seven-game look at High-A Wisconsin when the club needed a body in May/June. Listed at 5-foot-10, 160 pounds, Areinamo isn’t going to pop in a workout, or to anyone giving a quick look at the field, but he finds meaningful ways to contribute, starting with his work at the dish. The right-handed hitter is mature in his approach at the plate with a willingness to fight pitches off and go the other way when needed. He’ll flash some quick hands in his pre-swing setup but manages to control the bat well enough to find barrels and limit strikeouts. There isn’t much power in that frame, calling into question just how valuable he can be offensively. An average runner at best who earns some bonus points for making smart baserunning decisions, Areinamo has moved around from short to third to second as the Brewers have prioritized better pure defenders at the six. It’s just average arm strength too, and that makes it all the likelier he’ll land at second base if and when he needs to find a full-time spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suero moved from his native Bronx to the Dominican Republic as a teenager, a path that allowed him to sign with the Mets for $10,000 in March 2022. Despite the low bonus, he’s played his way into prominence since then, first with strong showings at two A-ball levels in 2024 and then at High-A and Double-A last season. He hit .233/.379/.407 with career highs in homers (16) and steals (35) over 115 games with Brooklyn and Binghamton before getting in 15 more contests in the Arizona Fall League. Standing only 5-foot-11, Suero flashes some fascinating traits that make him such an interesting prospect. He’s an above-average runner on any scale and especially quicker than other catchers; his 35 steals were tops among all Minor League backstops last year, and he went 8-for-8 on theft attempts in the AFL. That athleticism helps him behind the plate as he moves quickly out of the crouch and uses his above-average arm strength to register pop times in the 1.8-1.9-second range. He was relatively new to catching and still has room to grow back there, and the Mets plan to continue to rotate him between left field and first base, keeping other avenues open. Suero brings exciting bat speed from the right side and can pack a punch, maxing out with a 112.5 mph exit velocity in the AFL. There’s at least above-average raw power in there, but perhaps he swings with too much intent. While he shows discipline with his swing decisions, Suero can get wild with his hacks in the zone, and he posted just a 66.8 percent contact rate overall in 2025. Unless he finds a way to get the bat on the ball more consistently, he’s headed toward a backup (or even third) catcher role that can fill in elsewhere when needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of the Bronx, Suero was far from a significant addition when he signed with the Mets for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in March 2022 at 18 years old, but he’s caught the attention of many in the organization in short order. After two solid Complex-level seasons in the D.R. and Florida, Suero opened 2024 with Single-A St. Lucie and was promoted to High-A Brooklyn after only 25 games, having slashed .265/.390/.434 with a 141 wRC+. He continued to be productive in the South Atlantic League with a .228/.353/.350 line in 87 games to round out his age-20 season. A little undersized at 5-foot-11, Suero stands out more for his surprising athleticism. He’s at least an above-average runner, flashing plus times out of the box from the right side, and he stole 20 bags across both stops in 2024, fifth-most among Minor League catchers. He was relatively new to catching when he signed, and Suero focused mostly back there in his first two seasons but expanded his defensive resume to first base and left field last year. That has carried into 2025 at Brooklyn and Double-A Binghamton. Suero runs a simple operation as a hitter, looking calm before unleashing an uppercut swing. That helps him elevate on contact, aiding his pullside power but also leading to a good amount of harmless popups. He chased less at High-A than Single-A but whiffed more against soft stuff. It’s an OBP-driven hitting profile for now, but if he can play multiple premium positions at a high level, his future will only get brighter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After hitting .332 over his first two years at Virginia Tech with a little pop, despite a labrum injury that required offseason surgery in 2023, DeMartini turned on the power as a junior, slamming 21 homers for the Hokies in 2024 while sacrificing some of his approach. He joined the Phillies as a fourth-rounder in 2024 and had a solid debut after signing, then followed that up by hitting well with High-A Jersey Shore for the first half of 2025 before struggling with a promotion to Double-A Reading. A left-handed hitting infielder, DeMartini is capable of driving the baseball with a power-over-hit approach. He can register some big exit velocities, with over-the-fence pop mostly showing up to his pull side. His ability to take in information and make adjustments can be a blessing and a curse as he does have a tendency to tinker too much with his setup and approach. He draws walks, but he’ll need to figure out who he is and find a repeatable swing that allows him to cut down on his swing-and-miss, especially against softer stuff. He also really struggled against left-handed pitching. DeMartini continued to surprise people both with his baserunning acumen, stealing 45 bases despite having below-average speed, and his defense. He could be a plus defender at third and even got reps at shortstop during his first full season, though that’s not a long-term home for him. He could mix in some more second base to help him reach his floor as a power-hitting utility type, though it’s not out of the question he figures out upper-level pitching and settles in at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: DeMartini was part of an upsurge of hitting talent at Virginia Tech and put up numbers for three years with the Hokies. After a shoulder injury limited him in 2023 and required labrum surgery after the season, he returned to hit 21 homers last spring, though with the power uptick came a regression in his overall approach. The Phillies liked the offensive potential enough to take him in the fourth round, and while it was brief, he impressed during his pro debut with Single-A Clearwater, posting a .315/.385/.478 line over 104 plate appearances. While DeMartini has a power-over-hit profile from the left side of the plate, he has a good swing, doesn’t chase a ton and can hit the ball very hard. His strikeout rate jumped back up in his last year in college, but the Phillies were thrilled at how he integrated data and made adjustments during his pro debut. When told that his in-zone contact was particularly low in the spring, he turned that around with an in-zone contact rate of 87.6 percent with Clearwater, giving confidence that he’ll be able to get to his power more consistently, while a healthy shoulder should allow him to repeat his swing path. Perhaps the biggest surprise was how good DeMartini looked defensively. While the industry consensus may have been that he was an average defender at the hot corner, the Phillies think he has the chance to be at least plus with his glove and their defensive coordinator thought he had the chops to play shortstop. He may not have the quickness to stay there long-term, but how he showed on both sides of the ball made him the surprise of the Draft class.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted in the second round in 2020 out of Florida State, Van Eyk was one of the more encouraging long-term arms in the system before Tommy John surgery derailed his development and cost him the entire ‘22 season. Van Eyk returned to the mound in ‘23 and had a unique season, seeing some early spurts in Single-A and the Florida Complex League before a late assignment to Double-A New Hampshire, where he posted a 4.15 ERA with just seven strikeouts over 13 innings. A stint in the AFL brought some encouraging steps. Finally healthy and enjoying a “normal” season for the first time in years, Van Eyk has been circled by several people within the Blue Jays organization as one of the most exciting arms in the system, even at 25. Toronto is seeing all the building blocks that made him a second-round pick again, and now that he’s finally escaped the complex, Van Eyk can begin his long-delayed climb, even if it’s a few years behind schedule. Van Eyk is throwing two shapes of a fastball now, working in a two-seamer, and is sitting 93-95 mph. This sets up his curveball, an excellent pitch that could be effective against MLB hitters tomorrow, and a slider that plays well. Van Eyk’s workload will need to be closely monitored, given how his past few seasons have gone, but there is a surprising amount of internal belief that Van Eyk can get this back on track, and quickly, if his health cooperates.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Van Eyk drew plenty of attention prior to the 2017 Draft as a prep arm out of Florida, but missed some time with arm soreness as a senior and decided to head to Florida State instead of signing with the Mets, who selected him in the 19th round. Van Eyk developed into one of the best starters in the ’20 Draft class and was selected by the Blue Jays in the second round, signing to an above-slot bonus. After pitching to a 5.83 ERA over 80 1/3 innings in High-A Vancouver in ’21, though, Van Eyk underwent Tommy John surgery. The Blue Jays were immediately impressed with what they saw following the Draft in instructs, with Van Eyk showing a potential plus curveball and a low-90s fastball. His changeup slotted in as his third pitch while his slider, which was still developing, is key to his long-term success, especially if that can develop into a strikeout pitch. With strong reviews of Van Eyk’s poise and maturity on the mound, too, all of the right pieces are in place for when he returns from his rehab process. There will be a clearer timeline on Van Eyk later in the summer as he continues to work his way back, but once he’s fully healed, he’ll have an opportunity to move up the ladder as quickly as his workload will allow. The injury was an unfortunate setback for one of the more talented arms in the ’20 class.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Van Eyk generated some buzz prior to the 2017 Draft as a high school pitcher out of Florida, but missed time with some arm soreness as a senior and decided to head to Florida State instead of signing with the Mets, who selected him in the 19th Round. After developing into one of the top starters in the 2020 class, Van Eyk was picked by the Blue Jays in the second round and signed to an above-slot deal. The Blue Jays got another brief look at Van Eyk as part of their fall instructional league, and those within the organization already praise his poise and maturity. Van Eyk comes with a full arsenal that’s headlined by a plus curveball, while he spots his fastball well in the low-90s. Van Eyk’s changeup is his third pitch, and while it could benefit from some added depth, his arm speed keeps hitters off-balance. The development of that slider will be key long-term, especially late in counts. Van Eyk will have an opportunity to move quickly once he’s in full-season ball, given the depth of his arsenal and his maturity on the mound. The athleticism in his delivery, which the Blue Jays always love, leaves evaluators optimistic that he'll keep a clean, repeatable delivery. The Blue Jays are very comfortable with the right-hander sticking as a starter long-term, and the ’21 season will offer the first extended look at Van Eyk in pro ball. He’s a candidate to make a jump over the next season, especially as some of Toronto’s more advanced arms graduate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clemmey and Rocco Baldelli share a common Rhode Island high school alma mater in Warwick’s Bishop Hendricken HS, and the left-hander broke the former Rays outfielder’s state bonus record when he signed with the Guardians for $2.3 million out of the second round in 2023. Clemmey only lasted 19 Single-A starts in the organization before he was flipped to the Nationals for Lane Thomas at the 2024 Trade Deadline. Still only 19 for most of the 2025 season, he posted a 3.47 ERA and struck out 136 batters in 116 2/3 innings between High-A and Double-A in his second full campaign. Even as he enters his third full Minor League season, you have to view Clemmey as a large, 6-foot-6 piece of clay. He can use his athleticism to get down the mound well with good deception and extension and buzz a 92-95 mph four-seamer above bats. But he’s also worked in a two-seamer that works better with his natural supination, and it’ll be a goal to separate the two heaters even more in 2026. His mid-80s breaking ball has shown promise, moving away from a slurvier look toward a sharper version, but it still needs more consistent shape to be a true plus pitch. His upper-80s changeup increased in usage with effective results, though it lacks major velo separation from the fastballs. Clemmey struggled with keeping his delivery consistent in his early years of pro ball, leading to high walk rates at virtually every stop. He started to show signs of an improvement late in ’25 with Harrisburg, but was much more hittable when he filled up the zone. He’s only now entering his 20s and could be molded into a starting pitcher with swing-and-miss results, if he can strike the right balance of stuff and command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clemmey attended the same Rhode Island high school as Rocco Baldelli (Bishop Hendricken HS in Warwick) and broke the Twins manager’s bonus record for the state when he signed with the Guardians for $2.3 million as a 2023 second-rounder. The left-hander flashed raw stuff to begin his first full season with Single-A Lynchburg, where he had a 4.67 ERA and 97 strikeouts in 69 1/3 innings, but walks proved to be a problem. Cleveland traded him to the Nationals as part of a three-player return for Lane Thomas at the Trade Deadline, and his numbers were much the same with Fredericksburg. Standing at 6-foot-6, Clemmey still gets low down the bump with good extension and can generate a tough approach angle that gives hitters fits. His 92-96 mph fastball plays up in the top of the zone as a result, and there’s plenty of projection remaining to get him more velo as he works through pro ball. (He’ll still be only 19 for the majority of the 2025 season.) He's also worked with a sinker in 2025 to play into his natural supination. Clemmey has gone away from a slurvier breaking ball to more of a sharper 81-84 mph slider that he can land in the zone or generate chase running away from lefties or in on righties. An upper-80s changeup worked well at Single-A but is the third-best pitch in the arsenal. Clemmey has an uptempo delivery that can be hard to keep consistent at times, leading to the walk rates. Nationals officials would also like to see him work on getting ahead in counts, and they believe an approach change could just as well correct some of his control problems. Clemmey has youth and raw stuff on his side to become a future No. 2 or 3 starter with the right adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Clemmey signed for $2.3 million last July, he broke fellow Bishop Henricken HS (Warwick, R.I.) alum Rocco Baldelli's Rhode Island bonus record. He boasted some of the best stuff in the 2023 high school class, so the Guardians were surprised to find him available toward the end of the second round. He opened his first full season at Single-A Lynchburg and was then moved to the Nationals at the Trade Deadline for Lane Thomas. Clemmey already works with a 92-96 mph fastball that tops out at 99, and its high spin rates create good carry when he commands it at the top of the strike zone. His curveball combines power and depth, giving him a second plus pitch though it lacks consistency. He has added an 83-86 mph slider since turning pro, and it already looks like it will become at least an average offering. Clemmey still is working on gaining feel for a mid-80s changeup that features only modest sink. While his 6-foot-6 frame results in natural extension that lets his pitches get on hitters quicker than anticipated, he also has trouble keeping his long limbs in sync in his up-tempo delivery. He's going to need time to refine his repertoire and upgrade his control and command, but his upside as a potential frontline starter could make it worth the wait.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick in the 2021 Draft after he grew from a reliever into a starter at Tennessee, Chad “Cheese” Dallas opened his pro career with what you could call a learning experience in ‘22. That year with High-A Vancouver, Dallas posted a 4.60 ERA over 88 innings, with a walk rate of 5.2 BB/9 holding him back. Some improvements to Dallas’ body and repertoire helped him regain some momentum in ‘23, as he posted a 3.65 ERA over 123 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A, cutting that walk rate along the way. Dallas’ projection is still more about the overall package than overwhelming stuff, though his slider could be a plus pitch that misses serious bats in the big leagues. He threw the low-80s offering 40 percent of the time during his stint in New Hampshire. He’s added a bit of velocity over the years and is doing a better job of maintaining it now, but Dallas has been sitting near 93 mph and could benefit from a bit more because of the movement profile. He’ll need to spot that fastball with top-end precision to make everything else work. One new wrinkle is the cutter that Dallas has developed, which should help him against left-handed hitters. This is the type of pitcher the Blue Jays could benefit from developing in waves, particularly after a few years of thin rotation depth. Dallas may not match the ceilings of some of the names higher on this list, but he’s given himself a good shot with a strong floor and deep mix of pitches. He’ll have every opportunity to position himself well behind that first wave of Ricky Tiedemann, Bowden Francis, Yariel Rodriguez and others in Toronto’s depth picture if he gets off to a strong start. He’ll need to hit his spots, though, because Dallas won’t get away with as many misses on his fastball as some other starters might.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After striking out 71 batters in 39 innings as a freshman at Panola Junior College (Texas) in 2019, Dallas was recruited by Tennessee as a reliever. Instead, he developed into the Volunteers’ No. 1 starter and helped pitch them to their first College World Series since 2005. The Blue Jays made him a fourth-round selection in ’21 and signed him slightly over slot value at $497,500. Nicknamed “Cheese,” Dallas has gotten the velocity on his fastball to tick up since the Draft, and it now sits around 93 mph, touching 95 mph. There could be room for a bit more, too, which would leave Dallas’ arrow pointing up into ’22. The biggest addition for Dallas has been a mid-80s cutter that’s tough on right-handers while his low-80s curveball is a pitch he’s comfortable with in any count, too. At 5-foot-11, Dallas is a different look physically than many of the larger-built starters in the Blue Jays’ organization, but he makes it work by pounding the zone and competing. In '22, left-handed hitters will be one challenge to monitor, which is where an improved changeup would really benefit him. There’s bullpen potential here, of course, and that’s something Dallas would be familiar with, but he’ll be rolled out as a starter and could move quickly given his experience against quality NCAA competition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torin joined the D-backs organization with a $240,000 signing bonus out of his native Venezuela in January 2022 and has hit his way quickly through the system with a career .281 average and .391 on-base percentage entering 2026, his age-21 season. He slashed .287/.381/.385 with six homers over 122 games for High-A Hillsboro last season and ranked third among all batters at the level with 134 hits. Torin was promoted to Double-A Amarillo for the club’s postseason push in the Texas League, and he’ll head back to the upper Minors ahead of his upcoming Rule 5 eligibility after the ’26 campaign. If you just looked at Torin’s bat-to-ball skills, you’d think he’d be a future plus hitter. He stays straight to the ball with a slightly closed-off stance, unexaggerated load and quick hands from the right side of the box, and the data backs up the mechanics. He made contact on 86 percent of his swings with Hillsboro and sported a 91 percent in-zone contact rate, which would have ranked in the Top 25 among MLB qualifiers. The ball doesn’t come off the bat loud though; Torin set a career high with six homers but doesn’t project for the pop that would get him even double that total in the Majors. A below-average runner, Torin has the right actions and hands to be a defensive asset at shortstop, and his throws are strong on a line across the diamond. If he must move to second base permanently because of a more well-rounded player at the six, he could be a plus defender there. Torin’s lack of impact will be his biggest separator between being a regular on the dirt and a contact-heavy middle-infield option off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the D-backs for $240,000 out of Venezuela in January 2022, Torin has continued to move through the ranks of the Arizona system with a strong hit tool and approach. That was first evident in the Dominican Summer League, where he batted .333 with a .465 OBP over 50 games in '22, and he pushed through the Arizona Complex League after hitting .320 with a 9/21 K/BB ratio across 26 games a year later. After a dip with Single-A Visalia in the second half of ’23, Torin returned to the California League for all of last season and finished with a .255/.381/.344 line with four homers, 15 steals and almost as many walks (81) as strikeouts (84) across 108 games. There were 46 players aged 19 or younger to reach the qualifying standard at Single-A in 2024, and Torin ranked among the top six in on-base percentage, walk rate (15.8 percent), strikeout rate (16.4), hits (107) and total walks. As expected for those numbers, the right-handed hitter doesn’t expand the zone much and rarely misses when he does swing, staying straight to the ball. That approach has come with limited in-game impact to this point. Torin does lift and pull the ball but prioritizes contact at the detriment of power. Swinging with more intent could help that improve moving forward. D-backs officials note that Torin looked leaner entering ’25. He was just an average runner at best, but his actions and movements -- as well as his quick throws -- on the dirt portend a possible above-average shortstop. He’ll need to improve his consistency, though, as he can occasionally mishandle playable balls. The D-backs have gotten him some time at second base at each stop, but so much depends on Torin’s impact at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torin joined the Arizona organization in January 2022 and has moved fairly quickly on the strength of some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the entire system. After posting a .465 OBP and 1.85 BB/K ratio over 50 games in the Dominican Summer League in his first taste of the Minors, the infielder shot out of the gate with a .320/.437/.427 line, 21 walks and only nine strikeouts over 26 games in the Arizona Complex League last season, earning a mid-July callup to Single-A Visalia. Results were rougher in the California League, but it was notable that Torin was one of only 16 players to get more than 150 plate appearances at Single-A during their age-18-or-younger season in 2023, joining Top 100 prospects Ethan Salas and Samuel Basallo on that list. Regardless of level, Torin led all Minor Leaguers in that age bracket (min. 250 PA) with his 13.8 percent strikeout rate, and his 8.8 percent swinging-strike rate at Single-A ranked fourth among players 18 or younger at that level (min. 150 PA). That barrel control has been more about protecting the plate than driving balls in the early going, but there’s hope that the right-handed hitter could get to at least below-average power as he adds more oomph behind his hacks. The 5-foot-10 infielder has already shown some signs of physical maturation, and he’s trending toward being more of an average runner. He still shows great actions at shortstop, and while he has more than enough arm for the six, he’s gotten some looks at second base, too, because of Arizona’s deep group of middle infielders at the lower levels. Torin profiles as a potential high-contact, high-OBP option at a premium position, and power will be the biggest decider in his future role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2022 international signing window, eight players got higher bonuses from the D-backs than Torin’s $240,000, but in just one short year, the Venezuela native already looks like the most prominent player of the bunch. The right-handed-hitting middle infielder astoundingly walked 37 times and struck out on only 20 occasions in 50 games in the Dominican Summer League. That not only helped him bat .333 with a .465 OBP, but his 1.85 BB/K ratio ranked fourth among the 1,581 Minor Leaguers with at least 200 plate appearances in 2022. Arizona officials were instantly taken aback by how well Torin controls the strike zone and showed a mature approach by staying in the zone. He tended to make contact when he swung too, which helped keep the strikeouts low and the average high. While it may be notable that Torin didn’t homer in the DSL, the 5-foot-10 slugger can square balls up, and the D-backs believe at least some pop will come as he adds strength beyond his teen years. His decisions to swing only at balls he can drive certainly helps that case. One thing evaluators don't have to worry about is his ability to stick at shortstop, even though he got some looks at second. Torin does a good job of getting to balls all over the dirt, and plus arm strength means he can make throws from deep in the hole too. What’s more, Torin was aggressive on the basepaths (21 successful steals in 27 attempts), and with the new rules, he could continue to push the envelope on that side. His advanced approach and strong defensive acumen have already helped push him from the Arizona Complex League to Single-A Visalia in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 13 overall prospect of the 2020-21 international class by MLB Pipeline, Pineda signed with the A’s out of the Dominican Republic for $2.5 million in January of 2021. He spent most of his first summer as a professional in the United States, holding his own as a 17-year-old in the Arizona Complex League. Pineda appears to have a better understanding of the strike zone with less swing-and-miss than most young international signings by the A’s in recent years. His excellent bat speed was evident in Rookie ball, and as his mechanics improve at the plate, so should the power as his body continues to fill out. Pineda’s wide-ranging tools give him a high ceiling as an outfielder with the ability to play all three spots. He runs well enough to give him the chance to play center field and his arm would work well from right, as would his potential power profile. Described as one of the more fun players to watch in the organization, his long path ahead could result in him reaching the big leagues as an exciting everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $2.5 million out of the Dominican Republic in January, Pineda was considered to have some of the best tools in the 2020-21 international class and was ranked as the No. 13 overall prospect on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list at the start of the signing period. Pineda has been described as “explosive” and it’s easy to see why. He is raw, but has the potential to have several plus tools. Specifically, Pineda has been praised for his hands and excellent bat speed. For now, there’s some loft to his swing and his mechanics continue to improve. He also consistently hits the ball hard to all fields and can drive the ball out of the ballpark. Defensively, Pineda should shine at the corner outfield spots, but he is also comfortable in center field. He is learning how to contain his arm strength for improved accuracy. A’s fans will have to wait a long time to see a return on investment here, but the end result could be an exciting, toolsy everyday big league outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked in the top 20 of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list when the 2021 signing period opened, Acosta signed with the Padres for $1.8 million. After an impressive debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing, his first taste of life in the United States and the Arizona Complex League did not go as well. He was middling along with a .707 OPS when he was sent to the Reds at the 2022 Trade Deadline for Brandon Drury. While the numbers in his first full season with his new organization weren’t eye-popping, he more consistently showed off his solid tools with the move to the Florida State League. A switch-hitter, Acosta has shown the ability to swing the bat well from both sides of the plate with quick hands and bat speed, though he was a bit better from the left side with Daytona last year. While he keeps the strikeouts relatively in check and draws walks, he can get overly aggressive at times because he has such strong contact skills. He’s never going to be a huge power guy, but there were some good exit velocities coming off his bat in 2023, and he has the chance to find his way to some extra-base thump in the gaps. The hope is that Acosta, who is an above-average runner, will be able to stick at shortstop, and the Reds will likely keep giving him reps there for as long as possible. He has a decent arm and actions, but some see a move to second base eventually becoming necessary. How far his offense advances will determine if he can profile as an everyday guy at one spot in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Acosta was thought to be one of the better prospects available on the international amateur market when the 2021 signing period opened, with the Padres swooping in and signing him for $1.8 million on the opening day (Jan. 15). He made a strong first impression that summer with an OPS over .900, but he was having less success in his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League when he was sent to the Reds in the Brandon Drury Trade Deadline deal in 2022. In the early stages of his pro career, Acosta has shown some acumen for getting on base and making contact from both sides of the plate. He has quick hands and an aggressive approach, but he’s shown a willingness to see pitches and draw walks. There hasn’t been much power to speak of, and he needs to add strength to his frame, which could help him translate his contact skills into more extra-base authority. Acosta is a good athlete who runs well and possesses all of the defensive tools -- range, arm, footwork and instincts -- to stick at shortstop. He’ll keep getting reps on both sides of second base to potentially provide defensive versatility down the line and also to make sure he gets the at-bats he needs to reach his offensive ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 19 prospect in the 2020-21 international class, Acosta signed with the Padres for $1.8 million on Jan. 15, 2021. The early returns were promising as the Dominican Republic native flashes five-tool potential and hit .285/.431/.484 over 56 games in his Dominican Summer League debut, though he was having less impact offensively during his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League when he was sent to the Reds in return for Brandon Drury at the Trade Deadline. A switch-hitter, Acosta boasts an impressive set of tools. The teenager has quick hands and is an aggressive hitter with a swing-first mentality. As a result of the aggression, he handles fastballs better than off-speed pitches, though that’s not all that uncommon in young hitters. He doesn’t hit for a ton of power yet, but still has time to grow into his 5-foot-11, 170-pound frame and there’s hope he’ll tack on a bit more power as he develops. A projectable athlete, Acosta has the athleticism to stick at short, but could also wind up at second base. Above-average speed, which helped him steal 26 bases in 56 games last season, gives Acosta the range to make all the necessary plays up the middle, though the accuracy on his throws isn’t always consistent. He does, however, have plenty of arm strength and could develop into a middle of the diamond star if everything goes well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arguably the prize of their 2020-21 international haul, Acosta signed with the Padres for $1.8 million out of the Dominican Republic. He’s clearly worth dreaming on. Acosta boasts five-tool potential and is a twitchy athlete with lots of projection. A switch-hitter, Acosta has extremely quick hands, which should make his swing play from both sides of the plate. As he grows into his frame and perhaps adds an inch or two – at 16, he stands 5-foot-11, 170 pounds – the Padres envision Acosta growing into a bit of power. He’s raw at shortstop but can probably stick there, considering his athleticism and excellent arm. Acosta is a classic projectable athlete, and San Diego has had success in the past developing middle infielders. It’s unclear what position Acosta might end up playing, but he has all the tools necessary to stick up the middle somewhere. If his bat develops too, the Padres might have another big-time athlete to plug into the mix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a class that included Jesús Made and Luis Peña, Quintana was the Brewers’ top international signing in 2024 when he joined the organization for $1.7 million out of Venezuela. A solid first season in the Dominican Summer League led to a move stateside for 2025, though he didn’t head straight to Single-A like his fellow infielders. Quintana was hitting .264/.349/.403 in 50 Arizona Complex League games when Milwaukee moved him to San Diego alongside Nestor Cortes in a move for outfielder Brandon Lockridge. As is their wont, the Padres pushed Quintana aggressively to Single-A, and he struggled a bit with a 33.7 percent strikeout rate in 25 games with Lake Elsinore. Results aside, there are some interesting raw materials in Quintana’s profile.
