That performance helped him rise to a fifth-round selection by Seattle in 2025. A right-handed hitter, Dickerson stands out for his bat speed and ability to generate premium exit velocities. Scouts see at least plus raw power to all fields, though questions remain about his ability to consistently punish higher-velocity pitching. He tends to pull aggressively but could improve his offensive ceiling by being more selective. Defensively and athletically, Dickerson is a standout. With plus speed and 20/20 upside, he covers ground well in center field and shows the instincts and quickness that give him a chance to be a regular up-the-middle contributor. Arm strength is average but adequate for his position. His small sample in his debut season revealed a highly twitchy, athletic outfielder who aggressively tracks the ball -- a trait that excites evaluators despite a late-season hamstring and quad issue that limited reps. If Dickerson can remain healthy and continue to refine his approach at the plate, his combination of athleticism, speed, and emerging power could make him a dynamic center fielder in Seattle’s system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high schooler in Virginia, Stallings showed polish on the mound but not enough stuff to really register on the Draft radar, so he went to the University of Tennessee. He was pretty much the same pitcher with the Volunteers, but this time with three years of solid track record in the Southeastern Conference on his resume. That led to the Angels taking him in the fifth round of the 2019 Draft, though after not pitching that summer after a heavy college workload and the 2020 shutdown, he never threw an official pitch for the Angels before he was traded to the Orioles in the José Iglesias deal in early December. None of Stallings' offerings jump off the page, but he has a legitimate four-pitch mix. His fastball will top out at 93 mph and more often comes in at 88-91 mph, but he commands the pitch very well and throws it with a ton of sink. His changeup, which has similar movement, plays off it nicely and he sells it well. His curve got better during his junior year and he also has a slider/cutter at his disposal. Stallings’ stuff plays up because he tunnels his pitches effectively and can throw all four of them for strikes. He rarely hurts himself with walks, allowing just 1.3 per nine innings at Tennessee. That gives him a chance to fit into the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fajardo signed with the White Sox for $400,000 in February 2024 and has been a steady performer ever since, starting with his 26 percent K/BB rate in the Dominican Summer League that first season. The industry has taken notice as he’s been acquired in trades twice before his 20th birthday. The first came when he was moved to the Red Sox for the DFA’d Cam Booser in December 2024, and then one year later -- after climbing to Single-A in his first stateside season -- when he was traded to the Cardinals as part of the Willson Contreras deal. After adding strength, the 6-foot-3 right-hander pushed his four-seamer and two-seamer up to the 93-95 mph range, touching 96, before his move to the Cardinals. A lack of standout movement made them easier to touch at Single-A, but the velocity trajectory is promising. For now because the fastballs don’t really pop, Fajardo has leaned heavily on his mid-80s slider. He’s able to wear out the low, gloveside area with that breaking ball, and it could be a future plus pitch. Fajardo also delivers plenty of whiffs with his 85-87 mph changeup with fading action, and he appropriately ran equal splits in '25 because of it. Fajardo was pushed so aggressively by Boston because his control was more advanced than most 18-year-old pitchers (with many of them still pitching in American high schools). The chase on his secondaries helps him deliver strikes consistently, though that could be challenged when he reaches the Majors. There is an argument to be made for him as the headline of the return in the Contreras trade considering his ceiling as a potential No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The fact that Haley was a Top 100 prospect and one of the better high school lefties in the 2025 Draft class is a testament to his resilience. He had Tommy John surgery before high school, internal brace surgery on the elbow his junior year and a diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma in between. The Mississippi prep standout had a solid -- and healthy -- senior season and the Angels pulled their typical post-10th round magic by taking him in Round 12 and going way over slot with a bonus approaching $900,000 to keep him from heading to Vanderbilt. Haley has the chance to have a legitimate four-pitch mix and enough feel to be a starter. He sits in the low 90s with a fastball featuring plenty of carry and armside run, touching 97 mph during his senior year. His breaking pitches can blur into each other at times, but at their best he has a distinct hammer of a low-80s curve and a slightly harder slider. His low-80s changeup can kill spin, though he hasn’t thrown it a ton. Athletic on the mound, Haley moves down the mound well with good extension. He throws strikes and repeats his delivery, even if it has a bit of a head dunk. There’s no question about his makeup -- not only did he overcome that adversity, he learned to throw right-handed so he could keep playing as a position player while rehabbing his elbow and he played through his chemotherapy and radiation treatments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pence blew out his elbow pitching summer ball shortly before he enrolled at North Carolina, leading to Tommy John surgery and a redshirt year before he became one of the best relievers in college ball in 2023-24. Signed for an over-slot $350,000 as an 11th-rounder in 2024, he exceeded expectations during his pro debut last season. He logged a 2.73 ERA, .193 opponent average and 32 percent strikeout rate between two Class A levels while improving his secondary pitches. The key to Pence's success going forward will be if a fastball that parks at 91-93 mph and maxes out at 95 can continue to play as a solid pitch thanks to tremendous carry and fine command. He threw his heater three-quarters of the time while in college, and the Rangers had him dial back its usage so he could develop his sweeping slider and splitter/changeup. Both sit in the low 80s and missed more bats with more action last year than they had in the past. Pence uses his athleticism to get down the mound well, creating extension and a low release height. He repeats his delivery well and provides consistent strikes without catching too much of the plate. If he can continue to fool hitters with his fastball, he could be more than a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After helping host Mexico win a bronze medal at an 18-and under World Cup qualifier in November 2022, Gutierrez signed for $32,500 two months later. He batted .352 with a 12 percent strikeout rate in his first three pro seasons, though recurring back issues limited him to just 85 games. He was leading the Single-A California League in hitting (.351), on-base percentage (.445), runs (60) and hits (87) when his 2025 season ended after just 60 contests. There aren't any holes in Gutierrez's compact left-handed stroke or his approach. He rarely chases pitches or misses when he does swing, hangs in well against southpaws and handles all types of offerings while using the entire field. He's not very physical and doesn't pull or lift many balls, so his power upside may be limited to 12-15 homers per year. Gutierrez has solid speed and is an instinctive baserunner who swiped 38 bags in 42 attempts (90 percent) in his first three years as a pro. He may be quick enough to play center field, but he spent most of last season in right in deference to speedier Dakota Jordan. He has average arm strength and is a solid defender on the corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tejeda pitched at both Florida and Florida State in his two collegiate seasons with subpar results at both. After posting a 5.95 ERA in 19 2/3 innings primarily as a reliever in 2024, he headed to the Cape Cod League (where he also spent part of ’23) and struck out 16 in 11 1/3 frames. That performance in the premier summer collegiate league likely helped him go to the Nationals in the 14th round as a Draft-eligible sophomore in ’24, and he signed for $225,000. Washington moved Tejeda into a starting role in the pros, and he handled himself well with a 4.03 ERA, 1.23 WHIP and 79 strikeouts in 87 innings between Single-A and High-A. Entering his age-22 season, Tejeda will pop most for his size at 6-foot-8, and as you might expect, that leads to huge extension that gets him right on top of batters. He sat 91-94 mph with a pair of fastballs from his low three-quarters slot, and early spring reports indicate that he’s been sitting mid-90s more comfortably to begin his second full season, making at-bats even more uncomfortable for hitters. His low-80s sweeper and shorter mid-80s slider gives him two breaking ball variations, and the former is his best whiff generator as it runs away from righties. The fade on his 83-85 mph splitter shows promise, though lefties have given Tejeda a splits problem early in his career. Tejeda’s control numbers are significantly better on the pro side, though he relies on batters expanding the zone horizontally. Because of his limited usage in school and change in role, he’s more raw than the typical collegiate arm, especially one from the 14th round. Holding the velo and control gains would give him a decent shot at being a No. 4/5 starter in D.C.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Becker’s path to pro ball is rooted in baseball family ties and projection. A native of Thiells, New York, he crossed into New Jersey to attend Don Bosco Prep -- the same program that produced big leaguer Caden Dana -- following in the footsteps of his older brother, Eric. Their father, Jeff, played at Duke and logged time in Cleveland’s Minor League system, giving Nick a foundation in the game from an early age. Seattle believed enough in his upside to select him in the second round and sign him away from a commitment to the University of Virginia for $2.75 million, well above slot value. At 6-foot-4 with an athletic, projectable build, Becker already pairs present skill with long-term ceiling. A right-handed hitter, he shows advanced bat-to-ball ability and mature hitting instincts, consistently finding the barrel and making in-game adjustments. His swing is fluid and under control, and there’s confidence that more impact will come as he adds strength and learns to better leverage the ball in the air. The expectation is at least average future power without compromising his contact ability. Becker is a solid runner with room to grow into plus speed as he continues to mature physically. Defensively, he offers a strong foundation -- smooth actions, reliable hands and plenty of arm for the left side. All signs point to him sticking at shortstop long term, and he spent a few weeks with longtime Mariners infield coach Perry Hill in Arizona in early February. With his blend of tools, makeup and projection, Becker slots comfortably into Seattle’s deep infield pipeline with a chance to rise quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres parlayed a strong performance on the high school showcase circuit in 2017 into going 41st overall the following June, making him the second-highest New York prep arm taken in the last 25 Drafts (behind only 2016 No. 3 choice Ian Anderson). One of the youngest players in the 2018 Draft at 17 years and eight months, he proved more advanced than expected in his pro debut. He didn't pitch in another official game over the next two years, requiring Tommy John surgery in May 2019 and returning to the mound in instructional league last fall. Before he blew out his elbow, Torres displayed electric arm speed that generated fastballs that sat at 92-95 mph and topped out at 98 mph with riding action up in the zone. His low-80s slider also showed signs of becoming a plus pitch with power and high spin rates. He has a lot of work to do on a changeup that he didn't need much as an amateur, but it has some tumble and should become at least an average third offering. Torres isn't especially big for a starter, but he doesn't have much effort in his delivery and his athleticism helps him repeat it. While he pounded the strike zone in his brief debut, his command isn't as sharp as his control. He'll need to prove he can hold up when he takes a regular turn in the rotation, but the Indians believe his maturity and intelligence are two more assets that will help his cause.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the hardest-throwing pitchers on the 2019 international market, Mercedes already reached 95 mph before signing for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He has continued to add velocity and finally got a chance to make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League at age 18 last summer. While he recorded a 5.11 ERA, he also touched 98 mph and ranked fourth in the ACL with 62 strikeouts in 56 1/3 innings. Mercedes' fastball usually operates at 93-96 mph with running and boring action toward right-handers, and he could reach triple digits once he adds more strength to his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. His mid-80s slider moves in the opposite direction from his fastball, showing flashes of becoming a plus offering but also lacking consistency. His power changeup in the upper 80s is even more of a work in progress but eventually could give him an average third pitch. While Mercedes has a three-pitch mix to go with size and athleticism, he still may wind up in the bullpen in the long run. He has a slingy delivery with some effort and a long arm action, which compromises his control and command. He'll be 19 throughout the 2022 season, so he still has plenty of time to figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Franklin spent two years working out of the Kennesaw State bullpen and put himself on a semi-big stage in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2024, but he walked around one batter per inning in both places. That changed when he transferred to Tennessee for 2025. He still pitched out of the Volunteers' bullpen but walked only nine in 38 2/3 innings while posting a 4.89 ERA and 52 strikeouts. The Cardinals found his stuff promising enough to take him 72nd overall and sign him for full slot at $1,145,900. Franklin got in three starts between Single-A and High-A after signing. St. Louis intends to run Franklin out as a starter in the hopes that his stuff holds deeper into outings and makes him even more valuable on the bump. The 6-foot-5 right-hander showed a 94-98 mph four-seamer in Knoxville that got some of the best overall and in-zone whiff rates among all Division I heaters. The pitch can touch 102 but is especially untouchable because of its tremendous ride. It had an 18.5 inch induced vertical break during Franklin’s brief foray into the Florida State League. An 89-92 mph cutter was his most-used pitch beyond the fastball, but he’s shown the makings of a mid-80s sweeping slider and an upper-80s changeup. Franklin toned down the effort in his delivery in his one spring as a Volunteer, causing his walk rate to fall to 6 percent, and that aids St. Louis’ hopes for him as a starter. He’ll need to show he can hold those gains over longer stretches and prove he can be more than a two-pitch hurler in the expanded role. Otherwise, the fastball alone could be dangerous if he slides back to relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If you see the 6-foot-6, 255-pound Quick and think he looks like an offensive lineman, it’s because he was, in high school, and a good one who could have played college football. He opted to focus on pitching at Alabama, but after a solid freshman year as a reliever, needed Tommy John surgery as a sophomore in 2024. He made a speedy recovery and turned in 14 starts for the Crimson Tide helping him land with the Twins as the No. 36 overall pick in the 2025 Draft, signing for a full-slot bonus of $2.69 million. Quick’s stuff is downright electric, with a sinking fastball that sits at 96-97 mph and touches 99. He holds his velocity deep into his starts and was already sitting at 95 mph in early bullpens before Spring Training. The Twins are already working with him on his fastball usage, leaning on the sinker against right-handers and a four-seamer against lefties. They also want him to use his nasty secondary stuff more, especially in two-strike counts after he threw his heater almost 50 percent of the time in those situations in 2025 with Alabama. His mid-80s slider features two-plane depth and he can manipulate it into a harder cutter in the low 90s. Those two, and his upper-80s changeup that fades and sinks, miss a ton of bats. While he’s built like a workhorse, Quick doesn’t have a track record yet of handling a full workload, with just 87 total college innings on his resume entering pro ball. Learning routines as a professional starter, along with refining his command to maximize his raw stuff, will be keys for him to reach his ceiling as part of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roki Sasaki was the center of attention during the 2025 international signing period, and while the Blue Jays were in the running for the Japanese right-hander, they fell short to the Dodgers. Instead, Cristopher Polanco came in with the highest bonus at $2,297,500, but it’s another Dominican Republic infielder in Sanchez, a $997,500 signee, who has become the talk of the class. Sanchez was named a mid- and post-season All-Star in the Dominican Summer League after posting a .341/.439/.565 line with eight homers and 28 total extra-base hits across 56 games. Of the 304 DSL qualifiers, he was one of only seven with an ISO above .220 (.224) and a strikeout rate below 18 percent (17.4). Heading into his age-18 season, Sanchez already has plenty of size at 6-foot-3, but his plus power grades don’t come from physical projection alone. He’s already brought actualized pop into his game with loud contact in the DSL, and he combines his present strength with a balanced right-handed swing. He impressed Blue Jays officials with the way he reacted to being pitched around once the word got out on his ability, and that baseline of swing decisions should serve him well, if he can maintain it stateside. Sanchez will likely be a below-average runner at full maturity, and the Blue Jays have already given him the lion’s share of work at third base because of the amount of young talents they needed to get shortstop reps in the DR. While he’ll still work in time at the six, he’s a better fit at the hot corner, and his arm strength will work there. Sanchez’s early overall traits have already pushed him into prominence on the Toronto infield depth chart, and he’s a decent bet to see full-season ball before his 19th birthday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers saved international bonus pool money to pursue Roki Sasaki in 2025, and when he signed with the Dodgers, they pivoted and spent $1,200,001 on Kim in May. A two-way standout who projected to go in the first round of the Korea Baseball Organization draft, he played briefly in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League after signing before returning home to complete his high school education. After getting his diploma in January, he'll both play shortstop and pitch in his U.S. debut this year. Scouts are divided as to whether Kim is better as a position player or pitcher. He projects as an average hitter with a good approach and 15-homer power from the right side of the plate, and he could raise his offensive ceiling as he adds strength to his projectable 6-foot-2 frame. He's a solid defender at shortstop with a strong arm and average speed. On the mound, Kim displays a low-90s fastball that reaches 95 mph. He has a full complement of secondary pitches, with his low-80s slider ranking ahead of his mid-80s splitter and mid-70s curveball. He should add more power as he matures physically and his athleticism should help him throw strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lewis was a model-based pick by the Yankees as a power-speed athlete out of Queens College, and he quickly exceeded expectations after signing for $150,000 in the 13th round of the 2024 Draft. While old for Single-A and High-A in his age-22 season last year, he slashed .237/.321/.445 (120 wRC+) with 22 homers and 26 steals between the two levels. The Marlins acquired him along with Brendan Jones, Juan Matheus and Dylan Jasso in January for Ryan Weathers. Miami's front office was eager to add Lewis in no small part because of his power potential. The right-handed slugger produces top-of-the-line exit velocities, up to 113.9 mph last year, and has plenty of raw strength. That pop has come with swing-and-miss issues, which could be mitigated with better swing decisions. Lewis chased less as the 2025 season progressed, even against better competition, although some stiff swing mechanics make it likely that he'll maintain a below-average hit tool -- he's had particular struggles with in-zone contact. Lewis is an elite athlete who has been caught just twice in 29 stolen-base attempts in pro ball. Defensively, he shows good burst and speed and has a chance to be an average center fielder or above average in a corner -- likely left since he doesn't have ideal arm strength for right. Lewis earns praise for his makeup and has been a quick learner in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Belyeu really established himself as a college hitter to watch as a sophomore at Texas in 2024 when he hit .329 with 18 homers. He was off to a strong start to his junior year when he fractured his left thumb diving for a ball in March. Though he finished with nine homers and a .303 average in 32 games, it was really his sophomore production that got him drafted No. 74 overall by the Rockies. He struggled during his pro debut with High-A Spokane, though it was too small of a sample to draw any conclusions. A hamstring issue shut down any action at instructs for the outfielder. While Belyeu isn’t a total free swinger, he did get more aggressive during his junior year, and his strikeout rate did climb, something that continued during his stint with Spokane after signing. The left-handed hitter has some strike-zone awareness and there’s damage in there, with the ability to drive the ball to all fields, but he’s going to have to work to try not to do too much at the plate, which takes him out of his approach. The Rockies’ new hitting group values contact and will work with him to be a hitter first. Belyeu is a solid athlete with decent speed and should be able to handle a corner outfield spot capably, with a plus arm that fits in right field. He plays with intensity, sometimes being too hard on himself, and he’ll get to show what he can really do over a full, healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Obermuller had the chance to begin his pro career after his sophomore season at Iowa but opted to return to the Hawkeyes for his junior year rather than entertain signing with the Rangers, who took him in Round 19 of the 2024 Draft. It turned out to be a wise decision as the son of five-year big leaguer Wes Obermueller went in the same round as his dad did, the second, with the Phillies in 2025, signing for $1.2 million. Obermueller has a slender, wiry frame and is a plus athlete on the mound with a little bounce. The left-hander employs a low arm slot that helps provide excellent metrics on his fastball and slider. The heater sat at 91-94 mph, topping out at 98 and he’s able to manipulate the pitch for carry, run or sink coming from a flat approach angle. He’ll use his low-80s slider with a ton of horizontal break against hitters on both sides of the plate. He has a sinking mid-80s changeup he didn’t use much in college, but the Phillies think it can be a usable third pitch in the future. Standing around 6-foot even and 170 pounds, Obermueller will have to prove he can handle the workload of a starter. His improvement in the strike-throwing department as a junior helps his case there and he brings a very calm demeanor to the mound. He’ll get the chance to develop as a starter, but moving him to the 'pen would put him on a faster track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Memorial High School in Evansville, Indiana, will always be known for producing Don Mattingly, but Fisher represents the first player from the school to be drafted since 1993. While he didn’t quite surpass former Indiana prep pitchers Ashe Russell and Nolan Watson as a first-round pick, the two-sport standout -- he also starred at quarterback at Memorial -- did get close to second-round money ($1.25 million) from the Phillies to sign as a seventh-rounder in the 2025 Draft. Fisher is already a presence on the mound at 6-foot-3 with a combination of stuff and projection. He can really spin the baseball, both with his heater and a pair of distinct breaking balls. He tends to work in the 92-93 mph range, touching 95 with a high-spin fastball that has good carry and natural cut that allows it to play up. The spin rates on both his top-to-bottom upper-70s curve and traditional low-80s slider are also very high, and he can miss bats with both. It’s his fourth pitch, but he has some feel for a fading changeup as well. The athleticism that made him stand out on the gridiron helps him on the mound, where he repeats his delivery with good extension and throws a lot of strikes. He has room to add strength, which should lead to more consistent velocity, helping him reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones played football at Stanford, where he was a safety who played special teams, explaining his impressive speed, range in the outfield and pure strength. Once he focused on baseball as a sophomore, though, his ability began to shine through. He hit 18 homers and stole 14 bases for Stanford in 2021, played for Team USA that summer then turned things around as a junior to hit .324/.451/.664 with 21 homers in 65 games. As a result, the Rays selected him in the second round of the 2022 Draft and signed him for a full-slot bonus of $1,077,600. Jones has said he’s trying to “stop ‘athlete-ing’ baseball,” meaning he wants to further refine his all-around game. The biggest step will be cutting down his swing-and-miss rate, something that’s always been a part of his game but could be the only issue holding him back. But if he can hit enough to get to his power, pairing good swing decisions with his strong hands and pull-side power, there’s a potentially useful player here. Jones is close to maxed out physically, but he already has plus speed – with good instincts on the basepaths -- and raw power. Defensively, Jones plays center field like he’s in a one-high safety formation. He makes good reads and takes good routes to balls, with a fringy arm being the only drawback. Tampa Bay is also thrilled with Jones’ makeup, noting how he worked out with fellow prospect Xavier Isaac in Miami over the offseason. Maybe he settles into more of a platoon role eventually, but the Rays hope Jones can develop into an everyday center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ayers played three years at the State JC of Florida, Manatee-Sarasota and two at Marshall before he impressed the Cubs in a pre-Draft workout and signed for $50,000 as a 19th-rounder in 2024. In his first full pro season, he slashed .238/.341/.420 with six homers in 65 games as one of the oldest players (age 24) in the Single-A Carolina League before a broken right hand sidelined him in July. He came back and won the Arizona Fall League's breakout player award after hitting .357/.539/.591 with a league-best 22 walks in 20 games. Ayers uses a reasonably disciplined approach to find pitches he can launch in the air to his pull side. His solid raw power and impressive exit velocities portend 20-homer power, though he'll have to show he can do damage against more advanced and age-appropriate pitching. A switch-hitter, he's much better from the left side and has a glaring weakness against changeups. Because he didn't begin catching full time until his final year in college, Ayers needs a lot of work with his receiving and blocking, though he grades well in framing metrics. He regularly recorded sub-1.85-second pop times in the AFL, showing off plus-plus arm strength and a quick release. A below-average runner, he also has played briefly at first base and in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A position player at Junipero Serra (Calif.) HS, Garcia headed to Division III Chapman as an infielder. He appeared in just 24 games as a freshman then moved to the mound as a sophomore. He found immediate success in the bullpen, winning nine games and saving 12 more to help the Panthers win a national title, earning College World Series Most Outstanding Player honors in the process. After pitching well out of the pen on the Cape last summer, Garcia moved into the rotation at the start of his junior year and created a lot of early buzz in the process. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has shown glimpses of three pitches that have the chance to be above average. He came out of the gate this spring throwing much harder than in the past, showcasing a fastball consistently up to 97 mph. He backs it up with a mid-80s slider and an 86-88 mph cutter, though he hasn’t shown much of a changeup in the past. Garcia’s command has been spotty at times, but he’s generally around the strike zone, and given his athletic delivery and arm action, there’s some confidence he’ll improve on this front in the future. He doesn’t have a ton of track record against good competition – the stint on the Cape helped a bit – or as a starter, but he’s a relatively fresher arm with perhaps more projection than most college pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McDonough caught at Moeller High (Cincinnati), which has spawned 14 big leaguers including Hall of Famers Ken Griffey Jr. and Barry Larkin, but found himself blocked at that position at North Carolina State by future first-rounder Patrick Bailey. After transitioning to center field, he priced himself out of the shortened 2020 Draft as a sophomore-eligible and returned to help the Wolfpack place third at the 2021 College World Series, fashioning a 53-game on-base streak that spanned the two seasons. He signed for $828,600 as a third-rounder last July and batted .298/.397/.491 during a month in Low-A. A switch-hitter, McDonough has some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the system. He added strength and changed his approach in 2021, launching balls more consistently in the air (especially against left-handers) while continuing to control the strike zone well. He lost a half-step of speed as he gained muscle, but he's still a solid runner with good instincts on the bases. McDonough's quickness and savvy translate to center field, where he's a solid defender with average arm strength. He also saw action at second base in college and Boston plans on playing him in both spots and perhaps shortstop and third base. A potential super-utility man, he garners comparisons to former Red Sox fan favorite Brock Holt with his versatility and hard-nosed style of play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Summerhill might not have been available to the Rays with the 42nd overall pick in the 2025 Draft had he maintained the momentum he built as a sophomore at Arizona. He led the Wildcats in average, on-base percentage and extra-base hits in 2024 and followed that with an All-Star performance in the Cape Cod League. He played well as a junior, posting a 1.015 OPS and walking more than he struck out, but he missed more than a month with a broken hand and lost more time to a strained hamstring. He wound up with the Rays, signing for a below-slot bonus of $1,997,500, and played 10 Single-A games in his pro debut. When healthy, Summerhill has shown the potential to be a dynamic player on both sides of the ball. He’s strong and athletic, with a mature approach at the plate and a good sense of his strengths and weaknesses. He’s a pure hitter, having cut down on his tendency to whiff each year during his time at Arizona, although he does tend to chase pitches outside the zone. As strong as he is, his raw power hasn’t fully translated into game power since his hand injury, with most of his pop coming to the pull side regardless. Summerhill is an above-average runner but not a burner. He spent his junior season playing right field for Arizona, although the Rays seem inclined to use him in all three spots. He has the arm to play right field, but he’d likely be more valuable in center field if he can handle it in the professional ranks. The Rays generally give good athletes every chance to prove they can play center field, and their outfield philosophy has helped athletic players like Theo Gillen and Aidan Smith take massive strides as defenders. If all goes well, he could develop into a Jake McCarthy-type regular somewhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $40,000 out of Venezuela in 2024, Azocar started to attract attention after gaining strength following his pro debut and crushing balls in Minor League Spring Training last year. The Red Sox sent him to the Rookie-level Florida Complex League, where he batted .385/.448/.558 in 15 games before earning a promotion to Single-A at age 18. He has some similarities to Justin Gonzales but struggled more against significantly older competition. Azocar weighs closer to 195 pounds than his listed 168, and the added muscle allows him to produce higher velocities than most players his age. He generates plenty of bat speed from the right side of the plate and has the potential for at least 20-homer power once he matures as a hitter and learns to elevate balls more often. He chased too many non-fastballs in Single-A but showed the ability to do damage when he swung at strikes. Azocar has solid speed, can flash plus run times and displays the aptitude to steal a few bases. After playing most of his first season in left field, he spent much of his second in center. He has good instincts and average range in center, but he profiles better in right field and has the solid arm strength necessary there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shores has always been able to throw hard dating back during his Texas high school days, when he could have been a solid prep pick in the 2022 Draft if he wasn’t intent on honoring his college commitment at Louisiana State. His time with the Tigers was interrupted early by Tommy John surgery in April of his freshman year, and he missed all of 2024. The velocity came back, but he struggled to find a rhythm as a starter, though he did get two saves (including the championship winner) in the Men's College World Series last year en route to becoming the Angels’ second-round pick. Signed for a full slot bonus of $2.08 million, Shores brings a ton of arm strength to the Halos’ system. He’ll work his heater in the 94-98 mph range and touch triple digits, but upon his return from TJ, the fastball had less armside run and didn’t overpower hitters as much. His mid-80s slider still featured good depth and missed bats, but his command of the pitch wavered. He has an upper-80s changeup, but it hasn’t been an effective offering. Though he’s 6-foot 8 and 245 pounds, Shores is quite athletic on the mound and there’s optimism that the further removed from elbow surgery he gets, the more in sync he’ll become in order to repeat his low three-quarters delivery and find the zone more consistently. Similarly to Angels’ 2024 second-rounder Chris Cortez, Shores could get a chance to start, with most feeling he eventually lands in a bullpen where his fastball-slider combination could be nasty.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Grice homered 18 times and posted a 1.029 OPS over 60 games at the plate and posted a 3.35 ERA with 101 strikeouts in 78 innings during his junior year at Clemson -- numbers that won him the 2023 John Olerud Two-Way Player of the Year Award one year after Paul Skenes claimed the honor. He did punch out 26.9 percent of the time that spring because of his long left-handed swing, and that gave many evaluators pause about his potential at the plate entering the Draft. The D-backs selected Grice 64th overall in July and signed him for $1.25 million before declaring they preferred he stick to the mound. Beyond Grice's size at 6-foot-6, it isn't hard to see why Arizona would express the most excitement about the left-hander's pitching potential. He touched 95 mph in his final spring as a Tiger, and even though the fastball typically sat in the low-90s, there could be more in the tank once he turns his full focus to the bump. His upper-70s slider showed good depth, contributing to his whiff rate, and he sold his mid-80s sinking changeup well out of the hand. Grice doesn't need to show much effort out of his large frame, helping the belief that he'll limit walks even more so on the pro side. There's a lot more projection here than is standard for a college arm, especially of this size, and Grice's development -- particularly when it comes to adding velo -- should be followed closely in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wing appeared destined to play shortstop and pitch at Loyola Marymount before his stuff made a jump during his senior season at Scotts Valley (Calif.) HS, which also spawned Robbie Erlin. The Cubs liked his athleticism and projectability enough to select him in the fourth round last July and paid him more than double slot value at $1.5 million. The son of White Sox 2001 second-rounder Ryan Wing, a left-hander who topped out at Triple-A, he'll make his pro debut in 2026. Wing's fastball went from 88-90 mph at the 2024 Area Code Games to 90-96 with high spin rates plus nice carry and armside run last spring. He also tightened his curveball, which shows signs of becoming a plus offering in the upper 70s with downer break. His low-80s changeup has similar action and is still a work progress but looks like it will be a useful third pitch. More athletic than most pitchers, Wing moves down the mound well to create plenty of extension in his delivery, He repeats his mechanics well and provides strikes with ease. He'll need to add some strength but could develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally trained as an outfielder in Venezuela, Cayama didn't attract much scouting interest until he shifted to the mound and quickly began reaching the low 90s with his fastball. After signing for $147,500 in 2024, he had to overcome a bout with pneumonia before working in short stints in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He earned Rookie-level Arizona Complex League All-Star honors in his U.S. debut after leading the circuit in average-against (.191), WHIP (1.06) and strikeout rate (28 percent), then made a Single-A cameo at age 18. Cayama has more feel than most teenage pitchers, showing the ability to work up and down with his fastballs and throw his two secondary offerings with horizontal action in opposite directions. He rides four-seamers up in the zone and sinks two-seamers at the knees while working at 92-94 mph and touching 97 with his heaters. His solid low-80s slider has tight spin and breaks away from righties, while his mid-80s changeup fades and sinks toward them. Cayama uses his athleticism to repeat his three-quarters delivery and provide regular strikes. His control and fastball command weren't as sharp as usual when he got rocked at Single-A, though that was more a matter of fatigue than a long-term concern. He's not very physical but has the stuff and polish to succeed as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gallagher got off to a promising start at Santa Barbara, earning Big West Conference freshman of the year honors in 2022, but his progress was halted by Tommy John surgery that wiped out what would have been his sophomore season. He came back stronger than ever, posting a 2.22 ERA while leading all Division I pitchers in WHP (0.84), leading to the Cubs nabbing him in the sixth round of the 2024 Draft. He had just earned a promotion from High-A to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball when he was shipped to the Twins in the Willi Castro Trade Deadline deal, finishing off the season with Double-A Wichita. The 6-foot-4 Gallagher is more about his feel for pitching than wow stuff. His fastball sat around 91 mph during his first full season, but it has a chance to play above its velocity because of its impressive induced vertical break and his ability to command it well. He relies on his changeup and slider to miss bats, with an upper-70s cambio that has good depth and a low-80s slider that combined to elicit a 46-percent miss rate in 2025, per Synergy. He’ll still fold in a get-me-over upper-70s curve at times. With a simple and repeatable delivery, Gallagher has always been an excellent strike-thrower. The Twins are hoping there’s a little more velocity to tease out of him so he can be a starter long-term, with some chance of him being an effective multi-inning reliever or swingman, kind of like a Pierson Ohl type with better overall stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Yankees at the start of the 2018-19 international signing period for $350,000, Escotto jumped on prospect radars with an impressive debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019, when he finished with a .981 OPS. He was dealt to the Pirates before the 2021 season as part of the return for Jameson Taillon and while he scuffled at times with a leap to full-season ball, there were encouraging signs of development. In many ways Escotto held his own as a teenager in the Low-A Southeast and hit well out of the gate, though he ran into a bit of a wall and his production suffered as the season wore on. He’s strong and physical, showing bat speed and strength to impact the baseball from the right side of the plate. Registering excellent exit velocities, Escotto has the chance to hit for average and plenty of power. There was a good amount of swing-and-miss to his game last year, but the young infielder did offset it somewhat with a solid walk rate. There have been questions about whether Escotto can stick at shortstop given that he’s an average runner, but the Pirates like his footwork, hands and arm and think his body and frame give him the chance to stick there long-term. The makeup and maturity that made the organization feel confident in sending him to full-season ball last year should help him make adjustments from that season and take off from there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals took a liking to the state of Tennessee, taking players from there with their first three Draft picks in 2025. In between fifth overall selection Liam Doyle and 72nd Tanner Franklin -- both University of Tennessee pitchers -- St. Louis went with the state’s Gatorade Player of the Year in Mitchell out of Houston High School in Germantown. Mitchell signed for above slot with a $2.25 million bonus instead of heading to Georgia Tech. Some evaluators believe the left-handed-hitting Mitchell possesses one of the best pure hit tools among prep bats in the 2025 class. Starting with his hands held high, he coils like a spring to generate a quick stroke without much movement from his head. His strike-zone judgment was impressive as an amateur. There’s room to add strength in his 6-foot-2 frame too, and he could get to average pop by the time he reaches the Majors. Mitchell will flash plus speed, but scouts questioned whether he could stick at shortstop long term with average range and arm strength. The Cardinals announced him as a center fielder on Draft Day and intend to cycle him between the grass and dirt beginning in the Florida State League, where he’ll play along fellow shortstop Yairo Padilla. Mitchell took well to a throwing program that could aid his chances at being valuable at either spot up the middle as St. Louis tries to find the right defensive home for his athleticism.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After an uneven college career that began at Texas Tech, the Orioles drafted Wells in the fourth round out of Texas State in 2023, betting they could add polish to Wells’ tantalizing raw stuff. He struggled in his first full season of pro ball, finishing with a 6.71 ERA and .280 BAA over 60 ⅓ IP, but seemed to turn a corner last season following offseason workouts with Nathan Eovaldi. Wells returned to the mound throwing harder and proved more durable, seeing much better results by pitching his way to Triple-A by the end of the year. Wells is a right-hander with a bulldog mentality on the mound who throws everything hard. His fastball lives in the upper-90s and can hit triple-digits, and Wells has the ability to ride it up in the zone or sink it to generate ground balls. He’ll employ three secondary offerings with a low-80s curve that features depth and a harder sweeper, and he swapped in a 90 mph cutter last year in place of a changeup he grew out of the habit of using. Wells commanded everything better in his second season and throws enough strikes, but there is also a feeling his pure stuff is good enough to miss more bats than he did. Though the Orioles have developed him as a starter, Wells only completed more than five innings in two of his first 46 pro starts. His premium fastball and solid breaking stuff could be nasty in relief, and may destine Wells for more of a multi-inning fireman or swingman type of role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest bargain in the Dodgers' loaded 2023 international class, Nieves signed for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic that March. He repeated the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, logging a 5.43 ERA in two seasons there before taking off in his U.S. debut last summer. He was one of the more unhittable pitchers in the lower Minors, holding opponents to a .171 average with a 27 percent strikeout rate between Rookie ball and Single-A. Nieves' fastball velocity made a jump in 2025, sitting in the mid-90s and reaching 99 mph, and he found more success after switching from a fairly straight four-seamer to a two-seamer with run and sink. His mid-80s slider features devastating sweep at its best and he can also tighten it into a harder cutter. His nascent mid-80s changeup can flash some intriguing fade and sink. Nieves has a quick, whippy arm action and a lean 6-foot-3 frame that can add plenty of muscle, so there may be more velocity to come. He's still learning to keep his long limbs in sync and repeat his delivery, so the consistency of his secondary pitches and his control are still works in progress. But he has as much helium as any pitcher in the system and could become a future mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Queens native, Sime was a source of constant intrigue on the summer showcase circuit for his elite velocity, and he started to show a little more polish during his senior year at Brooklyn’s Poly Prep Country Day School, including in two outings at USA Baseball’s National High School Invitational. He made three appearances in the MLB Draft League (including one at Citi Field in an All-Star matchup against the Cape Cod League) to round out his résumé, and the Nationals selected him in the fourth round last July. The LSU commit signed for $2 million, almost triple the slot value for the 111th overall pick. The 6-foot-4 right-hander first touched triple digits when he was 16 years old, and he’s continued to pump premium heat since then, eclipsing 100 mph five times during his stint in the Draft League. Sime has good life on the four-seamer too, and he was able to blow it by batters in multiple settings. His low-80s curveball shows off his feel for spin with nice drop and a little sweep, and in his first spring, he’s toying with a gyro slider that would give him a harder breaking ball on top of that. His 85-88 mph changeup can fool batters with its velo differential and armside movement, but it’s likely to be his third pitch at best. Sime can have a long arm action, and he struggled as an amateur at times to land his stuff consistently in the zone. Professional batters will be more willing to lay off his power arsenal if he can’t throw more strikes, so there’s real reliever risk here even for someone who will still only be 18 on Opening Day 2026. Sime should be an interesting project for the Nationals’ new player development apparatus in its first year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bullard’s stock was on the rise heading into the 2025 Draft but he had what was considered a strong commitment to Texas A&M. The Blue Jays took a swing by selecting him in the 12th round and signed him for $1,697,500 ($1,547,500 of which counted toward their bonus pool), the largest bonus ever given to a player in that round. Since then, the club has only been more impressed as Bullard has packed on 15 pounds of muscle and shown an excellent work ethic in the early days of his development. Scouts who believe in Bullard like his bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate, but the left-handed swing is ahead of the right-handed swing at this point. He employs more of a gap-to-gap approach right now and makes a lot of ground-ball contact, but he also has bat speed and a projectable 6-foot-2 frame, giving the Blue Jays plenty to work with. The question becomes whether Bullard will have true standout tools or if he’ll be solid across the board. That said, Toronto has done well with the “solid” types, tinkering with offensive approaches to fit their identity. Bullard owns plus speed and knows how to use it on the bases and in the outfield. He displays good instincts in center field and should be able to remain there in Toronto's system. He has average arm strength and could handle the other two outfield spots if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a freshman reliever at Westmont College in California, Youngerman helped the Warriors win a NAIA Championship, then moved into the rotation as the school moved to Division II status. He went from a very strong showing in the Cape Cod League to Oklahoma State and put up impressive numbers while shuttling between the rotation and bullpen. The Phillies nabbed him in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft, signing him for right around slot. A strong 6-foot-3 right-hander, Youngerman could have the goods to start. He leans very heavily on his fastball – he threw it more than 70 percent of the time for the Cowboys last year – which that sat 92-94 mph and topped out at 96, with a little more in the tank when he’s relieving. He commands the pitch well, getting a fair amount of swing and miss as well as a lot of chase on the pitch. His other offerings – a tight mid-80s slider and a fading changeup he throws about as hard – are not as consistently effective, though both can miss bats. He limited walks throughout his college career, another reason why he should get every chance to refine his secondary pitches while developing as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Hechavarria, a Cuba native, out of the Dominican Republic in June 2024, nearly three months after his 21st birthday. He got his feet wet in the Dominican Summer League shortly thereafter with the results one would expect for an older arm in that circuit (1.84 ERA, 57 strikeouts in 49 innings) and jumped stateside for 2025, first in the FCL before moving to Single-A and High-A. With a combined 2.28 ERA and strong peripherals over 86 2/3 innings, Hechavarria’s second season as a pro was a success in nearly every way. Hechavarria stands 6-foot-4, bringing plenty of mound presence, and he throws from a high release. His four-seam fastball touches 96-97 mph and is generally 93-95 with good carry out of the high slot with some armside run to boot. He’ll mix in a sinker around the same velo for a different look, too. An upper-80s slider actually acts as his primary weapon. It’s a tight offering with less than an inch of gloveside movement on average and it tunnels well off the heaters until it’s too late, diving below bats. It gets a ton of whiffs against lefties, helping Hechavarria run reverse splits despite a subpar changeup. Coming off a nice jump in workload, the Blue Jays could look to push Hechavarria past 100 innings this season, and he’s ready to be challenged more. He has seemed to improve as the seasons went on -- and with each promotion in 2025 -- which left the Blue Jays very impressed. If Hechavarria can miss more bats, this is a different conversation entirely, but he currently profiles as a back-end starter who could eat some serious innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a freshman, Powell took over as UCLA’s closer and held on to the job until the 2020 season was ended prematurely. He racked up 26 saves, second in school history behind only David Berg, and was quickly becoming one of the best relief pitching options in the Draft class this spring, with a 20/2 K/BB ratio while allowing just three hits and no runs over 9 1/3 innings in eight appearances. Powell isn’t one of those college relievers you wonder about whether he could start at the next level. The nation’s Stopper of the Year as a sophomore, the 6-foot right-hander is bullpen only, but the type who could move quickly. He typically sits in the low 90s with his fastball and is regularly up to 96 mph. It’s his slider, though, that’s the real separator. It’s a filthy out pitch that gets a ton of swings and misses, a plus pitch for sure. Powell does have a changeup, but it’s that electric fastball-slider combination that has peaked scouts’ interest. With a loud delivery, he’s had trouble with command, but was finding the strike zone more consistently this spring and throws enough strikes to profile well in the back of a bullpen, a role he relishes, with the makeup to close games at the next level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers hadn’t used a Draft pick in the top two rounds on a college pitcher since Ty Madden in 2021 until they selected Witherspoon with the 62nd overall pick last summer. It was an interesting selection not just because of Detroit’s recent trend toward high school and college hitters on Day 1, but also the type of college pitcher selected. While Witherspoon’s twin brother and Oklahoma teammate Kyson was a sure first-rounder, Malachi’s mercurial results with a similar arsenal had dropped him to third-round projections in some places, with a potential reliever tag weighing on his stock. The Tigers are comfortable looking past results and more toward current and future arsenals, and Witherspoon, who turned down an over-slot bonus from the Diamondbacks as a 12th-rounder out of high school three years earlier, signed with them for a $1,448,700 bonus. There’s a lot to like about Witherspoon’s arsenal, from a power fastball that reaches the upper 90s to a buckling curveball and tight slider. The conundrum that teams faced with him in the Draft was an inconsistency throwing strikes and a struggle to repeat his mechanics. He walked 3.9 batters per nine innings for his college career, and hit 17 batters over 74⅓ innings in his final season at Oklahoma. He worked exclusively out of the stretch with a three-quarters arm slot in college, but there should be some refinement in the pros from the Tigers' pitching development department. The Tigers built a renowned pitching instructional group in part to help get value picks out of the Draft, and Witherspoon will be one of its most interesting tests. Team officials say he’ll get the chance to work as a starter. With improvements in command and a more refined delivery, he would have mid-rotation potential. If not, there are worse fates than getting a late-inning reliever from a second-round pick.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A breakout performance in the Cape Cod League in which he batted .344 with a .464 OBP and a strong junior year at the University of Michigan helped Elliott raise his stock in time for the 2022 MLB Draft, where the A’s selected him in Competitive Balance Round B. He was slated to get some action in the Arizona Complex League as part of his intro to the organization, but a quad injury sidelined him after just one game. Elliott has a quick bat that enables him to consistently hit quality fastballs for line drives all over the field. There has been some debate as to how much power he might develop, though an increase in home run totals from five in 2021 to 16 in 2022 should give some hope that he can grow into average power at the very least. He has shown some deficiencies against left-handed pitching that he’ll need to improve. Above-average speed and solid defensive skills make Elliott an asset anywhere in the outfield, though right field was his full-time position at Michigan. The A’s hope to get a good look at him as he enters his first full professional season for a better understanding of his overall game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of two North Atlanta (Ga.) HS players to fit in the first five rounds of the 2023 Draft, Anderson went in the third round to the Red Sox and outfielder Isaiah Drake got popped in the fifth by the Braves. Anderson's offensive upside attracted scouts early in his prep career and landed him a well-over-slot $1.5 million bonus. He made a 12-game pro debut, striking out 15 times and spending a week in Single-A. A switch-hitter, Anderson turns his swing loose more often and does more damage from the right side. He has a balanced setup and displayed the ability to make adjustments and deal with breaking pitches as an amateur. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to develop into at least a 20-homer threat, though he'll need to launch more balls in the air because he presently makes too much ground-ball contact. While Anderson played shortstop at North Atlanta, he has fringy speed and immediately moved to third base as a pro. His strong arm registered fastballs up to 91 mph as a high school pitcher and fits well at the hot corner. The best case is that he becomes an offensive second baseman, and Boston will see whether he has enough quickness for the keystone in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $100,000 by the Nationals at the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, Yean first provided a glimpse of return on that investment when he made his United States debut in 2019 and pitched his way from the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League to the short-season New York-Penn League. He created a lot of buzz at the Nationals’ instructional league program last fall, and the Pirates clearly noticed, acquiring the young right-hander in the deal that sent Josh Bell to Washington. His first year with his new organization, and his first taste of full-season ball, were uneven as he struggled with command in 2021. Yean has added a lot of strength since signing, which has led to some serious upticks in velocity. His fastball now touches 97 mph on a regular basis and will often sit in the mid-90s with life and good angle. He features both a power sinker and a four-seamer up in the zone. His upper-80s slider with depth might be a plus out pitch in time, and he’s shown good feel for his changeup, a pitch that’s come along nicely of late. While he’s gotten stronger and thrown harder, Yean has shown good athleticism on the mound and an ability to repeat his delivery, though he lost feel for the strike zone for much of 2021. He still has every chance to grow into a pitcher with average control of three above-average or better pitches eventually, a profile which could make him a future starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Thompson went undrafted out of high school in Texas in 2022 and instead headed to Vanderbilt, where he became a starter as a sophomore and the Friday night arm as a junior. He posted a 4.00 ERA and struck out 122 over 90 innings in his final spring as a Commodore, and his 32.1 percent strikeout rate ranked fifth-best among SEC arms (one spot ahead of Oklahoma’s Kyson Witherspoon). Thompson was selected by the Brewers in the second round of the Draft and signed for slot value at $1,560,200. The 6-foot southpaw doesn’t pop for velocity with a fastball around 91-94 mph (topping out at 96 in college), but it got incredible induced vertical break from his lowish release point. That, combined with the way he can hide the ball until late, led to a ton of whiff and chase on the four-seamer. He moved more toward a low-80s slider as a junior because it’s a breaking pitch he can throw in the zone more often than his upper-70s curveball. His low-80s changeup gets a ton of separation from the heater, leading to many empty swings in college, but pros may not chase it as much below the zone where the pitch lived frequently. Thompson’s control was solid in college thanks to his repeatable delivery, and if he can land in the zone with more intent, he could unlock perhaps above-average marks in that category in the Milwaukee system. A touch more velocity would send the fastball into easy plus territory with its movement metrics, but even as is, there could be enough here for a No. 4 starter profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A center fielder, first baseman, starter and closer at Tulane, Lombardi did it all in college. His Draft outlook was much better on the mound, where he saw a lot of improvement his junior year. That included a velocity increase and led to 73 strikeouts in 42 innings. Lombardi turned that into a second-round selection by the Royals in the 2025 Draft, and he received a $1,297,500 signing bonus. He began his professional career in Arizona, where he pitched in the Royals’ Bridge League and instructional league games. Mainly a reliever at Tulane, Lombardi got things done with his fastball and curveball, which both generated a lot of in-zone swing-and-miss. The heater sits 93-95 mph but runs up to 97 with lots of vert, while the 78-81 mph curveball has a sharp break. Lombardi has some feel for a changeup but he needs to develop it more to turn it into the above-average pitch some evaluators think it might be. He’s added a slider since joining the Royals mainly as a bridge pitch because his other pitches cover different parts of his movement plot, so the slider gives hitters something else to honor in the zone. Lombardi is very athletic -- which makes sense given his time in center field -- and brings that to his delivery, moving well down the mound. He didn’t throw a ton of strikes in college, so finding the zone will be a focus for him as a pro. Lombardi’s two-way status meant he hasn’t spent as much time on the mound as a typical college pitcher, so there’s development to be had here, both with his stuff but also his strength and throwing program. For that reason, the Royals might be a little more cautious with him, but there’s a ton of upside in his raw stuff and athleticism. He’ll develop as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Already 19 years old when the 2025 international signing period opened, Marquez signed that January for just $10,000 out of Mexico. The early returns point to him being a steal. The Phillies skipped him over the Dominican Summer League and sent him to the Florida Complex League for his debut. He threw so well over 10 outings there that he got moved up to full-season Clearwater and continued to miss bats there. Pitching all of this season at age 20, Marquez reminds some in the organization of a third- or fourth-rounder talent-wise. He can throw strikes with three pitches, the best being his 80 mph changeup that features a ton of sink and tailing action away from left-handed hitters, getting an absurd amount of swing-and-miss and chase while also eliciting weak contact on the ground. His fastball, which sits 92-94 mph and tops out at 96, is also a worm-killer, thrown with good sink. His feel for spin isn’t as strong, but there’s faith it will keep improving, with his slider being a bit better when he throws it harder with cutter-like action to it. The 6-foot-2 Marquez does have some projection remaining, and there could be more velocity to come as he fills out his frame. Marquez is athletic on the mound, and despite some excessive head movement, repeats his delivery well and fills up the zone. If he can find a breaking ball to trust and show he can handle the workload, he has the chance to be a back-end starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Washington state, Watson spent one season apiece at Cal Lutheran and San Joaquin Delta College and got drafted by the Mariners in the 20th round of the 2023 Draft before heading to USC. He moved from the Trojans' bullpen to their starting rotation, and he flashed enough promising stuff in the longer role for the Mets to take him in the seventh round and sign him for around slot at $281,300 in 2024. Watson climbed from Single-A to Double-A in his first full season and finished with a 2.60 ERA over 121 1/3 innings; his 142 strikeouts were fourth-most in the New York system. Despite the increased workload in the Minors, Watson experienced a velocity bump across the board in 2025. He averaged around 95 mph with a pair of fastballs, and his four-seamer shows promising ride and a flat approach angle from a relatively low release. His mid-80s slider gives him a gloveside option that can force opponents to expand the zone, while his upper-80s change moves even more horizontally armside. Because of the latter, he ran reverse splits last year, holding lefties to a .186 average and .561 OPS. Watson also shows an 88-91 mph cutter for a bridge pitch, but it can get hit hard with limited movement. With some length in his delivery, Watson lacks pinpoint accuracy with his arsenal, and he walked more than 10 percent of his batters faced at each level in 2025. As things currently stand, he may lack a true plus pitch, though it’s possible the fastball velo would play up in shorter stints. Still, a bevy of above-average options will keep getting him starting looks in a system loaded with upper-level arms.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A legitimate two-way player during his Mississippi high school days, Morris initially headed to college to both hit and pitch. He put down the bat after his freshman year in 2023 and struggled with his control over his first two seasons pitching out of Ole Miss’ bullpen. Things clicked more during his junior season, helping him land in the third round of the Draft to the Reds, who let him get his professional feet wet with Single-A Daytona. It was only a handful of innings, but he did toss three hitless frames in the playoffs to help catapult the Tortugas into the Florida State League Championship Series. While the Rebels employed him almost exclusively as a reliever, the Reds believe he has every chance to start, and will allow him to develop as such. Moving his arm slot higher helped him find more velocity, with a fastball that topped out at 99 mph, albeit with more downhill plane than life, so it doesn’t miss that many bats. His best pitch, though, is his low-90s cutter that dives, a pitch that led to a 45 percent miss and 40 percent chase rate in college last year. He has an effective upper-80s slider with similar shape that can also miss bats. Morris has a no-nonsense, super-competitive demeanor on the mound and showed in 2025 that he can find the strike zone consistently. He could use a changeup and some improved shape to his fastball, but he has the frame and other pitches to allow him to handle a starting workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: James had the look of a potential first-round pick after showing out as an underclassman on the showcase circuit and with Team USA’s 18-and-under team in 2023 but couldn’t replicate that same level of success in the summer before his senior year, including going 1-for-12 with six strikeouts at the East Coast Pro Showcase. He rebounded a bit in the spring at Davie County HS and won Gatorade’s Player of the Year honors in North Carolina as a result. Some scouts thought he was headed to Mississippi, but the Nationals selected him in the fifth round and signed him for $2.5 million, tied for the second-highest bonus in their 2025 class. A 6-foot infielder, James added weight going into his Draft year, trading off athleticism for strength in the process. With that additional impact, he profiles as a possible 20-homer hitter, especially if he can maintain his bat speed on the pro side. The focus on driving the ball also came with a regression in swing decisions, and he bit on a good number of non-fastballs outside the zone during his 2024 showcases. His right-handed swing has looked smoother in the past, and getting back to those mechanics would help his ability to hit for average in the pros. James has the actions, hands and above-average arm strength to handle shortstop, but his fringy speed limits his range on the dirt. With Eli Willits also in the organization, James is more likely to be a better fit at second or third base, and his arm could even work in a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox failed to sign Ehrhard as a 13th-rounder from a Florida high school in 2021, then nabbed him with a fourth-round selection in 2024 after his power blossomed during his junior season at Oklahoma State. He reached Double-A six weeks into his first full pro season, then went to Los Angeles along with fellow outfield prospect James Tibbs in a July trade for Dustin May. He batted .272/.374/.439 with 46 extra-base hits and 37 steals in 123 games between High-A and Double-A. While Ehrhard may be more of a good fourth outfielder than an everyday player, he can do a little bit of everything and his best attribute is getting on base. He controls the strike zone and grinds out at-bats, making consistent hard contact and showing the ability to launch balls in the air to his pull side. The Dodgers believe they can smooth out his right-handed swing and help him unlock some more hitting ability and power. Ehrhard has solid speed and good instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He has 41 steals in 46 attempts (89 percent) in 145 pro games and can play all three outfield spots while providing average arm strength. He's at least an average defender in center field and solid on the corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best contact hitters in the 2025 college class, Cohen set a Big Ten Conference record with 56 hits in league play (30 games) and a Rutgers mark with 24 doubles last spring while batting .387 with a 5 percent strikeout rate. He gave Rutgers a player drafted in the first three rounds for the third straight year, following Ryan Lasko and Joshua Kuroda-Grauer (both Athletics) and signed for an under-slot $847,500 in the third round. He batted .327 in 28 regular-season games and .438 in the playoffs to help Single-A San Jose win the California League championship. Cohen's efficient left-handed stroke and disciplined approach continued to translate into repeated contact during his pro debut. While he has undeniable bat-to-ball skills, he's also an extreme ground-ball and opposite-field hitter who totaled four homers in three college seasons and slugged .402 at San Jose. A 410-foot blast at the Draft Combine and surprisingly high exit velocities hint at perhaps average raw power, and San Francisco believes it can help him add some strength and elevate balls more often to get to 12-15 homers per season. Cohen enhances his solid-to-plus speed with keen instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He played mostly right field at Rutgers but has enough range for center, where he played well at Single-A, which prompted another club to tell the Giants he gave them Steve Finley vibes. While he has average arm strength and can play all three outfield spots, he'll profile best if he can stick up the middle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After shining with the bat as an All-Big Ten Conference first-team selection in each of his three seasons at Indiana, Taylor, who set the school's career home run record with 54, then followed that up with a strong showing in the Cape Cod League, was drafted by the A’s in 2025 as a second-round pick and signed over slot with a bonus of $2.5 million. Getting his professional career started at Single-A Stockton shortly after, he flashed some of that pop by hitting .264 with six home runs and five doubles in 28 games, making a solid first impression. Taylor has the tools to become a plus hitter for both average and power with a good feel for the zone. He’s very disciplined during his batting practice and sprays the ball around the field. Once game time rolls around, the power shows up, hitting the ball extremely hard and driving it out to all fields. There is some tendency to chase that he will need to cut down on, but the A’s see a hitter who also happens to bring a ton of power. Defense is a clear point of improvement for Taylor. His speed, arm strength and defensive instincts are lacking in the outfield, and some of that may have been due to limited practice on a regular basis in college. The A’s see some things they can clean up with his footwork and arm, and will work with him on improving that aspect of his game with the belief that he can become at least an average defender, likely in a corner outfield spot. But it’s the bat that has the organization extremely excited for his first full year of pro ball, and it will determine his ability to rise through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Livingston didn’t crack the Hebron Christian Academy (Dacula, Ga.) rotation until his senior year, but he had a lot of interesting traits, including a quick arm, good present velocity and a projectable body at 6-foot-4. The D-backs selected him in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft and signed him away from a Georgia commitment with a $1 million bonus, thus making Livingston the highest-selected prep pitcher from the Peach State since Dylan Lesko went 15th overall in 2022. The big right-hander showed he could sit 92-94 during his final spring as an amateur, and he showed two fastball looks in his four-seamer and two-seamer. He could be higher than that velo in some outings, and it was encouraging when he sat in the mid 90s and touched 97.6 at the Draft Combine in, of all places, Arizona. His feel for spin wasn’t always consistent, but his low-80s slider was ahead of his upper-70s curveball as a potential weapon. He also showed a low-80s changeup that could be effective as a pro. Livingston has added nice strength since signing, and that’s promising because some evaluators believed he was a future 100 mph candidate in high school. His athletic delivery looks like one that should bring at least average control and keep walks from holding him back. He’ll get plenty of runway as a starter in his new organization, and finding an above-average pitch to pair with the fastball will be a deciding factor in his future role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Mexican-born Gonzalez attended high school in Arizona and became a two-way player at New Mexico, where he won 11 games in three seasons. He stood out more as an outfielder, batting .361/.500/.598 with 14 steals and a school-record 58 walks in 2017. A third-round pick that June, he posted an .866 OPS (second in the system to überprospect Eloy Jimenez) with 40 doubles (fourth in the Minors) in his first full pro season. Gonzalez has a natural left-handed stroke and laces line drives all over the field with his disciplined approach. He's more hitter than slugger, but he uses his lower half well and should provide double-digit home runs annually along with a healthy amount of doubles. He's an average runner whose instincts outshine his potential as a basestealer. Gonzalez has bounced between all three outfield positions in pro ball, seeing the majority of his time in center field. He projects as an average defender up the middle, where he profiles best offensively, and as a solid one on the corners. He ran his fastball into the low-90s in college and has more than enough arm strength for right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mace almost signed with the Reds for fourth-round money as a 12th-round pick out of a Florida high school, and he could have gone in the first two rounds in 2020 if his price tag hadn't scared off teams in that shortened five-round Draft. After returning for a fourth college season at Florida, he improved his slider/cutter and posted a career-best strikeout rate of 11.3 per nine innings. Signed for a slightly over-slot $1.1 million in the supplemental second round, he'll make his pro debut in 2022. Mace struggled to find a reliable breaking ball in his first three years with the Gators, but now his mid-80s slider/cutter is his best pitch and grades as plus at its best. While his four-seam fastball can reach 97 mph, it's fairly straight and gets hit, and his low-90s two-seamer with sink is more effective. His 78-82 mph curveball has regressed and he doesn't have much trust in a mid-80s changeup that's too firm and has modest fade. While Mace lacks overpowering stuff, he uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create good extension that enables his pitches to get on hitters more quickly than expected.
