His track record of throwing strikes helps his chances of making it as a back-of-the-rotation starter, though he'll likely need a second better-than-average pitch to go with his slider/cutter. He'll be 23 when he throws his first professional pitch, so he could move quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Cutter: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Hardin spent two years at Daytona State College before transferring to Mississippi State, only to never break out of the Bulldogs' bullpen. The Brewers still took him in the 12th round in 2024, signed him for $147,500 and transitioned him to a starting role on the pro side with impressive early results. Hardin posted a 2.72 ERA and a 1.18 WHIP with 96 strikeouts over 96 innings between High-A and Double-A in his first full season. His 4.4 percent walk rate and 20.4 percent K/BB rate were tops among Brewers farmhands with at least 90 frames in ’25. The 6-foot-2 right-hander sits 92-95 mph with his four-seam fastball, and he makes up for the average velocity by generating decent ride from a low release and good extension. He’ll wear out the top rail of the zone with that four-seamer and then drop in a low-80s slider that gets good sweep to the lower gloveside corner. An upper-80s cutter isn’t quite as sharp as others in its pitch class, but the jump in velo from the slider allows it to sneak up on lefties, leading to soft contact. Hardin has an upper-80s changeup for opposite-side bats, but it’s too firm, leading to issues with splits. Hardin flows well on the mound and kept pumping strikes at each level in 2025. That type of control helped his case not only to start but to remain in a bulkier role in his first taste of the pros. Better batters might have more success against him in the zone, and that’s something that will be tested at the upper levels. If his gains continue, Hardin could factor into Milwaukee’s rotation depth by the second half of his age-24 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lamkin was on Draft prospect lists as a prep pitcher in 2022, but he was considered unsignable away from his Texas A&M commitment. He went to college and was an immediate contributor, pitching in big SEC and NCAA moments. Lamkin was one of the best college lefty options in the 2025 Draft, and the Royals selected him with their Competitive Balance Round B pick at No. 71 overall. He stayed in Arizona after he was drafted and pitched in the Royals’ fall instructional league. With some funkiness in his delivery, Lamkin’s 91-93 mph fastball plays up quite a bit, but he also showed up to spring in ‘26 with a little more velo. He’s big and strong and put on some good weight over the offseason, which helps, so whether that sticks throughout the season remains to be seen. His above-average, 83-85 mph gyro slider might look a little cutter-ish, but it’s short and tight. Lamkin sells his 84-86 mph changeup well and is continuing to work on that pitch, and he added an upper-70s curveball when he joined the Royals to give him something with more depth against right-handed hitters. Lamkin’s delivery has some moving parts to it, but it helps his game; he hides the ball well, has a short arm action and it gets on hitters quickly. He’s a solid strike thrower, so the delivery doesn’t seem to hinder him much right now. Lamkin has a good foundation and is advanced as a college pitcher who knows what he’s doing on the mound. He receives high marks for the way he evaluates himself and his outings. As long as those secondaries keep developing, he has back-end rotation potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paniagua was a little older than many international signees when he joined the Cardinals at 17 for $160,000 out of the Dominican Republic in December 2017. He didn’t reach full-season ball until 2021 and was primarily a reliever -- and a successful one with 62 strikeouts in 46 1/3 innings -- during that first spin at Single-A Palm Beach. Paniagua returned to the Florida State League as a starter in ’22 and impressed again with a 2.18 ERA, 0.96 WHIP and 107 K’s in 99 frames. He ended the year with eight more mundane outings for High-A Peoria, and the Cardinals chose to leave Paniagua off the 40-man when he was Rule 5-eligible, though he went unpicked. The 6-foot-1 right-hander works with a four-seamer and a sinker around 91-93 mph, occasionally touching 95, and there’s still the chance more velo could be coming because it looks like he still hasn’t fully grown into his figure. His upper-70s curveball showed great depth and 12-to-6 vertical break, and A-ball hitters -- especially righties -- couldn’t touch it. A mid-80s fading changeup could be helpful against batters from both sides, but lefties still had the lion’s share of success against Paniagua in 2022. Paniagua likely wasn’t much of a Rule 5 threat last year because he lacked success above the Single-A level, but with his three-pitch mix and solid ability to pitch in the zone, there’s still a potential starting pitcher here in the big leagues. That extra velo would go a long way toward helping that projection. Considering Paniagua is entering his age-23 season, the clock is ticking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best defenders in the 2022 international signing class, Gonzalez signed with Seattle for $1.3 million out of the Dominican Republic and could join a long list of success stories the franchise has had there. A slick-fielding shortstop, he projects to have the most potential to stick there long term as he grows and develops as anyone his age and rank within the organization. Despite being known more for his glove, Gonzalez does make hard contact and has a projectable body expected to add strength, which can ultimately add a little more pop to his bat. What he lacks in power, he makes up for in hitting ability and potential. He’s an average runner. On defense, he shows plus hands with smooth actions and is expected to be a plus defender. He projects to have an average arm and his range is improving. Gonzalez makes playing defense look easy. The Mariners are eager to see what he does in his first season of pro ball in the Dominican Summer League, which could put him on a fast track to the U.S. and the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League come fall.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2025 international signing period, the Dodgers’ gain turned out to also be the Pirates’ gain. When Los Angeles committed to signing Roki Sasaki, they could no longer also sign Morel. The Pirates were able to jump in and ink the infielder for $1.8 million, then watched him make a very solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, posting a .287/.425/.414 line to go along with 26 steals. Morel oozes athleticism and projection from his lean 6-foot-4 frame that he’s just starting to fill out. The teenager is a left-handed hitter who is already showing a solid approach. He’s willing to work counts, wait out at-bats and draw walks while also showing plenty of bat-to-ball skills. There’s plenty of bat speed to work with, and it’s easy to dream on him getting to his raw power as he gets more physical. Despite his size, Morel has a legitimate chance to stick at shortstop. He might only have average speed, but his instincts allow that to play up on the bases as well as defensively, showing excellent lateral range and more than enough arm for the premium position. Just 18 for the 2026 season, there’s the chance he’ll outgrow the spot, but there’s no need to worry about moving him yet. With his offensive upside, the Pirates are hoping perhaps Morel can follow a similar track to Top 100 prospect Edward Florentino.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Burlingame, Calif., Moss moved across the country to attend IMG Academy in Bradenton, Fla., when he was in eighth grade. He became a regular on the summer showcase circuit, including appearances at the East Coast Pro Showcase and the Area Code Games, and developed into one of the top-ranked Draft prospects in the state. The Rays reached into their backyard to select Moss with the 67th overall pick in the 2025 Draft, signing him for an above-slot bonus of $2,097,500. Moss’ hit tool is his finest trait, as he seemingly always found a way to get the barrel on the ball in high school despite a number of moving parts in his left-handed swing. He’s a twitchy athlete with plus bat speed, and he combines an ability to control the strike zone with an all-fields approach against all types of pitching. He’s hit-over-power right now, no surprise given his age and experience, but there is some raw power to tap into as he adds strength and learns to leverage his swing more effectively. Moss was primarily a center fielder in high school, and he has shown good instincts in the outfield. He has a solid arm, but the lack of plus speed could push him into a corner spot. The Rays generally give their outfielders a chance to prove they can stick in center, although they’re also quick to expose them to multiple spots in case a move is necessary. Time will tell if his bat can provide corner-outfield power, but the Rays clearly believed in his offensive upside enough to give him the chance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 45 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Ebel has baseball roots as the son of Dodgers third-base coach Dino Ebel, and he put them to good use as a showcase standout at the Area Code Games and High School All-American Game in 2024. He was part of a loaded and widely seen Corona High School squad featuring top 2025 picks Seth Hernandez and Billy Carlson, and while his stock may have slipped a bit as a senior, he still went 32nd overall to the Brewers with the Draft pick Milwaukee picked up for losing Willy Adames in free agency. Ebel signed just below slot at $2.75 million. Entering pro ball, the 6-foot-3 infielder may not have a lot of huge offensive tools, but there are enough pieces to like here. His left-handed swing is a smooth one with good barrel control, and he doesn’t need much of a load to get it going. Ebel faced many questions about his overall impact after hitting the ball on the ground too much as a Corona senior, but he has size to dream on. Average pop could come down the line with added strength under a pro program. Ebel played third base in high school because Carlson was such a wizard at shortstop, and as a below-average runner with a plus arm, he might just end up there long term. Brewers VP of amateur acquisition Tod Johnson noted after the Draft, however, that Ebel's shortstop actions mimicked Corey Seager, who worked with the senior Ebel in Los Angeles, and his overall IQ could paper over some of the other tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Forbes headed to Louisville as a potential two-way player and saw time as a DH/outfielder as a freshman in 2023, even getting at-bats in the Cape Cod League that summer. He broke his left hand in his lone plate appearance of 2024 and didn’t bat again as a collegian after shifting his focus to the mound exclusively that spring. He joined the Cardinals starting corps as a junior, and after working around a flexor strain, he finished with a 4.42 ERA and 117 strikeouts in 71 1/3 innings for Louisville’s College World Series squad. Arizona selected him 29th overall (the pick it received for losing Christian Walker in free agency) and signed him for $3 million. The 6-foot-3 right-hander throws from a low three-quarters delivery that can make him difficult to read. He picked up velocity in the summer before his junior year and sat 94-96 mph throughout the spring, touching 100, with impressive carry and high spin. He has continued to sit mid 90s in workouts heading into his first full season. An 81-85 mph slider shows promising sweep running away from righties and flashes plus. He could turn it into an upper-80s cutter for something sharper in college. Forbes’ upper-80s changeup will require refinement in pro ball as he’ll need a better option than the fastball alone against lefties. Forbes’ delivery comes with energy and verve, and while that might help his explosiveness, it’s also kept him from ever really showing average control to this point. That said, Arizona took him as an upside play considering he isn’t that deep into his time as a full-time pitcher. There could still be more development than your typical big-time college arm with the option of dominating out of the bullpen as a two-pitch righty always a fallback option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After his pandemic-shortened 2020 season saw him pitch sparingly at Florida State, Hubbart made a successful move into the Seminoles' rotation in 2021. He really put himself on the prospect map with a very strong performance in the Cape Cod League that summer, then served as FSU’s effective Saturday starter in 2022, showing enough for the Reds to take him in the third round of the Draft, where he signed for $522,500. As a lefty from the ACC, the easy thing might be to compare Hubbart to new organization-mate Andrew Abbott, though while the two have similar builds and resumes, they have very different personalities. Hubbart will use a three- or four-pitch mix to set up hitters well. His fastball only averaged around 90 mph in his last year at Florida State and topped out at 91 during his brief time with Single-A Daytona after signing, but it plays up a bit beyond the velocity thanks to solid spin rates and carry up in the zone. He can add and subtract from his stuff, manipulating his breaking stuff and showing a distinct curve and slider at times, though he showcased more of the latter during his pro debut. He does a nice job of killing spin on his 79-80 mph changeup. Hubbart profiles as a prototypical college lefty, one who has already impressed the Reds with his feel for pitching. He’s become a very good strike thrower, one who might have a ceiling as a No. 4 or 5 starter but could reach further if he adds some velocity or improves his secondary offerings with pro instruction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $200,000 signing out of Venezuela in 2023, Virahonda played in the Dominican Summer League in both '23 and '24, and with a .510 OPS in the latter campaign, he didn’t look like a player primed for a breakout with a move stateside. Fortunately, that’s exactly what happened after making adjustments heading into his age-19 season. He pushed past the Arizona Complex League in 2025 with a .347/.464/.455 line in 37 games and then held his own with a .256/.362/.357 performance and 108 wRC+ in 33 games at Single-A Visalia. Batting from the right side, Virahonda stays short to the ball with a simple operation and minimal load. He got a bit swing-happy against offspeed pitches in the California League, but nothing overly worrisome for a player making the large jump from the complex to full-season ball. It’s just average raw power right now, but Virahonda did a nice job of upping his line-drive rate with his move to the U.S., and he keeps the ball off the ground, good news for someone with below-average speed. His overall profile earns a boost for the fact that he looks like an above-average, potentially even plus defender behind the plate. Standing at 5-foot-11, he moves well back there to earn good reviews for his receiving and blocking, and he’s quick with his throws, getting the ball out efficiently to limit the opposing running game. Virahonda has blossomed into the best catching prospect in the Arizona system, but now it’s on him to hold onto that status.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When teams sign players from the international amateur free agent market, it’s obviously all about projection and the knowledge it may take years before the organization knows what kind of player they have acquired. In 2022, the Twins managed to get very good early returns on their top two acquisitions: Yasser Mercedes, who received $1.7 million to sign, and Acuña, who got the second-highest bonus from the Twins that period ($869K). Acuña, like Mercedes, found immediate success in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .310 with a .409 OBP. You only have to see Acuña swing once to realize he’s the younger brother of Braves star Ronald Acuña Jr., and that he has a similar setup and swing path. Following his success in the DSL, where Acuña showed an affinity for contact and a solid approach, the Twins won’t tinker with his swing much while letting him get acclimated to playing in the United States, though it’s been noted that he tends to flare balls in the upper half of the zone. It would probably be misguided to dream he’ll have his older brother’s power, but there should be some extra-base thump to come as he matures. Having grown up around the game, Acuña’s feel for what he wants to do is apparent on both sides of the ball. He has looked solid and athletic at shortstop, with excellent hands and a strong arm, and he could even be a plus defender at second should he move to the right side of the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ovalles signed a little later than many in his class when he joined the Mets in November 2019 out of the Dominican Republic, and he missed out on what would have been his first Minor League campaign due to the pandemic the following year. He got off to a solid start with a 2.83 ERA and 0.69 WHIP (third-lowest among the 257 pitchers on the circuit with at least 30 IP) over 35 frames in the Dominican Summer League in 2021 and took a step forward stateside this past season, posting a 4.05 ERA with 66 punchouts in 46 2/3 frames between the Florida Complex and Florida State Leagues. The 6-foot-3 right-hander gained velocity throughout his second pro campaign and was around 93-95 mph, topping out at 97, during his time with Single-A St. Lucie. If the heat wasn’t enough, Ovalles’ fastball also comes with a healthy amount of spin typically in the 2,500-2,700 rpm range, adding to the hope it can be a true plus pitch. His low-80s sweeping slider actually had a higher whiff rate and was dominant against righties. He’d fold in a get-me-over curveball occasionally, and his 83-86 mph changeup can get some swing-and-miss but was pounded by lefties, who had a .948 OPS against Ovalles in a small FSL sample. Ovalles has started and relieved at this early stage, and despite his improved stuff, he’s exhibited decent control too, adding to the hope the arsenal can play over a larger sample. His projectable frame at 6-foot-3 points to the possibility of another level of a repertoire still to come with more experience as he moves into full-season ball for good in his age-20 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a Venezuelan amateur, Cornielly endeared himself to scouts with his clean, athletic delivery and advanced feel for pitching. The Mets signed him for $25,000 at the outset of the 2017-18 international period, and he responded with a strong professional debut the next year in the Dominican Summer League. The right-hander didn’t fare as well last season in his return to the DSL, though he did perform better after a midseason jump over to the Rookie Gulf Coast League, where the 19-year-old impressed club officials with his endurance and aptitude on the mound. With a projectable frame and an innate ability for flooding the zone with strikes, Cornielly has a solid foundation as a starting pitcher. He doesn’t overpower hitters with his stuff, sitting in the low 90s with an above-average changeup and a fringy breaking ball, but he knows how to mix his pitches and commands his fastball better than most hurlers his age. He threw 84 percent of his pitches for strikes and posted a 52/9 K/BB ratio over 46 innings in 2019, all while inducing whiffs at an impressive 23-percent clip. Cornielly’s curveball is his least-advanced pitch, though club officials are optimistic that it will improve as he adds strength and refines his arm action. Cornielly is unique in the sense that he stands out more for his floor than ceiling even though he’s just 19 and has a projectable frame. Adding a bit more velocity could improve the effectiveness of his fastball-changeup combo, but even if he doesn’t, Cornielly still has enough starter qualities to profile to succeed at the back end of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An Alberta native, Piasentin rose up Draft boards in 2025 after showing off his tools in a swing through Arizona during Spring Training. Continuing to expand their presence with draft picks from their own backyard -- or at least their own country -- Toronto swooped in for him in the fifth round in July and signed him for above slot value at $747,500. At 6-foot-3 and 200 pounds, Piasentin is a presence in the box from the left side of the plate. He is all tools at this point and could continue to grow even stronger, so there’s some serious power upside for the Blue Jays to unlock in the coming years. There are some holes in his swing that come along with that, but Piasentin is the type of project that player development groups love, with an exciting combination of physical attributes and an eagerness to grow. The exit velocities will be interesting to watch early on, but his overall offensive game could be a slower burn. With a plus arm, right field feels likelier as Piasentin's long-term home, but he could continue to see some time at third base going forward. The more the Blue Jays can simplify the development process, the better. If his power really pops, then the sky is the limit, but there’s a wide range of outcomes here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in the 2019-20 international class for $290,000 at age-17 out of the Dominican Republic, Sanchez put together his first big year in the system, climbing all the way from the Arizona Complex League to High-A Everett. Why he’s been so under-the-radar and finally found himself is largely rooted in the Mariners’ player development program, which has constantly preached persistence and patience with the middle infielder. After he signed, Sanchez’s hips got a little wider and the defense and range took a dip. But he arrived in 2022 in much better shape, and it translated well into his profile at shortstop. He’s blossomed into a legit defender at the premium position -- arguably the best middle infielder in the system, which could greatly benefit his long-term trajectory. Beyond the glove, a big part of his step forward was simply trusting his approach at the plate. He may not hit for as high of an average as he progresses, but the sneaky power could lead to some surprising production that, coupled with his strong defense, will make up for it, and he’s definitely a high-ceiling player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers signed five high schoolers as nondrafted free agents following the shortened five-round Draft in 2020, compared to a total of 12 by the other 29 clubs. The two best prospects in Texas' group are right-handers Trevor Stephan and Curry, with the latter foregoing a commitment to Bucknell to turn pro for the maximum $20,000 allowed under pandemic rules. He spent two seasons in Rookie ball before making the leap to Single-A on a full-time basis in 2023 and winning Carolina League Pitcher of the Year honors after compiling a 2.30 ERA, .163 opponents' average against and 99 strikeouts in 82 innings. Curry's fastball parks at 92-94 mph and peaks at 96, playing better than its velocity because of its induced vertical break and the extension he creates with his 6-foot-5 frame. His best secondary pitch is a low-80s slider with horizontal and vertical action that overmatched Single-A hitters. His 82-86 mph changeup cuts and sinks, giving him a reliable third option. Curry has a clean delivery and did a better job of keeping his long limbs in sync in 2023, allowing him to throw more strikes. He still needs to add more muscle to his lanky build, and it's possible that he could have two plus pitches and perhaps solid control if he gets stronger and more consistent. He has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter and more upside than most of the Rangers' young pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lodise drew little scouting or recruiting attention as a Georgia high schooler before heading to NCAA Division II Augusta, where he batted .349/.450/.584 with 23 homers and 44 steals in two seasons. Posting similar numbers last spring after transferring to Georgia Tech propelled him into the third round of the 2025 Draft, and he spent a month in High-A after signing for $922,500. His cousin Alex made a similar small college to Atlantic Coast Conference breakout, winning the Dick Howser Trophy at Florida State last spring before the Braves selected him in the second round. Similar to organization favorite Sam Antonacci with his knack for contributing in many phases of the game without loud tools, Lodise has more physical gifts than Antonacci but a little less hitting ability. He's a right-handed hitter with a steady approach, using the entire field and producing surprising exit velocities for a 5-foot-11, 180-pounder. He did struggle in the Cape Cod League and hit .185 during his aggressive assignment to High-A last summer, so he still has to prove he can do damage with wood bats. Lodise combines solid speed with a high baseball IQ, which helped him steal 20 bases in 21 attempts between college and pro ball last year. His instincts also help him get the job done at shortstop, where he displays average range and arm strength. He's a better fit at second base and could wind up as an offensive-minded utilityman who provides constant energy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best Canadian prospects in the 2021 Draft, Bucknam turned down the Blue Jays as a 16th-rounder to attend Louisiana State (before transferring to Dallas Baptist). Toronto came calling once again in 2025, though, and selected Bucknam in the fourth round, signing him for $678,300. He immediately becomes one of the most exciting long-term projects for this development staff, especially given the recent success stories near the top of the system. Bucknam's tight 85-88 mph slider can reach 91, features high spin rates and is a legitimate wipeout pitch, while his low-80s curveball has more depth and is nearly as effective. His fastball stands out more for its velocity -- usually sitting near 94-95 mph -- than its life or ability to miss bats. He achieves some fade with his upper-80s changeup, though it's too firm and he struggles to land it for strikes at this point in his development. That pitch will be key to his repertoire long-term. The Blue Jays planned to give Bucknam every opportunity to start, but that was put on hold when he dealt with forearm tightness in the spring and later underwent season-ending elbow surgery before he even debuted in the system. Down the road when healthy, the organization could choose to max out Bucknam’s heater and impressive breaking ball in a shorter role, but his talent is worth exploring as a starter first, assuming the stuff and command returns after recovery and rehab.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After investing heavily in pitching at the top of the Draft from 2015 to 2021, the Tigers have pivoted toward offense in recent years with their early picks and pitching projects later on. Sears was a Day 2 pick in 2023 after struggling to a 6.24 ERA in his lone season at UConn despite 74 strikeouts over 62 innings. He has carried a relatively consistent strikeout rate as a pro while steadily improving his other fundamentals, including a drastic drop in his walk rate and deeper outings within the Tigers’ innings framework. Like former Detroit lefty prospect Brant Hurter, Sears brings a different look than a typical lefty with a low three-quarters arm angle and a fastball that sits around 93-94 mph but can play up to 97. He throws a four- and a two-seamer, and his arm angle accentuates the movement on his mid-80s sweeper. He has developed a split change as a third pitch, but it needs refinement to become more than a change-of-pace offering. He improved his command after moving to the third-base side of the rubber. Sears presents an interesting option for the Tigers in their search for pitching depth at the upper levels. Like Hurter, he could probably find a role as a lefty reliever who can hold his own against righties and cover multiple innings. With a little more development, though, he could fit as a backend starter, and that would be a win for a farm system that needs to develop more arms.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duran was traded to the Blue Jays in August 2022 as a player to be named later in an earlier swap involving relievers Anthony Bass and Zach Pop, and then top prospect Jordan Groshans. Looking back, it was an awfully savvy move to acquire a prospect who has developed into the top catcher in the system. The backstop spent parts of the 2023, '24 and '25 seasons with Single-A Dunedin before finally earning a promotion to High-A Vancouver last summer, where he hit a combined .275 with eight home runs and a .767 OPS over 100 games. Duran lost some steam in Vancouver, so the dip in his numbers could be more about fatigue than talent, but that’s something young catchers need to adjust to. Duran earns very high marks among teammates, coaches and development staff for his leadership and clubhouse presence. He speaks both English and Spanish and has worked on his ability to manage a pitching staff -- which is so often the final piece to the puzzle -- and his defense behind the plate profiles him as a future big leaguer. While Duran’s average exit velocity has crept up, it’s likelier that his power lands in the range of 10-15 home runs, with the majority of his value coming from an on-base ability and his presence behind the plate. A step forward at the plate could still change this, but Duran likely profiles as an MLB backup, which is still a valuable asset for a club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bracho received the highest bonus in Cleveland's promising 2017 international class, signing for $1.5 million out of Venezuela. Ticketed to come to the United States for his pro debut at age 17 in 2018 before he broke his right arm, he also missed a month with an oblique injury in 2019, when he would have ranked sixth in the Rookie-level Arizona League in slugging (.593) and OPS (1.009) if he had enough plate appearances to qualify. The youngest player (age 19) at the Indians' alternate training site last summer, he more than held his own against much more advanced pitchers. A switch-hitter, Bracho produces louder contact than would be expected from a player listed at 5-foot-11 and 175 pounds. He has a compact swing with plenty of bat speed and could produce 20 or more homers per season once he's fully developed. But after showing an advanced feel for the strike zone in his first taste of pro ball, he has been too aggressive following his jump to High-A this year and has been helpless against right-handers. The Indians planned on breaking Bracho into pro ball as a shortstop in 2018 but used him at second base during his debut a year later. Most international scouts thought he'd wind up at the keystone because he lacks true shortstop actions and possesses average arm strength and speed. His quick hands help him on the double-play pivot and even if he loses a half-step as he physically matures, he can become an average defender at second.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montero was one of three players to receive seven-figure bonuses from the A’s during the 2024 international signing period, with his $1.2 million bonus tying for the largest of the period for the organization with Jose Ramos. Learning from what they perceived as mistakes in years past when they moved high-money international prospects to the United States perhaps too quickly, the A’s gave Montero a second year in the Dominican Summer League after an underwhelming performance there in ‘24. The second time around in the DSL brought him much more success, as he slashed .313/.484/.580 with nine homers in 55 games last summer. Montero returned for his second year in much better shape and with an overall better understanding of his approach at the plate. The switch-hitting shortstop can impact the ball from both sides, showing he can hit for average and power. From the right side, he is more direct to the ball; from the left side, his swing is a lot more picturesque as he naturally has had more at-bats from that side. His solid approach has led to a good ability to draw walks and keep his strikeout totals relatively low. The A’s were very pleased with what Montero showed last year. Defensively, his instincts should help him stick at shortstop, especially with his improved conditioning, though he is obviously still growing into his 6-foot-2 frame as a teenager, which could eventually lead to a move to third. The next step for him is to make his debut in the United States and begin his climb up the organizational ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Cutter: 50 | Splitter: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Only three players have ever been drafted out of Cary-Grove HS in Illinois, and just two have ever signed. Both enter the 2026 season as Brewers: Major Leaguer Quinn Priester (2019) and Dorchies. The latter was much less heralded coming out of the prep ranks than his predecessor and went in the 10th round of the 2024 Draft before signing away from a University of Illinois-Chicago commitment with a $162,500 bonus. Only 17 on Draft Day, Dorchies came flying out of the gate in his first full season, blowing past the Arizona Complex League and reaching Single-A Carolina by mid-June. He finished with a 2.74 ERA, a 1.05 WHIP and 89 strikeouts over 82 innings between both spots. Dorchies checks in at 6-feet-5 and uses that size to generate around 7 feet of extension, putting his five-pitch mix right on top of hitters. His four-seamer and sinker only sit in the 90-93 mph range right now, but the ride on the former and the run on the latter help them play beyond the velo. Still only 19 for all of his second full season, Dorchies could stand to add strength and get that heat closer to the mid-90s with regularity in time. His low-80s, low-spin splitter dives late to generate whiffs at his best rates, but he’s been more focused on throwing a low-80s sweeping slider as his most-used secondary. An upper-80s cutter serves as a bridge pitch. The teenager’s walk rate inflated about four ticks once he got away from the complex, but he doesn’t overthrow and should deliver a decent amount of strikes, especially if that strength comes around. Dorchies already displays desirable traits and promising future projection for a 10th-round pick and could become one of Milwaukee’s better development stories by the time he reaches The Show.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the best high school catcher in a lean 2019 crop, Hearn figured to go in the top three rounds based on talent. Worries about the strength of his commitment to Mississippi State dropped him to the sixth round, though he was still the first prep backstop selected. He signed for $950,000, the equivalent of second-round money, then struck out 36 times in 80 at-bats while hitting .163 in his debut. Hearn offers plenty of bat speed and strength from the left side of the plate. Instead of letting his plus raw power to all fields translate into home runs naturally, he got too aggressive and pull-oriented in his introduction to pro ball, resulting in too many whiffs and rolled-over grounders to the right side of the infield. If he can settle down, he could develop into a decent hitter with 20 or more homers per season. Hearn runs like a typical catcher but moves well enough behind the plate. He had concentration lapses as an amateur but appeared more focused in his debut and should become an average to solid receiver. He has a plus arm with a quick release, and he has recorded 1.9-second pop times to second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hitt may have pitched his way into a prominent spot in the 2020 Draft as a high-schooler, if not for the pandemic-shortened spring and the shortened five-round process. Instead, he headed to Alabama and had rough results over his first two seasons before steadying the ship some in the Cape Cod League in 2022. Hitt's big breakout came in fall ball a few months later, and he became a high priority follow as a junior, only to get shut down in April with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. The D-backs took a swing on Hitt with a fourth-round selection and backed up their belief in him with a well-above-slot $1.2 million bonus. Hitt showed a 93-97 mph fastball with better action in the fall. That was up a few ticks from his 90-92 mph heater as a sophomore, and it was a sign that something was up health-wise when the fastball was back to averaging 92 in the spring. What also took the southpaw to another level was a plus upper-80s cutter that might be his best secondary now. Its biggest competition for that is a mid-80s slider, while a mid-70s curveball offers another breaker. Hitt's changeup goes virtually unused and needs to be located on the bottom edge of the zone to be at all effective. His control and command were also ticking closer to average in the fall, but that progress was certainly slowed by the lost TJ time. Hitt's pitch mix gives him mid-rotation upside, despite the injury history, and that's a big reason why Arizona went in for him last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Henderson was a two-time All-Mountain West First-Team selection during his time at Fresno State and was the Bulldogs’ Friday night starter as a junior in 2023, when he posted a 3.74 ERA with 100 strikeouts in 89 innings. The Cardinals took him in the eighth round that year and signed him above slot for $230,000. He enjoyed a solid first full season at two A-ball levels and held his own in the hitter-friendly Arizona Fall League to boost his status further. Henderson was the Texas League Pitcher of the Year in 2024 after finishing with a 2.59 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 134 strikeouts in 132 innings for Double-A Springfield. Standing 6-foot-2, the southpaw uses a diverse arsenal as the foundation for his success. The cornerstone of that is a fastball that took a velocity bump up to 93-94 mph and touching 96 in 2025. He can spot the heater well with carry up in the zone, driving above-average whiff rates, and makes the pitch work above its weight with a deceptive three-quarters arm slot. His 79-82 mph sweeping slider can be effective against batters from both sides, but a mid-80s changeup helps hold off splits issues the best. He doesn’t zone the cambio as well as the other two, but righties still couldn’t touch it for big impact. A mid-70s curveball and upper-80s cutter offer other (albeit less-used) looks. Henderson needs to live on the periphery of the zone, but in so doing, he hasn’t run into major issues with free passes at any pro stop yet in his career. The velo uptick made his future as a No. 5 starter more likely, but he hit a pause this spring with a flexor strain when he seemed ready to knock on St. Louis’ door.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gaston, a Cuba native, earned the No. 18 spot on MLB Pipeline’s list of top international prospects during the 2018 signing period due to his high-octane fastball. Back then, when he was taking part in a showcase circuit that once included fellow countryman Victor Victor Mesa, Gaston’s calling card was elite heat without much control. The Rays took a chance on that upside and signed him for $2.61 million that November, then he went on to strike out 31 with 27 walks and a 6.00 ERA over 27 innings in the Gulf Coast League. Gaston’s profile hasn’t changed that much – he’s all about his big fastball, and his control is still a question – but he took a massive step forward in 2021. He shortened his arm stroke to improve his command, but the 6-foot-3 right-hander maintained that 96-101 mph velocity on his heater because he has as much lower-body strength as any pitcher in Tampa Bay’s deep system. He also tightened up his slider, giving him a better chance to land it for strikes as opposed to it only being a two-strike chase pitch. After blowing away hitters in the Florida Complex League, he held his own with a 3.86 ERA, 38 strikeouts and 22 walks in 30 1/3 innings over seven starts for Low-A Charleston. Gaston also throws a curveball and a changeup, but his primary weapons are his fastball and slider. The Rays moved him to the bullpen in 2022 but insist they haven’t given up yet on Gaston’s starting prospects. The move was made to get him as many in-game opportunities as possible per week, in the hopes that the control could improve. If anything, it’s taken a step back. That said, Gaston still doesn’t turn 21 until December, and his heater gives him a lot of promise long-term as a high-leverage relief arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter pretty much out of the gate at Fresno State, Gray had solid freshman and sophomore seasons, earning Mountain West Freshman of the Year honors in 2023, but something really clicked in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2024, when he hit .329 and got an All-Star nod. When he got hot as conference play started in his junior season, he finished the year with an OPS of 1.037 and landed in Competitive Balance Round B with the Pirates, making him the first Bulldogs hitter to go in the top three rounds since Taylor Ward was taken in the first round in 2015. A big, 6-foot-4 right-handed hitter, Gray is all about impact and contact. He swings a lot, and chases too much (32 percent chase rate in 2025), but he doesn’t miss very often (19 percent miss rate last year). He has a ton of raw power to all fields, typically finding the seats to his pull side. He’ll need to work on some swing modifications and on his swing decisions, as professional pitchers are sure to take advantage of his desire to offer at just about anything near the plate. Where Gray’s bat will fit into a lineup remains to be seen. He has the arm to play third, where he played exclusively in college, but a lack of speed or first-step quickness may push him across the diamond to first base. He’s been working to get his body to be more explosive to give him a shot at the hot corner, but it’s going to be his bat that carries him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez showed plenty of upside when the Padres signed the Dominican outfielder for $300,000 at the start of the 2017-18 international period. Despite slashing just .176/.354/.270 with 80 strikeouts in 61 games in his first pro season in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, his knack for squaring up the ball impressed the club. Playing in the Rookie-level Arizona League in 2019 at age 17, Perez showed vast improvement as he hit .268/.349/.512 and tied for second-most in the league with 11 homers. That impressive bat enticed the A’s enough to nab him as the player to be named later in the 2020 deal that sent Jorge Mateo to the Padres. Perez could develop into a strong power bat given his physical frame. Like most young players, he’s still working through some swing-and-miss issues. That said, Perez does make a lot of quality contact with his quick bat and lofty swing. He has played mostly right field since 2019 and is destined for a corner outfield spot due to below-average speed. Perez's slightly above-average arm probably makes left field a better fit for the long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top position prospect in Tennessee's 2022 prep class, Godbout went undrafted because of his commitment to Virginia. An immediate starter for the Cavaliers, he became one of the best contact hitters in the college ranks, slashing .321/.415/.514 with an 11 percent strikeout rate in three college seasons. He posted similar numbers during a brief stint in High-A after signing for $1,093,800 as a supplemental second-rounder. Godbout's bat-to-ball skills derive from a compact right-handed stroke, disciplined approach and exceptional hand-eye coordination. He made a lot of groundball contact while producing pedestrian exit velocities in college, but he immediately incorporated some changes after signing and drove the ball in the air more frequently. Boston's demonstrated ability to help players improve their strength, bat speed and ball flight could help Godbout produce at least 15 homers on an annual basis. Godbout has fringy speed at best but compensates somewhat with a high baseball IQ. His average arm strength and range are best suited for second base, where he's a surehanded defender. The Red Sox gave him a little action at shortstop in his pro debut and plan on doing so again in 2026, though most scouts think that's a stretch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two years after producing a first-round outfielder in Jordyn Adams, Green Hope High (Cary, N.C.) has another early-round prospect in Norris. While Adams didn't break out until the National High School Invitational during his senior year, Norris has been famous on the showcase circuit for a while. He has the pitches and physicality to go in the first round but won't because he hasn't been able to harness them. Norris' powerful 6-foot-4 frame already produces fastballs that sit at 90-94 mph and peak at 96 with some late life. When he's on, both his upper-70s curveball and low-80s slider grade as at least plus offerings. He's in the early stages of developing a changeup with some sink. More strong than athletic, Norris has difficulty keeping his delivery in sync and staying online to the plate. He has 107 walks in 141 career innings at Green Hope and his command is shakier than his control. He might not go high enough in the Draft to divert him from a North Carolina commitment and his long-term role could be as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Oregon State, Forrester left campus with a career .326 average and a .970 OPS. A very strong junior season in 2023 made many scouts think he was one of the best college hitters on the West Coast in the class. The son of former Minor League infielder Gary Forrester, Garret went in the third round of the Draft and played briefly with full-season Bradenton during his pro debut after signing for an under-slot bonus of $772,500. Forrester is an advanced right-handed hitter who knows what he’s doing at the plate. He makes sound swing decisions and left Oregon State with more walks than strikeouts. He didn’t get to show it much during his stint in the Florida State League, but he has the ability to drive the ball to all fields with opposite-field power. He’s added some strength during the offseason, which hopefully will add to his power profile moving forward. Almost exclusively a first baseman in college, Forrester had seen a little time at third where his solid arm plays well, and the Pirates had him at the hot corner during his debut even though he’s not exactly fleet afoot. That will continue, as will another defensive wrinkle -- Forrester worked out at the Draft Combine behind the plate, and the Pirates have liked what they’ve seen from him at catcher, with plans to build him up and give him time there, first and third in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There was a dearth of college catching in the 2025 Draft class, and Carmichael stood out as one of the few who landed in the top 100 of MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 Draft prospects. Following his father, Darby, and brother, Braden, by playing his college ball at Oklahoma, Carmichael used his Cape Cod League All-Star turn (where he won game MVP honors) as a springboard into an outstanding junior season, when he posted an OPS north of 1.000 and showed off improved defensive chops behind the dish. The Pirates nabbed him in the third round and pushed him to High-A Greensboro for his pro debut, where a little wrist issue sapped his production. A right-handed hitter with the possibility of average tools across the board, Carmichael has a disciplined approach, making consistent contact and showing an ability to use the middle of the field. Most of his power -- he hit 17 homers for the Sooners last year -- comes to his pull side, and he has the strength to get to 20 homers annually if he can find a bit more loft. Carmichael is a solid athlete who runs better than most catchers and can steal a base now and again. The Pirates loved the leadership traits he showed right out of the gate, always a plus for the position, and his improved arm strength has already been apparent. There’s work to be done on his receiving in terms of his timing and glove positioning, but the pieces are all there to be a decent all-around big league backstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known as Leandro Calderon when he signed for $10,000 in 2021, Lopez spent his first two pro seasons at home in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and missed most of 2024 with shoulder fatigue. He improved his conditioning afterward, which led to a breakout 2025 season that earned him a spot on the 40-man roster. He compiled a 2.40 ERA, .198 opponent average and 111 strikeouts in 101 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. Lopez can create quality depth on two different breaking balls, and his upper-80s slider supplanted his low-80s curveball as his best pitch last year. His fastball operates at 93-95 mph and touches out at 97, albeit with more downhill plane than life and a tendency to catch the heart of the plate too often. He's still learning to locate his mid-80s changeup where he wants but it misses bats with tumble when it's on. Getting in better shape allowed Lopez to repeat his delivery, provide consistent strikes and maintain his stuff better than he had previously. His upright delivery and high arm slot help him stay on top of his breaking pitches but detract from his fastball shape. Upgrading his heater and continuing to refine his control would help enhance his chances of becoming a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player during his high school days in Maine, Bowker hit and pitched in the Appalachian League before heading to Georgetown. He did both as a freshman, then started focusing on pitching only in 2024. He was a Cape Cod League All-Star that summer before transferring to Vanderbilt and spending his junior year in the Commodores’ weekend rotation. Leaning heavily on his fastball, Bowker pitched well enough to land in the third round of the 2025 Draft, where the Phillies signed him for $700,000, a bit under slot. While his heater sat 92-93 mph and topped out at 95 at Vanderbilt, it plays up well beyond the velocity. Thanks to a drop-and-drive delivery and a low arm slot, he delivers the pitch from a low release height and a ton of carry. It rises above the barrel and he gets misses and chases on the offering. The rest of his repertoire isn’t as exciting, though he has average spin on his slider and it plays off his fastball pretty well. He has a slightly harder, shorter cutter that might just be a different version of his slider and he can sink a changeup but didn’t throw it much, something the Phillies plan to have him work on. While Bowker commands his fastball well, his control of his other offerings is not as consistent, though he does get a decent amount of chase out of the zone. He’ll need to refine his secondary stuff to have the chance to start long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing his high school ball at Calvary Christian in Florida, Nelson headed to Florida State rather than entertain signing with the Phillies, who had taken him in the 39th round of the 2019 Draft. A three-year starter for the Seminoles, Nelson didn’t show a whole lot with the bat until 2021 when he tied for the Division I lead with 23 homers. That earned him several collegiate accolades and landed him in the Competitive Balance Round A, where the Reds gave him full slot ($2.1 million) to sign. His pro debut was uneventful and brief, as a thumb injury on his glove hand limited him to just 10 games and he struggled with the bat during his first full season in 2022. Nelson has an exciting power combination in his bat and arm that many teams love to see from catchers. He’s capable of being short to the ball and drive it to all fields, with his plate discipline leading to walks and good hitter’s counts that help him get to his plus power when he was at Florida State. With the power does come some swing-and-miss and there are some holes in his swing he’ll have to continue to address at the pro level. Nelson’s plus arm is an asset behind the plate and has helped him control the running game wherever he’s been. He’s also shown flashes of good receiving and blocking skills, though he’s a bit streaky defensively. He needs to keep trying to find consistency on both sides of the ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Compton entered his redshirt sophomore season at Arizona State as a potential 2025 first-round pick after earning Pac-12 Conference freshman of the year honors, although his production regressed. His stock ticked back up after a record-setting Draft Combine performance with the three hardest exit velocities in the event's five-year history, and the Marlins signed him for an under-slot $2 million as a second-round pick. He got an aggressive assignment to High-A and posted a 112 wRC+ in 27 games while showing off his signature power. The lefty slugger is a stocky 6-foot-1 with incredible raw strength out of a crouched stance. Compton was able to access that power more in his first college season when he controlled the zone better, and the Marlins will work closely on his swing decisions. There is plenty of risk in his hit tool, though, especially considering he was just 2-for-21 with nine strikeouts against 95+ mph velocity and was quite vulnerable to sliders last year in college. Compton is a decent runner, and the Marlins have pushed him to be more aggressive on the basepaths. His range in the outfield is lacking, though, and combined with a fringy arm which required Tommy John surgery his first year at Arizona State leaves him limited to left field. He's likely to get time at first base in 2026 to increase his versatility, but that lack of defensive value puts lots of pressure on him to unlock his natural power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hugus’ path has been anything but linear, leading to a variety of opinions about him from scouts, other than the 80-grade put on his mustache. A two-way standout at Cardinal Newman High in West Palm Beach, Fla., he began his college career at Cincinnati as both a reliever and left-side infielder before transitioning to full-time pitching. After uneven results, he transferred to Miami, where a strong showing in the Cape Cod League earned him a rotation opportunity. And he seized it, opening the year as the Hurricanes’ Saturday starter before moving into the Friday night role by March and ultimately landing with Seattle in the third round, signing for under-slot at $640,000. The Mariners will have to wait to see what kind of pitcher they acquired as he blew out his elbow early in his first Spring Training and required Tommy John surgery. He doesn’t overwhelm with pure velocity, but Hugus offers the foundation of a starter’s mix. His fastball typically sits 92-93 mph and will touch 95-96 mph, playing better than the radar gun suggests because hitters struggle to square it up. His mid-80s slider is currently his primary weapon, though some evaluators believe his mid-70s curveball -- added during his time on the Cape -- could develop into the more consistent swing-and-miss offering. He also flashes a mid-80s changeup that could round out a legitimate four-pitch arsenal. Seattle’s interest goes beyond the stat line. Internally, there’s belief that Hugus fits the mold of a “posted” college arm -- someone with innings under his belt and room for targeted development tweaks, once he returns to the mound. The Mariners see areas where modest velocity gains or pitch-shape refinements could unlock another level. Pair that with strong makeup, curiosity and a reputation as a good teammate, and there’s quiet optimism that Hugus could take a meaningful step forward once fully integrated into the organization’s pitching program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Mann played at Louisville, scouts regarded him as a fine college player but didn't see a standout tool or think he fit the profile at second base. The Dodgers selected him in 2018's fifth round because they thought they could unlock some improvements, and he went from a .680 OPS in his pro debut to ranking seventh in the high Class A California League with 19 homers in 2019 despite missing a month with a sprained right knee. He got his 2020 development time at Los Angeles' alternate site. Mann hit just 15 homers in three years of college but looks like a different hitter these days after the Dodgers got him to use his legs more, add some loft to his right-handed stroke and seek out more pitches to attack. After focusing on making contact and reaching base at Louisville, he now looks to launch balls and shows at least average power to all fields. Though he has changed his identity at the plate, he still has maintained some discipline. Mann has transformed himself in the field as well, though his long-term defensive home is still uncertain. While he's still a fringy runner, he has quickened his footwork and strengthened his arm. He has sure hands but his actions are a bit stiff for second base, so he may fit better at third base, where his average arm might be a tick short.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feliz made a strong first impression in 2021 during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he had an .813 OPS and five homers in 46 games. Signed in 2019 for $900,000, the richest contract among that international class for Seattle, Feliz is still growing into his body and filling out, which has made him a more physical player in recent years. As his body continues to mature, it’s possible he can emerge with 55s for his tools across the board. None of those tools necessarily play above the other, making him one of the Mariners’ more well-rounded outfield prospects. Described as very smart and instinctual, Feliz has the potential to stick in center field due to those attributes. At the plate, Feliz’s swing mechanics are somewhat inconsistent and remain a work in progress. It’s not the cleanest or most compact swing and there are a lot of moving parts, especially in his lower half, but despite those hiccups, he showed more feel for hitting than scouts anticipated. However, it’s likely that he profiles more as a power than average hitter long term. Because of all of his tools projecting as above-average, Feliz probably has more upside than floor. But because his swing has a ways to go, his timeline for the Majors is probably a little longer too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas high schooler who saw his velocity spike during his senior year, raising his Draft profile in 2023, Ellwanger moved on to Dallas Baptist knowing he’d be eligible again in two years as a sophomore. A flexor strain in his elbow forced him out for a couple of months as a freshman, though he made up for lost time with a solid Cape Cod League performance that summer. He missed a ton of bats, albeit with spotty command, showing off enough ingredients for the Twins to take him in the third round of the 2025 Draft and sign him for $1 million, a bit over slot. Tall, projectable and athletic, the 6-foot-4 Ellwanger has some exciting raw stuff and can be dominant when he’s locked in. His fastball sat in the 95-96 mph range last year and flirted with triple digits and he’s capable of throwing it with good carry and armside run. His best secondary offering is his low-80s curve, a pitch that elicited a 41-percent miss rate, according to Synergy. He can land his mid-80s slider for strikes, but it got hit hard in 2025, so he started trying out a harder, low-90s cutter. He has a firm, seldom-used changeup as well. Ellwanger needs innings to develop from pure thrower to pitcher, starting with learning to repeat his delivery and compete in the strike zone more consistently. The Twins will work with him on some usage patterns to find the right mix, knowing there could be more velocity to come as he fills out. He has the stuff to pitch in a rotation if he can hone his command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts largely ignored Vradenburg during his California high school career and first two seasons at Michigan State, and he wasn't on their follow lists heading into 2023 even after leading the Coastal Plain League with 48 RBI in 32 games the previous summer. Then he exploded last spring to slash .400/.492/.721 with 13 homers, becoming the second player in Spartans history to earn athletic and academic All-America accolades in the same season. After signing for $916,000 as a third-rounder, he batted .236/.368/.291 in Single-A. Despite his hulking 6-foot-7, 230-pound build, Vradenburg's hitting ability overshadows his power. He doesn't chase pitches out of the strike zone and focuses on smacking them from gap to gap, though his strikeout rate did spike from 13 percent in his final college season to 28 percent in his pro debut. There's some question as to whether he can provide more than 15-20 homers per season because his pop comes more from strength and leverage than bat speed in his left-handed stroke, and the Marlins will try to help him add more muscle and explosiveness. Vradenburg moves surprisingly well for his size, recording average run times from home to first and showing solid quickness once underway. He doesn't have much twitchy athleticism and may not have the hands and footwork to remain at first base, where he made five errors in 26 pro starts. With his speed and fringy to average arm strength, he may be able to handle left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gelof is following the same path that took his older brother Zack to the big leagues with the Athletics, going to Virginia as a relatively unheralded recruit and blossoming into a second-round pick. Jake set Cavaliers records for single-season and career homers (23, 48) and RBI (90, 186) in 2023 before signing for $1,334,400. Rusty and not in peak shape after a layoff between the end of the college season and his pro debut, he hit .225/.314/.433 with five homers in 30 Single-A games. One of the best power prospects in the 2023 Draft, Gelof puts a charge into the ball with his combination of bat speed, strength and loft in his right-handed swing. He has an aggressive approach and focuses on launching balls in the air, yet he also uses the entire field and doesn't chase pitches or strike out excessively. He's a 30-homer threat who could hit for a decent average and he'll draw walks if pitchers won't challenge him. Gelof has below-average speed and lacks athleticism, so most of his value will come from his bat. There are questions about his ability to remain at third base, where he has been error-prone and his range and arm may be a bit light. If he has to move, left field and first base would be his fallbacks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing sparingly as a freshman and putting up middling numbers as a sophomore at Nebraska, Caron took off as a junior, finishing with a .968 OPS and 16 homers, hitting six in six Big Ten Conference Tournament games to earn tourney MVP honors. That allowed him to become a bigger fish in a small sea of college catchers, landing in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft to the Mariners, who sent him to full-season Modesto for a brief pro debut. As someone who was young for the Draft (just 20 as a college junior) and from a cold-weather region (he went to high school in Wisconsin before heading to Nebraska), Caron might have more ceiling that he can catch up to. There’s some rawness to his bat, with his rhythm and timing at the plate not great compared to other college juniors, though his swing works pretty well, and he has pretty decent pitch selection, though he can be prone to being over-aggressive and pull-happy. He’s physical and strong with a good amount of power to tap into and he swung the bat very well in helping Modesto win its second straight California League title. Caron already has a strong arm, and there might be more than met the initial eye defensively as well. Nebraska’s coaches were very regimented in how they told their catchers to set up and receive depending on the count. A decent athlete who runs well for a backstop, Caron could take a step forward in his overall receiving when given the reins to his own protocol behind the dish. If it all clicks, he could develop into a power-hitting regular in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Big left-handed starters aren’t exactly easy to find, so sometimes a team has to go a more unusual route to find one. Case in point is Prosecky, who went to Louisville with the intent to be in their rotation, but the pandemic limited that in 2020 and injuries sidelined him for most of '21. He threw relatively well as the Cardinals’ closer in 2022 and the Rockies took him in the sixth round of that summer’s Draft, then almost immediately converted him back into a starting role. The early returns were good as he led the Single-A California League in ERA (2.72), opponents' average against (.217) and strikeouts (125) in his first year of pro ball. The 6-foot-3 left-hander has a potential four-pitch mix that could work in a rotation. He throws his fastball with late life in the 91-96 mph range, showing the ability to move it around the zone well. His slider has late action with depth and could eventually evolve into a solid out pitch and he throws a slower curve that’s more of a show-me, get-me-over type of offering. He has feel for a changeup and the Rockies are urging him to throw it more. Considering how little Prosecky threw in college -- a grand total of 64 innings in three years -- he held up well over the course of a season and managed to surpass the century mark in innings pitched with plenty left in the tank while throwing better late in the year. He’s a solid strike-thrower who can finish hitters off late in counts who could stick in a rotation long-term if it clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cali’s path to pro ball was long and winding. It started at Florida State during the COVID year and he redshirted, not appearing any games. He transferred to Hillsborough Community College and then caught fire at the College of Central Florida in 2022, slashing .438/.533/.826 with 17 homers, which caught the eye of the University of Arkansas. After posting a .923 OPS with the Razorbacks in 2023, the Mariners took him in the 16th round of the Draft and he quickly hit his way from Modesto to High-A Everett, finishing with 16 homers, 81 RBIs and a 128 wRC+. Cali’s numbers do come with the caveat that he was old for the levels, turning 24 last August, but he did show off some savvy from the right side of the plate. It’s not premium bat speed or pop, but there is a little power there and he gives professional at-bats. The strikeouts were a little high (27 percent) but he also drew a ton of walks (14.3 percent). He’s not a slug on the basepaths, but he’s just fringy in terms of his speed. After playing third base almost exclusively with Arkansas, that is where Cali has seen most of his time in his year-plus of pro ball. He might be a little stretched thin there defensively, but he’s the kind of gamer who’ll do anything to help his team win. He’s probably best defensively at first, and he’ll keep getting reps there, but he’s unlikely to have the thump to profile as a right-handed regular at the spot. His best chance is to move around a little bit and hope he gets to enough impact to find a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Oliveto was on a path toward becoming an Ivy League catcher, having committed to Yale, when an eye-opening performance at the WWBA World Championship in the fall of 2024 changed his career trajectory. Oliveto not only climbed up Draft boards, he landed at the No. 34 selection with the Tigers, who selected him with their Competitive Balance pick and signed him for a $2,447,500 bonus. It was a reminder that good left-handed-hitting catchers are hard to find. Oliveto tracks as a power lefty bat at the plate, both in swing and in raw strength. He has work to do as a pure hitter, but his WWBA performance awakened some scouts to that potential. Oliveto had a commanding presence behind the plate in high school and embraced the position, while his raw skills as a catcher will require some work. He earned high marks on makeup and work ethic, which could become particularly important as he tries to balance the demands of development as a hitter and a catcher. The Tigers have recent history on the value of patience with catching prospects, having just seen Dillon Dingler become a Gold Glover in his first full Major League season after the better part of four years in pro ball -- and Dingler was a college pick. Oliveto should earn similar patience and will likely move slowly through the lower levels of the farm system. If he makes it, though, he could fill a big role behind the plate down the road in Detroit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Harber hit 54 homers in 206 college games between Georgia and North Carolina, he went undrafted before signing with the Yankees for $50,000 in July 2024. Though a wrist injury sidelined him for six weeks midseason, he still slashed .323/.420/.550 between two levels and ranked second in the Minors (minimum: 300 plate appearances) with a 173 wRC+. Sent to the Giants as part of a Trade Deadline deal for Camilo Doval, he terrorized the Arizona Fall League and led the developmental circuit with 12 extra-base hits in 17 games. A right-handed hitter, Harber generates high-end exit velocities and can drive balls out of the park from foul pole to foul pole. He doesn't pull or lift pitches consistently, however, so there's some question about how much his power will play at higher levels. He shows the patience to work counts and draw walks, though he does swing through some in-zone fastballs and struggles against sliders. While Harber has worked hard to improve his all-around game, almost all of his value will be derived from his bat. He's a limited athlete with well-below-average speed and average arm strength, which will make it tough for him to remain at third base. He has spent nearly as much time at first, a more viable option, while his lack of range makes the outfield corners a stretch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McGeary put up monster numbers at Colorado Mesa while winning consecutive NCAA Division II national player of the year awards in 2021 and 2022. He paced D-II in hitting (.481), on-base percentage (.579), slugging (1.061), OPS (1.640), hits (103), homers (35) and total bases (227) and became the level's career home run leader (75) in 2022. He gave up plans to transfer to Kentucky to sign with the Cubs as a 15th-rounder, then slammed 19 homers while advancing to Double-A in his first full pro season. One of the strongest and most physical Cubs prospects at 6-foot-4 and 235 pounds, McGeary produces some of the highest exit velocities in the system. More than just a raw masher, he has an easy right-handed swing with plenty of bat speed that generates plus raw pop from the left-field line to right-center. He makes good swing decisions and draws walks while looking for pitches to drive, and he could find more power if he can lift the ball in the air more consistently. Primarily a DH while also catching and playing briefly at first base and the outfield corners in college, McGeary doesn't offer much value outside of the batter's box. The Cubs had him catch a couple of games during his 2022 pro debut but he has been a first baseman/DH since. A well-below-average runner with limited range and decent arm strength, he has hard hands and is error-prone at first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners showed just how much they valued Aguilar when the 2020-21 international signing period opened by making him their highest-priced investment at $1.5 million. The Dominican Republic native hit the ground running in the DSL months later, but his numbers -- a .246/.359/.361 (.720 OPS) slash line with just two homers in 52 games -- didn’t exactly reflect as much. A third baseman by trade, Aguilar has drawn comparisons to Red Sox star Rafael Devers for many reasons beyond his position and left-handed-hitting swing. He worked with Devers’ trainer, the late Rudy Santin, and began living up to that comparison during his pro debut last season. Aguilar has shown an advanced hit tool, and he’s one of the top Minor Leaguers at embodying the Mariners’ mantra of “dominating the zone,” evidenced by a 13.2 percent walk rate. Yet he had just two homers and a .369 slugging percentage, which underscores that he, right now, is more of a hit-over-power type. However, the 17-year-old has decent pop and a 5-foot-11 frame that suggests he could grow into more power. Aguilar moved from shortstop to third after signing, and he worked diligently on his conditioning to handle the hot corner. That work appeared to pay off when he arrived at the Mariners’ high-performance camp in Arizona last fall. Seattle doesn’t necessarily expect him to blossom into Devers’ power profile, but Aguilar nonetheless has the upside to grow into more hard contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinckney was a three-year player at Alabama and broke out as an All-SEC Second Teamer in 2023. That led him to a fourth-round pick and below-slot $500,000 bonus from the Nationals that summer. The right-handed slugger aggressively opened his first full season at Double-A Harrisburg, in part because it was already his age-23 campaign, and then he touched Triple-A Rochester later in the year. He spent all of 2025 back in the International League and used a second-half surge to hit .269/.348/.431 with 20 homers and 34 steals in 125 games. Pinckney was one of only five 20-30 Minor Leaguers last season. Starting from an open stance that he closes with a leg kick, Pinckney is geared up to hit the fastball and generates exceptional exit velocities, topping out at 116.6 mph in 2025 and with a 90th-percentile EV of 107.6. Because of that pop, 20 of Pinckney’s 31 extra-base hits left the yard with Rochester last year. However, over half of his total batted balls were on the ground, and that kept him from getting more doubles, triples and even homers across the board. He also posted whiff rates above 40 percent against most non-fastballs, and he’ll likely always be someone who flirts with at least a 30 percent K rate in the Majors. Pinckney’s other skills are much like his power: loud. He’s a top-of-the-scale runner, eclipsing 30 ft/sec sprint speeds and posting occasional sub-4 home-to-first times. His arm strength allows him to touch triple digits from the grass, and his combination of that cannon and range from his wheels could make him an above-average defender from any outfield spot. A Major League team could live with some contact concerns given that skill set, but Pinckney still needs to clear that hurdle to push through to Washington.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinckney played four years at Alabama, and while he improved steadily with the Crimson Tide, his big breakout came in 2023 as an All-SEC Second Teamer with a .339/.442/.658 line and 18 homers in 64 games. The Nationals selected him in the fourth round, signed him for below slot at $500,000 and have aggressively pushed the outfielder up their chain ever since. After playing for four affiliates in his Draft year, Pinckney opened his first full season with Double-A Harrisburg and hit .259/.328/.366 with seven homers and 22 steals in 114 games. He was promoted to Triple-A Rochester in late August 2024, has been there throughout 2025 and caught fire in the second half with the Red Wings. Batting from the right side, Pinckney faced concerns heading into the Draft that he would struggle against non-fastballs at the next level, and those issues remain. He’s geared up for the heat, and he posts high whiff rates against sliders, curves and changes -- a trend that’s carried from 2024 to 2025 in Rochester. He’s capable of hitting the ball hard with exceptional exit velocities (with a 90th percentile EV of 107.6 entering early September) but needs to improve his elevation on contact -- starting with not clipping outside breakers -- to be a future 20-homer threat in the Majors. Speed is no concern in Pinckney’s game, as he’ll get up to Sprint Speeds above 30 ft/sec when charging down the line. He stole 27 bags in his first full season and cleared 30 bags in his second. He used those wheels and above-average arm strength to rotate through all three outfield spots, and he could be more than ample covering in center when needed. Washington is loaded with quality defenders in the middle of the grass, and Pinckney is likely headed toward a reserve role unless he drastically improves his contact and launch angles

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinckney showed steady improvement over his four years with Alabama and saw his big breakout come as a redshirt junior last year, earning Second-team All-SEC honors with his .339/.442/.648 line and 18 homers in 64 games. Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 216 Draft prospect, the Nationals liked him enough to select him in the fourth round in July and signed him for below slot at $500,000.
