He kept up his momentum by being one of the best post-Draft performers in his class, slashing .321/.415/.457 with four homers and 11 steals in 41 games across four levels, topping out at Double-A. Although Pinckney has grown more patient and cut down on his chase rate from 2022 to '23, he gave some evaluators pre-Draft concerns about his ability to hit non-fastballs with a 43 percent miss rate on swings against breakers and offspeed pitches. He did manage to keep the strikeouts slightly more in check on the pro side, but a lot of the wood bat contact came on the ground (63.2 percent). He still has the strength to be a 15-homer threat in the pros. The 6-foot-3 outfielder has the plus speed to impact the running game and man center field. The issue is that he was drafted into the same organization as Dylan Crews and James Wood -- each of whom has superstar potential in the middle of the grass. To prepare for this, the Nats got Pinckney more time in right field, where his arm can certainly play. Whether his issues with soft stuff return or are things of the past will determine if he can carve out an everyday role in that corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown continued the pipeline of Canadian talent flowing through the MLB Draft in 2019, going to the Blue Jays in the third round and signing for a bonus of $800,000 to keep him away from a commitment to Texas A&M. He eventually broke out in ‘22, reaching High-A Vancouver, but took a step backward in ‘23 and used ‘24 to reestablish himself. There have been some wobbles, but it feels like Brown finally has his footing underneath him and is coming off a year in which he posted a .246/.342/.381 line with eight home runs and 35 steals in 39 attempts. Brown may be the best athlete in the organization and one of the fastest players in Minor League Baseball, which is why he’s hovered on the back end of this list for years, even when his numbers dipped. The 23-year-old could be a big leaguer on speed and defense alone, and given his natural gifts in the outfield, he should be a great project for new special assistant Kevin Kiermaier to work with throughout the spring and summer. Brown’s problems at the dish seem to come when that athleticism doesn’t transfer into the box. He has been rigid at times as a hitter, but seems to have loosened up now and is embracing that athletic identity. When he’s on base, he can change games with his speed, so it’s all about OBP for Brown. Brown struggled against Double-A pitching over 32 games last season (.586 OPS), so he’ll need to prove that he’s capable of hitting more advanced stuff. As long as he can slap the odd hit, though, the pathway to the Majors will remain wide open. We know how much the Blue Jays value defense at the MLB level, so when you pair that with Brown’s elite speed tool, he’ll forever be a tempting prospect. Taking one more step forward in the box will determine whether he’s a fringe big leaguer or something more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown continued the pipeline of Canadian talent flowing through the MLB Draft in 2019, going to the Blue Jays in the third round and signing for a bonus of $800,000 to keep him away from a commitment to Texas A&M. Brown’s breakout finally came in ‘22, when he hit .283 with a .383 on-base percentage over 85 games and reached High-A, but the momentum from that year was lost in ‘23 when Brown hit just .218 with a .309 OBP with Vancouver. Still, Brown’s athletic talent is too rare to see him fall off this list. Brown is an elite runner, period. His speed serves him well in center field, where he can get to almost any ball, but it doesn’t show up in stolen bases as often as you’d think. Brown went just 26-for-37 in stolen base attempts last season, and while his speed really shines when going from first to third or home, he’s still developing as a true base stealer. If that part of his game develops, he’s a sure big leaguer based on speed and defense alone, but Brown is already close to that being the case. At the plate, Brown’s adjustments have been encouraging but they haven’t always carried over to game action. He doesn’t need to hit for power or bat .300, but if he can keep his on-base percentage in the .350 range or higher, that will let his skill set shine. This is a crucial season for Brown at 22, but his raw tools give him a path to the Majors already. He’ll just need to do enough with the bat to be playable as something more than a speed-and-defense specialist off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown continued the pipeline of Canadian talent flowing through the MLB Draft in 2019, going to the Blue Jays in the third round and signing for a bonus of $800,000 to keep him away from a commitment to Texas A&M. He briefly debuted in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League that year, appearing in 14 games before his development path shifted back to the complex through the lost 2020 season. The Blue Jays always viewed Brown as a long-term project with tremendous upside, and the 2021 season was still a learning experience. At Single-A Dunedin, he hit just .212 and stole 22 bases in 51 games as he worked to develop a more consistent plate approach and put more balls in play. In 2022, it clicked for Brown, posting a combined .283 average with a .383 OBP over 84 games split mostly between Single-A and High-A. Brown was also driving the ball more, embracing the natural athleticism in his swing as he began to grow more with the Blue Jays' assistance. Those gains haven't quite held in his return to High-A Vancouver, however. Brown’s speed is simply elite. On that alone, he has the potential to steal 40-50 bases over a full 140 games. If he can learn the instincts of a true base stealer, that number could be even higher. That speed makes Brown at least a plus defender in center field too, closing gaps in an instant. If Brown improves and reaches base at a decent clip, the door is wide open for his athletic gifts to take over. He's been challenged at High-A though and has to adjust if he's going to make an impact higher up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown continued the pipeline of Canadian talent in the Draft, going in the third round to the Blue Jays in ’19. Toronto signed him away from a commitment to play college ball at Texas A&M with an $800,000 bonus. Brown made a brief, 14-game debut in the GCL in ’19 and came back in ’21 to play 51 games in Low-A Dunedin, where he hit .212 with a .633 OPS and 22 stolen bases over 51 games. Brown is an elite athlete. His speed is unmatched in the organization and is one of the best speed tools in Minor League Baseball. This also allows Brown to be one of the top defenders in the organization, covering any ground necessary with a natural, quick jump. Brown’s throwing arm had a unique motion when the Blue Jays drafted him, but he makes it work and has smoothed it out over the past two years. The exit velocity readings on Brown show that he can certainly be more than a slap-and-sprint hitter, so the Blue Jays are excited to see what he’s capable of if he can improve his pitch selection and contact rates. If Brown can put the ball in play consistently, he becomes one of the highest-upside prospects in this entire organization. That’s no simple task, though, and Brown will be tested by more advanced pitching as he advances. He has done a better job of reaching base at Single-A and High-A in 2022, making it a little easier to see how he’ll squeeze out enough offensive value to help a Major League club someday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown continued the pipeline of Canadian Draft talent in 2019 when the Blue Jays selected the dynamic outfielder in the third round, signing him away from a commitment to Texas A&M with an $800,000 bonus. In his brief, 14-game debut in the Gulf Coast League in ’19, Brown hit .222 with an .800 OPS and six steals. Projections with Brown need to be viewed through a long-term lens, as he and the Blue Jays will be working to develop the other tools around his elite-level athleticism. As the fastest player in the system and the best defensive outfielder, though, there are already a pair of exceptional abilities in place. Brown ’s quick-twitch ability is evident in his bat speed, but there’s work to be done with his swing and pitch selection. As Brown matures physically, there could be some added pop to come along with it and he’ll have no trouble stretching doubles into triples. There are still several years of development ahead for Brown, but his physical tools are truly rare and the Blue Jays will be patient as they recognize his significant upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken fifth overall by the Nationals and signed for $6.5 million in 2022, the son of Pro Bowl tight end Eric Green was a high-ceiling prospect out of IMG Academy. It’s been a slow build through Green’s first two full seasons, both of which came at Single-A Fredericksburg. The outfielder was limited to 75 games due to a wrist issue in 2023 and returned to slash just .208/.293/.355 with 13 homers and 39 steals in 106 games last season. His .257/.332/.450 line and 127 wRC+ from July 1 onward provided a light at the end of the season, though it came with a 42.5 percent strikeout rate. For all the good that remains in his profile, you still can’t talk about Green without mentioning the strikeouts. Green’s 44.0 percent K rate on the season was tops among Minor League full-season qualifiers, and he missed on 47 percent of his swings. He especially struggled against non-fastballs, highlighting that part of the issue stemmed from pitch selection. Batting with a closed front side, a leg raise and his hands held out, Green is geared-up to shoot rockets when he does make contact, and the exit velos are some of the loudest in the Nats system, occasionally topping 115 mph. When Green’s bat meets ball, the ball tends to go a long way. Green has also retained the plus-plus speed that made him a huge Draft prospect. He’s a constant and efficient threat on the bases, and some believe he could play center field in the Majors tomorrow if needed. His plus arm has helped him pick up 15 outfield assists in the last two seasons. Washington believes in Green’s work ethic and desire to improve, but as his career continues, he’ll face tougher and tougher tests in the box.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Pro Bowl tight end Eric Green was MLB Pipeline’s No. 3 Draft prospect in 2022 because of a multi-tooled, high-ceiling profile he built at IMG Academy and various stops of the showcase circuit. The Nationals selected him fifth overall and signed him for slot at $6.5 million, hoping he could be the club’s next homegrown superstar. The right-handed slugger’s first full season, however, was a rough one. His 41.6 percent strikeout was fourth-highest among Minor Leaguers with at least 300 plate appearances, while walks and power helped him salvage a .218/.336/.327 line. He was limited to 75 games at Single-A Fredericksburg due to a midseason wrist issue. The Nats have cautioned anyone who would listen not to give up on Green because of just how loud four out of his five tools have been. He’ll pop the occasional exit velocity north of 110 mph because of his quick wrists and immense strength, and he can drive the ball to all fields when he gets the barrel on the ball. Green also makes 70-grade speed look easy on the basepaths -- he stole 30 bags in 2023 -- and he can track down balls all over center field. What’s more, he has a strong arm out there, registering seven outfield assists in 71 defensive starts from the grass. So much comes down to the right-handed slugger’s bat. Green can struggle with pitch recognition -- from missing on pitches outside the zone to sitting on hittable pitches inside it -- and he’s been off-kilter in his directionality at the plate, hurting his ability to make contact. Considering Green would be entering his sophomore year had he gone to school, there is time to correct the mistakes, but the climb to superstardom is a lot more uphill now than on Draft Day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Pro Bowl tight end Eric Green, Elijah Green had one of the highest ceilings in the 2022 Draft class after standout turns on the showcase circuit and at IMG Academy that spring. He headed into July as MLB Pipeline’s No. 3 Draft prospect, trailing only top two picks Druw Jones and Jackson Holliday on the board, and he eventually went fifth to the rebuilding Nationals, who could use all the ceiling they could get and signed him for slot money at $6.5 million. Green produced a .939 OPS in 12 Florida Complex League games but also struck out 40.4 percent of the time, heightening concerns about his biggest weakness. Start with Green’s strengths because there are many. His raw power could be double-plus in the end, and he makes it play in games with quick wrists and immense strength that drives the ball to all fields. What’s more, his speed is 70-grade now, giving him another elite athletic tool, and that will be a big help in his ability to stick in center for the long term. The same could be said for the plus arm strength that will be another asset from the grass. Green did show struggles against high fastballs even during his prep days, and his early swing-and-miss issues in the pros portend a long road of development ahead. The Nationals believe he just needs more exposure to advanced pitching to improve his swing decisions, and that will be the focus in the early days of Green’s budding career. The other four tools are ample enough to carry him until the bat comes around, and if it does, Green could have superstar potential in the capital.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were few college players in the 2024 Draft class better than Honeycutt in terms of his raw tools, and he left North Carolina as the Tar Heels' single-season (28) and career (65) home run leader. He turned in a 28-homer, 28-steal junior season, but it came with concerns about his ability to make contact after a 27.5 percent strikeout rate. The Orioles rolled the dice on the tools and took him No. 22 overall, and the contact concerns were warranted during his first full season, as he struck out more than 40 percent of the time and finished with a .171/.284/.275 line with High-A Aberdeen. Strikeouts are always going to be a part of Honeycutt's offensive profile, and it's going to be a question of whether he can control the zone just well enough to use his bat speed and leverage to get to his easily plus raw power enough to be a productive hitter. There were some signs this spring, aside from the four Grapefruit League homers in his first four at-bats, of improvement, with more consistent contact, less swing-and-miss and getting to deeper counts. A superior athlete, Honeycutt's speed still showed up despite his struggles, with 32 stolen bases in 2025. He uses it in center field as well as a two-time ACC Defensive Player of the Year and a potential Gold Glover. He'll try to hit the reset button in 2026, and if it clicks at all, his power-speed-defense combination could allow him to climb the organizational ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After almost a half-decade of lottery picks, the Orioles picked lower in the Draft the past couple of years as they grew into contenders in the American League East, and they’ve used those mid-to-late first-round picks on athletic outfielders with big tools. Honeycutt, who Baltimore grabbed with the No. 22 overall pick in 2024, is the embodiment of that idea. A high school quarterback who won North Carolina state titles in football and baseball, Honeycutt then posted multiple 20-20 seasons at the University of North Carolina and left college with both the school single-season (28) and career (65) home run records. He didn’t perform nearly as well during a very brief pro debut after signing for a slightly over-slot $4 million. A dynamic athlete with plus tools almost across the board, Honeycutt fell to the Orioles in the Draft because of concerns over his bat. At 6-foot-3 and 205 pounds, he generates enough bat speed, leverage and loft to create well-above-average raw power, though his armsy swing and pull-happy approach lead to serious contact issues that can make him too easy to pitch to. As it was, Honeycutt struck out in more than a quarter of his plate appearances in college and in 42.8 percent of his plate appearances during his 13-game pro debut. In college, Honeycutt was a two-time ACC Defensive Player of the Year and the first player from a Power Five conference to pair 60 career homers with 70 steals. His upside is providing similar impact at the highest level, where his well-above-average speed and plus arm make him a potential Gold Glover in center field. He simply needs to make more contact, enough for his big tools to play. How he develops in that area will determine if Honeycutt becomes a Drew Stubbs type or exceeds that production.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montgomery’s loud raw tools excited many teams as the 2021 Draft approached, but just as many were nervous about his unorthodox swing and whether it would work at the next level. The Rockies couldn’t pass on the skill set, taking him No. 8 overall. Injuries have cost him a lot of reps, as he played in just 62 games in 2022 because of a quad muscle issue and then missed nearly all of '24 after wrecking his shoulder diving for a ball in the outfield and needing surgery. He did return to get some reps in the Puerto Rican Winter League. Strong and athletic at 6-foot-5, Montgomery utilizes a leg kick and a hand pump from the right side of the plate. Rather than trying to remove those from his mechanics, the Rockies worked hard with Montgomery to get them synced up. It was something that started to click before he hurt his shoulder, and when they were in unison, he was more regularly on time for the fastball, which helped him adjust better to softer stuff. He’s always been able to register high exit velocities, but the ball was often on the ground. When he was in sync, he was able to get his barrel out in front more and drive the ball, with the hope that he’d tap into his raw power more organically. A nearly top-of-the scale runner, Montgomery took his rehab time seriously in the weight room and has continued to pack on strength to his frame without sacrificing that speed. He can play center, but will likely keep moving around all three outfield spots. If he can retain his timing and cut down on his swing-and-miss, there’s still untold offensive ceiling here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were five high schoolers taken in the top 10 of the 2021 Draft, two pitchers and three hitters. Montgomery was the fifth of the quintet to hear his name called. The Pennsylvania prepster went No. 8 overall to the Rockies, who took their second straight high school outfielder in the top 10 and signed him for $5 million. Over his first year-plus, he hit well, though a quad muscle injury knocked him out of action in 2022 for a couple of months. His performance at High-A Spokane in '23 wasn’t as inspired, though he did fare well in the Arizona Fall League to cap things off. He was off to a solid start in Double-A when a shoulder injury suffered from diving for a ball in the outfield required surgery and could keep him out for the remainder of the season. Still only 21 years old for the 2024 season, Montgomery has already done a lot of maturing, both physically and mentally. He’s put his Draft status in the rearview mirror and now has a firmer understanding of what he needs to do to be successful. He showed up to Spring Training with about 20 pounds of good weight added. That should lead to even more power, though his unorthodox mechanics at the plate still lead some to worry about him making enough contact to get to it. His strikeout rate hovered around 27 percent for the second straight year, but his walk rate did tick upward to help offset that and he’s shown tremendous raw power to all fields. Montgomery’s speed plays on both sides of the ball and the added strength could make him even more explosive. There’s no question he can play center field with plenty of arm, but he’ll get reps in all three outfield spots to keep options open. There’s so much potential to unlock here, and if Montgomery can continue to work on being just a little more efficient, he could be a dynamic everyday guy in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montgomery really put himself on the first-round map for the 2021 Draft with a strong performance on the summer showcase circuit before his senior year of high school. He went on to win Pennsylvania Gatorade player of the year honors, and his intriguing combination of power and speed landed him in the top 10, with the Rockies taking him No. 8 overall. After hitting well in a brief pro debut in the Arizona Complex League, he continued to perform well during his first full season but missed nearly two months with a quad injury. A lot of how Montgomery goes about it on the field wouldn’t be found in an instructional video. There are many moving parts to his swing, with concerns about that leading to too much swing-and-miss. While he made a lot of loud contact in 2022, his nearly 27 percent strikeout rate is worth noting and something he’ll have to show he can manage as he moves up the ladder. He’s continuing to add strength to his frame, and that, along with a continued focus on refining his mechanics, should help him keep tapping into his plus raw power. Montgomery routinely posts plus run times, but he does so in an unorthodox manner as well, leading to body resistance and perhaps contributing to him breaking down. He tried to play through the quad injury at first, but once he shut it down and came back, he was one of the better players in the California League. He’s learned a lot about how to train and take care of his body, which should help him reach his ceiling as a big league regular in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Pennsylvania high school standout who earned his state’s Gatorade player of the year honors in 2021, Montgomery climbed to first-round status the summer prior when his elite athleticism and raw power were on display. For the second year in a row, the Rockies went the toolsy high school outfielder front with their top 10 pick, taking Zac Veen in 2019 and then Montgomery last year, signing him for $5 million and letting him get his professional feet wet in the Arizona Complex League and in instructional league play. He moved up to full-season Fresno in 2022, but missed close to two months due to injury. Montgomery can do a lot of things well, albeit in somewhat unorthodox fashion. Some amateur scouts didn’t love how many moving parts he had in his swing, with a rigidity that had some worry about how it would work against better pitching. Still, he’s shown impressive contact skills at the start of his pro career, keeping his bat in the zone for a long time. The Rockies feel he’ll be able to get more efficient mechanically, with added strength helping him find better body control, which should help close some holes and help him get to his considerable raw power. An easily plus runner, Montgomery should be able to use his wheels on both sides of the ball. He has the chance to be a center fielder for a long time, with a plus arm. He likes to learn and brings a ton of energy and personality to the field, all of which should help him reach his ceiling as an impact up-the-middle player with an exciting power-speed combination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bateman played with Cubs manager Craig Counsell's son Brady at Minnesota, where he developed into one of the best contact hitters, fastest runners and top defenders in the 2023 college crop. But his utter lack of power affected his Draft stock, even after he batted .500 during a two-week stint in the Cape Cod League, and he dropped to Chicago in the eighth round. He overcame surgery on his right hamate last February to hit .261/.376/.307 at Double-A, ranking third in walk rate (15 percent) and sixth in on-base percentage. A left-handed hitter, Bateman rarely strays from the strike zone, rarely hits balls with authority and rarely lifts them in the air. He lacks strength and understands his limitations, so he focuses on reaching base by drilling grounders through holes in the defense and working walks. His approach comes at the expense of any power, and he's a career .315 slugger with three homers in 233 pro games. Bateman's game is built around his plus-plus speed, which he uses to beat out hits, steal bases and chase down balls from gap to gap in center field. A two-way player until he had elbow surgery following his freshman year with the Gophers, he has solid arm strength and has notched 22 assists in 223 starts in center. He has drawn comparisons to Orioles 2023 first-rounder Enrique Bradfield Jr. and Myles Straw.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best contact hitters and fastest runners in the 2023 college class, Bateman batted .355 with a nine percent strikeout rate that spring at Minnesota, where he played with now-Cubs manager Craig Counsell's son Brady. A lack of power depressed Bateman's Draft stock, even after he hit .500 during a two-week stint in the Cape Cod League, and he fell to Chicago in the eighth round. He ranked second in on-base percentage (.401) and fourth in batting (.283) in the High-A Midwest League before scuffling in Double-A during his first full pro season, becoming the subject of repeated trade inquiries because of his outstanding defensive metrics. Bateman is a study in extremes from the left side of the plate. He almost never chases pitches or swings and misses, especially in the zone, but he also rarely hits balls hard or in the air. Just 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds, he builds his offensive game around shooting grounders into gaps in the defense and getting on base at the expense of any power. He slugged just .324 last year, with one homer and 16 extra-base hits in 107 games. An intelligent player who understands his strengths and weaknesses, Bateman translates his plus-plus speed into beating out hits, stealing bases and covering wide swaths of ground in center field. A two-way player before elbow surgery following his freshman season with the Gophers, he has regained solid arm strength and recorded 14 assists in his first 136 pro starts in center. His biggest backers think he's a lesser version of Orioles 2023 first-rounder Enrique Bradfield Jr., while more skeptical evaluators think his ceiling is Myles Straw.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals had a $5,179,700 international signing pool in 2022 and used $4,925,000 out of it to add Cuba native Vaquero that January. The outfielder had learned how to switch-hit after a move to the Dominican Republic and was a solid producer in the Dominican Summer League and Florida Complex League over his first two seasons of pro ball. He jumped to Single-A Fredericksburg late in 2023 and returned to the Carolina League a year later with subpar results: a .190/.291/.303, five homers and 29 steals in 103 games. He injured his left shoulder diving back to the bag in a Championship Series game on Sept. 18 and underwent surgery. Vaquero’s strikeout rate exploded in his age-19 season from 20.4 percent to 34.2 percent, the eighth-highest mark among 111 Single-A qualifiers. It wasn’t exactly a splits issue either. He struggled to make consistent contact as a batter from either side of the box, though he did a slightly better job of handling breaking balls as a righty. He has a more pronounced leg kick as a lefty, one he’ll tone down with two strikes. Given his size at 6-foot-3, there’s still room for power in his frame, and he should muscle up balls better in his 20s. A plus-plus speedster, Vaquero played all three outfield spots with the FredNats but would have likely gotten more center-field looks if not for Elijah Green’s defensive skills up the middle. His plus arm strength plays everywhere as he registered 14 outfield assists in 2024. Getting Vaquero healthy will be the primary objective to begin this season, but until he adjusts to full-season pitching, the space between his ceiling and floor remains immense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known to swing big on center fielders in recent years, the Nationals used $4.925 million of their $5,179,700 international signing pool in 2022 to bring in Vaquero, a Cuba native who moved to the Dominican Republic before signing. He learned how to switch-hit in his second country and has been relatively solid in his two years of pro ball, first in the Dominican Summer League and then split between the Florida Complex League and Single-A Fredericksburg last season. He hit .279/.410/.393 with one homer, 15 steals and a 118 wRC+ over 42 games in the FCL before his late-August promotion to full-season ball. Standing at a listed 6-foot-3, 180 pounds, Vaquero still sticks out more for his projection and potential than current production. The son of an Olympic swimmer mother and judo-fighting father, Vaquero is a true plus-plus runner who should constantly give pitchers and catchers something to think about on the basepaths. His wheels also serve him well in center, and he has enough arm strength for right, where he played mostly in Fredericksburg because of the presence of Elijah Green. There’s still plenty of room for him to fill out as well, so while he’s managed only two homers to this point, Vaquero still projects for above-average power as he matures. It'll take some offensive development to get there, however, on top of the physical. Vaquero remains more advanced from the left side (where he has a more open stance) as he acclimates to switch-hitting; he struck out in 40 percent of his right-handed plate appearances over a relatively small 2023 sample. He shows continued patience at the dish though, and as he returns to the Carolina League for his age-19 season, the Nats will continue to exhibit their own patience in his ascent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals had $5,179,700 in their international signing pool for the 2022 period and used $4,925,000 on Vaquero alone, making him the highest signee in his class. The Cuba native had moved to the Dominican Republic, where he picked up switch-hitting before signing, and stayed in the DR for his first taste of the Minors, hitting .256/.379/.341 with nine extra-base hits and 17 steals in 55 games in the Dominican Summer League. Vaquero’s mother was an Olympic swimmer and his father a judo fighter, and it’s clear the 18-year-old picked up their athletic genes. He’s already a plus-plus runner, and the Nats leaned into that by placing him exclusively in center field in the DSL. His arm should work in center as well. However, Vaquero didn’t show a ton of power at the Minors’ lowest level, in part because he hit a plurality of balls on the ground, and the pop he did exhibit came from his natural left-handed side (slugging .358 there compared to .250 as a righty) as he continues to get comfortable as a switch-hitter. Listed at 6-foot-3, 180 pounds entering 2023, Vaquero has plenty of projection remaining to get to his at least above-average power potential, and his overall approach, in which he walked nearly as much as he struck out, adds to that promise. He’ll still only be 18 for much of his first summer playing stateside, where he’ll pick up the at-bats to develop into a potential star up-the-middle talent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Cuba, Vaquero comes from an athletic family -- his mother is an Olympic swimmer and his father is a competitor in judo. He moved to the Dominican Republic and learned to switch-hit there before becoming eligible for the latest international signing window. The Nats spent $4,925,000 of their $5,179,700 signing pool to add MLB Pipeline’s No. 2 international prospect to their potential farm-system rebuild in January. Vaquero, who turned 17 last September, is as skilled as Washington’s heavy investment would indicate. He has true five-tool potential, starting with plus speed that should translate well to the basepaths and center field in the pro game. Those wheels stand out all the more given Vaquero’s size at 6-foot-3. As he grows even more into that frame, true plus power at the plate should be possible as well. His move to switch-hitting has improved his pitch recognition, but he’ll need more time to prove he’s just as capable of hitting from the right side as he is from his more natural side on the left. Vaquero has the potential to be the face of the Nationals farm system for a long time. It’s worth remembering that he’s still the age of an American high-schooler as he begins his Minor League career, and he may need some developmental space to get his many tools in line, as most teenagers do. If it all clicks, he could be the organization’s biggest international success story since Juan Soto.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since Spikerman showed up on the University of Oklahoma's campus for his freshman season in 2022, he's shown off explosive speed and athleticism. But injuries have gotten in the way of his progress, missing two months as a freshman, then breaking his right hamate in March 2024, his junior season. That's continued as a pro since the Phillies took him in the third round of that summer's Draft, with a shoulder injury limiting him to just 62 games in an uneven first full season of pro ball. The Phillies were optimistic that the switch-hitting Spikerman was figuring things out thanks to a lot of work he put in during the offseason. While he should be all about making contact, getting on base and using his speed, he used to have way too big of a swing for someone with his size and offensive profile. He made some adjustments over the winter, showing a better understanding of how to use his elite athleticism in the box and engage his hands better when he hits. There have never been any questions about Spikerman's ability to use his speed to steal bags and play plus outfield defense. He's shown he can handle all three spots, and can play an outstanding center field long-term, with a plus arm only adding to his profile. That helps give him a decent floor as a backup outfielder, with a greater role if the bat comes along.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If it weren’t for injuries, Spikerman would have had three years of full-time starting on his Oklahoma transcript. He still left his mark, coming back from missing two months as a freshman to help the Sooners make the 2022 College World Series finals. After an up-and-down sophomore season that ended well, he was having a terrific 2024 campaign early until he broke his right hamate bone in March. He did make it back and landed with the Phillies as their third-round pick before making a brief debut with Single-A Clearwater. A switch-hitter, Spikerman is going to run his way up the organizational ladder. He has close to top-of-the-scale speed that he uses on both sides of the ball, stealing a ton of bases and beating out a lot of groundballs for hits on the offensive end of things. He cut down the swing-and-miss in his game considerably as a junior while continuing to draw walks and while he’s never shown much power, there is some strength and bat speed to feed hope he’ll have enough impact as he faces better pitching. Spikerman’s speed helps him cover a lot of grass and he should be able to patrol center field for a long time. He’s a plus defender in all three outfield spots, should he need to find a fourth-outfielder role, with a very strong arm that is playable from anywhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates went over slot to sign White away from playing football and baseball at Penn State in 2021, they knew they’d have to be patient with an athlete from a cold-weather state who had been splitting his focus among multiple sports. What they didn’t know is how hard it would be to keep him on the field. A number of injuries limited White to 11 total games in 2021 and 2022 but even though he didn’t get started until June of 2023, he saw his first extended action, mostly with full-season Bradenton, allowing him to finally to show a little bit of what the fuss was all about. White has teased with his physicality and athleticism since signing; in 2023, he got to put all of it to use for 61 games. Considering how much development time he missed, it was encouraging he shook off the rust and kept his strikeout rate under 30 percent while also drawing a lot of walks. He can be quick to the ball and find the barrel with pretty good power, with more to come. The former wide receiver is an easily plus runner, so his ability to get on base should help him be a threat to steal. It also helps him cover a lot of ground in center field, where he has a chance to be an excellent defender for a long time. He still has a ways to go, but last year was the first positive steps forward he’s been able to take. If he can put the injuries behind him and continue to stay on the field, he could really start sharpening all of those tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teams interested in White’s baseball ability knew he would be a tougher sign because he had the chance to go to Penn State to play football and baseball. Because the Pirates saved on signing Henry Davis atop the 2021 Draft, they were able to get not only two high-ceiling arms in Bubba Chandler and Anthony Solometo, but also White, giving him $1.5 million after selecting him in Competitive Balance Round B. Since then, it’s been tough for him to stay on the field, with injuries allowing him to play just 11 games since signing. Athletic and physical, White still has the raw tools that made him such an intriguing prospect in the first place. The former wide receiver can really run, which should allow him to steal bases and cover a lot of ground in center field. He’s shown glimpses of an approach at the plate, with a short swing from the right side and an ability to barrel up the baseball. Playing multiple sports meant he was a little more raw at the plate, but there’s power to tap into, and there’s been confidence things would smooth out with a baseball-only focus. What White has needed more than anything else as a multi-sport athlete from a cold-weather state is reps, and he’s missed a lot of development time because of what’s largely been soft-tissue kind of injuries. The Pirates don’t feel it’s a long-term concern and if he adjusts to the full-time baseball calendar, his body will respond, with the hope he can truly start showing what he’s capable of with a healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: White was a three-sport standout at his high school outside of Philadelphia, one who had the chance to go to Penn State to play football and baseball. The Pirates had other ideas, using their bonus pool wisely and taking the savings from signing No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis below slot and applying it to a number of high-ceilinged prep players. It took $1.5 million to sign White away from the Nittany Lions, and he went and had a brief pro debut in the Florida Complex League. As a former Division I football recruit as a wide receiver, White obviously brings athleticism and physicality to the Pirates system. And while some baseball tools are understandably raw given his previously split focus, he does have a shorter right-handed swing and tends to be on time at the plate. There are some swing-and-miss issues to iron out, but that might come with professional reps, and he has shown he can leverage the baseball and get to some solid power. White’s speed plays on both sides of the ball. He should be a basestealing threat and he can cover a ton of ground in center field with a combination of those wheels and excellent instincts. He might have a long way to go, but the Pirates are excited to see how his athleticism plays as a full-time baseball player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barriga signed for only $20,000 out of Mexico in January 2022 but pushed himself into notability with a strong debut in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old that year. A broken leg limited him to only 10 stateside games the following summer before he picked right back up in 2024, moving as high as Single-A Visalia as a teenager. He really struggled in his return to the California League last season, hitting just .199 with a 28.8 percent strikeout rate and 83 wRC+ over 99 games, but he's been much more productive at High-A Hillsboro to begin his age-21 campaign in ’26. The catcher may stand only 5-foot-9, but he can be a real standout to watch behind the plate. An above-average runner on the basepaths, he moves well behind the dish and often looks fluid at such an important position. This comes to bear most on steal attempts, during which Barriga gets into throwing position quickly and often delivers a throw right on target for the easy tag for his infielder. As of May 2026, his career caught-stealing rate was 43 percent, and that’s been consistent throughout his time in the Minors. A right-handed hitter, Barriga often flicks the bat in preparation for the pitch before getting into a leg raise in his load. He appears to be swinging with more intent in the Northwest League this season, and his power is ticking up as a result. He may never be a big homer threat given his size, but his swing and approach are so tailored to lift and pull that he could reach double-digit homers with everyday at-bats. Barriga is Rule 5-eligible this offseason, and his defense alone could get him a 40-man spot or Rule 5 look from another club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just a $20,000 addition out of Mexico in January 2022, Barriga immediately put up solid numbers in the Dominican Summer League that year with a .380 on-base percentage and 117 wRC+ over 42 games. He was going to make for an interesting follow as he headed stateside, but a broken leg ended his 2023 campaign after only 10 games in the Arizona Complex League. He returned to the ACL in ’24 and looked no worse for wear with a .276/.362/.432 line, four homers and 12 steals in 46 games. He joined Single-A Visalia for a seven-game spin after the ACL postseason. Just 5-foot-9, Barriga brings above-average speed to the table, a rarity for a full-time catcher. He could still learn to pick his stolen-base spots a little better, having gone 12-for-17 in his attempts in ’24, but no other qualified backstop on a domestic complex circuit had more than five thefts last year. He utilizes that athleticism well with good movement behind the plate, even for a smaller target, and his plus arm strength consistently nails attempted basestealers. Entering 2025, he has a 49.5 percent caught-stealing rate in his career. With a smaller strike zone, Barriga hasn’t punched out much yet in his career, but he was exposed for a high chase rate in that first bite of the California League. His bat-to-ball skills can make up for that, and his speed can help him beat out infield hits. He’ll need them with below-average power from the right side. Barriga will be 20 for the entire 2025 season as he tries to nail down his place as a potential athletic catcher for Arizona.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers had a quality international signing in 2025 when they added outfielder Cris Rodriguez for a franchise-record $3,197,500 and helped him develop gaudy power numbers (10 homers, .564 slugging percentage) in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. The organization didn't go quite that high on a signing bonus to bring in Santana -- in this case, $1,097,500 -- but they did go after a similar profile in the Dominican outfielder. Ranked as the No. 21 talent in the 2026 international class by MLB Pipeline, Santana flashes big-time power from the right side. He uses a leg kick to get into rhythm and generates a good amount of bat speed for a 17-year-old, and given that he stands 6-foot-3 already, there's projection for him to add strength and get to at least above-average pop at full physical maturity. Santana can show balance in his upper body that could help adjust to breaking balls and offspeed pitches, but he'll face higher quality secondaries as he climbs. It's a power-over-hit profile to begin his career, anyway. Santana's loudest tool at present is his cannon of a throwing arm with throws measured in the triple-digits before he joined the Detroit organization. The Tigers believe he could be a plus runner and stick in center, though that speed might slow a tick as he adds strength elsewhere. They intend to get him plenty of looks in center field, knowing that his arm strength and power would make him a fine fit as a right fielder if he needs to move.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Allan’s career started dramatically when he fell to the Mets in the third round in 2019, reportedly due to a high asking price, before New York coaxed him into pro ball with a $2.5 million bonus. What’s followed has been fascinating for all the wrong reasons. The right-hander was an alternate training site standout in 2020 but hasn’t pitched in a Minor League game since, after undergoing Tommy John surgery (2021), ulnar nerve transposition surgery (2022) and UCL revision surgery (2023). The latest procedure will knock him out until 2024 at the earliest. When healthy, Allan had all the makings of a potential ace. His four-seamer sat around 96 mph out of a clean delivery, and the Mets were pleased with how well he placed the heater high in the zone. His low-80s curveball had good spin rates and downward action, making it a second plus pitch, while his mid-80s changeup drew strong reviews coming out of his alt site work as it developed into another above-average offering. The Florida native will be coming up on the fifth anniversary of his Draft date by the time he’s able to take the mound for a full-season affiliate for the first time, and that’s if there aren’t any other setbacks. The window of a frontline starter is technically still open, but it’s closing more and more without Allan on the bump.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 13 Draft prospect in 2019, Allan became one of the most interesting follows of that process. He had a strong commitment to the University of Florida and a high asking price (reportedly $4 million), causing teams to look elsewhere in the early rounds. The Mets decided to pounce in the third and worked Draft mechanics (mostly by going heavy on college seniors later) to sign Allan for $2.5 million, roughly four times his slot value. The Florida native was an alternate training site standout in 2020 and was set to let loose on a full season in the Minors before tearing the UCL in his right elbow. He underwent Tommy John surgery in May 2021 and needed another procedure this offseason to transpose his ulnar collateral nerve. He isn’t expected to return to a Minor League mound in 2022, making his age-22 campaign next year his comeback. When he was healthy, Allan showed a clean delivery that helped him sit around 96 mph with his four-seamer. He was capable of touching higher than that when needed and drew strong reviews for his ability to locate vertically in the zone. His low-80s curve was another plus pitch with promising spin rates and good downward action. Mets officials praised Allan’s changeup, in particular, coming out of his alt-site workouts in Brooklyn, and the mid-80s offering flashed plus. Like everything else for a young pitcher, Allan likely needs more reps to nail down that third pitch. The pandemic and elbow procedures mean it could be around three years into his career until Allan officially suits up for a full-season team, and we still don’t fully know how or if his pitches will return when he is back on the mound. At his ceiling, he possesses No. 2 starting stuff. At his floor, we’ll be wondering what could have been if not for the elbow.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Many scouts who saw Allan during his senior year at Seminole HS (Sanford, Fla.) felt that he might have been the top high school arm available in the 2019 Draft. But with a reported price of $4 million on top of a strong commitment to the University of Florida, most teams did not feel comfortable risking their top Draft pick on the prep right-hander, and Allan went unselected on Day 1. The Mets took Allan with their third-round pick the next day and signed him for $2.5 million -- roughly four times slot value for the No. 89 overall pick -- thanks mainly to the money the team saved by selecting college seniors in Rounds 4-10. Allan stood out as one of the youngest players at the Mets’ alternate training site in 2020, performing well against the advanced competition, and he continued to improve during fall instructional league. Allan was set to start 2021 at High-A Brooklyn but was diagnosed with a torn ulnar collateral ligament in his right elbow before his first start. The resulting Tommy John surgery means he will miss all of the 2021 season and could be out for part of 2022 as well. When healthy, Allan’s athleticism and clean delivery allow him to generate easy velocity, as he’ll sit around 96 mph and touch higher at times with a four-seam fastball that explodes through the zone. He will drive the ball down in the zone, but he can pitch up and down with his heater well, commanding it both in and out of the strike zone. Allan features a second plus pitch in a high-spin-rate curveball in the low 80s that he throws with hard downer action. Allan’s mid-80s changeup was his most-improved pitch in 2020 and became a weapon for him at the alternate site, with some club officials even labeling it as a plus pitch in its current state. He repeats his mechanics well and is consistently around the plate with all three pitches, showing good command that should only continue to improve. With his combination of size, stuff and feel, Allan has all the ingredients needed to become a frontline starter. A better understanding of mixing his three pitches allowed the young right-hander to excel at the alternate site against Triple-A and Major League-quality hitters, and club officials were particularly impressed with Allan’s capacity for making quick adjustments. Allan will need to rely on that ability to adjust throughout his Tommy John recovery and rehab. If his stuff can return to the same level it was at prior to the procedure, the right-hander will have a shot at a prominent role in a future Mets rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia was one of the top prospects on the international amateur market when the 2019-20 signing period opened, but it’s taken him a while to sign and really get going in his professional career. Because of an age discrepancy, he didn’t sign with the Phillies until March 2020, getting a bonus of $2.5 million. Then the pandemic-related shutdown happened, so he was stuck in Venezuela for an extended period and played just 18 games with Single-A Clearwater in his official pro debut in 2021. The 2022 season wasn’t much better as a torn meniscus limited him to just 37 total games, depriving him of essential development time. Garcia still possesses the raw tools and athleticism that made him such a coveted prospect in 2019, but he has yet to really have the opportunity to learn how or show them in his performance. He has close to top-of-the-scale speed and is a major base-stealing threat, one who was on pace to steal 100 bases in 2022 before he got hurt. To use that speed he is going to have to work on improving his overall approach and gain strength so he can get on base and impact the ball from the right side of the plate more consistently. His explosive athleticism works very well in the outfield. He’s a plus defender who will be able to play center field for a long time, combining his speed and outstanding reads and routes to cover a lot of ground. There are a lot of similarities between him and fellow Phillies prospect Johan Rojas, both in terms of his tools and what he needs to work on, but he needs to start getting regular reps under his belt to show what he can do.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A discrepancy in his reported age kept Garcia from signing when many thought he’d be able to, in July of 2019, not joining the Phillies officially until March 2020 for $2.5 million. The toolsy outfielder had to stay at home in Venezuela, working out on his own for the rest of 2020, because of pandemic-related travel restrictions. He played just 18 games in his official debut in 2021, with just a .570 OPS to show for it. The Phillies are still very high on Garcia and his quick-twitch athleticism. The right-handed hitter needs reps to help him build focus from pitch-to-pitch and so he can learn a consistent approach. He’s worked to clean up his swing and connect his lower half to the upper half, with a bigger base, while gaining an understanding of the importance of controlling the strike zone. A plus runner who can steal a base, Garcia is a plus defender who can stay in center field for a long time, ranking behind only Johan Rojas in terms of route efficiencies in the outfield. More than anything, he just needs to play every day, something he’ll hopefully do in 2022 at the age of 20.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia was on the map as a prospect eligible to sign when the 2019-20 international signing period began on July 2, 2019, but a discrepancy with his reported age led him to have to wait until 2020. The Phillies were more than happy to be patient, signing the talented infielder for $2.5 million in mid-March of 2020 when he was 18 years old. He wasn’t able to participate in instructional league play in Florida last fall, working out at home in Venezuela. The Phillies love Garcia’s overall tool package, especially what they think he can do with the bat. He has a solid approach with the ability to send line drives to the gap, but there should be more power to come as he fills out. His super-quick hands standout more than anything, where he can let the ball get in on him and make late swing decisions, which should help him hit as he gets moving in the system. Garcia’s speed is currently his lone plus tool, with him having recorded 6.3-second 60-yard dashes in the past. That should help him on the basepaths and it really helps him play a very good center field, where he could be a plus defender in time. He plays with high energy and the Phillies can’t wait to unleash his talents on pro ball in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Espino is one of the hardest prospects to rank in the Guardians' system -- and perhaps across baseball -- because his upside is so tantalizing but his availability is a giant question mark. He was one of the most exciting arms in the 2019 Draft, when the Guardians selected him 24th overall and signed him for $2.5 million, and he quickly blossomed into one of the best pitching prospects in the sport. However, he essentially did not pitch for four consecutive seasons between knee tendinitis, shoulder soreness and a pair of shoulder surgeries. The Panama native, who moved to Georgia during high school, returned to face 26 batters across five outings in Triple-A and the Arizona Fall League in 2025, where his stuff was impressively close to its top form. While his fastball once peaked at 103 mph with impressive ride and run, he was still touching 100 last fall. His devastating slider with two-plane break had less power as well but should remain a weapon and could regain velocity as he builds back up. He'll also show a low-80s curve and mid-80s changeup, but the other two pitches are his bread and butter. Of course, the biggest hurdle will be health. The Guardians need to build up his workload slowly to make sure he stays on the mound, and there will likely be a natural push to use his bullets in the Majors as long as he's healthy. He still has No. 1 starter upside, but the Guardians will deploy a wait-and-see approach on his usage rather than make concrete plans. There's a chance he could be stretched out down the line -- and he previously showed enough command to start -- but given his age (25) and one remaining option, if he's dominating big leaguers in relief for a couple of innings at a time, that's a great outcome too. Espino has gold-standard makeup as far as work ethic and resilience, which is crucial given how much he's been through.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Espino had a mid-80s fastball when he moved from Panama to Georgia for his sophomore year of high school, then blossomed into arguably the most electric arm in the 2019 prep class. After signing for $2.5 million as the 24th overall choice, he developed the best all-around stuff in the Minors -- but he didn't pitch in an official game between April 2022 and September 2025. Initially sidelined by knee tendinitis, he developed shoulder soreness while rehabbing. He has had two shoulder surgeries since, getting a muscle strain and capsule tear repaired in May 2023 and damage to his shoulder capsule and rotator cuff fixed in March 2024. When last seen on the mound, Espino had a four-seam fastball that sat at 95-98 mph with a high of 103 with armside run, and he could blow it by Double-A hitters wherever he wanted in the strike zone. He also exhibited nice feel for a power slider, displaying the aptitude to spin it in the mid-80s with two-plane depth or push it up to 93 mph with more horizontal action. His low-80s curveball and mid-80s changeup with sink weren't as consistent but operated as solid pitches when they were on. Espino's combination of athleticism and strength allowed him to generate explosive stuff with little effort. He continued to improve his control and command as he rose through the Minors and was on the verge of joining the Guardians at age 21. He had all the ingredients to become a No. 1 starter but now he's a total wild card.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Panamanian-born Espino had a mid-80s fastball when he moved to Georgia for his sophomore year of high school and developed into one of the most electric arms in the 2019 prep class. After he signed for $2.5 million as the 24th overall pick, he kept improving to the point where he might have had the best overall stuff in the Minors -- but he has pitched just 18 1/3 innings in the last two years. Sidelined in May 2022 with knee tendinitis, he developed shoulder soreness while rehabbing and missed all of 2023 following May surgery to repair a muscle strain and capsule tear. He'll miss the entire 2024 season after having a second shoulder operation this March to repair damage to his shoulder capsule and rotator cuff. A healthy Espino can be unhittable with a top-of-the-scale fastball and plus-plus slider. In 2022, he was sitting at 95-98 mph and reaching 103 with a four-seam fastball that featured plenty of arm-side run, and he showed the aptitude to blow it by hitters at the letters with carry or leverage it down in the zone. He also has good feel for his two-plane slider, spinning it in the mid-80s with more depth or dialing it up to 93 mph with more horizontal movement. Espino's low-80s downer curveball and mid-80s sinking changeup can be solid pitches when they're working. His athleticism allows him to generate overwhelming stuff with little effort and also has enabled him to make adjustments to improve his control and command. If he can stay on the mound, he'll be a frontline starter, but his health remains a huge question mark.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Panama, Espino arrived with a mid-80s fastball when he moved to Georgia for his sophomore year of high school and developed into one of the best pitchers of the 2019 prep class. Signed for $2.5 million as the 24th overall pick, he has the most electric stuff among pro pitching prospects four years later. Poised to make his big league debut in 2022, he fanned 35 in 18 1/3 innings over four Double-A starts before getting sidelined by knee tendinitis, then got shut down with shoulder soreness. After his shoulder continued to bother him this winter, he was diagnosed with a muscle strain and a capsule tear that led to surgery in May and he isn't expected to return to game action until mid-2024. When healthy, Espino can destroy hitters with his top-of-the-scale fastball and plus-plus slider. He operates at 95-98 mph and tops out at 103 with a four-seamer with plenty of arm-side run, and he can use it up in the zone with carry or leverage it lower in the zone with downhill plane. He has good feel for his two-plane slider, showing the ability to work in the mid-80s with increased depth or reaching 93 mph with more horizontal action. Espino also owns a downer curveball in the low 80s and a sinking changeup in the mid-80s, both of which can be solid pitches when they're on. He came with reliever risk when he turned pro, but he had erased any doubts that he can be a frontline starter before he got hurt. His athleticism helps him generate premium stuff without much effort and also has enabled him to make adjustments to improve his control and command as he has risen through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Panamanian-born Espino had a mid-80s fastball when he moved to Georgia for his sophomore year of high school and developed the best heater in the 2019 prep class, topping out in triple digits. Signed for $2.5 million as the 24th overall pick, he reached short-season ball in his pro debut, the first high schooler in Cleveland's system to do so since Francisco Lindor in 2011. He made a spectacular full-season debut in 2021, striking out 152 in 91 2/3 innings between Low-A and High-A with double-digit whiffs in six of his last eight starts. Espino has one of the most electric arms in the Minors and easily overpowers hitters with his fastball and slider. He sits in the mid-90s and peaks at 101 mph with his heater, generating running action on his four-seamer. He shows feel for manipulating his slider, working in the mid-80s with more depth and in the upper 80s with more horizontal break, and missing a ton of bats with both versions. Espino also has a solid low-80s curveball and a sinking mid-80s changeup with similar promise, though the latter offering can get too firm at times. His athleticism helps him generate premium velocity without excessive effort, and he has made adjustments to shorten his arm action since turning pro. While he still battles the strike zone at times and comes with some reliever risk, he lowered his walk rate to 2.9 per nine innings in 10 High-A starts and has plenty of time to further improve his control in order to become a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Panama, Espino went from throwing in the mid-80s when he moved to Georgia for his sophomore year of high school in 2016 to becoming the most electric arm in the 2019 prep class. He regularly reached the upper 90s on the showcase circuit and earned a $2.5 million bonus as the 24th overall pick. He struck out 34 in 23 2/3 innings while becoming the first high schooler the Indians promoted to short-season ball in his debut summer since Francisco Lindor in 2011, but was limited to developing at Cleveland's alternate site in 2020. Espino works at 94-97 mph and can touch triple digits with his fastball, imparting running life on his four-seamer and heavy sink on his two-seamer. He backs up his heat with a pair of bat-missing breaking balls, with his low-80s slider sharper and grading better than his high-70s curveball. His changeup is more of a work in progress that gets too firm at times but also features some promising sink. Espino has a long arm action that leads to inconsistencies with his control and command, though his outstanding athleticism helps him find the strike zone. While he has more reliever risk than a typical first-round choice, he also has better stuff than most and definitely has closer upside if he winds up in the bullpen. The Indians envision him becoming a frontline starter and he could advance more quickly than initially expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of two national championship teams at Parkview HS (Lilburn, Ga.) before attending Troy, Cerny was one of the better college athletes in the 2021 Draft. He dropped to the Phillies in the 10th round because of signability concerns, but he turned pro for $146,100, then got traded to the Astros for Garrett Stubbs in November. He slashed .197/.293/.401 in Single-A during the first two months of 2022, then surged to .297/.404/.513 in the next two before getting shut down with a bruised right thumb. Cerny has some of the best all-around tools in the system but he also comes with swing-and-miss concerns. He has a busy right-handed swing geared to hit balls as far as he can, though his bat speed and strength would provide plenty of power even if he didn't swing for the fences. To reach his 25-25 upside, he'll need to learn to stop chasing balls out of the strike zone and figure out how to handle quality offspeed pitches, and he was making some mild progress last year when he got hurt. Cerny's aggressiveness carries over to the bases and the outfield as well. He has plus-plus speed and looks to steal and take extra bases. His quickness and instincts give him the range to remain in center field and his solid arm strength helps make him an asset at all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cerny played on two national championship teams at Parkview High (Lilburn, Ga.) before heading to Troy. One of the better college athletes in the 2020 Draft, he fell to the Phillies in the 10th round because of signability concerns and turned pro for $146,000. A thumb injury restricted him to 13 games in his pro debut, after which Philadelphia dealt him to the Astros for Garrett Stubbs in November. Cerny has 25-25 upside with bat speed and strength that creates legitimate pop from gap to gap. But he also comes with swing-and-miss concerns because he has a lot going on in his right-handed swing and a grip-it-and-rip-it approach. He can crush fastballs but chases too many pitches out of the strike zone and struggles with breaking balls and changeups. With plus-plus speed and an aggressive mindset, Cerny is a basestealing threat. His quick-twitch athleticism and instincts allow him to cover ground and play a quality center field. He also offers solid arm strength and some added intrigue with some catching experience in high school.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays preached patience with Santana even after selecting him 31st overall and signing him for $2 million out of south Florida’s Doral Academy in the 2023 Draft. They were impressed by the switch-hitting, slick-fielding shortstop’s defensive ability and a pre-Draft workout in which he hit well from both sides of the plate and drove four or five balls out of the park during batting practice. The Rays pushed him last year, assigning him to Single-A Charleston for his full-season debut despite him being a slightly built 18-year-old, and the results were about what they expected. Santana has shown the speed, baserunning acumen and hitting mechanics to add value offensively, although he hit just .240/.300/.305 over 103 games for Charleston last year. That much was no surprise to the Rays, considering he was dealing with the grind of his first full season against more experienced pitchers while still needing to fill out his 5-foot-11 frame. But he did impress on the bases despite his low OBP, stealing 51 bags while only being caught nine times, and his 15.8 percent strikeout rate reflects his solid bat-to-ball skills. It also stood out that Santana played 103 games, likely more than expected, and had his best offensive months in July (.782 OPS) and August (.648 OPS). Santana is an exceptional athlete and an excellent defender, likely behind only Carson Williams and Gregory Barrios in the Rays’ system in terms of his ability on the dirt. He has outstanding range with strong hands and clean footwork, with a plus arm to make all the throws he needs to make across the infield. His severely limited power will be an issue until he’s more physically developed, and it might further delay his progression if he can’t hit enough to move up the system. But the Rays know a thing or two about developing defensive-minded shortstops, and they will continue to be patient with this one.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays generally take an open-minded approach to talent evaluation -- especially in the Draft -- but a switch-hitting and slick-fielding shortstop is kind of their type. Santana, coming from Doral Academy in south Florida, further impressed the Rays during a pre-Draft workout in which he hit well from both sides of the plate and drove four or five balls out of the park during batting practice. Santana left that workout feeling like he’d wind up with the Rays, and sure enough, they called his name with the 31st overall pick and signed him for $2 million. Santana is a premium athlete with the potential to be a special baserunner and up-the-middle defender. He has enough bat-to-ball skills and smooth enough hitting mechanics to hold his own at the plate, even though his ability to hit for power will be severely limited until he fills out his 5-foot-11 frame. He’s also an excellent runner, even in a system with some true top-of-the-scale speed, which adds value to his offensive profile. Santana’s defense is his other strong suit. He’s got tremendous range at shortstop with strong hands and clean footwork, and his plus arm delivers strong and accurate throws across the infield. This year will challenge him, as he’ll be facing older and more experienced pitchers while dealing with the physical and mental grind of his first full season, so a successful season for him might not look the same as it would for a prospect of his caliber. His development might require some patience, but the Rays bet on Santana for a reason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres inked Contreras out of Mexico for $50,000 in July 2017, then watched as he became one of their steadiest risers. After posting a 3.61 ERA in 25 appearances (23 starts) at Class A Fort Wayne in 2019, Contreras’ stock continued to trend upward with a very impressive showing at the team’s instructional camp. That is, until he blew out his right arm during his final outing and underwent Tommy John surgery. Added to the 40-man roster last offseason, Contreras is still finding his footing in his post-procedure return to the mound at High-A Fort Wayne. Contreras doesn’t come with much physical projection to his thicker, undersized build, but his stuff has steadily ticked up since he entered the pro ranks. His fastball sits in the mid-90s, and he commands it with ease for a pitcher his age. He uses that heater to help set up one of the best curveballs in San Diego’s system, and he also has a quality changeup at his disposal to combat left-handed hitters. The clean and repeatable delivery that fuels Contreras’ strike-throwing ability also leads evaluators to project him for well-above-average command. Everything sounds promising, but first he needs to get back on the mound. Once he’s able to make up for lost time and get back on track, Contreras has the look of a future back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres inked Contreras out of Mexico for $50,000 in July 2017, then watched as he became one of their steadiest risers. After posting a 3.61 ERA in 25 appearances at Class A Fort Wayne in 2019, Contreras’ stock continued to trend upward with a very impressive showing at the team’s instructional camp. That is, until he blew out his arm during his final outing and required Tommy John surgery in November. Despite the setback, team officials remain high on Contreras, who should still be only 22 years old when he returns. Contreras doesn’t come with much physical projection to his thicker, undersized build. But his stuff has steadily ticked up since he entered the pro ranks. His fastball sits in the mid-90s, and he commands it with ease for a pitcher his age. Contreras uses that heater to help set up arguably the best the curveball in San Diego’s system, and he also has a quality changeup at his disposal to combat left-handed hitters. The clean and repeatable delivery that fuels Contreras’ strike-throwing ability also leads evaluators to project him for well above-average command. First thing’s first: Contreras needs to attack his rehab process. But with a knack for attacking hitters and an impressive blend of big league caliber pitches, Contreras has the look of a future backend starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An alumnus of MLB Develops programs like the Hank Aaron Invitational and Breakthrough Series, Drake was a toolsy outfielder from Atlanta who went to the MLB Draft League to test his mettle ahead of the 2023 Draft. He performed well over a small sample there ahead of the Braves taking him in the fifth round of that July’s Draft and going over slot -- close to $750,000 -- to sign him away from his commitment to Georgia Tech. The younger brother of former NFL running back Kenyan Drake, Isaiah really struggled in his first full season of pro ball, but made some great adjustments in 2025 to perform his way from Single-A Augusta to High-A Rome in his age-19 season. The Braves knew it might take a while for things to click for Drake, and when they sent him to Augusta in 2024 to sink or swim, he sunk, hitting .163 with a 35.5 percent strikeout rate in 69 games in the Carolina League. He slashed that last year with just a 21.3 percent K rate across two levels, and his overall miss and chase rates also went down. Strong and physical, the next step in his development with his improved ability to make contact might be tapping into his considerable raw power more consistently. Drake loves to run, swiping 46 bags last year, with some scouts putting an 80 run grade on him. That helps him go get the ball in center field and he’s improved in that facet of the game as well. There’s work to be done still, but he could be a plus defender when all is said and done. This was a bit of a lottery ticket for the Braves, but if his aptitude keeps trending in this direction, they could cash in.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drake’s older brother Kenyan has had a fairly lengthy NFL career, but Isaiah chose the baseball route. Playing his high school ball in the Braves’ backyard, it looked like he might be heading to Georgia Tech for college, but after performing well in the Draft League and the Combine, the Braves decided to go way over slot and give him close to $750,000 in the fifth round to sign him away from campus. He had a brief, and uneventful, debut in the Florida Complex League after signing. Young for his Draft class, Drake is a left-handed hitter who could develop an exciting power-speed combination. He might be the fastest player in the system now and that should help him on both sides of the ball. He has raw power aplenty to tap into and will have to work on his approach and his ability to barrel up the baseball to get to it as he advances. Drake’s speed allows him to cover a ton of ground in center field and he should be able to stick there, especially as he improves his reads and routes and doesn’t simply outrun the ball. Patience is going to be key here, as he’s a bit of a project, but the payoff could be considerable considering the raw tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $30,000 out of Panama in 2018, Ramos made an instant impression in his U.S. debut three years later, mashing a pair of homers with exit velocities of 111 and 114 mph in his first game in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. He has gone deep 44 times while advancing from Single-A to Double-A during the last two years, but the Dodgers have opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster either time. He was one of Panama's top performers at the 2023 World Baseball Classic, going 5-for-16 with a homer. Ramos weighed just 150 pounds when he turned pro at age 17, but he since has added 50 pounds and is one of the strongest players in the system. He also has tremendous bat speed and a pull-heavy mindset that contribute to well above-average raw power, tape-measure blasts and high exit velocities. However, his right-handed swing gets long and uphill and he chases too much, leading to too many strikeouts and rolled-over groundouts. Though he has slowed down some as he has gotten stronger, Ramos still possesses average speed. He spent most of 2023 in center field, where he has fine instincts and is an average defender. He's solid in right field, a good fit for his plus-plus arm strength that baserunners know better than to test.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $30,000 out of Panama in 2018, Ramos didn't make his U.S. debut until three years later but made an immediate impression by homering twice with exit velocities of 111 and 114 mph in his first game in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. He slammed 25 homers between Single-A and High-A at age 21 last season, but his batting average dropped from .329 to .249 and his strikeout rate rose from 25 to 31 percent compared to 2021. Los Angeles likes his upside but declined to protect him on its 40-man roster in November, successfully deducing that his bat was too raw to get plucked in the Rule 5 Draft. Just 5-foot-11 and 150 pounds when he signed as a 17-year-old, he has added two inches and 50 pounds and resembles fellow Dodgers outfield prospect Andy Pages in terms of physicality and tools. Ramos has tremendous bat speed and strength that allow him to hit tape-measure shots and could produce 30 or more homers per season in the big leagues.
