But his uphill right-handed swing and extremely aggressive approach make him vulnerable to breaking pitches and result in a lot of wasted at-bats and strikeouts, so he'll have to tone things down at higher levels. Ramos has slowed down as he has gained muscle, though he's still an average runner with good outfield instincts. He split time between right field and center field last season, and he's a solid defender at all three outfield spots. His plus-plus arm is a weapon that has notched 30 assists in 223 games in his first three pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A bargain signing at $30,000 out of Panama in 2018, Ramos didn't get a change to play in the United States before last season. He made an immediate impression, homering twice with exit velocities of 111 and 114 mph in his first game in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. He needed just three weeks to earn a promotion to Low-A at age 20 and batted .329/.396/.577 with 11 homers in 62 games between the two stops. Just 5-foot-11 and 150 pounds when he signed as a 17-year-old, Ramos has added two inches and 50 pounds since then and now resembles fellow Dodgers outfield prospect Andy Pages with his physicality and tools. Both offer well above-average raw power from the right side of the plate and arm strength to match. Ramos has an efficient swing and some feel to hit, though he'll need to tighten his strike zone and prove he can handle quality breaking balls at higher levels. Though Ramos has lost some speed as he has gotten stronger, he's still an average runner with good instincts in the outfield. He spent most of his early career in center field but played solely in right field in Low-A, projecting as a solid defender on the corner. Baserunners have not had much success testing his arm, as he recorded 20 assists in his first 112 outfield starts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howard led his Jackie Robinson West (Chicago) club to the Little League World Series Finals in 2014, six years before becoming just the third local product drafted by the Cubs in the first round. Signed for $3,745,500 as the 16th overall pick in 2020, he struggled offensively and missed time with a hamstring strain when sent to Single-A at age 19 to make his pro debut the following year. He didn't get much of a chance to rebound in 2022, severely injuring his hip in early May and requiring season-ending surgery. Howard's outstanding defense and makeup have prompted Chicago to challenge him with aggressive assignments. He hasn't disappointed with the glove, showing twitchy actions, range to both sides, quick hands and a plus arm capable of making strong throws from a variety of angles. He complements his tools with instincts and intelligence and looks like a future Gold Glover. Though amateur scouts had mixed opinions about Howard's offensive upside and he hit just .229/.287/.315 in 103 games during his first two pro seasons, the Cubs saw some encouraging signs before he got hurt last year. A right-handed hitter, he hit the ball significantly harder and controlled the strike zone better than he did in 2021. He could develop at least 15-homer power to go with his solid speed, but he's going to have to learn to recognize and deal with breaking balls and make adjustments to avoid producing weak ground-ball contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howard starred at shortstop on the Jackie Robinson West (Chicago) club that advanced to the Little League World Series finals in 2014, six years before the Cubs made him just the third Windy City-area product they've ever drafted in the first round. Signed for $3,745,000 as the 16th overall pick in 2020, he's so advanced defensively that he headed directly to Low-A for his pro debut at age 19 last year. Initially overmatched at the plate before rallying in the final two months, he didn't get much of a chance to develop further in 2022 because he injured his left hip in a baserunning mishap in May and required season-ending surgery. One of the best defenders in the entire Minors, Howard is a legitimate plus-plus shortstop. He has quick-twitch actions, fast hands and a plus arm capable of making quality throws from a variety of angles. He has instincts and intelligence to complement his physical tools, and the only reason he spent time at second base last summer was to give fellow teenager Kevin Made some time at shortstop. After Howard's offensive upside drew mixed reviews on the high school showcase circuit, he didn't answer any of those questions in his debut. He has some promising building blocks in a sound right-handed swing, the bat speed and projectable strength to have perhaps average power and solid speed. But he also has a long ways to go with his plate discipline and pitch recognition, which leads to too many strikeouts and too much ground-ball contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The starting shortstop on the Jackie Robinson West (Chicago) team that advanced to the 2014 Little League World Series finals, Howard became just the third Windy City-area product selected in the first round by the Cubs. The top true shortstop in the 2020 Draft, he followed in the footsteps of Brian Rosinski (1975) and Don Schulze (1980) when Chicago took him 16th overall last June. Signed for $3,745,500, he impressed the Cubs with his physical and mental maturity during instructional league. The best defensive player in the system, Howard is a no-doubt shortstop. He has smooth, athletic actions as well as quick hands and a solid to plus arm capable of making throws from a variety of angles. He has the high baseball IQ to make the most of his tools and the internal clock to slow the game down on both sides of the ball. While Howard drew some mixed reviews as a hitter on the high school showcase circuit and again while making his pro debut with a challenging assignment to Low-A, he has an efficient right-handed swing and mature approach that should allow him to make consistent contact. He generates promising bat speed and is adding strength to his projectable 6-foot-2 frame, so he could develop average power. He's a solid runner who's an asset on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Miller was a Wisconsin high schooler, scouts viewed him as a less physical but more athletic version of his older brother Owen, who has seen big league action with three teams in the past five seasons. After the Twins signed him for $1.7 million as a 2021 supplemental first-round choice, he has developed into a better defender and lesser hitter than anticipated. Swapped to the Dodgers for Manuel Margot and infield prospect Rayne Doncon in February 2024, he slashed .255/.290/.352 between Double-A and Triple-A last year. One of the best defensive shortstops in the Minors, Miller has all the ingredients to win a Gold Glove in the Majors. He has fluid actions, range in every direction, a strong and accurate arm, soft hands and good instincts. He's dependable too, committing just 11 errors in 212 games at short during the past two seasons. A switch-hitter who's more productive as a righty, Miller shows bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate but undermines his offensive game by chasing way too many pitches. While he doesn't strike out excessively, his aggressiveness cuts into his walk totals and produces a lot of weak groundball contact, and he offers well below-average power and just average speed. The best-case scenario is that he develops into something similar to World Series hero Miguel Rojas, as he'll have a difficult time cracking a loaded lineup in Los Angeles.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Rockies infielder Owen Miller, Noah profiled as a less physical but more athletic version of his sibling when he was coming through the Wisconsin high school ranks. Since signing with the Twins for $1.7 million as a 2021 supplemental first-rounder, he has provided much more defense and less offense than expected. Traded to the Dodgers for Manuel Margot and infield prospect Rayne Doncon in February 2024, he slashed .244/.318/.315 between High-A and Double-A last season. Some club officials believe Miller could win a Gold Glove in the big leagues this season if given the opportunity. With his slick actions, strong and accurate arm, soft hands and finely calibrated internal clock, there's not a play he can't make at shortstop. He's as reliable as he is spectacular, committing just six errors in 123 starts at short in 2024. A switch-hitter, Miller makes consistent contact but has provided little impact from either side of the plate. The Dodgers hope they can help him develop double-digit home run pop by improving his swing and approach, but he slugged just .317 in his first four pro seasons. He has average speed with good instincts on the bases, though he was a bit slower than that last year while playing through a meniscus injury in his left knee.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Miller was a Wisconsin high schooler, scouts considered him a less physical version of his older brother, big league utilityman Owen. Since signing with the Twins for a below-slot $1.7 million as a supplemental first-round pick in 2021, Noah has been more dazzling in the field and less productive at the plate than expected. The Dodgers acquired him and cleared some needed 40-man roster space in February by sending Manuel Margot and infield prospect Rayne Doncon to Minnesota. Miller won a Minor League Gold Glove in 2023 and is equipped to do the same in the Majors. He can make all the plays at shortstop with smooth actions, a strong and accurate arm, soft and reliable hands and an outstanding internal clock. He's a reliable and spectacular defender who could fit almost anywhere on the diamond if he winds up in a utility role like his brother. Though Miller batted just .220/.326/.318 in his first three pro seasons, Los Angeles hopes to unlock more impact by helping him improve his swing and his approach. He's a switch-hitter with bat speed from both sides of the plate and shows the patience to draw walks, but he makes a lot of soft contact and rarely drives the ball with authority. He's an average runner with good instincts on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller is trying to follow in the footsteps of older brother Owen, who was a big league regular for the Guardians in 2022. The younger Miller was the Twins’ pick in the 2021 Competitive Balance Round A, signing for $1.7 million. The Wisconsin high school standout showed some signs of an excellent approach at the plate, albeit without much impact, while playing strong defense in his first full season of pro ball with Single-A Fort Myers in 2022. There are ingredients for Miller to be a strong all-around infielder. The switch-hitter controls the zone well, drawing walks at an impressive clip, but as often as he was able to work counts, he wasn’t able to show an ability to do damage from either side. Some of that might come with added strength, and fatigue was certainly a factor, but Miller has also worked to make adjustments at the plate to create better angles and more impact. His right-handed swing had improved by the end of last season, but his left-handed one still needs some improvement. Miller’s calling card will always be his defense. His tools and plus instincts will enable him to play shortstop for a long time, with a strong, accurate arm and the chance to eventually be a plus defender at the premium position. Those bullish on Miller’s all-around skills look at fellow Badger state prep product Gavin Lux, who had modest offensive production in his first full season of pro ball then took off with the bat a year later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins went very college-heavy in the 2021 Draft, with 19 of their 21 picks coming from the four-year or junior college ranks. The first two, however, were high schoolers, with Chase Petty going in the first round, followed by Miller, from the Wisconsin prep ranks, going No. 36 overall. The younger brother of Guardians infielder Owen, Miller signed for $1.7 million and made his pro debut in the Florida Complex League last summer. When most talk about Miller, the first things that come up are his baseball IQ and instincts on both sides of the ball. While his contact skills were a bit behind as he adjusted to the speed of the game, he did show a good approach from both sides of the plate. He has shown the ability to make consistent contact in the past with a good bat path. He focused on his left-handed swing during the offseason as well as strengthening his lower half, and he did add good weight. As he works through minor tweaks in his swing, don’t be surprised to see more pop, though it’s hard to know yet where the hit-power balance will end up. Miller shows very good awareness on the dirt. While he’s not a burner, those instincts lead to good jumps and solid range. He has a good arm and a quick release with every chance to stick at the premium position for a long time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gastelum signed with the Cardinals for only $30,000 out of Mexico as a 21-year-old in April 2023 and headed stateside immediately. His big emergence came a year later when he posted a 2.81 ERA and struck out 34.5 percent of batters faced over 48 innings at Single-A Palm Beach, and he continued to dominate in the Mexican Winter League after that. The Cardinals pushed Gastelum past High-A for his age-23 season in 2025, and while his 4.02 ERA didn’t pop on the surface, his 35.4 percent K rate and 1.10 WHIP still did. Gastelum’s 28.8 K/BB percentage was sixth-best among 952 Minor Leaguers with at least 60 innings in ’25. Gastelum’s success to this point stems from one pitch: his low-80s changeup. It’s a mesmerizing offering with negative induced vertical break and plenty of armside run. It practically works like a left-handed breaking ball, but instead emerges from the 6-foot-2 right-hander’s low three-quarters delivery. Because of that action, the cambio was even more effective against righties than lefties last year with a 64 percent whiff rate against same-side bats. (Not that lefties fared that much better.) Gastelum can throw a mid-90s fastball, but with ordinary movement, it only works to set up his beast of a change. He’ll occasionally work in a mid-80s sweeper too for something with big gloveside movement. Gastelum has posted excellent walk rates at every stop to this point, and a big reason for that is that he consistently gets batters to bite on changeups diving out of the zone. He pitches exclusively out of the stretch, so this isn’t a complicated operation. Without an average fastball, Gastelum might have a limited ceiling, but his uniqueness should earn him some role in St. Louis’ bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Mexico as a 21-year-old in April 2023, Gastelum jumped stateside as a reliever and enjoyed a breakout season in 2024 in a 48-inning stint with Single-A St. Palm Beach. His 29.1 K-BB% led the Florida State League among 112 pitchers with at least 40 frames, while his 34.5 strikeout percentage ranked second and his 2.47 FIP third. Gastelum fanned three of his four batters faced (including the final one) in Palm Beach’s FSL championship clincher on Sept. 18, and he’s continued his momentum in the Mexican Winter League. The 6-foot-2 right-hander proved so dominant because of his special changeup. The 81-84 mph cambio averaged -1.6 inches of induced vertical break and 15.5 inches of armside movement, giving it two planes with which to menace hitters. Gastelum threw 317 changeups tracked by Statcast; 161 of them (50.8 percent) ended up as called strikes or whiffs. No one else in the FSL had a CSW rate higher than 41.1 percent (min. 50 changeups), and no one in the Majors had one higher than 41.0 (Angel Chivili) over the same minimum. Gastelum threw his change 47.9 percent of the time because it was so effective. The other side of the coin: the righty’s fastball is much less remarkable as a 91-93 mph offering with ordinary movement, and his mid-80s slider is the closest pitch to flashing above-average. Devin Williams comps would be misguided because at least the Yankees reliever has more fastball velo and usage, but that type of change-heavy profile out of the bullpen gives the righty a profile on which to dream. The Cards prospect will be 23 for the majority of the 2025 season, so it’ll be time for St. Louis to see just how quickly he can ride that changeup toward The Show.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bleis' five-tool potential earned him the largest bonus in Boston's 2021 international class, as he signed for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic. The consensus top prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League during his U.S. debut in 2022, he subluxated his left shoulder on a swing the following May, had season-ending surgery and hasn't made much impact at the plate since. He slashed .222/.300/.385 with 14 homers and 27 steals in 107 games between High-A and Double-A last year. The bat speed and loft in Bleis' right-handed swing create plus raw power that's more obvious in batting practice than during games. He chases too many pitches and tries to yank too many to left field -- his 62 percent pull percentage led the Minors in 2025 -- an approach that results in too many strikeouts and too much suboptimal contact. He hasn't been able to add strength as easily as the Red Sox hoped but still has the ingredients to generate 25 homers per season if he settles down at the plate. Even while struggling offensively, Bleis can impact a game on the bases and in the field. Boston's 2025 baserunner of the year, he displays consistent plus speed, flashes better than that and runs consistently hard. He has improved his defensive instincts and become a quality center fielder with a strong arm that registered 10 assists in 99 starts last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bleis showed five-tool center-fielder potential as an amateur in the Dominican Republic and parlayed it into the largest bonus ($1.5 million) in Boston's 2020-21 international class. He ranked as the consensus top prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League during his 2022 U.S. debut, but his progress came to halt when he subluxated his left shoulder on a swing the following May and required season-ending surgery. He slashed .221/.303/.354 with a system-best 38 steals in 95 games between two Class A stops last year while continuing to showcase the best all-around tools in the system. Bleis combination of electric bat speed, still-growing strength and the loft in his right-handed stroke give him more raw pop than most 21-year-olds. He could produce 25 or more homers per year without swinging for the fences, but he sells out for power with an overly aggressive approach focused on launching balls to his pull side. He generates impressive exit velocities when he connects but will need to improve his swing decisions to find consistent success. Though he has gained at least 25 pounds of strength since turning pro, Bleis has retained his plus speed and turns it loose on the bases. He makes some shaky decisions at times in center field but also has the quickness to overcome a lot of his mistakes and plays as a solid defender there. His plus arm strength helped him notch 22 assists in 174 outfield starts during his first four seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top signing in Boston's 2020-21 international class, Bleis earned a $1.5 million bonus on the basis of his electric bat speed and potential to become a five-tool center fielder. Excitement grew when the Dominican was clearly the best prospect in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in his U.S. debut in 2022, seemingly setting the stage for a full-season breakout last year. But he swings so hard that he subluxated his left shoulder last May and required season-ending surgery. Bleis already has jaw-dropping raw power at age 20 thanks to his bat speed, still-developing strength and the loft and leverage in his right-handed swing. He aggressively looks to launch balls to his pull side, producing high exit velocities for a 20-year-old but also leading to chases and strikeouts. He'll need to improve his swing decisions and his patience as he starts to face more advanced pitching. Evaluators give Bleis solid-to-plus grades for his speed, arm and center-field defense. He already has gained 20 pounds since turning pro and could lose a bit of quickness as he continues to add muscle, but even so his instincts will enable him to continue to be an asset as a runner and defender. He looks to make things happen on the bases and makes good reads in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bleis landed the largest bonus in Boston's 2020-21 international class, signing for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic as a center fielder with the potential for at least solid tools across the board. That's exactly what he looked like in his U.S. debut last summer, when he batted .301/.353/.542 with 23 extra-base hits and 18 steals in 40 games in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. The Red Sox's best international prospect since Rafael Devers, he subluxated his left shoulder on a swing in late May and had season-ending surgery. Built to hit for power, Bleis has a quick right-handed swing with loft and a 6-foot-3 frame with plenty of projectable strength and leverage. He also has an aggressive approach geared to launch balls to his pull side, which helps produce impressive exit velocities for a teenager but also portends the need for adjustments and better swing decisions against more advanced pitching. He does have some feel for recognizing pitches and discerning strikes, so there's optimism that he can become at least an average hitter, which would make him a star. Bleis' present speed earns 55-65 grades on the 20-80 scouting scale, and he likely will settle on the lower end of that range once he matures physically. He uses his quickness well, stealing and taking extra bases and effortlessly covering ground with long strides in center field. He also features solid to plus arm strength and would be an asset at any outfield position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bleis signed for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021, securing the largest bonus in Boston's 2020-21 international class. He made a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, batting .252/.331/.420 with four homers and seven steals in 36 games at age 17. He has one of the highest ceilings in the system with the potential for solid tools across the board. Bleis has a sound right-handed swing and a feel for the strike zone at a young age. His bat speed, projectable strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-2 frame give him plus raw power. He makes a lot of hard contact already and shows the ability to drive balls in the air to his pull side. Though Bleis currently has plus speed to match his raw pop, he likely will slow down a bit as he matures physically. His gliding strides eat up a lot of ground in center field, and he should have the quickness and instincts to stay there. If he had to move to a corner, his solid to plus arm strength would work in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going unselected in four straight Drafts while moving from Okeechobee (Fla.) HS to Florida SouthWestern State JC to Jacksonville, Adams led the Atlantic Sun Conference with 108 strikeouts in 90 innings in 2022. Signed for $75,000 as a 13th-round senior, he quickly established himself as one of the more polished pitchers in the system. On the verge of making the Majors in 2025, he injured his flexor tendon during Spring Training and had Tommy John surgery in April, costing him the entire season. Adams stands out with his ability to spin the ball and fill the strike zone. When healthy, he features a plus low-80s curveball with downer break and a solid if less reliable mid-80s slider with similar shape. He throws his breaking balls more than his fringy two- and four-seam fastballs, which park at 90-93 mph and peak at 94. He improved his upper-80s changeup in 2024, having more success with splitter action than the mild fade it had in the past. Adams excels at sequencing his pitches, working all four quadrants of the strike zone with the varying movement profiles of his offerings. He gets down the mound well, creating deception with extension and a flat approach angle. His No. 4 or 5 starter floor is more impressive than his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adams went unselected in four straight Drafts while going from the Florida high school ranks to Florida SouthWestern State JC to his junior season at Jacksonville. He finally got noticed when he led the Atlantic Sun Conference with 108 strikeouts in 90 innings in 2022, and the White Sox gave him $75,000 as a 13th-round senior sign. One of the most polished pitchers in the system, he paced Chicago farmhands with a 3.9 K/BB ratio last season and would have led the Double-A Southern League in ERA (2.44) if he hadn't fallen a few innings shy of qualifying. Adams had very good feel for spin, producing a plus low-80s curveball with downer break and a solid if less consistent mid-80s slider with two-plane break at its best. He uses his breaking ball as much as he employs his fringy two- and four-seam fastballs, both of which sit at 90-93 mph and top out at 94. He improved his upper-80s changeup, finding more success with improved depth rather than the mild fade he had in the past, though it's still a bit firm. A crafty right-hander, Adams mixes his pitches well and can work all four quadrants of the strike zone with the different movement profiles of his offerings. He creates deception with a flat approach angle and relentlessly fills the strike zone. He got roughed up in five Triple-A starts at the end of 2024, so he'll have to prove himself at that level, but he's not far from joining the big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 60 | Overall: 45 From his senior year as a Florida prepster to two seasons at Florida SouthWestern State JC to his first at Jacksonville, Adams went unselected in four straight Drafts. After he led the Atlantic Sun Conference with 108 strikeouts in 90 innings in 2022, the White Sox signed him for $75,000 as a 13th-rounder. He reached Double-A and established himself as one of the best strike-throwers in the system during his first full pro season. Adams' money pitch is his low-80s curveball with true downer break, a plus offering that he can locate for strikes or use to get chases outside the zone. His feel for spin extends to a mid-80s slider with two-plane depth, though it's not nearly as reliable as his curve. He uses both two- and four-seam fastballs in the low-90s, with his fringy sinker the more effective choice. Adams also has a mediocre mid-80s changeup with mild fade and not enough velocity separation from his heater. His ability to pound the strike zone and create deception with a flat approach angle help him get the most out of his less than overwhelming stuff. He could be a back-of-the-rotation starter if he can miss enough bats with his fastball, and a curveball-dependent reliever if he can't.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two years ago, Bitsko was considered a top prospect in the 2021 Draft class, but he chose to reclassify and become eligible for the Draft in 2020. Bitsko said he made the decision to reclassify “to further my career,” but he was dealt a significant setback before it really even began. In December 2020, a matter of months after the Rays took Bitsko 24th overall and signed him for an above-slot $3 million bonus, he underwent surgery to repair a torn labrum in his right shoulder. It’s been a slow recovery and return process for Bitsko since that procedure. He was healthy coming into the season, but the Rays have used him cautiously, beginning with an assignment to the Florida Complex League in early June. He’s made abbreviated and inconsistent starts in the Sunshine State since, though he was starting to show his old self in flashes entering late August. Still, the Rays picked Bitsko in the first round for a reason and remain confident in his upside. He’s big and strong, listed at 6-foot-4 and 225 pounds, and when he’s on, he has “now” stuff. His fastball reached 96-97 mph at the East Coast Pro Showcase, sitting between 92-96, and he throws a hard curveball that should be a plus, swing-and-miss pitch. He also throws a slider, shows a feel for his changeup and has the potential to develop plus command of all his pitches. He’ll need a lot of time to get healthy and develop, and the Rays are already hesitant enough to rush their young pitchers. But if he comes all the way back, he has a considerably high ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The scouting industry had seen a good amount of Bitsko, even though he was thought to be one of the top high school arms in the Class of 2021. But when the big right-hander from Eastern Pennsylvania announced that he'd be graduating early, that made him eligible for this year's Draft and put him right up with the top prep arms in the country. Bitsko is 6-foot-4, 220 pounds, with plenty of projection and now stuff. He stood out particularly at the East Coast Pro Showcase over the summer, but he has shown consistent ability at every stop. Bitsko was up to 96-97 mph at East Coast Pro, with all fastballs in the 92- to 96-mph range. He combines it with a hard breaking ball that shows plus shape, thrown in the 78- to 82-mph range to get a lot of swings and misses. While he doesn't throw it as much, he does have solid feel for a changeup. Bitsko isn't pure power, either, showing the ability to throw all three pitches for strikes with a chance for future plus command. Teams were going to have to play some catch-up with Bitsko this spring because they weren't bearing down on him over the summer as much as they were with the incoming senior class, something that couldn't happen beyond an early bullpen session because of the shutdown. He's committed to the University of Virginia, which could come into play, but he has the chance to be an early first-round pick.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers were one of the teams high on O’Rae coming out of Ontario ahead of the 2022 Draft. The organization liked what they saw from his high OBP stint with Canada’s Junior National Team and selected him in the third round that July. O’Rae signed around slot for $597,500 and backed up Milwaukee’s confidence with a solid first full season, hitting .349/.491/.394 with 44 steals in 60 games between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Carolina. His .491 OBP topped all Minor Leaguers with at least 250 plate appearances while his 1.54 BB/K ratio placed fourth. Standing just 5-foot-7, O’Rae doesn’t have a very big strike zone, and he does pitchers no favors by not going outside of it to swing. Starting from a slightly open stance, he shows quick hands from the left side that help produce a healthy amount of contact. It would be all the makings for a true plus hitter, if he had any modicum of power. His swing is geared toward ground balls -- 57.1 percent of his batted balls were on the dirt and grass -- and he punches a ton of them the other way with a 51.1 percent oppo rate that was second in the Minors. Only nine of O’Rae’s 84 career hits have gone for extra bases. The plus-plus speed the Brewers liked so much in the Draft has certainly played in pro ball, however, and O’Rae is efficient when it comes to stealing bags. Below-average arm strength pushed him from short to second base and he also tried center field in 2023, where he has more room to roam. There are pieces for an exciting prospect here, but the power needs to develop in his age-20 season and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Milwaukee felt like the industry was missing something on O’Rae. The Ontario native hit .257/.464/.343 with 17 steals in 25 games for Canada’s Junior National Team against advanced competition leading up to the 2022 Draft, and the looks he gave there provided the Brewers with enough confidence to select him in the third round and sign him for around slot at $597,500 -- an indication the pick was not made for pool-saving purposes. He played eight games in the Arizona Complex League after signing and showed much of the same skillset by going 8-for-26 with no extra-base hits and four steals. O’Rae already demonstrated to Milwaukee officials and scouts that he could control the zone in an advanced way as an amateur, and that continued with his 7/6 K/BB ratio in complex play. It’s a skill that could translate well at each Minor League stop when the teenager starts seeing full-season ball. Listed at 5-foot-9, 160 pounds, the left-handed batter has little in-game power in his current frame, but the Brewers believe there’s a chance for him to add strength as he matures. The Canadian’s plus-plus speed will help him pick up some extra-base hits for now -- on top of his ever-present threat to steal bags -- and it should help his case to stick up the middle, too. Milwaukee wanted to give O’Rae a try at short, but his limited arm strength made him a better fit in the Arizona Complex League this season. Being an average hitter with great speed is valuable anywhere up the middle, and becoming that should be a focus in the early stages of O’Rae’s career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals drafted Dabovich in the 18th round in 2018 after he flashed a 98 mph fastball as a Central Arizona CC freshman, but he turned them down to transfer to Arizona State. The Sun Devils shifted him from the rotation to the bullpen midway through his sophomore season and he became their closer before the Giants selected him in 2020's fourth round. He averaged 14.1 strikeouts per nine innings while advancing to Triple-A in his first two pro seasons but he worked just four games last April before undergoing season-ending hip surgery. Dabovich attacks hitters with two pitches, working up high with four-seam fastballs before dropping hammer curveballs through the bottom of the zone. His curve is a legitimate plus-plus pitch with mid-80s power and huge depth that produced a 52 percent swing-and-miss rate and 43 percent chase rate in 2022. His fastball also grades as a well-above-average offering at its best, though it's less inconsistent and parked at 93-96 mph with a peak of 97 two years ago. Hitters can't get comfortable against Dabovich, who works out of a high arm slot with a flat approach angle and doesn't always know where his pitches are headed. An intense competitor who has trouble repeating his delivery, he has walked 26 in 27 1/3 innings during his short time in Triple-A. He can show closer stuff but needs to prove he can harness it and stay healthy after also missing time in 2021 with back issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dabovich flashed a 98-mph fastball as a Central Arizona CC freshman in 2018, then turned down the Royals as an 18th-rounder and transferred to Arizona State. He transitioned from starter to reliever with the Sun Devils before signing as a fourth-rounder in 2020. He averaged 14.1 strikeouts per nine innings in his first two seasons while climbing from High-A to Triple-A. Both Dabovich's fastball and curveball can grade as plus-plus pitches when at their best, though his former wasn't as sharp in 2022, when he dealt with hamstring issues. He lost a bit of velocity and riding action on his heater, though he still sat at 93-96 mph. He likes to work up top with his four-seamer and then mess with batters' eye level by dropping mid-80s curveballs through the bottom of the zone. Hitters have trouble adjusting to Dabovich's pitches coming at a flat approach angle out of a high arm slot. He presents an uncomfortable at-bat because he has overpowering stuff but doesn't always know where it's going. He has trouble keeping his mechanics in sync, which led to 20 walks in 24 2/3 innings, and he'll need to throw more strikes to be a late-inning reliever in San Francisco.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals drafted Dabovich in the 18th round in 2018 after he touched 98 mph with his fastball as a Central Arizona CC freshman, but he turned them down and transferred to Arizona State. He transitioned from starter to closer while with the Sun Devils and pitched his way into the fourth round of the 2020 Draft. He struck out nearly two batters per inning and reached Double-A in his pro debut last summer, though his control disintegrated during a stint in the Arizona Fall League. Dabovich challenges hitters with a 93-97 mph fastball that peaks at 99 and has a flat approach angle coming out of his high arm slot. He works up top with his four-seamer, then changes batters' eye level by dropping mid-80s curveballs through the bottom of the zone. Both pitches can grade as plus-plus when at their best. It's tough for hitters to get comfortable against Dabovich because his stuff is overpowering and he doesn't harness it consistently. Counting the AFL, he issued 25 walks in 43 innings last year, and he'll need to get more dialed in to fill a high-leverage role in San Francisco. As soon as he gets his mechanics in sync and provides consistent strikes, he'll be ready for the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before Nolan McLean and Carson Benge were notable two-way prospects at Oklahoma State, Campbell was a finalist for the John Olerud Award -- given to NCAA Division I's best two-way player -- in 2021. The California native went on to focus solely on pitching and performed well enough as a junior for the Guardians to select him 37th overall and sign him for a below-slot $1.7 million in '22. However, Campbell did not make his pro debut until April 2026 because of May 2023 right elbow surgery to relieve pressure on his ulnar nerve, April 2024 Tommy John surgery on the same elbow and October 2024 right wrist surgery. Campbell was a polished arm in college and stands out at the start of his pro career for his broad five-pitch mix, with each offering at least average. After averaging 91-92 mph on his fastball at Oklahoma State, he's now sitting 94-95 mph and touching 97. He throws the pitch more than half the time, but opponents have trouble with it because of the extension he gets on his 6-foot-5 frame and the uncomfortable approach angle from his delivery. He pairs that well with a mid-80s changeup that can pick up a lot of whiffs and chase at its best. Campbell can spin a pair of promising breaking balls, with the curve currently ahead of the slider, in part because it gets nearly 40 inches of vertical separation from the fastball. His low-90s cutter is new since college and has been a promising fifth option. Campbell is an excellent strike-thrower, and his athleticism and delivery have helped him maintain his above-average control, even after all of those surgeries. The big question, though, remains health, since there are very few cases of pitchers not throwing for four years and developing into long-term starters, so the Guardians will continue to build him up slowly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Campbell was a finalist for the John Olerud Award given to NCAA Division I's best two-way player in 2021 before focusing solely on pitching as an Oklahoma State junior last spring. He ranked seventh in D-I with 141 strikeouts in 101 1/3 innings before going 37th overall in the Draft and signing for a below-slot $1.7 million. He has yet to make his pro debut, however, because he had surgery to relieve pressure on the ulnar nerve in his pitching elbow in May. Campbell has two secondary pitches that stand out more than his fastball: a plus upper-70s changeup with plenty of fade and a mid-70s curveball with significant depth. His heater sits at 91-93 mph and occasionally reaches 97, featuring high spin rates and armside run that generate a lot of weak contact. He can mix in a low-80s slider but usually works with three pitches. Due to his 6-foot-7 frame that creates unusual angle and deceptive delivery, hitters don't see the ball well against Campbell and take a lot of awkward swings against him. Very athletic for his size, he repeats his mechanics and pounds the strike zone. A tough competitor who had one of the highest floors among pitchers in the 2022 Draft, he should become at least a No. 4 starter with the chance for more if the Guardians can work their Shane Bieber magic on him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going unpicked in the truncated five-round 2020 Draft, Stephan bypassed his Stephen F. Austin State commitment and signed as a free agent because he wanted to launch his pro career despite pandemic rules capping his bonus at $20,000. He worked his way to Double-A at age 22 two years ago but missed two months that summer with a stress fracture in his back and two more last season with elbow inflammation. He returned to rank second in the Arizona Fall League with a 2.25 ERA, though the Rangers declined to protect him on their 40-man roster. Stephan’s slider easily stands out as his best weapon, a plus offering that sweeps at 82-85 mph, and he shown the ability to turn it into a tighter upper-80s cutter in the AFL. He throws strikes but doesn’t miss many bats with his fastballs, a sinking two-seamer that sits at 91-93 mph and touches 95 and a slightly harder four-seamer with carry. His mid-80s changeup gained velocity but lost some movement and effectiveness in 2024. Stephan’s deception and feel for pitching are the keys to his success. His low arm slot and release height add deception and life to his pitches, while his ability to repeat his easy delivery gives him plus control and the potential for solid command. He needs more strength, but if he can stay healthy, he has a future as a back-of-the-rotation starter or slider happy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just 17 high schoolers signed as nondrafted free agents in the wake of the shortened five-round 2020 Draft, and the Rangers landed five of them. The best of those is Stephan, who gave up a commitment to Stephen F. Austin State because he wanted to start his pro career despite pandemic rules capping his bonus at $20,000. He excelled in High-A last year with a 2.17 ERA, .175 opponents' average against and 73/12 K/BB ratio in 62 1/3 innings, but he sustained a stress fracture in his back during fielding drills after his first Double-A start and missed the final two months. His overall 0.84 WHIP led all Minor League pitchers who worked at least 60 innings. Stephan doesn't light up radar guns but he can really pitch with his low-90s fastballs, creating run and sink on a two-seamer that sits at 91-92 mph and carry and run on a four-seamer that's a tick harder. They tunnel well with his plus low-80s slider, which has more depth than horizontal action. He also has advanced feel for a fading low-80s changeup. Stephan features an easy delivery that he repeats well, giving him plus control and the makings of solid command. His low arm slot and release height create life and deception without costing him strikes. He needs to add some strength and falls in love with his slider at times, but his pitchability and competitiveness give him a high floor and the upside of a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the aftermath of the shortened five-round Draft in 2020, 17 high school players signed as nondrafted free agents and the Rangers grabbed five of them. A Texas high school product, Stephan had committed to Stephen F. Austin State but wanted to launch his pro career despite pandemic rules capping his bonus at $20,000. He impressed in his first extended taste of full-season ball in 2022, recording a 3.14 ERA and 115/31 K/BB ratio in 103 1/3 innings between Single-A and High-A at age 20. Stephan's low arm angle and release height create sink and run on a two-seam fastball in the low 90s and carry and run on a four-seamer than can sneak into the mid-90s. His heaters work well in tandem with his tight low-80s slider, which features more depth than sweep. He also exhibits good feel for a changeup with similar velocity and fading action. Stephan repeats his easy delivery, enabling him to fill the strike zone. He shows the makings of at least average command and his biggest need is to gain some strength so he can add more power to his stuff. One of the more advanced young pitchers in the system, he has a high floor and the potential to become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fabian left high school early to enroll at the University of Florida and was a second-round Draft pick by the Red Sox in 2021, but didn’t sign. The Orioles nabbed him in Competitive Balance Round B the following year, signing the toolsy outfielder for a full-slot bonus of $1.03 million. He’s since flashed the exciting combination of power and speed that made him a marquee name in college, mainly by enjoying a 24-homer, 31-steal performance in his first full season. But he has also struggled against better pitching at every level jump and seriously slumped after reaching Triple-A for the first time down the stretch in 2024. Belying Fabian’s enviable tools is all the swing-and-miss in his game, which was once viewed as a stomach-able tradeoff to his power-speed upside. But Fabian’s inability to make consistent contact has severely cut into his upside as he’s reached the higher levels, due to an uppercut right-handed swing that struggles against pitches at the top of the zone. Fabian struck out in 33 percent of his plate appearances at Double-A and in 41 percent at Triple-A. All those whiffs undercut his ability to get on base and get to his power regularly in games. No such glaring holes sabotage Fabian defensively. His plus speed and strong instincts give him excellent range, and his ability to read fly balls and run efficient routes make him a plus defender in center field. He also possesses one of the stronger outfield throwing arms in the O’s system. Given the athleticism, baseball IQ and purse of loud tools, Fabian could be an impact player if he makes enough contact against quality pitching; if not, the swing-and-miss might limit him to a part-time player capable of providing a spark off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 60 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Fabian has been a legit prospect since graduating high school early to enroll at the University of Florida for the 2019 season, and he was drafted twice: first by the Red Sox in the second round in 2021 and by the Orioles in Competitive Balance Round B the following year. He signed with Baltimore for a full-slot bonus of $1.03 million, and after an exciting debut, reached Double-A Bowie in 2023, though he struggled against better pitching. His entire career, Fabian has displayed a tantalizing combination of power and speed aside of the holes in his game. He generates legit bat speed and power from the right side of the plate and has good wheels and excellent instincts on the bases. He racked up 27 homers and 32 steals in only 142 Minor League games – including 15 and 12 respectively last summer in only a half season at Bowie. The tradeoff is his swing-and-miss, which was always a part of Fabian’s game. He struck out in 45 percent of his at-bats at Bowie. He’s shown he can make consistent contact without sacrificing power at times, but all the whiffs severely cut into Fabian’s upside. His speed and instincts benefit him as a defender. Fabian’s ability to read balls off the bat and run efficient routes point to a long-term future in center field, and he possesses one of the better outfield throwing arms in the Orioles system. The athleticism, baseball IQ and all those loud tools should enable Fabian to grow into a middle-of-the-field impact bat in the big leagues if he can consistently handle high-quality pitching and cut down on the swing-and-miss.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fabian graduated from high school early to enroll at the University of Florida for the 2019 collegiate season, then reestablished himself as a early-round prospect with a strong summer in the Cape Cod League. The Red Sox made him a second round draft pick in 2021, but he returned to campus after he and Boston could not come to terms. Fabian hit 24 home runs the next spring in Gainesville, this time lasting until the Competitive Balance Round B when the Orioles swooped in and signed him for a full-slot bonus of $1.03 million. Fabian then enjoyed an exciting debut, hitting .333/.455/.615 in 22 games across three levels and reaching High-A Aberdeen. Everywhere he’s played, Fabian has shown serious offensive upside as well as the holes in his game. He generates legit bat speed and power from the right side of the plate, connecting for 44 homers over his final two years in college. The tradeoff is some swing-and-miss; Fabian finished college with a 24.3 percent K rate, while also posting a strong 17.6 percent BB rate over his last two years. He’s shown he is capable of making more consistent contact without sacrificing power at times, including during his 2022 debut (19-21 BB/K ratio). Fabian isn’t a burner on the bases, but does possess above-average wheels and excellent instincts. His ability to read the ball off the bat and run efficient routes points to a long-term future in center field. Fabian will still be only 22 when he enters his first full season of pro ball, giving him significant upside; if he keeps cutting the whiff rate, he could grow into an up-the-middle impact bat at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Cuban defector, Vargas became eligible to sign in 2018 and seemed to have an agreement worked out with the Reds, who had to wait until the following year to get out of the international penalty box and pay him more than $300,000. But the Yankees wanted him too and pulled off a pair of trades to add bonus pool money, shipping Caleb Frare to the White Sox and Giovanny Gallegos and Chasen Shreve to the Cardinals in July '18 -- they also purloined Luke Voit in the latter deal -- and landed Vargas for $2.5 million two days later. He spent his first two pro seasons batting .251/.335/.382 in Rookie ball and is poised to jump to Low-A in 2022. At this point, Vargas stands out most with his speed and defense. He showcases plus to well above-average speed and can make things happen on the bases. He has quick feet and hands, plus arm strength and a good internal clock at shortstop, though he still makes youthful errors and needs more consistency. The question with Vargas is how much impact he'll make at the plate. He's a switch-hitter with good feel for the barrel and a relatively patient approach, but he lacks strength and doesn't hit the ball very hard. He has added 15 pounds since signing but still needs a lot more muscle and he's too pull-happy for someone with below-average power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds were prohibited from paying out more than $300,000 in international bonuses in 2018 but thought they had worked out a deal with Vargas for the start of the next year's signing period. The Yankees wanted him badly enough to pull off a pair of trades to add international pool money, sending Caleb Frare to the White Sox and Giovanny Gallegos and Chasen Shreve to the Cardinals in July 2018 (also stealing Luke Voit from St. Louis in the process), then swooping in and grabbing Vargas for $2.5 million a month later. He spent 2019 in Rookie ball and participated in New York's Dominican instructional league last fall. Vargas was advanced enough offensively and defensively to play in Cuba's 18-and-under league at age 15 before defecting. He's a switch-hitter with good feel for the barrel and the strike zone from both sides of the plate. While he won't be a slugger, he needs to continue to add strength and use his legs more in his swing in order to provide more offensive impact. A well-above-average runner, Vargas stole 15 bags in his 48-game pro debut and can be disruptive on the bases. His feet and hands are very quick, allowing him to get to balls many shortstops can't and to unload his throws in a hurry. His solid arm strength and good internal clock also enhance his ability to make plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A big-time international prospect (ranked No. 21 overall in the 2023 class), Valencia was hailed for his hitting tool when he signed with the Astros for $897,500. The Dominican Republic native's progress has been slow but steady with yearly promotions and league-average production. The Marlins acquired him along with Ryan Gusto and Chase Jaworsky at the 2025 deadline for Jesús Sánchez, and Valencia gave a glimpse of his offensive upside across 24 games with Single-A Jupiter by slashing .327/.367/.510 to raise his season OPS to .730. Valencia is a compact 5-foot-10 and deploys an extremely aggressive approach at the plate. He uses an unorthodox swing to cover the zone and has registered exit velocities up to 112 mph. But he also chases far too often and hasn't frequently tapped into his natural power. Valencia chased on secondary pitches well over 40 percent of the time, and he'll need to address that to bring his walk rate up to a sustainable level. Still, he is a very toolsy hitter with untapped potential. A fantastic athlete who can leg out hits and is an instinctual baserunner, Valencia can get overly aggressive at times while trying to steal. He has a real chance to stick in center field and has the arm to fit at any spot if he's relegated to a fourth-outfielder role. Valencia is quite a lottery-ticket prospect, and time is still on his side heading into his age-20 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros spent the majority of their 2023 international bonus pool allotment on three Dominican position players: shortstops Camilo Diaz ($2.25 million) and German Ramirez ($1.2 million) and Valencia ($897,500). The best pure hitter of the trio, he outperformed them both during their debuts in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He batted .262/.346/.388 with 11 steals in 46 games and had the lowest strikeout rate (15 percent) on either of Houston's two DSL clubs. A disciplined hitter, Valencia concentrates on making contact with a quick, compact right-handed stroke. He recognizes pitches, controls the strike zone and shows feel for the barrel better than most young international signees. While he needs to add strength and won't ever be a slugger, he does show some aptitude for pulling and lifting pitches and could grow into 15-homer power. Valencia will enhance his profile if he can remain in center field. While he's more of an average runner, his instincts help him cover ground in center. His plus arm strength would fit well in right field if he has to shift to a corner, and he had registered eight assists in his 42-game debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Playing at Alabama is a family affair for the Wilson brothers, with the oldest, Parker, playing football for the Crimson Tide, and Ross and Peyton playing baseball. The Royals drafted Peyton 66th overall in 2021, and he spent his second full season at Double-A Northwest Arkansas in ‘23, where he was the everyday second baseman and slashed .286/.366/.411 with a Texas-League leading 33 doubles in 128 games. He finished the year with a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League, posting an .822 OPS in 21 games. Small but mighty at 5-foot-8, Wilson has a strong frame with a short, compact swing that makes hard contact from both sides of the plate. However, it’s not power contact -- he’s not going to be hitting a ton of balls over the fence. Wilson is pretty aggressive in the strike zone for as little power as he has, although his 18 percent strikeout rate was the lowest of his career last year. What Wilson loses in power, he makes up for in speed as a plus runner who easily stretches singles into doubles. He has the speed to swipe more bags than he has so far, but that comes down to instinct. Defensively, Wilson’s above-average arm strength should allow him to play in the infield and outfield, but the Royals had him almost exclusively at second to get repetitions and settle in there. Wilson’s work ethic and makeup are off the charts, and there’s no question he’s mentally going to be able to move around to different positions in the field if that’s what the Royals need. He doesn’t possess the hit or power tool of an everyday player, so he could use more experience as a utility man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peyton comes from an athletic family, with his oldest brother, John Parker, a former Alabama quarterback and other brother, Ross, a former Crimson Tide baseball player. Peyton followed in Ross’ footsteps at Alabama, playing center field as a freshman and moving to second base in ‘21 before the Royals selected him in Competitive Balance Round B that summer. Wilson got off to a slow start because of a hamstring injury, missing about three weeks in April and running cautiously until later in the season. He finished strong with a .268/.359/.456 line at High-A Quad Cities. Wilson has a small frame at 5-foot-8, but he’s strong with a short, compact swing that makes hard contact as a switch-hitter. His best tool is probably his speed, which he can use on the bases and in center field. Wilson’s arm is plus-plus, too, which allows him to play center field without a problem, but he's gotten more time at second base, where he can also be a great defender. He’s still getting a feel for the strike zone and what pitches he can do damage on, so if he tones down the aggressiveness, he could unlock a high average with some sneaky pop. Of Wilson’s 14 homers in 2022, eight of them came in August and September last year, and of his 23 stolen bases, 15 of them came in the final two months of the season, too. So he and the Royals were looking forward to seeing what he can do over a full season, and he's been about league-average in the box in the Texas League in 2023. While center field has taken more of a backseat, he can still be a future utilityman for the big-league club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peyton was the third Wilson brother to star at Alabama; John Parker set records as a quarterback, and Ross still shares the freshman home run mark with 15. After catching and playing center field as a freshman, Peyton moved to second base in 2021 and hit .290/.353/.460 with nine homers in 58 games. The Royals selected him with the 66th overall pick and signed him for exactly slot at $1 million, and Wilson made his professional debut last summer, posting a .733 OPS between rookie ball and Low-A Columbia. At 5-foot-9, Wilson’s strength is deceiving, and his short, compact swing makes hard and loud contact from both sides of the plate. He has a chance to hit a lot of extra-base hits because of his speed, which earns plus-plus grades from scouts. If he tones down the aggressiveness he showed in college ball, he profiles as a leadoff hitter, allowing him to cause havoc on the bases. More toolsy than the typical second baseman, Wilson has great instincts and range at the position, and he has a well-above-average arm that has served him well as he’s gotten looks in the outfield this summer. With his athleticism, speed and overall scrappiness, Wilson fits the mold of a typical Royals player. After bouncing around as much as he did in college, the Royals’ plan is to get him as much time as he can at second base in full-season ball, and as he slows the game down, the organization will likely begin to move him around the field. If he can’t stick at one position, Wilson has the ability to play almost anywhere on the field as a utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The jewel of the Guardians' 2024 international crop, Arias, ranked as the No. 14 overall prospect in his class, signed for $1.9 million out of the Dominican Republic and is living up to his reputation as a potential leadoff hitter. He has thrived in two levels of Rookie ball, most recently leading the Arizona Complex League in stolen bases (29) and BB/K (1.32) while slashing .287/.389/.402. Arias is currently hit-over-power with a great feel for contact in his quick, left-handed swing. He has a discerning eye and makes good swing decisions, making him hard to beat in the zone as he sprays the ball to all fields. Arias has put on 30 pounds since signing and has more room to fill out his 6-foot-1 frame, which will be needed to tap into more power since he doesn't consistently put the ball in the air. His big selling point, though, is his elite speed. Arias can absolutely fly and has been very efficient on the basepaths, which suggests that he could be even more aggressive. His legs work well in center, too, although he's still learning the finer points of center-field defense, as one would expect of a teenager. The lefty thrower should have enough arm for center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Guardians annually give their highest international bonus to a player with advanced bat-to-ball skills, and Arias fit that bill when he signed for $1.9 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2024. That's the most Cleveland has paid an international amateur since giving Gabriel E. Rodriguez $2.1 million six years earlier. Arias hit .247/.367/.347 during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, ranking seventh in steals (29) and eighth in strikeout rate (8 percent). Arias recognizes pitches and controls the strike zone exceptionally well for an 18-year-old, allowing him to repeatedly find the barrel with a quick if unorthodox left-handed swing. He tends to slightly chop down on the ball, though he had no difficulty pulling pitches or lifting them in the air during DSL play. He'll need a lot of time to develop, but once he gets stronger and makes some adjustments, he could hit for a solid average while providing 15 or more homers per year. Arias has gotten a little faster since turning pro and now boasts well-above-average speed. He gets good jumps on the bases and in center field, and he definitely should cover enough ground to stay up the middle. He has average strength and gets to balls quickly, making it tough to run on him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: True to form, the Guardians gave the largest bonus in their 2024 international class to a prospect who stands out most with his hitting ability. Arias signed for $1.9 million out of the Dominican Republic, the most Cleveland has paid an international amateur since giving Gabriel Rodriguez $2.1 million in 2018. He'll make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. While Arias doesn't have the most picturesque left-handed stroke, he does have a knack for barreling balls. He's more advanced than most teenagers in terms of recognizing pitches and managing the strike zone. He tends to swing down on the ball, which isn't conducive to hitting for power, but he could have at least 15-homer pop if he gets stronger and makes adjustments. Arias should be able to handle center field, which will require less power production than if he were destined for an outfield corner. He's a twitchy athlete with solid speed and similar range. His average arm is playable at all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes there are college starters who are clearly ticketed for the bullpen. And sometimes, college relievers are given a chance to start at the next level. Then there are hurlers like Minacci, who did nothing but relieve in three years at Wake Forest, saving 13 games in 2023 en route to being the Angels’ sixth-round pick that summer, and will continue to pitch his way to the big leagues exclusively out of the bullpen. Minacci pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball last year, saving 18 games in the process. There’s nothing fancy about Minacci’s approach on the mound. He goes right after hitters with two plus pitches in his mid-90s fastball that peaks at 98-99 mph and his upper-80s slider. The heater misses a good amount of bats thanks to some serious armside run, and his slider misses even more with depth more than horizontal action. While Minacci’s delivery features some effort and he’s never likely to have pinpoint command, he’s tended to be around the strike zone. There’s some confidence that he’ll throw enough strikes to handle high-leverage situations in the big leagues, something he did effectively in multiple seasons with the Demon Deacons and in his first year of pro ball. It shouldn’t take him too much longer to be deemed big league ready.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wake Forest has developed into one of the best college baseball programs in the country, famous for its pitching lab and churning out starters like first-rounder Rhett Lowder (2023, Reds) and second-round pick Sean Sullivan (2023, Rockies). The Demon Deacons also produce relief prospects, with Minacci leading the way after serving as the school’s closer for two years and saving 13 games in 2023. That resulted in the Angels taking him in the sixth round of last summer’s Draft and sending him to Single-A Inland Empire for his debut. Minacci is a two-pitch reliever who could move pretty quickly through the Angels’ system, especially given their penchant for pushing college arms aggressively up the ladder. Both of his offerings are plus: a fastball with armside run that sits 94-96 mph and tops out at 99, and a mid-80s slider that touches 90 mph with more depth than horizontal action that misses a ton of bats. There is no third pitch in Minacci’s arsenal and there’s some effort in his delivery, so there’s no question of his future role. He has the intense mentality that can serve a reliever well late in games. His strike-throwing improved over the course of his college career, providing more confidence of him being able to handle high-leverage situations, perhaps as a future setup man in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite the Mariners’ possible logjam of quality arms competing for just a handful of bullpen spots, the club liked Clarke enough to pry him away from the Cubs in last December’s Rule 5 Draft, making him a strong candidate to contribute ASAP. Clarke’s numbers didn’t jump off the page at Double-A Tennessee last year, but Mariners GM Justin Hollander suggested that the under-the-hood metrics are above average, saying, “This is a guy we feel like there’s some dials to turn” at the Winter Meetings. Entering his age-25 season with three years of Minors experience, Clarke relies on his massive 6-foot-7 frame to his advantage, paired with a low three-quarters arm slot that creates a quirky angle and makes it challenging to decipher out of hand, especially for righties. And given his size, the repeatability of his mechanics and the athleticism and body control also stand out. He throws his fastball in the 92-94 mph range and tops out at 96 mph with much run and sink, making him one of the top ground-ball pitchers in the Minors. His best pitch is an off-the-table curveball, which is effective against both righties and lefties. He complements those with a mid-80s slider that ranks average. And he throws all of them for strikes, which makes him an ideal arm for the Mariners’ mantra of \"Dominate The Zone.\"

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs spent back-to-back 2019 Draft picks on college closers with starter traits, then moved Louisville's Michael McAvene (third round) and Southern California's Clarke (fourth) into the rotation as soon as they turned pro. Clarke got knocked around when he started for the Trojans early in his college career, but recorded a 1.96 ERA and a 26/4 K/BB ratio during his 23-inning pro debut. He participated in instructional league in 2020, making two game appearances there but spending most of his time in Chicago's pitching camp. He then missed the first three months of 2021 with with a hip impingement. Clarke's hammer curveball is the best in the system and works against both left-handers and right-handers while arriving in the low 80s with power downer break. His fastball sits at 92-94 mph and peaks at 96 with run and sink that produce groundouts. His mid-80s slider gives him another solid pitch and is further testament to his feel for spin, and he's refining a changeup with some sink. Clarke's 6-foot-7 frame and low three-quarters arm slot create unusual angle that makes it tough to pick up his pitches, especially for righties. He's athletic and has good body control, allowing him to repeat his delivery and provide consistent strikes. He can't match McAvene's pure stuff but has more polish and a better chance to succeed as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In many ways, Lara is already a success story. He signed for just $10,000 in June 2021 at age 18. Since then, he’s risen through the system, coming to the United States in 2023, reaching Double-A in '24, then hitting Triple-A in '25, missing bats -- and the strike zone -- along the way. He was added to the 40-man roster and recalled to the big leagues in September last year, but didn’t appear in a game. A 6-foot-3 right-hander, Lara has a huge arm, one the Braves were developing as a starter until last year, when he got more work out of the bullpen for the first time in his career. Lara features premium velocity with his fastball, especially out of the 'pen, averaging over 98 mph and topping out at 102 with the heater. But it’s his slider that’s the better of his two-pitch mix, a nasty, hard upper-80s breaker that misses bats at a very high rate. What kind of role Lara might fill will come down to how many strikes he can throw. He’s walked 6.6 per nine in his career, a rate that spiked to 8.5 per nine in 2025, and was even worse during his Arizona Fall League stint. His swing-and-miss stuff is legit (career 12.0 K/9 rate) and if he can find the zone a bit more consistently, he could carve out a slider-led Camilo Doval-like career in the back end of a big league 'pen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Still in the penalty for previous signing infractions when the 2021 signing period opened in January 2021, the Braves only had half of what their bonus pool would have been. They were able to add Lara’s talent to the system for just $10,000 in June. He was 18 when he signed, a bit older for the market, but he’s moved relatively quickly since, coming to the United States for the first time in 2023 and reaching Double-A in 2024. Lara will be 22 for all of the 2025 season and remains primarily a two-pitch pitcher. His fastball backed up a little bit in 2024, averaging more around 94-95 mph and topping out at 96-97. His upper-80s slider with good spin and sweep was excellent, with a 46 percent miss rate on the pitch last year, and he threw it almost as often as his heater. There’s talk of him playing around with a changeup at some point, but the focus remains on the consistency of his two potentially plus offerings. What kind of role Lara might have long-term will come down to his ability to repeat his delivery and throw strikes. There’s definitely reliever risk here given that he walked 6.5 per nine last year (5.9/9 in his career), but the Braves don’t want to pull the plug too quickly on him starting because his stuff holds up and misses bats consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves only had 50 percent of what would have been their bonus pool for the 2020-21 signing period because of their previous signing infractions, so finding bargains was a plus. They might have found one in Lara, who was 18 when he signed for just $10,000 in June of 2021. He made his debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2022 at age 18 and put his name on the map for the first time by pitching his way from Single-A Augusta to High-A Rome during his United States debut in 2023. Lara currently is a two-pitch pitcher, but they’re both really interesting offerings that miss a ton of bats (12.6 K/9 rate in 2023). His fastball was consistently 95-98 mph last year and often touched 99. His slider, a hard breaking ball with sweeping action he typically threw in the 88-90 mph range with solid spin rates, also had a high whiff rate. The 6-foot-3 right-hander didn’t show a changeup in game action, and while his ability to find the strike zone has improved, it’s definitely control over command. He’ll need to develop a third pitch and keep refining his strike throwing in order to give him a chance to start, something the Braves plan to let him keep doing in 2024. The fastball-slider combination could be downright nasty in shorter relief stints, but given how far Lara has come just in the last year alone, they don’t want to rule anything out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest notable shortstop prospect to come out of San Pedro de Macorís, Muñoz received the largest bonus ($1.45 million) of any international Marlins signing this year as the No. 27 prospect in his class. He's a dynamic athlete hoping to turn his basket of intriguing tools into production heading into his debut season. The Dominican Republic native offers electric hand speed from the right side of the plate and sprays line-drive contact to all fields. At 5-foot-11, he has a strong lower half and notable pull power. Time will tell whether he's able to get that raw pop to show up in pro ball since he has had trouble in the past making consistent contact, but the Marlins are confident they'll be able to improve his swing decisions. Muñoz is agile on the bases and in the field, and his quick hands and footwork point to him having a chance to stick at shortstop long term. He's played some second and third before and likely will in pro ball as well, and he has the arm to play anywhere. Muñoz is a safer prospect than Miami's other 2025 bonus baby, Santiago Solarte, but still offers plenty of upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bergolla has the same profile as his father William Sr., a contact-hitting, speed-and-defense middle infielder who played 17 games with the 2005 Reds. Signed for $2.05 million out of Venezuela by the Phillies in 2022, William went to the White Sox in a July 2024 trade for Tanner Banks. He won the High-A South Atlantic League batting title (.300) in 2024 and led the Minors in strikeout rate (5 percent) last season, when he hit .522 in the Double-A Southern League playoffs to help Birmingham win its second straight championship. With a compact left-handed stroke, Bergolla employs a contact-over-everything-else approach. He's not especially selective but almost never swings and misses, ranking second in the Minors in swinging strike percentage (3 percent) last year. He also rarely walks or drives the ball in the air, and he's a career .345 slugger with one homer in 293 pro games. He's an excellent bunter who laid down 36 bunts in fair territory in 2025, good for 14 hits and 21 sacrifices. Bergolla has plus speed and has become more comfortable stealing bases as he has gained experience, swiping 40 in 51 tries (78 percent) last year. Primarily a second baseman in the Phillies system, he has become a regular shortstop after switching organizations and has played solid defense at the more challenging position. He covers ground to both sides, and his ability to use his quickness to get behind throws helps his solid arm strength play up. The best-case scenario is that he's Luis Arráez with much more defensive value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: William Bergolla Sr. was a contact-hitting, speed-and-defense middle infielder who played briefly in the big leagues with the 2005 Reds. Signed for $2.05 million out of Venezuela by the Phillies in 2022, his son has a very similar profile. Traded to the White Sox for Tanner Banks last July, he won the High-A South Atlantic League batting title by slashing .300/.359/.381 with 27 steals in 89 games in High-A between the two organizations. Bergolla has a compact left-handed stroke and focuses on putting the ball in play, ranking seventh in the Minors in swinging strike percentage (4 percent) and eighth in strikeout rate (11 percent) last year. He generates extremely low exit velocities and a lot of opposite-field grounders, and he'll need to get a lot stronger and change his swing and approach to ever produce much power. He homered just once in 168 games and slugged .354 in his first three pro seasons. Growing up around the game, Bergolla developed a high baseball IQ that adds to his value as a runner and defender. He has plus speed and swiped 27 bases in 33 attempts last year after going 4-for-8 in his first two pro seasons. After playing primarily at second base in the Phillies system, he spent most of his time at shortstop with the White Sox. He has range to both sides and exhibits average to solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of the former big leaguer of the same name, Bergolla ranked fourth on MLB Pipeline's 2022 International Prospects list and signed with the Phillies that January for $2.05 million. He established himself as one of the best contact hitters in Philadelphia's system, batting .292 with an 8.7 percent strikeout rate in his first three seasons. The Phillies dealt him to the White Sox at this year's Trade Deadline to acquire Tanner Banks. The lefty-hitting infielder stands out with his high baseball IQ, plus instincts and innate knack for contact. Bergolla rarely chases pitches out of the strike zone and draws a decent amount of walks.
