There’s true setup potential entering Pacheco’s age-25 season, but even if that control backs up again, he could still be solid in middle relief shortly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals signed Pacheco as a 19-year-old out of Venezuela in November 2017 and immediately made him a reliever. The right-hander exploded on the scene in full-season ball in 2019 when he fanned 90 batters over 54 2/3 innings at Class A Peoria, but he walked more than a batter an inning there as well (56 free passes), leading to a 4.12 ERA and 1.72 WHIP. Pacheco was finally able to show modest control gains in 2021 and climbed from High-A to Triple-A, while finishing with a 3.67 ERA, 95 K’s and 29 free passes in 54 innings. His 44.0 percent K rate was second best among the 1,132 Minor League pitchers with at least 50 frames in 2021. Out of concern they’d lose him in the Rule 5 Draft, the Cardinals added Pacheco to the 40-man in November. It’s essentially a two-pitch arsenal from Pacheco but a very effective one. His fastball explodes out of his hand at 95-98 mph, and he lands it well up in the zone, befuddling hitters. The mid-80s slider can sometimes lose its shape and look more slurvy, but when it’s on, it buckles batters and can be dropped in for strikes against those sitting heat. Without much of a quality third pitch, lefties tend to hit him harder than righties. Five of his six homers allowed in 2021 came off the bats of left-handed hitters, and their .378 slugging percentage was nearly double the .193 of right-handers. Pacheco’s walk rate dropped from 21.5 percent in 2019 to 13.4 last season, but even that is dicey when trying to project it against Major League hitters. There is late-inning reliever potential, but barring split/control improvements, a middle-inning profile might fit best -- and it’s one Pacheco is close to reaching in his age-24 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Birdsell got drafted three times, pitched at three colleges (Texas A&M, San Jacinto JC, Texas Tech) and overcame Tommy John surgery and a rotator-cuff strain before turning pro as a Cubs fifth-rounder in 2022. He won the organization's Minor League pitcher of the year award while advancing to Triple-A in 2024, putting him on the cusp of the big leagues, before adversity struck last year. He missed the first two months of the season with a lat strain and blew out his elbow in August, leading to a second elbow reconstruction that will sideline him for all of 2026. Birdsell's 94-96 mph fastball can reach 98 with a mix of carry, armside run and command that yields plenty of chases and empty swings. His mid-80s slider also grades as a plus pitch at its best, featuring two-plan depth. His upper-70s curveball has similar shape and does a better job of throwing off hitters' timing than an upper-80s changeup with modest fade that he barely utilizes. Batters don't get a good look at Birdsell, who employs an upright delivery with one of the shortest arm actions in baseball and very little extension. He repeats his unusual mechanics well, enabling him to pound the zone and locate his fastball where he wants. He has No. 3 or 4 starter upside but will be 27 years old and coming off his second Tommy John surgery when he returns to the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Birdsell pushed his fastball into the low 90s as a Texas high school freshman, blew out his elbow as a sophomore, missed his junior season following Tommy John surgery and turned down the Astros as a 39th-rounder in 2018. He barely pitched as freshman at Texas A&M before spending a year at San Jacinto (Texas) JC and then strained his rotator cuff at Texas Tech in 2021. After avoiding surgery and spurning the Twins as an 11th-rounder that summer, he won Big 12 Conference Pitcher of the Year accolades and turned pro as a Cubs fifth-rounder in 2022. He won their Minor League Pitcher of the Year award in 2024, but he missed the first two months of this season with a lat strain before blowing out his elbow in August, resulting in Tommy John surgery that will cost him all of 2026. Birdsell gets a lot of swings and misses in and out of the strike zone with his fastball, which sits at 94-96 mph and tops out at 98 with a nice mix of carry, armside run and command. His mid-80s slider features two-plane depth and grades as a plus pitch at its best. His upper-70s curveball has similar shape and is a more effective change of pace than his actual upper-80s changeup with mild fade that he barely uses. Hitters don't see the ball well against Birdsell, who has an upright delivery with one of the shortest arm actions you'll see and precious little extension. He repeats his mechanics well, pounds the strike zone and locates his fastball with precision. His medical history may have hurt his stock in the 2022 Draft, but he has been healthy for the last three years and looks like an innings-eating No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Birdsell first attracted scouts when he reached the low 90s as a Texas high school freshman, but he blew out his elbow as a sophomore and missed his junior season following Tommy John surgery. He spurned the Astros as a 39th-rounder in 2018, barely pitched as a freshman at Texas A&M, spent a year at San Jacinto (Texas) JC and then strained his rotator cuff at Texas Tech in 2021. After avoiding surgery and turning down the Twins as an 11th-rounder that year, he returned to the Red Raiders, won Big 12 Conference pitcher of the year honors and finally turned pro as a fifth-rounder with the Cubs in 2022. He reached Double-A in his pro debut last year and contributed a postseason victory as Tennessee won the Southern League title. Birdsell's fastball sits at 93-96 mph and can reach 99, comes with plenty of carry and he commands it well. His best secondary offering is a mid-80s slider with good depth. He favors his upper-70s curveball with similar shape against left-handers and also has a below-average upper-80s changeup that will flash some fade on occasion. Though he has a stiff delivery, Birdsell repeats his mechanics well, throws plenty of strikes and locates his fastball where he wants. His medical history may have knocked him down a couple of rounds in the 2022 Draft, but he's not too far away from helping the Cubs as a back-of-the-rotation starter or multi-inning reliever. If Chicago shifts him to the latter role, he could arrive in Wrigley Field later this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vilorio signed for $1.75 million out of the Dominican Republic, landing the highest bonus in the Yankees' 2024 international class. He offered some of the best raw power on that market but had difficulty getting to it in his pro debut. He batted just .196/.294/.345 with a 33 percent strikeout rate in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Vilorio already is stronger and hits the ball harder than most 18-year-olds, and there's still room to add more strength to his 6-foot-4 frame. The bat speed he generates with his right-handed swing contributes to projections of plus-plus raw pop once he's fully developed. He has at least 30-homer upside, but he'll have to tone down his chase-heavy approach and make a lot more in-zone contact to succeed at the plate. With solid-to-plus speed and good instincts, Vilorio can steal a few bases and has a chance to remain in center field. He'll probably lose a step as he matures physically, which would dictate a move to the corners. His arm strength grades out as at least plus and easily would work in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Instead of investing most of their international bonus pool in one player like they often do, the Yankees spread their cash around their 2024 class. Their highest-priced signee was Vilorio, who turned pro for $1.75 million out of the Dominican Republic. He fits the classic right-field profile and will break into pro ball in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in June. A right-handed hitter, Vilorio is stronger than most teenagers and still has more room to add muscle to his 6-foot-3 frame, so he could have explosive raw power. He has plenty of bat speed as well and already exhibits 25-30 homer upside. There are some mixed opinions about his bat-to-ball skills, but the consensus is that he should be at least an average hitter. Vilorio's solid to plus speed gives him a chance to remain in center field. If he loses some quickness as he matures physically, his plus-plus arm strength is more than enough for right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tomas planned on signing with the Marlins until they fired the leaders of their international scouting department in August 2024, right when he hit a growth spurt and shot up to an ultraprojectable 6-foot-2. With the tooled-up Dominican back on the market, the Cubs scrounged up enough money in their bonus pool to pay him $1.1 million five months later. He struggled in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, hitting .186/.352/.301 with a 29 percent strikeout rate. Tomas has one of the highest ceilings in the system and has elicited comparisons to Elly De La Cruz because he's a switch-hitter with that starter tool kit. His lightning bat speed allows him to turn on pitches and produce high exit velocities -- when he connects. He was too passive in the DSL, when he couldn't recover after falling behind in counts and put the ball in play in just half of his plate appearances. With plus speed and twitchy athleticism, Tomas offers 30/30 upside and the ability to play almost anywhere on the diamond. He's more advanced as a defender than a basestealer, displaying smooth actions and solid arm strength at shortstop. There's no reason to expect that he'll have to change positions, but he also has the tools to become a dynamic center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tomas appeared headed toward a deal with the Marlins until they overhauled their international scouting department last summer, around the same time that he hit a growth spurt and shot up to a super-projectable 6-foot-2. The Cubs found enough money remaining in their bonus pool to sign him for $1.1 million out of the Dominican Republic. He's 17 years old and a long way from the Majors, but he might have the highest ceiling in the system with the possibility of plus tools across the board once he's fully developed. One scout called Tomas a potential Elly De La Cruz, and Tomas has that starter tool kit, as well as the switch-hitting ability. He features electric bat speed, hits balls exceptionally hard and his lanky frame has the room to add a lot more strength. Though his size creates some natural length to his swing, he has a relatively controlled stroke and approach at the plate. Tomas has plus speed and solid arm strength, and both of those tools could get better as he matures physically. He has 30-30 upside and the twitchy athleticism and solid arm strength to play anywhere on the diamond. Chicago believes he'll be able to play a solid shortstop, and if not, he could make for a dynamic center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2026 international signing period, the Reds jumped in by handing out a total of 11 bonuses of six figures or higher. At the top of that list was Nuñez, who came in at No. 6 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list and received $3 million to join the organization. A national team standout who starred for the Dominican Republic’s team in the U15 World Cup in 2024, hitting .350 with 11 RBIs across eight games, Nuñez brings a high energy and swagger that matches the vibrant and eclectic streets of his home city of Santo Domingo, to the Reds' system. A left-handed hitting 5-foot-10 sparkplug, Nuñez has already shown a feel to hit with an advanced approach at the plate. With an open and upright stance, Nuñez uses his quick hands to propel the bat through the zone, showing early acumen at spraying line drives to all fields. While he isn’t that big, there is some power for him to grow into, though it will likely be a hit-over-pop profile. Nuñez is easily a plus runner who has recorded some elite-level 60-yard dash times. He has the ability to use that speed on the basepaths, stealing nine bases in 10 tries during that World Cup, and in the outfield. He combines his wheels with excellent instincts to track down balls in center field, where he’ll be able to play for a long time with his strong arm an added bonus.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guilarte joined the Brewers system for $1 million out of Venezuela as part of the organization's 2021 signing class, the same group headlined by Jackson Chourio from the same country. The infielder missed out on his first season due to a left shoulder surgery but still jumped stateside in 2022, slashing .306/.403/.371 with eight steals in 36 games in the Arizona Complex League. Guilarte headed to full-season ball for the first time last summer and was roughly a league-average bat as a 19-year-old for Single-A Carolina with a .269/.377/.314 line, 107 wRC+ and 26 stolen bases in 58 contests. The right-handed hitter continued to demonstrate a strong knowledge of the strike zone in 2023 with a 13.2 percent walk rate -- equal to his BB percentage the season before -- and while his strikeouts climbed a bit, he still didn’t swing-and-miss much with an 8.8 percent swinging-strike rate that ranked 16th among 99 Carolina Leaguers with at least 250 plate appearances. The contact he did produce was generally weak, though, as 55.9 percent of his Single-A batted balls were on the ground and almost half were to the opposite field. Someone with Guilarte’s plus speed can still pick up hits on wormburners -- he had a .377 BABIP last season -- but the lack of impact is becoming glaring as he’s still yet to homer in pro ball. The good news is he has the range and actions to be an above-average defender at shortstop and plus arm strength to boot. The Brewers gave Guilarte more looks at second base at Carolina in deference to Gregory Barrios (a high-quality defender in his own right), and the youngster could be plus there if need be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jackson Chourio is likely going to be the headliner of the Brewers’ Jan. 15, 2021, international signing class for years to come, but Guilarte, who signed for $1 million out of Venezuela, is making a name for himself too. He moved stateside to the Arizona Complex League in 2022 with promising results – a .306/.403/.371 line and eight steals in 36 games against competition roughly two years older than him on average. Brewers officials quickly started paying more and more attention to Guilarte the longer he performed in the domestic complex circuit. He demonstrated a strong knowledge of the strike zone by walking in 13.2 percent of his ACL plate appearances, and he tended to make contact on pitches that did land in the zone. That contact was mostly on the ground, however; his 64.1 percent ground-ball rate was highest among all Brewers Minor League qualifiers. There is some physical projection remaining in his 6-foot, 160-pound frame, but it may take more than just added strength to give him anything close to average power. That said, Guilarte has a promising floor because of his overall athleticism. He’s a plus runner already, and his range, defensive actions and significant arm strengths should keep him at the six the higher he climbs. Those skills could also translate well at second and third base, where he got some looks in 2022. He’ll be an asset on the dirt no matter what, and any more impact out of the bat would send him flying up the Brewers' prospect ranks in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crawford led the Big East Conference with 13 homers at Connecticut in 2021 while pitching just 13 2/3 innings between the Huskies, the Cape Cod League and Team USA, yet he was a potential No. 1 overall pick on the mound until he blew out his elbow that fall and had Tommy John surgery in November. Though he missed all of 2022, the Giants spent the 30th overall choice and $2,297,500 on his massive upside that July. He has dominated pro hitters in the 37 1/3 innings he worked in 2023-24 while losing time to mononucleosis, an oblique injury, a lat strain and a labrum tear that required shoulder surgery last September, sidelining him for all of this year. Crawford throws harder than most left-handers, parking at 95-97 mph and peaking at 101 with riding action, and the extension he creates with his 6-foot-4 frame and athleticism make it even more explosive. His slider ranges from 82-88 mph with so much horizontal and vertical action that he struggles to land it in the strike zone. He has similar issues with a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks and could be a solid offering if he can harness it. While Crawford has the stuff and athleticism to become a frontline starter, he has seen just 57 1/3 innings of game action in the last five years, so it's unrealistic to project him as more than a reliever at this point. If he can stay healthy and improve his control and command, he could become a closer. Pitching exclusively out of the stretch in 2024, he still walked 12 batters in 18 1/3 frames.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An ultimate risk/reward first-round pick, Crawford went 30th overall in 2022 thanks to his immense ceiling and despite his limited track record. Though he led the Big East Conference with 13 homers at Connecticut in 2021 and pitched just 13 2/3 innings between the Huskies, the Cape Cod League and Team USA, he was a potential No. 1 overall pick on the mound. But he hurt his elbow that October, had Tommy John surgery in November and missed the entire 2022 season. Signed for $2,297,500, he struck out 32 in 19 innings between two Class A levels last year, while losing time to mononucleosis and an oblique strain. Few left-handers can match Crawford's power stuff. His fastball operates at 95-97 mph and reaches 100, with his 6-foot-4 frame and athleticism creating extension that helps his heater explode on hitters. His mid-80s slider tops out at 88 mph and can be just as devastating with its two-plane depth. He began working on a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink during his Tommy John rehab and while he's still learning to throw it for strikes, opponents managed a .000 OPS against the 43 cambios he threw in 2023. Crawford is more physical and athletic than most pitchers, leading to hope that he'll develop average control as he gets more experience. While he offers upside as a potential frontline starter, he pitched just 39 1/3 innings in game action (including summer ball) in the last four years and has been slowed by a lat strain and a tired arm in 2024. San Francisco may be tempted to expedite him to the Majors as a high-leverage reliever, but he lasted just six weeks pitching one or two innings every three or four days before getting shut down in early June. He does have at least plus raw power as a lefty-hitting first baseman but after getting sporadic at-bats in his first two pro seasons and in the Arizona Fall League, he's going to focus almost entirely on pitching this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: No player in the 2022 Draft could match Crawford's combination of lofty ceiling and limited track record. He topped the Big East Conference with 13 homers in 2021 but scouts liked him more as a pitcher. He totaled just 13 2/3 innings between Connecticut, Team USA and the Cape Cod League, striking out 30 of the 56 batters he faced. A potential No. 1 overall pick before he hurt his elbow that October and missed all of 2022 following Tommy John surgery, he still went 30th overall and signed for a slightly under-slot $2,297,500. Few left-handers can match Crawford's pair of power pitches, beginning with a 95-97 mph fastball that hits 100 with high spin rates and tremendous carry up in the strike zone. He also can overwhelm hitters with a mid-80s slider that peaks at 88 mph and features impressive depth. He's more physical and athletic than most pitchers and has thrown strikes during his limited experience on the mound. Because he has worked just 20 1/3 innings (counting summer ball) in three years of college and is coming back from elbow reconstruction, the Giants will handle him carefully in his 2023 pro pitching debut and just focus on getting him some reps and keeping him healthy. They'll worry about developing his changeup, refining his command and building up his workload in the future. He also offers at least plus raw power as a lefty-hitting first baseman and will continue to get some sporadic at-bats after going 3-for-19 in Rookie ball last summer, though his future definitely is on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: All of the Giants' best prospects from their 2023 international class were bargains: Keyner Martinez ($10,000), Carlos Gutierrez ($32,500), Luis de la Torre ($10,000) and Diaz ($50,000). The Cuban-born Diaz made the jump to Single-A at age 18 in 2024 and returned there last season to help San Jose win the California League championship. He batted .269/.320/.405 and topped the circuit in hits (139) and doubles (32). Diaz tries to do too much at the plate, chasing all types of pitches out of the zone and trying to yank them all to left field. The right-handed hitter somewhat makes up for those flaws with his ability to put the bat on the ball and generate high exit velocities when he makes contact, and he could develop 20-homer power if he tones down his approach. He crushes fastballs but flails against breaking balls, so he's going to have to make adjustments. A solid runner, Diaz enhanced his value by improving his basestealing aptitude and proving he could play center field in 2025. Mostly a corner outfielder in the past, he has good instincts and can remain in center going forward. His strong arm helped him notch 25 assists in 212 outfield starts during his first three pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cuban-born Diaz has exceeded expectations since signing for $50,000 in July 2023. He produced in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2023 and the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last year before making the jump to Single-A at age 18 in June. He slashed .279/.333/.434 with 21 extra-base hits in 55 games as one of the California League's youngest players. An aggressive right-handed hitter, Diaz looks to pull pitches and chases too many outside the strike zone. He hits the ball hard when he makes contact and already shows solid raw power that could grow as he continues to fill out his 6-foot-2 frame. He raked against fastballs but scuffled against breaking balls in Single-A, and he'll need to make adjustments to survive against more advanced pitching. Diaz has average speed and is a bit quicker once he gets going. He has a knack for chasing down balls in the outfield, providing solid range on the corners and warranting a look in center field. His strong arm adds to his right-field profile and he registered 11 assists in 40 starts there last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the harder-throwing pitchers in the 2021 international class, Maldonado touched 92 mph before signing for $145,600 out of Venezuela as a 17-year-old. He touched 97 mph during his U.S. debut the following year and 99 when he advanced to full-season ball in 2023. He blew out his elbow that July and had Tommy John surgery in December that sidelined him for all of 2024, but returned to reach 101 mph in Single-A last season. Now that he has regained his health, Maldonado sits at 96-99 mph with high spin rates, late hop and some armside run on his fastball. He didn't dominate Single-A hitters with his heater, however, as they slashed .261/.404/.326 against it in 2025. They had much more trouble handling his 82-85 mph slider, which features formidable sweep. Though he has been a starter to this point, Maldonado is a two-pitch guy who projects as a reliever, possibly a closer if he can learn to harness his stuff. He has a compact arm action that hides the ball from batters, but he has trouble keeping his mechanics in sync and logged a 16 percent walk rate last year. He carries at least 50 pounds more than his listed 170 and will have to watch his conditioning.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maldonado flashed a low-90s fastball when he signed for $145,600 out of Venezuela in 2021 and pushed it as high as 97 mph during his U.S. debut the following year. He reached 99 mph when he reached full-season ball in 2023 but blew out his elbow in late July and had Tommy John surgery in December. After rehabbing all of last year, he'll be ready to return to the mound at the beginning of this season. Before he got hurt, Maldonado was sitting at 95-97 mph with late hop and some armside run on his fastball. His 82-85 mph slider was more unhittable, generating a 54 percent swing-and-miss rate against Single-A hitters. He didn't show much feel for his fading upper-80s changeup, which was too firm and rarely found the strike zone. Maldonado's compact arm action hides the ball from hitters, making him even tougher to hit. He needs time to figure out his control and command and very well could end up in the bullpen, but he'd have closer upside if he does. At least 50 pounds heavier than his listed weight of 170, he'll have to stay on top of his conditioning.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller entered 2025 riding the momentum of a breakout 2024 season in the Tigers system and a spot in the Double-A Erie rotation alongside Troy Melton, among others. He started feeling back tightness early in the season, struggled to find the root cause of it and never really got going. After a rehab setback, he was diagnosed with hip issues -- first on the left, then on the right -- that required hip labrum surgery to repair. The Tigers added him on the 40-man roster in the middle of his rehab to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft, a hint at how highly Detroit regards him. When Miller is right, he creates deception from a three-quarters arm angle with a quick delivery. His fastball tops out in the mid-90s and sits more in the 93-mph range, but has good carry that sneaks up on hitters. His low-80s slider generates a high whiff rate with good spin, and his sweeper produces a good amount of movement. His changeup is a good swing-and-miss offering when he’s locating his fastball. He was also working on a sinker during his rehab from hip surgeries to complement the four-seamer. He became a more aggressive strike-thrower during his breakout 2024 season and looks to continue that. Miller has the opportunity to become this year’s version of Melton or Ty Madden, rising from Double-A to a brief stop at Triple-A to the big leagues for the stretch run. But he has to get back on the mound first, then get comfortable with how he’s delivering with two surgically repaired hips. Like Melton, Miller is comfortable as a starter or a reliever, but the Tigers will work him as a starter in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Jackson Jobe and Jaden Hamm were the pitching stars of the Tigers’ farm system in 2024, arguably no hurler in the organization did more for his stock than Miller, an eighth-round pick in 2022 out of Valparaiso who saw his pro career delayed by injuries in 2023. He began 2024 as a reliever at Single-A Lakeland but earned a rotation spot and dominated, rolling off seven straight wins and racking up strikeouts. He advanced to High-A West Michigan in a piggyback role, then made a spot start for Double-A Erie before going to the Arizona Fall League, where he gave up damage but posted a 24-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio in just 16 2/3 innings. Miller produces a lot of deception without a ton of velocity from his three-quarter delivery with an arsenal based around his 92-93 mph four- and two-seam fastballs with movement. His slider is a wipeout pitch with late action, and his changeup is difficult for right-handed hitters to pick up, with both producing high whiff rates. He shows solid command and an aggressive mentality, though the Tigers have yet to stretch him out far as a starter. The tricky part with evaluating Miller is determining what role he fills on a Major League team. He has the potential to become an impact reliever, but the Tigers want to see how far he can go as a starter. A back injury kept him from picking up from that momentum for much of 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better outfielders in the 2023 international signing class, Guanipa sat at the top of the Braves’ wish list, and they signed him for $2.5 million at the start of the signing period in January of that year. Things started off relatively well, with glimpses of his raw tools in the Dominican Summer League and stateside in 2024. There was hope he’d make adjustments from his tough move to Single-A Augusta that year into 2025 while repeating the level, but he managed to play in just 35 games because of a hand fracture from a hit-by-pitch and a quad strain. Guanipa will try to take a mulligan for his lost season while still being just 20 years old for all of the 2026 season. An aggressive hitter from the right side of the plate, he’s shown a knack for contact with plenty of bat speed. He limits his swing-and-miss but does have a tendency to chase out of the zone too much, especially on offspeed stuff. His game is about putting the ball in play, and it seems like it’s not going to come with a ton of impact, so it would serve him well if he could draw more walks to get on base more frequently. Then Guanipa could use his plus speed to greater advantage, something he wasn’t able to do last year. He has the chance to stay up the middle in center field, and the hope is his ceiling is an up-the-middle table-setter type who is a base hit machine.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guanipa was ranked No. 34 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list when the 2023 signing period opened up, and the Braves nabbed him as the gem of the crop they brought in, giving him a $2.5 million bonus to start his pro career. His raw tools were on display during his debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing, and he played well in the Florida Complex League to kick off his United States debut in 2024, though a bump up to full-season Augusta did not go well. Guanipa is an aggressive right-handed hitter who has shown off excellent bat speed and the ability to make loud contact at times. He swings at just about everything and chases too much, leading to a bit more swing-and-miss when he moved up a level (25.7 percent strikeout rate in 32 games with Augusta). It’s looking more like he’s not going to have that much power, so he’ll have to refine his approach and be a contact-oriented hit-over-pop type to succeed. While there might be questions about his bat, there’s confidence about Guanipa’s speed and defense. He should run well enough to be a threat on the basepaths and he has the chance to be at least an above-average defender in center field. He’s just 19 for all of 2025, with time to reach the ceiling expected of someone so highly regarded on the amateur market, with some seeing a bit of a Manuel Margot profile in him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 50 | Run: 65 | Arm: 45 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Since the Braves got out of the penalty box for international signing violations, they have not hesitated to go after high-end talent who commanded large bonuses. In 2021, that was Ambioris Tavarez. In 2022, Diego Benitez and Douglas Glod got seven-figure deals. When the 2023 signing period opened in January, the Braves targeted Guanipa, who was in the middle of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list and signed him for $2.5 million. He showed off his considerable tools, and his rawness, during his Dominican Summer League debut after signing. Guanipa plays bigger than his listed height of 5-foot-11. The Venezuelan outfielder has impressive bat speed and the ball can jump off his bat. He doesn’t get cheated at the plate and there’s plenty of raw power for him to continue to tap into as he matures, with the ability to drive the ball to all fields, though while he draws walks he will have to learn to refine his approach. A plus runner who has good defensive instincts, Guanipa should continue to be a threat on the basepaths after swiping 20 bags in the DSL a year ago while being able to stick in center field for a long time. The Braves are excited to see what he can do stateside for the first time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves are active players on the international market, giving a seven-figure bonus to Ambioris Tavarez in January 2021 and handing out a pair of seven-figure bonuses to Diego Benitez and Douglas Glod a year later. The top acquisition from the most recent international class is Guanipa, a toolsy Venezeulan outfielder who trained with Omar Alvarez and Johan Hidalgo. Guanipa’s potential of power and speed had him ranked among the best outfielders in the 2023 international signing class. The Braves certainly thought so, signing him for $2.5 million when the period opened in mid-January. While Guanipa is undersized, listed at 5-foot-11, he’s the kind of prospect who plays “big.” A lot of that assessment comes from his plus bat speed and how the ball jumps off his bat. He can drive the ball to the gaps now and has raw power that will certainly develop, with the ability to hit the ball to all fields. He’s also a plus runner, one who has excellent instincts defensively. That should allow him to stay in center field for a long time. There’s a lot to dream on here, with the hope that he can develop into a dynamic up-the-middle player who can both run and rake.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's No. 1 prospect in the 2022 international class. Arias signed for $4 million out of the Dominican Republic. Wrist and thumb injuries shortened his first two pro seasons, though he was one of the more dynamic players in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in 2023. He struggled in his first taste of full-season ball, batting .233/.335/.393 with 13 homers and Single-A Florida State League highs in steals (37) and strikeouts (171) last summer. While Arias will work counts and produces plus raw power with his bat speed and growing strength, he also has an overly aggressive, pull-happy approach that leads to many chases and empty swings, including on pitches in the zone. He's a switch-hitter who has a much better stroke from the left side (.776 OPS in 2024, compared to .544 from the right side), and all 22 of his homers in his first three seasons came as a lefty. He still could produce 20 or more homers per season, more than most shortstops, but he has created serious concerns about his bat and ability to make adjustments. A plus runner who's aggressive on the bases, Arias stole 64 bags in his first 183 pro games but needs to improve upon his 75 percent success rate. He has smooth actions and one of the strongest infield arms in the system, but his attention to detail slipped last year as he made 22 errors in 84 games at shortstop. He paled in comparison to Tampa teammate George Lombard Jr. at short and looked better at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2022 international crop, Arias turned pro for $4 million out of the Dominican Republic. His debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League was alarming, as he hit .194/.379/.370 with a 33 percent strikeout rate after missing the first month with a wrist injury. He looked much more dynamic in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in 2023, batting .267/.423/.505 with six homers and 17 steals in 27 games before he broke his right thumb. The switch-hitting Arias works counts looking for pitches to drive and has the bat speed and developing strength to punish them when he gets them. He has a pull-happy mentality and did a much better job of making hard contact and lifting balls in the air during his second pro season than he did in his first, though he has regressed in 2024. It's a power-over-hit approach that could produce 20-25 homers per season once he's fully developed. Arias not only possesses uncommon power for a middle infielder but also tools to impact the game in a variety of other ways. He's a plus runner who's very aggressive on the bases and has 30-30 upside. He's a solid shortstop with smooth actions, instincts and a plus-plus arm who could play almost anywhere on the diamond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's No. 1 prospect in the 2022 international class, Arias signed for $4 million out of the Dominican Republic. He may have the best all-around collection of tools among the Yankees' stockpile of shortstops, though he'll need time to develop. He missed the first month of the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with a wrist injury, then slashed .194/.379/.370 with a 33 percent strikeout rate in his pro debut. Though Arias didn't post big numbers in his introduction to pro ball, he showed the ability to use the entire field and hit the ball hard from both sides of the plate. He may have returned too soon and tried to do too much once he did, but he displayed a quick bat, the ability to identify breaking balls and promising patience. He drew walks at a 20 percent rate and could develop plus power once he gains more strength and experience. Beyond his offensive upside, Arias has exciting all-around ability. He has run the 60-yard dash in 6.5 seconds, should be at least a plus runner even after he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame and is aggressive on the bases. With his quickness, instincts, smooth actions and a plus-plus arm, he's a no-doubt shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2021-22 international class, Arias signed for $4 million out of the Dominican Republic in January. He added to the greatest position of strength in a Yankees system headlined by standout shortstops Anthony Volpe and Oswald Peraza. He has the potential for at least solid tools across the board and could be significantly better than that if he reaches his ceiling. Arias is extremely advanced at the plate for a teenager. A switch-hitter, he has feel for the barrel, recognizes pitches well, makes good swing decisions and uses the entire field. He makes consistent hard contact that could develop into plus power once he adds more strength and experience, and his pop currently plays better from the right side of the plate. Arias' secondary tools may be more exciting than his offensive gifts. He can run the 60-yard dash in 6.5 seconds and should retain at least plus speed once he's physically mature. He's also a no-doubt shortstop with instincts, smooth actions and a plus-plus arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor required surgery to remove a cancerous kidney at age 5 but recovered to become a multisport star, turning down college basketball offers to play baseball at Polk State (Fla.) CC. After starring for the Eagles and giving up a Florida State commitment to sign for an over-slot $300,000 bonus in the 11th round in 2023, he immediately stood out as one of the best all-around athletes in the system. He got off to good start in High-A last year before batting just .185 with a 29 percent strikeout rate in the final three-plus months, then fared even worse in the Arizona Fall League. As they have with several players, the Red Sox helped Taylor increase his strength and bat speed after he turned pro, and he's capable of producing high exit velocities. He's willing to work deep counts and led the South Atlantic League with 81 walks, but he also has a busy left-handed swing and doesn't make enough in-zone contact, especially against breaking balls and changeups. His solid raw power and ability to elevate balls to his pull side could translate into at least 20 homers per season, but he'll have to make significant adjustments at the plate to get there. One of the top defenders in the system, Taylor's plus speed and fine instincts allow him to chase down balls from gap to gap in center field. He'll flash plus raw arm strength but it plays down some because he lacks a quick release and throwing accuracy. He's an aggressive runner but still is learning the nuances of basestealing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor overcame surgery to remove a cancerous kidney at age 5 to become a multisport star as a Florida high schooler, receiving college basketball offers but turning them down to play baseball at Polk State (Fla.) CC. He helped Bourne win the Cape Cod League championship during a late-summer cameo in 2022 before hitting .353/.467/.620 and topping Florida juco players with 31 steals in 48 games as a sophomore the next spring. He gave up a Florida State commitment to sign for an over-slot $300,000 bonus in 2023, then won Red Sox Minor League defensive player of the year accolades in his first full pro season. Boston has helped Taylor improve his bat speed and strength since he turned pro, and his explosive left-handed swing generates high exit velocities. His pull-heavy mindset and uphill stroke allow him to turn on pitches and drive them in the air, contributing to his solid raw power. He makes good swing decisions but has a lot going on with his stroke and needs to improve his in-zone contact, especially against non-fastballs. If Taylor hits, he has the tools to be a star. He has well-above-average speed and is aggressive on the basepaths, giving him 25-25 upside. He's a no-doubt center fielder with the quickness and instincts to run down most flyballs and his fringy to average arm strength is more than playable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Phillies took Baylor in the third round of the 2019 Draft, signing him for a touch over-slot bonus of $675,000, they knew the Virginia high school product would need a lot of reps to sharpen his very raw tools. Those have been a bit hard to come by as he played in just four games in the Gulf Coast League after signing because of a hamstring injury and the 2020 season was wiped out. He did show signs of life in 25 Florida Complex League games in 2021, earning a late promotion to full-season ball, but wasn’t able to build on it much when he got hit in the thumb at instructs last fall. Baylor has a ton of athleticism at his disposal on both sides of the ball. His bat is a work in progress, but he’s made strides forward with his loose right-handed swing and his overall approach, though there are a lot of swing-and-miss and approach issues he needs to keep working on. He does have excellent bat speed and he started to show some ability to tap into his raw power in 2021. A shortstop when drafted, Baylor played on both sides of second base a year ago and his overall defensive play has improved. His arm and plus speed could work from shortstop, but some think he’d be best suited for second if he were to settle in at one position. It’s still too early to know exactly what Baylor could become, with a full year of games likely to help inform that evaluation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baylor had transferred to Benedictine College Prep, a military school in Virginia, a couple of years before the 2019 Draft. He could have been eligible in 2018 as one of the youngest players in the class, but he repeated 11th grade when he got to the school, which helped some of his raw tools come into focus. He moved up Draft boards firmly into Day 2 talk and went in the third round of the ’19 Draft, but hasn’t been able to play much since, with a hamstring injury forcing him out after just four Gulf Coast League games in 2019 and the pandemic wiping out the 2020 season. The missed reps hurt particularly for a player like Baylor, who is brimming with athleticism and raw tools, but still lacks refinement. When he has been on the field at all, he has shown a knack for making contact, with an ability to spoil pitches well. His right-handed swing is loose and athletic, with good bat speed, and there’s a chance he could have good power in the future, especially as he improves his overall approach, something he made strides with this past offseason. A plus runner who should be a basestealing threat, Baylor uses that speed and athleticism well on the defensive end of things. He moves well at shortstop and has an above-average arm that used to fire 92-mph fastballs from the mound in high school. Not everyone is convinced he can stick at short, with second base or perhaps the outfield an eventual home, but more than anything, he just needs to get out and play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For most of his pro career since the Padres took him in the third round and gave him an over-slot bonus of $3 million to sign, Head has been a bit of a cautionary tale about raw toolsy high schoolers who can’t quite figure things out at the next level. After a pretty solid pro debut after signing in 2019, he reportedly looked good at San Diego’s alternate site, but for most of his two years with the Pirates after they got him as part of the Joe Musgrove deal, it’s been a struggle. There might have been signs of life in 2022, however, as Head slashed a much more solid .264/.355/.472 from July 1 on after posting a .650 OPS in the season’s first three months. Head is a tinkerer at the plate, one who was constantly changing his setup to try to unlock his considerable raw tools. He moved his hands often and found a spot that helped him use his athleticism more, and rather than change it the second something went wrong in the second half of 2022, he stuck with it and found more consistency than he’d had previously. There are still approach issues, as he struck out more than 30 percent of the time, even when things were going better, but there’s a lot of potential impact in his left-handed swing. He also made progress on the other side of the ball. He’s always had good speed, but in 2021, his defensive metrics were not good. In 2022, he graded out very well in center field. It remains to be seen if Head’s mechanical changes and his commitment to his craft will allow him to climb to the next level, but it’s the first glimmer of hope in a while.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Head didn’t have a lot of experience against top competition as a two-sport standout who also was a quarterback at his Texas high school. He did show off some impressive tools as the 2019 Draft approached and the Padres jumped ahead of the industry by taking him in the third round and going way over slot to sign him for $3 million. He had a solid pro debut in rookie ball that summer and impressed the higher ups at the club’s alternate site in 2020. He made his full-season debut with the Pirates, who acquired him in Jan. 2021 as part of the Joe Musgrove trade, and he struggled offensively. The Pirates still feel Head has considerable tools; he just needs to learn how to unlock the shed. His power did show up, as he hit 15 homers, impacting the ball more than you would think someone with his smaller frame should be able to. In 2021, he struggled against good fastballs, leading to a lot of the strikeout issues, and most of his power came off of him crushing secondary stuff. He’s worked to stabilize his stance and let his natural athleticism play so he can more regularly time up velocity. Head also has very good speed, though it’s yet to translate to the basepaths, and his athleticism is a big asset in the outfield. He’s played all three spots thus far and might have the skills to play center field. He does have the arm for right and could have the power profile as well if he can learn to make more consistent contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport standout at his high school in Texas, Head jumped on scouts’ radars when he hit .615 as a senior. The Padres loved his athleticism and set a then-record for third-round bonuses by giving him $3 million in the 2019 Draft, despite his relative lack of track record. His pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League (.283/.383/.417) made it seem like a worthwhile investment, and even though he was slowed by a hamstring issue in 2020, he still showed off some loud tools during his time at the Padres’ alternate training site before joining the Pirates courtesy of the Joe Musgrove trade. Head has now become one of the best athletes in the Pirates' system. The left-handed hitter has tremendous bat speed and raw power, though he’ll have to keep working to rein in his swing to get to it. He does have a good overall approach at the plate with a feel for hitting, but the alternate training site has been the only time he’s really faced advanced competition heading into the 2021 season. With plus speed, Head should provide value on the basepaths, and he has a very good chance to play center field for a long time, especially as he gets more reps to work on his reads and routes. Should a move be needed, his arm, not to mention his potential offensive profile, could work well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins gave Mercedes, one of the highest-ranked outfielders in the 2022 international signing class, $1.7 million to sign in January of that year, banking on his raw offensive tools. He's shown glimpses, performing well in the Dominican Summer League after signing, then struggling stateside the following summer in the Florida Complex League. The next two years saw him hit well in the FCL but fail to figure out the Single-A Florida State League, with swing-and-miss troubles being a particular problem. The 2026 season opened as a different story, as he dominated FSL pitching and earned a bump up to High-A Cedar Rapids in May. Mercedes can be a very dangerous hitter from the right side of the plate, showing off outstanding bat speed and raw power he can get to, especially when he stays with his approach. The power has shown up mostly to his pull side, and when he's locked in, he limits the whiffs and draws a lot of walks, something he was doing well during the start of this season. While Mercedes have had some injuries that have hampered him in the past, and he might have slowed down a touch, but he's still an above-average runner who knows how to steal a base. He's still getting plenty of time in center field, and his plus arm -- he had 10 assists in 2025 -- works well from right field, where he continues to get reps. Still only 21 for all of this season, the Twins are hopeful Mercedes is starting to figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since joining the Twins in January 2022 for $1.7 million as an outfielder ranked in the top 20 of that year’s Top 50 international prospects list, Mercedes has shown off some very impressive tools in fits and bursts. He put up good numbers in the Dominican Summer League after signing, but struggled during his U.S. debut in the Florida Complex League in 2023. A return to the FCL went extremely well a year ago, earning a bump up to full-season Fort Myers, but he struggled there in a very small sample size. When he’s locked in, Mercedes has looked like a very dangerous right-handed hitter. He has excellent bat speed with a ton of raw power to tap into when he sticks to a gameplan. In the DSL and last year in the FCL, he made better swing decisions, limited his swing-and-miss and worked counts well to draw a lot of walks. When he got his feet wet for 10 games in full-season ball, the strikeouts spiked. Mercedes was nursing a quad strain at the end of the year that likely hampered him. Injuries have held back his development, including a minor hamstring issue during his debut and a shoulder injury that plagued him in 2023 and at the start of the 2024 season. He’s slowed down a touch, but he’s going to keep seeing a lot of time in center field while his plus arm would work well in right. For now, the focus will be for him to put in a full, healthy season of at-bats.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Puerto Rico but raised in the Dominican Republic, Mercedes was one of the top players on the international market when the signing period opened in January 2022. The Twins gave him $1.7 million to join the organization and he pushed past a hamstring issue to be one of the best offensive performers in the Dominican Summer League, finishing with a .975 OPS. His move to the United States and the Florida Complex League in 2023 did not go as well as he struggled with his approach while dealing with a nagging shoulder issue all summer. The Twins are optimistic they’ll see more of the DSL version of Mercedes now that he’s fully done rehabbing his right shoulder. He has plenty of tools to tap into, starting with outstanding bat speed. As he matures, the 6-foot-2 outfielder should grow into a whole lot of home run power, especially if he can get back to a solid gameplan at the plate, having shown better pitch recognition and swing decisions in the Dominican. Mercedes runs very well and is aggressive on the basepaths -- he stole 30 bags in 41 DSL games in 2022 -- and he has the chance to stick in center field. He did see some time in right in the FCL, which could become his eventual home if he outgrows center. Assuming his shoulder bounces back, he has the kind of hose that could fit well there and could grow into the corner outfield run-producing offensive profile as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2022 international signing period opened, Mercedes was one of the most highly rated outfielders in the class. A Puerto Rican native who grew up in the Dominican Republic, thus making him eligible to sign, received $1.7 million from the Twins when things got going in mid-January. Though he was initially slowed by a hamstring issue, he dominated the Dominican Summer League during his debut, finishing in the top 10 in batting average, slugging percentage, OPS and stolen bases. Mercedes is a veritable tool chest and it was encouraging to see him access them in competition right out of the gate. The projectable 6-foot-2 outfielder has tremendous raw power and impressed evaluators with his swing decisions in the DSL, showing a natural feel for the barrel and some strike-zone knowledge, even if his swing and overall approach are still a bit raw. It’s more extra-base thump right now, but there’s a good chance that will develop into plenty of over-the-fence pop as he physically matures and continues to develop his game plan. He runs well and is aggressive on the basepaths. Big and physical, Mercedes will continue to play as much center field as possible as he comes stateside. There is a chance he’ll outgrow the position and need to slide to a corner, but his easily plus arm, not to mention his potential offensive production, should profile fine in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Joining the organization for $750,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2022, Santana was Arizona’s third-highest signing of the class, trailing only Abdias De La Cruz ($1.1 million) and Yerald Nin ($900,000). It’s the same class that brought fellow infielders Jansel Luis and Cristofer Torin into the fold. Santana produced a 142 wRC+ in the Dominican Summer League during his first taste of the Minors that summer and moved stateside for 2023, slashing .316/.389/.487 with four homers and seven steals in 52 games in the Arizona Complex League. The right-handed slugger cut his walk rate nearly in half, going from 15.3 percent to 8.1 between the DSL and ACL, and his strikeout rate bumped slightly from 20.2 percent to 23.7, elevating some concerns that his hit tool will be more challenged by pitchers with better control and command. Santana still maintains above-average raw power in his 6-foot frame, and that could take another step forward if he can reel in some of the swing-and-miss concerns. Entering his age-19 season, Santana shows above-average speed for now, though concern that he’ll slow down eventually remains. That agility still serves him fairly well at third base, and his plus arm strength is an even bigger asset. The D-backs gave Santana seven starts at first base in the ACL, but any long-term move there remains far away. The power and early performance makes Santana an interesting follow ahead of his debut with a full-season affiliate in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abdias De La Cruz ($1.1 million) and Yerald Nin ($900,000) were the D-backs’ two highest-paid international additions on the first day of the 2022 signing period. Coming in right behind them was Santana as a $750,000 signee out of the Dominican Republic. The right-handed slugger proceeded to slash .316/.436/.436 with 10 extra-base hits, 15 steals and a 142 WRC+ over 43 games in the Dominican Summer League during his first pro season, solidifying his status as a Top 30 prospect in a deep Arizona system. Santana doesn’t get as swing-happy as many young players do when they enter the Minor League ranks, as proven by his 15.3 percent walk rate in 2022. That’s going to come in handy because he already has plenty of raw power from the right side and should grow to be above-average in slugging by the time he enters his 20s. The more selective he is on pitches he can drive, the better that pop will play. He’s also an above-average runner now but might still slow down a tick if he does add more bulk. Santana’s plus arm certainly plays well at third base -- his only defensive position in 2022 -- and his overall agility helps him make rangy plays and have quick reactions when needed. There are still some areas that need tightening, but he could be an average defender in the end. The long road ahead works both for and against Santana, but at the least, he deserves close following as he moves stateside this summer for his age-18 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins spread out their 2023 international bonus pool money by giving 17 different players six-figure bonuses. The best position prospect in that group is Valor, a Venezuelan whose $520,000 bonus was the third-highest. He offers one of the best power/speed combinations in the system and slashed .292/.367/.444 through two years in two Rookie-level circuits. Valor's quick right-handed stroke, the projectable strength in his projectable 6-foot-3 frame and his high-end exit velocities for a teenager portend plus raw power once he's fully developed. He already shows advanced aptitude for driving balls in the air to his pull side. He has a decent grasp of the strike zone, but more advanced pitchers may exploit his aggressive approach. Valor showed off his plus speed by finishing first in the Florida Complex League in triples (five) and second in steals (35 in 39 attempts) last summer. His quickness and instincts give him solid range in center field. Should he slow down as he fills out, his power and average-to-solid arm strength would fit the right-field profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miami opted to spread its 2023 international bonus pool money around rather than making a huge splashy signing, handing out seven-figure bonuses to 17 different players. Valor turned pro for $520,000, the third-highest bonus in the class. He was the top offensive performer on the Marlins' Rookie-level Dominican Summer League club in his pro debut, batting .294/.360/.466. A right-handed hitter, Valor has a large, projectable 6-foot-3 frame that should translate into significant power once he matures physically. He already exhibits promising bat speed and exit velocities, and he regularly launches balls in the air to his pull side. He shows some feel for hitting too, though his overly aggressive approach resulted in a 24 percent K rate in the DSL. Valor moves well for his size, posting solid to plus run times and using his quickness to steal bases and chase down balls in center field. If he loses some speed as he gains muscle, he might wind up moving to an outfield corner. He has average to solid arm strength and would profile well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers are the most productive organization at identifying, signing and developing young international talent, so when Frias joined the system as a $350,000 signee out of the Dominican Republic in January 2025, there should have been at least some intrigue about next steps for the outfielder. Frias was a solid performer in the Dominican Summer League with a .316/.411/.400 line and one homer over 27 games, prompting him to move stateside to the Arizona Complex League for his age-18 season this year. Upon his arrival this spring, the right-handed-hitting Frias quickly impressed Brewers officials with both his current power production and future pop potential, and that’s carried into the season, with him recording Statcast-measured exit velocities as high as 117 mph. That would be at least plus-plus raw power already. Frias has also displayed some early bat-to-ball skills, but his swing can be a little flat, keeping his rockets lower to the ground than needed to drive huge homer totals. If he can elevate more, then this level of loud contact would make him one of the best sluggers in a deep Milwaukee farm system. Frias doesn’t have the speed needed to play center field, with fellow 2025 signing Brailyn Antunez getting those looks instead. However, his arm strength makes him a perfect fit in right field, and he’s already proven capable of collecting outfield assists in bunches from out there. The slugging ability would slot in nicely in the corner, but with Frias still several years away, he still has much to prove that he can do more than light up Statcast tech.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers were scouting other players in the Dominican Republic when they stumbled upon Morel, whom they signed for $97,500 in 2023. He tore up the Dominican Summer League in his pro debut, hitting .344/.417/.644 and topping the Rookie-level circuit with 17 doubles, eight triples, 32 extra-base hits and 116 total bases. He continued to excel when he came to the United States last year, slashing .307/.407/.575 to rank third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in slugging and fourth in OPS (.982). Significantly larger and stronger than his listed 180 pounds suggests, Morel hits balls harder than most teenagers and has plus raw power. He has had less success tapping into it in 2025, when he hasn't launched balls in the air to his pull side as easily and his plate discipline has regressed. His right-handed swing can get too long at times and his aggressive mindset results in strikeouts. Morel draws comparisons to a more athletic version of Marcell Ozuna. He presently has solid speed and looks to make things happen on the bases, though he may slow down if he gets much bigger. His plus arm contributes to his right-field profile, though his defensive instincts and effort need improvement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sebastian Walcott's $3.2 million bonus absorbed most of Texas' 2023 international bonus pool, but they also may have found a bargain in Morel, who signed for $97,500 and was discovered while the Rangers were scouting other players in the Dominican Republic. He batted .344/.417/.644 in his pro debut, topping the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 17 doubles, eight triples, 32 extra-base hits and 116 total bases. He puts on one of the best batting-practice shows in the system and draws some comparisons to two-time All-Star Marcell Ozuna. Morel has a quick right-handed swing, more strength than most teenagers and room on his 6-foot-2 frame to add more muscle. He has plus raw power and gets to most of it, already showing the aptitude to drive balls in the air to his pull side. He'll need to tighten up his plate discipline as he faces more advanced pitching, but he doesn't strike out excessively. Morel is fairly athletic but could slow down a bit as he matures physically. He's presently a solid runner but hasn't shown much feel for stealing bases. He has arm strength to match, adding to his right-field profile, though his defensive instincts need some work.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz tied a Nationals record by signing for $3.9 million out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021, one that’s since been bested by Cristhian Vaquero. After hitting just .232 with a 73 wRC+ in the Dominican Summer League later that year, the young shortstop transitioned stateside with a little more offensive performance, batting .275/.320/.362 in 52 games in the Florida Complex League before getting a brief stint as an 18-year-old at Single-A Fredericksburg. The 5-foot-10 middle infielder continues to wow with his defensive work at a premium position, showing the footwork, hands and strong throwing arm that could play at any level in short order. Continuing the theme of his athleticism, Cruz is an above-average runner, though he needs to be a more efficient base stealer after going 6-for-11 in theft attempts last year. As good as Cruz’s glove prowess is, he’ll need to hit to become a larger part of the Nats’ future plans. He makes a good amount of contact -- again leaning into his quick hands -- as he proved with a 16.9 percent K rate in 2022, but that contact is far from loud with only 13 of his 48 hits going for extra bases. There could still be some power coming as he matures in his age-19 season and beyond, but as it stands, it would be a stretch for him to reach double-digit homers in the Majors. The 2023 campaign has only seen him be more challenged with the stick, and it's an open question how far he can get on his glove alone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz signed for $3.9 million out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021, tying him with Yasel Antuna for the highest international bonus in Nationals history at the time. (Fellow Top 30 prospect Cristhian Vaquero has since moved into the top spot.) He began his Minor League career, as did many in his signing class, in the Dominican Summer League, where his .232/.292/.305 line did not set the world on fire but established a baseline performance. Cruz made a lot of contact (13.7 percent K rate), at least, and swiped 11 bags in 15 attempts. Think of your favorite Major League glove-first shortstop, and that’s who Cruz is in very early form. His footwork and hands at such a premium position have drawn raves since before he signed, and he was considered the best defender of his class. He vacuums up balls, and he has more than enough arm to make proper throws across the diamond. That makes it a well-rounded defensive package. The jury remains out on how much he can hit. Cruz utilizes his quick-moving hands to make a good amount of contact already, and the Nationals came away from his DSL time optimistic that they can help him build an average offensive profile from here. He’ll need to add more strength to improve the quality of contact, but he’ll likely never hit for much power at the top level. Cruz’s glove gives him a floor as a backup infielder with the bat determining if he can do more than that. More professional at-bats will help that future take shape in 2022 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz was Washington’s biggest priority of the 2020-21 international signing period, and the organization proved it by signing the Dominican Republic native for $3.9 million, tying Yasel Antuna for the biggest signing bonus for an international prospect in club history. Because the opening of the international market was pushed back to Jan. 15 of this year, Cruz is still awaiting his first true introduction to the Nationals on the field. The 5-foot-10 infielder was arguably the best defender at any position in this year’s international group, and his glove will be his carrying tool in the early days of his career. Cruz draws praise for both his footwork and hands at the shortstop position, allowing him to get to most balls hit in his general direction, including those that result in highlight-level plays. His arm projects to be plenty strong enough to be a weapon as well. The bat remains the big question. His promising hands translate fine to the box and he could be an average hitter in time, though he doesn’t project to hit for much power. Cruz’s glovework at a premium position gives him a higher floor than most prospects who have just signed internationally. His ceiling will be determined by how well he can develop offensively and if he can get to the point where his bat is worth carrying in the lineup every day. Otherwise, a spot as a bench infielder who can provide value defensively might be in his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bostick and his older brother Marcus attended three junior colleges in three years, with Josh playing shortstop at Howard (Texas) in 2021, hitting and pitching at Hillsborough (Fla.) in 2022 and emerging as the best juco arm in Texas while at Grayson in 2023. He ranked third in the NCAA in strikeout rate (15.3 per nine innings) for the Vikings before signing for a double-slot $397,500 bonus as an eighth-rounder. He has led his circuits in strikeout percentage in his two pro seasons (26 percent in the Single-A California League in 2024, 28 percent in the High-A Northwest League last year), recovering from a rough start to log a 2.45 ERA in his final 11 starts in 2025. Bostick can miss bats with four different pitches when they're on, starting with a low-80s slider with impressive sweep. It pairs nicely with a mid-90s fastball that reaches 99 with huge induced vertical break. He made progress last season with his upper-70s curveball and low-80s changeup, which both drop at the plate. The Giants made changes to Bostick's delivery that spurred his second-half turnaround, moving his hands away from his body and changing his leg kick to enable him to get down the mound better and improve his extension. He works exclusively out of the strength, with his strength and athleticism allowing him to maintain his stuff and mechanics deep into games. He has only been a full-time pitcher for three years, so he has room to continue to improve, but his development will be put on hold after he ruptured an Achilles tendon while lifting weights during the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bostick and his older brother Marcus attended three junior colleges in three years, with Josh playing shortstop at Howard (Texas) in 2021 and pulling double duty at Hillsborough (Fla.) in 2022 before establishing himself as the best juco arm in Texas while at Grayson College. He ranked third in the NJCAA with 15.3 strikeouts per nine innings in 2023, and the Giants believed in his combination of stuff, size, athleticism and data to give him a double-slot $397,500 bonus as an eighth-rounder. He broke into pro ball by leading the Single-A California League in strikeout rate (26 percent) last year. Bostick blew away Cal League hitters with a four-seam fastball that parks at 92-96 mph, has reached triple digits in shorter stints and comes with significant induced vertical break and carry. His heater's movement pairs nicely with the depth on his sweeping low-80s slider, which can be a plus pitch when he commands it. He's gaining feel for his low-80s changeup with tumble as he uses it more regularly. After working out of the stretch at Grayson, Bostick did the same last summer and threw a decent amount of strikes. His combination of strength and athleticism allows him to maintain his stuff deep into games and should help him refine his control and command. He comes with reliever risk but also just started focusing on pitching in 2023, so he has more room for development gains than most 23-year-olds.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marceaux jumped on the national stage as a Louisiana prepster who pitched for Team USA’s 18U squad in 2017, then stayed home to play for Louisiana State. He spent three years in the Tigers rotation and saved the best for last, topping 100 innings and finishing with a 2.54 ERA to help him land in the third round of the Angels’ all-pitching Draft in 2021. He hurled his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season, though he was only able to make two starts for Rocket City because of back issues. He returned to Double-A in 2023 and was traded to the Mets in June in a package for Eduardo Escobar. Marceaux uses a combination of feel for pitching and a huge competitive streak to succeed. His fastball plays up a bit because it has good run and he can command it to both sides of the plate even though it averages around 91-92 mph. He has two distinct breaking pitches, manipulating the shape of his slider and curve and keeping hitters off balance with both. His low-80s changeup has very good fade and is often his best secondary pitch. As evidenced by his 1.72 groundout-to-flyout ratio and just a 7.2 per nine strikeout rate, Marceaux is much more about generating weak contact than missing bats. The Angels feel he might have the best pitch execution in the system, which he’s going to need to continue to have success with his average stuff at the upper levels and reach the big leagues as a No. 5-type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high schooler, Marceaux was one of many standout pitchers on USA Baseball’s 18-and-under team in 2017, a Louisiana area prepster who had an advanced feel for pitching with stuff that didn’t wow anyone. He came out of Louisiana State three years later very much the same pitcher, but with a much better resume. After adding a strong 2021 season to it, he landed in the third round in the Angels’ all-pitching Draft, but barely pitched after signing due to his heavy college workload. He jumped on the fast track in his first full season, however, pitching his way to Double-A in 2022. The six-foot Marceaux uses pitchability, command and competitiveness to get the most out of his four-pitch mix. His fastball averaged just a tick over 91 mph in 2021, topping out at 94, but it’s a successful pitch because it has good run to it and he commands it well. He throws both a slider and a curve in the low-80s, and both are above-average offerings. He has a fading changeup, also thrown in the low-80s like his breaking stuff, missing bats with all three and generating a lot of groundballs. Marceaux’s command coming from a simple and repeatable delivery, along with his makeup, are going to help him maximize his potential. The ceiling isn’t high, but his floor is, and he could move quickly and make it up to the big leagues as a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murphy pitched with Josiah Gray in the rotation for NCAA Division II Le Moyne (N.Y.) in 2018 and succeeded him as the Dolphins' ace the next two seasons while also winning New England Collegiate League pitcher of the year honors in 2019. Signed for $22,500 in the fifth round of the shortened 2020 Draft, he ranked third in the Minors in strikeouts (164), fourth in whiff rate (13.8 per nine innings) and sixth in K/BB ratio (6.3) while advancing to High-A. He wasn't nearly as effective last year, working just 42 1/3 frames while dealing with back and shoulder issues. Murphy's fastball plays better than its velocity thanks to his command and ability to create carry up in the zone, though it was less effective last season when it mostly parked at 88-92 mph after ranging from 91-95 in 2021. His most reliable offering is a solid low-80s slider with depth that he can turn into a harder cutter with more horizontal life. Both his upper-70s downer curveball and a fading low-80s changeup are decent pitches but nothing special. When he's 100 percent physically, Murphy repeats his compact delivery with ease and exhibits advanced control and command while mixing his pitches well. His ailments detracted from his ability to locate pitches with his usual precision in 2022, and he needs it to succeed with his mostly average stuff. If he can stay healthy and regain his 2021 form, he's a potential back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a freshman in 2018, Murphy was the No. 2 pitcher in NCAA Division II Le Moyne's rotation behind Josiah Gray and threw a no-hitter. He filled the strike zone for three years with the Dolphins and won New England Collegiate League pitcher of the year honors in 2019 before the Giants signed him for $22,500 in the fifth and final round of the 2020 Draft. He boosted his prospect stock immensely during his pro debut, when he ranked third in the Minors in strikeouts (164), fourth in whiff rate (13.8 per nine innings) and sixth in K/BB ratio (6.3) while reaching High-A. Though Murphy's fastball parks at 91-93 mph and tops out at 95, it plays much better than its velocity because he commands it so well and his high spin rates create carry up in the zone. His best secondary pitch is a low-80s slider with some depth, and he also can morph it into a harder cutter with more horizontal action. He also utilizes an upper-70s curveball with downer break and a low-80s changeup with some fade. Thanks to a compact delivery that he repeats with ease, Murphy has advanced control and command. He mixes his pitches expertly and throws them to all four quadrants of the strike zone. He competes and hides the ball well, making him that much tougher to solve, and has a high floor with a ceiling of a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles’ second-round pick in 2017, Hall signed for an above-slot $1.3 million bonus after starring for the Canadian junior national team, and seemed to put himself on the fast track with impressive seasons at Low-A Aberdeen in ’18 and Class A Delmarva in ’19. But he was affected more than most prospects by the pandemic, unable to attend Orioles’ secondary site camp in 2020 due to border regulations between the U.S. and Canada.
