He then experienced a down year at High-A Aberdeen in 2021, hitting .248 with three homers and a .672 OPS as a 22-year-old. The Orioles opted not to protect him from the Rule 5 draft in his first year of eligibility. Hall’s best tool is his plus speed, which he’s used to swipe at least 22 bases in each of his three full professional seasons. He’s more of an all-fields, gap-to-gap hitter than a power threat, with a quick bat and hand strength beyond his physical dimensions. Even so, the lack of power at High-A in 2021 was concerning, given how Hall’s walk rate and extra-base output also slid considerably when exposed to better pitching. Hall's a scrappy hitter who routinely puts together good at-bats, but he might need to add strength to compete more consistently at the higher levels. Hall couples his speed with savvy instincts on the bases, stealing 26 bases in 27 attempts last summer at Aberdeen. He’s also used his quickness to grow into a playable defender at short, though the bat might require him to move around the diamond at the highest level. The arm is good enough to play any of the three infield spots, and Hall also got some experience in center field with the Ironbirds. That versatility helps project Hall to reach the Majors in a utility role, especially if he adds muscle to his wiry frame and can stay out of the trainer’s room. That’s proven challenging in the past, with Hall having three of his four professional seasons disrupted by soft-tissue injuries.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hall has improved steadily since the Orioles, enamored with his play for the Canadian junior national team, landed him with an above-slot $1.3 million bonus in the second round of the 2017 Draft. An oblique injury limited Hall to just two games that summer, and he struggled initially in the New York-Penn League before breaking out down the stretch in 2018. Healthy again, Hall jumped a level and was one of the more productive hitters in the Class A South Atlantic League in 2019, hitting .298/.385/.395 with five homers and 33 stolen bases. He attended O’s instructional camp in 2020 and seems to be a fair bet to begin 2021 at Double-A. Hall benefits from a quick bat and hand strength beyond his physical dimensions, relying more on an all-fields, gap-to-gap approach rather than plus power. There are questions about whether he’ll grow into more, but Hall assuaged some of those doubts by improving his extra-base-hit output and walk rate at each new level. His best tool is his plus speed, which Hall couples with good instincts on the bases. He is a scrappy hitter who consistently puts together competitive at-bats and demonstrates strong on-base skills. He’s also used his quickness to grow into a playable defender at short, where Hall has a chance to stick at the highest level. Whether that’s on an everyday basis depends on how his bat develops as he adds muscle to what is still a wiry frame. Hall possesses enough arm strength to play all over the diamond if not, and has shown capable of handling second base and center field in small samples. This versatility leads him to project to reach the Majors in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramírez joined the Mets for $2.05 million out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019 and jumped straight to full-season ball in 2021 after missing out on his first full campaign due to the pandemic. Until this year, he had yet to make it out of A-ball and slashed .221/.310/.317 with seven homers and 21 steals in 120 games for High-A Brooklyn last season. The Mets added him to the 40-man roster in November 2023 but nontendered him just one year later after a down year at Double-A Binghamton. He re-signed as a Minor League free agent in December 2024. Ramírez can still flash the promising tools that once made him a Top 100 prospect. He can show promising raw power from the right side, especially on pulled fly balls, and at 6-foot-3, there is room for the 21-year-old to add more strength. His above-average speed helped him string together consecutive 20-steal seasons in 2022-23, and while his routes can be circuitous, he can still eat up enough ground with his long legs to be a potentially above-average center fielder. His strong arm, which enabled him to record 11 outfield assists in 2023, is another asset. But he’s going to have to hit to get those skills into a Major League lineup, and while he may have been more selective last season, he still had difficulty finding the barrel with a swing that can be vicious but tends to be all over the place. Only 29 of his 101 hits went for extra bases, and that wasn’t only because of Brooklyn’s pitcher-friendly environs -- he slugged .317 on the road too. Ramírez is still young for the upper Minors, but he's gone from exciting name to a questionable project in a short span.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez signed for $2.05 million as MLB Pipeline’s No. 26 international prospect on July 2, 2019, and after missing out on 2020 like everyone else, he’s only played full-season games, starting with Single-A St. Lucie in 2021. He repeated the Florida State League last year, hitting .284/.359/.443 in 67 games, before finishing up his age-19 season with a 106 wRC+ in 54 games with High-A Brooklyn. The Dominican Republic native is a toolsy center fielder that scouts and player-development types love to dream on. His biggest development in 2022 was cutting his K rate from 31.1 percent the previous year to 22.1 percent while still moving up a level, and that has strengthened the belief that he can hit enough to be an impact player, even if he has a noisy setup at the dish. He has wiry strength that should only increase as he matures, but it's still yet to show up in games. Standing at 6-foot-3, Ramirez uses his size and above-average speed to glide to balls in center, and he can make plays look effortless, sometimes to his detriment. He has enough arm strength for right field, giving him another route to Queens. While he’ll be Rule 5-eligible next offseason, Ramirez is still only 20 years old heading into his third campaign with a full-season club. He still has some road ahead of him, but the 2023 season has represented a step back in some ways.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets used their highest bonus of the 2019-20 international period on Ramirez (MLB Pipeline’s No. 26 prospect in that class) by signing him for $2.05 million. The Dominican outfielder has been moved about as aggressively as a player in that signing class could, going from instructional league play in 2020 straight to Low-A St. Lucie as an 18-year-old in 2021. Ramirez hit .258/.326/.384 with five homers in 16 steals over 76 games in his first taste of full-season (or any Minor League) action. The Mets remain enthusiastic about who Ramirez could be in time, but it’s still more about potential than present skills. Ramirez is an above-average-to-plus runner right now, one who is willing to use those wheels to good effect in center field and on the basepaths. (A strong arm will also help him move over to right field, if necessary, and he did play 22 games in that corner in 2021.) He stands 6-foot-3 and could fill out more than his current 170-pound frame. His power has started to show up in promising ways at Single-A and High-A this season, and there’s still room for more in-game pop as he matures and gains experience. Ramirez’s long-awaited breakout has begun to bear fruit in 2022, leading to his placement on the MLB Pipeline Top 100 for the first time. Ramirez doesn’t need to be added to the 40-man roster until November 2023, and another big jump could be coming before then, if he continues on this current trajectory.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cluff missed his sophomore and junior seasons at BYU because he was on a mission trip in Atlanta. When he returned to the Cougars as a senior in 2019, he batted .325/.458/.515 and had almost as many walks (37) as strikeouts (39), leading the Nationals to select him in the sixth round that year and sign him for below-slot at $200,000. Two years later, Cluff’s first full Minor League season was interrupted by a broken thumb and a broken hamate bone, and he managed only a .190/.278/.278 line in 35 games with Double-A Harrisburg. Cluff bounced back nicely (and healthily) in the Arizona Fall League, where he batted .342 in 22 games and was named the circuit’s Defensive Player of the Year. It would be too easy to get caught up in Cluff’s Harrisburg numbers and consider him a lost offensive cause, just like it would be too easy to see his resurgence in a hitter-friendly AFL and say he’s back. The answer, of course, lies somewhere in the middle, and we’ll need to see how the bat plays further away from multiple hand injuries. At his best, Cluff shows good bat-to-ball skills and incorporates some pullside power that could help get to double-digit homers in the Majors. The 25-year-old’s defense at shortstop remains stellar, thanks to solid range, good hands and a strong arm. That certainly helps lower his floor as a glove-first type, and these are defensive skills that could translate anywhere on the dirt if his offensive limitations force him into a utility role. More answers on the bat should be coming when Cluff returns to the upper Minors in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cluff was a senior sign out of BYU in the sixth round of the 2019 Draft, having spent the 2017 and 2018 seasons on a mission trip in Atlanta. His .325/.458/.515 line and 39/37 K/BB ratio that final spring on campus put him on the Nats’ radar, and the club signed him for a below-slot $200,000 bonus. Cluff immediately jumped to Class A Hagerstown, where he hit .229/.320/.367 with five homers and 11 steals in 62 games. The former Cougar is as good an infield defender as can be found in the system. His hands and plus arm work at any spot on the dirt, and he has the ceiling defensively of an everyday shortstop because of those skills. The bat will determine whether he deserves to get the at-bats that would come with such a profile. A late addition to the alternate site, Cluff showed average bat speed and a little more power than expected in Fredericksburg, but the pop remains solidly below average. His speed is above-average to plus, and that helps him cover a bit of ground on the dirt and pick up the odd extra base offensively. Because of the questions about how the bat will hold up, Cluff profiles right now as a utility infielder capable of providing value with the glove. Some more power in the upper levels would make an everyday spot more of a realistic option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Injuries have made it difficult to judge Zamora fully over the last three years. A two-year starter at Miami entering 2020, the Hurricane infielder didn’t play at all that spring in part due to a torn left ACL. The Brewers overlooked that, selected Zamora in the second round that summer and saw him get off to a slow start in his pro career at Single-A Carolina as he continued to try to gain strength coming off such a major knee issue. He entered 2022 with some momentum, only to hit .209 with a .556 OPS in his first 24 games at Double-A Biloxi, then suffer a season-ending subluxed left shoulder injury. Zamora’s best grades before the shoulder issue came on the defensive side. Given his above-average speed when fully healthy, he has the range to track down grounders at shortstop, and he also possesses the good hands needed to make plays. His plus arm strength is a big asset as well. Offensively, Zamora has a short swing geared toward making contact, and that’s helped keep his strikeout and swing-and-miss rates relatively in check in the Minors. Power is a real issue, and given he’s entering his age-24 season, there isn’t a ton of projection left to get him beyond scraping past double-digit home run totals at best. Shortstops who can put the ball in play tend to find regular places in lineups, and that gives hope that Zamora could still find his way into a Major League role. The No. 1 thing he needs is health, and if Zamora gets that in 2023, his future should be all the clearer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zamora started immediately upon arriving at the University of Miami in 2018 and put together a .300 average with more walks than strikeouts in his first two seasons. A torn left ACL, along with a minor team-rules violation suspension, kept the shortstop from appearing at all for the Hurricanes in 2020. The Brewers still selected him in the second round and signed him for just below slot at $1.15 million. Following some rehab work in the fall of 2020, Zamora needed some time to get acclimated to pro ball in his first full season and was a slow starter at Low-A Carolina. The healthier he got, the more he caught fire, and he finished with a .300/.404/.421 line, six homers and 10 steals between Low-A and High-A. Unfortunately, the injury bug bit again in 2022, and a subluxed left shoulder required season-ending surgery after only 24 games at Double-A Biloxi. Before the latest health concern, it was clear Zamora just needed to regain confidence in the knee for everything to click in 2021. When he’s on, he shows a contact-oriented approach with a short swing. Zamora has been trending in a positive direction with his slugging, but low double-digit home runs might be his ceiling because extra-base hits haven’t come in bunches. His above-average speed can help his offensive game. The Brewers saw more and more why Zamora will be a defensive asset at shortstop with good hands and range. His plus arm provides yet another reason why he can stick at the six. Prospects, like Zamora, who can play at a premium position and put the ball in play have a solid floor as low-impact starters/useful bench options.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a delayed start to pro ball due to the coronavirus pandemic and a knee injury, Freddy Zamora finally gets to follow his father’s footsteps in professional baseball. Freddy Zamora Sr. played professionally in Nicaragua, but his son has a chance to go much farther as one of the top pure talents coming out of the 2020 Draft. He was a collegiate starter at Miami from the moment he set foot on campus and went into his junior season with a chance to be a first-round Draft pick, only to fall to the Brewers near the bottom of the second round in 2020. Zamora was first suspended for a violation of team rules -- it emerged that the offense was minor -- then he suffered a left knee injury in practice that shelved him for the rest of the year and required ACL surgery. Still, the Brewers made Zamora their second-round pick and signed him for slot value. He wasn’t ready to play in the fall instructional league, but the Brewers assigned him to the program anyway to begin acclimating to pro ball, and about halfway through the program, Zamora was cleared for some light infield work and to track live batting practice. Despite some negative buzz about Zamora’s makeup at Miami, the Brewers found him to be a model rehabber. At his best, Zamora has the skillset to be an everyday player at a premium position. He can be a plus defender at times, with a lot of body control, range and wingspan and a plus arm. Zamora’s contact-oriented approach that makes him tough to strike out in college, and he started showing more extra-base pop during his sophomore year before tailing off late in the season. He has shown the ability to steal bases in his early days at Class A Carolina.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With some of the best all-around tools on the 2023 international market, Diaz landed a $2.25 million bonus, the highest in the Astros' class. It also ranks as the third-highest international bonus in franchise history and the most Houston ever paid an infielder from that talent pool. The Dominican broke into pro ball by hitting .209/.374/.353 with a 33 percent strikeout rate in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. The 6-foot-3, 208-pound Diaz looks the part of a power hitter, possessing electric bat speed and more present strength than most 18-year-olds. He has 30-homer upside but will need to make adjustments to get there. His right-handed stroke gets too long, he chases too many pitches and he has too many empty swings, so he'll have to adapt to succeed as he faces more advanced pitching. Diaz can flash plus speed but figures to lose a step or two as he continues to fill out his large frame. He doesn't have smooth actions at shortstop and didn't look very rangy there in the DSL, increasing the likelihood that he'll eventually move to third base. He saw some action at the hot corner and has the strong arm required there, but he'll need to settle down defensively after being erratic at both positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz featured some of the best all-around tools in the 2023 international class and landed the highest bonus in the Astros' crop, signing for $2.25 million out of the Dominican Republic. That's the third-highest international bonus in franchise history and the most Houston ever has paid an infielder in that market. He'll likely make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in June. More physical than most 17-year-olds at 6-foot-3 and 208 pounds, Diaz has electric bat speed to go with his present strength and already plus raw power. His size creates a naturally long right-handed stroke and he has an aggressive approach, so he'll have to prove he can make consistent contact against quality pitching. If he can, he could provide upwards of 30 homers per season. Diaz currently has plus speed but could lose a step as he continues to fill out his frame. Between his size and the fact that he has good but not smooth actions at shortstop, he could wind up moving to third base in the future, though the Astros are confident that he'll remain up the middle. With his strong arm and power, he'd profile well at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A projected 2023 first-rounder after transferring from Kansas to Tennessee, Ahuna fell to the fourth round after trying to do too much at the plate while dealing with a stress reaction in his back. The Giants saw a lot of parallels between him and another slick-fielding college shortstop who had fallen to them in the fourth round 15 years earlier: Brandon Crawford. Ahuna has had a difficult time making good on that comparison because he injured his elbow early in his 2024 pro debut, requiring Tommy John surgery, and played just 97 games in his first two seasons. Crawford earned four Gold Gloves with San Francisco and Ahuna has the talent to do the same. He has fluid actions, a quick first step, plenty of range and fast hands. He also possesses a strong arm, though it graded more as solid than its usual plus in his first year back from elbow reconstruction. Ahuna has sneaky pop for a 6-foot-1, 170-pounder and could provide 15-20 homers per season, but it comes at a price. He swings for the fences with a big leg kick and a left-handed stroke that gets too long and uphill, leading to too many empty swings on strikes and too many grounders when he does make contact, and he particularly struggles against southpaws. He has solid speed and some basestealing aptitude but needs to focus on reaching base more often to take advantage of them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ahuna transferred from Kansas to Tennessee for his junior season, entering 2023 as a projected first-rounder before trying to do much at the plate while playing through a stress reaction in his back. San Francisco pounced on him in the fourth round, just as they had done in 2008 with another slick-fielding college shortstop who stock fell after a down spring: Brandon Crawford. The Giants see a lot of parallels between the two, but Ahuna didn't get to show much in his 2024 pro debut after injuring his elbow and requiring Tommy John surgery. Crawford won four Gold Gloves with San Francisco and Ahuna has the same kind of defensive ability. He has smooth actions, outstanding body control, quick hands and a strong arm. If he doesn't hit enough to be a regular, his prowess with the glove and versatility would make him a useful utilityman. There are questions about Ahuna's bat because he sells out for power, letting his left-handed swing get too long and uphill while trying to pull every pitch he sees. He does have enough sneaky pop to translate into 15 homers per season, but he produces a lot of rolled-over grounders and struggles to make contact against non-fastballs. He has the quick first step and plus speed to steal bases but isn't especially daring in that regard.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brandon Crawford projected as a first-round pick in 2008, then had a rough spring at UCLA before dropping to San Francisco in the fourth round and developing into a two-time World Series champion, three-time All-Star and four-time Gold Glover. San Francisco is hoping that history will repeat itself with Ahuna, who slipped from a mid-first-rounder to signing for a below-slot $497,500 as a fourth-rounder last July after transferring from Kansas to Tennessee and trying to do too much at the plate while playing through a stress reaction in his back. The Giants were excited at how good he looked in camp after adding 20 pounds during the offseason, but his 2024 pro debut was marred by an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. Ahuna is similar offensively and defensively to Crawford and has the tools to win Gold Gloves of his own. The best shortstop in the system, including the big leagues, he can make all the plays and all the throws with smooth actions, outstanding body control and a strong arm. He has a quick first step and well-above-average speed, though he's not much of a basestealer. An aggressive hitter who employs a leg kick, Ahuna tried to do too much at the plate last spring, let his left-handed stroke get too long and didn't make adjustments. His college strikeout rate jumped from 21 percent in his final season with the Jayhawks to 31 percent with the Volunteers, and he's going to need to tone down his approach to succeed against pro pitching. His uphill swing produces some sneaky power that plays to all fields and could translate into 15 or more homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vazquez was the Royals’ top international signee in 2021 and signed for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic and the club sent him to Single-A Columbia right away in '22 as an 18-year-old. It has been a slow progression from there, spending three seasons in Columbia before making it to High-A Quad Cities in ‘25. He slashed .260/.333/.351 across 116 games, which also included six games on a rehab stint in the ACL and five games at the end of the year in Double-A Northwest Arkansas. Vazquez was the Royals’ best hitter in the Arizona Fall League, though, with a .928 OPS in 22 games and nearly as many walks (19) as strikeouts (20). Vazquez has always been a solid defender, but his bat has been slower to develop. It’s coming along, though, with harder contact recently. He’s gotten a lot stronger in the past year or so and really grown into his 6-foot-2 frame with broad shoulders. Vazquez is starting to have an understanding of the zone and hasn't been so fooled by breaking balls, allowing him to make more contact. He’s a potential plus defender with good hands and instincts with a strong arm to boot. Some think that as he’s filled out, he might be better suited for second base or even third, but you’d like to see a little more pop if you move him to the corner. An above-average runner with good instincts on the bases, Vazquez has the profile of a utility infielder if he can continue the positive trend with his bat. He was in big league camp this spring, which allowed him to learn a lot about the Major League routine.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals’ top signee in the 2021 international signing period, Vazquez signed out of the Dominican for $1.5 million. The team was aggressive with him early, sending him right to Single-A Columbia in 2022 as an 18-year-old. He has spent three seasons there making incremental progress with his game. In 2024, Vazquez slashed .253/.353/.289 with a 13.2% walk rate, 22.2% strikeout rate and a 99 wRC+. He missed about six weeks with a hamate injury and finished his season in the Arizona Fall League, hitting .298 with a .744 OPS in 14 games. Vazquez has always been a defense-first shortstop with good hands, instincts and agile movements that make the Royals believe he can stick at the position. Offensively, Vazquez has made slow but steady progress just with his hit tool and really increased his line-drive rate in ‘24. He’s in a better neutral position with his swing, which helps, and he’s also stronger and more physical after four seasons in pro ball. Vazquez flashed raw power when he was an amateur and still has good bat speed now, but the power has yet to show up in games. It might be more extra-base hit potential than anything. Vazquez has a strong arm and is an above-average runner. After three years, Vazquez headed up to High-A Quad Cities for 2025. His defense plays, and the Royals will stick with him as a shortstop, but he’ll have to show just a bit more offensively to reach his ceiling, which is likely as a utility player who can get on base unless he really finds something with his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vazquez was in high demand during the 2020-21 international signing period because of his tremendous upside, and he signed with the Royals for $1.5 million. He came to the United States a year later, which was ambitious for his age-18 season, and he was overmatched at Single-A Columbia in ‘22. He returned in ‘23 and made modest gains, with a .618 OPS, 15 doubles, 32 stolen bases, a 13.2 percent walk rate and 22.7 percent strikeout rate in 113 games. Vazquez is a glove-first prospect right now, although some evaluators still believe the power is coming because of the capability to add strength to his athletic frame. He shows good actions on the left side of the infield, makes agile movements and exhibits a plus arm with accurate throws. More repetitions will lead to fewer mental mistakes and make him a reliable defender over a flashy one. Vazquez had a line-drive profile when he first signed, and he’s slowly starting to get there with his smooth and repeatable right-handed swing. He needs to show improvement in his swing decisions to make the most of his physical gains. Still young with upside, Vazquez has had a slow start to his pro career, and the Royals knew they were being aggressive when they pushed him to Columbia. His defense will play, so it’ll be his hit tool that will determine his role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vazquez received comps to Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado during the 2020-21 international signing period and was coveted by teams because of his enormous upside. The Royals were able to sign him for $1.5 million and brought him over to the States a year later, where he went straight to Single-A Columbia in 2022. The Royals acknowledged that was ambitious for his age-18 season, and it wasn’t without struggles: Vazquez slashed just .195/.262/.229 with a 26.3 percent strikeout rate, 10 doubles and no homers in 77 games. He’s been sent back to the Carolina League for 2023 and has shown modest gains with the bat but still hasn’t been league-average. Vazquez looks the part with his athletic frame that has only added strength since he became a Royal. His defense wows with agile movement, exceptional reads, quick hands and good footwork. He profiles as a starting shortstop, but it remains to be seen what the Royals have with Vazquez offensively. He has a smooth, repeatable swing that should produce line drives as he matures. He’s shown nice rhythm and timing to his at-bats, but little has come into focus with the results. Vazquez looked overpowered and overmatched in Columbia last year as an 18-year-old facing a lot of older pitchers. The Royals were impressed with how Vazquez held himself despite the struggles last season. His tools give scouts something to dream on. Vazquez is still all upside in his projection and will need to show some offensive breakthroughs to be able to understand what kind of player he could be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2020-21 international signing period, Vazquez received comps to what Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado looked and played like when they were teenagers. The Royals signed Vazquez, who was ranked No. 12 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list, in the early days of the signing period for $1.5 million. After spending his first season in the Dominican Summer League, Vazquez skipped right over the Arizona Complex League and moved to Single-A Columbia for his age-18 season. Results with the Fireflies have been hard to come by, but the Royals maintain the teenager is just getting going with plenty of room to grow. Vazquez has already put on strength since he was signed, and that led to improved impact at the Dominican Academy last summer; despite the lack of results, reports mentioned how much louder the ball sounded off his bat. His smooth, repeatable swing makes a healthy amount of contact, and he should add more extra-base hits as he matures. He has average speed with above-average baserunning skills, and he’s an excellent defender with exceptional reads, a quick release and good footwork. He should remain at shortstop, and the Royals have yet to play him anywhere else in his first two seasons. Scouts see the long, lean and athletic prospect hitting at the top or even near the middle of the order as he develops, and he has a solid ceiling as a well-rounded player. Even with Vazquez’s 2022 struggles, Kansas City officials continue to point out that he moved to the Carolina League at the same age as an American high-school senior. A full-season breakout could be on tap for 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 12 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 International Prospects list in 2020-21, Vazquez is built like a young Fernando Tatis Jr. and compares favorably to a teenage Manny Machado. The Royals were able to sign the Dominican amateur in the early days of the international signing period, which was pushed back to January due to the pandemic. Long, lean and with an athletic frame, the 16-year-old Vazquez has a lot of room to grow. A smooth and repeatable swing makes consistent contact, and he projects to have average power. Some believe he will be able to hit around 15-20 home runs while hitting at or near the top of the batting over, and he has solid speed with projected above-average baserunning skills. Vazquez should remain at shortstop to start his pro career, with quick hands and great instincts. He gets exceptional reads on ground balls, features a quick release, has the ability to throw from all angles and shows good footwork at the position. Vazquez has reported to the Royals’ Dominican academy, and game action will determine more of a plan for his development. The projection is there but there’s still a long way to go for the young player. His hit tool and defensive ability give him a carrying asset.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perhaps it's a bit harsh to say that the 2025 season is a big one for someone who will play all year at age 21, but it might be true for Polanco. He's teased with some loud tools at times since he was considered one of the best prospects in the 2021 international class, getting $2.35 million from the Pirates as a result but has yet to provide any consistent production. He really struggled in his second season with Single-A Bradenton in 2024, finishing with a .623 OPS, but he did perform better with Leones in the Colombian Winter League over the offseason. Polanco has added a good amount of strength to his six-foot frame since signing and is capable of registering high exit velocities from the left side of the plate. He'll draw walks, but what he hasn't been able to do is stick with a consistent approach. He has a good swing, but he chases way too much (40 percent chase rate in 2024, according to Synergy), which contributed to a 31 percent strikeout rate with Bradenton last year. The outfielder runs well and can steal a base here and there, and there is a bit more confidence that he can stick in center field, where he's seen the majority of his reps. He'll probably continue to get time in all three spots, but his bat needs to come alive in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Polanco was in the top 10 of MLB Pipeline's international prospects list when the 2021 international signing period opened that January, and he got paid accordingly, receiving a $2.35 million bonus from the Pirates. He's made moderate progress each summer since, struggling in the Dominican Summer League after signing, showing some glimpses of his tools in the Florida Complex League in 2022 and then making a more substantial step forward, at least in the underlying metrics, with his first taste of full-season ball in 2023. The biggest positive signs Polanco showed came in terms of impact at the plate. The left-handed hitter has added considerable strength, and it started to show up in stretches in Single-A Bradenton, even though he missed a considerable amount of time with a quad strain. He started registering much higher exit velocities, and there should be more to come as he continues to mature. He's not afraid to draw a walk, though he could improve that area of his game, and he will need to cut the swing-and-miss down after striking out in 28.7 percent of his plate appearances last year. Even with the whiffs, though, he started showing the ability to get to his power. Polanco still runs well, and there's no expectation of the injury lingering moving forward. He's seen time at all three outfield spots, although he's looking more like a corner guy now in terms of his defensive acumen, strong arm and potential power profile. If things keep heading in the right direction, he could be an athletic run-producing right fielder in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2021 international signing period opened on Jan. 15 of that year, Polanco was heralded as one of the top outfield prospects in the class. His all-around tool set was the reason why the Pirates were willing to give him $2.35 million, one of the largest international bonuses the organization has ever given out. His production in the Dominican Summer and Florida Complex Leagues over the past two summers has been modest, but the raw tools have been apparent enough to have the Pirates excited for what's to come. Polanco has added some strength to his projectable frame, and that, along with good bat speed and loose hands from the left side of the plate, have enabled him to hit the ball hard frequently. He still needs to work on his overall approach and is too aggressive, but he has some feel for the strike zone and the Pirates feel his underlying metrics all improved in 2022, even if it wasn't reflected in his stat line. He's been more of a line-drive hitter to date, but there's power for him to tap into. An above-average runner with a strong arm, Polanco has seen time at all three outfield positions, but he has the chance to stick in center with solid reads and routes. More reps should help Polanco refine his considerable tools and he's a good candidate to be a breakout prospect in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez stood out as a teenager for a high baseball IQ befitting a player whose father, Jose, is a scout for the Brewers in their home country of Venezuela. Gabriel signed with the Guardians for $500,000 in 2024 and carried his amateur success over to his pro debut, where he posted a .904 OPS in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He played well in his stateside debut in the Arizona Complex League (.795 OPS) last year but only played 28 games between a hamstring injury and extra time in the weight room. Rodriguez, who was born in Florida, is taller than most Guardians infield prospects and continuing to grow. He signed with the team at 6-foot, 145 pounds, and has already grown an inch and added 25 pounds. Rodriguez does not yet hit for much power but has plenty of projectability in his lanky frame. He shows traits for an above-average hit tool with a pretty left-handed swing geared for low contact, good barrel feel and a discerning eye. Although the Guardians have played him at short, third and second, Rodriguez projects as at least an average shortstop, where his instincts and hands stand out, and his speed and arm strength are above-average. Added impact at the plate will determine his ceiling, but his impressive defense for his age gives him a solid floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Florida, Rodriguez grew up in Venezuela, where his father Jose scouts for the Brewers. As an amateur, he impressed with his performance against high-level competition (he batted .400 without a strikeout in 23 plate appearances at a 15-and-under World Cup qualifier in 2022) and the high baseball IQ he developed while being raised around the game. Signed for $500,000 in 2024, he ranked second in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with a .506 on-base percentage in his pro debut. Rodriguez recognizes pitches and makes better swing decisions than most players his age. A left-handed hitter, he uses the entire field well and shows some aptitude for pulling pitches and lifting them in the air. His bat-to-ball skills could translate into 20 homers per season once he fills out his lean 6-foot-frame. Rodriguez's instincts help him play quicker than his average speed on the bases and in the middle infield. More sure-handed than spectacular at shortstop, he committed just two errors in 26 games there last summer. He also saw action at second base, which may be a better long-term fit for his average range and arm strength, and has gotten some time at third base in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez signed out of Venezuela in 2018 for $2.1 million, which remains a Guardians record for an international position player. He batted .234/.300/.331 in his first two pro seasons, though he was younger than most of his competition. He made his U.S. debut at age 17 at the end of the 2019 season, and he was the fifth-youngest regular in the Low-A East last year at 19. The raw ingredients are there for Rodriguez to hit for some average with 20 or more homers per year. He has a compact right-handed stroke with bat speed that produces high exit velocities when he connects, and he shows a willingness to use the entire field. To reach his ceiling, he'll need to get stronger while improving his ability to recognize pitches and manage the strike zone. Rodriguez split most of his first full pro season between third base and shortstop while also getting brief action in right field and at first base. With average speed and solid arm strength, he fits best at the hot corner. He does have good instincts and body control for a youngster, but he probably won't have enough quickness and range at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez might have the highest ceiling among all of the international middle infielders in whom Cleveland has invested heavily in recent years. He signed out of Venezuela in 2018 for $2.1 million, which remains a franchise record for an international position player. He was advanced enough to venture to the United States at the end of his 2019 pro debut, though Rookie-level Arizona League pitchers exposed his lack of patience at the plate, and he participated in instructional league last fall. Rodriguez employs a compact right-handed stroke and shows a willingness to use the entire field. He has the hitting ability and solid bat speed for 20 homers per season as he continues to add strength, starts to pull more pitches and learns to drive more balls in the air. To reach his offensive potential, he'll have to do a better job of recognizing pitches and controlling the strike zone, two areas in which he struggled when he came to the AZL. Presently an average runner, Rodriguez could slow down as he fills out. Nevertheless, the Indians believe his actions, body control and solid arm may enable him to stay at shortstop. Scouts outside the organization think it's more likely that he'll move to third base, where he made 15 of his 48 starts during his debut, and he should provide enough offense to fit there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: May's winding college journey brought him to Oregon State -- his third school in as many years -- where he dominated as the Beavers' Friday night starter and raised his stock en route to going 70th overall to the Marlins in the 2023 Draft. The righty has barely seen the field since then, though. May did not pitch after signing for a below-slot $900,000 -- he had a heavy college workload and missed a month with a forearm injury -- and then arthroscopic elbow surgery delayed his pro debut until July 2025. He ended up logging 32 2/3 innings between Rookie ball, Single-A and the Arizona Fall League and heads into 2026 healthy for the first time in years. At 6-foot-2 with a low release point, May has a sinker-slider profile, although he's changed his pitch mix a bit since college. The sweeping slider remains his bread-and-butter pitch with biting action that he can land for strikes or get chases on, and his sinking fastball -- up to 96 mph in starts and 98 in short stints -- has almost equal horizontal movement in the opposite direction. This year, he's been incorporating a high-80s cutter, which is dangerous glove side and a weapon against lefties, and his upper-80s changeup has promise but needs to land for strikes more. May had solid control by the end of his college career, although he walked too many batters in his brief pro debut. Some of that can be chalked up to him working back from injuries in 2025. If he can stay healthy and improve his cutter or changeup as a platoon-neutral pitch, it's easy to see May becoming a back-end starter. If not, he could still profile as a reliever whose movement will play up even more in short stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: May's college career took him from Pima (Ariz.) CC to Arizona to Oregon State. His stuff and control looked better than ever with the Beavers last spring, when he missed a month with an elbow strain before recovering to permit just nine earned runs across his final seven starts. The Marlins signed him for a below-slot $900,000 as a supplemental second-rounder and believe he may emerge as one of the best pitching prospects when he makes his pro debut in 2025. May used his plus mid-80s slider almost half the time at Oregon State, and it comes with high spin rates and so much spin that it locks down both lefties and righties. While his two-seam fastball parks at 93-95 mph and reaches 98, it has more of a sink than carry profile and doesn't miss a lot of bats. His 87-90 mph changeup is firm but drops at the plate and rarely gets barreled. Working from a low arm slot, May creates deception with a flat approach angle but not much in the way of extension. Given his delivery, he might find more success with a four-seamer that carries up in the strike zone and plays better off his slider. He provides consistent success and has the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wolkow projected as a likely 2024 first-rounder before he reclassified during his sophomore year at a suburban Chicago high school. That made him one of the youngest and most physical prospects in the prep class in 2023, when he lasted longer than anticipated but received third-round money ($1 million) in the seventh round. The youngest regular (age 18) in the Single-A Carolina League in 2024, he returned there last year and ranked second in homers (13) and RBIs (69). At 6-foot-7 and 239 pounds, Wolkow has more strength and leverage than most players his age, and they combine with his bat speed and ability to launch balls in the air to give him as much raw power as anyone in the Minors. The big question is whether he'll make enough contact to tap into his pop, because he has a naturally long left-handed swing, chases too many pitches and has problems catching up to non-fastballs. He struck out 30 percent of the time in 2025, but that was down from 40 percent the season before, and the White Sox think he can continue to get improve by refining his swing decisions. While Wolkow looks more like a tight end than a typical baseball player, he has at least average speed once he gets going and pilfered 33 bases in 39 attempts (85 percent) last year. He moves well enough to provide average defense on the outfield corners and hasn't looked overmatched when he has filled in as a center fielder. He features plus arm strength and recorded 11 assists in 71 right-field starts in 2025. Besides his high ceiling, he also earns praise for his intelligence, maturity and competitiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rated as a probable first-rounder in 2024, Wolkow reclassified to the 2023 Draft during his sophomore year at a suburban Chicago high school. One of the youngest and most physical prospects in the '23 prep class, Wolkow lasted longer than expected but landed early third-round money ($1 million) in the seventh round. He tore up Rookie ball for two weeks to start his 2024 season, then slashed .241/.342/.428 with 11 homers in 76 games as the youngest regular (age 18) in the Single-A Carolina League. Wolkow has a massive 6-foot-7, 239-pound frame with more strength and leverage than most players his age. Add in his bat speed and he has as much power upside as anyone in the Minors. He's still growing and showing some aptitude for launching balls in the air, and he could produce 40 homers annually if he makes enough contact. That's a question, however, because his size results in a naturally long left-handed stroke. He'll miss some fastballs in the strike zone and chase non-fastballs more than he should, resulting in a 40 percent strikeout rate in 2024, though he improved throughout the year and the White Sox believe he'll make adjustments as he gains experience. Built like a tight end, Wolkow takes time to get out of the batter's box but moves well for his size and is at least an average runner underway. He played well at third base during the 2022 Area Code Games and some scouts think he could handle the hot corner, but he's more comfortable in right field and has the solid arm for the position. Club officials love his makeup, repeatedly praising his intelligence, maturity and competitive will.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Projected as a likely first-rounder in 2024, Wolkow reclassified to the 2023 Draft in March of his sophomore year at a Chicago-area high school. He lasted longer than expected before the White Sox selected him in the seventh round, though he landed top-of-the-third-round money ($1 million) to forego his commitment to South Carolina. He played briefly in Rookie ball and immediately impressed club officials with his maturity at age 17. One of the youngest and most physical prospects in the 2023 crop, Wolkow earns comparisons to Top 100 Prospect Spencer Jones of the Yankees. His massive 6-foot-7, 239-pound body gives him the strength and leverage that can produce top-of-the-scale raw power, and he's still growing. His size adds length to his left-handed stroke and his plate discipline is a work in progress, so he swings through some fastballs in the strike zone and gets fooled by offspeed pitches. Wolkow is built like a tight end and is athletic for his size, slow to get started out of the batter's box but displaying at least average speed once he gets going. He handled third base well at the 2022 Area Codes and some scouts believe he could make it there, but he's much more comfortable in right field and has the solid arm strength needed there. He'll be 18 throughout his first full pro season and will need time to develop, but his ceiling is as huge as his frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peluse, a ninth-round Draft pick by the A’s out of Wake Forest in 2019, transformed his body during the pandemic by strengthening his legs while also refining his mechanics, leading to a fastball that was up to 98 mph. The increased velocity helped him rack up 109 strikeouts in 101 combined innings between High-A and Double-A in 2021. He regressed a bit last season, posting a 5.38 ERA with only 92 strikeouts in 118 2/3 innings at Double-A Midland. Peluse’s fastball ticked down last season, sitting around 92-94 mph for the most part. He rounds out his three-pitch mix with an above-average slider and decent changeup, though both offerings were likely affected by the decrease in velocity. Command has always been a strength for Peluse dating back to his college days. Even in a down 2022, he only walked 28 batters at Double-A. Between his strong build and ability to consistently pound the zone with strikes, the A’s still see a path for him to stick as a starter, though they hope he can regain some of that lost velocity in the coming season. Given his repertoire, a move to the bullpen could also be in play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick by the A’s in 2019, Peluse went to the New York-Penn League later that summer and posted a 2.25 ERA. He utilized the pandemic as an opportunity to strengthen his legs and refine his mechanics, and the result was a return to baseball throwing a fastball harder than he’d ever thrown before. After lighting up the radar gun in the instructional league, the increased velocity helped him rack up 109 strikeouts in 101 combined innings at High-A and Double-A in 2021. Peluse’s 95-98 mph fastball is accompanied by a strong slider that has flashed plus at times and a solid changeup that continues to improve, giving him a good three-pitch mix to work with. Command is also a strength, evidenced by his low walk numbers that date back to his college days at Wake Forest. Proving to be durable with a big body and having just thrown by far the most innings over a single season in his baseball career, Peluse is expected to develop into a starter at the Major League level. His advanced repertoire and consistent ability to pound the strike zone should help him knock on the big league door soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick in 2019, Peluse has put himself on the prospect radar for the A’s after showing up to the instructional league that consistently hit 97-98. The increased velocity was a credit to his hard work during the baseball shutdown in 2020 as he focused on strengthening his legs. Now carrying a power fastball, Peluse also brings a strong slider that flashes plus, as well as a changeup that is still developing. His command has always been solid going back to his days at Wake Forest, and it showed up in his debut season in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League, walking just six batters across 24 innings. Approaching his first full season in the Minors in 2021, Peluse will get a chance to show what he can do with his improved repertoire. His repeatable delivery projects him to stick as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One would be hard-pressed to find another pitcher in Seattle’s system who has endured as many obstacles since Draft Day as Carlson. Since being selected in the second round in 2017 out of a Minnesota high school, the righty underwent Tommy John surgery one year later, then came back in an emotional return in Spring Training in ‘20 only to be shut down by the league-wide closure. More than one year after that, he finally began his first full pro season. That topsy-turvy start to his career gave him a more grounded mental approach, and in his first full season, he impressed by making every start. The quirky Minor League schedule actually helped ease him into a no-limits workload, and he reached 100 innings over 19 starts with a 4.77 ERA. Essentially, everything was finally consistent for the 23-year-old, who is in the same age range as some of Seattle’s other top arms, such as George Kirby and Emerson Hancock, who were drafted after him. That gives Carlson a good outlook and strong upside. Before the shutdown in 2020, Carlson had added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which allowed him to reach back into the high 90s on his fastball. His changeup has always been solid and thrown with a ton of fade, and his slider has been above-average at times, though it wasn’t as consistent as the changeup. There’s a lot to like about his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carlson was always going to be a case of patience for the Mariners, who selected the righty out of high school in Minnesota in the second round in 2017, given that he was raised in a cold-weather state. But they didn’t anticipate that he would weather the significant setbacks, with just three professional innings so far. He underwent Tommy John surgery in July 2018 and was sidelined all of ’19, but returned in Spring Training in ’20 only to be shut down by the league-wide closure. But Carlson enters 2021 completely healthy – and that will be the biggest thing for the 22-year-old. Beyond the physical toll, there’s the mental factor of being back on a field again consistently. It understandably will take time for Carlson to regain feel for his three-pitch mix, but there is confidence that it all will eventually come back. Before the shutdown, he’d added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which gives the Mariners optimism that he’ll be able to get back up to the 93- to 97-mph range he showed on his fastball as a high school senior. His changeup has always been solid and thrown with a ton of fade, and his slider has been above average at times, though it wasn’t as consistent as the changeup. Carlson is likely headed to High-A Everett or Low-A Modesto to start the regular season. He'll need time to get his command and control back to his pre-injury levels, but the Mariners are excited to finally see what kind of pitching prospect they have on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets weren’t necessarily big spenders during the 2021 international signing period, but the organization was excited to see what Díaz could do as he entered pro ball out of the Dominican Republic. He shot out of a cannon that summer, posting a 0.54 ERA with 63 strikeouts and only nine walks over 50 1/3 innings in the Dominican Summer League, making him the only qualified Minor Leaguer with an ERA below 1.00 in 2021. His 2022 was much bumpier following an aggressive assignment to Single-A St. Lucie (5.86 ERA in 55 1/3 frames), but it was notable that he pitched the entire 2022 campaign at just 18 years old. Díaz underwent Tommy John surgery in the spring, causing him to miss the entire 2023 season. The 6-foot-2 right-hander showed a touch-above-average velocity last year with a fastball around 92-95 mph, reaching as high as 97. The offering’s ride up in the zone makes it work well in this modern age of pitching, and the Mets are hopeful more velocity could still be in the tank. His 79-81 mph curveball flashes plus potential with some steep vertical drop. Díaz gained more confidence in his mid-80s changeup as the summer wore on, and the sink on the cambio was good enough to keep whiffs coming. In fact, Díaz didn’t allow a single extra-base hit on his change in games measured by Statcast. Díaz didn’t flash the same stellar control he had in the DSL, but there were no signs that strike-throwing should be a major issue when healthy. That control will be worth monitoring when he returns from the elbow procedure at some point in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets didn’t ink any of the big names or spend big money on Jan. 15, 2021, but if there was one new prospect the player development staff was most eager to see, it was Diaz. The 6-foot-2 right-hander backed up that excitement with one of the best statistical Minor League pitching performances of the year, sporting a 0.54 ERA (making him the only MiLB qualifier with a mark below 1.00) while striking out 63 and walking only nine over 50 1/3 innings in the Dominican Summer League. Since 2010, only Sixto Sánchez (0.50) has posted a lower qualified ERA in his age-17 season. Diaz’s fastball is the star of the show at this very early stage of his career. He throws it in the low-90s now and touches as high as 96. The pitch already shows impressive ride up in the zone, making it well-suited for modern pitching philosophy. Diaz flashes a little more than just the fastball with a curveball with solid vertical break and a changeup with decent sink. Both could be average to plus pitches in time, but he has room to grow with both. Strikes were not an early issue with a 4.7 percent walk rate, though it’ll be interesting to see how that holds up against more advanced hitters. Diaz is very much a lottery ticket at this early stage of his career. If the velocity holds over a fuller season and the secondary stuff improves, he could be a star of the system in short order. So much else (health concerns, loss of stuff, fluctuating command) could happen in the meantime that would challenge that status. At minimum, he should be a fun follow to see what he can do for an encore in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas was navigating through his first full year of full-season ball and setting a career high in innings (64) in 2023 when he hurt his elbow. That turned into Tommy John surgery and he missed all of the 2024 season as a result. The Rockies had invested $500,000 to sign Vargas out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021 and had the expectation bar raised after a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, followed by a summer that saw him pitch his way from the Arizona Complex League to Single-A Fresno in 2022. In an organization trying to uncover any gem in developing pitchers for the big leagues, his return is highly anticipated. Once he can really put the elbow surgery in his rearview, Vargas can get back to being one of the more exciting and projectable pitching prospects in the system. He has good command of his lively low-90s heater. It has good carry at the top of the zone and hitters don’t square it up, plus there’s hope for more consistent velocity in the future. He can really spin his breaking ball, a curve with bite and depth that misses a lot of bats. He has good feel for his tailing changeup as well. Vargas’ slender frame may not be able to add on that much weight and strength, but with more maturity, the hope is he can prove durable enough to handle a starter’s workload because he has the ability to throw his entire repertoire for strikes with a loose arm action. The first order of business is to get a full year in without incident, knowing he’s still only 21 for the 2025 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: July 2023 was not a great month for pitching development in the Rockies organization, with three pitchers having Tommy John surgery: Gabriel Hughes, Jackson Cox and Vargas, putting a pause on the promising start to Vargas’ pro career. Signed for $500,000 in January 2021, Vargas made a strong first impression in the Dominican Summer League that year, then pitched his way from the Arizona Complex League to full-season ball in '22. He was back with Single-A Fresno when he was shut down 13 starts into his 2023 season. When he’s healthy, Vargas might be the best pitching prospect in the system in terms of being able to pound the strike zone with a solid three-pitch mix. He can command his low-90s fastball to both sides of the plate, and the carry it has in the top of the zone helps it play up and keeps hitters from barreling it up. He can get a little fastball-heavy in his pitch mix, but he was making strides in his secondary offerings, especially in focusing in on one breaking ball. Instead of trying to create a distinct slider and curve only to have them run into each other, he’s recognized that the biting slider has a real chance to be an out pitch. There’s a solid changeup in there as well. With a narrow and slender frame, it remains to be seen if Vargas can put on weight and add strength in order to be durable enough -- and maintain his stuff enough -- to be a starter. There’s also work to be done in terms of professional maturity and not letting his emotions get the better of him on the mound. For now, though, rehabbing his elbow is the top priority with an eye towards a full return in 2025 when he’ll still be just 21 years old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dominican Summer League is typically known as being very hitter-friendly. Vargas, who signed for $500,000 in January 2021, didn’t get that memo and made a very strong first impression during his pro debut in the DSL. He came stateside in 2022 and showed that was no fluke, pitching his way from the Arizona Complex League to full-season Fresno. He had returned to the California League club to start the 2023 season but was shut down at the beginning of July and had Tommy John surgery at the end of the month. Just 19 for all of the 2023 season, Vargas has already impressed with his potential three-pitch mix and feel for how to use it to get hitters out. Coming from a slight and narrow build -- one evaluator said he’s built like a fungo -- he has a low-90s fastball that plays up a bit because of his ability to command it to both sides of the plate and the ride it gets at the top of the zone. Lower-level hitters haven’t been able to square it up, and he’ll have to learn not to rely on it as much as he faces better competition, having thrown the pitch close to 70 percent of the time in 2022. The good thing is he has secondary offerings to go to. He can really spin a breaking ball, and while it sometimes gets caught between a slider and curve, it has depth and bite. It’s a pitch he can land early for a strike and also use as an out pitch. He has good feel for his changeup too, and sometimes it’s better than the breaking ball. Vargas goes right after hitters and should be able to continue filling up the strike zone. It remains to be seen how much strength he can add to his wiry frame, with any physical maturity only adding to his potential starting pitcher profile, something he’ll try to continue building once he’s fully recovered from his surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big league reliever Yorkis Perez, Vargas signed with the Rockies for $500,000 when the 2020-21 international signing period opened in January 2021. The right-hander made an immediate impression by spending the summer dominating the Dominican Summer League at the age of 17, with a 1.30 ERA over 34 2/3 innings. Having thrown all summer, the Rockies didn’t bring Vargas to instructs last fall, building anticipation for his United States debut in 2022. He can already touch the mid-90s with his fastball, throwing it with good spin rates and resulting life. His curve has the chance to be a plus pitch, with outstanding downward action and spin. Working on a changeup will come with time. At 6-foot-3, Vargas has the type of projectible frame that should be able to handle a lot more strength, with more velocity highly likely as he matures. He already has a good idea of his delivery and is largely around the strike zone. Like a lot of young pitchers with premium stuff, he can get into trouble by hunting strikeouts, but as he learns to be more of a pitcher than a thrower, Minor League hitters better watch out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres took Williams in the third round of the 2022 Draft out of Duke despite him having Tommy John surgery about seven months beforehand. He worked his way back to the mound with Single-A Lake Elsinore in late May last year, and the Royals acquired him in the Scott Barlow trade at the Deadline. The Royals stuck to his post-rehab program when he joined Single-A Columbia, proceeding cautiously with his workload, and he made five starts (24 innings) with a 3.38 ERA, 22.8 percent strikeout rate and 12.9 percent walk rate. Williams was in the mid-90s with his fastball as an amateur, but he’s been more in the 92-94 mph range post-surgery, with officials believing there’s more velocity in there as he gets farther away from the procedure. His potentially plus slider is a short, tight, low-80s gyro shape with the chance for more power behind it. Williams also shows an average changeup and could show average control in time from his athletic delivery. Injury history might limit Williams’ upside if he’s unable to regain his stuff. If he does, he has a No. 4 or 5 starter ceiling. Williams is very cerebral, analytically-inclined and detail-oriented, and the Royals are already impressed with his execution and routine. His weapons and presence on the mound could find a fit in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres have no problem drafting a Tommy John pitcher if they believe the talent is there. They proved that by taking Dylan Lesko (perhaps the best prep arm in the class) in the middle of the first round last July, and they went back to the strategy in the third round, taking Williams out of Duke. The Connecticut native managed only 37 2/3 innings as a Blue Devil, but he was showing promising signs in the fall of 2021 before undergoing the elbow procedure that December. He still signed above slot at $800,000. Williams worked his way back to the mound with Single-A Lake Elsinore in late May and was still trying to regain his stuff when he headed to the Royals at the 2023 Trade Deadline. Part of the pre-TJ excitement with Williams was his added velo in the fall, as his fastball picked up from 90-92 mph the previous spring to regularly being around 94-95 mph. His low-80s slider could get a healthy amount of swing-and-miss as it dove down and away from right-handed batters. A mid-80s changeup also flashed above-average potential but could sit a little too close for comfort to his fastball velo at times. Williams stands 6-foot-5, making him a presence on the mound, and he has the athletic delivery to keep throwing strikes. The Tommy John surgery isn’t the only health issue on his docket, however, after arm soreness and a forearm strain popped up in 2020 and 2021 respectively. The elbow reconstruction could go a long way toward putting all of that in his past, and if he can stick on the mound, there’s mid-rotation upside. It’ll be on Kansas City to mold him into that moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays targeted Barriera with the No. 23 overall pick in the ‘22 Draft, signing him to an above-slot bonus of $3,597,500. Barriera had development staffers buzzing in early ‘24, but he suffered an elbow injury early in the season that required a hybrid Tommy John and internal brace procedure. Soon after he returned in ‘25, he was sidelined again with a fracture in his forearm, so this has been a long and frustrating stretch of Barriera being forced to start over. It’s time to begin again, though, and Barriera only turns 22 in March. There’s plenty of time for the Blue Jays to work with here and the optimism is back. He’s been living at 96-98 mph with his fastball on the backfields, but the key is for Barriera to find a consistent release point, which was a struggle in his brief time back on the mound in 2025 (eight walks in 5 2/3 innings). At this point, more game action is needed to see if Barriera’s plus slider is back to where it was before the injuries, but he finally has a shot at a healthy season. Expect him to be built up very carefully. The numbers won’t matter much for Barriera in 2026. The Blue Jays simply want the young left-hander to get out there and compete again, which would set him up with a foundation for ‘27. Barriera feels like an arm who could generate some serious buzz (again) a year from now if it all goes well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barriera was one of the top prep pitchers in the 2023 class and represented a sort of middle ground between high school and college arms with a rare combination of upside and polish. The Blue Jays targeted Barriera with the No. 23 overall pick in the ‘22 Draft, signing him to an above-slot bonus of $3,597,500. Barriera had development staffers buzzing in early ‘24, but he suffered an elbow injury early in the season that required a hybrid Tommy John and internal brace procedure. After losing a crucial year of development, Barriera is scheduled to return to game action in May or June. Prior to that injury, Barriera’s stuff was all the way back. He was hitting 97 mph in spring games a year ago, paired with a slider that projects as a legitimate out pitch at the next level. While the surgery was a major setback, Barriera used the time to get his body in better shape, and the Blue Jays believed they were getting the best version they’ve seen of him yet. He made five rehab starts in the Florida Complex League in 2025 before suffering yet another unfortunate injury -- this time a small fractured piece of his forearm -- and that ended his season in July. Barriera will still only be 22 entering 2026, but his prospect status is wearing thin, regardless of how he's looked in various comebacks. Getting healthy and sticking to the mound in games will be paramount next season, especially with the Jays' pitching pipeline getting all the stronger this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barriera had generated plenty of buzz on the showcase circuit leading up to the 2022 Draft and represented an exciting middle ground between the upside typically found in high-school arms and the polish typically found in NCAA pitchers. The Blue Jays targeted Barriera with the No. 23 overall pick in the ‘22 Draft, signing him to an above-slot bonus of $3,597,500. The organization has hoped to get Barriera to the same jumping-off point that Ricky Tiedemann experienced a year prior, but injuries slowed that process. That continued into 2024 when the southpaw made one Single-A start before suffering a left elbow injury that required a hybrid Tommy John and internal brace procedure. He will miss the rest of the season as a result. Barriera’s pro debut in 2023 was slowed by a separate pair of arm injuries, and his velocity lived more in the 92-93 mph range, a step back from the 95-96 fastball that excited scouts leading up to the Draft. Barriera had a reputation for a solid low-80s slider and upper-80s changeup, but as he continued to work around physical issues, the young left-hander never quite settled into a groove or found the momentum he needed. His 20 1/3 innings (3.98 ERA) didn’t offer much of a snapshot. Barriera got his body right this offseason and looked better physically than he did a year ago, but the elbow issue came all the same. Given that he only turned 20 in March, there is plenty of time for the development staff and Barriera to build something exciting together when he gets back on the mound in 2025. He should still have the polish to attack hitters and put up excellent numbers in the lower levels when healthy, but staying that way and maintaining his stuff are the keys for Barriera, now more than ever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: American Heritage High School in Plantation, Fla., has been known more for its hitters (Eric Hosmer, Triston Casas) than its pitchers over the years, but Barriera could change that. The southpaw was a showcase circuit standout heading into 2022, highlighted by a perfect inning at the High School All-American Game in Denver. MLB Pipeline’s No. 15 Draft prospect in 2022, Barriera went to the Blue Jays at No. 23 in July (eventually signing for an above-slot $3,597,500 bonus). While not a massive or projectable presence on the mound at 6-foot-2, Barriera does show promising stuff in his quest to be a Major League starter. His fastball sat in the low-90s as a high schooler, and after not pitching officially in the Minors post-Draft, he was touching 97-98 during fall bullpen sessions. The heater has late movement too, which can help it play up. He mixes in a low-80s slider with promising sweep that acts as his primary off-speed pitch, and his mid-80s changeup looks like the fastball out of the hand, giving it above-average potential too. Jays coaches have come to appreciate how Barriera isn’t afraid to attack hitters in the strike zone, and that mentality, mixed with the quality of his stuff, makes him a future rotation candidate. His size calls into question whether he’ll be durable enough to handle that load, and those questions have gotten louder as he's missed time in 2023 with elbow, shoulder and biceps issues. Gearing up for a true full season will be a priority moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $35,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2020, Monegro has compiled a 2.57 ERA and 33 percent strikeout rate since arriving in full-season ball in mid-2023. After shoulder weakness cost him most of the first two months of the 2024 season, he rebounded to not permit an earned run in his final 41 2/3 frames. He was thriving in Double-A last year when he blew out his elbow in June and had Tommy John surgery that will sideline him for all of 2026. Monegro spins the ball better than most Red Sox farmhands, producing upper-80s sliders/cutters and low-80s curveball that are hard to lay off and just as difficult to hit. He got overly slider-happy last year, preferring it to his two- and four-seam fastballs that both operate around 93-95 mph with a peak of 97. He also shows feel for an upper-80s splitter that serves as his changeup. Monegro has improved his control as he has cleaned up his delivery, and he has enough pitches and strikes to make it as a starter. He found more success with his fastball by emphasizing his sinking two-seamer over his fairly straight four-seamer, and he did a better job of maintaining his velocity before he got hurt. If he winds up in the bullpen, his stuff could tick up and give him the upside of a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Monegro turned pro for $35,000 out of the Dominican Republic in February 2020, a month before the pandemic shutdown that delayed his pro debut until the following year. He has thrived since arriving in full-season ball in mid-2023, logging a 2.55 ERA with 155 strikeouts in 116 2/3 innings between two Class A stops. After shoulder weakness cost him most of the first two months of last season, he went 41 2/3 consecutive frames without allowing an earned run from in the final two months. Monegro added a mid-80s slider/cutter in 2023 and it added depth and became his best pitch last year, though he fell in love with it so much that he used it 44 percent at the time. His four-seam fastball ranges from 92-96 mph early in games, but it loses velocity and lacks good shape, so he has begun using a low-90s two-seamer more often. His upper-70s curveball once ranked as the best in the system but has regressed since he started favoring his slider, while his improving upper-80s splitter/changeup is becoming an effective chase pitch. Though Monegro has size and athleticism in his favor and has toned down his delivery while improving his control, there are questions about whether he can survive as a long-term starter. He pitches backwards because his fastballs don't have much movement or deception, so he needs to find more life or add velocity as he continues to fill out his 6-foot-4 frame. If he can't, he'll probably be a slider-heavy reliever, and those concerns contributed to the Red Sox not protecting him on the 40-man roster during the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Monegro signed for $35,000 out of the Dominican Republic in February 2020, a month before the pandemic shutdown that pushed his pro debut to 2021. He reached full-season ball last June, pitching 18 straight scoreless innings upon arriving in Single-A. He posted a 2.06 ERA, .194 average-against and 93 strikeouts in 65 2/3 frames between three levels during the regular season and won his lone playoff start to help High-A Greenville capture the South Atlantic League championship. Monegro carved up lower-level hitters with one of the best curveballs in the system, an upper-70s bender with true 12-6 break that's effective against both lefties and righties. His four-seam fastball will range from 92-96 mph in the early innings, but it drops off later in games and lacks life, so he has begun to fiddle with a two-seamer as well. He also added an average mid-80s slider/cutter in 2023 but didn't make much progress with an upper-80s changeup that lacks velocity separation and life. The downside to Monegro's curveball is that he falls in love with it at the expense of developing is other offerings. He did improve his delivery and strike-throwing last season, adding to hope that he can become a No. 4 or 5 starter. There's still projection remaining in his athletic 6-foot-4 frame, so he could add velocity and boost his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Calabrese was slated to be a part of the 2021 Draft class when he reclassified to be eligible for 2020. He and Owen Caissie were two Ontario high school outfielders who went in the third round of the shortened Draft, the last in a seven-year run of Ontarians in the top three rounds. Calabrese’s debut in the Arizona Complex League didn’t stand out, but he took a nice step forward during his 2022 full-season debut at age 19. A left-handed hitter with a smaller frame, Calabrese has the feel of a potential table-setter if it all clicks. Only his speed is plus, and he can steal a base and cover a ton of ground in the outfield, but he does a lot of other things pretty well too.
