There isn’t going to be much power to speak of, but a full healthy season after dealing with some injuries in 2021 enabled him to develop a better approach at the plate and make more consistent contact. He cleaned up his bat path over the course of 2022 with outstanding results, slashing .331/.405/.514 from Aug. 1 on. Calabrese spent most of his time in 2022 in center field and he certainly has the ability to stay there. But he also showed he can handle either corner, which could be essential since he may best profile as a fourth-outfielder type, unless he can add strength and impact the ball more as he moves up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Calabrese reclassified to be eligible for the 2020 Draft rather than in 2021, though he couldn’t take advantage of the typical Canada National Team’s trip to Spring Training to raise his Draft profile. Nevertheless, his combination of hitting ability and speed intrigued the Angels enough to take him in the third round and give him full slot to keep him from attending the University of Arkansas. That made him one of three high school outfielders from Ontario taken in the top three rounds in the past two years, joining 2019 draftee Dasan Brown and fellow 2020 draftee Owen Caissie. A 5-foot-10, left-handed-hitting outfielder, Calabrese’s top tool is his speed. It’s received an 80 on the 20-80 scale from some scouts, the kind of top-of-the-scale wheels that should allow him to steal bases and have plus range in the outfield. He definitely has a hit-over-power profile at the plate, with a loose and easy swing that makes consistent hard contact. He should grow into more ability to drive the ball, but is more likely to have gap-to-gap extra-base authority than over-the-fence pop, though some see a little Andrew Benintendi in his profile if he gets stronger. Defensively, Calabrese has an average but accurate arm that works well in center field. He should have no problem staying up-the-middle long term. He’s just 18 for all of the 2021 season with plenty of time for him to develop into a top-of-the-order, table-setting type center fielder at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite signing for just $75,000 out of Venezuela, Mogollon has emerged as the best prospect from Chicago's 2023 international crop. He posted a .967 OPS in two different Rookie leagues during his first two pro seasons but didn't enjoy the same success in his full-season debut in 2025. He slashed .220/.347/.387 in 51 games, though some of that performance may be attributed to a hamstring injury that cost him most of May and ended his season in late June. Mogollon has the best all-around tools among the White Sox's relatively deep group of second-base prospects, though it remains to be seen if his approach will work against advanced pitching. He has a reasonable idea of the strike zone but a maximum-effort right-handed stroke that seeks to launch balls as far as he can to his pull side. That mindset results in shocking exit velocities for a player listed at 5-foot-8 and 160 pounds but also a lot of empty swings. Mogollon displays plus speed when healthy and looks to make things happen on the bases, stealing 42 in 50 attempts (84 percent) in his first 144 pro games. He has split his time between second base and shortstop, and while he has enough arm strength for the left side of the infield, his range is better suited for the keystone. He can get out of control at both positions and needs more reliability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite signing for just $75,000 out of Venezuela, Mogollon looks like the best prospect from Chicago's 2023 international crop. He batted .289/.412/.555 in Rookie ball during his first two pro seasons, ranking fourth in the Dominican Summer League with 10 homers in his debut and third in the Arizona Complex League with eight blasts last year. Though he's listed at 5-foot-8 and 160 pounds, he produces some of the best exit velocities in the system. After showing a more measured approach in the DSL, Mogollon adopted a leg kick and focused almost solely on launching balls in the air to his pull side in 2024. With his quick right-handed stroke, he still smoked balls hard and hit some tape-measure shots, but he also posted the third-highest strikeout rate in the ACL at 38 percent. He's not afraid to work deep counts and take walks, and he does show some feel for the barrel when he's not trying to do too much at the plate, but he'll have to tone down his aggressiveness when he faces better pitching. A plus runner with savvy on the bases, Mogollon stole 16 bags in as many attempts in 46 games last season. After playing more second base in his debut, he spent most of 2024 at shortstop. He has solid arm strength, though his range is just average at short and he needs to improve his defensive consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he signed for just $75,000 out of Venezuela, early returns indicate that Mogollon may be the best prospect in Chicago's 2023 international class. He slashed .315/.417/.582 in his pro debut, ranking fourth in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 10 homers. He stands just 5-foot-8 and is a long way from the Majors, but he offers one of the more intriguing combinations of hitting ability and power potential in the system. While he won't be a true slugger, Mogollon has stunning raw pop for his age and size, already producing occasional tape-measure shots -- at age 17, he had a maximum exit velocity of 105 mph. He has a quick right-handed stroke and already shows some feel for driving the ball in the air. He doesn't try to do too much at the plate and has a knack for putting the barrel on the ball. The rest of Mogollon's tools are average, though he's a savvy and aggressive runner on the bases. He plays under control in the middle infield, with his range and arm best suited for second base. He saw some action at shortstop in 2023 and the White Sox want to give him more time during his U.S. debut this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Conticello got a $500,000 bonus to sign out of Stoneman Douglas HS in Florida as an eighth-round pick in 2021, setting aside a South Florida commitment to do so. He’s essentially climbed one level per season from the Arizona Complex League in 2022 to Double-A Amarillo, where he spent all of his age-22 campaign in '25. He hit .275/.369/.435 with 12 homers in 121 games with the Sod Poodles, good for a 110 wRC+ while only getting 30 plate appearances against pitchers younger than him. The lefty batter, who has a long finish in his hacks a little similar to Cody Bellinger, still has above-average raw power and a good chance to get to it at full maturity, even if he didn’t post the big-time slugging others do in hitter-friendly Amarillo. Part of that is because of his approach. He expands the zone a lot against lefty sliders and righty changeups, essentially the pitches running away from him, but he doesn’t whiff as much as might be expected because of it. (His 21.3 percent K rate was actually pretty sensible for a power-first bat.) Being more selective than a 56 percent swing rate would help his strengths shine. An average runner with good arm strength, Conticello began his career as a third baseman, began to split time at both corner infield spots in 2023 and then moved to the outfield full-time in '24. He’s made some starts in center but fits better in right field, and the D-backs are comfortable enough in his progress there that he won’t have to move back down the defensive spectrum to first base. He’ll still have to slug in a corner though, and he’s added good weight ahead of his age-23 season to help his cause all the more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Stoneman Douglas HS in Florida, Conticello signed for well above slot with a $500,000 bonus as an eighth-round pick in 2021. He hit 17 homers between Single-A and High-A two years ago but put in a more well-rounded breakout campaign in 2024, hitting .282/.346/.428 with nine homers and 20 steals in 126 games for Hillsboro. He rounded out his age-21 season with six games for Double-A Amarillo, adding one extra dinger. The left-handed slugger cuts a lean figure in the box at 6-feet-3 and already shows raw power with good bat speed. Some believe he’s still growing into his strength and could continue to fill out as he gets deeper into his 20s. Moving back to the hitters' haven that is Amarillo for 2025 could find Conticello putting up career bests in most slugging categories. His overall contact rate was solid for his age despite a lengthy swing, but he struggled against lefties. None of his homers came against same-side pitching and he slugged just .302 against it. Conticello may just be an average runner, but he’s a lively one who knows when to pick his stealing spots. He began his career playing the two corner infield spots but moved to right field primarily in ’24. His reads and routes remain in transition there, but his plus arm strength and accuracy absolutely fit the position as he recorded 14 outfield assists last season. The former South Florida commit headed to the upper Minors for the first time in 2025, but his issues against lefties have continued.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: “A person’s a person, no matter how small,” is, of course, a quote from the Dr. Seuss classic “Horton Hears a Who?” Now, that wasn't about this Horton, a shortstop who ranked No. 9 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list and signed with the Angels for $2 million when the 2026 signing period opened in January. But the Dominican infielder is 5-foot-9, so perhaps the passage is apt after all. Hailing from the same town in the Dominican Republic that produced big leaguers like Hanley Ramirez, Horton is a super-athletic left-handed hitter with all the tools to stay up the middle. He has a smaller frame, but he’s already shown in competition that he has good balance at the plate and a natural feel for finding the barrel. He has a solid approach with above-average contact skills and has sneaky pop. It's more gap-to-gap right now, but he could grow into double-digit home run power in the future. Horton’s speed and twitchy athleticism are assets on the basepaths and in the field. He has the ingredients to stick at shortstop, with smooth actions. The Angels think he has plenty of arm for the position, with the chance to be a premium defender, but in a worst-case scenario, he slides over and becomes a plus second baseman. He gets very high marks for his makeup and high energy style of play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox handed seven-figure bonuses to two members of their 2026 international class, $1.4 million to outfielder Garielvin Silverio and $1.2 million to Brito. The latter has a similar package of tools to fellow Dominican shortstop Hector Ramos, one of the standouts from Boston's 2025 international crop. Brito will make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League at age 17. Scouts are split as to whether Brito is a better bet to hit for average or power, and he may do both. He has a quick right-handed stroke and hits the ball harder than most player his age, which could portend 20-homer power as he matures physically. He doesn't try to do too much at the plate and shows promising feel for the strike zone. A twitchy athlete with a projectable 6-foot-1 frame, Brito features solid speed and moves well to both sides at shortstop. His quick hands help him make plays at short, though his arm is merely average now and will need to get stronger in order for him to remain there. If he has to move, second base and center field are potential options.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a growing contingent of Bahamians in the Marlins organization, Lewis has drawn comparisons to countryman Jazz Chisholm for his package of power, speed and twitchy athleticism in a compact frame. Signed for $950,000 in 2019, he had his pro debut delayed until 2021 because of the pandemic. Personal issues and a broken hamate limited him to just 51 games in Single-A at age 19 last year and his performance has declined while he has repeated the level in 2023. A switch-hitter, Lewis has good bat-to-ball skills and a decent understanding of the strike zone. He exhibits electric bat speed from both sides of the plate and has gotten considerably stronger since turning pro, but he hits too many groundballs and has yet to figure out how to tap into his plus raw power. He can get overly pull-conscious and needs to make adjustments to better handle breaking balls. Lewis has well-above-average speed and uses it aggressively on the bases, stealing 16 in 17 attempts last season. His quickness doesn't play quite as well in the field, where he has average range at second base and perhaps a tick better than that at third. His average arm is better suited for second, where his fast hands help him turn double plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lewis signed for $950,000 in 2019, receiving the highest bonus among Bahamians in that international class. Though the pandemic wiped out the Minor League season and what would have been his pro debut the following summer, he impressed in instructional league that fall. When he finally got a chance to play in 2021, he batted .302/.354/.497 with 18 extra-base hits and nine steals in 43 games as an 18-year-old in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. Lewis is reminiscent of countryman Jazz Chisholm with his combination of twitchy athleticism, power and speed in a compact frame. A switch-hitter with a quick swing from both sides of the plate, he has gotten stronger since signing and opened eyes by displaying at least average power in his debut. His hand-eye coordination and patient approach allow him to make consistent contact, though he'll have to prove he can handle quality breaking balls at higher levels. With his well-above-average speed, Lewis is a base-stealing threat and covers ground in the middle infield. The Marlins believe he has the actions and solid arm strength to handle shortstop, though he probably won't get much of a chance as he rises through the Minors alongside Kahlil Watson and Jose Salas. Lewis spent most of last summer at second base, where his quick hands help him turn double plays, and he can become an average or better defender as he develops more consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $1.1 million out of Venezuela on his 16th birthday in July 2018, Garcia managed to play only 56 games through his first three seasons due to a broken ankle in 2019 and the pandemic-lost campaign in 2020. His first true full season came last year, as he opened with a .262/.309/.403 line in 85 games at Single-A Carolina before finishing his age-19 at High-A Wisconsin, where he was even more challenged offensively (.688 OPS in 26 games). The reason Garcia is a prospect at all is his defensive work at shortstop. The 6-foot-2 athlete may show below-average raw speed, but his combination of reactions, hands and overall footwork makes him a potential plus defender at a premium spot on the diamond. Once he vacuums up the ball, his impressive arm strength plays well deep in the hole, too, giving him yet another defensive weapon. Perhaps because of the missed time earlier, Garcia still hasn’t developed an approach that would make him a surefire everyday player. His 20.3 percent swinging strike rate was fifth-highest among the 387 Minor Leaguers with at least 450 plate appearances in 2022, and he didn’t walk in any of his 108 High-A plate appearances (while fanning in 40 of them). He can make loud contact when he does put bat on ball -- as evidenced by his career-high 15 homers last season -- but it isn’t often enough to justify the high K rate. Garcia was unprotected and unpicked when he became Rule 5-eligible last fall and needs to start showing more at the plate to prove he can be more valuable than his floor as a late-game defensive replacement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked 24th in his international class by MLB Pipeline, Garcia had to wait eight days until his 16th birthday on July 10, 2018, to sign with the Brewers for $1.1 million. He was off to a strong start in the Dominican Summer League a year later, going 10-for-32 (.313) with six walks in 10 games, before suffering a broken ankle that ended his first season early. He participated in Milwaukee’s alternate training site in 2020 and made his Minor League stateside debut in the Arizona Complex League, where he hit .252/.327/.474 over 150 plate appearances. Garcia finished his age-18 season with a brief cameo at Low-A Carolina. Brewers officials were impressed by Garcia’s glovework before he even signed, and he still projects as a surefire shortstop nearly four years later. Even without average speed, his reactions help him showcase promising range at the premium position. It’s that defensive work that drives the profile right now. Garcia has gotten more patient at the plate as he’s gained experience, and he’s tapping into more of his power as he’s matured physically. But his approach isn’t there quite yet -- he struck out 28.6 percent of the time in 2021 -- and he has some road ahead of him before he can project to be even an average Major League bat. The ankle and pandemic-missed season still make Garcia a raw prospect. He’ll get to experience a full Minor League season just before he’s eligible for the Rule 5 Draft next offseason. The defense will earn Garcia chances long after that, and some offensive improvements could make him a potential everyday player in time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in his class during the 2018-19 international signing period, Garcia signed with the Brewers for $1.1 million on his 16th birthday after MLB Pipeline ranked him as the No. 24 prospect for that period. The projectable Venezuelan shortstop impressed Brewers scouts with the across-the-board tools he showed during MLB prospect showcases in Colombia and the Dominican Republic and was off to a smashing start in the 2019 Dominican Summer League (.313/.450/.469 in 40 plate appearances) while impressing in the field and on the bases before his season ended abruptly after just 10 games in mid-June when he suffered a broken ankle while sliding into second base. He spent 2020 making up for lost time, first appearing with Major Leaguers during the 2020 Cactus League while on loan from Minor League camp, and then as a member of Milwaukee’s Alternate Training Site beginning in mid-August. When he signed, Garcia was considered one of the premier defenders on the international market, with all-around tools that projected to improve if he filled-out physically. At the onset, he drew physical comparisons to former Brewers shortstop prospects Alcides Escobar and Orlando Arcia, but those have waned as Garcia has filled out his frame, and it appears he will continue to get stronger. Garcia projects to stick as a shortstop long term thanks to a slick glove and plus arm strength, and club officials have been impressed with his composure and quick first step, which gives him more range than his average speed suggests. If his frame fills out too much, the Brewers think Garcia will eventually have the power to be a productive third baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres didn’t have too much time to show what he could do at North Carolina State, with the pandemic shortening his freshman year and him leaving after the 2021 season as a Draft-eligible sophomore. He played enough to convince scouts his glove alone was worth drafting, and his power production as a sophomore helped him land in the third round of that summer’s Draft. After a solid pro debut, his first full season in High-A in 2022 was rough offensively. There are some things Torres can do well from the right side of the plate when he stays within himself. He uses his hands well with some feel for the barrel, with some seeing a little Tim Anderson in his setup and mechanics. At his best, he’s shown good feel for the zone and a gap-to-gap swing, but he doesn’t see enough pitches and gets into trouble when he tries to do too much and sells out for power, leading to too many swings and misses. If Torres can simplify things at the plate, he’ll be able to impact a big league team sooner rather than later because of his glove. He’ll be a shortstop for a long time, with outstanding actions and hands to go along with a plus arm and terrific instincts. He saw a lot of time at second base in 2022, both because of personnel on the same team and the fact that the lack of offensive profile points to a likely career as a defense-first utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres was Maryland’s best high school prospect in 2019, but opted to head to North Carolina State for college. The Dominican-born shortstop was Draft-eligible in his second year of college in 2021 and while he didn’t go in the first round, like former Wolfpack shortstops Trea Turner and Will Wilson, he did land in the third round with the Reds, then went out and had an impressive pro debut, mostly in Low-A. Torres’ calling card in defense was, and continues to be, his work at shortstop. Though he’s a fringy runner, he has excellent instincts that help him cover a lot of ground to go along with smooth actions, plus hands and a plus arm. While there were concerns about how his bat would play at the next level, the Reds have been pleasantly surprised with his right-handed swing. He’s always had good bat speed and some sneaky power, but got into trouble in college by getting overly aggressive at the plate. In the brief sample of his pro debut, Torres showed good plate awareness, didn’t chase too often and showed off an excellent gap-to-gap line drive swing. If he can continue to perform offensively like that, he has the chance to be a big league regular at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez began his professional career after signing with the Yankees for $50,000 out of Venezuela. He quickly established his defensive bona fides in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and Florida Complex League while providing modest offensive production. The bat didn’t keep up with the glove when he moved to full-season Tampa, and that continued when he moved down the West Coast of Florida to Bradenton when the Pirates acquired him in the Trade Deadline David Bednar deal. At present, Perez offers two elite skills: his swing decisions and his defense. He’s shown an advanced knowledge of the strike zone, especially for his age, with more walks (18.8 percent rate) than strikeouts (17.8) in his young career, with the Yankees doing excellent work in teaching zone control to their young hitters. There is some impact in there, but Perez is more of a hit-over-power type and the Pirates think perhaps he was too focused on leverage, taking him away from making consistent contact. Defensively, Perez is a natural receiver with fantastic hands and excellent blocking and receiving skills to go along with plus arm strength and accuracy. Young Pirates arms are going to enjoy throwing to him, and he’s already shown a knack for calling a game. His glove gives him a high floor as a backup, and if he can find some offensive consistency, he could develop into more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees usually prefer offensive-minded catchers, but Perez stands out most for his ability behind the plate. Signed for just $50,000 out of Venezuela in 2023, he was arguably that system's best defensive backstop before making his full-season debut. He came to the United States last summer and placed second in walks (45) and third in on-base percentage (.444) in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. A move to full-season ball in 2025 has been a challenge, but he’ll get the chance to hit the reset button with the Pirates, who acquired him as part of the prospect package in return for David Bednar at the Trade Deadline. Taller and significantly stronger than his listed 5-foot-10 and 155 pounds, Perez has the upside of plus receiving and blocking skills. His arm strength already is at that level, and he boosts it with a quick release that helps him shut down the running game. More athletic than most catchers, he's agile behind the plate and shows below-average speed on the bases. Though his defensive prowess stands out the most, Perez has offensive potential as well. A right-handed hitter who's more disciplined than most teenagers, he has the strength to provide 15 homers annually once he learns to launch balls in the air to his pull side more often. His approach can border between patient and passive, but he makes his share of hard-hit contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves have half of what would have been their normal international bonus pool at the start of the 2020-21 signing period in January of 2021 as part of the penalty for previous signing infractions. That didn’t hold them back from going all in on Tavarez, giving the Dominican shortstop $1.5 million to sign. He didn’t debut until 2022, in the Florida Complex League, and that didn’t come until August because he had thoracic outlet surgery on his non-throwing shoulder. His full-season debut in 2023 was a struggle at the plate. It's still too soon to know exactly what Tavarez might be because of how much time he missed. There are some raw tools to work with, starting with excellent bat speed from the right side of the plate. He’s capable of driving the ball to all fields, with power to come, if and when he makes contact. That was the biggest issue in 2023 as he struck out in nearly 41 percent of his plate appearances. He’s continuing to work on quieting down his setup and swing, something that will have to improve so he can make more contact. At one point, there was concern that Tavarez would outgrow shortstop, but it’s seeming his athleticism, excellent hands and plus arm should allow him to stick at the premium position. That helps raise his floor, but he’s going to have to make some adjustments to make more contact in order to progress up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2020-21 international signing period finally began in January 2021, the Braves couldn’t wait to jump back into the market after the penalties levied as a result of their signing violations ended. They used a majority of that pool on Tavarez, giving the Dominican shortstop $1.5 million to join the organization. With no Braves affiliate in the Dominican Summer League, he didn’t make his pro debut until 2022 in the Florida Complex League, and he briefly performed well there after being delayed by thoracic outlet surgery on his left shoulder. Because of how little he’s played, Tavarez is a bit of a wild card, but the hope is the raw tools that made him a prime target of Atlanta's international scouting staff will start coming to the fore with more reps. While he’s working to learn to quiet down his setup and swing, the right-handed hitter has tremendous bat speed and can drive the ball to all fields, with the chance to have plenty of in-game power as he develops. There were some questions about whether Tavarez could stay at shortstop long term, with some thinking he’d outgrow it and need to move to third. He is a good athlete with a plus arm and the Braves got good reports on his defense from his stint in winter ball in Colombia. He’ll be given every chance to stick at shortstop as he really gets his pro career started.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The start of the 2020-21 international signing period was delayed until January of 2021, so the Braves had to wait to jump out of the penalty box that came as a result of their signing violations. Given half of what would have been their normal bonus pool, they used a huge chunk of it to sign Tavarez in January 2021 for $1.5 million. Because the Braves didn’t have a team in the Dominican Summer League, he wasn’t able to make his pro debut that summer. The start to his career was further delayed when he needed thoracic outlet surgery on his non-throwing arm before the start of Florida Complex League action this year, though he did return to the FCL to make his debut in August. The Braves are excited to see this athletic infielder in action, especially in the batter’s box. Tavarez’s right-handed bat has the chance to carry him up the ladder, with a ton of raw power he’ll learn how to get to as he physically matures. He can drive the ball to all fields with bat speed, but he’ll need to keep working on the moving parts of his swing so he can be sure to access that pop consistently. Tavarez is an excellent athlete with a plus arm and the Braves feel he has every chance to stick at shortstop, certainly with enough arm to play the premium spot. Should he slow down and need to move, it does look like he has the power profile to fit nicely at third.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hartle was one of the top prep lefties in the 2021 Draft class and entered his junior season at Wake Forest as perhaps the top college pitcher, but his stuff and control backed up and caused him to slip in the '24 Draft. He ended up signing for $850,000 as a Pirates third-rounder before the Guardians acquired him and fellow southpaw Michael Kennedy for Luis Ortiz. The North Carolina native made it to Double-A in his first full pro season and earned High-A Midwest Pitcher of the Year honors after logging a 2.35 ERA with 100 strikeouts and a 1.05 WHIP in 103 1/3 frames for Lake County. While he doesn't have overpowering stuff, Hartle throws strikes with a deep repertoire and creates unique angles from his 6-foot-6 frame and horizontal release. His best pitch is a slurvy slider that gets plenty of chase against lefties, and his changeup gets a decent amount of chase and miss but rarely lands for strikes. Hartle has a four-seam and two-seam fastball that each sit in the low 90s, although he could add more power as he fills out his 207-pound frame. He often works with his upper-80s cutter in the zone and limits hard contact on the pitch. Hartle repeats his delivery well and throws plenty of strikes. He profiles as a back-end starter currently, although the Guardians have had success developing this type of pitcher in the past. He's done a great job of preventing hard contact -- and home runs, in particular -- to date, but without velocity gains, that will be difficult against more advanced hitting. Hartle's 2025 season ended two weeks early with a shoulder injury, but he's unrestricted heading into 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some clubs rated Hartle as the best left-hander in the 2021 prep class, but he went undrafted because he was set on attending Wake Forest. Following an All-America sophomore season, he entered 2024 as a consensus first-rounder before all four of his pitches and his control regressed. The Pirates drafted him in the third round, then sent him to the Guardians five months later as part of a package for Spencer Horwitz. At his best, Hartle exhibits advanced feel for a plus slider, solid cutter and average fastball and changeup. His heater sat at 89-92 mph and topped out at 94 with less life and command last spring, and he became reluctant to throw it when it got pounded. His low-80s slider and upper-80s cutter weren't as sharp as in the past, and his sinking mid-80s changeup rarely landed in the zone. As a sophomore, Hartle used his athleticism to repeat his easy delivery and spot his pitches wherever he wanted. Diminished stuff with less command was a recipe for disaster in 2024, when he also gave up four runs and recorded just five outs in his lone pro outing. He once looked like a lock to be at least a No. 4 starter with the upside of a No. 2, and now he's a reclamation project for an organization renowned for its ability to develop pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies had 12 picks in the top 10 rounds of the 2022 Draft and they used 11 of them to take college-aged players. The one exception was Cox, their second-round selection who got a slightly over-slot bonus of $1.85 million to sign. He was just getting started finding his way in pro ball in 2023 when he needed Tommy John surgery and he missed all of 2024. He came back to log 85 innings under close medical supervision with Single-A Fresno in 2025 and the Rockies were very encouraged with what they saw. Cox’s stuff started coming back once he was on the mound, running his fastball up to 95 mph routinely and reaching back for more at times with good life up in the zone, but it’s his curveball that is still the talk of the town. He registers elite spin rates with the 1-to-7 breaking ball that features sharp bite, missing plenty of bats with it. He was way too fastball-heavy when he first entered pro ball, and in 2025, he found a better balance between the heater and the curve. He has a changeup, but it’s too firm and he doesn’t pronate all that well, leading some to think that he might be a candidate to add another pitch, perhaps bringing the cutter he had worked on previously back into his repertoire. There could be more consistent velocity from Cox as he gets further removed from Tommy John and he did a nice job of being around the zone and repeating his delivery well during his first season back. The gloves will come off a bit more and there’s a chance that Cox, at age 22, could reach a different plane as a pitching prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies had four picks in the top two rounds of the 2022 Draft and used the first three to take college players, one pitcher and two bats. Cox was one of the better high school pitchers on the West Coast that year and the Pacific Northwest native became the Rockies’ second-rounder and was signed away from his Oregon commitment for an over-slot $1.85 million bonus. The organization was excited to see what he could do in full-season ball after impressing in instructional league play the fall after signing, but after pitching in shorter stints over 10 outings with Single-A Fresno, he was part of the Rockies' Tommy John surgery trifecta with Gabriel Hughes and Jordy Vargas. It was Cox’s feel for spin that really helped him stand out as a prepster and during the infancy of his pro career. It’s a plus 1-to-7 curveball with elite-level spin rates, a true out pitch with sharp bite. His other offerings aren’t bad, either: a lively fastball up to 95 mph and some feel for a changeup. The athletic right-hander also tinkered with a slider and cutter after showing acumen for manipulating the spin and break on his curve. Added strength was already a plus for Cox and should help him get his stuff back -- and perhaps add more -- once he’s put the elbow surgery behind him. He has clean mechanics and the ability to pitch to both sides of the plate. It won’t be until 2025 before the Rockies know what they have on their hands, but he could still get back to reaching his ceiling as a mid-rotation type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts looking for good high school pitching in the state of Washington were busy in 2022, with both J.R. Ritchie and Cox getting a lot of attention as right-handers who had first-round potential. Ritchie went No. 35 overall to the Braves, while the Rockies were thrilled to get Cox in the second round, giving him an over-slot bonus of $1.85 million to sign him away from his commitment to Oregon. He didn’t pitch competitively after signing, but he did impress his new organization in instructional league play. He was being handled carefully during his first full season of pro ball in Fresno in 2023 when he needed Tommy John surgery in late July. One of the early things that stood out with Cox is his competitiveness on the mound, with a no-nonsense approach and a desire to attack hitters with what could be a very good three-pitch mix. He can get his fastball up to 95 mph with good running life, but it’s his curveball that has everyone buzzing. It’s a 1-to-7 breaking ball that registers elite-level spin rates and can be a real hammer out pitch with sharp bite to it. He has good feel for his changeup as well. Cox has already added strength to his athletic frame since signing, which could lead to more consistent velocity once he's back to full strength. He’s already shown an ability to command the ball to both sides of the plate and manipulate the spin and break on his curve, with some thinking he might eventually develop a distinct slider. His combination of pitchability and potential power stuff points to a future as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nezuh went from working just 18 innings in two seasons at Florida State to becoming Louisiana-Lafayette's top starter in 2023. The Astros put more stock in his pitch metrics than his 6.25 career ERA in college and selected him in the 14th round. He ranked 10th in the Minors with a 30 percent strikeout rate in his 2024 pro debut between two Class A levels but wasn't as effective while dealing with elbow issues in Double-A last year. Nezuh's upper-70s changeup has improved a lot since his college days, with its splitter action baffling both lefties and righties. It creates tremendous vertical separation from his fastball, which parks at 91-94 mph and touches 96 with huge carry. To remain a starter, he'll need to find a reliable third pitch from among a sweeping low-80s slider, a mid-80s cutter and a mid-70s curveball he has mostly shelved. Nezuh works from a higher arm slot that costs him some deception. Since battling the strike zone at Florida State, he has developed average control and good feel for playing his fastball and changeup off each other. Those two pitches alone could make him a useful multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nezuh worked just 18 innings in two seasons at Florida State before transferring and becoming Louisiana-Lafayette's top starter in 2023. He pitched well down the stretch and held his own in an NCAA regional playoff game against Texas, prompting Houston to draft him in the 14th round. He raised his stock with a strong pro debut that included leading the Single-A Carolina League with 105 strikeouts in 81 2/3 innings before his mid-July promotion and ranking 10th in the Minors with a 30 percent K rate. Nezuh has significantly upgraded his changeup since college and now owns one of the best in the Minors, a low-80s cambio that plunges at the plate and confounds both lefties and righties. It has tremendous vertical separation from his fastball, which sits at 93-95 mph and reaches 97 with the flat approach angle and carry that the Astros covet. He needs to improve his below-average breaking balls, a sweeping low-80s slider and upper-70s curveball with similar shape. After not throwing strikes in his two years with the Seminoles, Nezuh has done a better job of harnessing stuff since. His biggest need is to find a reliable third pitch, and he has begun toying with an upper-80s cutter. If he can't stick in the rotation, his fastball/changeup combination could make him a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 35 | Power: 60 | Run: 40 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 The Brewers took Bitonti out of the California prep ranks in the third round in 2023 when he was only 17 years old, signing him away from an Oregon commitment for $1.75 million, more than double slot value. He showed promise out of the gate with 16 homers (the second-most by a Minor Leaguer age 18 or younger) and a 147 wRC+ in 79 games between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Carolina in 2024 but came back to down to earth with a return to the Carolina League a year later. Bitonti hit .238/.341/.421 with 19 homers in 118 games with the Mudcats in ’25; his 33.5 percent strikeout rate was fourth-highest among Single-A qualifiers. Standing 6-foot-5, Bitonti cuts a massive figure from the left side of the box. He uses that size to generate big bat speed that comes primarily from his upper body, considering he only relies on a toe tap for the bottom half of his load. The levers in his swing create a lot of length despite the sheer velocity of his hacks, and he can run late on pitches, even fastballs in the zone. When he does make contact, it’s loud and often in the air to the pull side, giving hope that he could be a future 30-homer slugger. Originally taken as a shortstop, Bitonti has slid down the defensive spectrum since with some time at third base in 2024 and then primary duty at first in ’25. He makes for a big target there and still retains arm strength that will help on throws across the diamond. Bitonti will only be 20 for the duration of the 2026 season, but adjustments will have to come quick if he’s to power his way up the chain.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bitonti was an inconsistent performer on the showcase circuit in 2022 but received plenty of invitations and attention from scouts. The Brewers took the California native in the 2023 third round, signed him for above slot at $1.75 million and played it slow with him out of the gate considering he was still only 17 on Draft Day. Bitonti opened his first full season in the Arizona Complex League and laid waste to the Rookie level with a .320/.451/.580 line and eight homers in 51 games. He was promoted to Single-A Carolina in late July and continued to slug there with eight more homers in 28 games. His 16 total dingers were second-most in the Minors among players 18 or younger. Standing in the box at 6-foot-4, Bitonti already exhibits absolutely electric bat speed, registering in the mid-70s at times, and he’s already built like a house with the strength to turn most contact into loud contact. (Forty-two of his 83 hits in 2024 went for extra bases.) But with that comes a ton of swing-and-miss concerns at this early stage. His long levers contribute partly to the problem, and the Brewers hold out hope that shortening the swing some could lead to more overall contact. Bitonti was drafted as a shortstop but has primarily slid over to third in pro ball. The majority of his starts with Carolina came at the opposite corner at first base, and many believe that’s where he’ll land full-time as a fairly athletic defender and big target for his fellow infielders. Bitonti’s power will certainly play there as is, and he has plenty of runway to make other tweaks to unlock his hit tool in time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bitonti certainly made the rounds on the showcase circuit with stops at the PDP League, Area Code Games, Major League Baseball’s High School All-American Game and Perfect Game All-American Classic in 2022, and while his performance was inconsistent in those environments, he continued to draw scouts last spring. The Brewers selected the infielder in the third round and signed him with an above-slot bonus of $1.75 million. Bitonti went 7-for-39 (.179) with two homers, nine walks and 15 strikeouts during a 12-game run in the Arizona Complex League after signing. Standing in at 6-foot-4 already, Bitonti is certainly a presence on the diamond, and that shows up in his tools as well. The left-handed slugger already shows at least plus raw power, and given his size, he can make it translate into games fairly easily. While he has the plate discipline that can lead to walks, his long levers and swing have hurt his overall hit tool as he can struggle with swing-and-miss. Some amateur scouts believed he needed pro instruction to iron out those concerns. Though we live in the Age of the Big Shortstop, Bitonti has long been pegged for a move from the six to third base, and that’s what happened in the early days of his Brewers career. He had the body control to play an adequate short in school, and that, along with a plus arm, could make him a quality defender at the hot corner. Bitonti is only entering his age-18 season and has the tools (and room to grow) to be an interesting project for the Milwaukee pipeline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known more for his hitting and wrestling prowess than his pitching in high school in Virginia, Grammes became a two-way player at Xavier and showed enough promise on the mound to become a fifth-round pick in 2019. The four years since have been a rocky road, to say the least. He lost his first full season to the pandemic and then made eight High-A appearances before needing Tommy John surgery in July 2021. Grammes returned to Hillsboro late last July, and while the results were a mixed bag (17 earned runs, 33 strikeouts in 18 innings), his stuff still showed the same promise. The 6-foot-1 right-hander is back up to the upper 90s, touching triple digits, so velocity has not been a concern coming off the elbow procedure and long rehab. His upper-80s slider is a wipeout pitch too, making sure hitters can’t just sit on the heat, and it might be only a touch better than his low-80s curveball, at least when it comes to bite. The deuce is still at least an above-average pitch, which is more than can be said for a changeup he doesn’t use much in relief. Command was a relative difficulty for Grammes before Tommy John, and that continued to be true last year as he tried to play catch-up. In the offseason, the D-backs have worked with him on landing pitches more consistently. If he can, the quality of his arsenal could point to a high-leverage role out of the bullpen. Grammes was already left exposed to the 2022 Rule 5 Draft (and went unselected), so time is ticking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: More of a power hitter than a pitcher in high school, Grammes won nearly as many Virginia state wrestling titles (two) as he pitched innings (three), and he received a walk-on opportunity at Xavier only after emailing the program. While he has posted much gaudier numbers at the plate than on the mound with the Musketeers, he'll definitely become a full-time pitcher as a pro. He turned down the Orioles as a 35th-rounder last year as a sophomore and should go about 30 rounds higher this June. Grammes offers some of the best fastball velocity in the Draft, working at 95-99 mph as a reliever in the past and at 93-95 as a starter this spring. It doesn't feature a lot of life and he struggles to command it, so his heater can get hit when he leaves it over the plate. Similarly, he can throw some sharp low-80s sliders and also get into trouble when his breaking ball flattens out. Grammes has shown little feel for a changeup while trying to incorporate a third pitch as a starter this year, and he'll probably scrap it as a reliever at the next level. Though he throws with some effort, he has made some progress cleaning up his delivery and has the athleticism to continue to improve. He has little history of providing strikes or consistency, though he never has concentrated solely on pitching either.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The selection of Perez as a college senior out of Texas Christian in the 11th round of the 2022 Draft didn’t draw too much attention, and there wasn’t much buzz around him after a solid first full season of pro ball spent mostly at the Single-A level. He suffered through a tough 2024 campaign in High-A, but things started getting a little interesting last year, when he pitched his way from High-A to Double-A. The Mariners didn’t protect him on the 40-man roster, and he went unselected in the Rule 5 Draft. The 5-foot-10 Perez will never be confused with a flamethrower, but he does have a feel to pitch and for the strike zone. His fastball averaged around 93 mph last year, and he showed the ability to hold his velocity deeper into starts. But whatever success he has, he owes to his sliders. He throws them more than the heater, and he’ll use both a hard, short gyro-like pitch up to 87 mph as well as a low-80s sweeper. He’s tinkered with a variety of changeup grips and styles but hasn’t found one he can command. Perez continues to be an extreme strike-thrower, carrying a career 2.5 BB/9 rate into the 2026 season. He’ll get the opportunity to keep starting for now, but he’s pitching this year at age 26, so the clock is ticking. With younger starting pitching prospects coming behind him, there could be a time soon where the Mariners put Perez in a bullpen as a slider monster who maybe can gain a few more ticks in velocity in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez was selected as a reliever by the Angels in the late rounds of the 2021 Draft but he opted to return to Texas Christian University, then upped his stock to the 11th round, where the Mariners took him one year later and signed him for $125,000. He had a solid debut season in ‘23, making 15 starts at Single-A Modesto before a late-season promotion to High-A Everett. Undersized at 5-foot-10, Perez nonetheless possesses athleticism for his build. His fastball sits around 92-93 mph, with good ride and break, which allows it to play up more than the radar gun shows. It’s also possible that he continues to grow into more velocity. It’s the slider that really took off in his first year, particularly the command of the pitch that has good two-plane break. It’s already consistently missing bats in the pros. Perez has exclusively started in his short stint in the organization, but for him to remain there, he’ll need to fortify at least one more pitch, the clearest offering being the changeup that he’ll drop in occasionally. Even with just a two-pitch mix, there’s a good foundation for him to eventually work as a reliever in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of the Hawaiian baseball scene, Saltiban was one of the few high school players to compete in the 2023 MLB Draft League. He showed enough for the Phillies to take him in the third round of that summer’s Draft and there were some solid early returns. He was among the Single-A Florida State League’s leaders in home runs (17), slugging percentage (.428) and ISO (.191). He did not build off of that with a move up to High-A Jersey Shore in 2025, struggling to find a rhythm in a year interrupted by a nearly two-month stay on the injured list. He made up for lost time by hitting very well in the Australian Baseball League, winning Championship Series MVP honors as the Adelaide Giants won the title. With a quick right-handed swing that generates plenty of bat speed, the 5-foot-9 Saltiban is capable of doing damage when he’s swinging well. He can make loud contact with over-the-fence juice mostly to his pull side and is capable of driving the ball to all fields. His overall approach unraveled in 2025, with his strikeout rate increasing and his walk rate shrinking, though he made more consistent contact in Australia. Saltiban has plus speed and uses it efficiently on the basepaths, with 46 steals in 54 attempts in his career heading into 2026. He’s also back in the outfield, where he played in high school. The Phillies thought he had a chance to play second base, and while they’re not going to take him off the dirt entirely, they like how instinctive he looked in center field, where he played exclusively in Australia. That might take a little pressure off his bat and could be a better fit long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Saltiban was the best player from Hawaii in the 2023 Draft class. After he held his own as one of the youngest performers in the Draft League that summer, he was taken by the Phillies, who didn’t have a second-round selection, in the third round of that Draft, signing for an under-slot bonus of $602,500. After a brief debut in the Florida Complex League last year, Saltiban went to the Florida State League in 2024 and more than held his own, finishing in the top four in homers (17), slugging percentage (.428) and ISO (.191). Strong and compact, Saltiban has more juice in his 5-foot-9 frame than many anticipated. It’s a quick right-handed swing with plenty of bat speed, and he swings with intent to do damage, regularly registering high exit velocities. Most of his home run pop has come to his pull side so far, though he can drive the ball to all fields. He absolutely punishes fastballs and has shown a solid approach at the plate, drawing a good amount of walks, though he’ll need to improve against spin. A plus runner who went 22-for-24 in stolen-base attempts last year, Saltiban was an outfielder in high school, but the Phillies thought he had a chance to make it on the dirt and played second base exclusively in 2024. He’s probably a fringe-average defender right now, and though his athleticism points to him being average at the keystone in the future, he might get some reps in the outfield moving forward. He has as much upside as any hitter in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nearly all Hawaiian hitting prospects at some point work with Kaha Wong, Kolten and Kean’s father, and Saltiban was no different. The best player from the Aloha State in the 2023 Draft class, Saltiban held his own as one of the youngest players in MLB’s Draft League. He was nabbed in the third round by the Twins, no strangers to Hawaiian prep hitters having taken Kala’i Rosario in the fifth round of the 2020 Draft, making Saltiban the first from the state to go in the top three rounds since Shane Sasaki was a Rays third-rounder in 2019. While Saltiban isn’t the biggest player at 5-foot-10, he’s strong and compact. There is a lot of confidence in his right-handed bat. He has a quick swing and excellent bat speed that was on display during his brief debut in the Florida Complex League last summer. The Phillies believe there’s going to be power to come as well as he adjusts to professional pitching. An outfielder in high school, Saltiban now has the opportunity to show he can play on the dirt. He played shortstop in the FCL, and given that he’d never really played the position at any high level, he showed off good hands and a solid enough arm with his plus speed helping him cover ground. He’ll see most of his time at shortstop and second base, which could be his eventual home if the left side of second proves too much of a challenge, with perhaps him getting enough reps in the outfield to keep those skills sharp.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heredia joined the Phillies in the winter of 2021, signing for $300,000, and the early returns were very positive. He played well in the Dominican Summer League in '22 and performed well enough to climb from the Florida Complex League to full-season Clearwater the following year. He struggled with his approach -- and with staying healthy -- in '24, while better production in '25 with High-A Jersey Shore was cut short by a broken pinky. He got off to a solid start, albeit with similar approach issues, with a move to Double-A in '26. A strong and athletic right-handed-hitting outfielder, Heredia has shown glimpses of using all five tools, with hard contact from the right side of the plate and the ability to get to his power. He improved his bat-to-ball skills in 2025 after having worked with Luis Arraez's hitting guy in the offseason prior, but he'll have to watch his swing-and-miss and chase rates if he wants to keep being productive. Heredia isn't a burner and isn't much of a basestealing threat, but the strong and compact outfielder runs better than you might think. He has the kind of plus arm teams like to see in right field, and he continues to get work in both outfield corners. If he can refine his approach at the plate, he might have the offensive profile to fit in one of those spots at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies signed Heredia for $300,000 not long after the 2021 international signing period, but it wasn’t until 2022 that the organization got to see what he could do. He had a solid debut that summer in the Dominican Summer League, and then he really put himself on the map in the United States for the first time in 2023, going from the Florida Complex League to full-season ball and finishing with a .314/.392/.493 line, making him the most productive member of that signing class to date. A strong and athletic right-handed hitter, Heredia shows glimpses of all five tools. He can make hard contact and has impressive raw power that he is already showing he can get to. It’s a power-over-hit profile for sure, and he’ll have to cut his strikeout rate as he moves up the ladder and faces better pitching. He runs better than you might think given his strength/power profile. That speed helps Heredia be a solid defender in an outfield corner, which is where he’ll end up even though he’s seen some time in center early on in his career. His plus arm works from there, and if he can refine his approach, he could develop into that athletic right-field run-producer type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinto joined the Tigers organization for $897,500 out of Venezuela in January 2024, making him the second-highest-paid international signing by Detroit in that year’s window behind only Nestor Miranda ($1,497,500). Pinto hit the ground running nicely with a .275/.403/.438 line and four homers in 53 games in the Dominican Summer League in his first season but was limited by a hamstring issue in his move stateside in 2025. He did finish his age-18 campaign with Single-A Lakeland, however, and has returned to the Florida State League with more sustained results this season. A right-handed hitter, Pinto stays very much in control with the front side of his lower half, using just a toe tap to remain in rhythm and get himself in position to be short to the ball. He can kick out his back leg once he fires, and as a result, he has pushed the ball the other way a plurality of the time -- and on the ground the majority of the time at Single-A, to boot. Still, because of his quick movements, he has been among the FSL leaders in in-zone contact to begin 2026, and despite the subpar angles, his raw exit velocities have been solid too. Pinto is just an average runner right now, and while he has enough instincts to track down balls in center, he seems likely headed to a corner long term once he shares the grass with speedier defenders. That said, his arm is an absolute hose both in terms of strength and accuracy and remains an asset from anywhere on the grass. Pinto would need to show better slugging ability to be an offensive fit in left or right, but he still has plenty of development ahead as he won’t turn 20 until March 2027.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 A reliever for his first two years at Clemson, Weatherly moved into the Tigers’ rotation in 2020 and threw extremely well in four starts before the pandemic-induced shutdown. The Rockies saw enough to take him in the third round of the 2020 Draft and sign him for full slot, then saw him look extremely good in instructional league play last year. Shoulder issues have slowed him over his first two full seasons, but he’s shown glimpses of his overpowering stuff. Weatherly stands out for his pure stuff and his athleticism, to the point where the Rockies think he’s one of the best overall athletes in the entire system. The left-hander’s fastball touched 97 mph at instructs, but the high-spin heater sits more comfortably in the low 90s. His slider is his go-to pitch, a plus wipeout that gets both left- and right-handed hitters to swing and miss on a regular basis. He didn’t need his changeup much in college, especially when coming out of the bullpen, but it’s something he’s continued to work on to improve. The left-hander has had trouble commanding the baseball at times, often because of timing issues with his delivery, which can be remedied. He’s smart to a fault on the mound, sometimes thinking too much rather than just trusting his stuff. The Rockies think he has all the ingredients to be a Robbie Ray-like starter, but also know that he could get big league hitters out in the bullpen right now, with a Josh Hader-type career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clemson University has had more than its fair share of high-end Draft picks, including first-round bats like Logan Davidson in 2019 and Seth Beer in 2018. But Weatherly, who used a dominant move to the rotation in his shortened junior season in 2020 to climb up to the third round and sign for full slot with the Rockies, is the first pitcher to get taken in the top three rounds since the A’s selected Daniel Gossett in the second round of the 2014 Draft. The left-hander then went on to make a very good first impression during instructional league play last fall. Weatherly is all about power, with two potentially plus pitches at his disposal. His high spin-rate fastball was typically in the low-90s at Clemson, occasionally touching a bit higher, but he was up to 97 mph consistently at instructs. His best pitch is his wipeout slider that gets swings and misses from hitters on both sides of the plate. His changeup is behind -- he didn’t need it as much when he was pitching out of the bullpen for Clemson early in his college career -- but he showed improved feel for it as he used it more. There’s confidence that Weatherly has the stuff to start and the Rockies love his pitching IQ and competitive nature, but there are questions about him throwing enough strikes to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter. If not, he could become a very good lefty setup type out of a big league pen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Frasso showed first-round potential heading into the 2020 season at Loyola Marymount, but he strained his forearm during the pandemic-shortened schedule and dropped to the Blue Jays in the fourth round. He had internal brace surgery on his elbow in June 2021, returned to the mound in May 2022 and then joined the Dodgers along with lefty pitching prospect Moises Brito in a trade for Mitch White and infield prospect Alex DeJesus two months later. He blossomed into Los Angeles' best pitching prospect in 2023 before tearing the labrum in his pitching shoulder, necessitating surgery that November that sidelined him for all of last season. He has returned to the mound this year in Triple-A, and his ability to miss bats and throw strikes have regressed significantly. A healthy Frasso can overpower hitters with a fastball that parks at 94-97 mph and peaks at 100 with armside run and impressive extension that make it tough to barrel. He flashes a plus mid-80s changeup with fade and sink so hitters can't try to sit on his heater. His hard upper-80s slider features good depth and can be overpowering, though it lacks the consistency of his other two offerings. But none of those pitches have been as good in 2025 as they were two years ago. Frasso creates a lot of deception with his extension and crossfire delivery, and he has the athleticism to repeat his mechanics and pound the strike zone. He looked like a possible frontline starter before he got hurt, but he also had two major arm surgeries in 29 months and has worked just 152 innings in four pro seasons. Given his history and the Dodgers' rotation depth, he'll likely contribute as a multi-inning reliever in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A potential first-rounder going into his junior year at Loyola Marymount, Frasso strained his forearm during the truncated 2020 season and fell the to Blue Jays in the fourth round. He had the ulnar collateral ligament in his pitching elbow repaired with an internal brace in June 2021 and returned to the mound in May 2022 before getting dealt with lefty pitching prospect Moises Brito to the Dodgers for Mitch White and infield prospect Alex DeJesus two months later. He emerged as Los Angeles' best pitching prospect in 2023 before tearing the labrum in his pitching shoulder and having surgery in November that will sideline him for all or most of this season. Frasso’s fastball usually ranges from 94-97 mph and tops out at 100 with arm-side run, and the impressive extension he creates enables his heater to get on hitters more quickly than expected. His mid-80s changeup can be a plus pitch at its best, fading and sinking and confusing batters who are trying to sit on his heater. His mid-80s slider has the makings of a solid offering with sweep and depth, though it’s not as reliable as his fastball and changeup. Frasso has an extremely deceptive delivery thanks to his extension and crossfire action, and he also has the athleticism to repeat it. He has a long history of throwing strikes and held up while working a career-high 93 innings in 2023. Durability is the only real question he has to answer to become a mid-rotation starter, and he has the stuff to have a fallback as a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Contenders don't often acquire quality prospects at the Trade Deadline, but the Dodgers did just that last August when they grabbed Frasso and fellow right-handed pitching prospect Moises Brito from the Blue Jays in exchange for Mitch White and infield prospect Alex DeJesus. Frasso was a potential first-rounder entering his junior season at Loyola Marymount in 2020, but he strained his forearm during the shortened season and fell to the fourth round of the five-round Draft. He had elbow surgery in June 2021 but returned to the mound 11 months later and displayed an explosive fastball. Frasso can devastate hitters with his heater, which sits at 95-97 mph, touches 100 and plays even better than its velocity thanks to armside run and impressive extension in his delivery. His mid-80s changeup with fade and sink continues to improve as he uses it more often, showing flashes of becoming a plus pitch. His mid-80s slider also misses bats with a combination of sweep and depth, though he has trouble landing it for strikes. Frasso didn't go past four innings in an outing during his first two pro seasons, so he still has to prove that his stuff will last deeper into games and over a full season. He uses his athleticism to repeat his delivery well and has a history of throwing strikes. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter and his fastball alone could make him a high-leverage reliever if he winds up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming out of Palos Verdes Peninsula High School in Southern California, Frasso was a tall and gangly basketball player and a pitcher with a ton of upside, but who had difficulty making the transition from one sport to the next, which kept his velocity down for much of the spring. He looked like the type of pitching prospect who needed college, and that's proven to be true. Focusing on baseball at Loyola Marymount, Frasso started catching up to his upside over his first two years, though an elbow injury suffered before the shutdown put his Draft stock a bit more in question. He was reportedly throwing and working his way back when the season stopped, and the Blue Jays liked his untapped potential on the mound enough that they selected Frasso in the fourth round in June, signing him for below-slot value. Frasso’s athleticism is a plus, as you don’t often find starting pitchers who can dunk a basketball. His fastball has been sitting in the range of 93 mph but reaching up into the 95-97 mph area, and some added strength to his projectable frame could help his sustain that better going forward. That pitch is especially effective up in the zone. Frasso throws a sweeping curve that's an average pitch at this stage with a changeup that lags behind. With long arms, there’s plenty of extension on his releases, too. Frasso’s delivery isn’t the smoothest visually, but his athleticism allows him to repeat it well enough and get to his release point consistently. The physical development of Frasso’s wiry frame will be interesting to track now that he’s in the Blue Jays hands, and while there’s certainly bullpen potential down the road, the organization will explore his potential as a starter first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox were split on whether Cason had a brighter future as a right-hander or a shortstop when they drafted the Georgia prepster in 2024's eighth round and gave him the opportunity to do both after signing him for second-round money ($1.25 million). Most other teams preferred him on the mound, but he wanted the opportunity to play both ways. After a two-inning outing and a game at DH last May, he developed elbow soreness that eventually led to Tommy John surgery in August. He won't pitch in 2026 but possibly could get some at-bats. As an amateur, Cason showcased a 93-95 mph fastball, topped out at 97, and displayed the aptitude to carry it up in zone or sink it down at the knees. He showed better feel for killing spin on a split-grip changeup in the low 80s than producing it on a tight slider with similar velocity. His athleticism helps him get down the mound well, though he'll rush his delivery at times and lose some control.ss Cason also offers an intriguing combination of solid raw power and speed, though he comes with questions about his hitting ability. He struggled against breaking balls and changeups on the high school showcase circuit, and his right-handed stroke gets too long when he gets aggressive. He has fluid actions and an obviously strong arm at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest in a recent line of Georgia prep two-way talents that includes big leaguers Taj Bradley, Michael Harris and Josh Lowe, Cason starred in four sports at the Greater Atlanta Christian School. The Red Sox were truly divided on whether he was better as a right-hander or a shortstop and still aren't sure after signing one of the youngest prospects in the 2024 Draft for late second-round money ($1.25 million) as an eighth-rounder. Most clubs preferred him as a pitcher, but he wants to play both ways and Boston will make a sincere effort to let him try. Gatorade's Georgia high school player of the year, Cason features a 93-95 mph fastball that reaches 98 and shows the feel to ride it up in the zone or sink it down at the knees. He also has advanced aptitude for killing spin on his low-80s split-grip changeup, which tumbles at the plate and could become a plus offering. His tight slider has similar velocity and solid upside. While he's obviously athletic and gets down the mound well, he can rush his delivery at times and lose some control. Cason asked to showcase himself solely as a shortstop at the MLB Draft Combine, where he impressed scouts with his solid raw power and speed. There are some questions about his hitting ability after he struggled against non-fastballs on the showcase circuit, and his right-handed swing can get too long when he gets overly aggressive. There obviously aren't any questions about his arm strength at shortstop, where he displays fluid actions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nuñez joined the Twins for $25,000 in November 2019 and dominated the Dominican Summer League when he made his debut in 2021. He was off to another solid start in the Florida Complex League a year later when Minnesota dealt him to the Orioles as part of the four-pitcher return for Jorge Lopez at the 2022 Trade Deadline. He finally got a full season’s worth of innings (104 2/3) in 2023 between Single-A and High-A and was back with Aberdeen for 2024, posting a 2.45 ERA with 38 strikeouts in 29 1/3 frames when he went down with a shoulder injury. After going unprotected, Nuñez went to the Padres in the Rule 5 Draft but was returned to Baltimore at the end of Spring Training. The right-hander’s stuff plays bigger than his size at 5-foot-11. His fastball can touch the occasional 97 mph but typically settles in the mid-90s, though High-A hitters slugged .481 against it. Nuñez almost threw his gyro slider as often as the heater against righties, and they couldn’t much handle it with a 47 percent whiff rate and 35 percent chase rate. Thought to be a developing pitch entering the year, Nuñez’s changeup was a similar menace, tunneling well off the fastball only to dive armside late. It stood out more for its movement than its separation, but both lefties and righties couldn’t touch it in limited usage. Nuñez did a better job of cutting down walks in the short 2024 sample, but control had been a serious issue before that. The arsenal is interesting, but the hurler is also entering his age-24 campaign with only one season above 100 innings, no upper-level experience and a recent injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the four pitching prospects acquired by the Orioles when they sent Jorge Lopez to the Twins at the 2022 Trade Deadline, Nuñez had to wait two years before throwing his first official pitch after signing with Minnesota in November 2019 for just $25,000. The pandemic erased what should’ve been his debut in 2020, and he was throwing well in the Florida Complex League at age 21 when the Orioles picked him up. Nuñez then pitched his way from Single-A Delmarva to High-A Aberdeen in his first full season with his new organization, flashing power stuff but iffy control. He was off to a promising start back with Aberdeen this year before being shut down for the year in May with a shoulder issue. After Nuñez was left off the O’s 40-man in the offseason, the Padres selected him in the Rule 5 Draft, giving him a shot at the Majors for 2025. Nuñez may only be 5-foot-11, but his stuff is big. He has the ability to miss bats with everything in his four-pitch mix, working his secondary stuff off a fastball that can flash 96-97 but typically settles consistently in the mid-90s. He throws a power curve and a gyro slider that flash plus, as well as a developing changeup that could become at least an average pitch. He pitches with quick arm action but there is some effort to his delivery. While he’s strong and compact, sub-6-footers often have trouble making it to the big leagues as a starting pitcher. Control is also a problem after Nuñez walked 13 percent of batters last summer. He’ll need to reverse that trend and prove his health if he’s going to stick in The Show in ‘25, especially with San Diego’s plans for contention in mind.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a big junior season as Campbell’s Friday night starter, Keuhler was selected by the Braves with the No. 70 pick in the 2023 Draft, making him the third of three college pitchers the organization took to kick off their class. He was off to a solid start to his first full season, with Single-A Augusta, albeit without missing many bats. But after one start with High-A Rome, he was shut down and needed Tommy John surgery in July, so he’s likely out until the 2026 season. While he’s undersized at 6-foot, Kuehler has more than enough options in his repertoire. His fastball had been up to 98 mph in college, with excellent spin rates and carry, and while he was more 91-93 mph in 2024, the damaged elbow might have been the cause. He can mix in a two-seamer as well, and he backs up the fastballs with a mid-80s slider with depth that was plus pre-injury. He also throws a shorter, harder cutter and an above-average low-80s curve, and he’s toyed with both a splitter and a more traditional changeup. Kuehler’s size, short arm action and high three-quarters slot create deception, but he hasn’t always shown the ability to repeat it, leading to issues finding the strike zone. That combined with the elbow surgery may have some thinking he’s destined for a bullpen role, but he’ll have to get healthy before moving in any direction on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Campbell’s reputation for generating draftable talent has taken a large step forward over the past several years, starting with Seth Johnson going No. 40 overall to the Rays in 2019, followed by 2022 first-rounder Zach Neto and sandwich pick Thomas Harrington. Kuehler extended the run by landing No. 70 overall to the Braves in 2023 after pitching for the U.S. Collegiate National Team in the summer of 2022 and having a huge junior year as the Fighting Camels’ Friday night starter. He tossed seven shutout innings over two appearances during his brief pro debut with full-season Augusta. Kuehler can throw as many as seven pitches depending on when you see him. His four-seam fastball, which averaged 94 mph in 2023 and topped out at 98 mph, has plus spin rates and carry, and he’ll mix in some two-seamers as well. His mid-80s slider has depth that misses bats and he can manipulate it into a shorter, harder cutter. He has an above-average low-80s curve, a traditional low-80s changeup with fade and a mid-80s splitter/changeup, though he leaned on the fastballs and breaking balls mostly at Campbell. The six-foot right-hander can get hit at times when he’s not commanding his arsenal consistently. There’s deception stemming from his short arm action and high three-quarters slot, but he hasn’t always been able to repeat his delivery to throw strikes. Working from the stretch during his pro debut seemed to help, but he’ll have to prove he can find the zone enough to remain a starter as he moves up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ziehl turned down the Cubs as an 11th-rounder out of a New York high school in order to attend Miami, where he was the Hurricanes' best starter as a sophomore and junior. A Yankees fourth-rounder in 2024, he made his pro debut last year and logged a 4.12 ERA with a 90/19 K/BB ratio in 107 innings, mostly in Single-A and High-A. He already has changed organizations twice, going to the White Sox last July in exchange for Austin Slater and to the Red Sox in February as part of a Jordan Hicks salary dump. Ziehl's fastball got rocked last year, sitting at 91-94 mph and topping out at 96 with modest ride and run.
