He used his heater less than his sweeping mid-80s slider, which shows flashes of becoming at least a solid pitch, and an upper-80s cutter that's more ordinary. He pounds the zone with all three of those offerings but has less success controlling a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks. Though Ziehl had below-average swing-and-miss rates on all of his pitches last year, he can get chases with them. Considering his ability to fill the strike zone with ease, Boston might have something if it can help him improve his velocity. He's a tough competitor with a high floor but a current ceiling of no more than an end-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Cubs 11th-round pick in 2021 as a New York high schooler, Ziehl put his pro career on hold to attend Miami. He led the Hurricanes in appearances as a freshman, then became their best starter during the next two seasons before the Yankees took him in 2024's fourth round. He already has been traded twice, going to the White Sox last July in exchange for Austin Slater, then to the Red Sox along with a player to be named for Jordan Hicks, righty pitching prospect David Sandlin and two players to be named in February. Ziehl's ability to command his fastball stands out much more than its velocity and life, as it operates at 92-94 mph and reaches 96 with modest ride and run. He misses more bats with a sweeping mid-80s slider that grades as a plus pitch with two-plane depth at its best, and he used his slide piece and an upper-80s cutter more than his heater during his 2025 pro debut. He imparts fade and sink on a mid-80s changeup but has difficulty keeping it in the zone. At 6 feet and 223 pounds, Ziehl is compact but strong and durable. He's a tough competitor who repeats his high three-quarters delivery with ease, enabling him to rank seventh in the Minors last year (minimum: 100 innings) with a 4 percent walk rate. He comes with a high floor but his inability to keep hitters off his fastball limits his ceiling to back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $1.5 million signing by the Cubs in July 2019, Made skipped over complex-level ball completely with an assignment to Single-A Myrtle Beach in 2021 after the pandemic-canceled season. He was in the midst of a second season at High-A South Bend in 2023 when the Nationals acquired him in a three-player deal for Jeimer Candelario that also brought over DJ Herz. Made finished out the year in Wilmington and returned to the South Atlantic League for 2024, hitting .239/.353/.327 with one homer and a 103 wRC+ over 72 games. He was promoted to Double-A Harrisburg in early July but batted just .158 in 21 games there (albeit with a low .204 BABIP). Made was passed over for the 40-man roster when he was Rule 5-eligible in both 2023 and 2024 because of his distance from the bigs and overall questions about his bat. A right-handed hitter, he showed decent contact and chase rates in his High-A repeat but started to fan more against quality breaking stuff in Double-A. He’s generally been good at taking his walks, and even that started to dwindle with Harrisburg, though it’s still an early small sample. The Nationals had hoped he would add strength to bring closer to average power, but that hasn’t come to fruition yet. Made can fly open at times in his swing, thereby cutting on top of pitches and leading to heavy groundball rates. The Dominican Republic native is just an average runner, but his saving grace is on the defensive side. He plays a strong shortstop with a good first step and impressive reactions at hands, and his arm strength gives him another weapon. Made has a fallback as a utility infielder with that glovework, but he needs the bat to come around in his age-22 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Made signed with the Cubs for $1.5 million in 2019, and even after he missed out on a potential first full season because of the pandemic, Chicago got aggressive with the shortstop with a move to Single-A at 18 years old in '21. He returned to the level a year later and had his best offensive showing anywhere with a .266/.354/.450 line and nine homers in only 57 games for Myrtle Beach. He hit only .162 over 37 games after a midseason promotion to High-A, returned to the Midwest League in 2023 and was still slashing just .240/.328/.355 in 70 games when Chicago moved him to the Nationals in a three-player deal for Jeimer Candelario at last year’s Trade Deadline. He slashed just .137/.232/.192 after the swap, though he was hurt by a .182 BABIP. The Dominican Republic native has needed to be graded on a curve throughout his career because of the aggression of his assignments. On the optimistic side, he has developed a better approach at the plate and has produced solid contact rates. On the pessimistic side, it’s still gap power at best, and while the plurality of his batted balls are on the ground, even those he does elevate aren’t big threats to leave the park yet. The Nats are hopeful added strength will lead to better exit velocities and bat speed in his age-21 season and beyond. Made has the first step, reactions and hands to remain at shortstop, and his plus arm would certainly play at third, where the Cubs gave him some run. He could also slide over to second without issue. Made could be a future utilityman with that glove, but offensive work remains to get him there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Made signed for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2019, but the pandemic delayed his debut until 2021. Chicago's logjam of young shortstops resulted in them aggressively assigning him to Single-A at age 18 for his introduction to pro ball and pushing him to High-A at age 19 in mid-2022. The Cubs sent Made back to High-A for 2023, and he was roughly a league-average bat before being moved to the Nationals in a Deadline deal for Jeimer Candelario. Made's quick right-handed swing and advanced bat-to-ball skills have helped him survive against much older and experienced competition. He has shown the ability to make adjustments as he has gotten acclimated to a level and his walk rate soared from 2 percent in his debut to 11 percent last year, a very encouraging sign. He has projectable strength and shows the ability to turn on pitches, so he could provide 15-20 homers per season once he begins driving the ball in the air more regularly. A solid runner but not much of a base stealer, Made could be a big league regular with just modest offensive production because he's a gifted defender. He has smooth actions and quality instincts at shortstop, where he covers ground to both sides and has a well-above-average arm. He could play almost anywhere on the diamond if he winds up in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chicago added to its collection of promising young shortstops when they signed Made for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2019. The pandemic shutdown delayed his pro debut until 2021, when their depth at his position led the Cubs to send him straight to Low-A at age 18. He held his own by batting .272 as the second-youngest regular in the Low-A East, but he played in just 58 games while dealing with forearm and hamstring strains. With his quick right-handed swing and advanced bat-to-ball skills, Made was able to survive against much older and experienced competition last year. He has some projectable strength and already shows a propensity for turning on pitches, so he could hit 15 or more homers per season once he's fully developed. To reach his offensive ceiling, he'll need to develop some plate discipline and improve his quality of contact after posting a 2 percent walk rate and hitting a lot of grounders in his debut. Because he played on the same club as 2020 first-rounder Ed Howard, Made also saw some action at third base last summer, but he's a no-doubt shortstop. He has the actions and instincts to make all the plays and throws at short with an arm that garners well-above-average grades from some scouts. He's presently a solid runner but could add some quickness as he matures physically.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chicago spent the bulk of its $5.1 million international bonus pool in 2019 on two players from MLB's Trainer Partnership Program in the Dominican Republic, giving $2.9 million to catcher Ronnier Quintero and $1.5 million to Made. Though the coronavirus pandemic put his pro debut on hold, Made began to add some muscle during the layoff and stood out with his increased ability to drive the ball during instructional league last fall. The Cubs have a wealth of young shortstop prospects and he rivals 2020 first-rounder Ed Howard as the best defender in that group. Made makes consistent line-drive contact to all fields with a quick right-handed swing. He has a more advanced approach and better feel for the barrel than most 18-year-olds. While he'll always be a hit-over-power guy, his hitting ability, bat speed and projectable strength should translate into 15 or more homers per season. Presently a solid runner, Made could have plus speed once he's fully developed physically. He has the actions and instincts to play a quality shortstop and his tools will enable him to play all over the diamond as needed. His arm earns well above-average grades from some evaluators and plays better than its pure strength because he gets rid of the ball quickly and with impressive accuracy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top player in the Angels’ 2023 international signing class, Morrobel received $900,000 to sign. Perceived to be one of the better shortstops in the class and ranked on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list, Morrobel had a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing and was off to a good start during his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League, but he hurt his shoulder diving for a ball and was shut down after just 15 games. A switch-hitter, Morrobel has an extreme hit-over-power profile from both sides of the plate. He makes a ton of contact with good barrel control, striking out in only nine percent of plate appearances in his brief career so far. He needs to add strength to his frame so he can impact the ball a little. He has just seven extra-base hits in 57 professional games entering 2025, and his flat swing has led to too much groundball contact. It does look like Morrobel will be able to stay at shortstop long term. The arm is now plus, and while he’s an average runner, he has good actions and instincts for the premium position. With a clean bill of health, he’ll play this season at age 19, and there's hope that there’s a little more juice in his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels have never been shy about spending on the international market, often bringing in high-end players with seven-figure bonuses, something they’ve done in six of he last seven signing periods. The one exception was in 2023, but it’s not like they took the year off. They inked Morrobel, a Top 50 prospect in that class according to MLB Pipeline, for $900,000, and then saw him have a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League. Since signing, Morrobel has made a ton of contact from both sides of the plate. He’s slightly better left-handed, but he puts the ball in play from both sides. He has very good barrel control and delivers professional at-bats. There’s no power to speak of yet, with a line-drive approach, but he’s starting to grow into his body and there could be some thump to come. He’s a very aggressive hitter who rarely strikes out, but he also doesn’t draw many walks. Morrobel is an average runner, maybe a tick above, and is able to steal a base. It looks like he’s going to be able to stick at shortstop, with excellent actions and instincts, footwork and a potentially plus arm in the future. There’s some projection here, and if he can impact the ball more, he could grow into a legitimate everyday shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever at Southern Miss and in the Cape Cod League, the 2022 sixth-rounder moved to a starting role in the Mets organization and took off quickly with a 2.20 ERA and 112 strikeouts in 110 2/3 innings between High-A and Double-A in his first full season. He was off to a solid start back in Binghamton to open 2024 when he was traded to the Nationals in late July in a one-for-one deal for outfielder Jesse Winker. He split his remaining eight starts between Double-A Harrisburg and Triple-A Rochester, stumbling a bit with a 7.56 ERA at the Minors’ top level. At 6-foot-9, Stuart will be one of the Majors’ tallest pitchers immediately upon arrival; only Bailey Ober and Sean Hjelle were that height or taller in 2024. But he doesn’t stand out for his physical presence on the bump so much as he does for his special breaking stuff. Stuart twirls an 82-85 mph slider with good two-plane break. He commands the pitch well in spite of the movement, and the slider got a 41 percent whiff rate across all levels in 2024. He’ll use it like a primary pitch at times. That’s a sensible move considering his 93-95 mph sinker is more prone to be hit hard when it catches too much of the zone. There’s also an 85-87 mph changeup and harder 89-91 mph cutter to play with. Stuart’s walk rate climbed to 13.2 percent during his four-start stay in Triple-A, but the control has been at least average at every spot. Despite his large frame, it can look like he’s playing catch with the backstop. Stuart battled elbow issues for much of 2025, making only 10 appearances (nine starts) across three levels, before undergoing Tommy John surgery that will knock him out for much (if not all) of 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stuart worked mostly as a reliever at Southern Miss and in the Cape Cod League, but after his selection in the sixth round in 2022, the Mets transitioned him to starter -- and a statistically impressive one at that. The right-hander led full-season Minor League qualifiers with a 2.20 ERA and ranked 12th among the 183 on that list with his 1.10 WHIP over 110 2/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. That said, his numbers at the higher level were closer to pedestrian (3.60 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 19.3 percent K rate) as he faced more advanced bats. He was a solid starter back at Binghamton in 2024 and was dealt to the Nationals in late July in a straight-up swap for outfielder Jesse Winker. Standing 6-foot-9 (yes, 6-foot-9), Stuart tends to start with his low-80s slider, which he threw roughly half the time in 2023, and for good reason. The pitch can show good two-plane break and sweep, leading to above-average whiff rates especially when it’s located on the edges of the zone. But it can hang in the zone at other times and get thumped. His 91-94 mph fastball shows sink and run in the other direction and can be tough to square up from his low three-quarters arm slot, giving him two potentially above-average pitches. Stuart’s changeup remains a distant third option. Stuart didn’t walk more than 7.6 percent of his batters faced at either level in 2023, and he fills the zone better than expected for someone his size. That control is one reason why the Mets wanted to give him starting looks in the pros, but he needs a more well-rounded arsenal to lock in that status. He’ll continue that work at the upper levels of the Washington system with his sights set on a potential debut next spring.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds had the No. 7 overall pick and a Competitive Balance Round A pick heading into the 2023 Draft, giving them the sixth largest bonus pool, and they weren’t afraid to spread the money around. They went almost three times over slot in the fourth round to sign Schoenwetter away from his commitment to his hometown Santa Barbara Gauchos. It took a while for the Reds to see what they had on their hands as he headed straight into rehab mode in order to build shoulder strength after the Draft, eventually making his debut in the Arizona Complex League. Numbers aside, the Reds were thrilled he was able to make 18 healthy appearances and spend some time with full-season Daytona at the end of the year. This will be the first year Schoenwetter should be able to show if he can start reaching his potential. He does have three excellent pitches in his arsenal, with a fastball that sat 92-95 mph last year, playing up with good spin rates up in the zone. He has more of a true, hard power curve, thrown anywhere in the 78-84 mph range with good depth, and his 84-87 mph changeup features good fade and he sells it well with arm speed. All three offerings might grade out as average right now, but all three could be plus in time as he physically matures and gets more reps. He struggled a bit finding the zone during his debut, but that might have been the time away from competition as much as it was anything with his delivery, which does have a little effort to it at times. He still has the chance to develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schoenwetter made a name for himself on the summer showcase circuit in 2022, standing out on a national stage at the Perfect Game All-American Classic. A solid senior season at his Santa Barbara-based high school put him in top two round conversations based on talent, but there was a commitment to stay home and go to UC Santa Barbara to contend with. The Reds, by virtue of having the No. 7 overall pick and a Competitive Balance Round A selection, had one of the larger bonus pools in baseball and were able to snag the athletic right-hander in the fourth round by giving him $1.9 million to sign. A prototypical projectable prep pitcher, Schoenwetter enters pro ball with the foundations of an exciting three-pitch mix. His fastball currently sits in the low-90s, but not only could there be more in the tank, it already plays up because he throws it with high spin rates and misses a ton of bats up in the zone. He uses a spike curve to get swings-and-misses as well, typically thrown in the mid-70s with hard, downer depth to it. His fading changeup, thrown with excellent arm speed, is a third at least above-average offering. As the 6-foot-3 Schoenwetter adds strength to his frame, he should be able to continue to repeat his delivery -- which does have some effort at times -- and find the strike zone consistently. There are always things high school arms need to improve as they begin the climb, and if Schoenwetter can maintain his stuff and stay on top of his breaking ball consistently, he has the chance to grow into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because of his acumen behind the plate, Flores has been aggressively pushed by the Angels since they signed him for $280,000 at the start of the 2023 international period. After his debut in the Dominican Summer League, he advanced from the Arizona Complex League to full-season ball during his first year in the States. In 2025, he got pushed up to High-A and struggled on both sides of the ball over the first half of the season, but he played much better baseball in the second half, then performed well as one of the younger players in the Arizona Fall League. Flores is likely always going to be known for his work behind the dish ahead of what he does at it. This spring was his third big league camp in a row because he really knows how to handle pitchers. He’s a plus receiver who blocks well and already shows advanced game-calling skills. His plus arm wasn’t quite as effective as controlling the running game in 2025, but he gets rid of the ball and down to second base in a hurry. Flores was completely lost as a hitter over the first half of the season and was hitting just .158 with a .480 OPS and 46 wRC+ through June as he lost the strike zone completely while he tried to sell out for power. He still needs to refine his approach -- his strikeout rate in the second half remained high -- but he posted a .780 OPS and 113 wRC+, getting to his power more organically with eight of his 10 homers coming from July 1 on. His glove should get him to the big leagues. If he can replicate what he did at the plate in the second half, he could be a defense-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better defenders behind the dish in the 2023 international signing class, Flores received a $280,000 bonus to sign when the period opened that January. So far, he’s moved more rapidly up the ladder than shortstop Felix Morrobel, the top of the Angels’ crop that winter. Flores' ability behind the plate will enable him to keep advancing and he’s shown a little more acumen that could make him an even better prospect than expected. Compact and strong, Flores has shown some ability to drive the ball from the right side. He bested expectations with the bat in full-season ball to start off the 2024 season after skipping over the Arizona Complex League. He’s too aggressive at the plate and can chase too much, especially softer stuff, though he can punish a fastball. What pop he has shown has been to his pull side, and with too high of a ground-ball rate, he could stand to find ways to leverage the ball more in the air. The Angels have felt comfortable moving Flores aggressively and inviting him to big league camp in Spring Training two years in a row -- even though he just turned 19 in February -- because of his defense. His strong arm has thrown out 40 percent of potential basestealers in his pro career to date. He’s turning into an excellent receiver who blocks and calls the game well, looking like he’s going to be a plus overall defender with that plus arm and plus instincts. If he can get his bat close to average, he has the chance to be a standout regular in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Flores drew attention from scouts in Venezuela because of his advanced skills behind the plate. That’s a big reason why the Angels gave him $280,000 to sign at the start of the 2023 international signing period. He made his debut in the Dominican Summer League and showed that word of his defensive acumen was not greatly exaggerated, while he also shook off a slow offensive start to provide a little more with the bat than anticipated. Flores’ calling card will always be his glove work. The skills are there for him to perhaps be a plus receiver in the future and he already has a plus arm, one that threw out 53.1 percent of potential basestealers in the DSL during his debut. The Angels thought so highly of his work behind the dish they thought he’d be able to handle higher-level arms and invited him to big league camp this spring.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best college athlete in the 2019 Draft, Bishop went 10th overall to San Francisco, signed for a below-slot $4.1 million and had a solid pro debut. But he barely played in the next two years because the pandemic wiped out the Minor League season in 2020, when he came down with COVID-19 during Summer Camp, and he strained his right (throwing) shoulder in his third game of 2021, limiting him to just 16 contests. He's the younger brother of big league outfielder Braden Bishop, who spent most of last season at the Giants' Triple-A Sacramento affiliate. Bishop's bat speed, strength and the loft in his left-handed swing produce well above-average raw power that plays to any part of the ballpark, but he has yet to show that he can make enough contact or stay healthy enough to take advantage of his pop. He always has come with swing-and-miss concerns, and they've worsened in 2022 as he's gotten more aggressive and pull-happy. He also missed another month of needed at-bats with an oblique injury. A wide receiver who originally committed to play football as a recruited walk-on at Washington before deciding to concentrate on baseball at Arizona State, Bishop has plus speed and at least 25-25 upside. He's still learning to make the most of his quickness as a basestealer and a center fielder, and his inactivity hasn't helped. He should be at least a solid defender in center, where his fringy arm is playable and accurate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A wide receiver who originally committed to play football as a preferred walk-on at Washington, Bishop changed his mind and opted to play baseball at Arizona State. The younger brother of Giants Triple-A outfielder Braden Bishop exploded as a junior in 2019, batting .342/.479/.748 with 22 homers and 12 steals in 57 games, which prompted the Giants to draft him 10th overall and sign him for a below-slot $4.1 million. He recorded an .867 OPS in his pro debut, participated at San Francisco's alternate training site and in instructional league last year and missed most of the first three months this season with a right shoulder injury. Bishop had some of the best raw power in the 2019 Draft, with his bat speed, strength and the loft in his left-handed stroke enabling him to crush the ball out of any part of the ballpark. He did a better job of translating his pop into production once he settled down his approach, worked deeper counts and began using the opposite field, but he still comes with swing-and-miss concerns. He struck out in 27 percent of his plate appearances during his debut, though he also had an encouraging walk rate of 26 percent. Add in plus speed that he's still learning how to get the most out of on the bases, and Bishop has 30-30 potential. After playing the corners during his first two college season, he took quickly to center field in 2019 and should be at least a solid defender there. His arm is fringy to average but he makes accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two members of the Reds’ college-heavy 2021 Draft class have already made significant first impressions in the big leagues, with Matt McLain and Andrew Abbott turning in strong rookie seasons in 2023. Allen was the only high schooler taken in that class, signing for $2.4 million, selected with the compensation pick for losing Trevor Bauer to the Dodgers via free agency. After an excellent debut in the Arizona Complex League that summer, Allen has had trouble staying healthy and gaining any traction, missing time in 2022 with an oblique issue and a bulk of the 2023 season with a thumb injury suffered very early on. Because Allen split his focus among three sports in high school, there was an understanding that it might take time for his baseball skills to come to the forefront, so the fact he’s missed so much development time has been particularly unfortunate. He probably needs a mulligan for his at-bats last year because he likely wasn’t at full strength even when he came off the injured list. He seems to still be growing and filling out, so there could be some raw power for him to tap into if he can get into a groove. There’s some strike zone judgement as well, with decent walk rates, but there’s also been a lot of swing-and-miss. Allen’s plus speed makes him a legitimate basestealing threat and he can cover a ton of ground in center field. The goal is to try and keep the right-handed-hitting outfielder on the field for an entire season to see if he can start moving towards his very high ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds were super college heavy in the 2021 Draft, making all but one of their 22 selections from the college or junior college ranks. The one exception was Allen, a three-sport prep star from Florida who was taken No. 30 overall and signed away from his commitment to the University of Florida. He missed some time in his first full season with a minor oblique issue, but while he had mixed results at the plate, the Reds gave the chance to see how his athleticism would play up a level in High-A at the end of the year. Allen has good bat speed from the right side of the plate and a line-drive approach. He didn’t impact the ball as much as some had hoped, though there is raw power to tap into if he can continue to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame. He has a feel for the strike zone and drew a good amount of walks in 2022. His speed is a huge offensive asset, and he finished fifth in the Single-A Florida State League in steals even though he played in just 73 games there before his promotion. That speed also serves him well in center field where he can really go get the ball and has the chance to stay there long-term. Like with many multi-sport athletes, there’s a ton of unlocked potential here, with the full-time baseball reps he’s now getting sure to help him turn his plus athleticism into performance more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Allen was a three-sport star at his high school on the east coast of Florida, one who was a good enough football player to get college interest in that sport as well. He was committed to go to the University of Florida for baseball only, but the Reds liked his athleticism and overall tools enough to use the compensation pick they got for losing Trevor Bauer to the Dodgers via free agency to select him and sign him for just shy of $2.4 million before watching him make a very strong first impression in a brief pro debut in the Arizona Complex League. Allen is capable of doing a lot of things well on the baseball field with a chance to impact the game on both sides of the ball. He has the chance to be at least an average hitter, with a simple setup and good bat speed. Especially given how his focus was divided among three sports, he showed an advanced approach at the plate and feel to hit during his debut, making consistently hard contact from the right side of the plate. He’s sure to get to more power as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. He runs well, occasionally with plus run times, and showed in the ACL he isn’t afraid to steal a base. After playing center field in high school and during his pro debut, Allen does have the chance to stay up-the-middle, and the Reds believe he can stay there long-term, though some amateur scouts thought he’d be better suited for a corner in the future. He has the chance to be an everyday regular somewhere in a big league outfield if it continues to click.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wallace had an eventful two years at Arkansas, tying the school’s freshman homer record with 14 in 2021 and then helping the Razorbacks reach the College World Series a year later. He was Draft-eligible as a sophomore and went to the Royals in the second round in 2022. He reached Double-A Northwest Arkansas in his first full season and returned to the level to begin 2024, only to suffer a right oblique strain in late May. While rehabbing in Arizona, he suffered a broken rib on a hit-by-pitch and was traded to the Nationals eight days later as part of the return for Hunter Harvey. Wallace got in 11 games with Double-A Harrisburg and three more in the Arizona Fall League before being shut down with a back issue. All of the injuries made Wallace a difficult evaluation in 2024, though the main tenets of his profile remain true. His feel for the barrel from the right side helps him the ball to all fields, and there’s above-average raw power here that could make him a threat to hit 15-plus homers at peak. He chased too much against all pitch types during his Double-A looks last season and especially struggled to lay off (and make contact with) low-and-away sliders. Honing in that approach may be as simple as getting consistent at-bats again. The Royals were impressed by Wallace’s defensive gains before the trade, and the Nationals have come away from their early looks believing he won’t have any trouble handling the position for any club. His arm strength certainly fits there, and he has the accuracy to hit the target on a line. There’s everyday potential here at the hot corner, but Wallace will need the bat to catch up to the glove to reach that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wallace made an immediate impact at Arkansas when he tied the school's freshman home run record (14) for his home state Razorbacks. He led Arkansas to the College World Series as a Draft-eligible sophomore, and then the Royals took him in the second round of the 2022 Draft while giving him a $1.7 million signing bonus. In his first full pro season, the 22-year-old had a strong start in High-A before a late-season bump to Double-A. His performance dipped slightly at the higher level, but he slashed .254/.331/.414 over 130 games total in 2023, with 27 doubles, seven triples, 13 homers and 84 RBIs. Wallace was dealt to the Nats in July in a deal for Hunter Harvey. Wallace goes to the plate with a calm demeanor and simple mechanics, in addition to a compact and efficient right-handed swing. He has a true feel for the barrel and has power potential to all fields, although he struggled with breaking balls in 2023 and could have gotten pull-happy in an attempt to create more power. He projects as more of a gap-to-gap hitter than a home run hitter, but as he adds strength, he might tap into that above-average raw power. More than anything in 2023, Wallace showed he could handle the hot corner. He’s a natural third baseman with a strong, plus arm. His throws are accurate with good carry -- even the balls he fielded close to the line made it across the diamond with plenty of zip. Wallace has solid baserunning skills to help his average speed, which will lead to more stolen bases. Wallace, who has dealt with an oblique injury and broken rib after the trade, is now in an organization with other third-base options in Brady House and Yohandy Morales, but he has the well-rounded profile to carve out his own role in DC.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going undrafted in 2020 because of his commitment, Wallace made an immediate impact at Arkansas when he tied the freshman home run record (14) held by former first-round picks Zack Cox and Heston Kjerstad. After he led Arkansas to the College World Series, the Royals made Wallace, the Draft-eligible sophomore, their second-round pick and gave him a $1.7 million bonus. He made his pro debut last summer with three games in the Arizona Complex League before moving up to Single-A Columbia. There, he slashed .293/.379/.466 with two homers. Wallace has a compact and efficient right-handed swing with a traditional setup, and he has a true feel for the barrel. He generates impressive exit velocities and easy power with his bat speed and strength. Big and broad-shouldered, most of his power right now comes from the pull side, but he’s flashed the ability to go the other way. A point of emphasis will be his swing decisions and recognizing the pitches he can do damage with to let that power play. He has a strong arm and good instincts, impressing the Royals in the fall with his third-base defense. Wallace is about an average runner but will be able to steal bases. Wallace played a lot of outfield in college, but the Royals see him as a third baseman for the foreseeable future. As long as he makes the proper adjustments with his approach, Wallace should move quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Though he could have turned pro as early as January 2021, Burrowes waited until he nearly completed high school in Panama before signing for $75,000 in April 2022, and he returned home after his pro debut that summer to finish his degree. He broke his hand when hit by a pitch during Spring Training in 2024, which led to a disappointing first foray into full-season ball. He rebounded last year and also improved his effort level, earning a promotion to High-A at age 20. Burrowes has a quick right-handed stroke, makes reasonable swing decisions and hits the ball hard for his age. He does damage against fastballs and consistently turns on pitches, with most of his power playing to left field. He chases too many breaking balls and changeups and struggles to put them in play, so he'll have to make adjustments. Burrowes has plus speed and is an aggressive baserunner who stole 47 bases in 53 attempts (88.6 percent) last year. After spending most of his first two seasons in the United States at shortstop, where the game sped up on him, he looked more comfortable at second and third base in 2025. He has solid arm strength and also has seen action in left and center field. He could fill a super-utility role if he can become a more reliable hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was eligible to turn pro in January 2021, Burrowes waited to nearly finish high school in Panama before signing for $75,000 in April 2022. He attracted immediate attention when he made his pro debut two months later in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, with other clubs asking for him in trade talks. He completed his high school degree that fall before coming to the United States and hitting .259/.330/.386 in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last summer. Burrowes already produces impressive exit velocities for a teenagers and has the room to add a lot of muscle to his wiry 6-foot-2 frame. He has a sound right-handed swing with bat speed but is still a work in progress offensively. He was overly aggressive in his U.S. debut and wasn't able to turn on pitches consistently. Burrowes owns plus speed and likes to make things happen on the bases. His quickness gives him range at shortstop, where he displays solid arm strength but also a tendency to get flashy. An organization favorite, he's bilingual and stands out with his intelligence and leadership.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Eligible to sign in January 2021, Burrowes waited until he had nearly finished high school in Panama before turning pro for $75,000 last April. He made his pro debut two months later and immediately stood out in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, prompting other clubs to ask for him in trade talks. He returned home in the fall to complete his high school degree and will make his highly anticipated U.S. debut in 2023. Burrows' advanced hitting ability and projectable 6-foot-2 frame give him one of the highest offensive ceilings in the system. He recognizes pitches and manages the strike zone better than most teenagers, repeatedly barreling balls with a sound right-handed swing. He generates high exit velocities for someone so young and could develop at least 20-homer power as he gains strength and experience. A solid runner with good instincts on the bases, Burrowes went 12-for-12 stealing bases in the DSL but may slow a bit as he fills out. He has the athleticism and solid arm strength to possibly stick at shortstop, and if he outgrows the position, he'd profile well at third base. He's bilingual and draws praise for his intelligence and charisma in addition to his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lin is an international star back home in Taiwan, having stood out for Chinese Taipei at the 2021 U-23 World Cup before signing with the D-backs for $525,000 that December and throwing four scoreless innings against Japan just this winter in the WBSC Premier12 gold-medal game at the Tokyo Dome. In between, he’s been a steady performer in the Arizona system. His 2024 campaign was put on pause when he suffered facial fractures on a foul ball hit to the Double-A Amarillo dugout, but he still managed a 4.28 ERA with 90 strikeouts in 94 2/3 innings in the Texas League before making one start for Triple-A Reno. Lin rounded out his stateside season with three Arizona Fall League starts before heading abroad for Premier12. The 5-foot-11 southpaw steps to the side and rocks a bit to begin his delivery out of the stretch with a little flair. He throws both a four-seamer and a sinker in the 90-92 mph range (occasionally touching 95-96). Without stellar velocity, he needs the different movement profiles to keep hitters off balance. He also has to locate the pitches well, because when he doesn’t, they can be crushed. But the depth of the arsenal reveals more promising offerings, like an 80-82 mph changeup that fades well off the heat and a mid-70s curveball. Both are options against righties, while a 79-82 mph sweeper is his go-to secondary against lefties. Both breaking balls play with extreme spin with the curve, in particular, averaging above 3,000 rpm at Triple-A Reno in 2025. Lin has also worked on incorporating an upper-80s cutter to keep hitters guessing further. He needs to live on the edges of the zone if he’s going to achieve whiffs because he can’t blow pitches by batters. His four-seamer has been particularly crushed in the Pacific Coast League. Lin’s outing against Japan showed he doesn’t back down from challenges, though, and he has enough offerings to make it work as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 60 | Cutter: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 A standout performance at the 2021 U-23 World Cup for Chinese Taipei, along with his previous international experience, helped Lin sign with the D-backs for $525,000 in December of that year. He’s been dominant at virtually every level since and pitched his age-19 season at High-A and Double-A, finishing with a 3.86 ERA and an organization-best 140 strikeouts in 121 1/3 innings. Considering Amarillo is a hitter’s paradise, it was even more impressive that Lin posted a 3.89 ERA and 1.01 WHIP in six home starts (34 2/3 innings) for the Sod Poodles. Standing a mere 5-foot-11, Lin has one of the deepest and most interesting repertoires in the Minor Leagues. Rocking back in his throwing motion, he delivers a fastball that typically only sits in the 88-92 mph range. That said, the pitch has good ride up in the zone, making it play better than the velo alone, and he touched 94 at Double-A. D-backs officials believe the southpaw has added strength in the offseason, and even if he isn’t pumping mid-90s, a little more heat would go a long way. That’s because his secondaries are so impressive. A low-80s changeup shows tremendous fade and got a 49 percent whiff rate at Double-A. A 75-77 mph curveball is tough for hitters to track with its spin and vertical drop, while a low-80s slider glides more horizontally. He’s added a mid-80s cutter for a harder breaking ball as well. The Taiwanese left-hander got good chase rates on the changeup and cutter specifically, and while he spots the ball well, it’s worth wondering what happens when hitters lay off the low cambio. Still, the results at a young age, quality of stuff and early durability all give Lin mid-rotation upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lin’s ample international experience with Chinese Taipei certainly put him on the map, but his performance in the 2021 U-23 World Cup sealed his fate as a potential pro pitcher stateside. The southpaw led his country with 14 strikeouts over 8 2/3 innings against the likes of Cuba and Venezuela, all while just 18 years old. The D-backs signed Lin for $525,000 in December 2021 and he fanned 91 batters over 56 1/3 innings between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Visalia. His 40.3 percent K rate was sixth-best among the 1,343 Minor Leaguers with at least 50 frames in 2022, three spots behind Tink Hence (41.5) in a similar sample size. The 5-foot-11 left-hander is all about movement on the mound from the leg kick in his delivery to the profile of his pitching repertoire. His fastball is only around 89-92 mph, but there’s room for more velo if he adds strength, as Arizona expects him to do. The D-backs believed his vertically breaking curveball to be his best pitch entering the system, but his hard slider proved to be its equal in quality. Now his best offering looks to be a diving changeup with armside movement that makes hitters look silly. Driving home the kitchen-sink feel, Lin can add in a splitter and screwball-like pitch to keep hitters guessing. All that movement caught up to the lefty a bit in the California League, where he averaged a walk roughly once every two innings, but he still projects for average control. While Lin sends many low-level batters back to the dugout shaking their heads, his lack of velocity might catch up to him the higher he climbs. If he adjusts as he ages, he has at least mid-rotation upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Jaworsky impressed with his athleticism at the 2023 MLB Draft Combine, the Astros spent a fifth-round pick and an over-slot $847,500 bonus to lure the Colorado prepster away from a commitment to Utah Valley State. His top priority was to add muscle to his skinny 6-foot-1 frame and he has added about 15 pounds since turning pro. He showed steady improvement as a 19-year-old in Single-A last year and made the jump to High-A in 2025 before Houston sent him to the Marlins in a trade for Jesus Sanchez in July. A left-handed hitter, Jaworsky has good bat-to-ball skills but needs to improve his selectivity while continuing to gain strength. While he shows the ability to make adjustments and uses the entire field well, he currently makes a lot of soft groundball contact. Added physical development could result in 12-15 homers per year, though he'll always be a hit-over-power guy. Jaworsky's most obvious tool is his plus speed, which he used to steal 28 bases in 78 games last season. He has nice actions and range to both sides at shortstop, though there are questions as to whether his average arm will be enough to remain at the position. His quick release and good internal clock will help him, but some scouts think second base and center field are more realistic destinations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fellow shortstop Walker Martin (second round, Giants) claimed most of the high school scouting spotlight in Colorado last spring, but Jaworsky also went in the fifth round to the Astros, giving the Centennial State two prep position players drafted that early for the first time. Jaworsky, who impressed with his athleticism at the MLB Draft Combine, signed for an over-slot $847,500 to forego a commitment to Utah Valley State. His pro debut consisted of nine games in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. Though there were mixed amateur reports on Jaworsky's offensive upside, Houston likes his approach and believes he'll make consistent contact. He focuses on hitting the ball from gap to gap and shows the ability to make adjustments at the plate. He has a left-handed swing with promising bat speed but won't drive the ball with much authority until he adds some much-needed strength. Jaworsky also comes with questions about his future defensive home. He does have plus speed but just average arm strength that he enhances with a quick release and good internal clock. The Astros will give him every chance to stick at shortstop, while other clubs thought that second base was more realistic and center field will be the most likely destination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the younger players and considered one of the most advanced hitters on the 2025 international market, Cedeno received the largest bonus in the Yankees' class. After signing for $2.5 million out of the Dominican Republic, he endured a rough pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. He batted .183/.371/.305 and led the Rookie circuit with 76 strikeouts in 47 games. For someone who struck out 37 percent of the time in his first taste of pro ball, Cedeno has a surprisingly compact right-handed swing and relatively good bat-to-ball skills. His problems last summer stemmed from an overly passive approach that put him behind in too many counts and an extremely pull-happy mentality that leaves him vulnerable to pitches on the outer half. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to reach 15-20 homers per season provided he can overhaul his approach. Cedeno has plus speed and knows how to use it, swiping 21 bases in 23 tries (91 percent) last summer. He has fast hands and solid arm strength at shortstop, though his quickness translates into just average range. It's possible that he'll fit better at second base in the long, which would put more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: San Pedro de Macoris in the Dominican Republic may have produced more All-Star infielders per capita than any other city, including Robinson Canó, Tony Fernandez, Pedro Guerrero, Alfonso Soriano and Fernando Tatis Jr. Cedeno has the tools to follow in that tradition after signing for $2.5 million in January. One of the youngest prospects and most advanced hitters in the 2025 international class, he'll play most of the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League schedule at age 16. Cedeno has a compact right-handed stroke and is balanced at the plate, but he has struggled to make contact during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League because he has gotten way too pull-happy. He has shown a willingness to draw walks but also has gotten too passive at times. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to provide 15-20 homers on an annual basis if he refines his approach. Cedeno's infield actions are as smooth as his swing. His speed, shortstop range and arm strength all grade as solid and could get better as he physically develops. He uses his feet well at short and makes accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins' pick at No. 33 overall in the 2024 Draft out of Lousiana-Lafayette, DeBarge has a knack for stealing bases, something he did successfully 66 times during his first pro season. The rest of his offensive game was less consistent, but he also proved valuable by capably playing multiple positions as Cedar Rapids reached the High-A Midwest League championship series. During his huge junior season with the Ragin’ Cajuns, DeBarge had shown an advanced approach at the plate, a penchant for contact and a quick right-handed stroke with sneaky pop to his pull side that resulted in 21 homers. He still saw a lot of pitches and drew a ton of walks with Cedar Rapids in 2025, but his strikeout rate more than doubled compared to his last season in college, and the impact wasn’t present, with an inflated ground-ball rate. DeBarge is a 5-foot-9 sparkplug who isn’t just aggressive on the basepaths, he’s successful, going 66-for-74 in steal attempts in ‘25. He won a Minor League Gold Glove at second base, showed he can help out at shortstop occasionally and played a good center field, giving him a floor as a high-energy utility type. If he can get to a little more offensive impact, there’s still a chance he could be a regular presence in a lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If the Twins were trying to corner the market on college infielders who performed at the plate in the 2024 Draft, they did a very good job out of the gate, getting Kaelen Culpepper in the first round, Billy Amick in Round 2 and DeBarge right between them. The Lousiana-Lafayette standout had been a catcher at Barbe High School in Louisiana before moving to short and parlayed a huge junior season for the Ragin’ Cajuns (1.117 OPS) into being the No. 33 overall pick in the Draft. He got his professional feet wet with just over 100 at-bats with Single-A Fort Myers after signing. The Twin were clearly coveting advanced hitters with an idea of what they’re doing at the plate and DeBarge, like Culpepper, typically does a fantastic job at making a ton of contact without chasing out of the zone. He has a quick right-handed stroke with some sneaky pop to his pull side, but he does tend to hit a lot of ground balls with a flatter swing, something that happened more when perhaps he was pressing a bit during his brief pro debut. There’s confidence he’ll be able to rediscover his knack for finding the barrel and driving the ball without sacrificing his approach. An impressive athlete with plus speed, DeBarge should be able to steal bags as a pro. That quickness along with excellent hands, good instincts and a strong arm give him all the tools to play shortstop, but the Twins are eager to continue seeing how he looks at second, third and perhaps even in center field to expand his paths to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fox's father Blane reached Double-A as an outfielder and coached his son and Lakeland Christian HS to Florida's state 3-A championship in 2019. The Guardians selected Jake in the third round of the 2021 Draft and signed him away from a Florida commitment for an over-slot $850,000. He started slowly while dealing with an elbow injury in High-A last season but rallied to bat .288/.355/.443 in the final two-plus months. With his whippy left-handed stroke and fine hand-eye coordination, Fox has the tools to hit for average. He projects as more of a tablesetter than a middle-of-the-order masher, though he didn't control the strike zone as well in 2023 as he had in the past. While he has added strength and bat speed since turning pro and has learned to turn on pitches and lift them in the air, he still hasn't developed much power and may top out at 12-15 homers per season. Fox combines plus speed with constant energy, though he was less aggressive on the bases last year and still is figuring out the nuances of basestealing. A prep shortstop who spent most of his first two pro seasons at second base, he became a full-time outfielder in 2023. His high baseball IQ helped him make the transition easily, and he displays solid range with average arm strength in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Many evaluators inside and outside the organization tab Fox as their pick to click among Cleveland prospects in 2023. His father, Blane, reached Double-A as an outfielder and coached him to Florida's state 3-A championship at Lakeland Christian HS in 2019. A third-rounder in the 2021 Draft who signed for an over-slot $850,000, Fox ranked sixth in the Single-A Carolina League with a .381 on-base percentage at age 19 in his full-season debut and also impressed by taking quickly to playing center field. Fox has a whippy left-handed swing and the hand-eye coordination to barrel balls on a regular basis. He recognizes pitches well and controls the strike zone, and he could be an on-base machine who fits near the top of the lineup. He has improved his strength and bat speed since turning pro, surprised the Guardians with his exit velocities in 2022 and could hit 12-15 homers per season with more added muscle. A plus runner with a nonstop motor, Fox stole bases at a 90 percent success rate in his first two seasons. A shortstop in high school, he has spent the majority of his pro career at second base, where he's a surehanded defender with an average arm. Cleveland's stockpile of infield prospects at the lower levels necessitated trying him in center field last year, and his high baseball IQ helped him look so natural there that center will be his primary position going forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fox's father Blane got to Double-A as an outfielder and coached his son Jake to a 2019 Florida state 3-A championship at Lakeland Christian High. Two years later, the Guardians drafted Jake in the third round and signed him away from a Florida commitment for an over-slot $850,000. He batted .405 with seven steals in 13 games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League and continued to impress in instructional league. Though Fox has a hitch in his left-handed stroke, it's a whippy swing with bat speed and his hand-eye coordination allows him to barrel balls consistently. His feel for hitting exceeds his power potential, though he did add some strength during the offseason. If he improves at turning on pitches and launching balls in the air, he could deliver 12-15 homers per season. With solid speed and a high baseball IQ, Fox can make things happen on the bases. A shortstop in high school, he divided his time between second base, short and third base in his brief debut. With his first-step quickness and average arm strength, he probably fits best at second base, and some scouts think he could wind up in center field after seeing extensive action there in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 60 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Knoth and Marcus Stroman share an alma mater in Long Island’s Patchogue-Medford HS, but it was the former that became the first player to sign straight out of the school when he joined the Brewers as the 33rd overall pick in 2023. Knoth, who was 17 on Draft Day, signed below slot for $2 million. He struck out 96 and posted a 4.48 ERA in 84 1/3 innings with Single-A Carolina in his first full season but underwent Tommy John surgery the following offseason. He missed all of 2025 as a result but was back to throwing in the leadup to his third Minor League campaign. Before going under the knife, Knoth showed a 91-95 mph four-seamer that he could blaze by Single-A hitters with impressive ride to the top of the zone. Both his upper-70s curveball and mid-80s slider looked like potential plus pitches with exceptional spin rates, though the latter was better at getting batters from both sides to expand the zone the way Knoth worked it down and glove side. His changeup was rarely used, but he was still more effective against lefties than righties for Carolina. After walking 11.1 percent of his batters faced in ’24, Knoth projects for fringy control, and that’s if the command holds up post-TJ. He’ll still only be 20 years for much of the ’26 season, and the stuff is intriguing enough to make him a breakout candidate if he can maintain the quality of the arsenal over a likely innings limit. Knoth’s upside remains in the middle of a future Milwaukee rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knoth shares a high school alma mater with Marcus Stroman in Patchogue-Medford HS on Long Island, N.Y. But after Stroman chose to head to Duke after going in the 2009 18th round, Knoth headed straight to pro ball, becoming the school’s first player to sign as the 33rd overall pick in the 2023 Draft. His bonus came in below slot at $2 million. Knoth posted a 4.48 ERA with 96 strikeouts in 84 1/3 innings for Single-A Carolina in his first full season but dealt with elbow issues in his second offseason, leading ultimately to Tommy John surgery that will knock him out for the 2025 season. A little undersized at 6-foot-1 but strong for his frame, Knoth sat 91-95 mph with his fastball in the Carolina League but got whiffs with the heater because of good ride up in the zone. His breaking balls remained potentially plus pitches with an upper-70s curveball and mid-80s slider -- both of which came in with impressively high spin rates. The slider was better at generating chase, especially with two strikes. Knoth didn’t use much of a changeup with Carolina but will need one the higher he climbs. Knoth walked 11.1 percent of his batters faced in 2024, and how his control returns from surgery will be worth following upon his return in 2026. That’ll still just be his age-20 season, so time is very much on his side here. But it’s far from an ideal pause in development for a young pitcher who still has significant upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knoth hails from Patchogue-Medford HS on Long Island, N.Y. -- the same program that produced Marcus Stroman before he headed to Duke -- and the similarly undersized right-hander did enough to seize scouts’ attentions despite hailing from a cold-weather state. The Brewers made him the first player selected directly from his school since 2013 when they took him 33rd overall in July and signed him for a below-slot $2 million bonus. Strong for his 6-foot-1 frame, Knoth gained some velocity in his senior spring and was touching the upper 90s, though he was typically a few ticks below that. The real eye-opener was his feel for spin. His 77-80 mph curveball was easily the best in his Draft class -- high school or college -- because of its 3,000+ rpm spin rates and sharp downward action. He also showed a low-80s slider with similar dizzying spin and more two-plane break, though the pair of breaking balls can bleed into one another. Knoth’s changeup wasn't needed much in school and could be a focus in the pros. Knoth has a solid history of finding the strike zone with a repeatable delivery, and his ability to get chase outside of the zone with his breaking pitches should help hold walks relatively at bay. Having only turned 18 in August, he’s very much a lump of clay who could be molded into a reliever if the changeup never comes around or a high-end starter if the stuff takes off further.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2020-21 international signing period was delayed from opening until January 2021 because of the pandemic, and that’s when the bulk of the signings occurred and were announced. The Angels weren’t quite done though, as nine months later, they signed Marcheco for $35,000. After tossing nine hitless innings in the Dominican Summer League in his brief debut, he came stateside in 2022 and pitched his way from the Arizona Complex League to full-season Inland Empire. He reached High-A over the course of the 2023 season, piling up 121 2/3 innings in the process. The 6-foot-1 right-hander’s success comes from a combination of pitchability and deception. His fastball has below-average velocity, typically sitting 88-89 mph and touching 91, but he hides the ball so well that hitters have not fared well against it; he threw the pitch 70 percent of the time. Both the slider and the changeup will flash average to give him a three-pitch mix that plays beyond its individual grades. Marcheco might have the best command in the organization and uses the funk in his delivery and his understanding of how to keep hitters off-balance to get outs. He did wear down a bit by the end of the year; added strength would help with that and could give him the chance to gain enough velocity to give him the chance to reach the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The delayed 2020-21 international signing period might always be known in the Angels organization for the addition of Denzer Guzman to the system. But nine months after inking Guzman for $2 million when the period opened on Jan. 15, 2021, they also signed Marcheco, giving the Cuban right-hander $35,000 that September to start his pro career. He recorded two short hitless outings at the end of the month in the Dominican Summer League, then threw well in his U.S. debut in 2022, finishing third in the Arizona Complex League in strikeouts with 76 and earning a late bump up to full-season ball. Marcheco’s success has stemmed more from his pitchability than his pure stuff. He has a three-pitch mix with a fastball that currently sits in the 90-92 mph range and plays well because he locates it in the strike zone. He backs it up with an average slider and has decent feel for a changeup. The 6-foot-1 right-hander already has the ability to set up hitters and mix his pitches well, throwing a ton of strikes with all three offerings. There’s some funk and deception in his delivery, a reason why he was able to strike out 13.1 per nine and hold hitters to a .216 average-against in 2022. Now he’ll get to see how his average-stuff profile plays over an entire full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez was the fifth-ranked prospect in the 2021 international class as a big-bodied shortstop with power potential and signed with the Cubs for $3 million. The Venezuela native has yet to tap into his natural power in pro ball with just 24 homers in 430 games, but he's made slow, steady progress and posted a 99 wRC+ in his first full season in High-A at 21 last year. The Marlins acquired him as part of the return for Edward Cabrera and will be tasked with unlocking his potential after the one-time bonus baby was not protected from or selected in the Rule 5 Draft over the winter. The 6-foot-2 righty swinger has a wiry frame and plenty of room to add strength. Hernandez has excellent bat speed which should enable upward of 20-homer thump. However, he has consistently hit the ball on the ground, which could prevent him from reaching that power potential. He took a more aggressive approach in 2025, especially on pitches in the zone, which helped him strike out less but also cut into his walks. But a longer swing and mediocre footwork continue to hold his hit tool back. Hernandez has long been an above-average runner and performed better on the bases every season, culminating in a career-high 52 swipes on 61 attempts in 2025. He uses that quickness on defense well, although his footwork again can be an issue at short. That might force him to second base, where he would be an above-average defender. He should have plenty of arm for any infield position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez generated as much hype as anyone in the 2020-21 international class, drawing physical comparisons to Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado, while some scouts rated him the best prospect available. Signed by the Cubs for $3 million out of the Dominican Republic, he fared well in his 2021 pro debut but struggled in his first two seasons in the United States. He fared better at two Class A stops in the past two years before Chicago shipped him and two other prospects to the Marlins in exchange for Edward Cabrera in January. Hernandez has some of the best bat speed in the system and could translate it into 20 homers per season as he continues to add strength and learns to lift balls in the air more consistently. A much more disciplined approach fueled his growth at the plate in 2024, as he chased less and did a better job of using the entire field. The next step will be improving his timing and shortening his right-handed stroke so he can catch up to quality fastballs. A solid runner with good instincts, Hernandez has stolen 98 bases in 117 attempts (83.8 percent) in 315 pro games. He has the quickness and arm strength to play at least an average shortstop, though like most youngsters he needs to improve his defensive consistency. He's more than capable at second base as well and has the tools for third base if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez elicited physical comparisons to Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado as an amateur in the Dominican Republic, with some scouts rating him as the best prospect in the 2020-21 international class. When the Cubs signed him for $3 million, they believed he had a higher ceiling than any international amateur they had landed in years. But he has struggled since a successful pro debut, slashing .223/.302/.301 with a 27 percent strikeout rate in Single-A last year. With his lightning-fast right-handed swing, it's still easy to dream about Hernandez providing 25 or more homers per season. But he hasn't been able to make much of his plus power yet because he still lacks strength and makes too much ground-ball contact. He needs a more selective approach that concentrates on making hard contact because his pop should come naturally if he lets it. Hernandez has solid speed and is aggressive on the bases, stealing 27 bases in 32 attempts last year. With his quickness and solid arm strength he should be able to stay at shortstop, though he shifted over to second base once Jefferson Rojas came to Myrtle Beach in June. He's a fine defender at second base, more average at shortstop and should be able to handle third if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some evaluators considered Hernandez the top prospect in the 2020 international crop, and he drew physical comparisons to Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado. The Cubs signed him for $3 million out of the Dominican Republic in January 2021 and believe he has more upside than any international amateur they've signed in more than a decade. He made his U.S. debut last year, slashing .261/.320/.357 with a 30 percent strikeout rate in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. With electric bat speed from the right side of the plate, Hernandez has 25-30 homer upside. He's not tapping into his power yet because he needs to add strength and drive balls in the air more regularly. He has yet to learn to let his pop come naturally rather than pulling too many pitches and chasing too many out of the strike zone. Hernandez possesses solid speed and plus arm strength, and he should retain enough quickness and range to remain at short. He has seen more time at second base this year in deference to Jefferson Rojas and looked good there. If Hernandez slows down more than expected as he matures physically, he could wind up at third base or the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez drew repeated physical comparisons to a young Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado as an amateur in the Dominican Republic, and some scouts considered him the best prospect in the 2020 international class. The Cubs signed him for $3 million in January 2021 and believe he has more upside than any international player they've landed in at least a decade -- including Willson Contreras, Eloy Jimenez and Gleyber Torres. He debuted in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League at age 17, batting .285/.398/.424 with five homers and 21 steals in 47 games. An extremely advanced hitter for his age, Hernandez has a smooth right-handed stroke with plenty of bat speed. He has good feel for the barrel and exhibits patience at the plate as well as a willingness to use the entire field. While he should have plus raw power once his projectable 6-foot-2 frame fills out, he'll have to make some swing adjustments to make the most of it after sporting a 2.0 ground/fly ratio in his debut. Hernandez is a plus runner who can make things happen on the bases, though he could lose a half-step as he gets stronger. Even so, he should still be athletic and quick enough to remain at shortstop, where he displays the requisite actions and instincts as well as a plus arm. He'd also profile well at third base and on the outfield corners if he slows down more than expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some scouts considered Hernandez the best prospect in the 2020 international class. The Cubs say he offers more upside than any international player they've signed in recent memory -- including Eloy Jimenez and Gleyber Torres in 2013. The recipient of a $3 million bonus out of the Dominican Republic, he draws constant physical comparisons to a young Alex Rodriguez and Manny Machado. Hernandez has the tools to hit for average and power and could become a .300 hitter with 30 homers on an annual basis if everything comes together. He has a fluid right-handed swing with quality bat speed and also exhibits feel for the barrel and a mature approach. He has a track record of producing in game action and his projectable frame should allow him to add plenty of strength. Hernandez presently has plus speed, though he might lose a half-step as he matures physically. Even if that happens, he has the athleticism and actions to remain at shortstop for the long term. His quickness and arm strength would allow him to play all over the field if needed and he'd have no problem fitting the offensive profile wherever he winds up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs quickly became enchanted by Valdez's bat when they began scouting him in the Dominican Republic, and they signed him for $2.8 million after he developed into one of the best prospects in the 2023 class. When he turned pro, Chicago vice president of international scouting Louie Eljaua said Valdez had the potential to grown into a Starlin Castro build with Hanley Ramirez production. He scuffled in his pro debut, however, batting .234/.328/.477 with a 41 percent strikeout rate in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. A right-handed hitter, Valdez has quick hands that produce plenty of bat speed and allow him to control the barrel well. He undermined himself in the DSL by chasing way too many pitches and trying to launch them as far as he could to his pull side. He does have plus raw power and could produce 20 or more homers per season, but he's going to have to significantly tone down his approach to survive against more advanced pitching. Valdez possesses solid speed but still has a lot to learn about basestealing. His instincts and actions should enable him to stick at shortstop, where he displays solid arm strength. If he loses some quickness as he gains strength, he should be able to handle second or third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs fell in love with Valdez's bat soon after seeing him in the Dominican Republic. He blossomed into one of the top prospects in the 2023 international class and signed with Chicago for $2.8 million in January. Cubs vice president of international scouting Louie Eljaua said Valdez could grow into a Starlin Castro build and provide Hanley Ramirez production. While he doesn't have the all-around upside of fellow Dominican shortstop Cristian Hernandez, who signed for $3 million two years earlier, Valdez does have more pure hitting ability. A right-handed hitter, he's very advanced at the plate with gifted hands that produce plenty of bat speed and enable him to manipulate the barrel well. He uses the entire field and focuses on driving the ball from gap to gap with the promise of at least average power once he matures physically. An average runner, Valdez has good instincts and actions at shortstop. He should be able to remain at the position, but if he slows a bit as he gets stronger, he should have enough quickness and the solid arm strength to handle either second or third base. If he reaches his ceiling, he'll profile well offensively at any position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Rangers for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022, Vargas topped the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 11 homers, 27 extra-base knocks and 112 total bases during his U.S. debut in 2023. He made the jump to full-season ball last year and put himself all over the Single-A Carolina League leaderboard with 178 total bases (first), 108 hits (second), 40 extra-base hits (second), a .454 slugging percentage (second) and 14 homers (fifth). He's the best of the three prospects the Marlins acquired in exchange for Jake Burger at the Winter Meetings in December. Though he's just 5-foot-11 and 170 pounds, Vargas hits the ball much harder than most players his size. He uses a big leg kick and an aggressive right-handed stroke to turn on pitches and launch them in the air, allowing him to get the most out of his solid raw power. He'll need to tone down his approach against more advanced pitching after his chase rate ballooned to 42 percent last year and he struggled against non-fastballs. Vargas has solid speed and good instincts on the bases, giving him 20-20 potential. He has solid arm strength as well but more average range at shortstop, where the game sped up on him at times in 2024 as he committed 27 errors in 86 contests. He fits better at second base, also can handle third base and profiles as a power-hitting utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vargas lacks size and signed with the Rangers for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022, he had made an outsized impact at the plate in his first two pro seasons. He debuted by posting an .878 OPS and ranking fourth in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 28 extra-base hits in 54 games, then came to United States last year and topped the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 11 homers, 27 extra-base knocks and 112 total bases. Following his successful transition to Single-A in 2024, the Marlins traded Jake Burger to acquire him, fellow middle-infield prospect Max Acosta and left-hander Brayan Mendoza at the Winter Meetings in December. A right-handed hitter, Vargas uses a big leg kick and aggressive hacks to hit the ball much harder than expected from a 5-foot-11, 170-pounder. He has an affinity for turning on pitches and driving them in the air, allowing him to squeeze nearly every drop out of his raw power and giving him 20-homer upside. He has the hand-eye coordination to make that approach work without compromising his timing at the plate, though his strikeout rate did jump from 12 percent in the DSL to 22 percent in his first two seasons in the United States. Vargas has average-to-solid speed with good instincts and an aggressive nature on the bases. He has reliable hands and solid arm strength but limited lateral range at shortstop and is a better fit at second base. He's also a capable third baseman and projects as a slugging utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 11 prospect in the 2024 international class, Radney was Arizona’s top signing last year when he joined the D-backs for $1.85 million out of the Dominican Republic, just a smidge above the $1.8 million given to countryman Belfi Rivera. The outfielder split his time between both of the organization’s Dominican Summer League affiliates, hitting just .225/.331/.288 with three triples and two doubles in 34 games. It was a tale of two seasons for Radney. The outfielder batted .296 through his first 16 games, missed two weeks and then hit .158 in his final 18. He was going to be graded on a curve anyway since he turned 17 that June. On the positive side, he walked at a decent clip (10.8 percent) against wild DSL arms. The right-handed slugger’s value has always been in long-term projection as many believe he’ll fill out his 6-foot-3 form and become an above-average power threat. He’ll need to elevate better on contact too after putting the ball on the ground 54.1 percent of the time in 2024. Radney made 22 of his 23 defensive starts in right field. That’s typically not ideal for an athletic outfielder so young -- you’d rather have him in center -- but his power profile and above-average arm strength still fit in that specific corner.
