The 2025 season -- still just his age-18 season -- will bring more clarity on where the youngster belongs in Arizona’s outfield hierarchy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs had a $7,114,800 bonus pool for the 2024 international window and used a sizable allotment to target two of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 prospects in the class -- outfielder Belfi Rivera (No. 24) and Radney (No. 10). The higher ranked of the pair joined the organization for a $1.85 million bonus, just beating out Rivera’s $1.8 million mark to make him the official head of the D-backs' contingent. Radney doesn’t turn 17 until June of his signing year but he already stands in at 6-foot-3. There’s a ton of room to fill in that frame -- his official weight after signing was 180 pounds -- and that level of projection is something that excites Arizona officials. Batting from the right side, Radney has a relatively quiet approach that helps him hit for average, but once more muscle comes, his slugging ability should hit another level. The Dominican Republic native has solid speed for now, and it’s expected that he’ll get a good amount of center-field looks early in his career to keep that valuable lane open. His arm strength would certainly work in right field, however, should he need to move in deference to a better defender or if he loses a step, and the potential pop would play anywhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After eschewing the international market for years under previous management, the Orioles have become legit players in Latin America under GM Mike Elias and international scouting director Koby Perez, handing out seven-figure bonuses every year and reeling in some of the region’s top-rated prospects. Their biggest splash yet was Almeyda, who signed for a franchise-record $2.3 million bonus to headline the club’s 2023 class. Born in Paterson, New Jersey, Almeyda moved to the Dominican Republic as a 15-year-old and performed well in both the U.S. and the D.R. as a teen and was expected to transition more smoothly to pro ball than other international prospects. But Almeyda was limited to 19 games in the Dominican Summer League due to a left shoulder injury that required surgery in 2023, though he did play 53 games in the Florida Complex League in 2024. Almeyda is a tall, athletic shortstop with solid future tools across the board, but his impact will be made as an offensive player. He has a quick right-handed swing and hits the ball hard, generating a lot of line drives and power from a 6-foot-2, 180-pound frame that should strengthen as his body matures. He struggled with his approach in a small sample during his debut, but the injury played a big factor in that, and he is considered to have a good feel for the strike zone and hitting in general. He’s a good runner who can handle himself on the bases. Almeyda played most of his games during his debut at shortstop, and while he has the chance to play there long-term, there was always the possibility he’d outgrow the position, and he played a lot more third in 2024. He’s considered athletic enough to eventually adjust if necessary, given the strong arm, soft hands, good footwork and quickness he already shows in the middle of the diamond. Almeyda has flashed all five tools, but he needs time to develop on both sides of the ball for a better gauge of how high his ceiling really will be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: ﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ It took a while for the Orioles to get established in the international market after committing to doing so for the first time under general manager Mike Elias and international scouting director Koby Perez, but now that they are, they are legit players, handing out seven-figure bonuses every year. The latest example is Almeyda, who signed for a franchise-record $2.3 million as the headliner of their 2022-23 class. A native of Paterson, New Jersey, who moved to the Dominican Republic as a 15-year-old, Almeyda was a familiar name in amateur circles after performing well both in the D.R. and the United States as a teen. He is expected to transition more smoothly to pro ball than many international prospects given his familiarity with the U.S. A tall, athletic shortstop with a good approach at the plate, Almeyda generates power from a quick right-handed swing that could develop into a plus tool. His other tools are solid across the board, with a chance to improve as his body matures and he grows accustomed to professional pitching. He’s a good runner who can handle himself on the bases. Almeyda projects as a strong defender with a plus arm, soft hands, and good footwork in the middle of the diamond. He’ll play shortstop every day in pro ball, though at 6-foot-2 and 180 pounds, it’s possible he’ll outgrow the position in time due to his size. Even so, he’s considered athletic enough that an adjustment to a new position shouldn’t be a problem. He’ll need time to develop on both sides of the field, but Almeyda has a chance to develop into a five-tool player if everything clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even though he signed for just $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018, Ventura has been brimming with potential for years, beginning in 2019, when he climbed three levels out of the Dominican Summer League and into stateside ball. He missed all of 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic shutdown and Tommy John surgery respectively, and when he returned last June, it was only for four starts before a pectoral injury ended his 2022 early. Ventura went unprotected in the Rule 5 Draft, and while the Mets were concerned someone would grab and stash him, he went unpicked and stayed in the New York system. The 6-foot right-hander flashed his typical promise during his brief time in the Florida State League, striking out 10 of 29 batters (34.5 percent) before the most recent injury. He topped out at 97.3 mph on the radar gun and sat 93-95 mph from a high release slot. His mid-80s changeup got good separation off the heater, and while it did show some firmness, it projects as a potential above-average offering that got almost as many whiffs as the fastball and curve combined. Speaking of which, after Santos toiled with a breaking ball for years, his 79-81 mph curveball flashed as average with vertical drop, but he used it only 14 percent of the time. Ventura’s athletic delivery has long given Mets officials hope that he can throw strikes, and that didn’t change after the brief look in ’22. The right-hander still has the upside of a back-end starting pitcher, especially if he can lock the breaking ball into place, but he absolutely needs to get innings to meet that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for only $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018, Ventura shot up through three Rookie-level affiliates (one Dominican, two domestic) a year later and finished with solid numbers -- a 3.78 ERA, 54 strikeouts, 19 walks in 52 1/3 innings. Following the missed 2020 season, he had the potential to break into full-season ball last year but underwent Tommy John surgery in the spring, causing him to miss the entire 2021 campaign. The good news: Ventura returned to Single-A St. Lucie this season with a fastball that averages 94 mph. That’s even more promising because the 6-foot right-hander had really leaned on the heater to find his success early in his career. When he was previously healthy, he had also been working on finding a consistent breaking ball instead of one that showed slider shape at times and curveball depth at others. A mid-80s changeup has been his most oft-used secondary in 2022, and while it has a higher whiff percentage than the other two offerings, it does get too firm to be more than an average pitch. Ventura always earned points for an athletic and repeatable delivery that helped him throw strikes at the lower levels, and those characteristics should help him re-find the command post-Tommy John. A pectoral strain suffered in late June has put off that timeline a little further, but it’s less of a concern than the elbow was. Regained health and additional work on the secondaries could push him into becoming one of the Mets’ best prospect arms by the middle of 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ventura signed with the Mets for only $20,000 shortly after his 17th birthday in July 2018 and moved directly to the Dominican Summer League from there. He returned to the DR complex circuit in 2019 but was moved stateside after only three impressive starts. The right-hander climbed to Rookie Advanced Kingsport in that age-18 campaign, finishing with strong numbers (including 54 strikeouts against 19 walks in 52 1/3 innings) across the board at three levels. He underwent Tommy John surgery in the spring and won’t see a Minor League mound again until likely the middle of next summer. The Mets are fans of Ventura’s overall athleticism and repeatable delivery prior to the procedure. He uses both to throw a fastball around 92 mph that features some cut to it. The pitch alone has guided the 6-foot hurler’s early trips to the Minors to the point where he has used it 80-90 percent of the time at the lower levels. That pitch selection will change as he faces tougher bats, and the Mets are optimistic that his other offerings will be good enough to handle more usage. The breaking ball, particularly, will remain a focus. Sometimes, it can come out of his hand with slider-like action. Others, it has the depth of an above-average curveball. The Mets teamed with Ventura to find the breaking pitch that works best off his heater. The changeup can be an out pitch, but like any young pitcher, it needs to be thrown more to complete its true development. It wasn’t killer stuff from Ventura before Tommy John surgery. But it all came from a promisingly athletic frame, and Ventura’s ability to throw strikes across the board was a promising first step. A move away from the fastball and into the secondary pitches needed to get upper-level bats out should come next in his journey to find a spot in the back end of a Major League rotation, once he regains his elbow health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Pirates All-Star David Bednar, Will was named most outstanding player at the 2021 College World Series after dominating in three starts as Mississippi State won its first national title. After signing him for a below-slot $3,647,500 as the 14th overall pick that July, the Giants expected him to move quickly through the Minors. But his first full pro season in 2022 ended after two months because of a stress reaction in his lower back and related issues have sidelined him for most of this year. When he starred in college, Bednar bullied hitters with a 92-97 mph fastball that could feature either good carry up in the strike zone or heavy life at the knees and an 82-85 mph slider with horizontal and vertical action. Rarely at full health last year, he mostly worked at 90-93 mph with his heater and had less power and movement with the slider. His truncated season gave him little opportunity to work on a low-80s changeup with some fade and sink that he barely used in college and can struggle to throw for strikes. Bednar pounded the strike zone at Mississippi State but his back issues also took a toll on his control and command. He features some effort in his delivery but has a strong 6-foot-2 build that should lend itself to durability. His intelligence and competitiveness should help him get the most out of his ability, though he'll need to regain his health and his college stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Bednar brothers will remember 2021 fondly after David compiled a 2.23 ERA as a rookie reliever with the Pirates and Will won most outstanding player honors at the College World Series after leading Mississippi State to its first national title. The latter struck out 15 in six one-hit innings against Texas in his first CWS start and won the final with six more scoreless frames against Vanderbilt, then went 14th overall in the Draft and signed for an under-slot $3,647,500. His stuff and control haven't been as sharp in 2022 while he has battled some lower back issues. Bednar has spent much of his first full pro season working at 90-93 mph with his fastball after operating at 92-95 mph and reaching 97 in college. He can throw his heater with good carry up in the strike zone as well as with heavy life at the knees. His best offering is a slider that reaches the mid-80s with plenty of horizontal sweep as well as depth when it's on, and he'll occasionally dust off an upper-70s downer curveball to give hitters a different look. Bednar also has the makings of an average changeup with fade and sink, though he's still honing his ability to throw it for strikes. His physical frame should give him the durability to succeed as a starter, though there is some effort to his delivery and his control has wavered at times this summer. He also stands out with his intelligence and competitiveness and could be a late-inning reliever if starting doesn't work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: New York's best prep prospect in 2022, Kennedy worried clubs with his commitment to Louisiana State but turned pro for a well-over-slot $1 million when the Pirates drafted him in the fourth round. Pittsburgh handled him with care and he compiled a 3.11 ERA with a 158/44 K/BB ratio in 130 1/3 innings at the lower levels of the Minors in his first two pro seasons. After acquiring Spencer Horwitz from the Blue Jays in the Andrés Giménez trade at the Winter Meetings in December, the Guardians immediately spun Horwitz to the Pirates for Luis Ortiz, Kennedy and lefty pitching prospect Josh Hartle. Kennedy's fastball averaged just under 90 mph and peaked at 93 last season, though it was effective because he creates deception and carry with a flat approach angle. Hitters also can't sit on his heater because he has a pair of solid secondary pitches that elicit a lot of chases. His sweeping low-80s slider keeps left-handers in check and his sinking low-80s changeup keeps right-handers at bay. Kennedy's lack of overpowering stuff leaves him with little margin for error, but he rarely makes mistakes. More athletic than physical, he ranked third among teenagers in the full-season Minors (minimum: 80 innings) with a 6 percent walk rate last year, but his control has regressed in 2025. His floor stands out more than his ceiling, and he'll have to prove he can get higher-level hitters out without huge velocity, but his feel for pitching is impressive.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: New York's top high school prospect in 2022, Kennedy dropped to the fourth round because of his commitment to Louisiana State but signed with the Pirates for a well-over-slot $1 million. Pittsburgh handled him carefully and didn't turn him loose in full-season ball until 2024, when he pitched well at two Class A levels and posted a 95/19 K/BB ratio in 83 2/3 innings. The Guardians acquired him along with Luis Ortiz and lefty pitching prospect Josh Hartle in exchange for Spencer Horwitz at the Winter Meetings in December. Kennedy has good feel for a legitimate three-pitch mix, even if he lacks true wow stuff at present. His fastball tops out at around 92 mph, though it plays up a bit because of deception in his delivery and life up in the zone. He also shows a two-seamer with some sink at times, though not consistently. His slider is his best pitch, a low-80s offering that misses bats and is particularly effective against left-handed hitters. He sells his changeup with decent arm speed and it will be an area of focus to improve that pitch and get more velocity separation from his fastball. Kennedy’s ability to repeat his delivery, throw strikes and set up hitters creates a good foundation to be a big league starter, though at 6-foot-1, he doesn’t offer too much projection. There's hope that with natural maturation, there could be more in the tank, which could raise his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kennedy was the top talent in upstate New York in the 2022 Draft, having put himself firmly on the map with a strong summer showcase circuit, including pitching for USA Baseball’s 18U National Team. He was throwing well as the spring wore on, but many teams thought his commitment to LSU was too tough of an obstacle. The Pirates went well over slot in the fourth round of last year’s Draft to overcome that, giving the high school lefty $1 million to sign. Kennedy didn’t make his official debut in 2022, but the Pirates know they’ve gotten a prep arm with more of a college feel for pitching. He has a three-pitch mix, starting with a fastball that right now tops out at around 92 mph, but the combination of deception and riding life up in the zone helps it play up beyond the velocity. His upper-70s slider can miss bats, and he’ll throw his 80-81 mph changeup to all hitters, selling it with good arm speed. With a repeatable delivery, Kennedy should be able to throw a lot of strikes and has already shown a feel for how to set up hitters. The ceiling might be a little limited because of his size, but as a young pitcher who turned just 18 last November, there should be some projection to come from physical maturity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At Calvary Christian HS (Fla.), Carter pitched alongside Andrew Painter, who went 13th overall to the Phillies, in a rotation that scouts flocked to see. Carter’s commitment to play NCAA ball at Miami dropped him to the fifth round in 2021, but the Blue Jays made an aggressive play and signed Carter for $850,000, nearly $500,000 above slot value. Toronto had met with him multiple times prior to the Draft and prioritized this pick. Carter made his pro debut in 2022 and was hit hard at times, which the organization believes he’ll learn from. Between the Florida Complex League and Single-A, he posted a 5.48 ERA with 53 strikeouts over 47 2/3 innings. Carter was throwing strikes, but opposing hitters were simply finding a way to barrel him up consistently. Toronto still liked how his raw stuff looked, though, and the confidence he pitched with. There’s no shortage of that on the mound for him. With a fastball that lives in the 91-94 mph range and a slider that has the potential to be an above-average pitch, the building blocks are there. Carter is athletic in his delivery, even working in the odd hesitation or wrinkle. He’s the exact type of pitcher who should benefit from the Blue Jays’ physical program and resources at their new player development complex if he taps into those year-round. He still has immense upside, but his pro debut was a learning experience that shows there is some development ahead for the talented young righty.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pitching alongside Andrew Painter, who went No. 13 overall to the Phillies, Carter helped give Calvary Christian High School (Fla.) a formidable rotation and earned plenty of pre-Draft buzz in his own right. A commitment to pitch at Miami dropped him to the fifth round, but the Blue Jays selected him and signed him to an $850,000 bonus, nearly $500,000 above the slot value and the second-highest in their ’21 Draft class behind Gunnar Hoglund (Rd. 1). Carter had met multiple times with the Blue Jays prior to the Draft and worked out at their facility, identifying them as his priority fit. With an athletic, 6-foot-4 frame, physicality and natural arm strength, there’s a lot to like about Carter from the moment you see him throw. He was up to 94 mph coming out of the Draft, but a good offseason at the Blue Jays’ complex has him touching 96 mph early in ’22. His top secondary pitch is a slider, which lives in the mid-80s and could develop into an out pitch, while his changeup will be a focus over the next couple of years. Carter takes a page out of the Marcus Stroman and Johnny Cueto books with hesitations and wrinkles to his delivery, which he tries to use situationally to disrupt hitters’ timing. His control is still developing some consistency at this age, but he should have an average command of the plate, which is enough to let his stuff play. Carter is the exact type of pitcher that player development staffs love to work with, both because of his physical build and his eagerness to improve. His next steps will be managing a full season’s workload, both physically and mentally, but Carter represents one of the higher-upside arms in the system long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Phillips’ raw stuff has intrigued evaluators for some time, but injuries have largely kept it in the mythical category. The Braves took him in the second round of the 2022 Draft because of his upside despite the fact he had Tommy John surgery in April of his senior year of high school. He spent the 2023 season rehabbing and then was sent to the Mariners in the trade for Jarred Kelenic and others. Phillips had an eye on taking the mound competitively in 2024 when he needed a second TJ leading up to Spring Training, so he enters the 2025 season without having an official professional pitch on his résumé. It’s hard to know exactly what Phillips might be because it’s possible he hasn’t been truly healthy since his junior year of high school in 2021. The Texas native has shown high-octane stuff, with a fastball that has good run and sits in the mid 90s, touching close to 100. His breaking ball is a bit of a hybrid, thrown with slider-like velocity around 85 mph, but with curveball depth. There is feel for a fading changeup, but he hadn’t used it much nor had time to develop it. All of Phillips’ grades are hypothetical and on-paper numbers at this point. The hope is to get him on the mound at some point during the 2025 season, and while it will likely be '26 before anyone will be able to get any sense of what kind of pitcher he might be, the potential that intrigued the Braves three years ago is still too good to completely forget about him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Phillips was high on the Mariners’ radar ahead of the 2022 Draft, but the Tommy John surgery he underwent in April impacted his status and led him to being taken by the Braves in the second round for $1.5 million. He wound up in Seattle’s system as the upside return in the 2023 trade that sent Jarred Kelenic to Atlanta, but then he underwent a second TJ leading up to Spring Training in ‘24 that will further prevent him from making his pro debut. Part of what may have led to his injuries is also what made him so enticing, which is the fastball with elite velocity that sits in the mid-90s, flirts with triple digits and features strong running action. His best secondary pitch is a power breaking ball that he gets up to 85 mph, a pitch that has curveball depth with slider velocity. With that type of combination, he doesn’t often use the changeup that he has in his back pocket that possesses good fade. The most notable comparison Phillips has drawn is to Nathan Eovaldi, who was also high on Draft boards back in 2008 as a Texas high schooler before sustaining an elbow injury. The focus for Phillips in 2024 will again be to get healthy after another brutally unfortunate setback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Phillips was rushing up Draft boards in the spring of 2022 as reports flowed in of the Texas prep right-hander hitting triple digits with his fastball. He seemed like he had a shot at being a first-round pick until the train was derailed temporarily by Tommy John surgery in April. He had been scouted regularly prior to the injury and the Braves felt comfortable enough to take him as their third straight high school arm in the 2022 Draft, signing him for $1.5 million as their second-round pick. He never threw an official pitch for the Braves, who sent him and fellow right-hander Jackson Kowar to the Mariners in the December trade that sent Jarred Kelenic, Evan White and Marco Gonzales to Atlanta. The hope is that Phillips will get back to the improved stuff he showed before the elbow injury. His fastball can sit in the mid-90s, reach the upper 90s and touch 100 mph with good running action. His breaking ball, a power curve with depth thrown up to 85 mph, could be a plus pitch. Like many prep hurlers with that kind of fastball-breaking ball combination, he didn’t use his changeup much, but he has shown feel for a mid-80s offering with fade. Compared by some to big leaguer Nathan Eovaldi, a Texas high schooler who blew out his elbow as a junior, Phillips’ improved strength has led to a repeatable delivery and more strikes. He’ll get his first true professional test in his new organization in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas native who had a commitment to TCU lined up as a high school senior, Willems impressed the Orioles so much at a pre-Draft workout in Baltimore in 2021 that they convinced him to turn pro with a $1 million bonus as an eighth-round pick. After a difficult adjustment to pro ball, Willems began to turn a corner in 2023 and reached Double-A as a 21-year-old in '24, capping things off with an impressive showing in the Arizona Fall League. He spent all of 2025 back at Double-A. A left-handed-hitting catcher with plus raw power, Willems has produced at least 16 homers in each of the past three seasons. It’s power-over-hit in a strong and stocky package, with a simple swing built to drop the barrel on pitches low in the zone, but he can get pull-happy and prone to slumps when he strays from using the big part of the field. There is also some swing-and-miss, though Willems has cut his strikeout rate the past four years and kept it below 20 percent in ‘25. He’s not a liability on the bases despite poor footspeed. Willems has always had a strong arm -- he touched 90 mph from the mound as a prepster and recorded a 1.90-second pop time in the AFL -- but his future behind the plate is muddied by clunky mechanics, mobility issues and concerns about his receiving and blocking. Though he always played 60-70 percent of his innings at catcher, that number fell to around 50 last year as Willems saw more time at first base and DH. The power remains his driving tool as he reaches the upper levels, but Willems will need to improve defensively to catch everyday and/or probably hit a little more to become a regular at first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The impression Willems made at a pre-Draft workout in Baltimore convinced the Orioles to make him an eighth-round Draft pick in 2021, and an overslot $1 million deal convinced the Lone Star State native to bypass a commitment to Texas Christian and turn pro. The adjustment wasn’t the smoothest, but things began clicking at Single-A Delmarva in 2023 and Willems hit himself to Double-A in 2024 as a 21-year-old before capping the year with a solid stint in the Arizona Fall League. His 2025 was more uneven, though he did hit 16 homers, and the Orioles left him off the 40-man roster, but he was not selected in the Rule 5 Draft. Willems has an attractive profile as a left-handed hitting backstop with excellent raw power, and he’s been able to get to it in games to an impressive degree as a young player, socking 17 homers in each of his first two seasons, followed by the 16 last year. It’s power-over-hit in a strong and stocky package, with a simple swing built to drop the barrel on pitches low in the zone and drive them with authority. Willems can swing and miss quite a bit, but his approach is maturing and he sliced his strikeout rate in Double-A and the AFL, and still kept it under 20 percent in 2025. Willems is a decent baserunner despite poor footspeed, taking extra bases when he can and rarely running into outs. Willems touched 90 mph as a two-way prep player and that strong arm has kept him behind the plate despite questions about his receiving and blocking. He isn’t an elite defender, but he’s ironed out those edges somewhat and caught better than scouts expected in the Fall League. He’s also played about a quarter of his defensive innings at first base, though a full-time move there would put more pressure on the bat to develop even further.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 30 | Arm: 65 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 Willems was a two-way player as a Texas high schooler who appeared to be en route to Texas Christian for college ball before the Orioles swooped in and made him an eighth-round Draft pick in 2021. Baltimore kept Willems from heading to campus with an overslot deal of $1 million. He didn’t hit much at Single-A Delmarva in his first full season of pro ball, but things began clicking back at that level in 2023, when Willems hit his way to High-A Aberdeen and socked 17 homers between the two levels. Left-handed-hitting catchers are always a coveted demographic, and Willems brings youth and tremendous raw power to the profile. He is strong and stocky, using a simple swing to drop his barrel on pitches to drive them with authority, especially ones low in the zone. His results improved this year with a revamped approach and better pitch recognition skills. He also walked more, making him a productive hitter despite ample swing-and-miss. That element might always be a part of Willems’ game, but he also has a chance to grow into plus power by the time he’s fully developed. Willems had a strong enough arm as a high schooler to generate 90 mph velocity readings from the mound, and it’s still a weapon for him behind the plate even as questions remain about his receiving and blocking. He improved in both of those areas in 2023 while also seeing time at first base. If he continues his development behind the plate and with his approach in the box, he could develop into a power-hitting backstop at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of several Cubans signed by the Astros in recent years, Gomez landed a $775,000 bonus in 2022. He made a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before injuries limited him to 16 games when he came to the United States a year later. Jumping to full-season ball in 2024, he hit .267/.333/.403 with 37 extra-base hits and 20 steals in 107 games between two Class A stops. Gomez has the potential to hit for average and power, though he needs more selectivity at the plate. He keeps his left-handed swing in the hitting zone for a long time but chases all types of pitches off the plate too often. He's strong and shows the ability to pull and lift balls, yet he's still learning to be judicious about which ones he should attack. While Gomez has solid-to-plus speed, he's still learning the nuances of basestealing. His instincts are better in the outfield, where he gets better jumps and takes direct routes to flyballs. He's a plus defender with a playable arm in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros are more active in the Cuban market than most clubs and mined it for three players in the 2022 international class: shortstop Alberto Hernandez ($950,000), Gomez ($775,000) and right-hander Carlos Espinosa ($480,000). Gomez made an immediate impression with his advanced offensive and defensive skills. He batted .294/.402/.500 with 10 steals in 37 games during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Gomez prioritizes making contact at the plate with a disciplined approach and a left-handed swing that stays in the zone for a long time. Though he's a hit-over-power guy, he does have the bat speed and projectable strength in his compact 5-foot-11 frame to grow into 15-20 homer pop. He showed the aptitude to turn on pitches and drive them in the air against DSL competition. Gomez's plus speed will enable him to steal bases and remain in center field. He stands out with his instincts as well as his quickness in the outfield, making quality reads and taking efficient routes. He has fringy arm strength but it's playable in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A North Carolina prep product, Martin planned on going to East Carolina to play shortstop until Los Angeles spotted him on the mound at the end of his 2022 senior season, drafted him in the 17th round and signed him for $125,000. His stuff made a jump in his pro debut after he focused on pitching full-time, but an offseason car accident and other outside factors led him to regress physically in 2024. He got off to a poor start in High-A last April, necessitating a month to recalibrate at the Dodgers' training facility in Arizona, Martin's best pitch is a tight upper-80s slider that elicits plenty of chases and empty swings, and he trusts it and uses it more than a fastball that parked at 92-94 mph last year and peaked at 99. His heater has some carry but is fairly straight and gets pounded when he doesn't locate it well. He's still developing feel for a mid-80s changeup with some depth and has mostly shelved an upper-70s curveball. Martin has a quick arm and works with an up-tempo delivery that creates some deception. Though he's just 6 feet tall, he has the athleticism and strike-throwing to succeed as a starter if he can refine his fastball command and changeup quality. Added strength and durability would help as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally committed to East Carolina as a shortstop, Martin sporadically pitched as a reliever before making a handful of starts on the mound as a North Carolina high school senior in 2022. Los Angeles saw enough to take a flier on him in the 17th round, and his desire to join the organization led him to give up college for a $125,000 bonus. His stuff has made a significant jump since he started concentrating on pitching and began to add strength, and he posted a 2.04 ERA with 48 strikeouts in 39 2/3 innings in Single-A during his pro debut last summer. Martin's fastball velocity increased from the low 90s in 2022 to 94-96 mph with a high of 98 in his first full year as a pro, and his heater comes with carry and armside run. He always has shown feel for spinning the ball and has added power to a mid-80s slider that features plenty of depth. His upper-80s changeup is a bit firm but continues to improve as he uses it more often, grading as a solid offering at its best. The Dodgers loved Martin's athleticism when they scouted him as an amateur and haven't made any adjustments to his clean delivery. After showing the ability to throw all three of his pitches for strikes in 2023, he has fought his control and command throughout this season. He'll need to straighten out his strike-throwing and prove his durability but has the upside of a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hertzler teamed with Trey Yesavage at Boyertown (Pa.) HS ,and after three years of college, he went four rounds behind him in the 2024 Draft, joining the Astros as a fifth-rounder. A two-way player in his first two seasons at Liberty, he focused on pitching as a junior and became the Flames' No. 1 starter. He has worked just 21 innings as a pro because he sprained his forearm last April and made just one more appearance five months later. Hertzler's best offering is a low-80s changeup with significant fade. It helps him maximize the effectiveness of a fastball that sits at 91-94 mph and tops out at 97 with carry and armside run. He showed better feel for his tight mid-80s slider than his 78-82 mph curveball during his brief action last season. With a 6-foot-4 frame and high arm slot, Hertzler's pitches come out of a higher release point than usual. His control and command improved as he got more experience at Liberty, and he has no problem providing strikes. He'll need to show he can handle a starter's workload after totaling just 142 innings in the last four years but should be fully healthy for 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyertown (Pa.) High's 2021 pitching staff featured two arms who would go early in the 2024 Draft -- Blue Jays first-rounder Trey Yesavage and Astros fifth-rounder Hertzler. A two-way player in his first two college seasons at Liberty, Hertzler became the Flames' No. 1 starter when he focused on the mound last spring. His pro debut consisted of two brief appearances at Single-A. In his lone season as a college starter, Hertzler showed the ability to get chases and miss bats with four average pitches. His fastball operates at 91-94 mph and touches 97 with carry and armside run, and it could become a solid offering if he finds more velocity. His fading low-80s changeup is his best secondary pitch, followed by a tight mid-80s slider with occasional depth and a low-80s curveball. Hertzler's strong 6-foot-4 frame and high arm slot created a higher release point than hitters are accustomed to. As he got regular innings in 2024, he did a good job of cleaning up his delivery and providing strikes. He has more untapped potential than most college pitchers and could develop into a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guerrero pitched for three different Washington colleges in his home state, but it was a solid season for the Washington Huskies that caught the Royals’ attention and led them to select the lefty in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft. He was limited early in his pro career because of injuries but jumped onto the radar with two consistent seasons. Guerrero returned to Double-A in 2024 and posted a 3.69 ERA across 102 1/3 innings and 22 games (all starts). He jumped to Triple-A at the end of August and didn’t finish well, allowing 21 earned runs in 20 2/3 innings with 14 walks and 14 strikeouts in his final five starts. Armed with a four-pitch mix, Guerrero sits 91-93 mph with a fastball that runs up to 96. He has two breaking balls, an 83-84 mph slider and a 77-78 mph curveball, the latter of which has downer action and flashes plus on some nights. The slider with sweeping action is probably his best secondary right now and tunnels off his fastball well. His changeup is fringe average and still developing after an inconsistent year. Guerrero is usually a strikethrower who keeps the ball in the ballpark. Guerrero has more of a smaller build, but his stuff would probably tick up in the bullpen. There’s likely more opportunity there for him as a multi-inning reliever as he gets closer to Kansas City. He began the 2025 season in the Triple-A Omaha rotation but lasted only three starts before undergoing Tommy John surgery. Already left off the 40-man when Rule 5-eligible in 2024, he'll miss out on an opportunity to push for that status this season as he undergoes recovery and rehab for the remainder of the campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: From Lower Columbia (Wash.) CC to Washington State to Washington, Guerrero moved around his home state quite a bit in college, but his 2.96 ERA for the Huskies in 2021 led to the Royals selecting him in the 12th round that year. Guerrero had a limited start to his pro career because of shoulder injuries, but he stayed on the field in 2023 and had a solid year, making 18 appearances (17 starts) for High-A Quad Cities with a 3.63 ERA and 106 strikeouts with just 29 walks across 84 1/3 innings. He ended the season with a late promotion, making three starts for Double-A Northwest Arkansas. Guerrero sits 91-94 mph with his above-average fastball and throws a ton of strikes with the pitch. His best secondary pitch is a slider with sweeping action that grades out as plus and tunnels with his fastball well. His curveball differs from the hard breaking ball with downer action and low-80s velocity. Guerrero does have a changeup, but it’s inconsistent and will be a focus for him in Double-A. He’s an efficient strike-thrower with good control. Guerrero will need that changeup to neutralize right-handers, as hitters will challenge him more at the upper levels. But he has the tools and composure to keep starting, profiling as a back-end rotation pitcher. Evaluators could see Guerrero’s stuff ticking up in the bullpen, and he’d probably get to Kansas City quicker that way.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid prospect from the Pennsylvania high school ranks, Holman never seriously considered forgoing his commitment to Alabama by signing in 2021. After a year as a reliever and a solid season in the Crimson Tide rotation, Holman hit the transfer portal (following a good showing for the U.S. collegiate national team) and headed to Louisiana State. A strong junior season led to him being taken by the Reds at No. 71 overall in the 2024 Draft. He was sidelined by an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery just nine innings into his pro debut in 2025. A 6-foot-4 right-hander with a four-pitch mix when healthy, Holman won’t wow with velocity but had success in college thanks to his feel for pitching. At LSU, he maxed out at 95 mph and sat around 92, but a combination of induced vertical break, ride at the top of the zone and command helped the pitch play up. His low-80s slider with two-plane depth is his bread and butter, eliciting a ton of swing-and-miss, and while his upper-70s curve and mid-80s changeup are underutilized and underdeveloped, both can be effective at times. Holman has shown he can throw all of his pitches in and around the strike zone fairly consistently, and there could be some more velocity to come if he can add some strength to his long and lean frame. The first order of business is getting back to health so he can resume trying to develop into a future big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holman could have been a legitimate high school draftee in 2021, but didn’t go until the very end of the Draft because he was determined to go to Alabama. After relieving as a freshman, he had a successful turn in the Crimson Tide’s rotation in 2023 then was the U.S. collegiate national team’s top performer that summer, before transferring to Louisiana State. Another strong campaign at his new school helped him move up Draft boards and land in Competitive Balance Round B. The Reds shut him down, as they often do with their college arms, rather than send him out for a pro debut last summer. His debut was delayed even further when he missed all of 2025 following reconstructive elbow surgery. While Holman may never light up the radar gun, the 6-foot-4 right-hander has a good feel for using his four-pitch mix to get outs. His fastball sat 92 mph last year with LSU, topping out at 95, but excellent command, ride at the top of the zone and induced vertical break make it better than its pure velocity. He throws his low-80s slider with two-plane depth for strikes, eliciting a 48-percent miss rate according to Synergy in 2024. His upper-70s curve and mid-80s changeup aren’t as advanced in terms of his ability to land them for strikes or throw them frequently. With his long and lean frame, it’s possible that Holman’s stuff could tick up under pro instruction once he returns to health. Because of his fastball-slider and his command of them, Holman has every chance to stick in the back end of a big league rotation. If more velocity or better feel for his other secondary offerings come, he could be more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Juan showed an intriguing mix of power and speed as an amateur in the Dominican Republic, where he trained with three-time All-Star shortstop Rafael Furcal. He was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 16 prospect in the 2022 international class and signed with the Mets for $1.9 million -- more than a third of their pool money -- when the window opened on Jan. 15. Juan’s early results didn’t quite meet the hype as he hit .219/.310/.323 with a 77 wRC+ in 53 games in the Dominican Summer League, but his potential remains. The teenager’s plus speed certainly played early in his transition to pro ball, as he swiped 16 bags in 17 attempts and made 45 of his 47 defensive starts in center field. Batting from the right side, the 6-foot-2 slugger shows good raw power with impressive bat speed in his BP sessions. But to this point, that’s where much of his slugging ability remains, in part because he puts the ball on the ground a lot (51.1 percent GB rate in the DSL). Squaring up the ball a bit more and focusing on pitches he can drive should be focuses as he gains experience against pro arms. Juan drew early comparisons to Byron Buxton and George Springer as an amateur, and those certainly flatter him coming off the DSL time. The outfielder will only be the age of an American high school senior in 2023, so he has ample time to sharpen his considerable tools and become a potential everyday player at the top level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Power and speed working in combination will open any scout's eyes. Juan has the potential to show both in the pro game, and training with 3-time All-Star shortstop Rafael Furcal bolstered his case to be MLB Pipeline’s No. 16 prospect in the 2022 international signing period. The Mets made the right-handed slugger their biggest signing of the cycle when they inked Juan to a $1.9 million bonus, using more than one-third of their pool money to haul him in. Juan already shows at least above-average wheels in all aspects of the game, and that should give New York hope that he will be able to remain in center field for the long haul. As if that wasn’t enough, he already shows good power in batting practice, and there remains room for the lanky 6-foot-2 slugger to add more as he matures. His future value could come down to how well his hit tool plays, but early reports indicate Juan could be an average overall hitter if everything clicks. Juan drew initial comparisons to a young Byron Buxton and George Springer. That’s not exactly fair to a 16-year-old just about to get his professional feet wet, but it does paint a picture of who Juan could be at his absolute best in the pros. A word of caution, however: Buxton and Springer overcame severe strikeout concerns early in their careers. If those same issues pop up for Juan and he doesn’t properly adjust, it could be an uphill battle toward Queens, no matter how good the rest of his profile is.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After working as both a starter and reliever through his first three collegiate seasons, Saenz became a full-time member of the starting staff for Texas A&M in 2021, and while he was inconsistent that spring, he impressed enough late to get the Nationals to take him in the fourth round, signing for $500,000. He has worked his way methodically though the Washington system since with in-season promotions in each of his first two seasons after repeating the level from the campaign before. He dominated High-A early in 2023 and moved to Double-A, where he finished with a 4.44 ERA, 42 strikeouts and 19 walks in 73 innings. Saenz’s strikeout rate plummeted from 27 to 14 percent after the promotion, but he was still able to stay effective by throwing strikes and eliciting ground-ball contact. His 89-91 mph fastball certainly lacks velocity, but he hides the ball well to get it to play up, keeping it in line with his side just before release. His low-80s changeup separates nicely off the heater and drifts armside as it fades, getting some right-handers to chase down and away. He threw an 82-85 mph slider more than the changeup because of its movement away from lefties, but it could backfoot righties, too. An upper-70s curveball served as more of a get-me-over look to shake things up. The 5-foot-11 southpaw has thrown strikes consistently at every Minor League stop and won’t beat himself when it comes to allowing free passes. He’s proven plenty durable too, adding to the hope he can contribute to Washington’s starting depth; but without sharp stuff, it’s a limited ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Saenz worked as both a starter and a reliever in his first three seasons at Texas A&M, and after going undrafted in the truncated 2020 Draft, he officially moved into a starting role for good as a senior last spring. He was inconsistent for much of the season but ended on a high with striking out eight and allowing one run on two hits over eight innings against LSU in his final outing. The Nationals selected the southpaw in the fourth round a few weeks later and signed him for just below slot at $500,000. He made brief appearances (mostly in relief to save his arm) in the Florida Complex League and with Low-A Fredericksburg in his first taste of the pros. Saenz tends to lean on his low-80s slider because of its two-plane break. It’s easily his best pitch, and some analysts say it had some of the best metrics among similar pitches in the 2021 Draft class. His fastball doesn’t quite pop in terms of velo at 90-93 mph. It does come with some decent sink, however, and Saenz has little issue spotting to any side of the plate. A low-80s changeup with depth gives him enough to work as a starter, but he didn’t use that specific offering much at A&M. At just 5-foot-11, Saenz isn’t a classic candidate to add more gas in the pro game. There’s a chance the fastball could play up if he’s moved back to the bullpen and given shorter stints. For now, his promising command and control will give him a puncher’s chance to start, at least early in his journey through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas signed for $2,077,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2023 as MLB Pipeline's No. 3 international prospect. He batted .316/.415/.513 in his first two years as a pro, winning championships in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer and Arizona Complex leagues. His jump to full-season ball didn't go nearly as well in 2025, as he had hit .221 with a 30 percent strikeout rate in 29 games at Single-A, missing much of the year with a stress fracture in his left wrist. A switch-hitter early in his amateur career, Vargas now bats solely right-handed and creates plus raw power with his bat speed, growing strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame. His approach is geared to drive balls in the air to his pull side, but it's much too aggressive. He chased way too many pitches last year, fastballs and secondary pitches alike, and rarely made quality contact. Though Vargas moves well on the bases, he's bigger than most shortstops and still growing, so it's unclear whether he'll retain the quickness to remain at the position. He has good actions and his strong arm is beyond approach, but he's probably destined for third base in the long run. He could be a solid defender at the hot corner and has the power to fit the offensive profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's No. 3 prospect on the 2023 international market, Vargas signed for $2,077,500 out of the Dominican Republic that January. He played well in his first two seasons, hitting a combined .316/.415/.513 with 11 homers and 30 steals in 86 games. He also won a pair of championships in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer and Arizona Complex Leagues the past two years, homering three times in 10 playoff contests. A switch-hitter early in his amateur career, Vargas now bats solely from the right side of the plate with a quick, compact stroke that produces a lot of hard contact. He has a lot of leverage and room to gain strength in his 6-foot-3 frame, and he improved his ability to drive ball in the air consistently in 2024. He could provide 25 or more homers per season, though his strikeout rate rose from 15 percent in his first pro season to 23 percent in his second, so he'll have to prove he can do damage against more advanced pitching. Bigger than most shortstops, Vargas has average speed and good instincts on the bases, though he could slow down as he continues to add muscle. He has good actions and plenty of arm for shortstop, though his range could be an issue if he loses any quickness. If he eventually has to move, he could be a solid defender at third base and should have no problem fitting the offensive profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's third-ranked prospect in the 2023 international class, Vargas signed for $2,077,500 out of the Dominican Republic that January. He made a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, slashing .328/.423/.529 with seven homers and 19 steals in 48 contests. He also batted .310 with a pair of homers in seven playoff contests to lead the Dodgers Bautista squad to the championship. A former switch-hitter who now bats solely right-handed, Vargas owns a quick, compact swing and a mature approach. He controls the strike zone exceptionally well for his age and focuses on making hard contact. Once he fills out his 6-foot-4 frame and learns to lift balls in the air more frequently, he could provide 25 or more homers per season. Bigger than most shortstops, Vargas has good actions and range to both sides, giving him a chance to remain at the position. He's an average runner with good baserunning instincts, but he could lose a step as he matures physically. If he has to slide over to third base, he has the offensive profile and the plus arm to succeed there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers pull one of the top prospects out of nearly every international signing class, with Vargas the latest example. Ranked No. 3 in the 2023 crop by MLB Pipeline, he signed for $2,077,500 out of the Dominican Republic in January. He's just 17 years old and will need time to develop, but in a system loaded with shortstops, he has the highest ceiling of any of them. A former switch-hitter, Vargas now bats exclusively right-handed. He has a sound swing and an advanced approach, patiently stroking line drives to all fields. With his bat speed and the oodles of projectable strength in his 6-foot-4 frame, he could grow into 25-homer power while also producing high batting averages. Though he's bigger than most shortstops, Vargas has good actions, range to both sides, reliable hands and plus arm strength. He's one of the more polished hitters and defenders in his international class. An average runner who could lose some quickness as he matures physically, he'd profile well at third base if he had to move off shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coffey was a two-way prospect who touched 94 mph with his fastball, but the Red Sox preferred him as a position player when they took him in the second round of the 2022 Draft. Moved to the Blue Jays at the 2024 Deadline for Danny Jansen, Coffey is one of the Blue Jays’ most tooled up position player prospects. After struggling in High-A down the stretch in ‘24, Coffey looked better in ‘25, hitting .273 with 11 home runs and a .786 OPS over 99 games, and he carried some momentum into a strong performance in the Arizona Fall League (.328/.427/.406). There’s some serious power to be unlocked here if Coffey can put it all together, and many of these conversations feel like the same ones people had about Addison Barger a few years ago. Breaking balls were tough on Coffey, which is a hole he’ll need to shore up, but the Blue Jays feel he’s taking that next step and the tools are there for him to push past 20 home runs if he’s making more contact. Defensively, Coffey will be at third base with second base still part of his profile, and his throwing arm is more than enough for the hot corner. The athletic profile here is exciting. Coffey’s plate approach needs work, and those exceptional physical tools need to show up in games more consistently, but this is the type of prospect that development staffs love to work with. Coffey is one of the best bets to really pop if it all comes together.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better two-way high school prospects in the 2022 Draft, Coffey displayed a low-90s fastball and a sharp low-80s slider on the mound. Most clubs preferred him as a position player, however, and the Red Sox made him a full-time hitter after signing him for $1,847,500 in the second round. He's one of four California prep middle infielders whom Boston has given seven-figure bonuses in the past three Drafts. Coffey has more raw power than most middle infielders, and his bat speed and strength could produce 20 or more homers on an annual basis if he can develop more consistency at the plate. At times, he'll show the ability to recognize pitches and make adjustments, leading to hope that he'll be at least an average hitter. But his right-handed swing also can get long and he can struggle to handle velocity up in the strike zone, so he may be prone to strikeouts. In his 11-game pro debut, Coffey shuttled between shortstop, third base and second base. His athleticism, good infield actions and plus arm strength give him a chance to stick at short, though his fringy speed may land him elsewhere, especially if he loses a step as he continues to mature physically. He could become a solid-to-plus defender at the hot corner or wind up as an offensive-minded second baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinto originally signed with the Rockies out of Venezuela in July 2019 for $120,000, and came to the Blue Jays organization along with Raimel Tapia in the Randal Grichuk deal in '22. Since then, Pinto’s career has been defined by a string of injuries, but the flashes we’ve seen in between those moments have been tantalizing. Pinto appeared in just 19 games with High-A Vancouver in 2025, but launched seven home runs with a .985 OPS. Don’t expect Pinto’s power to look like that over the course of a full season, as he’s listed at just 5-foot-6. But his offensive upside, speed and ability to play multiple positions still have real value, even with so little game action in recent seasons. The Blue Jays are planning to simplify things for Pinto, focusing much more on second base alone, and you may not see him running as often, even though he has the ability to steal 30-plus bags a season. If the organization can get him to play in 100 contests, then they can expand his game again in ‘27 and beyond. Pinto remains a favorite among coaches and staff who have seen these glimpses. He plays the game with his hair on fire, which might not help on the injury front, but there’s still an exciting bench player in here -- and a fan favorite -- if he can stay on the field and develop some actual routines. That health aspect is one of the biggest “what if's” on this list, but Pinto’s raw ability keeps him ranked for at least one more season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinto originally signed with the Rockies out of Venezuela in July 2019 for $120,000, but due to the pandemic and the lost 2020 Minor League season, he didn’t make his professional debut until 2021. Pinto won the Dominican Summer League MVP award that season, batting .360 with a .487 OBP and 41 steals in 54 games. When Pinto was dealt to the Blue Jays with Raimel Tapia for Randal Grichuk, he was an immediate organizational favorite and that hasn’t changed, even as injuries slowed his development. This is a young player who Blue Jays staffers are extremely excited -- and hopeful -- to see for a full season. Pinto dealt with a rib injury in 2024, which limited him to just 26 games, but he hit .330 with a .951 OPS. He rolled that into an Arizona Fall League season nearly as long, at 25 games, in which he put up a line of .274/.392/.357. Now it’s time for the Blue Jays to see what Pinto can do across 100+ games as a prospect who could pile up stats in several categories. Pinto is just 5-foot-6, but generates enough power to be more than just a speed-and-contact threat. He’s focusing on becoming a better basestealer too, using the athleticism that also makes him a sharp defender all over the diamond. All of the raw tools and the flashes we’ve seen from Pinto have been very encouraging, but again, they’ve only been flashes. If it all comes together for Pinto, he could someday profile as a fantastic bench piece on a good MLB roster, bouncing between the infield, outfield and pinch-running spots. Pinto gives it everything he's got and surely would become an immediate Blue Jays fan favorite, but the first step is a full, healthy season. Games played will be the most important stat for Pinto in 2025, but if that number finally starts to climb, he’ll command some attention in this system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pinto originally signed with the Rockies out of Venezuela in July 2019 for $120,000, but due to the pandemic and the lost 2020 Minor League season, he didn’t make his professional debut until 2021. All Pinto did was win the Dominican Summer League MVP that season, batting .360 with a .487 OBP and 41 steals in 54 games. When Pinto was dealt to the Blue Jays with Raimel Tapia for Randal Grichuk, some within the organization believed this could eventually be known as “the Adrian Pinto trade.” Pinto was challenged with a Single-A assignment in 2022 and hit .242 with a .375 OBP, 24 walks and 32 strikeouts over 47 games. These numbers were a step back, but the Blue Jays loved the playing style they saw in Pinto, who buzzes all over the field at top speed. That matches well with his instincts, and despite the injury-shortened ’22 season due to a hamstring issue, he spent plenty of time at the complex over the winter to make up for lost time. Listed at just 5-foot-6, there isn’t much size or power projection to Pinto, but his speed and on-base ability should make him a leadoff man at each level. He’ll continue to move all over the diamond, where his raw athleticism gives him potential in both the infield and outfield. Pinto was a candidate to make a major jump in 2023 but quad injuries have kept him on the injured list again for much of the summer. He needs to stay healthy and on the field to reach his otherwise intriguing potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals took a risk selecting Charles in the final round of the 2022 Draft because it looked like he was headed to UC Santa Barbara, but they were able to lure him away from his commitment with a $429,000 signing bonus. He comes from a baseball family and actually impressed scouts just as much on the mound in high school, but the Royals have only had him hit in the three years since he was drafted. Charles improved upon repeating Single-A in 2024, slashing .257/.353/.386 with 10 homers, 15 doubles and 36 stolen bases in 117 games. Charles is an extreme athlete with tons of tools, including a plus arm and raw power. He’s tall at 6-foot-5, which doesn’t help his hit tool, but he made some adjustments with his swing this year, getting his hands to load back for a better firing position. The goal is to eliminate some of the length in his swing, helping him make better contact on fastballs and walk more. He still struggles with offspeed, but a tweak in his game planning helped him with his recognition and win counts. Finding stability in his swing will allow him to tap into his raw power. Charles’ frame doesn’t make him your typical shortstop, but he has good movements and a strong internal clock that helps him handle the position, while also getting time at third base in Columbia in ‘24. He’s an average runner, but quick-twitch movements help him on the bases. After two seasons in Single-A, Charles made significant progress but really struggled with a move to High-A in 2025 while also dealing with injuries. He is only in his age-21 season and still has untapped potential with his tools and athleticism, but the Royals are excited about what it all could look like if he turns things around as he develops.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Charles looked like he would honor his commitment to UC Santa Barbara before the conclusion of the 2022 Draft, but the Royals selected him in the 20th round and signed him for fifth-round money with a $429,500 bonus. He impressed scouts on both sides of the ball in high school, but the Royals are having him focus on being a hitter. Charles stayed behind in extended spring training last year and played two games in Rookie ball before he joined Single-A Columbia, where he slashed .230/.290/.356 with three homers in 69 games. Charles is one of the best pure athletes in the Royals' system, with a plus arm and raw power. There’s swing-and-miss in his game, and he struggles with breaking balls. But the Royals focused on functional strength with him last year before diving deep into his swing, and that allowed him to tighten up his body movements and find more stability. Now he’ll go into a full season stronger and making better contact. At 6-foot-4, Charles is not your typical shortstop, but he has the skills to handle the position with good movements and a strong internal clock. He saw time at third base because of the shortstop depth in the Royals’ system and he has the ability to become a solid defender on the left side of the infield. He could even move to center field because of his athletic ability and average speed. Charles faced older and better pitchers in Columbia and will likely go back there this season. There is tons of potential for Charles based on his tools and athleticism; he simply needs more time and development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just when it looked like Charles would honor his commitment to UC Santa Barbara last summer, Kansas City took him in the 20th round of the 2022 Draft and signed him for $429,500, roughly fourth- or fifth-round money. Charles impressed scouts with his skills on both sides of the ball, and the Royals were thrilled to get the high-upside high schooler in their system. Charles will stay as a shortstop, and he made his debut last year in the Arizona Complex League, going 3-for-11 in three games. A two-way player in high school, Charles is an elite athlete, with a plus arm and raw power. At 6-foot-4, he’s not your typical shortstop. But he's gotten some early looks there and has started to see more of third base because of Kansas City's loaded depth chart at short in the lower levels. Offensively, Charles is still tapping into his hit tool and raw power. The Royals will work with him on being more consistent at the plate, allowing him to make hard contact more often. Charles has the potential to be a dynamic player for the Royals, although it’ll likely take some time to develop him as he grows. He has all the tools to stay at shortstop, but he could play third base or the outfield as well. He was one of the Royals' best performers in extended spring training early in 2023 and forced his way to Single-A Columbia by early June.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis showed off monster power numbers in his final two seasons on campus at the University of Arizona, including a .742 slugging percentage and a 1.231 OPS as a Pac-12 All-Conference honoree in 2023. The Cardinals selected him 21st overall that July and signed him for slot at $3,618,200. St. Louis played it fairly passively with Davis out of the gate in 2024 with an assignment to Single-A Palm Beach, and he didn’t crack out of the level for 74 games, hitting .232/.337/.401 with eight homers in that span. He was much better after a late July promotion to High-A Peoria (.301/.388/.451 in 30 games) and even finished things out with a quick trip to Double-A Springfield. The left-handed slugger worked through numerous swing and approach changes in his first full season but appears to be at his best with a swing that often draws comparisons to Carlos Gonzalez with his hands starting high near his head, his stance open and his front leg kicking to generate forward momentum. His raw power numbers are still clearly above average and he can pull the ball well, especially heaters. But soft stuff tailing away from him can be an issue when it comes to whiffs or quality contact. Even during the good times at High-A, he ran a 55.6 percent ground-ball rate, and he's continued to miss on a ton of offspeed pitches in 2025. Davis gets most of his reps in center field, but with average speed and plus arm strength, he figures to land in a corner full time as he closes in on St. Louis. That puts added pressure on the raw power to come through in games, and with his whiff rates with Springfield, that's becoming a tall order.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going undrafted in 2020, Davis hit 39 homers between his sophomore and junior years at Arizona, sandwiching those powerful performances between summer excursions in the Cape Cod League and at Team USA trials. A Pac-12 All-Conference member and tournament MVP, Davis led the conference with his .742 slugging percentage and 1.231 OPS in 2023. The Cardinals snagged him with the 21st overall pick and he signed for slot at $3,618,200. Davis slowed down post-Draft with a .212/.366/.269 line in 34 games with Single-A Palm Beach. Putting that first pro stint aside, the left-handed slugger still stands out most for his impressive raw power that can play to all fields. It’s a fast, twitchy swing that often draws comparisons to Carlos González. He improved his approach as a junior in order to get to that power more, but swing-and-miss concerns remain, especially after that first trip through the Florida State League. An average runner, Davis was pushed to left field with the Wildcats, but the Cardinals kept him exclusively in center after the Draft. His plus arm strength would certainly work in right too if he needs to move again, and his power-first profile fits either corner. The Cardinals like getting their outfielders versatility early and have moved Davis around the grass in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After pitching well as a reliever at South Carolina, Mahoney had to wait until 2023 to show what he could do for an encore after Tommy John surgery knocked out his sophomore season, though he did get some at-bats while he was rehabbing. He was an effective starter in the Gamecocks rotation upon his return in 2023, showing enough stuff and athleticism to land in the third round with the Rockies. He spent most of the year with Single-A Fresno and earned a late bump up to High-A Spokane, showing good command of his stuff over 120 innings. With a sturdy 6-foot-3 frame, Mahoney appears built to eat innings. He can run his fastball up to 97 mph, sitting more around 93 mph, and it has good natural sink to it that helps him get ground-ball outs. His changeup might now be his best secondary offering, thrown in the mid-80s with good fade and the ability to miss bats and get weak contact. His slider, also around the mid-80s, can also be an out pitch at times, with horizontal and vertical break. A former high school quarterback and position player, Mahoney’s athleticism helps him repeat his delivery and fill up the strike zone, providing a good combination of pitching to contact to get ground balls and miss bats. His time with Spokane wasn’t as smooth, so he’ll have to work on his overall command within the zone, but he has the makings of a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mahoney started putting his name on the map for the 2023 Draft back in '21 with a dominant freshman year spent mostly in relief. But he became a question mark when he blew out his elbow that May and Tommy John surgery kept him off the mound for all of 2022. He was in the Gamecocks' rotation in 2023 and was their best starter, showcasing a three-pitch mix and athleticism on the mound that helped him land in the third round with the Rockies, who didn’t have him do much after signing following a heavy workload during the spring in his first year post-surgery. A 6-foot-3 right-hander, Mahoney saw his stuff bounce back pretty well upon his return. It starts with a fastball that tops out at 97 mph and sits in the 92-95 range with late natural sink to it. His mid-80s slider can be inconsistent, but at its best, it has horizontal and vertical break. He throws his changeup with the same velocity, and when it’s on, it features good fade. He has the ability to get outs early in counts on the ground, as well as strike guys out. Mahoney is a good athlete who quarterbacked his high school football team and even hit a couple of home runs in 2022 for South Carolina while he was rehabbing his elbow. He has a feel of what he wants to do on the mound, though he’ll need to keep refining his command and control of his repertoire. It’s a pretty good rotation piece starter kit, with perhaps a leap forward to come another year removed from the elbow surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shoulder problems limited Ingrassia to 10 innings in two seasons at San Diego State before he transferred to Cal State Fullerton and became the Titans' closer in 2023. A 14th-round pick that July, he dominated in his 2024 pro debut, topping all Minor League pitchers who worked as many as his 58 1/3 innings in strikeout rate (40 percent) while finishing second in strikeout minus walk rate (31 percent) and compiling a 1.85 ERA. He missed six weeks in the second half of that season with elbow inflammation, then didn't pitch after April last season because of more shoulder woes, though he did return for the Arizona Fall League. Ingrassia's fastball has below-average velocity, sitting at 91-94 mph and reaching 95, but it plays better than that because he operates from a low slot with crossfire and extension and creates plenty of carry, armside run and deception. He's throwing a harder, tighter slider in 2026, working with a mid-80s breaker and occasionally turning it into an upper-80s cutter. He produces a ton of fade on his mid-80s changeup, generating a lot of empty swings but also having difficulty landing it for strikes. Ingrassia doesn't have a pretty delivery and throws with some effort, yet he generally throws strikes. He began his pro career as a reliever before earning an opportunity as a starter. His lack of size and durability probably will land him back in the bullpen, though he could move quickly in that role if he stays healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shoulder problems held Ingrassia to 10 innings in two seasons at San Diego State before he moved to Cal State Fullerton and became the Titans' closer in 2023. A 14th-round pick that July, he dominated in his 2024 pro debut while earning Single-A Carolina League All-Star honors. He led all Minor League pitchers who worked as many as his 58 1/3 innings in strikeout rate (40 percent) while ranking second in strikeout minus walk rate (31 percent) and posted a 1.85 ERA. Though Ingrassia's fastball sits at 91-93 mph and tops out at 95, it plays better than its below-average velocity because he throws from a low slot with crossfire and extension that create sink, horizontal action and deception. His low-80s slider has similar movement with more break and works as a back-foot pitch against right-handers. His best offering is a plus mid-80s changeup that fades in the opposite direction as his heater and slider. Ingrassia throws with some effort and doesn't have the most picturesque delivery, yet he's able to trick hitters without costing himself control. He began 2024 as a reliever before getting stretched out as a starter, thriving in both roles but missing six weeks in July and August with elbow inflammation. His size and durability questions probably will land him in the bullpen, but he could move quickly in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carela created some buzz by pushing his fastball to 96 mph shortly after signing with the Yankees for $335,000 in July 2018, but he hasn't picked up any additional velocity since. He now leans heavily on his slider and it helped him record a 3.71 ERA with 145 strikeouts in 106 2/3 innings between High-A and Double-A in 2024, his first full season in the White Sox system. They picked him up in a 2023 Trade Deadline deal for Keynan Middleton and added him to their 40-man roster last November. He was on track to reach the big leagues this year but instead will miss the season after having Tommy John surgery in March. The Yankees specialize in teaching pitchers to throw sweeping sliders, and Carela's low-80s version induces plenty of chases, though it does get pounded when he doesn't locate it down in the zone. He uses his slider more than his two-seam fastball, which usually ranges from 92-94 mph and generates a lot of weak groundball contact with its sink. He also mixes in a cutter and an occasional fading changeup, both of which arrive in the mid-80s. Carela has the athleticism to repeat his delivery and provide consistent strikes. If he can improve his command and develop a second better-than-average pitch, he could become a No. 4 starter. If not, he has a future as a slider-happy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carela's fastball touched 96 mph shortly after he signed with the Yankees for $335,000 in July 2018, but it hasn't added any velocity since. He logged a 6.90 ERA in his first two pro seasons before improving his slider, which has allowed him to successfully navigate both Class A levels the last two years. The White Sox acquired him in an August trade for Keynan Middleton. The Yankees love sweeping sliders, and Carela picked up a solid low-80s version that he can turn into a more traditional slide piece in the mid-80s. He falls in love with his sweeper too much and will have to use his 91-96 mph two-seam fastball with sink more often against more advanced hitters. His upper-70s curveball and mid-80s changeup are average offerings. Carela is athletic and has a clean delivery that he repeats well, allowing him to throw consistent strikes. If he can refine his command and find a second better-than-average pitch, he could slot in the back of a rotation. Otherwise, he'll probably wind up as a slider-happy middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $10,000 find in the Dominican Republic by the Dodgers in 2021, Batista pitched well in the Rookie ball the next two summers.
