When Los Angeles needed extra international bonus pool money to sign Korean right-handed Hyun-Seok Jang in August 2023, it packaged Batista with fellow righty pitching prospect Maximo Martinez to acquire $1 million from the White Sox. He had a strong first season with his new organization, but after he made his first start in 2025, a stress fracture in his elbow sidelined him for 4 1/2 months. When he's fully healthy, Batista has a pair of 92-94 mph fastballs that top out at 96, favoring sinking two-seamers down at hitters' knees to running four-seamers at their letters. He has one of the best changeups in the system, a mid-80s weapon with fade and tumble that creates a lot of weak contact. His mid-80s slider is effective and features two-plane depth at its best. Batista is deceptive too, operating from an extremely low arm slot that doesn't prevent him from providing strikes. His stuff was down when he returned late last August to make seven brief appearances, so he'll need to prove he can recapture what he had. He's a potential No. 4 starter who could boost his ceiling if he adds more strength and velocity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2021, Batista fared well in Rookie ball during the next two summers. Los Angeles needed more international bonus pool money to sign Korean right-hander Hyun-Seok Jang in August 2023, so it traded Batista and fellow righty pitching prospect Maximo Martinez to the White Sox for $1 million in funds. He has pitched well at two A-ball levels since while displaying one of the system's best changeups. Batista utilizes two fastballs that operate at 92-94 mph and max out at 96, preferring sinking two-seamers down at hitters' knees to running four-seamers past them at the letters. He slings mid-80s changeups that fade and tumble, generating a lot of weak contact. He has an effective mid-80s slider that will flash some two-plane depth at its best. Batista is athletic and works from a low slot that's a tick above sidearm, creating deception without harming his ability to throw strikes. If he can add more muscle to his slender 6-foot-2 frame, he might add more velocity and boost his stuff and ceiling. He has the upside of a No. 4 starter but will need some development time to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz came out of the shortstop factory of San Pedro de Macoris in the Dominican Republic that produced All-Stars such as Tony Fernandez, Jose Offerman and Fernando Tatis Jr., signing with the Cubs for $2.3 million as the headliner of their 2025 international class. He was in the midst of his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League when the Orioles acquired him at the ‘25 Deadline for reliever Andrew Kittridge in what turned into a low-risk deal for Baltimore after it reacquired Kittridge last offseason. That means the Orioles are playing with house money with De La Cruz, who commanded the ninth-highest bonus in the entire ‘25 international class. He’s a switch-hitter with a disciplined approach and the offensive upside to profile as a regular at several positions, with scouts divided over whether his hit tool or power will outshine more in the long run. He has room to grow and fill out his athletic 6-foot-2 frame, hinting at the potential for plus raw power in the future. Adding muscle could slow down De La Cruz, who right now is only an average-to-solid runner, and perhaps move him to the hot corner as he matures. He has enough arm strength to be a quality defender at the position if necessary but features the hands, instincts and footwork to remain a shortstop at least for the moment.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz signed for $2.3 million in January, landing the largest bonus in the Cubs' 2025 international class and the ninth highest on the entire market. He's part of the shortstop factory of San Pedro de Macorís in the Dominican Republic that has produced All-Stars such as Tony Fernandez, Jose Offerman and Fernando Tatis Jr. De La Cruz may eventually move off short but has the offensive upside to profile as a regular at several positions. He got off to a slow start during his debut in the Dominican Summer League but then started figuring some things out, posting an OPS of 1.031 in July when he was sent to the Orioles in return for Andrew Kittredge at the Trade Deadline. Scouts debate whether De La Cruz will stick out more with his hitting ability or power in the long run. He's a switch-hitter with a disciplined approach who focuses on making line-drive contact rather than swinging for the fences. His stroke also features promising bat speed and loft and his still-growing 6-foot-2 frame can get stronger, so he could grow into plus raw power and provide 20 or more homers per season. De La Cruz's twitchy athleticism, smooth actions, soft hands and solid arm strength are suited for shortstop. Presently an average-to-solid runner, he could slow a bit as he develops physically, which would dictate a move to third base. He has the tools to be a quality defender at the hot corner and meet the offensive demands of the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays signed Colmenarez, a highly regarded Venezuelan shortstop, for $3 million as the headliner of their 2021 international signing class. It’s been a tough road for him so far, with most issues completely out of his control. He couldn’t join the Rays in 2020 because the signing period was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, couldn’t properly train with them during the shutdown, then fractured his right hamate before his first season began. Still young (he’ll be 19 all season) and plenty raw, Colmenarez will likely be further challenged with a necessary but challenging promotion to Single-A Charleston this year. It's easy to write off the .247/.319/.289 slash line Colmenarez produced as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League, because the hamate injury sapped his strength even after he returned for 26 games. His numbers were better, but not dominant, as he moved to the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. He hit .254/.379/.381, still displaying a sweet left-handed swing, but his 26.8 percent strikeout rate and lack of power inspired some concerns about how he’ll fare against upper-level competition. He should gain more power as he grows into his projectable frame, and that would enhance his overall offensive profile. It's the rest of Colmenarez’s game, though, that suggests he still has a big league future. He looks like an above-average shortstop with soft hands, good actions, a strong arm and impressive instincts. That would make him, at worst, a lefty-hitting utility infielder if he hits enough -- and it’s not hard to find a place for those on Major League rosters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Look no further than his $3 million signing bonus to understand the Rays’ optimism regarding Colmenarez, a highly touted Venezuelan shortstop who headlined their 2021 international signing class. And understand the number of obstacles that he faced leading up to his professional debut: He couldn’t join the Rays during the first summer of the COVID-19 pandemic due to the delayed signing period, couldn’t properly train during the shutdown, then fractured his right hamate bone just before his first season began. With his debut pushed back to mid-August in the Dominican Summer League, Colmenarez hit for essentially no power as the hamate injury sapped his strength. That led to a .247/.319/.289 slash line in 26 games for the 17-year-old, but the Rays remain excited internally about his potential despite those pedestrian numbers. His hamate is not considered a long-term issue, and Tampa Bay expects him to bounce back as he moves to a domestic affiliate this year. Colmenarez is still projectable, listed at 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds. He has a sweet left-handed swing with a balanced profile, a good blend of hitting for contact and power, that should include more pop as his body continues to mature. Colmenarez has displayed soft hands with good actions at shortstop, and evaluators expect he’ll remain up the middle as an above-average shortstop even as he grows. He also has plus arm strength, enhancing his defensive potential. Despite a delayed and disappointing debut, there’s still plenty of reason to believe Colmenarez will develop into a well-rounded shortstop with above-average tools across the board.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Hit: 40 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 The Padres were one of the finalists for Roki Sasaki in 2025, and if they had landed him, he would have fit right in alongside Ethan Salas (2023) and Leo De Vries (2024) as top international prospects who joined the San Diego system in successive seasons. When they didn’t land the big fish, the Padres pivoted and added three of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects, including No. 35 Coronil, who signed for $900,000 out of Venezuela. He got his career off to a slow start in the Dominican Summer League, where he slashed .186/.327/.214 with no homers in 45 games. A switch-hitter, Coronil shot up to 6-foot-3 before signing and is still maturing physically as he builds out that frame, so some growing pains were to be expected out of the gate. That said, his 27 percent strikeout rate would set off alarms at any level, especially the DSL where pitchers are equally raw. Coronil barely got work as a righty bat and went 3-for-22 (.136) from that side, highlighting how he’ll need many more reps. He could get to average power as he adds strength but will need to improve the contact alongside the slugging development. Coronil drew strong reviews for his actions and instincts as an infield defender as an amateur, and with above-average speed, he should have decent range too. He actually spent the bulk of his time at third base in the DSL, and he has the arm strength for the deep throws there. But his athleticism should get him looks at shortstop throughout his Minor League time. Coronil will still be the age of an American high-school senior in his second pro season, so he isn’t worth writing off yet as he continues to build a foundation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two straight years of taking big international swings with Ethan Salas and Leodalis De Vries, the Padres changed tact after losing out on the Roki Sasaki sweepstakes to begin 2025. The organization had its complete $6,261,600 international signing pool open to it and spread the signings around, including giving $900,000 to Coronil – a Venezuelan shortstop who had trained with David Concepción Jr. at his academy in Cagua. A switch-hitter, Coronil moves quickly through the zone from both sides of the plate, though he looked inconsistent in the box at times before signing. His impact potential is very much dependent on his projection. Only 17 at time of signing, he shot up in height to 6-foot-3 and is still working to add on muscle. He has the frame for at least average pop, but his swing was geared for contact as an amateur, making some believe he’d work best as a future tablesetter. Even as he’s grown, Coronil has still drawn strong reviews for his defensive work at shortstop. He has fluid actions for the premium spot on the infield, and his instincts give him another leg up. Mix in above-average speed and arm strength, and there’s the potential for him to be an elite fielder. If he can improve his strength to go with the overall athleticism, there is tremendous upside and ceiling in Coronil’s profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming out of Southern California, Baro joined Capistrano Valley HS to play in a more competitive environment as a senior in 2023, and the move worked. The Mets took him in the eighth round but gave him $700,000 (third-round money) to sign away from an UCLA commitment. In his first full season, he finished second in the Florida State League with a .288 average and fourth with a .767 OPS before rounding out his age-19 season at High-A Brooklyn. His return to the Cyclones was a rough one as he finished with a .224/.282/.321 line, four homers and 84 wRC+ in 103 games before a hamstring injury ended his ’25 season in late August. Baro’s biggest step back last season was that he bit a lot more on non-fastballs out of the zone with chase rates above 40 percent on both sliders and changeups. Batting from an open stance before working with a toe tap, he still made a good amount of contact on fastballs, and his in-zone contact rate was impressive at 88 percent. That’s all to say there’s hope Baro could get back to an average hit tool with better swing decisions. Entering his age-21 season, the power in his 6-foot frame is still more projectable than actualized. The former Bruin recruit can move well, and he was efficient on the basepaths, going 28-for-30 in his steal attempts last year. He rotated between shortstop, second base and third with Brooklyn and improved his actions as ’25 went on, giving hope he could be an above-average fielder on the dirt (especially away from short). He’ll show a cannon of an arm but needs to work on his accuracy. Baro is trending toward utility man territory, pending him finding enough plate discipline to reach that status.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Southern California native headed to Capistrano Valley High School to play in a more competitive environment after a standout 2022 summer and boosted his stock enough to sign for $700,000 as a 2023 eighth-rounder, essentially getting third-round money to go pro instead of head to UCLA. He was a solid performer in his first full season and finished second in the Florida State League in average (.288) and on-base percentage (.368) while placing fourth in OPS (.767) over 84 games. Baro rounded out the year with 11 contests with High-A Brooklyn. Standing in the box at 6-foot-even, Baro runs a loose and easy operation as a left-handed hitter, starting with a slightly open stance while looking to jump on balls. He didn’t expand the zone often in the FSL and found the barrel well on pitches inside the zone, helping the belief he’ll be at least an average hitter. Baro didn’t stand out for his pop, however, topping out with a 104.4 mph exit velocity with St. Lucie, but there’s still a good amount of projectability in his frame. He could shoot balls harder if he’s a late bloomer as some scouts expect. Baro is expected to be an average runner by the time he reaches the Majors, and he’s shown good defensive actions as an infielder. The Mets were loaded on the dirt in the lower levels, causing him to move around with stops at shortstop, third base and second. He’d be even more valuable up the middle, though he has the arm strength for the hot corner, and New York officials plan to give him plenty of looks at the four and six, especially as he proves himself with the stick.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from a family of Boston-area sports fans, Baro headed to Southern California’s Capistrano Valley High School after a standout 2022 summer, and he continued to help his stock in a more competitive environment. He was committed to UCLA and looked like he was headed there before the Mets selected him in the eighth round in July and signed him well above slot at $700,000 – money typically associated with the late third round. Baro played seven games in the Florida Complex League after signing and went 6-for-19 (.316) with five walks and only one strikeout. Baro shows a loose and easy left-handed swing from his athletic 6-foot-2 frame, and Mets officials noted how much more physically developed he looked this winter after participating in the Get Wright position-player camp. His offense is aided by his excellent approach, and while the power only plays to the gaps now, he might still make enough contact to be a solid overall hitter at peak. The Golden State native is right on the cusp of being an above-average runner and could get faster if and when he adds strength as he enters his 20s. He has good actions on the dirt and showcases decent arm strength – attributes that would normally get him long looks at shortstop. However, the Mets are particularly loaded at the six at the lower levels, and Baro already has experience at second and third base. His best fit might be at second, where he can remain up the middle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring on the high school showcase circuit in 2019 and winning Gatorade's national baseball player of the year award in the shortened 2020 season, Kelley established himself as a first-round talent. But signability questions and the industry's reluctance to take prep right-handers that high dropped him to the second round, where he signed for $3 million. Poor conditioning led to a dreadful 2021 pro debut, but he looked significantly better last season, which he concluded by pitching well in Double-A during the organization's Project Birmingham. Kelley can run a four-seam fastball up to 98 mph but is more comfortable and generates more weak contact with a 92-96 mph two-seamer. He has regained his feel for a changeup that ranked among the best in the 2020 Draft, a low-80s weapon with fade and tumble. He lacks natural feel for spin but has made strides with an 82-85 mph slider with more than depth than sweep, and it could become at least an average third option with more consistency. Kelley was significantly overweight during his pro debut, which cost him arm speed and led to shoulder fatigue and forearm tightness. After improving his shoulder and core strength and dropping some weight, he did a better job of repeating his deliberate delivery in 2022. He cut his walk rate from 9.9 per nine innings in his debut to 5.5 last season, but his control and command still have to get much better for him to remain a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelley dominated the high school showcase circuit in 2019 before winning Gatorade's national baseball player of the year award the following spring. Though he was a consensus first-round talent, his signability and the industry's general skittishness about prep right-handers dropped him to the second round in the 2020 Draft, and the White Sox signed him for $3 million. His 2021 pro debut went poorly, as he dealt with shoulder fatigue and forearm tightness while logging a 7.61 ERA with 26 walks in 23 2/3 innings between Rookie ball and Low-A, but he has fared better this season. Kelley still shows the pure stuff that scouts loved as an amateur, starting with a four-seam fastball that ranges from 93-98 mph with running action and a low-90s two-seamer that induces groundball contact. His mid-80s changeup remains an advanced weapon with fade and sink. After showing inconsistent feel for spin in high school, he has made some progress with a sweeping slider that shows flashes of becoming at least an average third option. Kelley's conditioning started to go south during his truncated senior year and got worse in 2021, when he was significantly overweight and lost some arm speed. His ability to repeat his delivery and locate the strike zone also fell apart. He focused on improving his shoulder and core strength during the offseason, which has helped him throw more strikes, but he's going to have to make significant further gains with his control and command to be a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 55 | Overall: 55 Refugio (Texas) High never has produced a drafted player, though that's about to change in a big way in 2020. Kelley entered the year rated as the nation's top high school prospect and is regarded as Texas' best prep pitcher since Jameson Taillon went No. 2 overall in 2010. He repeatedly dominated on the showcase circuit last summer, including an Area Code Games performance that some scouts said was the best in the long history of the event. Few pitchers can create as much velocity with as little effort as Kelley, who can pump 93-96 mph fastballs and reach 98 with some running action. He already owns an advanced changeup with fade and sink, and he's willing to throw it in any count. His third-best pitch at the moment is a hard slurve in the low 80s that lacks consistency but should develop into at least a solid offering. Kelley combines his now stuff with feel for pitching. The Texas recruit pounds the strike zone and has the look of a frontline starter who could reach the big leagues before he turns 21. His strong, physically mature frame and the ease of his delivery should allow him to log plenty of innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bruns has teased with his upside since his days as an Alabama high schooler, when he displayed one of the best arsenals in the 2021 prep class but rarely the ability to harness it. Since signing for $2,197,500 as the 29th overall selection, he has continued to mitigate enticing stuff with a lack of control and health. He has totaled 235 strikeouts and 139 walks in 174 2/3 pro innings over four seasons, missing a month with a lat strain in 2022 and three months with back and rib issues last year. Bruns can overmatch hitters with three different offerings, including a mid-90s fastball that climbs as high as 98 mph with significant induced vertical break that carries it past barrels. His mid-80s slider with depth can be a wipeout pitch at its best, and he favors it over an upper-70s downer curveball that can be a hammer at times. He'll also flash an interesting mid-80s changeup with fade and sink but struggles to land it in the zone and doesn't trust it much. Though the Dodgers have helped Bruns clean up his mechanics, switching him from an over-the top delivery to a high three-quarters slot, that and working more out of the stretch hasn't produced more strikes. He might become a No. 3 starter if he could develop even fringy control, but he has yet to show that he can do that or handle a rotation workload. He's still intriguing as a lefty reliever with power stuff, though he'd have to locate his pitches better to be trusted in a high-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the biggest enigmas in the 2021 Draft, Bruns showcased some of the best pure stuff in that prep class but rarely displayed the ability to harness it on a consistent basis. He did win Gatorade's Alabama prep player of the year award as a senior and the Dodgers loved his upside enough to select him 29th overall and sign him for $2,197,500. He continued to display a tantalizing arsenal and a lack of control while going 0-12 with a 4.92 ERA in 51 starts over his first two-plus years as a pro. Bruns throws harder than most left-handers, operating in the mid-90s and topping out at 98 mph with a fastball that's tough to barrel thanks to its combination of velocity and carry. Both of his breaking pitches grade as well above average at their best, as his upper-70s curveball can be a true hammer and his mid-80s slider features plenty of sweep. His fading mid-80s changeup has the potential to become average, though he doesn't use it very often. Bruns has made some strides with his pitchability, cutting his walk rate from 9.1 per nine innings in his first full pro season to 6.2 in his second, though he'll need to refine his control much more to remain a starter. Los Angeles has helped him clean up his strong 6-foot-2 frame and his mechanics, having him use a high three-quarters slot rather than the over-the-top delivery he employed in high school. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter but a greater likelihood of becoming a power reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bruns was an enigma as an Alabama high schooler, displaying some of the best pure stuff in the 2021 class but also little track record of taming it. He showed more consistency as a senior, winning Gatorade state player of the year honors before Los Angeles selected him 29th overall and signed him for $2,197,500. He opened his first full season with 18 strikeouts versus just two walks in 8 1/3 innings in April before his control fell apart in May, and he never got back on track after missing a month with a mild lat strain. Bruns continues to show three pitches that can grade as well above average when they're on. His fastball can sit in the mid-90s and top out at 98 mph with good carry up in the zone, his upper-70s curveball can be a hammer and his mid-80s slider can sweep past hitters. He shows the makings of an average low-80s changeup with fade but barely has used it while working abbreviated outings as a pro. The Dodgers have helped Bruns clean up his body and his delivery, and he now throws from a high three-quarters slot rather than straight over the top like he did in high school. He still needs to improve the timing and consistency of his mechanics. He has the stuff to pitch in the front half of a rotation with even fringy control and command but has a long ways to go after walking 52 batters in his first 49 1/3 pro innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bruns had some of the best pure stuff in the 2021 high school class but also a mixed history of being able to harness it. After struggling to find the strike zone on the showcase circuit, he did a better job last spring en route to being named Gatorade's Alabama high school player of the year and becoming the Dodgers' first-round pick. The first of 14 straight pitchers selected by Los Angeles last July, he walked seven in five innings in Rookie ball after signing for $2,197,500. When Bruns is dialed in, he can work with a mid-90s fastball for several innings and reach 98 mph with good carry up in the strike zone. He also can spin a pair of plus breaking balls, an upper-70s downer curveball with quality depth and an 83-85 mph slider with nice tilt. He didn't need his low-80s changeup much as an amateur and will have to use it more often and improve its action against more advanced hitters. Bruns has a dynamic delivery with a high three-quarters arm slot and the ingredients to become a frontline starter if he can develop reliable control and command. He repeatedly lost feel for the zone in the summer before his senior season and had to dial his pitches back in order to try to get them over the plate. The Dodgers have a track record of helping prospects maximize their talents and were encouraged by the early returns from instructional league and winter camp.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shim was MLB Pipeline's second-highest ranked pitcher in the 2023 international class, and he opted to sign with the Pirates for $750,000 rather than stay home and get drafted in South Korea's KBO League. He has barely pitched since turning pro, with his debut limited to four Rookie-ball outings because of a right pectoral strain. A shoulder injury had sidelined him for all of the 2024 season when Pittsburgh included him in a July trade that brought Bryan De La Cruz from the Marlins. At 6-foot-4, Shim has the chance to grow into a big power pitcher with a four-pitch mix. His live arm can fire fastballs that flirt with triple digits and comfortably sit in the mid-90s. He generates high spin rates on a pair of solid breaking pitches: a curveball with 12-to-6 break at its best and a harder slider. He’s still working on gaining consistency with his changeup. Shim has a clean arm action overall and a feel for landing his stuff in the zone, but he needs reps to hone his craft after winding up on the shelf for much of his first two pro seasons. He also missed time with elbow issues in Korea in 2021, so there are legitimate questions about his durability. If he can stay healthy, he has the stuff to pitch in the front half of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shim decided to forego the draft in the Korean professional league (KBO) so he could sign with a Major League organization, and many were interested in one of the top arms in the 2023 signing class. Ranked No. 10 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospect rankings when the period opened on Jan. 15, Shim signed with the Pirates for $750,000, officially joining the organization on Jan. 26. The second highest-ranked pitcher in this year’s class, Shim has the chance to have a four-pitch mix with a very live arm. His fastball sits in the 94-96 mph range and can touch triple digits. It plays thanks to good spin and riding life up in the zone, reminding some of the heater of former Pirate Gerrit Cole, who Shim grew up idolizing. He has a really good feel for spinning a breaking ball, with a curve that has true 12-to-6 characteristics, and also is developing a harder slider. He has an emerging changeup that could give him a fourth viable option. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has a good feel for the strike zone and scouts liked his clean arm action and athleticism on the mound. He’ll be 19 for the 2023 season and it will be interesting to see what he can do with pro instruction to go along with strength and conditioning.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suarez signed for only $10,000 out of Venezuela in May 2018 but became a name to know after posting a 1.79 ERA with 47 strikeouts in 40 1/3 innings in the Gulf Coast League a year later. He missed 2020 due to the pandemic and then had his momentum further stifled by Tommy John surgery six starts into his 2021 campaign. Suarez didn’t look fully back on track until early summer 2023 and truly took off in his final 15 appearances between High-A Brooklyn and Double-A Binghamton, posting a 2.53 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 98 strikeouts and 21 walks over 74 2/3 innings in that span. To boot, he tossed back-to-back hitless outings over 13 innings in his first two starts in the Eastern League. The 6-foot-3 right-hander averaged 95.2 mph with his fastball in three Binghamton starts, proving he was still strong toward the end of first season with 100+ frames. His command of the pitch seemed to jump once he made a midseason adjustment of moving from the first-base side of the rubber to the third-base side. He also ditched a cutter that acted more like a bad fastball and went toward an 82-85 mph gyro slider that got more swing-and-miss in the zone, leading him to throw it 31 percent of the time at Double-A. Suarez also still has an upper-70s curveball and upper-80s changeup for additional looks. Suarez’s walk rate plummeted from 16.6 percent in his first nine starts to 7.2 percent over those final 15 following the mound change. That’s much more palatable for his rotation chances. He’s ticketed to become a Minor League free agent after 2024 and has a number of similarly aged starters ahead of him on the depth chart. But Suarez’s momentum makes him an interesting follow at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $10,000 signing out of Venezuela in May 2018, Suarez made a name for himself when he posted a 1.79 ERA with 47 strikeouts over 40 1/3 innings in the Gulf Coast League a year later. After working out stateside during the canceled 2020 season, the right-hander returned to make six starts for Low-A St. Lucie but managed just a 7.66 ERA in 24 2/3 innings. Elbow issues may have been to blame, and he underwent Tommy John surgery in June, ending his 2021 season there. During his Low-A time last season, Suarez was around 92-94 mph with the fastball, and he touched 95.5 mph with his hardest-thrown pitch of the season. Once he’s fully recovered, he could add more velocity, as some do following Tommy John. An upper-80s changeup remained his most-used secondary pitch because he’s shown the most feel for it early in his career, and a developing mid-70s curveball showed some promise with its vertical drop. The 6-foot-3 right-hander did take a step back in terms of his control with a 13.6 percent walk rate in the short 2021 sample, but that could have been related to the elbow issue. The Mets are still hopeful that Suarez, who is back on an early throwing program this spring, can be a serviceable starter in time. He’ll try to back up that optimism with an expected return to the mound in late 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suarez was far from a big name in the 2017-18 international signing period, when he signed for only $10,000 out of Venezuela in May 2018. His stock has steadily risen since then, aided by a promising first trip stateside in 2019. During that campaign, Suarez finished with a 1.79 ERA, 47 strikeouts and 16 walks over 40 1/3 innings in the Gulf Coast League. The right-hander spent the 2020 shutdown at the Mets’ facility in Florida with his fellow Venezuelans. He made six starts for Low-A St. Lucie before undergoing Tommy John surgery at the start of the summer. Suarez will likely next see a Minor League mound for his age-22 season in 2022. The 6-foot-3 right-hander threw in the low-90s with his fastball in the early days of his career, and given his size, there is some hope he could add more gas to the tank. He was up to 93-94 last fall. The changeup earned solid marks in the early days because of his feel for the offering, while the curve had been the secondary in need of the most development. The Mets were most pleased with how the breaking pitch came along in 2020 after it had been a focus during the entire summer and hope it can grow beyond being just a show-me pitch. Like so many others, Suarez just needs a chance to prove how far his stuff has come against actual competition. It’s unfortunate that the elbow surgery will cause him to miss more opportunities for experience, but the raw ingredients remain there for him to pick his progress back up once he does return.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: JSerra Catholic HS (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) has sent Austin Hedges and Royce Lewis to the big leagues and featured 13 NCAA Division I recruits on its 2021 team. The highest pick among that group was Silva, who gave up a UCLA scholarship to sign for $1,497,500 (nearly triple slot value) in the third round. Though he got tagged for a 5.88 ERA in Single-A during his first full pro season, he impressed scouts with what could be the best four-pitch mix in the system. Silva's quick arm generates 92-95 mph four-seam fastballs that reach 97 with a low release height that produces plenty of riding action up in the zone. He has good feel for spin and his plus 82-85 mph slider with horizontal and vertical life misses more bats than his solid upper-70s curveball with more depth. He's making progress with a mid-80s changeup with fade, though it gets too firm at times. Silva isn't very physical at 6-foot-1 and 185 pounds, and his control and command wavered when he tired in the second half of 2022. He needs to get stronger so he can do a better job of maintaining stuff and strikes. More shortstop than pitcher at the start of his high school career, he's a quality athlete.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: More of a shortstop than a pitcher when he first got to Laguna Beach (Calif.) High, Silva knew his future was on the mound when he transferred to JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) for his 2021 senior season. The Lions have spawned Austin Hedges and 2017 No. 1 overall pick Royce Lewis, and Silva was one of 13 NCAA Division I recruits on their team last spring. The highest pick among that group, he gave up a UCLA commitment to sign for $1,497,500, nearly triple his slot value in the fourth round. Silva isn't particularly physical at 6-foot-1 and 185 pounds, yet he has a quick arm that produces 92-95 mph four-seam fastballs that peak at 97 and feature a flat attack angle that provides tough carry up in the zone. He has a pair of quality breaking balls that miss bats, with his low-80s slider with horizontal action and depth perhaps slightly better than his upper-70s curveball with more downer break. He shows some feel for throwing a changeup with fade, though it needs more consistent velocity separation from his fastball. Silva provides strikes but like most young pitchers, he'll need to refine his command as he faces more advanced hitters. Despite his size, his arm speed and athleticism can help him remain a starter. To do so, he'll have to show that his stuff will hold up over a long pro season, and he has done that in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hicks starred for two years at Crowder (Mo.) JC before transferring to South Carolina for 2022, only to blow out his elbow in his second start and have Tommy John surgery that March. He turned down the Orioles as a 15th-rounder, came back for his redshirt junior year and joined the Astros as a 13th-rounder in 2023. A line drive broke his right forearm in April last season, costing him three months, though he returned to win Arizona Fall League pitcher of the year honors with 19 strikeouts in 14 scoreless innings. Hicks succeeds with command over pure stuff, with his two- and four-seam fastballs ranging from 91-94 mph but playing as average pitches because he locates them so well. His stuff is mostly average across the board, with his sweeping low-80s slider and fading mid-80s changeup his best secondary offerings. He also mixes in a tight mid-80s cutter and a fringy upper-70s curveball. While he lacks a true weapon, Hicks' arsenal is more effective than the sum of its parts because he mixes pitches and locations so well. He creates some deception with an upright delivery and low three-quarters slot that creates wide angle and a flat approach on his pitches. He has one of the highest floors among the system's pitchers and could help Houston at some point this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring for two years at Crowder (Mo.) JC, Hicks transferred to South Carolina for the 2022 season but blew out his elbow in his second start and had Tommy John surgery that March. The Orioles still selected him in the 15th round, but he returned to pitch well in a variety of roles for the Gamecocks the following spring before signing with the Astros as a 13th-rounder. He demonstrated some of the best command in the system while reaching Double-A midway through his first full pro season last year. Hicks' best pitches are his low-90s two-seam fastball with sink and a mid-80s changeup with fade and depth. Since turning pro, he has added a slightly harder four-seamer and a low-80s slider with more sweep to an arsenal that also includes a curveball in the upper 70s and a more traditional slide piece in the low 80s. His breaking stuff pales in comparison to the rest of his repertoire. None of Hicks' six offerings grades as better than average, but they work because he sequences them well and works all four quadrants of the strike zone. His low three-quarters slot creates wide angle and a flat approach trajectory that provides deception. He's on track to help the Astros as a back-of-the-rotation starter or middle reliever sooner than initially expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 45 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 As an amateur, Haskin drew comparisons to George Springer, another toolsy right-handed center fielder who starred at Avon (Conn.) Old Farms School. He was drafted in the 39th round in 2018 by the A’s and then by the Orioles with the 39th pick in 2020 out of Tulane, signing with Baltimore for full pick value ($1,906,800) after shooting up Draft boards as an eligible sophomore. He’s displayed both power and speed, but rarely both at the same time. A hamstring injury and then a left hip impingement that required surgery kept him from showing much in 2023, leading the Orioles to leaving him unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft, though Haskin went unclaimed. Haskin stood out in college for excelling with an unorthodox swing, featuring a dynamic, divey load that sometimes resulted in an awkward finish. He’s quieted his front side quite a bit since then, but has tinkered with his swing continuously as a pro. Standing taller and ditching the leg kick led to a breakout year in the power department at Double-A Bowie. Haskin then resurfaced an abridged version of the leg kick last year at Norfolk. He’s always managed the strike zone well (career .376 on-base percentage) and barreled balls consistently, and his power spike at Double-A came without any increase to his strikeout rate. However, Haskin did swing-and-miss a lot more in a small sample at Triple-A before the injury last spring. Haskin broke Springer’s stolen-base record in high school and his best tool is still his speed. He has good defensive instincts and a nose for the ball in the outfield, and is athletic enough to potentially remain in center field long term. He’ll need to get past his rash of injuries and prove durability behind a mass of outfield depth in the big leagues and at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming out of high school and then the 2020 Draft, Haskin was compared to All-Star outfielder George Springer, another toolsy right-handed center fielder who starred at Avon (Conn.) Old Farms School. Unlike Springer, though, Haskin was drafted twice — first by the A’s in the 39th round in 2018 and then by the Orioles with the 39th pick in the 2020 Draft. The O’s signed Haskin for full pick value ($1,906,800) after he shot up draft boards as a draft-eligible sophomore at Tulane. Haskin then displayed both power (five homers) and speed (22 steals) during a solid debut season in 2021, despite being limited to 83 games by a thumb fracture. He built on those results in 2022 at Double-A Bowie, where, propelled by a three-homer game in April, Haskin socked 15 homers with a .821 OPS in 109 games. The uptick in power didn’t come at the expense of plate discipline (.367 OBP), but Haskin did run much less (five steals in eight attempts) at Bowie than he did at lower levels. While Haskin did reach Triple-A in 2023, he missed time early with a hamstring injury, then was shut down again in late June and ended up requiring surgery to repair a left hip impingement. Haskin excelled in college with an unorthodox swing, utilizing a dynamic, divey load and sometimes awkward finish that drew comparisons to Hunter Pence. He’s quieted it up significantly since college, ditching the leg kick he used at Tulane and starting from a taller, less crouched position that allows him to leverage his contact against better pitching. Haskin has always managed the strike zone well and barreled balls consistently; with that better leverage, the power he used to flash showed up more regularly in 2022. In addition to that offensive potential, Haskin’s best tools are his glove and his speed. He’s a plus runner who broke Springer’s school stolen-base record in high school, with good instincts and a nose for the ball in the outfield. His athletic skillset suggests he will be able to remain in center field long term, giving Haskin the ceiling of a big league regular who can do a little bit of everything offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An athletic center fielder with both power and speed, Haskin has long drawn easy comparisons to All-Star outfielder George Springer, who preceded Haskin at Avon (Conn.) Old Farms School by a decade. One difference between them is Haskin was drafted twice, first by the A’s in the 39th round in 2018 and then by the Orioles with the 39th pick in the 2020 Draft. Haskin signed for full pick value ($1,906,800) after two years at Tulane, rocketing up draft boards as a draft-eligible sophomore. Haskin held his own at Baltimore’s instructional camp in 2020 and then enjoyed a solid debut season in 2021, posting a .381 on-base percentage with five homers and 22 steals while reaching High-A Aberdeen. He was, however, limited to 83 games by a thumb fracture. The easiest thing to notice about Haskin is his unorthodox swing, which has drawn comparisons to Hunter Pence. It’s dynamic and divey, with Haskin striding from a significantly crouched stance and sometimes finishing in awkward positions. He’s quieted it up some since college, ditching the leg kick he used at Tulane for better timing after showing some swing-and-miss during his first pro season. But Haskin also manages the strike zone well and barrels the ball consistently, and the power he flashed at Tulane showed up in spurts during his debut summer as well. He is a potential double-plus runner who broke Springer’s stolen base record at Avon Old Farms, and shows good instincts and an average arm defensively. The athleticism and skillset lead many to believe Haskin will be able to stick in center field long-term, giving him the ceiling of a big league regular who can do a little bit of everything offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Avon (Conn.) Old Farms School produced an athletic center fielder in 2008 who went on to become a first-round pick after three years in college and an eventual star with the Astros -- George Springer. A decade later, the Beavers spawned another toolsy center fielder who should go early in the 2020 Draft as a sophomore-eligible. A 39th-round pick by the Athletics in 2018, Haskin batted .372/.459/.647 as a Tulane freshman and helped his cause by performing well with wood bats in the New England Collegiate Baseball League during the summer. Though Haskin's right-handed swing can get long at times, he still manages to barrel the ball consistently. His stroke is quick and has nice loft, and once he fills out his lean 6-foot-2 frame he could produce 20 or more homers annually. He manages the strike zone well, though his ability to make contact with ease does cut into his walks. Haskin's speed grades as at least plus. Though he broke Springer's stolen base record at Avon Old Farms, he hasn't been especially aggressive on the bases in college. He tracks balls well in center field, showing good instincts and an average arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 When they signed Tavera in January 2022, his $1.7 million bonus constituted the largest the Orioles had ever given to an international prospect. An alum of the Zorilla Baseball Academy in the Dominican Republic, Tavera was one of the more highly coveted players in his class, with a good feel for hitting, emerging power and a plus run tool. He’s shown all of those qualities since entering Baltimore's system, performing well in the Dominican Summer League in his debut and even better in the Florida Complex League in 2023 as an 18-year-old. Scouts see a potential five-tool prospect in Tavera. A tall and athletic right-handed hitter, he stands out for his smooth swing and advanced approach at the plate at this early stage in his career. His plate discipline and pitch recognition skills enabled him to walk nearly as much as he struck out in the Florida Complex League last summer. Tavera also showed a tendency to get the ball in the air which should result in more power as he continues to fill out physically, and he is already one of the faster players in the system. He did miss some time due to nagging injuries last summer, limiting those will be a goal as he learns how to handle the physical demands of full-season ball in 2024. Tavera’s speed and athleticism give him a chance to be a plus defender in center field long term, with an average arm that doesn’t hint at a move to the corners. He is skilled enough defensively to handle himself at either if necessary, though. The test of better competition awaits, and if everything clicks, his ceiling could be of a first-division center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more highly coveted international players in his class, the well-rounded Tavera signed with Baltimore for a then-franchise record $1.7 million in January 2022 after catching the eye of team scouts while training at the Zorilla Baseball Academy in the Dominican Republic. He swung the bat well in the Dominican Summer League, showing strong plate discipline and pitch recognition for a young hitter. Tavera is a right-handed hitter with a smooth and effortless swing, and he has good bat-to-ball skills that complement a solid approach and sound fundamentals. His lean and athletic build produces emerging power that projects as a plus tool if his body continues to develop, and he’s already one of the faster players in the Orioles’ system. Those factors hint at a tantalizing combination of impact speed and power at the highest level. Defensively, Tavera profiles in center field with a strong chance to stick at the position. But he’s also athletic enough to move around, though his fringy arm might be suited better for left than for right. Like all players his age, Tavera’s skill set and instincts are expected to develop as he gets more experience in pro ball. He has a chance to blossom into a five-tool player if everything clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more well-rounded international players in the 2021 class, the highly coveted Tavera caught the eye of Orioles scouts while training at the Zorilla Baseball Academy in the Dominican Republic. He signed with Baltimore for a franchise-record $1.7 million bonus, the latest signal of continued growth the organization longed to see in Latin America. Tavera shows a solid approach and sound fundamentals from the right side of the plate, with a good feel for hitting and improving pitch recognition. His swing is smooth and effortless and the bat-to-ball skills are already there. He also features emerging power that projects as a plus tool if his body continues to develop as expected. Indeed, Tavera’s lean and athletic build makes him a strong runner with plenty of room to grow, hinting at the combination of impact speed and power at the highest level. A right-handed thrower with an average arm, Tavera profiles defensively in center field, with an ability to play all three outfield positions. Like all players his age, Tavera’s skillset and instincts are expected to develop once he enters pro ball. But he has a chance to blossom into a five-tool player with above-average tools across the board.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baum’s pro career is playing out as quite the feel-good story. Selected by the A’s in the second round of the 2019 Draft after three years at North Carolina as a starter, he returned from the pandemic unable to even play catch and spent nearly two years at the club’s Minor League Complex in Arizona trying to figure out how to throw a strike again. Sent to High-A Lansing to begin the 2023 season, he took off by posting a 2.59 ERA with 37 strikeouts and 14 walks in 31 1/3 innings before ending the year at Double-A Midland. Baum’s strong three-pitch mix suits his role as a reliever. He sits between 95-98 mph with his fastball and also brings a 12-6 curveball that flashes plus and a lights-out changeup that has been described by some as Trevor Hoffman-esque when it’s on. Baum utilizes his unorthodox over-the-top arm slot to his benefit since regaining his feel for pitching. His command was scattered early last season yet was still around the zone enough to get hitters to chase, and it improved as the year went along. After virtually two lost seasons, he is back on the big league radar, and it would not be a surprise to see him pitch his way to Oakland’s bullpen at some point in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After forgoing a chance to be a possible first-rounder in the 2016 Draft out of high school, Baum turned in three solid seasons at the University of North Carolina before the A’s selected him in the second round in 2019. He debuted in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League and posted a 4.70 ERA in 11 starts. Baum carries a solid four-pitch mix, bringing a fastball that can touch 94, and reached a bit higher at the A’s alternate camp in 2020, to go with two distinct breaking balls, an upper 70s curve and a low 80s hard slider that breaks low. He also throws a changeup that has some fade to it. Baum’s velocity mysteriously curtailed last year at the A’s alternate training site. After getting cleared during medical examinations, Oakland opted to shut him down for the year rather than sending him to the instructional league. A strike-thrower who has shown good command in the past, Baum projects as a mid-rotation type, though his fastball-breaking ball combo could eventually make him a candidate for the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies were investing in McGowan’s stuff and upside when they went over slot to sign the junior college product in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft. Injuries have prevented him from providing any true sense of what the return on that investment might be, with Tommy John surgery ending his first full season after two starts. He returned to toss a combined 42 2/3 innings between the regular season and the Arizona Fall League in 2023 and was limited again to 40 1/3 IP in 2024, this time because of a back issue. He did make it back to the AFL again to make up for some lost mound time but was shelved with a labrum injury that will likely cost him all of 2025. When he’s been healthy, McGowan still teases with a legitimate arsenal. It’s almost all sinker-slider, with a two-seamer that averaged north of 95 mph and topped out at 98 mph in '24 and it’s a worm-killer, leading to a career 1.70 GO/AO heading into 2025. His slider has gotten harder, now more consistently in the upper-80s with depth, and it can miss bats, and his firm upper-80s changeup is a third pitch he doesn’t use as frequently. McGowan needs more mound time to hone his craft and refine his command, and his strike-throwing regressed in '24, though it’s hard to know how much his injury impacted his ability to repeat his delivery and land his stuff in the zone. He has the mentality to fit in the bullpen should the Phillies move in that direction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at Eastern Oklahoma State Junior College, McGowan was a Top 200 Draft prospect in 2021 and went in the seventh round to the Phillies, who more than doubled the slot value to sign him for $577,000. They haven’t truly gotten a sense of what kind of pitcher they have because he needed Tommy John surgery after two starts of his first full season. He did return to throw 25 2/3 innings in 2023 before adding 17 more in the Arizona Fall League, but had his 2024 interrupted by nearly two months on the injured list with a back issue. Strong and physical, McGowan has legitimate power stuff when he’s fully healthy, led by a very effective sinker-slider combination. His two-seam fastball tops out in the upper 90s and sits around 94-95 mph with excellent sinking action that generates high ground-ball ratios. He can miss bats with his low-80s slider with good depth, and he has shown decent feel for a changeup, but he throws it too hard. Because of the three-pitch mix, the Phillies thought McGowan had a chance to start, and he could continue to get the opportunity to do so now that surgery is firmly in his rearview mirror. He could end up in the bullpen -- given the injury, the lack of consistent command and the fact that he’s strong but not that big -- where his competitiveness and sinker-slider duo could play up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McGowan spent two years pitching at Eastern Oklahoma State Junior College, opting to return to the Mountaineers' rotation rather than transfer to Kansas State for the 2021 season. He pitched well as part of a deep staff and caught the eye of the Phillies, who went over slot in the seventh round to sign him away from heading to Texas Tech for $577,000. There’s been very little return on investment so far as he barely pitched during his summer debut and then needed Tommy John surgery after just two starts in his full-season debut in 2022. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has the build and the three-pitch mix that should point to a future as a starter. At full strength, he can touch the upper-90s with his fastball, though he tends to comfortably sit around 93-94 mph and he’ll show both a two- and four-seamer. There’s good depth on his low-80s slider and he has shown solid feel for a fading mid-80s changeup, though he hasn’t thrown it as much and it can get too firm at times. McGowan gets high marks for his athleticism and competitiveness on the mound and while he can be around the zone, there was a lot of effort and recoil in his delivery as he entered pro ball, which impacted his command. Adding strength to his frame will help him iron out some of those delivery issues, with hope he can reach his big league starter ceiling once he fully returns from the elbow injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Only two pitchers cracked MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international list in 2024, and the highest-ranked arm on the list came at No. 25 in Franco. The Dominican right-hander signed with the Cardinals for $800,000, and while he’s since been outshined by other members of his signing class in Rainiel Rodriguez and Yairo Padilla, it’s worth remembering that he was the one who received St. Louis’ highest bonus in 2024. Franco didn’t flash impressive numbers out of the gate with a 6.16 ERA, a 1.63 WHIP and 37 strikeouts in 38 innings in the Dominican Summer League, but he showed some of the promise that made him a notable addition in the first place. Officially 16 on signing day, Franco was all about projection when he first joined the St. Louis system, and his arsenal has already shown an upward trajectory in year one. After sitting 91-93 mph with his tailing fastball as an amateur, he’s closer to the 93-95 mph range now, and entering his age-18 season, there’s still likely more room for velo. He improved a high-70s slurve to be more of a low-80s sweeping slider while his mid-80s changeup needs more refinement. DSL pitchers are typically wild, and Franco was no exception with a 13.3 percent walk rate in year one. Harnessing his pitches will be just as important as improving their individual pitch quality, and that’ll be part of the process as he expands his professional workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2024 international class was much more heavy on bats than arms. In fact, only two pitchers featured among MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international list this offseason, and the highest-ranked of the pair was Franco at No. 25. The Dominican Republic native signed with the Cardinals for $800,000 at the start of the signing window on Jan. 15, becoming the organization’s most high-profile addition of the period -- one in which it was down $500,000 in pool money after signing Willson Contreras in 2022. Having only turned 17 back in February, Franco is all about projection. He already stands 6-foot-3 and is expected to fill out as he heads toward and into his 20s. Even so, he already sits 91-93 mph with a tailing fastball that can help generate ground balls now, and considering his present arm speed, there’s a good chance he could be adding a few more ticks to that heater in time. He can sell his 85-87 mph changeup well out of his three-quarters arm slot, and he shows a high-70s slurve that he uses as his preferred offspeed weapon for now. The right-hander can pitch in the zone well from a fairly low-effort delivery at his current stage of development, though that deserves following if he does end up adding velocity. Creating better separation across his fastball and changeup will help too, but in general, he has the tools to be a potential Major League starting pitcher down the road.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Galiz originally agreed to sign with the Yankees for $1.5 million, but they backed out of the commitment in November 2020, nine days after his father Edgar died of COVID-related complications. Two months later, the Dodgers signed the top-rated catcher in the 2020-21 international class for the $812,500 they had remaining in their bonus pool, adding him to their collection of Venezuelan catching prospects that also includes Diego Cartaya and Yeiner Fernandez. Galiz made his U.S. debut at age 18 last year and slashed .235/.343/.471 in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. A former middle infielder, Galiz is quicker and more athletic than most catchers. He moves well behind the plate, has the hands to become at least a solid receiver and can deter the running game with plus arm strength. He impressed with his framing ability during his first season in the United States and also earns praise for his intelligence and maturity. Galiz's defense is ahead of his offense at this point. He does offer 20-homer potential from the right side of the plate thanks to his bat speed, growing strength and feel for driving balls in the air to his pull side. But he'll need to address swing-and-miss concerns because he gets overly aggressive and tends to pull off pitches, resulting in a 25.3 percent strikeout rate last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top catching prospect in the 2020-21 international crop, Galiz originally committed to sign with the Yankees for $1.5 million. But they backed out of the agreement in November 2020, nine days after his father Edgar died of covid-related complications. The Dodgers signed him two months later for the $812,500 they had left in their bonus pool, adding him to a collection of Venezuelan catching prospects that also includes Diego Cartaya and Yeiner Fernandez. Galiz's .218/.286/.287 batting line in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League belies his offensive potential. He's a right-handed hitter with bat speed and a patient approach who already makes consistent contact. He shows some feel for launching balls in the air and could develop 20-homer power once he gets stronger. A former middle infielder, Galiz is more athletic than most catchers. He's quick and agile behind the plate, where he shows soft hands and solid arm strength. He'll need time to develop but has the intelligence and maturity to make the most of his physical gifts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Galiz's world was shattered last November, when both his father Edgar died of covid-related complications and the Yankees backed out of an agreement to sign him for $1.5 million out of Venezuela. The top catching prospect in the 2020 international class, he wound up joining the Dodgers in January for the $812,500 they had remaining in their bonus pool. He adds to the club's strong collection of Venezuelan catching prospects that also includes Keibert Ruiz, Diego Cartaya and Yeiner Fernandez. Galiz is advanced enough on both sides of the ball that he could have come to the United States for his debut this summer. A patient hitter with a quick right-handed stroke, he's content to spray line drives to all fields. As he gets stronger and gets more aggressive with his swing, he could develop 20-homer power. A former middle infielder who's quite athletic for a catcher, Galiz is quick and agile behind the plate. He has the soft hands to become at least a solid receiver and has the arm strength to match. He also earns praise for his intelligence, leadership ability and maturity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After three collegiate seasons with at least a .300 average and 1.000 OPS, Taylor became the highest position player drafted in TCU history when he went 19th overall to the Rays in 2023. He was a Midwest League end-of-season All-Star in his first full season after slashing .269/.389/.513 with 14 homers and 26 steals in 84 games at High-A Bowling Green and overcame a 36.8 percent K rate to produce a 113 wRC+ in a late 30-game assignment to Double-A Montgomery. With 20 total homers and 29 steals, he was one of two 20/20 players in the Tampa Bay system alongside Carson Williams. Batting in the left side of the box, Taylor raises his right leg fairly high and stamps it down in time to generate lift and pull consistently. It helped make him a power threat both in college and the early days of the pros, and it was notable that 11 of his 21 hits went for extra bases (including six homers) during what may have been an otherwise tough time in the pitcher-friendly Southern League last year. He’s returned to Montgomery for 2025 with even more struggles, often whiffing through secondary pitches or popping the ball up leading to a low BABIP and overall average. Taylor may be just an average pure runner but he’s a solid athlete, capable of picking his stolen-base spots and moving around the infield. In other words, he’s a good fit for the Rays. He stopped playing shortstop after the promotion in deference to Carson Williams, and he’s a capable fit at third base with his arm strength. He also moves well enough for second, though that will take some transitioning to learn to read balls on the other side of the dirt. The Rays still have hopes that Taylor can move past the first baseball lumps of his life and adjust to upper-level arms, but his stock has undoubtedly taken a hit in his second full campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of his Utah high school, Taylor went to Texas Christian University and developed into the program’s first-ever position player selected in the first round. A well-rounded infielder without the loud tools of his fellow top prospects in the system, Taylor’s bat stood out as he finished with double-digit home runs, a batting average north of .300 and an OPS higher than 1.000 in each of his three collegiate seasons. The Rays selected him with the 19th overall pick in the 2023 Draft and signed him for a slot-value bonus of $3,880,100. Taylor’s ability to hit is his carrying tool, as he features a sweet left-handed swing with excellent bat-to-ball skills. He uses the entire field, controls the strike zone and rarely chases outside the zone. He’s willing to work deep counts but since he’s more of a hitter with power than a power hitter, he sacrificed some batting average while looking to pull and drive more balls near the end of his time at TCU. That trend followed him into the Rays’ system, as he hit just .242 with a 31.5 percent strikeout rate, but he managed 12 extra-base hits (including five homers) in his 25-game professional debut. Taylor is an average runner and a solid defender. He is probably best suited for third base, where he spent most of his time in college, but he’ll play some shortstop in his full-season debut. He’s not the quickest player in the field, but he has the instincts and arm to make it work on the left side of the infield. The Rays were quickly impressed by Taylor’s makeup, and while he likely won’t wow you with any one tool, his overall value and high floor put him near the top of a system loaded with infield prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hendrick had an up-and-down summer showcase circuit in 2019, at times looking like one of the top high school power hitters in the country and at times looking lost, though he did play for USA Baseball’s 18U team that won silver at the World Cup in Korea. His 2020 season in the Pittsburgh area was all but wiped out by the pandemic, but the Reds bought his power potential at No. 12 overall that summer and signed him for $4 million. Since then, the outfielder has had trouble finding his groove at the plate. After shaking off an injury-riddled first full season, Hendrick’s prodigious power did show up in games in 2022 as he homered 21 times in 388 at-bats. That unfortunately also came with a 37.2 percent strikeout rate across two levels of A ball, but there were some signs of things clicking, albeit inconsistently, cutting down the swing-and-miss a little and getting to his power over the last month and change of last season. He needs to slow himself down and let his barrel stay in the zone a bit longer, with more than enough strength if he can focus with a left-center-field approach, the left-handed hitter has a chance to produce more regularly. Hendrick is a good athlete who runs pretty well and can steal a base. While he’s best suited in right field -- where his strong arm also profiles well -- he’s shown he’s more than capable of playing center field if needed. He’ll need to find a way to make consistent contact to profile well as a regular in either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds certainly haven’t been afraid to take hitters with their top pick in Drafts over the years, going the position player route with their first selection in five of the last seven years. Three of those have been college players and two have been high school, with catcher Tyler Stephenson going No. 11 back in 2015 and Hendrick going No. 12 overall in 2020. The Pittsburgh area prep standout’s debut in 2021 was a bit of a mixed bag, showing off some of the offensive tools that made him worth a $4 million bonus, but also struggling to make contact and dealing with a leg injury that limited him to just 63 games in Low-A in 2021. Healthy in 2022, the power showed up, but consistency remained elusive. Hendrick still has the raw tools as a left-handed hitter that got scouts excited when he was in high school, with elite bat speed and strength which leads to tremendous raw power. He showed flashes of getting to that power during his debut, and while he showed patience (19.2 percent walk rate) he also struck out way too much (37.6 percent), a trend that continued in 2022. It was more about focusing too much on launch angle power to his pull side than it was about chasing out of the zone or poor pitch recognition, and there’s hope he can make adjustments to get back to a gap-to-gap approach that allows him to get to his power more naturally. Hendrick has trimmed down and is more agile and mobile than he’d been previously, with some thinking he’s moving well enough to play center field. He likely fits better in right field, where his above-average arm would play well, with the hope that he can find a level of consistency to fit the power profile for the corner spot as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Pittsburgh area isn’t exactly known as a huge amateur baseball hotbed, there have been some first-round quality bats to come out of the high school ranks in the region. Back in 2003, the Pirates took Neil Walker No. 11 overall and more recently, Alex Kirilloff went 15th to the Twins in 2016. In 2020, it was Hendrick’s turn when the Reds took him at No. 12 and signed him for $4 million, then saw him impress late in the alternate camp and during instructional league play. At his best, Hendrick’s left-handed bat is what stands out the most. He has as much raw power as anyone from the 2020 Draft and when he’s on time at the plate, it’s shown up in games against very good competition. He has very quick hands and plus bat speed, with leverage and loft and the ball jumps off his bat, while the bat head going through the zone sounds like a helicopter. He has, at times, listened to too many people in terms of his setup at the plate, forcing him get out of sync and leading to more swing-and-miss. There’s some rawness to his game, but that will be offset by the plus work ethic that was on display last summer after he signed. Hendrick isn’t a burner, but he is very athletic and runs well. The Reds will let him continue to play center field for now until he shows he can’t handle staying up the middle, but he has the arm and bat to profile well in right, so don’t be surprised to see him get time in both spots in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays handed MLB Pipeline's No. 23-ranked prospect in the 2021 international class a $2.35 million bonus due to their faith in Beltre's maturity as a player and a person. He was one of the most experienced players in the class, which showed in his approach soon after his pro debut with more walks (42) than strikeouts (33) over 53 games in the DSL. The past two seasons have seen Beltre continue to develop a strong base with his already-impressive fundamentals, but the focus has shifted to getting more out of him offensively. Beltre hit just .231 with Single-A Dunedin in 2023 with his six home runs and .675 OPS representing the ceiling of his power potential at the time. The Blue Jays have challenged Beltre to increase his exit velocities and start impacting the baseball more consistently. The early reviews are positive, as Beltre has put on nearly 15 pounds, but we’ll need to see if that can translate to power in actual games. Thirty home runs isn’t the goal here, but if the Blue Jays can get Beltre to drive the ball, some of those will start sneaking through the infield and some singles could turn into doubles. He has impressive zone control, so if there’s any power to come, he should have no trouble getting to it. Beltre is not a flashy defender, but he could stick at shortstop. This projection is all about his power, frankly, because Beltre’s entire profile is being a solid, across-the-board prospect otherwise. If the ball starts leaving his bat at 100 mph more often, his ceiling could change, and there’s still time for that to happen as he enters his age-20 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays handed MLB Pipeline's No. 23-ranked prospect in the 2021 international class a $2.35 million bonus due to their faith in Beltre's maturity as a player and a person. He was one of the most experienced players in the class, having played internationally with the Dominican Republic and travel ball teams in Florida. That summer, Beltre got in 53 games in the Dominican Summer League, where he hit .225 with a .391 OBP. In 2022, Beltre played 54 games, mostly in the Florida Complex League, and hit .250 with a .357 OBP. He’d begun driving the ball more, which will be key to his long-term value as a smaller hitter at 5-foot-9, but his exceptional fundamentals give the Blue Jays optimism on multiple fronts. He’s praised widely for his worth as a teammate and many within the organization believe these traits will enable him to raise his game with each promotion he earns. Beltre should be able to stay at shortstop, where his athleticism and instincts mesh well. There’s still plenty of development ahead for him, but he’s earned plenty of trust and profiles as a player who should self-teach well, absorb good coaching and make the proper in-game or in-season adjustments. It hasn't been a stellar season for him at Single-A Dunedin in 2023, but he is taking his walks and putting the ball in play at good rates as he establishes himself in full-season ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 24 prospect in the 2021 International class by MLB Pipeline, Beltre signed with the Blue Jays for $2.35 million. He was arguably the most experienced prospect in that class after playing internationally with teams from the Dominican Republic and playing extensively with travel ball teams in Florida. Debuting in the Dominican Summer League in ’21 at 17, Beltre hit .225 with two home runs and a .737 OPS, but impressed by taking more walks than strikeouts and finished strong. Many within the organization view Beltre as a potential “culture driver” given his natural leadership abilities and charismatic personality at such a young age. He pairs this with advanced fundamentals across the board. There is still room for him to mature physically, but Beltre should have enough arm to stick on the left side of the infield. His power is worth monitoring as he develops to see whether that develops into line drives or home runs, but he’s already shown the potential for an advanced plate approach and strong contact rate. While his athleticism is slightly above average now, that’s also worth monitoring as his 5-foot-9 frame fills out. At this point, Beltre simply needs reps. The Blue Jays are looking forward to seeing a full season from him, given his ability to analyze and adjust from game to game. He’s still far off with years of development ahead of him, but his sound fundamentals give the Blue Jays player development staff an exciting package with which to work.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 24 prospect in the ’21 international class by MLB Pipeline, Beltre signed with the Blue Jays for a bonus of $2.35 million. Beltre was arguably the most experienced 16-year-old in the class, having played internationally with teams from the Dominican Republic and moving on to travel ball teams in Florida. Many who have seen Beltre play immediately point to the charismatic teenager’s personality, work ethic, and dedication to his own growth, which they feel will help develop Beltre into an excellent leader as he matures. At the plate, Beltre is a natural hitter with a quick, efficient swing. It's a hit-over-power profile for now, but that could change as he matures physically. His throwing arm is just ahead of his fielding tool right now, but the Blue Jays believe he’ll stay up the middle long-term. Beltre has plenty of development ahead, but it’s easy to see the appeal of his tools and his intangibles fit what the Blue Jays love. In a system that’s not lacking for talent up the middle, Beltre represents the next wave with his bat as his likeliest carrying tool.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Rhodes became one of the top sophomore-eligible hitters in his class after the 2021 Draft was moved from June to July that year, going in the third round to the Orioles and signing for an above-slot $1.38 million. Rhodes was coming off a down year at Kentucky after breaking out as a freshman the previous year and raking in the Northwoods League that summer. The Orioles decided to bet on that small sample and then saw Rhodes enjoy a solid debut and reach Double-A down the stretch in 2022. He plateaued a bit back at Bowie in 2023 and didn’t hit much during an extended stay in the Arizona Fall League.
