Rhodes did tap into his raw power more in ‘23, hitting 17 homers with 22 doubles in 108 games at Bowie. But more than two full seasons in, he’s yet to duplicate his early success at Kentucky. The power stood out last summer as the most improved of the blend of tools that have always been Rhodes’ calling card and still has a chance to be solid across the board. But he’ll need to keep working to refine his overall approach and avoid the extended slumps that have zapped his productivity for long stretches. Where Rhodes is not searching for success is on the bases. He doesn’t run all that often, but when he does, he’s used his plus straight-line speed to convert 30 of 31 stolen-base chances as a pro. That speed and his strong arm help him profile at either corner outfield spot, and while he is athletic enough to handle center in a pinch, those opportunities dried up entirely last year. The versatility is a plus, and points to a possible fourth-outfielder role in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles went all-in on college outfielders in the 2021 Draft, selecting four with their first five picks in executive vice president and general manager Mike Elias’ third Draft at the helm. Their third-round selection was Rhodes, who had become one of the top sophomore-eligible hitters available after the Draft was moved from June to July that year. Rhodes was coming off a down year at Kentucky, after bursting onto the scene with a .426/.485/.672 line in 17 games as a freshman and then raking in the Northwoods League that summer. The Orioles signed him for an above-slot $1.38 million, and after a solid debut, watched him reach Double-A Bowie down the stretch in 2022. He slumped initially at the level after hitting .259/.389/.428 with five homers in 58 games at High-A Aberdeen, despite missing three weeks with a minor wrist injury. Rather than one otherworldly tool, Rhodes’ calling card is a blend of tools with the potential to be solid across the board. He’s strong enough to flash power that could be at least average, with a quick right-handed swing but an inconsistent approach that leads to slumps. He’s always had the ability to work the count and showed good plate discipline both at Kentucky and throughout his Minor League career. Rhodes began using his plus straight-line speed more on the bases last summer, swiping 16 bags without being caught (he owns a 100 percent SB success rate in pro ball, with 16 steals in 16 tries). He shifted from third base to left field to right field during his time at Kentucky but is strictly an outfielder now, playing predominately right during his first two seasons. His strong arm profiles well out there, and he’s athletic enough to move across all three spots and even play center in a pinch. That versatility should help him develop into a bat-first regular who swings his way into the lineup if he continues to hit consistently at the higher levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles have shown an appetite for drafting college bats under executive vice president and general manager Mike Elias and in 2021 went big on college outfielders, selecting four with their first five picks. Their third-round pick was Rhodes, who became eligible for the 2021 Draft after it was moved from June to July and quickly became one of the top sophomore-eligible hitters available in his class. Rhodes had turned heads by hitting .426/.485/.672 in 17 games during his shortened freshman season at Kentucky, and continuing to rake in the Northwoods League that summer. Then his slumped in ’21, but still signed for an above-slot $1.38 million. Rhodes next got his feet wet at Low-A Delmarva, posting a .343 on-base percentage and two homers in 23 games alongside fellow ’21 draftees Colton Cowser, Reed Trimble and Donta’ Williams (all outfielders), then reached Double-A in his first full season in 2022. Rhodes stands out for his potential for solid tools across the board, with the strength for at least average power and a strong but inconsistent approach. Rhodes’ slumps at Kentucky came when he tried selling out for power, compromising the quick right-handed swing that made him look like an advanced hitter as a freshman. He’s always had the ability to work the count and showed good plate discipline at Delmarva, walking at an impressive clip in a small sample. Rhodes has plus straight-line speed but doesn’t show it much on the bases, and a strong arm that’s allowed him to move around defensively since starting college. He shifted from third base to left field to right field during his time at Kentucky, and played mostly right field during his pro debut. The Orioles also gave Rhodes some early reps at first base; he’s athletic enough for the versatility to be a good thing, with some believing he may be quick enough to even merit a look in center field. If Rhodes hits consistently, he has a chance to develop into a bat-first regular who swings his way into the lineup every day at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: What's better than one member of the De Los Santos family in your system? Two. The Pirates signed Yordany De Los Santos in 2022, then circled back to sign his younger brother Johan in 2025, who was No. 23 on MLB Pipeline's Top 50 International Prospects list for that signing period. After getting $2.25 million to join his brother in the system, Johan had a very strong professional debut in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .353 with a .911 OPS while not turning 17 until late July. He came stateside and got off to an equally solid start in the Florida Complex League in 2026. Swinging the bat from the left side of the plate, De Los Santos has a feel for the barrel with a line-drive approach and solid bat speed. He's athletic and twitchy in the box, and while he's hit-over-power, he could add strength to his 5-foot-11 frame with impact to come. He's an above-average runner who has already shown he likes to be aggressive on the basepaths. Primarily a shortstop as an amateur, De Los Santos has the actions and an above-average arm to give him a chance to play the premium position going forward. He's been splitting time between short and second base thus far in his blossoming pro career, as the Pirates like to encourage versatility to their young prospects, giving them options if De Los Santos' bat develops like it looks like it might as he rises through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The De Los Santos family must be doing something right. At least the Pirates think so. In 2022, they gave Yordany De Los Santos $1.2 million to sign. Three years later, at the start of the 2025 international signing period, they signed his younger brother Johan for $2.25 million. The younger De Los Santos ranked No. 23 on MLB Pipeline's 2025 Top 50 international prospects list and was one of the youngest players in the class, not turning 17 until late July. A left-handed hitter with a feel for finding the barrel, De Los Santos has a line-drive approach with a sound swing and bat speed. He's athletic with twitchy actions and could add strength to his 5-foot-11 frame with perhaps more impact to come, though he's likely to always be a hit-over-power type of offensive performer. He has good speed with the chance to make plays on the basepaths. With good actions and an above-average arm, De Los Santos has largely played only shortstop and will likely get plenty of reps at the premium position as he embarks on his professional career. The Pirates like to introduce multiple positions to players at a young age to encourage versatility, so don't be surprised if the younger De Los Santos sees some time at second base in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Marlins for $17,500 out of Mexico in May 2022, Vargas was an on-base machine at the Dominican and Florida complexes in his first two Minor League seasons, and he popped enough to be included in the July 2023 trade with the Mets for David Robertson. His first full season in the Mets organization was limited to only 37 games because of wrist tendinitis, but he got a fuller workload in 2025, where he zoomed past Single-A St. Lucie after 13 games and finished with a .239/.328/.296 line, one homer and 38 steals in 95 contests with High-A Brooklyn. At 5-foot-11, Vargas isn’t a commanding presence in the box, and his best offensive asset is the fact that he doesn’t expand the zone much at all for someone his age. After he slugged just .238 in the Florida State League in 2024, he got a mulligan for his power because of the wrist injury, but the pop didn’t show up much at all in ’25 either. That wasn’t just an issue with Coney Island (where lefty sluggers tend to struggle); he slugged .330 at home and .260 on the road, in part because of a batted-ball profile that’s overly focused on going the other way. There’s still an intriguing floor here. Vargas can flash impressive home-to-first times when he gets a jailbreak run out of the box, and while he won’t slug, he can add extra bases by stealing bags in bunches. Some consider him the best defensive shortstop in the system with good hands and range, and because of roster crunches, he got time at second base in Brooklyn. He could be above-average to plus with the glove at either spot, lowering his need to show much more than a strong OBP at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas may have signed for only $17,500 out of Mexico in May 2022, but he hit the ground running in the Marlins system with a .319 average, .421 on-base percentage and .877 OPS in 53 games as a Dominican Summer League All-Star that season. He was again an on-base fiend in the Florida Complex League in 2023, and that was enough for the Mets to acquire him that July in a deal for David Robertson. Vargas got a little time at Single-A late in 2023 and was set to take on full-season ball for a longer stretch but was limited to only 37 games because of various bouts with wrist tendinitis. The left-handed hitter slashed just .208/.369/.238 over 168 plate appearances in his age-19 season, but the wrist problems basically made that campaign a wash. When Vargas did play, he continued to display the advanced approach at the plate that excited New York officials in the first place, and his 20.2 percent walk rate was ninth-best among 499 Single-A hitters with at least 100 PA. His already below-average power was sapped by the wrist problem , and it didn’t exactly return during his run at High-A in 2025. Vargas has fringy speed but has shown solid baserunning acumen to this early point in his career. He split his time between shortstop and second base in 2024 with some time at third mixed in, and he’s likely a better fit at second, where he could be above average if he sticks there. He might be best served as an OBP-driven middle-infield option off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas signed with the Marlins for only $17,500 out of Mexico in May 2022 (the same month he turned 17) and instantly became of Miami’s best lower-level hitters, producing a .319/.423/.456 line over 53 games in the Dominican Summer League that helped become a league All-Star. Vargas kept producing stateside during his time in the Florida Complex League and joined the Mets in the David Robertson trade at the Trade Deadline. New York got the infielder time with Single-A St. Lucie before the year was out, and he finished 2023 with a .275/.432/.389 line with two homers, 53 walks and 38 strikeouts over 54 games. The 6-foot left-handed slugger was the only Minor Leaguer aged 18 or younger who walked more than he struck out over 250 plate appearances or more, emphasizing how strong his approach and plate discipline were compared to his peers. If anything, Vargas may not have swung enough on pitches in the zone, leaving some potential hits on the table in favor of those walks. While his power value comes more in the gaps, he makes that profile work by distributing the ball almost evenly to the pull side, center and opposite way. Vargas will swipe some bags with his fringy speed, but that’s more out of savvy than wheels. Both the Mets and Marlins have moved him around the dirt with time at short and third base, but he’s best fit for second where his actions and arm strength are a solid fit. He projects as a high-OBP-type who can play up the middle, while adding strength to his profile would make him an even more complete offensive threat.

Vargas has fringy speed but has shown solid baserunning acumen to this early point in his career. He split his time between shortstop and second in 2024 with some time at third mixed in, and he’s likely a better fit at second, where he could be above-average if he sticks there. mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Hit: 35 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Tears didn’t get consistent playing time until his junior year at Tennessee and broke out for that Men’s College World Series championship team, hitting .324/.427/.643 with 20 homers in 71 games. The Padres used their first compensation pick after the fourth round (a selection they received for losing Josh Hader in free agency) on the outfielder and signed him for $525,200. Tears dealt with a right hamstring strain in his first spring and never quite got going at Single-A Lake Elsinore, finishing with a .227/.320/.385 line, 13 homers and a 96 wRC+ in 107 games. The left-handed slugger gets going with a big leg kick that helps him generate big bat speed, but he got exposed for being too rotational and getting too long with his swing in his first campaign against pro pitching. Tears especially struggled against changeups with a whiff rate of 58 percent against them, per Synergy, often showing an inability to manipulate the barrel going down and away from him, and that led to reverse splits in the California League. When he does make contact, it can be loud, and there’s still hope to be found in his exit velocities. Tears is a better runner underway than he is out of the gate, and he was only 6-for-11 in stolen-base attempts in 2025. Once he gets the legs going -- and isn’t being bothered by the hamstring -- he can get moving in the outfield and he has the arm strength for right field. Tears spent much of last season at DH, however, and even mixed in three starts at first base. His priority in year two will be tightening up the swing in search of getting back to being the toolsy star he was as a Volunteer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 55 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 Tears redshirted at Tennessee in 2022 and then got only 56 at-bats due to hamstring and oblique injuries in 2023. No bother. Facing Draft eligibility last spring, the outfielder became one of college baseball’s toolsiest players and was a force for a Volunteers squad that went on to win the Men's College World Series. He finished with a .324/.427/.643 line and 20 homers in 71 games. The Padres selected Tears with their first compensation pick after the fourth round (the selection they got for losing Josh Hader in free agency) and signed him for slot value at $525,200. Standing tall in the box as a left-handed hitter, Tears loads with a big leg kick and generates big bat speed that helps him drive the ball all over the park. He has at least plus raw power that helped him generate impressive exit velocities, even when adjusting for college and metal bats, and that pop was a huge piece of his Draft profile. There are more questions about his overall hit tool. He showed improved swing decisions as a junior but still ran just a 69.6 percent contact rate on his swings. A flat bat path could be partly to blame and could cap his overall offensive profile. Tears is a better runner underway than he is out of the box or off the bag, so he may not be a huge stolen-base threat. But the running ability certainly helps him in the outfield. For Tennessee, he played mostly right field, where his plus arm strength certainly is an asset, but he could be average in center as well. Tears hasn’t played an official Minor League game entering 2025, and pro pitching will test just how much he can rely on his pure strength as a hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds jumped into the college pitching pool with both feet at the start of the 2023 Draft, taking Wake Forest’s Rhett Lowder No. 7 overall and then going from the ACC to the SEC to nab Floyd out of Louisiana State at No. 38. He had an uneven year that did include a record-tying 17 strikeouts in a nine-inning College World Series game in the finals against Florida. So far, the Reds are 1-for-2, with Lowder already reaching the big leagues. Floyd has yet to throw a professional inning following shoulder surgery in late May 2024. Given a clean bill of health, Floyd should be able to show the Reds what he’s all about in 2025. In 2023, his fastball had been up to as high as 98 mph, averaging around 94. It’s a heater that plays well because of its spin rates and carry up in the zone to go along with good induced vertical break. He hadn’t been throwing his low-80s slider for as long as his upper-70s curve, but it became more of a go-to pitch with good depth. He didn’t throw his changeup that frequently, but he showed good feel for the low-80s cambio. Floyd has a quick arm and a delivery without too much effort with the kind of repertoire that could fit in the middle or back of a rotation, especially if he can refine his command and land his secondary stuff in the zone more. His fastball and slider would play in a relief role if it comes to that, but step one will be for him to get through a healthy season, with the Reds monitoring his workload carefully in a first year after missing 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid prospect when he pitched for his Georgia high school, Floyd went on to Louisiana State after he wasn’t taken in the shortened 2020 Draft. He pitched well out of the Tigers’ bullpen as a freshman and showed flashes -- albeit inconsistently -- in a Draft-eligible sophomore year, and came back to campus when he went unselected a second time. He was a full-time starter in 2023 with mixed results, though he tied a College World Series nine-inning record with 17 strikeouts in the finals against Florida. The Reds took him No. 38 overall and signed him for $2.1 million. As was the case with all the college arms the Reds took in 2023, Floyd didn’t throw a competitive pitch after signing, and he didn’t throw one for all of 2024 either as shoulder surgery ended his year before it began. His fastball velocity had ticked up from 2022 to 2023, when he averaged 94 mph and topped out at 98. The pitch plays up because of its induced vertical break and high spin rates that produce carry up in the zone. His newer low-80s slider has good depth, and he relies on it more than his upper-70s curve. There’s feel for a fading low-80s changeup, but he doesn’t mix it in that often. With a quick arm and easy velocity, Floyd has the stuff to remain a starter in the middle-to-back of a big league rotation. He’ll need to refine his command while tightening up his secondary offerings and landing them for strikes more consistently. He has a pretty high floor as a reliever who relies on his fastball if starting doesn’t work out, but the first order of business will be to get him on a mound for healthy, competitive innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De Jesus was one of the top prospects from the 2018 international class, and he started to play some shortstop after the Dodgers signed him for $500,000. He eventually came to the Blue Jays in a ‘22 trade from the Dodgers along with Mitch White and made good on his potential in ‘23 with a full-season assignment to High-A Vancouver. There, De Jesus put up an .806 OPS and played through a shoulder injury which required a procedure at the end of the season, so it will be interesting to see how his game develops when fully healthy. De Jesus played more freely in ‘23, letting his natural athleticism show. He’s far likelier to end up at third base long term than shortstop and will work in some first base in 2024. He has a very strong arm, which helps at the hot corner. Some added power would bolster this projection after he hit 11 home runs a year ago, and while his start to ‘24 could be slowed by last year’s injury, there’s enough pop in there for De Jesus to hit at least 15 annually. There’s still belief that De Jesus, who turns 23 in March, could take another step as he climbs to Double-A, but he’ll need one of his skills to pop if he’s going to stand out from the rest of Toronto’s infield depth. He did a better job of limiting strikeouts in ‘23, but that was an issue for him the year prior (151 in 114 games), so that is worth monitoring as he faces more advanced pitching. This feels like a fork-in-the-road season for De Jesus.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De Jesus was one of the top prospects from the 2018 international class, and he started to play some shortstop after the Dodgers signed him for $500,000. He chased power at times early in his Rookie-level debut, batting .281 with a .732 OPS over 57 games, but he came on strong late. Some of that power came in 2021 at Single-A Rancho Cucamonga, where he hit 12 home runs while posting a .268 average and .834 OPS over 87 games. De Jesus was in the middle of another nice season at High-A in 2022 when the Blue Jays acquired him from the Dodgers alongside Mitch White. While his Blue Jays debut was underwhelming over 24 games at High-A Vancouver, the club was very impressed with his maturity, as the fully bilingual De Jesus quickly bought in and became a good teammate. Toronto’s program has also helped him physically, with optimism that more power will follow at the plate. Defensively, De Jesus can play short and third base but is likelier to end up at the hot corner, where his plus arm can make any necessary throw. He’ll need to cut down his strikeout rate at the plate, though, after whiffing 151 times in 113 games last season. If that happens alongside a power surge, De Jesus is another candidate to jump in 2023. Alongside Adrian Pinto, the Blue Jays have done a solid job of acquiring prospects in Major League trades recently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top third-base prospects in the 2018 international class, De Jesus moved to shortstop after signing for $500,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His 2021 full-season debut as a 19-year-old was a tale of two halves. He got too power-hungry early on and batted .210/.315/.395 with a 38 percent strikeout rate in the first two months, then made adjustments and hit .314/.440/.490 with a 25 percent whiff rate afterward. De Jesus has enough strength and bat speed that he doesn't have to lengthen his right-handed stroke and swing for the fences to hit for power. He did a better job of using the opposite field in 2021 and could become an average hitter with solid pop if he stays under control. He drew 45 walks in his final 54 games and made more consistent hard contact once he started making better swing decisions. Six-foot-2 and more physical than his listed 170 pounds, De Jesus started getting more looks back at the hot corner in 2022. He has below-average speed, though his surprisingly smooth actions and well above-average arm strength help him make plays at shortstop. His range projects as fringy at best at short but he could be at least an average defender at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best third-base prospects in the 2018 international crop, DeJesus moved to shortstop after signing for $500,000 out of the Dominican Republic. When he made his pro debut the following summer, he earned a swift promotion to the Rookie-level Arizona League and didn't look overmatched despite being the circuit's second-youngest batting qualifier (age 17). The coronavirus pandemic robbed him of a chance to build on that momentum in 2020, though he did attend the Dodgers' Dominican instructional league program. Though DeJesus is young and inexperienced at the plate, he shows the potential to hit for both average and power. He has a compact right-handed stroke and already has begun to add strength and bat speed that eventually could pay off with 20 homers per season. To reach his offensive potential, he'll need to improve his pitch recognition and tone down his aggressiveness. Presently a fringy runner, DeJesus will have below-average speed at best once he fills out. He's smoother and has more range at shortstop than expected thanks to a quick first step, and he has reliable hands and solid arm strength. While he has a chance to stick at short or handle second base, most scouts outside the organization think he'll end up on the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Graham and Jace Jung were good friends, college rivals and even roommates on their way into the 2022 Draft, and the Tigers made them organizational teammates by following their first-round pick of Jung with a second-rounder on Graham. His 20-homer, 34-steal season at Oklahoma was historic, but Graham has struggled to translate that dynamic offensive package to the pros, partly due to injuries that limited him to 84 games over a year and a half in the Tigers' system. Though Graham has learned to temper his aggressive approach at the plate, it has yet to translate into consistent quality contact, particularly against breaking balls and offspeed pitches. He still hits a fair amount of balls on the ground. He had surprising struggles against left-handed pitching last year, from strikeout rate to limited extra-base power. Though the Tigers moved Graham around the infield last year, they had him primarily at his natural position at short, where his athleticism, body frame and arm play better than at third. This could be a key season for Graham, who needs to start moving up the system. His reputation as a hard-nosed player and tough competitor is well-earned, so watching him take on the challenge should be interesting to watch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers went heavy on college bats in the 2022 Draft, and while Jace Jung was the highest-profile one, Graham fit their hitters' prototype. Though he wasn’t a top recruit and went undrafted out of high school, he made himself into a top-class college bat, becoming the first NCAA Division I Player in 18 years with 20 homers and 30 stolen bases in the same season. The Tigers selected him in the second round, signed him to an above-slot $1.8 million bonus and assigned him to Single-A Lakeland for a challenging introduction to pro ball. Though Graham has a solid line-drive swing that produces power without having to push for it, he can still fall into bouts of overaggressiveness at the plate, hunting fastballs at the expense of vulnerability to breaking balls. His plus speed plays well on the basepaths, but that hasn't translated into doubles and triples yet. He showed an ability to hit to the opposite field during his short stint in Lakeland. He has been rated average defensively at shortstop, but his strong arm could lead to a move to third base, especially if he adds more strength. He even played outfield in the Cape Cod League during college. Ultimately, Graham’s athleticism could fit him into the Tigers’ mold of infielders who can play all over the diamond and provide offensive impact at multiple positions. Ankle issues and muscle strains have kept him from truly getting going in 2023, but the raw pieces of his profile remain exciting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Many saw Moore, the son of current Rangers senior advisor Dayton Moore, as a potential first-round pick after he posted a .942 OPS and smashed 16 homers for Arkansas in 2021. He did not back that up with another strong season in 2022 as his OPS dipped to .801 with a .232 average. The Brewers liked his bounceback potential enough to take him No. 72 overall that July, but his first full season in High-A was fairly nondescript. He’ll get to try to rediscover his groove with a new organization after joining the Phillies in November in the trade that sent Oliver Dunn to the Brewers. At his best, Moore is a savvy middle infielder whose whole maybe be better than the sum of his parts. He switch hits but has historically been better with more thump from the left side, though he was a bit more impactful the other way during what was largely a rough first full season. Even though he’s listed at 5-foot-9, there is some raw pop in there and he tends to have a solid idea of the strike zone, limiting strikeouts and drawing his fair share of walks. With solid contact skills, he’ll need to rediscover the ability to impact the ball to take the next step. Moore is showing he is a very capable defender on both sides of second base, where his instincts, hands and ability to slow the game down are assets. An above-average runner, he has more than enough range for short, but if he’s going to stick in one spot as an everyday player, it’s likely going to be second base because of his fringy arm strength. His feel for the game and defensive acumen give him a high floor as a utility infielder-type in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Royals exec and current Rangers advisor, Dayton Moore, Robert looked like he was hitting his way to Draft prominence when he homered 16 times and finished with a .942 OPS in 61 games in his first full season at Arkansas in 2021. His dinger output halved the following spring, and he hit just .232 with an .801 OPS, causing his stock to fall. But he was still taken in Competitive Balance Round B by the Brewers in July 2022 and signed for a little below slot at $800,000. After playing at Single-A Carolina during his pro debut, Moore went to Australia for winter ball and showed signs of his old self with a .294/.378/.516 line in 40 games with Brisbane. He wasn’t able to follow that up with a move to High-A Wisconsin in 2023, finishing with a .682 OPS, and is now hoping a change of scenery will help ignite his bat after he got traded with Hendry Mendez to the Phillies in return for Oliver Dunn in November. A switch-hitter, Moore has been more powerful and productive from the left side, though that trend flipped a bit in 2023. Listed at 5-foot-9, it’s sneaky pop overall but likely to be below-average compared to his peers. He typically does a good job of not expanding the zone and should make enough contact with good bat speed from either side to be a potential average overall hitter in the end, though his High-A experience was relatively rough. The former Razorback has the hands, internal clock and instincts to be an impressive defender up the middle. He moved over to second in college in deference to Jalen Battles but got a few more looks at the six in his first taste of the Minors. Fringy arm strength will likely keep him at the keystone long term, and he could be an absolute asset there. That glovework and his high motor give him a high floor, and he could be everyday quality if he can swing it like he did in Australia.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morales was a solid performer in his first two seasons at Miami but broke out even bigger with a .408/.475/.713 line and 20 homers as a junior in 2023. The Nationals were pleased to see him still available in the second round, took him there and signed him for $2.6 million. Morales’ first full season was limited by a serious left thumb injury, and he returned to Double-A Harrisburg briefly to begin 2025. After an early promotion to Triple-A Rochester, he hit .249/.330/.401 with 11 homers in 95 games at the Minors’ top level. A productive stint in the Puerto Rican Winter League (three homers in 15 games) helped buoy his stock heading into 2026. A hulking presence, Morales still brings the plus raw power that made him a college star. His 105.9 90th-percentile exit velocity and 48.8 percent hard-hit rate at Triple-A both rated above the Major League average and speak to his slugging ceiling. But when he did make contact, so much was on the ground or hit the other way because of a long swing that it kept his power from showing up as it should have in games. The same length also made him late on fastballs, leading to heavy whiffs on four-seamers, and he looked at times more ready to swing hard than to swing at good pitches. Morales looked like he was pulling the ball in the air more efficiently in PR this winter, a hopeful sign for his age-24 season. Though he has plus arm strength, he’s been trending toward first base since reaching Rochester. The Nationals plan to get him time at both corners but note that Morales could be more of a defensive asset as a big target at the cold corner, where the offensive bar to slug is even higher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morales performed all three years at the University of Miami and exploded in his junior year with a .408/.475/.713 line and 20 homers in 61 games. The Nationals were happy to take him when he was available in the second round in 2023 and signed him for above slot at $2.6 million. Continuing with that enthusiasm, Washington opened Morales at Double-A Harrisburg in his first full season, only for the corner infielder to suffer a serious left thumb injury on a plate at the plate in his 37th game on May 18. He didn’t return to the Senators lineup until Aug. 9 but hit .304/.412/.426 over his final 32 games. So much of Morales’ 2024 was defined by the thumb, even after he returned because of the mental battle dealing with an injury to a key piece of the hitting apparatus. There’s hope that a full offseason of additional rest and recovery will help take away the concerns of a ghost injury and get Morales’ plus raw power to play in games again. At his best, he’s a large presence in the box with significant strength that could produce loud contact. At his shakiest, he struggles against sliders and changeups and gets on top of the ball too much, leading to groundball contact. With his good arm strength, Morales could sprinkle in some third base still, but with Brady House ahead of him and Cayden Wallace acquired last year, his best chance for upper Minors at-bats is at the first base spot. He’s still learning the nuances of the position but will need the power to return to collegiate levels soon if he’s going to be valuable at the cold corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 131 prospect in the 2020 Draft, Morales had a strong commitment to the University of Miami and went undrafted in the shortened process as a result. He was a three-year performer for the Hurricanes -- with some Team USA time sprinkled in -- and enjoyed his best spring as a junior in 2023, slashing .408/.475/.713 with 20 homers in 61 games. The Nationals selected Morales (now ranked 20th in his second class) in the second round of the 2023 Draft and went above slot to sign him for $2.6 million. Morales experienced four levels of Washington's system in his first taste of the pros, going 58-for-166 (.349) while finishing out at Double-A Harrisburg. He returned to the Senators for his first full season but a left thumb injury caused him to miss much of 2024. Washington officials were excited that they were able to take Morales with their second pick and that they were able to add his significant raw power to their rebuild. The right-handed slugger can be aggressive as he tries to lean into that power, and he experienced some swing-and-miss in college, especially against breaking stuff as a junior. Still, Morales was trending in the right direction with his hit tool in school and struck out only 19 percent of the time in his early taste of the pros, adding to the belief he’ll be an average hitter thanks to his screaming line drives and other loud contact. Morales was a shortstop as an amateur and still retains some of that athleticism. The Nationals drafted him as a third baseman, and he certainly has the arm strength for that position. However, the presence of Brady House at the hot corner has pushed Morales to more full-time duty across the dirt at first base. He could still see time at both corners, but the need for Morales’ power to play is heightened if he remains at first for the long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles signed Martinez out of the Dominican Republic for $950,000 as a headliner of their 2024 international class, and he impressed with a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, collecting 13 extra-base hits in 41 games as a 16-year-old. Martinez then made his way stateside and reached full-season ball by the end of his first full season in 2025, the Orioles challenging him more aggressively than is typical for teenage international signs. He had a tough go of it at Single-A Delmarva, but as a just-turned-18-year-old he was also extraordinarily young for the level. Martinez shows better on-base ability and can hit the ball harder than most players his age. At 6-foot-4 and nearly 200 pounds, he’s strong and athletic and capable of producing 90th percentile exit velocities as high as 108 mph, which hint at a chance at plus raw power. Martinez generates similar hard-hit metrics as Samuel Basallo did at his age and can drive the ball to all fields. His bat-to-ball skills are less advanced, with swing-and-miss tendencies evident even before he was overmatched during his short stint with Delmarva. He’ll need to learn to recognize spin and understand the strike zone better to develop into an average hitter. Martinez got reps at all three outfield spots in each of his first two seasons, but his size and fringy speed make him look more suited for a corner spot, where his plus arm would play. Martinez’s ability to impact the baseball gives him the chance to grow into a run-producer, but he will need to work to develop his all-around offensive profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles now have an established presence on the international amateur market, and at the beginning of the 2024 international period handed out six-figure bonuses to 16 players, including Martinez, an outfielder who signed for $950,000 as one of the headliners of that year’s crop. Martinez was ranked on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list entering the period and then enjoyed a solid debut, collecting 13 extra-base hits during a stint in the Dominican Summer League played mostly as a 16-year-old. Strong and athletic with a knack for hitting the ball hard, Martinez stands out particularly because of his raw power. He’s shown he is capable of producing uncommonly high exit velocities for a hitter his age, registering readings as hard as 108 mph off the bat during his pro debut. Those numbers are comparable to the type of pop Orioles top prospect Samuel Basallo exhibited as a young prospect, when he was a little-known teenager turning heads by lighting up the exit velo radars at the O’s training facilities. Martinez generates similar numbers and can already drive the ball to all fields, showing better feel for hitting to the opposite field than Basallo did at that age. It’s clear that Martinez’s 6-foot-4, almost 200-pound frame will be able to add more strength as he matures, but he’s also aggressive at the plate and will need to cut down on the swing-and-miss as he advances to develop into an average hitter. Martinez played mostly center field in his debut and has an easily-plus arm. But he’s only an average runner, and though it's possible he could stick in center, the size and power potential make his ceiling look more like that of a run-producing corner outfielder given the chance he grows out of the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Unsigned during the 2018-19 international period, Dominguez moved from Venezuela to the Dominican Republic to focus on improving his velocity. The venue change paid dividends when the Mets inked the right-hander just before his 18th birthday in November 2019. The 2020 shutdown kept Dominguez from seeing the Minors in his first season, though he did stay stateside that summer and work out with other Venezuelans at the Mets’ Spring Training facility. Dominguez remained in Florida in 2021 but was highly limited, making only 10 appearances (12 innings) in the Florida Complex League while the Mets had him focus on developing routines and getting in better shape to handle the rigors of a starting role. Dominguez underwent Tommy John surgery in March and is in line to return for 2023. There remains ample stuff on which to dream here. Dominguez stands 6-foot-5 and uses every bit of that size to throw in the mid-90s, touching as high as 99. The heater works well up in the zone too, when Dominguez is at his best with his command. A low-80s slider -- previously deemed a curve -- shows promising spin and break, but it lacks consistency compared to the fastball. He technically possesses a changeup with some movement, but it has a long way to go to become an average offering. Between last year’s and this year's surgery, Dominguez’s inexperience could mean there’s still room for ample growth, especially when it comes to his secondary pitches. But early results make the 20-year-old look more and more like a future reliever who relies on his velocity to blow by hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It isn’t often a great sign when an international player (outside of Cuba) signs a year after he is first eligible, but the plan has worked out well for Dominguez so far. Originally eligible for the 2018-19 signing period, the Venezuela native finally inked a deal with the Mets in November 2019 following a move to the Dominican Republic, where he focused on improving his velocity. Dominguez has yet to appear in a Minor League game but has some experience stateside after the coronavirus pandemic forced him and other Venezuelans to work out of New York’s Spring Training facility in Port St. Lucie last summer. The 6-foot-5 right-hander uses his size to his advantage to sit in the mid-90s and has touched as high as 99 in the past. The Mets have been pleased with the way his breaking ball – previously classified as a curveball but now looking more like a slider – has progressed because of the way he can spin it. It shows above-average potential with late break. The changeup made strides in 2020 and now shows promising movement of its own. The command needs to be the next thing to come for the tall righty, and New York hopes improvements with his release point will aide in that category once he is able to get in games more consistently. Dominguez has the pieces and physicality in place to be a starter. He just needs the game action to put all of those into place against actual opponents. If the command doesn’t quite come around, the velocity gives him a good shot at seeing Major League time in a bullpen setting, but as a pitcher still only entering his age-19 season, that conversation remains far off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hawkins was limited by COVID protocols at the University of British Columbia in 2021 and turned to a stint in the MLB Draft League (where he struck out 32 and walked only two in 24 innings for Trenton) to boost his stock. The Padres took him in the ninth round that summer, and he was on a steady climb through the San Diego system when he underwent Tommy John surgery in August 2024. Hawkins returned as a full-time reliever at High-A and Double-A and dominated in the role, posting a 1.50 ERA and 0.85 WHIP with 80 strikeouts in 60 innings. The Padres added him to the 40-man roster when he became Rule 5-eligible last offseason. There’s a reason why they call the fastball numero uno. The 6-foot-5 Hawkins really leans into his four-seamer and for good reason. It’s a pitch that can sit in the mid-90s with exceptional ride up in the zone, thanks to his over-the-top mechanics. He threw the pitch at least 69 percent of the time against both sides of batters, and Midwest and Texas League hitters couldn’t help but swing under it. A low-80s sweeper was his most-used secondary as a chase pitch versus righties, and there were the makings of a changeup that lacked consistent results. Hawkins pumped strikes at High-A but saw his control take a hit in a 13-game sample at Double-A, but considering he’s sticking in relief anyways, he can live with some walks. Ideally, he’ll need the slider to take a step forward to make him less predictable, but the heater is so good that he should get a chance to be at least a middle reliever in the San Diego bullpen beginning in his age-26 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canadian COVID protocols meant that Hawkins had a limited NAIA career at the University of British Columbia. His path took a trip to Trenton in the MLB Draft League, putting him on the radar in 2021, and he did so with a 2.63 ERA and 32/2 K/BB ratio in 24 frames. The Padres made him a ninth-round pick that July, signed him for $75,000 and moved him straight to full-season ball a year later. Hawkins dominated at Single-A Lake Elsinore, leading the California League with a 16.7 percent swinging-strike rate but was humbled with a move to High-A Fort Wayne (8.80 ERA, 2.09 WHIP in 15 innings). The 6-foot-5 right-hander owns a 92-95 mph fastball that explodes up in the zone from his high delivery point and tall frame. That helps it play above its already solid velocity, and Single-A hitters stood no chance. His mid-80s changeup plays well off the fastball with the way it drops late off anyone thinking they’re getting the high heat, and it was a big reason why lefties posted just a .661 OPS against him (compared to .830 for righties). He also shows a slider, but it isn’t nearly as close to the other two. Hawkins has a history of throwing strikes, and while that control backed up on him at High-A, that may have been the result of fatigue at the end of a long season. The bigger concern might be his lack of a quality third pitch, and that will determine whether he can find a spot in the back end of a Major League rotation or is better utilized as a two-weapon reliever. He made four starts back in Fort Wayne to begin 2023 before an oblique and forearm strain moved him to the IL, stopping his development chances for a time this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Robberse signed with the Blue Jays for $125,000 out of Zeist, Netherlands in July 2019, a few months shy of his 18th birthday and methodically climbed the Toronto system over the next four years. He was with Double-A New Hampshire in 2023 when Toronto dealt him to St. Louis as part of the return for Jordan Hicks at the Trade Deadline. He immediately headed to Triple-A for the first time and was added to the 40-man roster when he became Rule 5 eligible that offseason. Robberse returned to Memphis for 2024 but was limited to 84 1/3 innings there due to elbow tightness, posting a 4.59 ERA with 76 strikeouts in that span. The 6-foot-1 right-hander still hasn’t managed to add much velocity as he’s aged and was still sitting only 90-92 mph and topping out at 93.7 mph with his four-seamer at Triple-A. It was his primary pitch, technically, but without great movement, he only threw it 29.3 percent of the time. That’s a sound strategy considering his sweeping 82-84 mph slider (with an average 12.9 inches of gloveside break) and 86-89 mph changeup were much better at generating whiffs. The latter is particularly interesting because it may not have a ton of separation from the four-seam but has enough run to make Robberse a reverse-splits righty. An upper-80s cutter rounds out the arsenal but was hit hard in Triple-A. Without elite velo, Robberse needs to be able to hit his spots, and his 7.8 percent walk rate at Triple-A was a nice improvement from his 10.6 percent mark at all levels in ’23. The more he leans on the slider versus righties and changeup against lefties, the better chance he’ll have to be a No. 5 starter. The pursuit of such a role will be delayed following the May news that Robberse needed Tommy John surgery. He will miss the remainder of the 2025 season and could be out for a chunk of 2026, too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Robberse signed with the Blue Jays out of Zeist, Netherlands, in July 2019, and he stayed stateside during the lost 2020 pandemic season. Since then, he's followed a pattern of playing for two teams per season following a repeat of a level and an in-season promotion. In 2023, the 21-year-old had a 4.06 ERA and 86 strikeouts in 88 2/3 innings for Double-A New Hampshire when Toronto dealt him to the Cardinals alongside Adam Kloffenstein for Jordan Hicks at the Trade Deadline. St. Louis moved Robberse to Triple-A Memphis after the transaction, and he posted a 4.84 ERA with 44 K’s and 24 walks in 35 1/3 innings there. With his Rule 5 eligibility looming, the Cards added Robberse to their 40-man roster in November. There has long been hope that the 6-foot-1 right-hander would add velocity as he’s aged, and that hasn’t quite manifested yet. His fastball primarily sat 91-93 mph in 2023, and without much movement, it wasn’t much of a bat misser. However, his secondaries showed a good amount of promise, starting with an 82-86 mph breaking ball with sweep and depth that helped him wear out the low, gloveside corner. An upper-80s changeup may not have the separation of a typically great pitch of that designation but the armside fade was good enough to fool batters en route to a 43 percent whiff and chase rate. Robberse also worked with an upper-80s cutter right around the 0 horizontal movement mark. Because he doesn’t overthrow from his three-quarters slot, the Dutch hurler hasn’t suffered many control issues outside of Triple-A, where ABS may have played a role. Any velo/movement improvement on the heater could get him to St. Louis before his 23rd birthday. He was dealing with elbow tightness in June that led to an extended IL stint.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Robberse is a unique development story, originally signed out of Zeist, Netherlands, in 2019. He was able to make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League that season, allowing just one run over 10 1/3 innings. When the pandemic stopped baseball, Robberse was unable to return to the Netherlands and stayed at a hotel near the Blue Jays’ complex with a group of prospects, including many of the Venezuelan players. This added yet another interesting wrinkle to his growth as he was often forced to work out by himself. Coming out of that, Robberse posted a 4.36 ERA over 88 2/3 innings in 2021, split between Single-A Dunedin and High-A Vancouver. Each number moved in the right direction in 2022, as Robberse climbed another level to Double-A and finished with a cumulative ERA of 3.23 over 111 1/3 innings, striking out 97. Much of Robberse’s game is self-taught, which gives him a unique ability to adjust on the fly, and the Blue Jays were encouraged with some of his physical growth, too. After trying to keep on weight for years, Robberse finally packed it on in ’22 and is now up above 200 pounds, which was the goal. There’s hope this can bump his fastball up closer to the 93-94 mph range eventually. An increased strikeout ability would serve Robberse well, as at this point he relies on finesse with a promising package of secondaries. Now with the Cardinals after a Jordan Hicks trade at the 2023 deadline, the Futures Game participant can carry his momentum forward in hopes of joining a future St. Louis rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in 2019 out of Zeist, Netherlands, Robberse is one of the most unique development cases in Toronto’s system. The right-hander appeared in just five GCL games as a 17-year-old back in ’19, but when the COVID shutdown hit in ’20, he was unable to return to the Netherlands and instead stayed at a hotel near the Blue Jays’ complex along with other prospects, including a large Venezuelan group. Robberse worked to keep weight on and train his arm with workouts provided by the club, but this threw a wrench into some valuable development time. Back on the mound in ’21, Robberse split time between Low-A and High-A, posting a 4.36 ERA over 88 2/3 innings with 90 strikeouts. Robberse had his fastball up to 93-95 mph at the end of ’21, but dropped a bit of weight and has been building that back up. His curveball sits just ahead of his slider and has the potential to be an above-average pitch while his developing changeup trails behind. The Blue Jays like Robberse’s feel for pitching and his athletic delivery, which comes naturally and is more self-taught than other prospects in these ranks. Coaches also compliment Robberse’s ability to take feedback and immediately implement it on the mound, which lends to their belief that his development will continue at this rate through the upper levels. He also used much of the down time during the shutdown to develop his mental game, diving into pitch sequencing and mound strategies. Now 20, Robberse still needs to add muscle to his frame and sustain that over the course of a full season, but he’s already exceeding expectations, especially when you consider the disruptions he’s been forced to deal with. Now one of the highest-upside arms in the system, Robberse does still have a wide range of outcomes from here, but he’s put himself in a very good place entering ’22.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in late July 2019 as an international free agent out of Zeist, Netherlands, where he spent the entirety of his amateur career and competed for his country internationally, the young right-hander opened eyes quickly in his pro debut. Though he only got into five games in the rookie Gulf Coast League, Robberse offered a flash of what the Blue Jays hope they’ll see more of in the future, posting a 0.87 ERA over 10 1/3 innings, walking none and striking out nine. Given that much of Robberse’s game is self-taught, the right-hander’s delivery is a natural movement that the Blue Jays believe comes with plenty of projection. Robberse’s fastball velocity has moved from the high-80s to the low-90s with room for more growth, and his curveball, a pitch he throws confidently, is well ahead of his developing changeup when it comes to secondaries. One could argue that his mid-80s slider has overtaken the curve as his best breaking pitch in 2021, and it’s helped take his profile to a new level. When Robberse signed with the Blue Jays, he had an extremely wide range of potential outcomes, and that remains true. The potential is there for a breakout, though, especially as he develops his 6-foot-1, 160-pound frame. Robberse is one of the more intriguing long-term rotation projects in the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A soccer and baseball standout at his Ohio high school, Ross wasn’t heavily recruited and stayed in state, traveling northeast to Division II Notre Dame College outside of Cleveland. With a .405 average and an OPS north of 1.200, he became the first player in program history to be given All-American honors and left campus after the Twins took him in the fifth round of the 2022 Draft. He didn’t quite put up those kinds of eye-popping numbers in his first full season, but he was productive with High-A Cedar Rapids and earned a late bump up to Double-A. Lanky and athletic, Ross has some legitimate tools on both sides of the ball. His profile changed a little bit during his first full season, as there was a bit more swing-and-miss than expected. But he also got to his excellent raw power a bit more, finishing tied for second in the Midwest League with 19 home runs. He’s working on refining his approach and swing angle as he especially had a tendency to hit the ball in the air too much on fastballs up in the zone, with the hope he can keep a line-drive angle on those. Ross’ speed and arm do work well at shortstop, his primary position in college, and he’ll continue to see time as he nears the upper levels. He’s also shown the ability to move around the field as needed, even playing more first base than anticipated because of other high priority infielders in Cedar Rapids. His future is likely as a utilityman, but one who can stay up the middle at short and even in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Notre Dame College is a Division II school that doesn’t exactly have a long track record of producing professional talent, with only lefty Travis Scott previously coming from the school, and he transferred to a junior college for his Draft year. So when the Twins took Ross, who was considered to be the best college hitter in Ohio in his class, in the fifth round of the 2022 Draft, he became the first Falcons product to be drafted. He left Notre Dame with a career .405 average and an OPS over 1.200, then held his own with Single-A Fort Myers in his pro debut. Ross brings some twitchy athleticism, speed and a feel for the barrel to the Twins organization. The right-handed hitter doesn’t chase a ton and draws walks. He can drive the ball, but he entered the pro ranks with a setup at the plate with his lower half that made it difficult for him to cover the outer half. He’s made some small adjustments to have better direction to the middle of the field and a better bat path overall. Tall and lanky, he’s already added at least 10 pounds of strength, which could help him impact the ball more. Primarily a shortstop in college, Ross has a strong arm and plus speed that not only should enable him to be a threat on the bases but give him range defensively. He’ll keep getting reps at the premium position, but like he did during his pro debut, he’s going to move around the infield and see more time in the outfield, where his athleticism might really play well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hansen was Mr. Reliable during his days at Texas, especially when he moved into the rotation as a sophomore and junior. He posted a 3.76 ERA with 120 strikeouts and only 19 walks over 107 2/3 innings as a junior in 2022, despite limited velocity, and that was enough to make him a third-round pick that summer. He signed for exact slot at $629,800. Hansen spent his first full season with Single-A Palm Beach, where he had a 3.12 ERA and 126 K’s in 112 2/3 frames in a rather lax assignment. He did make one late-season appearance for Triple-A Memphis, retiring all three batters he faced. The 6-foot-2 southpaw continued to sit in the 88-92 mph window with his four-seam fastball but didn’t shy away from the pitch because he could command it so well. He also showed a sinker around the same velocity. Hansen played off those with his best pitch -- a 78-82 mph sweeper that batters missed both in and out of the zone. His mid-80s changeup got a healthy amount of his chase and helped him limit righties to a .594 OPS (compared to .722 for lefties). An upper-70s curveball was a distant fifth pitch in terms of usage, but it was good for the occasional swing-and-miss too. Given his profile, Hansen needs to be able to spot the ball well if he’s going to stay effective, and so far so good on that score. He’s a pitchability lefty through and through who could settle into the back-end of a rotation, but he needs bigger challenges than the FSL to prove himself.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If \"pitchability lefty\" was in the dictionary, you might find Hansen’s picture right next to it. The southpaw was an effective hurler in all three of his years at Texas despite limited velocity, and he took a 3.76 ERA, 120 strikeouts and only 19 walks over 107 2/3 innings as a junior into the 2022 Draft. He went to the Cardinals in the third round, becoming the organization’s third straight collegiate southpaw at the top of the Draft, and signed for exact slot at $629,800. Hansen’s fastball barely reached over 90 mph for much of his time as a Longhorn and was in the 88-92 mph range, occasionally tickling mid-90s, in his final spring in Austin. But his 78-82 mph slider helped drive up his K count, thanks to plus horizontal and vertical action that made it difficult to touch against batters from either side. He also mixed in an 72-76 mph curveball, though he's mostly pocketed it so far at Single-A Palm Beach. His low-80s changeup with decent fade keeps righties honest. The former Texas ace makes it all work because of his control coming out of a near-effortless delivery. He knows exactly where he wants to put it, and he puts it there with relative ease. That feel for location gives hope that he could be a potential No. 5 starter, even without the velocity, but he needs to see higher levels soon heading into his age-23 season in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zanetello compiled an impressive resume on the 2022 showcase circuit that that included winning MVP honors at the Breakthrough Series and leading Team USA in hitting (.429) at an 18-and-under World Cup qualifier. The Red Sox loved his five-tool potential and makeup, drafting him in the second round and paying him first-round money ($3 million). He struggled with a hamstring injury and pro pitching in his first full season, batting .157/.279/.279 with a 44 percent strikeout rate that ranked third-worst in the Minors (minimum: 300 plate appearances). Zanetello's bat speed, projectable strength, the loft in his right-handed swing and his exit velocities give him at least plus raw power, but he'll have to show that he can get to it. His hands drift and his stroke gets long, completely throwing off his timing at the plate. He'll need to make adjustments to his swing and his approach, because he's both too pull-happy and passive, falling behind in counts and finding himself unable to recover. Though he didn't steal much while dealing with hamstring woes in 2024, Zanetello possesses at least solid speed and flashed plus-plus run times as an amateur. He has the athleticism and arm strength to make plays at shortstop, but he didn't look comfortable there while committing 24 errors in 48 games last summer. He could outgrow the position but has the tools to become a solid center fielder or third baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zanetello repeatedly starred on the high school showcase circuit in 2022, winning MVP honors at the Breakthrough Series in June and standing out during athletic testing at the PDP League in July. He mashed at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October and led Team USA in batting (.429) at an 18-and-under World Cup qualifier in November. Scouts touted his five-tool potential and personality before the Red Sox signed him well over slot for $3 million as a second-rounder last July. With impressive bat speed, strong hands and wrists and a projectable 6-foot-2 build, Zanetello generates high exit velocities and has the ingredients for at least 25-homer power. Though he had a track record of producing against quality pitching and controlled the strike zone well as an amateur, he'll need some time to develop as a hitter. He doesn't have the smoothest right-handed swing and will have to improve his timing and rhythm at the plate after striking out 15 times in 38 at-bats in his brief pro debut. Zanetello has posted run times that grade anywhere from 45-70 on the 20-80 scouting scale, and he'll probably settle in as a solid-to-plus runner once he fills out his wiry frame. His athleticism and strong arm enable him to make plays at shortstop and center field, and he projects as a solid defender at either spot. He also should be an asset at third base if he outgrows shortstop and stays on the dirt.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Houck was a two-way star at Parkview HS in Liburn, Ga., the same school that produced Matt Olson and Jeff Francouer. He threw for 2,189 yards as a senior quarterback, earning Power 5 football offers along the way, and was named Gatorade’s Georgia Player of the Year for baseball. The Mets selected the Mississippi State commit with the 32nd overall pick in 2023 and signed for him above slot at $2.75 million. Houck spent his entire first full season with Single-A St. Lucie but struggled with the jump to full-season ball, hitting just .206/.304/.306 with five homers and 171 strikeouts in 112 games. Houck’s 171 K’s were tied for third-most among Single-A batters, and his 36.3 percent K rate was fourth-highest among qualifiers at the level. The punchouts came in a variety of ways. On one hand, the right-handed hitter couldn’t handle breaking and offspeed pitches, whiffing on 53.9 percent of his swings against secondaries. On the other, he had 59 called third strikes because of his passivity; no one else in the FSL had more than 42. When he did make contact, there was still decent pop in there for his age and experience level. An average runner, Houck has plus arm strength, and that helps him on the left side of the dirt. He remains a work in progress defensively, however, and saw time at third base earlier than expected. He can rush plays at the corner, either forcing him to bobble on a transfer or throw inaccurately. Houck will be 20 for the entire 2025 Minor League season, making him the age of a college sophomore, but he needs to prove he can adjust off these early issues to get anything close to the potential he showed heading into the 2023 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While at Parkview (Liburn, Ga.) HS – the school that produced Matt Olson and Jeff Francoeur – Houck threw for 2,189 yards and 24 touchdowns as a senior quarterback and was also named Gatorade’s Georgia Player of the Year for his work on the diamond. He turned down Power 5 football offers to commit to Mississippi State only to go 32nd overall in the Draft to the Mets. New York signed Houck for just above slot at $2.75 million and sent him to the Florida Complex League, where he went 7-for-29 (.241) in nine games. Batting from the right side, the 6-foot-2 Houck has had a flummoxing first full season at the plate with Single-A St. Lucie. He's looked passive at the plate at times, even with two strikes leading to a ton of strikeouts looking, and his contact rate against pitches in the zone is general has been rough. He's especially struggled against non-fastballs as he's dug in against pro pitchers over an extended amount of time. His exit velocities when he has managed to make contact have been average at least, which is more in line with his pre-Draft scouting report. Houck has at least average speed, and he has the body control and obvious arm strength to handle plays at shortstop. Some project him to trend more toward third base as he matures, but there will be added pressure on the bat should he need to move to the corner. Houck will seek to rebound, likely back in the Florida State League, in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Petersen was an all-Big Ten honoree as an Iowa sophomore in 2023 and looked set to achieve similar status by hitting .333 and slugging .571 in 33 games as a Hawkeyes junior, only to see his ’24 season cut short by stress reactions in both his shins. The Nationals took him in the eighth round and signed him for slot at $230,900, and a similar story of good results mixed in with injuries carried over to pro ball. Petersen missed the start of his first full season with a hamstring issue and managed only 44 games with High-A Wilmington, hitting .297/.398/.490 with a 161 wRC+ in that span. He made up for the lost time in the Arizona Fall League with a .305 average and a .934 OPS in 17 contests there. The right-handed hitter is constantly shifting in the box, making him look eager to get things going. There were some red flags in his Fall League performance, despite the promising surface-level numbers. He carried only a 65 percent overall contact rate on his swings and tended to get overzealous to expand the zone against fastballs. That said, he did surprise by showing better impact at the plate, a continuation of a trend from college, and his swing can come with optimal angles that make some swing-and-miss easier to stomach. Petersen is a plus runner who went 18-for-18 in steals attempts with Wilmington, though he didn’t push the envelope in the AFL. He could be an average defender in center field with that speed but would be above-average if he needs to land in a corner. Left field seems like his best fit due to subpar arm strength. Petersen’s potential as a fourth outfielder will be tested further with his first move to the upper Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Iowa rotation drew plenty of attention in recent years, especially for Brody Brecht, but Petersen stood out in his own right among the position-player group. An all-Big Ten selection in 2023, the outfielder got off to a strong start as a junior last year, hitting .333/.459/.571 with five homers and 17 steals in 33 games before stress reactions in both his shins ended his season in late April. The Nationals selected him in the eighth round, signed him for slot at $230,900 and got him seven games later in the summer with Single-A Fredericksburg. Batting from the right side, Petersen can make for a kinetic at-bat as a constant waggler in the box. He improved his plate discipline over time in college, and he also made harder consistent contact. He slugged just .329 with wood bats in a trip to Cape Cod in 2023, and he struggled against velocity above 94 mph even with metal. There might just be enough power for 12-15 homers, and it was notable that, while he didn’t go deep with the FredNats, four of his eight hits went for extra bases in the small sample. Petersen is a plus runner who has good baserunning instincts; he had a 90.9 percent success rate in steals in college and was 5-for-5 in the pros. Subpar arm strength pushed him primarily to left field with the Hawkeyes, and he might need to stay in a corner with superior defenders like Dylan Crews and Elijah Green options up the middle. With Petersen’s on-base ability and speed alone, he could fit nicely as a Major League fourth outfielder – a solid return for his Draft spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of college baseball's best two-way performers as a sophomore in 2023, Mathis topped the College of Charleston in OPS (1.014) and ERA (3.45) before ranking second in the Cape Cod League with 11 homers in 38 games. He focused on hitting as a junior while dealing with an elbow injury, became the highest pick in school history (second round) and had Tommy John surgery shortly after signing for $1,681,200. Rehab and a subsequent elbow sprain limited him to 29 Single-A games in his 2025 pro debut, and he didn't play the field until the Arizona Fall League. Mathis has an easy right-handed stroke and the upside of a solid hitter with raw power to match, though he hasn't gotten much of a chance to show what he can do when fully healthy in pro ball. He strings together quality at-bats and hangs in well against breaking balls and changeups. He was more aggressive at Single-A than he was in college, showing the ability to elevate balls to his pull side but not hitting the ball as hard as he did at Charleston. Though the Cubs announced Mathis as a third baseman when they drafted him, he spent just one game there in college and most scouts think he lacks the quickness and athleticism to handle the hot corner. He has a chance to be an average first baseman but won't cover a lot of ground at either corner. Before he got hurt, he had a low-90s fastball with armside run and a mid-70s downer curveball that he located well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mathis broke out as one of college baseball's best two-way players as a sophomore in 2023, when he led the College of Charleston in OPS (1.014) and ERA (3.45) before finishing second in the Cape Cod League with 11 homers in 38 games. He concentrated on hitting last spring while dealing with an elbow injury, bouncing back from a slow start to slash .335/.472/.650 en route to becoming the highest pick in Cougars history. After signing for $1,681,200 as a second-rounder, he had Tommy John surgery in August. Mathis employs an effortless, if not picturesque, right-handed stroke and a very patient approach to produce hard contact to all fields. He rarely strayed from the zone or swung and missed in college, though he may need to turn his bat loose more often in pro ball because he takes a lot of strikes. He has enough pull power to get to 20 homers per season, drives the ball the other way for doubles and draws a healthy amount of walks. The Cubs announced Mathis as a third baseman when they selected him, but he played just one game at the hot corner at the College of Charleston and his fringy quickness and athleticism seem like a stretch for the hot corner. Most clubs thought he was strictly a first baseman despite his strong arm. As a pitcher, he featured a low-90s fastball with armside run and got outs with a mid-70s downer curveball that he located well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodden’s professional profile is built around versatility, competitiveness and high baseball IQ. After two years at Seminole State College in Oklahoma, he transferred to Wichita State, where he posted a huge senior season that earned him American Athletic Conference Player of the Year honors. Though originally drafted as a junior in the 10th round by the A’s in 2022, he returned to school and elevated his stock, leading to a fifth-round selection in 2023 by the Mariners, who signed him for $200,000. Rodden hit well with High-A Everett in his full-season debut, earning a bump to Double-A. He returned there in 2025 and kept the bat going, finishing with an .822 OPS despite injuries getting in the way. An undersized switch-hitter, Rodden has consistently shown bat-to-ball skills and plate discipline, though the jump to Double-A saw strikeouts rise and contact become less consistent. Over two years at Wichita State he hit 34 home runs, and he added 14 in his first full pro season. But Rodden projects as a low-power bat as he moves up, with just five homers at Arkansas. His game will rely heavily on making consistent contact and drawing walks to create offensive value, and he did a better job at that while hitting .342 during an 11-game stint in the Arizona Fall League. Defensively, Rodden has the versatility to play second base, third, shortstop and potentially the outfield, and his plus speed helps him defensively and on the basepaths, where his strong instincts make him a base stealing threat. Scouts are particularly encouraged by his sneaky utility potential at the Major League level. Among big league comps, Leo Rivas has been floated. Beyond tools, Rodden brings leadership and a grinder mentality that sets the tone for younger teammates, making him a candidate to contribute as a versatile, switch-hitting option on a future big-league roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodden took the junior college route out of high school, then went to Wichita State after two years at Seminole State College in Oklahoma. He was one of just three players taken in the Top 10 rounds of the 2022 Draft that opted to go back to school, returning to the Shockers after the A’s took him in Round 10. He had a huge senior year to win American Athletic Conference Player of the Year honors and he jumped up to the fifth round, where the Mariners signed him for $200,000. After hitting very well with High-A Everett during his full-season debut, he got pushed to Double-A at age 24, though he struggled at the level. An under-sized switch-hitter, Rodden has shown good bat-to-ball skills and a disciplined approach at the plate, though that unraveled a bit and the strikeouts piled up more once he got to Arkansas. He hit 34 homers over two years at Wichita State and finished his first full pro season with 14, but there’s not going to be a ton of power as he keeps moving up, so he’s going to have to really make a ton of contact and draw a lot of walks. Rodden is a plus runner and combines that with good instincts on the basepaths. He’s best suited to play second base defensively, but his bat is unlikely to profile as an every day player at the position. He’s seen time at third and at shortstop, which also won’t work at the highest level, so there’s a chance the Mariners give him the chance to see how his athleticism plays in center field so that he can possibly carve out some kind of utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in the Dominican Republic, Cepeda grew up in New Jersey and played well on the high school showcase circuit, attracting interest from major college programs. Rather than wait for the 2023 Draft, he returned home and signed six months earlier with the Cubs for $1 million. After posting an .826 OPS in two years of Rookie ball, he made his full-season debut last year and slashed .249/.339/.375 at age 19 in Single-A, good for a 116 wRC+. Cepeda's quick right-handed stroke and growing strength give him more raw power than most middle infielders and 20-homer upside if he can make more contact and elevate balls more consistently. While he makes reasonable swing decisions, he struggles to do damage against non-fastballs. At Single-A, he logged an .844 OPS with a 24 percent swing-and-miss rate against heaters vs. a .571 OPS and 44 percent miss rate against everything else. Though Cepeda has slowed down as he has started to mature physically and now possesses just average speed, he has good baserunning instincts. The question is whether he'll maintain enough range to stay at shortstop, his primary position where he's a sure-handed defender with a strong arm. He's a solid gloveman at second base but the game is too fast for him at third base, where he has 18 errors in 54 career games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cepeda grew up in New Jersey and stood out on the showcase circuit as early as age 14, garnering interest from major college programs. He decided to bypass the Draft by moving back to his native Dominican Republic and signing with the Cubs for $1 million in 2023.
