A second season in the Dominican Summer League helped him get his bat going in 2019, and while he’s had trouble producing consistently at the plate since, he did reach Double-A in 2022 and opened some eyes with a strong performance in the Colombian Winter League this past offseason. While it’s taken him a while to get going, Vellojin has the chance to be a solid all-around big league backstop. Already working in his favor offensively -- even if the surface stats don’t always reflect it -- is his outstanding approach at the plate. He’s walked in 16.9 percent of his plate appearances, including 15.5 percent in 2022 across three levels. The left-handed hitter is capable of making hard contact, and there’s raw power he’s starting to tap into, with it really showing up over the winter as he slugged .597 while walking as much as he struck out. He also caught for Colombia in the Caribbean Series. Vellojin continues to improve as an overall receiver and blocker, but he has always impressed with his plus arm strength and his willingness to take charge behind the dish. It might be a backup profile, but a big year at the upper levels could change that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vellojin joined the Reds out of Colombia for just $10,000 in Jan. 2018 and proceeded to struggle in his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League the summer after signing. A return engagement to the DSL led to better results and a postseason All-Star nod. Post-shutdown, Vellojin skipped over rookie ball and went to Low-A Daytona and was named an organizational All-Star by MiLB.com The Reds think they might have gotten a potential big leaguer behind the plate at a bargain price. Defensively, his plus arm is his carrying tool, and he threw out nearly 43 percent of potential basestealers in 2021. While there’s work to be done on his blocking and receiving, he does have good hands, already calls a good game and has that “it” factor teams like to see from their backstops. A left-handed hitter, Vellojin is just starting to come into his strength. He makes good, hard contact and has a very good approach that saw him walk nearly as often as he struck out a year ago. There could be more power to come as he continues to get more physical. He has the floor of a Major League backup, but the Reds aren’t ruling out continued growth into a solid all-around regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two former Rangers pitchers helped shape Figuereo: his father, Victor, who made it to short-season ball in the early 2000s, and Edison Volquez, an All-Star and the key player in the trade that brought Josh Hamilton to Texas, who trained him in the Dominican Republic. Signed for $80,000 in 2021, Figuereo worked with Volquez after a decent pro debut and added significant strength. He ranked second in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with nine homers in 35 games in 2022 but scuffled in Single-A last year. Figuereo's left-handed stroke and hitting ability initially attracted the Rangers, and he still shows good feel for the barrel at times. But he also chases too many pitches and gets too focused on trying to launch balls to his pull side, resulting in a 29 percent strikeout rate at Single-A. His combination of bat speed and strength -- he weighs much more than his listed 165 pounds -- creates plus raw power but he's going to need to make adjustments to solve quality pitching. Figuereo has below-average speed and limited range at third base, where he committed 23 errors in 104 games a year ago. He has plus arm strength but also some issues with throwing accuracy that he made some progress with over the course of last season. He'll need to watch his thick lower half in order to remain at the hot corner, and he might move to an outfield corner anyway.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Figuereo has connections to two ex-Rangers pitchers -- his father, Victor, topped out in short-season ball in the early 2000s and former All-Star Edinson Volquez (who was traded to bring Josh Hamilton to Texas) trained him and helped him transform his body after his decent 2021 pro debut. Signed for $80,000 out of the Dominican Republic that year, Gleider was significantly stronger last summer. He ranked second in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with nine homers in just 35 games before a late promotion to Single-A. The Rangers liked Figuereo's left-handed swing and bat-to-ball skills when they signed him, and he immediately demonstrated the aptitude to pull and drive balls in the air. Now that he has added muscle and weighs significantly more than his listed 165 pounds, he's displaying plus raw power and 25-homer potential. He hits the ball hard but may need to tone down his approach against more advanced pitchers because he focuses so much on launching balls to his pull side. Figuereo spent his first two pro seasons at third base but may not stay there. He has fringy speed and range and his plus arm strength is mitigated by accuracy issues that resulted in 28 errors in 77 games. The Rangers could decide to expedite his bat by lessening his defensive responsibilities with a move to an outfield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally a walk-on at Brigham Young, Pintar played his way into a Diamondbacks fifth-round pick in 2022 despite losing much of that year to a right shoulder injury that required two surgeries. A broken ankle truncated his first full pro season, but he returned to earn High-A Northwest League all-star honors (.304/.403/.516) before scuffling in Double-A in 2024. Sent with slugging prospect Deyvison De Los Santos to the Marlins for A.J. Puk at the Trade Deadline in July, he won Arizona Fall League defensive player of the year accolades during the offseason. When he's on, the righty-hitting Pintar controls the strike zone, gets on base and shows the ability to drive homers to his pull side and doubles to right field. He got abused by non-fastballs in Double-A, however, and did little damage while making contact against heaters. He has flashed hitting ability and 15-homer power, but he'll need to make adjustments or else be relegated to a platoon role. Finally healthy in 2024, Pintar turned his plus speed loose on the bases and swiped 33 bases in 35 attempts (94 percent) between the Minors and AFL. A middle infielder in college, he made a smooth transition to full-time center fielder last year. His reads and routes continue to improve and he's at least a solid defender in center, though his shoulder issues left him with below-average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pintar went from a BYU walk-on in 2020 to one of the program’s best performers a year later after he slashed .333/.433/.556 with nine homers and more walks (32) than strikeouts (29) in 48 games. He hit just .209 with a .613 OPS in 17 games to begin his junior year and then underwent shoulder surgery that shut him down the rest of the way. Relying mostly on what they saw in 2021, the D-backs took Pintar in the fifth round and signed him for below slot at $316,950. The former Cougar was back to hitting and taking ground balls as part of his rehab process heading into the spring, adding to Arizona’s optimism. How much the shoulder affected his 2022 performance remains in question, but the raw tools are certainly enticing enough. He’s a plus runner running down the line and has some promising raw power from the right side. Pintar drew praise from BYU coaches for his improving approach in college, starting with laying off breaking stuff below the zone, and if that upward trajectory continues, it should help ease his transition to the Minors. A shortstop in 2021, Pintar moved to second base-only last year out of concern for his below-average throwing arm. The D-backs say they expect to continue to move him around the infield, hoping to take advantage of his athleticism and range, but second still seems most likely in the long run. If the shoulder was nothing but bad timing and Pintar can get his performance to match his tools again, he could be a mid-round steal for Arizona.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Serrano comes from the same Jaime Ramos Academy in San Cristóbal, Dominican Republic, that helped produce Top 100 prospects in Dodgers shortstop Emil Morales and Giants shortstop Josuar Gonzalez. The outfielder was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 26 prospect in the 2026 international class, and he signed with the Nationals for $1,969,000, becoming the organization’s biggest January 15 addition this year. Isaias Suarez (No. 40) was the only other prospect from MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 to join Washington. The left-handed hitter repeatedly earned praise from Nationals officials for his sweet swing from the left side. He can maintain his timing despite a wider stance than most of his peers, and he can repeat his swing with impressive loft. He already stands at 6-foot-3 entering his age-17 season, and with the right strength gains, he could get to at least average power, given that propensity to put the ball in the air already. Serrano is just an average runner as he enters the affiliated ranks, but he has a nose for the ball in center field and takes clean routes to generate outs. The Nationals should give him plenty of looks in center field to begin his career, knowing that he could be above-average in a corner should he need to move when he bumps into speedier defenders higher up the chain. That will add some pressure to the bat, though there’s enough promise there to make him a potential average regular in the years to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2021, the Angels used all 20 of their Draft picks on pitchers. Albright was the only high schooler from that group, a Maryland native who moved to IMG Academy and got a way-over-slot bonus of $1.25 million to sign as a 12th-rounder rather than head to Virginia Tech. His first full season was full of bumps, but he returned to Single-A in 2023 and was having much better results when he was sent to the Rockies at the Trade Deadline in the deal for Randal Grichuk and C.J. Cron. He finished the year with a five-start look at what High-A Spokane was like. None of Albright’s four pitches jump off the page, but he has a pretty good feel for how to use all of them effectively. The six-foot lefty usually sits in the low-90s and it’s effective because he has good fastball command and hitters don’t pick it up because of deception in his delivery. When he stays on top of his breaking ball, it’s an effective pitch. He has good feel for a fading changeup and he can mix in a cutter as well. In the past, Albright has been plagued with a long arm action in the back and some inconsistency out front with his delivery that hurt his overall command. But was able to shorten his arm action and find the zone much more regularly in 2023. As his walk rate went down, his stuff ticked up and so did his strikeouts. The ceiling is limited, but if those trends continue, he could land in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2021 Draft might always be remembered as the one in which the Angels used all 20 of their picks to select pitchers. All but one were from the college ranks, with the lone exception being Albright, a Maryland native who moved to Florida to get exposure at IMG Academy. The left-hander received a way over-slot bonus of right around $1.25 million, second-round money, to join the organization rather than head to Virginia Tech. He tossed eight scoreless innings in the Arizona Complex League in his pro debut before getting more work in at instructs. Albright is not your prototypical high school projection case, as the six-footer is more about his feel for pitching than raw stuff. His fastball typically has been sitting in the 90-92 mph range, though he has shown a little more velocity in the past. It does play up because he can command it and misses bats thanks to deception in his delivery. His curve has the chance to be a solid pitch, though it can get slurvy at times, and he has feel for his changeup. While the southpaw can throw all three pitches for strikes, there is some concern about his long arm action in the back and his consistency out front with his delivery that hampered his stuff and his command. He’s young enough to correct some of those mechanical issues and land in the back end of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After getting hammered for a 6.79 ERA in three seasons at Cal State Fullerton, Knorr transferred to Coastal Carolina in 2022, added velocity and pitched his way into the third round of the Draft. He struck out 125 in 98 innings while advancing to Double-A in his first two pro seasons but has had a hard time staying healthy. Persistent shoulder issues sidelined him for the final two months of the 2023 season and the last three months in 2024. Knorr works at 93-95 mph and reached 98 mph with carry on his fastball, though it lacks movement and got rocked last year when he threw it over the plate. His tight mid-80s slider was his most effective chase pitch last year, but it too got hit when he didn't locate it well. He also has an upper-80s curveball and a low-80s changeup with fade and depth, and the latter could be his best weapon if he can command it better. Knorr works exclusively out of the stretch and his short arm action and extension bolster his deception. He pounded the strike zone in college but his walk rate has doubled from 5 percent at that level to 10 percent in his first two pro seasons. His mound presence adds to his starter's package, and the Astros believe they can help him get more out of his stuff, though they're going to have to keep him healthy first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knorr got knocked around en route to a 6.79 ERA in three years at Cal State Fullerton before transferring to Coastal Carolina and discovering more velocity and success in 2022. He topped the Sun Belt Conference in K/BB ratio (6.6), finished second in strikeout rate (11.2 per nine innings) and worked his way into the third round of the Draft. He fanned 78 in 58 1/3 innings between two Class A levels during his 2023 pro debut but missed the final two months with a shoulder injury. Knorr's fastball jumped from 90-92 mph in 2021 to 93-96 and topped out at 98 the following spring, albeit with more downhill plane than carry. He has maintained that velocity in pro ball while adding more power to his breaking pitches, a tight mid-80s slider and an upper-70s curveball with more vertical movement. They're both average offerings, as is his low-80s change with fade and depth. Working exclusively out of the stretch, Knorr features a short arm action that adds deception without detracting from his ability to throw strikes. His control wasn't as sharp in his debut as it was at Coastal Carolina, and he needs to refine his command because his pitches don't have a lot of life. A tough competitor, he could become a back-of-the-rotation starter if he develops a solid second offering and refines his ability to locate his arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knorr got rocked for a 6.79 ERA in three seasons at Cal State Fulllerton before transferring to Coastal Carolina and finding more velocity and success in 2022. He led the Sun Belt Conference in K/BB ratio (6.6) and was second in strikeouts per nine innings (11.2) before signing for an under-slot $487,500 in the third round. As they did with all three of the college pitchers they took in the top four rounds last July, the Astros gave him the summer off and will have him make his pro debut in 2023. Knorr went from pitching with a 90-92 mph fastball with the Titans in 2021 to parking at 93-96 mph and peaking at 98 with the Chanticleers. His heater comes with more downhill plane than life, so he has to rely on his ability to command it well to keep it off barrels. His 83-85 mph changeup with fade and depth is his best secondary pitch, and he adds to its deception by selling it with fastball arm speed. Though Knorr missed some bats with his breaking pitches in college they were too soft, and the Astros have helped him add more power to what are now a mid-80s slider and an upper-70s curveball. He works exclusively out of the stretch and employs a short arm action that creates deception without detracting him from solid control. If he can continue to pound the zone while developing a more reliable breaking ball, he could fit in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lantigua was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 42 prospect in the 2024 international signing class and joined the Mets for $950,000 out of the Dominican Republic when the window opened that January. He performed well in the Dominican Summer League with a .397 OBP and 123 wRC+ over 45 games in his signing year and continued to build on that as a Florida Complex League end-of-season All-Star in 2025. He hit .288/.433/.399 with three homers, 33 walks and 29 strikeouts in 49 games as an 18-year-old in his first stateside campaign. Given his projectable 6-foot-1 frame, Lantigua was expected to be power-over-hit, but to this early point in his career, he’s been quite the opposite as his K/BB ratio last year would attest. His 14.9 percent K rate and 17 percent BB rate ranked eighth and 10th among FCL qualifiers, respectively, but that will be tested when he faces full-season arms that can pitch in the zone more easily. Lantigua also hit 55.5 percent of his batted balls on the ground. Some have noted he’s begun to look more physical this spring, and that could mean the promised power is around the corner. Oddly, Lantigua performed better against fellow righties in the FCL (.900 OPS) than lefties (.584), though the latter came in a much smaller sample. Lantigua hasn’t been an efficient baserunner to this point and went only 13-for-23 in steal attempts in the FCL last year. He’s been a primary center fielder, but if he slows down as he adds bulk (as he’s expected to), then he’ll slot into a corner. Lantigua, who is still only 19 for all of 2026, will then need the power to start playing more in games to lock down a starting MLB role in left or right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 42 international prospect in the 2024 class, Lantigua joined the Mets for $950,000 out of the Dominican Republic. Only Yovanny Rodriguez ($2.85 million) signed for more in the organization last year. Making his pro debut in his home nation, Lantigua was arguably New York’s top performer in the Dominican Summer League as he slashed .263/.397/.395 over 45 games, giving him a 122 wRC+. The outfielder was named a DSL midseason All-Star and went 1-for-3 with a steal in the circuit’s version of the midsummer classic. As good as Lantigua’s first taste of the pros was, he still stands out more for his future projection than current skills. At 6-foot-1 and having turned 18 in November, he still has room to mature physically -- a great sign for a right-handed slugger who already produces strong top-end exit velocities. He took his fair share of walks against the typically wild DSL arms (and was even one of the most plunked players in the league with 14 HBPs) and kept strikeouts in check for his age and experience, but he’ll likely need to tighten his swing to keep that contact rate coming against more experienced arms. A solid runner now, Lantigua spent the bulk of his DSL time in center field. There’s always a chance he slows as he ages, and the Mets did give him looks in the corners already, specifically more right than left. The power could certainly play there if it continues to develop as hoped. Lantigua’s move stateside will be closely followed at Single-A St. Lucie and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As one of the more highly regarded international prospects available for the 2019-20 signing period, Vera commanded a $2 million bonus in July 2019, then was basically stuck in his Arizona apartment and unable to stay in shape during 2020 because of the pandemic. In 2021, he turned his conditioning around and went out and hit well during his pro debut in the Arizona Complex League to earn a late bump up to full-season ball. The 2022 season, however, was a disaster, as Vera struggled out of the gate and let it snowball. Still only 20, there’s time for Vera to right the ship, but after a year in which he finished with a .572 OPS, he has a lot to work on. A 6-foot-2 athletic switch-hitter, Vera had shown a strong feel for making contact in the past, and there was belief he could tap into some raw power as he added strength. In 2022, he chased out of the zone much more than he should have and didn’t make enough contact to overcome that, with a 27 percent strikeout rate far too high for someone without big-time power. He’ll have to work to make better swing decisions moving forward. Vera is still a good defender with excellent actions and a strong arm, enough for him to play shortstop going forward. For now, the emphasis will be on him finding a better approach at the plate if he’s going to have a chance to fulfill his potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vera was ranked in the top 10 of MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospect list when the 2019-20 signing period began and the Angels gave him $2 million to join the organization in July of 2019. The pandemic not only kept him from making his debut in 2020, but he was pretty much stuck in an Arizona apartment for an extremely long time and gained weight as a result. He was able to return to his conditioning, shedding those pounds in time to hit .317/.384/.469 in the Arizona Complex League in 2021, earning a late promotion to Low-A ball at age 18. Vera reported to camp this spring in even better shape and the Angels were thrilled with where he was physically, though that didn’t help his offensive profile as he struggled to find consistency in full-seson ball. He’s still hit over power, and has shown the ability in the past to make contact from both sides of the plate. He doesn’t draw a ton of walks and his strikeout rate crept upward in 2022. There’s plenty of bat speed and his added strength should allow him to start tapping into his raw power, even if he always has a contact-first approach. There is a chance Vera’s 6-foot-2 frame will fill out too much and he’ll become too big for shortstop, though he shows very good actions and more than enough arm for the premium position. He could be a plus defender if he eventually has to move to third and there’s confidence the extra-base authority will come to profile well at the corner spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A dozen prospects got bonuses of $2 million or more during the 2019-20 international signing period. Vera, one of two to get seven-figure bonuses from the Angels over that time, was at the bottom of that dozen, getting $2 million even to sign on July 2. The shutdown kept him from making his professional debut in 2020. Because he was stuck in one place, he wasn’t able to work out, so he came to instructs with some added weight. The good news is that he still showed off tremendous tools and already has shed the excess pandemic-induced weight. The Angels gave Vera that kind of bonus because they feel he can be an impact player at a premium position. He swings the bat well from both sides of the plate, with excellent bat speed and an advanced feel for the strike zone that’s geared for contact. There’s definite raw power to tap into, but he’s hit over power for sure, with the chance for him to be a plus hitter in time. While Vera is an average runner, he might be as close to a true shortstop as the Angels have in the system. He moves very fluidly with outstanding actions and instincts, a strong arm and very true hands. The only thing that will keep him from being an above-average defender at short is if he slows down too much in the future, which eventually could necessitate a move to another infield position, though that’s not something being discussed at all internally at this point.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for $75,000 out of Aruba in 2022, Albertus slashed .303/.449/.415 in his first three pro seasons. He fractured his left tibia a month after getting promoted to Single-A at age 19 in mid-2024 and joined the White Sox shortly thereafter in a three-team trade that shipped Erick Fedde and Tommy Pham to the Cardinals and Michael Kopech to Los Angeles. He had surgery on his leg in November 2024 and has been slow to recover, playing just eight games on a rehab assignment in Rookie ball last year. One of the more advanced young hitters in the system, Albertus recognizes pitches well and employs a disciplined approach. He makes regular contact to all fields with a quick right-handed stroke and hangs in well against breaking balls. He was making progress learning to drive balls in the air when he got hurt and should provide 15 homers per year once he returns to health and adds more strength. While Albertus had below-average speed even before his leg injury, his high baseball IQ allowed him to play better than that on the bases and in the field. He has the solid arm strength, reliable hands and enough range to get the job done at third base. He has worked hard to improved his defense and also has seen action at shortstop and second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Dodgers for $75,000 out of Aruba in 2022, Albertus flew under the radar while spending most of his first two pro seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. After he gained some strength and made his U.S. debut in late July 2023, teams repeatedly asked about him in trade talks. The White Sox acquired him last July in a three-team swap that sent Erick Fedde and Tommy Pham to the Cardinals and Michael Kopech to Los Angeles. He didn't play after the deal because of a fractured left tibia that required surgery in November. A career .303/.449/.415 hitter in three years at the lowest levels of the Minors, Albertus stands out with his quick right-handed swing, disciplined approach and bat-to-ball skills. He continues to improve at lifting balls in the air and did a better job of using the opposite field last year. The next step will be to add more muscle to his 6-foot-1 frame so he can develop 15-homer power to go with his hitting ability. Though Albertus has below-average speed, his high baseball IQ helps him play a bit faster than that on the bases and in the field. His solid arm strength, reliable hands and lack of quickness make him best suited for third base, where he's a decent defender with the work ethic to become better. He divided his time equally between the hot corner, second base and shortstop in his first two years as a pro, and Chicago plans on giving him a chance to show what he can do in the middle infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Albertus initially flew under the radar in the Dodgers' 2022 international crop, signing for $75,000 out of Aruba and hitting a soft .304 in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. After starting to add some much-needed strength, he batted .309/.447/.479 last summer between the DSL and the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. Other teams took note and his name came up repeatedly in trade talks until the White Sox landed him in the three-team deal in July that shipped Erick Fedde and Tommy Pham to the Cardinals and Michael Kopech to the Dodgers. Even taking into consideration that Albertus has yet to face much in the way of advanced pitching, he has one of most patient approaches in the system, drawing 70 walks versus just 40 strikeouts in his first 85 pro games. He improved the quality of his contact last year, hitting the ball harder and launching it in the air much more consistently. A right-handed hitter, he can get pull-happy at times but offers the upside of a high on-base percentage guy who provides 15-20 homers per season. Albertus has a high baseball IQ that allows him to play faster than his fringy speed on the bases and in the field. He has solid arm strength and divided his time almost equally between third base, second base and shortstop in his first two pro seasons. He profiles best at second base and could be an average defender there or at the hot corner, while sticking at short is more of a stretch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Soler was the D-backs’ third-largest signing in the 2023 international class when he joined the organization for $425,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He’s been solid at every stop since then, though he’s still searching for a true full season of Minor League success. Soler was slow out of the gate as a 19-year-old with Single-A Visalia but caught fire after May, hitting .278/.386/.494 with eight homers and a 143 wRC+ over his final 48 games with the Rawhide. The right-handed slugger has a relaxed look in the box to the point where he’ll actually lay the bat down briefly on his back shoulder as he awaits the pitch from the mound. He’ll coil and get a leg kick going before unleashing his cuts. His strikeout rate has climbed about five percentage points per year, to the point where he fanned 22.3 percent of the time in the California League. Some of that is Soler’s willingness to jump on pitches outside the zone, leading to ground-ball contact, though he got a tad less aggressive during his hot streak. He has a compact build in his 5-foot-11 frame, and there’s already present strength there that could lead to 18-20 homers per year in the future if he can improve his angles off the bat. Soler isn’t any kind of a stolen-base threat with below-average speed, but he’ll show in flashes that he has the right hands for third base, the only position he’s played in pro ball so far. His above-average arm strength certainly fits the position, but he’ll rush his whippy throws sometimes, leading to inaccuracy. Soler is entering his 20s in 2026, just as he’s putting together the sum of his pieces as a classic power-first corner infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $425,000 signing out of the Dominican Republic in 2023, Soler was the D-backs’ third-largest addition in that class in terms of bonus and has continued to carve out an impressive standing for himself in the organization. He was a solid performer in the Dominican Summer League in his first season with a 97 wRC+ in his first 37 games and took off more stateside last year. The third baseman hit .303/.351/.472 with six homers in 53 games in the Arizona Complex League in his age-18 campaign and even got in a pair of games with Single-A Visalia to round out 2024. Soler looks relaxed from the right side of the box, lifts his lead leg a little and then relies on his hands to fire. It works because he’s able to manipulate the barrel well and put bat on ball consistently. His 17.2 percent strikeout rate in the ACL was solid for a player with his age and experience, though he did start to expand the zone much more than he had in the DSL. He’s already well built in his 5-foot-11 frame, and the raw power is above average. But he gets on top of the ball too often (50.3 percent ground-ball rate in the ACL), and he’ll continue to need to add lift to get to that pop. Soler has been third base-only at this early stage in his career, and D-backs officials feel like he’s a good fit for the position with good reads and reactions off the bat and plenty of arm strength for throws across the diamond, despite below-average speed overall. He’ll head to full-season ball for a longer look in 2025 and to potentially solidify his standing in Arizona’s infield corps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Buelvas signed with the A’s out of Colombia during the 2018-19 international signing period for $100,000. He has experienced several ups and downs while developing in the organization. Last season saw a bit of a resurgence for him as a prospect, as he moved back to High-A Lansing to begin the year before advancing to Double-A Midland. Between the two levels, he combined to hit .267/.352/.421 with eight home runs, 28 doubles, seven triples and 62 RBIs in 113 games. Then he went back home to play winter ball and was one of the top hitters in the Colombian Winter League, hitting .361 with a .986 OPS, nine homers, seven doubles and 35 RBIs in 34 games. Buelvas still strikes out a ton, but his overall approach has improved, leading to an ability to draw a decent amount of walks. His power is below average, though he can drive the ball to all fields. Keeping that line-to-line approach is how the A’s believe he can maximize his potential at the plate. The A’s are still dreaming of a Ramón Laureano-type defensive arc for Buelvas. Though he may not ever reach that kind of physicality, he is still a very good defender in his own right who can handle all three spots. His ability to cover ground with good speed and a solid arm have helped him stick at center field in the Minors. The intriguing tools are still there for Buelvas, even if they have developed a bit slowly, and a carryover of his recent success could boost his chances of getting another bump through the system, with the potential to develop into a fourth outfielder at the Major League level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Buelvas signed out of Colombia for $100,000 in 2018 and got off to a hot start in 2019 by hitting .300 as a 17-year-old playing in the Rookie-level Arizona League. After an encouraging 2021 in which he showed off his raw tools with 31 extra-base hits, 16 home runs and 17 stolen bases over 88 games with Low-A Stockton, he took a bit of a step back last season, hitting just .195 in 69 games at High-A Lansing. He continued to play into the winter with Vaqueros de Monteria in Colombia and hit .214 with four homers and 15 RBIs in 33 games. Buelvas has displayed qualities of a good approach at the plate at a young age with a decent ability to draw walks, even in a down season last year. He has shown off an intriguing speed and power combo, with the hope he can tap into that pop as he develops more into his wiry 5-foot-11 frame. A very good outfielder who can play all three spots well, Buelvas likely will continue to move around out there to maintain that versatility. The A’s are not too concerned about his down year, partially attributing the struggles to him being a bit worn out from his workload the previous year, which also included winter ball. They still see a bit of a Ramón Laureano-type skill set with him and hope he can bring more energy throughout the 2023 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $100,000 out of Colombia in 2018, Buelvas quickly made a good impression in 2019 by hitting .300 in the Rookie-level Arizona League as a 17-year-old. He really showed off his raw tools in 2021 with a total of 31 extra-base hits, 16 home runs and 17 stolen bases over 88 games in his first full season at Low-A. He spent some time in the Caribbean Series playing for Colombia and hit .273 with three RBIs in seven games, but didn’t carry that over to 2022, when he struggled offensively and missed considerable time with a hamstring injury. The A’s think Buelvas has the chance to have a good approach at the plate. For a player his age, he’s shown good plate discipline at times with his ability to draw walks. While the solid speed has always been there, the uptick in power was a pleasant surprise, given his wiry 5-foot-11 frame. With time, he has the chance to develop into a very good hitter. Able to play all three outfield spots, Buelvas projects to stick in center field, with the A’s believing he could evolve into a Ramón Laureano-type player without the amazing arm. His passion for the game is clear, which should help him advance through the system and ultimately establish himself as an everyday player at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Buelvas signed for $100,000 out of Colombia in July 2018 and put himself firmly on the prospect map in 2019, when he went to the Rookie-level Arizona League as a 17-year-old and shined with a .300/.392/.506 slash line and 20 extra-base hits in 44 games. He made a fairly successful jump to full-season ball as a teenager in 2021, reaching double-digits in home runs and stolen bases. The A’s have been impressed with how well Buelvas has handled everything that's been thrown at him at such a young age. He’s expected to develop into a plus hitter in due time, already showing an advanced approach with a willingness to draw walks. He’s an aggressive runner on the basepaths with a touch above average speed. He struggled some in the instructional league in 2020 after perhaps putting extra pressure on himself, but it appears he was able to learn from older players and use those lessons during his full-season debut. Buelvas can play all three outfield spots well, though he has the chance to stick in center field. The A’s love the passion he plays with just as much as his tools, which showed up consistently in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fountain became the Nebraska high-school career home run record holder when he was a junior at Norris HS and finished with 31 total blasts. An LSU commit, he went to the Padres in the fifth round of the 2024 Draft but signed for second-round money with a $1.7 million bonus. His time in the San Diego system has been marred by injuries – Tommy John surgery in his first pro fall, hamstring and knee injuries in his first full season. He played only 65 games split between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2025, hitting .226/.346/.309 with three homers and 21 steals. Big-framed at 6-foot-5, Fountain still hasn’t found a solid foundation in the San Diego system because of the unfortunate piling up of his injuries. His size and strength still give him tons to dream on, but he hit too many balls on the ground and swung through too many sliders in his California League stint. To his credit, he didn’t expand the zone as much as other high-schoolers jumping to the pros, and those swing decisions point to a more promising offensive future. Fountain can show above-average speed at times, and he was an efficient basestealer in 2025, only getting thrown out once in 22 attempts. He spent the vast majority of his time last year at first base, where he’s a big target, but the Padres moved him to the outfield for '26 in hopes of tapping into his athleticism. Fountain suffered a left shoulder injury in April that required season-ending surgery, adding another health issue to his growing list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 60 | Run: 45 | Arm: 55 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Fountain set the Nebraska high-school career home run record as a junior, surpassing Cole Stobbe (25) and Jakson Reetz (24), and finished with 31 total dingers when he graduated in 2024. He also set state career records with 154 RBIs and 84 stolen bases. On top of the individual success, Fountain helped Norris High School win a state Class B championship as a senior. After all that fanfare, the third baseman went to the Padres in the fifth round of the Draft but signed for second-round money with a $1.7 million bonus. He underwent Tommy John surgery in the fall, slowing his early ability to show out in pro games. Fountain stands at 6-foot-5 and brings massive right-handed power. He has tremendous bat speed and strength, and he can launch balls with loft and leverage in his swing. That cuts both ways in his case. Fountain had rough showings on the summer showcase circuit between his junior and senior years, and some scouts worry that his uphill stroke and strike-zone discipline will hold him back against pro pitching. On the plus side, he didn’t swing-and-miss too much, but that could come without proper adjustments. The Padres were aware of a potential elbow issue because of Fountain’s throwing motion out of school, but at his best, he shows at least above-average arm strength. Some scouts think he should be able to handle third base when healthy, but others believe he doesn’t have the range for the spot and will land at first long term. He's been primarily at the cold corner in his first taste of Minor League action while he's been tested early by full-season arms. The Padres rave about Fountain's makeup, and his work ethic will be put to the test as he moves beyond injuries and the early rough numbers with Single-A Lake Elsinore.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Righty-hitting catchers can be fighting an uphill battle in terms of Draft status, and you have to go back to Reds backstop Tyler Stephenson from the 2015 class to get a player in that profile who's found good MLB success. (Harry Ford, of the 2021 class, could join that list in time.) Like Stephenson, Harvey showed out in front of southeast scouts – this time coming from the Florida ranks – and he was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 153 prospect in the 2025 Draft. The Padres took him right around that slot in the fifth round but gave him their second-highest bonus at $1.5 million to sign away from a Florida State commitment. Harvey has strength and power in his 6-foot-2 frame and continually showed that off in high school, summer showcases and the Draft Combine. At the latter event, he hit three balls at 400-plus feet, tied for the most on Day 2 and maxed out with an exit velocity of 110.5 mph. Scouts were split on whether he would have the hit tool to get to that pop before the Draft, and Harvey’s limited contact in a short seven-game sample with Single-A Lake Elsinore didn’t help the cause. In that time however, he didn’t expand the zone much, and there’s hope the dip in the California League could open him to adjustments in his first full season. Harvey’s good hands and receiving skills will get him plenty of looks behind the plate, and his above-average arm strength fortifies the case, especially if he can clean up some of his mechanics. The Padres took fellow prep backstop Truitt Madonna in the Draft last year and will have to balance the workloads for both, but Harvey has more upside with his slugging advantage.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A growth spurt and some mechanical adjustments put Reyes on international radars a bit later than others in his 2025 international signing class. So while he wasn’t ranked on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50, his arm strength got him a $1.8 million bonus from the Braves, the second-largest figure given to a pitcher in the class behind only Roki Sasaki. He showed off his arm's potential, along with just how much he has to work on, during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. Reyes is now a 6-foot-4 pure thrower, one who will be 17 for nearly all of the 2026 season. It’s all about his fastball, and he can crank it into triple digits consistently, having topped out at 102 mph in the past. He doesn’t have much else he can rely on yet, but he started taking a step away from being a one-trick pony by improving his slider over the course of his DSL debut. Giving him grades on that and his control would be pure projection. He walked 29 (while striking out 35) in 27 DSL innings last year, so there’s obvious work to be done on learning how to repeat his delivery and find the zone. The Braves will let him keep starting for now so he can get reps in, but he likely will be a fireballing short reliever in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2025 international amateur class was extremely hitter-heavy, with only four pitchers in MLB Pipeline’s Top 50. That quartet was headlined, of course, by Roki Sasaki. Reyes wasn’t on the list, but thanks to a growth spurt and some tweaks in his mechanics, his arm strength got some late love from teams. The Braves, who also signed highly regarded outfielder Diego Tornes for $2.5 million, swooped in to get Reyes for just under $1.8 million, the largest bonus given to a pitcher not named Sasaki in the class. Now standing 6-foot-4 and 210 pounds, Reyes is all about arm strength and not much else at this point. He was one of the youngest players in this class, will be 16 for most of the 2025 season, and he enters pro ball about as raw as a pitcher can be. What he can do is throw very, very hard. His fastball has already touched triple digits, maxing out at 102 mph with some riding life coming from a three-quarters arm slot. The rest of Reyes’ repertoire is a bit of guesswork. He does have the makings of an 86-90 mph slider with cutting action and a mid-80s changeup with some fade, and the Braves think he has the feel to spin to add a power curve. He’ll hit the ground running, motivated to learn secondary stuff and how to find the strike zone consistently, though the Braves say he has an idea of how to command the baseball overall and a fierce desire to move up the ladder quickly. The Braves player international scouting staff gave their player development colleagues an impressive piece of clay. Now it’s up to them, and Reyes, to see how it gets sculpted.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Porter had a decorated high school career at St. Mary's Prep (Orchard Lake, Mich.), winning three state championships in three seasons, Gatorade state player of the year honors in 2021 and 2022 and Gatorade's national award in his senior season. Though he was MLB Pipeline's top-rated pitching prospect in the 2022 Draft, the Rangers managed to float him to the 109th pick, where they used the savings from taking Kumar Rocker at No. 3 to pay Porter a fourth-round-record $3.7 million. He logged a 2.47 ERA with a .160 opponent average and 95 strikeouts in 69 1/3 Single-A innings during his 2023 pro debut, though he also walked 42. Porter's fastball and changeup ranked among the best in the 2022 prep class, and the latter pitch continues to confound hitters with its tumble and fade. But after operating at 94-97 mph and touching 100 with his four-seamer in the past, he has sat at 90-93 mph for much of 2024, and his command and confidence with his heater have plummeted as well. He made just three starts in High-A in April before Texas sent him to the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, where he didn't appear in a game for another two months and continued to struggled when he returned. After showing inconsistent feel for spinning the ball in high school, Porter has scrapped an upper-70s curveball to focus on a mid-80s slider that's becoming a solid offering. But his control has gone from below average last year to a disaster this season, making him a wild card as a prospect. He once looked like he'd pitch in the front half of a rotation, but even before his struggles in 2024, several scouts outside the organization were projecting him as more of a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's top-rated pitching prospect in the 2022 Draft, Porter won three state titles in three seasons at St. Mary's Prep (Orchard Lake, Mich.) and was Gatorade's state player of the year in both 2021 and 2022. He also earned Gatorade's national award last spring, when he went 9-0 with a 0.41 ERA, 115 strikeouts in 58 innings and three no-hitters for a 44-0 team. After the Rangers saved money by taking Kumar Rocker with the third overall pick last July, they floated Porter all the way down to pick 109, where they destroyed the fourth-round bonus record by paying him $3.7 million. Porter had the best fastball and one of the best changeups in the 2022 high school class. He's able to sit at 94-97 mph for several innings at a time and reach triple digits with plenty of run and carry on his four-seamer. He achieves excellent velocity separation between his fastball and his low-80s changeup, which has devastating tumble and fade. Porter upgraded his slider significantly as a high school senior, flashing some plus mid-80s slide pieces, and also has a downer curveball in the upper 70s. His strong 6-foot-4 build should lend itself to durability and still has some remaining projection, and he does a nice job of repeating his low-effort delivery. Though Texas decided to defer his pro debut until 2023, he still should advance quickly for a prep pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A catcher at the outset of his high school career, Hurd blossomed into a top-two-rounds prospect on the mound but went undrafted in 2021 because he was determined to attend UCLA. He fared well as a Bruins freshman before coming down with a stress fracture in his lower back, then transferred to Louisiana State. Inconsistent as a sophomore before winning the clinchers in the semifinals and finals of the College World Series, he entered 2024 as a projected first-rounder but battled his control and command while getting hammered for a 6.55 ERA. After he went in the third round, he had Tommy John surgery in February 2025 and won't make his pro debut until this year. When he's healthy and dialed in, Hurd can overmatch hitters with a 93-96 mph fastball that climbs to 98 with significant armside run and carry. If they try to sit on his heater, he can make them look bad with a high-spin mid-80s slider that touches 91 mph with plenty of horizontal and vertical action. He threw just two changeups as a LSU junior, preferring to attack hitters with a 78-82 mph curveball with formidable depth but little consistency. Hurd is athletic and there's nothing glaringly wrong with his delivery, so he should have at least average control and be able to pitch in the front half of a rotation. But he never provided consistent strikes at LSU and working exclusively out of the stretch didn't help, and his lack of command meant he got hit harder than his pure stuff indicated he should. The Yankees develop pitchers better than most organizations, and he'll be an interesting project.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hurd started his prep career as a catcher before moving to the mound and would have been a top-two-rounds pick in 2021 if he wasn't set on attending UCLA. He pitched well as a Bruins freshman before missing the final two months with a stress fracture and transferring to Louisiana State, where he was inconsistent throughout 2023 before rallying to win the clinchers in the Men's College World Series Semifinals and Finals. Projected as a likely first-rounder in 2024, he once again battled his control and pitched his way out of the Tigers' rotation, which dropped him to the third round and an $836,400 bonus. He won't make his pro debut until 2026 after having Tommy John surgery in February. Hurd has a pair of quality pitches when healthy, beginning with a fastball that parks at 93-96 mph and reaches 98 with significant armside run and carry. His high-spin slider sits in the mid-80s and reaches 91 with plenty of horizontal and vertical movement. He threw just two changeups as an LSU junior, trying instead to combat left-handers with his 78-82 mph curveball. With his athleticism and a delivery that features arm speed rather than effort, Hurd should have at least average control, which would land him in the front half of a big league rotation. But he never has shown the ability to provide consistent strikes, his slider gets bashed when he doesn't command it and he hangs his curve too often. Many scouts believe his lack of reliability will land him in the bullpen, where his fastball and slider could become well-above-average offerings in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: To be filed under “pitching talent can come from anywhere,” Erla was a 17th-round pick of the Angels in their all-pitching 2021 Draft, signing for slot value ($125,000) after spending five years at Michigan State. The organization first thought that perhaps it had a Draft bargain when he was the most exciting arm at instructs the fall after he signed. He missed the first two months of the 2022 season with a shoulder issue but threw well across 16 starts in Double-A once he was healthy. Erla’s arsenal starts with what can be a plus fastball. He sat in the mid-90s during instructs in shorter stints and was around 93-94 mph, touching 97 with the Trash Pandas last year, but the organization thinks there’s more velocity in the tank. With a lower release, he does a good job of sinking it down in the zone to get ground-ball outs but also can get guys out at the top of the zone because of his unique release height. He flashed a solid mid-80s slider and he’s worked on a new one this offseason in the hopes of finding a true out pitch. He has a changeup that can miss bats and get contact on the ground, though it’s too firm at times. The 6-foot-4 Erla has shown he can repeat his delivery well and fill up the strike zone with all of his pitches. He’ll be 25 for most of the 2023 season, so the clock is ticking, and the Angels will continue to let him start because of his strike-throwing ability and the hope he can sharpen his two secondary offerings, knowing the fastball-slider from his slot could be nasty coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Erla spent five years at Michigan State, not getting drafted in 2019 after a rough season in the Spartans rotation and not getting selected in the shortened five-round Draft in 2020. He put up decent numbers in that fifth year to attract a little attention and the Angels made him pitcher No. 17 in their 20-pitcher Draft in 2021. He threw a handful of innings last summer in the Arizona Complex League to get his professional feet wet, then opened some eyes with his performance in instructional league play. The 6-foot-4 Erla may have been the most impressive arm at instructs for the Angels last fall. He’s more about arm strength than anything, with a fastball that sat 95-96 mph and touched 98 at instructs. After that, it’s a bit of a question mark. He showed a good hard slider in the mid-80s that has the chance to be a solid secondary offering and he has a changeup, but it’s well behind the other two as a below-average pitch. While Erla was generally around the plate at Michigan State, he didn’t have great command, but he’s been filling up the strike zone since joining the Angels. He’s already 24, but there’s an interesting combination of velocity and size here. He’ll get the chance to start for now and any future role will depend on the consistency of his secondary stuff and his ability to land them for strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of four baseball-playing brothers, Southisene has a twin (Tee) who pitches at CC of Southern Nevada, a younger sibling (Tate) whom the Braves drafted in 2025's first round and an even younger brother (Troy) who's a 2026 prep prospect committed to Oregon State. A fourth-rounder in 2024, Ty was one of the least physical players in his class but earned an over-slot $1 million bonus thanks to his high baseball IQ and long track record of performing well with USA Baseball and on the showcase circuit. He batted .244/.387/.276 with 41 steals in 90 Single-A games during his pro debut, ranking fifth in the Carolina League in runs (69) and on-base percentage. Southisene employs a very patient and sometimes passive approach to make a lot of contact, especially against fastballs, and get on base. But his flat right-handed swing and utter lack of strength resulted in the third-worst isolated power (.032) and seventh-worst ground-ball rate (60 percent) in the full-season Minors last year. He can put the bat on the ball vs. secondary pitches but rarely hits them with any authority, slashing .159/.261/.167 against them in 2025. Southisene's profile is similar to Nick Allen's with better on-base skills and quickness but not quite the Gold Glove-caliber defense. Not only does he have solid speed and twitch athleticism, but he also has the instincts to make the most of them. He compensates for his average arm strength with a quick release and was drafted as a shortstop, though he spent all of his time in Single-A at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Southisene was one of the least physical players in the 2024 Draft class at 5-foot-9 and 170 pounds, he stood out with his high baseball IQ and long track record of performance on the showcase circuit and with USA Baseball. The Cubs popped him in the fourth round and paid him an over-slot $1 million bonus to lure him away from a Tennessee commitment. His twin brother Tee is a right-hander at Southern California and younger sibling Tate was the Braves' 2025 first-round pick. More advanced than most prep products, Southisene has a disciplined approach and a penchant for using the opposite field. He has a good feel for the barrel, though his relatively flat right-handed swing and lack of strength may cap his power production at 10 homers per season and he has made next to no impact at the plate in his pro debut. He lapses into swinging for the fences at times and must recognize that his role is to make contact and get on base. Southisene's instincts allow him to make the most of his solid speed and twitchy athleticism on the bases and in the field. He has quick hands and feet and he makes up for merely average arm strength with a fast release. Though he was drafted as a shortstop, Chicago's system is overflowing with shortstop prospects, so he has spent 2025 at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baumeister was a highly touted prospect coming out of The Bolles School in Jacksonville in 2021, ranking among MLB Pipeline’s Top 100 Draft prospects that year despite the former catcher’s fairly recent (at the time) move to the mound. But he revealed on Draft Day that he would honor his commitment to Florida State, so he went undrafted until the Orioles took him 63rd overall in 2023 and signed him for an over-slot bonus of $1.61 million. They sent the advanced prospect to High-A for his full-season debut, and the Rays watched him dominate for Bowling Green after acquiring him in the Trade Deadline deal for starter Zach Eflin. Baumeister is coming off an odd year that delayed a widely expected breakout. He had a terrible April and an up-and-down May before going on the injured list with a shoulder injury that kept him out until August. When he returned, he was lights out, with a 0.78 ERA and 20 strikeouts compared to seven walks in 20 innings over five starts for Double-A Montgomery. Then came an underwhelming stint in the Arizona Fall League, where he was fine despite taking a comebacker off his head. The righty leans mostly on his fastball, a mid-90s heater with good life and upper-90s velocity in the tank if needed. His arsenal has evolved to the point where his cutter/slider is now his top secondary pitch, although his curveball has typically been his out pitch. The Rays were encouraged with the work he did on his changeup in the AFL, and he’ll need it to create separation with his fastball, especially against lefties. Baumeister is big and strong, standing 6-foot-4 with plenty of extension down the mound, and his physicality paired with his fastball can create uncomfortable at-bats for hitters. If he can stay healthy, improve his changeup and limit walks, he’ll give the Rays another starting pitching prospect to watch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baumeister could have been picked pretty high in the 2021 Draft out of high school, having ranked among MLB Pipeline’s Top 100 Draft prospects that year as a former catcher who moved to the mound. But the Jacksonville native announced on Draft day that he would honor his commitment to Florida State and, thus, went unselected. Two years later, the Orioles took him 63rd overall, signed him for an over-slot bonus of $1.61 million and pushed him to High-A for his first full season. He was off to a nice start there before the Rays landed him as part of a three-prospect haul for starter Zach Eflin, and he turned in a dominant stretch to finish the year. Baumeister’s arsenal isn’t quite as elite as fellow Trade Deadline pickup Brody Hopkins, but he features a good combination of stuff, strike-throwing and command. He’s a fastball-dominant starter, using his heater more than half the time, and he throws that pitch in the mid-90s with good life and 97 mph in the tank if he needs it. But his curveball is his go-to out pitch, and it’s up there with the best benders in the Rays’ system. The right-hander has a starter’s frame, listed at 6-foot-4 and 224 pounds, and he’s got the makings of a full arsenal with a cutter-y slider and a changeup. It's a little bit challenging to get a read on Baumeister, in part because of how his performance fluctuates. He struggled to limit his walks as a reliever early in his college career, then he got them somewhat under control in the rotation as a Draft-eligible sophomore despite mixed overall results. He was averaging 5.5 walks per nine innings in Baltimore’s system before the trade, then only walked five batters in 29 innings (while, by the way, striking out 44 and only allowing 12 hits) with the High-A Bowling Green. A shoulder injury has kept him from taking that next leap in his first full season as a Ray.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A converted catcher ranked as a high school prospect on MLB Pipeline’s Top 100, Baumeister had a chance to be picked fairly high in the 2021 Draft. But he went unselected after announcing on the day of the Draft that he was honoring his commitment to Florida State, and it wasn’t until two years later that the Orioles took him in Competitive Balance Round B with the 63rd overall pick in 2023. Baumeister signed for an over-slot $1.61 million bonus and moved to High-A Aberdeen for his first full season, posting a 3.06 ERA with a 29.5 percent strikeout rate over 70 2/3 innings. The Rays picked him up as part of a three-prospect return for Zach Eflin at the Trade Deadline. At 6-foot-4 and 224 pounds, Baumeister is a tall, physical right-hander with exciting raw stuff. His best pitches are a low-to-mid-90s fastball that can get as high as 97 mph and a playable mid-70s curve he uses to keep hitters off balance. He also can dunk in a developing cutter-like slider at times as well as a fringy changeup, but both those pitches are behind his primary offerings. The fastball shows some good riding quality up in the zone, and it’s not hard to believe Baumeister will be able to get to consistently plus velocity with it as he grows and develops. Baumeister began his college career pitching in relief and then had mixed results in the rotation as a Draft-eligible sophomore, in part because he’s had trouble at times limiting walks. He might be able to clean up those issues because of his fairly simple delivery and his size suggests he can be durable. That remains a work in progress on the pro side, but his overall pitch shapes should make for exciting additions to the Tampa Bay pipeline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last and least expensive player signed in the Astros' 2021 international crop, Fleury turned pro for $10,000 that December out of the Dominican Republic. He made a spectacular pro debut in 2022, compiling a 1.42 ERA and 60/4 K/BB ratio in 38 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, then jumped from Single-A in 2023 to Double-A the following year. He posted a 1.82 ERA in Double-A in the first half of 2025, missing a month with shoulder issues, then tasted adversity for the first time when he got rocked for a 6.95 ERA in Triple-A. Fleury's success stems from his changeup, which sits around 80 mph with plenty of fade and depth, parachuting through the bottom right-hand corner of the strike zone. He struggled in Triple-A when hitters sat on his cambio because his other fringy pitches couldn't make them pay. His fastball features good carry but sits around 90 mph and peaks at 94. His low-80s cutter, 78-82 mph slider and mid-70s curveball all lack power and get barreled. The 6-foot Fleury lacks physicality but his athleticism helps him repeat his high arm slot and provide regular strikes. It also allows him to get down the mound well and create atypical extension for his size. He has some of best feel for pitching in the system but will have to upgrade his arsenal to claim a regular role in Houston.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The final and cheapest player signed in Houston's 2021 international class, Fleury turned pro for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic that December. He broke into pro ball by logging a 1.42 ERA with a 60/4 K/BB ratio in 38 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2022. He continued to dominate in Single-A in his U.S. debut the following year, then skipped a level and held his own in Double-A last year despite a thigh injury that sidelined him for two months. Fleury's changeup has fueled his success, operating in the low 80s with fade and huge depth while deceiving both lefties and righties. It drops through the bottom of the strike zone and pairs nicely with a 90-92 mph fastball that tops out at 94 and stands out much more with its carry than its velocity. He trusts his low-80s slider more than his upper-70s curveball, though neither is as effective as his cambio or heater. Fleury makes up for a lack of physicality with athleticism and a fluid, high three-quarters delivery that he repeats well. He adds deception by getting down the mound well and creating a low-release height with quality extension. He doesn't have a high ceiling but can be a No. 4 or 5 starter if he can find a little more velocity or improve his breaking stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last and least expensive player signed by the Astros in their 2021 international class, Fleury turned pro for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic that December. He made a spectacular pro debut in 2022, recording a 1.42 ERA with a 60/4 K/BB ratio in 38 innings in the Dominican Summer League. He came to the United States last year and earned All-Star accolades in the Carolina League, where his strikeout rate (12.7 per nine innings) and average-against (.181) would easily have topped the Single-A circuit if he hadn't fallen just short of qualifying. Fleury's low-80s changeup has significant fade and has keyed his early career success. It helps him make the most of a fastball that stands out more for its induced vertical break and carry coming out of a low release height than it does for its velocity, operating at 90-92 mph and topping out at 94. He throws two breaking balls, with his upper-70s curveball grading better than a tight 78-82 mph slider, though both need work. Though he lacks physicality, Fleury is athletic and repeats his delivery well. While his walk rate jumped from 0.9 per nine innings in his debut to 4.4 in 2023, he should have at least average control once he's fully developed. Adding some velocity and refining his breaking stuff would help raise his ceiling, but he's on a promising path to becoming a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fleury was the last and least expensive player signed by the Astros in its 2021 international class, turning pro in December for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He broke into pro ball in spectacular fashion, posting a 60/4 K/BB ratio with a 1.42 ERA in 38 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He continued to impress during instructional league, building anticipation for his U.S. debut in 2023. Fleury's best offering is his low-80s changeup, which features plenty of fade and plays well off his fastball. He doesn't throw especially hard, sitting at 90-92 mph and touching 94, but his heater has outstanding vertical movement and good carry coming out of a low release height. His breaking pitches need significant work because his 75-78 mph curveball gets slurvy and blends with his tight 78-82 mph slider. Though young DSL hitters don't exactly have refined plate discipline, Fleury's strike-throwing numbers are nonetheless impressive. He lacks physicality but is athletic and repeats his delivery well. He needs to refine a better breaking ball and is years from the Majors, but he has starter traits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz’s long journey in pro ball began all the way back in February 2017 when he signed with the Dodgers for $60,000. He advanced to full-season ball as a starter in 2019, then had to wait through the pandemic to return in 2021. He threw just 11 2/3 innings before needing Tommy John surgery, and between that and other injury setbacks, didn’t throw another competitive pitch for three years. After 11 innings in 2024, he pitched his way from High-A to Triple-A in 2025 as a reliever and earned a spot on the 40-man roster. The Dodgers faced a roster crunch and sent him to the Mariners this past offseason in a trade for Minor Leaguer Tyler Gough. Now 26, Ortiz has the chance to impact a big league bullpen soon. The Mariners really liked his slider, a firm mid-80s breaker with good action to it -- a pitch they think could have even better characteristics. He pairs it well with a 94-95 mph fastball that gets a decent amount of miss and chase. He’ll also work in a hard 90 mph cutter. Command has been one issue for Ortiz, and that might limit what his ultimate bullpen role is, but he also missed so much time from the mound that there could be some improvement to come in terms of his strike-throwing ability. He could fit the Mariners’ need for a lefty reliever this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz signed for $60,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the end of the 2016-17 international period. He helped win a championship in the Rookie-level Arizona League in his 2018 U.S. debut, then made a successful jump to low Class A at age 19 in 2019. He opened eyes with improved velocity during Spring Training last year but didn't participate at Los Angeles' alternate site or instructional league program after the coronavirus pandemic cancelled the Minor League season. Ortiz worked at 94-97 mph during live batting practice last spring after previously operating at 90-93 and topping out at 95 with running action on his fastball. He uses his heater to set up a solid changeup with fade and sink that he throws with the same arm speed. His slider has its moments but gets slurvy at times and is clearly his third-best pitch. Ortiz isn't especially big or projectable but he's athletic and repeats his delivery well, which should allow him to throw strikes. His walk rate nearly doubled from 2.2 per nine innings in his first two pro seasons to 4.2 in low Class A, but Los Angeles believes some minor mechanical adjustments will improve his consistency. He has a ceiling of a No. 4 starter and has elicited comparisons to a smaller version of Caleb Ferguson, though a strained forearm in May put Ortiz's development on hold once again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Oklahoma's top high school prospect in 2018, Franklin missed most of his senior season with a broken foot yet still landed third-round money ($450,000) as a sixth-round pick. The nephew of former All-Star closer, Ryan Franklin, he significantly improved his stuff during his first full pro season, then didn't pitch at all the next two years because of the pandemic shutdown (2020) and oblique and shoulder issues (2021). He never got into a rhythm making abbreviated starts every six or seven days last season in High-A, recording a 6.88 ERA with 75 strikeouts in 69 1/3 innings. Franklin had no trouble regaining his fastball velocity in 2022, hitting 99 mph in his first live batting practice in Spring Training and working at 94-97 mph and touching 99 during the season. His fading changeup was still his best secondary pitch, albeit a little less lively because it got a bit too firm at 83-86 mph. After showing limited feel for spin as an amateur, he has developed a 78-82 mph knuckle-curve that's at least a solid pitch when it's on, and he has added a similarly effective sweeping low-80s slider in 2023. While his stuff returned, Franklin had difficulty locating his pitches, issued too many walks and got crushed when he caught too much of the zone. His fastball has more downhill plane than life and gets hit when he doesn't command it, and he can have trouble throwing his secondary pitches for strikes. He still flashes mid-rotation upside, but he's also 23 years old with just 120 innings in his first five years as a pro and may wind up as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of former All-Star closer Ryan Franklin, Kohl ranked as Oklahoma's top prep prospect in 2018 but missed most of his senior season with a broken foot. After selecting him in the sixth round and paying him third-round money ($450,000), the Cubs were delighted by the progress he made in his first full pro season in 2019. But he didn't pitch at all the next two years because of the pandemic shutdown in 2020 followed by oblique and minor shoulder maladies in 2021. As Franklin has added muscle to his 6-foot-4 frame, his fastball has increased from 86-89 mph in 2017 to 89-93 in 2018 to 93-96 in 2019, and he worked at 97-99 during his first live batting practice in Spring Training 2022. His best secondary pitch is a low-80s changeup with fade that plays well off his four-seamer. He lacked feel for spin as an amateur but added an upper-70s knuckle-curve in 2019, and it shows signs of becoming at least a solid offering. Franklin has the athleticism to repeat his delivery and fill the strike zone, though his control and command have been erratic in High-A this year. He uses his size and high three-quarter arm slot to create downhill plane on his pitches, and club officials praise his maturity and competitiveness. He has the ingredients to become a mid-rotation starter but must prove he can handle the workload after totaling just 50 2/3 innings in his first four pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of former All-Star Ryan Franklin, Kohl emerged as Oklahoma's top high school prospect in 2018 but missed most of his senior season with a broken right foot. The Cubs took him in the sixth round and paid him third-round money ($450,000) to divert him from a college commitment to Oklahoma. His stuff took a jump forward during his first full pro season in 2019 but the coronavirus pandemic scuttled plans to build up his workload in full-season ball last year and he has yet to pitch in 2021 while dealing with an oblique injury. As he fills out his 6-foot-4 frame, Franklin continues to add fastball velocity, going from 86-89 mph in 2017 to 89-93 in 2018 to 91-97 the last two years. The Cubs think he eventually could sit at 93-96 mph and back up his heater with a pair of solid to plus secondary pitches. He has advanced aptitude for a hard changeup with fade and has taken to a knuckle-curve he adopted in 2019 after showing inconsistent feel for spin as an amateur. Franklin's athleticism and ability to repeat his delivery allow him to provide consistent strikes. He uses his size and high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill plane on his pitches. He offers hope for a mid-rotation starter to an organization that has had difficulty developing homegrown pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox might have taken Kath with their 2021 first-round pick if Colson Montgomery hadn't been available, so they were delighted to grab him as their second-rounder with an over-slot $1.8 million bonus. Gatorade's Arizona player of the year, he led Desert Mountain HS (Scottsdale) to the state 5-A title and crushed a long home run at the Angels' Spring Training stadium in the championship game. He hasn't thrived in pro ball, batting .227/.325/.367 with a 35 percent strikeout rate in his first two pro seasons. Scouts considered Kath one of the more advanced hitters in the 2021 prep class, but he has struggled to catch up to quality fastballs and to recognize breaking balls as a pro. Chicago helped him simplify the load with his left-handed swing, and while he did a better job of drawing walks and avoiding ground-ball contact last season than he did in his debut, his propensity for swinging and missing remains a huge concern. He still has plus raw power that could translate into 20 or more homers per season if he can put the bat on the ball more regularly, but he also needs to add more strength after his bat speed diminished late in the year. Kath played shortstop in high school but his below-average speed and quickness prompted an immediate move to third base in pro ball. He has the potential to become at least an average defender with soft hands and plus arm strength at the hot corner, though he'll have to improve his agility and consistency. He has a ways to go to catch Bryan Ramos as Chicago's third baseman of the future, which eventually could prompt a move to first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kath factored into the White Sox's possibilities for the first round of the 2021 Draft, so they were thrilled to find him available in the second. Gatorade's Arizona player of the year, he carried Desert Mountain High (Scottsdale) to the state 5-A title and smashed a long homer at the Angels' Spring Training park in the championship game. Signed for an over-slot $1.8 million, he hit just .212/.287/.337 with a 37 percent strikeout rate during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. Kath was one of the more advanced hitters in the 2021 high school crop, employing an easy left-handed swing and a mature approach to make consistent hard contact to all fields. He tried to do too much in the ACL, chasing and trying to pull too many pitches and producing a lot of weak contact when he did connect. If he gets back to focusing on driving the ball from gap to gap and can add some loft to his stroke, he could become a solid hitter with average or better pop. A shortstop in high school, Kath immediately moved to third base after turning pro. Though he's a below-average runner, he has enough range to go with soft hands and plus arm strength at the hot corner.
