mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles tend to sign more position players than pitchers from the international market, but they’ve made good decisions with the hurlers they’ve targeted, seeing prospect success with arms like lefty Luis De Leon and righty Esteban Mejia. They think Hidalgo is more advanced at his age than either of those guys were, making him a highlight of their 2026 class when they signed him out of the Dominican Republic for $700,000. A 6-foot-4, 170-pound left-hander, Hidalgo has a great frame for a 16-year-old pitcher, more space to fill out and already features premium stuff for his age. His fastball gets up into the mid-90s, and he also throws a sharp slider that has potential to be a plus pitch. He may work to develop a changeup down the line as he faces better competition but doesn’t need one very much right now. Hidalgo is still learning to control his body and throw strikes consistently, but he has a low-effort, repeatable delivery and creates some deception with his long limbs. He was young for his class and has a long road of development ahead but has an extremely high ceiling if the command part clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player who played shortstop and was largely a reliever at Hanover High School in Virginia, Keller jumped on prospect map as a pitcher with a 16-strikeout performance at the 2022 National High School Invitational and then continued to raise his profile in Hanover’s rotation the rest of the spring. His athleticism and arm strength helped him land with the Braves in the sixth round of that summer’s Draft, getting well over slot to sign him away from his commitment to Old Dominion. It was looking like a wise investment when he posted a 1.17 ERA and .180 batting average against over his first six outings with Single-A Augusta, but after a month on the injured list due to elbow inflammation, his stuff backed up and he got hit hard in the 23 innings he pitched the rest of the year. Keller is hoping to hit the reset button as he continues to learn how to be a pitcher only. The sub-six footer has quick-twitch athleticism working in his favor on the mound, and when he’s right, he’s shown a low-90s fastball with run that he can crank up to 95 mph. He’s shown good feel for a low-80s changeup with fade and thrown with deception thanks to Keller’s arm speed. A low-80s slider with 11-to-5 break gives him a third at least average pitch. While his athleticism should help him repeat his delivery, Keller struggled with his command and control, especially after he came off the injured list. There is some effort there and that, along with his size, had some evaluators dubious about his ability to start long-term and he did a fair amount of relief work during his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Keller might have been known to area scouts in Virginia as a high school shortstop who also served as a reliever at Hanover High School. His profile changed when he stepped in as a starter at the 2022 National High School Invitational and struck out 16 early in the spring, then taking over in the rotation when Levin Huesman got hurt. The Braves liked the two-way standout’s athleticism and arm strength on the mound enough to go well over slot -- close to $700,000 -- to sign him in the sixth round of last summer’s Draft. The Braves are banking on Keller’s quick-twitch athletic actions playing as he focuses on pitching only for the first time. The undersized right-hander can touch the mid-90s with his fastball, though he’s not up there consistently, sitting a tick below that with good run. The Braves think his low-80s fading changeup is his best secondary pitch, which comes with good deception thanks to Keller being able to maintain his arm speed well. He has a solid low-80s slider with decent 11-to-5 break as well. There is optimism Keller’s stuff will mature as he adds strength, and he should be able to repeat his delivery well and find the strike zone consistently thanks to that athleticism. There’s been some effort in the delivery in the past and because of his size, he’ll have to show he can handle a starter’s workload, but that’s not a conversation the organization has to worry about yet.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes slow and steady can win the race in player development. That’s what the Phillies are hoping is true with Graves, who they took as a raw high school pitching prospect back in the sixth round of the 2022 Draft. There have been some bumps along the way, like with his pro debut in the Florida Complex League in 2023, but he bounced back with a move to Single-A Clearwater in 2024. Another rung up the ladder in High-A Jersey Shore in 2025, Graves started slowly, with a 6.50 ERA, .270 BAA and 1.83 WHIP through June, but he turned a corner once July hit, posting a 1.93 ERA, .189 BAA and 1.18 WHIP for the remainder of the season. A 6-foot-6 southpaw, Graves’ fastball typically sits around 90-91 mph, topping out at 94-95 mph, and he’ll throw both a four-seamer up in the zone and an occasional two-seamer with sink, though he’s yet to grow into more consistent velocity. His bread-and-butter is his ability to spin the baseball, with elite-level spin rates on his breaking stuff, an upper-70s sweeper and a harder cutter-like slider, both of which miss a lot of bats. Graves has a low-80s changeup that can be effective against right-handed hitters, but the Phillies are working with him to commit to throwing his best pitch -- that slider -- against hitters on both sides of the plate. He’s going to need to be more consistent in the strike zone to remain a starter, though it would be interesting to see if he gains a few ticks on the fastball in shorter stints and uses that slider to neutralize lefties.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies rolled the dice in the 2022 Draft when they took Graves, a tall project of a high-school left-hander out of South Carolina, in the sixth round, and it’s looking like a gamble that could pay off. They slow-rolled him, with Graves not making his pro debut until 2023 in the Florida Complex League, and that didn’t go well. But a move to full-season ball in 2024 provided the first glimpse of what the future might look like, with a 31.8 percent strikeout rate over 84 innings with Clearwater as a 20-year old. There are few players in the Phillies system who made more strides in one year than Graves did in 2024. The 6-foot-6 southpaw can attack hitters with as many as five pitches. He’ll throw both a four-seamer up in the zone and a two-seamer with sink in the 90-95 mph range, getting a lot of groundballs with the latter. He’s already added some strength, with room for more, so it’s easy to dream on him living more in the 93-95 mph range and holding it, making the fastball more playable. Graves can really spin a breaking ball, registering spin rates north of 3,000 rpm with his slider. He has a separate cutter, though the two pitches run into each other, both missing a ton of bats in the low-80s. His changeup took a nice step forward, killing spin with it. Graves also improved dramatically in finding the strike zone, lowering his walk rate to 3.9 per nine in 2024. Continued work on his command, especially the secondary stuff, along with expected velocity gains, could allow him to keep evolving into a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sikkema’s Draft stock soared his junior year at Missouri, when he posted a conference-leading 1.32 ERA that spring and demonstrated a strong makeup and feel for pitching. The Yankees took him in Competitive Balance Round A that summer, signing him for nearly $2 million, but his full-season debut didn’t come until 2022 because of injuries. He made 18 starts last year and posted a 4.83 ERA over 69 innings, splitting his time between High-A with the Yankees and Double-A with the Royals, who acquired Sikkema and two others in July for Andrew Benintendi. Sikkema has a funky delivery to throw at hitters, throwing crossfire coupled with his stocky frame. He varies his arm angle and manipulates his pitches to see them play up more. His two-seamer sits in the upper 80s or low 90s and is thrown from a low three-quarters arm slot. His four-seamer is 93-95 mph and comes from an overhand slot. His slider has tight spin, and his changeup has sink to it in the low 80s. Sikkema’s strikeout rate fell to 18.7 percent in the jump to Double-A. He got hit around a lot more at the next level, but the Royals are hoping as he settles into his new organization, so will his stuff. Sikkema’s ceiling is as a back-end starter, but his stocky body might present problems. Many scouts see his delivery and mix as a good fit in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sikkema demonstrated some of the best feel for pitching and strongest makeup in the 2019 Draft, and he topped the Southeastern Conference and ranked third in NCAA Division I with a 1.32 ERA at Missouri that spring. He figured to move quickly after signing for $1,949,800 but had yet to make his full-season debut nearly two years later. His conditioning regressed during the pandemic layoff and he missed all of 2021 with shoulder and lat issues that didn't require surgery. He was back to pitching consistently at High-A in 2022 before the Yankees moved him to the Royals in the Andrew Benintendi trade in July. Sikkema's aptitude to vary his arm angle and manipulate his pitches has led club officials to compare him to a southpaw version of Orlando Hernandez. He can produce 88-91 mph two-seam fastballs with plenty of run and sink from a low three-quarters angle and hit 93-95 mph with four-seamers from a more overhand slot. He can alter the shape of a 78-83 mph slider with high spin rates and keeps right-handers at bay with a sinking changeup in the low 80s. While Sikkema's stocky body and crossfire delivery are less than ideal, he attacks the strike zone and commands his pitches well. His stuff plays up because of the angle and extension he creates and his abundant confidence and willingness to challenge hitters on the inside part of the plate. Now that he's healthy and in better shape, the Royals will take on the responsibility of molding him into a potential back-end starter. He turned 24 in July so the clock is ticking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Missouri has produced 11 big league pitchers (most prominently Max Scherzer) and six arms taken in the top two rounds since 2003, including Sikkema last year. He led the Southeastern Conference and ranked third in NCAA Division I with a 1.32 ERA, demonstrating some of the best feel for pitching and strongest makeup in the 2019 Draft. Taken with a supplemental first-round pick acquired from the Reds in the Sonny Gray trade, he signed for $1,949,800. Sikkema's ability to vary his arm angle and manipulate his pitches reminds some Yankees officials of a left-handed version of Orlando Hernandez. He operates at 88-91 mph with quality run and sink on his fastball from a low three-quarters slot and can reach back for 93-95 mph from a more overhand look when needed. He can change the shape of his 78-83 mph slider, which features high spin rates and is a plus offering at its best. Sikkema also trusts his sinking changeup, which keeps right-handers honest. His stocky build and his crossfire delivery aren't pretty, but his stuff plays better than its grades because of his angle, extension and supreme confidence. He's not afraid to attack the strike zone or pitch inside, adding to a package that gives him a high floor with the upside of a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Acker pitched at three colleges in three years, bouncing from Rice to San Jacinto (Texas) JC to Oklahoma before joining the Athletics as a fourth-rounder in 2020. Because of the pandemic shutdown, he didn't make his pro debut until after he got traded with Jonah Heim and Khris Davis to the Rangers for Elvis Andrus and Aramis Garcia in February 2021. His four-seam fastball soared to 94-99 mph and his curveball jumped into the mid-80s that spring, but he blew out his elbow two starts into the season and hasn't shown that stuff again since having Tommy John surgery that May. More of a low-90s two-seamer guy in college, Acker settled in at 92-94 mph and topped out at 96 with carry and run on his four-seamer last summer after missing the first six weeks of the season with shoulder issues. He has good shape on his curveball, though it's back to sitting at 78-82 mph. His fading mid-80s changeup was easily his best pitch in 2023, both in terms of landing in the zone and missing bats. Acker continues to stand out with his intelligence and mound presence, though he hasn't fully regained the feel for pitching he had before his elbow reconstruction. He struggled to throw both his fastball and slider for consistent strikes last year, though he still managed to compile a 2.54 ERA, .182 average-against and 76 strikeouts in 67 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. He may not have the same mid-rotation ceiling he flashed in 2021, but the Rangers still like his potential as a starter and could expedite him to the Majors as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Acker spent three years in college at three different schools, moving from Rice to San Jacinto (Texas) JC to Oklahoma before signing with the Athletics as a fourth-rounder in 2020. The pandemic shutdown meant that he never pitched in a game in Oakland's system before he got traded along with Khris Davis and Jonah Heim to Texas for Elvis Andrus and Aramis Garcia in February 2021. He created a lot of excitement with dramatically improved stuff that spring, but he blew his elbow out after two Single-A starts and had Tommy John surgery in May. A sinker/slider guy who operated in the low-90s and threw four pitches for strikes at Oklahoma, Acker suddenly whipped out a 94-99 mph four-seamer and a low-80s curveball with improved power and spin in his two 2021 starts. When he returned to the mound last summer, neither pitch was nearly as overwhelming. He did show more consistency with a fading mid-80s changeup that earned plus grades and also worked in some average low-80s sliders. Acker didn't fully regain his feel for pitching last season, typical for pitchers in the early stages of coming back from elbow reconstruction, but he has the potential for plus control with at least average command. The Rangers will have a better idea of what exactly they have in him when he pitches a full season in 2023 and are encouraged that his stuff looked stronger during offseason workouts. His intelligence and competitive drive will help him get the most out of his ability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 Acker pitched at three colleges in three years, going from Rice to San Jacinto (Texas) JC to Oklahoma and turning down the Diamondbacks as a 23rd-rounder in 2019 before signing with the Athletics as a fourth-rounder in 2020. He never played for Oakland, which traded him along with Khris Davis and Jonah Heim to acquire Elvis Andrus and Aramis Garcia in February 2021. He displayed spectacular stuff in two Low-A starts before blowing out his elbow and having Tommy John surgery in May. In his last college season with the Sooners, Acker was a sinker/slider guy who worked in the low 90s and relied on throwing four pitches for strikes. In his two pro starts -- admittedly a small sample size -- he unveiled a four-seam fastball that ranged from 94-99 mph and a low-80s downer curveball with improved power and spin. He also flashed some plus upper-80s changeups and average mid-80s sliders. Acker returned to the mound this summer with a little less fastball and curveball but a more consistent changeup. He's an intelligent and competitive pitcher who repeats his delivery and throws strikes, so he doesn't need overwhelming velocity to succeed. Once considered a floor-over-ceiling guy, he now has a shot at pitching in the front half of a big league rotation if he regains the stuff he showed in his brief pro debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before Orioles executive vice president Mike Elias took over baseball operations and hired Koby Perez as his international scouting director, the team had long-eschewed Latin America from a scouting standpoint. They were one of the few teams without a presence in the talent-rich region, and their system suffered for it. As it was, the franchise had never given out a seven-figure bonus until Hernandez received one of two in 2020-21, when the 17-year-old Venezuelan signed for $1.2 million. So far Hernandez is yet to deliver on that promise, after struggling in his first two seasons in Rookie ball. Hernandez is tall, graceful and strong at 6-foot-3, with a smooth right-handed swing and an all-fields approach some believe cuts into the raw power he flashes in batting practice. That power is nonexistent in games at this point, with Hernandez going homeless in his first 82 professional contests, but he’s still young enough to grow into more as his body matures. He is an average runner but quick with strong baserunning instincts. Hernandez is more advanced on defense, where his athleticism complements an above-average arm and smooth hands. He cut down his errors significantly in his second year in Rookie ball, without undercutting the good footwork and impressive range that make him a standout defender. There is still a chance he may have to move off the position because of his size, depending on his growth in the coming years. But the bigger question mark right now is whether Hernandez will hit enough to eventually make that a conversation. This is a big year for Hernandez to work on re-setting his ceiling, which when he signed was arguably as high as anyone in the Orioles’ system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles made the international market a priority for the first time under executive vice president and GM Mike Elias and international scouting director Koby Perez, hoping to establish themselves in the talent-rich region after hardly tapping into Latin America for decades. They had a headliner for those burgeoning efforts last year in Hernandez, a lean and athletic shortstop who received one of the first two seven-figure bonuses in franchise history. Hernandez signed for $1.2 million as a 17-year-old out of Venezuela, then showed promise despite choppy results in his first season at Rookie ball. At 6-foot-3, Hernandez is tall, graceful and strong, reminding some scouts of a young Alex Rodriguez or Carlos Correa because of his body type. His right-handed swing is smooth and easy, with flashes of raw power potential that have yet to show up in games. He can hit to all fields, make consistently hard contact and show a prescient understanding of the strike zone. He walked more than expected in the Dominican Summer League despite the lack of power. His discipline, and strength are expected to develop as his body matures. He is an average runner but quick with good instincts on the bases. Tool-wise, Hernandez is more advanced at this point on defense, where his athleticism shows in abundance. He has an above-average arm, smooth hands and good footwork, despite committing his share of errors in the DSL. That’s not uncommon for young infielders with impressive range, and the Orioles don’t want to undercut his aggressive instincts on the dirt. If Hernandez must move off the position eventually it’ll probably be because of his size, depending on his growth in the coming years. But as Correa, Rodriguez and others have shown, there is certainly a place for tall shortstops in the Majors — and their upside often outweighs the risk. Hernandez’s size, athleticism and youth enable the Orioles to dream on him as a player with that kind of ceiling; while his floor is probably as a utilityman at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles were dormant for years in the international market, eschewing it almost entirely before Mike Elias became general manager in 2018 and immediately hired Koby Perez as his director of international scouting. Come international signing day 2021, Hernandez was the main headliner of a record-setting class for which the Orioles shelled out their first two seven-figure bonuses in franchise history. A lean and athletic shortstop, Hernandez, 17, signed for $1.2 million out of Venezuela. At 6-foot-3 and 175 pounds, Hernandez reminds some scouts of a young Alex Rodriguez and Carlos Correa because of his body type. His right-handed swing is smooth and easy, with flashes of raw power potential and an ability to hit to all fields. He already makes consistent hard contact and shows an early understanding of the strike zone, although he would benefit from improving his plate discipline as he develops. Hernandez’s athleticism shows most obviously on defense, where he displays an above-average arm, smooth hands and good footwork. There is belief he’ll stay at the position as he grows, but could require an eventual move to third base depending on how his body matures in pro ball. More important to scouts is the upside, which gives Hernandez the ceiling of an impact regular in the big leagues with a utility man floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Blanco began his pro career when he signed with the Pirates for $900,000 in January 2022. The son of the late Tony Blanco, who spent 17 years in pro ball, Blanco Jr. has shown that he can get to his immense power with 18 homers over 362 career at-bats but he’s had trouble both making contact and staying healthy. He’s yet to play more than 40 games in a season, and while he did reach full-season ball for the first time in 2025, he missed much of the year with a hamstring injury. He made up for some lost time in the Arizona Fall League, where he put on a show in winning the Fall Stars Home Run Derby. A mountain of a young man at 6-foot-7 and over 240 pounds, Blanco’s calling card is, and always will be, his immense raw power. He hits the ball extremely hard, with a max EV of 120 mph in the Florida State League last year. When he makes contact, it’s impactful, and even when the ball isn't hit squarely, he can send it out of the park to all fields with elite-level barrel and hard-hit percentages. Unfortunately, he doesn’t make enough contact to establish confidence that it’s going to work even if he can stay on the field and move up the ladder. He has a career 35.1 percent strikeout rate, and that’s just at the lowest levels of the Minors. Continuing to work on his conditioning so that he can keep working on that approach and avoid the injured list is essential. While there had been talk of him playing some corner outfield, where his strong arm would profile well, his limited time has been at first base, a more likely long-term home.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tony Blanco spent 17 years in pro ball, several in Japan, getting a cup of coffee with the Nationals back in 2005. Now his namesake is trying to work his way through the Pirates’ system. Blanco Jr. signed for $900,000 back in January 2022 and since then has shown glimpses of his tremendous offensive potential along with what he needs to work on, spending two years in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and then making progress in his first taste of playing in the United States, with a .890 OPS in 30 Florida Complex League games, but that came to an end with a hamstring injury in July. Blanco is a monster of a human now standing at 6-foot-7 and more than 240 pounds. With that frame comes an absurd amount of raw power, huge exit velocities and leverage. But that's only when he makes contact, something that has been an issue in his early career. The good news is he cut his strikeout rate by about 10 percent in 2024, leading to better numbers overall. He's always going to be power-over-hit, and the Pirates will live with some swing-and-miss, knowing that if he can even find the barrel at a fringy rate, he's going to put up big power numbers. More than anything for his development, Blanco has to stay on the field so he can get reps in order to refine his approach. He worked this offseason on his conditioning to enhance the odds of him staying healthy. Playing a corner outfield spot still isn't completely out of the realm of possibility, but he'll be getting a lot more time at first to keep his bat in the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The fact that Curtis is not only pitching professionally but doing it well is somewhat miraculous. He had ulnar transposition surgery that forced him out for the 2021 season, then he needed a second surgery because stitches from the first procedure were on his nerve. Doctors thought he was done. But he moved to Arizona State for the 2023 season and showed enough for the Pirates to give him $500,000 in the 12th round to start his pro career. He missed time again in 2024 with a hamstring injury, but a healthy 2025 campaign enabled him to pitch his way to Double-A for the first time. Curtis has some of the best overall stuff in the entire system, all coming from a 6-foot-5 frame. He misses a tremendous amount of bats with a number of offerings, and his mid-90s fastball isn’t even the best one in that regard. His 90-mph cutter with gyro slider-like shape elicited a 41 percent miss rate last year. His depthy slider, which is thrown in the mid-80s and more horizontal, missed bats at a 47percent rate. His low-80s changeup plays really well off his fastball with a ton of armside run to produce a 45 percent miss rate, and he’ll fold in an occasional upper-70s curve to boot. What’s even scarier is that Curtis has been working on a cut-ride fastball, up to 96 mph with 18 inches of vertical break. He can get into trouble when he doesn’t trust his stuff, leading to walks, but his BB/9 rate was just 2.44 from July 1 on last year. If that trend continues, he has every chance to be a starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Curtis' path to pro ball has not been an easy one. He had unlar transposition surgery that kept him from the mound in 2021 and then needed a second surgery because stitches from the first were on his nerve and doctors thought he may never throw again. He transferred to Arizona State for the 2023 season and stayed healthy, albeit with uneven results. His size and pure stuff as a redshirt sophomore intrigued the Pirates enough to pay him $500,000 in the 12th round of that summer's Draft. A hamstring injury sidelined him for a spell during his first full season, but he showed off serious swing-and-miss stuff with Single-A Bradenton and then in the Arizona Fall League. Curtis has as many as five pitches in his arsenal, many of which miss a very high number of bats. It starts with his 95-96 mph fastball, a pitch that touches 98-99 mph. When he holds the vertical break on his heater, it can be 16 inches and above, everything else plays off of that, though sometimes his mechanics get out of whack and his fastball lacks life and impact. Every other pitch he throws elicited a miss percentage north of 45 percent in 2024, led by a 90-91 mph cutter (51 percent miss rate), but he also has a mid-80s slider and upper-70s curve that confound hitters, as does his fading changeup. What Curtis has not done consistently is find the strike zone with his electric stuff. The 6-foot-5 right-hander walked 4.7 per nine last year, and his fastball got hit when his delivery wasn't in sync. He needs to maintain his posture to hold the heater, and if he can corral his secondary offerings better, he has a chance to start long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A well-regarded high school pitching prospect, Champlain honored his Southern California commitment in 2018 and stayed close to home. Three years later, the Yankees selected him in the ninth round of the 2021 Draft and then traded him to the Royals as part of a three-pitcher package for Andrew Benintendi in 2022. Champlain returned to Double-A in ‘24 and showed he had mastered it with a 3.50 ERA, a 0.92 WHIP and a 34.5% strikeout rate in seven starts. The move to Triple-A was more challenging; Champlain made 28 appearances (27 starts) there for a 5.61 ERA, 15.5% strikeout rate and a 1.56 WHIP while batters hit .283 against him. Champlain’s average cutting fastball sits 91-94 mph, touching 97 in 2024. He spins the ball well and has improved his upper-70s curveball into a solid weapon. That pitch is different from his low- to mid-80s slider which has good depth and got some chase in ‘24 in a limited sample. Champlain also shows a cutter, which could be an out pitch eventually because of his natural movement, and his mid-80s changeup is still a work in progress, as it has been for several years. The lack of a pitch against lefties has hindered Champlain as he’s faced better hitters. He has some effort in his delivery which affects his command at times, but he showed up to Spring Training over 10 pounds lighter. Champlain has the look and mentality of a workhorse on the mound and has proven durable in the Minors, throwing 135 and 140 innings the past two seasons respectively. But he’ll need to develop a weapon against lefties for him to reach his ceiling, otherwise there’s thought he would have more in the tank as a multi-inning reliever with a fastball-curveball combination. He wasn’t added to the 40-man when eligible for the Rule 5 Draft, but he’ll return to Triple-A, be part of the Royals’ depth and could make his debut in ‘25.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Well-regarded as a pitching prospect at a Southern California high school, Champlain struggled for three years at USC, but he showed enough stuff for the Yankees to take him in the ninth round in 2021. A year later, he was traded to the Royals as part of a three-pitcher package for Andrew Benintendi at the ‘22 Deadline. Champlain had a tough first impression in High-A Quad Cities, but his 2023 season was much better. With 25 starts and 135 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A Northwest Arkansas, Champlain posted a 3.33 ERA with a 22.8 percent strikeout rate and a 7.8 percent walk rate. Champlain spins the ball extremely well and has a 91-94 mph cutting fastball that showed improved velocity last year. He can throw his upper-70s curveball for strikes, and it has above-average spin and good shape to it. His 83-86 mph slider shows some sweep and got better last year. He’s shown a feel for a changeup, but it needs more work. The split-finger grip he had last year on the change had moderate success in limited usage, but he struggled to master it, leading to a grip change this spring. The mental side of changing speeds is something that will be a focus for Champlain this year. At 6-foot-5, Champlain has the look of a workhorse and he has been able to pitch innings. There is a little bit of effort in his delivery, but he has deception. Champlain profiles as a back-end starter, and without overpowering stuff, he will have to continue to locate well and keep working on his changeup to stick there. Otherwise, Champlain has the weapons and presence to fit in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Champlain was a top high school pitching prospect out of California in 2018, but he went to USC instead, where things didn’t go quite as expected. He wasn’t a starter until his junior year, but the Yankees still saw enough to draft him in the ninth round in 2021, signing him for around slot at $150,000. He didn’t make his debut until last year and was solid for Single-A Tampa until the Royals acquired him as part of a three-pitcher package for Andrew Benintendi at the Trade Deadline. After some inconsistencies at High-A after the trade in 2022, Champlain returned to Quad Cities to begin 2023 and has taken off with Double-A Northwest Arkansas in the second half of the season. Champlain spins the ball extremely well and has a cutting fastball that sits in the mid-90s with flashes of upper 90s when he’s fresh. His upper-70s curveball has above-average spin and good bite, while his slider also features tight spin and two-plane movement while sitting 82-84 mph. Champlain has shown feel for a changeup that could be an occasional weapon for him, but it needs more development. He is 6-foot-5 and sturdy, certainly looking the part. He has a quick delivery, which helps his deception off the mound. Champlain has done a nice job of rebounding in 2023 and has been almost unhittable at times following his midseason promotion to the Minors' second-highest level. His ceiling is as a back-end starter if he can iron out his fastball command and develop another secondary pitch, but his weapons and presence could fit in a bullpen as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A decision to give up hitting and focus on pitching only at Gonzaga catapulted Hughes into first-round conversations in 2022, and he ended up landing with the Rockies at No. 10 overall. When he reached Double-A in his first full season, it was looking like a wise pick, but then he got shut down in July that year and had Tommy John surgery. He made it back to shake off the rust in the Arizona Fall League and pitched his way to Triple-A in 2025. The Rockies saw enough to add him to the 40-man roster during the offseason. While some of Hughes’ surface results were decent in 2025, his stuff has yet to come all the way back post-surgery. His rehab went very well, with no setbacks, but issues started popping up once he was back. He struggled to stay in the same slot, then was shut down with a shoulder issue because of how he was over-compensating. He still gets good sink on his two-seamer to get groundball outs, but his fastball only averaged around 91-92 mph last year, down a few ticks. He does have solid secondary stuff, with a mid-80s slider and a changeup that has a chance to be a solid offspeed offering. His slower, upper-70s curve did miss bats last year, though his strikeout rate tumbled overall. Hughes really struggled with the move to Albuquerque last year and overall, his stuff just wasn’t quite as crisp as it had been pre-surgery. This is a big year for him as the gloves come off a bit and he gets a chance to show if things can bounce back further removed from TJ. There’s still a starter package in here if it clicks, but there is some thought to his sinker-slider combination working in a multi-inning relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After splitting his focus as a two-way player for Gonzaga in his first two seasons of college ball, Hughes took a big step forward when he put the bat down for good and focused on pitching only as the Zags’ Friday night starter in 2022. That led to him beating Marco Gonzales as the highest pick in school history, going No. 10 overall to the Rockies. Hughes reached Double-A in his first full season in 2023, but got shut down in July and needed Tommy John surgery. He returned in time to make six starts in the Arizona Fall League in 2024. Hughes was able to use his 17 1/3 innings in the AFL to shake some of the rust off and the good news is that his stuff looked pretty much back to where it was pre-injury. His fastball averaged 93 mph and touched 96, thrown with good sink to frequently get ground-ball contact. His cutter-like slider was regularly in the mid 80s, a hard breaker that flashed plus in the past, and he has some feel to spin a slower 80-82 mph curve, though it’s behind the harder breaking ball. HIs upper-80s changeup is starting to improve as well. Throw out Hughes’ surface numbers in the AFL given they came from his first post-surgery innings. He generally was around the zone previously, though his up-tempo delivery could get out of sync and cause timing issues, which in turn would lead to control problems. His ceiling might be somewhat limited, but once he really puts TJ behind him, he could be a big league back-end starter soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hughes spent two years in Gonzaga’s rotation and took a big step forward as their Friday night guy in 2022, allowing him to become the Zags’ first first-round pick since the Cardinals took Marco Gonzales No. 19 overall in 2013. Hughes became the highest pick in school history when the Rockies took him tenth overall in the 2022 Draft, thinking there might be some upside from a guy who had been a two-way player for his first two college seasons. He did touch Double-A in his first full year of pro ball but needed Tommy John surgery in July. When he’s healthy, Hughes brings an intriguing combination of size and stuff -- with feel for it -- to the mound. Even right before the elbow injury in Double-A last year, he was up to 97 mph with his fastball, though he sat at around 93. His short and hard mid-80s slider, that has cutter-like action to it, flashes plus and he’s shown feel to spin an effective upper-70s curve as well. He has an 87-88 mph changeup as well, but it’s clearly a fourth pitch. Hughes uses an up-tempo delivery and goes right after hitters. He can sometimes run into timing issues and there’s unintentional cut on his fastball occasionally, and both can impact his command, though he’s generally around the strike zone. All of that is on hold, of course, with Hughes not expected to do much competitively until 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It may go counter to what people think, but the Rockies have had some success when they’ve taken a college pitcher with their first pick, with hurlers such as Tyler Anderson, Jon Gray and Kyle Freeland having some big league success. The Rockies had gone the college arm route just once since Freeland was taken in 2014, with Ryan Rolison in 2018, until they selected Hughes No. 10 overall in 2022. The Gonzaga standout signed for an under-slot $4 million and pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season before getting shut down in early July with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. A former two-way player, Hughes only started pitching full-time in 2022, so there could be some serious growth potential once he's healthy. He already has the makings of a very good three-pitch mix coming from a solid starting pitcher’s frame. His fastball touches the upper 90s with some riding life to it, with more velocity to come. His slider is short and hard with cutter action to it, a pitch that flashes plus and misses bats. His changeup is probably his worst pitch, mostly because he didn’t throw it much in college, but there’s feel for it. Hughes has already impressed the Rockies with his mound presence, work ethic and intelligence -- he was a biology major who was on pace to graduate in three years. He goes right after hitters, and there’s confidence he’ll continue to be a solid strike-thrower the more time he has focusing on the craft, though first he'll focus on rehabbing post-surgery. He’s the type of college arm who could move pretty quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $900,000 out of Venezuela, Velasquez received the highest bonus in the Giants' 2021 international class thanks to his advanced bat-to-ball skills. He earned All-Star accolades in the Single-A California League in 2023 and in the High-A Northwest League last season, which he concluded by hitting .313 in 42 Double-A games at age 20. He's not overly toolsy but has the highest ceiling among San Francisco's middle-infield prospects. Velasquez has a controlled approach at the plate, making consistent contact to all fields while rarely chasing pitches out of the zone. A switch-hitter with a quick, compact swing from both sides, he does more damage as a righty. He did a better job of lifting pitches in 2024 but still lacks the strength to hit more than 10 homers per season. Velasquez's instincts allow him to play a bit quicker than his average speed on the bases and in the field. He has been a steady defender at shortstop in the past but his average arm and range are better suited for second base, where he has spent almost all of 2025. He'll project more as a contact-hitting utilityman than a big league starter unless he can provide some more offense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Velasquez signed for $900,000 out of Venezuela, landing the highest bonus in the Giants' 2021 international class because of his advanced hitting ability. He earned a promotion to Single-A at the end of the 2022 season at age 18 and earned California League All-Star honors when he returned there last year. He topped the circuit in hits (127) and doubles (32), while ranking second in batting (.298), extra-base hits (41) and total bases (185). A switch-hitter, Velasquez has a quick swing and makes consistent contact from both sides of the plate. He controls the strike zone well and his on-base skills give him a high floor, but his power potential remains in question because he lacks strength and has yet to show much affinity for pulling pitches or driving them in the air. He'll need to add muscle and make some adjustments to even provide 10 homers per season. Velasquez has average speed and looks to make things happen on the bases, stealing 23 bases in 29 attempts a year ago. After spending most of his first two seasons at shortstop, he split time between short and second base in 2023. He has sure, quick hands but his range and arm are better suited for the keystone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in the 2022 international class, Cabrera signed with the Reds for $2.7 million when the signing period opened that January. He first provided an early return on the investment when he came stateside in 2023, finishing with an OPS over 1.000 and touching full-season ball for the first time. His full year at Single-A Daytona in 2024 wasn’t as dynamic, though he held his own, but he wasn’t able to create any momentum with a move to High-A Dayton when a slow start was stopped 21 games in by a knee injury that ended his season. Given the struggles he had in the Midwest League and the injury, this is a big season for the 21-year-old. There’s plenty of bat speed and raw power to tap into for the right-handed hitter and Cabrera has shown in the past an ability to jump on fastballs. He’s always been an aggressive hitter, though he seemed to have more of an overall approach when he first came to the United States, something that regressed as he moved to full-season ball. He chases far too much and struggles against spin, things he’ll have to address if he wants to progress through the system. Signed initially as a shortstop, Cabrera last saw playing time at the premium position in 2024, focusing on third in 2025 while also getting reps at second base. That will continue to be the plan, and how he bounces back from the knee injury and maintains his athleticism will determine where on the dirt he ultimately lands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cabrera came in at No. 3 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list ahead of the 2022 signing period. When the period opened in January, the Reds jumped in, giving him a bonus of $2.7 million to join the organization. After getting his feet wet in the Dominican Summer League after signing, Cabrera had a huge United States debut with a 1.028 OPS in the Arizona Complex League and a late bump up to full-season ball. That’s where he spent the season in 2024, and while the numbers didn’t jump off the page in the same way, he still finished in the top 10 in the Florida State League in OPS and wRC+. It’s clear that Cabrera’s most comfortable spot is in the batter’s box. The right-handed hitter has terrific bat speed and can absolutely punish fastballs, though he’s not nearly as productive against spin and softer stuff. He’s a very aggressive hitter and while he largely manages his strikeouts, he chases too much, with a 43-percent chase rate in 2024 according to Synergy. There’s plenty of power for him to tap into, with most of it showing up to his pull side. While he signed as a shortstop, got some time at the premium spot in 2024 and will keep getting reps there for flexibility-sake, he won’t be able to stay there long term. His strong arm would work very well from third and he’s going to continue to learn how to play second base, but it’s looking more and more like he’s going to have to hit his way to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered one of the best prospects on the 2022 international market, Cabrera officially joined the Reds when that signing period opened on Jan. 15 for $2.7 million. While his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League was relatively nondescript, he started to show what all the fuss was about during his United States debut. Cabrera finished second in the Arizona Complex League in OPS (1.028) and wRC+ (158) while hitting .350. That earned him a late bump to Single-A Daytona, where he hit in four of the five games he played. Cabrera’s right-handed bat is clearly going to be his calling card. He has an advanced feel for hitting with outstanding bat speed and the ability to use all fields. His overall approach improved some, with an increase in walks as his strikeout rate ticked down a bit in 2023. Like with many young hitters, he’ll need to keep working on recognizing spin, but he can really punish a fastball. Signed as a shortstop, Cabrera split time between short and third base in the ACL, and his plus arm will definitely work from the left side of the infield. He has decent hands, but he’s slowing down some so the move to the hot corner may eventually become permanent. That would put more pressure on the raw power to show up, and he’ll keep getting reps up the middle for as long as possible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2022 international signing period opened in January of that year, Cabrera was No. 3 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list. The Reds signed him right when the period opened for $2.7 million, tied for the fourth-highest bonus handed out for the period. He had a modest debut in the Dominican Summer League but showed some of what all the fuss was about as an amateur. Right now, Cabrera’s bat is ahead of his glove. While his statline didn’t jump off the page in the DSL, he did display an early ability to use the whole field from the right side of the plate. He has bat speed and raw power to tap into with an idea of what he wants to do as a hitter, though he’ll have to continue to make more consistent contact to get to it as he advances. Cabrera runs well, and the Reds will let him stay at shortstop for as long as possible. He has the arm, hands and footwork to play there for now. There’s a chance he’ll outgrow the spot and have to move to third, where the Reds think his bat will profile well. The teenager’s offseason focus was on getting in the weight room, establishing a pro routine and showing up for his United States debut as athletic as possible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While training with Denny Suarez, a member of Major League Baseball’s Trainer Partnership program, in Venezuela, Cabrera’s tools caught the eye of all 30 teams. He was ranked No. 3 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list when the 2022 signing period opened in January. The Reds were all in, signing the shortstop for $2.7 million on Jan. 15, the first day of the signing period. Cabrera has the chance to have every tool in the proverbial toolbox. He has a good idea of what he’s doing at the plate, with the right-handed hitter using all fields and making hard contact. He has good raw power and some idea of how to access it already, creating backspin. With solid average speed, Cabrera should have the range to stick at shortstop for a long time. He has more than enough arm for the position, with good hands and footwork. If the 17-year old outgrows the position, he has the chance to hit enough to profile well at third. The Reds were impressed with his work at their strength camp in the Dominican Republic and think they got a first-round talent on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bedell was part of the Cardinals’ 2020 Draft class that produced Jordan Walker, Masyn Winn, Tink Hence and Alec Burleson, but Tommy John surgery limited him to only eight appearances in his first two Minor League seasons. He rebounded to win 2023 Midwest League Pitcher of the Year honors after posting a 2.44 ERA with 106 strikeouts in 96 innings with High-A Peoria and was a strikeout maven again to begin 2024 with 79 in 64 2/3 innings at Double-A Springfield. His performance fell apart following a promotion to Triple-A, and he finished with a 5.02 ERA, 31 strikeouts and 24 walks in 43 frames. At least part of Bedell’s slide stemmed from his transition to the Major League ball. He lost a little velocity with his fastball, going from 92-96 mph in Double-A to 90-92 in Triple-A, and International League batters took advantage. His low-80s gyro slider was still a relatively effective pitch with sharp downward action, despite low spin, and it could be even better with a little more velo as well. He used an upper-80s cutter that typically ran a little armside, so getting it back to gloveside will be a priority as well. Bedell’s low-80s changeup was a distant fourth pitch but could be effective with its own armside fade. Bedell’s walk rate jumped from 7.1 percent in Double-A to 12.7 at the Minors’ highest level, and he joined after Triple-A went to the full challenge system so ABS isn’t fully to blame. That said, it was still a small sample, and Bedell will head back to Memphis with a full offseason to prepare. He’s been left off the 40-man for two straight Rule 5 cycles and will have to prove he can serve as a starter or long man in relief in his age-25 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bedell was taken in the fourth round of the Cardinals’ 2020 Draft class -- which also includes Jordan Walker, Masyn Winn, Tink Hence and Alec Burleson -- as a reliver-turned-starter out of Missouri. After signing for above slot at $800,000, he made it two outings into his first full season with High-A Peoria before he needed Tommy John surgery. He didn’t return to a Minor League mound until August 2022 and then only in abbreviated outings. Back with no IL stints in 2023, he was named the Midwest League Pitcher of the Year after posting a 2.44 ERA and 1.15 WHIP with 106 strikeouts in 96 innings for Peoria. Getting through the season healthy was perhaps the biggest win of all for the 6-foot-2 right-hander, but he showed a potential starter’s repertoire too. His four-seam fastball and sinker can sit 91-94 mph, and he’ll run the former up the ladder for the occasional high whiff. He’s worked on adding a low-80s gyro slider that’s become his best breaking ball, giving him a gloveside option that plays off the armside sinker, and his mid-80s changeup can show promising fade, though it remains inconsistent. He has a curveball -- arguably his best pitch in college -- in his back pocket as well. Bedell walked 8.7 percent of his batters faced last year, giving him solid control. That’s a good sign for someone with so much missed time, and the command may only improve as he adds innings. St. Louis didn’t protect him from the Rule 5 Draft when he was eligible in the offseason, and no team selected him either, a sign of how far the industry believes he still has to go. Bedell’s age-24 season in 2024 will be go time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals’ 2020 Draft has a chance to become a legendary one. The organization’s top four picks (Jordan Walker, Masyn Winn, Tink Hence, Alec Burleson) entered 2023 as Top 100 prospects. Fourth-rounder Bedell has had a bumpier entrance into pro ball. The Missouri product used a breakout performance in the 2019 Cape Cod League to command an above-slot $800,000 bonus three years ago, but got in only two High-A appearances in 2021 before needing Tommy John surgery. He returned last August and struck out 10 over 5 2/3 innings between the Florida Complex League and Single-A Palm Beach. During that brief return to full-season ball, Bedell sat 90-93 mph with four-seam and sinking fastballs, maxing out at 94.9. That’s roughly in line with where he was pre-surgery, and he leaned heavily on the heat as he worked to find his command again as he built back up. He used his 75-79 mph curveball as his most featured off-speed pitch, and while it didn’t elicit many whiffs in the small sample, it has enough break to do so in the future. A mid-80s fading changeup had the makings of an above-average pitch in the past, but he’ll need to find it again with experience. He also used to possess a mid-80s cutter that he didn't use in the FSL, and he's added a low-80s slider that has helped him rack up strikeouts nicely in 2023 with High-A Peoria. The 6-foot-2 right-hander walked 7.1 percent of batters he faced in college, and that level of control, along with a relatively deep pitch mix, has given hope that he can be a future Major League starter. This will be Bedell’s 40-man decision year, so he needs to show both health and a return to pre-TJ form to press the issue with St. Louis. He's certainly helped his case with a strong showing at High-A Peoria to begin 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a reliever in his first two seasons at Missouri, Bedell broke out most at the Cape Cod League in 2019, where he sported a 0.59 ERA and 36/3 K/BB ratio in six starts for Wareham. He slotted into the Tigers rotation the following spring and got off to a solid start, which included a 12-strikeout performance against Western Illinois in his final outing before the 2020 season was canceled due to the pandemic. The Cardinals grabbed Bedell in the fourth round of the shortened Draft that summer and went over slot to sign him to an $800,000 bonus. The right-hander only got in two appearances at High-A Peoria before needing Tommy John surgery in May 2021. He returned to the Minor League mound this August. Before the procedure, Bedell threw in the low 90s with both his four-seam and two-seam fastball and showed promising movement. His low-80s changeup and curveball were equally in the discussion for his best off-speed offering, with the former having perhaps a few more fans because of its fade. A mid-80s cutter gave him a desirable fourth pitch for a complete arsenal. Utilizing a strong delivery, the 6-foot-2 hurler hasn’t had any issue filling the zone at the collegiate or pro level, and if that returns post-procedure, that control will grease the wheels of his charge toward St. Louis. That’s still a large assumption, even with the recent successes of Tommy John. Given the timing of last year’s surgery, he should be back on a Minor League mound by the height of the summer, and the Cardinals have been pleased with the progress of his rehab. We may have to wait until 2023 to determine whether he remains on track to be a starter or if he might be better served with a move to the bullpen in his search for a true plus pitch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bedell, who graduated high school a semester early to enroll early at Missouri, tallied 11 2/3 innings as a freshman in 2018 and then took off as a sophomore, when he racked up 36 strikeouts over 40 1/3 innings out of the bullpen while holding opponents to a .193 batting average against. The righty followed that up with a dominant showing in the Cape Cod League. Moved to the rotation in 2020, Bedell fanned 35 over 24 1/3 innings and struck out a career-high 12 over six innings in his final start before the coronavirus pandemic halted the season. The Cardinals selected Bedell in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft and signed him to an over-slot $800,000 bonus. He made his professional debut in 2021, but appeared in just two games before having Tommy John surgery. Bedell works his fastball in the low 90s and throws two- and four-seamers, both with movement. There’s debate as to what his best secondary pitch is, but he throws a low-80s changeup with fade and a curveball around the same velocity. He also possesses a mid-80s cutter and pitches with confidence because of his above-average command and strong delivery. The 6-foot-2, 198-pound right-hander is viewed as a pitcher with a high floor who could move quickly through the Cardinals’ system. Bedell’s fastball could tick up a bit in short bursts if he’s moved to the bullpen, but he’ll be developed as a starter first and could find a home in the middle or back end of a rotation in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lin moved to the U.S. to play in the 2022 Northwoods League and 2023 MLB Draft League. Despite rough control, he flashed premium velocity and signed with the Cardinals for $500,000 in July 2023, becoming the first player out of Taiwan to sign with St. Louis. The righty stormed out of the gate in his first full season with Single-A Palm Beach in 2024 but was limited to only 50 1/3 innings across three levels in ’25 by forearm issues and a midseason left oblique injury. Lin made five starts in the Arizona Fall League to make up for the lost time and posted a 19/8 K/BB ratio in 12 1/3 frames. Standing 6-foot-7, Lin flashed premium velocity less frequently, sitting more in the mid 90s during his time in Arizona. He still touched 100 mph during the regular season, and with 7 feet of extension, he doesn’t always need to live above that threshold to get his fastball on batters quickly. There’s also plenty of ride and run on the pitch to make it a moving target. Lin works with both a changeup and a splitter. The former moves a ton to his arm side to generate whiffs, while the latter really kills spin but can be more unpredictable. He focused on throwing a low-80s slider harder in the AFL, but it’s still a low-spin backside pitch with armside run rather than gloveside break. After making huge progress with his control in ’24, Lin struggled to find the strike zone consistently in his second full season, a trend that carried into the desert. His long limbs give him a lot that needs to be in sync. With Rule 5 eligibility looming, he is likely best served with a move to the bullpen in the upper Minors, where he can let his stuff truly fly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Taiwan, Lin pitched stateside in the 2022 Northwoods League and 2023 MLB Draft League, where he showed flashes of brilliant stuff with really rough control. But after posting the Draft League’s best fastball velocity, the right-hander signed with the Cardinals for $500,000 in July 2023, thus becoming St. Louis’ first player signed out of Taiwan. He opened his first full season at Single-A Palm Beach and dominated the Florida State League with a 2.79 ERA and 123 strikeouts in 116 innings. Lin was the only Palm Beach pitcher to exceed 100 mph in 2024, and he did it 12 times and touched 101 on May 25. He typically stayed more in the 95-98 mph range with his four-seamer, and while the heater had ample armside run, it didn’t come with great ride, causing it to play below the velo. His 86-89 mph changeup was a much better whiff-heavy pitch with 50.8 percent of swings coming up empty against it. The separation off the fastball and similar horizontal movement befuddled many hitters. Lin could also work in a mid-80s slider, but without high spin rates, it will likely be less effective higher up the chain. None of Lin’s pitches averaged gloveside break in the FSL, and that will be a focus entering year two. For a pitcher who once walked 24 batters in 15 2/3 innings in the Northwoods League, Lin showed a spectacular turnaround when it came to control in the FSL with just a 7.8 percent BB rate. That will be challenged against more patient hitters at High-A and above, but entering his age-23 season, Lin is more raw than many arms his age and could continue to hone his sharpness on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burns flashed first-round stuff and won Gatorade's Alabama high school player of the year award in 2017, but dropped to the Yankees in the 37th round because he was strongly committed to Auburn. He succeeded 2018 No. 1 overall pick Casey Mize as the Tigers' No. 1 starter in his final two seasons before signing for a below-slot $1.6 million as a supplemental first-rounder in 2020. He performed well while advancing to Double-A in his first two years as a pro but missed time with a sore elbow in 2021 and a shoulder strain last season. After working with a 92-95 mph fastball and touching 97 with some armside run on his fastball in 2021, Burns spent much of last year operating more at 90-93, though he still commanded his heater well. His most dependable pitch is a mid-80s slider with depth, and he can turn it into a harder, tighter cutter as well. He lands his upper-70s curveball for strikes and also mixes in a low-80s changeup with sink. Burns flashed solid control in the past but his walk rate jumped from 3.4 per nine innings in his first pro season to 4.6 last year, when he didn't challenge hitters as much with slightly diminished stuff. He's small for a starter and has durability concerns that date back to college, where he had shoulder issues in 2019. If he can regain some velocity and stay healthy, he might be a No. 4 starter, though he's starting to trend toward becoming a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burns flashed first-round stuff as Gatorade's Alabama high school player of the year in 2017, but he was strongly committed to Auburn and followed 2018 No. 1 overall pick Casey Mize as the Tigers' Friday-night starter in his final two college seasons. The Guardians selected him 36th overall in 2020, the highest pick they've spent on a college arm since taking Drew Pomeranz at No. 5 a decade earlier, and signed him for a below-slot $1.6 million. They handled him carefully in his successful 2021 pro debut, starting him once a week in High-A and giving him two weeks off when he came down with elbow soreness in midsummer. Burns usually works at 92-95 mph and touches 97 with some run on his four-seam fastball, and his ability to spot it on either side of the plate may be more impressive than its velocity (which fluctuated after his stint on the injured list) or life. His best secondary pitch is his plus slider/cutter, which arrives in the upper-80s and helped him to have more success against lefties than righties in High-A. He also throws a 78-82 mph downer curveball that has gotten more consistent in pro ball and has some feel for a low-80s changeup with some sink. With the ability to throw four pitches for strikes and advanced command of his fastball, Burns has a high floor as well as the upside of a mid-rotation starter. The biggest concern is his durability because he's small for a starter, had shoulder issues in 2019 before his elbow flared up last year and his stuff has declined at the end of his last two full seasons. If he can stay healthy, his biggest backers believe he could be similar to fellow former Southeastern Conference standout Sonny Gray.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burns flashed first-round stuff when he was Gatorade's Alabama High School Player of the Year in 2017, but worries about his size and signability dropped him to the Yankees in the 37th round. He didn't sign with New York, then worked his way into Auburn's rotation as a freshman and succeeded 2018 No. 1 overall pick Casey Mize as the Tigers' ace during the next two seasons. The Indians signed him for a below-slot $1.6 million as the 36th overall choice last June, the highest they've taken a college arm since grabbing Drew Pomeranz at No. 5 a decade earlier. When he's on, Burns can feature two plus pitches in his fastball and breaking ball. His four-seamer sits at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with some run, and he shows the ability to locate it on either side of the plate. His breaker can combine curveball depth with slider velocity in the low 80s at times and devolve into a slurve at others. Burns also has a sinking changeup that can become an average third offering. He throws strikes but comes with some durability concerns because he's 6 feet tall, had shoulder problems in 2019 and his stuff tends to dip late in the season. The highest-ranked college pitcher on this list, he has a higher floor than the high school arms ranked ahead of him and his biggest backers see similarities between him and another smaller former Southeastern Conference standout, Sonny Gray.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best college bats in the 2021 class and the Pacific-12 Conference Player of the Year that spring at Oregon, Zavala went in the second round that July. A post-Draft physical revealed a mass at the top of his cervical spine, a medical anomaly that left him with a well-below-slot $830,000 bonus but hasn't affected him in pro ball. After a successful first full pro season in 2022, he blew out his right (throwing) elbow in the Arizona Fall League and had internal brace surgery that cost him the first six weeks of last season. His left-handed swing got out of whack and he never recovered, slashing .194/.343/.284 with a 37.3 percent strikeout rate at Double-A. Known for making consistent hard contact with bat speed, hand-eye coordination and a disciplined approach, Zavala never looked like himself in 2023. He got too passive and his contact rate and exit velocities plummeted when he did swing the bat. Assuming that he does return to previous form, to win an everyday job he'll have to demonstrate that he has more than fringy power and that he can handle southpaws after they dominated him in each of the past two seasons. Zavala is a decent athlete with average speed but he isn't very daring on the bases. He gets the job done on the outfield corners and has seen more action in right field during pro ball, though his average arm may be better suited for left. The Rangers are stacked in terms of young outfielders, so he risks getting buried if he doesn't bounce back quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zavala established himself as one of the best college bats in the 2021 Draft, winning Pac-12 Conference Player of the Year honors after setting Oregon records for on-base percentage (.525), runs scored (64) and walks (50). The Rangers selected him in the second round, making him the highest-drafted Ducks position player since the program resumed in 2009, but a post-Draft physical revealed a mass at the top of his cervical spine. The medical anomaly left him with a well below-slot $830,000 bonus but wasn't an issue last year, when he led qualified hitters in the system in OBP (.420) and ranked second in OPS (.873) while reaching Double-A in his first full pro season. Zavala makes contact with ease thanks to his quick left-handed stroke, hand-eye coordination and patient approach. Though he's clearly a hit-over-power guy and lets balls travel deep while judiciously using the entire field, he does hit the ball hard and could produce 20 homers per season if he turns on and lifts pitches more regularly. The only concern with him at the plate is his ability to handle left-handers after he slashed .183/.318/.269 against them last year, compared to .309/.454/.515 versus right-handers. An average runner and athlete, Zavala has decent instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He has spent most of his college and pro career in right field, though his average arm may be better suited for left. He injured his right (throwing) elbow in the Arizona Fall League, requiring internal brace surgery that cost him the first six weeks of the 2023 season, and he hasn't looked like his normal self at the plate for much of the year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best bats in the 2021 college class, Zavala was named Pacific-12 Conference player of the year after setting Oregon records for on-base percentage (.525), runs (65) and walks (50) last spring. The Rangers popped him in the second round, making him the highest-drafted Ducks position player since the program was brought back in 2009. After a medical anomaly was revealed during his post-Draft physical, he signed for a well below-slot $830,000, but he looked like his normal hitterish self while advancing to Low-A in his pro debut. Zavala has advanced bat-to-ball skills and makes repeated contact with his quick, compact left-handed swing and disciplined approach. He concentrates on drilling line drives from gap to gap and controlling the strike zone, but Texas thinks he has untapped power. He worked on some adjustments to his stance and setup during instructional league to unleash some more pop, and he might be able to deliver 15-20 homers on an annual basis if he looks to launch more balls in the air. Zavala's speed, arm and outfield defense all grade as average and he fits best in left field despite spending most of his 22-game debut in right field. He also caught in high school and played mostly third base during the truncated 2020 college season. His hitting ability and strong makeup could allow him to rise quickly through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bastardo had grown into one of the Red Sox highest-upside pitching prospects since they signed him out of Venezuela for $35,000, but underwent Tommy John surgery in July 2024. The Blue Jays, chasing his long-term upside, selected him in December’s Rule 5 Draft. Bastardo sported a 5.36 ERA through 10 starts at Double-A before going under the knife, but now that he’s with the Blue Jays, he’ll have most of the 2025 season to round out his rehab process. When healthy, Bastardo has a very advanced changeup for his age, potentially his best offering. That was one of the Blue Jays’ main attractions to Bastardo, on top of a heater that sat 93-95 mph while touching 97. His breaking balls are closer to average, but there’s clearly a starter’s arsenal in there, and if that doesn’t work down the road, the Blue Jays could try to max out his arm talent as a reliever. The rehab will slow any process, of course, but Bastardo got up to 119 1/3 innings in 2023. This is a fascinating piece of roster management by the Blue Jays, who tend to get creative the odd time they dip into the Rule 5 Draft. If they can find a way to keep Bastardo long term, it’ll be a major win for the organization as it looks to add high-upside pitching talent any way possible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest bargain in Boston's 2018-19 international class, Bastardo signed for $35,000 out of Venezuela. He didn't reach full-season ball until 2022 but has been one of the better Red Sox pitching performers in the lower Minors the past two years. He had one of the best outings in their system last year, striking out 14 in a seven-inning shutout in High-A in late July, but tired down the stretch. He made 10 starts for Double-A Portland in 2024 before needing Tommy John surgery. When the Red Sox left Bastardo off the 40-man in the offseason, the Blue Jays selected him in the Rule 5 Draft as an upside pick. Bastardo's best offering is a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink that helped him limit left-handers to a .190 average last season. He sets it up with a 93-95 mph fastball that reaches 97, though it doesn't feature good shape and gets pounded when he doesn't locate it well. He sports a pair of average breaking balls, with his low-80s curveball perhaps slightly better than his tight mid-80s slider. If Bastardo can develop more consistency with his arsenal and his ability to command it, he could be a back-of-the-rotation starter. He’ll spend much of his Rule 5 year rehabbing, allowing Toronto to keep closer eyes on him without the Major League pressure out of the gate. But he’ll still have to prove his stuff has returned post-TJ to give himself a true MLB shot in his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bohrofen was a highly ranked player out of high school in 2020 and could have landed in the top three rounds but opted to play college ball at Oklahoma. A strong showing in the Cape Cod League and a strong finish in ‘23 with Arkansas revived his Draft stock. The Blue Jays landed Bohrofen in the sixth round and they were thrilled with the value. Coming off an impressive start to his pro career that year, Bohrofen hit 14 home runs with a .796 OPS over 116 games in High-A Vancouver in 2024. Down the stretch in ‘24, Bohrofen turned a corner and was one of the hottest hitters in the Blue Jays’ system, which has reignited the optimism around his long-term potential. Bohrofen has made an adjustment with his front foot to help him see the ball better and it’s been paying off. He’s built to mash, with excellent upper-body strength, but he isn’t too rigid in the field. The Blue Jays believe he’ll be just fine in the outfield and play solid defense, allowing his bat to shine if he takes that next step. The power numbers haven’t quite been there yet, but if Bohrofen ever truly breaks out, that’s going to be his headlining tool. Cutting down on his swing-and-miss will continue to be a priority, but Bohrofen is still a fine candidate to climb a couple of levels in 2025 and could give the Blue Jays an outfield depth option by next spring. His power will need to pull him up the ladder a bit, so this is a major season for Bohrofen and he’ll need to carry that strong finish from ‘24 over.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bohrofen was a highly ranked player out of high school in 2020 and could have landed in the top three rounds but opted to play college ball at Oklahoma. A strong showing in the Cape Cod League and a strong finish in ‘23 with Arkansas revived his Draft stock, and the Blue Jays landed Bohrofen in the sixth round, where they were thrilled with the value. He carried the power of his 16-homer season in college right into pro ball, putting up a 1.080 OPS and seven home runs over just 24 games between the complex league and Single-A. Bohrofen balances the Blue Jays system well. Many of their higher-ranked hitters, like Alan Roden or Spencer Horwitz, profile more as contact hitters who reach base at a high rate, while Bohrofen has the potential to mash. The big, well-built outfielder moves well enough to play a sturdy corner outfield position and let his bat shine. Bohrofen has excellent upper body strength and can produce power in multiple zones, which leaves the Blue Jays optimistic that this area of his game will sustain itself as he climbs levels. This will be challenged in High-A Vancouver, where he will face the same pitchers over and over. There’s nothing complicated about Bohrofen’s projection. He’ll go as far as his bat takes him, and so far that bat looks exciting, though swing-and-miss against softer stuff presents some reason for pause. He should continue to benefit from the Blue Jays’ player development complex to hone his swing and represents one of the higher-upside power bats outside of the Orelvis Martinez and Arjun Nimmala tier.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz was the 19th-ranked international prospect in the 2018 class, according to MLB Pipeline, before the Tigers signed him for a $1.8 million bonus. His much-anticipated debut in the States was delayed a year by the pandemic and arguably led to him being rushed to Low-A Lakeland, where his .127 average and 74 strikeouts over 158 plate appearances promoted a midseason second-guessing. He had a much more respectable second half one level down in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. As an athlete, De La Cruz is a physical specimen who keeps getting stronger; he already boasts some of the best raw power in the organization. As a hitter, he’s still unrefined with a violent, uppercut swing. He has enough power to go to all fields. He has shown improvement in his plate discipline but struggles against offspeed pitches. He runs well for his body but isn’t an instinctive base stealer. He has the strong arm to play a corner outfield spot but needs time to hone his accuracy. Considering De La Cruz’s age, he has plenty of time to learn the skills necessary to take advantage of his raw skills, but the Tigers have to avoid the temptation to push the timetable with him. His second chance at the Florida State League hasn’t quite proven that much better than the first, and the 20-year-old is in danger of never meeting his ceiling of a power-first Major League bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before the Tigers spent just shy of $3 million each to sign Roberto Campos and Cristian Santana, they gave De La Cruz – then the 19th-ranked international prospect by MLB Pipeline – a $1.8 million bonus out of the Dominican Republic. He made a strong first impression in 2019 in the Dominican Summer League, batting .307 with 11 home runs, 16 stolen bases and a .931 OPS in 225 at-bats. He was on track to compete in the Gulf Coast League when the pandemic scuttled the Minor League season. De La Cruz continues to fill out his athletic frame, reporting to instructional ball last fall with more muscle following the shutdown. He has all-fields power with an aggressive approach at the plate, possibly too aggressive given his 75 strikeouts in the DSL. The Tigers believe his approach will mature, allowing him to maintain average while adding power. He played center field in the DSL but will likely shift to a corner as he continues to fill out. Though the recent Campos and Santana signings have overshadowed De La Cruz, the Tigers see similar upside with a stronger body than expected out of a teenager. He opened 2021 at Low-A Lakeland but bounced down to the Florida Complex League in late June to find his offensive stroke.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There have been eight high schoolers drafted and signed out of Hawaii to make it to the big leagues this century, the most recent coming in 2017 (Joey Cantillo). The last two prep hitters to come from the Aloha State to reach the highest level were both taken in 2013: Kean Wong and Isiah Kiner-Falefa.
