Rosario, the Twins’ final selection in the shortened 2020 Draft hopes to end that drought. He’s provided up-and-down production since winning Midwest League MVP honors in 2023, then missed a chunk of '24 with an elbow injury that dampened his output. He bounced back with 25 homers in Double-A during his age-22 season. It’s becoming clear that Rosario’s power is for real, with 20-plus homers in two of his last three seasons while being young for his level. The right-handed hitter routinely hits the ball hard, with plus bat speed, and can find the seats to all fields. With that power comes a healthy dose of strikeouts (27.5 percent K rate in 2025), especially against softer stuff, but he also draws a ton of walks (12.6 percent). He has fringy speed, but for the first time in his career, he used what he has to swipe 32 bases last season. Rosario hasn’t been protected on the 40-man roster and hasn’t been selected in the Rule 5 Draft largely because of those strikeouts and his fringy, at best, defense. If he can improve that part of his game, his power could profile as a big league corner outfielder soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario was the top prospect in Hawaii ahead of the shortened 2020 Draft and ended up being the second one taken when the Twins selected him in the fifth round. (The Red Sox took pitcher Jeremy Wu-Yelland in Round 4.) Rosario has shown flashes of offensive potential, like when he won the Midwest League MVP and then tied for the Arizona Fall League lead in home runs in 2023. That raised expectations for 2024, but an elbow injury that forced him out of action for two months somewhat derailed his progress, though he did make up for lost time with a return engagement in the AFL. Since entering pro ball, Rosario has displayed the ability to hit the ball very hard, but he’s also been one to get off to slow starts and then heat up as the year goes on. That was happening again in 2024 when he landed on the injured list as he started to show he could make adjustments to the sharper breaking balls he saw in Double-A. Early on, his swing had gotten flatter and he was chasing more than he used to. There is always going to be swing-and-miss to Rosario's game with a power-over-hit profile, but he was starting to figure things out and he always offsets the K’s with a healthy dose of walks. As a right-handed-hitting corner outfielder, Rosario is on the wrong side of a platoon and he’s going to have to really consistently mash to be an everyday player. The Twins didn’t protect him from Rule 5 Draft last December and he wasn’t taken, but he has the kind of work ethic in which he can use that to earn a 40-man spot this year, when he’ll still be just 22 for most of the season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There have been just two Hawaiian prep hitters who signed out of high school to go on and make any real impact in the big leagues: Shane Victorino, a 1999 sixth-round pick, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa, who went in the fourth round in 2013. Rosario is hoping he can join that short list after the Twins took him with their final pick in the shortened 2020 Draft and has moved one rung at a time. He's gone from the Florida Complex League in 2021 to Single-A Fort Myers in 2022 and then on to High-A last year, when he had his most productive year to date, earning Midwest League MVP honors. He finished off 2023 by tying for the Arizona Fall League lead in home runs. The Twins’ patience with Rosario’s development appears to be paying off. He made a big adjustment with his setup at the end of 2022 and it really clicked in 2023, using a spread out base to cut down his movement, recognizing he didn’t need to do that much to tap into his natural strength and raw power. He also cut down on his chase rate and drew a lot more walks as his overall approach improved, helping him to lead the Midwest League in homers. While he did a really good job at punishing fastballs, he still missed breaking stuff at a pretty high clip, his front hip can leak out early, leading to struggles with pitches away, and he’s still learning to be adjustable with his swing. Now a corner outfielder only, Rosario has shown off an accurate arm that racked up 14 assists with Cedar Rapids. Upper level pitching will be the next challenge, but he seems to make improvements at each step as well as anyone in the system and could very well profile well as a power-hitting right fielder in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Messina became the starting catcher at South Carolina as a sophomore and hit 17 homers that season in 2023. He upped his game in 2024, hitting 21 more long balls and winning the Johnny Bench Award, given to the top catcher in college baseball. The power potential and defensive work were enough to get him selected in the third round of that summer's Draft and he made it to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball. It's a power-over-hit profile for Messina, with more strength than bat speed in his right-handed swing. He can punish mistakes, though he didn't get to much power in 2025, and he did limit his strikeouts while drawing walks. There are a lot of moving parts to his swing with a leg kick, and at times, a bat wrap to go along with questions about his ability to make adjustments. Because of his catch-and-throw skills, Messina has a high floor as a future backup at the big league level. More athletic than you'd think -- he stole 14 bases in 2025 -- pitchers love throwing to him. He's an excellent receiver who calls a good game and has an arm that threw out 40 percent of potential basestealers last year. If he can iron out his swing and his approach to improve the offensive part of his game, he could be a glove-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After not playing much as a freshman at South Carolina, Messina became the Gamecocks' starting catcher as a sophomore, smashing 17 homers in 2023. He won the Johnny Bench Award as the top NCAA catcher in 2024, hitting 21 more homers and finishing with a 1.166 OPS. That helped him land in the third round with the Rockies. He then got to watch younger brother Carson, a high school pitcher, go in Round 12 to the Blue Jays. Messina is a strong right-handed hitter who put up those good power numbers despite struggling with his approach during his junior season. There was a lot more swing-and-miss overall compared to his 2023 campaign, with higher whiff rates against fastballs than previously, and he's always had a hard time with softer stuff. There's plenty of power for him to tap into, especially to the pull side, and he may always have a power-over-hit approach with some walks thrown in. With a take-charge attitude behind the plate, Messina has the right mentality to catch at the next level. He's a solid receiver with an average arm and shows enough agility to block well even though he's not fleet of foot. He didn't hit during his pro debut after signing, but a 15-game sample is not enough to draw any conclusions from.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Breaux smacked 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC while also hitting 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever, a combination that made him the best junior college prospect in the 2018 Draft. After signing for $1,497,500 in the second round, he missed half of his first full season with elbow problems that dogged him at McLennan and lost all of 2020 to the pandemic. He returned last year to homer 23 times in 90 games while advancing to Double-A, though the Yankees declined to protect him on their 40-man roster in November. Breaux resembles recently traded Gary Sanchez offensively, defensively and physically. He has a strong presence at the plate, where his well above-average bat speed and extremely aggressive approach create plus-plus raw power but also a propensity to swing and miss. He did a better job of turning on pitches to crush them out of the park last season, but his swing decisions still leave a lot to be desired. His elbow issues prevented him from catching much in 2018 or 2019 before the pandemic wiped out the 2020 season, so Breaux still has considerable work to do behind the plate. He's still raw in terms of receiving and blocking, while his slow transfer and inconsistent accuracy mean that his arm plays down and he threw out just 17 percent of basestealers last year. He's a bottom-of-the-scale runner, so his only other defensive option would be first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top junior college prospect in the 2018 Draft, Breaux bashed 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC while also clocking 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever. He went homerless in his 30-game pro debut after signing for $1,497,500 in the second round but bounced back to go deep 13 times in 51 low Class A contests in 2019, missing half the season with elbow problems that also bothered him at McLennan. His on-field development last year consisted of five games in the independent Constellation Energy League. Similar to Gary Sanchez offensively, defensively and physically, Breaux has a lofty ceiling but is a long ways from reaching it. His well-above-average bat speed and strength coupled with an extremely aggressive approach give him the raw pop to deliver 35 or more homers per season. But he also swings and misses excessively, and he'll need to make better swing decisions and loft more balls in the air to fully tap into his power potential. Elbow soreness meant Breaux spent more time at DH than at catcher in 2018-19 and he had next to no game reps last year, costing him the time behind the plate he needs to improve his receiving and blocking. While few catchers can match his pure arm strength, he has a slow transfer and inconsistent accuracy that led to him throwing out just 16 percent of basestealers in his first two pro seasons. He's a well-below-average runner, so his only other position options would be first base or DH.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Guardians went under slot to sign their first three selections in the 2022 Draft, they splurged on Humphries in the eighth round, giving him fourth-round money ($600,000) to convince him to forgo his commitment to Campbell. Early returns were positive in his first full season, as he showed his strikeout stuff in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, but the next two years were a wash. An illness caused him to lose significant weight in 2024, and he could not find his control in '25 and walked nearly a batter per inning. Humphries is starting to look like his old self again now that he's diligently grown stronger over the offseason and refined his delivery. While he used to have an extreme over-the-top delivery, he's dropped his release point to a high-three-quarters slot that still enables him to reach nearly 20 inches of induced vertical break on his fastball while also adding more armside run. The southpaw throws his heater about half the time and sits 91-93 mph -- he can reach back and touch 96 mph -- and the hope is that his added strength will help him maintain velocity late into the season. The North Carolina native has a pair of distinct breaking balls -- an upper-80s slider and high-70s curve -- that each have a chance to be plus. His changeup has rare vertical movement and pairs well off the fastball because of 10 mph of velocity separation. However, much of his value will come down to his control. After throwing strikes just 54 percent of the time in 2025, he's been consistently in the zone in 2026, thanks in part to a less effortful delivery and better direction to home plate. Humphries' stuff could play up in relief if the walks don't dissipate, but he has the foundation to be a mid-rotation starter, and Cleveland is likely to keep developing him in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Humphries flashed top-three-rounds talent as a North Carolina high schooler before an inconsistent senior season in 2022 dinged his stock a little bit. The Guardians still gave him third-round money ($600,000) as an eighth-rounder that July, and he responded by standing out as the best pitching prospect in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League during his pro debut the following summer. He had a lost season in 2024, coming down with a virus early in the season that cost him 20 pounds as well as significant velocity and athleticism. When he's at full strength, Humphries shows the potential for three plus pitches. His fastball can operate at 92-95 mph and touch 97 with sink and run, and he can show a pair of high-spin breaking balls, an upper-70s curve with quality depth and a sharp low-80s slider. Even his low-80s fade changeup could become a solid offering. Last year, Humphries worked around 90 mph with his fastball and lost power on his curve and slider, though he still managed to strike out 97 in 79 Single-A innings. His arm action isn't the cleanest and he doesn't repeat his delivery on a consistent basis, so he might be limited to average control and fringy command at best. Assuming he can regain the stuff he had before he got sick, he has a higher ceiling than most of the system's other pitching prospects as a potential mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Humphries looked like a potential top-three-rounds pick when he led Fuquay-Varina HS to the North Carolina 4-A state championship as a junior and impressed at the Super 60 Showcase in February 2022. An up-and-down senior year dinged his stock a bit, though the Guardians gave him third-round money ($600,000) in the eighth round to divert him from a Campbell commitment. He stood out as the best pitching prospect in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League during his 2023 debut, then displayed improved control following a mid-August promotion to Single-A. While Humphries shows the potential for three plus offerings once he's fully developed, he rarely has been at his best in 2024 while battling a stomach virus that sapped his strength. His fastball already sits at 92-95 mph and reaches 97 with sink and run. He creates high spin rates on two distinct breaking pitches, an upper-70s curveball with quality depth and a low-80s slider with sharper action. Humphries has just begun focusing on his low-80s changeup, which fades and shows flashes of solid upside. He doesn't have the prettiest arm action or most consistent delivery, so he may never have more than average control or fringy command. While he'll need time to develop, he has a higher ceiling than most of Cleveland's mound prospects and could blossom into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vaz transferred to Vanderbilt from Louisiana State Eunice junior college for his final two seasons of eligibility and played his way to a starter’s role by his senior season. The Royals took him in the 15th round of the 2022 Draft, but he was quickly labeled an underrated pick and jumped onto the scene his first full pro season. In 2024, Vaz spent the entire campaign at Double-A, logging 115 games and slashing .263/.375/.379 with eight homers, 22 doubles, 16 stolen bases and more walks (73) than strikeouts (60). That walk-to-strikeout ratio is Vaz’s game as one of the best pure hitters in the system with a keen understanding of the strike zone. His swinging-strike rate was 4.1% in ‘24, fourth-lowest among Minor Leaguers at all full-season levels. Vaz operates from a solid setup with a higher hand position, and his bat path plays well and is consistent, covering most of the strike zone. His contact ability is elite, but it will have to carry him because of his well-below-average power and low exit velocities, although he started to take advantage of counts and drive some balls late in ‘24. Vaz is also a plus runner with good instincts and mentality on the bases. His best position is second base, where he’s an above-average defender, and he’s gotten more work in left field, where he’s fringe-average right now. His below-average arm limits him in the field, but his tools play up because of his effort. Vaz gets high marks for his leadership and clubhouse presence, and he was the recipient of the Mike Sweeney Community Impact Award in 2024. He should be able to find a role in the big leagues in a utility role, but broken fingers in this spring got him off to a late start and hampered his offensive progress back with Northwest Arkansas.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vaz’s dad, Roberto, played college ball for Alabama and is now a coach in the Cubs’ system. Vaz followed in his dad’s Southeastern Conference footsteps when he transferred from a Louisiana junior college to Vanderbilt and played his way to a starter’s role by his second season. The Royals drafted him in the 15th round of the 2022 Draft, but he quickly jumped onto the scene in his first full pro season. Between High-A Quad Cities and a late-season promotion to Double-A Northwest Arkansas, Vaz slashed .279/.373/.400 with 30 stolen bases, a 119 wRC+ and more walks (64) than strikeouts (50). One of the best pure hitters in the Royals’ system, Vaz rarely swings and misses. His 3.3 percent swinging-strike rate ranked third-best among qualified hitters across all levels of the Minors. The left-handed hitter drives balls to the gaps at times, but he has well-below-average power. He makes that small-ball profile work since he’s a plus runner with aggressiveness that makes him a threat on the bases. Vaz is a versatile defender and got looks at second base, shortstop, center field and left field in ‘23, although second is his natural and best position because of his below-average arm. Players and coaches rave about Vaz’s clubhouse presence and leadership skills. He’ll embrace any role, which makes him suited for a super-utility spot if he can add enough strength to play the outfield and learn the routine of moving around the diamond. Vaz won the inaugural Alex Gordon Heart & Hustle Award last year in the Royals organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Tommy John surgery as a high school senior in 2020, Carr redshirted in his first college season at San Diego and barely got on the field as a two-way player in his second. He transferred to Palomar (Calif.) JC, emerged as the top junior college prospect in the 2023 class and became a third-round pick. His stuff has regressed since he turned pro, though that didn't stop him from becoming the 2025 South Atlantic League pitcher of the year and leading the High-A circuit in ERA (1.96) and opponent average (.190). Carr worked with a 91-97 mph fastball at Palomar and now operates at 90-92 and maxes out at 95, and while he doesn't miss many bats with his two- and four-seamers, he also generates a lot of weak contact. His slider has lost some power and sweep as well, going from the low 80s to the upper 70s, and it's now more of an average offering. He has switched to a harder changeup that sits in the mid-80s with decent sink. Carr compensates for a lack of physicality with athleticism and arm speed. He pounded the strike zone in junior college but has become more of nibbler working with a diminished arsenal against pro hitters. He has flashed bigger stuff in offseason workouts the last two years, so the Yankees hope he'll show improved velocity in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following Tommy John surgery as a California high school senior in 2020, Carr redshirted at San Diego in his first year in college and got a brief run as a two-way player in his second. He pitched well in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2022, transferred to Palomar (Calif.) JC and ranked as the best junior college prospect in the 2023 Draft after going 12-1 with a 2.31 ERA and 111/19 K/BB ratio in 78 innings. A third-round pick, his stuff and control regressed during his pro debut last year at High-A. After dealing at 91-95 mph and touching 97 with his fastball at Palomar, Carr worked more at 88-92 and topped out at 94 with his two- and four-seamers in 2024. His once-solid low-80s sweeper also lost some velocity and life, playing as more of an average pitch. He has yet to show much aptitude for a changeup that dropped into the low 80s last year while featuring inconsistent depth. Carr's walk rate also doubled from 6 percent in junior college to 12 percent at High-A as he became reluctant to attack hitters with diminished stuff. His athleticism and arm speed help him overcome a lack of physicality, and offseason workouts have the Yankees optimistic that he's recapturing his Palomar form. If that happens and he adds some strength and polish, he still could become a No. 3 or 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carr had Tommy John surgery as a California high school senior in 2020 before redshirting at San Diego in his first college season and seeing brief action as a two-way player in his second. He pitched well in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2022, then transferred to Palomar (Calif.) JC and became the top junior college prospect in the 2023 Draft after going 12-1 with a 2.31 ERA and 111/19 K/BB ratio in 78 innings. He bypassed a Texas Christian commitment after the Yankees selected him in the third round and will make his pro debut in 2024. Carr's stuff has backed up in his first full pro season, and he has lost about 3 mph off his two- and four-seam fastballs, averaging around 90 mph and topping out at 94. He doesn't always stay on top of his slider, which has dipped in terms of both velocity and spin and now sits around 79 mph. His mid-80s changeup gets too firm and has only mild fade, so he doesn't trust it much. Carr's athleticism and arm speed help him compensate for a lack of physicality. After filling the strike zone at Palomar, he has been more tentative in 2024. He'll need to improve his strength and polish to make it as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez signed with the D-backs for $1.25 million in January 2023, making him Arizona’s top international addition of that year. A strong introduction in the Dominican Summer League complete with a .363 OBP caught the attention of many, including the Mets, who acquired him in a one-for-one swap for Tommy Pham at the ’23 Trade Deadline. Rodriguez caught even more fire with New York's DSL affiliate after the deal and had a solid stateside debut in the Florida Complex League last season, slashing .282/.355/.400 with three homers and 17 steals in 50 games. A left-handed hitter, Rodriguez stays on time with a leg lift and snaps into place at the right moment to drive his impressive bat-to-ball skills. With a 17.1 percent K rate, he was one of only two players aged 17 or younger to strike out less than 18 percent of the time in stateside complex ball in 2024 -- Phillies catcher and preseason Top 100 prospect Eduardo Tait (14.6) was the other. Rodriguez’s slugging output did drop a touch from the DSL to the FCL and his exit velocities weren’t exactly at a promising level. Considering he’s still only entering his age-18 season, he has time to mature physically and produce more than gap power, but the trend lines aren’t established yet. Rodriguez possesses above-average arm strength that remains his best defensive asset at shortstop, but even as an average runner, he has the footwork and hands to handle the position at this early stage in his career. He continues to get looks at second base to keep him up the middle, and he even played a few games at third, where the arm would work as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez was the D-backs’ biggest international addition in 2023, signing with the club for $1.25 million out of the Dominican Republic in January. He didn’t last long in the organization after a strong walk rate and OBP in the Dominican Summer League caught the Mets’ eye, and New York acquired him in a one-for-one swap for Major League outfielder Tommy Pham at the Trade Deadline. Rodriguez went 19-for-45 (.422) with eight extra-base hits, 11 walks and four strikeouts in 13 games for a Mets’ DSL affiliate after the move, further solidifying his status as a prospect to watch in his new organization. Batting from the left side, Rodriguez was nearly stellar at protecting the plate in his first professional season, especially considering he didn't turn 17 until July. His 1.06 BB/K ratio ranked third among the 15 qualified DSL players playing in their age-16 seasons in '23. With only three of his 18 extra-base hits leaving the yard, his power plays best to the gaps, but it was always likely he’d need some time to get the pop to play in games. The 6-foot infielder boasts above-average arm strength needed for long throws from shortstop, and while he’s just an average runner, he has the hands and footwork to keep getting work at the six. Notably, the Mets got him some looks at second base to keep his athleticism up the middle. Rodriguez will take his advanced approach stateside with plenty of development still to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bright was a key member of Auburn’s 2022 College World Series team and signed with the Orioles for a below-slot $400,000 as a senior after they made him a fifth-round selection in that year’s Draft. After a brief debut, Bright struck out more than one-third of the hitters he faced at High-A Aberdeen in 2023, though he wasn’t young for the level, and reached Double-A by the end of his first full pro season. He spent all of 2024 sort of stagnating back at the level, pitching to a 4.18 ERA but missing fewer bats and finishing with an ugly 0-11 record. Bright has always stood out more for his pitch traits than his stats, which weren’t sensational in college either. He’s a 6-foot-4 righty with a traditional delivery and a four-pitch mix, the best of which is a plus curve that he learned to spin harder in ‘24. He pairs it with an average heater that lives between 92-95 mph but can play up because he tunnels it well and throws it with carry at the top of the zone. He also throws a harder breaker that’s morphed from a slider into more of a pure cutter and an improving changeup that has a chance to be an average pitch. Bright has never been a very good strike thrower, and the Orioles were hoping he’d improve at limiting free passes and learn to come out of the gate stronger over a full year at Double-A. But that didn’t necessarily happen. Bright’s walk rate stayed on the high side, his strikeout rate declined, and falling behind often in counts made him more predictable, leading to more hits allowed. With more consistency, he still has a chance to develop into a back-end starter, but if the control issues persist, they limit his upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bright never put up overwhelming numbers in college, but he was a mainstay in Auburn’s weekend rotation in 2022 and helped the Tigers pick up their first College World Series win since 1997. That helped him catch the attention of the Orioles, who were intrigued enough with his pitch shapes to select him in the fifth round of that year’s Draft and sign him for a below-slot $400,000. He became the highest drafted pitcher Baltimore signed that year after it failed to bring third-rounder Nolan McLean into the fold. Bright then broke out at High-A Aberdeen, where he struck out more than one-third of the hitters he faced before finishing his first full season strongly at Double-A Bowie. Bright is a 6-foot-4 right-hander with a traditional delivery and over-the-top slot who spent his first full season adding to his pitches and learning how to best utilize them. His 92-94 mph fastball is average velocity-wise but plays up by getting above barrels due to its plane and carry. Bright’s best secondary offering is a plus mid-70s curveball that he tunnels well off the heater and can throw to both sides of the plate with depth. He also incorporates a changeup that flashes above average and two sliders, including a hard mid-80s gyro. If Bright can improve his feel for them, all three of those pitches have a chance to be average offerings. The area Bright needs to improve the most on is his command. He’s had high strikeout rates in college and through his pro career so far, but that comes with high walk rates that threaten to limit his upside. Cutting down the free passes and learning how to come out of the gate stronger in the first inning could lead to better consistency overall and give Bright a chance to develop into a back-end rotation option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez began his college career at Miami Dade, pitching two years at the JC level before moving on to be a part of the University of Miami rotation. He missed bats, but with inconsistent command, something that continued in his first year of pro ball after the Braves took him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft. He spent the past year with High-A Rome, finishing second in the South Atlantic League in strikeouts (127) and would have been among the leaders in batting average against (.193), ERA (3.57) and K/9 (11.1) had he thrown enough innings to qualify. A bit undersized at 5-foot-10, Hernandez does have some traits that give him a chance to start. Pitching last year at 21, he flashed an effective four-pitch mix. His fastball is an average offering which sat around 93 mph and touched 97, a tick more than in college, and it does miss some bats with good riding life to it. His slider is his go-to, a low-80s breaker that elicited a 40 percent miss rate according to Synergy. He has an upper-70s curve that he doesn't throw as often, and he started showing signs of a solid splitter, though he's still getting the feel for it. The Braves think there's more upside to tap into given that Hernandez really didn't pitch much until he got to Miami Dade. He'll have to find the strike zone a lot more consistently after walking 5.9 per nine in his first full year to have any chance of starting, though that fastball-slider combination could work really well in a relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 After two years at the junior college level, pitching for Miami Dade, Hernandez headed to the University of Miami rather than sign with the Reds as a Day 3 draftee in 2023. He had an inconsistent season pitching in the Hurricanes' weekend rotation, but the Braves liked his arsenal enough to take him in the fourth round of the Draft, then sent him out to get his professional feet wet with a few innings with Single-A Augusta and High-A Rome. While he's just 5-foot-10, Hernandez could have the chance to be a left-handed starter thanks to a robust repertoire. At Miami, he had four pitches he could go to, though he might simplify it a bit at the next level. He has an average fastball that averaged just over 92 mph in 2024, topping out at 95 mph. His feel to spin breaking stuff really supports his heater, with his low-80s slider that missed bats at a 43-percent rate last year perhaps being the focal point in pro ball. He had a distinct upper-70s curve that missed bats too, though he didn't command it as well. HIs firm changeup is his fourth pitch. For Hernandez to stick as a starter, he'll have to improve that offspeed offering and cut down on the walks. Though he's undersized, he's strong and has the chance to be a durable innings-eater, though there is some reliever risk, with the chance of his breaking stuff really playing well out of the pen should that move be necessary.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Messinger spent most of his college career as a reliever at Virginia before the Yankees signed him for an above-slot $225,000 as a 13th-rounder in 2021. They had him spend that summer reshaping his fastball and slider before making his pro debut in 2022. His improved stuff has translated into 232 strikeouts in 194 innings over his first two seasons, and he finished last year with a start in Double-A. After sitting at 90 mph with his fastball in his final year with the Cavaliers, Messinger now deals at 92-94 mph with bat-missing run and carry, and he touched 99 in 2022. His slider also has jumped from the upper 70s in college to 81-84 mph with high spin rates and nasty sweep. He also has increased the power and gets good depth on an upper-70s curveball, though he doesn't use it very often. Messinger's sinking mid-80s changeup lags behind the rest of his repertoire because it doesn't have enough velocity separation from his fastball and he struggles to throw it for strikes. He uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create angle and extension that make life difficult for hitters, but he's still learning to harness his upgraded stuff. He has a ceiling of a No. 4 starter with a fallback of becoming a multi-inning reliever who could lean even more heavily on his slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a reliever in college at Virginia, Messinger signed for an over-slot $225,000 as a 13th-rounder in 2021. He spent time remaking his fastball and slider before embarking on his pro debut last season in Single-A. He showcased some of the most interesting stuff in the lower levels of the Yankees system while moving into the rotation in late May and striking out 112 in 83 2/3 innings. After averaging 90 mph with his fastball in his final college season, Messinger operated at 92-94 and touched 99 with armside run and carry on his four-seamer in 2022. His slider went from parking in the upper 70s with the Cavaliers to sitting at 81-84 mph with high spin rates and dastardly sweep. He also has good shape on an upper-70s curveball that added power but doesn't find the strike zone consistently. Messinger's changeup is a work in progress, showing some sink but coming in too firm in the mid-80s. He uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create difficult angle and extension, though he's still learning to harness his improved arsenal. He has the ceiling of a No. 4 starter but will have to refine his changeup, control and command to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: White was only 17 on Draft Day when the Nationals selected the South Carolina native in the fifth round and signed him for above slot at $400,000, knowing he was raw but had tremendous upside. Despite his age, the switch-hitting slugger held his own at Single-A Fredericksburg in his first full season, and because of its belief that he’d carve out a role in the organization’s future, Washington moved him to first base to get him away from the outfield logjam and place more emphasis on his offensive potential. That potential wasn’t realized in 2023 as White slashed just .170/.277/.279 with six homers in 77 games at High-A Wilmington. The former Indiana commit has a few things going for him. His raw power is still among the best in the system, and when he gets the bat squarely on the ball, it can be sent screaming into the night. He actually showed decent swing decisions, too, and took his share of walks (12.2 percent) when pitchers went wild. But overall, his barrel control needs work, and pitchers found it easier to beat him with velocity up in the zone, leading to a rough 36.4 percent strikeout rate and hurting the belief that his pop will play without the proper adjustments. White is still a work in progress at first base and won’t be a threat to steal bases, solidifying power and patience as his saving graces. But it’s also worth noting that he was one of only six players aged 19 or younger who received more than 250 plate appearances at High-A in 2023. Everyone involved with White’s development acknowledges 2024 will be a big, deciding year for him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: White was 17 entering the 2021 Draft, making the South Carolina native a high-upside, extremely raw talent. The Nationals bet on that potential with a fifth-round pick and signed the Indiana commit with an above-slot $400,000 bonus. White spent 92 games at Single-A Fredericksburg in his first full season and held his own with a .258/.353/.432 line and 11 homers -- all while being the second-youngest Carolina Leaguer to qualify for the batting title. A switch-hitter, White’s ceiling is tied directly to his plus raw power that derives from impressive strength and a leg kick that helps him get the most of it when he’s in sync. Strikeouts continue to be a concern with a relatively high 27.4 percent K rate with the FredNats, but there was positive growth in that area as White adjusted -- particularly on balls lower in the zone -- and he fanned 22 percent of the time in the 2022 season’s final two months. The hit-tool concerns have reared their head again in 2023 at High-A Wilmington, unfortunately, causing White's stock to drop as the season has gone along. White doesn’t have the same speed as other low-level outfielders in the system like James Wood, Elijah Green and Jeremy De La Rosa, and as such, all 86 of his starts not at DH came in left field in 2022. A deep group on the grass forced White to grab a first baseman's mitt, and that put a bigger strain on his slugging output. His power, youth and relatively even splits still remain big points in his favor toward becoming a lineup regular wherever he lands defensively (or even DH).

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: White didn’t turn 18 until July 23, nearly two weeks after the 2021 Draft, so the South Carolina native was always going to be one of the rawest talents in his class. The Nationals were the ones to jump at the opportunity to mold White’s skillset and selected him in the fifth round. The organization signed White away from his Indiana commitment with an above-slot $400,000 bonus, and he rewarded that confidence by going 15-for-53 (.283) with four homers during his foray into the Florida Complex League. White’s raw power might have been the best among prep players in the 2021 class, and it’s that pop that gets Washington so excited in the early stages of its development work with him. His slugging ability plays from both sides as a switch-hitter, alleviating some splits concerns. He doesn’t have a history of varying his bat path much, however, and that could dull his overall offensive performance without an adjustment. The 6-foot-2 outfielder is a below-average runner and might lose more of a step as he matures. As such, the majority of his early pro looks have been in left field, and that’s where his defensive skills profile best at this stage. First base is also a possibility down the road, though that discussion is likely years away. White will need to make the most of his power to be of value in either left or at first, but given how high the ceiling is with that tool, he could be in for a few homer-filled years of fun development in the Nats system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Strumpf played in the same JSerra Catholic HS (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) infield as 2017 No. 1 overall pick Royce Lewis and 2019 supplemental first-rounder Davis Wendzel before becoming an immediate starter at UCLA. The best second-base prospect in the 2019 Draft, he homered in an NCAA regional playoff game immediately after Chicago took him in the second round, later signing for $1,050,300. More of a hit-over-power guy in the past, he sold out for power in 2022 and batted .236/.378/.463 with 22 homers and 162 strikeouts in Double-A. Amateur scouts compared Strumpf to Cubs 2018 first-rounder Nico Hoerner because both were right-handed hitters who drilled line drives from gap to gap and controlled the strike zone while starring in the Pacific-12 Conference. Strumpf has gone from using an inside-out stroke and the entire field at the start of 2021 to looking to pull and launch almost every pitch he sees. He does have real 20-homer power and mitigates his strikeouts with a healthy amount of walks, but he's extremely vulnerable against offspeed pitches. A fringy runner with average arm strength, Strumpf has split his pro career between second and third base. He improved his range at second last season and grades a solid defender there. Chicago has a greater need at the hot corner, where he does a passable job.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the same JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) infield as Royce Lewis (No. 1 overall pick by the Twins in 2017) and Davis Wendzel (a Rangers supplemental first-rounder in 2019), Strumpf became an immediate starter at UCLA. The consensus top second base prospect in the 2019 Draft, he homered in an NCAA regional playoff game immediately after the Cubs drafted him in the second round. Signed for $1,050,300, he earned a promotion to Double-A one month into his first full pro season in 2021 but hit just .211/.335/.380 at that level. Amateur scouts likened Strumpf to fellow Pacific-12 Conference star and Cubs 2018 first-rounder Nico Hoerner because both were right-handed hitters who focused on driving balls from gap to gap while controlling the strike zone. Strumpf has been a different guy in pro ball, however, and his production has suffered as he has aggressively tried to launch balls out of the park to his pull side. He's still drawing walks and making hard contact when he connects but Chicago would like to see him make some adjustments to keep his bat in the zone longer. Because he's a fringy runner with average arm strength, Strumpf derives most of his value from his bat. He's not particularly notable on the bases or in the field, and he played mostly third base last year because of team needs in Double-A. The Cubs still view him as more of a second baseman, though he did prove capable at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Strumpf starred in the same JSerra Catholic High (San Juan Capistrano, Calif.) infield with Royce Lewis (the No. 1 overall pick in 2017) and Davis Wendzel (a Rangers supplemental first-rounder in 2019), playing shortstop and pushing Lewis to second base. He immediately started at second base for UCLA as a freshman and was the consensus top prospect at the position in the 2019 Draft. He homered in an NCAA regional playoff game immediately after the Cubs drafted him in the second round and reached Low-A in his pro debut after signing for $1,050,300. Coming out of the Draft, Strumpf was considered similar to fellow Pacific-12 Conference product and Cubs 2018 first-rounder Nico Hoerner, a right-handed hitter who focused on lining balls from gap to gap while controlling the strike zone. But he has been a different guy in pro ball, struggling to provide consistent production while getting too caught up trying to pull and lift pitches. He has the hitting ability, bat speed and strength to hit 20 homers per year if he lets his power come naturally. Most of Strumpf's value will come from his bat, so his early-career difficulties have been alarming. He has fringy speed and won't rack up many stolen or extra bases. He has fringy to average range and arm strength at second base, his position at UCLA and in his debut, and his arm has been stretched at third base, where he has seen most of his action in Double-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a baseball family that includes a father (Wilton), uncle (Fernando Tatis Sr.) and cousin (Fernando Tatis Jr.) who played in the big leagues, Veras signed for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2019. He led the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with a .949 OPS in his pro debut two years later and bashed his way to Double-A over the next three seasons. He batted .267/.319/.424 and led the Southern League in hits (131) and total bases (208) in 2024. There's nothing subtle at the plate about Veras, who has some of the best raw power and one of the most aggressive approaches in the system. With the bat speed in his right-handed stroke and the strength in his 6-foot-2 frame, he offers the upside of 30 homers on an annual basis. But his pull-happy mentality and willingness to swing at everything results in an excessive amount of strikeouts and rolled-over groundouts. Veras is a deceptively effective baserunner who has parlayed his average speed into 49 steals during the last two seasons. He can look lackadaisical on the outfield corners at times but some of that is trying to bait opponents into testing his solid strength. He played the infield corners in his first two years as a pro but lacks the hands for the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: His father Wilton, uncle Fernando Tatis Sr. and cousin Fernando Tatis Jr. all reached the big leagues, and Veras could do the same in the next couple of years. Signed for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2019, he topped the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with a .949 OPS in his pro debut two years later. He finished strong after a promotion to Double-A last August, hitting .309/.346/.533 with six homers in the final six weeks as one of the youngest players (age 20) in the Southern League. Veras possesses some of the best raw power and one of the most aggressive approaches in the system. He has a quick right-handed swing and huge strength that provide pop to all fields and 30-homer upside, though his lack of selectivity also leads to a lot of strikeouts and rolled-over grounders. He whiffed nearly five times as much as he walked in his first two years in full-season ball and hasn't met a pitch he won't chase out of the zone. Veras spent his two pro seasons on the infield corners, but he had limited range and the game sped up too much on him at third base. He has below-average speed and doesn't cover much ground in right field, but his average to solid arm is an asset there. He threw out 10 runners in 101 starts in right last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Veras has extensive baseball bloodlines as father Wilton, uncle Fernando Tatis Sr. and cousin Fernando Tatis Jr. all have played in the big leagues and cousin Elijah Tatis is a fellow White Sox infield prospect. Signed for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2019, Veras has some of the best raw power in the system. He led the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with a .949 OPS in his 2021 pro debut, ranked fourth in the Single-A Carolina League with 17 homers last season and went deep three times in 12 Double-A games as a part of the organization's Project Birmingham. Veras has well-above-average raw power, the product of bat speed, strength and an aggressive right-handed swing. While he can crush fastballs, his pull-happy mindset leaves him vulnerable to breaking pitches and results in too many rolled-over ground balls. He posted a 132/30 K/BB ratio in his first full season, further underscoring his eventual need to tone down his approach against more advanced pitching. Veras has below-average quickness and average arm strength, which limits his defensive utility. He divided his first two pro seasons between first base, where he's a fringy defender with limited range, and third base, where the game speeds up too much on him and his tools aren't good fits. He has spent 2023 playing an adequate right field and showing a knack for throwing out runners who challenge him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 3 in the 2024 international class by MLB Pipeline, Santana earned Julio Rodríguez comparisons for his tools and personality before signing for $1,297,500 out of the Dominican Republic. After performing well in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and winning MVP accolades in the DSL all-star game during his pro debut, he faced more adversity when he came to the United States in 2025. He was decent in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League but overmatched as an 18-year-old in Single-A, where he struck out 29 times in 60 at-bats. Santana controlled the strike zone well in the DSL but didn't in his U.S. debut, struggling to recognize pitches and getting completely bamboozled by non-fastballs in Single-A. He has a quick right-handed stroke but swung through too many offerings when he wasn't chasing them out of the zone. He hit the ball hard when he did connect, and his bat speed and projectable strength give him the chance to develop 20-homer power. Santana has solid speed but still is learning the finer points of basestealing. He got most of his DSL action in center field but spent more time in left field last season, and he may fit better on a corner unless he refines his instincts. He has fringy but playable arm strength at either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born and trained in the Dominican Republic, Santana spent some time on the U.S. high school showcase circuit and performed well at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in Florida in October 2024. No. 3 in MLB Pipeline's 2024 international rankings, he garnered comparisons to Julio Rodríguez for his five-tool potential and personality. After signing for $1,297,500, he slashed .292/.465/.364 in the Dominican Summer League and won MVP honors in the Rookie-level circuit's All-Star Game. An advanced right-handed hitter, Santana showed the ability to recognize pitches, manage the strike zone and make adjustments at the plate in his pro debut. He had much more difficulty making contact when he came to the United States in 2025, with his strikeout rate doubling from 15 to 30 percent. He didn't homer in 53 games in the DSL but has the bat speed and projectable strength to grow into at least 20-homer power. Santana has plus speed and the instincts to make use of it on the bases and in center field. He has solid range in center along with a playable if fringy arm. He's bilingual and earns plaudits for his high baseball IQ and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 2 prospect in MLB Pipeline's 2024 international rankings, Santana signed out of the Dominican Republic for $1,297,500. He got better as the signing period approached and earned comparisons to Julio Rodríguez for both his five-tool potential and his personality. He's advanced enough to possibly reach Single-A during his pro debut, just as the gem of the Rangers' 2023 international class (Sebastian Walcott) did last summer. Santana performed well at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in Florida last October, showing the potential to hit for average and power while competing against top U.S. high school prospects for the 2024 Draft. A right-handed hitter, he controls the strike zone with an extremely mature approach and shows the ability to make adjustments at the plate. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to grow into plus pop and drives the ball to all fields. Santana also has the plus speed to make an impact on the bases and in center field. The only obvious weakness in his game is his arm, which grades as below-average-to-fringy but should be playable in center. He's bilingual and earns raves for his work ethic and intelligence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Andujar got the largest bonus the Rockies handed out during the 2024 international signing period, joining the organization for $1.7 million. He fared well during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, hitting .292 with a .376 on-base percentage. He was still 17 when his United States debut began in the Arizona Complex League, and the Rockies were thrilled with how he carried himself, as he once again hit well (.319) and got on base (.370 OBP), but with virtually no impact either summer. Andujar is a switch-hitter who has already has shown an ability to make a lot of contact. He carries a career strikeout rate of just 13.9 percent into the 2026 season, routinely finding the barrel. He's better from the left side, but some of that is that he just hasn't gotten many reps the other way against left-handed pitching. What he's lacking more than anything else is strength. He has just 17 total extra-base hits in his two stops so far and has not shown the ability to drive the ball. He does have every chance to stick at shortstop with terrific hands and enough arm for the spot. He had a little trouble with the speed of the game when he first got to the ACL, but as he got his legs under him, his internal clock kicked in and he let his defensive instincts take over. This one may take some patience as a deep projection, with the strength piece critical for him to reach the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies don't shy away from going after middle infielders on the international market, with Ezequiel Tovar the biggest success story of the past several years. They added Andujar to the system when the 2024 signing period opened, giving him $1.7 million to sign. One of the top infielders in the class, he went to the Dominican Summer League for his pro debut and showed off some good contact skills, hitting .292 with a .376 on-base percentage, but leading to some concerns about future impact. One of the youngest players in the class who didn't turn 17 until late July, Andujar certainly has time to figure things out. He starts out with a pretty good feel for hitting from both sides of the plate. He can find the barrel routinely and makes a ton of contact. He struck out just 13.5 percent of the time, isn't afraid to hit behind in the count and even drew some walks. He needs to add strength so he can impact the ball more, even if power isn't ever a big part of his game after slugging .352 in his debut. More strength should also augment Andujar's speed. He likes to run despite having just average speed at present and he moves well defensively at shortstop. He has good hands and an arm that could develop into a plus for him at the premium position. His ability to slow the game down gives him an even better overall defensive package and something he can lean on to help his team win if his bat is slow to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In July 2017, it was Ezequiel Tovar. Two years later, Adael Amador led the class. Dyan Jorge was next up in 2022. So it should have come with little surprise when the Rockies again went after, and signed, one of the top shortstops in this year's international amateur class. Andujar, who was No. 17 on MLB Pipeline's Top 50 International prospect list when the 2024 signing period opened in January, got $1.7 million to sign, and like Tovar and Jorge, he will get his pro career started in the Dominican Summer League. Andujar is a switch-hitter who has shown some offensive upside from both sides of the plate. He finds the barrel consistently with high contact rates, rarely strikes out and isn't afraid of hitting with two strikes. Right now it's gap-to-gap thump, at best, but if he can add strength to his frame, there should be more power to come in the future. While he isn't a burner, that added strength should allow Andujar to add speed as he matures as well, and he's already aggressive on the basepaths and likes to steal. He has all the makings of a solid shortstop, with soft hands and an arm that could eventually be plus. His defensive tools play up because he has excellent instincts and awareness to go along with a good internal clock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After losing out on Roki Sasaki as the cream of the international crop to begin 2025, the Padres moved to build out their system with depth by adding three of MLB Pipeline's Top 50 international prospects: left-hander Carlos Alvarez, shortstop Deivid Coronil and De La Cruz, who checked in at No. 21 on the list. He signed with the Friars for $1 million out of the Dominican Republic on Jan. 22. De La Cruz spent his entire first Minor League season in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, where he hit .259/.477/.360 with one homer and 11 steals in 51 games. The most promising part of the switch-hitter's DSL performance was that he walked more times (46) than he struck out (45) and finished with a 23.2 percent walk rate, 18th-best among the 304 qualifiers on the complex-level circuit. The DSL can sport some raw, wild arms, and De La Cruz choosing to take his free passes instead of forcing swings is a good sign. That said, he'll be much more tested in the zone when he comes stateside, and considering he stands just 5-foot-9, a lack of impact could make that an uphill climb. He'll also need more reps as a righty hitter to even out his early splits. De La Cruz is considered an above-average runner, and his footwork, instincts and range should land him in the middle of the infield somewhere. He got ample starts at both shortstop and second base in the D.R. De La Cruz's profile will get more answers during his age-18 season in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tons of talent has hailed from San Pedro de Macorís, Dominican Republic, over the last few decades, including current Padres star Fernando Tatis Jr. The San Diego organization hopes to unearth another star from the area in De La Cruz, who signed with the club for $1 million at the start of the 2025 international period. De La Cruz was one of three of MLB Pipeline's Top 50 international prospects to sign with the Friars, joining left-hander Carlos Alvarez and fellow shortstop Deivid Coronil at the top of the class. The switch-hitter showed quick hands as an amateur, helping him drive the barrel through the zone quickly. He also drew good reviews for his strike-zone awareness for his age, signaling that he could have an average hit tool as a professional. De La Cruz would occasionally try to sell out for power, but at 5-foot-9, he doesn't project for a ton of pop. He's at his best when he sends the ball to all fields from both sides of the dish. De La Cruz has the right defensive instincts on the dirt, and his footwork should help him stick up the middle. He has just average arm strength, which might portend a move to second base long-term, and it will be interesting to see how San Diego balances him and Coronil in their introductions to pro ball. He could be a decent basestealing threat, especially if he's able to maintain his speed as he fills out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Repeating the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League used to be a developmental kiss of death. But it’s been happening more in recent years, with fewer short-season options in the United States and sometimes it really helps a young prospect figure some things out. Arguelles, whose $700,000 bonus in January 2024 was the second-highest the Rockies handed out during that international signing period, held his own during his pro debut in the DSL the summer after signing, but without any impact. He stayed for a second summer, and after adding some strength, earned DSL MVP honors after winning the batting title (.422) and leading the circuit in OPS (1.180). Arguelles hit so well the Rockies considered flying him stateside last summer, but they’re excited to have him in country now. He already has a very strong feel for hitting, using the whole field. He grinds out at-bats, takes walks and shows excellent balance at the plate. The left-handed hitter is going to keep getting stronger and has mistake-type power with a hard rate of contact, but it’s more gap than over-the-fence kind of pop. While he’s not a runner, he has solid instincts defensively and his average arm can play up a little when he attacks the ball. He’s played mostly center field thus far, and the Rockies will still give him reps there to maximize his athleticism, but he’ll start getting time at all three spots, with a corner the most likely home for him long term if he develops into a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays made Bonilla one of their biggest international signings in years, handing the young Dominican slugger a $4.1 million bonus in 2023. Bonilla was billed as one of the top offensive talents in that year’s class and showed some early flashes in the Dominican Summer League, where he hit .307 with an .836 OPS over 50 games. Bonilla’s numbers took a significant step back in ‘24, though, which was surprising after he’d generated so much positive buzz coming into the year. In the Florida Complex League, Bonilla hit just .186/.257/.299. The organization isn’t putting too much stock into those results and still believes in Bonilla's physical upside, which remains among the highest in the organization. Bonilla was a popular breakout pick a year ago for a reason, and many of those reasons still apply, but in 2025 that stat line will start to matter. Bonilla’s profile is all about his bat. He could develop into a dynamic offensive threat with legitimate plus power, but he’ll need to cut down on the swing-and-miss significantly to be more consistent. At 19, he remains a bit of a long-term project, but is still a name that brings out as much excitement as nearly any hitting prospect in the system. Likely destined for a corner outfield spot, the Blue Jays are still rolling out Bonilla in center field for now. A year ago, Bonilla felt like a dark-horse pick to catapult himself into the Top 100 conversation, and while the exact opposite happened, Bonilla is a talent worth being patient about. Few prospects in this system have a bigger gap between their potential floor and ceiling than Bonilla, so this should be a fascinating 12 months for him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays made Bonilla one of their biggest international signings in years, handing the young Dominican slugger a $4.1 million bonus in 2023. Bonilla was billed as one of the top offensive talents in that year’s class and showed some early flashes in the Dominican Summer League, where he hit .307 with an .836 OPS over 50 games. His game power hasn’t quite shown up (three homers) and his 55 strikeouts were an issue, but at 18, Bonilla is still one of the highest-upside prospects in this organization. It’s already jarring to see Bonilla in person. After having the image of a baby-faced teenager when he signed with the Blue Jays, there's a double-take upon seeing Bonilla walking around the Blue Jays’ complex with braids and a full, thick beard. There are raw elements to his game, but the exciting power he flashes in batting practice should start spilling into games this season. His exit velocities are already showing progress from 2023, and while he isn’t quite at the level of Orelvis Martinez in that area, he’s getting there. Bonilla seems destined for a corner outfield spot, which will need to be a greater focus for him in the coming seasons. He still moves very well for his size, so even if the Blue Jays can get Bonilla to the point that he’s playing a passable corner outfield, that’s enough to let his bat truly shine. His plate approach and strikeout rates are worth monitoring this year, but much like Arjun Nimmala, Bonilla is a dream project for this development staff and should benefit as much as anyone in the organization from the resources at the new complex. The long-term nature of said project remains a point of emphasis after Bonilla has struggled in the Florida Complex League this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays made Bonilla one of their biggest international signings in years, handing the young Dominican slugger a $4.1 million bonus in 2023. There are years of development ahead for Bonilla, but the Blue Jays came away impressed with him after he took part in their instructs in the Dominican Republic after the signing. At 6-foot-1, 180 pounds, Bonilla will continue to add strength and size to a physical frame that is already very impressive. His hit tool will need to develop in the coming years as he learns about himself as a hitter and develops a professional plate approach, but his raw power and bat speed were among the very best in the ’22 international class. He will play some center field coming up, but as he continues to mature, Bonilla could soon profile as a corner-outfield thumper, and he’s athletic enough to be a solid fielder in left or right. We’re still a couple of years away from seeing Bonilla with a full-season affiliate, but with his physical tools and age, he is a prospect the organization can dream on. He’ll benefit from climbing the ladder with the Blue Jays’ new player development complex at his disposal as he gets into the team's training program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perdomo was No. 4 on the 2024 Top 50 International Prospects list when that year’s signing period opened up, the second-highest ranked shortstop behind only Leo De Vries. The Braves went all in, giving Perdomo $5 million, the highest bonus awarded in the class, to join. Since then, they haven’t really gotten a true look at who he is; hamstring issues shut him down after just eight games during his debut in the Dominican Summer League and limited him to 54 more in the Florida Complex League in 2025. The injury bug hit again, though this time it was his knee, an injury suffered in his second game of 2026 that will cost him the season. The Braves really don’t know what kind of player they have on their hands at this point, not wanting to put too much weight on 62 total games and a combined .546 OPS. When he was entering pro ball, he was considered to be one of the best pure hitters in his signing class, a right-handed hitter who is capable of making hard contact. He’s overly aggressive and can chase too much, but there had been a semblance of a plan at the plate with decent pitch recognition, which didn’t necessarily show up stateside last year. All of the missed reps certainly didn’t help him find a rhythm or get to any of his raw power. It remained to be seen if Perdomo, once he got past the hammy bug, could utilize his above-average speed on the basepaths, something even more in question now with his knee injury. Before he went down again, there was confidence he could play a reliable shortstop with a good arm. His age-19 season now scrapped, he'll try to get the ship moving in the right direction in 2027, at age 20.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Imagine getting a premium sports car but not being able to see how it runs for an entire year because it broke down seemingly before you drove it off the lot. That’s kind of how the Braves are feeling with Perdomo, considered one of the best prospects in the 2024 international class who received the largest bonus anyone in the class received, $5 million, to sign. But he suffered a hamstring injury that shut him down after just eight games, leaving the Braves a little unsure what kind of player they actually have on their hands. The good news is that Perdomo should have a clean bill of health and be able to truly get going in 2025. Thought to be one of the best pure hitters in his signing class, the right-handed hitter does not swing-and-miss much and can make consistently hard contact. With his knack for finding the barrel comes an over-aggressive approach at times, chasing out of the zone, but he seems to have good pitch recognition skills and the ability to handle all kinds of stuff. He can drive the ball to all fields and there could be plenty of power to come as he matures. Perdomo was at least an above-average runner before the injury and the hope is that will still be an asset on the basepaths post-injury. He also has a good foundation to play shortstop long-term thanks to good range and arm strength. He’s just 18 for the 2025 season, so there’s still plenty of time for him to reach his ceiling, with the Braves eager to see him get through a full, healthy year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perdomo was ranked No. 3 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list when the 2024 signing period opened in January. The Braves had a bonus pool of $5.284 million for the period and put nearly all of their chips in, giving the shortstop $5 million -- the largest bonus anyone in the class received -- to join the organization. A right-handed hitting infielder, Perdomo was considered to be one of the best pure hitters in this international signing class. He rarely strikes out and has a knack for making hard contact with a quick and simple swing. While he’s an aggressive hitter, he has a solid approach, showing good pitch recognition skills and an ability to drive fastballs and soft stuff to all fields, with his power just starting to come. He’s at least an above-average runner who should be able to impact the game on the basepaths as well. It's looking now like Perdomo will be able to play shortstop for a very long time. He’s fundamentally sound with plenty of range and enough arm for the premium position. He’ll be 17 years old for the entirety of his pro debut this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Padres signed Suero for $325,000 at the start of the 2022 international signing period, he's shown glimpses of his tools coming from a frame that now stands 6-foot-6. He had a solid enough debut in the Dominican Summer League, but was struggling to find consistent production during his United States debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in 2023 when he was sent to the Pirates in the Rich Hill/Ji Man Choi deal. He wasn't able to have much more success with a return to the Florida Complex League in 2024, with what turned out to be a broken hamate sapping his impact and shutting him down at the end of July. Suero will be just 19 for nearly all of the 2025 season, and there are ingredients to work with. He's a switch-hitter who has shown the ability to make hard contact with good bat speed from both sides of the plate. He has a decent approach, draws walks and generally makes good swing decisions. What he doesn't do is make enough contact, as he struck out close to 30 percent of the time at the rookie levels. He'll need to find a way to cut down on the swing-and-miss so he can tap into his raw power, with more of that to come as he adds strength to that huge frame. Right now, Suero runs well enough to man center field, and it could be an option moving forward. There is a pretty good chance he outgrows the position and needs to move to a corner, and he's seen time in both. The focus now is staying healthy and getting enough reps to find some offensive consistency to fit the corner outfield profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres signed Suero for $325,000 at the start of the 2022 international signing period, and he went out and performed fairly well during his debut in the Dominican Summer League. The move to the United States and the Arizona Complex League was a little bumpier, then he was dealt to the Pirates as part of the return for Rich Hill and Ji Man Choi. He finished up his summer in the Florida Complex League and then got some more work in the Dominican Instructional League. It's hard to miss Suero, now standing at 6-foot-5 and just starting to grow into that frame. As modest as his numbers have been, it should be noted he was still 16 when he played in the DSL and there's a ways to go in terms of his physical development. The upside, though, is considerable. A switch-hitter with all the raw tools, he can make hard contact from both sides and has good bat speed, even with his long arms. He'll need to work on his approach and cut down on the swing-and-miss, but does show some feel for barreling up the baseball out in front. Suero runs well, too, potentially providing an exciting speed-power combination in the future. That speed gives him a chance to play center field, but he could fill out enough where moving to a corner spot will be necessary. He could take off as he learns how to polish those tools, but just ask Oneil Cruz: The Pirates know a little bit about helping a tall, lanky and toolsy player reach the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Top 50 international prospect in 2023, Martinez signed with the Mariners for $600,000 when that signing period opened in January. He pitched well, albeit with poor control in his first two stops as a pro, the Dominican Summer and Arizona Complex Leagues. His transition to full-season ball was rough, plagued by poor command in and out of the zone. His July was much better and then he was sent to the Pirates in return for reliever Caleb Ferguson. Martinez is a big, physical 6-foot-4 right-hander with a huge fastball. His heater sat around 95 mph in 2025, touching 97, and he can throw it with decent sink to get ground-ball outs. His mid-80s slider has the chance to be an out pitch, but it was very inconsistent and the Pirates sent Martinez to pitch design camp to help turn it into more of a bat-misser. He’ll flash a good upper-80s changeup but didn’t throw it a lot last year and really struggled to land it in the zone. That’s the biggest thing standing in Martinez’s way. Per Synergy, he threw just 58 percent strikes overall in 2025, leading to a 5.8 BB per nine rate, and when he was in the zone, he got too much of the plate, leading to getting hit. He’ll pitch at age 20 for all of 2026, so there’s time for him to work with the Pirates to turn this upside play into a big league contributor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez was one of just seven pitchers on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list when the 2023 signing period opened. While the Mariners may have made more noise in signing some elite-level hitters on the international market, they weren’t afraid to go after Martinez, whom they signed for $600,000 in January 2023, adding to a class headlined by Felnin Celesten. In Martinez's two stops heading into 2025, the Dominican Summer League and the Arizona Complex League, he showed his raw stuff can get hitters out -- when he knows where it’s going. He struggled to find consistency for much of his first taste of full-season ball this year, but was having his best month in July when he was sent to the Pirates in the Caleb Ferguson trade. There are still plenty of reasons to be high on Martinez: his athleticism, his size -- he’s 6-foot-4 -- and his power stuff. The teenaged right-hander has seen velocity gains in the early stages of his career, and his fastball now sits around 94-95 mph and touches the upper 90s, and he can really sink it to get ground-ball outs. While his changeup was his better secondary pitch in the DSL, his slider has now caught up and surpassed it. In the DSL, Martinez did a nice job of being in and around the strike zone, even with his upticks in velocity. He didn’t replicate that when he came stateside and his command issues after walking seven batters per nine in the ACL -- and 5.5 per nine in the California League at the time of the trade -- have raised some reliever-risk flags. He's pitched all of the 2025 season at age 19, so there’s no reason to restrict him just yet, but he’ll need to seriously refine his command to remain in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez ranked No. 42 among MLB Pipeline’s international prospects when he signed with Seattle for $600,000 out of Mexico in 2023. He blossomed onto many teams’ radars after playing in the showcase circuit in the U.S., with long-term starter potential -- particularly after a stellar debut season in the Dominican Summer League, where he carried a 1.72 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 30.7 percent strikeout rate in 47 innings. At just 17 years old during his debut, while leveraging a huge 6-foot-4 frame, Martinez’s fastball made a huge velocity jump in just one year, from sitting in the 89-90 mph range all the way up to 93-94, even touching 97 thanks to a combination of getting onto the Mariners’ Dominican campus and making a small mechanical tweak. Through it all, Martinez retained his plus strike-throwing ability, which can often be sacrificed among youngsters growing into velocity. Among his secondaries, the changeup was better than the slider in the DSL. The Mariners haven’t had nearly as much success with pitchers on the international market in the Jerry Dipoto era -- those have mostly come via the Draft -- but there’s more than a strong chance that Martinez could blossom into one of the organization’s best in the coming years, with the ceiling of being a mid-to-high-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paul Skenes was not the only 6-foot-6 right-hander the Pirates took in the early rounds of the 2023 Draft. They also selected Mueth out of the Illinois high school ranks No. 67 overall, going over slot to sign him for $1.8 million. Starting him out cautiously, Mueth pitched very well in his debut in 2024, making his way from the Florida Complex League to Single-A Bradenton. A return to the level in 2025 was disastrous, both in terms of production and staying healthy, as he missed a good chunk of the season with shoulder and abdominal strains. With his size, home state and low arm slot, Mueth gets compared to big league right-hander Tanner Houck. That low three-quarters slot delivers a three-pitch mix with movement and deception. His fastball sits around 94 mph and will touch 97-98 mph at times, often with so much horizontal movement he has trouble landing it for strikes. He backs it up with a hard gyro slider that has the chance to be an out pitch, and while his mid-80s changeup is his third offering, it features sink and can also miss bats. Mueth had worked to clean up his arm stroke, cutting down what had been a long, loopy action in back in the hopes that a shorter arm circle would create a more repeatable delivery. He missed too much time to really get in sync last year and carries a career 7.1 BB/9 rate into the 2026 season. In the rare times he finds the zone, he can be dominant and a full, healthy season is important to get the reps he sorely needs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a huge right-hander from the Illinois high school ranks (not to mention a lower arm slot), Mueth has drawn comps to big leaguer Tanner Houck. Houck went on to college before embarking on his pro career, but the Pirates stepped in with an over-slot bonus in Competitive Balance Round B of the 2023 Draft to lure Mueth away from heading to Mississippi.
