The Pirates often start their high school arms slowly, with time in the complex league in their first full season, and Mueth made a very strong first impression there, pitching his way to full-season Bradenton before the end of the summer. With a low three-quarters arm slot, Mueth’s stuff offers a ton of movement and deception. His fastball sat around 94 mph and was up to 97. It’s a four-seamer, but has two-seam characteristics, often with 8-9 inches of vertical break, along with up to 20 inches of horizontal. HIs mid-80s slider has a chance to be a true out pitch, a gyro-like breaker that misses a ton of bats, and his mid-80s changeup has a chance to be a solid third pitch with sink. There will be work ahead to add more depth on his slider and to make sure the changeup remains a viable option against left-handed hitters, but the biggest step Mueth needs to take in his development to remain a starter is to land his stuff in the strike zone more consistently. All of it moves so much that it will take time for him to harness it, but the Pirates are excited to see how he builds off his strong 2024 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tanner Houck was a tall right-hander with a low slot from an Illinois high school not far out of St. Louis who decided to go on to Missouri for college ball, an eventual first-round selection and the big leagues. Naturally, Mueth drew comparisons to Houck as a 6-foot-6 right-hander from 20 minutes south of where Houck was a prepster. Rather than follow in Houck’s footsteps and head to college, in this case Mississippi, he joined the Pirates organization as the No. 67 overall pick in the 2023 Draft, getting an over-slot bonus of $1.8 million. He focused on training and preparation rather than game action after signing to hopefully set him up for a solid first year of pro ball. Mueth’s unusual low three-quarters slot leads to a ton of deception and horizontal action. His fastball has topped out at 97 mph and sits 92-94 mph, playing up because of its sink and run. His low-80s slider has huge break, a sweeper that can miss bats, though commanding it has been an issue at times. He has a mid-80s changeup that he’ll need to keep working on to separate velocity-wise from his fastball and add more sink to, but it has the chance to be a third at least average offering. There isn’t a ton of effort in Mueth’s unusual delivery and whippy arm action, but like with many pitchers his size, it can be difficult to sync everything up. The metrics on his stuff are very good and he physically has starting pitcher traits if he can improve that third pitch and find the strike zone consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 100 innings that Tredwell pitched in 2025 nearly matched his total from the previous five years. He missed his final two high school seasons after Tommy John surgery in January 2020, then lost much of his 2023 Draft year at UCLA to back issues and the last two months of his 2024 pro debut to a shoulder strain. He finished last season in Double-A, where he logged a 3.18 ERA with 40 strikeouts in 22 2/3 innings. Tredwell's fastball operated at an ordinary 90-93 mph and topped out at 95 last year, but it still played as a solid pitch because it features tremendous carry. His upper-70s curveball and low-80s slider both feature good depth that work well in contrast to the shape of his heater, and they too can be solid offerings at the best. He doesn't trust his mid-80s changeup with fade enough to use it very often. Tredwell's huge 6-foot-8 frame creates natural extension and angle that create difficulty for hitters. While he has good body control and keeps his long limbs in sync, his control has regressed from solid at UCLA to fringy in pro ball. He has a ceiling of a No. 3 or 4 starter, and improving his fastball velocity, changeup and/or his strike-throwing would help his cause.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tredwell has barely pitched the past four years, missing his junior and senior high school seasons following Tommy John surgery in 2020, working 47 innings as a UCLA freshman reliever in 2022 and just 45 1/3 as a starter last spring before a back injury sidelined him. The Astros still liked his combination of size, stuff and pitchability to select the sophomore-eligible in the second round last July and sign him for an over-slot $1,497,500. He posted an 8.10 ERA in the first two months of his pro debut this spring, then got on a roll before getting shut down with a shoulder strain in mid-July. Tredwell's fastball parks at 91-93 mph and tops out at 95 yet plays as a solid offering because his 6-foot-8 frame, high arm slot and flat approach angle create a lot of deception. Both of his breaking balls feature good depth and can miss bats, with his low-80s slider eliciting more chases out of the zone than his upper-70s curveball. He hasn't used his fading mid-80s changeup much, so it's not as effective as the rest of his arsenal. His size lends itself to unusual extension, enabling his pitches to get on hitters quickly, and Tredwell also has exceptional body control for such a tall pitcher. He keeps his long limbs in sync, repeats his delivery and pounds the strike zone, logging a 113/18 K/BB ratio in college. He has a high floor as a potential No. 4 starter if he can remain healthy, and Houston's knack for helping pitchers bolster their stuff could raise his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez was far from a big name on the international stage when he signed with the Cardinals as a 19-year-old in January 2016, but he commanded attention after hitting .322/.400/.580 with seven homers over 40 games in the Dominican Summer League in his first Minor League season. He climbed steadily through the system and earned a Florida State League midseason All-Star spot in 2019 before jumping to Double-A Springfield. He was set to return to that level in 2021, only to break his hamate bone playing winter ball back home in the Dominican Republic. Following February surgery, he played briefly for Springfield in May, suffered a setback and came back for good in late July. The right-handed slugger hit just .196/.252/.299 with three homers over 29 games in Double-A last season, numbers that were clearly affected by the hamate injury, which can typically sap players of their power in the early stages of recovery. Still, Rodriguez has a history of being aggressive at the plate, and while his bat-to-ball skills keep the strikeout rates from being high, that aggression also keeps him from developing much power. It’s an all-defensive-type profile anyway. Rodriguez’s arm has always been effective at limiting the running game, and even with the hand issues, he threw out 9 of 14 (64 percent) of attempted basestealers with Springfield last season. He’s a quality blocker and receiver out of his 6-foot, 245-pound frame, and it’s clear Cardinals pitchers enjoy working with him behind the plate. It’s a clear glove-first backup profile, and after Rodriguez was passed over twice for a 40-man spot when Rule 5-eligible, a healthy 2022 could get him closer to achieving that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in January 2016 as a 19-year-old, Rodriguez was initially expected to be an organizational roster-filler but has surpassed expectations thanks in large part to his offensive development. He hit .322 with seven homers over 40 games in the Dominican Summer League in his professional debut and has continued his upward trajectory in the Cardinals’ system, including midseason All-Star honors in the Florida State League in 2019. Rodriguez suffered a broken hamate bone after being hit by a pitch in winter ball. He underwent surgery in February and after getting off to a late start in his 2021 campaign, he found himself on the injured list once again, though he returned in early August. Rodriguez’s defensive skillset is what drew the Cardinals to him initially. The backstop has a strong, accurate arm and has thrown out 69% of attempted basestealers over the first four years of his professional career. Offensively, Rodriguez has an overly aggressive approach, but flashes some power -- he hit a combined 16 homers in 2017 and ’18 -- and has made noticeable strides since signing. There’s certainly value to having a defensive-minded catcher like Rodriguez in a system keen on developing pitching prospects. If he continues to improve his overall game and reaches the Majors, it’s likely he’ll do so in a reserve role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lesko underwent Tommy John surgery in April 2022, a tough break for someone who had earned a ton of buzz after becoming the first-ever player to be named the Gatorade National Baseball Player of the Year as a junior the year before. Still, the Padres believed in the hype enough to select him 15th overall and sign him for $3.9 million. Lesko worked his way back from surgery and debuted in June 2023, flashing signs of dominance and reaching High-A despite posting a 5.45 ERA over 33 innings. He struggled even more last season, walking 19.2% of the batters he faced and hitting 14 more in 84 innings. The Rays saw an opportunity to buy low and landed him as part of their return for reliever Jason Adam. Lesko’s apparent loss of control since returning from surgery is an obvious issue. His stuff isn’t. He has an elite changeup, which clocked in around 79 mph last year with incredible movement off his fastball. It’s a devastating swing-and-miss pitch, and he showed the ability to land it for strikes despite his otherwise problematic control. He throws a tighter-spinning slider that shows some promise as well as a curveball. His fastball has the velocity and movement profile to be effective, too, sitting in the mid-90s and touching 97 mph. Joining the Rays didn’t immediately solve his issues with strikes, as he walked 31% of the batters he faced with Bowling Green. The Rays have been evaluating Lesko since his Draft year, though, and learned a lot from a pitching coordinator in their system who came over from the Padres. The hope is that he can shake off the post-TJ rust and get back to Top 100 form as a potential mid-rotation starter. If not, he’s bound for the bullpen, where perhaps he can command his fastball enough to let his changeup play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 70 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 Lesko entered his senior season at Buford (Ga.) High School in 2022 with plenty of hype after becoming the first-ever junior Gatorade National Baseball Player of the Year the prior spring. He was delivering on his promise, only to undergo Tommy John surgery in late April. The Padres still selected the right-hander 15th overall and signed him for just under slot at $3.9 million. Lesko made his pro debut in June 2023 – nearly 14 months after surgery – and despite a 5.45 ERA, showed his high potential again with 52 strikeouts over 33 innings across three levels, ending the season at High-A Fort Wayne. He returned to High-A for 2024 but never dominated as he was capable of doing, and the Padres traded him to the Rays at the Trade Deadline as part of a three-player package for reliever Jason Adam. Lesko sits 92-96 mph with his fastball, touching 98, and makes the offering play even better with impressive carry up in the zone. That’s not even his best pitch. That remains his low-80s changeup with tremendous separation off the heater and movement that gets some silly swings, earning it consistent plus-plus grades. (Lefties hit just .186 with a 38.8 percent K rate off Lesko in 2023 as a result.) His mid-70s curveball shows with 12-to-6 movement and promising spin rates but is still developing consistency. A mid-80s slider might end up becoming the better of his two breaking pitches as he gets to work with the Rays pitching group. The 6-foot-2 right-hander experienced control problems in his first year back from surgery in 2023, and those issues have continued into this summer. That created an opportunity for Tampa Bay to buy low, with the Rays hoping to harness his promising stuff and get Lesko back to filling the zone with more regularity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lesko was the first junior to win the Gatorade National Baseball Player of the Year award in 2021 after posting a 0.35 ERA with 112 strikeouts in 60 innings at Buford (Ga.) High School, the alma mater of Brandon Marsh and Joey Bart. Lesko continued to shove the following spring as a senior, heightening the belief that he could be the top arm drafted in the Class of 2022, but Tommy John surgery in late April made him a question mark. He still ended up being the first prep pitcher taken when San Diego selected him 15th overall and signed him for just under slot at $3.9 million. Before the elbow procedure, the 6-foot-2 righty was already throwing 92-95 mph, touching 97, with a fastball that carried up in the zone, and as he builds back up, there’s the chance he adds even more velo with age and physical maturity. His low-80s changeup was arguably the best of the Draft and will be one of the best in the San Diego system once he throws it again, on account of its separation and two-plane movement that can make hitters look downright silly. His upper-70s curveball will need work to reach consistency, but its high spin rates carry promise. Lesko will have to show he can pitch with the same strong command as he continues to build back innings. That’s easier than it once was for Tommy John pitchers, but still no small task. The good news is he’s been getting innings at both the Arizona Complex and California Leagues and could be primed for a bigger takeoff in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After drafting Vrieling in 2022's third round out of Gonzaga, the Yankees had him focus on gaining muscle, and he added 20 pounds in advance of his planned pro debut in 2023. He missed all of that season with a stress fracture in his pitching elbow, however, before returning to the mound in the Arizona Fall League. He finally broke into the Minors last season at Double-A, leading the Eastern League in wins (13) while ranking second in innings (147 1/3) and sixth in strikeouts (132). Though Vrieling's best attribute is his feel for spin and his 78-82 mph curveball and mid-80s slider/cutter both can grade as plus pitches at their best, they were merely average in Double-A. He gets some carry on his low-90s fastball that maxes out at 96 mph, but it can straighten out at times. His upper-80s changeup is too firm, and he has trouble landing it in the zone despite its modest movement. A reliever for the first two years of his college career, Vrieling held up under a full starter's workload last summer and threw more consistent strikes than ever before. He's doing a better job of repeating his three-quarters arm slot as a pro. He looked like a potential No. 3 starter in the first part of his junior season at Gonzaga, but he'll have no more than a back-of-the-rotation ceiling unless he can develop a better-than-average offering.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzaga's 2022 weekend rotation produced three early picks in that year's Draft, with Hughes going 10th overall to the Rockies and Vrieling (Yankees) and William Kempner (Giants) factoring in the third round. New York had Vrieling focus on adding strength after signing and he gained 20 pounds in advance of his planned 2023 pro debut. He wound up missing all of last season after coming down with a stress fracture in his pitching elbow, though he did return to work 10 2/3 innings in the Arizona Fall League. Vrieling has good feel for spin, with both his 78-82 mph curveball and mid-80s slider/cutter grading as plus pitches at their best, though they've played as more average in Double-A this season. He fell in love with his breaking pitches too much while transitioning from the bullpen to the rotation at Gonzaga in 2022, costing him run and sink on a low-90s fastball that tops out at 96. He's vulnerable without his best life on his heater but has recaptured it since turning pro. Vrieling has a lot to prove to remain a starter, beginning with durability. He needs to improve an upper-80s changeup that's much too firm, as well as his fastball command and overall control. If that doesn't work out, his breaking balls could make him a useful multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: All three members of Gonzaga's 2022 weekend rotation went in the first three rounds of the Draft, with the Rockies taking Gabriel Hughes 10th overall before Vrieling (Yankees) and William Kempner (Giants) became third-rounders. Vrieling spent his first two years with the Bulldogs as a reliever before overpowering hitters as a starter early last spring, then tailed off in the second half of the college season when he got away from using his fastball. New York had him focus on building strength after signing and he added 20 pounds before making his pro debut in 2023. Vrieling has high spin rates on his low-80s downer curveball, his best chase pitch, and his tight mid-80s slider, his top offering in terms of getting swings and misses. Both can be plus offerings at their best and he can turn his slider into a harder cutter with even more upside. When he fell in love with his breaking pitches last spring, he lost some of the sink and run on a fastball that parks at 90-93 mph and peaks at 96, and it got hit. To survive as a starter in pro ball, Vrieling will need to find some more velocity or life for his heater, and his strength gains should help. He also needs to improve and develop more trust in his changeup, which is too firm in the upper-80s, and throw more strikes. If he returns to the bullpen, his breaking stuff could make him a multi-inning weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending two years at Sacramento City Junior College, Costeiu transferred to Arkansas and showed off the ability to miss bats in a relief role in 2021. The Angels took him that summer in the seventh round and decided to stretch him out as a starter. There were some positive early returns with High-A Tri-City, but he blew out in July and needed Tommy John surgery. He missed all of the 2023 season and returned to amass 74 1/3 innings in a solid post-surgery return. One of the reasons why the Angels thought he had a chance start despite being a six-footer is because he does have a real four-pitch mix, even if he doesn’t have one offering that jumps off the page. His low-90s fastball can be effective because of good spin rates and carry up in the zone. His changeup might be his best pitch, a low-80s cambio that can get swing-and-miss and groundball outs. His upper-70s curve was his go-to when he started his career, and he’s since added a distinct slider. Costeiu was an outstanding strike-thrower in 2022 before he got hurt and he wasn’t as sharp upon his return in 2024. If this command returns, he could have a chance to start, though the size and the elbow history will have some thinking a move to the bullpen is in the offing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Costeiu’s work in relief at Arkansas in 2021 -- transferring there after two years at Sacramento City JC -- helped him land in the seventh round of the Angels’ all-pitching Draft. After a solid debut missing a ton of bats out of the bullpen after signing, he was given the chance to start with High-A Tri-City in his first full season, but his early success was cut short by an elbow injury in July that required Tommy John surgery, knocking him out for all of the 2023 season. Though he’s a bit undersized, the 6-foot right-hander’s combination of stuff and feel for the strike zone has some evaluators thinking he has the chance to start. When he was stretched out, he was throwing his fastball in the 92-94 mph range, with good life and carry up in the zone thanks to high spin rates. His low-80s changeup flashes plus, a pitch that misses bats and gets weak contact. He entered pro ball with a big upper-70s curve, but he had started working on a slider that might be a better option long-term. In his brief time starting, Costeiu did a very nice job of throwing his arsenal for strikes, leading to an impressive 4.26 K/BB ratio, which makes it tempting to exhaust the starting pitcher possibilities. But between his size and the elbow surgery, there are a lot of reliever profile signs here, and his stuff would tick up in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at Sacramento City Junior College, Costeiu moved on to the University of Arkansas and missed a ton of bats pitching out of the Razorbacks bullpen. His arm strength was enough to land him in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft with the Angels. He struck out close to 16 per nine innings in his pro debut that summer, then got the chance to start with a move to High-A for his first full season. He pitched effectively, though his season ended prematurely in July due to an elbow issue and he didn’t throw a pitch in 2023 because of the injury. As a starter, Costeiu’s stuff did back up a bit. His fastball was more in the 92-94 mph range with Tri-City in 2022. There could be more consistent velocity for him to rediscover, especially if he eventually ends up with shorter stints again. The fastball plays up because of its high spin and carry up in the zone. His low-80s changeup can miss bats and get weak contact on the ground, and he brought an upper-70s big curve with him from college. He’s also worked on adding a slider this offseason. Because of the chance to have a complete repertoire and the fact he’s generally around the zone, Costeiu could keep getting the opportunity to start. But the 6-footer does have more of a reliever profile, where the stuff would likely tick back up once he returns to full strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Echavarria dominated his senior season at Millburn (N.J.) HS by going 8-1 with a 0.28 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 50 innings as a senior. That, along with a strong showing on the showcase circuit, led to the A’s selecting him in the third round (72nd pick) of the 2023 Draft, swaying him away from a commitment to the University of Florida by signing him for first-round money at $3 million. After spending his first professional season with Single-A Stockton, he began the 2025 campaign at High-A Lansing and spent the entirety of his year there. Echavarria’s stuff is tantalizing. His fastball can touch 99 mph, while his mid-80s slider has the makings of a plus pitch. His upper-80s changeup has shown promise as a third offering but remains inconsistent. This past season, he experimented with a low-80s curveball, but it's largely a work in progress. Overall command of his pitches is still an issue at times, which often leads to him running his pitch count up early in his outings. Consistency is something Echavarria is still working to find, which is not uncommon for a high school arm at this point in his career. When he’s on, he’s really good; when he’s off, he really struggles. The A’s worked with him over the second half of ‘25 on relying more on his scouting reports instead of overthinking things by trying to dissect weaknesses of hitters. The arm talent is there, and the club hopes to see some more polish as he continues to rack up more innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout in the New Jersey high school ranks, Echavarria put himself on the Draft radar by impressing on the showcase circuit and dominating his senior season at Millburn High School by going 8-1 with a 0.28 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 50 innings. Selecting him in the third round (72nd pick) of the 2023 Draft, the A’s were able to snag him away from his commitment to the University of Florida with first-round money at $3 million. Getting his pro career underway last season at Single-A Stockton as an 18-year-old, he went through some ups and downs and posted a 6.55 ERA in 19 starts with 59 strikeouts and 36 walks over 57 2/3 innings. The A’s believe Echavarria’s stuff played better than the overall numbers might suggest. His fastball reached 98 mph and sat 95-96 with good ride up in the zone. The issue was struggling to command his arsenal when he would fall behind in counts. His mid-80s slider flashes plus, and his upper-80s changeup continues to improve. He also throws a two-seamer in the 92-93 mph range. He clearly dealt with some control issues, but the A’s are not at all sounding the alarm, instead patiently working with the teenager on adjustments. Echavarria profiles as a starter for the long-term with his 6-foot-1 frame and sound delivery. Previously having shown an ability to consistently throw all of his offerings for strikes prior to the Draft, he will continue to work to rediscover that control in his second season of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Echavarria boosted his Draft stock on the strength of his performances on the showcase circuit and an uptick in velocity that helped him dominate his senior season by going 8-1 with a 0.28 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 50 innings. Though he was committed to the University of Florida, the A’s managed to sway him with first-round money ($3 million) as a third-round selection (72nd pick) in the 2023 Draft. The A’s liked what they saw in the handful of innings he pitched in the instructional league, and there is a lot of anticipation within the organization about watching his first season of pro ball unfold. Echavarria brings a four-pitch mix that features a fastball that consistently hits 96 mph and has reached up to 98, carrying ride up in the zone that lends to a good amount of swing-and-miss. Other pitches in the arsenal include a sweeping slider, curveball and low-80s changeup. He also throws a 92-93 mph two-seamer down in the zone, which should develop more consistent velocity as he grows into his 6-foot-1 frame. For a prep arm in a cold-weather state, Echavarria shows off very good pitchability with an ability to consistently throw all his offerings for strikes. Continuing the recent run of early-round Draft picks from the New Jersey high school ranks, headlined by first-rounders Anthony Volpe in 2019 and Chase Petty in 2021, he enters his first full year as a pro with high expectations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Joseph received the fourth-highest bonus of anyone in the 2024 international signing class, getting $3.3 million from the Mariners in January of that year as one of the perceived best shortstops in the entire crop. He had grown since first being scouted years prior, sprouting up to 6-foot-2 and 185 pounds, but he wasn’t able to use his size or tools with any consistency during a rough professional debut in the Dominican Summer League, when he hit just .133 with a 29.1 percent strikeout rate. The Mariners would like to give Joseph a mulligan and hope he can hit the reset button in 2025, but there could be a long way to go for the right-handed-hitting infielder to figure things out. There were always some concerns for his pure hit tool, but the raw power was significant and something to work on tapping into. But Joseph didn’t show much feel for contact during his debut, and even when he did, he wasn’t squaring up the ball with much impact. Additionally, it appears like Joseph might outgrow shortstop. He’s slowed down after growing, and as he fills out, it seems more likely that he won’t have the quickness to stay at the premium position. If he can hit the reset button and start tapping into that power the Mariners liked, perhaps he can eventually profile as a third baseman, though there’s a lot of work to be done.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners started following Joseph three years ago, when he was just 5-foot-10. By the time they brought him in during the 2024 international signing period for $3 million, he had grown to 6-foot-2 and 185 pounds. Given that young frame, most weren’t sure if he’d profile as an outfielder or infielder, with some thinking he had a similar build to Twins center fielder Byron Buxton. Joseph now exhibits much more body control, with better hands at shortstop. It's more of a power-hitting offensive profile than before, and overall, he’s a physical athlete who projects to play a position up the middle. And just as importantly, he can really control the zone with a simple swing, direct mechanics and projectable power. He’s lost some of the top-end wheels through his growth spurt but still is touted with at least above-average speed, with the ability to be a threat on the basepaths. Now for the No. 7 prospect from his international class will come the opportunity to play in the Dominican Summer League, where he’ll face stiffer competition and look to incorporate some of the work he’s done with respected trainer Cristian Batista, a member of MLB’s Trainer Partnership Program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feliz was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 24 international prospect in the 2024 class and signed with the Nationals for $1.8 million that January. Only outfielder Victor Hurtado ($2.7 million) signed for more. Feliz was a Dominican Summer League mid-season All-Star in his first taste of the pros after hitting .310/.381/.468 with four homers and 27 steals in 49 games and handled himself decently well with his move stateside for his age-18 season in 2025. The infielder produced a .264/.366/.358 line in 53 games in the Florida Complex League and produced a 96 wRC+ with Single-A Fredericksburg following a late July promotion. It was notable that Feliz was one of only 30 age-18 prospects to get more than 100 plate appearances in Single-A last season and the only Washington player to meet that criteria. Already standing at 6-foot-3, there’s hope that he can add some strength to that frame and get to at least average power, but to do that, he’ll have to lift the ball at a much better rate. He doesn’t chase pitches outside the zone much for his age, but when he does, it’s often with an empty swing, especially against soft stuff. Starting with his hands held above his head, he can yank over breaking pitches beyond the outer third of the plate right now, but it’s still plenty early in his development cycle. Feliz will flash decent home-to-first times when he’s really pushing it out of the box, but many expect him to land at fringy speed at best by the time he fills out. He isn’t the twitchiest defender, though Nats officials have praised him for his hands on the dirt and arm strength. With Eli Willits likely in his path, Feliz remains a priority infielder, albeit one likely to move to third long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals went for two of MLB Pipeline’s Top 25 international prospects in the 2024 signing class, adding Dominican outfielder Victor Hurtado for $2.8 million and Feliz for $1.8 million out of the same country. The young shortstop was the better performer out of the gate in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .310/.381/.468 with four homers and 27 steals in 49 games. He led qualified DSL Nats in average, slugging, isolated slugging (.158), hits (53) and doubles (nines) and tied for the lead in homers on his way to mid-season All-Star honors. At 6-foot-3 already so early in his development cycle, Feliz drew excitement for his projectable power potential when signing and already put it to use in the DSL, specifically to the pullside. The exit velocities should only get louder from here, and if he can use added strength to elevate more on contact, there’s even the possibility for above-average pop here in time. Concerns about the length of Feliz’s swing were quieted some with good contact rates, but he’ll face much tougher tests against stateside pitching. Feliz ran wild in the DSL but is expected to have below-average speed by the time he reaches the Majors. The Nationals have stuck to their word about intending to play him at shortstop as much as possible, but the thought that he might have to move over to third base eventually remains. His arm strength will fit there. But everything is trending well enough offensively that Feliz moved to Single-A Fredericksburg for a late-season came at the end of his age-18 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Starting with a $5,284,400 signing pool, the Nationals came away with two of MLB Pipeline’s Top 25 international prospects in the 2024 class. Dominican outfielder Victor Hurtado (No. 20) was the headliner with a $2.8 million bonus, but not far behind him was Dominican infielder Feliz (No. 23) with a $1.8 million deal of his own. Both are expected to begin their careers in the Dominican Summer League. Standing in already at 6-foot-3 at just 17 years old, Feliz stood out to Nationals evaluators for his projectable size and strength. His promising pullside power should play pretty quickly when he first sees pro pitching. That right-handed swing can get a bit long, so tightening that up might be one of the early focuses for Washington’s hitting instructors, but the pop alone gives them plenty of positives to work with. The Nats say they believe Feliz can make impressive defensive plays up the middle at for his size, and given that we live in the age of the big shortstop, it’s possible he could stick there in time. It does seem more likely, however, that he’ll eventually have to move to third base, where he’s a more stereotypical fit. His arm strength -- which also drew praise as an amateur -- should help with that transition if and when it comes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez was sought after when he defected from Cuba toward the end of the 2023 international signing period, but not every club interested had squirreled away as much money for these types of situations as the Orioles, who signed him for $450,000 that December. Sanchez then enjoyed a standout debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2024 and had an excellent first full pro season in 2025, reaching Class-A Delmarva by the end of the year and homering twice in his first four games there. Though his unique situation made him old for the lower levels, he’ll be 20 for the entire 2026 season. The bat is the carrying tool for Sanchez, a left-handed-hitting outfielder with tremendous raw pop. He has natural loft to his swing and a good feel for the strike zone for his age, which has enabled the power to show up early -- he’s collected 47 extra-base hits and 13 homers in his first 96 professional games. When Sanchez connects, he hits the ball hard and rarely puts it on the ground. But there is real swing-and-miss alongside the exit velocity and on-base ability, with Sanchez running a 25 percent career strikeout rate in the low Minors. Sanchez’s slugging profile and fringe-average speed make him best suited for a corner outfield spot, with left field looking more likely given his average arm. He needs to refine his approach and prove he can hit advanced pitching as he climbs the system, but there is no reason he can’t develop into a middle-of-the-order run producer even if he’s never more than an average hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez defected from Cuba and wasn’t eligible to sign until late in the 2023 international signing period, and the Orioles had enough pool money laying around to ink him for $450,000 in December of that year. Sanchez then had a standout debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2024, pairing 21 extra-base hits with a 1.037 OPS, though his unique situation did make him old for the circuit and his season was cut short due to an injury. A left-handed-hitting outfielder, Sanchez has tremendous raw power that he’s already showing an ability to tap into with both extra-base and over-the-fence authority, and because of the loft to his swing, he produced one of the lower ground-ball rates in the Orioles' system. The hit tool is less polished but he shows some strike zone recognition and ability to work counts, and it wouldn’t be surprising if he developed into an average hitter with above-average power. The bat is the carrying tool as Sanchez is just a fringe-average runner. Sanchez saw time at all three outfield positions during his debut, but his bat-first profile is best suited for a corner, possibly left field because the arm is just average. Based on his age and abilities, Sanchez is like an everyday corner outfielder starter set: he’ll need to refine his approach at the plate and show he can hit more advanced pitching, but his precocious ability to barrel pitches and hit the ball hard give him the ceiling of a middle-of-the-order run-producer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Soto signed with the Angels for $250,000 in January 2023, he was still only 16 and didn’t celebrate his 17th birthday until he was already into his Dominican Summer League debut. He ended up spending two years in the DSL, adding strength and stuff so that he’d be ready to come stateside in 2025. His U.S. debut was a mixed bag of big stuff, missed bats and iffy command, though he had more success in six outings with Single-A Inland Empire than he did in the Arizona Complex League. As he’s filled out his 6-foot-2 frame, Soto has added velocity to his fastball, beginning his career in the upper 80s and now sitting in the low 90s and touching 97 mph. The four-seamer plays up because he gets really good extension and there could be more consistent velo to come. Beyond the heater, things are a bit more inconsistent. His low-80s changeup does miss bats and could be a solid offspeed offering but his upper-70s curve wasn’t as effective in 2025, and he could be a candidate to add a slider. At times, Soto has shown enough feel for the strike zone where it’s possible to project him as a starter, but that too was inconsistent last year. If he can refine his command and find a better breaking ball, he still could profile in a rotation, with plenty of time for him to figure it out in his age-19 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 The Angels gave out five six-figure bonuses to hitters at the top of their list at the start of the 2023 international signing period before they got to their first pitcher. Soto received $250,000 to be that arm and he was still only 16 when he made his professional debut in the Dominican Summer League. While his surface numbers looked good (like his 1.64 ERA), his youth and lack of velocity led to the Angels erring on the side of caution and sending him back to the DSL, where added strength and stuff led to even better results in 2024. After packing some weight onto his 6-foot-2 frame, Soto's velocity jumped from sitting 86-89 mph and touching 92 to more in the 92-94 mph range and topping out at 97. At first it seemed like his 82-85 mph changeup was his best secondary offering, but more power behind his curve -- now up to 77-80 mph from the low 70s in 2023 -- might have caught it up to the cambio. Both have chances to be solid-to-average pitches for the right-hander. In addition to missing a fair amount of bats overall, Soto improved his feel for the strike zone, cut his walk rate down considerably in 2024 and is showing some feel for pitch usage. All of this has added excitement over what he might do for an encore as he pitches in the United States for the first time this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Genovés family in Venezuela produced a pair of brothers who became professional catchers in Ernesto, who spent six years in the Astros system before getting released in 2014, and Ricardo, who signed for $500,000 in 2015. The latter posted the best offensive numbers of his career last year, though his line dipped from .338/.441/.552 in Low-A to .217/.294/.364 in High-A. Though the Giants didn't reserve him on their 40-man roster last November, he has a path to the big leagues as a backup. Known more for his defense, Genovés got an early taste of handling pro-caliber pitching when he caught current Cubs prospect Anderson Espinoza when both were amateurs in Venezuela. He moves well behind the plate despite well-below-average speed, but he needs to clean up his receiving after committing 26 passed balls in 91 games last season. He has plus arm strength and makes accurate throws. Genovés focused on making contact and pulling the ball early in his career before adding some loft to his right-handed stroke while driving the ball from gap to gap in 2019. Once he reached High-A last year, he got overly aggressive and produced too many strikeouts and weak grounders. His strength stands out more than his bat speed, but if he can regain his past plate discipline, he could hit for a decent average with 15 homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Genoves family in Venezuela sent two catchers into pro ball in older brother Ernesto, who spent six years in the Astros system, and younger brother Ricardo, who signed for $500,000 in 2015. Initially known more for his defense, Ricardo homered four times in 148 games and produced a .664 OPS in his first three pro seasons before going deep nine times in 51 games with an .804 OPS while reaching low Class A in 2019. His 2020 development was limited to instructional league. Catching for Cubs pitching prospect Anderson Espinoza as an amateur helped prepare Genoves for handling quality stuff as a pro. He moves well behind the plate and is becoming a solid receiver, albeit in need of more consistency. He has a strong and accurate arm that helped him erase 40 percent of basestealers in 2019. Early in his career, Genoves had a contact-oriented, pull-happy approach that produced a lot of weak groundouts to the left side. He has added some loft to his right-handed stroke and now drives the ball more regularly to all fields, showing 15-20 homer potential. He's a decent hitter who could use more plate discipline but should produce offense to serve as a useful big league backup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming out of Weatherford High School in Texas – the alma mater of Zack Britton – Kemp went to the Padres in the eighth round of the 2023 Draft and signed away from an Oklahoma commitment with a $625,000 bonus. He started to experience shoulder issues shortly after signing and needed surgery to address a labrum tear in the spring of what should have been his first full season. His pro debut finally came in May 2025 in the Arizona Complex League, followed by a move to Single-A Lake Elsinore. He posted a 5.56 ERA with 64 strikeouts in 77 2/3 innings between the two spots and added six brief appearances in the Arizona Fall League. By the time he reached the desert, the 6-foot-6 right-hander’s story was no longer just about projection but also about present stuff. His velocity slowly ticked up throughout his age-20 season, and in the Fall League, his fastball sat 96-98 mph, topping out at 99.5, from his short arm action. The movement was more pedestrian, as was the extension, but the additional heat was certainly necessary to get it to play better. He throws both a four-seam and two-seam. An upper-80s bullet slider acts as his breaking ball with tight break, and his 88-91 mph changeup shows a good amount of armside run, sometimes so much Kemp can’t command it in the zone. For all the promise in his individual pitches, Kemp didn’t miss bats in standout ways in any of his stops in 2025, and he still must prove he can maintain the late velocity increase over a longer period. But with another year removed from the shoulder issues, he could be in for a much-awaited breakout when he’s the age of most college juniors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from Weatherford (Texas) HS – the same school that produced Zack Britton, Beau Burrows and no-hitter legend Hippo Vaughn – Kemp put himself on the radar the fall before his senior year when he started touching 94 mph at the Texas State Games and the World Wood Bat Association World Championship. He maintained that momentum into the spring and was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 209 Draft prospect in 2023. The Oklahoma commit fell to the eighth round, but the Padres signed him for $625,000, giving him their second-highest bonus of the class to talk him away from college ball. Kemp was back to the 89-92 mph range for the most part, still touching 94, in his final spring as an amateur, but he started flashing a little more velo under the Padres’ watch, though he didn’t pitch in an official game for the organization. His low-80s slider was also improving, but because of a short arm action, some scouts doubt it would be better than average in the pros. A mid-80s changeup also showed too much firmness, though it’ll occasionally fade nicely giving hope it too could be a decent third option. Kemp stands out most for his size at 6-foot-6, and there’s still projection remaining, so this might be only the start of his velo gains. The stronger he gets, the more likely he is to repeat his delivery and get strikes too, giving him breakout potential entering his first full season. Because Kemp signed, the Padres can oversee his development how they see fit, but shoulder issues have kept him from getting going in earnest in what should have been his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While it’s too early for the 2018-19 international signing class to have made a big league impact in Colorado, the Rockies' efforts during that period are showing up on the prospect landscape. Warming Bernabel is in the organization’s top 10 and Juan Brito was dealt to bring in Nolan Jones. Guerrero, who signed for $650,000 in July of 2018, is perhaps a step behind Bernabel, but has pretty much hit everywhere he’s been, from his Dominican Summer League debut in 2019 to his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2021 and his step up to full-season ball in 2022. Since signing, Guerrero has displayed a knack for finding the barrel. It’s kind of a controlled aggression at the plate as he’s not one to see a ton of pitches, but he rarely strikes out, with a 15.6 percent K rate heading into the 2023 season. He’s slight and wiry, but he started tapping into some raw power more consistently in 2022, though it still remains to be seen how much strength he can add to maintain that extra-base authority. Though he’s just an average runner, Guerrero is an aggressive baserunner and can steal a base. He’s played all three outfield positions since moving from the infield in 2021, but is mostly likely a corner guy long term and his defense has improved markedly. That puts more pressure on his bat, but the Rockies like his confidence and his response to things like late-game pressure to make them a bit more bullish about his offensive upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies handed out nine bonuses of six figures or higher during the 2018-19 international signing period. Guerrero was closer to the top of the list when he received $650,000 to sign out of the Dominican Republic at the start of the period. Since then, he’s done nothing but hit, with a .319 average in the Dominican Summer League for his pro debut in 2019 and then a .318 average in his United States debut in 2021 in the Arizona Complex League. Guerrero has already shown a very good feel at the plate and even though it’s more of a “see the ball, hit the ball” approach, he’s limited his strikeouts and even drawn some walks. How much he can add muscle to his ultra-lean frame will help determine how much impact he has at the plate, with the Rockies expressing confidence he’s going to grow into more extra-base thump. Signed as a shortstop, Guerrero mostly played third during his DSL debut and shifted to the outfield in 2021 where he used his athleticism more than he exhbited any idea of how to actually play the position. He’s an aggressive baserunner who plays with super-high energy but has average speed, so a corner spot makes the most sense. He might just be scratching the surface, with the ceiling to eventually grow into a big league regular with an exceptional bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Padres out of the Dominican Republic for $300,000 in 2018, Angeles jumped out to a promising start in his pro career by hitting .301/.359/.376 and striking out just 19 times in 44 games the next year in the Dominican Summer League. A continued breakout in 2021 in which he hit a combined .329/.392/.445 between Low-A and High-A made him an attractive prospect for the A’s, who acquired him last March along with Adrián Martínez as part of the Sean Manaea deal. Playing his first season with Oakland at High-A Lansing as a 20-year-old, he hit .278/.316/.353 in 97 games. Angeles is a strong, physical player despite what his 5-foot-11, 175-pound frame might suggest. While there’s not a ton of power to his game, the ball really comes off his bat hard and he uses a quick swing to hit high quality line drives. He has continued to post low strikeout totals, demonstrating good bat-to-ball skills throughout his Minor League career. Angeles can utilize his above-average speed to steal bases. He still plays shortstop and second base, though he does get lackadaisical defensively at times. With an overall talent the A’s remain high on, he’ll get a chance to continue progressing through the system, with second likely his future full-time role should he settle into one spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres, as a penalty for overspending in the 2016-17 international signing period, were unable to sign anyone for more than $300,000 in 2018, but that didn’t stop the organization from inking Angeles. Signed for the full $300,000, the infielder has looked like a bargain and is off to a fast start in his pro career. He hit .301/.359/.376 with only 19 strikeouts in 44 games in the Dominican Summer League during his 2019 pro debut, then raked over 105 games in 2021, hitting .329/.392/.445 over two levels of Class-A ball. The contact skills caught the eyes of the A’s, who acquired him along with Adrian Martinez in the April trade that sent Sean Manaea to San Diego. Listed at 5-foot-11 and 175 pounds, Angeles doesn’t hit for a ton of power, but puts that ball in play with strong bat to ball skills and an aggressive approach. The right-handed hitter hit .354 against right-handers in 2021, suggesting he’ll be tough to match up against as he continues to climb the ranks. There’s some uppercut in Angeles’ quick swing, but that translates more to doubles and triples as he uses his above-average speed to take the extra base. He also knows how to steal a bag when the opportunity presents itself, swiping 36 over his first 149 professional games. While Angeles is most comfortable at shortstop, the position he played prior to signing, it’s likely he’ll wind up at second base. He’s played second, third and shortstop early in his career and that versatility may help expedite his path to the big leagues -- especially if he keeps hitting at his current pace. Angeles has quick feet, solid hands and the arm strength to play anywhere on the infield, though his accuracy needs to improve. Of course, if he continues to rake, the A’s will find a spot for him to play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Liranzo trained with Fernando Tatis Jr. before signing with the Orioles for $500,000 as part of their international class, and raised his stock enough during his first year in the system to the point where he was targeted by clubs in trades the following winter. A solid showing in his pro debut as one of the youngest players in the Dominican Summer League gave him helium heading into 2024, but he lost most of the year to a knee injury. The younger brother of Tigers prospect Thayron Liranzo, Joshua’s tenacious style of play earned him a killer early-career nickname: “Animalito” (“Little Animal”). The bat is Liranzo’s loudest tool. He turned heads after signing by showing the potential for plus raw power, producing high exit velocities and barreling balls consistently for a young player. His bat speed and strength hint at the potential for plus raw power, and he’s drawn comps to Teoscar Hernández at the same age, only with better bat-to-ball and pitch-recognition skills. That package gives Liranzo a chance to develop into an average hitter with more reps and polish. His bat will carry him further than his legs, as Liranzo was a below-average runner before the knee issue. Liranzo signed as a shortstop, outgrew the position quickly and settled at third, where he has adequate arm strength to project as an average defender, assuming the knee problem doesn’t hinder his mobility. He’s still young and inexperienced, but with enough seasoning, Liranzo could still develop into an impact run-producer at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Nicknamed “Animalito” (“Little Animal”) for his tenacious style of play, Liranzo is the younger brother of Dodgers prospect Thayron Liranzo as well as the offseason roommate and training partner of Padres star Fernando Tatis Jr. He wasn’t the headliner of the Orioles’ 2023 international class, but Liranzo showed enough potential to command a $500,000 bonus and raised his stock so much during his first year in the system that he was targeted by clubs for trades this winter. Liranzo turned heads in his debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he finished with a .393 on-base percentage as a 16-year-old and one of the youngest players on the circuit. The debut reminded some observers of fellow Dominican Republic native Samuel Basallo, who enjoyed similar success in the DSL a few years prior before rocketing up prospect lists, giving Liranzo helium heading into what should be his stateside debut in 2024. The most exciting thing about Liranzo is the way the ball leaves his bat. He hits it harder than most players his age, using above-average bat speed to produce excellent exit velocities while driving the ball consistently. He’s already grown about 3 inches and gotten considerably stronger since signing, now standing 6-foot-3 and using his strength to leverage his right-handed swing. His precocious power draws comparisons to Teoscar Hernández at that age, but Liranzo’s approach and hand-eye coordination are more advanced than Hernández’s were then. Liranzo is not a burner with below-average speed. The converted shortstop has already outgrown the position and profiles better at third base, with the arm strength, footwork and reaction time to succeed at the hot corner. He projects as an average defender there but his ceiling is of a bat-first player who can grow into a middle-of-the-order run producer at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez’s signing, initially scheduled to take place in the 2018-19 international window, had to wait until June 2020 due to the pandemic and an age discrepancy. After joining the Cardinals for $525,000, he moved to Single-A Palm Beach in 2021 and couldn’t break past the Florida State League until '23 when he was promoted to High-A Peoria in late June after showing significant control improvements. Nunez finished with a 3.39 ERA, 65 strikeouts and 30 walks in 63 2/3 innings between the two stops and got in eight more appearances in the Arizona Fall League where he held his own. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has always been on the St. Louis radar because of his velocity. Despite leaving the club midseason, he threw 24 of the 30 hardest pitches for Palm Beach in 2023, topping out at 99.9 mph. He averaged 96-98 mph with the heater, which acts like a sinker, and the lack of rising movement makes it more hittable than the velo alone would indicate. His upper-80s changeup is better at generating swing-and-miss with nice armside fade, and FSL hitters chased it out of the zone 43.1 percent of the time. He’ll throw a low-80s slider too, but even low-level hitters knew to lay off it given his poor command of the breaker. Nunez worked on staying within his delivery, allowing for the overall control improvements last season, but it’s going to take more for him to move beyond 40 control. He has the present stuff to be a quality reliever, and last year’s results give him solid momentum heading into his Rule 5 decision year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez was meant to sign during the 2018-19 international signing window but was declared ineligible by MLB because of an age discrepancy. The Cardinals were finally able to sign him for $525,000 in June 2020, after a pandemic-related pause in the international market. The Dominican Republic native jumped right into full-season ball the following year and showed enticing stuff with lackluster results. There are two ways to best describe Nunez’s experience at Low-A Palm Beach. First, he threw the 109 fastest pitches thrown by Palm Beach pitchers as recorded by Statcast in 2021 -- all at 98.2 mph or above and topping out at 101.1 mph. Second, he walked 56 batters in 53 2/3 innings, nearly equaling his output of 59 strikeouts in the same span. It’s a lot of gas, very few brakes from the 6-foot-3 hurler. Nunez also sports a mid-80s curveball that can flash above-average with decent spin rates and an upper-80s changeup that he doesn’t sell very well just yet. The Cardinals like Nunez’s clean delivery and work ethic and believe his control struggles were the result of inexperience due to lost time and an aggressive assignment. The righty pitched almost exclusively out of relief in 2021, and that’s where his big-time velocity profiles best anyway. If he can even find just 45-grade control in the Minors, his future as a back-end reliever will become even clearer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Three seasons at Vanderbilt both starting and relieving as well as a strong MLB Draft Combine showing led the Royals to take Owen in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft, signing him for $631,700, He might have gone higher if not for injury concerns in his final season at Vandy. Owen put those aside by throwing 102 innings across 23 games (22 starts) for High-A Quad Cities in his first pro season. He had a 4.20 ERA with a 1.20 WHIP, an 18.9% strikeout rate and a 7.5% walk rate. Owen is a presence on the mound at 6-foot-6 and 260 pounds. His fastball is 90-94 mph with solid carry and vert to it and uses the top of the zone well. His 86-89 mph slider is smaller, almost cutter-like, misses bats and has potential to be his out pitch, while his 75-76 mph curveball is still developing after he wasn't able to land it much in 2024. His 83-85 mph changeup is near average with sink and gets some chase on it. Owen’s delivery is simple but does have some effort because of his bigger frame, although he likes using that strong presence to his advantage on the mound. Owen looks the part of a big-bodied rotation guy who’s built like a workhorse, so it was good to see him stay healthy across a full season with a lot of innings and a jump from what he had in ‘23. He’ll head to Double-A in 2025 and projects as a back-end starter if he can keep developing his secondaries, but that stuff might tick up in a bullpen, especially against lefties.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Owen was Maine’s top prep prospect in 2020, but he opted to attend Vanderbilt rather than turn pro right away. He was a reliever his first two seasons, then a starter in ‘23, but he could not stay healthy with a tired arm after flashing first-round stuff in the spring. A strong showing at the MLB Draft Combine eased some concerns, and the Royals took him in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft. Owen didn’t pitch last year with the Royals after the up-and-down nature of his season. All of the stuff Owen flashed early on last spring was impressive. His 92-94 mph fastball has good carry, while his upper-70s curveball is above-average. A mid-80s slider missed bats with a whiff rate of 46 percent as a junior, and a mid-80s sinking changeup grades out as average but has potential to improve. Owen is an effective strike-thrower with all his pitches. He’s a big guy at 6-foot-6 and 261 pounds, but he has a simple and athletic delivery despite the sometimes uneven tempo to it. The former Commodore faces major question marks about his health and durability entering his pro career. As a college pitcher coming out of a program like Vanderbilt, one might hope to accelerate his development a bit quicker, as long as he can stick on the mound. He’ll begin his career as a starter, but his stuff and presence would fit in a bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aliendo has been one of the biggest enigmas in the system since signing for $200,000 out of Venezuela in 2018. He has solid raw power and the tools to be a quality defender, yet he's inconsistent on both sides of the ball and the Cubs declined to protect him on their 40-man roster in each of the last three offseasons, during which he's gone unselected in the Rule 5 Draft. He hit 10 homers in 58 Double-A games last year, missing two months with a broken right wrist. Though Aliendo has soft hands and is quicker and more agile than most catchers, he loses focus behind the plate and his receiving and framing skills still need more refinement. He has at least plus arm strength -- some evaluators give him plus-plus grades -- yet surrendered 66 steals in 74 attempts (89.2 percent) in 50 starts last season. He does a good job of calling games and running a pitching staff but should be better behind the plate than he is. Stronger than his listed 170 pounds, Aliendo could provide 15-20 homers per season without swinging for the fences. But he's overly aggressive at the plate and his right-handed stroke gets too long as he tries to crush every pitch he sees in the air to his pull side. He chases and swings and misses too much, doing little damage against non-fastballs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $200,000 out of Venezuela in 2018, Aliendo showed little with the bat during two years in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and didn't reach full-season ball until 2021. A key part of championship clubs the past two seasons at High-A South Bend in 2022 and Double-A Tennessee in 2023, he's also something of an enigma. His 16 homers last year exceeded his total of 13 from his first four pro seasons but he also batted just .231, and he hasn't gotten the most out of his defensive tools. Quicker and more agile than most catchers, Aliendo is very flexible and has soft hands, yet his receiving and blocking skills remain inconsistent. He has plus arm strength yet surrendered 118 stolen bases in 86 starts last year and erased just 16 percent of basestealers. He does earn praise for his game calling and leadership but needs to improve his focus behind the plate. The wiry Aliendo is doing a better job of tapping into his solid raw power as he gets stronger and drives the ball in the air more frequently, giving him at least 15-homer upside. His approach needs refinement, however, as his right-handed stroke gets too long and he chases too many non-fastballs while shooting for the fences. There's a potential starting catcher in here if he can make adjustments on both sides of the ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $200,000 out of Venezuela in 2018, Aliendo scuffled offensively in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League for two years before losing the 2020 season to the pandemic shutdown. He made his U.S. and full-season debuts in 2021, advancing to High-A and impressing with his athleticism and his defense. Though he still has plenty of work to do at the plate, he ranks as the Cubs' top catching prospect. Quicker and more agile than most catchers, Aliendo actually saw brief action at shortstop and third base last season. He's extremely flexible and has soft hands, which should allow him to develop into a quality receiver with more experience. His solid arm strength adds to his defensive package. Aliendo has added muscle and improved his plate discipline since signing and if he can continue to do so, he could hit enough to become an everyday player. He shows some promising bat-to-ball skills from the right side of the plate, though he needs to improve his swing decisions. He has some deceptive wiry strength that might turn into 15-homer power if he makes some adjustments to launch more balls in the air.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Simpson was selected by the Pirates in the 18th round of the 2019 Draft but opted to honor his commitment and play at Washington. He didn’t generate enough excitement to get drafted again after his junior season and instead returned for his senior year. He was eventually taken by the A’s in the 15th round (436th overall) and immediately delivered encouraging results in the A’s system, reaching Double-A by the end of his first full season. Looking to add right-handed power to their system, the Rays acquired Simpson along with two pitchers and a Draft pick in return for lefties Jeffrey Springs and Jacob Lopez. Batting with a slightly open stance and his hands high, Simpson makes good use of all the power in his 6-foot-3, 225-pound frame. The 23-year-old has legitimate power, ranking up there with the top hitters in the Rays’ system in terms of bat speed and exit velocity. With the A’s, assistant GM Billy Owens compared his hitting profile to former All-Star Garrett Cooper, another big right-handed slugger. The 23-year-old can barrel balls to all fields, but he’s also shown a good sense of what he’s doing and the adjustments he needs to make during at-bats. Simpson has mostly played first base, but he’s more athletic than many might assume. He could split time between first and the outfield this season, and he even got some work at third base with the A’s. As a right-handed-hitting first baseman who won’t add value on the bases, Simpson’s bat will obviously have to carry his profile. From what he’s shown, it could carry him pretty far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A’s selected Simpson in the 15th round of the 2023 Draft following four solid years at the University of Washington. Shortly after, he began his pro career in the Arizona Complex League and ended the year at Single-A Stockton, where he hit .322/.373/.544 with four homers, 11 doubles and 16 RBIs in 29 games, leaving a strong first impression before embarking on his first full season in 2024. Simpson is a cerebral player with a good understanding of the analytics side of the game and how to gameplan for every at-bat. This advanced approach should help him maintain a decent walk rate while keeping strikeout totals relatively low. There is some good power potential, as evidenced by his 18 homers as a senior at Washington, and his big 6-foot-4 frame has drawn some comparisons to Garrett Cooper. Despite his bigger size, Simpson is a decent defender at first base and is also plenty capable of handling the corner outfield spots thanks to his sneaky effective athleticism. He plays the game hard, which caught the eye of many within the A’s organization who look forward to watching him go through his first full season after a productive first look.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's Maryland High School Player of the Year in 2021, Heubeck offered one of the best curveballs and was one of the most polished pitchers in that year's prep class. Since the Dodgers signed him away from a Wake Forest commitment with an over-slot $1,269,500 bonus in the third round, he has gained velocity but lost some feel for pitching. He missed the last two months of the 2025 season with rotator-cuff inflammation, and his strikeout rate (28 percent) ranked fifth in the Double-A Texas League and his walk rate was the eigth-highest (12 percent) among pitchers who worked at least as many as his 66 1/3 innings. Heubeck's fastball operates at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with huge induced vertical break that helps it ride by barrels up in the zone. Both of his breaking balls grade as plus pitches and get lefties and righties out when they're on, though he also has difficulty landing his upper-70s downer curveball and tight mid-80s slider for strikes. He also struggles to locate a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks. Heubeck filled the strike zone as an amateur and should have at least average control given his athleticism and clean arm action. Instead of his letting his stuff play naturally, he'll lapse into overthrowing his fastball and overspinning his breakers. Though Los Angeles still hopes to develop him into a starter, it's more realistic to project him as a bat-missing reliever whose ability to throw strikes will determine what role he fills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's Maryland high school player of the year in 2021, Heubeck stood out with one of the best curveballs and some of the best polish in that year's prep class. Since signing for an over-slot $1,269,500 as a third-rounder, he has retained his feel for spin while adding velocity and losing control. He posted a 3.05 ERA at High-A last year with the best average-against (.181) and second-highest strikeout percentage (30 percent) among Midwest League pitchers with at least 90 innings, but he also had the worst walk percentage (17 percent). Heubeck now operates with a 92-95 mph fastball that reaches 97 with huge induced vertical break that creates significant carry. Both his upper-70s downer curveball and his tighter mid-80s slider can be plus pitches that work against both lefties and righties when he lands them for strikes, which he hasn't done consistently in pro ball. He also has a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink that could be an average pitch if he learns to harness it. Heubeck has a clean arm action and an athletic delivery that should be conducive to at least average control. He sometimes overspins his breaking balls and needs to find a better balance between trying to create nasty stuff and throwing strikes. The Dodgers still think he could develop into a No. 3 or 4 starter, even if takes longer than they expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heubeck earned Gatorade's 2021 Maryland high school player of the year award after leading Gilman School (Baltimore) to the state Class A title, fanning 15 in a complete-game victory in the semifinals and saving the finale. The Dodgers drafted him in the third round, making him the Old Line State's highest prep pitcher pick since 2005, and signed him away from a Wake Forest commitment for an over-slot $1,269,500. He quickly stood out with his aptitude during his four-inning pro debut and in instructional league, with one club official describing him as \"plug and play.\" Heubeck already possesses a plus curveball with upper-70s velocity and legitimate 12-6 break. It plays well off his fastball, which sits at 90-93 mph and tops out at 95 with good induced vertical break and carry up in the strike zone. He also shows promising feel for a low-80s changeup with some fade and sink. With a clean arm action and athletic delivery, Heubeck should provide at least average control. His strike-throwing and velocity should improve as he adds some much-needed strength to his skinny 6-foot-3 frame. A potential No. 3 or 4 starter, he could move through the Minors more quickly than most high school pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout on Cuba’s 15U national team back in 2016, Nunez signed with the Cardinals for $300,000 in July 2018 and immediately dominated the Dominican Summer League and won a batting title with his .415 average. He hasn’t been able to reach that very high bar since, scuffling a bit during his United States debut in 2019 and putting up pedestrian numbers in 2021. He found his footing with Double-A Springfield a year ago before being sent to the Pirates in the José Quintana deal and finished the year in Triple-A. The Bucs rolled the dice and didn’t put him on the 40-man roster, but he wasn’t selected in the Rule 5 Draft. His case to land a spot on the roster in 2023 wasn’t helped by missing two months of the season with a shoulder impingement. Compact and strong, Nunez tapped into his considerable raw power more consistently in 2022 than he has since that stunning DSL debut. He makes a lot of contact, with a strikeout rate under 20 percent for his Minor League career and even his small uptick in whiffs during his power breakout last year was offset by a walk rate of 14 percent. While he still tends to hit the ball on the ground too much, the improved patience has given him better counts to drive the ball on a regular basis. Although Nunez doesn’t have the footspeed to play third on a regular basis, he does have more than enough arm for the hot corner, and he’ll continue to get some reps there. He has really good hands, which will help him be a solid defender at first, where he’s most likely to fit long term if he’s going to play one spot every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nuñez posted Cuba’s best batting average during a gold medal-winning turn at the 2016 15U World Cup in Japan and won the 2018 Dominican Summer League slash-line triple crown (.415/.497/.774) after signing with the Cardinals for $300,000 that July. Following some stateside stumbles as an 18-year-old in 2019, Nuñez popped much better at High-A Peoria to open last season, hitting .285/.351/.453 over 151 plate appearances. He was pushed once more to Double-A Springfield, and while his 91 wRC+ was below-average, his 224 plate appearances were second-most among 20-year-olds at Double-A in 2021 behind Riley Greene’s 373. He was spending a full season at Double-A and showing more power when he was sent to the Pirates in return for José Quintana close to the Trade Deadline. Listed at 5-foot-11, 205 pounds, Nuñez shows impressive raw power and bat speed out of his boxier frame, and it’s that pop that will continue to fuel his ascent toward the big leagues. He shows good bat-to-ball skills as well with strikeout rates regularly below 20 percent. That said, the lack of K’s had been in part due to his overly aggressive nature at the plate, and that leads to more ground balls than should be expected of someone with his strength. Experience has helped and he started showing more patience and tapping into his power more consistently as a more age-appropriate for his level in 2022. Nuñez has the strong arm for third base, but he lacks the speed or relative athleticism to make him a surefire fit for the position. He seems destined for a first base/DH role or even left field where the arm could be of use, and he’ll have to hit to be valuable at any of those spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez put himself on the international radar while playing in Cuba’s youth national leagues and then recorded the team’s highest batting average as he led Cuba to a gold medal during the 2016 15U World Cup in Japan. He signed with the Cardinals for $300,000 in July 2018 and won the Dominican Summer League triple crown (.415/.497/.774) in his professional debut. The Cardinals pushed Nunez to Low-A Peoria in 2019, but some holes in his game were exposed and he was demoted to the Rookie Appalachian League, where he hit .254 over 37 games. That experience proved fruitful for Nunez as he made adjustments to his approach and worked his way up to Double-A as a 20-year-old in 2021. Nunez’s calling card is his raw power and ability to impact the baseball. The 5-foot-11 Nunez generates impressive exit velocities, but doesn’t hit a ton of balls in the air, something he worked on at the alternate training site in 2020 and has continued to work on this season. Nunez’s approach can get overly aggressive at times, though that can be attributed to his lack of experience and he’s been receptive to coaching early in his career. Defensively, questions remain about Nunez’s long-term home. While he has spent the vast majority of his career at third base, he’d need to both refine his mechanics and improve his athleticism to stick at the hot corner. Nunez, who possesses a solid arm, may ultimately wind up at first base, with left field also being a potential option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boston College's only two-time baseball All-American, Morissette fell short of pulling off the trifecta in 2021 after injuring his hand in a home-plate collision with Louisville catcher and No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis. He did rally to finish his college career with a 16-game hitting streak before Miami selected him in the second round and signed him for $1,403,200. He batted just .234/.312/.401 in his first full pro season, though he did homer six times in June just before fouling a ball off his left ankle and sustaining a fracture that sidelined him for six weeks. After standing out with his bat-to-ball skills in college, Morissette has made changes to his left-handed swing to help him drive the ball more consistently as a pro. Instead of focusing on making line-drive contact and using the entire field, he has concentrated on launching balls to his pull side since joining the Marlins. His new approach might result in 15 or more homers per season, but he also batted just .226/.311/.372 in his first two professional years. That kind of production won't cut it for a player projected as an offensive second baseman. His instincts are more notable than his average speed on the bases and in the field. He has a quick first step and gets the job done at the keystone, but his average arm is stretched at third base and he doesn't have the range desired at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boston College's only two-time baseball All-American, Morissette didn't put up loud numbers last spring, in part because he injured his hand in a home-plate collision with Louisville catcher and No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis. He rallied to finish the season with a 16-game hitting streak before signing for $1,403,200 in the second round.
