Former All-Star Joe Panik was his favorite player growing up and Morissette projects as a steady player in the same mold. Though Morissette batted just .204/.308/.299 while making his pro debut in Low-A, the Marlins remain confident in his bat-to-ball skills. He employs a compact left-handed swing with a patient all-fields approach that should enable him to produce high batting averages. His power is more in question because he has solid but not plus bat speed, needs more strength and frequently hits the ball on the ground, which may limit him to 10-12 homers per season. Morissette's instincts on the bases and in the field stand out more than his average speed. After he spent most of his college career at second base while also seeing action at third for the Eagles and at shortstop in summer ball, the Marlins plan on trying him all over the infield. He's a solid defender at second base, but his range is a bit lacking at shortstop and his average arm is stretched on the left side of the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Viars entered his senior season of Texas high school baseball as a bit of an unknown because he wasn’t a presence on the summer showcase circuit, but his power and athleticism opened the eyes of some scouts in the spring of 2021. That led to the Phillies taking him in the third round of that summer’s Draft and going a little over slot to sign him away from his commitment to Arkansas, and they were encouraged by early returns from his pro debut. He was greatly slowed in 2022 by a bad ankle sprain and by getting hit in the hand by a pitch. The Phillies are still high on Viars’ set of tools. He’s a strong and physical right-handed hitter who has the chance to hit, and hit with power. He sees the ball very well and has a decent overall approach, and while he was out of sync for much of the 2022 season, he still showed the ability to impact the ball when he made contact. His swing features bat speed to go along with leverage and loft that points to solid future power. Viars runs well for his size, with decent straight-line speed, though he might slow down a bit as he physically matures. After playing first base and the outfield during his summer debut, he was exclusively a left fielder last year, which could be a good long-term fit. The Phillies are hopeful a full, healthy season will help Viars tap into his considerable offensive potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Viars was a bit of an off-the-radar prospect out of the Texas high school ranks as the 2021 Draft approached, albeit one with a commitment to Arkansas, mostly because he didn’t hit the summer showcase circuit before his senior year. A strong senior season brought some interest and the Phillies nabbed him the third round and signed him away from heading to play for the Razorbacks. He had a solid, but brief, debut in the Florida Complex League. A left-handed hitter and thrower, Viars is big and physical with a ton of now strength. He sees the ball really well and uses a swing with leverage and loft that has the chance to deliver a lot of power. It started to show up during his senior year of high school and he showed a solid overall approach during his summer debut. Viars is a better athlete than you’d think and is a pretty good straight-line runner, though he might slow down some as he fills out his 6-foot-4 frame. He’s shown some positional versatility, with the ability to play some center field, the outfield corners (a more likely long-term fit) and some first base, but it’s his power bat that will carry him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meza was one of the top catchers on the 2022 international market and signed with the Blue Jays for a bonus of $2,050,000. The No. 33 prospect in that class per MLB Pipeline, he joined a system that had recently produced Gabriel Moreno and Alejandro Kirk as potential stars after signing each to much smaller bonuses. Meza’s 2022 debut was a learning experience. Pressing at times as he tried to produce early, he hit .229 with a .559 OPS over 28 games in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old. The Blue Jays still like his foundational tools, though, and expect him to bounce back. There will be plenty of patience too as catchers typically take longer to develop, and he still has years of growth ahead of him. It still may be a year or two until you see Meza with a full-season affiliate, but the Blue Jays will continue to bring him along at his own pace. Like all new international signings, he should benefit greatly from having access to the Blue Jays’ new player development complex and their physical program from such a young age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meza was one of the top catchers available on the International market, signing with Toronto out of Venezuela in January of ’22 for $2.05 million. The young backstop was ranked as the No. 33 overall prospect in the class and joined a system that’s begun to regularly produce talent at the premium position. The Blue Jays were attracted to Meza’s potential as a defender behind the plate, where he’s showing early signs of strong catch-and-throw skills along with the potential to be an above-average receiver and blocker. Scouts are also high on Meza’s baseball IQ and fundamentals across the board for a player his age. While he’s listed at 5-foot-10, Meza comes with a broad frame that should allow him to add some muscle and hold up against the wear and tear of catching as he develops. Meza can drive the ball to all fields, but the development of his power long term will be worth monitoring. At such a young age, Meza is further from the Major Leagues than any prospect on this list, but he has some high-upside building blocks for the Blue Jays’ development staff to work with.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a relatively pedestrian freshman season at Virginia Tech, Schobel hit over .300 in the Cape Cod League that summer, using that as a springboard into a big Draft-eligible sophomore season. Hitting in the middle of the Hokies' powerful lineup, he smashed 19 homers and posted a 1.134 OPS while playing shortstop and ended up being taken by the Twins No. 68 overall. He performed well enough with High-A Cedar Rapids during his first full season to get a bump up to Double-A in mid-July, though he scuffled a bit up a level. Schobel is the kind of player whose whole might be greater than the sum of his parts, one who can do a lot of things pretty well, but nothing plus. Even when the results didn't stand out in Wichita, his underlying numbers were good, including his penchant for making a ton of contact from the right side of the plate and limiting his strikeouts. He controls the zone well and draws plenty of walks and has worked to add depth to his swing, allowing him to drive the ball a little more effectively. While Schobel played shortstop at Virginia Tech and could fill in there if needed, his best position now is second base, where he could be an excellent defender, and he split time between the keystone and third base in 2023, something that should continue to maintain his positional flexibility moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schobel put himself on the map as one of the top Draft-eligible sophomores in the 2022 class after hitting well in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2021. He kept on raking as Virginia Tech's shortstop the next spring, hitting in the middle of a potent college lineup, finishing with 19 homers and a 1.134 OPS, enough to land him in the Competitive Balance Round B and the Twins signed him for $1 million. He spent most of his pro debut with Single-A Fort Myers. A right-handed-hitting infielder, Schobel's contact skills already stand out. He struck out in just 14.2 percent of his plate appearances and registered an overall miss rate of just 14 percent on all pitches, according to Synergy, during his sophomore year with the Hokies. He displayed that skill, as well as his ability to control the strike zone, during his relatively modest pro debut. He worked during instructs to add some depth to his swing, as he had a tendency to be too out in front with a pushy swing, with the hope he can impact the ball more as a pro and adjust to breaking stuff more consistently. Schobel is a good athlete who could potentially play shortstop with decent actions and a solid arm. He played a lot of second base during his pro debut, and he'll likely keep moving around, with the Twins' depth at shortstop as much of a reason for that as Schobel's inability to stick there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Serna signed with the Yankees for $10,000 out of Mexico in 2019 before the pandemic delayed his pro debut until 2021, allowing him to play the first two seasons of his career alongside his cousin, righty pitching prospect Luis Serna. After two years in Rookie ball, Jared broke out with 19 homers in 95 Single-A games in 2023, then climbed to Triple-A by the end of last season. After acquiring him in a three-prospect package for Jazz Chisholm Jr. last July, the Marlins protected him on their 40-man roster in November. Though he's just 5-foot-7 and 168 pounds, Serna surprisingly has solid raw pop and wants to make the most of it. He focuses on hitting balls hard to his pull side, and he might reach 20 homers per season if he learns to drive them in the air more consistently. Despite his power-seeking mentality, he still makes consistent contact with his compact right-handed stroke, though more patience would help against more advanced pitching. Serna's max-effort swing slows him down coming out of the batter's box, but he can flash solid speed underway and looks to make things happen on the bases. More dependable than flashy at shortstop, he has fringy range and arm strength, making him better suited for second base. He also has seen action at third base and both outfield corners in the past, adding to his versatility as a potential utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The cousin of Yankees pitching prospect Luis Serna, Jared signed with New York for $10,000 out of Mexico in 2019 but didn't make his pro debut until two years later because of the pandemic. He made the Single-A Florida State League postseason All-Star team after batting .283/.350/.483 with 19 homers in 95 games there in 2023, though he didn't go deep in 27 contests following a promotion to High-A. He rediscovered his pop at that level this year before the Yankees included him in a three-prospect package to acquire Jazz Chisholm Jr. from the Marlins in July. Serna has a naturally compact right-handed stroke and makes good swing decisions, allowing him to make repeated contact. He looks to pull the ball and hits the ball harder than expected for a 5-foot-7, 168-pounder, creating surprisingly solid raw power. He can get too pull-conscious and will put pitches in play that he'd be better off avoiding, leading to some suboptimal groundball contact. Though he's slow out of the batter's box, Serna can flash plus speed once he gets going and is aggressive on the bases. With average range and arm strength, he's best suited for second base, but has seen more action at shortstop in 2024. He made 11 errors in 52 games at short last year, compared to just one in 60 contests at second, and also has played third base and both outfield corners in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Twins prospect Jake Rucker, Carson was a two-time winner of the Mr. Tennessee award as the state’s top prep baseball player. He seemed poised to stay in the state and play collegiately at Tennessee like his older brother, until the Tigers selected him in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft and signed him above slot for $772,500. Injuries have stalled his career since then, including labrum surgery on his left shoulder last summer that limited him to 13 games at the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. Rucker earned his status on Draft boards with right-handed pull power but has had precious few opportunities to show it as a pro. The pull-heavy approach is still apparent, along with a good eye at the plate. Though Rucker has been primarily a shortstop when he has played, he is expected to eventually shift to third base. The Tigers still believe in Rucker’s potential despite the injuries. He’ll turn 21 in August, but in many ways, 2025 is an introductory season for Rucker to develop an everyday routine as a pro player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first Draft under president of baseball operations Scott Harris and amateur scouting director Mark Conner saw a number of high school players signed away from college commitments. One of them was Rucker, a two-time Mr. Tennessee winner who looked set to join the Vols until the Tigers went above slot to sign the fourth-rounder for $772,500. He made his pro debut with nine games in the Florida Complex League, showing a mix of run production, plate discipline and aggression. Rucker earned his status on Draft boards with right-handed pull power. Despite a 43.5 percent ground-ball rate in his brief 2023 stint, he had virtually equal rates of pull and oppo hitting in his small sample size. The power should become more apparent as he physically matures without having to sell out what is a productive swing and keen eye at the plate. Though Rucker is expected to eventually shift to third base, he stayed at shortstop for most of his FCL stint with good numbers. While top picks Max Clark and Kevin McGonigle project to be high-risers up the Tigers' system, Rucker could involve more patience. That’s even truer after he suffered a separated shoulder four games into his 2024 season, prompting a move to the full-season injured list. Once he returns to play, his upside for pure hitting and power could prove well worth the wait.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers invested big in signing the Cuban-born Campos in 2019 with a $2.85 million bonus, then a franchise record, knowing there was mystery in a player with all the tools for success but with three years out of competitive baseball after defecting in 2016. That mystery remains; while dreams of Campos becoming the Tigers’ next star talent have been tempered, he shows signs his athleticism and steady improvement can lift him to the big leagues in time. Though Campos has flashes of light-tower power from his muscular 6-foot-3 frame, he has yet to translate that into consistent results over a full season. His 10 home runs at High-A West Michigan last year marked his first season in double digits, and his .425 slugging percentage was his highest since his 39-game stint in the Florida Complex League in 2021, resulting in an impressive 120 wRC+. He improved his approach against breaking balls and has worked to add more lift to his swing while increasing his pull rate, but at his best, he might be a better line-drive hitter. He runs well for his size and put that to work on the basepaths last year, which could add to his offensive toolset. His speed and athleticism allow him to run down balls in center field, but he might grow his way into a corner. Campos’ progress in repeating High-A is a reminder that he’s still learning his game and how to adjust, something current Tigers Parker Meadows and Wenceel Perez had to experience at a similar stage. How Campos’ power swing plays in more hitter-friendly dimensions at Double-A Erie will make an intriguing watch against the tougher pitching of the Eastern League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For years, the Tigers had shied away from big-bonus international signings, opting to spread out their money across several smaller deals and leverage the odds that some of them would make it. Detroit veered off script for Campos, a strapping athlete who defected from Cuba as a 13-year-old in 2016 but went three years without competitive baseball while working out in the Dominican Republic. His $2.85 million bonus was a Tigers record at the time, but he couldn’t join competitive ball until 2021. After three seasons in the Minors, the mystery around his game remains. Campos’ 6-foot-3 frame profiles as a power hitter, but he has just 18 home runs in 239 professional games, including back-to-back five-homer seasons in larger ballparks. He’s capable of majestic power when he gets around on a pitch. He has worked on his lower body to stay back on pitches and generate lift in his swing, but his search for power has coincided with a drop in walks. He shows a knack for situational hitting and an awareness for how pitchers are approaching him. Campos runs well for his size and has played primarily in center field, where his athleticism helps him outrun some reads, but he profiles as a corner outfielder. The Tigers’ decision to leave Campos available in the Rule 5 Draft created some buzz, but it reflected a reality: He’s a young hitter with raw talent who needs time to match his game to his abilities. The Tigers have had recent success playing the long game with prospects, Parker Meadows being the top example. Campos has similar athleticism with a longer adjustment. He remains very much a mystery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Campos was a mystery man when the Tigers signed him in 2019 for a $2.85 million bonus, a franchise record at the time for an international prospect. At the time, he hadn’t played competitive baseball in three years since defecting from Cuba, instead training in the Dominican Republic under former Major League outfielder Alex Sanchez. After losing another year of play to the pandemic, Campos finally made his pro debut in 2021 with a home run in his first at-bat in the Florida Complex League. His first full pro season in 2022 showed more of his raw talent and athleticism, this time for Single-A Lakeland, but still left questions about just how good of a prospect he’ll become. Though Campos was billed as a budding young slugger upon signing, his pro career to date has been a bit of a departure. He hits balls hard, but more for line drives and grounders than fly balls, and toward the middle of the field. He actually hit as many triples as homers (five) while collecting 26 doubles in 2022. He also impressed by keeping a relatively low strikeout rate despite a long swing and a tendency to chase pitches outside the zone. Scouts expect more power as he matures and learns to lift the ball a little more. He’s athletic and instinctive enough to play center field in the Minors, but projects to move into a corner spot where his arm could play. One evaluator compared Campos to Juan Rivera, who had similar build and athleticism but was hampered by injuries over a 12-year Major League career. Campos has a wide range of potential outcomes based on his combination of athleticism and instincts, but will need to avoid falling into the trap of selling out too much for power and launch angle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Once the owner of the largest signing bonus the Tigers had ever given an international prospect, Campos was a $2.85 million mystery man until he homered in his first pro at-bat in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in 2021. Campos defected from Cuba at age 13 in 2016 after winning MVP honors at the Punta Cana International Tournament, but he went three years without playing competitively while training in the Dominican Republic under guidance from former Major League outfielder Alex Sanchez. The COVID pandemic cost Campos a crucial year of development in the Dominican Summer League, but the Tigers kept him at their Dominican academy to work. While Campos’ deal went against the Tigers’ historic trends of spreading their international money across several smaller deals, one look at Campos’ frame shows why Detroit took the risk. His big, strong frame looks like he could’ve stepped out of a video game, and he has the fluid swing to go with it. While his home run power is primarily to the pull side, he has shown a willingness to slash line drives to the gap in right-center. His bat sits just besides his neck in his stance, giving him a long bat path to travel that leaves him late on some fastballs but creates power. He has worked on hitting breaking balls and staying within his strike zone, but at age 18, he still needs more work. He played primarily center field in the FCL but projects to settle into right. The mystery around Campos created an aura of potential stardom around him, complemented by a physique that reminded some of former Tiger Avisail Garcia. Time and development will tell whether he approaches those lofty hopes, but Campos has the physical tools to be an impact hitter given time. He’s played at Single-A Lakeland this season as he just gets his full-season career going.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even as he just gets going at the complex level this season, there is still an air of mystery that has surrounded Campos since the Tigers signed him for a then team-record $2.85 million bonus in July 2019. Though Campos defected from Cuba three years earlier at age 13 after winning MVP honors at the Punta Cana International Tournament, he virtually disappeared for that time while training in the Dominican Republic with former Tigers outfielder Alex Sanchez. The Tigers saw enough in him to go big for an unranked prospect and brought him to their Dominican academy for instructional ball in 2020 after the COVID shutdown of the Minor Leagues cost him a season in the Dominican Summer League. Even a passing look at Campos shows why the Tigers believed in him. He has an imposing frame for a teenager and grew even stronger working out during the shutdown. More than one Tigers official has compared his frame to Avisaíl García when he broke into the Majors with Detroit a decade ago. He has shown the ability to hit for power to all fields, though not in actual games yet. He has good speed for his size, allowing him to play center field, but projects to settle into right, where his arm should play best. Campos is the kind of high-risk international prospect the Tigers have historically avoided. Even if he makes it, he’s going to need time to develop his game and hone his skills. He has the physical tools to be an impact hitter who can make Comerica Park seem small and make the Tigers lineup more like Detroit’s heyday a decade ago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paulino turned 16 the same day the 2018 international signing period opened, and he celebrated by turning pro for $205,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He made his U.S. debut by batting .336 in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in 2021 and led the Single-A Carolina League in doubles (35), triples (10), extra-base hits (58) and total bases (217). He made the jump to full-season ball the following year, and his numbers weren't as big in 2023 but he held his own in High-A at age 20 and helped Greenville win the South Atlantic League championship. He was a solid performer at Double-A Portland to begin 2024 and was traded to the Blue Jays in a four-player deal involving Danny Jansen at the Trade Deadline. Paulino has the ingredients to hit for average: a pretty left-handed swing, fine hand-eye coordination and more discipline than most players his age. But he hasn't been able to add much muscle to his slight 5-foot-10 frame, so his quality of contact dipped against better pitching last year. His hitting ability should enable him to tap into most of his average raw power, so he could deliver 15 or more homers per season if he gets stronger. Though he has just average speed, Paulino can steal bags, though he became less efficient at that skill in 2024. Almost half of his starts last year came at shortstop, though he has fringy range there and his arm stands out more for its accuracy than its strength. He also saw action at second base (his best position) and third (where his arm is a bit light), and he played briefly in center field in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paulino celebrated his 16th birthday in 2018 by signing with the Red Sox for $205,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His best attribute was his pure hitting ability, and that has translated into a .281/.377/.468 slash line through his first three pro seasons. He made his full-season debut at age 19 last year and led the Single-A Carolina League in doubles (35), triples (10), extra-base hits (58) and total bases (217). After recognizing pitches well and repeatedly making good swing decisions in 2022, Paulino has been less patient and productive in High-A. His sweet left-handed stroke and fine hand-eye coordination should allow him to make consistent contact, but he has regressed and has been feeble against southpaws. There are some questions about his lack of physicality and how much power he'll have, though he should have the hitting ability to get to most of his raw pop and produce at least 15 homers per season. Paulino plays faster than his average speed on the bases thanks to his instincts and aggressive nature. Signed as a shortstop, he started games there and at second and third base, and left and center field in 2022. With his average quickness and arm strength along with his hit-over-power profile, he fits best at the keystone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paulino turned 16 on the day the 2018 international signing period opened, and he celebrated by turning pro with the Red Sox for $205,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His biggest selling point was his pure hitting ability, which was evident when he batted .336/.436/.549 as a 19-year-old in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League making his U.S. debut last summer. Originally signed as a shortstop, he moved to third and second base in the FCL to accommodate slicker defenders Marcelo Mayer and Brainer Bonaci. Paulino is built to hit for average with a smooth left-handed stroke, fine hand-eye coordination and advanced pitch recognition and swing decisions for a teenager. He makes a lot of contact but also shows the ability to work walks. Though he didn't homer in his first two pro summers, he did have 20 extra-base hits in 36 FCL games and his bat speed and ability to barrel balls could produce 15 or more homers annually once he adds some much-need strength. An average runner, Paulino displays good instincts on the bases. He has reliable hands and some twitchy athleticism but his quickness and average arm strength are a bit stretched at shortstop. He profiles best as an offensive second baseman and also might see some outfield action to enhance his versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Panzini was part of the trio of prep pitchers the Royals took high in the 2021 Draft, with his selection in the fourth round following Frank Mozzicato (first) and Ben Kudrna (second). It took Panzini until 2025 to reach the upper levels of the Minors, mainly because of a lat/oblique injury that caused him to miss significant time in ‘24. He bounced back well in ‘25, moving up three levels from High-A to Triple-A and ending the year with a 3.39 ERA in 26 games (17 starts) and 109 innings. In Double-A, where he made 13 appearances (10 starts), Panzini had a 27 percent strikeout rate and an 8.7 percent walk rate. With the injury slowing him down some, it wasn’t until 2025 that Panzini looked and felt healthy, and his velocity started to pop. His above-average fastball sits comfortably in the mid 90s and flashes into the upper 90s with good vert. Panzini has two breaking balls: an upper-70s curveball that has good depth and grades as slightly below average right now but could be above average down the line, and a mid-80s slider that is average and gets sweepy at times -- he’s working on tightening it up. Panzini is still developing a changeup that he doesn’t use much. Alongside health, Panzini has really worked on his body the last few years and is taller, leaner and stronger. He moves better now, which has helped to smooth out his delivery. Panzini made so many starts in ‘25 because he needed to throw innings following the injury, and then the Royals needed more depth in Triple-A when he made it up there at the end of the year. But it’s likely that Panzini returns there this year and makes the reliever transition; that’s where he can make an impact at the big leagues, and it can be in multi-inning stints with his arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Panzini became the highest Draft pick out of Red Bank Catholic High School in southern New Jersey when the Royals selected him in the fourth round in 2021 and signed him for well-above slot at $997,500. He fit right in with the two high school pitchers the Royals took in earlier rounds, Frank Mozzicato and Ben Kudrna, and the three pitched in instructional league together last fall. The Royals viewed Panzini as an under-the-radar pick based on how many arms were in the Northeast last year and were thrilled to get him in the fourth round because of his ceiling. Pitching largely off his fastball, Panzini hovers around 94-95 mph consistently and throws the pitch with plus life and high spin. Although there’s not much projection left in his 6-foot-3, 220-pound frame, some believe there is more velocity in there. Panzini has a slider that could be above average in time, and he mixes in a changeup, though not consistently. He threw that pitch in the Royals’ fall camp and flashed some deception with it, which should help him get through a lineup multiple times. Panzini will need to learn how to land his breaking balls for strikes consistently to eliminate the reliever risk some scouts saw during the Draft process. He could fill a bullpen role with his fastball/slider combo and aggressive mindset, but he also has a durable frame that will be able to log innings. The Royals love his quiet competitiveness and plan to start him, taking their time to see what they have, but he could be someone who does move quickly as things begin to click.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels gave out nine bonuses that were six figures or higher at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period. Placencia got the second-highest bonus the organization awarded, signing for $1.1 million. After the lost 2020 season, the infielder made his pro debut in the Arizona Complex League and struggled, though he had more success moving to full-season ball in 2022. Moving up one rung on the organizational ladder in 2023, Placencia showed off some patience at the plate before getting a late taste of Double-A and heading to the Arizona Fall League for some extra work. In some ways, Placencia is ahead of the curve in hitting the upper levels of the system and not turning 21 until June. A switch-hitter who was much better from the right side with Tri-City last year, he has shown some thump and high exit velocities. He’s drawn a ton of walks in his two years of full-season ball, with a career 16.1 percent walk rate heading into 2024. He’s going to have to tone down the strikeouts (29.4 percent career K rate); better swing decisions will help him with that and doing more damage at the plate, as will added strength. Signed as a shortstop, Placencia can still play there in a pinch, but it’s clear that second base is his best spot defensively and where he would play should he be able to develop into an everyday guy at one position. That will only happen if he can refine what he does at the plate and make more consistent contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels went aggressively after middle infield talent at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, giving Arol Vera, Jose Bonilla and Placencia bonuses of $600,000 or above. Placencia got $1.1 million to sign and after a rough-looking line in his professional debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2021, he started showing off the offensive skills that made him an intriguing amateur prospect with a move to full-season ball in 2022. As one of the youngest players in the Single-A California League in 2022, the switch-hitting Placencia consistently hit the ball hard, routinely posting high exit velocities. Though he needs to get stronger, he did tap into some power during his full-season debut. With that increased extra-base authority came some more swing-and-miss, with a strikeout rate north of 30 percent, but he does have good knowledge of the zone and showed it with a 16.2 percent walk rate. Placencia continues to get reps at both middle infield positions, but because of his lack of speed, most see him settling in as a second baseman if he is going to play one spot full time. He spent most of the offseason working out in Arizona, and if he can continue to focus on getting stronger, he has the chance to be a big league regular on the right side of the infield with some offensive impact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a perfect world, the 2019-20 international signing class will provide the Angels with their future big league double play combination, with Arol Vera and his $2 million bonus at shortstop and Placencia, who got $1.1 million, at second base. The Angels liked Placencia’s feel to hit, one he showed off at instructs after the pandemic-induced layoff, but he struggled to replicate that when he hit .175/.326/.343 during his pro debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2021. Despite the rough line, Placencia did show some signs of a decent approach with patience from both sides of the plate. At times, he’d see a lot of pitches and drew walks, but then he’d get out of his approach and the swing and miss was concerning. Some of the teenager’s metrics are encouraging, with promising exit velocities, but he needs to add strength in order to be able to impact the ball more consistently. Signed as a shortstop, Placencia saw more time at second base during his pro debut. He’ll likely keep getting reps on both sides of second base, but his below-average speed points to the keystone as a more likely destination if he’s going to develop into a big league regular in one spot. His ability to refine his approach at the plate and drive the ball with more authority might dictate just what kind of role he’ll fill in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were six teams that handed out more than one seven-figure bonus during the 2019-20 international signing period. The Angels were one of them, giving out a total of $3.1 million to a pair of middle infielders: Arol Vera, who got $2 million, and Placencia, who signed for $1.1 million. Like most from the signing period, Placencia didn’t get to do much baseball-wise until the Angels held instructs last fall. During his time in front of player development staff, Placencia impressed with how he handled himself in the batter’s box. Both boxes, actually, as the switch-hitter showed he can have competitive at-bats from both sides of the plate. He has an advanced feel to hit and a better approach than many players his age, showing good knowledge of the strike zone. There isn’t a ton of strength right now to help him impact the baseball, but there is some raw power to tap into down the road as he matures. While Placencia scuffled a bit defensively at instructs, that was more as a result of rust than anything else, as the infielder has good hands and instincts that should allow him to stick up the middle. Because of below-average speed, many feel his best chance at sticking at a regular spot will be at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles think they might be in the process of unearthing a diamond in the rough from their 2022 international class in Sosa, who signed for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. Sosa flashed enough potential in the Florida Complex League the next year that the Orioles began challenging him, assigning Sosa to affiliates where he has routinely been one of the youngest players. He seems destined for a big league role of some kind after reaching Double-A in 2025 as a 20-year-old. Sosa is a left-handed-hitting, left-handed-throwing outfielder with size, projectable power and upside, garnering early comparisons to former Pirates outfielder Gregory Polanco. He consistently registers some of the organization’s best 90th percentile exit velocities and hard-hit rates, though issues making contact and with his approach have made the power slow to show up in games so far. He proved to be a better runner than expected by stealing 30 bases in 2024, but was limited on the bases last year due to a knee injury. Defensively, Sosa became more or less a full-time corner outfielder last season and seems suited to right field, where his plus throwing arm profiles well. Otherwise, this is a bat-first skillset, with Sosa’s ceiling dependent on the extent to which he can polish his approach and develop into a well-rounded hitter, rather than a panoply of pop and potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 40 | Overall: 40 Sosa wasn’t one of the highest-ranked players in the 2022 international class and didn’t get an earth-shattering signing bonus ($400,000), but the Orioles feel they may have struck gold with the Villa Mella, Dominican Republic, native. After a forgettable debut, Sosa turned heads in the Florida Complex League in 2023 and performed well at Single-A Delmarva in '24. He earned a late-season promotion to High-A Aberdeen but experienced growing pains there as a 19-year-old. Sosa has been compared to former Pirates outfielder Gregory Polanco because he is a left-handed-hitting, left-handed-throwing outfielder with size, projectable power and intriguing upside. He generates loud contact and produces high exit velocities with probably plus raw power, though it's yet to really show up in games because Sosa’s swing and approach remain unrefined. He’s already gotten bigger and stronger since signing, with room to add more size and strength, and Sosa also might be a better runner than expected after totaling 30 stolen bases in 93 games in his first season stateside. Defensively, Sosa gets reps at all three outfield positions, including center field, though he’s probably destined for a corner. His plus arm strength profiles well for right field. Sosa is raw enough that there is still real risk here, but his skill set is the kind that could develop into a bat-first regular if a few things go right, and a star if everything clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Villa Mella, Dominican Republic, Sosa signed with the Orioles for $400,000 at the start of the 2022 international signing period. He didn’t hit much in his Dominican Summer League debut that summer but began turning heads in 2023 in the Florida Complex League, where he showed an intriguing mix of upside and production as part of a talented Baltimore club. A left-handed hitting, lefty-throwing outfielder, Sosa draws comparisons to former Pirates outfielder Gregory Polanco for his size, build, stance and makeup. He is long and lanky with a solid approach and flashes of line-drive power that should increase as his body fills out. That’s already begun to happen as he’s grown a lot in the two years since signing, adding at least 3 inches and 20 pounds. He’s a solid runner at this point with good instincts on the bases. A natural center fielder, Sosa got experience at all three outfield spots last year and could potentially move to a corner one day. If that happens, he has the power and arm strength to profile well at either left or right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from Puerto Rico, Luciano used good performances at the PDP League and MLB Draft Combine to help his Draft stock going into his senior year in 2024. The D-backs selected the then-17-year-old in the second round that July, making him the highest prep player selected from the island since Edwin Arroyo also went in the second round in 2021. After signing for $990,000, Luciano spent most of his first full season in the Arizona Complex League, hitting .275/.398/.382 with two homers and a 31/28 K/BB ratio over 44 games. He was promoted to Single-A Visalia for three games in the final week of the season. Luciano seems to see the ball well out of a simple left-handed setup in the box, featuring a load with his legs. He was willing to take his walks against wild ACL arms, not an unexpected skill for a backstop who sees so many pitches on defense anyways. Standing only 5-foot-10, he isn’t a big power threat at this very early stage of his career, but he’s impressed D-backs officials with how he’s hitting the ball harder in early spring work, thanks to improved lower-half strength and body efficiency. His best defensive asset entering Year 2 is his above-average arm strength, and he used it to throw out 28.8 percent of attempted basestealers in the ACL. That improved lower-half foundation should help his work behind the plate too, and he briefly shared a Puerto Rican Winter League roster with Gold Glove winner Martín Maldonado in the offseason. Tackling a true full summer season will be Luciano’s next hurdle as he gains steam in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most famous Puerto Rican catcher to enter professional baseball through the Draft is potential future Hall of Famer and 2000 fourth-rounder Yadier Molina, but others like Geovany Soto, Martín Maldonado and Christian Vázquez give the list extra heft. Luciano could be next in line after good showings in the PDP League and MLB Draft Combine pushed him into the second round to the D-backs last July. He signed below slot for $990,000, the seventh-highest bonus given to a Puerto Rico native since the bonus-pool era began in 2012. Left-handed-hitting catchers will always garner attention from scouts, and Luciano checks that box straight out of the gate. He can make consistent hard contact and shows a solid approach. It’s hit-over-power right now, but he showed a better ability to tap into his pullside pop as a senior heading into the Draft. Though he’s a below-average runner, Luciano has enough athleticism to keep the carousel moving when he’s on base. The 5-foot-10 backstop brings plenty of arm strength to the table, and if he can improve his exchanges, he could give opposing runners plenty to consider. His receiving and framing will also need attention as he enters pro ball, but it’s important to remember he was only 17 at the time of the Draft. Luciano even worked on the defensive side of his game with Molina, notable considering Arizona thought of him as a bat-first catcher at the start of his career. Luciano will have plenty of time and space to become a well-rounded player at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There was already a Perez-Brewers connection considering Hedbert’s father, Robert, played for the club in 2001. The younger Perez joined Milwaukee for $700,000 out of his native Venezuela in July 2019, and after the lost pandemic season, he got off to a quick stateside start in 2021, slashing .333/.394/.575 with six homers in 32 games in the Arizona Complex League before a brief promotion to Single-A Carolina. He returned to the Mudcats for his age-19 season last year and showed some pop (15 homers) but struggled overall with a .216 average, .272 OBP and 82 wRC+. There is an obvious positive in Perez’s game in his raw power. He’s bulked up in his 5-foot-10 frame from his days playing back home, and the result has been loud exit velocities and a significant portion of his hits going for extra bases when he puts the bat on the ball. Pitch recognition and selection have been issues at this early stage, and those problems not only led to a 29.9 percent K rate in Carolina, but also have kept him from reaching the hitter’s counts that would allow him to swing away more freely. As Perez has grown out at the lower levels, he’s become progressively less toolsy overall. Once a 55 runner, he’s closer to average now and isn’t likely to be a huge stolen-base threat moving forward. The lack of speed and a weak arm have made left field his primary position, and he’ll face a higher offensive threshold there. There are worse places to start than with plus raw slugging ability, and considering Perez will still only be 20 for the entire upcoming season, he has time to improve his overall approach at the dish.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of six-year Major Leaguer Robert Perez signed with the Brewers -- for whom his father played briefly in 2001 -- for $700,000 out of Venezuela in July 2019. It hasn’t taken Perez long to stand out in an organization getting more loaded with outfielders by the year. In 2021, the left-handed slugger slashed .333/.394/.474 with six homers over 32 games in the Arizona Complex League and earned a bump to Low-A Carolina in his age-18 season. Full-season pitchers were able to keep him much more off-balance (25 strikeouts in 65 PA), thus ending Perez’s 2021 on a sour note. An alternate training site participant at just 17 in 2020, Perez struggled with pitch selection and found himself down in a lot of counts at Carolina, leading him to fight off pitches instead of putting good swings on hittable offerings. He is capable of making good strong contact, and he exhibits a good amount of raw power from a bulky 5-foot-10 frame. It plays in games as well, as he showed in Arizona. The Brewers are hopeful that the Carolina bumps are growing pains because if it does come together, Perez still has the chance to be an average hitter at the top level with the way he can pound the ball on contact. Perez looked toolsier upon signing, but as his body has matured, his power remains his only plus skill. His speed and fielding ability are above-average now, though they could grade downward if he continues to prioritize strength, and his arm isn’t seen as much of a weapon these days. While he has years of development ahead of him, Perez is trending toward becoming a power bat in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prince Fielder moved fast through the Brewers’ Minor League system thanks to a mix of talent and pedigree; he knew his way around professional baseball because he grew up in the game. Now along comes another left-handed hitter with eye-popping tools and impressive poise for his age in Perez, whose father, Robert Perez, wasn’t a player the caliber of Cecil Fielder but nonetheless logged six seasons in the Major Leagues with five different teams including the Brewers in 2001. Hedbert Perez received the second-highest bonus ($700,000) among players signed by Milwaukee during the 2019-20 international period and immediately made an impact during a batting practice session in Milwaukee, launching a series of long home runs to Fielder’s former landing spots before departing for that fall’s instructional league. Despite being denied his official pro debut in 2020, Perez continued to impress with tools on both sides of the ball. At 17 years old he was the youngest player at the Brewers’ alternate training site, getting experience against far more experienced pitchers and some of the Brewers’ tough left-handed pitching prospects like Antoine Kelly and Aaron Ashby. Perez finished the year in the instructional league, then once again was the youngest player in the room when the Brewers included him among 15 players invited to their Minor League mini-camp at the start of Spring Training. Perez has a quick, compact left-handed swing and advanced plate discipline for his age combined with the raw power. In the field, he has an arm for the corners but the speed and instincts to play center field. The Brewers, who prioritize up-the-middle defenders, believe he will stick in center. If his tools and poise lead to production in his long-awaited pro debut, then Perez could continue to rise to the top of the Brewers’ prospect list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Madden needed Tommy John surgery during his senior of high school, he opted to take the junior college route and head to Northwest Florida State instead of South Carolina. He showed off some intriguing power stuff in his return to the mound in the fall of 2021 and it showed up in games, albeit inconsistently, in the spring of '22. He was planning to head to Alabama to keep pitching when the Angels went over slot in the fourth round to sign him for $1 million. His first full season of pro ball was similar to his JUCO season in terms of his stuff playing, but with inconsistent results, when he was sent to the Rockies with lefty Mason Albright for C.J. Cron and Randal Grichuk at the Trade Deadline. Madden’s pitching resume is still a bit light, with 47 2/3 innings in junior college in 2022 and 79 1/3 professional innings under his belt heading into '24. But there’s no doubt he has size -- he’s 6-foot-6 -- and arm strength working in his favor. He can be up to 98 mph with his heavy fastball, a pitch that breaks bats and gets ground ball outs. He also gets a lot of swing and misses with the pitch because of the sink, and his mid-80s slider can miss bats as well, a breaker that could be a put-away pitch in the future. He has feel for an upper-80s changeup as well. If Madden can add some strength to his frame, it can help in multiple ways. Obviously, it will allow him to be more durable and hold up to a full-season workload as a starter. It could also help him land his delivery more consistently, which could aid his command and control, an issue after he walked 5.4 per nine in his pro debut. There’s a long way to go, but there could be a big payoff as a starter if it all clicks, knowing the sinker-slider combination could be nasty out of the bullpen as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After needing Tommy John surgery his senior year of high school in 2020, Madden switched gears and decided to head to Northwest Florida State rather than South Carolina and opened some eyes in the fall of 2021, the first time scouts in the Florida Panhandle had seen him. He had an up arrow next to his name when his stuff played in competition, even though trying to pitch through a blister issue hurt his stat line. The Angels took him in the fourth round, giving him an over-slot bonus of $1 million to keep him from heading to Alabama. He was having an up-and-down pro debut in 2023 with Single-A Inland Empire when he was sent with Mason Albright to the Rockies close to the Trade Deadline in return for C.J. Cron and Randal Grichuk. There isn’t much track record with Madden, but there is a lot to work with. The 6-foot-6 right-hander has a loose arm and a starting pitcher’s repertoire. He was up to 98 mph with his fastball last spring and it can be heavy, getting ground-ball outs when he keeps it down in the zone, breaking bats when he isn’t missing them. His mid-80s slider has improved and could be a true out pitch if he stays on top of it, and he misses bats with his upper-80s changeup as well. The two main areas of developmental focus for Madden are his command -- he walked more than 4.5 per nine innings in his junior college season and was at 5.5 BB/9 at the time of the trade -- and his physicality. Added strength will help him repeat his delivery and could lead to better strikes moving forward. More than anything, he needs to get on the mound and beef up his pitching resume with a high ceiling to try to reach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in Puerto Rico's 2020 high school class, Ceballos went unpicked in the shortened five-round Draft and spent two years at San Jacinto (Texas) JC. He declined to turn pro with the Angels as a 14th-rounder in 2022, then set Oregon records for homers (18) and RBI (70) the next spring before the Braves signed him in the third round. Traded to the Giants last July in a package for Jorge Soler and Luke Jackson, he boosted his High-A OPS from .707 before the deal to .914 afterward and was Puerto Rico's best hitter (.412/.500/.882) at the Premier12 tournament in November. A physical 6-foot-3, 225-pounder with bat speed and strength, Ceballos hits balls hard but has yet to fully tap into his power potential with wood bats. He did a much better job of driving the ball in the air after switching organizations and could offer 20 or more homers per season if he can sustain it. A right-handed hitter, he controls the strike zone reasonably well but struggles against curveballs and sliders. Ceballos' value will be tied to his defensive home. He has a strong arm but has well-below-average speed that hampers his agility and range at third base. His only realistic alternative may be first base, which would increase the demands on his bat, though he did catch briefly in the MLB Draft League in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better prospects in Puerto Rico's 2020 high school class, Ceballos spent his first two college seasons at San Jacinto (Texas) JC. After turning down the Angels as a 14th-round pick in 2022, he transferred to Oregon and set school records for single-season homers (18), RBIs (70) and slugging (.643) the following spring before turning pro as a third-rounder with the Braves. The Giants acquired him in July as part of a package for Jorge Soler and Luke Jackson. Though he's a physical 6-foot-3, 225-pounder with a quick right-handed swing, Ceballos is a hit-over-power guy. He does a reasonable job of managing the strike zone and making the contact, and he has the upside of a .275 hitter with 15-20 homers per year. He did a better job of driving the ball in the air after the trade, and San Francisco is eager to see if he can maintain that improvement in 2025. Ceballos' best pure tool is his plus arm strength, which enables him to make all the necessary throws from third base. He's a well-below-average runner who lacks range and agility, however, and first base may be his only realistic alternative. Some scouts are intrigued by the idea of using his arm behind the plate, and he caught briefly in the MLB Draft League in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reyzelman underwent Tommy John surgery as a San Francisco freshman in 2020 and couldn't find the strike zone as a sophomore, then overpowered hitters as a reliever after transferring to Louisiana State and worked his way into 2022's fifth round. He worked just 8 2/3 innings in his first two years as a pro while dealing with a cyst on his back that required three operations before compiling a 1.16 ERA, .136 opponent average and 41 percent strikeout rate while rocketing to Double-A in 2024. His stuff and strikes went way backward in Triple-A last season, when he missed the final two months with a mild back strain. When he was rolling two years ago, Reyzelman paired a 94-97 mph fastball that hit 99 and featured good carry with a tight low-80s slider with significant horizontal action. In 2025, his heater dropped 2 mph and lost life while his sweeper lost 4 mph and often didn't come close to the strike zone. He had an effective low-80s changeup with huge fade in 2024 but it became so unreliable that he abandoned it last season. Reyzelman works solely out of the stretch and uses a three-quarters arm slot to create a low release height and wide angle that's tough on right-handers. He struggled to keep his mechanics in sync last year, when his walk rate spiked to 22 percent from 12 percent the season before. He may never have more than below-average control and command, so he'll need to regain his sizzling stuff from 2024 to succeed in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reyzelman had Tommy John surgery as a San Francisco freshman in 2020 and couldn't throw strikes as a sophomore before transferring to Louisiana State in 2022. His mid-90s fastball and success as a reliever got him drafted in the fifth round that July, but he barely pitched in pro ball before last year because of a cyst on his back that required three operations. Finally healthy in 2024, he posted silly numbers (1.16 ERA, .136 average-against, 41 percent K rate) in 31 appearances between three stops, mostly at Double-A. When he dominated in 2024, Reyzelman showcased two plus pitches in a 94-97 mph fastball that touched 99 with more ride than armside run and a tight low-80s slider with significant horizontal break that worked against both lefties and righties. His changeup showed similar velocity and big fade in the opposite direction, though it lacked the consistency of his other offerings. But his arsenal has backed up this year, with his fastball losing 2 mph, as well as life, his sweeper often missing the zone by a wide margin and his changeup becoming unreliable. After throwing 94 percent fastballs at LSU, Reyzelman has changed his approach and cleaned up his mechanics in pro ball. He works out of the stretch, creating a flat approach angle with a low three-quarters arm slot. If he can recapture his 2024 stuff and do a better job of keeping his delivery in sync and providing more strikes, he could join New York's bullpen in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers planned to sign Mata in July 2015 before a groin injury scuttled the deal, and he turned pro with the Red Sox instead six months later for $25,000. He blossomed into Boston's best pitching prospect before losing 2020 to the pandemic and 2021 to Tommy John surgery. He recaptured his stuff and pitched well in Triple-A by the end of 2022, but he worked just 27 innings last year while plagued by shoulder inflammation and an inability to throw strikes. Mata sits at 94-96 mph and reaches triple digits with both his two-seam and four-seam fastballs, and the former is more effective because of its power sink. His mid-80s slider can be a plus pitch with significant sweep, though he turned it into more of an upper-80s cutter last year. He lost trust in his mid-80s changeup with late fade as well as in an ineffective upper-70s curveball he should discard. Mata's delivery features effort, and he has trouble keeping it in sync, resulting in a lack of fastball command and an inability to land his secondary pitches for strikes. He walked just two batters in nine Arizona Fall League innings, but he also surrendered nine runs on 11 hits. Once viewed as a mid-rotation starter, he's out of options and likely will stick with the Red Sox in a relief role that won't give him the innings he needs to work out his issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mata originally agreed to sign with the Brewers in July 2015 before they declined after he suffered a groin injury, so he turned pro with the Red Sox for $25,000 six months later. He established himself as Boston's top pitching prospect before losing two years of development to the pandemic in 2020 and Tommy John surgery in 2021. He returned to the mound last June and recaptured his previous stuff, but he has been waylaid by shoulder inflammation and control woes this season. Though Mata can run his four-seam fastball up to 101 mph, it lacks life and isn't nearly as effective as his 94-96 mph two-seamer with power sink. While his heaters generate more weak contact than swings and misses, his upper-80s slider dodges plenty of bats with its horizontal action. His mid-80s changeup grades as a plus pitch with late fade at its best, though it can get too firm and straight at times, and he should scrap his ineffective upper-70s curveball. Despite three quality pitches, Mata isn't a slam-dunk starter. He's not as dominant as his stuff suggests he should be, and he's not efficient because he lacks consistent control and doesn't command his secondary pitches well. There's an increasingly strong possibility that he's more of a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mata planned on signing with the Brewers in July 2015 before they backed out when he suffered a groin injury, and he inked with the Red Sox for $25,000 six months later. The Venezuelan was the youngest pitcher (age 19) in the 2018 SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and established himself as Boston's top pitching prospect while reaching Double-A the following year. He lost two years of development to the 2020 pandemic shutdown and 2021 Tommy John surgery but should return to the mound by the middle of this season. Before he got hurt, Mata had electric sink and unusual velocity on a two-seam fastball that sat at 93-97 mph and created a lot of weak groundball contact. Both his upper-80s slider and fading mid-80s changeup graded as plus pitches at times, with his slider more reliable because he trusted it more. He also has a four-seam fastball that reaches 100 mph but lacks life and a slurvy curveball he never has shown much feel for. Boston brought Mata to its alternate training site in 2020 to work on simplifying his delivery so he could provide more frequent and better strikes. His control had gone haywire in 2018 and his command regressed when he reached Double-A the next summer, so he's seeking more consistency. He still has the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter but could end up as a multi-inning reliever if he can't add more polish.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Brewers backed out of a deal to sign Mata in July 2015 when he came down with a groin injury, the Venezuelan landed with the Red Sox for $25,000 six months later. He was the youngest pitcher (age 19) in the 2018 SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game but also dealt with a sore back and severe control issues that summer, then dominated high Class A but struggled in Double-A in 2019. Throughout those ups and downs, he has established himself as Boston's best pitching prospect, and he reinforced that status with his performance at the club's alternate site last year. Mata has electric sink and unusual velocity on his two-seam fastball, which sits at 93-97 mph and generates more weak groundball contact than swings and misses, and he also throws a four-seamer that reached triple digits in the Arizona Fall League in 2019 but features ordinary life. Both his upper-80s slider and fading changeup can be plus pitches at times, with his slider more reliable because he uses it more. He never had much feel for spinning a curveball that predates his slider but still has the curve in his repertoire. While Mata slashed his walk rate from 7.3 per nine innings in 2018 to 3.6 in 2019, he got knocked around when his control and command weren't as sharp in Double-A. The Red Sox helped him simplify his delivery at their alt site and were impressed by the increased frequency and quality of his strikes. He has the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter, but his development is on hold after he was diagnosed with a small ligament tear in his elbow during Spring Training and underwent Tommy John surgery in April.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros are adept at finding worthwhile older international pitchers at bargain prices. Tamarez signed for $15,000 out of the Dominican Republic as a 19-year-old in March 2019, lost a year to the pandemic and since has climbed from Single-A to Triple-A in three full seasons. His control and command regressed last season, but he did make some progress while posting a 3.32 ERA in the final two months in Triple-A. Tamarez has one of the deeper repertoires among Houston's pitching prospects, starting with a fastball that sits at 94-96 mph, reaches 100 and comes out of a high arm slot with plenty of induced vertical break. His heater pairs well with his tight upper-80s slider/cutter that grades as a plus pitch at its best, parking at 86-88 mph and peaking at 92. He can flash a solid upper-80s changeup with fade, though his low-80s curveball doesn't fool many hitters. Tamarez's up-tempo delivery provides power and deception, yet it also hampers his ability to throw strikes. He's better at getting chases than landing pitches in the zone, and he averaged 5.1 walks per nine innings through his first four pro seasons. He's athletic and has three viable pitches but probably is less a starter and more a multi-inning reliever -- a role in which he might help the Astros this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Another older pitcher whom the Astros uncovered in the international bargain bin, Tamarez signed for $15,000 out of the Dominican Republic as a 19-year-old in March 2019. He made his U.S. debut four months later and rose from Single-A to Triple-A in the two seasons following the 2020 pandemic layoff. He ranked second in the system last year in innings (121 1/3), strikeouts (142) and average-against (.191), finishing the season with a 2.50 ERA in four Triple-A starts. Tamarez uses a quick arm and high slot to unleash mid-90s fastballs that top out at 99 mph with uncanny vertical movement and boring action in on right-handers. His heater works well in tandem with his mid-80s slider, which reaches 90 mph and features more vertical than horizontal action. His upper-80s changeup is a bit firm but gets swings-and-misses as well as groundouts thanks to its combination of plane and fade. Tamarez is athletic but his high-tempo delivery produces more deception than strikes. He works solely out of the stretch yet averaged 5.2 walks per nine innings in 2022. He has enough pitches to start but likely will become a multi-inning reliever if he can't do a better job of locating them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros have repeatedly hit on signing older pitchers for small bonuses on the international market, uncovering Luis Garcia, Cristian Javier and Framber Valdez. Tamarez may follow the same path after signing for $15,000 out of the Dominican as a 19-year-old in March 2019. He made his U.S. debut four months later and impressed at two Class A levels in 2021, whiffing 103 in 76 2/3 innings with a 3.76 ERA. Tamarez's fastball parked in the low 90s during instructional league in the fall of 2020, then jumped to the mid-90s and touched 99 mph last season. His heater has a flat approach angle and good carry up in the zone, and it plays well in tandem with a mid-80s slider that overmatched lower-level right-handed hitters. He also can flash a solid changeup with fade and mix in a power curveball with more depth than his slider. Tamarez battled the strike zone until he got to High-A, where he issued just 10 walks in 33 2/3 innings. He has the athleticism and strength to develop average control, though he'll have to prove he can provide consistent strikes in more than just a sample size. He has a ceiling of a No. 4 starter but could wind up as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles’ foray into the international market under executive VP and GM Mike Elias has resulted in some flashy acquisitions and some of the biggest bonuses handed out in franchise history. The team is seeking success developing bargain gems such as Bencosme, who signed for only $10,000 in August 2020 and then played his way to High-A Aberdeen as a 19-year-old the following year. After jumping three levels in 2022, he was given all of 2023 to develop at High-A and held his own, walking nearly as much as he struck out and swiping 28 bases in 34 attempts. Bencosme is a left-handed batter with excellent contact skills that could make him an average hitter. He rarely strikes out, displaying an approach, understanding of the strike zone and ability to draw walks uncommon in hitters his age. He’s also a really good bunter. The drawback is a dearth of pop. Bencosme generates enough strength from his wiry frame to drive the ball into the outfield and leg out some extra-base hits, but his below-average exit velocities and only average wheels emphasize his need to hit line drives at a high clip. His below-average raw power is only to the pull side, though he might grow into a little more as he continues to add strength to his projectable frame. His strong decision-making on the bases enables him to collect more steals than other players with similar footspeed. Bencosme is primarily a shortstop, but his actions could be cleaned up a little and he’s athletic enough to move around the infield. He essentially split 2023 between short and second base, sprinkling in some time at third as well. His average arm is accurate and strong enough to handle the throws necessary at all those positions. He could probably be average at second and slightly below average but playable at short or third. If he can add a little more thump to his game, Bencosme’s age, athleticism and advanced bat-to-ball skills give him the ceiling of a future infield regular with a useful utility-type floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles’ transformation under executive VP and GM Mike Elias from absentees to legit players in the international free-agent market took some time to result in high-end acquisitions. But they might have found themselves a bargain gem after signing Bencosme for only $10,000 in August 2020. He made a strong first impression in the Dominican Summer League in 2021, then after playing only two games at the Rookie-level Florida Complex League, jumped to full-season Delmarva and hit .336 in 59 games in 2022. He finished the year at High-A Aberdeen as a 19-year-old. A left-handed hitter with elite bat-to-ball skills, Bencosme is a career .311 hitter in 117 games across four levels already. He almost never strikes out, showing a precocious approach and willingness to draw walks not often seen in very young hitters. So far he does so without much pop, though there is hope he can add more extra-base impact as he continues to grow and add strength to his wiry build. Bencosme’s primary position is shortstop and he played most of his games there at both affiliates last summer, but has also moved around the infield and looks comfortable at second and third as well. He’s a good runner who is already showing some ability to steal bases. Hope remains he can grow into a 8-to-10-homer guy as he matures at the plate. If he’s able to add that thump to his game, he looks like a future regular on the infield with the floor of a useful utility-type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Braves during October of the 2018-19 international period for just $35,000, Salinas blossomed into an intriguing talent who the A’s coveted as part of the prospect haul they received in the three-team Sean Murphy deal in December 2022. With injuries limiting him to just 71 2/3 innings this past season, he was sent to the Arizona Fall League for extra work, making six starts and striking out 23 batters while walking 12 in 19 innings. He reached Triple-A in 2024, but his season ended at the end of May with a shoulder injury that required surgery. Salinas is a true power arm with a fastball that touches 98 mph. His power slider is also an electric offering that generates a lot of swing-and-miss with good sinking action. He rounds out his arsenal with a crisp curveball and a developing changeup that is a clear fourth pitch. Salinas continued to work on refining his command in the Fall League, though he still has work to do in order to prove he can stay in the zone consistently. After showing up to Minor League camp out of shape last season, it was encouraging that he arrived at his first big league camp this year appearing trimmer and more prepared. He remains in a starting role, though his high-octane arm could eventually lead him to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Salinas was a diamond in the rough during the 2018-19 international period, signing with the Braves for just $35,000 in October 2018. Joining the A’s as part of the prospect haul they received in the three-team Sean Murphy deal in December 2022, he was hoping to build on what was a strong campaign last year when he racked up 175 strikeouts and a 3.55 ERA in 109 innings across two levels of A-ball, but a forearm strain limited his progress. Salinas is a prototypical power pitcher with his 6-foot-3, 205-pound frame. His repertoire features a fastball that can touch 99 mph and a power slider that has flashed plus and seems to be developing into a wipeout pitch. He also throws a curveball and changeup, though usage of both is mostly limited to when he’s facing left-handed hitters. The high three-quarters delivery that Salinas utilizes requires a lot of effort and could very well be what is leading to his high walk rate throughout the Minors. The A’s plan to keep him in a starting role, though staying there for the long term is likely going to require a serious polishing of his arm slot. Given his impressive fastball-slider combo, it might not be the worst thing in the world to move him to the bullpen, where he could really stand out as a high-octane reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite exhibiting two-way potential and earning a scholarship offer from the University of Alabama, Ford reclassified ahead of the 2022 Draft and oozed with projectable potential as a 6-foot-3 righty who was already hitting 96-97 mph. It led to the Mariners selecting him in Competitive Balance Round B and signing him over-slot at $1.25 million. So far, the transition to the pros has been shaky. Ford experienced a notable drop in velocity (into the high-80s) during his debut season in the Arizona Complex League in ‘23, which led to the Mariners giving him extra rest in between starts in an attempt to see if his stuff would see an uptick. He showed decent run suppression (3.57 ERA) but surrendered consistent contact (.789 OPS against) and had a high walk rate (9.7 percent). More than anything this season, the focus for Ford will be to regain some of that velocity -- and confidence -- while staying healthy. As one of the youngest members of his class -- he reclassified to be eligible for 2022 -- he’s entering his age-19 season, the time where some pitching prospects begin heading to their first Spring Training, so there’s still plenty of time to get back on track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Already popular with Mariners fans for his exuberant social media personality, Ford has the makeup of a prototypical projectable high school right-hander. At 6-foot-3 and just age 18 for all of the 2023 season, Ford has the potential to grow into an even bigger and more physical power pitcher, with velocity that’s reached up to 96-97 mph already, a big reason why the Mariners were bullish enough to give him a $1.25 million over-slot bonus after landing him in Competitive Balance Round B of the 2022 Draft. Ford began the preceding summer as a two-way talent from Alabama, possessing legitimate raw power as an infielder. But his stuff on the mound had too much potential, which led Ford to reclassify for the 2023 Draft and move back to his hometown of Pace, Fla., for his senior season. Ford experienced some inconsistencies last spring, specifically issues with repeating his delivery and occasionally trying to overthrow, leading to some sporadic command. But again, because he was one of the youngest players in last year’s class, there’s plenty of room to make those fixable corrections. His fastball sits comfortably in the low-90s and features good riding life in the zone, though his velocity backed up a little in the spring. He throws a solid low-80s slider that misses a lot of bats, and while his feel for a changeup is fringy, it could develop into an average offering in the future as he commits to throwing it more. Like the rest of the Mariners’ high school arms taken, Ford did not make an in-game appearance the rest of 2022, a by-design effort to keep them healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros lost their first two picks in the 2020 Draft as part of their punishment for sign stealing, and they spent their top selection (supplemental second round) and an over-slot $1.25 million bonus on Santos. Though he was one of the best high school arms to come out of New York City in the last decade, his conditioning, stuff and control all regressed in the early years of his pro career. He got hammered for a 7.83 ERA in Double-A during the first month of the season before getting sidelined by an elbow strain, but he looked like a different pitcher when he returned to tie for the Arizona Fall League lead with 26 strikeouts in 17 2/3 innings. Small sample size aside, Santos' AFL performance provided cause for optimism as he averaged 95 mph and touched 98 with his fastball, getting good carry on his four-seamer and effective sink and run on his two-seamer. His low-80s slider was unhittable at times with two-plane depth and he mixed it with a tighter upper-80s cutter. His upper-70s curveball wasn't as reliable as his other offerings, and he didn't throw a single changeup. Houston had Santos lower his arm slot a bit, and he looks more comfortable while throwing with greater velocity and spin. He also demonstrated better control in the Fall League than he had in the Minors. If he can sustain that stuff and strike-throwing, he still might be a big league starter if he can find a way to get lefties out reliably.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best high school arms to come out of New York City in the last decade, Santos didn't get a chance to pitch as a senior in 2020 because of the pandemic. He had performed well on the showcase circuit the previous summer, which was enough for the Astros to spend their top pick (supplemental second round) and an over-slot $1.25 million on him. They handled him carefully in his pro debut last year, when he struggled to throw strikes during 41 2/3 innings in Low-A. Santos reached 96 mph with his fastball in 2021 but sat more around 90-91 later in the season, though he still had good carry on his four-seamer and nice sink on his two-seamer. His curveball has greater potential, showing signs of becoming a plus pitch with upper-70s velocity and plenty of depth. He's gaining aptitude for using a fading changeup that should give him an average third offering. Though Santos is athletic and doesn't have much effort in his delivery, he had difficulty repeating his mechanics in his introduction to pro ball.
