The hope is that he'll get more consistent as he fills out his lean 6-foot-4 frame, allowing him to provide enough strikes to remain a starter. He'll be 20 throughout the 2022 season, so he has plenty of time to figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros lost their first two choices in the 2020 and 2021 Drafts as sign-stealing punishment, and they used their first choice (supplemental second round) last June on Santos. Scouts consider him and 2018 Indians supplemental first-rounder Lenny Torres the two best prep arms to come out of New York City in the last decade. Santos didn't get a chance to pitch in the spring because of the coronavirus shutdown, but he proved himself enough on the high school showcase circuit the previous summer to earn an over-slot $1.25 million bonus. Santos has the type of high-spin four-seam fastball that Houston emphasizes, usually dealing at 90-94 mph and touching 96 with little effort in his delivery. His curveball may have even more upside, flashing as a true plus pitch with upper-70s velocity and quality depth. He shows aptitude for throwing a changeup with fade despite having little use for the offering as an amateur. Santos is athletic and has plenty of projection remaining in his 6-foot-4 frame, so he could have a plus fastball and curve along with a solid changeup as he gets stronger and more consistent. He repeats his delivery well and should have no difficulty throwing strikes. He's one of the better bets to make it as a starter among Astros pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays selected Messina in the 12th round and signed him away from his commitment to South Carolina for $550,000 in 2024, a sharp move by Toronto’s amateur scouting team to add a top prep arm to the system. Unfortunately, Messina was limited to just one outing in the Florida Complex League and dealt with arm issues throughout the summer, so we’re still left with his Draft profile and little competitive data to work with. When the Blue Jays landed Messina, he’d been up to 97 mph in high school and had touched 99 soon after, which he’s working to get back to now at the club's complex. His slider was showing the potential to be a legitimate plus pitch, with a changeup that trailed behind, all of which is a fairly standard profile for a top prep arm. But it still remains to be seen how these pitches play against young pro hitters. Messina has a thick, powerful build that should hold up to workloads as long as his arm can stay healthy. For 2026, getting into competitive games with some level of regularity would be a success, setting him up for a big ‘27 season. Whether he starts long-term is for his health to determine, but the base-level tools are there for an exciting relief profile down the road, too. Messina remains one of the biggest projects for the development staff in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It looked like Messina would play NCAA ball for South Carolina like his brother, Cole, whom the Rockies drafted in the third round in 2024, but the Blue Jays selected him in the 12th round and signed him away from that commitment for $550,000. This was a smart, aggressive move by the Blue Jays' Draft team, adding another high-upside high school arm to the system, where they hope he can benefit from their player development complex and new pitching philosophy. His 2025 was severely limited, though he was back to throwing bullpens by the end of the season. Messina was touching 97 mph in high school and regularly sits in the 93-95 range with his heater. (He's been up to 99 since then.) His breaking ball is his most advanced secondary pitch right now and shows legitimate potential, but like most high schoolers, he'll need to develop his feel for a changeup in the coming years. Messina has a strong build at 6-foot-2, 225 pounds, so while that may already be toward the ceiling of his physical projection and leads to Messina throwing with max effort, there's plenty to work with here. When fully healthy, Messina will be developed as a starter, of course, but if his control doesn't hold up to that consistently, there's some real potential for Messina to excel as a maxed-out, back-end bullpen arm. One advantage the Blue Jays have right now is time, making Messina one of this development staff's most important projects in 2026 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A steady riser in the 2024 Draft as an athletic righty out of Mountain Vista HS, Shepardson landed an over-slot $897,500 bonus from the Marlins in the fifth round of the 2024 Draft. In the process, he and brother Blake, a White Sox 11th-rounder out of San Francisco, became the first set of Colorado brothers to be selected and signed from the same Draft. The younger Shepardson made a strong first impression in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League with a 3.67 ERA and 47 strikeouts to just 18 walks in 41 2/3 innings before earning a late-season promotion to Single-A, where his control regressed in relief. Shepardson has added velocity since his prep days with his fastball averaging 94 mph and touching 96. With a low and wide release from his 6-foot-1 frame, he's able to impart intriguing ride and armside run on the pitch, which plays well up in the zone due to its flat approach angle. It's been hit hard in the past, although the pitch shape is improving. Because of that, he leans heavily on a sweeping 82-85 mph slider and an 86-88 mph cutter that both display excellent spin, with the former his best weapon to pick up swings-and-misses. Shepardson will show an 87-88 mph changeup with nice downward movement, and incorporating that pitch more should enable the other pitches to play up. His command is a work in progress, but he has the athleticism to repeat his drop-and-drive delivery consistently. Although questions will linger about his size and high school pitching remains a risky demographic, his strike-throwing and changeup could improve enough to the point that he projects as a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Shepardson brothers would have pitched together in college this spring at San Francisco if they hadn't both signed in the 2024 Draft. The Marlins paid Grant third-round money ($897,500) in the fifth round out of a Colorado high school, while the White Sox gave Blake $150,000 in the 11th round after he touched 100 mph as a Dons junior. Grant, who touched 98 mph after gaining 15 pounds as a prep senior, will make his pro debut in 2025. Added strength allowed Shepardson to add about 4 mph to his high-spin fastball, which now operates at 91-95 mph with carry and armside run. He also generates high spin rates on his low-80s slider, which shows signs of possibly becoming a plus pitch. With his 6-foot-1 frame and fastball/slider combination, he has elicited comparisons to Lance McCullers Jr. Shepardson also owns an intriguing mid-80s changeup that he throws with a Vulcan grip, and he can use an upper-70s curveball as a get-me-over pitch. His control and command are still works in progress, but he has the athleticism to provide consistent strikes as he continues to mature. He has no red flags with his delivery but lacks the prototypical size of a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It looked like Hettiger, who starred on the Los Angeles high school scene, was going to head to Oregon for college ball as the 2023 Draft wore on and he didn’t hear his name called. The Phillies had other ideas, using some extra bonus pool money when Day 3 started, going over slot to sign him for close to $400,000. He hasn’t put up big numbers as of yet, but he made some progress along the way in a rough first full season with Single-A Clearwater, then earning a promotion to High-A Jersey Shore while finishing the year in Double-A in 2025. A former switch-hitter who is now only hitting left-handed to help simplify things at the plate, Hettiger does have the makings of a solid approach at the plate, seeing a lot of pitches and drawing a lot of walks as evidenced by his career walk rate north of 16 percent heading into 2025. He finds the barrel a lot, and there’s some power for him to get to, but while he limits chase, the swing-and-miss is concerning (29.1 percent K rate). When he first entered pro ball, there were questions about Hettiger’s ability to catch long-term, especially because he hadn’t played much behind the dish in high school. He continues to get reps at first, but he’s become one of the better defenders at the position in the organization, with more than enough arm. If that continues, he could end up catching in the big leagues one day, getting at-bats against right-handed pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the first two days of the Draft came and went in 2023, Hettiger may have thought he was headed to Oregon for college ball. But the Phillies hadn’t quite used up their bonus pool money over the top 10 rounds and were able to nab Hettiger in Round 11, going over the Day 3 slot ($150,000) to sign him for just under $400,000. He made his very brief pro debut in the Florida Complex League last summer after signing. A switch-hitter, Hettiger appears to be better from the left side than the right, though he sees the ball well and has good at-bats from both sides of the plate. He’s used a small trigger in his swing in the past, but tends to be on time and has an advanced approach with excellent pitch recognition. There’s plenty of raw power to tap into, and that shows up more when he’s hitting left-handed. Strength gains this offseason could start showing up at the plate during his first full season. Hettiger didn’t catch a ton in high school, as the solid athlete moved around and played the infield corners quite a bit. There’s work to be done on his receiving, but he sets up well behind the plate. He’s already shown that he has more than enough arm to remain behind the plate, throwing out several potential basestealers in the FCL, with the Phillies having a bit more faith that he can stick there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Villarroel has an unusual profile as a 5-foot-8 catcher who can flash solid speed once he accelerates and has started games at five different positions in each of the last two seasons. Originally signed by the Astros for $10,000 out of Venezuela in 2022, he batted .259/.351/.388 with 20 steals in 100 games between two Class A levels in 2025. The Giants acquired him straight up for Kai-Wei Teng in January. For a compact guy, Villarroel has a quick right-handed stroke that generates surprising exit velocities and at least average raw power. He makes decent swing decisions and enough contact, but he gets so pull-conscious that he produces too many rolled-over grounders. He oddly struggles against lefties, and 17 of his 18 homers in his first four seasons came against righties. Quicker than most catchers, Villarroel will lose some speed as he spends more time behind the plate. He's not a lock to stay at catcher, however, because his receiving, blocking and throwing all need considerable work. He does have solid arm strength and has played every position in pro ball except for shortstop and pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $10,000 out of Venezuela by the Astros in 2022, Villarroel features one of the more unusual profiles in the Minors. He's a 5-foot-8 catcher with solid speed who started games at five different positions over the past two seasons. The Giants acquired him in a trade for Kai-Wei Teng in January. Despite his lack of physicality, Villarroel packs surprising strength in his compact frame and has a quick right-handed swing that generates higher exit velocities than most players his age. He could produce 15-20 homers per season once he adds more muscle and starts driving balls in the air more regularly. He has decent plate discipline though he can get pull-happy and roll over grounders to the left side. If Villarroel remains at catcher, the physical demands of the position will take a toll on his offensive production as well as his quickness. He has solid arm strength but will need time to polish his receiving, blocking and throwing. He also has seen action at every other position besides shortstop and pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hightower was a pop-up player out of the North Carolina prep ranks, and San Diego surprised many by swooping in to take him in the third round of the 2024 Draft, paying him slot money at $852,300 to go pro. He looked like one of the best players in the Arizona bridge league the summer after he signed, but then scuffled out of the gate in his official pro debut at Single-A Lake Elsinore. He was traded to the Orioles as part of the return for Ryan O’Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the Trade Deadline and didn’t hit much in 24 games with his new organization at Single-A Delmarva to finish the year. Scouts were bullish on Hightower’s offensive potential coming out of the Draft. He looks athletic and hitterish in the box with a high leg kick, has good bat speed and barrel control and a good feel for the strike zone. There was hope he could develop into at least average power, but he didn’t impact the ball much in his debut as he struggled to square balls consistently against advanced pitching. Hightower does show on-base acumen, as well as a mature approach and a strong baseball IQ that hint at an ability to make the necessary adjustments. Hightower can impact the game with his legs, as he is at least an above-average runner who has run the 60-yard dash in 6.6 seconds. He played exclusively shortstop with the Padres but split time between short and second base after the trade. He should still get opportunities at short, though he looks more like a second baseman long term. Wherever he ends up defensively, it’ll be the bat driving the profile -- that is, if he can develop offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hightower helped lead East Rowan High School to a 3A North Carolina state championship last spring and was a consistent performer during his time in school but tended to be overlooked in many Draft circles. Padres area scouts had interest in him, however, and he popped all the more in a South Carolina workout before the Draft. Still, San Diego surprised many when it swooped to take Hightower in the third round last summer and paid him slot money at $852,300 to go pro. After hanging back in extended spring training, Hightower scuffled over his first two months with Single-A Lake Elsinore, but had righted the ship with a solid July when he was sent to the Orioles as part of the return for Ryan O’Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the Trade Deadline. The former UNC commit stays back on balls well with a high leg kick and can find the barrel with a repeatable swing. His strike-zone knowledge is solid for his age, adding to the belief he could be an above-average hitter in time. There’s at least average power potential too, especially if he can continue to square balls against more advanced pitching. A 6.6 runner in the 60-yard dash, Hightower can also impact the game with his speed. He should get every chance to play shortstop for the time being, but some view him as a future bat-first second baseman too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers’ international scouting department did an excellent job finding Herrera and signing him for just $10,000 in August of 2019. It wasn’t until 2023 that he gained any real traction, pitching well in his second go-round in the Single-A Carolina League. Things clicked more the following year as he made his way to High-A ball when he was sent to the Rockies in the Nick Mears trade that July. He threw very well upon his arrival, but got shut down after six starts and he needed Tommy John surgery, so he missed all of the 2025 season. Herrera did return in time for instructional league play and was providing some optimism by dialing his fastball up to 97-98 mph in shorter stints. Before the injury, he was usually in the 92-94 mph range, getting groundball outs when he sinks it, but relying on his hard slider as his main out pitch. His feel to spin also helps him land a slightly slower curve and he has a changeup that he hadn’t committed to before he got hurt. The new pitching group with the Rockies are excited about working with Herrera because of his ability to shape different pitches, all coming out of the same slot. He got in some competitive innings in winter ball and he’ll pitch most of the 2026 season at age 22, trying to show he has the stuff and command to stick in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herrera got just $10,000 to sign with the Brewers in August 2019 and didn’t really make any significant waves until 2023 when he turned in a solid season in the Carolina League, his second year at the level. He broke out in 2024, pitching his way to High-A when he was sent to the Rockies as part of the return for Nick Mears in a July trade; Herrera then made six more solid starts for his new organization. Excitement for Herrera’s acquisition was dampened when he needed Tommy John surgery at the end of the year, forcing him out for all of 2025. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has three pitches in his arsenal that he was just starting to really learn how to use effectively when he went down. He typically throws his fastball in the 92-94 mph range and uses his hard above-average slider with bite as his go-to pitch. He misses plenty of bats with the pitch, showing the ability to backfoot lefties with it. He has a changeup, but it’s behind the other two offerings. Because of that slider, Herrera’s strikeout rate took a nice step forward in 2024 and he uses the two-seam variation of his heater to get a lot of ground-ball outs. He threw a lot more strikes as well last year, but the Rockies will have to wait until 2026 to see if that sticks and if he can refine a third pitch so that he can stick in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Already 21 years old when he signed with the Angels for just $10,000 in late June of 2022, Hurtado brought his arm strength to full-season ball in 2023 after a brief Dominican Summer League debut after signing. He had inconsistent results as a swingman type with Inland Empire, and a move to full-time starting up a level with High-A Tri-City led to similar surface numbers. Things clicked a bit more in Double-A in 2025, with Hurtado walking far fewer batters while also striking out less, finishing with a solid start in Triple-A. The Angels rolled the dice and didn’t protect him on the 40-man roster and nobody took him in the Rule 5 Draft. Hurtado has always been able to throw hard, and that didn’t change last year despite missing two months of the season. His fastball sits at around 95 mph and typically tops out in the upper-90s, though he’s no stranger with triple digits. The two-seamer is the effective one, thrown with good sink to routinely elicit groundball rates of 50 percent or higher. He has an 85-86 mph hard slider that can be effective but doesn’t miss as many bats as it should, especially since his fastball isn’t about whiffs. He’s continued to try to find a changeup that works, with limited success. The 25-year-old right-hander did improve his strike-throwing considerably last year, with just a 2.7 BB/9 rate all season. That, plus the ability he’s shown to log innings and hold his stuff deep into outings, gives him the chance to start, though he needs a third pitch and more missed bats to thrive. He could otherwise find some success as a sinker-slider type out of a bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Several months into the 2022 international signing period, the Angels landed Hurtado for the bargain price of $10,000. He was older, already 21 when he signed, so after getting started in the Dominican Summer League after signing, he went straight to full-season ball in 2023, starting very slowly but then figuring things out in the back end of the season. After starting and relieving with Single-A Inland Empire, he was a mainstay in High-A Tri-City’s rotation in 2024 with mixed results, though he did lead the Northwest League in innings pitched (138 2/3) and strikeouts (134). Now 24, it feels like in many ways Hurtado is still figuring out who he is as a pitcher. The 6-foot-2 right-hander can light up the radar gun, flirting with triple digits and sitting in the mid-90s with ease, throwing two-seamers with sink to get groundball outs. His slider, which he can run up into the upper-80s, has become his breaking ball – he’s all but scrapped a slower get-me-over curve – and he misses a lot of bats with it. He continues to try to find a third pitch, some kind of change-of-speed, that can work for him. Hurtado’s ability to land his two potentially plus pitches for strikes regressed in 2024 and he walked 5.3 per nine as a result. The Angels may not want to pull the plug on him starting just yet so he can work on his command and that third offering, but it’s hard not to dream about him as a sinker-slider reliever who’s throwing 100 mph-plus in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2022 international signing period opened in January of that year, the Angels found some high-price-tag talent right out of the gate, signing outfielders Nelson Rada and Randy De Jesus for seven figures apiece. They did some bargain shopping later on, getting Hurtado (then already 21 years old) for $10,000 at the end of June. He got his feet wet in the Dominican Summer League after signing and then came stateside for full-season ball in 2023. After really struggling out of the gate, he was very effective with Inland Empire, capping things off with seven innings of one-hit, shutout ball in a playoff start. After giving up 19 runs in six innings in April 2023, Hurtado posted a 3.50 regular-season ERA from May 1 on, striking out 10.3 per nine while walking just 2.8. He does it mostly with a fastball-slider combination. He sits around 95-96 mph with his heater and can flirt with triple digits, and he started throwing more two-seamers with sink as the year went on. Hurtado's mid-80s slider, which can touch 88-89 mph, is his go-to breaking ball that can miss bats. He has a little get-me-over 82-84 mph curve, and he’s working on a changeup, though he didn’t bring it into games in 2023 much. As Hurtado gained confidence and got stretched out as a starter during his U.S. debut last year, he started filling up the strike zone more consistently. Continued development on that front, along with finding an offspeed offering, could give him a chance to stay in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves were excited to see what Bagwell could do in his first full season of pro ball in 2025 after giving him third-round money ($822,500) in Round 6 to sign him away from his Missouri commitment. The Illinois high school standout had shown glimpses of upper-90s velocity early on in his senior season but didn’t maintain that. He hasn’t shown a return to that kind of crisp stuff since, though an oblique injury that cost him three months didn’t help and put the organizational enthusiasm on hold. Bagwell is a big, strong 6-foot-4, 230-pound right-hander with a feel for pitching and a potentially deep repertoire. When he was on the mound in 2025, his fastball sat at around 92 mph and topped out at 95, with some carry up in the zone. He needs to sharpen his secondary offerings, though his low-80s slider that features some sweep can miss bats at times and was particularly effective against right-handed hitters. He does have an 86 mph changeup he’ll use more against lefties that he’s still learning to trust, but it can get groundball outs. With a football player’s build, Bagwell’s physicality is a plus, even if there’s not much projection in there. There’s some effort in his delivery, though he managed to be around the zone more often than not. He’ll need to find a true out pitch as he looks to turn in a full, healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It seemed likely that Bagwell, a strong right-hander from the Illinois high school ranks, was going to honor his commitment to Missouri as the 2024 Draft approached. He had opened eyes by touching the upper 90s at the very start of his senior season but did not keep that kind of velocity up all year. He did head to the Draft combine and hit 96 mph during his brief outing. The Braves, never one to shy away from high-ceiling prep arms, took him in the sixth round and were able to keep him from heading to Mizzou by giving him $822,500, third-round money. For most of his senior season, the 6-foot-4, 230-pound Bagwell sat 89-94 mph with his fastball with decent carry up in the zone. His secondary stuff isn’t as consistently effective, with his 78-82 mph sweeping slider the best of his options. His upper-80s changeup is too firm, and like with many prep arms, he hasn’t thrown it a lot nor does he trust it much. Bagwell’s delivery does have some effort to it and that has led to command and control issues at times, even when pitching out of the stretch full time. He doesn’t offer much projection to his frame, but he’s more physical than many high schoolers, giving him upside to go along with some reliever risk.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dohm worked out of the bullpen at both Ball State and Mississippi State as a freshman and sophomore, respectively, before joining the Bulldogs rotation as a junior in 2024. A forearm strain slowed an otherwise hot start, but after re-establishing his health later in the spring and participating in the MLB Draft Combine, he went to the Mets in the third round and signed for below slot at $797,500. He put up solid numbers at Single-A and High-A to begin his first full season in 2025 and was moved to the Cardinals at the Trade Deadline as part of the return for closer Ryan Helsley. Dohm couldn’t find similar results at High-A Peoria after the deal and returned to the Midwest League to begin ’26. The 6-foot-4 right-hander shows a 93-96 mph four-seamer that can zip past batters at the top of the zone with impressive carry. He could reach 99 as a reliever in college in a sign that the pitch could be even more explosive in shorter stints if and when he needs to head back to the bullpen. His 83-86 mph slider can flash hard, late bite to get something move gloveside and similarly generate whiffs. He has much more trouble landing a changeup for strikes, and lefties have become a concern in pro ball without the third pitch. Dohm had started to show improved control as a Mets starter but hasn’t been able to replicate that in either of his Peoria stints so far. He needs batters to chase the high heaters and diving breaking balls to be effective, and that could be a challenge as he climbs. He has the chance for two above-average, bat-missing pitches though and could let them fly to their full potential with a move back to relief, if the control never comes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dohm pitched in relief at Ball State as a freshman in 2022 and transferred to the Mississippi State bullpen a year later. He finally got a chance to start with the Bulldogs as a junior and started fast with a 1.50 ERA and 32/4 K/BB ratio through his first four starts. But a forearm strain slowed him for much of the spring, and he mostly made short appearances when he fully returned in late May. He helped his case with two dominant innings against Texas A&M in the SEC tournament, participated in the MLB Draft Combine and went to the Mets in the third round before signing for below slot at $797,500. After Dohm posted solid numbers at Single-A and High-A to begin his first full season, New York traded him to St. Louis in a big move for closer Ryan Helsley at the Deadline. The healthy version of Dohm utilizes a 93-95 mph fastball with impressive carry to blow past hitters up in the zone. He ran the heater up to 99 in shorter stints as a sophomore reliever -- a sign of what’s in the tank -- and he relied heavily on the heater throughout his college career. His 82-85 mph slider plays off the heater well, darting late gloveside to get a healthy amount of whiffs. He’s mostly kept his upper-70s curveball in his pocket as a pro, but the offering gives him a vertical option too. His upper-80s changeup is often too firm and doesn’t stand as a huge weapon against lefties, leading to splits concerns. Dohm was a tremendous strike-thrower in his two years in Starkville, but because of the forearm issues -- including more during his sophomore campaign -- evaluators hadn’t seen that control hold up over long stints as a starter. He quieted some of those concerns in the first half of the 2025 season before the trade. The lack of a cambio could hurt him down the line, but there’s still starter upside here given his ability to fill the zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hidalgo began his pro career almost as an afterthought for the Angels at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, joining the organization for just $30,000. He wasn’t able to make his official pro debut until 2021, logging just 27 Arizona Complex League innings and missing some time with arm issues. He moved to full-season ball in 2022, but the injury bug bit again, with a rotator cuff strain shutting him down for the year in June. He returned for instructs before getting dealt to the Twins in November in return for Gio Urshela. While Hidalgo’s pure stuff doesn’t necessarily jump off the page, he does have some good ingredients to work with. His fastball sits around 92 mph, but it has some good riding life to it and he attended the Twins’ velocity camp to streamline his delivery in order to squeeze a little more velo out of him. His changeup is now his best secondary offering, a low-80s offering sold with good arm speed that elicited a 44 percent miss rate last year. In the past, Hidalgo has had more of a curve-like breaking ball that was slurvy and blurred into a slider at times. He’s worked with the Twins to scrap the curve action and focus on a firmer, harder true slider. His walk rate ticked up in 2022 to 4.4 per nine innings, but he has shown an overall feel for pitching and an ability to find the zone, with the streamlining of his delivery sure to help his overall control and command. If he can find a few ticks of velocity for the heater and continue to tighten up his breaking stuff, he could find his way into the back end of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels were aggressive on the international market when the 2019-20 signing period opened, handing out seven-figure bonuses to a pair of shortstops in Arol Vera and Adrian Placencia. At the other end of the spending ledger was Hidalgo, who joined the organization for just $30,000. After throwing well at instructs during the fall of 2020, he made his official pro debut in the Arizona Complex League, missing a little time with some arm issues. He made his full-season debut in 2022 with Single-A Inland Empire, though he was shut down for the year in late June. He did return to throw at instructs, and the Angels sent him to the Twins in a deal for infielder Gio Urshela in November. Not turning 20 until May, Hidalgo currently uses a two-pitch mix to get hitters out. His fastball sits in the low-90s, touching 94 mph at times, and he has a curve that he has a good feel to spin -- a breaking ball that could be above-average in time. He does have a changeup and sells it well with good arm speed, but it’s fringy right now. Hidalgo has impressed with advanced pitchability at times, especially for his age, showing an ability to throw his arsenal for strikes with a repeatable delivery. While his walk rate ticked up in 2022, he has the chance to have average overall command. He gets high marks for his competitiveness on the mound. Advancements in his fastball execution and development of his third pitch could help determine his future role with the Twins.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shortstops were all the rage for the Angels in the 2019-20 international signing period, with Arol Vera, Adrian Placencia and Jose Bonilla at the top of the bonus list for the organization when the period opened on July 2. That class also netted the Angels Hidalgo for $30,000, and he already opened eyes with his performance at instructs last fall. Hidalgo packs a combination of an advanced feel for pitching for his age and projection into his athletic 6-foot-1 frame. While he averaged around 92 mph and topped out at 94 with his fastball at instructs, added strength should lead to more velocity in the future. He features both a curve and a changeup, with good feel for spin for the former and a good idea of how to sell the latter with good arm speed, giving him two secondary pitches that also have some upside. What stood out more than anything at instructs was Hidalgo’s pitching know-how. He lands all three pitches for strikes, and he has a simple and athletic delivery he repeats well. If his first impression is any indication, Hidalgo should see his name rise up prospects lists as he continues to physically mature.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor set a Central Michigan record with 125 strikeouts while winning Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year honors as a sophomore in 2021, then encored by breaking his own mark with 126 the following spring. The Astros selected him in the supplemental second round, making him the Chippewas' highest pick since 1986 second-rounder Kevin Tapani. His strikeout rate (13.5 per nine innings) in his 2023 pro debut ranked fourth among Minor Leaguers who worked as many as his 84 innings. Taylor's low-90s fastball features outstanding metrics because he has a 6-foot-5 frame with a high arm slot and plenty of extension, plus he backspins the ball so well that it has tremendous carry up in the zone. He has added significant strength since turning pro, weighing closer to 225 pounds than his listed 190, and the Astros hope that results in added velocity that will make his heater even more effective. After throwing roughly 80 percent fastballs in college, he's trying to refine the rest of his repertoire. His best secondary pitch is his low-80s slider, though he'll switch to a tighter version after having difficulty controlling a sweepier version in 2023. Both his upper-70s curveball and low-80s changeup are fringy and leave him vulnerable against left-handers, who batted .313/.405/.458 against him last season. He repeats his delivery well enough but will need to provide more strikes to reach his ceiling as a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2021 Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year, Taylor set a Central Michigan record with 125 strikeouts and then broke the mark with 126 whiffs last spring. He left two starts early with elbow tightness but didn't miss a turn in the rotation and looked good in the NCAA regional playoffs against Florida. The Chippewas' highest pick since 1986 second-rounder Kevin Tapani, he signed for $804,700 as a supplemental second-rounder and will make his pro debut in 2023. Taylor's fastball sits around 90 mph and tops out at 94, yet it rarely gets squared up. His heater is an analytical darling because his high spin rates produce tremendous carry and he uses his 6-foot-5 frame to create plenty of extension that throws hitters off. He relied on his fastball roughly 80 percent of the time in college, with his seldom-used 78-82 mph changeup with fade and sink serving as his most reliable secondary pitch. The Astros will work with Taylor to improve his breaking pitches and add strength. His tight 78-82 mph slider is average at best, while his soft mid-70s curveball is more of a fringy offering. He does a good job of keeping his long limbs in sync and repeating his delivery, though he has battled the strike zone more than expected in his first taste of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $350,000 in January 2022, Plaz immediately raised the expectations bar by hitting .382 with a 1.206 OPS in 32 Dominican Summer League games. There were some bumps, both of the production and injury variety, when he came to the United States, though he did start to find his power stroke in 2024 when he homered 15 times in the Florida State League, albeit with a ton of swing-and-miss. The injury bug bit again in 2025 with a fractured finger on his left hand limiting him to just 66 games, though he made up for lost time and swung the bat well in the Arizona Fall League. When Plaz is healthy and squares up the ball, the right-handed batter hits the ball really hard. He was in the upper echelon of Florida State League hitters in terms of data like exit velocity, barrel and hard-hit percentages. In 2025, he even cut down his strikeout rate, which had been an issue, while sticking to a better overall approach. There’s plenty of power to spare and to all fields, but he’s going to have to learn better pitch recognition after a 40 percent chase rate last season. There’s work to be done for Plaz on the defensive side of things as well. He has plenty of arm for the position, but the consistency of his receiving has been lacking. His power bat might profile at first base, but there aren’t too many sub-6-foot right-right players at that infield corner in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yordany De Los Santos and Tony Blanco Jr. were the top two bonus-getters in the 2022 international class for the Pirates, but they gave out 14 bonuses of six figures or higher. Plaz, hailing from San Felix, Venezuela, was in that mix, getting $350,000 in January and then putting up huge numbers in the Dominican Summer League. He followed up that 1.206 OPS summer with a rough go of it stateside, limited to 33 games because of injuries and finishing with a .144/.359/.237 line. He was one of the better power hitters in the Florida State League in 2024, finishing with 15 homers, but also showed what he needs to work on both in the box and behind the plate. Strong and compact, Plaz can really impact the ball with quality hard contact from the right side of the plate. He has good bat speed but is a bit of a free swinger, leading to a 28.4 percent strikeout rate and overall high miss-and-chase rates while with Bradenton. He does draw walks, but he'll need to refine his approach so he can get to his power more consistently with the ability to drive the ball to all fields, though most of his over-the-fence pop has come to his pull side. Plaz's best tool defensively is his arm, which is at least above average, but the rest of his catching needs work. Some of it is focus-related and could improve with maturity and more reps, but he doesn't always block or receive well and has seen time at first, where a right-right 5-foot-11 profile might be tough. If the light switches on, he could be a power-first, power-armed backstop in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles tend to covet bat-to-ball skills at the top of the Draft, but they pivoted big time by taking toolsy outfielder Vance Honeycutt with their first pick of the 2024 Draft. Ten picks later, they reverted back to their comfort zone by selecting O’Ferrall with the PPI pick they were awarded for Gunnar Henderson winning 2023 AL Rookie of the Year Award. O’Ferrall was fresh off a college starring turn for Team USA and the University of Virginia, where he set the single-season hits record as a sophomore and was named the nation’s top shortstop as a junior. But he was challenged in his first full season of pro ball, finishing with a .626 OPS, though he briefly reached Double-A at the end of the year. In college, O’Ferrall’s contact skills made him a steady performer whose excellent fundamentals elevated his game. He’s shown good plate discipline in the pros, as well as an ability to grind out at-bats and get on base. But his lack of impact at the plate drags down his overall offensive ceiling. He doesn’t hit the ball particularly hard despite making a lot of contact, and needs to drive the baseball more consistently to be an average hitter. His footspeed is a tick better than average but plays up because he’s a smart baserunner, helping him swipe 42 bases last season. O’Ferrall has enough quickness and range defensively to handle shortstop, though his just-average arm may fit better at second. His strong instincts, makeup and baseball IQ should help him move around, enhancing his floor. Though he lacks eye-popping tools, O’Ferrall plays hard and does a lot of little things well, making him the kind of player who is greater than the sum of his parts, but he probably needs to hit more to be an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest in a long line of quality Draft talent to come out of the University of Virginia, O’Ferrall set the school’s single-season hits record as a sophomore, starred for Team USA that summer and was named the nation’s top shortstop as a junior. The Orioles took him with their second Day 1 selection in the 2024 Draft (No. 32 overall), using the PPI pick they were awarded for Gunnar Henderson winning Rookie of the Year to bring in a steady performer whose excellent fundamentals elevate his game and allow him to get every ounce out of his ability. While he showed good plate discipline during his first full season, he lacked impact, finishing with a .626 OPS, almost entirely with High-A Aberdeen. From Adley Rutschman to Colton Cowser to Enrique Bradfield Jr., the Orioles have consistently coveted bat-to-ball skills at the top 42 b of the Draft (with a few exceptions) under their current regime. O’Ferrall has impressive abilities in this category. He walked more than he struck out in college, has very good feel for the barrel and makes sound swing decisions, which allow him to grind out at-bats and get on base. That continued in 2025, with an 11.4 percent walk rate and just a 14.9 pct K rate. He relies on being a tough out because his power is limited, and while the lack of pop might drag down O'Farrell's overall offensive ceiling, he could develop into an above-average hitter. His footspeed is a tick better than average, and he can steal bases and rarely makes mistakes between the lines, leading him to swipe 42 bases last season. Defensively, too, O’Ferrall is greater than the sum of his parts. Good footwork, positioning and quickness help him overcome a just-average but accurate arm, and while he has enough range to stick at shortstop, those skills would help him move around the infield if necessary, and he saw time at second base in 2025. While O’Ferrall doesn’t have eye-popping tools, he has plus instincts, makeup and a high floor with probably enough upside to develop into an everyday player, and a floor as a utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery limited Ray to bullpen duty as a Draft-eligible sophomore at Alabama in 2022, but he used an impressive showing in the Cape Cod League that summer to push himself into the fourth round, where he signed with the D-backs for slot money at $565,800. Ray looked the part of a starter as a Northwest League All-Star in his first full season, posting a 3.81 ERA with 123 strikeouts in 99 1/3 innings for High-A Hillsboro and made three late starts for Double-A Amarillo in the summer of ’23. A right forearm flexor strain delayed his 2024 debut until June, and he didn’t make it out of the Texas League in his return, finishing with a 5.22 ERA and 68 strikeouts in 70 2/3 frames. Ray made up for the lost time with five starts in the Arizona Fall League. Take Ray’s time in Double-A with ample grains of salt because pitching in hitter-friendly Amarillo – where he allowed 11 of his 16 homers and had a .560 slugging-against -- is no joke. But whether it be the conditions or time coming back from the injury, the former Crimson Tide hurler’s stuff took a step back in effectiveness in 2024. His 92-94 mph fastball shows average velocity for the modern era, and while his 83-86 mph slider and 82-84 mph changeup both flash above average, neither did much to fool hitters outside the zone. His upper-70s curveball offered another breaking look. The continued forearm issues likely didn’t help Ray’s control numbers, nor did the more advanced hitting approaches. It’s still worth wondering what the righty can do in a healthier campaign, and he could use one ahead of his Rule 5 eligibility next offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ray underwent Tommy John surgery before he could throw a pitch for Alabama in 2021 and worked as a reliever in his return as a Draft-eligible sophomore a year later, striking out 49 in 31 1/3 innings. After a standout turn in the Cape Cod League to help boost his Draft stock, he went to the D-backs in the fourth round in 2022 and signed for exact slot at $565,800. Ray proved to be durable and effective in his first full season, posting a 3.81 ERA with 123 K’s in 99 1/3 innings for High-A Hillsboro (where he was a Northwest League All-Star) before getting three starts for Double-A Amarillo to round off the campaign. The 6-foot-3 right-hander could run his fastball into the upper-90s at times in college and the pros, but his velocity can be inconsistent all over the 90-96 mph range. He typically aims to work the four-seamer high, allowing his secondaries to play lower in the zone. Ray can snap a sharp upper-80s slider down and away from righties, and he’s added a nice 82-85 mph changeup that drops armside below lefty bats. Thanks to that development, he had a higher K rate against lefties (36.4 percent) than righties (23.7) last season. An upper-70s curveball and upper-80s cutter round out the arsenal. Ray walked 7.9 percent of his High-A batters but saw more control issues after his Double-A promotion. He generally spots his pitches well, and that command may only get better as he moves away from TJ surgery and builds up more of a starting résumé. With this deep a repertoire, he has pushed relief further into the rearview and has the upside of a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ray was meant to begin his collegiate career at Alabama in the spring of 2021 but needed Tommy John surgery before throwing his first official pitch for the Crimson Tide. He returned as a Draft-eligible hurler in 2022 and worked exclusively out of the bullpen, earning eight saves while posting a 4.60 ERA with 49 strikeouts in 31 1/3 innings. In an attempt to win over clubs, he kept pitching in the Cape Cod League and was a standout for Yarmouth-Dennis, striking out 17 while walking only two in 11 frames. The D-backs were convinced enough to make him a fourth-round pick and signed him for exact slot at $565,800. Ray made eight Minor League starts to round out his summer but suffered in the hitter-friendly California League, where he surrendered five homers in 11 2/3 innings. The 6-foot-3 right-hander touched as high as 97 mph in the spring of 2022, but his fastball should settle in a little lower than that with some carry. His mid-80s slider was his best pitch in college and provided the biggest boost to his high K rate, while a high-70s curveball provided a different kind of breaking look. He’ll need to develop a changeup of some sort as he gets lengthened out in pro ball and sees left-handers multiple times per outing. From the moment they drafted him, the D-backs believed Ray’s pitch mix and solid control could help him become a starter in the pros. While his limited innings may hurt his current stock, they also amp his potential to grow and improve the quality of his stuff with additional experience. The work to become a No. 4/5 starter will begin in earnest in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz signed with the Rangers for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent out of Puerto Rico in July 2021, and after training with Carlos Delgado and wearing contact lenses in games, he really started to take off by the 2023 season. He was named South Atlantic MVP and Rangers’ Minor League Player of the Year that campaign after going deep 33 times and slugging .619 across 109 games (80 of which were with High-A Hickory). Ortiz needed a second-half rebound with Double-A Frisco in ’24, returned there in ’25 and hit .283/.388/.565 with nine homers in 41 games with Triple-A Round Rock after an early August promotion. The Rangers added him to the 40-man roster as Rule 5 protection and traded him to the Nationals in January as part of the prospect return for MacKenzie Gore. Standing 5-foot-10, Ortiz packs a punch from the left side of the box with significant strength. It’s already plus raw power (as evidenced by a 106.6 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity), and he gets to it in games with strong lift-and-pull tendencies. There is 25-30-homer potential here at peak. Ortiz isn’t the most selective hitter though, and he’s struggled against left-handers in the upper Minors. He’s also liable to really undercut balls, leading to a lot of infield popups that hurt his BABIP and overall production. Ortiz is a bottom-of-the-scale runner too, so he won’t pick up extra bags on balls to the gap or many infield singles. Any production from his bat will come from its thunder. He’s moved between first base and right field in recent years, but his lack of range and arm make him a better fit for the cold corner. Washington has an opening there, and he could slide in as the broad (and powerful) side of a platoon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2021, Ortiz looked overmatched in his first full pro season before improving rapidly once he started training with fellow Puerto Rican Carlos Delgado, shortened his left-handed stroke and began wearing contact lenses during games. He won High-A South Atlantic League MVP and Rangers Minor League player of the year honors in 2023, when he topped the Minors in slugging (.619) and ranked fourth in homers (33) and OPS (.990). He recovered from a rough first half at Double-A last year to bat .309/.412/.636 with 15 homers in his final 43 games. Ortiz’s power took him to Triple-A in 2025, and after he was added to the 40-man roster in November, he was traded to the Nationals two months later as part of the MacKenzie Gore deal. Ortiz's bat speed in his lefty stroke and his strength give him well-above-average raw power that plays to all fields, and he began to tap into it more often when he stopped swinging for the fences. A more selective approach helped him find better pitches to attack, enabling him to hit them harder and drive them in the air more frequently. He tightened his strike zone in 2024, cutting his K rate to 22 percent from 27 percent the year before, but struggled against breaking balls and left-handers. Most of Ortiz's value will come from his offense because he's a well-below-average runner with fringy arm strength. He's a decent defender at first base, though he needs to reduce his errors. While he has looked better than expected as a right fielder in the Arizona Fall League and Double-A, the outfield corners are still a stretch because of his limited range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz attended high school and trained at the Carlos Beltran Baseball Academy in his native Puerto Rico before following the program's pipeline to Florida Southwestern State JC. Signed for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2021, he didn't do much in his first full pro season but has taken off since shortening his left-handed swing and beginning to wear contact lenses during games. He led the Minors in slugging (.619) and ranked fourth in homers (33) and OPS (.990) in 2023, then shook off a rough first half in Double-A last season to slash .309/.412/.636 with 15 homers in his final 43 games. Ortiz's strength and bat speed create well-above-average raw power. He began to tap into it more in games by toning down his approach, which allowed him to hit the ball in the air and with premium exit velocities on a more regular basis. Strikeouts always will be part of his package but he's showing more discipline than he had in the past and will draw his share of walks. Because Ortiz is a well-below-average runner with fringy arm strength, there's a lot of pressure on his bat. He's an adequate defender at first base who needs to cut down on his errors. He looked better than expected in right field during the Arizona Fall League and in Double-A, but the outfield corners are still a stretch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Urbina was ranked No. 6 on MLB Pipeline’s international prospect list when the 2018-19 signing period began, and the Twins gave the outfielder $2.75 million to sign right out of the gate on July 2, the third-highest bonus given to a player in the signing period. He’s shown some glimpses of ability, especially in terms of his approach at the plate, but it’s come without much impact and his development has been impeded by the pandemic in 2020 and then visa issues that kept him from playing in 2022 until late June. There is no question the right-handed-hitting outfielder knows how to control the strike zone. He makes a ton of contact and draws walks, bringing a 17 percent strikeout rate and a walk rate just over 11 percent with him into the 2023 season. But he’s yet to show a consistent ability to do any damage or tap into any power. He did hit the ball a bit harder in 2022 with more line drives and fly balls, but he’ll have to show more to live up to the initial power projections. Urbina has slowed down some since signing and will have to stay on top of his body and conditioning to maximize his ability. He’s a center fielder by trade, but there is growing concern he won’t maintain his speed to stay up the middle. A move to a corner might be necessary, which puts even more pressure on him to be a more productive hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in the 2018-19 international signing class, Urbina got $2.75 million to sign with the Twins right at the start of the signing period. He showed off his advanced feel to hit and speed during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 and got pushed up to full-season ball in 2021, an aggressive assignment that didn’t go so well as the outfielder finished with a .585 OPS. His 2022 debut was delayed until late June because of visa issues. Despite the struggles, Urbina still showed off a strong knack for making contact and controlling the strike zone, with a 12.3 percent walk rate and a strikeout rate of just 18.7 percent. The issue was the quality of contact, with a lack of physicality leading to a lack of impact. He did work this offseason in Venezuela on adding strength and engaging his lower half more to give him a more impactful swing. Adding angle to that swing while having better pitch selection in terms of which ones to put into play will also help his offensive upside. While Urbina appeared to slow down a tick, the strength and conditioning work he put in this offseason should help in that regard as well. He has good instincts on defense and can still play center field even if he’s not quite the burner he was when he first signed. Urbina could have benefitted from a summer in a short-season league last year, but given how young he is, there’s time for him to reach the ceiling the Twins thought he had when they signed him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Urbina was ranked No. 6 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list when the 2018-19 signing period began, and he got the third-highest bonus in the class, $2.75 million, to sign with the Twins. He showed off an exciting offensive skill set in his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 and continued to impress with how he carried himself during his time at instructs last fall. Though he’ll be just 19 for nearly all of the 2021 season, Urbina really stands out for his feel for the game. He has incredible bat-to-ball skills and controls the strike zone very well, walking more than he struck out in the DSL and whiffing in just 6.5 percent of his plate appearances. He has a good swing from the right side of the plate and tends not to chase out of the zone. The only question is how much impact he’ll have, as he needs to add strength to get to what could be decent power in the future. Urbina is a plus runner right now, but beyond his pure speed, his tempo in the game helps him both be a basestealing threat and to play excellent outfield defense. While he played mostly center field during his debut, he looks very comfortable in all three outfield spots, with good instincts and routes, with the Twins thinking he could end up a plus defender in whatever spot he settles into.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 De Andrade was in the top half of MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 International Prospects list when he signed with the Twins in January 2021 for $2.2 million. After a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, he held his own stateside in the Florida Complex League. In 2023, he moved to full-season ball for the first time and showed off some of his tools with 11 homers and 20 steals in pitching-friendly Fort Myers. He wasn’t able to build off that in 2024 when an ankle injury that required surgery ended his season with High-A Cedar Rapids after just 29 games. He was supposed to head to the Arizona Fall League, but wasn’t ready, though he’s been given a clean bill of health for 2025. With the injury behind him, the hope is De Andrade can get back to building off a decent foundation of contact skills and ability to control the zone. He limits strikeouts, draws walks and was making better swing decisions overall, though his knack for contact has led to higher chase rates. He’s continued to try to get better swing angles, and while the surface numbers don’t show it during his small Midwest League showing in cold weather, his ground-ball rate went down as he started leveraging the ball in the air more. De Andrade was a fringy runner before the injury and he’ll have to work to maintain his athleticism. He has the hands and arm to play shortstop, which is where he’ll mostly play in 2025, though he’ll continue to get work at third and second as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects on the international market when the signing period opened in January 2021, De Andrade received a $2.2 million bonus from the Twins to sign then went about showing off his solid fundamental skills, even if they didn’t show up in eye-popping numbers. He was solid in the Dominican Summer League during his debut, showed some abilities to make adjustments when he came to the United States and played in the Florida Complex League in 2022 and continued making some progress during his full-season debut in 2023. His move to High-A in 2024 ended after just 29 games with an ankle injury that required surgery. From the outset of his pro career, De Andrade has shown off excellent bat-to-ball skills. He had stretches early on when he was making too much contact, chasing pitches out of the zone and getting himself out. Work he started putting in during his FCL season to cut his chase rate carried over to the Florida State League last year as he continues to refine his approach, make better swing decisions and draw more walks, all while still keeping the strikeouts relatively in check. He also made some subtle adjustments with his mechanics to get better swing angles and not hit the ball on the ground as much. He’s continuing to learn how to get the ball in the air more and hit the ball harder, which should help increase his power output. With good hands and a strong enough arm, combined with excellent instincts, De Andrade has a chance to stick at shortstop even though he’s a fringy runner. He’ll have stay on top of his conditioning so he doesn’t slow down too much to stay at the premium position. Though he played short exclusively in 2023, he has seen some time at third, which would put more pressure on his bat to produce.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 14 on MLB Pipeline’s Top International Prospects list when the signing period opened in January 2021, De Andrade was one of two players to get seven-figure bonuses from the Twins. The Venezuelan infielder signed for $2.2 million and had a solid, if unspectacular, debut in the Dominican Summer League. He came stateside in 2022, and after a rough start, showed improvement as the Florida Complex League season wore on. De Andrade’s knack for making contact is a blessing and a curse. He has very impressive bat-to-ball skills, having struck out in just over 15 percent of his plate appearances over his first two summers of pro ball. The down side is that he’s fallen into the habit of expanding the zone too much, something he got away with in the DSL, but then he was chasing and missing at the start of the FCL season. He focused on hunting pitches over the plate after his first month, and that cut his chase rate in half while sharply boosting his walk rate. He’s made some small swing adjustments as well, because he used to enter too steeply, which led to too many ground balls. That tweak plus added strength should help him turn his contact into more impact. While De Andrade doesn’t run particularly well, his instincts, hands and arm give him the chance to stick at shortstop, especially if he follows through with his conditioning. He’s seen time at third base already and could slide over if he slows down more, though that will put a little more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the good things about the international signing deadline not starting until January the last couple of years is that teams can get an almost immediate first impression of their new player that summer. That’s what happened with De Andrade, a Venezuelan infielder who had been training in the Dominican Republic. Ranked right in the middle of MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list, De Andrade signed with the Twins for $2.2 million and then went out and had a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League. De Andrade has the chance to be a plus hitter in time from the right side of the plate and stood out with his ability to control the strike zone, especially given his age (17) and lack of experience. There is bat speed and the ability to use all fields, though he’s content right now to focus on contact, and he did that well, rarely striking out even if he was a bit over-aggressive. The next step in his offensive development will be to work on driving the ball and doming more damage, something that will come as he physically matures. The teenaged infielder saw time at shortstop and third during his debut. The Twins think he has the chance to play up the middle for a while because of his actions, hands, arm and instincts. He’s not particularly speedy, so there is some thought that sliding over to the hot corner eventually might be in his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2020-21 international signing period, which officially opened in mid-January, featured a class that was particularly deep at shortstop. De Andrade, a Venezuelan infielder who had been training in the Dominican Republic, was ranked No. 16 overall on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects rankings, the eighth shortstop on the list. The Twins liked his size and athleticism enough to give him $2.2 million to sign. De Andrade has the ingredients to develop into an impact hitter. He shows off excellent bat speed from the right side of the plate and can drive the ball to all fields. There are flashes of average power now, with above-average pop in the future possible as he adds strength to his lean frame. Added strength would also help him get close to being an average runner. Because of his soft hands, good footwork and arm, there’s a chance De Andrade could stick at short. It’s more likely, given his speed, that he’ll eventually slide over to third as he physically matures, where his actions and instincts could make him an above-average defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A California prep product, Barber earned an over-slot $1 million bonus as a 2019 fourth-rounder because the Astros were intrigued by his power/speed combination. But his pop hasn't fully developed and he has lost some quickness, in large part because of shoulder, ankle and hip injuries that limited him to 189 games in his first five years as a pro. He played in a career-high 79 contests in 2023, batting .244/.358/.433 in Double-A. When fully healthy, Barber has shown the ability to work counts, launch balls in the air and employ the entire field from the left side of the plate. He has the bat speed and strength to provide 20 homers per season, and his power plays to all parts of the ballpark. He hasn't produced high batting averages outside of 2022 and he hasn't done much damage against southpaws, so he might not be more than a platoon option. Barber once flashed plus speed but now is an average runner who doesn't take a lot of chances on the bases. After dividing time between all three outfield positions but seeing more action in center field earlier in his career, he only had duty on the corners in 2023. With fringy arm strength, he's better suited for left field than right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros have been waiting for Barber to take off since signing him to an over-slot $1 million bonus as a fourth-rounder from a California high school in 2019. He has shown one of the best power/speed combinations in the system when he has taken the field, but the pandemic (2020), shoulder surgery (2021) and shoulder and ankle ailments (2022) limited him to 110 games in four years as a pro. He batted .294/.400/.439, mostly in High-A, while playing in a career-high 66 contests last season. When healthy, Barber has shown a promising ability to work counts, lift balls in the air and use the entire field. He's still learning to drive balls to his pull side, though he has enough bat speed and strength to produce 20-homer power from the left side of the plate. He hasn't been effective against southpaws, though he's an intelligent hitter who could make adjustments once he gets regular at-bats. Barber has settled in as a solid runner as he has matured physically. He's aggressive on the bases and has improved his reads and routes in center field, where he's an average defender. He has arm strength to match and divided his time almost equally among all three outfield spots in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barber's combination of power potential and speed earned him an over-slot $1 million bonus as a fourth-round pick in 2019. Because of the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and labrum surgery on his right (non-throwing) shoulder in 2021, he accrued just 141 at-bats in his first three years as a pro, including only 42 in full-season ball. The Astros still have high hopes for him and believe his tools and work ethic will allow him to rebound from all that lost time, and one club official likens his intensity to Alex Bregman's. Despite his youth and inexperience, Barber already shows the ability to work counts and launch balls in the air. He has the bat speed and strength to produce at least average power from the left side of the plate, though he can get too pull-conscious. Houston has had him focus on driving balls from gap to gap and he did a better job of using the entire field during his brief 16-game stint last season before getting hurt. Barber presently flashes plus speed but likely will be more of a solid runner once he matures physically. He makes the most of his quickness with an aggressive nature on the bases and in center field, where his reads and routes have improved. His average to solid arm strength fits at all three outfield positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barber had one of the better power/speed combinations in the 2019 prep class, which helped him garner an over-slot $1 million bonus as a fourth-rounder. He finished strong in his pro debut and divided his 2020 between the independent City of Champions circuit (where he was the youngest player at age 19), a brief appearance at Houston's alternate site and instructional league. Besides his tools, he has impressed the Astros with his work ethic and focus, with one club official comparing his intensity to Alex Bregman's. Barber has a mature offensive approach for a youngster, showing the ability to work counts and use the entire field. With his quick left-handed swing, projectable strength and propensity for launching the ball in the air, he should develop at least average power. Houston had him focus on driving the ball from gap to gap during instructional league and was pleased with his progress, though his development was limited to just 16 games this year before he injured his shoulder and required season-ending surgery. With present plus speed and an aggressive nature, Barber is a potential 20-20 player. He may slow down a bit as he fills out, which might dictate a move from center to right field. He played all three outfield positions during his pro debut and has the solid arm strength and offensive ability to profile in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After turning down the Pirates as a sophomore-eligible 40th-rounder at Indiana in 2019, Dunham raked in the New England Collegiate League and as a junior, only to go unpicked in the five-round 2020 Draft. Since signing, he quickly became an organization favorite with his hard-nosed play, and he concluded his first pro season by winning the Arizona Fall League's 2021 Breakout Player of the Year Award. He starred in the playoffs as Double-A Somerset won the Eastern League championship last season. Dunham doesn't have a true standout tool but can do a little bit of everything offensively. He makes hard contact with his compact left-handed stroke, has the bat speed and strength to generate 20-homer power and owns the discipline to take walks if pitchers try to work around him. Though he has fringy speed, he's instinctive and aggressive on the bases and finished third in the Eastern League with 37 steals in 44 tries last year. Dunham began his college career as a first baseman but has played mostly left field since. He has decent range and fringy-to-average arm strength that's a bit stretched when he gets time in right field. While his ceiling seems to be that of a second-division regular, he plays with constant energy and continues to exceed expectations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dunham turned down the Pirates as a sophomore-eligible at Indiana taken in the 40th round in the 2019, then performed well in the New England Collegiate League and as a junior, only to go unpicked in 2020's shortened five-round Draft. After signing for the maximum $20,000 permitted for a nondrafted free agent, he quickly became an organization favorite with his play and his intensity. He advanced to High-A during his 2021 pro debut before winning the Arizona Fall League's breakout player of the year award. Dunham provides a little bit of everything as an offensive player. He makes repeated hard contact with a compact left-handed stroke and disciplined approach. He has enough bat speed and strength to produce 20 homers on an annual basis, will take walks if pitchers refuse to challenge him and used his average speed and aggressiveness on the bases to swipe 39 bags in 45 tries last year between the Minors and AFL. After starting his college career as a first baseman, Dunham spent his last two years with the Hoosiers and most of his debut in left field. He's a decent outfielder with fringy to average arm strength that doesn't really fit in right field. His ceiling might be as a second-division regular, but he's an overachiever who could exceed that expectation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arias trained with Sandy Nin, a member of MLB’s Trainer Partnership Program, in the Dominican Republic before signing with the Orioles for $600,000 as part of their 2022 international class, one of their first handing out six and seven-figure bonuses. After a solid debut that year, he emerged as one of the top performers in the Florida Complex League a year later. And though he didn’t tear the cover off the ball stateside in 2024, he held his own as one of the youngest players in the Carolina League and reached High-A Aberdeen as a 19-year-old by the end of the year. One of the O’s more intriguing international pickups since entering the market, Arias is a switch-hitting infielder with solid tools across the board and projectable athleticism. He’s hit-over-power, with a strong understanding of the strike zone and approach at the plate for his age, which is why he has a chance to develop into an average hitter despite not impacting the baseball much yet. That might change as Arias adds strength, as his wiry frame still has room to fill out and he can already find the barrel and produce high exit velocities for his size. He’s an average runner but can get too aggressive on the bases and run into outs. Defensively, Arias isn’t a finished product, but he has enough range and quickness to stay up-the-middle and an arm that is a tick above average and would serve him well at either shortstop or second base. Even without any standout tools, Arias’ projection and profile give him a high floor as an up-the-middle regular if he continues developing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 40 | Overall: 40 One of the Orioles' most intriguing pickups of the 2021-22 international signing period, Arias signed for $600,000 out of the Dominican Republic after working with Sandy Nin, a member of MLB’s Trainer Partnership Program. He had a decent debut and boosted his profile significantly in 2023 in the Florida Complex League, where he grew into more power and looked like one of the circuit’s better all-around players, though he struggled to find similar results with a move to full-season Delmarva in 2024. A switch-hitting infielder, Arias controls the strike zone well and demonstrates good bat-to-ball skills while flashing raw power that could be a plus tool in the future. He’s not the biggest guy, but he’s able to generate pop thanks to an excellent approach from both sides of the plate. Arias also displays on-base acumen advanced for a player his age. He’s an aggressive hitter who swings at strikes, and while that could continue to work for him, he will need to fine-tune his swing decisions at the higher levels to avoid being exploited against better pitching. There is still plenty of room for his wiry frame to fill out, and he’s athletic enough to maintain his speed as he adds strength. He’s an average runner whose good instincts enable his speed to play up and he knows how to steal a base. Arias’ defense has been a work in progress since he signed as a shortstop, and he saw almost equal time at short, second base and third in 2023. His above-average arm strength fits well at other spots and he still has the chance to grow into a bat-first infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Another product of the Orioles’ growing presence in Latin America, Arias signed for $600,000 out of the Dominican Republic to profile as one of the club’s more intriguing players of its 2022 class. A switch-hitting shortstop with power potential, Arias trained with Sandy Nin, a member of MLB’s Trainer Partnership Program, prior to signing. He then showed on-base acumen and good wheels during a decent debut in the Dominican Summer League. Arias’ ceiling is tied up in his hitting ability. He demonstrates an advanced approach and good bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate, while flashing power that projects as a plus tool in the future. At 6-foot-1, 155 pounds, he’s tall and wiry, with plenty of room to fill out as his body matures. Adding strength should also allow him to drive the ball more consistently from both sides of the plate, and he’s athletic enough to remain a good runner with additional weight. Arias showed more base-stealing acumen than expected during his debut, going 10-for-13 in stolen base attempts across 46 DSL games. His defense is still a work-in-progress, with actions that need to be fine-tuned but enough arm strength to stay at shortstop at least in the short-term. Even if the Orioles’ shortstop depth forces a move to second or third, Arias could develop into a switch-hitting middle-of-the-field player with a varied skillset in the Erick Aybar or Elvis Andrus mold.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles have spent years improving their scouting presence in Latin America under executive vice president general manager Mike Elias and international scouting director Koby Perez, resulting in the franchise’s deepest class of international signings in 2021. One of the more intriguing players in that class was Arias, a switch-hitting shortstop with power potential, who signed for $600,000 out of the Dominican Republic. Arias trained with Sandy Nin, a member of MLB’s Trainer Partnership Program, prior to signing. Arias’ signature tool is his hitting ability. He demonstrates an advanced approach and good bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate, while flashing power that projects as a plus tool in the future. He’s tall but lanky, with plenty of room to fill out as his body matures and enough athleticism to remain a solid runner with additional weight. Added strength should also allow him to drive the ball more consistently both right-handed and left-handed. Arias is still fine-tuning his actions on defense, but is expected to have enough arm strength to stay at shortstop as he progresses through Baltimore’s system.
