The sweeping action on his upper-70s slider and mid-70s curveball made them difficult to barrel, though his fading low-80s changeup remains a work in progress. Gray also drew scouting interest as an outfielder in high school, is one of the best athletes in the system and throws without much effort. Yet he struggles to keep all the moving parts of his delivery in sync and when he misses the strike zone, he often does so by such a large margin that hitters aren't tempted to chase. He has the ingredients for mid-rotation starter ceiling, but will be ticketed for the bullpen if he can't improve his control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray drew interest as both a hitter and pitcher before performing better on the mound on the high school showcase circuit in 2020. He was Illinois' top prep prospect before transferring to IMG Academy (Bradenton, Fla.) for his senior year, where his stock dipped amid control problems and rumors of arm issues. He signed for an over-slot $900,000 in 2021's third round, blew out his elbow the following February and had Tommy John surgery that sidelined him until mid-2023. Gray's fastball operated at 88-92 mph at IMG and now sits at 92-95 with good carry up in the zone, and the extension he creates in his delivery allows his heater to get on hitters more quickly than expected. He attacks left-handers with a sweeping low-80s slider and uses an upper-70s downer curveball against right-handers, and both of his breaking balls are solid offerings. His mid-80s changeup with fade is still a work in progress. The biggest item on Gray's to-do list is to upgrade his strike-throwing after issuing 29 walks in 34 innings last season. He's athletic and his delivery doesn't contain much effort but he doesn't keep all of its moving parts in sync. He also hasn't topped three innings or 60 pitches in an outing three years into his pro career, so he'll have to establish that his arm and stuff will hold up over a full season's workload to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts were undecided as to whether they liked Gray more as a hitter or a pitcher before he blossomed on the mound while on the high school showcase circuit in 2020. Illinois' top prep prospect before he transferred to IMG Academy (Bradenton, Fla.) for his senior year, he saw his Draft stock drop among command woes and rumors of arm issues. The Cubs still signed him for an over-slot $900,000 in 2021's third round, only to see him blow out his elbow in February 2022 and require Tommy John surgery. Gray spent most of his high school senior season working with an 88-92 mph fastball before dealing at 91-95 during instructional league in the fall of 2021, and his heater plays better than its velocity thanks to quality carry up in the strike zone. He has good feel for spinning a mid-70s downer curveball from a high arm slot, and he also employs a sweeping low-80s slider that shows promise. He was just starting to develop a fading changeup when he got hurt. Gray has a projectable 6-foot-3 frame, and if he adds more velocity after gaining strength and rehabbing from his elbow reconstruction, his fastball, curveball and slider all could become plus pitches. He doesn't feature much effort in his delivery, though he needs to do a better job of keeping all of his moving parts in sync. His athleticism should help him as he looks to refine his changeup, mechanics and command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray drew legitimate interest as both a hitter and pitcher before taking a step forward on the mound while on the high school showcase circuit in 2020. He ranked as Illinois' top prep prospect before deciding to transfer to IMG Academy (Brandenton, Fla.), where inconsistent command and rumors of arm issues dinged his Draft stock. The Cubs signed him away from an Arkansas commitment for $900,000 in the third round, only to see him blow out his elbow this February and require Tommy John surgery. After working at 88-92 mph for much of last spring, Gray sat in the low-90s and touched 95 with nice carry on his four-seam fastball during instructional league. He has impressive feel for spinning a mid-70s curveball that could be a plus pitch once he adds more power, and he also has a sweeping low-80s slider. He's in the early stages of developing a changeup with a bit of fade. Though his elbow reconstruction four innings into his pro career is a setback, Gray still has a bright future. He's loaded with projection and athleticism, which should help him add more power to his pitches and make the necessary adjustments to refine his changeup and command. He's doesn't have much effort in his delivery but still is learning to keep all his moving parts in sync and won't return to game action until 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Fitterer one of the more polished high school pitchers in the 2019 Draft, and he drew comparisons to Kyle Hendricks with better stuff. Since signing for an over-slot $1.5 million as a fifth-round pick, he has been slower to acclimate to pro ball than expected. He lost the 2020 season to the pandemic and missed time with back and shoulder issues in 2021 before finally getting a full season in High-A last year. Fitterer's fastball usually ranges from 92-95 mph with natural sink and cut, and it stands out more for its ability to generate weak contact than for missing bats. His best secondary pitch is a sinking low-80s changeup that helped him have more success against left-handers than right-handers in 2022. He has some feel for spinning the ball, though his upper-70s curveball and low-80s slider can blend together at times. Fitterer's athleticism hasn't translated into reliable strike-throwing. He doesn't attack hitters, and his average stuff doesn't leave him with much margin for error when he catches too much of the plate. He needs to get stronger and more consistent to make it as a starter, and he faces an important year in Double-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more polished prep pitchers in the 2019 class, Fitterer slid to the fifth round amid concerns about his UCLA commitment but signed for $1.5 million (the equivalent of early second-round money). He has been compared to Kyle Hendricks with better stuff, though he has only pitched 53 innings in three years because of the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and back issues last season. The Marlins tried to get him more innings in the Arizona Fall League, only to see him develop shoulder soreness after two starts. Fitterer imparts a lot of natural sink and cut on a fastball that ticked up a bit last year, when it sat at 92-94 mph and touched 96 while generating a lot of weak grounders. He has aptitude for spinning the ball, producing solid 78- to 82-mph curveballs with good depth and some tighter sliders in the low 80s. He's also making progress with a sinking low-80s changeup. A good athlete who offered some intriguing right-handed power as a two-way player in high school, Fitterer repeats his delivery with ease and provides consistent strikes. He exudes a calm demeanor on the mound and has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter with three solid pitches and control to match. To reach it, he'll need to get stronger and prove he has the durability for the role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Fitterer one of the more polished high school pitchers in the 2019 Draft, but his UCLA commitment clouded his signability. He fell to the fifth round before signing with the Marlins for $1.5 million, the equivalent of early second-round money. He posted a 2.38 ERA in his 2019 pro debut in Rookie ball and performed well in instructional league last fall while continuing to draw comparisons to Kyle Hendricks with better stuff. Fitterer uses a fast arm to generate 91-93 mph fastballs and top out at 95 with natural sink and cut that produce weak grounders, and he could add more velocity as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. His best secondary pitch is an upper-70s curveball with good shape. He also has a tighter slider in the low 80s and a changeup with similar velocity and some sink. A good athlete who flashed some intriguing right-handed power potential as a prep hitter, Fitterer repeats his delivery consistently and throws strikes. If he adds strength and refines his arsenal, he could fit into the middle of a big league rotation. His polish will help him make the jump to full-season ball in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox more than doubled Dalquist's third-round slot value, paying the California high schooler $2 million to forgo an Arizona commitment. After getting just three innings in his first two years as a pro because the pandemic wiped out the 2020 Minor League season, he stayed healthier and outperformed fellow big-money prep right-handers Jared Kelley and Matthew Thompson at Low-A Kannapolis. He didn't exactly dominate, however, with a 4.99 ERA and 56 walks in 83 innings. Dalquist has added velocity since signing and now sits at 92-94 mph and reaches the mid-90s more often with his fastball, with the extension in his delivery adding deception that's more notable than his heater's life. His low-80s slider with depth has surpassed his mid-70s downer curveball as his best breaking pitch, though he hangs it too often. He's also making progress with a fading low-80s changeup that can get too firm at times. Dalquist stood out more with his polish than his pure stuff as an amateur, but the reverse was true in 2021, when he struggled to harness his improved stuff. Fastball command was a particular problem, as he regularly missed up and to his arm side. He's a potential four-pitch mid-rotation starter if he can figure things out, but he has yet to show many signs of doing so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox invested heavily in high school right-handers in the last two Drafts, spending $2.1 million on Matthew Thompson and $2 million on Dalquist in 2019 and $3 million on Jared Kelley in 2020. A California high school product, Dalquist received more than double his slot value in the third round to give up an Arizona commitment. He pitched three innings in his pro debut before spending 2020 at Chicago's alternate training site and instructional league program. Though Dalquist stands out more with his polish than his pure stuff, his pitches have gotten better as he has gained strength. He's reaching the mid-90s more often with his fastball and sitting around 92-94 mph, with the extension in his delivery creating deception that's more notable than the life on his heater. His mid-70s curveball and harder slider both have gotten sharper since he turned pro and show flashes of becoming plus offerings. Dalquist also shows some feel for a changeup that he didn't need much as an amateur. More athletic than physical, he has a whippy arm action, repeats his delivery and usually fills the strike zone, though he has had difficulty harnessing his improved stuff in 2021. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of former Astros great José Cruz and son of former first-round pick and longtime MLB center fielder José Cruz Jr., Trei Cruz was a third-round pick in the shortened 2020 Draft whose career seemed stalled at Double-A Erie, where he spent parts of four seasons. After adding outfield to his position list and becoming more of an impact hitter, Cruz won over Tigers officials by becoming the pinnacle of versatility, a switch-hitter who can play all over the field and defend well nearly everywhere. That didn’t get him to Detroit in 2025, but it earned him a spot on the 40-man roster in the offseason and a long look in Spring Training. While Cruz has always been a switch-hitter, he’s much more dangerous from the left side, where he hit all of his home runs in 2024 and 2025. He adjusted his swing two years ago with help from his dad to produce more power from his hips and lower body, yet he doesn’t chase home runs, taking more of a doubles mentality. He has the bat speed to keep up with rising velocity and produce a high hard-hit rate, yet stays very disciplined at the plate with a low chase rate and swing rate overall. His high walk rate, even against lefties, enables him to utilize above-average speed on the bases. While he doesn’t have a standout defensive position, he’s athletic and instinctive enough to play just about everywhere. As a switch-hitter who can be that versatile, Cruz profiles as the ultimate player for manager A.J. Hinch’s bench. Hitting a little stronger against lefties would help his cause, but it’s not hard to envision Cruz as a fill-in for an injured Zach McKinstry should the need arise.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz may have the most extensive big league pedigree in this year's Draft, as his father Jose, grandfather Jose and great-uncles Hector and Tommy all played in the Majors. His uncle Enrique started at second base for the 2003 College World Series champions at Rice, where Trei has spent the last three seasons. Selected in the 35th round out of high school by the Astros in 2017 and in the 37th round as a sophomore-eligible by the Nationals in 2019, he should fit in the first five rounds after improving several aspects of his game. A switch-hitter, Cruz has toned down his approach after selling out for home runs in the past. He has modified a big leg kick he used from the left side of the plate and displayed better strike-zone discipline during the truncated 2020 season. Scouts see him as a hit-over-power guy who could provide 15 homers on an annual basis. Cruz posted below-average running times in the past but now flashes average speed, especially once he gets going, and shows aggressiveness and savvy on the bases. His average arm and fringy range don't lend themselves to sticking at shortstop, though he may get a chance to play there for a while in pro ball after displaying more quickness this spring. His best fit is at second base, where he played well as a freshman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After earning national freshman of the year accolades at Arizona in 2021, Berry followed coach Jay Johnson to Louisiana State and had another monster year. He offered one of the best combinations of hitting ability, power and plate discipline in the 2022 Draft, so the Marlins selected him sixth overall and signed him for $6 million. He has surprisingly struggled at the plate in his first three years as a pro, though he did have his best stretch of success yet in the second half of 2024. A switch-hitter, Berry has a quality swing from both sides but lost his patient approach and chased too many pitches out of the zone while trying to make up for a slow start in 2023. The same was true when he posted a dismal .155/.205/.217 line in the first two months of this season, but he looked more like his college self while batting after the all-star break. There were some worries that his pedestrian exit velocities in college might mean that he'd be more of a hit-over-power guy as a pro, and he looks like he might top out at 15-20 homers per season. Drafted as a third baseman, Berry has below-average speed and average arm strength at the hot corner, with most scouts questioning whether he was athletic enough to remain there. He has decent range and can make some nice plays, but he also made 20 errors in 69 starts at third in 2023. Miami had him play more first base in Double-A last season to lessen his defensive load, and he started to hit better once he became primarily a right fielder in the second half of this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Berry earned national freshman of the year honors at Arizona in 2021 before following coach Jay Johnson to Louisiana State. He continued to thrive in Baton Rouge, posting a 1.094 OPS with more extra-base hits (24) and walks (27) than strikeouts (22), en route to going sixth overall in the 2022 Draft and signing for $6 million. He shockingly has struggled to make much impact at the plate in his first two pro seasons. Berry offered perhaps the most tantalizing combination of hitting ability, power and patience in the 2022 college crop, drawing comparisons to a switch-hitting version of Andrew Vaughn. He has a quality swing and advanced approach from both sides, showing more pop as a left-handed hitter, though those attributes have yet to translate into pro production. His relatively pedestrian exit velocities were the lone concern about him in college and he hasn't hit the ball hard in the Minors, while his approach has regressed significantly. After Berry spent most of his freshman year at DH and split his sophomore year between third base and right field, there are questions about where he will wind up defensively. He has below-average quickness and average arm strength, and most scouts think he lacks the athleticism to play the hot corner in the big leagues. He could be adequate in an outfield corner and most likely will wind up at first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A player born in New Zealand has never made it to the big leagues. Andy Skeels was the first New Zealand-born player to be drafted and went on to be a very successful career managing in the Minor Leagues, and Scott Campbell was a Futures Game participant. Pouaka-Grego, who signed with the Phillies for $250,000 in January 2022, hopes to be the first to reach The Show. He put his best foot forward during his pro debut in the Florida Complex League at age 17, hitting .301/.424/.466. His progress was halted when he tore his ACL in the Australian Baseball League that offseason, forcing him to the sidelines for the entire 2023 season. Now healthy, Pouaka-Grego can go back to hitting his way to Philadelphia. The left-handed-hitting infielder has a unique ability to make contact, with a strikeout rate under 13 percent in his pro debut. He has good plate discipline and pitch recognition, drawing walks as often as he strikes out. His feel for the barrel helps him get to some extra-base authority, and there could be some decent pop as he moves up the ladder. Pouaka-Grego was a shortstop when he signed but split time between second and third base in the FCL in 2022. He’ll likely see more time at the keystone than the hot corner moving forward, with the chance to develop into an offensive-minded regular at second at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies handed out six bonuses of six figures or higher to infielders during the 2022 international signing period, led by William Bergolla’s $2.5 million. They also added Pouaka-Grego from New Zealand for $250,000, then he hit .301/.424/.466 during his pro debut as a 17-year old in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. That raised excitement for his first full season in 2023, but he suffered a knee injury in the Australian Baseball League during the offseason that turned out to be a torn ACL and put his development on a serious hold. A left-handed-hitting infielder, Pouaka-Grego has shown a very good feel for hitting from the left side of the plate. He has a knack for contact, striking out in less than 13 percent of his plate appearances during his debut, and a solid overall approach, walking as much as he whiffed. He showed some extra-base thump in the FCL and there should be more as he physically matures, with a chance to get to it courtesy of his feel for the barrel. Originally signed as a shortstop, Pouaka-Grego spent most of his time shuttling between second and third during his debut, and that’s likely where he’ll stay once he’s healthy. He doesn’t have a ton of range, but he can catch what’s hit to him. First up will be to get him healthy to see what he might evolve into with maturation and more professional reps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Toman grew up around the game as the son of longtime college coach Jim Toman, so it’s no surprise that he was one of the most polished and mature high school hitters in the 2022 Draft class. Toman was committed to play NCAA ball at LSU, but the Blue Jays selected him 77th overall and signed him for a well-above-slot $2 million. Trusting Toman’s pedigree, the Blue Jays assigned him to Single-A Dunedin for his first full season in 2023, when he hit .208 with five home runs and a .633 OPS. Those numbers, including Toman’s 135 strikeouts in 114 games, were underwhelming, but the Blue Jays came away impressed with how he dealt with the challenge at the very least. His maturity showed, and while the numbers need to improve significantly, the organization continues to believe in Toman’s upside because of those intangibles and his dedication to his development. The switch-hitter continues to find more success hitting from the left side (.658 OPS in 2023) than the right (.549). Toman’s body is in a better spot than when he was drafted and he’s looked sharp at third base, which feels like his future home over shortstop. Still just 20, there’s still plenty of time for him to develop into a solid all-around prospect, but the numbers will need to improve in 2024. For now, Toman’s foundation and some positive internal evaluations on how he’s managed his first year-and-a-half in pro ball keep him afloat in rankings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Toman grew up around the game as the son of longtime college coach Jim Toman, so it’s no surprise that he was one of the most polished and mature high school hitters in the 2022 Draft class. Toman was committed to play NCAA ball at LSU, but the Blue Jays selected him 77th overall and signed him for a well-above-slot value of $2 million. Toronto gave the switch-hitting Toman a taste of pro ball in the Florida Complex League, where he hit .290 and worked seven walks over 11 games. He’s already earned rave reviews throughout the organization for how much time he’s spent at the club’s player development complex. In fact, the Blue Jays sent him home at one point over the offseason for a mental break from baseball, but they love what they’ve seen early. He’s expected to continue to split time between shortstop and third base, but his instincts give him a shot to stick at short. His body will play a role in that too, as he’s already added some natural build and is benefiting from the Blue Jays’ program. Toman has a smooth, sweet swing from the left side. His right-handed swing wasn’t as fluid, but that had taken noticeable strides since he was drafted. However, Toman has struggled out of the gate with Single-A Dunedin, where he's walked a decent amount but has also punched out at a higher rate than desirable. There's still the potential for an all-around game here, but it's going to be a longer climb than first envisioned when Toman entered the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boeve was a king of contact over his three years at University of Nebraska-Omaha, and that was never clearer than in his junior campaign when he finished among the top five nationally with a 4.3 percent K rate and a 0.28 K/BB ratio while hitting .401 over 47 games. The Brewers took him in the second round in 2023, making him the highest pick in school history, and he came firing out of the gate in his first full season by going 21-for-38 (.553) in his first 13 games with High-A Wisconsin. Milwaukee promoted Boeve to Double-A Biloxi in late April, and he slashed .306/.374/.447 with six homers in 66 games the rest of the way while missing some time with a right shoulder injury. Batting from the left side, Boeve gets into a slight crouch, using only a minimal load and whipping a short swing to put the barrel on the ball. Even at Double-A, he’s shown an ability to handle most pitch types, and he’s as comfortable shooting balls the other way as he is pulling them down the line. However, his current power projection is for 10-12 homers over a full season because most of his pop comes on doubles to the gaps. Whether it's due to the shoulder or the Southern League, Boeve hasn't been as sharp at the plate in 2025 and has mostly been carried by a decent OBP. Boeve is a below-average runner and a non-threat to steal bases. He can still get his glove to balls at third base but won’t wow anyone there with his range or arm strength. The Brewers gave him more looks at first base in the Southern League, and he has a better chance of being average there, albeit with an added need for power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boeve was one of the best contact hitters in Division I baseball in 2023, ranking fifth among qualifiers with a 4.3 percent K rate and third with a 0.28 K/BB ratio at Nebraska-Omaha. He finished with a .401/.512/.563 slash line over 47 games in his junior spring. Those numbers, along with strong summer performances in the Cape Cod and Northwoods Leagues, pushed Boeve to become the highest UNO player ever drafted when he went in the second round to the Brewers and signed below slot for $1.25 million. He got his feet wet in pro ball with stops in the Arizona Complex and Midwest Leagues. Batting from the left side, Boeve shows a quick and compact swing that prioritizes putting the ball in play. His ability to focus on balls in the zone helps him build a solid on-base percentage on top of the strong average, and that’s the entire foundation of his offensive profile. Because he does focus so much on protecting the plate over driving the ball with his short swing mechanics, he doesn’t get into his average raw power as much as he could, and his exit velocities suffer. He did tee off with four homers in nine games against less-advanced ACL competition but was back to hitting the ball on the ground 60 percent of the time in his short High-A sample. A below-average runner, Boeve improved defensively over time at third base in school but still lacked the arm strength to pop there. He was also drafted into the same organization as Brock Wilken, and as a result, the Brewers tried Boeve out more at second in pro ball where his arm is a better fit. His lack of wheels could push him to first or left field in time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baez went from a $10,000 signing in June 2022 to a must-follow Brewers prospect just one year later after hitting .370 in an All-Star year in the Arizona Complex League. He ended his age-18 season with Single-A Carolina and returned to the Mudcats for 2024 but was limited to 81 games due to an injured right shoulder suffered on a dive back to the bag. He hit .272/.331/.361 with only one homer in that span, good for a 106 wRC+ in the Carolina League. To make up for the lost at-bats, Baez headed to the Arizona Fall League and thrived as one of the younger players in the desert with a .295/.402/.474 line and two homers in 22 games. Baez starts from an open stance as a right-handed hitter and closes into place with a big leg kick that looks like something designed to launch balls beyond the left-field fence. Despite all that movement, he has good hand-eye coordination that helps him put the ball in play. He handled fastballs well with Carolina but was more prone to being blown away by heat against more advanced AFL arms, and while his walk rate improved nicely overall in ’24, he still looked prone to chasing soft stuff. He doesn’t wow with exit velocities at this stage, and there is some concern he’s already maxed out physically. An average runner, the Dominican Republic native went just 11-for-22 in stolen base attempts last year during the regular season but was uncaught in three AFL attempts. Roster requirements pushed him to second base in the Fall League, but he’s still a better fit at third with relatively limited range. It’s possible Baez takes another jump in a healthier 2025 as he’ll still be a teenager for half the summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It was easy for Baez to get lost in the international shuffle when he signed with the Brewers for only $10,000 in 2022, but his first stateside season cemented his place as a Top 30 prospect in a burgeoning system. The infielder was named an Arizona Complex League All-Star after finishing second on the Rookie-level circuit with a .370 average and 71 total hits over 48 games. He ended his age-18 season with nine more contests with Single-A Carolina, where he was humbled by going 7-for-30 (.233). Baez has a pronounced leg kick to begin his swing from the right side, but the noise hasn’t affected his ability to make contact in the early going -- his 11.2 percent K rate was lowest among ACL qualifiers. Because of his good hand-eye coordination, he can tend to go hunting for that contact and expands the zone, hurting his walk rate (just 3.9 percent in the ACL) and OBP in the process. He flashed decent raw power at the complex, and getting more patient in search of drivable pitches could help that pop play even better in games. The Dominican Republic native is an average but aggressive and savvy runner, swiping 19 bags in 21 attempts in 2023. His relatively limited range was likely going to push him more toward third base full-time in an organization loaded with low-level shortstops, and overall defensive inconsistencies -- even on simple plays like transferring the ball out of the glove -- put his glovework behind his bat. He’ll head back to the Carolina League for his age-19 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starting his college career at Clemson, Amick transferred to Tennessee so he could play third base. He manned the hot corner all spring, slammed 23 homers and helped the Volunteers win the College World Series. His production helped him land in the second round of the 2024 Draft, where he signed for a full-slot $1.45 million. While he hit .310 with an OPS of .873 with High-A Cedar Rapids in his first full season of pro ball, oblique and shoulder injuries limited him to just 59 games for the entire season. An attempt to make up for lost time in the Arizona Fall League went poorly as Amick went 1-for-30 with 20 strikeouts. Amick’s plus raw power and ability to tap into it to drive the ball to all fields were supposed to be his calling cards as a pro. He showed some glimpses here and there during the regular season but never consistently, and the injuries didn’t help him get in sync. While he cut down his chase rate some compared to his season with Tennessee, his miss rate went up. The damage he did do came against fastballs, and he struggled to do much with breaking and offspeed stuff. It was generally thought that Amick would hit as a pro, but there was less clarity about his defensive home, and he’s yet to answer those questions. A combination of lack of range and inconsistency with his hands makes a move to first base, where he’s played some as a pro, possible. He works hard to improve his defense at the hot corner, and there’s more pressure on his power bat should he become a first baseman only.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Amick spent the first two years of his college career at Clemson, barely playing as a freshman, then being stuck in a DH/first-base role once he finally got a shot to play as a sophomore. After a strong showing in the Cape Cod League, the son of former NASCAR driver Lyndon Amick transferred to Tennessee, where he hit 23 homers and helped the Volunteers win the College World Series. The Twins bought the power potential in the second round, signing him with a full-slot $1.45 million bonus and letting him get his feet wet with Single-A For Myers. With bat speed and plenty of strength, Amick’s offensive calling card entering pro ball was his plus raw power and ability to get to it to all fields. Though he can be very aggressive at the plate and often chased pitches out of the zone in college, he showed he could routinely barrel up the baseball, and the Twins were pleased during his pro debut that to see him do a better job at laying off bad secondary stuff, showing better pitch recognition than anticipated. The other question surrounding Amick is whether he will be able to stick at the hot corner, which he finally got to play with the Volunteers. Though he’s a below-average runner with fringy-to-average defensive tools, the Twins are bullish on that part of his game as well after seeing him make solid strides in his brief time with the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yet another international pitcher signed at a lower price and higher age by the Astros, Ullola turned pro for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic at age 18 in 2021. He reached Single-A in 2022, and in his first four years in full-season ball, he posted the lowest opponent average (.189) and highest strikeout (30 percent) and walk (15 percent) rates among pitchers with at least 400 innings. Houston has developed him as a starter, but his big league future almost certainly will be as a reliever. Ullola has one of the most unhittable fastballs in the Minors even though it sits at 92-94 mph and tops out at 97. With its combination of a flat approach angle and exceptional carry, it seems to explode at the plate. His secondary pitches vary in quality, with his upper-80s cutter and sweeping low-80s slider his most effective options in 2025. His low-80s curveball features depth and his upper-80s changeup has some fade but neither is very reliable. Ullola isn't tall but he has a strong 6-foot-1 frame, plenty of arm speed and the athleticism to get down the mound and create a low release height with quality extension. He has no glaring red flags in his delivery but never has been able to repeat it well enough to provide consistent strikes, and he landed his fastball in the zone just 36 percent of the time last season. He's on the same career path as Bryan Abreu, who battled his control as a starter in the Astros system before claiming a vital role in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Finding older international pitchers at bargain prices and developing them into big leaguers has played a large role in the Astros' eight consecutive playoff appearances, and Ullola could be the next in line. Signed for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic at age 18 in January 2021, he struck out 32 percent of the batters he faced in his first four pro seasons while climbing from Rookie ball to Triple-A. He led the Minors in opponents average (.163) while ranking third in strikeouts (171 in 130 1/3 innings) and sixth in K rate (31 percent) last year. Ullola's electric fastball can be unhittable, parking at 92-96 mph and peaking at 98 with a flat approach angle and tremendous carry up in the zone. He sharpened his mid-80s slider and threw more strikes with it in 2024, giving him a solid second offering. His low-80s curveball has more depth but isn't as devastating or reliable, while his upper-80s changeup has its moments but lacks consistent movement. Ullola has a quick arm and gets down the mound well, creating premium extension with a low-release height. He's athletic and his delivery isn't glaringly effortful, but he never has provided regular strikes and his 14 percent walk rate last year represented his career best. He has a special fastball and could become a mid-rotation starter if he can find more control, or perhaps will follow the Bryan Abreu path to Houston's bullpen if he can't.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros have had a lot of success signing older pitchers on the international market and refining them into big leaguers. If he can add some polish, Ullola could follow that same path after signing for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic as a 18-year-old in January 2021. He averaged 13.2 strikeouts but also 6.7 walks per nine innings in his first three years as a pro. Ullola has an electric fastball that he can throw repeatedly and still leave Minor League hitters helpless to do much against it. His four-seamer can sit at 92-95 mph and reach 97 with a flat approach angle and exceptional carry up in the zone, though he often has to dial back his velocity in an attempt to throw strikes. His next-best pitch is a short slider that stands out more for its power (peaking in the upper 80s) than its shape. Ullola also sports an improving mid-80s changeup and a fringy low-80s curveball, though he doesn't trust either offering. He has a quick arm but lacks a smooth delivery, so he has no history of throwing strikes despite working out of the stretch all the time. There's a low probability that he makes it as a big league starter, but his fastball is special, and Bryan Abreu had similar early career control issues before becoming a key part of Houston's bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros have made a habit of signing older international pitchers to modest bonuses and turning them into big leaguers. They have another candidate in Ullola, who signed for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic at age 18 in January 2021. He fanned 120 batters in 72 Single-A innings last year, finishing second in strikeout rate (15.0 per nine innings) among all Minor Leaguers with at least that many frames. Reminiscent of when Cristian Javier was advancing through the system, Ullola can throw his fastball over and over again and batters are helpless to do anything with it. He sits at 93-95 mph and reached 98 with a four-seamer that features a flat approach angle and tremendous carry. His second-best offering is a short slider that stands out more for its ability to climb into the upper 80s than its shape. Ullola's low-80s curveball and mid-80s changeup don't have as much upside and he doesn't trust them as much as his fastball and slider. He has a quick arm but doesn't have a smooth delivery, and he has trouble finding the strike zone even while working out of the stretch on a full-time basis. He needs a lot more polish and comes with considerable reliever risk, but it's difficult not to fall in love with his electric fastball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the first 10 rounds of the 2021 Draft, the Braves had a little extra bonus pool money to go after some talent on Day 3. That’s how they were able to sign Shoemaker, a native of Ontario, away from his commitment to St. John’s University, with an over-slot bonus of $477,500 in the 11th round. It’s been slow going for the projectable lefty, not surprising given how little he got to pitch in high school, both because of the weather and COVID protocols in Canada, spending the last two summers in the Florida Complex League. At 6-foot-6, Shoemaker is very much a \"baby giraffe\" type on the mound, one who’s thrown just 43 1/3 innings over his first two summers, missing time in 2022 with some minor shoulder issues. There’s plenty of ceiling to reach, with a fastball that touches 94-95 mph but doesn’t live in that range, a mid-80s slider that has the chance to become a solid offering and some feel for a changeup that he needs to throw more. Shoemaker is definitely still growing into his body, and the Braves are hopeful that added strength will lead an uptick of stuff. It will also help him repeat his delivery and command the baseball more consistently. He needs reps more than anything, as Atlanta was very cautious with this project, with the hopes that he can be a late-blooming left-handed starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Big projectable left-handers are often a hot commodity in the Draft, but not as much when they can’t be seen. A native of Ontario, Shoemaker couldn’t pitch much and couldn’t be seen much because of strict pandemic protocols in Canada. He was able to get to the States a bit to show what he could do and the Braves thought his size and potential were enough to go over slot in the 11th round of the 2021 Draft for $477,500 to sign him away from his commitment to St. John’s. While there’s a lot of unknown about Shoemaker, one thing is certain: there is definite upside potential. The 6-foot-6 southpaw can throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range, shows a pretty solid mid-80s slider and does have some feel for a changeup, but hasn’t thrown it much to date. He attended Braves strength camps during the offseason and if he can keep becoming more physical, those strength gains could translate into more velocity. Shoemaker is a solid athlete with the chance to repeat his delivery and throw a decent amount of strikes. He’s pitched so little over the last couple of years that the Braves are sure to proceed cautiously, with a huge variance of potential outcomes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A big-time college performer who started three years at NC State and helped lead the Wolfpack to a Men's College World Series, Cozart went in the second round of the 2024 Draft and signed with the Guardians a hair over slot for $2,050,000. After his first taste of pro ball was a disappointment offensively following a long college campaign, he bounced back in his first full season with a .235/.341/.371 slash line between High-A and Double-A. Despite being large for a catcher at 6-foot-3, 214 pounds, Cozart stands out most for his defense. Not only is he a strong framer and receiver, but he receives rave reviews for soft skills such as his communication with pitchers, game planning and leadership -- perhaps unsurprising since he comes from a baseball family. He has a strong throwing arm, although he only caught 23.9 percent of attempted runners last year because his throws were sometimes off the mark. Cozart may be no threat to steal bases, but he's plenty nimble behind the plate. His offense trended in the right direction last season, although swing-and-miss is holding him back. Cozart's longer, steep swing can make it difficult to cover the zone, and his strikeout and walk numbers regressed against more advanced pitching; his overall improved production from High-A (106 wRC+) to Double-A (113 wRC+) can largely be attributed to BABIP luck. He has solid raw strength, but his lack of bat speed caps his in-game power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An immediate starter as a freshman at North Carolina State, Cozart earned All-America honors last spring after hitting 19 homers and leading the Wolfpack to the College World Series. The fourth catcher drafted in 2024, he signed for $2,050,000 as a second-round pick. He went just 5-for-42 (.119) in a 13-game pro debut in High-A, though he did throw out eight of 15 basestealers. A left-handed hitter, Cozart works counts in search of pitches that he can drive. He's a potential 15-20 homer hitter whose power plays from left-center to the right-field line, though he generates it more with strength than bat speed. His swing can get long and he has difficulty barreling non-fastballs, so he'll have to prove he can do consistent damage against quality pitching. Taller than most catchers at 6-foot-3, Cozart is an average receiver with good framing skills. While he'll flash solid pop times, his arm plays more as average. He's a baseclogger with well-below-average speed, though he moves well enough behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Selvidge's performance on the mound and during team interviews at the inaugural MLB Draft Combine in 2021 served as a springboard to the third round and a well over-slot $1.5 million bonus. He pitched well in his first three pro seasons and earned a spot in the Futures Game in 2024, but he missed the event with a pinched nerve in his left biceps that required surgery that September. His stuff wasn't the same while he posted a 4.92 ERA with 61 strikeouts in 75 Double-A innings last year, and internal brace surgery this March will cost him all of 2026. At his best earlier in his career, Selvidge had three solid pitches in a 92-95 mph fastball that hit 97, a low-80s slider and an 85-89 mph cutter. Last season, his heater averaged 91 mph, topped out at 94 without much life and got crushed when he didn't locate it up in the zone. He didn't lose any velocity off his slider or cutter, but they weren't as effective as they were in the past. Selvidge had more of a reliever look in 2025, throwing more sliders than fastballs and barely using a sinking mid-80s changeup he couldn't land for strikes. His once-solid control has backed up as well, with his walk rate rising from 7 percent in his first three years as a pro to 12 percent in the next two. Scouts like his athleticism and mound presence, and the Yankees hope he can get back on the path to becoming at least a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After his stuff and strikes regressed during his Arizona high school senior season in 2021, Selvidge salvaged his prospect stock with a strong performance on the mound and in interviews at the inaugural MLB Draft Combine that June. Signed for a well-over-slot $1.5 million, he spent his first two years as a pro in Rookie ball before pitching well at two Class A levels in 2023. He starred at another new event in 2024, pitching four shutout innings with eight strikeouts against the Blue Jays in a Spring Breakout game, but rarely looked that sharp at Double-A before his season ended in July with biceps inflammation. The Yankees had Selvidge lean heavily on his best pitch last season, when he threw his sweeping low-80s slider nearly half the time, and he'll also mix in an upper-80s cutter as well. That usage and his biceps injury may have contributed to the loss of a tick or two of fastball velocity, as he operated at 91-94 and peaked at 96, and his heater straightens out and gets hit when he doesn't locate it up in the zone. His mid-80s changeup has impressive fade but won't be a reliable option until he can land it for strikes consistently. While Selvidge's walk rate jumped from 7 percent in his first three pro seasons to 11 percent in 2024, he has the athleticism and clean delivery to have at least average control and command. He earns praise for his mound presence and has a higher floor than most of New York's starting pitching prospects. He's a good bet to become a No. 4 or 5 starter, and his slider alone would make him a useful lefty reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After his stuff and strikes went backward during his senior season as an Arizona high schooler in 2021, Selvidge helped himself more than anyone at the inaugural MLB Draft Combine that June. He threw three shutout innings, interviewed well and worked his way into the third round and a well over-slot $1.5 million bonus. He repeated Rookie ball as his stuff regressed in 2022, then bounced back last year to earn Single-A Florida State League All-Star honors and pitched well in High-A. Selvidge struggled in 2021 when his high school coach changed his mechanics and found more success when he returned to his previous delivery, but he saw his fastball drop to 87-91 mph and his slider flatten out in his first full year as a pro. They rebounded in 2023, with his heater sitting at 92-95 mph and touching 97 and his low-80s slide piece regaining its shape. Both are solid offerings, as is an 85-89 mph cutter that he picked up last year. Selvidge also has a low-80s changeup with fade but hasn't been able to land it for strikes consistently. His athleticism helps him repeat his clean delivery easily, giving him average control and command. He's a tough competitor who could begin to move quickly and develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Selvidge put himself into top-two-rounds consideration with his performance on the 2020 summer showcase circuit, his stock dropped when his stuff and control regressed during his Arizona high school senior season the next spring. He rebounded with a strong performance at the inaugural Draft Combine in June 2021, working three shutout innings and impressing teams during interview sessions, leading the Yankees to spend a third-round pick and a well-over-slot $1.5 million bonus on him. His stuff backed up again when he repeated Rookie ball in 2022 but has bounced back this year as he has thrived at two Class A levels. Selvidge struggled in 2021 when his high school coach changed his delivery and found success again when he returned to his previous mechanics, displaying a 91-95 mph fastball and a low-80s slider. His fastball dipped to 87-91 mph and his slider flattened out last season before rebounding in 2023, when he also has added a solid 85-89 mph cutter. He's working on a low-80s changeup with encouraging fade. Selvidge's athleticism and clean delivery result in quality control and at least average command. He compiled a 2.95 ERA in the Florida Complex League last summer, a testament to his ability to compete without his best stuff. There's still some projection remaining in his 6-foot-3 frame, so he could continue to improve his arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Selvidge established himself as a top-two-rounds talent on the 2020 summer showcase circuit, then saw his stock dip when his stuff and control regressed last spring. But he helped himself more than any other player at the inaugural MLB Draft Combine in June, pitching three scoreless innings and wowing teams in interviews. The Yankees selected the Arizona prep product in the third round and lured him away from a Louisiana State commitment with a well over-slot $1.5 million bonus. Selvidge struggled after his high school coach changed his mechanics but regained his quality stuff once he went back to his previous delivery. His fastball bounced back to the low 90s and touched 95 again, while his slider returned to the low 80s and was sharper as well. He's beginning to learn a changeup with promising fade and velocity separation from his heater. With his athleticism and clean delivery, Selvidge should have at least average control and command. His stuff could add more power as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-3 frame and he's already starting to add strength. He impressed with his performance and work ethic during instructional league, fueling hopes that he can become a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former standout at Seminole State (Junior) College of Florida, Levenson moved into a DH/bench role for Miami in 2022 and became a starting outfielder with a .292/.397/.554 slash line and 14 homers over 63 games as a junior. The Cardinals took him in the fifth round of the 2023 Draft and signed him for exact slot at $381,300. Levenson put in a solid turn at Single-A Palm Beach in his first taste of the pros and spent his first full season with High-A Peoria, slashing .215/.317/.367 with eight homers and a 100 wRC+ over 70 games. He didn’t play after July 20 after being hit by a pitch on the left wrist. It was a perplexing year for Levenson. On one hand, his contact numbers were generally solid with some struggles against changeups in particular, and his 11.2 percent walk rate was above-average for the Midwest League. That’s notable because he tends to stay back in his stance and use a quick toe tap for a load, and pitchers will attack him outside because of that. On the other, he popped a ton of balls up; his 41.9 percent infield flyball rate was third-highest among 1,312 Minor Leaguers with at least 250 plate appearances in 2024. He had shown above-average exit velos in the Florida State League in ’23, and there is still decent raw power in his 6-foot frame, but he needs to improve the quality of contact to get to it. With fringy speed and glovework, Levenson got most of his looks in left field, and many expect that’s where he’ll remain. Being in a corner means he’ll need to hit all the more, and after being robbed of an opportunity to improve in the second half, he’ll be under a microscope in his second full campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Levenson went from a junior college standout at Seminole State College of Florida in 2021 to a solid DH/bench option for Miami in 2022 to a starting outfielder/team captain for the Hurricanes in 2023. He made the most of his playing time in his final spring on campus, slashing .292/.397/.554 with 14 homers and a decent 18.8 percent strikeout rate over 63 games. The Cardinals selected Levenson in the fifth round in July and signed him for exact slot at $381,300. He was an above-average hitter during a 34-game spin with Single-A Palm Beach, slashing .268/.331/.480 with six homers and a 114 wRC+. The right-handed hitter’s setup at the dish isn’t overly complicated. He stays back in his stance, slightly lifts his legs and lets his arms and hands fire. It’s a process that works for him as he pulverized fastballs as a Miami junior and didn’t even whiff on a pitch 95 or above in that collegiate season. The misses he did experience came more on breaking stuff, and that trend continued in the Florida State League. Levenson will show average power -- standing more to the pullside -- and ran a 40 percent hard-hit rate at Single-A at a time when many other college picks show fatigue. The Florida native needs to hit because with speed and arm strength that can both be called fringy, he’s likely locked into left field long-term. That’s where he made 21 of his 27 defensive starts with Palm Beach with fellow 2023 picks Chase Davis and Travis Honeyman also on the roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lizarraga signed for $1 million out of Mexico in March 2021 at 17 years old, moved stateside immediately and has moved up exactly one level a year since. He struggled with his mechanics in 2023 and struck out only 78 batters in 94 2/3 innings for High-A Fort Wayne but bounced right back a year later. The right-hander spent the entire ’24 campaign with Double-A San Antonio and finished with a 4.03 ERA and 102 K’s in 96 frames in his age-20 season. He was one of only four 20-year-olds to throw more than 90 innings at the Minors’ second-highest level, joining Caden Dana, Robby Snelling and Yu-Min Lin on the list. Standing 6-foot-3, Lizarraga has good size on the mound but doesn’t possess stellar velocity yet, averaging just 90.1 mph on his fastball in the Texas League. He can run it up to the mid-90s, and there’s decent carry on the pitch that makes it play better than that. The Padres have hoped he would add some heat as he matures, and considering he’s still only the age of a typical American college junior, that could still happen. His 75-78 mph curveball and 77-79 mph slider drew most of his whiffs down and gloveside, while his mid-80s changeup acted mostly as a show pitch to lefties. Because he isn’t overthrowing, Lizarraga should have average control out of his lower three-quarters delivery, though his walks crept up at Double-A in 2025, and his improved K numbers will help his case to remain in a starting role. Without a true plus pitch, he could really use that extra velocity sooner rather than later as he knocks on the door of the Majors. He will be Rule 5-eligible for the first time next offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Mexico, Lizarraga joined the Padres for $1 million on March 1, 2021, and he moved up the chain pretty aggressively from there, playing his whole age-18 season with Single-A Lake Elsinore in '22 and then moving up to High-A Fort Wayne last year. The right-hander struggled with his mechanics early on in 2023 and finished with a 4.09 ERA and only 78 strikeouts in 94 2/3 innings with the TinCaps. However, he provided over his final four starts, in which he posted a 1.17 ERA with 26 K’s and only five walks in 23 frames. Lizarraga can run it up to 94-95 mph occasionally, but he’s much more typically throwing his fastball in the low-90s. He really needs to climb the ladder with the pitch too because when his command drifts lower, Midwest League batters had little issue putting it into play. Optimistic evaluators believe the 6-foot-3 hurler can still add some strength and a few ticks to that heater as he gets into his 20s. Lizarraga will spin both an mid-70s curveball and upper-79s slider that can play off the high heat well at the best of times, and his changeup can look firm but helps keep lefties at bay. When locked in, the righty doesn’t need a ton of effort to be effective, and considering how young he’s been for every level, he’s kept the walks in check through the first three years of his career. But simply put, he needs to start missing bats with more regularity to hold onto the promise he showed earlier on, making 2024 a big year for him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: January 15 is now the big signing day at the start of the international window, but the Padres managed to add Lizarraga to its class when they signed him for a $1 million bonus on March 1, 2021. The Mexico native immediately moved stateside for 11 starts in the Arizona Complex League, where he fanned 35 in 30 innings, and took things to another level (literally and figuratively) at Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2022, finishing with a 3.43 ERA and 95 K’s. His 94 1/3 frames with the Storm were the most among any 18-year-old Minor Leaguer last season. The fact that Lizarraga’s stuff held up over such a comparatively long season speaks well to his future. His low-90s fastball already has the makings of an above-average pitch and plays well up in the zone, and he grew even stronger this offseason as he started to fill out the 6-foot-3 frame that Padres officials always said pointed to more velo coming. His mid-80s changeup has become arguably his best present pitch with good last-second drop. It helped the righty hold left-handed hitters to just a .611 OPS in 2022, compared to a .756 OPS by batters on the other side. That reverse split might also be a result of a curveball that lacks the consistency of the other two options. Lizarraga has long limbs that can make his pitches deceptive to hitters, but, notably, his strike-throwing improved from year one to two in the Minors. Only 19 for the duration of the 2023 season, the right-hander has seen his K rate crater at High-A Fort Wayne, but there's still enough to dream on moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for a $1 million bonus on March 1, 2021, Lizarraga was certainly one of the more intriguing names in the Padres' 2020-21 international class. Regarded as the top pitching prospect from Mexico, the 18-year-old features an exciting three-pitch mix and struck out 35 over 30 innings in Rookie ball during his brief professional debut. Lizarraga’s fastball sits in the low-90s, but Padres officials believe his velocity will tick up as he adds strength to his 6-foot-3, 180-pound frame. The right-hander also shows some feel to spin his upper-70s curveball, though the pitch needs more refinement to reach its ceiling. He rounds out his arsenal with a changeup that features downward action and shows flashes of becoming a real weapon in the future. Confident from competing against older competition in Mexico, Lizarraga shows good poise on the mound. His natural athleticism is apparent in his smooth delivery, which allows him to command his pitches and throw plenty of strikes. Referred to by some as a “projection dream”, it’s easy to see a high ceiling as a starter for Lizarraga. In order to get there, he’ll need to add some strength and continue to improve both his off-speed offerings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After landing a few prospects when the international market opened, the Padres were thrilled to add Lizarraga on a $1 million signing bonus in late February to put a cap on what they feel was a strong 2020-21 international class. Regarded by many as the top pitching prospect out of Mexico, Lizarraga features an intriguing blend of athleticism and three pitches. Lizarraga’s fastball currently sits at 89-92 mph with solid life, and as he grows into his lean frame – he enters his debut season at 6-foot-4 and just 185 pounds – the Padres believe that fastball could reach the mid- to high-90s. To go along with the heater, Lizarraga has feel for a changeup that projects as at least average, with fade and drop. His current go-to secondary weapon is a curveball that bites hard. Lizarraga’s delivery is smooth and repeatable, and his raw athleticism is readily apparent. Combine that with a three-pitch mix, and it seems fairly clear that he’s destined for a starter’s role in the long-term. First, however, Lizarraga needs to bulk up a bit to get the most out of his fastball, while continuing to progress in developing his two offspeed weapons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hamm looked like a Draft steal in his first full pro season, earning Midwest League Pitcher of the Year and Tigers Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors in an impressive 2024 season that included a 2.64 ERA and 11.1 strikeouts per nine innings. Still, his second-half fade that year had some curious whether he could keep it up. Those concerns were realized in 2025, when Hamm struggled to make the jump to the more hitter-friendly surroundings of Double-A Erie and the Eastern League. He regressed in virtually every statistic, and looked no better after missing more than a month at midseason with injury. Hamm has always been a unique pitcher as a pro with an over-the-top delivery, and part of his struggles in 2025 came from an alarming drop in velocity on his fastball. What had been firmly in the low 90s and approaching 94-95 mph at times dropped into the upper 80s for a stretch. That loss of heat had a trickle-down impact on his changeup. Without the base pitches to pound the strike zone and get ahead in counts, Hamm’s 12-to-6 curveball and sweepish slider became less of a worry for hitters. He could still get strikeouts with lesser stuff, particularly against right-handed hitters, but it took more work to get them. Hamm still has the potential to be a Major League pitcher, but he’ll need to add strength and durability to regain and maintain his velocity, especially if he wants to be a starter. If his struggles carry into 2026, his best fit might be in the bullpen, where shorter outings could help bring his fastball back.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers benefited from several pitching prospects graduating to Detroit last year, but defining the next wave was difficult. Then came Hamm, Detroit’s fifth-round pick from the 2023 Draft after a solid but unspectacular career at Middle Tennessee State. The Tigers signed him for below slot, had him throw more high fastballs, worked with him on developing a slider, then saw him dominate hitters at High-A West Michigan for his first full pro season. He posted a 0.96 ERA, .188 batting average and 51-to-6 strikeout-to-walk ratio over his first 10 outings before hitters began to adjust. He seemed to wear down over the home stretch but still finished with impressive ratios of 11.1 K/9 and 6.6 H/9. Hamm doesn’t look imposing at 6-foot-1, but his high arm angle allows his fastball to play up at the top of the zone. His velocity sat 92-95 mph in 2024 but has been down a few ticks (while maintaining the elite ride) while he's worked around an IL stint this summer. While the high heaters set up his buckling curveball, his slider has more horizontal movement than vertical, going in on left-handed hitters and away from righties. His changeup works as an occasional look but has upside. While he has the stuff and command to get through a lineup multiple times, the physical riggers of his first full pro season took their toll on his fastball and set him off-balance. Hamm has the range and grasp of pitches to reach the big leagues, but how he maintains his pitches over a full season could determine whether he slots in as a starter or eventually moves into the bullpen. The 2025 velocity dip puts that into greater question.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maroudis played shortstop at Calvary Christian HS in Florida when he wasn’t pitching and shot up Draft boards with evaluators enamored by how his physical upside could take off while focusing full time on pitching. Toronto selected the 6-foot-3 Maroudis in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft and signed him away from an NC State commitment with a $1.5 million bonus. Maroudis was off to a strong start in 2024 with Single-A Dunedin but needed surgery to address his right UCL with an internal brace in late May. Until that surgery, Maroudis had as much upward momentum as any pitcher in this system. It wasn’t quite to the level of Ricky Tiedemann a couple of years ago when he made his big jump, but it was getting there. The surgery was a setback, yes, but Maroudis is still just 20 years old with plenty of development time ahead of him. That's important to note with his pair of fastballs sitting only 89-91 mph following the surgery. He's gone his mid-80s slider a ton for whiffs, and his 78-80 mph curveball gives him another quality breaking ball. The control simply hasn't been there in his return with more walks than strikeouts at times. The Jays prefer to focus on the fact that Maroudis is getting in any work at all against Minor League batters after the lost 2024, and with a full healthy offseason to prepare, there is hope Maroudis could look much more like himself in 2026 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Calvary Christian HS in Florida had one of the deepest high school pitching staffs in the country with right-hander Liam Peterson, lefty Hunter Dietz and Maroudis. Also the club's shortstop when he wasn't pitching, Maroudis entered the spring third on the depth chart, but many evaluators believed he had vaulted to the top of the list based on his performance and upside. Toronto selected the 6-foot-3 hurler in the fourth round and signed him away from an NC State commitment with a $1.5 million bonus. Maroudis was off a strong start in 2024 with Single-A Dunedin but needed surgery to address his right UCL with an internal brace in late May. Before the injury, Maroudis did exactly what the Blue Jays hoped for, leaning into everything their complex has to offer. It helped that he already lived nearby, so he was one of the organization’s most dedicated pitchers over the offseason. He quickly started to transform his body into a pitcher’s build, with immediate results. He was already sitting in the 93-95 mph range, which is where he topped out at in high school, and showed a promising changeup already at age 19. His breaking balls will be the real difference-makers here, and he leaned plenty on a mid-80s slider and 78-81 mph curveball in his first taste of the Florida State League. Maroudis has plenty of runway to develop those offerings. Like with so many of the other high-ranked teenagers -- including Arjun Nimmala and Enmanuel Bonilla -- the Blue Jays hope their investment in player development will pay huge dividends with Maroudis once he can reestablish his health in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Long Branch, N.J. native, Reilly would’ve been one of the more interesting prep arms of the 2020 Draft but went to Vanderbilt instead, and then became a fifth-round pick of the Pirates in 2023. He was pitching well at High-A when the Pirates traded Reilly to the Orioles in a prospect-for-prospect deal for Billy Cook at the 2024 Trade Deadline, and Reilly finished the year at Double-A in his new organization. Reilly made three starts at the level in 2025 before suffering an elbow injury and undergoing Tommy John surgery in May. He is likely to miss most, if not all, of 2026. Before the injury, Reilly was a high-octane righty with a power arsenal but poor command, liable to generate whiffs in bunches but dogged by high walk rates. He threw a high-spin fastball with rise that flashed triple-digits and sat comfortably in the low-to-mid-90s, complementing the heater with a slider he could snap for swings-and-misses and morph into more of a cutter against left-handed hitters. He also toyed around with a changeup, though that pitch was less developed than his other offerings. It remains to be seen what level the stuff returns to post-injury. Reilly threw from a high arm slot and with a high-effort delivery that was at the root of his difficulty throwing strikes, and potentially the elbow injury. It’ll be notable if he simplifies his mechanics to make his delivery more repeatable and put less stress on his arm. All of that could factor into Reilly’s potential role post-surgery, as his profile already hinted at a possible move to the ‘pen down the line. It could behoove his long-term health and power stuff for him to pitch in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reilly went from one of the better prep arms of the 2020 Draft class to a fifth-round pick of the Pirates in 2023 after honoring a commitment to Vanderbilt, where control issues led to an uneven career. The New Jersey native was having a solid first full season with High-A Greensboro when he was dealt to the Orioles in a prospect-for-prospect deal for Billy Cook at the 2024 Trade Deadline, and he pitched to a 3.73 ERA at Double-A over his first eight appearances with his new organization. He made just three outings with Double-A Chesapeake in 2025 before being shut down with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery in May. A 6-foot-3 right-hander with a power arsenal, Reilly's ultimate role once he returns to action will be based on his ability to command his high-octane stuff. He's been dogged by fringy control since college, where a consistently high walk rate led Reilly to pitch mostly out of the bullpen. His high-spin fastball flashes as high as 100 mph in relief and sits comfortably in the low-to-mid-90s as a starter, and he uses its impressive induced vertical break to generate a ton of whiffs up in the zone. Reilly compliments the heater with a power slider that he can morph into a cutter against lefties, and he played around with a bigger sweeper and a gyro-type changeup after the trade. Either could develop into average offerings with more usage. Reilly's high-effort delivery is at the root of his difficulty throwing strikes, notably a high arm slot that gives his pitches more movement but also makes his mechanics tough to replicate. Though the walk rate crept back up with the Orioles, they were going to give him a chance to develop into a back-end starter even if his profile hints at an eventual move back to the 'pen, especially post-surgery, where his stuff could play even better in short stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reilly went undrafted in 2020 as a New Jersey prepster because of his commitment to Vanderbilt. He was enigmatic over his three years there, showcasing electric stuff but seldomly harnessing it. Opportunities to start, like the one he was given in 2023, didn’t go well and he spent most of his time in the bullpen. The pure stuff was too much for the Pirates to look past in the fifth round of that summer’s Draft, and Reilly pitched briefly in the Florida State League to get his professional feet wet after signing. He was having a solid first full season with High-A Greensboro when he was sent to the Orioles in return for prospect Billy Cook. A 6-foot-3 right-hander, Reilly’s profile is similar to former organization-mate Kyle Nicolas, with huge grades on his stuff and questions about what kind of role he can fill because of his lack of command. In college, he leaned heavily on his fastball, which was 95-99 mph during his pro debut, and for good reason. With high spin and ride at the top of zone along with impressive induced vertical break, it’s a tough pitch for any hitter to square up, let alone make contact with. His mid-80s slider flashes plus, though he only landed it for a strike half the time at Vanderbilt in 2023, and he can also turn it into an effective harder cutter. He doesn’t use the changeup much, but it also could be an average offering. He’s even thrown a two-seamer in the past and toyed with a curve. Reilly throws with quite a bit of effort, having trouble repeating his delivery and keeping his mechanics in sync, which is why he’s had such difficulty throwing strikes. He’s been working to simplify things to see whether he can get stretched out, and he was throwing more strikes, giving him a fighting chance to start.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bergner was a highly rated pitcher out of high school who had an up-and-down college career at North Carolina before the Tigers took a chance with a ninth-round pick in 2019. After beginning his pro career as a long reliever, he took advantage of a starting opportunity at High-A West Michigan with a strong stretch run in 2021, building momentum that carried into Double-A Erie with an outstanding first half. He began a late-season stint at Triple-A Toledo with five scoreless innings against Iowa, but largely struggled the rest of the way. Bergner pitches with a polished, easy delivery out of his tall frame. His fastball approaches the mid-90s, but was more often around 91-93 mph last season. His changeup ranges from the low-to-mid-80s depending on whether he’s looking for speed differential or movement. He has a slow, buckling curveball and tweaked his slider last year with help from Tigers pitching director Gabe Ribas to develop more bite. Bergner needs to hit the corners, work ahead and throw his secondary pitches for strikes to be effective at the upper levels, something he struggled to do at Triple-A. The Tigers did not add Bergner to their 40-man roster at season’s end, opting to keep other pitching prospects instead. His arsenal and grasp of pitching give him the potential to take the next step, but this is probably a make-or-break year for him with his 26th birthday in May. With other starting prospects coming, Bergner might be better off with a move to the bullpen to see whether his fastball plays up in shorter doses.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers hit the jackpot with a college pitcher in the ninth round when they drafted Tarik Skubal in 2018, and they’d love to find fortune again with Bergner, their ninth-round pick in 2019. Bergner had been on pro teams’ radars since he was a highly rated pitcher in high school. He followed through on his commitment to North Carolina, but had an up-and-down career with the Tar Heels. He was a high-strikeout long reliever in Low-A Lakeland, posting an 8-for-34 walk-to-strikeout ratio over 24 1/3 innings, then got his opportunity as a starter at High-A West Michigan after Beau Brieske was promoted to Double-A. His performance opened eyes, as did his 110 strikeouts over 83 1/3 innings for the season. On the flip side, he thrived in West Michigan despite high fly-ball and pull rates. Bergner has a nice, easy delivery out of his 6-foot-5 frame. He pitches off a fastball that approaches the mid-90s. As a reliever, he could pair that with a fading changeup and mix in a slow curveball. He later revamped what had been a hard slider, took some velocity off it and added some depth in hopes of making it a swing-and-miss fourth pitch in his arsenal. Bergner has a good understanding of pitch design and mental approach. While Bergner enjoyed a breakout season at West Michigan, he was also older than the vast majority of hitters he faced. He continued to be successful at Double-A Erie to begin this season and is getting a late-season look at Triple-A. Bergner is eligible for the Rule 5 Draft this offseason and just might be on the cusp of pitching his way onto the 40-man roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $700,000 signing out of Mexico City in January 2022, Verdugo has shown what can be exciting and cautionary about pushing a young prospect quickly early in his career. He ran a 116 wRC+ over 52 games in the Arizona Complex League in his age-17 season in ’22 after skipping over the Dominican Summer League completely, but his move to Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2023 was a struggle with a .220/.308/.332 line in 113 games. He returned to the Storm with much better numbers (.250/.363/.407 in 81 games) before hitting another wall as a 19-year-old with High-A Fort Wayne, finishing with a .561 OPS and 29.4 percent strikeout rate in 25 games. Watch Verdugo hit, and you can see why the Padres have pushed him so far. He doesn’t overly complicate matters with his setup from the right side, keeping things nice and quiet until he unleashes quick hands through the zone for a sound swing. He showed a better understanding of the strike zone between his first full season and his second, cutting down his chase by a good margin, but he still struggled to make consistent contact. When he did, he got under the ball too much. Without significant strength, many of his batted balls were catchable flies rather than stung line drives. In 2025, he's started to drive more of those balls over the wall back with Fort Wayne and looks more like a 15-plus homer threat as he enters his 20s. A below-average runner, Verdugo has had to move away from shortstop and spend time at second and third. He continues to see time at those last spots, and even the departure of Leo De Vries won't likely lead to more Verdugo looks at the six moving forward. He's still building his offensive game, but the home run gains are promising at this still early stage.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 47 international prospect, Verdugo was considered the top player from Mexico in the 2022 signing class, and he joined the Padres for $700,000 out of the Diablos Rojos del Mexico academy in Mexico City. After Verdugo turned 17 in February, San Diego moved him straight stateside to the Arizona Complex League, and he was the only person with a 2005 birthdate to get enough at-bats to qualify for a batting title in the circuit. He finished with a .251/.338/.467 slash line, seven homers and a 116 wRC+ over 52 games. The right-handed slugger showed loud contact in the ACL that mostly played in-game to the pull side, but that's backed up some with a move to Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2023. He isn’t a hulking presence in the box at a listed 6 feet, but perhaps power could return as he ages and gets more upper-level experience. His strikeout rate has dropped around 10 points year to year, so that's a positive sign of development at the plate.
