That would be a good fit for such a hard thrower with that release point, but picking up such a unique pitch isn’t as easy as Paul Skenes or Jhoan Duran make it look. Still, Chalas’ continued breakout has many across the industry intrigued, including Arizona, which won’t rule out trying Chalas as a starter the more he proves himself stateside. His control was solid for a reliever, especially late in the 2024 season, and it’s worth trying out Chalas’ stuff in a longer role before he knocks on the door of the desert.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes teams take a college senior early on Day 2 of the Draft solely to save money for other signings. Occasionally, those bargains turn out to be pretty good. That might be the case for Cranton, who signed for just $50,000 in the third round of the 2024 Draft after a solid season saving games for Kansas. The right-hander was sent to Modesto for his pro debut, and after throwing well in the regular season, tossed four hitless innings and picked up three saves to help the Nuts win the California League title. His 2025 debut was delayed by a concussion suffered on a comebacker in Spring Training, but he was in the midst of dominating at High-A Everett when the Mariners traded him to the D-backs in the Eugenio Suárez deal in July. Cranton has all the makings of a big league reliever. His fastball has interesting characteristics in terms of ride up in the zone and it’s a pitch that sits 97-98 mph and can top out in triple digits. His upper-80s gyro-like slider can be a plus out pitch at times, though it flattened out and got hit at Kansas occasionally. The 24-year-old right-hander has a long arm action and moving parts in his delivery, which can impact his control and command. That improved with the Jayhawks in 2024, but it’s definitely a work in progress. If he can get to throwing more consistent strikes -- and early returns were good in that regard -- he could find himself in the back end of a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roberts went undrafted after his junior year at Utah in 2023, when he batted just .266 with three homers over 46 games, but he started to show out for Mankato in the Northwoods League that summer (.346/.476/.555), creating some momentum for himself. He built on that with a Pac-12 All-Conference nod after slashing .356/.430/.562 with seven homers in 55 games for the Utes as a senior. His 33 steals were most among Pac-12 players. The Padres selected him in the seventh round and signed him for just $10,000, but Roberts continued to show out with a .340/.414/.470 line in 24 games with Single-A Lake Elsinore in his first taste of the Minors. Roberts cuts a stunning figure in the field at 6-foot-5, 205 pounds, and he moves exceptionally well for that size, notching 60-yard dashes in the 6.5-second range. He was a perfect 14-for-14 in steal attempts during that short run in the California League, and the Padres don’t have much doubt that his speed will continue to play as he reaches higher levels. With those wheels, Roberts is a comfortable fit in center field and has just enough arm for the position, too. That said, the left-handed hitter hasn’t been a huge power threat despite his size, though San Diego officials were intrigued by the good weight he put on during in his first offseason. He struggled to make contact against sliders and changeups as a senior and will need his speed to help run high BABIPs that can make up for some of the contact issues. Roberts already enters his first full season at age 24 and doesn’t have a long runway, but his best skills could be useful in the Majors in short order.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Compared to George Springer as an amateur in Venezuela, Rivas signed for $950,000 in January 2025. He flashed five-tool potential during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, where he hit .258/.393/.384 with 12 extra-base hits and 18 steals in 46 games. He'll make his U.S. debut shortly after turning 18 this year. Rivas stood out with his ability to recognize pitches, make consistent hard contact and draw walks in his first taste of pro ball. The next steps will be to add strength and make adjustments to his bat path so he can tap into his potential plus raw power. His right-handed swing is more notable for its bat speed than its loft, resulting in a lot of groundball contact. Rivas' speed, arm and defense all earn plus grades from evaluators, giving the upside of a 20-20 center fielder. He's an aggressive baserunner who has posted 6.5-second times in the 60-yard dash. His quickness and instincts leave no doubt that he can handle center, where his unusually strong arm for the position notched seven assists in 42 games last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Owusu-Asiedu had a background in the United Kingdom, Canada and Wisconsin before landing at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville. A promising turn in the 2022 Appalachian League (.965 OPS) preceded a junior year breakout with the Cougars in ’23 (.986 OPS, 15 HR, 24 SB), and both performances helped push him to the ninth round that July. Owusu-Asiedu really struggled with Single-A Clearwater in his first full season with a 36.1 percent strikeout rate, but he cut that by more than 12 points in his return in ’25 and then held his own in High-A Jersey Shore after an in-season promotion. He was dealt to the D-backs in the offseason in a straight-up swap for lefty reliever Kyle Backhus. Listed at 6-foot-4, the right-handed slugger has an interesting profile from a tools standpoint. He moves quickly as a plus-plus runner and regularly posted sprint speeds above 30 ft/sec in the Florida State League. That helps him cover ground well in center field, and he’s seen some time in the corners, where evaluators believe he’d be plus if he has to slide over full-time eventually. Clocked up to 97 mph from the grass, he can give opposing runners something to think about and he even threw out top prospect Konnor Griffin on a play at the plate last season. The bat could be what holds him back. Owusu-Asiedu can post impressive exit velocities -- topping out at 112.7 mph with Clearwater in 2025 -- but he struggles more on making contact in the zone than is desirable, in part because said zone is so big. The trend line is promising, but entering his age-23 season, he’s still yet to be tested in the upper Minors. He’ll make for an interesting development case in his second organization as Arizona tries to get him enough bat to be a potential fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lambert didn’t stay long at any one location as a collegian, moving from North Iowa Area CC to Missouri State to Oklahoma between 2022 and '24. He also worked as a closer in the MLB Draft League ahead of his Draft eligibility in 2024. The Mets took him in the eighth round that July and signed him for below slot at $172,500, but it didn’t take long for Lambert to look like a mid-round steal. He moved quickly through High-A Brooklyn after striking out 17 in eight innings there to begin 2025 and spent the rest of the season with Double-A Binghamton, finishing with a 1.62 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 50 innings between both spots. His 39.5 percent strikeout rate was fifth-highest among 1,383 Minor Leaguers with at least 50 innings last season. Lambert describes himself as “an adrenaline guy,” and it isn’t hard to see why. Working exclusively out of the stretch, he throws a 95-98 mph four-seamer with a ton of spin and carry that’s capable of touching triple digits. The heater had a 38 percent whiff rate in 2025, giving it the swing-and-miss tendencies of a breaking ball rather than a primary pitch. When the fastball is that good, you don’t need a ton of secondaries, and Lambert only has one: an 86-88 mph slider that breaks sharply downward and keeps batters from looking for the high four-seam alone. Lambert’s lack of a third pitch leads to predictable left-right splits, but opposite-side bats swing through their fair share of heaters and sliders too. The former Sooners reliever has the look and walk rates of a grip-it-and-rip-it reliever, and no one will confuse him for a pinpoint artist anytime soon. But with two absolute MLB-quality weapons, Lambert has high-leverage upside and could get important outs in Queens.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mikolajchak set a Sam Houston freshman record with 13 saves in 2017 and split the next two seasons between the bullpen and the rotation before the Guardians selected him in the 11th round of the 2019 Draft. They sent him to Double-A for his full-season debut after the pandemic layoff and he responded by posting a 3.18 ERA with a 57/9 K/BB ratio in 39 2/3 innings. Mikolajchak has upgraded his stuff since turning pro, beginning with a fastball that has gone from 92-95 mph in college to 94-97 with riding action and induced vertical break that make it tough for hitters to get on top of. He has turned an average low-80s slider into a plus mid-80s slide piece, and he also can morph it into a shorter, harder cutter. His upper-70s curveball has become an average offering and he also can mix in a low-80s changeup with some fade. Not only does Mikolajchak have more pitches than most relievers, but he also throws more strikes. His biggest need is to find a way to hold left-handers in check after they battered him for an .835 OPS (compared to .555 by right-handers) in 2021. Though he'll open 2022 with just 64 2/3 frames in the Minors, he may not need many more before he's ready to help Cleveland.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers originally signed the two best big league pitchers from Korea in Chan Ho Park and Hyun Jin Ryu, and they hope Choi can follow a similar path. He might have been the No. 1 overall pick in the Korean Baseball Organization draft out of high school if he hadn't opted to sign with Los Angeles for $300,000 in August 2018. He made a successful full-season debut in 2021, winning organization Minor League pitcher of the year honors after advancing to High-A and leading the system in ERA (3.55) and WHIP (0.97). Choi's fastball sits in the low 90s and peaks at 94, but plays as a solid pitch because he can locate it on either side of the plate or sneak it by hitters at the top of the zone. His heater pairs well with his changeup, a low-80s offering with sink that can be a plus offering at its best. He throws two distinct breaking balls, with his average low-80s slider with depth more effective than his mid-70s curveball. Choi thrives with control and command more than stuff. He ranked ninth in the Minors in walk rate (1.5 per nine innings) last season, putting pitches where he wants while operating from a low three-quarters slot that adds deception. His floor is more notable than his ceiling, as he's a safe bet to make it as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez left Cuba in 2024 but took a while to get cleared by Major League Baseball, so he didn't turn pro until January. He signed for $900,000, the second-highest bonus in the Cubs' 2026 international class. He stands out with his all-around ability and high baseball IQ. A switch-hitter, Martinez has a slight 5-foot-10 build that seems built more for contact than profile. While he does focus on lining balls to all fields and getting on base, he also hits balls surprisingly hard for his size. He won't be a slugger but could provide 15 homers per season once he gets stronger. Martinez has quick-twitch athleticism and plus speed that serves him well on the bases and in the field. He has good actions and solid arm strength at shortstop, where he should have no difficulty remaining. He also earns praise for his makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cermak had some of the best all-around tools from the college ranks in the 2022 Draft class, which led the Rays to select him 71st overall out of Illinois State and sign him for a below-slot $750,000 bonus, but he’s still raw in some ways. He led his college team with 11 homers during his first full season in 2021 then became a more well-rounded player in his final spring by controlling the strike zone better. He spent most of his first college season and the beginning of his second at third base, then moved to the outfield and became Missouri Valley Conference’s defensive player of the year two years in a row. Wrist and knee injuries limited him in 2023, but he was productive for Single-A Charleston, finishing with a 129 wRC+ in 39 games. Cermak hit for big-time power in college but still hasn’t faced a lot of high-level competition. His right-handed swing comes with effort and an uphill path, leaving him vulnerable to high fastballs, although he’s done more consistent damage by cutting down on his chases outside the zone. He looks to drive the ball, and he has the bat speed and pure strength to generate above-average power. He’s shown a pull-heavy mindset that can lead to strikeouts. Cermak has well-above-average speed, having been clocked down the first-base line in less than 4.1 seconds, and an arm that lit up the radar guns up to 95 mph during a brief stint on the mound in college. The Rays gave him time at all three outfield spots in 2023, but the majority of his looks came in right because of the arm. That will put more pressure on his bat to help him climb through the Minors as he works to stay healthy for a full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants drafted Heliot Ramos in the first round out of the Leadership Christian Academy (Guaynabo, P.R.) in 2017, then went back there six years later to take Ortiz in the 13th round. He impressed with his athleticism on the U.S. high school showcase circuit and continued to do so in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League the last two years. Promoted to Single-A last August, he banged up his knee running into the outfield wall in his first game, ending his 2024 season. Ortiz isn't very physical, so he focuses on making contact and getting on base. He has good feel for his right-handed swing and the strike zone and looked more comfortable against pro pitching during his second stint in the ACL. He did a better job of turning on pitches and lifting them last summer, so he could grow into 12-15 homer power once he fills out his 5-foot-11 frame. Ortiz earns plus grades for his speed, arm and center-field defense. He has the mentality and aptitude to steal bases, and the instincts enhance his range in center. His arm is stronger than most at his position, adding to his credentials as the system's best defensive outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tom Wideman was a four-year starting center at Clemson and played basketball in multiple countries overseas, including Spain where his son Ryan was born. The younger Wideman was a standout for two years at Georgia Highlands JC but went undrafted before heading to Western Kentucky, where he was the Conference USA Player of the Year in 2025. He notched 36 extra-base hits and 45 steals in 60 games for the Hilltoppers, becoming the first Division I player to eclipse 35 and 45 in those categories since 2001. The Padres selected Wideman in the third round, signed him for below slot at $650,000 and gave him 26 games at Single-A Lake Elsinore. Standing at 6-foot-4, Wideman was one of the most physical players in his Draft class and instantly became one of the most athletic in the San Diego system. He can show plus-plus speed and uses his size to display plus raw power from the right side. He can go and get balls in the gaps from center field with those wheels, and tellingly, the Padres only played him in the middle of the grass after the Draft. With average arm strength, he could be a fit anywhere in the outfield. But so much will come down to his hitting mechanics and approach. Wideman chased out of the zone a ton in his one season at the Division I level, and there were only slight improvements during his time in the California League. He typically uses a giant leg kick to get going – though he’ll sometimes tamp it down – and can chop at the ball, leading to a lot of groundball contact that dulls his power. The Padres have hopes they can alter Wideman’s directionality, and there’s everyday upside if he can improve that and his selectivity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kevin Alvarez wasn't the only Astros outfield prospect to make a strong impression in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League last year. Signed for $472,500 out of Venezuela, Millan had a history of performing well at amateur events, so his easy transition to pro ball wasn't much of a surprise. He batted .279/.407/.419 with 11 extra-base hits and 13 steals in 42 games. More advanced than most 17-year-olds, Millan controls the zone and makes consistent contact. While he's not very physical at 5-foot-11 and 170 pounds, he hits the ball surprisingly hard for his size and generates plus raw pop. His right-handed-stroke is relatively flat, so he'll need to add some loft to fully tap into his 20-homer potential. A plus runner, Millan uses his quickness well on the bases and in center field. He has the instincts to steal bags and chases down balls from gap to gap. He also features solid arm strength and recorded six assists in 40 outfield starts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 6-foot-7 Storm was better known for his basketball exploits than his pitching at Madison (Miss.) Central HS, where he worked just 14 varsity innings in four years. He put himself on the prospect map with a crucial victory over Louisiana State to help send Southern Mississippi to the NCAA Super Regionals in 2022, then won the Sun Belt Conference tournament finale and three of the Golden Eagles' five NCAA playoff wins last spring. He made four relief appearances in Rookie ball after turning pro as a seventh-round pick last July. Solely a reliever, Storm gets ahead of hitters with his fastball and puts them away with his slider. Though his fastball usually ranges from 90-93 mph and maxes out at 95, it plays better than its pedestrian velocity because it comes out of a very high release point and features plenty of carry up in the zone. His plus slider is his best pitch, sitting at 82-85 mph and missing bats with a combination of horizontal and vertical action. His unusual arm angle and crossfire delivery create plenty of deception without costing Storm control. He has the upside of a set-up man and could move quickly through the system. He had repeated success in long outings in the last two NCAA postseasons, so there could be some temptation to try him as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed Barrios for $1 million out of Venezuela in January 2021, but a fellow Venezuelan of the same age turned out to be the biggest prospect in that international class for Milwaukee: Jackson Chourio. While Chourio rocketed to the Majors, Barrios advanced one level per season from the Dominican Summer League in 2021 to High-A ball in ‘24. As they began a summer sell-off in July, the Rays sent starter Aaron Civale to the Brewers and landed Barrios in the one-for-one swap. Barrios’ greatest strength is his defense. He’s a no-doubt shortstop, grading out in the Rays’ system behind only top prospect Carson Williams. His movements are smooth and fluid, his instincts are impressive for his age and his actions are clean. He also has a strong arm, giving him the ability to make most every throw, including many from deep in the hole. The Brewers pushed the 6-foot shortstop to High-A Wisconsin despite subpar results in Single-A primarily to let him play the position every day, and he proved to be more than up for the challenge in the dirt. Barrios uses his speed well on the bases, swiping 90 bags in his first four seasons while only being caught 18 times. He gave up switch-hitting after the 2022 season and didn’t hit much in the Carolina League the next year, but he got off to a hot start with High-A Wisconsin in 2024 by slapping the ball around the field for singles and the occasional double. Barrios doesn’t swing and miss much, with a roughly 13 percent strikeout rate in the Minors, and he can hit with two strikes. So if he improves his pitch selection to key in on the stuff he can do damage against, he could hit for a decent average as a bottom-of-the-order hitter with some baserunning value and plus-plus defense at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coley faced plenty of adversity in his college career at Rhode Island, striking out in more than half his at-bats as a freshman in 2019, losing most of the 2020 season to the pandemic, missing all of 2022 because of a school credit snafu and half of 2023 after breaking his jaw in a collision at first base. He homered eight times and stole six bases in 25 games last spring, graduated with a mechanical engineering degree and signed with the Marlins for $50,000 as a 17th-rounder. He made his pro debut by batting .265/.395/.480 in Single-A and helping Jupiter win the Florida State League title. Coley's bat speed and strength rank among the best in the system and create plus raw power. A right-handed hitter, he looks to make the most of it by launching balls to his pull side, though his approach also yields strikeouts and rolled-over groundballs. More raw than most 23-year-olds because he had only 305 at-bats in five years in college, he could do a lot of damage if he learns to be more selective. He didn't run much at Rhode Island but Coley possesses plus speed and swiped nine bases in 10 tries during his 33-game pro debut. His quickness allows him to cover plenty of ground of center field and he has solid arm strength that could improve a tick if he cleans up his throwing motion. Besides his tools, he draws raves for his intelligence and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barnett headed to Division II Wingate as a two-way player before exploding offensively as a junior in 2024. His 26 homers were second-most for that level of collegiate baseball, while his .739 slugging percentage placed 32nd among qualifiers. He posted a .349 average and 1.138 OPS over his 59 games with the Bulldogs while also making six appearances out of the bullpen, striking out seven and walking six over five frames. The Padres took him in the 11th round in the '24 Draft and signed him for $175,000 ($25,000 of which counted toward their bonus pool). Barnett only hit and played corner outfield with Single-A Lake Elsinore after joining the organization, but he pitched in late workouts and turned more than a few heads on the mound. He ran his fastball up to 97 and averaged closer to the mid-90s. His slider sat in the upper-80s with a hard cutter-like break, and that pitch could easily be a weapon, too. The ball comes out of his 6-foot-2 frame easily, and his delivery isn’t overcomplicated. With his position-player background and athleticism, he could get to average control with the right professional instruction. As much as many in the organization prefer Barnett’s work on the mound, the Padres will still give him a chance to DH part-time to begin his first full season. His power is undeniable from the right side, but he really struggled against non-fastballs in the California League last year. Had Barnett shown this level of stuff more consistently, some believe he would have gone several rounds earlier as a pitcher alone, and that’s likely where his future lies.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending four years at St. John’s, Antico transferred to Texas as a pandemic senior for the 2021 season and made sure he was on the Draft map this time by hitting .273/.437/.489 with 10 homers while leading Division I with 63 walks and ranking second with 41 steals. The Cardinals took him in the eighth round and signed him well below slot at $20,000. Antico split his first full season between High-A Peoria and Double-A Springfield, hitting .245/.344/.395 with 14 homers, and his 67 steals led all St. Louis farmhands and tied for sixth-most in the Minors. Antico finished up with 23 more games in the Arizona Fall League as a taxi-squad member. Dating back to his college days, Antico’s whole offensive role has been about getting on base. He has a normal, quiet setup at the plate, and the lack of noise helps him see the ball well and take his walks (11.9 percent BB rate in 2022). Standing at 5-foot-10, there isn’t a ton of power, but he could threaten for double-digit homers over a full Major League season with an uphill swing that put the ball in the air 46.7 percent of the time -- the highest fly ball rate among Cardinals full-season qualifiers last year. That also takes away his ability to snap up infield hits, though. A plus-plus runner, Antico’s value will stem from his feet. He’s the perfect type of base runner to take advantage of new rules encouraging stealing, as he proved in 2022, and he can track down balls between the gaps in center too. Because of his extensive collegiate experience, his second full season will be his age-25 campaign, so he’ll need to get to his ceiling as a speedy fourth outfielder soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing Christopher Morel for $800,000 in 2015, the Cubs added his younger brother and fellow Dominican shortstop Rafael for $850,000 in 2018. They're two of the toolsier players in the system, with Rafael smaller and sturdier than his sibling. He broke into pro ball with an .821 OPS, 25 extra-base hits and 23 steals in 60 games in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Morel has a sound right-handed swing, manages the strike zone well and makes consistent hard contact. He shows the aptitude to turn on pitches and drive them in the air, displaying solid raw power that already is starting to translate into games. He has the plus speed and the instincts to be a basestealing threat. When Morel was an amateur, scouts were split on whether he'd be better off playing shortstop or center field. The Cubs don't think he'll have any problem staying on the dirt with his athletic actions, quickness and strong arm. Should he wind up in a utility role, he has the tools to play almost anywhere on the diamond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in the 2019-20 international class for $350,000, Labrada made his debut among the Mariners’ Top 30 prospects for the first time in spring 2022 after wowing with his speed the season prior. Though the consensus is that Jonatan Clase might be the fastest player in Seattle’s system, Labrada led all Mariners Minor Leaguers with 32 stolen bases last year over 99 games. At 5-foot-9 and 165 pounds, he may be short in stature but he packs physicality. He possesses a good, compact swing from the left side, but is certainly more of a hit-over-power prospect. With his glove, Labrada profiles in center field given that he has advanced range, great jump, and again, elite speed. After graduating in 2021 from Low-A Modesto to High-A Everett, Labrada saw a dip in offensive production, but not an astronomical one. He still showed decent on-base skills and will continue to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peterson bounced from Purdue to Wabash Valley (Ill.) CC to Connecticut in four years of college, earning All-America honors in his final season in 2022 when he ranked second in NCAA Division I with 11 wins and third with a Huskies-record 147 strikeouts in 110 1/3 innings. His performance stood out more than his stuff, so he lasted until Cleveland drafted him in the ninth round. He shook off a so-so 2023 pro debut to lead the Minors with 14 victories and a 0.89 WHIP last year while placing second in K/BB ratio (7.6) and walk rate (4 percent) and advancing to Double-A. Relying heavily on deception, Peterson uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create plenty of extension and has the feel to manipulate the ball to produce three solid secondary pitches. His low-80s slider and upper-70s curveball both feature downward action, as does his fading mid-80s changeup, and all three elicit a lot of chases. He has added strength since turning pro and his fastball has gained a couple of ticks velocity to average 92 mph and top out at 95, and it's effective when he locates it up in the zone. Repeating his easy three-quarters delivery with precision, Peterson has the best control and command in the system. He'll still have to prove he can keep Triple-A and big league hitters off his fastball and get them to fish outside the zone for his secondary pitches, which he can fall in low with a bit too much at times. He comes with a high floor as a likely back-of-the-rotation option, and the Guardians believe they can help him find more velocity and ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Draft picks taken after the 10th round are automatically assigned a slot value of $150,000. When a college senior gets taken in Round 11, as Clohisy was out of St. Louis in 2024, and signs for that exact slot amount, it tends to fly under the radar. But when that senior plays his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season and finishes third among all Minor Leaguers with 79 steals before stealing 22 more to lead the Arizona Fall League, as Clohisy did in 2025, folks tend to sit up and take notice. Clohisy’s future in the big leagues is directly connected to his legs. In 2025, regular season and AFL combined, he stole 101 bases in 120 attempts (84.2 percent success rate) in 152 games. Not only does he have great speed, he’s aggressive in using it, wreaking havoc at all times. His wheels also help him cover a ton of ground in the outfield. He can no doubt play center field, but has and will continue to get time in all three spots. That’s important because his future role would be as a fourth or fifth outfielder if it all clicks. And that will depend on how the left-handed hitter swings the bat. There is a little extra-base ability, but his job will always be to put the ball in play and get on base, and it will be interesting to see whether he can carry over the offensive success he had in Double-A and Arizona to lift him up to Atlanta.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2019-20 international signing period, the Braves weren’t allowed to sign any amateur free agents for more than $10,000 as part of the penalty for previous signing infractions on the market. That doesn’t mean they weren’t able to find any talent. They nabbed Joseph in November 2019 when he was already closing in on his 19th birthday, and he wasn’t able to make his pro debut until 2021. He spent three years either in the Florida Complex League or with Single-A Augusta until 2024, when he managed to pitch his way from High-A Rome to Double-A Mississippi. It’s not difficult to figure out what Joseph, 24 for all of the 2025 season, is all about. He’s a two-pitch-only reliever who offers power and more power. His fastball sat at 98 mph in 2024 and touched triple digits, missing bats at a 36 percent clip thanks to good ride up in the zone. He unfurled his slider, topping out at 89 mph, more than his fastball and it’s easy to see why: The nasty breaking ball produced a 45 percent miss rate last year, according to Synergy. The one thing that has held Joseph back has been his control, and he enters 2025 with a career 5.9 BB/9 walk rate to go along with his 12.2 K/9 rate. He found the zone a bit more consistently to start the year, which enabled him to reach Double-A for the first time, but there’s a reason why the Braves didn’t put him on the 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft and why he wasn’t taken. It’s clear his stuff would be good for the backend of a bullpen, but he won’t see any high leverage situations unless he can improve his command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Leach had two elbow surgeries in high school and a third to remove screws from the joint while in college, where he compiled a 5.50 ERA in 54 innings during two seasons at Creighton and one at Miami (Ohio). His medical history and lack of success left him unselected in the 2023 Draft, but his arm strength and feel for spinning the ball spurred the Astros to sign him for $125,000 as a nondrafted free agent. He missed most of last May and June with a shoulder strain but also added 4 mph to his fastball last year, which helped him shoot from High-A to Triple-A before he impressed in the Arizona Fall League. Leach can exceed 3,000 rpm on a power curveball that operates in the low 80s, features huge downer break and can be unhittable when it's on. His heater went from sitting at 91-94 mph in 2024 to working at 95-97 and touching 99 with nice carry and some mild armside run. He also employs an upper-80s cutter that stands out more for its velocity than its action. Pitching solely out of the stretch, Leach has a drop-and-drive delivery that provides a low release height and good extension. The depth of his curve can make it hard to harness and Triple-A hitters punished his fastball and cutter when he didn't locate it well. If he can improve his control, he could contribute to Houston's bullpen this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marquis Grissom was a two-time All-Star and four-time Gold Glover across his 17 seasons in the Majors. His son headed to Georgia Tech to make it as a starting pitcher but didn’t produce high-quality results, leading to him being taken by the Nationals (the same organized that selected his dad as an Expo in 1988) in the 13th round as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2022. He’s been a reliever in the Washington system ever since and a dominant one at that. Grissom split 2024 between High-A Wilmington and Double-A Harrisburg, finishing with a 2.21 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 56 strikeouts in 53 innings. The 6-foot-2 right-hander’s best pitch is easily his 82-85 mph changeup. It gets roughly 10 mph separation off Grissom’s 92-95 mph fastball and also fades incredibly well to the armside, holding lefties at bat. Even right-handed hitters whiff on 49 percent of their swings against the changeup last season, per Synergy Sports. The fastball has just average life but can touch 96 when Grissom really needs it. A mid-80s slider gives him a breaker with gloveside action. Grissom struggled with strikes over longer outings as a collegiate starter but has reined that in as a pro. He can use the fastball to steal early strikes and then put batters away by getting them to chase over and over with the changeup. More fastball velocity would help his case to be a high-leverage reliever, but the cambio alone should help him punch his ticket to working out of an MLB bullpen. Considering when he was drafted, he might have more runway of development than a typical college relief arm anyways.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivera was already well past 19 years old when the Astros signed him in October 2016 for just $10,000 and he didn't break out as a prospect until his 2019 full-season debut, when he struck out 11.3 per nine innings in low Class A. His only development in 2020 came in instructional league, after which Houston opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster because he was 23 and had yet to advance to the upper levels. The Angels selected him in the Rule 5 draft in December but returned him to the Astros in March, and he has barely pitched this year while dealing with persistent shoulder soreness. Rivera has one of the better fastballs in system after its velocity shot up from 89-93 mph in his 2018 U.S. debut to 94-98 and touching 100 a year later. His changeup is his best secondary offering, showing signs of becoming a solid weapon with splitter action. His slider has similar velocity but lacks consistency. The Astros have used Rivera in a hybrid role and most scouts think he's destined to become a multi-inning reliever. He features a lot of effort in his delivery and has a long arm action that compromise his control and command and ability to maintain his stuff over longer stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pardinho signed with the Blue Jays out of Brazil for $1.4 million as a 16-year-old in 2017 and immediately became one of the more unique arms in the systems, but injuries have held the right-hander back through his early years of development. Now 20, the right-hander is coming off Tommy John surgery and is expected to make his return to the mound in 2021. Pardinho last pitched in ’19, when he posted a 2.41 ERA over 33 2/3 innings with Class A Lansing. He returned for two Florida Coast League rehab starts this July but suffered a setback that has slowed his comeback attempt. When healthy, Pardinho has a feel for pitching well beyond his years, and he improved his physique over the past year while recovering from surgery. After reaching the mid-90s with his fastball in the lower levels, Pardinho’s velocity had dipped a bit prior to the surgery, so those radar readings and his ability to sustain them will be a key factor in his return. Pardinho pairs that live fastball with a plus curveball, a useful slider and a changeup that has potential. With a repeatable delivery that generates plenty of drive from his strong lower body, Pardinho has all of the building blocks to remain a starter. Although undersized at 5-foot-10, that hasn’t held Pardinho back and he could fully revive his prospect stock with a strong return to the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because Sanchez had a 5-foot-11, 150-pound build and a mid-80s fastball as an amateur, he received just a $17,500 bonus when signing out of Venezuela as an amateur. He's still not very physical, but his stuff has improved dramatically in pro ball. He posted a 46/7 K/BB ratio in 34 1/3 innings during his U.S. debut last summer at age 18, spinning four shutout frames in a playoff start to help the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League Dodgers win a championship before becoming the youngest pitcher to make a start in the Single-A California League. Sanchez now operates at 92-94 mph and can push his fastball to 97 while producing difficult carry from a high arm slot. He has advanced feel for killing spin and creating sink on a plus mid-80s changeup that already ranks among the best in the system. He's still refining his breaking pitches with a mid-70s curveball with more depth than power and a tight low-80s slider that blend into each other at times. More advanced than most pitchers his age, Sanchez repeats his efficient delivery and pounds the strike zone. He needs to add more strength and has to prove he can handle a starter's workload. He generates his stuff with arm speed, athleticism and little effort, which helps his cause.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the last players signed in the Guardians' 2018-19 international class, Antunez turned pro for $10,000 out of Venezuela in April 2019. He played 15 games in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League that year, then lost 2020 to the pandemic and didn't see any game action in 2021 while dealing with leg injuries. He got back on the diamond last season and impressed scouts with his all-around tools but hurt his leg again on an awkward slide shortly after arriving in Single-A in late July. Antunez has the potential to hit for both average and power. He possesses a quick left-handed stroke and works deep counts looking for pitches he can drive. While he's aggressive, he also makes a lot of hard contact, shows the ability to drive the ball in the air and draws walks. Antunez likes to use his plus speed on the bases, swiping 13 bases in his first 41 pro games and exuding 20-20 upside. With his quickness, instincts and solid arm strength, he can provide quality defense at all three outfield spots. He has spent most of his early pro career in center field and should be able to remain there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A true gamer who rose to prominence at Kansas State for his speed, discipline and defense -- he led the Big 12 in steals (40) and walks (55) as a junior while being named a Gold Glove finalist -- Jones signed with the Yankees for $150,000 as a 2024 12th-rounder. He's hardly missed a step in pro ball with 69 stolen bases and nearly as many walks (111) as strikeouts (130) across his first two seasons of pro ball, and ended 2025 at Double-A. The Marlins acquired him along with three other prospects in January for Ryan Weathers to add to their outfield depth on the farm. Jones holds his hands high and maneuvers his barrel around the zone to make frequent contact on all pitch shapes. He controls the zone well and rarely chases, taking pride in getting on base. The Tennessee native has not made much hard contact, though, and doesn't have much projection left in his 5-foot-10 frame. The Marlins hope a mechanical change will make him more powerful so he can at least fill a Brett Gardner-like role. Not only does Jones possess impact speed, but he's also highly efficient and isn't afraid to take an extra base. He's similarly an intellectual defender in center field -- and a quality defender in the outfield corners -- with a good sense of how to position himself and average arm strength. Jones is a high-character player who gets high marks for his motor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez was working his way back from a knee injury in the spring, but despite not being scouted much, he still looked like the best Draft prospect out of Puerto Rico in the 2023 class. That status was cemented when he headed to the Draft Combine in June, and by Draft day, he'd established himself as MLB Pipeline’s No. 213 prospect in the class. The Padres liked him even more than that, selecting him in the third round and signing him for $550,000. Gonzalez became the first Puerto Rican catcher selected in the first 10 rounds since 2017 (Santis Sanchez, A’s). He opened with Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2024 and was traded to the Rays at the Deadline as part of a three-player return for reliever Jason Adam. There are plenty of interesting parts of Gonzalez’s profile, starting with his status as a left-handed-hitting backstop. The Combine was the perfect place for him to show above-average raw power with a steady rate of exit velocities above 96 mph, and there’s a chance he could add even more pull-side pop in pro ball. The biggest raves he earns are reserved for his arm strength, with one evaluator noting he has a “bazooka” behind the dish. His blocking and receiving skills could end up being solid with professional work, and therein lies the rub. Having only turned 18 in October of his Draft year, Gonzalez faces a potentially long developmental path, and the history of prep catchers isn’t terrific across the game. But the building blocks, in this case, are worthy of some early excitement and intrigue, and that’s what the Rays were buying into with this acquisition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the top 10 rounds of the 2025 Draft, the Phillies took nine pitchers, eight of them from the college ranks. The lone hitter in the group was Ferrara, a high school shortstop from Toms River East High School in New Jersey. The athletic middle infielder had shown off some tools on the summer showcase circuit and turned in a strong season in the New Jersey Shore Conference. The Phillies had some bonus pool money to play with in the ninth round when they took Ferrara, who signed for an over-slot bonus close to $600,000, or fourth-round money. The Phillies pushed the six-foot right-handed hitter to full-season Clearwater for a 15-game debut that did not go particularly well, though little should be read into thrusting an 18-year old kid from the Northeast into that level of competition. What was impressive was that even in the small sample, he was starting to make some small adjustments that should help him in the future. He wasn’t on time, launching his barrel too late, which led to poor barrel accuracy. When he got more synced up, his barrel accuracy and zone contact improved. He’s already added strength and physicality since signing, which could help him get to more impact. While Ferrara only played second base during his debut, the Phillies think his athleticism gives him the chance to stick at short. He’s an easily plus runner with decent actions defensively. He’ll continue to see time on both sides of second base, and it’s not out of the question that he gets some run out in center field at some point in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyd didn't get on the field during the pandemic-shortened 2020 season in his first year at Oregon State and made just 19 starts in his second. But he broke out last spring, hitting .373/.490/.577, and led the Pac-12 Conference with 24 steals before the Reds signed him for a slightly under-slot $847,500 as a supplemental second-round pick. He spent most of his pro debut in Single-A before Cincinnati traded him to Cleveland for Will Benson in February. A disciplined right-handed hitter, Boyd focuses on making contact and reaching base. He features at least plus speed, which he uses to beat out bunts, turn grounders into singles and create havoc on the bases. He has a bit of pull power but makes a lot of ground-ball contact and hasn't shown much power with wood bats, so he could max out at 10-12 homers per season. Boyd's quickness, solid arm strength and keen instincts give him plenty of versatility. Though he played primarily right field at Oregon State, he spent most of his pro debut in center and the Guardians project that he'll develop into a quality center fielder. The Beavers recruited him as a shortstop and it's possible he could handle second or third base in a super-utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kling displayed five-tool potential as a Pennsylvania high schooler and could have gone in the first three rounds in 2022 if he hadn't withdrawn from the Draft to head to Louisiana State. He was part of a national championship team as a freshman but after struggling for two years and going unselected as a sophomore-eligible, he transferred to Penn State. He slashed .358/.470/.632 with 13 homers and 15 steals with the Nittany Lions, spurring the Rangers to sign him for an over-slot $375,000 as a seventh-rounder last July. A right-handed hitter, Kling tried to do too much at the plate at LSU, getting pull-happy and struggling to make contact against non-fastballs. He did a better job of using the entire field at Penn State, though he still swung and missed at a 40 percent clip against non-heaters. His plus raw power and ability to drive balls in the air give him 25-homer upside, though his hitting ability remains a question. Kling possesses plus speed but isn't especially daring on the bases. He's a versatile defender with the range to cover center field and the arm strength to handle right. He has a higher ceiling than most Rangers prospects but also a lot to prove at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best pitcher ever at Navy, Song led NCAA Division I in strikeouts per nine innings (15.4, the sixth-highest rate in D-I history) in 2019 and finished his career with school records for career wins (32), innings (334 1/3) and whiffs (428). He became the highest pick in Navy history when the Red Sox took him in the fourth round, and he would have gone much higher and signed for more than $100,000 if not for his two-year military commitment. He dominated in his brief pro debut and with Team USA at the Premier 12 tournament that November, then reported to flight school in June 2020 and hasn't petitioned for an early release, which he could have in May 2021. Song has first-round stuff, starting with a four-seam fastball that sits at 93-96 mph and reaches 99 with late riding action. His mid-80s slider grades as his best secondary pitch and can be a legitimate wipeout offering at its best. He gets good depth on an upper-70s curveball that shows flashes of being a plus pitch and surprised the Red Sox with the quality of his fading changeup during his debut. Song uses his 6-foot-4 frame and high three-quarters slot to create downhill plane on his pitches. He doesn't feature much effort in his delivery and throws strikes, though some evaluators quibble with his arm action and whether he'll ever have better than average command. He has as much upside as any Boston pitching prospect, but it's unclear when he might return and how much his long layoff will affect him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Colleran wasn’t really on a ton of radars entering the 2024 Draft after an inconsistent season at Northeastern. But the Royals were intrigued by his fastball and selected him in the seventh round that summer. He climbed three levels in 2025, ending the year with an inning in Double-A and with a 2.85 ERA across all affiliates. He was especially dominant in High-A Quad Cities, where he made 21 appearances, posted a 1.83 ERA and struck out batters at a 25 percent clip. He also pitched in the Arizona Fall League, where he struck out 11 in 7 2/3 innings. Colleran’s heater is probably the best in the Royals’ system, given that it sits upper 90s and touched 101 mph in 2025. It’s a plus-plus pitch with really good sink and is hidden well in his delivery with his big leg kick. He throws an above-average 90-91 mph cutter that sometimes registers as a slider depending on the location, as well as an average mid-80s sweeper with big horizontal break. Colleran can get a little wild with high walk rates, but consistency with his secondaries could help with that. He’s focusing on the breaking ball especially, as well as controlling the running game; that big leg kick gives him some deception and power, but it can also get him in trouble. There’s obviously a lot to like with the velocity on Colleran’s fastball, and he has setup man or closer upside if he can continue to develop the secondary weapons and have better command. The Royals had him in big league camp this spring, so he’s on the radar and could move quickly if he keeps improving.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Werner pitched and hit his first two years of college at Texas A&M before transitioning to hitting full-time in ‘22 and ‘23. Scouts were still intrigued by his 90-plus mph arm, and the Royals drafted him as a two-way player in the seventh round of the 2023 Draft. But he made his pro debut as a hitter with four games in the Arizona Complex League before heading to Single-A Columbia. There, he simply produced and produced some more. Werner won the Carolina League Player of the Month in September, when he had a 1.328 OPS and paced the league in hits (15), runs (12) and RBIs (14). There were some questions about the swing-and-miss in Werner’s game leading up to the Draft, and he did strike out at a 23 percent clip in the small sample at Single-A last year. Werner holds his hands high, and he’s not totally smooth in his setup or follow-through. But he’s done a good job of freeing up his swing with the work he did this offseason, and that should help to unlock his impressive power. Werner has athleticism and an ease with which he moves about third base, although he made eight errors in 20 games at Single-A. He has a cannon of an arm and should be able to stick there at least for now. Werner receives high praise for his work ethic and cerebral approach to the game, his routine and his preparation. He’s a physical presence at 6-foot-3 and 225 pounds. It certainly was a small sample size in Columbia last year, but it rightfully garnered some attention. Werner has some tools to work with, which excites the Royals long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lara joined the Mets for just $25,000 in June 2021 and has been a level-per-year player since. After posting an OPS below .700 in both the Dominican Summer and Florida Complex Leagues the previous two seasons, he broke out some in his first trip to full-season ball with a .264/.362/.452 line, 14 homers and 17 steals in 99 games with Single-A St. Lucie last summer. His 122 wRC+ tied for seventh-best in the Florida State League while he was one of only seven players in all of Single-A ball with at least 14 homers and 14 steals. The right-handed slugger keeps his lower half relatively quiet in his batting setup, relying on his arms and wrists to fire through the zone. He can be caught chasing occasionally and was especially prone to whiffing on offspeed stuff, but he was aggressive on fastballs for good reason, slugging .653 off four-seamers. His exit velocities were roughly league average for the Florida State League, a solid showing for a 19-year-old, and his 90th percentile EV (101.5) was in the same neighborhood as more notable prospects Jett Williams (102.2) and Jacob Reimer (101.6). Lara ranked in the 82nd percentile for speed among his fellow FSLers, and the Mets put those wheels to use all over the diamond with time everywhere except for pitcher and catcher. He has the arm strength for either right field – where he topped out with a 100.5 mph throw – or third base, but a more permanent move to a corner puts a strong focus on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kohn immediately claimed a role in Mississippi State's bullpen as freshman before missing all of 2023 following Tommy John surgery. He showed average stuff when he came back as a starter and went undrafted in 2024, then improved his stuff and strike-throwing as a redshirt junior last spring. One of the best fourth-year collegians in the 2025 Draft, he went in the fourth round and will make his pro debut this year. Though Kohn's fastball has pedestrian velocity at 91-95 mph, hitters don't see it coming out of his low three-quarters arm slot and flat approach angle, and he has the aptitude to work it with carry up in the zone or spot it down at the knees. He also has advanced command of a sweeping low-80s slider that he can locate on either side of the plate. While he works almost exclusively with those two pitches, he does show a promising low-80s changeup with fade that could give him a third solid offering. Kohn improved his athleticism in 2025, allowing him to get down the mound better and repeat his delivery more consistently. That led to improved extension and deception as well as control and command. He has a high floor as a three-pitch lefty starter with advanced feel for his craft and strong mound presence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After turning down the Phillies as a 14th-rounder in 2024 to transfer to Texas, Spencer emerged as the best college senior in the 2025 Draft before injuring his shoulder in April and undergoing season-ending surgery. The Blue Jays selected him in the 11th round last summer and signed him for $165,000, a big swing on landing a talent who could have landed in the top three rounds of the Draft if he was healthy. There’s risk, but these are the types of gambles organizations should be taking outside of the first 10 rounds. Spencer added two mph to his fastball in the spring of 2025, sitting at 93-96 and touching 98 while maintaining his velocity deep into games, albeit with more downhill angle than carry or run. His sweeping slider always has been his best pitch, and it became a wipeout offering after it picked up five mph compared to a year ago, averaging 88 and reaching 91. His changeup had developed into a solid, mid-80s offering before the surgery. Spencer will open 2026 on the IL, so if he simply gets into some game action and sets himself up for a “regular” offseason next winter, that will be a success. This is a longer-term project for the Blue Jays, which is rare to say about a senior pick, but this has the potential to pay off in a major way if Spencer returns to his old self following rehab.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hedges was a presence in Southern Cal’s lineup for nearly all of his three years on campus. He turned in a big junior season, not only as the best hitter on the team who posted a .346/.462/.619 line with 14 homers but also serving as the Trojans’ closer and racking up nine saves. With former big leaguer Andy Stankiewicz at the helm, there tends to be a comfort level from MLB teams in terms of taking USC infielders, and the Rockies didn’t shy away from nabbing Hedges in the third round of the 2025 Draft, sending him to High-A Spokane for a brief pro debut. While his time at instructs after the season was cut short because of a concussion, the Rockies are intrigued with what Hedges might bring to the table. He has a good feel to hit from the right side of the plate, with a line-drive approach and a knack for barreling up the baseball. It can be loud contact at times and while it’s more extra-base authority right now, the hope is the jump in the bat the Rockies saw can translate to more over-the-fence pop in the future. Hedges moves well enough to play third base capably, though it’s the arm that fired low-90s fastballs as a reliever for the Trojans that really stand out. His instincts help all of his tools play up across the board.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Floyd pitched only one year at Texas Tech, following two years of JuCo in the same state, but he made enough of an impression as a reliever to get the Brewers to select him in the 10th round of the 2019 Draft. Following the 2020 Minor League season cancelation, he made his full-season debut last year and was effective at both the High-A and Double-A levels, posting a 2.89 ERA and 1.11 WHIP with 84 strikeouts in 56 innings across the two spots. He also made nine appearances in the Arizona Fall League, but he suffered tougher results in the hitter-friendly circuit (seven earned runs, 10 K’s in 8 2/3 innings). The 6-foot-1 right-hander throws out of a low sidearm slot that borders on being a submarine delivery. There’s nothing secondary about his slider. Floyd often goes to the 77-79 mph offering as his primary pitch, because its hard break leads to a ton of swing-and-misses. His 90-92 mph fastball won’t wow with velo, but it does feature a ton of sink, causing batters to hit the ball straight into the ground when they do make a contact. He only occasionally will sprinkle in a low-80s changeup and can sometimes be left vulnerable by batters not willing to swing on movement out of the zone. Floyd ranked among the top three Brewers Minor League pitchers (minimum 50 innings) in both strikeout rate (37 percent) and groundball rate (50.4 percent) in 2021, highlighting his strengths perfectly. The Brewers feel he’s capable of pitching in high-leverage situations because of those typical outcomes, even if it isn’t high-octane stuff, and Floyd might not be far off from helping the Milwaukee bullpen with his version of funk.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After barely playing during the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, Sprinkle was co-Big West Conference freshman field player of the year the following spring and played for the U.S. collegiate national team during the summer. UC Santa Barbara's best position prospect since 2006 third-rounder Chris Valaika, Sprinkle entered 2022 with first-round buzz but slipped to the fourth round after struggling at the plate. He batted .237/.290/.301 in a month in Single-A after signing for $452,900. Scouts considered Sprinkle the best defensive shortstop in the 2022 college class. He's quick with range to both sides and reliable hands, and he increased his arm strength last year to where it now grades as solid to plus. He enhances his throwing ability with a fast release and has a good internal clock. Sprinkle batted .353/.402/.536 at UCSB in 2021 but got out of whack when he added strength and hunted home runs for much of his draft year. He has bat speed but gets overly aggressive at the plate, lengthens his right-handed swing and leaves himself vulnerable to offspeed pitches. He needs to focus on getting on base to take advantage of his plus speed and basestealing aptitude.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star who excelled on the football field in high school, Campbell focused on baseball only when he headed to the University of Texas. He improved each year and the Dodgers took him in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft after he posted a 1.039 OPS as a Longhorns junior. He spent his first full season of pro ball with High-A Great Lakes and was one of a handful of hitters in the Minors to hit 20 doubles and 10 homers while stealing 40 bases. The Dodgers sent him to the Phillies in January to get international bonus pool money used to sign Roki Sasaki. Strong and compact, Campbell has a well-deserved reputation for spraying line drives to all fields and was among the best in the Dodgers system last year with his 24.3 percent line-drive rate. His strikeout rate did go up, but he typically has had good pitch recognition and a solid approach, making good swing decisions and there’s confidence he’ll be able to make adjustments as he progresses. He’s not a burner, but he runs well and used his instincts to steal 42 bags in 2024. While he saw some time on the dirt at the start of his college career, and played a few games at second last year, Campbell has developed into a defensive outfielder. He used his plus arm to pick up 11 outfield assists a year ago and his speed allows him to cover a lot of ground. Right field might be his best spot, but his ability to play all three outfield positions points to a future career as a fourth-outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Spence spent his first two college seasons at Black Hawk (Ill.) CC, where he batted .368/.442/.600 while also seeing action on the mound. He continued to play both ways at Southern Illinois-Edwardsville, where he won the Ohio Valley Conference batting title (.385) in 2024 before the Astros signed him for $150,000 as a nondrafted free agent. He reached Double-A in his first full pro season, hitting a combined .244/.368/.403 with 10 homers and 27 steals in 116 games between three levels. Spence rarely chases pitches and could fit at the top of the order with his on-base skills and basestealing ability. While the left-handed hitter doesn't miss fastballs, he struggles to make contact against breaking balls and changeups and has been overmatched by southpaws in pro ball. He has some sneaky pop but also hits a lot of grounders, so he'll probably top out at 10-12 homers per season. Though there's some question about how much offense Spence can provide, he can help a team win in a variety of ways. He knows how to use his plus speed to reach base, steal bags and chase down balls in the outfield. He's a solid defender in center with plus arm strength that translated into a low-90s fastball in college.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The 2019 Draft class was deep in terms of college shortstops and the spring began with Holland looking like he could be one of the first ones taken, especially after a very strong Cape Cod League showing the summer prior. But the Auburn product struggled during his junior year, allowing him to slide to the fifth round, where the Twins were able to sign him for $575,000. He continued to scuffle with the bat during his pro debut in the rookie-level Appalachian League. Holland is an impressive athlete with speed and plenty of raw power. His biggest problem is that he hasn’t incorporated his athleticism into his swing. He seemed uncomfortable and unnatural at the plate during his pro debut using a setup some felt was too spread out. He spent the offseason hitting with fellow Twins prospect Brent Rooker in the hopes of finding some rhythm and timing from the right side of the plate. Getting the bat going would allow Holland to become an intriguing all-around player. He plays good defense at short, with a strong arm and his plus speed helping him with enough range. He continued to work on his swing at the Twins’ minicamp and if he can take that into his first full season of pro ball, he could shoot up this list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: By the standards of a drafted high-school player, Cox may have been a relatively late bloomer. He was a member of the JV team as a sophomore at Rock Hill High School (Texas), and it took breakouts as a junior and senior to make pro scouts think he could be signed away from playing at the University of Texas. The Nationals took on that risk by selecting Cox in the fourth round and inked him to a nearly double-slot $1 million bonus. With his upright stance, Cox sports a classic left-handed swing that could translate nicely on the pro side. He went 10-for-35 with a homer in 10 Rookie-level Florida Complex League games to boost that argument, and it’s notable that he only batted out of the leadoff spot there. There isn’t a ton of power at present, but his 6-foot-3 frame indicates more pop could be in store as he matures physically. Cox was a two-year starting quarterback and touched 94 mph on the mound during his prep days, so he should be able to handle any of the three outfield spots from an arm perspective. On top of that, he’s a plus runner and impressive overall athlete. Cox has already bumped a bit into Washington’s logjam of athletic outfielders -- he made eight of his 10 starts in left field in deference to Elijah Green -- but while he’s raw, he still has the skill set to elbow his way further into the conversation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs have long loved their athletic and toolsy center fielders with Corbin Carroll and Alek Thomas graduating in recent years, Druw Jones joining as the second overall pick in 2022 and Adriel Radney entering the fold internationally this January. Zapata fit the description in January 2023 when he signed with Arizona for $950,000. The teenager debuted in the Dominican Summer League and was a midseason All-Star there before finishing with a .254/.364/.522 line and 126 wRC+. The left-handed-slugging outfielder measured in at 6-foot-4 and 195 pounds upon signing, and his size led to belief that he’d get to above-average power down the line. That pullside pop actually came quickly in 2023 with nine home runs and a .269 ISO, each of which ranked fifth in the DSL. Zapata, however, struck out in 29.1 percent of his plate appearances, and he’ll need to reel in that approach significantly as he heads stateside. The Dominican Republic native runs well for someone with his frame, and the D-backs gave him the majority of his defensive starts in center field. He also got ample time in right because of his plus arm strength, and he might end up there long-term should he slow down a tick as some expect. His powerful profile would play in a corner, but he’ll have to make adjustments at the plate as he climbs the ladder toward Phoenix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Preparing for the possibility that Roki Sasaki might sign at the end of the 2024 international period, New York stockpiled bonus pool money and acquired some more from the Red Sox in the Carlos Narvaez trade that November. When Sasaki opted to wait, the Yankees spent $1.65 million on Dec. 17 to sign Marinez, who had planned to turn pro in 2025. He batted .275/.424/.375 and looked good at shortstop in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. A left-handed hitter, Marinez has a sound stroke and patient approach. He drew 41 walks in 47 DSL games but also can get too passive and fall behind in counts more than he should. He needs to add significant strength so he can turn on more pitches and hit them harder, but New York believes he can grow into at least 15-homer power with more muscle and some adjustments to his swing path. Marinez features plus speed and likes to turn it loose on the bases, stealing 22 bases in 28 attempts (79 percent) in the DSL. His quickness helps him cover ground to both sides and he has the solid to plus arm strength to finish plays. Like most teenage infielders, he needs more defensive consistency, which should come with experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Neville’s commitment to Arkansas as a Las Vegas high school standout pushed him to the end of the 2022 Draft, so he headed to play for the Razorbacks. After getting just 27 at-bats as a freshman, he transferred to Oregon and immediately showed he could get to some power with 16 homers as a sophomore. He tightened up his swing as a junior, cutting down his strikeouts, which helped him tie for the Division I lead with 26 homers. Worries about his feel for hitting followed him into the Draft, so he was available for the Reds in the fourth round and his debut with Single-A Daytona, albeit brief, did not assuage those swing-and-miss concerns. Neville does offer up ever-exciting raw power from the left side of the plate to go along with excellent overall athleticism. After striking out 33.5 percent of the time as a sophomore with the Ducks, he trimmed that to 23.6 percent as a junior before whiffing 31 times in 90 pro plate appearances during his debut. He can impact the ball for extra bases to the gaps, with his over-the-fence thump showing up mostly to his pull side. He can feast off fastballs but one of his areas of focus as a pro will be to recognize spin and cut down whiffs on softer stuff overall. Neville played a solid center field at Oregon and there are those who feel he has a chance to stick there. He’ll get time at all three spots as he gets going in earnest and might best be suited for right, where his above-average arm would play well. His ceiling is directly tied to how much he can manage the strike zone and make contact in order to get to his very real power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally drafted by his hometown D-backs as a 19th-rounder in 2022, Turley instead opted to play college ball at Oregon State, where he had a big year as a freshman with 14 home runs and an OPS above 1.100. After crushing another 19 homers in 2024 and performing well in the Cape Cod League that summer, the A’s drafted him in '25 as a fourth-round pick, following a 20-homer junior year, signing him below slot at $600,000. Ahead of his first full professional season, Turley got his feet wet with 27 games at Single-A Stockton. Turley falls in line with similar A’s draft picks in recent years -- like Denzel Clarke and Rodney Green Jr. -- as a toolsy outfielder with some concerns about his ability to make consistent contact. He’s got big power and is able to drive the ball out to all fields with great bat speed, but his strikeout rates throughout his career with the Beavers were somewhat alarming. The question over whether he can hit enough to tap into that raw power is something he’ll have to prove early in his pro career. He has a tendency to chase breaking stuff often, though he mitigates that issue somewhat with his strong ability to draw walks. A big knock on Turley coming out of college was poor defense, but the A’s believe he is plenty athletic and speedy enough to improve and envision that happening as he grows into his 6-foot-1 frame. His body type and look in the box remind some within the organization of Mark Canha, and he’ll look to move through the system as a power-hitting corner outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rincon was three months shy of his 17th birthday when he signed with the Cardinals for $70,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2019. His stateside debut didn’t come until three years later, and while he looked like a workhorse with back-to-back seasons of 132 2/3 innings in ’23 and ’24, he didn’t become a breakout arm with swing-and-miss stuff until this past season, in which he posted a 3.92 ERA with 108 strikeouts in 96 1/3 frames at High-A and Double-A. Despite that, he went unprotected and unselected in the Rule 5 Draft when eligible in the offseason. The 6-foot-2 right-hander bumped up his velocity just a bit to sit 91-94 mph with his fastball, but the pitch only gets ordinary ride and doesn’t come with big extension. While it doesn’t produce whiffs, he can spot it well to get ahead in counts and bring in his more dangerous weapons. Rincon tinkered with his changeup grip and clearly found something that worked because the mid-80s pitch shows a lot of armside run and generated a ton of whiffs. (Lefties pounded the heater though, making splits still an issue.) He’d also work in a low-80s gyro slider with nice drop versus righties, who’d often lunge at breakers low and away from them. Rincon throws free and easy from a fluid delivery, and he’ll even use a bounce in his right knee when he gets into the windup that gives him a throwback look from a different era. He was better at limiting walks in his climb to Double-A Springfield, something Cardinals officials credit for better sequencing rather than any overhaul in mechanics. Entering his age-24 season, Rincon may need to rely even more on his secondaries if he’s going to break through to the Majors because they are the moneymakers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more athletic players in Illinois' 2025 high school crop, Wheeler played third base and pitched for Morris (Ill.) HS, while also pulling duty as a wide receiver and defensive back in football and setting the school's career scoring record in basketball. His varied sporting interests didn't leave much time for the prep showcase circuit, so he flew a bit under the scouting radar. The Rangers waited until the sixth round to take him and paid an over-slot $525,000 to sign him away from an Illinois commitment. Texas believes in Wheeler's offensive upside because he makes good swing decisions and consistent contact while producing better exit velocities than most players his age. He has a simple right-handed stroke and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. Once he adds more strength to his athletic 6-foot-5 frame and learns to elevate balls more regularly, he could produce 20 or more homers per year. Wheeler presently has solid speed but may lose a step as he fills out. He moves well at third base and features a strong arm that ran fastballs up to 92 mph when he took the mound. If he can't stay on the dirt, his power and arm strength would profile well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Geraldo received the sixth-highest bonus ($600,000) in the Cubs' 2026 international class, he may have a higher offensive ceiling and a stronger arm than any of his counterparts. A late bloomer physically out of the Dominican Republic, his stock was rising as the January opening of the signing period approached. Geraldo has the ingredients to develop 25-homer power. He has a quick right-handed stroke, a knack for barreling balls and room to add plenty of strength to his 6-foot-1 frame. He's an advanced hitter for his age who shows some ability to recognize pitches. An average runner who doesn't have typical shortstop quickness, Geraldo compensates with plus arm strength. Given the four of the five Cubs 2026 signees who landed higher bonuses also play shortstop, he likely will get some reps at second and third base when he makes his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He probably fits best at the hot corner in the long run and should have the pop to profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tillero signed for $497,500 out of Venezuela, making him the most expensive pitcher in the Dodgers' 2023 international class. Los Angeles hadn't spent that much on an arm in that market since giving Jerming Rosario $650,000 and Osvanni Gutierrez $600,000 five years earlier. In his pro debut, Tillero earned the starting nod in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League's All-Star game and logged a 1.47 ERA with 34 strikeouts in 30 2/3 innings. Before he tired later in the summer, Tillero displayed a 94-95 mph fastball that touched 97 with plenty of induced vertical break. His slider parks at 83-86 mph at its best and could become a solid or better offering once he improves its consistency. He also has the makings of a decent changeup but hasn't used it much in game action. Tillero already repeats his sound delivery with ease and walked just six batters in 10 DSL starts. He's not very big or physical, so he'll have to prove that he and his stuff can hold up over a full-season workload. But he's off to a promising start and could turn heads when he makes his U.S. debut in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A mainstay in UNC Wilmington’s rotation over his four years there, Taylor produced one of the best seasons in school history as a senior in 2025 by leading NCAA Division I in K/BB ratio (9.6) and WHIP (0.76), while also ranking second in walk rate (1.0 per nine innings) and fourth in ERA (1.98). Entering the 2025 Draft as one of the top senior arms in the class, he was selected in the fifth round by the A’s and signed at a full-slot bonus of $513,900, becoming the highest-drafted pitcher out of UNCW since supplemental first-rounder Bradley Holt in 2008. With Triple-A Las Vegas in need of a starter at the end of the season, Taylor was called upon for his pro debut with a start for a playoff-bound Aviators squad. Taylor pleasantly surprised the A’s by showing up with a bit more velocity than they expected, working with a fastball that reached up to 98 mph and sat 93-95. His low-80s changeup has good fade and is probably his best secondary pitch right now. He also brings a low-80s curveball, mid-80s cutter and a sweeper he learned shortly after getting drafted. He has good command of all his pitches and was one of the top strike-throwers in all of college baseball. Taylor is a bit undersized, reminiscent to some within the A’s organization of Sonny Gray in that aspect. He will enter his first full season as a professional as one of the more intriguing A’s pitching prospects, and given that he’s basically a finished product, the potential is there for him to rise quickly through the system and eventually reach the Majors, where he profiles as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
