mlb_pipeline.text: Abeldt was one of college baseball's best relievers in his first two years at Texas Christian, recording a 2.81 ERA with 125 strikeouts in 99 1/3 innings and spending both summers with the U.S. collegiate national team. The Horned Frogs planned on turning him into a starter in 2025, but he blew out his elbow just before the beginning of the season and required Tommy John surgery in February. The Rangers still popped him in the fifth round and signed him for $450,000. Abeldt relies heavily on a 91-94 mph fastball that peaks at 96 and is much more effective than its ordinary velocity would indicate. His heater has riding action and plenty of deception coming out of a crossfire delivery, and it's nearly impossible to lift when he works down in the zone. He can't overpower hitters with a slider that sits around 80 mph, but it can baffle them with its sweeping action when it's on. While he doesn't use it much, Abeldt has the makings of an effective low-80s changeup with sink. He looks like a shorter, stronger version of Chris Sale with his slingy delivery, and it generates a lot of empty swings and groundballs. It remains to be seen if he can succeed as a starter, but he comes with a high floor as a quality lefty reliever once he returns to full health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $42,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2024, Laroche pitched just three innings during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He returned to the DSL last year and stood out with some of the best stuff in the circuit, posting a 2.11 ERA with a 34/6 K/BB ratio in 38 1/3 frames. He'll make his U.S. debut in 2026 and could push his way to full-season ball at the end of the summer. LaRoche features an explosive sinker that operates at 93-95 mph and maxes out at 97, and he also uses a four-seam fastball with similar velocity and armside run. His tight 82-85 mph slider has the potential to become a solid offering. While he has yet to use it very often, he also shows some feel for a mid-80s changeup. Though Laroche stands just 5-foot-11 and doesn't have a smooth delivery, he's very athletic and deceptive. He flies down the mound, producing plenty of extension for his size as well as a unusually low release height. He has no problem filling the strike zone but will need to refine his command as he climbs the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Contreras signed with the Royals as part of their 2025 international signing class for just $147,000 out of the Dominican Republic, and he didn’t turn 17 until Aug. 10 -- right before he wrapped up an excellent Dominican Summer League season. He posted a 3.30 ERA there, striking out 37 batters across 30 innings with 13 walks. He also started for the American League in the DSL All-Star Game, although he allowed four earned runs and recorded just two outs. Listed at 5-foot-11, Contreras might not be super tall in stature, but he’s very strong and throws effortlessly from the mound. Answering the questions about his durability and velocity because of his smaller size, he already sits 95-98 mph with his heater, pairing it with a downer curveball that has great spin and an average changeup that plays off his fastball well. Contreras threw strikes in the DSL and has a repeatable delivery that helps with his command, as the ball comes out of his hand free and easy. Contreras is young and still has far to go with his development, but there’s upside of a mid-rotation starter. He arrived stateside for the 2026 season but suffered an elbow injury that required season-ending UCL surgery in the spring. Contreras will likely still only be 18 by the time he returns to a Minor League mound with plenty of promise still ahead.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Romero received the second-largest bonus in Chicago's 2026 international class, signing for $1.5 million out of Venezuela in January. He's a more advanced hitter than most 17-year-olds, and his tools are roughly comparable to those of Jaden Fauske, who landed an above-slot $2,997,500 bonus as second-rounder last July. He'll likely spend his first pro season in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. A left-handed hitter, Romero has a fluid stroke and showed the ability to put together quality at-bats and make consistent contact as an amateur. He has a projectable 6-foot-2 frame that could add significant strength, and he should develop at least 15-20 homer power. He'll require time to develop but could blossom into one of the best offensive prospects in the system. Romero has solid speed and athleticism, which should allow him to steal some bases. He also should be able to handle center field and has the arm strength to handle right field if he shifts to a corner. He has been clocked up to 88 mph on throws from the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Tanner hit 15 homers as a sophomore at Mississippi State, including one in the game that clinched a 2021 College World Series title against Vanderbilt, he was more known for his work behind the plate. He didn’t hit as well as a junior in 2022, but his glove work was the main reason why the Reds took the Bulldogs standout in the second round of last year’s Draft. Tanner is always likely to be a defense-over-hit backstop. He loves to throw and who can blame him, with one of the strongest arms in the Minors. It’s plus-plus with some amateur scouts hanging an 80 on it, the kind of hose that can shut down a running game. A good leader behind the plate who works well with pitchers, Tanner is a solid receiver and blocker, giving him all he needs to catch in the big leagues for a long time. How often he’s able to do that will depend on how his bat develops. There’s strength and bat speed from the right side, with a solid knowledge of the strike zone and a willingness to draw walks, although he needs to get the ball in the air more to put that raw power to better use. In his brief pro debut, he was a little pull happy; the Reds think an emphasis on staying in the middle of the field, trusting his hands and believing he has the goods to stay on the fastball away and breaking stuff moving away from him to go opposite field will serve him well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Grinsell made a big leap between his sophomore and junior seasons at Oregon, lowering his ERA by a full run and cutting his walk rate in half while becoming just the sixth pitcher in Ducks history to post 200 career strikeouts. While he wasn’t overpowering, his ability to miss bats and his athleticism -- he was a very good two-way player in high school -- led the Tigers to take a sixth-round pick on him in the 2025 Draft and sign him for $297,500. Deception is the name of the game for Grinsell, who doesn’t have a dominant pitch but has a good feel for sequencing and reading hitters. His fastball sits in the low 90s but plays up thanks in part to extension and location. It also sets up an 80 mph changeup that he hides well with a similar delivery. His slider was his third pitch in college. While he fits into the Tigers’ pitching philosophy of commanding the strike zone, he could also add velocity if the club can improve his delivery. Projection can be difficult with a college pitcher, but Grinsell’s athleticism provides some potential for upside if he can find another tick or two on his fastball, which could then make his changeup that much better. He’ll need an effective breaking pitch to make it as a starter, but a good fastball-changeup combination could be the foundation for a potential crafty lefty reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Like Fernando Rodney, a fellow native from Samana, Dominican Republic, De Jesus was a wild card in the Tigers farm system. He spent two-plus years in the Dominican Summer League and didn’t reach full-season ball until 2019, three years after signing. From there, his power fastball and high strikeout rate caught attention, allowing him to advance quickly. By the end of 2021, he was closing at Triple-A Toledo, and combined for 80 strikeouts over 64 2/3 innings with just 38 hits allowed between the Mud Hens and Double-A Erie. De Jesus’ fastball picked up some life last year, sitting in the mid-90s but topping out at 97-98 mph. There’s enough late movement on it and enough deception in his three-quarter delivery that hitters struggle to pick it up. He complements that with a mid-80s slider that moves late. Command and consistency have always been his questions; he rarely gives up home runs in part because he rarely leaves mistakes over the middle of the plate. The Tigers thought enough of De Jesus’ potential to add him to their 40-man roster at the end of last season. Detroit has had success turning hard-throwing but inconsistent relievers into Major Leaguers, including Gregory Soto and Jose Cisnero. With a little work, De Jesus could be next up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $10,000 back in July 2018, Castellano didn’t pitch officially until 2021 in the Dominican Summer League and then spent two years in the Florida State League, mostly as a reliever. In 2024, he jumped on the map when he was given the chance to start, pitching his way to Double-A while recording a 31-percent miss rate. The Phillies didn’t protect him on their 40-man roster, and the Twins selected him in December’s Rule 5 Draft, but he was returned to the Phillies on March 25. A huge amount of that 2024 swing-and-miss came from Castellano’s curveball, an 80-82 mph pitch with power and depth that showed a lot of improvement in 2024, eliciting a 49 percent miss rate. His changeup has long been an effective offering for the 6-foot-3 right-hander, thrown in the mid-80s with sink and fade that also can be an out pitch (39 percent miss rate, according to Synergy). He mixes both of them well with a fastball that averaged just over 94 mph last year, touching 98, and is thrown with good extension. The biggest leap forward for Castellano has been his command and control. After walking 4.1 per nine in his two years in Single-A Clearwater, he cut that rate to 2.5/9 last year, while still racking up strikeouts (11.8 K/9 in ‘24), giving him the potential to start long term, something he’ll get back to doing with the Phillies.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The maternal grandson of former Orioles outfielder and 1965 AL Rookie of the Year Curt Blefary, Servideo played sparingly as a Mississippi freshman in 2018, then spent most of 2019 shuttling between right field and center field for the Rebels before posting the worst batting line (.149/.228/.277) in the Cape Cod League. He looked like a different player as a junior, starting on Opening Day by singling, doubling and walking against Louisville left-hander Reid Detmers, the eventual No.10 overall pick. Servideo emerged as one of college baseball's better shortstops, slashing .390/.575/.695 in the shortened season. That showed the Orioles enough to take him in the third round and give him a slightly above-slot $950,000 bonus to sign. Servideo’s plus speed and selective approach allowed him to play a table-setting role in college, where he drew 24 walks in 17 games during his junior year and then routinely created havoc on the bases. He’ll need to add strength and cut down his left-handed swing to remain at the top of the order at the next level, where it’ll be necessary to make more consistent contact. He's not big and won't be a slugger, but he displayed more pop as a junior, homering five times after going deep just four times in 100 previous contests. While there are mixed opinions on how much impact Servideo will have at the plate, there are no questions about his ability to play shortstop. He’s a flashy defender, with smooth hands, quick feet and enough arm strength to profile at the position long-term. His athleticism and strong instincts up the middle should give him time to grow into more of an offensive threat. If he doesn't hit enough to be a regular, he'd be capable of playing anywhere in the infield and outfield as a utility man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Callahan was a career .351 hitter at St. Joseph’s and posted an OPS above 1.000 in both his sophomore and junior years with the Hawks. But questions about how he’d hold up against better competition dropped him to the 13th round in 2023, and the Tigers picked and signed him for $197,500. He’s shown flashes of dominance at virtually every stop since but has struggled with injuries, including a dislocated finger and right lower leg hematoma in 2024 and a pulled quad in 2025. He finally cracked Double-A to begin 2026 -- his age-24 season -- with positive results out of the gate. A left-handed hitter, Callahan has long shown promising raw power as a professional, and he proved that this spring in limited Grapefruit League looks with a pair of home runs hit above 105 mph and one batted ball at 112.2 mph. But an overly aggressive approach early in his career seriously put into question how much of that pop translated into game action at the upper levels. Callahan, who has gone from an open stance to one more straight-on while keeping his leg kick, has been less swing-happy to begin ’26, allowing his walk rate to double in the season’s first month and making a potential MLB future all the clearer. Standing 6-foot, the former Atlantic 10 first-teamer can get moving out of the box, and he’s proven capable of making strong throws from the grass. The Tigers have rotated him around the outfield because of both skillsets, and he could prove to be above-average defensively in a corner. Much will come down to maintaining his early swing-decision improvements, especially with Rule 5 eligibility coming up this offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Another reason 2025 was a very strong international signing class for the Royals, Calcaño ranked as the 38th-best prospect on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international list heading into the signing period. The Dominican native signed for $1,847,500. His 2025 season was cut short because of a shoulder injury, but he stood out in his nine-game sample, hitting .346 with a 1.052 OPS, seven stolen bases and eight walks to 10 strikeouts. A switch-hitter, Calcaño is a bit better from the left side but overall possesses a line-drive approach and good understanding of the strike zone. He has a wiry and lean frame, and as he adds strength, there’s power potential beyond doubles in the gap. But the early excitement about Calcaño comes on the dirt. He’s a plus defender with good hands and he'll be able to stick at shortstop. There are questions about how his arm strength returns following the shoulder injury, but it was plus before. Calcaño also has good speed and instincts on the bases. Because of their position and ages, there will be comparisons between Calcaño and Ramcell Medina as they grow up through the system together. Calcaño probably is the better defender, while Medina has the higher upside with his bat. Calcaño could make his stateside debut in ‘26.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barreto received the next-highest bonus behind Josuar Gonzalez in San Francisco's 2025 international crop, signing for $1,118,700 out of Venezuela. Though he received more attention for his shortstop play as an amateur, he slashed .322/.449/.394 in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He also spent most of his time at second base in deference to Anthony Marquez. A right-handed hitter, Barreto has advanced bat-to-ball skills. He makes good swing decisions though he can get overly pull-happy, resulting in too many rolled-over grounders. Though he only went deep once in his first 53 pro games, he packs some sneaky pop in his compact frame and could provide 15 or more homers per year if he improves his quality of contact. An average runner with a thick lower half, Barreto could lose some quickness as he matures physically. He has the actions, hands and plus arm strength to play shortstop if he maintains his current quickness. The Giants will give him some time at short but project him as more of an offensive second or third baseman. rate of just 8.9%. He didn’t make much impact on contact, however, and most of his power will likely be limited to doubles on balls to the gaps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Webb spent two seasons as a starter at Sinclair (Ohio) CC and two as a reliever at Miami (Ohio) before the Red Sox picked him in the 14th round in 2021. In his first full pro season, he compiled a 3.18 ERA with 88 strikeouts in 56 2/3 innings while rising from Single-A to Double-A. The first pitcher from Boston's 2021 Draft to reach Double-A, he also performed well in the Arizona Fall League. Webb works with two pitches and misses bats with both of them. His fastball sits at 93-96 mph and touches 98 with significant carry and some arm-side run. He backs it up with a low-80s slider that has good sweep at times and is tighter with more depth at others. Physically imposing at 6-foot-5 and 246 pounds, Webb has an extremely low release point for someone so large and creates good extension. There's effort in his crossfire delivery and his short arm action isn't the prettiest, but they provide a lot of deception and his pitches get on hitters in a hurry. He threw strikes in college but has lacked reliable control as a pro, and he could help Boston's bullpen in the near future if he can find the zone more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last 40-round Draft could very well be the 2019 edition. One year before that, the Mets used their 40th-round selection on Metoyer out of NAIA program Louisiana State University of Alexandria. He was dominant in relief for High-A Brooklyn in 2021 with a 2.18 ERA, 0.91 WHIP and 46 strikeouts in 33 innings with the Cyclones and made a late two-game appearance at Double-A Binghamton. The right-hander closed out his age-24 season in the Arizona Fall League, where he fanned 17 but walked 10 while allowing 12 earned runs in 10 1/3 innings. Lanky at a listed 6-foot-3 and 173 pounds, Metoyer earns the biggest praise for his curveball, a plus-plus offering that could play in the Majors right away. The 79- to 81-mph deuce regularly pops 3,000-plus rpm, and he posted the 35 highest spin rates as measured by Statcast in last year’s Fall League. The vertical break toward the bottom of the zone helps generate a high ground-ball rate, and his 69.2 GB percentage was tops among Mets pitchers with at least 30 innings in 2021. The right-hander is typically around 94-96 mph with a cutting fastball, helping keep balls on the dirt. Metoyer went to the AFL to work on a changeup, but that remains a distant third pitch. Because of all the movement, Metoyer can struggle to stay in the zone. That lack of control (along with the lackluster third pitch) keeps him in relief, and it played into the Mets’ decision to leave him off the 40-man roster last November when he became Rule 5-eligible. The velocity and spin of the curveball give him enough of an arsenal to feature in a Major League bullpen, and a back-end role is possible if he can land more strikes in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Facundo has worked just 148 innings in his first five years as a pro after signing for $20,000 out of Venezuela in May 2021. He missed all of 2022 with shoulder issues and had Tommy John surgery in May 2024. He may be worth the wait, however, because he's the rare left-hander who can reach triple digits with his fastball. Coming back from his elbow reconstruction, Facundo threw harder than ever, working at 94-96 mph and touching 100 with his heater. He has more success with a two-seamer with sink because his four-seamer is fairly straight and doesn't miss many bats. His mid-80 slider lacks consistency but could become a solid offering with more development, while he barely uses a changeup that sits around 90 mph without much action. Because he's currently a two-pitch guy who has yet to show any durability, Facundo projects more as a reliever than a starter. He works solely out of the stretch and with an upright delivery and three-quarters arm slot. The Yankees opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster this offseason, and his relative inexperience allowed him to sneak through the Rule 5 Draft without getting popped.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels may have found a real sleeper in Quintero, whom they signed at the start of the 2024 international signing period for just $25,000 out of Panama. He immediately established himself as one of the best catch-and-throw backstops in the system, first in the Dominican Summer League after signing in a year truncated by a broken hamate, and then when he came stateside in 2025, helping the Angels win the Arizona Complex League championship. Following that, he moved up to Single-A Inland Empire to play a part in the 66ers’ playoff run. Quintero is always going to lead with his glove. Compact at 5-foot-8, he’s agile behind the dish with excellent receiving and blocking skills. His arm is at least plus, using its strength and accuracy to throw out 49 percent of potential basestealers across both stops in 2025. Playing all of 2026 at age 19, Quintero does have some offensive qualities to work with. He has a line-drive approach to all fields and his exit velocity took a nice step forward last year. He doesn’t strike out much, but he needs to cut down on his chase to become a more complete hitter. That will determine his ultimate ceiling because his defensive work might be special enough to carry him to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the better two-way players in the 2022 Draft, Mule displayed raw power, arm strength and athleticism at shortstop and hit 100 mph with his fastball on the prep showcase circuit. He displayed increased polish as a pitcher during his New Jersey high school senior season, leading most clubs to believe he had more upside on the mound. He gave up a Miami scholarship to sign for an above-slot $1 million in the fourth round, but Tommy John surgery in March 2023 will push his pro debut back to mid-2024. Though Mule can reach triple digits with his fastball, he has learned that he's better off ignoring radar guns and working at 93-96 with increased riding action. He showed a more consistent slider last spring and his low-80s breaker features more depth than sweep. He barely needed a third pitch as an amateur but can flash a low-80s changeup with intriguing fade. Mule did a better job of pitching under control as a high school senior, and his athleticism should help him throw strikes. Though he'll need plenty of time to refine his secondary pitches, control and command, he has one of the more electric arms in the system. The Cubs have said they plan to develop him as a pitcher but will remain open-minded about how his role might evolve.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pena has been a reliever in the Padres system ever since signing for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2022, 10 days before his 21st birthday. After one season in the Dominican Summer League, he’s been on a fast track toward San Diego, having played for all five stateside affiliates between 2023 and ’24. In his most recent campaign, he finished with a 2.43 ERA and 64 strikeouts over 63 innings across the top three levels of the Minors. Like many Padres pitching prospects, his numbers jumped at hitter-friendly El Paso but not enough to be overly concerning. Pena cuts a thin figure at 6-foot-1, setting up out of the stretch from the first-base side of the rubber. But he generated over 7 feet of extension at Triple-A, putting himself close to the plate with dynamic stuff. He throws a pair of fastballs, both in the 94-97 mph range -- a sinker with more than 11 inches of armside run and a straighter four-seamer. He leaned on the former more at Triple-A, which makes sense given his other offering. In 2025, his most oft-used secondary is an 86-89 mph two-plane slider that he uses to get a ton of whiffs. Walks weren't a huge issue for Pena in the Minors until his extended time at Triple-A in '25. The sinker helps him run a heavy ground-ball rate. The lack of a changeup may make him a questionable fit against lefties at the top level, but the slider has served him well enough so far. He has to find more strikes if he's going to earn that MLB debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meola was named Atlantic Sun Conference Tournament MVP as a sophomore after homering three times in four games and earned ASUN defensive player of the year accolades as a junior in 2025. The cousin of former U.S. national soccer team goalie Tony Meola, he went in the fourth round, making him Stetson's highest-drafted position player since 2003 first-rounder Brian Johnson. He took over at shortstop for an injured Maui Ahuna at Single-A San Jose and helped win a California League title. With solid speed and quick feet, Meola covers plenty of ground at shortstop. His smooth actions, soft hands and strong arm help make him a plus defender at short. Factor in some sneaky power, and some Giants officials think he has J.J. Hardy upside. Meola hits the ball surprisingly hard for a 5-foot-11, 172-pounder and can drive the ball out of the park to all fields, giving him the potential for 15-20 homers per season. He does get overly aggressive and pull-happy, however, resulting in strikeouts and rolled-over ground balls. He's most effective when he focuses on driving balls from gap to gap.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Copen's 6.30 ERA in three seasons at Marshall belied his power and physicality, which the Dodgers liked enough to grab him in the seventh round of the 2023 Draft. A line drive struck him in the face and cost him the vision in his right eye in August 2024, but he returned for Opening Day last year. He ranked 12th in the Minors in strikeout rate (29 percent) and opponent average (.200) while splitting his year between High-A and Double-A. After working with a 91-94 mph fastball during his final college season, Copen now operates at 95-98 mph and touches 100 with bat-missing carry. His high-spin mid-80s slider has so much depth that it's difficult to hit and even harder to land in the strike zone. He uses a low-90s cutter as his third pitch and threw just four changeups in 2025. The 6-foot-6 Copen has a long arm action with a deep plunge in the back, and he has trouble keeping his long limbs in sync. He walked 13 percent of the batters he faced at Marshall and 15 percent his first three years as a pro. He may never harness his stuff well enough to make it as a starter, but his fastball and slider could make him a dynamic bullpen weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyle was a reliever for much of his college career at Suffolk (N.Y.) CC and Dallas Baptist before signing for $10,000 as a 25th-round senior in 2018. He consistently has outperformed expectations as a pro and finally became a full-time starter last year. He led the system in wins (13), innings (155 1/3) and strikeouts (160) while successfully navigating Double-A and Triple-A, though he was left off New York's 40-man roster for the second straight offseason. Boyle relies heavily on the type of sweeping slider that the Yankees love, operating in the low 80s with enough horizontal action that it works against both righties and lefties, and he also can morph it into an upper-80s cutter. His two-seam fastball sits around 90 mph and maxes out at 94, and while it doesn't miss bats, its sink does create weak ground-ball contact. His fading mid-80s changeup shows flashes of becoming a solid offering but he needs to do a better job of controlling it and creating velocity separation from his sinker. His lack of overpowering stuff leaves Boyle little margin for error and he was tagged for a system-high 25 homers last year. He helps his cause by minimizing his mistakes and pounding the strike zone, though his floor always will stand out more than his ceiling. He continues to beat the odds associated with his Draft pedigree and could find a role as a slider-heavy middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners’ activity in the 2024 international signing period started with Dawel Joseph being the headliner, getting $3.3 million in January. Six months later, they added Shen, signing the Taiwanese right-hander, for $175,000 in July. Pitching at age 21, Shen was rolled out cautiously, making his debut in the Arizona Complex League last May. After 28 dominant innings over seven appearances, he earned a bump up to full-season ball for nine more starts. Right out of the gate, Shen displayed a feel for commanding all three of his pitches. His fastball sits in the low 90s, touching 95 mph now and again, and he throws it with sink to help get ground ball outs. His mid-80s changeup also gets weak contact on the ground and gets a lot of chase. He can spin an 81 mph slider decently, and it missed bats at the lower levels, but a little more power could make it even nastier. Shen filled up the strike zone in both stops during his debut, though he was getting too much of the plate during his time in Modesto. Some added strength to his 6-foot-3 frame would help not only that slider, but all of his offerings trend upwards. He has back-of-the-rotation potential based on his pitchability and projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Curley was a 16th-round pick by the Pirates in 2024 after two years at Virginia Commonwealth but didn’t sign and instead transferred to Georgia. He began as the Bulldogs’ closer but became the club’s No. 1 starter later in the spring, finishing with a 3.55 ERA, 1.05 WHIP and 85 strikeouts in 66 innings. That pushed him into the third round last summer, and he signed with the D-backs for below slot at $700,000. The 5-foot-10 right-hander sure makes for an interesting watch. When pitching out of the windup, he looks like he hesitates a bit in his gather before rushing toward the plate with high effort. (In the stretch, he gets things moving a lot quicker, as you’d imagine.) He runs his fastball up to 100 mph and generally sits 94-97 with high spin rates, thanks to added velo as a junior. He can work a few different breaking ball looks -- the best of which is a mid-80s slider with good depth. There’s a harder version in the upper 80s with cutter-like tendencies too and a 79-81 mph curveball with more vertical snap. Curley didn’t show a changeup or other armside offspeed pitches in Athens, using his curve to neutralize lefties instead. That, along with the exertion in his delivery for his size, give him a relief projection in the Majors. But in their search for depth, the D-backs should still give him plenty of starting chances to open his career, knowing the stuff could be high-leverage quality if Curley needs to slide back.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Like his father, Eric, the 1992 National League Rookie of the Year, Karros played collegiately at UCLA before turning pro with the Dodgers. He pitched just 41 innings in three years with the Bruins because of the pandemic and persistent back issues that sidelined him for all of 2022, when Los Angeles drafted him in the 16th round. He has filled the strike zone while climbing from Single-A to Double-A the past two seasons, though he missed nearly three months last summer with mild flexor soreness. Karros' fastball parks at 91-93 mph and reaches 96 but stays off barrels because his 6-foot-7 frame creates an unusually high release point and plenty of extension. He'll spot his heater where he wants, then catch hitters off balance with a solid low-80s changeup that he leverages down in the zone. He also can miss bats with a low-80s slider that has depth and occasionally will flip in a fringy upper-70s curveball. Karros stands out more for his pitchability and deception than his pure stuff. He repeats his simple delivery with ease and provides consistent strikes, though he nibbled at the zone a bit too much when he got hit harder in Double-A. He has a high floor and could become a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hood overcame some pandemic-impacted challenges at Penn, mainly in that his 2020 season was cut short after just eight games and that it was canceled altogether in ‘21. His performance as the 2019 Ivy League rookie of the year caught some eyes, including those of the Red Sox, who drafted him in the 20th round in 2021. But Hood instead opted to transfer to NC State, where he jumped on Seattle’s radar and prompted the club to take him in the sixth round in 2022 and give him $250,000 to sign. The 22-year-old has above-average raw power and has the chance to remain an infielder, perhaps even at shortstop, though he profiles better at third. He also plays a decent outfield defense, which collectively has drawn comparisons to big league super utilityman Dylan Moore but with more power. That type of versatility could only help his case to ascend quickly. Hood has legit strength and an aggressive approach, with some impressive exit velocities already. But one critique is that he can too often hunt the homer. He’ll also need to make adjustments against secondary pitching, especially as he rises the ranks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Keith won Western Athletic Conference Player of the Year honors in 2021, posting a 1.021 OPS and leading the league with 13 homers before Los Angeles drafted him in the 18th round. He has the tools to become the first California Baptist position player to reach the big leagues. In his first full pro season, he slashed .277/.411/.478 with 17 homers between two Class A levels. Not only does Keith have one of the best right-handed swings in the system, he also features one of its best combinations of power and patience. His combination of bat speed and strength produces plus raw power that he'll tap into more efficiently if he can lift the ball in the air more consistently. While he struggled in the final six weeks last season following a promotion to High-A, he continued to work counts and draw walks. Keith has solid speed but isn't much of a basestealer. He needs to upgrade his reads and routes in the outfield, though he's a decent defender on the corners and has the plus arm strength for right field. He also has seen action in center field and might have enough quickness for the position if he can improve his instincts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur, Mathison showed off some legitimate pop at various stops, first as a high school senior and then when he stayed in-state to play college ball for the Hoosiers, homering 19 times as a freshman. He was more inconsistent his next two years but he still finished sixth on Indiana’s career home run list with 42 and the Phillies took the power potential in the fifth round of the 2024 Draft, going a little over slot to sign him and sending him to full-season Clearwater for a very brief pro debut. It remains to be seen what kind of impact Mathison can ultimately have at the plate. The left-handed hitter has plus raw juice and can drive the ball to all fields, but while he was willing to take walks in college, he also got too passive at times and took too many strikes. His swing also got long and he’ll have to show he can be dangerous with a wood bat after not doing much during his time in the Cape Cod League in 2023. Mathison has plus speed but wasn’t much of a basestealer with the Hoosiers, but his wheels were a definite asset in the outfield. He has every chance to play center field for a long time and might be plus there when all is said and done. He can play all three outfield spots well, something he did during his debut and which should continue while he works to develop his offensive game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two seasons at Samford, Walton transferred to Arizona, where he had a career-best season with a 1.026 OPS, 14 homers and 19 stolen bases. Cleveland snagged him with the 66th overall pick in the 2025 Draft and signed him for $1.1 million, after which he played 16 games at Single-A with a solid .238/.324/.397 slash line but surprising strikeout issues after big improvements through his college years. Walton is a power-speed threat from the right side who is built at 6-foot-3 like Captain America -- and he has the makeup to match. His bat speed is among the best in the Guardians' system, which he deploys with a big leg kick and a closed-off stance. Walton has become more selective with time, and how his somewhat noisy swing fares against more advanced pitching will be key, especially given how he has been vulnerable to pitches away. Walton uses his swift legs well on the bases and in the field. He pushed 2025 supplemental first-rounder Brendan Summerhill off of center at Arizona, and Cleveland will give him every shot of sticking there, even if he may fit better in a corner. The Tennessee native is fearless and has solid instincts, but there are mixed reviews about his routes. Right-right outfielders who can even pass in center are rare, though, which gives him a decent floor as a bench bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jimenez bounced around Florida as an amateur with four years at Archbishop McCarthy HS followed by one season each at Miami and Central Florida. After only limited playing time with the Hurricanes, he was an All-Big 12 Second Team selection with the Knights in 2025 after hitting .329/.407/.575 with 11 homers and 11 steals in 55 games. He was Draft-eligible as a sophomore, and the Mets, who love such a profile, took him in the third round with their second overall choice of last year. Jimenez signed for below slot at $564,000 before getting in 26 contests with Single-A St. Lucie. Jimenez has strength in his 6-foot-1, 200-pound frame, and his above-average raw power was something the Mets highlighted as a reason they took him where they did. It’s not exactly all-fields pop though, and he’s at his best when he’s getting out in front of balls and driving them with authority to the pull side. (Ten of the right-handed slugger’s 11 homers in 2025 went to left or left-center.) Jimenez handled fastballs well with UCF but expanded the zone against sliders and changeups, and both trends carried over into the Florida State League. Entering his first full season of pro ball, Jimenez earns his strongest grades for his plus arm strength as he’ll unleash absolute ropes from anywhere on the dirt. He has the right actions for shortstop right now after improving his defensive game in college, and while he can look too flashy at times, he should get plenty of chances to stick at the six. An above-average glove would lessen the need for him to improve his plate discipline at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros play the Cuban market as much as any team and handed the largest bonus in their 2024 international class to an outfielder from the island. Hernandez signed for $1.7 million and likely will make his pro debut in the United States this summer. As an 18-year-old in 2022, he batted .233/.398/.301 as a semi-regular in Cuba's top league. Houston is bullish about Hernandez's potential to hit for both average and power. He already has produced maximum exit velocities of 110 mph and has plus raw pop that plays to all fields. There's more question about his hitting ability because some scouts with other organizations don't love his left-handed swing. Hernandez has plus speed and is plus-plus once he gets going, giving him 25-25 upside. He projects as a center fielder, though his reads and routes could use some improvement. With average arm strength, he's capable of playing all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Musgrove played both ways at the NAIA program at the University of Mobile, and in his three years with the Rams, he finished with a .398/.505/.668 line over 489 plate appearances and a 4.70 ERA with 103 strikeouts in 99 2/3 innings. The Padres took him in the seventh round in 2023, signing him for just below slot at $175,000, and initially intended to keep him on a two-way path. However, Musgrove underwent Tommy John surgery soon after signing and didn’t appear in a game for a San Diego affiliate until April 2025, by that time cementing his place as a pitcher-only. He managed 20 innings for Single-A Lake Elsinore (striking out 26 in that span) before continuing to build up with six more appearances in the Arizona Fall League. The 6-foot-3 right-hander can run his fastball up to triple-digits, and he has a few of them – a four-seamer with good riding action up in the zone and a sinker that can equally come in the 97-99 mph range over shorter outings with more armside run. He also possesses a cutter for another fastball look. Musgrove pitches with upwards of seven feet of extension, shortening the decision window further for hitters. He can spin a mid-80s sweeper with impressive horizontal break and can mix in another slider with more vertical drop and a slower curveball in the low-80s. After dropping a splitter, he’s working on a rarely thrown changeup. Dating back to his days as a collegiate center fielder, Musgrove has athleticism to work with on the mound but is still finding his command post-surgery. He’s come back stronger though and with enough velocity to garner attention across the game in his initial relief looks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morfe wasn’t a headliner of the Orioles’ 2023 international class, signing for $207,500 out of Venezuela as an undersized right-hander, and he struggled to throw strikes in his Dominican Summer League debut later that year. But he made a big leap forward in 2024, proving quickly he was too good for the DSL in his second go-around there before finishing the year with four starts at Single-A Delmarva as an 18-year-old. He racked up 49 strikeouts over 32 2/3 innings across the two levels, the equivalent of 13.5 strikeouts per nine. Morfe surprised a lot of evaluators with his ascent last summer and has surprisingly high-octane stuff for a pitcher his size. He only stands around 5-foot-8 but can dial his fastball up near triple digits, and it consistently lives in the upper 90s. What Morfe lacks in height he makes up for in athleticism and flexibility, using those qualities in tandem with a whippy arm to generate velocity that belies his size. His two secondary offerings are both hard, too: a mid-80s sweeping slider that can miss bats and a low-90s changeup with fade. The change especially showed big improvement last summer, going from a fringy offering to a potential plus pitch. It’s an advanced arsenal in an unpolished package, as Morfe’s command remains a work in progress. That’s not unusual for a young power pitcher, and Morfe was better at throwing strikes last year than his stats might imply because they were skewed by one ugly blow up start at the very end of the season. His three plus pitches and bulldog mentality remind some evaluators of Carlos Martinez, but to reach that ceiling, Morfe will need to prove he can throw enough strikes and that his body can handle a starter’s workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Patick stood out more with his projection than his present stuff when the Dodgers made him an 18th-round pick out of a suburban Los Angeles high school and signed him for an over-slot $347,500 in 2023. An illness requiring hospitalizing sidelined him for what would have been his first Spring Training and limited him to 31 2/3 innings in 2024, but he bounced back to successfully navigate Single-A last year. His 27 percent strikeout rate ranked third in the California League among pitchers who worked at least as many as his 85 1/3 innings. Patick's fastball sits at 92-94 mph and touches 96 with more downhill plane than life, and he uses it to set up a wide variety of secondary pitches. His best offering is a mid-70s curveball with depth that confounds both lefties and righties but also makes it difficult to land for strikes. He also utilizes a low-80s slider with plenty of sweep that he can turn into a tighter cutter that climbs as high as 93 mph, as well as an 85-88 mph changeup with some fade. Patick has good feel for spinning the ball and mixing his pitches. He creates deception by utilizing a big leg kick, rotating his upper half and throwing from a crossfire angle, and that doesn't stop him from throwing strikes. He has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter and his ability to neutralize hitters from both sides with his breaking pitches could make him a useful bullpen piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holton’s commitment to Vanderbilt meant he slid out of serious Draft consideration in 2021, and he headed to Nashville and established himself immediately in the Commodores’ weekend rotation. After a solid start to his final college season in 2024, he faded and saw his stuff diminish, missing the SEC Tournament and making just one relief appearance in Regional play. He made one appearance as a pro after signing with the Braves as a second-rounder, then needed Tommy John surgery, meaning he’ll miss the 2025 season. When he’s healthy, Holton has a legitimate four-pitch mix, starting with a fastball that sits 93-95 mph and tops out at 98. His low-80s slider -- a plus breaking ball with horizontal and vertical action that misses bats -- is particularly effective against left-handed hitters. He’s had a solid upper-70s curveball in the past and can throw a sinking changeup in the mid-80s. Holton is super competitive on the mound, but there are questions about whether he can be a starter at the next level. The 5-foot-11 lefty has an unorthodox delivery and high arm slot, and his mechanics haven’t always led to consistent strike-throwing. For now, the focus is on rehab, and the Braves will get their first real look at what he might be in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tatum spent his first three seasons at North Carolina State as a part-time player, then hit .317/.423/.543 with 12 homers and 16 steals as the Wolfpack reached the College World Series semifinals in 2021. He hit a massive home run to beat Jack Leiter and Vanderbilt, 1-0, in Omaha shortly before the White Sox made him a 16th-round pick. He played just 42 games in his first full season because he drew a 50-game suspension after testing positive for amphetamines, and an ankle injury limited him to just six contests in the Arizona Fall League. Tatum collected just 600 at-bats in the past five years between college and the Minors, so he has more untapped potential at the plate than most 23-year-olds. He has a quick left-handed swing and a willingness to work counts and draw walks, but he also strikes out way too much (30 percent of his plate appearance in his first two pro seasons), puts the ball on the ground far too often (28 percent) and uses the opposite field almost to a fault. He has enough bat speed and wiry strength to produce at least 15 homers per season but will need to turn on and lift more pitches to get there. With his well-above-average speed, Tatum is dangerous on the bases and covers plenty of ground in center field. His below-average arm is playable in center and left but limits his usefulness in right. His speed and defense could help make him a useful fourth outfielder if he doesn't provide enough offense to be a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the stricter penalties for their international signing violations weren’t levied until the 2019-20 signing period, the Braves still couldn’t sign any prospect for more than $300,000 during the 2018-19 period, the typical penalty for having exceeded their bonus pool (in 2016-17). That doesn’t mean they didn’t find talent, such as prospects like Royber Salinas -- traded to the A’s for Sean Murphy -- and Quintero, who signed in February 2019 for just $40,000 and is coming off a solid full-season debut that allowed him to reach High-A in 2022. Quintero is a bit of a throwback type player as an undersized infielder who can do a lot of little things well on the diamond. A switch-hitter, Quintero has shown a knack for making contact and getting on base, walking in 11.8 percent of plate appearances and striking out just 16.2 percent of the time in his brief pro career. That’s going to have to be his game because there’s not much power there, with relatively low exit velocities. Quintero’s best tool is his speed, and he’s registered some 30 ft/sec sprint speed times, something that should become more of an asset the more he learns the nuances of basestealing. He doesn’t have the actions to play shortstop, with second and maybe third base the best options, and a future as a speedy utility-type the most likely outcome.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Venezuela native didn’t sign with the Mets until he was a 19-year-old in August 2021 but moved quickly, reaching Single-A St. Lucie the following year. New York used him as a reliever that first full season in the Florida State League with promising results: a 3.78 ERA and 54 strikeouts in 47 2/3 innings. Gomez generated a ton of buzz in his second Spring Training, averaging 100 mph during one backfields outing. He made three starts for High-A Brooklyn as the Mets hoped to see him transition into a rotation, but he needed Tommy John surgery after that and missed the rest of the season. Gomez’s fastball sat 96-98 mph before surgery and regularly touched triple digits. The heater had plenty of ride up in the zone too, making it more than just a radar-gun darling. He also showed an upper-80s slider that could break over two planes, leading to some buckled knees from anyone trying to time their swing on the fastball. An upper-80s changeup remained very much a work in progress, and that will continue when he returns in 2024. The 6-foot-2 right-hander’s velo increase coincided with control issues as he walked nine batters in his seven innings with Brooklyn. The ability to limit walks was closer to average at the lower levels, and there’s hope it would have improved as the sample grew larger in the South Atlantic League. Regardless, Gomez had arguably the best two-pitch profile in the Mets system pre-injury, and he could be dominant in a move back to the bullpen when healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz signed with the Yankees for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022 and was one of several standouts on a prospect-laden team in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer. The youngest batting qualifier in the circuit at age 17, he led the FCL with 47 RBI and ranked second with 10 homers. The Marlins acquired him in a three-team trade in March, sending Jon Berti to New York and also receiving outfield prospect Shane Sasaki from the Rays. After looking launch-happy and passive during his 2022 pro debut, Cruz displayed a better approach and more power last year. His quick left-handed stroke produces loud contact when he connects, and he could grow into plus pop if he fills out his projectable frame and adds more polish as a hitter. He controls the strike zone fine for a teenager, but his aggressiveness leads to less-than-ideal contact. Cruz presently has solid speed but is still learning to make the most of it on the bases and in the outfield. He's not an instinctive defender and spent most of his FCL time in right field, where he displays solid arm strength. To make it in center, he'd need to improve his reads and routes while retaining his quickness as he matures physically.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highlight of Boston's 2024 international crop, Asencio signed for $1 million out of the Dominican Republic. He trained at the same Mejia Top 10 facility that also spawned Miguel Bleis, the top signee in Boston's 2020-21 class. He'll make his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League later this year. Asencio's advanced bat-to-ball skills are his calling card. He recognizes pitches, consistently barrels balls with his sound right-handed swing and already has a penchant for using the opposite field. His lack of physicality leads to questions about his power potential, and he may top out at 15 homers per season -- and he'll have to add muscle to get there. Asencio's speed earns average-to-solid grades from evaluators, and he could get quicker as he gets stronger. His instincts enhance his range in center field, and he should be able to stay there long term. With average arm strength, he's capable of handling all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Keener logged a 6.31 ERA in his first two seasons at Wake Forest before earning all-star honors in the Cape Cod League. He allowed just three earned runs in his first 42 2/3 innings last spring and ranked second in NCAA Division I in WHIP (0.87) and third in opponent average (.167) while serving as a swingman on college baseball's best pitching staff. The White Sox signed him for $800,000 in the third round and definitely see him as a full-time starter on the pro level. The key to Keener's success is a mid-80s slider with two-plane depth that can be a wipeout pitch, and he has the aptitude to both throw it for strikes and get chases outside the zone. He used his slider more than his fastball at Wake, a pattern he'll need to reverse as a starter. He has a 91-95 mph heater that maxes out at 97 with riding action and uses a fading mid-80s changeup to keep left-handers in check. Keener has the sound delivery and strike-throwing ability to make it as a starter. To do so, he'll have to prove he can maintain his stuff and control deeper into games and over the course of 150 innings in a season. If Chicago changed course and deployed him as a reliever, he'd probably race through the Minors and could become a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Texas high school all-state performer, Peters began at Temple Junior College before transferring to Dallas Baptist University, where he earned second-team All-Conference USA honors. Primarily a reliever, he led the Patriots with four saves and made key spot starts, including a six-inning, 10-strikeout outing as part of a combined no-hitter against Liberty to close the regular season. Strong performances in Regional play helped propel him to Seattle’s fourth-round selection in 2025, when he signed for below slot value at $550,000. At 5-foot-11, Peters is an athletic left-hander with the potential to develop into a starter. His fastball sits around 93 mph and can touch 96 mph, featuring natural ride that challenges hitters up in the zone. Behind it, he mixes an upper-70s curve that generated high whiff rates in 2025 and a low-80s sweepy slider, though the slider is used less consistently. Peters pairs his repertoire with a repeatable delivery and solid arm action, allowing him to command all his pitches and attack the strike zone effectively. The next step for Peters as a starter will be refining a changeup and demonstrating he can handle a rotation workload, as he did not report to an affiliate after being drafted. Even if that path proves challenging, he projects as a high-floor left-handed reliever with three effective pitches. Paired with other top picks like Griffin Hugus and Kade Anderson, Peters represents another promising pitching piece in Seattle’s 2025 Draft class, offering both present value and long-term upside out of the bullpen or potentially in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: German signed for $400,000 last year out of the Dominican Republic, giving him the joint fourth-highest bonus of Washington’s 2025 international class but well behind the seven-figure deals for Brayan Cortesia ($1.92 million) and Daniel Hernandez ($1.1 million). Only year later, the switch-hitting infielder has surged in stock to become the best prospect of the group at this very early stage of his career. German was a Dominican Summer League mid- and post-season All-Star with a .283/.479/.513 line, eight homers and 33 steals in 53 games. While many of his age can be undisciplined at the plate, German showed an advanced approach from both sides of the plate, leading to a 42/43 K/BB ratio. He shows better ability to slug from the left side to this point -- all eight of his dingers came against righty pitchers – but that might also speak to his lack of gametime against southpaws (only 49 plate appearances in 2025). German stands only 5-foot-10, but what he lacks in stature, he makes up for in his early tendency to lift and pull the ball, helping the pop show in games. By getting on base so much, German gives himself plenty of chances to steal bags, and he certainly took advantage by showing off his above-average wheels in the DSL. That athleticism has helped him stay up the middle on the dirt to this point, and he has the arm strength to make that a defensive asset as well. Nationals instructors have been impressed by his teenage work ethic and aptitude with the glove early on, and he should be a priority middle infielder at the Florida complex when he arrives stateside this spring.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s important not to put too much stock into Dominican Summer League numbers as the Rookie-level circuit tends to be very hitter-friendly. But when a new prospect has a huge debut there, it also shouldn’t be ignored. Beltre put a huge first foot forward after signing for just under $1.5 million, shaking off an early wrist injury to post a 1.071 OPS and finished tied for second on the circuit with 11 homers. Beltre showed, at least during his debut, that his right-handed swing can do a lot of damage. He makes hard contact to all fields, and it’s clear he can already get to his raw power. He entered pro ball with a reputation of being a very aggressive hitter, and his strikeout rate was a little high (23.8 percent), but he also had better plate discipline than expected, offsetting those K’s with a healthy dose of walks (15.5 pct). Strong and compact, Beltre’s athleticism stood out on both sides of the ball. He was introduced to all three outfield positions in the DSL, and while it was once thought he was certainly destined for a corner where his strong arm would work well, there’s now some conviction that he could stick in center field. He’ll be 18 for all of his U.S. debut in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ozuna was the latest standout to train at the Niche Baseball Academy in Santo Domingo North, Dominican Republic, where stars such as Juan Soto, Elly De La Cruz and others have trained at under Cristian Batista. Drawing rave reviews by those who watched him closely there, he came in at No. 16 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list for 2025 and signed with the A’s for $850,000 when the signing period opened in January. He got his feet wet in pro ball with 35 games in the Dominican Summer League but was limited production-wise because of a hamate injury. Listed at 6-foot-3 and 185 pounds, Ozuna is a presence that is hard to miss when walking through the A’s Dominican complex. He reminds some within the organization of a young Vladimir Guerrero Sr. in terms of how he looks standing in the box for batting practice. His physical attributes lend to impressive power as a right-handed hitter that could reach plus-plus levels as he continues growing into his body. Ozuna’s cannon of an arm and natural athleticism gives him a shot at being a decent defensive right fielder. The obvious question here is whether he will make enough contact to fully unleash that tremendous raw power. The A’s are hopeful that he will come back this year in a healthier form and continue his valuable development time as a teenager.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Quebec native, Langevin came to the United States for college ball at Wabash Valley (Ill.) Community College before transferring to Louisiana-Lafayette his junior year. He struck out the world there, maintaining a nearly 40 percent strikeout rate. The metrics on his fastball in particular were part of the reason the Royals took Langevin in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft, signing him for $597,500. It’s no secret that Langevin’s fastball is what makes him stand out. It’s a unique pitch that has baffled hitters so far, although not because of velocity -- it sits 92-96 mph. The pitch has extremely high spin rates and features plenty of ride and run from a lower vertical approach angle. Langevin’s deceptive delivery definitely helps the pitch play up too, as does his quick arm. His secondaries are fringe average at best, as he didn’t really need or use them in college, so that will be a focus for him in his first pro season. The slider has some sweeping action to it, but it varies in speed and he needs to work on landing it in the zone. He has a feel for a changeup but needs to develop it more. If it translates to results in pro ball, Langevin’s fastball could dominate, and he could move quickly as a reliever. Officials love his makeup and fiery competitiveness on the mound. He’s a one-trick pitcher right now, though, and needs to improve his secondaries and control to reach his ceiling as a potential back-end bullpen arm. Langevin will likely begin his pro career at High-A in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Guardians landed two talented high school arms with well-over-slot bonuses in the middle rounds of the 2022 Draft, signing left-hander Jackson Humphries for $600,000 in the eighth round and Zibin for $1.2 million in the 10th. The top Canadian prospect and youngest player in the Draft, Zibin set a record for his round and received the equivalent of second-round money. A veteran of the Canadian junior national team, he spent his senior season at the TNXL Academy (Ocoee, Fla.) to increase his exposure. Zibin already works at 92-94 mph and touches 97 with armside run on his four-seam fastball, which should gain more velocity as he adds weight to his projectable 6-foot-4 frame. He has advanced feel for a low-80s changeup with fade and sink, selling it well with deceptive arm speed. His 77-82 mph slider can flash some promising sweep but also gets slurvy at times. While Zibin throws strikes, he can refine his delivery and command. He'll focus on gaining strength and building up innings early in his career. He'll need time to develop but has the upside of a mid-rotation starter, especially if he can upgrade the consistency of his slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If you’re a high-ceiling high school pitcher who hasn’t heard his name called in the top 10 rounds and think you’re headed to college, the Angels can always give you hope. On an almost annual basis, extra bonus pool money is available to take and sign some prep arms. In 2025, they targeted a pair of intriguing high school lefties, taking Talon Haley in the 12th round and Mitchell a round later. Rather than head to Texas, Mitchell signed for $872,500, heading down a baseball path despite coming from a football family that includes an uncle who quarterbacked in the Canadian Football League and a brother who was a wide receiver at Arizona. After pitching for Team USA the summer before his senior year, Mitchell got off to a good start back at school but was shut down with shoulder fatigue after a month, so building up strength will be a key. He can sit 90-92 mph with his fastball, touching 94, and the fastball plays up because of deception in his delivery and carry up in the zone. He has a good feel to spin an upper-70s curve with depth that works well off of his heater. Like with a lot of high school pitchers, he hasn’t used a changeup much, but he’s shown glimpses of a decent cambio in the low-80s with fade and sink. Mitchell is athletic on the mound, repeating his delivery well and filling up the strike zone. There’s room to add muscle to his 6-foot-3 frame, which could help all of his stuff tick up as he gets his pro career going.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De la Rosa signed with the Yankees out of the Dominican Republic for $400,000 last April, receiving the third-highest bonus given to any left-hander on the 2025 international market. He quickly stood out with his stuff and strikes during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, drawing immediate trade interest. Three months after he turned pro, the Giants acquired him in a four-prospect package in exchange for Camilo Doval. De la Rosa works with a 92-94 mph fastball that reaches 96 with significant carry as well as armside run. Both of his secondary pitches also show promise. He throws both a tight slider and a sweepier version in the low 80s, and his fading changeup is a tick harder. While De La Rosa has three legitimate pitches and posted a 7 percent walk rate in his first taste of pro ball, there are questions about his ability to remain a starter in the long run. He's undersized and works uphill with some funk in his arm action, though his delivery provides deception without costing him control. If he does land in the bullpen, he has the upside to work in a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Whitaker is the latest prospect to come out of Bishop Gorman High (Las Vegas), which has spawned 10 big leaguers, including Joey Gallo and former American League Rookie of the Year Marty Cordova. He was a shortstop/right-hander before shifting to the outfield last spring and winning Gatorade's Nevada player of the year award. Signed for a well over-slot $1.5 million as the Astros' top pick (third round) in the 2021 Draft, he batted .202/.263/.327 with a 35 percent strikeout rate in his pro debut in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. Whitaker's bat speed and the leverage in his 6-foot-4 frame create plus raw power with the potential for more as he gets stronger. He made a more concerted effort to drive the ball in 2021, though his right-handed stroke gets too long at times, leading to swing-and-miss concerns. To make the most of his pop, he'll need to make more contact and learn to turn on more pitches and drive them in the air. A quality athlete, Whitaker offers solid to plus speed and a strong arm. While he played right field in a loaded Bishop Gorman outfield, he shifted to center field in pro ball and may have enough quickness and instincts to stay there. Houston also was pleasantly surprised at how he looked in brief action at third base during his debut and has played him at shortstop this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Right-hander Nehomar Ochoa Sr. pitched in the Expos system from 2003-05 until falling off a horse and injuring his shoulder, and his son was born in Venezuela shortly before his career ended. The younger Nehomar moved to the United States at age 10 and blossomed into a physical and toolsy outfielder at a Houston high school before signing with the local Astros for $300,000 (double slot value) as an 11th-rounder in 2023. In his first full pro season, he slashed .222/.317/.359 with 10 homers and 17 steals in 103 games as the second-youngest batting qualifier (age 18) in the Single-A Carolina League. Extremely physical at 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, Ochoa has a quick right-handed swing and at least plus raw power that plays mostly to left field because of his pull- and launch-heavy mindset. He has enough natural pop to hit 25 or more homers per season without swinging for the fences. He'll have to moderate his approach as he advances because he chases too much and is overmatched by breaking balls from righties. Very athletic for his size, Ochoa has average speed and is aggressive on the bases. He's still a work in progress as a corner outfielder, but he has the quick reactions to become at least an average defender and may get a trial in center field. He has plus arm strength, reaching 95 mph with his fastball as a prep pitcher and throwing out 12 runners in 76 starts in right field last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a deep Red Sox international class headlined by shortstop Dorian Soto, outfielder Harold Rivas and right-hander Sadbiel Delzine, Ramos signed for $500,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He offers an interesting combination of shortstop defense with unusual switch-hitting pop for the position. He batted .254/.384/.443 with four homers in 36 games during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Ramos hits the ball hard for a teenager and already shows feel for driving balls in the air to his pull side, so he could become a 20-homer threat once he adds more strength to his projectable 6-foot-1 frame. He has good hand-eye coordination, which allows him to turn his swing loose and still make consistent contact. In his first taste of pro ball, he displayed power from both sides of the plate but did a much better job of controlling the strike zone as a lefty. Though Ramos possesses just average speed, he runs the bases well and plays a smooth shortstop. He has good actions, range to both sides, quick hands and a strong, accurate arm. Though it's possible he could slow a bit if he gains considerable muscle, Boston believes he's stay at short.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Etzel spent a semester at Texas A&M then played two seasons at Panola (Texas) JC, but it was actually a stint in the MLB Draft League that set him up for his professional future. He slashed .371/.463/.586 with 25 steals in 33 games there in 2022, putting himself on scouting radars a year before signing with the Orioles as a 10th-rounder out of Southern Mississippi. Baltimore sent him to the Rays as part of a three-prospect package for starter Zach Eflin in July 2024, then Tampa Bay shipped him to the Marlins for Nick Fortes a year later. Etzel’s performance dipped after a promotion to Double-A and fell off when he joined the Rays, as he batted .232 with a .692 OPS and a 35 percent strikeout rate in 36 games for Montgomery. The swing-and-miss jump was somewhat alarming, as Etzel typically makes a fair amount of contact (especially against fastballs) and already puts a lot of balls on the ground. Granted, he has the speed to make that work and added value by stealing 45 bases over 119 games last year, but it will require him to boost his slugging percentage with doubles and triples, not home runs. Despite his above-average speed, Etzel seems likely to settle in at a corner position. He played all three outfield spots at an almost exactly even rate last year and even saw time at first base in an effort to keep his bat in the lineup. He hasn't made much progress at Double-A this year, a telling sign that probably caps his ceiling as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The two best prospects signed by the Giants in their 2017 international class are Dominican right-handers who turned pro for just $50,000 each: Randy Rodriguez and Cruz. The latter didn't stand out in his first three pro seasons but progressed rapidly in 2022, leading all Minor League relievers (minimum 50 innings) with a .119 average-against and ranking second with a 43 percent strikeout rate. Though he spent the entire season in Single-A at age 22, San Francisco protected him on its 40-man roster in November rather than risk exposing him to the Rule 5 Draft. Cruz creates exceptional armside run with his fastball and changeup, both of which are consistent plus pitches and sometimes better than that. His heater sits at 94-96 mph and touches 98 while running away from left-handers and in on right-handers, and his low arm slot creates carry up in the zone. His mid-80s changeup has a tad more horizontal movement and also some tumble, helping him limit lefties to a .085/.207/.169 line last season. Cruz doesn't have as much feel for spinning the ball, as his third pitch is a tight mid-80s slider that's fringy at best. Though his career has moved slowly to this point, San Francisco will begin expediting his path to the big leagues in 2023. He'll have to prove that his stuff will play at higher levels and also needs to improve his control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watters transitioned from pitching in the bullpen his first two years at West Virginia to starting in 2022. The stuff he showed in the Mountaineers' weekend rotation was tantalizing, highlighted by a 15-strikeout performance against Texas, and it was enough for the A’s to take him in the fourth round of the 2022 MLB Draft. Getting his feet wet with a couple of outings at High-A Lansing, he’ll look to begin his ascent as a starter through the system in his first full season as a pro. Watters is a strong presence on the mound at 6-foot-4. His fastball was up to 99 mph during his junior year and touched triple digits in his time as a reliever. He also possesses a plus pitch in his power curve, missing plenty of bats as a true 12-to-6 that sits in the mid-80s. There’s also a mid-80s changeup in there, though it’s less polished compared to his other two offerings. Command will need to improve for Watters to have a chance to start at the next level. While the stuff was high-octane in college, he usually had little idea of how to locate it. Given his track record as a reliever, there’s a strong chance he ends up back in the bullpen, where he can rear back and overpower hitters with two plus pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the last players the Astros signed in their 2018-19 international class, Batista signed for $25,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His career started slowly, with a pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League followed by the pandemic shutdown and then a 7.46 ERA in a brief stint in the United States in 2021. He took a huge step forward last year, posting a 2.67 ERA with a .178 opponents' average against and 127 strikeouts in 107 2/3 innings while earning a late promotion to High-A at age 20. Batista works at 91-94 mph and tops out at 96 with the projectability to add more velocity, and his fastball also features the flat approach angle with carry and armside run that's in vogue. His best pitch is a plus low-80s slider with two-plane break and he also throws an upper-70s curveball with similar shape. He shows some feel for a low-80s changeup with some fade but it's still a work in progress. More polished than most of Houston's younger pitching prospects, Batista has a sound delivery and generally repeats it well. He could have average control and at least decent command once he's fully developed. He has the ingredients to become a four-pitch starter and also could be a bullpen asset who concentrates on his fastball and slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery ended Patteson’s 2022 college season early at Central Florida, but the Royals were convinced enough in their scouting of him and his makeup that they still drafted him in the fifth round that year. It took Patteson time to come back from the injury and start to make an impact, but his stuff shot up in 2025. He made 13 starts in High-A with a 1.99 ERA, while holding batters to a .199 average. He finished the year with 11 appearances (eight starts) in Double-A, where he had a 4.41 ERA. Patteson’s fastball hovered around 90-92 mph over the past few years, but once he got to Double-A in ‘25, he started running it up to the mid 90s and touching 97. The velo spike, which was more about a return to his pre-TJ form, also helped his main breaking ball become more firm as a mid-80s average slider that tries to be gyro but can get a little sweepy. Patteson also throws a curveball with good depth and feel to land it for strikes. His best weapon, though, is a mid-80s changeup with plus potential. Patteson throws strikes and has a clean delivery, hiding the ball well with short arm action. Lauded for his pitchability and being a student of the game, Patteson might be a late bloomer but is really coming into his own now that he’s reached the upper levels. He needs to show more consistency at Double-A and continue to refine his secondaries, but if the stuff continues to look like what it did there in ‘25, he has back-end rotation potential. The Royals might try him in the bullpen to see whether the stuff ticks up even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Wisconsin high schooler with a big fastball, Snead started his college career at Wichita State, but then moved on to Tennessee where, as a sophomore, he helped the Volunteers win the 2024 Men's College World Series, picking up a key save and hold in the Finals. He came out of the bullpen again as a junior, but his combination of a full arsenal and ability to throw strikes could give him the chance to start, something the Angels no doubt were contemplating when taking him with their compensation pick following the third round of the 2025 Draft. There’s no doubt that Snead can throw hard -- he sat around 95-97 mph and touched triple digits. But the heater often lacked life, with sink over carry, so if he wasn’t locating it down in the zone well, it was very hittable. He’s already gotten to work on differentiating his two- and four-seamers (which often blended together), as well as improving his low-90s cutter. His low-80s curve evolved into his best secondary offering in 2025. There’s also a mid-80s slider and low-90s changeup in Snead’s bag of tricks, though he didn’t pull them out often. He has a bit of a slinky delivery coming from a low three-quarters slot, and while he finds the strike zone, it’s control over command. The Angels could give him a chance to start out of the gate, knowing that he could also develop into a late-inning reliever with better fastball characteristics.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees' decision to select Jackson in the fifth round last July drew criticism after reports surfaced that he drew a swastika on the dorm room of a Jewish student when he was a freshman at Nebraska in 2021.
