He transferred to South Mountain (Ariz.) CC as a sophomore and spent his final two college seasons at Utah, where he was charged with impaired driving in 2024. He batted a combined .363/.455/.577 and earned first-team all-conference honors in his two years with the Utes before signing for a well below-slot $147,500. A left-hander who made consistent hard contact college despite an aggressive approach in college, Jackson was unusually passive in High-A during his pro debut. He usually crushes fastballs but had trouble making contact against in-zone heaters last summer, though he may have been overwhelmed by his challenging assignment. He has the ingredients for at least 15-homer power, especially if he can learn to elevate more pitches. Jackson was more impressive defensively in his first taste of pro ball. He displays smooth actions, solid range and plus arm strength, leaving no doubt he can remain at shortstop. He has average speed with good baserunning instincts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners took Beilenson as a money-saving senior sign in the fifth round of the 2024 Draft, with his $25,000 under-slot bonus helping pay to sign Ryan Sloan. But Beilenson had success in college, especially once he moved to Duke after three years at Brown, saving 12 games for the Blue Devils while getting a pair of graduate degrees. While he was old for the High-A level where he began his first full season of pro ball, he pitched well enough to earn a promotion to Double-A after 20 appearances, putting him on the prospect map. Now 26, Beilenson is more a sum-of-his-parts kind of pitcher than a reliever who is going to blow hitters away. He has a foundation of three pitches but manipulates them into different shapes to give him a repertoire of as many as five. He’ll throw both a four- and a two-seam fastball, averaging around 93 mph. His best pitch is his kick-change that has splitter-like action to it. He’ll throw both a sweeper and a shorter, harder slider around 81 mph with cutter-like action. Beilenson can throw a ton of strikes with all his offerings, but it’s control over command, and he got hit more once he got to Double-A. If he can find a bit more consistency from one outing to the next, he could be knocking on the door to a big league bullpen job.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres are one of the most heavily involved -- if not the most heavily involved -- teams in Mexico as part of the international signing process. That’s where the club headed to sign Serna in January, two months before the southpaw turned 17. Serna gained some international notoriety at the 2024 WBSC U15 World Cup in Colombia, where he struck out 12 and allowed only one earned run on one hit and four walks in seven innings against the host nation. He signed for $1 million. The 6-foot-3 southpaw throws free and easy from a smooth delivery, and while he only sits 88-91 mph with his fastball now, he has the size to add strength and get that velocity up to at least Major League average in the years to come. His best present pitch is an upper-70s slider with short, controllable depth, and it should help fuel any immediate Minor League success. There’s a feel for a low-80s changeup too, though he barely used it in the World Cup. Serna excelled on the international stage because he could hit his spots at an advanced level, and he was willing to go right after hitters. The Padres brought up his strike throwing on signing day as the most exciting part of the early profile, and if Serna can sharpen his stuff with physical maturity -- not a given considering the wide error bars on young arms -- he could be a midrotation option in the Majors in the next decade.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Of the 16 prospects who received six-figure bonuses from the Pirates at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, Tsung-Che Cheng has jumped out as the best prospect to date. Castillo was close to the bottom of that list, getting $140,000 to sign in July 2019. He jumped on the map when he won the Florida Complex League batting title (.352), and while he wasn’t nearly as productive with a move to full-season Bradenton in 2023, he joined teammate Termarr Johnson as two of the eight players in the Minor Leagues to walk 100 or more times. Since signing, Castillo has shown off impressive bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate. He’s registered very low strikeout rates at each stop, carrying a 17.3 K rate into the 2024 season. He doesn’t give away at-bats and isn’t afraid to hit with two strikes. He couples that with excellent patience to be an on-base machine, when he can then use his speed to be a basestealing threat. What he lacks, however, is any impact at the plate, and he’s working to get more physical without taking away his all-fields approach, though he’s never going to have more than gap power. Castillo is so sound defensively, the sentiment is that he could handle playing in a Major League game at shortstop if need be. He’ll continue to get plenty of reps there, but he’s also proven to be a bit of a Swiss Army knife, one who did everything but catch for Bradenton in 2023. The Pirates love his aggressive style of play and his contact skills. If he can add just a little strength, he could carve out a future as a utility player in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez was a July 2019 signing out of the Dominican Republic who joined the Mets as part of the same international class as Alex Ramirez. The southpaw missed out on the 2020 season like every other Minor Leaguer, but New York showed enough confidence in him to push him to the Florida Complex League and Single-A St. Lucie in 2021, when he fanned 16 in 12 1/3 innings. Rodriguez was set to take off in 2022, only to undergo Tommy John surgery in March that knocked him out for the entire campaign. There was promising stuff to generate excitement in Rodriguez’s abbreviated stateside look before he hurt his elbow. He typically sat in the mid-90s with his fastball and touched 97 mph during his brief turn in the Florida State League. His low-80s slider showed promising sweep to help him generate whiffs and give him another above-average offering. He didn’t throw his changeup at all with St. Lucie, and it will remain a major point of focus moving forward. Tommy John surgery isn’t what it used to be in terms of scariness, but the Mets have experienced another concern with Rodriguez getting shut down in August due to forearm inflammation. There's still enough stuff here for the southpaw to develop into a potential backend starter, but New York will be extra cautious with him as arm issues continue to pile up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pitts was a “famous” high schooler in the Atlanta area at a very early age, and he actually committed to the University of South Carolina as a shortstop before he even began his high school career. By the time his Draft year came around in 2025, he had moved to the outfield and changed his college commitment to the University of South Florida. He might have had the chance to move up boards more during his senior year, but a hamstring issue slowed him considerably. After being able to work him out a couple of times and getting to know more about his makeup, the Reds rolled the dice and took him in the fifth round, going a little over slot at $575,000 to sign him. Pitts didn’t make his pro debut after signing and he was slow coming out of the spring as he continued to nurse his hamstring back to health. The Reds think this was a good upside play based on his athleticism and potential to stay up the middle. A right-handed hitter and thrower, Pitts’ carrying tool is the speed he wasn’t able to showcase much his senior year, getting 70 grades from some evaluators when he’s healthy. He’s shown off solid raw power at times and a decent feel for hitting that gives some hope he can tap into that pop consistently in the future. That plus speed is also an asset defensively, and Pitts has the athleticism to play center field at the next level, albeit with an arm that needs work. It’s a bit of a lottery ticket given that he wasn’t seen that much in 2025, but if he can get past the hamstring problems, there’s some ceiling for him to grow into.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phoenix-born De La Torre grew up in Mexico before attending high school in Utah and showcasing himself to big league teams in the Dominican Republic. Signed for $10,000 in July 2023, De La Torre spent two seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before making his U.S. debut last year. He was leading the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 62 strikeouts in 38 2/3 innings when he was promoted in early July to Single-A, where he logged a 1.77 ERA in seven starts before starring in the playoffs as San Jose won the California League title. De La Torre's 94-96 mph fastball touches 98 and explodes on hitters because the extension and low release height in his delivery create plenty of carry. His heater generated a 32 percent swing-and-miss rate at Single-A; to put that in perspective, big league left-handers Aroldis Chapman and Brendon Little posted identical marks in 2025. He backs it up with a mid-80s slider that can be a plus pitch with big sweep at its best. De La Torre operates mainly with two pitches and has yet to show much faith in his fading mid-80s changeup. He compensates for a lack of physicality with some of the best athleticism in the system, getting down the mound very well and filling the strike zone. If he's as good as he looked last year, he could be a mid-rotation starter and climb quickly through the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kouba spent his first two college seasons at North Central (Texas) CC and opened 2021 in Dallas Baptist's bullpen, pitched his way into the rotation by midseason, earned all-Missouri Valley Conference honors and became a 12th-round pick. He doesn't dazzle anyone with his stuff but compensates by being the best strike-thrower in the system. He was named Double-A Texas League pitcher of the year in 2023 and finished the season in Triple-A. Kouba's fastball sits at 89-92 mph and tops out at 94 but doesn't get hit hard because he has all the traits the Astros target with pitchers: low release height, flat approach angle, significant extension in his delivery. It also plays up because he keeps batters off balance with his best pitch, a solid low-80s changeup with fade and sink. He has a pair of ordinary breaking balls, a sweeping low-80s slider he uses vs. righties and an upper-70s curveball he employs against lefties. With his combination of deception and control, Kouba could be a No. 5 starter. His stuff works better than it grades because he mixes his pitches well, commands his fastball and throws his secondary offerings for strikes. He was in line to get an opportunity if Houston needed rotation help in 2024 before missing two months with an elbow injury that didn't require surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dombroski established himself as a prospect while winning Cape Cod League most outstanding pitcher accolades in 2021, when he led the summer circuit in ERA (0.85), strikeouts (45 in 31 2/3 innings) and K/BB ratio (22.5). He set a Monmouth record with 120 whiffs in 95 frames and ranked seventh in NCAA Division I with an 8.6 K/BB ratio the next spring, becoming the third-highest pick in school history when Houston selected him in the fourth round. He topped the Single-A Carolina League in strikeouts (148), average-against (.216) and WHIP (1.12) in his 2023 pro debut. Dombroski's lone better-than-average pitch is his low-80s changeup with depth, but he succeeds thanks to his ability to command his entire four-pitch arsenal. His fastball is nothing special, sitting in the upper 80s and topping out at 93 mph with some riding action. His breaking balls both can flash average and have added a bit more power since he turned pro, with his downer upper-70s curveball maybe a tick ahead of his 78-81 mph slider with sweep. A classic finesse left-hander, Dombroski depends on his ability to locate and mix his pitches. His control wasn't as sharp as usual in the first two months of his debut before he locked in and issued just 15 walks in his final 14 starts. He's a high-floor guy who profiles as a No. 5 starter for now, though the Astros have helped several pitchers unlock more velocity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals signed Rodriguez in July 2019 out of the Dominican Republic, and the start of his pro career was bumpy because of the pandemic. It didn’t seem to slow him down, as he was named the DSL Royals Blue Player of the Year in 2021 and then brought his high energy to the States in 2022, slashing .306/.395/.514 between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A. Rodriguez’s best tool is hitting, with innate bat-to-ball skills, an efficient swing and a simple approach at the plate. He doesn’t fear velocity and has an excellent idea of the strike zone for someone who just finished his age-19 season -- his 10.8 percent walk rate and 16.2 percent strikeout rate were better in Columbia than Rookie ball. The switch-hitter has a good approach from both sides of the plate, but most of his pop -- which is below average right now -- comes from the left side. That could change with more reps on the right side and more strength. Rodriguez is an above-average defender at second base with quick hands and good footwork. Rodriguez has tools and youth on his side right now. The ingredients are there to make good on that upside as long as his contact skills and zone control continue. He seems to be limited to second base right now, but he could probably handle the left side of the infield if needed; certainly if he gets stronger and there’s emphasis on versatility. As a second baseman without a lot of thump, Rodriguez has a high floor as a utility infielder, but if the high average and on-base numbers continue against better pitching, perhaps there’s a leadoff candidate in his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Venezuela natives Brayan Rocchio (Guardians) and Ezequiel Tovar (Rockies) have taken their slick-fielding ways at shortstop to the Majors in recent years with varying levels of effectiveness. Cortesia is several years behind his countrymen at the position but could very well follow in their footsteps in time. The 17-year-old was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 14 prospect in the 2025 class and became Washington’s top international signing at the start of the 2025 period when he joined the organization for $1.92 million. Nationals officials said they targeted hit tools at the top of this year’s international group, and Cortesia has a solid one with a level right-handed swing that can send the ball all over the diamond. It’s been hit-over-power at this early stage, but he’s been growing into his frame, adding to the hope that average pop could be in the tank by the time he fully matures. Cortesia earned his best amateur grades on the defensive side. His hands, footwork and arm strength all look above-average at this early stage, and as the brother of a member of the Venezuelan national track-and-field team, he’ll flash plus-plus run times in the 60-yard dash right now. Even if he slows down as he fills out, he should still be good for above-average wheels. The Nationals will take that defensive profile and hope to build a stronger and sustainable hitter in Cortesia, starting with their Dominican Summer League program.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fernandez is yet another small, contact-oriented, switch-hitting infielder for the Guardians, having exceeded expectations after signing for $215,000 out of Venezuela in 2024. He looked overqualified for the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last year as he hit .333/.398/.558 with six homers and 16 steals in 43 games before a brief cameo at Single-A Lynchburg. This well-rounded skillset starts with strong contact skills. Fernandez is an aggressive swinger who puts the ball in play a lot, which causes him to rarely strike out -- or walk. He is undersized and doesn't have a ton of physical projection, but his line-drive approach could lead to 15 homers at maturation with added strength, since he's still plenty athletic. To date, he has been much more productive from the left side, partially a product of seeing far more consistent playing time against right-handers. Fernandez has played across the infield and will likely continue to do so as the Guardians try to find his long-term home. His above-average speed that plays well on the basepaths is also an asset at second, short and third, and he has ample arm strength too. He has been somewhat error-prone and looks most comfortable to date at second base but has a real chance to stick at short.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed from the Mexican League's Yucatan Lions in May 2021, Serna landed a $50,000 bonus and has excelled ever since. He posted a 2.25 ERA in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in his pro debut and a 1.96 mark in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer. He topped the FCL with 56 strikeouts in 41 1/3 innings, while whiffing 32 percent of the batters he faced. Serna has confounded younger hitters with a mid-70s changeup that drops at the plate and has huge velocity separation from his fastball. His heater operates at 90-91 mph and reaches 93 and he could throw harder if he adds more strength to his small frame. His sweeping upper-70s slider stands out more for its spin rates than its power and he also throws a mid-70s curveball with more depth. Serna has a clean delivery, throws strikes, misses bats and generates weak ground ball contact. Listed at just 5-foot-11 and 162 pounds, he'll have to prove he can handle a starter's workload over a full season. He has gained nearly 20 pounds since turning pro and is the most polished of the Yankees' teenage pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The prize acquisition for the Braves during the 2023 international signing period was outfielder Luis Guanipa, who got $2.5 million to sign. But the organization handed out seven additional six-figure bonuses when the period opened in mid-January, including the $240,000 they gave to Baez. A strong debut in the Dominican Summer League is not a full return on investment just yet, but the infielder made a very good first impression by posting a .311/.393/.422 line with 24 steals. A 5-foot-9 sparkplug kind of a player, Baez is a right-handed hitter who has shown a knack for making contact in the early going. He struck out in just 12.1 percent of his plate appearances during his debut and showed a solid approach, walking nearly as often, especially for someone who didn’t turn 17 until the end of March. He’s never going to be mistaken for a cleanup hitter, but there is some extra-base authority in his compact swing. Baez is a plus athlete who has already shown a propensity for effective basestealing. That speed and agility helps him defensively as well. He’s a little undersized for what most big league teams are looking for at shortstop, but his above-average arm plays there and the Braves will keep running him out there until it no longer seems viable, at which point a move to second base would make the most sense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly bounced around a bit as an amateur, going from a two-way high school standout in Northern California to starting his college career at Texas A&M. After a redshirt year, he moved to McLennan Community College and played both ways, then was on the move again, this time to Arizona State as a pitcher only. He missed a bunch of bats as a reliever, helping him land in the sixth round of the 2025 Draft, and he headed up to High-A to get his feet wet professionally. He capped things off by striking out the side to get the save that gave Everett a Northwest League championship. The 6-foot-4 Kelly is strong and physical and comes at hitters largely with a two-pitch mix and a funky delivery. His four-seam fastball topped out at 99 mph in college, and it misses bats thanks to its carry up in the zone. He backs it up with his 79-84 mph slider that can have good depth and bite to it at times, a breaking ball that could be at least above average if he can find the strike zone with it more. He had a changeup for lefties on occasion at ASU, but he might not need it, and there was some talk of him bringing a two-seamer he used to feature back into his repertoire. Kelly’s unusual mechanics come with a ton of effort and a low three-quarters arm slot and cross-body delivery. But he tends to get down the mound well and throw a decent amount of strikes. If he can be around the zone enough, especially with his slider, it’s not out of the question to see him in high-leverage relief situations in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Florida high school product, Hermann was headed to play college baseball at South Florida before the Yankees took him in the 14th round and gave him a slightly over-slot $135,000 bonus in 2021. Because he was the lightest player in the Draft at 160 pounds, they had him initially focus on adding strength before making his pro debut in 2022. He needed little more than a month before earning a promotion from Rookie ball to Single-A, where he recorded a 2.66 ERA in four starts. Hermann's fastball sits at 89-92 mph and peaks at 94, playing better than its velocity because it has a flat approach angle that produces carry up in the zone. He has advanced feel for a sinking 83-88 mph changeup that yields ground-ball contact, though it could use more velo separation from his heater. He also utilizes a low-80s slider with encouraging shape and spin rates that he can morph into an upper-80s cutter. While he lacks physicality, Hermann is athletic and has projection remaining. He has good extension in his delivery, allowing his pitches to appear quicker than they are, and he provides plenty of strikes. If he can get stronger and add more power to his stuff, he could become a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds are always active players on the international market and it was no different during the 2024 international signing period. They focused much more on bats, with seven of their top bonuses – all six figures or more – going to hitters. Down the list was Torres, a six-foot right-hander who got $30,000 to sign with the organization when the period opened in January of that year. He was among the Dominican Summer League’s leaders in ERA, WHIP and batting average against, then came stateside in 2025 and was equally dominant over 38 1/3 Arizona Complex League innings. While a bit undersized, Torres is strong and stocky and his intriguing combination of feel for pitching and solid all-around stuff points to a future as a starter. He has three usable pitches, all of which are average but could be better as he progresses. His fastball sits in the 91-94 range, and he’s shown the ability to maintain his velocity throughout outings, he spins a low-80s curve very well and has good feel for an 85-87 mph fading changeup. All of his offerings play up because he’s shown a very strong feel for throwing them all for strikes, especially for his age. He’s walked just 1.9 per nine in his brief pro career heading into 2026, with the hopes of him having at least above-average command in the future. He’s yet to show he can answer the bell in a full-season rotation, but the Reds are bullish on his ability to start long term. Other organizations have definitely noticed his early success as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The big splash, headline-grabbing international signings every year tend to happen right when the period opens in January. But sometimes hidden gems are found, and the Reds are hoping Villafana is one of them. Signed in July 2024 for $20,000, Villafana was older than most international prospects, signing at age 21. He made his brief pro debut after joining the Reds in the Dominican Summer League, then came to the U.S. and posted a nifty 42/9 K/BB ratio in the Arizona Complex League, though he also gave up 78 hits over 46 2/3 innings. Villafana has a legitimate three-pitch mix that he’ll throw to hitters on both sides, coming from a projectable 6-foot-4 frame that points to more in the tank to come. Coming from a three-quarters slot and upright delivery, his fastball typically sits in the 92-96 mph range, occasionally touching as high as 98. It doesn’t offer a ton of life, typically offering more horizontal than vertical break, and proving to be hittable in the ACL. He lands his 85-mph changeup for strikes consistently, getting above-average chase and a ton of groundballs with the cambio. His 82-mph gyro slider isn’t a super-high spin breaker, but it has a little sweep because of his arm slot and also elicits a good amount of chase. It’s an interesting package, with solid shapes for his secondary offerings and a clear ability to fill up the zone with all three pitches. The key to his success will be some kind of pitch design for his fastball to keep it away from barrels, especially as he starts to move up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hamilton played little in his first four seasons at Wright State, redshirting when he arrived, coming off the bench the next two years and having the 2020 season shortened by the pandemic. He finally got a chance to show what he could do in 2021, when he was named Horizon League Player of the Year and ranked third in NCAA Division I in runs scored (78) and OPS (1.306). Signed for a well-below-slot $47,500 in the fifth round that July, he slashed .308/.425/.508 between Single-A and High-A in his first full pro season before dropping to .206/.320/.341 in the final six weeks in Double-A. Hamilton has one of the best approaches among Astros farmhands, controlling the strike zone while making consistent contact and drawing a healthy amount of walks. His left-handed swing is geared more for hitting line drives than launching balls, but he has enough bat speed and strength to generate 12-15 homers per season. He handles same-side pitchers well, adding to his usefulness as a potential fourth outfielder. Hamilton has plus speed and uses it well on bases, swiping 27 bases in 31 tries last year. He possesses average range in center field, where he played most often in 2022, and could be a solid defender on the corners, where he also saw a lot of action. He has average arm strength, gets rid of throws quickly and registered 11 assists last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Benitez's $225,000 bonus ranked fourth among left-handers in the 2023 international class, and the Dominican has emerged as the best prospect from the Marlins' crop that year. He made his U.S. debut last May but needed just three starts in Rookie-ball to merit a promotion to Single-A four days after his 18th birthday. He logged a 3.12 ERA with 58 strikeouts in 57 2/3 innings as the youngest starter in the Florida State League. Extremely advanced for his age, Benitez already owns a plus low-80s changeup with significant fade and sink. He has added 20 pounds since turning pro, boosting his two- and four-seam fastballs into the low 90s with a peak of 96 mph, though both could use more consistent action. He improved the shape of his upper-70s slider last year, turning it into a sweeper that should become a solid pitch once it gains more power. With a quick arm and explosive movement down the mound, Benitez creates more extension than most 6-foot-1 hurlers. His control and command can waver at times, but he's athletic and repeats his delivery well, so he should gain more consistency as he gets stronger. Another member of Miami's deep stable of potential lefty starters, he could fit in the middle of a big league rotation once he's fully developed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Milwaukee has been hailed as one of the most effective clubs when it comes to international scouting in recent years, and its top signing from the start of the 2025 international window was Fenelon out of Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic. The 17-year-old signed for $1.3 million, making him one of only two seven-figure additions for the Brewers’ 2025 class. Brewers director of international scouting James Armstrong described Fenelon’s power as “top of the market” when his Jan. 15 signing was announced. The right-handed slugger uses an uppercut swing to bring the pop into his game, though some evaluators have expressed concern about how his mechanics will play against pro-level arms. Power isn’t his only above-average tool, however. Fenelon also draws excitement for his wheels, and that power-speed combination could be special if it all comes together offensively. Standing at 6-foot right now, Fenelon earns quality reviews for his work in center field. He already shows the instincts to get good jumps on balls and then can track those in the gaps with his speed as well. That should help him get long looks at the position moving forward. Below-average arm strength might point to a future in left if and when he bumps into bigger talents up the middle, but the power should still be valuable in that spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Florida State, Parrish did enough to warrant the Royals’ attention in the 2019 Draft, when they took the southpaw in the eighth round and signed him for slot at $184,700, shortly after he dominated Arkansas in the College World Series. After the 2020 season was canceled due to the pandemic, Parrish shoved in Double-A Northwest Arkansas last year, striking out 95 in 83 innings with a 3.36 ERA across 18 games as one of the most consistent starters in the Royals’ system. He even earned a spot with Team USA’s Olympic Qualifying team. Parrish might have been overlooked in the Draft due to his 5-foot-11 frame and lack of velocity, throwing in the high 80s for most of college, but he’s up to low 90s consistently now -- and even flashed 94-95 mph in 2021. Parrish’s headliner is his changeup, an upper-70s pitch that consistently misses bats. He didn’t have to use his curveball much as an amateur, but he’s significantly improved the pitch to be at least average. Parrish doesn’t have a fast arm, but it’s extremely efficient. He can spot the ball to all four quadrants and walked just 25 batters in 83 innings in 2021. Parrish’s ceiling may be limited because of his velocity, but Royals officials love the way he pitches and his overall craftiness. His dominance last season also proved that velocity isn’t everything. A back-end starting role is an attainable goal, but Parrish could end up filling a lot of roles for the Royals -- starter, bulk pitcher out of the bullpen or a middle-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After LaCombe posted a 1.74 ERA with 97 strikeouts in 67 1/3 innings at Cochise (Ariz.) CC in 2023, he became the second native of France ever drafted when the White Sox took him in the 12th round. Signed away from a Louisiana-Lafayette commitment for fifth-round money ($450,000), he dealt with a shoulder impingement and lat issues and didn't make his pro debut until 2025. He thrived in Rookie ball but battled the strike zone in Single-A. LaCombe has a pair of bat-missing weapons, beginning with a fastball that parks at 93-95 mph and touches 98 with carry and armside run. He has improved his low-80s slider since turning pro, and it features some of the best sweeping action among Chicago's farmhands. His mid-80s splitter has nice tumble when it's on but lacks consistency. LaCombe's low arm slot produces wide angle and a low release height, not to mention life on his pitches. It also makes it difficult to stay on top of his secondary offerings, and he struggled in Single-A when he landed his slider and splitter in the zone just 30 percent of the time. He looks like a mid-rotation starter when he's at his best, but he'll also be 24 this season and has pitched just 17 2/3 innings above Rookie ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dominican-born Reyes' $450,000 bonus was the fifth-highest given to a pitcher on the 2024 international amateur market. He broke into pro ball by not allowing a run in four June starts in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, striking out 17 and walking just two in 16 innings. He came down with a tired arm and worked just one more frame in the next two months as the Red Sox had him concentrate on gaining strength. Reyes already can park in the low 90s and reach 94 mph with run and sink on his fastball while exerting little effort, and he could operate in the mid-90s once he fills out his extremely projectable 6-foot-5 frame. Just 18, he already has the makings of a pair of solid mid-80s secondary pitches in a slider and a fading and sinking changeup. Boston may have him add a cutter to his arsenal as well. Quite advanced for his age, Reyes does a nice job of keeping his long limbs in sync and producing a clean delivery that he repeats well. In his pro debut, he not only provided strikes but also showed the ability to command his pitches and manipulate their shapes. He'll need time to add muscle and develop, but his combination of stuff and pitchability gives him one of the higher ceilings among Red Sox pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cardenas walked right into UCLA’s starting lineup as a freshman in 2019 largely because of his defense and surprised a lot of people with a .976 OPS that season. He didn’t come close to that kind of production again over his next two years as the Bruins’ backstop, but his glove enabled him to go in the eighth round of the 2021 Draft to the Twins. He’s largely been the same player professionally, moving one rung at a time. Possessing the kind of skills that could point to a long career in the big leagues, Cardenas is a plus receiver with plus instincts that go along with excellent blocking skills. He also has a huge arm, one that has thrown out 30 percent of potential basestealers heading into the 2024 season. Pitchers love throwing to him, and it’s not a big surprise that he was behind the dish when High-A Cedar Rapids won the Midwest League title. It isn't that Cardenas is a complete zero as a hitter. He makes a ton of contact and draws a lot of walks, leading to lofty on-base percentages. It’s an unorthodox swing that might make hitting coaches cringe, but he puts the ball in play, albeit without much impact. He’s worked to clean up his swing to get to a little more thump, which would help him stick as a big league backup for a long time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles under Mike Elias love to draft college players, and the 2024 Draft was no different, with Baltimore taking each of their first six picks from the collegiate ranks. But they tend to break that pattern once or twice per Draft for a prep player they really believe in, and in 2024, that was Layton. An athletic infielder from Charlotte Christian HS in North Carolina, Layton was the only high schooler the Orioles took in the top 10 rounds when they made him a sixth-rounder. They then went more than twice over slot to sign him away from his commitment to Southern Miss for $715,800. The Orioles decided to wait for 2025 for Layton to make his pro debut. But they are bullish on the athletic switch-hitter with a few interesting raw tools. He’s shown some ability to make consistent contact from both sides of the plate, and he uses all fields with a gap-to-gap approach and a solid swing. Layton’s athleticism plays on both sides of the ball, and on the basepaths, he has the kind of speed that should make him a basestealing threat. Layton was clocked at up to 93 mph as a prep pitcher, plus arm strength that would help him play anywhere in the middle of the field. Though he was drafted as a shortstop, he lacked defensive polish and area scouts weren’t convinced Layton had the chops to stick there. Even if he gets the chance to prove them wrong off the bat, Layton’s speed, athleticism and arm strength may be best suited long-term for center field, where those raw tools can play more freely.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for only $17,500 out of Colombia in January 2022, Liñan spent his first three years in the Los Angeles system primarily working out of the bullpen. His big breakout came as a starter in 2025, and he had a 2.78 ERA with 101 strikeouts in 74 1/3 innings across three levels heading into the Trade Deadline, when the Dodgers moved him to the Nationals as part of the Alex Call deal. Washington dealt him again eight months later, shipping him to the Yankees for Jorbit Vivas right before the start of the regular season. Liñan has a legitimate claim for the best changeup in Minor League Baseball. The 6-foot right-hander throws the 79-82 mph offering like a screwball with significant drop and armside run, and oddly, it’s also his highest-spin pitch. Batters whiffed on 60 percent of their swings against the cambio that earns Devin Williams comps from virtually all that witness it. But how far can Liñan can go on that one pitch alone? He throws a 90-93 mph four-seamer and sinker with ordinary movement that got crushed in ’25; at their best, he can sneak them by batters waiting for the lower-velo changeup. Liñan also has a mid-80s cutter/slider with only slight armside movement. Liñan looked like he could deliver enough strikes at Single-A and High-A, but his brief runs in Triple-A and the Fall League made that less of a certainty. He could stand to add some extra velocity, and considering he’s only entering his age-21 season in 2026, that remains a possibility. But for now, he’s trending a one-pitch relief role, albeit with that one pitch being excellent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Belgrave's lack of polish led to him redshirting in his first college season at Maryland and recording a 6.79 ERA with 51 walks in 51 2/3 innings during the next two. The Marlins still saw enough promise to draft him in the 15th round last July and he posted a 2.16 ERA in Single-A during his pro debut, though he still battled the strike zone. He allowed one run in three playoff appearances during Jupiter's run to the Florida State League championship. Both of Belgrave's pitches looked better than ever during his brief debut. His primary weapon is a late-biting slider that sat at 86-88 in his first taste of pro ball after parking at 82-84 mph during the spring. His fastball also jumped form 93-95 mph with the Terrapins to 95-97 with the Hammerheads, and its heavy life induces groundouts. Belgrave has a short arm action and considerable effort in his delivery, so he has trouble repeating his pitches and throwing strikes. He's going to work on adding a changeup as Miami considers trying him as a starter, but he's probably going to wind up as a two-pitch reliever. If he can improve his control and command, he could be a seventh- or eight-inning option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Girton played three springs at Texas Tech but never found a regular spot in the rotation -- an injury-marred 2022 didn’t help -- and transferred to Oklahoma in '24. Ten of his 16 appearances with the Sooners were starts, but success was still limited with a 7.32 ERA, 47 strikeouts and 31 walks in 35 2/3 innings. The Mets selected him in the 10th round -- two rounds after taking OU teammate Ryan Lambert -- and signed him for below slot at $122,500. Girton dominated High-A Brooklyn in his first full season, posting a 2.59 ERA with 91 strikeouts in 76 1/3 innings, before slowing down in his final four starts with Double-A Binghamton. The 6-foot-1 right-hander pitches with bounce in his delivery and throws from a high three-quarters slot. His four-seam fastball can move in the mid 90s and acted like a downright weapon with cut-ride action at the top of the zone, getting whiffs on one-third of opponents’ swings against it across both levels in 2025. Girton works with two slider variations -- a mid-80s sweeper with a ton of horizontal break and a tighter upper-80s option that practically acts like a cutter. He has talked about adding a splitter but went to very little offspeed last season. Luckily for him, the sweeper can backfoot lefties well and helped fend off splits issues. Girton really struggled to deliver consistent strikes in school and looked to correct course midseason in ’25, only to struggle again after his move to the Eastern League. He’s already entering his age-24 season and might not have too long of a leash for starting, now that he’s seen the upper Minors, unless the control is ironed out or he finds a split/change. Even so, the fastball/sliders could put him on the fast track to Queens on their own.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paplham went undrafted after only 12 appearances at the University of New Orleans in 2022 and had a rough go with Mahoning Valley in the MLB Draft League shortly after, giving up seven earned runs in four innings. Still, the Padres believed there was enough to work with there because of elite velocity and signed Paplham as a free agent that August. He was a quick mover in his first taste of the pros, jumping from Single-A Lake Elsinore to Double-A San Antonio while finishing with 11 saves, a 3.60 ERA and 36 strikeouts over 30 innings. Paplham rounded his first full season with eight appearances in the Arizona Fall League. Always pitching out the stretch, the 6-foot-3 right-hander threw a 95-97 mph fastball -- touching 99 -- during the regular season, carrying over that velo he showed in the Draft League. His 85-87 mph sweeping slider could also look like a plus pitch at times with promising break, and it was a good enough second pitch on its own to help Paplham limit lefties to a .489 OPS in the Minors. Paplham walked 12 batters in 21 innings in the California League, and while he didn’t run into as many control issues higher up in-season, the AFL was a good reminder that his let-it-fly look on the mound will be an issue against more advanced batters. Still, he already has the two-pitch profile needed to be a solid Major League reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Entering the 2021 season, Ferguson was considered Tennessee’s best hitting prospect since Nick Senzel, who was selected second overall in 2016, but he slumped and fell to the Padres in the fifth round of the Draft. Just like he did in his final season with the Volunteers, he has drawn walks and made things happen on the bases but also has been too passive at the plate in pro ball. He was batting .221 and ranked third in the Minors with 55 steals in 91 games between two Class A stops in 2022 before the Padres sent him to the Red Sox with Eric Hosmer and outfield prospect Corey Rosier in exchange for 2016 first-rounder Jay Groome at the Trade Deadline. When at his best in college, Ferguson displayed a sweet left-handed swing, controlled the strike zone and barreled balls with ease. In the past two years, he has tried to drive the ball in the air more often, his stroke has looked slower and he has made less contact. He needs to add some strength, stop worrying about power and focus on getting on base. Ferguson has good instincts and makes the most of his plus speed on the bases. A quality defender at the keystone in his pro debut, he has seen more action at shortstop in 2022 and looks solid there. His finely tuned internal clock helps him compensate for average arm strength at short, and he also should be capable of playing all three outfield spots if he winds up in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ravelo signed for $545,000 out of the Dominican Republic, landing the third-highest bonus in Boston's 2021 international class. Though he batted just .197/.303/.265 in his U.S. debut last summer, his defense earned him a promotion to Single-A for the final week of the season at age 18. His offensive game needs more work, though he shows some promise as a switch-hitter with bat speed from both sides of the plate. Despite his youth, Ravelo already displays the consistency to make routine plays at shortstop and the tools and instincts to produce web gems. He has twitchy athleticism, classic shortstop actions, quick hands and solid arm strength. He's an average runner at best, but still shows range to both sides and is one of the best infield defenders in the system. More effective as a left-handed hitter, Ravelo needs to make adjustments to his offensive approach. He employs a leg kick and is overly pull-conscious, leading to too many strikeouts and weak ground balls. If he can get stronger and improve his pitch recognition and swing decisions, he could produce 10-15 homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peck was an undersized shortstop in high school until a senior-year growth spurt and a visit to Pepperdine’s camp earned him his only Division I option. Former Tigers shortstop Danny Worth, then a coach on Pepperdine’s staff, recruited Peck to the Waves and then reworked his swing to get more impact. It paid off with an all-West Coast Conference sophomore season in 2022, but a tough summer in the Cape Cod League and a subpar junior season sent him falling down Draft boards. The Tigers were the beneficiary, getting him in the seventh round in 2023 and then watching him break out in 2025 to climb all the way to Double-A Erie and earn a non-roster invite to Major League camp, where his work made an impression on Detroit’s staff. While Peck’s calling card is his defense, he has enough impact at the plate to punish pitchers for mistakes. He has a relatively quiet swing other than a leg kick for timing, but he’s capable of hard contact for line drives around the field. His walk rate dropped a bit last year as he took a slightly more aggressive approach, but his strikeout rate remained relatively steady. He’s opportunistic on the basepaths and capable of sneaky speed to take an extra bag. Peck is an elite defender with smooth movements, good pitch anticipation and a fairly strong arm. He can play around the infield. Though Peck might be the best defensive shortstop in the Tigers system, his bat will determine how much Detroit can do with that, whether he has a chance to compete for a shortstop role in the big leagues or fits better as a utility infielder who can hit lefties hard. He’ll likely open the season back at Double-A Erie but could advance quickly given his age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last New Hampshire high schooler to make it to the big leagues was outfielder Ryan McKenna, an Orioles fourth-rounder back in 2015. Carey, who was a two-sport star in the Granite State (hockey), signed with the Braves for $150,000 as a 15th-round pick in the 2024 Draft and opened eyes with a very solid first full season of pro ball, playing all year with Single-A Augusta. Especially for a teenager from New England, Carey showed off a good feel to hit from the left side of the plate. He displayed excellent contact skills during his first full season, striking out less than 16 percent of the time, with a smooth stroke. He hit the ball on the ground too often, but there’s a feel for loft and raw power for him to tap into, even if it hasn’t shown up yet. He uses a leg kick that can help him get the ball in the air to his pull side, but there hasn’t been any resulting in-game production in-game yet. Carey will have to find a way to elevate consistently and do more damage in order for him to fit a corner-outfield profile. He’s a good defensive outfielder who saw time at all three spots and has above-average speed, but he probably doesn’t have the chops to play center field regularly, putting a bit more pressure on the power to materialize at some point during his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castro signed out of the Dominican Republic for $450,000 in 2024 with a prototypical slugging corner outfield profile, and he's beginning to fulfill that potential after a second stint in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. After struggling to make contact as a 17-year-old, he became one of the most productive players on the circuit in 2025 with a single-season-record 16 homers (six more than any other player last year) and a .264/.399/.585 slash line. At 6-foot-3, Castro was already larger than most Rookie-ball players, but his power began to show up in games after he added 20 pounds in the past year. The right-handed slugger has plenty of raw strength and bat speed -- with further room to fill out his frame -- and his pull-happy approach plays up the game power even more. Swing-decision issues that plagued his debut season have lessened but remain, and refining his approach to key in on hittable pitches in the zone should enable him to tap into his team-best exit velocities more consistently. Castro is fairly athletic for his size but has not been an efficient basestealer. Defensively, he stands out most for his strong arm, which fits well in right field and could get even stronger as he adds weight. He's occasionally played in center but is a better fit for a corner long term. Castro is an organizational favorite and gets high marks for his makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Armas played in the 2015 Little League World Series before attending San Diego, where he hit a soft .265 in three seasons but won Rawlings NCAA Division I Gold Glove recognition in 2024, when he permitted just 15 steals and allowed only one passed ball in 55 games. His prowess behind the plate led the Cubs to draft him in the fifth round that July and he has ranked among the best defensive catchers in the Minors ever since. He slashed .234/325/.347 at High-A during his first full pro season. While Armas has below-average speed, he moves exceptionally well behind the plate. His framing metrics are outstanding, and he's also a quality receiver and blocker who committed just two passed balls in 79 games last year. He has a strong arm and makes accurate throws, erasing 34 percent of basestealers in 2025. Armas profiles as a quality backup because he's unlikely to provide enough offense to become a big league regular. He has a sound right-handed stroke and a decent approach, but he struggles against changeups and is hapless against breaking balls. He showed some aptitude for launching balls to his pull side in 2025, but he doesn't barrel enough to provide more than 8-10 homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wichrowski worked as both a starter and a reliever as a junior at Bryant in 2023 and didn’t wow scouts with a 4.50 ERA and 64 strikeouts in 50 innings. The Brewers took him in the 13th round that July, signed him for $100,000 and were taken aback by the jumps in stuff Wichrowski showed that fall and the following spring. He was promoted from High-A Wisconsin to Double-A Biloxi after only four starts (in which he struck out 21 and walked three) and posted a 4.12 ERA with 61 strikeouts in 74 1/3 frames in the Southern League the rest of the way. He ended the year on the injured list with a dead arm but is expected to be good to go to begin 2025. The 6-foot-2 right-hander reminds some of Joe Kelly for his ability to light up radar guns from a lither frame. He was touching triple-digits at times before the season started and still touched 98 at times, though his velocity wavered a bit because of the arm down the stretch. He’ll throw a pair of heaters too between a blazing four-seamer and a sinker to give batters different looks. Wichrowski can twirl an 83-85 mph sweeping slider down and gloveside to elicit some funky swings against batters from both sides. There are two upper-80s pitches in his cutter and changeup, but the latter isn’t nearly as reliable as the others. Wichrowski walked 11.1 percent of his batters faced in Double-A, and even as his stuff has jumped, there remains a concern that he won’t corral it well enough to remain a starter. Milwaukee is already enthused by his early jumps in pro ball, however, and some in the organization believe the righty can build on 2024’s gains with a fully healthy ’25.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets added Fañas -- then on the older side at 18 -- for $1.5 million as their second-biggest signing of the 2022 international period, behind Simon Juan, who joined for $1.9 million. The Dominican Republic native didn’t get off to the greatest statistical start in the Dominican Summer League, hitting just .257/.330/.297 with a 79 wRC+ over 32 games, but he did flash enough potential to keep Mets player development officials excited. It’s all about potential with Fañas heading into his second Minor League campaign. Listed as 6-foot-2, 190 pounds, the outfielder has plenty of power projection remaining, so while he didn’t homer at all in the DSL, there’s hope that at least average pop is coming down the line as he gains strength and experience against pro arms. A switch-hitter, he did a decent job protecting the plate and had fairly even splits from both sides in a small sample. Fañas’ athleticism and above-average running ability helped him swipe 10 bags in 13 attempts and provide him with another avenue to be valuable until the overall hitting ability comes around. Even if he needs to move from center field to right, his arm strength should help ease that defensive transition. Fañas turned 19 in January, making him the same age as many American collegiate freshmen, and he stands to move stateside for the first time. The larger the sample on his Minor League playing time, the more answers Mets' and other club evaluators will receive on his chances to turn potential into performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Michigan's top high school prospect in 2021, Mooney elicited top-two-rounds interest but ultimately went undrafted because of his commitment to Duke. He stood out as one of the best position players in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2022 and earned all-Atlantic Coast Conference honors as a sophomore last spring before signing for a well-over-slot $1 million in the seventh round. He batted just .152/.263/.212 in his 17-game pro debut in Single-A. A right-handed hitter, Mooney initially struggled as a college freshman but found consistent success after settling down his approach. He's making more consistent and higher quality contact, though he'll still chase pitches and struggles with changeups. He has bat speed, some sneaky strength and feel for driving the ball in the air to his pull side, giving him 15-homer potential. Like many of Cleveland's middle-infield prospects, Mooney distinguishes himself with his fine instincts, and he also earns praise for his nonstop energy and leadership ability. He has solid speed and is opportunistic on the bases. He has good hands and solid arm strength but just average range at shortstop, so he projects more as a second or third baseman in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing as a 17th-round pick from a Puerto Rican high school in 2023, Rodriguez spent his first three seasons in pro ball in Tampa. Minor injuries limited him to 90 plate appearances in 2023-24 with the Yankees' Rookie-level Florida Complex League team there, and he returned to the FCL to start last year. He earned a promotion to their Single-A Florida State League affiliate after six weeks and slashed .237/.342/.392 with two homers in 30 games before missing the final month with a sprained wrist. Rodriguez has a quick left-handed stroke, makes reasonably good swing decisions and generates a lot of contact and promising exit velocities. Overly pull-conscious in his first two years as a pro, Rodriguez settled down his approach in 2025. He began to understand that he doesn't have to launch every pitch he sees to right field, which resulted in fewer rolled-over grounders, and he should develop 20-homer pop as he continues to get stronger. Rodriguez possesses solid speed and some basestealing savvy. He has spent most of his early pro career on the outfield corners, where he's a solid defender with average arm strength. He may be quick enough to handle center field and should get more of an opportunity to show what he can do there in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies handed out a dozen six-figure bonuses when the 2025 international signing period opened in January of that year. Espinosa, who was still 16 years old at the time he signed, was on the back half of that list with his $250,000 bonus. He more than held his own during his debut in the Dominican Summer League, finishing with a .282/.363/.430 line over 41 games to set the stage for his United States debut in 2026. Tall and wiry with long levers, the 6-foot-4 Espinosa reminds many of a young Elly De La Cruz in terms of his physical build. The young infielder's athleticism stands out more than anything else, and that permeates all parts of his game. The right-handed hitter showed off very solid bat-to-ball skills during his debut and his bat speed graded out as above-average as one of the youngest players in the DSL. There should be a lot more power to come in the future as he packs on strength to that long frame. He's raw in some facets of the game, particularly in chasing too much and not recognizing spin. Even with his size, the Phillies think he has a good chance to stick at shortstop because of that athleticism, actions and enough arm, not to mention at least above-average sprint speed. He's a little bit of a lump of clay, but there's plenty to be molded with the chance for an exciting big leaguer when all is said and done.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lara wasn’t a big-time prospect when the Marlins signed him for just $85,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of their international signing class in January 2023. But his performance as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League caught the Rays’ attention, and they landed him from Miami as part of a three-prospect return for infielder/outfielder Vidal Bruján and reliever Calvin Faucher. This could be the latest in a long line of moves in which the Rays have acquired a young Complex League prospect and watched him take off. Lara, hailing from Bani, has excellent bat speed and a loose, whippy swing from the left side of the plate that allows him to drive the ball well. He had enough skills and polish to perform in his professional debut in the DSL, slashing .305/.416/.445 with 23 walks and 37 strikeouts in 154 plate appearances. He’s skinny, at 6-foot-2 and 165 pounds, but he could develop above-average power as he fills out his frame. Where Lara lands defensively is another question. He started most of his games at shortstop last year, and he has the arm strength to handle the left side of the infield. It’s not out of the realm of possibility that he’ll stick at the six, but if he gets big enough, he might be a better fit at third base and could be athletic enough to handle a spot in the outfield. He’ll likely spend the season at the Rays’ Spring Training complex, first for extended spring camp then in the Florida Complex League. The Rays love his upside, but it’ll be years before his developmental path is totally clear.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams took off after transferring from Alabama to Florida State and hammered 33 homers with a .975 OPS across his sophomore and junior seasons. Known for his massive raw power and free-swinging approach, he was a natural fit for the Marlins in the third round of the 2025 Draft and signed for a below-slot $897,500. He finished the year at Single-A with a .269/.359/.284 slash line across 19 games. The lefty slugger can produce plenty of thump from a crouched stance as he fires his hands with impressive speed. Williams was able to succeed in college with an overly aggressive approach -- he chased all secondary pitches at least 40 percent of the time -- but will have to tighten that up in pro ball. Although the power didn't show up in his brief pro cameo, success in wood bat leagues while in college gives hope that it will come. He did make more contact than usual at Single-A and frequently walked, which will be key to his offensive profile. Despite being a solid athlete, Williams didn't use his average speed much on the bases in college. He'll play all three outfield positions but will be more suited for a corner long term unless he improves his routes. Williams' offense will drive his profile, so sticking in center would merely be a plus, and he could be an above-average defender in right with a strong arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After showing the ability to command his fastball and miss bats with his secondary pitches as a freshman at Cloud County (Kan.) CC and a sophomore at Nebraska, McConnaughey positioned himself as an early-round pick in 2025. But his elbow gave out after three starts last spring and required Tommy John surgery in March. He still rated as the top prospect in the Cornhusker State and went in the fourth round to the Rangers, signing for a below-slot $495,825. McConnaughey's fastball sits in the low 90s and peaks at 95 mph, though it plays up a bit because he can ride it up in the zone and sink it down at the knees. He can manipulate his low-80s slider, landing a tight version for strikes and getting chases by burying them in the dirt or sweeping them away from righties. He also has good feel for a tumbling 82-85 mph changeup that neutralizes left-handers. McConnaughey has an easy, clean delivery that he repeats well, allowing him to place his pitches where he wants. Pitchers often throw harder after adding strength during the Tommy John rehab process, and adding more velocity to his present polish would raise his ceiling. Scouts praise his mound presence and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson missed almost all of his 2024 Mississippi high school senior season while recovering from internal brace surgery before staying local to pitch at Pearl River (Miss.) CC. In his lone season with the Wildcats, he tied a school record with 12 wins while posting a 2.28 ERA with 70 strikeouts in 71 innings. The Rangers paid him a double-slot $300,000 bonus in the 11th round last July to divert him from attending Auburn. Johnson's fastball sat at 89-90 mph at the end of his high school career before parking at 90-93 mph and touching 96 last spring, generating a lot of grounders with its heavy sink and armside run. He backs his heater up with a tight low-80s slider that he can land for strikes or use to create chases. He barely uses his mid-80s changeup with fade but controls it well. With Johnson's long, whippy arm action and ultraprojectable 6-foot-3 frame, Texas believes more velocity gains are in his future. He's athletic and moves down the mound well, creating deception with extension and a low arm slot and release height. He'll be just 19 at the start of the 2026 season, so the Rangers will be patient with his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez signed with the D-backs for $50,000 as a 17-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in January 2023, and entering 2026, he’s yet to post a seasonal ERA above 4.00 during his steady climb through the lower Minors. In 2025, his 2.40 ERA in 105 innings between Single-A Visalia and High-A Hillsboro was best among D-backs Minor Leaguers (min. 100 IP) and ranked 10th among MiLB hurlers who met that requirement. He accomplished that despite striking out only 88 in that span. The right-hander returned to the Northwest League for his age-20 campaign in ’26 and poured on the strikeouts at much better rates, furthering his push into Arizona prospect prominence. The 5-foot-10 hurler shows a pair of promising pitches in his four-seam fastball and sweeping slider. The heater comes in at 92-94 mph, giving it just below MLB average velocity, but it plays above that with cut-ride action and enough induced vertical break to keep it consistently above bats. The mid-80s breaking pitch comes with high spin and good horizontal movement and has regularly fooled batters, getting both ample whiffs and chases early on this season. Sanchez has worked on incorporating a bridge cutter and a changeup, though the latter hasn’t quite helped him fend off splits issues against lefties at this stage of his career. Starting from the extreme first-base side of the rubber, Sanchez has steadily improved his control numbers throughout his time as a pro, aided by opponents expanding the zone against the slider in particular. He lacks the power stuff to blow his arsenal past opponents, and given his size, it’s unlikely that will ever come, so he’ll need to keep locating well. The results are becoming undeniable though, and he looks more like a possible backend MLB starter with each passing year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray chose baseball over the chance to be a Division I quarterback, thinking he had more of a future on the mound. Raw but electric, the athletic right-hander excited scouts with what he could potentially become once he left the gridiron behind. The Angels' scouting department was definitely in that camp, giving him third-round money -- a bonus of $1.25 million -- to sign the North Carolina high schooler as a fifth-rounder in the 2025 Draft. With tremendous arm speed, Gray can light up radar guns with his fastball up to 98 mph, sitting in the 92-96 range with sink. He featured an upper-70s sweeper of a slider in high school, often having trouble harnessing it, and leading some to think his power profile would be better suited for a tighter, harder slide piece in the future. Surprisingly, he has some feel for an 80 mph changeup with some fade. Gray’s athleticism helps him drive down the mound, but his mechanics are rarely in sync and he has trouble repeating his delivery, leading to poor control and command. This is a bit of a lottery ticket that might take extra time to cash in, but the payout could be huge eventually.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins' Rookie-level Dominican Summer League roster is filled with big pitchers with upside, including 2025 signees Kevin Defrank and Adrian Pena, who have some of the best stuff in the system. Santana, who signed for $67,500 in 2023, fits right in as a 6-foot-7 physical specimen. The Dominican Republic native showed plenty of promise early on before undergoing Tommy John surgery in 2024, 13 games into his pro career. He returned 13 months later to make five starts with even more velocity. Santana was touching the high 90s before his elbow injury and spent his time rehabbing adding significant muscle. The right-hander is now up closer to 250 pounds, compared to his listed weight of 200, enabling him to top out at 102.6 mph on his fastball with impressive ride. His upper-80s cutter-like slider is his best secondary pitch with the potential to be plus, and his low-90s changeup also has promise. Santana's control has wobbled before and after the injury, but the hope is that added strength will make his delivery more consistent and coordinated. This is one of the highest-upside arms in the system, albeit one who turns 21 in October, has yet to pitch stateside and has to be added to the 40-man roster after the 2027 season or be exposed to the Rule 5 Draft. This will be a key season, more than a year after the surgery, to see how his powerful stuff plays against better competition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals landed two of the top infield prospects in the 2016-17 international class with seven-figure bonuses, signing Yasel Antuna ($3.9 million bonus) and Luis Garcia ($1.3 million) as part of a larger haul. They added another promising infielder the following year in Pena, inking the undersized switch-hitter for $150,000. The Dominican native has done nothing but hit since entering Washington’s system and batted .359/.455/.481 over 37 Rookie-level Gulf Coast League games in 2019, making his stateside debut at age 18. Pena’s ability to repeat his swing and barrel the ball from both sides of the plate already ranks among the best in the organization and could help him develop into an above-average hitter in the big leagues. He has a small frame and will never much in the way of home-run power, he does have the bat speed and strength needed to turn around good velocity and is comfortable hitting to all fields. A solid-to-plus runner, Pena’s quickness and speed help him on both sides of the ball. Though he’s seen time at shortstop, second and third base early in his career, Pena’s best long-term fit might be at the keystone based on his size and offensive profile. If it all clicks, he could develop into a scrappy, top-of-the-order catalyst type who wears out pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After turning down the Phillies as 31st-rounder out of an Arizona high school in 2019, Murphy worked just 14 innings in three years at Chandler-Gilbert (Ariz.) CC because of the pandemic and Tommy John surgery. The younger brother of former big league pitcher Patrick Murphy, he parlayed a short stint in the MLB Draft League into getting drafted by the White Sox in the 14th round in 2022. He flew under the radar until last season, when he reached Triple-A, led the Minors in WHIP (0.89) and ranked second in ERA (1.66) and eighth in walk rate (5 percent). Murphy's success came despite not having a single pitch that grades as average. He has the best control and command in the system, and he keeps hitters off balance by expertly sequencing his offerings and locations. He's a tremendous competitor who studies scouting reports and reads swings to exploit opponents' weaknesses. Murphy's fastballs sit at 90 mph and don't exceed 94, avoiding hard contact thanks to the carry on his four-seamer, the sink on his two-seamer and the precision with which he spots them both. His best secondary offering is a mid-80s changeup with depth, followed by a low-80s slider that he can turn into a mid-80s cutter and an upper-70s curveball. Whether all that's enough to get big leaguers out remains in question, but he has put himself in position to find out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After pitching out of the bullpen as a freshman, Marriott joined Baylor’s rotation for two years beginning in 2023 but didn’t find consistent success in that role and finished his junior season with a 5.94 ERA, 65 strikeouts and 37 walks in 69 2/3 innings. The D-backs still found some intriguing traits and selected him in the sixth round in 2024 before signing him for below slot at $241,000. Marriott was playing a different tune in his initial taste of pro ball with a 2.29 ERA, 25 K’s and eight walks in his first four starts with High-A Hillsboro to open his first full season, but he needed Tommy John surgery after that. Before undergoing the elbow procedure, Marriott could run his fastball up to the mid 90s, often sitting a touch below that for basically average fastball velo. His high release point helped him command the ball better to the upper part of the zone, where he could get some swing-and-miss. His best pitch was a low-80s, high-spin curveball, and its tight break was toughest on lefties who struck out 15 times in 41 plate appearances against him in the small sample. His feel for spin should help him find at least an average slider, and he’s flashed a changeup that could give him something arm side. Marriott showed much better control in pro ball, having tamed some of the rushing he did late in his delivery in college. He is expected back in the middle of the 2026 season, and the D-backs believe he should continue his upward trajectory toward the back end of an MLB rotation once he’s returned to full starting status.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: High school pitching can be one of the riskiest demographics in the Draft, but occasionally a late-round flier can emerge as a true gem. That appears to be the case with Payne, whom the Marlins signed away from his George Mason commitment for $235,000 as a 2024 18th-rounder and now looks like a bargain. The southpaw cruised through the Rookie-level Florida Complex League by striking out more than a third of the batters he faced and ended the year with six solid Single-A outings. Payne can really spin a pair of breaking balls and leaned on his low-80s slider and high-70s curve to rack up whiffs and chases. Both pitches have significant downward movement from his higher three-quarters delivery, which has helped mitigate platoon concerns. His fastball is still a work in progress, though, with a 91 mph average and sinking shape in 2025. He was more consistently hitting 95 over the offseason and has the build to add more velocity. Payne has a little-used cutter and a changeup with splitter-like movement that have had modest success in the mid-80s, but the breaking balls remain his meal ticket. The Marlins tried to ramp up his stuff at the cost of his control early on, and it will be key to see him throw more strikes to avoid bloated walk rates. Still, Payne has No. 4 starter upside thanks to his workhorse size, repeatable delivery and breaking balls -- or perhaps more if his added velocity sticks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green showed off an exciting power-speed combination across three seasons at Cal by swiping 45 bases and crushing 34 home runs in 151 games. The A’s had plenty of looks at those raw tools while scouting him just down the road over the years and were thrilled to land him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft, going over slot value to sign him for $1 million. Getting his feet wet at Single-A Stockton last year, he hit .289 with an .832 OPS, three homers, eight doubles and nine stolen bases in 24 games. Green falls in line with recent A’s Draft picks such as Denzel Clarke and Henry Bolte who stand out for their exciting raw tools. The ball really jumps off the bat with his ability to drive it to all fields, and the A’s still believe there is more raw power he will tap into. The big concern has always been his lack of consistent contact, as his strikeout rate hovered around 30% in college, which could be attributed to his unorthodox mechanics at the plate. But the A’s have been encouraged by his improvements in that respect, and he has shown a decent eye by drawing a fair amount of walks. A plus runner who can cover a ton of ground with a solid arm, Green has a chance to stick in center field, though some scouts see an eventual move to left. The A’s saw Green as a first-round talent with a ceiling that is just about as high as any other prospect in the organization, but he will have to overcome the swing-and-miss issues that plagued him throughout his amateur career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roki Sasaki took up virtually all of the pitching oxygen in this year’s international class, and much of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 ranking was loaded with players at other premium positions. The second-highest ranked arm – and the only left-hander on the list – was Alvarez out of Santo Domingo East, Dominican Republic. The southpaw was one of two players to sign with the Padres for $1 million, shortstop Jhoan De La Cruz being the other. Alvarez would stand out plenty for his handedness and his size at 6-foot-4, but he caught plenty of scouts’ attentions as well with a fastball that already works consistently in the low-90s. It isn’t hard to envision him adding a few ticks more as he ages and matures more physically. He also shows a biting slider and fading changeup that could become average pitches in time. A former outfielder who only recently converted to full-time pitching, Alvarez is still raw on the mound, but that works to his credit here as he still has a fresh arm. Using a short arm action from his big frame, he can land strikes decently well for his experience level, and that will help his starting chances early in his career. Alvarez will be 17 for the entirety of his first professional season and has plenty of time to develop into a promising young lefty in the San Diego system alongside Kash Mayfield and Boston Bateman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hynes took a leap as the top Canadian prep pitcher in the 2025 Draft by adding four ticks of velocity last spring and performing well against professional teams, including a group of Guardians prospects. Months later, Cleveland drafted him in the second round and signed him away from his Wake Forest commitment for $950,000. He did not pitch after signing, similar to how the club has treated high school hurlers in the past. Considering how few reps he had as a teenager from Ontario heading into pro ball, Hynes has quite a good feel for his delivery and creating spin. His best pitch to date is a potentially plus slider that operates in the low 80s with plenty of horizontal movement from his low three-quarters release. Hynes' sinking fastball now touches 95 mph and figures to have another gear in it, as he has a lot of room to fill out his 6-foot-2 frame. His changeup fits his arsenal well with sink and run but has a ways to go to reach its potential. Hynes is a quality strike-thrower, and his athleticism and sound delivery portend above-average command to pair with his promising control. The Guardians are generally cautious with prep arms, so he will likely start in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, but he has the pitchability to take off pretty quickly and a solid chance to stick as a starter. While Hynes lacks the high-end traits of 2024 picks Braylon Doughty and Joey Oakie, he's a nice combination of the two.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top seven bonuses the Twins handed out at the start of the 2025 international signing period were all given to hitters. You have to go down to a tie (with another bat) for eighth to find Castellanos, who signed in January of that year for $247,500.
