He opened a lot of eyes with a sizzling Dominican Summer League debut, where he finished with a 2.79 ERA, .215 batting average against, 1.10 WHIP and 11.2 K/9 rate over 29 innings. If Castellanos fit the 6-foot-3 projectable mold, he might be considered the best pitching prospect in the DSL. The 5-foot-10 right-hander was still just 16 when he got things going and showed off an exciting four-pitch mix at times during his debut. His fastball currently sits in the low 90s, occasionally bumping up to 95-96, but it plays up because of its life and deception, getting some swing-and-miss. His sweeper is his best pitch with huge horizontal break, an offering that produced a 63-percent miss rate in the DSL. He also has shorter and harder cutter to go along with an effective changeup. While Castellanos threw a good amount of strikes, his in-zone rates weren’t great, with a lot of that swing-and-miss coming from chasing that sweeper out of the zone. He’s athletic on the mound, and if he can show he can get his fastball to sit in the 94-95 mph range, he has a solid starting pitcher package.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ibarguen was announced as a shortstop when he signed with the Brewers for only $60,000 out of Venezuela in January 2023, but he’s yet to play there in pro ball as he’s bopped around all three outfield spots as well as second and third base. His bat did the early talking at the outset of his career anyway, as he hit .311/.437/.447 with three homers and seven steals over 43 games with Milwaukee’s Dominican Summer League affiliate. Batting from the right side, Ibarguen did a nice job of adjusting to pro-level pitching and was named the Brewers’ Complex Player of the Month in August, when he hit .341/.436/.659 with more extra-base hits and walks (seven each) than strikeouts (five) over 14 games. With a slight leg kick and early bat movement, his swing is geared to provide pullside power, and that’s where most of his batted balls land. There’s the potential for at least average power eventually, though his size is a little limited at 5-foot-10. (Note: Ibarguen turned 17 in July after signing, so time is on his side when it comes to physical maturation.) The Brewers’ 2023 international class was too loaded at shortstop and pushed Ibarguen all over the diamond. He has the arm strength to play anywhere in the outfield and even some third base. The majority of his looks came on the dirt as Milwaukee wanted to try him up the middle. If he does land in a corner, he’ll have to replicate his DSL numbers or develop even more power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Reds 2023 rookie standout Matt McLain and Dodgers infield prospect Sean McLain, Nick redshirted at UCLA (Matt's alma mater) with a back injury in 2022 before transferring to Arizona State (Sean's alma mater). He broke his right hamate in 2023 and his left hamate last spring before finishing his college career with a 20-game hitting streak. Signed for an under-slot $800,000 as a third-rounder, he'll break into pro ball in 2025. A switch-hitter with bat speed and solid raw power from both sides of the plate, McLain ranks sixth in Sun Devils history with a career .658 slugging percentage. Though he's relatively compact at 5-foot-10 and 190 pounds, he drives the ball in the air with authority as both a lefty and righty. He makes consistent contact while controlling the strike zone and produced with wood bats in the Cape Cod League. McLain lost a touch of speed as he gained strength while in college, but he's still an average runner out of the box and quicker underway. While he's not a burner, the White Sox believe his instincts and fearlessness give him a chance to play center field in pro ball after he barely did at Arizona State. If he can't, his solid arm strength will fit well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gordon began his time at Oregon as a two-year reliever before undergoing internal brace surgery that wiped out his junior year in 2023. He returned to the Ducks as a starter but posted a 5.13 ERA in that role, leading him to land in the 13th round to the Mets in ‘24. He enjoyed a breakout first full season in the High-A and Double-A rotations, finishing with a 3.36 ERA and 147 strikeouts in 128 2/3 innings. Gordon was one of only 13 Minor League pitchers to post a K rate above 27 percent (27.3 in his case) over at least 120 frames. The 6-foot righty isn’t going to blow many batters away with his 91-94 mph fastball, but he has the strong set of secondaries to get outs as a starter. His 83-86 mph slider was his most-used pitch in 2025 (per Synergy), and that’s understandable because he commands its tight break to the gloveside edge of the zone so well. An upper-70s curveball gives him something with a bit more of a hump that he can get for swings below the knees. Gordon deserves credit for moving to a kick-change after barely using a cambio in his last year at Eugene, and the 83-85 mph pitch is a natural fit for his supination tendencies. With the addition of the armside offering, he ran reverse splits in ’25. Gordon used his breaking pitches to get batters to expand the zone in Binghamton and actually improved his walk rate as he climbed up the Mets' system. His mechanics are loose and easy, and he could even get to above-average control if this trend holds. Gordon’s lack of velo holds back his ceiling, but his development into a backend starting option would be a massive win for a 13th-rounder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres were considered one of the three finalists for 2025’s top international prospect Roki Sasaki, only to see the Japanese right-hander sign with the NL West rival Dodgers. San Diego still signed three members of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects in Carlos Alvarez, Deivid Coronil and Jhoan De La Cruz but managed to have international pool money left over come October when it signed Su for $775,000. The Taiwanese right-hander had most recently pitched for Chinese Taipei in the 18U World Cup in Japan in September, when he struck out 14 batters and held opposing batters to a .192 average in 7 1/3 innings. Drawing comparisons to fellow past top international signing Humberto Cruz, Su is super projectable at 6-foot-1 and a rail-thin 150 pounds at the time of signing. His fastball works 89-94 mph right now, but there is ample room for that velocity to jump as he adds strength within the Padres development program. He showed good feel for spin with a pair of breakers in his upper-70s curveball and 79-83 mph slider in the World Cup, and there were the makings of a decent changeup that he can sell well out of the hand, though it was a distant fourth offering in terms of usage. Because he isn’t overthrowing, Su has a natural feel for throwing strikes, and that will aid his starting chances as he moves stateside. Maintaining that control while adding a few ticks of velocity will be key in the early years of his career, but at a time when the farm system needs depth after years of aggressive trades, the Padres are excited to add Su to their pitching depth.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2022 international signing class’ Top 50 list included two players from Panama: The first was catcher Adan Sanchez, who got $1.5 million to sign with the Cubs. Pineda stayed in the NL Central as well, as the No. 49 prospect received $800,000 to join the Reds organization. He had a solid, albeit brief, debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing and then continued to show some hitterish tendencies in his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2023. A former standout in international youth competition, Pineda is a compact and strong right-handed hitter. He has a good feel to hit with the ability to find the barrel consistently while hitting the ball hard. He hasn’t started finding the seats yet, but he did start tapping into his extra-base authority in the ACL with a bunch of doubles. As he moves along, those could translate to long balls and he could eventually have average power. Pineda is a corner outfielder only because he’s a fringy runner and not overly athletic. His plus arm fits in right field and he’s a capable defender there. Now it’s a question of whether his run-producing capabilities manifest as he matures so he can profile as an everyday guy in that spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest in the line of pitching Leiters, Cam has a father (Kurt) who reached Double-A and two uncles (Al, Mark) and two cousins (Jack, Mark Jr.) who took the mound in the Majors. After spending his first college season at Central Florida in 2023, he transferred to Florida State and showed first-round stuff early in his sophomore season before developing shoulder issues in March 2024. He underwent cleanup surgery that October and never pitched again for the Seminoles, but the Dodgers still took him in 2025's second round and signed him for $1,346,600. When he last pitched for the Seminoles, Leiter worked with a 95-96 mph fastball that touched 99 mph and featured carry and armside run at times and heavy sink at others. His 78-82 mph curveball and 85-89 mph slider/cutter both graded as plus pitches with quality depth at their best. He even showed signs of a solid upper-80s changeup/splitter that earned more strikes than either of his breaking balls. Besides his health, the biggest question with Leiter is whether he can provide enough strikes to remain a starter. More physical than athletic, he operates from an upright delivery that lacks deception and carried a 15 percent walk rate in college. He comes with a lot of risk but also has a huge ceiling and was back throwing in the mid-90s and reaching triple digits during the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After an up-and-down freshman year at Clemson in 2023, mostly in relief, Smith really put himself on scouts' radars with an outstanding performance in the Cape Cod League that summer. The Draft-eligible sophomore had an up arrow next to his name with how he was throwing during the 2024 season, but an ankle injury that forced him out for a month slowed his progress a bit. The Reds made him the third college pitcher they took in last summer's Draft, going over slot in the fifth round to sign him for $600,000. As they typically do with their college arm draftees, the Reds didn't pitch Smith competitively after he signed and he managed just a handful of outings in 2025 after dealing with illness then knee discomfort following his return. In some ways, Smith is the same pitcher who was a top South Carolina prep talent, a left-hander with a fastball that sits 91-94 mph and touches 96 mph, one who can ride it up in the zone or sink it down. His low-80s slider has a lot of sweep, and he lands it in the zone consistently with high spin rates to miss a good amount of bats. He had a really good feel for a slinking low-80s changeup in high school, and he's not afraid to throw it to hitters on both sides of the plate. While he has the arsenal to start long-term, it remains to be seen if he can throw enough strikes to be in a big league rotation. His delivery can get out of sync, and he loses his direction to the plate, impacting his control and command. The Reds will have to wait until 2026 to get their first prolonged look at him, and he still has a starting pitcher ceiling if he can repeat his delivery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Smith's combination of stuff, athleticism and arm speed landed him in the third round of the 2023 Draft, the Tennessee high school product had Tommy John surgery shortly after turning pro. He missed all of 2024 and worked just 21 innings in his pro debut last year, but he's finally making regular starts this season. While he'll need time to develop and to add some strength to his projectable 6-foot-2 frame, he has some of the best upside among Los Angeles' starting pitching prospects. Smith has advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks, and he shows the ability to land it for strikes or use it as a chase pitch. His fastball sits at 93-96 mph and touches 98 with quality carry and should join his cambio as a plus offering once he learns to command it better. His upper-80s slider, low-90s cutter and upper-70s curveball are all works in progress but show some promise. Smith explodes off the mound and tunnels his pitches well from a three-quarters arm slot. He still has to prove that he can maintain and harness his stuff, and the Dodgers think his athleticism will help him do so. They'll try to bring him along carefully while also realizing that he'll need to be protected from the Rule 5 Draft following the 2027 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After splitting time as a starter and reliever at Illinois, Lavender headed to the MLB Draft League with Mahoning Valley in 2021 for another opportunity to boost his stock. The Mets selected him in the 14th round, signed him for $125,000 and immediately gave him a full-time role in the bullpen. The southpaw appeared for all five domestic affiliates in his first three seasons, topping out at Triple-A Syracuse in 2023. After posting a 3.27 ERA with 67 strikeouts in 44 innings in the International League and ranking second among Mets Minor Leaguers (min. 50 IP) with a 36.9 percent K rate last season, Lavender was diagnosed with ligament damage this April. Lavender is the rare reverse-split reliever -- he held righties to a .164/.265/.336 line in 2023 compared to .241/.366/.374 for lefties. A big reason is the deception in his three-quarters-slot delivery. He hides his 90-92 mph fastball (touching 95) exceptionally well, and it sneaks up in the zone against righties, who missed on 48 percent of their swings against the heater. For that reason, Lavender went to the fastball 66 percent of the time against righties and 65 percent overall in 2023. His 78-81 mph changeup got an even better whiff rate (56 percent) against other-side batters because of the velo separation and way he sells it out of his hand, but its usage lags well behind the fastball. He also has a low-80s slider with some sweep, but it’s not nearly as effective as batters slugged .463 off it in ’23. The effort in Lavender’s delivery can get him off line at times, and he’ll run into some problems with location and control. That – and his lack of standout velo – may keep him from serving a prominent role in future Mets bullpens, but he’s essentially ready to get out Major League batters from both sides now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Tunink enticed scouts with his left-handed stroke and athleticism as an Illinois high schooler, his strong Notre Dame commitment clouded his signability in the 2024 Draft. The Dodgers floated him down to the eighth round and were able to land him for $412,500, the equivalent of fifth-round money. He earned Arizona Complex League All-Star honors in his pro debut last summer after finishing fourth in the Rookie circuit in wRC+ (152), slugging (.550) and OPS (.967), but he also struck out at a 30 percent rate. Tunink's bat speed, growing strength and propensity for driving the ball in the air to his pull side generate high exit velocities and plus raw power. He's not overly aggressive in terms of chasing pitches, but he has holes in his swing that lead to too many in-zone misses. Viewed as more of a hit-over-power guy as an amateur, he flipped that projection in the ACL. Tunink features at least plus speed that makes him a basestealing threat and a solid center fielder. He has below-average arm strength and didn't record an assist in 35 outfield starts last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have made a habit in recent drafts under amateur scouting director Mark Conner and assistant general manager Rob Metzler of targeting high school pitchers with second-day picks and signing them away from college commitments. Schiefelbein was one of the more notable ones last year, a California prep star at Corona High School and seemingly headed for UCLA before Detroit selected him 72nd overall and signed him above slot for a $1,797,500 bonus. While Schiefelbein is neither physically imposing nor overpowering, he has an advanced pitch mix that hitters do not like to face, based around a low-90s sinker and two breaking balls. He used his mid-70s looping curveball more often in high school, flipping it into the zone to steal strikes and burying it for chase with a delivery that sometimes left him falling off the mound. His harder slider might have more potential as a swing-and-miss pitch in the pros with more deception. His low-80s changeup plays well off his fastball. Physical maturation will be big for Schiefelbein as he gets into the pro ranks, but his ability to adapt and adjust provides more than typical upside. While he could end up as the prototypical crafty left-hander, his grasp of pitching could create a hurler who outperforms his stuff. He's battled a shoulder strain in his first full season that limited him to only three Rookie-ball appearances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he signed for just $10,000 out of Colombia, Bella is the best pitching prospect from the Cubs' 2022 international crop. He compiled a 3.21 ERA with 91 strikeouts in 89 2/3 innings in Single-A during his full-season debut last year, surrendering just five runs in his final seven starts. The Astros acquired him in the January trade that sent Ryan Pressly to Chicago. Bello's best weapon is a mid-70s curveball that generated a 50 percent swing-and-miss rate in 2024 thanks to its huge downer break and some horizontal action as well, and it could become a plus pitch with more power. His fastball also could use more velocity but works while sitting in the low 90s and topping out at 94 because he commands it well up in the zone with carry. He gets chases with his low-80s slider and mid-80s changeup but doesn't consistently land them for strikes, which is also the case with his curve. Bello operates with a lower three-quarters arm slot and a flat approach angle, and he'll have to show that he can succeed against better hitters who are less likely to stray out of the strike zone. He's not very physical at 6-foot-1 and needs more strength so he can work deeper into games and hold up over a full season's workload. Added muscle could provide a boost to his stuff and bolster his chances of making it as a four-pitch starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pentecost was one of the NAIA's top pitchers in 2025, ranking among the national leaders in wins (12, sixth), strikeouts (116, sixth), K/BB ratio (5.5, second), K rate (13.1 per nine innings, fifth) and walk rate (2.4 per nine innings, third). He set Taylor (Ind.) school records for victories and whiffs and became the Trojans' first Draft pick in a decade. After he signed for a below-slot $297,500 in the sixth round, a shoulder impingement delayed his pro debut until 2026. Pentecost's four-seam fastball averages 92 mph and tops out at 96 with more carry than life, but it plays up because of his command and extension. He also has good feel for locating a sweeping low-80s slider that he can use to get both chases and in-zone strikes. His 78-82 mph curveball and low-80s changeup with fade are decent complementary pitches. His athleticism allows Pentecost to repeat his delivery and get down the mound well, leading to a lower release height and consistent strikes. He'll need to prove himself against more rigorous competition, but he exhibits some of the best feel for pitching in the system. A potential back-of-the-rotation starter, he'll attempt to join Dave Wickersham as the only big leaguers ever to come out of Taylor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 40 | Slider: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 The Rangers made Hales the third reliever taken in the 2023 Draft, selecting him in the fourth round out of Santa Clara. He finished his pro debut in the High-A South Atlantic League playoffs, then advanced to Double-A midway through his first full season before getting some extra work in the Arizona Fall League. He could reach the big leagues in 2025 if he can find a reliable pitch to complement his fastball, which can be unhittable at times. Hales turns to his heater about two-thirds of the time, operating at 94-97 mph and reaching 100 with tremendous carry and deception as well as some armside run. His mid-80s slider is his most trusted secondary pitch and features sharp horizontal action at its best, though it doesn’t result in many chases or empty swings. He got roughed up in the AFL while fiddling with a low-80s curveball he couldn’t throw for strikes and an upper-80s cutter that didn’t fool anyone. Hales works from a low slot with a short arm action in back, and his mechanics allow his fastball to get on hitters more quickly than they expect. He has a history of filling the strike zone when he comes out of the bullpen, and his competitiveness contributes to his ceiling as high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After working just 19 1/3 innings in two seasons at Oklahoma State, Reid transferred to Abilene Christian and set the program's NCAA Division I record with 112 strikeouts in 88 1/3 innings last spring. He allowed only one run in his final starts, including seven shutout frames with 12 whiffs against Utah Valley in the Western Athletic Conference tournament, and worked his way into the third round of the 2025 Draft. He signed for a below-slot $649,125 as the Wildcats' highest selection since 1969 third-rounder Bill Gilbreth, the lone big leaguer in school history. Reid led all NCAA D-I pitchers with 66 strikeouts via a changeup. His plus cambio operates at 82-84 mph with fade and sink, and he'll double and triple up on it, even against same-side hitters. He sets it up with a 91-94 mph fastball that touches 96, and he can create carry at the letters or sink at the knees. He's mainly a two-pitch guy, showing little faith in a slurvy low-80s breaking ball that doesn't fool hitters. Reid has a strong 6-foot-3 build that lends itself to durability and an athletic delivery that he repeats well and translates into regular strikes. His fastball doesn't overpower hitters and can catch too much of the plate, so he needs to command it well to set up his changeup. Set to make his pro debut in 2026, he probably will need a better breaker to remain a long-term starter as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Growing up in a suburb of Montreal, Pitre admitted he was “kind of an outlier” in one sense: He never played hockey. The Quebec native preferred soccer and, of course, baseball. Specifically, he loved hitting. He played travel ball as a teenager, his first time playing in the United States, and starred on Canadian provincial teams before playing for the National Junior Team. That made him Quebec’s top position player prospect in 2021, but the undersized infielder -- he said he weighed 130 pounds in high school -- needed an opportunity to grow in college. He learned English in Ontario during the pandemic and wound up playing at Kentucky, despite having never visited the campus, where he eventually turned into the Rays’ second-round pick in the 2024 Draft. Pitre went straight to Single-A Charleston to make his professional debut, and he was as advertised there. He has a mature approach, excellent hand-eye coordination and a lot of strikezone awareness. All that allows him to make contact to all fields, and his surprising strength gives him playable power at the plate even though his flat left-handed swing might top out at 10 homers per season in the professional ranks. Pitre is a solid runner and uses his speed aggressively on the bases, like when he swiped 26 bags for Kentucky in his final season there or when he stole seven down the stretch for Charleston. He is regarded as a quality defensive second baseman, and he showed enough range in the Rays early looks that he could get some time at shortstop this year. His arm strength will likely limit his overall effectiveness if he winds up in a utility role, but he has the defensive ability and offensive profile to hold down a job at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Milwaukee’s 2024 international class came with a big seven-figure name in Jorge Quintana ($1.7 million) and a future Top 100 prospect in Jesús Made. Anderson’s $60,000 bonus out of the Dominican Republic barely would have registered from an outside perspective. But Brewers evaluators had Anderson down as an early breakout candidate, and he achieved that status by leading Milwaukee Dominican Summer League prospects in homers with eight (two more than Made) while slashing .283/.403/.512 over 201 plate appearances. His .916 OPS was fifth best by a Brewers DSL prospect since 2010. Anderson has impressed Milwaukee hitting instructors with his ability to stay balanced at the plate, especially compared to other teenagers with his level of pro experience. That helps his above-average power play in games already, and there could be even more coming as he continues to fill out his 6-foot frame. Anderson walked 14.4 percent of the time against often wild DSL pitchers but has seen that approach challenged more with an aggressive jump to Single-A Carolina this season. Anderson is a solid runner at this stage and swiped 15 bags in 19 attempts in 2024. He might slow down a touch as he matures, and he's already seen time in both center and right at this early stage of his career. He’s expected to head to a corner full-time as he joins clubs with faster players up the middle, and his arm strength and power would be fine fits in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Warwick’s path from Downers Grove North High School in Chicago to Michigan State took a detour when Detroit drafted him in the 12th round in 2024 and wooed him away from Big Ten baseball with a $247,500 bonus. He did so well at the Florida Complex League that the Tigers gave him a chance at full-season ball at Single-A Lakeland, where his command of the strike zone was tested. He still showed plenty of reason to climb the prospect rankings and became the latest shortstop in the Tigers’ potential pipeline. Warwick is a speedy, solid-fielding shortstop with a disciplined approach at bat. His parents enrolled him in dance classes as a child, which reflects in his solid footwork and ample range at short, though he also saw time at second. At the plate, Warwick stays upright in his stance before employing a toe tap to generate some momentum in his swing. He showed solid swing decisions and contact rates in the FCL but struggled with the jump. That said, he needs to add strength to his 6-foot-1 frame. He’s at least an above-average runner with both aggression and savviness in picking his spots on the basepaths. The Tigers have enough shortstop prospects that Warwick can easily get overlooked, and he’ll likely continue to until he makes a bigger offensive impact. That could require physical growth. Even if it doesn’t happen, his left-handed bat and defensive range could ultimately find him a utility infield role in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After growing up in the Dominican Republic, Rodriguez moved to Boston in 2020 and lived in New England for two years before heading to the Georgia Premier Academy. He became the program’s first hitter to be drafted when the Angels took a $100,000 flyer on him in Round 19 of the 2023 Draft. Following two uneventful summers in the Arizona Complex League, things clicked in 2025 with a move up to the Single-A California League, where he finished among the league leaders in several categories and his 130 wRC+ was good for third in the circuit and led the Angels' organization. He wasn’t done, either, going to the Arizona Fall League and hitting .433 while taking home Fall Stars Game MVP honors. The Angels think Rodriguez’s leap forward isn’t an anomaly. There’s a good amount of swing-and-miss in his power-over-hit game, but he has an approach and takes his walks to help offset the strikeouts. He’s just scratching the surface in getting to his power in games, with excellent bat speed producing high-end exit velocities and allowing him to drive the ball to all fields. Not only did he hit 14 homers in 2025, he also legged out 14 triples, a sign of his speed and athleticism. The speed that allowed him to swipe 38 bases last year should help him defensively in the outfield as well. He’s probably a corner guy long-term, but he’s shown it’s not out of the question that he could spend some time up the middle. If he can keep the whiffs in check, he has the chance to have big league value as an athletic corner outfielder with pop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boissiere arrived on the University of Arizona campus in the fall of 2018 and never stopped hitting from there, finishing with a .355/.434/.488 line over 117 career games with the Wildcats. His best numbers (.369/.451/.506, five homers) came as a junior, prompting the Nats to select him in the third round and sign him for below slot at $600,000. Boissiere stumbled out of the gate at Low-A Fredericksburg, going 17-for-85 (.200), but that’s not unheard of for a college player settling into the pro game after a long spring. Boissere earned solid reviews in the Grand Canyon State for his impressive approach against collegiate pitchers. He posted near-equal K/BB ratios all three years, an indication of his willingness to work a walk while limiting his punchouts. His slugging numbers won’t open any eyes on their own, but he’s capable of above-average raw power from the left side. It’s pop that plays to all fields too, so he could see 15-20 homers in the Majors at his peak. The left-handed thrower, who will be 22 for the entire season to come, had some experience as a corner outfielder in his early NCAA days but was a full-time first baseman in college and the pros last year. He possesses the agility to be an above-average glove at the cold corner, adding another way he can provide value. He’ll still need to fulfill every bit of his hitting potential and maybe squeeze a little more power to meet the offensive requirements of the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs took Giesting in the 11th round of the 2022 Draft after he’d struck out 104 in 74 1/3 innings that spring and signed him for $400,000 (roughly fifth-round money) as a Draft-eligible sophomore with leverage. He spent his entire first season with High-A Hillsboro, where he posted a 4.00 ERA with 124 strikeouts and 71 walks in 117 innings, and returned to the Northwest League with much more dominance and control (1.50 ERA, 67 K, 13 BB in 60 IP) in 2024. Giesting rounded out his age-22 season with 15 starts for Double-A Amarillo, and his 154 strikeouts across 141 1/3 total frames were tops in the Arizona system and tied for 13th-most in the Minors. Setting up from the first-base side of the rubber, the 6-foot-4 left-hander gets down the bump well, creating some flat angle on his 89-91 mph fastball and enabling it to play above velocity alone. His 78-82 mph slider can be a menace with ample sweep; even righties whiffed on 45 percent of their swings against it, per Synergy. His feel for spin also ties into a curveball that can bleed into the slider but is as effective. Giesting added an upper-80s cutter in 2024 and used it with solid effect when he needed more of a pinpoint offering to get back into a pitcher’s count. His 85-87 mph changeup is too close to the fastball to be truly effective. Giesting significantly improved his control numbers year to year at High-A, and even his 8.7 percent walk rate at Double-A shouldn’t scare anyone. He’s proven plenty durable through two Minor League seasons and moves well enough in his mechanics that he could be a backend starter, even with subpar velo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the D-backs out of the Dominican Republic three months after his 18th birthday in January 2021, Yan worked his way through the organization’s Dominican and Arizona Complex-level affiliates, combining for 50 2/3 innings between the two spots before enjoying his breakout performance this past season. Pitching in his age-20 campaign, the right-hander tied for third in the organization with 138 strikeouts over 103 2/3 innings and led D-backs Minor Leaguers (min. 100 IP) with a 31.9 percent K rate between Single-A Visalia and High-A Hillsboro. It's all about east-west movement for the projectable 6-foot-4 right-hander. Coming out of a lower slot, his fastball only touches the low-90s currently, but it’s a sinker that can run in hard on the hands of right-handers, making it play above the velo. It also helped lead to a 51.3 percent ground-ball rate, 24th best among 272 Minor Leaguers with at least 100 frames in 2023. Yan’s best pitch is a sweeping slider that darts the opposite way of the sinker and can make hitters look foolish if they guess wrong because of the deceptive delivery. His low-80s changeup can flash above average, but it remains inconsistent in terms of location. Notably, lefties slugged .428 off Yan in 2023, compared to only .197 for righties. After early control issues in the DSL, Yan didn’t get too much in his way in terms of walks last season, and that helped him stay in a starting role. More advanced hitters might lay off the slider, though, causing walks to creep back up, along with relief concerns. He could absolutely continue to dominate righties in shorter stints, but given his trajectory and projection, the D-backs have every reason to keep him in the rotation moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smaller-college outfielders like Strong can easily get overlooked in the Draft, but the numbers he posted during his junior season at Canisius got attention, from an 1.104 OPS and 11 home runs to more walks (41) than strikeouts (38) and 42 stolen bases in 48 games. That combination of athleticism and plate discipline drew the Tigers to take a shot with a seventh-round pick in 2024, signing him for a $222,500 bonus to see whether his skills could translate to pro ball. After a cameo appearance at Single-A Lakeland in 2024, he posted a respectable first full season, including a .370 on-base percentage, 20 stolen bases and 20 doubles between Lakeland and High-A West Michigan, all while playing solid defense. Strong shows good bat speed from his left-handed swing and produces high line-drive and lift rates for a hitter with below-average power. He’s a patient, disciplined hitter with a low swing rate, but there was a concerning uptick in strikeouts last year due to a low contact rate and a high number of called strikes. He has very good speed that he uses on the bases as well as in the outfield, where his defense is the strength of his game. Strong profiles as a fourth outfielder in the Majors given his defensive versatility. He’ll have a chance to roam the vast outfield gaps of West Michigan this spring, but his offensive improvement -- particularly in contact -- will determine how quickly he advances up the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murphy was technically still a freshman in 2021, despite him being Draft eligible and in his third year as a Vanderbilt student. The right-hander had needed Tommy John surgery after his senior year in high school, so he redshirted and rehabbed with Vandy in 2019, then threw two innings total in the shortened 2020 season. He emerged as the Commodores’ closer in 2021, saving nine games and performing very well in postseason play. The Angels loved the arm strength and took him the fourth round of their pitching-only 2021 Draft, going over slot to sign him for around $750,000. While he didn’t pitch much for the Angels after signing, Murphy has the chance to move quickly through the system in a relief role. He gained velocity in his time at Vanderbilt and now features a four-seam fastball that touches 99 mph and has good riding action up in the zone. His slider is his go-to second offering, a power breaking ball thrown in the low-80s that misses bats, but that he hasn’t always commanded so well and that can flatten out when he overthrows. He does have feel for a sinking changeup that could be a good option against left-handed hitters if he can find the strike zone with it more consistently. The 6-foot-5 right-hander creates good plane and uses his high three-quarters arm slot well to stay on top of his breaking ball. He’s never going to have pinpoint control, but he doesn’t need it in a bullpen role. Because of the chance to have three pitches, he could develop into an intriguing multi-inning reliever in a hurry.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonzagni worked just 23 1/3 innings in two seasons at Weatherford (Texas) JC after coming back from Tommy John surgery, then operated mostly out of the bullpen after transferring to Southern Illinois in 2023. The Rangers thought he had one of the best sinkers in that Draft and selected him in the 12th round. In his first full pro season, he compiled a 3.64 ERA with 95 strikeouts in 89 innings between two Class A stops. Bonzagni’s two-seam fastball operates at 92-94 mph and tops out at 96 while burrowing at the plate, and its heavy sink is the reason why he posted an excellent 2.0 groundout/airout ratio in his first two pro seasons. He also throws a four-seamer that reaches 98 mph with more armside run and carry. He gets good depth on a sweeping low-80s slider, giving him a solid second offering. A good athlete, Bonzagni repeats his simple side-step delivery and provides a steady stream of strikes. He has yet to show much feel for his too-firm changeup in the mid-80s and almost never uses it. He’ll project more as a sinker/slider multi-inning reliever unless he can refine his cambio, but he might advance quickly in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates handed out 17 six-figure bonuses during the 2018-19 international signing period. Nolasco was right in the middle, getting $235,000 to sign out of the Dominican Republic. He immediately opened eyes with a very strong Dominican Summer League performance in 2019, finishing with a .302/.373/.472 line. His highly anticipated United States debut was delayed, first by the pandemic in 2020, and then a minor injury in the spring of 2021 that kept him from going to full-season ball. He spent the summer posting a .961 OPS in the Florida Complex League. Nolasco has the chance to be an impact hitter from the right side of the plate. He has ridiculous raw power, with the chance for it to be plus in time as he improves his approach. Already showing present strength, he needs to refine his movements in the box so he can get the bat head out front more, but he does show some strike zone discipline and the willingness to draw walks and work counts to get to pitches he can do damage with. In his short time as a pro, he’s already put up impressive Trackman data in terms of things like exit velocity. Not particularly speedy, Nolasco is limited defensively to an outfield corner. He does have enough arm for the prototypical right fielder and he’ll likely see time moving forward in both spots to see which is a better fit. Wherever he plays, it’s the bat that has the chance to move him up the ladder, with physicality and youth on his side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trying to prove that a local kid can make good, Tolve went from the Georgia high school ranks to Kennesaw State for college. He parlayed a solid 2021 season (.319/.393/.498) to get drafted by his hometown Braves in Round 17 of the 2021 Draft. He showed off some interesting tools during a solid first full season with High-A Rome in 2022, but his climb to Double-A in 2023 was interrupted by a quad strain that limited him to just 50 games. He made up for some lost reps in the Arizona Fall League. When he’s healthy, Tolve has been an athletic left-handed hitting catcher, a demographic that’s often in high demand. He is capable of making loud contact, though there’s too much swing-and-miss in his game. He did improve his strikeout rate a bit in 2023 (27.2 percent, compared to 32 percent in 2022), and he will draw some walks. There’s raw extra-base pop there if he can be a bit more consistent in finding the barrel at the plate Tolve runs very well, especially for a catcher, and he’s been athletic enough to play other positions in the past. His agility is an asset as a backstop; he’s a solid receiver with good arm strength. If he can continue to refine his approach at the upper levels, he could be a solid big league backup in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McKenzie looked like he was well on his way to Draft prominence after hitting .389 his first two seasons at Baylor, only to drop off with a .225 average and .561 OPS in 30 games on the Cape in the summer of 2021. He got off to another slow start back with the Bears before a late surge allowed him to finish with a .288/.388/.517 line in 54 games as a junior, albeit with a 26.3 percent strikeout rate. The Nats grabbed him in the fifth round, and McKenzie looked like his old self by going 28-for-70 (.400) with 10 extra-base hits and 11 steals in 17 games at Single-A Fredericksburg. McKenzie has a sweet-looking swing from the left side, one designed to spray line drives all over the field. That said, the same swing hasn’t done a great job the past two years of generating power, especially in wood-bat leagues, as he seems to prioritize contact over impact. McKenzie can get too aggressive in trying to put his bat on the ball, and that approach found him walking only once in 73 plate appearances with the FredNats. An above-average runner, McKenzie got more aggressive on the basepaths in the Carolina League, and he would be a decent bet to stick in center in most systems because of his instincts and jumps from the grass. However, James Wood’s presence pushed him to the corners last summer, and because of fringy arm strength, he’s a better defensive fit in left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fisher redshirted at Mississippi in 2020, helped Walters State (Tenn.) CC make the Junior College World Series in 2021 and cranked 18 homers (including two grand slams in one game) at Charlotte in 2022 but went undrafted because of worries about his stroke and strikeout tendencies. Then he set 49ers marks for single-season (30, third in NCAA Division I) and career homers (48), including a record six while winning MVP accolades at the Conference USA tournament, powering his way into the fourth round. He batted .273/.396/.500 with five homers in 31 games in Single-A in his pro debut. There's nothing subtle about Fisher's approach. He stands upright at the plate and looks to launch balls to his pull side with an uphill left-handed stroke. His combination of bat speed and strength, extreme pull-focused mentality and high exit velocities led one amateur scout to call him the mid-major version of Kyle Schwarber. Though he ranked fifth in D-I with 64 walks and generally makes good swing decisions, his mentality results in a lot of strikeouts and some difficulties against non-fastballs. Fisher isn't the prettiest runner, but he has surprisingly solid speed and succeeded on all 15 of his steal attempts between college and pro ball last year. His athleticism should translate into defensive ability as well, but he's just adequate as a corner outfielder with an average arm. A part-time catcher in junior college, he played mostly right field at Charlotte and in his debut but is better suited for left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing Dominican shortstop Cristian Hernandez for $3 million in January 2021, the Cubs came back a year later and inked his younger brother, Alexis, for $1.3 million. He wasn't as physical or considered as advanced at the plate as his older sibling at the same stage, but Hernandez had a much productive U.S. debut. He batted .315/.407/.515 in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last summer, while Cristian managed a .261/.320/.357 line in the ACL in 2022. Hernandez's .494 average on balls in play was the second-highest in the Minors (minimum: 150 plate appearances) last year and obviously isn't sustainable. A right-handed hitter, he'll need to show more patience after striking out at a 33 percent rate in 2023 but he has a knack for making hard contact when he connects. He shows some aptitude for driving balls in the air to his pull side, so he could grow into 15-20 homer power. With solid speed, Hernandez will steal an occasional base. He's an average defender with a solid arm at shortstop, though like many youngsters he needs to play more under control. He also has seen action at second and third base, and some scouts who saw him as an amateur thought he might wind up in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest-ranked member of Florida's 2019 recruiting class to make it to Gainesville, Rivera could have factored in the top five rounds had he been signable. He did little offensively in his first three years with the Gators or with wood bats in the Cape Cod League, then broke out with 19 homers to help Florida reach the College World Series finals in 2022. He proceeded to High-A almost immediately after turning pro as a third-rounder and slashed .250/.320/.402 in 25 games. Rivera was aggressively pushed to Double-A Tennessee for his first full season but struggled (in part due to a low BABIP) before being traded to the Blue Jays in late July in a deal for Nate Pearson. Rivera developed more patience and hit the ball significantly harder in 2023 than he had previously. He always had displayed a quick right-handed swing and he did a better job of keeping it on plane, allowing him to drive the ball with authority to all fields. He has the upside of a .260 hitter with 15-20 homers per season, but he’ll need to do a better job against upper-level pitching to get there. Rivera plays quicker than his average speed thanks to his instincts. More steady than spectacular at shortstop, he has decent range and solid arm strength. The Jays like his defense at the six and are hopeful they can squeeze enough offense out of their acquisition with more exposure to the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lovich was one of the older players in the 2024 prep class and carried just 185 pounds on his 6-foot-4 frame, so most teams viewed him as a projectable project they'd like to see develop in college at Arkansas. A couple of clubs were intrigued enough to try to lure him away from the Razorbacks, and the Cubs did so by selecting him in the 11th round and paying him a fourth-round bonus ($650,000). He fared well during the instructional league and will make his official pro debut in 2025. With a quality left-handed stroke that's relatively short considering his size and the ability to recognize pitches better than most players his age, Lovich is equipped to hit for average. He shows promising bat speed that should increase once he adds some much-needed strength, giving him the potential to develop 20-homer power. Some evaluators aren't as sold as much on his pop because he doesn't turn on many pitches and the fact that he hit a lot of opposite-field grounders on the showcase circuit. Lovich is more athletic than his gangly frame might indicate and has solid speed. The Cubs were impressed by how well he tracks ball in the outfield and will give him every chance to stick in center field, though he projects more as a right fielder with solid arm strength. He also created some interest as a three-pitch left-hander with an upper-80s fastball in high school, though his future clearly was brighter as a position player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Dyan Jorge may have been the cream of the Rockies' crop at the start of the 2022 international signing period, getting $2.8 million to sign. But Hidalgo, another middle infielder who received a $500,000 bonus, has jumped to the forefront a bit more. It didn’t happen overnight as Hidalgo repeated the Dominican Summer League, but things really clicked for him in Round 2 in 2023, finishing with a .980 OPS en route to being named the DSL MVP. He performed well during his U.S. debut in 2024, earning a late bump up to Single-A Fresno, albeit with less impact at the plate. A right-handed-hitting infielder, Hidalgo showed a knack for finding the barrel in the DSL. But while he still made some loud contact in 2024, more chase showed up in his game. There’s a good amount of raw power for him to tap into, but he’ll need to tone down his approach more so he can get pitches to drive, instead of wave at soft stuff out of the zone too much. Hidalgo is a solid runner with good instincts on the basepaths, which helps him be a threat to steal. There is some question over whether he’ll be a shortstop long term -- his arm works from the left side of the infield and no one is pushing him off short for the time being, but he likely will get introduced to second base this year after he’s also received time at third at the outset of his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 45 | Run: 45 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Hailing from Carabobo, Venezuela, the same hometown as former All-Star and World Series champion Pablo Sandoval, León is the son of longtime Twins scout Jose León. So it should have come as no surprise that Minnesota was the team that landed the shortstop ranked No. 24 on MLB Pipeline’s 2025 Top 50 International Prospects list when the signing period opened on Jan. 15. León, one of four Top 50 players signed by the Twins, received just under $1.7 million to join the organization. Some of the Twins staff have known León since he was a little kid, so they didn’t have to do too much digging to understand what makes him tick. He’s a right-handed hitter who shows that he grew up around the game with an advanced aptitude for contact and having a selective approach, standing out as the top performer in the 2024 Carabobo Prospect League. He’s hit-over-power right now, but some scouts think there could be a lot more pop to come as he continues to refine his strike zone and understands when he can drive the ball. An average runner now, León has good actions, hands and enough arm for the left side of the infield. He could slow down a tick as he matures, which might mean a move to third base eventually. For now, though, he’ll focus on getting his professional feet wet this summer at age 17.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCollum spent three seasons at Division II Wingate University, pitching almost entirely out of the bullpen and helping the team win a national championship in 2021. He went undrafted, but signed a free agent contract following the Draft and made his pro debut that summer with full-season Clearwater, recording inconsistent results over nine appearances. A return to the Single-A level in 2022 reaped much better results with a 1.45 ERA and a .111 average-against before a bad ankle sprain ended his season at the end of June. The 6-foot-5 right-hander might end up with three quality pitches. He throws his fastball in the 94-97 mph range with solid carry and offers a hard and short slider. His splitter is a developing third pitch, but there’s a chance it could become an out pitch in time. Command and control have held McCollum back, though. He walked more than seven per nine in college and really struggled during his pro debut. But he’s already improved his ability to find the zone since he signed, dropping that walk rate to 4.6 in 2022 while striking out 15.1 per nine. More strides in that direction could give him the chance to impact a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watson utilized a low slot at Virginia Commonwealth before the Yankees selected him in the 15th round in 2021. Following his lackluster first full pro season in Single-A, they had him drop down further and overhaul his arsenal. The changes paid off as he led all Minor League relievers (minimum: 60 innings) with a 1.58 ERA and ranked second with a .138 opponent average while reaching Double-A. Watson creates unique deception as a 6-foot-7 sidearmer with an upright delivery. Batters struggle to barrel his fastball, which parks at 90-92 mph and tops out at 94 but features tremendous carry and armside run. He has scrapped a tight slider and a changeup and now works with a mid-80s cutter that shows flashes of becoming a solid offering and a fringier 78-82 mph sweeper. The new arm slot not only upgraded Watson's stuff, but he's also throwing more strikes. The changes also helped him log a .393 OPS against left-handers in 2023 after they teed off on him for a 1.019 OPS the year before. He could reach New York in 2024 if his unusual look can continue to baffle hitters in Triple-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holiday bounced between two Florida junior colleges in 2022 and 2023, leading JuCo pitchers with 141 strikeouts in 88 innings for Junior College World Series champion Central Florida the latter year. He moved to Oklahoma State as a junior and led the Big 12 with 128 punchouts in 113 frames. Holiday delivered a complete-game two-hitter in the postseason against Florida in the NCAA Regionals, and the Cardinals selected him in the third round that July. He signed for $800,000, a little below slot, as St. Louis’ second pick of the 2024 Draft. The 5-foot-11 right-hander may have only sat 90-93 mph (touching 95) with his fastball in college, but his impressive command of the pitch, particularly with carry up in the zone, made it closer to an average offering. His low-80s slider caused batters from both sides of the plate to expand the zone, and he could land it especially well low and to the gloveside. His mid-70s curveball was a serviceable third pitch, while his low-80s changeup was used only against lefties and with unreliable results. Holiday uses an extremely high leg kick that could rival that of Bronson Arroyo and he makes a stabbing motion with his front foot as it lands, adding some deception. At his size, he isn’t a candidate to add a ton of velocity in pro ball, so he’ll need to continue to pound the zone and throw hitters off in other ways to stick as a starter. Holiday underwent Tommy John surgery last spring and has yet to make his pro debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kohlhepp is a unique all-around pitcher, from his delivery to his background. He was the top-rated shortstop in Wisconsin out of high school, but pitched effectively -- and hard -- out of the same sidearm angle he threw as an infielder. The package earned him a chance at the University of Tennessee, but his command woes left him little used as a freshman. He was wild again at Iowa Junior College, but his 30 batters faced over 21 1/3 innings caught the attention of Notre Dame, which slotted him into a bulk relief role and gave him a chance to thrive. He became one of the best pitchers in the ACC and helped the Irish reach the NCAA Super Regionals. The Tigers have sought unique bullpen arms in recent years, but viewed Kohlhepp as a potential starter when they drafted him in the fourth round and signed him for a $400,000 bonus. Kohlhepp generates a lot of velocity from his near-sidearm delivery with late whip action. His fastball sits in the mid-90s with movement and can top out higher in a pinch. He throws a changeup in the mid-80s out of the same slot to attack left-handers and a harder slider to eat up right-handers. The question with Kohlhepp has always been command of the strike zone. The result isn’t necessarily a high-strikeout arsenal, but hitters struggle to square him up. Kohlhepp already has the ingredients to become an effective reliever, providing a different look in a Tigers bullpen currently stocked with traditional hard-throwing righties. However, team officials are open to giving him a chance to start and see how he can mix his pitches. Either way, he has a chance to fit in on a Major League staff in some role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hunt never found a full-time spot in the Mississippi State rotation during his four years in school, and after choosing not to sign with the Pirates as a 12th-rounder in 2022, he posted an 8.54 ERA as a reliever the following spring. He boosted his stock with a solid showing as Falmouth’s closer in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2023 and signed with Milwaukee as a nondrafted free agent in July. He broke out in a big way in his first full season of pro ball, moving from Single-A Carolina to starting spots with High-A Wisconsin and Double-A Biloxi. His 2.03 ERA and 0.93 WHIP each ranked fourth best among Minor Leaguers with at least 100 innings, while his 34.7 percent K rate placed fifth. The former Bulldog’s dominance stemmed from heavy slider usage last season. Hunt can wear out the low, armside corner with the 84-86 mph pitch that has gyro shape, dipping below bats at just the right moment. Hunt threw it almost half the time against righties, but the breaker was also effective against lefties, who batted just .163 against the hurler during the season. His 91-93 mph fastball (occasionally touching 96) doesn’t pop for velo but can work well at the top of the zone, especially to set up the slider. Hunt also works with an upper-70s curveball and a firmer mid-80s changeup. Hunt really struggled with control in college but was a control artist last season with a 6.2 percent walk rate. That will likely creep up if hitters can hold off against the sliders outside the zone, but the improvements have helped his case at reaching -- and sticking in -- a pro rotation as a potential future No. 5 in the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Elissalt had an outstanding first pro season after the Tigers made him a Day 3 Draft pick and wooed the former Chipola College hurler away from Southern Miss with an above-slot $187,500 bonus. The lanky right-hander opened the season in the Single-A Lakeland bullpen before moving to the rotation by the end of April. He allowed just two earned runs in a 40-inning span from mid-May to the All-Star break, including 21 2/3 consecutive scoreless innings, before securing a promotion to High-A West Michigan's run to the Midwest League title. He earned Florida State League Pitcher of the Year honors, vaulted up prospect rankings and worked his way into the Tigers’ long-term pitching picture. Elissalt isn’t an overpowering pitcher, but uses his long frame for extension that gets his pitches on the hitter sneaky quick. His fastball generally sits around 91-93 mph but still gave up little damage despite a pedestrian whiff rate. His dominant pitch is a 77-80 mph curveball with good spin, nearly 5 feet of drop and another foot of gloveside movement. His lesser-used slider generates a similar whiff rate with less spin and good vertical movement, while his kick change has potential against left-handed pitchers. He has occasional off nights for command but generally attacks the strike zone when he’s in form. Part of Elissalt’s standing comes from projection for a velocity bump with refinements and physical growth; he won't turn 22 until July. He has potential as a back-half starter if he gets a tick more on his fastball and continues to locate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gavin Lux, Jarred Kelenic and JD Dix have been the most prominent high school bats to come out of Wisconsin in the last decade, and the state deserves credit for being the home of 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin before he shipped off to Missouri State. But the Badger State has been considerably lighter on prep arms, at least until 2025. Kussow was Wisconsin’s top prospect heading into last year’s Draft and ended up being the only player from the state selected when the Mets took him in the fourth round. His $897,500 bonus was more akin to mid-third-round money and was the highest-ever paid to a Wisconsin high school pitcher. New York has favored college arms higher up in the Draft in recent years, but it isn’t hard to see what they see in Kussow to change strategy. Standing 6-foot-5, the right-hander generates good extension and gets down the mound to create a low release point that make him difficult to read. He showed a low-90s fastball as a prepster and touched 97 with carry and armside run. An upper-80s, high-spin slider gives him a breaking-ball weapon that could take off under the Mets’ guidance, and there are the workings of a mid-80s changeup in there. Kussow’s delivery was under some scrutiny as an amateur, and he’ll likely need to smooth out his mechanics to deliver strikes consistently on the pro side. As a cold-weather arm, he has a lot of potential that the Mets, who have made tremendous gains in pitching development in recent years, could tap into in the coming years. That in-game development will have to wait until 2027 after preseason labrum surgery on his pitching shoulder pushed him to the full-season injured list for '26.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies are no strangers in trying to find bullpen help via the Rule 5 Draft. Anthony Molina was a 2023 selection who spent parts of the next two seasons in the big leagues. Back in 2020, they gave Jordan Sheffield a shot, and he appeared in 30 games the following season. This year, they’re hoping Petit will be their Rule 5 lightning in a bottle. While he was a starter in his last year at Charleston Southern, Petit has done nothing but relieve as a pro since the Tigers drafted him in the 14th round in 2021. After reaching Triple-A in 2025, he was left off the 40-man roster for the second straight year, and the Rockies made him the No. 1 pick in the Major League phase. Petit is a mountain of a man, standing at 6-foot-8 and 300 pounds, though he’s a good athlete, especially for his size. He can touch as high as 98 mph with his fastball, sitting around 95 and using a steep downward plane to get ground-ball outs. His 84-mph gyro slider is his out pitch, missing a lot of bats and getting a lot of chase, a breaking ball the Rockies think might work in Coors Field. He does have an upper-80s changeup that tunnels off the fastball effectively. The big right-hander has shown an ability to get hitters on both sides of the plate out and has kept his walk rate in check. His best chance of sticking with the Rockies will likely be as a bulk reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Cutter: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 Dalena shares an alma mater of Montoursville Area (Pa.) HS with Mike Mussina and was mentored by the Hall of Fame pitcher growing up in the Keystone State. After a stint at Monmouth in 2021-22, he played both ways at Division II Shippensburg in 2023, turned toward pitching in ’24 and posted a 3.36 ERA and a 1.17 WHIP with 99 strikeouts in 83 innings as a graduate student in ’25. The Padres took him in the sixth round, making him the first Shippensburg player selected since 2018 and the highest since 1999, and signed him for $10,000. Dalena made three brief appearances for Single-A Lake Elsinore in his pro debut. The 6-foot-3 right-hander is entering his age-24 campaign in his first full season but has some upside given his limited background. He was sitting mid-90s with impressive ride up in the zone after signing, and it’s a pitch he uses to set up the rest of his repertoire. It’s likely to be a true north-south look with an upper-70s curveball that drops off the table and a low-80s slider that stands out more for its drop than sweep. The deuce has better action and got more whiffs in his final collegiate season, but finding a consistent preferred breaking pitch will be a priority in ’26. Dalena also worked with a cutter and a changeup, the latter of which he struggled to command in his brief pro look in the California League. Dalena has a history of landing multiple pitches in the zone though, and he’d come up in offseason trade talks with other clubs intrigued by his early mix. He must prove his stuff can play beyond Division II, but the quality of the arsenal could make him a quality low-money, middle-round sign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were certainly bigger names and bigger players than the 5-foot-9 Rivero in the Nationals’ 2018-19 international signing class, and in part because of the 2020 canceled season, it took the shortstop a little longer to prove himself within the system. That opportunity came last summer when Rivero hit .270/.409/.416 with three homers and more walks (19) than strikeouts (17) over 32 games in the Florida Complex League. Rivero was signed in the first place primarily because of his glovework at the premium position of shortstop. He shows exciting fluidity at the six and has looked like a smooth natural at that spot on the diamond ever since he entered pro ball. He gets rid of the ball quickly with a good arm too, giving him multiple ways to impact the game defensively. What earned Rivero his spot on this list, however, was his offensive improvements. He thrives on making a good amount of contact, and the Nationals have been enthused by how well he’s protected the plate at this early stage. The bat doesn’t come with much power, however, and for all Rivero’s defensive strengths, he isn’t much more than an average runner underway. Good, if light, hitters that are also no-doubt shortstops tend to find their ways onto Major League rosters. Rivero’s fit of that profile will be tested when he sees full-season ball for the first time in 2022, just before he becomes Rule 5-eligible in the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A California high school product, Huezo didn't turn 18 until three months after the Astros signed him for $397,500 as a 12th-round pick in 2023. Injuries and strikeout issues resulted in him spending most of his first three years as a pro in Rookie ball, but he does offer one of the more interesting combinations of power and speed in the system. After overcoming hamate surgery early in 2025, he played the final month of last season at Single-A, where he batted .301 with a pair of homers in 22 games, then led the Australian Baseball League with a 1.031 OPS during the offseason. One of the strongest hitters in the system, Huezo hits balls exceptionally hard with a left-handed swing designed to crush balls to right field. He has 30-homer upside, but to get there he'll have to make a lot of adjustments at the plate after striking out at a 32.7 percent clip his first three pro seasons. His stroke gets too long and uphill, he chases too many pitches and he struggles to connect with non-fastballs. Huezo has solid speed and is aggressive on the bases, swiping 27 bags in 35 tries (77.1 percent) in 127 pro games. He played all three outfield spots in 2025, spending the bulk of his time in center field, where he's an average defender. He profiles best in right with his power and solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A South Carolina high school standout who stayed nearby to go to Clemson for college ball, Gordon was an outstanding reliever for the Tigers as a freshman, then spent his sophomore year in their weekend rotation. He lost his starting gig as a junior, though he did get into a bit of a groove closing games, finishing with 11 saves. The Angels sent him out as a starter in his first full season after taking him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft and he missed bats and limited walks, but he got hit over the course of the year with High-A Tri-City. Gordon has a potential four-pitch mix coming from a 6-foot-5 frame, ingredients to be a starter long-term if things click. Nothing in his repertoire is better than average at present, limiting his ceiling. He’ll typically throw his fastball in the 92-93 mph range, occasionally touching 96-97. He still has two breaking balls -- a mid-80s slider and upper-70s curve -- and both can miss bats but don’t profile as true out pitches. He still doesn’t throw the mid-80s changeup he has very often. Gordon can fill up the strike zone, walking just 2.9 per nine during his pro debut. It’s definitely control over command, and he often got too much of the zone, with Northwest League hitters combining for a .260 average against him. There’s a starter profile in there, but he’ll have to improve his secondary offerings to get to the big leagues as a back end of a rotation type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Dominican Republic native, Sanchez was the Orioles’ highest-ranked signee (No. 31 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list) and received the highest bonus of their 2024 international class at $1.3 million. He made his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he walked more than he struck out and ran rampant on the basepaths in his first taste of professional baseball. Sanchez is a left-handed hitter with athleticism and an advanced approach at the plate for his age. His pitch recognition and plate discipline stood out in his pro debut, as Sanchez drew 13 more walks than strikeouts over his first 203 plate appearances, and though he didn’t impact the baseball much, his patience and bat-to-ball ability hint at a solid offensive skill set. Adding strength as his body matures should help Sanchez develop more raw power, though he’s already showing signs of some to the pull side. He’s a strong runner who swiped 29 bases in 31 attempts in the DSL. Sanchez flashes his athleticism on the basepaths and in the infield, where his actions, range and arm could give him the chance to stick at shortstop. At 6-foot-1 and 160 pounds, he still has room to grow and fill out, and he’s already seen some time at third base if that happens and requires him to move to the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pacheco headlined the 2022 international signing period for the Athletics, signing out of Caracas, Venezuela, as a 17-year-old for $1.2 million. Confined to the Dominican Summer League for his first two professional seasons as he acclimated himself to pro ball, he stood out in extended spring training and finally made his way to the Arizona Complex League last season. He held his own as a 19-year-old by hitting .257 with an .801 OPS, three homers, 10 doubles and 11 stolen bases in 48 games. On the smaller side at 5-feet-11, 150 pounds, Pacheco makes up for his lack of size with dynamic fast-twitch athleticism. He is selective at the plate with decent on-base skills, particularly for his young age. He has an athletic swing and good bat speed, which lead to good contact rates. His power numbers have been below average thus far, though he can spray line drives to all fields, giving the A’s hope that he could develop into 20-homer potential as the 20-year-old grows into his body. With plus speed that enables him to cover plenty of ground and a solid arm, Pacheco is gifted enough as a defender to stick at center field for the long term. With a well-rounded set of tools and a strong foundation to work with, Pacheco will get an opportunity to continue honing those physical tools in full-season ball as he looks to climb toward reaching his high and exciting ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Butterworth started his college career at Western Carolina, spending two years as the Catamounts' second baseman before transferring to North Carolina State for his junior year. He got the chance to play shortstop every day for the Wolfpack, and while he put up pedestrian numbers offensively, he showed enough for the Padres to take him in the 12th round of the 2024 Draft. He was having a solid first full season of pro ball in High-A, playing both middle infield positions, when he was sent to the Orioles at the Trade Deadline as part of the prospect package received in return for Ramon Laureano and Ryan O'Hearn. The Orioles bumped him up to Double-A after the trade, and that's where he started his first full season in the organization in '26. An undersized and athletic right-handed hitter, Butterworth has the makings of a future utility-type in the big leagues. He can find different ways to beat opponents offensively, starting with a contact and on-base-oriented approach at the plate. His swing is geared for line drives, and he puts the ball in play a lot, while also showing solid plate discipline and an improved walk rate. It's going to be hit over power, but there are some flashes of pop, particularly to his pull side, registering exit velocities up to 108 mph. Butterworth is a plus runner who can steal a base, and that athleticism helps him move around the diamond defensively. He'd been an infielder exclusively in college and at the outset of his pro career, and the Orioles have continued using him on the dirt. They've also given him time in center field because of that agility and he'd seen action at five positions over the first month of the 2026 season, pointing to a future as a flexible role player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The win-now Padres didn’t seem like an obvious Rule 5-picking club at the start of the 2022-23 offseason, but San Diego decided it was worth a small risk to take Lopez, a $100,000 signing by the Rays out of the Dominican Republic in October 2016 -- who now has a real Major League opportunity. The left-hander earned his chance to The Show with a full-time move to the bullpen in 2022, when he posted a 2.60 ERA with 91 strikeouts in 55 1/3 innings at Double-A Montgomery. His 38.7 percent K rate and .164 average-against ranked fourth and fifth, respectively, among Double-A pitchers with at least 50 innings pitched. Lopez’s move to relief corresponded with added velocity, and he was around 94-96 mph as he got deeper into his new role. The 6-foot-1 southpaw paired that with a low-80s sweeping slider that also was a plus pitch last year and was downright unfair to lefties, who often flailed as it dove down and away from their whiffing bats. His upper-80s changeup may have lacked much separation off the heater, but it was effective enough to help him limit righties to a .170 average and .522 OPS last season. If there’s one aspect of Lopez’s game that will truly hinder his Rule 5 chances, it’s his rough control. A 14.9 percent walk rate in Montgomery showed the troubles the southpaw can face against more advanced and patient hitters, and those will only increase against Major League bats. The contending Padres won’t be able to carry Lopez should strike-throwing continue to be that much of an issue, but his two plus pitches, promising splits and whiff-heavy tendencies give him a solid floor as a bullpen arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur in Cuba, Martinez hit over .400 in the island country’s 18U national league in 2016 to win the batting title and trailed only current White Sox outfielder Luis Robert in slugging percentage. Martinez joined the Angels in August 2017 for $250,000 and reached full-season ball in his first year in the United States, hitting over .300 across two levels. More power showed up with a move to High A in 2019. Though he wasn’t added to the 40-man roster after the 2020 season, no one took him in the Rule 5 Draft. Martinez is the kind of prospect whose whole is greater than the sum of his parts. He doesn’t have a plus tool, but instead can do a lot of things well, the type of player you like the more you see of him. He has a smooth left-handed swing with a solid overall approach, making a lot of contact and drawing some walks along the way. There might be a bit more power to come beyond what started showing up in 2019, but he’s more a contact-first kind of hitter. Still just 23 for all of the 2021 season, Martinez runs well enough, though he’s not really a basestealing threat. He can play all three outfield spots well and while he may never win a Gold Glove, he has very clean and efficient routes. Any surprising offensive gains could make Martinez a big league regular, but it’s looking like he has a pretty high floor as a fourth outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brailer Guerrero was the big name in the Rays’ 2023 international signing class, but they may have landed another player to watch in Monzon. The infielder from La Guaira, Venezuela, was signed for $300,000 by Rays scouts Marlon Roche and William Bergolla. Initially viewed as a defensive-oriented shortstop who could also make contact at the plate, he immediately performed well in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old and jumped onto the prospect radar. Monzon is one of the Rays’ best young players coming out of the DSL, and his .281/.395/.421 batting line reflects some of the things he does well. His hit tool stands out ahead of his power, which is more gap to gap at this point, but he controls the strike zone well from the left side of the plate and he ultimately had more walks (35) than strikeouts (30) in 205 plate appearances during his 46-game professional debut. Considering he was signed as a glove-first prospect, it’s an especially interesting offensive profile for someone his age -- but he’s obviously yet to be tested by even Florida Complex League pitching. Monzon played 25 games at shortstop, 10 at third base and nine at second last season. He’s a shortstop for at least the short term, with above-average actions, solid instincts in the field and enough arm to hold down the spot. The question is more about how he grows physically, as he bulked up quickly to 6-foot and 160 pounds with some projection remaining on his frame. If he gets bigger, it’s more an issue of lateral quickness and whether he’s better suited for one of the other infield positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers paid eight of the nine largest bonuses in their 2022 international class to Venezuelans, including $247,500 to Torres.
