He ranked third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 23 steals and fifth with seven homers in his U.S. debut last summer, the only player in the league to place in the top five in both categories. He was overmatched in a 10-game promotion to Single-A as an 18-year-old, going 4-for-37 (.108) with 18 strikeouts. Torres has one of the quickest bats among Rangers farmhands, and the loft in his left-handed stroke and his growing strength produce some of the best raw power. There are some questions about how much contact he'll make because his swing can get long and uphill, and he didn't do much damage against southpaws last year. He does display some characteristics of a good approach, mostly concentrating on balls from gap to gap and showing reasonable patience for a teenager. Torres flashes plus straight-line speed but projects to be more of an average runner once he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. He steals more with savvy than quickness, so he likely won't be as much of a factor on the bases at higher levels. He's an average defender with similar arm strength in left and right field and at first base, the three positions he played (in order of frequency) in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Active players in the international amateur market, the Phillies have handed out at least one seven-figure bonus in each of the past four signing periods, with three signees in the previous two alone already ranked highly in the organization’s Top 30. Arias became the latest addition, signing for $1.45 million when the 2024 signing period opened in January. Already 6-foot-3 and having added strength, Arias is a long-limbed outfielder who has the chance to hit for a ton of power. The right-handed hitter uses an explosive uppercut swing and has gap-to-gap pop, with more certainly coming as he continues to fill out his frame. While he does have an idea of what he wants to do at the plate, he will have to watch the swing-and-miss, especially with those long arms. He has a power-over-hit profile right now. Arias runs well enough for his size and is a solid athlete with smooth defensive actions and an average arm. He might have the chance to play some center field at least early on, but chances are he’s going to continue to slow down a bit as he matures and will need to slide over to a corner. There he’ll have the chance to fit the power-hitting profile well if everything clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best sleeper in the Giants' 2024 international class, Tejada signed for $147,500 out of the Dominican Republic. Known most for his power when he turned pro, he turned in a nifty all-around offensive performance in his debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He slashed .300/.405/.488 with 19 extra-base hits, 22 walks and 13 steals in 46 games. Tejada has plenty of strength in his stocky 5-foot-11 frame and generates impressive bat speed and high exit velocities with a simple right-handed stroke. In the DSL, he showed the ability to drive balls in the air to his pull side and the possibility of 25-homer seasons in the future. Though he has a power mentality, he also displayed some feel for hitting and for managing the strike zone. Tejada makes the most of his average speed with an aggressive nature on the bases and good instincts in the outfield. He spent his pro debut in center field, yet his quickness is better suited for the corners in the long run. Though he has average to solid arm strength, he didn't record an assist in 42 games last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz has a lot of similarities to Bryan Ramos, as both are power-over-hit third baseman who starred as youngsters in Cuba before signing with the White Sox. The MVP at the 15-and-under world qualifying tournament in Venezuela in 2022, Cruz played with Cuba's 18-and-under team at age 16 the following year. Signed for $2 million shortly after turning 18 this January, he's expected to begin his pro career in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Cruz has a projectable 6-foot-3 frame with a relatively compact right-handed swing with loft. He already shows some aptitude for working counts and using the entire field. He has present pull power and could produce 20 homers annually as he gains strength and experience. While Cruz currently has plus speed and shows some basestealing ability, he'll probably lose a step and be more of an average-to-solid runner once he matures physically. He displays good actions at third base and could be a better defender than Ramos in the long run. He earns average to solid grades for his arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A top prospect in the Royals’ stacked 2025 international class, Medina slipped onto MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 list at No. 49, and he signed with the Royals for $947,500 out of the Dominican Republic that January. Medina earned an All-Star selection in the Dominican Summer League in 2025, slashing .260/.398/.404 in 44 games with two homers, seven doubles and four triples. He walked more (31) than he struck out (26), not uncommon in the DSL, but still impressive and a nod to his skill set. He came to the States after the ‘25 season for the Royals’ fall instructional league program. Medina already looks leaner and has gotten stronger in his short time as a pro, and there’s plenty of projection in his frame still as an 18-year-old. A twitchy athlete, he has a compact right-handed swing with power potential, along with a good approach at the plate for such a young hitter. Defensively, Medina probably profiles best as a corner infielder, likely third base because of his arm strength, range and quickness. The Royals do want to see how he handles shortstop, though. Because of their position and ages, there will be comparisons between Medina and Warren Calcaño as they grow up through the system together. Calcaño is probably the better defender, while Medina has the higher upside with his bat. Medina figures to see plenty of reps stateside in ‘26.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lindsey took a truly unique path to the Rays’ Minor League system. He pitched for two years at Walters State (Tenn.) CC and struggled a bit the following season at UNC Charlotte, at which point he decided to give up baseball. He took a job digging ditches and repairing roads and took the spring of 2022 off, but coaching a youth team renewed his love of the game. He pitched in the Appalachian League that summer, transferred to Tennessee and pitched his way into the Volunteers' rotation. He wound up being their most reliable starter, logging a 2.90 ERA in 21 outings, and went to the Marlins for a below-slot bonus of $340,000 in the fifth round of the 2023 Draft. He only made two professional starts in the Florida Complex League before Miami flipped him to Tampa Bay alongside Erick Lara and Jake Mangum for Calvin Faucher and Vidal Bruján. Lindsey added velocity across the board as a fifth-year college pitcher last spring, and he’s now a power sinker/slider-type starter who covers the entire width of the plate and hides the ball well before throwing from a lower arm slot. His fastball sits in the mid-90s with the potential to reach back for more. But the Rays were more enamored with his slider, a tight upper-80s breaker that can tick above that while landing in the zone for strikes or outside for chases. It’s a different profile for the Rays, who often target pitchers with big fastballs that carry up in the zone. Lindsey also throws a curveball and a lesser-used changeup, giving him a starter’s arsenal. He also has the physical strength to log innings in the rotation. He could evolve to handle a variety of roles for the ever-creative Rays, with the ceiling of a starter and a solid floor as a sinker/slider reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A transfer from Kirkwood (Iowa) CC, Krob ascended to the TCU starting staff in his second year there in 2021 and placed at No. 250 on the MLB Pipeline Draft rankings that summer. No team took him, however, and he returned to the Horned Frogs, only to flip between the rotation and bullpen in '22. The Padres believed in him enough to take the left-hander in the 12th round that July and signed him for $125,000, the max allowed without dipping into their bonus pool. Pitching in his age-23 season, Krob was dominant for both Single-A Lake Elsinore and High-A Fort Wayne in his first full season, finishing with a 2.72 ERA, 1.34 WHIP and 124 strikeouts in 109 1/3 innings. In many ways, Krob dominated those levels as he should for someone his age and experience, but the Padres came away believing he set himself up for a potentially solid pro career. The 6-foot-3 southpaw still has his 81-85 mph sweeping slider that’s gotten an even longer tail in pro ball and helped him pick up consistent K’s. His low-80s changeup also shows decent fade, and it was notable that Krob held righties to a .316 slugging percentage and .629 OPS across his 22 outings last season. The sinking fastball only sits 89-92 mph, but the action on it helped force a lot of weak contact as Krob ranked ninth among Minor League qualifiers with a 55.2 percent ground-ball rate. The former Horned Frog pitches out of the stretch, beginning with his back almost turned to the batter, and his delivery looks relatively free and easy, heightening the belief that he’ll stick as a starter. After making a pair of Double-A postseason appearances, Krob has faced more challenges upon his Texas League return this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Randall was a catcher growing up before taking his strong arm out from behind the plate and onto the mound. After two years in the bullpen at the University of Arizona, he transferred to the University of San Diego and became a workhorse starter and hit the scouting radar. The Tigers selected him in the third round and signed him for a $700,000 bonus. Randall made 16 starts at Single-A Lakeland in his first full season before earning a promotion to High-A in late July. He was traded to the Nationals shortly after in a Deadline move for Kyle Finnegan. Randall is a classic power sinker-slider pitcher with a low three-quarter delivery and rotation, but he actually saw an uptick in his strikeout rate when he became a starter at San Diego. His heavy sinker sits around 94-95 mph but can ramp up to 98 and induce a ton of ground balls. His high-spin slider is a nice swing-and-miss pitch off the sinker. He has a feel for a changeup, but his ability to develop it could determine whether he ends up a starter or reliever as he advances. Part of what separated Randall as a starter in college was his ability to repeat his stuff and hold his velocity late into starts. Randall, who threw a ton of strikes in Lakeland, drew comparisons to former Cleveland starter Justin Masterson during his time in the Detroit system. But with Randall’s big body frame and sinker/slider approach, there’s still a decent chance he ends up in a bullpen role down the road with Washington, one who needs to play in front of a good defensive infield given his propensity for grounders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith pitched at a Houston-area high school (Bellaire) and college (Rice) before the Astros selected him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft. The Owls' top starter in his last two college seasons, he didn't make his pro debut until late May 2025 because of a back injury. He fashioned a 3.32 ERA with 55 strikeouts in 59 2/3 innings in Single-A. While Smith doesn't miss a lot of bats with a low-90s sinker that can reach 96 mph, its movement yields a lot of harmless grounders. His best offering is a mid-80s changeup that grades as plus at its best but also has so much fade that he can struggle to land it near the zone at times. His low-80s slider stands out more for his ability to throw it for strikes than its sweep. At 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, Smith is strong but also maxed out physically and unlikely to add much more velocity. His slingy, low three-quarters delivery adds life to his pitches without costing him control. He stands out more of his floor than his ceiling and projects as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It has been well documented several times on the current Angels' Top 30 that this organization likes rolling the dice on high-end high school pitchers in later rounds of the Draft. In 2025, they did it five times, acquiring a group that included LaCourse in Round 6, making him the first Michigander prep pitcher to be taken in the top 10 rounds since Brock Porter was a fourth-rounder in 2022. The Angels went about $120,000 over slot to sign the right-hander away from his commitment to Michigan State. LaCourse’s size, projection and feel for spin all stood out to the Angels scouting staff. The 6-foot-3 starter routinely hits elite spin rate levels with his slider, registering consistently north of 3,000 RPMs with what could be a true out-pitch in time. While he had touched 93-94 mph in short stints in high school, he was more around 88-92 mph with his fastball as a starter, though Angels player development staff have been pleased to see that his velocity is starting to creep up. He throws the heater with a lot of spin for good carry up in the zone to miss bats. His changeup has also improved under pro supervision in the early going. A strong athlete who played basketball in the winter and shortstop when he wasn’t pitching as a prepster, LaCourse does an excellent job of filling up the strike zone with all of his offerings. If the early gains are for real and he can continue to add strength and velocity, he could turn into an inning-eating starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After racking up seven saves as Ohio State’s closer as a freshman, then being named a Cape Cod League All-Star in 2023, Beidelschies led the Buckeyes’ rotation as a sophomore. A transfer to Arkansas didn’t go well from a results perspective, as the left-hander lost his spot in the Razorbacks’ rotation. Once considered a potential top-five round pick, Beidelschies went in the sixth round in the 2025 Draft, signing for just under $300,000, a little below slot. With a potential three-pitch mix, Beidelschies does have the ingredients to start at the next level. His fastball sat in the 92-94 mph range with Arkansas and topped out at 96, occasionally missing bats with armside run up. He can throw his 83-85 mph slider with a lot of depth, a pitch he uses a lot against left-handed hitters. He has a mid-80s changeup that isn’t as consistent, but it has good fade and tumble when it’s on. There’s some hope that the 6-foot-3, 230-pound Beidelschies might have some untapped velocity and stuff to come as he gets pro instruction, strength and conditioning, and he was up into the mid 90s during fall practice with the Razorbacks. He repeats his short-armed delivery and fills up the strike zone, though it’s more control over command. His ceiling is probably as a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Choate led NCAA Division II with 16.3 strikeouts per nine innings in 2022, including games with 19 and 18 whiffs, the Giants took him in the ninth round, making him the first Assumption (Mass.) player drafted in 29 years. Signed to a discount $87,500 bonus, he breezed through the lower levels of the system with a 2.59 ERA before arriving in Double-A last August. His finesse approach didn't translate immediately at that level, as he got tagged for a 5.82 ERA in eight starts. Using his 6-foot-6 frame and low arm slot to create extension and a flat approach angle, Choate manages to get chases and miss bats with a fastball that operates at 89-92 mph and peaks at 94. His 78-82 mph changeup baffles hitters with its sweeping shape and grades as his best pitch. His slider features similar velocity and shape with more horizontal action, and though he can struggle to throw it for strikes or get batters to chase it, they don't catch up to it when lands it in the zone. The 6-foot-6, 249-pound Choate patterns his mechanics after Chris Sale's and uses his athleticism to keep his long limbs in sync. His repertoire gives him little room for error, so he got into trouble when his control and command wavered in Double-A, allowing hitters to tee off on his fastball when he didn't locate it well. A classic crafty lefty, back-of-the-rotation type, he'll have to make adjustments when he returns to that level in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quinn had an uneven two-year tenure at Mississippi, cracking the Rebels’ weekend rotation as a freshman but battling blister and oblique issues as a sophomore, before transferring to Georgia. He found success as a swingman for the Bulldogs before the Orioles took him in Competitive Balance Round B in the 2025 Draft and signed him for $1.15 million. He didn’t pitch for the organization after the Draft. Quinn is a 6-foot-6 power righty. He throws a fastball that lives in the mid-90s and touches 98 mph with armside run, and his main putaway pitch is a mid-80s slider that breaks down and away from right-handed hitters. He throws a curveball in the upper 70s with significant depth but has trouble landing it with any consistency. He has a much better grip on his fastball command, as he’s able to run that pitch past hitters up in the zone or throw it with downhill plane toward the bottom of the zone to induce ground balls. Overall, it’s fringy control of what is basically a fastball-slider package at this point, and Quinn also operates exclusively from the stretch -- all of which gives him the look of a power reliever who would be best running his raw stuff wild in short sprints. It stands to reason he’d need to learn to throw more strikes and develop an offspeed pitch to succeed as a starter in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Cutter: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 The Brewers have set up a connection in New Jersey by taking four pitchers from the state in the past two Drafts, including top-70 picks Bryce Meccage and Chris Levonas in 2024 and Cairone and Sean Episcope in ’25. Cairone joined the organization from Delsea HS as the 68th pick last year -- the same selection Milwaukee picked up for not inking Levonas -- and signed him below slot for $1,097,500. The 6-foot-2 left-hander struck out 94 batters in 44 innings as a senior and helped his cause with a nice showing at the MLB Draft Combine in Arizona. His fastball touches 95 mph but plays up with ride generated from a low release, and his extension close to 7 feet puts that heater right on top of batters. Holding the velocity will be a test on the pro side. Cairone’s low-80s slider sat between 2,900-3,000 rpms during the Combine, making it easy to dream on the breaking ball as a future plus pitch with good sweep. A solid cutter acts as a bridge pitch, and he can kill spin with a mid-80s changeup that still sits behind his other pitches in quality. Only 17 on Draft Day, Cairone fits a lot of the Milwaukee bill when it comes to Draft arms: young for the class, projectable and armed with pitches that plug nicely into models. Unfortunately, he was hospitalized after a serious car accident in the middle of the offseason, and while reports have been good about his initial recovery, he’ll likely need to be eased into his first full season. Once fully healthy and built up, Cairone will get plenty of runway to take off as a Brewer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After one year in the George Mason bullpen, Salina – a native of Rochester, N.Y. – moved closer to home with a transfer within the Atlantic 10 to St. Bonaventure ahead of the 2024 season. He pitched out of the Bonnies rotation in his first spring and became the team’s No. 1 starter as a junior. His time atop the depth chart didn’t last long; he struck out 26 batters over 17 1/3 innings in his first four starts but suffered an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery in April 2025. The Padres selected him in the fourth round and signed him for slot value at $571,500. The 6-foot-1 righty was showing steady gains with his fastball velocity during his days as a collegian and was sitting 94-96 with his heater as a junior, even touching as high as 102 mph. He also got excellent extension that made the fastball play better than the heat alone and generate a healthy amount of whiffs. His mid-80s slider shows short, hard break and looks like an absolute weapon against fellow righties. There was some feel for an upper-80s changeup, but he’ll need a better option against lefties in the pros. Salina pitches exclusively out of the stretch and used a fair amount of effort late in his delivery to squeeze that velocity. That said, he was showing a little better control before TJ, and the Padres are hopeful that a year of recovery and rehab may only make him stronger, as can happen for pitchers after the elbow procedure. Salina should be an interesting arm with upside when he debuts in the San Diego system in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $20,000 out of Venezuela in 2021, Agreda spent the first four years of his career in Rookie ball, including three straight seasons in the Arizona Complex League. He made a successful jump to Single-A in 2025, fashioning a 2.64 ERA with a .163 opponent average and 95 strikeouts in 82 2/3 innings. The Rangers opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster during the offseason, surmising correctly that his distance from the big leagues would sneak him through the Rule 5 Draft. Agreda relies heavily on a mid-90s fastball that reaches 100 mph with good carry but not much armside run. He creates high spin rates on his heater as well as a mid-80s slider and low-80s curveball that can be unhittable but also catch the zone only one-third of the time. He dabbles with an upper-80s changeup with fade and depth, though he almost never lands it for strikes. The 6-foot Agreda lacks starter size, and his short arm action has more of a reliever look. He can miss bats with four different pitches yet struggles to throw any of them for consistent strikes. He has the upside of a No. 4 starter or late-inning reliever, though he also has pitched just one game above Single-A five seasons into his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mikulski had offers to go toward the end of 2020's shortened five-round Draft, but he decided to bet on himself and return to Fordham. He improved his delivery and control, led NCAA Division I in strikeout rate (16.3 per nine innings), set Rams records for season (124) and career (272) whiffs and won Atlantic 10 Conference pitcher of the year honors last spring. The Giants signed him for $1,197,500 in the second round, making him the second-highest pick in school history behind only 1987 supplemental first-rounder Pete Harnisch. After shortening his arm action and making his delivery more compact, Mikulski saw his stuff get better across the board in his final college season, with his fastball sitting in the mid-90s and reaching triple digits with plenty of carry up in the zone. His velocity has backed up in his first full year as a pro, with his heater parking around 90 mph and his formerly mid-80s slider and changeup dropping into the low 80s. His slider still shows flashes of being a solid offering with sweep and depth, while his sinking changeup is more average. Cleaning up his delivery also helped Mikulski improve his control, though he still has lapses at times and will need to refine his command. His new mechanics have given him more deception as well, as his pitches jump on hitters quicker than they anticipate. The funkiness in his delivery has helped him miss bats in Single-A, but he also has been hit hard and looked more like a future reliever than a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes buying low on a prospect can provide a huge payoff. That's what the Pirates are hoping they can get from Ager, who had dropped to the sixth round of the 2024 Draft after a subpar junior season at Santa Barbara. Considered one of the top college arms on the West Coast heading into the year after pitching for Team USA over the summer, his stuff and performance regressed, though he did settle in as the Gauchos closer. It turned out he had been trying to pitch through an oblique issue, so the Pirates are hoping a healthy Ager will rebound quickly in pro ball. When he was at his best, Ager had a solid four-pitch mix and the ability to throw strikes with all of them, with a fastball in the 92-93 mph range that topped out at 96. His low-80s slider flashed plus in the past, with the potential to miss a lot of bats. He uses a slower mid-70s curve as a get-me-over type of breaking ball, and while his changeup has been his fourth pitch, it has the chance to be an average offering. As a sophomore, Ager repeated his delivery and threw a lot of strikes, giving him the chance to start long term. He's 6-foot-6 with some projection, and the Santa Barbara program has a history of producing solid big league rotation pieces, with the Pirates curious to see what he might do now that he's 100 percent healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If you wanted to see young outfielders who really had a feel to hit, you should have headed to Inland Empire in the California League in 2023. That’s where Nelson Rada and Ruiz called home as teenagers. Rada was a big-ticket purchase prospect who got seven figures in January 2022; Ruiz got just $10,000 to sign in May 2021, but he’s hit every where he’s played, going one rung at a time to date: the Dominican Summer League in '21; the Arizona Complex League in '22 and Single-A last year. He was hitting over .300 in July when a wrist injury sustained while diving for a ball in the outfield ended his season. Like Rada, Ruiz has shown in the early stages of his career that he has a knack for getting the barrel to the ball. Because of that impressive contact skill, he’s shown the ability to hit righties and lefties alike with a line-drive, all-fields approach. He rarely strikes out (12.8 K rate heading into 2024) with a firm knowledge of the zone and the ability to get on base. There’s never going to be much power, but a little added strength would help him impact the ball more. While he’s not a burner, Ruiz is capable of stealing a base, and while he played left field mostly in deference to Rada at Inland Empire, he could be at least an above-average defender in center if given the opportunity. He could be a fourth outfielder type with an old school slashing contact profile, the kind of guy who finds his way into the lineup more than expected because of that feel to hit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez turned pro for $250,000, earning the largest bonus given to a Dominican catcher on the 2019-20 international market. Because of the pandemic and two years in Rookie ball, he didn't reach full-season ball until 2023. He batted .299/.360/.393 between Single-A and High-A but tired noticeably down the stretch and wasn't protected on the 40-man roster in November. One of the best contact hitters in the system, Perez laces balls to all fields with a compact right-handed stroke. He has enough strength and bat speed for at least 12-15 homer power, but his approach yields a lot of soft contact and he went deep just four times in 158 games over his first three seasons. He does make good swing decisions and controls the strike zone well. Perez needs to clean up his defense after giving up 24 passed balls in 62 games a year ago, and he may never be more than an adequate receiver and blocker. He has well-above-average arm strength but can improve how quickly he gets rid of throws. Despite below-average speed, he managed to steal 23 bases in 27 attempts in just 75 games last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An inability to throw strikes limited Potter to 8 2/3 innings in two seasons at Crowder (Mo.) JC. He still battled the zone after transferring to Wichita State in 2025 but also established himself as one of the harder throwers in NCAA Division I. The Astros signed him for a below-slot $336,600 as a fifth-rounder and will have him make his pro debut in 2026. Potter used his fastball three-quarters of his time with the Shockers, operating at 95-97 mph and reaching 100 with impressive carry. He complements his heater with a tight 82-85 mph slider that could become a solid offering if it adds more movement. He threw only a handful of cutters and changeups during three years in college, and Houston will look to expand his arsenal this season. Potter works exclusively out of the stretch, with a big leg kick and a long arm action that help him generate power but hurt his ability to find the zone. He'll work as a tandem starter to get him regular innings to work on his arsenal and his control, but he projects as a two-pitch reliever. He'll need to add considerable polish to become a late-inning option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mariners management was relieved when Kuhn remained in the organization after clearing the Rule 5 Draft despite not being added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. That’s because they view him as a possible big league bullpen piece, perhaps as soon as 2023. It was emblematic of his career path to this point, because wherever the big righty has played, he’s had to prove that he belonged, dating all the way back to when he was a walk-on at the University of San Diego. Kuhn’s fastball is a legit heater, sitting 95-96 mph and topping out near 99 mph with good run and sink on it. He also throws a hard, short slider that lands in the upper-80s and has become a true out pitch in the Minors. Both offerings from his small yet stocky frame make him the prototypical come-right-after-you reliever. Entering his age-25 season, Kuhn is a little older and one of the many whose development was stalled due to the Minors season being canceled in 2020. But if the command takes a step forward, he could be a viable shuttle guy between the Majors and Triple-A Tacoma sooner than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered one of the best left-handed high-school pitchers in the country headed into the 2020 Draft, Savino was so committed to the University of Virginia that he graduated a semester early and headed to Charlottesville that spring instead. He wasn’t wowing scouts the same way in college, but after some promise in the fall of 2021, he enjoyed the best spring of his brief Cavaliers career, posting a 3.69 ERA with 79 strikeouts in 78 innings. The D-backs selected him in the third round and signed him for just below slot at $700,000. Savino underwent shoulder surgery before his first full season began, meaning his pro debut will wait until 2024. The 6-foot-3 southpaw added some velo to his fastball last spring, ranging from 90-94 mph after it averaged just 87.4 mph in 2021, and his slider also moved from the upper 70s to the low 80s while showing more sharpness. An effective changeup rounded out the pitch mix, and as the stuff looked better, so did his punchout rates. That said, Savino wasn’t always consistent with the velocity as a junior, and scouts had serious questions about who he would be over a larger sample in the pro ranks. The good news is he largely throws strikes, having walked 9.4 percent of his batters faced in 2022, and his delivery is simple and athletic enough that that shouldn’t change even against more advanced bats. Even if it’s just average stuff across the board, that’s enough to make Savino a possible Major League backend starter with the possibility for more if the D-backs can squeeze more velo out of him upon his return next season .

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The pandemic and injuries limited Wehunt to 11 innings in three years at Southern Mississippi before he transferred and became Kennesaw State's Friday-night starter in 2023. His combination of size and strikes attracted the Red Sox, who signed him for a below-slot $100,000 in the ninth round that July. He posted better numbers in his first full pro season than he did with the Owls and finished 2024 in Double-A. Wehunt added a little velocity and missed more bats with his fastball as a pro, operating at 92-94 mph and touching 96 while showing the ability to carry it by hitters at the letters or leverage it down in the zone for grounders. He has switched from a low-80s changeup in college to a mid-80s splitter in pro ball, and it could become a plus pitch if he learns to harness it better. He threw his sweeping low-80s slider almost as much as his heater last year, and he also can morph it into an upper-80s cutter. Wehunt is more athletic than most 6-foot-7, 240 pounders and gets down the mound extremely well, producing plenty of extension that allows his pitches to get on hitters quickly. He keeps his long limbs in sync and repeats his three-quarters delivery well, providing consistent strikes. Boston believes he can add more strength to his frame and more power to his pitches, which would enhance his chances of becoming a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cebert spent his first three college seasons at South Florida before transferring to Texas Tech for his senior season last spring. He led the Raiders with seven wins as a long reliever before the Yankees selected him in the 15th round. His stuff jumped during his brief pro debut, during which he struck out 11 of the 25 batters he faced at High-A. At Texas Tech, Cebert sat in the low 90s and topped out at 96 mph with a two-seam fastball that he backed up with a 78-82 mph slider and an upper-80s cutter. He didn't miss a lot of bats with any of his offerings, relying on throwing strikes and inducing ground balls to succeed. At High-A, he went to a four-seamer that averaged 95 mph and touched 98. His high-spin slider added a couple of ticks of velocity and some sweep, while his cutter parked around 90 mph. Cebert started as a sophomore and a junior in college, and New York may return him to the rotation in 2026. He'll have to refine a mid-80s changeup with occasional fade to keep left-handers in check. His control is more impressive than his command, and he'll have to improve his location against pro hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lohman was a steady buildup at Fort Zumwalt North HS, northwest of St. Louis. He didn’t show much velocity with a fastball only in the upper 80s as a junior, and that initially made him a low priority with many figuring he was set to honor his commitment to Missouri. Instead, he turned heads with a little extra heat as a senior, along with a pair of interesting breaking balls, and he attended the MLB Draft Combine in Arizona. The Mets selected him in the eighth round and signed him for well above slot at $797,500 (late third-round money) to keep him out of the SEC. That improved velo pushed Lohman’s fastball into the 91-95 mph range, and with his size at 6-foot-4, he can create downhill plane from a high release point. He’ll work with both a mid-70s curveball and low-80s slider that have promising two-plane depth. The curveball might be a better fit for his over-the-top delivery, but both pitches have the chance to become at least average Major League quality. His low-80s splitter was a work in progress but looks like a pitch with some promise. Lohman uses short strides on the mound, rather than getting big extension, and that’s what leads to the high release. He’ll either need to improve the shape of his fastball and slider or locate them exceptionally well in pro ball to get the most out of both offerings against pro bats, but as a prep arm, he’ll be given plenty of time and space to work on both goals. There could be even more strength coming in his projectable frame, and the Mets, who have a run of pitching development success, could be the right org to get the most out of Lohman’s budding potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An accomplished amateur player who starred for the U.S. national team that won a gold medal at the 2017 18-and-under World Cup, Young nonetheless went undrafted as a Washington high schooler after slumping offensively on the showcase circuit the following summer. He hit 16 homers in his first full season at Vanderbilt but also led NCAA Division I in strikeouts while battling a left shoulder injury that required offseason surgery. Healthy again, his offensive struggles persisted last spring as Young continued to sell out for power and pile up whiffs, batting .207/.327/.383 as a junior. The Orioles took a no-risk flier on him in the 17th round in the 2022 Draft, signing him for just over $1.3 million when it became clear they weren’t going to be able to come to terms with third-round pick Nolan McLean. Young got his feet wet but didn’t hit much during a brief debut in pro ball, finishing the year at Single-A Delmarva. Young is a different player than he was in his prep days, having added 20 pounds and a more upward angle to his swing from both sides of the plate. He now has average power that plays to his pull side as a righty and to all fields as a lefty, but it comes with a ton of swing-and-miss due to poor pitch recognition. He’ll need to tidy up his approach and stop chasing pitches out of the strike zone if he’s to realize his 20-homer potential in pro ball. Young is much more polished defensively, with advanced instincts and a strong internal clock that allows him to play quicker than his average speed. Good range and a strong arm help make him a solid and reliable defender. Right now it’s a glove-over-bat profile, with questions about whether Young will hit enough to develop into a regular. If not, he has the versatility and skills to fill a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herrera not only earned a berth on Venezuela's team at the 2022 18-and-under World Cup qualifiers when he was just 15, but he also led the squad with a homer and nine RBI in eight games. One of the best power hitters in the 2024 international class, he signed in January for $1.8 million, the top bonus in the White Sox crop. He'll probably make his pro debut this summer in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Already 6-foot-3 and 212 pounds at age 17, Herrera is built to hit for power. He has a relatively effortless right-handed stroke with plenty of bat speed and leverage that produce pop to all fields. His pure hitting ability draws mixed reviews, earning below-average grades from some evaluators while others laud his ability to make adjustments and handle offspeed pitches. Herrera moves OK considering his size, but he's a below-average runner who could lose more speed if he continues to add muscle. He already has outgrown shortstop and could develop into an average defender at third base if he can retain his present quickness. He has solid arm strength and some experience at catcher, though Chicago would rather expedite his bat than try him behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top acquisition for the Angels in the 2025 international market was the highest-ranked catcher in the class, Gabriel Davalillo. But the organization was also jazzed to get De Paula, a shortstop from Santo Domingo, for $900,000. He got off to a hot start on offense, one that was equally as encouraging as Davailillo’s, in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .387/.525/.484 over his first 10 games. But his debut ended when he hurt his left shoulder diving for a ball on defense. The Angels are excited to see what a healthy De Paula can do stateside. He’s shown an early penchant for contact, with solid knowledge of the strike zone, limiting strikeouts and taking some walks. He’s a switch-hitter with some ability to drive the ball, though it’s a hit-over-power profile. De Paula runs well and can steal a base, and that athleticism will help him stay up the middle defensively. He has the chance to be a plus defender at shortstop in the future, one with a table-setter type of offensive profile. He might be a half step ahead of 2026 international signee Jeyson Horton for now, and it will be interesting to see which one of them sticks at the premium position and which one slides over to the keystone, a competition the Angels won’t have to worry about for a while.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Big league caliber talent can be found just about anywhere and Diaz has the chance to prove that true. Taken in the 27th round of the 2019 Draft out of Michigan State, where he relieved for a year after two years at Iowa Western Community College, Diaz put himself on the map in 2021 with a huge full-season debut that saw him earn a promotion from High-A to Double-A and strike out 16.6 per nine for the year. He wasn’t as dominant post-promotion and he struggled to find the strike zone during his time in the Arizona Fall League, a trend that continued in Double-A in 2022. Diaz is a 6-foot-5 right-hander who profiles as a reliever only. He can get his fastball up to 97 mph, but typically sits around 92-93 mph. It plays up because of its carry in the zone and his extension coming down the mound. His power breaking ball can get slurvy, and it has good depth, but because of the mid-80s velocity, it plays more like a slider. Diaz generally had shown a penchant for throwing strikes somewhat consistently, generally attacking the zone and going right after hitters, but his walk rate continued to climb with Mississippi in 2022. He doesn’t need pinpoint command to fill a prominent role in a big league bullpen, something he should be able to do once he shows he can handle the upper levels of the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: William Bergolla was the crown jewel of the Phillies’ international signing class in 2022, getting over $2 million to sign. Segura received just $80,000 to sign when the period opened in January, but if early returns are any indication -- he was one of the better pitching prospects in the Dominican Summer League -- he could help make it a bumper crop. The right-hander out of San Pedro de Macorís is all about projection, though he has some new offerings that helped him succeed in his DSL debut. The 6-foot-3 hurler hits 92-95 mph with his fastball, throwing it with good life especially down in the zone, which enabled him to get a good amount of ground-ball outs. It’s easy to dream on him adding strength to that frame, and there should be an increase in velocity as he physically matures. He already has a solid slider with good depth that could eventually develop into a true out pitch. There’s a long developmental road ahead for Segura, but he doesn’t turn 18 until December, so the Phillies can be as patient as needed. If it all comes together -- the added velocity, harnessing of his stuff, adding a third pitch -- he could rise up the rankings as he gains experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners went shopping for hard-throwing senior signs on Day 2 of the 2024 Draft and may have found a couple of potential big league bullpen pieces in Hunter Cranton and Moore. Moore bounced from Danville Community College to Menlo College in the NAIA ranks to Oregon for his final collegiate season at age 24. He brought a ton of velocity to the system and to Single-A Modesto for his pro debut after signing in the seventh round, posting four shutout relief innings in the Nuts’ championship run. Moore is all about power coming from his enormous 6-foot-6 frame. His fastball averaged around 96-97 mph at Oregon, and after seeing him hitting 101 on pull-downs in early pitching camp, the Mariners think he could sit in the 99 mph range out of the bullpen. He can also really spin his firm 82-85 mph sweeper and he has a firm 85-88 mph changeup, though it’s unclear if feel for it will be there long term. That won’t matter if Moore can find a way to limit the walks just a little bit. He does not have a great record of strike-throwing, with a career 4.9 BB/9 rate at Menlo and Oregon combined. He’ll need to be tested quickly at the upper levels given his age, but the physical talents are too impressive to ignore.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays have done some great work on the nondrafted market in recent years and Coleman looks like one of their gems. Coleman had some hype going into his time with LSU, but ran into some injuries along the way and never quite established himself with the Tigers. Something has been unlocked with Toronto, though, and Coleman is suddenly the top lefty among the organization's pure bullpen prospects. Between Single-A and High-A in 2025, Coleman posted a 3.00 ERA with 85 strikeouts over 54 innings. Coleman got stronger as the season went on, too, leaning on a fastball that sits 94-96 mph and can reach a tick higher. That fastball comes from a bit lower of a release point than you typically see and it has some deception to it; when paired with a slider that can at least be a solid pitch in the future, it’s an intriguing package. Coleman pitches with an edge, too, and feels like a perfect fit for a true relief role. That role should also allow him to climb the ladder quicker than as a starter. If Coleman can keep his walk rate close to where it was in his pro debut (3.8 BB/9), that’s a safe enough number to let his strikeout rates shine. Expect to see him remain in one-to-two inning stints, and while others on this list have the advantage of starting, Coleman’s path to the big leagues is shorter and straighter than many others.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reed didn’t get much traction as a swingman over his first two years at West Virginia, but he really opened eyes with his power stuff as the Mountaineers’ closer in 2023. Reed always felt he had the ability to start, even going to the Draft League to do it a few times as the Draft approached; the Pirates agreed, taking the right-hander in the fourth round of that summer's Draft, allowing him to develop in a rotation out of the gate. The early returns were better than expected as he pitched his way from Single-A Bradenton to High-A Greensboro while leading all hurlers in the system with at least 100 innings pitched in ERA (1.99) and BAA (.173). With two fastballs and very real secondary offerings coming from a 6-foot-4 frame, Reed does have a future rotation piece starter kit. His fastball sat around 93-94 mph last year, and touched 97, and it wouldn’t surprise anyone if there was a velocity jump coming. He throws a four- and two-seamer, missing some bats up and getting ground-ball outs down. Both of his secondary offerings -- an 83-84 mph sweeper with high spin and his spin-killing changeup -- miss bats and could be plus pitches in the future. The one thing that could keep Reed from remaining a starter is his command, as his longer arm action has led to high walk rates. He’s ironed out some issues with his delivery, and he did a better job of finding the zone in his six Greensboro starts, perhaps a sign of things to come away from the ABS system. There’s currently no talk of moving to the 'pen, with the Pirates excited to see what he does for an encore.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Salcedo was arguably the revelation of the Tigers organization on the pitching side with a spectacular stateside debut. Signed for $70,000 out of Venezuela in January 2023, he spent two years in the Dominican Summer League, then dominated the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer, racking up more than twice as many strikeouts (53) as hits allowed (22) over 45⅓ innings, including a 10-strikeout gem over five scoreless innings of one-hit ball against the Blue Jays. He jumped to Single-A Lakeland for the stretch run and helped the Flying Tigers win a Florida State League title, not allowing more than one run in six of his seven starts and two hits or fewer in all of them. Salcedo has a good fastball and sinker that average around 95 mph and top out at 97-98 but don’t miss many bats. His secondary pitches were the key to his high strikeout rate, including a mid-to-upper-80s slider with sharp movement and a better than 50 percent whiff rate, plus a split change that plays off of it with even better swing-and-miss. His walk rate was a concern in the FCL as well as in the DSL, but he tempered it upon promotion to Single-A. His body has filled out since turning pro, enabling him to maintain his best stuff deeper into games but could lead to delivery issues if he gets too big. The Tigers need pitching depth in their system to go with their abundance of bats, and Salcedo has a chance to be the next to emerge. He’ll likely return to Lakeland to begin the season but could move to High-A West Michigan if he makes improvements with command while maintaining his high-strikeout arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rossi spent six years in college, bouncing from West Florida to the State JC of Florida (Manatee-Sarasota) to UNC Charlotte. After missing all of 2023 following Tommy John surgery, he came back to reach 97 mph with his fastball and destroy college hitters with his slider in 2024 but went undrafted because he was 25 years old. Signed as a nondrafted free agent for $10,000, he posted a 2.18 ERA, .119 opponent average and 34 percent strikeout rate in his pro debut last season. Rossi's slider tore up hitters at two Class A levels with its combination of mid-80s velocity and huge sweep, producing an elite 52 percent swing-and-miss rate. His fastball works in the mid-90s and maxes out at 98 mph with armside run. He works east and west with his heater and slider, then can drop an upper-80s splitter though the bottom of the zone. A physical 6-foot-3, 230-pounder, Rossi combines a low release height and extension to provide deception. He can't always maintain his delivery and has little history of providing consistent strikes. If he can develop decent control, he certainly has the stuff to find a bullpen role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels may have a reputation of drafting college players who can get pushed to the big leagues in a hurry, but they broke away from that script when Day 3 of the 2023 Draft commenced. They had some bonus pool money left over to sign Wimmer -- a toolsy but raw high school shortstop from South Carolina -- away from his commitment to The Citadel as their 11th-round pick for close to $400,000. He got his feet wet with a handful of games in the Arizona Complex League. It's likely going to require patience for Wimmer to grow into his raw tools. He’s a plus quick-twitch athlete and right-handed hitter who can use the whole field. His swing works and there might be some power to tap into in the future if he can add some strength to his lean frame. An above-average runner, he shows good instincts on the basepaths. While there’s work to be done on his footwork defensively, there’s some confidence he can stick at shortstop in the long run. It’s possible the Angels will move him around the diamond some, but don’t be surprised to see him stick up the middle -- at second or in center field -- if shortstop doesn’t work. He’s a bit like a piece of unmolded clay, one that the Angels can dream on becoming a Rodin.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Robert Calaz was the big get for the Rockies when the 2023 international signing period opened in January of that year. Four months later, the organization might have found a bargain in Dali, who signed for $70,000 in May. It took a while for him to get going, spending two summers in the Dominican Summer League, but he hit .327/.445/.450 there in his second summer, then showed it might not be an aberration by coming stateside in 2025 and hitting his way from the Arizona Complex League up to Single-A Fresno, finishing with a combined .308/.399/.468 line. Dalis gets some high praise from those who have been around the Rockies a while, earning comps to Ezequiel Tovar at a similar age in terms of how he plays the game. The switch-hitter has shown the ability to swing it from both sides of the plate, though he was stronger as a left-handed hitter in 2025, with a hit-over-power profile. He has gap power now with doubles-type pop, but he also isn’t close to being physically mature, so there could be more power to come in the future. Hopefully, that doesn’t come at the expense of his speed and athleticism. He can steal a base and he has the agility to stay up the middle defensively, with an ease of operation defensively that’s fun to watch. He’ll keep seeing time at three infield positions and while he played he’s played mostly on the left side of the infield, some think second base might be his best shot as a long-term home if he turns into a table-setting every day type of player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starting his college career at Southern Mississippi as a two-way player in 2023, Monistere focused on hitting and played six different positions as a sophomore. He became a full-time second baseman in 2025 and won Sun Belt Conference player of the year honors after slashing .323/.410/.623 with a league-best 21 homers. The Astros made him a fourth-round pick because they liked his athleticism and versatility, though he looked less refined than expected on both sides of the ball during his introduction to pro ball. Monistere uses an aggressive right-handed swing to produce high exit velocities, though he needs to tone down his approach. He rolls over on too many fastballs and comes up empty while chasing too many breaking balls and changeups. His solid-to-plus raw power could translate into 20 homers per season if he can become more selective and less pull happy. Monistere features average quickness and solid arm strength that produced fastballs up to 94 mph when he pitched as a freshman. The game sped up on him when he spent most of his pro debut at shortstop and third base, and he began 2026 by mainly playing second base. That's his best position and he projects as an average defender there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s way too soon to know what kind of return the Angels will ultimately get for their investments in the 2023 international market, but the early signs are encouraging. The class, led by shortstop Felix Morrobel, also includes Juan Flores behind the plate and Texido on the mound. The left-hander signed for $250,000 in March and then found himself all over the leaderboard in the Dominican Summer League, finishing in the top 10 in strikeouts (61), WHIP (0.95), ERA (2.31) and strikeouts per nine (10.8) as the Angels' club in the league went 37-18 and made the playoffs. None of Texido’s three pitches currently jump off the page, but he already has an idea of how to use them. The left-hander’s fastball sat around 88-89 mph and touched 92. His 80-82 mph changeup has the chance to be an above-average pitch with some sink and he’ll need to add some power to his 75-78 mph slider, a pitch he also struggled to command in the zone consistently. Other than those issues with his breaking ball, however, Texido did a very nice job in throwing strikes overall. There’s a little funk in his delivery, which helps in the deception department, and he has a projectable frame, giving the potential for him to add strength and some oomph to his fastball-slider combination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted by the Blue Jays out of McNeese State in the 11th round of the 2023 Draft, Rogers’ development has slid under the radar because there are no eye-popping strikeout numbers or 100 mph radar readings. Rogers is a throwback, a starter who already has the ability to eat serious innings by filling up the zone and letting his defense work behind him. This is the type of prospect who coaches and teammates will always appreciate more than some external rankings do. Rogers works quickly, and despite his massive frame at 6-foot-7, he repeats his mechanics well and rarely “loses it” mid-start. Between High-A and Double-A in 2025, Rogers posted a 3.47 ERA over 150 1/3 innings, and while his strikeout rate (6.9 K/9) won’t blow anyone away, his walk rate (2.3 BB/9) was very impressive. Rogers leads with a fastball that can reach up to touch 94-95 mph and typically lives just below that, but he has a great feel for his repertoire and adjusts well throughout games. Prospect lists are stocked with hard-throwing arms who run into health problems or end up in bulk roles, but Rogers is a different profile entirely. This almost feels like a pitching prospect from the 1980s and 90s, one capable of throwing 170-plus innings each season and posting every five or six days. If Rogers can miss more bats, that opens up more conversations about his big league potential, but even with his current traits, he has a path towards being a reliable depth arm from Triple-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gutierrez signed with the Padres for $750,000 out of Venezuela on July 31, 2019 -- the day he turned 16 years old. The timing couldn’t have been tougher since he missed out on a professional debut in 2020 due to the pandemic and repeated the Dominican Summer League in 2021 and 2022. He was still at Single-A Lake Elsinore to begin 2025 but zoomed up all four full-season levels, posting a 3.31 ERA with 115 strikeouts in 125 innings. The 6-foot left-hander showed he could spot his 91-95 mph fastballs extremely well, and he added a little extra zip to touch 97 in his age-21 season. The sinker he showed in his one Triple-A start was in the deadzone, and the life on his four-seamer wasn’t all that much better, so Gutierrez needs to land those on a dime to be effective as he pushes toward San Diego. His low-80s slider shows nice depth, and it’s a pitch that he can glide nicely away from lefties. An upper-80s changeup has similar armside movement to the sinker but more drop; however, it wasn’t quite as effective against righties as it needs to be. No one will accuse the southpaw of overthrowing any time soon, as his delivery looks relatively free and easy albeit maybe a bit rushed in its final movements. He sets up on the extreme first-base side of the rubber, giving that slider the full width of the plate over which to break. Gutierrez may have gone unprotected and unpicked in last year’s Rule 5 Draft, for which he was eligible, but he’s still young at only 22 entering 2026. With the right adjustments, he could be a part of San Diego’s MLB depth soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers spread out their international spending during the January 2023 window, adding Dominican outfielder Yophery Rodriguez ($1.5 million) and a pair of Venezuelan shortstops in Kevin Ereu ($1.4 million) and Di Turi ($1.3 million). Di Turi started the Dominican Summer League strongly, batting .338 over 19 games in June, and even when he faded over his final 13 in August, he was still walked 14 times and struck out only seven. He finished with a .282/.414/.354 line, 12 steals, 38 walks and 32 K’s in 52 games on the international complex circuit, good for a 119 wRC+. The switch-hitter has a smooth and mechanically sound swing that helped him make a healthy amount of contact in his first pro campaign. He also showed a relative unwillingness to expand the zone against wilder DSL arms. That will certainly be tested against arms with much better command, but the Brewers were pleased with the foundation he set with his approach. Power remains a question mark. Di Turi put 47.6 percent of his batted balls on the ground and only picked up 11 extra-base hits in his 52 games, none of which were homers. Standing 5-foot-11, Di Turi doesn’t have burning speed and might be asked to ease up on stolen bases if he doesn’t become more efficient (60 percent success rate). His best defensive weapon is his plus arm. That helped him get the majority of his starts at shortstop, but the Brewers also tried him at second base to keep him up the middle. He could also see time at third down the line based on his cannon, but Di Turi will need more pop to be a viable offensive option at the corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene signed for just $17,500 as a South Alabama senior when the Yankees took him in the eighth round of the 2019 Draft. After missing out on his first full season due to the pandemic, he proved to be a steady performer as a reliever at the High-A, Double-A and Triple-A levels in 2021 and 2022. He spent all of last season with Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, posting a 3.42 ERA, .199 average-against and 96 strikeouts in 68 1/3 innings, but he was still left off the Yankees' 40-man roster when he became Rule 5-eligible due to a roster crunch. The Mets swooped in during the Rule 5 Draft, and in order to keep him, Greene must remain in their Major League bullpen for all of 2023. The 6-foot-1 right-hander pitches out of the stretch at the extreme first-base side of the rubber, and he fires in a low-90s fastball that can be deceptive with its apparent rise and cutting action. Despite the fastball being closer to average velo, that ride can make the heater extremely difficult to pick up, and hitters often hopelessly swung below the pitch at Triple-A. An upper-70s slider kept opposing batters from sitting on the fastball and played well into the Yankees’ pitching philosophy of prioritizing sweep on breaking pitches. An upper-80s changeup kept lefties honest but was a distant third pitch. If hitters can learn not to chase the high heat or the solid breaker, they can earn the occasional free pass from Greene, who walked 11.1 percent of the batters he faced in 2022. That control has been one reason why the righty has stayed in relief in the pros, but his two best pitches make him an MLB-ready bullpen option for the Mets.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most advanced prospect in Miami's 2022 international crop, de la Cruz turned pro for $150,000 out of the Dominican Republic. Making his U.S. debut last summer, he needed just two starts in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League to earn a promotion to Single-A. The only 18-year-old to work double-digit innings in the Florida State League, he held his own with a 4.57 ERA and 42 strikeouts in 43 1/3 innings. While de la Cruz still is refining his entire repertoire, both his fastball and curveball show the potential to become plus pitches once fully developed. His riding fastball parked at 92-95 mph and touched 97 before he tired late in his first full pro season, and he should add more velocity as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. His mid-70s curveball has good shape with plenty of depth and some horizontal action but also would benefit from more power. De la Cruz's changeup has some interesting fade, though it gets too firm in the mid-80s and he needs to use it more often so he can refine it. He's not as physical as Edward Cabrera was as a teenager, but he reminds some club officials of their big league starter with his repertoire and delivery. His control was spotty versus much older competition in the FSL but should be fine as he adds more strength and experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prior to his senior season, Steinmetz wasn’t known that well outside the region of Long Island, New York. The big projectable right-hander opened a lot of eyes, however, by heading the ELEV8 Baseball Academy in southeast Florida and became the first Orthodox Jewish player ever drafted when Arizona selected him in the third round. He signed for a below-slot $500,000 and showed more polish than expected in subsequent workouts. There’s plenty of projectability with Steinmetz and the teenager already shows the potential to develop two plus pitches. The fastball sits in the low 90s now, but it’s believed that number will tick up as he adds muscle to his 6-foot-5 frame. Steinmetz’s best secondary offering is his high-spin-rate curveball and his sinking changeup also shows promise. As a Northeast prep pitcher without a track record against top competition, Steinmetz is understandably raw. He’s struggled at times in finding the strike zone consistently, though scouts like his delivery and arm action enough to think he’ll figure it out with reps and instruction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 65 | Control: 40 | Overall: 40 The Rangers have had more success than any organization with signing high schoolers as nondrafted free agents in recent years. Curtis gave up a commitment to Barry University (Fla.) to turn pro for $125,000 in 2022, working just 6 2/3 innings in his pro debut the following summer because he was too wild. His control was still sporadic last year but he posted a 2.85 ERA with a .194 average-against at Single-A. Much of Curtis’ success stems from his high-spin low-80s changeup that dives and fades under barrels, generating a 56 percent swing-and-miss rate in 2024. He also does a good job of spinning a solid upper-70s curveball and a tight low-80s slider that get chases but landed in the zone only a third of the time last year. His fastball has some carry but misses few bats, sitting in the low 90s and topping out at 96 mph in the early innings but parking at 88-90 by the middle frames. While Curtis is a good athlete, he has yet to figure out how to harness his stuff. He could become a No. 4 starter if he gets stronger and discovers more strikes, though he also has to prove he can do more than trick Single-A hitters with his array of secondary pitches. Texas will continue to be patient with his development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tom Candiotti rode the knuckleball to a 16-year career in the Major Leagues. His son, Clark, utilizes a very different arsenal that took him on an interesting ride as a college player. Candiotti played for five schools in five years between St. Mary’s (2020), Vernon (Junior) College (2021), Grayson County Community College (2022), Wichita State (2023) and finally Arizona (2024). He was a Pac-12 All-Conference selection after posting a 3.39 ERA with 103 strikeouts in 95 2/3 innings with the Wildcats, and that helped push him to Padres with the 135th overall pick in the '24 Draft, where he signed for $80,000. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has the look of a durable starter. He added fastball velocity between his time at Wichita State and Arizona, averaging around 93 mph with the latter while touching 96. The heater can feature good carry, eliciting chase above the zone. Candiotti, however, leaned even more heavily on his 83-85 mph slider, throwing it 45 percent of the time and using it against batters from both sides. It has sharp, short movement, allowing him to wear out the gloveside half of the plate. He mixed in a 78-82 mph curveball for a different breaking look and barely used his mid-80s changeup in ’24. Candiotti did a great job of throwing strikes in each of his last two collegiate seasons, but a significant portion of that was getting batters to expand the zone. That ability will be tested against pro bats. There is a certain temptation to throw Candiotti in the bullpen because of his age -- he'll be 24 entering his first full season -- but given his late college trajectory, he could have a fighting chance to stick in future rotations, too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two seasons at Southeastern Louisiana, Burke transferred to Miami and earned all-Atlantic Coast Conference accolades in 2022 before the White Sox selected him in the 11th round. He missed the first month of last season with a lower back injury, then returned to hit .294/.392/.439 between two Class A levels. He made up for some lost at-bats in the Arizona Fall League and will advance to Double-A to begin 2024. Burke looks to smack line drives to all fields with his quick right-handed swing. He projects to hit in the bottom third of a big league batting order because he has only modest pull power that may not translate into more than 10-12 homers per season and his aggressive approach doesn't yield many walks. He doesn't strike out excessively but can improve his quality of contact. Burke makes the most out of his solid speed on the bases and in the outfield, enhancing his chances of making it as a fourth outfielder. He has spent most of his pro career in center field, exhibiting solid range and playable if fringy arm strength. A two-time all-state linebacker as a Louisiana prepster, he plays baseball with a football mentality and endears himself to club officials and coaches with his intensity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia signed for $500,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of the Orioles’ 2024 international class and he made an impact immediately, producing a .943 OPS with 12 steals and more walks than strikeouts in the Dominican Summer League in one of the organization's best debut performances of the year. That set the stage for the switch-hitting shortstop to come stateside in 2025. Garcia is an athletic infielder with a line-drive swing and a knack for making solid contact, with a varied skill set that can make him intriguing as he matures and adds strength. He’s hit-over-power, but he has an advanced approach for his age and can work deep counts, avoid strikeouts and barrel balls from both sides of the plate. He’s a good runner and his athleticism serves him well on the basepaths. He is an advanced fielder with good instincts, actions and quickness up the middle, and a strong arm that gives him a chance to stay at shortstop long-term. Garcia will be 18 for the entire '25 season and there is a lot of projection here, but if he continues to develop, he has a chance to grow into an up-the-middle regular in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fairly anonymous when he signed with the Yankees for $30,000 out of Venezuela in 2022, Ramirez batted .319 in two seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before attracting attention in his U.S. debut last year. He earned Florida Complex League All-Star accolades after ranking second in the Rookie-level circuit in hitting (.348) and on-base percentage (.447) and fourth in OPS (.960). The Marlins acquired him as part of a three-prospect package for Jazz Chisholm Jr. at the Trade Deadline last July. Ramirez employs a leg kick at the plate and makes consistent contact with a disciplined approach and a compact right-handed stroke. He's learning to turn on pitches but hits a lot of ground balls and may not provide more than 10-12 homers per season. Though he puts the bat on the ball with ease, he makes good swing decisions and draws a healthy amount of walks. Ramirez's solid speed plays better on the bases than in the field, though he's not a prolific basestealer. His average arm and range are best suited for second base, though he spent the majority of his time last year at third base, where he committed nine errors in 36 starts. He also has seen action at left field and shortstop and projects as a utilityman with a sparkplug mentality.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Michigander during his high school days, Steensma headed to Boone, North Carolina, home to Appalachian State, for college ball. After pitching out of the bullpen as the Mountaineers' closer, racking up seven saves as a freshman in 2023, he moved into the rotation as a sophomore, finishing among the Sun Belt Conference top 10 in a host of pitching categories. An elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery in December 2024 kept him off the mound in '25, but a combination of Mariners scouts and their analytics department saw enough potential from his performance the year prior to take him in the ninth round of last July's Draft. Now healthy, he got off to a very good start during his pro debut at Single-A in 2026. A strong 6-foot-4 right-hander, Steensma has a potential four-pitch mix that gives him a chance to start. While his fastball sits 92-93 mph and touches 95, it plays up and misses bats thanks to riding life that comes as a result of the combination of good extension and low release height. His tight mid-80s slider has ticked up since his college days and could be an out pitch in time. He'll mix in an 80 mph curve, and while he does have a potentially serviceable changeup, he wasn't throwing it much at the outset of his pro career. The Mariners are bullish about Steensma because he's still learning how to mix his pitches effectively. He was throwing a ton of strikes out of the gate, with the organization thinking he could have future plus command. They don't want to put unfair expectations on him, but the Mariners have done excellent development work with formerly injured college arms taken later on Day 2 of the Draft, like sixth-rounder-turned-All-Star Bryan Woo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roberts placed himself squarely in the Draft conversation by slashing .270/.442/.476 with 10 homers and more walks (44) than strikeouts (41) over 55 games as a UNC junior outfielder in 2021, and the D-backs selected him in the fifth round that July, announcing him as a catcher, where he had summer league experience. After spending most of his first full season at High-A, the left-handed slugger broke out some with Double-A Amarillo in 2023, slashing .278/.383/.523 with 17 homers over 97 games. The former Tar Heel rarely expands the zone with a strong approach, resulting in a 13.4 percent walk rate last season. He particularly shows strong contact skills against fastballs, thanks to a simple and quick swing, but swing-and-miss issues against softer stuff and right-left splits (.930 OPS vs. .751) will likely keep him from being an average hitter at higher levels. Roberts also took advantage of Amarillo’s friendly confines, hitting 14 of his 17 homers there with a .677 SLG at home, but he has solid raw power and the lift needed to push for 12-15 dingers annually. Roberts rotated through the outfielder corners and catcher at Double-A and during a stint in the Arizona Fall League. His arm strength helps play at those spots, but he’s still a work in progress behind the plate with his bat pushing him faster than his glove can follow. His left-handed stick, power potential and multiple mitts would give him value on a Major League bench should his offensive trends continue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Angelo spent three years at Cal State Bakersfield, finally cracked the Roadrunners’ rotation in 2021 and then transferred to Fresno State for two more years. Playing as a COVID senior in 2023, he was an All-Mountain West Second Team selection with a 4.39 ERA and 72 strikeouts in 80 innings with the Bulldogs but didn’t get drafted. The D-backs signed him as a free agent in July, and a year later, he ranked second in the system with 151 strikeouts while sporting a 3.49 ERA over 121 1/3 innings between Single-A and High-A. A 6-foot-5 right-hander, Angelo gave Arizona some size to dream on despite his advanced age, and he put that to good use early in his career. He averaged just 90.1 mph on his fastball in his final collegiate season but was typically up closer to the 93-94 range at Visalia and Hillsboro. He throws different types too between his four-seamer and sinker. It’s a deep arsenal as well, highlighted by a mid-80s changeup that ran a 51 percent whiff rate in his first taste of the pros. His slider was his next-best option for swing-and-miss, and he’ll also incorporate curveballs and cutters for different shapes. Angelo walked 17 in 25 innings with Visalia before his promotion but showed much closer to average control at the higher level. He can rush his delivery a bit, and given that he’s already entering his age-25 season, he won’t have a super-long leash as a starter. But the ingredients are there, and he has enough offerings to keep hitters constantly on their toes as he heads toward the upper Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds handed out 10 bonuses of six figures or more at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, including two north of $1 million. In terms of early returns, it’s been Confidan, who signed for $200,000 out of the Domincan Republic, who has stood out. He came to the United States to make his professional debut in 2021 and promptly hit .315/.359/.573 to earn Arizona Complex League MVP honors. The left-handed hitting outfielder has the chance to be a very good offensive performer. He has a handsy swing and manipulates the bat well and has a ton of raw power, especially to the pull side. The biggest surprise may have been how much he accessed it right out the gate, with 11 homers in 178 at-bats in 2021. He will need to work on his overall approach as he advances to cut down on his tendency to chase, though there may always be some swing-and-miss to his game. Defensively, Confidan has a strong arm that might be plus in time, one that allowed him to pick up seven outfield assists in the ACL. Improvement on his reads and routes will come with more reps and he could fit the athletic right fielder profile well. Just 19 for all of the 2022 season, he reminds some of fellow Reds prospect Elly De La Cruz as an under-the-radar prospect whose tools translated better, and faster, than expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best prospect in Boston's 2022 international class, Encarnacion signed for $1.1 million out of the Dominican Republic. He debuted as a 17-year-old in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, hitting .255/.355/.369 and leading his club with three homers in 41 games. He'll need plenty of time to develop but features some of the best power potential in the system. With a quick right-handed swing and a projectable 6-foot-2 frame, Encarnacion could have at least plus raw power once he matures physically. He can lift pitches without selling out for home runs, and his pop plays to all fields. He also shows promising feel for hitting and managing the strike zone.
