Presently a fringy-to-average runner, Encarnacion could slow a bit as he adds muscle. Reduced quickness could push him from shortstop, where he spent most of his pro debut, to third base, where he also got some playing time. His quick hands and strong arm would be well suited to the hot corner, and he should be able to fit the offensive profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of the former All-Star shortstop of the same name, Ramirez was born in New Jersey but grew up in the Dominican Republic. He signed with the Guardians for $800,000 in 2022 and is one of the more physical middle-infield prospects in the system. He made his U.S. debut last summer in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, where he ranked second in walks (50) and seventh in on-base percentage (.453). He was off to a slow run with Single-A Lynchburg to begin his age-18 season when Cleveland dealt him and two other youngsters to Washington for Lane Thomas. At least 15 pounds heavier than his listed 159, Ramirez has the developing strength and the bat speed to produce 15-20 homers per season. He already displays the aptitude for turning on pitches and launching them in the air. He'll need to make more consistent contact after logging a 28 percent strikeout rate in the ACL, but he has the sound left-handed stroke and bat-to-ball skills to do so once he refines his approach. Like many sons of former big leaguers, Ramirez has a high baseball IQ. He's an average runner who gets the most out of his speed on the bases. He exhibits quick hands and solid arm strength at shortstop, though he may slow a bit as he matures physically and wind up at second or third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scull’s father, Antonio, won three Olympic medals playing as a first baseman for Cuba. Anthony started his own path in baseball by signing with the Angels for $235,000 in September 2021. It took a while for the outfielder to show the Angels anything, getting into just 10 games in the Dominican Summer League after signing, then missing most of the 2022 season with a shoulder injury sustained when diving for a ball in the outfield. He did play a full slate of Arizona Complex League games in 2023, showing glimpses of some playable tools. Scull has a strong and athletic frame with the ability to do some damage from the left side of the plate. He makes a lot of hard contact, registering some of the better exit velocities in the lower levels of the Angels' system. He doesn’t strike out a ton, but he can be a bit too aggressive at the plate. It’s more of a line-drive swing right now, but there’s raw power to tap into with the potential to hit around 15 homers annually once he matures physically and with his approach. An above-average runner, Scull can play all three outfield spots with an average arm. He saw more time in center field than anywhere else in 2023 and he does have a chance to stay there should he develop into a regular at one position. A more likely outcome is for him to be a solid fourth outfielder type who moves around and provides a left-handed bat off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Foster rated as the second-best shortstop in the 2020 Texas high school class behind Masyn Winn (who reached the Majors in 2023), but he went unselected in the shortened five-round Draft and attended Auburn. He barely played as a freshman and started at second base as a sophomore, then boosted his stock considerably last spring by improving his approach and returning to shortstop. He scuffled offensively and defensively after turning pro as a third-round selection, batting .230 with a 32 percent strikeout rate in Single-A. After Foster took off at Auburn by focusing on making consistent contact to all fields rather than trying to launch out of the park, he got too aggressive and his swing got too uphill in his first taste of pro ball. He'll need to settle back down to reach his ceiling of a .260 hitter with 15-20 homers per season and a decent amount of walks. A switch-hitter, he did damage from both sides of the plate in college but went just 1-for-24 with 12 strikeouts against southpaws in his debut. Foster's instincts allow him to play quicker than his average speed on the bases and in the middle infield, though he's not much of a threat to steal. While he's a sure-handed defender with a strong arm, his average range at shortstop may not be enough to keep him there. He's a solid defender at second base and also could handle third base if he winds up in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals’ 2024 international class was headlined by shortstop Yandel Ricardo, ranked No. 17 on MLB Pipeline’s international prospects list, and the club handed Ugarte a $1,312,500 bonus to sign out of the Dominican Republic just two months before he turned 17. Ugarte jumped onto the radar later that year in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .299 with an .818 OPS and nearly as many walks (30) as strikeouts (36) in 46 games. He then participated in the Royals’ instructional league that fall. Ugarte has an efficient bat path and line-drive swing, with some quickness to the hands as he makes contact. He starts in an athletic stance with his front foot slightly back, using a toe tap to get into a firing position. He’s already grown into a sturdy frame, but there might be another level he can get to with his power. While DSL pitchers can get wild, Ugarte has already shown a good awareness for the strike zone, although he struggled with breaking balls like many young hitters do. Ugarte is strong and looks more like a third baseman or even a corner outfielder, but the Royals will develop him as an infielder. He has above-average arm strength and good instincts, and he should be a solid defender wherever he lands. Ugarte doesn’t turn 18 until March, after which he’ll make his stateside debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2025. He’s young and his development will take time, but the potential for an everyday third baseman is certainly there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz hails from La Vega, Dominican Republic, the country’s fourth-largest city and hometown of Major Leaguers Jonathan Villar and Ronald Guzmán. The outfielder was the biggest prospect from there in the 2025 international class and ranked No. 27 in MLB Pipeline’s list heading into the January signing period. He was Arizona’s biggest addition -- and only seven-figure signing -- with a $1.1 million bonus. The right-handed slugger brings an uphill swing from a stance that features an inward-facing front foot. He gets into his power through his back leg, generating good bat speed ahead of the point of contact, and some evaluators said he reminded them of Marcell Ozuna as a player who uses his pop as his carrying tool. There’s a solid approach here too, although the plane of the swing might be challenged against pro pitching. With decent wheels, De La Cruz could cover center field, but many expect he’ll be pushed to a corner by rangier players. The D-backs happen to have plenty of those already in the system between Slade Caldwell and Druw Jones, among others. He could play closer to average defensively once he moves, and his wheels should be good enough to make him a potential basestealing threat. De La Cruz has a long way to go, but the pieces are there for him to be a middle-of-the-order bat who also adds value in other areas.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Munoz joined the Mariners during the 2019-20 international signing period for $195,000, then was among the many impacted by COVID interrupting the following season, which prevented him from pitching competitively until an assignment to the Dominican Summer League, where he spent 2021-22. The first year was inconsistent, but he rebounded in the second and made the midseason All-Star team. A projectable righty with room to keep adding strength, Munoz is another arm that Seattle’s player development staff has been banging the drum on. He’s up to the mid-90s on his fastball with decent arm-side run and above-average hop. He’s also shown flashes of a plus slider that generated a ton of whiffs and strikeouts with. It’ll probably need more depth as he progresses, but, so far, he commands it better than the heater. Now it’s a matter of if he can develop a third pitch and remain a starter, because there were a lot of positive signs with his strike throwing. It’s a changeup right now, but he doesn’t throw it often because of how good the other two have been. If he does go down a relief road, his path to the Majors could be accelerated.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Overshadowed in a deep 2022 Wisconsin high school class headlined by future first-rounder Gavin Kilen, Fox was also an all-state quarterback on a championship football team. Recruited by Notre Dame primarily as a shortstop, he didn't play much as a freshman before becoming a full-time starting pitcher the next two seasons. After he led the Atlantic Coast Conference in opponent average (.187) last spring, New York signed him for an over-slot $411,100 in the sixth round. As a Fighting Irish junior, Fox operated at 91-94 and topped out at 96 with bat-missing carry and armside run on his fastball. His best offering is a tight low-80s slider that yields a lot of called strikes and in-zone misses. He also employs a mid-80s changeup with sink and fade and an upper-70s curveball that both need more refinement. The younger brother of Dodgers lefty pitching prospect Luke Fox, he's more athletic than most pitchers and has a long history of throwing strikes. There's room to add more strength to his 6-foot-3 frame and the Yankees are known for their ability to help pitchers upgrade their stuff. He already has pushed his fastball to 98 mph during offseason workouts and could have the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson spent his first three years of collegiate ball with Division III North Carolina Wesleyan and transferred to UNC Greensboro for the 2024 season. He spent two additional years with the Spartans and closed out his time there with a 3.79 ERA and 87 strikeouts in 61 2/3 innings as a reliever. The Blue Jays took him in the eighth round as a fifth-year senior sign, and his $5,000 bonus was the lowest in Toronto's 2025 class. Thompson popped nicely at Single-A Dunedin with one run allowed and 15 K's in 13 2/3 innings after the Draft, and he has joined the High-A Vancouver staff in his first full season, showing enough stuff to get his first extended starting look since 2023. The 6-foot right-hander has already taken nice steps forward in his professional development under the Blue Jays' guidance. His fastball velocity is up a bit in his first full season, sitting 93-95 mph, and he can staple the four-seamer to the top of the zone from a lower-than-average release height, making it tough for High-A hitters to pick up. Thompson also works with a promising upper-80s slider with harder action, and he's folded in a sweepier breaker in '26 too (one he calls a curveball but is likely closer to a sweeper). He's struggled to land his upper-80s changeup in the zone. It might be more of a command-over-control profile for Thompson moving forward. He can place the ball in the right spot to miss bats consistently, but if batters can learn to lay off the fastballs up and the sliders down, Thompson could find more trouble the higher he climbs. As it sits early in '26, he's been a K-BB% standout with a possible back-end starter profile and another potential win for the improved Toronto pitching department.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed a then 17-year-old Aquino for only $16,000 out of the Dominican Republic on the first day of the 2021 international period and have seen him steadily climb the ranks one level a year since. After stints on the Dominican and Arizona Complex circuits, the right-hander posted a 2.75 ERA and 1.26 WHIP with 86 strikeouts over 88 1/3 frames for Single-A Carolina this summer. That inning output more than doubled his total from 2021 and '22 combined (78 1/3), so Milwaukee officials found it particularly promising that Aquino was still growing into himself toward the end of his age-20 campaign. Aquino shows largely average fastball velocity around 92-94 mph but can crank it up as high as 96 at times. His low-80s slider is his best pitch with impressive two-plane movement that can drive his whiff rate. Despite averaging less than a K per inning, his 14.5 swinging-strike percentage was ninth-best among 29 Carolina Leaguers with at least 80 innings in 2023. The vertical drop, in particular, can make the breaker look closer to a curveball at times, but it’s still effective. Aquino’s mid-80s changeup remains behind the other two offerings, and without a quality third pitch, lefties batted .288 with a .381 OBP off the hurler in 2023. The 6-foot righty found the zone with better regularity as the season wore on, walking only five batters in his final six outings (27 IP). More disciplined upper-level hitters could hold off chasing the diving sliders out of the zone, pushing that walk rate back up in years to come, but the improvements at least help Aquino’s odds of starting for now. Even so, his best chance of being an impact Major Leaguer might be as a two-pitch reliever who leans into his best tools in shorter appearances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heuer had some of the best physicality and projectable fastball velocity in the 2023 Draft, but he turned down the Guardians as a 16th-rounder to attend Texas Tech. He served as the Red Raiders' No. 1 starter and pushed his fastball to 98 mph last spring, but he also logged a 6.28 ERA as a Draft-eligible sophomore. That didn't deter the Yankees, who signed him for an over-slot $400,000 in the eighth round. Heuer operates at 93-95 mph with cut and carry on his fastball, which is effective up in the zone but gets pounded when he doesn't command it well. His mid-80s slider with sweeping action can be a solid offering when it's on, though he has trouble landing it for strikes and it sometimes flattens over the heart of the plate. His mid-80s changeup with fade and depth was his most effective offering as a sophomore, though he didn't use it much. Scouts don't love Heuer's delivery, which features a short arm action, high release point and some crossfire. He presently has fringy control and below-average command, which may make him more of a reliever than a starter in the long run. If he doesn't make it in baseball, he has his own livestock business with his brother and raised ewes that won grand champion titles at the 2020 and 2022 Georgia National Fairs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Had things gone differently, Barr might now be a part of the University of Tennessee rotation. But the top junior college player in the 2025 Draft class threw well enough at Niagara County Community College, now known as SUNY Niagara, to catch the attention of the Twins. They went over slot in the fifth round to sign the right-hander for $762,500, making him just the second Thunderwolves player to go in the top five rounds, joining 2023 Brewers fifth-round pick Ryan Birchard. The 20-year-old Barr is a 6-foot-6 poster child for projection with some good now stuff. He can run his fastball up to 97 mph and it features very good life up in the zone. He has a pair of distinct breaking pitches with his slider and curve, and both missed a lot of bats en route to him dominating the NJCAA DIII level. His breaking stuff registers elite-level spin rates and his heater plays up because of spin on that as well. Barr has a loose, easy and athletic delivery, so there’s belief that he can improve what’s been spotty command and control. He’s on the raw side and as good as he is at spinning the ball, he hasn’t always had a feel for consistent grips. There’s a lot of upside here, given that he has plenty of room to fill out both his frame and his repertoire.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Finding big lefties with good stuff isn't always so easy, so Eaton got plenty of attention during his time at George Mason University. He worked out of the Patriots' rotation for two years, missing bats but with poor command. The Rockies thought he was worth a flier with their sixth-round pick in the 2024 Draft, and after sending him out that summer as a reliever for a brief pro debut, there was a lot of internal talk about putting him in the bullpen. That thinking has been shelved, however, after Eaton made 27 starts and amassed 140 innings while reaching Double-A in his first full season of pro ball, leading the organization in strikeouts, K/9 and strikeout percentage. Eaton is now showing an ability to throw three pitches for strikes and that, along with showing acumen for finishing hitters, gives him a chance to start. His fastball sits around 93 mph and he can reach back for 95-96. He'll carry his velocity deep into starts, and the pitch has occasional cut or tail to it. His mid-80s slider is his best pitch, eliciting a miss rate north of 40 percent last year. He'll manipulate its shape, sometimes throwing it with sweep, sometimes with the tilt and depth of a more traditional slider. A big reason for his success thus far has been his conviction in throwing his low-80s changeup more. The big left-hander struggled with the strike zone throughout his college career, a big reason why the Rockies weren't the only ones thinking he belonged in a bullpen. It's not pinpoint command, but he's around the zone enough where the organization thinks he might have the ability to stick in a rotation for a long time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mullins ranked among the best high school left-handers in the 2019 Draft but had elbow problems that spring that persisted through his three seasons at Auburn, where he worked just 53 1/3 innings before having Tommy John surgery in 2022. A 12th-round pick that July, he posted some of the best numbers (2.21 ERA, .177 opponent average, 30 percent strikeout rate) in the Red Sox system last year despite missing three weeks with shoulder fatigue in May. Boston gambled by not adding him to its 40-man roster in November and was glad that he slipped through the Rule 5 Draft without getting taken. Mullins has one of the better bat-missing fastballs among Red Sox farmhands, thanks to tremendous carry that helps it play significantly better than its 91-95 mph velocity. While his low-80s slider can feature big sweep and grade as a plus pitch at its best, it was more of an average offering last year. His sinking low-80s changeup is similarly effective, and he also has begun working on a cutter with similar velocity. There's a lot going on in Mullins' delivery, which features a big leg kick, a twist that hides the ball behind him and a low release point. All of that provides deception but hampers his ability to find the zone, and he never has demonstrated better than fringy control or command. He could be a No. 4 starter if his secondary pitches and strikes improve, and he may be of more immediate big league help as a multi-inning lefty out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally recruited as a catcher by Boise State, Buxton moved to the mound with the Broncos, redshirted in 2019 and pitched in just four games during the shortened 2020 season. Boise State dropped baseball afterward, so he transferred to Lipscomb, where he led the Atlantic Sun Conference with seven wins in 2022 before getting drafted in the 15th round that July. He reached Double-A for one start at the end of his first full pro season and soaked up more experience in the Arizona Fall League afterward. Buxton relies heavily on his fastball, a power sinker that operates at 93-95 mph, reaches 97 and creates a ton of groundball contact -- his 2.06 groundout/airout ratio would have ranked fourth in the Minors last year if he had enough innings to qualify. He can flash a solid low-80s slider with nice sweep at times but he struggles to land it in the zone. He has made some strides with an 82-85 mph changeup with similar sink to his heater, and it could become an average offering if he uses it more often. To remain a starter, Buxton will need to throw more strikes. His control improved a bit during his six weeks in High-A last summer but remains fringy at best. He could wind up fitting toward the back of a big league rotation or wind up as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Almost all of Boston's promising catchers are congregated at the lower levels of their system, and Rodriguez is the best of the bunch. Signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela in 2023, he was advanced enough to defensively to get a taste of Single-A the following year at age 18. After adding strength and bat speed before last season, he showed more power and finished with three homers in 22 games in Single-A during the final month. A right-handed hitter with good bat-to-ball skills, Rodriguez will be more effective at the plate as he becomes more selective. He doesn't strike out much but chases more pitches than he should, lowering his quality of contact. He not only added muscle but also improved his ability to drive balls in the air, giving him 12-15 homer potential. Rodriguez is stocky but has some sneaky athleticism, moving well enough on the bases and showing agility behind the plate. His receiving needs more consistency but he blocks and frames well to project as a solid defender. He has at least as much arm strength to match and erased 35 percent of basestealers in his first three pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers appreciated Lopez's defensive ability as a catcher and signed him for $347,500 out of Venezuela in 2022. He made his U.S. debut last summer and homered three times in four games at the end of June but played just once more before getting shut down with a sore arm. He slashed .289/.396/.644 in 13 games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. A no-doubt catcher, Lopez looks natural and more advanced than most teenagers behind the plate. He moves well, receives and blocks well and threw out 39 percent of basestealers in his first two seasons thanks to plus arm strength and impressive accuracy. He's intelligent, already exhibits good feel for calling pitches and can communicate with hurlers in either English or Spanish. There's nothing subtle about Lopez's left-handed stroke and approach, which are geared to launch balls to his pull side. His strength and exit velocities portend 15-20 homer power, with strikeouts a product of his swinging for the fences. He does exhibit some patience at the plate and could provide enough offense to go with his quality defense and become a starting catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates handed out a pair of seven-figure bonuses to hitters Bralyn Brazoban and Adbiel Feliz at the start of the 2024 international signing period, but a couple of prospects a bit further down the list have come to the forefront a bit more. One is Edward Florentino, now a Top 100 prospect, and the other is Navarro, an electric left-hander who got $270,00 to sign, the third-highest bonus given to a lefty in the class. In both his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2024 and in his first trip to the United States in '25 (where he reached full-season ball), he showed that he is very tough to hit, if he can find the plate. There is no doubt that Navarro has the stuff to dominate hitters, with a 15.8 K/9 rate and .120 batting average against over 56 total innings heading into the 2026 season. Thus far, it’s been all about the lefty’s fastball-slider combination. He’ll throw his heater in the 95-100 mph range, and the four-seamer elicited a 47 percent miss rate. His mid-80s slider has been even nastier, with a 50 percent miss rate. He does have a seldom-used changeup that he didn’t throw last year, but the plan is to be intentional to up his usage on the pitch this season. As unhittable as Navarro is, his inability to command his stuff makes it hard to project what he might be. He only threw his fastball for strikes 54 percent of the time last year and his slider came in under the 50 percent mark. If the walks start to trend down, he could start to move. He’s almost certainly a reliever long-term, but the Pirates will keep him on a starting routine so the 19-year-old can work on harnessing all three of his pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays selected Jennings in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft out of Louisiana Tech, and while it’s taken some patience, he's developed into one of the most interesting arms in the upper levels of Toronto’s system. It all came together for a healthy Jennings in 2024, when he opened the season at High-A Vancouver and eventually slid into a bullpen role with Double-A New Hampshire, posting a combined 1.93 ERA with 68 strikeouts over 60 2/3 innings. He followed that up with an excellent showing in the Arizona Fall League (10 IP, 0 ER, 14 K). Jennings leads with a fastball that sits 95-96 mph, reaching up to touch 98, and while his mid-80s slider projects as a legitimate MLB pitch, the depth of his arsenal (with an added curveball and changeup) is what continues to tempt the Blue Jays to keep him stretched out. Jennings could help the MLB bullpen in the short term, but if he stays in the rotation and reaches 100 innings in 2025, that could give the Blue Jays some attractive depth going forward. Team need will dictate this to a certain extent, but Jennings has developed from a stuff-first pitcher into one with a better feel for his own game. Jennings turns 26 in June, so there’s no need to slow play anything development-wise. Regardless of how he gets there, he is a good bet to be a big leaguer and is getting close to being a success story for the player development staff. Jennings is a name that comes up often around the organization as a prospect who deserves some more shine.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies had spent $6.1 million of their close to $6.7 million international bonus pool as the 2026 season opened, but they knew they wanted to land Park, a projectable 17-year-old right-hander from South Korea, to their organization. So they traded Griff McGarry to the Dodgers and Andrew Baker to the Rockies for a total of $750,000. That gave them enough room to sign Park for just over $1.2 million in May and keep him from being one of the top pitchers in the KBO Draft. Park wanted to pursue a career in the United States rather than head to the top league in Korea, and now he'll get his chance. He's still growing and now stands at 6-foot-3 and 195 pounds with as many as five pitches in his arsenal. Throwing from a three-quarter slot, he can get up to 94 mph with his fastball, generally sitting in the 91-93 range, with late ride at the top of the zone. He can also run and sink it occasionally against right-handed hitters. He has feel to spin two distinct breaking pitches in his curve and slider, the latter registering 2,800 rpm spin rates. He has a changeup and splitter for offspeed options to kill spin -- using the fading change more frequently -- against hitters on both sides of the plate. The Phillies really like Park's ease of operation on the mound, showing an ability to repeat his delivery. He's athletic, with a feel to pitch and an ability to execute that belies his years. That gives him a very good chance to start long-term, and given how much strength he can add to his frame, there's excitement about his ultimate ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Olson earned second-team all-Big Ten Conference honors and an invitation to try out for the U.S. national team as a Nebraska sophomore in 2022. He boosted his Draft stock with a strong performance against Michigan in front of a crowd of scouts last April and went in the fourth round, where he signed for a well below-slot $460,000. He made just one brief appearance after turning pro. A finesse left-hander, Olson has his most success when he's in command of his breaking pitches. His mid-70s curveball has a lot of downer break but lacks power and rarely lands in the zone, while his low-80s slider is more reliable in terms of strikes and chases. His fringy low-90s fastball peaks at 95 mph and doesn't miss many bats, and his mid-80s changeup has depth but gets too firm. Olson features a high-three-quarters arm slot and provides consistent strikes with all of his pitches except for his curve. He's physically maxed out at 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, so he's unlikely to add significant velocity. He has a decent floor as an end-of-the-rotation starter with little margin for error with his stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez has built a reputation for outstanding bat-to-ball skills ever since his high school days in Georgia. He brought them with him to Georgia Tech, where he hit .332 and had a .932 OPS the spring after finishing second in the Cape Cod League with a .331 average. The skillset intrigued the Pirates enough for them to take him in the fifth round of the 2022 Draft and he continued to do his thing, hitting .325 during his pro debut in Bradenton. He quickly made his way from Bradenton to High-A Greensboro while he continued to build on his hit-over-power profile. The left-handed-hitting outfielder has a fairly high floor because of his knack for contact and lack of strikeouts, especially when combined with his plate discipline and willingness to draw walks. What’s lacking thus far has been impact; his exit velocities have been a little light and he’ll need to find a way to add more physicality and drive the ball more without sacrificing his contact skills. Gonzalez is a better baserunner than his average speed would indicate, and those instincts make him a thread on the basepaths. The lack of speed makes it seem unlikely that he can stick in center field, and he’s seen time in all three outfield spots. If he can’t play center, the offensive profile without more extra-base thump is a little tougher, but his feel for hitting gives the chance to perhaps be a fourth or fifth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of La Romana, Dominican Republic, in 2017, Nunez put up underwhelming numbers in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in 2019, but there was already some early intrigue with his power potential heading into the lost 2020 season. Nunez grew into some of that in 2021, hitting six home runs with an .848 OPS between the Florida Complex League and Single-A, then his breakout finally came in 2022. Last summer, Nunez climbed from Single-A to High-A, hitting a combined 19 home runs with a .304 average and .824 OPS. He carried this into a successful Dominican Winter League stint, showing some of the pop that the Blue Jays have long dreamed on. At 6-foot-3 with a big frame, Nunez is limited to first base, where he’s just an OK defender. He needs to improve his chase rate at the plate and work more walks, but his exit velocities are among the best in the organization. Nunez will be challenged by more advanced pitching, especially as older arms use more polished breaking balls against him, but there’s no denying his pop from the right side. Much like Spencer Horwitz or any other prospect in the organization likely to stick at first base, he’ll need to hit his way up the ladder. The Blue Jays believe there’s far more potential in there physically, though, making Nunez a name many are watching for another potential breakout if he can clean up his plate approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a long winding path for Mejia, who started his college career by redshirting at Arizona in 2019, then transferred to Pima Community College in 2020, but made just five starts there because of the pandemic. The right-hander went to New Mexico State after that, mostly relieving in 2021 then stepping into the rotation in 2022. He signed for $100,000 as an 11th-round pick that summer, spent all year with High-A Rome in 2023 and then had another solid, and durable, season with Double-A Mississippi in 2024. Mejia’s feel for pitching and the ability to mix his offerings to keep hitters off-balance stands out more than any of his pure stuff. His fastball averaged around 92 mph last year and maxed out at 94 mph. It doesn’t feature a ton of life, but he commands the pitch consistently. His low-80s slider is his go-to pitch, and he threw it almost as much as his heater in 2024, missing bats at a 42-percent clip. His 83-84 mph changeup is a decent third offering and he’s been working on a splitter as well. The 6-foot-3 Mejia does a nice job of repeating his delivery and has a history of throwing strikes, especially in 2022 with the Aggies and during his first pro season. His walk rate did jump a bit in 2024, but he’s posted consistently, topping 120 innings in each of his two full seasons. His ceiling is probably as a No. 5 type starter because of the lack of wow stuff, but he’s close to showing if it can work in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis never could claim a regular turn in Oklahoma State's rotation, battling injuries and his control and command while logging a 5.61 ERA in three seasons. As a junior, he missed fall practice after breaking his collarbone in a fishing accident and lost a month last spring to shoulder issues. But he was still a 6-foot-9 right-hander with power stuff, so the White Sox selected him in the fifth round last July and signed him for an over-slot $587,500. Davis can work at 94-97 mph and touch 100 with his fastball, which features more downhill plane than armside run, so it can get hit when he doesn't command it. His tight upper-80s slider climbs as high as 92 mph, and he can turn it into a harder cutter. His mid-80s changeup lacks consistency but will flash some intriguing fade and tumble. With room to add more strength to his huge frame, Davis could add even more velocity. He still has starter upside, but to get there he'll have to prove he can stay healthy and keep his long limbs in sync well enough to put his pitches where he wants them. If he does head to the bullpen, he has the fastball and slider to fill a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Foley worked as a freshman reliever for Indiana and got his collegiate career off to a solid start with 42 strikeouts in 29 innings. After a quick spin in the Appalachian League, he moved to the Hoosiers rotation for 2024 and got off to a strong start with four scoreless starts in his first eight only to suffer a back problem in his ninth. He missed two weeks and didn’t show the same control in his return, eventually finishing with a 4.71 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 82 strikeouts and 49 walks in 63 frames. The D-backs selected him in the fifth round as a Draft-eligible sophomore and went well above slot to sign him for $1 million. Foley touched 99 and showed a 93-95 mph fastball in both of his roles at Indiana, and the fact that his velocity held despite the back issues was promising. The heater plays well with good induced vertical break out of his over-the-top delivery, and batters from both sides struggle with it up in the zone. He plays off it nicely with a low-80s changeup that tumbles away arm side with so much separation it can look like it’s in slo-mo compared to the fastball. His short mid-80s slider was reserved for right-handers and was less effective. Standing 6-foot-5, Foley is a former all-state tight end in Indiana and brings a physical presence to the mound, but his command and control woes after the back issue heightened the concern that he’s still a reliever long term. Eliciting more chase outside the zone would help alleviate some of that as he gets going in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins were very active at the start of the 2023 international signing period, inking three members of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list. That trio was led by Castro, the Cuban outfielder, who was No. 11 in the rankings. After training with Jaime Ramos in the Dominican Republic, Castro signed with the Twins for $2.4 million. Castro stands out because of his raw tools, projectable frame and left-handed swing. He has a good knack for contact and has shown off a solid approach at the plate at times with a smooth stroke. From time to time, he will get overly aggressive, which is common for a hitter his age. He has the kind of body that should be able to add plenty of strength and some project above-average power when all is said and done. He already displays excellent raw pop in batting practice. Reminding some in the organization of outfield prospect Yasser Mercedes, Castro has the opportunity to stick in center field, where he has good instincts. There is a chance he’ll slow down more as he physically matures and he could slide over to be a run-producing athletic right fielder with a solid arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After putting himself on the Draft radar with three solid years at South Florida, Boser transferred to the University of Florida and boosted his stock as a senior with an impressive season. Entering the 2025 MLB Draft on MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 list, Boser landed with the A’s as an 11th-round pick. Ahead of his first full season as a pro, he got his feet wet with 32 games at Single-A Stockton. Boser has an intriguing profile as a hitter. He’s got some power to all fields and showed he can do some damage with the bat in college with good bat speed and balance at the plate. There’s also a bit of swing-and-miss to his game, which he’ll have to improve to tap into that power as a pro. Boser fits the mold of a versatile utility player who can provide strong defense at multiple positions that the A’s traditionally value highly, similar to past prospects such as Jeremy Eierman and Max Schueman. He has a good, accurate arm that should allow him to get plenty of reps at shortstop, third base and second base. He also worked to improve his athleticism in college, and that shows through on the bases as a decent runner. There is a solid floor here as a productive super-utility type, and the A’s liked what they saw from him at first glance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While big-money international signings are usually wrapped in January, De La Cruz didn’t officially join the Nationals organization until April last year. All the same, the Dominican Republic native’s $500,000 bonus was the third-highest for a new Nationals prospect in the 2025 signing cycle. He backed that up quickly in the Dominican Summer League, where he hit .294/.448/.450 with two homers, 15 steals, 30 walks and only 17 strikeouts over 39 games. A left-handed hitter, De La Cruz certainly put up a performance that would jump off any page at any level. His 1.76 BB/K ratio was 13th-best among 363 hitters with at least 140 plate appearances in the DSL last year. However, evaluators believe some of that success came from an all-too passive approach at the plate. In a league with young, wild arms like the DSL, oftentimes the best decision is not to swing. That can be promising discipline. It can also be worrisome if it’s a trend that carries over to leagues with arms that boast much better control. De La Cruz could also get to at least average power if he adds strength to his 6-foot frame in his move stateside. An average runner, De La Cruz got the vast majority of his starts in center field in the DSL, as one might expect for the bigger-money signing on the grass, but he also saw time in both corners. He seems likely to slide over to left or right more permanently higher up the Nats’ chain. De La Cruz has certainly put himself on the map entering year two, and how he answers the passivity question will determine his place in Washington’s growing outfield depth chart.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly was a two-sport standout who didn't stop playing football until his senior year of high school. He was on scouts' radars in southern California but headed to pitch at UC Irvine. Although Injuries interrupted his progress over his two first years with the Anteaters, a chance to move into their rotation in March of his junior year allowed him to take off. He landed in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft, and while he didn't pitch officially after signing, he got in some good work during instructs. An athletic 6-foot-5 right-hander, Kelly entered pro ball with three pitches and might now have four at his disposal. The Rockies are hoping there might be another tier of velocity to reach with his fastball, which currently sits in the 91-94 mph range, occasionally touching 96. It has some good metrics with some ride and finish to the pitch. But Kelly's really all about the spin. His upper-70s curve has 11-to-5 shape and regularly tops 3,000 rpm, and he can miss bats with his low-80s changeup as well. During instructs, he found a slider grip that works for him, giving him a fourth pitch that could be Major League average. Kelly started throwing better quality strikes when he became a starter during his junior year, and the hope is that trend continues. He has the pitch mix to start and will be given the opportunity to stick in a rotation if he can hold the zone consistently throughout his outings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies have long sought potential impact hitters on the international market, with an eye on up-the-middle-type players. Ezequiel Tovar is a recent success story, while others have reached the big leagues -- like Adael Amador -- without establishing themselves yet. They're hoping De Los Santos can rise through the ranks as well after they signed him for $1 million at the start of the 2026 international signing period in January. One of the younger players in the class, De Los Santos doesn't turn 17 until right before the Dominican Summer League season starts. He's already started adding some strength to his projectable and lean 6-foot-1 frame, which should help his overall offensive profile. He has clean mechanics in the box, showing he can be on time with his smooth left-handed swing. He uses a slight front-foot toe tap for timing, and there's some ability to drive the ball starting to surface. The hope is that De Los Santos, with a good first step and improving arm strength, will be able to stick at shortstop. Some scouts feel he doesn't always have the cleanest slot and might eventually need to move to third as a result, though that's obviously not something the Rockies have to worry about just yet.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hainline spent two seasons at Washington State before transferring to Oregon State, where he formed a double-play combination with No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana in 2024. A below-slot seventh-rounder that July, he played at all four levels of the Dodgers system in 2025, counting the Double-A Texas League playoffs. He earned All-Star honors in the High-A California League and played well enough during an emergency Triple-A assignment in June that the Oklahoma City coaching staff wanted to keep him. A right-handed hitter, Hainline has a good eye at the plate but swings and misses at strikes more than he should, especially against non-fastballs. His sneaky raw power and ability to turn on pitches could translate into 15 or more homers per season, though he produces more groundballs than are desirable. He hits the ball consistently hard but needs to improve his quantity and quality of contact. Hainline has average speed and good instincts on the bases, and he swiped 31 bases in 39 attempts (79 percent) last year. He played shortstop, second base and third base and his glovework earned differing reviews from inside and outside the organization. The Dodgers see him as a solid defender with arm strength to match, while other scouts grade him as more average in both regards.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: High school catching is a tough demographic, with perhaps as much risk as prep pitching. The Braves weren’t afraid to roll the dice after seeing Montgomery excel on the summer showcase circuit, at events like MLB’s PDP League and the Area Code Games, along with the Draft Combine. They took Montgomery in the fifth round but went way over slot to sign the California high schooler away from his Arizona State commitment, giving him third-round money to begin his pro career. The 6-foot-4 Montgomery’s standout offensive tool is his raw power from the right side of the plate. He showed he can get to it against good pitching at showcase events, using a small leg kick for timing. There is some length in his swing and he opens up prematurely at times, leading to some questions about his overall feel to hit, though there was some confidence from scouts that he would make enough contact to get to that pop as a pro. Given his size, it’s unclear if Montgomery will be able to catch. He has at least an above-average arm that plays, and he’s not a terrible receiver, but his lack of agility could have the Braves looking at first base or maybe a corner outfield spot in the future, which would put more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz slugged .771 with 34 homers in his two years at Walters State CC in Tennessee and showed out nicely in separate stints in the Appalachian (2023) and MLB Draft Leagues (2024) to establish himself on the Draft radar. The Cardinals took him in the 16th round and dipped a little into their bonus pool to make him a JUCO signing for $200,000. Ortiz ripped through the Florida State League in his first full season with a .285/.406/.446 line and 10 homers in 77 games and produced a .938 OPS over 30 contests with High-A Peoria following a July promotion. The 6-foot-1 right-handed slugger has an interesting stance at the plate that starts with him leaning back and then launching forward with a leg kick. It’s a swing designed for contact in the air, and his 29.7 percent line-drive rate was highest among Cardinals full-season qualifiers, while his 29.3 percent ground-ball rate was lowest. His 105.3 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity in the FSL was also comfortably above average, and Ortiz could be a threat to hit 20+ homers pretty easily if trends hold. Ortiz was beatable with good velocity and sliders in the zone, however, and that will be a more worrisome trend against better arms in the upper Minors. The Puerto Rico native ran subpar sprint speeds in the FSL but picked his spots well against Single-A catchers, going 31-for-34 in steal attempts there. (That dropped to 8-for-14 in the Midwest League, perhaps a better sign of what to expect.) The Cardinals believe Ortiz has enough athleticism to keep getting looks at third base, where his above-average arm strength fits, but have already mixed in plenty of first. It’s likely he lands down the defensive spectrum and needs to keep his offensive production high to be valuable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Johnson jumped on scouts’ radars as the 2019 Draft approached, most felt the Mississippi prep right-hander was going to head to Mississippi State. The Braves, however, thought they had a chance to keep him from going and were able to do so by taking him in the 14th round and going over slot to sign him for $257,500. He threw well during his brief debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League that summer, but while he missed bats with the jump to full-season ball in 2021, he struggled in other areas of his craft. He’ll have to wait to refine those things, as Tommy John surgery this spring will knock out his entire 2022 season. Johnson added strength to his 6-foot-2 frame during the 2020 shutdown, helping him throw harder than he had before the Draft. He can sit in the mid-90s and has been up to as high as 99 mph with his fastball at times. He also has a solid power slider, which flashes above-average with good sweep to it. His changeup remains his third pitch, something Johnson will have to focus on if he wants to start long-term. He’s also going to have to throw more strikes after walking 5.6 per nine innings in 2021. He needs reps to find consistency in repeating his delivery and landing his secondary stuff in the zone, because even at the lower levels, people can hit a fastball. He’s still young -- just 21 for the 2022 season -- so there’s time for him to come back from surgery and show the Braves what kind of pitcher they have on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 50 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Japanese-American Balzer was primarily a position player growing up in Japan but saw time on the mound as a high schooler, and that’s where he got interest from evaluators on both sides of the Pacific. The Padres signed him for only $10,000 in January 2023, and Balzer spent the start of his career rehabbing from Tommy John surgery. He didn’t debut until July 2024 and went to Single-A Lake Elsinore last season, posting a 7.92 ERA and a 1.78 WHIP with 49 strikeouts in 50 innings. The 6-foot-1 right-hander is still plenty raw, but he generated excitement by reaching the upper 90s last spring. He worked closer to 93-96 mph, touching 98, with a running sinker in the California League. Despite some nice movement on the heater, he couldn’t command it well, often leaving it to be slammed in the zone. His mid-80s sweeper was his best swing-and-miss offering, mirroring the horizontal movement of the sinker (plus a few extra inches) while running away from righties. His split-change is very much a work in progress to find consistency, and lefties teed off on Balzer with a .971 OPS against him at Single-A. At this stage, Balzer, who pitches solely from the stretch, is a control-over-command arm. His 11.6 percent walk rate with Lake Elsinore was modest for someone with such little pro experience, but his misses were in sluggable spots for opponents. He’ll be 21 for the 2026 season and enters the campaign still two years away from Rule 5 eligibility, meaning he’ll be given ample time and space to find the results that match the quality of his fastball-slider mix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Millar’s stock rose quite a bit during his senior season at Alhambra HS in Martinez, Calif., and the Royals jumped at the chance to get him in the third round of the 2025 Draft. He signed for an over-slot $1,497,500 bonus to keep him from an Arizona commitment. Millar didn’t go out to affiliate ball after he was drafted, but he did pitch in the organization’s instructional league games in the fall. Similar to a lot of prep pitchers the Royals have drafted recently, Millar is young and raw with intriguing stuff that needs development. His fastball was in the low-to-mid-90s in high school until it spiked to 97 mph his senior year, and the Royals have seen that velocity recently, along with good ride. Millar’s slider hovers around 83-85 mph and is more bullet-like and not quite average yet. His changeup was his best pitch in high school, a low-80s offering with lots of tumble. He’s working on throwing it from a more consistent slot, and one of his cues is to throw it harder and more like his fastball. Millar pitches from a higher slot. although there’s some inconsistency he’s working on, but it’s mostly a clean delivery with a quick arm. He went to the Royals’ strength and conditioning camp over the offseason with hopes that some of the benefits could be found in his delivery and velocity. Millar’s development will be a slower one, but it’ll be as a starter to begin his career with the potential for a mid-to-back-end rotation member there. He gets high marks for his competitiveness on and off the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2024, the Mariners signed Chia-Shi Shen out of Chinese Taipei. They hit that pitching market again in 2025, signing Lin for $460,000 when the signing period opened in January. A former two-way player who pitched well in international competition, Lin looked really good in Spring Training after signing, but then wasn’t able to make his pro debut because of a lat strain, though he did get some innings in the bridge league at the end of the year, once again raising expectations. Lin had played both the infield and outfield previously, and he brings that athleticism to the mound. The 5-foot-11 right-hander has the chance to have a full starter’s repertoire, with his splitter the standout pitch. It flashes plus and can fall off the table with excellent depth while also throwing a distinct changeup. His fastball sits around 92-93 mph, but he’s shown the ability to reach back for more, and there could be more velocity in the future. He has some feel to spin with a more traditional slider, though it’s behind the other offerings, and there’s been some talk of adding a sweeper to his mix. Lin’s athleticism helps him repeat his delivery and find the strike zone consistently. His stuff may never wow anyone, but his feel for pitching and full array of offerings gives him the chance to start, with the Mariners getting to see what he’s like in competition this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the advanced age of 18 in 2023, Florentino drew little attention while spending his first two pro seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He made a spectacular U.S. debut in 2025, earning Cubs Minor League Pitcher of the Year accolades. He posted a 2.43 ERA, .201 opponent average and a 30 percent strikeout rate despite a lack of physicality and velocity. Florentino has a slender 6-foot frame and a fastball that sits around 90 mph with a peak of 92 without notable carry or run. But lower-level hitters haven't done damage against his heater because his low arm slot and ability to get down the mound produce an elite low release height and quality extension. His slider parks in the mid-70s but missed a lot of bats last summer with high spin rates and plenty of sweep. Florentino relies mainly on his fastball and slider, occasionally turning the latter into a mid-80s cutter and also fiddling with a mid-80s changeup with fade, though neither of those offerings fool hitters at this point. He has a simple, effortless delivery that has allowed him to provide consistent strikes throughout his career. He could be very intriguing if he can find some more power for his main two weapons, and the fact that his heater gained 5 mph from 2024 to 2025 is an encouraging sign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rogers bounced from Southeastern Louisiana to Jones (Miss.) JC to Southern Mississippi in three years of college. Used exclusively as a reliever by the Golden Eagles in 2022, he struck out 57 in 37 innings while limiting opponents to a .128 average. After he made two short starts in the Cape Cod League, the Red Sox drafted him in the third round and signed him for a below-slot $447,500 with the intention of moving him into the rotation. Rogers threw 85 percent fastballs at Southern Miss and the metrics on the pitch are elite. His 5-foot-11 frame and drop-and-drive delivery result him in delivering at an extremely low height and flat plane that create exceptional carry on his heater, which also has some running action while sitting at 91-94 mph and topping out at 96. His low-80s changeup plays off his fastball well because of its velocity separation and depth, though he struggles to throw it for strikes. To succeed as a starter, Rogers will need to refine his breaking ball and control. He shows some feel for changing the shape of his low-80s slider depending on whether he's facing a lefty or a righty, but he rarely used it as an amateur because he could dominate with his fastball alone. He averaged 5.5 walks per nine innings in college and will have to be much more efficient to be able to handle a rotation workload, especially considering his slight build.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cohen spent five years at George Washington and was the Colonials' best starter in the final three before signing for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2022. Since missing the first half of the 2024 season with a back strain, he has been one of the most unhittable relievers in the Minors during the past two years, logging a 1.62 ERA and .155 opponent average. Though the Yankees declined to protect him on their 40-man roster this offseason, he slipped through the Rule 5 Draft and will compete for a big league bullpen job in 2026. Cohen's money pitch is a tight mid-80s slider that hitters can't lay off or catch up to when it ventures into the strike zone. His fastball is fairly ordinary, ranging from 92-94 mph and reaching 96 with nice carry at times but also below-average command that can make it vulnerable. His mid-80s changeup with fade and sink can be a solid offering at it's best. Cohen hides the ball well with an up-tempo, upright delivery with a high leg kick. While his mechanics provide deception, they also hamper his control and have resulted in a 12 percent walk rate in pro ball. He profiles more as a middle reliever than a high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hansell was in the Royals’ backyard at Wichita State before he transferred to Arizona State for his sophomore and junior years, and they selected him in the 16th round of the 2023 Draft, signing him to a $150,000 bonus -- the max allowed without dipping into their bonus pool. A reliever mostly in college, Hansell pitched in the bullpen during his first full season in 2024, but he transitioned to a starter’s role in '25. He made eight starts at both Single-A Columbia and High-A Quad Cities but saw a better ERA at the higher level with a 2.81 mark for the River Bandits. A stress reaction in his back ended his season in July. Hansell came to the Royals fairly raw in his development, even as a college pitcher, but with really intriguing stuff. His fastball sits around the low-to-mid-90s but can run up to 97 mph. His potentially plus curveball is in the upper 70s with good downer action, getting consistent whiffs. Hansell has a harder breaking mid-80s slider that is average on most days, while his mid-80s changeup is still developing but can get some chase if he’s ahead. Hansell has some work to do on his delivery, which is inconsistent in its tempo. The Royals are working with him on moving quicker and more efficiently. There’s still a bit of development to go with Hansell, but the Royals really like his weapons and potential. While he needs reps and innings to help with that development, Hansell may end up as a reliever by the time he reaches the Majors, with his stuff ticking up in shorter spurts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Juan was relatively unheralded when he signed out of the Dominican Republic with the A’s for just $10,000 in 2017 as an 18-year-old. Struggling through some command issues early in his professional career, he returned from the year off due to the pandemic and unexpectedly broke out in Single-A in 2021, showcasing an uptick in velocity that led to a promotion to High-A Lansing before a flexor strain cut his season short. The A’s liked his power arm enough to add him to the 40-man roster this past offseason, but they had to release him after designating him for assignment in early May, then re-signed him a week later. He again missed time rehabbing the same arm issue, but showed similar ability to miss bats when he was on the mound. Juan utilizes his big 6-foot-8 frame to fill up the zone with a fastball that can reach up to 99 mph and consistently hits 95-97 mph. He also brings a wipeout slider and an offspeed pitch that has the makings of a solid changeup but can be thrown too hard at times, which is why the A’s had encouraged him to focus on it by throwing the pitch more over the past year. When he did pitch in 2022, Juan did a better job of finding the strike zone, but command still remains an overall issue. That, combined with his injury history, could lead to him moving to the bullpen full-time in the future, where that fastball-breaking ball combination could play up in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport standout in high school who didn’t start pitching until he was 17, Natera had three uneven seasons at New Mexico State where he missed a lot of bats and walked a lot of hitters. The Angels took a low-risk flyer on the left-hander in the 17th round of the 2022 Draft, and he kept striking guys out and giving them free passes during his pro debut with High-A Tri-City in 2023. A sprained elbow kept him off the mound for all but 15 innings during the regular season, but he opened a lot of eyes with his work over five Arizona Fall League outings. It was a small sample size spanning just 12 innings, but Natera’s combination of size, stuff and better feel for the zone made people sit up and take notice. His fastball averaged around 94-95 mph and touched 98, and it plays up because of its life that allows it to get a lot of swings and misses. His 82-85 mph slider has good sweep to it, giving him another bat-missing offering. He has a changeup, but he doesn’t throw it very often. While Natera is already 25, he has very low mileage on his arm between starting late, the pandemic and the missed time in 2024. In his brief mound time last year, he was finding the strike zone with more consistency, raising the bar a little bit more. Left-handers who are 6-foot-4 and have two out pitches tend to make it to the big leagues, so everyone is intrigued to see how Natera follows up his AFL breakout.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Cardinals for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019, Saladin still didn’t see the Dominican Summer League until 2021 due to the pandemic and repeated the level after becoming a starter in 2022. He moved stateside in 2023 and enjoyed a breakout season in 2024 with a 2.62 ERA that ranked second among St. Louis Minor League full-season qualifiers. He also struck out 134 and walked 33 over 123 innings between Single-A and High-A. He was Rule 5-eligible in the offseason but went unprotected and unpicked due to his distance from the Majors. Standing only 5-foot-11, Saladin still stands out for his fastball that comes out of a low release height and has a flat vertical approach angle, causing more swing-and-miss than expected for most four-seamers. The pitch played in the 92-94 mph range in the Florida State League but lost some steam late with Peoria, understandable considering Saladin’s workload. His mid-80s changeup comes with enough armside run and deception off the fastball to get some whiffs too and hold lefties relatively at bay. A low-80s slider and upper-70s curveball aren’t at the same standard. Saladin kept his walk rates fairly low at both levels in 2024, and while he relies on some chase on all of his pitches (particularly the changeup), he has the control to remain a starter. Despite his Rule 5 status, the hurler is only entering his age-22 season and should get heavier 40-man consideration if he enjoys repeat success in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Armbruester wasn’t very well known coming out of the Seattle prep ranks. He turned into quite an accomplished collegiate pitcher, first at Division III Pacific Lutheran and then at New Mexico State, for whom he claimed WAC conference pitcher of the year honors in 2021. That success caught the attention of the Orioles, who took him in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft and signed him for $100,000. He pitched well enough to reach Double-A in his first full season and Triple-A in 2023, but stalled a little in Norfolk down the stretch last summer. At 6-foot-5 and 250 pounds, Armbruester is a big, physical right-hander with intriguing stuff that he tinkers with frequently, sometimes with immediate success. He added an upper-80s cutter in 2022, and missed more bats with it that year than any other pitch in his arsenal. Last season, he shelved his changeup and added a curveball. In 2024, he plans to revive the change to give him another weapon against left-handed hitters. The cutter is the best of those offerings. Armbruester plays them all off a hoppy low-to-mid-90s fastball with ride and a sweepy slider, both of which he demonstrates plus feel for. Armbruester uses an awkward delivery and funky arm slot to hide the ball well, using that deception to help his stuff play up. His success really hinges on that and his command. When he locates everything well, he controls the zone and can miss bats with multiple pitches. But he can sometimes get hurt throwing too many strikes when ahead in the count and his walk rate spiked down the stretch last year against Triple-A hitters. If he can continue developing his secondary stuff and throwing strikes with all his offerings, he could still fit in as a back-end rotation piece at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of Corona Del Mar High School in California, Schwartz headed to UCLA, where he redshirted his freshman year and only saw 15 games in the shortened 2020 season. His big breakout finally came last spring when he hit .396/.514/.628 with eight homers and a 28/37 K/BB ratio in 44 games for the Bruins. Those numbers made him the Pac-12 batting champion and earned him a spot on the All-Conference Team. The Mets selected Schwartz in the fourth round and went slightly under slot to sign him for $475,000. He walked more than he struck out (13 vs. 12) but otherwise saw minimal results with a .195 average and a .576 OPS in his first 25-game trip to the Minors with Low-A St. Lucie. Despite standing in the box at 6-foot-4, Schwartz isn’t your typical slugging first first baseman. He’s shown an advanced approach everywhere he’s played over the last four years, including in summer-ball circuits, and as he proved in his final season on campus, he makes enough quality contact to sustain a good batting average. However, he doesn’t have a long history of hitting the ball over fences, and before the Draft, some evaluators were concerned that previous shoulder, knee and hip problems would keep him from showing even average power in games. Schwartz is first-base only on defense, and the Mets secured that by giving him all 24 of his defensive starts at the cold corner with St. Lucie. He faces a high offensive threshold there, and simply producing a solid average and OBP might not be enough to meet it. Schwartz is staring up at Pete Alonso on the Mets’ first-base depth chart, so he needn’t press to expedite his route toward Citi Field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After getting $600,000 to sign with the Pirates out of the Dominican Republic at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, Terrero couldn’t play until 2021 because of the pandemic. He showed off a solid approach during his Dominican Summer League debut that year, then posted an .890 OPS in the Florida Complex League when he came to the United States for the first time. He was streaky during his full-season debut in 2023, fading down the stretch, but showing off some of his offensive potential. With a smaller frame, Terrero has yet to display a ton of impact from the left side of the plate. But there were some gains in terms of exit velocity last year, which gave the Pirates hope there could be more of that to come with some pop to his pull side. He’s made a ton of contact in his brief career, though his strikeout rate did climb a bit in Single-A Bradenton. He tends to have a consistent approach and draws walks, with a 13 percent walk rate in 2023. Terrero runs well enough to steal some bags, and it also gives him the potential to stick in center field. He’s an average defender there now who still needs to work on his reads and routes. He’s actually a plus defender in an outfield corner, but he’s not going to have the kind of offensive impact teams like to see from that spot, which could make him a bit of a tweener if center doesn’t work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After selecting just two position players in the 2021 Draft, the Dodgers needed some more bats and farm director Will Rhymes liked Gauthier's swing and selectivity. Signed for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent, he has ranked in the top 10 in the Minors in both walks and on-base percentage in each of his two full pro seasons. He batted .316/.435/.475 with 12 homers and 19 steals while reaching Double-A in 2023, and he soon could become Hofstra's first big leaguer since mid-1970s Mets right-hander Hank Webb. Gauthier understands the strike zone and makes better swing decisions than most players, rarely giving away an at-bat. He understands his right-handed stroke and doesn't try to do too much with it, lacing line drives while using the entire ballpark. He focused on adding strength after his first full season and hit the ball harder in the second, though he won't have more than 12-15 homer power unless he looks to turn on pitches and drive them in the air more frequently. While Gauthier doesn't have loud tools, he makes the most of them and is surprisingly versatile for someone with average speed and arm strength. He started 18 or more games at five different positions in 2023: third base, shortstop, second base, left field and right field. He fits best and provides averageish defense at second base, grades as fringy elsewhere and profiles as an offensive-minded utilityman who excels at getting on base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After saving $1.3 million in bonus pool with 2024 first-round pick PJ Morlando, whom they coveted, the Marlins used most of that cash to sign Johnson in the second round for a well-over-slot $2.8 million. The latter garnered some comparisons to fellow Alabama prep shortstop Gunnar Henderson, though the 2023 American League Rookie of the Year had more athleticism and power potential at the same stage of their careers. The game sped up a bit on Johnson in his pro debut, when he batted .221 with a 33 percent strikeout rate and made nine errors in 24 games as one of the youngest players (age 18) in the Single-A Florida State League. Johnson earned a reputation as one of the better hitters in the 2024 prep class by making consistent contact to all fields with a controlled left-handed swing and advanced approach. He didn't look like himself in the FSL, chasing pitches out of the zone much more than normal and struggling with non-fastballs. He doesn't stand out in terms of bat speed, present strength or exit velocities, but his hitting ability could translate into 15 or more homers annually once he matures physically. Though he'll flash slightly above-average speed, Johnson probably will slow down a bit as he gets stronger, and he isn't adventurous on the bases. He has smooth actions, reliable hands and a solid arm at shortstop but may not have the quickness or range to stay there. He'll return to the FSL in 2025 on the same team with gifted defenders Starlyn Caba and Andrew Salas, so he'll also see action at second and possibly third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The state of Missouri produced three quality prep shortstop prospects in the 2024 class. D-backs fourth-rounder Tytus Cissell was seen as having the best athleticism of the trio, Drew Dickerson was the most physical but went undrafted on his way to the University of Oklahoma and Snyder – Missouri’s Gatorade high school player of the year -- had the most polish and highest floor. He went to the Mets in the fifth round (12 picks after Cissell) but signed for roughly second-round money with a $1,322,500 bonus. Snyder played in six games with Single-A St. Lucie to mark his pro debut. The former Tennessee commit impressed amateur scouts with his good swing decisions as a righty hitter. That hit tool is part of the reason why New York decided to give him a quick look at the Florida State League, and the approach could help him take off even more quickly in a return there this spring. There was some concern about his power coming into his senior year, and that remains to some degree even after he added strength. His exit velocities have run cold in 2025, but he is doing a better job of limiting chase and making contact in the zone. Snyder could flash plus run times when he really got going as a high schooler, but his added strength did slow him down some when it came to going home to first. He has the hands and internal clock for shortstop, while his arm strength and limited range have seen him move to second and third in his first full season back in the FSL.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Undrafted in 2021, Bazzell was slated to head to Dallas Baptist out of high school but transferred to Texas Tech after only one semester, causing him to miss the 2022 season. He hit the ground running as a Red Raiders third baseman in 2023, hitting .343 with a 1.025 OPS, and transitioned to the catching spot when it became open for 2024. He dealt with mononucleosis early in the spring but managed a .307/.401/.473 line in 49 games, and that performance pushed him to the Nationals in the third round. He got in 19 games for Single-A Fredericksburg, including the postseason, after signing. Batting from the right side, Bazzell keeps things simple in the box with a controlled stroke and calm load. He rarely swung and missed in college, especially against fastballs, but started to whiff a bit against more high-quality sliders in his early looks in the pros. Still, he brings discipline to a lineup and could carry high OBPs at each stop moving forward. He’ll hit balls hard but without optimal launch angle, dulling his power projection to more of the gap variety until he adjusts for more elevation. Bazzell is fairly athletic – a big reason why he could play both third and catcher in college – but will likely slow down the more he focuses behind the plate. He’s still wet behind the ears back there, and the Nationals intend to prioritize getting him work there to improve his receiving. He has a quick release to help keep runners in check, and his arm strength could be useful elsewhere should he need to move again later in his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jimenez’s $480,000 bonus was the fourth-highest the Mariners handed out in the 2019-20 international signing period. Like with all signees from July 2019, he had to wait through the pandemic to make his pro debut in 2021, spending two summers in the Dominican Summer League. He then ended up in the Arizona Complex League for parts of another two years before having a bit of a breakout in 2024 that allowed him to reach full-season ball for the first time. He repeated the level in 2025 and showed off an intriguing, if still unpolished, set of tools. While he’s not the biggest guy in the world at 5-foot-10, Jimenez has shown that he can impact the baseball at times from the left side of the plate. He started barreling up the baseball more consistently in 2025 and can show solid bat-to-ball skills overall when he sticks to his approach. He also tapped into his power more effectively last year, showing leverage to his pull side, but has to make sure he doesn’t sell out for that pop and lose his approach. He can get caught in between being a guy to drive the ball with some swing-and-miss and a guy to get on base -- he does draw a good amount of walks -- who puts the ball in play. The Mariners would love to see him be more of the second guy, letting the power come naturally, so he can keep taking advantage of his speed and athleticism on the basepaths. He can also run the ball down in center field but will likely be the kind of guy who sees time in all three outfield spots as a potential fourth outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 Dickinson certainly had an interesting path to pro ball. He didn’t make his varsity team at Kennewick HS (Wash.) until he was a junior and headed to Utah Valley for college as a walk-on. He was a two-time All-Western Athletic Conference first-team honoree with the Wolverines and set school records with 18 homers and 32 steals in 2024. He had stints in Cape Cod and with the U.S. Collegiate National Team that summer and transferred to LSU as a junior, helping the Tigers win a Men's College World Series title while hitting .315/.458/.525 with 12 homers and a 42/40 K/BB ratio in 68 games. The Brewers took him in the sixth round and signed him for $325,000. Batting from the right side, Dickinson looks relaxed at the plate and employs a simple right-handed swing and excellent hand-eye coordination to put lots of pitch types into play. His chase rate in his final year of college was just a tad below the MLB average, and his ability to get that bat on the ball kept strikeouts in check. His raw power is just average at best, however, and he didn’t slug much with wood bats before his move to Baton Rouge -- something worth watching in his introduction to the pros. As an average runner with average arm strength, Dickinson bounced around a good amount defensively as a collegian with most of his looks for Utah Valley and LSU coming at second base. With other priority shortstops Jesús Made, Luis Peña and Cooper Pratt already in the system ahead of him, it’s likely Dickinson will settle in back at the keystone. Down the road, he might project best as a contact-heavy utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hodge is a product of Crespi Carmelite HS (Encino, Calif.), which has sent seven players to the big leagues, most notably Rick Dempsey, Jeff Suppan and Trevor Plouffe. He was considered the most athletic catching prospect in the 2025 Draft , just as White Sox starter Kyle Teel was in the 2023 class.
