A fourth-round pick, he foresook a Louisiana State commitment to sign for a well-over-slot $1,097,500. Hodge has a disciplined approach geared to work balls from gap to gap. While he has a quick, compact left-handed swing, he comes up empty on pitches in the strike zone more than he should, especially fastballs on the outer third. He had contact issues against quality pitching on the prep showcase circuit and will need to improve his timing and add strength to realize his ceiling of an average hitter with 15-homer pop. With his agility behind the plate, developing receiving skills and solid arm strength, there's no doubt that Hodge can stay at catcher. He can get better with the technical aspects of his craft and has the work ethic to do so, not to mention strong leadership skills. An average runner, he's quick enough to play second base or the outfield corners if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis began his pro career back in 2015 when the Dodgers took Davis in the fifth round out of his California high school, going way over slot ($918,600) to sign him away from his commitment to Cal State Fullerton. He was traded to the Rangers at the 2017 deadline in the Yu Darvish deal and he moved to Double-A in 2019, though he struggled there. Left unprotected in 2020, the Angels took Davis in the Minor League phase of the Rule 5 Draft and he broke out in a huge way, going from High-A to Triple-A, hitting 30 homers and earning a spot on the Angels’ 40-man roster. While Davis has always been willing to draw walks, his overall approach, or lack thereof, kept him from maximizing his offensive tools. In 2021, he cut down his strikeout rate and was able to access his considerable raw power, more than doubling his career home run total in the process. The 6-foot-4 right-handed hitter can create leverage and loft, though there will always be swing-and-miss in his game. An average runner who is a smart baserunner, Davis was drafted as a shortstop and continues to see time there. His power profiles at third, where he’s also played a good amount, and he’s added in second base and left field over the years, pointing to a potential future as a bat-first utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For years, scout Billy Milos scoured independent leagues and found quality players for the Twins. Now with the Rockies, Milos’ last hurrah for his old team might be Eeles, who spent four years at Division II Cedarville University in Ohio, then got a fifth season at Coastal Carolina because of the pandemic. He was 23 and only 5-foot-5, so he went undrafted and headed to the American Association and then the Atlantic League to start 2024. That’s where Milos found him and he joined the organization for just $500, then became one of the best stories of the year, hitting his way to Triple-A and finishing with a system-leading .932 OPS. The left-handed-hitting Eeles combines a terrific feel for hitting with a “hair on fire” approach to the game. He really controls the strike zone, drawing walks and limiting his swing-and-miss (16 percent in 2024). It’s a hit-over-power approach, but he barrels up baseballs routinely and uses all fields. There’s surprising pop, and he has shown the ability to hit the ball out in all directions. Eeles doesn’t have plus speed but he’s smart and aggressive on the bases, which enabled him to steal 41 bases last year. He played every position but first base and catcher during his debut season, and his path to the big leagues is probably as a super-utility type. No one wants to undersell him at this point, though, and second base seems like his most likely landing spot should he be an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crossland bounced from Division II Ouachita Baptist (Okla.) to Weatherford (Texas) JC to the University of Oklahoma in a three-year collegiate period. Just when he was about to show off with the Sooners, he strained a back muscle in fall practice, and it affected his performance with a 6.32 ERA in 68 1/3 innings. He struck out 26.6 percent of his batters faced, though, and buoyed himself with nine strikeouts and just one unearned run allowed in seven innings against Nebraska in the NCAA Regionals. The Cardinals selected him in the fourth round and signed him above slot at $729,500. The 6-foot-2 southpaw touched 98 mph in his one SEC spring but generally sat 91-94. He could elicit a healthy amount of chase by climbing the ladder effectively with the heater from a simple side-step delivery. Holding bigger velocity without the back problems should be a goal in pro ball. Crossland’s most dominant pitch was easily his 83-85 mph changeup that generated special fade, and hitters swung over it again and again. He sells it well out of the hand, only for it to die just as it reaches the plate. His low-80s breaking pitches didn’t have great spin rates or feel for the zone, but he could work a slider or humpier curveball in for different looks. Crossland slowly improved his control rates during his various stops in school, but even with the simple mechanics, he still walked 10.4 percent of batters faced with OU. At least the changeup should help him run reverse splits in the pros, and that’ll help his chances of finding a spot in the back of a future St. Louis rotation, especially if he gets to a little more velo with full health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming out of San Diego’s St. Augustine HS, Boles got time on the showcase circuit in 2024 and even started the High School All-American Game in his native city at Petco Park that August, picking up a pair of strikeouts in his lone frame. He had a commitment to Texas and looked likely to head to Austin as the 2025 Draft passed before the Royals selected him in the 18th round. Kansas City eventually signed the right-hander for $500,000 ($350,000 of which counted toward its Draft pool), and that was the sixth-highest bonus in the organization’s 2025 class. Already standing in at 6-foot-5, Boles is all about projection. He ran his fastball up to 94 mph in his final amateur season, and it’s easy to dream on him sitting mid-90s more regularly as he fills out that frame with strength in the pros. His low-80s slider also shows present and future promise with impressive spin and sharp movement to the glove side. He can also flash a solid mid-80s changeup to give him an offspeed pitch going the other way while his slow curveball doesn’t look like a true weapon. Boles could be all around the zone at times heading into the Draft, and tightening up his slinging delivery should be a focus on the pro side. The Royals tend to take things slowly with prep arms early in their careers, and Boles will be no exception as he’ll open his age-19 season in the Arizona Complex League with the goal of cracking Single-A Columbia at some point in 2026. He has received positive reviews from Royals officials for his willingness to take pro-level instruction, and that combined with his stuff gives him higher upside than a traditional 18th-round flier.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Um’s father, Um Jong-soo, played one season in the Braves’ system back in 2001, and with Um’s signing with the Royals in 2022, it made the pair the first South Korean father-son duo to join Major League organizations. After going back to Rookie ball in Arizona to start ‘24, Um showed he was ready for the next level by hitting .310 with a .900 OPS. In his final 50 games of the season in Single-A Columbia, Um slashed .205/.333/.307 with four homers and a 100 wRC+ while sharing catching duties with 2023 first-rounder Blake Mitchell. Um has a simple setup with a little bit of a higher positioning with his hands, getting them back in a decent position to hit, and a leg kick that lifts and coils into his hip for a better load. It’s an efficient swing from the right side with line-drive power right now and the potential for more extra base hits and average power as he grows into his frame. His solid bat speed and quick hands help him get to pitches on the inner half of the plate. Um is still learning how to navigate an at-bat and can struggle with breaking balls. Defensively, Um is athletic and moves well behind the plate. His receiving is a work in progress, but he has above-average arm strength and the foundation to stick at backstop. Um adds to the Royals’ catching depth in their system with four catchers in the preseason Top 30. With a strong makeup, he is smart and wants to learn, and the Royals are eager to get him to a full-season affiliate. With time and more development, Um has the potential to be a backup Major League catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves had a compensation pick after the fourth round of the 2025 Draft after losing Max Fried to free agency. They used it to pick up Williams, a middle infielder who was coming off a solid junior season at East Carolina, finishing with 14 homers and an OPS over 1.000 before going 8-for-20 and being named to the all-tournament team at the NCAA Greenville Regional. He signed for just under $500,000, a bit under slot, becoming the earliest-drafted hitter from the Pirates program since Connor Norby was a second-rounder in 2021. Williams brought his solid approach from the left side of the plate with him during his relatively brief 28-game pro debut last summer with Single-A Augusta. He could be an average hitter in the future with solid on-base skills and strike zone control. He drew more walks than strikeouts in his last year of college, part of what helped him get to his power more, with his over-the-fence pop coming mostly to his pull side. His debut with Augusta was solid, but the Braves think the underlying data points to even better contact rates to come. A plus runner who swiped 22 bases in 25 tries last year at East Carolina, Williams could have a potentially intriguing power-speed combination in the future. Where he ends up defensively is still up in the air. He played second and third in college, and his arm might be a tad short for the hot corner. His best bet long term to stick in one spot might be as an offensive-minded player at the keystone. But he’ll likely move around some, with center field one day not out of the question for a more likely utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCoy should make for one of the most interesting prospect follows in the Padres system in 2026, and not just because he stands 6-foot-5 and is listed at 260 pounds. The Baltimore-area native spent two years at the University of Maryland-Eastern Shore before transferring to Hofstra, where former 14-year Major Leaguer Frank Catalanotto coached him. After going unselected in the 2024 Draft, McCoy signed as a nondrafted free agent with the Padres. He dealt with hamstring and quad injuries in his first full season but he left a mark in his time with Single-A Lake Elsinore, hitting .318/.394/.513 with six homers in 53 games. The right-handed slugger's raw power is the best in the San Diego pipeline and some of the best in the entire Minors. There's a ton of strength in his base and upper body, and he maxed out with an 118 mph exit velocity in the California League -- a number that would fit at the top of many teams' leaderboards in the Majors. There is some feel for hitting here too. McCoy doesn’t lash out to get to that pop, and his swing can be short and controlled to whack stuff inside. He did swing a fair amount through sliders and changeups away, and upper-level pitchers will try to take advantage of that. McCoy is a decent mover under way -- someone who can push for extra bases on balls to the gaps -- but can take a bit to get moving up the first-base line. He was primarily in left field last year in Lake Elsinore, a decent fit for his speed and arm strength, but could eventually become a bigger target at first base, where he spent the first two years of his NCAA career. McCoy will need to mash at either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top infielder in Miami's 2018 international class, Rodriguez signed for $300,000 out of Venezuela. Though he batted just .229/.321/.346 in Rookie ball during his first two pro seasons sandwiched around the pandemic shutdown, those numbers belie his offensive upside. Rodriguez still is figuring out his left-handed swing but generates plenty of bat speed and could produce 20 or more homers on an annual basis. To do so, he must improve his ability to recognize pitches and control the strike zone. He uses the opposite field almost too much and puts the ball in play on the ground too often. Signed as a shortstop, Rodriguez split time between there and third base in his pro debut and played mostly at the hot corner in 2021. He has nice infield actions, soft hands and solid arm strength, but his fringy speed and quickness limit his range at shortstop and he could slow down further as he matures physically. He makes some youthful mistakes at third base, just like he does at the plate, but time is still on his side because he'll be just 20 throughout the 2022 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Martinez out of Venezuela in 2018 and started him in the Dominican Summer League the next summer, when he hit .239 with a .664 OPS over 58 games but showed some raw tools that kept the organization intrigued through the lost 2020 season. In 2021, Martinez played in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League and got a brief taste of Single-A, hitting .330 with as many walks (22) as strikeouts in 34 games. Last summer, Martinez broke out over the course of 96 games, mostly with Single-A Dunedin and High-A Vancouver, hitting .293 with an .832 OPS. Most impressive was his power jump, as he launched 14 homers after showing very little pop earlier in his pro career. This placed Martinez squarely on the radar for the Blue Jays, who have been starving for a star outfield prospect for years. Martinez has borrowed some swing mechanics from Bo Bichette. They help him tap into his natural athleticism, and he showed a very good feel for the barrel of his bat before a difficult 2023 season with High-A Vancouver, where he still hasn't struck out much but has lacked impact. Defensively, his range in the outfield needs to improve, which likely limits him to a corner spot, but his bat-first profile puts the young Venezuelan on the map in the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted in the seventh round as a Puerto Rican high schooler in 2023, Melendez gave up a Rice scholarship to sign for an over-slot $400,000. He spent his first two years as a pro in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, slashing a combined .263/.374/.410 with 22 extra-base hits and 11 steals in 63 games. He's still raw but is one of the more intriguing young hitters in the Cubs' system. Melendez has a relatively compact left-handed swing considering his gangly 6-foot-3 frame and he produces better exit velocities than most teenagers. He shows some feel for driving the ball in the air to his pull side and could grow into 25-homer power once he gains some much-needed strength. He comes with contact concerns because he chases pitches and swings through strikes, so he'll have to prove he can handle more advanced pitching. Presently an average runner, Melendez will lose some quickness as he fills out. He displays quick hands and solid arm strength at shortstop, but his fringy range will necessitate a change of position at higher levels. He played more under control at third base and second base than he did at short last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pedro Strop pitched eight seasons as a reliever for the Cubs and even had a brief run in the Reds bullpen in the COVID-shortened season of 2020. His son Royelny, at least to begin his career, is sticking in the NL Central. The outfielder, who trained with his father in their native Dominican Republic, signed with the Cardinals for $1.4 million in January, becoming St. Louis’ top international addition in the 2025 signing period. Only 16 at the time of his signing, Strop is seen as mighty projectable moving forward as a lefty-hitting, lefty-throwing outfielder. St. Louis scouts dream that he’ll have at least average power at full maturity once he bulks up, and he already shows quality pullside pop. His hit tool is somewhat split with some seeing strong present bat-to-ball skills and others concerned about his mechanics. If he can continue to hit the ball hard, he could live with a few strikeouts. With that ability to bulk up also brings questions about where Strop lands defensively. He’s a good runner right now who can handle center, but he may slow down as he ages, necessitating a move to the corners. It’s likeliest that his bat is what pushes him through the St. Louis system in the years to come, and Strop got to show that off late in the Dominican Summer League, going 13-for-26 (.500) with seven extra-base hits in his final six games after sporadic opportunities throughout the summer. He hit for the cycle in his final contest of 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2023 NCAA Division II player of the year after batting .408/.506/.901 with a school-record 28 homers at Point Loma Nazarene (Calif.), Christian transferred to San Diego for his Draft year. The Toreros' best power prospect since Kris Bryant, he slashed .364/.460/.828 with 26 homers to win West Coast Conference player of the year honors. He played briefly in Single-A after signing for $397,500 as a fifth-rounder. Christian's 6-foof-5, 225-pound frame gives him tremendous strength and leverage, and his right-handed stroke provides plenty of bat speed and loft. That combination results in well above-average raw power that allows him to smash balls out of any part of the ballpark. He does come with an aggressive approach and swing-and-miss concerns, especially against non-fastballs, and he struggled to produce with wood bats in college summer leagues. Christian moves well for his size, displaying fringy speed with decent instincts on the bases. After playing first base at Point Loma Nazarene, he moved to right field at San Diego and spent most of his short pro debut in left field. He has adequate range and average arm strength on the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dumesnil looked like he could be a high-round Draft pick after an eye-opening sophomore season at Cal Baptist, including a .362/.440/.702 slash line with 19 homers, and an All-Star season in the Cape Cod League, hitting .311 and leading the circuit in steals (26). A difficult junior season changed his momentum, but the Tigers snagged him in the eighth round, signed him for $214,300 and immediately put him at Single-A, where he made an impact for Lakeland in the Florida State League playoffs. Strong and athletic, the 6-foot-2 Dumesnil showed the ability to hit with power in college, but his 2025 season came with struggles against spin, notably sliders, and inconsistent power. Both of those continued in Lakeland, where he hit fastballs well but not for much power while whiffing on breaking balls. He’s not a fluid runner but has enough speed and aggressiveness to swipe bases, which he did often in a small sample size for the Flying Tigers. Dumesnil’s speed does help him cover ground in the outfield and he’s shown he can be solid at all three spots defensively. Some feel he can play center long term, but others feel he’s best suited for a corner, with left being a better option because of his fringy arm strength. Even with the struggles he’s had, the Tigers will try to get him back to 2024 Cape form.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nankil was a seventh-round selection by the A’s out of Cal State Fullerton in the 2023 MLB Draft as part of a class headlined by No. 6 overall pick Jacob Wilson. After a strong first full professional season, he began 2025 at High-A Lansing and ended with Double-A Midland, combining to hit .278 with a .724 OPS in 124 games. Nankil’s overall approach at the plate is solid, having shown a good ability to draw walks and limit the strikeout totals at a decent rate. His raw power excited the A’s when he entered the organization, but that aspect of his game has yet to fully show through. While he does hit the ball hard, he tends to hit the ball on the ground too often. He also has some trouble picking up on offspeed pitches at times. Nankil is an average defender who can cover a decent amount of range in the outfield with his athleticism, while also bringing a strong arm. He ideally profiles as a corner outfielder, but he will have to hit for more power to continue progressing through the system. The A’s believe he has at least 20-homer power potential, and they plan to work with him on getting the ball in the air more to try to unlock some more of that pop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $47,500 out of Venezuela in 2022, Osorio spent his first two years as pro in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League and his third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. When he finally made his full-season debut in 2025, he ranked third in the Single-A Carolina League with a .393 on-base percentage at age 20. He returned to Hickory this spring and was one of the top offensive performers in the early part of the season. Osorio's skills stand out more than his physical tools, beginning with his ability to put the bat on the ball. With a compact left-handed stroke and advanced feel for the barrel, he rarely swings and misses. He's hitting balls harder and launching them in the air to his pull side more frequently in 2026, allowing him to homer 10 times in his first 45 games after going deep just six times in 178 contests during the previous four seasons. Osorio has fringy speed but good baserunning instincts. His high baseball IQ has also led to some playing time in center field despite his lack of quickness, though he's better suited for the corners. He's an average defender in left or right field with decent arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Benny Agbayani spent parts of five seasons in the big leagues after being a late-round Draft pick out of Hawaii Pacific University in 1993. When the Twins took his son Bruin out of the Hawaiian high school ranks in the sixth round of the 2025 Draft, he beat his dad by 24 rounds, signing with the Twins for just over $380,000. He got his feet wet with a handful of games with Single-A Fort Myers after signing. A 6-foot-2 left-handed hitter who earned Hawaii Gatorade Player of the Year honors last year, Agbayani enters pro ball with a very good feel to hit. He routinely finds the barrel with outstanding bat speed and while he’s a hit-over-power type, there is some thump, especially to his pull side, which was on display when he ripped a 106 mph triple to right-center field in the MLB Draft Combine High School Game last June. There should be extra-base impact to come in the future as well. Agbayani likes to use his above-average speed on the basepaths, but few think he has the ability to stay at shortstop -- his high school position -- not only because of a lack of range, but also because he doesn’t possess the actions or hands for the premium spot. He’ll still get reps there, but his best chance of staying on the dirt will likely be second base, though some amateur scouts thought an outfield corner will make the most sense long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mobley established himself as one of the best prep pitchers in the 2024 Draft early in his career at Durant HS (Plant City, Fla.) and stood out last spring as one of the youngest, most projectable and hardest-throwing high school hurlers available. Armed with the largest bonus pool ($18,334,000) since those rules came into play in 2012, the Guardians floated Mobley all the way down to the 295th overall pick, where they signed him for $1.8 million. That obliterated the 10th-round bonus record Cleveland set two years earlier by paying Jacob Zibin $1.2 million. Mobley already reaches 92-95 mph and reaches 99 with armside run and carry on his fastball, which gains deception coming out of a low three-quarters arm slot and low release height. Because he could overmatch most high schoolers simply by using his heaters, he didn't need to rely on or develop his secondary pitches very much. His slider and tumbling changeup both park in the low 80s and have solid upside, while his mid-70s curveball needs more power. There still plenty of projection remaining in Mobley's 6-foot-5, 205-pound frame, so he could add even more velocity as he gets stronger. He's still in the process of learning how to keep his long limbs in sync, maintain a consistent regular point and land his secondary pitches in the zone. He comes with some reliever risk and will need time to add polish but could develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels clearly have a thing for two-way players. We all know about Shohei Ohtani, and Jared Walsh got to the big leagues in 2019. In 2018, they drafted William Holmes and are letting him both hit and pitch as a pro. They took Rivera from the Puerto Rico high school ranks in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, giving him an above-slot $597,500 bonus to sign him away from his Florida International commitment. He only hit during his pro debut in the Rookie-Level Arizona League, but the plan is to let him follow in Holmes’ footsteps. Rivera has some serious raw power to tap into from the left side of the plate, but there’s question about whether he’ll make enough contact to get to it consistently. There are some swing-and-miss issues -- he struck out in more than 37 percent of his plate appearances during his pro debut -- and he’ll have to refine his approach. But Angels hitting instructors like his swing and think that will come with experience. On the mound, Rivera has been up to 95-96 mph with his fastball, sitting more in the low 90s, with plenty of room to add strength and consistent velocity. He’s shown both feel for spinning his breaking ball and for a changeup, but he’ll need to work on improving his secondary stuff along with his command of all his offerings. Like with his swing, Angels instructors like the biomechanics of Rivera’s delivery, leaving it a bit of a tossup which area he might have the better chance with if he had to choose one to pursue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his four years at Princeton, Smith both relieved and started. He had his strongest year in the Tigers' rotation as a senior, enough for the Angels to take a low-risk flier on the left-hander in Round 18 of the 2019 Draft, signing him for just $3,000. After pitching out of the bullpen during his pro debut that summer, Smith took the opportunity to start in 2021 and ran with it, pitching across four levels to finish in Triple-A. Smith does have four pitches at his disposal, all coming from his strong, though undersized, 5-foot-11 frame. His fastball averaged around 92 mph in 2021, touching 94, but it plays up some because it has good ride up in the zone. His slider, a sweeper with a ton of horizontal movement, is his best secondary offering that can miss bats, a big reason why he struck out 10.6 per nine last season. His slower curve isn’t as good, but serves as a good get-me-over pitch for strike one and he uses his changeup effectively while starting to mix in a new cutter as well. Throughout his college career, Smith struggled with command, walking 4.4 per nine. He threw a ton more strikes in 2021, nearly cutting that walk rate in half. He’s on the map now, with the chance to serve as a No. 5 starter/long reliever type in the big leagues soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels gave seven-figure bonuses to outfielders Nelson Rada and Randy De Jesus at the start of the 2022 international signing period, but they also brought in some intriguing young pitching talent. No one got a higher bonus than Encarnacion, who signed for $500,000 and then struck out nearly 11 per nine innings during his Dominican Summer League debut. A plus athlete on the mound, Encarnacion’s fastball currently sits around 92-93 mph and can touch 96. His slider is his best secondary offering, a low-80s breaking ball that has the chance to be better than average in the future. He’ll throw his changeup up to 87-88 mph, giving him a true three-pitch mix, though he could use some more separation between his heater and the offspeed offering. The two things Encarnacion needs to work on the most are his command and physicality. He walked 5.3 per nine in his debut and adding strength to his 6-foot-2 frame will help him repeat his delivery, which in turn will lead to more strikes. There’s projectability here to go along with some intriguing stuff, giving him the chance to develop into a starting pitcher long term as he comes stateside for the first time in 2023 at age 18.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted coming out of high school despite being a standout in the Louisiana area and as a Breakthrough Series alum, Huggins continued his baseball career at Chipola Junior College in Florida, where he became teammates with Cam Collier. The two went on to be Draft classmates for the Reds in 2022, with Collier going to Cincinnati in the first round and Huggins in the fourth. After Tommy John surgery in June 2023, he returned near the end of the ‘24 campaign. Beginning the 2025 season at Single-A Daytona, he was dealt to the A’s at last year’s Trade Deadline for Miguel Andujar, finishing his season at High-A Lansing. Huggins has an electric arm with a fastball that can reach up to 97 mph and sits 95-96. His hard slider is by far his most effective secondary pitch. He also recently reintroduced an upper-80s changeup into his repertoire. All this comes from a high release point that creates some good deception. Command has been an issue for Huggins in the past, though he seems to be emerging as more of a consistent strike thrower the further removed from surgery he gets. He’ll get a chance to continue starting for now, but his limited pitch mix could lead to him in a bullpen role long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trentadue spent a season at NCAA Division III Southern Virginia before moving to the JC of Southern Idaho, where he topped national junior college pitchers in strikeout rate (16.0 per nine innings) in 2023. A 14th-round pick that July, he earned High-A South Atlantic League honors in 2025 after posting a 1.15 ERA, .148 opponent average and 34 percent strikeout rate in the first four months of the season. He got roughed up in seven Double-A starts to finish the year, so he'll return there in 2026. As Trentadue has gotten stronger, his fastball has gone from averaging 88 mph at Southern Idaho to sitting at 92-95 mph and touching 97. Beyond its velocity, hitters have trouble handling his heater because it features quality carry and bores in on right-handers. He also made improvements with his sweeping low-80s slider and sinking mid-80s changeup, though he's still figuring out how to locate the latter where he wants. Trentadue uses his athleticism to get down the mound very well, creating a low release height and extension that add to his deception. He has decent control but looked more tentative while getting knocked around in Double-A. He has the ceiling of a No. 4 starter but his ability to make adjustments against advanced hitters will determine whether he stays in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montgomery was well-known as an Orlando-area high schooler and slotted in at No. 34 on MLB Pipeline’s 2020 Draft rankings. The shortened Draft and his strong commitment to Florida State kept him from being drafted that year, but he never found consistent success with the Seminoles as a starter or a reliever. The Padres still took him in the 11th round in 2023 and signed him for $200,000. Montgomery needed Tommy John surgery after only three appearances with Single-A Lake Elsinore in '24, and he didn’t return to a mound in an official setting until the 2025 Arizona Fall League, where he allowed two earned runs, struck out seven and walked seven in 10 1/3 frames. He has opened his age-23 season as a starter with High-A Fort Wayne. The 6-foot-1 right-hander showcases both a four-seamer and sinker. He can sit 92-95 mph with the heat, though he’s been below that at times in the cold Midwest League this spring. The sinker has decent tail running in on righties, while the four-seam will flash promising ride, and both were significant chase pitches in the AFL. His 83-86 mph slider is back as a whiff generator in 2026, flashing enough depth to look like a potential above-average offering, while his upper-80s changeup lacks enough separation to be a serious weapon against lefties at this stage. Montgomery had control problems dating back to his first year in Tallahassee but has actually tightened up his command coming out of his TJ recovery and rehab, enough to keep getting starting looks. He’s already facing Rule 5 eligibility this upcoming offseason though, and unless there’s a significant jump in stuff in 2026, he might not be far off from seeing if the sinker-slider combo can play up as a righty-heavy option in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: “I am tomorrow, or some future day, what I establish today. I am today what I established yesterday or some previous day.” The other James Joyce could have very well been talking about pitching prospects, including the Mariners one who shares his name. This Joyce has always flown under the radar among a pitching-heavy pipeline, particularly given that he was a 16th-round pick in 2021, signed for just $25,000 and entered his pro career on the heels of struggling to find consistency at Hofstra University. Those challenges continued in his first full pro year at High-A Everett, but he took a notable leap forward in 2023 despite missing the season’s first two months with a forearm strain, climbing all the way to Double-A Arkansas. Joyce operates with a three-pitch mix via a funky delivery. His fastball sits around 93 mph from a lower arm slot, and it's thrown with plenty of life. His 83-84 mph changeup runs and has hard fade to it and his 82-83 mph curveball gets big top to bottom action on it. That combination of funk and movement has allowed him to miss a fair amount of bats despite less than plus stuff. The cause for Joyce’s turnaround last season? A big step forward with command. He dropped his walk rate from 10 to seven percent in the span of a year while keeping hitters in the ballpark, with just one homer surrendered in seven starts after the Double-A promotion. With many questions about his trajectory entering the year, he probably steered back into an arm with starter upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more unheralded Day 3 picks of the 2023 Draft by the A’s who signed for $150,000 as a 13th-rounder out of Texas A&M, Johnston exceeded expectations after an inconsistent four-year career with the Aggies, beginning his first full pro season at Single-A Stockton and continuing through High-A Lansing before finishing at Double-Midland. Combined at the three levels, he posted a 3.88 ERA in 27 games (15 starts) with 137 strikeouts and 40 walks over 99 2/3 innings. Johnston appears to have a much better feel for his three-pitch mix than he did in college. His fastball velocity typically varies from 89-94 mph and can touch up to 96. His split-changeup flashes plus as it continues developing as a true out pitch. His low-80s slider is improving but still a work in progress as it sometimes gives off the look of a slurvy-type offering. Big-bodied at 6-foot-3 and 215 pounds, Johnston has the size and arsenal to stay in a starting role, something that may have seemed like a long shot before he was drafted. His strike-throwing ability has clearly improved as a professional, which helped him quickly rise through multiple levels last season. Maintaining that control along with tightening up the breaking ball as a solid third pitch will be the keys to developing into a possible back-end rotation piece, with a floor of a multi-inning lefty reliever out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Waddell’s first experience with the Draft came in 2019, when he was eligible as a sophomore at Georgia Tech and was selected in the 32nd round by the D-backs. He went back to school, only to see the season shortened by the pandemic and did not have his name called in the truncated five-round Draft in 2020. He had a solid 2021 season and was taken in the fifth round this time around as a senior sign, and the Braves saved some bonus pool money by signing him below slot. He went straight to High-A and hit six homers in 21 games before getting a bump to Double-A and then finishing off his long year with a strong performance in the Arizona Fall League. He began the year in Double-A to start his first full season, but a back strain forced him out of action at the end of May. Waddell has a contact-first approach from the left side of the plate with excellent strike zone judgment, leading to very low strikeout rates and good walk rates, something he brought with him during his pro debut and in the AFL. He added some strength that helped him impact the ball more in 2021, though he’s likely never going to be a huge home run guy. The infielder showed he can play a capable shortstop at Georgia Tech, then spent time at three infield positions during his debut. He likely has the ceiling of a utilityman, but his floor is pretty high and it shouldn’t take him too long to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Signed for $300,000 in January 2021, Perez toiled away in relative anonymity for two summers in the Dominican Summer League. He opened some eyes in his first Spring Training stateside in 2023 and held his own with a jump to full-season Fresno, albeit without much offensive impact. The Rockies sent him back to Single-A to start the 2024 season and some of that impact started showing up, which earned him a late nudge up to High-A Spokane, where he played shortstop for a championship-winning team. Perez is a left-handed hitter who is gradually and continually adding strength. He’s considerably bigger than his listed height and weight, with team officials thinking he’s closer to 6-foot-4 and 210 pounds now. The left-handed hitter has a strong offensive foundation built on making a ton of contact, and despite chasing too much, he rarely strikes out. There’s confidence the combination of that added strength and a little more refinement in his approach will lead to a greater power output after he took a big step forward by hitting 10 homers in 2024. An average runner, Perez can steal a base. And even at his size, he moves very well on the dirt defensively. There is conviction internally that he can stay at short for the long term, but if the impact at the plate keeps coming, he could profile well even if he has to move to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taurek redshirted his freshman year at St. Mary’s in 2023, then played sparingly the next season. He made it count in 2025, earning second-team All-West Coast Conference honors while hitting .328 with 11 homers and helping the Gaels win the WCC tournament and reach NCAA Regional play. The Mariners liked his swing enough to take a $150,000 flier on him in the 13th round of the Draft, and he went out and hit some more, posting a .336 average over 27 games with Single-A Modesto during his pro debut. The one thing that seems certain about Taurek is that he can make a lot of contact with a chance to hit at this level. He’s small and compact and so is his right-handed swing, with simple mechanics and direct to the ball action. He does not strike out much -- just 9.5 percent with the Gaels in ‘25 -- and while he’s very aggressive at the plate and doesn’t walk a ton, he also limits chase. He’s not all that projectable from a physicality standpoint, and it’s unclear whether he’ll have that much impact. Taurek is a bit of a tweener defensively. He doesn’t have enough speed to play center field regularly -- he played left exclusively at St. Mary’s, and that’s where he spent most of his time during his pro debut. But he doesn’t have enough thump to profile as an everyday guy in a corner. The right-right undersized profile is a tough one, but he’s swung the bat well enough to make him interesting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies spread their 2025 international bonus pool money around when the signing period opened in January, handing out a total of 19 six-figure bonuses to help restock the lowest levels of the farm system. Blanco got the fourth-highest bonus ($600,000) to join the organization, and he’s the one who has jumped to the foreground in the early going after a terrific Rookie-level Dominican Summer League debut. The infielder slashed .345/.449/.453 over 54 games to raise excitement for his United States debut in 2026. Blanco is a 6-foot-1, solidly built middle infielder who has already shown a solid approach and feel for hitting. He walked nearly as often as he struck out during his debut, really limiting his swing-and-miss. He has bat speed with a short right-handed swing and has already displayed some ability to drive the ball with carry off his bat. He made good swing decisions during his debut which led to a ton of quality contact, and there could be more power to come as he fills out. The infielder, who will play all of 2026 at age 18, manned shortstop almost exclusively last year and has a chance to stay there with average speed and excellent instincts. He likely could handle moving anywhere on the infield in the future because of his feel for the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A shortstop in Venezuela before changing positions and becoming the top catching prospect in the 2016 international class, Garcia signed for $800,000. He struggled with the physical demands of his new position and pro ball in his first two seasons before he began hitting the ball with more authority and earned short-season Northwest League all-star accolades at age 19 in 2019. Though he has yet to make his full-season debut, the Rangers protected him on their 40-man roster in November. Garcia has soft hands and has become a solid to plus receiver as he has added some much-needed strength. With a strong arm and a quick release, he erased 35 percent of basestealers during his first three years as a pro. He's quicker and more athletic than a typical catcher, and he has remarkably advanced defensive instincts for someone who didn't move behind the plate until 2015. Garcia has put on 30 pounds since turning pro and made some swing changes in 2018 to unlock his bat speed, improving the likelihood that he provides enough offense to become a regular catcher rather than a defensive-minded backup. A switch-hitter with a compact stroke, he has started launching balls in the air more often and could become a 12-15 homer threat. He has been more productive hitting left-handed but club officials think his swing is better from the right side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he signed for a mere $45,000 out of the Dominican Republic, Luciano quickly has become one of the most intriguing players in Houston's 2022 international class. He earned Rookie-level Dominican Summer League All-Star honors in his pro debut, then ranked second in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League with 10 homers after coming to the United States last summer. He smokes balls harder than most teenagers, already producing average exit velocities by big league standards and maxing out at 110 mph. Luciano's power is his most obvious tool, as he not only hits balls hard from the right side of the plate but also has a penchant for driving them in the air to his pull side, giving him at least 25-30 homer upside. Though he batted just .238 in his first two pro seasons, the Astros are encouraged by his bat-to-ball skills. His swing got out of whack and he was making too much suboptimal contact in the first half of the 2024, so Houston had him spent a month on the development list to get back on track. Heftier than his listed 170 pounds, Luciano currently has fringy speed and will have to watch his conditioning so he doesn't lose his quickness and limit his defensive options. Houston would like to see him get leaner and more athletic to enhance his chances of sticking at third base, where he has average-to-solid arm strength. Right field would be Plan B if he slows down and he saw action there last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia, a cousin of Wilmer Flores (both the Giants infielder and the Tigers pitching prospect), joined the Mets system out of Venezuela in June 2021 and made it to full-season ball last year with mixed results. His 5.04 ERA in 80 1/3 innings between Single-A St. Lucie and High-A Brooklyn didn’t quite pop, but he did strike out 106 batters in that span. His 31.9 percent K rate in the Florida State League ranked third among the 46 pitchers on the circuit with at least 60 frames. The 6-foot right-hander throws a 92-94 mph two-seam fastball (topping out at 96.7) out of a low slot that lower-level batters just found difficult to pick up, leading to a strong whiff rate and some weak contact. He primarily paired that with a low-80s sweeping slider that gave him an option with good gloveside break as compared to the armside movement of the two-seamer. He showed the occasional low-80s curveball and mid-80s changeup too, but he understands which pitch is his bread and butter. Garcia walked 14.6 percent of batters faced between those two levels. That’s a slight improvement from 15.6 percent in 2022 but an example of why many believe he’ll remain in a relief role. He’ll still only be 21 years old as he heads back to the High-A level, and there are some in the organization who believe he’s on the precipice of a breakout as he continues to rack up K’s and finetune his command with more stateside experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivas earned NCAA Division II All-America accolades at Indianapolis in 2022 before transferring to Mississippi, where he was the Rebels' best starter as a junior before missing all of 2024 following Tommy John surgery. The Yankees still drafted him in the 16th round because they were intrigued by the deception of his pitches. He returned to the mound last year and recorded a 3.38 ERA with a .166 average-against and a 31 percent strikeout rate while advancing from Rookie ball to High-A. Rivas doesn't fool hitters with a riding fastball that sits at 90 mph and maxes out at 92, but he utilizes it well enough to set up a pair of baffling secondary pitches. He does an excellent job of killing spin on a low-80s changeup with splitter action that generated a 41 percent chase rate and 57 percent swing-and-miss rate in his pro debut. Hitters also consistently swung over the top of his tight low-80s slider. Though Rivas spent his first pro season as a starter, he profiles better as a tricky left-handed reliever. He has to nibble with his below-average heater and get chases with his slider and changeup, so only a third of his pitches landed in the strike zone last year. His competitive makeup also would work well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ross moved all over the collegiate spectrum with time at Eastern Kentucky (2020), Northwest Florida State College (2021) and Georgia (2022). But he lasted only two starts with the Bulldogs before needing Tommy John surgery, and the elbow procedure pushed him down into the 13th round, where the Mets took and signed him for $125,000. A TJ revision pushed his pro debut back to September 2024, and after a trip to the Arizona Fall League, he was ready for a healthy breakout in ’25. Ross accomplished just that, posting a 2.17 ERA with 80 strikeouts in 54 relief innings across three levels before getting called up (but going unused) by New York in late September. The 6-foot-5 right-hander came back with a vengeance in 2025. He ran his four-seamer up to 102 mph and generally sat 96-98 with it. The heater also came with roughly seven feet of extension on average, putting it right on top of hitters. But the velocity is the biggest standout there, and it didn’t miss as many bats as expected in his 28 Triple-A outings, making it more plus than plus-plus. Ross uses his 88-91 mph splitter as his primary weapon against lefties; it averaged only 708 rpm at the Minors’ top level, making it a real spin killer. Ross’ upper-80s slider dominated righty bats with limited gloveside movement, just enough to give him something the other way. He also occasionally flipped in a mid-80s curveball. Ross’ walk rate exploded to 17.3 percent at Syracuse; without a big breaker or armside runner, the movement profile might make him more predictable horizontally, limiting the chase he needs to dominate. His control will be the biggest determining factor in his future MLB role because batters can’t touch his stuff when they do swing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former catcher, Hall redshirted his freshman year at Division II Central Missouri and moved into the Mules’ bullpen as a sophomore with rough results (9.20 ERA in 14 2/3 innings) in 2024. He was showing signs of a big breakout as a junior starter, fanning 19 of the 62 batters he faced, before suffering an elbow injury that required season-ending internal brace surgery. He showed enough in that limited look for the Mets to take him in the sixth round and he signed for below slot at $297,500. Some evaluators believe that, if healthy, Hall could have gone closer to the third round based on his talent. He showed a four-seam fastball up to 98 mph in February before getting hurt, and he threw the pitch out of a low release height, generating a good vertical approach angle. If that velocity -- he was typically closer to the mid 90s early in starts before tapering off -- and movement hold, it could be a plus pitch at maturity. Hall also flashed some good low-80s sliders and upper-70s curveballs with promising depth, and he showed he could at least turn over a decent changeup. The 6-foot-3 right-hander is still very much finding his way as a pitcher, and the elbow surgery put his collegiate development on pause. Mets officials have praised how well Hall has tackled his rehab, and coming out of the Draft, they believe he has enough promising athleticism to deliver strikes and earn starting looks. Hall could be a fun pick to click if his stuff returns to form and holds up in his first taste of the pros in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knipp spent most of his time over his time at Campbell University as a catcher, becoming the starter and putting up big numbers at the plate in 2024. He also returned to the mound to make four relief appearances that year, showing off tremendous arm strength that intrigued several teams. The Mariners initially announced him as a two-way player when taking him in the sixth round of the 2024 Draft, but it seemed like they were inclined to have him focus on the mound only. He didn’t make much progress as elbow trouble in Spring Training resulted in Tommy John surgery, and he missed the 2025 season. Not only is Knipp coming back to pitch at some point in 2026, the Mariners have decided to let him also get at-bats as a DH after seeing him swing it well last spring, taking since-traded prospect Jurrangelo Cijntje deep twice. As a hitter, he’s strength over bat speed with raw power and questions about him making enough contact to get to it. On the mound, he had been up to 96 mph with his fastball last spring, showing good ride and induced vertical break on the pitch to go along with an interesting sweepy 84-85 mph slider. It will be interesting to see how long the Mariners conduct this two-way experiment, with Knipp in his age-24 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a Panamanian pipeline to Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro, Ga.) highlighted by Guardians 2019 first-rounder Daniel Espino, Rodriguez was one of the older prep prospects (19 years, seven months) in the 2023 Draft. The Cubs didn't mind his age because they had some third-round grades on him, and they took him in the 13th round. His development has progressed more slowly than expected, but he finally reached Double-A at the end of last season. Rodriguez operates at 92-95 mph and touches 99 with his fastball, but he's often tentative with it because it lacks good shape and gets whacked when it grabs too much of the plate. He shows much better feel for strikes with his upper-80s changeup that fades and sinks. Like the rest of his arsenal, his tight mid-80s slider plays as an average pitch. Rodriguez works solely out of the stretch with a low release height that creates some deception. He has improved his strike-throwing every season as a pro, though his control and command still need more work if he's going to succeed as a starter. He gets more ground balls than he misses bats and is more likely to wind up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies targeted college pitching in the 2025 Draft, using 13 of their 20 selections on that demographic. Their first six picks were all college arms, with Tallon the last of the half-dozen. The big left-hander spent three years at Duke, almost entirely as a reliever, showcasing swing-and-miss stuff albeit without the ability to command it consistently. A 12.5 career K/9 rate for the Blue Devils stood out and the Phillies took a chance on his bat-missing arm in the sixth round, signing for right around slot. While there was some talk about Tallon being given the chance to start out of the gate, it’s looking like he’s going to be a reliever to kick off his pro career. The 6-foot-5 southpaw is all about his unhittable fastball, a pitch he threw more than 70 percent of the time last year at Duke. It sits in the low 90s and tops out at just 95 mph, but it elicited a miss rate of 34 percent and a 35-percent chase rate in 2025 thanks to a deceptive delivery and a low release height. He’ll need to improve his breaking ball, though his cutter-like slider did miss bats at times. Tallon did throw a mid-80s changeup now and again in college, but will likely focus on his top two pitches as a professional reliever. He needs to harness his command after walking 4.7 per nine last year, but if he can do that and improve his ability to spin the ball, he could move pretty quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top high school left-handers in the 2021 Draft, Coppola went undrafted because he was strongly committed to Florida. He struck out 38 percent of the batters he faced with the Gators, but he also worked just 49 1/3 innings in four years because of back and shoulder ailments. After the Cubs made him a seventh-round pick last July, he fanned 14 in eight innings at Single-A. Coppola uses his huge 6-foot-8 frame and a low arm slot to create wide angle on his fastball, which sits in the low 90s and tops out at 96 with carry and armside run. He could have more velocity in the tank if he can stay healthy and add strength. He also operates with an upper-70s slider with sweep that made it unhittable in college, though it may need more power to succeed in pro ball. Though Coppola has toyed with a mid-80s splitter, he's mainly a two-pitch guy. He doesn't have a smooth delivery and doesn't repeat it well, which has led to injuries and below-average control. He'll begin his pro career as a starter to get some much-needed innings, but the likely best-case scenario is that he cleans up his mechanics and adds some power en route to a bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Auerbach turned down the Rockies as a 40th-rounder out of Saddleback (Calif.) CC in 2018 and transferred to Alabama instead. The co-MVP at the 2019 Cape Cod League All-Star Game, he batted .388 with 12 steals in 17 games while making starts at four positions during the shortened 2020 college season before signing for $20,000 as an undrafted free agent. His offensive production and versatility quickly made him a favorite among Giants officials during his pro debut in 2021, when he forced a promotion to High-A after two months and hit .288/.379/.529 overall. A classic greater-than-the-sum-of-his-parts type, Auerbach is a gritty right-handed hitter who works deeps counts and repeatedly finds his way on base. Though he's just 5-foot-9 and comes with ordinary bat speed, he understands how to turn on pitches and launch them in the air, giving him at least 15-homer power. He possesses fringy speed but has outstanding instincts on the bases, allowing him to steal 30 bases in 37 attempts last year. Auerbach's savvy is obvious on defense as well. He started games at second base, catcher, third base, left field and center field in his first year in pro ball and also appeared in right field. He has average arm strength and profiles best at second base, though he's a legitimate option behind the plate and likely has a super-utility role in his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres signed Cedeño for $300,000 out of Venezuela in July 2018, the max they were allowed due to previous overages in the international period. He showed a good approach in the 2019 Dominican Summer League with a nearly equal K/BB ratio but hit just .193 in 47 games. There was hope a breakout would come when he moved stateside in 2021, only for a meniscus tear to limit him to 18 games in the Arizona Complex League. He jumped to a full-season affiliate last year in Single-A Lake Elsinore and produced a .256/.362/.400 line in 71 contests before getting 12 games in during the Arizona Fall League. Because of his distance from the Majors, the Padres left Cedeño unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft. Cedeño is still more about potential than production. To watch him take batting practice and even swing during the game is to see a switch-hitter with a patient approach, promising bat speed and enough power to reach around a dozen homers in a Major League campaign. In reality, he still hasn’t hit above .256 in a season, perhaps because he trades line drives for more catchable fly balls and still looks a little more comfortable hitting from the left side. An average runner with a decent arm, Cedeño has seen time at all four infield spots, including a little bit of first base in 2022. He’s adequate enough with the glove to handle second base, and that would represent his best opportunity to provide value. Cedeño will be 21 for all the 2023 season, and that will be a proving ground to show his physical gifts can turn into actual performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs signed only one player to a seven-figure bonus when the international window opened in January 2021, and that was Pena, who inked for $1.2 million out of the Dominican Republic. He got off to a solid start at the Dominican Summer League in his first Minor League campaign. Arizona got aggressive with the infielder in 2023, sending him to both the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Visalia in his age-18 season. That aggression caught up to Pena in the California League, where he slashed just .248/.344/.314 in 36 games, but that early taste of full-season ball could set him up well for a return in 2023. The pieces that Arizona evaluators first loved from Pena as an international amateur are still there, for the most part. He shows a smooth swing from the left side, and even when he was struggling with Visalia, he was still taking walks at a 12.7 percent clip. The power remains in the projectable department, considering he homered only four times in 2022 (none of them in Single-A), but his size at 6-foot-1, 170 pounds gives hope that at least average pop is coming. Pena’s lack of speed at this early stage of his career has pushed him from shortstop to second base, and he might end up being average there with the lesser defensive demands. D-backs coaches and evaluators have always loved Pena’s baseball IQ, and that’s part of the reason why they’ve pushed him so quickly to this point. He’ll get a crack at his first full Minor League campaign during his age-19 season in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some teams might have been content with nabbing the No. 5 prospect in the 2024 international class, like the Reds did by signing Adolfo Sanchez for $2.7 million. But Cincinnati was able to go big a second time, nabbing the No. 42 prospect in Mariano for $1.65 million, both of whom they got when the signing period opened in mid-January. It’s the second time in three years the Reds have doled out multiple seven-figure bonuses in one signing period, having done so to bring Ricardo Cabrera and Anthuan Valencia into the fold in 2022. Mariano is a long and lean 6-foot-3 infielder with lots of room to add strength. He’s already shown good contact skills from the right side of the plate, though like with many young players, improved plate discipline and pitch recognition will help. With his aggressive approach, he’s shown the ability spray the ball in the gaps and the thinking is he’s going to fill out that frame and plenty of power is going to come. That will be an important part of his development because most feel he isn’t destined to stick at shortstop long-term. He has good hands and plenty of arm for the premium position, but if he matures physically as expected, he’s likely to slow down too much and will need to move to third, where he should be a capable defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brazoban was ranked No. 38 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international prospects list when the 2024 signing period opened this past January. The Pirates made him their top target, and he became one of nine prospects in the class to get a bonus of $2 million or more by getting that amount exactly. He’ll get his first taste of professional baseball in the Dominican Summer League. A left-handed-hitting and -throwing outfielder, Brazoban has already shown a solid approach and strike-zone knowledge to go along with a knack for consistent hard contact. He has quick hands with excellent bat speed, allowing him to drive the ball line-to-line with authority. There are flashes of over-the-fence power, with more to come as the teenager matures. Lean and athletic, Brazoban runs well, especially underway. He has the kind of frame that should be able to add strength, which could mean more pop and speed. He looks like he could have a chance to stick in center field, but if he slows down as he gets older, a move to the corner isn’t out of the question.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Columbia, Mo., native and Missouri State product, Nivens was the Royals’ fifth round selection in the 2023 Draft, signing for just above slot at $472,500. He was slowed out of the gate in ‘24 with High-A Quad Cities, dealt with a hamstring strain in April and didn’t hit well in the first half with a .168 average through June and a high strikeout rate. He absolutely turned it on in the second half, though, and especially in August, when he hit 13 home runs alone. In all, Nivens slashed .243/.333/.475 with 20 homers and 17 doubles. Nivens clearly has power, especially pull side, and can drive the ball, but he was more aggressive in his first full season of pro ball than what he showed in college, striking out at a 26.9% clip. A lot of that was the inconsistency in his stance with a hand pump, a leg kick that can turn into a hang and a lot of moving parts that get exposed as a pro. He toned that down some in the second half and is continuing to simplify and sync up the movements to get on time, because when he does, it’s above-average power. Nivens fits best in the corner outfield with his power, and most likely left field with his below-average arm strength and average speed once he gets going. There weren’t many hitters who did what Nivens did in August 2024, and his second half surely could give him momentum as he likely heads to Double-A in ‘25. Nivens needs to stay consistent with his movements and keep hitting to reach the big leagues and stick there as a fourth-outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Regarded as one of the top infielders of the 2025 international signing period, Johnson, a Nassau, Bahamas native, received a $1.5 million signing bonus from the A’s. His arrival to the organization comes with considerable hype, with some talent evaluators labeling him as arguably the Caribbean nation’s most polished prospect to ever enter pro ball. Johnson is fully bilingual and has been training with Jose Fortuna, which afforded him the opportunity to play in the United States and the Dominican Republic. Joining his brother, Paris -- a current member of the Dodgers organization -- in the pro ranks, Johnson will get his career started in 2025. Johnson is a bat-first prospect. He has a clean setup at the plate from the right side and utilizes a quick and crisp bat path, which leads to spraying the ball to all fields. He hunts for his pitch and looks to do extra damage, and the power should start to show up as he continues to grow into his 6-foot-2 frame. Johnson is not a burner but his speed is solid. While some evaluators see him as an eventual third baseman, the A’s will get him plenty of reps at shortstop, where he is considered a steady defender up the middle, to begin his journey as a professional.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 The Reds have had success on the international market in recent years finding talent among five-figure signings, headlined by Elly De La Cruz. Jimenez looks to add to that collection after joining the organization in April 2024 for $82,500. After an impressive five-game showing in the Dominican Summer League later that year, the D.R. native got a full run through the circuit last season and posted an .819 OPS across 35 games. He played for the Sydney Blue Sox in the Australian Baseball League over the winter and hit four home runs with 18 RBIs across 38 contests while being nearly 6 years younger than the average competitor. A right-handed hitter, Jimenez shows excellent athleticism in the box and a feel for extra-base pop, although it’s not appeared consistently during game action. There’s some length to his swing and he’ll need to become more selective after running a 25.9 percent strikeout rate (with just a 9.5 percent walk rate) during his extended look in the DSL. But when he squares the ball up, it can really jump off his bat. He posted a 29.2 percent line-drive rate in 2025, which ranked him fourth among all Reds Minor Leaguers with at least 100 plate appearances. As can often be the case at the lower levels, he’s a pull-side fiend with a 58.5 percent rate for his balls in play last year. Jimenez played strictly shortstop during his time in Australia, but the Reds split his time almost 50/50 last year between there and the hot corner. With premier defensive shortstops at the lower levels like Liberts Aponte and Steele Hall, it’s likely that Jimenez moves around a bit, including seeing time at second base. He has average actions on the infield but a solid arm and quick first step, the latter evidenced his 16-for-17 mark on stolen-base attempts through his first 40 pro games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gourson spent three years starting for UCLA (mostly at second base), earning a reputation as a gamer who maximized what tools he had, even earning a spot on Team USA after his sophomore campaign in 2023. He had a solid, albeit unspectacular junior season, finishing with a .909 OPS, and the Pirates took a low-risk flyer on him in the ninth round of the 2024 Draft, signing him for a touch under $190,000. After a nondescript pro debut after signing, he was one of the pleasant surprises of the Pirates' system in 2025, performing well in all facets of the game with High-A Greensboro and Double-A Altoona. Gourson earned a ticket to pro ball because of his approach at the plate, swing decisions and contact skills. There was enough bat-to-ball skill to think he had a chance, and that was apparent in 2025; he kept his strikeouts relatively low, despite a little more swing-and-miss once he got to Double-A, while also posting a walk rate north of 10 percent. What wasn’t expected was the increased impact from the left side of the plate. He gained a few miles per hour in bat speed and that resulted in a huge uptick in exit velocity, allowing for more quality contact. Gourson's instincts and aggressiveness make him an average runner or perhaps a slight tick above that as he stole 31 bags in 34 tries in 2025. He’s seen time at three infield positions -- all but shortstop -- and he should get some reps in the outfield corners as well. If he takes another step offensively, he has a utility role kind of future in the big leagues, and it’s hard to bet against him given his intangibles.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estanista joined the Phillies after signing for just $10,000 in November 2019. Because of the pandemic, the Curacao native wasn’t able to debut professionally until 2021, but he made a solid first impression in the Dominican Summer League. He followed that up with perhaps an even more impressive showing during his U.S. debut in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League in 2022. The right-hander screams projection from his 6-foot-3 frame. He’s long and loose, coming at hitters with a high slot delivery. He can already run his fastball up to 97 mph, and it’s easy to dream on more consistent velocity to come. The pitch has good carry to it and cuts because of that arm slot. His secondary stuff is a work in progress, and while he’s shown some feel to spin a decent slider, his best secondary offering might end up being a newer cutter he throws in the upper 80s, a tight pitch with late depth to it. He’ll continue to work on developing his changeup as well. Between extended spring training and the FCL last year, Estanista probably topped out at around 50 innings, and he needs a lot more reps to improve his command. When he’s in the zone, hitters do not square up the baseball, and the Phillies are excited to see what he can do as he builds up his innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a Marlins' 2024 Draft class filled with prospects hailed for their bat-to-ball skills as amateurs, Trimble stands out as the club's best selection as a fourth-rounder who signed for a below-slot $550,000. After amassing high OBPs with few strikeouts at James Madison, he carried that over to pro ball. Trimble reached Double-A in his first full season and slashed .253/.372/.402 between three levels in his age-22 season. Although he missed two months with a strained hamstring, he made up for lost time with a strong Arizona Fall League performance. While he doesn't have any single standout tool, Trimble is above average in many aspects of the game. Chiefly, he does a lot of the small things quite well. Trimble makes good swing decisions, takes his walks and rarely whiffs. Pitchers haven't found an easy way to get him out, and he proved even more disciplined against more advanced pitching. But while his swing is smooth, he doesn't offer a ton of bat speed. Until he can elevate the ball more, there are questions about his ability to hit more than 10-15 homers in a season. Trimble uses his above-average speed well on the bases to leg out hits and take extra bases. He's a solid athlete on defense who has a chance to stick in center and could be very good in left, even if his arm strength is fringy at best. Trimble is a well-rounded prospect who is quite likely to be a Major Leaguer, even if he may top out as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Karpathios played both ways in his one season at Maryland’s Harford Community College in 2022, and the Padres (via area scout Danny Sader, who scouted Jackson Merrill from the same area) preferred his bat. Looking to go pro rather than stay in school, Karpathios signed with San Diego as a nondrafted free agent that July, just one month after his 19th birthday. While he was a decent performer early in his career, his big breakout came in 2025, when he hit .249/.357/.413 with 15 homers and 73 walks in 124 games between High-A and Double-A. Karpathios ended the year with time in the prospect-rich Arizona Fall League. The Pennsylvania native stands tall from the left side of the box before getting into a leg kick. He rarely chased pitches outside the zone during the 2025 regular season despite increasing his overall swing rate a tad. His exit velocities were loud with a 90th-percentile EV of 105.8 mph, leading to a jump in home-run production. He can hit the ball well to all fields too, although he went the opposite way more than he pulled the ball once he reached Double-A. Getting the barrel out front more often will be a focus when he returns to the upper levels, or else he’s probably limited to 15ish homers per season. Karpathios also whiffs at high levels against non-fastballs, and he swung and missed more across the board in the Fall League (albeit after a long summer). A below-average runner, he has experience in all three outfield spots but is the best fit in right, thanks to his above-average arm strength. Ahead of his Rule 5 decision year, Karpathios is trending toward a lefty bench bat/fourth outfielder, and that’d be a nice development win for an NDFA signing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Colon grew up in Puerto Rico and came to the United States for his senior year of high school in the Miami area. He caught the attention of the Reds, who had some bonus pool money left over as Day 3 began in 2024. They went about $100,000 over the post-10th-round slot to sign him in Round 11. He learned a lot in going to full-season ball during his first full season in 2025, then returned to Daytona and was making big strides in the Florida State League to kick off 2026. A strong and athletic right-hander who is about an inch taller and 20 pounds heavier than his listed height and weight, Colon has future rotation potential if he can improve his command. Right now, he leans heavily on his fastball-split-change combination. It's a plus heater that currently sits around 96 mph and touches 98 mph, getting outstanding induced vertical break on the pitch to elicit strong swing-and-miss rates. He can kill spin and gets good horizontal action on his upper-80s changeup that also can miss bats. His slider thrown at about the same velocity continues to improve. Colon is athletic on the mound, with a short stride that leads to less-than-optimal extension. In addition to rounding out his arsenal with a dependable breaking ball he trusts, Colon needs to continue to improve his control and command. He showed some improvement in that regard to kick off 2026 and he gets high marks for his maturity at age 20, providing optimism he can figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vasquez signed for only $50,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2023, and three years later, he’s proved to be a lesson in the power of patience. Vasquez sported an unseemly 13/24 K/BB ratio over 27 innings in his first pro season, forcing him to repeat the Dominican Summer League in 2024. With a better foundation under him, he found success stateside in 2025 with a 3.80 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 64 innings between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Visalia. His 28.1 percent strikeout rate was 10th-best among 42 Minor Leaguers aged 19 or younger (min. 60 IP). The 6-foot-2 right-hander sits 94-96 mph with his four-seamer and can run it up to 98 already, a big driver of the excitement on his profile. There’s room for even more power behind the heater as he enters his 20s, and he mixes in a sinker for a different fastball look too. His slider shows good sweep and spin, running away from righties with regularity. It flashes at least above average, but Vasquez’s command of it could use improvement with too many missing the mark. He added a kick-change that shows early promise but wasn’t often used in the California League. Vasquez clearly has arm talent, the type that earns you long looks at starting. But until he establishes more consistent command of the breaking ball, his control is going to be a major question mark. Entering 2026, he’s walked at least 11 percent of the batters he’s faced at every level, and that number was up to 15.4 in his five Single-A starts. He’ll be the age of a college sophomore as he returns to Visalia this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arias originally signed as a shortstop for $10,000 with the Blue Jays in July 2018, but he never played in an official game before getting released in May 2020. The Cubs picked him up as a pitcher in January 2021 and he spent most of the next two seasons figuring out how to throw strikes in Rookie ball. He broke out in 2023, fanning 110 in 81 1/3 innings between two Class A stops, but his control regressed significantly during a rocky 2024 season before the Cubs designated him for assignment this January and dealt him to the Yankees for cash considerations. Arias presents an unusual look to hitters, working from a nearly sidearm slot and slinging fastballs that sit at 94-97 mph and touch 99 with heavy sinking and tailing action. He struggled to locate his heater well in 2024, however, and it got pounded. His changeup shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch with upper-80s velocity to go with fade and sink and his low-80s slider devours righties when he stays on top of it and creates some late bite, though he often missed badly with both offerings.
