While Arias' low arm slot and whippy arm action create deception and electric life, they also limit his ability to provide strikes. The movement on his pitches makes them difficult to land in the zone at times and he may never have enough control or command to be a starter. Making him a full-time reliever in 2024 didn't improve his strike-throwing, but he could become a late-inning option if he figures it out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of Georgia's best prep pitching prospects in 2019, David slid to the Diamondbacks in the 35th round amid signability concerns and opted to attend Auburn instead. He never pitched for the Tigers during the pandemic-truncated 2020 season before bouncing from Gordon State (Ga.) JC to Northwest Florida State JC to NAIA program Southeastern (Fla.) before the Astros drafted him in 2024's 10th round as a fifth-year senior. He moved from Single-A to Double-A in his first full pro season, compiling a 3.47 ERA with 87 strikeouts in 85 2/3 innings. David's fastball parks at 95-96 mph and peaks at 98, and he maintained that velocity throughout 2025. It features carry and armside run. His tight mid-80s slider doesn't get a lot of chases but does generate a lot of in-zone swings and misses, and he can turn it into an 89-91 mph cutter on occasion. After focusing primarily on his heater and slider in college, he has worked on incorporating a low-80s curveball and an upper-80s changeup with depth but has trouble landing both for strikes. There's effort in David's delivery that has prevented him from throwing consistent strikes, so he's more of multi-inning reliever than a starter in the long run. He spent the first two months of 2025 in the rotation at Single-A Fayetteville before shifting to the bullpen. He'll pitch at age 25 this season, and the less challenging role will accelerate his timetable to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Molina stood out in two years at Texas Tech and transferred to Arkansas as a junior in 2024. He dealt with ankle and control issues with the Razorbacks, causing him to go to the Brewers in the seventh round of the 2024 Draft. The Rangers acquired him in his first offseason in a deal for Grant Anderson, and he was moved again to the Cardinals at the 2025 Trade Deadline as part of the Phil Maton return. He finished with a 3.10 ERA, 119 strikeouts and 43 walks in 95 2/3 innings across Single-A and High-A in his first full season. The 6-foot-2 southpaw sat 90-93 mph with his four-seamer in 2025 but got a healthy amount of whiffs on it thanks to impressive ride up in the zone. He showed improved velocity this spring, averaging 93.2 mph on the heater (touching 95.8) in a pair of Grapefruit League outings, and with the 18-20 inches of induced vertical break, the extra heat could make the fastball a plus pitch in his age-22 season. Molina typically earns his best grades for his low-80s changeup that gets almost exactly 10 mph separation from the four-seamer and a ton of fade and armside run, but he drops the release enough on the pitch that it could become a tell for upper-level bats. He showed both 82-85 mph sliders and 79-82 mph sweepers this spring and occasionally sprinkles in a slow mid-70s curve. Even with the improved stuff, Molina must show he can find the zone more consistently as he climbs the ladder. His walk rate moved to the double-digits at High-A before the trade and escalated to 16.1 percent. He’ll need the breaking stuff, particularly the sweeper, to help keep batters off the predictability of his fastball-changeup mix and improve his starting chances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A year after signing Bryce Bush for $290,000 in the 33rd round of the 2018 Draft, the White Sox used an over-slot bonus and late pick to snag another high school third baseman from the Midwest, nabbing Gladney for $225,000 in the 16th round. Gladney stayed on Bush's path by hitting for power in the Rookie-level Arizona League during his pro debut, going deep eight times in 50 games. His 2020 development was restricted to instructional league after the coronavirus pandemic wiped out the Minor League schedule. Gladney's carrying tool is his plus raw power, which he creates with bat speed, projectable strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame. He already has a feel for driving the ball in the air with his right-handed stroke and exhibits pop to all fields. He comes with serious swing-and-miss concerns, however, posting a 37 percent strikeout rate in his debut because his approach and pitch-recognition skills are rudimentary. Though Gladney moves well for his size and can flash average speed, he figures to lose a step as he matures physically. The White Sox had him focus on improving his footwork and the consistency of his arm stroke during instructs and think he can become an average third baseman. While he has solid arm strength and decent hands, scouts outside the organization question his range and reliability at the hot corner and project him as a left fielder or first baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers saw a chance to build organizational depth and some offensive upside at catcher when they drafted Crouch in the 11th round in 2021 following a breakout junior season at Central Florida. But even they weren’t expecting how well he adjusted to the pro game. After two strong weeks at Single-A Lakeland, Crouch moved to High-A West Michigan and helped lead a Whitecaps turnaround, taking ownership of a young pitching staff while providing clutch hits. That earned him a September promotion to Double-A Erie following a season-ending injury to Dillon Dingler. Crouch doesn’t really have one standout tool so much as he does a lot of things well. He’s sneaky athletic behind the plate with a strong enough arm to control a running game. He improved his receiving skills as the season went on but still has a lot of room to grow there. Similarly, he has enough power in his quick swing to punish mistakes but is more effective as a situational hitter. He batted .346 with 51 RBIs with runners in scoring position at West Michigan despite just eight extra-base hits. More impressively, he struck out just 14 times in those situations. Crouch was one of the more intriguing players in the Tigers system for some evaluators, thanks in part to his sudden emergence. With a strong work ethic and an effort to get stronger, he has a chance to reach the Majors in time, likely profiling as a backup. It’ll be interesting to see how the Tigers move Crouch and Dingler, who aren’t far apart in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez flew under the radar in the 2016-17 international class, signing for just $75,000 out of Venezuela. He took a few years to find his footing, but he absolutely wowed in 2022, especially when making the jump to High-A Everett, where he slashed .342/.477/.583 with seven homers and 27 RBIs in 35 games to give him 27 homers and 114 RBIs (second among all Minor League hitters) in total. There’s a chance he taps out because of his speed and defense, but the Mariners are bullish on how he finished the season, which he capped off with time in the Arizona Fall League. The big focus for him into 2023 will be finding better counts to continue to do damage, which should help him better tap into his considerable raw power. He can be aggressive and expand the zone too often at times, though he offsets the swing-and-miss with a willingness to take walks. When he’s putting the ball in play, he’s found far more line drives and fly balls, a big reason why he surpassed his 2021 season home run total by June last year. Likely destined for first base, Perez has legit pop from the right side and the exit velocities to show for it, but he’ll need to continue raking to progress -- his big league trajectory depends on it, especially given the defensive limitations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's 2025 Delaware high school player of the year, Mitchell won a state championship at Cape Henlopen HS (Lewes), a program that has produced big leaguers Mason Fluharty and Zack Gelof. The Astros drafted him in the seventh round, making him the state's highest selection since 2012 Rangers second-rounder Jamie Jarmon. Mitchell signed for $797,500, tripling his slot value and breaking Jarmon's Delaware record of $601,500. More physical than most high schoolers at 6-foot-3 and 205 pounds, Mitchell features plus raw power. He needs to learn to let that pop come naturally rather than hunting home runs, which leads to his left-handed stroke getting too long and uphill. He hits balls hard but doesn't have much experience facing quality pitching, so he'll have to prove that he can hit premium velocity and breaking pitches. As a catcher, Mitchell stands out most with solid arm strength that will play better once he improves his footwork. He needs to clean up his receiving and blocking and may need some time to adjust to handling pro pitchers. He's a below-average runner but not bad for his position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guedez headlined a group of 2025 international signees for the A’s along with Shotaro Morii and Ayden Johnson, signing out of Venezuela for around $1.5 million. He was regarded as one of the top hitters in the class, and that showed through in a very successful pro debut as he hit .359 with an .885 OPS in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old. Next up for him is to make his stateside debut. Guedez has a knack for hitting. His swing is smooth through the zone with good barrel control and impressive hand-eye coordination that allows him to get to pitches both inside and outside of the zone. He does tend to chase at a high rate, though that is not uncommon for a teenager. There isn’t much power to his game at this point, and the A’s are unsure how much will come even as he fills out his 5-foot-11 frame. Guedez’s defense is considered average with an average arm, which likely limits him to a corner outfield spot. He was one of the more fun players to watch for the A’s player development staff down in the Dominican Republic this past summer, but with his no standout defensive attribute and underwhelming power, he will have to rely on his strong hit tool to carry him through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s not always a straight line of progress and development for young players -- especially pitchers -- and repeating a level can be just what the doctor ordered. Such seems to be the case for Acosta, who didn’t make any waves when he signed for $10,000 in April 2022 and struggled with his first professional action in the Dominican Summer League. But a return to the DSL last year paid dividends as he led the hitting-friendly circuit with a 1.17 ERA while striking out 12.4 per nine. Acosta is a strong and athletic 6-foot-1 right-hander who might have the chance to stick in a rotation. He improved the command of his 92-96 mph fastball in 2023, a big reason for his more consistent success. He complements the heater will with a low-80s slider that flashes above-average and served as an out pitch. He continues to work on finding a changeup, but it’s a distant third. Being able to find that third offering will be key for him if he wants to remain a starter. So will his ability to find the strike zone more consistently. He made strides in that regard in 2023 and continued refinement will help him stay in games longer. Still a teenager, there’s time for him to iron those things out as he comes stateside for the first time, with his fastball-slider combination likely playing up in shorter stints should he need to move to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The big catch of the 2023 international signing period for the Phillies is no doubt Starlyn Caba, who fetched a $3 million bonus. But it might be a much more productive class than just the shortstop and the Phillies have done it with some bargain shopping, getting Eduardo Tait for $90,000 and De La Cruz for just $20K. The big right-hander put his name on the map with a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, striking out nearly 12.5 per nine over 31 1/3 innings of work. De La Cruz has size and arm strength already working in his favor at 6-foot-6. He already had plenty of fastball, getting his heater routinely into the mid-90s. He couples it with a solid mid-80s slider with sweep that misses a lot of bats. He has shown some feel for a changeup, but it’s well behind the other two offerings. A former basketball player, De La Cruz is relatively new to pitching, so while he needs to refine his command, the fact that he showed any feel for pitching out of the gate is encouraging. His athleticism plays on the mound in a Taijuan Walker kind of way (Walker’s first sport was also basketball) and the Phillies are excited to see what he can do stateside for the first time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers swiped Pacific Northwest prep pitchers away from Oregon State commitments in consecutive Drafts. The more recent, Swanson, was a two-sport star in Washington, the son of a high school basketball coach who was the top-ranked high school player in the state. The Tigers drafted Swanson in the ninth round and wooed him to pro ball with an above-slot $722,500 bonus. Swanson’s athleticism has allowed him to blossom as a pitcher at a later stage than others. His fastball ranged from the low-to-mid 90s in high school but is more of a power offering with carry since working with the Tigers’ pitching department to refine his delivery. His high-spin slider has a lot of movement and depth. His changeup needs work but could be the difference between starting and relieving. The Tigers drafted Swanson fully knowing he could take longer to develop but believing in the athlete and competitor. His introduction to pro ball will be delayed after he underwent Tommy John surgery ahead of the 2025 campaign, knocking him out for what would have been his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 While Joswa Lugo received the highest bonus of any player from the Angels’ signing class at the start of the 2024 international signing period, De La Rosa received the most of any pitcher signed by the organization, getting $300,000 to get his pro career started. He did that in the Dominican Summer League and put his best foot forward out of the gate, finishing with a 2.79 ERA, .211 BAA and a 9.9 K/9 rate in a typically hitting-friendly environment. At 6-foot-4, the hope is De La Rosa can develop into an innings-eating workhorse-type starter. His fastball maxes out at 96 mph and typically sits 91-94, though the hope is more velocity will come as he matures. He has a solid 77-82 mph slider that flashes above average and could develop into an out pitch. There’s an upper-80s changeup in there, but it’s too firm and it’s behind the other two offerings. For his first time out, De La Rosa did a decent job of being in and around the strike zone. He’ll be just 18 as he comes stateside for the 2025 season and he’s a long way away, but with improved command and velocity to go along with a solid third pitch, he has a big league starter ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years of inconsistent work at the University of Maryland, Staine transferred to Central Florida for the chance to have a more certain role. While a minor back issue and a blister slowed him down some, his ability to pitch well -- mostly as the Knights’ Friday night starter -- allowed him to land in the fifth round with the Rockies. While he didn’t pitch competitively after signing, he did make a good impression with the club's player development staff during instructs. A 6-foot-4 right-hander with a loose arm and some athleticism on the mound, Staine has four pitches that give him the chance to start. His fastball averages around 93 mph and touches 96 and it features good ride to it, which plays well at the top of the zone when he needs it to. His low-80s slider should be an average breaking ball, and he has a slower curve he can land early in counts. He’ll flash a decent changeup, but will need to commit to it more after not throwing it much in college. More than anything, the Rockies love how Staine goes right after hitters with a repeatable up-tempo delivery. He’ll need to refine his command to remain a starter long term, but the organization feels like he has the mentality to develop into a guy who can navigate through a lineup multiple times and be a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coba wouldn’t have popped on many radars as a $10,000 signing out of Venezuela in May 2024, and he was initially used out of the Tigers’ Dominican Summer League bullpen in his first season with rough results (14 ER, 11 BB, 14 K in 12 1/3 innings). He returned to the DSL as a starter in ’25 and was much more in control there. Coba has moved to the Florida Complex League this season for his first taste of affiliated stateside ball, and his early work in the Sunshine State has solidified his standing as one of the more intriguing young arms in the Detroit system. All three of the 6-foot right-hander’s pitches show promise. Coba can run his four-seamer into the mid-90s while generating 18-20 inches of ride, but right now, he can leak some of that velocity over the length of his outings. If he can continue to build strength and sit 94-96 rather than 92-95, the heater would become a true plus pitch. His 79-83 mph slider shows gyro shape, dropping more downward than to the gloveside, but it can play well off the heat running up and in on righties. His 83-86 mph changeup kills spin while showing similar armside run to the four-seamer except it tumbles more, leading to empty swings when it’s on. Coba throws with some energy on the bump -- the arm speed helps sell the changeup -- and when he misses, it’s because he’s yanking the ball a bit too much to his gloveside. Still, it was promising to see him cut his walk rate by more than half between his two DSL stints, and with three potentially above-average pitches in his arsenal, he’ll deserve more starting looks as he climbs the domestic ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Kahle first got to the University of Washington in 2017 after playing his high school ball in Southern California, he got to learn under the wing of Joey Morgan, who ended up being a third-round pick of the Tigers that June. Kahle took over as the Huskies' everyday backstop the following year, then led the team in all three triple-slash categories (.339/.506/.532) during a breakout junior campaign before signing with Milwaukee as a fourth-round pick in 2019. Kahle's uptick in production during his sophomore and junior years has the Brewers believing that he'll at least hit for average in pro ball. He's shown the ability to catch up to good fastballs with solid bat speed and recognizes breaking stuff well. He has an advanced approach and takes his share of walks, giving him strong on-base skills on the top of the natural hitting ability. While Kahle’s power plays mostly to the gaps, he does stay inside the ball well and shows some ability to turn on pitches for some over-the-fence pop. Short and stocky, Kahle is a below-average runner and doesn't have that much agility behind the plate. But he has improved his receiving and blocks well, and while his arm strength is fringy, it's accurate. Whether Kahle can unlock all of his hitting ability will likely determine his ultimate role. If he can make the necessary offensive gains, Kahle has the chance to play a long time, with a floor as a very good backup and the chance to be a solid regular if everything clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wherever Anthony has been, he’s hit. Over two years at Iowa, he posted a combined .372/.476/.686 line, but he wasn’t drafted because he had been suspended for betting on college sports (not his own team). Since the Phillies signed him as a nondrafted free agent in the summer of 2023 for $125,000, he’s continued to rake, making his way all the way to Triple-A in 2025 and carrying a career .324/.402/.467 line as a pro into the 2026 season. Anthony is a smart right-handed hitter with a knack for contact. He limits his swing-and-miss, with a career 17.8 percent miss rate as proof, and loves going the other way for base hits. He’s cleaned up his body and added some strength, registering better hard-hit rates last year, and he can drive the ball to all fields for extra bases. But he has a tendency to hit the ball on the ground too much, and his chase rate (38 percent) went up when he went to Triple-A. He’s a hit-over-power guy for sure, but finding a bit more loft and leverage would help. That’s because he’s limited to first base only, putting pressure on him to be more of a run producer. He’s a fine defender at first, but he’s not super athletic, and the right-right profile at the position is tough. Because of that, he gives off some Darin Ruf type vibes, and Ruf did carve out a career that included parts of nine seasons in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guzman signed for only $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in September 2022 and played in the Dominican Summer League the two following seasons without standing out much statistically -- his highest seasonal OPS down there was .691. He came stateside all the same for 2025 and broke out in a big way with a .302/.375/.524 line and 10 homers in 75 games between the Florida Complex League and Single-A St. Lucie. His 18 extra-base hits in 26 games following his debut in full-season ball on July 25 were second-most in the Florida State League over that span, trailing only Top 100 prospect Alfredo Duno’s 22. Standing 6-foot-4 and batting from the right side, Guzman begins with his hands held high above his head before loading up with a toe tap to unleash his power. He’s up there to hack -- he ran a 43 percent chase rate in the FSL -- but he can show adaptability on spin inside the zone too. When he runs into a ball, he really runs into it with his strength. Guzman ran a 108.5 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity at Single-A, better than Konnor Griffin’s 107.7 in the same league. It’s always going to be that pop that intrigues most, though the overall approach will be a restrictor plate unless he makes more adjustments. A well-below-average runner, Guzman has seen time at all four corners of the infield and outfield during his three professional seasons. His primary focus was at first base in 2025 with some left and right field mixed in. He’s almost certainly going to be locked into the cold corner long-term, but his slugging ability gives him a fighting chance to clear the high offensive bar there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kent State is an underrated pitching factory that has produced multiple big leaguers over the past decade. Albright should be the next in line after making a successful transition from relieving to starting. The D-backs selected Albright in the sixth round of the 2021 Draft and signed him for slot value ($301,600) before sending him to Low-A Visalia to begin his professional career. His debut was brief as he threw just 23 1/3 innings, but he struck out 22 and posted a 3.47 ERA. A hard worker, Albright throws a low-90s fastball which is expected to increase in velocity as he tightens up his mechanics. As is, the pitch plays up because he uses his 6-foot-4 frame and three-quarters arm slot to create downhill plane. An upper-70s curveball and sinking changeup are Albright’s best offspeed weapons, with both offerings grading out as above average. He rounds out his arsenal with a sharp, low-80s slider, though sometimes the pitch has more cutterish actions. A fully developed slider will give Albright an intriguing mix of four above-average pitches. His command could still use some refinement, though he has shown an ability to adjust as necessary. His competitiveness adds to his No. 4 starter upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Endersby was recruited as an infielder but moved to the mound at Cal State Fullerton, where he totaled 16 2/3 innings in three years before transferring to Concordia (Calif.). He made just five starts at the NCAA Division II level during the shortened 2020 season, yet impressed the Astros enough to sign for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent. He spent most of his 2021 pro debut in Double-A and struck out 110 in 97 innings. Endersby employs the north-south attack pattern that Houston favors. He goes after hitters with a 92-95 mph four-seam fastball with high spin rates and carry up in the zone and an upper-70s curveball with downer break. He also has a harder slider with sweeping action and a nascent changeup that lags behind the rest of his offerings. Endersby lacks physicality but he's athletic and has a quick arm. His control and command come and go, as does the consistency of his secondary pitches, so it's more likely that he winds up as a reliever than a starter. If he moves to the bullpen and concentrates on his fastball and curveball, he could reach the big leagues in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While fellow infielder Nestor Miranda was the Tigers’ headline signing of the 2024 international class, Dickson had the better introduction to pro ball after signing for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He was one of the more impressive performers for the Tigers in the Dominican Summer League and earned a spot in the DSL All-Star Game. Dickerson has a lanky, athletic build with a solid swing that becomes more formidable as he physically matures. He had a leg kick when he signed, but the Tigers worked to quiet his stance. He was pull heavy in the DSL with a high rate of ground balls and fly balls and good extra-base power without a home run, but his aggressive approach was tempered by a good eye at the plate for his age. He’s an opportunistic baserunner whose high stolen-base total in the DSL came with a good success rate. He moves well at shortstop but could move positions as he fills out. Dickson’s success in the DSL should move him to the Florida Complex League as an 18-year-old. He has the tools to become a promising prospect, but his physical maturation will have a big impact on his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fontenelle bounced around during his college days, starting at the University of Washington in 2021, then moving to McLennan Junior College the following year and then on to Texas Christian for his Draft year in 2023. He went to the College World Series that year and finished with an OPS over 1.100, helping him land in the seventh round with the Angels. In a very unsurprising development for anyone who follows the organization, Fontenelle went up to Double-A to start his first full season and was playing well when his season ended after just 22 games after a slide into second caused both a dislocated ankle and fractured fibula. He made it back to play in the Arizona Fall League, where he really struggled to shake off the rust at the plate. A big switch-hitter the Angels think just fell through the cracks as teams focused on Horned Frogs teammate Brayden Taylor, Fontenelle has the chance to fit the corner-infield profile well offensively. When he’s healthy, he can hit the ball very hard with excellent exit velocities. He didn’t swing and miss much in college with a solid overall approach, and while his strikeout rate ticked up during his pro debut and in the AFL, it’s too small of a sample size to draw any conclusions there. Fontenelle has only played third with the Angels, and while he’s big and a below-average runner, he has good instincts (which help him steal some bases despite the lack of quickness) and actions, with enough arm to have a chance to stick at the hot corner. He’s played first base and even a little left field in the past, so there are some options should a move be needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After not being recruited during his high school career, Yeaman took the junior college route to play for College of the Canyons. Though he missed a lot of time over two years there because of multiple injuries and non-throwing shoulder surgeries, he did manage to hit .400 and showed enough in his limited time for UC Irvine to join the Anteaters lineup. He had a big 2025, finishing with an OPS over 1.000, and as college performers tend to do, he rushed up Draft boards. The Orioles took him in the fourth round and signed him for just over $600,000, sending him out to get his professional feet wet with Single-A Delmarva. Yeaman brings a strong track record of hitting to the Orioles organization. He's adept at finding the barrel, doesn't chase and draws walks. He can really punish fastballs, and he puts up good in-zone contact numbers. There's some strength and bat speed, helping him drive the ball to all fields, with some home run juice to his pull side. He's a fringy runner who likely won't be a basestealing threat at the next level. Because of that lack of speed, Yeaman's range is a bit shy for shortstop long term, and his average arm also could hold him back. He played more third than short during his brief debut with Delmarva. Carving out a career as a utility type might be the best outcome, though he could potentially be an offensive-minded second baseman should the O's shift him to the right side of the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Southern California’s Notre Dame HS helped produce Hunter Greene and Giancarlo Stanton, and Gurevitch is aiming to be the next big name from the program, though his path took him in state to the University of San Diego before the pros. He showed steady gains over his three years with the Toreros before exploding with a .371/.477/.681 line and 17 homers in 56 games as a junior. The Cardinals took him in the third round, signed him for slot at $879,000 and sent him to Single-A Palm Beach for 22 games where he struggled in the late summer. Gurevitch has a straight-on stance from the left side of the box, featuring a crouch and hands held high. He relies on those hands to drive his contact, without a big load in his lower half, but that was enough to make lots of loud impact during his final spring on campus. His clean mechanics made him look like a potential above-average hitter coming out of school with at least average pop. Fair or not, some of his reddish flags from college glowed crimson in the Florida State League, namely his high chase and whiff rates on sliders and his inability to catch up to pitches at 94 mph or above. That exposure, along with an offseason to prepare, could help Gurevitch erase those concerns in his first full campaign in ’26. Gurevitch got some time at third base with San Diego, but many believed he was always headed to first base. Indeed, all of his starts with Palm Beach came at the cold corner. He’ll need to hit to be valuable there, but he earned good reviews for his leadership coming out of school, adding to the belief that he could take well to St. Louis’ hitting development department.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays found Shaw in the ninth round of the 2023 Draft out of Lambrick Park Secondary School in British Columbia and signed him away from an NCAA commitment to Xavier with a $282,500 bonus. This was a strong piece of scouting by the Blue Jays' staff, who knew Shaw well going back to his appearance in their Canadian Futures Showcase. Shaw got a brief look at pro ball in ‘23, appearing in nine games in the FCL. Shaw profiles between second base and the outfield defensively, with some projecting the outfield as his likeliest landing spot after he’s worked out some throwing issues. The Blue Jays already like the style of at-bats they see from Shaw, grinding out deep counts and competing consistently. He’s naturally athletic in the box, too, not getting bogged down by rigid mechanics. Right now, Shaw’s contact tool is comfortably ahead of his power, but the Blue Jays are optimistic that he can develop some pop in the coming years. Shaw represents upside, which is exactly what the Blue Jays need more of in their system, particularly when it comes to players with the potential to play the outfield long-term. This will be a fun development project for the Blue Jays’ staff, particularly if Shaw’s pop can step forward as his leading tool and pull him up through the Minor Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading Vanderbilt with 15 homers as a junior and turning down the Marlins as a 31st-rounder in 2018, Scott bashed 14 more longballs and won a College World Series championship with the Commodores the next spring. A $50,000 senior sign taken in the 10th round of the 2019 Draft, he became an organization and fan favorite last year when he raked in Low-A and High-A while living in a camper with teammate Joe Davis. He finished his first full pro season by batting .338/.430/.606 with eight homers in 39 games in High-A. Scott not only has one of the better bats in Boston's system, but he also has one of the best approaches as well. He has an efficient left-handed swing, controls the strike zone and uses the entire field. His strength creates plus raw power and he lets his home runs come naturally rather than swinging for the fences. Scott made 39 starts at first base, 25 on the outfield corners, 18 at catcher and 14 at DH last year. Boston will give him more time behind the plate in 2022 and he has the desire and work ethic to make it as a backstop. He's a potentially average to solid receiver with some aptitude for framing, though he has fringy arm strength at best. With well below-average speed and a subpar arm, he doesn't offer much defensive value elsewhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing high school baseball at Westlake HS (Ga.), Nowlin went to Chipola Junior College in Florida, and while he didn’t throw a ton -- 60 innings in total over two seasons, almost all in relief -- he impressed with his ability to miss bats. The left-hander didn’t hurt his stock by throwing well in the Cape Cod League in 2021, with the Twins taking him in the 19th round of the Draft that year and going a bit over the Day 3 slot to sign him for $160,000. Developing him cautiously, he both started and relieved in his first full season, reaching High-A at the end of the year. Because of Nowlin’s lack of deep resume, he’s still pretty raw, but his performance as a pro has spoken for itself. He struck out about 36 percent of batters he faced in 2022. His fastball averaged around 92 mph and topped out at 95-96 with high spin and good arm side life, with the potential for more consistent velocity as he gets more physical. He missed a ton of bats with both his low-80s slider, which is more of a north-south pitch with depth than a sweeping breaker, and a mid-80s changeup that was effective more because of the velocity differential than the action of the pitch. Nowlin is going to have to refine his command, with an inflated walk rate (4.6 BB/9 in 2022), especially as he moves up the ladder and faces hitters less likely to chase out of the zone. If he does that, he has the chance to start. If not, his stuff could play well as a lefty reliever in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After three years of relief work at Kansas State, including a junior season that catapulted him onto Draft boards, he went in Round 14 in the Angels’ all-pitching Draft in 2021. Los Angeles challenged him with a Double-A assignment in his first full season and he responded. The left-hander led the Southern League in saves and was named its Reliever of the Year, missing a ton of bats and giving up very few hits in the process. Torres does it from a 6-foot frame and with average stuff, but his combination of a lower slot -- the ball looks like it’s coming from the first-base dugout -- and feel for using what he has helped him strike out 14.3 per nine innings and hold hitters to a .143 average in 2022. His fastball only sits around 90 mph, but the angle and carry up in the zone helped it elicit a 36-percent miss rate last year. His low-80s slider can also miss bats, a sweeping breaking ball that flashes above average. He continues to work on a changeup to give him another look for right-handed hitters, but no one squared him up from either side in the Southern League. The Angels love Torres’ athleticism and competitiveness on the mound, and while he could stand to cut the walk rate down a little, he’s around the zone enough to project future success. The overall stuff might mean he doesn’t get the ball in high-leverage situations in the big leagues, but he’s not far from getting the chance to impact the Los Angeles bullpen and he’s shown he is far from afraid of the spotlight.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The University of North Carolina at Pembroke has never had a player from its Division II program make the big leagues, though it now has two pitchers in pro ball with that chance. River Ryan is getting close to Los Angeles with the Dodgers. Bowen has just one year of pro ball on his résumé after the Mariners took him in Round 13 of the 2022 Draft, and he spent the year with Single-A Modesto after an up-and-down college career in which he mostly started as a sophomore and mostly came out of the bullpen as a junior. The Twins saw enough upside potential to get the right-hander in the late January Jorge Polanco deal. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has more projection than the typical college arm. With a lanky and wiry build, Bowen is a terrific athlete with room to add strength to his frame, giving hope that his stuff could tick upward as he matures. Right now he has a fastball that’s typically in the 91-94 mph range but touched as high as 97 at times in 2023. He has both a sweepy upper-70s slider that could eventually be an out pitch as well as a shorter, harder cutter that's thrown around 85 mph. He also has a changeup with depth typically around 84 mph. Bowen will need to refine his control and command for him to have the chance to start at the next level. He’s a good athlete on the mound, so there’s hope he can learn to repeat his delivery and find the zone more consistently. He’ll get the chance to prove he can stick in a rotation, though his stuff would tick up even more in shorter stints coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seven years after the Tigers took a Draft flier on a college pitcher with mixed results a year removed from Tommy John surgery (Tarik Skubal), they went a similar route with Leys, who missed the 2024 season recovering from surgery before taking the mound for the University of Maine in 2025. Leys won America East Pitcher of the Year with a 2.69 ERA and 74 strikeouts in 67 innings, better than his first two seasons with the Black Bears. The Tigers drafted him in the fourth round, five rounds earlier than Skubal, and signed him for $574,900. While Leys isn’t big for a pitcher, he has a quick, fluid delivery with a big leg kick and a three-quarters arm angle. His fastball can touch 96 mph, setting up a slider and a changeup both in the low 80s. Leys greatly improved his strike throwing and command upon his return from surgery, cutting his walk rate in almost half from his first two seasons while ticking up his strikeout rate. The Tigers have been aggressive at times starting out college pitchers in full-season ball, and could do the same with Leys, who made an impression in Spring Training. If he can hold his command while adding more swing-and-miss, he could force his way up the system quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Olejnik started his college career at Triton College in Illinois before heading to Oklahoma for his sophomore year. After pitching sparingly for the Sooners, he was on the move again, this time to Miami (Ohio), where he missed bats in a swingman/multi-inning reliever role. He threw really well over five starts in the Draft League in 2024, helping him land in the sixth round with the Angels, where he signed for a below-slot bonus of $197,500. He proved to be durable during his first full season of pro ball, amassing 128 2/3 innings with Single-A Inland Empire, capping things off with a playoff win. The thing that stands out the most with Olejnik is his size, with the right-hander coming in at 6-foot-11. He does a solid job with his four-seam fastball, coming from a lower slot. He backs it up with a decent sweeper and a changeup, both of which can flash above-average at times. He needs tighter action to miss more bats on his breaking ball and his changeup needs more depth. There are some who feel the addition of a cutter and a two-seam fastball would help round out his repertoire. For a guy his size, Olejnik does a decent job repeating his delivery and he tends to be around the zone. Timing up his mechanics will always be an issue, as they are for any super-tall pitcher. There are starter characteristics here, especially if Olejnik can get some more bat-missing action out of his secondary offerings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Puerto Rico, Ortiz slid over to Florida’s IMG Academy for high school ball as a two-way player who was initially known more as a shortstop. The Nationals took him in the 20th round of the 2022 Draft, as a pitcher, but he opted to head to junior college instead, playing both ways for Chipola. The Reds took him as a draft-and-follow in 2023, then saw enough progress on the mound back at Chipola to sign him for $225,000 that May. He got his feet wet the summer after signing, then threw over 90 effective innings with full-season Daytona in 2025. An athletic six-foot right-hander, Ortiz continues to get better the longer he’s been focused on pitching only. His fastball is gaining velocity and he throws it mostly in the 90-95 mph range with some armside run, and there could be more consistent velo to come in the future. The Reds feel his 84-87 mph changeup is ahead of his 83-86 mph slider but not by much, and there’s conviction he could end up having three above-average pitches down the road. In addition to the stuff ticking up, Ortiz used his athleticism to find the strike zone more consistently in 2025 and it’s not difficult to believe that he will eventually display average command. He has full-time starter upside with the organization excited to see how he handles a climb up the ladder and a heavier workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers spent much of the 2022 Draft stocking up on college bats. Gold was among the most polished, a three-year performer at Boston College who posted a .940 OPS as a sophomore and .958 as a junior. The Tigers’ front office has changed since drafting Gold, but his combination of hitting ability and zone control fit the mold of hitter that new president of baseball operations Scott Harris has touted as the model for the organization. Though Gold struggled in a late-season stint at Single-A Lakeland last summer, his quick swing and line-drive approach to all fields is expected to translate well once he gets acclimated to pro ball and develops a routine. The bigger question might be power. He never reached double digits in home runs at BC, and just two of his 13 pro hits last summer went for extra bases, both doubles. He doesn’t tend to chase much. Gold alternated between second and third base in Lakeland, but his strong arm and body frame could work better at third. Gold turned 22 last fall, and the Tigers could aim to push him if he can handle pitching in Lakeland early in the season. He’ll have to fight his way through a crowded group of infielders in the Tigers farm system, but for an organization that badly needs offense, Gold’s hit-first resume should get a fair shot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis worked out of the Sam Houston State bullpen for two years, got a taste for starting in the Cape Cod League in 2023 and transferred to Oklahoma for the '24 season. He posted a 4.30 ERA with 117 strikeouts in 92 innings during his time in Norman, and the Cardinals took him in the fifth round that summer before signing him for $485,700. He led all Cardinals farmhands with 153 strikeouts and finished with a 2.85 ERA over 110 1/3 innings between Single-A Palm Beach and High-A Peoria last season. The 5-foot-11 southpaw picked up velo from his days as a Sooner and sat 90-94 mph with his fastball, touching as high as 96.9 in the Florida State League. There was a ton of ride and run on the pitch that lower-level hitters just couldn’t handle. But its below-average velo also comes with below-average extension, and it’s likely that more experienced bats will read it better. Davis’ best pitch is a killer 80-82 mph changeup that had a 61 percent whiff rate across both levels. It moves much like the heater and has only a smidge less spin, but the velo differential fooled batters and led to dominance against righties. A low-80s slider also showed some depth as an option moving gloveside, and a mid-80s cutter bridged the repertoire. As untouchable as he could be in terms of hits and strikeouts, Davis struggled to stay in the strike zone consistently, and his 16.6 percent walk rate was the highest among any Minor League full-season qualifier. He can pitch like he’s trying to be fine at the corners, only to miss with uncompetitive pitches. The reverse splits and nasty changeup still make him intriguing, but the lack of control could shorten his leash as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Indiana State might best be known for producing NBA great Larry Bird, but there have also been more than 20 big leaguers to come from the school, most recently left-hander Sean Manaea. Hayden hopes to be the next after the Reds took him in the eighth round of the 2024 Draft. He started his college career at Indiana before transferring to start for the Sycamores, where he had his real success, albeit with command issues. He made four relief outings for full-season Daytona after signing. Hayden’s best offerings are his fastball-slider combination. While he sat in the low-90s as a starter during his junior season, he’s already shown he can push his fastball up to 98 mph. His mid-80s slider is actually better than the heater, a pitch that elicited a 45 percent miss rate during his junior season, according to Synergy. He does have a firm changeup up into the upper 80s, but it’s a distant third pitch he doesn’t rely on. The Reds may let Hayden develop as a starter for now so he can work on his entire repertoire and try to refine his command after his 5.4 walk per nine rate in 2024 was an improvement from his first two seasons of college ball. He profiles best as a reliever and he could see his stuff tick up while moving quickly through the system, if and when he gets shortened up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Binelas established himself as a potential first-rounder when he slugged 14 homers as a Louisville freshman in 2019, but he played just two games in the shortened pandemic season before breaking the hamate bone in his right hand and slumped at the start of his junior year. He recovered to hit 19 homers in 50 games before the Brewers selected the Wisconsin native in the third round and signed him for $700,000. After he batted .314/.379/.636 with nine blasts in 29 games in Low-A, Milwaukee traded him along with Jackie Bradley Jr. and shortstop prospect David Hamilton to the Red Sox for Hunter Renfroe in December. Binelas' strength and bat speed create solid power to all fields. While he has a reasonable approach at the plate, drawing his share of walks and avoiding chasing too many pitches, he's also a streaky hitter who batted just .272 in three college seasons. His left-handed stroke can get long and uphill, leading to concerns about his ability to handle velocity up in the zone and prolonged slumps when his timing gets out of whack. Where Binelas plays with his fringy speed and average arm remains to be seen. He's erratic and lacks range at third base, his primary position in his debut, and scouts don't like his hands, footwork or funky throwing motion. Louisville moved him to first base three weeks into this junior season but he also looked rough there and may wind up in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2019-20 international signing period might always be known for the addition of Francisco Álvarez for $2.7 million in July. One month later -- after New York added international bonus pool money in a deal that sent Jeurys Familia to Oakland -- the club also picked up Lugo for $475,000 as an infielder out of the Dominican Republic. After a mundane introduction to stateside ball, Lugo broke out offensively in 2022 with Single-A St. Lucie, hitting .261/.347/.427 with 10 homers in 84 games before moving up to High-A Brooklyn, where he was also an above-average hitter with a 115 wRC+ in 28 contests. Lugo’s power is better than his Florida State League numbers indicate as he regularly registered exit velocities above 95 mph. His 41.1 percent hard-hit rate on that circuit was on par with Major League sluggers like Ian Happ and C.J. Cron in 2022, and the 20-year-old -- who stands out for his strength more than bat speed -- may only get stronger from here. Batting from a slightly closed stance, Lugo can sometimes expand the zone, leading to strikeouts in about one-quarter of his plate appearances, and hitting for average likely won’t be a strong suit. At 6-foot-3, Lugo was large for shortstop, even by modern standards, and as a below-average runner, he’s a better fit at third base. He has the arm for that spot, and he has enough pop to provide offensive value away from a premium position. The 20-year-old was Rule 5-eligible this offseason but went unprotected and unpicked as he’s at least two years away from the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Teams generally want junior college hitters to prove they can handle better pitching, so Miller went undrafted despite batting .394 in two seasons at Bishop State (Ala.) CC and winning a Perfect Game Collegiate League MVP award in between. He had no problem making the jump to the Southeastern Conference last spring, batting .381/.474/.702 at Alabama before the Marlins signed him for $800,800 as a third-rounder. He expanded his strike zone during his pro debut, resulting in a .240/.305/.298 line between two Class A stops. Miller found success throughout college and in Single-A by understanding how pitchers were trying to attack him, adjusting accordingly and making consistent hard contact to all fields. He diverted from that approach when he got off to a slow start in High-A, aggressively tried to pull everything and piled up strikeouts and weak groundballs. When he's not trying to do too much, he shows the feel for the barrel, bat speed and strength to hit for a high average with 20 homers per season from the right side of the plate. It's unclear where Miller, who has below-average speed and fringy arm strength, will wind up defensively. He was adequate at best at third base for the Crimson Tide and may not have the quickness for second base, where he spent most of his debut. The Marlins believe his work ethic will help him get the job done at the keystone, while most scouts project him as a left fielder or first baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hipwell played just 76 games in three seasons at Santa Clara and had little experience with wood bats in summer ball, so he was tougher to evaluate than most collegians in the 2024 Draft. He lost the final three weeks of his sophomore year and the first two months of his junior season to a suspension for performance-enhancing drugs, which he attributed to an over-the-counter supplement. Signed for $345,700 as a sixth-rounder, he batted .196/.360/.402 with five homers and 40 strikeouts in his 29-game pro debut in Single-A. Hipwell is built to hit for a power with a quick left-handed stroke with loft, a strong 6-foot-3 frame and a pull-focused mindset. He has a patient-bordering-on-passive approach that results in walks, but it also leaves him behind in counts too often and leads to strikeouts. He pounds fastballs but had a 38 percent swing-and-miss rate against non-heaters in his debut. With below-average speed, Hipwell offers little value on the bases and limited range at third base. His solid arm strength fits the hot corner, but he's an erratic defender who may have to move. He played some right field and first base with the Broncos and also dabbled at second base in the MLB Draft League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A's got a close look at Diaz as a local amateur when he played at Acalanes HS (Calif.) and liked what they saw back then, leading to his selection by the club years later coming out of Vanderbilt in the eighth round of the 2024 MLB Draft. He's been on a steady climb through the system since joining the organization. Jumping from Single-A Stockton to High-A Lansing in 2025, he made another leap early on in '26 with a promotion from High-A to Double-A Midland after a strong performance in first 29 games with the Lugnuts. Diaz stands out at the plate for his impressive bat-to-ball skills and overall patience in the batter's box. That has translated to a low strikeout rate and solid on-base numbers early in his pro career. The contact skills help mitigate the lack of power he's shown thus far, though he has increased his frequency of extra-base hits this season, which gives some hope that there is some more pop in that bat to unlock. The A's raised some eyebrows when they decided to utilize Diaz, primarily a third baseman in college, as a catcher, a position he hadn't played since high school. So far, that decision is looking great as he's demonstrated clean mechanics behind the dish along with a strong arm and ability to control the run game. Still showing off his versatility by getting some time at third, second and even some first base, Diaz is quickly emerging as an intriguing super-utility player with enough tools to eventually make a big league impact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cleveland didn’t get much mound time at Central Arkansas until 2021, his third year on campus, becoming the Bears’ closer and saving nine games. He pitched well as a starter in 2022 to close out his college career, and the Mariners took him in the 14th round that July. He actually spent the 2023 season still working as a starter, but a combination of moving to the bullpen and dropping his arm slot even further has helped him get some traction, and he made it to Double-A for the first time in July 2025 before capping things off in the Arizona Fall League. Nothing Cleveland does is conventional on the mound, and while his mode of operation isn’t the same, his stuff -- and the surprising effectiveness of it -- evokes some Tyler Rogers vibes. Once just a sidearmer, Cleveland has dropped down further to submarine levels, and there’s even more deception with a delivery that has him stepping all the way to the third-base side of the mound while slinging his two-pitch mix back across his body. His fastball hovers around 85 mph but hitters don’t pick it up, his sweepy low-70s slider also misses a fair amount of bats and he was virtually unhittable in 2025 (0.87 ERA, .128 BAA). Cleveland throws enough strikes with his funk to believe it’s something that could work at the highest level. It might have to be in limited stints, but teams are often seeking out different looks coming out of the 'pen to keep hitters off balance, and Cleveland is as different as they come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Merejo was born in Florida and grew up there before moving to the Dominican Republic late in his high school career and signing for $340,000 in 2023. He followed up a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League by coming to the United States at age 18 last year. After beginning the season in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, he concluded it by batting .282/.372/.466 in the final month Single-A as one of the Carolina League's youngest players. Unlike most of the Guardians' international signings, Merejo stands out more for his power than his hitting ability. His physicality and the bat speed in his right-handed stroke produce plus raw pop, and he taps into most of it by concentrating on driving balls in the air to his pull side too. He has some feel to hit and is willing to take walks, though he'll have to tone down his approach because it leaves him vulnerable to non-fastballs. Most of Merejo's value will come from his bat. Though he stole 11 bases in 77 games last year, he's a below-average runner who's probably limited to first base. He committed 10 errors in 53 starts there in 2024 while also getting time on the outfield corners, where he displayed solid arm strength but substandard range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aracena was a long play for the Mets when they signed him out of the Dominican Republic for $70,000 as part of their 2022 international class. He was super raw, even for a young pitcher, walking 20.2 percent of his batters as recently as 2024. But Aracena took a big step forward as a 20-year-old in the Florida State League in 2025 and was pitching very well when the Orioles acquired him as part of the return for Gregory Soto near the Trade Deadline. He pitched to a 1.95 ERA over his first 27 2/3 innings in his new organization, finishing the year at High-A Aberdeen, but was traded again in the offseason to the D-backs as part of the return for Blaze Alexander. Aracena’s stuff makes it clear why he was a project worth waiting for. The 6-foot-3 right-hander brings serious heat to the mound, sitting 96-99 mph with his four-seam fastball and topping out at 101. He also throws a razor-sharp cutter at 92-94 mph with significant gloveside run, as well as two breaking balls: an upper-80s slider with depth and a developing curve. He’s had a two-seamer and a changeup, but throws neither pitch often enough to be a factor. The control of those offerings was so erratic that Aracena’s 13.6 percent walk rate in ‘25 indicated marked improvement. He’s still able to blow his stuff past batters for now, but upper-level hitters won’t provide that luxury. As it stands, it’s a high-risk/high-reward package -- when Aracena commands his stuff, he dominates; when he doesn’t, the walks make him vulnerable to implosion. How well he learns to locate will ultimately dictate his true ceiling, though he looks like a high-leverage reliever in the making if he can learn to harness even a fraction of his tantalizing stuff consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clarke tied for the Division I lead with 23 homers as a junior for South Carolina in 2021, apt timing considering he missed much of his sophomore campaign the previous year due to the pandemic. The Brewers selected him in the 10th round that summer and signed him below slot at $75,000. The right-handed slugger was a solid performer between High-A and Double-A his first full season, finishing with 14 homers and a 116 wRC+ in 99 games, but truly took off in a return to Biloxi this summer with a Southern League-best 26 homers and an .889 OPS that placed third on the circuit. A strong Arizona Fall League campaign solidified the breakout. Power, power, power -- that’s long been Clarke’s calling card and will continue to be the closer he gets to Milwaukee. His uphill swing enables the pop to play as 50.2 percent of his batted balls were flyballs in 2023, but it also can affect his overall contact rate as he struck out 29.2 percent of the time. Clarke balances the punchouts with a lot of walks, but even he’s admitted he needs to get to the power earlier in counts to keep the offensive profile balanced. A well-below-average runner, Clarke initially impressed Brewers officials with his improvements behind the plate, but he’s still viewed as a long-term first baseman, especially as he plays next to Jeferson Quero and bumps into William Contreras’ shadow. He has decent arm strength but lacks accuracy on throws, leading to a 10.3 percent caught-stealing rate in 2023. A full-time right-right first baseman has a high offensive bar to clear, but Clarke just might have the power to handle it. If he can serve as a third catcher on the roster too, all the better.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signing as a 17-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in May 2018, Rodriguez began his career in the bullpen because of major control issues (51 walks in 50 1/3 innings) during his first two years in the Dominican Summer League. After the lost pandemic season, he moved into the rotation at Single-A Palm Beach and had success with a 3.36 ERA and 88 strikeouts in 69 2/3 innings. His 2022 season in High-A Peoria (4.59 ERA, 119 strikeouts in 121 2/3 frames) was a bumpier ride, but it was notable that he nearly doubled his previous career-high workload. The Cardinals did not add him to the 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible in the offseason, and he went unselected in that process. The 6-foot right-hander’s velocity has picked up in recent years as he’s matured and gotten stronger. He can sit 95-96 mph earlier in outings but typically settles in closer to 93-94 as he goes deeper, which makes sense for a pitcher still getting built up as a starter. He’ll showcase a quality mid-80s slider that he can work to either side of the plate while also mixing in an upper-70s curveball offering a slower breaking look. His mid-80s changeup still lacks consistency, and there are the makings of a cutter for another diversified offering. Rodriguez doesn’t have the same control issues he did earlier in his career, but his delivery lacks consistency and can make him to fly open, causing his command to waver. His career might go full circle with a return to the bullpen as a result, which could allow him to open the velo even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest acquisition for the Reds on the international market when the 2023 signing period was catcher Alfredo Duno, who received $3.1 million, and the organization gave a seven-figure bonus later in the period to ink Sheng-En Lin. Third on the 2023 bonus list was Alcantara, signed initially as a shortstop out of the Dominican Republic for $640,000 in January of that year. He performed well enough during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League to come stateside in 2024 and struggled with the Arizona Complex League assignment. A return to the level the year after paid dividends, and he earned a bump to full-season Daytona for the first time. The Reds saw enough to move him to High-A Dayton to kick off his age-20 season in 2026. Alcantara, an undersized infielder at 5-foot-9, is a right-handed hitter with an aggressive approach at the plate. After striking out over 36 percent of the time during his U.S. debut, he's worked to refine his approach, cutting down on his swing-and-miss considerably in 2025. He has gap-to-gap power right now, with some ability to impact the ball, and limiting chase and continuing to see pitches and draw walks should help him maximize his offensive potential. While he was signed as a shortstop and saw plenty of time at the premium position over the first three summers of his career, Alcantara doesn't have the range to stick there long-term. He has the arm strength for third, and he's splitting time between the hot corner and second base, which might be the best option for him should he settle into one position permanently in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros paid the two highest bonuses in their 2025 international class to a pair of players who trained together in Santo Domingo, D.R. Cuban outfielder Kevin Alvarez signed for $2 million, while Venezuelan infielder Manzueta turned pro for $847,500. The latter slashed .224/.405/.392 with 42 walks in 47 games during his pro debut as one of the youngest players (age 16) in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Manzueta stands out with his advanced feel for the barrel and his control of the strike zone. He has a sound right-handed stroke and recognizes pitches well. He won't be physically imposing and needs to add strength to his 5-foot-10 frame, but his ability to turn on pitches and square them up gives him some sneaky power that could translate into 12-15 homers per season. While Manzueta trained as a shortstop, his below-average speed and average arm strength aren't suited for the position. He played there briefly in the DSL while spending most of his time alternating between second base and third base. He profiles best at the keystone and could wind up a utilityman who derives much of his value from his on-base skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With fewer options for Rookie or short-season ball available to teams, it’s become more common for young international signees to spend multiple seasons in the Dominican Summer League. The Reds did just that with their top three signings from the 2024 class: Adolfo Sanchez and Naibel Mariano, who both got seven-figure bonuses, and Morillo, who signed for $420,000. Morillo put up solid numbers both summers and is ready to come stateside. Morillo is a switch-hitting catcher who will play all of his 2026 season in the United States at age 19. His bat is definitely ahead of his glove, with an advanced approach that led to more walks than strikeouts over two summers in the DSL and helped him hold his own against older competition in the Australian League this offseason. His swing works from both sides of the plate with more gap-to-gap thump right now, though there’s power for him to get to. He needs to tighten up his zone a little bit and his swing can get long, but there are building blocks for him to be an average hitter with average power. While Morillo has more work to do behind the dish with maybe an average arm and more rudimentary receiving skills, the Reds love the intangibles and leadership qualities he possesses, including improving his English and showing up in Arizona early to get to work for the season ahead. There might come a time when they’ll want to move him from behind the plate so his bat can advance, but that decision isn’t coming any time soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were two Indiana natives on the World Cup-winning US 18-and-under national team in 2022: Max Clark and Tilly. While Clark went third overall to the Tigers in the 2023 Draft, Tilly was unselected as MLB Pipeline’s No. 208 prospect in the class and headed to Auburn instead. He pitched primarily out of the bullpen in his two years in the SEC and sported a 5.48 ERA with 58 strikeouts in 46 innings as a Draft-eligible sophomore last year. The Mets took him in the seventh round and signed him for above slot at $397,500 to keep him from heading back to school. The Mets have early interest in developing Tilly as a starter because of his interesting pitch mix. His fastball sits at 92-94 mph, touching 97, and because of the average velocity, he was willing to go liberally to his secondaries in his final season on campus. Since his amateur days, Tilly has earned praise for the high spin rates on his low-80s slider, and he’s developed his mid-80s splitter into arguably an even better pitch, one with enough dip and movement to cause lefties fits. Tilly also worked in another high-spin curveball in the mid 70s with Auburn but saved it mostly for early counts. Tilly walked 13.4 percent of the batters he faced in his two years at Auburn -- a rate that would keep anyone in the bullpen early in their collegiate career -- but the Mets believe there’s untapped pitchability there, especially if they can tame some of his spinnier options. There’s a good chance Tilly would have gotten starting looks as junior anyways, and now that can happen under the eye of a New York organization that has specialized in pitching development in recent years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stovall could have had the chance to be an early-round selection out of the Louisiana high school ranks in 2021 but chose to keep his commitment to play for Arkansas. He under-performed over his first two seasons with the Razorbacks, trying to play through a torn labrum in his throwing shoulder in 2023. He missed the start of the 2024 season with a broken left foot, but when he returned, his bat clicked, finishing with a .944 OPS, and he played better second base defense. He landed in the fourth round with the Reds, who sent him to full-season Daytona for a brief pro debut after signing. Stovall’s left-handed swing still stands, out and he used it to find the barrel much more consistently during his junior year at Arkansas. He has excellent strike zone awareness and showed more overall patience in 2024, allowing him to get to better pitches to drive. The power hasn’t shown up as much, but he does have extra-base authority to the gaps and some over-the-fence juice to his pull side. While speed isn’t a part of his game, Stovall makes the most out of that and his fringy arm thanks to plus makeup and excellent instincts. He should be able to stay on the right side of the infield, at second base and perhaps at first, where he played exclusively as a freshman in college. He could even see a little time at third, though his arm strength will likely limit him there. The plan is to let him go hit and find ways to get that bat into the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Van Scoyoc comes from Iowa baseball royalty, with a grandfather who was a coach immortalized in the film “The Final Season,” a dad who played pro ball and a brother who was drafted by the Phillies in 2019. Connor was committed to Arizona State after earning Iowa Gatorade Player of the Year honors, but the Angels went well over slot, giving him $400,000 in the 11th round of the 2018 Draft to keep him from heading to campus. He didn’t make much noise over his first couple of years, but he found some success in A-ball in 2022 and got some exposure in the Arizona Fall League. He was pitching well at High-A in 2023 when he was sent to the Rockies in exchange for Mike Moustakas and he finished the year with eight starts at Double-A. A 6-foot-6 right-hander, Van Scoyoc could have a three-pitch mix that gives him the chance to start. His fastball averages around 92 mph, though he can reach back for a few more ticks on occasion. It can be an effective pitch because of it’s cut and sink, a reason why he produces solid ground-ball rates. He’s shown the ability to spin a decent upper-70s curve that can flash above-average at times. He has a mid-80s changeup, but he doesn’t throw it much and it’s well behind the other two offerings. Pitchers this size can often find it difficult to repeat their delivery and Van Scoyoc struggled with finding the zone consistently in the early stages of his career. He improved dramatically on that front in 2022 and was a decent strike-thrower in '23. He was left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft last offseason and wasn’t selected, making this a big year for the 24-year old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round selection by the A’s in the 2024 MLB Draft out of Boston College, Leary underwhelmed a bit in his first taste of pro ball upon joining the organization. His first full season as a pro went much better, as he began the year at Single-A Stockton and earned a promotion to High-A Lansing, where he held his own over a 33-game stint. Between the two levels, Leary hit .269 with a .798 OPS in 126 games. Leary has above-average power potential which showed up in stints last season, with an ability to hit to all fields after working with the A’s to tighten up his swing. He can draw a decent amount of walks, but his 130 strikeouts last year highlight some swing-and-miss issues that will need to be corrected for him to fully take advantage of that power. Leary might be one of the better baserunners in the entire organization, evident by his 56 stolen bases in ‘25 while getting caught only eight times. Defensively, he can move around well, but his below-average arm likely limits him to left field, though the A’s plan to work with him on his quickening up his release to see if his positional versatility could expand to the other two outfield spots. The A’s are still trying to figure out just what type of player Leary might end up being, but there were some encouraging signs in his first full year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-round pick in 2022 out of Iowa, Williams has always been an upside play on his long-term power. Nicknamed “The Iowa Meat Truck”, you won’t find a larger human being in the Blue Jays’ organization … or many organizations. Listed at 6-foot-5, 255 pounds, Williams looks even larger than that in the box, but it hasn’t turned into the eye-popping power numbers you’d expect just yet. He homered 14 times in 2023 (83 games) and 11 times last season (87 games), but with a strong finish and a successful stint in the Arizona Fall League, there’s buzz in the system about him finally unleashing more of that pop. Outside of Vladimir Guerrero Jr., there may be no player in the organization who hits the ball harder than Williams. He’s still a proper hitter, fully capable of shooting a line drive when the situation calls for it, but the Blue Jays are eager to get Williams taking more shots in the right counts. There’s also been a focus on getting him to drive the ball in the air more often. While Williams is a sturdier defender at first base than you’d expect, all of the upside here is clearly and fully tied to his bat. The Rowdy Tellez comps are easy, and given the breakout season Tellez had at Double-A New Hampshire in 2016, you’ll probably be hearing more of them. Similar to outfielder Dasan Brown, whose value leans on elite speed and defense, Williams gets on this list because he does one thing extremely well. He’ll need to hit his way to the top, but there’s a chance he does just that. He’s already an organizational favorite and would be a fan favorite in Toronto if he ever puts on that uniform.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor split time between catcher and first base in two seasons at Virginia Tech, and he was one of college baseball's top performers (.431/.541/.690) during the shortened 2020 season. A Draft-eligible sophomore, he went in the fourth round that summer and made his pro debut in 2021. He batted .278/.371/.433 in High-A and posted similar numbers as a late replacement in the Arizona Fall League. First and foremost an offensive player, Taylor controls the strike zone, puts together some of the best at-bats in the system and makes a lot of line-drive contact. A switch-hitter, he had a loopier swing from his natural left side when he entered pro ball but has tightened that up. He has solid raw power that currently translates mostly into doubles, but he could produce 15-20 homers on an annual basis if he learns to pull more pitches in the air. Taylor's 55 starts at catcher in High-A more than doubled his total at Virginia Tech, so he's still a work in progress behind the plate. His receiving has improved significantly and could become solid or better, but he's not particularly agile and still is learning the nuances of blocking balls in the dirt and calling pitches. He has average raw arm strength but needs to upgrade his accuracy after throwing out just 19 percent of basestealers last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thach could have started his pro career out of high school when the Giants took him in the 18th round in 2022, but the great-nephew of Hall of Famer Catfish Hunter headed to UNC Wilmington instead. He's all over the Seahawks' record books, setting the freshman home run mark (15) in 2023 and then the single-season record with 27 as a sophomore. The power kept showing up with wood bats in the Cape Cod League (eight homers), but enthusiasm dampened a bit when the pop didn't show up as much in 2025. Still, his 54 career homers are a school record, and the Rockies took a flier in the eighth round of last summer's Draft, going a bit over slot to bring him into the fold. He got off to a very good start during his first full season of pro ball with Single-A Fresno. The big left-handed hitter offers an intriguing combination of strength and bat speed coming from his 6-foot-4 frame that provides optimism he can send the ball a long way and catch up to good velocity. He hits the ball very hard, registering high exit velocities and his well-above-average raw power can show up to all fields, though most of his home run thump comes to his pull side. He doesn't strike out a ton, especially given his power, but he does chase out of the zone too much, something that will have to improve as he moves up the ladder. A former two-way player who was up to 90 mph on the mound, Thach's well-below-average speed almost certainly limits him to first base, though he has seen a little time in right field as a pro. He'll have to keep getting to that raw pop to profile well in either corner spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels drafted McIntosh in the 34th round after he swatted 16 homers as a Motlow State (Tenn.) CC freshman in 2018, but he chose to transfer to West Virginia rather than turn pro. He had modest success with the Mountaineers but performed well in the inaugural year of the MLB Draft League in 2021, landing him a $20,000 bonus from the Marlins as a nondrafted free agent. He quickly has become an organization favorite and spent his first full pro season in Double-A, where he helped Pensacola win the Southern League championship. A right-handed hitter, McIntosh produces some of the best exit velocities in the system and works deep counts in search of pitches he can drive to his pull side.
