Though he fits the power-over-hit profile, he draws plenty of walks and doesn't strike out excessively. He's surprisingly quick for a catcher, can flash solid run times and displays good instincts on the bases. It may be a stretch for McIntosh to remain behind the plate, however. He earns raves for his leadership and preparation skills, but he's a decent receiver at best, struggles to block balls and has below-average arm strength. He surrendered 97 steals (at an 85 percent success rate) in 67 games last year, and Miami plans on giving him time at first base to get him more at-bats in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Moss has spent most of his baseball career flying under the radar. After playing sparingly over two years at Seton Hall, he transferred to Division II St. Leo University in Florida and hit .340 with an 1.107 OPS in his final season there. He cemented his unofficial title as the \"Mayor of the Appalachian League\" and earned Player of the Year honors by posting a 1.254 OPS there in 2024, his third summer in the wood-bat MLB-run collegiate league. That led to a contract with the Royals as a nondrafted free agent. Moss was in the middle of his first pro season when the Pirates acquired him from Kansas City at the 2025 Trade Deadline in the Bailey Falter deal. A right-handed first baseman, Moss absolutely raked in the Pirates organization post-trade, hitting .339 with a .993 OPS over 30 games with High-A Greensboro. He's always shown excellent contact quality, but he could be poised to take another step forward as he registered high-end max exit velocities all spring. When that's combined with good bat-to-ball skills, solid plate discipline and decent chase rates, Moss has the chance to add up to a solid overall hitter. Moss has below-average speed but is an excellent baserunner, with his instincts allowing him to swipe 17 bags last year. He's worked hard to become a capable defender at first, but his bat will always be his calling card. For him to have the chance to be a big league regular, he'll have to get to more power, but if he doesn't, it won't be from lack of effort. Moss plays with a chip on his shoulder and gets praise for his work ethic and leadership characteristics as he enters his age-22 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: No player had been drafted from Seattle’s Ballad HS since 1997 and no one had signed from there since 1989 before Madonna headed to the MLB Draft League out of hope he could build up his stock to end both streaks. He hit .279/.360/.512 with two homers and four doubles in 12 games for Frederick on the summer showcase circuit while being roughly four years younger than its average player. The Padres saw enough from there and his time in the Pacific Northwest to take him in the 11th round and sign him away from a UCLA commitment with a $654,000 bonus (closer to fourth-round money). Madonna flashed good power in that short time with the Keys, topping out with a 107.8 mph exit velocity on one of his two dingers and finishing with a 90th-percentile EV of 104.3 (close to MLB average) in the small sample. It's gap-to-gap power that led to six of his 12 hits falling for extra bases. The right-handed slugger was left exposed against high-end velocity, and he struggled against Draft League breaking stuff. That was a trend that carried into his short spin with Single-A Lake Elsinore, where he had just a 57.3 percent overall contact rate in 14 games. All that said, Madonna faced aggressive assignments as an 18-year-old amateur and pro last summer and deserves to grow into more age-appropriate competition in his first full season. Defensively, some scouts believe he's close to maxed out physically and might have to move to first base eventually in his 20s, though his average arm strength and good accuracy should help limit opposing running games behind the plate. The Padres will rotate Madonna with 2025 fifth-rounder Ty Harvey at catcher while getting them enough at-bats to develop offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally recruited by Auburn as a left-handed pitcher, Snell redshirted there while injured in 2021 before transferring to Wallace-Dothan (Ala.) CC and becoming the national junior college player of the year in 2023. He played both ways on Alabama in 2024 before becoming a full-time left fielder in his final college season. As a Southeastern Conference performer with intriguing data and no college eligibility remaining, he was one of the better discount hitters available in the 2025 Draft and went in the fifth round. After displaying one of the best combinations of swing decisions, contact and exit velocities in the 2025 college crop, Snell continued to stand out in those areas even while slashing just .167/.268/.219 at High-A during his 27-game pro debut. He drives the ball to all fields and handles all types of pitches with a quality left-handed swing. His biggest need is to learn to launch balls in the air more regularly, or else he'll be a hit-over-power corner outfielder who will top out at 15 homers per season. Snell can show close to average speed at his top end but he's more of a below-average runner with limited outfield range. He reached 93 mph with his fastball as a redshirt junior and the Cubs deployed him on both outfield corners after Alabama utilized him solely in left field. Most of his value will come from his bat, though he also receives high marks for his leadership skills and competitiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 30 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 An All-Big Ten Second Teamer for Penn State in 2021, Wood followed up a solid sophomore year with a stellar junior campaign in which he finished second in the conference in average (.379) and OPS (1.147) and helped Nittany Lions pitchers strike out a program-best 503 batters. Milwaukee made him the highest-picked position player in Penn State history when it selected him in the fourth round and signed him for below slot at $347,500. Already known for a strong approach, Wood boosted his stock by walking more times (36) than he struck out (26) during his final spring on campus, and his jump from four to 12 homers opened some eyes as well. His current power plays best to the pullside and comes more as a result of his natural strength than his overall bat speed. That brings along some concerns about how the bat will translate, and some evaluators believe Wood’s performance says more about his quality of college competition than his own potential. Wood can be a solid catcher but isn’t likely to wow anyone with his defensive work. Decently quick pop times and solid arm strength will be helpful, and he’ll need an adjustment period to handling better stuff day in and day out in the pros. That said, lefty-hitting catchers who can reach base at a good clip are always in demand, so there’s a path to being at least a Major League backup here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If the early returns mean anything. Pena might be the bargain of the Twins’ 2023 international signing class. Signed for just $40,000 out of the Dominican Republic, Pena has done nothing but hit at two stops. He batted .382 with a .949 OPS in 39 Dominican Summer League games during his debut after signing, then came stateside and slashed .282/.386/.410 as an 18-year old in the Florida Complex League. An undersized right-handed hitter, Pena makes an almost absurd amount of contact. In his first two summers of pro ball he struck out in just 6.5 percent of his plate appearances, obviously reminding many of former Twin Luis Arraez in his knack for finding the barrel. He has shown a willingness to draw some walks (11.8 BB percentage) and while he’s never going to be a big power guy -- how much he does end up impacting the ball is a question -- he did show a bit more extra-base authority in the FCL and can drive the ball to the gaps. Finding a spot for Pena’s bat in the lineup might be more of a challenge. He’s played second base, his most likely full-time home should he land in one spot, as well as third and left field. He’ll likely spend most of his time at the keystone and in left, but it’s been a bit of an adventure defensively thus far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts and recruiters mostly ignored Bush when he was a Texas prepster, but he went in the 16th round of the 2023 Draft after slashing .357/.510/.615 as a freshman at Tyler (Texas) JC. He earned High-A South Atlantic League all-star honors last year, though his OPS dropped from .812 there to .671 after he was promoted to Double-A in early August. He profiles as an offensive-minded backup catcher. The strength in Bush's 6-foot-4, 235-pound frame and the loft in his left-handed stroke give him solid to plus raw power that translates into high exit velocities and plays to all fields. He could provide 20 homers on an annual basis if he makes enough contact, though he has to prove he can catch up to quality fastballs and handle spin. Strikeouts will always be part of his package, though his patient approach also yields a fair amount of walks. Bush needs reps behind the plate to improve receiving and blocking skills, but those were hard to come by when he played alongside 2024 first-rounder Walker Janek in High-A. He's a well-below-average runner who isn't very agile as a catcher or at first base. His solid arm strength is his best defensive attribute, though he needs to improve his throwing accuracy after erasing just 17 percent of basestealers last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Mason Martin, a former Pirates farmhand who ranked fourth in the Minors with 35 homers in 2019, Martin also stands out with his well-above-average raw power. Signed for an over-slot $250,000 in 2023 as an 11th-rounder from a Washington high school, he struggled for two years in Rookie ball before doing more damage in Single-A last year and drawing significant trade interest from other clubs. He earned Carolina League all-star honors after leading the Single-A circuit in extra-base hits (43) and ranking second in slugging (.440) and third in homers (12) and OPS (.783). Martin can drive the ball out of the park to all fields with an impressive combination of bat speed and strength, and he hits the ball harder and farther than most Rangers farmhands. In 2025, he did a better job of attacking hittable pitches in early counts and launching them in the air to his pull side, allowing him to make better use of his pop. How much he'll be able to tap into his 25-30 homer upside at higher levels will depend on his ability to improve his swing decisions and handle secondary pitches. Though Martin stole 15 bases in as many attempts last year, he has fringy speed with good instincts on the bases. He has limited range and below-average arm strength, relegating him to left field and diminishing his value outside of the batter's box. He's adequate at first base and can fill in in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez reached a deal with the A’s for $800,000 during the 2022 international signing period, a figure that was only topped among the club’s agreements that year by outfielder Carlos Pacheco, who signed for $1.2 million. After playing 44 games in the Dominican Summer League last year, his second summer there, he should make his United States debut in 2024. Gonzalez has outstanding bat-to-ball skills and an overall advanced approach at the plate. He has been described as hitterish in the box with an ability to drive the ball to all fields, and his power should show up more as he grows into his 6-foot-2 frame. Though young, he does seem to already be drawing his fair share of walks while also limiting the strikeout totals. While Gonzalez is considered more of a bat-first catcher, the A’s have been pleased with his defensive skills thus far, though there is certainly room for improvement behind the plate. He has an above-average arm and should stick as a backstop, but the A’s also will get him some time at first base this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Powell got just 35 at-bats as an Oklahoma freshman, prompting him to transfer to Seminole State (Okla.) JC, where he became the national junior college player of the year as a sophomore in 2024. He topped NJCAA Division I in slugging (1.088), OPS (1.649), homers (32) and RBI (104) before giving up an Oklahoma State commitment to sign with the Astros as sixth-rounder. He slashed .264/.331/.442 in Single-A before breaking his left hamate last May, then missed two months and hit just .209/.358/.358 afterward. Powell features well above-average raw power, the product of a fierce right-handed stroke and an aggressive mindset that looks to crush balls to his pull side. He exhibits reasonable plate discipline and hits balls extremely hard when he makes contact -- but there are major questions about whether he can do so consistently against advanced pitching. He had a swing-and-miss rate of 29 percent against the strikes he saw in 2025, including 33 percent against in-zone fastballs. While Powell is slower out of the batter's box, he flashes solid speed underway and stole 32 bases in 38 attempts (84 percent) in 84 games last year. He played mostly shortstop in junior college and spent the majority of his time there last year, but his quickness is better suited for third base. He was erratic at both spots in 2025, committing 16 miscues in 61 starts, and has average arm strength. The organization will focus on getting him reps in the outfield this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez-Gomez pitched one season each at San Bernardino Valley (Calif.) JC and Temple (Texas) JC before the Cubs signed him for an under-slot $100,000 in the 10th round, using some of the savings to land since-traded Zyhir Hope with their next pick. Used primarily as a reliever as a pro, he got torched in his debut and spent most of his first two seasons in Rookie ball. He broke out in 2025 with a 1.46 ERA and 29 percent strikeout rate at two Class A stops, which may earn him a chance to show what he can do as a starter this year. The key to Martinez-Gomez's success was developing a low-80 splitter that's a weapon, as he does an excellent job on killing spin before it dives under barrels. The splitter plays well off his fastball, which parks at 93-95 mph and touches 97 with sink and armside run. He also spins a fringy slider in the low 80s. Martinez-Gomez's athleticism helps him get down the mound well and create extension in his delivery, though it hasn't helped him repeat mechanics well enough to provide regular strikes. He has a career 16 percent walk rate in pro ball before slicing that mark to 6 percent at High-A during last season's final month. If he can maintain average control, he might become a back-of-the-rotation option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: St Joseph’s most successful product has been left-hander Jamie Moyer, who spent a quarter century in the big leagues. There’s been one other catcher, Brian O’Keefe, who touched the Majors in 2022-23, but Cossetti is hoping to be the next. After four years at the Philadelphia-based school, Cossetti certainly didn’t hurt his stock with a strong showing in his second stint in MLB’s Draft League in 2022, helping him land in the 11th round of that year's Draft. He posted a .960 OPS across two levels of A ball in 2023, with a 163 RC+ that placed second among all catchers with more than 300 plate appearances, before finishing up with a defense-focused stint in the Arizona Fall League. Cossetti has the chance to be a productive right-handed hitter because he has a solid combination of strength and approach at the plate. He limits strikeouts and draws a ton of walks, getting him into better counts where he did fairly consistent damage. He registers high exit velocities, and there’s good power he should be able to continue to get to. Whether he can defend well enough to stay behind the plate is more of a question. He’s improved his arm strength to average, and he works very hard at his craft, but he’ll need to keep grinding to become an adequate receiver. The Twins don’t want to bet against his work ethic, but they’ll also keep getting him some reps at first base to get his bat in the lineup more regularly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schubart has been a major power prospect for years, falling two hits shy of the Big 12 Conference triple crown as a sophomore before finishing his Oklahoma State career with 59 homers and a 1.169 OPS. His prodigious power has come with swing-and-miss concerns, though, which led to Cleveland grabbing him in the third round of the 2025 Draft and signing him for just under slot ($730,000). The Michigan native made a brief cameo at Single-A, where, true to his three-true outcome profile, 63.6 percent of his plate appearances ended with a homer, walk or strikeout. Standing at a hulking 6-foot-5, 223 pounds, Schubart has double-plus raw power -- where the vast majority of his value derives. It's more than just brute strength; the lefty slugger's bat speed and penchant for pulled air contact make him a home run machine. He's selective and waits for pitches he can hunt, which leads to impressive walk rates, but he often struggles to make contact in the zone. The Guardians are working to shorten his swing to counteract that problem, especially early in counts, even if whiffs will likely always be a part of his game. Schubart was still fairly productive against fellow southpaws in college, and maintaining that will be key to his future deployment. Given his massive size, Schubart is likely a first baseman long-term, although the Guardians will give him a chance to play an outfield corner several times per week. He doesn't have a great first step or the speed to make up for it, and his arm likely limits him to left if he can pass in the outfield. His lack of range also leaves him as a below-average defender at first. The good news is that if he's limited to DH, he has the type of raw power to still potentially make an impact there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Campos shot out of the gate with a .357 average and an .869 OPS over 45 games as a freshman at Arizona State and never much looked back. He finished with a career .369/.465/.554 slash line over his three springs as a Sun Devil and had significantly more walks (94) than strikeouts (66) over the 147-game span. He was a two-time Buster Posey National Collegiate Catcher of the Year Award semifinalist. The Cardinals selected him in the fourth round in 2024, signed him for exact slot at $669,300 and assigned him to the Florida State League, where he slashed .319/.396/.407 with a 13/13 K/BB ratio over 26 contests. It's astounding how consistent Campos has been, both in the pros and in college. As a left-handed hitting catcher, he’d hold a certain value already, but he adds to that with good swing decisions, excellent pitch recognition and strong bat-to-ball skills. He doesn’t whiff on many pitch types and especially succeeds against fastballs. However, the 5-foot-8 backstop doesn’t project for much pop at all, despite an uptick in collegiate homers in ’24, and he’ll likely always be hit-over-power. At that size, Campos doesn’t make for a huge target, and his defensive skills – from his receiving to his arm strength – are considered fringy. He played some corner outfield in school, but his best value will be behind the plate. Evaluators rave about his baseball IQ though, and his overall offensive approach gives him a good shot at being a future backup catcher in the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After his high school career in Champaign, Illinois, Munroe stayed in-state to keep playing at the junior college level, setting both single-season and career home run records at John A. Logan College. He parlayed that to an invite to play for Louisville in 2025 and continued to perform with an OPS over 1.000 and a spot on the College World Series All-Tournament Team. The Angels took him in the fourth round of last summer's Draft, signing him for an under-slot bonus of just less than $600,000. He got his professional feet wet with a dozen games in the California League after signing and got off to a solid start with High-A Tri-City in his first full season. Munroe is a 6-foot-2 right-handed hitter who has shown a feel to hit throughout his college career and early on with the Angels. With more of a choppy approach as an amateur, even though he found the seats at that level, he profiles more as a contact-first bat with good plate discipline, one who uses the whole field with some gap power, though he was showing some over-the-fence juice early in 2026. A below-average runner who didn't show much in the way of quick-twitch athleticism at Louisville, there were some concerns about his ability to stick at third base at the pro level. So far, though, he's shown off average defensive tools with an average arm, giving him the chance to stick at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cerda was born in the Bronx but signed out of the Dominican Republic when he joined the Rays' system for $325,000 in July 2019. He debuted in the Dominican Summer League in 2021 due to the pandemic and was in the midst of his first stateside campaign in 2022 when the Rays dealt him to the D-backs for outfielder David Peralta at the Trade Deadline. Finally in full-season ball last year, Cerda slashed .247/.402/.397 with 11 homers over 108 games between Single-A and High-A. His 93 walks ranked second among all Minor League catchers, trailing only Harry Ford's 103. That knowledge of the strike zone and unwillingness to expand it remain Cerda's best offensive attributes. The right-handed slugger starts with his lead leg slightly open from a hunched-over position but he drags the toe into place instead of incorporating a leg kick. The muted movement keeps him seeing the ball well and allows the free passes to pile up. When he does make contact, Cerda tends to hit the ball in the air with an uppercut swing; his 44.4 fly-ball percentage was second-highest among Arizona full-season qualifiers. There's enough raw power, too, that he should challenge for double-digit homers over a full year. Through his background, Cerda is bilingual, and he earns strong reviews for his ability to work with a pitching staff. He still has some room to grow with blocking and receiving, but the pieces are there for at least an average Major League defensive backstop. Cerda has arm strength, but a lack of accuracy helped opposing runners steal 139 bags off him in 2023. Despite being left off Arizona's 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible in 2024, Cerda is trending upward and could serve as an adequate backup in The Show in time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Valencia is the latest example of catchers sometimes needing more time to develop, though his development seemingly came out of nowhere. Far from a top prospect, the Venezuelan was a 2018 international signing for a $10,000 bonus. After five seasons in the States, he had played one game above A-ball, often serving as a backup or platoon mate. Then came 2025, when he got in better shape, looked for more launch angle, found his power stroke at the plate at Double-A Erie, then carried it to Triple-A Toledo. The breakout earned him a spot on Detroit’s 40-man roster in November, at the additional position of first base to help keep his bat in a lineup. Valencia, with help from Tigers instructors, changed his swing after the 2024 season to lower his hands and add more lift. A big leg kick helps with his timing, but he also became more selective with pitches, looking for balls he can launch after struggling with ground-ball rates for years. He has solid pitch recognition and can read what pitchers are trying to do against him, though he still struggled against breaking balls. Defensively, Valencia receives well but isn’t especially agile, and he struggled to control the running game in Toledo. Valencia’s work ethic and resulting rise made him one of the more popular players in the organization among coaches and instructors who worked with him over the years. He’s clearly in the Tigers’ sights, possibly even as a third catcher behind Dillon Dingler and Jake Rogers if he continues to hit, but shoring up his work behind the plate could be his best ticket to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palma trained in the same Venezuelan program that produced Willson Contreras and Keibert Ruiz. He signed for $300,000 in 2018, receiving the maximum bonus the Astros could pay while in the penalty box for blowing well past their international pool two years earlier. He batted .274/.340/.409 in High-A last year while missing seven weeks with a calf strain, then struggled offensively and defensively in the Arizona Fall League. Palma provides quality work behind the plate, where he moves well and is one of the best receivers, framers and blockers in the system. He also earns praise for his game planning, pitching calling and leadership ability. His lone drawback defensively is his below-average arm, which led to 112 steals in 129 attempts (87 percent) in 48 games at catcher between the Minors and AFL in 2023. Young for every league he's played in, Palma has shown the ability to manage the strike zone. He has some raw power but struggled to turn on pitches or lift them in the air last season compared to the past. The right-handed hitter doesn't have a huge offensive ceiling but could bat .250 with 10-15 homers per year with solid defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Older than most Draft picks, Kopps had to bide his time before bursting onto the radar. He redshirted in 2016, missed 2018 after undergoing Tommy John surgery and then the pandemic shortened his 2020 campaign. However, he was nearly unhittable in 2021, pitching to a 0.90 ERA with a 0.76 WHIP, both of which led NCAA Division I. After racking up 131 strikeouts in 89 2/3 innings, Kopps was named the SEC Pitcher of the Year and also won the Dick Howser Trophy as the College Player of the Year. The Padres grabbed the Arkansas product in the third round and signed him to a below-slot $300,000 bonus. As a result of his workload in college, Kopps only threw 14 2/3 innings in his professional debut, but was just as dominant. Kopps has four pitches in his repertoire, but it’s his cutter that’s been the key to his success. The mid-80s offering has late movement and the right-hander is able to vary its depth depending on whether he wants to throw it in the zone, or try to get a hitter to chase. He also throws a low-90s fastball, an average curveball and a developing changeup. Kopps has shown decent control early in his career, but doesn’t always command his fastball as well as he’d like. Kopps has been 25 for the duration of the 2022 season and hasn’t moved as quickly as many would have hoped coming out of college, having been just OK at Double-A thus far. He’ll need to work on getting more swing-and-misses against advanced bats if he’s going to break through to San Diego as a 26-year-old in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rios was the Pac-12 Player of the Year in 2023 after finishing with an OPS of 1.191 while helping Stanford reach the College World Series. This was an amazing development given the fact that Rios appeared in eight games combined over his first two years in college. He became one of the more intriguing college bats on the West Coast last year and the Angels were piqued enough to take him in the third round of the Draft. It was a small sample, but he struggled out of the gate during his pro debut, mostly with Single-A Inland Empire. Even though his résumé was light, amateur scouts had some conviction that Rios would hit at the next level. The right-handed hitter is short and quick to the ball and he displayed a very advanced approach, drawing a ton of walks, as well. The combination of pitch recognition, discipline and finding the barrel enabled him to use his raw power consistently, with 18 homers last spring. For Rios to make it, he’s going to have to hit because he doesn’t have a real defensive home. He played left field at Stanford but the Angels started working with him behind the plate -- he spent a lot of his non-playing time catching bullpens in college -- and they liked his leadership and his good hands behind the dish, though his arm is below-average. He’ll still get some reps in the outfield, but he’d obviously have more value -- and there’d be less pressure on his bat -- if he can catch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castañon broke out with a 1.208 OPS during his senior year at UC Santa Barbara in 2021 but was limited to only 28 games by a broken hand, hurting his Draft stock. The Padres picked the infielder in the 12th round that summer, signed him for $125,000 and have seen him hit at every Minor League stop since. Castañon was a California League end-of-season All-Star for Single-A Lake Elsinore in his first full campaign, then slashed .287/.352/.491 with 13 homers in 77 games for High-A Fort Wayne to begin 2023. His numbers at Double-A San Antonio were much closer to average (.280/.335/.436) over a 54-game stint to end the year. The right-handed hitter has put up solid batting averages at every stop, staying on time with the ball even with a large leg kick. That leads to hard contact that helps fuel the numbers, despite below-average speed that would otherwise help pick up extra hits here and there. Castañon was especially good at elevating and spraying the ball to all fields at Fort Wayne but got more pull- and ground-ball heavy at San Antonio, hurting his power. There’s still potential for 15-plus homers though, if he can even out those approaches. Castañon needs to hit because he’s a major question mark defensively. His lack of agility makes him a rough fit for second base, and his lack of arm strength makes him a stretch for third base. Those have been his two primary positions in pro ball, and barring a full-time move to first base, there isn’t a great place to hide his glove. Castañon might be best at being a right-handed part of a DH platoon and bench infielder, provided he carries his previous results to the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Hall of Famer Jeff Kent, Kaeden has the same profile as an offensive-minded infielder who fits best at second base. He was a part-time player for most of this first two years at Texas A&M before an injury to first-round pick Braden Montgomery thrust him into the lineup during the 2024 NCAA tournament, and Kent provided a grand slam in the super regionals before hitting .417 in the College World Series. He started at shortstop for the Aggies as junior, then went in the third round and struggled during an aggressive pro debut assignment to High-A. Kent's best attributes are his high baseball IQ, quality left-handed swing and penchant for making line-drive contact. He tries to do much at the plate at times and got too more chase- and pull-happy in High-A, though he still put balls in play fairly easily. He could enhance his offensive profile if he drove more balls in the air and tapped into more of his 15-20 homer potential. Kent makes up for below-average speed with advanced instincts on the bases and in the field. Though the Yankees will give him every chance to stay at shortstop, his fringy range and average arm are better suited for second base. He's at least an average defender at the keystone and his internal clock allows his arm to play up enough that he may be able to handle third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bowen could have played baseball and football at Michigan State coming out of an Ohio high school, but the Pirates tempted him into pro ball instead with an over-slot $392,500 bonus as an 11th-rounder in 2019. He flashed an intriguing power-speed combination in the Bucs' system -- most evident in a 23-homer, 26-steal campaign at High-A and Double-A in '23 -- but didn’t reach Triple-A until '25. The Padres signed Bowen as a Minor League free agent back in November and saw him take off in Spring Training and the first month of action at Triple-A El Paso. The right-handed-hitting outfielder bops his front leg in his slightly open stance before getting going with a leg kick. He’s been hitting the ball harder with El Paso with a max exit velocity of 112.6 mph and a 90th-percentile EV of 106.4 entering late April. He can elevate well to help him pick up extra-base hits in bunches too; in fact, he hit for the cycle in just his fifth game of 2026. But while he’s reeled in some of the aggression he showed early in his career, he still expands the zone too much, which would limit that power and overall hitting potential in The Show, and he’s particularly vulnerable on breakers down and away out of the zone. Even so, Bowen is at least an above-average runner capable of pushing for extra bases on balls to the gap or stealing bags when opportunities arise. That athleticism helps him on the grass too, and the Padres have played him at all three outfield spots to take advantage of it with an early emphasis on center field. With his twitchy toolset, Bowen could finally be pushing for an MLB debut as a fourth/fifth outfielder in his age-25 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There’s long been a complaint that baseball hasn’t been doing enough to attract premium athletes to the pro game. The Pirates did their part at the start of Day 3 of the 2019 Draft when they took Bowen, a two-sport star from the Ohio high school ranks, in Round 11. They went over slot with a $392,500 bonus to sign him away from playing football and baseball at Michigan State. He’s shown off an improving power-speed combination in three years of full-season ball, reaching Double-A in 2023 and capping things off with a solid showing in the Arizona Fall League. Bowen brings a football mentality to how he attacks the game, both in terms of his work ethic and how he’d run through a wall while playing center field. While his numbers were no doubt helped by hitting-friendly High-A Greensboro in 2023, the metrics under his 20-20 season were very good. He routinely registers high exit velocities with quality contact and does damage more consistently from the right side of the plate. There’s still work to be done on his approach as he continues to focus on not chasing and expanding the zone, with sweepers from right-handed pitchers particularly his kryptonite. With above-average speed and that aggressiveness a plus on the basepaths, Bowen continues to be a legitimate basestealing threat. He’s an excellent defender who can definitely play center and also looks good in the corners with a strong arm, and he’s also proven to be a capable first baseman. He likely profiles as a fourth outfielder, but the quality of his at-bats in the AFL was encouraging, and if he can cut down the K’s and up his walk rate, there could be more here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arroyo was one of the youngest players in the 2021 Draft class when he was the best player coming out of Puerto Rico and selected by the Mariners in the second round. He was having a solid first full season of pro ball at age 18 when he was part of the prospect package sent to the Reds for Luis Castillo at the 2022 Trade Deadline. Arroyo made a nice step up in 2023, reaching Double-A briefly, but then was derailed by a torn left labrum that cost him his 2024 season. He turned in a full 2025 campaign, and though reduced impact at the plate has led to some questions about his ultimate ceiling, he was added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. The Reds view the fact that Arroyo played 120 games at Double-A in 2025 as a win coming off that injury, then he added some more productive at-bats playing winter ball in Puerto Rico. He’s a switch-hitter who can make a ton of contact from both sides of the plate. It looked like added strength was contributing to more power, which didn’t reappear in 2025, perhaps because of the injury. He’s an aggressive hitter who is prone to chase too much and can struggle with softer stuff, but he also didn’t elevate the ball nearly as consistently last year compared with his pre-injury performances. One thing that has never been questioned is his defense and he still very much has the chops to play shortstop, with the actions and arm to stay there for a long time. He did get introduced to second base last year and he’ll continue to focus on both sides of the bag, giving the Reds options should they need help in Cincinnati now that he’s on the roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because Arroyo was just 17 years old when the Mariners drafted him in 2021, the native of Puerto Rico has always been very young for every level he's reached so far. So even after two full seasons in 2022 and 2023, the latter of which including getting dealt to the Reds in the Luis Castillo deal, and a missed 2024 season because of a torn left labrum suffered in Spring Training, he'll still be only 21 years old for the bulk of the 2025 season. Arroyo had touched Double-A in 2023 with a big up arrow next to his name, and he was able to shake off the rust from the layoff by holding his own in the Arizona Fall League in 2024. Arroyo’s time in the AFL was more about him starting to get his timing back at the plate while proving to himself that he put the injury behind him, so even though his offensive numbers were modest, those missions were accomplished. The switch-hitter swings the bat well from both sides with a contact-first approach that allows him to send line drives to all fields. Before the injury, his power started to show up more consistently and there should be more of that in the tank to come. A very aggressive baserunner with above-average speed, Arroyo likes to steal bags and take extra bases. The one thing that wasn’t rusty at all during his Fall League stint was Arroyo’s glovework. He’s a smooth defender with excellent body control, showing the ability to make all the plays and throws from all angles, with evaluators thinking he could play shortstop defensively in the big leagues right now. For now, though, he’ll get to focus on playing a full healthy year at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest members of the 2021 Draft class, Arroyo got more exposure to scouts when he relocated from Puerto Rico to Florida for his senior year of high school. Drafted at age 17, he went in the second round to the Mariners and was having a solid first full season of pro ball when he was sent to the Reds in the Deadline deal for Luis Castillo. He struggled initially after the trade and had just a .576 OPS through the end of May 2023, after which he righted the ship. He slashed .276/.356/.474 the rest of the way, including a bump up to Double-A to close out the season. That momentum came to a halt when he needed surgery to repair a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder in March, ending his 2024 season before it began. Before the injury, the Reds felt everything was trending up for the switch-hitting shortstop, who was set to play at age 20 for almost all of the 2024 season. He has a good swing from both sides of the plate, with a line-drive approach that produces hard contact to all fields. He started really coming into some \"man strength\" as the 2023 season progressed, and he started tapping into his extra-base authority more consistently, with some thinking he’s going to have at least average power eventually. After his rough start, he tightened up his approach and cut his strikeout rate considerably, all while raising his walk rate. Arroyo has swiped 56 bases over his first two full seasons of pro ball and should be a threat to steal as he continues to the upper levels of the Reds' system. He’s worked very hard on his defense at short, especially on balls to his glove side, exhibiting impressive body control and leaving no doubt about his ability to play the premium position. The Reds were impressed with his emotional maturity as much as his physical growth, leaving some thinking he’s primed for a breakout season once he’s fully returned from the shoulder injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arroyo was just 17 when the 2021 Draft rolled around and after impressing on the summer showcase circuit, the Puerto Rican infielder relocated to Florida for his senior year of high school for more exposure. The Mariners liked what they saw and took him in the second round of that summer’s Draft, and he was giving an early return on investment with a strong first full season in the Single-A California League when he was sent to the Reds in the Luis Castillo deal. Still only 19 years old for nearly all of the 2023 season, Arroyo has the chance to be a dynamic up-the-middle player. He swings the bat well from both sides of the plate and was productive each way, showing the ability to make hard contact with a line-drive approach. He’s added a good amount of strength to his wiry build already, and that led to more power than anticipated out of the gate, though he’s still more of a hit-over-power type. He could become even more of an impact hitter as he tightens up his approach, something that got away from him post-trade as he was likely pressing too much. If he continues to hit at all, Arroyo could be an elite-level player because there’s no doubt he’s going to be able to play shortstop for a long time. He has excellent hands and actions at the premium position, with more than enough arm to make throws from all over the infield. Assuming he gets his bearings with his new organization, he should continue to prove he has the tools to be an everyday shortstop in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the younger players in the 2021 Draft class, at age 17, Arroyo quickly established himself as the best player from Puerto Rico on the showcase circuit the summer prior. The potential shortstop got the chance to be evaluated more closely last spring after coming to Florida to attend Central Pointe Christian Academy for his senior season, which led to the Mariners taking him in the second round in 2021 and signing him for $1.65 million. He was having a stellar first full season, sitting in the Top 10 among California League hitters in a host of offensive categories when he was sent to the Reds as part of the package for Luis Castillo. Arroyo has an intriguing package of athleticism, defense and offensive potential, and he was making a quicker-than-expected transition to full-season ball in 2022. A switch-hitter who is a bit better from the right side, Arroyo has good contact skills and is a solid line-drive hitter. While he entered pro ball lacking strength, Arroyo has been praised for his sneaky wiry-strong build, and he was already starting to grow into some extra-base pop, with potentially more to come. Defensively, Arroyo has every chance to stick at shortstop, with plenty of arm strength, good hands and easy actions at the premium position. Arroyo can actually throw with both hands and has pitched left-handed, though that doesn’t necessarily mean he’ll do so professionally. Arroyo certainly had a wake-up call with his first taste of pro ball in the Arizona Complex League in 2021, hitting .211/.337/.324 (.661 OPS) with a 30.2% strikeout rate in 21 games, and used that lesson to work on his offensive game. If the bat continues to come along, he has the chance to eventually be an everyday shortstop in the big leagues.

just_baseball.label: JB 2026 Preseason
just_baseball.text:
Height/Weight: 5’11″, 175 | Bat/Throw: S/R | 2nd Round (48), 2021 (SEA) | ETA: 2026

Arroyo missed the entirety of the 2024 regular season due to labrum surgery during Spring Training. He turned in a fine 2025 campaign, but struggled to produce much power. Mechanical adjustments and added strength have helped Arroyo tap into much more power in 2026 as the glove and defensive versatility continue to stand out.

A switch hitter with a similar set up from both sides of the plate, Arroyo simplified his operation from both sides. Previously featuring a very crouched setup that would cause his weight to sway, pushing onto his front side prematurely. Arroyo is now more upright with his setup, coiling over his back side, rather than teetering over it and pushing out.

Staying taller on his back side has helped him leverage the ground more effectively, aiding both his raw power and batted ball angles. His setup was even more dramatically crouched from the left side, with his front knee bowed and open. His hands are also closer to his launch position from both sides, compared to the previous lower starting point, below his back shoulder.

The quality of contact shift through the first half of 2026 is impossible to overlook, not just on the surface where he nearly matched his career-high home run total through his first 50 games, but in the raw power and batted ball angles as well.

Arroyo upped his 90th percentile exit velocity by two MPH, while cutting his ground ball rate by nearly 20% and doubling his Air Pull percentage. Previously featuring below average exit velocities, Arroyo’s now average raw impact paired with the improved angles makes 20 home runs an attainable plateau.

The contact skills are above average for Arroyo from both sides of the plate, with the aforementioned swing adjustments improving his ability to handle secondaries as well. Though the contact skills are strong, Arroyo can hurt himself with his aggressive approach, consistently running a chase rate at or around 35%.

Above average hit and leaps in the power department give Arroyo the upside to be an above average contributor offensively, but the swing decisions could hold him back some.

An above average runner and sure-handed defender with a plus arm Arroyo provides plenty of value in the infield, with the ability to play an above average shortstop with comfort moving all over the diamond. Arroyo has improved his efficiency as a base stealer and should be a threat for around 20 bags annually.

Though losing out on his 2024 campaign was a tough blow for his development, Arroyo proved to have his feet back under him in 2025 before appearing to really put things together in his age 22 season in 2026. Arroyo’s offensive improvements give him the upside of an everyday shortstop, as even league average production with his glove and speed should give him a reasonable path to 3-WAR. If the bat stalls at the highest level (would likely be due to swing decision issues and the power uptick perhaps not translating against big league competition), Arroyo has the fallback of a quality infield utility piece, giving him a high probability of sticking on a big league roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Juenger worked almost exclusively as a reliever at Missouri State, striking out 31 batters over 21 innings in his final season with the Bears. The Blue Jays picked up Juenger in the sixth round in 2021, and he made an immediate impression in Draft camp, which convinced the Blue Jays to challenge him out of the gates with an assignment to High-A Vancouver. In his pro debut, Juenger posted a 2.70 ERA over 20 innings with 34 strikeouts. In 2022, the Blue Jays stretched out Juenger into a bulk relief role, something the club has worked to develop consciously as the role grows more popular at the MLB level. Making 19 starts and 19 relief appearances while typically working in the range of three innings, Juenger posted a 3.76 ERA with 100 strikeouts over 88 2/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A. This quickly put Juenger on the MLB radar entering 2023. Juenger’s best pitch is his fastball, which sits near 95 mph. He plays an upper-80s cutter off of that, and his mid-80s changeup is developing nicely to the point where it's become more of his second pitch. He's opened 2023 in the same bulk role as ’22 -- in part because his stuff tends to fade the deeper he gets into outings -- and with the ability to grow or shrink that workload, he’s given himself multiple paths to the bigs if the results are there. Juenger’s development case from a workload standpoint is one the Blue Jays are hoping to repeat with many other young arms in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Working almost exclusively as a reliever at Missouri State, Juenger struck out 31 batters over 21 innings with a 3.86 ERA as a junior coming off a strong sophomore season and stint in the Northwoods League. The Blue Jays selected Juenger in the sixth round, and he made one of the best first impressions in his class -- immediately convincing the organization he was ready for a challenge in ’21. Toronto sent him to High-A Vancouver, where Juenger posted a 2.70 ERA with 34 strikeouts over 20 innings, walking just four batters. Juenger leads with a fastball that now sits at 95-96 mph and features a good slider as his top secondary pitch. His changeup has developed nicely, is getting whiffs on its own and will be key for Juenger long term, while his fastball-slider combo is advanced for this point in his development. Juenger has a smaller build to his six-foot frame, and that’s been tested some in 2022. To his credit, the 22-year-old right-hander looked solid in an aggressive opening assignment to Double-A New Hampshire and moved to Triple-A Buffalo already in his first full season Juenger has been limited to two-to-four innings per outing at both of his stops in 2022, and the move has helped his stuff play up. It’s a promising enough arsenal to work through a lineup at least once, and that’s valuable in the modern game where roles are constantly evolving. Juenger is already knocking on Toronto’s door and could be a Major League option less than two years after his Draft date.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez starred in college at Mississippi, winning national freshman of the year accolades in 2021 and a College World Series championship in 2022 while also starting for the U.S. collegiate national team both summers. When questions about his athleticism creeped up during his junior season, he slipped from a potential top-five pick to No. 15 overall, where he signed for an under-slot $3.9 million. He has done little damage as pro, slashing .232/.310/.335 in his first three seasons while reaching Triple-A. While Gonzalez has continued to control the strike zone and consistently put the ball in play just like he did with the Rebels, he has lapsed into a defensive approach at the plate and makes too much soft contact. After displaying 25-homer power potential in college, he rarely turns his left-handed stroke loose and rarely drives the ball with authority. Adjustments to quicken his load, improve his bat path and allow him to pull more pitches won't make much difference unless he swings with more intent. Gonzalez has below-average speed but his instincts allow him to play better than that on the bases and in the field. He has sure hands, solid arm strength and a finely calibrated internal clock, though he's not particularly rangy. Primarily a shortstop in his first two years as a pro, he spent more time at second base in 2025 and may not be more than utilityman unless he gets his bat going.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez had a decorated college career at Mississippi, winning national freshman of the year honors in 2021, helping lead the Rebels to their first-ever College World Series title in 2022 and starting for the U.S. collegiate national team during both summers. Questions about his athleticism arose during his junior season, so he dropped to the 15th overall pick, where the White Sox signed him for $3.9 million. He has slashed just .233/.313/.326 while reaching Double-A in his first two pro seasons, though he did star in the Southern League playoffs last September as Birmingham won the championship. After controlling the strike zone and making consistent contact in college, Gonzalez has continued to do the same in pro ball. But the 25-homer upside he showed as an amateur hasn't translated, and it now looks like he'll have to add some strength and use a more selectively aggressive approach to produce 12-15 per year. Even after making adjustments to quicken his load and give him a better left-handed swing path, he still struggled to pull pitches or drive them with much authority in 2024. Gonzalez is a below-average runner with solid instincts on the bases but questions about his ability to remain at shortstop. He's a sure-handed defender with solid arm strength and a good internal clock, and the White Sox think he can cover enough ground at short. Others think he's better suited for second base (where he saw some action last season) or third base, which would put more demands on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez earned national freshman of the year honors at Mississippi in 2021, helped lead the Rebels to their first-ever College World Series championship in 2022 and started at shortstop for the U.S. collegiate national team both summers. He continued to star last spring but teams began to question his athleticism, so he lasted until the 15th overall pick, where Chicago signed him for $3.9 million. He slugged just .260 in his pro debut, though the White Sox believe some offseason adjustments will restore his power. Gonzalez exhibited fine bat-to-ball skills and plate discipline throughout his college career, and he walked nearly as much as he struck out in his first taste of pro ball. As an amateur, his strength plus the bat speed and leverage in his left-handed stroke were thought to give him 25-homer potential, with most of his power playing to his pull side. After struggling to turn on pitches in his debut, he's standing more upright at the plate in hopes that will translate into a quicker load and better swing path, but he's not hitting the ball with much authority in 2024. Because Gonzalez's pure speed is below average at best, there are questions about his ability to remain at shortstop. His proponents -- the White Sox among them -- think he covers enough ground with his long strides and makes more than enough plays with his keen instincts, quick hands and solid arm. Others think he's most likely to wind up at second or third base, which would put more pressure on his ability to hit for power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After tearing up junior college pitching for two years at Butler (Kan.) CC and Eastern Oklahoma State JC, Cox led Oral Roberts to the Men's College World Series in 2023, topping NCAA Division I with 114 hits and fashioning a 47-game hitting streak (the third-longest in D-I history). The Athletics drafted him in the sixth round that July and dealt him to the Giants for Ross Stripling seven months later. He stole 58 bases in each of his first two seasons in San Francisco's system before suddenly becoming one of the hottest hitters in the Minors in the first two months of 2026, earning a promotion from Double-A to the big leagues. The son of former big league catcher Darron Cox, Jonah has improved his right-handed stroke and his swing decisions this year. He's chasing fewer pitches and hitting the ball harder than ever, and has looked much more dynamic at the plate. He's doing a better job of getting on base, and while he won't be a slugger, he now appears more likely to translate his bat speed and strength into 15-homer power. Cox's best tool is his plus-plus speed and he uses it to wreak havoc on the bases. A shortstop in junior college, he began playing center field at Oral Roberts and has developed into a solid defender there as he has gained more experience. He has fringy arm strength but gets to balls quickly and recorded 10 assists in each of the last two seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 40 The Pirates found McAdoo all the way down in the 13th round of the 2023 Draft and eventually dealt him to the Blue Jays for Isiah Kiner-Falefa at the 2024 Trade Deadline. While McAdoo struggled with New Hampshire down the stretch in 2024, his full line between High-A and Double-A left him with an .843 OPS and 17 home runs over 124 games. In ‘25, McAdoo put up a .732 OPS with 16 home runs over a full season (121 games) at Double-A. That doesn’t quite capture McAdoo’s power ceiling, but that’s going to be his ticket up the ladder if it all comes together. He produces much of this naturally with his big, physical frame, so he’ll be a fun project for the Blue Jays hitting coaches as they work to get him driving the ball in the air as consistently as possible. McAdoo’s defense at third base is still a work in progress, but the organization believes that it can at least be playable; he’ll start to mix in more corner outfield reps this season, which should be a nice addition to his profile. McAdoo has bat speed, an ability to handle high velocity and legitimate power bona fides. That all combines to create an impressive amount of upside, but the Blue Jays will need to see that come together in a jump year as he turns 24 in 2026 with plenty of other infielders coming up in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates found McAdoo all the way down in the 13th round of the 2023 Draft out of San Jose State, a pick that immediately paid dividends with his hot start in the Minors. McAdoo was eventually dealt to the Blue Jays for Isiah Kiner-Falefa at the Trade Deadline, and while he struggled with Double-A New Hampshire down the stretch, his full ‘24 line between High-A and Double-A left McAdoo with an .843 OPS and 17 home runs over 124 games. That doesn’t quite capture McAdoo’s power ceiling, which is his calling card. Beyond Orelvis Martinez, McAdoo has one of the best power tools in the system and immediately impressed the Blue Jays with his bat speed. McAdoo produces much of this naturally with his big, physical frame, so he’ll be a fun project for the Blue Jays hitting coaches as they work to get him driving the ball in the air as consistently as possible. McAdoo’s defense at third base is still very much a work in progress, so it remains to be seen whether he’ll stick there, try more second base or eventually slide to first. He tried out right field in both systems last year too. McAdoo will need to hit his way up the ladder, but he has one of the highest-upside bats in the system, so that’s a fine starting point. His pure bat speed should help him handle velocity and more advanced breaking balls, but he’ll likely always be a “power-over-hit” prospect. With that in mind, sorting out McAdoo’s defensive profile will be a big priority in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Weston had an accomplished college career at Michigan before the Orioles made him an eighth-round pick in 2022, and he’s been one of their systems most consistent performers since debuting that summer. He spent most of his full season debut at High-A Aberdeen and had his most impressive year yet in 2024, pitching to a 2.97 ERA and 1.01 WHIP across 109 innings, mostly at Double-A. The 6-foot-2, 215-pound Weston is a sinker/slider righty with a three-quarters arm slot, a four-pitch mix and some polish. He operates off a low-90s two-seamer that generates weak contact and high ground-ball rates, and uses a high-70s sweeping slider to miss bats when he needs to. He also uses a splitter against righties and a changeup against lefties, throwing both with a deceptive delivery that makes his low arm slot difficult to pick up. Paired with above -average control and the ability to locate all of his pitches, Weston is able to miss bats without breaking the radar gun. He walked only 2.4 batters per nine at Double-A. If Weston maintains his level of performance, he has a chance to fulfill his ceiling as a durable back-end starter. But there is a chance the stuff proves less vexing for more advanced hitters, particularly the second and third time through a lineup. If that’s the case, Weston could profile as the type of valuable multi-inning reliever that tends to always be in demand and consequently enjoy lengthy careers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of an all-prospect Eastern Oklahoma State JC rotation along with current Phillies prospects Christian McGowan and Andrew Walling in 2021, Sandlin transferred to Oklahoma and starred in the postseason as the Sooners finished runner-up at the 2022 Men's College World Series. The Royals paid him an over-slot $397,500 as an 11th-round pick that July and dealt him to the Red Sox for John Schreiber in February 2024. Though he struck out 189 in 163 1/3 innings in two years in Boston's system, he also logged a 4.79 ERA and was sent to the White Sox as part of a Jordan Hicks salary dump this February. Sandlin's fastball sits at 95-97 mph and reaches 100 mph, but it can get rocked when he doesn't command it well because it lacks consistent run and carry. He began using a sweeping mid-80s slider in 2024 and switched to an upper-80s cutter as his third pitch last season. He used to get good tumble on an upper-80s splitter that he employed as a changeup, though he barely used it in 2025. Sandlin repeats his delivery well and provided plenty of strikes until he reached Triple-A, where he posted a 7.61 ERA while working out of the bullpen as a potential callup last summer. But he also lacks command and gets hit much harder than his stuff indicates he should. He comes with mid-rotation starter ceiling but also a lot of reliever risk, and he has to prove his durability after missing time in 2023 (oblique) and 2024 (forearm strain).

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a loaded rotation in 2021 at Eastern Oklahoma State JC with Christian McGowan and Andrew Walling (both now in the Phillies system), Sandler transferred to Oklahoma for 2022. After an inconsistent regular season with the Sooners, he struck out 10 in a win over Kansas State in the Big 12 Conference tournament, beat Florida in the NCAA regionals and fanned 12 in a College World Series victory over Texas A&M to earn an over-slot $397,500 bonus as a Royals 11th-rounder. He dominated Single-A hitters last season but strained his oblique in his second start after a promotion to High-A and missed the final three months, then joined the Red Sox in a February trade for John Schreiber. Sandlin's four-pitch mix and strike-throwing ability allowed him to post a 79/13 K/BB ratio in Single-A in 2023. His fastball parks at 93-95 mph and peaks at 98 with riding action that's effective when he operates up in the zone. He always has demonstrated nice feel for spin and has a pair of solid breaking balls, favoring his mid-80s slider over his low-80s curveball with downer break. Sandlin also gets good depth on his upper-80s splitter, though it doesn't have enough velocity separation from his heater to serve as a true change of pace. While he never has had any issues providing strikes with his easy delivery, his command isn't as sharp as his control and his fastball gets hit when he doesn't locate it well. He'll need more consistency and refinement, but he immediately became one of the best starting pitching prospects in a Boston system thin in that commodity.

mlb_pipeline.label: TJ Pre-Season 2026
mlb_pipeline.text: Jump was a top 50 prospect coming out of the California high school ranks in 2021 but decided to head to UCLA for college rather than entertain starting his pro career. He pitched briefly before needing Tommy John surgery, then missed all of the 2023 season. After transferring to Louisiana State, he threw well enough to land with the A’s in Competitive Balance Round B in 2024. Their over-slot $2 million investment in the lefty seems to be a good one as he pitched his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season, represented the organization in the Futures Game in July and established himself as one of the better left-handed prospects in the game. The 6-footer’s fastball has always played up because of deception stemming from his lower arm slot, and his velocity has taken a nice step forward as well. After sitting in the 92-94 mph range at LSU, Jump’s heater averaged 94.6 mph, according to Synergy, reaching the upper-90s and touching triple digits occasionally. He has distinct breaking stuff, and he went to his low-80s slider with cutting action frequently in his first year of pro ball, eliciting a 36-percent miss rate with the pitch, while also throwing his upper-70s curve with downer break effectively. His fading changeup is clearly his fourth pitch, but it has some depth to it. Given his size and unorthodox delivery, there have been questions about Jump’s ability to hold up as a starter, and some still see some reliever risk in him. But he throws a ton of strikes and maintains his stuff with good arm speed, so there’s no reason to keep him from trying to reach his mid-rotation ceiling now, with a chance of him impacting a big league staff in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rated California’s top high school pitching prospect coming out of JSerra Catholic High School, Jump was committed to UCLA when the Padres drafted him in 2021. Opting for the college route, he pitched in seven games for the Bruins in 2022 before sustaining an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. Shelved for over a year, he transferred to Louisiana State and pitched well over a healthy 2024, posting a 3.47 ERA in 17 games (15 starts) with 101 strikeouts over 83 innings. That standout sophomore campaign led to the A’s selecting him with their Competitive Balance Round B pick and going over slot for a $2 million signing bonus. After going through instructs, Jump is set to begin his first season as a pro in 2025. Jump’s fastball is difficult for opposing hitters to pick up with an arm angle that creates some deception. The heater sits about 92-94 mph and can reach up to 97 with good carry up in the zone. His upper-70s curveball has significant downer break, and his low-80s slider has cutting action. His fading low-80s changeup is used far less than his other three offerings. Listed at 6-foot, Jump lacks the size of a typical starter, though his growth since the surgery and ability to generate his stuff with arm speed helps his potential outlook as a long-term starter. The ceiling of a mid-rotation starter is there, though some scouts believe he might be better suited in a bullpen role. To start out, the A’s will develop him as a starter and look to see him maintain good health and strike-throwing ability.

espn.label: ESPN 2026 Preseason
espn.text: Type : Potential middle-of-the-rotation starter, if he can stay healthy Jump was a strong prospect out of high school with second-round interest whose price wasn't met, pushing him to UCLA. He threw 16⅓ innings before needing elbow surgery that knocked out the rest of his freshman year and all of his sophomore year before he transferred to LSU for his draft year in 2024. Jump finished the season strong, showing above-average stuff and strong data, but a limited track record of bulk innings and more solid-average off-speed stuff than any truly plus secondary pitch. The A's gave him an overslot $2 million bonus at the 73rd pick and that paid off with a big 2025. Jump's velocity spiked almost 2 mph, which helped firm up his above-average slider and curveball, but his fastball remains his best pitch. Jump's heater sits 93-96 and touches 98 mph with plus shape. After throwing 112⅔ innings in 2025 and 83.0 innings at LSU in 2024, Jump now seems durable enough to be a starter in the mold of Robbie Ray .

just_baseball.label: JB 2026 Preseason
just_baseball.text:
Height/Weight: 6’0″, 200 | Bat/Throw: L/L | CB-B (73), 2024 (ATH) | ETA: 2026

One of the most biggest breakout arms of 2025, Jump has seen his fastball velocity climb by two ticks as a pro while finding a much better feel for his breaking balls.

Jump’s fastball leads the way, now sitting in the mid 90s with plus carry, averaging 18 inches of induced vertical break from a below average release height. He also has a slight hesitation in his delivery that seems to only add to the uncomfortable nature of his fastball for hitters. The velocity and life it features makes it a big whiff pitch within the zone as well as a chase pitch at the top.

Working off of his plus fastball is a pair of breaking balls with the sweeper leading the way at 82-84 MPH. Jump’s breaking ball shapes have some variance that seems to be unintentional, but he still has little trouble landing them for a strike consistently. Sometimes it’s more of a true sweeper, other times it’s shorter horizontally with a bit more depth vertically.

Jump’s curveball is a bit more consistent shape wise, featuring two-plane break at 79-81 MPH. He prefers to throw it to righties, showcasing a good feel to back door it as well as bury it towards the back leg of hitters.

Lagging well behind is Jump’s changeup, which he only mixes in around five percent of the time with a strike rate below 50%.

Jump’s uptick in stuff and improved pitchability helped him breakout in a big way in the early going of the 2025 season and he did not miss a beat after quickly being pushed to Double-A. His standout fastball will easily be a plus pitch at the highest level and with a pair of breaking balls that he has developed a great feel for to go with it, Jump now looks like a potential No. 3 starter who should at least land as a quality No. 4 option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dion earned Southland Conference pitcher of the year accolades and set a McNeese State record with 121 strikeouts in 99 2/3 innings in 2021 before the Guardians made him a ninth-round pick that July. Though he doesn't light up radar guns, he thrived in his first two-plus years as a pro, logging a 2.14 ERA with 307 strikeouts in 256 2/3 innings. He needed just two months to earn a promotion to Double-A last season, when he led the system with a 2.39 ERA. Cleveland persuaded Dion to stop trying to completely emulate Clayton Kershaw's delivery and helped him gain a bit more velocity on his fastball, though it still sits at 88-90 mph and tops out at 92. His heater is effective enough with his combination of carry, command and deception, working well in tandem with his best pitch, a tumbling 78-82 mph changeup. He also mixes in a pair of fringy breaking balls, a low-80s slider against lefties and a soft mid-70s curveball against righties. While Dion no longer looks like a shorter exact replica of Kershaw, he still hides the ball well behind his body and utilizes a higher arm slot. He has tremendous feel for his craft, mixing his offerings and locations and sometimes adding a pause in his delivery to throw hitters' timing off. Though he's just 5-foot-10 and not very physical, he has a track record of strikes and success that could make him a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s not often that a pitcher enters pro ball via the international free agent market and pitches only in relief. That’s what Herrera has done since signing with the Rockies for $200,000 in January 2021. The Rockies have allowed the left-handed to develop slowly, and he spent two years in the Dominican Summer League and one in the Arizona Complex League, finally reaching full-season ball in 2024. After pitching well in the Dominican Winter League, things clicked more in 2025 when he reached Double-A for the first time, represented the organization in the Futures Game and pitched in the Arizona Fall League, all en route to be added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. He continued his upward trajectory by starting the year in Triple-A and then making his Major League debut in late May, but he tore his UCL in his third big league outing, ending his season. When you combine a funky delivery with velocity, you might get a very valuable left-handed reliever. Herrera cranked his fastball up to 99 mph in 2025, averaging around 95 and he throws it from a low three-quarters slot that allows it to carry above barrels, resulting in a lot of misses and chases. He leans on the heater, sometimes too much, and will have to keep using his slider more, because it has the chance to really have teeth. He threw it around 86 mph across all stops last year with depth to it when he finishes it and it missed bats at a 44-percent rate, according to Synergy. He actually has an upper-80s changeup that could be useful against right-handed hitters, but it’s not as consistent. Herrera will still only be 23 for all of the 2027 season, when he'll hopefully be able to return to the mound post-injury. If he can continue to hone his craft in areas like holding runners and fielding his position, not to mention committing to throwing that slider, he still has high-leverage reliever upside when healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Teams interested in signing young amateur pitchers tend to look for clean deliveries and arm actions, guys who look like future starters. Perhaps that’s why some teams didn’t consider Herrera when the 2021 international signing period opened. The Rockies were willing to think outside the box and bring the smallish lefty with the funky mechanics into the organization; initial progress was slow. Herrera spent two years in the Dominican Summer League and one in the Arizona Complex League, but he started taking off in 2024, pitching his way from Single-A Fresno to High-A Spokane, where he finished things off with three perfect innings during the team’s championship run. He tacked on 10 strong appearances in the Dominican Winter League. Used only as a reliever, Herrera relies largely on his fastball-slider combination to go right after hitters. His fastball sits around 95 mph and touches 97 and it comes from a low three-quarters arm slot, an upshoot heater that has carry above the barrel that gets a lot of swing-and-miss. He can get too fastball-reliant and will have to keep learning to trust his 84 mph slider. It's a pitch he has improved by more consistently staying on top of; it flashes better than average while dropping below barrels. He actually has feel for a changeup with depth, but he doesn’t throw it much. Herrera pounded the strike zone during his time with Fresno, but he wasn’t as sharp with Spokane. He’s made adjustments before, so there’s confidence he’ll be able to become another legitimate big league bullpen piece for the Rockies.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mautz didn’t become a full-time starter at the University of San Diego until his junior year but was good enough in 2022 to push into the second round, where the Cardinals took him and signed him for $1.1 million. He has steadily climbed one level per season from Single-A in 2023 to Double-A in '25, and it was with Springfield last year that he enjoyed his best professional campaign yet. Mautz was a Texas League All-Star with his 2.98 ERA, 1.11 WHIP and 134 strikeouts in 114 2/3 innings, and the Cardinals protected him from the Rule 5 Draft with a spot on the 40-man roster in November. The 6-foot-3 left-hander throws from a low three-quarters slot that gives him a little deception and a flat angle on his fastball. The heater came with some extra velocity in Mautz’s age-23 season and sat in the 91-95 mph range, and even with that increase, he still commanded it well to stave off hard contact. His mid-80s slider gets good depth that leads to some truly ugly swings from batters from both sides, but especially lefties. Mautz can work in an upper-70s curveball with slurvy tendencies too, and he barely used a mid-80s changeup. That lack of an armside weapon could be an issue as Mautz heads to Triple-A and beyond. For now, his control has actually improved at each stop up the St. Louis chain, and he’s surpassed the 100-inning mark in each of his three seasons. That combination of durability and effectiveness should keep him on St. Louis’ starting depth chart, but his upside is limited to the back end of a rotation. The fastball-slider mix would work in a relief setting if he can’t break in as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years in relief, Mautz moved into a starting role at the University of San Diego in 2022 and thrived with a 3.87 ERA, 129 strikeouts and only 22 walks in 90 2/3 innings. The Cardinals selected him in the second round that July and signed him for below slot at $1.1 million. Mautz threw 104 innings in his first full season, but all of them came at Single-A Palm Beach, where he finished with a 3.98 ERA, 1.34 WHIP and 115 strikeouts. The 6-foot-3 left-hander was 89-93 mph with his pair of fastballs, using both a four-seamer and a sinker. He could get 15-17 inches of horizontal movement with those heaters, and the sinker in particular helped him run a 49.5 percent ground-ball rate that was 13th-best in the Florida State League (among hurlers with at least 50 innings). His 78-82 mph slider remains his best pitch -- a two-plane breaker that can be hard to pick out of his deceptive slot -- and it dropped below the zone to get significant chase in 2023. His mid-80s changeup flashes promise with similar horizontal movement to the sinker but it's generally too firm, and per Statcast, he didn’t throw it all in August or September. Mautz also has an upper-70s curveball with more drop and sweep than the slider, and he picked up usage of that as the year wore on. The former Torero was better at limiting walks in college, as he worked with a 9.9 percent walk rate with Palm Beach. He would make for an interesting relief candidate with the slider, but that decision might be at least another year away.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mautz was primarily a reliever in his first two years at the University of San Diego, and that bullpen work extended to a stint in the Northwoods League in the summer of 2021. He joined the Toreros as a junior and thrived in the role, posting a 3.87 ERA with 129 strikeouts and only 29 walks in 90 2/3 innings.
