mlb_pipeline.text: Monteverde started his college career at NCAA Division III Virginia Wesleyan in 2017 before moving to Division II Seton Hill (Pa.) and missing much of 2019-20 because of Tommy John surgery and the pandemic. He landed at Texas Tech as a graduate transfer in 2021, became the Red Raiders' top starter and went in the eighth round of the Draft despite being almost 24. He has led the system in ERA in each of his two full pro seasons and was the organization's Minor League pitcher of the year in 2023, when he also worked in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game. Monteverde outperforms his stuff, thanks in large part to his lone plus pitch, a low-80s changeup with depth that keeps right-handers off balance. His only other average offering is a tight low-80s slider that holds left-handers in check, and he'll occasionally turn it into a harder cutter. He throws strikes with an 88-90 mph fastball that peaks at 92, using four-seamers for early-count strikes and two-seamers to get grounders, and will mix in a soft mid-70s curveball. The quintessential crafty lefty, Monteverde relies on changing speeds and locations because he can't overpower anyone. He has good control but his walk totals have risen as he has advanced through the Minors and had to nibble more often against more advanced hitters. He got pounded for 15 runs in two Triple-A starts last summer, so he's still going to have to prove himself at that level before he gets a shot as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Monteverde began his college career at NCAA Division III Virginia Wesleyan in 2017 before transferring to NCAA D-II Seton Hill (Pa.), where he lost most of 2019-20 to Tommy John surgery and the pandemic. He moved on to Texas Tech as a graduate transfer, became the Red Raiders' Friday-night starter and despite being nearly 24, went in the eighth round of the 2021 Draft. He reached Double-A and led all Marlins Minor League starters in ERA (3.20) during his first full pro season. Monteverde uses an 89-92 mph four-seam fastball to get ahead in counts and a two-seamer with similar velocity to get groundballs and chases out of the strike zone. His best pitch is a low-80s changeup with depth that helps him keep right-handers from sitting on his below-average heater. His tight low-80s slider has similar movement and works as a back-foot pitch against righties, and he also can turn it into a harder cutter or even mix in a soft mid-70s curveball. A classic crafty left-hander, Monteverde keeps hitters off balance by changing speeds and working both sides of the plate. He can't overwhelm hitters with his stuff but helps his cause by pounding the strike zone and commanding his arsenal well. He comes with a low ceiling but a high floor as a potential back-of-the-rotation starter or multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Young signed with the Orioles as an undrafted free agent in 2020 following stints at the junior college level, Howard College (Texas) and Louisiana-Lafayette, where he excelled both in the rotation and out of the ‘pen. He enjoyed a solid pro debut but made only three starts in 2022 before being sidelined by elbow surgery for more than a year. Young returned in July 2023 and moved quickly from Double-A to Triple-A, where he spent most of '24 before the Orioles added him to their 40-man roster prior to the Rule 5 Draft in November. Young is a 6-foot-6 right-hander whose performance exceeds the sum of its parts. His repertoire might not feature a truly above-average offering, but it’s a legitimate four-pitch mix that Young augments with excellent command, and he throws enough strikes to be effective without earth-shattering stuff. His fastball is an effective pitch that lives 93-95 mph but plays up because he throws everything out of the same window, and he keeps hitters off balance with a slider, cutter and changeup that can all be average offerings. The fading changeup is particularly important for Young, as it helps neutralize left-handed hitters. Young doesn’t miss a ton of bats, and his lack of a true out pitch probably limits his ceiling. But the pitch mix and ability to command his entire arsenal give him a solid floor as a dependable strike-thrower who figures to factor into Baltimore’s big league mix in 2025, perhaps in a swingman role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The only thing that apparently can slow down Keaschall’s bat is his elbow. After hitting well in two years at University of San Francisco, and especially as a junior after transferring to Arizona State, he was taken by the Twins in the second round in 2023. He quickly earned a promotion from High-A to Double-A in his first full season after slashing .335/.457/.544 with 14 steals in 44 games with Cedar Rapids. The 2024 Futures Gamer performed well in Double-A, though a torn UCL limited him to DH duties before the decision was made for him to have Tommy John surgery in August so he would be ready to go in 2025. The right-handed-hitting Keaschall has quickly developed a reputation as one of the better pure hitters in the Minors. He routinely barrels up the baseball and has an advanced approach at the plate, continuing a trend he had in college by limiting strikeouts (17.2 percent K rate in 2024) and drawing nearly as many walks (13.4 pct). He recognizes spin well and has long been a solid two-strike hitter. He’s hit over power, but because of his approach and his knack for contact, seeing him get to average pop eventually isn’t out of the question. Keaschall runs well, with good instincts, so he should continue to be a base-stealing threat. His athleticism has allowed him to move around the field some, though it’s unclear where his best long-term home defensively will be. Assuming the elbow comes all the way back, he’ll be just fine at second, where he played regularly at ASU, but he has the chops to play center or left field as well. The flexibility might come in handy as his bat is going to be ready soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two seasons at the University of San Francisco, and two solid summers with Orleans in the Cape Cod League, Keaschall entered the transfer portal and landed at Arizona State for his junior season in 2023. His 1.168 OPS, 18 homers and 18 steals helped him land in the second round of the Draft, where he signed with the Twins for a just-under-slot bonus of $1.5 million. He had a solid pro debut that saw him touch High-A at the end of the year, then turned in a terrific first full season that saw him reach Double-A and play in the Futures Game before he was shut down in August to have Tommy John surgery so he could be ready to swing the bat again at the start of 2025. Keaschall has a long amateur résumé of having a feel for the barrel, both in college and with a wood bat in his hands on the Cape. He left college with a strikeout rate under 11 percent while walking nearly as much, and he’s kept those trends during his brief pro career. He has a very solid approach and is a good two-strike hitter. The power really started to show up in Arizona, but while he should have extra-base authority at this level, he's likely to be a hit-over-power type of right-handed hitter. With above-average speed and good instincts, Keaschall can turn his on-base skills to extra bases by stealing some bags, and his athleticism is an asset defensively, though it hasn't been totally clear where he'll profile long-term. He went to Driveline during the offseason to work on his arm action, with very encouraging results. He played second base exclusively at ASU, and that's mostly where he saw time during his debut, and he started seeing time in center field as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Division III standout at Washington University in St. Louis, Durbin signed for $50,000 as a Braves 14th-round pick in 2021 but lasted only one full season in the Atlanta system before he was traded to the Yankees in a three-player deal for Lucas Luetge in December 2022. He was a high-average, high-steal performer in pinstripes and batted .287 with 29 thefts in 82 games at Triple-A last summer. The 5-foot-6 infielder was a two-time Arizona Fall League standout to make up for lost at-bats – most recently for a broken right wrist – and set the AFL single-season SB record with 29 steals this fall. The Yankees added him to the 40-man in November and traded him a month later to the Brewers in a deal for Devin Williams. The right-handed hitter starts from a slightly open stance before unleashing a big leg kick. That said, his hand-eye coordination is so good that he thrives on making contact in the zone, running Z-contact rates above 90 percent on every pitch type he saw more than 40 times at Triple-A (per Synergy Sports). He doesn’t expand the zone much either, keeping walk rates healthy and K rates low. Power is very much in question. He ran a 100.5 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity (similar to Sal Frelick in the Majors) but shows enough lift and pull to pick up extra-base hits. Durbin’s plus speed, combined with his baserunning acumen and aggression, is a major asset and fits well with the modern game. The Yankees got him time at second, third and shortstop and even some looks in center and left to give him room to roam. His arm is a touch light, making the keystone his best spot, but he profiles best as a utilityman that can help virtually everywhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quero left Cuba in 2019, signed with the Angels for $200,000 in February 2021 and won California League MVP honors a year later after leading the Single-A circuit in slugging (.530) and OPS (.965) at age 19. His numbers dropped when the Angels skipped him a level to Double-A in 2023, though he performed better after joining the White Sox as part of the Lucas Giolito/Reynaldo López trade in late July. He reached Triple-A at age 21 last year and led all Minor League catchers his age or younger in OPS (.829) and wRC+ (139). An offensive-minded catcher, Quero is a switch-hitter who has been more potent from the right side of the plate against upper-level pitching. He has a more advanced approach than most players his age, rarely chasing pitches out of the zone and making repeated contact. He did a better job of pulling pitches and hitting them harder in 2024, fueling optimism that he'll get to most of his average to solid raw power and become a 20-homer threat. Quero will have to maintain the conditioning of his thick 5-foot-10 frame because he's a baseclogger who needs to hold onto his so-so agility behind the plate. He's making progress with his receiving, framing and blocking but may not become more than a fringy defender. He has average arm strength but needs to improve his accuracy because throwing errors have been a repeated issue, including 10 in 75 games last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of Cuba's top hitters at the 2018 15-and-under World Cup, Quero left the island a year later and signed with the Angels for $200,000 in February 2021. He won Single-A California League MVP honors in 2022, slashing .312/.435/.530 at age 19, before skipping a level to Double-A last season. While he posted less gaudy statistics as the third-youngest regular in the Southern League, the White Sox acquired him to be their catcher of the future as part of the Lucas Giolito/Reynaldo López trade in late July. A switch-hitter, Quero did much more damage from the right side in 2023 after offering more production as a lefty the year before. He controls the strike zone, makes consistent contact and uses the opposite field well from both sides of the plate, and that didn't change even when his numbers dipped last season. He struggled to launch balls in the air in 2023 but is driving them with more authority this year, creating optimism that he can get to 20-homer power. Quero has a thick 5-foot-11, 210-pound build, lacks quickness and looked slower on the bases and behind the plate in 2023 than he did previously. An offensive-minded catcher, he's working to improve his receiving, framing and blocking, but he may not be more than a fringy defender. He features average arm strength and erased 24 percent of basestealers last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A regular on Cuban youth teams, Quero left the island in 2019 and signed with the Angels for $200,000 in February 2021. After a promising pro debut, he won MVP honors in the Single-A California League in 2022, batting .313/.435/.530 as a 19-year-old. He jumped to Double-A this season and was the third-youngest regular in the Southern League when the White Sox acquired him and left-hander Ky Bush in exchange for Lucas Giolito and Reynaldo López in late July. A switch-hitter with more power from the left side of the plate, Quero barrels up the ball consistently from both sides. He has an advanced approach with excellent plate discipline, drawing a ton of walks in the early stages of his pro career. He has the chance to be at least an above-average hitter when all is said and done, and his ability to tap into his raw pop took a nice step forward in 2022, with more over-the-fence ability to come as he continues to figure out when to attack pitches in the zone. Quero moves well behind the plate and has a solid arm. There's still work to be done on other facets of his defensive game, from his receiving to his game-calling, though he's still just 20 and has plenty of time to arrive. The White Sox acquired him with hopes that he'll be their starting catcher of the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quero initially made a name for himself in international competition with Cuba, starring on the national team in the U-15 World Cup in 2018. Part of a signing class by the Angels that was led by Denzer Guzman and his seven-figure bonus, Quero got $200,000 to sign in February 2021 and made his pro debut in the United States, playing his way from the Arizona Complex League up to Low-A. He continued raising his profile with a strong full season with Single-A Inland Empire in 2022. A switch-hitting catcher, Quero has a good feel for the barrel with the ability to make a lot of contact. He already shows he can consistently have professional at-bats and isn’t afraid to walk. He’s more contact-oriented now, but he’s started to tap into some extra-base pop, with most of it showing up on the left side so far. Quero has a solid arm and threw out 37 percent of potential basestealers in his debut. He needs to continue to work on his receiving and managing of a game, but all of the tools are there for him to be a decent defender behind the dish. He’s not flashy, but he’s rapidly becoming one of the better catching prospects in the Minors, one who has the chance to be a solid big league regular if it all clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners went over slot to sign their first two picks in the 2023 Draft, Colt Emerson and Jonny Farmelo, then went way over slot to sign another high school bat, Aidan Smith, in the fourth. To make their bonus pool work, they used their second-round pick on a college senior and signed him for $600,000, more than twice less than slot value. But Williamson is far from just a money-saver, going from William & Mary to playing his way to Double-A in his first full season. A right-handed hitter, Williamson has a definite hit-over-power profile. He makes a ton of contact, with just a 20 percent miss rate overall in 2024, according to Synergy. He's typically content to shoot line drives up the middle or the other way, but without a ton of impact. He may never be a huge power guy, but if he can get the bat head out in front a little more, it could change his profile a bit. More thump would help him fit the third baseman offensive mold, and there's no question he can play the hot corner for a long time. He offers elite-level defense at third with a strong arm and excellent instincts. He's so gifted there that the Mariners might continue testing it out at shortstop like they did last year, and if that works, he could turn into a Jared Triolo type of player if he doesn't have enough thump to play third every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2023, the Mariners were able to snag Williamson for well-under slot value ($600,000) despite being such a high pick (second round), a byproduct of their aggressive strategy to swing for the fences with their top three picks that year, all high school bats (Colt Emerson, Jonny Farmelo, Tai Peete). They did so on the heels of Williamson's sold senior season at William & Mary, where he had a 1.175 OPS and 12 homers in 55 games, leading to him being named the Colonial Athletic Association Player of the Year. Because he went to a smaller school and he doesn't necessarily possess big-time power at a run-producing position, the third baseman has flown a bit under the radar. He's hit-over-power, with good contact ability to all fields. He does so with a more flat, right-handed swing, which could be why he's not gotten the ball in the air as consistently yet, but exit velocity readings have suggested that he could grow into power in the 12-15 homer range. It's his glove that could carry him, though. He's a plus defender at the hot corner who will prevent runs for whatever pitching staff he plays behind, and he can even move to shortstop when needed. His success is rooted in his body being in sync, having the instincts to read tough hops to go along with above-average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Health concerns have dogged Henry since his LSU days when he suffered an upper-arm stress reaction and had elbow concerns. The Nationals still took him in the second round in 2020 when he was a Draft-eligible sophomore, but over three seasons since, he’s yet to throw more than 47 innings in a single Minor League year. His most recent issue was his most serious -- surgery to address thoracic outlet syndrome before the 2023 campaign. Henry returned to the mound in May and made 14 appearances (10 starts) between Single-A, High-A and Double-A with mixed results (6.21 ERA, 37 strikeouts in 33 1/3 innings), though the whole point was getting him throwing regularly again. The 6-foot-4 right-hander touched 98 mph with his fastball in his return and was in the 93-96 range pretty consistently, so velocity wasn’t an issue post-TOS. Command was an issue, however, and he left some of the heaters right over the plate for Double-A hitters to bang (they slugged .641 with three homers in 10 games off the fastball alone). His low-80s slider was his most whiff-heavy pitch with sharp two-plane break, and a mid-80s changeup continued to show promising separation. Henry walked 14.3 percent of the batters he faced in the Eastern League, but it’s hard to judge both the command and control so soon after the surgery. The Nationals hope to keep him in a starter’s role to preserve that path for him, knowing they can move him into relief when necessary. They liked him enough to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft with a 40-man spot in November, so that role decision might not be far off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Similar to Jackson Rutledge, who is also in the Nationals' Top 30, Henry’s amateur and pro careers have been mixed with promise and injuries. In this case, the latest news was tougher to swallow, though. Washington overlooked Henry’s upper-arm stress reaction and elbow concerns at LSU to snag him in the second round of the 2020 Draft as an eligible sophomore. The right-hander battled an elbow strain again in 2021, but was off to a stellar start with a 1.71 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 34 K’s in 31 2/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A last year before hitting the IL again. This time, he required surgery to address thoracic outlet syndrome, a condition that has limited Stephen Strasburg and Matt Harvey, among others in recent years. Before the procedure, Henry featured a pair of promising fastballs – a four-seamer that could touch the high 90s and a mid-90s two-seamer with good armside sink. A late-breaking curveball gives him another weapon against righties (who went only 6-for-66 with no extra-base hits off that Henry pitch in ’22), and a low-80s changeup holds lefties at bay. Other than a five-walk outing for Harrisburg, the former LSU star threw more than enough strikes to suggest control won’t be an issue. It all comes down to health. Henry’s injury concerns were well documented, and that was before last year’s TOS surgery. It has been historically difficult for pitchers to return from that with stuff similar to their pre-surgery levels. The good news is that Henry has gotten back on the mound with three different affiliates in 2023. But his starting status remains a major question until he can pitch without issue for a full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A strong commitment to LSU kept Henry from signing with the Tigers as a 37th-round pick in 2018. His time in college mixed both brilliance (3.03 ERA, 95 strikeouts in 77 1/3 innings) with missed time (upper-arm stress reaction, elbow, COVID-canceled season), but the Nationals saw plenty of promise to pop him in the second round and sign him for $2 million as a 2020 Draft-eligible sophomore. The story remained much the same in pro ball. Henry was dominant in nine appearances for High-A Wilmington in 2021, posting a 1.88 ERA and 0.79 WHIP with 63 K’s in 43 frames, but was again limited due to another elbow strain. He ended the season on a high in the Arizona Fall League, where he finished second in the circuit with 30 strikeouts in 19 innings. The 6-foot-4 right-hander throws both a four-seamer with more velocity (touching high-90s) and a two-seamer with more arm-side sink and run (sitting mid-90s). He locates both well from a high arm slot and has a solid understanding of when to go to either offering. Henry entered pro ball with a better late-breaking curve than his changeup, but both project to be at least above average now. The low-80s changeup, in particular, dives well enough to his arm-side to fool hitters while looking much like the heaters out of the hand. It’s a desirable three-pitch mix, and as Henry showed both at High-A and the AFL, he can throw more than enough strikes to stick as a starter. Consistent health will continue to be a concern until the former SEC star can prove he’s capable of throwing 120-plus innings in a season. Injuries have been an issue again in 2022 with Henry dealing with shoulder tightness starting in mid-June. Getting through a full 2023 has to be a major goal for both hm and the Nats.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Henry was touching the high-90s (though not with regularity) as a senior in the Alabama high-school ranks but chose to head to LSU, where he had a strong commitment, instead of signing with the Tigers as a 37th-round pick in 2018. His freshman year was mixed with flashes of brilliance as a Friday starter and injuries, including a stress reaction in his upper arm in the fall and an elbow issue that limited him to 58 1/3 innings in the spring. He was back to his dominant ways in 2020, posting a 1.89 ERA with 23 strikeouts in 19 innings before the pandemic-related shutdown, and was selected in the second round as an eligible sophomore. This time, the Nats convinced him to join the pro ranks with a $2 million signing bonus, comfortably higher than the slot value of $1.31 million. Another elbow strain limited Henry to only five High-A starts in 2021, though he is expected to pitch again this season. The 6-foot-4 right-hander typically sits closer to 94 these days with the heater but is capable of throwing both the four-seam up in the zone and the two-seam with run and sink. The curveball can be a late breaking pitch that makes for an impressive secondary, and his changeup fades well, giving him the well-rounded package needed to be a starter. He tends to work up and down in the zone using an over-the-top delivery that can bare down on hitters, thanks to his size. The Nationals believe Henry is a firm part of their Big Three behind Cavalli and Rutledge. He might lack the pure power stuff of the other two, but his arsenal gives him a comfortable starting projection. The more innings he picks up and the further he gets from the 2018/19 injury issues, the higher his stock could climb.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The pandemic and a shoulder injury restricted Meidroth in his first two college seasons before he starred in the wood-bat Northwoods League during the summer of 2021 and as a San Diego junior the next spring. Signed by the Red Sox for a well-below-slot $272,500 in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft, he led Boston farmhands with a .408 on-base percentage in his first full season, then topped the Minors with 105 walks and the Triple-A International League with a .437 OBP in his second. He's the most big league-ready of the four prospects the White Sox acquired in the Garrett Crochet trade at the Winter Meetings in December. Meidroth's compact right-handed swing and advanced feel for the barrel give him some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the Minors. He rarely chases pitches or swings and misses, though some scouts point to the fact that he swings less than almost any prospect and could be too passive. He uses the entire field and has a history of getting on base, but he doesn't hit the ball hard, puts it on the ground too often and doesn't have more than 10-homer power. Meidroth comes with just one tool that grades as average or better. He has fringy speed and arm strength, and he's not adventurous on the bases or especially in the range. He may open the season as Chicago's shortstop despite below-average range there, and he fits best at second base because his arm is stretched at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The pandemic and a shoulder injury limited Meidroth to 32 at-bats in his first two college seasons, but he broke out in the wood-bat Northwoods League in the summer of 2021 and earned all-West Coast Conference accolades at San Diego the following spring. The Red Sox selected him in the fourth round of the 2022 Draft and signed him for a well-below-slot $272,500. He reached Double-A and led Boston farmhands with a .408 on-base percentage in his first full pro season, topped the Triple-A International League with a .437 OBP in his second, then joined the White Sox as part of the Garrett Crochet trade at the Winter Meetings in December. Meidroth's bat-to-ball skills and strike-zone management got him drafted and stood out in his first taste of pro ball. He has a compact right-handed swing and tremendous feel for the barrel, and he rarely chases pitches out of the zone. His bat speed and strength are ordinary, however, so he only has modest pull power. With fringy speed and arm strength, Meidroth doesn't offer much value on the bases or in the field. He's best suited for second base but primarily played third in Double-A and shortstop in Triple-A because of team needs. He can get job the done at second but lacks the arm for the hot corner and has below-average range at short.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because of the pandemic and a shoulder injury, Meidroth got just 32 at-bats in his first two college seasons at San Diego, but he started to catch the attention of scouts when he hit .345 with three times as many walks as strikeouts in the wood-bat Northwoods League in the summer of 2021. His hitting ability and strike-zone management earned him all-West Coast Conference honors last spring before the Red Sox signed him for a well-below-slot $272,500 in the fourth round. His 22-game pro debut (mostly in Single-A) featured more of the same, as he batted .316 with 14 walks vs. 11 whiffs. Somewhat of a college version of Boston 2020 first-rounder Nick Yorke, Meidroth is a righty-hitting second baseman whose ability to put the bat on the ball outshines the rest of his tools and limited athleticism. He has excellent feel for the barrel and the strike zone, using a compact stroke and disciplined approach to spray line drives to all fields. His bat speed and strength are ordinary, so he may not deliver more than 12-15 homers per season, but his on-base skills could land him at the top of a lineup. Meidroth's fringy speed and arm strength may restrict him to second base, where he's a sure-handed but not especially rangy defender. He may have a better chance to play second on a regular basis than Yorke, though Meidroth has spent most of his time at third base since joining Yorke in Double-A. He lacks the arm for the hot corner, so left field may be his best fallback position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Cheng signed back in 2019 for $300,000, the Taiwanese infielder didn’t make his professional debut until 2021 because of the pandemic. He’s moved quickly through the system since, riding his defense and his speed a rung at a time, with a summer in the Florida Complex League and a season with Single-A Bradenton in 2021 and '22, respectively. He put up big numbers in High-A and earned a bump up to Double-A in 2023, earning a spot on the 40-man roster that offseason. The bat regressed with a return there in 2024, though he finished with a flourish up in Triple-A. At his best, Cheng is a left-handed-hitting table-setting type, one who is more of a gap-to-gap contact hitter who gets on base while using his plus speed to his advantage. He started thinking his ticket to the big leagues was to hit homers and got too pull-happy, and his strong finish was him getting back to understanding who he is in the box. He should use the whole field, work counts and be a strong two-strike hitter rather than sell out for pop he doesn’t have. Cheng has seen time on both sides of second base as he’s moved up, but make no mistake that he could play shortstop defensively in the big leagues right now. He’s quick, with outstanding range and actions, terrific hands and a solid and accurate arm. He’ll get the chance to right his offensive ship in 2025 and still has time to develop into an everyday player at the premium position while being able to fill in at either middle-infield spot when the need arises.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Cheng signed at the start of the 2019-2020 international signing period, getting a $380,000 bonus, it marked the start of stronger interest in the Asian amateur market for the Pirates, who went on to sign Hung-Leng Chang in 2022 out of Cheng’s home country of Chinese Taipei and Jun-Seok Shim out of Korea in 2023. Cheng couldn’t get going until 2021 because of the pandemic, made his full-season debut in 2022 and then really took off by playing his way from High-A Greensboro to Double-A Altoona in 2023. Cheng absolutely dominated during his time in Greensboro and while the easy thing might be to credit the hitting haven of his home ballpark, it should be noted that his 1.066 OPS on the road was nearly 200 points higher than his home mark and he held his own in Altoona once he got his feet under him. The left-handed hitter has the makings of a solid table-setter, one who makes a ton of contact and knows how to get on base. He’s not a big power guy, but he did impact the ball more in 2023, showing an ability to find the gaps for extra bases. He’s a plus runner who should be able to keep stealing bags. While Cheng has played shortstop, second and even a little third, he’s the best defensive shortstop in the system and should be able to stay there long-term. That’s where his value is, with an average, but very accurate arm, excellent hands and plenty of range. If the offensive gains in 2023 continue at the upper levels, he could be a big league regular at the premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates have become more active in the Asian amateur international market of late, handing out six-figure bonuses to right-hander Jun-Seok Shim out of Korea in 2023 and Taiwanese righty Hung-Leng Chang in 2022. Cheng, a shortstop also from Chinese Taipei, may have started the run, getting $380,000 to sign in 2019. Since then, he’s hit and defended nearly everywhere he’s been, including for Colombia in winter ball and the Caribbean Series and in his full-season debut with Single-A Bradenton in 2022. Since joining the Pirates, Cheng has shown a knack for making contact and getting on base. He limits strikeouts and draws free passes, with a walk rate just north of 15 percent heading into 2023. The switch-hitter is never going to be mistaken for a power hitter, but he has added some strength and shown an improved ability to impact the ball, particularly from the left side of the plate, with some extra-base authority to all fields. A plus runner who should continue to be a base-stealing threat, his quickness is an asset defensively as well and he has every chance to stick at shortstop for a long time. The key for him being more than a utility-type player will be to show continued improvement in the offensive impact department as he moves up the organizational ladder and faces better pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s not been the most direct path for Veen ever since the Rockies made him the No. 9 overall pick out of the Florida high school ranks in 2020. He reached Double-A at age 20 in 2022 but stalled out due to a combination of lack of production and injury. He played in just 110 games in 2023 and 2024 combined, showing enough in ‘24 to earn a spot on the Rockies’ 40-man roster. His brief big league debut in 2025 did not go well, though he performed decently back in Triple-A for most of the season. Now playing at age 24, this is a big year for Veen, who needed to mature as a player and a person. The good news is he showed up for Spring Training with a ton of added strength to his 6-foot-3 frame and what seemed to be more intent in going about his business. There’s still offensive upside in his left-handed swing, and 2023 wrist surgery and a 2024 thumb injury certainly did not help him find consistency. There has been some focus in getting him back to the contact-oriented hitter he was early on, with the hope that he’ll get to his raw power more organically without selling out for it with more loft and the elevated strikeout rates that came with that at the upper levels. Veen has worked with the Rockies on improving his ability to pick up and track balls defensively, with a chance to be a solid corner outfielder. If he can keep on the muscle, something he’s had trouble doing in the past, and maintains his intent, he could finally live up to the promise of being a former top 10 pick.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since going No. 9 overall as one of the best high school hitters in the 2020 Draft class, Veen has shown off very impressive raw tools, and often the ability to use them in games. His first signs of real struggle came when he got to Double-A in 2022 at age 20. A strong Arizona Fall League seemed to hit the reset button for him to head into 2023, but he’s had trouble staying healthy since. He played just 46 games in 2023 due to wrist surgery and while he performed a bit better in '24 (and reached Triple-A for the first time to earn a spot on the 40-man roster), thumb and back issues limited him to 65 games for the year. The 23-year-old outfielder still offers plenty of projection in his 6-foot-3 frame and game, if he can stay on the field. His 2023 wrist injury definitely wreaked some havoc with his swing mechanics, but it was encouraging that he started to get to some of his power again in '24, albeit sporadically. He’ll have to be cognizant of not trying to get to too much loft, something that has happened in the past, also the reason why his strikeout rate is north of 25 percent at the upper levels. Earlier in his career, he offered better bat-to-ball skills. A solid runner who squeezes every ounce of his speed by being aggressive with good instincts on the basepaths, Veen probably fits best in an outfield corner if he were to settle in as a regular. He’ll see time in all three outfield spots to provide options for when the need arises, but more than anything, he has to show that he can answer the bell over the course of a full, healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Veen was the top-ranked high school player in the 2020 Draft class, going one pick behind fellow prep outfielder Robert Hassell III to the Rockies and getting $5 million as the No. 9 overall pick. A solid first full year with Single-A Fresno (.901 OPS) raised the bar and he came out of the chute well in 2022, hitting 11 homers and stealing 50 bases in 92 games with High-A Spokane before struggling after a promotion to Double-A. He reversed that with a solid Arizona Fall League performance but couldn’t carry that over back with Hartford in 2023 as wrist surgery ended his season after just 46 games. When he’s healthy, Veen has shown the ability to do a lot of things well on the baseball field. Still only 22 years old for all of the 2024 season, there is plenty of projection in the 6-foot-3 left-handed-hitting outfielder. It’s hard to know exactly what his power potential is because his attempts to play through his wrist injury changed his mechanics. The Rockies like where his swing is now, staying more on a plane; but when his top hand wrist was hurt, he couldn’t finish balls and had gotten way too steep with his swing. While Veen has above-average pure run speed, his instincts and aggressiveness on the bases make him a plus basestealing threat. He’s improved defensively and should see time in both outfield corners, with the organization excited to see what a truly healthy Veen can do at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first seven selections in the pandemic-shortened 2020 Draft were college players. The Padres took the first high schooler off the board at No. 8 (OF Robert Hassell III) and the Rockies doubled up on prep outfielders by taking Veen out of the Florida high school ranks. He showed what the fuss was about by posting a .901 OPS with 15 homers and 36 steals in his first full season and hit well enough in High-A in 2022 to earn a bump to Double-A, where he struggled. He finished off on a high note by hitting .333 with 16 steals in 21 Arizona Fall League games. He was off to a slow start back with Hartford in 2023, when surgery to repair his left extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) tendon, an issue he had been trying to play through since the second half of 2022, ended his season. Though he’s reached the upper levels, there’s still a lot of projection in the tall, lanky left-handed hitter. He’s shown the ability to hit the ball hard to all fields, and when he’s on time, there’s plenty of juice. There should be more over-the-fence power as he adds strength to his 6-foot-4 frame. He’s shown a solid approach, with an ability to draw walks, and his strikeout rate actually went down a tick in 2022 despite the fact he got out of his approach in Double-A, struggling especially against breaking stuff. Veen generally is thought to have above-average speed, though he did record some plus sprint times in the AFL. Combine that with excellent instincts and a passion for baserunning and he’s become a legitimate threat to steal. He’s improved his defense and looks very much like the protypical athletic right fielder, one who will grow into the power and run production teams like to see from the outfield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite having a pandemic-shortened senior season of high school in Florida's Daytona Beach, Veen went from being a solid prospect to one of the best prep players in the country, leading to his selection at No. 9 overall by the Rockies in the 2020 Draft. They didn’t get to really see what Veen was capable of until he made his pro debut in 2021, and he didn’t disappoint, posting a .301/.399/.501 line and helping Fresno reach the Low-A West playoffs. Though Veen finished his first full season with 15 homers and 36 steals, he might still be scratching the surface of his offensive potential. The left-handed hitter has a very sustainable swing that did not require a ton of tinkering, though an ability to stay on his legs more and not lunge enabled him to start driving the ball more consistently as the 2021 season wore on. When he’s balanced and on time, he has power to all fields, with more to come as he matures. His ability to not carry over poor at-bats should serve him well. While he might have a smidge above-average speed as a runner, Veen is super-aggressive on the basepaths, showing an affinity for stealing bases and taking the extra base. He also dedicated himself to his corner outfield play and liked showing of his plus arm in the process. A natural leader, Veen has the chance to become an elite-level corner outfielder in the big leagues if he continues to follow this development path.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Spruce Creek High School in the Daytona Beach area in Florida, a school that previously had just one draftee, Veen came out of the summer showcase circuit as a solid prospect for the Class of 2020, an outfielder who ranked No. 22 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 100 Draft prospects the December before the Draft. The 2020 season may have been cut short, but Veen made the most of it, coming out on fire and jumping all the way up to No. 7 by the time the Draft rolled around. He ended up being the second prep bat taken, going No. 9 overall and signing with the Rockies before making his unofficial pro debut in instructional league play. Long and lean, Veen has already shown off plus hitting ability and plus raw power, with much more to come as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-4 frame. The left-handed hitter has a pretty swing with plus bat speed and can create leverage and loft when he stands more upright, drawing some Cody Bellinger comps along the way. A good athlete who is a solid average runner, Veen has played center field in the past and the Rockies certainly could let him play up the middle until he shows he can’t. He has the arm, and the future offensive profile, to look very good in right field should he slow down enough to necessitate the move.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After one year at Georgia Southern to start his college career, Dollander transferred to Tennessee and was named the Southeastern Conference’s pitcher of the year in 2022, setting the stage for him to potentially go at the top of the 2023 Draft. His inconsistency as a junior kept that from happening, but he still went No. 9 to the Rockies and pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season with a trip to the Futures Game mixed in. Dollander has the chance to have four at least above-average offerings at his disposal. His fastball sits around 96 mph and touches 98-99, and it’s a bat-misser thanks to his approach angle, extension and induced vertical break. At its best, his upper-80s slider is hard and tight and can be an out pitch, though the right-hander tinkered with a variety of grips for the breaking ball in 2024 and wasn’t always thrilled with where it was. As a result, he did go to his upper-70s curve more frequently, especially to get ahead in counts quickly. His upper-80s changeup features fade and can also be very effective. A solid athlete on the mound, Dollander has shown the ability to repeat his delivery well and find the strike zone consistently, though there’s room for improvement in terms of overall command. The struggles of that junior year far behind him, Dollander has the stuff and work ethic to give the Rockies a future potential frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dollander was under recruited as a Georgia high schooler, one who didn’t have enough time in the truncated 2020 season to impress big college recruiters, and he headed to Georgia Southern to begin his college career. He threw well enough as a freshman to transfer to Tennessee and was Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year as a sophomore in 2022. That set the stage for him to be considered the top pitcher in the Draft as the 2023 season approached, but inconsistent results knocked him from that perch. He didn’t fall too far, landing No. 9 overall and signing with the Rockies for full slot. Dollander’s pure stuff was still pretty exciting during his junior season, with a fastball that averaged around 96 mph and touched 99, a heater with good carry that elicits a lot of swings-and-misses. His mid-80s tight slider can touch the low 90s and is often a plus pitch with sweep. He has a bigger mid-70s curve and an upper-80s changeup with fade, and both can be effective, even if they aren’t as reliable a go-to as the fastball-slider combination. While Dollander didn’t walk a ton of guys as a junior, the command of his premium stuff, both in and out of the strike zone, regressed compared to his dominant sophomore campaign. He’s a good athlete on the mound and has shown the ability to repeat his delivery, with the hope that the Rockies can help him right the ship and use his frontline starter stuff more effectively as he embarks on his pro career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dobbins logged just 46 1/3 innings in three years at Texas Tech because of the pandemic and blowing out his elbow just before he was poised to become the Red Raiders' Friday-night starter in 2021. The Red Sox drafted him in the eighth round that July despite his Tommy John surgery and have nurtured him into one of their higher-floor mound prospects. They named him their Minor League starting pitcher of the year and added him to their 40-man roster in 2024, when he led the system with a 3.08 ERA between Double-A and Triple-A. Dobbins has added velocity and remade his repertoire as a pro, dropping a sinker and changeup and adding two versions of a slider and a splinker. His four-seamer was gaining steam when his elbow gave out in college and now operates at 93-98 mph with some carry and armside run. He turned his former splitter into a harder splinker (a sinker/splitter hybrid) late last season, and it averaged 90 mph while serving as his best pitch down the stretch. Both Dobbins' 82-85 mph sweeping slider and cutterish 86-89 mph version can be solid offerings at times, while his upper-70s curveball has more depth and reliably produces strikes. Scouts worry about the effort in his funky mechanics, though it adds deception without harming his control. There's a good chance he can become a No. 4 starter and he should help Boston in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dobbins worked just 46 1/3 innings in three years at Texas Tech, losing time to the pandemic in 2020 and then blowing out his elbow just before the 2021 season started. Undeterred by his Tommy John surgery, the Red Sox drafted him in the eighth round and brought him back to the mound in 2022. After missing the first month of last season with vertigo, he walked just five batters in seven High-A starts to earn a promotion to Double-A. Dobbins employs a four-pitch mix highlighted by a solid mid-80s slider with horizontal and vertical action. It plays well off his fastball, which parks at 92-95 mph and peaks at 97 but lacks life. He added a promising if inconsistent low-80s splitter in 2023 and also has a decent upper-70s curveball with depth. Scouts don't love the considerable effort in Dobbins' delivery, but it adds funk without compromising his ability to provide strikes. His control outstrips his command, however, and he'll have to improve his ability to locate his fastball to succeed against upper-level hitters. He could become an end-of-the-rotation starter or a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A dominant athlete in both football and baseball as an Oregon high schooler, Tawa played four years at Stanford -- two of which were affected by a shoulder injury and the 2020 pandemic-shortened season. He recovered enough as a senior in 2021 to go to the D-backs in the 11th round, first reaching Double-A Amarillo in 2022 and staying there three straight seasons. He actually opened 2024 at Triple-A Reno but was sent down and dominated the Texas League with 21 homers and a .487 slugging percentage in 105 games. He returned to Triple-A in late August, finished with 31 homers on the season and was added to the 40-man roster as Rule 5 protection last November. A right-handed hitter, Tawa has an upright stance at the plate and chokes up a little on the bat, enabling him to stay quick to balls, particularly heaters. That causes him to pull the ball a ton, and that’s part of what allowed him to lead the organization in homers last year. His top-end exit velocities won’t stand out, but he gets the barrel to the ball often enough that there should still be at least average pop in there. (Surprisingly, he slugged just .416 in Amarillo and .541 away from that particular launching pad at Double-A in ’24.) Troubles with offspeed pitches and overall selectivity might hold him back offensively. Tawa played every position but pitcher and catcher in 2024. He focused more on first base down the stretch in Reno, but with decent speed and an average arm, he best fits at second base in an everyday role. Then again, his athleticism and power make him a candidate to be the last man on the roster who can fill multiple roles in a pinch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Harrington established himself as an extreme strike-throwing starting pitching prospect as a Draft-eligible sophomore at Campbell in 2022, when the Pirates made him the highest-drafted Fighting Camels hurler ever at No. 36 overall. He cemented his reputation as he climbed the ladder, reaching Triple-A by 2024 and posting outstanding K/BB and BB/9 rates along the way. Those wheels came off, however, in 2025, both in the big leagues across three rough outings and back in Triple-A. He struggled with his command and some injuries, limping to a 5.34 ERA with Indianapolis. Not armed with plus stuff, Harrington needs to get back to the right-hander who could put the ball on a dime to all quadrants of the strike zone and pitch backwards to keep hitters off-balance. He still has a full array of pitches but was getting too much of the plate and missing the zone with them last year. His fastball sits in the low 90s and touches 95 mph and can have run and carry when it’s right. He’ll throw both a low-80s sweeper and an upper-80s cutter, with the former a better bat-misser, and he’ll fold in an 80-mph curve. His tumbling 84-85 mph splitter might be his best secondary offering now. A groin strain shut Harrington down twice later in the year, and he had his hip cleaned up during the offseason. He’s the type of cerebral pitcher who can learn from adversity, and with the injuries hopefully behind him, he can reset his high floor as a back-end starter or be well-suited for a swingman/bulk inning type of role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a span of two years, Harrington went from being a walk-on at Campbell to a mainstay in the Fighting Camels rotation to an early-round option as a Draft eligible sophomore. He became the earliest drafted pitcher from the program when the Pirates took him No. 36 overall in the 2022 Draft, and he’s climbed the ladder relatively quickly, reaching Triple-A in his second full season and leading the organization in K/BB ratio for the second straight season while also topping all Pirates pitching prospects in BB/9 and WHIP. Sometimes lost in the shadow of the premium stuff coming from right-handers like Paul Skenes, Jared Jones and Bubba Chandler, Harrington combines solid stuff with an easily plus feel for pitching. He has as many as five pitches in his arsenal, and he’s not afraid to pull any arrow from his quiver. While his fastball averages between 92-93 mph and tops out at 95, it plays up because of its run and carry. He backs the fastball up with an array of secondary offerings, with his 83-84 mph sweeper with excellent spin rates the best of his breaking balls. His 84-85 mph splitter with tumble also serves as an above-average pitch that misses bats. His upper-80s cutter provides a shorter power breaker that plays well off of his sweeper, and he uses a low-80s curve effectively as well. Helping all of his pitches play up is Harrington’s ability to fill the strike zone, as he was one of the best in the Minors in strike percentage in 2024, and he’s adept at keeping hitters off-balance with his pitch mix. He has as high a floor as a future big league starter as anyone in the system as a result.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport standout in high school who was also a quarterback, Harrington was a walk-on at Campbell but quickly landed in the Fighting Camels rotation. He was the Big South Conference Freshman of the Year and then won the conference’s Pitcher of the Year award in 2022 as a Draft-eligible sophomore. He became the school’s highest-drafted pitcher ever when he went No. 36 overall to the Pirates in that summer’s Draft. He showed his stuff would play at the next level by leading the organization in several pitching categories including K percentage and K/BB ratio. Of all the highly-rated pitching prospects in the system, Harrington has the most advanced pitchability of the group. He can throw as many as five distinct pitches for strikes, though he uses his slower curve only sparingly. His fastball tops out at 95 mph, sitting 93-94 mph, but it’s run and carry allows it to play up. He mixes in a big mid-80s sweeping slider with big spin rates that flashes plus and his mid-80s changeup features tumble and can also miss bats. He added a cutter last year and it might eventually be another above-average offering as a shorter slider-ish pitch that plays well off of his sweeper. Harrington uses his athleticism on the mound to repeat his low three-quarters delivery well, and he commands and mixes all of his pitches well. That gives him a high floor as a big league starter, with the potential for a little more velocity to allow him to take another big step forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the span of two years, Harrington went from unknown walk-on to one of the best pitchers in Campbell history, earning Big South Conference Freshman of the Year honors in 2021. He was then named the conference’s Pitcher of the Year in 2022, when he set school records in wins (12) and strikeouts (111). He surpassed Seth Johnson, who went No. 40 overall in 2019, as the highest-drafted pitcher in Fighting Camels history when he went No. 36 to the Pirates and signed for just over $2 million. Harrington has a four-pitch mix that points to a future in a big league rotation. His fastball averaged around 92 mph at Campbell last year, touching 96, and it plays up because of its excellent run and carry. He has a plus mid-80s changeup with tumble that gets a lot of swings and misses and chases. His mid-80s slider has depth and flashes plus, though it’s not as consistent as the changeup, and he will fold in a slower, get-me-over curve as well. A former high school quarterback, Harrington’s athleticism is a big plus on the mound, helping him repeat his low three-quarters delivery, leading to excellent command. There’s some projection to go along with his feel for pitching, giving him a high floor and the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a Cape Cod League all-star performance put Koss in position to go early in the 2019 Draft, he slumped for most of his junior season at UC Irvine and dropped to the Rockies in the 12th round. He batted .332/.447/.605 in his pro debut in the launching pad that was the Rookie-level Pioneer League, then lost a season to the pandemic shutdown and went to the Red Sox in a deal for Yoan Aybar in December 2020. He overcame a slow start at High-A during his first year in Boston's system to hit .295/.338/.531 with 14 homers in his final 66 games. Koss is a steady hitter who makes consistent contact to all fields with a compact right-handed swing. His ability to barrel balls combines with his sneaky strength to give him 12-15 home run potential. He's not overly aggressive but rarely walks, and more advanced pitchers might be able to exploit his impatience. Koss' high baseball IQ helps him make the most of his average to solid speed on the bases and in the field. Club officials admit they didn't realize how good he was defensively when they traded for him, as he impressed last year with his athleticism, range and plus arm strength. He's capable at second base and third base as well, and he also saw some action on the outfield corners in college.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 45 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Cruz signed with the Padres as an 18-year-old out of Mexico in July 2017, headed to the Pirates in the Joe Musgrove deal in January 2021 and returned to the San Diego organization as a Minor League Rule 5 pick in December 2023. He moved from a starting role to relief at Double-A in 2022 and stayed at that level for three straight seasons, finally making it to Triple-A last year. He finished with a 3.96 ERA and 118 strikeouts between San Antonio and El Paso in 2024. The Padres added him to the 40-man roster in November to protect him from the Major League phase of the Rule 5 Draft. The 6-foot southpaw’s standout pitch is easily his changeup. His fastball velocity is down to 90-92 mph in 2025, but he'll occasionally zip the four-seamer past hitters. What it might do best is set up the cambio. Cruz’s 79-82 mph change comes from almost the exact same release spot as the fastball and looks very much like the heater with similar armside run until it’s too late and batters are swinging through or over it. The pitch had a 48 percent whiff and 49 percent chase rate across both levels in 2024. Cruz will mix in a mid-70s curveball that can surprise batters with good spin, but it’s way behind the other two offerings in usage. Cruz’s walk rate jumped from 6.6 percent at Double-A last season to 13.8 with the Major League ball in Triple-A. He especially doesn’t throw the breaker in the zone as much, but the left-hander doesn’t overthrow and can generally command pitches where they need to be for minimalized damage. He entered the 2025 season at 26 years old with a few looks out of the San Diego bullpen but has even made some starts with El Paso to add much-needed rotation depth.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz was one of six players given $100,000 bonuses by the Padres to sign out of Mexico at the start of the 2017-18 international signing period and made a very strong first impression. The left-hander reached full-season ball as a 20-year-old in 2019, showing a feel for pitching well beyond his years. After faring well for San Diego in instructional league play, he was sent to the Pirates as part of the return for Joe Musgrove. The quintessential lefty with pitchability, Cruz commands all three of his pitches very well. He can move his low-90s fastball in and out, showing no fear in going right after hitters and throwing inside. He really knows how to spin a breaking ball, an overhand curve with top-to-bottom shape, and he has good feel for his average changeup, thrown with good deception thanks to arm speed. There might not be a ton of ceiling with Cruz, though he will be just 22 for all of the 2021 season and some more velocity could change his profile a bit. Even if he stays as is, with his feel for pitching and strong and durable frame, he has the chance to pitch in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fluharty was a three-year reliever at Liberty and notched 83 strikeouts in 50 2/3 innings as a junior in 2022, leading the Blue Jays to take him in the fifth round. Since then, he’s developed into one of the most interesting prospect debates in the system. While he doesn’t light up laptop screens like some other pitchers on this list, he’s one of the best bets in the organization to be a big leaguer. He gets outs, which is the metric that matters most, and in 2024 with Triple-A Buffalo, Fluharty put up a 3.63 ERA with 76 strikeouts over 67 innings. Fluharty’s deception is impressive from the left side, leading with a mid-80s slider that has a ton of sweep (averaging 17 inches in Triple-A) and a cutter that creeps into the low 90s. He’s been tougher on lefties, but handles right-handed hitters just fine with backfoot sweepers and should be able to chew through multiple innings when needed. All of the pieces are in place for Fluharty to make an impact on the Blue Jays’ bullpen in 2025, whether that comes early in the season or down the stretch. The club has a wave of bullpen options coming, which should simplify its roster building in the years to come, but many in the organization believe Fluharty could take a job and run with it. This isn’t the flashiest profile on the list by any means, but Fluharty’s name is consistently brought up by player development staff as a prospect who needs to be talked about more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith worked just 10 1/3 innings in three years at Wake Forest, redshirting in 2019 and losing most of 2020 to the pandemic before having Tommy John surgery in 2021. Signed as a nondrafted free agent by the Brewers for $20,000, he returned to the mound in August 2022 and quickly climbed to Triple-A during the next two seasons. The White Sox selected him in the Rule 5 Draft in December, so he'll have to remain on their big league roster all season or else be exposed to waivers and offered back to Milwaukee for half his $50,000 draft price. Smith's best pitch is a fastball with natural cutting action that sits at 92-95 mph and touches 97, losing a tick of velocity when he works as a starter rather than a reliever. Both of his breaking balls are average, and he favors his upper-70s curveball over his tighter mid-80s slider. He has trouble landing his curve and slider for the strikes, but the bender showed flashes of becoming a plus pitch and missed more bats in 2023. Combining a low release height with quality extension, Smith creates plenty of deception and has no difficulty providing strikes. Scouts are split as to whether he can make it as a starter with three average pitches and control to match, or whether he'd provide more value as a reliever who might get a boost to his fastball and breaking stuff in shorter stints. He should be able to stick with the pitching-strapped White Sox, who will give him an opportunity to make their rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A potential high pick out of Massachusetts in 2018 if not for an arm injury, Vasil was inconsistent during his three years at the University of Virginia and dropped to the Mets in the eighth round in 2021. He threw 71 1/3 innings in his first full season while working around forearm tightness and bone spurs in his elbow and added six more appearances in the Arizona Fall League. Vasil’s healthier breakout came in 2023, when he opened with a 3.71 ERA, 0.84 WHIP and 57/8 K/BB ratio through 10 Double-A starts (51 innings). His numbers (5.30 ERA, 1.48 WHIP, 38 walks in 73 innings) took a drop at Triple-A Syracuse, but his career-high 124 total frames was a solid positive. Vasil transitioned from a two-seam fastball in college to a four-seamer, and while the pitch touched 97 mph last season, it’s typically closer to the 92-95 range. Vasil’s velocity did tick down as the season wore on – he averaged around 92.7 mph in September – but the workload may have played a part. His mid-80s slider acts like a two-plane cutter and gets swing-and-miss down and away from fellow righties, fueling his strikeout rate at the upper levels, and he'll also show a breaker with more sweep. He can mix in a 78-81 mph downer curveball as a breaking-ball option for lefties, while his mid-80s changeup has some fade but is a clear fourth option. The 6-foot-5 hurler’s walk rate jumped from 4.1 percent at Double-A to 11.7 at Triple-A, where he had to deal with the ABS system. He should still throw enough strikes to remain a starter and could get even better as he gets more comfortable working 120+-inning seasons. Vasil hasn't pushed for the Majors quite as hoped in his age-24 season in 2024 and is trending more toward being a depth arm than a key piece of future rotations in Queens.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A possible high 2018 pick out of Boston College High School, Vasil opted to head to the University of Virginia following an arm injury that may have dinged his stock. He was inconsistent in his three years as a Cavalier, causing him to fall to the eighth round to the Mets in 2021. He sported a 3.53 ERA with 85 strikeouts in 71 1/3 innings last season, mostly at Single-A and High-A, but he was limited due to forearm tightness and bone spurs in his elbow. He made up for the lost time with six Arizona Fall League appearances. The Mets immediately got to work on getting Vasil more athletic in his delivery and eliminating the two-seamer that sat 91-92 mph in college. He averaged 93-95 mph with his newly reworked four-seamer, though velo could be inconsistent, and he had good spin in the 2,300-2,500 rpm range. He also credited New York for working on his upper-80s cutter-ish slider, making it more vertical to help play off the high heat. His low-80s curveball with good downward bite accomplishes the same goal, while his mid-80s changeup is a clear fourth pitch that shows some potential. Vasil’s walk rate was downright stellar at Double-A Binghamton to begin 2023, giving added faith that he can be a future Major League starter. The control has gone a little wayside as he's been squeezed by the ABS system at Triple-A, but he should still throw enough strikes to compete for a job in the New York rotation coming out of next spring.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There was talk of Vasil going high in the 2018 Draft out of Boston College High School, but after suffering an arm injury, he told clubs that he was planning to head to the University of Virginia. He put up rough numbers as a freshman with the Cavaliers, seemed to rebound in 2020 before the shutdown and was inconsistent in his junior spring. He finished that final season with a 4.52 ERA and 73 strikeouts in 81 2/3 innings. Despite being MLB Pipeline’s No. 111 Draft prospect last summer, Vasil fell to the eighth round and signed with the Mets for exact slot at $181,200. It’s too early to say for sure, but Vasil is already showing the makings of being a pro-development success story. Previously a two-seam fastballer in college who sat around 91-92 mph, Vasil worked with the Mets right away on transitioning toward the four-seam fastball. His velocity appropriately picked up, and he’s now around 92-95, topping out around 97. That’s closer to what he looked like in his more promising high-school days. His upper-80s slider and low-80s curve draw at least average reviews, and it’s to his credit that he can show multiple breaking ball looks. A mid-80s changeup looked like his best secondary coming out of school, but the hard slider might overtaken it at this stage. Even when his stuff didn’t stand out, the 6-foot-5 right-hander was showing promising gains in his strike-throwing in Charlottesville, and the Mets have worked with him on becoming even more athletic in his delivery. Vasil might need to show that his improvements can hold up for an entire season before he makes a massive jump in the rankings, but he may have already bumped up his ceiling some from a back-end starter to a mid-rotation one.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After never making the varsity team at his North Carolina high school, Gusto walked on at Broward (Fla.) JC in 2018 before transferring to Florida SouthWestern JC as a sophomore, when he led the state's junior collegians with 110 strikeouts in 75 innings. Signed for an over-slot $421,699 as an 11th-rounder in 2019, he lost the next two seasons to the pandemic and Tommy John surgery. He has gotten better every year since, earning Pacific Coast League All-Star accolades in 2024 after leading the Triple-A circuit in ERA (3.70) and strikeouts (141) and winning the league title. Gusto's four-seam fastball sits at 92-94 mph and touches 98, playing better than its velocity and eliciting a lot of chases thanks to its riding action. He mixes four secondary pitches equally, the best of which are a mid-80s changeup with plenty of fade and sink and a sweeping low-80s slider. The changeup could become a solid offering with more consistency, while his upper-70s curveball and upper-80s cutter are more fringy. Gusto provides consistent strikes from a simple side-step delivery with a three-quarters arm slot. None of his pitches or his control grades as better than average, but he keeps hitters guessing by sequencing well. An organization favorite with impeccable makeup, he's a potential back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 40 | Slider: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 McDaniels only made three outings for Division II Mt. Olive in 2021 before needing Tommy John surgery, but the Dodgers signed him as an undrafted free agent in May 2022 as he was rehabbing on the recommendation of area scout Jonah Rosenthal. They didn’t get a full look at a healthy version of the left-hander until 2024, when he pitched across three levels and finished at Double-A with impressive combined numbers (3.19 ERA, .229 BAA, 10.3 K/9), mostly as a reliever. They did not, however, protect him on the 40-man roster and the Angels took him in the Rule 5 Draft in order to give him a chance to make their big league staff. A 6-foot-2 left-hander, McDaniels likely profiles best coming out of the bullpen, which he has done for most of his pro career. He typically sits 94-95 mph with his fastball, dialing it up to 97. He can spin two different breaking balls, with his 87-89 mph slider showing glimpses of being a potential out pitch, and he’ll mix in a slower curve as well. He’s shown a propensity for missing bats (10.5 career K/9 rate) and getting ground-ball outs (2.35 GO/AO). McDaniels doesn’t have pinpoint command but is generally around the zone and that could continue to improve the further removed from TJ surgery he gets. He did make seven starts to begin the 2024 season, and while Angels GM Perry Minasian talked about how hard it is to find good left-handed relievers following the Rule 5 Draft, he didn’t rule out giving McDaniels the chance to start down the road.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mangum was a rare three-time college Draft selection but chose to return to Mississippi State the first two times, in part to aid his hunt for the SEC all-time hits record. He achieved that aim as a senior and finished with 383 knocks over his four years in Starkville. The Mets, who also picked Mangum in 2018, selected the outfielder in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft and signed him for just $20,000. The switch-hitting slugger finally saw full-season ball in 2021 and spent most of the year at Double-A Binghamton, where he hit .294/.337/.454 with seven homers and 14 steals in 75 games. The former Bulldogs star has rarely had issues making contact and showing off impressive bat-to-ball skills. That worked to his detriment at times in his first tastes of pro ball when he was just trying to spray around the field, leading to weak batted balls and lower slugging percentages. Mangum spent 2021 working on improving his swing decisions and generating a less-grooved bat path, and his nine homers were four more than his entire college total in 178 fewer games. It’s still not average pop because of a close-to-50 percent ground-ball rate, but the adjustments were noteworthy. An above-average runner, Mangum is arguably the best defender in the Mets system with enough range and arm strength to play a quality center field. He’s also likely to swipe double-digit bags over a full big league season. All that said, Mangum is entering his age-26 season, so the clock is working against him. He needs to prove the power improvements can hold at Triple-A. Otherwise, the other tools are good enough to eke out a fourth/fifth outfielder role in Queens.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A transfer from Santa Fe College, Lord posted pedestrian numbers as a University of South Florida starter in 2021 and 2022. The Nationals took him in the 18th round in the latter year, and after spending a solid but not spectacular first full season in 2023, it looked like he was trending organizational pitching depth. Instead, he broke out after winning an opportunity to join the Double-A Harrisburg rotation early in April and led Washington full-season qualifiers in ERA (2.43) while finishing second with 135 strikeouts over 129 2/3 innings across High-A, Double-A and Triple-A. The 6-foot-3 right-hander throws for a low three-quarters release that helps him generate around 17 inches of armside movement on his 91-94 mph sinker. His four-seamer is right around the same velocity but is straighter; it had a higher whiff rate at Triple-A in part because it caught batters off-guard. Lord’s 83-85 mph changeup also features similar horizontal movement to the sinker with a little more dip, and even his gyro slider doesn’t move much to the gloveside with more dip than the changeup. Lord makes that arsenal play up with above-average command, spotting the ball where he needs to miss bats. Nationals coaches credit him with putting on muscle and striving to make the right physical gains that would help him stick as a starter, and the work has paid off to this point. He doesn’t have a stellar ceiling without a true plus pitch, but he isn’t far from being a No. 5 starter or swingman for the big club in DC.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murdock had Tommy John surgery during his sophomore year at Virginia but returned to action 10 months later, and the Royals were already familiar with his dynamic stuff after scouting teammate Daniel Lynch a year earlier. They took Murdock in the seventh round of 2019, but he’s yet to pitch more than 37 1/3 innings in a Minor League season. Injuries in 2021 limited him to 22 2/3 innings at High-A Quad Cities, where he made seven appearances (six starts) and posted a 3.18 ERA with 19 strikeouts and 11 walks. Murdock’s 6-foot-8 frame is imposing, and the extension gives his mid-90s fastball deception. His main secondary pitch is a high-spin curveball that he improved his grip on at the alternate site in 2020. He has an improving feel of a power slider that the Royals believe would have been more defined if he’d been healthy this year, and while his changeup isn’t plus, it plays up because of his big fastball. The 23-year-old is working on repeating his delivery, which lacks consistency and can get out of sync quickly. Murdock was one of the more impressive pitchers at the alternate site in 2020 with increased velocity and added muscle, and he likely would have made big strides in ’21 if not for the pectoral injury that held him back. His size and stuff still give him a back-end rotation projection, but his health will determine his plan going forward. If he doesn’t reach that projection, Murdock’s fastball and curveball are weapons that would fit in the big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Tommy John surgery his sophomore year at Virginia, Murdock returned to action 10 months later and delivered 15 starts as a junior, flashing dynamic stuff that he had a hard time harnessing. The Royals saw his 6-foot-8 frame and mid-90s fastball and took him in the seventh round in 2019, and he has shown improvement with his control since his pro debut. He worked out remotely during the 2020 season and got back on the field at the Royals’ fall instructional program in Kansas City, where he showed significant strides in his strength, arsenal and control. Murdock’s velocity has only increased since he’s entered the Royals system, and he now can touch 99 mph while sitting comfortably in the mid-90s. His frame is imposing on the mound, and his extension gives his fastball deception. Murdock’s main secondary pitch is a high-spin curveball, with a newer grip that has made it a different-looking pitch than what he showed before 2020. He has improving feel of a power slider, and while his changeup isn’t plus, it plays up because of the fastball deception. Murdock has work to do in repeating his delivery because of his long frame. He has a fast arm, but he needs to improve the sync and consistency in his delivery. Murdock receives praise for how smart he is on and off the mound. His size, stuff and low-mileage arm give him a back-of-the-rotation projection, and he’ll keep starting until he shows he can’t command his stuff deep into his starts. If he doesn’t reach that projection, Murdock’s power arm could make him a bullpen weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If the last time you saw Thomas was at Triple-A Memphis, then you may have been surprised that the Cardinals chose to protect the 2019 fifth-rounder from the Rule 5 Draft with a 40-man roster spot in November. The southpaw had a rough return to the International League last year -- where he made 22 appearances in 2021 -- and finished with a 5.47 ERA, .307 average-against and 110 strikeouts in 135 innings with the Redbirds. However, St. Louis sent Thomas to the Arizona Fall League for extra work, and he was the showcase circuit’s Pitcher of the Year with a league-best 34 strikeouts in 25 2/3 frames. The secret to success? A cutter he added on the advice from Mike Maddux and Jason Isringhausen. Thomas’ velocity typically sat around 88-90 mph with heavy sink, and while his mid-80s slider could flash plus, he needed something even tighter to keep upper-level hitters more off balance. The cutter did the trick in the AFL, sitting with enough velo to look like the heater, moving just late enough to elicit whiffs.
