As a starter, Montgomery featured a low/mid-90s fastball that played well because of its vertical movement, an effective slider and a useful changeup with a deceptive delivery. But his stuff ticked up when he shortened his outings to one or two innings, to the point that his fastball averaged 97.3 mph during his September stint in the Majors while his slider registered in the upper 80s. Both pitches were comically effective, with his fastball generating a 43.1% whiff rate and his breaking ball checking in at 56%. He still struggled with walks, the one area of concern for the lefty, but he offset that by striking out 17 of the 37 hitters he faced. The knock on Montgomery as a starter was that his best stuff would come and go, not only from start to start but from inning to inning. If he can more effectively harness his stuff as a reliever, as he did last September, he has the arsenal and composure to be a highly effective high-leverage reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For nearly a decade, the Rays have had at least one pitcher in their system who looks like the Next Big Thing. In fact, they’ve had at least one arm on MLB Pipeline’s preseason Top 100 list nearly every year since MLB.com began ranking prospects in 2004, which the exceptions being ’04, ’06, ’07, ’15 … and now, this year. Montgomery is Tampa Bay’s top-ranked arm heading into the season, but he isn’t riding quite as high as he was this time last year. A sixth-round pick out of Texas Tech who signed for a below-slot bonus of $225,000 in 2021, Montgomery followed his brief but dominant professional debut by rocketing to Double-A Montgomery in his first full season. He posted a combined 2.10 ERA with 171 strikeouts against 43 walks in 124 innings over 27 starts that year, good enough to be named the organization’s Pitcher of the Year. But he took a step back performance-wise last season, logging a 3.98 ERA with 144 strikeouts and 60 walks in 124 1/3 innings over 29 starts between Double-A and Triple-A Durham. The uptick in his walk rate is concerning, because he typically tends to use his stuff on the edges of the zone even when he’s putting the ball where he wants it. More alarming is how often Montgomery’s best stuff would come and go, both from start to start and throughout the course of a game. When he’s on, he offers a dominant mid-90s fastball, an effective changeup and a useful slider that play up due to his deceptive delivery from a 6-foot-2 frame. The Rays were encouraged by how Montgomery finished the season, and he’s close to being a big league option. The challenge is proving he can consistently maintain his stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montgomery wasn’t a high-profile prospect in the Draft coming out of Texas Tech, having started all three seasons with solid numbers in the spring of 2021: a 3.82 ERA, a 1.18 WHIP and 84 strikeouts over 63 2/3 innings. The Rays picked him in the sixth round and signed the lefty for a below-slot bonus of $225,000. But the southpaw almost immediately proved to be something special, following a brief but dominant professional debut by flying from High-A Bowling Green to Double-A Montgomery in his first full season, posting a combined 2.10 ERA (best in Tampa Bay’s system in 2022) with 171 strikeouts (sixth-most in the Minors) in 124 innings over 27 starts. The 6-foot-2 Texan has proven capable of dominating hitters with mostly just his fastball, a pitch that sits in the low to mid-90s but touches 97 mph. That one-note success is a function of his delivery, as he hides the ball exceptionally well, and the riding life on his heater. Montgomery also uses an effective, mid-80s changeup and successfully implemented a slider that gives him a full arsenal of three average-to-plus pitches. Montgomery walked 8.6 percent of the hitters he faced in 2022, but his control is probably better than his rate stats indicate. He tends to use his stuff on the edges of the zone, but he’s typically putting the ball where he wants it. He has a consistent enough delivery and throws enough strikes to remain a starter, and he showed last year he can already handle a decent workload. The next step for the lefty is sustaining his top-level stuff throughout outings, as he did in some of his best starts but not every time out during his full-season debut. When he has it all going, there’s little doubt he looks like the organization’s 2022 Minor League Pitcher of the Year, though consistency has been a bigger issue at Double-A in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sabrowski played sparingly as a two-way player at Cisco (Texas) JC in 2017, then transferred to Cloud County (Kan.) CC, where he set a school record with 117 strikeouts in 66 innings and also led the Thunderbirds with 11 homers. An 18th-round pick by the Padres in 2018, he didn't make his pro debut until three years later because he needed Tommy John surgery soon after signing and also lost time to the pandemic. He pitched in just eight games in 2021 before needing his elbow reconstructed for a second time, after which the Guardians plucked him in the Minor League phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December. He returned to the mound in 2023, breezed through Double-A and Triple-A over the next two seasons, then made eight scoreless appearances with Cleveland last September and logged a 1.69 ERA run in five playoff outings. Sabrowski's fastball parks at 93 mph and tops out at 96, but it's all but unhittable because he has elite extension, active spin and induced vertical break that produce tremendous carry up in the zone. His upper-70s curveball plays extremely well off his heater with its downer action, and he featured 34 inches in vertical separation between the two pitches while with the Guardians -- 10 inches more than the MLB average. His tight upper-80s slider/cutter also has more ride than most slide pieces. The key to Sabrowski's long-term success will be control and command. He doesn't have a history of throwing strikes and walked 15 percent of the batters he faced in the Minors last year before cutting that rate to a more manageable 10 percent in the Majors. Cleveland loves his fearlessness and will trust him in high-leverage roles if he can land his pitches in the zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $75,000 out of Venezuela in 2018, Iriarte blossomed into one of the best arms in the Padres system and was pushing for a big league promotion as a 21-year-old in 2023. After the White Sox acquired him in a three-prospect package for Dylan Cease in March 2024, he ranked third in the Double-A Southern League in opponent average (.228) and WHIP (1.28) and fourth in ERA (3.71) and strikeouts (122 in 126 innings). He posted a 1.50 ERA in six relief appearances with Chicago at the end of the season. After parking in the mid-90s and peaking at 100 mph in the first half of 2023, Iriarte's fastball has settled in at 92-94 mph with a high of 96, and its excessive armside run now stands out more than its velocity. His sharp 82-85 mph slider has good horizontal action in the opposite direction and plays well off his heater. So does his upper-80s changeup with fade, giving him a third solid offering. While Iriarte wasn't as overpowering as the year before he did throw more strikes, though his control and command still need more work. He's athletic and creates plenty of extension with his delivery, adding to his deception. He could be a No. 3 starter if he improves his location, perhaps more if he recaptures some velocity, but he also could wind up as a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $75,000 out of Venezuela in 2018, Iriarte developed into one of the best arms in the Padres system. He posted a 3.49 ERA with 128 strikeouts in 90 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A last year, and San Diego temporarily shifted him into a relief role to prepare for a potential big league callup that didn't come. He went to the White Sox along with prospects Drew Thorpe and Samuel Zavala plus Steven Wilson in the Dylan Cease trade in March. Iriarte's fastball sat in the mid-90s and touched 100 mph in 2023, showing good ride and run and allowing him to effortlessly hit the high armside corner consistently, but he has operated more at 92-95 mph this season. His sharp low-80s slider can dive to the opposite end of the zone, moving away from righties and backfooting lefties. His low-90s changeup doesn’t have great velocity separation but does have the fade needed to run away from opposite-side bats. Iriarte doesn’t necessarily control those darting pitches well, however, especially the breaker and cambio, and Double-A hitters laid off the stuff outside the zone, leading to a career-high 14 percent walk rate at that level. He did whiff a career-best 41 percent of the batters he faced in Double-A, and the quality extension he creates in his delivery makes his pitches even more difficult to barrel. He has the ceiling of a No. 3 starter and while he comes with reliever risk, he has closer upside if he changes roles.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite being limited to $300,000 max bonuses during the 2018-19 international signing period, the Padres still managed to land a potential future rotation candidate in Iriarte for just $75,000. The right-hander worked in both starting and relief roles in his first two seasons before emerging on the scene as a full-blown starter last year at Single-A Lake Elsinore. His 5.12 ERA, affected by the hitter-friendly California League, may not have jumped off the back of his baseball card, but 109 strikeouts and a 26.7 percent K rate established him as a bona fide arm. The 6-foot-2 right-hander has added velocity as he’s matured and now sits near the mid-90s with good extension to put that fastball right on top of hitters. His upper-80s changeup also forced Padres officials to take notice in his first full season because of the way he sells it out of his hand just before it fades successfully below swinging bats. His mid-80s slider breaks hard -- and often backfoots lefties -- but he doesn’t often land it well, which could be an issue against more advanced bats. As deep as his three-pitch mix is in pure quality, Iriarte can often battle himself with commanding his offerings. More patient batters will let him fight himself, and it was notable that his walk rate went up in 2022. Still only 21, the Venezuela native continued his upward trajectory with a dominant run at High-A Fort Wayne in 2023 and started to get Double-A bullpen looks as San Diego considered him as a relief option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two dominant junior college seasons in Kansas, Helman transferred to Texas A&M to boost his stock and went to the Twins in the 11th round of the 2018 Draft, signing for above slot at $220,000. He first reached Triple-A St. Paul in 2022 but had to repeat the level in '23 and '24 after dealing with three separate hamstring strains and a dislocated shoulder. He slashed .271/.350/.487 with 14 homers in 72 games with the Saints last season and was called up to join the Twins in September, going 3-for-10 in nine games total for the big club. Minnesota traded him to St. Louis for cash in the offseason. Helman is entering his age-29 season in 2025, making him much older than the typical prospect, but the injury setbacks delayed parts of his development. He’s a plus runner who has stolen as many as 40 bags in a full campaign when healthy, and that agility has helped him move all around the diamond. He played every position but first base and catcher in 2024, and while the plurality of his Triple-A starts came at shortstop, he’s a better fit in center (with more space to roam) or second (with fringy arm strength). As a hitter, Helman showed below-average in-zone contact rates, and his top-end exit velocity was a smidge below ideal as well. But he gets to his power well with a strong tendency to lift and pull the ball, and he’d be a threat to hit 15-plus homers over a full MLB campaign. In the midst of a transitional year for the Cardinals, Helman could plug many holes as a pinch-runner, defensive replacement all over the diamond or right-handed bat off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Through the 2024 season, four members of the Angels’ 2022 Draft class had already touched the big leagues. Three were among the 18 college players (of 19 total selections) taken by the organization that July. The fourth was Dana, a New Jersey high school product who wasn’t taken in the first 10 rounds because of his commitment to Kentucky, but thanks to the Angels’ under-slot deals early, they had $1,497,500 to sign the big right-hander. He spent most of the 2023 season in High-A then really took off in Double-A in 2024, leading the Southern League in ERA, WHIP and strikeouts. He went to the Futures Game and made his big league debut in September at age 20. While Dana might look like Noah Syndergaard in terms of his frame and hair style, he doesn’t profile as the same kind of pure-power pitcher, though he has plenty of now stuff. His fastball sits at 94 mph, topping out at 96 mph, with good riding life to it. His slider has really taken off in pro ball and it’s now a plus pitch with depth that elicited a 41-percent miss rate in Double-A last year, according to Synergy. His changeup continues to make strides and could eventually be an average offering, and he still has the slower, upper-70s curve that he featured more in high school. In his two years of pro ball, Dana has registered solid in-zone rates, but his strike-throwing took a very nice step forward in 2024 and his walk rate tumbled. He’s strong and athletic, so he should be able to keep trending upward in terms of repeating his delivery and commanding his arsenal, pointing to a long career as a No. 3 type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels’ ability to save money in the first 10 rounds of the 2022 Draft left them with some cash to be aggressive at the start of Day 3. Dana, a New Jersey high school standout, was considered to be a top four-round talent, but slid because of his commitment to Kentucky. The Angels went over the $125,000 slot in the 11th round more than tenfold, giving Dana $1.5 million to sign. While operating on a limited workload to ease him into pro ball, Dana still quickly made it up to High-A for most of his 2023 starts. Dana is polished for a high school pitcher, especially one from a cold-weather state, already showing that he has an idea of what he wants to do on the mound. He has the potential for a three, or maybe four, pitch mix. His fastball averaged around 94 mph and topped out at 96 in 2023 and it’s not hard to see his 6-foot-4 frame and dream of more consistent velocity to come. He entered pro ball as a curveball guy, and he still has it, but his focus has turned to a slider with depth which has the chance to be an above-average pitch. He’s still working on the changeup, and it’s clearly his fourth pitch coming off a year that was fastball-slider heavy. For someone his size -- he’s elicited comps to Noah Syndergaard both for his frame and his hair -- he does a decent job staying around the zone and strike-throwing shouldn’t be an obstacle in the future. The gloves could come off a bit in 2024, and especially if his stuff ticks up, he can reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Given Dana’s size -- he’s 6-foot-4 -- and arm strength, the New Jersey high school product had several teams interested as the 2022 Draft approached. When he didn’t go in the top 10 rounds, most felt he was heading to the University of Kentucky for college ball. But the Angels had other ideas and bonus pool money available, so they grabbed him at the start of Day 3 in Round 11 and went way over slot to sign him for $1.5 million. He made his brief pro debut in the Arizona Complex League and got a bump up to full-season ball to close out the year. Dana received Noah Syndergaard comps in high school, partially because of his strong, physical frame and partially because of his Thor-like flowing locks. He has the chance to have a power arsenal as well, with a fastball that gets up to the mid-90s regularly and can touch a bit higher and velocity he’s shown he can hold deep into starts. His mid-70s curve is a hard downer that has the potential to be a plus pitch, especially if he can command it better. He’s shown a little feel for a changeup, but like with a lot of prep power arms, he didn’t need it much in high school. For a big teenaged right-hander, Dana does a solid job of being around the zone, with decent fastball command, and when he stays on top of the breaking ball, it’s an out pitch. He needs reps and pro instruction to add polish to go along with his power arsenal and physicality. If it all clicks, he could pitch in the middle of a big league rotation in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout closer in the 2019 Cape Cod League, Brzykcy went unselected in the shortened 2020 Draft after seven difficult appearances for Virginia Tech that spring. He signed with the Nationals for $20,000 and was a dominant force in the Minor Leagues by 2022, when he posted a 1.76 ERA with 95 strikeouts in 61 1/3 innings across High-A, Double-A and Triple-A. He underwent Tommy John surgery in April 2023, halting his progress, but returned to a Minor League mound in late May 2022. After climbing his way steadily through four different levels, he debuted with the Nats on Sept. 1, 2024, and made six hot-and-cold appearances out of the Washington bullpen. The 6-foot-2 right-hander saw his velocity drip from the 94-97 mph range before surgery to 92-95 last season. There’s still explosive life up in the zone on the heater out of his near over-the-top delivery, and the pitch averaged 18.3 inches of induced vertical break in the Majors. Throw in good extension, and Brzykcy doesn’t need stellar velo to blow the four-seamer past hitters. His 81-84 mph curveball plays well off the verticality of the fastball, and an upper-80s changeup can be firm but fairly effective as a pitch for lefties. Brzykcy’s control fell back in line with his pre-TJ levels, but he’ll have to live more on the edges of the zone if the velocity isn’t going to be quite what it was. He should be a candidate for the Major League bullpen again right out of the gate in his age-25 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brzykcy was going to be a close follow in 2020 after serving as a standout closer in the Cape Cod League, but he struggled in seven Virginia Tech appearances and then couldn’t regain momentum once the season shut down. He signed with the Nationals for $20,000 as a free agent after going undrafted in the five-round process, found his bearings at High-A Wilmington in 2021 and then absolutely took off in '22 with a 1.76 ERA, 1.01 WHIP and 95 strikeouts in 61 1/3 innings across the top three levels of the Minors. He would have been a Major League candidate in 2023 had Tommy John surgery not ended his season in April. The Nats still protected him from the Rule 5 Draft with a 40-man spot last November. Before the procedure, the 6-foot-2 right-hander showed an explosive heater up in the zone with great induced vertical break. He lived in the 94-97 mph range, touching 98, but it was the riding action that pushed it into plus-plus territory among heaters and led to Brzykcy throwing it as high as 71 percent of the time at Double-A. He also showed a low-80s curveball that could help him work north and south and an upper-80s changeup that faded armside. The breaking pitch was seen as the more advanced of the two, but the cambio actually generated more whiffs and helped Brzykcy keep lefties in check. Brzykcy found it difficult to control the velo and movement at times in 2022, resulting in an 11.7 percent walk rate, and it’s still yet to be seen how well he’ll command the ball coming off all the lost time. If his stuff gets back to 2022 levels, he’ll be a weapon in Washington’s bullpen by summer’s end.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After notching seven saves in 10 appearances on the Cape the previous summer, Brzykcy entered the spring of 2020 with some momentum, only to get rocked in seven Virginia Tech appearances before the pandemic shutdown. He went unselected in the five-round Draft and ended up signing with the Nationals for $20,000. Brzykcy needed to find his footing at High-A Wilmington in 2021 (5.20 ERA in 62 1/3 innings) before taking off last year, climbing three levels to finish with a 1.76 ERA, 1.01 WHIP and 95 strikeouts in 61 1/3 frames. He concluded his age-22 season with a pair of scoreless relief outings at Triple-A Rochester, putting him on the cusp of the bigs. Before he could push for the Majors this season, Brzykcy underwent Tommy John surgery in April, meaning that debut won't come until 2024 at the earliest. The 6-foot-2 right-hander releases from a high over-the-top angle that can be difficult enough on hitters, and while doing so, he blazes in a 95-98 mph fastball with the rise needed to play extremely well at the top of the zone. The heater fueled his 19.4 percent swinging-strike rate in 2022, best in the system and ninth-best among the 905 Minor League hurlers with at least 60 innings. Brzykcy can keep hitters guessing by dropping in a low-80s curve or high-80s changeup at the bottom of the zone, though the former’s two-plane movement makes it the better pitch of the two. As with many fireballing relievers, Brzykcy isn’t likely to develop stellar control anytime soon with a career 10.5 percent walk rate, and he can overthrow in spots too. He was basically Major League-ready before the surgery, and any improvements in landing pitches in (or close to) the zone could be the separator between him becoming a high-leverage arm or a middle-relief option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For now, fans might know Baker most as Dusty’s son and as the bat boy who was saved from a potential collision by J.T. Snow during the 2002 World Series. But the 2021 10th-rounder is carving out a path as a legitimate prospect in the Nationals' rebuilding system. He placed himself squarely on the radar by hitting .280 with 15 steals in 105 games between High-A and Double-A in 2022 and then slashed .273/.338/.340 with three homers and 19 thefts in 99 games for Triple-A Rochester last year. Baker is a throwback player in a few ways. He’s a classic slap hitter who sprays the ball around the field, particularly the opposite way toward left field. The former Cal Golden Bear lives heavily on the ground with a 58 percent GB rate at Triple-A, in part because he prioritizes contact with solid bat-to-ball skills against pitches of all types. He’s also a skilled bunter that can push the defense with his plus speed up the line to first. All of this to say, he has near-bottom-of-the-barrel power with just a 100.1 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity. The 25-year-old makes some rangy plays at second base, including one behind-the-back glove save on a deflected ball to his left that served as one of the best Minor League highlights of 2023, but his arm strength limits his defensive ability. The Nats gave him some time in left field to give him more space to run. Baker will return to Rochester in his 40-man roster decision year, and the Nationals are hoping he can maintain his approach and add a little more impact to force their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two seasons at North Carolina as a two-way player, Casparius transferred to Connecticut, focused on pitching and led the Big East Conference with 127 strikeouts in 91 2/3 innings in 2021. A fifth-round pick that July, he posted a 5.13 ERA in his first three pro seasons before doing a better job of dodging barrels in 2024. He made his big league debut in August, delivered three scoreless outings and won the clincher in the National League Championship Series, then started Game 4 of the World Series as the opener. Casparius' money pitch is a mid-80s slider that has quality horizontal and vertical break, and he also can morph it into an upper-80s cutter that has been clocked up to 94 mph. His fastball has only modest carry and armside run but played better when he added velocity last season, and he now operates at 94-96 mph and touches 99. His third pitch is a low-80s curveball with more depth but less effectiveness than his slider. Though Casparius has been developed as a starter, he's more likely to be a multi-inning reliever in the big leagues. Not only do the Dodgers have as much rotation depth as anyone, but he also doesn't use a changeup and doesn't have a history of throwing strikes or commanding his fastball. His slider is a legitimate strikeout pitch and he can lean on it more in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lowder stepped into Wake Forest’s weekend rotation right when he arrived, turning an inconsistent freshman year into a successful one as a sophomore that led to him winning 2022 ACC pitcher of the year honors. He was the conference’s top arm again in 2023 and one of the best in the country, leading to him being the second pitcher taken in that summer’s Draft behind No. 1 pick Paul Skenes. The No. 7 overall selection started his pro career in 2024 with High-A Dayton and ended it with some early success in the big leagues. The right-hander has long had a reputation for his advanced feel for pitching, so much so that his stuff often gets short shrift. His fastball averaged around 93-94 mph at all levels in 2024, topping out at 96-97 and he throws both a four- and a two-seamer, the latter featuring solid sink to elicit a good amount of ground-ball outs. He has an outstanding changeup, thrown 86-87 mph with a ton of fade and to both sides of the plate when at its best, though he didn’t throw it as much nor was it quite as effective as during his junior year at Wake Forest. He’s leaned more on his mid-80s slider as a pro, throwing it as often as his four-seamer during his big league debut. One thing the Reds can be sure of is that Lowder is going to be in the strike zone consistently. He repeats his three-quarters arm slot and delivery extremely well and continues to be seen as the pitching prospect with the best pitchability in the game. He showed the ability to make adjustments and succeed as he climbed the ladder quickly, something he’s sure to do when he settles into the big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lowder spent three years in Wake Forest’s weekend rotation, improving considerably each year. After posting a 6.12 ERA as a freshman, he brought that down to 3.08 as a sophomore to win ACC pitcher of the year honors and pitched for Team USA that summer. He repeated as the ACC’s top arm in 2023, leading Division I with 15 wins and ranking fourth in ERA (1.87) and strikeouts (143) as the Demon Deacons reached the Men's College World Series for the first time since 1955. Lowder was the second pitcher taken in the 2023 Draft behind No. 1 overall pick Paul Skenes, with the Reds selecting him seventh overall and signing him for $5.7 million. The right-hander didn’t pitch competitively in 2023 after signing but made a strong impression at instructs in the fall, mostly participating in velocity work as well as an early January check-in camp. Lowder’s feel for pitching is so good that sometimes his pure stuff is underrated. His fastball can tap out at around 97 mph, sitting easily in the 92-95 mph range, and it has more sink than ride, getting a lot of weak ground-ball contact. He brings one of the best changeups in the college game to the Reds, a mid-80s offering with huge fade that he’ll throw to hitters on both sides of the plate. His low-80s slider has more depth than sweep, and it flashes plus. Lowder is athletic on the mound, repeating his delivery well and using a three-quarters arm slot to fill up the zone. He has a keen understanding of how to set hitters up with his complete repertoire, and he received the most votes for “best pitchability” in MLB Pipeline’s executive poll in 2024, a big reason why there’s an expectation he could move very quickly through the Reds system.

espn.label: ESPN 2026 Preseason
espn.text: 72. Rhett Lowder , RHP, Cincinnati Reds Age: 23 | Bats: Right | Throws: Right Type : A likely No. 3/No. 4 starter who missed most of 2025 but didn't need surgery Lowder was the No. 7 pick in the 2023 draft out of Wake Forest, and he debuted in the big leagues in 2024. He seemed poised to return and maybe stick in the big league rotation for good in 2025, but he threw in only five regular season games because of forearm strain and oblique issues. His four-seam and two-seam fastballs are roughly average pitches, while his slider, changeup and feel for locating his stuff are above average. Unless there's another stuff/command jump in here, a healthy Lowder will be a reliable No. 3/No. 4 starter.

just_baseball.label: JB 2026 Preseason
just_baseball.text:
Height/Weight: 6’2″, 200 | Bat/Throw: R/R | 1st Round (7), 2023 (CIN) | ETA: 2024

Lowder made his closing argument as the second best college arm in the 2023 draft by going toe-to-toe with Paul Skenes in a winner-take-all semifinal game in Omaha. As expected, Lowder flew through the minor leagues, making his MLB debut after just 22 starts where he showed well. Lowder is a high floor arm with middle-rotation upside.

A four pitch mix, Lowder wields a pair of fastballs: a four seamer that averaged just above 94 mph in 2024 and a sinker a tick slower. Lowder utilizes the four seamer more frequently to lefties and while nothing jumps off of the page, he varies the shape between run and ride and true ride, throwing hitters off. Across all levels, Lowder held left-handed hitters to an OPS right around .600. The sinker is his preferred weapon to righties, averaging 17 inches of horizontal break while picking up a ground ball rate north of 60%.

Lowder’s mid 80s slider is his best pitch. The gyro action it features and his feel to consistently locate it resulted in a ground ball rate north of 50% in 2024 with high chase figures. His 86-88 mph changeup has not been as consistent as a pro, but has the potential to be a comfortably above average pitch.

Plus command of a quality four pitch mix makes Lowder a high probability MLB starter. The effectiveness of his duo of fastballs in his pro debut and MLB debut only help his case. If Lowder can regain his the feel for his changeup he flashed at Wake Forest, he has the upside of a No. 3 option. His ability to get contact on the ground and prevent free passes makes him a great fit to handle the offensive haven that is Great American Ball Park.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Halvorsen was the best pitching prospect in Minnesota in the 2018 Draft class but wanted to head to Missouri to pitch and hit, so he was only a courtesy pick of his home-state Twins in the 30th round. He had Tommy John surgery after four relief outings in his freshman year, so he redshirted, then played some outfield as a sophomore before the 2020 season was shut down. He started for the Tigers in 2021, then transferred to Tennessee to serve as a reliever and pitched well enough for the Rockies to take him in the seventh round and sign him for an under-slot $200,000 bonus. He raced up the system as a reliever, saving nine games in 2024 and made his Major League debut just over a year after being drafted. Now 25, Halvorsen has the power repertoire and mentality to pitch late in games. Across three levels in 2024, his fastball sat close to 99 mph and routinely got into the triple digits. It has plenty of life when he’s at the top of the zone, but he also can show it to the bottom when he wants to. He throws both his slider and splitter in the upper 80s and they both can miss bats. Halvorsen's command was iffy in the Minors in 2024, but he was locked in during his big league debut, allowing just two walks in his 12 outings, giving up an earned run in only one of them. He’s ready for high-leverage situations in the back end of the Rockies' bullpen and it wouldn't surprise any one if he ended up closing games in the big leagues soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Aldegheri came from Verona, Italy, to pro ball when he signed with the Phillies in June 2019 for $100,000. The pandemic kept him off of a stateside mound until 2021 and then a shoulder issue shelved him for much of the following season. He started to figure some things out in 2023, then reached Double-A for the first time in '24 before being sent to the Angels along with George Klassen in the Carlos Estévez deal. He’s touched the big leagues in each of the last two seasons, though he spent most of 2025 in Double-A while his stuff regressed. When he’s at his best, Aldegheri looks like the kind of pitchability lefty who could fit in the back end of a big league rotation. But with that profile comes a lack of margin for error and he struggled when his repertoire, and his feel for it, backed up. His fastball sat around 92 mph and topped out at 95 and didn’t miss many bats for most of the year. His secondary stuff can get outs, with a low-80s changeup his best of the lot. His low-80s slider can be effective and he folds in a mid-70s curve, too. Early in the 2025 season, Aldegheri struggled with command of his entire repertoire, but some of that did bounce back later in the year, leading to his bump up to Triple-A and then his second trip to the big leagues. He’s now walked 4.0 per nine in his Minor League career and he needs to be much more precise in order to become a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 45 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Back in 2017 and '18, Aldegheri joined older brother Mattia in international competition for Team Italy. The two gentlemen of Verona soon parted ways, with Mattia setting up shop in the Italian professional league and Samuel signing with the Phillies in July 2019 for $100,000. He didn’t make his pro debut until 2021 and missed most of '22 with a shoulder issue. Things started to click a bit in 2023 then really took off last year, when he reached Double-A for the first time, got traded along with George Klassen in the Carlos Estévez deal and made his big league debut with the Angels. In many ways, Aldegheri is the anti-Klassen, the pitchability lefty vs. the flame-thrower. But he does have a legitimate four-pitch mix and a very good idea of what to do with it. His fastball sits around 92-93 mph and can touch 95-96, and it has decent spin and carry up in the zone. All three of his secondary offerings have bat-missing potential, led by an 84 mph slider that was his go-to breaker. His low-80s changeup has improved to the point that it might be better than the breaking stuff, and he throws a 76 mph curve as well. Combined, they elicited a 44 percent miss rate in 2024, according to Synergy. Aldegheri does an excellent job mixing his pitches and keeping hitters guessing and off balance. While his walk rate hasn’t been akin to a “pitchability” guy, he’s around the zone a lot and there’s better command to come for the southpaw. He’ll be just 23 for most of the 2025 season and it’s looking more and more like he’ll fit into a big league rotation soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 The last Italian-born pitcher to make it to the big leagues was Marino Pieretti, who appeared in 194 games with Washington, Chicago (AL) and Cleveland, a career that ended in 1950. Signed for $210,000 in July 2019 a few months shy of his 18th birthday, Aldegheri could break that 70-plus year schneid. He couldn’t make his Phillies debut until 2021 because of the pandemic, then missed most of '22 with shoulder soreness. He followed up a solid performance across two levels of A ball in 2023, then took another step forward in 2024, reaching Double-A for the first time before traded in the Carlos Estévez deal. The left-hander’s profile has been upgraded from a back-end rotation or spot-starter type to one who has a real chance to start games in the big leagues. He’s always had four pitches with decent feel for them, and that’s continued as his stuff has ticked up a bit this year. His fastball sits in the low 90s and is up to 95 mph, a high-spin heater that has solid carry in the zone. He has both a slider and a curve, and Aldegheri throws the former a lot more than the latter, a solid low-80s breaking ball. The curve is more of an upper-70s pitch that's improving. Further commitment to his changeup has been a big reason for his improvement, as it’s been very effective against right-handed hitters. Aldegheri’s walk rate hasn’t been great, but he’s shown more feel for the zone than the numbers might indicate, and there was belief in the Phillies organization that he’ll be a solid strike-thrower as he gets more time on the mound. Now it will be the Angels who can try to help him put the finishing touches in his development as he logs more innings at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If he hadn't barely missed qualifying, Kelly would have led all JUCO pitchers in strikeout rate (19.1 per nine innings) as a Wabash Valley (Mount Carmel, Ill.) CC freshman in 2019. After the Brewers signed him as a second-rounder that summer, his development stalled because of the pandemic, thoracic outlet syndrome surgery in November 2020 and a lack of strikes. He earned a berth in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game in 2022, got traded to the Rangers in a deal for Matt Bush shortly afterward and was the organization's Minor League Relief Pitcher of the Year in '23 after logging a 2.04 ERA with 79 strikeouts in 57 1/3 innings. A forearm injury and a loss of feel for the strike zone in 2024 derailed his progress, but the Rockies felt he was worth rolling the dice on when they claimed him off of waivers in July. Kelly uses his 6-foot-5 frame and a low arm slot to produce unusual shape on a pair of pitches that elicit a lot of empty swings and weak contact. He can sustain fastball velocity, working at 95-97 mph and hitting 99 with tremendous induced vertical break. He throws his heater about three times as much as his slider, a plus mid-80s sweeper with so much movement that it eats up both lefties and righties. After making a huge step forward in finding the strike zone in 2023, Kelly walked 22 in his first 17 1/3 innings of work in 2024, leading to him being taken off the 40-man roster after earning a spot for the first time last offseason. If the Rockies can help him hit the reset switch, he does have the stuff to be a high-leverage reliever in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly popped up late in the spring as an Illinois high schooler in 2018, prompting the Padres to try to sign him for an above-slot bonus in the 13th round. He turned them down to attend Wabash Valley (Ill.) CC -- where he would have led all JUCO pitchers in strikeout rate (19.1 per nine innings) in 2019 if he hadn't fallen just shy of qualifying -- then turned pro with the Brewers as a second-round pick. The pandemic shutdown, plus thoracic outlet surgery in November 2020, have stymied his development, but he pitched in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game last July shortly before getting traded with Mark Mathias to the Rangers for Matt Bush. With his 6-foot-5 frame and a low arm angle, Kelly creates difficult shape on a pair of plus pitches that generate a lot of awkward swings. His four-seam fastball sits at 94-96 mph and tops out at 98 with plenty of induced vertical break and carry up in the zone. He complements his heater with a sweeping mid-80s slider with so much movement that it works against both left- and right-handers. Kelly never has demonstrated much feel for pitching, however, and working just 160 2/3 innings in his first four years as a pro hasn't helped his cause. He doesn't repeat his delivery easily, leading him to battle his fastball command and struggle to land his slider, and his third pitch is an upper-80s changeup that's more of a batting-practice fastball. Despite his upside, he's almost certainly a reliever and he went unpicked in the Rule 5 Draft after Texas declined to protect him on its 40-man roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly was a late popup before the 2018 Draft as an Illinois high schooler, impressing scouts enough with his size and projectability that the Padres made a run at signing him to an over-slot bonus in the 13th round. He chose instead to attend Wabash Valley (Ill.) CC, where he averaged 19.1 strikeouts per nine innings in 2019 before the Brewers made him a second-round pick. He recovered from thoracic outlet surgery in November 2020 to pitch in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game this summer, shortly before Milwaukee shipped him and Mark Mathias to the Rangers for Matt Bush. Kelly has regained the stuff he had before his surgery. His fastball sits at 94-96 mph and reaches 98 with a flat approach angle that creates difficult carry up in the zone. He backs up his heat with a sweeping mid-80s slider that can be a wipeout pitch when he commands it, and he also has the makings of a decent changeup with some sink. With his 6-foot-5 frame and low arm slot, Kelly creates unusual angle on his pitches, but he also has difficulty repeating his mechanics. He has no real history of throwing strikes, though his control has improved to fringy as he has gotten regular innings for the first time as a pro this year. Few left-handers can match his fastball/slider combination, which gives him mid-rotation starter upside if he adds some polish and make him a high-leverage option if he lands in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly was a 6-foot-6 project when the Brewers drafted in him the second round in 2019 out of Wabash Valley (Ill.) Community College, where he led all junior college pitchers with a whopping 19.1 strikeouts per nine innings but little in the way of secondary pitches. The Brewers signed Kelly for slot value, sent him to the Arizona Rookie League and watched him strike out 41 batters in 21 2/3 promising innings while striking an imposing figure; after adding 20 pounds as a high school senior to fill-out his tall frame and power a fastball that jumped from the low 90s to the upper 90s, he pitched almost exclusively with a fastball that immediately became one of the best in the Brewers’ system. In 2020 at the Brewers’ alternate training site, Kelly took the next step by honing his changeup into a legitimate weapon to pair with his fastball and a slider that could be above average in time. It may have been a matter of necessity, since Kelly pitched against veteran hitters with Major League experience who were accustomed to handling big velocity. After seeing Kelly make strides to his arsenal and the rest of his game, including learning to hold runners, some club officials considered Kelly the team’s unofficial alternate site MVP. He made only one appearance in the fall instructional league, however, before being sidelined by thorasic outlet syndrome. Kelly underwent surgery in early November. Kelly has surprisingly good control for a hurler with such long levers and should continue to make gains on that front given his fluid delivery and remaining physical projection. Whether or not he can develop enough feel for a breaking ball and changeup will likely dictate Kelly’s long-term role, but the Brewers are believers in the big left-hander’s potential as a starter and view him as a possible mid-rotation starter if it all clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crews finished his three-year spin at LSU with a lengthy resume that included the 2022 SEC Co-Player of the Year, the 2023 Golden Spikes Award and the 2023 College World Series title. His phenomenal junior campaign captured scouts’ attentions not only for posting gaudy numbers, but also for honing his plate discipline. The Nationals selected him second overall that July and signed him for $9 million. Crews proved to be as advanced as expected in his first full season in 2024, hitting .270/.342/.451 with 13 homers and 25 steals in 100 games between Double-A Harrisburg and Triple-A Rochester and debuted in the Majors on Aug. 26. The right-handed slugger may not have popped statistically in the pros in the same ways he did in college, but the overall scouting report remains. He was chase-heavy early at Triple-A but reeled that in as his sample expanded, in part because of improved hand placement and a more efficient load, and his chase rate was above average over his 132 plate appearances in the bigs. That has much been Crews’ MO as a prospect. Given enough time at a level, he tends to figure out pitchers, adjust and exceed the competition. An improved approach also helps because he packs a significant punch from his 5-foot-11 frame, thanks to good strength and bat speed, and his Triple-A exit velocities specifically (112.6 mph max, 106.3 90th- percentile) point to a player with 30+ homer potential. Crews has already brought his plus-plus motor to The Show with 12 steals, and the wheels give another level to his offensive game. He moves well in all directions defensively and won a 2024 Rawlings Minor League Gold Glove for his efforts. With his plus arm strength, he’s a natural fit for center field but may continue playing right in deference to Jacob Young to begin his MLB career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year performer in Baton Rouge, Crews enjoyed one of the most decorated careers in LSU baseball history, nabbing SEC Co-Player of the Year honors in 2022. He then won the award outright along with the Golden Spikes Award a year later as he led the Tigers to the 2023 Men's College World Series title. He ranked among the Division I leaders in average (.426, fourth), OBP (.567, second), OPS (1.280, 11th), hits (110, second) and walks (71, first) over 71 games, all while cutting his strikeout rate from 18.2 percent as a sophomore to 13.4 as a junior. The Nationals snagged Crews with the second overall pick in July and signed him for $9 million, the second-highest bonus in Draft history. He ended the season at Double-A Harrisburg, where he started to show fatigue from the long spring and summer. Crews thrust himself into the conversation as the top talent in the 2023 Draft on the strength of his improved plate discipline in college, rarely going outside the zone while teeing off on the pitches he could drive (particularly fastballs). He struggled a little more with offspeed stuff on the pro side, but his ability to adjust during his time as LSU speaks well to his chances of improvement in his first full season and beyond. Batting from a well-coiled right-handed stance, Crews packs at least plus power in his 6-foot frame. A plus runner, Crews doesn’t have a history of stealing bags, but he can make defenses think twice once he gets moving. He has the athleticism to stick in center field, but the former Bayou Bengal saw some time in the corners in Harrisburg as he joined a roster with James Wood and Robert Hassell III. His bat should play anywhere in Washington’s dream of a homegrown outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Go ahead and try to find an upper-level pitching prospect with the kind of roller-coaster ride that Madden endured in 2024. The former supplemental first-round Draft pick spent April repeating Double-A Erie with instructions to hone his newly-developed splitter. After four SeaWolves starts, Madden moved to Triple-A Toledo, where he posted a 7.97 ERA and allowed 17 homers in 79 innings but also fanned 102 batters, 11 of them over a 5 2/3-inning loss in which he gave up 12 hits. The Tigers, needing pitching, believed in the stuff over results and called him up at the end of August. Though he mainly worked out of the bullpen, his seven strikeouts over five innings of one-run ball earned him his first Major League win Sept. 8 at Oakland. He also made Detroit’s postseason bullpen. Madden’s mid-90s fastball and snappy slider form a dynamic duo that has been his weapon against hitters ever since his days as a starter at the University of Texas. His heater plays up beyond its 94 mph average with good ride, allowing it to play at the top of the strike zone and set up the slider to change eye levels. An upper-80s cutter was an effective pitch at Triple-A with mixed results in limited Major League use. Though Madden’s new splitter improved as a swing-and-miss pitch on his way up the Minors, he’s still learning when to use it and how to set it up. Madden missed more bats later in the season after lowering his arm angle a tad and changing his positioning on the mound at Toledo. The Tigers have left the door open for Madden to compete for a starting job, but Detroit’s wealth of pitching could ultimately leave the bullpen as his best route to stick in the big leagues. His ability to take constructive criticism and adapt his game impressed coaches and higher-ups last year. A right rotator cuff strain kept him from being part of the equation through the first half of 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The rise of Reese Olson, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe, Sawyer Gipson-Long and Brant Hurter in the Tigers system overshadowed Madden, who spent the entire 2023 season at Double-A Erie and overcame a middling first half to put together a sneaky strong year that backed up the club's faith in the former supplemental first-round pick as a starter. The University of Texas product finished second to Hurter among Eastern League pitchers in ERA (3.43), third in strikeouts (146), fifth in opponents' average against (.233) and seventh in WHIP (1.28), all while having his innings watched (he tossed six or more innings in just three of 25 starts). It wasn’t flashy, but it put Madden squarely in Detroit’s long-term pitching pipeline. Madden has gotten back to his roots as a fastball-slider dominant arm at Triple-A Toledo in 2024, with mixed results. His fastball sits 93-95 mph, topping out around 98, and though the pitch comes with some carry, hitters have feasted on it at the Minors' top level. His 82-85 mph slider is better at getting whiffs with snappy glove-side action. Those two pitches alone account for 75-80 percent of his usage at Triple-A this summer, but he'll also mix in an 82-85 mph changeup, upper-70s curveball and upper-80s cutter for different looks. Given his age and proximity, Madden has a decent floor as a two-pitch reliever, but the Tigers want to keep getting him starting opportunities before completely changing his role. The former Longhorn is Rule 5-eligible this winter and could force Detroit's hand if he's able to finish the year on a stronger note.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have a history of using first-round Draft picks on college pitchers with upside, from 2018 top overall pick Casey Mize to 2017 College World Series hero Alex Faedo. Madden was slightly different, but the Tigers were opportunistic when the former University of Texas star fell out of the traditional first round and into the Competitive Balance picks in 2021. While some clubs saw a reliever’s arsenal, the Tigers thought he had a chance to make it as a starter. Madden’s first pro season seemed to reward that faith, with 7.1 hits and 9.8 strikeouts per nine innings between High-A West Michigan (19 starts) and Double-A Erie (seven). While Madden’s strength is a combination of mid-90s fastballs and mid-80s sliders, his arsenal has evolved under Tigers director of pitching Gabe Ribas. He has worked in more high fastballs to change hitters’ eye level after entering pro ball with a reputation for pounding the bottom of the strike zone. He also mixed in his changeup more often. When his pitches are on, he can get swings-and-misses in the strike zone in addition to getting hitters to chase off the outside corner. After off-and-on strike-zone issues during the summer, including his first couple Double-A starts, he allowed one walk in each of his final five outings in Erie in 2022, posting a 35-to-5 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 25 2/3 innings. Scouts seem split on whether he can make it as a starter; how the changeup progresses could be a factor. Madden will get a chance to build on that progress at the front of the Erie rotation this year. The Tigers have enough pitching depth to be patient with the 23-year-old as he refines his game, but a strong SeaWolves stint likely would put him in a strong position among Detroit's internal rotation answers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Madden hadn’t faced a hitter since pitching in the College World Series for Texas until the Tigers invited their supplemental first-round pick to Minor League minicamp in February. His first matchup with live hitting was Riley Greene, whom he sent down swinging and missing on three straight pitches. Neither Spencer Torkelson nor Ryan Kreidler could do anything against him either. It was an impressive arrival for the reigning Big 12 Conference Pitcher of the Year, who fell to the Tigers near the end of the first round and signed for a $2.5 million bonus. One of the critiques on Madden going into the Draft was that he thrived pitching down in the zone in college, creating question of whether he could successfully change eye levels on hitters in the pros. He seems to have taken that to heart and was more willing to challenge hitters with high fastballs in Spring Training. If he can do that consistently, it should set up his mid-80s slider as an effective swing-and-miss pitch with late bite. He has shown progress with an upper-70s curveball as a potential third pitch, and also throws a fading low-80s changeup. The Tigers have had success bringing college pitchers through their system quickly with Casey Mize and Tarik Skubal. There’s enough pitching depth in Detroit to give Madden more time, and he could benefit greatly from working with new pitching director Gabe Ribas. There’s enough in his arsenal to make a solid Major League starter if he can adapt to pro hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Jeff Conine became known as \"Mr. Marlin\" while winning a pair of World Series with the franchise, and son Griffin is trying to follow him to Miami. He signed for $1.35 million with the Blue Jays as a 2018 second-rounder from Duke and went to the Marlins as the player to be named in an August 2020 trade for Jonathan Villar. He has a track record of hitting for power, leading the Cape Cod League with nine homers in 2017 and the Low-A Midwest League with 22 in his first full pro season before ranking second in the Minors with 36 last year. Conine is a feast-or-famine hitter who combines plus-plus raw power with poor contact skills, topping the Minors with 185 strikeouts in 2021 and posting a 36 percent whiff rate in his first three pro seasons. He batted just .176 with a 47 percent strikeout rate following a mid-July promotion to Double-A and struck out against a batting machine during a fall minicamp, underscoring the need to make adjustments in order for his pop to play at higher levels. His bat speed and strength produce tape-measure shots and jaw-dropping exit velocities from the left side of the plate, but his homer-happy approach leaves him vulnerable to velocity up in the zone as well as breaking pitches. Though he's a below-average runner, Conine has acceptable range on the outfield corners. He has plus arm strength and recorded 29 assists in 211 games during his first three seasons. His power and arm fit the classic right-field profile, though it remains to be seen whether he can make enough contact to get to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Conine led the Cape Cod League with nine homers in the summer of 2017 and smacked 18 more the following spring at Duke, earning a $1.35 million bonus from the Blue Jays as a second-rounder. He was suspended for the first 50 games of 2019 after testing positive for a stimulant but still managed to top the low Class A Midwest League in homers (22) and slugging (.576). He joined Miami, the club his father Jeff won two World Series with while becoming known as \"Mr. Marlin,\" last September as the player to be named in the deal that shipped Jonathan Villar to Toronto. Conine generates well above-average pop that plays to all fields with bat speed, strength, loft in his left-handed swing and an aggressive mentality. His approach needs some work, however, because he gets pull-happy and his stroke gets long as he hunts home runs. He logged a 36 percent strikeout rate during his introduction to full-season ball in 2019 and needs to understand that his power will come naturally if he lets it. Though he's a below-average runner, Conine covers enough ground to get the job done defensively on an outfield corner. His plus arm and power potential fit the traditional right-field profile. The Marlins loved what they saw of his work ethic at their alternate site and instructional league camp, and they may expedite his development in 2021 because he'll turn 24 at midseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gentry was the Royals’ third-round pick out of Alabama in the shortened 2020 Draft. He’s had an up-and-down Minor League career in part because of the pandemic, a knee injury and performance. But he was added to the Royals’ 40-man roster after the 2023 season and made his debut on Aug. 25, 2024. He only had five at-bats in the Majors and is still looking for his first hit there. Gentry spent most of the season at Triple-A Omaha, slashing .251/.338/.422 with 16 home runs, 24 doubles and a 99 wRC+. Gentry has made several swing changes over the course of his Minor League career and continued to tweak it last season, modifying the toe tap for a more balanced swing, easier operation and better firing position. Gentry is strong and physical but has only shown average power so far, and his main struggle is his aggressiveness. He struck out at a 30.5% clip while only walking 10.8% of the time in 2024. His issue seems to be more timing-based, fouling off pitches he should drive. Gentry can really play right field with one of the strongest arms in the Royals’ system, and he’s aggressive out there, giving him average-to-above-average defense. Likely headed back to Triple-A to serve as depth for the Royals in 2025, Gentry has to find a way to cut down on his strikeouts if he wants to break into the big leagues, much less take over an everyday role. He has typically started slow each season and comes on in the second half, so he needs to find better consistency to reach his potential as a reserve outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a college career that began at Walters State (Tenn.) CC followed by two seasons at Alabama, Gentry became the Royals’ third-round pick in the shortened 2020 Draft. He had an inconsistent start to his pro career because of the pandemic and a knee injury that shortened his first full season. He took a big jump in ‘22 but had a slow start to ‘23 before getting back on track, leading to the Royals adding him to their 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft this past offseason. From June 15 to the end of the year with Triple-A Omaha, Gentry hit .266 with an .851 OPS and 119 wRC+, cutting his strikeouts down; he finished the year with 16 homers and 28 doubles. Gentry made several adjustments to his swing that helped him break out in ‘22, taking to the Royals’ hitting department philosophy of hunting drivable pitches in the zone. In the second half of last year, Gentry made better swing decisions and simplified his mechanics to get back to his smooth, efficient right-handed swing. He’s strong and physical with average power. Gentry has one of the strongest arms in the Royals’ system and brings solid and aggressive defense to right field, although it would be good to see more power from him for his profile to fit the position. Eyeing his Major League debut at some point in 2024, Gentry got off to a rough start back in Omaha to begin the season but proved, once again, to be a second-half performer with strong showings from July onward. On one hand, that speaks well to his ability to make adjustments. On the other, he'll need to be more consistent to carve out a potential everyday role at some point behind his age-26 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After he began his college career at Walters State (Tenn.) CC, Gentry led Alabama in most offensive categories his final two seasons. His professional career started when the Royals drafted him in the third round of the 2020 Draft. A knee injury ended Gentry’s first full season in ‘21 early, but he was 2022’s breakout player of the year in the Royals system. He beat High-A quickly by slashing .336/.434/.516, then was promoted to Double-A on June 14. He was even better there, crushing 16 homers and posting a .972 OPS. Another product of the Royals’ successful hitting development program, Gentry’s improvement in 2022 was not just health -- it was his approach. Gentry slashed his strikeout rate from 25.7% at High-A to 19.9% at Double-A. Gentry became more patient and learned the best pitches to drive and the best part of the zone to do damage. Big, strong and physical, Gentry generates solid power from his right-handed smooth swing. He displays solid defense in right field and has one of the strongest arms in the Royals system. Speed won’t be a major part of Gentry’s game, but his instincts will allow him to swipe a bag here and there. No Royals prospect took a bigger step forward in 2022 than Gentry. He went from a fringe-prospect and likely fourth outfielder to someone who could hit his way into a starting outfield job in the big leagues by the end of 2023. After a slow start at Triple-A Omaha, he began to look more like himself in the second half, showing both a high OBP and good power. If Gentry doesn’t become an everyday player, he could provide value as a lefty-masher off the bench. He profiles best in right field but will see time in both corner outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gentry’s college career began at Walters State (Tenn.) CC and ended at Alabama, where he led the Crimson Tide in most offensive categories his final two years. His bat led the Royals to taking him in the third round of the 2020 Draft, and he joined their Arizona instructional league in the fall. In his first full season, Gentry continued his momentum for the first part of the year. He posted a .844 OPS with six homers in 44 games for High-A Quad Cities before knee injuries shut him down in August. Big, strong and physical, Gentry’s best tool is his right-handed pop with a smooth swing that carries the ball to all fields. The swing is also aggressive, so he’ll have to maintain better plate discipline. But if he does that, he could hit for both average and power in the big leagues. Gentry displays solid defense in right field with one of the stronger arms in the Royals' system. With solid speed, he profiles best as a right fielder, but it wouldn’t be surprising to see him in left field, either, given how the Royals value left field defense at Kauffman Stadium. Fully healthy in 2022, Gentry has also been fully productive with consistent results at both High-A and Double-A this season. He turns 24 in February, and given the way he’s put the pedal to the metal of late, his mix of hit and power tools could send have him knocking on Kansas City’s door by the middle of next season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After hitting 18 home runs as a freshman at Walters State (Tenn.) CC in 2018, Gentry led Alabama in most offensive categories the past two years. He hit .429/.554/.750 in the shortened 2020 season, ranking among NCAA Division I leaders in all three stats. That led the Royals to taking him in the third round, and he joined their Arizona instructional league in the fall for his first look at the organization. A big, strong and physical player, Gentry’s offensive profile stands out the most. His right-handed pop is his best tool. The ball carries to all fields, but he has an aggressive swing and approach and will have to maintain the improved plate disciple he showed during the shortened college season last year. If he can do that, Gentry could hit for both average and power. Gentry’s defense is solid, too, with one of the stronger arms in the Royals system. Gentry profiles best in right field with his bat and arm strength. Like all the 2020 Draft picks, this year has been important for Gentry to get onto the field and see how his raw power holds up against opposing pitchers. Early reviews from High-A Quad Cities are solid, though not stellar in that regard. Gentry has solid speed, but his success as a big leaguer is going to come down to his bat and how productive it can be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Freddy Peralta has become the anchor of the Brewers rotation and a 2021 All-Star. His younger brother, Luis, is ready to establish himself as a big leaguer too, albeit as a reliever. The younger Peralta’s journey started in 2017 when he signed with the Pirates and then spent two years starting and relieving in the Dominican Summer League. He made it to full-season ball for the first time in 2022 as a starter, then started to see more time in the bullpen back at that level in 2023. Things clicked as a full-time reliever in 2024 as Peralta dominated at High-A and Double-A before getting moved to the Rockies in the Jalen Beeks trade. Less than a month later, he was in the big leagues and pitching his way into future bullpen plans. A 5-foot-11 lefty, Peralta comes right at hitters with a two-pitch mix. His fastball sat 95 mph during his big league stint and touched 97 and that doesn’t appear to be a mirage. He can miss bats with his low-80s slider. The uptick in his stuff over the past year contributed to a 14.2 K/9 rate at all Minor League stops in last year. Before starting to find the strike zone more consistently in 2024, command had long been an issue for Peralta, who will pitch at age 24 this season. If he can keep landing his slider in the zone, something he did more of last year, that could be a potentially plus pitch and help him not just make a big league bullpen, but get high leverage innings out of it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Criswell began his career at Michigan as a reliever, then moved into the Wolverines rotation as a sophomore, pitching well enough then and in his shortened junior season to land in the second round of the 2020 Draft with the A’s. He missed nearly all of his first full season, though he did pitch in the Arizona Fall League and then pitched his way from High-A to Triple-A in 2022. The Rockies acquired him at the Winter Meetings in return for Chad Smith. With a bit of an unorthodox delivery, Criswell has shown he can use four distinct pitches to get people out. His fastball averages around 93 mph and tops out at 96. He throws his low-80s fading changeup a good amount and it misses bats while his slider, thrown around the same velocity, can also be a swing-and-miss pitch. He’ll fold in a slower upper-70s curve effectively as well. While Criswell has simplified his delivery some since entering pro ball, there is still some herky-jerky effort to it. He’s managed to be around the strike zone enough to give faith that he can remain a starter. His ceiling might be limited to someone who pitches in the back end of a big league rotation, but assuming health, he’s close to reaching it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Criswell’s success as both a starter and reliever at the University of Michigan led to him landing a $1 million signing bonus from the A’s as a second-round pick in the 2020 Draft. After injuries limited him to just 12 innings pitched at High-A in what would have been his first full season with the organization, he did manage to end his year on a high note by returning in time to play in the Arizona Fall League and ranking among the league’s top strikeout leaders, using that as a springboard to a healthy 2022 season that saw him go from High-A to Triple-A. The Rockies took notice and acquired him in a Winter Meetings trade for Chad Smith. Criswell’s mechanics could use some cleaning up to eliminate some herky-jerky movement, but overall they are repeatable. His fastball sits in the low-90s, though he can reach back for more and brings a changeup with some fade that has swing-and-miss possibilities. His arsenal is rounded out by a power slider and tight curveball, giving him a solid four-pitch mix. Once he cleans up the mechanics, Criswell does project as a starter at the big league level if he can stay healthy. He’s been described as “Bassitt-ish” in reference to Chris Bassitt for similarities in their athletic builds. A bullpen role, where his stuff could play up even more, is also not out of the question.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Flashing dominance both as a starter and reliever at Michigan, Criswell was given a $1 million bonus as a second-round pick in the 2020 Draft. Once he joined the organization for instructional league last year, his mechanics appeared even better than advertised. Criswell is a hard thrower with repeatable mechanics whose fastball works between 93-96 mph. He also throws a slider and a changeup, both of which flash plus, giving him a good starter mix with two secondary pitches that sit in the low 80s. Criswell’s stuff makes him one of the more exciting pitching prospects the A’s have had in recent years, though he does tend to overthrow at times, causing his delivery to go out of whack. He will be developed as a starter and projects as a mid-rotation type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ginn was a second-round pick by the Mets in the 2020 MLB Draft out of Mississippi State and joined the A’s in 2022 as one of two players acquired from New York for Chris Bassitt. After arm injuries became an unfortunate theme, including a forearm strain in ‘22 and bicep tendinitis in ‘23, he finally got to a good place with his health last season and took advantage of his first big league opportunity. Pitching in eight games (six starts) for the A’s, the right-hander posted a 4.24 ERA and ended the year as a member of their starting rotation. The sinker is Ginn’s bread and butter, with some in the organization likening it to that of former Big Three member Tim Hudson for the mid-90s velocity and frequent ability to generate ground balls. He also brings a good swing-and-miss slider in the mid-80s, giving him a strong power sinker-slider combo as his base. The changeup has improved but can still get him in trouble when the velocities are too similar to his fastball readings. He came into Spring Training working on adding a cutter to his pitch mix. Control has always been a key part of Ginn’s game. He is able to maintain low walk rates and has a strong ability to keep all of his pitches around the plate consistently. After showing some promise in his limited look as a Major League starter, he has the chance to impact the big league rotation long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round Draft pick by the Mets in 2020 out of Mississippi State, Ginn joined the A’s last year as part of the return from the Mets in the Chris Bassitt trade. Dealing with a forearm strain early in the season, the A’s were cautious with the right-hander, who was only a couple of years removed from Tommy John surgery. Appearing in 12 combined games in the Arizona Complex League and with Double-A Midland, he finished the season with a 6.17 ERA but was able to redeem himself a bit in the Arizona Fall League, where he posted a 2.25 ERA in five outings and earned a spot in the Fall Stars Game. He wasn’t able to carry over that success into the 2023 season as he once again spent considerable time on the injured list with bicep tendinitis. Ginn’s fastball is more of a power sinker that has been described as “Tim Hudson-like” and comes in the low 90s with good action, which has led to his high ground-ball rates in recent seasons. He also throws a mid-80s slider with good two-plane break that helps him generate swing-and-miss. His changeup is a decent third offering, though it can get him into trouble when its velocities become too similar to the fastball readings. Having demonstrated good control throughout his career as evidenced by his low walk rates, Ginn has a chance to emerge as a mid-rotation starter at the big league level, though staying healthy will be vital in order for that to materialize. The A’s had hoped 2023 would be a breakout year until the injury bug struck again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mississippi native was selected by the Dodgers at No. 30 in 2018, but he headed to Mississippi State instead. He lived up to the hype early with the Bulldogs, earning SEC Freshman Pitcher of the Year honors with 105 strikeouts in 86 1/3 innings, but only got in one 2020 start before requiring Tommy John surgery. The Mets grabbed the Draft-eligible sophomore in the second round in 2020, signed him to an over-slot $2.9 million bonus and had him back on the mound a year later. Ginn’s early Minor League stats have been promising -- 3.03 ERA, 1.05 WHIP, 81 strikeouts in 92 innings between Low-A and High-A. The A’s noticed his return to the mound and acquired him in March as the top prospect in the Chris Bassitt trade. The right-hander, who will be 23 for much of the 2022 season, has morphed into a ground-ball specialist in the pros. His fastball mostly sat in the low 90s last year with lots of sink, leading to a 61.6 percent ground-ball rate (second-best in the Minors among pitchers with at least 90 frames). The Mets were encouraged that the velo could return even more this spring, it was back to touching 97. Ginn’s mid-80s slider is his best swing-and-miss pitch with good two-plane break and another mid-80s changeup rounds out the arsenal, though it gets a little too close to fastball velocity at times. With a 5.9 percent walk rate in 2021, Ginn’s control was not a concern coming back from surgery. Ginn was hoping 2022 would be go-time after proving he was healthy, but forearm issues forced him out of action for more than two months. A sinker-heavy style has some benefits in the modern game, but it’s not as desirable as a profile that can elicit more whiffs. A few more ticks of consistent velo could be what solidifies Ginn as a mid-rotation type. Otherwise, he has a decent floor as a No. 5.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Neely's college career took him from Texas to Iowa Western CC to Ohio State before the Yankees signed him for a slightly over-slot $150,000 bonus in 2021. They immediately moved him to the bullpen and he has dominated ever since, ranking in the top five in strikeout rate among Minor League relievers (minimum: 50 innings) in each of his three full seasons: fifth in 2022 (40 percent), fourth in 2023 (39 percent) and fifth again last year (37 percent). Traded to the Cubs along with infielder Ben Cowles in exchange for Mark Leiter Jr. at the Trade Deadline in July 2024, he gave up six runs in six relief appearances with Chicago and has seen his stuff and control regress this year. Neely's slider can be virtually unhittable, posting elite chase (42 percent), swing-and-miss (55 percent) and swinging-strike (30 percent) rates between Double-A, Triple-A and the Majors in 2024. His slide piece averages 87 mph and reaches 91 with tight spin and two-plane depth at its best but hasn't been as sharp this season. He sets it up with a four-seam fastball that ranges from 94-98 mph and has bat-missing carry, though it's fairly straight and can get pounded when it catches too much of the plate. With his massive 6-foot-8 frame and low three-quarters arm slot, Neely creates more angle and extension than most pitchers. The Yankees helped him learn to keep his long limbs in sync and throw more consistent strikes but he has averaged nearly a walk per inning in 2025. He looked like a potential setup man when the Cubs acquired him but his future is more muddled now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Neely pitched at three colleges in three years, bouncing from Texas to Iowa Western CC to Ohio State before the Yankees signed him for a slightly over-slot $150,000 in the 11th round in 2021. New York immediately moved him to the bullpen and he has dominated in that role, ranking fifth among Minor League relievers (minimum: 50 innings) with a 40 percent strikeout rate in 2022 and fourth with a 39 percent K rate last year while climbing to Double-A. The Cubs acquired him along with infield prospect Benjamin Cowles in a July trade for Mark Leiter Jr. Though Neely's mid-80s slider is a tighter version than the sweeper that's the rage in the Yankees organization, it's a plus-plus weapon nonetheless. It does feature some two-plane break at times and overwhelmed Double-A hitters in the final six weeks of last season, registering a 57 percent swing-and-miss rate and a 47 percent chase rate. He sets it up with a fastball that parks at 95 mph and peaks at 97 with significant armside run and induced vertical break, though it generates more weak contact than empty swings. Neely's massive 6-foot-9 frame creates a natural angle and extension that provides deception. He lowered his walk rate from 4.6 per nine innings in his first full pro season to 2.7 in his second. If his slider-heavy attack continues to work against upper-level hitters, he could help Chicago in the near future and eventually settle into a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If things had gone according to plan, Aguiar would have graduated off this list last year.
