His fastball played better than its fringy velocity in college because of the deception and sink he created with his lower arm angle, and it has been more effective since gaining 2 mph and parking 91-95 in pro ball. While Roupp's changeup has some interesting fade, it's too firm in the mid-80s and he relies on his curve to get left-handers out. He throws strikes with a clean delivery and has shown more upside than the long reliever/No. 5 starter ceiling he entered pro ball with. His breaking pitches give him a high floor as a bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some scouts believed that Beeter had the best stuff of any college starter in the 2020 Draft, but his long medical history (Tommy John surgery in December 2017, a follow-up arthroscopic procedure seven months later) and limited track record at Texas Tech dropped him to the Dodgers in the supplemental second round, where he signed for an over-slot $1,196,500. Acquired in an August 2022 trade for Joey Gallo, he ranked eighth in the Minors with 165 strikeouts in 131 2/3 innings in his first full season in the Yankees system. He opened 2024 in the Majors and made one appearance before heading to Triple-A, where he missed nearly four months with shoulder issues before getting back to New York for two games at the end of the season. He moved to relief for good in 2025, made two more MLB appearances for the Yanks in July and was dealt to the Nationals before the Trade Deadline in a move for Amed Rosario. In his role over shorter bursts, Beeter sits 94-97 mph, touching 99, with impressive carry on his four-seam fastball. He also overpoweres hitters with an upper-80s slider with downer break that plays very well off the shape of his heater. (It had a 48.9 percent whiff rate at Triple-A at the time of the trade.) He can flash a plus 78-82 mph curveball and has a mid-80s changeup with some fade, but he has mostly scrapped both pitches. Beeter’s move to the bullpen made sense considering his two reliable pitches and below-average control and command. He operates with a high three-quarters delivery that includes a deep plunge in back, which helps him stay on top of his slider but compromises his ability to land pitches in the zone. If he can find a way to provide more strikes, he could fill a high-leverage role in the nation’s capital.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beeter was so dominant at Texas Tech during the shortened 2020 season that some scouts believed he had the best stuff of any college starter in the Draft. He also came with a long medical history (Tommy John surgery in December 2017 before his first college season, a follow-up arthroscopic procedure seven months later) and limited track record, so he lasted until the Dodgers took him in the supplemental second round and signed him for an over-slot $1,196,500. Traded to the Yankees for Joey Gallo in August 2022, he earned Double-A Eastern League all-star honors, pitched a career-high 131 2/3 innings and claimed spots in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and on New York's 40-man roster in his first full year in his new organization. While Beeter's stuff cooled off a bit in 2023, he still can show flashes of three plus pitches. His best offering is an 82-86 mph slider with two-plane depth that hitters can't barrel or lay off, and he now favors it heavily over a 78-82 mph curveball with similar shape that he can't land for strikes. His fastball sits at 92-94 mph and peaks at 97 with more carry up in the zone than true life, and it can get tagged when he doesn't command it. Beeter's mid-80s changeup is too firm and he barely uses it, making him primarily a two-pitch guy. He worked deeper into games last year and made some mild progress throwing strikes, increasing his chances of remaining a starter. He still has below-average control and command, however, so he might have more success focusing on his fastball and slider in a relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beeter dominated in four outings for Texas Tech during the shortened 2020 season and some scouts thought he had the best stuff of any college starter in the Draft, but he dropped to the Dodgers in supplemental second round because his medical history was longer than his track record. He had Tommy John surgery in December 2017 before his first college season and a follow-up arthroscopic elbow procedure seven months later. Los Angeles signed him for an over-slot $1,196,500 and handled him with extreme care, letting him work as many as four innings just four times in 43 starts before dealing him to the Yankees for Joey Gallo last August. The Dodgers initially had Beeter shelve his slider to focus on his curveball, but his mid-80s slide piece was his best pitch in 2022, a well above-average offering generating a 53 percent swing-and-miss rate thanks to its combination of velocity and two-plane depth. His fastball also can be dominant, sitting at 93-96 mph and reaching 98 mph with nice carry up in the zone, as well as some armside run. His low-80s downer curveball can be a plus pitch at times but isn't as reliable as his slider, and his low-80s changeup has regressed because he barely uses it. His high arm slot creates downhill plane and deception, and his ability to tunnel his pitches makes him even harder to hit. No Minor League pitcher who worked as many innings (77) as Beeter had as high a strikeout rate (15.1 per nine innings) in 2022, but he has yet to prove he can handle a starter's workload or provide consistent strikes. He looks like more of a reliever and has the stuff to become a high-leverage option if he improves his control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beeter showcased stuff arguably as good as any college starter in the 2020 Draft, but the Dodgers were able to grab him in the supplemental second round because his medical record was more extensive than his track record. He had Tommy John surgery in December 2017 before his first season at Texas Tech and a follow-up arthroscopic elbow procedure seven months later before leading the Red Raiders' 2019 College World Series semifinalists with eight saves and dominating in four starts as a redshirt sophomore. Los Angeles signed him for an over-slot $1,196,500 and handled him with great care before trading him to the Yankees for Joey Gallo this August. Beeter has a pair of pitches that grade as well above-average when at their best. He sits at 93-96 mph and touches 98 mph with a fastball that has good carry, and a high-spin low-80s curveball that plays off his heater well by dropping through the bottom of the zone. He also had a plus mid-80s slider that the Dodgers had him shelve in order to focus on his curve, and he can flash a solid low-80s changeup with some sink and fade but doesn't use it very often. Using an overhand slot that creates deception and downhill plane, Beeter tunnels all of his pitches well. With the exception of the shortened 2020 college season, he has exhibited fringy control at best, and his delivery may not be conducive to throwing more strikes. If he can't make it as a starter, he has the stuff to become a high-leverage reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some scouts who saw Beeter during the brief 2020 college season thought his stuff was as good as any in the Draft, but he lasted until the supplemental second round because of his medical history and lack of track record. He had Tommy John surgery in December 2017 before his first season at Texas Tech and a follow-up arthroscopic elbow procedure seven months later. After leading the Red Raiders' 2019 College World Series semifinalists with eight saves, he exploded as a starter last spring by recording nearly twice as many strikeouts (33) as baserunners allowed (18) in 21 innings. Beeter's pitches and control actually got better when he worked longer outings last year, though he was inconsistent at Los Angeles' alternate site and during instructional league after signing for an over-slot $1,196,500. Dodgers big league hitters said he was as good as any pitcher at their alt site when he was on. His fastball can park at 93-96 mph and reach 98 with good carry though the top of the strike zone, his high-spin low-80s curveball can be an absolute hammer and the organization has had him shelve his mid-80s slider for now to focus on his other pitches. Beeter also shows flashes of a solid changeup with some sink and fade, and he tunnels all his pitches well with an overhand delivery that creates deception and downhill plane. Without making any significant mechanical changes, he reduced his walk rate from 8.7 per nine innings as a reliever in 2019 to 1.7 as a starter last year. If he proves he can maintain his wipeout stuff and his improved control over a long season, he could be the steal of the 2020 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round pick by the Yankees in the 2019 Draft, Spence was part of an impressive Day 2 class for the Yankees in which they took a pair of college arms who are now big leaguers, Ken Waldichuk and Hayden Wesneski. Moving quickly through New York’s system, Spence's solid ‘23 campaign in which he posted a 4.47 ERA at Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre and led all Minor Leaguers with 163 innings led an A’s club in search of pitching this offseason to select him first overall in the Rule 5 Draft in December. Spence can dial up his fastball to 95-96 mph at times but mostly sits 91-92. That lower velocity is aided by his good feel for pitching as a strike-thrower. In addition to his effective cutter, good curveball and developing sweeper, he has been tinkering with a sinker in A’s Spring Training that is still a work in progress. Spence’s good arm action and sound delivery remind some in the organization of Derek Lowe. His 2.9 walks per nine innings rate shows his ability to command the ball well. His Rule 5 status means he should get a good shot to stick with the A's as a first-time big leaguer in 2024, either as a starter or a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers selected Keith in the fifth round of the shortened 2020 Draft and talked him out of an Arizona State commitment with an above-slot $500,000 signing bonus. Injuries -- including to his right shoulder in 2022 -- limited him to only 113 games over his first two full seasons, though he did stand out in the Arizona Fall League in '22. Finally healthy for much of 2023, Keith broke out with a .306/.380/.552 line and 27 homers in 126 games between Double-A and Triple-A. His 68 extra-base hits and 280 total bases ranked third and fifth among Minor Leaguers, respectively. In January, the Tigers rewarded him with a six-year, $28,642,500 contract extension with club options through 2032. Using a quick and short left-handed swing, the Mississippi native does a nice job of marrying quality contact rates with noticeable impact at the dish. He elevates well and rarely expands the zone, leading to the high slugging percentages and extra-base-hit rates. With Triple-A Toledo, he maxed out with an exit velocity of 110.1 mph and slugged a 473-foot homer (per Statcast) that ranked as the fifth-longest in the International League last season. Higher EVs and more tape-measure shots should be in his future as he grows more comfortable getting through long seasons. The Tigers moved Keith -- a below-average runner with a stocky frame -- from third base to second on a near-full-time basis by mid-August last season out of the belief his reaction times and throwing motion work better at the keystone. He’d be a bat-first player at either place, but there is a clear lane for Keith to seize a spot in the Majors and join Spencer Torkelson and Riley Greene as homegrown premier talents in Detroit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Keith looked on his way to Arizona State before Detroit selected him in the fifth round of the shortened 2020 Draft and signed him for above slot at $500,000. The left-handed slugger got hot late in his first full season and seemed to be carrying that performance into 2022, when he hit .301/.370/.544 with 26 extra-base hits in 48 games with High-A West Michigan. A June 9 shoulder injury, suffered when he dove back to the bag on a pickoff attempt, knocked Keith out for the remainder of the regular season, but he made up for the lost time by hitting .344/.463/.541 with a 16/16 K/BB ratio over 19 Arizona Fall League contests. The Mississippi native has added even more size to his 6-foot-3 frame since his Draft days, and that’s starting to translate into more power, as he proved in the AFL, where he had multiple batted balls with a 105-plus mph exit velocity (as measured by Statcast). His quick left-handed swing should help him hit for healthy averages too, and it was a promising sign for his developing approach when his K rate dropped to 19.4 percent in the Midwest League last season. Keith has seen some time at second base in the Minors, but a lack of footspeed, which may only get worse as he ages, should keep him at third. The plus arm that had him throwing 89-93 mph off the mound in high school is best utilized at the hot corner anyways. Keith has managed only 113 Minor League games over his first two seasons, so getting him those defensive reps -- and proving how well his bat can play over the long term -- should go a long way in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers wooed Keith away from an Arizona State commitment with a fifth-round pick in the 2020 MLB Draft and a $500,000 bonus, a nifty pickup amidst a pandemic-shortened amateur season and Draft. His rust showed with a slow start last summer at Low-A Lakeland, but once he caught up, he tore up the Florida State League with a .356 average in July (compared to .225 in June). His success earned him a late August promotion to High-A West Michigan, a week and a half after his 20th birthday. Keith is athletic for his big frame. He was a two-way talent in high school and drew interest from some clubs as a pitcher. His size hasn’t yet translated into power, but he has a nice line-drive approach and advanced plate discipline for his age thanks in part to a quick, efficient left-handed swing that enables him to wait to commit. His .320 average at Lakeland included a .437 on-base percentage; followed by eight walks in 18 games at West Michigan. He doesn’t chase breaking balls out of the zone often, though he can be challenged by high velocity in the strike zone. He has quick reactions and a strong arm, but will need to continue working to stick at third. Though Keith’s career is off to a nice start at a good level, the Tigers can afford to be patient and let him find his identity as a hitter. He’s in a system deep in third basemen, yet the Tigers will find a place for him if he hits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not only did the Tigers select two Arizona State players in the 2020 Draft, they wooed a recruit away from the Sun Devils when they selected Keith in the fifth round and signed him for a $500,000 bonus. The Gatorade 2019 Mississippi high school player of the year was a two-way talent, with some scouts valuing him more as a pitcher, but the Tigers quickly committed him to third base, a natural move from his high-school spot at shortstop given his body frame. Keith has a line-drive, left-handed swing with bat speed but is expected to develop power as he matures. Some evaluators wonder whether that could come at the cost of more strikeouts. His potential maturation mirrors that of Nick Castellanos, who made a similar transition in the Tigers system after he was a first-round pick as a high-school shortstop in 2010. Keith’s strong pitching arm serves him well in the field, complementing his quick reactions for plus potential defensively. If the hot corner doesn’t work out, his arm could play well in an outfield corner. The Tigers system is deep in third basemen, including several recent Draft picks out of college, but Keith presents a higher upside, especially on offense. Detroit can afford to be patient with him as he just entered his 20s in August.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted as a Trenton (Fla.) HS third baseman in 2020, Langford got just four at-bats as a Florida freshman before destroying college pitching the next two seasons. He topped the Southeastern Conference with 26 homers in 2022 and led NCAA Division I with 28 doubles and 52 extra-base hits in '23, hitting .373/.498/.784 last spring while helping the Gators reach the College World Series finals. Signed for a Rangers-record $8 million as the No. 4 overall pick, he continued to rake in his pro debut, slashing .360/.480/.677 with 10 homers and 12 steals in 44 games while reaching Triple-A. A complete package at the plate, Langford stands out most with his plus-plus power to all fields, which he generates with an easy right-handed stroke that lets him launch balls in the air. By letting his massive strength, electric bat speed and natural loft work for him without swinging for the fences, he makes consistent loud contact and projects as a .280 hitter with 35 or more homers per season. He makes sound swing decisions and controls the strike zone, walking more than he struck out during his college career and his first taste of pro ball. Though he's a good athlete with solid to plus speed, Langford spent most of his college days and his first pro summer in left field. While there's some thought that he could handle center field, Texas has more capable defenders at that position in Leody Taveras and Evan Carter. With fringy to average arm strength, Langford likely will remain in left and should make his presence felt in the big leagues at some point in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scott didn’t break out until his junior season at West Virginia, when he batted .278 with a Mountaineers' record of 38 steals in 55 games. The Cardinals saw plenty to work with, selecting the outfielder in the fifth round in 2022 and signing him for exact slot at $350,400. That faith was rewarded quickly. Scott tied for the Minor League lead with 94 steals between High-A and Double-A in his first full season and led all Cardinals Minor Leaguers with 166 hits while slashing .303/.369/.425 over 618 plate appearances. He kept that train moving with a .286 average and .805 OPS over 23 games in the Arizona Fall League. Scott might be one of the fastest players in all of baseball, regardless of level. He’s always a threat to steal second base the moment he reaches first, and there’s little opposing defenses can do about it. With rule changes meant to encourage movement on the basepaths, Scott has been open about his desire to steal 100 bags, something that hasn’t happened in the Majors since fellow Cardinal Vince Coleman swiped 109 in 1987. Those same wheels make Scott a plus-plus defender in center field, where he tracks down balls in all directions, and he already has a Minor League Gold Glove on his résumé. The left-handed hitter didn’t strike out more than 17 percent of the time at either Minor League stop in 2023. Instead, he pelted line drives through much of the ballpark and even thrived at times by bunting for singles to let his best tool play from the batter’s box. On the negative side, Scott may not hit for much power, especially against lefties (two extra-base hits against LHP in 2023). But his spark in other areas overshadows that drawback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scott hit .222 and .232 respectively as a freshman and sophomore at West Virginia, but showed signs of a well-timed breakout as a junior last year, finishing with a .278/.397/.454 line and six homers in 55 games. His 38 steals broke the WVU single-season record and ranked sixth in Division I for the 2022 campaign. The Cardinals took notice and selected Scott in the fifth round, signing him for exactly slot at $350,400. The outfielder moved to Single-A Palm Beach for 31 games, finishing with a 115 wRC+ and 13 steals in his first go with a full-season affiliate. The son of a pair of collegiate track athletes, the former Mountaineer instantly became one of the fastest, if not the fastest, player in the entire St. Louis system. Statcast measured him with multiple sub-4 home-to-first times in the Florida State League, and he recorded 11 of the 12 highest Sprint Speeds on the Palm Beach basepaths despite his relatively late start. That's carried into his first full season as he's been consistently near the top of the Minor League SB leaderboard all summer. The wheels make him a natural center fielder with tons of range, and he could be a future Gold Glover in center, if given the ample playing time at the top level. Scott struck out more than you’d like to see in college, something he chalked up to getting out of his approach to chase homers, and he's adjusted nicely to more of a line-drive approach with High-A Peoria and Double-A Springfield in 2023. While he used to sell out for power with an uphill swing, he hasn't shown as much pop with the adjustments in the pro game, but that still suits his way of playing just fine. If Scott can hit around .270-.280 with his other skills, he could be a valuable outfield asset for St. Louis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Alexander had a commitment to head from IMG Academy to the University South Carolina in 2018, but the D-backs took him in the 11th round that summer and talked him out of it with a $500,000 signing bonus. His breakout season didn't come until 2022 when he slashed .306/.388/.539 with 17 homers in 88 games at Double-A Amarillo, and when he became Rule 5-eligible that offseason, Arizona added him to its 40-man roster. Alexander suffered a broken right thumb in the first month of the 2023 campaign with Triple-A Reno and returned in June to slash .291/.408/.457 with eight homers over 73 games. That Triple-A slash line masks some of the major concerns in Alexander's offensive profile. His 27.2 percent K rate was already on the high side, and beneath that, he had just a 78.1 zone-contact percentage, lowest among Reno batters with at least 100 plate appearances. He especially struggled on fastballs in the zone, missing on 30 percent of his swings against those, and that'll be a concern moving forward. When he did make contact, he showed above-average raw power, fueling the other numbers. Alexander didn't steal much in '23, but he showed off his speed in other ways, often on bunt attempts and in the field. His plus-plus arm strength makes him a weapon on the dirt, and he has the hands and range for shortstop. With added experience at second and third, Alexander could contribute to Arizona's infield depth in his age-25 campaign, but it's possible his struggles with velo keep those opportunities limited.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Alexander was an 11th-round pick out of the IMG Academy in 2018, but the D-backs showed what they really thought of him by giving him a $500,000 bonus to sign away from his South Carolina commitment. It was a slow road through the lower Minors for the shortstop until 2022, the same year he became Rule 5-eligible. After hitting just .218 with a .688 OPS in 92 games a year earlier, Alexander broke out with a .306/.388/.539 line and 17 homers in 88 games at Double-A Amarillo. He made seven late-season appearances for Triple-A Reno and was added to the 40-man in November. The move to an extremely hitter-friendly environment in Amarillo explained part of the power jump for Alexander in 2022, but he still slugged .446 in Texas League road games. Added strength in his age-23 season had just as much to do with the improvements, and his above-average pop now profiles as his best offensive asset. His strikeout rate dropped seven percentage points, but concerns about his whiffs inside the zone hurt the belief that he'll hit consistently against more advanced arms. Alexander is known to make flashy plays with great hands and movements at shortstop, and his plus-plus arm -- easily his loudest tool -- helps him unleash fireballs across the dirt to erase runners on close plays. Arizona has given him some time at second and third to boost his overall defensive versatility, but he still profiles best at the six. The glove work gets him close to being an everyday player, and his increased pop could push him over the edge as he closes in on the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs took Alexander in the 11th round out of the IMG Academy in 2018 and signed him away from his South Carolina commitment with an above-slot bonus of $500,000. He immediately rewarded the organization with a strong pro debut, slashing .329/.417/.538 across two Rookie levels, and followed it up with a promising, although inconsistent, full-season debut at Class A Kane County in 2019. His lone action of 2020 came during Instructional League, which ended prematurely due to a rib injury. Alexander put on several pounds of muscle prior to the 2021 season and hit a career-high 10 homers with High-A Hillsboro, but his overall numbers were disappointing. He's rebounded nicely in 2022 at Double-A Amarillo, putting himself in line to see Arizona potentially next year. The tools are there, but consistency is a problem for Alexander, who sometimes gets away from his approach and becomes a streaky hitter. His strikeout rate spiked to 32.4% last season, but has settled a little lower than that this season. He has a high ceiling if everything clicks Alexander's best tool is his plus-plus arm, which is possibly the best of any position player in the Arizona system. The arm qualifies him to play anywhere on the diamond and while he's an athletic shortstop with the hands and feel for the position, the D-backs have bounced him around several infield spots over the past few seasons, giving him semi-regular reps at the keystone and also working him at third base. He has the tools and instincts for either of three positions but stands to offer the most value as a shortstop. Alexander flashes all his tools and has impressed with the glove since being drafted. The D-backs feel he can become an everyday shortstop in the future, the key now being experience and reps. If he puts it together on a consistent basis, he could be an average hitter with double-digit home run power at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs took Alexander in the 11th round out of the IMG Academy in 2018 and ultimately were able to sign him away from his South Carolina commitment with an above-slot bonus of $500,000. He immediately rewarded the organization with a strong pro debut, slashing .329/.417/.538 across two Rookie levels, and followed it up with a promising, if inconsistent full-season debut at Class A Kane County in 2019. His lone action of 2020 came during Instructional League which ended prematurely due to a rib injury. Alexander put on several pounds of muscle prior to the 2021 season, which he's spent with High-A Hillsboro. The skills are there, but consistency is a problem at times for Alexander, who sometimes gets away from his approach and becomes a streaky hitter. He has shown an ability to make adjustments and has a high ceiling if everything clicks. Alexander's best took is his plus-plus arm, which is possibly the best of any position player in the Arizona system. The arm qualifies him to play anywhere on the diamond and while he's an athletic shortstop with the hands and feel for the position, the D-backs bounced him around several infield spots in 2019, giving him semi-regular reps at the keystone and also working him at third base. He has the tools and instincts for either of three positions but stands to offer the most value as a shortstop. The D-backs have been pleased with Alexander's defensive progress in 2021 and feel he can become an everyday shortstop in the future. The key now is experience and reps. If he puts it together on a consistent basis, he could be an average hitter with double-digit home run power at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Puerto Rico who grew up in El Paso, Texas, Hernaiz was originally drafted by the Orioles out of Americas High School in the fifth round of the 2019 Draft. The A’s were excited about acquiring him from Baltimore in the Cole Irvin deal in January 2023, and he still somehow managed to exceed expectations in his first year with the organization by combining to hit .321 with nine home runs, 32 doubles and 71 RBIs over 131 games between Double-A and Triple-A. He was in his second big league stint in May when he suffered an ankle injury that kept him sidelined for two months, though he was back with Oakland in August. Hernaiz displays strong bat speed and tremendous bat-to-ball skills with an ability to drive the ball across the field. His homer total was down a bit from the previous year, though the A’s still believe there is more power to be tapped into. He also cut down his strikeouts while upping his walk total. Hernaiz demonstrates a strong competitive nature whenever he takes the field. He only swiped 13 bags last year, but he has shown enough speed in the past to make him a real threat on the basepaths. As good as he’s looked at the plate, his biggest improvement has come on the defensive end, demonstrating qualities that just might keep him at shortstop, though the A’s also like what they have seen from him defensively at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Puerto Rico and growing up in El Paso, Texas, Hernaiz was a fifth-round pick by the Orioles out of Americas High School in the 2019 MLB Draft. Impressed by his tools while scouting him in recent seasons, the A’s were excited about acquiring him from the Orioles in the Cole Irvin deal in January 2023. He built up a good track record of success at each level he played in Baltimore’s system, most recently combining to hit .273 with 12 homers, 21 doubles and 62 RBIs in 105 games across three levels in a 2022 campaign that ended at Double-A. Athleticism is the first thing that stands out about Hernaiz. Last season brought encouraging improvements to his offensive game, as he displayed strong bat speed and a solid ability to make contact, while also tapping into more of his power than he’s shown in the past. Having swiped 32 bags last season, Hernaiz is a real threat on the basepaths. He could use some refining on the defensive end, with an average arm that eventually could lead to him moving off shortstop. With the A’s always placing an emphasis on versatility, he’ll likely see plenty of time at second base and maybe even third in addition to short, depending on other personnel.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Miller one of the Midwest's best high school pitchers in 2016 but also unsingable because he was committed to Stanford, where he became a fourth-round pick of the Phillies three years later. Acquired by the Giants in a January 2023 trade for Yunior Marte, he led all Double-A/Triple-A relievers (minimum: 60 innings) with a .143 opponent average and grabbed a 40-man roster spot in November. He can miss bats with three different plus pitches but can't throw any of them for strikes on a consistent basis. Miller gets his most strikes with a four-seam fastball that added velocity in 2023, sitting at 95-97 mph and reaching 99 with good carry up in the strike zone. His low-80s slider combines horizontal and vertical action and is his best swing-and-miss offering. And both take a back seat to his mid-80s changeup, which plummets at the plate and elicits the most chases. The 6-foot-5, 240-pound Miller is much more physical than athletic and has trouble repeating his stiff delivery. He surrendered more walks (45) than total bases (42) in 62 1/3 innings a year ago and averaged 5.8 walks per nine frames during his first four pro seasons. If he could develop even below-average control, he could be a high-leverage relief option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller was one of the top high school pitchers in the Midwest in 2016 but unsignable because of his commitment to Stanford, where he spent three seasons before signing with the Phillies as a fourth-rounder in 2019. He worked just 97 innings in his first four years as a pro, with his development hindered by the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and shoulder issues in 2021. He remained healthy last season before the Giants acquired him for Yunior Marte in January. A legitimate three-pitch mix gives Miller the chance to start, though he spent most of 2022, and reached Triple-A, pitching out of the bullpen. He tends to sit in the low 90s with the fastball, though he’s up to 97 mph, especially in shorter stints. He’s always had a very good changeup, killing spin with it effectively, and he’s worked to tighten up his breaking ball, a low-80s slider that can miss bats. The biggest thing holding Miller back is his ability to throw strikes. He has worked to incorporate improvements to his delivery, cleaning up his arm stroke, but he still struggled to repeat it and battled his control throughout 2022. He doesn’t have to have pinpoint command to pitch in relief and his stuff should continue to tick up in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: From a pure stuff and size standpoint, Miller was one of the best college lefties in the 2019 Draft class. Concerns about command and reliever risk led to him being the seventh-ranked college southpaw on the Draft Top 200 list and he was the eighth one taken when the Phillies made him their fourth-round selection. The stuff played very well during his summer pro debut as he pitched his way to full-season ball. During his first pro offseason, Miller worked hard on all of his stuff, starting with adding velocity to an already effective fastball. A heater that sat around 93 mph when he entered pro ball, he’s been more around the 95- to 96-mph range, throwing it with a lot of riding life through the zone with a slightly higher arm slot that’s generated above-average spin. His slider is still his best pitch, a put-away breaking ball that misses a ton of bats and he continues to work on developing his changeup, which he does a nice job of killing spin with. Miller has worked on adding a distinct 12-to-6 curve which plays well against right-handed hitters, with the chance for that to be an average pitch eventually. He’s cleaned up his delivery, which has led to more strikes, giving the Phillies more faith in his ability to start long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Rays for $240,000 back in July 2018, Molina progressed slowly through their system, debuting in the Dominican Summer League in '19 and pitching in the Florida Complex League in '21 following the 2020 shutdown. While he was pitching mostly in relief in 2022, he did approach 100 innings across two levels of A ball, then was given an opportunity to start full-time in '23. He piled up 122 frames and reached Triple-A, but when the Rays didn’t protect him on their 40-man roster, the Rockies nabbed him in last December’s Rule 5 Draft. While Molina lacks wow stuff, there might be enough in the tank for him to fit into a big league rotation. His fastball sat around 94 mph last year and touched as high as 97 as he’s added some velocity over time. His changeup is his best secondary offering, a splitter he has enough confidence in to throw at any point in the count that helps neutralize left-handed hitters in particular. His mid-80s slider is fringy, but it has gotten better. Molina has a simple and repeatable delivery, with a clean arm action that points to a future of strike-throwing, and he brings a career 2.2 BB/9 rate into the 2024 season. He could be eased into big league life in a bullpen, but don’t be surprised if he gets a chance to start at some point, a la Brad Keller and the Royals.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of 2014 second overall pick Tyler, Kolek was a three-year pitcher for Texas A&M before the Dodgers grabbed him in the 11th round in 2018. He was traded to the Mariners in April 2021, was a full-time starter at Double-A Arkansas in '22 and then transitioned back to the bullpen in '23, finishing with a 3.76 ERA, 1.21 WHIP and 76 strikeouts in 69 1/3 innings between Arkansas and Triple-A Tacoma (making 44 of his 49 appearances at the latter). The Padres selected the 26-year-old in this offseason’s Rule 5 Draft, giving him a shot to stick as a Major League reliever for the first time. As he pitched exclusively in the bullpen, the 6-foot-3 right-hander saw a nice velocity uptick in 2023 with a pair of fastballs in the 94-96 mph range, topping out close to 98. He prefers the sinker of the two heaters, and the movement on the pitch made him effective at keeping the ball on the ground. His 57.5 percent ground-ball rate was tops among 62 Pacific Coast Leaguer hurlers with at least 60 innings in ’23. His above-average slider also ticked up as the season progressed, going to 83-85 mph with good sweep and depth. Kolek throws an upper-80s changeup that can get too firm but helped hold lefties at bay too. Kolek’s velocity improvements didn’t coincide with a major loss of control as he walked 11.4 percent of his Triple-A batters faced, but that’ll keep him in relief. He’s a sinker-slider righty that is Major League-ready -- a true Rule 5 option -- but he might face a tall task sticking with a hopeful contender in San Diego.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest Maryland high school position player selected since 1986, Merrill went 27th overall to the Padres in 2021 and signed for below slot at $1.8 million. He put himself on the Top 100 radar at Single-A Lake Elsinore the following year despite being limited by wrist and hamstring injuries, and he made up the lost time with an aggressive move to the Arizona Fall League. He got off to a slow start with High-A Fort Wayne in '23 but slashed .310/.342/.474 over his final 50 games with the TinCaps, earning a mid-July bump to Double-A San Antonio. He slashed .273/.338/.444 with 104 wRC+ over 46 games the rest of the way in the Texas League. Batting from the left side, Merrill uses an all-fields approach to pepper the ballpark with base knocks while protecting the plate. He doesn’t whiff often for his age and experience with an 8.1 percent swinging-strike rate that ranked 10th-best among qualified full-season Minor Leaguers aged 20 or younger in 2023. He did a better job of elevating balls last season, cutting down his ground-ball rate from 59.6 percent to 42.5, and that helps the belief that he’ll settle into above-average power later in his 20s. Merrill is on the taller side for shortstop at 6-foot-3 but has improved his quickness enough in pro ball to help the belief that he can stick at shortstop. However, as Merrill climbed into the upper levels, San Diego gave him looks at second base, left field and even one start at first to see if he can get out of the shadow of more options at short. He is expected to move around more because of his proximity to the bigs. That underlines how much belief the club has in the bat and how quickly Merrill could move in his age-21 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Merrill became the highest Maryland high-school position player selected since 1986 when he went 27th overall to the Padres in the 2021 Draft. After signing for below slot at $1.8 million, the left-handed hitter produced a solid .722 OPS in the Arizona Complex League that summer and was showing major signs of a breakout with Single-A Lake Elsinore (.325/.387/.482), though wrist and hamstring injuries limited him to only 45 games in the California League. San Diego made an aggressive move in sending the 19-year-old to the Arizona Fall League, and Merrill responded by being one of the most talked about prospects in the advanced loop, despite modest numbers. On the taller side for a shortstop at 6-foot-3, Merrill showed a promising mix of discipline and an all-fields approach in the early stages of his career and took those to the next level everywhere he played in 2022. To prove the point, his pull (38.5 percent) and opposite-field (39.1) rates were nearly equal at Lake Elsinore. He should still add muscle as he matures and could grow into above-average power at his Major League peak, especially if he starts to elevate batted balls more. While it was once a question of if Merrill would have to move off short someday, he’s improved his lateral quickness enough to erase those concerns, and San Diego officials were often wowed at how much his arm strength improved in his first full season. The next step will be keeping Merrill on the field for a full campaign after last year’s injury concerns, and if he does that, the Padres could be even more ecstatic that he was the big-name prospect they kept around following the Juan Soto blockbuster trade.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prior to Merrill, there had been just two high school position players from Maryland who have been drafted in the top five rounds this century, outfielders Troy Stokes Jr. in 2014 and Matt McPhearson in 2013, both taken in the fourth round. Merrill became the highest pick of that group when San Diego called his name 27th overall in 2021. Merrill passed on his Kentucky commitment and signed for below slot value at $1.8 million and then put together a solid professional debut, slashing .280/.339/.383 with nine extra-base hits over 31 games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. A 6-foot-3, left-handed-hitting infielder, Merrill has a good feel for hitting and some power that he’ll grow into as he continues to develop. He improved his timing at the plate last summer and utilizes the whole field when he’s in the box. He can have more of an inside-out swing at times and will have to learn how to turn on pitches to get to his power more consistently. While there’s a chance Merrill could outgrow shortstop and eventually move to second or third, the Padres do plan on keeping him at shortstop for the time being. With an above-average arm and soft hands, Merrill has the tools needed to stick at shortstop. The organization has also been impressed with his maturity and mental makeup as he’s drawn strong reviews for his work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres drafted Pauley in the 13th round in 2022, his only season as a full-time starter at Duke, then watched him lead their system in batting (.308), slugging (.539), OPS (.931) and homers (23) while reaching Double-A in his first full pro season. He continued to impress in the Arizona Fall League that offseason and made San Diego's Opening Day roster last March, though he looked overwhelmed in the big leagues while going 4-for-32 with 15 strikeouts. He never heated up following a demotion to Triple-A, or even after the Marlins sent him to Double-A after acquiring him in the Tanner Scott/Bryan Hoeing trade in July. During his breakout year in 2023, Pauley made consistent contact with a compact, smooth left-handed stroke with loft and looked like a high-average hitter who would get to most of his solid raw power. He became less disciplined last season and did little damage against non-fastballs. His ability to launch balls to his pull side still could translate into 20-homer pop, but he needs to let it come naturally and let his swing do the work for him. Pauley has to hit because he's a below-average runner with fringy arm strength and questionable defensive value. He doesn't have the agility or arm for third base, his primary position, and also saw time at second base, first base and the outfield corners last year. The most realistic hope is that he becomes an adequate first baseman or left fielder, though those positions will put more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pauley didn’t become a full-time starter for Duke until his junior year, and he was still somewhat of an afterthought heading into the 2022 Draft before going in the 13th round to the Padres. In his first full pro season, he led San Diego farmhands in batting (.308), slugging (.538), OPS (.931), hits (148) and homers (23). He hasn't been as productive in 2024, though he made his big league debut in March before getting sent to the Marlins four months later as part of the Tanner Scott/Bryan Hoeing trade. The left-handed slugger has a short and sweet swing that’s helped him make a healthy amount of contact since his collegiate days. Midway through last year, Pauley began to prioritize elevating the ball more on contact with a swing change meant to cut down on over-rotation and increase the amount of time his bat stayed in the strike zone. The result was a motion that added loft and allowed the pop to truly play to the pull side, and it’s easier to project Pauley getting to average power in the Majors. Signed as a third baseman, Pauley has below-average speed and fringy arm strength that limit his effectiveness with the glove. Before the deal, he spent 2024 dividing his time between the hot corner, second base, first base and left field. He's a below-average defender at third and second and may not have the bat to profile as a regular at first or in left, so he may be destined for a reserve role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jensen battled the strike zone for two seasons at Fresno State before winning the Mountain West Conference pitcher of the year and tournament MVP awards in 2019. Though he had one of the best fastballs in that year's Draft, he wasn't a consensus first-round talent, but the Cubs selected him 27th overall and signed him for a below-slot $2 million. He has had only sporadic success as a pro starter and spent six weeks in the middle of the 2022 season changing his mechanics at the club's training base in Arizona. Jensen owns one of the harder two-seam fastballs in the Minors, operating at 94-96 mph and reaching 98 with power sink, and he trusts it more than a four-seamer with more velocity and less life that gets rocked when he doesn't keep it up in the zone. He has yet to find a reliable complement to his heater, with his low-80s curveball serving as his second-best pitch last year. He also has an upper-80s slider and changeup, but the latter lacks movement, and he doesn't throw either for strikes. After shortening his arm action and stride and reworking how he uses his lower half in his delivery, Jensen gained a tick more velocity, but his secondary pitches still weren't effective, and he still struggled with his control and command. Chicago still believed in him enough to add him to the 40-man roster last November, but it may be time to move him to the bullpen. His path to the big leagues is as a fastball-heavy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jensen struggled to throw strikes in his first two seasons at Fresno State before dominating in his third, winning the Mountain West Conference's pitcher of the year and tournament MVP awards in 2019. Though he was not a consensus first-round talent, the Cubs selected him 27th overall that June and signed him for a below-slot $2 million. He has continued to showcase power stuff and inconsistent control and command in pro ball while reaching Double-A at the end of his first full pro season in 2021. Jensen throws his two-seam fastball with atypical velocity, working at 94-96 mph and topping out at 98 with quality sink, and he trusts it more than a harder four-seamer that lacks life and gets pounded when he doesn't locate it up in the zone. His slider has gotten harder and sharper in pro ball, sitting in the mid-80s and touching 90 mph, and he has added a low-80s curveball to give him a softer option with more downer break. He's still refining a mid-80s changeup with fairly ordinary life. The Cubs still believe Jensen can translate his athleticism into enough control and command to be an effective starter. But he also has a funky delivery with a lot of moving parts that he struggles to keep in sync, preventing him from locating his pitches where he wants on a consistent basis. Most scouts outside of the organization believe he's destined for the bullpen, where he could focus on his fastball and slider and perhaps become a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After recording a 5.84 ERA while battling the strike zone in his first two seasons at Fresno State, Jensen dominated in 2019, winning his final nine starts en route to Mountain West Conference pitcher of the year and tournament MVP awards. He wasn't a consensus first-round talent but the Cubs made him the first Bulldogs arm selected that high since Matt Garza in 2005, signing him for a below-slot $2 million as the 27th overall pick. He comes with a good deal of upside but also a hefty amount of reliever risk. Jensen had the best fastball in the 2019 college class, working with sinking two-seamers and riding four-seamers while sitting in the mid-90s deep into games and peaking in the upper 90s. At Fresno State, he relied heavily on his heaters and his slider, an 82-85 mph offering that got sharper when he altered his grip midway through his junior season. The Cubs have had him develop a curveball with more depth to play off his four-seamer and also have encouraged him to use his changeup more often. Jensen's long-term role and success will come down to his ability to throw strikes. Chicago believes his quality athleticism will translate into control and command and enable him to remain a starter, though he averaged 4.2 walks per nine innings in college (2.4 as a junior) and issued 14 free passes in his 12-inning pro debut. Scouts outside the organization believe his long arm action and the effort in his delivery eventually will land him in the bullpen, where he could become a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gómez has gone from a $40,000 signing with the Rays out of Venezuela in April 2015 to a player on a 40-man roster entering 2023, albeit for a different organization. The right-handed slugger first showed signs of a breakout with his 19-homer season at Single-A Bowling Green in 2019, but severe strikeout issues at higher levels led to his release by Tampa Bay in October 2021. St. Louis signed Gómez as a Minor League free agent and he promptly became the Minor League leader in home runs with 39 between Double-A and Triple-A. The Cardinals protected him from the Rule 5 Draft (and additional free agency) with the 40-man add in November. Gómez always posted some of the best exit velocities in the Rays system when he made contact, and both the player and St. Louis coaches got to work on tamping down some of the moving parts of his swing (namely a large leg kick) to get that double-plus raw pop to play in games. The proof was certainly in the pudding with the way he slugged .705 at Springfield and .541 in Memphis. That said, Gómez still sold out for power too often, leading to a 34.7 percent K rate -- highest among Cardinals qualifiers. Though he was signed as a center fielder, the 24-year-old has slowed out of the position and now profiles in the corners, where he’s still a below-average defender. A strong arm helped him earn nine assists from right field in 2022. Now with his best Major League chance ever, Gómez profiles as a potential right-handed power bat off the bench who can wow crowds with moonshots and frustrate them with punchouts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Rosa signed for $300,000 in July 2018, and the Dominican Republic native was already impressing in instructs that fall. He later got another advanced assignment when he was included in the club’s alternate training site at just 18 years old in 2020. He slashed .315/.394/.505 with 10 homers in 69 games at Single-A Fredericksburg in 2022 and after he got a dip at High-A Wilmington, he was added to Washington’s 40-man roster as Rule 5 protection. That roster spot lasted one year. De La Rosa slashed just .240/.324/.361 with seven homers in 93 games back in Wilmington last season and was outrighted off the 40-man in November. The left-handed slugger is capable of showing off above-average raw power in batting practice sessions, and he’ll run into the occasional high-end exit velocity, thanks to the strength in his 6-foot, 215-pound frame. Notably, he was a victim of Wilmington’s hitting graveyard, slugging .288 there compared to .422 on the road in 2023. But his bat path -- starting from a semi-open stance -- needs to be better geared for loft. Instead, it led to a majority of ground balls, and that’s when he made contact, factoring in his 33.7 percent strikeout rate. De La Rosa still runs decently well, and he’s workable in center field. However, he played more games than ever in right field in 2023 because of his organization’s logjam in the middle of the grass, and his arm can work there. De La Rosa is still only entering his age-22 season, so he has time to make adjustments, but he’s already been on the wrong end of roster churn once.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just a $300,000 signing out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018, De La Rosa has impressed Nationals officials at nearly every stop, earning advanced assignments to instructs in fall 2018 and the alternate training site in the lost 2020 campaign. After a down age-19 season in 2021, the left-handed slugger showed promise by hitting .315/.394/.505 with 10 homers over 69 games back at Single-A Fredericksburg. He suffered a broken hamate at High-A Wilmington, and his numbers plummeted (.195/.273/.271), but the non-injured portion was enough to get him added to Washington’s 40-man when he first became Rule 5-eligible last November. Batting from an open stance, De La Rosa does a good job of staying back on balls, and his Single-A strikeout rate notably improved from 34.1 percent to 24.8 in his return to the Carolina League. Even while he struggled with the hamate, he still only punched out 27.8 percent of the time with Wilmington, though that trend has reversed course in 2023. De La Rosa has long shown above-average raw power, and it started to play even more in games in 2022 (see the .505 slugging), even if he still puts the ball on the ground more than most would like at this stage. A plus runner who swiped 39 total bags last year, the 21-year outfielder has gotten the majority of his looks in center field, where he covers ample ground. The trouble is that the Nats are becoming more and more loaded in the middle of the grass, and he may get squeezed to a corner. Though Wilmington is a notorious tough place to hit, De La Rosa has to get back on track offensively or else risk getting lost in Washington's increasingly deep pool of outfielders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Rosa wasn’t a huge name when the Nationals signed him for $300,000 in July 2018 but has shown a strong base level of skills in the close to four years since. Washington liked him enough to send him to American instructs the same year he signed and then to the Gulf Coast League in 2019. At 18, he was one of the Nats’ youngest alternate-training-site participants in 2020 and moved back to Fredericksburg for Low-A play last summer. Even the Nats would agree that may have been a bit too aggressive for the 19-year-old, and De La Rosa backed that up by hitting just .209/.279/.316 with five homers and a 34.1 percent K rate in 87 games with the FredNats. De La Rosa’s scuffles at the plate were mostly approach-based in 2021. Once the strikeouts began to pile up because of chased pitches, the youngster became perhaps too passive and sat back on pitches he could drive. It’s a seesaw battle that many teenaged hitters wage, and without being able to fall back on a non-complex short-season club to find success, De La Rosa rode that up-and-down for much of the summer. The good news is that the raw tools remained in place, and he’s enjoyed a much more productive 2022 back at Fredericksburg and at High-A Wilmington. The left-handed slugger still shows above-average raw power to all fields, and decent speed is an asset he puts to use in center field, where he gets the bulk of his looks. The Nationals came away from De La Rosa’s first taste of full-season ball enthused by his reaction to the lows of the game. He showed strong makeup by acknowledging struggles are part of a budding career and still acted like a leader as the season wore on in Fredericksburg. His rebound in 2022 has gotten him right back on track to be a piece of Washington’s brighter future

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals went a bit under the radar when they signed De La Rosa out of the Dominican Republic for $300,000 in July 2018 and have been fairly aggressive with his assignments ever since. He moved stateside for instructs in his signing year, then played 26 games in the Gulf Coast League in 2019, when many others of his class were in the Dominican Summer League. The 5-foot-11 outfielder played at the alternate site in Fredericksburg last year, during what would have been his age-18 season. De La Rosa’s swing from the left side remains a work in progress, particularly when it comes to getting his hands into position early, but the pieces are there for a solid hit tool. The bat speed produces impressive raw power that can go all over the field, and that should show up more in games as he grows older. His speed is also above-average at present, giving him a promising mix on the offensive side. That run tool helps him in center, where he typically tracks down balls well. But if he needs to move to a corner, the rest of his profile shouldn't make that a problem. The Nats like to challenge De La Rosa because he can show solid tools across the board. All the pieces are there for a solid-hitting outfielder, regardless of exact placement on the grass, and his time against advanced competition at the alternate site in 2020 should help him reach that ceiling moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Many pegged Cronin as a potential quick mover when the Nationals selected the former two-year Arkansas closer in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft. The canceled 2020 campaign got in the way of the southpaw’s first full season, and then he was limited to 30 innings in 2021, in part due to a non-arm-related health issue. Ten walks in 11 1/3 Double-A innings didn’t help matters. Back to being fully healthy, Cronin returned with 14 scoreless appearances at Harrisburg before finishing out with a 3.53 ERA and 34 K’s in 35 2/3 innings at Triple-A Rochester. The 6-foot-2 left-hander’s velocity has backed up a little bit to the low 90s, but it still plays well with good vertical break and spin efficiency. Though he isn’t a commanding size on the mound, Cronin’s high-slot delivery can make it seem like he’s putting the ball right on top of hitters. He shows good feel for spin with an upper-70s, 11-to-5 curveball that can keep opponents off the fastball, while his low-80s changeup provides a third option. Cronin isn’t a typical lefty reliever -- he sported fairly even splits between righties (.174 average, .542 OPS) and lefties (.216 average, .581 OPS) in 2022. He can still run into occasional bouts of wildness, but his control actually improved as 2022 wore on. Having been added to the 40-man roster in November, Cronin is a high-floor bullpen arm who won’t need much seasoning in Rochester before getting his chance to help the Washington relief corps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cronin was dominant in all three seasons at Arkansas and took over the closer’s role for the Razorbacks in his final two years on campus. He finished with 16 saves, a 2.08 ERA and 91 strikeouts in 52 collegiate innings before the Nationals selected him in the 2019 fourth round, a rarity for a relief-only talent. He continued his strong run of form at Low-A Hagerstown (0.82 ERA, 41 K in 22 innings) that summer before taking his 2020 work to the alternate site and instructs. Cronin moved quickly from High-A to Double-A last season but hit a wall with control in Harrisburg and missed six weeks with a non-arm-related health issue. The 6-foot-2 left-hander’s present and future in the bullpen is clear based on his arsenal. His heater comes in the mid-90s and earns extra points for its vertical break and spin efficiency. It can be a truly explosive pitch on its own. His 12-to-6 curveball shows promising depth and can flash plus when he locates it. A split-change is a distant third pitch and won’t be what pushes the southpaw to Washington. Cronin ran into control issues with Harrisburg (10 walks in 11 1/3 innings) against more patient Double-A hitters. Landing the curve in the strike zone will become even more important at the upper levels or else batters will be able to take lengthy free passes/feast on the heaters. The two pitches alone give the former Razorback true late-inning potential, but it hasn’t been as quick a trip to the Majors as may have been expected when Cronin first entered the system three years ago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Relief-only types have to show something special to go in the first five rounds of the Draft, and that’s exactly what Cronin accomplished at Arkansas before the Nats took him in the fourth round in 2019. The 6-foot-2 southpaw recorded 26 saves in his final two years on campus and fanned 101 batters in 77 1/3 innings over that span. He didn’t miss a beat in the pro ranks, posting a 0.82 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 41 K’s in 22 frames at Class A Hagerstown the summer of his Draft year. Cronin pitched at both the alternate site and instructs in 2020. The former Razorback is a classic two-pitch bullpen arm who could move quickly when regular play resumes. The heater comes in at the mid-90s, and he’s able to rely on it heavily because of a 20-inch vertical break and perfect spin efficiency. Those latter aspects are what give the offering explosive life. The 12-to-6 curveball gives another impressive look because of its depth, though Cronin has needed to focus on throwing it more in the strike zone. He has also worked on a split-change that the Nats admit he’ll likely use sparingly. Control, in general, will remain a point of emphasis – as is typical of relievers – after Cronin walked 11 of the 85 batters he faced in Class A two years ago. Cronin’s two best pitches are nearly as Major League-ready as any you’ll find on a pitcher two years out of the Draft – his fastball especially. He has late-game upside in the back of a traditional Nationals bullpen or could be used earlier in bigger spots. Barring any significant setbacks, his stay in the Minors could be a short one.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gómez made his big league debut at the end of 2023, seven years after signing for $50,000 out of Venezuela. He spent most of his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball before losing 2020 to the pandemic and most of 2021 to shoulder and elbow issues, with the latter requiring internal brace surgery that August. He also missed time with shoulder tendinitis in 2023 but stayed healthy throughout last year, working a career-high 95 2/3 innings and spending three short stints in New York. Gómez mixes five different pitches and relies heavily on his two solid offerings, a low-90s fastball that tops out at 96 and plays better than its velocity thanks to its carry and the elite extension in his delivery and a sweeping low-80s slider. He also spins a downer curveball at 79-82 mph and a mid-80s cutter, both of which grade as average. His upper-80s changeup has some fade but is too firm and lags behind the rest of his arsenal. With his velocity and spin rates decreasing a bit in recent years -- he touched 98 mph before his elbow surgery -- Gómez lacks a true plus pitch. His control has slipped a bit as well, and he never has been especially durable. He probably fits best now as a multi-inning reliever in the big leagues, with the possibility of regaining some power if he pitches in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, Gómez pitched just 277 innings in the next seven years, including two with the Yankees last September. He spent most of his first three seasons as a pro in Rookie ball, lost 2020 to the pandemic and has battled arm issues since. He had shoulder issues in early 2021, tore the ulnar collateral ligament in his elbow and required internal brace surgery that August and missed the first two months of last season with shoulder tendinitis. Gómez's fastball sits at 92-94 mph and tops out at 97 with some riding action and carry that keep it off barrels. His most effective secondary offering is his 78-82 mph curveball, though he uses it a lot less than his 83-85 mph sweeping slider and upper-80s cutter. He'll throw an occasional changeup to left-handers, but it's too firm in the upper 80s and features just mild fade. Gómez's velocity and spin rates have ticked down a bit in the last couple of years, leaving him without a true plus pitch. His control has regressed too, and outside of his cutter he doesn't have a secondary pitch that he reliably can land for strikes. He once flashed mid-rotation upside but now looks more like a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $50,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, Gómez spent most of his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball before losing 2020 to the pandemic. He dealt with shoulder issues early in 2021 and had a torn ulnar collateral ligament in his elbow repaired with an internal brace that August, but he returned last June and finished the year with a crucial victory in the Double-A Eastern League Finals to help Somerset win the championship. He missed the first two months of this season with shoulder issues. Gómez spins the ball exceptionally well, creating quality carry on a fastball that ranged from 92-96 mph last year and has touched 98 in the past. His feel for spin extends to his breaking pitches, a sweeping 82-85 mph slider that grades as plus at its best and a 79-82 mph curveball that can be a solid offering. His upper-80s changeup has some fade but needs more velocity separation from his heater. Gómez looked rusty last year and his control and command haven't returned to where they were before his elbow surgery. His delivery hasn't been as tight and repeatable, and the Yankees hope he'll return to the best version of himself when he's fully healthy. He worked a total of just 209 2/3 innings in his first six seasons as a pro -- and never more than 56 1/3 in a single year -- so there are questions about his ability to hold up as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela as a projection right-hander in 2016, Gomez spent almost all of his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball. The Yankees still added him to their 40-man roster after he lost 2020 to the pandemic shutdown and kept him on there after he worked just 23 2/3 innings in 2021, when he had shoulder troubles early in the season and elbow surgery in August. Despite his lack of development opportunities, he still has the best feel for pitching among New York's international pitching prospects. Gomez has added about 5 mph to his fastball since signing and now operates at 92-95 mph and peaks at 98 with high spin rates that create a lot of carry and riding action. He also generates plenty of spin on his breaking pitches, and his 82-85 mph slider has supplanted his 79-82 mph curveball as his best secondary offering. He trusts his fading changeup but it needs more consistency. Gomez is doing a better job of repeating his clean delivery as he gets stronger. He throws strikes but needs more innings in order to polish his command. He returned to the mound in June and still has mid-rotation upside, though he has to prove his durability after never pitching more than 56 1/3 innings in a single year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest bargain in the Yankees' 2016 international crop, Gomez signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela as a projection right-hander. He spent almost all of his first three pro seasons in Rookie ball, skipping a level to jump to low Class A at the end of 2019. New York didn't invite him to its alternate site and didn't hold instructional league in 2020, crimping his opportunity for development last year, but did add him to its 40-man roster in November. Gomez has gained about 5 mph on his fastball since turning pro and usually deals at 92-95 mph and peaks at 97. His heater plays better than its velocity because its high spin rates create riding action and his size and high three-quarters delivery produce downhill plane. He also generates plenty of spin on a hard curveball that's his best pitch, has added a low-80s slider in 2021 and already has learned to trust his fading changeup. Gomez has better feel for pitching than any of the Yankees' top pitching prospects. He has a clean delivery and is doing a better job of repeating it as he adds strength. He's on track to have three solid or better pitches with similar control and command, and he still has projection remaining in his lanky frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bowlan followed in his dad’s footsteps and went to the University of Memphis, pitching his way into the second round of the Royals’ pitching-heavy 2018 Draft. His dad, Mark, was a 19th-round pick by the Cardinals in 1989. Jonathan was on a fast track to the big leagues in 2021 until Tommy John surgery stopped him. He returned at the end of ‘22 to make nine starts in Double-A, but his stuff wasn’t all the way back, which the Royals expected after elbow surgery. He’s fully healthy now and on the 40-man roster. Bowlan has a massive mound presence standing at 6-foot-6, with broad shoulders and an imposing frame. Before his surgery, he was an extreme strike thrower, pounding the zone with his 95 mph fastball that speeds up on hitters down in the zone. His 87-89 mph breaking ball tunnels well with his fastball, and his changeup continues to improve. All of his pitches played up before the surgery because he was so aggressive in the strike zone and uses his long extension down the mound to his advantage. Now that he doesn’t have an injury holding him back, the Royals believe he’ll get back to that style of pitcher. Before his surgery, Bowlan was tearing up Double-A. If his stuff comes back in 2023, he’ll likely get back on that track. The Royals truly see him as a starter in their future because of his pitch mix and physicality. If he can stay healthy and get back in the zone, he could see time in Kansas City this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mark Bowlan was a star pitcher at the University of Memphis and 19th-round pick by the Cardinals in 1989, spending two years in pro ball. Three decades later, his son Jonathan followed in his footsteps to Memphis and pitched his way into the second round of the Royals’ college pitching-heavy 2018 Draft. In 2021, the right-hander was on the fast track to the Major League rotation when he suffered an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. He returned to the mound in mid-June and reached Double-A again by the end of July. An extreme strike-thrower, Bowlan was off to an impressive start in Double-A last season, posting a 1.59 ERA with 25 strikeouts in 17 innings. His star offering is his 93-96 mph fastball that has deception and can be sneaky quick because of his imposing 6-foot-6 frame. His low-80s slider tunnels well with his late-breaking fastball, and his changeup continues to improve as a solid offering in his arsenal as a starter. The biggest change for Bowlan in ’21 was the addition of a curveball that has potential, giving hitters a different look than his slider. Bowlan commands the ball extremely well with a clean delivery, which allows all his pitches to play up as he gets aggressive in the strike zone. If Bowlan can stay healthy after his surgery, the Royals truly see him as a starter in their future. Officials rave about his makeup and work ethic, which should help during rehab. If Bowlan can’t stick as a starter, his physicality and weapons would fit well in a big league bullpen. His command hasn’t been great coming off the rehab, but the Royals expect him to return to form by 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Mark Bowlan, a star pitcher at the University of Memphis and a 19th-round pick by the Cardinals in 1989, Jonathan also attended Memphis and pitched his way into the second round of the 2018 Draft, the last of five consecutive college arms the Royals took that year. The big right-hander had a breakout year in 2019, with a 150/23 K/BB rate and a nine-inning no-hitter on July 15 at Class A Advanced Wilmington. Bowlan was a late addition to the Royals' alternate training site in 2020 before taking part in instructional league at Kauffman Stadium. He made four impressive starts at Double-A Northwest Arkansas to open 2021 before suffering an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. He will miss the remainder of the 2021 season and at least part of 2022 as a result. Bowlan, whose 6-foot-6 frame is imposing on the mound, is an extreme strike thrower, pounding the zone with all three of his pitches. He has a plus fastball, which sits at 92-95 mph and can be sneaky quick, getting on hitters more deceptively. His low-80s slider tunnels well with the fastball, has some cutter action to it and will flash plus with tilt and a late break to it, though he needs to work on the consistency of the pitch. Bowlan’s changeup was a major focus of his work in 2020, developing into a solid offering in his arsenal as a starter. His command is excellent, and while he’s learning how to throw inside to right-handers better, he can throw the down-and-away strike as well as anyone in the Royals system. Bowlan might seem more under the radar compared to the pitchers who went higher than him in his Draft class, but the Royals truly see him as a starter in their future. Officials rave about his makeup. Still, much will depend upon his return from Tommy John. If Bowlan is unable to stick as a starter, his fastball-slider combination and physicality would fit well in a big league bullpen, where his stuff could play up in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2017-18 international signing period was coming to a close, the Angels took a low-risk flier on Caceres, signing him for $10,000 in May 2018. Working as a starter and reliever at the outset, he did little to distinguish himself at Rookie-level stops in 2018 and '19, nor did he make much noise when he returned to competitive action following the pandemic in '21. Things started to click a bit with a full-time move to the bullpen in 2022, and after being left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft that offseason, he pitched his way from High-A to the big leagues in '23. While Caceres does have three pitches, he’s definitely a reliever-only now. It’s a power arm from a small, but strong frame, starting with a fastball that sits around 95 mph and touches 99. He has both a four- and two-seamer, the latter of which can get groundball outs. His out pitch is his hard 82-84 mph curve, but he also misses bats with his 88-89 mph changeup. Caceres’ command did improve in 2023, but that’s still a work in progress after he gave up 5.3 walks per nine in the Minors. He doesn’t need pinpoint control to be an effective big league reliever -- something that could happen this year with more ease now that he’s on the roster. If he can find the strike zone a little bit more consistently, his power stuff could help get some high-leverage outs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Veneziano has had a rollercoaster of a professional career ever since the Royals drafted him in the 10th round in 2019 out of Coastal Carolina. The pandemic eliminated his first full season, and he was a breakout player in ‘21, when he struck out 127 batters in 93 2/3 innings for High-A Quad Cities. Then he got out of whack in ‘22 with a 5.72 ERA at Double-A Northwest Arkansas. Veneziano got back on track last year and was one pitcher who really benefited from the Royals’ revamped pitching department. He started his 2023 season in Double-A and ended it with 2.1 innings in the Majors. Veneziano’s walk rate dropped to three percent in Double-A last year while his strikeout rate jumped to 28.4 percent. He was challenged more in Triple-A, in part because of the ABS system, but he posted a 4.22 ERA in 18 games (17 starts). Veneziano is 6-foot-5 with long limbs, which helps the deception on his 92-94 mph fastball. He pairs that with an 82-85 mph tight, gyro slider -- still his best out pitch. He worked hard on his 85-87 mph above-average changeup, especially on establishing the velocity separation. This spring, he came into camp with a new ‘slurve,’ that sometimes looks like a sweeper. It’s a get-me-over pitch that he can drop in for strikes, especially against right-handed batters. Veneziano can get out of his three-quarters-slot delivery at times, and cleaning that up helped him immensely last year. Fighting for an Opening Day roster spot, Veneziano built up as a starter this spring, but he's been used in a variety of roles during the season -- a starter, multi-inning reliever, one-inning arm. Considering he turns 27 in September, the southpaw is seeing the clock tick on his time as a rotation option for Kansas City, be his overall stuff could still be helpful in other ways.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A year after Coastal Carolina won the College World Series in 2016, Veneziano joined the program and saw things start to click during the playoffs of his sophomore year. His Draft stock increased during his junior year, and the Royals took him in the 10th round of the 2019 Draft. After spending 2020 working out at his home in New Jersey, Veneziano broke out in ’21 for High-A Quad Cities, posting a 3.75 ERA in 93 2/3 innings and striking out a whopping 127 batters.
