At 6-foot-5 and 205 pounds, Veneziano is deceptive on the mound and elevates his fastball, which saw a burst in velocity over last season, averaging 94-95 mph with late life and at times hitting 98-100 mph. Working off his fastball, he possesses an above-average slider that gets whiffs and an average changeup that is a major focus for improvement this season. Tall and lanky, Veneziano had some kinks in his delivery to work out last season, mainly not dropping his front arm and staying loaded in his back leg so he could drive through the baseball. He saw it all click around June and took off from there as one of the bigger surprises of the Royals’ Minor League season. There’s no denying what Veneziano showed as a starter last season, so he will continue on that track for now. While he did throw more strikes in ’21 and was able to repeat it, lack of fastball command as a power lefty could eventually drive him to the bullpen, especially if he doesn’t develop that changeup. But even then, a 100-mph throwing lefty would certainly be welcomed in the big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming off a strong year as South Florida’s closer in 2021, scouts were excited to see what Kerkering could do as a starter in 2022. It might have worked to the Phillies’ benefit that the transition didn’t go well and the right-hander returned to the bullpen, enabling them to select him in the fifth round of that year's Draft. His brief pro debut that summer did nothing to prepare anyone for what was to come in his first full season, when Kerkering pitched across all four levels of the Minors, landed in the big league bullpen in September and made seven postseason appearances. Kerkering is already staking a claim to be a true Slider Monster at the highest level. The upper-80s sweeper routinely registers an rpm north of 3,000. It missed bats at every single level, including in the big leagues, registering a 45 percent miss rate from Double-A on up. He threw the breaking ball a lot more than his fastball, especially once he reached Philadelphia, but that doesn’t mean his heater isn’t also a weapon. That pitch with sink flirted with triple digits and elicited a 29 percent miss rate at those same levels. The stuff is good enough to get hitters out in The Show, but Major Leaguers have not yet seen the above-average command of a slider-fastball combination that will make him more than just any old reliever. That, combined with deception in his delivery and the mentality of wanting the ball in tough situations, gives him the chance to eventually pitch in the back of a bullpen and close out games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his first two years at South Florida, Kerkering pitched out of the Bulls’ bullpen, closing games effectively in 2021. He got a chance to start on Friday nights and broke out of the gate well, but returned to relief work when things went sideways. The Phillies were able to add him to their system with an under-slot bonus of $322,500 as their fifth-rounder in the 2022 Draft and he made his brief pro debut, mostly with Single-A Clearwater, last summer. The right-hander’s velocity fluctuated during his final year at South Florida depending on what role he was in. In shorter stints, he can be expected to be consistently in the mid-90s and he’s been working on the playability of his fastball so it’s not as hittable as it has been at times. He has what might end up being one of the best sliders in the system. It has the chance to be consistently plus, with high spin rates, feel to shape it, and the ability to land it in the zone and get hitters to chase it. He does have a mid-80s changeup he doesn’t use as much, but it could be an option against left-handed hitters. Pitching solely from the stretch, Kerkering’s stuff plays up because of deception in his delivery and his ability to hide the ball well. He’s improved his strike-throwing ability and he doesn’t need pinpoint command to serve in what is likely to be a relief role long term. He’ll get the chance to be a multi-inning guy in his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Caminero signed with Cleveland in July 2019, but because of the pandemic, he didn’t debut in the Dominican Summer League until two years later, slashing .295/.380/.534 with nine homers in 43 games. Tampa Bay acquired him for Tobias Myers in a 40-man-clearing move in November 2021, and Caminero's breakout came in a big way during his age-19 season in 2023. His 31 homers between High-A and Double-A tied for sixth-most in the Minors (no other teenager hit more than 24). His .591 slugging percentage ranked fifth among MiLB full-season qualifiers, and his .324 average placed 11th. The Rays called up Caminero from Montgomery on Sept. 22 and kept him on their postseason roster as a bench bat. Starting from an open stance, the right-handed slugger routinely unloads on pitches of all kinds (especially fastballs) with exit velocities that would pop up Major League leaderboards right now, nevermind ones adjusted for age. It’s near top-of-the-scale power that plays to all fields -- eight of his 20 Double-A homers went the other way to right -- and it’s a big reason why Tampa Bay wanted him nearby in the playoffs. His plate discipline also improved as he climbed the ladder, and that, combined with his loud contact, should help him be a plus overall hitter, too. A fringy runner, Caminero moved from shortstop to third base more full-time in 2023, and Tampa Bay officials were enthused by how he improved his reactions at the hot corner as the season wore on. He has enough arm for either spot on the left side and should be at least average defensively. Caminero’s bat is what gives him such an elite ceiling, however, and he should be a talent the Rays make room for, even with an already loaded infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays followed a familiar playbook to land Caminero. To resolve a roster crunch before the deadline to protect eligible prospects from the Rule 5 Draft, they traded a nearly MLB-ready pitcher and in return targeted a young infielder with little experience outside of complex-league ball. That’s how they acquired Curtis Mead from the Phillies, and it’s how they snagged Caminero from Cleveland in exchange for right-handed pitcher Tobias Myers in November 2021. Signed by the Guardians in 2019 out of the Dominican Republic, Caminero almost immediately proved to be another hidden gem following Mead’s path into the upper tier of a loaded Tampa Bay system. Only 19 at the start of the 2023 season, Caminero possesses elite bat speed that generates a ton of power to his pull side and impressive bat-to-ball ability that allows hard line-drive contact to all fields. His plus raw power led to 11 homers over 62 games as he hit .314/.384/.498 between the Rookie-level FCL Rays (where he was the organization’s team MVP) and Single-A Charleston in 2022, but there may be more over-the-fence production coming as he continues to grow. Evaluators rave about his offensive traits and mature feel for what he’s doing in the batter’s box, painting the picture of a potentially special bat. Caminero’s best spot defensively is third base, where he spent most of his time in his first season with the Rays and all his time in the Australian Baseball League over the winter. He profiles as an average defensive player at the hot corner in the future, with a solid-average arm, which is more than enough to stick there given his offensive ability. Caminero will have to be added to the Rays’ 40-man roster in December 2023, and the organization has gotten aggressive with him in 2023 by sending the teenager to Double-A already, backing up its confidence with its assignments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: This story might sound familiar: Facing a deadline to protect eligible prospects from the Rule 5 Draft, the Rays flipped an intriguing, nearly MLB-ready pitcher who didn’t fit on their 40-man roster and received a young infielder with no experience outside of complex-league ball. Yes, it sounds like how they acquired a pre-breakout Curtis Mead. But in this case, we’re talking about how the Rays landed Caminero from Cleveland in November 2021. Tampa Bay traded Rule 5-eligible righty Tobias Myers for Caminero, a Santo Domingo native and part of the Guardians’ 2019 international signing class. Caminero barely has any professional experience but showed some intriguing traits while performing well at the plate during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, leading some evaluators to believe the Rays might have unearthed another hidden gem. With a right-handed swing and impressive bat speed, the 5-foot-11 Caminero generated a lot of power to his pull side – he pulled 55 percent of the balls he put in play last year – and hit the ball in the air roughly 60 percent of the time. Caminero projects to have plus power at the plate, although the question for now is whether he’ll continue to make enough contact to get to that power as he’s challenged by higher-level pitching, better stuff and more complex sequencing. Caminero profiles as a future corner infielder, another potential parallel to Mead, although he worked all around the infield in his debut with 18 games at third, 10 at first and the rest up the middle. He has split his time between third and short this season in the Florida Complex League. He has a solid-average arm and is projected to be an average runner. Caminero hit well in the FCL, showing both power and a solid contact rate, and Tampa Bay decided to test him with a move to Single-A Charleston a month after his 19th birthday. In a system loaded with infielders, Caminero has given himself plenty of helium and could shoot higher up prospect boards during his true full-season debut in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Mike Fitzgerald, a first-round pick in the 1983 January and 1984 June secondary Drafts who played briefly in the Majors, Tyler was a fourth-rounder out of Louisville in 2019. He has produced consecutive 20-20 seasons in the upper Minors, earning Triple-A Pacific Coast League All-Star recognition in addition to making his big league debut in 2023. He started nine games in center field for the Giants despite not playing there prior to last year and homered off Ryan Yarbrough and Clayton Kershaw. Fitzgerald homered just 11 times in three college seasons but has developed average power in pro ball by concentrating on launching balls to his pull side. He has a quick right-handed swing and plenty of strength and leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame, and his aggressive approach helps him do damage when he connects. He chases too many pitches out of the zone and doesn't make consistent contact against non-fastballs, so he may not hit enough to be a regular. Fortunately for Fitzgerald, he's well suited for a utility role with his plus speed, solid arm strength and fine baserunning and defensive instincts. He has average to solid range at shortstop -- his primary position -- and quickly took to covering ground in center. He's a quality defender at second base, though the game speeds up a bit on him at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estes was a 16th-round pick in 2019 out of Paraclete High (Lancaster, Calif.) by the Braves and signed over slot with a bonus of $497,500. He joined the A’s in March 2022 as part of the Matt Olson deal. Beginning 2023 at Double-A Midland, he worked his way up to Triple-A and earned his first call to the big leagues in September, making two starts for Oakland the final month of the regular season. Estes possesses a pitch repertoire that includes a fastball that tops out at around 96 mph with significant ride, a mid-80s slider that varies in shape and a changeup that continues to make strides. He also incorporated a cutter with some late tilt last season, giving him a four-pitch mix that helps him generate a good amount of swing-and-miss. All of this comes from a compact and athletic delivery. The A’s have long been impressed by Estes’ strike-throwing ability and admire his competitiveness on the mound. After getting his feet wet with a couple of Major League starts, he should play a bigger role on Oakland’s pitching staff in 2024, with his improving four-pitch mix giving him a good chance to stick as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estes was committed to Long Beach State out of high school in California until the Braves signed him well over slot value with a bonus of $497,500 as a 16th-round pick in the 2019 Draft. After making his pro debut at age 17 the summer he was drafted, he earned 2021 Low-A East Pitcher of the Year honors in his first full season of professional baseball, making him an intriguing talent for the A’s, who acquired him from Atlanta as part of the Matt Olson deal in 2022. The A’s liked what they saw from Estes as a 20-year-old at High-A Lansing, where he posted a 4.65 ERA with 92 strikeouts in 91 innings. He upped his fastball to around 95-96 mph. He also brings an effective mid-80s slider with good depth and mixes in a changeup that he made strides with last season. Estes is aggressive on the mound and fills up the zone with strikes, continuing to develop a better feel overall for pitching as he matures. He doesn’t necessarily have a plus pitch in his arsenal at the moment, though that could come with time. His ultimate role will likely be determined by how much he can polish his secondary stuff. For now, the A’s are content with keeping him in a starting role and seeing just how much better he can get.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estes was a solid high school pitcher in California who looked like he might end up honoring his commitment to Long Beach State. But the Braves swooped in the 16th round of the 2019 Draft and were able to sign him for a well-over-slot bonus of $497,500 before he turned 18. He made the move to full-season ball in his first true full season in 2021 look easy, earning Low-A East Pitcher of the Year honors after leading the circuit in ERA, strikeouts, WHIP and batting-average-against. That clearly caught the eye of the A’s, who acquired him as part of the prospect package they received from the Braves in return for Matt Olson. All of Estes’ stuff is trending in the right direction. He averaged 93.5 mph with his fastball in 2021, a good tick or two harder than in 2019 when he first entered pro ball, and it has unique characteristics and good life. At times, he relied on overpowering Low-A hitters just with the fastball, and other times, he mixed in an effective slider with better depth as well. There was some variability to it, thrown anywhere in the 82- to 87-mph range, with Estes having more success with it when he started throwing it a little harder. His changeup also improved, though it’s still his third pitch. As encouraging as the stuff gains were, it was equally impressive that Estes filled up the strike zone as much as he did as a teenaged starter. How much the consistency of his secondary stuff improves could dictate his ultimate role, but for now those who thought he was sure to be a reliever have been quieted.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since his college days at Ball State, Nicolas has shown off premium stuff without always known where it was going. He landed in Competitive Balance Round B of the 2020 Draft with the Marlins after throwing more strikes before the shutdown and pitched his way to Double-A in 2021 before getting sent to the Pirates that offseason in the Jacob Stallings deal. He spent all of 2022 back in Double-A and seemed to have stalled back at Altoona in 2023, but he eventually moved up to Triple-A and a switch to a bullpen role helped him reach the big leagues for the first time. The 6-foot-4 Nicolas still has some of the most exciting stuff in the system. It starts with a fastball that averaged close to 96 mph in 2023 and touched 98-99 in shorter stints. It plays up even more because it has a ton of induced vertical break. He has two distinct breaking pitches, with the upper-80s slider that topped out at 92 mph a plus pitch that misses a ton of bats and a low-80s curve that provides a different look to hitters. He typically relied on those three pitches, infrequently bringing out his mid-80s changeup. The biggest thing that’s continued to hold Nicolas back has been his command. Not only does he have the repertoire to start, he’s shown he doesn’t wear down and his stuff holds up deep into starts. But he’s walked 4.6 per nine innings in his Minor League career, and the fact his offerings continue to tick up without as much concern for control in shorter stints could land him a job in the big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nicolas moved back and forth between relieving and starting in his three years at Ball State, showing off good raw stuff but struggling with command. He made only four starts before the shutdown in 2020, but his ability to find the strike zone more consistently helped him land with the Marlins in Competitive Balance Round B. He pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season in 2021, then pitched all season at the level with the Pirates in 2022 after coming over in the Jacob Stallings deal. Nicolas has the stuff to start, with a fastball that has some elite characteristics and two distinct breaking balls. While he’s not throwing quite as hard as he once did, averaging around 93.5 mph and topping out at 97, he maintains the velocity deep into starts, showing the ability to reach back for that 97 mph heater late in games. It plays up because it has 20 inches of induced vertical break, among the highest IVBs in the Minors. Both his mid-80s slider and low-80s curve will show glimpses of being above-average to plus. He does have a changeup, but it remains behind the other three offerings. The one thing that might keep Nicolas from reaching a big league rotation is his inability to land that premium stuff in the strike zone consistently, with a 4.6 walk per nine rate entering 2023. His ability to maintain his stuff will afford him more chances to start, but if the strikes don’t come more consistently, there’s comfort knowing his fastball-breaking ball combination would tick up in a relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two years at Ball State, Nicolas had a reputation as a big right-hander who could throw really hard, but didn’t always know where it was going. When he found the strike zone with more regularity during the shortened 2020 season, his Draft stock soared, landing him with the Marlins as a supplemental second-round pick. He used his power repertoire to pitch his way to Double-A in his first full season, then was sent to the Pirates in the Jacob Stallings trade last November. Nicolas’ ability to maintain his stuff deep into games could give him a chance to start. He touches triple digits in shorter outings and holds mid-90s with his fastball in most starts. The heater plays beyond just velocity because of it’s carry up the zone and heavy life when he’s down. He misses bats with a slider that can top out at 90 mph with sharp break and while his breaking pitchers run into each other, he will show a good, distinct curve. His changeup is a distant fourth pitch. The 6-foot-4 right-hander had simplified his delivery at Ball State to improve his command and cut his walk rate. He walked 4.5 per nine in his first full pro season and continued refinement could help his cause as a future starter. If his control doesn’t come along, that premium fastball and slider are plenty to serve a high-leverage role out of a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of former NFL quarterback Todd Blackledge, Nicolas used his strong arm to become one of the hardest-throwing starters in the 2020 Draft. He showed improved control during his truncated shortened junior season at Ball State, where he struck out 17 in seven one-hit innings in his final start before the Marlins signed him for $1,129,700 as a supplemental second-rounder. He showcased one of the best arms at Miami's instructional league program last fall and used that to have a successful first full season of pro ball, reaching Double-A, before getting sent to the Pirates at the end of November as part of the Jacob Stallings trade. Nicolas maintains mid-90s velocity deep into games with his fastball, which has reached 100 mph in shorter stints and features good carry up in the strike zone and some heavy life when he works the bottom half. He also can overpower hitters with a slider that parks in the mid-80s, touches 90 mph and has sharp break when it's on. He also flashes an interesting curveball, though his breaking balls blend together at times, while his changeup is very much a work in progress. After simplifying his delivery and understanding that he doesn't have to maximize his velocity to get hitters out, Nicolas slashed his walk rate from 7.6 per nine innings in his first two college seasons to 2.7 in his third and walked 4.5 per nine in his first pro season. More improvements with strike-throwing should allow him to continue to move quickly. He also earns praise for his intelligence and graduated from Ball State in just three years with a degree in business administration.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyle was a bit of an enigma for three years at Notre Dame as a flamethrower who missed a lot of bats and walked a lot of hitters. The Reds took a chance on his power stuff in the fifth round of the pandemic-shortened 2020 Draft. Missing most of the 2021 season due to injury, he got going in 2022 as a starter who reached Double-A. Struggling with command when he was traded to the A’s for Sam Moll in 2023, Boyle figured something out in his new organization and dominated his way to the big leagues, making three starts for Oakland and posting a 1.69 ERA with 15 strikeouts and five walks in 18 innings. Boyle consistently pushes triple digits with an high-octane fastball that also has some riding action to it. That, along with an upper-80s power slider that misses plenty of bats and a solid low-80s curve, gives him a solid three-pitch arsenal to work with as he’s continued to operate in a starting role for the A’s. This upcoming season will reveal whether Boyle’s newfound control is fluky or legit. There is some thought that Boyle’s command issues earlier last season may have had something to do with the experimental baseballs that were being utilized in the Southern League he was pitching in. It could also be that something just clicked for the 6-foot-7 right-hander. Whatever the case, Boyle is now viewed as a potential frontline starter if he can keep this up, while a high-leverage bullpen role could still be in the cards if the command falls apart again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Reds took Boyle out of Notre Dame with their fifth round, and final, selection of the 2020 Draft, they knew what they were buying. Boyle had spent three years pitching out of the Fighting Irish bullpen, using power stuff to rack up strikeouts while typically not having much of an idea of where the ball was going. While he spent a good portion of his first full season on the injured list, he did make his pro debut in August, cautiously making his way to Low-A. Healthy in 2022, Boyle pitched his way to Double-A. Boyle has shown off the high-octane velocity that made him a Draft prospect, typically sitting 97-98 mph and touching triple-digits. There’s good riding action on the pitch but his delivery doesn’t offer much in the way of natural deception, so he won’t be able to rely on power alone. That means his upper-80s slider, which does have good power and tilt, will have to keep trending upwards, and he did miss plenty of bats in 2022. The biggest question mark around Boyle is his control. He walked a whopping 12 batters per nine innings in his Notre Dame career, and walked 9.2 per nine in his 12 2/3 innings with Daytona. That’s trended in a better direction as the Reds have let him start and if he can find the strike zone even moderately well, he could be a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyle spent three years pitching out of Notre Dame’s bullpen, missing a ridiculous amount of bats and walking nearly as many along the way. A stronger Cape Cod League showing in the summer of 2019 provided a glimpse into what he was capable of, though it didn’t carry over into his shortened junior season. Still, he had the best arm strength in the Draft class of 2020 and the Reds decided to roll the dice on it by taking him with their final selection in the fifth round. The 6-foot-7 right-hander can now compete with fellow Reds prospect Hunter Greene for most velocity in the organization. He’s topped triple-digits on a regular basis and has shown the ability to sit in the upper-90s over multiple innings, with good riding action on the pitch. He couples it with an 85-88 mph slider that has missed a lot of bats, with Boyle leaving Notre Dame with a 14.3 K/9 rate. The issue with Boyle has been, and will likely continue to be, his ability to land either pitch in the strike zone. He walked 12.0 per nine in college and even in his successful turn on the Cape in 2019, he still walked 7.7 per nine. His size helps in terms of being imposing on the mound, but it’s also made it hard for him to repeat his delivery. That will be the biggest focus in his development, and he does have some athleticism to provide hope he can throw enough strikes to pitch in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kjerstad was off to a hot start (1.304 OPS) at Arkansas in his Draft year, but his season was cut short by the pandemic in 2020. While most of the industry saw him as a legitimate first-rounder, the Orioles reached a little bit to take him at No. 2 and sign him well under slot so they could aggressively go after other talent in the later rounds. He wasn’t able to play until June 2022 because of a diagnosis of myocarditis, a viral inflammation of the heart. That summer was mostly about just getting him on the field, but he showed he was ready to make the next step when he won Arizona Fall League MVP honors that fall. It carried over to a 2023 season in which he posted a .904 OPS between Double-A and Triple-A while making his big league debut in September. With the ailment clearly in his rearview, Kjerstad is looking very much like the left-handed power bat the Orioles hoped they were picking up. He has a combination of strength and bat speed and makes a ton of hard contact, showing the ability to drive the ball over the fence and for extra bases to all fields. His overall approach improved in 2023, and while he’s an aggressive swinger, he also managed his strikeouts well (18.4 percent K rate in the Minors), giving hope that he might not be as much power-over-hit as some anticipated. While he’s a fringy runner, Kjerstad is an athletic outfielder and fits nicely in right field with an above-average arm. It’s looking like his bat will profile well there in the big leagues too, and he should get every opportunity to prove that soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kjerstad had put his name on the map as a potential impact college bat by hitting 31 homers over his first two seasons at Arkansas. When he broke out of the gate in 2020 by posting a 1.304 OPS over his first 16 games, his Draft stock took a bigger leap and while it surprised many when the Orioles took him No. 2 overall to save money and manipulate their bonus pool, he was a bona fide first-rounder. A diagnosis of myocarditis, a viral inflammation of the heart, and its lingering effects, kept him off the field until June 2022. He made quick work of Single-A ball, struggled a bit with the move to High-A but definitely righted the ship with an MVP performance in the Arizona Fall League. More than anything, the 2022 season was a win for Kjerstad simply because he got on the field and competed for the first time in over two years. Beyond that, he started to show that his left-handed power bat has the chance to have an impact at this level. There’s strength and bat speed and even though there’s some swing-and-miss that’s still a part of his game that might always make him more power-over-hit, he showed a willingness to work counts and take walks as well as the ability to punish the baseball. His approach suffered a bit when he moved up to High-A and his K rate went up in the AFL, though he hit the ball consistently hard in Arizona. Defensively, Kjerstad fits nicely into an outfield corner, with a strong arm that works in right field. It’s his bat that will continue to carry him up the ladder, though, with the hope that his AFL experience serves as a springboard.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles sent shockwaves through the industry when they selected Kjerstad out of the University of Arkansas second overall in the 2020 Draft, as part of a strategy to manipulate their bonus pool and spend on upside picks later on. The fifth Razorbacks hitter to be taken in the first round of the Draft, Kjerstad signed for more than $2.5 million below-pick value after accumulating 37 homers over parts of three seasons in Fayetteville, where he emerged as one of the top sluggers in college baseball. Due to the lingering effects of myocarditis, a viral inflammation of the heart that surfaced shortly after the Draft, Kjerstad didn't make his pro debut until June 2022. Because of those unforeseen circumstances, Kjerstad remains something of an unknown quantity to the Orioles and the baseball world at large. He was seen as the best left-handed power bat among college hitters in his Draft class, with significant strength and bat speed and well-above average raw power to all fields. He was an aggressive hitter in college with some swing-and-miss attributed to the moving parts in his swing. It’s a herky-jerky swing with a hitch that sometimes made it tougher for Kjerstad to be on time consistently, but that may have been altered in the 23-some months since he left campus. Whether he’s tailored that swing to make more contact and how well he maintained strength during the layoff will be two points of emphasis for the eyes on Kjerstad as he gets acclimated to pro ball. Kjerstad resumed baseball activity at the Orioles’ training complex late last year, and while he went more than two years without playing in a competitive game, he managed to hit his way from Single- to High-A in short order in 2022. He’s just 23, plenty young enough to make up the time missed and climb up the Orioles’ system. He’s still seen as a potential middle-of-the-order hitter, a bat-first corner outfielder with an above-average arm and who moves well enough to profile in right field long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A total of five hitters have been taken from the University of Arkansas in the first round of the Draft, starting with Kevin McReynolds in 1981 and No. 1 overall pick Jeff King back in 1986. After setting a freshman home run record with 14 in 2018, hitting 17 more as a sophomore and starting out his junior year on fire, Kjerstad looked like he was ready to join that pair and 2015 No. 7 overall pick Andrew Benintendi as a Top 10 selection. The Orioles, loving the bat and knowing they could save some money, reached a little to sign him for more than $2.5 million below pick value at No. 2 overall. He was unable to participate in the club’s alternate camp or instructional league last summer after he was diagnosed with myocarditis, a viral inflammation of the heart. Kjerstad resumed physical activity at the club's Sarasota complex in August and has yet to play a game as a professional. Kjerstad had the best left-handed power bat among college hitters in the 2020 Draft. With strength and bat speed to spare, he has well-above-average raw power to all fields. An aggressive hitter who has some swing-and-miss to his game – a sacrifice the Orioles will have to make to get his power production – Kjerstad has a lot of moving parts to his swing, which makes it a little tougher for him to be on time consistently. It’s a setup that worked at Arkansas and he made strides during his shortened junior year to simplify and make more contact. Speed will never be a big part of his game, but Kjerstad is better underway and moves well enough to be a solid corner outfielder. An above-average arm and potential to hit in the middle of a big league lineup should profile well in right field in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals believed they were making a high-upside pick when they selected the 6-foot-8 San Jacinto (Texas) JC product 17th overall in 2019, and four years later, he made his Major League debut, though it was a bumpy ride in between those two points. That path was marked by a lost 2020 season, a shortened 2021 due to shoulder and blister issues, a 2022 spent entirely at Single-A and a 2023 climb through three levels. Rutledge posted a 3.71 ERA with 106 strikeouts in 119 innings at Double-A and Triple-A before his September arrival in the bigs, where he was much more roughed up (6.75 ERA, .304 average-against in four starts). The towering righty throws both a four-seamer and a sinker in the mid-90s and can touch 98-99 mph with both. However, he doesn’t get great extension out of his large frame, giving batters just a little longer to react to the heaters. His 82-86 mph slider posted his best whiff rate across all three levels, and even Major Leaguers couldn’t manage much off it because of its two-plane break. He left his upper-80s changeup up too much in The Show, and it got subsequently pounded, while his 79-81 mph curveball only got five percent usage. Although his walks ticked up under the ABS system in Triple-A, Rutledge was a control-over-command type in 2023 as he continued to adjust away from the short arm action of earlier in his career. Major League hitters were happy to take advantage of pitches in the zone, and after taking his MLB lumps, Rutledge has to either work more at the edges or sharpen his pitches if he’s going to stick in future Washington rotations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rutledge moved from Arkansas to San Jacinto JC (Texas) for the 2019 collegiate season after tearing a hip labrum as a freshman, and he showed enough stuff to become the 17th overall pick. His pro career has featured a similar mix of injuries and promise. The 6-foot-8 right-hander missed the 2020 season like everyone else in the Minors, then was limited to 36 1/3 innings by shoulder and blister concerns. The Nats kept him at Single-A Fredericksburg for all of 2022, hoping to establish a base layer of success, and Rutledge finished with a 4.90 ERA, 1.39 WHIP and 99 strikeouts in 97 1/3 frames. A large presence on the bump, Rutledge regularly sits 94-96 mph with both his four-seam and two-seam fastball and can touch the upper-90s in starts. The development of the two-seamer, in particular, has given his heater some needed movement and helped drive up his ground-ball rate to a career-best 50.7 percent. His mid-80s slider can be his swing-and-miss pitch with its promising hard break, while his upper-80s changeup and vertical curveball are average, though he's been throwing the changeup more and more as 2023 has rolled along. While there were previous concerns about short arm action in his delivery, Rutledge has added a little more length and that hasn’t come at the cost of throwing strikes. His control (6.9 percent BB rate) was at its best in the Minors so far last year, giving the Nats further belief he could be a starter. He’s on the 40-man roster, having been added in November, and is in his age-24 season, but he's been able to hold off a potential move to the bullpen to this point.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rutledge began his collegiate career at Arkansas but moved to San Jacinto (Texas) Junior College after suffering a torn hip labrum as a freshman. He was lights-out following the transfer (0.87 ERA, 134 strikeouts in 82 2/3 innings), prompting the Nationals to grab him 17th overall in the 2019 Draft. Like so many picks that year, Rutledge was forced into alternate-site action in 2020. Shoulder and blister issues limited him to 36 1/3 innings across three levels last summer, and he struggled with results, finishing with a 7.68 ERA and 20 walks. He made up for the lost time in the Arizona Fall League, where he was again inconsistent but finished on a high with seven strikeouts and 13 swings-and-misses over 3 1/3 relief innings in the championship game. Standing at 6-foot-8, Rutledge can be an imposing figure on the mound. He uses that frame to sit comfortably in the mid-90s with his fastball, and he can reach triple-digits when he rears back. He showed in the Fall League why his 82-85 mph slider is his best secondary; the breaker, which he can manipulate to add more or less break as he desires, led to nine of the 13 whiffs in the AFL championship. He’ll also mix in an upper-80s changeup and low-70s curveball, both of which could be average Major League pitches. The former shows a little more promise with the way it plays lower in the zone. Look at Rutledge’s stuff, and you could see a Major League starter. A short-arm-action in his delivery puts that projection into question, and inconsistencies with his location don’t help either. Few Nationals pitchers need innings more than Rutledge, or else it could be time to start looking at him as a power bullpen arm beyond this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rutledge was a juco success story. Jumping from Arkansas to San Jacinto (Texas) after suffering a torn hip labrum as a freshman, the right-hander showed big-time stuff and results, posting a 0.87 ERA with 134 strikeouts in 82 2/3 innings in 2019. The Nationals swooped for him at No. 17 and signed him to a $3.45 million bonus, only a little below slot for the pick. He saw action at three Minor League levels in 2019 and was an alternate-site standout at Fredericksburg during the lost 2020 season. Shoulder and blister problems have limited Rutledge further in what could have been his first full campaign in 2021. The St. Louis-area native can be a daunting presence on the bump, given his 6-foot-8 frame and power stuff. The fastball typically sits in the mid-90s but can touch higher with a ton of spin, and Rutledge can command it well in the strike zone. The slider is his clear second pitch, and the Nationals have been impressed with the way he can play with the looks of it, coming harder or shorter depending on need. The curve and change were two clear focuses at the alt site and could be solid Major League pitches in time. The changeup might be ahead of the two right now with Rutledge’s ability to throw it low in the zone and induce ground balls, while the curve remains more for show at this stage, though he can occasionally spike it. But both have the chance to develop with more pro experience. Improved control was another point of emphasis in Fredericksburg, and it should be an average skill by the time Rutledge reaches the Majors. The pieces are in place for him to fit comfortably in a Major League rotation. He needs just one of the changeup or curveball to click to fully round that future into place, and that could come as he picks up more Minor League innings than the 37 1/3 he possessed entering 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hurt flashed first-round potential as a California high schooler in 2017 before injuring his knee, and he turned down the Phillies as a 34th-rounder to attend Southern California, where he enjoyed only sporadic success. The Marlins selected him in the fifth and final round of the shortened 2020 Draft, then spun him along with Alex Vesia to the Dodgers for Dylan Floro eight months afterward. He finally broke out in 2023, leading all Minor Leaguers (minimum: 90 innings) in strikeout percentage (39 percent), strikeout minus walk percentage (28 percent) and swinging strike percentage (20 percent) before making his big league debut with two scoreless innings that September. He opened 2024 with Los Angeles but went on the injured list with shoulder inflammation in late April and succumbed to Tommy John surgery in July. Hart's fastball operates at 94-97 mph and touches 99, playing better than its impressive velocity thanks to his low release height and carry up in the zone. His changeup can be a well-above-average weapon at its best, arriving in the upper 80s before fading and tumbling at the plate. He dialed back his breaking ball usage from 21 percent in '23 to just 3 percent last year, but he has shown a solid upper-80s cutter and a decent upper-70s curveball in the past. Hurt has little track record of throwing strikes, though he's learning that his fastball and changeup are good enough that he doesn't have to be precise with them. He has the raw stuff to project as a starting pitcher, but he hasn't shown the control or durability to work more than 94 innings in a season. He'll miss all of 2025 rehabbing his elbow, and when he returns at age 28 in 2026, it almost certainly will be as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A potential 2017 first-rounder as a California high schooler before injuring his knee, Hurt flashed quality stuff but recorded a 5.06 ERA in three college seasons at Southern California. The Marlins took him in the fifth and final round of the shortened 2020 Draft, only to trade him with Alex Vesia to the Dodgers for Dylan Floro eight months later. After battling wrist and knee ailments as well as the strike zone during his first two years as a pro, Hurt led all Minor League pitchers who worked as many as his 92 innings in strikeout rate (14.9 per nine innings), strikeout percentage (39.2) and strikeout minus walk percentage (27.8) in 2023. Los Angeles' 2023 Minor League Pitcher of the Year, he made his big league debut with a perfect two-inning outing in September, but barely pitched this year before requiring midseason Tommy John surgery. Before his elbow gave out, some club officials believed Hurt had the best stuff in the Dodgers' system, beginning with a fastball that operates at 94-97 mph, touches 99 and plays even better than its velocity thanks to its low release height and carry. His changeup remains his best secondary pitch and gives him a second well above-average weapon at its best, arriving in the upper 80s before dropping at the plate. His tight mid-80s slider/cutter improved and became a reliably solid offering last year, and he also has a decent upper-70s curveball with bigger break. Hurt averaged 5.6 walks per nine innings in college and 6.7 per nine in his first two pro seasons, but he cut that rate to 4.2 last season. Staying healthy helped his control and command, and so did understanding that he doesn't have to be perfect with his quality stuff to get hitters out. If he can regain his health and stuff, he has a ceiling as a mid-rotation starter, and also could develop into a high-leverage reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of actors Matthew Armstrong and Ashley Crow (who played the mother in the baseball movie \"Little Big League\"), Crow-Armstrong repeatedly starred on U.S. national youth and junior teams before signing with Mets for $3,359,000 as the 19th overall pick in the 2020 Draft. His 2021 pro debut ended after six games when he tore the labrum in his right (non-throwing) shoulder during a baserunning mishap that May, and New York traded him to the Cubs for Javier Báez and Trevor Williams two months later. Crow-Armstrong has since developed into the game's best defensive prospect, displayed a higher offensive ceiling than expected and made his big league debut last September at age 21. Crow-Armstrong was more of a line-drive hitter with limited power as an amateur, but Chicago helped him alter his quick left-handed swing so that he could lift and pull balls more easily. He's hitting the ball harder than ever and now looks like a 20-homer threat. He's still learning to curb a tendency to become overly aggressive, a trait that was obvious when he went 0-for-14 with seven strikeouts with the Cubs, but he'll also show a willingness to use the entire field and patiently work counts at times. Crow-Armstrong's combination of plus-plus speed, outstanding instincts and fearlessness allow him to cover a tremendous amount of ground in center field and make plays most defenders can only dream of. He adds to his defensive package with solid arm strength and accuracy on his throws. His aggressiveness carries over to the bases as well, and he stole 39 bags in 51 attempts last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crow-Armstrong entered the summer of 2019 as the top-rated high school prospect, and while his stock dipped slightly, he still went 19th overall in the 2020 Draft and signed with the Mets for $3,359,000. The California high school product's pro debut ended after six games when he tore the labrum in his non-throwing shoulder during a baserunning mishap in May 2021, and New York traded him to the Cubs for Javier Baez and Trevor Williams two months later. In his first year in the new organization, he demonstrated newfound power at the plate, established himself as the game's best defensive prospect, played in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and helped South Bend win the High-A Midwest League championship. As an amateur, Crow-Armstrong used his quick left-handed stroke and a disciplined mindset to lace line drives to all fields. Chicago helped him incorporate some swing changes designed to allow him to pull and lift balls more easily, and he responded last year by making increased hard contact and showing at least 20-homer potential. He did become noticeably more aggressive, striking out nearly five times as much as he walked following a promotion to High-A, and will need to tone down his approach to succeed against more advanced pitching. As exciting as Crow-Armstrong's enhanced offensive upside is, it pales in comparison to his defense. Scouts give top-of-the-scale grades to his center-field skills, as he exhibits tremendous range from gap to gap with his combination of plus speed and precision reads and routes, and he completes the package with solid arm strength. He's aggressive in the outfield and on the bases, stealing 32 bags in 43 tries last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a Harvard-Westlake (Studio City, Calif.) program that has produced seven big leaguers -- including Jack Flaherty, Max Fried and Lucas Giolito -- Crow-Armstrong ranked as the best high school prospect in the 2020 class entering the showcase circuit the previous summer. While his stock dipped slightly, he still went 19th overall in the Draft and signed with the Mets for $3,359,000. His pro debut lasted just six games before he tore the labrum in his right (non-throwing) shoulder in a baserunning mishap and required season-ending surgery last May, two months before New York traded him to the Cubs for Javier Baez and Trevor Williams. Crow-Armstrong's quick left-handed stroke and mature approach is built for spraying line drives all over the park. He could fit near the top of an order with his hitting ability and on-base skills, not to mention his plus speed and baserunning savvy. While it initially was believed he might not have more than average raw power, he has made some swing changes that are allowing him to launch and pull balls more easily, and he now may have 20-homer pop. The top outfield defender in the 2020 Draft, Crow-Armstrong is a no-doubt center fielder with Gold Glove potential. He covers tremendous ground with his quickness and instincts, and he also possesses solid arm strength. He has a similar profile to former Cubs center fielder Albert Almora, though he bats left-handed and should be a better hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best examples of the progress the Tigers have made in pitching development and pitch design under Scott Harris came from the last prospect acquired by former general manager Al Avila. Gipson-Long was a relatively obscure prospect in the Twins system who came over in the Michael Fulmer trade, but his cerebral approach and eagerness to tinker served him well in his new organization. After posting high strikeout and home run rates between Double-A Erie and Triple-A Toledo, Gipson-Long earned a September callup when the Tigers needed starters. He beat the White Sox in his MLB debut, then fanned 11 Angels over five innings of one-run ball nearly a week later. His 2024 campaign was marred by injuries, and he underwent Tommy John surgery in April and a hip procedure in July. Though Gipson-Long showed a mid-90s fastball at times during his late-season stint in Detroit, he uses it more at 92-93 mph with command. He leverages his long frame to get outstanding extension, allowing the fastball to play up while setting up a mid-80s changeup. A low-80s slider with good depth is his secondary pitch of choice. His Minor League success coincided with the development of a cutter, but he didn’t use it much in his late-season stint in Detroit. Though Gipson-Long was homer-prone on his way up the system, he gave up just two home runs over 20 innings in Detroit despite a 47.9 percent fly-ball rate. The sudden rise of Gipson-Long in 2023 made him the rare player who made his MLB debut before his first Major League Spring Training camp. His timeline was set back by the lost year, but Detroit officials still talk about him being part of the big club’s starting depth in ’25.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even when he was just starting his pro career after the Braves took him out of high school in Round 14 of the 2018 Draft, Vodnik had a reliever’s profile. He did get an opportunity to start for a while in 2021 but had trouble staying on the mound then and in '22. A permanent move to the bullpen that season helped things click as he reached Triple-A. He was back in Double-A in 2023 when he was acquired by the Rockies in the Pierce Johnson trade. Vodnik then made two stops at the upper levels of Colorado’s system before making his big league debut last September. In shorter stints, Vodnik can focus on using his two plus pitches to miss a whole lot of bats. His fastball averaged around 97 mph and hit 100 in 2023 with good life. He throws his changeup around 89 mph with excellent deception thanks to good arm speed and it serves as a strikeout pitch, as well as getting weak contact. His mid-80s slider can be serviceable at times, though it gets slurvy. It wasn’t going to work for Vodnik as a starter mostly because of his command as he’s carried high walk rates throughout his Minor League career. It doesn’t have to be pinpoint for him to carve out a big league bullpen role. It’s clear his stuff is good enough, with a 10.8 K/9 rate across all levels, so if he can be around the zone just enough, he should get opportunities.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Braves went over slot in the 14th round to sign Vodnik for $200,000 out of the California high school ranks, he’s had a bit of an odd profile as a prepster who looked best suited for a relief role. The Braves did let him start in 2021 after he performed well at the team’s alternate site in 2020, mostly to let him get innings and work on his repertoire. Injuries got in the way in 2021 and kept him off the mound again for a good bit in 2022, but he seems to have found a home in the bullpen. He was pitching fairly well in relief in Double-A, albeit with poor command, when he was sent to the Rockies in the trade for Pierce Johnson in July. A bit of an undersized right-hander at 6 feet tall, Vodnik has more than enough stuff to be an effective reliever. It’s mostly a two-pitch mix with his fastball and changeup, both of which are plus pitches. His lively heater has averaged over 96 mph over the past two seasons in shorter stints, and he’s flirted with triple digits. He can miss bats and get a ton of weak contact on the ground with his upper-80s changeup, which he sells well with good arm speed. He does have a slurvy slider, but it’s a distant third pitch. In addition to the injury history, the main reason for a permanent move to the bullpen is Vodnik’s difficulty finding the strike zone. He walked 4.9 per nine innings in 2022 to bring his career average up to 4.2 BB/9 heading into 2023, and that number trended upwards this season. The Braves left him off the 40-man roster in the offseason and he wasn’t selected in the Rule 5 Draft, and now he’ll get the chance to show he can learn to throw enough strikes to earn a roster spot with a new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves went over slot to sign Vodnik away from his Cal State Northridge commitment in the 14th round of the 2018 Draft, giving him $200,000. Easing him into pro ball, he pitched almost exclusively in relief in his first full season, and many felt he had a reliever's profile. After pitching well late at the team’s alternate site in 2020, he gave starting a try in 2021, but an elbow issue, blisters and COVID all got in the way, limiting him to 33 2/3 regular season innings. He made up for lost time in the Arizona Fall League. Despite his smaller stature, Vodnik has a big arm. The right-hander was firing his live fastball in the 95-100 mph range when he was healthy. His changeup has become his best secondary offering, one that often flashes plus and misses a lot of bats. His slider can get slurvy and is still a work in progress. One of the reasons evaluators have felt he was destined to be a reliever was his command, or lack thereof, and he’s walked four per nine since being drafted, a tick more in the AFL. His delivery can get of whack, leading to issues with finding the strike zone consistently. The Braves would love for him to have a full, healthy season to truly get a sense of what he is, with the plan to let him keep developing as a starter at age 22 for all of the 2022 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Braves took Vodnik from Rialto High School in California in the 14th round of the 2018 Draft and gave him $200,000 to sign him away from Cal State Northridge, the right-hander has had an unusual profile: a prep arm who looked like a reliever. Vodnik has almost exclusively come out of the bullpen for the Braves since signing, though often in multi-inning outings, but that doesn’t mean he’s definitely destined for the bullpen. He advanced his profile by throwing well late at the Braves’ alternate training site and during instructs in 2020. Vodnik’s stuff is much bigger than you might expect to see given his six-foot stature. His stuff all ticked up in 2020, with a live fastball now sitting more in the mid-90s and touching 98-99 mph on occasion. His slider can miss bats when it’s tight enough, though it can get a bit slurvy at times. His changeup had been an experiment previously, but he showed off a pretty good one at the alternate site last year. The right-hander will need that third pitch to go along with continued improvement with his command and control if he wants a chance to start. The Braves view him as a starter and will let him develop all three pitches as such, but there wouldn’t be any shame if he ends up fitting that initial profile as a power reliever who could get the ball late in games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because he attended few showcase events and played just three games as an Elizabethton (Tenn.) HS senior before the pandemic ended his 2020 season, Carter was a relative unknown when the Rangers shocked the industry by drafting him in the second round that June. Area scout Derrick Tucker and Texas' upper-level evaluators believed he had five-tool potential when they signed him away from a Duke commitment with a $1.25 million bonus, and he quickly impressed other teams with his ability and polish once he began his pro career. He sparked the Rangers to the 2023 playoffs by posting a 1.058 OPS during a September callup, then slashed .300/.417/.500 while also starring defensively in the postseason as the franchise won its first World Series championship. Carter's offensive game centers around his preternatural ability to recognize pitches and discern strikes, which has earned him the nickname \"Full Count Carter\" and allowed him to record a 16.1 chase rate in his big league debut (including the postseason) -- better than the MLB-leading 16.6 mark of official qualifier Juan Soto. Though he was more pull-happy in his first taste of the Majors, he focuses on making hard contact to all fields with a quick left-handed stroke and should have at least average power as he gains more strength and launches more balls in the air. His lone offensive weakness is his production versus left-handers, against whom he slashed .242/.349/.253 in 2023, though the Rangers think he'll improve as he faces more southpaws. Carter has well-above-average speed and uses it well on the bases, stealing 32 bags in 43 attempts at all levels last year. His quickness and savvy are also assets in center field, where he chases down balls from gap to gap with long, gliding strides. He spent most of his big league debut in left field in deference to Leody Taveras, and his average arm strength allows him to play all three spots. The valedictorian of his high school class, he also impresses with his intelligence and makeup and handled baseball's biggest stage in October with aplomb.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carter didn't get scouted heavily as an amateur because he attended few showcase events and played just three games as an Elizabethton (Tenn.) HS senior before the pandemic ended his 2020 senior season. But area scout Derrick Tucker and the Rangers believed he had five-tool potential and made him a surprise second-round pick, signing him away from a Duke commitment for an under-slot $1.25 million. He has wowed pro scouts with his ability and polish ever since, advanced to Double-A shortly after turning 20 last summer and helped Frisco win the Texas League championship. The Rangers' 2022 Minor League player of the year, Carter stands out most for his advanced approach at the plate, where he recognizes pitches and controls the strike zone well beyond his years and uses the entire field. He makes consistent contact with a clean left-handed swing, and his bat speed and the leverage in his lanky 6-foot-2 frame should lead to at least average power once he adds some needed strength and pulls pitches more frequently. He completes his offensive package with plus speed and the savvy to use it well on the bases. His instincts also are apparent on defense, where Carter uses his quickness and long strides to chase balls down with ease in center field. His arm strength grades as average to solid, so he's capable of manning all three outfield positions, but there's no reason he won't stick in center. The valedictorian of his high school class, he also earns praise for his intelligence and makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carter went overlooked by many clubs in the 2020 Draft because he hadn't attended many showcase events and played just three games as an Elizabethton(Tenn.) High senior before the pandemic ended his season. But area scout Derrick Tucker and the Rangers saw enough to believe Carter had five-tool potential and selected him in the second round, signing him away from a Duke scholarship for an under-slot $1.25 million. He shed his anonymity with an impressive 2021 pro debut, with some teams evaluating him as Texas' top position-player prospect considering his performance relative to age as an 18-year-old in Low-A. Though he was one of the youngest players in full-season ball and hadn't faced much pro-caliber competition in the past, Carter wowed scouts with his advanced approach at the plate. Before a stress fracture in his back ended his debut prematurely, he drew 34 walks in 32 games, recognizing pitches and managing the strike zone with aplomb while using the entire field. He has a lean 6-foot-4 frame but has enough bat speed and leverage to produce 20 or more homers on an annual basis once he adds some strength and turns on more pitches. He not only possesses plus speed but Carter also has the instincts to steal bases and chase down balls in center field. His arm strength grades as average to solid, so he's capable at all three outfield positions. The valedictorian of his high school class, he stands out with his intelligence and makeup in addition to his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Most clubs didn't rate Carter as highly in the 2020 Draft as the Rangers, who took him in the second round and signed him away from a Duke commitment for an under-slot $1.25 million. Led by area scout Derrick Tucker, they scouted him heavily and believe other teams would have bought into what they see as five-tool upside if the coronavirus hadn't ended his final high school season after three games. He flew under the radar because he didn't attend many showcase events and he played in an out-of-the-way northeast corner of Tennessee. One of the youngest and most projectable players in the 2020 Draft, Carter didn't turn 18 until late August and entered pro ball with 190 pounds on a lean 6-foot-4 frame. His loose left-handed swing features plenty of bat speed and leverage, and he impressed with his ability to control the strike zone during instructional league. He could hit for both average and power once he adds more muscle, which he began to do as a high school senior. With solid to plus speed, Carter can steal some bases and cover ground in center field. His arm earns average to solid grades and would fit in either outfield corner as well. The valedictorian of his Elizabethton (Tenn.) High class, he also draws praise for his intelligence, instincts and makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going sixth overall in the 2021 Draft, Lawlar zoomed through the D-backs system in his first two full seasons. He earned most of his 2023 accolades in the Texas League, where he picked up Top Prospect and All-Star honors and a spot in the All-Star Futures Game. The Texas native made his Major League debut for Arizona that summer at 21 years old, and though he went just 4-for-31, Lawlar cracked the club's postseason rosters and walked in his lone World Series plate appearance. Thumb and hamstring injuries limited him to only 23 Minor League games in 2024, and after not appearing in The Show, he made up for the lost at-bats with Licey during winter ball in the Dominican Republic. The missed time only gave evaluators a 58-plate-appearance sample in Lawlar's return to Triple-A, but some of his strengths remained, namely his above-average ability to focus on pitches inside the zone. The Pacific Coast League's (and Reno's, specifically) hitter-friendly environs flattered his .592 slugging percentage as his exit velocities didn't meet those standards; his xSLG was .317. But the long layoff and thumb issue did him no favors, and he should have the bat speed to settle into at least average power long term. Before missing time again with a hamstring strain in 2025, Lawlar showed real struggles against breaking stuff during his second foray into the big leagues. Lawlar can really fly, especially underway, and he should be a threat to steal 30+ bags for much of his career. He's grown more consistent at shortstop over the years, doing more than just relying on his athleticism to make plays, and his throwing has improved with the professional reps. He sprinkled some time in at third base in both the summer and winter, and the D-backs say that will continue, along with some potential work at second, as they try to find him an MLB home.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline's No. 3 prospect in the 2021 Draft, the Gatorade Texas High School Player of the Year went to the D-backs with the sixth overall pick before signing for well-above-slot at $6,713,300. A left shoulder injury limited him to only two Minor League games that summer, but he showed signs of being a quick mover with time at four levels -- including Double-A Amarillo -- in 2022 while finishing with a .303/.401/.509 line, 16 homers and 39 steals. He returned to the Texas League for 2023 and caught fire midseason, leading to an August promotion to Triple-A Reno and a quick September hook to the Majors. Lawlar appeared in three games in Arizona's playoff push to the World Series, serving as a pinch-hitter and runner. Lawlar's quick and compact swing means he can catch up to velocity, although he exhibited some swing-and-miss issues with offspeed stuff in 2023. Having turned only 21 last July, he might just need more exposure to high-level non-fastballs to iron out those issues. Lawlar also rarely expands the zone and has posted at least a 10 percent walk rate at each of his Minor League stops thus far. He did a better job of elevating on contact in his return to Amarillo (an extreme hitter's park), and he should quickly be a 20-homer threat in the Majors. The 6-foot-1 infielder moves extremely well and smartly picks his stolen-base opportunities, leading to back-to-back 30-plus steal seasons in 2022 and '23. That athleticism has treated him well at shortstop, too, and the D-backs believe he's solidified his standing at the position with improved consistency across the board. Arizona will have a good problem with Geraldo Perdomo manning the six, but with his pop advantage, Lawlar has the higher long-term ceiling. Before challenging Perdomo in 2024, Lawlar will need to return from right thumb surgery that is expected to keep him out for the first two months of the regular season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fresh off being named Gatorade's 2021 Texas High School Player of the Year, Lawlar went sixth overall to the D-backs and signed for the Draft's third-highest bonus at $6,713,300. After a shoulder injury ended his first dip into the Minors after only two games, the right-handed slugger came out firing in 2022, batting .351/.447/.603 with 22 extra-base hits in 44 games at Single-A Visalia. Eager to press the shortstop, Arizona gave him looks at High-A Hillsboro, Double-A Amarillo and the Arizona Fall League before a fractured left scapula knocked him out again in the autumn. Lawlar's compact right-handed swing is already helpful in his pursuit to square up balls, and his advanced pitch recognition aids that ability to produce solid averages and walk rates. (He notably walked at least 10 percent of the time at all three full-season stops in 2022.) The former Vanderbilt commit established a solid power base with 16 homers in his first full season and could build on that as he matures into his 6-foot-2 frame. Even now, the power plays well to all fields as he can go the other way with authority when pitch location calls him to do so. Using his plus speed, Lawlar took advantage of Minor League rules to swipe 39 bags across three levels, and even if he doesn't reach those heights in the bigs, he should be a baserunning threat for much of his career. He's still a work in progress defensively, particularly when it comes to the accuracy of his throws. Good range and promising arm strength still give him an impressive five-tool ceiling, but the D-backs will have to balance the need to challenge Lawlar's bat and develop his glove in future assignments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a five-tool shortstop from a Dallas-area high school, Lawlar inevitably draws parallels to Bobby Witt Jr., the No. 2 overall pick in 2019 by the Royals. While Witt had louder tools and was more advanced after growing up around the game as the son of a 16-year big leaguer, Lawlar entered 2021 as the consensus top high school prospect and won Gatorade's Texas high school player of the year award. The D-backs selected him with the sixth overall pick and signed him away from his Vanderbilt commitment with an above-slot bonus of $6.71 million. But a shoulder injury ended his professional debut after just two games (five at-bats) in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. Lawlar is a more polished hitter than Witt was at the same stage with a quick, compact right-handed swing and a mature, patient approach, though he struck out more than expected as a senior. He focuses on working the gaps and has a knack for inside-outing balls to right field. With his bat speed and the projectable strength in his 6-foot-2 frame, he should develop solid power once he adds strength and starts turning on more pitches. Lawlar's plus speed plays well on the bases and in the field, and he'll even clock some well-above-average run times on occasion. With plenty of range, quick hands and a strong arm, there's no doubt he'll stick at shortstop, though like most youngsters he needs to improve his consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Daniel could have signed with the Brewers as a Draft-eligible sophomore taken in the 11th round in 2018 but instead decided to head back to Auburn for his junior season. That campaign lasted just two innings before he blew out his elbow and had Tommy John surgery, though the Angels thought they were getting a bargain by nabbing him in the seventh round of the 2019 Draft. Post-pandemic, he pitched his way to Triple-A in his first pro season, and while he didn’t make his debut in 2022, he did get called up to the big leagues for the first time. His 2023 was nearly ruined by a shoulder strain that landed him on the 60-day injured list, though he did return to make his actual big league debut in September before throwing very well in four Arizona Fall League starts. There’s not a ton of ceiling with Daniel because he lacks true wow stuff, but he does have a legitimate four-pitch mix and knows how to use it when he’s healthy. His fastball sits around 92 mph, but it gets more swings and misses in the zone than you’d expect thanks to high spin rates. His mid-70s curve provides a solid north-south option, and he can bury it down in the zone. His low-80s slider is a solid pitch, and while it’s a bit behind the others, he does have a mid-80s changeup that can be effective. Very small big league sample aside, Daniel has shown the ability to mix all of his pitches well and land them all for strikes, utilizing a simple delivery he repeats well. There’s long been concern about the 6-foot-1 right-hander’s physicality and durability, so he’ll have to show he can stay healthy, but he could get the chance to do that in Los Angeles soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken by the Brewers in the 11th round of the 2018 Draft as a Draft-eligible sophomore, Daniel opted to return to Auburn for his junior year. He threw just two innings in his first start in 2019 before his elbow blew out and he needed Tommy John surgery. The Angels feel like they might have gotten a steal by taking him in the seventh round that June, seeing him first open eyes in instructional league play in 2020, then pitching his way across three levels to finish the year in Triple-A. While none of Daniel’s stuff jumps off the page, he has a good idea of what to do with his entire repertoire. His fastball may touch 93 mph on occasion, usually sitting lower, but it plays up because of high spin rates that lead to swings and misses up in the zone. He creates good north-south separation with that four-seamer and his 74-75 mph curve that he can bury down. He has a low-80s slider and a changeup to give him a legitimate four-pitch mix. Daniel throws a lot of strikes with a simple and repeatable delivery and while he hit a wall when he got to Triple-A, that’s not so alarming since he threw 114 2/3 innings in his first year of competition after surgery. The Angels would like for the 6-foot-1 right-hander to get a little more physical so he can handle the workload of a back-of-the-rotation type starter

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a solid high school career in Alabama, Daniel stepped right into Auburn’s rotation as a freshman, then both started and relieved as a Draft-eligible sophomore when he was taken in the 11th round of the 2018 Draft. He was set to be a part of Auburn’s rotation in 2019 but got shut down after two innings in his first start, undergoing Tommy John surgery in April 2019. The Angels took him in the seventh round of that June’s Draft anyway, signing him for a bit under slot. He didn’t pitch in any capacity for the organization until instructs last fall, where he made a very strong first impression. A 6-foot-1 right-hander, Daniel uses a very efficient and smooth delivery to deliver a solid, if unspectacular, three-pitch mix. His fastball tops out at around 93 mph, but he gets swings and misses on it thanks to high spin rates up in the zone. He complements his fastball with a solid breaking ball and good feel for a changeup. When he was healthy, Daniel did struggle with his command and control, walking 4.3 per nine innings as a sophomore. His repertoire and feel for pitching point to the potential to start, but his fastball did tick up when he pitched out of the pen for Auburn in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants signed Canario for $60,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2016 and traded him and Caleb Kilian to acquire Kris Bryant from the Cubs five years later. He ranked second in the Minors with 37 homers while reaching Triple-A in 2022, but he broke his left ankle and dislocated his left shoulder in the Dominican Winter League that November. Originally expected to miss most of 2023, he returned at midseason and celebrated his big league debut in September with a grand slam off Kyle Nicolas in his first start. Canario is strong -- weighing closer to 215 pounds than his listed 165 -- and doesn't get cheated at the plate, turning his right-handed swing with electric bat speed and loft loose with the intention of crushing the ball great distances. While he did curb his extreme pull-happy tendencies a bit last year, strikeouts will always be a byproduct of his plus power. He may not produce high batting averages but his power plays from the left-field pole to right-center and against both lefties and righties. Though Canario is athletic for his size, he didn't run as well last year, exhibiting below-average speed compared to average-to-solid quickness in the past. He has played all three outfield positions throughout his career, spending more time in right field than center in 2023 for the first time since his pro debut. He's an average defender in right and would perhaps better if he regains some speed, and he has the strong arm required at the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Giants for $60,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2016, Canario didn't make it to full-season ball until 2021. He has belted 55 homers in the past two years and ranked second in the Minors with 37 while moving from High-A to Triple-A in 2022. He joined the Cubs in July 2021, arriving along with Caleb Kilian in the Kris Bryant trade. A baserunning mishap in the Dominican Winter League last November left him with a broken left ankle and a dislocated left shoulder, both of which required surgery that cost him the first half of the 2023 season. Big leaguers took note of Canario's well-above-average raw power when he played at the Giants' alternate site in 2020. He's geared to hit for power with lightning-fast bat speed, formidable strength and plenty of loft and leverage in his right-handed stroke. He's overly aggressive and pull-happy at the plate, so he will pile up strikeouts, but he did make strides with his swing decisions last season and boosted his walk rate from 7 percent in the first half to 15 percent in the second half. Though he weighs closer to 215 pounds than his listed 165, Canario is athletic for his size. An average runner out of the batter's box, he's quicker once he gets going and swiped 23 bases in 26 tries last year. He has spent the majority of his career in center field but his range fits best in right and his plus arm strength is an asset there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Giants for $60,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2016, Canario spent his first two seasons and the start of his third in Rookie ball. He blossomed into one of San Francisco's better prospects when he slammed 16 homers in 59 games at the lower levels in 2019 and ultimately became a trade chip who went to the Cubs along with right-hander Caleb Kilian in exchange for Kris Bryant last July. He went deep in four straight games shortly after the deal and has challenged for the Minor League lead in homers this season while advancing to Double-A. Several big leaguers noticed Canario's well-above-average raw power when they saw him at the Giants' alternate site in 2020. He has electric bat speed, plenty of strength and lots of loft and leverage in his right-handed stroke. The downside is that he hunts homers too much at times, getting overly aggressive and pull-happy and compromising his ability to make contact. Canario weighs significantly more than his listed 165 pounds and is quite athletic for his size. He shows average speed out of the batter's box, is faster underway and looks to steal when given the opportunity. He played the majority of his games in center field during his first four pro seasons, but his range is better suited for right, where his strong arm is an asset.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite sitting in the international spending penalty box in 2016 after signing Bahamian shortstop Lucius Fox for $6 million the year before, the Giants still found a bargain by signing Canario for $60,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He won MVP honors at the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League's all-star game during his 2017 pro debut and really broke out two years later by batting .318/.377/.623 with 16 homers in 59 games between Rookie and short-season ball.
