mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of 16-year big leaguer Juan Uribe, Tena signed for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2017. After losing a full season to the pandemic, he broke out in 2021 by batting .281 with 16 homers as a 20-year-old in High-A and leading the Arizona Fall League in hitting (.387). His bat wasn't as potent the next two years, though he did make his big league debut last August. With a quick left-handed stroke and the hand-eye coordination to barrel balls with ease, Tena has the tools to hit for average with decent power. But he struggles to catch up to fastballs up in the zone and chases too many offspeed pitches, resulting in a 29 percent strikeout rate last year. He's doing a better job of driving balls in the air, but he won't realize his 12-15 homer potential unless he becomes more selective. One of the better defenders among Cleveland's middle-infield prospects, Tena has a quick first step, reliable hands and solid arm strength. He's an asset at both shortstop and second base and also can fill in at third base. On the bases, his instincts stand out more than his average speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of Cleveland's 2017-18 international crop that included Top 100 prospects George Valera and Brayan Rocchio, Tena signed for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. The nephew of 16-year big leaguer Juan Uribe, he broke out by hitting .281 with 16 homers as a 20-year-old in High-A and winning the Arizona Fall League batting title (.387) in 2021. He held his own in Double-A last year and made a five-game cameo at Triple-A at the end of the season. With his quick left-handed swing and quality hand-eye coordination, Tena is built to hit for average. But he's too aggressive at the plate, repeatedly chasing offspeed pitches down in the zone and struggling to catch up to good fastballs at the top, and he makes too much weak contact while rarely walking. Adding strength during his pandemic layoff in 2020 translated into more bat speed and power that could pay off with 15 homers per season in the Majors. Tena has solid speed and is a good base runner, albeit not a prolific base stealer. He has a quick first step and reliable hands, and he enhanced his chances of sticking at shortstop by also upgrading his arm strength during his pandemic downtime. He's at least an average defender at short and better than that at second and third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The nephew of 16-year big leaguer Juan Uribe, Tena signed for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of what could be a special Guardians 2017 international class. After batting .319 with two homers in Rookie ball in his first two pro seasons, he used his pandemic downtime to get stronger in 2020. He added 15 pounds before hitting .281 with 16 homers as a 20-year-old in High-A last year, then won the Arizona Fall League batting title (.387) and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster. Tena has a well-rounded game but stands out most for his hitting ability, the product of a sweet left-handed swing and outstanding hand-eye coordination. His extra muscle translated into more bat speed and higher exit velocities last year, and while he won't be a slugger he should be able to provide 15 or more homers per season. Though he showed more patience in 2021, his walk rate still was just 6 percent because he makes contact so easily. An aggressive runner with solid speed, Tena can steal an occasional base. He also improved his arm strength to solid during his layoff, enhancing his changes of staying at shortstop. He covers ground with a quick first step, has reliable hands and is a solid defender at short and third base and perhaps plus at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a potentially special Indians 2017 international class, Tena signed for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. The nephew of 16-year big leaguer Juan Uribe, he's one of several sweet-swinging middle-infield prospects in the system. After hitting .319 in Rookie ball during his first two pro seasons, he had his development limited to instructional league in 2020. Tena's smooth left-handed stroke and outstanding hand-eye coordination give him some of the best bat-to-ball skills among Cleveland prospects. He almost puts the bat on the ball too easily, resulting in a 3-percent walk rate and inconsistent quality of contact during his U.S. debut in 2019, so he'll need to develop better plate discipline. After showing little power in his first two years in pro ball, he used his pandemic downtime to get stronger and is driving the ball with more authority in 2021. Tena has solid speed and is as aggressive on the bases as he is at the plate. He covers ground at shortstop with a quick first step, has dependable hands and bolstered his arm strength from average to solid during his layoff last year. He should be able to stay at shortstop and might be a plus defender at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mead stood out in the Australian Baseball League at a young age and signed with the Phillies for $200,000 in May 2018. He was flipped to the Rays for reliever Cristopher Sánchez 18 months later after two season of complex ball and then broke out with a .321 average and .911 OPS over 104 games across three levels in 2021. He was productive -- though limited by a right elbow strain -- at Double-A and Triple-A in 2022, and broke through to the Majors last season while slashing .294/.385/.515 in 61 games back in Durham. The Adelaide native was Tampa Bay’s second-base starter during Games 1 and 2 of its Wild Card Series loss to the Rangers. Batting out of a simple, upright stance, Mead sees the ball well out of opposing pitchers’ hands and has the hand-eye coordination to put bat on ball with relative ease. The Rays have prioritized Mead hunting for pitches on which to do damage as he’s gotten closer to the bigs, but that hasn’t made him a free swinger either. There’s the potential for decent power if he can turn some of his doubles into dingers, but he still profiles closer to average pop for now. Because his bat is so advanced, the 23-year-old himself has emphasized his glovework to get it Major League-ready. Below-average arm strength has caused him to add reps at second base over his natural position of third, and while his range has improved since the early days of his career, he still isn’t likely to add much defensive value. Luckily, Mead’s pure hitting ability should make him a piece of Tampa Bay’s puzzle in 2024 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mead has become a poster child of why organizations should run if the Rays come asking after a Complex League performer. An Australian Baseball League standout at a young age, Mead signed with the Phillies for $200,000 in May 2018 and was dealt to the Rays for lefty reliever Cristopher Sánchez 18 months later. Mead’s breakout came in 2021 when he hit .321 with a .911 OPS across three full-season levels and produced an 18-game hitting streak in the Arizona Fall League. His 2022 performance at Double-A and Triple-A solidified his standing as a consistent hitter, and if not for a late-season right elbow strain, he would have pushed for St. Petersburg already. The Australia native bats out of an upright stance, and its simplicity allows him to see the ball well and react to most pitches. He doesn’t strike out a ton by modern standards, but the Rays have been enthused by the way he’s become more selective in seeking out pitches on which to do damage, rather than making contact for the sake of making contact. That change in approach, along with the 22-year-old’s increasing strength, should help him settle into 20-25-homer power over the next decade. Mead’s arm strength has been an issue throughout the Minors, and that was before last year’s elbow injury. He got the bulk of his starts at third base in 2022 but is likely a better fit at second or first because of the arm. As is their M.O., the Rays plan to keep moving Mead around as long as they can to keep any hope of versatility because they, and many in the industry, believe his bat will be an impactful presence in any lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Australian Baseball Leaguer Tim Mead, Curtis was a quality ABL hitter himself, batting .373/.411/.471 over 20 games as a 16-year-old in the 2017-18 season. The Phillies signed him the following May, then dealt him to the Rays in November 2019 for left-handed reliever Cristopher Sánchez before he left the Florida complex. An instructs participant in 2020, Mead was one of the Rays system’s best hitters last season with a .321/.378/.533 line and 55 extra-base hits in 104 games across three levels. He impressed further in the Arizona Fall League with an 18-game hitting streak. The right-handed slugger stands upright in his stance and commands the strike zone with a mix of discipline and bat control that leads to few strikeouts. (His 15.5 percent K rate was fourth-best among Rays full-season qualifiers in 2021.) Mead is also able to show plus raw power from the box. His contact mostly results in line drives and doubles to the gap for now, but the Rays believe those will go over the fence as the 21-year-old matures and gains experience. Tampa Bay wants to keep him away from a full-time first base role as long as possible and made third base his primary position in 2021, though he’s far from fluid there. His arm strength is also tested across the diamond. He has seen more game time at second base this season, and that has replaced first as his secondary position. The bat will play anywhere he lands, and that notion has gotten truer with each passing level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Selected in the 28th round in 2017 out of Eastern High School (Voorhees, N.J.), Schneider has earned every bit of playing time along the way. Given his Draft position and profile, though, that didn’t always come easily in his early years. Schneider opened in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in 2017 and Appalachian League in ’18 before getting a taste of short-season ball with Vancouver in 2019. There he showed a knack for reaching base and playing multiple positions along the way. Schneider brought along a bit more power in 2021, hitting nine home runs with an .812 OPS over 49 games spent mostly in High-A. In 2022, Schneider finally earned his way into everyday reps in High-A, Double-A and eventually Triple-A, hitting a combined .253 with a .366 OBP and .457 slugging percentage, including 16 homers. Add in 17 stolen bases and a broad defensive profile, and Schneider simply found a way to impact the game. A favorite among the Blue Jays’ development staff for his hard work and commitment as he earned bigger roles, Schneider now demands playing time, and on the cusp of a 30-homer season in the Minors, he joined Toronto's Major League club in August. It may not be a flashy brand of baseball, but Schneider has an advanced plate approach and knows how to get on base. There’s some legitimate pop in there too from his strong build. After 17 games at Triple-A in ’22, he handled the test provided by pitchers at that level, where he played second base, the corner outfield spots, first and third. Even if there aren’t true standout tools here, you don’t have to squint too hard to see how Schneider could continue to be a utility option for Toronto as a right-handed bat off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-year starter at Miami, Cecconi did enough for the Hurricanes to become the 33rd overall pick in 2020 as a Draft-eligible sophomore. Wrist and elbow injuries limited his first full season, and he enjoyed a fuller campaign in 2022, posting a 4.37 ERA with 127 strikeouts in 129 2/3 innings for Double-A Amarillo. He jumped to Triple-A Reno last year -- a trial through hellfire for any pitcher -- and posted a 6.11 ERA in 116 1/3 innings there, though he did have 118 strikeouts and only 36 walks. The D-backs rewarded Cecconi with his Major League debut in August, and he made seven regular-season appearances (four starts) for the club with mixed results before adding a pair of scoreless relief outings in the NLCS. The 6-foot-4 right-hander ran his fastball up to 99.9 mph in Triple-A in 2023 but was generally closer to 93-95 during his time at both stops. The pitch has some armside run, but its ordinary movement profile made it play below the velocity, allowing upper-level bats to take advantage. Cecconi's 81-84 mph slider remains his best pitch -- a true two-plane snapper that darts glove-side late to fool hitters. His mid-70s curveball has some promising break of its own, but it can be another hittable pitch if not buried below the zone. Still, Cecconi's increased usage of the curve helped him fight off some splits issues since his low-80s changeup remains a distant fourth pitch. Cecconi has yet to post a walk rate below 8.1 percent for any Arizona affiliate, and his 7.1 percent mark in Triple-A was notable given how ABS increased free passes in 2023. The former Hurricane has already contributed to Arizona's starting depth, but he could use sharper stuff to carve out a more permanent role or else he could be a fastball-slider reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cecconi started both of his two seasons at Miami, though his second campaign lasted only four outings because of the pandemic, and that was enough to push him to be the 33rd overall pick as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2020. Wrist and elbow concerns limited him to only 59 innings at High-A Hillsboro in his first full season, and he made up for the lost time with 15 additional frames in the Arizona Fall League. Cecconi spent all of 2022 at Double-A Amarillo and was healthy throughout, posting a 4.37 ERA with 127 strikeouts and only 32 walks in 129 2/3 innings. As is typical for Amarillo pitchers, his road splits (3.27 ERA, 1.23 WHIP) were significantly better than his home numbers (5.74, 1.43). The former Hurricane can ramp up his fastball to the upper 90s, but he typically settles in the 92-94 mph range, especially deeper in starts. Part of that decreasing velo could be explained by his hefty workload in 2022 after missing so much time in '20 and '21, but it is a cause for concern. His mid-80s slider is his best pitch, one that darts gloveside quickly and late for whiffs. His curveball (coming in 10 mph slower than the slider) offers a more vertical -- if occasionally loopy -- breaking pitch, while his low-80s change isn't enough of a weapon against lefties, who slugged .539 off Cecconi in '22. The right-hander's 5.7 percent BB rate ranked fifth among Double-A qualifiers, and he's been trending in the right direction in that regard. But he needs a consistent third pitch to become a true rotation option, and as he enters his Rule 5 year, it might be worth seeing how the fastball-slider combo plays in shorter spurts soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cecconi likely would have been a high pick out of high school, but the combination of an injury that kept him off the mound for most of his senior year and a strong commitment to the University of Miami forced him to slide to the 38th round in 2018. After spending his freshman year in the Hurricanes' rotation, Cecconi was one of the more intriguing Draft-eligible sophomores in the country in 2020 and showed enough stuff for the D-backs to take him in Competitive Balance Round A and sign him for a slightly above-slot bonus of $2,384,900. His 2021 professional debut was delayed by a minor injury to his left wrist, though once healthy, Cecconi pitched as expected for High-A Hillsboro. He found himself back on the injured list in early August, but was able to make up for some lost time with 15 innings over five appearances in the Arizona Fall League. At 6-foot-4, Cecconi has a prototypical pitcher frame and an electric upper-90s fastball to go with it. His slider, which some feel is his best pitch, is a true out pitch that is right up there with Levi Kelly's for the best in the system. He also throws a curveball and a changeup that has shown improvement since he was drafted. Cecconi has been dominant in flashes and his stuff plays, but his overall consistency will need to improve as he works his way toward Arizona. Cecconi has all the makings of a big league starter once he further refines his curveball and changeup and tightens up his mechanics, though his fastball-slider combination would play well out of the bullpen. While injuries derailed his 2021 season, the D-backs don’t have any questions about Cecconi’s long-term durability. He’s been much healthier in 2022 with Double-A Amarillo, playing in a notoriously hitter-friendly park, and could be in line for a debut next summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cecconi likely would have been a high pick out of high school, but the combination of an injury that kept him off the mound for most of his senior year and a strong commitment to the University of Miami forced him to slide to the 38th round in 2018. After spending his freshman year in the Hurricanes' rotation, Cecconi was one of the more intriguing Draft-eligible sophomores in the country in 2020 and showed enough stuff for the D-backs to take him in the Competitive Balance Round A and sign him for a slightly above slot bonus of $2,384,900. His professional debut was delayed by a minor injury to his left wrist, though once healthy, Cecconi pitched as expected with High-A Hillsboro. However, he found himself back on the injured list in early August. Cecconi has the prototypical pitcher frame at 6-foot-4 and he has an electric fastball to go with it, touching 97-98 mph this past summer. His slider is a true out pitch and is right up there with Levi Kelly's for the best in the system. He also throws a curveball and changeup that has shown improvement since he was drafted. Cecconi has all the makings of a big league starter once he further refines his offspeed pitches. If he can stay healthy, Cecconi is viewed as someone who could move quickly through the system. Given his fastball-slider combination he could transition into an effective reliever if necessary.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Back in 2018, which might seem like an eternity ago in the scouting and player development worlds, the Angels rolled the dice on Adams’ athleticism in the middle of the first round, signing him away from a chance to play football and baseball at North Carolina. He came out of the gates performing well, but he stumbled post-pandemic with a combined .629 OPS in 2021-22 and he was left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft after the '22 season. He landed on the 40-man roster anyway in 2023 when an uptick in production with Triple-A Salt Lake led to his first big league callup, though he looked overmatched in a very small sample size. There were some encouraging signs of offensive life from Adams, starting with a little bit of extra-base impact, and while some of that can be attributed to his hitter-friendly home ballpark and the Pacific Coast League in general, he did register some better exit velocities. There’s still too much swing-and-miss in his game as he chases and tinkers with his swing too frequently, but that improved some as the year went on. With 80-grade speed, Adams listened to the Angels’ push for him to be more aggressive on the bases and he led the PCL with 44 stolen bases while continuing to play outstanding defense in center field. He’s 24 for the entirety of the upcoming season, waiting for a longer chance to show what kind of big leaguer he can be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former multi-sport star who could have played football and baseball at North Carolina, Adams was a surprise first-round pick by the Angels, who were betting on his premium athleticism when they went over slot to sign him in 2018. The early returns were promising, with a better-than-expected approach helping him put up a solid first full season of pro ball. It’s gone backward since he returned to competitive action in 2021, slashing just .230/.306/.352 combined the past two years. Because of his athleticism and top-of-the-scale speed, it’s hard to give up on Adams as a prospect, though the Angels did not protect from the Rule 5 Draft in the offseason, figuring teams were unlikely to take a high-risk outfielder who has barely played above A ball and hasn’t figured out a plan at the plate yet. The right-handed hitter changes his swing too often and he needs to focus on putting the ball in play, getting on base and using his speed to his advantage. There’s too much swing-and-miss and he doesn’t drive the ball consistently. He does know how to use his speed on the basepaths, going 33-for-36 in theft attempts in 2022 despite his offensive struggles, and he’s an outstanding defender in center field as well. He’s still only 23, so if he can start making better swing decisions and contact, there’s time for him to get back on the right track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels surprised some when they took Jordyn Adams in the middle of the first round of the 2018 Draft and went over slot to sign him away from playing baseball and football at North Carolina. Adams, in turn, surprised some who thought the athletic, but raw outfielder, would take a long time to produce by showing a much better feel to hit over his first year-plus of pro ball. His move to High-A in 2021, however, wasn’t nearly as successful, as he regressed and finished with a .600 OPS in a 71-game season that was shortened by a leg injury. For much of the time he was on the field with Tri-City, Adams looked lost at the plate. He didn’t have much of an approach, striking out in 37.8 percent of his plate appearances. There’s plenty of raw power to tap into, but he’ll need to tamper his free-swinging ways to work better counts and give him a better chance to get to it. As he struggled, Adams tinkered with his swing too much and needs some clarity and consistency in terms of his gameplan. There’s no doubt about Adams’ athleticism, and he’s continuing to learn to use his top-of-the-scale speed to his advantage on the basepaths. It certainly helps him be a plus defender in center field, where he will be able to play long-term. His future is tied into his hit tool; if the 22-year-old can commit to and stick with a more refined approach, his tools will carry him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Angels selected Jordyn Adams in the first round of the 2018 Draft and went over slot to sign him away from playing both baseball and football at the University of North Carolina, many felt it would take the premium athlete’s raw tools a while to show up in terms of production on a professional diamond. But while he hasn’t come close to reaching his very high ceiling, he showed a more advanced feel for the game than many two-sport stars exhibit by playing well during his first full season of pro ball in 2019 and taking a very big step forward as one of the youngest players at the Angels’ alternate site in 2020. A quick-twitch athlete, Adams showed off an advanced approach at the plate to go along with all of his raw tools during his first full season, one that led to a 11.6 percent walk rate. That carried over to the alternate site, making quick adjustments to the highest level he’d ever faced. He made strides in tapping into his raw power, with it showing up in alternate site games, and has the chance to tap into at least average in-game pop in the future. Some think he eventually could be power over hit when all is said and done. Adams is one of the fastest players in the Minors and he’s continuing to learn how to use that skill to be a threat on the bases. He’s also gone from being an outfielder who made errors early in his first full season and outran mistakes to one who is a plus defender making highlight-reel plays in center. There’s an up arrow next to his name as he plays all of the 2021 season at age 21.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants dominated the international market in the 1950s but have had little success since, with Pablo Sandoval and Camilo Doval their only homegrown All-Stars to come from that source in the last 60-plus years. They have hopes that Luciano will herald a reversal in fortune after signing for $2.6 million as the top middle infielder in the 2018 crop. Despite losing 2020 to the pandemic and dealing with back issues in '22 and '23, the Dominican native needed just 280 games in the Minors before making his big league debut at age 21 last July. Few players have more bat speed than Luciano, whose electric right-handed stroke produces huge exit velocities and plus-plus raw power to all fields. He'll use the entire field and work his share of walks, but he's also an extremely aggressive hitter whose plate discipline has wavered as he has rushed through the Minors. He pummeled lefties but struggled against breaking balls from righties last season, and he also had difficulty avoiding chasing changeups out of the strike zone. Though San Francisco is counting on Luciano to win its shortstop job in 2024, most evaluators outside the organization think he's better suited for third base or right field. He has solid arm strength but just fringy speed and range at short, where he's a bit error-prone and an average defender at best. But if his power translates as expected, he'll be a star no matter where he plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top middle infielder available in the 2018 international class, Luciano has demonstrated electric power since signing for $2.6 million out of the Dominican Republic. Perennially one of the youngest players in his leagues, Luciano has looked raw at times against older pitching but the only thing that really has slowed him was a back injury that limited him to 57 full-season games in 2022. He still posted a .798 OPS with 10 homers as a 20-year-old in High-A. Luciano's most notable asset is his lightning-fast bat speed from the right side of the plate, which produces plus-plus raw power to all fields. While he looks to do damage and can get overly aggressive, he does use the entire field and will accept walks when pitchers decline to challenge him. He'll always be a power-over-hit guy but his natural ability and aptitude for making adjustments could mean that he's a .270 hitter with 35 homers per season. Though Luciano has a strong arm and a high baseball IQ, most scouts outside the organization believe he'll have to move off shortstop. He has fringy speed and range that are better suited for third base or right field, where he could be a solid defender. His offensive game will profile at any position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top-rated middle infielder in the 2018 international crop, Luciano signed for $2.6 million out of the Dominican Republic. He reached the short-season Northwest League as a 17-year-old in his 2019 pro debut, then jumped to full-season ball last year and matched his age with 19 homers between Low-A and High-A. He scuffled against more advanced pitching as the youngest player in the Arizona Fall League, though his huge raw power was still apparent. Luciano generates electric bat speed from the right side of the plate and excels at hitting the ball hard and in the air. He does a nice job of using the opposite field and will take his share of walks, but he also can get overly aggressive at times and get himself out by chasing pitches. Though he'll always be a power-over-hit guy, he has enough natural ability to hit for a solid average once he matures. Despite plus arm strength and a high baseball IQ, Luciano probably won't stay at shortstop. The Giants will give him every chance to do so, but his speed and range are fringy. The good news is that he has the tools to play a solid third base or right field and the bat to be a superstar at either position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following two years of international spending restrictions after signing Lucius Fox for $6 million in 2015, the Giants came out of the penalty box and were able to land Luciano for $2.6 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2018. The top-rated middle infielder in that year's international class, he came straight to the United States for his pro debut in 2019 and batted .302/.417/.564 while reaching the short-season Northwest League at age 17. He spent last year getting exposed to much more experienced pitching at San Francisco's alternate training site and getting more reps in instructional league. Luciano's bat speed and raw power rank among the best in the Minors and stand out in particular for a middle infielder. He has a lightning-fast right-handed stroke with loft and his strength continues to increase as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame. He also has the hitting ability to get the most out of his pop, already showing a willingness to use the entire field and take walks when opponents pitch around him. In addition to his offensive promise, Luciano also offers plus arm strength, a high baseball IQ and good actions at shortstop. There's still some question as to whether he can remain at short because he has fringy speed and could lose a step as he gets more physical, but the worst-case scenario is that he shifts to third base or right field. He has the tools to be a solid defender at either spot and his bat makes him a potential superstar anywhere he plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams attended baseball powerhouse Rancho Bernardo High School in the San Diego area, but scouts felt he needed to add strength to raise his offensive profile and that college would allow him to develop. While he was taken by the Yankees in the 32nd round in 2017, he did head on to Arizona State. After an ordinary freshman year, he took a nice step forward as a sophomore, then followed that up with a strong summer on the Cape and for Team USA. Even in high school, Williams showed the ability to control the strike zone and make consistent contact from the right side of the plate. He doesn't swing and miss much, and walked more than he struck out during his sophomore year. While power will never be a huge part of his game, he has added some strength and showed extra-base ability last year with the Sun Devils and with wood in his hands for USA Baseball. He's not a burner, but he runs better than average and he has a good first step defensively. With above-average hands, range and ability to throw on the run and from different angles, he should have no problem staying at shortstop long term. Williams reminds some in the area of Kevin Newman, the University of Arizona shortstop who went in the first round of the 2015 Draft and is now the Pirates starter at the position. Williams has the chance to also be an everyday player at the premium position at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 After parts of two seasons pitching in Cuba as a teenager, Hernandez left for Mexico for a chance to make it to the big leagues. He eventually was able to sign with the Braves for $190,000 in September 2017 and went straight to full-season ball in 2018, brushing off a long layoff to pitch across two levels of Class A ball. He was dominant in a return to the Florida State League in 2019, but had trouble throwing strikes in the Arizona Fall League that fall. After pitching well at instructs in 2020, he was able to get some work in the Mexican Winter League. A 5-foot-10 right-hander, Hernandez fits the power short reliever profile perfectly. His fastball sits easily in the mid-90s and hits 98-99 mph consistently, thrown with excellent riding life. He backs that up with a slider that flashes plus with bite when it’s tight enough, though it can get loopy at times and he can have trouble landing it in the strike zone. Hernandez has had trouble with his control on and off since signing with the Braves, but he threw strikes fairly consistently during his time at instructs. He doesn’t need pinpoint command for him to get to the big leagues, and with the improvements with his slider, he could get some high-leverage innings in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Frelick excelled in football and hockey at Lexington (Mass.) High School but went to Boston College for baseball. The move paid off after his breakout junior year, when he parlayed a .359 average and 1.002 OPS into becoming the 15th overall pick by the Brewers in the 2021 Draft. The left-handed hitter had one of the best first full seasons of anyone in his class as he climbed from High-A to Triple-A while pushing his average up and his K rate down at each stop up the ladder. He hit .365/.435/.508 while fanning only 7.4 percent of the time during his 46-game Triple-A stint with Nashville. The former Eagle has shown stellar plate discipline dating back to his college days, and with a short left-handed swing, he can turn on pitches in any spot of the zone. Those bat-to-ball skills come in handy for a player with plus-plus speed, and Frelick can beat out infield dribblers or pick up extra bases on balls to the gaps. That last part is important because, while Frelick is fairly strong for his size, he hasn’t shown power yet, and he may not have the over-the-fence pop to challenge for 15 homers when he reaches the Majors. A former ACC Defensive Player of the Year, Frelick can be a fit in center because of his speed, but he is still working on his reads and routes. Since he's debuted with the Brewers in July, he's actually played more right field in deference to fellow rookie Joey Wiemer, who has been a great defender up the middle, and he's exhibited better arm strength from that corner than was expected when he first entered pro ball. Frelick's ability to put the ball in play and bring energy to the lineup has helped energize a Milwaukee hitting corps that needed the boost.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Listed at 5-foot-9, Frelick went undrafted out of Lexington (Mass.) High School, where he also won Massachusetts' Gatorade Football Player of the Year award in 2017-18 and excelled in hockey. He headed to Boston College, where he quickly grabbed scouts’ attention by hitting .367/.447/.513 with 18 steals in 39 games as a freshman before undergoing knee surgery. He didn’t perform at the same level during his pandemic-shortened season, but was a force as a junior, finishing with a .359 average and a 1.002 OPS. Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 11 Draft prospect, Frelick went to Milwaukee at No. 15 overall and signed for $4 million. The organization sent him to three affiliates (Rookie, Low-A, High-A), and he posted a combined slash line of .329/.414/.466 with 12 steals in 35 games. Frelick’s athleticism remains a big part of his game. His best grades are reserved for his plus-plus speed that’s been put to good use on the basepaths at every level. The left-handed slugger exhibits impressive contact ability and discipline, having earned a 50/60 K/BB ratio in college and a 25/21 in the Minors. That approach drives his impressive ability to pick up hits because while he’s stronger than his frame might indicate, he doesn’t show a ton of in-game power. Most of his future extra-base hits could come as products of his speed picking up an additional bag on balls to the outfield. The former Eagle saw some time in the corners in college but moved to center for good in 2021, earning ACC Defensive Player of the Year honors. He might continue to improve defensively as he gets more used to the routes required to play up the middle. With his offensive skill set, he could be Milwaukee’s leadoff man of the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wolf spent four seasons at West Virginia, returning for a final year in 2021 after not getting drafted during the pandemic-shortened 2020 campaign. He had a huge year for the Mountaineers and was a quality senior sign for the Padres in the fourth round, picking up a $300,000 bonus. After spending most of his first full season at High-A Fort Wayne, he was with Double-A San Antonio in 2023 when he got called up for a one-start debut in July and then got traded to the Pirates in the deal for Rich Hill and Ji-Man Choi. He finished the year with Double-A Altoona, was designated for assignment in late March and traded back to the Padres in April. While none of Wolf’s offerings register as truly plus, the combination of his feel for mixing pitches and the funky, long levers that create deception have made him effective. That said, a velocity jump of some sort would give him a better chance of finding a role as a big league starter. His fastball averaged 89 mph in 2023 and he’s touched 94 mph, but fatigue at the end of the year sapped him of a few ticks. If he can get to consistently sitting 91-93 mph with his elite extension, he could be in business. Both Wolf’s upper-70s sweeping slider and his softer north-south curve play well off his fastball. He’s continued to work on his changeup, but it needs a little more separation from the heater and more depth, something that would help him even out what’s been an unkind righty-lefty split in terms of right-handed hitters’ numbers. He throws a ton of strikes, and if some added strength to his 6-foot-7 frame adds some oomph to his stuff, he could be a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wolf had a 1.05 ERA with 27 strikeouts in 25 2/3 innings as a junior before that spring season ended early due to the pandemic, and without a larger sample of success, the southpaw went unselected that summer. After he punched out 104 in 89 frames as a senior, Wolf went in the fourth round a year later and signed for $300,000. He spent much of his first full season at High-A Fort Wayne, posting a 4.01 ERA with 134 K’s in 119 innings, and made two late Double-A starts to top off his 2022. He spent the year back in San Antonio, earning a one-start callup for his big league debut in July before being sent to the Pirates as the top prospect in return for Rich Hill and Ji-Man Choi. Despite standing in at 6-foot-7, Wolf doesn’t flash huge velocity, sitting in the 88-92 mph range. However, he can make for an uneasy at-bat with the way he stays in almost constant motion on the mound before firing in from a low arm slot. The sinking motion on the heater has traditionally made it play better lower, but the Padres have worked with Wolf on throwing higher in the zone in line with modern practices, leading to the solid K rates the past two seasons. His sweeping slider and vertical curveball are his two actual above-average offerings, both playing well off the heater, while he’s worked to establish a more consistent changeup. Because he’s more reliant on the breakers, Wolf posted harsh righty-lefty splits last season – 16 of his 17 homers allowed came against opposite-side hitters – and that’ll be a concern. Despite the movement, he could still throw enough strikes to provide starting depth for the Pirates.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s not often a 28-year old is considered a prospect, but Winans has gone the unconventional path throughout his career. He started in junior college, then moved on to pitch for two years for Campbell before joining the Mets as a 17th-round pick in 2018. He served as a reliever for a pair of seasons, reaching Double-A in 2021, before the Braves took him in the Minor League phase of the Rule 5 Draft that December. He transitioned to a starting role in 2022 and pitched extremely well in the Triple-A Gwinnett rotation in 2023, leading to his first big league callup at age 27. There’s nothing flashy about what the 6-foot-2 right-hander does, but he’s managed to make it work thanks to an advanced feel for his entire repertoire. His fastball is below-average from a velocity standpoint, sitting around 89 mph and topping out at 92, but his sinking two-seamer gets a lot of groundball outs, and he has a four-seamer as well. His best pitch is a plus changeup that gets both weak contact on the ground and misses bats. He has a 79-80 mph sweeping slider as well that can get hitters to chase. Winans’ ability to land all of his offerings for strikes and to keep hitters off-balance helps him pitch beyond his raw stuff. He’s already shown the ability to provide starting depth for the big league staff with the belief that he could handle a No. 5 spot should the opportunity arise.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After working out for teams as an infielder in the Dominican Republic, Berroa shifted to the mound in 2016 and shifted to the Twins for $200,000 in July. He since has been traded three times, going to the Giants in 2019 as part of a package for Sam Dyson, to the Mariners in 2022 for Donovan Walton and to the White Sox in February along with outfield prospect Zach DeLoach and a supplemental second-round pick in exchange for Gregory Santos. He has a very similar profile to Santos and dominated Double-A and made his big league debut with two scoreless outings after moving to the bullpen full-time in 2023. Though he's far from physically imposing at 5-foot-11, Berroa can overmatch hitters with a pair of power pitches. He throws his upper-80s slider about 60 percent of the time, and it gets a lot of empty swings and chases while showing tight break at times and more depth at others. His four-seam fastball sits at 95-98 and touches 100 with armside run, though it can straighten out at times and get hittable. Berroa struggled as a starter because he lacked feel for a changeup he since has scrapped and struggled to provide consistent strikes. He still battles the zone because he has an effortful delivery that he struggles to repeat. He should claim a role in Chicago's bullpen this year, and how much he can improve his control will determine if he'll eventually reach his ceiling as a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Berroa originally signed with the Twins for $200,000 as an infielder out of the Dominican Republic but never got a professional at-bat before converting to the mound. He has been traded three times: to the Giants in 2019 as part of a deal for Sam Dyson, to the Mariners in 2022 for Donovan Walton and to the White Sox along with outfield prospect Zach DeLoach and a supplemental second-round pick in February for Gregory Santos. Berroa moved to the bullpen full-time in 2023 and carved up Double-A hitters before making his big league debut with a pair of scoreless appearances in Seattle. Berroa’s heater sits in the mid-90s and has touched 99-100 mph with arm-side run, and the slider sits at 82-85 mph with a shorter, cutter-like shape. Both generate a ton of whiffs and groundouts. He also had an ineffective changeup that he scrapped after becoming a reliever. Though Berroa is athletic, he never has provided consistent strikes, averaging five walks per nine innings throughout his career and giving up free passes to three of the eight big leaguers he faced. He has the stuff to handle a high-leverage role for the White Sox if he does a better job of locating his pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marlowe’s ETA very well could’ve been 2022 had the Mariners included him on their postseason roster, a legitimate consideration after he traveled to Toronto for the AL Wild Card Series. Ultimately, they deemed that the pressure of debuting on such a grand stage would’ve outweighed his potential contributions, so they opted against it. But the calculus underscored how much they value the outfielder -- and that he almost certainly will contribute in ‘23. After considering a career in biology, Marlowe turned his baseball trajectory around with a stellar 2021 in which he crushed 26 homers and was one of only two Minor Leaguers to drive in more than 100 runs, earning the Ken Griffey Jr. Minor League Hitter of the Year Award. He followed that up with another 23 homers in ‘22 while swiping 42 bases, tangible evidence to the front office’s assertion that he’s one of the system’s best runners. For a prospect that flew under the radar at a smaller school, Marlowe continues to show that he has all the real tools. This will be his age-26 season, which dings him a bit, but he could be a legitimate fourth outfielder in the Majors, especially for a solid lefty hitter against righty pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marlowe wowed everyone in the Mariners’ front office -- and even himself -- with a stellar 2021 in which he hit .275/.368/.566 (.935 OPS) with 26 homers, and he was the only Minor Leaguer to drive in more than 100 runs. He also stole 24 bases, making him the first Seattle prospect with a 20-20 season since Jarred Kelenic in 2019. For all those efforts, he was named the Mariners' Ken Griffey Jr. Minor League Hitter of the Year for ‘21. Marlowe has had as rapid a rise as any player in Seattle's system. He advanced from Low-A Modesto to Triple-A Tacoma last season, just two years after the club selected him in the 20th round out of the University of West Georgia, where he was on a fast track to becoming a doctor after graduating cum laude with a 3.87 GPA from the University of West Georgia. Yet he just kept hitting. From the left side of the plate, Marlowe has continued to add strength to his 6-foot-1, 210-pound frame, which explains the power spike. He’s still working on translating that athleticism to his glove in the outfield. On the older side, entering his age-24 season, Marlowe’s ceiling is likely a fourth or fifth outfielder in the big leagues, which perhaps could come sooner than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Speas owned one of the most electric arms in the 2016 Draft but carried so much reliever risk that he dropped to Texas at the end of the second round. He blew out his elbow and had Tommy John surgery in June 2018, and he left baseball after walking 52 batters in 30 2/3 innings in 2021. He regained his love for the game while spending a year as a high school coach, rejoined the Rangers last February and climbed his way to the big leagues, where he walked five, struck out four and allowed three runs in two innings. Chicago claimed him on waivers in October. It's easy to dream on Speas' pure stuff, starting with an explosive fastball that averages 98 mph and touches 102 with carry that makes it almost impossible to hit up in the zone. His most effective pitch is a sweeping slider that parks at 90 mph and peaks at 94. His most-used offering last year was a harder cutter that tops out at 98. Though Speas is extremely athletic, he never has been able to maintain a consistent arm slot or keep his delivery in sync on a regular basis. He threw only 46 percent of his fastballs for strikes last year and has averaged 7.7 walks per nine innings through his first six pro seasons. The rebuilding White Sox can give him more opportunity and patience than the defending World Series champion Rangers, and his arm is worth the gamble.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Priester was one of the best high school pitchers in the 2019 Draft, one who played multiple sports at his Illinois school, but the Pirates liked his upside and feel for pitching enough to take him in the first round of the 2019 Draft. After a brief summer debut, he had to wait until 2021 to really get going and he led his league in ERA and went to the Futures Game in that first full season. He was slowed in 2022 by an oblique injury and didn’t make his debut until June, but he still managed to pitch his way to Triple-A and then made up for lost innings in the Arizona Fall League. While the projectable Priester hasn’t quite taken the big steps forward stuff-wise some might have expected, he’s shown that his legitimate four-pitch mix can get hitters out in a number of ways. The right-hander, who will be just 22 for nearly all of the 2023 season, has plenty of time for more velocity to come. His fastball touched 97 mph in 2022 and averaged just over 93. His two-seamer features plenty of sink and has led to a ton of ground-ball outs and he also has a four-seamer he can throw up in the zone to change eye levels. His curve is still his best pitch, a high-spin upper-70s breaker that misses a ton of bats, and he also has a low-to-mid 80s slider as he continues to fold in a mid-80s changeup. Priester is super-athletic on the mound and at times has shown he can be a very efficient strike-thrower, something that will only improve with more reps at the upper levels. Even with his missed development time, he’s knocking on the big league door at a very young age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Typically when a high school pitcher -- especially one from a cold-weather state who played multiple sports -- is taken in the first round of the Draft, there’s a healthy dose of patience that comes along with watching his development. That should certainly have been the case with Priester, the 2019 first-rounder from the Illinois prep ranks, given that there was no competitive 2020 season. But word of his advancement at the Pirates’ alternate site in 2020, coupled with dominant stuff in instructional league play that fall, created a ton of buzz. His first full season was a little up-and-down, but he still led the High-A East in ERA and went to the Futures Game. He was slowed by an oblique issue at the end of Spring Training in 2022, keeping him from making his Double-A debut for more than a month. The Pirates actually feel Priester’s 2021 couldn’t have gone better, scuffles and all, when considering his age (20 for all of the ’21 season) and the fact he’d never come close to the 97 2/3 innings he threw for Greensboro. While his stuff might have backed up a bit, he still showed a very strong four-pitch mix, starting with a fastball that sat mid-90s for most of the year. He can sink it, leading to a lot of ground-ball outs, and throw his four-seamer up in the zone. He has two distinct breaking balls: a plus curve with high spin rates and a newer slider that should be at least average. He’s continuing to work on mixing in his changeup consistently. Priester’s athleticism on the mound points to a future of strike-throwing. The Pirates feel the young right-hander learned valuable lessons about handling fatigue, sticking with his routine and getting outs without his best stuff. All of that still points to him having the chance to be a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before the Pirates took Priester in the first round of the 2019 Draft, No. 18 overall, the last time an Illinois high school player had been taken in the first round was when Mike Foltynewicz was the No. 19 overall pick in the 2010 Draft, taken by the Astros. A two-sport star as a prepster, Priester’s athleticism was not only on display during his pro debut in 2019 but also during his time at the end of the alternate training site and in instructional league play in 2020. It’s clear Priester used his first offseason to add strength and the stuff he displayed in 2020 had taken a step forward. Over the summer and fall, he was up to 98 mph, averaging a touch over 97 mph, a four-seamer thrown with a spin rate north of 2,200 rpm in a matchup against Phillies 2020 first-rounder Mick Abel at instructs. He also features a sinking two-seamer that gets ground ball outs. He worked on distinguishing between two breaking balls, a plus low-80s curveball with 2900 rpm spin rate metrics and a slider that could eventually be at least above-average. He has growing feel for his changeup as well. Big, broad and athletic, it’s easy to dream on Priester’s physicality and stuff. The work he did in 2020 on how and when to use all of his pitches and in sharpening all his offerings has as big of an up arrow next to his name as any pitching prospect in baseball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The three-team trade that sent Joe Musgrove to San Diego in 2021 netted the Pirates All-Star closer David Bednar, but there’s a good chance that getting Rodríguez from the Mets in the deal will be the real steal. Signed for just $10,000 by the Mets in 2018, Rodríguez didn’t reach full-season ball until 2021 and immediately took a leap forward in terms of offensive production, something that continued in a huge way with a 2022 season that saw him play across three levels of the Minors and be named the catcher on the MLB Pipeline Prospect Team of the Year. A switch-hitter, Rodríguez is now looking like he has the chance to be a true impact bat in the middle of a big league lineup. Even as he’s moved up the ladder, he’s continued to show a very good approach at the plate, drawing walks (11.4 percent BB rate in his two full seasons in the Pirates' organization) and limiting the swings-and-misses (18.4 K rate in 2021-22 combined). The power continues to come, and after hitting 25 homers and slugging .590 in 2022, it’s looking like he should have at least above-average pop in the big leagues. More athletic than most catchers, Rodríguez has seen time at both second base and the outfield. His flexibility is a plus, even if it initially slowed his catching skills from developing, but the Pirates noticed a marked improvement with more consistent reps in 2022, especially with his pop times and his throwing. He’ll get most of his time behind the plate this year, but he will still move around some, showing average defense in the outfield and a bit below that at second.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez was a little bit older than most international free agents when he signed at age 18 with the Mets for just $10,000 in July 2018. He spent parts of two summers in the Dominican Summer League before coming to the United States and the Gulf Coast League in 2019. The Pirates noticed his upside and athleticism back then and during his time in instructional league play in 2020, managing to get him from the Mets in the three-team deal that sent Joe Musgrove to the Padres in January 2021. Rodriguez’s abilities on both sides of the ball in his full-season debut, and his first with the Pirates, was one of the biggest revelations of the 2021 season. A switch-hitting catcher, Rodriguez has shown a solid feel to hit and an idea of what he’s doing from both sides of the plate since he signed. Not only did that continue in Low-A in 2021, the power started to show up more consistently without sacrificing any of his plate discipline or approach, especially as the year went on, with an OPS of .970 from July 1 through the end of the season. His willingness to draw walks (11.1 percent) and knack for contact (17.7 percent K rate) should help him maximize his offensive tools. Rodriguez was equally impressive behind the plate, where his athleticism and agility play well and he’s shown excellent catch and throw skills. His maturity and presence might stand out even more than his tools, so while he’s athletic enough to play the outfield and first base, committing to him as a backstop might maximize his value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez joined the Mets organization for just $10,000 at the start of the 2018-19 international signing period and he immediately set out to outperform the moderate expectations that come with a bonus of that size, making a nice transition from the Dominican Summer League to the Gulf Coast League in 2019. He showed off his athleticism with the Mets during instructional league play in 2020, then headed to the Pirates in the three-team deal that sent Joe Musgrove to the Padres and Joey Lucchesi to the Mets, giving the Pirates their first catcher in the top 30 since 2017. The switch-hitting Rodriguez has already showed off an advanced approach at the plate, with impressive contact skills and the ability to use all fields. There’s more extra-base pop from the left side right now, with good raw power that should show up as he matures physically. He’s hit-over-power right now, but there could be a lot more juice to come in the future. Super-athletic, Rodriguez has played first base and the outfield in addition to catching in games. He's also gotten reps elsewhere, but his value is obviously higher if he can stick behind the plate. He’s very agile back there with a strong enough arm that will get better as he focuses on the craft more. He has a long way to go, but the ingredients for an everyday catcher might be in there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years at Yavapai, a junior college in Arizona, Encarnacion-Strand moved on to Oklahoma State and put up big numbers there, hitting 15 homers and posting an OPS north of 1.100. The Twins thought they had a fourth-round steal on their hands as he posted a 1.022 OPS during his brief pro debut after being drafted in 2021, then hit his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season (.987 OPS). They weren’t the only ones paying attention; the Reds liked his bat enough to make sure he was included in the return for Tyler Mahle at last year’s Trade Deadline, then watched their new acquisition continue to rake after the trade. The Reds knew they were getting someone with very impressive raw power who was already tapping into it, with Encarnacion-Strand finishing his 2022 breakout with 32 homers, a .587 slugging percentage and 114 RBIs to boot. What impressed them even more was a better feel to hit than many expected when he entered pro ball. Sure, he swings and misses some, with a K rate of 25.5 percent in 2022 and he can cut down on his chasing of soft stuff out of the zone, but there’s an advanced approach here. He uses all fields and can hit the ball out everywhere, showing a willingness to go the other way with two strikes. Encarnacion-Strand has more than enough arm strength to stick at third, and he’ll keep getting plenty of reps there, but the strong and physical infielder can be too stiff there at times. He’ll keep getting time at first, mostly to give the Reds options of ways to get him into the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: All Encarnacion-Strand did as an amateur was hit, spanning two seasons at Yavapai (Ariz.) College in the JUCO circuit and one year at Oklahoma State, where he was Big 12 Conference newcomer of the year after hitting .361/.442/.661 with 15 homers. He didn't slow down after the Twins selected him in the fourth round in 2021, hitting .391/.424/.598 in A-ball across 22 games in the notoriously pitcher-friendly Low-A Southeast. The bat kept coming during his first full season, and he had hit his way from High-A to Double-A shortly before being sent to the Reds as part of the return in the Tyler Mahle Trade Deadline deal. Encarnacion-Strand can chase outside the zone a little too much, perhaps borne of seeking contact and hits instead of waiting for his pitch, but he's got solid bat-to-ball skills and the ability to drive the ball hard to all fields. The results have obviously spoken for themselves throughout his amateur career and early pro career and he’s made some strides with his plate discipline and selectivity, with some mechanical adjustments with his stride also in play to help his consistency. Though he mostly played first base in his first professional season, the 22-year-old also opened eyes with his defense at the hot corner, where he moves well with his big frame and features strong instincts and angles to the ball and good hands. If he can address the plate discipline, his bat could carry him up the system, with the ability to contribute from either corner infield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2017-18 international signing period, the Phillies handed out 19 bonuses of six figures or more, topped by the $2.5 million they gave Luis Garcia. They found a bargain later on in the period, in January of 2018, when they inked Rojas for just $10K. In each of his two years of full season ball, he’s started slowly but finished well offensively, showing off his plus speed and defense at all stops. He made it to Double-A for the first time in 2022 and then finished with a strong performance in the Arizona Fall League before getting added to the 40-man roster. Rojas has shown he can be an impact player on both sides of the ball thanks to his near-top-of-the-scale speed. He’s an elite baserunner, one who stole 62 bases in 67 tries last season and then went 13-for-13 in the AFL. His speed is an obvious asset in the outfield, where he is a premium defender in center field, one who could be a Gold Glove contender because of his range, instincts and above-average arm. The young outfielder’s ceiling is tied to what advancements he can make at the plate. The right-handed hitter is very adept at making contact, striking out in just 16.6 percent of his plate appearances entering 2023. He’s too often been content to hit the ball on the ground and use his legs to get on base, though he did get the ball in the air a bit more in 2022. The Phillies would love to see him make more hard contact, with line drives to the gaps turning into doubles and triples, to give him a real chance to be a table-setter atop a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the international signing periods typically opened in July before the pandemic, Rojas didn’t sign with the Phillies until January of 2018 and did so for just $10,000. He immediately showed he might be the biggest bargain of that 2017-18 class by putting up a .321/.421/.797 line in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and hit his way across two levels of rookie ball during his United States debut the following year. He had a solid, if unspectacular, full-season debut in 2021 until he absolutely raked after getting moved up to High-A for the final month of the season. Since signing, Rojas has shown an innate ability to make contact, and he struck out in just under 18 percent of his plate appearances in 2021. That standout skill has also been an obstacle, as he’s been too over-aggressive from the right side of the plate. He’s been working on his approach and swing decisions to keep him from not expanding the zone too much, all while learning to get the ball off the ground more. He’s made strides in getting better counts and not being content to beat the ball into the ground. Using his elite-level speed has allowed him to start tapping into his considerable raw power. That speed makes Rojas a very impressive center fielder, with plus range and instincts to go along with a strong arm, with no doubt he can stay up the middle long-term. Rojas could have been even further ahead had he not missed a year of reps because of the pandemic, but he’s the player who often gets asked about when teams call to talk trades.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017-18 international signing period has the chance to be a successful one for the Phillies at both ends of the spending spectrum. At the top end, there’s Luis Garcia and his $2.5-million bonus. At the bottom end, there’s lefty Jordi Martinez, now a Top 30 prospect, and Rojas, who jumped on the map by hitting .320 in the Dominican Summer League in 2018, then hit his way from the Gulf Coast League to the New York-Penn League during his United States debut in 2019. He was one of the top standouts during instructional league play in 2020. Rojas has already impressed with his ability to make consistent hard contact from the right side of the plate, displaying plus bat-to-ball skills along with one of the highest exit velocities in the system. Because of his knack for contact, he’s been very aggressive at the plate. While he doesn’t strike out much, he doesn’t draw walks and is still working on his overall approach so he can get to better hitters' counts and utilize his raw power more effectively. With a strong arm that works well for a corner, Rojas’ plus speed and instincts give him a very good chance to stick in center, showing the ability to play shallow and go deep with ease. He’ll keep getting time at all three outfield spots, with one of the highest ceilings in the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2021 West Coast Conference Pitcher of the Year as a senior at Gonzaga, Jacob dropped to the 16th round because scouts were concerned his low-velocity funk wouldn’t translate to the Minors. Two years after his Draft day, he made his Major League debut on July 15, 2023, and struck out Alec Bohm as his only batter faced. In between, the right-hander transitioned to a relief-only role, climbed three levels in 2022 and posted a 1.32 ERA with 32 strikeouts in 27 1/3 innings for Double-A San Antonio in '23. A minor flexor strain and UCL sprain in his right elbow limited him to only three Major League appearances last summer, but he is back healthy for this season. Throwing out of a low sidearm slot, Jacob is all about running pitches east and west with what can look like Bugs Bunny stuff. His mid-80s sinker won’t light up any radar guns, but it slices enough armside to make right-handers at least a little uncomfortable and drops enough to generate plenty of ground balls. His low-70s sweeper breaks just as hard going the other way, forcing some awkward diving swings from righties, and was his most-used pitch during his limited MLB run. A changeup also fades armside but somehow has the 11-12 mph separation to make it a potential plus pitch too. Despite all the movement, Jacob hasn’t posted a walk rate above 7.5 percent at any Minor League level because he locates to both sides of the plate so well. Entering his age-26 season, Jacob won’t be a back-end Major League option necessarily, but he’s definitely capable of getting outs as a reliever in The Show so long as his command holds.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There are funky pitchers, and then there is Jacob. A four-year hurler and 2021 West Coast Conference Pitcher of the Year at Gonzaga, Jacob fell to the 16th round in 2021 because of concerns over his lack of velocity, and he joined the Padres system with a $75,000 signing bonus. Despite those issues, he was one of the quickest risers of his Draft class, climbing from High-A to Triple-A in his first full season and ending it with an assignment to the Arizona Fall League. The bulk of Jacob’s work came at Double-A San Antonio, where he finished with a 1.83 ERA, 1.08 WHIP and 43 K’s in 34 1/3 innings as a reliever. About that lack of velo: Jacob’s fastball only sits in the upper-80s -- atypical for the modern game where bullpen arms throw harder than ever. A difficult sidearm angle, heavy sink and arm-side run make the fastball difficult to barrel, however, and it’s a better pitch than the radar gun alone will tell you. His best offering, however, is a low-70s, Bugs Bunny-esque changeup that stands out for its separation from the sinker and its own fade going down and to Jacob’s right. A slider around the same velocity dives the other way toward his glove side, and the opposite movement can have batters tied up in knots. Though Jacob is capable of filling up the strike zone, the Padres have kept him in relief roles, thus limiting how many times batters can sit on his softer stuff. Right shoulder soreness in the offseason had him delayed to start the season before he earned a Major League debut in July. A minor flexor strain and UCL sprain in his right elbow placed him on the IL soon after, but there's no denying the goofy stuff could still be useful in relief in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big league pitcher Steve Soderstrom, Tyler was one of the best high school bats in the 2020 Draft class, coming out of Steve’s alma mater, Turlock High School. The A’s went over-slot to sign him for $3.3 million at No. 26 overall and despite missing a large part of his first full season, he immediately showed off his offensive upside in 2021, then started in High-A and ended in Triple-A in 2022, mashing 29 homers and driving in 105 runs in the process. A left-handed hitter, Soderstrom has long displayed an excellent feel for the barrel and solid overall approach at the plate. He can make consistent hard contact to all fields, and his combination of strength and bat speed point to the kind of power and run production consistent with his 2022 output, with the ability to hit the ball out to all fields. His strikeout rate did tick up last year, but he spent the first month of the season playing through a thumb injury and the A’s are confident that his feel for hitting will allow him to be more consistent contact-wise as he faces better pitching more consistently. Where Soderstrom plays defensively long-term is more of a question. He has solid arm strength, and while his glove is still behind his bat, the A’s have been pleased with his progress behind the plate. He split time between first base and catcher in 2022 and that should be the case moving forward, giving the organization options to get his bat into the lineup if his blocking and receiving aren’t big league ready, not to mention the presence of Shea Langeliers ahead of him on the depth chart.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Steve Soderstrom came out of Turlock High School in Northern California, went to Fresno State and was the No. 6 overall pick by the Giants in 1993, pitching in the big leagues for them in 1996. His son Tyler went to the same high school, but instead of heading to college, in this case UCLA, he signed with the A’s for an over-slot bonus of $3.3 million as the No. 26 pick in 2020. While an oblique injury limited him to just 57 games and kept him from playing in the Arizona Fall League, he showed off his offensive tools by posting a .957 OPS and went to the Futures Game. While playing as a teenager in the Low-A West, Soderstrom showed off why he was considered one of the more advanced high school hitters in the 2020 Draft class. The left-handed hitter works counts and draws walks (10.6 percent walk rate in 2021), allowing him to drive the ball hard to all fields. There’s plenty of strength and bat speed, to the point where Soderstrom could have plus game power when all is said and done. Soderstrom entered pro ball without a ton of catching experience and that part of his game is still behind the bat, leading some to wonder if it would be better to move him to first, a position he saw some time at in 2021 and played a lot more in 2022, to let his bat advance more quickly. There’s still work to be done, but he had made some progress with his blocking and receiving, as well as using his above-average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Steve Soderstrom, a former big league pitcher who was the sixth-overall pick in the 1993 Draft by the Giants out of Fresno State, Tyler carved out his own path as one of the top high school catchers in California. Concerns from teams over whether he would sign out of high school or continue his amateur career at UCLA led to him dropping to No. 26 to the A’s, who went nearly $650,000 above pick value to sign him for $3.3 million in 2020. Soderstrom’s offense is ahead of his defense at this point. The left-handed hitting catcher has an offensive game that is quite mature for a 19-year-old, with supreme strike zone recognition and plenty of pop in his bat. Though there was talk of a potential move to third base or outfield in the future, the A’s saw a solid improvement behind the plate both at the club’s alternate site and in the instructional league and expect him to stick at catcher. How Soderstrom progresses with his blocking and game management -- two areas he is still raw in -- will determine his long-term position. He has already shown off a strong arm, which helps his cause.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2021 college season, Gelof looked like one of the more intriguing college bats in the Draft class, one who could land in the first round. He got off to a very slow start, hurting his stock, though he righted the ship as the season wore on and he landed in the second round with the A’s. He had a huge pro debut and got off to a very good start in Double-A in his first full season before a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder derailed his train. He did return and made up for lost reps in the Arizona Fall League. When he’s locked in, Gelof provides an exciting combination of approach and raw power from the right side of the plate to any lineup. His swing is a bit unorthodox, but he understands it well and he shows good knowledge of the strike zone. His strikeout rate was a bit high in 2022 (27.5 percent), but it was offset by a healthy walk rate (11.4 percent). The latter helped him get to his power more consistently, even late in the year when he was out of sync overall post-injury. While his speed is just a bit above average, he’s a good baserunner and his overall athleticism is an asset on the field. A third baseman out of college, he shifted over and played a lot of second late in the year and exclusively in the AFL, where he showed solid overall defensive skills. That should be his spot most of the time going forward, though he could see some time in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a strong finish to an uneven junior season at the University of Virginia, Gelof entered the 2021 Draft considered to have some of the best raw power of any hitter in the class, leading to his signing with the A’s for $1,157,400 as a second-round pick. That power bat immediately showed up in pro ball, as he homered seven times in 36 games and was rewarded with a call-up to Triple-A in the final week of the Minor League season. Along with power that is expected to show up even more as he progresses through the system, Gelof brings an advanced approach at the plate with strong strike zone recognition and a good understanding of his swing. While he’s not a burner, he runs well enough and has excellent instincts, making him a legitimate threat on the basepaths. Gelof’s supreme athleticism could lend to him playing multiple infield positions, though the A’s were impressed with his defense at third base, particularly his throwing arm, which had been a question mark entering the Draft due to some injuries. Also earning high praise for his confidence and presence in the clubhouse, Gelof has the makings of a player who could soon find himself on the fast track to Oakland.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a journey since Uribe signed for only $85,000 as an 18-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018. His stock began to soar at Single-A Carolina in 2021, when he used his elite velo to fan 52 in 33 2/3 relief innings, but that campaign was limited by a torn meniscus. Following a trip to the Arizona Fall League, he was about to pop again at Double-A Biloxi in 2022, only to suffer another torn meniscus in his left knee in April that required season-ending surgery. A second (and even more productive) trip to the AFL pushed him onto the 40-man roster last November, and he worked in three more appearances in the Dominican Winter League. The 6-foot-2 right-hander is a prospect first and foremost because of his fastball. It was back to sitting 98-99 mph during his Arizona Fall League stint, and he had eight of the 11 hardest pitches thrown in the showcase circuit (in games measured by Statcast) -- all at 100-plus mph. He has been known to touch 103 in the past too, when healthy. Uribe has plenty of confidence in his upper-80s slider with two-plane break and will sometimes lean on it more than the heater because he can land it better in the zone. Therein lies the rub. Like many elite fireballers, Uribe has a mixed history when it comes to throwing strikes. However, he walked only two batters (while fanning 14) in 10 innings during his AFL return, giving hope that he may have turned a corner in that department. His high-tempo delivery may keep him from ever being truly average there, but there’s upside as a high-leverage arm on the quality of his stuff alone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed Uribe for $85,000 just a month after his 18th birthday in July 2018 and moved him straight to the Dominican Summer League. His first two seasons, which included trips to the Arizona and Pioneer Leagues, brought uninspiring results (28 strikeouts, 21 walks in 18/13 innings; multiple 9-plus ERAs), but the right-hander’s stock began to shoot up as he added strength with the velocity to match. He posted a 4.01 ERA with 52 strikeouts in 33 2/3 frames for Low-A Carolina in 2021, missing some time with a torn meniscus, and he ended the year in the Arizona Fall League, where he fanned 16 in nine innings but also walked 17. Unfortunately, he suffered another torn meniscus in his left knee early in 2022 and underwent season-ending surgery on April 26 to address the issue. It’s the velo that will always pop for the 6-foot-2 righty, when he is healthy. There were outings when Uribe sat 100-101 mph last season, and he threw 13 of the 14 hardest-thrown pitches of the 2021 AFL as measured by Statcast, all above 98.9 mph. His high-80s slider, which some systems call a cutter, can actually be his best pitch some days, too, and he sometimes relies on that over the heater in tough situations because of his ability to land it in the zone. He used to mix in a changeup, but the fastball and slider have become almost co-primary pitches. It’s going to come down to control. Like many young pitchers, Uribe can chase radar-gun readings and overthrow, causing him to miss the zone with regularity. Considering his delivery is pretty smooth without any major red flags, it might just take a change in mentality and approach for Uribe to improve and find even average control. If that (no small task) happens and everything else returns post-surgery, he could be impactful in the back end of a Major League bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Uribe signed out of the Dominican Republic as an 18-year-old in 2018 for $85,000, so he was eligible to finish that year with the club’s Dominican Summer League team, then came stateside in ‘19 and logged limited innings in the Arizona League and the Pioneer League.
