His mid-80s slider can be devastating with two-plane break that makes it effective against left-handers and right-handers. He relies heavily on those two pitches but also will mix in a low-80s curveball and an upper-80s changeup that gets too firm and has modest fade. Even though he has added strength, Dubin is still shorter and skinnier than a typical starter, and the effort in his delivery creates additional concerns about his ability to hold up in that role. He provides a decent amount of strikes but his control and command are average at best, another reason that he'll likely wind up in a big league bullpen. His fastball/slider combination can be electric when he's healthy, so he could succeed as a high-leverage reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dubin concluded a nomadic college career that included one year at Erie (N.Y.) CC and two at Buffalo by spending his 2018 senior season at Georgetown (Ky.), where he won NAIA all-America honors and became the school's first Draft pick (13th round) in 21 years. Signed for $1,000, he boosted his stock tremendously in his first full pro season, when he led the high Class A Carolina League with 132 strikeouts in just 98 2/3 innings. He continued to open eyes at Houston's alternate site and pitched his way into the club's 40-man postseason pool, though he was not on the active roster for the playoffs. Dubin has added 25 pounds and done a better job of incorporating his lower half in his delivery since turning pro, and his four-seam fastball has gone from sitting around 90 mph to parking at 93-97 mph and approaching triple digits. His mid-80s slider is an even better pitch, featuring so much movement that it tied up left-handers and right-handers alike in the lower levels of the Minors. He also has added power to his curveball and is working to improve his changeup. Because Dubin is smaller and skinnier than a typical starter and has some effort in his delivery, there are concerns about his ability to hold up as a starter. To remain in the rotation, he'll also have to upgrade his fringy control and command. The Astros could choose to expedite his path to the big leagues as a multi-inning reliever who has the fastball and slider to succeed in high-leverage situations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a fifth-year senior in 2021, Hartwig led Miami (Ohio) pitchers -- a group that included 2021 first-rounder Sam Bachman -- in innings pitched (73 1/3) and finished with a 3.42 ERA and 82 strikeouts, but he went unselected in that July's 20-round Draft. The Mets snagged him as their first non-drafted free-agent signing and moved him to the bullpen. Hartwig led Mets Minor Leaguers with 13 saves and finished with a 1.75 ERA, 1.09 WHIP and 83 K’s in 56 2/3 frames across all four full-season levels in 2022. He added seven more appearances in the Arizona Fall League to end the season. The 6-foot-5 right-hander’s 35.5 percent strikeout rate led Mets Minor Leaguers with at least 50 frames in 2022, and a big reason for that was his low-80s slider with good vertical and horizontal break. The pitch could dive away from lunging right-handers or cut sharply to the back foot of a lefty hitter, and it was actually the latter who struggled most against Hartwig, hitting just .150 with a 38.5 percent K rate against him in the regular season. His 93-95 mph fastball played closer to average, but sinking action on it helped him keep healthy ground-ball rates and allow just one homer over his 39 appearances. His mid-80s changeup lags behind the other two in usage but offers at least something of a third option. Hartwig’s walk rates got worse the higher he climbed as hitters knew to lay off the breaking stuff out of the zone. The slider is still so good it’s worth the risk going for that chase, and it has the former RedHawk on the doorstep of the New York bullpen entering 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Balazovic started his pro career as the Twins’ fifth-round pick in the 2016 Draft out of the Canadian high school ranks, he was a projectable right-hander who quickly gained strength and put his name on the map as a Top 100 prospect who went to the Futures Game in 2019. He was added to the 40-man roster after the 2020 shutdown and he pitched pretty well in Double-A in 2021, though a back issue kept him from pitching until June. A knee injury in 2022 sidelined him until May and he clearly wasn’t ready for Triple-A as he struggled for most of the year. He did finish the year well, but was delayed building off of that in 2023 when he suffered a broken jaw in an off-field altercation at the start of Spring Training. When Balazovic first returned from his knee injury, he was not as physical as he had been and his stuff regressed across the board. His upswing at the end included an uptick of his velocity in the right direction, though his average fastball dipped from 96 mph in 2021 to about 94 mph. His power breaking ball can still miss bats but wasn’t as sharp, and his changeup also got hit hard. Not only did Balazovic’s walk rate jump, his command within the zone wasn’t sharp, leading to him giving up 13 hits per nine innings in 2022. All of the numbers looked a bit better in the season’s final month and the hope is that once he returns to the mound in 2023, he can get back to looking like he'll be headed to the middle of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best prospect in Canada from the 2016 Draft class, Balazovic inspired the Twins to take him in the fifth round and go over slot value to sign him. Then, he was a thin, super-projectable high school right-hander. He’s made steady progress since, making his full-season debut in 2018, pitching across two levels of A-ball and going to the Futures Game in 2019 and pitching well at the Twins’ alternate training site and in instructs in 2020 to earn a spot on the 40-man roster. Although a back issue kept him from making his Double-A debut until June 2021, he still managed to miss bats while setting a career high in innings pitched. He was slowed out of the gate in 2022, this time by a knee injury, and never really got on track. As Balazovic has advanced, he’s gotten stronger and thrown consistently harder. That trend continued once he returned to the mound in 2021, with a fastball that averaged 96 mph in Double-A and has good life up in the zone to miss bats. His power breaking ball is also harder and flashes plus to give him another swing-and-miss offering. Balazovic started throwing a splitter as his changeup, with good results, a pitch with more depth off his fastball. Balazovic’s walk rate went up in 2021, and his command in the zone suffered a bit, leading to a higher hit rate, partially because he’s learning to harness his now firmer stuff. But he repeats his delivery well, and there’s deception, making for a tough at-bat. Further refinement of his splitter to go along with a return to his excellent command should allow him to reach his mid-rotation ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the past 10 years, there have been five pitchers drafted and signed in the top five rounds of the Draft out of Canada. Only one, the Braves’ Mike Soroka, has made it to the big leagues. Balazovic, signed as a thin, projectable high school right-hander as a fifth rounder in 2016, has the chance to be the next. After pitching across two levels of Class A ball, and in the Futures Game, in 2019, Balazovic joined the Twins’ alternate training site late in the summer of 2020, throwing well there and in instructional league play last fall, impressing enough to get added to the organization’s 40-man roster. Balazovic has add two inches in terms of height and a ton of good weight since he’s signed, with his stuff ticking up as a result. His fastball now sits consistently in the mid-90s and he can get swings and misses at the top of the zone with life on his four-seamer. When he’s down in the zone, it has good life and generates weak contact, with his high front glove side providing deception for his fastball so hitters don’t pick up the ball well. He throws a hard breaking ball that looks like a slider when he’s locked in, flashing plus and missing more bats. His changeup, once a distant third pitch, has caught up and might be a tick above-average when all is said and done. All of his stuff plays up because of his penchant for throwing strikes, with his fastball command really separating him from other young power arms. Balazovic worked hard to earn his way up to the alternate camp last summer, paving the way to the upper levels of the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 24th round doesn’t even exist anymore, but that’s where the Blue Jays grabbed Horwitz after three productive years at Radford, and he’s carried that level of success throughout the pros. Sporting a career .302 average and .407 OBP in the Minors, the 26-year-old pushed his way onto the 40-man roster in November 2022. He backed that up with his best season yet at Triple-A Buffalo, where he posted a .337/.450/.495 line with 10 homers and more walks (78) than strikeouts (72) over 107 games. He got in 15 contests with the Major League club over two separate stints in June and September. The left-handed slugger has built a reputation on his strong knowledge of the strike zone, and that’s a big reason why he thrived in Triple-A, where the automated ball-strike system helped define that zone more clearly. His .450 OBP was third-highest among full-season Minor League qualifiers. Horwitz rarely whiffed on fastballs with Buffalo and continued to show an all-fields approach that helped him pick up hits aplenty, although his swing lacks the lift that would help him push for average power production. A well-below-average runner, Horwitz has made some strides defensively at first base but has also gotten looks in left field (away from Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s shadow) as the Jays try to find a spot for his bat in the lineup. He remains a better fit at the cold corner, and given his pressing age and roster status, he’s likely a left-handed bat-first option off the bench in the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Horwitz put together three productive seasons for Radford in the Big South Conference, and while he didn’t have a flashy Draft profile, he has made the Blue Jays’ scouting crew look smart after selecting him in the 24th round in 2019. Horwitz’s NCAA experience immediately translated that summer as he split 60 games between the Appalachian and Northwest Leagues, batting .307 with an .808 OPS. Following the lost 2020 Minor League season, Horwitz spent most of 2021 at High-A Vancouver before earning a taste of Double-A, batting .294 with 12 home runs and an .862 OPS over 110 games. That included more walks (70) than strikeouts (68). Then Horwitz starred in the Arizona Fall League, where he hit .375 over 16 games. In 2022, Horwitz split 114 games between Double-A and Triple-A, batting .275 with a .391 OBP. He has one of the best plate approaches and abilities to control the strike zone in the organization. That hitting tool and plate approach will need to carry Horwitz, who is solid at first base but may not move well enough to play the outfield in the big leagues. Horwitz offers a very mature at-bat at 25, though, and should adapt quickly to Major League pitching if injuries open up an opportunity for him at some point in 2023. He profiles as a player who will continue to play up to the level he’s assigned to.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Horwitz put up some nice, consistent numbers at Radford University in the Big South, hitting .288 with 25 home runs and an .850 OPS over three seasons. The Blue Jays picked him up all the way down in the 24th round, which has proved to be one of their best selections in the ’19 Draft. Horwitz debuted that summer, hitting .330 over 51 games in the Appalachian League and getting a taste of Low-A. He kept hitting in ’21, batting .294 with 12 homers and an .862 OPS over 105 games in High-A and five in Double-A, but really broke out in the AFL. There, Horwitz hit .375 with a .944 OPS against some of baseball’s best prospects. An above-average plate approach allowed Horwitz to walk (70) more than he struck out (68) in ’21, and that’s where everything starts for him. With good control of the zone, Horwitz works his walks and hits for average, but unlocking more power will be the next step, especially for a prospect splitting time between first base and left field. Horwitz answered that bell by slugging .517 and posting a .930 OPS in 70 games at Double-A New Hampshire to open 2022 -- production that carried him to Triple-A. Without adding surplus value as a defender or runner, Horwitz’s value will be tied closely to his bat, so he'll need to keep the power coming. First base remains the primary position for Horwitz, but he’ll continue to experiment with the corner outfield. He’s earned plenty of fans within the organization with his plate approach and overall offensive improvements.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for an over-slot $247,500 in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft, Amaya quickly made an impression with his plate defense and plate discipline. He set a career high with 17 homers and reached Triple-A in 2022 before the Marlins acquired him in a trade for Miguel Rojas in January 2023. He made his big league debut over four games with Miami last June, but got designated for assignment this April and traded to the Astros for right-handed pitching prospect Valente Bellozo. Amaya is a quality defender at shortstop with smooth actions, quick and sure hands, a solid and accurate arm and a good internal clock. He has average speed but solid range and is working to enhance his first-step quickness so that he can cover more ground. He's also quite capable at second and third base. A right-handed hitter, Amaya is at his best when he keeps his stroke under control and focuses on getting on base. He added strength during the pandemic layoff, which enhanced his power but also has led to lapses where he starts hunting home runs and chasing pitches. He makes consistent contact when he swings at strikes and could provide on-base ability with 15 homers per year if he maintains a disciplined approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers signed Amaya out of a suburban Los Angeles high school for an over-slot $247,500 in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft, and his plate discipline and defense quickly made him an organization favorite. He bounced back from his worst pro season in 2021 to hit a career-best 17 homers between Double-A and Triple-A last year before the Marlins acquired him for Miguel Rojas in January. He could be Miami's shortstop of the very near future and for the long term. Amaya is most effective when he employs a controlled right-handed stroke and concentrates on getting base. He got stronger during the pandemic layoff, but his newfound power can get him into trouble when he starts hunting home runs and chasing pitches. He settled down more in 2022 and projects as a .250 hitter with 12-15 homers per season and plenty of walks. That type of production would be more than enough to make Amaya a big league regular at shortstop, because he's a quality defender. Not only does he have quick, reliable hands and a strong, accurate arm, but his high baseball IQ and nonstop energy allow him to get the most out of his physical tools. He also is an asset at second and third base and would be a useful utility man if he doesn't hit enough to play regularly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of former Dodgers middle-infield prospect Frank Amaya, Jacob signed for an above-slot $247,500 out of a suburban Los Angeles high school in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft. His keen batting eye and his glovework quickly made him an organization favorite, and he bounced back from his worst season as a pro in 2021 to hit a career-high 17 homers in 2022. The Marlins acquired him in a January deal for Miguel Rojas. Amaya walked nearly as much as he struck out in his first three pro seasons, but he got away from his approach in 2021 after homering five times that April and seeking more power. He's most effective when he employs a controlled right-handed stroke and focuses on hitting line drives and getting on base. He could hit .260 with 12-15 homers per season if he can refrain from chasing pitches; he did show more discipline in 2022. Even when he slumped, Amaya continued to provide quality glovework at shortstop. His high baseball IQ and constant energy allow him to maximize his tools and play faster than his average speed. His quick, reliable hands and a strong, accurate arm help make him a plus defender at shortstop and will serve him well in a projected utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of Frank Amaya, a middle infielder in the Dodgers system during the late 1950s, Jacob signed for an above-slot $247,500 as an 11th-rounder in 2017. He stood out at the National High School Invitational that spring but his commitment to Cal State Fullerton scared off several clubs. When he made his full-season debut in 2019, he ranked second in walks (74) and seventh in OPS (.775) in the low Class A Midwest League at age 20 and batted .563 in the high Class A California League postseason. Amaya possesses one of the best batting eyes in the system and hit .273 with nearly as many walks as strikeouts during his first three pro seasons. He has a sound right-handed swing and a mature, all-fields approach. He's making harder contact as he continues to get stronger but likely will be more of a doubles threat than a home run hitter. Amaya's high baseball IQ and nonstop energy allow him to make the most out of his tools and play faster than his average speed on the bases and in the field. He has quick, reliable hands and a strong, accurate arm, and he's the best infield defender among Dodgers prospects. He's a legitimate shortstop who also has seen action at second and third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A rare 23rd-round pick who signed out of high school, Robinson took a few years to find his footing in pro ball and started showing improved velocity heading into 2021. The improved stuff helped him post a 3.08 ERA with 62 strikeouts in 49 2/3 innings across three levels in that first post-pandemic season. He was even better last year, finishing with a 2.49 ERA and 84 K’s in 65 frames at High-A, Double-A and Triple-A while leading all Minor Leaguers with 25 saves. The Brewers added Robinson to the 40-man roster in November to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. Throwing from a near-extreme over-the-top delivery, Robinson can make for an uncomfortable at-bat with the way he puts his 93-95 mph fastball on top of hitters. Since the pandemic off year, the heater has a natural cut to it, and while it looks like a hard cutter, Robinson says it’s his natural fastball. All the same, the improvements helped fuel his 2022 successes, including a 63.2 percent ground-ball rate that was fourth-highest among 905 Minor Leaguers with at least 60 innings in 2022. He’ll also drop in a 79-82 mph curveball with solid spin rates and good bite that can hold off any batters sitting on the high cheese, and he’s been working on developing a slider with a longer tail to differentiate it from the cutting fastball. Robinson’s overall control improved last season, but his 11.3 percent walk rate – raised by a 12.9 mark in Triple-A – was still a touch high. Despite all the saves, his strike-throwing and overall quality of stuff point more toward a middle-relief role, and it’s one he could fill quickly in Milwaukee, given his run of success and newfound roster status.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers talked Robinson out of a University of South Florida commitment with a $125,000 bonus as a 23rd-round pick out of University High School (Orlando, Fla.) in 2017. The right-hander’s career sputtered in the early years as he didn’t pitch above Rookie ball, and he hadn’t posted an ERA below 5.50 at any level as a reliever. With the rubber about to meet the road in 2021, he showed an uptick in velocity last spring, throwing more in the low-90s. He rode that to climb three levels from Low-A to Double-A in his first taste of full-season ball. He finished 2021 with a 3.08 ERA, 62 strikeouts and 30 walks in 49 2/3 innings, but he was left off the 40-man roster when he became Rule 5-eligible in November. After throwing in the 94-96 mph range last spring, Robinson settled in closer to 92-94 as the 2021 season wore on. His delivery is very over the top, and the fastball can get right on top of batters (especially right-handers) as a result. He also sports a 12-to-6, upper-70s curveball that pairs really well with his elevated fastballs. An upper-80s cutter -- some systems read it as a slider -- provides another option to keep hitters off-balance. The big break on Robinson’s curve makes it difficult for him to earn calls in the zone, and a lack of consistent fastball command doesn’t help matters either. There’s a reason why Robinson has been in Minor League bullpens since signing. That said, he changed his trajectory in 2021, and it’s much easier now to see Robinson’s fastball-curve combo playing a useful role in a Major League bullpen someday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Now in his third organization after being drafted by Cleveland in 2016, Taylor was part of Kansas City's return for Whit Merrifield in the August 2022 trade with the Blue Jays. Things started to click for Taylor in Double-A in 2021, when he hit .294 with a career-high 16 home runs and 30 stolen bases. He was off to a solid start in 2022 in Triple-A but missed half the season with an oblique injury. He didn’t make his Royals debut until the Arizona Fall League, but the club saw enough to add him to the 40-man roster in the offseason to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. Taylor is a toolsy player, with a good combination of speed and power for a second baseman. His natural bat speed is enticing, but he’s still learning to control it and remains aggressive at the plate. Taylor is working with the Royals’ hitting department on the strike zone, letting pitches get deeper before committing, as well as in-game adjustments that will enable his bat-to-ball skills to play. Even at 5-foot-8 and 160 pounds, he does have power in his swing, but that can lead to holes if he’s trying to hit it over the fence. There is value solely in putting the ball in play for him because of his plus-plus speed and ability to run the bases. Taylor is a better defender at second base with his quick instincts, but he can be an average defender in the outfield. The Royals have moved Taylor around the infield and outfield this year to increase his versatility. His speed and defense can give him a utility role in the big leagues, with everyday playing time dependent on whether it clicks offensively. Taylor has gotten sporadic Major League time in KC as that versatility has opened up holes for him with the big club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted by Cleveland out of Corona High School in 2016, Taylor debuted in the Rookie Arizona League as a 17-year-old and in ’17 advanced to the short-season level. That’s the summer he was traded to the Blue Jays along with Thomas Pannone for reliever Joe Smith, a deal that could still pay off for Toronto. In ’18, Taylor spent the full season in Low-A, hitting .228, then continued into ’19 hitting just .216 in High-A. Finally, in ’21 with an assignment to Double-A, Taylor’s physical gifts began to click. He hit .294 with a career-high 16 home runs, an .888 OPS and 30 stolen bases, showing the all-around skillset the Blue Jays had been waiting on. In the midst of a steady Triple-A season, Taylor was traded to the Royals at the Trade Deadline in a swap that sent Whit Merrifield north of the border. With a combination of speed and some power for a second baseman, Taylor excites the organization with his natural bat speed. The next step will be trusting that bat speed, allowing pitches to get a bit deeper in the zone before committing. His overall approach and in-game adjustments will be part of this next step, too, but the raw tools continue to be tantalizing. Defensively, Taylor was solid enough at second base, but he spread his focus to play third, shortstop, center field and left field in Double-A in ’21. If he can prove to be a competent defender in a utility role, that only gives him more paths up the ladder. Left off the 40-man roster this past offseason, Taylor still has a chance to impress from Triple-A at some point in ’22. Between defensive versatility and his speed, which remains his best tool, Taylor can create an opportunity for himself in a few different ways. While the Blue Jays believed that ’21 was the true Taylor, it’s now on Kansas City to develop him into a potential fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After pitching just 28 1/3 innings in his first two years at Boston College, Sheehan became the Eagles' ace in 2021, setting a school record with 15 strikeouts in his penultimate start and finishing one whiff shy of the season mark with 106 in 76 2/3 innings. He has been even more unhittable since turning pro as a sixth-round pick and reached Double-A at the end of his first full pro season despite missing the first six weeks with mild arm soreness. He stood out in the Arizona Fall League with the induced vertical break on his fastball and his quality changeup, tore up Double-A for the first two months of the 2023 season and then broke into the big leagues with six no-hit innings against the Giants. Sheehan's fastball sat at 91-94 mph in his final college season but now operates at 94-97 and reaches 99, and his low release point and the extension in his delivery create outstanding carry up in the strike zone. He entered pro ball with advanced feel for his changeup, which arrives in the low 80s before diving at the plate. The Dodgers had him mostly shelve a soft curveball in favor of a short low-80s slider has made a jump this year to become a solid third pitch. Sheehan has the upside of a mid-rotation starter but has a number of things to check off his to-do list to get there. He has refined a reliable breaking ball, but he still has to improve his strike-throwing and prove he's durable enough to handle a 150-inning workload. If he can't, he could be a multi-inning relief weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two years at South Carolina, Mlodzinski saw his role change as a freshman and had a broken foot that cost him most of his sophomore season. He was hoping to use a very strong Cape Cod League performance as a springboard into the Gamecocks’ weekend rotation, only to have the pandemic cut short his junior year after a strong four-start beginning. The Pirates used their Competitive Balance Round A pick on him that summer, but a shoulder issued limited him to 14 starts in 2021. He moved up to Double-A in 2022, with mixed results. At his best, Mlodzinski does have three pitches to attack hitters with. His fastball will now touch 96-97 mph, but he sits more comfortably in the 92-94 mph range. He’s worked on getting his four-seamer up in the zone and can still sink his two-seamer, but his heater was very hittable in 2022. He can manipulate the shape of his breaking ball, but at its best, it’s a low-80s slider with decent cutter-like action that misses a fair amount of bats. He has a mid-80s changeup that can be effective. Mlodzinski did top 100 innings for the first time in 2022 and he was generally around the strike zone, but it remains to be seen if he can command his arsenal well enough to start long term. If he has to move to the bullpen, his fastball-breaking ball combination could tick up in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mlodzinski threw just 81 2/3 innings over three years at South Carolina, serving as a swingman as a freshman, missing nearly all of his sophomore year in 2019 with a broken foot and then having to deal with the pandemic-shortened 2020 season. He showed off enough stuff, especially with a very strong turn in the Cape Cod League in ’19, to land at pick No. 31 overall to the Pirates in the 2020 Draft. He threw well in his pro debut with High-A Greensboro but was limited to 50 1/3 innings because of a shoulder issue. He made up for lost time with seven relief outings in the Arizona Fall League. With a legitimate three-pitch mix, Mlodzinski does have a chance to start. He’ll typically sit around 94-95 mph but can reach back for upper-90s. In the past, he leaned on a heater with sink and run to it, but he’s worked on getting a four-seamer up in the zone as well. He throws his slider in the low-80s and it features cutter-like action. His changeup is a third above-average pitch at times, thrown with good deception and sink. Mlodzinski has to prove he can handle a larger work load and stay healthy, as well as command the baseball more effectively for him to start long-term. The Pirates still view him as a future member of the big league rotation, with a move to the upper levels a true test.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The University of South Carolina’s plans to have Mlodzinski serve as their No. 1 starter in 2019, a year after serving as a freshman swingman, went awry when the right-hander broke his left foot in his third start of the season. He came back to dominate the Cape Cod League that summer, and that helped put him in first-round conversations. He landed No. 31 overall to the Pirates in Competitive Balance Round A and he got his career unofficially started by working on a throwing program for a few weeks at instructs in the fall. During his dominant turn on the Cape, Mlodzinski’s fastball sat in the 92-96 mph range, and he showed he can reach back for upper-90s heat during the fall of 2019, throwing the pitch with good sink and run. His power low-80s slider has depth and often has cutter-like action to it, to the point where some scouts see them as two distinct pitches. He has good feel for a changeup with sink, giving him three pitches that project to be at least above average. Mlodzinski’s command had been an issue early on in his college career, but he threw a ton of strikes on the Cape and showed the ability to repeat his delivery more consistently. Athletic and physical, there’s faith he’ll have average control, which should help him reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation-type starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a baseball family with a father (Jose), uncle (Malvin) and several cousins (Luis Alexander Basabe and Rays prospect Osleivis Basabe among them) who played professionally, Matos starred at international tournaments for Venezuela before signing for $725,000. He stood out in his first two pro seasons, posting a 1.004 OPS in his 2019 debut and won Low-A West MVP honors in 2021, when he led all players at that level in hits (141), extra-base hits (51), doubles (35), total bases (223) and RBIs (86). He struggled last year after injuring a quadriceps early in the season, losing his swing and batting just .211/.275/.344 in High-A, but looked like his old self and quickly surged to Triple-A in 2023. Before 2022, Matos displayed a smooth right-handed stroke and the best bat-to-ball skills in the system. Though he still made consistent contact, a lot of it came in the form of harmless fly balls that emphasized his need to add significant strength. He has displayed a more disciplined approach this season, once again looking like a potential .300 hitter in the big leagues, though he still needs to add some muscle if he's going to provide 15-20 homers per season. Matos also wasn't as potent athletically in 2022 as he had been previously. He still showed solid speed but was less dynamic on the bases. His high baseball IQ was evident in the outfield, where he has fine range in center field along with average-to-solid arm strength, and he won defensive player of the year honors in the Arizona Fall League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants landed their best international crop in years in 2018, when they signed shortstop Marco Luciano and outfielders Matos and Jairo Pomares for a combined $4.3 million. Matos raked at international tournaments as a Venezuelan amateur and has continued to do so since signing for $725,000, posting a 1.004 OPS in his 2019 pro debut and winning Low-A West MVP accolades when he made the jump to full-season ball last year. His father and uncle played pro ball, as do several of his cousins, including former Giants outfielder Luis Alexander Basabe and Rays infield prospect Osleivis Basabe. Matos owns the best bat-to-ball skills in the system but has turned in a baffling performance in 2022 while dealing with a quad injury that cost him a month. The right-handed hitter still is recognizing pitches and controlling the strike zone, but he's making a lot of harmless flyball contact that underscores his need to get stronger. Club officials believe he still has the ceiling of a .300 hitter with 20 homers per season, but to reach it he'll have to add some muscle and refine his approach. Besides providing value at the plate, Matos is also an asset on the bases and in the outfield with his athleticism and high baseball IQ. He features solid to plus speed and has a knack for stealing bases, succeeding on 42 of 50 attempts in 169 games during his first two pro seasons. He continues to improve his reads and routes in center field, giving him a chance to stay up the middle, and his average to solid arm strength will fit on either corner should he have to move.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following two years of limitations on their bonus spending after paying Bahamian shortstop Lucius Fox $6 million in 2015, the Giants came out of the penalty box in 2018 and assembled their best international class in years, highlighted by shortstop Marco Luciano and outfielders Matos and Jairo Pomares. Signed for $725,000, Matos had performed well in international events for Venezuela and continued to do so in his 2019 pro debut, ranking third in hitting (.362) and OPS (1.000) in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before coming to the United States and going 7-for-16 in the Rookie-level Arizona League. He has several cousins in pro ball, including Giants outfielder Luis Alexander Basabe and Rays shortstop prospect Osleivis Basabe. Matos is such an advanced young hitter that one Giants official described the organization's plan for him offensively as \"just don't screw him up.\" He excelled in instructional league last fall, continuing to display precocious bat-to-ball skills, pitch recognition and plate discipline. He has a quick right-handed swing and has gotten stronger since turning pro, producing high exit velocities that could lead to 20-homer power. Matos has the chance for average or better tools across the board and the high baseball IQ to make the most of them. He's a solid to plus runner with the aggressiveness and aptitude to steal bases. He focused on improving his reads and routes in center field during instructional league, and his average to solid arm allows him to play anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Like Beau Brieske and Garrett Hill in previous years, White enjoyed a breakout season out of relative obscurity last season. The former 26th-round pick advanced from struggling starter at High-A West Michigan to a do-everything workhorse in the Double-A Erie bullpen, posting 9.8 strikeouts and 2.3 walks per nine innings while dropping his hit rate by better than 3. The Tigers, fearing another club snatching him in the Rule 5 Draft, added him to their 40-man roster over higher-ranked prospects, a feel-good story for a small-college product who read up on Tom House’s pitching philosophies and worked with other athletes as a certified personal trainer. White isn’t big but generates deception out of a slightly lower delivery with an ability to manipulate pitches. His out pitch is an extreme high-spin slider that tops 3,000 rpm, which would compare with top prospect Jackson Jobe and the best Major League pitchers. His four-seam fastball has natural cut and good spin that plays above its low-to-mid-90s velocity and beat hitters at the top of the strike zone. His sinker works off the slider to give him another look when needed. He has added a cutter to play off the four-seamer at a slower velocity, while a splitter acts as an occasional offspeed pitch. White has yet to move levels at midseason in his pro career, but a strong start at Triple-A Toledo could put him in position to become the next homegrown pitcher added to a young bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Winn struck out 59 in 36 1/3 innings as a sophomore reliever at Iowa Western CC in 2018, then gave up a Mississippi State scholarship to sign for an over-slot $500,000 in the fifth round. He performed well in Single-A during his first full pro season in 2019, then didn't pitch again until 2022 because of the pandemic and Tommy John surgery. He rocketed from Single-A to San Francisco in 14 months, making his big league debut last June and logged a 4.68 ERA in nine appearances (five starts). After turning pro, Winn scrapped a regular changeup for a splitter that has become a plus-plus devastator, arriving at 87-90 mph and topping out at 92 before tumbling at the plate. He also has upgraded a fastball that peaked at 94 mph in college and now works at 94-97 and reaches 99, while using both a two- and four-seamer. He favors the latter but it gets hard if he doesn't locate it up in the strike zone, and his sinker was much more effective in 2023. He pitches almost exclusively with his fastballs and splitter, mixing in an occasional mid-80s slider that lands in the zone but doesn't miss many bats. Winn has a strong 6-foot-4 frame and repeats his easy delivery well, which has led to a history of pounding the strike zone. He entered Spring Training as a favorite to claim a spot in the big league rotation, though mild elbow soreness slowed him at the beginning of big league camp. He has the upside of a No. 4 starter but also could be an asset as a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 2018 fifth-round choice from Iowa Western CC, Winn spurned a commitment to Mississippi State to sign for an over-slot $500,000. After a decent first full pro season in 2019, he didn't pitch in a game again until 2022 because of the pandemic shutdown and Tommy John surgery. He came back last year and recorded a 4.08 ERA with 125 strikeouts in 108 innings between three levels, reached Double-A and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster. Mostly a reliever at Iowa Western, Winn has adapted well to starting in pro ball and his stuff has gotten better. His fastball topped out at 94 mph in junior college but now operates at 94-96 mph and reaches 100 with carry and armside run. He scrapped a standard changeup for a mid-80s splitter that results in a lot of chases and empty swings. While Winn can throw his mid-80s slider for strikes, it lags behind his other two offerings. With a strong 6-foot-4 frame and the ability to repeat a simple delivery, he has a long track record of filling the zone. He could be a useful starter if he improves his slider and command, but he also could reach San Francisco sooner and perhaps see another uptick in stuff if he returns to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for an above-slot $1.5 million as a 2018 second-rounder from a North Carolina high school, White didn't make his pro debut until May 2021 because of Tommy John surgery in May 2019 and the pandemic shutdown. He broke his pitching hand in his first start when he slammed it on the ground after making an error, costing him two more months, but he looked spectacular while winning Arizona Fall League Pitcher of the Year accolades in 2021. He missed two months with a tired arm in 2022 and his stuff regressed last year, though he did make his big league debut and work a career-high 112 2/3 innings. Each of White's five pitches can grade at plus or better when at their best, though that rarely has been the case in 2023 and 2024. His best offering is an upper-80s cutter that he added last year, but his low-80s slider is now more of an average offering than a weapon with two-plane break. He throws two- and four-seam fastballs that sit at 93-95, top out at 97 and get hit hard. White has trouble landing his big-breaking upper-70s curveball and has lost some feel for his too-firm upper-80s changeup. He's throwing less strikes with his diminished stuff, though the athleticism that helped him draw interest from college football programs has translated into solid control in the past. He has shown the ingredients to become a frontline starter but not on a consistent basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-sport star as a North Carolina high schooler, White drew college football interest as a quarterback before signing with the Rangers for an above-slot $1.5 million as a 2018 second-rounder. Tommy John surgery in May 2019 and the pandemic shutdown delayed his pro debut until May 2021, when he broke his pitching hand in his first start when he slammed it on the ground after making an error, costing him three more months. He has taken off since then, winning Arizona Fall League pitcher of the year honors in 2021 and making his big league debut this summer. White has a complete arsenal of four pitches that each can grade as at least plus when at its best, though his stuff has ticked down in 2023. His four-seam fastball has sat at 92-94 mph and topped out at 96, down about 2 mph from 2022, and features armside run and carry. His best offering may be a slider that parks at 82-86 mph and reaches 89 with a combination of horizontal action and two-plane depth, though it hasn't been as consistently sharp this year and he has had more success when he turns it into an upper-80s cutter. He imparts more downward break on an upper-70s curveball that also has lost a bit of velocity and owns a fading 86-88 mph changeup, though the latter gets too firm at times. White was one of the more athletic pitchers in his Draft class, and that trait allows him to repeat an easy delivery -- though his strike-throwing also has regressed this year. He's an intense competitor who got to the Majors after pitching just 169 innings in the Minors. He has the ingredients to be a frontline starter if he can remain healthy and his stuff bounces back to 2022 levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more athletic high school pitchers in the 2018 Draft, White was a three-sport star who drew college football interest as a quarterback before signing with the Rangers for an above-slot $1.5 million in the second round. Tommy John surgery in May 2019 and the pandemic delayed his pro debut until May 2021, when he broke his pitching hand in his first start when he slammed it on the ground after making an error. Once healthy again, he finished the season with three straight double-digit strikeout efforts in Low-A and then won Arizona Fall League pitcher of the year honors. White dominated in the AFL and showed that he had regained the stuff that made scouts fall in love with him as an amateur. His fastball operates at 92-96 mph with armside run and good carry up in the strike zone, and he may find more velocity as he gets stronger and puts his elbow reconstruction further behind him. His best secondary pitch is an 82-86 mph slider with horizontal and vertical action that makes it effective against left-handers and right-handers. Both White's 78-82 mph curveball and 85-88 mph fading changeup can be solid offerings, though the latter gets too firm at times. He'll also mix in some two-seam fastballs and shows feel for pitching despite all his lost time. His athleticism helps him repeat an easy delivery and his control and command should continue to improve as he gains more experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: White drew interest from college football programs as a quarterback but opted to focus on pitching as a high school senior in 2018, when the Rangers signed him for an above-slot $1.5 million in the second round. They put him in a deloading program in his first pro summer, holding him out of game action to focus on conditioning and learning, but he still blew out his elbow the next spring before making his official debut. He had Tommy John surgery in May 2019 and returned to the mound in instructional league last fall. White showed he had regained his stuff in instructs, working with a 92-96 mph fastball with arm-side run and a high-spin curveball. He has a lot of athleticism and projection in his 6-foot-3 frame, so he could gain more velocity as he puts his elbow reconstruction further behind him. He also has promising feel for a changeup and flashed a plus slider in high school, though Texas has had him focus on his curve as his primary breaking ball. A three-sport star in high school who would have hit and pitched for South Carolina had he gone to college, White uses his premium athleticism to repeat his delivery and throw strikes. He needs more strength and plenty of innings -- his pro debut came three years after he was drafted -- but he has the makings of a No. 2 or 3 starter. He didn't help his cause by breaking his right hand when he slammed it on the ground after he made an error during his first start in May, costing him three months, though he did pitch at 95-97 mph in his first game back.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adcock’s long journey to the Majors -- from eighth-round Draft pick in 2019 who sustained a shoulder injury and then Tommy John surgery -- culminated in ‘23 when he was called up in June and made 12 appearances out of the bullpen before suffering another setback in August after returning to Double-A Arkansas. He finished the year on the IL with an arm injury but arrived at Spring Training healthy. Adcock, who played at Elon University with George Kirby, is a two-pitch specialist, with the slider being his primary weapon, one that he throws with a hard, two-plane break in the mid-to-high-80s. But in a small Major League sample size, it was teed off on for a .613 slugging percentage and four homers among the 116 he threw. The four-seam fastball saw more success, with opposing batters hitting just .148 against it. The heater ranked in the 89th percentile in velocity, per Statcast, with an average of 96.6 mph. At age 27, Adcock might be past the older end of the prospect spectrum and is likely facing a make-or-break year for his career. If he can throw strikes and miss bats -- as simple as it sounds -- he could carve out a contributing role within a bullpen always open to new arms.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adcock almost certainly wouldn’t have emerged on the Mariners’ radar had it not been for scouts pursuing George Kirby at Elon University. The righty started there as a catcher and played some outfield after redshirting his first college season in 2016. But in ’18, he began attempting a two-way path, playing right field and coming out of the bullpen. And by ’19, he was hitting and closing. He homered 12 times that year, but it was clear his future was on the mound, and Seattle thought so too, taking him in the eighth round of that year’s Draft. However, he’s yet to throw a pitch against an opposing team for the organization – though that should change in ’21. Adcock has big-time potential as a reliever when healthy, with a power fastball and slider combination. He’s retained some of his outfielder profile in his over-the-top delivery, with fastballs in the 94- to 98-mph range -- topping out near 100 -- that offer cut-and-ride at times. He’s also added some velocity to a slider that has plus potential, sitting in the 88- to 92-mph range. The righty has a high-effort delivery but also some command issues. There’s no question Adcock is a reliever all the way. But now, the Mariners will need to build the sample size with him once he returns. He worked out all summer in North Carolina after being drafted and then the pandemic ended his 2020 before it started -- but they really like his competitive nature on the mound and believe the metrics on his slider give him the chance to get big league hitters out in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murphy set a San Diego record and led the West Coast Conference with 12.2 strikeouts per nine innings in 2019, yet he lasted until the sixth round because of unreliable control. He has moved quickly through the Minors, reaching Triple-A at the end of his second full pro season in 2022. But after posting a 2.58 ERA in Double-A during the first three months of last season, he got crushed for a 5.50 ERA following his promotion. Murphy's four-seam fastball plays better than its velocity thanks to its flat approach angle, but it wasn't as effective when it dropped from sitting at 92-94 in early 2022 to 90-92 by season's end. His best pitch is his low-80s changeup with sink and fade that helps him keep right-handers off his four-seamer. His low-80s slider shows flashes of becoming a solid offering and is more dependable than his upper-70s curveball, which gets slurvy when he doesn't stay on top of it. After making some mechanical adjustments and challenging hitters more often, Murphy improved his strike-throwing during his first two pro seasons. But he started nibbling around the plate again last year, especially when he got roughed up in Triple-A. The deception in his delivery and feel for mixing pitches give him a chance at becoming a No. 4 starter if he can maintain his stuff and improve his control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Murphy led the West Coast Conference and set a San Diego record by averaging 12.2 strikeouts per nine innings in 2019, he lasted until the sixth round because he exhibited below-average control. After a dominant pro debut and a year lost to the pandemic, he made the jump to full-season ball in 2021 and reached Double-A. He and 2016 first-rounder Jay Groome posted almost identical numbers at the two levels, and there are mixed opinions as to who projects as the better southpaw starter in the long run. When at his best, Murphy can flash a plus fastball that tops out at 98 with tough vertical approach angle, a plus changeup in the low 80s with fade and a solid slider with similar velocity and short break. But there also are times when his four-seamer sits in the low 90s with less life, making it vulnerable and leaving his changeup less effective with reduced velocity separation. He also has an upper-70s downer curveball that gets slurvy when he doesn't stay on top of it. Thanks to some minor mechanical adjustments and more of an attack mindset, Murphy issued 2.9 walks per nine innings in his first two pro seasons after averaging 4.8 in college. He has some deception in his delivery and feel for mixing pitches, and he's working on tunneling his slider and changeup so they near the plate in the same fashion before moving in opposite directions. He's a potential No. 4 starter and perhaps better in that if he can maintain his best stuff more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murphy led the West Coast Conference and set a San Diego record with 12.2 strikeouts per nine innings as a junior in 2019, but he lasted six rounds in the Draft in large part because he had severe control issues. He had no problems finding the strike zone in his pro debut, posting a 1.08 ERA while working on 60-pitch limits in short-season ball. Poised to move quickly in 2020, he had to settle for a trip to instructional league when the coronavirus pandemic cancelled the Minor League season. Murphy has upgraded his fastball velocity and command as a pro, going from sitting at 90-92 mph in college to now working at 92-93 mph and topping out at 96 with riding action. The consensus is that his best secondary pitch is a low-80s slider that he has refined in pro ball, though some scouts prefer his fading changeup with similar velocity. He also has an upper-70s curveball that features good depth when he stays on top of it and gets slurvy when he doesn't. The Red Sox attribute Murphy's improved control to minor mechanical adjustments and a new mindset in which he attacks hitters more often. While he lacks a true plus pitch, he has a deceptive delivery and feel for sequencing his four offerings. Easily the best lefty pitching prospect in the system beyond 2016 first-rounder Jay Groome, he could beat Groome to Fenway Park and become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout sprinter and long jumper as a California high schooler, DeLuca could have accepted track scholarships or signed with the Twins as a 39th-rounder in 2017, but he opted instead to play college baseball at Oregon. Although he hit just .226/.296/.354 in two seasons with the Ducks, the Dodgers liked his athleticism enough to sign him for $300,000 as a 25th-rounder in 2019. After making several adjustments, he has totaled 47 homers and 37 steals in his two full pro seasons, earning a spot on Los Angeles' 40-man roster in November. The Dodgers had DeLuca give up switch-hitting and helped him upgrade his right-handed swing and his approach. He also has gotten considerably stronger since turning pro and developed solid raw power that he maximizes by looking to pull and lift pitches. His pop also plays to the opposite field and he's able to drive the ball without sacrificing contact. DeLuca uses his plus speed well on the bases, succeeding on 46-of-50 steals attempts in his first three pro seasons. His quickness helps him compensate for so-so instincts in the outfield, where he has an average arm and can play all three spots. He's a solid defender on the corners and more average in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Kessingers will be a three-generation family of big leaguers if Grae can follow his grandfather Don (a six-time All-Star with the Cubs) and uncle Keith (who played briefly for the 1993 Reds) to the Majors. A steady player with unremarkable tools, Grae pushed himself into the second round of the 2019 Draft by batting .405 in Southeastern Conference play that spring. He hasn't been able to replicate that success as a pro, batting .219/.307/.321 in his first two seasons. Kessinger's contact-oriented bat was his best attribute in college and the Astros thought he could tap into some more power with some adjustments to his right-handed stroke. He's hitting the ball harder than ever and in the air more often, but he's also swinging and missing more frequently. Houston had him spread out his stance to simplify his timing last July, and he responded with six homers in his final 43 games but also batted just .234. Kessinger's high baseball IQ stands out more than his athleticism. He's a fringy runner with savvy on the bases and possesses an average to solid arm, yet his instincts and knack for positioning allow him to get the job done at shortstop. A solid defender at second base who can hold his own at third base, he's more likely to become a utilityman than a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Grae could make the Kessingers a three-generation family of big leaguers, following his grandfather Don (a six-time All-Star with the Cubs) and uncle Keith (who played briefly for the 1993 Reds). Regarded as a steady player with unremarkable tools in his first two college seasons at Mississippi, he hit .405 in Southeastern Conference play as a junior to push himself into the second round of the 2019 Draft. He spent most of his pro debut in low Class A, where he hit .224/.333/.294, and participated in instructional league last fall. Kessinger got drafted for his contact-oriented bat, though he was just a career .248 hitter in college before entering the SEC schedule as a junior. His controlled right-handed swing is geared more for line drives, but the Astros believe he has the bat speed and untapped pop to produce 15 or more homers per year if he quiets some pre-swing movements and gets his front foot down quicker. He has the instincts to make the most of his fringy speed on the bases. He's not the twitchiest or flashiest athlete, yet Kessinger makes plays at shortstop with his knack for positioning and high baseball IQ. His arm earns average to solid grades and many scouts believe that his reliable defensive package fits better at second base. A high-floor guy with a good chance to at least be a utilityman, he features a work ethic and coachability that allow him to get the most out of his relatively modest tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $65,000 in July 2018, De La Cruz performed capably enough in the Dominican Summer League in 2019, but had to wait through the pandemic to make his United States debut in 2021. That’s where the legend began to grow, and quickly, as he dominated the Arizona Complex League so much that scouts from other teams started advocating for him to be a Top 100 prospect. He finished that year in full-season ball and then charged up prospect rankings by hitting his way to Double-A in 2022, finishing with a .945 OPS, 28 homers and 47 steals. There are few prospects more dynamic than De La Cruz, both in terms of his five-tool potential and the joy and passion he brings to his game. The switch-hitter’s plus bat speed has been amplified as he’s added strength, and he has legitimate plus power, especially from the left side of the plate. He can still be over-aggressive at times, striking out in more than 30 percent of his plate appearances in 2022, but he showed improved patience while more than holding his own in the Dominican Winter League against much older competition. Because of his size, he’s drawn some comparisons to the Pirates’ Oneil Cruz, and like Cruz, De La Cruz is eager to show he can stick at shortstop. He has the actions and plus arm to stay there for sure while also having no problems playing third and saw time at second with Licey this past winter. Just 21 for the 2023 season, he’s the kind of player who should have no ceiling placed on him, with the chance to be a true five-tool All-Star sooner rather than later.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It would be hard to find a prospect who has gone from unknown quantity to Top 100 more rapidly than De La Cruz. Receiving a modest bonus of $65,000 at the start of the 2018-19 international signing period, the Dominican infielder performed well during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019, but nothing that tipped anyone externally off about what was to come. He showed that the Arizona Complex League was no challenge for him with a 1.235 OPS in 11 games, then kept on hitting with a push to full-season ball to close out his United States debut in 2021, then kept going by hitting his way to Double-A in 2022. De La Cruz has the chance to be a true five-tool player. He showed off bat speed and athleticism in the DSL, but added strength was the huge contributor to his explosion on the scene in the U.S. He can swing it from both sides of the plate, looking a little more comfortable from the left side. He can be very quick to the ball, but he’ll have to continue to refine his approach as he advances as he can get over-aggressive. He started to show he can tap into his considerable raw power in 2021, with some believing he might eventually be a plus hitter with plus power. While De La Cruz is markedly bigger than his listed height and weight, there is little doubt he can play shortstop, with a plus arm and above-average defensive actions. He can play third and has the athleticism to play center field as well. As loud as his tools are, his makeup, feel for the game and passion while playing it all give him the chance to maximize those tools in terms of performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abbott spent nearly all of his first three seasons at the University of Virginia, including the pandemic-shortened campaign, pitching out of the bullpen. His Draft profile increased when he made an effective move into the Cavaliers' rotation, helping him land in the second round of the 2021 Draft to the Reds. He made quick work of the High-A Midwest League to kick off his first full season in 2022 and spent most of the year, with a trip to the Futures Game mixed in, with Double-A Chattanooga. It was clear pretty quickly Abbott wasn’t being challenged enough in Dayton, so the Reds promoted him so he could face a better level of hitters, feeling that the learning experience was worth the struggles the southpaw faced at the level. While his fastball sits mostly in the low 90s, it can play up thanks to deception in his delivery and the cutting action to the pitch, though he needs to trust it and come in on right-handed hitters more frequently. He always has had a plus curve that he manipulates well in terms of velocity and shape, but in 2022, he added a distinct slider with more sweep. It's thrown a tad harder than his curve, which still has good depth, and might be a tick better at this point. His changeup could be a very effective pitch, but he needs to throw it more. Abbott struggled with his command in Double-A, though he did finish off with three impressively efficient outings in September. He gets high marks for his IQ and competitiveness on the mound, giving confidence he’ll learn from the bumps in the road to keep developing as a future big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Throughout his career, mostly as a reliever, at the University of Virginia, scouts often thought Abbott had the stuff to start. The former member of USA Baseball’s Collegiate National Team got the chance to be a part of UVa’s rotation in 2021 and showed that he might indeed have a future as a starter after posting a 2.87 ERA and 13.7 K/9 rate, leading to the Reds taking him in the second round of the Draft. Abbott has a very intriguing combination of solid stuff and intense competitiveness on the mound, with a good idea of how to gameplan. He’ll throw his fastball up to 95 mph, sitting in the low-90s, and it’s particularly effective at getting swings and misses because there’s deception in his delivery and it has good cutting action to it. The lefty’s curve is his best pitch, a plus breaking ball he deftly adds and subtracts from, making it a more slurvy offering to run away from left-handed hitters. He started using his changeup more last year when he became a starter and he’ll need to continue to refine it to give him a true three-pitch mix. Like many college pitchers, Abbott has an advanced idea of how to prepare, as well as how to set up and attack hitters. He was a solid strike-thrower a year ago and repeats his delivery well, so that shouldn’t be an issue going forward, with the chance to move pretty quickly through the Reds system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a little hard to evaluate where Smith-Shawver is as a prospect and future big leaguer because of how quickly he moved through the Braves system. Signed out of high school and away from a chance to play baseball and football at Texas Tech back in 2021 for close to $1 million, he went from an inconsistent first full season to going from High-A to the big leagues in 2023 at age 20. He spent more time with Atlanta in 2024, though an oblique injury shelved him for a stretch, and he enters the 2025 season with just 257 2/3 professional innings since signing. The good news is that Smith-Shawver is still just 22 for all of this season and still has big stuff coming from an athletic 6-foot-3 frame. His fastball averaged just over 95 mph in 2024 and touched 100 mph, and he did an outstanding job throwing his lively heater for strikes. His low-80s spin-killing changeup progressed a lot in 2024, maybe more so than his mid-80s gyro slider, though both are capable of missing bats. He still has a slower upper-70s curve he can fold in, though he didn’t land it for strikes as consistently as his other offerings. While there’s still work to be done in terms of his command, Smith-Shawver’s walk rate in Triple-A last year actually registered as above-average compared to others at the level and the Braves think there’s an up arrow next to his overall strike-throwing abilities. He would have been a junior in college a year ago, something to remember in recognizing he’s far from a finished product.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith-Shawver went to high school with Bobby Witt Jr., playing baseball with him and also quarterbacking for the football team, with the chance to play both sports at Texas Tech. The Braves gave him the equivalent of a Competitive Balance B bonus in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft, close to $1 million, to sign him away from that opportunity. Focusing only on baseball for the first time, he showed glimpses of his pure stuff during an uneven first full season in 2022, then took everyone by surprise by going from High-A Rome all the way to the Majors in 2023. He was back in the big leagues in late May, but landed on the injured list for over a month with an oblique strain, returning to find his footing back in Triple-A. Just 21 for all of the 2024 season, Smith-Shawver is far from a finished product. He now has the makings of an electric four-pitch mix. His fastball sits around 95 mph and touched triple-digits last year, with good life, and it’s not difficult to dream on more consistent velocity as he matures. His mid-80s gyro slider that misses a ton of bats is still his best secondary offering, and his changeup also served as an out pitch and got weak contact, giving him two east-to-west pitches. He reintroduced a curve, and the upper-70s breaker isn’t far behind, playing well off his fastball for another north-to-south look. While he landed on the Braves’ Division Series roster, Smith-Shawver still has work to do in terms of his command and control. His athleticism should help him continue to repeat his delivery and, given how little he’s pitched, he still might be just scratching the surface of his potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During his time at Colleyville Heritage High School in Texas, Smith-Shawver was a legit quarterback recruit while also playing baseball with Bobby Witt Jr., and he could have gone on to Texas Tech to play both sports. His upside and athleticism on the mound was too much for the Braves to pass up and they went well over slot to sign him as a seventh-round pick in the 2021 Draft. He showed off his impressive stuff during his first full season with Single-A Augusta, though with a lack of polish not surprising for a two-sport star. Smith-Shawver is big and projectable and already has an electric fastball-slider combination. His heater sits in the mid-90s and touches 98 mph, with a ton of run and life. His slider flashes plus at 88-92 mph and has the chance to be a special out pitch. There’s some feel for his changeup, but he hasn’t thrown it a ton, and it’s behind the other two pitches. He once had a curve but didn’t use it at all last year. The 2022 season marked the first time Smith-Shawver focused on baseball (and pitching) full time, so there will be an obvious learning curve. The Braves are optimistic about his ability to harness his stuff and find the strike zone more consistently than he did in his first full season. Of the young high school arms the Braves have selected over the past couple of Drafts, Smith-Shawver might have the highest ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith-Shawver was a teammate of Bobby Witt Jr.’s at Colleyville Heritage High School in Texas, but was known more for his work on the gridiron than the diamond for much of his high school career. A highly-touted quarterback recruit who had the chance to play football and baseball at Texas Tech, Smith-Shawver instead joined the Braves organization when they went well over slot to sign him for $997,500 in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft. The 6-foot-3 Smith-Shawver has big stuff coming from a big, projectable athletic frame and the Braves think he’s just scratching the surface since he really didn’t pitch that much in high school before his senior season. He’s already added velocity, with a fastball that sat in the low-90s at Colleyville but now touches 98 mph with armside run. He’s now focusing on a hard slider that could be above-average in time and he’s already shown some feel for his changeup. Being devoted to baseball has already paid dividends as Smith-Shawver’s stuff has ticked up and he’s starting to learn to harness that stuff and repeat his delivery. His athleticism will be a huge asset in that endeavor, though his development comes with the usual high risk/high reward label that accompanies high school right-handers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baker’s time at TCU was riddled with injuries, including an arm strain, a hairline fracture in his left arm, a broken fibula and torn ankle ligaments. The maladies caused him to go from a two-way prospect to a full-time masher, and he overcame them to finish with an NCAA OPS of 1.026 over three seasons. The Cardinals took him with the 75th overall pick in 2018, and he proved to be an above-average bat (albeit with less pop than expected) at Class A Advanced Palm Beach in 2019. His breakout came last season with a career-best 26 homers and .248/.322/.530 line at Double-A Springfield, and he earned a brief move to Triple-A Memphis. He was curiously left off the 40-man roster ahead of his Rule 5 eligibility. Batting from the right side, Baker uses every bit of his size at 6-foot-4, 280 pounds to show off impressive raw power. His .282 isolated slugging percentage was third-best among Double-A qualifiers in 2021, and his 48.4 percent flyball rate is a strong indication that he can make the most of that strength with his lift. While he takes his walks, his strikeout rate did tick up to 26.3 percent in 2021, and he projects for a below-average hit tool. The former Horned Frog has bottom-of-the-scale speed, and while he did make some defensive gains last summer in Springfield and still has his strong arm from college, he isn’t likely to add much value with the glove at the cold corner. Baker is a classic first-base/DH type and, 40-man status aside, may need only a little more runway to bring his powerful performance to the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Once an interesting two-way prospect, an arm strain at Texas Christian University pushed Baker off the mound, and he’s continued to develop solely as a position player since. The arm strain foretold things to come as injuries -- including a hairline fracture and ligament/muscle damage in his left arm, a broken fibula and torn ankle ligaments -- caused him to miss time in both 2017 and ’18. Despite the numerous setbacks, Baker impressed with a .347 average in college and went to the Cardinals with the 75th pick in the 2018 Draft. He performed well in his 2019 full-season debut and developed into a slugger in 2021 as he mashed 23 homers through his first 78 games at the Double-A level. Baker’s 6-foot-4, 280-pound frame screams power-hitting first baseman, and that’s exactly the role he fills. Baker started to tap into that power bank late in 2019, finishing with five homers and 13 doubles over his final 30 games in the pitcher-friendly High-A Florida State League. The power surge continued in 2021 as he set a career high for homers, including 11 in July alone. The slugger also features an advanced approach at the plate and drew 52 walks (122 games) in his first full season. Defensively, Baker is limited to first base. While he possesses a strong arm, which contributed to him being an enticing two-way prospect coming out of high school, his speed and range are limited. The Cardinals feel Baker can be a serviceable defender at first, which should be plenty if his bat continues to develop along its projected path.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After rehabbing from Tommy John surgery, Woo wowed in his debut season with Seattle in 2022, becoming one of the most coveted trade targets in the organization. And it’s been the more progressive teams that are making those calls. A starter and reliever at Cal Poly, Woo sat at 95 mph with his fastball last year but touched 99 mph with excellent ride, missing bats at a slightly lower release point. All said, it helps the rest of his stuff play. The slider is also a really solid pitch, albeit less impactful than the heater. He’s begun to throw it slightly harder as he’s gotten more reps and distanced himself from surgery. Woo only had 69 1/3 innings of college experience, then just 57 innings last year, but he was among the standouts in the Arizona Fall League. He possesses a solid delivery and is athletic enough, but there are times where he can be scattered with location, though it’s possible that could be chalked up to early stages of development and coming back from elbow surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It hasn't exactly been a straight path for Soriano, who originally signed with the Angels back in March 2016. He had early success at the lower levels of the system and spent three consecutive years in the top half of the Angels’ Top 30. He needed Tommy John surgery in February 2020 and missed development time he might have had as a result. When the Angels didn’t protect him on the 40-man that offseason, the Pirates took him with the top pick in the 2021 Rule 5 Draft. He made just two rehab appearances with Pittsburgh before he needed a second elbow surgery in June 2021. The Pirates designated him for assignment and eventually he was sent back to the Angels. The right-hander returned in 2022 to throw 13 encouraging innings, this time earning a spot on the Angels roster. Soriano has always sported a big arm, one that reaches triple digits with his fastball and sits around 96 mph, though that was back in 2019 before the double Tommy John treatment. He still shows flashes of two very good breaking balls and there is some feel for a changeup. Soriano appears to be healthy and was throwing well at the end of last year and into the fall. He's showed a better feel for pitching than he has in the past, when command had been very elusive. He’ll only be 24 for all of 2023, but he’s also yet to throw a pitch above A ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Soriano signed for just $70,000 in March 2016 and based on his upside alone, that might already be a bargain. After Soriano's stellar United States debut in '17, the Angels pushed Soriano to full-season ball after extended spring training in 2018, where the teenager struggled at first, but finished relatively strongly. Soriano screams projectability and high ceiling, and he's starting to put his considerable tools together on the mound. His electric fastball will touch 97-98 mph and there's still room for more consistent velocity as he grows into his 6-foot-3 frame. He's always been able to spin his breaking ball, but he improved the consistency in throwing it effectively as it trends towards being a plus pitch. The Angels pushed him to throw his changeup more, and he did it 15 percent of the time in 2018, and it took a big step forward as a result, showing a much better feel for the off-speed pitch. While Soriano's walk rate spiked in 2018, there is confidence he'll get to average command and control eventually thanks to a very athletic delivery. All he needs are innings and the gloves should come off a bit in 2019, with a chance for him to make a nice leap up this list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers’ struggle to garner premium prospects in trades was among many factors that slowed the organization’s rebuild, but getting Olson from the Brewers for Daniel Norris at the 2021 Trade Deadline was one of former GM Al Avila’s better deals during his tenure. Milwaukee's 13th-round pick in 2018 became one of Double-A Erie’s best pitchers in 2022, raising his strikeout rate from 9.8 to 12.6 per nine innings while dropping his walk rate. A midseason bout with home run balls and fastball command was the one major blemish on his season, raising his ERA, but Olson established himself among the next crop of Tigers pitching prospects. When Olson is on, his four-seam fastball approaches the mid-90s with enough command to hit the corners and get him ahead in counts. That sets up an impressive combination with an upper-80s changeup and a mid-80s slider, and he can get strikeouts without chasing them. When Olson isn’t on, he overthrows the fastball and either gets hurt in the zone or falls behind in counts, limiting his use of secondary pitches. His changeup plays well off his fastball despite a smaller velocity gap, while the slider has supplanted his curveball as his preferred breaking ball, though he can steal strikes with the curve when he has a feel for it. He recently added a sinker to change eye levels off his four-seamer and give him another pitch against right-handed hitters. Though Olson could eventually become a high-strikeout reliever, the Tigers are giving him a chance to show his wares as a starter first. Either way, he has the chance to give Detroit well more than it bargained for out of a deadline deal in 2021. A bump to Triple-A Toledo should test his command against more veteran hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Tigers had hit-and-miss results on trades going into their rebuild, Olson is an example of the kind of smaller deals with which they’ve had better success. The Brewers’ 13th-round pick in 2018 was enjoying a midsummer resurgence at High-A Wisconsin last year when he became the return prospect in the Daniel Norris deal at the July 30 Trade Deadline.
