All he had to do was change teams in the league and head to West Michigan, where he tossed 11 scoreless innings with 14 strikeouts over two starts before joining Double-A Erie for the final month. While Olson doesn’t profile as a power pitcher, his fastball can get to the mid-90s and a tick above when he wants, an improvement from the start of his pro career. His next step is to sustain velocity improvement without sacrificing command. Though his curveball was a preferred secondary pitch earlier in his career, he found success with a slider and a changeup last season, and is trying to sharpen the slider to play off the curve. Though Olson has a compact delivery, he can also struggle to get back in form when he falls out. He had eight outings with seven or more strikeouts, but he also had six outings with four-plus walks. Only once did he reach both in the same outing. A goal of the Tigers’ revamped player development staff is to use mechanics tools to get more out of prospects beyond the top echelon. In that sense, Olson is an interesting project. His rising strikeout rate is worth following, but refinement is still needed before he can profile in a Major League rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Is Joyce the flame-throwing equivalent of Bigfoot? Often buzzed about but rarely sighted? The 2024 season may go a long way toward answering that question. By now, most baseball fans know about Joyce's ability to routinely hit triple digits, and there’s the legend of him touching 105 mph in his one season with Tennessee. But he had Tommy John surgery in 2021 after multiple issues slowed him down previously and even in '22, he couldn’t pitch on back-to-back days. Still, the Angels couldn’t ignore that kind of power and took him in the third round of that summer’s Draft. He did reach the big leagues in his first full season, but he also missed three months due to ulnar neuritis. Even with all the missed time, Joyce averaged 100.4 mph with his fastball between Double-A and the big leagues in 2023. When it straightens out, it’s more hittable than it should be, but it can feature some armside run coming from a lower slot when it’s at it’s best. He actually has two distinct breaking balls, both in the slider class -- one a sweeper, and one that’s harder and shorter that’s now up to 90-91 mph. He’s all but shelved his changeup. Because Joyce has yet to show he can handle pitching multiple days in a row, it’s hard to project him pitching in high-leverage situations, not to mention that his walk rate took a big jump up in 2023. The Angels are hopeful that his taste of the big leagues will help him slow things down and trust his stuff, which is plenty good enough to pitch in those late-inning situations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When you throw 105 mph, people are going to notice. That’s what Joyce did in his lone season for Tennessee in 2022 after transferring from Walters State CC (Tenn.), but he missed the 2021 season because of Tommy John surgery. Even though his resume was short, the Angels decided they couldn’t pass up his fastball and took him in the third round of the 2022 Draft, and he pitched well in Double-A during his pro debut. After averaging 101 mph with his fastball at Tennessee, he hovered around 100 mph with Rocket City. Though the heater can get hit because it straightens out at times, it can feature some armside run, and when he works up in the zone, it’s tough to square up coming from a lower arm slot. He can miss bats regularly with his slider, which averaged around 83 mph, and the Angels are working to get him to throw his breaking ball harder and close the velocity gap between it and his heater. Joyce has mixed in a changeup in the past with some effectiveness, but it’s a distant (and not often used) third offering. While he has the stuff to pitch late in games and in high-leverage situations, he doesn’t have a track record of doing so. The injury history -- he missed most of 2018-19 with shoulder, elbow and growth-plate issues -- and the fact that he had multiple days off between outings in college means he’s going to have to prove he can handle a professional reliever workload while moving away from being so fastball-reliant after throwing the pitch 80 percent of the time in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year member of the Miami (Ohio) rotation, Bachman’s Draft stock soared when his stuff did in the spring of 2021. He might have had the best pure stuff of any pitcher in the class, a big reason why the Angels made him the first of 20 straight arms they took in the 2021 Draft, signing him for a below-slot bonus of $3.85 million with the ninth pick. He wasn’t able to put that stuff to good use in 2022 as he only collected 43 2/3 innings due to back and biceps issues, causing a regression in his repertoire. The good news for the Angels is that, now healthy, Bachman was back to showing off the elite-level velocity at instructs and in early bullpen sessions this spring. After only averaging around 93 mph with his fastball in Double-A last year, he was back over 100 mph in those sessions, the rarified air he was in regularly during his 2021 dominant college season. His mid-80s slider still missed bats in 2022 and was a plus breaking ball, even though it wasn’t quite as sharp as it has been. His mid-80s changeup has heavy sink and gets a lot of weak contact on the ground. In addition to his stuff backing up, Bachman struggled to find the strike zone consistently when he was on the mound last season, something he had improved tremendously in his last two years at Miami. With health, Bachman has gotten back to the preparation that made him jump up boards as an amateur, with many in the organization thinking he’s poised for a breakout.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: From a pure stuff standpoint, there may not have been a better pitcher available in the 2021 Draft than Bachman, a starter at Miami (Ohio) from his freshman year on. That stuff took a jump forward after the 2020 shortened season, leading to the right-hander moving up on many boards to the upper half of the first round. He was among the most dominant college starters in the game, leading to the Angels taking him No. 9 overall and signing him to a below slot bonus of $3.85 million. His first full season was interrupted by nearly two months on the injured list with biceps issues. Bachman saw his fastball climb from the low 90s during the first stages of his college career to sitting 94-97 mph and topping out at 101-102 with a ton of armside run and sink. He throws his slider harder now, too, a mid-80s breaking ball with more bite that neutralized hitters from both sides of the plate. He didn’t throw his changeup as much, but he has good feel for the mid-80s offspeed pitch, throwing it with heavy sink. As impressive as Bachman’s swing-and-miss stuff was (14.0 K/9 in 2021), it was even better because he made big strides in his ability to find the strike zone, thanks to improved conditioning and athleticism. The combination of his size (6-foot-1), his lower slot, arm action and effort in his delivery does bring some reliever risk, and there was some concern when he missed two early starts in his junior year with arm fatigue. The Angels, though, are confident he can start with frontline starter stuff that holds up deep into outings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vásquez joined the Yankees for $10,000 when he was 19 years old in May 2018, and his breakout didn’t truly come until after the lost pandemic season when he struck out at least 120 batters in both '21 and '22 while reaching Double-A. The right-hander finally climbed to the Majors in his age-24 campaign last year, splitting time between New York (where he both started and relieved) and Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, and after he didn’t quite catch on in the Bronx, the Bombers sent him to the Padres as part of the Juan Soto blockbuster. Undersized at 6-foot, Vásquez mixes and matches with a full arsenal that can go as many as six pitches deep. The two that pop the most are his sweeper and curveball -- two breaking pitches that hover around 80 mph and averaged more than 3,000 rpm in the Majors. The curveball tends to have more drop than the sweeper, and that’s the main separator as their high-spin profiles can bleed into each other otherwise. His 93-95 mph fastball and sinker give him a pair of distinct, if average, heaters, and he’ll also show an upper-80s cutter that too often found the heart of the zone in The Show. An upper-80s changeup may lack separation, but its fade made it tough to touch. Without much extension in his delivery, the Dominican Republic native is easier to follow out of the hand, and he didn’t miss many bats in his first taste of the bigs. Given his age, he is trending toward being a reliever with enough weapons to get through a lineup once before handing the ball over.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vásquez went from signing for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the relatively old age of 19 in May 2018 to becoming one of the Yankees' better pitching prospects. Initial reports had him going to the Rangers as part of the Joey Gallo trade in July 2021 before New York decided to hold onto him. He capped his 2022 season with eight no-hit innings in the deciding game of the Double-A Eastern League playoffs before getting added to the 40-man roster in November. After making his MLB debut and 11 total appearances for the Yanks in 2023, Vásquez was included in the Juan Soto blockbuster and joined San Diego in December. Vásquez owned the nastiest curveball in the Yankees system, combining low-80s power with vertical and horizontal movement produced by spin rates that top 3,100 rpm. His low arm slot imparts difficult induced vertical break on four-seam fastballs that park at 93-95 mph and reach 100. He also can mix in a slider with more velocity and sweep but less consistency than his curve and possesses a fading upper-80s changeup that needs more separation from his heater. While Vásquez is athletic and has a clean delivery, he's also 6-feet tall and lacks physicality, so there are questions about his ability to hold up as a starter. He has helped his cause by improving his strike-throwing while rising through the Minors and now flashes average control, though it needs further refinement. He worked as both a starter and reliever during his debut season in the Bronx and could work in either role -- depending on that control -- as he establishes his future with San Diego.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was first eligible to sign in the 2015-16 signing period, Vasquez waited more than two years for a deal before signing out of the Dominican Republic for $10,000 at the relatively old age of 19 in May 2018. He made a successful jump to full-season ball last year, moving from Low-A to Double-A while posting a 2.52 ERA with 130 strikeouts in 107 1/3 innings. Initial reports had him heading to the Rangers as part of the Joey Gallo trade last July, but the Yankees ultimately decided to hang on to him. Vasquez's best pitch is a curveball that combines power (78-82 mph) and depth produced by excellent spin rates that consistently top 3,100 rpm, and it's an absolute hammer at times. He works from a lower arm slot that produces nifty induced vertical break on a four-seam fastball that sits at 93-95 mph and touches 98 and imparts sink on a two-seamer in the low 90s. He also has a slider that's harder but less consistent than his curve, and a changeup that looks like a solid pitch at times but gets too firm (upper 80s) and misses the strike zone at others. Vasquez has done a better job throwing strikes as he has climbed through the Minors, issuing just 15 walks in 57 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A in the second half of 2021. He's athletic and has a relatively easy delivery, but he's also 6 feet tall and lacks physicality, leading to questions about whether he's better suited for the bullpen. He has the stuff to thrive in short stints and his curveball works against both left-handed and right-handed hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller didn't crack Louisville's rotation until partway through his sophomore year and the pandemic ended his junior season after four starts, so several teams had concerns about his delivery and risk. That allowed the Dodgers to grab him with the 29th overall pick in the 2020 Draft and a $2,197,500 bonus, which looks like a steal now that he has a four-pitch repertoire that rivals that of any mound prospect in the Minors. He hit 100 mph while striking out Shohei Ohtani in an exhibition last April and again while fanning the side at the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game, highlights from a season in which he whiffed 145 in 112 1/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A. Miller throws exceptionally hard and maintains his velocity, parking at 97-99 mph for innings at a time and topping out at 101 with a running four-seamer -- and he also can unveil a two-seamer that reaches triple digits. His upper-80s slider can climb to 92 mph and is a plus-plus weapon with two-plane depth at its best. His upper-80s changeup fades and sinks, giving him a third well above-average pitch at times, and his low-80s curveball is a solid fourth offering. Since turning pro, Miller has calmed down his delivery and provided more strikes, and there no longer are questions about his ability to remain in the rotation. He needs to improve his pitch sequencing, because he can get too predictable and his fastball sometimes gets hit harder than it should. While he still can refine his overall command and do a better job of finding the zone with his changeup, he's pretty much big league ready and looks like a future frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Questions about his delivery and reliever risk made Miller available to the Dodgers with the 29th overall pick in the 2020 Draft, and he has looked like a steal since signing for $2,197,500. Los Angeles kept him on tight pitch counts during his 2021 pro debut, when he reached Double-A while fashioning a 2.40 ERA and .192 opponent average while striking out 70 in 56 1/3 innings despite dealing with an oblique injury. He showcased the best stuff of any starter in the Arizona Fall League after the season, though he did surrender 11 runs in 10 innings. Miller can sit at 97-98 mph for innings at a time and reach triple digits with his riding four-seam fastball and he also can mix in a heavy 93-96 mph two-seamer. Both his two-plane slider and fading, sinking changeup operate in the mid-80s and grade as well above-average pitches at their best. Los Angeles had him shelve his spike curveball early last season and he developed better shape and command when he brought back a low-80s bender with a more traditional grip later in the year. The Dodgers have helped Miller tone down his delivery and throw more strikes since turning pro. After averaging 3.6 walks per nine innings in three college seasons at Louisville, he cut that rate to 2.1 in his first year in the Minors. Hitters struggle to barrel his quality stuff, he's locating his pitches better than ever and he has a strong 6-foot-5 frame built to handle innings, so he has all of the ingredients to become a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller enjoyed nothing but success and continually improved after joining Louisville's weekend rotation as a sophomore in 2019, yet there mixed opinions about his delivery and where exactly he belonged in the 2020 Draft. Though he improved his control during the shortened college season, he was available with the No. 29 overall pick, which the Dodgers gladly spent along with a $2,197,500 bonus to land him. He since has raised expectations with the way he pitched at Los Angeles' alternate site and in instructional league last year and in his pro debut in 2021. Miller throws harder than most starters, working into the mid-90s deep into games, topping out at 99 mph with a riding four-seamer and operating at 93-95 with a heavy two-seamer. He also dodges bats with a sharp mid-80s slider that grades as well above-average at its best, and he can morph it into a cutter that reaches 90 mph. He trusts his mid-80s changeup, which features fade and sink and shows signs of becoming a plus pitch, and has added a spike curveball since turning pro. While there's some effort in Miller's delivery, the Dodgers believe it has improved significantly as he has gotten more acclimated to starting. His control and command continue to get better, and his strong 6-foot-5 frame is built for durability, so they see him as a definite starter. Instead of wondering if he might wind up in the bullpen like some did in the past, scouts now ponder whether he'll become a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: San Francisco used two first-rounders in three years on Atlantic Coast Conference catchers, selecting Georgia Tech's Joey Bart at No. 2 in 2018 and North Carolina State's Bailey at No. 13 in 2020. Signed for $3,797,500, the latter has batted .247/.355/.425 while battling back issues in his first two pro seasons. Evaluators inside and outside of the organization note his underlying data and performance against right-handers (.264/.373/.458) are more encouraging than his raw overall numbers. A switch-hitter, Bailey make more consistent and higher quality contact from the left side of the plate, and the Giants believe he'll be productive enough to at least form the strong side of a platoon. He may never hit for a high average but has the strength and the ability to launch balls to his pull side to provide average power against right-handers. He draws a healthy amount of walks and San Francisco hopes he'll improve vs. left-handers as he gets more at-bats against them. Though he shows little speed on the bases, Bailey moves well for a catcher and is agile behind the plate. He's a quality receiver and blocker who frames pitches well, though that skill may mean less with an automated strike zone. His solid-to-plus arm strength enabled him to throw out 31 percent of base stealers in his first two years as a pro, and he also stands out with his game-calling and leadership skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two years after taking Joey Bart with the No. 2 overall pick in the 2018 Draft, the Giants took another Atlantic Coast Conference catcher in the first round when they selected Bailey 13th overall in 2020. Signed for $3,797,500 out of North Carolina State, he struggled with back issues and an assignment to High-A at the outset of his 2021 pro debut, batting just .185/.290/.296 in 33 games. He rebounded after getting healthy and heading to Low-A, where he hit .322/.416/.531 in 47 contests before getting more at-bats in the Arizona Fall League. Compared to Bart, Bailey puts together higher quality at-bats but produces less power. A switch-hitter who's more proficient from the left side of the plate, he works counts and uses the entire field. He's strong and did a better job of driving the ball after resetting in Low-A, and he could provide 20 or more homers per season with healthy on-base percentages if not high batting averages. Similar defensively to Bart, Bailey moves well for a catcher and is an agile receiver and blocker. He exhibits plus arm strength and erased 33 percent of basestealers in his first pro season. He has strong leadership skills that help him take charge of a pitching staff and he's an advanced game-caller who selected his own pitches in college.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite spending the No. 2 overall pick in 2018 on Joey Bart, San Francisco couldn't resist taking another Atlantic Coast Conference catcher in the first round two years later. A veteran of the U.S. national 18-and-under and collegiate teams, Bailey was a three-year starter at North Carolina State who slammed 29 homers in 131 college games. Signed for $3,797,500 as the 13th overall choice last June, he impressed with his steady professionalism at the Giants' alternate site and instructional league program. Though he's a switch-hitter with power from both sides of the plate, Bailey may be more impressive with his defense than his offense. He's athletic for a catcher, moving well behind the plate while providing solid receiving skills and arm strength. He has all the intangibles teams want in a backstop, exhibits the ability to take charge of a pitching staff and called his own pitches with the Wolfpack. Bailey's 20-25 homer potential stands out more than his hitting ability, but he makes consistent contact and walked nearly as much as he struck out in college. While his lefty swing is better than his righty stroke, he's capable of doing damage from either side. Though the coronavirus pandemic delayed his pro debut until 2021, the Giants believe exposing him to advanced pitching at their alternate site last summer may expedite his offensive and defensive development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: College World Series fans will know who Kauffman is after he played a huge part in the University of Michigan’s runner-up finish in the 2019 College World Series. The Rockies had drafted him in the Competitive Balance Round B that June, No. 77 overall, and opted not to have him pitch that summer because of the postseason-extended workload with the Wolverines. A shoulder issue slowed him at the club’s alternate site in 2020, and he struggled in 2021 when he was rushed up to Double-A after two starts with High-A Spokane. Kauffman is all about pitchability and mixing his repertoire to keep hitters off-balance. The right-hander’s velocity is down a tick from his college days, with a sinker that usually sits in the low-90s, but he still can get up to 94 mph on occasion. He gets a ton of groundballs with it, but would run into trouble when he would get frustrated by giving up hits on the ground, then would leave a ball up and would pay the price. His changeup also has sink, and he separates it well from his fastball with good arm speed deception. He’s worked to tighten up his slider, giving him a third average or better pitch. The spike in walk rate (4.5 BB/9) Kauffman had in Double-A isn’t indicative of his strike-throwing abilities. He’s a thinker on the mound, to a fault, with over-analysis sometimes being his worst enemy. When he’s been able to go out and trust his gameplan, he’s shown the feel for pitching that could make him a No. 4 or 5 type starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kauffmann spent three years on the University of Michigan’s staff, the last two as a starter, and was instrumental in helping the Wolverines finish the 2019 season as the College World Series runners-up. The Rockies had drafted him in the second round that June and because of the lengthy postseason run, opted to not have him pitch that summer. He had to deal with a shoulder issue at the Rockies’ alternate training site in 2020, something he rehabbed at instructs last fall, so he enters 2021 with a zero in the innings pitched column. After rehabbing and offseason bullpens, Kauffmann is ready to begin his pro career and see how his three-pitch mix plays against professional hitters. While he hasn’t missed a ton of bats, he commands his low 90s two-seam fastball very well, maintaining his velocity throughout starts and throwing the pitch with very good run and sink. His changeup is his best secondary pitch, an above-average offering that features similar sink, but that he separates well from his fastball and sells with arm speed. He’ll get his slider up to 86 mph and it isn’t as consistent a weapon, but when it’s firm it flashes above-average. The right-hander got better at finding the strike zone over his three years at Michigan and he gets high marks for his competitiveness on the mound. He just needs to get out and pitch, with a ceiling as a workhorse starter and a floor of a reliever who can come in and get ground ball outs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Although Rocchio received just the ninth-highest bonus ($125,000) in Cleveland's 2017 international crop, he has emerged as the best prospect of the bunch. He quickly earned the nickname \"The Professor\" for his high baseball IQ, which helped him make his U.S. debut at age 17 and arrive in the big leagues last May at age 22. After the Guardians got little production out of their shortstops in 2023, he's expected to stabilize the position for them this season. A switch-hitter, Rocchio has become more proficient from the left side of the plate as he has gained more experience. Though he uncharacteristically tried to do too much in his first taste of the Majors, he generally employs a disciplined approach to stroke line drives to all fields. He's not very physical but has some sneaky pop that could translate into 15 homers per season if he lifts the ball more consistently. Despite just average speed, Rocchio stole 25 bases in 32 attempts last season thanks to his savvy. His instincts and quickness give him quality range at shortstop, where he compensates for an average arm with a fast release. A smooth defender with Gold Glove potential, he could play all over the infield in a utility role if he doesn't hit enough to be an everyday shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $125,000 out of Venezuela as part of a banner 2017 international crop reeled in by Cleveland, Rocchio quickly earned the nickname \"The Professor\" for his high baseball IQ. Unable to come to the United States to play at the Guardians' alternate site or instructional league program during the pandemic shutdown in 2020, he nonetheless reached Triple-A at age 21 last season while hitting a career-best 18 homers. In a system overflowing with infield prospects, he stands out as the most talented offensive player among them. A switch-hitter, Rocchio recognizes pitches well, barrels them easily and lashes line drives to all fields. He already had a quick bat and then gained muscle during his pandemic layoff, which has helped him develop average power (solid pop as a righty, more fringy as a lefty). He could be a .275 hitter who produces 15-20 homers annually when he's a finished product. Though Rocchio has solid speed, he's not a prolific basestealer and succeeded on just 64 percent of his attempts in his first four pro seasons. His quickness is more apparent at shortstop, where he has smooth actions and soft hands and enhances his average arm with a fast release. He wore down late last season while playing a career-high 132 games, so he needs to add some more strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Guardians' stellar 2017 international haul that could yield a half-dozen big league position players, Rocchio has the highest floor among that group and rivals fellow Top 100 prospect George Valera for the highest ceiling as well. Signed for just $125,000 out of Venezuela, he quickly became known as \"The Professor\" because of his excellent baseball IQ. Unable to come to the United States to play at Cleveland's alternate site or instructional league program in 2020, he returned last year to hit .277 while tripling his previous career high with 15 homers and reaching Double-A in his full-season debut at age 20. Added to the 40-man roster in November, Rocchio is a switch-hitter who recognizes pitches well and drills line drives to all fields. He's not big but got stronger during his pandemic layoff and smoked the ball with more authority in 2021, displaying quick hands, at least average raw power and the ability to get to most of it during games. The youngest regular in the Double-A Northeast during the final two months of the season, he more than held his own against advanced pitchers and his feel for the barrel should allow him to continue to hit for average. Rocchio's quickness and instincts are apparent on the bases and in the field. He has the plus speed and aggressive nature to steal and take extra bases. He's a gifted defender with smooth actions and soft hands at shortstop, where he enhances average arm strength with a fast release and impressive accuracy on his throws, and he also can handle second and third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians assembled a potentially special international class in 2017, highlighted by outfielders George Valera and Alexfri Planez and middle infielders Rocchio, Aaron Bracho and Jose Tena. The biggest bargain of the group at $125,000, Rocchio batted .335 in his 2018 pro debut, which included coming to the United States at age 17, and held his own as the short-season New York-Penn League's youngest regular the following summer. After going home to Venezuela after Spring Training shut down in 2020, he was unable to return to play at Cleveland's alternate site or instructional league program. Rocchio has earned the nickname \"The Professor\" because of his outstanding baseball IQ. It's apparent at the plate, where he's a switch-hitter with precocious bat-to-ball skills and pitch recognition. He may never walk much because he makes contact so easily, but his hitting ability and quick, strong hands should yield double-digit home run totals once he adds some needed strength. Rocchio's quickness and instincts also make him an asset on the bases and in the field. He has the plus speed and aggressiveness to steal bases, though he succeeded in only 63 percent of his attempts in his first two pro seasons. He's a reliable defender who covers plenty of ground at shortstop, where he compensates for an average arm with a quick release.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After beginning his college career at North Iowa Community College, Williamson moved to Texas Christian and served as part of the Horned Frogs weekend rotation in 2019. The big left-hander showed off premium stuff, albeit with some mixed results, but it was enough for the Mariners to take him in the second round of the Draft that June. He pitched his way to Double-A in 2021, his first real full season and then was sent to the Reds prior to the 2022 season in the trade that sent Jesse Winker and Eugenio Suarez to Seattle. He split time between Double- and Triple-A, with mixed results, in his first year with the Reds. Though some of it regressed a little in 2022, Williamson’s stuff is all still very good. He has four legitimate pitches at his disposal, starting with a fastball that averaged just over 92 mph and touched 95. It didn’t elicit quite as much swing-and-miss this year compared to the season prior, but there’s still good carry with it up in the zone. He has a true 12-to-6 type of curve, thrown in the mid-70s, and a harder, mid-80s cutter-ish slider that misses bats while also mixing in an effective low-80s changeup. Williamson’s ability to locate it is what suffered more than anything else and the Reds feel some of that had to do with him trying to impress his new organization too much. They added him to the 40-man roster in the offseason and think he’ll be able to settle in, trust his stuff and reach his ceiling as a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williamson had re-established himself at Texas Christian University after transferring from North Iowa Community College ahead of the 2019 Draft. He had solid stuff across the board, but it came with inconsistency, and he also had some injury risks, having undergone surgeries to repair both hip labrums the fall before the Draft, in ’18. That led him to falling to the second round and Seattle, which signed the left-hander for below-pick value. A strong summer debut led to a big first full season in 2021, when he pitched his way to Double-A. He was the top prospect sent to the Reds in March’s deal for Jesse Winker and Eugenio Suarez. Williamson has four legitimate pitches that fill up the zone -- and his stuff just keeps ticking up, as did his pitchability and command until he struggled with the strike zone in the move to the upper levels in 2022. During his debut in 2019, his fastball had one of the best swing-and-miss rates in the entire Minor Leagues, thanks to its riding life and his excellent extension, and in many ways, Williamson grew into his velocity, which now reaches up to 96 mph when he really rears back. But it’s the sweeping, 12-6 curveball that has many dreaming on the possibility of him developing into a legit mid-to-high rotation starter. Williamson also throws a slider that has cutter-like action and a blossoming, mid-80s changeup. Lefties with a 6-foot-6 frame and overpowering stuff are the types of pitchers that organizations dream on, and floor wise, Williamson’s development will come down to command. Given the severity of his injury history, it’s been a pleasant surprise that he’s had no hiccups. Maintaining that health, along with his durability to go deeper into games, will be the focal part of his development, with the chance for him to knock on the big league door in the very near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Left-handers with a 6-foot-6 frame and overpowering stuff are the types of pitchers organizations dream on. Texas Christian had two of them in 2019 in Nick Lodolo (who went No. 7 overall to the Reds) and Williamson, who had transferred from North Iowa Area Community College. He showed good stuff across the board but was inconsistent, and he came with the risk of having had surgery to repair both hip labrums the previous fall. But the Mariners felt he was worth the risk and drafted him in the second round in 2019, signing him for below-pick value and watching him strike out 25 of 61 batters in his pro debut at short-season Class A Everett. He kept trending upward during his full-season debut in 2021, pitching his way to Double-A, leaving many in the front office thinking they’d acquired a steal. The Reds noticed, too, acquiring the left-hander in the trade that sent Jesse Winker and Eugenio Suarez to Seattle. Williamson has four pitches that fill up the strike zone, and his stuff ticked up during his debut, albeit in a small sample size. In that time, his 91- to 96-mph fastball had one of the best swing-and-miss rates in all the Minor Leagues, thanks to its riding life and Williamson’s excellent extension. In many ways, he grew into his velocity. Williamson's curveball is his breaking pitch, which he throws with good depth, and while he didn’t throw the slider as much, the Mariners like the cutter-like action the lefty has on it, and the pitch will be a focal point in 2021. He threw his changeup more during his pro debut than he did in college, and it was better than previously advertised. In his final year at TCU, Williamson wasn’t a pure command-and-control guy, but he was outstanding in these areas during his pro debut. Floor-wise, his development will come down to command, but that’s an area that can improve with Minor League development. That gives more hope that he can advance as a starter, with a ceiling of perhaps a No. 3 in a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Walker was used as a reliever at Division II University of New Haven after transferring from the University of South Florida and showed enough there to be selected by the Mets in the 37th round of the 2017 Draft. The left-hander didn’t see full-season ball until 2021, partly due to a 2019 car collision that left him with nerve issues in his throwing arm, but he took off in that age-26 campaign, reaching as high as Triple-A. He was one of only five Mets Minor Leaguers with 100-plus innings, and his 1.02 WHIP across three levels was best among New York Minor League qualifiers. Despite his sizable frame at 6-foot-6, Walker thrives more on pitchability than stuff, and that’s helped him make the transition from relieving in college to starting in the pros. His fastball sat in the low-90s last season, and he could place it well within the zone. The southpaw has emphasized adding velocity this offseason to force his way into the Majors, so that will deserve following. An upper-70s curveball gives him a more vertical look, though the organization has tried to get it to show more break, and he possesses a serviceable changeup for right-handers that could use a little more separation off the heater. Walker has admitted that harnessing his control was his biggest point of emphasis in 2021, and a 6.5 percent walk rate and 3.4 K/BB ratio helped fuel his rise up the system last year. It still wasn’t enough to get him on the 40-man roster, when he was Rule 5-eligible, so he’ll need that velo and sharper stuff to come around in 2022 if he’s going to force the issue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A first-round pick out of high school in 2018, McLain headed to UCLA rather than sign with the D-backs. After posting an OPS over 1.000 in both the shortened 2020 season and then in a solid 2021 campaign with the Bruins despite a thumb injury, McLain landed in the first round again, this time signing with the Reds for $4.625 million as the No. 17 overall pick in that summer’s Draft. Thought to be an advanced college hitter who could move quickly, McLain struggled at the plate with an aggressive move to Double-A for his first full season and didn’t hit well in the Arizona Fall League. After striking out in just 15 percent of his plate appearances at UCLA in 2021, that rate skyrocketed to just over 28 percent in 2022 with the Reds. Much of that stemmed from McLain trying to do too much at the plate as he was trying to figure out who he is as a pro hitter and he sold out for power too often. The right-handed hitter does have a feel for the strike zone -- he had a 15.5 percent walk rate in Double-A -- and there’s confidence he’ll learn to make better swing decisions and get back to his high-contact rate overall approach at the plate. McLain’s speed has played well as a pro and that should continue to be an asset. He also showed he can handle shortstop with a solid arm, good range and excellent instincts. He also played a very good second base, which might be the best fit long-term, and that versatility could help him given the organizational depth at shortstop if he can get back on track offensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The eldest of three baseball-playing brothers -- Sean is a legitimate 2022 Draft prospect at Arizona State and Nick is a freshman at UCLA -- Matt McLain was a first-round pick out high school in 2018 who headed to UCLA instead of signing with the D-backs, then turned a solid junior season in 2021 into becoming a mid-first-round pick, despite a thumb injury that sidelined him. The Reds gave him an over-slot bonus of $4.625 million, then saw him perform as advertised during a pro debut spent mostly in full-season ball. The cliché “a real baseball player” might get used way too often, but it really fits for the 5-foot-11 infielder, who maximizes his solid tools with outstanding instincts on both sides of the ball. He has a compact swing and outstanding bat-to-ball skills and his approach improved at UCLA to the point where he walked as much as he struck out in 2021, then posted a .389 OBP during his pro debut. While he’s geared for hit over power, there’s enough strength for him to have plenty of pop moving forward, with some seeing a bit of Alex Bregman in him. Just like Bregman, McLain will play shortstop at the outset of his career, though he might not be there long-term. The Reds are happy to let him stick there or play his way off, and he has the chance to stay thanks to his plus speed, above-average arm strength, quick release and those plus instincts. The Reds feel his bat will profile at third or second as well if there’s a better defensive option at the premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After winning Big 12 Conference pitcher of the year and co-tournament MVP honors as a Baylor sophomore, Bradford projected as a top-two-rounds pick for 2019. But he made just three starts that spring before having thoracic outlet surgery and wound up signing for early third-round money ($700,000) as a sixth-rounder. He ranked sixth in the Minors with a 6.1 K/BB ratio in his 2021 pro debut, but he struggled much of last season in Double-A before rallying with a 2.63 ERA in his final seven starts and six shutout innings in the Texas League semifinals. A classic crafty left-hander, Bradford has a four-seam fastball that sits at 89-92 mph and touches 95, but generated a 27 percent swing-and-miss rate last year because of command and carry at the top of the zone. It pairs well with a plus low-80s changeup that he works closer to the knees with some fade and sink. The Rangers had him scrap the soft curveball he used in college to go with a low-80s slider, but the slider got hammered in 2022 and he shifted to a more promising mid-80s cutter down the stretch. Bradford has better feel for pitching than any Texas farmhand and keeps hitters uncomfortable by mixing his pitches and locations. He repeats his clean delivery at will and provides quality strikes, and he creates elite extension that provides deception and enables his stuff to play up. If he can continue to miss bats with a fastball with below-average velocity, he could slot into the back of the big league rotation at some point this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bradford seemed destined for the top two rounds of the 2019 Draft after winning Big 12 Conference pitcher of the year and co-tournament MVP awards as a Baylor sophomore the previous spring. But he made just three starts the next spring before needing surgery to alleviate thoracic outlet syndrome, after which the Rangers took him in the sixth round and signed him for early third-round money ($700,000). He looked like his usual polished self in his 2021 pro debut, ranking ninth in the Minors with a 6.1 K/BB ratio while advancing to Double-A, but struggled for much of this season before finishing strong in August and September. Bradford's best pitch is a plus low-80s changeup with sink that he sells with fastball arm speed. His cambio tunnels well with his four-seam heater, which sits at 90-91 mph and tops out at 95 but is effective because of his command and deception. Texas had him scrap the curveball he used at Baylor in favor of a low-80s slider that got rocked in 2022 before he switched to harder, shorter cutter down the stretch. Thanks to his ability to provide quality strikes and the elite extension he creates in his clean delivery, Bradford is greater than the sum of his individual pitches. An intelligent and competitive pitcher, he keeps hitters off balance by mixing his pitches and locations. He's a high-floor type who could fit in the back of the big league rotation in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Six-foot-4 and 175 pounds when the Marlins signed him for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2019, Pérez added four inches and 45 pounds by the time he made his pandemic-delayed pro debut in 2021. He almost immediately asserted himself as one of the best pitching prospects in baseball and dominated as a 19-year-old in Double-A last season. A lat strain cost him a month late in the summer, but he returned to help Pensacola win the Southern League championship. Pérez's combination of size, stuff and polish is tough to top, starting with a fastball that parks at 94-97 mph and peaks at 100 and plays even better than its velocity thanks to its shape, running action and induced vertical break. His deceptive upper-80s changeup is just as nasty, generating an outstanding 61 percent swing-and-miss rate in 2022 thanks to its fade and tumble. After featuring an upper-70s curveball in the past, he added a tighter mid-80s slider last season that grades as plus more consistently than his bender. Considering his youth and size, Pérez is incredibly advanced on the mound. He has uncanny body control that allows him to keep his long limbs in sync, repeat his delivery and fill the strike zone. The Marlins also praise his maturity and mound presence, two more factors that should allow him to make his big league debut as a 20-year-old at some point this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez has grown four inches and 45 pounds to 6-foot-8 and 200 since signing for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2019. His stuff has gotten bigger as well. After standing out in instructional league in 2020, he made a spectacular pro debut last year, posting a 1.96 ERA, .158 opponent average and 108/26 K/BB ratio in 78 innings while reaching High-A at age 18. He hasn't advanced nearly as far as Edward Cabrera, Max Meyer and Sixto Sánchez, but some evaluators inside and outside the organization believe he could eclipse them all in the long run. After displaying a mid-80s fastball when the Marlins first scouted him, Perez worked at 91-95 mph during instructs in 2020 and operated at 93-96 last season, topping out at 98. His extra-long, super-lean frame still features plenty of projection, so there could be more velocity to come, and the shape, running action and induced vertical break on his heater could make it a plus-plus offering when he's a finished product. He also owns a pair of promising secondary pitches, with his mid-80s changeup featuring some fade and tumble and grading as plus more consistently than an upper-70s curveball that he lands for strikes. Perez produces his intriguing stuff with a smooth delivery and little effort. He keeps his long limbs in sync with outstanding body control for someone his size and age and locates his pitches where he wants. He excelled while facing much older competition, exuding maturity and mound presence, and should continue to move rapidly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez didn't immediately stand out when he signed out of the Dominican Republic for $200,000 in July 2019, and the coronavirus pandemic prevented him from making his pro debut last summer. But he has grown four inches and 45 pounds to 6-foot-8 and 200 since turning pro and opened eyes in instructional league last fall. He was both the youngest (17 years, six months) and most impressive pitcher in Marlins camp. Perez worked in the mid-80s when first spotted in the Dominican but operated with a 91-95 mph fastball during instructs and has reached 97 this season. There's still a ton of projection remaining in his extra-tall frame, so his heater could sit in the mid-90s once he matures physically. He also shows feel for spinning a curveball and some aptitude for using a changeup. In addition to his stuff, Perez also impresses with how easily he generates it. He has a smooth delivery, keeps his long limbs in sync with surprising body control for such a tall teenager and fills the strike zone. He wasn't fazed by facing older hitters at instructional league, displaying mound presence that adds to his mid-rotation starter upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best two-way prospect in the 2020 college class, Schmitt stood out with his power, defense and fastball/splitter combo while earning Cape Cod League all-star and playoff MVP honors the summer before. He became the highest-drafted San Diego State player since Stephen Strasburg went No. 1 overall in 2009, signing for an under-slot $1,147,500 in the second round and becoming a full-time third baseman. After a broken nose and left wrist injury marred his 2021 pro debut, he hit .293/.365/.489 with 21 homers while advancing to Triple-A last year. Schmitt showed more power with wood bats than metal bats as an amateur, and he began hitting balls harder and driving them more consistently in 2022. He showed a quicker right-handed swing than in the past and tapped into his solid raw power more easily by not swinging for the fences. He crushes fastballs but still has to prove he can handle quality offspeed pitches at the upper levels. Though he's a below-average runner out of the batter's box, Schmitt moves well at third base and is a potential Gold Glover. He has range to both sides, reliable hands and a strong arm that produced fastballs up to 96 mph and some devastating mid-80s splitters when he closed games in college. His defensive tools translated into solid shortstop play when the Giants needed him to take over for an injured Marco Luciano at High-A Eugene last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schmitt impressed as a slugger, third-base defender and closer in the Cape Cod League in 2019, winning playoff MVP honors and establishing himself as the top college two-way prospect in the 2020 Draft. He became the highest-drafted San Diego State player since Stephen Strasburg went No. 1 overall in 2009, signing for an under-slot $1,147,500 in the second round and becoming a full-time third baseman. He dealt with adversity in his 2021 pro debut, overcoming hitting .121 in May and playing through a broken nose sustained when he was hit by a pitch until his season ended in August when another errant pitch injured his left wrist. Despite his offensive potential, Schmitt turns more heads with his defense. The third baseman on MLB Pipeline's 2022 All-Defense team, he has range to both sides, soft hands and well above-average arm strength that all translated well to shortstop when the Giants needed him to fill a hole there this season. When he closed games in college, he showcased a low-90s fastball that reached 96 mph and a mid-80s splitter that was devastating at its best. As an amateur, Schmitt showed more power with wood bats on the Cape than he did with metal bats with the Aztecs. After focusing too much on trying to drive the ball in the air last season, he's doing a better job of using the whole field and letting his solid raw power come naturally. He's a below-average runner with good instincts on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schmitt hit for power while also closing games in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2019, winning playoff MVP honors and establishing himself as the best college two-way prospect in the 2020 Draft. The highest-drafted San Diego State player since Stephen Strasburg went No. 1 overall in 2009, he signed for an under-slot $1,147,500 in the second round and saw his first pro action in instructional league. Though he tied for the NCAA Division I lead with six saves during his shortened junior season, the Giants plan to develop him solely as a third baseman. Schmitt's bat speed and strength create plus raw power, and he did a better job of using it with wood bats on the Cape (five homers in 36 games) than he did with metal bats with the Aztecs (six longballs in 132 contests). The issue is that he has good bat-to-ball skills but doesn't always make quality contact, and San Francisco believes he can be at least a 20-homer threat if he develops a more selective approach and adds some loft to his right-handed stroke. While he has below-average speed, he has good instincts on the bases. The Giants love Schmitt's defense at third base, where he has soft hands and an easy plus arm. If he doesn't make it at the hot corner, he has pitching as a fallback. As a reliever, he displayed a low-90s fastball that topped out at 96 mph, a mid-80s splitter that could be devastating at times and a fringy breaking ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player at Duke who became more pitcher than hitter as his career progressed, Mervis became a priority free agent when he went unselected in the shortened five-round 2020 Draft. Signed for the maximum $20,000 allowed under pandemic rules, he struggled in his 2021 pro debut but broke out the next year to lead the Minors with 78 extra-base hits, 310 total bases and 119 RBIs and rank second in doubles (40), third in homers (36), fifth in slugging (.605) and eighth in OPS (.984). He got a shot at the Cubs' first-base job last May but hit just .167 with a 32 percent strikeout rate in six weeks before spending the rest of the year in Triple-A. Mervis offers the best combination of power, patience and contact in Chicago's system, though he tried to do too much in his big league debut and struggled when his approach fell apart. He got back on track when he returned to Triple-A, letting his combination of bat speed and strength translate into solid left-handed power without swinging for the fences. He has handled lefties well in the Minors the past two seasons but struck out 11 times in 19 at-bats against them in the Majors, and some evaluators believe he's more of a platoon partner than an everyday player. With well-below-average speed, Mervis is limited to first base, where he's an adequate defender. As a college pitcher, he displayed a strong arm that produced low-90s fastballs with high spin rates and solid low-80s sliders. If Michael Busch winds up at first base after joining the Cubs in a January trade, Mervis may need a deal of his own to get a chance for a starting role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player at Duke, Mervis spent most of his first two college seasons as a pitcher before focusing on hitting in his final two years. A priority free agent after getting shut out in the shortened five-round 2020 Draft, he had offers from several clubs and signed with the Cubs for the maximum $20,000 permitted under pandemic rules. He quadrupled his home run output from nine in his 2021 pro debut to 36 last season while leading the Minors with 78 extra-base hits, 310 total bases and 119 RBIs and ranking second in doubles (40), third in homers (36), fifth in slugging (.605) and eighth in OPS (.984). Mervis features the best combination of power and contact in the Cubs system, and he took off when he improved his bat path and his swing decisions -- though he tried to do too much and struggled during his first big league callup this summer. His bat speed and the strength in his 6-foot-4, 225-pound frame are obvious, but he's more than just a masher. His relatively compact left-handed swing enables him to make consistent hard contact and he did a much better job of handling same-side pitchers in 2022 than he did in his debut. Though he's a well-below-average runner, Mervis moves well enough to play an adequate first base. He has a strong arm that produced low-90s fastballs with high spin rates and solid low-80s sliders when he pitched in college. He played some third base at Duke but lacks the range to play there or in left field as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shewmake left Texas A&M with a career OPS of .868 after three years playing every day, performing well enough in his junior season to land a $3,132,300 bonus from the Braves as the 21st overall pick in the 2019 Draft. He then fared so well in his pro debut that summer that he got on the fast track by earning a double jump to Double-A. He hasn't replicated that offensive success since, and went to the White Sox as part of a five-player package for Aaron Bummer in November 2023. A left-handed-hitting infielder, Shewmake’s best characteristic at the plate is his knack for making contact. He shook off a rough start and elevated strikeout rate in his first full season and now carries a career K rate of just 18.5 percent heading into the 2023 season. While he is capable of hitting the ball hard, there are questions about whether he can drive it enough and also get on base more consistently to be more of an impact offensive player. Shewmake’s defense has improved to the point at which the metrics point to him being one of the better defensive shortstops in the Minor Leagues. He’s not flashy, but he has great hands, plus instincts and an above-average arm, leading other teams to ask about him because of his glovework. How much he hits will determine whether he can reach his ceiling as an everyday player at the premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shewmake was a three-year starter at Texas A&M, manning second base as a freshman and shortstop the next two seasons. He played well enough as a junior in 2019 to become the Braves’ second of two first-round picks, going No. 21 overall. A strong debut in Low-A earned him a double jump to Double-A to close out his pro debut. That’s where he spent all of his first full season in 2021, starting incredibly slowly, but righting the ship after a horrific first month, then spending the 2022 season in Triple-A. Throw out a May in which Shewmake hit under .100 and the infielder posted a much-more-respectable .253 and slugged .436 with 11 homers. Known coming into pro ball for his bat-to-ball skills, he also made a lot more contact, dropping his strikeout rate below 20 percent after whiffing more than 30 percent of the time that opening month. Though he’s lean and wiry, he can make surprisingly loud contact with solid exit velocities from the left side, even if his overall power profile is somewhat in question. One thing that’s no longer in doubt is his ability to stick at shortstop. While he’s not a burner, he’s a very instinctive defender with great hands and an above-average arm. It’s not flashy, but he makes all the plays. He’ll need to prove he can consistently impact the baseball for a full season, and if he can, he has the chance to be a solid, if unspectacular, big league regular at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The second of two college hitters taken by the Braves in the first round of the 2019 Draft, Shewmake hit the ground running during his pro debut after being taken No. 21 overall out of Texas A&M. He showed off advanced skills on both sides of the ball after heading straight to full-season Rome, posting an .862 OPS to earn a double-jump up to Double-A. He lost his approach a bit with that challenge, albeit in a small 14-game sample size, but rediscovered it during his time at the Braves’ alternate training site in 2020. Since his freshman year with the Aggies, Shewmake has shown an impressive feel for the barrel and an ability to make consistent hard contact without striking out. He left college with a strikeout rate under 10 percent, a trend that largely continued in Rome, but climbed in that first taste of Double-A. He regained his approach in 2020, almost walking as much as he struck out. He’s added strength to his 6-foot-4 frame and he should continue to learn how to drive the ball with excellent leverage in his left-handed swing. While he’s not a burner, Shewmake does have some sneaky speed that allows him to be an aggressive baserunner who can steal a base. It also gives him a chance to stick at shortstop, with his instincts and game clock allowing all of his actions to play up, not to mention an above-average arm. His plus makeup and leadership skills should allow him to continue to move quickly up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $1.3 million out of Panama in 2015, Amaya quickly became the Cubs' best catching prospect and played in consecutive SiriusXM All-Star Futures Games in 2018 and 2019. But the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and a forearm strain that led to Tommy John surgery in November 2021 limited him to just 63 games (and only 12 behind the plate) in the past three years. Chicago hoped to get him more work in the Arizona Fall League last offseason, but he suffered a Lisfranc fracture in his left foot in September. Amaya has worked diligently to become a solid receiver, and he frames and blocks pitches well. He also has improved his arm strength from average when he turned pro to at least solid before his elbow blew out, and he has erased 38 percent of base stealers in his career. He won't be able to show well his arm has bounced back from Tommy John surgery in game action until some point this year. Though Amaya batted just .243/.342/.379 in his first six years as a pro, the Cubs believe he can provide above-average offense for a catcher. He offers a sound swing and plenty of bat speed from the right side of the plate and employs a patient all-fields approach. But those ingredients haven't cooked up much production because he chases too many offspeed pitches and rarely does damage against them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Amaya quickly emerged as the Cubs' best catching prospect after signing for $1.3 million out of Panama in 2015 and earned berths in back-to-back SiriusXM All-Star Futures Games in 2018 and 2019. But his development has been stuck in neutral ever since, thanks to the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and a forearm strain that limited him to 22 games in Double-A last year. Tommy John surgery last November means that he won't catch during the 2022 season, though he was able to DH by midsummer. Amaya's defense is ahead of his offense at this point. He has worked to become a solid receiver, and he blocks and frames pitches well. He possessed average arm strength when he first signed but now has a solid-to-plus arm that has helped him erase 38 percent of base stealers as a pro. Though Amaya batted just .241/.339/.371 in his first five seasons, he has controlled the strike zone well and made consistent contact as one of the youngest regulars in his leagues. He has feel for the barrel and uses the entire field from the right side of the plate, though he may not have more than average power. He projects as a possible .260 hitter with 15 homers per season and quality work behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs ranked second in international spending in 2015-16 with $16.4 million in bonuses (and another $13.2 million in penalty tax), and the best player from that crop is Amaya, who signed for $1 million out of Panama. A participant in the last two SiriusXM All-Star Futures Games, he was also the youngest batting qualifier (age 20) in the high Class A Carolina League in 2019. He spent 2020 at Chicago's alternate training site, improving his pitch-calling and communication under the tutelage of veteran backstops Jose Lobaton and P.J. Higgins. Amaya stands out most with his work behind the plate. He demonstrated more consistency as a receiver last summer while continuing to frame and block pitches well. His arm rated as average when he turned pro and now grades as solid to plus, and he erased 35 percent of basestealers in 2019. Though Amaya batted just .243/.334/.375 in his first four pro seasons, he has been younger than most of his competition and has shown the ability to manage the strike zone and get on base. He has good feel for the barrel and uses the entire field well, though most of the right-handed hitter's pop comes to his pull side. If he learns to drive the ball more consistently, he could develop into a .260 hitter with 15-20 homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There have been 13 big leaguers who hail from Mercer University, the most recent being Mariners outfielder Kyle Lewis. Cox could be No. 14. In the college-pitching-heavy 2018 Draft, Cox was the Royals’ fifth-round pick and had one of the best full-season debuts in ’19, walking only 38 batters in 130 2/3 innings. Back in game action in 2021, Cox posted a 3.00 ERA with 56 strikes and 25 walks across 63 innings at Double-A Northwest Arkansas. He worked through some arm fatigue, which led to a lower average on his fastball and struggles with control. Cox’s arsenal includes three above-average pitches, starting with his low-90s fastball that has good life to it and misses bats on both sides of the plate. His main secondary pitch is his curveball, which is one of the best in the system. It has true 12-to-6 action to it and flashes plus with power behind it. Cox’s feel for spin allows him to have a new distinctive slider in the low-80s, and he rounds out his arsenal with a changeup that’s he’s been working on getting a feel for on the mound. Cox features a repeatable delivery and arm action. While he hasn’t moved as quickly as some of the others from his Draft class, Cox put together a solid year in Double-A despite the arm fatigue and higher walk rate. The Royals were faced with a roster crunch this past offseason and left Cox off the 40-man, exposing him to the Rule 5 Draft, but he’s still high on their radar and has a future in the big league rotation if he can get completely healthy. He also wouldn’t be out of place as a big arm in the bullpen, especially if he’s limited to his fastball and curveball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cox’s alma mater, Mercer University, has produced 13 big leaguers since the program’s inception in 1897. Mariners outfielder Kyle Lewis is the most recent. Cox could be next. The Royals drafted him in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft, and the lefty was a model of efficiency in his first full season between Class A and Class A Advanced. Cox had a tough summer working at the Royals' alternate training site in 2020, adjusting to more advanced hitters and working on his secondary pitches, but he left in a good spot heading into 2021. Cox operates with three Major League-caliber pitches that he controls well. He usually sits in the low 90s with his fastball, but he can dial the above-average pitch up to 95-96 mph. His curveball is one of the best in the system, a true plus pitch thrown with power and 12-to-6 downer action that gets him whiffs on both sides of the plate. His feel for spin also translates into a distinctly different slider that sits in the low 80s and can be a solid pitch at times. His average changeup has improved, and he’s been able to command it better recently with fastball-like arm speed in the mid-80s. His stuff shows natural bat-missing ability, and he’s able to repeat his delivery and arm action, which has lowered his walk rate from college. Cox bulked up some before going to the alternate training site, and it might have led to some of his battles in 2020. He struggled with getting the ball down, which led to a ton of contact against him. But the Royals were encouraged with where he left things, and he's enjoyed a bounceback year for the most part at Double-A Northwest Arkansas. He has the makeup and talent to project as a big league starter but would not be out of place as a big arm near the back of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following standout turns in the Northwoods and Cape Cod Leagues, Pfaadt became the second-highest player selected in Division II Bellarmine history when he went in the fifth round to the D-backs in the shortened 2020 Draft. He established a good baseline by playing at three levels in his first full season in 2021 before exploding last year. The Arizona hurler became the first Minor League pitcher to strike out more than 200 batters since 2011 when he fanned 218 batters over Double-A and Triple-A, and his 167 frames also led the Minors. The 6-foot-4 right-hander topped out at 96.2 mph in the Pacific Coast League but is typically more around 93-94 mph with his fastball. The pitch has enough carry to work up in the zone, giving another tick or two of quality. Pfaadt utilized his mid-80s slider the most among his secondary pitches (roughly 28 percent of the time at the Minors’ top level), and it got a healthy amount of swing-and-miss because of its promising sweep across the zone. A mid-80s changeup moved the other way toward his arm-side and dove enough out of the zone to have a higher whiff percentage than the slider, while his upper-70s curveball is mostly used for show and little else. Pfaadt had the lowest walk rate (4.8 percent) among D-backs full-season qualifiers, and while his ability to pitch in the zone made him hittable in the past, he did a better job of working its periphery and letting the quality of his stuff do the work. His arsenal, durability and strike-throwing prowess have gotten Pfaadt to the Majors in 2023, and he needs to build on what he showed in the Minors to stick as a prominent piece of the Arizona rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from NCAA Division-II Bellarmine, Pfaadt made a name for himself in the Northwoods and Cape Cod leagues over the 2018 and ’19 summers. He was off to a strong start in 2020 (1.38 ERA with 27 strikeouts over 26 innings) before the coronavirus pandemic canceled the rest of the season. The D-backs selected the 6-foot-4, 220-pound right-hander in the fifth round of the 2020 Draft and signed him for a below-slot $100,000. It didn’t take long before the pick looked like a steal as Pfaadt pitched his way across three levels and worked his way up to Double-A in his 2021 professional debut. Pfaadt operates with a 92- to 97-mph four-seam fastball that cuts and a 93- to 95-mph two-seamer with armside run. The heavy sink generates a lot of ground-ball outs for the 6-foot-4 right-hander and he complements the fastballs with a changeup and a pair of breaking balls. Some evaluators feel the fading changeup is his best pitch, while the curveball and slider grade out as average offerings. The two breaking balls used to blend together at times, but Pfaadt has begun to separate them, getting vertical break on the curveball and more horizontal action on the slider. As the two pitches become more defined, he may be able to miss even more bats after posting a 10.9 K/9 in 2021. A throwback pitcher who brings both hands up over his head in his delivery, Pfaadt can throw all of his pitches for strikes and holds his velocity deep into his starts. With above-average-to-plus command, he’s been guilty of throwing too many strikes on occasion and will work his way through the system as a starter. He has the potential to develop into a mid-rotation starter, but if he has to transition to the bullpen, his heavy fastball and ability to miss bats would play well in high-leverage situations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever in his first two years at Central Arkansas, Stone got just four starts as a junior in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season but finished with a 13-strikeout no-hitter and became the highest-drafted pitcher in Bears history. After the Dodgers signed him for a well below-slot $97,500 with the penultimate pick in the truncated five-round Draft, they helped him significantly upgrade his stuff, which allowed him to lead the Minors with a 1.48 ERA in 2022. He regressed a bit last season as he struggled through a rough first half, yet he made his big league debut in May and spent four stints in Los Angeles. Stone barely employed a fading changeup in college before the Dodgers outfitted him with a more powerful mid-80s version with devastating tumble at its best that grades as a plus-plus weapon. The only downside is that he falls in love with his cambio, using it more often than any of his other pitches, and big leaguers weren't fooled by it as much as Minor Leaguers were. His low release point produces good carry with a 93-95 mph four-seam fastball that reaches 97, but his heater lacks life and got mashed in 2023, when he had more success with a little-used sinker with similar velocity. His mid-80s slider shows flashes of becoming a solid pitch but lacks consistency, and he has a less effective 89-91 mph cutter that he can throw for strikes more easily. Stone's fastball dodged more barrels and his slider had better shape when he dominated in 2022, and he still could be a No. 3 or 4 starter if he can recapture that form. Using his heater more often could help him improve its movement and command, which would make his changeup even more effective. He's not very physical but his athleticism and efficient delivery help him maintain his stuff and throw strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stone led Central Arkansas with six saves as a sophomore in 2019 before moving to the rotation, where he authored a 13-strikeout no-hitter against Southeastern Louisiana in his fourth and final start of the pandemic-shortened 2020 season. Though he didn't get a lot of scouting exposure, the Dodgers made him the highest-drafted pitcher in school history, selecting him in the fifth round with the penultimate pick in the truncated Draft. His stuff has made a huge leap since he signed for a well below-slot $97,500, and he ranked first in the Minors in ERA (1.48) and fifth in strikeout rate (12.4 per nine innings) in 2022. Stone barely used a fading changeup in college but he now has a harder, mid-80s cambio with devastating tumble, a plus-plus pitch that he threw more than his four-seam fastball in 2022. After averaging 92 mph with his heater at Central Arkansas, he now sits at 94-96 mph and peaks at 98, and his low release point creates plenty of induced vertical break. He also has scrapped a downer curveball and developed a solid slider that showed improved shape while parking in the mid-80s last season. While Stone is less physical than desired for a starter, he's athletic and has an efficient delivery that helps him hold his stuff and provide consistent strikes. His biggest need is to add some life to his fastball, which doesn't miss as many bats as metrics suggest it should. He has little left to prove in the Minors and projects as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading Central Arkansas with six saves and a 1.52 ERA in 2019, Stone moved to the rotation as a junior and spun a 13-strikeout no-hitter against Southeastern Louisiana in his final outing of the shortened 2020 college season. The Dodgers made him the highest-drafted pitcher in school history, selecting in the fifth round with the penultimate pick of the truncated Draft. Signed for a well below-slot $97,500, he showed improved stuff in his pro debut while reaching High-A and averaging 13.6 strikeouts per nine innings, which would have ranked fifth in the Minors if he weren't five innings short of qualifying. Stone went from working with a 90-94 mph fastball as a college starter to averaging 94 mph and touching 98 in his first season as a pro, and his low release point creates induced vertical break that leaves hitters scuffling to get on top of his heater. He barely used a mid-80s changeup with some fade in college but now has a harder, devastating cambio that drops off the table. He has scrapped his downer curveball to focus on a harder mid-80s slider/cutter and is working to add more sweep to help combat right-handers. Stone aggressively attacks hitters with all three of his pitches and provides strikes. Though he's less physical than a typical starter, his efficiency and twitchy athleticism may help him remain in that role. Los Angeles also could try to expedite him to the big leagues as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Irvin overlapped with top Nationals pitching prospect Cade Cavalli on the 2018 Oklahoma staff and went to the Nationals in the fourth round that year after two solid seasons as a Sooners starter. After spending all of his first full season at Single-A, he missed out on 2020 like everyone else and then didn’t pitch in a Minor League game in 2021 due to Tommy John surgery. Irvin returned to the mound last year and lasted 103 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A, posting a 4.79 ERA over 15 starts with a more promising 25.5 percent K rate at Harrisburg. The 6-foot-6 right-hander showed encouraging velocity in his return from the elbow injury, sitting in the mid-90s while topping out around 97 mph. The velocity waned as he worked deeper into games, but that likely had something to do with the workload after such a long layoff. A low-80s curveball displayed promising break, and he landed it for enough strikes and whiffs outside the zone to help push his strikeout-an-inning pace. An upper-80s changeup remains fringy but hasn’t hurt him too badly against lefties. Irvin’s 6.6 percent walk rate ranked second among Nationals Minor Leaguers with at least 100 frames in 2022, and that will keep him in a starting role. Washington added him to its 40-man in November, and he is entering his age-26 season -- signs he’ll need to push for the Majors soon, perhaps as a two-pitch reliever if he runs into starting snags in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It will be some time before we see results from Irvin on the mound. The 6-foot-6 right-hander was a standout at the University of Oklahoma, where he pitched Friday nights. Irvin posted a 3.41 ERA with 115 K’s and 28 walks in 95 innings as a junior, prompting the Nationals to grab him in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft. He spent his first full season at Class A Hagerstown and held his own in the South Atlantic League with a 3.79 ERA, 1.25 WHIP and 113 strikeouts in 128 1/3 frames. Irvin looked like he was making improvements at the Nationals’ alternate site in Fredericksburg, but developed forearm and elbow issues that required Tommy John surgery in October. He will be out for the entire 2021 season as a result. Before the injury, the former Sooner was showing promising signs of using his size to pump fastballs with increased velocity in the mid-90s, touching 97 mph at times. The high-70s curveball has been a plus pitch at times and was only held back by its inconsistency, while the changeup sat behind the heater and breaker. Irvin’s arm action could get long at times, but the Nationals weren’t overly concerned that would inhibit his stuff over the long term. It all comes down to what kind of pitcher Irvin can be coming back from the surgery. Returning from Tommy John is not as difficult as it once was, but Irvin will have the added task of proving he can maintain the velocity jump he showed in 2020. If he does, his Major League chances are all the better. If that fastball doesn’t hold, there is much more pressure on the secondaries to prove his worth as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller began his college career at Blinn College, a junior college in Texas, then moved to Texas A&M after one year. He pitched out of the Aggies' bullpen for two years before getting the chance to start in 2021. He showed his premium stuff could potentially play enough as a starter to go in the fourth round of the Draft to the Mariners, then jumped on the fast track by pitching his way to Double-A in his first full season, finishing with a combined .195 batting average against while striking out 11 per nine.
