Over the course of a full season and more than 133 innings, Miller showed his stuff will hold up. He has at an easily plus fastball with high spin, a pitch that averaged 95 mph in Double-A and touched triple digits. He has a distinct hard mid-80s slider with power and depth and a slower upper-70s curve that can both miss bats, with the slider ahead of the curve. He also has an effective heavy mid-80s changeup. There were those who thought Miller was destined to head back to the bullpen because he had struggled with command and has a high-tempo delivery. But he’s made huge strides in his ability to find the strike zone while repeating his delivery that features a ton of arm speed, giving him a very good chance to join a big league rotation soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite being just a fourth-round pick less than 12 months ago, Miller has more makings than arguably any pitcher in the system to make an aggressive leap. He flashed 99 mph in Minor League Spring Training and has a gnarly slider that could probably play in a big league bullpen sooner than later. His trajectory will likely be determined by what profile the Mariners view him as long term. Miller went the JUCO route in college, transferring from Blinn (Texas) after one season to Texas A&M, where he had to prove himself a full-time reliever before finally getting the chance to start in his final season. That opportunity was a big part of why he turned down his 38th-round selection by the Marlins in 2018 and other opportunities in the shortened ‘20 Draft. Despite the transition from the bullpen, Miller held his velocity and featured some of the best fastball metrics in last year’s Draft. He has three effective secondary offerings, the best of which is a mid-80s slider with power and depth. He also utilizes an upper-70s curveball as an offspeed pitch and mixes in a heavy mid-80s changeup. Though he has a high-tempo delivery, Miller generates his stuff with arm speed more than effort. He has shown the ability to maintain the quality of his pitches deep into games. His arm action is a bit long and leads to some inconsistencies with his control and command that he'll need to iron out to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 2018 supplemental first-rounder from a Florida high school, Edwards signed with the Padres for an over-slot $2.6 million and quickly established himself as one of baseball's top second-base prospects. After the Rays acquired him in the Jake Cronenworth trade in December 2019, he lost 2020 to the pandemic before his performance took a downturn the next two seasons. Tampa Bay declined to protect him on its 40-man roster in November, instead dealing him and J.T. Chargois to the Marlins for righty pitching prospects Marcus Johnson and Santiago Suarez. Edwards displayed advanced feel for the barrel while hitting .320 in his first three pro seasons, then slumped to .246 while striking out at a 19 percent clip in Triple-A last season. The switch-hitter lost his approach and got too aggressive in 2022 but has gotten back to what makes him successful this year while ranking among the Minor League leaders in hitting and contact rate. He matched his previous career total of six homers in four years by early August, though he still features well below-average power. While Edwards once had double-plus speed, he was more of a plus runner in 2022 before ticking up a bit this season, when he has shown better basestealing aptitude than ever. His quickness allows him to cover ground in the infield but his fringy arm strength limits his effectiveness at shortstop and third base. He's more reliable than flashy at second, the position at which he has the best chance to become a big league regular, and the Marlins have deployed him in center field for the first time in his pro career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres paid Edwards an over-slot $2.6 million as a 2018 supplemental first-rounder from a Florida high school, then traded him along with Hunter Renfroe and Esteban Quiroz to the Rays in December 2019 to acquire Jake Cronenworth and Tommy Pham. After losing the '20 season to the pandemic, Edwards has seen his prospect stock dip significantly in the last two seasons. Rather than protect him on its 40-man roster in November, Tampa Bay dealt him and J.T. Chargois to the Marlins for right-handed pitching prospects Marcus Johnson and Santiago Suarez. A career .320 hitter entering 2022, Edwards batted just .246 in Triple-A. While he exhibited elite bat control in the past, he struck out at a career-high 18.8 percent clip this year. He has limited offensive upside because he rarely drives the ball and produces little power, and his ability to make contact cuts into his walk totals. Edwards' best tool remains his plus-plus speed, though he never has been a particularly prolific basestealer and ran less than ever this season. While his quickness gives him range, his fringy arm strength limits his effectiveness on the left side of the infield and leaves him best suited to play second base. He may be more utilityman than regular, and he'll have to regain his past hitting ability to claim a role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres went well above slot value to get Edwards in the 2018 Draft, signing him for $2.6 million and away from a Vanderbilt commitment after selecting him No. 38 overall. He followed up his strong pro debut with an even better first full season, batting .322 with 34 steals between Class A Fort Wayne and Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, while also finishing tied for the third in the Minors with 162 hits. After the season, the Padres traded Edwards to Tampa Bay, packaging him with Hunter Renfroe to get Tommy Pham and Jake Cronenworth in a December 2019 deal. The Rays added Edwards to their alternate training site group in August, then got their first extended look at the young infielder in fall instructional league. Edwards has several leadoff-man qualities in his natural hitting ability, approach and speed. He will hit the ball to all fields from both sides of the plate, showing a penchant for making quality contact and a discerning eye, with an approach that leads to minimal swing and miss. Edwards is a threat to run whenever he gets on base and stole 56 bases with an 82.4 percent success rate across his first two seasons. The Rays think Edwards will develop more pop as he gets stronger and learns to generate more bat speed, but even then, he’s unlikely to offer anything more than well-below-average home-run power. Edwards is a capable shortstop but profiles as more of a true second baseman in the pro ranks. He’s at least an above-average defender at the keystone, one with smooth actions, soft hands and average arm strength that was stretched thin as a shortstop. Edwards isn’t flashy but does all the little things needed to help a team win, projecting as a top-of-the-order regular at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fletcher was one of college baseball's best outfield defenders during his three seasons at Arkansas and the Razorbacks' top hitter at the 2018 College World Series, where they lost in the finals to Oregon State. A 2019 supplemental second-round pick by the Diamondbacks, he batted .301/.350/.441 in his 28-game big league debut last summer before breaking his left index finger in late August. The younger brother of the Braves' David Fletcher, he joined the White Sox in a February trade for righty pitching prospect Cristian Mena. Fletcher continues to stand out most with his defense. Though he's just an average runner, he's faster under way and possesses tremendous instincts, allowing him to cover a lot of ground in center field. A plus defender at all three outfield spots, he also has solid arm strength and recorded four assists in 24 starts in the Majors. Because he offers less impact at the plate, Fletcher projects more as a fourth outfielder than a regular. He has some sneaky strength in his 5-foot-6, 185-pound frame but ordinary bat speed and not the smoothest left-handed swing. He fishes for too many pitches outside the strike zone and doesn't turn on pitches or drive them in the air on a consistent basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter in center for Arkansas and key part of the 2018 College World Series finalist squad, Fletcher became the 75th overall pick in 2019 when he joined the D-backs. Arizona added Fletcher to its 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible in November 2022, and Team Italy selected him for the World Baseball Classic roster (along with brother David) last spring. He made his big league debut in 2023, slashing .301/.350/.441 in 28 games, then went to the White Sox in a February trade for righty pitching prospect Cristian Mena. Fletcher’s improvements in picking his pitches and protecting the plate correlated with his offensive performance in 2022 and continued last season. The hitter-friendly environments flatter his power performance as a 5-foot-9 left-handed hitter who is better known for spraying the ball the other way, but there’s still enough pop for him to hit double-digit homers in The Show. While Fletcher is just an average runner, he gets great reads off the bat and is efficient with his routes to the ball, translating into outs for his team. He has the plus range and arm strength to handle all three outfield positions. He's 26 and doesn't come with a high ceiling, but he should get the chance to establish himself with a rebuilding White Sox club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter in center for Arkansas, Fletcher was the Razorbacks' best hitter at the 2018 College World Series, where they lost to Oregon State in the Finals. As with older brother, David, an infielder with the Angels, Dominic’s skills still stand out more than his pure physical ability. The D-backs took Fletcher 75th overall in the 2019 Draft and sent him straight to Low-A, where he produced an impressive .318/.389/.463 line with 20 extra-base hits in 55 games. Bumped up to Double-A for his 2021 full-season debut, Fletcher got off to a slow start and had a bit of an up-and-down season, but made some adjustments throughout the year and finished strong, hitting nearly .400 in September. Arizona likes Fletcher’s left-handed swing and is pleased with the way he uses the entire field. The 5-foot-9, 185-pounder has surprising power for his size and could develop into a 15-homer guy in the Majors. He’s still improving and fine-tuning his approach, but overall Fletcher is a polished hitter who puts together quality at-bats. He makes up for his average speed with tremendous instincts. Fletcher consistently gets good jumps and some club officials believe he’s one of the best defenders in the entire organization. He’s primarily played center, but has the skill set to be an above-average defender at all three outfield spots with a strong, accurate arm. Fletcher has a floor of a fourth outfielder and the D-backs have fallen in love with the way he plays. Given the career his brother has put together and the fact that Dominic has superior tools, the D-backs are bullish on his chances to finish closer to his ceiling than his floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter in center for Arkansas, he was the Razorbacks' best hitter at the 2018 College World Series, where they lost to Oregon State in the finals. As with his older brother David, an infielder with the Angels, his skills still stand out more than his pure physical ability. The D-backs took Fletcher with the last of their seven picks on Day 1 of the 2019 Draft and sent him straight to Class A Kane County, where he produced an impressive .318/.389/.463 line with 20 extra-base hits in 55 games. Fletcher got off to a slow start in 2021 as he was bumped up to Double-A, but after a few weeks, he adjusted to the new level and started to perform better offensively. Though he won't wow you with any one of his tools, the combination, along with his instincts, should carry him far. The Diamondbacks like Fletcher’s left-handed swing and how he uses it to hit to all fields with some surprising power for a 5-foot-9 guy. He puts together very consistent at-bats and competes hard. He could develop into a 15-homer guy in the big leagues. Fletcher is an average runner but receives above-average grades for his center-field defense because he has excellent instincts and consistently gets good jumps that allow him to track down balls from gap to gap. While he’s primarily played center, he has the skill set to be an above-average defender at all three outfield spots and possesses a strong, accurate arm that flashes plus at times. Fletcher has a floor of a fourth outfielder and the D-backs have fallen in love with the way he plays and think he could have more potential than that. Given the career his brother has put together and the fact that Dominic has superior tools, the D-backs are bullish on his chances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bolton was a projectable high school right-hander from California who would have headed to the University of Michigan had the Draft not worked out. The Pirates, never an organization to shy away from high-upside prep arms, kept him off campus by going slightly over slot to sign the right-hander in the sixth round of the 2017 Draft. Despite missing much of his first full season with a forearm issue, Bolton was able to pitch his way to Double-A in 2019 and then pitched well at the Pirates’ alternate training site in 2020. Bolton has a three-pitch mix that’s trending upwards -- four considering he uses two distinct fastballs effectively. His four-seamer is up to 97 mph and thrown with high spin rate that leads to ride up in the zone. His two-seamer is more in the 93-95 mph range with good sink that has led to a lot of ground-ball outs. His slider has become sharper and less slurvy, flashing signs of being an out pitch and his changeup gives him another at least average offering. While he’s a good strike-thrower, Bolton needs to continue to refine his fastball command within the strike zone. That, plus continued sharpening of and trust in his secondary stuff, should allow him to reach his ceiling as a No. 3-type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: New Mexico State is a college hitters' paradise, so scouts weren’t sure what to make of Ortiz’s gaudy numbers as a three-year starter there, particularly his .422/.474/.697 line as a junior. The Orioles figured at least his defensive acumen was worth taking in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, but it took a while to really know what kind of all-around player they had on their hands, between the pandemic in 2020 and a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder cutting his 2021 season short. He took a big step forward with a healthy 2022 in which he reached Triple-A, then hit .321/.378/.507 with Norfolk last year while making multiple stops in Baltimore. He was traded to the Brewers as part of the Corbin Burnes blockbuster in February. Since being drafted, Ortiz has added a lot of strength that’s enabled him to consistently register high exit velocities. He hasn’t sacrificed any of his elite bat-to-ball skills, striking out just 17.2 percent of the time in his Minor League career while showing the ability to drive the ball to all fields with solid in-game pop. There’s never been any question about his ability to defend. He has plus hands, actions, instincts and the ability to slow the game down, not to mention more than enough arm for shortstop. He’s shown the ability to play a plus second base and can even slide over to third, something that could come in handy given Milwaukee’s larger need at the hot corner with Willy Adames handling short. Adames is a free agent next season, however, and Ortiz could slide over to his natural position for the long haul in Milwaukee.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Looking to beef up their system with up-the-middle players, the Orioles made Ortiz the highest-drafted player taken out of New Mexico State when they picked him 108th overall in 2019. The selection came after Ortiz starred for the Aggies, leading the country in hits and runs as a junior while turning heads with his defensive prowess at shortstop. That plus glovework remains Ortiz’s calling card, and after a slow start offensively, he seemed to be coming into his own at the plate before his season ended prematurely due to shoulder surgery, though he was heating up again as the season wore on in Double-A in 2022. Now amid a system brimming with up-the-middle players, Ortiz is regarded by many as perhaps the best defensive prospect of the bunch. He is a true shortstop, with a good clock, strong hands, slick actions and a natural ability to read balls off the bat. He has a plus arm that’s improved since his college days (the 2021 surgery was to his non-throwing shoulder), and remains athletic enough after adding strength during quarantine to move around the diamond if necessary. Whether that happens probably depends on his bat, which briefly came to light last summer. After homering just once in his first 75 professional games, Ortiz celebrated his promotion to Double-A by homering four times in 16 contests at the level before injury struck. He doesn’t run particularly well, so it’ll be important for Ortiz to continue translating those power strides. If he does he could grow into a big league regular, or perhaps a defensive-minded utility player at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cal State Fullerton's No. 1 starter as a sophomore and junior, Bibee was better known for his strike-throwing than his stuff when the Guardians made him a fifth-round pick in 2021. Cleveland initially had him focus on refining his delivery and his pitches, deferring his pro debut until 2022 -- and the results were spectacular. He reached Double-A in July and finished the season ranked among the Minor League leaders in ERA (2.17, sixth), K/BB ratio (6.2, sixth), WHIP (0.97, eighth) and walks per nine innings (1.8, 10th). The Guardians had Bibee focus on throwing with more intent, which freed up his delivery and allowed his stuff to take off. His fastball went from sitting at 90-93 mph and peaking at 95 in college to operating at 93-97 and touching 99 with carry and run. His sweeping slider went from parking around 80 mph to the mid-80s, becoming a plus pitch, and his fading changeup made similar velocity gains while continuing to confound left-handed hitters. Bibee also can mix in an upper-70s curveball to give hitters a different look and pounds the zone with all four of his offerings. He was able to upgrade his stuff without costing himself control or command, going from a high-floor, back-of-the-rotation option to at least No. 3 starter upside and a Top 100 Prospect in short order. He's yet another example of the Guardians drafting a polished college pitcher and helping him raise his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the return from the Yankees for Frankie Montas and Lou Trivino at the 2022 Trade Deadline, Medina struggled to find the strike zone with any sort of regularity upon joining the A’s organization. He walked 22 batters in 20 2/3 innings with Double-A Midland, posting an 11.76 ERA in seven starts. Insisting on getting extra work over the winter, he performed much better in the Dominican Winter League by limiting the walks and posting a 2.57 ERA in 10 starts for Toros del Este. Medina’s stuff has never been in question. He possesses an electric arm with a fastball that averaged a tad over 96 mph and touched 102 in 2022. His low-80s curveball is just as unhittable, and his changeup -- which averaged around 89 mph -- has also flashed plus at times with good splitting action. All of this comes with an athletic delivery. Command continues to be what keeps Medina in a holding pattern regarding what type of role awaits him in the big leagues. The ceiling is as a frontline starter, and the A’s still believe in his starter mix coming off his showing in winter ball, but a high-leverage relief role is the likely outcome unless he can drastically improve the control issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Medina began hitting 100 mph with his fastball as a 16-year-old in June 2015, a month before he signed for $280,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He has showcased some of the best pure stuff in the Minors for years but never has been able to locate the strike zone consistently, which is why he carried a 4.73 career ERA into 2022. He made some progress with his mechanics and control toward the end of 2019 and while earning Puerto Rican Winter League pitcher of the year honors in 2020, but he regressed last year while reaching Double-A. Back in Double-A in 2022, he was continued to miss bats, and walk hitters, when he was sent to the A’s as part of the return for Frankie Montas near the Trade Deadline. Medina features electric arm speed and produces premium stuff with little effort, beginning with a fastball that sits at 96-99 mph and peaks at 103 with natural cutting action. At its best, his low-80s curveball is a true hammer that can be more unhittable than his heater. His changeup also grades as a well above-average offering at times, sitting around 90 mph and diving at the plate with splitter action. Though Medina is athletic and has no glaring flaws in his delivery, he averaged 6.3 walks per nine innings in his first five seasons as a pro and 5.1 walks per nine last year. He doesn't require pinpoint command to succeed with his arsenal, but he won't be able to stay in the rotation unless he becomes more efficient. While he still has a ceiling of a frontline starter, it's becoming increasingly more likely that he'll wind up in a relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Medina first reached triple digits with his fastball as a 16-year-old in the Dominican Republic a month before he signed for $280,000 in July 2015. He unquestionably has the best pure stuff in the system but it translated into a 5.51 ERA with 144 walks in 183 innings during his first four years in pro ball. He maintained a more consistent release point and started finding the strike zone much more regularly at the end of the 2019 season, then spent 2020 at the Yankees' alternate site before earning pitcher of the year honors in the Puerto Rican Winter League. With little effort and electric arm speed, Medina generates stuff that sounds almost too good to be true, beginning with a heater that parks at 96-99 mph and reaches 102 with natural cut. His low-80s curveball can be a plus-plus hammer and more unhittable than his fastball when it's on. His changeup is also a well above-average pitch at its best, sitting around 90 mph with devastating splitter action. Medina is athletic and has no glaring mechanical flaws, so there's no obvious reason he shouldn't have average control. He has had trouble repeating his delivery in the past, though some observers believe his problems have been more mental than physical and he may be turning a corner as he has matured and learned to trust his stuff. The gap between his ceiling (frontline starter) and floor (not enough strikes to contribute) is as large as any prospect's, but he could take off if he can sustain his recent progress.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Busch has lived up to his reputation as one of the best all-around offensive prospects in the 2019 Draft since signing with Los Angeles for $2,312,000 as the 31st overall pick out of North Carolina. He had his best season yet in 2023, winning Pacific Coast League MVP and prospect of the year honors after topping the Triple-A circuit in slugging (.618, second in the Minors) and OPS (1.049, second), finishing second in batting (.323) and placing third in on-base percentage (.431, eighth). Though he also made his big league debut, he had no avenue to regular playing time with the Dodgers, so they dealt him and Yency Almonte to the Cubs for prospects Jackson Ferris and Zyhir Hope in January. Busch is a well-rounded hitter who stands out most for his plus power to all fields, which he creates with a combination of bat speed and strength. With his disciplined approach, smooth left-handed swing and fine hand-eye coordination, he's built to hit for average as well. He draws a healthy amount of walks and has an offensive profile that resembles Max Muncy's but with more hitting ability. Primarily a first baseman in college, Busch moved to second base as a pro and worked diligently to improve his quickness and arm strength. He was still fringy at best in both regards and was never going to be more than adequate at second, so Los Angeles deployed him more at third base in 2023, but he faced the same issues there. He's best suited for first base, where he'll have an opportunity with Chicago, or left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best all-around offensive prospects in the 2019 Draft, Busch fell to the Dodgers at No. 31 amid questions about his defensive home and signed for $2,312,000. He dominated the upper levels of the Minors in the last two seasons, winning Pacific Coast League MVP honors in 2023 after leading the circuit and ranking second in the Minors in both slugging (.618) and OPS (1.049). He also made his big league debut but didn't have the road to much playing time with Los Angeles, which traded him and Yency Almonte to the Cubs for prospects Jackson Ferris and Zyhir Hope in January. With his sweet left-handed stroke, patient approach with good balance, uncanny hand-eye coordination, bat speed and strength, Busch is equipped to hit for both average and power. He focused more on the latter in 2022, more aggressively attacking pitches early in counts and driving the ball with authority to all fields. He continued to draw walks and present an offensive profile similar to Max Muncy's, though Busch is a better pure hitter. Though Busch has fringy speed and arm strength, he has worked hard to improve his quickness and arm since turning pro. Evaluators inside and outside of the Dodgers organization were impressed at how he has transformed himself into an adequate defender at second base, though Los Angeles deployed him primarily at third base in 2023. The game speeds up on him at the hot corner, however, and he's still best suited for first base and capable of playing a passable left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Other clubs lament that talented players keep falling to Los Angeles at the end of the first round, starting with Busch in 2019 and followed by Bobby Miller and Maddux Bruns the last two years. One of the best all-around offensive prospects in his Draft class, Busch signed for $2,312,000 as the 31st overall selection. Injuries to his right hand after he was hit by pitches ended his pro debut after 10 games and hampered him early last season, but he rallied to bat .300 with 14 homers in his final 61 games. His profile is similar to Dodgers All-Star Max Muncy, though Busch is a better pure hitter. He controls the strike zone while waiting for pitches to punish, employing a sweet left-handed swing and good balance at the plate to drive balls from gap to gap. He barrels balls with ease and draws plenty of walks, and his biggest needs are to be more aggressive early in the count when opportunities present themselves and to launch more balls in the air to get the most out of his plus raw power. Like Muncy, Busch fits best defensively at first base (his primary position in college at North Carolina) but can get the job done at second base. His stockiness belies his deceptive athleticism, and he has worked hard to improve his quickness and arm strength since turning pro. His speed and arm are still fringy, but he has impressed scouts inside and outside of the organization by his transformation into an adequate defender at second, and he also has seen some action in left field in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best all-around hitters in the 2019 college crop, Busch signed for $2,312,000 as the 31st overall pick. Though he broke his right hand when hit by a pitch 10 games into his pro debut and had the 2020 Minor League season wiped out by the pandemic, he has still impressed the Dodgers with the improvements he has made to his defense and athleticism despite the lack of game action. Scouts from other organizations who saw him during instructional league raved about his hitting ability and gave him a better chance to play second base than they had previously. Busch employs a polished approach at the plate, controlling the strike zone while waiting for pitches he can do damage against, and he's willing to take walks if pitchers try to work around him. With a pretty left-handed stroke and good balance, he can drive the ball to all fields. He squares up the ball consistently and should hit for average and power while getting on base at a high clip, giving him one of the best offensive ceilings and floors from the 2019 Draft. Though Busch mostly played first base and some left field in college at North Carolina, Los Angeles saw him at second base in the Cape Cod League and will give him the chance to make it there. He's stocky but has some deceptive athleticism and has gotten quicker and added some arm strength since signing. His speed and arm are still fringy, but he's looking more comfortable at the keystone and could become a Max Muncy type with a higher batting average.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In three years as a starter at Division II Shepherd University in West Virginia, Doyle showcased his power and speed, hitting 32 homers and stealing 52 bases. That was enough to catch the attention of the Rockies, who took him in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, then saw him lead the Pioneer League in OPS in his debut. It’s been a little up-and-down in terms of production since, but he did reach Triple-A at the end of 2022 and was added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. Doyle is a tooled-out athlete who “looks the part” on the diamond, one who can do everything well, at times. The plus raw power is very real, and he started tapping into it more in 2022, hitting 26 homers. There’s still a ton of swing-and-miss, with a 31.2 strikeout rate last year, but he made some adjustments in his setup at the plate, with more separation to create space. He made more contact as a result, one of the first times he’s made successful adjustments in-season. A plus runner who finished with a 20-20 season last year, Doyle is one of the best defensive outfielders in the system, one who can play center field for a long time and whose arm is a real asset in throwing out runners. How much he can carry over the adjustments he made at the plate will determine just what kind of big leaguer he can become.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A total of four players have ever been drafted out of Division II Shepherd University, and none earlier than when the Rockies took Doyle, a super-toolsy and athletic outfielder, in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft. When he led the Pioneer League in OPS during his pro debut, he answered an early question about whether or not he could handle pitching at the next level. His full-season debut, in High-A, in 2021, was a bit more uneven, interrupted by welcoming a baby daughter into the world, but he still showed off his exciting suite of tools. Doyle’s premium athleticism and conditioning were still on full display in 2021, despite the inconsistency of his results. With an upright stance that helps him leverage the ball more, he’s still learning to tap into his plus raw power on a regular basis. He gets over-aggressive at the plate and expands the zone too much, rarely drawing walks (7.1 percent rate in 2021). That, in turn, led to a spike in his strikeout rate (31.6 pct), and while there’s work to be done to find a sustainable approach, it should be noted he was much more productive after he returned from home and the pressure of impending fatherhood was lifted. Doyle won a Rawlings Gold Glove for his defensive work in center field, and his plus speed will allow him to stay there, with a plus arm to boot, for a very long time. If he can refine his approach, he has the chance to bring an exciting power-speed combination to Colorado.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Players who come from smaller college programs, particularly below Division I, always have to prove themselves at every level. That’s likely to happen with Doyle, the Rockies’ fourth-round pick in the 2019 Draft out of Division II Shepherd. If the early returns are any indication, including winning the Pioneer League batting title during his pro debut and performing very well at instructs in 2020, it will continue to become clear why the Rockies coveted him enough to go a bit above slot to sign the outfielder. Doyle stands out for his athleticism, his premium conditioning and his very loud tools. He certainly looks the part and in terms of his frame and strength, looked like a big leaguer on a rehab assignment during instructs the last two years. Big and spread out in the box in college, Doyle is now more upright, allowing him to use his legs better and leverage the ball more frequently. Having more time to see the pitch and make decisions has also helped his pitch recognition, giving him a better chance to get to his plus raw power consistently. Doyle’s plus speed should continue to allow him to steal some bases and it also contributes to his above-average defense in the outfield, where the Rockies think he could stick in center field but also know one of the best arms in the systems would profile well in right. The power-speed combination reminds some of Preston Wilson with the organization excited about seeing what Doyle can do as he moves up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player at Florida International, Allen became the first Golden Panther ever to make the U.S. collegiate national team. Signed for $1,125,000 as a second-rounder in 2020, he made his pro debut the following year and led Guardians farmhands with a 2.26 ERA while advancing to Double-A. He continued to thrive in Akron last season but got pounded for a 6.49 ERA in Triple-A following a promotion in June. Allen ran into trouble in Columbus because he lost some command and deception with his fastball, which has added 2 mph since his college days and now ranges from 90-94 mph. His low-80s changeup remains his best pitch, with fade and sink that make it effective against left-handers and right-handers. He has increased the sweep on his low-80s slider, which has become a solid offering, and he has begun morphing it into a mid-80s cutter on occasion. Though Allen doesn't have the physicality of a typical starter, he should have the durability to last in a rotation because he's more athletic and efficient than most pitchers. He repeats his easy delivery, which features good extension that helps his pitches get on hitters quicker than expected, and has a history of providing precision strikes. He nibbled around the strike zone when he struggled in Triple-A but should be able to make the adjustments necessary to become a mid-rotation option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A year after acquiring a left-hander named Logan Allen in a three-team Trevor Bauer trade, the Guardians signed a second one for $1,125,000 in the second round of the 2020 Draft. He starred on the mound while also starting at first base at Florida International, becoming the first Golden Panther to play for the U.S. collegiate national team. He made a spectacular pro debut in 2021, leading the system with a 2.26 ERA while cruising to Double-A. One of the most polished pitchers in the 2020 college class, Allen expertly mixes three pitches, the best of which is a plus low-80s changeup with fade and sink that's effective against both left-handers and right-handers. His fastball has picked up 2 mph since his college days and now sits at 90-94 mph while playing better than its velocity thanks to his extension and command. His low-80s slider isn't particularly sharp but works because he locates it well. While Allen is less physical than a typical starter, his athleticism and efficiency should allow him to hold up in a rotation. He repeats his easy delivery, which provides some deception without compromising his ability to place his pitches where he wants. He's a dogged competitor whose pitchability gives him a high floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not to be confused with the left-hander Logan Allen who joined the Indians in the 2019 Trevor Bauer trade and graduated to the big leagues in 2020, this one signed for $1,125,000 as a second-round pick out of Florida International last June. He starred on the mound for three years in college while also playing regularly at first base, becoming the first Golden Panther to play for the U.S. collegiate national team. He offered some of the best pitchability in the 2020 Draft and should move quickly after breaking into pro ball in instructional league. Allen keeps batters off balance by mixing three pitches, the best of which is a plus changeup that fades and sinks, producing empty swings and weak groundouts against both lefties and righties. He works around 90 mph and peaks at 93 with his fastball, which plays better than its velocity because of his extension and command. His curveball can be a decent third offering but also gets loopy at times. Though he's just 6 feet tall and thin, Allen still profiles as a starter because of his athleticism. He repeats his delivery easily and provides plenty of strikes. His floor stands out more than his ceiling, as he's a good bet to become at least a back-of-the-rotation option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first Stanford freshman pitcher to start on Opening Day since Mike Mussina in 1988, Beck entered 2017 as a Draft-eligible sophomore with first-round potential but missed the entire year with a stress fracture in his back. He returned in 2018 and signed with the Braves for an over-slot $900,000 as a fourth-rounder, then went to the Giants a year later along with Dan Winkler in a trade for Mark Melancon. He pitched well in high Class A and the Arizona Fall League following the deal, then continued to impress in instructional league last fall, but missed three months early this season with more back problems. San Francisco encouraged Beck to employ more four-seam fastballs up in the strike zone, and he went from working at 91-92 mph at the start of 2019 to dealing at 92-95 and hitting 97 in the AFL. His downer curveball plays well off his four-seamer and showed consistent low-80s velocity during instructs. He also utilitzes a slider/cutter and a changeup with some run and sink that both sit in the mid-80s and grade as average. An intelligent pitcher, Beck has one of the higher floors among Giants mound prospects and could move quickly in 2021. He has no issues throwing strikes but will need to upgrade his command to succeed with less-than-overpowering stuff against more advanced hitters. If he can stay healthy, he could be a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller’s journey to pro ball was truly inspirational. After he was diagnosed with Type 1 juvenile diabetes in 2018 and weighed around 150 pounds, he found a diet and strength program that helped him bulk up to about 220 pounds. Transferring from Waynesburg (Pa.) to Gardner-Webb University (N.C.) in 2021, his 3.30 ERA and 121 strikeouts in 92 2/3 innings that year led to the A’s signing him for $599,100 as a third-round Draft pick. Generating plenty of buzz last spring, he earned his way to the big leagues in 2023 after seven dominant outings in the Minors and posted a 3.78 ERA in 10 Major League games, six of which were starts, with 38 strikeouts and 16 walks across 33 1/3 innings. Already sporting an overpowering fastball that frequents triple digits, Miller integrated a cutter into his repertoire that sits around 94-96 mph and has the makings of a devastating primary secondary pitch. He also brings a wipeout slider that generates plenty of swing-and-miss and utilizes an improving changeup that serves as a solid fourth offering. As impressive as Miller is at lighting up the radar gun, he also fills the zone with a bunch of strikes, qualities that give him the ceiling of a frontline starter. His 6-foot-5, 220-pound frame seems durable enough to hold up as a starter, though injuries continue to be a major concern for the A’s, the most recent being the UCL sprain that sidelined him for nearly four months in 2023. The plan is to move him to the bullpen in 2024. How he holds up as a reliever over a full season will determine his long-term role in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller overcame severe obstacles in a truly inspiring journey to pro ball, going from being diagnosed with Type 1 juvenile diabetes in 2018 and weighing around 150 pounds to finding a diet and strength program that helped him bulk up to about 220 pounds. Transferring from Waynesburg to Gardner-Webb University in 2021, his 3.30 ERA and 121 strikeouts in 92 2/3 that year led to the A’s signing him for $599,100 as a third-round Draft pick. Though a scapula strain in his right shoulder kept him out of action until the end of August, he received some much-needed extra work in the Arizona Fall League and impressed with a 3.24 ERA and 20 strikeouts across 16 2/3 innings. A power arm who can light up the radar gun at triple digits, Miller also brings what is looking more and more like a wipeout slider. He continues to work on integrating a mid-80s changeup as a third offering, though that pitch still could use some developing. There’s no question Miller can throw a bunch of strikes with his big arm, and his 6-foot-5, 220-pound frame seems durable enough to hold up as a starter. A quicker path to Oakland, however, could come in a bullpen role as a reliever with all the makings of a flame-throwing closer. Whether he reaches the Majors as a starter or reliever likely hinges on how far he can refine that changeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fastball: 70 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Miller’s path to the professional ranks is truly inspirational. Battling Type 1 juvenile diabetes he was diagnosed with in 2018 and weighing around 150 pounds, he worked hard to transform his body. Discovering the right diet and strength program, he bulked up to 220 pounds and transferred from Waynesburg to Gardner-Webb University. Miller went 8-1 with a 3.30 ERA and 121 strikeouts in 92 2/3 innings in 2021 and forced his way onto the Draft radar, with the A’s signing him for $599,100 as a third-round pick. He was mostly unable to showcase his stuff in 2022 as a scapula strain in his right shoulder kept him out of action until the end of August. Miller is a power arm that can light up the radar gun as high as 100 mph and also holds what at times can show up as a wipeout slider. His mid-80s changeup has shown promise but needs to develop more consistency in order to solidify his pitch arsenal. Miller has a big league arm that can throw a ton of strikes. The question is what role awaits him. The A’s could choose the long route to build him out as a starter or fast track him in a bullpen role. His big body suggests a starting role could suit him well, even if it means slightly decreased velocity, but that would only come if he can fully develop the changeup as his third pitch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros believed in Valdez's hitting ability enough to sign him for $450,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, but he didn't reach full-season ball until 2018 and didn't take off until he returned from the pandemic layoff in 2020 with a more disciplined approach. He has slugged 54 homers in the last two seasons and batted a career-best .296/.376/.542 between Double-A and Triple-A in 2022. The Red Sox acquired him and outfield prospect Wilyer Abreu in exchange for Christian Vazquez last August and added both to their 40-man roster in November. More patience at the plate has paid off with more production for Valdez, as he's making higher quality of contact and drawing more walks. He combines a quick left-handed stroke with strength in a compact frame, which allows him to regularly drive the ball with authority to his pull side. He doesn't see the ball well against left-handers, however, chasing all types of pitches and batting just .261/.315/.388 against them last season. Valdez has below-average speed and fringy arm strength, which limits his effectiveness as a defender. He lacks range at second base, his primary position, and has played everywhere but center field and pitcher as a pro. Boston also gave him brief looks at third base and left field after the trade, though he doesn't have enough arm for the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stoudt spent three years pitching in Lehigh University’s rotation, putting himself on the radar enough to get the Mariners to take him in the third round of the 2019 Draft. Elbow soreness that had plagued him with the Mountain Hawks turned out to be a torn UCL, and he had Tommy John surgery before throwing a professional pitch. He made his debut in May 2021 and reached Double-A and was having an up-and-down 2022 at that level when he was sent to the Reds as part of the Luis Castillo trade. After finishing the year in Triple-A, he was added to Cincinnati’s 40-man roster. Stoudt has the chance to have a legitimate four-pitch mix and an idea of how to use it. He’s throwing harder since putting TJ surgery in his rearview mirror, consistently reaching 97 mph with some riding life up in the zone. He throws distinct breaking pitches, with a slower, get-me-over curve and a harder slider that has flashed plus at times. His changeup features good depth and fade. While the Reds didn’t think they saw the best version of Stoudt post-trade, they were impressed by his poise and mound presence, and he showed enough to earn a roster spot. Even though he got the chance to impact the big league staff in 2023, his ability to find the strike zone regressed, limiting his success both in Triple-A and with Cincinnati.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A quick ascent at Lehigh University to the conference’s all-freshman team showed Stoudt had early potential, and he went on to become the staff ace, leading the team in innings, complete games and opponents' batting average. That potential appeased the Mariners, who took him in the third round in 2019, but shortly after the Draft, the righty experienced elbow fatigue, which eventually led to Tommy John surgery almost right after he signed. He recovered incredibly well, pitching in the Mariners’ fall developmental league in '20 and making his pro debut for High-A Everett in ’21, finishing in Double-A. He was having more uneven results back in Double-A in '22 when he was packaged with three other prospects and shipped to the Reds in return for Luis Castillo. Stoudt has been described by one scout as an “incredibly stuffy guy,” with a fastball that has touched 98-99 mph frequently and that has a ton of ride up in the zone. The changeup is the pitch that had really excited the Mariners, particularly with its depth and fade, as well as his ability to land it for strikes. His slider can flash plus and he also has a solid curveball. Stoudt was linked to many rumors ahead of last year’s Trade Deadline as the Mariners were looking to buy, but Seattle decided to hang on to him until close to this year’s Deadline. As Stoudt continues to distance himself from elbow surgery, he’ll be stretched out further in terms of workload. The workman-like, reserved righty’s upside is as a back-end starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A quick ascent at Lehigh University to the conference’s all-freshman team showed Stoudt had early potential. He followed it up with a stellar sophomore campaign, not allowing a single homer over his first two seasons, and he capped it as the ace of the staff while leading the team in innings, complete games and opponents' batting average. That potential appeased the Mariners, who took him in the third round of the 2019 Draft, making him one of four college pitchers Seattle selected in the Top 100 picks. Shortly after the Draft, the righty experienced elbow fatigue, which eventually led to Tommy John surgery. After undergoing the procedure right after he signed, Stoudt recovered incredibly well, pitching in the Mariners’ fall developmental league, where his fastball was as high as 97 mph with a ton of ride up in the zone. Though it doesn’t have a ton of movement, he’s located it well in short stints. The changeup is the pitch that has Mariners scouts drooling, particularly with the depth and fade Stoudt delivers it with, as well as his ability to land it for strikes. His curveball and slider have a ton of potential, too. Following his performance in Arizona last fall, if Stoudt continues to recover positively, he could be stretched out further to a full season in the Minors. His upside has back-end starter ceiling potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Headrick spent three years starting at Illinois State and was taken by the Twins in the ninth round of the 2019 Draft. He had a relatively nondescript year in Single-A in 2021, but jumped on the map by dominating the High-A Midwest League and earning a promotion to Double-A in 2022. He pitched well enough to earn a spot on the Twins’ 40-man roster. A 6-foot-6 left-hander, Headrick has managed to miss a ton of bats at each level despite not having any pitches that wow scouts. He’s added a few ticks to his fastball, from an average of 88 mph in his last year of college to 91 mph in 2022, and there could be a little more in the tank. He entered pro ball with a slider that didn’t inspire people, but he’s worked to add some juice to that as well. It averaged 80 mph last year and produced a 48 percent whiff rate in Double-A, getting the pitch up to 83-84 mph could make it close to an out pitch. He misses bats with his changeup, though he doesn’t always land it for strikes. Headrick made huge strides in 2022 in terms of his strike-throwing ability and looks like he should have at least average command. His 32 percent strikeout rate in Double-A is a sign that what he’s doing might work at the upper levels. His ceiling is limited, but the Twins have a good track record of turning college arms into big leaguers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $55,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, Soriano missed all of 2017 with a forearm strain and didn't reach full-season ball until his fourth year as a pro in 2019. Following the pandemic layoff, he emerged as one of the Marlins' better lower-level starting pitching prospects in 2021, but they declined to place him on their 40-man roster. His stuff found another gear when he became a full-time reliever in June, prompting Miami to protect him on its 40-man in November. Soriano's fastball sat at 92-94 mph and peaked at 97 when he was a starter in 2021, then jumped to 96-98 mph and reached 100 without losing any of its riding action in shorter stints last season. His tight mid-80s slider grades as a plus pitch at its best and helps him overmatch right-handers. He exhibits some feel for an upper-80s changeup, though his lacks consistency and he needs to refine it to help him combat left-handers. Soriano worked just 383 innings in his first seven years as a pro, and his inexperience shows at times on the mound. He doesn't always repeat his mechanics well, which hinders his ability to throw strikes and command his fastball. Once he does a better job of locating his pitches, he'll get the chance to contribute to Miami's bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 Part of a Marlins 2015 international class highlighted by Edward Cabrera, Soriano drew little attention after signing for $55,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He missed all of 2017 with an injury and didn't reach full-season ball until his fourth year as a pro in 2019, then the pandemic wiped out the 2020 Minor League season. He emerged as one of the organization's better pitching prospects at the lower levels last year, when he successfully navigated Low-A and High-A, though Miami opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster. Soriano operates at 92-94 mph and peaks at 97 with riding action on his four-seam fastball. It grades as a plus pitch at its best, as does his low-80s slider. He exhibits some feel for a changeup, though his lacks consistency and he needs to refine it to help him combat left-handers. Because he totaled just 307 innings in his first six years as a pro, Soriano isn't as polished as might be expected. He did a better job of hitting the strike zone after his promotion to High-A, but he still needs to upgrade his control and command. He has the upside of a back-of-the-rotation starter, but might be on a more realistic path to becoming a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Neto first jumped on the radar as a sophomore at Campbell University in 2021, hitting over .400 and earning Big South Conference Player of the Year honors. He won the award again in 2022 thanks to a 1.283 OPS, after showing it worked with a wood bat against tougher competition in the Cape Cod League the summer prior. Belief in that bat, especially at his position, is a big reason why his name was popping up regularly in first-round conversations before he was eventually taken No. 13 overall by the Angels. Signed to a below-slot $3.5 million bonus, Neto looked like he might be a bargain by jumping on an early fast track and hitting .320 in 30 Double-A games during his pro debut. Neto’s setup and mechanics at the plate, including a big leg kick and an uphill swing from the right side, might not be what coaches would teach young hitters, but he’s made it work as he relies on tremendous hand-eye coordination to make consistent hard contact. He doesn’t strike out a ton, while his bat speed and ability to loft the baseball point to solid power, especially to his pull side. Just an average runner, Neto’s aggressiveness makes him an asset on the basepaths. His quick feet and hands, when combined with solid arm -- he was in the low 90s as a reliever at Campbell -- and instincts, give him a good chance to stick at shortstop, though he’s seen time all around the infield and could find a home as a second baseman who hits his way to the big leagues in a hurry.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted by the A’s out of the University of Louisiana at Lafayette in the third round of the 2018 MLB Draft, Harris had been plagued by injuries throughout most of his professional career, including a 2021 season that was wiped out as he recovered from Tommy John surgery. In 2022, he finally stayed healthy and skyrocketed up the prospect radar with a solid campaign in which he pitched at three different levels and combined for a 3.42 ERA with 105 strikeouts over 73 2/3 innings, ending the season at Triple-A Las Vegas. Harris has a thick build at 6-foot-3, 220 pounds. His fastball can reach up to 97 mph and sits around 94-95. His changeup flashes plus and serves as a strong secondary pitch, and he also mixes in a slower get-me-over breaking ball. Harris’ high walk totals indicate there is still some work to do in order to improve his command. A true feel-good story for his perseverance, the time is now for him to make or break as he’ll be entering his age-26 season. The A’s are encouraging him to add a hard cutter/slider-type pitch, as they believe such an addition will help him stick as a starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 The last Louisiana-Lafayette pitcher of any kind to reach the big leagues was B.J. Ryan, who last pitched in 2009. Harris, a third-round selection by the A’s in the 2018 Draft, hopes to break that drought soon, though a rash of injuries has impeded his development recently. Harris has shown he can really fill up the zone with a three-pitch mix. His fastball sits in the low 90s with some run to it. He also brings a slurvy breaking ball that looks more like a curveball. His changeup gives him another solid pitch to work with. The injuries continue to pile up for Harris, as he entered 2021 once again having to deal with an elbow injury. When he’s on the field, he can be a very good left-hander. The problem is keeping him healthy for a full season. If Harris can work out the health issues, his repertoire projects him to be a starter in the long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Having turned 17 that March, Bradley was young for the 2018 Draft class when the Georgia native was selected in the fifth round by Tampa Bay. He started to show signs of a breakout during 2020 instructs following the pandemic-canceled season, and he carried those promising signs into becoming the Minor League ERA leader (1.83) in 103 1/3 innings at two A-ball levels in 2021. Bradley built upon that further with a 2.57 ERA and 141 K’s in 133 1/3 innings at Double-A and Triple-A in 2022, on his way to becoming the AL starter in the All-Star Futures Game at Dodger Stadium. He was an easy 40-man addition when he first became Rule 5-eligible in November. After experiencing a velocity bump in late 2020, the 6-foot-2 right-hander now throws 94-96 mph with his heater, touching 98, and he spots it well around the zone. He calls his best secondary pitch a cutter, and we’ll do the same, even though it could land in the slider territory. All the same, the mid-80s offering breaks late and plays well off the fastball. An 89-91 mph split-finger changeup doesn’t offer a ton of separation but has given Bradley another suitable fading option against lefties, while his mid-70s curve is more for show in early counts. Bradley hasn’t averaged more than 2.7 BB/9 in any of his full-season stops, and his athletic delivery should continue to help keep him throwing strikes. With 59 Triple-A innings already on his résumé, he doesn’t need much more Minor League experience in his age-22 season before he’ll be ready to join the rotation in St. Petersburg and step closer to his ceiling as a No. 2/3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays took Bradley in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft out of Redan High (Stone Mountain, Ga.) -- a program known for Domonic Brown, Brandon Phillips and Wally Joyner -- and signed him for $747,500 (slot: $343,600). Young for his class, the right-hander spent his first two seasons in Rookie ball before starting to show signs of a breakout at 2020 fall instructs. That came to fruition in 2021, when Bradley led the Minors with a 1.83 ERA over 103 1/3 innings at Low-A and High-A. He also fanned 123 and walked 31 in that span. Bradley has picked up right where he left off in 2021 and has been just as effective this season, having reached Triple-A at just 21 years old in July. Known for an athletic delivery dating back to his prep days, Bradley worked to become more efficient last season, and the result was a velocity bump. He sat comfortably in the mid-90s and touched higher than that at times. His upper-80s cutter -- previously deemed a slider but Bradley himself uses this designation -- features tough, late break, and the Rays have preached to him how well they like it playing off the heater. He pocketed a curveball in 2021 but has since brought it back to give hitters another look while his changeup usually serves as his typical third pitch. Bradley regularly throws strikes with his improved delivery, and the Rays were pleased with how consistent he was in that department, even when taking on a new level in the middle of the season. His fastball and cutter give him a decent floor, but given how well he works within his profile, Bradley has star potential as a starter for Tampa Bay.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bradley was one of the youngest players in his class, seemingly bound to honor his commitment to South Carolina, but he would not be a Gamecock. The Rays selected Bradley in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft out of Redan High School in Stone Mountain, Ga., a program that produced All-Stars like Domonic Brown, Wally Joyner and Brandon Phillips, and signed him to an above-slot bonus. Also an outfielder in high school, Bradley turned out to be a better prospect on the mound and has continued improving as a pitcher. He spent last fall in the Rays’ instructional league camp, wowing evaluators with his stuff. Bradley has made impressive gains with his velocity in 2021, throwing more comfortably in the mid-90s while touching the upper regions of that velo band thanks to a more efficient delivery. He’d made strides with his curveball in 2019, throwing it with more power and a tighter, 12-to-6 shape. His slider is his primary breaking ball, but the curveball adds an interesting wrinkle to his arsenal. Next up on his list is a changeup, which could come quickly based on the aptitude he showed in improving his curveball and his natural athleticism on the mound. If Bradley can keep improving his command and round out his arsenal, he could eventually reach his upside as a starting pitcher. His steadily increasing velocity and sharpening breaking stuff would seem to give him the floor of an intriguing reliever, though, even if the rest of his game lags behind. His development will take time, as the Rays are typically patient with their high school pitchers, but he’s put himself on a positive forward track this summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a slightly unusual path for Julien, a one-time standout on Canada’s junior national team who went from Quebec to play college ball at Auburn. He hit 27 homers over his first two seasons and was deemed eligible for the Draft after Major League Baseball ruled that his secondary school year in Canada counted as a year of college. The power potential was enough for the Twins to go well over slot in Round 18 to sign Julien for $493,000. He led the Minors in walks in 2021, showing off some pop in A ball, then took a step forward in Double-A by batting .300 with 17 homers and 19 steals before capping things off by hitting .400 in the Arizona Fall League. Julien is proving to be a more complete hitter than he was at Auburn. The power is still very much there, with bat speed and strength helping him drive the ball to all fields and nearly as many homers hit out to left field as to his pull side. No one in the Minors has walked more than he has over the previous two seasons combined and he walked more than he struck out in the AFL. But while his plate discipline is a plus, he can get too passive at times in his desire to see pitches. While it’s becoming pretty apparent Julien is going to hit in the big leagues, where he’s going to play defensively is still a bit of a question. After moving around quite a bit at the outset of his career, he focused on second base exclusively in 2022. It may never be pretty, but he’s worked to be competent enough so his bat has a place in a big league lineup every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Moore’s numbers at Arkansas-Little Rock certainly didn’t jump off the page, as he posted a walk rate of 11.8 per nine and a 7.95 ERA over three seasons. The White Sox saw a 6-foot-6 reliever with impressive arm strength and took a flier on him in the 14th round of the 2019 Draft and signed him for $100,000. He pitched across two levels of A-ball in his first full season and then was sent to the Phillies in the Adam Haseley trade prior to the 2022 season and Moore made more strides in a move to Double-A with his new organization. A reliever all the way, Moore is all about going right after hitters with power stuff. He relies mostly on his fastball-slider combination, a heater that flirted with triple digits and averaged 97 mph last year, with decent carry up in the zone, and a slider that flashes plus with cutter-like action thrown typically in the upper-80s. Both pitches can miss bats, though his fastball can get hit at times when it flattens out. He will fold in a changeup to give left-handed hitters a different look, but at 90-91 mph, it’s often too firm. Moore is never going to have pinpoint command, but he doesn’t need it with his stuff out of the ’pen. After really struggling in the walks department out of the gate in ’22, he walked 3.6 per nine from May 1 on. More of that improved strike-throwing could allow him to impact a big league bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Moore went winless in three seasons at Arkansas-Little Rock while posting a 7.95 ERA with 64 walks in 48 2/3 innings. The White Sox bought into his size and arm strength enough to select him in the 14th round of the 2019 Draft and sign him for $100,000. The strike zone still remains a mystery to him at times but he advanced to High-A during his first full pro season in 2021 and held his own in the Arizona Fall League, something the Phillies noticed as they acquired him from Chicago in the Adam Haseley trade in late March. There's no subtlety to Moore, a 6-foot-6, 225-pounder who works at 93-96 mph and peaks at 98 mph with his four-seam fastball. It can straighten out at higher velocities but features plenty of carry up in the strike zone. He complements his heater with a mid-80s slider/cutter that shows glimpses of becoming a plus pitch, though he lacks anything soft or particularly effective against left-handers. Moore's pure stuff stands out much more than his ability to locate it. More physical than athletic, he doesn't have the smoothest delivery but has toned it down since signing, and he reduced his walk rate from 11.8 per nine innings in college to 6.9 in his pro debut to 4.6 in 2021. If he can continue to improve his control and command, he has a chance to fill a setup role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies gave Ortiz $4 million to sign at the start of the 2015-16 international signing period, the fifth-highest bonus given to an international amateur player during that period. Since then, he’s tantalized with his offensive potential, though not consistently. He wasn’t added to the 40-man roster in 2020, but then had a turn-around season with High-A Jersey City in 2021, got bumped up to Double-A and earned that roster spot. A return to Reading in 2022 saw some regression and he didn’t perform well in the Arizona Fall League. In 2021, Ortiz’s pitch recognition improved, as did his walk and strikeout rates, but in 2022, he struggled in those departments, whiffing in 32.7 percent of his plate appearances and walking in 8.5 percent of them. His high chase and overall swing-and miss rates kept him from tapping into his plus plus raw power. When he does make contact, it’s loud, and he still managed to hit 17 homers in 2022, mostly to the pull side, but the right-handed hitter is going to have to rediscover a better overall approach to use his best tool more consistently. Ortiz has proven to be a better athlete than many had expected and he’s a capable enough defender in the outfield corners, with the offensive power profile and strong arm to fit in right field in the big leagues. Whether he gets the chance to do that as a big league regular will be determined by his ability to make more contact at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz, who signed with the Phillies in July 2015 for $4 million, was not added to the 40-man roster in the fall of 2020 after a rough 2019 season and getting time in instructional league play in 2020, but he also wasn’t selected in the Rule 5 Draft that December. After really improving his conditioning, he had a big 2021 in a return to High-A, slugging .521 there to earn his first trip to Double-A. The Phillies saw enough this time around to add him to the 40-man following the season. While there’s still work to be done in terms of his overall approach, Ortiz’s pitch recognition improved in 2021, with better walk and strikeout rates. That allowed the right-handed hitter to get to his easily plus power more consistently, though there will always be a good amount of swing-and-miss to his game. Ortiz’s cleaned up body also led to better defensive play, including considerable time in center field. Long-term, Ortiz is destined to play a corner spot, with the kind of arm that works well in right. If the 23-year-old’s approach gains are for real, he could have the power profile for the spot as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz was No. 10 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list at the start of the 2015-16 signing period and received one of the year’s highest bonuses, getting a $4 million bonus to sign with the Phillies. Since then, he’s shown off his power, to go along with approach issues, while being young for his level. He participated in instructional league play in 2020, but wasn’t added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. There’s absolutely no question about Ortiz’s raw power from the right side of the plate, which is close to top of the scale. It helped him finish second in the Florida State League in home runs in 2019 as a 20-year-old, but worries about the swing-and-miss in his game abound. He’s struck out in nearly 32 percent of his plate appearances in his two years of full-season ball. He’s had a tendency to chase breaking stuff out of the zone in particular and he has worked on shortening his swing a bit, with the Phillies preaching that he’s strong enough with above-average bat speed that the power will come naturally with more contact. The 6-foot-3 Ortiz is a much better athlete than anyone anticipated and moves very well in the outfield, seeing some time in center field in 2019. With a plus arm and that power, he still could develop into a run-producing right fielder type, but he’s going to have to prove he can cut down on the K’s first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles took some by surprise when they selected Rodriguez out of the Texas high school ranks with the No. 11 overall pick in the 2018 Draft, but if his performances in the Minor Leagues are any indication, it might end up being a steal. As he’s gotten bigger and stronger, the 6-foot-5 right-hander has dominated hitters at every level with a combination of pure stuff and tremendous feel for pitching. A Grade 2 right lat strain that landed him on the injured list last June might be the only reason why he didn’t join the 2022 turnaround in Baltimore and graduate off prospect lists. Rodriguez has an outstanding four-pitch mix with the chance to have at least three plus pitches in his repertoire. His high-spin fastball touches triple digits, can sit easily in the mid-to-upper 90s deep into starts, and he throws the pitch with plus life. He might have the best changeup in the Minors, a mid-80s off-speed pitch that he tunnels well off his fastball to create deception and hard, late life. He misses bats with his mid-80s slider, and even his fourth pitch, a tighter low-80s curve, has improved. If his pure stuff wasn’t impressive enough, Rodriguez has refined his command across the board and fills up the strike zone with all of his offerings. This has resulted in him striking out nearly 13 batters per nine innings in his career heading into 2023, while walking just three per nine and keeping hitters to a combined .173 batting average. He returned healthy at the end of 2022 and should impact the Orioles' rotation soon, with the potential to lead it in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As parting gifts go, Rodriguez looks like he’s going to be a very big one. Taken a bit earlier than the industry had him at No. 11 overall in the 2018 Draft, Rodriguez was the last first-rounder selected by the front office replaced that November by Mike Elias. The 6-foot-5 Texas high school product has continued to become bigger, stronger and a more complete pitcher as time has passed. He overwhelmed lower-level hitters during his 2019 full-season debut with pure stuff, learned a lot at the alternate site in 2020 and showed a real feel for his craft in reaching, and dominating in, Double-A to become the best pitching prospect in the game. He was putting the finishing touches on his Minor League career in Triple-A this season when a Grade 2 right lat strain landed him on the injured list in early June. Rodriguez has always had a legitimate four-pitch mix at his disposal, and all four have continued to get better as he’s learned how to use them more consistently. In 2021, he threw his fastball in the 95-101 mph range, commanding it extremely well with high spin rates and plus life. His mid-80s changeup continues to improve; it’s hard, late and really deceptive, especially coming off of his fastball. His slider is a plus out pitch, also in the mid-80s and he’s tightened his curve a bit to provide a fourth, low-80s, offering. Rodriguez has always been able to throw strikes and the right-hander walked just 2.4 per nine in 2021. His steps forward came in his ability to further refine his command of all his offerings within the zone, a big reason why his strikeout rate climbed to 14.1 per nine and his batting average against dropped to .159. All he needs is a bit more experience against better hitters and he’ll be ready to reach his potential as a front-of-the-rotation type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles took some people by surprise when they took Rodriguez, the 6-foot-5 right-hander from the Texas high school ranks, No. 11 overall in the 2018 Draft. As he’s continued to add strength, he’s shown they were right in taking him so early as he dominated his full-season debut in 2019 that included a perfect Futures Game inning, then took more positive development steps during his time at the Orioles’ alternate training site in 2020. Rodriguez’s four-pitch mix continues to get sharper as he progresses. He’s now up to 99 mph with his fastball, averaging around 95 mph over the summer, and he throws it with good downhill plane and heavy sink. The Orioles now think his changeup might be his best secondary offering, thrown in the low 80s with more proper spin for a change than he’d had previously, looking like a fastball coming out of his hand before it disappears, diving and running under the barrel. His slider, thrown around 82 mph, is still a plus out pitch and he folds in an upper-70s curveball effectively as well. During the summer of 2020, Rodriguez continued to make strides in consistently executing all of his pitches. Despite his size, he repeats his delivery well and should be a solid strike-thrower. He’ll be just 21 for all of the 2021 season and his combination of size, stuff and feel for pitching all look like a future frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There have been money-saving college senior signs in the Draft bonus pool system who are taken in the top 10 rounds simply to manipulate the pool and afford higher-ticket players. Then there are those who, while saving money, have a legitimate shot at making it to the big leagues. Dodd was identified as being in the latter group as the Draft approached in 2021, signing for way under-slot in the third round with the Braves, but being a ranked prospect. He pitched across three levels in 2022 and while his 2023 wasn’t as dominant, he did spend considerable time in the big leagues. Dodd’s feel for pitching allowed the left-hander to move quickly and be in position to make the Opening Day roster when the need arose. The left-hander’s stuff is largely average across the board, with a fastball that sits around 92 mph and had played well in the past with decent life and high spin rates, but got hit at the highest level. His changeup and slider are both low-80s offerings and will flash above-average, but also weren’t quite as sharp in 2023. He added a mid-80s cutter that could give him a fourth usable offering. As Dodd learned in 2023, he doesn’t have a huge margin for error given how his stuff plays. He repeats his delivery well and throws a lot of strikes from a higher arm slot, which helped him reach Atlanta relatively quickly. He’ll have to find another gear in order to stay there, with a ceiling of a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Draft bonus pool system began, teams have drafted college seniors in the top 10 rounds as money-savers in order to use their pools to go after tougher-to-sign talent in other rounds. Sometimes there are “priority senior signs,” ones who come at a bargain but are more than that. Dodd fit that description, hitting MLB Pipeline’s Draft Top 250 list as a Southeast Missouri State senior while also saving the Braves money by signing for $122,500 as a third-rounder in 2021. It’s looking like a very savvy selection as the left-hander pitched his way from High-A to Triple-A and led the organization in K/BB and walk percentage last season. In many ways, particularly the feel for pitching without wow stuff, Dodd is like the left-handed version of fellow Braves prospect Darius Vines. While Dodd’s fastball sits around 92 mph, it’s a bit more playable than Vines’ heater because it has more life and higher spin to it. He throws his changeup and slider in the low 80s, and both are at least above-average offerings. The former has good depth and deception, and the latter is a sweeper that also misses bats. He can fold in a slower curve as well. A former two-way player, Dodd’s athleticism is an asset on the mound, helping him repeat his delivery and higher arm slot, which leads to an ability to fill up the strike zone.
