That’s enabled him to move quickly through the system, and he’s close to reaching his ceiling as a No. 4 or 5-type starter in a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his second professional season went 12-9 with a combined 3.36 ERA in 26 starts between three levels of the Braves farm system. Went 9-5 with a 3.44 ERA (34 ER/89.0) in 16 starts with High-A Rome…Was named the South Atlantic Pitcher of the Week (5/20) after tossing a combined 13.0 scoreless innings with nine strikeouts between two starts. Pitched to a 3.11 ERA (16 ER/ 46.1 IP) with 55 strikeouts in nine starts with Double-A Mississippi. Made one start with Triple-A Gwinnett on 9/25 … Allowed three runs in 6.2 innings pitched in his G-Stripers debut. Dodd was a solid two-way player at Kankakee Community College in Illinois, where he helped the school win the Division II Junior College World Series in 2017. From there, he moved on to Southeast Missouri State as a pitcher only, starting for three years. A strong senior season led to him being one of the more highly regarded senior signs, and the Braves took him in the third round and signed him for $122,500 before making brief stops at two levels of A ball, then pitching his way to Double-A in his first full season. The big left-hander rode his changeup to Ohio Valley Conference pitcher of the year honors in 2021, and it’s a dandy, thrown in the low-80s with good depth. He’ll throw them at any point in the count and trusts the off-speed pitch enough to double up. He’s added some velocity since his junior college days, sitting in the 90-93 mph range and occasionally reaching back for a tick or two more with his high spin-rate fastball that misses bats with good riding life. He has two distinct breaking pitches, with his low-80s slider a bit better than his upper-70s curve. Dodd has shown an ability to repeat his delivery and high three-quarters arm slot consistently, which should allow him to keep throwing strikes. His best outcome is as a back-end starter, but his feel for pitching could allow him to move pretty quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shuster was dominant on the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2019 and carried that over to a strong start to the 2020 season with Wake Forest before the pandemic shut things down. His uptick in stuff and overall command were enough for the Braves to take him at the end of the first round of that summer’s Draft. He made it to Double-A in his first full season, then made his way from Double-A to Triple-A in 2022 while pitching in the Futures Game along the way. While the velocity gains Shuster showed at Wake Forest haven’t continued to come for him as a pro, Shuster has a solid three-pitch mix and a strong knowledge of how to use it to get hitters out. His fastball averaged around 91 mph in 2022, topping out at 94, and while he commands it well, it doesn’t feature much life and can get hit at times. In many ways, he uses it to set up his best pitch, a plus 80-81 mph changeup with a ton of tumble to it. It elicited a 45 percent miss rate and a lot of weak contact on the ground. His low-80s slider has developed into a solid swing-and-miss pitch as well. All of his stuff plays up because he fills up the strike zone consistently, walking just 2.5 per nine innings heading into 2023, and he’s learned how to set up -- and finish off -- hitters more consistently. He’s more of a high-floor than high-ceiling arm, but he’s very close to being ready to help out a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two relatively nondescript years at Wake Forest, Shuster turned in an outstanding performance in the Cape Cod League in 2019 and carried it over to a dominant start to his 2020 season before the shutdown. The Braves liked his combination of improved stuff and feel for pitching enough to take him No. 25 overall and sign him for a below slot $2.2 million. He pitched well enough to earn a promotion from High-A to Double-A in his first full season, though he got hit upon the move to the new level. He mastered that level in 2022, earning a promotion to Triple-A and heading to the Futures Game to boot. Shuster’s velocity had ticked up in 2020 and he was touching 97 mph before the shutdown. While he hasn’t continued that as a pro, sitting more in the low-90s, he does command the pitch well. He has the best changeup in the system, thrown around 80 mph with excellent tumble. He’s willing to throw it in all counts and routinely misses bats with it. His slider, which had been a bit of a question coming out of the Draft, has improved, and it elicited a good amount of swing and miss as well. Shuster has continued to throw strikes throughout his climb up the ladder. He’s learned how to repeat his delivery well and improved his pitch sequencing. He might not have the highest ceiling in the world, but his feel for pitching gives him the chance to be a solid big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2020 Draft approached, there were a number of college left-handers most slated to get taken in the first round. Shuster, who was ranked No. 77 on MLB Pipeline’s Draft Top 200 at the time of the Draft, making him the No. 8 ranked college southpaw on the list, wasn’t one of them. But after a big step forward in the Cape Cod League the summer prior and a very strong start with Wake Forest before the shutdown, the Braves believed enough to take him No. 25 overall then let him make up for lost innings with work at the alternate training site and in instructional league play. The Braves saw a lefty in the spring of his junior year with a lot more velocity than he had previously, going from someone who topped out at 92 to someone who regularly hit 95 mph and could reach back for 97 mph, thanks to the offseason work he put in at Cressey Performance. He once featured a sinking two-seamer, but now relies on a riding four-seamer with good success. His changeup immediately became one of the best in the Braves system, an 80-mph offspeed pitch with tumble that he’ll throw at any point in the count. His breaking ball is his third pitch, but the Braves think there’s upside in his slider. Control had been a major issue over his first two years at Wake Forest (5.2 BB/9), he walked only 1.4 per nine on the Cape and during his junior season. It’s not the smoothest delivery, but he repeats it well enough to point to a future of throwing strikes, giving him a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $35,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, Brito had Tommy John surgery three years later and didn't reach full-season ball until 2019. He has taken off since losing 2020 to the pandemic, establishing himself as one of the system's best strike-throwers while reaching Triple-A. The Yankees added him to their 40-man roster in November. Brito's fastball velocity made a jump in 2022, with his four-seamer parking at 94-96 mph and peaking at 98 while exhibiting some running action. Hitters had to guard against his hotter heater, leaving them more vulnerable against his solid mid-80s changeup with fade. He doesn't have as much feel for his breaking pitches, with his tight mid-80s slider more effective than his low-80s curveball. Brito has pounded the strike zone throughout his pro career, averaging 1.9 walks per nine innings -- though that rate rose to 2.8 between Double-A and Triple-A last season. He generates weak contact more than he misses bats and may be more of a multi-inning reliever than a starter unless he can develop a better breaking ball. He earns praise for his work ethic and continuing improvement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wiemer showed some tools in his three seasons at Cincinnati but hadn’t managed more than six homers in a spring. The Brewers were still willing to bet they could turn him around with a fourth-round selection in the shortened 2020 Draft, and that move paid off a year later when the right-handed slugger broke out for 27 homers and a .958 OPS across two A-ball levels. He got off to a slower start at Double-A Biloxi in 2022, prompted by a 30.2 percent K rate, but ended much brighter at Triple-A Nashville with a .287/.368/.520 line and 19.5 percent K rate over 174 plate appearances. Wiemer’s swing has calmed down from his collegiate days, in part due to a move to a toe tap over a large leg kick, but he still generates a good amount of movement and torque -- some of which has caught up to him in the upper levels. His 19.2 percent swing-and-miss rate was 20th-highest among the 609 Minor Leaguers with at least 400 PA in 2022. When Wiemer does make contact, he absolutely pounds the ball with elite exit velocities, and improvements in his ability to elevate have helped drive his increased homer output. A plus runner who has 61 Minor League steals, Wiemer would already be a defensive asset, and his absolute cannon of an arm seals that fate. The Brewers believe he could play a solid center field, but the presence of Sal Frelick and Garrett Mitchell has pushed him to right, where he’s a natural fit. It will all come down to contact. Wiemer hits the ball so hard that he could be simply below-average with his hit tool while the rest of his tools make him an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wiemer was a steady, if unspectacular, performer in his three years at Cincinnati, where he hit .264/.379/.408 with 12 homers over 122 career games. The Brewers grabbed him in the fourth round, betting they could help him make the most of the impressive raw power. The proof came quickly. Wiemer hit .276/.391/.478 with 13 homers and 22 steals in 75 games with Low-A Carolina to begin his first full season and then was scorching with 14 homers and a .719 slugging percentage in 34 games for High-A Wisconsin. A bruised left thumb ended his standout turn in the Arizona Fall League after two weeks. Everything Wiemer does on the diamond is loud. That starts with a kinetic, tornado-like swing to which the Brewers made some adjustments for 2021. The biggest change was transitioning to a toe tap, rather than a large leg kick. Wiemer credits the move with helping him focus on his hands, where he’s able to generate more bat speed. That has also helped the right-handed slugger lift the ball and make the most of his plus-plus raw pop. He is at least an above-average runner and that helps him cover good ground in the outfield. The Brewers gave him some looks in center, but his plus-plus laser of an arm is tailor-made for right, where he picked up eight assists in 2021. It all comes down to the hit tool. Wiemer’s strikeout rate has climbed since he saw the upper Minors in 2022, heightening concerns that his moving parts may hold him back offensively. His walk rate has dipped as well. However, when everything comes together, Wiemer brings as much electricity to the plate as he does the outfield grass and the basepaths. His dynamic profile gives him a chance to be a solid everyday Major Leaguer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fifth-round pick out of Central Florida in 2018, the former Red Sox Spring Training bat boy got off to a fast start by winning Boston's 2019 Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors with a 2.14 ERA and 157 strikeouts in 126 1/3 innings between Single-A and High-A. He missed 2020 due to the pandemic and then underwent Tommy John surgery after only two Double-A starts the following year. Ward returned to Portland for seven starts in 2022, posting a 2.43 ERA with 41 K’s in 33 1/3 innings, and continued to make up for lost time in the Arizona Fall League. But he was left unprotected in the Rule 5 Draft and went first overall to the rebuilding Nationals. The 6-foot-3 right-hander’s best pitch remains an 81-85 mph slider that bites late and lands typically where he wants. It’s his true plus pitch, but a 92-96 mph two-seam fastball shows some promise too with its ability to induce ground balls (a 49.4 percent Double-A GB rate in 2022). The Nationals believe there could be even more velocity in the tank the farther Ward gets from the elbow surgery. Ward can sport a kitchen-sink arsenal with a cutter, curveball and changeup, but none of them quite show the same promise of being above-average Major League pitches. Even after the long layoff, Ward throws enough strikes to stick in a starter’s role. Washington intends to use him out of the bullpen to begin his Major League journey, thus improving his chances of sticking as a Rule 5 pick, but given the organization’s rebuild, it wouldn’t be a shock to see him starting games midway through 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ward served as a Red Sox bat boy during Spring Training while growing up in Fort Myers, Fla., and became a full-time employee when they selected him in 2018's fifth round out of Central Florida. Converted from college reliever to pro starter, he won Boston's Minor League pitcher of the year award in his first full pro season after logging a 2.14 ERA with a system-best 157 strikeouts in 126 1/3 innings between Low-A and High-A. After sitting out all of 2020 like most Minor Leaguers, Ward missed almost all of 2021 due to Tommy John surgery before returning to Double-A for seven starts last summer. The Nationals made him the first pick of the Rule 5 Draft in December. Ward displayed one of the Boston system's best sliders, an 81-85 mph weapon with late bite that he could use for strikes and chases and also turn into an upper-80s cutter. He set up his slider with a hard two-seam fastball that ranged from 92-96 mph with good sink to induce groundball contact. He has worked on improving his changeup, flashing some solid ones in the low-80s with fade. Left off Boston's 40-man roster each of the last two years, Ward would have been a possible Rule 5 pick in 2021 before becoming the real thing this winter. Also a college basketball prospect in high school, he's a good athlete who repeats his easy delivery and should have at least average control. He still has a ceiling of a No. 4 starter with the fallback of becoming a multi-inning reliever who relies heavily on his slider and sinker if and when he sees the Majors with Washington.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ward grew up in Fort Myers, Fla., and served as a Red Sox bat boy during Spring Training as a youngster. He became a full-time member of the organization when the Red Sox drafted him in the fifth round in 2018, converting him from a reliever at Central Florida to a starter as a pro. He posted a 2.14 ERA and led the system with 157 strikeouts in 126 1/3 innings between two Class A stops in his first full season, but his 2020 encore was limited to instructional league and he had Tommy John surgery after two Double-A starts this year. Ward's best weapon is a late-biting 81-85 mph slider, and he has the feel to land it for strikes, get hitters to chase it out of the zone and to turn it into an upper-80s cutter when he wants. He sits at 92-94 mph and tops out at 96 with his two-seam fastball, using sink to produce groundouts. He focused on his changeup during instructs and is improving his feel for the pitch, which helped him shackle lefties to a .179/.289/.224 line in 2019. A good athlete who had college basketball scholarship offers, Ward repeats his easy delivery and should have at least average control. His walk rate jumped from 3.1 per nine innings in low Class A to 5.3 in high Class A, and adding 10 pounds of strength last year may help him maintain his ability to throw strikes over a whole season. Assuming a return to full health, he has a ceiling of a No. 4 starter while his slider gives him a high likelihood of becoming at least a useful reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best high school pitching prospects in Delaware's history, Bilous missed his 2015 senior season following Tommy John surgery but still got offered $600,000 by the Dodgers after they selected him in the 29th round. He went to Coastal Carolina, where he contributed to a 2016 College World Series championship but struggled to throw strikes throughout his college career before signing for an over-slot $185,000 in the 13th round of the 2018 Draft. He made significant progress with his control in 2021, pitching his way to Double-A and claiming a spot on the 40-man roster. After throwing in the mid-90s as a Chanticleer, Bilous settled into the low 90s early in his pro career but bounced back to 92-97 mph with riding action last season. He can miss bats with his heater as well as his low-80s slider, which can be a plus pitch at its best. He also uses a hard curveball that varies between a downer and a slurve, and a low-80s changeup with fade that shows some flashes of becoming a solid pitch. Bilous is making progress with repeating his delivery and staying online toward the plate. He averaged 7.1 walks per nine innings at Coastal Carolina and 5.4 per nine in his first two pro seasons before slicing that rate to 3.6 in 2021, but he has regressed this season. If he can continue to improve his secondary pitches and his control, he could become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A local product, Julks played at a suburban Houston high school and the University of Houston before the Astros drafted him in the eighth round in 2017. He had 17 homers in 300 games as a pro when the club sent him from Double-A to its training base in West Palm Beach, Fla., in June 2021 to make some swing changes to unlock some power. He has gone deep 43 times in 179 contests since, including 31 times in Triple-A, though Houston declined to protect him on its 40-man roster. Julks had shown a patient approach and made good swing decisions in his early years as a pro, but he was stalling at age 25 because he made too much soft contact. After doing a better job of incorporating his lower half with his right-handed stroke, he began driving the ball harder and farther. He has gotten more aggressive while looking to turn on more pitches, resulting in more swings and misses, but he doesn't strike out excessively and still takes his share of walks. Julks has solid speed and uses it to steal an occasional base and provide average defense at all three outfield spots with arm strength to match. He had played one game at third base in the previous six years when the Astros decided to try him at the hot corner to increase his versatility in 2022, but that 49-game experiment didn't go well. He also saw action at second base, where he made three errors in four contests, and the verdict is that he's an outfielder only.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A local product who played at a suburban Houston high school and the University of Houston, Julks joined the Astros as an eighth-rounder in 2017. After he slumped in Double-A last June, they sent him to their training base in West Palm Beach, Fla., to make some swing changes. Once he returned, he batted .297/.369/.545 with 12 homers in his final 49 games. The Astros always appreciated Julks' swing decisions and patient approach, but he was stalling at age 25 because he was making too much soft contact. He bought into the alterations they wanted him to make to his right-handed stroke, and he started hitting the ball harder and in the air more often. His more aggressive mindset resulted in more strikeouts, but they're worth the uptick in production. Julks uses his solid speed to steal a few bases and cover ground in center field. An average outfield defender with an arm to match, he has spent most of his career on the corners. He fits the fourth-outfielder profile and has seen brief action at third base last September and again this spring.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After teaming with future No. 2 overall pick Jack Leiter to lead the Delbarton School (Morristown, N.J.) to a state non-public Class A championship in 2019, Volpe turned down the opportunity to join him at Vanderbilt to sign with the Yankees for $2,740,300 as the No. 30 overall choice. Mononucleosis contributed to a lackluster pro debut that summer before he used the pandemic layoff in 2020 to rework his swing and add strength. He has been a different player since, winning MLB Pipeline's Hitting Prospect of the Year award in 2021 and encoring last season by recovering from a slow start to become the first 20-homer, 50-steal Minor Leaguer since Andruw Jones in 1995. Volpe stood out as much for his intangibles as his tools when he entered pro ball, but that's no longer the case after he transformed himself physically. He still has as much pure hitting ability as anyone in the system, but he now has a right-handed stroke geared for loft and produces high exit velocities and power to all fields. He struggled at times against sliders in 2022 and occasionally looked like he was trying to do too much at the plate, but he made adjustments over the course of the year. Volpe's work ethic and instincts continue to allow him to get the most out of his physical ability. His solid speed and aggressive nature on the bases led to 50 steals in 57 attempts last season. The lone question is whether his finely tuned internal clock can help him stay at shortstop with average range and arm strength (albeit with a quick release) that may be better suited for second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Delbarton School (Morristown, N.J.) featured a pair of future first rounders in 2019, with Volpe signing for $2,740,300 as the 30th overall pick that summer and Jack Leiter going No. 2 overall last year after two seasons at Vanderbilt. Mononucleosis limited Volpe to 34 game in a ho-hum pro debut but he blew away all expectations in his first full pro season in 2021. MLB Pipeline named him the Hitting Prospect of the Year after he batted .294/.423/.604 with 27 homers and 33 steals in 109 games between Low-A and High-A while topping the Minors in runs (113) and ranking second in OPS (1.027) and ranking third in extra-base hits (68). Left on his own for development in 2020 after the pandemic shut down the Minor League season and the Yankees didn't stage a domestic instructional league program, Volpe added significant strength and reworked his right-handed swing to allow him to hit balls harder and drive them in the air more easily. Once he was fully healthy, he made more consistent contact against all types of pitching and showed the patience to wait for pitches he can punish and to take walks when he doesn't get them. Originally projected as a hit-over-power type, he now looks capable of hitting .280 with 25-30 homers per season. Volpe also comes with outstanding makeup and quality instincts that help his tools play up on the bases and in the field. His solid speed and aggressive nature translated into 33 steals in 42 attempts last season. His arm earns fringy to solid grades but he compensates with a good internal clock and a quick release. He has the fast hands and feet to play at least an average shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Volpe teamed with right-hander Jack Leiter at The Delbarton School (Morristown, N.J.) in 2019, with both establishing themselves as premium prospects whose signability was clouded by strong commitments to Vanderbilt. The Yankees selected both, landing Volpe for $2,740,300 as the 30th overall pick and taking an unsuccessful 20th-round flier on Leiter, who went No. 2 overall in the 2021 Draft. Mononucleosis limited Volpe to 34 games in his pro debut before the coronavirus and New York's lack of a domestic instructional league program left him on his own for development in 2020, but he has hit the ball with more authority than expected when he returned to the field this summer. While Volpe isn't physically imposing, he's an advanced hitter with a compact right-handed swing. After posting an uncharacteristic 25 percent strikeout rate in his debut, he has made much more consistent contact during his first full season. And after initially projecting as a hit-over-power guy who might reach double digits in home runs once he added strength, he's now driving the ball more, hitting it harder than ever and looking like at least a 20-homer threat. Volpe's instincts help him play above his tools on the bases and at shortstop. He's a solid runner who recognizes and makes the most of opportunities to steal or take an extra base. Though his arm earns average to solid grades, he figures to stick at short because he has a good internal clock and a quick release.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s an open question just how high Walker would have gone if not for a pandemic-shortened spring in 2020. After showing off in the small sample at Decatur (Georgia) High School, the right-handed slugger went 21st overall to the Cardinals, who signed him away from his Duke commitment with a $2.9 million bonus. Walker has done nothing but hit since, posting averages above .300 and slugging rates above .500 in each of his first two full seasons. After producing a 128 wRC+ as a 20-year-old at Double-A last year, the Peach State native got more time against advanced competition in the Arizona Fall League. Standing in at 6-foot-5, Walker makes repeated loud contact with a fairly simple, if long, swing and consistently puts up the highest exit velocities at every stop he makes, including the AFL, where he had the four highest exit velos measured by Statcast. While his current career high is 19 homers, he should challenge for 30-plus in the Majors in short order. A swing-heavy approach does lead to some chase concerns, but his overall average and K rates should still be at least solid because of his ability to find the barrel. Walker is moving to the grass to get out of Nolan Arenado’s shadow, and he’s still a work in progress out there with his reads and routes. He’s a better runner than his size would indicate, and even if he slows down as he matures, he could be a serviceable corner outfielder. He displayed a cannon of an arm in Arizona, maxing out with a 99.5 mph laser, so right is likely his best spot. Walker should hit enough to feature anywhere and might not need much more offensive seasoning in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Walker already had an upward trajectory, having posted a 1.555 OPS in 16 games at Decatur (Georgia) High School, before the pandemic canceled his 2020 senior season. The Cards swooped to take him 21st overall that summer and signed him away from Duke with a $2.9 million bonus. The right-handed slugger quickly established himself as one of the game’s top corner-infield prospects in his first taste of the Minors. Having posted a .374/.475/.687 line in 27 games at Low-A Palm Beach, he was promoted to High-A Peoria in late June and finished with eight homers and a 124 wRC+ in 55 games there. The 6-foot-5 masher already showed elite exit velocities in his first taste of the Minors. He maxed out at 116.2 mph in Low-A Southeast (a similar max to Juan Soto, Fernando Tatis Jr. and Javier Báez among others in 2021) and had 21 batted balls come in at 100-plus mph there. Despite a long swing built to make the most of his strength, Walker walked and struck out in nearly equal measures at Palm Beach, only for that ratio to go south in Peoria. He’s answered quite nicely to an aggressive assignment to Double-A Springfield in his age-20 season, hitting above .300 for much of the season and making hard contact again at that. St. Louis was also pleased with Walker’s defense at the hot corner, and officials praised his instincts and arm at a difficult position. The Cardinals have started to give Walker looks in all three outfield spots to get him out of Nolan Arenado’s shadow. He has some work to do on the grass, but that’s part of the learning process. The Peach State native will go as far as his bat takes him, and so far, that route looks to be toward an All-Star-caliber hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2019-20 Georgia Gatorade Baseball Player of the Year, Walker hit .457 with four homers and posted a 1.555 OPS through 16 games before the coronavirus pandemic forced the cancellation of the rest of his senior season. He had already established himself as the top corner-infield prospects in the 2020 high school class and passed up a commitment to Duke after the Cardinals selected him 21st overall and signed him for $2.9 million. Walker drew rave reviews for his performance at the alternate training site in 2020 and showed why in 2021. He got off to a fast start with Palm Beach and worked his way up to High-A Peoria at 19 years old. At 6-foot-5 and 220 pounds, Walker has easy bat speed and frequently posts exit velocities over 100 mph. The power potential is obvious, but the big frame creates a naturally long swing and there are questions about his ability to hit breaking balls. While there is some swing and miss in his game, he did shown an improved ability to make contact in 2021. With a strong work ethic and willingness to learn, so he should hit enough to be able to produce the desired power numbers. Athletic for his size, the hope is for Walker to remain at third base, where he has spent the entirely of his brief professional career. However, if he loses some quickness and he continues to grow, his above-average arm and power bat would profile well at either first base or a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Colas spent three years splitting time between Cuba's Series Nacional and Japan's minor Western League, getting a seven-game cup of coffee with Japan's big league Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks. A dispute over the legality of his contract with the Hawks resulted in him being granted free agency in December 2020 and he elected to wait until the following signing period for the White Sox to have enough money in their international pool, landing a $2.7 million bonus in January 2022. Yet another potential Cuban star in the organization, he impressed in his U.S. debut by batting .314/.371/.524 with 23 homers and getting better at each level while rising from High-A to Triple-A. Colas is an aggressive hitter who combines a quick left-handed stroke and impressive strength to create well-above-average raw power, with most of his home run pop going to his pull side. Yet he also shows adaptability at the plate, using the entire field and toning down his approach with two strikes and also against left-handers. He worries less about power in those situations and just lets his hands work, and he batted .362 versus southpaws last year. Though he moves well for a 6-foot-1, 220-pounder, Colas possesses just fringy speed and will have to maintain his conditioning to retain it. He spent most of his first U.S. season in center field but is destined for right field, where he’ll have average range and a well-above-average arm. Hyped as \"The Cuban Ohtani\" before signing with Chicago, he pitched only briefly in Cuba and Japan and showed off a fastball that reached 95 mph.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Colas played parts of three seasons in Cuba's Serie Nacional as well as three years in Japan's minor Western League and seven games with that nation's big league Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks. A dispute with the Hawks led to him being declared a free agent in December 2020, but he elected to wait until January 2022 to sign with the White Sox for $2.7 million. Chicago didn't have enough money left in its 2021 international bonus pool for him, but he was willing to wait to join a Cuban contingent that includes José Abreu, Yasmani Grandal, Yoán Moncada and Luis Robert in the Majors and prospects Yoelqui Céspedes, Norge Vera and Bryan Ramos in the Minors. Compared to fellow outfielder Céspedes, Colas is a better hitter with similar power and less athleticism. Though it's unclear how much time it will take him to adjust to U.S. pitching after a two-year layoff from meaningful competition, Chicago believes he can be a solid hitter whose quick left-handed stroke and strength could translate into 30 or more homers on an annual basis. He may need to tighten his plate discipline after striking out four times as often as he walked in the Japanese minors. The 6-foot-1, 209-pound Colas moves well for his size and possesses average speed. Though he was hyped as \"The Cuban Ohtani\" in the past, he pitched only sporadically in Cuba and Japan, where his fastball was clocked as high as 95 mph. He fits the right-field profile nicely with his well-above-average raw power and arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Turang has been pushed aggressively through the Milwaukee system ever since the Crew selected him 21st overall in 2018 and signed him above slot at $3,411,100. After reaching Triple-A as a 21-year-old in 2021, the infielder repeated the level last year with a slight uptick in results: a .286/.360/.412 line and career highs in homers (13) and stolen bases (34) over 131 games with Nashville. The Brewers added Turang to the 40-man roster when he first became Rule 5-eligible in November. The left-handed hitter typically does a nice job of working within the strike zone by limiting his chases and posting above-average walk rates. That continued in 2022, though it was noteworthy that he traded some strikeouts for a power increase. Some of that jump in pop came from naturally increased strength as part of the physical maturation process, and some from a more open stance that helped him launch more balls on contact. He still doesn’t project for average power, but at least there’s increasing evidence that double-digit homer seasons are possible in the Majors. Turang hails from an athletic family that includes a Major League dad, a Long Beach State softball star mom and four NCAA athlete sisters, and he puts his athletic ability to good use defensively, where he’s shown increased range at shortstop. He would be a good bet to stick there, if not for the presence of Willy Adames, and while he has experience in center field and at third base, his best bet to become a Brewers regular is at second, where he easily could be a plus defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Turang was in the discussion as one of the best prep players in the 2018 Draft class but fell back some after not meeting lofty expectations in the spring. The Brewers gladly selected him 21st overall in July and went above slot to sign him for $3,411,100. Milwaukee has gotten aggressive with his assignments ever since and pushed him to both Double-A and Triple-A in his age-21 campaign last year. He was about league average with a 99 wRC+ at both spots and finished with a .258/.347/.362 line, six homers and 20 steals in 117 games. Turang works well within the strike zone with walk rates typically above 10 percent across his Minor League career and strikeout rates that are above-average for the modern game. He is capable of hard contact, but it hasn’t translated into game power just yet. That could be because he’s yet to be age-appropriate for a league, and the Brewers are hopeful he can add strength as he matures, leading for the potential for around 15 home runs per season in the Majors. He’ll have to reverse a 53.3 percent groundball rate for Nashville to send balls over the wall with that regularity. As slugging questions remain, the 6-foot infielder has provided more answers on defense. He projects to be at least an above-average shortstop, thanks to improved range and overall playmaking ability. Where there were once concerns about moving over to second, he’s actually played more center field in 2022 as the Brewers have tried to take advantage of his athleticism. His steady bat and other array of skills could make him a solid regular by next summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brice’s father, Brian Turang, played in 78 games with the Mariners from 1993-94 as part of his eight-year career in pro ball. Those bloodlines put Brice on scouts’ radars at a young age, while standout performances on the summer showcase circuit and with Team USA made him a likely first-round pick in 2018. The Brewers were elated to find Turang still on the board ahead of their first pick (No. 21), and even more so when they signed him away from an LSU commitment with a $3,411,100 bonus. He looked like one of the more advanced prep players from his Draft class in his first full season, garnering midseason All-Star honors at Class A Wisconsin at age 19 before finishing the year in the Class A Advanced Carolina League. He built upon that progress in 2020, standing out as the most impressive hitter at Milwaukee’s alternate training site. Plus hitting ability and speed is at the heart of Turang’s offensive game. He makes a lot of hard line-drive contact from line to line using a smooth left-handed swing that he controls well. Turang’s on-base skills are fueled by his mature approach and ability to identify pitches -- a combination which helped him lead Milwaukee’s system in walks (83) in his first full season -- and he earns high marks from club officials for how he consistently puts together strong at-bats. He knows how to put his plus wheels to use on the basepaths and was successful in 30 of 35 steal attempts in 2019. Turang has continually added strength in pro ball and showed improved exit velocities at the alternate training site. He has enough pop to project double-digit home run totals in his prime, though he’s more likely to rack up doubles and triples than clear fences consistently as a big leaguer. The Brewers have few doubts about Turang’s ability to remain a shortstop. He has solid defensive tools across the board, including actions, hands and arm strength that are above average for the position, and he possesses the type of high baseball IQ and makeup that could help him exceed expectations and projections as a big leaguer. At the least, Turang looks like a future regular who will hit for average, get on base and steal some bags, all while providing quality defense at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even though he signed for just $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic, Vargas was actually Cleveland’s top international addition in the 2016-17 period. He hadn’t even made it above short-season ball -- a big reason being the lost pandemic season -- when the Guardians added him to their 40-man roster in November 2020 because they believed the quality of his stuff would make him a Rule 5 target. Vargas underwent Tommy John surgery the following spring and returned to post a 3.67 ERA with 37 strikeouts in 34 1/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A in 2022. The D-backs acquired him in a November deal for Ross Carver. The 6-foot-4 right-hander worked as a starter in his early career but moved to the bullpen full time following elbow surgery in a move that was likely always coming. His fastball now sits 96-99 mph, occasionally touching triple digits, and that Major League-ready velo explains why Cleveland wanted to protect him all those years ago. His 89-92 mph slider gives him another near plus-plus pitch, one that tunnels off the fastball before dropping below a swinging bat. The pitch notably has vertical break, rather than horizontal sweep. Like many hard-throwing receivers, the 23-year-old typically can struggle to locate. He specializes on pitches lower in the zone and can become hittable if batters know that and target that area. Still, Vargas arrives in the Arizona system with upper-level experience, renewed elbow health and the dangerous stuff needed to become a Major League bullpen factor quickly in his first season as a D-back.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas signed out of the Dominican Republic for $275,000, the largest bonus in Cleveland's 2016 international class. Though an elbow strain pushed his pro debut back to 2018, he quickly attracted attention by hitting 100 mph with his fastball at age 18. He added some polish in 2019, but his development was limited to instructional league year and he had Tommy John this surgery this April that will sideline him for all of 2021. Usually ranging from 94-97 mph with some run and sink on his fastball, Vargas has been clocked as high as 101 mph and still has some projection remaining in his athletic 6-foot-3 frame. His mid-80s slider is gaining more consistency and grades as a plus pitch with sharp break at its best. He's still learning to use and trust a changeup he needs to better deal with left-handed hitters. Vargas has a quick arm and doesn't feature much effort in his delivery, which he did a much better job of repeating in his second pro season than in his first. But his command pales in comparison to his control, so he doesn't miss as many bats as his power stuff suggests he should. If he can refine his changeup and do a better job of locating his pitches, he eventually could fit in the middle of Cleveland's rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Englert looked like a quintessential Texas baseball story, a high-school legend in the Lone Star State who broke David Clyde’s record for consecutive scoreless innings before the Rangers drafted him in the fourth round in 2018. Unfortunately, an elbow injury in his first Spring Training led to Tommy John surgery and delayed his pro debut for two years. Despite a solid second half in 2022 that included 14 consecutive hitless innings and a promotion to Double-A, the Rangers opted not to add him to their 40-man roster in November. The Tigers took advantage with a Rule 5 Draft pick, believing he can stick on their staff for a year. Englert’s arsenal has improved the further he gets past surgery. His fastball ticked up to 96 mph last year after a midseason adjustment to his delivery, complemented by a hard slider that he developed around the same time. However, he’s more effective throwing 92-94 mph with command and playing it off his sinker and mid-80s cutter. His low-80s changeup has been his most effective pitch in the pros, with healthy velocity gap off his fastball. He has been working on a curveball in the upper 70s. Though Englert is a Texas legend, he spent part of his offseason in Michigan on a workout program that included a daily dip in the Grand River. If he can crack Detroit's staff, he’ll feel even more at home in the state. The Tigers will use him in the bullpen starting out, but haven’t ruled out a future as a starter given his pitch range and upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Originally taken by the A’s in the 14th round of the 2018 Draft out of Concordia University -- the same Division II attended by his brother and Twins prospect Louie -- Varland moved to the Dodgers in Feb. 2021 as part of a four-player swap. He played at Double-A Tulsa in both the 2021 and 2022 seasons with rough results (a 5.98 ERA, 1.59 WHIP in 105 1/3 innings) but was flashing more prominent stuff down the stretch last summer. Facing a loaded 40-man, Los Angeles left Varland unprotected for the Rule 5 Draft, and he was scooped up by the Brewers in that December process. Most notably, he was up to 96-98 mph as a reliever in the second half of the 2022 season, up a few ticks from where he opened the year as a member of the Tulsa rotation. An upper-80s slider not only came in hard, but its break made it another quality pitch. The 6-foot-1 right-hander can land a changeup, but it isn’t likely to ever be as notable as the other two. As Varland’s arsenal improved, he closed out his time in Tulsa with a 3.44 ERA, 31 strikeouts and five walks in 18 1/3 innings over his final two months. While he has some experience working deeper into games, Varland, who underwent Tommy John surgery in 2019, is likely best-suited for shorter bursts. He’ll need to translate his promising repertoire into actual results in 2023 and do it in the Majors no less if he’s going to be a Rule 5 success story.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wisely starred as a two-way player at Gulf Coast CC (Fla.), batting .363 and recording a 2.86 ERA in two seasons before the Rays drafted him in the 15th round in 2019 -- 19 rounds earlier than the Guardians selected his older brother, Alec. Most of the clubs interested in Brett liked him more as a pitcher, but Tampa Bay preferred him as a hitter and he batted .284/.364/.471 in his first three pro seasons. Faced with a 40-man roster crunch, the Rays traded him to the Giants for outfield prospect Tristan Peters in November. Wisely has a sound left-handed swing, knows the strike zone and uses the entire field. While he's more hitter than slugger, he uses a leg kick to help him drive the ball in the air and trades some strikeouts to get to most of his fringy raw power. He has the upside of a .275 hitter who provides 15 homers per season while also drawing a good amount of walks. Though he has fringy speed, Wisely is an opportunistic runner who has stolen 63 bases in two full seasons. He played all four infield positions as well as left field in 2022, spending most of his time at second base. He's a surehanded, if unspectacular, defender with decent range and solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The key return in the 2020 Trade Deadline deal that sent Taijuan Walker to Toronto, Rodriguez’s timeline has taken longer than perhaps the Mariners would’ve envisioned. After a decent 2021 in which he climbed to High-A Everett, Rodriguez stalled in '22, leading to him being designated for assignment. He wound up clearing waivers and had a nice bounce-back in 2023, with a 241-point jump in OPS to .973 at Everett, which led to a promotion to Double-A Arkansas. Some of the challenges that Rodriguez has experienced are rooted in conditioning, though the Mariners have liked his progress in this area. When he’s going really well and making impact to all fields, it’s because his strides are more out front and he’s not opening himself up early. The question is whether he can sustain the success -- and the mechanics in question -- from ‘23 throughout ‘24. Rodriguez’s calling card is his bat, which will continue to be under more of a microscope as he climbs the ranks. Aside from that, he doesn’t have an above-average tool, though he does run and throw better than his body profile might suggest. At his best, he profiles as a productive player off the bench, and his ceiling is probably as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Most of Rodriguez’s projectability hinges heavily on his bat, and the bat was average at best in 2022. That played a part in the club designating him for assignment in order to clear a 40-man roster spot in January, though he wound up clearing waivers and being outrighted, thus giving him another chance in the organization after arriving as the key return in the 2020 Trade Deadline deal that sent Taijuan Walker to the Blue Jays. With unorthodox mechanics, Rodriguez still shows flashes of all-field hitability, but at the same time, he struggled making consistent contact pull side on optimum pitches to do so, part of a greater issue of challenges staying in the strike zone. There are enough encouraging signs that the bat can still be solid, but he’ll need to show it more consistently against better pitching. Rodriguez also shows some athleticism, but physical conditioning and high performance efforts will be a big part of him getting back on track. If he has no legit outfield position to play, there’s that much more pressure on the bat to be elite.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The key return in the 2020 Trade Deadline deal that sent Taijuan Walker to the Blue Jays, Rodriguez was pried away from Toronto reluctantly. Shortly after his arrival, the Dominican Republic native drew a lofty scouting report from another top Mariners prospect, Noelvi Marte, who compared Rodriguez to Barry Bonds. Now, the 21-year-old probably doesn’t have 700-homer potential, but he does show consistent contact and he’s quick to the ball with a strong recognition of the strike zone. With direction from the club to become more lean, the left-handed-hitting outfielder had a solid season at High-A Everett in 2021, hitting .295/.383/.484 (.867 OPS) with 10 homers in 93 games before earning a promotion to Double-A Arkansas for the season’s final two weeks. Known for a solid approach at the plate, Rodriguez also possesses sneaky power for his 5-foot-11 frame, thanks to improved and more disciplined conditioning. A toe-tap hitter, Rodriguez is touted for maximizing his impact to the baseball, as well as solid pitch-recognition ability. Defensively, he has average speed and range and an above-average arm that will likely have him slated for a corner spot long-term. Rodriguez was coveted enough by the Mariners for the club to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft by adding him to the 40-man roster in November, even if he is a few seasons away from contributing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The key return in the 2020 trade that sent Taijuan Walker to the Blue Jays, Rodriguez was pried away from Toronto reluctantly, particularly after he hit .301/.364/.422 as an 18-year-old for the Jays' Rookie-level affiliate. He was last listed at 5-foot-11 and 186 pounds, but he came to Seattle with direction from the club to become more lean. Rodriguez was highly touted within the Mariners’ farm system by one of their own: top prospect Noelvi Marte, who grew up with the outfielder in the Dominican Republic. When asked for a loose scouting report on what big league comps the up-and-coming outfielder projected as, Marte had lofty praise for Rodriguez, likening him to Barry Bonds. Rodriguez probably doesn’t have 700-homer potential, but he does show consistent contact and he’s quick to the ball with a strong recognition of the strike zone. The Mariners don’t have much more to go on beyond Marte’s recommendation, given that Rodriguez did not play at the alternate training site last year. Because of his young age and uncertainty, it’s likely he will begin the season at a lower-level Minor League affiliate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more highly regarded high school arms in the Draft Class of 2017, Enlow had a higher pricetag because of his commitment to pitch for LSU. The Twins were willing to meet that price, taking him in the third round, but giving him end of first round money ($2 million) to sign. While he wasn’t as overpowering as he was as a prepster, he had relative success at each level of A ball over his first two full seasons of pro ball. The stuff started ticking back up in 2020 and he looked like he was making a huge stop forward in 2021 when he blew out his elbow and needed Tommy John surgery in June. The Twins liked what they saw from Enlow before he got hurt, with a fastball that was trending in the right direction, averaging 94 mph and touching 97, with better movement. He was continually working to add velocity back to the curve and those two improved pitches led to a much higher strikeout rate. He has a cutter-like slider as well and he was working to slow down his changeup to separate it from his fastball more and give it more depth. With the increased stuff had come a small uptick in his walk rate, but Enlow had an internal brace put in his elbow to hopefully shorten the recovery time post-surgery. He was able to return to get innings starting in May and the Twins hope he’s back to his pre-surgery improved self by 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2017 Draft approached, Enlow was the fifth-highest-rated high school right-hander in the Draft class, one who many felt could go in the first round in that June’s Draft. There was a commitment to LSU to contend with, a big reason why he landed in the third round, where the Twins went well over slot to sign him for $2 million. Though his stuff backed up a bit as a pro, he did pitch his way to High A ball in 2019, his second full season, then saw the stuff tick back up during his time in instructional league play in 2020. His progress was halted when an elbow injury turned out to be a torn UCL that required Tommy John surgery in June. Before the injury, all of Enlow’s stuff was pointing in the right direction. His fastball, which had dipped to the low 90s in 2019, was back up and touched 97 mph at instructs, albeit in a small sample size. He’s worked on fastball movement along with adding velocity. He’s gotten more depth on his curve again, up to 80 mph, with more vertical movement than he’d shown previously as a pro. He has a slider with cutter action that’s effective, and his changeup gives him the chance to have four average or better offerings. Enlow has generally been around the strike zone and shows a good overall feel for pitching, so sharpening his stuff will be key to miss more bats as he moves up the ladder. He was just 22 for all of the 2021 season, so there's time for him to come back from the surgery, room for growth and the ability for him to be a mid-rotation type starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $75,000 signing out of the Mexican League in July 2016, Carrillo looked the part of a breakout star during his years in the Dodgers system, even earning a 40-man spot in November 2020 after only throwing at the alternate site and instructs that year. While pitching in the upper Minors for the first time in 2021, the right-hander went to the Nationals as a key prospect piece in the Max Scherzer-Trea Turner Trade Deadline blockbuster and finished up at Double-A Harrisburg. He was set to move to the bullpen because of control woes when right shoulder discomfort knocked him out for three months in 2022, and the Nationals designated him for assignment in December. Carrillo made up for lost time with 11 appearances in the Mexican Pacific League this offseason, and he’s been up to 94-95 mph in those looks. The Nationals are hopeful even more velocity will return as he puts the shoulder woes further in the rearview, and he has a history of nearing triple digits. His mid-80s slider shows promising break to remain his best secondary and could be an even more prominent pitch in short spurts. An upper-70s curveball and mid-80s changeup with tumble flash average but remain behind the other two. Listed at 5-foot-11, Carrillo has always struggled with throwing consistent strikes because of a high-effort delivery, leading to his placement in the bullpen, and the shoulder concerns did him no favors. He has the pure stuff of a future Major Leaguer but will need to show health and results in 2023 to squeeze his way back onto the 40-man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers scouted Carrillo out of the Mexican League, where he played for Tijuana, and signed the then-17-year-old for only $75,000 in July 2016. He became a pop-up name in his first two seasons at the lower levels but met resistance at Class A Advanced Rancho Cucamonga in 2019 (5.44 ERA, 51 walks in 86 innings). A lat injury was partly to blame, and he bounced back nicely in the Arizona Fall League that autumn. After seeing him at the 2020 alt site and instructs, the Dodgers added Carrillo to the 40-man that November and sent him to the upper Minors for the first time last season. He moved to the Nationals system as part of the Trea Turner-Max Scherzer deal last July and finished 2021 with a 4.76 ERA, 101 strikeouts and 50 walks in 96 1/3 innings at two Double-A affiliates. Carrillo sits around 93-96 mph with his fastball and can flirt with triple-digits on occasion. The heater comes with plenty of life and can be difficult for any hitter to track. A mid-80s slider is easily his best secondary with lots of good break that can give hitters on either side a fit. An upper-70s curveball and tumbling changeup round out the arsenal, and both could be average pitches. The 5-foot-10 right-hander features a fair amount of effort in his delivery, and that hasn’t helped his control over the last three years. The Nationals decided to make Carrillo a full-time reliever at the start of the season, and shoulder discomfort led to nearly three months on the IL, essentially locking him into that role. The stuff certainly plays in shorter spurts, and it may just be health that keeps Carrillo from seeing DC before the end of next season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers spotted Carrillo while he was training with the Mexican League's Tijuana Toros and signed him for $75,000 in 2016. He cruised through his first two pro seasons before stumbling in high Class A in 2019 while dealing with a lat injury, though he bounced back as one of the best starting pitching prospects in the Arizona Fall League that offseason. After spending time at Los Angeles' alternate site and instructional league program in 2020, he joined the 40-man roster in November. While at Double-A Tulsa this summer, he was dealt to the Nationals as part of a four-prospect return for Max Scherzer and Trea Turner at the Trade Deadline. Carrillo operates with a 93-97 mph fastball that tops out at 100 with life as impressive as its velocity, displaying heavy sink at times and plenty of armside run at others. He sometimes will command his upper-70s curveball better than his heater, and his mid-80s slider is superior to his curve. His changeup has some nice tumble but isn't as trustworthy as the rest of his repertoire. Though the Dodgers developed Carrillo as a starter, there's a good chance that he winds up in the bullpen with the Nats in the future. His lack of physicality leads to questions about his durability and he has yet to prove he can provide consistent strikes. He earns praise for his intelligence and competitive nature, and his mentality could help make him a late-inning asset as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez made Colombia's 2013 national 18-and-under team as a 15-year-old infielder, then became a full-time catcher after signing with the Rays for $225,000 the following July. He emerged as one of baseball's top catching prospects when he hit 21 homers as a 20-year-old in Low-A in 2018, but he slumped the next season and Tampa Bay traded him and infield prospect Nick Sogard to the Red Sox for Chris Mazza and Jeffrey Springs in February 2021. Hernandez responded with 16 homers in Double-A and reached Triple-A in September. Hernandez looks to drive the ball with a pull-heavy approach that maximizes the plus raw power created by his bat speed, strength and loft in his right-hander stroke. He lacks selectivity at the plate, however, putting balls in play that he should avoid and rarely drawing walks. Though he hit .291 through his first six pro seasons, scouts question how effective he'll be in the big leagues unless he tones down his aggressiveness. Though Hernandez possesses a plus-plus arm and has erased 42 percent of basestealers as a pro, the rest of his catching requires significant improvement. He's not particularly agile, his receiving and framing are fringy at best and he committed 14 passed balls in 66 games last year. He's a well below-average runner whose only other defensive option would be first base, where his lack of range would work against him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An infielder on Colombia's 2013 national 18-and-under team at age 15, Hernandez became a full-time catcher after signing with the Rays for $225,000 the following year. He broke out as one of the game's best catching prospects when he hit 21 homers in the low Class A and notoriously pitcher-friendly Midwest League in 2018, but his stock slumped when he went deep just nine times in high Class A as an encore. After designating journeymen Chris Mazza and Jeffrey Springs for assignment in February, the Red Sox dealt them to Tampa Bay for Hernandez and infield prospect Nick Sogard. Hernandez is geared to hit for power, with bat speed, strength, loft in his right-handed stroke and a pull-heavy mindset. His hand-eye coordination allows him to make consistent contact but sometimes to his detriment, because he gets himself out by putting balls in play that he should avoid and he rarely walks. If he can improve his pitch recognition and develop some patience, he could be a .260 hitter with 20 homers per season. Hernandez also needs to upgrade his defensive play. He does have plus-plus arm strength and threw out 46 percent of basestealers in his first five pro seasons, but he's a shaky receiver who also committed 63 passed balls in 253 games. He's a well below-average runner who doesn't move particularly well behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals signed Antuna for $3.9 million in July 2016, about three times what they gave fellow infielder Luis García who has since cracked the Majors and graduated from prospect status. Antuna’s road to The Show has been longer, in part due to injuries. He underwent Tommy John surgery in August 2018 and then dealt with leg problems a year later that allowed him to play only three games in the Gulf Coast League. Antuna forced his way onto the 40-man roster as an alternate-site standout in 2020 but struggled immensely in the first half of last season, hitting just .149 with a .531 OPS in the first two months at High-A Wilmington. He righted the ship from July onward and finished with a .227/.307/.385 line over 106 games. Antuna’s second-half improvements saw him get more into his lower half in his swing, and that helped the then-22-year-old make more hard contact. A switch-hitter, Antuna exhibits promising bat speed from both sides but is a better slugger as a lefty, where he hit 11 of his 12 homers in 2021. He has enough raw power to hit 20-plus homers someday but will need to lock in his adjustments to threaten that mark. Washington has always liked Antuna’s athleticism, but the organization is moving him from shortstop into a full-time corner outfield spot to lessen the burden on his glove and allow for more focus on the bat. That plays into Antuna’s strengths as a hitting-first profile, but entering his second 40-man year, he needs to be much more consistent at the plate to get near his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Antuna was considered MLB Pipeline’s No. 21 international talent in the July 2, 2016, signing period, thanks to his ability to switch-hit and show multiple tools. The Nationals signed him out of the Dominican Republic for $3.9 million, making him their top international acquisition that year. By comparison, Luis Garcia – a former Top-100 prospect who made the Majors in 2020 – signed with the club for $1.3 million. But Antuna’s time in pro ball has been marred by injuries; first Tommy John surgery in August 2018 and then leg issues that limited him to only three Gulf Coast League games in 2019. Insofar as anyone could break out in 2020, a healthy Antuna certainly fit the bill at Washington’s alternate site and instructs. The Nationals like Antuna’s consistent hit tool from both sides of the plate, highlighted by his promising bat speed and ability to keep the bat through the zone for a long time. The contact is mostly resulting in low line drives at this point in his development, but the pieces are there for above-average power as he gets deeper into his 20s. The plan is to stick with him at shortstop for a while longer, but his average speed likely portends a move elsewhere. He worked out at second base and third in 2020, and his arm would work well at either spot. Washington added Antuna to the 40-man in November, fearing a potential Rule 5 pick even with all of the lost time. He will still be only 21 for the entire 2021 season, meaning there remain more opportunities for development despite the roster situation. If Antuna can take what happened behind closed doors last year and implement it into gameplay, his future as a solid hitter anywhere on the dirt becomes all the clearer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies signed Olivarez for just $65,000 just over a month into the start of the 2016-17 international signing period and the lefty proceeded slowly, spending two full summers and part of a third in the Dominican Summer League. When he finally came stateside in 2019, he showed off his outstanding stuff and shaky command in the rookie-level Pioneer League. The lefty earned a spot on the 40-man roster after throwing well at the club’s alternate site in 2020, but struggled with a jump to High-A ball in 2021. There’s nothing wrong with the 6-foot-3 southpaw’s stuff. His fastball easily sits in the mid-90s and he couples it with a power curve that might be a plus out pitch in time. He throws his changeup with good arm speed, and it should be a solid third pitch for him. All of his pitches come from a strong, physical frame. As Olivarez grew into that frame quickly, he developed a delivery that was tough to repeat and he would cross over one time and fly open the next. He spent last fall at instructs not pitching in any games, but working on his delivery, his timing and his direction to the plate. If he can harness that and his arm slot, he has the chance to head back in the right direction.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies gave eight players bonuses of six figures or higher during the 2016-17. Some are no longer with the organization and none are on the Rockies’ Top 30. But Olivarez, who got just $77,000 in August of 2016, has as big of an arrow next to his name as any pitching prospect in the organization in some time. Though he’s yet to pitch above a rookie-ball level, the left-hander did impress as the youngest player at the team’s alternate site in 2020, showing enough to get added to the 40-man roster this offseason. At 6-foot-3 and around 200 pounds, Olivarez has the prototypical pitcher’s body teams covet, especially coming from the left side. He consistently sat 95-97 mph at the alternate site and instructs in 2020, complementing it with good feel for spinning a power curve, which shows glimpses of being a plus pitch and he continues to work on his changeup, which does show good action at times. More than anything, Olivarez needs to work on gaining more consistency, especially in repeating his delivery in a controlled way. He’s generally around the strike zone, but he can get sped up, leading to a loss in command. The Rockies love his work ethic and baseball IQ, giving more confidence he’ll be able to reach what appears to be a very high ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nearly 18 when he signed for $60,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, Rodriguez didn't reach full-season ball until his fourth pro season, in part because he missed most of 2017 to a 75-game suspension for testing positive for a banned diuretic. He dominated in Low-A in 2019, though he was shut down that July with a sprained elbow. After a season lost to the pandemic, he excelled as a starter in Double-A (2.67 ERA) but got crushed pitching mostly out of the bullpen in Triple-A (8.01 ERA). Rodriguez deals 92-96 mph fastballs and occasionally reaches 98 with high spin rates, arm-side run and carry up in the zone. His low-80s changeup has splitter action and consistently misses more bats than his other offerings, but he didn't use it as much as a reliever. He relied more heavily on a low-80s slider that he hung too often and was less sharp than it had been in the past. After averaging 1.9 walks per nine innings during his first four pro seasons, Rodriguez saw that rate nearly double to 3.6 in 2021. He has a deceptive delivery with a flat approach angle and the athleticism to repeat it consistently. He's trending more to reliever than starter at this point, and he has yet to exceed 81 2/3 innings in a single season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez took a while to get noticed because he was nearly 18 when he signed for $60,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015 and he missed most of 2017 with a 75-game suspension after testing positive for a banned diuretic. He posted an 82/8 K/BB ratio in his 2018 U.S. debut, then logged a 2.08 ERA in low Class A the following season. He was shut down that July with a sprained elbow but returned to the mound during instructional league last fall and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster. Rodriguez generates some of the best spin rates in the Rangers system and shows flashes of three plus pitches. He operates at 92-96 and touches 98 mph with his heater, producing riding action at the letters or sink at the bottom of the zone. Some scouts think his changeup with splitter action will be his best offering in the long run, and he also has a breaking ball that combines curveball depth and slider velocity. If he can prove he can stay healthy and maintain quality stuff every fifth day -- he's 23 and never has pitched more than 73 2/3 innings in a season -- Rodriguez will rocket up this list and to the big leagues. He has an athletic delivery that provides some deception without compromising his ability to throw strikes and command his fastball to both sides of the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: UC Santa Barbara has generated a good amount of Draft talent over the past several years, from Shane Bieber in 2016 to 2021 first-rounder Michael McGreevy. In between those two, Davis looked like another starter who had the chance to do well, especially after a strong 2017 Cape Cod League performance. Instead, he was shut down just three appearances into his junior year in 2018 and needed Tommy John surgery. The Reds took him in the 11th round that June and helped him rehab back from surgery, though he missed development time with the shutdown in 2020. He was throwing well in High-A in 2021 when he was sent to the Rockies in the Mychal Givens trade and the Rockies added him to the 40-man roster following the season. Davis has a four-pitch repertoire that gives him the chance to start long-term. His fastball sits in the low-90s and can touch 94-95 mph, with good sink and tail to it. The Rockies would like him to increase his fastball usage up to around 50 percent after he threw his heater only around 27 percent of the time with the Reds at the time of the trade. He knows how to spin a breaking ball and loves to throw his 83-85 mph slider and can also throw a mid-70s curve. He throws his fading changeup with good deception. The right-hander has an up-tempo delivery that adds deception, and he threw more strikes post-trade than he did earlier in the year. The Rockies saw enough upside to add him to the roster, thinking there’s a future big leaguer here, either as a back-end starter or an interesting bullpen piece

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year member of the rotation at UC-Santa Barbara, Davis hoped to turn a solid Cape Cod League performance in 2017 into a strong junior season in 2018. Instead, he ended up needing Tommy John surgery after just three appearances. Nevertheless, the Reds took him in the 11th round of that June’s Draft and helped him work his way back to the mound. He made his pro debut the following summer in two Rookie-level leagues, but wasn’t able to build much upon that because of the shutdown in 2020, though he did get some instructional league work in last fall. He was having a fairly solid full-season debut in High-A when he was one of two prospects sent to the Rockies in the July Mychal Givens trade. Davis has the chance to have a usable four-pitch mix. His fastball typically sits around 92-93 mph with decent sink and tail to it, and he can reach back for 94-95 mph on occasion. He throws both a slider, 83-85 mph, and a curve, 73-77 mph, with the former a touch ahead of the latter. He has feel for a changeup with fade and deception, giving him a fourth potentially average offering. In the past Davis has been around the plate, both before and after the surgery, though his walk rate spiked in 2021. It’s been more control over command, something that will have to be refined for him to reach his ceiling as a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An athletic and projectable high school right-hander from Texas, Woods Richardson entered pro ball as the Mets’ second-round pick in 2018. He got off to a strong start at the lower levels of the Minors when he was sent to the Blue Jays in the deal that brought Marcus Stroman to New York. He was on the move again at the Trade Deadline when he was dealt to the Twins, along with Austin Martin, in the José Berríos trade in 2021. Though his stuff overall has backed up, he has touched the big leagues for a game in 2022 and another one in 2023. While Woods Richardson will only be 23 for nearly all of the 2024 season, the hopes that his lost velocity would return as he added strength have largely quieted. His fastball can still touch an occasional 95 mph, but it averaged just over 90 mph in 2023, though the cutter-like life it often has helps. He throws his low-80s changeup a lot, selling it with good arm speed and plenty of fade. His 83-84 mph slider can miss bats and he’ll still fold in a bigger, slower (73-74 mph) overhand curve. With his stuff not as sharp, Woods Richardson’s strikeout rate dipped again in 2023, while his walk rate went up. There are those who still believe he has the chance to start in the big leagues, but it’s now as a No. 5 type as opposed to what people dreamed of when he was coming out of high school.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Woods Richardson started his pro career as a second-round pick of the Mets in 2018, he looked like an athletic and projectable right-hander who would continue to develop plus stuff across the board. He’s been traded twice, first going from the Mets to the Blue Jays in the 2019 Marcus Stroman deal and then heading to the Twins in 2021 as part of the return for Jose Berrios, and his fastball’s velocity has backed up. He’s learned to be a better pitcher, though, one who earned a big league callup late in the 2022 season. While he used to throw harder, Woods Richardson has been able to make a fastball that averaged 91 mph last year work. It topped out at 94 mph, but its life still led to a decent amount of swing-and-miss. His low-80s changeup is still his best secondary offering, a plus offspeed pitch with good fade and deception that generated a 38 percent miss rate last year. He’s long had a solid upper-70s downer curve, and he worked in 2022 to throw his slider harder. It now averages 83 mph, getting more swings-and-misses as a result. Only 22 for nearly all of the 2023 season, Woods Richardson worked this offseason in terms of his strength and conditioning program and refining his delivery to be more efficient in his direction to the plate in order to perhaps get a little more velocity out of him. That might raise his ceiling a touch, but he has a pretty high floor as a back-half-of-a-rotation type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally a second-round pick of the Mets in 2018, Woods Richardson has already been involved in two big trades, first getting sent from the Mets to the Blue Jays in the Marcus Stroman deal in 2019, then going from Toronto to Minnesota as part of the Jose Berrios trade at the 2021 Deadline. After a breakout in 2019, Woods Richardson’s stuff backed up in 2021, and he only pitched briefly for the Twins after being on Team USA’s pitching staff for the Olympics. At his best, Woods Richardson is an intriguing combination of size, stuff and feel for pitching. The Twins are working with him to regain the velocity on his fastball, which still features good movement but averaged only around 91 mph in 2021. He touched 96 mph, so the organization thinks more consistent velocity is in there if he can access it. His curve, an upper-70s downer, is a tick better than his low-80s slider, but it’s his changeup that is his only plus pitch right now, thrown with good fade and deception. Prior to 2021, Woods Richardson was an extreme strike-thrower. While he still missed a lot of bats a year ago, his walk rate more than doubled in his first taste of Double-A. The good news is Woods Richardson will be just 21 years old for the 2022 season, giving him time to right the ship as a legitimate starting pitching prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players (17) in the 2018 Draft, Woods Richardson signed with the Mets for $1.85 million after they selected him in the second round. He jumped straight to full-season ball the next year at age 18 and was having a strong campaign in the Class A South Atlantic League when the Mets packaged him with lefty Anthony Kay to get Marcus Stroman from Toronto ahead of the ‘19 Trade Deadline. The Blue Jays promoted Woods Richardson to Class A Advanced Dunedin upon acquiring him, and the young right-hander responded to the challenge by making six impressive starts down the stretch. He continued to add polish while pitching at Toronto’s alternate training site in 2020. The move to Double-A in 2021 had been a bit more uneven, and Woods Richardson was in Tokyo as part of Team USA’s Olympic pitching staff when he was packaged with Austin Martin and sent to the Twins for Jose Berrios at the Trade Deadline. At his best, Woods Richardson gets great extension over his front side because he’s an excellent athlete who repeats his clean delivery well. That extension gives Woods Richardson’s 91-95 mph four-seam fastball riding life, and he did a better job of pitching up in the zone with it at the alternate site, though his stuff backed up a bit in 2021 overall. He commands his heater better than most, showing the potential for plus command, and it's easy to envision the right-hander adding velocity as he grows into his ultra-projectable frame. Woods Richardson throws two distinct breaking balls in a top-to-bottom, downer curveball in the upper 70s and a sharp low-80s slider. He can locate the latter down in the zone as a chase pitch and showed better action and command of his curveball in 2020. Woods Richardson completes his four-pitch mix with a plus changeup that is regarded as one of the best in the system.
