Woods Richardson’s size, stuff and pitchability at a young age all bode exceptionally well for his future development, and he already demonstrates plus control and command of four pitches. He's more advanced and polished than the typical prep hurler and still has the potential to grow into a No. 2 or 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Josh (12th overall, 2015) and Bo (29th overall, 2018) are the only Canadian siblings both selected in the first round, and younger brother Myles is Canada's top prospect in the 2023 Draft. Signed for $2,578,137, Bo was considered one of the best pure hitters in his prep class but lacking an obvious defensive home. His development didn't go according to plan, as he emerged as the best defensive catcher in the Guardians system while struggling at the plate, but he improved dramatically in 2022 and joined his brother in Cleveland in October. Naylor snapped out of his offensive doldrums and hit .263/.392/.496 between Double-A and Triple-A last year, taking off once he understood how pitchers were trying to attack him. He made better swing decisions and allowed his plus raw power to come naturally rather than trying to lift and pull pitches out of the park. He generates impressive exit velocities with his combination of a quick left-handed stroke and strength, and he has the tools and approach to produce 20 homers per season with a healthy amount of walks. Not only will Naylor provide more offense than most catchers, he's also faster and more athletic than most players at his position. He didn't become a full-time backstop until he turned pro yet quickly took to receiving, framing and blocking pitches. He also does a nice job of running a pitching staff and used his strong arm to erase 32 percent of basestealers last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Naylor went 29th overall in the 2018 Draft, three years after the Marlins popped his older brother Josh 12th overall, making them the first Canadian siblings both selected in the first round. One of the best pure hitters in his prep class, Bo came with questions about his future defensive home when he signed for an above-slot $2,578,137. His development has not gone nearly as anticipated, as he became the best defensive catcher in the system but also batted .188 with a 31 percent strikeout rate in Double-A last year -- but he has improved dramatically at the plate in 2022 and soon could join his brother in Cleveland. Naylor displays a quick left-handed swing and good feel for the barrel. He got himself into trouble when he focused too much on trying to launch balls out of the park, but he snapped out of it this year by using a much more disciplined approach and utilizing the opposite field more often. His bat speed and strength give him plus raw power and he produces impressive exit velocities. When Naylor turned pro, Cleveland had to decide whether to maximize his positional value by keeping him at catcher or his offensive value by playing him at a less demanding spot like third base. He's quicker and more athletic than most backstops and has become adept at receiving, framing and blocking pitches. His solid arm strength enabled him to throw out 31 percent of basestealers last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Naylor starred with the Canadian junior national team, winning MVP honors in both 2017 and 2018, and also reached the High School Home Run Derby finals at the 2017 All-Star Game. One of the best pure hitters in the 2018 prep class, he went 29th overall that June and joined his brother Josh (drafted No. 12 overall by the Marlins in 2015, acquired by the Indians last summer) to become the first Canadian siblings both taken in the first round. Since signing for an above-slot $2,578,137, he has taken to catching better than anticipated. Naylor has a quick left-handed stroke and good feel for the barrel, which should allow him to hit for both average and power. His bat speed and strength helped him rank fifth in the low Class A Midwest League with 39 extra-base hits in his first full pro season in 2019, and he showed off more speed than most catchers by leading the MWL with 10 triples. But when he skipped a level to Double-A this season, he tried too hard to launch balls and began striking out an alarming rate. The Indians will have to decide whether to maximize Naylor's positional value by keeping him at catcher or tapping into more of his considerable offensive upside by moving him to a less demanding position. For now, he'll stay behind the plate because his receiving has been better than advertised. Though he threw out 37 percent of basestealers in 2019, the Indians had him work with their pitching instructors on his arm strength and throwing mechanics at their alternate site and during instructional league last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Having signed for $2.7 million out of Venezuela in July 2018, Álvarez lived up to early hype by jumping straight to stateside ball and posting a .917 OPS between two Rookie-level circuits a year later. After spending 2020 at the alternate site in Brooklyn, the right-handed masher put in a strong full-season debut with a .272/.388/.554 line and 24 homers in 99 games at Single-A and High-A in 2021 and continued to show immense power with 27 blasts in 112 games at Double-A and Triple-A in his age-20 season last year. Álvarez debuted for the Mets late on Sept. 30 and likely would have gotten more time if not for a right ankle injury that eventually required post-season surgery. Álvarez’s swings on contact can be some of the most entertaining in the Minor Leagues. He utilizes impressive strength and bat speed from a whip-like swing to tap into his near-top-of-the-scale raw power, and as a result, his exit velocities and home run totals can both be eye-popping. Like many catchers, Álvarez knows the zone well and will take his walks -- also like many young hitters, he’s still working overall on swing decisions. The combination of loud contact and ever-improving approach could make him an above-average hitter in the end. While the Mets consistently note how Álvarez has improved his framing, he remains below-average defensively because of his limited athleticism. The ankle injury may hamper that development further, though that’s yet to be seen, but he does possess the pure arm strength to give himself a defensive weapon. Álvarez enters 2023 still only 21 years old with a Major League-ready bat, and if he does continue to refine his work behind the plate, he has the potential to be a multi-time All-Star.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Álvarez was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 13 international prospect during the 2018-19 signing period, and the Venezuela native signed with the Mets for $2.7 million that July. The hype continued at Rookie-level Kingsport and the alternate training site in 2019 and 2020, respectively. Álvarez’s stock rocketed again last season, and he climbed from Double-A to the Majors at just 20 years old this summer. The backstop did miss some time with a right ankle injury and had surgery to address cartilage damage in October. He is expected to be ready for Spring Training. Even if he didn’t play a premium position at catcher, Álvarez would be one of the most exciting offensive prospects in baseball. His swing is whip-like from the right side and helps him barrel balls easily to all fields. He has tremendous raw power that is already been of use in games. His 24 total homers in 2021 were second-most among Minor League teenagers, and he would have hit for more if he didn’t play at pitcher-friendly Coney Island. Buck Showalter’s Major League staff certainly took note of Álvarez’s plus-plus pop in the spring, noting that his homers looked Major League-quality even then. All that said, Álvarez’s profile does get a boost from his ability to play behind the plate. New York officials acknowledge he has been working diligently to become even an average defensive backstop, hoping his framing and blocking can at least come close to his bat. His plus arm is an asset at least, though he needs to improve his throwing. Regardless, Álvarez’s power could help the youngster become one of the game’s best offensive backstops once he reaches Queens for good, and he has the bat to make multiple All-Star trips (and perhaps a few Home Run Derby appearances as well).

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Alvarez checked in as MLB Pipeline’s No. 13 prospect for the 2018-19 international period before inking a $2.7 million pact with the Mets on July 2. The Venezuela native emerged as one of the better young catchers in the Minors in 2019, slashing .282/.377/.443 over 35 games in the Rookie Appalachian League at age 17 to conclude his pro debut. The Mets sent Alvarez to their alternate training site in Brooklyn in 2020 -- a challenge to which the teenage catcher responded by showing better than any hitter in camp. With his exceptional physical strength and explosive swing, Alvarez appears poised to do damage each time he steps to the plate. He has massive raw power and knows how to get to it during games, making hard, fly-ball contact using a leveraged right-handed swing. Alvarez also finds the barrel consistently and is comfortable hitting to all fields, thanks to an approach that belies his age and experience. Alvarez still has gains to make defensively with his blocking and catch-and-throw skills, but the arm strength is plus, and he’s worked hard to improve his athleticism and mobility behind the plate. On top of the impressive physical tools, Alvarez earns high marks for his makeup and leadership skills and his desire to improve in all facets of the game. mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies have had a strong connection to Long Island, finding several players from the New York area in the Draft over the years. Best among those is likely to be O’Hoppe, taken in Round 23 of the 2018 Draft and given an over-slot bonus of $215,000. After being a surprise addition to the Phils’ alternate site to catch big league pitchers, he started to take off in 2021, reaching Triple-A. He went to the Futures Game in 2022 before he was dealt to the Angels for Brandon Marsh at the Trade Deadline; he went off in Double-A with his new organization and earned his first big league callup later that year. He had made the Angels’ Opening Day roster, but suffered a torn labrum in his left shoulder in late April, requiring surgery and potentially keeping him out for the remainder of the season. Since a relatively humble beginning to his pro career, O’Hoppe has worked tirelessly to improve his offensive profile. He now has an outstanding approach, greatly limiting strikeouts (16.6 percent in 2022) while drawing a ton of walks. That’s helped him tap into his considerable raw power more consistently, with his 26 homers and .544 SLG in 2022 the kind of production the Angels might be seeing from the backstop in the big leagues. While O’Hoppe’s defensive tools don’t jump out as plus, he is a very solid all-around receiver, with a quick release, an accurate arm and excellent blocking skills. Pitchers love throwing to him, and his worth ethic and makeup are off the charts, the kind of leader teams covet behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Most thought O’Hoppe was destined to head to East Carolina, where his father and uncle attended, after graduating from his Long Island high school in 2018. But the Phillies’ scouting department, which has found draftable talent on Long Island consistently over the last several years, was able to sign him in the 23rd round of that June’s Draft for an over-slot bonus of $215,000. After playing rookie and short-season ball his first two summers, O’Hoppe gained invaluable experience catching at the Phillies’ alternate site in 2020, using those lessons to go from High-A to Triple-A before finishing with a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. He was having a solid season in Double-A, one that included a trip to the Futures Game, when he was sent to the Angels in return for Brandon Marsh at the Trade Deadline. O’Hoppe has put in a lot of work to refine his approach from the right side of the plate. He trimmed his strikeout rate down considerably in 2021 (17.4 percent), then walked more than he struck out in the AFL. All of that has allowed him to tap into his raw power more consistently and it’s easy to think he could top 20 homers annually in the future. He’s already proven to be a very capable defender, one who receives and blocks well and whose arm plays up because of his quick release and accuracy. The backstop’s work ethic will help ensure he makes the most out of his tools. He was named the Dernell Stenson Sportsmanship Award winner in the AFL because of his makeup and pitchers love working with him. There’s a big up arrow next to his name, with every chance of him being a starting catcher in the big leagues soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If it sounds strange for a 23rd-round pick in the 2018 Draft out of the Long Island high school ranks to get invited to a team’s alternate site camp in 2020, you’re not wrong. O’Hoppe did get an over-slot bonus of $215,000 to sign, then went out and posted a .367/.411/.532 line in the Gulf Coast League during his pro debut. He didn’t fare as well with the bat with a move to the short-season New York-Penn League in 2019, but the Phillies love the way he carries himself and they were short on catching at the alternate site, so O’Hoppe chipped in and really held his own. Over his first two summers of pro ball, O’Hoppe has shown the ability to impact the baseball from the right side of the plate. He has tremendous raw power, especially to his pull side, though he hasn’t always gotten to it with a raw approach leading to swing-and-misses, particularly with the move to short-season ball (27.7 strikeout rate in 2019). His strikeout rate went down and walk rate went up during his time in the Australian Baseball League after the 2019 season and that continued at the alternate site, where he doubled his walk rate compared to his previous Phillies totals. O’Hoppe is an excellent receiver, showing agility to get the low pitch and blocking well. He has an average arm now, but his quick release has helped that play up and he continues to add strength. He gets very high marks for his baseball rat mentality and leadership behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rockies scouts first spotted Tovar when he was 13 years old and playing beyond his years in the Dominican Republic, so they were sure to sign him when he was eligible, giving him $800,000 in August of 2017. Known initially as a glove-first shortstop, Tovar performed well enough to make his way from the Dominican Summer League in 2018 to Rookie ball in the U.S. the following summer. After spending all of the shutdown in Arizona, Tovar's bat started to catch up to his glove in 2021, and he finished in the Arziona Fall League. Another big step came in Double-A in 2022 and despite missing more than two months because of a groin injury, he made his big league debut in September. As Tovar has added strength to his six-foot frame, he’s become more of an offensive threat. He’s still very much an aggressive swinger from the right side of the plate and doesn’t walk a ton, but he also limits his strikeouts. He’s shown the ability to hit for average and with burgeoning power, slugging .540 in 2022, mostly in Double-A Hartford. While he’s not a burner in terms of pure speed, he’s an excellent baserunner who knows how to steal a base. Tovar had every chance to make it to the big leagues based on his defense alone. He’s long been the best glove in the system, with easy plus actions at shortstop that point to a very long career at the premium spot. He makes all the plays with excellent footwork and a plus arm, and he has every chance to show off his Gold Glove potential as a big league regular in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since signing with the Rockies for $800,000 in August 2017, Tovar has been pushed fairly aggressively. And more often than not, he’s responded. After performing well in the Dominican Summer League in his 2018 debut, Tovar worked his way from rookie to short-season ball in 2019. He got stuck in Arizona for around 18 months during the pandemic, playing well at instructs, making his full-season debut and earning a promotion to High-A in 2021 before finishing up in the Arizona Fall League, where he showed glimpses of what he could become -- and what he has to work on -- before finally being able to return home to Venezuela. There is absolutely no question that Tovar could play defensively in the big leagues right now. He’s the best defender in the system, showing an ease of operation in his actions at the premium position. He makes the routine and the flashy plays consistently, with outstanding actions, footwork and a plus arm he saves for only when he needs it. He’s shown he can seamlessly move over to second base, if needed, but he has Gold Glove potential at short. Just 20 for most of the 2022 season, Tovar continues to add strength to his frame and that showed up in an improved ability to drive the ball at all stops. He still needs to refine his aggressive approach, and he did chase pitches out of the zone more in High-A and the AFL, but he also was very young for those levels. He’s now on the 40-man roster and has the chance to be the Rockies’ everyday shortstop for a long time once he’s ready.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Of the 17 players the Rockies gave six figure bonuses to in the 2017-18 international signing period, the top three were all shortstops. The Rockies had to wait until Aug. 1, 2017 to give Tovar the highest bonus in their class, $800,000, on his 16th birthday. He’s been pushed fairly aggressively after making his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, making his way to short-season Boise in 2019 during his United States debut as one of the youngest players in the league. He was a standout performer at instructs in 2020. Tovar is, according to some in the organization, a defensive wizard. He has the best actions of any infielder in the system, one who makes routine plays as well as highlight-reel ones. He has a consistently plus arm that he doesn’t feel he has to show off all the time. Though he’ll see time around the infield, there’s no question he can stay at the premium position for a very long time, even if he settles into being more of an average runner. Tovar’s ceiling is hinged on how his bat, or more specifically, his strength, develops. He gave up switch-hitting to focus on his right-handed swing and he is capable of making consistent contact. There was more impact in his bat at instructs, including a home run at Chase Field in the last game of the fall. He’s always going to be a glove-first infielder, but if that trend with the bat continues, he could be an everyday shortstop instead of just a utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves had originally come to terms with Bae back in 2017, but part of the fallout for their international signing violations was the voiding of that deal. The Pirates brought him aboard in the spring of 2018, giving him $1.2 million to sign. He was suspended for 30 games in 2019 after being convicted of assaulting his former girlfriend in Korea. Once he returned to the field, he performed well, winning a batting title with Greensboro in ’19, moving up to Double-A in 2021 and making a very good impression during his big league debut last season. The left-handed-hitting Bae continues to excel based largely on his knack for making contact, striking out in just 18.6 percent of his plate appearances in the Minors heading into the 2023 season. He also draws a fair amount of walks, increasing his on-base impact and allowing him to use his easily plus speed to be a legitimate threat to steal. While he’s never going to compete for a home run title, he has added enough strength to impact the ball more than he did in the early parts of his career. Adding to Bae’s versatility is his defensive flexibility. He started out as a shortstop and can still handle filling in there, and he's proven to be a solid second baseman, while also showing his speed plays very well in center field. He’s ready to impact a big league team in a super-utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bae originally agreed to sign with the Braves in 2017, but had the deal voided as part of Atlanta’s penalty for international signing violations. That allowed the Pirates to sign him for $1.2 million in the spring of 2018. Things haven’t always gone smoothly, as a conviction for assaulting his former girlfriend in Korea led to a 30-game suspension in 2019. He came back to hit .323 and win a batting title in his first taste of full-season ball and then after playing at the club’s alternate site, he jumped up to Double-A and performed well there, missing time due to a sprained knee, capping it off with a solid showing in the Arizona Fall League. The two things that will carry Bae to the big leagues are his speed and his ability to make contact. He stole 28 bases between Altoona and the AFL last year and the Pirates have challenged him to use his close to top-of-the-scale speed to swipe 40 bags in 2022. Bae draws a good amount of walks and limits his strikeouts, putting the ball in play at a very high clip and letting his legs do the work. He’ll never be confused for a power hitter, but he has added strength and showed the ability to impact the ball more in 2021. Originally a shortstop, Bae started seeing more time at second in 2019 and then played there almost exclusively for most of the 2021 season. The Pirates started folding in center field, both in the regular season and in the AFL, with the plan for him to get reps in both spots and a potential future role as a utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Bae’s deal with the Braves in 2017 was voided in the wake of Atlanta’s violations on the international market, it worked out to the Pirates’ benefit as they signed the middle infielder for $1.2 million in March 2018. He ran into trouble off the field in 2019, serving a 30-game suspension after being convicted of assaulting his former girlfriend in Korea, but returned to win the South Atlantic League batting title with a .323 average in his full-season debut. He spent the summer of 2020 at the Pirates’ alternate training site in Altoona. Bae’s offensive profile is all about his ability to make contact and get on base. The left-handed hitter has a slasher kind of approach, going the other way and putting the ball on the ground a lot (well over 50 percent groundball percentage) to allow his nearly top of the scale speed work to his advantage. He doesn’t strike out much and draws a fair amount of walks, getting on to be a true basestealing threat. There’s not a ton of power there, though he can make loud contact at times, with roughly a third of the balls he put in play in Altoona last summer registering exit velocities of 95 mph or higher. Defensively, Bae continues to see time both at shortstop, his original position, and second, where he’s seen most of his time. There are some questions as to whether he’ll stay on the dirt long term, with some curious to see how his speed might play in center field. If everything clicks, Bae could turn into a David Fletcher type performer in the big leagues in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since Siani emerged as top high school Draft prospect for the Class of 2018, there’s been confidence he could play center field in the big leagues. There was certainly upside with the bat, a big reason why the Reds went well over slot to sign the Pennsylvania prepster for $2 million as their fourth-round pick that June. His profile has stayed somewhat the same in his Minor League career, though he did find a greater level of offensive consistency in 2022, allowing him to make his big league debut last September. He struggled some in a return to Triple-A Louisville in 2023, was designated for assignment in late August and was picked up by the Cardinals off waivers on Sept. 2. In 2021 in particular, Siani had bought into the launch angle and loft craze a bit too much, which led to too much power-sellout to his pull side and taking him out of his overall approach. He righted the ship a bit in the Arizona Fall League following that year, and that carried over to 2022, when he got back to being more of a line-drive, hit-the-gaps, use-his-speed kind of a hitter. He did get to some of his power more naturally with 14 homers, all coming to his pull side, while cutting his strikeout rate down and continuing to draw walks. Getting on base more allowed Siani to steal more bags, and he led the Southern League with 49 steals. That speed, along with his natural feel for reads and routes, also continues to help him cover ground in center field, with his strong arm a plus as well. He’s trending toward being a defense-and-speed fourth outfielder at best, but considering he turned 24 in July before the DFA, there’s still some time for development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds went well over slot to land Siani in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft out of the Pennsylvania prep ranks, signing him for $2 million. Since then, the older brother of Pirates prospect Sammy Siani, has had some difficulty finding a level of consistent performance on the offensive side of things. That remained true with a move to High-A in 2021, though the Reds were encouraged with a strong performance in the Arizona Fall League. Siani was a plus defender in high school and nothing has changed. He could play center field defensively in the big leagues right now, with his plus speed enhanced by his outstanding instincts and good reads and routes, not to mention his plus arm. He’s used that speed on the basepaths as well, swiping 75 bases in 2019 and 2021 combined, then 10 more in the AFL. Questions arise when it comes to what kind of hitter he might be. He likely profiles better as a line-drive, all-fields player, one who can drive the ball to the gaps and use his legs. In the past, he’s bought too much into the launch angle and loft movement, selling out for power to his pull side, without much to show for it. If he can settle into being an average hitter who gets 12-15 homers over the fence, and he took steps in that direction in the Fall League, he still can develop into a big league regular with Gold Glove potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Three players have come out of West Penn Charter School in eastern Pennsylvania and made it to the big leagues, with outfielder Ruben Amaro the most recent (his last year in the Majors was 1998) and pitcher Mark Gubicza the most successful. Gubicza is the only one of the trio who signed out of high school and Siani, who got an above-slot $2 million bonus as a fourth-rounder in 2018, hopes to be the next. After a first full season that saw him struggle early, but finish more solidly, he played both at the Reds’ alternate training site and in the instructional league in 2020. Siani entered pro ball known especially for his defensive work in center field, and he’s done nothing but solidify his reputation as the best defensive outfielder in the Reds’ system, especially in terms of his reads and routes, not to mention his plus speed and strong arm. The questions were more about how much he would impact the baseball offensively. He showed the ability to make adjustments in the second half of the 2019 season and that continued in 2020. He’s using his legs more effectively and staying back more while showing overall improvement with his bat path. One thing Siani has worked on has been to not just hit the ball on the ground and let the plus speed that led to 45 steals in 2019 work for him. He’s using more of the field, with gap power showing up more consistently. If that trend continues, he has every chance to be a starting center fielder in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Guardians may have another Steven Kwan-esque success story in the works, as Brennan is making a similar journey from overlooked college contact hitter to potential big league regular. He stood out with his finesse more than his power as both a hitter and pitcher at Kansas State, where he had a career 5 percent strikeout rate and topped NCAA Division I in at-bats per whiff (18.6) in 2019, when Cleveland popped him in the eighth round. He led the Minors with 166 hits and ranked second with 40 doubles in 2022, made his big league debut in September and earned a spot on the postseason roster. With outstanding hand-eye coordination and a compact left-handed swing, Brennan continues to make contact seemingly at will and placed second in the upper Minors last year in strikeout rate (12 percent). While his flat stroke and approach aren't conducive to power, the Guardians have helped him make some adjustments to pull more pitches in the air. He jumped from six homers in 2021 to 14 last season, though he still may max out at 10-15 per year. Brennan's solid speed enables him to steal a few bases and cover ground in center field. He's a capable defender up the middle and more of an asset on the corners. Clocked up to 92 mph as a college pitcher, he has solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the Rangers for just $10,000 at the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, Henriquez has continually surpassed expectations, starting with a dominant debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2018. A jump to full-season ball in 2019 didn’t slow him down, and he pitched his way to Double-A in 2021, earning a spot on Texas’ 40-man roster. He moved to the Twins courtesy of the March 2022 Mitch Garver trade and had mixed results in Triple-A, though he did open some eyes with a solid big league debut in September. An undersized right-hander, Henriquez tends to pitch backward much of the time, leaning heavily on his slider and throwing his changeup nearly as much as his fastball. He utilized his secondary pitches more than the heater when he was up with the Twins. The slider is a true weapon, a mid-80s breaking ball with excellent depth, which along with his upper-80s changeup, miss a good amount of bats. His slider is fine velocity-wise, averaging around 94 mph in Triple-A last year, but it’s been too hittable, and he's working to throw it in the top half of the zone more after it initially was more down in the zone. Because he has three usable pitches, fills up the strike zone and is still so young, the Twins don’t want to pull the plug on him starting just yet. Some of that will depend on big league need, and he can let that slider really do damage in a relief role if that’s what he’s called upon to do.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Henriquez largely flew under the radar as a prospect in the 2017-18 international signing class because of his diminutive stature, but the Rangers liked his live arm enough to sign him for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2017. He provided a very early return on that small investment, with a 12.3 strikeout-per-nine rate that led the Dominican Summer League and then continuing to miss bats and not walk hitters with a jump to full-season ball in 2019. The right-hander was able to pitch his way to Double-A in 2021, though he struggled at that level, showing good enough stuff to get added to the Rangers’ 40-man roster last fall. He got a fresh start with the Twins in 2022 as he was sent to them in mid-March in exchange for Mitch Garver as Spring Training opened, and while he missed bats, he struggled in Triple-A. As small as Henriquez is -- 5-foot-10 and 155 pounds -- he has a big arm and three very good offerings. His four-seam fastball leads the way, touching 98 mph and sitting regularly in the 92-96 mph range. His heater registers high spin rates and has good carry up in the zone. His hard slider has good depth, as does his changeup and while the breaking ball is a bit ahead, both will flash plus at times. Because of his size, there will be questions about Henriquez’s durability as a starter until he shows he can handle a big league workload against more advanced hitters. In his favor, he has a low-effort and repeatable delivery and goes right after hitters, consistently filling up the strike zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Henriquez's small stature worked against him on the 2017 international market, though the Rangers saw enough arm strength to take a $10,000 flier on him out of the Dominican Republic. He led the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in strikeout rate (12.3 per nine innings) and placed second in K/BB ratio (9.9) during his 2018 pro debut, and he continued to throw strikes and miss bats when he made the jump to Low-A in 2019. He did the same in instructional league last fall while focusing on the development of his secondary pitches. The Twins were impressed enough to acquire him in the March 2022 Mitch Garver deal. Though Henriquez is listed at just 5-foot-10 and 155 pounds, he shows flashes of three plus pitches and scouts can't agree on which is his best. His most consistent is a 92-96 mph four-seam fastball that tops out at 98 and features high spin rates and good carry. He achieves quality depth with his hard slider as well as his changeup, with the former a more reliable offering at this point. Despite his lack of size, Henriquez is able to generate velocity without expending much effort in his compact delivery. He attacks hitters and fills the strike zone, enhancing his chances of remaining a starter. He still needs to prove he can hold up over a 150-180 inning workload and handle more advanced hitters as he gets acclimated to the Minnesota system, but the early returns are quite encouraging.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hollowell spent three years pitching out of St. John’s bullpen in college, saving 17 games in the process. Though he wasn’t as dominant as a junior, when he saved nine games, he still went in the sixth round of the 2019 Draft to the Rockies and started closing immediately. He finished second in the Double-A Eastern League with 16 saves in 2022 while making his big league debut in September. Perhaps fueled by some of the lumps he took with the Rockies late last season, Hollowell wowed everyone by transforming his body and adding around 30 pounds of muscle to his 6-foot-7 frame and leaving everyone excited to see what that might do to his stuff. He was already missing a ton of bats, with an 11.8 K/9 rate in Double-A last year, using his fastball-slider combination effectively. His fastball sat around 93-94 mph, touching 97-98, a four-seamer with high spin rates that hitters didn’t square up and he missed a ton of bats with his low-80s slider that has good, hard break to it. While his command eluded him during his first taste of big league life, Hollowell has been an outstanding strike thrower as a pro and there’s no reason to think he can’t settle in to having average command in the big leagues. If his stuff ticks up thanks to his newly found conditioning, he could pitch in high-leverage situations in a big league bullpen full time soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A member of St. John’s bullpen for three years, Hollowell’s junior year in 2019 wasn’t as dominant as his first two. The Rockies thought he looked like a future big-league reliever, taking him in the sixth round in that June’s Draft and watched him pitch very well in his debut that summer in the rookie-level Pioneer League. He was slowed in 2021 by an elbow issue, but was extremely impressive once he got to full-season ball for the first time. The 6-foot-7 Hollowell is a two-pitch reliever, but they are two very good pitches. His fastball reaches the mid-90s with ease and after working with the Rockies to stand up taller on the mound, he delivers the pitch with better plane and angle. He couples the heater with a nasty slider that tops out in in the mid-80s, a pitch he adds and subtracts from to give it hard, tight, cutter-like traits and a bigger, sweeping breaker. Hollowell does a good job of throwing both pitches from the same slot, a lower angle that is hard for hitters to pick up. He goes right after hitters with his stuff, filling up the strike zone and missing a ton of bats (12.4 K/9 in 2021). With concerns about his elbow behind him, he has the chance to move quickly up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hollowell spent three years pitching out of St. John’s bullpen, dominating as a freshman and sophomore before struggling a bit as a junior. The Rockies liked his reliever profile enough to take him in the sixth round of the 2019 Draft and he immediately rewarded their faith in him by saving seven games and striking out 14.5 hitters per nine innings during his Pioneer League debut that summer. The first thing the Rockies did with Hollowell is get the 6-foot-7 right-hander to stand up tall on the mound to create plane and leverage as he came to them with a crouched-over delivery. At instructs last fall, he was sitting 94-95 with his fastball, now with a lot better angle. He couples it with what’s best described as a power slurve. It has mid-range break with long three-quarter tilt to it, coming in at 83-84 mph. It plays very well, and misses a lot of bats, from his release point. Hollowell is a two-pitch reliever, but one who has thrown both for strikes since joining the Rockies. He was repeating his new delivery well and there’s a chance he could start moving quickly, with his power stuff giving him the ceiling of a seventh- or eighth-inning setup type if it all clicks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While he was a two-way player over his first two years at Southern Miss, Wallner quickly established his power-hitting bona fides with 19 homers as a freshman. By the time he left school as the Twins’ selection in the 2019 Competitive Balance Round A, he held the school career homer record after smashing 23 in his Draft year. Despite missing a lot of time with a broken hamate in 2021, that pop has carried him to the top of the Twins system, with Wallner making his big league debut last September. Wallner’s raw power gets an 80 on the 20-to-80 scale in that category. And while he does tap into it -- he hit 29 home runs combined in 2022 -- the question has always been whether he can make enough contact to do it regularly in the big leagues. He offsets it with a lot of walks, drawing 97 of them in the Minors in 2022 and carrying a 12.8 percent walk rate into the 2023 season, but he’s also struck out more than 30 percent of the time. He’s always struggled with fastballs at the top of the zone, and to that end, he has worked to spread out at the plate more to provide a more stable base and simplify movements, which will hopefully cut down on his in-zone miss rate. Wallner had a mid-90s fastball as a reliever in college and that arm plays very well in right field, though he’s not going to battle for a Gold Glove any time soon. If his mechanical adjustments at the plate can provide just a little more contact, his three true outcomes profile could make him a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a three-year starter at Southern Miss, Wallner hit for power consistently, even when pitching his first two years. He set the school’s career home run mark when he hit 23 out as a junior, leading to him being taken in the Compeititive Balance Round A by the Twins. The pop has shown up as a pro, along with the swing-and-miss concerns, even despite missing a good chunk of 2021 with a broken hamate. He made up for lost time and showed off his carrying tool in the Arizona Fall League. While it’s possible Wallner came back too soon from the hamate fracture, thus impacting his hit tool, the power did come back and he slugged .606 in the AFL. He has as much raw pop as anyone in the system and despite some swing issues, he’s shown he can get to it. There will likely always be high strikeout rates, but he has shown a better hit tool in the lower part of the strike zone, and the Twins have worked with him to tone down his swing so he can be more consistent at the top of the zone. Wallner has a plus arm that fired mid-90s fastballs as a reliever in college that works well in right field, though he’s a fringy, at best, defender. If he can continue to shrink the zone in order to increase the damage he can do when he puts the ball in play, he does have a Joey Gallo-esque offensive ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2017, the Twins went the college power route with their pick in the Competitive Balance Round A when they took Brent Rooker. Two years later, they hit the same pool in the CBA, when they selected Wallner, Southern Miss’ career home run leader. After hitting 23 homers in his junior year, the outfielder hit eight more while reaching full-season ball in his pro debut in 2019. Wallner has a bit of a three true outcomes feel to him as a hitter, with a tremendous amount of raw power to tap into, a lot of swing and miss and a willingness to draw walks. He struck out in 27.5 percent of his plate appearances during his pro debut, leaving some to question if he’ll make enough contact to get to that power, which could be plus in-game pop should he cut down on the K’s a little bit. That will be the key to him fitting the profile of a power-hitting right fielder, the spot he played in the summer of 2019. He has the arm for the position -- he was up to the mid-90s as a reliever as a freshman and sophomore – but has work to do in refining his approach if he wants to have success as he faces better professional pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Soto originally signed with the Braves for $1 million in July 2016 but was one of the many prospects made free agents as part of the penalty the Braves paid for their international signing infractions. He joined the Angels in December 2017 for $850,000. He’s advanced slowly through the system mostly because of his defensive acumen, but a step forward offensively in Double-A in 2022 led to him making his big league debut in September. Soto’s glove work will always be his calling card. He has great hands, good footwork and plus instincts that allow all of it, including his average arm, to play up at shortstop. While he almost exclusively played the premium position in the big leagues, he’s seen a good amount of time at second base and even has played third, showing an ability to move all over the dirt and play outstanding defense. That’s important because Soto is almost certainly a utility type in the future. He’s gotten a little stronger and gained some more confidence at the plate, and the left-handed hitter has a patient approach, drawing a ton of walks to offset a little swing-and-miss to his game. He’s never going to hit for power, but a little more strength could help him impact the ball more. That, when combined with his above-average speed and plus defense, gives him a better chance at carving out a big league bench role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels netted two big prospects from the Braves after a dozen of their players were made free agents as a penalty for international signing infractions in November 2017. The headliner was Kevin Maitan, but they also got Soto, who signed for $850,000 in December of that year. After a solid Angels debut in the Pioneer League in 2018, the infielder didn’t fare as well offensively with a push to full-season ball in 2019. While Soto is a defensive-minded player, he does have some offensive tools from the left side of the plate. He has exceptional bat-to-ball skills, with a very low 13.1 percent strikeout rate, to go along with an advanced approach that has led to nearly as many walks as strikeouts in his career. While he can really barrel up the ball, it’s been without much impact or exit velocity. He’s added some strength since joining the Angels, but needs to hit the weight room more if he wants to be able to hit, albeit without power, as he moves up the ladder. There are fewer questions about his glove work. Soto has more than enough arm, not to mention very good hands and footwork, to play shortstop for a long time. He continues to play second base to help maintain versatility, which raises his floor as a utility type. If he can start impacting the baseball more consistently, there’s still plenty of time for him to develop into a glove-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees selected German in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft after he increased his velocity and ranked fifth in NCAA Division I in ERA (1.58) and sixth in WHIP (0.83) as a North Florida junior. They shipped him to the Red Sox in January 2021 as part of the Adam Ottavino salary dump, and Boston dealt him to the White Sox for righty pitching prospect Theo Denlinger in February 2023. He stalled before a move to the bullpen in late 2021, then climbed from Double-A to Fenway Park in 13 months. German's fastball velocity has progressed from the low 90s in college to the mid-90s with the Yankees and now sits at 96-98 mph and touches 100 in shorter stints. He relies heavily on his riding heater, throwing it about two-thirds of the time, and has tightened what was a slurvy breaking ball into a tighter mid-80s slider with depth. He uses a splitter with similar velo as a changeup against left-handers, but he has trouble landing it for strikes. German lacked consistent control as a pro starter but is providing more strikes as a reliever. Scouts never have loved his arm action and he wasn't especially durable in the rotation, so he seemed headed to the bullpen for a while. If he can do a better job of commanding his fastball and slider than he did in his brief look with the Red Sox, he could handle a seventh-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Like his fellow 2019 pick Ryne Nelson, Jameson has ridden a roller coaster since entering pro ball out of Ball State. His first full season in 2021 was a success as he posted a 3.98 ERA with 145 K’s in 110 2/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. He spent a good chunk of the season at Triple-A Reno, where pitchers tend to struggle in dry air and elevation, and he was no different with a 6.95 ERA, .299 average-against and 109 strikeouts in 114 innings. The D-backs still gave Jameson four late-season starts in the Majors, and he lasted at least 5 1/3 innings and allowed no more than two earned runs in all four outings. The 6-foot right-hander may lack some size, but his super athleticism enables him to zip four-seam fastballs high in the zone at 96-98 mph, touching triple digits on occasion. His sinking mid-90s two-seamer plays better in the lower third and gives him a different movement profile on the heat. His mid-80s slider, however, is arguably his best pitch -- a two-plane breaker that elicits whiffs from batters on both sides. Major Leaguers went just 2-for-10 with 10 strikeouts and a 46 percent whiff rate against the slider in the limited sample. His mid-80s changeup flashes average, while he rarely broke out a mid-70s curveball as the season wore on. Jameson moves his arm incredibly quickly through his delivery, and while it was a concern that control woes would pop up, that hasn’t been the case in pro ball to this point. He has a deep enough arsenal to be a part of Arizona’s rotation mix in 2023, though it could get tempting to see how the fastballs and slider would play in shorter spurts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs selected Jameson with one of the comp picks they received when A.J. Pollock left via free agency, and they signed the Ball State right-hander for below-slot value in 2019. They sent him to Class A Short Season Hillsboro, where he made eight starts and threw just 11 2/3 innings due to his college workload. He got some work at instructs in 2020 and was recognized as the High-A Pitcher of the Month in July 2021 before he worked his way up to Double-A in an impressive first full season. Jameson struck out 145 over 110 2/3 frames last season and showed he was durable enough to handle a big workload, a key development as there had been concerns that his 6-foot, 165-pound frame portended a future in the bullpen. An explosive athlete, Jameson has a lightning-quick arm and sits in the mid-90s, with the ability to touch triple digits with his four-seam fastball. He also added a two-seam fastball to his repertoire last season, which is turning into another solid offering and some feel it may be better than his four-seamer. He complements the fastballs with an effective changeup and a pair of hard breaking balls. The sinking changeup, which profiles well with the two-seam fastball, is currently Jameson’s best off-speed pitch, though his slider could eventually take over that role. There had been concerns that Jameson’s slider and curveball blended together in the past as he uses the same group for both pitches, however he’s able to manipulate his wrist angle and the pitches no longer blend the way they used to. The curveball shows good depth, while the slider has more of a sweeping action. Some scouts suspect Jameson will ultimately wind up in the bullpen, but his 2021 performance went a long way toward showing he can hold up as a starter. Not only did he log over 100 innings, but he also improved his command and showed the ability to hold his velocity deep into starts. He certainly has the stuff needed to start, but if he needs to move to the ‘pen, his stuff would play well in a high-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs selected Jameson with one of the comp picks they received when A.J. Pollock left via free agency, and they signed the Ball State right-hander for below-slot value in 2019. They sent him to Class A Short Season Hillsboro, where he made eight starts and threw just 11 2/3 innings due to his college workload. He was not part of the team's 60-man player pool in 2020, but did get some work in during Instructional League and worked his way up to Double-A with increased stuff in an impressive 2021 campaign. At first glance, Jameson doesn't look like the explosive athlete that he is. He's somewhat undersized, but he may be the fastest player in the D-backs system. He has a lightning-quick arm that helps him generate a fastball that sits 93-96 mph and can touch triple digits. He complements his big fastball with a pair of hard breaking balls and has a really good feel for how to spin the ball. He’ll throw a curveball with depth and a slider with more lateral break. Both pitches have above-average, bat-missing potential. He has worked to separate the two breaking pitches, which had tended to blend together at times. The breaking balls play well off his riding fastball. Jameson rounds out his pitch mix with a changeup, which has taken a big step forward this season. Some scouts worry that Jameson doesn’t have the physicality needed to handle the rigors of starting in pro ball, but he does have the stuff for the role. Jameson showed a lot in 2021 to give the D-backs confidence that he can hold up as a starter long-term. His stuff plays out of the rotation, but if he needs to move to the ‘pen, his stuff would also play well in a high-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays spent $5.85 million on Magnolia (Texas) HS teammates in the 2018 Draft, paying Groshans $3.4 million as the 12th overall pick and Adam Kloffenstein $2.45 million as a third-rounder. A foot injury in 2019, the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and a sore back in 2021 severely cut into Groshans' development time, and his power hasn't materialized as expected. He homered just three times in 98 Triple-A games last year and once in his 17-game big league debut after the Marlins acquired him for Anthony Bass, Zach Pop and catching prospect Edward Duran in August. One of the better pure hitters in the organization, Groshans has a controlled right-handed stroke, a disciplined approach and a willingness to use the entire field. Listed at 6-foot-3 and 200 pounds, he hasn't added meaningful strength since turning pro, doesn't drive the ball in batting practice and produces ordinary exit velocities during games. He projected to have 25-homer power when Toronto selected him in the first round, but he has had increasing difficulty lofting balls in the air as he has risen through the Minors. Groshans needs to find more pop, because the Marlins plan on making him more of a third baseman than a shortstop. He played credible defense at short despite his size and fringy speed, but he is better suited for the hot corner and has the plus arm desired there. He played all four infield positions in 2022 and may be trending toward a utility role if he can't produce more home runs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays invested $5.85 million in Magnolia (Texas) HS teammates Jordan Groshans and Adam Kloffenstein in the 2018 Draft, paying the former $3.4 million as the 12th overall pick and the latter $2.45 million as a third-rounder. A foot injury in 2019, the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and a sore back in 2021 limited Groshans to just 146 games in his first four years as a pro. He hasn't hit for much power in the last two seasons, and the Marlins bought low on him by acquiring him in August for Anthony Bass, Zach Pop and a player to be named. Projected as a power-over-hit guy coming out of the Draft, Groshans has seen his profile flip the last two seasons. He continues to make regular contact to all fields while controlling the strike zone. But his right-handed swing seems slower and he's not hitting the ball as hard as he used to or doing any damage against left-handers. A taller shortstop at 6-foot-3, Groshans showcases decent mobility and the strong arm needed to stick on the left side of the dirt. He has fringy range at shortstop and figures to wind up at third base, which will put more pressure on his bat. His ceiling as an above-average regular remains intact, though his likelihood of reaching it has decreased.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays drafted a pair of Magnolia (Texas) High School teammates with two of their first three picks in 2018, taking shortstop Jordan Groshans, one of the top prep hitters in the class, in the first round, followed by right-hander Adam Kloffenstein in the third. Groshans’ bat has been as advertised in the pro ranks when he’s been healthy, as he built upon his strong pro debut by hitting .337/.427/.482 in his first 23 games at Class A Lansing in 2019 before succumbing to a season-ending foot injury that May. He recouped some of that lost time with a healthy ‘20 campaign, making strides on both sides of the ball as a standout at Toronto’s alternate training site. Groshans has all the raw ingredients to become a plus hitter with plus game power. The ball jumps off his right-handed bat because he combines a balanced swing with plus bat speed and a knack for barreling the baseball. He consistently hits hard line drives with backspin carry to all fields, has no problem turning around quality velocity and employs an approach that's advanced for his age. Groshans led all Blue Jays hitters at the alternate training site in home runs and should find even more power as he grows into his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. He’s athletic for his size, possessing average speed. Groshans has the hands and arm strength to play shortstop and worked hard to improve his footwork in 2020. Still, many evaluators believe that his size and actions make him better suited for third base at the highest level. He has the type of hitting ability and power needed to profile there, with the potential to develop into a middle-of-the-order run producer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A bout of forearm tightness as a high school senior in 2014 hurt Ortiz's Draft stock, but he still received a $1.75 million signing bonus from the Rangers after they drafted him late in the first round. He had already reached the Double-A level as a 20 year old in 2016 when the Brewers acquired him and Lewis Brinson in the Jonathan Lucroy-Jeremy Jeffress Trade Deadline deal. Two years later, Ortiz was on the move again at the Deadline, this time heading to Baltimore with Jonathan Villar and Jean Carmona in return for Jonathan Schoop. Bumped up to Triple-A after the trade, he pitched well there and made his big league debut as a reliever in September. Making his first MLB start the following week, Ortiz suffered a hamstring injury while covering first base that ended his season and raised more questions about his already suspect durability. Ortiz's stuff was down across the board during his brief big league stint as he sat around 92 mph with his fastball and showed little feel for his slider and changeup. The big right-hander has been up to 97 mph with his heater in the past, though, with a low-80s slider that flashes plus and a changeup that might be average once fully developed. While throwing strikes has never been an issue for Ortiz, his ability to command his pitches has backed up at higher levels, in part because he's struggled to stay in shape. The concerns that scouts had about Ortiz's weight and conditioning prior to the Draft have continued in the pro ranks, and he was especially out of shape at the time he was traded to the Orioles. The good news is that Ortiz is now committed to improving physically and has shed 20-plus pounds from his 6-foot-3 frame during the offseason. He doesn't have the ceiling he once did, but the ingredients are all still there for Ortiz to become a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Waites' mid-90s fastball helped him rank in the NCAA Division II top five in strikeout rate in 2018 and 2019 at West Alabama, prompting San Francisco to draft him in the 18th round. He pitched just 30 2/3 innings in his first three years as a pro because of the pandemic and meniscus surgery on his knee in 2021, then rocketed from Single-A to the big leagues last year. He had the second-highest strikeout rate among Minor League relievers (minimum 40 innings) at 16.4 per nine frames and claimed Mookie Betts as his first K victim in the Majors. The Giants have helped Waites find more velocity by improving his mechanics, and his fastball now operates at 95-98 mph and tops out at 100 with plenty of carry while boring in on right-handers. His slider can be a plus offering in the mid-80s with two-plane depth when he can land it for strikes, but he doesn't do so consistently. He throws about 75 percent heaters and doesn't have anything remotely resembling an offspeed pitch. While Waites' delivery and control have improved in pro ball, he still works with a lot of effort and battles the strike zone. If he could do a better job of commanding his fastball and controlling his slider, he might be a closer. He still has less pro experience than most pitchers his age, so he has room for more growth.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vientos was only 17 when the Mets selected him in the second round of the 2017 Draft, and after a few years of buildup (including the lost 2020 season), he broke out in a big way with 25 homers, a .581 slugging percentage and .933 OPS in 83 games between Double-A and Triple-A in 2021. He continued to show plus pop in Syracuse last season with 24 blasts in 101 games and debuted for the Mets in September, when they were in dire need of righty designated hitter options. He went just 6-for-36 (.167) during that span and didn’t crack the club’s Wild Card roster. The slugger is capable of exhibiting at least plus raw power with exit velocities going above 110 mph, and his 45.8 percent hard-hit rate was about equal to Pete Alonso’s in the Majors, albeit over a much smaller sample. That said, Vientos started putting the ball on the ground more than ever in 2022 -- 48.4 percent of the time, 14th-highest among 107 Triple-A qualifiers -- and his power comes more from natural strength than bat speed, calling into question how he’ll handle big league arms. Like Brett Baty, the Mets have tried moving Vientos around from third base to left field, hoping his plus arm could give some defensive value at either spot. He’s still a below-average runner, however, and lacks the agility to stick at the hot corner or quickness to properly track down balls from the grass. He got more looks at first than ever in 2022 but still might be best-served as a DH for the Mets as long as Alonso is around.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets took a 17-year-old, bat-first shortstop in Vientos in the second round of the 2017 Draft. After signing him for $1.5 million, the organization put him on the slow road with stops at Rookie-level Kingsport in 2018 and Class A Columbia in 2019. He showed classic signs of a power bat waiting to bloom before the 2020 pandemic forced him to continue his progress at the alternate training site and fall instructs. His big breakout came at last in 2021, when he hit .281/.352/.581 with 25 homers over 83 games at Double-A and Triple-A, and he was added to the 40-man roster as a result. It’s scary to think what kind of heights Vientos’ home run total could have reached in 2021, had he seen a fuller season that wasn’t so impacted by coronavirus delays and cancelations. He’s slugging above .500 again in 2022, making the most of his significant strength at Triple-A, but he’s also striking out more than 30 percent of the time again while also posting a groundball rate close to 50 percent, a regression from previous trends. The raw power will always make Vientos a middle-of-the-order threat, but his overall hit tool could limit that impact. Vientos’ plus arm works at third base, but his glove and actions aren’t nearly at the same level. The Mets worked him out in left field in 2021, and as of now, early reports aren’t encouraging that it’s a solid fit. He has gotten more looks at first base this season, and that’s his likeliest defensive home if and when he isn’t DHing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 American Heritage (Fla.) High has produced a number of professional prospects, headlined by first baseman Eric Hosmer. Vientos, who slid a bit after an up-and-down senior season but got an above-pick value of $1.5 million from the Mets to sign, has the chance to eventually join Hosmer as a big league slugging alumni of the school. He flashed his high offensive ceiling in 2018 at Rookie-level Kingsport, where he overcame a slow start to finish among the Appalachian League leaders with 11 home runs (fourth) and 52 RBIs (third). One of the youngest players in the 2017 Draft class, Vientos has only scraped the surface of his offensive potential. With bat speed and strength, Vientos produces exit velocities that are among the best in the system, up there with the likes of slugger Peter Alonso. That innate ability to impact the baseball gives him a chance to hit for average and power, and the latter is already showing during games. Vientos' timing can get out of whack at times, resulting in some swings and misses, but his approach is advanced for his age, and he's demonstrated a willingness to work deep into counts and take walks. After playing both spots on the left side of the infield during his debut, Vientos manned the hot corner exclusively at Kingsport in 2018. He has below-average speed and lacks range, but he's athletic and has the requisite hands and plus arm strength needed for the position. There's little doubt that he has the bat to profile there, too, and the final product could be that of a bat-first regular who hits in the middle of a lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jung went eighth overall in the 2019 Draft to the Rangers after starring at Texas Tech, and his younger brother Jace went 12th last July to the Tigers after doing the same. Josh played just 153 Minor League games in his first four years as a pro because of the pandemic, a stress fracture in his left foot and a labrum tear in his left shoulder, delaying his anticipated arrival in Texas until last September. He homered off Ross Stripling in his first big league at-bat and went deep five times in 26 games. One of the most advanced hitters in his Draft class, Jung has the sound right-handed swing, bat-to-ball skills and pitch recognition to produce high batting averages. After hitting .322 in his first two pro seasons, he was noticeably more aggressive in 2022 and batted .239 with a 74/11 K/BB ratio between Triple-A and the Majors. He did hit balls harder and drove them in the air more frequently than in the past, displaying plus power, and still has the upside of a .300 hitter with 25 or more homers per season. Though he's known mostly for his ability at the plate, Jung has worked to improve the other aspects of his game. He's a below-average runner out of the batter's box but has developed the athleticism, instincts, hands and strong arm to become a solid defender at third base. The Rangers also have played at him second base, shortstop and in the outfield during instructional league in the past, but the hot corner definitely is his home.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Jung family produces talented hitters -- Josh went eighth overall in the 2019 Draft after consecutive consensus All-America seasons at Texas Tech, and his younger brother Jace went 12th to the Tigers in July after also starring for the Red Raiders. Signed for $4.4 million, Josh might have made his big league debut in 2021 if he hadn't missed time because of a stress fracture in his left foot and coronavirus protocols. His development is on hold again this year after he tore the labrum in his left shoulder while lifting weights in February, necessitating surgery that kept him out of game action until late July. Jung was one of the most advanced hitters in his Draft class and his bat-on-ball skills, ability to recognize pitches and strike-zone management all have been as good as advertised. He has a sound right-handed stroke and after struggling to lift and pull pitches in his 2019 pro debut, he has adapted and is doing a much better job of translating his bat speed and strength into power. He's driving balls in the air more often and hitting them harder than in the past, and he could become a .300 hitter who produces 25 homers per season. Jung also has worked diligently to improve at third base. While he's a below-average runner, he has the athleticism, instincts, hands and strong arm to provide at least average defense at the hot corner. The Rangers have also tried him at second base, shortstop and in the outfield during instructional league to enhance his versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best position player in Texas Tech history, Jung went eighth overall in the 2019 Draft after consecutive consensus All-America seasons and leading the Red Raiders to their best finish ever, third place at the College World Series. He spent most of his pro debut in low Class A after signing for $4.4 million and could join the Rangers as early as this year despite being limited to alternative camp and instructional league in 2020. He figures to open the season in Double-A and could advance rapidly if he can build on the offensive improvements he made last year. One of the most advanced hitters in his Draft class, Jung recognizes pitches and manages the strike zone well while barreling all types of pitching on a regular basis. He has a sound right-handed stroke and the bat speed and strength to hit at least 20 homers per season. After he had trouble pulling the ball for power in his first taste of pro ball, he made adjustments in 2020 to enable him to drive more balls in the air to left field. Though Jung has below-average speed, he has the athleticism, instincts, hands and strong arm to play at least an average third base. He spent the second half of the 2019 college season at shortstop and saw time there again in alt camp and instructs, where he also got reps at second base and in the outfield. Texas believes in Jung at the hot corner enough to move Gold Glover Isiah Kiner-Falefa to shortstop for 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pineda is coming up on the eighth anniversary of his $450,000 signing out of Venezuela, and it’s been a roller coaster of a development process since then. The peak came in 2022 when he set a career high with 16 homers in 99 games across three levels and made his Major League debut that September. He entered another valley in 2023, however, in part after being severely limited by a fractured right pinkie and strained left oblique. Pineda slashed just .153/.215/.214 with one homer in 28 games for Double-A Harrisburg, was designated for assignment in January and cleared waivers shortly after. It's hard to tell how much of the backstop’s on-field performance was affected by the injuries and how much he was pressing to make up for lost time. In terms of approach, he chased pitches out of the zone 39 percent of the time at Double-A and was especially vulnerable against breaking balls. That led to a Minors-high 31.8 percent strikeout rate and kept him from tapping into his above-average raw power. Even with his well-below-average speed, the .219 BABIP that dragged down the overall line was still quite low in the small sample. Pineda’s framing was improving leading up to 2023 but was stilted by the injuries. His arm remains easily his best asset with a 40.6 percent caught-stealing rate in the Minors and a 33 percent mark during a 13-game spin in the Arizona Fall League. There’s still the potential for Pineda to be a backup catcher, but he needs to prove he can return to 2022 form when healthy to regain his 40-man spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pineda is a prime example of why you shouldn’t give up on prospects just because they weren’t added to the 40-man when Rule 5-eligible. Signed for $450,000 out of Venezuela in July 2016, he wasn’t protected after the 2020 or 2021 seasons despite showing skills that could make him a future big league backstop. After returning to High-A Wilmington for 2022, Pineda ended up playing at three Minor League levels, finishing with a .258/.325/.458 line and a career-high 16 homers over 99 games, and he finally got the call for four Major League games in September. Pineda has been severely limited in 2023 due to a fractured right pinkie and a left oblique strain. A hit-over-power player earlier in his career (perhaps because of hand injuries), Pineda has flipped the switch the past two seasons and now shows enough raw pop to project for around 15 homers over a full Major League season (his average over his last two MiLB campaigns). He can get overly aggressive while trying to take advantage of that power, leading to strikeouts that blunt his overall offensive ceiling. Ever since signing, the 5-foot-11 catcher has been adept at limiting the running game with caught-stealing rates of at least 38 percent in his five Minor League seasons on account of his plus arm strength. His framing has improved over his time in full-season ball, and that helps his case to back up Keibert Ruiz in the nation’s capital. A bench role -- as a right-handed power bat and No. 2 catcher -- is likely his ceiling, but one he’s close to reaching once he stays healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $450,000 out of Venezuela in July 2016, Pineda burst onto the scene as a New York-Penn League All-Star two years later when he hit .273/.341/.388 in 46 games for Class A Short Season Auburn. His offensive results hit a wall in full-season ball in 2019, and after trips to the alt site and instructs, he wasn’t protected from the Rule 5 Draft in November 2020. He met the same fate this offseason after hitting just .208/.280/.389 in 77 games for High-A Wilmington and a nine-game Arizona Fall League stint. He did set a career high with 14 homers during the regular season and has hit for even more power at High-A and Double-A in 2022. That has been perhaps Pineda’s most interesting development of late. Listed at 5-foot-11, 190 pounds, the backstop went from a hit-first profile in previous seasons to more of a power bat last year. Hand injuries in 2019 could have been behind the delay in slugging numbers, but there’s enough raw power there now for around 15 homers in the Majors. Pineda’s arm has helped him throw out around 40 percent of attempted baserunners at every Minor League stop, and it’s easily his best asset. He still has some room to grow defensively, but the Nats were encouraged by his framing gains last season, noting how much their pitchers liked throwing to him in Wilmington. Pineda will be 22 for the entire 2022 Minor League season, and despite some prospect fatigue, it’s always worth remembering that catchers can face a longer developmental path. Now in the upper Minors for the first time, Pineda’s future as backup catcher is looking clearer than ever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pineda falls in behind Yasel Antuna as another member of the July 2, 2016 signing class to make this year’s list. The backstop was signed for $450,000, but was pushed aggressively soon after, first stateside to the Gulf Coast League in 2017 and eventually to Class A Hagerstown during his age-19 season, two years later. Pineda took a step back offensively in full-season ball, hitting just .217/.278/.305 with seven homers in 101 games. He participated at the alternate training site and instructs, but was left unprotected and unpicked in the Rule 5 Draft. As is true of many catchers, Pineda just needs more time in his development. He was able to scrape some of that back working with advanced pitchers at last year’s alternate site, but he could have used a full season’s worth of at-bats to get over the struggles of 2019, which were partly due to hand injuries. The right-handed slugger focused on staying up the middle with the ball and keeping his bat in the zone as much as possible. Once a hit-over-power batter, that equation flipped in 2021 as he’s shown more pop than overall hitting ability at High-A Wilmington. His arm is his best defensive weapon and as he continues to work with more experienced arms, the Nationals believe he has the aptitude to be at least an average backstop in time. With an early April birthday, Pineda has only been 21 for the entire 2021 season. He has posted rough offensive numbers again this campaign, but some of that may have been bad luck (e.g. a low .211 BABIP entering late August). The power jump has been encouraging as has been a caught-stealing rate around 40 percent. The pieces are still there for Pineda to be a solid backup backstop in time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burleson pitched three seasons at East Carolina but always stood out most for his hitting. That was never more true than in 2019, when he hit .370 with a .972 OPS on his way to becoming a John Olerud National Player of the Year finalist. The Cardinals selected him 70th overall in the shortened 2020 Draft, and a year later, Burleson’s bat helped him push up three levels from High-A to Triple-A. He returned to Memphis in 2022 and performed well enough with the stick to earn a Major League debut down the stretch in September. The left-handed-hitting slugger had a solid case as the most productive hitter in Triple-A last season. He won the International League batting title with a .331 average over 109 games and was one of only two hitters at the level to finish with a .300 average and 20 home runs (exactly that amount in his case). The other was Wynton Bernard, who played in the high elevation of Albuquerque. With a 14.3 percent K rate (ninth-best in Triple-A), Burleson protected the plate by relying on his stellar bat control to spray line drives with two strikes. His typical exit velocities point more toward average pop in the end. A below-average runner, Burleson is stuck in the corners when he plays in the grass, and he even picked up a first baseman’s mitt (last used in college) for six games in the Majors. With Paul Goldschmidt locked in at the cold corner and Jordan Walker nearly claiming an outfield spot himself, the Cardinals might have to rotate Burleson through OF/1B/DH to get him regular plate appearances, but after 2022, it should be a goal to get his bat in a lineup regularly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burleson played four different positions at East Carolina, including pitcher, but it was the bat that did the talking. After hitting .370/.399/.573 with only 24 strikeouts in 64 games as a sophomore in 2019, he was named a John Olerud National Player of the Year Award finalist. The pandemic robbed him of his chance to reproduce those numbers, but the Cardinals saw enough to select him 70th overall in 2020. Burleson opened his first full season at High-A, looked much too talented for the level and earned a promotion to Double-A after only two weeks. He hit .288/.333/.388 with 14 homers in 63 games with Springfield and finished the season at Triple-A Memphis, where he’s been one of the level’s most consistent performers in 2022. Making contact has always been Burleson’s hitting strength. Once seen as a gap hitter, he has shown improved slugging ability in the Minors, and 20 homers seem like a solid target in The Show. (He hit 22 across three levels in 2021 and was already at 20 through mid-August this season.) Burleson crushes righties much better than he does lefties, but he still makes enough contact against southpaws to not be a total splits concern. Burleson flipped between the two corner-outfield spots throughout 2021, and the Cardinals plan for that to continue in his return to Memphis and beyond. He has just enough arm for right, but that’s about the most he can contribute defensively as a below-average runner.
