Burleson’s bat will be what sends him to St. Louis, once he can fight his way past a crowded outfield, and the 23-year-old has enough hit and power tools to be a solid offensive contributor for years to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burleson put together an impressive resume at East Carolina, where he contributed on both sides of the ball, was a finalist for the 2019 John Olerud National Player of the Year Award and earned 2020 First-Team All-American honors from Collegiate Baseball as a utility player. He struck out 22 batters over 23 1/3 innings on the mound for ECU, but the Cardinals viewed him as a better offensive prospect when they grabbed him with the 70th overall pick in the 2020 Draft. Burleson’s bat played right away as he consistently made loud contact and worked his way across three levels, reaching Triple-A, in his professional debut. Burleson makes plenty of contact, and although he was more of a gap-to-gap hitter in college, he slugged 18 homers over his first 74 professional games. The Cardinals had hoped Burleson would tap into his power more as he focused solely on hitting, and early on that’s been the case as he’s consistently produced impressive exit velocities. A basketball player in high school, Burleson has some athleticism but doesn’t possess a ton of speed. The Cardinals plan to give him some work in the outfield -- he played both corner spots in college -- but a future at first base seems likely with his bat ultimately determining his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pitchers taken in the 15th round of a Draft out of a Division II schools do not enter pro ball with much in the way of expectations. Varland, who was selected by the Twins in that round in 2019, a year after brother Gus went in Round 14 to the A’s, never got that memo. He pitched across two levels of A ball in 2021, his first full season, then made it up from Double-A to the big leagues in 2022 to become the first Concordia University product to reach the highest level since 1951. No one in the Twins system has worked harder to improve than Varland has since signing. He routinely posts the most impressive weight room scores in the organization, and that, plus a refined delivery, has translated into harder -- and better -- stuff across the board. He now flashes a plus fastball, one that averaged around 94 mph in 2022 and touched the upper 90s. He continues to work on two distinct breaking balls, though he didn’t throw his curveball much in 2022, with his 83-84 mph slider becoming closer to an out pitch that can routinely miss bats. His 83-84 mph changeup has good action to it Varland needs to keep working on throwing his breaking stuff for strikes consistently and is focusing on delivering his shorter, harder slider with more depth and sweep while keeping it in the zone. His ceiling might be limited to that of a No. 4 or 5 starter, but he’s already exceeded expectations and has made it very clear that underestimating him might be a mistake.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There have been a grand total of four players ever drafted from Division II Concordia University in St. Paul, Minn., and two of them are named Varland. Gus went in round 14 in 2018 and is now with the Dodgers, while younger brother Louie went a year, and one round, later. He was a revelation in his first full season in 2021, showing improved stuff and dominating across two levels of A ball en route to being named the organization’s Minor League pitcher of the year, then has followed that up by pitching his way to Triple-A in 2022. A focus on changing his arm action to reduce joint stress led to increased velocity and movement on his fastball, not to mention nastier secondary stuff. Varland entered pro ball maxing out at 92 mph, but averaged 94 mph in 2021 and touched 98 mph. His changeup is his best secondary offering, thrown with really good action to it, but his slider might be catching up. He throws it in the mid-80s and will continue to work on adding side-to-side movement in order to miss bats with it. He can still fold in a get-me-over slower curve to give hitters a different look. Even with the increased velocity and action, Varland did a very nice job of filling up the strike zone with all of his offerings. He was the fastest riser in the system in 2021 and the Twins are excited about what he’s done for an encore.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wesneski led NCAA Division I freshmen with 10 wins at Sam Houston in 2017 and set a school D-I record with 110 strikeouts in 2019, when the Yankees selected him in the sixth round. Though his on-field development opportunities were limited during the pandemic shutdown in 2020, he managed to improve the velocity on his fastball and the quality of his secondary pitches while training on his own. Acquired in the Scott Effross trade last August, he posted a 2.18 ERA with 33 strikeouts in as many frames with the Cubs and spun an immaculate inning against the Pirates in his second big league start. Wesneski had one of the best sinkers in the 2019 Draft and has since increased the velocity on his heavy two-seam fastball to a consistent 92-94 mph while also developing a four-seamer that reaches 98 mph and misses more bats. He also has upgraded his low-80s slider, which features tremendous horizontal action and moves in the opposite direction of his sinker. He can morph his slider into a harder upper-80s cutter and owns a fading mid-80s changeup, his two main secondary pitches against left-handers. No Cubs pitching prospect has a higher floor than Wesneski, who also comes with the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter. He gets quality extension in his delivery, creating deception without compromising his solid control. He's a tough competitor whose only real need is to refine his changeup, which can get firm and doesn't always find the strike zone on a consistent basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After turning down the Rays as a 33rd-round pick out of high school, Wesneski led all NCAA Division I freshmen with 10 wins at Sam Houston in 2017 and set a school D-I record with 110 strikeouts two years later. A Yankees sixth-round pick in 2019, he had limited on-field development opportunities during the pandemic shutdown the following year but nevertheless improved his fastball velocity and the quality of his secondary pitches while training at home. His stock soared as he advanced from High-A to Triple-A in his full-season debut a year ago, and New York traded him to the Cubs for Scott Effross this August after he continued to perform well. Wesneski featured some of the best sink in the 2019 Draft, and he since has boosted the velocity on his two-seam fastball to where it now sits at 92-94 mph. He's also added a four-seamer that can reach 98. He has upgraded his low-80s slider as well, adding more sweep that gets a lot of swings and misses by playing well off his sinker, which moves in the opposite direction. He can turn his slider into a harder cutter and is making progress with his fading low-80s changeup -- two pitches that could increase his effectiveness against left-handers. Wesneski pounded the strike zone throughout his college career and has continued to do so in pro ball, even as his stuff has made a leap forward. He's deceptive, too, and hitters don't get good swings against him and struggle to lift the ball when they do make contact. His competitive demeanor is another asset and he could help Chicago in the big leagues in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wesneski turned down the Rays as a 33rd-round pick in 2016 and made an immediate impact at Sam Houston the following spring, leading the Southland Conference and all NCAA Division I freshmen with 10 victories as the Bearkats advanced to their first super-regional in program history. He set a school D-I record with 110 strikeouts as a junior in 2019, when the Yankees selected him in the sixth round. While the coronavirus pandemic curtailed his on-field development opportunities last year, he did push his fastball to 98 mph in workouts. Wesneski's fastball stood out in college, but not for its velocity. His heater ranged from 88-95 mph with some of the best sink in the 2019 Draft, which he created by using a low three-quarters arm slot and opening early in his delivery. He missed bats and induced groundouts while still showing the ability to control his fastball despite its well-above-average movement. Adding a mid-90s four-seamer to his lively two-seamer gives him a four-pitch mix that also includes a sweeping low-80s slider that moves in the opposite direction as his sinker and a fading changeup that shows flashes of becoming a solid offering. He has no problem throwing strikes and could be a No. 4 starter if he can refine his secondary offerings and upgrade his command. He also could move quickly as a fastball-heavy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Overlooked as a suburban Detroit high schooler, Brown didn't become a starter at nearby Wayne State until his junior season in 2019, when he matched Anthony Bass as the NCAA Division II program's highest draft pick ever (fifth round). He was the most dominant pitcher in the Triple-A Pacific Coast League last season and easily would have led the circuit in ERA (2.55), opponent average (.186) and strikeout rate (11.4 per nine innings) if he hadn't fallen short of qualifying because the Astros called him up in September. He posted a 0.89 ERA in 20 1/3 regular-season innings with Houston, then contributed three scoreless outings in the postseason as the franchise won its second World Series championship. Brown maintains premium velocity deep into games and throughout a long season, operating at 95-97 mph and peaking at 100 with plenty of carry and run on his four-seam fastball. The Astros helped him add a power curveball during the pandemic layoff in 2020, and his bender is now a devastating low-80s pitch that falls off the table coming out of his high three-quarters arm slot. His curve is more of a chase pitch and he does a better job of landing his low-90s slider/cutter for strikes, giving him a third offering that grades as plus or better. Brown doesn't have much trust in his upper-80s changeup, which has a bit of fade, and he barely used it in his relief role with the Astros. He has improved his strike-throwing throughout his pro career but may never have more than average control or command, though the quality of his stuff lessens the need for precision location. Houston's depth may prevent him from cracking the Opening Day rotation, but he's primed to become one of the club's top starters in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown's only college offer as a suburban Detroit high schooler came from nearby Wayne State and he didn't become a full-time starter at the NCAA Division II school until his junior season. He dominated that spring and went in the fifth round of the 2019 Draft, matching Anthony Bass as the Warriors' highest pick ever. After making huge strides with his curveball during the pandemic shutdown, he made his full-season debut in Double-A last May and earned a promotion to Triple-A three months later. Brown showed that he could maintain premium velocity in college and continued to do so over a long pro season in 2021, when he still sat in the mid-90s and hit 99 mph with some riding action on his four-seam fastball in September. But his most devastating weapon is a power curveball that sits in the low 80s and seems to drop off the table coming out of his high three-quarters arm slot. He also has a mid-80s slider with more horizontal action and a fading changeup with similar velocity that's most effective when he leverages it down in the zone. While there's no question about Brown's pure stuff, he's still working on his feel for pitching. He doesn't fully trust his changeup or repeat his delivery consistently, though his control did improve during his two months in Triple-A. The Astros love his work ethic, citing the gains he made while pitching off a homemade mound in his backyard during the 2020 layoff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown's only college offer out of a suburban Detroit high school came from nearby Wayne State, and he didn't become a full-time starter at the NCAA Division II level until his junior season in 2019. He didn't permit a run in six of 14 starts while fanning 114 in 85 1/3 innings en route to matching Anthony Bass as the Warriors' highest pick ever (fifth round). Though his development was limited to instructional league last year, he made huge strides with a curveball that has become his best secondary pitch. Brown's fastball topped out at 91 mph when he was a freshman, but he consistently added velocity throughout his college career and now shows the ability to maintain a 96-98 mph heater for three innings and work at 92-96 deep into games. His four-seamer can get straight but arrives on a steep downhill plane from his high three-quarters slot, and he also uses a sinking two-seamer in the low 90s. While his No. 2 pitch in college was a sharp mid-80s slider that shows flashes of becoming a plus offering, it has been passed by a power curveball with depth that plays better off his four-seamer. In order to remain a starter at higher levels, Brown will have to add some polish. He needs to refine a changeup that gets too firm and repeat his delivery more consistently so he can locate his pitches better. If he winds up in the bullpen, his fastball/curveball combination could make him a high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Both a shortstop and reliever in Oregon, Nelson showed the D-backs enough signs that he could be a future professional starter and became a second-round pick in 2019. He finally got his first taste of full-season action in 2021 and dominated with a 3.17 ERA and 163 strikeouts (fourth-most in the Minors) in 116 1/3 innings between High-A and Double-A. He traversed the rough roads of Triple-A Reno with the numbers to match (5.43 ERA, 25 homers allowed in 26 starts) in 2022, but ended the season with three Major League starts, allowing just three earned runs in 18 1/3 frames (1.47 ERA). Nelson’s velocity was ticking down at the beginning of last season, with his fastball sitting around 92 mph in April. As he made adjustments, the 6-foot-3 right-hander got back to his usual self with a heater averaging 94.8 mph in the Majors, touching 98.1 in his MLB debut on Sept. 5. He relied heavily on the four-seamer, throwing it 70 percent of the time in the bigs, and his establishment of numero uno – and its ability to work up in the zone -- laid the foundation for his early success. He mixes in a 75-78 mph curveball with good vertical break that works against batters from both sides, while his low-80s slider shows cutting action for righties. An average low-80s changeup gives Nelson a full arsenal. The former Duck throws out of the stretch exclusively, which helps him stay in line with where he wants the ball to go, and that control should keep his relieving days in the rearview. The wavering velocity and his age (25) bring some pause on his prospect status, but he’ll at least enter 2023 practically ready for another crack at the Arizona rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nelson showed his athleticism at Oregon, where he spent two years as an infielder and reliever. Initially given the chance to start as a junior, Nelson moved back to the bullpen largely to help the Ducks' pitching staff. His premium power stuff was as good as ever, and he finished fourth in NCAA Division I with an average of 14.4 strikeouts per nine innings. Intrigued by Nelson’s athleticism and powerful low-mileage right arm, the D-backs took him in the second round of the 2019 Draft and signed him for $1.1 million, slightly below slot value. After an impressive pro debut in 2019, Nelson dominated in 2021. He posted 163 strikeouts over 116 1/3 innings and was named the D-backs Minor League Pitcher of the Year after working his way up to Double-A. Nelson has an explosive fastball that jumps on hitters. He could once touch triple-digits, but the velocity has backed up a little in 2022 to the point where he’s averaging around 93 mph with the pitch at Triple-A Reno. The heater still pairs well with a knee-buckling curveball. Some inside the D-backs organization feel the slider, which took a step forward in 2021, will be his best pitch when more consistency is established. Nelson rounds out his repertoire with an average-to-above-average changeup. The pitch is his fourth best offering, but it’s a usable pitch that has improved over the years as he’s tinkered with the grip and gained confidence in throwing it. Naturally tough to hit, Nelson’s command has continually progressed since signing, giving the organization confidence he’ll be able to stick as a starter long term. Improved mechanics have also helped him establish more consistency, which, combined with the improvements he’s made to his secondary stuff heightens the chances he’ll ultimately be able to reach his ceiling. If he’s unable to stick as a starter, Nelson can be an effective reliever with his enticing mix of swing-and-miss stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nelson showed his athleticism at Oregon where he spent two years as an infielder and reliever. Initially given the chance to start as a junior, Nelson moved back to the bullpen largely to help the Ducks' pitching staff. His premium power stuff was as good as ever, and he finished fourth in NCAA Division I with an average of 14.4 strikeouts-per-nine. Intrigued by Nelson’s athleticism and powerful, low-mileage right arm, the Diamondbacks took him in the second round and signed him for $1.1 million, slightly below slot value. Nelson has an explosive fastball that jumps on hitters. He’ll sit in the upper 90s and bump triple digits with a fastball and pairs it with a knee-buckling curveball. The curveball plays nicely off his high-carry fastball, giving him a nasty two plus pitch combination in shorter stints. He also throws a slider and a splitter, with most scouts preferring the former to the latter. Nelson can miss a ton of bats and is naturally tough to hit. Nelson has cleaned up his mechanics, which has improved his command and allowed him to be more consistent. That combined with continuing to improve his secondary stuff has the D-backs optimistic that he can be a starter long term. Otherwise he can be an effective reliever with his fastball/curveball combination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 After missing the 2017 season at Wright State following Tommy John surgery, Burdick bounced back to win the Horizon League tournament MVP honors in 2018 and player of the year accolades in 2019, when he batted .407/.538/.729 with 15 homers and 24 steals. The Marlins loved his performance, metrics and makeup so they took him in the third round -- and he has exceeded expectations ever since. He posted a .949 OPS with 64 RBIs in 69 games while leading Low-A Clinton to the Midwest League Finals in 2019, then topped the Double-A South in homers (23), runs (71) and walks (76). Burdick combines bat speed, strength and patience to produce plus power to all fields while drawing plenty of walks. He takes an aggressive hack from the right side of the plate, which results in extremely loud contact when he connects but also led to a 30 percent whiff rate last year because his swing can be long and his approach can get pull-heavy. He settled down some toward the end of his first full pro season before a late promotion to Triple-A. Burdick moves well for his size and gets the most out of his average speed thanks to good instincts on the bases and in the outfield. He spent the majority of his time in center field last year because he's fearless and has a nose for the ball, but he most likely will land in right, where he profiles well with his power and solid defense and arm strength. He swiftly became an organization favorite, and club officials laud his competitiveness and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burdick missed the entire 2017 season at Wright State following Tommy John surgery, then returned to win the Horizon League's tournament MVP award in 2018 and player of the year award in 2019, when he batted .407/.538/.729 with 15 homers and 24 steals. Though \"stocky 22-year-old corner outfielder\" isn't a coveted Draft demographic, the Marlins loved his performance, metrics and makeup to take him in the third round and sign him for a below-slot $397,500. He responded by hitting .308/.407/.542 with 11 homers and 64 RBIs in his 69-game pro debut while leading low Class A Clinton to the Midwest League finals, then continued to rake in instructional league last fall. Burdick generates well above-average raw power via bat speed and strength and he has the hitting ability to translate it into home runs to all fields in game action. While he takes aggressive cuts from the right side of the plate, he makes plenty of hard contact and will take walks if pitchers refuse to challenge him. He moves well for his size and makes the most of his average speed with good instincts and aggressiveness on the bases. Capable of providing at least average defense on either outfield corner, Burdick spent most of his first pro summer in left field. He has solid arm strength and notched 10 assists in 65 outfield games during his debut. With his combination of tools, performance and work ethic, he comes up frequently when other clubs inquire about trades with the Marlins.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a storied amateur career that included 18-and-under World Cup MVP honors and the World Baseball Softball Confederation player of the year award for 2017, Casas reclassified into the 2018 Draft as a Florida high schooler and went 26th overall. One of the game's top power prospects since signing for $2,552,800, he tied for the tournament lead with three homers at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. He recovered from a high ankle sprain last summer to make his big league debut at age 22 in September, homering five times in 27 games -- including a 411-foot, opposite-field blast off Gerrit Cole. A left-handed hitter, Casas creates huge raw pop to all fields with a combination of bat speed, strength and leverage in his massive 6-foot-4 frame. He's somewhat reminiscent of Aaron Judge in that he never topped 20 homers in a Minor League season because he focused on making hard contact to all fields and letting his power come naturally. He patiently works deep counts and draws walks if he doesn't get pitches to attack, and he could become a 40-homer threat if he launches balls in the air more aggressively. Casas is a solid defender with soft hands at first base, and his arm is stronger than most at the position after producing low-90s fastballs when he pitched as an amateur. He also stands out with his cerebral approach and competitive fire. The only shortcoming in his game is his well below-average speed, which is understandable considering his size.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since reclassifying into the 2018 Draft as a Florida high schooler and signing for $2,552,800 as the 26th overall pick, Casas has been one of the best young power prospects in the Minors. After a storied amateur career with Team USA that included 18U World Cup MVP honors and the World Baseball Softball Confederation Player of the Year award in 2017, he won a silver medal at the Tokyo Olympics last August, when he tied for the tournament lead with three homers in six games. He also reached Triple-A at age 21 and topped the Arizona Fall League with a .495 on-base percentage, paving the way for a likely big league debut in 2022. While Casas' combination of bat speed, strength and leverage in his massive 6-foot-4 frame give him plus-plus raw power to all parts of the park, he resists the temptation to sell out for power. He controls the strike zone extremely well, focuses on making hard contact to all fields with a sound if naturally long left-handed swing and shows the aptitude to make adjustments at the plate. He made progress last season with his ability to work counts and launch balls in the air to his pull side, and he could become a 35-40 homer threat if he continues to do so. Just as he's more than a one-dimensional hitter, Casas also offers value beyond the batter's box. While he's limited to first base, he's a solid defender with soft hands and a strong arm that produced low-90s fastballs when he pitched as an amateur. The only real knock on his game is his lack of speed, though he moves well for his size, and he also earns praise for his makeup and competitive nature.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a storied international career that included winning 18U World Cup MVP honors and the World Baseball Softball Confederation Player of the Year award in 2017, Casas reclassified from the 2019 Draft to '18 and went 26th overall. He tore a ligament in his right thumb two games into his pro debut after signing for $2,552,800, but he rebounded to rank second in extra-base hits (49), third in homers (19) and fourth in slugging (.472) in the Class A South Atlantic League at age 19 in '19. Despite being one of the youngest players at Boston's alternate training site last summer, he impressed with his power and his approach there and during instructional league. Casas has as much raw power as anyone from the 2018 Draft, launching balls to all fields with his combination of bat speed, strength and leverage in his still-growing 6-foot-5 frame. He's more than just a masher, however, as he's an advanced hitter for his age who controls the strike zone and uses the entire field rather than trying to yank everything out of the park. His size adds some length to his left-handed swing, but he provides plenty of hard contact and displays the ability to make adjustments. Casas moves well for his size, but he is huge and will slow down as he fills out, so he'll be limited to first base. He still can be an asset defensively, however, because he has soft hands, presents a huge target and has a strong arm that produced low-90s fastballs when he pitched as an amateur. He draws praise for his makeup as well and earned respect at the alternate training site when he was drilled by a Tanner Houck pitch, declined to take first base and then crushed a home run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montes de Oca was one of the biggest enigmas of the 2018 Draft as a hard-throwing right-hander, and even as he enters his age-27 season, he remains a fascinating question mark. The former Mizzou righty, who previously turned down two opportunities in the Draft, went in the ninth round to the Mets that year and has since undergone surgery to address shoulder, back and knee issues. He didn’t officially play in the Mets system until 2021 but climbed through Double-A and Triple-A to debut with New York last year, making three bullpen appearances. On a pure stuff level, Montes de Oca is very exciting. His sinker sits (!) 98-100 mph and maxed out in the Majors at 102.4 mph. Put another way, 44 of the 50 hardest-thrown pitches by Mets pitchers came from either Edwin Díaz or Jacob DeGrom in 2022. The other six were by Montes de Oca, even though he only pitched 3 1/3 innings in the bigs. He also offers a mid-90s cutter that comes in hard and breaks late -- and he actually throws the cutter more than the sinker -- and an upper-80s slider with a long tail. Those three pitches could make Montes de Oca a dominant bullpen arm, and he was just that in some ways with a 34.6 percent K rate last year. He also walked 16.5 percent of batters faced as upper-level hitters dared him to pitch in the zone. It’s a difficult proposition with Montes de Oca’s delivery containing a lot of moving parts that can be tough to keep in sync. A stress reaction in his right elbow this spring required surgery, and during that procedure, it was also determined he needed Tommy John. Even as injuries continue to pile up, his quality of stuff leaves him with an intriguing ceiling when he is able to come out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Peraza showed the potential for solid or better tools across the board, the Yankees were able to sign him for just $175,000 out of Venezuela in 2016. The pandemic layoff delayed his development but he has broken out since returning, totaling 38 homers and 73 steals in the last two seasons. He slashed .306/.404/.429 during his first callup last September, claimed a spot on the American League Championship Series roster and is the favorite to claim New York's starting shortstop job in 2023. Peraza has more bat speed and strength than most shortstops, and he began translating it into average game power when he added loft to his right-handed stroke in 2021. Most of his home run pop is to his pull side and he has become more aggressive about looking to turn on pitches. He displayed a more patient, contact-oriented approach in his first month in the big leagues and likely will turn his swing loose more often as he gets more acclimated. With superior speed, range and arm strength to more famous Yankees shortstop prospect Anthony Volpe, Peraza likely will push Volpe to second base when the latter arrives in the Majors. Peraza has smooth actions and advanced instincts at short and could play all over the diamond if needed. His aggressiveness and savvy are also evident on the bases, and he has succeeded on 82 percent of his steal attempts as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though New York was in the international spending penalty box in 2016 and limited to bonuses of no more than $300,000, it still landed a strong crop that included Peraza ($175,000 out of Venezuela), right-hander Yoendrys Gomez and trade pieces Jose Devers (sent to the Marlins in the Giancarlo Stanton deal) and Roansy Contreras (shipped to the Pirates in a package for Jameson Taillon). Club officials have touted Peraza's ceiling for years and he broke out in 2021, reaching Triple-A at age 21 while batting .297/.356/.477 with 18 homers and a system-best 38 steals in 115 games. He has louder physical tools than fellow Yankees shortstop prospect Anthony Volpe, should arrive in the big leagues first and could push him to second base. Pound for pound, Peraza hits the ball as hard as anyone in the Yankees system and he began to launch balls in the air much more consistently last year after adding some loft to his right-handed swing. He has a penchant for squaring balls up and could produce 20-25 homers per season. After controlling the strike zone well in the past, he got more aggressive in 2021 but should still hit for average if he can reclaim some of his patience. Peraza has the upside of a shortstop with four plus tools and solid power. He's a smooth defender at shortstop, where he has soft hands, a strong arm and keen instincts. He looks to make things happen on the bases with plus speed and savvy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite facing international spending restrictions in 2016, the Yankees still assembled a solid class highlighted by Peraza ($175,000 out of Venezuela), shortstop Jose Devers (shipped to the Marlins in the Giancarlo Stanton trade) and right-handers Yoendrys Gomez and Roansy Contreras (sent to the Pirates in the Jameson Taillon deal). New York has pushed Peraza with aggressive assignments and he proved up to the challenge as a 19-year-old in low Class A in 2019. His only on-field development last year came in a half-dozen games in the Venezuelan League during the winter. Added to the 40-man roster in November, Peraza has the best all-around tools among Yankees infield prospects. He has quality bat-to-ball skills and controls the strike zone well, allowing him to make consistent line-drive contract from the right side of the plate. He needs to get stronger but already generates some of the highest exit velocities in the system and could develop 15-20 homer power once he learns to drive the ball in the air more frequently. Peraza could have four plus tools once he's fully developed. He has smooth actions at shortstop, the arm to make any throw necessary and a good internal clock that helps him slow the game down defensively. He makes good use of his plus speed and stole 44 bases in 54 attempts in 159 games over his first three pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz has hit ever since signing with the Guardians for $25,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2016, batting .294 in his pro debut and never less than .302 in four seasons in the United States. Cleveland traded him to Houston along with Phil Maton in exchange for Myles Straw in July 2021, after which the Astros didn't protect him on its 40-man roster that offseason. He showed increased power and improved defense last year, made his big league debut in September and could wind up in an offense/defense timeshare with Martin Maldonado in Houston in 2023. A career .321 hitter with a 14 percent strikeout rate through five seasons in the Minors, Diaz has a fluid right-handed swing and outstanding bat-to-ball skills that produce constant contact to all fields. His exit velocities jumped about 5 mph as he demonstrated plus raw power during his first full season in the Astros organization. The only concern with his offensive game is that he swings at a lot of pitches that he shouldn't, both in and out of the strike zone, resulting in excessive ground-ball contact and very few walks. Diaz never has started more than 51 games behind the plate in a season and scouts are somewhat divided as to whether he can become an average defender. His receiving, blocking and preparation are all getting better but still need more work, though his plus arm is an asset in terms of controlling the running game. His well-below-average speed leaves first base as his only realistic alternative and he spent almost as much time there as he did at catcher last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with Cleveland for $25,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2016, Diaz finished second in the Rookie-level Arizona League batting race (.355) during his U.S. debut two years later. He continued to hit for average afterward and was batting .314 in Low-A last July when he went to Houston along with Phil Maton in exchange for Myles Straw. Though the Astros declined to reserve him on their 40-man roster in December, they definitely will this time around after he showed more power than ever and made some defensive progress in 2022. Diaz's natural hitting ability and fluid right-handed swing allow him to make consistent contact, producing a .328 batting average and 13 percent strikeout rate through his first four pro seasons. He hits the ball hard and his exit velocities have jumped about 5 mph this summer, and though he still hits too many grounders, he's doing a better job of tapping into his plus raw pop. Though he doesn't swing and miss, he could use a more selective approach because he rarely walks and makes some sub-optimal contact. Diaz features plus arm strength to keep the running game in check. He caught just 148 games through his age-22 season, so his inexperience sometimes shows with his receiving and blocking, but he's on course to become an average defender behind the plate. He moves like a typical catcher, leaving first base as his only alternative.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at the University of Oregon, Steer had a huge junior season in 2019, finishing with a .958 OPS and walking nearly as often as he struck out, helping him land with the Twins as a third-round pick that June. He changed his hit-over-power profile thanks to work during the 2020 shutdown to drive the ball more and that led to 47 homers over the next two seasons. A 2022 Futures Game participant, Steer had made it from Double- to Triple-A when he was sent to the Reds as part of the return for Tyler Mahle, then made his big league debut with Cincinnati last September. Steer is still very much a hitter who focuses on contact, one who has not sacrificed his feel for the barrel to get to his newfound power. The right-handed hitter still struck out in less than 20 percent of his plate appearances in 2021-22 combined and he continued his on-base acumen by walking 10.8 percent of the time. Using his lower half consistently, he is capable of driving the ball to all fields, though most of his over-the-fence pop has been to his pull side. Steer brought a reputation as a ‘gamer’ with him to the Reds and he lived up to that billing with his new organization. He’s seen time at all four infield positions, including playing first base for the first time after the trade, and he was even willing to go to the outfield when the Reds asked him to. Third base is likely his best destination if he were to land in one spot, but his ability to move around the diamond could come in handy in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Power was never a significant part of Steer's skillset as a three-year starter for the University of Oregon, where his .349/.456/.502 slash line and control of the strike zone as an everyday shortstop during his junior year earned him a third-round selection in the 2019 Draft. After Steer maintained that profile with four homers and a .385 on-base percentage in '19, the Twins worked with him during the shutdown to drive the ball more effectively, and he responded with 24 homers in his first taste of full-season ball. There was more power in 2022, as well, with Steer hitting his way to a Futures Game appearance before being dealt to the Reds as part of the return for Tyler Mahle. Steer doesn’t have any big tools, but his natural affinity for putting the barrel to the ball helps his skillset play up. The swing tweaks didn't affect his bat path or approach too much but allowed him to use his lower half more effectively to transfer force from the ground into his bat speed. He didn't trade off too much of his excellent discipline, maintaining a .348 on-base percentage with 55 walks in '21, and while the strikeout rate jumped he had cut it back down in 2022 as he hit the upper levels. He’s an average runner, but isn’t really a base-stealing threat. Though Steer's collegiate shortstop experience has helped him play three infield positions with good hands, his throwing needs work and his focus has been more at second and third than at shortstop, with continuing uncertainty as to where he'll fit best. Previously, he likely profiled best as a utility type at the highest level, but with this newfound power, he could push into consideration as a regular with defensive versatility, with third base becoming more realistic if the power stays and his arm improves.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kreidler was the surprise gem of the Tigers farm system in 2021, a 2019 fourth-round pick out of UCLA who blossomed into an everyday shortstop and 22-homer slugger at the upper levels. He entered 2022 seemingly needing just finishing touches at Triple-A Toledo before getting a chance in Detroit, but an inside pitch broke a bone in his right hand, costing him the better part of six weeks. Just when he healed, he strained his groin fielding a ground ball, costing him another month. He made it back in August and reached Detroit in September, but the combined injuries cost him development opportunities and hitting reps, which showed in his brief Major League stint. Kreidler is a pupil of noted hitting instructor Doug Latta, who works with young hitters on simplifying their swing with a focus on hard contact. He generates good bat speed to produce surprising pull power. He has been a streaky hitter in his career, but some evaluators believe he could benefit more if he found a way to keep his bat in the zone a bit longer. Defensively, Kreidler handles shortstop very well for his size, showing solid instincts, a strong arm and the agility to meet low grounders without having to reach too far. He looked good at third base in a late-season stint in Detroit and appears comfortable at second, but some wonder if he loses value moving away from shortstop. One evaluator compared Kreidler to former Tiger Jordy Mercer, who played solid shortstop for years with a similar build while showing enough offense to be productive for his position. If not for Javier Báez, Kreidler could well be a long-term answer at short in Detroit. As is, Kreidler will fight for playing time at other spots, including some center-field work, while trying to prove he can hit enough to stick in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Tigers farm system has struggled to find quality position prospects beyond the first round, no hitter had a better breakout than Kreidler, a fourth-round pick in 2019. The former UCLA shortstop used an impressive Spring Training to skip both A-ball levels and open 2021 at Double-A Erie, where his power surpassed anything he had done in college or the pros. He followed top prospects Riley Greene and Spencer Torkelson to Toledo, where he adjusted quickly to Triple-A pitching and posted a .926 OPS down the stretch. Kreidler’s power emerged after he worked with private hitting instructor Doug Latta to simplify his swing and focus on hitting the ball hard. Kreidler keeps his arms close in his stance, then turns quickly on the ball to generate pull power. His strikeout rate rose with his power, but he had tougher at-bats as the season went on, battling his way into walks. While Kreidler’s 6-foot-4 frame makes him big for a shortstop, smart positioning and sure hands allow him to make routine plays consistently. He has enough arm strength to handle third base. Kreidler worked his way into the fringe of the long-term conversation at shortstop before the Tigers signed Javier Báez. With Gage Workman and Cristian Santana among the shortstop prospects at the lower levels and no long-term answers at second base, Kreidler’s future could be as a versatile infielder who gets regular playing time. He’ll have a chance to show his fit back at Triple-A Toledo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have collected big, versatile middle and left-side infielders with defensive skills in their system in recent years. Kreidler, a fourth-round pick in 2019, fits the profile at 6-foot-4. The former UCLA shortstop took a big offensive jump in his junior season with career highs in nearly every offensive category, including a .300 average and .872 OPS. He hit .232 with a .658 OPS at Class A Short Season ball after the Draft, then made some occasional appearances as an extra infielder in Spring Training before the pandemic shut down camps and eventually the Minor League season, costing him a move up to full-season play. Kreidler moves well for his size with good instincts and a very strong arm that affords him an extra step, a defensive skill set that has been consistent over the years while his offense has ebbed and flowed. His right-handed swing shows power capability in stretches but vulnerability to strikeouts in others, which has shown up in his college career and his brief Minor League sample. He can grind his way into walks. Kreidler combines enough speed with good instincts to be a solid, opportunistic baserunner. He used the lost 2020 season to add some strength to his frame. The Tigers rated Kreidler highly enough to add him to their Minor League minicamp in March to give him an introduction to Detroit’s new coaching staff. While the organization has kept him primarily as a shortstop, recent history suggests he could become a versatile infielder at the top level, similar to what Detroit did with Don Kelly years ago. His aggressive start at Double-A Erie and August promotion to Triple-A Toledo speaks well to his chances at reaching that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Initially a fifth-round pick by the Yankees out of Saint Mary’s in 2018, Waldichuk’s prospect profile grew as he started throwing consistently harder as a pro, making a noticeable jump after working out on his own during the 2020 shutdown. His full-season debut in 2021 was the stuff legends are made of, throwing shutout ball over his first 30 2/3 innings and finishing fourth in the Minors in strikeouts. He made another big leap forward in 2022, reaching the upper levels and going to the Futures Game before being sent to the A’s in the Frankie Montas deal near the Trade Deadline. He made four starts in Triple-A before he was called up to finish the season in the big leagues, making seven starts for the A’s. Once the owner of a two-seam sinking fastball in college, Waldichuk now wields a four-seamer with good spin that has excellent shape and carry up in the zone that enables it to play up even beyond its velocity. He throws plenty hard enough, frequently touching 96-97 mph in the big leagues last summer, and gets hitters to swing under the pitch with regularity. He’s added more sweep to his slider as a pro and has an excellent fading changeup. Both are thrown in the low 80s and flash plus, and he also folds in an upper-70s curveball that does blend with his slider at times. There’s deception in the 6-foot-4 lefty’s delivery thanks to his lower three-quarters arm slot, not to mention his angle and extension. He’s struggled with his command at times, but made some nice strides in the strike-throwing department in 2022, helping him look more and more like a mid-rotation big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a dominant sophomore season at Saint Mary's in 2018, Waldichuk scuffled the following spring as he tried to throw harder, allowing the Yankees to draft him in the fifth round. He has found more velocity since turning pro and hit 98 mph while working out on his own during the pandemic shutdown in 2020. That led to a spectacular full-season debut in 2021, when he opened the year by not allowing a run in 30 2/3 innings in High-A. He finished fourth in the Minors in strikeouts (163 in 110 innings) and strikeout percentage (36.0). He was having another big season in 2022, reaching Triple-A and being named to the Futures Game, when he was sent to the A’s as the top prospect in the Frankie Montas deal close to the Trade Deadline. Waldichuk has scrapped the 89-92 mph two-seam fastball he had in college in favor of a four-seamer that sits at 92-95. His heater's shape and carry up in the strike zone are even more impressive than its velocity, and hitters repeatedly swing under it. He also has made progress with his slider, adding sweep to it since signing, as well as his fading changeup, and both low-80s offerings grade as plus at their best. Waldichuk also employs an upper-70s curveball to give him a pitch with more depth, though it gets slurvy and blends with his slider. He does a nice job of using his 6-foot-4 frame and low three-quarters arm slot to enhance his deception, and his angle and extension are especially tough on left-handers. He throws a reasonable number of strikes but is still learning how to command his improved stuff, which could make him a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Saint Mary's has sent Kyle Barraclough, Corbin Burnes and Tony Gonsolin to the big leagues in the last decade and could have a fourth pitcher on the way in Waldichuk. After dominating as a sophomore in 2018, he got caught up seeking more velocity, which led to a so-so junior season that allowed the Yankees to get him in 2019's fifth round. He posted a 49/7 K/BB ratio in 29 1/3 Rookie-ball innings in his pro debut that summer and hit 98 mph in bullpen workouts on his own last year during the pandemic shutdown. After operating with an 89-92 mph two-seam fastball during his college career, Waldichuk has adopted a four-seamer and repeatedly has hit 95-96 as a pro. His heater plays as at least a plus pitch because it features quality shape and life, and hitters just don't seem to be able to see it well. Scouts debate which of his breaking balls is better, but both his upper-70s curveball and low-80s slider show the potential to become solid offerings. Waldichuk also displays some feel for a changeup with fade, though it still needs more work. He uses his 6-foot-4 frame and low three-quarters arm slot to create angle and extension that makes it difficult to pick up his pitches, especially for left-handers. He has a history of throwing strikes but will need to refine his command to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a while since the state of Alabama has produced a high school player who was drafted, signed and had a big impact in the Major Leagues, with the 2005 tandem of Colby Rasmus and Desmond Jennings the most recent. Henderson is ready to jump to the front of the list. The Orioles’ second-rounder in 2019, Henderson had a strong year in 2021, his first full season due to the pandemic and then really took off in 2022, dominating Double- and Triple-A, going to the Futures Game and holding his own over the last month-plus of the season as a 21-year old in the big leagues. Following his first promotion to Double-A in 2021, Henderson struggled, particularly with his approach at the plate. In an indication of his future ability to make adjustments, the left-handed hitter greatly upped his walk rate and cut his strikeout rate in 2022 compared to the previous year, eliminating much of his chasing out of the zone. That let his impressive bat speed play with even more consistent hard contact and extra-base power, with additional over-the-fence pop certainly coming. A premium athlete who was a basketball star as well in high school, Henderson’s solid speed makes him a threat to steal, and he couples aggressiveness and instincts to take extra bases. That athleticism, along with an easily plus arm, could help him continue to play shortstop despite his size, and Henderson has Gold Glove potential at third, where he played mostly for Baltimore last year. If he’s not on your short list for Rookie of the Year honors, he should be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2019 Draft may always be known in Baltimore as the one where Adley Rutschman became an Oriole, but it would be short-sighted to forget the scouting staff also managed to bring in Henderson to kick off the second round. A tremendous high school athlete who starred in basketball and baseball in Alabama, Henderson signed for an over-slot bonus of $2.3 million and had a solid pro debut that summer. After playing well as one of the youngest players at the O’s alternate site in 2020, Henderson started the 2021 season in Low-A and finished in Double-A, then made it up to Triple-A, and the Futures Game, in 2022. Henderson has always been young for his level and the Orioles have been pleased with how he's responded with the challenges each promotion presented. The left-handed hitter is capable of making loud contact with at least plus power potential. Questions about whether he could cut down on his swing and miss to reach that ceiling have abated as he’s whittled down his strikeout rate and continued to make strides on pitch selection, chasing out of the zone and maintaining his emotions in the box as he's moved up the ladder. With a cannon for an arm and off-the-charts athleticism, there is confidence Henderson could play shortstop long-term despite his size. He’s also shown he can handle playing third base and has gotten enough work in the outfield for the Orioles to believe he could play all three spots if needed. He has superstar potential if he can continue to refine his approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first pick of the second round in the 2019 Draft, Henderson was the Alabama basketball and baseball player of the year before the Orioles signed him for $2.3 million to forgo his commitment to Auburn. Henderson showed well in the Gulf Coast League as an 18-year-old, then turned as many heads as anyone at the O’s alternate training site and instructional camp in 2020. There, he impressively flashed an array of loud tools against exclusively older and more advanced pitching than he would’ve faced during a normal season. A physical left-handed hitter, Henderson produces good bat speed from his projectable 6-foot-3 frame, which has elicited comparisons to Corey Seager. The power upside is big, potentially plus at the highest level. He also has a plus arm, good speed for his size and strong instincts on the bases, to go along with strong makeup and work ethic. The jury is still out on whether Henderson sticks at shortstop or will require a move to third as his body continues to mature. But the Orioles believe there is enough athleticism there to move him around out of choice, not need, after he held his own defensively at third and even center field at times during instructional camp. Henderson’s age and athleticism should give them more than enough time to sort out those particulars; at this moment, he owns the highest ceiling of any O’s position player prospect not named Adley Rutschman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter for three years at UCLA, Toglia’s power showed up in a big way when he slugged 19 homers as a junior in 2019, helping him land in the first round with the Rockies, who had taken a late-round flier on him out of high school three years prior. He reached Double-A and hit a home run at Coors Field in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game in his first full season in 2021, before tapping into his power enough to hit 30 homers in the Minors in 2022 en route to making his big league debut. The signs are pointing towards Toglia being a three true outcomes kind of hitter. He has at least plus raw power from both sides of the plate, and he’s shown he can get to it at all levels and hit the ball out to all fields. While he did that more consistently in 2022, he also struck out at a 30.1 percent clip in the Minors and he’ll need to cut down on his tendency to chase early in counts to have lasting success in the big leagues. He does offset the K’s by drawing a lot of walks (13.1 percent walk rate in his Minor League career). Defensively, Toglia has the chance to be a Gold Glover at first base, moving with ease and excellent range, terrific hands and a very strong arm. He’s played some right field, including during his time up in Colorado and is more than athletic enough to handle a corner outfield spot as needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies liked Toglia when he was a high schooler coming out of the Pacific Northwest, taking him in Round 35 in 2016 before he went on to UCLA. His Bruins career was inconsistent, but his power surge as a junior in 2019 was well-timed, helping him land in the first round and once again with the Rockies. His first full season in 2021 after the shutdown brought mixed results, though he did reach Double-A and hit a home run in his future home ballpark during the Futures Game. Toglia’s offensive profile is all about his power. He’s a threat to leave the yard in every at-bat and can do so from both sides of the plate, hitting 22 homers in 2021. He might always be a higher walk, higher strikeout kind of hitter, as he walked in 13 percent of his plate appearances a year ago and struck out in 28.5 of them. At times he can be too patient and find himself quickly behind in the count, especially when he faced more advanced pitching in Double-A, and the key will be continuing to eliminate swings and misses in the strike zone. Toglia is athletic enough and has solid instincts to be a good corner outfielder, but he has the chance to be a Gold Glove caliber first baseman. He does everything with ease in and around the bag with excellent hands and a strong arm to boot. He could be Colorado's first baseman of the future if he can make enough adjustments to hit the ball out of the park consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid, but raw, high school prospect from Washington State, Toglia went to UCLA rather than entertain signing with the Rockies as a 35th-rounder in 2016. He had an up-and-down college career with the Bruins and didn’t hit well in two summers in the Cape Cod League, but got hot in his junior season in 2019, finishing with 17 homers. This time, the Rockies got their man, drafting and signing Toglia in the first round of the Draft, then watched his pop translate to the Class A short-season Northwest League during his pro debut. A switch-hitter, Toglia’s power from both sides of the plate stands out. The 6-foot-5 first baseman can drive the ball to all fields with tremendous raw pop. The question has always been his ability to make enough contact to tap into that power in games consistently because even though he draws walks, he does swing and miss quite a bit. He did make some small adjustments, particularly to his right-handed swing, at the Rockies’ alternate training site last summer, with positive results in terms of in-game power production. Very athletic, especially for his size, Toglia could play an outfield corner, something he did at times in college and on the Cape, but he’s a very good defender at first with an above-average arm and excellent hands. If he can continue to make adjustments at the plate, he should fit the profile of a power-hitting, run-producing first baseman in the big leagues quite well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: North Carolina gave Little just four innings of work as a freshman in 2016 but he impressed scouts with electric stuff in the Cape Cod League that summer. He transferred to the State JC of Florida, Manatee-Sarasota in order to become eligible for the 2017 Draft as a sophomore, and the Cubs signed him for $2.2 million as the 27th overall choice. Like Alex Lange, Chicago's other 2017 first-rounder, he saw his stuff decline in his first full pro season. At his best, Little has two plus offerings in a low-80s hammer of a curveball and a 91-96 mph fastball with life and downhill plane. He rarely overwhelmed hitters in 2018, often sitting around 90 mph with his heater and having a good-not-great curve, though his stuff has bounced back somewhat this season. He's slowly making progress with his changeup, which the Cubs have emphasized after he had little need for one as an amateur, and he also has added a slider. Because Little had just 89 innings of college experience, Chicago knew he would require time to develop. For now, he's focusing on repeating his delivery and keeping it in sync so he can maintain his best stuff. He throws with effort and has little history of throwing strikes, so he may have average control at best.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs rated Estrada as a second-round talent in the 2017 Draft and were elated to get him with a sixth-round pick and a $1 million bonus. He barely pitched in the next five years, working just 40 innings while dealing with a sore elbow (2018), Tommy John surgery (2019), the pandemic shutdown (2020) and a bout with COVID (2021). Finally healthy last year, he ranked second among Minor League relievers (minimum 40 innings) with a 1.30 ERA and struck out 86 in 54 innings while zooming from High-A to the big leagues. With his physical issues behind him, Estrada worked with a fastball that sat at 95-97 mph, touched 99 and seemed even harder thanks to its vertical movement and the extension in his delivery. His 82-85 mph slider can reach 89 and also has unusual life with both sweep and carry. His fading mid-80s changeup also can miss bats though he doesn't use it very often, and he has a mid-70s curveball that he utilizes as a chase pitch. While he has a four-pitch mix, Estrada works mostly with his fastball and slider and is purely a reliever. After not always being dedicated to his conditioning in the past, he got in better shape in 2022 and did a better job of throwing strikes with his two primary pitches. If he can stay healthy and locate his arsenal with more precision, he might be Chicago's closer of the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered one of the best athletes of the 2019 Draft class, Carroll has consistently performed when he’s been on the field since. The 2020 canceled season and a 2021 labrum tear in his right shoulder kept him out of games, but his true breakout came last year, when he hit .307/.425/.610 with 24 homers and 31 steals between Double-A Amarillo and Triple-A Reno (two hitter havens). Following a late August promotion to the Majors, the outfielder more than held his own in virtually all phases of the game, and he heads into 2023 as a National League Rookie of the Year favorite. Carroll is already in the conversation for the fastest player in the Majors; his 30.7 ft./sec. average Sprint Speed on competitive runs was tops in the bigs (min. 10 opportunities), while his 31 Bolts (runs at 30+ ft./sec.) were second-most on the Arizona roster despite his late start. He puts that speed to good use on the grass, where he can cover acres in any direction, and after making arm strength a focus, he’s above-average in that area and can keep runners honest. The wheels and glove would be enough to make Carroll a special prospect, but what places him among the best in the game is his work in the box. Starting from an upright stance, the left-handed hitter then drops down to look almost springloaded, which helps generate the bat speed necessary to spray the ball all over the park. His slugging performance has improved as he’s added strength in pro ball, and he could be capable of multiple 20-homer seasons if this progress continues. Even if the presence of Alek Thomas or (way down the line) Druw Jones pushes Carroll to a corner, he carries the offensive capability to provide across-the-board impact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts generally agreed Carroll was among the best hitters and better athletes in the 2019 high school class. After an MVP-winning performance at the Perfect Game All-American Classic, the Pacific Northwest prep star solidified his spot in the first round with a strong senior season at Lakeside High in Seattle. The D-backs took Carroll 16th overall that June, then gave him $3,745,500 to forgo his commitment to UCLA. Carroll looked advanced during his pro debut, posting a .299 average with an .896 OPS and 18 steals while reaching Class A Short-Season Hillsboro. He was even more impressive at Arizona’s alternate training site in 2020, standing out against much more advanced competition in the uniquely competitive environment. It then came as no surprise that he got off to a fast start in 2021, slashing .435/.552/.913 through seven games at the High-A level before shoulder surgery abruptly ended his campaign. Carroll has all the qualities scouts look for when projecting a player as a plus hitter. He has an advanced approach and controls the zone well, showing the ability to make adjustments and excellent swing decisions at a young age. Carroll makes consistent hard contact and drives the ball to all fields from the left side of the plate. The strength Carroll has added since signing has already helped him unlock more power. He may always have more of a hit-over-power profile, but there’s enough pop in Carroll’s left-handed bat to project him for double-digit home runs in the big leagues. Carroll’s plus-plus speed is a game-changing tool. He’s a threat to steal and swiped 21 bags (he was caught just twice) over 49 games in his first two seasons. That speed also gives him plenty of range defensively, where he’s an easy plus defender in center field. Carroll’s across-the-board tools and overall maturity could help him reach the Majors faster than the typical prep pick. Developing more power could heighten a presently lofty ceiling, as he already shows the hitting ability, speed and defensive prowess needed to become a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts generally agreed that Carroll was among the best hitters and better athletes in the 2019 high school class. After an MVP-winning performance at the Perfect Game All-American Classic, the Pacific Northwest prep solidified his spot in the first round with a strong senior season at Lakeside High in Seattle. The D-backs took Carroll 16th overall that June, selecting him with the first of their seven picks in the top 75 slots, then gave him $3,745,500 to forgo his commitment to UCLA. Carroll looked advanced during his pro debut, posting a .299 average with an .896 OPS and 18 steals while reaching Class A Short-Season Hillsboro. He was even more impressive at Arizona’s alternate training site in 2020, standing out against much more advanced competition in the uniquely competitive environment. Carroll was off to a fast start in 2021, but season-ending shoulder surgery halted his campaign in May. Carroll has all the qualities scouts look for when projecting a player as a plus hitter. He has an advanced approach and controls the zone well, showing the ability to make adjustments and excellent swing decisions at a young age. Carroll makes consistent hard contact and drives the ball to all fields from the left side of the plate. The strength Carroll has added since signing has already helped him unlock more power, and some D-backs club officials felt that he showed as much raw power as any player at the team’s alternate site. He may always have more of a hit-over-power profile, but there’s enough pop in Carroll’s left-handed bat to project him for double-digit home runs in the big leagues. Carroll’s plus-plus speed is a game-changing tool. He’s a threat to steal whenever he gets on base and has range for days as an easy plus defender in center field. There is no doubt that he will be able to stay at the position long term. Carroll’s across-the-board tools and overall maturity could help him reach the Majors faster than the typical prep pick. Developing more power could thrust Carroll into the conversation as one of baseball’s best prospects, as he already shows the type of hitting ability, speed and defensive prowess needed to become a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly won 27 games in 46 starts over four years at NCAA Division II Concord (W.Va.) and Newberry (S.C.) before hooking on with the Athletics for $500 as a nondrafted free agent in 2017. After getting released by Oakland the next spring and the Angels in 2020, he had elbow surgery and signed with the Red Sox in January 2021. He became a full-time reliever, struck out 141 batters in 95 Minor League innings the next two seasons and made his big league debut last August. Kelly's fastball dodges barrels because it features good carry coming out of a lower release height, and he has boosted it from the low 90s as a starter to 94-95 mph with a peak of 97 as a reliever. It pairs well with his low-80s changeup, a plus offering that drops at the plate with plenty of velocity separation from his heater. He'll also work in a fringy mid-80s slider against right-handers. Though Kelly's control can get inconsistent at times, he can throw strikes with all three of his pitches and had no issues while recording a 3.95 ERA in 13 appearances with Boston. He's not overpowering but generates a lot of swings-and-misses as well as weak contact. Following his humble beginnings in pro ball, he's positioned to become an effective middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 6 Draft prospect heading into the shortened 2020 process, the UCLA star ended up going to the Brewers with the 20th overall pick, in part because of concerns around his Type 1 diabetes. It only took him two years to reach the Majors, having risen from Double-A Biloxi and Triple-A Nashville (while missing some time with an oblique injury) to Milwaukee in 2022. He went 19-for-61 (.311) with two homers and eight steals in 28 games following his Aug. 27 ascent to The Show and enters 2023 as the internal favorite to be the club’s Opening Day center fielder. Mitchell became one of the Majors’ fastest players the second he arrived. His 4.01 home-to-first time (as measured by Statcast) was fastest among 529 qualifiers, and his 30.2 ft./sec. average Sprint Speed on competitive runs was sixth-highest, one spot behind Trea Turner. Those wheels certainly come in handy in center field, where he can track down balls gap to gap. If that wasn’t enough of a defensive weapon, he also has plus arm strength that helps limit the opposing run game. Batting from an open stance, the former Bruin tends to slice the top of balls, and as a result, his 59.5 percent ground-ball rate was ninth-highest among the 1,251 Minor Leaguers with at least 250 plate appearances last season. He has raw power and made solid contact with an average exit velocity of 92.9 mph in his small sample of the Majors, but constant worm burners hurt that slugging output. An increase in launch angle and consequent power production would seal Mitchell’s place as an outfield regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mitchell came into his own as a UCLA sophomore in 2019, hitting .349 with a .984 OPS, and he was off to a strong start before the 2020 season was cut short. The California native was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 6 2020 Draft prospect but fell to the Brewers at No. 20, in part due to concerns about his Type 1 diabetes. He dominated High-A to open his Minor League career in 2021 but hit a wall following a July promotion to Double-A. He finished with a .186/.291/.264 line at the higher level and was limited to only 64 games overall between the two spots by a knee injury and non-COVID illness. What makes Mitchell such a promising prospect is his athleticism. He’s a plus-plus runner who can steal a base (17 in 19 attempts last season) and turn balls hit to the outfield into extra-base hits. He covers lots of ground in center and showcases a plus arm that makes him an overall defensive asset. The bat remains in question, even more so now after the trip to Biloxi. The left-handed slugger can show good raw pop in batting practice, but his in-game swing leads to a lot of ground balls. His 61.7 percent GB rate was highest in the system (min. 200 PA), blunting his overall offensive impact. Worth noting: his 17.2 percent walk rate was also third-best. The Brewers don’t want to get Mitchell too far away from what made him successful in college. That could be delaying an inevitable swing change, but a healthier 2022 would go a long way toward that return to hitting promise. The rest of the tools give Mitchell a promising floor as a fourth outfielder with burning speed and plenty of glove.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Mitchell was a solid high school prospect at Orange (Calif.) Lutheran and firmly in the middle of the Draft Top 100 in 2017, concerns about his ability to consistently tap into those tools and his strong commitment to UCLA led to him not being selected until the 14th round (by the A's). He started to make good on his potential during a strong sophomore season with the Bruins and was expected to play for USA Baseball’s College National Team before a leg injury forced him off the roster. The injury continued to limit Mitchell the next fall, but he still impressed scouts with his batting practice sessions, then showcased his across-the-board tools in earnest early in his junior year. The Brewers were thrilled to land Mitchell, whom MLB Pipeline had ranked as the sixth-best 2020 Draft prospect, with the 20th overall pick, and they signed him for slot value. He got his first taste of pro ball during Milwaukee’s fall instructional league, though a quad injury limited his time on the field. Mitchell has done his part to assuage concerns about his hitting ability by making real strides with his left-handed swing. He hit consistently for the first time in 2019, and he was doing it again early in his junior season, even transferring the plus raw power he showed in batting practice to games. Big and strong, Mitchell is an easy plus runner who can steal bases and cover a ton of ground in center field, a premium position he'll be able to play long term, with the chance to develop into at least an above-average defender in time. Mitchell has been playing with Type 1 diabetes since being diagnosed in third grade and has shown he can be a premium athlete while dealing with the disease. He featured perhaps the best collection of tools in the entire 2020 Draft class, and the Brewers believe he will be able to use those tools consistently in games once he’s healthy. If it all clicks, Mitchell could become an above-average regular at the pro level, perhaps even more if he can come close to reaching his offensive ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former two-way player at Oklahoma, Cavalli showed better potential on the mound, pushing to the 22nd overall pick with the Nationals in the shortened 2020 Draft. He led the Minors with 175 strikeouts and reached Triple-A in his first full season but didn’t find the same level of consistency back in Rochester in 2022, though he was able to make his Major League debut at home on Aug. 26 that year. It remains his only MLB outing after Tommy John surgery wiped out his 2023 season, and after three rehab starts in 2024, he didn’t pitch again last summer due to the flu and dead arm, according to the organization. Both Cavalli and the Nationals as a club have cautioned that not every pitcher recovers from TJ on the same timeline. After building back up late in the season, Cavalli is expected to be ready to go for a healthier 2025. Before the surgery, he had a 95-97 mph fastball that touched triple-digits but lacked stellar movement. His 82-85 mph curveball had good bite, leading to plenty of whiffs, while an 85-88 mph slider had gyro movement with ample drop to keep hitters off. An upper-80s changeup also flashed plus with ample swing-and-miss and helped stave off lefties. Command issues have dogged Cavalli as a pro and are the second thing to keep him from his considerable ceiling, beside the injuries. He was still feeling his way back to form during his abbreviated rehab looks, and that work will continue headed into his age-26 season in 2025. If everything clicks, he could be a key contributor to Washington’s rotation, but after the missed time, it’ll be an uphill climb to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cavalli transitioned from being a two-way player at Oklahoma to sticking to the mound only, and after flashing great potential before the 2020 shutdown, the Nationals selected him 22nd overall that summer. He led the Minors with 175 strikeouts in 123 1/3 innings in his first full season but was much more inconsistent at Triple-A Rochester in 2022, though he did make his Major League debut that August. Right shoulder inflammation ended that campaign early, and as Cavalli worked toward an MLB return in spring 2023, he suffered a Grade 3 UCL sprain in his right elbow that required Tommy John surgery. His rehab has been a slow process in 2024, in part because he's dealt with the flu and a bout with \"dead arm.\" Before the procedure, the 6-foot-4 right-hander showed off a 95-97 mph fastball that could tickle the occasional triple digits. It was a velo-over-movement offering, but that type of heat is still rare. A mid-80s curveball was his best bat-missing pitch in 2022, earning whiffs on 41 percent of swings, thanks to its sharp downward bite, while his upper-80s cutterish slider could get chase down and on the gloveside. An upper-80s changeup also developed enough fade to keep lefties relatively in check. Cavalli fought off command issues early in his Triple-A tenure in 2022 but was trending upward by the time he reached The Show. His first priority this year will be getting healthy, and it’s possible that his location still wavers as he refinds his form in rehab outings. There’s still a high degree of upside if he hits his spots and remains on the mound, but even with the high TJ success rate these days, nothing is guaranteed coming off the surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player at the start of his NCAA career with Oklahoma, Cavalli settled best on the mound and looked like he was on the precipice of a breakout as a junior in 2020, when his season was canceled after only four starts. The Nationals saw enough promise to grab him 22nd overall, and the former Sooner showed how worthy he was by leading the Minors with 175 strikeouts in 123 1/3 innings across three levels in his first full season. The 2022 campaign was one of fits and starts at Triple-A Rochester (3.71 ERA, 104 strikeouts in 97 innings), but Cavalli did manage to improve enough to earn a Major League debut on Aug. 26. He suffered right shoulder inflammation shortly after and didn’t pitch again in 2022. The injury bug bit again this spring when Cavalli suffered a Grade 3 sprain of the UCL in his right elbow, an issue that required Tommy John surgery. He will miss the 2023 season as a result. The 6-foot-4 right-hander sits 95-97 mph with his fastball and is capable of touching triple digits. The four-seamer relies more on velocity than movement, considering it can come in fairly straight, but that level of heat still makes it a promising pitch. His mid-80s curveball breaks sharply downward and has separated itself as Cavalli’s best breaker over his upper-80s slider that features late cutterish break. His upper-80s changeup has been a work in progress in pro ball but has developed enough fade to be a pitch to hold off lefties. Though he usually avoids walks in large bunches, Cavalli struggled most in 2022 when he couldn’t find consistent fastball command. He was trending in the right direction before his injury with a 1.47 ERA in his final seven Rochester starts. The elbow procedure throws another wrench in that progress, but the rebuilding Nats have said they plan on Cavalli playing a prominent role in future MLB rotations after his return in '24.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
