mlb_pipeline.text: Originally drafted in the 29th round by the Braves in 2017, Cavalli instead headed to the University of Oklahoma, where he opened as a two-way player. He moved to the mound full-time as a sophomore, suffered a stress fracture in his arm that season and then showed exciting results as a junior before the pandemic ended his 2020 spring after four starts. The Nationals saw enough to take him 22nd overall and gave him long looks at the alternate training site and fall instructs. He had one of the most promising debut seasons in 2021, leading the Minors with 175 strikeouts in 123 1/3 innings while climbing three levels. Cavalli has added velocity and now sits around 96-97 mph with the heater. He’ll touch triple digits, as he did three times in last year’s All-Star Futures Game (the most of any participant). The 6-foot-4 hurler also can manipulate the ball well, with both his mid-80s curveball and upper-80s slider showing plus potential. The curve has more depth while the slider has some cutter action to it, and both were big pieces in driving Cavalli’s K rates. An upper-80s sinking changeup is still a work in progress, but Washington was pleased with its growth. Where Cavalli struggled in 2021 was in his ability to fill up the strike zone, especially against upper-level bats. Lower-level hitters were flummoxed by his velocity and movement, but those in Double-A and Triple-A were more patient, leading to a 13.2 percent walk rate. The Nationals are hopeful Cavalli can continue to refine his command and work on his pitch sequencing. If it all clicks, they could have the next big piece of their rebuild.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cavalli was Oklahoma's top prep pitching prospect in 2017, but he turned down the Braves as a 29th-rounder to attend the University of Oklahoma. After spending the early part of his college career as a two-way player, he shifted his focus more to pitching as a sophomore and emerged as a likely first-rounder in ‘20 after his stuff had ticked up early in his junior year. Viewing Cavalli as someone who is only scraping his potential on the mound, the Nationals took the right-hander with the No. 22 overall pick and signed him for $3,027,000. The electric stuff Cavalli showed at Washington’s alternate training site and fall instructional camp left an indelible impression on club officials, and there even was some speculation that the hard-throwing righty might have finished the year in the Nationals’ big league bullpen had the team stayed in the playoff race. Despite being relatively new to pitching, Cavalli already has shown that he can both throw strikes and miss bats with his entire four-pitch mix. Cavalli knows how to use his powerful 6-foot-4 frame and lightning-quick right arm to generate easy velocity. He sat comfortably in the mid-90s and topped out at 99 mph with his riding fastball in his first pro exposure. Cavalli can make hitters look bad with his 82-85 mph curveball, a plus pitch that he throws with power and depth, and he has developed an upper-80s slider/cutter that has similar out-pitch potential. An upper-80s changeup that Cavalli throws with conviction gives him yet another weapon, and some within the organization think it could become the right-hander’s best secondary offering. Where Cavalli has struggled at times is in the command department. Lower-level hitters were flummoxed by his velocity and movement, but those in Triple-A have been more patient, leading to a higher walk rates and some punished balls that are more squarely in the zone. The Nationals are hopeful Cavalli can continue to refine his command and work on his pitch sequencing. He’s shown modest gains there as the season has gone along, and he still holds No. 2 starter upside..

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres signed Rosario for $300,000 in August 2015 but he didn’t find full-season success until joining High-A in 2019. After climbing a level per year, his best statistical season came with Triple-A El Paso in 2022, when he hit 22 homers and stole 21 bags while slashing .288/.368/.508 in a hitter-friendly environment. He got in seven games with the Major League club that summer, but a broken ankle sustained during Winter League workouts kept him out for a chunk of the 2023 campaign. He delivered a .769 OPS in 43 games back in the Pacific Coast League and managed 11 more contests in The Show after rosters expanded in September. With a small zone due to his 5-foot-7 stature, Rosario has never been a huge strikeout type, but he still swung and missed at his fair share of breaking stuff and offspeed. Still, he can generally find contact with good bat speed, especially against fastballs, and he could hit for a decent average if given enough at-bats. Rosario has decent raw power with an 111.3 mph max exit velocity, but he won’t challenge for 20 homers again outside the PCL in all likelihood. The Dominican Republic native showed improved wheels the further he got from the ankle issues in 2023, and his home-to-first and sprint speeds point to him being an above-average runner again. That agility comes in handy as he’s moved around the dirt and does well been moving in on grounders. He can handle third with his arm strength or second with his quickness, but at this juncture, he best profiles as a bench infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in August 2015, Rosario didn’t grow into a full-season success until four years later at High-A Lake Elsinore in 2019, when he finished with a .743 OPS over 122 games. He has climbed one level per season since (excluding the missed 2020 pandemic campaign) and is coming off his most successful year yet when he was a 20-20 player at Triple-A El Paso, including a career-best 22 homers, .508 slugging percentage and .876 OPS. The Dominican Republic native was called up to the Majors for seven games in August and September but was only used minimally as infield depth. He suffered a broken ankle during Winter League workouts and has been slow to get going during his return in 2023. Rosario lacks size at 5-foot-7, but his good bat speed from the right side, along with improving pitch selection and bat control, have helped turn him into a high-contact hitter. His 19.3 percent K rate as a 22-year-old at Triple-A last year was his lowest mark with a full-season affiliate and coincided with his jump in power. That said, don’t expect Rosario to be a 20-plus homer guy moving forward, considering a good part of that jump was related to extreme hitter-friendly conditions in El Paso (he slugged just .416 on the road). Rosario has acted more like a below-average runner at Triple-A coming off the ankle injury. He’s moved around the dirt a lot in recent years, and while he has a strong arm for third base, his traditional athleticism might be best served at second base; that’s if he needs a full-time position. Rosario’s versatility and hit-over-power profile point toward a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in August 2015, Rosario posted gaudy numbers in both rookie ball and the Dominican Summer League. It took some time for that bat to translate as he progressed, but he put forth a solid 2019 season at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, hitting .278/.331/.412. After losing the 2020 season to the pandemic, Rosario played in the Venezuelan Winter League, where he hit .327 with an .821 OPS in 27 games. He continued to hit in 2021, mashing a career-high 12 homers and slashing .281/.360/.455 over 114 games in his first taste of Double-A before finishing up the year in the Arizona Fall League. Rosario, listed at 5-foot-9 and 150 pounds, is undersized, but he has an innate feel to hit, showing good bat speed from the right side of the plate and the ability to drive the ball all over the field. Improved pitch selection helped him set a career-high for homers last season, but he's still more of a hit-over-power type who drives the ball into the gaps. When he reaches base, Rosario knows how to use his speed and has swiped 20 or more bases in four of his five Minor League seasons. A plus arm stands out as Rosario plays all over the diamond defensively. He spent the bulk of his time in Double-A at second base and shortstop, though also got plenty of reps at the hot corner in the Arizona Fall League. Third base may wind up being his best position long-term, but the overall versatility will certainly help Rosario carve out a place on a roster, especially if his bat keeps trending upward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in August 2015, Rosario posted gaudy numbers in rookie ball and the Dominican Summer League. It took some time for that bat to translate as he progressed, but he put forth a solid 2019 season at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, hitting .278/.331/.412. After losing the 2020 season to the pandemic, Padres officials were pleased to see Rosario challenge himself in the Venezuelan Winter League. He thrived there, too, hitting .327 with an .821 OPS in 27 games. Rosario is undersized, but he has an innate feel to hit, showing good bat speed from the right side of the plate and the ability to drive the ball from line to line. He has gap-to-gap pop -- though his pitch selection and overall contact rate leave something to be desired. Rosario has a strong arm, and when he reaches base, he knows how to utilize his plus speed as a baserunner. After splitting time mostly between second and third base early in his career, Rosario was deployed in a utility role in 2020. He's played primarily at second and short this season at Double-A San Antonio as the Padres cling to the hope he can stick up the middle. If Rosario’s bat continues its upward trajectory, he has the makings of a big league-caliber utility piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Waters was taken in the second round of the 2017 Draft by his hometown team, was the Southern League MVP in ‘19 and made the Futures Game roster in ‘21. But the jump to Triple-A was rough, and he again struggled in Triple-A Gwinnett to start ‘22. The Royals have had their eye on Waters since he was in high school, though, and in July 2022, they were able to land him and two other Minor Leaguers by sending a supplemental first-round Draft pick to the Braves. Waters made an immediate impact, posting a .940 OPS with Omaha before finishing the year in Kansas City, where he had an .803 OPS with five homers in 32 games. The change Waters made when he came to Kansas City was not mechanical. Rather, the Royals emphasized his approach and making better decisions at the plate. His walk rate nearly doubled from Gwinnett to Omaha and then settled at 11% in Kansas City. Waters has power from both sides of the plate and is continuing to tap into that despite his lean frame. He is still too aggressive at times, but that will be a work in progress as he gets into his second Major League season. Waters has elite speed that allows him to swipe bags and play center field, where he can showcase his plus fielding skills and plus arm. The Royals see 2023 as the year to find out if they have their center fielder of the future in their organization, and Waters is still in that conversation despite a left oblique strain wiping out his spring and delaying his season. He can also play right field or serve as a valuable defensive replacement if his bat doesn’t hold up in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken in the second round of the 2017 Draft and signed for a slightly below-slot bonus of $1.5 million out of the Georgia high-school ranks, Waters moved rapidly up his hometown team’s ladder, picking up accolades along the way. He was the Southern League MVP in 2019 and made the Futures Game roster in 2021. Outside of that trip to Denver in the midst of a very strong July, however, Waters' production dipped considerably in Triple-A last year, though the Braves were sure to protect his five-tool potential on the 40-man roster during the offseason. In the midst of another rough year, Waters was traded to Kansas City in early July, and he’s shown promising signs of a turnaround in the weeks since. After the lost 2020 season, Waters tried too hard to show he was ready for the big leagues in 2021, and he didn't consistently drive the ball from both sides of the plate. He’s always been an aggressive hitter, one who swings and misses a good amount, with plenty of raw power he still is learning to get to. He actually cut his strikeout rate and upped his walk rate in Triple-A in 2021 compared to his time there in 2019, and also cut down his chase rate considerably, even if that didn’t show up in his other numbers. A positive sign of maturity in 2021 was that Waters didn’t let his offensive struggles impact the other aspects of his game. He swiped a career-high 28 bags and played plus defense consistently in all three outfield spots. He still doesn’t turn 24 until December and will use the time before then to press upon his new organization just how much of a piece of its future he can be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Braves went into their own backyard to draft Waters, a Georgia high schooler, in the second round of the 2017 Draft, he’s done nothing but perform well, showing off all five tools as he’s made a quick ascent up the organizational ladder. Often playing alongside, or a half step behind, fellow Braves outfield prospect Cristian Pache, Waters has won a batting title and MVP award, both in the Double-A Southern League in 2019, while reaching Triple-A at age 20. He spent 2020 working on his game at the Braves’ alternate training site. Waters is a switch-hitter, better from the left side, but able to drive the ball to all fields from both sides of the plate. An aggressive hitter, he can use his quick, whippy swing to hit for a high average. He spent much of his time at alternate camp working on his overall approach, one that has produced a career 26.2 percent strikeout rate and just a seven percent walk rate, and the Braves feel his time facing so many advanced arms last summer will benefit him and allow him to be a more advanced hitter and to tap into his raw power more consistently. Because of Pache, Waters might not play center field in the same outfield as him, but he certainly has the skills, with plus speed, excellent range and strong instincts. He’s played all three spots and would be a plus defender with a very strong arm in any spot he plays. If the gains in his approach are for real, he’ll be an impact player on both sides of the ball soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Anyone going from a $5,000 signing as a 19-year-old to a Major League starter is a success story, and Butto certainly fits the bill. The right-hander has been a steady performer throughout his time in the Mets system since signing in June 2017 and earned a 40-man spot in November 2022 after reaching Double-A. He sported a 3.56 ERA with 138 strikeouts in 129 innings between Binghamton and Triple-A Syracuse last year to continue his string of successful seasons, and he made his Major League debut on Aug. 21 in Philadelphia, surrendering seven earned runs on nine hits over four rough innings against the future National League champions. The Venezuela native touches 97 mph with his four-seam, high-spin fastball but is more likely to sit around 92-95 mph in most starts. The heater might be best when it’s setting up his 82-85 mph changeup, which has long been the best in the Mets system because of its separation and depth. Butto added a low-80s slider to fend off concerns about his lack of a true biting breaking pitch, but both that and his curveball still don’t do much to fend off righties. He continued to do better against lefties (.742 OPS) than righties (.747) in ’22. On one hand, Butto has a history of Minor League success and is already a starting depth option for the Major League club. On the other, he has a limited ceiling as a two-pitch hurler who isn’t a clear option to have his stuff play up in shorter spurts. He could be valuable as a bulk pitcher out of the bullpen and occasional emergency starter, a role he could handle right away for New York.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Butto signed for just $5,000 as a 19-year-old in June 2017. Five years later, he has worked his way to New York’s 40-man roster and now stands on the cusp of the Majors. After starting 2021 at High-A Brooklyn, the 6-foot-1 right-hander sported better numbers at Double-A Binghamton with a 3.12 ERA, 1.04 WHIP and 50 strikeouts over 40 1/3 innings. That performance helped earn him Rule 5 Draft protection when he became first eligible in November. The Venezuela native is around 92-94 mph with his fastball, touching 96 mph at times, and it comes with an above-average spin rate as well. Perhaps the fastball’s greatest asset, though, is the way it plays off Butto’s low-80s changeup, which is easily his best offering. The change already gets tremendous separation off the fastball and fools hitters further with its depth. The righty will also mix in a low-80s curveball, but throws it with below-average consistency and bite. Butto hides the ball well in his delivery and throws a healthy amount of strikes, aiding his quest to be a potential Major League starter. The changeup keeps his splits in line -- lefties had a .712 OPS against him in '21, compared to a .699 OPS for righties -- but the lack of a third pitch means he might struggle seeing Major League hitters a second or third time through the order. Now on the Mets' 40-man roster, Butto, who was promoted to Triple-A Syracuse in August, should be knocking on Queens’ door by the first half of next year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Butto signed late out of Venezuela as a 19-year-old in June 2017 and signed for very little with just a $5,000 signing bonus. It didn’t take long for him at all to look like a bargain. The 6-foot-1 right-hander posted sub-2.00 ERAs in the Dominican Summer and Appalachian Leagues before stumbling some with Class A Short Season Brooklyn in 2018. He regained ground again in 2019 by showing durability and promising results with a 3.62 ERA and 109 strikeouts in 112 innings at Class A Columbia. Only two Mets full-season pitchers posted a WHIP lower than his 1.17. Any discussion of Butto’s repertoire must begin with the change. The 6-foot-1 right-hander really sells the pitch with the same hand speed upon delivery, only for it to show 10-11 mph of separation from the fastball with depth thus making hitters look bad when they swing early. Speaking of the heater, Butto was averaging 93 mph on the fastball during his time at last year’s instructs, about in line with what he showed early in 2019 (when he had also been touching as high as 96). That left the Mets enthused after concerns he might lose some velocity in the otherwise lost year. Butto also sports a two-seamer that the organization has worked with him on, making sure it provides different movement from his four-seam. The breaking ball is a work in progress. It had shown slurvish tendencies with some sweeping action, and both he and the Mets have tried to give it more vertical break. Butto throws a good amount of strikes with the entire repertoire. The promising velocity and near-elite changeup have given Butto a much brighter future than the one predicted for him when he first signed. He will need the breaker to become more of a consistent pitch if he’s going to face batters multiple times at the top level, but the two pitches he does have could eventually work in middle-relief role at the bare minimum.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Comparably old as a 19-year-old high-schooler, Baty’s age may have caused him to slip some in the 2019 Draft, but his considerable tools have shone brightly at every Minor League stop. He hit .312/.406/.544 with 19 homers in 89 games at Double-A last season, prompting an August promotion to Triple-A. He lasted only six games in Syracuse before joining the Mets in The Show, where he homered in his first at-bat. The Texas native struggled to reproduce that magic over his 11 total games in the Majors and was shut down after that time due to a torn UCL in his right thumb that required surgery. Baty finished his 2022 Minor League season with a .315 average between his two stops on the strength of a smooth left-handed swing and an approach that doesn’t see him expand the zone too often. His biggest bugaboo throughout his career has been his ground-ball rate, and that did drop to a more manageable 43.5 percent (down from an organization-worst 55.8 percent in 2021) after he made it a priority to get behind the ball more and lift it more efficiently on contact. That’s important because Baty can hit the ball hard with at least plus raw power, and more airtime means more extra-base hits. A three-sport athlete in high school, the 23-year-old still looked rough around the edges defensively when he made the Majors, and increasing his range will remain a priority perhaps for much of his career. A plus arm certainly helps his defensive case and also eases his time in left field, where he’s made 29 Minor League starts. Baty’s ceiling is at its highest at the hot corner, however, and after the Mets’ Carlos Correa deal fell through, his path to third in Queens should be clear for the taking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baty’s age at 19 might have been the only thing that allowed him to slip to the Mets at No. 12 overall in the 2019 Draft. He quickly got to work across three affiliates that first summer, finishing with a trophy-raising turn with Class A Short Season Brooklyn. He returned to Coney Island for the alternate site in 2020 and played once more with the Cyclones as a High-A affiliate last summer. He hit .292/.382/.473 with 12 homers at High-A and Double-A and picked up more at-bats in the Arizona Fall League. Baty works well to all fields utilizing a smooth swing from the left side. He typically has little issue staying behind the ball and making solid contact off the bat, and when he doesn’t, he can still work a walk. The Texas native is capable of putting on a powerful show in batting practice, but it hasn’t translated into eye-popping slugging numbers. A 50-plus percent ground-ball rate has kept him from making the most of that strength, but there’s hope that more upper-level experience could iron out those issues. A better runner than one might expect given his size, Baty has grown to be a capable defender at third base, where his plus arm fits the bill. The Mets gave him time in left field in Binghamton, and he has enough athleticism to work there. Notably, he was third-base-only in the Fall League. If Baty can turn his dreamlike raw pop into actual game power, New York could have its next long-term third baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baty was old for his class as a 19-year-old high school senior, and that deterred some clubs from taking him early in the 2019 Draft. The Mets weren’t one of them, as they made Baty the first third baseman to be taken by the organization in the first round since Chris Donnels in 1987, selecting the Lake Travis (Texas) High product No. 12 overall. Baty posted a .821 OPS with 25 extra-base hits (seven homers) while climbing three levels in his pro debut after signing for $3.9 million, then arrived at the Mets’ alternate training site in '20 looking physically stronger and leaner. Hitting for power from line-to-line from the left side is Baty’s calling card. He’s shown early in his career that he can get to it during games, even hitting his longest and most impressive home runs to the opposite field, though he’s still learning how to turn on the ball. Baty’s swing mechanics and bat path do lead to swing-and-miss issues that raise questions about his hit tool, but he also employs a patient approach and controls the zone well enough to project him as an average hitter with plus game power. The athleticism that made Baty a three-sport standout as a prep shows up on the diamond, and he showed improved agility and more speed last summer at the alternate site. He could develop into an average defender at third base, where his plus arm strength -- he was clocked at 92 mph off the mound in high school -- is an asset, though, overall, Baty will need time to develop on both sides of the ball to reach his ceiling. Having climbed to Double-A in 2021, Baty has seen some time in the outfield with the Mets hoping to get his bat in the lineup anyway they can in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tarnok was a two-way player for most of his amateur career at Riverview High School in Florida, but success on the mound as a senior led to the Braves going well above slot with a bonus of nearly $1.45 million as a third-round Draft pick in 2017. After a brief Major League stint in 2022, he was traded to Oakland that December in the Sean Murphy deal. Working his way back from a Spring Training shoulder issue, he made five appearances (one start) in 2023 for the A’s before a calf strain cut his season short. Tarnok’s low-80s changeup has emerged as a solid put-away pitch that misses plenty of bats, complementing a fastball that sits around 95 mph and can top out at 98. His curveball continues to be an effective pitch, while a newer slider showed encouraging signs during his time in the big leagues last season. Tarnok’s repeatable, athletic delivery helps him consistently stay around the zone and command the ball well. The A’s continue to build him up in a starting role, though recent injury history -- he entered 2024 Spring Training recovering from hip surgery last August -- could lead to considerations for a possible bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player for most of his amateur career at Riverview High School in Florida, Tarnok’s success as a pitcher in his senior year was enough for the Braves to go well above slot, signing him for nearly $1.45 million as a third-round Draft pick in 2017. Utilizing the pandemic in 2020 as an opportunity to work on his body and refine his mechanics, he rapidly ascended through Atlanta’s system upon returning, reaching Triple-A in 2022 and making his Major League debut before getting traded to Oakland in the Sean Murphy deal. Tarnok increased his stock in the Braves’ system thanks to a return of his stuff that had regressed earlier in his pro career. His fastball sits around 95 mph, topping out at 98. While his curveball has long been an effective pitch and he added a slider more recently, he did struggle a bit landing them for strikes in 2022, but his low-80s changeup took a nice step forward and missed a good amount of bats. Tarnok tends to be around the zone with a repeatable, athletic delivery and commands the ball well enough to get plenty of swing-and-miss, evidenced by his 10.5 whiffs per nine innings in ‘22. With a 6-foot-3 frame that looks to be durable, he figures to get a good look in Oakland’s pitching staff at some point in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Tarnok hadn’t pitched a ton in high school as a two-way player at Riverview High School in Florida, he did have some helium in his senior year on the mound. The Braves liked his projection and athleticism enough to give him double slot and sign him for nearly $1.45 million. He showed glimpses early on, then regressed, both in terms of velocity and effectiveness, in 2019. His home workouts in 2020 seemed to pay off as he reached Double-A and pitched well there, earning a spot on the 40-man roster. He made it to Triple-A in 2022 and made his big-league debut before being sent to the A’s in the three-team deal that brought Sean Murphy to Atlanta. Tarnok was one of the most improved pitchers in the Braves’ system prior to the trade. His stuff ticked back up after that early regression, starting with his fastball that averages around 95 mph. He’s long had an effective curve and, like many pitchers in the system, he more recently added a slider, with positive results. His average changeup is effective, especially against left-handed hitters. He’s missed a lot more bats over the past two seasons, including whiffing 10.5 per nine in 2022 and while his command isn’t pinpoint, he’s generally around the strike zone. His athleticism should help him continue to repeat his delivery and refine his command and he should get the opportunity to impact the A’s big league staff at some point in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player from the Florida high school ranks who seemed likely to head to Division II Tampa for college, Tarnok’s athleticism on the mound, though raw, caught the attention of the Braves, who went well over slot in the third round of the 2017 Draft to put the infielder on the mound full time. He’s been able to move fairly well, especially considering how little time he spent pitching as an amateur, hitting full-season ball in 2018 then moving up to High-A in 2019. He pitched well there after returning from a lat injury. Working out at home on his own during the shutdown, Tarnok continued to fine-tune a delivery that’s been a work in progress. After his velocity backed up a bit in 2019, the first year he topped 100 innings, it was trending back up, sitting more in the mid-90s while maxing out at 99 mph in bullpen sessions. There’s room to keep adding strength to his 6-foot-3 frame so he can maintain those velocity gains. He complements the heater with a power breaking ball with tight spin, a pitch that could be better than average in time, and an average changeup he uses mostly against lefties. Tarnok has improved his strike-throwing as he’s developed in the Braves system, something he’ll have to keep doing as his stuff ticks up. He’ll have to show better command within the zone as well as he gets to the upper levels if he wants to reach his ceiling as a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees signed Cabrera out of Venezuela for $100,000 in 2015, a year after they signed his older brother Leobaldo for $250,000. While they released Leobaldo in 2018 -- he's now an outfielder in the Twins system -- Oswaldo has slowly developed into one of their better prospects. After totaling 22 homers in his first four years as a pro, he broke out with 29 in 2021, winning Double-A Northeast League MVP honors and going deep five times in nine Triple-A games at the end of the season. A switch-hitter, Cabrera returned from the 2020 pandemic layoff with more strength and more pronounced loft in his swing. His power surge only came from the left side, where he batted .290/.350/.612 compared to .227/.277/.333 as a righty. He's using his legs more at the plate and has taken a more aggressive approach without sacrificing much in the way of contact, though he's a fringy hitter at best. Cabrera's added muscle cost him some quickness, though he's still an aggressive runner who makes the most of his fringy to average speed on the bases. His quick hands, solid arm and finely-tuned internal clock help him make plays in the field, though his range is a bit stretched at shortstop. He saw more action at second and third base in each of his last two seasons, and he's a solid defender at both spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thanks largely to his defensive prowess behind the plate, Langeliers was thought to be the second-best catcher in the 2019 class, behind only eventual No. 1 overall pick Adley Rutschman. The Braves were a bit ahead of the industry when they took him No. 9 overall and signed him for an under-slot $4 million bonus. A solid debut in full-season ball and a strong performance at the Braves’ alternate site in 2020 allowed Langeliers to jump to Double-A in 2021, finish in Triple-A and earn the trust of the organization enough to be the catcher on the club’s taxi squad throughout its postseason run. It’s also why the A’s wanted Langeliers to be one of the headliners in the deal that sent Matt Olson to Atlanta. Langeliers’ power bat and arm were on full display during his first full season. His right-handed pop started to show up at the alt site in 2020 and continued in Mississippi, where his 22 homers stand out even more because it’s such a tough place to hit. While there is some swing-and-miss to his game (26.8 percent K rate), that was right about average for his level and he routinely registered high exit velocities, was near the top of the organization in terms of the quality of his contact and showed the ability to recognize and hit breaking stuff. Improvement in handling velocity up in the zone will help his development as a hitter. Even if he doesn’t hit, Langeliers’ defense will make him a big leaguer. He has one of the best arms of any Minor Leaguer at any position and he threw out 42 percent of potential basestealers a year ago. He’s a strong leader and works very well with pitchers and after his experience on the postseason taxi squad, he’s close to being ready for a job as a big league regular, receiving his first call up in mid-August.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For most of his college career at Baylor, Langeliers was known as a glove-first backstop and for good reason. Even though he missed part of his junior year with a broken hamate in his left hand, he answered enough questions about his offensive profile to make him the second best catcher in the class, behind No. 1 overall pick Adley Rutschman. Thought by many to be more of a middle-of-the-first-round type of player, Langeliers ended up going No. 9 overall to the Braves, who signed him for below pick value. He held his own with a debut assignment to full-season Rome in 2019 and performed very well at the club’s alternate camp in 2020. He hit 22 homers in Double-A his first real full season, then spent the entire postseason on the big league club’s taxi squad. He was in Minor League Spring Training when he was part of the quartet of prospects sent to the A’s for Matt Olson. There’s no question that Langeliers’ defense is still his calling card. His athleticism and agility allow him to be a plus blocker and receiver and he perhaps has the best arm of any catcher in the Minor Leagues, one that allowed him to throw out 42 percent of potential basestealers heading into 2022. He is a strong leader who worked very well with more advanced pitchers at the alternate training site and frames pitches extremely well. While his glove is ahead of his bat, the Braves loved the strides Langeliers made from the right side of the plate. He has a good setup and solid swing mechanics that point to consistent hard contact and plenty of raw power, which he got to fairly consistently in 2021, with excellent velocity on balls in play to the opposite field. He has every chance of being an outstanding starting catcher in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The MVP of the 2016 Connie Mack World Series as an Atlanta high schooler, Curry stayed home to pitch for Georgia Tech for three years before the Guardians selected him in the seventh round of the 2019 Draft. Between shoulder inflammation that summer and the pandemic, he didn't make his pro debut until 2021. It took him just 15 months to climb from Single-A to Cleveland, where he made a pair of starts last summer. Curry's 91-94 mph fastball reaches 96 and plays better than its average velocity because it has all the characteristics the Guardians crave, coming out of a high arm slot with plenty of induced vertical break and efficient spin. His four-seamer overmatched hitters in the lower Minors but wasn't nearly as dominant in Triple-A or the big leagues. He has helped himself by improving the velocity and depth on what is now a mid-80s slider, giving him a second solid offering. Curry's mid-70s curveball lacks power and his mid-80s changeup often is too firm and straight, and both grade as fringy. His lack of a reliable third pitch and physicality leads to questions as to whether he's more of a back-of-the-rotation starter or a multi-inning reliever. He has a history of throwing strikes but his control regressed a bit last year when he became reluctant to challenge more advanced hitters when they knocked him around.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Curry won MVP honors at the 2016 Connie Mack World Series before pitching for three years at Georgia Tech and going in the seventh round of the 2019 Draft. Shoulder inflammation that summer and the cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season delayed his pro debut until May 2021, but he made up for lost time quickly. He reached Double-A and ranked third in the Minors in K/BB ratio (7.7) and sixth in ERA (2.30) and walks per nine innings (1.5). Curry's fastball sits in the low 90s and touches 96 mph, playing as a solid to plus pitch with all the characteristics that the Guardians covet. He releases it from a high arm slot with plenty of efficient spin and induced vertical break, and hitters couldn't catch up to his heater last year. He relies heavily on his four-seamer, with his low-80s slider showing flashes of becoming an average pitch because he locates it well and his downer curveball and changeup grading as fringy. Just 5-foot-11 and 190 pounds, Curry lacks the physicality desired as a starter, though he repeats his delivery well and pounds the strike zone. He's riding a lot of momentum from last season, but he still needs to find a reliable secondary pitch or two in order to make it as a big league starter. Otherwise, he'll wind up as a fastball-heavy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hall was one of the best high school lefties in the 2017 Draft class, ranking only behind MacKenzie Gore. The Orioles drafted him accordingly, taking him No. 21 overall that June. Throughout his climb up the organizational ladder, which included his first trip to the big leagues in a relief role, he’s shown off elite-level stuff that dominates hitters, though his ability to find the strike zone has hampered him at times. He put an elbow strain that sidelined him for much of 2021 in his rear view with a healthy 2022, largely in Triple-A, to earn that first callup. Throughout the 2022 season, Hall continued to show off a four-pitch repertoire and an ability to miss bats. Hall’s fastball touches triple digits and averages over 96.5 mph. His fading mid-80s changeup is a plus offering at times and it elicited a 49 percent miss rate. He still has two separate breaking balls, throwing his upper-80s slider a lot more frequently than his slower curve. No one has questions Hall’s stuff and ability to get big league hitters out, but there are concerns about his ability to find the strike zone enough to do it as a starter. His walk rate ballooned to 5.3 per nine in the Minors in 2022, though he was more efficient during his big league debut. The O’s still think he can use his athleticism to improve his command and start, with the stuff to pitch in the front half of a rotation, though there is still some reliever risk here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Orioles took Hall out of the Georgia high school ranks No. 21 overall in the 2017 Draft, the left-hander has shown off premium pure stuff and the ability to dominate Minor League hitters. The 2019 Futures Gamer had gone a level at a time, spending all of 2018 in Low-A and all of 2019 up a level with High-A Frederick before pitching at the alternate site in 2020. His 2021 in Double-A was off to a very good start, but an elbow strain limited him to just 31 2/3 innings all year. The Orioles added him to the 40-man roster in the offseason and a healthy 2022 led to his first call up to the big leagues in August. At full strength in 2022 after a rebuilding program and the organization erring more on the side of caution with holding him out for so long a year ago, Hall’s stuff has continued to be absolutely nasty, with a fastball routinely up to 101 mph and a fading changeup that flashes plus. He does have distinct breaking pitches, throwing the slider more frequently than the curve. Hall’s main obstacle, other than health, has been his command. He did throw more strikes in 2021 (4.6 walks per nine) and he’s worked to streamline his delivery, though his walk rate ticked back up in 2022. He’s one of the best athletes at any position in the system, something that should help him continue to find consistency in that regard. Further refinement will allow him to reach his ceiling as a dynamic lefty starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were three high school lefties taken in the first round of the 2017 Draft: MacKenzie Gore, who went No. 3 to the Padres; Trevor Rogers, the No. 13 pick by the Marlins who made his big league debut in 2020; and Hall, the Orioles' pick at No. 21. He’s shown dominant stuff across Class A and Class A Advanced during his first two full seasons of pro ball, adding in a perfect Futures Game inning in '19 for good measure, before spending the summer of '20 at Baltimore’s alternate camp. As Hall has progressed through the Orioles' system, he’s continuously added velocity. He was consistently at 96-99 mph last summer, throwing his heater with excellent life. His changeup can be a true out pitch, thrown in the low-80s with good fade. Hall has worked hard to separate his curve and slider and has defined the shape and speed of each pitch consistently now, with the curve flashing plus with excellent spin and bite. One of the few things holding Hall back has been his command, as his walk rate spiked along with his strikeout rate in 2019. The Orioles liked what they saw in terms of improvements in his delivery during his work at the alternate training site, and he showed a greater capacity to make in-game adjustments. He’s yet to top 100 innings in a season, so he needs more reps, but there’s an up arrow next to his name in terms of his starting pitcher ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick out of Oklahoma State in 2019, Battenfield already has been traded twice, by the Astros along with outfield prospect Cal Stevenson to the Rays for Austin Pruitt in January 2020 and to the Guardians for D.J. Johnson and Jordan Luplow last July. After relieving in college, he has found success as a starter in pro ball, logging a 2.53 ERA with a 131/19 K/BB ratio in 103 innings while advancing to Double-A in his first full season last summer. He struck out 10 in seven innings of one-hit ball in the opener of the Double-A Northeast championship series to help Akron win the title. Battenfield's fastball sat around 90 mph in shorter stints in college, but now he's operating at 91-95 and touching 97, with his four-seamer playing up thanks to its carry and his command. His heater pairs well with his upper-70s downer curveball and an upper-80s cutter/slider with short horizontal break, both of which can be solid offerings. He also has a low-80s changeup with fade that flashes similar upside. The younger brother of White Sox pitching prospect Blake Battenfield, he keeps batters off balance by mixing four pitches that move in four different directions and locating them where he wants. He has improved his conditioning and athleticism since turning pro, resulting in improved stuff and a better ability to repeat his delivery. He doesn't have the prettiest arm action but he pounds the zone and misses bats, giving him a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter and a high floor of a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Casey was a two-way player at Boston College but told teams he preferred hitting, despite posting better numbers on the mound. He fell to the Dodgers in the 20th round in 2017 as a result. Inconsistent success marked his first two seasons in pro ball before he managed 23 homers at High-A and Double-A in 2019. He was hitting .296/.362/.462 over 73 games as a 25-year-old back in Tulsa last season when Los Angeles sent him to Washington in the six-player deal involving Trea Turner and Max Scherzer. Shortly after, Casey ran into a roadblock at Triple-A, hitting .179 with a 38.8 percent K rate over 38 games. Eligible for the Rule 5 Draft for a second time, he was added to the 40-man in November after strengthening his case in the Arizona Fall League. Casey still possesses a strong arm from his days as a BC pitcher, and he uses it to great effect from the outfield grass. He also boasts plus speed that makes him an annual candidate to swipe 15-plus bags in a full season. While he played a lot of right field in the Dodgers system, it was notable that Casey played primarily in center for the Nationals following the trade. He could likely step right into the Washington outfield mix without the MLB club missing a beat defensively. There are legit questions about Casey’s bat, however. He has shown K rates right around 30 percent for much of his time in the upper Minors. That hinders his ability to tap into his solid raw power, as does his history of putting the ball primarily on the ground. Casey isn’t far from being a fourth-outfield type in the Majors because of his wheels and defense. But his age at 26 and performance in the box might keep him from ever being more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2019, the main attraction at Hagerty High School in Florida was Riley Greene, who went No. 5 overall that June to the Tigers. Grissom was that school's shortstop, and while he wasn’t as highly regarded, the Braves liked him enough to go over the $125K limit in the 11th round and sign him for $347,500. He’s rewarded their investment by hitting pretty much everywhere as a pro -- from his summer debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League to the alternate site, where he was one of the youngest players, to a full-season debut in 2021 in which he raked in A ball and earned a late promotion to High-A. Grissom routinely displays outstanding bat-to-ball skills with a very good approach. He has a strong feel for the barrel from the right side of the plate, manages his at-bats well, draws walks and rarely strikes out. He’s short to the ball with relatively simple hitting mechanics and has solid bat speed. The Braves hope he’ll continue to fill out his 6-foot-3 frame and grow into more power as he matures. As solid as Grissom has been at the plate, it’s been less clear where he might belong long-term defensively. He’s still seen more time at shortstop than any other position, but he’s also played a fair amount at third as well as a little at second. He has the arm to stay on the left side of the infield, where he’s more comfortable and while he doesn’t always have silky-smooth actions, he’s a solid defender. If he can’t play short, he might need to raise his power profile a bit to be a fit at the hot corner as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the 2020 season, Hagerty High School now has two big leaguers on its alumni list, with Orioles outfielder Ryan Mountcastle joining Phillies right-hander Zach Eflin at the highest level. Chances are Tigers 2019 first-round pick Riley Greene will be next, but Grissom, his teammate and 11th-rounder that same June, might not be far behind him. After getting an above-slot bonus to keep him from attending Florida International, he had a solid pro debut in the Gulf Coast League, then performed well as one of the youngest players at the Braves’ alternate site in 2020 before continuing his good work at instructs. Facing a slew of 40-man roster-caliber arms at the alternate site, Grissom showed that the advanced approach he displayed in the GCL was for real. He consistently had quality at-bats, with the ability to repeat a simple load and swing with good bat speed. He’s simplified his setup from his days as an amateur and that should help him make hard contact and tap into his power more as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. Just how much he does that might help decide what infield position he ends up at long term. A shortstop in high school and during his pro debut, he has good hands and a strong arm. He’ll likely see time at second, third and short moving forward, with the hot corner the most likely landing spot should he develop enough to be a regular at one position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Charles has steadily climbed up the organization since signing with the A’s in March 2015 out of the Dominican Republic. The right-hander’s breakthrough came in 2019, when he rose through three levels to end the season at Double-A Midland as a reliever. Possessing the highest average velocity in the organization, Charles is still learning how to pitch as he looks to graduate to the highest level. Bringing a power fastball that can touch triple digits to go along with a wipeout slider, Charles showed improvement at both the A’s alternate site and in the instructional league. If he can put it together, Charles has the makings of a strong-armed reliever who can fill the back end of a bullpen. Lowering his walk rate and throwing more strikes could speed up his call to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first Georgia State player ever to make the U.S. collegiate national team, Gaddis also became the highest pick in school history when Cleveland drafted him in the fifth round in 2019. He topped the High-A Central with 127 strikeouts in 97 1/3 innings during his first full pro season in 2021, then scooted from Double-A to the big leagues last season. He allowed seven homers and 15 runs in 7 1/3 innings over two starts with the Guardians, who believe he was tipping his pitches by altering his arm angle when he threw his changeup. Gaddis' best pitch is his upper-70s change, which elicits a lot of empty swings with plenty of fade and some sink as well. His changeup pairs well with his four-seam fastball, which parks at 92-95 mph, can reach 98 in short stints and has effective carry when he maintains his high three-quarters arm slot. His mid-80s slider/cutter plays as a solid pitch because he locates it well and is much more effective than his mid-70s curveball. Gaddis throws strikes and uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create deceptive angle that is tough on right-handers, but he struggled against left-handers in 2022. He's vulnerable to home runs when he doesn't locate his pitches well, and he gets in trouble when he drops his arm slot and loses action on his fastball and depth on his breaking balls. He could serve as an innings-eater at the back of a rotation or a long reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A quarterback who totaled 43 touchdowns as an Alabama high school senior and sparked interest from Southeastern Conference football programs, Thompson decided to focus on baseball. The Rangers spent the 26th overall pick in 2017 and $2.1 million to land his athleticism and upside, but a series of injuries (tendinitis in both knees, broken hamate, ankle) and the cancelled 2020 season held him to just 171 games in his first four years as a pro. He enjoyed full health and the best season of his career in 2021, though his plate discipline remains an issue and Texas opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster in November. Thompson's best tool remains his well-above-average speed. It helped him lead the Double-A Central with nine triples and 48 extra-base hits last season, and he also swiped 25 bases in 33 attempts. He has improved his reads and routes and become a plus defender in center field, though the former quarterback surprisingly lacks arm strength and didn't register a single assist in 93 games a year ago. With his hand-eye coordination, bat speed and strength, Thompson has the physical tools to be productive at the plate. But his lack of pitch recognition and plate discipline continue to hold him back, and the right-handed hitter may not do enough damage against same-side pitchers to be more than a platoon player. His work ethic and personality have made him an organization favorite and earned him its True Ranger Award in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vargas starred as an amateur in Cuba, driving in the gold medal-winning run off Team USA's Hunter Greene at the 2014 15-and-under World Cup, before defecting with his father Lazaro (the DH on Cuba's 1992 and 1996 Olympic champions) in November 2015. He waited nearly two years before signing with the Dodgers for $300,000 and has established himself as the best hitter in the system. A career .313 hitter in the Minors, he won the Double-A Central batting title (.321) in 2021 and doubled off Alex Cobb in his first big league at-bat last August. Vargas is an extremely advanced hitter with elite bat-to-ball skills and a good understanding of his right-handed swing and what he's trying to do at the plate. He controls the strike zone, uses the entire field and handles fastballs and breaking balls with ease, though he did struggle a bit against changeups in 2022. He's more hitter than slugger, but his bat speed, strength and penchant for making hard contact should allow him to get to all of his solid raw power and produce 20-25 homers per season. Known mostly for his bat, Vargas has put in the time to improve his speed, athleticism and defense. Regarded as a fringy to average runner, he nonetheless recorded sprint speeds in the 94th percentile during his introduction to the Majors. He has fringy range but solid arm strength at third base, his primary position, but spent most of his big league time at first base and left field. He's decent at first base, a work in progress in left field and comfortable (albeit with subpar range) at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Lazaro Vargas, the DH on Cuba's 1992 and 1996 Olympic champions, Miguel drove in the gold medal-winning run off Team USA's Hunter Greene at the 2014 15-and-under World Cup in Mexico. After defecting with his father in November 2015, he waited nearly two years before signing with the Dodgers for $300,000. The best pure hitter in the system, he owns a career .316 average in his first three years as a pro and won the Double-A Central batting title last season at .321 as a 21-year-old. Vargas is well equipped to accrue more batting championships in the future because he has advanced bat-to-ball skills, understands the mechanics of his right-handed swing, controls the strike zone and hits balls where they're pitched. He's figuring out how to tap into his solid raw power, improving from seven homers in 2019 to 23 last year by turning on and lifting more pitches. He has shown the ability to handle high-velocity fastballs and isn't fazed by quality breaking balls. Vargas' bat definitely should play but the question is where because he lacks speed and quick-twitch athleticism. He has improved his conditioning and his range at third base since turning pro, and he does possess solid arm strength. The Dodgers also have given him time at left field, second base and first base the last two seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a Cuban team that also included Adrian Morejon and Athletics outfield prospect Lazarito Armenteros, Vargas drove in the gold medal-winning run at the 2014 15-and-under World Cup in Mexico. He defected in November 2015 with his father Lazaro, the DH on Cuba's 1992 and 1996 Olympic champions, and waited nearly two years before signing with the Dodgers for $300,000 in September 2017. He hit .314/.387/.447 while reaching high Class A in his first two pro seasons before spending 2020 in instructional league. Los Angeles has pushed Vargas aggressively because he has the advanced bat-to-ball skills to handle the challenge. He understands his right-handed swing mechanics, controls the strike zone and uses the entire field. He began driving the ball in the air more regularly in 2019 and has shown solid power this year as he has gotten more aggressive and turned on more pitches. Because Vargas lacks speed and quick-twitch athleticism, his defensive home is in question. He has worked diligently to improve his conditioning and his range at third base, where he displays solid arm strength. The Dodgers are pleased with his progress at the hot corner, while scouts in other organizations wonder if he's destined for first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A supplemental second-round choice out of a Southern California high school in 2017, Freeman has established himself as one of the best pure hitters in the Minors. He hit .292 or better in each of his first four pro seasons, won the short-season New York-Penn League batting title at .352 in 2018 and entered 2022 with a career .319 mark along with a tiny 9 percent strikeout rate. He was contending for another batting crown in the Double-A Northeast last June when he slightly tore the labrum in his left shoulder on a swing, leading to surgery that ended his season after 41 games, but he still claimed a spot on Cleveland's 40-man roster in November. His younger brother Cody is a catcher in the Rangers system with similar tools. A right-handed hitter, Freeman possesses exceptional bat-to-ball skills that produce line drives to all fields on a regular basis. He rarely swings and misses, but the ease with which he makes contact cuts into his on-base ability because he owns a career 4 percent walk rate. He also homered just nine times in his first 272 pro games, so he might fit a Nick Madrigal high-average/low-impact profile, though he does drive some balls to the gaps and offers some doubles power. Freeman's bat is his lone plus tool, and his speed, arm and defense all grade as average. He does have good instincts that allow him to play above his physical ability on the bases and in the field. He's an aggressive baserunner and a sure-handed fielder with a quick release on his throws, though many scouts think he'll eventually shift from shortstop to second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of Southern California's best high school hitters in 2017, Freeman gave up a Texas Christian scholarship to sign with the Indians as a supplemental second-round Draft pick. One of several sweet-swinging infielders with a high baseball IQ in Cleveland's system, he won the short-season New York-Penn League batting title (.352) in ‘18 and batted .306/.368/.410 between two Class A levels as an encore. He continued to excel in Double-A this year, but sustained a slight tear in his labrum in his left shoulder on a swing, necessitating surgery that ended his season after 41 games. His younger brother Cody was a Rangers fourth-rounder in ‘19 and possesses similar tools. While Freeman's hitting ability is his only plus tool, he does have some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the entire Minor Leagues. He batted .319 with a 9 percent strikeout rate in his first three pro seasons, lashing line drives to all fields from the right side of the plate. He could develop 15-homer power if he adds strength and learns to drive the ball in the air more often, though he may never walk much because he makes contact so easily. Freeman's instincts allow him to play quicker on the bases and at shortstop than his average speed. He's an aggressive baserunner with a knack for stealing bases and is a reliable defender with sure hands at short. He enhances his average arm strength by getting rid of the ball quickly, though many scouts think he's destined for second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Henry vaulted onto the radar with his first five starts of 2019, including a complete-game one-hitter with 13 strikeouts against The Citadel on just 88 pitches. The D-backs took Henry with the No. 74 overall pick in the Draft, then watched as the southpaw fired a 10-strikeout three-hit shutout against Florida State to help lead Michigan into the College World Series Finals. Henry’s stuff ticked up at the alternate training site in 2020 and he carried that momentum into 2021, when he made his full-season debut with Double-A Amarillo. Pitching in an offense-friendly league, Henry posted a 5.21 ERA and struck out 135 over 115 2/3 innings with multiple D-backs officials saying he threw better than the numbers indicated. Henry's stuff has improved since his time at Michigan. After throwing in the mid-80s as a freshman and sophomore, his fastball now sits between 90-94 mph and can touch 95-96. He locates the fastball to both sides of the plate and impressed with his ability to miss bats in Double-A (10.5 K/9). His fading changeup has grown more than any of his other offerings over the past two seasons and his low-80s slider serves as his out pitch. Henry has also developed a curveball, and although it needs refinement, it shows promise. An underrated athlete, Henry has an easy delivery -- though his mechanics, and therefore his velocity, fluctuate at times. That being said, plus control allows Henry to throw all his pitches for strikes. He fared well when the D-backs challenged him with an aggressive assignment to Double-A in his professional debut, showing growth throughout the season and improving as the year went on. A consistent performer, Henry has already pitched his way to Arizona with a strong season at Triple-A Reno and should get consideration for a long-term Major League rotation spot the rest of the way in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Henry was steady as a freshman reliever and sophomore starter at Michigan, but he wasn't a priority target after sitting in the mid-80s with his fastball in the Cape Cod League. Then he was spectacular in his first five starts of 2019, including a complete-game one-hitter with 13 strikeouts against The Citadel on just 88 pitches, looking like the Wolverines' best pitching prospect since Jim Abbott. The D-backs took Henry with the No. 74 overall pick in the Draft, then watched as the southpaw fired a two-hit, 10-strikeout shutout against Florida State to help lead Michigan into the College World Series finals. Henry’s stuff ticked up at the alternate training site in 2020 and he carried that momentum into 2021, when he made his full-season debut with Double-A Amarillo. Henry's stuff has improved since his time at Michigan. While his fastball still sits in the low 90s, he’s also shown an ability to dial it up to 95-96. He locates the fastball to both sides of the plate and has impressed with his ability to miss bats in Double-A. He also throws a changeup with good fading action and a slider with depth, with both offerings registering in the upper 70s to low 80s. He’s a good athlete with an easy delivery that he repeats well. Henry is an underrated athlete, one of those guys who can drive a golf ball or kick a field goal and he has a tremendous competitive streak. The D-backs challenged Henry, assigning him to Double-A in his first full season, and he responded well. A consistent performer, he has a chance to move quickly through the system and develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite hitting just .249 in three seasons at Sacramento State, Outman showcased an interesting package of tools that enticed Los Angeles to select him in the seventh round of the 2018 Draft. He homered 11 times in the final month of the 2019 season in Single-A and has continued to get better after returning from the pandemic layoff in 2020. He batted .294/.393/.586 with 31 homers between Double-A and Triple-A last season, leading all Dodgers farmhands in slugging and OPS (.978), and homered off Germán Márquez in his first big league at-bat in July. Outman has taken off at the plate after making significant adjustments to his left-handed swing, gained a better understanding of it and calming down his approach. He still prioritizes damage by looking to launch balls to his pull side, but his ability to tap into his bat speed and strength could result in 25 or more homers per season. His aggressive hunt for power does lead to strikeouts, though he offsets his whiffs by consistently drawing walks and getting hit by pitches to post high batting averages. Outman has the ability to contribute in all phases of the game. One of the best athletes in the system, he has plus speed and has stolen bases at a 77 percent clip in the Minors. He's a quality center fielder who can fit anywhere in the outfield with his ability to cover ground and his strong arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Outman batted just .249 in three seasons at Sacramento State, the Dodgers bought into his intriguing all-around tools and selected him in the seventh round of the 2018 Draft. He began to break out with 11 homers in the final month of the 2019 season in Low-A and took another step forward in the second half of 2021, batting .297/.392/.568 while advancing to Double-A. He built on that momentum in the Arizona Fall League and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster. Outman began to perform better at the plate as he gained a better understanding of his left-handed swing. He still aggressively looks to launch balls to his pull side, but slowing things down enabled him to chase fewer pitches out of the zone and access his plus raw power more consistently. He still strikes out too much to post high batting averages, though he compensates by drawing plenty of walks and hit by pitches. One of the best athletes in the system, Outman is a 6-foot-3, 215-pounder with plus speed and arm strength. He has aptitude for stealing bases and swiped 23 in 27 attempts last season. He has instincts to go with his quickness in center field and provides plus defense at any of the three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Orioles assistant general manager Sig Mejdal broke into baseball with the Cardinals, he famously targeted a college infielder for the team’s top pick in the 2005 Draft, believing the player was undervalued. That player was Jed Lowrie, whom St. Louis passed on and who went on to enjoy a productive big league career as a versatile switch-hitting second baseman. Mejdal never forgot that oversight, and now, the system he oversees sports a player with a similar profile in Terrin Vavra. The story goes a long way toward explaining why the Orioles targeted Vavra as part of their return package in the 2020 Mychal Givens trade with the Rockies. A bat-first second baseman who can also play some outfield, Vavra was Colorado’s third-round pick in 2018 out of the University of Minnesota. His baseball family ties run deep: He is the son of former Twins and Tigers hitting coach Joe Vavra, and has two brothers who also played pro ball. He had a standout career at Minnesota and built on that success immediately, earning South Atlantic League MVP honors in ’19. He then had a productive but incomplete first year in Baltimore’s system, posting a .388 on-base percentage at Double-A Bowie in ’21 but missing more than two months with back issues. The Orioles added him to their 40-man roster in November. On the field, Vavra’s natural feel to hit stands out more than anything else. He works counts and knows the strike zone extremely well, walking nearly as much as he's struck out in his Minor League career. He’s known as a gamer who manipulates the bat head well and rarely gets fooled, consistently squaring up the baseball from both sides of the plate. The power is only fringe to average, though he’s shown more from the left side of the plate thus far. Defensively, Vavra profiles best at second but also showed well in center field in a small sample last summer. He’s likely to move around at the highest level rather than settle at one position, profiling as an offensive-minded utility type who hits his way into the lineup every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies' 2018 third-round pick after a standout career at the University of Minnesota, Vavra built on that success immediately in pro ball, earning South Atlantic League MVP honors in 2019. He arrived in the Orioles system the following year, as part of the Mychal Givens trade prior to the 2020 Deadline. Vavra is known as a gamer whose baseball bloodlines run deep: He is the son of former Twins and Tigers hitting coach Joe Vavra, and has two brothers who also played pro ball. On the field, Vavra’s natural feel to hit stands out more than anything else. He works counts and knows the strike zone extremely well, walking as much as he struck out in 2019. The switch-hitter manipulates the bat head and doesn’t get fooled, consistently squaring up the baseball and spraying line drives to all fields from both sides of the plate. It is a hit-first profile with fringe to average power, though he’s shown more from the left side of the plate thus far. Described by Orioles people as a “Moneyball-style second baseman,” Vavra profiles better defensively at the position than at short. The likelier scenario is that he moves around, seeing time at third and in the outfield as well in ’21, with an eye toward maximizing his versatility. Even if he doesn’t settle into one position, he could easily be an offensive-minded utility type who hits his way into the lineup every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading Vanderbilt to the 2019 College World Series title while pacing NCAA Division I with 27 homers and 192 total bases, Bleday signed for $6.67 million as the No. 4 overall pick in the Draft. He was overly aggressive in his pro debut in High-A and batted just .212/.323/.373 with 12 homers in 110 Double-A games last season, when he generated a lot of harmless flyball contact. He did rake in the hitter-friendly Arizona Fall League and looked more like the guy who dominated in college, but has exuded a power-over-hit vibe while earning his first big league callup in 2022. Bleday has said that he tried to do too much in 2021, when a slow start snowballed on him, and he believes he has made the necessary adjustments (lowering his hands, using his legs more, regaining a disciplined approach) to be productive going forward. With his smooth left-handed swing and his bat speed, strength and leverage, he has the tools to hit for both average and power. After reporting to Spring Training looking stronger than ever after adding 20 pounds of muscle, he has launched more fly balls to his pull side than in the past while also striking out at a higher rate than ever before. While his offensive performance has been puzzling, Bleday has upgraded other aspects of his game such as his quickness and defense. He's a fringy runner out of the batter's box but average underway, and his instincts help him play faster on the bases and in the outfield. He's a capable center fielder but fits best in right field, where he's at least a solid defender with a plus arm that once made him a two-way prospect as a Florida high schooler.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts voted Bleday the top prospect in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2018 and he rode that momentum to a banner junior season, leading Vanderbilt to a College World Series championship while topping NCAA Division I in homers (27) and total bases (192). The Marlins put him on the fast track immediately after drafting him fourth overall and signing him for a then-franchise-record $6.67 million, sending him to high Class A for his pro debut. Though his only experience last year came at Miami's alternate training site and the instructional league, he seemed on course to reach the big leagues at some point in 2021 but instead has endured a rough season in Double-A. In college, Bleday first emerged as an advanced hitter with a quality left-handed swing and a disciplined approach. His power began to emerge on the Cape and he projected as a potential 30-homer threat thanks to his bat speed, strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame. While the Marlins aren't overly concerned with his performance this year and attribute it to struggling with some mechanical adjustments, evaluators outside the organization note that he has lost weight and isn't making quality contact as much as he did in the past. Bleday used his pandemic downtime to improve his conditioning and quickness. He's a fringy runner whose instincts allow him to play faster than that on the bases and in the outfield. While he saw time in all three spots last summer, he fits best in right field, where he can be a solid defender with a plus arm that made him a two-way prospect as a Florida high schooler.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring for three seasons at Minnesota, Meyer matched Hall of Famer Paul Molitor as the highest pick in Golden Gophers history when he went third overall and signed for $6.7 million in 2020. He won Double-A South pitcher of the year accolades and ranked fifth in the Minors with a 2.27 ERA in his 2021 pro debut before reaching the bigs the following July. His elbow gave out in his second start with the Marlins, leading to Tommy John surgery that sidelined him throughout 2023, but he made a triumphant return to the Majors this April. Meyer long has been famous for his wipeout slider, which sits in the upper 80s with plenty of horizontal movement as well as two-plane depth. His fastball sits at 94-96 mph with riding action and reached triple digits when he worked shorter stints in college. He has improved his feel for his changeup since turning pro, a solid offering that can get a bit firm in the upper 80s. Though Meyer lacks size and his elbow reconstruction will add to questions about his long-term durability as a starter, he helps his cause with his strength and athleticism. He has a fluid delivery that he repeats well and never has had any issues throwing strikes. His competitiveness enhances his package as possible No. 2 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meyer starred for three seasons at Minnesota before going third overall in the 2020 Draft, matching Hall of Famer Paul Molitor as the highest pick in Golden Gophers history and signing for a Marlins-record $6.7 million. Sent to Double-A for his 2021 pro debut, he answered the challenge by winning Double-A South pitcher of the year honors and ranking fifth in the Minors in ERA (2.27). He missed a month with nerve irritation in his elbow last season yet still made his big league debut in July, only to have his elbow blow out in his second start with Miami and result in Tommy John surgery that will sideline him for all of 2023. Meyer's slider wasn't quite as dominant as advertised in his pro debut but returned to wipeout status last year, sitting in the upper 80s with outstanding horizontal action and two-plane depth as well. His fastball added a couple of ticks of velocity, parking at 94-96 mph with riding action, and he has reached triple digits in shorter stints in the past. He also upgraded his feel for his changeup, which is a bit firm in the upper 80s but features good fade and serves as a solid third pitch. His lack of size did lead to concerns about Meyer's durability, and his elbow reconstruction will create more questions, though he does have the strength and athleticism to remain a starter. He repeats his fluid delivery well and made progress with his control and command in 2022. If he can't last in the rotation, he has the stuff and competitiveness to be a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meyer tied a Minnesota record with 16 saves as a freshman in 2018 before dominating as a starter in his next two college seasons. He went third overall in the 2020 Draft, matching Hall of Famer Paul Molitor as the highest pick in Golden Gophers history, and he signed for a Marlins-record $6.7 million. Challenged with a Double-A assignment at the outset of his 2021 pro debut, he responded by capturing Double-A South pitcher of the year honors and ranking fifth in the Minors in ERA (2.27), including two overpowering starts in Triple-A to cap his year. Meyer made his big league debut this July but two weeks later was diagnosed with a torn elbow ligament that required Tommy John surgery. Meyer's slider was the consensus best pitch in the 2020 Draft, and while it wasn't quite as dominant last summer, it was still a well-above-average offering that usually ranged from 85-89 mph with tremendous horizontal break and some depth as well. His fastball sits at 92-95 mph and can reach 100 with riding action up in the strike zone. While he had little need for a changeup in college, his fading mid-80s cambio shows potential but needs more consistency. Though he's just 6 feet tall, Meyer is strong and athletic and repeats his fluid delivery well. After battling the strike zone in his first two months as a pro, he did a better job of trusting his stuff afterward. Now the next step will be refining his command. While there's no reason he shouldn't pitch in the front half of a big league rotation, his stuff and competitive makeup could make him a lights-out closer if so desired.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meyer made an immediate impact at Minnesota, tying a school record with 16 saves as a freshman in 2018 and leading the U.S. collegiate national team with seven that summer, then continued to dominate after moving into the rotation as a sophomore. He posted a 1.95 ERA with 46 strikeouts in 27 2/3 innings during the truncated 2020 college season and went third overall in the Draft, matching Hall of Famer Paul Molitor as the highest pick in Golden Gophers history. After signing for a Miami-record $6.7 million, he participated in alternate camp and instructional league. Meyer had the best pitch in the 2020 Draft, a wipeout slider that reaches the low 90s and with which he can add and subtract depth. He also can blow away hitters with a four-seam fastball that sits at 93-97 mph, clocked at 98 in the ninth inning of one start last spring and tops out at 100. He surprised the Marlins with his feel for a changeup that he didn't need much in college, and his mid-80s offering with fade could give him a solid third option. Though Meyer is listed as just 6 feet tall, he has erased any concerns about whether his size would prevent him from becoming an impact starter. He's strong and athletic, showing the ability to repeat a fluid delivery and fill the strike zone with premium stuff. A tough competitor who got semiregular at-bats in Minnesota's lineup, he should move quickly through the Minors.
