mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As Garcia has risen in the Royals’ farm system, so has his potential. The cousin of Royals postseason hero Alcides Escobar and Braves star Ronald Acuña, Garcia signed with the Royals out of Venezuela in 2016. He burst onto the scene in 2021 as he got stronger and developed a contact-oriented approach at the plate, leading the Royals to add him to the 40-man roster. His stock only continued to rise in 2022, when he made his debut on July 15, playing in nine big league games. He finished the year in Triple-A Omaha, where he posted an .804 OPS. Over the winter, he just kept hitting: Garcia slashed .323/.444/.498 in 58 games in winter ball, walking more times (46) than striking out (31). With an unorthodox setup at the plate, Garcia is a contact-oriented hitter who has excellent hand-eye coordination and uses the entire field. He hit 11 homers in 2022 -- six more than the previous four seasons combined -- but he isn’t a home run hitter. Instead, he relies on his gap-to-gap power with speed, which helped him to 34 doubles last year. He brings a consistent approach to the plate and gets on base, where he can then cause trouble because of his plus speed. Garcia is one of the best shortstops in the Royals’ system with a quick first step, above-average arm and great range. He is instinctual at the plate and in the field. There is still projection in Garcia’s wiry frame, but he showed up this spring stronger as he continues to physically mature. Evaluators see strength as the difference between him becoming a utilityman or a starting middle infielder. Garcia will compete for a roster spot this spring, but it’s likely he returns to Triple-A and serves as infield depth knowing he’ll get a callup at some point in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The cousin of Royals postseason hero Alcides Escobar, Garcia signed with the Royals during the 2016-17 international signing period and is looking to follow in his cousin’s footsteps with Kansas City in the coming years. Like Escobar, Garcia is a shortstop, and he burst onto the scene in 2021 with a lot of contact and tons of walks between Low-A and High-A this year. That ability, plus his defense, earned him a spot on the 40-man roster in the offseason for protection from the Rule 5 Draft. Garcia’s skillset is contact over power -- he hit .291 last season with only four home runs -- and he can get on base, posting a .380 on-base percentage across the two levels in 2021. As he’s risen in the system, he’s seen his walk rate improve and his strikeout rate decrease. And when he’s on base, he creates havoc with his speed. He stole 35 bases last season and has 83 in his Minor League career. Defensively, Garcia is as consistent of a shortstop as the Royals have in their system with a quick first step, above average arm and great instincts. The Royals aren’t lacking depth at shortstop, and Garcia is near the top of that list. Some see the lack of physicality in his small frame as the biggest hurdle for him to be a big leaguer. But he does have wiry strength, and being only 21 years old, there’s still projection in his body. The Royals put Garcia on the 40-man because of his contact skills and glove, and that’s already born fruit as they gave him his Major League debut on July 15. Bobby Witt Jr.’s presence at short complicates matters a little, but Garcia gives Kansas City another potential everyday player at the six -- a good problem to have for a team building around its youth.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Massey -- no relation to the Royals second baseman of the same name -- was a dominant reliever at Wake Forest in 2023, striking out 76 batters over 41 2/3 innings while holding opponents to a .161 average before converting to a starter in his junior season with mixed results. After hamstring and back injuries, he moved back to the bullpen in late May, but he dropped to the fourth round of the 2024 Draft, where the Tigers signed him for a $522,500 bonus. Massey combines the core ingredients of a potentially dominant reliever with secondary pitches that could allow him to grow into an effective starter; the Tigers tweaked his pitch usage to aid him in the latter. His fastball ranges from 93-97 mph but plays big with a lot of ride, allowing him to beat hitters to the top of the strike zone. His 82-85 slider has plenty of drop, allowing him to work the bottom of the zone. His starting arsenal includes a changeup to attack left-handed hitters and a curveball. The Tigers plan on having Massey work as a starter to begin his pro career. Still, they have a history of finding successful late-inning relievers out of converted starters, from Michael Fulmer to Shane Greene to Alex Lange. How Massey develops his secondary pitches will likely determine his career path.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A back injury that limited his time in the field during his junior year at Illinois caused Massey’s Draft stock fall, but he was still able to post an .831 OPS. The Royals jumped at the chance to take him in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, signing him for just below slot at $312,500. Massey was still hindered by the back injury during Rookie ball and his first instructional league, but his work with the Royals' training staff and increased focused on his mobility saw him enjoy a strong and healthy campaign in High-A Quad Cities in 2021 -- with his 21 homers more than he hit in all three years at Illinois. The Royals knew Massey had power as an amateur, but they didn’t know what they would get after the canceled 2020 season. Finally healthy, Massey tapped into his power after working with the Royals hitting development program, but he didn’t lose the contact skills that got him drafted, either, posting an .882 OPS in 99 games for the Bandits. He employs a sweet swing from the left side and makes hard contact to all parts of the field. He may be limited to second base defensively, but he’s made himself into one of the best second basemen the Royals have, winning the Minor League Gold Glove at the position in 2021. He has more range there now that he’s healthy and has shown improved arm strength. Massey picked up right where he left off in 2021 with another powerful season this year at Double-A and Triple-A, where he slugged above .500 and posted an OPS above .900 before joining the big club potentially for good in early August. The offensive improvements over the last two years, along with Massey’s steadiness at second, could make him another sizable piece in KC’s youth movement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pratto entered last year in a similar bucket to his fellow 2017 draftee MJ Melendez. That year’s 14th overall pick had a solid first full season at Class A Lexington, only to hit .191 with nine homers over 472 plate appearances at Class A Advanced Wilmington in 2019. The Royals believed Pratto learned from the experience and were pleased with his performance at the alternate training site in 2020, preceding his breakout. The left-handed slugger swatted 36 homers and finished with a .265/.385/.602 line in 124 games at Double-A and Triple-A last summer. His 71 total extra-base hits were second-most in the Minors, trailing only teammate Bobby Witt Jr.’s 72. Kansas City added Pratto to the 40-man roster in November, protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft. Pratto’s jumps in 2021 were more based in changes to his approach than physical adjustments. Beginning at the alternate training site, he learned to avoid pitches below the knees and mash those more up in the zone. As a result, his ground-ball rate went down, and his fly-ball rate jumped, leading to better power numbers. He also became a more patient hitter. That patience and intent to drive the ball have kept his K numbers high, and that blunts his hit tool. But overall, he possesses an above-average offensive ceiling with the potential for 30-plus homers. His speed is fringy, but he has strong instincts that have helped him swipe 10-plus bags every season thus far. Since his Draft days, the California native has been considered a gifted defender at first base and should provide value there with his athleticism and plus arm. Now back on track, Pratto has the pieces in place to play a large role in the Royals’ next foundation of contention.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pratto was a two-way standout at Huntington Beach (Calif.) High School before emerging as a better hitting prospect as a senior in 2017, when the Royals selected him in the first round of the MLB Draft. He looked like one of the more advanced prep players from his class in his first full season, turning in a strong second half at Class A Lexington to finish with 14 homers and 22 stolen bases, though he lost much of that progress with the move up to Class A Advanced Wilmington in ‘19. Pratto was one of the organization’s most improved and impressive players at the alternate training site in ‘20. After deviating from his strengths in 2019 as he tinkered with several components of his left-handed swing to no avail, Pratto looked like a different hitter in 2020, and that carried into 2021 as well. Employing a more confident approach that led to better decisions, Pratto’s hard-hit rate has shot up, and his whiffs have decreased sharply. After hitting only nine homers at Wilmington two years ago, he cleared 20 with ease in 2021 and shows at least 25-homer potential for the future. One of the best and most efficient baserunners in Kansas City’s system, Pratto compensates for his fringy speed with excellent instinct on the basepaths. Pratto has long been revered for his defensive prowess as a first baseman, with many evaluators giving his glove a 70 grade on the 20-80 scouting scale. His athleticism translates well at the position, while the plus arm that he used to fire upper-80s fastball as a prep is an underrated weapon. Given that defensive ability and his increased offensive production, Pratto has turned himself back into one of the best first-base prospects in baseball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ruiz signed with the Royals in July 2015 out of the Dominican Republic for $100,000. He was sent to the Padres two years later in a six-player trade in the midst of a standout year that earned him 2017 Arizona League MVP honors after slashing .350/.395/.602 with 34 extra-base hits and 26 stolen bases in 52 games between two organizations. Moved again in a 2022 Trade Deadline deal with the Brewers for Josh Hader, it was his overall performance last season that featured a Minor League-leading 85 stolen bases that really caught the attention of the A’s, who acquired him in the three-team deal that sent Sean Murphy to the Braves last December. Ruiz improved across the board as a hitter in ‘22, even showing an uptick in power. His chase rate also went down with better decision-making on pitches outside of the strike zone, which in turn led to career highs in several categories over his 114 games between Double-A and Triple-A. Ruiz’s 80-grade speed is his most tantalizing attribute, and the value shows up in his Minor League stolen-base totals. His legs have also enabled him to transition from second base to center field, a position the A’s feel confident in his ability to handle on an everyday basis. He’ll likely get a shot to prove that belief with Oakland in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Multi-sport high school stars are not uncommon, but those who stand out in hockey and baseball are a bit more unusual. Jones played hockey at a high level before leaving the ice to become one of the best high school hitters in the 2016 Draft class and getting first-round money as Cleveland’s second-round pick that June. He was buzzing his way through the Minors, including going to the Futures Game in 2019, when a combination of struggles and a serious ankle injury slowed him in 2021. Ankle surgery slowed his return in 2022, but he did make it up to the big leagues for the first time and then was sent to the Rockies for Juan Brito during the offseason. Big and strong with tremendous leverage in his left-handed swing, Jones’s raw power has always been apparent, though he hasn’t always been able to tap into it. There’s some length to his swing, which leads to some swing-and-miss, and while he draws walks and works deep counts, that can lead to him being too passive at the plate. He made some adjustments last year to handle breaking stuff better, and he spent the offseason in Scottsdale, with the Rockies preaching more aggression at the plate. The Guardians had moved Jones to the outfield, largely because of the presence of José Ramírez in Cleveland. He’ll still get reps in both outfielder corners, with the athleticism and arm to do so, but he’ll get back to seeing time on the dirt, both at his natural third as well as first base, with the chance to get his bat into the big league lineup regularly while moving around the corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout hockey center before concussion issues forced him to leave the sport, Jones emerged as one of the best high school hitters in the 2016 class and landed first-round money ($2.25 million) as a second-rounder. After performing well throughout the Minors, including leading the short-season New York-Penn League in OPS (.912) in '17 and the Minors in walks (96) in '19, he spent time playing the outfield during instructional league in '20 and appeared on the verge of filling a void in Cleveland. Jones struggled in Triple-A in '21 and sustained a left high ankle sprain that required surgery that kept him sidelined until May 2022, but he bounced back to solve Triple-A pitching and earned his first big league callup in July before being sent to the Rockies for Juan Brito in November. With his bat speed, strength and the leverage in his left-handed swing, Jones has tremendous raw power and a patient approach. At the same time, his naturally long stroke and willingness to work deep counts always will result in strikeouts. He has made some adjustments to better deal with breaking balls in 2022, though the Guardians protected him by using him almost exclusively against right-handers in the Majors. Though he possesses below-average speed, Jones is reasonably athletic for his size and worked hard to become a competent third baseman. His arm strength never has been a question, and he has improved his footwork, agility and range. Cleveland had moved Jones to the outfield because of José Ramírez at the hot corner, and he's at least an adequate defender in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A standout hockey center before concussion issues forced him to focus on baseball, Jones developed into one of the best prep hitters in the 2016 Draft and signed for first-round money ($2.25 million) in the second round. He has performed well everywhere he has played as a pro, and in 2019 he led the Minors with 96 walks, advanced to Double-A at age 21 and played in both the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and the Arizona Fall League's Fall Stars Game. His only action in 2020 came at alternative camp and in instructional league, and he stood out in both places with his offensive approach and dedication to improving his defense. Jones exudes patience at the plate, waiting for pitches he can hammer and taking walks if pitchers decline to challenge him. His combination of bat speed and strength plus the loft and leverage in his left-handed swing give him well above-average power that plays to all fields. His willingness to work deep counts and the length in his naturally long stroke do lead to strikeouts, an acceptable tradeoff for his pop and on-base ability, though he'll have to make adjustments to solve left-handers after hitting .167/.316/.286 against them in his first two years of full-season ball. Jones has more athleticism than his below-average speed would indicate and has worked to transition from a high school shortstop into an acceptable third baseman. He has the strong arm desired at the hot corner and his footwork, agility and range all have gotten better since he turned pro. Because the Indians have José Ramirez at third and need outfielders, they began working him at the latter position during instructional league.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bello has gone from getting passed over in the 2015 and 2016 international signing periods to turning pro for a mere $28,000 in 2017 to ranking as Boston's top pitching prospect five years later. He initially struggled when he skipped two levels and jumped to Low-A in 2019, but he finished strong that summer and then looked better than ever at the Red Sox's instructional league program in 2020 following the pandemic layoff. He maintained his improved stuff throughout 2021, when he reached Double-A, pitched in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster. After using his pandemic downtime to get stronger, Bello has seen his fastball go from sitting at 92-95 mph in 2019 to parking at 95-97 and pushing triple digits. His heater is fairly straight and is vulnerable when he doesn't locate it where he wants, so he might benefit it from mixing in some two-seamers with sink. He has refined his changeup into a consistent plus offering in the mid-80s with fade and depth, and his slider features similar velocity and upside. Bello has three quality pitches, throws enough strikes and generates plenty of swings and misses as well as weak groundball contact. He has the potential to pitch in the front half of a big league rotation, and to get there he'll have to refine his command and show that his fastball will work well against more advanced hitters. If not, he still has a high floor as a multiple-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bello signed for $28,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the relatively advanced age of 18 in 2017. He dominated the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in his pro debut the following year but struggled for three months when he skipped two levels and jumped to low Class A in 2019. He finished strong down the stretch that summer and showed some of the best pure stuff at Boston's instructional league program in 2020. Bello's four-seam fastball sat at 92-95 mph during the 2019 season and parked at 95 while touching 98 in shorter stints during instructs. His heater features modest life and can get hammered when he struggles to command it, so he might be better off trying to sink a two-seamer, which he has shown some aptitude for. Both his slider and fading changeup reside in the mid-80s and show flashes of becoming plus pitches, with the changeup having the most upside in his entire arsenal. With the ability to throw strikes, miss bats and elicit ground-ball contact with three solid or better pitches, Bello has mid-rotation upside. Some scouts don't love his fastball characteristics and wonder how well it will play against more advanced hitters, however. He's athletic and still has some projection remaining, so he could add some more velocity in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hill was a bit of a late bloomer in the Tigers system, though not for lack of results. He was 22 years old when Detroit drafted him in the 26nd round in 2018, posted a 2.25 ERA and 129 strikeouts across Class A ball in 2019, lost 2020 to the pandemic, then fanned 99 batters over 75 2/3 innings between High-A West Michigan and Double-A Erie last year. He backed it up with 21 strikeouts over 13 2/3 innings in the Arizona Fall League, which caught scouts’ attention. Hill’s fastball sits in the low 90s, but he has an assortment of breaking balls to go with a nasty splitter. When he does allow contact, it tends to be on the ground. He has allowed just eight home runs over 237 1/3 innings in his Minor League career. The big question with Hill has been how much advantage he has gained being an older pitcher at each level, though he looked solid against Detroit’s top prospects in Minor League minicamp. Despite Hill’s success, the Tigers left him off their 40-man roster going into 2022. He forced his way onto it with impressive upper-level performances to begin the season, earning his Major League debut on July 4. Because of his solid command, he’s been able to overcome a lack of standout stuff and could continue to be a reliable backend starter for Detroit in the years ahead.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stefanic put up huge numbers at Westmont College, an NAIA school in California, leaving the school as the career leader in a host of offensive categories, including hits and total bases. Despite hitting .392 his senior year, he went undrafted in 2018, signing as a free agent with the Angels. He managed to hit his way to Triple-A in 2021, finishing the breakout season with a .336/.408/.493 line across two levels. As the numbers show, Stefanic has pretty much hit wherever he’s been. He makes a ridiculous amount of contact, with a miniscule 12.7 percent strikeout rate in his pro career heading into 2022. He didn’t sacrifice any of that in 2021 even with some power starting to show up. There’s a little more pop to his pull side, but he showed in Triple-A (where he hit 16 of his 17 homers last year) that he can drive the ball the other way as well. While there is growing confidence that Stefanic would hit Major League pitching, there are large questions about how to get that bat into the lineup. He’s a below-average defender with a below-average arm who has played several positions in the Minors. He’s played second base the most and the hope is he can be acceptable enough there to earn big league at-bats.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A part-time player in his first two college seasons at California, Lee had a huge year in 2019 batting behind No. 3 overall pick Andrew Vaughn. Most clubs regarded Lee as more of a third-round talent, but the Astros loved his massive raw power and arm strength and made him a surprise first-round pick, signing him for a below-slot $1.75 million at No. 32. He made his big league debut with 12 games with Houston in 2022 but spent all of this season in Triple-A before getting traded to the White Sox for Kendall Graveman in late July. The Astros worked with Lee to quiet his load and shorten his stride after he turned pro, but he was still an extreme power-over-hit guy before 2023. After previously trying to get the most out of his well above-average raw power by launching balls to his pull side, he has settled down this season. Though he's making more contact, he's doing a lot less damage. Lee didn't become a full-time catcher until 2019 and has yet to start more than 73 games behind the plate in a pro season. While he's quicker and more athletic than most backstops and features plus-plus arm strength, his receiving and blocking skills draw mixed reviews. He has done a better job in 2023 and the consensus is that he's an average defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lee went from posting a .724 OPS as a part-time player in his first two college seasons at California to batting .337/.416/.619 in 2019 while batting behind No. 3 overall pick Andrew Vaughn. Though most teams evaluated Lee as more of a third-round talent, the Astros bought into his raw power and arm strength and selected him 32nd overall, where he signed for a below-slot $1.75 million. After losing a year of development to the pandemic layoff, he moved from High-A to Triple-A during his 2021 full-season debut and demonstrated improvement on both sides of the ball. Since turning pro, Lee has quieted his load, shortened his stride and added more balance at the plate, which has allowed him to drive balls in the air from gap to gap more easily. A right-handed hitter, he still can tap into more of his well above-average raw power if he can further reduce his tendency to make ground-ball contact. His approach has deteriorated in 2022, as he has gotten more pull-happy and looked helpless against breaking balls. Lee didn't become a full-time catcher until 2019 and continues to develop behind the plate. He's quicker and more athletic than most backstops and the hope is that he can become an average receiver and blocker as he gains more experience. The Astros have helped him get more out of his plus-plus arm strength by shortening his throwing stroke, and he erased 43 percent of basestealers last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After batting .243/.332/.392 as a part-timer in his first two college seasons at California, Lee surged to a .337/.416/.619 line in 2019 while hitting behind No. 3 overall pick Andrew Vaughn. Though most clubs viewed Lee as a third-round talent, the Astros loved his raw power and arm strength and made him a surprise first-rounder, signing him for a below-slot $1.75 million at No. 32. He bought a pitching machine for his home, which enabled him to work on his hitting and receiving during the pandemic layoff, before making a brief appearance at Houston's alternate site and participating in instructional league last fall. While in instructional league, Lee focused on maintaining some mechanical changes at the plate. He has quieted his load, shortened his stride and improved his balance, allowing him to drive the ball from gap to gap more easily. His bat speed and strength give him raw pop to all fields from the right side of the plate, and home runs should come naturally if he just concentrates on making hard contact and managing the strike zone. Lee also saw time at both infield corners and DH in college and didn't become a full-time catcher until 2019. He has the athleticism and quickness to remain behind the plate and is making strides with his receiving, which should become at least average with more experience. The Astros have shortened his arm stroke, making him even more effective at deterring the running game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Winder entered pro ball as a pitchability right-hander, a seventh-rounder in 2018 from Virginia Military Institute who carved up lower-level hitters because of his impressive feel for pitching. Since that time, his stuff has consistently improved, and in 2021, he showed that the physical gains he made during the shutdown were for real as he pitched his way from Double-A to Triple-A and appeared in the Futures Game. Only a shoulder strain, which ended his season in late July, put a cloud over the breakout performance, but he was still added to the Twins’ 40-man roster and given a clean bill of health. The 6-foot-5 Winder has seen his velocity uptick since signing, sitting in the low-90s during his first full season in 2019 and averaging 95 mph (touching 98 mph) last season, maintaining the burst he had shown in instructional league play after the shutdown. His mid-80s slider flashes plus, and he has very good feel for his changeup, an offspeed pitch that doesn’t offer huge speed differential but does feature excellent depth and elicited a 53-percent swing-and-miss rate last year. He folds in an average curve as well. Winder’s improved stuff has not come at the sacrifice of his command as he walked just 1.6 per nine a year ago. The biggest question is the health of his shoulder. If he can put the injury behind him, he has the chance to be a mid-rotation type big league starter in the very near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins’ seventh-round pick in the 2018 Draft out of Virginia Military Institute, Winder provides an interesting test case in terms of how to evaluate developmental progress during 2020’s lost season. A touch-and-feel kind of right-hander entering pro ball, one who led the Midwest League in ERA and WHIP during his first full season, Winder showed up for instructional league play last fall more physical and throwing a lot harder, something that carried over into his 2021 season, and he earned a Futures Game nod for his efforts. Winder worked hard during the shutdown to add strength to his 6-foot-5 frame, and it showed. After sitting in the low 90s throughout the 2019 season, he was up to 98 mph consistently during instructs, albeit in a smaller sample size, throwing it with good riding life. He added velocity to his curve as well, touching the low 80s with more spin, giving him a second above-average pitch. He still throws a distinct slider, and his average changeup now potentially has a better separation in terms of velocity from his fastball. The big right-hander has always had a knack for finding the strike zone, with a 2.0 BB/9 rate in the Minors entering the 2021 season after a 1.7 rate at VMI. The velocity and stuff gains seem to be for real, allowing Winder to keep climbing the charts as one of the biggest starting pitcher sleeper prospects in the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Proctor was already an interesting enough prospect for the Rays entering the 2020 season. A third-round pick out of Rice University in the 2018 Draft, the infielder was viewed as a great teammate with a high baseball IQ, good defensive skills at multiple positions and a solid bat. He hit .290/.383/.402 with 29 doubles in 121 games for High-A Bowling Green in 2019, hardly numbers to scoff at. Last year, perhaps seeing the writing on the wall with the number of infield prospects in the Rays’ system, Proctor came to the Rays with an intriguing idea: What if he moved behind the plate? The Rays believed Proctor possessed a lot of the leadership skills and instincts they value in their catchers, so they gave it a shot. And unlike most Minor Leaguers in 2020, Proctor had chances to prove himself behind the plate. The Texan played in the Constellation Energy League, at their alternate training site and instructional league camp, and for Perth in the Australian Baseball League, giving him plenty of time to practice his swing and, more importantly, work on his new position. By the end of the year, the Rays saw encouraging early returns that suggested he was already among their best catchers, and he was still hitting the ball about as hard as anyone at their alternate site. Proctor is a line drive-spraying left-handed hitter with an all-fields approach, and he’s an above-average defensive infielder who could mold himself into at least an average defensive catcher. The Rays were thrilled by not only his willingness to add a position to his repertoire, but the mindset he took toward finding additional avenues to playing time. He doesn’t have to be an everyday catcher, but he could carve out a niche on any roster with that skill-set. With the exceedingly rare, Austin Barnes-type versatility as an infielder and catcher, he made himself into a potentially valuable player during a season viewed as “lost” for many prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maryland's top high school prospect in 2015, Morris had Tommy John surgery a week before the Draft and redshirted during his first college season at South Carolina. He has performed well since the Guardians made him a seventh-round pick in 2018, but he also has worked just 106 innings combined in the past two seasons because of repeated shoulder issues. He made his big league debut last September, allowing a total of five runs in five starts and pitching two scoreless frames against the Yankees in the American League Division Series. Morris threw harder than ever in 2022, working at 93-95 mph and peaking at 98 with high spin rates and good carry on his four-seam fastball. He has a second plus pitch in a tumbling 81-85 mph changeup that dies at the plate, and big leaguers went 2-for-18 with 11 strikeouts against it. His breaking balls lag behind the rest of his arsenal, though both his 87-92 mph cutter and 78-82 mph curveball are average offerings. Though Morris has a long arm action, he repeats his delivery well, provides strikes and locates pitches well. With his arsenal and history of throwing strikes, he could fill a variety of roles in Cleveland from mid-rotation starter to late-inning reliever. The Guardians would like to deploy him as a starter but his inconsistent health may land him in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maryland's best high school prospect in the 2015 Draft, Morris had Tommy John surgery a week before the Draft and redshirted in his first year of college at South Carolina. A seventh-round pick in 2018, he made a strong pro debut the following year but lost 2020 to the pandemic shutdown and came down with a sore shoulder last spring. He looked better than ever when he returned to the mound last July, logging a 1.62 ERA with 93 strikeouts in 61 innings between Double-A and Triple-A to earn a spot on the 40-man roster. When he's 100 percent, Morris works at 92-95 mph and reaches 97 with high spin rates and good carry on his four-seam fastball. His tumbling 82-85 changeup disappears at the plate and gives him a second plus pitch at its best. After he showed little feel for a slider in college, he has reshaped it into a solid upper-70s curveball with downer break, and he's also beginning to unveil an upper-80s cutter. While Morris has a long arm action, he did a better job of repeating his delivery and commanding his repertoire in 2021. With three solid or better offerings and a history of throwing strikes, he offers the upside of a mid-rotation starter. To get there, he'll have to show that he can stay healthy and maintain quality stuff throughout a full pro season, and he missed the first three months of this season after straining his shoulder during Spring Training.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Logue pitched in a few different roles at Kentucky, moving between the bullpen and rotation, and put up a very strong Cape Cod League showing in ’16 as a reliever. His junior year at Kentucky wasn’t his strongest (4.97 ERA), but the Blue Jays selected him in the ninth round of the ’17 Draft, signing him to a $125,000 bonus. After a strong pro debut in ’17, Logue hauled 154 1/3 innings in ’18 with a 3.15 ERA between Low-A and High-A. He spent most of ’19 in Double-A before the lost ’20 season, then split ’21 between Double-A and Triple-A with a 3.67 ERA over 125 innings. He’ll now get the chance to make the next step with the A’s, who acquired him as part of the four-prospect package they received for Matt Chapman in March. “Solid” is the word you’ll hear for Logue. While none of his pitches or velocities stand out as truly dominant, the lefty has an advanced feel for pitching and has already shown at multiple stops in the Minor Leagues that he’s not only capable of handling a full workload, but adjusting his way through a season. With his fastball up to the 92- to 93-mph range, a recent addition for Logue is a cutter in the mid-to-high 80s that morphed out of his slider, which helps against lefties. Add in that slider and a plus changeup, and you’ve got a deep arsenal coming from the left side with good control of the zone and a very low walk rate (1.9 BB/9 in ’21). Logue was added to the 40-man roster this past offseason and he should be in line to help the A’s big league rotation soon. The addition of that cutter has helped him bump his strikeout rate (10.4 K/9 in ’21), which gives him a real opportunity to develop into a back-end Major League starter long-term instead of as a depth piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Named Jeter Deion Downs in honor of a couple of iconic athletes, Downs signed with the Reds for $1,822,500 as a 2017 supplemental first-round pick before becoming part of two blockbuster trades in the next three years. The Dodgers acquired him as part of a package for Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Alex Wood and Kyle Farmer in December 2018, then used him as the key prospect in the Mookie Betts/David Price trade in February 2020. He endured the worst season of his career in 2021, batting .190/.272/.333 with a 32 percent strikeout rate in Triple-A, before getting added to the 40-man roster in November. Downs was claimed off waivers by the Nationals in December. When he was posting an .888 OPS with 24 homers and as many steals while reaching Double-A as a 21-year-old in 2019, Downs displayed a simple right-handed swing with quick hands and nice loft and controlled the strike zone well. But after getting off to a slow start last year, he began pressing and never recovered, as his plate discipline deteriorated and he struck out and made weak contact much more than before. He homered in five straight games in the Arizona Fall League but otherwise scuffled there as well, adding to the concern that he might be more of a streaky power-over-hit guy rather than someone who can provide consistent all-around production. Downs continues to make the most out of his average speed thanks to baserunning instincts that help make him a 20-20 threat. His high baseball IQ is evident in the field as well, where he has good hands and solid arm strength. His merely average range at shortstop likely will dictate a move to second base, where he could be an asset with his glove.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 2017 Reds supplemental first-rounder who signed for $1,822,500, Downs was part of two blockbuster trades in his first three years as a pro. The Dodgers acquired him in December 2018 as part of a package for Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Alex Wood and Kyle Farmer, then sent him to the Red Sox in February 2020 as the top prospect in the Mookie Betts/David Price deal. Coming off a 2019 season in which he posted an .888 OPS with 24 homers and as many steals while reaching Double-A at age 21, he's having the worst year of his career in 2021 at Triple-A. Named after Derek Jeter and the younger brother of Boston first-base prospect Jerry Downs, he's chasing more pitches than ever before as his strikeout and ground-ball rates have spiked. In 2019, he did a better job of working counts and using the entire ballpark, and he started displaying the ability to drive the ball to the opposite field. At his best, he has a simple right-handed swing with quick hands and deceptive strength, and he shows the potential to hit for average and power while drawing a healthy amount of walks. Downs has average speed but plays quicker than that on the bases and in the middle infield thanks to his high baseball IQ. He has the hands and enough arm strength to play shortstop, though his range probably fits better at second base. The Red Sox already have Xander Bogaerts at short but Downs could fill their void at second that has existed since Dustin Pedroia got hurt in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Once a top-rated high school quarterback in Texas who was thought to be a serious NFL Draft prospect, Thomas arrived at the University of Oklahoma as a two-sport star who ended up switching his focus to baseball as an outfielder. Signing with the Dodgers for $297,500 as a 13th-round Draft pick in 2016, Thomas was dealt to the A’s alongside left-hander Adam Kolarek in February 2021 and performed well at Triple-A Las Vegas last season, hitting .289 with 18 home runs, 20 doubles and 52 RBIs. Thomas’ raw power immediately ranked at the top of the A’s prospect list upon joining the organization. That tool has carried him through his pro career, showing an ability to launch home runs against both left-handers and right-handers. He does have a bit of length to his left-handed swing, which leads to high strikeout rates, but he did show an improved ability to work the count while at Triple-A last year. Thomas moves surprisingly well for a 6-foot-4, 211-pounder. Though he can play center, he seems to have settled in as a right fielder. He’s right in the mix of Oakland’s outfield depth and could find himself getting some Major League at-bats in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thomas was a top-five-rounds prospect for the 2013 Draft as a Texas high schooler, but he was also a prized quarterback recruit who some scouting services rated ahead of future NFL No. 1 overall pick Jared Goff. He turned down the Yankees after sliding to the 30th round and went to the University of Oklahoma, where he started just three football games in three years but caught the eye of the Dodgers as a part-time outfielder. Signed for $297,500 as a redshirt sophomore in the 13th round of the 2016 Draft, he slugged 62 homers during his first three full seasons of pro ball. The A’s acquired that power, along with lefty Adam Kolarek, in a February trade that sent Sheldon Neuse and Gus Varland to the Dodgers. Thomas' raw power is his carrying tool and it immediately puts him among the best in the A’s system in that category, and he translates it into production against both left-handers and right-handers. However, Thomas' long, left-handed stroke and aggressive approach limit his ability to make contact and have resulted in a 29 percent strikeout rate as a pro. He showed a better understanding of his swing during Spring Training in 2020, fueling optimism that he could break out before the coronavirus canceled the Minor League season. Thomas moves well for a 6-foot-4, 211-pounder, showing average speed once he gets going. He ran well enough to play mostly center field in his first two years in pro ball, though he has settled in right field since. He's an average defender on the corners with a solid arm, and his power fits the right-field profile well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player at the University of Arkansas, Lee was selected as a pitcher by the Nationals in the 15th round of the 2018 Draft. He has since become a two-way prospect in a different sense. The 6-foot-1 southpaw was used primarily as a reliever at Class A Short Season Auburn in 2019 but enjoyed a strong instructional league during his relatively short 2020 looks. Washington decided to move him into a starting role last season with good results: a 4.32 ERA and 104 strikeouts in 77 innings at High-A Wilmington. Following a stint out of the bullpen in the Arizona Fall League, he was added to the 40-man roster in November when he was first Rule 5-eligible. Lee works primarily in the low-90s with his fastball, earning solid reviews for the pitch’s spin rate and life up in the zone. A high-70s curveball can tickle the bottom of the zone -- a nice contrast to the high fastball -- and it’s the pitch that gets the most whiffs in his current arsenal. He added a cutter in 2021 that he used primarily on lefties, and a low-80s, show-me changeup provides another less exciting option. The former Razorback’s athleticism dating back to his college days has aided his full-time transition to the mound, and his raw nature for a college pitcher has helped Washington develop him how it sees fit. That development has led to healthy strikeout rates and some Major League looks in 2022 before an elbow injury put him on the IL. A full-time move to the bullpen upon his return seems likeliest.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lee was a two-way player during his two years at the University of Arkansas, working as an outfielder on his days in the field. The Nationals were more interested in his pitching, however, even after he posted a 5.00 ERA in 15 appearances his final spring on campus. Washington took the 6-foot-1 southpaw in the 15th round of the 2018 Draft and put him on the slow road with assignments to the Gulf Coast League and Class A Short Season Auburn in his first two professional seasons. He pitched primarily out of the bullpen in the New York-Penn League, but after a strong instructional league, the Nationals hope to move him to a rotation full time in 2021. The 6-foot-1 southpaw’s heater sits 92-94 mph in longer outings but was touching 95-96 at instructs. The fastball draws solid reviews for its high spin rate, and Washington was pleased with his ability to throw it with life up in the zone. The curveball looks like the pitch most likely to be plus with the way it can get swings-and-misses coming off the high fastball. Lee has worked on a cutter to give the fastball a different look, and his changeup is mostly just a show pitch right now. Lee entered pro ball plenty raw for a college arm, allowing the Nationals to shape him in his professional development. It’s worth trying him as a starter when he moves to a full-season club for the first time in 2021, but the fastball and curve are good enough that he should move quickly if and when he slides back to relief, his likely destination in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since the Pirates acquired Smith-Njigba in the Jameson Taillon deal in January 2021, he’s shown glimpses of his offensive upside while having trouble staying healthy. Originally a fourth-round pick of the Yankees in 2017 out of the Texas high school ranks, he put his name on the map with a strong full-season debut in New York’s system in 2019. He jumped to Double-A with the Pirates in 2021, though he missed time with a thigh injury, and was added to the 40-man roster. He hit well enough in Triple-A to get his first callup to the big leagues in June, then suffered a broken wrist that ended his season. Smith-Njigba’s biggest asset at the plate continues to be his knowledge of the strike zone; he had reached base in 40 of 41 games during a stretch in Triple-A in 2022. He limits strikeouts and draws a ton of free passes, with a walk rate of 15.2 percent in his Minor League career entering the 2023 season. He’s capable of hitting the ball hard to all fields and has shown extra-base authority the other way, but the left-handed hitter is still learning how to tap into his raw power and needs to elevate the ball more in order to do so. A fringy runner who has good instincts on the basepaths, his speed plus lack of arm strength probably means Smith-Njigba is best suited for left field in most ballparks. Healthy once again, he should get the chance to see whether his on-base skills can help him stick in a big league outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees liked Smith-Njigba’s strength and advanced bat, especially for a high schooler, to take the Texas prep outfielder in the fourth round of the 2017 Draft and go a bit over slot to sign him. He showed tremendous on-base skills and some flashes of power, jumping on the scene more with an OPS of .871 in his full-season debut in 2019. Sent to the Pirates in the Jameson Taillon deal, he showed glimpses of the same offensive potential with a move to Double-A, though he missed about six weeks with a thigh injury. The Pirates saw enough in Smith-Njigba’s left-handed swing to add him to the 40-man roster this past offseason. Now they want to keep him healthy so he can really reach his potential. He’s long had outstanding strike zone judgement and has a career .387 OBP entering the 2022 season to show for it. There’s definitely power to tap into, though he’s still learning how to access it successfully. While he has fringy speed, he’s a smart baserunner with excellent instincts and the Pirates think his baseball IQ is off the charts. He’s in knocking on the door range if he can stay on the field, with the potential to be at least a productive fourth outfielder or on the long side of a platoon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After kicking off the 2017 Draft with three pitchers, the Yankees took Smith-Njigba in the fourth round, signing the high school outfielder for an over-slot $497,500 bonus. He lived up to his reputation as an advanced hitter by leading the Gulf Coast League in walks during his pro debut that summer. He struggled in 2018 but turned it around with a very strong full-season debut in 2019, finishing among the top three in the South Atlantic League in a number of offensive categories. He’s continuing his development with the Pirates, who acquired his bat as part of the return for Jameson Taillon. Smith-Njigba has the chance to hit for both average and power thanks to his bat speed, present strength and that advanced approach from the left side of the plate. He’s learning to drive the ball in the air more and to use all fields, with more power to come as he learns to leverage his swing more. He’s walked in nearly 15 percent of his plate appearances through 2019, but doesn’t hesitate when he gets a good hitter’s pitch. While he’s an average runner at best with a stocky build, Smith-Njigba is more athletic than one might think. He runs better underway and he’s aggressive on the basepaths, allowing him to steal some bags. His arm is probably best suited for left field in a normal ballpark, and he should be an acceptable defender in either corner, though it’s his bat that will eventually get him to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 2017 16th-rounder out of Division II Florida Southern, Walsh opened his career in the Cardinals system as a starter, but Tommy John surgery in 2019 and a ticking roster clock moved him to the bullpen in recent years. He showed promising enough results at Double-A, Triple-A and the Arizona Fall League in 2021 to earn a 40-man spot when St. Louis feared he would be a Rule 5 option for another club. After opening the 2022 season as the Memphis closer, he earned his Major League debut in May. A month later, he hit the injured list with elbow soreness and didn’t pitch again the rest of the season, though he said this offseason he’s back to full health heading into 2023. Walsh’s velocity slipped a bit before his trip to the IL, but he was still around 94-96 mph with his sinker. If he is indeed back to full health after getting a PRP injection last year, he could have a chance to threaten triple digits again upon his return in ’23. Four of his six K’s in the Majors came on his 81-84 mph curveball with a tight break that makes it tough to pick up, especially against right-handers. His low-80s change is used to keep lefties honest, while an upper-80s slider was mostly for show. While he’s leaned more into the power action of his stuff, the 6-foot-1 hurler still has the relative control of a former starter. It’s just his building history of injury concerns that has kept him working in shorter stints. The 2023 season should be a make-or-break season for Walsh in that regard as he’ll turn 28 in July.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Promising performances following a transfer from Jacksonville State to Division II Florida Southern helped Walsh get taken in the 16th round of the 2017 Draft. He showed solid results as a starter in the lower levels but suffered a torn UCL in his right elbow in 2019 and underwent Tommy John surgery late that summer. He returned as a reliever in 2021 (his first year of Rule 5 eligibility) and shoved once again, posting a 1.50 ERA with 25 strikeouts in 18 innings. He was hit around much more at Triple-A Memphis (four earned runs in four innings) and the Arizona Fall League (nine earned runs in 10 innings) -- where he was sent to make up for innings lost to a midseason IL period. The Cards still saw enough to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft with a 40-man spot in November. Walsh operates 95-97 mph with a sinking fastball and threatens triple-digits when he needs extra gas. An 83-84 mph curveball shows a lot of promise as a 12-to-6 breaker, and its tight break works wonders against right-handers. He also possesses a mid-80s changeup that can flash average but isn’t typically his go-to secondary. The 6-foot-1 right-hander fell into some control issues in the small samples of Triple-A and the AFL, but that hasn’t been a huge concern for him at earlier stops. Talking to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, he likened the move to the bullpen to “painting with a sledgehammer,” and indeed, the change in role has allowed him to lean into his power stuff. He just needs to show it for longer stretches, having thrown only 23 2/3 regular-season innings since the start of 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: On Day 3 of the 2018 Draft, the Braves did some excellent work scouting and signing some big arms. Woods, who was selected in the 23rd round out of Dyersburg State Community College in Tennessee, was one of them. A forgettable pro debut that summer turned into a promising full-season debut in 2019, thanks to an uptick in velocity. Between the pandemic and arm issues in 2021, he hasn’t been able to spend too much time on the mound, throwing just 10 2/3 innings during the regular season, though he did make a Double-A postseason start. He did show enough with additional innings in the Arizona Fall League that he earned a spot on the 40-man roster. A move to the bullpen in 2022 led to him making his big league debut in April, but he again missed a chunk of the season, this time with an ankle injury. After Atlanta designated Woods for assignment in November, the Mets claimed him off waivers. Everything Woods throws is generally hard, though he lost a touch of velocity in 2022. After flirting with triple-digits in the past, he can still touch around 96 (as he did in his second trip to the AFL this autumn), but he was more in the 93-95 mph range with good life up in the zone. He has a power slider that might eventually be an above-average swing-and-miss pitch and a firm changeup that’s clearly his third pitch, but has the chance to be usable. The key for Woods is going to be continuing to improve his command, though it doesn’t have to be as pinpoint in a relief role. If he can regain a little more velo once fully healthy again in 2023, he has a chance to crack New York’s bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Braves took Woods from Dyersburg State Community College in the 23rd round of the 2018 Draft, he became just the second draftee ever from the two-year school in Tennessee. After struggling during his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League that summer, he could have become just a footnote, but an uptick in velocity and stuff led to better results in full-season ball in '19 and he gained valuable experience at the Braves’ alternate training site in '20. Woods has the chance to have a solid three-pitch mix, led by mid-90s fastball with decent life up in the zone. He can reach back for more, and as he continues to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame, there could be more consistent velocity to come. A power slider is his best secondary offering and it will show glimpses of being an above-average out pitch. He has a changeup, but it’s behind the other two and can be too firm at times. If Woods wants to have a chance to start, he’s going to have to improve his command, which led to him walking 4.9 per nine in the first year-plus of his career. He can have the chance to start for now to iron those issues out, but looks like he has a floor of being a power-armed reliever if it doesn’t click.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following his stint in the summer collegiate Alaska Baseball League, the Mariners signed Kerr for $5,000 as an undrafted free agent out of Lassen (Calif.) Junior College in August 2017. As he added strength to his 6-foot-3 frame, the lefty’s velocity started to increase and he hit 100 mph for the first time in 2019 with High-A Modesto. The canceled 2020 season halted Kerr’s momentum and he was left exposed to the Rule-5 Draft, but went unpicked. The reliever got off to a fast start in 2021 and pitched to a 3.18 ERA with 60 strikeouts over 39 2/3 innings with Double-A Arkansas and Triple-A Tacoma. The Mariners added him to the 40-man roster in late November and nine days later, the Padres acquired him in a three-player deal that sent All-Star infielder Adam Frazier to Seattle. Kerr’s fastball is easily his best pitch, sitting in the upper-90s and consistently touching triple digits. He also throws a low-80s wipeout slider, which plays well off his fastball and helped him rack up a 13.6 K/9 rate last season. Kerr’s long limbs led to some control problems early in his career, but he ironed them out in 2021 and his BB/9 dropped from 5.1 in 2019 to 3.9 in ‘21. Consider that increase in strikeouts and the decrease in walks and it’s easy to see why the Mariners added him to the 40-man, and why the Padres were excited to acquire him. Age may be the biggest thing working against Kerr at this stage as he’ll be 27 for the bulk of the 2022 season. That said, he’s nearly a finished product and ready to contribute out of a Major League bullpen. With two above-average offerings and plus velocity it’s likely Kerr will get some looks in high-leverage situations for the Padres.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A third baseman when the Yankees first drafted him out of high school in the eighth round of the 2015 Draft, he moved behind the plate for his first full season of pro ball and showed very little upward mobility, struggling both at and behind the plate. He was unprotected and ignored in multiple Rule 5 Drafts and stayed home during the shutdown before things suddenly clicked in 2021, a year that saw Sands go from Double-A to Triple-A with an improved bat and glove. That landed him a spot on the 40-man roster, right before he was traded to the Phillies. Utilizing quick hands and smooth swing from the right side of the plate, Sands had always been a contact-first kind of hitter with a line-drive mentality. The power came in 2021 as he added loft to his swing and started getting the ball in the air more, leading to 18 homers in 94 games in 2021. Sands’ defense has also greatly improved since his humble beginnings. He’s a good and agile receiver now with an average arm. It’s a backup catcher profile, but one he should be able to bring to the big leagues soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If looking for evidence of the progress the Orioles system has made in the last few years, it would be instructive to use D í az’s status as a guide. It wasn’t that long ago the Cuban outfielder was widely considered Baltimore’s best prospect, the centerpiece of the 5-for-1 trade that sent Manny Machado to the Dodgers in 2018. D í az was fresh off an impressive two-homer performance in the Future Games game that summer, and a few years removed from signing for $15.5 million as a 19-year-old (the Dodgers actually laid out $31 million to get him, incurring a 100% penalty tax in the process). He looked like a rising star. These days, that outcome seems less assured. D í az never turned promise into production in the Orioles’ system, eventually stalling at Triple-A last summer. He’s been consistently undercut by injury along the way, missing time to hamstring and quad issues in ’19 and toe problems in ’21, when he was limited to 65 games and hit .161. A subsequent Arizona Fall League stint was also cut short, this time by shoulder woes. The Orioles still protected him from Rule 5 eligibility by adding him to the 40-man roster for 2022. At his best, D í az’s calling card is a blend of tools highlighted by his pure hitting ability. His arm is also plus, best suiting D í az to a corner outfield spot, though he could play center in a pinch. D í az has also showed above-average power and speed at times, though his stolen base percentage is poor and he’s never hit more than 11 home runs in a season as a pro. It’s a skillset that allows D í az to project in the aggregate — when he’s on the field, he can do a little bit of everything at least pretty well. The questions surrounding him now concern whether he can stay healthy and put it all together. If so, he still has a chance to grow into an everyday corner outfielder who hits for both average and power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been more than three years since Diaz was the centerpiece of the 5-for-1 trade in July 2017 that sent Manny Machado to the Dodgers, and his big league moment is imminent. The Dodgers signed Diaz for $15.5 million out of Cuba in November 2015 but actually laid out $31 million total to get him, incurring a 100% penalty tax in the process. Excelling at Double-A at the time, Diaz introduced himself to a national audience by hitting a pair of impressive home runs in the 2018 Futures Game, a few days before the Orioles acquired him for Machado. He's yet to match his initial production at Double-A (.314/.428/.477) in two separate stints at the level in the Orioles' system, though hamstring and quad injuries cut into his 2019 campaign. Diaz likely would’ve debuted had the 2020 season not been cut short; as it was, he spent most of the summer binging at-bats at the O’s secondary site. Diaz’s best tool is his pure hitting ability, but his calling card is a blend of tools -- they project as average or above across the board. The question remains whether he will hit for power; Diaz has hit exactly 11 home runs in each of the past three seasons. But he has an advanced feel for the strike zone, doesn’t punch out much and still walks at a decent clip, even if that declined during his second crack at Bowie. Still young and projectable, Diaz is seen as a potential No. 5- or 6-hole type who hits for both average and power. Defensively, Diaz’s above-average arm makes him playable at all three outfield positions, though he’s probably best suited long term at one of the corners. He possesses average speed and that’s translated to just a 42 percent stolen base success rate as a professional. The Orioles hope he can clean that up and stay healthy, knowing Diaz can become a staple in their outfield for years to come if things click.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bannon signed for $122,500 as an eighth-round pick in 2017, the year he earned Big East Conference Player of the Year honors after a monster junior season at Xavier. He immediately hit enough for the Dodgers to place him at Class A Advanced Rancho Cucamonga for his first full pro season, when Bannon broke out to the tune of 20 homers in 89 games. He was leading the California League in homers and slugging when the Orioles acquired him in a five-prospect package for Manny Machado in July 2017. They immediately promoted Bannon to Double-A, where he slumped at first. Bannon then performed well enough in 2019 to earn a midseason promotion to Triple-A Norfolk and a ticket to the Arizona Fall League. A compact but strong hitter, Bannon controls the strike zone very well, as evidenced by big on-base numbers throughout his professional career. But there is also an all-or-nothing element to his offensive game, with some significant swing-and-miss involved. He has a unique swing for his 5-foot-7, 180-pound frame, using a big leg kick and uppercut path to generate above-average raw power. It has translated into game action less, though, as Bannon has been exposed to better pitching. Defensively, Bannon possesses good first step quickness and a strong but sometimes erratic arm. He played almost exclusively third base upon arriving in the Orioles’ system, then predominately second base in 2019. He’ll probably always be a bat-first player, but is going to get some exposure to shortstop this year in an effort to improve his versatility even further. All told, he profiles a valuable utility player at the Major League level, who should be able to provide some thump off the bench against left-handed pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the Phillies in July 2016 for $720,000 as one of the top pitchers in the 2016-17 international signing class, Morales began his development largely as a starter with mixed results, though he did touch Triple-A in 2021 after having been added to the 40-man roster the previous offseason. A move to the bullpen in 2022 seemed to net good results as he dominated Double-A. Called up to the big leagues out of need, Morales’ wheels kind of came off after his debut. Though he righted the ship a bit after being sent from Triple-A back down to Double-A and to the Arizona Fall League, he was designated for assignment in the offseason, with no other team claiming him. Still just 23 for all of the 2023 season, Morales has the stuff to be an effective reliever in the big leagues. There’s plenty of fastball there, up to 97 mph in the Minors last year, though it often gets hit more than it should because of a relative lack of life. His bread and butter is a mid-80s slider that missed bats at a 53 percent rate in Double-A and Triple-A in 2022, the main reason he struck out 12.4 per nine innings for the year. He’s worked on adding a cutter to give a different look, especially to left-handed hitters, without finding something that consistently works. More than anything, Morales’ strike-throwing must improve for him to pitch in higher-leverage situations in the big leagues. Even if you throw out his time in Triple-A, he still walked 5.0 per nine last year and has walked 5.6 per nine in his Minor League career. No longer on the roster, Morales still has time to learn to find the zone enough to get another crack at the Phillies' bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Considered to be one of the top pitchers in the 2016-17 international signing class, Morales joined the Phillies in July of 2016 for $720,000. He moved incrementally, making a solid full-season debut in 2019. After the shutdown, he pitched well during instructional league play and earned a spot on the 40-man roster, but struggled mightily with a move to hitter-friendly Reading in 2021. He fared better in returning to the level in Double-A, and with a move to the bullpen, made his big league debut in May. Morales still has size and two plus pitches to rely on as he hits the reset button, and he can miss bats with both his fastball and slider. His fastball has been up to 98 mph at times and typically sits in the mid-90s. His slider, up to 88 mph, is a true out pitch and the two offerings are why he struck out 11.5 per nine in 2021, right in line with his career rate. The big right-hander does have a changeup, though it’s a below-average offering, but more than anything a regression in his strike-throwing is the most concerning. Morales walked 6.6 per nine in 2021 and that trend continued in 2022 as he struggled to repeat his high-effort delivery. The good news is he doesn’t have to have great command now as a reliever, though better feel for the zone could help him pitch in high-leverage situations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies handed out a total of 15 six-figure bonuses during the 2016-17 international signing period. Morales, who was ranked No. 23 on MLB.com’s Top 30 international prospects list heading into the period, received the organization's second-highest bonus that summer, getting $720,000 in July 2016. After making his professional debut in the Gulf Coast League in 2017 and moving up to short-season ball in 2018, the big right-hander had an outstanding full-season debut in a piggyback system in 2019. He was one of the best pitching prospects on hand in instructional league play for the Phillies in 2020. Coming from a strong 6-foot-4 frame, Morales easily has two plus pitches in his arsenal now. He was consistently up to 98 mph with serious life to the fastball during instructs and he couples it with an absolutely filthy slider that generates a ton of swing-and-miss. His changeup continues to improve and he throws it with good arm speed and depth. Command has been an issue for the right-hander in the past, he walked 4.3 per nine in 2019, but he made very good strides in that area at instructs last year. Just 21 for all of the 2021 season, Morales learned how to start and finish games in the piggyback system in 2019. As he continues to add polish, he has every chance to do the former for a very long time in the middle of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Muzziotti begain his professional career with the Red Sox, but he was made a free agent in 2016 after having played in 17 Dominican Summer League games as part of Boston’s penalty for international signing infractions. The Phillies jumped in and signed him for $750,000, and he finished out the summer in the DSL. He’s moved slowly up the ladder since, with the pandemic and visa issues forcing him to miss 2020 and most of 2021, but he did make it to the big leagues in 2022 and had arguably his best Minor League season in Triple-A in 2023. At this point in his development, Muzziotti is set as a left-handed contact-oriented hitter. He has struck out in just 13.1 percent of his career plate appearances in the Minors heading into 2024. What’s been missing has been extra-base thump, and while there has been tireless work on adding strength (and he did impact the ball a bit more last year), it’s clear he’s never going to have much pop. Because of his knack for contact, he chases pitches out of the zone too much. An above-average runner who is a threat to steal, Muzziotti is a savvy defender who can play a strong center field, though he saw more time in left with Triple-A Lehigh Valley than anywhere else. He likely has a ceiling as a fourth outfielder who moves around, though he’s blocked a bit in Philadelphia.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After initially signing with the Red Sox in 2015, Muzziotti became a free agent the following year as part of the penalty for Boston’s international signing infractions. He joined the Phillies for $750,000 shortly thereafter and started to gain traction as a prospect with High-A Clearwater in 2019. Since then, he’s had trouble staying on the field, losing 2020 to the pandemic and nearly all of 2021 when visa issues kept him in Venezuela. While he did make his big league debut in 2022, he also missed another large chunk of the season with a knee injury. Despite all the missed time, Muzziotti is just about ready to contribute to a big league lineup. He continues to show off impressive bat-to-ball skills, with just an 18 percent miss rate in the Minors in 2022 and a 12.3 percent strikeout rate in his Minor League career entering 2023. How much he can impact the ball has long been an issue, and while he’ll never be a power guy, he has shown some glimpses of extra-base ability and stayed in Clearwater this past offseason to work out and added a little weight and strength. Muzziotti runs well and can steal a base, though his speed shows up best when he’s patrolling center field. He’s a plus defender out there and still could be an everyday player up the middle if he can raise his offensive profile. If not, he could prove to have value as a fourth outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Muzziotti started his pro career with the Red Sox, signing for $300,000 in 2015, but was made a free agent when he was in the Dominican Summer League as part of Boston’s penalty for international signing infractions. After signing with the Phillies for $750,000, he started moving steadily up the ladder, but after turning in a solid season in High-A in 2019, he lost nearly two years of development time, first because of the pandemic-caused shutdown in 2020 (though he was added to the 40-man roster that fall) and then because of visa issues that kept him stuck in Venezuela for nearly all of 2021. The left-handed-hitting outfielder did make it back for 20 regular season games and then 20 more in the Arizona Fall League, getting back to doing what he does best: making contact. He has professional at-bats with improved plate discipline and has a knack for putting the ball in play. Adding strength continues to be one of his bigger challenges as he has shown very little in the way of extra-base authority. An above-average runner, Muzziotti has shown he can play an excellent defensive center field with good reads and routes. He has the ability to play all three outfield spots well, a good thing because he likely profiles best as a fourth outfielder given his limited offensive ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed for $300,000 out of Venezuela by the Red Sox in 2015, Muzziotti had begun his pro career in the Dominican Summer League when he was declared a free agent as a penalty for Boston’s breaking of international signing rules. The Phillies jumped in and Muzziotti got $750,000 to join their organization. He’s moved steadily up the ladder, spending a year at each full-season A level in 2018-19 before attending instructional league play and landing a spot on the 40-man roster in 2020. Muzziotti has always been a contact machine from the left side of the plate, one who has struck out in just 11 percent of his plate appearances entering the 2021 season. As he’s worked to improve his knowledge of the strike zone, he’s become more selective, and he walked as much as he struck out at instructs in 2020. That’s allowing him to hit in better counts and added strength has enabled him to drive the ball more effectively, though he’s likely never to be a huge home run guy. Still just 22 for all of the 2021 season, Muzziotti is a plus defender in center field with outstanding jumps and reads off the bat. He’s also shown the ability to handle the corners very well, with the ceiling of being an everyday player up the middle and a very high floor as a productive fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Solomon started his college career at Alderson Broaddus, the small West Virginia school that produced Twins right-hander Randy Dobnak. He transferred to Lackawana Junior College in Pennsylvania for his sophomore year and his arm strength caught the eye of the Reds, who went over slot in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft to sign him. Developed as a starter, he pitched across two levels of A ball in 2019 and looked like he was taking a big step forward stuff-wise during instructional league play in 2020 when he blew out his elbow and needed Tommy John surgery. Despite the injury, the Reds added Solomon to the 40-man roster this offseason, believing his gains in the fall will be for real once he returns. His fastball had sat in the mid-90s as a starter, with good spin, with the ability to reach back for a bit more, but that tracked up to 99 mph at instructs. His slider also improved, an above-average breaking ball with good depth. He has a changeup, but it’s well behind the other two pitches. Before the injury, command and control had been an issue, with a 4.3 BB/9 rate through the 2019 season. That, plus the surgery, could point to a future in the bullpen, where that fastball-slider combination could play up even more in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Cardinals back in Aug. 2014, Montero jumped on the prospect map when he posted an OPS of .875 in his full-season debut in 2018. A broken left hamate bone contributed to a stumble with a move to Double-A in 2019, but the Cardinals added him to the 40-man roster following the season anyway and sent him to the alternate training site in 2020. He found a new home when he was the top prospect sent to the Rockies in the Nolan Arenado blockbuster prior to the start of the 2021 season. After taking a while to get his bearings. Montero looked more like his 2018 self by hitting 28 homers and slugging .529 between Double- and Triple-A. It took a little while for Montero to get comfortable in his new organization. Once he settled in and connected with organizational coaches like Andy Gonzalez and Darin Everson, he got back on track, making incredible strides in pitch recognition and cutting his chase rate. Increased patience allowed him to elevate the ball and get to his prodigious raw power more consistently, and Montero loves talking about and studying hitting. In addition to refining his approach, the Rockies worked with Montero on adding first base to his defensive portfolio. He has really good hands and moves very well for his size, but first base might be the best spot for him long term. At the very least, the positional flexibility gives added options to get his bat into the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2014-15 international signing period is best known as of now for the quartet of Cuban players who received more than $55 million combined to sign, led by Yoan Moncada’s $31.5 million bonus from the Red Sox. Montero received a more modest bonus of $300,000 from the Cardinals that August and it looked like he’d provide plenty of return on that investment when he won the Midwest League MVP in 2018 in his full-season debut. He couldn’t replicate that in 2019 with a push to Double-A, as injuries -- most notably a broke left hamate – hampered him. Added to the 40-man roster, he participated in the Cards’ work at their alternate site in 2020, but was sent to the Rockies as the top prospect in the Nolan Arenado deal in February. Montero has the combination of bat speed, strength and the ability to make hard contact that point to a future as a Major League hitter, with outstanding raw power from the right side. He needs to work on his approach at the plate, as his aggressive style led to a lot of swing and miss in Double-A in 2019. If he can cut down on the strikeouts with more time facing advanced pitching, he has plenty of leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame to hit for a lot of power in the future. The infielder’s plus arm works just fine from the hot corner, but the jury is out about whether he can stay there long-term, with concerns he lacks the range and footwork to play third at the big league level. That could mean a move to first, but he does have the power/run-producer ceiling to profile at that infield corner as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fox is on his fifth organization since the Bahamas native signed with the Giants as an 18-year-old in July 2015. He was traded to the Rays a year later in the Matt Moore trade, moved to the Royals at the 2020 Trade Deadline and was picked up by both the Orioles and Nationals in waiver deals in November 2021. Washington seems to be where he’s settled now, and as a member of the 40-man roster, he will get an opportunity to find a place in a Nationals infield that remains very much in flux.
