A switch-hitter, Fox has thrived on spraying line drives around the field at his best, but he got away from that approach some last season with a 56.5 percent groundball rate and .242 average for Triple-A Omaha. He is capable of squaring balls up and making hard contact, but by putting the ball on the ground, he blunts his power. Fox’s best offensive assets remain his willingness to take a walk (13.1 percent in 2021) and his plus-plus speed that allows him to earn infield hits and be a 20-plus stolen-base threat. An impressive defender at shortstop, Fox saw more time at second base in deference to Bobby Witt Jr. in Omaha and even played center field for the first time over the season’s final month. His athleticism will allow him to play up the middle, and that’s what so many teams have bet on in the last seven years. Without a significant offensive adjustment, Fox, who was called up by the Royals briefly but was never given his official MLB debut, remains a bench piece at best, albeit one that is ready now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After he moved from Florida’s American Heritage High to his native Bahamas ahead of his senior year, Fox signed with the Giants as an 18-year-old in 2015. Less than a year later, the Giants traded him to Tampa Bay for Matt Moore at the Trade Deadline. Fox earned an All-Star Futures Game selection in ’17. After opening the 2020 season at the Rays’ alternate site, he was traded to Kansas City for Brett Phillips and joined the Royals' alternate site before seeing time during fall instructs. A member of the 40-man roster, Fox struggled for part of the year at Triple-A Omaha but used a hot run in the closing weeks to end up a league-average bat at the Minors’ top level. He was recalled by Kansas City briefly in July but is still awaiting his official Major League debut. He was claimed off waivers twice this offseason, first by the Orioles and most recently by the Nationals. Fox can spray line drives from both sides of the plate. Prior to Fox’s most recent moves, the Royals learned that his hard-hit rates were better than what his power numbers suggest; he hits hard line drives, they just don’t find themselves over the fence. Fox shows patience at the plate and has quality chase rates, and his on-base skills have continued as he’s moved levels and organizations. He also knows how to use his plus-plus speed on the bases. He stole a career-high 39 bases in 2019 and added 19 in 57 games with Omaha this past summer. Fox’s running and defensive profile have made him attractive to multiple clubs in the past few years, and he’s a quick learner with a high baseball IQ. He was considered an above-average shortstop with good hands and a strong arm entering 2021, but the rise of Bobby Witt Jr. has made him more of a utility option. Fox saw time at second base and center field with the Storm Chasers, and his athleticism helped in that transition. Now a part of Washington’s quick rebuilding efforts, Fox’s proximity to the Majors and ability to help out in multiple areas off the bench could make him a better option for the Nats than your typical waiver claim.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals say they were lucky to snap up Pasquantino in the 11th round of the 2019 Draft. The Old Dominion slugger broke out late with the power for the Monarchs, slugging .573 with 16 homers in 56 games as a junior. He carried that to Rookie-level Burlington, where he hit .294/.371/.592 with 14 homers in 57 contests, but his momentum stopped momentarily in 2020. When he returned in 2021, Pasquantino was arguably better than ever, producing a .300/.394/.563 line, 24 homers, 64 walks and 64 strikeouts in 116 games at High-A and Double-A. His 64 total extra-base hits were sixth-most in the Minors. Pasquantino was a remarkably consistent hitter at two different levels and racked up more walks than strikeouts after his move up to Northwest Arkansas. Batting from a slightly open stance, Pasquantino stays on time and sees balls well through the zone. He draws positive reviews for the way he utilizes his lower half to create the necessary lift on contact that leads to extra-base hits by the bunches. He doesn’t quite create the same damage against fellow lefties (three of his 24 homers came off southpaws), but the overall package of contact and pop is refreshingly rare in today’s game. His makeup and clubhouse presence are often the first things mentioned by Royals officials, even above his hitting exploits. A well-below-average runner, Pasquantino is locked into first base, but those in Kansas City believe he’s more athletic there than he’s gotten credit for in the past. Sticking there or slotting into DH keeps the offensive bar high. The 24-year-old has shown he can clear it to this point, and anything close to a repeat performance in 2022 should get him to Kauffman Stadium by season’s end.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After joining the Rays out of Mexico as a 17-year-old during the 2015-16 international signing period, Aranda eased into his professional career. He didn’t play in a full-season league until 2019, and even that year brought only 273 plate appearances of a fine average, a respectable on-base percentage and little power. But the Rays were encouraged with what they saw from Aranda in the Mexican Pacific Winter League after the canceled 2020 Minor League season, as the infielder hit .333/.390/.458 over 40 games. That, it turns out, was just the start of Aranda’s breakout. Aranda put together a 1.004 OPS in 21 games for High-A Bowling Green last year and earned a promotion to Double-A Montgomery, where he hit .325/.410/.540 over 79 games. Aranda was named the 2021 Double-A South Most Valuable Player and the Rays’ team MVP for Montgomery, and his big year ended with him on Tampa Bay’s 40-man roster. He’s not a prototypical left-handed slugger, standing at just 5-foot-10, but he has a simple swing and has always possessed a good approach with plenty of bat speed. He’s still a hit-over-power player, likely only reaching solid-average power, but he started hitting the ball in the air more over the last year and set a career high with 14 homers in 2021. He’s lined up plenty at second and third base, but his most likely long-term home is at first base, where he made most of his starts in Montgomery. Aranda’s track record doesn’t scream “highly touted prospect,” but if he can sustain the gains he made last season in Triple-A and the Majors this year, his hit tool and defensive flexibility should carry him into the Majors with a pretty high floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a senior at Lee's Summit West High in 2013-14, Harrison accounted for 29 touchdowns on a Missouri Class 5 state champion football team and averaged 16.4 points per game on a basketball squad that finished third in the state. He turned down a scholarship to play wide receiver at Nebraska to sign with the Brewers for $1.8 million as a second-round choice in 2014, then came to the Marlins as part of the Christian Yelich trade in January 2018. He led the Minors with 215 strikeouts in his first season with his new organization, then showed some progress in 2019 before fracturing his right wrist in June. Few players can match Harrison's all-around tools, though he'll have to prove he can make consistent contact in order to reach his lofty ceiling. He did tone down his leg kick and do a better job of using the whole field in 2019, reducing his strikeout rate to 29 percent from 37 percent the year before. The bat speed in his right-handed swing and the strength in his 220-pound frame create well above-average raw power and exit velocities, though his career 1.6 groundout/airout ratio (2.1 last year) reduces his effectiveness at driving balls over the fence. Harrison has plus speed and knows how to use it, stealing bases at an 84 percent success rate in his first six pro seasons and projecting as a 30-30 threat if he can continue to make adjustments at the plate. His quickness makes him at least a solid defender in center field, where he has spent most of his pro career, and an easy plus on the corners. His plus-plus arm strength ranks among the best in baseball for his position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $325,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, Sosa came to the United States at age 17 for his pro debut the following summer and has consistently been one of the youngest players in his leagues. He finally broke out in 2022 after adopting a more disciplined approach, leading the system in hitting at .315 while slamming 23 homers (more than double his previous career high) between Double-A and Triple-A at age 22. He had two brief stints with the White Sox, homering off Jonathan Heasley in August and making himself a candidate for their open second-base job in 2023. Sosa's hand-eye coordination and bat-to-ball skills allow him to make a lot of hard contact despite an aggressive mindset. He settled down his right-handed stroke and made better swing decisions in 2022, and while he's still not patient, his walk (7 percent) and strikeout (17 percent) rates were easily his best in three years in full-season ball. He has the bat speed and strength for average power, and he might find more than that if he can become more selective. Sosa displays good actions and reliable hands as an infielder, but his below-average speed leads to fringy range, and his arm strength is merely average. He has played primarily shortstop in the Minors, but his range would be stretched at that position in the big leagues, and his arm may be a bit light for third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox have promoted Sosa aggressively since signing him for $325,000 out of Venezuela in 2016. They brought him to the United States for his pro debut the following summer, have consistently made him one of the youngest regulars in his leagues and sent him to Double-A at age 21 last August. He finally caught his breath in 2022, breaking out as one of the system's top prospects and making his big league debut in June. A right-handed hitter, Sosa owns some of the best hand-eye coordination and bat-to-ball skills in the system. He began to reach his offensive potential this year by making better swing decisions, and while he still doesn't walk much, he's not getting himself out by making weak contact. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to deliver 15-20 homers per season if he can maintain a decently selective approach. Sosa has good actions, reliable hands and solid arm strength at shortstop, but his below-average speed leads to subpar range. He fits better at second or third base, though those positions will demand more offense. Given the strides he has made this year, that shouldn't be a problem.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox considered Sosa advanced enough to come to the United States for his pro debut in 2017, a year after he signed for $325,000 out of Venezuela. He held his own as one of the youngest regulars in his league in each of his first three seasons and ranked second in the low Class A South Atlantic League with 35 doubles at age 19 in 2019. His development experience last year consisted of instructional league. Sosa already shows the ability to make consistent contact thanks to his fine hand-eye coordination. The next step will be to add some strength and some loft to his right-handed swing to make the most of what could be 15-20 home run power. Developing more patience to wait for better pitches to put into play also would help his cause. Sosa's fringy speed throws his ability to remain at shortstop into question, though his instincts help him get to balls and make plays. He has reliable hands and solid arm strength and may fit best at third base, with second base another possibility. He'll likely spend this year in high Class A as a 21-year-old and could wind up as a bat-first utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 70 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Signed for $450,000 in July 2012, Barrera took a long journey through the A’s system before really breaking out in 2016. After earning Texas League All-Star Game MVP honors in ‘19, a left shoulder injury temporarily hindered his ascent. Making a full recovery and standing out at the alternate site in 2020, Barrera finally got his first taste of big league action in 2021, appearing in six games for the A’s. Barrera is a pure hitter with an ability to slash the ball from line to line. While the home run totals have been low, he is able to use his left-handed stroke to hit line drives to all fields. His great hand-eye coordination allows him to put the ball in play often and keeps his strikeout rate low, even if he does not draw a ton of walks. Not only is he a speedster on the bases, he’s also displayed good instincts when running, allowing him to consistently put up double-digit stolen base totals. Barrera’s passion for the game makes him one of the more fun A’s prospects to watch. He plays good defense, though he is a little slow in his transition getting the ball out of his glove. The A’s still love his athleticism, and he projects as an outfielder who can play all three spots in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barrera signed for $450,000 in July 2012, but it wasn’t really until 2016 that he really took off in the A’s system. The outfielder played across two levels in both ‘17 and ‘18, earning a spot on the 40-man roster following his ‘18 campaign. The Texas League All-Star Game MVP in ‘19, Barrera’s rapid push to the big leagues took a hit later that year due to a left shoulder injury that required surgery. He made a full recovery in 2020 and was by far considered the best performer at the alternate site by A’s officials. A slasher from line to line, Barrera is a pure hitter. Although there isn’t a ton of power there, he brings a level left-handed stroke and the ability to hit line drives to all fields. His plus speed comes with good instincts on the bases, and his solid defense allows him to play all three outfield spots. Barrera plays with a lot of passion and brings excitement. He does not walk much, but he also does not strike out at a high rate due to great hand-eye coordination. Barrera will chase sometimes, which could expose him at the higher levels, though he seems determined to work on improving that area of his game. Once that comes, Barrera should develop into a starter at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Encarnacion didn't land a deal in the 2014 international signing period, and the Marlins were tracking other players in the Dominican Republic when they stumbled upon him and inked him for $78,000 in September 2015. Nagging injuries and a propensity for strikeouts dogged him until he broke out in 2019, when he led the system with 71 RBIs and ranked second in with 43 extra-base hits before clubbing the decisive home run in the Arizona Fall League's championship game. He reached Double-A last year but hit just .222 with a 38 percent whiff rate while knee issues and a broken finger limited him to 63 contests. Encarnacion fits the right-field profile with some of the best power and arm strength in the system. His combination of bat speed and the strength and leverage in his massive frame give him 30-homer upside that he has yet to fully tap into. A long right-handed swing and pitch-recognition issues prevent him from making consistent contact, and he'd be more dangerous if he turned and lifted pitches more consistently. Though Encarnacion is more athletic than the typical 6-foot-4, 250-pounder, he's still a fringy runner who doesn't provide much value on the bases. He has decent range in right field and notched 33 assists in his first 200 starts there, but he's also error-prone. He played on a Double-A Pensacola team last year that also featured outfield prospects JJ Bleday, Peyton Burdick and Griffin Conine, so he saw semi-regular action at first base, allowing enough at-bats for everyone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miami stumbled upon Encarnacion while pursuing other players in the Dominican Republic and signed him for $78,000 in September 2015, a month before he turned 18. Nagging injuries and swing-and-miss issues prevented him from making much of an impact until 2019, when he led the system in RBIs (71) and ranked second in extra-base hits (43) while playing at two Class A levels and swatted the decisive home run in the Arizona Fall League championship game. He spent 2020 at the Marlins' alternate site before they protected him on the 40-man roster in November. Encarnacion generates at least plus raw power with his combination of bat speed, strength and leverage in his 6-foot-5 frame. He did a better job of translating his pop into production in 2019, when he improved his plate discipline and pitch recognition, but he regressed in those areas this year in Double-A. He also has made adjustments to help him pull and lift pitches more frequently. Though Encarnacion is more athletic than most players his size, he doesn't do much on the bases with his fringy speed. He has a plus arm that helped him register 18 assists in 118 games in 2019, though he must improve his decision-making and accuracy after committing 15 errors. Once he settles down, he should be an average defender on the outfield corners, and he also has seen time at first base this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene was an impressive prep hitter, leading to a gold-medal-winning turn with USA Baseball's 18-and-Under National Team in the Pan-American Championships in 2018. The Tigers grabbed him with the fifth overall pick the following year and signed him to a slot $6.18 million bonus. The Florida native saw three levels in the summer of 2019, was a standout at Major League camp the following spring and continued to the alternate training site before his 20th birthday. In 2021, the slugger hit .301/.387/.534 with 24 homers and 16 steals over 124 games at Double-A and Triple-A. A trip to the Arizona Fall League was canceled after he experienced concussion-like symptoms, but he cleared protocols in October. Greene exhibits a potent combination of hit and power tools from the left side. His swing is often described as fluid, but it also comes with plenty of violence, thanks to the way he utilizes his lower half. He exhibits a mature approach as well, one that helps him pick up walks at a good clip. While his strikeout rate has sat on the high side, there is hope it will trend back down as he sees more upper-level pitching. Perhaps most promising in his development has been the power that has gone from raw strength to in-game prowess with some added muscle. Primarily a center fielder at Double-A, Greene played all three outfield spots with Toledo. His instincts help make up for average speed, and he has the arm to work anywhere on the grass. The Tigers have sought new challenges for Greene since signing him, only for him to clear every bar. Whether it’s in center or a corner, he’ll be an impact bat alongside Torkelson in the heart of a Detroit lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a standout turn with USA Baseball's gold-medal-winning 18-and-Under National Team in the Pan-American Championships, Greene strengthened his case as the best pure prep hitter in the 2019 Draft by batting .422 with eight homers as a Hagerty HS (Oviedo, Fla.) senior. The Tigers took Greene with the No. 5 pick that June, signing him for $6.18 million, then watched him climb three levels to finish his pro debut at Class A West Michigan. He was the biggest standout among Tigers prospects in his first big league camp, slashing .417/.611/.917 with two homers and six walks in seven games, and continued to make an impression on Tigers officials during Summer Camp and at the alternate training site. Scouts love Greene's left-handed swing because it’s as fluid and balanced as it is explosive. His bat speed and path through the zone yield plenty of hard contact, and he already demonstrates an advanced approach. He shows huge raw power in batting practice, especially to the pull side, and has started to get to it more regularly as he’s gotten stronger. He should have at least above-average game power, along with a plus hitting ability, once developed. Greene is an above-average runner who can hold his own as a center fielder, although most scouts believe he eventually will move to an outfield corner. His strong arm would fit in either left or right, as would Greene’s offensive profile. Greene is advanced for a recent high school pick, possessing a unique combination of tools, skills and instincts that could help him move through the Minor Leagues relatively fast. The final product could be that of an above-average Major League player, if not better, who hits for average and power from the middle of a lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a tale of two competitive seasons for Peguero since he came to the Pirates from the D-backs in the 2020 Starling Marte trade. After impressing as one of the youngest players at the team’s alternate site that year, he made the leap to High-A in 2021 and helped Greensboro make the playoffs as one of the youngest regulars in the league. The move to Double-A in 2022 wasn’t as kind, though he was called upon to be an emergency fill-in and make his brief big league debut and was still very young for his level. Peguero started his Double-A debut with a hot bat, albeit one that was too aggressive, with an OPS of .853 through May. But when the Eastern League adjusted, he largely wasn’t able to. He needs to see more pitches at the plate, and the right-handed hitter often chased out of the zone, relying too much on his knack for making contact and thus diminishing his ability to impact the ball consistently. It’s still in there, with good bat speed, but his power only came to his pull side last year, and he struggled against breaking stuff. Peguero’s speed is still an asset on both sides of the ball, and he likes to run, with 56 steals over the past two years combined. While he has plenty of range and arm strength, he’s struggled with defensive consistency but will continue to see time at shortstop while adding in second base and perhaps even some outfield moving forward. The good news is at just 22 years old for all of 2023, there’s plenty of time for him to figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates looked to trade Starling Marte before the 2020 season, they wanted to make sure they got some high-end talent, even if it meant waiting for a return on the investment. They found what they were looking for with the D-backs, sending the All-Star outfielder to Arizona in return for right-hander Brennan Malone and Peguero, who had signed for $475,000 back in July 2017 and was coming off a scintillating United States debut in Rookie ball in 2019. After Peguero opened a lot of eyes at the Pirates’ alternate training site in 2020, he was challenged in '21 with a move to High-A, where he was the regular shortstop of a playoff team and nearly three years younger than his contemporaries in the league. A right-handed hitter, Peguero routinely shows the ability to hit the ball with outstanding exit velocities and premium bat speed, giving him the chance to eventually be a plus hitter. He continues to get stronger as he matures and could also have at least average power, especially if he can figure out who he is as a hitter. He can get over-aggressive and try to do too much in each at-bat, but he improved in terms of his consistency from AB to AB as the 2021 season wore on. Peguero is a plus runner who has shown he can steal a base and uses that speed to cover plenty of ground at shortstop, a position he should be able to play long term. He gets as high marks for his aptitude and passion for the game as he does his tools, and he’ll play all of 2022 at age 21, with the Pirates excited to see him continue bonding with his future double-play partner, Nick Gonzales.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs signed Peguero for $475,000 back in July 2017, and it didn’t take him long to put himself on the map, playing his way from the Dominican Summer League to the United States in his debut summer in 2018. In 2019, he was impressive as one of the youngest prospects at his level, earning a promotion from the Rookie-level Pioneer League to the Short-Season Northwest League. The Pirates took notice, making sure to get him as part of the return for Starling Marte before the 2020 season began. He was the youngest, and perhaps the most exciting, prospect at the Pirates’ alternate training site in 2020. After getting his footing at the alternate site, Peguero’s performance really stood out and carried over to his play during instructional league play. The right-handed hitter posted elite-level exit velocities consistently at instructs, topping out over 109 mph. Because of his bat speed and knack for barreling up the baseball, he has the chance to be a plus hitter down the line. The power will come more as he keeps adding strength to his 6-foot-1 frame, and his advanced approach for his age has separated him from other young prospects. Peguero’s speed is an asset on both sides of the ball, with the chance to steal bases and the ability to cover a ton of ground at shortstop, a position he could play for a very long time because of his instincts, footwork, hands and arm. If he outgrows the position, his offensive profile could work in a lot of places and his infectious energy will be welcomed wherever he’s penciled into the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first player to be selected out of Millville (N.J.) High School since Mike Trout in 2009, the D-backs picked Kennedy in the fifth round of the 2017 Draft. He signed for $500,000, forgoing his commitment to North Carolina, then impressed over 50 games in his professional debut. Kennedy was named a Pioneer League midseason All-Star and slashed .327/.396/.465 over 57 games in 2018. He put together another solid campaign in 2019 and added strength to his frame before the 2021 season. The results were obvious as he slugged a career-best .523 and more than tripled his previous best of seven homers with 22. Listed at 6-foot-1 and 190 pounds, there’s a lot to like about Kennedy’s offensive profile. His quick bat and barrel control enable him to consistently square up the baseball and make line-drive contact. While he started to hit the ball more in the air last season, his biggest improvement came with his approach. Kennedy drew more walks and gained confidence working pitchers and hitting in deeper counts. He projects to be an average hitter who gets on base and collects 20 or so homers at the highest level. A decent athlete, Kennedy is an average runner with good instincts on both sides of the ball. He’s not a burner, but he uses his speed well and swiped 16 bags last season (he was caught four times). He’s made strides defensively since signing and has spent time at first, second and third in the Minors, paving the way for him to ultimately be someone who can fill a variety of needs for a club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Talk about perseverance. Bride was nowhere near the prospect radar as a 23rd-round pick by the A’s in 2018. In fact, his struggles in 2019 as a 23-year-old had the A’s thinking they might need to demote him to Low-A. However, he returned from the pandemic and put together a solid 2021 season in which he showed supreme versatility while hitting .265 with nine home runs and 49 RBIs for Double-A Midland. Bride is considered to have the best fastball contact of any player in the entire system, particularly against fastballs in the zone. There is some power in his game, and he’s always been able to get on base at a high clip. The definition of super-utility, Bride can play third, first, second and left field well. This past season, he added catcher to his list of positions, getting extra reps behind the plate in the Fall League due to the injury to Tyler Soderstrom. Known to be a great teammate who is hard-nosed and has already overcome several challenges in his career, he’s moved his way up the system and reached the big leagues in June as a solid utility man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles have binged on college outfielders in the Draft under executive vice president and general manager Mike Elias, adding a bevy of such players to their system during their current rebuild. The first was Stowers, whom the Orioles took out of Stanford with the No. 71 overall pick in 2019, the first of three Cardinal players they’d select with their first 12 picks that season. He also was the first of that group to reach the Majors after leading Baltimore’s system with 27 homers and reaching Triple-A Norfolk in 2021, then getting called up for the first time in mid-June. The surfer-haired, sweet-swinging Stowers showed as much growth as any prospect in Baltimore’s system last season, jumping three levels and sharing its co-Player of the Year honors with Adley Rutschman. Most of his damage came at Double-A Bowie, where Stowers hit .283/.377/.561 with 17 homers in 66 games. Stowers’ loudest tool is plus raw power, which results in consistently strong exit velocity readings and translates better to the pull side of his left-handed swing. He generates it with good bat speed, though there is some length to his path that creates some swing-and-miss in his game. Stowers struck out at a 32-percent clip in 2021 but his 14-percent walk rate also indicated refinement in his approach. Stowers is an average runner with a decent arm who projects best as a bat-first corner outfielder. The likeliest landing spot is left field, especially if he can develop the type of all-fields approach he’ll need to hold his own against left-handed pitching. If it all clicks, Stowers could grow into an everyday, impact bat at the highest level -- as early as this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a breakout sophomore season at Stanford, Stowers shot up Draft boards with a strong showing in the Cape Cod League the following summer, when he ranked among the premier wood-bat league’s leaders in hitting and homers. He got off to a slow start offensively as a junior, but the Orioles saw enough maturation and promise to snag Stowers with the No. 71 overall pick in the 2019 Draft, making him the first of three Cardinal players they’d choose with their first 12 picks. Stowers then got off to a slow start in his pro debut, hitting .216 with six home runs and 53 strikeouts in 55 games with Class A Aberdeen. He participated in Orioles instructional camp in 2020. The Orioles are confident Stowers’ numbers at Aberdeen don’t reflect the quality of contact he made, citing consistently strong exit velocity readings and bad batted-ball luck. Stowers’ loudest tool is his plus-raw power, which translates better to the pull side of his left-handed swing. He generates it with good bat speed, though there is some length to his path that creates some swing-and-miss issues at times. Stowers is an average runner with a decent arm who projects best as a bat-first corner outfielder. The likeliest landing spot is left field, especially if he can develop the type of all-fields approach he’ll need to hold his own against left-handed pitching. If it all clicks, Stowers could grow into an everyday, impact bat at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Moreno for only $25,000 out of Venezuela in August 2016, and he has recently blossomed into one of the game’s most promising catching prospects. He first got onto external scouts’ radars when he hit .413 over a 23-game span in the Gulf Coast League, prompting a push off the complex in his age-18 season. He followed that up with a strong showing at Class A Lansing in 2019 and was a standout at the alternate training site a year later. His biggest breakout came last summer when he hit .373/.441/.651 with eight homers in 32 games at Double-A New Hampshire before a fractured left thumb cut that short. He returned in time for the Arizona Fall League (where he led the circuit in doubles) and a short spell in the Venezuelan Winter League. The Jays gave the 22-year-old his Major League debut this summer, but a crowded catching group has caused him to stay at Triple-A Buffalo for much of the summer. The right-handed slugger shows a quick and compact swing that he uses with promising hand-eye coordination to make a good amount of contact, and he should always hit for a decent, if not impressive, average. His .600-plus slugging percentage flattered him last year, and a high groundball rate could take the shine of what would otherwise be at least average pop. Moreno has made promising developments behind the plate as well. An infielder at the time of signing, the 22-year-old puts his athleticism to use with blocking, receiving and throwing. He has a plus arm with a quick release, capable of controlling the running game as he did with a 40 percent caught-stealing rate last year. Moreno saw some time at third base in the AFL, but his ceiling behind the plate is immense as a potential All-Star.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 60 | Power: 55 | Run: 35 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 55 One of the organization’s savviest international signings in recent years, the Blue Jays landed Moreno for $25,000, seeing the fundamental tools and athleticism to develop into a catcher. Five years later, Moreno is one of the most intriguing young players in the organization, and teams around baseball are quickly taking notice of what the Blue Jays have seen for years. After a rough debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2017, Moreno hit everything he saw in the GCL in ’18, earning him a bump up to the Appalachian League. With Class A Lansing in ’19, Moreno put himself squarely on the prospect map by hitting .280 with 12 home runs and an .823 OPS over 82 games. He was off to a killer start in 2021, hitting .373/.441/.651 with eight homers in 32 games at Double-A New Hampshire before he suffered a fractured thumb in June. At the alternate training site in 2020, Moreno didn’t just turn coaches' heads. Fellow players raved about the young catcher, who was making louder contact and consistently driving the ball in the air with his quick, compact swing. With low strikeout and walk rates, Moreno puts plenty of balls in play with his very advanced hand-eye coordination and has added even more power as he’s matured in the pro game. He should be above-average in both the hit and power categories, a scary scenario considering his position. Behind the plate, it’s Moreno’s quickness and athleticism that appeal most to evaluators. Those skills, along with an above-average arm, are what give the Blue Jays confidence in Moreno as a catcher not just today, but in his development going forward, as well. Moreno is young with development still ahead of him, but he has a path to becoming a Major League starter. Even with the lost time due to injury this year, Moreno is young and looking like he may not be far from helping Toronto at the top level. He’s become one of the game’s most exciting catching prospects before his 22nd birthday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The tools Swaggerty displayed in three years at South Alabama, most notably his power-speed combination and his defense, were why he rose up boards as the 2018 Draft approached. He landed No. 10 overall to the Pirates, signed for $4.4 million and showed glimpses of what he could do in his first full season. He then missed the better part of two years of competitive reps, first because of the pandemic and then because of a shoulder injury in 2021 that ended his season after 12 games, though he was still added to the 40-man roster that offseason. He had considerable rust to shake off in 2022, and while his overall season was up and down, there were some glimmers of hope while at Triple-A. With the injury and rehabbing of his shoulder now hopefully completely in his rearview, the aim is that Swaggerty can get back to showing why he was a Top 10 pick. He’s quieted his swing down since his college days and has a better understanding of using his lower half, which gives him a chance to tap into his raw power better, but he still has a tendency to produce too many ground balls. He’s a patient hitter who sees pitches and draws a fair amount of walks. Swaggerty still runs very well and that helps him be a stolen-base threat and to be an above-average defender in center field. This is his age-25 season and it’s a big one, with the chance to provide a return on investment for the organization at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Swaggerty checked off a lot of boxes during his career at South Alabama, with power (28 homers, .506 SLG), speed (48 steals) and patience at the plate (.457 OBP), combined with excellent defense. The outfielder went No. 10 overall to the Pirates, signed for $4.4 million and had an inconsistent season in High-A in 2019, though he finished strong. That carried over to his work at the Pirates’ alternate site in 2020, but he didn’t get much of a chance to show off his gains to the public as a shoulder injury ended his season a dozen games into the Triple-A schedule. The dislocation to his non-throwing shoulder is not expected to hamper Swaggerty going forward. Prior to getting hurt, the left-handed-hitting outfielder had worked hard to quiet down his swing and improve the use of his lower half. That helped him time his swing better and drive the ball more consistently, with plenty of raw power to tap into. Swaggerty walked more than he struck out in college and has a solid 10.6 percent walk rate as a pro heading into 2022. Swaggerty’s speed and plus defense in center field make him an asset, with the ability to cover a lot of ground and stay up the middle for a long time with an above-average arm. The tools are why the Pirates added him to the 40-man roster last fall; now he just has to go out and show he can use them consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In three years at South Alabama, Swaggerty hit 28 homers and stole 48 bases, and it was that power-speed combination that landed him at No. 11 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 200 Draft Prospects list as the 2018 Draft approached, and he was taken No. 10 overall that June by the Pirates. His first full season in the Florida State League was uneven at best, as he finished with a .728 OPS, though he did hit .328 over the season’s final two months. His lone action in 2020 came at the Pirates’ alternate training site. Swaggerty’s issues in 2019 largely stemmed from too many moving parts in his setup and swing, leading to the swing-and-miss issues that had concerned some scouts as the Draft approached. He was able to quiet things down late in that season, getting a better feel for his lower half, which led to better results. When he’s on time and not moving too much, he’s able to drive the ball consistently, which should let the left-handed hitter’s power show up more. After walking more than he struck out in college, Swaggerty still showed the ability to work counts and draw walks. While there are questions about what kind of hitter Swaggerty will be, there aren’t concerns about his defensive ability. His plus speed, also an asset on the basepaths, helps him play a plus center field with a strong arm. The upper levels should provide a good test to see if Swaggerty can be an everyday center fielder at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Walker established himself as one of the best hitters in college baseball during three seasons at Oklahoma, where he played alongside Heisman Trophy winner and two-sport first-round pick Kyler Murray in the outfield. The White Sox signed him for an above-slot $2 million as a second-rounder in 2018, then traded him to the Rangers for Nomar Mazara at the Winter Meetings a year later. Part of Texas' recent emphasis on more polished hitters, he spent a month at the club's alternate site last summer before attending instructional league. Walker is an advanced hitter with outstanding hand-eye coordination who recognizes pitches well and controls the strike zone. He made repeated hard contact to all fields from the left side of the plate in college but has yet to produce high batting averages as a pro, perhaps because he has looked to add more power to his game. He has the bat speed and strength to provide 15-20 homers per season, though he has yet to show much pop against left-handers in the Minors. Walker makes the most out of his physical ability and his all-around game garners comparisons to Mark Kotsay's. He plays quicker than his average speed, stealing and taking extra bases and getting the job done in center field. He projects as an average defender in center and solid on the corners, where he fits better in left field with his fringy arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Duran was old enough to sign out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, problems with the registration process delayed his entry into pro ball until 2017, when the Yankees gave him $10,000. He led the short-season New York-Penn League with 13 homers in 2019, then smacked 19 in his full-season debut last year. He changed organizations in July in the Joey Gallo/Joely Rodriguez deal, headlining the four-prospect package the Rangers received in return, and continued to mash in the Arizona Fall League during the offseason. Added to Texas' 40-man roster in November, Duran has strong hands and wrists and creates explosive bat speed from the right side of the plate. He's an aggressive hitter who looks to drive the ball in the air to his pull side, allowing him to make the most of his plus raw power. He may never walk much but he's making progress with his pitch recognition and swing decisions, so he should hit for a decent average. Duran has average speed and runs as hard as he swings, giving him the potential to steal 15 bases on an annual basis. In 2021, he played predominantly at second base before the trade, shortstop afterward and third base in the AFL -- flexibility that will come in handy after Texas invested $500 million in Corey Seager and Marcus Semien. Duran has quick hands and a strong arm, but his range is a bit limited at shortstop and he likely will fit best at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Duran was old enough to turn pro out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, issues with the registration process pushed his signing back until 2017, when he received a $10,000 bonus from the Yankees. After posting the third-lowest OPS (.562) in the Rookie-level Appalachian League during his U.S. debut in 2018, he bounced back to lead the short-season New York-Penn League with 13 homers the next summer. One of the more impressive players at the Yankees' Dominican instructional league last fall, he tore up High-A in the first half of 2021 before going to the Rangers as part of a four-prospect package for Joey Gallo and Joely Rodriguez in July. Duran produces some of the best exit velocities in the system and legitimate power to all fields because his hands and wrists are strong and create explosive bat speed from the right side of the plate. In order to fully tap into his pop, he'll need to chase pitches out of the strike zone less frequently and learn to solve quality breaking balls. He made some progress toning down his aggressive approach in the NYPL and continued to do so at Dominican instructs. Add in his solid speed, and Duran has 20-20 potential. While his average arm is best suited for second base, New York's infield instructors thought he showed enough range and carry on his throws in the Dominican last fall to merit time at shortstop in the future. His quick hands help him in the field as well as at the plate, especially with turning double plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Giants 2019 eighth-round pick out of Texas Tech, Kilian lost 2020 to the pandemic shutdown before dominating in his first full pro season. He led the Minors in K/BB ratio (8.6) in 2021 while coming to the Cubs in July along with outfield prospect Alexander Canario in the Kris Bryant trade, and he capped his year by fanning eight in six perfect innings to win the Arizona Fall League Championship Game. Though he made his big league debut with three starts in 2022, his stuff and control regressed significantly. Kilian succeeds when he commands his fastball and uses three distinct versions, favoring his 91-95 mph sinker over a slightly harder four-seamer that can touch 98 and an 88-93 mph cutter. All three can be solid offerings, as can his 75-78 curveball, though he missed fewer bats when he didn't command them as well last season. Lefties pounded him in part because he lost faith in his ineffective low-80s circle changeup, which he didn't use at all in the Majors. Kilian seemed tentative while with Chicago and rarely looked comfortable in 2022, when he didn't use his lower half well and leaked open in his delivery. The Cubs hope he'll resume pounding the strike zone after making some adjustments to stay more directional to the plate. He has a ceiling of a No. 4 starter but looked more like a middle reliever last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An eighth-round pick out of Texas Tech in 2019, Kilian didn't give up an earned run in his 16-inning pro debut and was one of the better pitchers in the Giants' instructional league program after the pandemic shutdown in 2020. He led the Minors in K/BB ratio (8.6) in 2021, his first full pro season, dominating in the first three months before San Francisco dealt him and outfielder Alexander Canario to the Cubs for Kris Bryant. He caught COVID-19 shortly afterward and missed the final month, then returned to excel in Arizona Fall League, where he struck out eight in six perfect innings to win the championship game. Kilian got stronger during the pandemic layoff and added more power to his pitches. He now works at 94-98 mph with his four-seam fastball with riding action and 90-96 mph with his two-seamer with sink, and his ability to command his heater helps it play as a plus offering. His upper-80s slider is slightly better than his upper-70s curveball, though both are solid pitches, and he also is refining a low-80s circle changeup. Kilian repeats his athletic delivery well, allowing him to provide quality strikes and locate each of his four offerings where he wants. His control and command haven't been as sharp in 2022 as they were a year ago, and he looked tentative in his first three big league starts in June. Club officials acknowledge that he's even better than they realized at the time of the Bryant trade and he eventually could settle in as a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter on back-to-back College World Series teams at Texas Tech, Kilian turned down the Orioles as 20th-round sophomore-eligible in 2018 before signing with the Giants for an over-slot $397,500 in the eighth round a year later. He didn't surrender an earned run in 16 innings during his pro debut and might have begun to advance quickly in 2020 if the coronavirus pandemic hadn't shut down the Minor League season. He was one of the better pitchers in San Francisco's instructional league camp last fall and dominated in the first three months of this season, reaching Double-A before going to the Cubs with outfield prospect Alexander Canario in a trade for Kris Bryant in July. Kilian added strength during his layoff and showed increased velocity in short stints at instructs, topping out at 98 mph after usually ranging from 90-95 with his four-seam fastball in college. After battling inconsistency with his breaking balls at Texas Tech, he has added some power to his curveball and scrapped his slider in favor of a shorter, harder cutter. He also exhibits feel for an average changeup. Kilian's lanky 6-foot-4 frame gave him more projection than a typical college pitcher, and if he continues to make the gains he has early in his career, he could develop into a No. 4 starter. He repeats his athletic delivery and throws all four of his pitches for strikes. He could push for a spot in Chicago's 2022 rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: St. Louis made an organizational decision to push their prospects aggressively in 2021 in hopes they would develop and grow into their assignments. Perhaps no one was pushed into the deep end more than Thompson, a 2019 first-rounder out of Kentucky. Due to the pandemic, Thompson entered the 2021 season with only 15 1/3 Minor League innings and some alt-site experience but opened up the campaign with Triple-A Memphis. His numbers floundered (7.06 ERA, 82 strikeouts, 57 walks, 18 homers allowed in 93 innings) as a result. The Arizona Fall League offered a reset, and all involved came away optimistic heading into 2022. Thompson’s velocity dropped some while he was in Triple-A, but it settled back into the 92-94 mph range in the AFL. That was even more promising considering the bump came after a long summer when many pitchers are losing velo. The 6-foot-2 southpaw’s mid-70s curveball is the star of the show with good spin rates as high as 3,000-plus rpm and impressively tight break. He’ll show a mid-80s cutter/slider as well, and a mid-80s changeup can drop off and be useful against righties. The stuff is there on its day, but perhaps the most worrisome trend of Thompson’s 2021 was the decline of his control and command. He walked 12.8 percent of the batters he faced with Memphis and 18.5 percent during his nine appearances (17 1/3 innings) in the Fall League. The Cardinals attributed that to rust, coming off the lost 2020, but it’s still concerning for a pitcher entrenched in the upper Minors. Thompson will return to Triple-A as a 24-year-old, and if he can take his AFL stuff with finetuned strike-throwing ability to the second go-round, he still has a chance to be a No. 4 starter in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson was a promising Draft prospect coming out of Wapahani (Ind.) HS in 2016, but shoulder concerns and his strong Kentucky commitment kept him on the board until the 11th round. After failing his post-Draft physical, the lefty went to college, where injury concerns showed up once again as a sophomore. He was healthy and dominant in 2019 as he turned in one of the best seasons in school history. His 130 strikeouts surpassed James Paxton for the most in school history by a lefty and he finished the year with a 2.40 ERA. The Cardinals selected Thompson 19th overall that June and after he spent the bulk of his pro debut pitching with High A Palm Beach, he spent 2020 at the Cardinals’ alternate training site and was bumped all the way up to Triple-A in 2021. Thompson, an athletics southpaw with four pitches, struggled with the jump to Triple-A and didn’t miss as many bats as he has previously. The 6-foot-2, 215-pounder has a fastball which typically sits in the low 90s, though he’s able to tack on a bit more velocity when he needs it. He also throws a pair of breaking balls: an above-average curveball that flashes plus and generates good spin rates, and a mid-80s slider. An average changeup completes his repertoire. Polished and intense on the mound, Thompson not only has an impressive arsenal, but knows how to use his pitches. His walk rate increased in 2021, though some feel part of that was related to rust from the canceled 2020 season. Although his command wavered a bit in 2021 and the strikeouts dipped, Thompson’s ceiling is still high. He has the potential to move quickly through the system and establish himself as a key cog in a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers opened the third round of the 2018 Draft by selecting the third of Cy Young winner Roger Clemens’ sons coming off a Big 12 Player of the Year season at the University of Texas. After grinding through three levels in two years, he spent the canceled 2020 Minor League season playing independent ball. The extra work set him up for a 2021 jump to Triple-A Toledo, where his left-handed power made him a regular in the Mud Hens lineup. After a difficult 2019 season led him to a line-drive, all-fields approach, Clemens came out of the pandemic season slugging in Toledo and became pull-heavy by season’s end. His 18 Hens homers -- two-thirds of them on the road -- led to a career-best .458 slugging percentage, but while his triples rate remained steady, his doubles total dropped into the teens. Perhaps swinging big in hopes of a late-season callup, Clemens endured a rough final month that sank his batting average under .250. After shifting from third base in college to second in the pros, Clemens became more of a right-side utility player by season’s end in Toledo, adding right field and first base to his primary work at second. While Clemens’ award-winning season at Texas looks more like a career year than a breakout, he has a chance to carve out a Major League career as a left-handed hitting utility player if he can solidify his offensive approach. The Tigers already have several utility infield types, but thought enough of Clemens’ chances to add him to the 40-man roster after the 2021 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The third of Cy Young winner Roger Clemens’ sons to enter pro ball, Kody defied the pitching legacy and became a slugger, winning Big 12 Conference Player of the Year honors at the University of Texas in 2018. The Tigers drafted him with the first pick of the third round that summer, signed him to a $600,000 bonus and assigned him to Class A West Michigan. He quickly adjusted to Midwest League pitching and hit .302 with an .864 OPS. He had a tougher time at High-A ball, batting .238 in 2018 and 2019 at Lakeland, but finished the 2019 campaign at Double-A Erie. When the pandemic closed down the Minor League season, Clemens played for his dad and older brother in the independent Constellation Energy League, where his .233 average, four homers and 12 RBIs in 28 games earned him a league All-Star spot and ranked him among his team leaders. Clemens’ grinder mentality has helped him in pro ball. After working to become a pull-power hitter in college, he adjusted his approach following his struggles in Lakeland and began to use more of the field and focus on line drives. His pitch recognition improved while facing older pitchers in the Constellation League, allowing him to stay on more breaking pitches. He was never a big basestealer in college or the low Minors until he swiped 11 bases in 14 tries at Lakeland, most of them early in the season. With average speed and quickness, he relies on positioning and instincts in the field to hold his position at second base. He can also play at either infield corner. Though Clemens has to show he can hit at higher levels, he’ll get a chance to move up the system and fill a need for infield help. If he holds his own, cuts down on strikeouts and can play multiple positions, he could fit a utility role in the Majors as a left-handed hitter with some pop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins originally signed Palacios for $75,000 in September 2013, and he toiled away in relative anonymity in the lower levels over four summers before he was traded to the Rays prior to the 2018 season in return for Jake Odorizzi. After two rough seasons in the Rays organization and the 2020 shutdown, he came back to the Twins as a Minor League free agent prior to the 2021 season, where he had a breakout with the bat in Double-A while continuing to provide his typical strong defense, something that continued at Triple-A and earned him a September callup to the Majors this year. The Tigers claimed him off waivers from the Twins in October. Palacios’ outburst with the bat was a bit of a surprise as the right-handed hitter controlled the strike zone better and tapped into his raw power more consistently, setting a career high in home runs with 19 and showing an improved ability to make hard contact. His success continued in the Venezuelan Winter League, where he posted a .987 OPS in 150 at-bats, but he was overmatched with a .143/.184/.229 line over 77 plate appearances in the bigs. Palacios has always been an excellent defender with very good hands, instincts and a plus arm. He has the tools to play shortstop defensively on a daily basis, but any big league future lies in his ability to move around the field. He focused mostly on short and second during his brief stint in the Majors but also saw time at all four infield spots in 2022. Already 26 years old, time is pressing for Palacios to prove he can be a quality bench infielder for Detroit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a stress reaction in a lumbar vertebra limited him to six games as a Louisiana State sophomore in 2018, Smith bounced back the next year and went to the Yankees in the second round of the 2019 Draft. Clubs pursued him in trade talks as soon as he raked in his pro debut, and the Rangers landed him last July in a four-prospect package for Joey Gallo and Joely Rodriguez. He advanced to Double-A shortly after switching organizations and continued to hit, staying on course for a big league debut in 2022. Smith possesses some of the best bat-to-ball skills and strike-zone judgment in the Texas system, regularly delivering hard contact to all fields. He has a quick bat and began launching more balls in the air last season, giving him 20-homer upside, though he put too many grounders in play during his month in Double-A. He has solid to plus speed and the savvy to steal bases. Scouts debate whether Smith has enough range to stay at shortstop in the long run, and his chances probably ended when the Rangers signed Corey Seager and Marcus Semien this offseason. He's a reliable defender with soft hands, solid arm strength that plays up with a quick release and a finely tuned internal clock. He'll see time at second base, third base and the outfield this year as Texas determines where to fit his bat into its lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith started at third base on Louisiana State's 2017 College World Series runner-up team as a freshman before moving to shortstop the next year, when a stress reaction in a lumbar vertebra limited him to six games. He returned to lead the Tigers in all three slash categories (.346/.433/.533) as well as steals (20) in 2019, elevating himself into the second round of the Draft. He raked in his pro debut with the Yankees that summer and other clubs began asking about him in trade talks ever since -- until the Rangers landed him as the top prospect in the four-player package they received from New York for Joey Gallo and Joely Rodriguez this July. Smith has outstanding bat-to-ball skills, controlling the strike zone well while making hard contact to all fields. His bat speed and the loft in his left-handed stroke create solid raw power that could translate into 20-homer power as he gets stronger. He could provide a similar amount of steals thanks to his solid to plus speed and his instincts on the bases. While many scouts think Smith's range would fit better at second base, he has a chance to stick at shortstop. He's more of a steady than a flashy defender with reliable hands and a good internal clock that helps him get the job done. His solid arm strength plays up with his quick release.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Espinoza was signed by Boston for $1.8 million during the 2014-15 international signing period, a record for a Venezuelan prospect, doubling the amount that Francisco Rodriguez had received in 1998. His immediate success as a teenager against full-season competition caught the Padres' attention, and they acquired him for Drew Pomeranz during the 2016 All-Star break. Unfortunately for both Espinoza and the Padres, the right-hander's 2017 season was over before it began, as he opened the year on the disabled list with right forearm tightness before undergoing Tommy John surgery in August. Though he may be small in stature, there's nothing diminutive about Espinoza's stuff when healthy. His smooth delivery and lightning-quick arm produce a heater that can touch triple digits, though he typically works in the 94-97 mph range with late movement. Espinoza's curveball shows plus potential but lacked consistency at times in 2016, while his changeup, thrown with fastball-like arm action as well as considerable sink, gives the teenager a true chance for three plus pitches once he matures. Beyond the stuff, Espinoza repeats his mechanics well and demonstrates advanced control and command for a hurler his age. Espinoza had progressed to throwing bullpen sessions in July before it was announced he would require season-ending surgery. He's throwing from 120 feet as part of his rehab program and should soon be back on the mound, although the Padres are unlikely to deploy him during games until fall instructional league as they continue to exercise caution.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Declared ineligible for what would have been his senior season at Lake Worth (Fla.) High in 2017, Velazquez returned to his native Puerto Rico and caught the attention of the Cubs, one of the few clubs with an area scout (former big leaguer Edwards Guzman) on the island. A fifth-round pick, he flashed intriguing tools but didn't break out until 2021, when he led the system in extra-base hits (45), total bases (191), RBIs (73) and slugging (.496) while reaching Double-A. He continued to mash in the Arizona Fall League, where he was named MVP after topping the development circuit in homers (nine) and OPS (1.191), cementing a spot on Chicago's 40-man roster. Velazquez is loaded with bat speed and strength that has produced some of the best raw power and exit velocities in the system for a while. He spent his pandemic downtime honing his ability to identify and punish breaking pitches, which previously had been a weakness, and also toned down what had been a busy right-handed swing. He's still an aggressive hitter who will accrue strikeouts, but he's doing a better job of tapping into his pop and driving balls in the air to all fields. Though Velazquez lost a step as he has matured physically and now has just average speed, he uses it well on the bases and in the outfield. He swiped 17 bags in 19 attempts last season and continued to see action at all three outfield spots. A solid defender on the corners and more average in center, he has a strong arm that erased 16 runners in 121 games between the Minors and the AFL last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2019 SEC Pitcher of the Year after fanning 176 in 107 innings at Mississippi State, Small got hot at the right time to vault himself into the first round, where Milwaukee took him 28th overall. His first full season was delayed due to the pandemic, but he didn’t skip a beat with a 1.98 ERA and 92 strikeouts in 77 1/3 innings in 2021, mostly at Double-A and Triple-A. His numbers regressed in his return to the Minors’ highest level (4.46 ERA, 1.36 WHIP in 103 innings back at Nashville) in 2022, but he did get a chance to debut with a pair of Major League starts -- neither of which lasted beyond the fourth inning. Small’s fastball typically only plays around 90-92 mph, touching 95, but it plays up because of the angular deception and extension coming from his 6-foot-4 frame. His changeup, hovering right around the 80 mph mark, remains his best pitch by far -- looking like the fastball out of the hand, only to slam on the brakes and dive below swinging bats before it reaches the plate. The Brewers have tried to get Small to find a breaking pitch, but his upper-70s slider just hasn’t become much of a weapon, and he doesn’t use it often as such. The southpaw’s walk rates have sat around 13-14 percent in the upper Minors, hurting his chances to start, and Major Leaguers hammered that point home by walking eight times in his 6 1/3 frames in The Show. In his age-26 season, Small has become a full-time reliever but one who can get outs against batters from either side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After undergoing Tommy John surgery as a Mississippi State sophomore in 2017, Small was the SEC Pitcher of the Year in 2019 after leading Division I with 176 strikeouts in 107 innings, and that performance led the Brewers to take him 28th overall that June. His 2020 duty was limited to the alternate training site, and he roared into his first true full season in 2021, posting a 1.98 ERA with 92 strikeouts and 42 walks in 77 1/3 innings primarily at Double-A and Triple-A. Small was shut down for part of the summer with a strained tendon in his left hand, but he made up for the lost time with 20 additional frames in the Dominican Winter League. The 6-foot-4 southpaw’s fastball sits just in the low-90s, but it plays up because of good spin, deception and ability to work up in the zone. His changeup looks a lot like the heater out of the hand, only to dive low and armside for a healthy amount of whiffs. Small’s slider has moved ahead of his curve in terms of effectiveness, but neither looks much like an average pitch just yet. He’s thrown the fastball and change as much as 85 percent of the time because of that. Small’s control took a step back in 2021 as he issued free passes to 13.3 percent of the batters he faced. The Brewers chalked that up to facing more advanced hitters for the first time, and it was notable that the skill looked more average in the Dominican this winter. Small needs to throw strikes to keep himself in a starting role. The fastball-changeup could get him to be a No. 4/5, and if either breaking ball truly catches on, a higher rotation slot is possible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Of the trio of left-handed pitching prospects in the Brewers’ Top 10, Small might not have the highest ceiling but he probably has the highest floor. After undergoing Tommy John surgery that wiped out his entire 2017 at Mississippi State, Small returned as a redshirt sophomore in 2018 and emerged as one of the most accomplished pitchers in college baseball, leading the Bulldogs to a College World Series appearance in '19 and winning Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year honors after finishing first and second among NCAA Division I hurlers with 176 strikeouts and 14.8 K/9, respectively. Hoping to reverse their history with touted college pitchers drafted in the first round (see: Eric Arnett, Taylor Jungmann, Jed Bradley), the Brewers took Small with their 2019 first-round pick and signed him for $1.8 million, below slot value for the No. 28 overall pick ($2.49 million). Early returns were promising. Small posted a 0.86 ERA and 36 strikeouts versus four walks over 21 innings that summer, mostly at low-A. He pitched at the team’s Alternate Training site in 2020 and was back in big league camp in ’21. Small’s fastball does not produce particularly big velocity since surgery (89-92 mph at the start of his pro career), but it plays up thanks to Small’s command, his deceptive and varied delivery with crossfire action, the extension from his 6-foot-3 frame, and his knack for going right after hitters, leading to surprising whiff rates and weak contact in the strike zone. Small sells his above-average changeup in the mid-70s with fastball arm speed, turning it over well to imparting late fading action on the pitch. Small also throws a curveball. None of those offerings stand out a’la Antoine Kelly’s fastball or Aaron Ashby’s slider, but Small’s polish and ability to fill up the strike zone should help him move quickly toward being an effective middle-of-the-rotation starter in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Regardless of who’s in charge, the Braves have long prided themselves on drafting players from their own backyard. While most scouts liked Harris, a two-way talent from the Georgia high school ranks, as a left-handed pitcher, the Braves knew Harris wanted to hit and liked him better as a position player, so they took him as an outfielder in the third round of the 2019 Draft. He immediately responded to the faith they had in him by reaching full-season ball during his debut, then had a very successful season in High-A at age 20, including an invite to the Futures Game. Even the Braves have to admit Harris has gotten a lot better a lot faster than expected, though they saw improvement internally during 2020 and some of the gains showed up in the public eye in 2021. An aggressive hitter from the left side of the plate, Harris has shown an innate ability to make a lot of hard contact. There has been concern about his chase rate, but he made strides in that area in 2021, upping his walk rate considerably and seeing that rate decrease, all of which will help him tap into his raw power. The Braves feel Harris is one of the better defensive outfielders in the Minors, on par with Cristian Pache and Drew Waters. He has impressive instincts and a quick first step. While he’s not a pure burner, he gets very good reads and routes and the arm that made him an intriguing pitching prospect is plus from center field. Harris has rapidly become one of the more intriguing outfield prospects in baseball as he reaches the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2019 Draft approached, many teams saw Harris, who likely would have played two ways had he gone on to Texas Tech, more as a pitcher than a hitter. But much like they did with Austin Riley, whom most liked on the mound more than at the plate, the Braves were a bit of an outlier in liking Harris’ upside as a position player. So they drafted the Georgia prepster in the third round as an outfielder, then saw him hit well enough to get a large bump up to full-season ball. He was one of the youngest players at Atlanta's alternate site in 2020, then had a successful move to High-A that included a trip to the Futures Game. Outside of the players at the very top of the Braves’ Top 30, there might not be any prospect with as much upside potential as Harris. He has good bat speed and the ability to make hard contact from both sides of the plate. While he’s been more of a line-drive hitter, there is plus raw power to tap into as he improves things like pitch recognition, and it has started showing up a bit at the alternate site and in 2021. An instinctive plus runner, he should be able to steal bases. That speed also plays in the outfield, where he should have no problem manning center field for a long time. He played mostly center and right, where his plus arm looks good, during his pro debut and should keep seeing time in all three spots. The Braves love how well he’s competed so far, thinking it’s a harbinger of things to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays drafted Winckowski in the 15th round out of a Florida high school in 2016 and he didn't reach full-season ball until three years later, when he led the system with a 2.69 ERA. After the 2020 pandemic shutdown, he stood out during instructional league that fall and got traded twice in the first two months of 2021, joining the Mets in a package for Steve Matz and to the Red Sox in a three-team swap that sent Andrew Benintendi to the Royals. The most advanced of the four prospects Boston landed in the Benintendi deal, he made two successful Triple-A starts at the end of last season and got added to the 40-man roster. Winckowski's velocity rose in his first year with the Red Sox, with his four-seam fastball sitting at 93-95 mph and 97 with good induced vertical break. His four-seamer does get straight at times, so he'll mix in some two-seamers in the low 90s with some sink down in the zone. His best offering is a power mid-80s breaking ball that he calls a slider but drops straight down like a curve, and he can morph it into a harder cutter. Winckowski requires a reliable third pitch to remain a starter and has come up with an upper-80s splitter that he uses as a changeup, though it doesn't have much velocity separation from his fastball and hasn't helped him keep left-handers in check. He throws strikes but also will need to improve his command in order to stay in the rotation. If he can't, his breaking ball could make him an effective multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hicklen initially planned to play two sports at Alabama-Birmingham, but when the football program was shut down in 2015, Hicklen put his wide receiver dreams aside and focused on being an outfielder. He parlayed that into being a seventh-round pick and had a strong pro debut. When he was held back in extended spring training because of an outfield logjam, he sulked and struggled. To his credit, he put it behind him, hit his way out of Lexington once he was assigned, but then willingly returned there to help win a South Atlantic League title as the Legends' cleanup hitter after Seuly Matias got hurt. Hicklen's power-speed combination makes him a very intriguing prospect. He has plus raw power that is eye-popping when he is on time at the plate, and he'll have to continue to refine his approach in order to make enough contact to tap into that power. His speed is also a game-changer -- he finished third in the organization in stolen bases in just 104 games in 2018 -- and if it all comes together, he has 20-20 potential. His speed also gives him plenty of range to play center field, but he's likely destined for left field because of his below-average arm. The good news is he looks like he might have the offensive game to profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since signing with the Cardinals for $200,000 out of Panama in July 2016, Herrera has moved rather quickly through the St. Louis system with typically solid numbers across the board. He put himself on the cusp of the Majors in 2021 with a career-high 17 homers in 98 games with Double-A Springfield. He managed to make his Major League debut a year later, lasting 11 games with the big club. However, his offense and defense seemed to step back at Triple-A Memphis in 2022 as he posted a .268/.374/.396 slash line with six homers and just a 17.7 percent caught-stealing rate, sixth-lowest among the 17 International League backstops with at least 60 steal attempts faced. Herrera’s best offensive asset remains his discerning eye at the plate and his ability to protect the strike zone, as he proved with a 13.7 percent walk rate and 18.7 percent K rate at Triple-A. It’s when he makes contact that he’s run into trouble over the past year. Though he possesses at least average raw power, the right-handed slugger has struggled to lift the ball on contact, leading to grounders on more than half of his batted balls in 2022. The Cardinals have worked with Herrera on improving his blocking and framing since he signed, but his defense appears to have settled around fringy and he was a below-average framer during his small sample in the bigs. It was certainly telling that St. Louis, facing Yadier Molina’s retirement, chose to sign Willson Contreras to a five-year deal instead of handing the reins over to Herrera. But the backstop is still just entering his age-23 season and has some development time ahead of him to become a backup to Contreras or a lower-ceiling starter elsewhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herrera has been pushed so aggressively since signing with the Cardinals for $200,000 out of Panama in July 2016 that it’s important to remember he’ll still only be 22 on 2022 Minor League Opening Day. He hit at least .330 in each of his first two seasons, produced a solid .284/.374/.405 over 106 games at two A-ball levels in 2019 and earned a 40-man spot in November 2020 after standing out at the alternate training site. The right-handed slugger’s .231 average at Double-A Springfield last season may seem like a steep drop, but it was driven in part by a .261 BABIP that was considerably lower than Herrera’s career numbers. He still took plenty of walks (13.7 percent BB rate) and showed improved ability to tap into above-average raw power with a career-best 17 homers in 98 games. In all, he was a league-average bat in a circuit where he was three years younger than the norm. Herrera can typically control the zone well -- no surprise for a catcher with a good eye -- and was starting to barrel balls better as 2021 wore on. He is a candidate to bat in the upper-.200s at the top level, should that trajectory continue. St. Louis officials have long been enthused by Herrera’s defensive growth and the work he’s put in on that side. His blocking has gotten better in the last two years, but there is still room to improve in that area. Once put on a throwing program by the Cardinals, Herrera now projects to have an above-average arm behind the plate. The Cardinals haven’t needed a Yadier Molina replacement yet, but they will after 2022. With solid tools across the board, Herrera could be the guy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals have challenged Herrera at every stage in his career after signing the Panama native for $200,000 at the outset of the 2016-17 international period. He received a brief taste of the Double-A level in 2018 during his impressive U.S. debut, then advanced to full-season ball the next year to produce a .284/.374/.405 line between Class A Peoria -- where, at age 18, he was the Midwest League’s third-youngest player on Opening Day -- and Class A Advanced Palm Beach. Herrera performed well in that year’s Arizona Fall League, once again standing out as a younger player against the advanced competition, and he continued to improve at the Cardinals’ alternate training site in 2020 and earned a spot on the 40-man roster.
