The jump to Double-A proved troublesome initially in 2021, though once he settled in, he began to perform better in the second half. Herrera makes hard contact with a quick, compact right-handed swing. He knows how to use his hands to stay inside the ball and find the barrel, showing above-average raw power to his pull side during batting practice. He began to tap into that power more in the second half of 2021. Herrera has long demonstrated an advanced approach, recognizing spin well and controlling the zone better than most his age, with little swing and miss. Herrera’s most significant gains as a pro have come defensively. His blocking improved in 2020, thanks in part to the time he spent around Yadier Molina at the alternate training site, and his arm strength has continued to improve after the Cardinals put him on a throwing program early in his career. Herrera also earns high marks from club officials for his work ethic and dedication to improving on and off the field. A bilingual catcher, he began learning English early in his pro career and takes pride in communicating with his teammates and coaches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from San Diego high school powerhouse Rancho Bernardo, Mitchell was a second-round pick of the Pirates back in 2017. He’s moved methodically through the system since, spending a year at each level and showing off glimpses of offensive potential. After the shutdown, Mitchell reached Double-A for the first time and touched Triple-A for the final week of the season, but the Pirates did not protect him on the 40-man roster this past offseason. Mitchell’s value all comes from what he can do with his bat. He has a smooth left-handed swing with leverage and plenty of extra-base authority. He has plenty of raw power, but in the past he’d try to sell out to get to it, impacting his approach and ability to make consistent contact. He cut his strikeout rate way down in 2021, though he still didn’t draw many walks and the 23-year-old will need to find a balance between contact rate and impacting the baseball. The outfielder has mostly played right field in the Minors, perhaps because PNC Park’s left field is so cavernous. He’s worked to make his arm passable and he’s a capable enough defender, but it’s the bat that will give him opportunities and it shouldn’t surprise anyone if he uses the lack of a 40-man roster nod as motivation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rancho Bernardo is a high school baseball powerhouse that has produced All-Stars like Cole Hamels and Hank Blalock, with 2014 first-rounder Alex Jackson the most recent to make it to the big leagues. Mitchell, the Pirates’ second-round pick in 2017, hopes to be the next after showing off his offensive skills across two levels of A ball in his first two full seasons of pro ball, then participating in instructional league action in 2020. As Mitchell has developed, and he showed up for Spring Training this year clearly having added strength, he’s become more of a power-over-hit kind of hitter. He still has a pretty left-handed swing with leverage and there’s plenty of raw power he’s still just learning to tap into. One thing he’ll have to be sure of as he moves up is to avoid his tendency to sell out for that power. While his 15 homers in the pitching-friendly Florida State League in 2019 were impressive, they were all to his pull side and he got too aggressive at making his decisions to swing too early. That took him out of his approach and led to a spike in his strikeout rate and drop in his walk rate. It will be Mitchell’s bat that gets him to the big leagues. He’s worked very hard on improving his throwing, which has been below-average, with some progress being shown, and he’s a fringy defender destined to a corner. He’s only 22 for all of the 2021 season and is ready to take on the challenge of the upper levels of the Pirates system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: File was far from a big name coming out of Division II Dixie State in Utah, but he signed for $75,000 as a 21st-round pick by the Brewers in 2017. He instantly slotted into low-level rotations and showed the most promise in 2019, when he posted a 3.24 ERA with 136 strikeouts and only 22 walks over 147 innings at High-A and Double-A. After seeing him more at the alternate training site, the Brewers added File to their 40-man roster in November 2020 only to see him need surgery to repair a stress fracture in his right elbow three months later. File didn’t return to a Minor League mound until July, and he finished with a 5.27 ERA in nine starts (42 2/3 innings) at Triple-A Nashville. The 6-foot-1 right-hander’s velocity was back into the low-90s when he did return to the mound. The velocity still doesn’t quite pop, but he was able to pitch in the strike zone regularly, tapping back into his best overall strength -- strike-throwing. An upper-70s slider with late life gives him a good breaking ball alongside a more vertical curveball that provides a different spinning look. A low-80s changeup shows occasional promise to give File enough pitches to keep a starting role in view. Milwaukee anticipates having more answers on File as 2022 gains steam. The organization had hopes of using the righty to build up its Major League depth in 2021, but File needed the year to re-establish his health following the elbow surgery. He’ll need every bit of his stuff to click into place if he’s going to start for the Brewers, or else a move to long relief doesn’t seem far off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: File compiled a 20-4 record and a 3.12 ERA but didn’t miss many bats during three seasons at Division II Dixie State. The Brewers saw enough starter qualities in the right-hander that they selected him in the 21st round of the 2017 Draft after his junior year, and File rewarded the organization by making strides in his first full season. In 2019, File was perhaps the most improved pitcher in the system, making a successful climb from Class A Advanced Carolina to Double-A Biloxi to lead all Brewers Minor League pitchers in wins (15) while ranking second in innings (147) and fourth in strikeouts (136). And in 2020, File impressed the organization with an uptick in velocity at the alternate training site, earning him a 40-man roster spot in November and a chance to contribute in the Major Leagues in 2021. Unfortunately, File was denied a chance to impress in Spring Training by a stress fracture in his right elbow that required Feb. 4 surgery. It was expected to sideline File for 3 1/2 to 4 months. File’s effectiveness is rooted in his ability to command four quality pitches. Working from a slightly lower arm slot, the right-hander sat in the low 90s with his fastball prior to 2020’s uptick and spots it with aplomb, working both sides of the plate and challenging hitters in the zone. That helps to set up a swing-and-miss slider that serves as his out pitch, registering in the upper 70s with late bite. File also throws a top-to-bottom curveball to give hitters a different look, and he can mix in a fringy but effective changeup against left-handed hitters. Like fellow 2017 mid-round pick Alec Bettinger, File projects either as a No. 5 starter or a long reliever, provided he overcomes the elbow injury. Those versatile relief roles are especially valuable to the Brewers, who like to make liberal use of pitchers on the 40-man roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ashcraft began his college career at Mississippi State in 2017, but hip problems and surgery forced him to miss some of that year and all of 2018. He returned to the mound in 2019 with Alabama-Birmingham and showed off enough power stuff to offset concerns about his command and get taken in the sixth round of the 2019 Draft. Ashcraft worked hard during the 2020 shutdown and was a much more effective pitcher, making his way from High-A to Double-A in 2021. There’s no question about Ashcraft’s stuff and the ability to get professional hitters out. He has two plus pitches in his fastball and slider and he isn’t afraid to go after hitters with them. His fastball touches triple digits and easily sits in the mid-90s, a pitch that has a ton of natural cutting action to it. His slider is almost more of a power curve, with more up-down tilt than most sliders, and it’s nasty. He misses a ton of bats and generates a lot of groundballs as well. While his changeup is his third pitch, he’s improved that offering as well. Ashcraft has made huge strides in finding the strike zone more consistently and that, with his ability to maintain his stuff during an outing, does give him the chance to start. His all-power repertoire to go along with his super-aggressive approach does point to a more likely reliever outcome, where he could get to the big leagues fast.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid high school prospect in Alabama as the Draft approached, Ashcraft was drafted by the Dodgers in the 12th round of the 2016 Draft, but he headed to Mississippi State. He appeared in 10 games as a freshman, five as a starter, but hip issues that required surgery kept him out of action for a year and half. The right-hander transferred to Alabama-Birmingham and showed off the same raw arm strength he had as a high schooler, enough for the Reds to take a flier in the sixth round of the 2019 Draft and send him out for a solid pro debut in the Appalachian League. After the 2020 shutdown, Ashcraft took a huge step forward, pitching his way to Double-A. Ashcraft has a power repertoire that gives him the chance to be successful if he can harness it. He’s been 93-97 mph with his fastball consistently, touching triple digits, throwing the pitch with solid sink and ride. His slider might not wow anyone with big-time depth, but there’s enough projection in the 84-87 mph pitch to believe it will be above-average, and he throws both the heater and breaking ball with good spin rates. He’ll flash a changeup, but it’s fringy at best. The key to success for Ashcraft is going to be his command, which is fringy, and his control, which has a chance to be average. While his tempo on the mound points to a future in the back end of a bullpen, where his fastball-slider combination could be nasty, his ability to maintain his stuff gives him the chance to start.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rutschman was the clear-cut choice to be the top pick in the 2019 Draft, winning both the Gold Spikes and Dick Howser Awards as the best player in college baseball that season. The Oregon State product really got to show what all the fuss was about in 2021 after a solid pro debut in ’19 and spending 2020 at the Orioles’ alternate training site. All that time with advanced players clearly helped, as the future face of the franchise hit 23 homers with an OPS of .899 between Double- and Triple-A, went to the Futures Game in Denver and was named co-organization player of the year by the Orioles. Bringing an advanced feel for the game on both sides of the ball with him from college, Rutschman has only matured more in learning what it takes to get through a long professional season. He’s learned to manage his energy at the plate and showed the ability to make adjustments from both sides of the plate against high-level pitching in the Minors. He has easily raw power from both sides of the plate and thanks to an advanced approach that saw him walk in 14.5 percent of his plate appearances and strike out in just 16.6 percent of them, he gives himself every opportunity to do damage. His defense continued to improve, starting with a very strong foundation, and he threw out 27.8 percent of potential basestealers while showing plus receiving skills and continuing to get very high marks for his rapport with his pitchers. As much as his plus tools stand out, his humility and work ethic get even higher marks, giving him every chance to become the superstar people expect to see. That thud Baltimore is hearing is Rutschman banging on the big league door.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes a player enters his Draft year as the front-runner to be the No. 1 overall pick and then doesn’t live up to expectations. Then there are players like Rutschman, who won both the Golden Spikes and Dick Howser Awards as the best player in college baseball as a junior in 2019, a year after helping Oregon State win the College World Series. He was the clear choice to go No. 1 overall, receiving a then-record $8.1 million dollar bonus to sign. After reaching full-season ball during his pro debut that summer, Rutschman was the best prospect at the Orioles’ alternate training site in 2020. During his time with the Orioles in Bowie, Maryland, last summer, Rutschman had the chance to sharpen what was already a pretty full suite of plus tools. The switch-hitter has an incredibly advanced approach, walking more than he struck out in college. He can drive the ball from both sides of the plate, with a ton of over-the-fence pop, while never selling out for power and showing the ability to make rapid adjustments against a higher level of competition last summer. His already-plus defense also got better in his first full year of pro ball as he acclimated well to working with high-level pitching talent. He knows how to call a game, works very well with pitchers and has soft hands and excellent agility behind the dish. He couples that with a very strong arm, which should help to control the running game and is already exhibiting the kind of leadership teams covet from a big league backstop, something he should be in the very near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 16th overall pick in 2018, Liberatore has gained more notoriety in recent years for the January 2020 deal that sent him from the Rays to the Cardinals and included future postseason hero and AL Rookie of the Year Randy Arozarena. The left-hander was a part of St. Louis’ alternate training site in the lost 2020 season and was pushed aggressively to Triple-A Memphis for his age-21 campaign. He repeated the level in 2022, posting worse numbers (5.17 ERA, 1.38 WHIP), but he did get his Major League debut, though he couldn’t quite stick with a 5.97 ERA and .304 average-against in nine appearances (seven starts). Last season, Liberatore’s four-seamer averaged 93.7 mph in the Majors and his sinker 92.8, putting him right around average, but he did touch 97.7 mph at his peak, showing there was something in the tank. That’s continued to be evident in 2023 as he’s been closer to sitting 94-96 mph with his pair of heaters. A mid-70s curveball remains his true plus pitch with real bite and swing-and-miss potential against batters from either side. He also uses his hard mid-80s slider and upper-80s changeup, though the latter has been reserved exclusively for righties. Generally a good strike thrower, Liberatore saw his control back up against the advanced competition of The Show, but he still projects to be average in the category. It’s how he pitches in the zone that could next be a focus. His diverse pitch mix should always give him a chance to start, and his slight uptick in velo in 2023 gives him a much better chance at being a mid-rotation starter in St. Louis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Slotted in at No. 4 among 2018 Draft prospects, Liberatore was the top prep pitcher on MLB Pipeline’s board that summer following a strong showcase season and a gold-medal turn with the U.S. National Team. Tampa Bay grabbed him with the 16th pick and signed him right around slot at $3.5 million. The Rays eased Liberatore in with 78 1/3 solid innings at Class A Bowling Green the following season, only to move him to the Cardinals in January 2020 for a package that included Randy Arozarena. Following a year at the alternate training site, Liberatore was pushed aggressively to Triple-A Memphis for a full age-21 season and held his own after some early bumps with a 4.04 ERA and 1.25 WHIP over 124 2/3 innings. He got more trips to big stages in Olympic qualifiers with Team USA and at the All-Star Futures Game in Denver. The 6-foot-4 southpaw thrives on pitchability to eat up innings. His fastball sits in the low-90s in most outings, and he’ll touch 95-96 when he rears back. He used to be best known for his upper-70s, 12-to-6 curveball, but an upper-80s slider with good, late breaking action has arguably surpassed it among his breaking pitches. The Cardinals are pleased with how he can go with either depending on need and feel, and his low-80s change pairs well with the fastball to give right-handers another look. Liberatore walked only 6.3 percent of the Triple-A batters he faced, and that control should continue to be a strength. What he lacks in a true plus pitch, he makes up for in a diverse pitch mix. The lack of elite velocity has kept him from sticking in St. Louis after multiple Major League looks this summer, but at just 22 years old, Liberatore could still overcome those lumps and find a more secure spot in a future St. Louis rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts viewed Liberatore as one of top prep hurlers in the 2018 Draft ahead of his senior year at Mountain Ridge (Ariz.) High, after the left-hander had turned in strong performances on the summer showcase circuit and as a member of the gold-medal-winning 18U U.S. National Team. The Rays ended up taking him with the No. 16 pick, and he pitched well at Class A Bowling Green in his first full season. But Liberatore’s time in the system was short-lived, as the Rays traded him in January 2020 to the Cardinals in the deal that sent Randy Arozarena to Tampa Bay. Liberatore impressed at the alternate training site in 2020, but struggled with a jump to Triple-A in 2021. The lefty also pitched for Team USA in the Olympic qualifiers and represented the Cardinals in the Futures Game. Liberatore has both stuff and pitchability, boasting a four-pitch mix that includes three future above-average-or-better pitches. He sits comfortably in the low 90s with a fastball that can touch 95-96 mph, and it's easy to envision Liberatore adding a few more ticks as he fills out his 6-foot-4 frame. His best secondary pitch is a plus curveball in the upper 70s that he throws with 12-to-6, downer action. A changeup that plays nicely off his heater gives Liberatore an above-average third pitch, and he has made progress developing a slider after adding the pitch to his arsenal in 2019. Tall and athletic, Liberatore does an excellent job repeating his delivery and arm action to throw consistent strikes. He will need time to develop physically and hone his craft in the Minors, but he still has the ceiling of a No. 1 starter, despite his struggles in 2021. Even if he doesn’t reach that lofty ceiling, his high floor also offers value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gorman was notorious for his power going into the 2018 Draft, having been a showcase star in home run derbies the previous summer. The Cardinals grabbed the slugger with the 21st overall pick in June, and he justified his profile with 17 homers in his first taste of the Minors. He was challenged with moves to two Class A affiliates in 2019 and tackled the upper levels as a 21-year-old in 2021, hitting .279/.333/.481 with 25 homers at Double-A and Triple-A. Spurts in the All-Star Futures Game and Arizona Fall League put Gorman on more prominent stages this past season. The left-handed hitter’s power potential remains as great as ever. Aggressive assignments by St. Louis -- designed to challenge Gorman -- have kept the slugging numbers from popping just yet, but he remains capable of busting out tape-measure shots, thanks to exciting bat speed and overall strength. Something to watch will be his batted-ball data after he reverted to hitting more balls on the ground with Memphis and landed at a 45 percent groundball rate. He did strike out less there too (dropping his K rate from 26.2 to 19.7), giving St. Louis hope he’ll be more than a one-trick offensive player. The biggest news of Gorman’s 2021 was his full-time move to second base, which kicked into gear at Triple-A, following the acquisition of Nolan Arenado. He worked hard with infield coordinator Jose Oquendo to improve his footwork and range, particularly on balls to his right, and he could be average there in time. All of this was done to ensure his bat can be in a St. Louis lineup someday, and that opportunity could come not long after his 22nd birthday in May.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gorman was widely regarded as the top high school slugger in the 2018 Draft after putting on prodigious power displays during home run derbies as part of the summer showcase circuit, including the prestigious MLB All-Star High School Run Derby in Miami. The Cardinals took the Arizona prepster with the No. 19 overall pick that June, then watched him belt 17 homers while reaching full-season ball in his pro debut. Gorman fell two homers shy of matching that total during a challenging first full season that saw him advance to Class A Advanced Palm Beach at age 19, but also struck out nearly 30 percent of the time. He homered in big league camp for a second straight spring in '20 and worked his way up to Triple-A, while also representing the Cardinals in the Futures Game in 2021. Gorman has all the ingredients teams covet in a young power hitter, possessing a high-end blend of physical strength and bat speed, with a left-handed swing that’s conducive to make fly-ball contact. Gorman's swing-and-miss tendencies can get exposed by elevated velocity and well-sequenced secondary pitches, and the approach can become too pull-heavy at times, but he drives the ball to all fields with plus-plus raw power at his best, and scouts generally like his chances of becoming at least an average hitter with plus game power. Gorman's biggest gains have come on the defensive side, thanks mainly to his dedicated work with infield coach José Oquendo. Gorman, who came up as a third baseman, has received the bulk of his playing time at second base with Memphis. With Nolan Arenado manning the hot corner in St. Louis, a switch to second is Gorman’s quickest path to the Majors and he’s handled the switch well. While there are questions about his first step, his plus arm certainly plays at second base and his bat should more than make up for any defensive shortcomings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs signed Morel for $800,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, three years before signing his brother Rafael, an infielder, for $850,000. Christopher cut his right arm in a household accident after turning pro, delaying his debut until 2017, but he has moved quickly and reached Triple-A last year at age 22. He's the most versatile Cubs farmhand and one of the most athletic, though he batted just .223/.303/.427 between Double-A and Triple-A in 2021. Morel produces impressive bat speed and exit velocities from the right side of the plate and can drive the ball out of any part of the park. Yet instead of letting his plus raw power manifest itself naturally, he overswings and struggles to get to fastballs up in the zone. He did increase his walk rate from 4 percent in 2019 to 10 percent, an encouraging sign, but he still needs to focus on just driving the ball from gap to gap rather than shooting for the fences. Morel notched 18 steals in 21 attempts last year, a testament to his plus speed and aggressive nature on the bases. His quickness and well above-average arm strength allow him to play almost anywhere on the diamond -- and he has, making double-digit starts at center field, third base, right field, shortstop and second base last year. He covers solid ground at all three outfield spots and is a rangy if erratic infield defender.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs have invested heavily in the Morel brothers, signing Christopher for $800,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015 and Rafael, a fellow infielder, for $850,000 three years later. Christopher cut his right arm in a household accident after turning pro, delaying his debut until 2017. He has some of the best all-around tools in the system and was added to the 40-man roster in November after spending 2020 at Chicago's alternate site and instructional league. Morel's right-handed swing produces some of the best bat speed and exit velocities among Cubs prospects. Once he improves his pitch recognition and strike-zone judgment and adds some more strength, he could become a decent hitter with plus power, but he has struggled mightily after jumping two levels to Double-A in 2021. He has legitimate opposite-field pop and is most effective when he drives balls from gap to gap rather than lapsing into a pull-crazy mindset. A quick-twitch athlete, Morel has plus speed and is aggressive on the bases. His arm is his best pure tool, earning plus-plus grades from some evaluators, and he's equipped to play all over the diamond. He split his first two pro seasons between shortstop and third base, settled at the hot corner in 2019, and has seen the majority of his time this year in center field while also making several starts on both outfield corners as well as shortstop, second base and third.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Grove missed his junior season at West Virginia while recovering from Tommy John surgery, yet the Dodgers still drafted him in the second round of the 2018 Draft and signed him for a well over-slot $1,229,500 -- effectively costing them first-rounder J.T. Ginn. He posted a 7.12 ERA in his first two pro seasons but began to take off in late 2021 after a midsummer adjustment to lower his arm slot resulted in dramatically improved control and command. He made his big league debut last May and allowed a total of 12 runs in six spot starts over five callups. Although Grove's fastball sits at 93-96 mph and peaks at 98 that misses bats with carry when he locates it up in the zone, it gets hit hard when he doesn't command it well. His best pitch is a plus mid-80s slider that drops out of the strike zone, and he also has a solid upper-70s curveball with even more depth. He doesn't have much feel for and barely uses a mid-80s changeup with more downhill plane than life. After Grove quickly adapted to a three-quarters arm slot, he started throwing a lot more strikes and getting a lot more chases with his pitches. He'll need to get more consistent with his fastball command and develop some semblance of a changeup to remain a starter in the Majors. It's more likely that he settles into a multi-inning reliever role in Los Angeles.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Grove missed his entire junior season at West Virginia following Tommy John surgery, the Dodgers still popped him in the second round of the 2018 Draft and signed him for a well over-slot $1,229,500 -- leaving them without enough bonus-pool money to land first-rounder J.T. Ginn. He has produced mixed results in his first two pro seasons, compiling a 7.12 ERA with 161 strikeouts in 122 2/3 innings while advancing to Double-A. But a midsummer adjustment to lower his arm slot led to dramatically improved control and command last August, prompting Los Angeles to protect him on its 40-man roster. After pitching with a 92-96 mph fastball at the end of his 2019 pro debut, Grove dipped to 90-93 mph early last season before his mechanical changes resulted in him pitching in the mid-90s and touching 99 with better carry up in the zone. He owns a pair of high-spin breaking balls with depth that lack consistency but can overwhelm hitters when they're on, with his slider that can reach the upper 80s grading better than his low-80s curveball. He doesn't have much trust in his changeup, which has some fade at times but usually lacks much life or velocity separation from his fastball. The Dodgers marvel at how quickly Grove adapted to more of a three-quarters slot and started getting more strikes and chases out of his arsenal. He maintained his improved stuff and ability to locate it for five innings at a time and will continue to develop as a starter at the outset of 2022. Scouts believe his lack of an effective changeup or a track record of providing quality strikes will make him a reliever, though it's not out of the question that he could get to Los Angeles this year in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest surprise pick on the first day of the 2018 Draft, Grove went in the second round despite missing his entire junior season at West Virginia while recovering from Tommy John surgery. The Dodgers valued him enough to sign him for a well over-slot $1,229,500 -- which left them without enough bonus-pool money to meet first-rounder J.T. Ginn's asking price. Grove posted a 6.10 ERA while making his 2019 pro debut in high Class A, but his stuff started to come all the way back at the end of that season and continued to do so in Spring Training and at Los Angeles' alternate site last year. Grove regained his 92-96 mph fastball with good carry up in the zone by the end of his debut and showed a tick more velocity and the ability to hold it for longer stints in 2020. He refined an upper-70s curveball in 2019 when his trademark slider abandoned him, then saw his mid-80s slide piece with high spin rates return last year. He barely used a changeup as an amateur but is making some progress with it. Since Rancho Cucamonga pitching coach Connor McGuiness helped him smooth out a wrist wrap and some hook in the back of his delivery in 2019, Grove has provided more consistent strikes. He could develop into a No. 3 starter if he refines his secondary pitches and command, but he's also 24 and never has pitched more than 51 2/3 innings in a college or pro season. Expediting his development by moving him to the bullpen could make sense, and he could have a dominant fastball/slider combo as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels made some waves in the 2021 Draft when they took 20 pitchers with their 20 selections, all but one of them coming from the college ranks. It would be difficult to find anyone who predicted that Silseth, who went from Tennessee to the College of Southern Nevada and then to the University of Arizona before being selected in Round 11 of that Draft, would not only be the first Angels player from the class to reach the big leagues, but the first player from any team to do so. He began the year in Double-A and was dominant at the level, getting called up for the first time in May and making seven starts for Los Angeles. Silseth has always had good stuff, even if his results at Arizona were a bit uneven, but it all ticked up during his first year of pro ball. His fastball sat at 95 mph and ran up to 98-99, with good spin up in the zone. His 83-85 mph slider missed bats at a 42 percent rate in 2022, and while his slider used to run into his curve more, forcing him to cut back on throwing the latter, he still would throw the 80-81 mph slower breaking ball occasionally. His offspeed pitch is a splitter, and some think it’s his best pitch, an upper-80s offering that missed bats and got ground-ball outs. Generally a solid strike-thrower, Silseth’s command wasn’t as sharp in the Majors as it was in Double-A, both in and out of the zone. Because of his size, some projected a move to the bullpen, but his stuff and his early success will afford him every opportunity to show he belongs in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Silseth had a bit of a meandering college career, starting at the University of Tennessee in 2019, then moving to the College of Southern Nevada when he didn’t get the chance to start for the Volunteers. After five starts at the junior college, the pandemic ended the 2020 season, and he moved on to Arizona and served as their Friday night starter. While his stat line didn’t stand out, he showed off enough stuff to intrigue the Angels, who took Silseth in the 11th round – the 11th of 20 straight pitchers taken by the club – and signed him for an above-slot bonus of $485,000. It’s already turned out to be a worthwhile investment as he became the first player from the Draft class to reach the big leagues. A four-pitch mix gives Silseth the chance to start, and he showed off all four offerings during instructional league play last fall. He can run his fastball up to 96 mph and he backs it up with both a curve and slider. They have at times run into each other, but he was separating them better at instructs, the slider up to 85 mph and the curve sitting more in the low-80s. He didn’t use the changeup much in college, but that flashed as an above-average pitch last fall at times. Because he’s a bit undersized at six-foot, there have been questions about his durability, with some thinking he’d be best suited to be a power-armed reliever. But he generally throws strikes and if he can show his stuff can hold up deep into outings, his full repertoire will at least afford him the opportunity to stick in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Wentz was once a first-round Draft pick, he has been among the least heralded of Detroit’s pitching prospects ever since arriving from the Braves in the Shane Greene trade in 2019. Being teammates with fellow top prospects Casey Mize, Tarik Skubal, Matt Manning and Alex Faedo didn’t help. Still it’s a shame, because a left-hander with Wentz’s body frame and control should command some attention. He began to get it last summer, when he made his Major League debut in Detroit. Shoulder issues cost him most of the summer, but a strong five-start stretch in September -- followed by an impressive Arizona Fall League -- put him squarely in the Tigers’ pitching depth plans for 2023. Though Wentz has thrown his fastball as hard as 97-98 mph following Tommy John surgery in 2020, he’s more comfortable working in the low-to-mid-90s and locating the pitch for strikes. His tall frame and high arm slot leave hitters struggling to keep up. His changeup is above-average and works as an out pitch when he has an effective fastball to set it up. He had success with the curveball in the Minors, but it looked at times like a throwaway pitch before Triple-A pitching coach Doug Bochtler worked with him on spinning it. Adding in an average 83-85 mph cutter, it’s a good arsenal, but he needs to command it and mix segments of the zone to be effective. Wentz’s success down the stretch last year put him in line for the Tigers as an insurance starter this season. But given Detroit’s youth movement, he has a chance to eventually settle in at the back end of the rotation behind Skubal, Manning and others, much like in Erie a few years ago. Considering the Tigers acquired him for a rental reliever, that would be value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wentz, a former supplemental first-round pick out of high school, was looking like a gem of a find from Atlanta in the Shane Greene trade in July 2019 until Tommy John surgery halted his 2020 season in Spring Training. His rehab year coincided with the lost Minor League season, and he returned to game action in May 2021 at Low-A Lakeland before heading back to Double-A Erie, where he had ended 2019. He had a typical first season post-surgery, getting his old velocity back before his old command, but he looked much better by season’s end. Considering Wentz’s game hinged on command before surgery, it was impressive he pitched as effectively as he did, albeit inconsistently. He was prone to bad innings or stretches more than bad nights, often depending on command of his low-90s fastball. His upper-70s changeup hinges on the fastball’s effectiveness. He throws a curveball and a slider, and could do so anytime in counts before surgery, though stingy pitch counts limited how often he could mix his full arsenal last year. The second season back from Tommy John surgery is often when a pitcher feels more like his old self, and the Tigers were counting on that from Wentz. He did make his Major League debut in May, but unfortunately, a shoulder injury caused him to miss two months in the heater of the summer. The southpaw turns 25 in October and needs to find innings and health if he’s ever going to meet his ceiling as a backend starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers already had a deep system in pitching prospects before acquiring Wentz from Atlanta as part of the Shane Greene trade in July 2019, but he became the kind of big surprise who could round out a very good rotation. An inconsistent half-season at Double-A Mississippi made Wentz expendable in the Braves system, but he blossomed upon joining Casey Mize, Matt Manning, Tarik Skubal and Alex Faedo at Double-A Erie, posting a 37-to-4 BB/K ratio in five starts. Just when Wentz seemed poised to push for a debut in Detroit in 2020, his first Major League camp ended abruptly with Tommy John surgery in March 2020, costing him the season. Wentz doesn’t have the power arsenal of Manning or Skubal, nor does he have a pitch as dominant as Mize’s splitter. His strength is his overall command of his pitches and ability to change speeds to set them up. His fastball sat in the low 90s before surgery with enough life to draw swings-and-misses while setting up an upper-70s changeup that works as a putaway pitch. His curveball is a third pitch with promise, one he’s willing to use as a first pitch or to finish at-bats. Wentz returned to action in the summer of 2021 but has needed time to find himself on the mound at Double-A Erie. Expect the Tigers to continue to be cautious with him, but his overall mix and less reliance on velocity should help him adjust further down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pepiot set Butler records for single-season (126) and career (306) strikeouts in 2019, when he went in the third round and eclipsed two-time All-Star Pat Neshek (sixth round, 2002) as the highest-drafted Bulldog ever. He arrived with the best changeup in his Draft class, and the Dodgers have helped him upgrade his fastball and slider. He reduced his Triple-A ERA from 7.13 in 2021 to 2.56 last year, when he also posted a 3.47 ERA in nine appearances (seven starts) during four different stints with Los Angeles. He made the Opening Day roster in 2023 but went on the disabled list with an oblique strain that delayed the start of his season. Pepiot lost some feel for his changeup last year, throwing it harder at 86-88 mph and for strikes less often, and it played more as a plus offering than one that earned some top-of-the-scale grades with greater fade and tumble in the past. His best pitch in 2022 was his four-seam fastball, which has added 3 mph since his college days to sit at 93-95 and top out at 98, and it plays better than its velocity thanks to impressive spin, carry and extension. He has added power and sweep to an upper-80s slider that he can land for strikes or use as a chase pitch, and it grades as average to solid. The final step for Pepiot will be to refine his control and command after he made strides in Triple-A last summer but walked 27 in 36 1/3 big league innings. He has worked to add more balance in his delivery but still battles the strike zone at times and gets hit harder than his stuff suggests he should. His ability to locate his pitches will determine whether he works in the front of a rotation or is more of a back-end option or multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pepiot established Butler records for single-season (126) and career (306) strikeouts in 2019, en route to surpassing two-time All-Star Pat Neshek (sixth round, 2002) as the highest pick in school history when the Dodgers popped him in the third round. His stock soared in 2020 at the Dodgers' alternate site, where he stood out as the best pitcher while overmatching big league hitters with improved stuff and control. His 2021 was a tale of two seasons, as he logged a 2.87 ERA in Double-A but got knocked around for a 7.13 ERA in Triple-A when his control and command faltered. Pepiot owns the best changeup in the Minors, earning top-of-the-scale 80 grades from some evaluators for a low-80s weapon that fades before dropping at the plate. He has improved his fastball significantly since turning pro, gaining about 3 mph to sit at 94-96 and touch 98 while boosting its induced vertical break and carry up in the zone. He has added sweep and power to his slider, which now parks in the upper 80s and moves in the opposite direction from his changeup, and he also can turn it into more of a cutter. While Pepiot has tremendous feel for his changeup, he struggles to locate his fastball with precision and to throw his slider for strikes. Los Angeles has worked with him to create more balance in his delivery, and he made strides with his control and command in 2020 before regressing in the second half of 2021. He could pitch in the front half of a big league rotation if he can add some polish, and his fastball/changeup combination is so good that he should be at least a valuable multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pepiot set Butler records for strikeouts in a season (126) and career (306) in 2019, when he rode the best changeup in that year's Draft class into the third round, surpassing two-time All-Star Pat Neshek (sixth round, 2002) as the highest pick in school history. He reached low Class A in his pro debut that summer before really opening eyes as the best pitcher at the Dodgers' alternate site in 2020. He overmatched big league hitters while showing improved stuff and control, and he has continued to dominate in the upper levels of the Minors in 2021. Pepiot's changeup is a legitimate weapon that he sells with fastball arm speed, only to have it arrive at the plate in the low 80s with a ton of fade. After working at 91-94 mph and touching 96 with high spin rates on his fastball in 2019, he sat at 93-96 with increased vertical movement in shorter stints last year and has averaged 96 mph as a starter this season. He has added power and sharpness to his slider, which is now a solid pitch in the upper 80s, and he uses his upper-70s curveball to get early-count strikes. His crossfire delivery enables Pepiot's pitches to get on hitters more quickly than expected, though it also contributes to control and command lapses at times. Los Angeles has helped him stay more balanced over the rubber, which led to better location of his pitches last summer. He's on the path to becoming at least a No. 3 starter and the Dodgers rebuffed several inquiries for him at the Trade Deadline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Minor League outfielder Allen Thomas, Alek grew up around baseball. The three-sport star at Chicago's Mount Carmel High School was set to honor a commitment to Texas Christian before the D-backs selected him in the second round of the 2018 Draft and signed him to an above-slot bonus of $1.2 million. Thomas looked like one of the more advanced prep players from his class during his first full season, hitting his way up to Class A Advanced Visalia at age 19 while earning a SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game nod along the way. He spent 2020 at Arizona’s alternate training site and carried that experience with him in 2021, when he worked his way up to Triple-A, set career highs in multiple offensive categories and represented Arizona for a second time at the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game. It didn’t take Thomas long to live up to his reputation as one of the better prep hitters in his Draft class. A compact left-handed swing that yields hard, line-drive contact to all fields along with an advanced approach fuels Thomas' projection as a plus hitter. His approach and his power took steps forward in 2021 as he showed more discipline and hit a career-high 18 homers. While it’s unlikely he’ll ever be a slugger, Thomas has shown the ability to drive the ball and could rack up between 15-20 homers a year once he’s in the Majors. Outstanding instincts, along with a strong baseball acumen, enhance Thomas’ plus speed on the bases and in center field, where he has a chance to stay. Thomas could move to left if needed, but his below-average arm would likely keep him out of right. Thomas receives some comparisons to 2019 first-rounder Corbin Carroll for having an advanced, well-rounded game that could enable him to move quickly. He has an incredibly high floor, and club officials like his chances of developing into at least a well-rounded regular at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Minor League outfielder and current White Sox director of strength and conditioning Allen Thomas, Alek spent his early years around the game. He became a three-sport star at Chicago's Mount Carmel High School and was set to honor his commitment to Texas Christian before the D-backs selected him in the second round of the 2018 Draft and signed him to an above-slot bonus of $1.2 million. He looked like one of the more advanced prep players from his class during his first full season, as Thomas hit his way up to Class A Advanced Visalia at age 19 while earning a SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game nod along the way. He spent 2020 at Arizona’s alternate training site and carried that experience with him in 2021. Thomas put together an impressive campaign with Double-A Amarillo, represented Arizona for a second time at the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game in Denver and was promoted to Triple-A in August. It didn’t take Thomas long to live up to his reputation as one of the better prep hitters in his Draft class. A compact left-handed swing that yields hard, line-drive contact to all fields along with an advanced approach fuels Thomas' projection as a plus hitter. His approach took a step forward this season as he’s shown an ability to control the strike zone and swinging at better pitches. It’s a hit-over-power offensive profile, but there’s also enough pop in Thomas’ bat to forecast 12-15 homers, and he started to tap into it more this season. Outstanding instincts, along with a strong baseball acumen, enhance Thomas’ plus speed on the bases and in center field, where he has a chance to stay. His below-average arm strength qualifies him to play either center or left field but is stretched thin in right. Thomas receives some comparisons to 2019 first-rounder Corbin Carroll for having an advanced, well-rounded game that could enable him to move quickly. He has an unusually high floor for a high school player, and club officials like his chances of developing into at least a well-rounded regular at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The second of three straight college right-handers taken in the first round by the Mariners, Kirby came out of Elon University as a strike-throwing machine, a command-over-stuff guy who walked just 1.9 batters per nine innings over three years. After a brief debut in 2019, time at the Mariners’ alternate training site in 2020 and a full-season debut that saw him reach Double-A in 2021, Kirby still fills up the strike zone, but his prospect stock has skyrocketed thanks to his stuff improving exponentially since signing. Kirby appeals to evaluators of all types thanks to the quality of stuff and the ease with which he does it, blowing up any and all internal metrics in terms of things like velocity, movement, command, swing and miss and lack of hard contact. He can now run his fastball up to 100 mph, turning what was a low-90s heater into one that sits in the 96-98 mph range consistently. He has two distinct breaking pitches, both of which are plus at times, and he sinks a solid changeup as well. The velocity gains have done nothing to hamper Kirby’s ability to drop the ball on a dime, as the right-hander walked just 2.0 per nine in 2021. The only thing that’s holding him back is experience, and he did miss some time with shoulder fatigue, but he’s looking more and more like a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s now been five Drafts in a row that the Mariners have gone with a college player in the first round, the last three coming in the form of right-handed pitchers. Kirby, the No. 20 overall pick in 2019, was the first-ever first-round pick out of Elon University and was sandwiched by Logan Gilbert in 2018 and Emerson Hancock in 2020 as the Mariners try to draft and develop a future rotation. Kirby gave a glimpse of what he’s about during his pro debut in short-season ball in 2019, then threw well at the Mariners’ alternate training site last year. While Kirby is known more for his command than anything else, he has more than enough raw stuff at his disposal. He delivers a four-pitch mix from a 6-foot-4 frame, starting with a fastball that sits in the low-90s with good running life, but that he can get up to 98 mph at times. He’s worked on adding strength which will lead to more consistent velocity as well. Kirby throws both a curve and a slider, with the former slightly ahead, and both have the chance to be out pitches. He does a nice job of selling his sinking changeup with excellent arm speed. All of Kirby’s stuff plays up because of his command, which might be as good as any pitcher in the Minor Leagues. He walked virtually no one during his last season at Elon and then walked literally no one over 23 innings of his pro debut in 2019. His combination of improving stuff and elite-level control all point to him moving very quickly up the organizational ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Back in 2017, Lewis was a bit of a surprise No. 1 overall pick, though the Twins coveted him. He made a very strong impression playing across two levels of A ball in his first full season. After a rougher 2019 campaign, Lewis won MVP honors in the Arizona Fall League, but then didn’t play a game for two years because of the 2020 shutdown and a torn ACL in 2021. He hit well upon his return in Triple-A in 2022 to earn his first callup to the big leagues. The comeback story was short-lived as he tore the same ACL after crashing into the center-field wall during his second time up with Minnesota, knocking him out for another year. All of the tools that made Lewis a potential All-Star caliber player are still there. It remains to be seen if his elite-level speed will still be intact after his second knee surgery, but Lewis’ rehab work following his first injury actually increased his speed. He had struggled with his approach at times during the early stages of his career, particularly in 2019, but was much more refined and patient at the plate in 2022, with simpler swing mechanics -- minus his old leg kick -- allowing him to barrel up the baseball more consistently and get to what could be above-average or better power in the future. Lewis has continued to primarily play shortstop as a pro and has the defensive chops to stay there long-term, with more than enough arm and range for the premium position. He showed off the ability to play a very good center field in the AFL and then in 2022, though there might be some concern given that’s where he reinjured his knee in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 1 pick in the 2017 Draft, out of the Southern California high school ranks, Lewis played up to advanced billing in his first year-plus of pro ball, with a .292/.352/.451 slash line across two levels of A ball in his first full season. He struggled in '19, though he went to the Futures Game and reached Double-A. He seemed to right the ship with an MVP performance in the Arizona Fall League, but he didn’t play a competitive game for two years because of the pandemic and a torn ACL suffered in Spring Training of '21. He made a triumphant return to competitive play in '22, earning his first callup to the big leagues, only to tear the same ACL when he crashed into the center-field wall in his second Major League stint. Lewis has tremendous upside when he’s healthy. He had close to top-of-the-scale speed before he hurt his knee that made him a dangerous baserunner. With a lot of moving parts to his swing and a big leg kick, Lewis got out of sync in 2019, but he seemed to get his timing back in the AFL and at the Twins’ alternate training site in '20. He’s worked to quiet his setup and smooth out his swing, and losing the leg kick helped his timing before his second knee injury. He is capable of driving the ball to all fields and there’s plenty of raw power for him to tap into. Drafted as a shortstop, Lewis has mostly played the premium position as a pro, and had made enough improvements for most to believe he and his above-average arm can stick there in the big leagues. He also showed off positional flexibility in the AFL, including some plus defensive ability in center field. He was added to the 40-man roster this past offseason, but now Lewis and the Twins will have to wait 12 months from his June surgery to get him back into action again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While it was a mild surprise when Lewis was the No. 1 pick in the 2017 Draft, he certainly played like the top player in the class during his pro debut that summer when he reached full-season ball as a high school draftee and continued excelling across two levels of Class A ball during his first full season. He dealt with failure for the first time in 2019, though he did reach Double-A, finishing with a .661 OPS. Lewis erased some of that with an MVP performance in the Arizona Fall League that fall and continued to play well at the Twins’ alternate camp in 2020. His progress was derailed when he required surgery for a torn right ACL at the start of Spring Training. When he’s locked in and healthy, Lewis shows off all five tools on the field, all of which can play up because of his plus makeup and instincts. The main variance might be with his hit tool. He spent most of 2019 struggling being on time at the plate as he utilizes a big leg kick and has a busy swing, leading to a loss of approach. He was able to get it back for his time in the AFL and it carried over to his alternate camp work this past season. Lewis is able to drive the ball with hard contact to all fields and the power is just starting to show up. Lewis’ plus speed makes him a basestealing threat and his athleticism helps him on the defensive side. He showed he can move seamlessly around the field in the AFL, seeing time at second, third and center field in addition to shortstop. That’s the spot he played exclusively at the alternate camp, working with infield coordinator Billy Boyer and has every chance to stick there long-term, though the Twins know they can plug his bat into any number of positions when it’s deemed ready.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hjelle is on the cusp of making it to San Francisco, and when he does, he'll match Jon Rauch as the tallest big leaguer ever at 6-foot-11. The Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year as a Kentucky sophomore in 2017, he signed for $1.5 million as a second-round pick after his junior season. After mostly breezing through the Minors, he got rocked for a 5.74 ERA in 10 starts after he arrived in Triple-A last August, though that didn't dissuade the Giants from placing him on their 40-man roster. Hjelle's biggest weapon remains his hard knuckle-curve, an 82-85 mph breaker with power and depth that was his lone effective pitch in Triple-A. His fastball continued to sit at 92-94 mph and top out at 96, but the extension and angle that his extra-large frame creates didn't throw Triple-A hitters off as much as it had lower-level opponents. His sinking changeup can be an average third offering when he keeps it in the low 80s and lands it in the zone, but it lacks consistency. With excellent body control for his size, Hjelle has a long track record of providing strikes, though his walk rate jumped from 2.3 per nine innings before he got to Triple-A to 4.9 afterward. He keeps batters off balance by sequencing his pitches well, but he must locate his fastball and changeup with more precision in order to succeed. He has displayed No. 4 starter ceiling in the past but looked more like a future curveball-dependent reliever at the end of 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year as a sophomore in 2017, Hjelle signed for $1.5 million as a second-round pick the following year and advanced to Double-A in his first full pro season. Despite the lack of a Minor League season in 2020, he wasn't invited to the Giants' alternate site (because they focused on pitchers who could help in the Majors imminently) or instructional league (because they didn't want to ramp him back up and alter his offseason program in advance of big league camp). While throwing simulated innings at home, he was on hand for the birth of his first child and completed his college degree from Kentucky. If Hjelle makes it to The Show, he'll match Jon Rauch as the tallest big leaguer ever at 6-foot-11, but unlike a lot of gargantuan pitchers he's more polished than intimidating. His fastball parks around 92-94 mph and tops out at 96, playing better than its velocity because of the extension and angle his huge frame creates. His low-80s knuckle-curve can be a plus pitch at times and he has made progress with a sinking changeup since turning pro. Hjelle has exceptional body control for his size, which allows him to provide consistent strikes and pound the bottom of the zone. He sequences his pitches well, adding to his ability to keep hitters off balance. He should help the Giants in the near future and comes with a high floor as a good bet to become a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: No one in the Cardinals' system did more to put himself on the radar in 2021 than Yepez. Originally signed for $1 million by the Braves in July 2014, the Venezuela native was traded to St. Louis in May 2017 for Matt Adams. He didn’t hit more than 10 homers or sport an OPS above .789 until that 2021 breakout, where he sported a .286/.383/.586 line with 27 blasts between Double-A and Triple-A. The Cards added Yepez to the Major League roster for the NL Wild Card Game against the Dodgers and afterwards sent him to the Arizona Fall League, where he hit .302/.388/.640 in 23 games. Yepez added muscle in 2021 and used it to fuel his power increase at the upper Minors. He also shortened his swing to make the most of that pop and make more quality contact. The result was a strikeout rate below 20 percent, not typical for someone with that much power. Improved strike-zone awareness and an advanced approach could make him an above-average hitter at the top level, should this trajectory continue. The Cardinals have given Yepez time at all four corner spots -- left, right, third and first. A lack of speed and his increasing strength make him more of a first baseman, and it was noteworthy that 16 of his 20 defensive starts in the AFL came at that spot. He might need to access the versatility (or a DH) to find playing time with Paul Goldschmidt on the roster, but the hitting gains and new roster spot should mean he’ll help St. Louis in some way soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves signed Yepez as a 16-year-old for $1 million in 2014. He made his full-season debut in 2016, but missed nearly three months with an injury. The Venezuela native continued to work his way up the ladder in the Braves’ system, but was dealt to the Cardinals in exchange for Matt Adams in 2017. Yepez showed an advanced approach and promising hitability upon his arrival to the Cardinals organization. Yepez shed some fat and added some muscle to his frame, which quickly paid dividends as things really started to come together for him in 2019 and continued in 2021 as he set a career high for homers and reached Triple-A Memphis. While he doesn’t always get to it in games, there is power in Yepez’s 6-foot-1, 200-pound frame. Yepez drives the ball well to the gaps and consistently posts high exit velocities, so the Cardinals expect more home runs to come as he continues to make adjustments in the batter’s box. Among those adjustments, Yepez has shortened his swing since the Cardinals acquired him and also increasingly shown a better understanding of the strike zone as a whole, as well as which pitches he’s able to drive. The fact that he’s been able to transform both his body and offensive approach speaks to a work ethic that could help speed up his timeline. Yepez’s size and lack of speed limits him on the defensive side of the ball, but he’s still shown some good versatility. Originally signed as a third baseman, Yepez also spent time at first base early in his career and added outfield to his skillset in 2019. While his arm will play at any of the positions, his range will likely limit him to first base in the future. The development of his power will certainly be important if Yepez is to profile at first base. While his bat will allow him to contribute, the power may determine whether he’s an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Faedo is nearly five years removed from his dominant run through the College World Series at the University of Florida. He was once among a quartet of pitching prospects who comprised the heart of the Tigers’ rebuilding effort, but the combination of the pandemic and a torn elbow ligament that led to Tommy John surgery halted his progress the last couple of years while Casey Mize, Tarik Skubal and Matt Manning graduated to Detroit. Faedo’s slider has always been his out pitch, which he has leaned on to varying degrees since his college days at the University of Florida. He can throw it like two different pitches, whether he’s trying to spot it for a strike or induce a hitter to chase. His fastball dropped to 90-91 mph in 2018 but bounced back to the mid-90s with an improved spin rate thanks to a more upright delivery and consistent arm slot. How that pitch mix, especially his slider use, changes after surgery will be closely followed. The Tigers will have to weigh carefully how to progress Faedo. He hasn’t thrown a regular-season pitch since 2019 at Double-A Erie, and he’ll likely face the same growing pains with command that many pitchers -- including fellow Tigers prospect Joey Wentz last year -- encounter their first year back from surgery. Faedo is also 26 years old, and with the Tigers ready to progress into contention, the organization has to figure out where he fits in its plans.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Faedo’s career has progressed in stops and starts since the summer of 2017, when he was the Tigers’ first-round pick and the Most Outstanding Player of the College World Series just weeks apart. Faedo didn’t pitch the rest of that year, struggled through his first pro season in 2018, matured into a more polished prospect in 2019, then saw a chance at the Majors vanish during baseball’s spring shutdown. Last year included a COVID bout that cost him a spot in Summer Camp, a forearm strain that shut him down at the alternate training site and eventually a diagnosis of a torn elbow ligament. He underwent Tommy John surgery and will miss the 2021 season while rehabbing. Faedo’s slider has always been his out pitch, which he has leaned on to varying degrees since his college days at the University of Florida. He can throw it like two different pitches, whether he’s trying to spot it for a strike or induce a hitter to chase. His fastball dropped to 90-91 mph in 2018 but bounced back to the mid-90s with an improved spin rate thanks to a more upright delivery and consistent arm slot. How that pitch mix, especially his slider use, changes after surgery will be closely followed. Tigers officials were impressed with Faedo’s progress and maturity and saw him as a real contributor for the near future, until an essentially lost 2020 was followed by a lost 2021. He’ll be 26 years old when he resumes pitching in 2022, at which point former Double-A Erie teammates Casey Mize, Tarik Skubal, Matt Manning and even Joey Wentz all might be in Detroit. How he reacts will determine whether he’s left behind or pulled forward to join them. If he doesn’t crack the rotation, his arsenal could play in a bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few Minor Leaguers did more to rebuild their stocks in 2021. The Florida native was a Royals second-round pick in 2017, signing for above slot at $2.1 million, and enjoyed a solid first season at Class A Lexington a year later. His 2019 season, however, was a massive offensive struggle. Melendez hit just .163 with nine homers and a 39.4 percent K rate at Class A Advanced Wilmington. He spent 2020 reworking his swing and approach at the Royals’ alternate training site and put that to good use in his breakout 2021. Melendez led the Minors with 41 home runs and finished with a .288/.386/.625 line and 21.7 percent strikeout rate over 123 games at Double-A and Triple-A. The bulk of the left-handed slugger’s improvements came down to him lessening the severity of his leg kick and improving his pitch recognition with the added time at the plate. His power plays to all fields, and Melendez can really drive balls the opposite way when needed. He has been considered a plus defender behind the plate since his prep days, though his framing still needs work entering his age-23 season, and his arm is right there with his pop as his loudest tool. Melendez threw out 31 percent of attempted Double-A and Triple-A basestealers and owns a career 40 percent caught-stealing rate in the Minors. Melendez is back to being one of the most complete catching prospects in the game. With Salvador Perez still in the frame, Melendez’s ceiling as a first-division backstop only gives the Royals a good problem -- one they might have to solve early in the summer of 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a 2017 Draft light on catching prospects, Melendez stood out as MLB Pipeline’s No. 72 prospect. The Royals took him No. 52 overall and signed him well above pick value to get him away from playing for his father, Mervyl, at Florida International. While Melendez has always performed well behind the plate, he struggled offensively in 2019 and posted a .163/.260/.311 slash line in Class A Advanced. He spent the summer at the Royals’ alternate training site followed by instructs at Kauffman Stadium to get as many at-bats as possible while also working on mechanical changes to his swing, and the work has showed up in a big way in 2021 as Melendez has chased the Minor League home run lead for much of the summer. Melendez has serious raw power that even the Royals say might be the best in the system. In 2020, he toned down the big leg kick that causes him to over-rotate with his upper half and commit to pitches earlier -- which hurt pitch recognition and had been a reason for his 39.4 percent strikeout rate in the Minors. The Royals don’t want to take away the leg kick completely and have worked with Melendez to improve his posture in the box, trying to get him to be squarer with the pitcher and calm the movement in his swing down. He worked hard to improve his contact point and reduce the amount of pitches he chases out of the zone. Melendez’s best tool defensively is his cannon of an arm with a quick release that helps stymie the running game. He already has impressive blocking and receiving skills, and he knows how to call a game and manage a staff. The Royals were confident in his offensive adjustments made last year and have been elated to see them turn into production in 2021. Melendez always had the defensive ability to be a Major League catcher, but these improvements make his future as a starting backstop all the clearer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins took Miranda in the Competitive Balance Round B of the 2016 Draft and the Puerto Rican high school product progressed slowly, spending two summers in rookie ball and putting up moderate numbers across two levels of A ball in 2018 and 2019, though he did touch Double-A at the end of the year. He wasn’t put on the 40-man roster following 2020, nor was he selected in the Rule 5 Draft, decisions all 30 teams might be regretting after Miranda had one of the best offensive seasons in the Minor Leagues in 2021, leading the Minors in hits and finishing with a .973 OPS between Double- and Triple-A. Miranda has always been a contact machine with a very low whiff rate. In 2021, he was much more selective, drawing more walks and working counts in his favor, which allowed him to use his plus bat-to-ball skills to drive the ball much more frequently and finish with 30 or more doubles and homers for the season. The power came without a sacrifice in terms of strikeouts as he whiffed in just 12.5 percent of his plate appearances. He rarely misses a fastball, and he registered above-average exit velocities during his time in Triple-A. As certain as the Twins are now about Miranda’s bat, and yes, he was added to the 40-man this past offseason, it’s less clear where Miranda might fit defensively. He has good hands and has worked this offseason to improve his arm strength, but he’s very limited range-wise. He’s played mostly third and second, with some first base mixed in of late, though few doubt he’ll get his bat into the lineup more often than not in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins drafted and signed at least one player from Puerto Rico every year from 2007-18, with Eddie Rosario ('10) and José Berríos ('12) the most successful to date. Miranda, a 2016 draftee, was the first Puerto Rican player taken in the top two rounds by the club since Berríos and is one of four players taken from the island in rounds 1 or 2 from 2016-20. He’s made incremental progress, touching Double-A for the first time in 2019. He wasn’t protected on the 40-man roster and wasn’t taken in the Rule 5 Draft last December, but turned in a good instructional league performance last fall and hit well in a brief stint in the Puerto Rican Winter League, something that has carried over to a breakout 2021 performance. Miranda’s biggest strength, and perhaps weakness, had been his ability to make contact. He’s struck out in less than 12 percent of his plate appearances over the course of his career entering 2021, using a short, compact swing to drive the ball to all fields. The flip side of that coin is that he swings at virtually everything, often putting balls out of the zone into play and rarely working counts. The Twins challenged him to work on his approach and tighten up his strike zone at instructs, with positive results that helped lead to his power breakthrough in 2021. Miranda has mostly played second and third defensively, and has seen time at those two positions as well as first base in 2021. It’s now looking like there might be enough pop to profile at an infield corner, but he could still fit a role as an offensive-minded utility player whose bat finds its way into the lineup on a daily basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Sands missed a lot more bats in his third year as a starter for Florida State in 2018, that led to him creeping up Draft boards, landing to the Twins in the fifth round. He’s missed some time with injuries -- some arm-related, some not -- but has shown he can get professional hitters out. He pitched across two levels of A-ball and touched Double-A in 2019, then came back post-pandemic in 2021 and found success in Double-A, where his 2.46 ERA would have led the Double-A Central had he pitched enough innings to qualify. Sands was a consistent performer pretty much from start to finish, using a solid, if unspectacular, three-pitch mix in the process. He doesn’t have the more typical north-south profile, with a lower slot bringing fastballs that averaged 93 mph and topped out at 97. He worked in the offseason to add more movement and there was good run on the pitch last year, leading to missing more bats. His curve is a bit slurvy, with more of a sweepy break at around 80 mph, and he’s worked to throw it a bit harder, but it’s a successful pitch, and his changeup features solid fade. With a very repeatable delivery, Sands was a big-time strike-thrower in the early stages of his career and his uptick in walks in 2021 caught some by surprise, though that might be attributed to the 2020 layoff. His ceiling might be limited to the back end of a rotation, but he could be ready to help out in that role very soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sands spent three years in Florida State’s rotation with somewhat uneven results. A combination of two strong summers in the Cape Cod League and a junior season that saw him miss bats at a much higher rate led to the Twins taking the right-hander in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft. He didn’t make his professional debut until '19 because of some arm issues and even though his workload was somewhat limited during that first full year, he pitched his way across three levels to Double-A. His official work in '20 was limited to instructional league play. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has the chance to have three at least average pitches, all of which he can throw for strikes. After featuring more of a sinker down in the zone in college, Sands has found success with a low-90s fastball that touches 95-96 mph with life up in the zone. His breaking ball, a curve with solid three-quarters break to it, has improved, and he continues to work on adding velocity to it and commanding it in the strike zone more consistently. His changeup gets swings-and-misses as well as weak contact. While Sands’ control was intermittent in college, he was an extreme strike-thrower during his first full season of pro ball, walking just 1.8 per nine innings, with a very repeatable delivery. His ceiling might be limited as a back-end starter, but he’s not far from reaching it, with the chance to be a bit more than that if his stuff keeps ticking upwards.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles opted for a bulk package of pitching prospects when they traded Dylan Bundy to the Angels in December 2019, acquiring Bradish along with Kyle Brnovich, Zack Peek and Isaac Mattson. All have a chance to reach the big leagues (Mattson already has) in short order. But the highest ceiling of the group belongs to Bradish, a sizable righty with a starter’s build and a developing four-pitch mix. A former fourth-round pick of the Angels in 2018, Bradish spent three years as a weekend starter at New Mexico State before impressing in his only season in the Angels’ system. He was one of the top performers at Orioles’ instructional camp in 2020, then spent most of 2021 at Triple-A Norfolk, posting a 4.26 ERA with 105 strikeouts in 86 2/3 innings. Baltimore added him to its 40-man roster in November. At 6-foot-4 and 220 pounds, Bradish is an imposing presence on the mound with a max-effort delivery that creates natural deception and an uncomfortable look, especially for right-handed hitters. His fastball sits in the mid-90s and touches 97 at times, pairing with a power curve in the mid-80s he uses to miss bats. Bradish also features a hard changeup and slider-like cutter, which he throws in the high 80s and darts away from righties. The changeup has made strides and gives him an additional weapon, though it remains a work in progress. Bradish struggled with command at times as a younger pitcher due to his size, stuff and all-out delivery. Control remains a growth area, but improved at Triple-A to quiet speculation about a potential long-term move to the ‘pen. He may end up there or as a swingman in the short term, given his chance to break camp with the Orioles this spring. But his four-pitch mix gives Bradish the ceiling of an impact starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick of the Angels in 2018 after spending three years as a weekend starter at New Mexico State, Bradish was the highest rated of the four prospects the Orioles acquired from the Angels for Dylan Bundy in December 2019. He performed well in one season in the Angels system, compiling 120 strikeouts in 101 innings in the Class A Advanced California League, looking like a potential mid-rotation starter when he was sent to Baltimore along with Isaac Mattson, Kyle Brnovich and Zack Peek. There is a sense now, though, that Bradish could grow into much more. His fastball velocity increased from 88-94 mph before the trade to 92-97 mph after, numbers Bradish showed regularly at the O’s alternate training site in 2020 and has largely maintained into the 2021 season. The 6-foot-4 righty pairs it with a power curve in the mid-80s he uses to miss bats, and features a hard changeup and slider-like cutter as well. The slider, which Bradish throws in the high 80s, may develop into his best secondary pitch with time. He fires it all from a unique delivery that creates natural deception and an uncomfortable look, especially for right-handed hitters. The combination of Bradish’s size, stuff and max-effort delivery gives him a lot of moving parts on the mound; as a result, he’s struggled with command and control issues both in collegiate and pro ball. He has enough weapons though, at this point, to silence any prior chatter about potentially ending up in the ‘pen. He advanced to Triple-A after three Double-A starts at the beginning of 2021, moving quickly thanks to his four-pitch mix and impact starter ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: First drafted out of Chipola College by the D-backs in the 18th round of the ’16 Draft, Francis went in the seventh round to the Brewers the next summer and signed for an above-slot bonus of $235,000. Francis’ first full season in Milwaukee’s system (’18) saw him post a 4.50 ERA between Low-A and High-A, but he came back with a stronger ’19 season between High-A and Double-A, posting a 3.97 ERA with 165 strikeouts over 142 2/3 innings. The Blue Jays acquired Francis alongside reliever Trevor Richards in a deal for Rowdy Tellez in July of ’21.
