Francis filled a valuable role for the Blue Jays immediately in terms of upper-minors depth. With a sinking fastball that comes from his 6-foot-5 frame in the low-90s, Francis works to set up his slider, which has been his most effective pitch of late when he needs a strike. He’ll feature a curveball and changeup to a lesser extent, but Francis’ value lies mostly in his steady outings. Much like former rotation-mate Zach Logue, who was traded to Oakland in the spring, Francis doesn’t do much in a flashy manner but gets the job done consistently. Also added to the 40-man roster this past offseason, Francis should be one of the first young arms the Blue Jays turn to if they have a need at the Major League level. After needing to convert starters into relief roles in recent seasons, the Blue Jays are now looking at a nice Triple-A depth group. Turning 26 in March, Francis could be called on at any point in ’22.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Taft High School in Chicago, most thought Suwinski was headed to Indiana for college. But the Padres swooped in, taking him in the 15th round of the 2016 Draft and signing him for an above-slot $550,000 to keep him from ever suiting up for the Hoosiers. He spent two years in Low-A ball and one up a level in 2019, with little success, before having a bit of a breakout in 2021 in his first taste of Double-A, then getting sent to the Pirates in the Adam Frazier deal at last year’s Trade Deadline. The Pirates liked the bat enough to add Suwinski to the 40-man roster in the offseason. The left-handed-hitting Suwinski showed off an improved approach at the plate in 2021 that led to much better results. His walk rate went up and his strikeouts decreased, which helped him get to his plus raw power on a more regular basis, and he set career highs in several offensive categories. He hits the ball hard and with loft, especially to his pull side, and it’s not hard to dream about how his left-handed swing might work with the short porch in right field at PNC Park. Suwinski has average speed, but moves well for his size. He’s never going to wow anyone with his outfield play, but should be capable enough to play an outfield corner in the big leagues. He might be more of a platoon or fourth-outfielder type, but don’t be surprised if he works his potent bat into a lineup more often than not.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palacios comes from a baseball family that already has produced a pair of big leaguers in his uncle Rey and brother Josh. The highest-drafted player in Towson history, he set school records for single-season (32) and career (76) steals before the Guardians selected him in the third round of the 2018 Draft. After missing all of 2019 following labrum surgery on his right (throwing) shoulder and losing 2020 to the pandemic, he came back last year to reach Triple-A in his first full pro season and grab a spot on Cleveland's 40-man roster. Palacios posted a career .318 batting average and .409 on-base percentage in his first two seasons as a pro, thanks to his quick left-handed stroke, bat-to-ball skill and patient, all-fields approach. He uses his plus speed to get on base and is a threat to steal, adding to his tablesetter profile. He has added some strength since signing but prioritizes contact over power and won't provide more than 12-15 homers per year. Though he spent most of his first two pro seasons at second base and has more than enough quickness for the position, he doesn't have smooth infield actions and possesses fringy arm strength. Cleveland has an abundance of middle-infield prospects, so he's probably headed for the outfield. He played some center field last season and only left and center in the Arizona Fall League, showing the potential to become an average to solid defender if he moves.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-round pick out of South Alabama in 2018, Donovan was one of the Cardinals' breakout stars in 2021. Playing in his age-24 season, the left-handed slugger climbed three levels to Triple-A Memphis and finished at the top of the system in average (.304), OBP (.399), OPS (.854) and wRC+ (134). He continued to hit during a trip to the Arizona Fall League, where he went 16-for-52 (.308) with more walks (10) than strikeouts (eight) and won a fan vote to be named to the Fall Stars Game. The Cardinals rewarded Donovan for his efforts with a spot on the 40-man roster ahead of his Rule 5 eligibility. Utilizing the smallest of toe taps, Donovan relies on the quickness of his hands to generate a healthy amount of contact from the left side. He shows a patient approach that also helps drive his walk rates, and the shortness of his swing keeps him from striking out all that often too. Since the approach is geared toward contact, he doesn’t exhibit a ton of power, and his 12 homers from 2021 are about what to expect from him in a potential full Major League season. Donovan doesn’t exhibit great speed by any means but knows how to pick his spots on the basepaths; he finished with 19 steals in 2021, third-most among St. Louis full-season farmhands. Donovan saw time at six different positions last season -- all four infield spots, along with left and right -- and that was almost out of necessity because the Cards wanted his bat in the lineup somehow. With his below-average speed and arm, he isn’t a natural fit anywhere and is likely best served to continue moving around based on daily need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Riley Greene wasn’t exactly a surprise as the Tigers’ Minor League Player of the Year in 2021, nobody would’ve expected Brieske -- a 27th-round pick in 2019 -- to win Pitcher of the Year honors going into the season. He didn’t begin pitching full-time until his senior year in high school, then went to Glendale (Ariz.) Junior College before his high strikeout rate caught scouts’ attention at Division II Colorado State-Pueblo. A solid introduction to the Tigers system in 2019 backed up the pick, and after losing a season to the pandemic, he returned to action in 2021 as a more well-rounded pitcher and hit the fast track up the system. By season’s end, he was arguably the most effective starter at Double-A Erie, and in the conversation for pitchers who could eventually contribute in Detroit. With a high arm angle and a delivery that starts on the first-base side of the rubber, Brieske essentially takes the shortest path to home plate and throws downhill from there. His four-seam fastball averages 92-94 mph, but he commands it well to all parts of the strike zone and complements it with a changeup about 10 mph slower. That was his primary arsenal when he entered pro ball, but his breakout 2021 season came after adding a tight slider that he can locate and a 12-6 curveball that can freeze hitters as it breaks. The total package is four pitches at different speeds with different movement. Brieske is the kind of pitching prospect who can make a good organization great if he makes the big leagues. His cerebral approach and work ethic have enabled him to better his game and earned him an opportunity to tap the Tigers’ player development resources. Brieske came to Spring Training intent on adding an extra mph or two of velocity on his pitches through training and technique. If he can do so without sacrificing the rest of his game, that could be the factor that eventually lands Brieske in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Padres' $78 million international spending spree in 2016-17, Arias signed for $1.9 million out of Venezuela. He had the highest ceiling among the six youngsters San Diego sent to the Guardians in the nine-player Mike Clevinger trade in August 2020, and he may have more upside than any of Cleveland's position prospects. His performance dipped in 2022, in part because of a broken right hand that cost him eight weeks in Triple-A, but he still made his big league debut, homered off Tyler Glasnow in September and started three American League Division Series games at first base in October. With impressive bat speed and strength, Arias has more raw power than most shortstops and 30-homer upside. To reach that potential, he'll need to develop a more selective approach and do a better job of driving the ball in the air. He doesn't strike out excessively, but he gets himself out on pitches he should avoid and rarely walks. Arias gets average-to-solid grades for his speed, which plays better in the field than on the bases. He's a quality defender at shortstop with range to both sides, reliable hands and double-plus arm strength that ranks among the best in the Minors. He played all four infield positions in Cleveland last year as well as left field in Triple-A, and he might be able to claim a role as a slugging super-utilityman on a big league club loaded with infield options.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arias has the highest ceiling of the six players the Guardians acquired in the nine-player Mike Clevinger trade with the Padres in August 2020 -- and some evaluators believe he has the highest ceiling of any position player in Cleveland's system. He was part of San Diego's $78 million spending spree on the 2016 international market, signing for $1.9 million out of Venezuela. The youngest batting qualifier (age 21) in the Triple-A East last season, he posted an .802 OPS with 13 homers while also standing out with his defense. A right-handed hitter, Arias has impressive bat speed and strength that give him more raw power than most shortstops, but he'll need to make some adjustments at the plate to reach his 25-30 homer upside. While he doesn't strike out excessively, he's overly aggressive at the plate and makes too much weak groundball contact. He'll have to make better swing decisions and learn to launch more balls in the air to his pull side. Arias earns average to solid grades for his speed, which is more apparent in the field than on the bases. He has good actions and instincts at shortstop, where he's a plus defender, and he's also an asset at third and second base. He has one of the strongest arms in the Minors and is capable of making any throw needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres shelled out $78 million in bonuses and penalty taxes for their 2016 international class, with Arias' $1.9 million bonus ranking as just their seventh-highest. They promoted the Venezuelan aggressively, sending him to high Class A at age 19 in 2019 and watching him hit .302/.339/.470 and lead the California League with 224 total bases. He has the highest ceiling of the six players acquired by the Indians in the nine-player deal that sent Mike Clevinger to San Diego in August 2020. Loaded with tools, Arias has more raw power than most shortstops and is capable of driving the ball out of the park to all fields thanks to his bat speed, strength and leverage. How much he'll tap into his 25-30 homer potential will depend on his ability to refine his approach at the plate. He needs to improve his pitch recognition, keep his right-handed swing from getting too long and curb a tendency to chase pitches out of the strike zone. An average to solid runner, Arias makes better use of his quickness in the field than on the bases. He's a plus defender at shortstop, where he displays quality instincts and actions, and he also gets the job done at second and third base. His best pure tool is his arm, which earns top-of-the-scale grades from some evaluators and ranks among the very best in the game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Allen’s defensive prowess as a high schooler was enough for the A’s to go well above his slot value as a third-round pick in the 2017 Draft with a $2 million bonus. In addition to the defense that continues to shine, Allen has gradually improved his offensive game, hitting a combined .288 at Double-A and Triple-A in a 2021 campaign that also saw him help Team USA to an Olympic silver medal over the summer. He was added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. Continuing to refine his skills with the bat, the A’s believe Allen is starting to find himself as a hitter, now focused on keeping the ball on the lines and hitting it to all fields, with added strength helping him drive the ball more consistently. He has a knack for making a lot of contact and while he doesn’t walk a ton, he also limits strikeouts. His speed also allows the potential for double-digit stolen base numbers. Allen has seen some time at second base, but there’s no question his big league future is at shortstop as a superb defender who could win multiple Gold Gloves. With the questions about his bat now fading away, he’s just about ready for his call to the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A’s thought so much of Allen’s impressive showing on defense as a high schooler that they went well over his third-round slot value with a $2 million bonus in the 2017 Draft. While maintaining his defensive prowess, Allen has made strides in his offensive game, getting off to a strong start at the plate in 2019 until a high ankle sprain ended his season prematurely. He returned from the injury in time for the Arizona Fall League. Allen’s defense will always outshine his offense. He is spectacular in every facet of the position, whether it be range, hands or footwork. He also has a strong arm that lends to him making any throw from any angle. All put together, Allen has the makings of a future Gold Glove Award winner at shortstop. He is still refining his offense, which took a step in the right direction prior to the ankle injury. Allen projects as a No. 8 or 9 hitter in the big leagues, though that could improve with more success at the higher levels of the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gore helped lead Whiteville (N.C.) High to three state titles and capped his outstanding prep career by garnering Gatorade National Player of the Year honors as a senior in 2017. The Padres took him with the No. 3 overall pick that June, signing the left-hander for $6.7 million. Gore was bothered by a blister problem in his first full season, landing on the injured list twice at Class A Fort Wayne, but emerged as baseball’s top pitching prospect in 2019, finishing his age-20 season in Double-A as the Minor League leader (min. 100 IP) in ERA (1.69) and WHIP (0.83). Seemingly poised to impact the Padres’ rotation in 2020, Gore instead spent the season at the alternate training site, working on mechanical issues. He opened 2021 at Triple-A El Paso but those same issues persisted and he was then sent back to the Padres’ Arizona complex to try and get back on track before he pitched in a trio of Arizona Fall League contests. When everything is clicking, it’s easy to see why Gore has been so highly regarded. The lefty has good life on his 92-96 mph fastball and complements it with a mid-80s slider and an above-average curveball. Gore also throws a plus changeup with late sink in the low 80s. He’s shown an ability to pound the strike zone and command all four of his pitches, but that command wavered as he lost his mechanics over the past two seasons. Regaining and further developing that consistency will be key to his future. Gore’s ceiling remains high, but his floor may now be lower than initially thought. After he showed flashes of his 2019 self in the Arizona Fall League, the Padres are hopeful he’ll round into form in 2022 and was just experiencing the type of failure most prospects have to overcome early in their careers. However, the longer Gore’s struggles persist, the less likely it becomes that he reaches what was once thought to be a very lofty ceiling as a frontline starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gore helped lead Whiteville (N.C.) High to three state titles and capped his outstanding prep career by garnering Gatorade National Player of the Year honors as a senior in 2017. The Padres took him with the No. 3 overall pick that June, signing the prep left-hander for $6.7 million. Gore was bothered by a blister problem in his first full season, landing on the injured list twice at Class A Fort Wayne, but emerged as baseball’s top pitching prospect in 2019, finishing his age-20 season in Double-A as the Minor League leader (min. 100 IP) in ERA (1.69) and WHIP (0.83). Seemingly poised to impact the Padres’ rotation in 2020, Gore instead spent the season at the alternate training site, working on mechanical issues. He opened 2021 at Triple-A El Paso but still didn’t look consistent in his mechanics or stuff, and the Padres actually moved him back to their Arizona complex to work on those issues away from games. When he’s on, the extension Gore generates towards the plate gives the left-hander’s 92-96 fastball big carry and life through the zone, and hitters generally struggle to time the pitch. Gore’s mid-80s slider has become his go-to breaking ball, having surpassed his curveball in the eyes of many evaluators, although the latter is still above average. He rounds out his four-pitch mix with a plus changeup in the low 80s that he can locate down in the zone with late sink. Gore pounds the strike zone and recorded one of the Minors' better swinging-strike rates in 2019, and the Padres have hopes he can get back to that level despite these recent stumbling blocks. Gore has been one of the biggest prospect enigmas of the 2021 season. His backers believe that the 2019 version of him is still inside him and that he’s going through struggles that most pitchers must overcome earlier in their careers. To that point, Gore is only 22 and was ahead of the age curve prior to these latest issues anyways. On the other hand, the longer he struggles both on and away from Minor League mounds, the more his stock drops along with the hopes that he can be a frontline Major League starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Plummer was considered a long-term project coming out of a Michigan high school when the Cardinals selected him 23rd overall in 2015. The road looked even longer after a broken hamate cost him the 2016 season, and offensive struggles kept him from breaking above High-A in the three seasons that followed. After spending the lost 2020 campaign and early 2021 focused on changing his approach in the box, Plummer took off like a rocket in 2021, hitting .283/.404/.489 with 13 homers in 90 games at Double-A and .267/.455/.440 with more walks (20) than strikeouts (18) in 27 games a Triple-A. St. Louis still allowed him to become a free agent, and the Mets swooped in to sign the outfielder to a Major League contract, guaranteeing him a spot on the 40-man for the first time in his career. The right-handed slugger’s improvements at the plate came after he lost a significant leg kick that often threw off his timing. As a result, his strikeout rate plummeted, and he did a better job of doing damage on pitches inside the zone. Plummer’s 15 homers in 2021 were a new career high, but without above-average raw power, that is likely his limit in the category. He’s flashed above-average speed since his Draft days, and he’s used it in all three outfield spots. A fringy arm likely makes him a left fielder, if he does nail down an everyday spot. The Mets’ outfield picture needed depth, and Plummer certainly provided some coming off his breakout, earning his Major League debut in April. His offensive numbers have regressed in Syracuse, however, because his strikeouts have returned. The 26-year-old can still be a quality depth piece for the organization, and he has shown an ability to turn his game around before.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees signed Severino for $7,500 in 2013 and he drew a 50-game suspension for testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs before he threw his first pro pitch. He never climbed higher than High-A before qualifying for Minor League free agency following the cancelled 2020 season. He issued more walks (four) than he threw strikes (three) in his first game in the White Sox system last May, but made progress with his control over the course of the season and compiled a 2.36 ERA with 53 strikeouts in 45 2/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A. Added to the 40-man roster last November, Severino offers high-octane stuff. He sits at 97-99 mph and regularly reaches triple digits with a four-seam fastball that doesn't have much life but is tough to catch up to at the top of the strike zone. He mainly attacks hitters with heat but also uses a pair of breaking balls, providing more strikes and getting more chases with his upper-70s curveball than his low-80s slider. Purely a reliever, Severino has an effortful delivery that can easily get out of whack. He averaged 5.4 walks per nine innings in his first seven pro seasons, including a rate of 7.1 in Double-A last year that he cut to 4.5 once he got to Triple-A. His ability to locate his pitches will determine how much of a high-leverage role Chicago will entrust to him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A top 50 selection out of high school by the Pirates in 2016, Lodolo went on to Texas Christian University instead of signing and turned himself into one of the best college pitchers in the country, one who went No. 7 overall to the Reds in 2019. The 2021 season turned out to be his first real pro season and he was often dominant when he was on the mound, including a strong performance in the Futures Game, but was sidelined by a blister early in the year and a shoulder strain late, though he did reach Triple-A. Completely healthy, Lodolo can get back to using three at-least above-average pitches with plus command and control. While his fastball typically sits in the low-90s, the left-hander easily touched 96-97 mph at times, with some believing he could end up sitting closer to 95 mph in the future, and he usually throws it with a ton of sink. His slider flashes plus, a low-80s breaking ball that showed much more cross-plane depth than it had previously. He’ll throw an occasional plus changeup as well, with good deception and fade/tumble, as he continues to work on using it more effectively. Lodolo’s pitches play up because of his ability to locate all of them, and the Reds were pleased with how much he learned about how to attack hitters and mix his stuff to keep them guessing. The hope was that the shoulder issue is something minor that popped up after he tried to do too much coming off the blister issue and that he can keep pairing with Hunter Greene as a dynamic duo in the big league rotation soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lodolo opted to honor his commitment to Texas Christian University rather than sign with the Pirates, who selected him in the Competitive Balance Round A of the 2016 Draft. Three years later, he was one of the best arms in the 2019 Draft class and was the first pitcher taken that June, when the Reds took the southpaw with the seventh overall pick. He gave a glimpse at how his advanced feel for pitching would work by not allowing a walk in 18 1/3 innings during his pro debut that summer, then made good strides during his time in the Reds’ alternate camp in '20. While Lodolo fits the “advanced college lefty” label extremely well, he’s not just a pitchability guy with no stuff. He has three pitches that are consistently above average. He throws his fastball, which can touch 96 mph at times, downhill with good sinking movement, using his 6-foot-6 frame well. His low-80s slider is a tight breaking ball and has greater depth and bite now than it used to, with excellent late action. He specifically worked on his changeup during his time at the alternate training site, and he made strides in matching his arm slot to how he throws his fastball more consistently, providing more deception with very good fade and tumble. Though he's known as a strike-thrower, Lodolo improved the command of his fastball to attack hitters’ weaknesses more effectively. While he has an extremely high floor as a starter who can move quickly through the system, there’s still some upside here as he continues to add strength to his frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sears blossomed as a junior at The Citadel in 2017, striking out 20 in one game versus Virginia Military Institute and ranking among the NCAA Division I leaders in strikeouts (142, fifth) and strikeout rate (13.4 per nine innings, third). The Mariners signed him for a slightly over-slot $160,000 in the 11th round, only to trade him five months later to the Yankees along with right-hander Juan Then (since dealt back to Seattle) in exchange for Nick Rumbelow. He opened 2021 as a Double-A reliever but finished it as a Triple-A starter, logging a combined 3.46 ERA with 136 strikeouts in 104 innings to grab a spot on New York's 40-man roster. He made his big league debut in April of 2022 and pitched well in his brief time there and in Triple-A before being sent to the A’s in the Frankie Montas deadline deal. Though Sears' fastball sits at just 90-93 mph and maxes out at 95, hitters don't get good swing against it. He's just 5-foot-11 and his low arm slot makes it seem like he's throwing uphill, producing a flat approach angle and lots of riding action up in the zone. His slider also lacks power, parking at 78-81 mph, but it too misses bats because it has plenty of sweep as well as two-plane depth when he stays on top of it. He'll use a decent changeup with fade to give batters a different look, but it's often too firm. Sears doesn't have much margin for error and succeeds by avoiding mistakes. He has a fairly simple delivery and repeats it well, enabling him to locate his pitches where he needs to. His size leads to long-term durability concerns if he remains a starter, though that's probably a moot point because he seems destined to be a multi-inning reliever who concentrates on his invisiball and slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Elder went from the University of Texas bullpen as a freshman to being the Longhorns’ top starter in 2019 and 2020. He pitched well enough in his shortened junior season to land in the fifth round, where the Braves gave him better than twice pick value to keep him from returning to school for his senior year. He quickly showed he was a worthwhile investment by leading the Minors in innings pitched and advancing from High-A to Triple-A in his first full season of pro ball. He moved to Triple-A and made his big league debut in 2022. The right-hander has a four-pitch mix and can throw strikes with all of them. His fastball averages around 92 mph and will be in the 90- to 95-mph range on any given day. It’s a steep fastball with a ton of sink. He backs it up with a really good slider, a pitch that took a big step forward at the alternate site in 2020 and kept missing bats in his pro debut. He can manipulate spin to fold in a curve and his changeup is now a tick above-average, with a lot of depth, an offspeed offering he’ll throw to lefties and righties. Elder has a simple delivery he repeats well, allowing him to be in and around the strike zone on a regular basis. It all plays up because of his competitiveness on the mound and feel for pitching, getting him close to reaching his ceiling as a durable No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A bit of a late bloomer as a pitcher, Elder found a spot at the University of Texas as a high school senior in the Lone Star State. After a year pitching out of the Longhorns’ bullpen, Elder served as Texas’ top starter in 2019 and the shortened 2020 season. He came out of the gates very strongly in his four starts before his junior season was ended, landing him in the fifth round of last year’s Draft. The Braves went way over slot to keep him from returning to Texas for his senior season and he impressed in instructional league play, albeit in a brief look. Elder’s bread and butter is his slider, a quick mid-80s breaking ball he’ll throw at any point in the count. His advanced feel for manipulating spin allows him to also throw a curve with more downward break to it. His sinking fastball typically sits in the low 90s and can touch 95, and his changeup gives him a fourth at least average pitch. Strong and durable, Elder throws a lot of strikes with all of his offerings with a repeatable delivery. He stood out in his short time at instructs with his feel for pitching and understanding of how to use his stuff, which help give him the chance to be a workhorse No. 4-type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brash received some attention coming out of Niagara University, enough to land with the Padres in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft. The Canadian right-hander pitched briefly in his pro debut that summer, then his first full season of pro ball was canceled by the pandemic. Seemingly an afterthought as the player to be named later sent to the Mariners for reliever Taylor Williams, who was waived by San Diego in 2021, Brash took everyone by surprise by dominating in High-A and Double-A to earn a callup to Seattle near the end of the year. He didn't make his debut, though. Watch Brash on any given night without looking at data and you might be tempted to hang 70s or 80s on his stuff because he elicits so many swings-and-misses. He struck out 13.1 per nine innings while holding hitters to a .180 batting average across two stops in 2021. Hitters just don’t see his fastball, which averaged 96.4 mph in 2021 and is thrown with high spin rates and excellent extension down the mound. His slider is virtually unhittable with a lot of length to it, the type of breaker that will start on a right-handed hitter’s hip and end up on the opposite corner. He mixes in a curve and shows an effective changeup as well. While Brash didn’t appear in a big league game in 2021, he created buzz among fellow pitchers with his electric bullpen sessions. There’s still some reliever risk here given the effort in his delivery and how much of his success comes from hitters chasing out of the zone, but suffice it to say neither the Padres nor the Mariners knew what he could become.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Romero has often been overlooked, but wherever he’s gone, he’s performed. The right-hander pitched for two junior colleges before the Mariners selected him in the 15th round of the 2017 Draft. He stood out in the low levels of Seattle’s system, and Tampa Bay took notice. The Rays acquired him alongside Andrew Moore in a May 2018 deal for Alex Colomé and Denard Span. New organization, same results: Romero was named the 2019 Florida State League Most Valuable Pitcher after posting a 1.89 ERA in 23 outings for Charlotte. Romero didn’t pitch in 2020, save a handful of outings in the Puerto Rican Winter League, but picked up where he left off by producing a 2.61 ERA between Double-A Montgomery and Triple-A Durham in 2021. That was more than enough for Romero to earn a spot on the Tampa Bay 40-man roster. Romero has seen his stuff tick up a bit, with his fastball jumping from about 90 mph to sit around 92-94. But it’s the good spin on his heater that helps it play up, especially for swinging strikes at the top of the zone, making hitters feel like they’re facing a fastball with much higher velocity. That was the key to his eye-catching strikeout rate (33.3 percent) last year. The 6-foot-2 right-hander’s other pitches, a curveball and changeup, aren’t necessarily remarkable on their own. But they drop vertically to play well off his fastball and keep lefty hitters at bay, at least in the Minors. Romero also stays out of trouble and avoids beating himself by consistently throwing strikes and hitting his spots; his 4.68 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 2021 was the best of his career. Romero has managed to make the most of his pitch counts by working 128 innings in 2018, 125 1/3 innings in ’19 and 110 1/3 innings last year. His career 2.52 ERA and 9.5 K/9 would make him an absolute standout in most organizations, but he gets a little bit lost in the shuffle of high-end arms with the Rays. That might not be the case for long, as Romero -- a low-key favorite of rival scouts -- is likely to debut this year. He doesn’t have big, top-of-the-rotation stuff, and he might need to get more out of his offspeed stuff to turn over a lineup multiple times at the next level. But his effective fastball, pitchability and past performance make him a safe bet to stick on Kevin Cash’s pitching staff soon as a back-end starter, bulk pitcher or multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Unrelated to the Reds reliever of the same name, Marte signed with the Royals for $77,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022. He didn't reach full-season ball until late in his third pro season, then posted a 2.91 ERA with 96 strikeouts in 102 innings in Single-A last year. The Giants acquired him in a July 2025 deal for Mike Yastrzemski. Marte's fastball has added velocity this season, sitting at 94-97 mph and touching 100 with carry and armside run. His tight mid-80s slider locks up righties but isn't as effective against lefties. He uses a mid-80s splitter as his primary secondary pitch versus left-handers and is gaining more aptitude for the pitch as he throws it more often. Marte's 6-foot-5 frame creates some natural extension in his delivery, which features some effort. He repeats his mechanics well enough to provide consistent strikes, but he'll need to improve the command of all three of his offerings to succeed as a starter. He'll be eligible for the Rule 5 Draft following the 2026 season, so San Francisco may try to expedite his development a bit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene was the top-ranked prospect in the 2017 Draft, a high schooler who featured a triple-digit fastball but also could have been selected in the first round as an infielder. He went No. 2 overall to the Reds and was having a strong first full season of pro ball in 2018, one that included a buzz-inducing outing at the Futures Game, when an elbow strain in July led to Tommy John surgery. While he pitched at the Reds’ alternate site in 2020, his official return to the mound didn’t come until 2021, when he pitched his way from Double- to Triple-A. Greene made quick work of Double-A in 2021, using his power repertoire to move up to Triple-A after just seven starts, a promotion that certainly provided more of a challenge. Every bit of Greene’s premium fastball came all the way back post-surgery, hitting 100-plus routinely and averaging close to 99 mph. Overall, he located his fastball much more consistently and when it was down, it both missed bats and generated groundball outs, and he showed more ability pitching in with it. He got into trouble in Triple-A when he got too much of the zone without a ton of life, and experienced hitters did a lot of damage. His upper-80s slider showed improved bite and often flashed plus. The right-hander will have to keep committing to throwing his changeup more. He mixed in some effective cutters as well, things that help give hitters a different look, and he can throw all of them for strikes. Now added to the 40-man roster, Greene is just about ready to see how his premium stuff plays against big league hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Touching triple-digits in high school, Greene was at or near the top of most boards as the 2017 Draft approached. A two-way standout in the California high school ranks who might have been a first-round pick as an infielder, Greene went No. 2 overall to the Reds and spent his first summer of pro ball both hitting and pitching before taking to the mound full-time. He created huge buzz by lighting up the radar gun at the Futures Game in 2018, but an elbow strain suffered that July led to eventual Tommy John surgery that negated his 2019 season. He returned to the mound in 2020 and threw well at the Reds’ alternate training site. More than anything, Greene proved he’s healthy and ready to go in 2020. The premium stuff that made him such an elite Draft prospect and Futures Gamer was back on display at the alternate camp, leaving little doubt he’ll be back up to his 98-102 mph fastball full-time. He flashed his plus slider, a future go-to out pitch and continued to work on feel for his changeup. Over the summer, he focused on the consistency of both offerings, both in terms of quality and landing them in the strike zone. Greene also learned a new cutter, thrown 91-93 mph, that could give hitters another look, though he’s yet to use it in a game that counts. He also learned a tremendous amount in terms of preparing and making a gameplan from the older pitchers at the alternate camp, something that should help carry him up the organizational ladder now that he has a clean bill of health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lavastida batted .393 in two years at Hillsborough (Fla.) CC and began catching as a sophomore in 2018 before the Guardians drafted him in the 15th round and signed him away from an Alabama commitment for an over-slot $150,000. The pandemic shutdown in 2020 wasn't great for his defensive development, but he has hit .305 in three pro seasons and reached Triple-A last year. The Guardians protected him on their 40-man roster in November. With a calm, balanced approach from the right side of the plate, Lavastida makes consistent hard contact and manages the strike zone well. His swing is geared more for line drives, which limits his power production, but he did do a better job of launching balls in the air in 2021. He hit nine homers in 84 games last year after going deep just three times in 92 previous pro contests, and he could provide 12-15 homers and 30 doubles on an annual basis. Lavastida runs better than most catchers and turned his below-average speed into 16 steals in 24 attempts last season. He continues to improve behind the plate and might become an average receiver once he's fully polished. Though he has average arm strength, he gave up 58 swipes in 59 games last year and threw out just 22 percent of basestealers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lavastida hit .393 in two years at Hillsborough (Fla.) CC, spending his freshman year at third base before splitting time between the hot corner and catcher in 2018. Intrigued by his bat, the Indians drafted him in the 15th round that June and signed him away from an Alabama commitment for an over-slot $175,000. He batted .319 in his first two pro seasons but played just 64 games behind the plate and only one in full-season ball, so being limited to instructional league in 2020 wasn't great for his development. Lavastida employs a calm, balanced approach from the right side of the plate. He has a history of making repeated hard contact throughout his junior college and pro careers and manages the strike zone well. While his stroke is geared for line drives and 12-15 homer power at this point, he has enough bat speed and strength to do more damage if he more aggressively pulls and lifts pitches. Quicker and more athletic than more catchers, Lavastida desperately needs reps behind the plate to see if he can handle the demands of the position on a regular basis. He needs to improve as a receiver and has yet to deal with advanced pitchers. He has average arm strength and threw out 33 percent of basestealers in his first two years as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pallante was a dominant starter in his final two seasons at UC Irvine, particularly as a sophomore in 2018 when he posted a 1.60 ERA with 115 strikeouts in 101 1/3 innings. The Cardinals selected the right-hander in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft and sent him to Double-A Springfield for much of his true first full season in 2021. Pallante posted a 3.82 ERA with 82 strikeouts in 94 1/3 frames in the somewhat aggressive assignment and earned a brief two-game look with Memphis late in the season. He opened a lot of eyes as one of the few pitching standouts of the 2021 Arizona Fall League, where he finished with a 1.29 ERA and 22 K’s in 21 frames. The 6-foot right-hander’s velocity gains were what popped most last season. Coming out of an extremely over-the-top throwing motion, Pallante sits in the mid-90s comfortably now, and he got as high as 99 mph in the autumn. There is some cut to it too, making the pitch all the more uncomfortable for hitters. His slider draws solid reviews as well as it dives away from lunging right-handed hitters, while a high-spin curveball (that can get loopy at times when he isn’t spiking it) and a serviceable changeup add to his mix. Because of the long nature of his delivery, Pallante doesn’t always find the strike zone with regularity. It’s a deep enough arsenal to keep him starting, and the Cardinals are enthused to see what he can do in a Triple-A rotation coming off the AFL. If he needs to move to the bullpen, his velo and breaking pitches could be even tougher weapons in short bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high school junior in 2015, Pallante helped San Clemente High School win the National High School Invitational, then went on to join the Irvine pitching staff. After a freshman season spent largely in the bullpen, he jumped on the national radar as a sophomore All-American starter. He kept on performing as a junior as the Anteaters' Friday night starter and signed for slot value after the Cardinals selected him in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft. He pitched well in his pro debut, posting a 2.78 ERA with 38 strikeouts in 35 2/3 innings in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League. While he's not the prototypical starting pitcher in terms of height, the 6-foot right-hander does have a lot of arm speed and strength. And he's worked hard to turn himself into more of a pitcher compared to the thrower he was earlier in his amateur career. He can still go get 96-97 mph at times, but is more comfortable sitting in the 91-94 range with a fastball that has cutting and some sinking action to it. He throws both a slider and a curve, and while the former might be a tick ahead of the latter, some feel he might be better served focusing on the curve to differentiate from his fastball more. He sells a future average changeup well and knows how to pitch backwards when needed. While Pallante doesn't have the cleanest arm action, with a little stab in the back, he repeats his delivery well and tends to be in sync, leading to a lot of strikes. That gives him the chance to stick in a rotation long-term, with the ceiling of a No. 4 type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 2008 bonus-skimming scandal derailed the White Sox's international program for years, and they didn't sign another big-money player until they landed Adolfo for $1.6 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2013. He played just 465 games in his first eight years as a pro because of ankle and hamate injuries, two elbow surgeries and the pandemic. He stayed healthy in 2021 and bashed a career-high 25 homers between Double-A and Triple-A, putting him on the cusp of the Majors. Even after the additions of Cuban sluggers Yoelqui Cespedes and Oscar Colas, Adolfo still might have the most raw power in Chicago's system. With his bat speed, strength, the loft and leverage in his right-handed stroke and an extremely aggressive approach, he can crush balls great distances form the right side of the plate. His career 33 percent strikeout rate raises concerns about his ability to make enough contact to get to his pop against big league pitchers, and his swing gets long and too uphill when he hunts home runs. Adolfo's arm has bounced back from Tommy John surgery in 2018 and follow-up elbow arthroscopy in 2019 to regain its plus-plus strength, though he registered just 21 assists in 310 outfield starts over his first seven pro seasons. He moves well for a 6-foot-4, 225 pounder but still has fringy speed and doesn't do much on the bases. He's a decent defender on the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Unfortunately for Adolfo and the White Sox, the coronavirus pandemic meant that 2020 was yet another lost year of at-bats as his action was limited to Chicago's alternate training site. Signed for $1.6 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2013, he was the franchise's first big international amateur acquisition following a bonus-skimming scandal five years earlier. But he has played only 364 games since turning pro while dealing with ankle and hamate injuries in his first two seasons, Tommy John surgery in 2018 and follow-up arthroscopic elbow surgery in 2019. Adolfo's bat speed, strength and the loft and leverage in his right-handed swing create some of the best raw power in the system. He encouraged the White Sox by doing a better job of recognizing pitches and using the whole field in 2017-18, when he slugged 27 homers in 191 games between two Class A levels, but he regressed and struck out in 39 percent of his plate appearances between the Minors and the Arizona Fall League in 2019. He has drawn more walks in recent years but there still are questions as to whether he's too aggressive to get enough out of his pop. Adolfo's arm ranked as one of the strongest in the Minors before his elbow reconstruction and it has bounced back, though he has recorded just 15 assists in 233 games in the outfield. He moves well for a large man, though if his fringy speed declines as he gets older, it will limit him in the field. He's a decent defender in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of an athletic family that includes an older brother (Henry) who has reached the Majors and another (Hector) who played professional soccer, Heliot offered one of the best power/speed combinations in the 2017 Draft. A Puerto Rican high schooler who was one of the youngest players in that class, he signed for $3,101,700 as the 19th overall pick. He hasn't been as productive offensively since the pandemic shutdown and posted the worst numbers of his career in 2022, though he did make his big league debut at age 22. Still trying to figure out his right-handed stroke and approach, Ramos was too aggressive and too passive at different times in 2022, when he made too much opposite-field and ground-ball contact. He worked this offseason to try to hit the ball more out in front of the plate, make his swing less inside-out and get his lower half more involved. He has at least solid raw power but needs to pull and lift more pitches to make the most of it. After displaying plus speed as an amateur, Ramos has gotten stronger and thicker as a pro and is now more of a fringy-to-average runner. He played all three outfield positions last year, and though he spent most of his time in center field, he's still honing his defensive instincts and his range is better suited for the corners. His plus arm strength is suitable for right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramos comes from an athletic family with one older brother (Henry) who made his big league debut as a Diamondbacks outfielder in 2021 and another (Hector) who played professional soccer. Heliot was one of the youngest players and owned one of the better power/speed combinations in the 2017 Draft, in which he went 19th overall and signed for $3,101,700. One of the youngest regulars (age 21) in Double-A and Triple-A last year, he batted .254/.323/.417 with 14 homers and 15 steals in 116 games. While Ramos hasn't posted huge numbers since leaving High-A, he almost never has been older than the pitchers he has faced and still has some of the best raw power in the system. His bat speed and strength enable him to drive the ball out of the park to all fields, though he won't maximize his pop until he turns on more pitches and adds some loft to his right-handed stroke. He has decent plate discipline but needs to make adjustments to better handle right-handers, who ate him up with sliders in Triple-A. Ramos had plus speed as an amateur but has lost a step as he has begun to fill out and now plays closer to average. Though he has spent almost all of his pro career in center field, his instincts and reduced quickness are better suited for a corner. He could fit well in Oracle Park's expansive right field and has the plus arm strength for the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramos comes from a family of athletes that includes older brothers Henry, an outfielder who made his big league debut with the Diamondbacks in 2021, and Hector, a former professional soccer player. Heliot parlayed strong performances on the showcase circuit and one of the best power/speed combinations in the 2017 Draft into going 19th overall and signing for $3,101,700. After posting an .850 OPS, playing in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and reaching Double-A at age 19 in 2019, he continued his development last year at San Francisco's alternate training site and in instructional league. Though Ramos doesn't have much loft in his right-handed swing, he has so much bat speed and strength that he can drive the ball out of the park to all fields. He's a power-over-hit guy, though he should produce at least decent batting averages now that he's becoming more disciplined at the plate. While he didn't get any official game action in 2020, he focused on handling offspeed pitches, maintaining patience and sticking to a gameplan. A plus runner when he turned pro, Ramos has slowed as he has matured physically and his speed now grades closer to average. The Giants have used him mostly in center field and believe he has a chance to stay there, though most scouts think his instincts and reduced quickness will fit better on a corner. With his offensive upside and plus arm strength, he profiles well as a right fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a long, methodical march to the big leagues for Bautista, who first signed as a teenager with the Marlins in 2013 and reached Triple-A Norfolk in 2021 for the first time. He’ll also turn 27 in June, making him about a decade older than the youngest prospects in the Orioles’ system. That’s not a typical profile, but Bautista is not a typical prospect. He is a 6-foot-5 right-hander who jumped three levels in ’21, striking out 40 percent of the batters he faced to leapfrog from obscurity onto the Orioles’ radar. The club added Bautista to their 40-man roster in November; prior to ’21, he’d never pitched above Class A. Now, Bautista looks not only like a candidate to make Baltimore’s Opening Day roster, but to potentially be closing games come 2022. He’s an imposing presence on the mound with an electric arm, sporting a triple-digit fastball and a slider in the low 90s. That arsenal led to eye-popping strikeout numbers in the Minors but remains very raw, with Bautista issuing 30 walks in 46 2/3 innings last summer. The control issues are nothing new; Bautista spent five seasons in Rookie ball and remained in the low Minors into his mid-20s largely due to spotty command. The upside with Bautista is that when he does throw strikes, his stuff is virtually unhittable. The question is whether he can do it consistently at the highest level, where hitters quickly learn to time even the hardest heaters. With a little polish, Bautista profiles as a late bloomer who might be able to dominate late in games, particularly in short stints. For a rebuilding team like the Orioles with persisting bullpen issues, it’s a gamble worth taking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best athletes in the 2016 international class, Rosario signed out of the Dominican Republic for $1.85 million as part of the Padres' $78 million spending spree. The third-youngest regular (age 19) in the high Class A California League in 2019, he never put up big numbers while being promoted aggressively during his first three years in pro ball but did post consistently high on-base percentages. The Red Sox acquired him and infield prospect Hudson Potts in exchange for Mitch Moreland in August. Rosario has natural hitting ability thanks to a combination of bat speed, barrel control and hand-eye coordination. But his left-handed swing has a few moving parts, which makes it tricky to repeat. If he can simplify things, Rosario has quick hands and makes a lot of hard contact from the left side of the plate, and he could grow into some power. Rosario’s above-average speed enables him to cover ground with graceful strides in the outfield, giving him a good chance of remaining in center. He still needs time to develop in the Minors, mostly to fill out his lean and athletic frame. But the finished product could be that of a big league regular, with the athletic capabilities to do dazzling things on the baseball field -- including his trademark backflips to celebrate victories.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After redshirting his freshman year at Santa Clara and missing his senior season because of Tommy John surgery, Wilson was granted a sixth year of collegiate eligibility and used that year to establish himself as the Broncos’ No. 1 starter. The Padres selected Wilson in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft and pushed him aggressively because of his age. He went from High-A Lake Elsinore straight to Triple-A El Paso during his 2019 full-season debut, then spent most of this past season in El Paso again, pitching to a 3.21 ERA with 71 strikeouts over 42 innings out of the bullpen. Wilson has a prototypical bullpen profile, attacking hitters with a pair of above-average offerings. His fastball is notable for its velocity and movement, sitting in the mid 90s and touching 97 mph with late action that helps him miss barrels and generate whiffs. Wilson also throws a solid slider in the low- to mid-80s. Wilson’s command has improved considerably since he was drafted. After issuing 5.66 walks per nine innings in 2019, that number dropped to 3.20 in 2021. He doesn’t have the truly elite stuff a team would expect from a closer, but his fastball-slider combination plays well enough to translate into a role as an effective reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilson’s amateur path made him a late arrival to pro ball. He redshirted his freshman year at Santa Clara, then missed his senior season due to Tommy John surgery, before receiving a sixth year of NCAA eligibility. It was in that sixth season where he emerged as Santa Clara’s top starter and became an eighth-round pick of the Padres in 2018. They pushed him quickly. He thrived at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore in 2019 and made the leap to Triple-A El Paso. Then, after spending the ’20 season at the team’s alternate site, he was excellent in the Dominican Winter League, where he posted a 1.88 ERA across 14 outings. Wilson has a prototypical bullpen profile, attacking hitters with two pitches. His plus fastball is notable for its velocity and movement, sitting in the mid 90s and touching 97 mph with late action that helps him miss barrels and generate whiffs. Wilson pairs his heater with a solid slider in the low to mid 80s. Wilson has refined his command of both pitches significantly since the Padres drafted him. But he’ll need to prove he can keep his walk rate down at the higher levels. Though he may not have closer stuff, Wilson’s profile is unique enough and he misses enough bats to become an effective big league reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marinaccio missed what would have been his first college season at Delaware in 2014 while recovering from Tommy John surgery, then became a mainstay in the Blue Hens' rotation the next three years. The Yankees signed the redshirt junior for $100,000 as a 19th-rounder in 2017 -- they took Garrett Whitlock the round before -- and have watched him develop into one of their best relief prospects. He recorded a 2.04 ERA with 107 strikeouts in 66 1/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A last season to grab a spot on New York's 40-man roster. Marinaccio's fastball went from sitting around 90 mph before the pandemic layoff to averaging 94 mph and topping out at 97 with improved carry up in the zone last season. His best pitch is a plus changeup that approaches the plate at 82-85 mph before taking a dive. He also has a sweeping low-80s slider that flashes as a solid offering at times. While he generally throws strikes, Marinaccio gets so much action on his changeup and slider that he can't always locate them where he wants. He utilizes a low arm slot that provides deception and adds life to his pitches. He's old for a prospect at 26 but is ready to help the Yankees as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roberts broke Tennessee Tech's saves record with 13 as a sophomore and again with 15 as junior in 2018, when he helped the Golden Eagles win their first NCAA regional playoff tournament ever. The Cubs made him the highest pick in school history that June, signing him in the fourth round for a below-slot $130,000 that helped them afford outfielders Brennen Davis and Cole Roederer and right-hander Kohl Franklin. He has continued to thrive as a pro, reaching Triple-A and grabbing a spot on the 40-man roster in 2021 before making his big league debut this year, though he blew out his elbow in June and required Tommy John surgery. Roberts is a spin-rate monster who can top 2700 rpm with his fastball and 3100 rpm with his breaking ball. His heater sits in the low 90s and peaks at 95 but plays well above its velocity because it features natural cut and appears to rise as it nears the plate. His breaker combines slider velo in the low 80s with curveball depth, playing nicely off his fastball. Roberts lacks physicality at 5-foot-10 and 180 pounds, but his size works for him by contributing to a flat approach angle for his heater and a compact delivery that he repeats well. He's a competitor who challenges hitters, though getting touched up for a 4.50 ERA in Triple-A underscored his need to refine his command. He doesn't have the overpowering stuff or ceiling of fellow Cubs relief prospects Ben Leeper and Cayne Ueckert, but he does have a higher floor with a longer track record of success and strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While there’s no question Rodriguez has made the $1.75 million investment the Mariners made in him back at the start of the 2017-18 international signing period seem very shrewd, there were some question marks surrounding the uber-talented outfielder heading into the 2021 season. He had broken his wrist at the Mariners’ alternate training site and did not perform well in winter ball upon his return. Rodriguez answered those questions and then some by hitting .347/.441/.560 between High-A and Double-A, while also going to the Futures Game and helping the Dominican Republic earn a bronze medal in the Olympics. Outside of that small sample in winter ball, Rodriguez has hit pretty much wherever he’s been, carrying a career .331/.412/.543 line into the 2022 season. He’s long had an advanced approach at the plate with impressive pitch recognition and plate discipline and can hit the ball hard to all fields. He has prodigious power he’s tapping into more and more, but he doesn’t sell out for that pop, giving him every chance to be a double-plus hitter with double-plus pop. Not content with just being a bat, Rodriguez has worked hard on his speed and is an excellent and aggressive baserunner who can steal a base. Rodriguez has played more right field than anything, which should be a very good long-term home for him that will allow him to use his plus arm, though he’s also shown he can handle roaming center field when needed. All of his incredible tools play up because of his makeup, work ethic and passion for the game. Loved by old-time scouts and analytics-minded folks alike, he has all the makings of a big league superstar.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2017-18 international signing period began, Rodriguez was ranked No. 10 on the MLB Pipeline Top 30 international prospects list. The Mariners were thrilled to sign him for $1.75 million on July 2 and the outfielder quickly served notice that he was one of the best players in the class by posting a .929 OPS in the Dominican Summer League in 2018. Despite a left hand fracture in 2019, Rodriguez played across two levels of A ball during his United States debut before playing in the Arizona Fall League. He was playing well in the Mariners’ summer camp last July when he fractured his wrist diving for a ball in the outfield, though he recovered in time to get some winter ball at-bats under his belt. Rodriguez has every chance to be a plus hitter with plus power at the big league level. The Mariners felt comfortable pushing him as a teenager across levels and to the AFL largely because of his advanced approach from the right side of the plate, something that allows the big, physical outfielder to already tap into his tremendous raw power. While he’ll never be a big basestealing threat, Rodriguez has worked very hard to improve his speed and moves very well for his size. Just 20 for all of the 2021 season, Rodriguez has played both center and right field during his pro career. He can handle playing up the middle, but is better suited for a corner, where his plus arm plays well, especially given other personnel in the organization. In addition to his obvious on-field tools, Rodriguez brings a passion and joy to the game that should help him become a superstar in short order.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torkelson broke Barry Bonds’ Arizona State freshman record with 25 homers in 2018. He led the Pac-12 in dingers as a freshman and sophomore and slugged at least .700 in all three seasons as a Sun Devil. Mix in star turns in Cape Cod and two Team USA stints, and Torkelson entered the 2020 Draft as a consensus No. 1 talent. The Tigers agreed and made him the first corner infielder to go No. 1 overall since Adrian Gonzalez in 2000. Torkelson signed for $8,416,300, which still stands as a Draft record. He backed up that investment with a stellar first season, climbing from High-A to Triple-A while hitting .267/.383/.552 with 30 homers over 121 games. He finished the year in the Arizona Fall League before a right ankle sprain cut that assignment short after only seven games. Thanks to impressive physical strength, Torkelson has some of the best raw power in the Minors, and it shows in both batting practice and game settings. He isn’t just a modern free swinger either. Torkelson is patient in the box, willing to take a walk and able to control the zone with a sound swing. The Tigers were impressed that he didn’t seem willing to rest on his previous laurels and constantly found ways to improve as he moved up the chain, including an added emphasis on going the other way at Triple-A. During the Draft, Detroit announced Torkelson as a third baseman, and he was OK there. However, he primarily stuck to first base in Toledo, and in September, Tigers manager A.J. Hinch said, “there’s no secret that the first baseman of the future is going to be Spencer Torkelson.” The 22-year-old has the offensive capability to be an elite middle-of-the-lineup talent in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torkelson was a three-sport standout as a California prep but went unselected in the 2017 Draft and ended up at Arizona State, where he hit 25 home runs to shatter Barry Bonds’ freshman record. Torkelson continued to perform well for USA Baseball and in the Cape Cod League, then led the Pac-12 in home runs (23) as a sophomore before another turn with Team USA. After an abbreviated junior campaign in 2020, the Tigers made Torkelson the first corner infielder in 20 years to be drafted No. 1 overall, announcing him as a third baseman. He signed for $8,416,300, becoming the first No. 1 pick in the bonus-pool era (since '12) to receive more than slot value, then spent the summer at Detroit’s alternate training site before participating in the team’s fall instructional program. Torkelson has a special bat, with the ability to hit for both average and power from the right side. He’s extremely patient and controls at-bats well, drawing plenty of walks. When Torkelson does swing, he combines physical strength and bat speed to generate massive power from line to line, including elite raw power to his pull side. He gets to that power during games with relative ease, too, thanks to natural hitting ability that allows him to hit all different pitch types to all fields. Torkelson had not manned the hot corner since high school before the Tigers drafted him as a third baseman and deployed him there at the alternate site. Club officials were surprised by how agile and athletic Torkelson looked at the position, noting that he improved over the summer thanks to his work with Alan Trammell. Being able to stay at third base will only maximize Torkelson’s future offensive value, and he should have no trouble meeting the offensive demands that come with playing first base at the highest level should he be forced to move down the defensive spectrum.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abrams was named Georgia’s Gatorade High School Player of the Year as a senior at Blessed Trinity Catholic High (Roswell, Ga.) in 2019, when he also separated himself from his Draft class peers with his elite blend of athleticism, speed and pure hitting ability. The Padres took Abrams with the No. 6 overall pick that June and signed him for a below-slot $5.2 million. Abrams continued to garner accolades as he won the Rookie Arizona League MVP Award after hitting .401 and stealing 14 bases over 32 games. He built on that success in ‘20, impressing at the Padres’ alternate training site and held his own when aggressively pushed to Double-A as a 20-year-old in 2021. However, a fractured left tibia and sprained left MCL limited him to just 42 games last season. Abrams’ 80-grade speed allows him to impact the game on both sides of the ball and he’s shown an early ability to use that speed, swiping 28 bags over his first 76 professional games. He’s also added strength to his 6-foot-2, 185-pound frame and projects to have at least average power in the future. A plus hitter, Abrams is still fine-tuning his pitch selection, but possesses good bat-to-ball skills and has shown the ability to make adjustments in the box. A naturally gifted athlete, Abrams has made big strides defensively since signing. That top-of-the-scale speed gives him plenty of range, and his hands, coupled with his strong arm, give him the tools needed to make all the necessary plays. He has the skills to stick at shortstop and be an impact player long-term, but a position change may ultimately occur if San Diego keeps Fernando Tatis Jr. at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abrams garnered honors as Georgia’s Gatorade High School Player of the Year as a senior at Blessed Trinity Catholic High (Roswell, Ga.) in 2019, when he also separated himself from his Draft class peers with his elite blend of athleticism, speed and pure hitting ability. The Padres took Abrams with the No. 6 overall pick that June and signed him for below-slot value at $5.2 million, then watched him win the Rookie Arizona League MVP Award -- batting .401 with 23 extra-base hits and 14 steals in 32 games -- and reach Class A Fort Wayne in his pro debut. He was even better in ‘20, showing more polish and strength to go along with his loud tools, albeit at the Padres’ alternate training site and fall instructional league camp. San Diego pushed Abrams to Double-A for his age-20 season. He held his own despite his youth, but a fractured left tibia and sprained left MCL suffered in early July ended that campaign early. Abrams’ top-of-the-scale speed is a game-changing tool that makes him an impact player on both sides of the ball. The strength Abrams has added to his ultra-projectable frame since signing shows in his ability to drive the ball and do damage from the left side, and scouts now like his chances of developing at least average game power to go along with a plus bat. Abrams’ speed and penchant for making hard contact give him both a high ceiling and floor as a hitter -- the latter a product of his ability to steal hits on the infield and stretch singles into extra bases. Abrams’ biggest improvement in 2020 came on the defensive side thanks to his work with the coaching staff at San Diego’s alternate training site. His speed and quickness give him tremendous range in all directions, and he has the hands, actions and plus arm strength needed to make all the plays. And while a move to either second base or center field in deference to Fernando Tatis Jr. may be unavoidable, any such position change shouldn’t keep Abrams from reaching his potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After putting up solid numbers in three years at UNLV, Stott became the first Rebels first-rounder in five years, and the first position player from the school to go that high since Matt Williams went No. 3 overall back in 1986. Strength gains made during his time at the Phillies’ alternate training site in 2020 paid dividends in his first full season of pro ball, as the infielder went from High-A to Triple-A before capping it off as one of the best prospects in the Arizona Fall League and topping the circuit in RBIs. Since his college days, Stott has exhibited an advanced approach from the left side of the plate with the ability to hit the ball hard to all fields. He draws a ton of walks and walked more than he struck out in the AFL, much like he did in college. That helps him get in more favorable counts to let him drive the ball with more extra-base authority than he’s had in the past, with the chance to get to average in-game power in the future. Stott has the arm, hands, footwork and instincts to play shortstop at the big league level, with enough speed and range to stay there long term. He’s also shown he can slide over to second or third with ease should the need arise, giving the Phillies many options of getting his solid bat into the Major League lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at UNLV, Stott parlayed a huge junior season in which he finished with a .997 OPS to land in the middle of the first round, where the Phillies took him No. 14 overall in the 2019 Draft. He had a solid debut, mostly in the short-season New York-Penn League, then showed improved strength facing a much higher level of competition at the Phillies’ alternate site in 2020. A left-handed-hitting shortstop, Stott has shown a knack for making contact and using all fields and an advanced approach at the plate that enabled him to walk more than he struck out in college. He uses all fields well and the added strength led to an increased ability to drive the ball at the alternate site, something that only will improve as he continues to mature. The Phillies were particularly impressed with his recognition of spin and his ability to handle left-handed pitching. A solid runner, Stott is a natural shortstop who got some experience playing second and third at the alternate site to add versatility to his resume. But he has the range, arm and instincts to stick at shortstop long-term and the upside to be a big league regular at the premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins acquired Duran from the D-backs, who had originally signed the right-hander for just $65,000 in 2018, when he was making his full-season debut. He pitched his way to Double-A and onto the Twins’ 40-man roster in 2019 and after pitching well at the club’s alternate training site in 2020, he seemed poised to contribute to the big league staff in 2021. However, elbow issues limited him to 16 Triple-A innings, though he was healthy and throwing extended live batting practice sessions at the end of the year. Duran has long had a dominant combination of pitches in his fastball and hybrid splitter-sinker called a “splinker.” Even in his brief time on the mound in 2021, his fastball touched 101 and averaged 96.4 while the splinker averaged 90 mph and touched 94. Both pitches miss bats and generate a ridiculous amount of ground balls. He started working on a slider last year to go along with the big, hard curve he’s always thrown, but that he hadn’t always landed consistently in the strike zone. Duran didn’t have enough time to see if the slider would be a usable weapon in game action, though there were positive early indications. He’ll have to show his elbow is sound, but if he can throw that slider for strikes and continue to refine his overall command, he still has a good chance to start in the long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duran originally signed back in Dec. 2014 with the D-backs for just $65,000 and originally moved slowly, finally reaching full-season ball in 2018 when he was sent at that year’s Trade Deadline to the Twins in the Eduardo Escobar trade. The right-hander took off in his first full year with the Twins, pitching his way to Double-A and getting added to the 40-man roster following the 2019 season, then was the best pitching prospect at the Twins’ alternate site in 2020. Physically imposing at 6-foot-5, 230 pounds on the mound, Duran attacks hitter with an exciting power arsenal featuring two pitches that could get big league hitters out right now. The first is his fastball, a heater that sits around 97 mph and hit triple-digits regularly at the alternate site. He complements it with a a filthy “splinker,” a splitter-sinker hybrid pitch he cranks up to 94 mph that gets both swings and misses as well as weak contact on the ground. The key to Duran reaching his ceiling will be the continued development of his hard curve. He’s made strides in throwing it for strikes more consistently and his overall command has improved. There isn’t concern internally about reliever risk, with belief Duran will have the three-pitch mix to be a very successful big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez hit 98 mph with his fastball and flashed a plus slider as a Florida high school senior in 2017, but he had a sore shoulder for much of the spring and learned right before the Draft that he would require Tommy John surgery. The Astros were one of the few teams that preferred him as a hitter when he was healthy, so they took him in the second round and signed him for an above-slot $1.6 million. More injuries and the pandemic pushed his full-season debut back until 2021, but he rose from Single-A to Houston in 11 months, getting an at-bat with the Astros last April while providing emergency depth. Perez creates at least plus raw power with a combination of bat speed, strength and leverage in his right-handed stroke. He hasn't been able to tap into it consistently at higher levels, however, producing a lot of ground-ball contact and just 15 homers in 567 at-bats across Double-A and Triple-A the past two years. He has matured as a hitter during that time, showing more discipline at the plate and using the opposite field more often. Though Perez works hard on his conditioning, he's still limited athletically and defensively. He's a well-below-average runner who lacks range at third base and on the outfield corners. He has regained his arm strength but is erratic at the hot corner and could wind up at first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez drew plenty of pitching interest as a Florida high school senior who reached 98 mph with his fastball and flashed a plus slider in 2017, but he battled shoulder soreness that spring and learned just before the Draft that he required Tommy John surgery. One of the few teams that preferred him as a position player when he was healthy, the Astros still selected him in the second round and signed him for an above-slot $1.6 million. Further injuries and the pandemic delayed his full-season debut until 2021, when he slammed 18 homers and forced his way to Double-A and onto the 40-man roster. Perez has well above-average raw power thanks to his bat speed, strength and the loft in his right-handed stroke, and he created optimism that he'll be able to tap into it by maturing as a hitter last season. He did a better job of controlling the strike zone and using the entire field, though he still can get more consistent in both regards. His swing can get long and uphill, so he'll always be a power-over-hit guy. Though Perez used the pandemic layoff to improve his conditioning, he's still limited athletically. He's a well below-average runner who lacks range at third base, where he made 21 errors in 88 games last year. He has recovered his arm strength but probably will wind up at first base in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez hit 98 mph with his fastball and flashed a plus slider as a Florida high school senior in 2017, but he came down with a sore shoulder in March and learned just before the Draft that he needed Tommy John surgery. That didn't deter the Astros, one of the few teams that preferred him as a position player when he was fully healthy, and they signed him for an above-slot $1.6 million in the second round. Because of his elbow reconstruction, some soft-tissue injuries and the coronavirus pandemic, he played just 54 games in his first four years as a pro. Perez's bat speed, strength and the loft in his right-handed swing give him easy plus raw power, though he still has to prove he can tap into it. His stroke gets too long and uphill, and he gets too aggressive and pull-focused, which led to a .188 batting average and a 28 percent strikeout rate in short-season ball in 2019. He produces high exit velocities when he connects, and he has done a better job of making contact while advancing to Double-A in his full-season debut in 2021. The Astros were pleased that Perez used the pandemic layoff to improve his conditioning, and he reported to instructional league in the best shape of his career. He's still a well below-average runner and has limited range at third base but has a better chance of becoming at least an adequate defender there. He still has well above-average arm strength, so pitching could still be a fallback if needed.
