mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sousa compiled a 5.50 ERA in four college seasons as a reliever at Virginia, turning down the Nationals as a 34th-rounder in 2017 before signing with the White Sox for $10,000 in the 10th round the following June. He has thrown a lot more strikes in pro ball than he did in college, and his stuff made a leap when he returned from the pandemic layoff last season. He claimed a spot on the 40-man roster in November after recording a 3.61 ERA with 71 strikeouts in 47 1/3 innings between Double-A and Triple-A. Sousa's money pitch is a plus slider that went from parking in the low 80s at the start of 2021 to averaging 88 mph and touching 91 in Triple-A. It features both horizontal and vertical action, destroys same-side hitters and is effective against right-handers. His fastball velocity also improved over the course of the year, ranging from 94-98 mph in Triple-A, though his four-seamer gets straight and doesn't dodge a lot of bats. Outside of an early-2021 blip in Double-A, Sousa has had no control issues as a pro, averaging 2.4 walks per nine innings in his first three seasons -- down from 5.8 at Virginia. He hides the ball well in his high three-quarters delivery, making it harder for hitters to get good swings against him. If he continues to dial in the strike zone and maintains his Triple-A stuff, he could play a key role in Chicago's bullpen this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of a 16-year Major League pitcher, Witt already had a high stock before he saw his first pro pitch as a star in showcase and international events. The 2019 Gatorade National High School Player of the Year was selected second overall by the Royals and signed for a franchise-record $7,789,900. An early trip to the Rookie-level Arizona League provided lackluster statistical results (but strong underlying data), and Witt built on that with standout trips to Kansas City’s 2020 alternate site and fall instructs. He busted out for good in 2021, hitting .290/.361/.575 with 33 homers and 29 steals at Double-A and Triple-A. He fell one theft shy of being the Minor Leagues’ ninth 30-30 player since 2000. Little Witt does on the diamond is surprising anymore. Utilizing a slightly open right-handed stance and small leg kick, the Texas native generates impressive bat speed with a compact swing capable of generating power to all fields. He also gets good lift through the zone, and that -- combined with improved strength -- helps him to project for plus-plus power. He has shown that additional pop while cutting his K rate down from 24 percent at Double-A to 22.5 percent at Triple-A. A plus runner coming out of high school, Witt has already put his wheels to good use, and he should continue to be a base-stealing threat. Witt covers ground well, shows quick hands and makes the most of his plus arm from the premium position of shortstop. He’ll bump up against Adalberto Mondesi and Nicky Lopez quickly in 2022 and could move to third, where he made 17 starts in 2021. The rest of the tools make Witt, who only turns 22 in June, a potential star and the future (if not the present) face of the franchise.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline ranked Witt Jr. as the 2019 Draft’s No. 2 prospect behind Oregon State catcher Adley Rutschman. The two players came off the board in that order, with the Royals taking Witt, the son of former 16-year Major League pitcher Bobby Witt, at No. 2 and then signing him to a franchise-record bonus worth $7,789,900. He produced mixed results during his pro debut in the Rookie Arizona League, but the 20-year-old proved advanced beyond his years in 2020, excelling in the face of older, more advanced competition at the alternate training site and the Royals’ fall instructional program at Kauffman Stadium. Witt drives the ball to all fields with excellent barrel control and outstanding bat speed. He has made significant gains in improving his approach in pro ball, becoming more aggressive while also trimming swing-and-miss tendencies from his game, and he already knows how to make difficult adjustments within at-bats. Witt has long shown plus raw power to his pull side and tapped into it more consistently in 2020, applying it from line to line against advanced pitching. He should generate even more power as he adds strength to his projectable frame and continues to refine his approach. Witt is also a plus runner who is aggressive on the basepaths, giving him a high-end combination of power and speed at a premium position. There’s no question Witt will also be able to stay at shortstop, with that speed allowing him to have plenty of range. He has very quick hands and an arm that allowed him to throw in the mid-90s off the mound in high school. Club officials rave about his makeup, instincts and passion for the game as much as his tools, giving him as much chance as anyone to reach his enormous potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The highest-drafted position player in University of Maine history, Peña went in the third round in 2018, when he was considered one of the best college defenders in his class. The son of former big league second baseman Geronimo Peña, he has gotten stronger and provided more offense than expected since turning pro. He injured his left wrist diving for a grounder in Spring Training last year and had surgery that cost him much of the season, but he returned to set a career high with 10 homers in just 30 Triple-A games and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster. Peña remains the best defender in the Astros system, getting to plenty of balls at shortstop with his quick first step and plus range. He has solid arm strength, unloads the ball quickly and makes accurate throws. He also has soft hands and sound fundamentals and is capable of playing anywhere in the infield if needed. After looking feeble with wood bats in college summer leagues, Peña has gotten much stronger and is hitting the ball much harder as a pro. He also has gotten better at controlling the strike zone and does a nice job of using the entire field, though he still needs to add more loft to his right-handed swing because he makes a lot of groundball contact. Factor in his solid speed and basestealing mentality, and he has the upside of a 20-20 player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While his father Geronimo played seven seasons in the Majors as an offensive-minded second baseman, Pena is best known for his glove at shortstop. One of the top college defenders in the 2018 Draft, he became the highest-drafted position player in University of Maine history when the Astros took him in the third round. He has proven a better hitter than expected in pro ball and batted .306/.349/.430 in the Dominican League this winter, but he didn't get a chance to build on that in 2021 because he injured his left wrist diving for a grounder in Spring Training and required surgery that cost him most of the season. The best defender in Houston's system, Pena is a legitimate shortstop with a quick first step and plus range. His arm strength draws grades anywhere from fringy to plus, but the bottom line is he has a quick release and doesn't have any problems making the necessary throws. He has soft, reliable hands and can provide quality glovework all over the infield should he wind up as a utilityman. Though he struggled with wood bats in college summer leagues, Pena has gotten much stronger in pro ball and now is making more frequent and higher quality contact from the right side of the plate. The Astros believe he'll hit enough to be a regular on contending teams and see some untapped power that eventually could produce 15 or more homers per season once he incorporates some mechanical changes. A solid runner out of the batter's box, he's faster once he gets going and has a basestealing mentality.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A steady performer but overshadowed on an Oregon State 2018 College World Series championship team that included three first-round picks, Kwan went in the fifth round that June. He did little to shed his reputation as a slap-hitting complementary player in his first two years as a pro before coming back as a different guy after the 2020 pandemic shutdown. He batted .328/.407/.527 with 12 homers in 77 games between Double-A and Triple-A, prompting the Guardians to place him on their 40-man roster. Kwan has elite contact skills, the product of a short left-handed swing, uncanny hand-eye coordination and a disciplined approach. He added a more pronounced leg kick in 2021 and began pulling more pitches and hitting them harder, and his 12 homers last year doubled his total from three years in college plus his first two in the Minors. He's not very physical and scouts still question how much impact he'll provide at the plate, with most believing he'll top out at 12-15 homers per full season. A solid runner out of the batter's box and quicker once he gets going, Kwan projects as a leadoff type who can provide high on-base percentages and a few stolen bases. His quickness and instincts allow him to cover plenty of ground in center field, where he has a fringy but playable arm. If he doesn't offer enough thump to be a regular, his broad array of skills would make him a useful fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees went all-in during the 2014-15 international signing period, handing out a total of seven seven-figure bonuses. After that tier came 15 six-figure bonuses with Castillo at the higher end of that group, getting $750,000 to sign out of Venezuela. Outside of a solid Dominican Summer League debut in 2015, the Yankees didn’t get a whole lot of return on their investment until 2021, when his bat took off in Double-A in time for him to be included in the return the Pirates got for Clay Holmes at last year’s Trade Deadline. He hit his way to Triple-A and on to the Pirates’ 40-man roster last fall. Castillo earned his way onto his first 40-man roster because of advancements he made at the plate. He’s always made a ridiculous amount of contact, with a career strikeout rate under 11 percent, but added strength and more patience, combined with a willingness to add loft, led to a power outburst of 19 homers, more than double his career total heading into last season. That it came without sacrificing contact rate points to it being something that could be sustainable. His bat is going to have to carry him to the big leagues because it’s unclear where he fits defensively. Signed as a shortstop, he’s seen time at all three infield spots over the last few seasons. He might fit best as an offensive-minded second baseman, and maybe he’s developing the power to fit the third base profile, but it’s more likely he carves out a role as a bat-first utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Potts bypassed his Texas A&M commitment and signed with the Padres for $1 million in 2016 as the No. 24 overall pick, making him Southlake Carroll (Texas) High's highest-drafted player ever. After finishing his professional debut in the Class A Short Season Northwest League, Potts spent his first full season with Class A Forty Wayne, where he and Fernando Tatis Jr. became the first 18-year-olds to hit at least 20 home runs in the Midwest League since 1987. Potts finished with an even 20 homers, 14 of which he hit during a torrid second-half stretch that also saw him slash .278/.325/.512 over 65 games. Potts has a knack for making hard contact at the plate, with a quick right-handed bat and plenty of strength to his frame, though there is some swing-and-miss to his game. He projects as fringe-average hitter, but scouts expect him to develop at least average power as he continues to add strength. San Diego drafted Potts as a shortstop but has since shifted him to third base, where he shows the necessary hands, footwork and arm strength for the position. Potts has proved to be more advanced than expected early in his career, most notably in his capacity to make adjustments and get to his power during games. Though he'll need to tighten his approach and clean up his defensive some, Potts appears on the right path towards becoming a future middle-of-the-order third baseman at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Solis moved faster than expected after signing for $450,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, reaching the Rookie-level Appalachian League during his pro debut the following summer. He overcame some early-season control issues to pitch well in Class A in 2018 until he blew out his elbow in August. He had Tommy John surgery and may not return to game action until 2020. Solis went from working with an 89-91 mph fastball when he signed to sitting at 93-95 mph and touching 97 with late hop and cutting action when he got hurt. He could add more velocity because he still has physical projection remaining and Tommy John rehab often leaves pitchers stronger than ever. His hard slider has the potential to become a plus pitch and he also shows promising feel for his changeup. His long arms allow Solis to create good extension and downhill plane on his pitches. He repeats his delivery well and had a history of throwing strikes until his elbow began to give out. If he can regain his health and upgrade his secondary pitches, he has a chance to become a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery wiped out Moss' first two college seasons at Florida, and he pitched sparingly on a loaded 2016 Gators staff that included five future first-rounder. But the Reds saw enough to take him in the fourth round that June, and he has proven healthy and durable since. He led the Minors with 15 wins in 2018 and made a successful jump to Double-A this year before going to the Indians in a three-team trade in July that sent Trevor Bauer to Cincinnati. Moss won't be a pitcher who wows people with his stuff because all three of his pitches grade as average. But he has a 91-92 mph fastball that gets on hitters quickly because he commands it well and gets excellent extension in his delivery. Scouts liked his slider more than his changeup in 2018, but the latter pitch has been more effective this year. Though Moss struggled with his control early in the 2019 season, he settled down and resumed throwing strikes. His ceiling is somewhat limited, but he knows what he's doing on the mound and misses enough bats to eventually be a fifth starter or swingman in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels were limited to signing players for $300,000 during the 2015-16 international signing period after going over their limit the previous year. But they were still active, and the top six bonuses they handed out were all to pitchers. Only two got more than Yan’s $80,000 bonus and Reyember Mendoza is out of baseball while Wilkel Hernandez is with the Tigers. It took Yan awhile to get going, spending three summers in three different Rookie-level leagues, but he dominated once he got to full-season ball, finishing second in the Midwest League in strikeouts in 2019 and earning a spot on the 40-man roster. There were two very tangible things that led to Yan’s step forward in 2019. His fastball velocity once again ticked up, averaging a bit over 93 mph all year, up from 92 mph in 2018. And his curve got even better, with added velocity and more depth to it, giving it a chance be a plus pitch eventually. His changeup is definitely his third pitch, but he has shown some feel for it, something that will have to keep improving to give him a chance to start. Yan has a very deceptive delivery which leads to uncomfortable at-bats for hitters, but it’s also tougher to repeat and has led to control issues. He did cut his walk rate down considerably while seeing his strikeout rate soar, perhaps a sign of things to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Intrigued with his upside, the Padres took Lawson 71st overall in the 2016 Draft and signed him for $1.9 million, more than double the slot value. The right-hander struggled to find consistency in 2017 and 2018, but flashed plus stuff and gave glimpses of his high ceiling. Lawson impressed late in the 2019 season and then dominated in the Arizona Fall League, but underwent Tommy John surgery in March 2020 and was limited to just 6 2/3 innings in 2021. Lawson sits in the mid 90s with his fastball and complements it with a mid-70s curveball that can be a hammer at its peak. Scouts believe the curve will continue to improve, but he's yet to show great command of the offering. Lawson also features a promising changeup that has quickly become a third weapon for him. An excellent athlete, Lawson has grown into his muscular 6-foot-4 frame. He's made strides with the consistency of his delivery, too, but he needs to cut down the walks. Lawson has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency, but the Padres feel he's only scratching the surface of his potential. Once he harnesses his talents and logs some consistent innings, he could develop into a back-end starter or a dominant bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres gambled on Lawson’s upside, giving him $1.9 million (more than twice slot value) after selecting him with the 71st overall pick in the 2016 Draft. In his two full Minor League seasons, Lawson never found any measure of consistency, with an ERA hovering around 5, but he continued to flash promising stuff and a high ceiling. His overall numbers are hardly indicative of his potential, and he showed signs of a breakout late in 2019 -- only to have his ‘20 campaign wiped out by Tommy John surgery. Lawson operates in the mid 90s with a mid-70s curveball that can be a hammer when thrown right. Scouts believe the curve will continue to improve, but he's yet to show great command of the pitch. Lawson also features a promising changeup that quickly has become a third weapon for him. An excellent athlete, Lawson has grown into his muscular 6-foot-4 frame. He's made strides with the consistency of his delivery, too, but he needs to cut down on his walk totals. No question, Lawson has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency, but the Padres feel he's only scratching the surface of his potential. Once he harnesses his talents, he could develop into a back-end starter or a dominant bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best all-around talents in the 2016 international class, Nova saw his $2.5 million agreement with the Marlins fall apart after he tested positive for performance-enhancing drugs that February. Signed for $1.2 million by the Astros out of the Dominican Republic that July, he has plenty of raw tools but needs game reps to polish his skills. His only action in 2020 came in instructional league, after which Houston added him to its 40-man roster. Nova has drawn comparisons to the likes of Hanley Ramirez and Edgar Renteria but has a long way to go to get there. He barrels balls with his quick right-handed swing and has the bat speed and loft to create plus raw power, but he chases out of the strike zone too much and gets himself out by putting balls in play that he should take. He needs to improve his pitch recognition and plate discipline in order to approach his ceiling. Nova has lost a half-step as he has matured physically but still has solid speed and is aggressive on the bases. He remains quick enough to play shortstop, where his hands and plus-plus arm are assets. He also has seen action at second and third base and still must learn to slow the game down defensively.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Nationals for $35,000 out of Panama in 2013, Fuentes pitched to mixed results in multiple roles early in his career but began to put it all together in 2018. He built upon that success during a breakout age-22 campaign in 2019, excelling as a reliever at Class A Advanced Potomac and then as a starter at Double-A Harrisburg. But after compiling a 2.23 ERA with 89 strikeouts and 22 walks in 80 2/3 innings between the two stops, Fuentes was slapped with a 50-game suspension in early August after testing positive for Heptaminol, a banned stimulant. Fuentes succeeds with an intriguing blend of stuff and pitchability. His fastball can touch 95 mph and sits in the low 90s with heavy sinking action that fuels the right-hander’s extreme ground-ball tendencies. He posted a 58 percent ground-ball rate in Double-A before the suspension and has induced grounders at 54.2 percent clip since the start of the 2017 season, his first in full-season ball. Both his average slider and his above-average changeup improved when he moved into the rotation, and he generated whiff rates of 41 and 40 percent, respectively, with the two pitches in the Eastern League. He can throw all three pitches for strikes and doesn't hurt himself by issuing many free passes. Fuentes' ability to work effectively in various roles is an asset, and club officials view him as a potential multi-inning reliever much like former Nats hurler Yusmeiro Petit. At the same time, it wouldn't surprise anyone in the organization if Fuentes were to continue to excel as a starter en route to a spot in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for only $50,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2016, Adon has already bounced around numerous roles in the Nationals system. He was a reliever only in 2017 and 2018 and then moved into the Low-A rotation at Hagerstown in 2019 with solid, if unspectacular, results. Adon still made the most of his trip to the 2020 alternate site and earned a 40-man roster spot in the process. He spent the bulk of 2021 at High-A Wilmington with middling numbers (4.97 ERA, 1.25 WHIP, 91 strikeouts in 87 innings), got bumped up briefly to Double-A Harrisburg and jumped to the Majors for his debut against Boston in the last game of the season. He fanned nine Red Sox and scattered two earned runs on three hits and three walks in 5 1/3 frames, showing he wasn’t perhaps as out of his depth as the initial promotion made him look. Adon averaged 95.0 mph on his four-seam fastball in that lone MLB appearance, and that’s right in line with where his velocity was throughout 2021. It’s been a back-and-forth over the years on which of his two secondary pitches will be his best. As of now, it looks like the slider is winning out as a low-80s pitch with promising depth. The high-80s changeup drew positive reviews in the past for its separation from the fastball, but it’s more of a third pitch now and was utilized sparingly as such in that brief Major League look. Adon has battled control issues for much of his Minor League career, and an 8.8 percent walk rate in 2021 demonstrated only modest maturation in that department. His late 2021 surge, coming at the end of a 110-plus-inning workload, carried some promise that he could be a back-end starter, but it seems more likely that he’ll take the fastball and slider and settle into a prominent role in the Washington bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adon’s career is already somewhat of a success story. The 6-foot-2 hurler was signed for only $50,000 coming out of the Dominican Republic in July 2016. After he worked exclusively out of the bullpen in his first two Minor League seasons, Adon moved to a starting role with Class A Hagerstown and found success, posting a 3.86 ERA with 90 strikeouts in 105 innings. He continued his development at last year’s alternate site and stood out enough to earn a 40-man roster spot ahead of his Rule 5 eligibility in the offseason. Adon pumps the velocity to work in any pitching role with a fastball that sits 94-96 mph. His changeup developed last year to the point where it’s his best secondary option. The Nationals particularly point out that the pitch has better separation and action than it did at this point a year ago. The slider, previously his best offspeed offering, has backed up some in terms of its consistency with his release point. It can still be above-average in spots because of its cutter action, but the changeup has moved past it in the arsenal. Adon’s control can still be an issue. He has walked 10.4 percent of the batters he faced in his Minor League career. The control and development of the secondaries will determine Adon’s future role, now that he has experience both in a rotation and bullpen. The Nationals say he would have started in a normal 2020, perhaps reaching as high as Double-A, but they remain open on his future role. If he moves back to relief, he could reach the capital quickly, a notion aided by his roster status. A road to a back-end starter would take longer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since Cruz shot up to 6-foot-7 after signing with the Dodgers for $950,000 back in July 2015, people have been waiting for him to get moved off of shortstop. He played both short and third with the Dodgers early and after the Pirates acquired him for Tony Watson at the 2017 Trade Deadline. He’s played only shortstop since, putting up big numbers in Double-A in 2021, and despite missing a big chunk of the season with a forearm injury, he made a very strong first impression in his brief big league debut, highlighted by his first Major League home run. Cruz has a toolbox that would make any evaluator excited. He has immense raw power from the left side of the plate, with the ability to hit the ball as hard, if not harder, than anyone in the system. Work on his approach started to pay off more in 2021, with a lower strikeout rate and better walk rate, allowing him to start tapping into that power more. The long and lanky infielder runs well and knows how to steal a base. For some time, the Pirates were keeping Cruz at shortstop mostly to help him maintain his focus on the field. But there he was becoming the tallest starting shortstop in big league history last year, and there isn’t talk of him moving off the premium position now. He has plus-plus arm strength, and his athleticism still plays, giving him the chance to stay there as long as he continues to work on his mechanics.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Dodgers for $950,000 back in 2015, Cruz was the key part of the return sent to the Pirates for reliever Tony Watson at the 2017 Trade Deadline. Having grown three inches since signing, the now 6-foot-7 shortstop used incredibly loud tools to get to Double-A in 2019 despite a foot fracture before struggling in the Arizona Fall League. After participating in the Pirates’ alternate camp in 2020, his future was clouded during the offseason when he was involved in a car accident that killed three people, though no charges were filed and he was able to participate in winter ball as planned. Cruz continues to be one of the most fascinating prospects in baseball because of his size, position and, more than anything, offensive potential. The raw power and ability to barrel up the baseball is readily apparent, with an average exit velocity off the bat in 2019 of 92.4 mph equaling that of former Pirates first baseman Josh Bell that season. The Pirates spent a lot of time with Cruz talking about chase rates and committing to a gameplan and approach for each at-bat during his time at the alternate camp last summer, with positive results. For years now, especially since he’s grown to 6-foot-7, everyone has been waiting for Cruz to move off of his position at shortstop. His close to top-of-the-scale arm works just fine and despite his size has shown the ability to make plays. One of the reasons to keep him in the infield for now is to encourage him to stay engaged in every pitch, with maturity perhaps the only thing keeping him from truly unlocking his tremendous potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves had just four total picks in the shortened 2020 Draft, with Strider going in the fourth round despite having missed the 2019 season because of Tommy John surgery and having thrown just 12 innings during that abbreviated ’20 collegiate campaign. It turns out the gains he showed velocity-wise that brief spring were legit and he went from Low-A up to the big leagues in his first full year of pro ball. Working with the Braves to simplify his arsenal, Strider dominated mostly with his fastball-slider combination. His electric heater touched triple digits on occasion and was routinely in the upper 90s. He made big strides with his power breaking ball, focusing on a true slider that enabled him to strike out 14.6 per nine in the Minors a year ago. He throws the occasional changeup, but it is clearly his third pitch. Strider’s competitiveness and work ethic have as much to do with his surprising climb as his pure stuff. He knows what he’s good at and will continue to rely on his fastball-slider combination to get outs. How consistently he finds the strike zone (3.8 BB/9 in 2021) and if he can start folding in that offspeed offering more might determine whether he can start long term, though there are no plans to change his role any time soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Strider got some attention as a Tennessee high schooler and was selected by the Indians late in the 2017 Draft. He headed to Clemson and worked mostly as a reliever as a freshman, but didn’t throw a pitch in 2019 because of Tommy John surgery. He came back for four outings in 2020 before the shutdown, showing enough of the old arm strength for the Braves to take him in the fourth round and then send him to their alternate site after he signed. He pitched his way up to Double-A in his first full season in 2021. It was a brief look, only 12 innings, but Strider’s velocity had crept back up pre-Draft with Clemson, up to 95 mph. There were more velocity gains after he signed, averaging 95 mph at the alternate site and touching 99 mph there and at instructs, and he’s maintained it in ‘21. His secondary stuff has gotten sharper, with a changeup that showed glimpses of being above average with good velocity differential and a power breaking ball that looks like an average offering. Strider really had trouble throwing strikes during his freshman year and in the Cape Cod League in 2018 but was much more efficient during that 2020 season small-sample size. He’s largely been around the zone with the Braves as well (though less so in Double-A), giving some hope that he could start in the future, though the arm strength would certainly play up in shorter stints out of the 'pen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zerpa has been on a steady progression since the Royals signed the young Venezuelan during the 2016-17 international signing period for $100,000, and he’s yet to flinch at any big moment. He hadn’t pitched above rookie ball before the Royals protected him from the Rule 5 Draft in 2020. He had spent less than half a season in Double-A before he made his Major League debut in ‘21, a day after he turned 22. Zerpa spent 2022 jumping from Double-A (4.36 ERA), Triple-A (1.17 ERA) and Kansas City, where he made three appearances and had a 1.64 ERA in 11 innings. A knee injury slowed him down at the end of last year, and a shoulder issue sidelined him for part of 2023. Zerpa has good velocity for both of his fastballs, which generate sink and weak contact. His short and tight slider sits around 84 mph and has downward bite, while his upper-80s changeup hasn't quite been as effective in 2023. He commands each pitch well and is a natural strike-thrower. Zerpa has a short-armed delivery out of a lower slot, and he throws his pitches with good arm speed. He has a shorter frame, but he does not lack conviction, pitching fearlessly and aggressively. The Royals see Zerpa more as a back-end starter and he made starts at Double-A and Triple-A in 2023, but the southpaw has pitched out of the bullpen in the Majors entering early August. He presents KC with options but needs to stay consistently healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals signed Zerpa out of Venezuela during the 2016-17 international signing period for $100,000, and the young lefty hadn’t pitched above rookie ball before the Royals protected him from the Rule 5 Draft and added him to their 40-man roster in 2020. Zerpa dominated High-A Quad Cities in 2021 with a 2.59 ERA in eight starts, but he struggled more when the Royals promoted him to Double-A Northwest Arkansas. Three days after he turned 22, Zerpa made his MLB debut in late September and showed how capable he is already, allowing just three hits and two unearned runs in five innings. Zerpa’s fastball has seen an uptick in velocity lately, sitting at 93-96 mph. It generates weak contact and has plenty of sink, and Zerpa has a natural feel for the strike zone with the pitch. His fastball is paired with a breaking ball that could be categorized as a slurve -- a pitch that has some loop to it but still lands sharply like a slider. Zerpa rounds out his arsenal with an above-average mid-80s changeup. Hitters have a hard time picking the ball up out of Zerpa’s hand given his short-armed delivery out of a lower slot, and despite his shorter frame, he pitches aggressively and fearlessly. The Royals gave Zerpa a tall task when they brought him up at the end of last season, but he wasn’t scared of the environment and impressed in all aspects. His pitchability gives him another level, and he gets high marks for his mound presence and ability to field his position. Zerpa needs to get more innings under his belt in the Minors, but he’ll be pitching depth for the Royals in 2022. His makeup and three-pitch mix give him a chance to start with the ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Zerpa was signed out of Venezuela for $10,000 in July 2016, the third-largest bonus the Royals gave out during the 2016-17 international period. Zerpa had good results in the Dominican Summer League and Rookie Arizona League, but he really showed his potential in 2019 as a starter in the Appalachian League. Despite not pitching past Rookie levels, the Royals added him to their 40-man roster in 2020 because they didn’t want to lose him in the Rule 5 Draft. A natural strike-thrower, Zerpa can generate weak contact with his fastball, which now sits 94-96 -- up significantly from previous years. He has a breaking ball that’s more of a slider shape, one that’s hard and lands sharply, and commands the pitch well. His mid-80s changeup has good drop and plays well off the fastball. Zerpa’s delivery is from a lower arm slot, which makes it hard for hitters to pick the ball out of his hand. The Royals have helped him with working from the stretch, to keep him compact and quicker to the plate while not diminishing his stuff. Zerpa has promising stuff, but his pitchability is what puts him on another level. Even at a young age, the Royals are impressed by how he’s able to use his repertoire past just the pure talent to get hitters out. He also gets high marks for his mound presence, his confidence, and his ability to field his position. That, plus the physical maturity and three-pitch mix, gives him a chance to remain a starter for now, but there’s also a path to a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed for $250,000 by the Yankees at the start of the 2016-17 international signing period, Contreras had a very strong year in Low-A in 2019 and was added to the team’s 40-man roster in Nov. 2020 as what appeared to be a high-floor type starting pitcher. Sent to the Pirates in Jan. 2021 as part of the Jameson Taillon trade, Contreras saw his stuff -- and his stock -- skyrocket, despite missing a large chunk of time with a forearm strain. He capped things off with a strong big league debut and a turn as one of the better pitching prospects in the Arizona Fall League. Contreras has seen his fastball go from a solid offering to an explosive one that touched 97-98 mph with ease and averaged around 96 mph with excellent life and high spin rates in 2021. He has both a high-spin 80-mph curve and a mid-80s slider, showing the ability to miss bats with both of them on a regular basis. While he doesn’t use it as much, his changeup features good sink and should be a legitimate above-average fourth offering. The right-hander finds the strike zone consistently with all of his pitches, and he’s very athletic on the mound, so he could have better-than-average command eventually. There are concerns about health and durability, especially given the injury in 2021, but the Pirates were erring on the side of caution, and Contreras is strong even though he’s undersized, giving confidence he’ll be able to hold up as a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees were not allowed to spend more than $300,000 on any free agent during the 2016-17 international signing period, but they were able to find a potentially good value in Contreras, who signed for $250,000 at the opening of the period. He pitched his way to the United States in his debut summer in 2017 and made it to the full-season South Atlantic League the following year. He spent all of 2019 at that level and was one of the best pitchers in the circuit despite still being a teenager and was added to the 40-man roster following the season. He was part of the package of prospects the Pirates received for Jameson Taillon, then went out and showed much better stuff than anticipated in 2021, though a forearm strain shelved him for a good part of the season. Contreras has the chance to have three solid or better pitches when all is said and done. His fastball, which sat 92-95 mph previously, was consistently in the 95-96 range in 2021, thrown with high spin rates and riding action. His changeup is his best secondary pitch, coming at hitters in the mid-80s with heavy sink. His breaking ball is more of an average offering that he can add and subtract from to give it different shape and he’s added a distinct slider. Contreras’ uptick in stuff has not compromised his feel for pitching. He repeats his delivery well and throws strikes. He’s gotten better with his command within the zone and, assuming healthy, his age, pitchability and stuff all provide confidence he’ll be a big league starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A transfer from Everett (Wash.) Community College to the College of Idaho, O’Brien became the first player from that NAIA school to be taken in the top 10 rounds when the Rays took him as a money-saving senior sign for $7,500 in the eighth round of the 2017 Draft. He looked like more than a bargain pickup when he pitched his way across two levels of A ball in 2018, then up to Double-A the following year, though the 2019 season ended early with elbow soreness. He hadn’t been pitching in 2020 when he was sent to the Reds for Cody Reed in late August. O’Brien was put on the Reds’ 40-man roster following the 2020 season because of his athleticism and the potential of his stuff, even if he wasn’t quite as electric at Reds instructs following the trade. O’Brien had added strength to his 6-foot-4 frame and was cranking his fastball up to 98 mph at times, sitting more in the 92-95 mph range in the past, though his fastball was more average last fall. Scouts differ on his breaking stuff, some preferring the shorter slider with bite, others preferring what they saw as a hard curve. The changeup is a work in progress, though he has been able to work in some usable ones at times. The slender right-hander has had fringy control and command, though the Reds liked his strike-throwing ability at instructs and think there’s still projection while loving his athleticism and makeup. There’s upside despite the fact he’s 26 and the Reds will let him keep working on his repertoire as a starter. They know that the fastball-breaking ball combination might play up out of the 'pen and other evaluators think that’s the best spot for him given his slender frame and effort in his delivery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanmartin’s pro career began way back in 2015, when the Colombian lefty signed with the Rangers for just $10,000 at the start of the 2015-16 international signing period. He’s been since traded twice, first to the Yankees in November 2017 and then to the Reds in January 2019 when Cincinnati also acquired Sonny Gray from New York. That 2019 season was the first time Sanmartin made it out of A ball and he had even more success in 2021, pitching his way from Double- to Triple-A before being called up to the big leagues for the first time in September. Sanmartin definitely falls under the “whole is greater than the sum of his parts” category. His fastball is fringy, averaging around 89 mph, topping out at 92 mph, though it plays up a bit because of deception and his ability to command the pitch very well. His best offering is his above-average changeup, giving him an excellent weapon against right-handed hitters, an offspeed pitch that led to a 44-percent whiff rate in Triple-A and the big leagues in 2021 and also elicited a lot of groundball outs. His 80-mph slider is average, but effective. All of Sanmartin’s stuff plays up because of his ability to command all three offerings in the strike zone and his strong feel for pitching. He has a limited ceiling because of the nature of his stuff, but he also has the chance to fill a number of roles, from No. 5 starter to lefty specialist and has impressed Reds staff with his willingness to take the ball at any time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crouse showed off first-round stuff and a super high-energy personality during his California high school days, and was taken by the Rangers in the second round of the 2017 Draft. Since then, he’s shown glimpses of that stuff while being shelved several times with different injuries with the Rangers and the Phillies, who acquired Crouse at the 2021 Trade Deadline. He made his big league debut that summer and got more work in during an Arizona Fall League stint but made just five Triple-A appearances in 2022 because of biceps tendinitis. It's hard to know exactly what Crouse can be after missing so much time, but when he has been healthy, he still shows four solid offerings. The velocity on his fastball has dipped because of the injuries, dropping down to an average of around 91 mph in his brief active time in 2022. His low-80s slider also lost some crispness, though it still missed bats and he can manipulate it when he’s feeling right. He has a fading changeup and more of a slower, truer curve as well. Crouse’s command and control has ebbed and flowed over his years in the Minors, though it’s more the injury history -- bone chips in his elbow with the Rangers, shoulder issues, and most recently, the biceps injury -- that point to a future as a reliever. He’ll likely work as a multi-inning guy in 2023 to build back up as the Phillies hope his stuff will tick back up with continued health and shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An electric, if a bit mercurial high school product from California, Crouse and his first-round stuff went in the second round of the 2017 Draft to the Rangers. He’s shown the ability to dominate Minor League hitters, but only in limited innings as bone spurs shelved him for parts of the 2019 season. He had them removed that offseason, sat out 2020, but came out throwing well in Double-A in 2021 and was part of the group sent to Philadelphia in return for Spencer Howard. Crouse made his big league debut at the end of the season and got some extra work in the Arizona Fall League, but missed nearly all of the 2022 season due to biceps tendinitis. Even though Crouse’s stuff backed up a little bit as the 2021 season wore on, he still has some big stuff that can get Major League hitters out. His velocity dipped a bit, but he was still averaging around 93 mph and touching 96 with riding life. His second plus pitch is his best one, a nasty mid-80s slider that can be a wipeout pitch. He started to throw it more again after his elbow was cleaned out. He’ll change the velocity on it, so it can have cutter-like action, or he can make it a bigger breaking ball. His fading changeup improved when he focused on that instead of his slider while battling the elbow issues and he can still fold in an average true curve. Ever since high school, because of Crouse’s high energy on the mound and effort in his delivery, there has been some reliever risk, with the injuries only adding to that potential move. He has thrown strikes for the most part and does have four legitimate pitches, so he does have the ingredients to start if he can stay healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crouse had the stuff and performance track record to go in the first round of the 2017 Draft, but he also had a lot of moving parts and effort in his delivery and was emotional on the mound, so the Rangers were able to land him in the second. He worked just 162 1/3 innings in his first three seasons after signing him for $1.45 million, in part because he was limited by bone spurs in his elbow in 2019. He had them removed that October and then sat out alternate camp and instructional league in 2020 for undisclosed personal reasons that the club says aren't a concern. He was back and throwing well, handling a push up to Double-A in 2021, when he was sent to the Phillies in a Trade Deadline deal that also brought Kyle Gibson and Ian Kennedy to Philadelphia. It looks as if Crouse has regained the electric stuff he had when he was last fully healthy in 2018. His fastball sits at 92-97 and reaches 99 with riding life. His slider can be a wipeout pitch with mid-80s velocity and two-plane break, though it was less sharp and he used it less frequently in 2019 because it bothered his elbow. Relying less on his slider forced Crouse to spend more time on his changeup, which has the potential to become a solid offering with fade and sink, and he can also manipulate his breaking ball into more of a true curve to use as a fourth pitch. Though he still has a lot going on in his delivery, including some head whack, he keeps everything in sync and averaged just 2.0 walks per nine innings in 2019. He's entertaining to watch because he'll talk to himself, groom the mound a la Mark Fidrych and employ a Johnny Cueto shimmy, and some scouts think his energy would be best directed in a late-inning relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a starter at Missouri State, Coleman had above-average velocity that would drop off late in games, so the Padres, who took Coleman in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft, moved him to the bullpen. While his numbers were good in his first two seasons, his velocity tumbled from 97 mph down to the upper 80s. Many wrote him off, but the Royals remained intrigued and selected him as the player to be named later in the Trevor Rosenthal trade in 2020. After an offseason searching for answers to the velocity drop, Coleman’s stuff jumped to another level in 2021, culminating in his MLB debut in late September. Coleman’s fastball now regularly sits 98-100 mph and has even flashed as high as 102 mph on radars last season. He complements that with a hard slider, and his work with the Royals’ pitching development team found a few more ticks of velocity on the pitch, making it more of a power slider than the looping shape it had before. Coleman is still working on consistency with the pitch, as well as his fastball command when he tries to blow it by hitters -- although he impressed in his short stint in the Majors with just one walk in 6 1/3 innings. The Royals have discussed working in a third offering as another look against lefties. With the obvious velocity, Coleman has the ceiling to be a dominant closer at the highest level, and his 6-foot-5 frame helps with that projection. How close he gets to that role will be about fastball command and slider consistency, but he factors into the Royals’ plans for their bullpen now and in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken 12th overall in the 2017 Draft, Baz was the player named later alongside Austin Meadows and Tyler Glasnow in the Pirates-Rays trade that sent Chris Archer to Pittsburgh a year later. The Rays immediately got to work on making Baz their next big pitching prospect, and the early results showed in 2019 at Class A Bowling Green and the Arizona Fall League. After spending time at Tampa Bay’s alternate training site in 2020, Baz took another huge leap last summer as one of the Minors’ most dominant pitchers, posting a 2.06 ERA with 113 strikeouts and 13 walks in 78 2/3 innings at Double-A and Triple-A. He also mixed in a silver-medal-winning trip to the Olympics with Team USA. The Rays gave him his debut on Sept. 20 and made him their Game 2 starter in the ALDS. Baz was one of 12 Major Leaguers to throw 100 fastballs and average at least 97 mph and 11.4 inches or less of vertical movement, putting him on a list that includes Aroldis Chapman, Gerrit Cole and Jacob deGrom. That's why he threw it 54.5 percent of the time in the Majors. Baz’s mid-80s slider remains his best secondary, thanks to its bite that makes it a menace for right-handers. His low-80s, loopier curveball seemed like a distant fourth pitch in the past, but he threw it almost equal to the slider at the top level with similar whiff rates. His high-80s changeup is reserved almost exclusively for lefties. The 6-foot-2 hurler’s biggest gains came in the control department. His Minor League walk rate dropped from 10.8 percent in 2019 to 4.4 percent last summer, while his 8.7 K/BB ratio led the Minors (minimum 70 IP). Outside of some small improvements to his curve and change, there’s little polishing left to be done for Baz.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baz emerged as one of the hardest-throwing high school pitchers in the 2017 Draft as a Concordia Lutheran High (Tomball, Texas) senior, even generating some buzz as a possible top 10 pick. Pittsburgh ended up taking Baz with the No. 12 pick and signed him for $4.1 million, slightly above slot value. He had been in the Pirates’ system for a little more than a year when the organization sent him to Tampa Bay in August 2018 to complete the Chris Archer trade that had already netted the Rays Tyler Glasnow and Austin Meadows. Baz made a smooth transition to full-season Class A Bowling Green in 2019 and showcased his high-octane stuff after the season as one of the Arizona Fall League's youngest pitchers. He gained even more experience at the Rays’ alternate training site in 2020. From cleaning up his delivery to refining his pitch mix, Baz has only improved since he entered the Rays’ system. He scrapped his two-seam fastball and dialed back his curveball usage upon joining the organization in favor of a four-seamer that can touch triple digits and sits in the mid-90s and a hard, biting slider that is perhaps the best in Tampa Bay’s system. He can generate whiffs with both pitches, albeit while operating with fringy command, and he also shows the makings of having a solid changeup. Baz rounds out his arsenal with a fourth-pitch curveball that receives below-average grades from evaluators. The Rays worked with Baz to improve his delivery after acquiring him and he showed more control in 2019, walking one fewer batter per nine innings (4.1) compared to his first two seasons (5.1). That improved control and command took another jump in 2021, solidifying Baz’s place as one of the best pitching prospects in baseball when everything is working. If he can keep hitting his spots with premium stuff, he has the potential to lead future Tampa Bay rotations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Frias was a strong-armed third baseman when he signed out of the Dominican Republic for $50,000 in November 2015. Seeing the potential in that arm, the D-backs moved him to the mound early in his career and watched him blossom. He showed flashes of dominance in 2018 during his first stateside campaign and was the organization’s most improved pitching prospect in ’19, riding a jump in velocity and sharper secondary pitches up to Class A Kane County. Frias spent the bulk of 2021 in Double- and Triple-A, and while there are still bouts of inconsistency, he’s made noticeable strides. He put everything together in a seven-inning no-hitter for Double-A Amarillo on Aug. 1. He was called up in late September and made a trio of appearances in the Majors. A prototypical power pitcher with a combination of physicality and stuff, Frias generates big-time velocity with a lightning-quick arm. He touches 99 mph with a fastball that sits in the mid-to-upper 90s deep in starts. A spike curveball gives Frias a second plus pitch. It's thrown with huge vertical depth and hard 12-to-6 downer action that challenges right-handed hitters. He continues to make progress with that pitch, and his enormous hands enabled him to add a split-changeup in 2019. The pitch registers in the upper 80s and bottoms out as it nears the plate, giving him a potential weapon against left-handed hitters. Frias threw more strikes and also showed an ability to hold his velocity deep into starts in 2021. As he’s matured, he’s begun mixing his pitches and has become less of a thrower and more of a pitcher. That said, the D-backs moved him into relief for good this summer in the hopes that the fastball-curve combo can play up even more in short settings. If he can maintain the stuff and hone in on the control just a bit more, the right-hander could be a high-leverage bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Frias was a thick-framed, strong-armed third baseman when he signed out of the Dominican Republic for $50,000 in November 2015. Seeing the potential in that combination, the D-backs moved him to the mound early in his career and watched him blossom. He showed flashes of dominance in 2018 during his first stateside campaign and was the organization’s most improved pitching prospect in ’19, riding a jump in velocity and sharper secondary pitches up to Class A Kane County. He worked his way up to Triple-A in 2021 and while there are still bouts of inconsistency, he’s made noticeable strides and put everything together on August 1, when he threw a seven-inning no-hitter. Frias is your prototypical power pitcher with his combination of physicality and stuff. He generates big-time velocity with a lightning-quick arm, touching 99 mph with a fastball that sits in the mid-to-upper 90s deep in starts. A spike curveball gives Frias a second plus pitch, thrown with huge vertical depth and hard, 12-to-6 downer action that befuddles same-sided hitters. He continues to make progress with that pitch and his enormous hands allowed him to add a split-changeup in 2019. The pitch registers in the upper 80s and bottoms out as it nears the plate, giving him a potential weapon against left-handed hitters. Frias has thrown more strikes in 2021 and has also shown an ability to hold his velocity deep into starts. As he continues to mature, Frias has begun mixing his pitches better becoming less of a thrower and more of a pitcher. While some evaluators mention a high-effort delivery, Frias is athletic for his size, and shown an ability to consistently repeat his motion. If he continues to command his secondary pitches and stick with the adjustments he’s made this season, it's easy to see him as a future starter, but if not he could be a valuable backend bullpen piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Friedl set a record for a bonus given to a non-drafted free agent ($735,000) when teams discovered in 2016 that he was Draft eligible while he was playing for Team USA the summer after that Draft. Following a strong debut that summer, he moved slowly through the lower levels during his first two full seasons of pro ball, then missed a large chunk of the 2019 season because of an ankle injury. He wasn’t protected from the Rule 5 Draft in either 2019 or 2020, but wasn’t selected. He finally reached Triple-A in 2021 and was called up to make his big league debut with the Reds last September. When Friedl remembers who he is as a hitter, he has success. The left-handed hitter is at his best when he focuses on working counts, getting on base, making hard contact with line drives to all fields and using his plus speed and high energy to be a table-setter. He got into trouble trying to get to his pull side power with too much lift rather than going gap-to-gap and let his power come naturally. Friedl can play all three outfield spots extremely well. A fringy arm would make it tough for him to play right field on a daily basis, but it’s playable in center and left. If he can commit to maintaining his approach, he has the chance to be a solid fourth outfielder in the big leagues in the very near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a sophomore at Nevada, Friedl hit .401 and finished with an OPS over 1.000, but no team realized he was a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2016. That information came to light as he was playing well for the U.S. Collegiate National Team that summer and the Reds, who had some bonus pool money left over, were able to sign him for $735,000, a record for an undrafted free agent. After a scintillating pro debut after signing, he methodically made his way up to Double-A and was scuffling there in 2019 when an ankle injury that required surgery ended his season early. Friedl, who was at the Reds alternate site in 2020, but was left off the 40-man roster and not selected in the Rule 5 Draft both after the 2019 and ’20 seasons, won’t wow anyone with his size or tools. He does have a very good feel for contact and keeps his strikeouts down while drawing a fair amount of walks. Some saw a little Adam Eaton in the left-handed hitter when he first entered pro ball, but he lacks the same kind of bat speed, which limits how much he can impact the ball. From a pure speed standpoint, he might just be above-average, but it plays up on the basepaths because of his instincts and aggressiveness. Friedl has seen time at all three outfield spots and can play all of them very well, albeit with a fringy arm. That bodes well for him as his profile is likely as a fourth outfielder type, but one who could be valuable in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies’ first selection in the 2017 Draft, Vilade was a high school product from Oklahoma who was taken in the second round. Since that time, the son of former coach and scout James Vilade moved steadily up the organizational ladder, spending a year at each A ball level, performing well at the Rockies’ alternate site in 2020, then jumping to Triple-A, going to the Futures Game and making his brief big league debut in 2021 before wrapping things up with a trip to the Arizona Fall League. He spent a so-so year in Triple-A in 2022, and when the Rockies put him on waivers in November, the Pirates decided to buy low and claim him. Throughout his professional career, Vilade has always shown an innate knack for contact. He rarely strikes out, with a career 17.4 percent K rate to show for it, and he’s not afraid to work counts or draw walks. He’s long been hit over power, not changing his approach too much by adding launch angle that would diminish his hit tool. He’s added a lot of strength as he’s matured, so there’s still confidence the power, which hasn’t shown up consistently, will come, especially if he can start making contact out front more regularly. Initially an infielder, Vilade made the move to the outfield in 2020 and played there almost exclusively a year ago, with a little first base mixed in. He’s likely a left fielder when all is said and done, with the chance for the power to come as he’ll play all of 2023 at age 24.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies didn’t have a first-round pick in 2017, thanks to the free-agent signing of Ian Desmond. But they feel they may have gotten a first-round talent in Vilade, the son of former college coach and current Marlins scout James Vilade, who signed for full pick value as the No. 48 overall selection, and has moved one level per year in his first two full seasons, making progress offensively at both stops. That continued in 2020, as he was the best hitting prospect at the Rockies’ alternate site in Denver. Over the last year and a half, Vilade had evolved from a good hitter with solid bat-to-ball skills and an advanced approach to one who can really damage the baseball. He’s added strength and very good weight without sacrificing any athleticism and might now have 70 raw power from the right side of the plate. Because of his approach and plate discipline, he’s a safer bet to get to that power, with the Rockies thinking he might be a 25-30-homer guy in the future. Vilade has moved around a bit defensively, starting his pro career at shortstop, moving to third and then focusing more on playing left field, where he could be an average defender. He’s likely done with the hot corner, but he could get some reps at first, where he played a bit during instructs. He does have the chance to be an everyday run producer in left field, reminding some of former Rockie Matt Holliday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 40 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 Fortes didn't become a full-time starter behind the plate until his third college season at Mississippi in 2018, when he won Southeastern Conference tournament MVP honors and went in the fourth round. He stood out defensively but did little offensively as a pro, batting .232/.318/.333 in three Minor League seasons, until the Marlins called him up in mid-September last year when Jorge Alfaro injured his calf. He homered in each of his first two starts and four times in 34 plate appearances. Fairly athletic for a catcher, Fortes is agile behind the plate and a capable receiver and blocker. His arm strength is merely average but plays better than that because he has a quick transfer and makes accurate throws. He also has the leadership and intelligence desired in a backstop, and he graduated from Mississippi with a finance degree in just three years. Despite his power outburst in September, Fortes is more a guy who ambushed some fastballs from unsuspecting big leaguers than a real slugger. He did start launching balls in the air more often in 2021 and does have enough bat speed and strength to perhaps produce 15 homers per season from the right side of the plate. While he won't hit for a high average, he does make consistent contact and has a knack for getting on base via walks and hit by pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heasley fell to the 13th round in the 2018 Draft after posting a 6.98 ERA in 15 starts at Oklahoma State, but the Royals saw something in the right-hander and went above slot to sign him. He’s steadily improved in stuff, pitchability and presence since he became a Royal. His 3.33 ERA across 105 1/3 innings in Double-A last year earned him a jump to the Majors, where he impressed in three starts. Heasley’s velocity keeps ticking up since he became a pro; he can dial his fastball to 97-99 in short bursts and was averaging 94 mph in the Majors as a starter. He has four pitches, and his best secondary pitch is his above-average, 12-6 curveball. He didn’t throw his slider as much in the Majors, but it should be a solid offering for him moving forward. And he rounds out his arsenal with an effective changeup that he can use on both sides of the plate. Heasley has a repeatable delivery and walked just 34 batters in Double-A with 120 strikeouts, although he faced tougher hitters in the bigs and lost a feel for fastball command at times. Heasley gets high marks for his ability to field his position and control the running game, boasting one of the best pick-off moves in the organization. He received praise for how he handled the jump from Double-A to the Majors last year, and his competitiveness and talent will see him help the starting group this year and even compete for a spot in the Opening Day rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heasley had mixed results in two years at Oklahoma State and posted a 6.98 ERA in 15 starts as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2018. He fell to the 13th round, but the Royals thought he was better than his performance and went above-slot to sign him. He showed better stuff and improved pitchability in 2019 and was a late addition to the alternate training site in 2020 before finishing the year at Kauffman Stadium for the Royals' instructional league program. Heasley has unlocked more velocity as a pro thanks to a higher arm slot. His fastball sits at 92-95 mph with high spin but can get up to 97 mph. His 12-to-6 curveball is an above-average pitch, and he also has a slider that’s distinct from his other breaking ball. Heasley rounds out his arsenal with an effective changeup, and he’s not afraid to throw to either side of the plate with it. He has done a great job of repeating his delivery, and he gets whiffs not only because of his stuff, but also because he knows how to be successful with his sequencing. Heasley receives praise for his competitiveness on the mound and his ability to control the running game and field his position. He’s tightened up his body since he was drafted and looks more like a starter now after a solid beginning to 2021 at Double-A. The Royals project him as one still with his arsenal and makeup giving him the potential to be at the back end of the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Moran remained in the Twins' organization despite being unprotected in the Rule 5 Draft following the wiped-out 2020 season, and the left-hander's performance shone across Double-A and Triple-A following an initially shaky taste of the high Minors in '19. His 109 strikeouts and 2.41 ERA in 67 1/3 innings earned him a late-season promotion to the Twins, where his control issues flared up and made for a challenging first MLB stint, though the stuff is there for the young Puerto Rican to join the Twins' recent pipeline from the island that has featured José Berríos, Eddie Rosario and Jose Miranda. A season missed due to bone chips in Moran's elbow spurred his move to the bullpen in 2017, and that's allowed him to lean heavily on his superb, disappearing changeup that generates huge swing-and-miss numbers against both lefties and righties. His fastball averages 93 mph with life, and he's worked hard to improve his slider from an essentially nonexistent pitch to a somewhat competitive in-game offering, though there's still work to be done there. To this point, his changeup has been good enough that the slider hasn't really mattered as much. He has the chance to occupy a leverage role in the Twins' bullpen sooner rather than later if he continues to progress with the slider and throws more strikes, though walks will always be a part of his game. He has struggled at times when deviating from his routine -- say, with a promotion to a new level -- and could benefit from his '21 MLB cameo in that regard.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cal State Fullerton keeps sending strike-throwing machines to the big leagues, with Seabold following in the footsteps of Noe Ramirez, Dylan Floro, Thomas Eshelman and Justin Garza when he made a start for Boston in September. A Phillies third-round pick in 2017, he reached Double-A midway through his first full pro season and boosted his stock by starring in the Arizona Fall League in 2019. After the Red Sox acquired him in an August 2020 deal for Brandon Workman and Heath Hembree, he missed most of the first three months last year with elbow inflammation. Seabold's best pitch is clearly his changeup, a true plus offering (and sometimes better) in the low 80s with late fade and tumble that confounds hitters from both sides of the plate. He sets it up with a four-seam fastball with high spin and induced vertical spin, and though his velocity dipped a bit to 88-92 mph with a peak of 94 in 2021, his heater still didn't get hit hard. He could use a better breaking ball because his low-80s slider is merely average and he lacks trust in his softer curveball. Because he can't overpower hitters, Seabold tricks them by mixing his pitches and locations. He has a simple, efficient delivery and pounds the strike zone, though his control and command weren't quite as sharp last year as they had been in the past. He has a high floor as a likely back-of-the-rotation starter, though he'll have to prove he's durable enough dealing with oblique (2019) and elbow issues in his last two full seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Phillies took Seabold in the third round of the 2017 Draft, the hope was the Cal State Fullerton product would be the kind of advanced college starter who could move rapidly through the system. While he did struggle a bit when he first got there, he did live up to his advanced billing by reaching Double-A in his first full season. Seabold is all about mixing his pitches, his overall feel for pitching and his command, rather than pure stuff, with three offerings that typically grade out as average. He will show an above-average fastball on occasion, with a tweak to his delivery helping him add a tick, though he usually sits in the 90-93 range. He mixes in his average changeup effectively and he'll show an average breaking ball. His ability to keep hitters guessing and fill up the strike zone will continue to be key for him moving forward. After initially struggling in Reading, Seabold made solid adjustments and pitched very well over the season's final month. If he can continue to show that kind of command and crispness of his pitches, he'll be ready to impact the back end of the Phillies rotation soon now that he's put the injury in his rearview mirror.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beer became a national sensation in his first year at Clemson, garnering honors as the consensus 2016 Freshman of the Year while also taking home the Dick Howser Trophy as national player of the year. He continued to produce over the next two years to finish his Tigers career with a .321/.489/.648 line and 56 homers in 188 games, during which he totaled more walks (180) than strikeouts (98). The Astros took Beer 28th overall in the 2018 Draft, and he continued to mash, hitting 12 homers over 67 games in his pro debut. He, along with J.B. Bukauskas, Corbin Martin and Josh Rojas, was dealt to Arizona as part of the Zack Greinke deal in the middle of the 2019 season. Beer impressed at Arizona’s alternate training site in 2020 and then continued to excel in Triple-A last season. He was called up to make his Major League debut last September, but appeared in just four games before hurting his shoulder diving for a ball and undergoing season-ending surgery. Some initial mechanical tweaks that Beer made to his swing upon entering Houston’s system have paid off considerably for the left-handed slugger. He applies his booming raw power from line to line, making loud contact with a leveraged swing that’s conducive to hitting fly balls. He projects as an average hitter, one with an advanced approach, though there is some swing-and-miss in his game. To his credit, Beer made strides in this area in 2021, reducing his strikeout rate to 17.5 percent over 100 games, his lowest mark since his 67-game professional debut in 2018. He’s a below-average runner but moves better once underway. The jury is still out on Beer’s long-term defensive home. He saw some time in the outfield early in his pro career but has primarily played first base in the D-backs’ system. While his initial performance in the outfield was discouraging, Beer dedicated himself to improving defensively and has made notable gains over the past few seasons, giving club officials hope he’ll be at least serviceable in the outfield long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beer became a national sensation in his first year at Clemson, garnering honors as the consensus 2016 Freshman of the Year while also taking home the Dick Howser Award as national player of the year. He continued to produce during the next two years to finish his Tigers career with a .321/.489/.648 line and 56 homers in 188 games, during which he totaled more walks (180) than strikeouts (98). The Astros took Beer at the back end of the first round in the 2018 Draft, and he had already clubbed 16 homers at the Double-A level the following year before Arizona acquired him, along with J.B. Bukauskas, Corbin Martin and Josh Rojas, in the Zack Greinke deal. Beer was a standout at Arizona’s alternate training site, showing more consistency on both sides of the ball, and continued to impress with Triple-A Reno in 2021. Some initial mechanical tweaks that Beer made to his swing upon entering Houston’s system have paid off considerably for the left-handed slugger. He applies his booming raw power from line to line, making loud contact with a leveraged swing that’s conducive to hitting fly balls. He projects as an average hitter, one with an advanced approach that nets him walks, although there is some swing-and-miss in his game. He’s a below-average runner but moves better once underway. The jury is still out on Beer’s long-term defensive home. He saw some time in the outfield early in his pro career but has played first base almost exclusively in the D-backs’ system. While his initial performance at the new position was discouraging, Beer dedicated himself to improving defensively at the alternate site and did just that. Club officials are pleased with the progress they’ve seen this season and are now bullish about Beer’s capacity to play the position, viewing his defense as at least serviceable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays selected Lowe 13th overall in 2016 on the strength of his athleticism and gave him some early looks at third base. A year later, Lowe moved to the outfield full-time and has remained there ever since. He climbed one level per season from 2017 to 2019 but had yet to post an OPS above .800 until his breakout 2021 campaign at Triple-A Durham. The left-handed slugger produced a .291/.381/.535 line with 22 homers and 26 steals in 111 games and received a two-game cup of coffee with the big club in early September. Lowe sports arguably the loudest collections of skills in a deep Rays system. The 24-year-old has emphasized shortening his swing in recent years to cut down on strikeout issues, and while he can still get lengthy at times, those adjustments (along with some added strength) have helped buoy the hope that he can hit for a decent average. The next step could be evening out his splits with 17 of his 22 Triple-A homers coming off right-handers and a difference of 200 points between the two sides (.763 vs .996). The power could lead to 25-plus homers at the top level. Elsewhere, he is an easy plus runner who has always been a threat to steal in the pros. He draws strong reviews for his ability to cover ground in center, and his plus arm gives him another asset when playing the grass. He could stick up the middle or switch over to right without issue as he did at times for Durham. Lowe has the tools necessary to elbow his way more into a longer Major League look this summer and hold down a spot once there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way standout in high school, Lowe garnered Georgia Gatorade player of the year honors as a senior and was one of the more impressive all-around athletes available in the 2016 Draft. The Rays liked him more as a hitter and selected him with the 13th overall pick, then lured him away from a Florida State commitment with a $2.6 million bonus. He overcame a sluggish start in his full-season debut the next year and ultimately finished on a high note, hitting .296/.350/.415 with 24 extra-base hits and 14 steals over his final 72 games. The performance led to high expectations for Lowe's 2018 campaign, though he was unable to build upon that progress in the Florida State League, where his feel to hit backed up and resulted in below-average production. Lowe's athleticism and physical tools suggest he'll eventually make an impact at the plate, but right now he's still figuring out what type of hitter he is. He knows how to create leverage through the hitting zone and has added some loft since signing, though, so far, it hasn't yet translated to any uptick in usable power. But even as he's scuffled at the plate, Lowe has worked to improve his approach and become more selective. That progress was evident in 2018, as he trimmed his strikeout rate by nearly 3 percent from the previous year while simultaneously improving his walk rate from 8.3 to 10.3 percent. It gives him a solid foundation for further offensive development, and club officials are still bullish about Lowe's potential to hit for average and power. After struggling at third base during his pro debut, Lowe was shifted to center field and immediately proved a natural, covering huge amounts of ground with his plus speed and long, graceful strides. He's developed into the best defensive outfielder in the system and looks like a lock to stick in center field, where his offensive profile offers the most value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not only did Ortega get just $10,000 to sign, he did so in the middle of the 2014-15 international signing period in February. He was also 18, nearly ancient for that market. Suffice it to say that this signing came with little fanfare or expectations and Ortega was basically off the grid for the first four years of his pro career, spending a summer in the Dominican Summer League and one in the Arizona League before missing all of 2017 with injury. He pitched well enough, again with no attention, during his full-season debut in 2018, but then officially jumped on the radar with an All-Star season in the California League and a late promotion up to the Double-A Southern League in 2019.
