Ortega generates a ton of swing and miss with his fastball and curve, finishing last season with 10.9 strikeouts per nine innings. His fastball sits in the mid-90s now and touched as high as 99 mph last season, showing he can hit those upper levels regularly in relief stints. His curve also flashes plus and he took a big step forward in his feel for both pitches working off each other. While those two pitches are his bread and butter, he does have a slightly below average changeup. His biggest area of focus going forward is his command and control a year after walking 4.6 per nine innings. Ortega could succeed as a starter, even with a fringy changeup, if he can throw strikes because his other stuff is so good. If his control doesn’t improve, watching that fastball and breaking ball come out of the bullpen could be a lot of fun.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring at Jacksonville alongside future Orioles outfielder Austin Hays, Baumann became a third-round selection of Baltimore in 2017, signing for below-slot value ($500,000) and rising quickly. Baumann reached Class A Advanced in his first full season and threw a 10-strikeout no-hitter in ’19 at Double-A Bowie, where he blossomed into a standout in the O’s fast-improving system. But the pandemic and some arm trouble delayed Baumann’s debut until 2021, when he made four inconsistent September relief appearances. He touched the big leagues again in 2022, again in relief, spending most of his time in Triple-A in the bullpen as well. The 6-foot-4, 225-pound righty is an imposing presence on the mound, with broad shoulders and a strong lower half he uses to create a downhill plane that accentuates his stuff. His fastball sits in the mid-90s and flashes 98-99 mph at times. It has angle and carry that generates plus vertical movement, enabling him to miss bats up in the strike zone. Baumann has a simple, repeatable delivery but the arm action is long, leading to inconsistent command at times and risk of injury. Indeed, he was on the fast track before being shut down with a flexor strain late in 2019, and he was limited at the Orioles’ 2020 alternate site due to the issue. Those durability concerns mean Baumann could ultimately end up in the bullpen, where it's easy to envision his heater and plus power slider presenting a dominant combination late in games. But he also has the pitch mix to start, with an improving changeup and developing curve that remains a work in progress. Baumann showed an ability to maintain velocity deep in games in the Minors when healthy, but also struggled with walks, especially post-injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Atlantic Sun Pitcher of the Year at Jacksonville in 2015, Baumann caught the eyes of Orioles scouts when they arrived in north Florida to see former college teammate Austin Hays. The O’s tabbed Baumann in the same round as Hays a year later, signing him for below slot value ($500,000), thus beginning the big, physical righty’s quick climb through the system. Baumann reached the Class A Advanced Carolina League in his first full season, then pitched to a 2.31 ERA and threw a 10-strikeout no-hitter at Double-A Bowie in 2019. Baumann had his 2020 cut short due to an elbow strain that did not require surgery, and it isn’t expected to hinder his status for 2021. Standing 6-foot-4 and 225 pounds, Baumann uses his frame and simple, repeatable delivery to create a downhill plane that accentuates his stuff. His fastball sits 94-95 and flashes 98-99 mph at times, with late life that he maintains deep in games. A plus power slider is the better of his two breaking balls, thrown in the high 80s to elicit swings and misses. Baumann’s changeup has improved immensely since his college days, and he is still working to develop a fringy curve. Both will be integral in whether he ultimately sticks as a starter at the highest level. Baumann’s longer arm action has also led to command issues at times. If those are refined, Baumann’s durability and potential four-pitch mix give him a chance to be a mid-rotation starter in the big leagues. If not, his fastball-slider combination could be devastating late in games, making his floor that of an impact reliever. He’s next in line to debut in a group of exciting young Orioles pitchers that includes Dean Kremer, Keegan Akin, Zac Lowther and others.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castro grew up in Venezuela as a catcher and switched to pitching just three months before San Francisco signed him for $100,000 in July 2015. Tommy John surgery in 2017 restricted him to one inning in two years and he didn't make his full-season debut until 2021, when the Giants challenged him with a full-season debut in Triple-A last May. He responded by earning a September callup, allowing just a single unearned run in 13 1/3 innings in the Majors before making a couple of scoreless Division Series appearances, but scuffled this season before the Cubs claimed him on waivers in August. Castro displayed inconsistent fastball velocity and parked around 91-92 mph as a starter in 2019, then used his pandemic downtime to add strength and showed up at the instructional league in 2020 with a 92-97 mph four-seamer. He maintained that heat as a reliever last season, topping out at 98 mph and getting good carry up in the strike zone. He always has demonstrated good feel for his curveball, a low-80s offering with power and depth despite below-average spin rates. Though Castro repeats his simple delivery well and showed solid control in the past, he had bouts of wildness in Triple-A last year with his improved stuff and has struggled to throw strikes in 2022. He flashed an average changeup as a floor-over-ceiling starter and theoretically could try to make it as a starter if a need arose. If he can rediscover the strike zone, he can bolster Chicago's bullpen after the club dealt three relievers at the '22 Trade Deadline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castro grew up catching in Venezuela and moved to the mound just three months before the Giants signed him for $100,000 in July 2015. Tommy John surgery in 2017 cost him all of that season and limited him to one inning in the next, so he didn't make his U.S. debut until 2019. Though he worked just 89 2/3 frames in his first five pro seasons -- none in full-season ball -- San Francisco added him to its 40-man roster in November after he used his pandemic downtime to get stronger and his velocity trended up at instructional league. After Castro's fastball sat around 91-92 mph and its velocity wavered in his first year back from elbow reconstruction, his four-seamer operated at 92-95 and reached 97 last fall. He long has demonstrated feel for spin, and his curveball showed improved power and depth during instructs. His changeup needs more consistency but shows the makings of an average third pitch. Before his stuff took off this fall, Castro impressed the Giants with some of the best control in the system. He repeats his simple delivery well and led the short-season Northwest League in walk rate (1.7 per nine innings) in 2019. He'll remain a floor-over-ceiling starter to open 2021 but could shift to the bullpen in the near future if San Francisco looks to expedite his development now that he's on the 40-man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 22nd-round pick by the Yankees out of Seattle University in 2017, Junk is now on his third organization, having moved from New York to the Angels for Andrew Heaney at the 2021 Trade Deadline and then the Halos to the Brewers in a November 2022 deal for Hunter Renfroe. The right-hander’s breakout came in 2021, when he posted a 1.78 ERA with 68 K’s at Double-A Somerset in his final stop in the Yanks' system, and he spent most of 2022 at Triple-A Salt Lake, where he posted a 4.64 ERA with 69 strikeouts and only 18 walks in 73 2/3 innings. Junk made seven appearances (six starts) during his two years with LA but couldn’t manage to stick in Anaheim. Junk sits around average velocity with a 91-93 mph fastball, but a decent spin rate helps it play better up in the zone. His low-80s slider has become his best offspeed pitch with good sweep across the zone, and he upped its usage in 2022 to the point where he was throwing it about as equally as the fastball. As a result, he relied less and less on his upper-70s, 12-to-6 curveball and was barely using his firm upper-80s changeup by season’s end. Throwing strikes hasn’t been an issue for the 6-foot-1 hurler over the last two seasons, and his 5.8 percent BB rate was sixth-best in the Pacific Coast League (min. 70 IP) in 2022. That will keep Junk a part of Milwaukee’s starting depth heading into his first campaign in the system, and any further uptick in stuff, whether it be more velo or a sharper curve as a third offering, could earn him a longer look as a No. 5.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For the first few years of his pro career after the Yankees took Junk out of Seattle University in the 22nd round of the 2017 Draft, he did little to distinguish himself as a prospect. Using the shutdown as a time to really get to work, he emerged in '21 as a different pitcher, one who had a 1.78 ERA and .185 batting average against in 14 Double-A starts when he was sent to the Angels for Andrew Heaney at the Trade Deadline. He took a perfect game into the ninth inning in his fifth start with his new organization, then was called up and made four September big league starts. He jumped between Triple-A and the Majors in '22 before being traded again in November, this time to the Brewers in a four-player deal for Hunter Renfroe. Junk leans heavily on his low-90s fastball, a four-seamer that can touch 96 mph and has high spin rates and carry up in the zone. He features both a slider and a curve, thrown roughly around the same velocity in the 78-81 mph range, with the former a bit better with excellent sweep. As a result, he threw the slider around 38 percent of the time in 2022, almost three times as often as his other breaker. He throws his fringy upper-80s changeup much less frequently than his other three offerings. The 6-foot-1 right-hander’s control took a big step forward in 2021, a big reason for his consistent success. At 26, he’s a bit old for a prospect, but the late bloomer is ready for a more consistent big league role, either as a back-end starter or perhaps in the bullpen where his four-seamer and slider might play up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltner both started and relieved during his three years at Ohio State, with mixed results, though he was virtually unhittable as a closer in the Cape Cod League in 2017. When the Rockies took him in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft, it was because they thought he had the goods to start at the next level. His development on that front was slow going at first, but things clicked a bit more in 2021 as the right-hander started the year in High-A and made his big league debut last September. The 6-foot-4 right-hander does have a solid enough three-pitch mix to give him the chance to start, though there’s still work to be done in terms of command and execution for him to stick in that role. While he can crank his fastball up into the mid-90s in shorter stints, he’s more likely to sit in the low-90s as a starter. Even without premium velocity, he misses bats up in the zone and the Rockies want him to be effective down as well so he isn’t so predictable with his heater. He can land his mid-80s slider for strikes and also will take something off to fold in a get-me-over slower curve on occasion. He has feel for a changeup, but the Rockies would like to see him use it more. Tweaks to shorten his arm action in back paid dividends in 2021 as he repeated his delivery more effectively and showed signs of being able to pitch to both sides of the plate. There’s still hope he can land in a rotation, even if the fastball-slider combination would look very good in the 'pen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltner’s three-year career at Ohio State was up-and-down, serving in both starting and relief roles. He was, however, lights out closing in the Cape Cod League in 2017, which undoubtedly opened a lot of eyes. So even though his junior season as a starter for the Buckeyes was inconsistent, he landed in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft. The Rockies have been developing him as a starter and after a strong summer pro debut, he struggled pitching in the hitting haven of Asheville in 2019. He was dominant, albeit as a 24-year-old, during his time in instructional league play last fall. The progress Feltner made in workouts over the summer and then at instructs revolved around his delivery and ability to command his power stuff. He was 95-97 mph with his fastball at instructs and his slider played a lot better than it did in 2019, an 86-87 mph breaking ball with better action and lateness to it. He’s always had a good changeup with good fade. Feltner shortened up his arm circle in back, allowing him to get to a more consistent release point and he was repeating his delivery more last fall. That helped his stuff tick up while he was able to command his pitches relatively well. He has the stuff to start, but if the command gains don’t stick, his fastball-slider combination could be really nasty in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Tigers 2013 first-rounder Jonathan Crawford, Kutter taught himself a cutter during Christmas break in 2016 before posting the second-best ERA (1.71) and third-most strikeouts (99, trailing two seasons by Chris Sale) in Florida Gulf Coast history. A 16th-round pick in 2017, he reached Double-A before blowing out his elbow late in the 2019 season. Following Tommy John surgery that fall and a second operation to remove bone chips from his elbow in the summer of 2020, he looked better than ever last season and made his big league debut with a September start. Crawford's returned from his elbow reconstruction with a better fastball and curveball than before. His heater added a couple of ticks of velocity, sitting at 92-95 mph and reaching 97 with carry up in the zone, while his upper-70s curve went from an offering he could land for strikes to flashing as a plus offering with improved depth. His mid-80s cutter was his best weapon before he got hurt but played mostly as an average pitch in 2021. Crawford also has a mid-80s changeup with splitter action, but he doesn't trust it much because he struggles to throw it for strikes. He has good control of the rest of his repertoire, though he got knocked around in Triple-A and the Majors when his command faltered. He could be a back-of-the-rotation starter or useful multi-inning reliever if he can figure out a way to handle advanced left-handed hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Reds for $70,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2012, Siri set a Midwest League record with a 39-game hitting streak in 2017, when he topped the Low-A circuit with 46 steals and added 24 homers, but he couldn't replicate that success. He bounced to the Mariners and Giants on waivers in the spring of 2020 before the Astros signed him as a free agent that November. He tore up Triple-A last summer to earn his first big league callup in September, homered four times in 46 at-bats and wound up starting two games in the World Series. Siri has demonstrated impressive raw tools for years but hasn't been able to find consistent success at the plate. His approach didn't change much in 2021, as he was still very aggressive and pull-happy and struck out at a 31 percent clip. He was able to get to his plus raw power and reach base more than ever before, though it's unclear how sustainable his performance will be if he doesn't add more plate discipline. Siri doesn't have to hit for a high average to help a team. His plus-plus speed makes him a weapon on the bases -- he stole 27 bags in 31 attempts last year -- and an asset in center field. He has the quickness and strong arm to provide quality defense at all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez piqued the interest of White Sox scouts in high school before batting just .262 in three college seasons at Miami, though he did perform well with wood bats and earn all-star honors in the Cape Cod League in 2017. Looking for a versatile defender in the later stages of the 2018 Draft, Chicago signed him for $125,000 in the 18th round, but he didn't do much while primarily playing the outfield in his first two pro seasons. He shifted to the middle infield last year after coming back from the pandemic layoff, and he batted .283/.364/.532 with 24 homers and 24 steals in 93 games between Double-A and Triple-A to earn his first big league callup. At 6-foot-2 and 215 pounds, Gonzalez is bigger and more powerful than most middle infielders. His strength and bat speed create solid to plus raw pop, and he taps into it with an aggressive approach. His right-handed stroke can get long and leads to swings and misses, so he'll probably always be a power-over-hit guy. Gonzalez has solid speed and translates it into stolen bases. His hands and arm grade as average, and he's more capable of playing several positions than a standout at any of them. He's a decent shortstop who probably profiles best at second base, and he also has seen action everywhere but catcher in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted as a senior out of Division II Cal State Stanislaus in the seventh round of the 2018 Draft, Ryan quickly showed he was much more than a money-saving senior sign when he pitched his way to Double-A in his first full season. He was pitching well in Triple-A for the Rays when he was sent to the Twins in the Nelson Cruz deal, then helped the United States earn a silver medal in the Olympics before returning home and eventually making a solid five-start big league debut for Minnesota. Ryan continues to live and die with his fastball more than anything else, and while it doesn’t light up radar guns -- his four-seamer averaged 91.2 mph and reached 96 mph in 2021 -- it has crazy life up in the zone and elicited a 27 percent miss rate last year. It’s a good thing since he threw it 72 percent of the time during the season. The Twins hope he can continue improving his 80-mph slider, a pitch that did miss bats at a 35-percent clip, though that was more because hitters didn’t look for it than any strong characteristics. He less frequently mixes in a low-80s changeup and low-70s curve. A former water polo player, Ryan’s athleticism plays well on the mound in terms of repeating his delivery and his three-quarters arm slot creates deception. His stuff plays up because he commands his repertoire very well and while his ceiling might be somewhat limited because of the lack of wow stuff, he’s ready to be a No. 3 or 4 starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs eyed Rivas, a two-way player on Arizona's 2016 College World Series runners-up, in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft only to have the Athletics beat them to the punch. Chicago eventually landed him in a January 2020 trade for Tony Kemp. The pandemic and an early-2021 hamstring injury delayed Rivas' debut with his new organization until last June, but he arrived at Wrigley Field two months later and batted .318 with one homer in 18 games before tearing a tendon in his right middle finger. Rivas has a smooth left-handed swing, tremendous feel for the barrel and a disciplined approach that allow him to spray line drives to all fields. He's built for making contact as opposed to driving the ball, and he's a rare first baseman whose power ranks as his worse tool. He produces middling exit velocities and rarely launches balls to his pull side, so he'll probably max out at 12-15 homers per season. Quicker than most first basemen, Rivas is a below-average runner out of the batter's box but closer to average underway. He's a solid to plus defender at first base with soft hands, plenty of range and a strong arm. He moves well enough to play the outfield corners, where his range is a bit limited.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Although Otto starred as a reliever at Rice, the Yankees turned him into a starter after drafting him in 2017's fifth round, a transition that went slowly because of shoulder and ribcage issues and the pandemic. He finally broke out with a dominant first half in 2021, prompting the Rangers to acquire him as one of four prospects in the Joey Gallo/Joely Rodriguez trade in July. He became the first of that group to reach the Majors, logging a 9.26 ERA in six late-season starts. Otto's four-seam fastball sits at 92-94 mph and touches 96 with riding action up in the zone. Before 2021, his best pitch was a 78-81 mph spike curveball that could be a hammer at times, but he now favors a low-80s sweeping slider that plays better off his heater. He doesn't have great feel for a fading changeup that's often too firm in the mid-80s. Otto's 119 innings last year exceeded his total from his first four years as a pro, and his stuff dipped a bit in the second half. He did display much better control than ever before and continued to throw strikes even while getting pounded with the Rangers. He could wind up as a multi-inning reliever who focuses on his fastball and slider, and he has reached 98 mph in shorter stints in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Otto starred as a reliever and made just four starts in three seasons at Rice, the Yankees took him in the fifth round of the 2017 Draft with the plan of making him a starter. His transition has been slowed by surgery to remove a blood clot in his pitching shoulder that cost him most of 2018, a ribcage injury in 2019 and the pandemic shutdown of the Minors last year. He finally stayed healthy in the first half of 2021 and worked his way to Triple-A before New York sent him to the Rangers in the Joey Gallo/Joely Rodriguez trade in July. Otto's out pitch is a spike curveball that ranges from 78-81 mph and also in effectiveness, as it's a hammer with true 12-6 break at times and less sharp and hard to control at others. He sets up his curve with a four-seam fastball that sat at 92-94 mph and reached 96 with riding action in 2019 but has touched 98 in the past. He barely used a changeup in college and needs more consistency with the pitch, which lacks enough velocity separation from his heater at times. Because Otto will be 25 throughout this season and injuries have hampered his progress as a starter, it was believed that he may be better suited to a return to the bullpen. While his past success was based much more on stuff than polish, he has displayed much better control this year than he ever had before. He still has a floor as a multi-inning reliever but now looks like a viable rotation option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCarthy broke out during his sophomore season at the University of Virginia, and although a broken wrist cut short his junior season, the D-backs had already seen enough and selected him 39th overall in 2018. After signing for $1.65 million, slightly below slot value, McCarthy impressed in his professional debut, hitting .288/.378/.472 over 55 games with Class A Short Season Hillsboro. Multiple stints on the injured list limited him to 53 games during the 2019 campaign, though he put up good numbers when healthy and was sent to the Arizona Fall League to make up for some of those missed at-bats. He added 15 pounds of muscle on his 6-foot-2 frame during the canceled 2020 season, then went out and hit a career-high 15 homers in 2021 before being called up in late August for his Major League debut. More of a hit-over-power type throughout his career, McCarthy showed an ability to tap into his power last season and elevated the ball more than he’d done previously. A .337 career hitter in college, he followed that up by averaging .270 over his first three pro seasons. While his bat path can get flat at times, he generates impressive exit velocities and has a strong approach at the plate. His strikeout rate did spike once he was promoted to the Majors, but that was a small sample size and can likely be attributed to adjusting to a new level. Once on the bases, he is a plus runner who swiped 29 bases last year and is 68-for-82 (83 percent) in stolen-base attempts over the past three seasons. Defensively, McCarthy uses his speed well and his instincts help him grade out as an above-average defender. He doesn’t have the loudest collection of tools, but he does have a high floor and the potential to become an everyday outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peguero signed with the Yankees for just $50,000 back in July 2015, at an older-than-usual age of 18. It took him a while to gain any traction, with the pandemic-related shutdown not helping, not reaching full-season ball until the 2021 season. Having been moved to the bullpen in 2019 was a smart move as the right-hander began the year in High-A and was in Double-A when the Yankees included him in the deadline deal that brought Andrew Heaney to New York. Peguero went from Double- to Triple-A and made his big league debut in late August. The 25-year-old Peguero fits the two-pitch power reliever mold. His fastball is a heavy two-seamer that averages 96 mph with plenty of sink. That and the fact that he throws downhill with his 6-foot-5 frame leads to a ton of groundball outs. His slider flashes plus, a breaking ball with good bite that touches 90 mph and generates a lot of swings and misses. Command has long been the largest obstacle for Peguero, though he did find the strike zone much more consistently last year, a big reason for his ability to advance like he did. He doesn’t need pinpoint command, so if he can throw strikes like he did in 2021, he has the chance to serve as an effective middle reliever in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cabrera didn't find any takers when he first became eligible to turn pro in 2014, then signed with the Marlins for $100,000 a year later. He broke out in 2019, his fourth pro season, and was on track to make his big league debut in 2020 before minor shoulder soreness intervened. Biceps inflammation sidelined him until June last year, but he recovered to make it to Miami in late August and logged a 5.81 ERA in seven starts. Cabrera has a diverse repertoire with four pitches that grade as solid or better, headlined by a heavy fastball that averaged 97 mph in the Majors, climbs into the triple digits and features heavy life that generates a lot of weak grounders. His best secondary weapon is a darting upper-80s slider with depth as well as lateral break, and he also has a power curveball in the low 80s with even more downer action. He throws his changeup harder than most, sitting in the low 90s with plenty of fade, and it was unhittable in Triple-A last year but flattened out and was his least effective offering in the Majors. While Cabrera has learned that he can produce premium stuff without overthrowing, his control and command weren't as sharp as usual in 2021 and big leaguers made him pay when he didn't locate his pitches well. He could be an ace if he develops more precision and should be at least a mid-rotation starter with average control. He still has to prove he can handle a full-season workload because his career high is 100 1/3 innings in five pro seasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Sixto Sánchez is the more famous prospect, there are Marlins executives who believe that Cabrera has a brighter future. A late bloomer in the Dominican Republic, he went unsigned when first eligible in 2014 before turning pro for $100,000 a year later. He made huge strides with harnessing his electric stuff in 2019, when he excelled in Double-A at age 21, and almost certainly would have made his big league debut last year if he hadn't been bothered by minor shoulder soreness. Cabrera's best weapon is a fastball that sits at 93-97 mph and climbs into triple digits, with its heavy life and the downhill plane he creates with his 6-foot-5 frame leading to a lot of weak groundball contact. He improved the reliability of his slider in 2019, continuing to deal at 82-85 mph with increased bite. He also maintained more consistent velocity separation between his heater and changeup, which has become a solid third pitch. Cabrera has learned that he doesn't need to overthrow to generate premium stuff, though he'll still lapse on occasion. Now that he's throwing more strikes and doing a better job of locating his pitches within the zone, he has erased talk that he might land in the bullpen. Instead, he and Sánchez should pitch at the front of Miami's rotation for much of this decade.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Lopez signed with the Blue Jays in 2016, he already had Canadian roots as a Dominican-born player who lived in Montreal, Quebec, when his father was a teacher there. For years now, Lopez has been one of the most consistent producers in Toronto’s system, but he is still looking to establish himself at the MLB level after making brief appearances as a bench player the past two seasons. Lopez hit at the lower levels, but he really put himself on the prospect map with a strong 2021 campaign in Double-A and Triple-A, proving his contact ability could hold up against more advanced pitching. That year, Lopez hit .315 with a .379 OBP. He kept rolling in ’22 at Triple-A Buffalo, where he hit .297 with a .378 OBP over 91 games. He impressed with the big club too, going 6-for-9 (.667) in his limited time. Lopez tends to hit the ball on the ground plenty, but his above-average speed has helped him cover for that. Lopez’s power trails well behind his contact rate, but he doesn’t need to be a home run hitter. Producing more line drives would translate his approach well to the MLB level, and his defensive versatility gives him many pathways back to the big leagues. Lopez can play across the infield and outfield, and when you factor in his contact ability and speed, he’ll have every opportunity to compete for at least a part-time role in Toronto again at some point in 2023 and beyond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lopez already had Canadian roots as a Dominican Republic-born kid who moved to Montreal when his father took a teaching job there. He has been a constant producer in the Jays' system since signing in July 2016 with a career batting average of .312 and OPS of .802 in the Minor Leagues. The 2021 season was his best yet as the 5-foot-10 utility player hit .315/.379/.437 with five homers and 22 steals over 113 games at Double-A and Triple-A. He made his Major League debut on Aug. 17 but managed only one at-bat before being sent down to Buffalo. As Lopez’s numbers would indicate, he shows ample offensive promise with his ability to make consistent contact. He has posted groundball rates above 50 percent with each of his last three affiliates, but his plus speed means he can earn plenty of hits with his legs. He’s a stolen-base threat as well and has improved his success rate on the basepaths since 2019. Lopez isn’t much of a power bat though, and he may struggle to reach double-digit home runs over a full season. The Blue Jays have tried to put Lopez’s athleticism to good use by utilizing him in multiple positions, including second, short and all three outfield spots. He sports just an average arm, and that might limit him to second base if he ever needs to stick to one place on the diamond. He might not, however, and Lopez’s best value might be as a speedy contact hitter worth carrying in the lineup in any way, regardless of where his glove plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Santo Domingo and raised for several years in Montreal after his father’s teaching job took the Lopez family to Canada, Otto signed with the Blue Jays back in 2016 and has quietly put up numbers ever since. Starting in the Gulf Coast League in ’17, Lopez posted a slash line of .275/.361/.360, then stepped into a little more power in ’18 with Vancouver. Lopez’s breakout came in ’19 with Lansing, where he won the Class A Midwest League batting title with a .325 average while playing second base, shortstop and the corner outfields. Lopez does a little bit of everything, and does most of it quite well. His offensive profile is certainly hit-over-power, but he’s added some strength over the past year and is starting to impact the baseball with more authority. With good speed and athleticism, Lopez can also be a threat on the bases and fill the gaps in the outfield. As one of the most versatile players in the organization, Lopez has super-utility potential, which opens up several different avenues for him to reach the Major Leagues. His arm plays well enough at infield and outfield positions, too. Added to the Blue Jays’ 40-man roster this past winter to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft, Lopez was tested in the upper Minors this season and performed well at both Double-A and Triple-A, putting himself on track for a Major League debut in August. He’s a comfortable fit with the organization’s emphasis on positional versatility, and that should help his case for future looks at the top level. His power tool is worth monitoring in ’21, but he’s a comfortable fit with the organization’s emphasis on positional versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick in 2017 out of Virginia Tech who tended to be a bit too hittable during his college career, Naughton had an up-and-down first full season of pro ball with the Reds. While he finished second in the organization in strikeouts and capped off his year with a good start up a level in the Florida State League playoffs, the left-hander gave up more hits (168) than innings pitched (154) in the Midwest League. Naughton can be prone to creating his own big innings with one mistake. He often fought his delivery, causing his stuff to not be as sharp. That was particularly true of his breaking ball, which can get caught between a curve and a slider. He needs to rely on movement, deception and command because of his lack of plus stuff, starting with an 87-94 mph fastball that can sneak up on hitters due to his deception, but often lacks movement. He might need to pick one breaking ball to help define it better and give him a third solid pitch, behind his above-average changeup. He goes right after hitters and fills up the strike zone (2.0 BB/9 in 2018). Naughton finished off his first full season much more strongly than he started it. His ceiling might be limited, but if he can carry those adjustments over, he has the chance to be a No. 5 type starter or an effective middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shortly after signing with the Twins for $90,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, Gil had shoulder surgery that cost him all of the following season, and he didn't reach full-season ball until 2019. He joined the Yankees in a March 2018 trade for Jake Cave and quickly blossomed into one of the hardest throwers in their system. He didn't allow a run in his first three big league starts after arriving in New York in August 2021, but he got rocked that September and again early in 2022 before having Tommy John surgery in May. Before he got hurt, Gil averaged 96 mph and reached 100 with a fastball that stood out not just for its velocity, but also for its high spin rates, carry and the extension in his delivery that allowed it to get on hitters quickly. His mid-80s slider can be a plus pitch with sharp horizontal action at its best, though he loses his feel for it on occasion. He also has a low-90s changeup with some fade and sink, but it's too firm and he doesn't trust it. While his quick arm produces high-octane stuff without much effort, Gil never has harnessed it consistently. He averaged 5.4 walks per nine innings and worked 100 innings just once in his first six pro seasons, so it's becoming increasingly likely that he's more reliever than starter. He has closer upside if he can improve his control, though he may not pitch much this season and will turn 26 in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Soon after signing with the Twins for $90,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, Gil had shoulder surgery that cost him the following season. The Yankees acquired him in a March 2018 trade for Jake Cave, three months before he made his U.S. debut, and he quickly turned into one of the hardest throwers in their system. He made his big league debut last August and didn't allow a run in his first three starts before getting knocked around in his last three, and he spent most of 2022 in Triple-A before injuring his elbow in May and requiring Tommy John surgery. Gil has more velocity than most starters, averaging 96 mph with his riding fastball in the Majors while topping out at 100 in the Minors, and holds it for several innings at a time. He has tightened his mid-80s slider into a plus pitch with sharp horizontal break when it's on, though he sometimes loses feel for it. His third option is a low-90s changeup with some fade and sink but he doesn't trust it much or use it very often. Though Gil can light up radar guns without much effort in his delivery, he has trouble harnessing his high-octane stuff. He averaged 5.3 walks per nine innings last year (5.8 in the big leagues) and 5.4 in his first five pro seasons. He'll have to throw a lot more strikes and improve his changeup in order to last as a starter but has closer upside if he lands in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $90,000 out of the Dominican Republic by the Twins in 2015, Gil missed the following year after shoulder surgery. After he showed signs of a mid-90s fastball when he came back in 2017, the Yankees acquired him in a trade for Jake Cave the next spring. He averaged 12.1 strikeouts per nine innings in his first two years in New York's system before spending last summer at the club's alternate site and pitching briefly in the Dominican League during the winter. Gil has higher-octane stuff than most starters, beginning with a fastball that operates at 95-98 mph for several innings at a time and regularly reaches triple digits with significant riding life up in the strike zone. He made progress last year with his power breaking ball that features slider velocity in the mid-80s and sometimes has more of a curveball shape. He also has a hard changeup that parks around 90 mph with fade and sink, though it lacks consistency. Gil generates premium velocity with relatively little effort but has difficulty harnessing his stuff. He reduced his walk rate to a career-best 4.2 per nine innings in low Class A in 2019 but will have to throw more strikes and continue to refine his secondary pitches in order to make it as a starter. His live arm potentially could make him a closer if he winds up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting Grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 55 Detmers moved full-time into Louisville’s rotation as a sophomore and cemented his bona fides as one of the top college lefties in the Draft class of 2020 with four dominant starts before the shutdown. The Angels saw enough to take him No. 10 overall and he jumped to Double-A for his professional debut in 2021, moving up to Triple-A and then the big leagues in his first season. He was greeted rudely during his Major League debut, though he did shut down the Astros in mid-August for his first big league win. Landing on the COVID injured list may have been the only thing that kept him from losing his rookie status. Detmers is still a strike-throwing machine with four legitimate offerings at his disposal. He throws a touch harder than he did for most of his Louisville days, with a fastball that touches 95 mph and sits comfortably at around 93 mph. When he’s in sync, it plays up even more thanks to deception in his delivery and good command of the pitch, though he lost some of that during his time in Los Angeles, getting too much of the zone and getting hit hard. His go-to is still his curve, a low-70s breaking ball that missed bats in the big leagues. He effectively mixes in a mid-80s slider, a relatively new pitch, and has a solid sinking changeup as well. The left-hander may have tried to do a bit too much during his debut, causing uncharacteristic command issues both in and out of the zone. But there’s plenty of reason to be confident in Detmers’ ability to make adjustments and reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: and Grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 55 Prior to 2020, the Angels had taken college players in the first round in four of the previous six Drafts. All but one of them, lefty Sean Newcomb, had been hitters. Detmers became their second college southpaw in seven Drafts when they took the Louisville standout No. 10 overall after he had established himself as one of the best college arms in the class. He was the second left-hander from that crop to get taken in 2020, after Asa Lacy went No. 4 overall, and then was as good as advertised during his time at both the Angels’ alternate camp and in instructional league play. Detmers has the chance to have a solid four-pitch mix, with his feel for using all of them ahead of how the stuff grades out. He’ll usually throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range and was more consistently at the upper end of that spectrum with the Angels after he signed. It plays up because of deception and Detmers’ ability to command the pitch well, something that was on display in the summer and fall, particularly after he settled in. His 72-76 mph curveball is his best offering, a plus out pitch with good shape. He uses an effective sinking changeup and he worked on developing a slider he threw occasionally in college after signing, giving him another very serviceable pitch. Detmers should be able to continue to fill up the strike zone thanks to a delivery he repeats consistently. His pitchability helped him strike out 47 batters in 30 innings at the alternate camp and that feel for his craft should allow him to move fairly quickly through the Angels system to a career as a durable mid-rotation starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brendan McKay won the 2017 Golden Spikes Award and was selected fourth overall in that year’s Draft, but it was Ellis who led the University of Louisville squad in average, home runs and RBIs that season. The D-backs selected the infielder in the second round that year and he has methodically worked his way through the system. The advanced bat he showed in college took a while to translate to the professional game as Ellis hit under .250 in his first three professional seasons. He made good use of the canceled 2020 campaign, leaning out a bit, and with a more athletic frame, Ellis got off to a fast start in 2021. His efforts were rewarded when he made his Major League debut on July 30. A physically strong right-handed hitter, Ellis has easy raw power to all fields and has shown a solid approach. He didn’t always use his lower half, which led to weak contact and inconsistent swings early in his career, but the D-backs believe his swing is in better shape now after addressing those inefficiencies. Ellis draws his share of walks and shows good plate discipline, though his strikeout rate did tick up when he was called up to the Majors. On the plus side, Ellis’ walk rate remained the same, showing he was staying within his approach despite the lack of hits. Early concerns about Ellis' defense had some thinking he'd eventually move to first. Instead, he's improved the most in that area as a pro, so much so that he's now regarded as an above-average defender at the hot corner, where his plus arm strength profiles well. Ellis has played some first and also spent some time at second with the Major League club, but it’s clear third is his long-term home. The defense and raw power give him a chance to succeed there, but Ellis will need to continue to make strides as a hitter to establish himself as an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since the start of the Draft bonus pool system, teams have used the middle rounds of Day 2 to take money-saving seniors, using that savings to go after other higher-priced talent. Sometimes, those bargains pay off, as it appears to have with Warren, a former infielder who started pitching late and turned a solid senior season at UNC-Wilmington into a sixth-round selection in the 2018 Draft, signing for just $7,500. The reliever reached Double-A and pitched well in the Arizona Fall League in 2019, then shook off a rough start in Triple-A in 2021 to get hot late in the year, earn his first callup to the big leagues and pitch as well as any reliever on the Angels' staff to close out the season. Warren is pretty much a two-pitch pitcher, with his fastball and slider. The heater averaged around 93 mph in 2021, touching 95, and he throws both a four-seamer up and a two-seamer that gets a ton of groundball outs. He misses bats with his slider that flashes plus, a sharp breaker that falls off the table. Warren leaned heavily on the pitch during his successful big league debut, eliciting a 37-percent whiff rate with the upper-80s pitch. He has a seldom-used below-average changeup that can provide a different look. The six-foot reliever threw a lot more strikes in Los Angeles than he has in the Minors. If that trend continues, he has the chance to get the ball late in games and he was already getting trusted in high-leverage situations late last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The power Terry showed as a Georgia high schooler intrigued scouts but his righty-hitting, first-base-only profile did not, so he lasted 13 rounds in the 2015 Draft. After giving up a Georgia State commitment to sign for $100,000, he didn't reach full-season ball until his fifth pro season, but once there he batted .293./.362/.537 with 25 homers between two Class A stops in 2019. He was the Rangers' best hitter in instructional league last fall, though they opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster for the second straight year. Terry still sticks out most for his prodigious pop, which he creates with bat speed and the strength and leverage in his massive 6-foot-2, 258-pound frame. Though he primarily looks to pull balls in the air, he makes a reasonable amount of contact for a slugger -- and most of it's loud. He doesn't draw many walks, however, and may need more patience when he faces more advanced pitchers. Though he works hard to maintain his conditioning and improve his defense, Terry is still an all-bat player. He's a well below-average runner with limited range at first base, and he has a below-average arm while throwing from a low slot. He's not the slam-dunk DH he looked like when he entered pro ball but he's really going to have to hit to become a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a shortstop in his first two seasons at NCAA Division II Le Moyne (N.Y.), Gray became a full-time pitcher in the Cape Cod League during the summer of 2017. He went 11-0 and ranked third in D-II with a 1.25 ERA in ‘18, when he joined the Reds as a supplemental second-round pick in June and went to the Dodgers as part of the Yasiel Puig/Matt Kemp trade in December. Gray reached Double-A and won the Los Angeles' Minor League Pitcher of the Year Award in his first full pro season and spent his second refining his secondary pitches at the club's alternative training site. He made his Major League debut on July 20, 2021, but he was moved to the Nationals nine days later in the Max Scherzer-Trea Turner Deadline blockbuster. Having been traded twice already, Gray has been on the move very much because of other organizations looking to bring him in rather than anybody trying to get rid of him. Hitters have difficulty catching up to Gray's 92-97 mph fastball, which seems to explode at the plate with riding and rising life. He sharpened both of his breaking balls at the alternate training site, tightening up and adding some power to his mid-80s slider while improving his feel for his upper-70s curveball. His changeup is more of a work in progress because he didn't use it much in college, and it features some sink but gets too firm at times. The athleticism that made Gray a shortstop translates well to pitching. He repeats his delivery well and shows the ability to harness his electric fastball and slider. He was one of the toughest competitors in the system and brings that tenacity to a Nationals pipeline in need of potential stars.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Mets for an over-slot $150,000 in the 18th round of the 2015 Draft, Humphreys was breaking out during his full-season debut two years later when he blew out his elbow, requiring Tommy John surgery in August 2017. A second operation to address an ulnar nerve issue in his elbow delayed his return until June 2019 and he pitched only two innings in Rookie ball last year, but he allowed just one run in 11 2/3 Arizona Fall League frames and landed a spot on New York's 40-man roster. He was designated for assignment twice in 2020 and changed organizations each time, going to the Giants in a trade for Billy Hamilton in July and to the Indians via waivers in November. Humphreys' best pitch is his fastball, which plays better than its 90-94 mph velocity because of its riding life and his ability to command it to any quadrant of the strike zone. Both of his secondary pitches presently grade as average but show flashes of becoming better than that. He has a tight upper-70s curveball with promising spin rates and a changeup that he sells well with fastball arm speed. Humphreys pounded the strike zone before he got hurt, averaging just 1.6 walks per nine innings in his first three pro seasons before issuing five in 13 2/3 innings in 2019. He offers the upside of three solid pitches with plus control, though he's also 24 years old and has worked just 11 innings above low Class A. Cleveland probably won't know exactly what it has in Humphreys until he returns to game action in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Buford High School, Marsh’s alma mater in Georgia, has produced some solid baseball talent in the past, namely Joey Bart, who went on to Georgia Tech and became the No. 2 overall pick in the 2018 Draft. Marsh is the first player to get taken from Buford in the top two rounds, taken No. 60 overall by the Angels. A two-sport star who helped Buford win state titles in football, Marsh’s combination of athleticism and feel for hitting have allowed him to climb to the top of the organizational ladder, though some minor injuries have slowed his ascent. Throughout his pro career, Marsh has shown an ability to make hard contact and get on base, with a walk rate over 10 percent to show for it. With strength and bat speed, there’s always been raw power to tap into, but he hadn’t done much of that until 2019, when a change in his setup at the plate -- standing more upright -- helped him slug .520 in August and .522 in the Arizona Fall League. He continued to get to his power at the Angels’ alternate camp in 2020, hitting seven homers in just over 100 at-bats, showing power to all fields, while still walking at a 20-percent clip. Marsh’s other three tools -- his speed, arm and defense -- are all plus and were all consistently on display at the alternate camp. He has the goods to play center field long-term, but can easily handle either corner to flank Mike Trout in the Angels’ outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duran has blown away expectations since the Red Sox drafted him in the seventh round out of Long Beach State in 2018. He had a scintillating pro debut that summer, played in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and reached Double-A in his first full pro season and arrived in Boston halfway through his second after playing for Team USA in an Olympic qualifier. He struggled in his first taste of the big leagues, however, striking out in 36 percent of his plate appearances. The best athlete and fastest runner in the Red Sox system, Duran has plus-plus speed that allows him to beat out routine grounders and wreak havoc on the bases. Boston has helped him rework his left-handed swing since he has turned pro, allowing him to drive the ball much more consistently as he has added some loft and is doing a better job of using his lower half. While he's now a legitimate 20-homer, 40-steal threat, his stroke got too uphill during his Red Sox debut and he'll have to prove he can make consistent contact to reach his potential. A second baseman in college and during his first month in pro ball, Duran lacks experience in center field and it shows. He has improved his reads and routes but they still need more work, and he often relies on his speed to overcome his mistakes. His fringy arm strength is playable in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duran has raised his profile significantly since Boston made him a seventh-round pick out of Long Beach State in 2018. He posted a .910 OPS in his pro debut and hit .387 in high Class A during the first two months of 2019 before appearing in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game and spending the second half of his first full season in Double-A. The Red Sox are excited by the offensive and defensive gains he made at their alternate site last summer, which paid off with an MVP award in the Puerto Rican Winter League playoffs and a .400/.500/.640 line at the Caribbean Series. Duran's best offensive tool is his plus-plus speed, which helps him routinely beat out grounders and makes him a dangerous basestealing threat, as evidenced by his 70 swipes in 199 games during his first two pro seasons. Though he showed some ability to backspin the ball, scouts had concerns about how much impact he might have when he slugged just .325 in Double-A. But after he added some loft to his left-handed swing and started better incorporating his lower half at the plate at the alt site, some club officials believe he could produce 20 or more homers per season. Because he spent his college career and his first month as a pro at second base, Duran still is learning the nuances of outfield play. He's making progress with his reads and routes in center field, and his speed helps him overcome some of his mistakes. He has fringy arm strength but could compensate by getting to balls more quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Raleigh, whose uncle played for a long time in the Minor Leagues and father played and coached college ball, has more than lived up to the expectations typically laid upon players who grew up around the game. The Mariners’ third-round pick in 2018 out of Florida State, Raleigh made it to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball and led all Minor League catchers with 29 home runs. He followed that up with nine homers at the alternate training site in 2020 in what was perhaps the best offensive performance of any player there. Raleigh has been tabbed as an offensive-minded catcher, and the power he showed at Florida State has carried over to the pro game. He definitely has a better power tool over hit, but he controls the strike zone well enough that his tremendous raw power shows up from both sides of the plate. He can drive the ball to all fields, with more success from the left side. From a raw power numbers perspective, Raleigh ranks right up there with elite catching prospects like Joey Bart. His biggest area of improvement would be cutting down his 23% strikeout rate, but he will likely show better strike zone command with more Minor League reps. Despite his reputation with the bat, Raleigh has made significant strides with his defense. His receiving metrics have been off the charts and his blocking has been great. He also has wowed with his ability to communicate with and lead a pitching staff. Having already formed a close bond with Logan Gilbert, Raleigh has helped pitchers learn their game plans and held them accountable -- signs of a big leaguer in the making. Raleigh’s lowest floor would be a platoon backstop in the big leagues, while his ceiling could be a starting regular, particularly given his switch-hitting ability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reetz had a decorated prep career, garnering MVP honors at the 2013 Perfect Game All-America Classic before starring for the 18U U.S. national team in the World Cup in Taiwan. The Nationals drafted him in the fourth round the following year, making Reetz the first Nebraskan prep to be picked in the top five rounds since 1996. While he has made progress in the subsequent years, especially as a defender, injuries in back-to-back years have kept Reetz from developing as hoped. Despite having a quick right-handed swing that yields line drives across the whole field, Reetz has struggled to hit for average as a pro. The same can be said about Reetz's power, though he does hit the ball consistently harder now after learning how to better apply his lower half in 2016. Reetz continues to show plate discipline and a solid approach at the plate, qualities that some within the organization believe will help his bat to eventually come around. Defensively, Reetz stands out most for the arm strength and catch-and-throw skills that produced a career-best caught-stealing rate of 31 percent in 2017. He continues to earn high marks for his makeup and work ethic, and club officials are quick to note his great relationship with Nats catching coordinator Michael Barrett, who has helped him to improve as a receiver and game-caller. But after logging just 230 games across his first four seasons, Reetz now faces an uphill battle towards reaching the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knehr saw time as a two-way player at Fordham, but he showed more promise as a pitcher and the Padres drafted him as one in the 20th round in 2018. He reached Class A Fort Wayne in his pro debut and spent his first full season at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, where he averaged 11.3 strikeouts-per-nine over 17 appearances (12 starts). The Padres had Knehr work out of the bullpen exclusively in that year’s Arizona Fall League, and he built upon that progress with a standout performance at fall instructional camp in 2020. Knehr built on that success in 2021 and made his Major League debut in July, appearing in 12 games and throwing 29 innings. Knehr’s stuff has improved in the pro ranks as the right-hander has shifted his focus to pitching only. He throws his high-spin fastball around 93-95 mph with late movement that helps him induce a mixture of whiffs and weak, ground-ball contact. His changeup is effective against hitters on both sides of the plate, flashing plus on occasion and playing nicely off the fastball. He rounds out his arsenal with an above-average slider. Knehr looks the part of a Major League reliever, with his 6-foot-2 frame, crisp stuff and natural strikeout tendencies, but he will need to improve his control in order to reach his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knehr saw time as a two-way player at Fordham, but he showed more promise as a pitcher and the Padres drafted him as one in the 20th round in 2018. He reached Class A Fort Wayne in his pro debut and spent his first full season at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore, where he averaged 11.3 strikeouts-per-nine over 17 appearances (12 starts). The Padres had Knehr work out of the bullpen exclusively in that year’s Arizona Fall League, and he built upon that progress with a standout performance at fall instructional camp in 2020. Knehr’s stuff has improved in the pro ranks as the right-hander has shifted his focus to pitching only for the first time. He throws his fastball around 93-95 mph with late movement that helps him induce a mixture of whiffs and weak, ground-ball contact. His changeup is effective against hitters on both sides of the plate, flashing plus and playing nicely off the fastball, and he can miss bats with a useful slider as well. Knehr looks the part of a future Major League reliever, with his 6-foot-2 frame, crisp stuff and natural strikeout tendencies, but he will need to develop more control in order to succeed at higher levels. He showed improvement on that front late in 2020, giving the right-hander some helium heading into the 2021 season and his eventual Major League debut in July.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 55 | Power: 45 | Run: 70 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 55 Bruján signed for just $15,000 out of the Dominican Republic in October 2014, and he stood out as a steal almost immediately. When he completed his first full season in 2018, he posted a .320 average with 55 steals (second-most in the Minors) at Class A and Class A Advanced. After a 48-theft season in 2019, he was added to the 40-man roster and spent 2020 at the alternate training site and on the postseason taxi squad. Bruján was with Triple-A Durham for the majority of 2021 (hitting .262/.345/.440) and featured in 10 games with the big club in his debut campaign. Bruján puts bat to ball often, although the drop in average with Durham takes some shine off a plus hit-tool projection, and is a better overall hitter from the left side. Thanks to an increased fly-ball rate, his power did take a jump with a career-best 12 homers in 2021, and he showed off better exit-velocity numbers, enough to bump up his pop ceiling. His best asset remains his plus-plus speed, and he’s as good as anyone in the Minors at putting it to use on the basepaths. The majority of Bruján’s starts came in the outfield for the first time in 2021, and he played all three spots in both the Majors and Minors. His infield work was concentrated at second base -- partly in deference to Wander Franco -- but he saw time at third and short as well. Bruján’s athleticism and above-average arm will make him an option anywhere for the Rays, and his best chance at getting in the lineup every day might be to keep bopping around based on need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brujan came with little fanfare as an international amateur, signing with the Rays for $15,000 in 2014. He looked like one of the biggest steals from that year’s class when he led the Minors in runs (112) and finished second in stolen bases (55) in his first full season, then solidified his top-prospect status by reaching Double-A at age 21 in 2019. The Rays added Brujan to their 40-man roster after the season, and he spent the 2020 campaign at the alternate training site before joining Tampa Bay’s taxi squad in the postseason. Brujan structures his game around the plus-plus speed that helped him rack up 103 steals in his first two full-season campaigns. His quickness is as impressive as his pure speed, and they both allow him to get out of the box well and create hits from both sides of the plate. Solid bat-to-ball skills with a knack for making line-drive contact fuel Brujan's projection as a plus hitter, and he has long demonstrated that he can control the strike zone. He drives the ball more consistently while showing some sneaky pop from the left side of the plate -- all 13 of his home runs in 2018-19 were against righties -- while his right-handed stroke is geared toward putting the ball in play to utilize his wheels. Those wheels also make Brujan a rangy defender on the infield. He profiles as a near plus defender as a second baseman and can hold his own at shortstop even though his solid arm strength is stretched thin there. The Rays also began trying him out in the outfield during Spring Training, giving him starts in center and right field, with the idea of potentially making him an even more versatile, Ketel Marte-type up-the-middle player. He profiles better at the keystone long term and looks the part of a future top-of-the-order hitter with his blend of hitting ability, on-base skills and speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fairchild's intriguing mix of power and speed prompted the Reds to take him in the second round of the 2017 Draft and pay him full slot value. He had a solid, albeit unspectacular first full season of pro ball, playing across two levels of Class A ball, but then jumped up the rankings after making good strides at the plate and reaching Double-A in 2019. The D-backs were able to acquire him at the Trade Deadline in 2020 in the Archie Bradley deal and, he made his Major League debut with the club on July 6, 2021. Fairchild doesn't have a big flashy set of tools, but he does everything well. He got off to a slow start in 2019 as he made adjustments to his swing that allowed him to recognize pitches sooner and get to the ball quicker. Once he found his swing consistency, it clearly started clicking for him, with an .824 OPS after his promotion in the second half of the season. He controls the strike zone well, hits the ball hard and has above-average speed. Fairchild has a lot of attributes the D-backs value -- strike zone judgement, versatility and good instincts for the game. He can play all three outfield positions and his floor is that of a backup outfielder, but he could grow into more. He spent the winter hitting almost every day with fellow prospect Corbin Carroll. D-backs manager Torey Lovullo values players he can trust and Fairchild is that type of player -- you know what you're going to get from him every game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox signed Burger for $3.7 million as the 11th overall pick in 2017, making him the first Missouri State position player ever selected in the first round and envisioning that his power would get him to Chicago quickly. Instead, he ruptured his left Achilles tendon running out a ground ball in February 2018, tore it again during rehab three months later and severely bruised his left heel in 2019. After losing those two seasons to injury and 2020 to the pandemic shutdown, he returned last year to bash 18 homers in 82 Triple-A games and go deep once during his 15-game big league debut. Burger's significant strength and solid bat speed create plenty of raw power from the right side of the plate, though he'd be able to tap into more of it if he could shed a propensity for hitting balls on the ground that has marked his brief pro career. He does make a lot of hard contact, as evidenced by his average exit velocity of 98 mph and maximum of 115 mph during his stint with the White Sox, and he uses the entire field. He was more aggressive last year than he was in college or during his pro debut, and he may need a more disciplined approach to succeed against big leaguers. Though he's a stocky 230-pounder and can look awkward at times, Burger is deceptively athletic and got into better shape while recovering from his leg injuries. He can flash average speed out of the batter's box, but he doesn't make much happen on the bases. While his range might be a bit limited at third base, he has soft hands and solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first Missouri State position player taken in the first round, Burger has had a star-crossed pro career since signing for $3.7 million as the 11th overall choice in 2017. After a modest debut that summer, he didn't play in an official pro game the next three years after rupturing his left Achilles tendon running out a grounder in February 2018, tearing it again during rehab three months later and severely bruising his left heel in 2019. He did see action last year in the CarShield Collegiate League and at Chicago's alternate site and instructional league program. Added to the 40-man roster in November, Burger generates at least plus raw power with strength and solid bat speed. He made hard contact and drove the ball to all fields while training at the alt site and instructs in 2020. He evokes comparisons to Todd Frazier because he's a stocky right-handed hitter with some arm bar in his swing, though he manages the strike zone better and makes more consistent contact than the two-time All-Star. Burger can look awkward at times, but the White Sox believe he has recaptured most or all of the deceptive athleticism he had before he tore his Achilles. Before he got hurt, he displayed average speed out of the batter's box and was a little quicker once he got going. He has the soft hands, solid arm and enough range to stick at third base, though it won't be easy to displace Yoan Moncada from the hot corner in Chicago.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jackson performed better as an outfielder than a pitcher at Utah before requiring Tommy John surgery that wiped out his 2017 season. The Dodgers still drafted him in the 12th round and signed him for an over-slot $247,500 that June, brought him along slowly for a year and have seen him make rapid progress since. He led their system in strikeout rate (11.1 per nine innings) in 2019, spent 2020 at the club's alternate site and instructional league program, then rocketed from Double-A to Los Angeles last year. Jackson has more athleticism and arm speed than most pitchers and can reach 98 mph with a four-seam fastball with late finish, though he operated more in the low 90s in 2021. His best offering for much of last season was a plus mid-80s changeup that drops off at the plate. He has replaced a soft downer curveball with a mid-80s slider that has more power than bite in his efforts to find a reliable breaking ball, and he might turn to more of a cutter in the future. Raw on the mound when he began his pro career, Jackson has worked hard to develop a more compact and consistent delivery. It has paid off with better control, as he went from averaging 5.0 walks per nine innings during his first two seasons in the Minors to 2.8 in his third. He could be a useful starter if he regains some velocity and refines a third pitch, and more of a multi-inning reliever if he can't.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jackson had more success in college at Utah as an outfielder than he did on the mound, posting a 6.53 ERA in brief action over two seasons before having Tommy John surgery that sidelined him for all of 2017. The Dodgers still drafted him in the 12th round and signed him for an over-slot $247,500 that June, then didn't have him make his pro debut until May 2018. He led the system in strikeout rate (11.1 per nine innings) in 2019, then jumped on the 40-man roster last November after seeing time at Los Angeles' alternate site and instructional league program. More athletic than most pitchers, Jackson has a quick arm that generates 92-96 mph fastballs that top out at 98 with some late finish. He presently shows more feel for his changeup than he does for spinning the ball, and his low-80s changeup is a plus offering with some sink. His 78-82 mph curveball has its moments and he has developed a mid-80s slider/cutter since turning pro. Still raw on the mound at the start of his pro career, Jackson has worked to develop a more steamlined and consistent delivery. After averaging 5.0 walks per nine innings during his first two pro seasons, he's doing a much better job of attacking hitters and providing strikes in 2021. He has erased questions about whether he can remain a starter and drew a lot of interest from other clubs at the Trade Deadline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of several left-handers who debuted in Baltimore in 2021, Lowther made the jump without Triple-A experience, then spent the summer bouncing between Norfolk and the big league club to mixed results. It was a bumpy debut for the burly southpaw, who rose quickly through the Orioles system after they made him a second-round selection out of Xavier in the 2017 Draft. But he finished strong, using his first extended look to post three strong starts in September. Lowther enters 2022 in competition for a back-end rotation job in Baltimore. To claim it, it’ll be key for Lowther to miss bats, which he showed a talent for in the Minors on the strength of his pitchability and high-spin fastball. Lowther led the Eastern League in strikeouts and finished second in ERA in 2019. After battling an oblique injury in 2020, he compiled 30 punchouts in 29 2/3 big league frames despite considerable hard contact. Lowther relies more on deception than pure stuff, using big extension and a low release point to augment his low-90s fastball and three offspeed pitches. The fastball is his main weapon, but it was crushed by big league hitters last summer. Lowther also features an above-average spike curve, a useful changeup and a developing slider. He is a polished strike-thrower who draws high marks for his competitiveness and makeup, with the size, frame and skills to suggest a durable mid-rotation-starter ceiling. Whether Lowther gets there probably depends on how well he can balance his pitch mix, become less predictable and get big league hitters off his fastball more effectively. He should get plenty of opportunity in 2022, either as a starter or in a swingman role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles’ second-round pick in 2017 out of Xavier, Lowther made a name for himself as a strikeout artist in the Big East Conference and hasn’t stopped missing bats since entering pro ball. The burly left-hander has risen quickly through the O’s system on the strength of his pitchability and ultra high-spin fastball, which helped him lead the Eastern League in strikeouts and finish second in ERA in 2019. He was slowed by an oblique injury in 2020, but not enough for the O’s to rethink protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft last November. Lowther doesn’t have dominant pure stuff, instead relying on a combination of deception and his signature heater, which only regularly registers between 87-91 mph but can click slightly higher at times. What it does do is play up due to Lowther’s low release point and big extension, which gives the heater an “invisible” element he uses to get swings and misses both in and above the strike zone. He pairs it with an above-average spike curve and serviceable changeup, and has worked to incorporate a slider into his arsenal. Lowther is considered a polished strike-thrower who draws positive reviews for his competitiveness and makeup. His size, frame and skills suggest a durable back-end starter at the highest level, though Lowther has a chance to surpass those projections as well. His first chance could come in 2021 if Lowther shows well at Triple-A to begin the year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Deichmann had some of the best power in the 2014 high school class, but a so-so senior season and signability concerns left him undrafted and headed to Louisiana State. After barely playing as a freshman, he slugged 30 homers over the next two seasons and went to the Athletics in the second round of the 2017 Draft. He broke the hamate bone in his left hand during his first full season and hurt his right shoulder diving for a flyball in his second, but he finally stayed healthy in 2021 before joining the Cubs along with righty pitching prospect Daniel Palencia in a July trade for Andrew Chafin. Deichmann's best attribute is his considerable raw power from the left side of the plate, which he generates with bat speed and strength. After batting .232 in his first three years as a pro and leading the Arizona Fall League with nine homers in 23 games after the 2019 season, he has employed a more selective approach in Triple-A this year. He's making more contact and drawing more walks but also homered just four times in 60 games before the deal, and he's no longer clearly a power-over-hit guy. Though he possesses fringy speed, Deichmann has good instincts on the bases and will swipe bags if the defense forgets about him. An infielder in his first two college seasons, he has developed into an average defender on the outfield corners. His solid arm strength plays well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Reds are no strangers to being aggressive on the international market, particularly when Cuban players become available. They jumped at the chance to sign Gutierrez, who was No. 4 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International Prospects list when he got $4.75 million from the Reds to sign. After impressing early with his bullpen sessions and showing initial polish similar to fellow Cuban Raisel Iglesias, the right-hander appeared to get away from his strengths during a rocky first pro season in 2017. The 2018 season was a nice step forward for Gutierrez. He did a good job of finding his delivery, which enabled him to stay on top of the ball better and created a better angle. As a result, he had better action on his pitches and a more consistent break on his curveball, which lost its sharpness when he would get under or on the side of the ball. But he wasn't able to repeat that success in 2019. An improved tempo also increased Gutierrez's ability to pound the strike zone in 2018, though his walk rate spiked the following season.. With a three-pitch mix that gives him a good chance to start, Gutierrez's fastball touches as high as 97-98 mph. If he can get back to what led to his success in '18 and continues to refine his pitches, he might not be far from reaching the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers signed Alexy for a well-over-slot $597,500 as an 11th-rounder in 2016, then shipped him along with Willie Calhoun and infield prospect Brendon Davis to get Yu Darvish from the Rangers a year later. After making just five starts in 2019 because of a lat injury and losing 2020 to the pandemic shutdown, he came back and moved from Double-A to the big leagues last year. He won three of his four starts with Texas, logging a 2.79 ERA, though he was shelled in his lone relief appearance.
