As a starter, Alexy works with a 92-95 mph four-seam fastball that reaches 97 with good carry in the strike zone. He flashed a plus curveball with power and depth in the past, but it parked more in the mid-70s and he didn't use it as much in 2021. He has started using a tight low-80s slider and owns a mid-80s changeup with modest life, and both are fringy offerings. Alexy never has been a prolific strike-thrower and issued as many walks as he had strikeouts (17) in his 23 innings in the Majors. He sat at 97 mph and touched 100 with his fastball in short stints during instructional league in 2020, and he might be better suited as a two-pitcher reliever than a starter. For now, he'll contend for a rotation job in Texas.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers signed Alexy for a well-over-slot $597,500 as an 11th-rounder out of a Pennsylvania high school in 2016, then traded him along with Willie Calhoun and infield prospect Brendon Davis to Texas for Yu Darvish a year later. He was progressing nicely until getting shut down with a lat injury five starts into the 2019 season, and his only action since has come at instructional league in each of the last two falls. He showcased maybe the best pure stuff at Rangers instructs in 2020, prompting his addition to the 40-man roster. When last seen as a starter in early 2019, Alexy dealt with a 92-95 mph four-seam fastball that topped out at 97, but in shorter instructional league stints he has parked at 97 and touched 100. He has high spin rates on both his heater and his curveball, which combines power with legitimate 12-6 break. His changeup lacks the upside of his other two offerings but can be an average pitch at times. Though Alexy has a big frame and has quieted his delivery since turning pro, he may be better suited for the bullpen than the rotation. In addition to refining his changeup, he also needs to improve his control and command to remain a starter. He could move very quickly as a reliever and become a high-leverage option if he can carry his instructs stuff into the regular season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player as a Virginia high schooler, Lee went to the Royals in the third round in 2016 and became strictly a position player. Pre-pandemic, he was moved aggressively up the system due to his speed (stealing as many as 53 bags at Double-A in 2019) and strong on-base skills. After Lee was added to the 40-man roster in November 2020, Kansas City traded him three months later to the Mets as part of a three-team deal that brought in Andrew Benintendi from the Red Sox. Lee was a statistical Triple-A standout in Syracuse, leading full-season qualifiers with a .451 OBP while finishing with 14 homers and a .951 OPS in 23 games. He was used for an 11-game Major League cameo in May but went 1-for-18 with 13 strikeouts. As his 18.3 percent walk rate indicated in 2021, Lee can be patient at the plate, but that borders too much on passivity. He did get more aggressive as the season wore on and will need that to continue to make the most of his offensive potential. The left-handed slugger has always shown above-average raw power. A high ground-ball rate blunts that slugging potential, and while some gains were made in that department last year, he still hit the ball on the ground 51.5 percent of the time. Lee’s above-average speed and plus arm (dating back to his pitching days) give him defensive assets, and he profiles best in right field, where he spent most of last season. The 5-foot-10 prospect isn’t far from his floor as a bench outfield bat, and he’ll need to continue his improvements on aggression and launch angle to have a chance at being a Major League fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lee was a third-round pick by the Royals in 2016 after a stellar two-way showing out of a Virginia high school. Kansas City kept him as a position player only and moved Lee aggressively up the chain, including an assignment to Double-A in 2019 when he opened the season at just 20 years old. Lee held his own with a 112 wRC+ in that campaign but stood out most for his 53 stolen bases, which ranked second in the entire Minors behind only then-fellow Royal Nick Heath’s 60. Lee was added to the 40-man last November and was traded to the Mets three months later in a three-team involving the Red Sox and Andrew Benintendi. Lee is no stranger to two of three true outcomes, having struck out in 28.2 percent and walked in 11.9 percent of his plate appearances at Double-A. That balances out the offensive profile. He loses a few points as well for hitting the ball primarily on the ground with a 59.3 percent ground-ball rate that led the Texas League in 2019. That keeps him from playing into what could be above-average power. As such, elevation was a key focus during his time at the Royals’ alternate training site last year, and it deserves watching whether he can reverse that trend when he returns to play. The other tools are the standouts of the profile right now. Lee showed in 2019 that he can steal bags by the dozens, and that speed gives him a good shot at sticking in center. The arm is even better than the glove and is a true plus tool, so if some route-running issues push him to a corner, he can still help any club defensively. The Mets inserted themselves into the Kansas City-Boston trade in order to pick up Lee, so they were obvious admirers of the outfielder’s skill set. However after a few games with the Major League club in the first half of 2021, Lee has been overlooked while positing an impressive on-base percentage and overall OPS at Triple-A Syracuse. This remains his age-23 season, and after establishing a little more consistency at Triple-A, he could still very well carve out a role as a fourth outfielder in the Majors down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones both started and relieved at Washington State, with very mixed results, but the Phillies felt his size, raw stuff and left-handedness was worth a flier in the 18th round of the 2017 Draft. After pitching out of the pen during his pro debut that summer, Jones had two fairly successful seasons starting, touching Triple-A in 2019. After being added to the 40-man roster in 2020, he moved back to a relief role in 2021 and made his big league debut before a very strong turn in the Arizona Fall League. The 6-foot-5 lefty has the stuff to get big league hitters out; it’s just a question of landing that stuff in the strike zone enough to do so. His fastball easily touches 95-96 mph and averaged around 94 in 2021 and it often has cutting action to it, leading to solid groundball ratios throughout his career. He’s thrown both a curve and slider in the past, but he focused on the slider especially in the AFL with good results, with the chance for it to be a true out pitch. He’s also had a changeup in his repertoire, but he may not need it as a reliever. That’s the role he’s going to have from now on as his walk rate spiked in 2021. He threw better strikes in the AFL, though he still walked 6.1 per nine in a small sample. With his swing-and-miss stuff (11.3 K/9 in his career in the Minors), he doesn’t need pinpoint command to play a role in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2021 The 2017 Draft has already produced some late-round big leaguers, like Cardinals’ 27th-rounder Kodi Whitley and Angels 30th-rounder Jeremy Beasley, a list that also includes Phillies’ 10th-rounder Connor Brogdon. Jones, a Phillies flier taken in the 18th round that June, is about ready to join them after a 2019 season that saw him pitch his way to Triple-A and a 2020 that included time at the Phillies’ alternate training site and a spot on the 40-man roster. Jones typically uses three pitches, all of which can get outs. It starts with a fastball that’s up to 96 mph with natural cut to it, a pitch that has gotten a groundball percentage well over 50 percent. He misses bats, 12 of them per nine innings in 2019, with a plus curve and a slider that’s above-average. He does have a below-average changeup, but he doesn’t throw it much at this point. That, combined with command issues, he’s walked 4.6 per nine innings, means the 6-foot-5 lefty’s future is very likely in a bullpen. The good news is the combination of that lively fastball and his array of breaking stuff could allow him to play a significant role if he can find the strike zone a bit more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers selected the Puerto Rican backstop out of Carlos Beltran Baseball Academy with the 75th overall pick in 2016. His breakout campaign came in 2019, when he was named Carolina League MVP after hitting .270/.323/.473 with 19 homers for High-A Carolina. He followed that up with a strong showing at the alternate training site a year later. Milwaukee added Feliciano to its 40-man roster in November 2020, but 2021 was a rough season for him. Feliciano, who appeared in one Major League game in May, missed nearly two months with a right shoulder impingement and hit just .210/.246/.314 (46 wRC+) over 114 plate appearances with Triple-A Nashville. A trip to the Arizona Fall League (.318/.348/.432) helped end the year on a brighter note. Ever since he was drafted, Feliciano has used his bat to raise his prospect profile. He utilizes a compact right-handed swing to drive the ball with authority, and he has the above-average raw power to threaten for 15-20 homers over a full Major League season. Among reasons for optimism in 2021, his strikeout rate did drop a touch at Triple-A, but he isn’t the most cautious swinger with just a 3.5 percent walk rate. Feliciano’s shoulder troubles weren’t a first last season -- he also needed arthroscopic surgery in the 2018-19 offseason -- and it’s becoming a concern whether his injury history will affect his ability to stay behind the plate. At his best, he’s an agile catcher with above-average arm strength, and the Brewers are optimistic he can get back to that level. He needs consistent reps to find that form, and those should come in his second 40-man season in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers have not hit big drafting and developing catchers. The last home-grown catcher to represent them at an All-Star Game was Jonathan Lucroy in 2014 and ‘16. Before that, it was Dave Nilsson in 1999, but Nilsson was already an established pro in Australia before he signed with the Brewers. But now the Brewers have a relatively deep crop of backstops led by Feliciano, the No. 75 overall pick in the 2016 Draft. After nagging injuries ruined his 2018, including a shoulder flare-up in the Arizona Fall League that required arthroscopic surgery in the offseason, Feliciano got back on track during a breakout 2019 at the advanced Class A level; he was Carolina League MVP after leading the circuit in home runs (19), RBIs (81), slugging (.477) and total bases (210) at age 20, and he was added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. Feliciano’s strength is his bat. His clean and compact right-handed swing yields consistently hard contact as well as above-average game power that plays from the left-center gap to the right-field line. There is great potential for more if Feliciano can bring down his 28.8 percent strikeout rate from 2019 and cut down one of the Minors’ highest swinging-strike rates (19.7 percent). Defensively, Feliciano has enough tools to be a catcher long-term, particularly his arm. He’ll be a bat-first guy, but should be able to stick behind the plate at the highest level. A shoulder impingement has limited both his production and game experience in 2021, but the Brewers are still believers that Feliciano can be a productive catcher when fully healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bettinger was more of a reliever than a starter during his four years at the University of Virginia, and he worked exclusively out of the bullpen as a senior in 2017. The Brewers still liked this strike-throwing ability enough to select him in the 10th round and transition him into a starting role. Early results were inconsistent until Bettinger’s breakout season for Double-A Biloxi in 2019, when he finished second in the Southern League with 1.07 WHIP and 157 strikeouts in 146 1/3 innings. The Brewers added the former Cavalier to the 40-man roster in November 2020, and he was solid at Triple-A Nashville last year with a 4.75 ERA, 98 strikeouts and 26 walks in 96 2/3 innings. He made four appearances (one start) for the Brewers in the first half of the 2021 season but is still seeking consistent Major League success. The Virginia native doesn’t boast a true plus pitch as part of his arsenal, but he makes the most of a deep pitch mix. His heater averaged 91.5 mph in the Majors last season, and he’s typically right around that 89-92 mph velocity range. The pitch plays up with some deception out of Bettinger’s 6-foot-2 frame, aided by decent extension toward home plate. He adds in a mid-70s curveball with good break and an upper-80s cutter that works well off the fastball and can be effective against either hitters on either side of the plate. A low-80s changeup remains below average. Bettinger, who turns 27 in July, is yet to walk more than 7 percent of his batters faced at any full-season level, including Triple-A and the Majors, where his BB rates were below 6.3 percent. He will still get starting looks because of that control, but he might be most effective soon as a long reliever for Milwaukee.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round pick in 2017 who signed for $10,000 after a strong senior season as a long reliever at Virginia, Bettinger was moved into a starting role upon entering pro ball and has surged to the brink of the big leagues thanks to his penchant for throwing strikes. He struggled in his first full season in ‘18, recording a 5.45 ERA between the two Class A levels, but the Brewers still decided to push the right-hander up to Double-A Biloxi in 2019. After Bettinger got off to another shaky start, he pitched increasingly well and showed more velocity as the season unfolded, putting him on the organization’s prospect map. He finished among Southern League leaders in starts (T1st, 26), strikeouts (2nd, 157), WHIP (2nd, 1.07), innings (2nd, 146 1/3), opponent average (4th, .223) and ERA (6th, 3.44). The Brewers added Bettinger to the 40-man roster in November 2020 and president of baseball operations David Stearns predicted he would contribute at the big league level in 2021. That proved prescient when Bettinger made his Major League debut back in May. Though Bettinger has always featured some deception with crossfire action in his delivery, he found a new level of effectiveness in Double-A thanks an uptick in velocity. With Biloxi, the right-hander was touching 94-95 mph with his fastball early in games and sitting in the low 90s consistently, and that continued in 2020 at the Brewers’ alternate training site. He throws two different breaking balls -- a curveball that flashes above average and a slider with cutter-like action that plays nicely off his fastball. A changeup gives Bettinger a usable fourth pitch. He knows how to mix his pitches and throws a lot of strikes, showing above-average control and solid command. Bettinger could become a back-end starter, though most evaluators believe he will end up pitching as a multi-inning long reliever. That’s a valuable role for a Brewers team known for using the full 40-man roster and blending the lines between starters and relievers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Stoneman Douglas High School in Florida, Welker was a fourth-round pick back in 2016 and the Rockies went about $300,000 over slot to sign the infielder. He didn’t hit below .329 over his first three summers of pro ball, establishing self as one of the better pure hitters in the Minors. A shoulder injury didn’t help him with a move to Double-A in 2019, though he did earn a spot on the 40-man roster following the shortened 2020 season. He served an 80-game suspension in 2021 for Dehydrochlormethyltestosterone (DHCMT), a performance-enhancing substance, returning late and making his big league debut last September. At his best, Welker still shows off the skills of a very gifted hitter. Even when he’s struggled, he’s shown a willingness to work counts and draw walks, keeping his strikeout rate relatively low. He has a knack for contact and can drive the ball to all fields, showing an aptitude for making adjustments during an at-bat. There is raw power to tap into, but he’s struggled when he’s tried to sell out for power and would be better suited just letting it come naturally from his right-handed swing. While Welker has solid hands and a strong arm that work at third, his lack of speed might mean first base is a better home long-term. Either corner puts pressure on his bat and he’ll have to be more consistently productive to profile well as a regular at either corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 35 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 The best player to come out of Stoneman Douglas High School to date has been Anthony Rizzo, who was a sixth-round pick in the 2007 Draft. Thirteen years later, Jesus Luzardo was a third-round pick and the most recent alum to make the big leagues. Welker was part of that same 2016 Draft, going a round later than his lefty teammate. For much of his Minor League career, he lived up to his offensive potential, hitting .337 over his first two-plus years of pro ball. He hit a wall, and dealt with a shoulder injury, after a hot start in Double-A in 2019, then struggled in the Arizona Fall League. Still believing in his bat, the Rockies added him to the 40-man roster following the 2020 season, though Walker was given an 80-game suspension after testing positive for Dehydrochlormethyltestosterone (DHCMT), a performance-enhancing substance, in May. Still just 23 years old for the 2021 season, there’s plenty of time for Welker to rediscover the swing and approach that made him look like a future plus hitter from the right side of the plate. When he’s in sync, he combines his knowledge of the strike zone with his ability to drive the ball to all fields. He’s willing to draw walks and doesn’t strike out a ton, even when he struggled in 2019. He gets into trouble when he gets out of his game plan and tries to hit for power, rather than let it come naturally. While Welker doesn’t run well, he has the tools to play a solid third base, with good hands and enough arm for the hot corner. He started seeing more time at first base in 2019 because of his lack of speed and, of course, Nolan Arenado. The latter is gone, but Welker should still get reps at both infield corners, once he returns from his suspension.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $320,000 at the start of a 2016-17 international signing period that saw the Padres spend more than $40 million on the international market, Marcano hit .366 in his first taste of pro ball in the United States in 2018. He hit well in full-season ball in 2019, then jumped from Low-A that season to the big leagues to start the 2021 season. That may have been too tall of an order to fill, and Marcano struggled, though he righted the ship a bit back in Triple-A when he was sent to the Pirates in the deal for Adam Frazier at last year’s Trade Deadline. Contact has, and always will be, the name of Marcano’s game. He carries a strikeout rate of under 10 percent in his Minor League career into the 2022 season and has drawn more walks (152) than strikeouts (135). His knowledge of the strike zone is elite and his short swing from the left side can spray line drives to all fields. There isn’t much power to speak of and it’s unclear how much he’ll drive the ball, though he’ll still be just 22 years old for nearly all of the 2022 season. Marcano’s above-average speed helps him defensively and he’s shown the ability to play shortstop, with good hands. His arm fits better at second and he played all four infield spots as well the two corner outfield positions in 2021, with an eye towards a future as a super-utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres' 2016-17 international spree garnered attention for the money spent, but some of the best pieces from that class weren't big-bonus signings at all. Marcano is a perfect example. Named for the town of Tucupita, where he's from in Venezuela, Marcano signed for $320,000. He’s already shown some of the most advanced knowledge of the strike zone in the organization. Marcano batted .366/.450/.438 at the lower levels in his first full season, while striking out 16 times and walking 30. At Class A Fort Wayne in 2019, he continued to hit -- but not for much power -- and that continued in 2021 as he jumped to Triple-A and made his big league debut before being included as the top prospect in the deal that sent Adam Frazier to San Diego Marcano is a slender and wiry middle-infield type, who still needs to fill out his 6-foot frame. As he has, he has grown into a bit of pop. But his contact skills are the defining characteristic. Marcano's short left-handed stroke produces line drives all over the field. At times, his hand-eye coordination is almost too good, and he’d be better served being more selective within the strike zone, swinging at pitches he can do damage with. Still, Marcano can differentiate balls from strikes as well as anyone, and he complements his excellent plate approach with above-average speed. Defensively, some feel Marcano can remain at shortstop, and he's got the quick hands necessary to be a solid defender. His arm projects as merely average, and that could force a move to second base. But his plate skills could develop into him being a serious on-base threat as a bat-first middle infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Newcastle, Australia, Wells has a chance to become the third Orioles player to hail from Down Under after signing for $300,000 in August 2015. He’s risen steadily through their system since, his only hiccup coming due to no fault of his own in 2020, which he spent almost entirely in Australia due to the coronavirus pandemic. Wells was the organization’s Minor League Pitcher of the Year in 2017, a SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game selection in 2018, and went 8-6 with a 2.95 ERA and 1.07 WHIP at Double-A Bowie in 2019 before turning heads with a stellar showing in the Arizona Fall League. The Orioles added Wells to the 40-man roster in November, hinting at a potential 2021 debut. With three quality pitches and plus control, Wells succeeds despite a fastball that used to live in the upper 80s, though it consistently clocked in at 90-91 mph late in ’19. His above-average changeup is an equalizer and he pairs it with an improving 12-to-6 curveball that helps keep hitters off balance. Both play up due to Wells’ ability to throw them for strikes to both sides of the plate, and he’s added a serviceable slider to use predominatly against right-handed hitters. Plus-command allows Wells to limit free passes and keep the ball in the ballpark; he’s averaged 1.4 walks-per-nine in over 475 career innings and allowed just 10 homers across 153 innings in 2019. While he will never miss many bats, Wells’ ability to spot three distinct pitches gives him a high floor that should translate to a back-end starter or swingman at the very least. Some believe he has a chance to exceed those projections and potentially become a mid-rotation starter in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During his college days, Dohy lived up to the “have left arm, will travel” adage, attending three schools in three years. The Phillies took Dohy, a starter at Division II Cal Poly in 2017, in the 16th round in that June’s Draft and immediately put him in the bullpen with good results. The lefty reliever made it to Double-A in his first full season and up to Triple-A in 2019, though he didn’t pitch particularly well there. Though he didn’t pitch at the alternate training site or in instructional league play, the Phillies still decided to protect his left arm on the 40-man roster this past offseason. The 6-foot-2 lefty brings an intriguing combination of deception and stuff to a future big league bullpen. There’s funk in his delivery, making it hard for hitters to pick the ball up, contributing to his 13.8 strikeout per nine rate in his career heading into 2021. He’s typically topped out in the mid-90s, but was up to 98-99 mph on Rapsodo during offseason workouts. It remains to be seen if those are real velocity gains. He has one of the best changeups in the system, with good separation from his fastball and thrown with excellent deception. At times, his slider is a wipeout pitch, though it’s less consistent. Dohy has shown the ability to miss bats with all three pitches. What he hasn’t been able to do is find the strike zone consistently enough. He’s walked 7.0 batters per nine innings, which will keep him from having any lasting impact in the big leagues. If he can find the strike zone a bit more frequently, his stuff is more than good enough to be a reliever at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick by the Braves in the 2016 MLB Draft out of the Texas high school ranks, Muller progressed through a farm system that was stacked with pitching talent and earned his first call to the big leagues in 2021. After another short stint in the Majors in ‘22 as the organization’s top-rated prospect, he was one of five players dealt to the A’s in a three-team deal that sent Sean Murphy to Atlanta in December. Muller brings a strong four-pitch mix that includes a fastball that consistently hits 95-97 mph with good carry. His two breaking pitches -- a low-80s curveball and recently added power slider that averages around 87 mph -- have both flashed plus and can generate plenty of swing-and-miss. He’s also developed a fourth offering in a changeup that comes in handy when he lacks a feel for his breaking stuff, though he uses it much less frequently than his other three pitches. Muller’s walk rate improved considerably at Triple-A in 2022, and he often succeeded in limiting damage whenever he found himself in a tough spot. While his path to a starting role was going to be difficult in Atlanta’s loaded rotation, the move to Oakland should allow him plenty of opportunity to build on that early Major League experience and establish himself as a starter with the A’s.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2016, the Braves took four high-school pitchers with their first six picks. While first-rounder Ian Anderson has spent considerable time in the big leagues, the Braves had traded two others from that class, Joey Wentz and Bryse Wilson, previously. Muller, the fourth-round pick, made his Major League debut in 2021, touched the big leagues again in 2022 while making strides on his overall pitchability in the Minors. He then became the third member of this quartet to get dealt, going to the A’s in the three-team deal that brought Sean Murphy to Atlanta in December. The 6-foot-7 southpaw now has four pitches in his arsenal. It starts with a fastball that averaged 93.5 mph in Triple-A and the big leagues in 2021, consistently reaching 95-97. It's a pitch that plays well up in the zone with high spin rates and good carry. He has two distinct breaking pitches and he leaned on his newer power slider more in 2021, a pitch that flashed plus, averaging almost 87 mph and missing a ton of bats. He still threw his low-80s curve and generated swings-and-misses with it, though he threw it for strikes less consistently. His changeup is definitely his fourth offering, one he doesn’t use frequently, but did help him at times when he lost feel for his breaking stuff. Muller is never going to have pinpoint control, but his walk rate dropped considerably in 2022 in Triple-A, and he did a good job of limiting damage. The advancement of that slider is a big reason why he had early success in the big leagues and if he can continue to make strides in finding the strike zone, he has more than enough stuff to be a Major League starter, something he should get to do in Oakland.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Two other high school pitchers taken by the Braves in the 2016 Draft had already made it to the big leagues through the 2020 season. Fourth-rounder Bryse Wilson was the first to get there and Ian Anderson, the No. 3 overall pick, made a huge contribution in the regular and postseason in 2020. Muller, a lefty taken from the Texas prep ranks who got an above-slot deal to sign in the second round, doesn’t look like he’s too far behind after dominating Double-A hitters in 2019 and throwing well enough at the Braves’ alternate training site in 2020 to get added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. Muller started throwing harder back in 2018 and velocity gains have continued since. He was sitting in the upper 90s and touched triple digits during his time at the alternate site in 2020, throwing his four-seamer with a lot of spin and carry to miss bats up in the zone. Already equipped with a curve that can be above-average, Muller added a harder slider last year and it could end up being as good as, if not better than, the curve. He continued to show improvement on his changeup, giving him the chance to have a legitimate four-pitch mix. The one thing that’s held Muller back has been his command -- he walked 5.5 per nine in Double-A in 2019 -- but the big left-hander has worked hard on the consistency of his delivery and was finding the strike zone with some more consistency last summer. If that trend continues, he has more than enough stuff to join Anderson in the Braves rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rondón signed for only $25,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2016 and needed two-and-a-half seasons before jumping to full-season ball. His breakout came in 2019 when he was named Cardinals Minor League Pitcher of the Year, having posted a 2.93 ERA with 159 strikeouts in 160 innings between High-A and Double-A. He moved to Triple-A for his age-23 season and put up more pedestrian numbers (4.58 ERA, 68 strikeouts in 76 2/3 innings), but he did make his Major League debut with a pair of relief outings in June. The 6-foot-1 right-hander averaged 93.1 mph on his heater in those brief MLB looks, and that’s around where his fastball was in the Minors as well. He can touch the mid-90s when needed, and the fastball plays up because of some natural deception and late movement. Rondón pitches a bit backward with much better splits against lefties than righties (.223 average-against vs. .329, respectively, at Triple-A) in part because of a low-80s fading changeup. His slider and curveball can flash average with the former looking slightly better than the latter at this stage, but both have suboptimal spin rates and can hang a bit too much, leading to the punishment from fellow righties. To Rondón’s credit, he did improve his control rates in 2021, dropping it from 8.9 percent in 2019 to 6.5 percent. He also deserves plaudits for working with a four-pitch mix that he can sequence well, keeping hitters off even when the raw stuff doesn’t stand out. His pitchability makes him a potential No. 5 starter, and entering his age-24 season, he isn’t far from reaching that role. A focus on just one breaking ball to go with the fastball-changeup could also work in a bullpen setting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rondon’s career got off to a bit of a slow start after he signed with the Cardinals as an 18-year-old for $25,000 in 2016. The native of the Dominican Republic spent two seasons in Rookie ball before he started to rise up the ranks. Rondon reached full-season ball in the second half of the 2018 campaign and followed up the strong showing with an award-winning 2019. He began the year with Class A Advanced Palm Beach, where he was named a midseason All-Star before being promoted to Double-A Springfield and ultimately named the Cardinals’ Minor League Pitcher of the Year after posting a 2.93 ERA with 159 strikeouts over 160 innings split between the two levels. The 2021 season got off to a rough start as Rondon was hit hard and struggled in his first Triple-A experience, though he did make a couple of scoreless appearances in the Majors. Rondon impressed at the Cardinals’ alternate training site in 2020, facing advanced hitters and showing a good understanding of how to sequence pitches. His delivery creates natural deception, which often helps his fastball play above its velocity. The fastball features late movement and sits in the mid 90s, but can also touch 97 mph on occasion. Rondon can vary the shape of his curveball, a pitch with heavy downward action that reminds some of a slider. He’s also shown an ability to keep hitters off-balance with an average changeup. The right-hander needs to improve his command and control, but he has shown he’s capable of handling a starter’s workload. The 2021 numbers have been a bit of a disappointment, but it’s important to remember he’s still just 23-years-old. Rondon’s ceiling seems to be at the back end of a rotation, though his fastball/curveball combo, paired with his pitchability, could also play well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a breakout campaign as a Louisville sophomore that he followed with a strong performance for the U.S. collegiate national team, Ray solidified his status as a future first-round pick by hitting 15 homers and swiping 44 bags as a junior. The Brewers made him the fifth overall pick that June, and Ray signed for $4.125 million, the largest bonus in club history. Knee surgery delayed the start of Ray's pro debut, and he never looked right upon returning, hitting for neither average nor power while spending the entire season in the High A Carolina League. Challenged with a Double-A Biloxi assignment in 2018, Ray finally looked like the player the Brewers had drafted, hitting 27 home runs and swiping 37 bags en route to honors as the Southern League's Most Outstanding Player. He was slowed early in 2019 by an avulsion fracture in his right hand that he tried to play through all spring before finally requiring a month-long stint on the injured list in May. Ray's power-speed combo is among the best in the Minors. It didn't show in his first full season because Ray struggled to control the strike zone, often chasing pitches well out of the zone with a lengthy swing that produced a Carolina League-high 156 strikeouts. With an emphasis on picking specific pitches to hit in 2018, Ray regained his confidence at the plate and returned to his strengths, showing above-average game power and feel for using the entire field. He still struck out quite a bit and finished second in the Southern League with 176 whiffs, but the overall quality of his contact, as well as the results, were markedly better. A plus runner, Ray's 37 steals were an improvement over the 24 in his pro debut, and he's a candidate to steal 30 bags at the highest level. Ray's wheels also serve him well in center field, where he's an above-average defender with at least average arm strength. Strikeouts will always be a concern with Ray, but his combination of strong game power, speed and defense should ultimately help to offset concerns about his low batting averages. Overall, it's the profile of potential above-average everyday player, with a fourth-outfielder floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peters has posted big power numbers everywhere he has gone in the last three years, starting with setting school records at Western Nevada CC for batting (.419) and homers (16) in 2016, when Los Angeles signed him as a fourth-rounder. He topped the Rookie-level Pioneer League in runs (63), total bases (161) and OPS (1.052) during his pro debut, then encored by winning California League MVP honors and leading the Class A Advanced circuit in extra-base hits (61) and slugging (.514) during his first full season. He followed up in 2018 by pacing all Double-A hitters in homers (29) and the Texas League in extra-base hits (55) and total bases (232). Compared to Jayson Werth for his power and surprising athleticism in a big frame, Peters can knock the ball out of any part of any ballpark thanks to his strength and leverage. His 6-foot-6 build comes with a naturally long right-handed swing that, coupled with his aggressive approach, resulted in a Texas League-worst 192 strikeouts and 34 percent whiff rate in 2018. He went through five different batting stances during the season as he searched for a way to make more contact, and the Dodgers think he'll be able to do that after reworking his stroke during the offseason. Peters displays average speed out of the batter's box and is a step quicker once he gets going, which enabled him to play center field for the majority of his first three pro seasons. He's an average defender up the middle but better suited for a corner. His strong arm fits perfectly in right field, as does his power profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of the New Hampshire prep ranks, McKenna was committed to Liberty before the Orioles drafted him in the fourth round and signed him for slot value. He showed well in his first full season, tallying 42 extra-base hits and 20 steals at Class A Delmarva, and then broke out in earnest in 2018 with a torrid first half in the Class A Advanced Carolina League (.377/.467/.556) before a bump up to Double-A in June. While he didn't fare as well in the Eastern League (.239/.341/.338), McKenna did get back on track in the Arizona Fall League, finishing fifth in the batting race (.344) and second in OPS (1.064). McKenna's quick bat and natural feel for finding the barrel helps him make consistent line-drive contact, and he's become increasingly comfortable hitting to all fields as he's faced better pitching. He's also made strides in refining his approach, demonstrating a combination of patience and aggressiveness that fuels his ability to both hit for average and get on base at a solid clip. While McKenna projects for more gap power than true over-the-fence pop, some evaluators believe he could have seasons with double-digit homers in his prime. McKenna gets out of the box exceptionally well for a right-handed hitter and routinely posts plus-or-better home-to-first run times. That speed also gives him the chance to stay in center field, and he has more than enough arm strength for the position. Overall, McKenna has the ceiling of a center fielder who hits at either the top or bottom of the lineup, and his well-rounded game gives him a realistic fourth-outfielder floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies dipped into their own backyard in the 2014 Draft to find Padlo, a Colorado prep whom the club signed to an above-slot deal after taking him in the fifth round. His time in Colorado’s system was short-lived, however, as the Rays acquired the young third baseman after the 2015 season in the Jake McGee-Corey Dickerson trade. Below-average production and injuries defined Padlo’s first two years with the Rays, but he bounced back with a career-best performance in 2019 as he led the farm in home runs (21) while making a smooth transition from Double- to Triple-A. After the season, the Rays added Padlo to their 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. Padlo generates high-end exit velocities from the right side of the plate by combining bat speed and physical strength with a forceful stroke. His plus raw power plays to his pull-side during games, and he showed that he could get to it more than ever in 2019 during his first taste of the upper Minors. A career .359 OBP across six pro seasons speaks to Padlo’s mature approach and willingness to take a walk, though his patient approach does come paired with strikeout issues that give scouts pause in projecting him as anything more than a below-average hitter. Padlo is a sound defender at the hot corner, with the necessary hands, range and arm strength for the position, and he's also seen time at first base. He runs and moves better than most corner infielders. A better performer against left-handed pitchers (1.240 OPS, 9 HR) than righties (.823, 12 HR) in 2019, Padlo exhibited the type of strong platoon splits that the Rays tend to covet on their big league roster. Though he appears ticketed for such a role in 2020 after being added to the Rays’ 40-man roster in November, a career as a late-blooming, second-division regular isn’t out of the question.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big leaguer and current Yankees third-base coach Phil Nevin, Tyler was selected by the Rockies in the supplemental first round of the 2015 Draft as a high schooler with an advanced bat. He’s largely lived up to those expectations when on the field, notably at hitter-friendly Lancaster in 2018 and the Arizona Fall League in 2019, when he won the circuit’s batting title. Although Nevin missed significant time to injury in ’16 and ’17, and slumped a bit at Double-A in ’19, the Orioles traded for him on the eve of the 2020 Trade Deadline as part of the Mychal Givens deal. He was added to the Rockies' 40-man roster the previous year. Everywhere he’s played, Nevin displayed strong plate discipline and an ability to make hard contact consistently. He shows good raw power but it doesn’t always translate into games, leading many to believe there is more to unlock from his 6-foot-4, 225-pound frame. Even so, Nevin matched his career high with 13 homers at Double-A in ’19 while drawing a ton of walks and keeping his strikeouts down, and showing glimpses of being able to use the whole field. It’s a right-handed swing with more of a hit than power profile at this point, though Nevin could grow into an impact bat if he learns to drive the ball more consistently. That would be important given his position. Nevin has been moved around defensively quite a bit in pro ball, between third and first base and seeing some time in the outfield as well. But he projects best at first base, where he is a solid defender right now with room to get better. Ultimately, though, it’ll be the bat that gets Nevin to the big leagues — and dictates how well he sticks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2018, the southpaw dominated for Crowder (Mo.) Junior College, where he led JuCo pitchers with 156 strikeouts in 74 2/3 innings as a sophomore. The Brewers took Ashby in the fourth round and signed him above slot at $520,000. Ashby kept the K’s coming with 135 in 126 frames between Low-A and High-A in 2019, earning Brewers’ Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors. He was an alternate training site participant in 2020 and jumped to Triple-A in 2021, making only 12 starts before seeing the Majors in June. He traveled back and forth between Milwaukee and Nashville for much of the summer and made two relief appearances for the NL Central champs in their NLDS loss to the Braves. Ashby averaged 96.5 mph on his sinking fastball in the Majors and touched as high as 99 later in the season. The shorter relief stints had something to do with that, but the left-hander’s velocity gains have been clear. He should continue to sit in the mid-90s with the fastball, even if he stays a starter. Ashby’s best pitch easily remains his plus slider. It’s an 82- to 85-mph offering that has hard break and bite and led to 42 percent whiffs in the Majors. An upper-80s diving changeup gives him a third above-average pitch that gets swings-and-misses, while an upper-70s looping curve is mostly kept in his back pocket. What may hold back Ashby from a bona fide starting role in Milwaukee is command. The fastball can be too hittable at times, and he doesn’t always find the strike zone with regularity. The Brewers open 2022 with hopes of keeping Ashby as a starter, and at the least, the fastball-slider-change triad should make for a quality arsenal in any role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Like fellow left-handed prospect Antoine Kelly, Ashby posted eye-popping strikeout numbers in the junior college ranks before the Brewers drafted him in the fourth round in 2018. The nephew of 14-year Major Leaguer Andy Ashby, Aaron was one of the top junior college pitching prospects that year, leading Division I JUCO pitchers in strikeouts (156) and strikeout rate (18.8 per nine innings) at Crowder JC in Missouri. And like Kelly a year later, Ashby immediately performed. He had a 3.50 ERA in 126 innings between the two Class A levels in 2019 and was the Brewers’ Minor League pitcher of the year, finishing among the system leaders with 135 strikeouts (fifth) and a 25.5 percent strikeout rate (third). After taking part at the Brewers’ Alternate Training Site in 2020, he was invited to his first big league Spring Training in 2021 and has been used as a spot starter for the Major League club this summer. Ashby’s calling card is his athleticism and his best pitch is a nasty slider, one of the best breaking balls in the system, which highlights a potential five-pitch mix and produces swing-and-miss. He sets up the slider with a 92-95 mph fastball that has riding life and some armside action. Ashby’s changeup has come along quickly in the pro ranks, giving him a third big league-caliber pitch, and he also shows feel for keeping hitters off-balance with a slow curveball. In 2020, Ashby began incorporating a sinker beginning in Spring Training, and after sending updates to Brewers instructors via video over the summer he made significant strides on the pitch at instructs. An athletic but funky delivery adds a layer of deception to everything Ashby throws and makes him especially tough against lefties, who slashed .183/.292/.229 against him in 2019. And his athleticism plays in helping to disrupt hitters’ timing by adding and subtracting with his pitches and by varying the leg lift and stride in his delivery. If he keeps his complicated delivery in check, Ashby has the arsenal and know-how to be a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mets fans largely know Szapucki’s story at this point. The 2015 fifth-rounder has thrown only 145 Minor League innings in his entire career entering 2021 due to lost time caused by a back issue, a shoulder injury, Tommy John surgery, its subsequent rehab and the coronavirus pandemic. Szapucki showed enough promise along the way to get added to the 40-man roster back in November 2019 and was a participant in New York’s alternate site. He made his Major League debut in June but underwent season-ending ulnar transposition surgery on his left elbow a month later. He is expected to be ready for Spring Training in 2022. Szapucki’s velocity ebbed and flowed during his 2020 time in Brooklyn. There were times, especially early in the program, when he was only sitting in the high 80s. Occasionally, he would touch 93, and the Mets say he’s touching even a bit higher than that this spring. Historically, he has sat around 91-92 after Tommy John, and that seems like a better expectation for the fastball going forward. The curveball is the main show here and what gives him such promise. The breaker features impressive depth and good spin and is tough to handle for both righties and lefties. The changeup is well behind the other two as an offering around 84-85 that features some sink but can get firm at times. It's odd to say that projection for a 24-year-old pitcher is a tough call, but that’s the case for Szapucki simply because of all the lost time. The fastball-curveball combo has been good enough that he should see the Majors in some role. He needs to prove he can handle a starter’s workload though, and that just hasn’t come yet, nor will it until next season at the earliest. Those innings will need to come consistently for Szapucki in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former big leaguer Larry Sheets, his coach at Baltimore's Gilman High, Gavin topped NCAA Division I with 84 RBIs and the Atlantic Coast Conference with 21 homers as a Wake Forest junior in 2017. Signed for an over-slot $2 million as a second-rounder that June, he didn't hit for much power until the second half of the 2019 season in Double-A, where he slugged .478 while doing a better job of using his legs in his swing. Disappointed at not getting invited to Chicago's alternate site last summer, he dedicated himself to improving his athleticism and did so enough to earn playing time in left field during instructional league. Added to the 40-man roster in November, Sheets is doing a better job of tapping into his well above-average raw power and performed well at the plate in his first taste of the big leagues this summer. He stands out more for his strength than his bat speed, and he doesn't have much of a track record of doing damage against premium velocity or against left-handers. While he has a fluid lefty swing and controls the strike zone, he may not be more than a platoon player. Sheets moves decently for a 6-foot-5, 230-pounder but still has well below-average speed. He has worked hard on his defense at first base, where he has soft hands and a stronger arm than most at the position. The White Sox played him more in right field because of team need during his first extended callup, but his lack of range makes him a liability on the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been an unusual path to the big leagues for Lopez. Born in Mexico City, his family sent him to Canada to go to school and play baseball. He went from Alberta to Phoenix for high school and had committed to Arizona State, but when the Reds took him in the 27th round of the 2015 Draft, he decided he wanted to begin his pro career. He was moving one rung at a time before completely bursting on the prospect scene in 2021, hitting .320/.401/.447 across Double- and Triple-A and making his big league debut in late June. Lopez has a magic wand from both sides of the plate, with uncanny contact skills. There hasn’t been much power to speak of, but he can make enough impact to keep pitchers honest. He almost never strikes out, with a 10.9 percent strikeout rate entering 2022, but also shows an ability to draw walks, making him an on-base machine (.375 career OBP in the Minors). A fringy runner, Lopez is never going to wow anyone defensively, but he should be capable enough to move around a bit as a big league utility man. He’s largely played second and third, but also saw some time in left field in the big leagues last year. He could find his way into fairly consistent at-bats in Cincinnati because of his innate hitting ability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kranick was a solid high school prospect from Pennsylvania, one who most figured would be heading to the University of Virginia as the 2016 Draft approached. The Pirates had some bonus pool money left over and a good feel for what Kranick wanted to do, enabling them to go over the $100,000 pick value for a post-10th round pick and giving him $300K to sign in the 11th round. While his first full season was limited by some shoulder fatigue early, he did advance to full-season ball in 2018 and finished strong there. Strong and physical, Kranick has the chance to have three usable pitches he can throw for strikes. He was up to 96 mph with his fastball in 2018, sitting mostly in the 92-93 mph range, using both a four- and two-seamer. What he profiles as in the future will be about how his secondary stuff continues to develop. The 6-foot-3 right-hander entered pro ball with a bit of a hybrid power breaking ball that's become more of a firm slider that flashes above-average. His changeup is still a work in progress. The Pirates have managed Kranick's workload carefully, not sending him to full-season ball in 2018 until late May. He'll continue to start for now, with the gloves coming off as he moves up a rung, with the possibility he ends up as an effective fastball-slider reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Trevor Megill, a Rule 5 Draft pick by the Cubs in 2019, Tylor transferred to the University of Arizona after his freshman year at Loyola Marymount. Though he pitched to mixed results out of the Wildcats’ bullpen as a junior and senior, Megill’s large frame and high-spin fastball suggested that there was more potential to unlock. The Mets were willing to find out, and they signed the senior right-hander for $50,000 after taking him in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft. He rewarded the organization with a promising pro debut, then climbed from Class A Columbia to Double-A Binghamton while averaging 11.6 strikeouts-per-nine in his first full season. At 6-foot-7, 230 pounds, Megill, much like his 6-foot-8, 235-pound brother, is an imposing presence on the mound. Though he averaged a little better than 93 mph and touched 96 with his fastball in 2019, Megill’s heater consistently plays at a higher effective velocity due to its high spin rate and the right-hander’s massive extension toward the plate. He complements his impressive fastball with a hard, mid-80s slider that flashes above-average with a ton of spin, and together the two pitches helped Megill strike out 30.5 percent of the batters he faced in ’19. A changeup gives him a third pitch, albeit a below-average one that will need to be developed. The crossfire in Megill’s delivery helps to enhance his stuff, and hitters seldom look comfortable in the box when facing the towering right-hander. It can detract from his fastball command at times, causing him to miss arm-side with the pitch, but scouts generally like his arm action and ability to generate velocity without too much effort. He will continue to work as a starter for the time being, but could reach the big leagues in a hurry if the Mets move him to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 A switch-hitting shortstop with deep baseball ties in his family, Franco ranked as MLB Pipeline's No. 2 international prospect before signing with Tampa Bay for $3,825,000 at the outset of the 2017-18 period. The Dominican Republic native made the jump stateside for his pro debut last season and promptly established himself as one of baseball's better prospects by winning the Rookie-level Appalachian League's MVP Award at age 17. Playing against considerably older competition, he produced a .351/.418/.587 line with 11 home runs in 61 games and led the circuit with 85 hits and 57 RBIs. Franco's robust production during his pro debut reflects his high offensive ceiling. He consistently impacts the baseball from both sides of the plate, showing a combination of bat speed, strong wrists/hands and elite bat-to-ball skills that leads some scouts to project him as a plus-plus hitter. He should offer above-average over-the-fence power, too, especially from the left side of the plate, from where he hit all but one of his home runs in 2018. Franco's approach, much like his physical tools, is advanced beyond his years, and he receives raves for his ability to recognize spin and control the zone. In the field, Franco has impressed evaluators with his hands, range and actions at shortstop, not to mention the high level of confidence he exudes. He could outgrow the position and shift over to second or possibly third base, though such a move would do little to detract from his All-Star-caliber ceiling. While the Rays have historically employed a patient approach in developing young talent, Franco could be the rare exception, as many have already identified him as the next teenage wunderkind to reach the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prior to his San Diego days, Thompson required Tommy John surgery as a junior in high school and pitched just one inning as a senior. But the Padres liked Thompson enough to make him a third-round pick in 2016, taking him 85th overall, then giving him a $1.75 million bonus. Injuries continued to affect Thompson, who missed time early in his pro career with biceps tendinitis, shoulder inflammation and a leg injury after he was hit with a comebacker. But his stuff didn’t get any less electric. Fully healthy for the first time as a pro, Thompson was a standout during the Padres’ 2020 instructional camp pitching in a relief-only role for the first time. Bigger and stronger after the shutdown, the 6-foot-7 right-hander showcased explosive stuff in an upper-90s fastball and a power slider, missing bats with both. He still has a curveball and changeup at his disposal from his days as a starter, though both secondary offerings are likely to take a back seat in his role. Thompson has a clean delivery despite his injury history, though questions remain about his durability. The Padres were so impressed with Thompson’s performance during instructional league that they added him to the 40-man roster in November rather than risk exposing him to the Rule 5 Draft. They later gave him his Major League debut in 2021, and the Nationals thought enough of Thompson to make him the main prospect piece in a Deadline deal for Daniel Hudson. Still early in his transition to full relief, Thompson could become an eventual bullpen force down the line in Washington.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wong started at shortstop for Houston as a freshman before moving behind the plate for his final two years of college and going to the Dodgers in the third round of the 2017 Draft. He hit 43 homers in his first two full seasons as a pro and exploded for a .349/.393/.604 line in the final six weeks of 2019 following a promotion to Double-A. He came to the Red Sox along with Alex Verdugo and infield prospect Jeter Downs in the Mookie Betts/David Price trade in February 2020, then saw action at Boston's alternate site and instructional league program. Wong used more of a controlled approach in college before the Dodgers encouraged him to turn his right-handed swing loose and look to drive the ball in the air. His wiry strength and the loft in his stroke give him solid raw power that plays to all fields, but his swing also gets long and uphill, which led to a 31 percent strikeout rate in his first three pro seasons. It remains to be seen whether he can succeed against big league pitchers without toning down his aggressiveness. Faster and more athletic than most catchers, Wong showed plus speed in the past but is running closer to average as he spends more time as a backstop. The Red Sox worked with him on his stance behind the plate last summer, and he projects as an average thrower and receiver. He's also capable of playing second and third base, enhancing his value as a backup if he doesn't make it as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vierling had a solid, if unspectacular, career as a three-year starter at Notre Dame, turning a .906 OPS as a junior into a fifth-round selection by the Phillies. The outfielder made it to full-season ball in his debut, spent an inconsistent year in High-A in 2019, then came back after the shutdown with some added strength and a renewed approach, which helped him hit his way to the big leagues, where he had a stirring .324/.364/.479 line in his 71-at-bat debut. A right-handed hitter, Vierling has shown a knack for making a lot of very hard contact, consistently recording very high exit velocities. He’s been more hit over power with a line drive approach and fairly high ground ball rates in his career so far. He started tapping into his raw power a bit more in 2021 and a commitment to elevating the ball could lead to more extra-base authority. The 6-foot-3 Vierling is a better athlete than people may have initially thought, one who runs well and covers a decent amount of ground in the outfield, giving him the chance to play center field. His strong arm would play from a corner and his ability to crush left-handed pitching gives him the chance to at least be a solid platoon, fourth-outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2017, the Royals acquired a pair of pitchers via the Rule 5 Draft, Brad Keller and Burch Smith, with Keller moving into the Royals' rotation and being very consistent there. Kansas City was at it again in '18, getting McWilliams and Chris Ellis. The organization sees some of Keller in McWilliams, a big right-hander originally drafted and signed by the Phillies who has been traded twice prior to his Rule 5 selection. The 6-foot-7 McWilliams has always been intriguing because of his size and power projection. As a starter, he's proven durable, topping 130 innings in his last two seasons of full-season ball, though he struggled a bit with a promotion to Double-A in 2018. He'll throw both a two- and four-seam fastball, the former in the low 90s with sink and the latter climbing into the mid-90s with good running action. The Royals really liked his slider as they were evaluating players for the Rule 5 Draft, and his breaking ball took a step forward last year, enabling him to miss more bats. His changeup continues to be a work in progress. While not wanting to give up on him as a starter because of his durability and ability to fill the strike zone, his best chance of initially pitching in the big leagues will likely be out of the bullpen, a la Keller. There could be an uptick on his stuff if he becomes a fastball-slider reliever with an intimidating presence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Tigers knew that Manning might be a bit of a project when they signed him for slightly above slot value after taking him in the first round of the 2016 Draft. Manning's father, Rich, is a former NBA player, and Matt was a two-sport prep star who could have gone on to play both sports at Loyola-Marymount. After initially being eased into pro ball, Manning's development took flight in 2018 as he pitched his way from Class A to Double-A and led Tigers Minor Leaguers with 154 strikeouts as a 20-year-old. The 6-foot-6 right-hander generates easy velocity, sitting in the low-90s and touching 95-96 mph, and his fastball plays up because he gets so much extension toward the plate. His power curve is a low-80s hammer that has the chance to be a plus pitch in the future, and while his changeup lags behind, he's shown some feel for it, giving him a third at-least-average offering at his disposal. He's capable of missing bats and inducing weak contact with all three pitches, especially his plus fastball-curveball pairing. The Tigers have worked with Manning to clean up his mechanics and it's already led to better fastball command, though, overall, he's still learning to repeat his delivery and arm slot. Manning's athleticism and remaining physical projection should go a long way in helping him with that. He has as much upside as any pitcher in the Tigers' system, with athleticism, size and stuff that point to him becoming at least a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a little tough to figure out exactly who Santillan is as a professional pitcher ever since the Reds took him in the second round of the 2015 Draft. His first two summers of pro ball were rough, but he broke out in the Midwest League in 2017 and pitched his way to Double-A in 2018. His stuff backed up with the move to Double-A in 2019, though he was added to the 40-man roster following that season., Reports from the Reds’ alternate training site in 2020 were that the right-hander was back trending in the right direction. When Santillan was in Double-A, his fastball was sitting 91-92 mph in most starts, partially because of some arm issues and partially because he was trying to do too much on the mound and his mechanics got out of whack. At the alternate site, he looked more like the Santillan of 2018, sitting closer to 93-95 mph and touching 97 mph. His secondary stuff looked sharper as well, especially his slider, which flashes as an out pitch at times. He does have a changeup that has developed slowly and is clearly a third pitch. Santillan is still young enough to right the ship and show he can start at the big league level and the improvements in both his velocity and command at the alternate site are good signs. Though he has a large frame, he’s fairly athletic and the stuff, with control, should come naturally if he stays within himself.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adams was one of the more intriguing high school catchers in the 2014 class given his size and athleticism -- a black belt in karate -- but he opted to honor his commitment to San Diego when selected by the Cubs in the 37th round. A strong performance in the Cape Cod League and big junior campaign eventually landed Adams with the Blue Jays in Round 3 of the 2017 Draft, and the 6-foot-4 backstop got off to a strong start with Vancouver. Adams’ power didn’t show much in High-A Dunedin the next season with just four home runs in 99 games, but he launched 14 between Dunedin and Double-A New Hampshire in ’19. He made his Major League debut with the Jays in May and served as catching depth for Toronto but was dealt to the Nationals for reliever Brad Hand at the Trade Deadline. Adams has a rare physical profile for a catcher at 6-foot-4, 235 pounds, which led many to question his long-term future behind the plate coming out of the Draft. He’s made strides in that area recently and has a strong arm, but there’s room to improve with his receiving. Adams’ IQ and game management are the primary reasons the Blue Jays believed he’ll stick behind the plate, and it'll be interesting to see how he takes to a rebuilding Nats system. The power tool is what’s so appealing about Adams, though. Given his ability to handle the position and hit for legitimate power, it’s easy to envision Adams sticking at the Major League level as a power-hitting backup, but there’s room for him to grow into a more consistent role and he hasn’t yet hit the ceiling of his development. There are reasons why Washington acquired him this July, and he should get every opportunity to stick as part of a new era in the capital.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Kowar and Brady Singer headlined a loaded University of Florida rotation as sophomores during the Gators’ College World Series title in 2017, they were both viewed as first-round Draft picks going into the following spring. The Royals were able to get both in the first round, selecting Singer and Kowar with the Nos. 18 and 33 overall picks, respectively. Both have moved quickly, with Singer making his Major League debut in 2020 while Kowar made progress at the alternate training site and the Royals’ fall instructional program at Kauffman Stadium. Kowar’s fastball-changeup combo is the gem of his arsenal. His mid-80s plus-plus changeup is his signature pitch, generating swings and misses from hitters on both sides of the plate. It has a fading action, and Kowar throws it with superb deception and arm speed, He sits in the 94-97 mph range with his fastball but can dial it up to 98-99 mph with command that’s improved since he was drafted. Kowar’s developing curveball was the focus for him throughout his time at the alternate site in 2020, and that remains the case after he was roughed up a bit in brief Major League looks. The Royals believe the pitch, which he throws with better spin and shape now than he did in college, can be above average and the key that brings Kowar’s game to another level. Kowar gets high marks for holding runners to the bag and fielding his position, along with praise for his competitiveness on the mound. Despite not getting Minor League game action in 2020, Kowar still made significant strides in his development and has gained confidence both on the mound and in the organization with the added experience. He’s been nothing but durable as a Royal, and the final product could be that of a mid-rotation workhorse with a higher ceiling if his curveball continues to improve.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Foley had relatively mundane numbers at Sacred Heart University before an outstanding summer-ball campaign following his junior season caught the attention of the Tigers, who signed him as an undrafted free agent. His rise as a hard-throwing reliever was interrupted by Tommy John surgery in 2018, then the canceled Minor League season in 2020, but a strong Spring Training and impressive stretch at Triple-A Toledo earned him his big league debut in June 2021. Though Foley climbed the Tigers system with a fastball that approached 100 mph, he has settled in with a heavy two-seamer that sits in the mid-90s and produces more ground balls than swings-and-misses. He has to be precise with it to avoid hard contact and launch angle. A mid-80s slider is his main secondary pitch but didn’t throw off Major League hitters much. Whether it’s the slider or a split-change he has tinkered with for a couple years, Foley needs something to disrupt hitters’ timing from the fastball. The Tigers like different looks in their bullpen, and Foley has a chance to provide one if he can round out his arsenal. He’s still relatively young, and his arm hasn’t had much wear and tear since surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sánchez began his career with the Rays, signing for $65,000 back in 2013. He didn’t reach full-season ball until 2019, but that was a breakout season for the left-hander, as he pitched well across both levels of A Ball. Tampa didn’t have room on its 40-man roster that offseason, so they sent him to the Phillies in exchange for Curtis Mead. The Phillies added him to the 40-man, and while he had an uneven year in Triple-A in 2021, he did make his big league debut. Sánchez does have the stuff to start, led by a fastball that averaged around 93 mph between Triple-A and the big leagues in 2021, but touched 97 mph, thrown with a ton of sink that has led to very high groundball rates. His low-80s changeup, thrown with a split grip and sold well, and his sweeping slider, thrown around 83 mph last year, both missed bats at a very high rate. The left-hander has both started and relieved throughout his career, including in 2021, when he started in the Minors and mostly came out of the bullpen during his time in the big leagues. His ultimate role might be determined by his ability to find the strike zone, which regressed last year, pointing to the possibility of greater success in shorter stints as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It took Sanchez three summers in the Dominican Summer League after signing with the Rays for $65,000 back in July 2013 before he made his debut in the United States in 2017. The left-hander didn’t really pop onto radar screens until a strong 2019 across both levels of A ball, split between starting and relieving. Without room on their 40-man roster, the Rays dealt him to the Phillies in November 2019. Added to the 40-man roster, Sanchez spent 2020 at the Phillies’ alternate site. The star of Sanchez’s repertoire is a two-seam fastball that he can crank up to 97 mph. It has incredible run to it, a big reason why he’s posted very high groundball rates over the course of his career. His best secondary pitch might be his changeup, thrown with a split grip, that Sanchez does a nice job of selling and killing spin with, providing big separation from his fastball. His sweeping slider gives him a third at least average offering, and he’s worked on a spike grip for a curveball as well. Command had been a huge obstacle for the 6-foot-5 left-hander, though he took a nice step forward in lowering his walk rate during that 2019 breakout and the Phillies were pleased with the strike-throwing progress he showed last year. While his ultimate role is yet to be determined, he does have the look of a middle reliever, perhaps one who can soak up multiple innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 After two pedestrian seasons at Loyola Marymount, Abbott changed the course of his career by altering the grip on his cut fastball while watching video of Noah Syndergaard. As a junior in 2017, he threw the first perfect game in Lions history, had a 43-inning streak without allowing an earned run and set school records for strikeout rate (11.9 per nine innings) and opponent average (.173). He has breezed through pro ball since the Cubs drafted him in the second round, leading the system with a 2.50 ERA in his first full season in 2018. Abbott relies heavily on his cut fastball, command and deception. His cutter sits in the upper 80s with sharp lateral break that keeps it off barrels. He works from 90-93 mph with a four-seam fastball that's more effective than its velocity because he spots it on the edges of the strike zone. Abbott will flash some solid changeups and curveballs but they're mostly average offerings. He always has attacked hitters, even before he had his nasty cutter, and fits the profile of a durable back-of-the-rotation starter. He also could make for an interesting reliever who could lean more heavily on his out pitch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros were aggressive on the international market during the 2015-16 signing period, handing out five bonuses of six figures or more. Celestino was the prize acquisition and got a $2.5 million bonus to sign out of the Dominican Republic after starring for a number of youth teams in international competition. He had made it to the short-season New York-Penn League in 2018 and was thriving there when he was sent to the Twins as part of the Ryan Pressly deal. Celestino finished the rest of the summer in the Appalachian League and the coaching staff in Elizabethton felt he was one of the best defenders they've seen at that level. He has tremendous instincts in center field with an above-average arm, allowing him to play a plus center field despite not being a burner speed-wise. The bigger question is whether his bat can catch up to his glove. He has shown plenty of ability to make contact, but it's a more line-drive to the gaps oriented approach right now. Some of that is because of his swing path and some of that stems from his need to add strength. Just 20 for all of the 2019 season, there's plenty of time for Celestino to grow into some power, and he has the bat speed to get there. If that part of his game develops, he could be a dynamic regular playing up the middle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Manoah was a two-way player out of high school in the Miami area in 2016 but went undrafted and headed to West Virginia. The big right-hander worked more out of the bullpen than in the rotation over his first two seasons but opened a lot of eyes as a starter in the Cape Cod League, leading the circuit in strikeouts. He's been that pitcher ever since and shot up Draft boards with a dominant junior season for the Mountaineers. The Blue Jays took Manoah with the No. 11 overall pick, making him the second pitcher to come off the board in the 2019 Draft. A physical beast at 6-foot-6, 260-pounds, Manoah has always shown glimpses of solid power stuff, but without consistency or command of it. That changed this spring as he showed above-average control for most of his junior season. He typically sits in the 94-97 mph range with his fastball, missing a ton of bats thanks to good sink. His slider flashes plus at times and has been a more reliable weapon for him. He has a solid changeup, on which he relied in the Cape Cod championship game, but he didn't use it as much during the spring. Manoah has managed to keep his large frame in sync and has repeated his delivery in order to fill up the strike zone more effectively. Given that he doesn't have that many starts on his resume, he's a rare college pitcher with projection. With three pitches, power stuff and natural strike-throwing ability, Manoah has all the ingredients needed to become an impactful Major League starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As if the Indians didn't already have a surplus of sweet-swinging infielders, they added another by grabbing Miller from the Padres as part of the nine-player Mike Clevinger trade last August. The second-highest position player ever drafted out of Illinois State, he went in the third round of the 2018 Draft and hit .336 in his pro debut. He jumped to Double-A for his first full season and batted .290 with 43 extra-base hits, then spent 2020 at San Diego and Cleveland's alternate sites before heading to the instructional league. Miller's forte is making consistent line-drive contact to all fields with a compact right-handed stroke and control of the strike zone. It's a hit-over-power approach, though his strength gives him some pop to his pull side and could result in 12-15 homers on an annual basis. He's an average runner and a little quicker underway but not a threat to steal. Miller spent most of his first two pro seasons as a steady if unspectacular shortstop with reliable hands, decent range and fringy arm strength. He also saw action at second base, where he profiles best, and third base, where his arm is light. He reminds scouts of Mark Loretta, who hit .295 in 15 big league seasons while playing all four infield positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last time Florida State had a shortstop who garnered early-round consideration was in 2004, when Stephen Drew was in the conversation for the No. 1 overall pick and ended up going No. 15 overall to Arizona. Walls has continued to perform at Class A Bowling Green in his first full season, when he ranked among the Midwest League leaders in average (.304, fifth), hits (142, third), on-base pct. (.393, fifth) and runs (87, second). Walls' best offensive skill is his plate discipline. After compiling more walks (178) than strikeouts (145) during his 196-game college career, Walls posted 66 walks against 80 strikeouts at Bowling Green. He's a switch-hitter who grinds out at-bats, with a line-drive approach and some extra-base ability, albeit with below-average over-the-fence power. An above-average runner with strong instincts, he tied for second in the organization with 31 stolen bases.
