While he's not a flashy defender, Walls makes all the plays at shortstop, with arm strength and range that both grade as a tick above average. He was named the Defensive Player of the Year by the Rays Baseball Operations department last season and should be able to stay up the middle long-term, either at short or second base. Walls might profile best eventually as a super-utility type, but has a chance to succeed as an everyday player up the middle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ivey transferred from Texas A&M to Grayson County (Texas) CC to become Draft-eligible in 2017, when he ranked second among national juco pitchers in strikeout rate (14.1 per nine innings) and went in the third round. He has pitched just 65 innings in the last three years, losing time with a suspension for using a foreign substance and an elbow sprain in 2019 and missing out on alternate camp and instructional league after coming down with COVID-19 in 2020. He made his big league debut last May, then went on the injured list for four months with persistent elbow soreness that he hid from the Astros. Ivey adheres to Houston's pitching blueprint, featuring high spin rates that help him change hitters' eye level with fastballs that carry at the top of the zone and curveballs that drop through the bottom. His four-seamer sits at 90-93 mph and tops out at 95, while his downer curve is a consistent plus offering in the upper 70s. He also employs a short slider and a fading changeup, both in the low 80s. Scouts never have liked Ivey's complicated and effortful delivery, though it provides a lot of deception without hindering his control. It's difficult to know what to make of him because his durability and makeup don't inspire much confidence. He was diagnosed with thoracic outlet syndrome but avoided surgery and was healthy again in Spring Training this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ivey pitched in Texas A&M's rotation for part of his freshman season before transferring to Grayson County (Texas) CC to become Draft-eligible as a sophomore in 2017, when he went in the third round after ranking second among national juco pitchers with 14.1 strikeouts per nine innings. He has averaged 11 whiffs per nine innings as a pro but has been limited the last two years. He worked just 52 innings in 2019, when he got suspended after umpires found a foreign substance on his glove and was sidelined for six weeks with an elbow sprain, and he missed out on alternate camp and instructional league last year after coming down with COVID-19. Added to the 40-man roster in November, Ivey fits nicely into the Astros' preferred mold of pitchers who have high spin rates and miss bats by changing opponents' eye level. He'll work at the letters with 90-93 mph fastballs that top out at 95 with riding life, then lock hitters up with plus downer curveballs in the upper 70s that drop through the bottom of the zone. He also mixes in a slider/cutter he has honed since turning pro and a usable changeup. Scouts don't care for Ivey's delivery, which is busy and features a lot of effort, and question whether he'll be durable enough to start every fifth day. He made just three appearances in 2021, including his first big league start, before getting shut down with persistent elbow pain that he admitted dates back to his sprain two years ago. At the same time, his mechanics add a lot of deception and don't prevent him from throwing strikes, so they add to his effectiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Ober looked like he would be an exciting Draft prospect in 2016 when he won 10 games and posted a 1.52 ERA as a College of Charleston freshman in 2014, a year that landed him on USA Baseball’s Collegiate National Team. He got derailed by Tommy John surgery in 2015, didn’t sign with the Dodgers as a 23rd-round pick in 2016 and eventually got his pro career started after a so-so 2017 season when the Twins took him in the 12th round. Though he’s battled minor arm issues since, he did pitch his way to Double-A in 2019 and the Twins liked him enough to add him to the 40-man roster after the 2020 season. The 6-foot-9 Ober won’t wow anyone with pure stuff, but he does have four distinct pitches and throws them all for strikes. His fastball averages around 87 mph, but it has excellent cut and carry to it. It plays up better than his velocity, which actually upticked in 2019. His changeup is his best pitch, thrown typically around 79 mph, with unusual carry and arm-side action. Both of his breaking pitches are OK, with an average slider that has unusual action to it and a curve with moderate depth. In addition to his size, extension and rare movement to all of his offerings, Ober might have the best command in the system, walking just one batter per nine innings in his pro career. His ceiling is limited to that of a back-end starter, but pitch life and that plus control give him a good chance to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Kelenic was one of the top high school hitters, if not one of the best pure overall bats, in the 2018 Draft class, one whose stock soared as the Draft approached and he heard his name being mentioned as a potential top 10 pick. It was the Mets who took the two-time U.S. national 18-and-under team member No. 6 overall, signing him for more than a million under pick value. The Mariners, who picked 14th, had brought Kelenic in for a pre-Draft workout and liked him so much, they made sure to get him as part of the return for Robinson Cano and Edwin Diaz in December. Kelenic's outstanding feel for hitting from the left side of the plate, with an advanced approach, was on display during his summer debut, when he earned a promotion from the Gulf Coast to the Appalachian League. He has a knack for barreling up the baseball with solid raw power some feel will eventually translate to above-average in-game pop as he matures. An above-average runner, Kelenic is a very smart baserunner who can steal a base. The Wisconsin prep product was a center fielder in high school and that's where he played during his pro debut with the Mets. While the jury is still out about his ability to stay there long-term, he does have the arm for right field should he have to slide over. Kelenic is mature beyond his years and gets high grades for his makeup and work ethic, so making the transition to his new organization shouldn't be too difficult. He has the kind of offensive profile that could allow him to move a little more quickly than some high school hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Slider: 55 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 55 | Overall: 55 The two best draftees ever out of Stetson University are currently carving up hitters in the big leagues. Gilbert, whom the Mariners took in the middle of the first round after a slightly up-and-down junior season as he pitched through a bout of mono, hopes to be the next in line after Corey Kluber and Jacob deGrom. The right-hander didn't pitch at all in his first summer as a pro after signing for full pick value. Gilbert has a strong track record of using a solid four-pitch mix and throwing them all for strikes. He showed just what he's capable of when 100 percent healthy while winning Atlantic Sun Pitcher of the Year honors as a sophomore, then being named a Cape Cod League All-Star that summer. He sat in the mid-90s, touching 97 mph on the Cape and then saw his velocity dip while he was sick, though it ticked back up closer to Draft time. He's gotten bigger and more physical this offseason, so don't be surprised to see some 70-grade fastballs in there in 2019. He can throw two distinct breaking balls, with the harder slider better than the curve, and can mix in an effective changeup as well. With a history of throwing strikes, Gilbert could have plus control when all is said and done. He did something Kluber and deGrom didn't: get taken in the first round. Now it's time for him to get going towards catching them in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Poteet was a freshman on a 2013 UCLA team that won the College World Series and has sent four pitchers to the Majors. A fourth-round pick in 2015, he advanced to Triple-A by 2019 without making a blip on any prospect radars. He returned from the pandemic layoff and was the organization's most improved pitcher last year, making his big league debut in May and holding his own in seven starts before missing the final three months with a sprained right knee. After sitting at 90-92 mph with his four-seam fastball in 2019, Poteet operated at 92-95 and touched 98 last season, producing high spin rates with good carry up in the zone. His heater plays well with his changeup, a heavy 85- to 88-mph sinker that was his most effective secondary pitch in the Majors. He also features a lot of spin on his 78- to 81-mph curveball (which he mainly uses against lefties) and his 84- to 87-mph slider (his primary weapon against right-handers), both of which flash as solid pitches but got hit hard by big leaguers. Poteet throws strikes but will need to be more precise with his breaking balls to survive as a long-term starter in the Majors. He has pitched to contact more than missed bats during his pro career, which could indicate he's better suited for a multi-inning relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 College hitters who perform as juniors, particularly for big programs, always rise up Draft boards. Larnach was a prime example of this, going from interesting bat to sure-fire first-round pick as he helped Oregon State win the College World Series. The Twins liked his offensive profile enough to make him the 20th overall selection of the Draft and after his long college postseason run, he turned in a solid pro debut, reaching full-season ball even though he was running out of gas. Larnach had shown an advanced approach at the plate and the ability to hit for average as a sophomore and in the Cape Cod League, but took a huge step forward as a prospect when he added power to his resume thanks to some tweaks to his swing mechanics. The added power hasn't taken anything away from him potentially being a plus hitter, one who draws walks and doesn't strike out a ton, when all is said and done. Larnach's above-average arm works well from the outfield and he looked fine in right field during his debut, though some feel his below-average speed will land him left. In the end, though, it will be his bat that will carry him quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of three first-round pitchers taken by the Royals in the 2018 Draft, when the club selected eight college pitchers in the first six rounds, Lynch was pitching well at Class A Advanced Wilmington in 2019 before a minor arm issue interrupted his first full season. But the 6-foot-6 lefty made a healthy return in late July to finish the regular season on a high note, then opened eyes as one of the best pitchers in the Arizona Fall League. Lynch made even more progress at the alternate training site in 2020, with some club officials pegging him as the camp’s biggest standout. The Royals suggested Lynch throw more fastballs upon entering the pro ranks after he had pitched with a breaking-ball-heavy arsenal in college. It immediately helped Lynch unlock more velocity, and he's been averaging around 95 mph on his fastball this summer. A plus, mid-80s slider represents the left-hander’s best secondary pitch and plays nicely off his fastball with its big depth and sharp bite. Lynch’s changeup was a major focus of his work at the alternate site, and he became more comfortable throwing it against hitters on both sides of the plate. He completes his four-pitch mix with an average curveball that he can throw for strikes but doesn't go to very often. That Lynch also got better at repeating his delivery and arm slot while at the alternate site has inspired even more confidence in his capacity to develop at least average command on top of his present above-average control. Lynch’s feel for locating his power stuff speaks to his high ceiling as a starter, and the Royals have been committed to getting him looks at that role in the Majors in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Cubs made Thompson a third-round pick in 2017 in large part because of his long track record of success. He won two gold medals with U.S. national teams while in high school and sandwiched three productive seasons at Auburn around missing all of 2016 while recovering from Tommy John surgery. He reached Double-A midway through his first full pro season and after a tough debut, he allowed a total of five runs over his next eight starts before tiring down the stretch. Thompson's best pitches are his curveball and his slider. His upper-70s curve flashed plus more often in college, while his low-80s slider was his more consistent breaker in 2018. He uses 89-92 mph two-seam fastballs with sink and can reach back to hit 95 when he turns to his four-seamer. Thompson also demonstrates feel for a changeup with some sink. He can't blow the ball by hitters but instead keeps them off balance by mixing his pitches and pounding the strike zone. He has one of the higher floors among Cubs starting pitching prospects, projecting as a workhorse toward the back of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mills was the Mariners’ yo-yo in 2021, having been recalled from Triple-A Tacoma seven times during his first season in The Show. As such, his rookie status remained intact after pitching just 12 2/3 innings in mostly low-leverage scenarios, yet it was a bit of a stumble, as Mills was scoreless in just four of the 11 outings and had a 9.91 ERA overall. Seattle is still bullish on his makeup, though. He’s another example of the Mariners’ excellent job of finding money-saving college seniors in the Draft who really perform, having signed for well under slot value at $125,000 after being taken in the third round in 2017. Mills’ low three-quarter-slot delivery has been described as funky, and he’s primarily relied on a fastball-slider combination to miss bats and generate a ton of groundouts. The Mariners want to see Mills continue to use all of that to his advantage and remain in “attack” mode. His fastball sits in the low 90s with sink, and his slider has been his main strikeout pitch, especially against righties. Both offerings have high spin rates and his developing changeup gives lefties a different look, but it’s not a go-to pitch yet. Mills doesn’t need to be pinpoint accurate to be a right-handed specialist or a sixth-inning type of reliever, but if he can improve his changeup and refine his command a bit, he still has the chance to have a larger role. The Mariners love the makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mills is another example of the Mariners’ excellent job of finding money-saving college seniors in the Draft who really perform. Infielder Donovan Walton and reliever Sam Delaplane are other cases, but Mills is an even later selection who has risen through the ranks. A third-rounder in 2017, Mills signed for $125,000 – more than $45,000 under slot value -- then he proceeded to carve up Class A hitters and reached Double-A in his first full season. He scuffled some during the first half of ’19 when returning to Double-A, but he was able to turn things back up and he finished in Team USA’s bullpen during Olympic qualifying that fall. Mills’ low three-quarter-slot delivery has been described as funky and he’s primarily relied on a fastball-slider combination to miss bats and generate a ton of groundouts. The Mariners want to see Mills continue to use all of that to his advantage and remain in “attack” mode. His fastball sits in the low 90s with sink, and his slider has been his main strikeout pitch, especially against righties. Both offerings have high spin rates, and his developing changeup gives lefties a different look, but it’s not a go-to pitch yet. Mills essentially missed all of 2020 after not being selected to Summer Camp or the alternate training site, which may have served as a wakeup moment for him, but he made up for lost time at the club’s fall developmental league in Arizona and wound up on the 40-man roster, showing a nearly 4-mph uptick in fastball velocity. Hitters were said to have no chance with the 97-mph heat with movement. Typically around the strike zone, Mills' walk rate went up a bit in Double-A. He doesn’t need pinpoint accuracy to be a right-handed specialist or a sixth-inning type of reliever, but if he can improve his changeup and refine his command a bit, he still has the chance to have a larger role. The Mariners love the makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the advanced age of 18 in 2016, Uceta recorded a 6.59 ERA in his U.S. debut a year later. He did improve over the course of the summer and pitched well in the playoffs to help Ogden win the Rookie-level Pioneer League championship. His 2018 season unfolded in a similar fashion, as he struggled after an August promotion to high Class A but won a crucial postseason game with 5 2/3 scoreless innings to contribute to Rancho Cucamonga capturing the California League title. Uceta's best pitch is a hard changeup with fade and late tumble, and he throws it with the same arm speed as his fastball. His four-seam heater parks at 90-93 mph and reaches 95 with riding life up in the strike zone. He improved the shape of his curveball last year, giving him an average third offering. Uceta has thrown strikes throughout his pro career, and his command improved once the Dodgers got him to stop throwing across his body and take a more direct path to the plate. A dogged competitor, he must be precise with his pitches and confuse hitters by throwing them from the same release point because he doesn't have overpowering stuff or deceptive angle. As a slender 6-footer, he'll have to prove he can maintain his stuff over the course of a full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafting high school catchers can be a risky business, and teams need to play the long game patience-wise in terms of development. That's even more true when that catcher hailed from a cold-weather state. The Twins knew all of this when they took Rortvedt in the second round of the 2016 Draft out of the Wisconsin prep ranks. His defensive work has been exemplary and he took a step forward with the bat in 2018, playing across two levels of Class A. There are few questions about Rortvedt's ability to defend at this point. He's an outstanding blocker and receiver, with some thinking he'll be a plus defender overall. His above-average arm plays up because of its accuracy and his ability to transfer quickly as well as throwing from his feet or his knees, as he's thrown out 32.6 percent of potential basestealers heading into 2019. There could be more in Rortvedt's left-handed bat as well. While he's big and strong, he employs a more conservative, contact-first swing. He did improve offensively in 2018, but the Twins would like to see him let loose a little more to unlock more of his raw power. If that happens, then the Twins could have a very intriguing every day catcher on their hands. But even if he stays the course, he has the tools necessary to have a successful backup backstop career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Reds scouted Hendrix at Texas A&M, they thought his stuff as a reliever could have placed him in the top two rounds of the 2016 Draft. But he struggled in his junior year, so he was still on the board when the Reds picked in the fifth round that June. His power stuff has played well in the lower levels of the Minors, and he was a Florida State League All-Star in 2018. With big stuff that projects well for the Major Leagues as a reliever, Hendrix has two effective pitches with a plus-plus 94-98 mph fastball and an above-average power curveball that ranges from 87-90 mph. There is no question he has swing-and-miss stuff, with a 12.3 K/9 ratio entering 2019. He also gets a lot of weak contact on the ground, as evidenced by his 1.60 GO/AO ratio through the 2018 season. Hendrix still has work to do to sharpen his command and control after he had 4.9 walks-per-nine innings last season at Daytona while he posted a 1.76 ERA in 44 games. He doesn't need to have pinpoint control in short relief, but more consistent strikes could lead to him getting high-leverage innings late in games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox signed Santos for $250,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, and then he went with Shaun Anderson to the Giants in a trade for Eduardo Núñez two years later. He showcased power stuff early in his career and kicked it up a notch during instructional league in 2020, propelling him to the big leagues in April 2021. He drew an 80-game suspension that June after testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs and never could claim a full-time job in the Majors the last two seasons, after which San Francisco dealt him to Chicago for right-handed pitching prospect Kade McClure in December. Santos featured a heavy 92-98 mph fastball and a plus 82-85 mph slider as a starter earlier in his career, and he has lit up radar guns even more since becoming a full-time reliever in 2021. His slide piece is a true plus-plus pitch that sits at 87-90 mph and touches 93 with two-plane depth, and it generated a 45 percent swing-and-miss rate last season. His heater averages 99 mph and peaks at 102, though it lacks life and gets barreled more than his slider. Now that he's in the bullpen, Santos no longer has to refine what was a mediocre changeup, but he does need to improve his control and command if he's going to play a high-leverage role. After he averaged 2.5 walks per nine innings as a starter in the Giants system, that rate has jumped to 5.4 the last two seasons, during which big leaguers tagged him for three homers in just 5 2/3 frames. The White Sox hope he'll figure things out like Tommy Kahnle did after they acquired him in a 2015 trade for Yency Almonte.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox signed Santos for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015 before shipping him to the Giants along with Shaun Anderson in a deal for Eduardo Núñez two years later. His stuff took a leap during instructional league in 2020 and landed him in San Francisco in April 2021, but he drew an 80-game suspension that June after testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs. After he was unable to land a permanent role in the big leagues the last two seasons, the Giants traded him to the White Sox for right-handed pitching prospect Kade McClure in December. Santos had a heavy 92-98 mph fastball and flashed some plus 82-85 mph sliders in the past, then kicked his stuff up a notch during instructs and maintained it after becoming a full-time reliever in 2021. Working in shorter stints, he now parks at 97-99 and regularly climbs into triple digits with high spin rates that produce carry, though his heater is somewhat straight. His slider now operates at 88-90 mph with wicked horizontal and vertical action and both offerings grade as plus-plus. Santos no longer has to worry about refining a mediocre changeup that he scrapped after moving to the bullpen. His biggest need is to improve his control and command after he battled the strike zone last year and big leaguers teed off on him when he didn't locate his pitches well. If he can add some polish, he could become a late-inning weapon and perhaps a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Red Sox for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, Santos came to the Giants along with Shaun Anderson in a trade for Eduardo Nunez two years later. He made his full-season debut at age 19 in 2019 but made just eight starts because of shoulder tightness. His only 2020 development experience came in instructional league, where he performed spectacularly to cement a spot on the 40-man roster. Santos already had showcased some of the best stuff in the system prior to last fall, working with a 92-96 mph fastball that touched 98 with heavy sink and flashing some plus sliders at 82-85 mph. In shorter stints at instructs, he dealt at 97-100 mph and displayed a plus-plus slider with increased velocity and sharpness. His stuff looked ready for a high-leverage role in a big league bullpen. When Santos continued to display an overpowering fastball and slider this spring, the Giants promoted him to their bullpen in late April, though he got demoted a week later and drew an 80-game suspension in June after testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs. As a reliever, he won't have to worry about refining his changeup or his command as much as he would if he remained a starter. Working in shorter stints may help him stay healthier after he accumulated just 174 1/3 innings in his first five years as a pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Short put himself on the prospect map by leading the Northeast Conference with nine homers and 33 walks as a Sacred Heart sophomore in 2015, only to slump in the Cape Cod League that summer and again as a junior. He fell to the 17th round of the 2016 Draft, signed for $80,000 and didn't do much in his pro debut. But he has opened eyes since with his power and patience, combining for 30 homers and 176 walks in his first two full seasons while reaching Double-A. Short has quick hands and a pull-heavy approach, giving him more pop than a typical 175-pounder. He's an extreme flyball hitter who makes a lot of loud contact from the right side of the plate, though the Cubs would like to see him cut down his swing and make more regular contact. He works deep counts and draws a lot of walks, giving him healthy on-base percentages despite subpar batting averages. With solid speed and an aggressive nature, Short can steal an occasional base. Some club officials believe he's the best defensive infielder in the system, and his quickness and arm strength allow him to play second and third base and serve in a utility role if needed. If he can put the bat on the ball more consistently, he could be an everyday shortstop in the mold of Zack Cozart.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Switch-hitters with power potential who have the chance to play up the middle aren’t easy to find, so the Pirates were excited when they landed Castro for $150,000 in the 2015-16 international signing period. Since then, Castro has shown glimpses of that pop, but has often struggled with other facets of his offensive game. After hitting 19 homers across two levels of A ball in 2019 and performing well at the club’s alternate site in 2020, Castro was added to the 40-man roster. He made headlines when his first five big league hits were home runs in 2021. An extremely physical infielder who has packed on a lot of strength to his six-foot frame since signing, there are no questions about his raw power from both sides of the plate. He’s tended to be better from the right side, though he hit bunch of homers left-handed in 2021. He can hit the ball out to all fields, but the question remains if he can make enough contact to get to it his power consistently. He hits the ball very hard, but also swings and misses a great deal, giving away at-bats and not recognizing spin all that well. Castro is an average runner who used to play a lot of shortstop, but now focuses on second and third, where he’s a fringy defender. It’s possible he could be an offensive-minded second baseman in the big leagues, but it’s more likely that he moves around a bit to find ways to get his power potential into a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bukauskas' velocity and prospect status took off in 2014, when he reclassified from a high school junior to a Draft-eligible senior, yet he turned down early-round overtures from clubs in order to attend North Carolina. Many scouts believed his fastball and slider were the best combination of pitches in the 2017 Draft, where he went 15th overall and signed for $3.6 million. An automobile accident in his first Spring Training left him with a slipped disc and limited him to three appearances in the first three months of the 2018 season, but his overpowering stuff was apparent down the stretch and in the Arizona Fall League. He was having an inconsistent season in Double-A, albeit while missing plenty of bats, when the Astros packaged him with Seth Beer, Corbin Martin and Josh Rojas to Arizona to get Zack Greinke at the 2019 Trade Deadline Bukauskas' best offering is his slider, which combines mid-80s power with late, sharp bite, though he can fall in love with it and lose some feel for his fastball. His heater is also formidable, sitting in the mid-90s, topping out at 98 mph and featuring some sink and run. He flashed a plus changeup with fade in the AFL, though he needs to throw it more often to improve its consistency, and he also can mix in a cutter. The debate over whether Bukauskas is better suited to be a starter or reliever dates to his high school days. He has settled down his delivery somewhat since then but still throws with effort, and his lack of size and reliable command could point him toward the bullpen. He could move very fast in a relief role, though others see him as a Sonny Gray type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top prospect in Minnesota in 2014, Hentges was a high school two-way star who became a full-time pitcher after signing for an over-slot $700,000 in the fourth round. He spent most of his first two years as a pro in Rookie ball before blowing out his elbow in '16, with Tommy John surgery sidelining him for most of the subsequent season as well. He finally broke out in 2018, leading the Class A Advanced Carolina League in strikeout rate (9.3 per nine innings) and ranking second in ERA (3.27). Hentges doesn't have a true plus pitch, but he has the potential for four solid offerings. He has shown more arm speed since having his elbow reconstructed and now works at 91-94 and touches 96 mph with his fastball. An upper-70s downer curveball is his second-most reliable option, a mid-80s cutter he began throwing in 2018 has promise and his changeup features some fade and should improve if he uses it more often. Hentges uses his 6-foot-6 frame and high-three-quarters delivery to create steep downhill plane on his pitches, which helped him top the Carolina League in home-run rate (0.3 per nine innings). He has a fairly smooth delivery for an extra-large pitcher but has yet to prove he can throw strikes on a consistent basis. If he can do that and refine his secondary offerings, he could be a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If nothing else, the Maton brothers know how to overachieve. Older brother Phil was a 20th-round pick of the Padres in 2015 and has spent the last two years pitching out of their big league bullpen. Nick was a 40th-round pick out of high school in the same Draft as his brother and after a year at Eastern Illinois, transferred to Lincoln Land Community College. A huge season there landed him in the seventh round of the 2017 Draft and he had a solid, albeit unspectacular, first full season in 2018 that included a South Atlantic League All-Star nod. Maton has the chance to have four at least average tools. As a legitimate 6-foot-2 infielder, the easy thing to say is he won't be able to stay at shortstop long-term, but the Phillies haven't seen any reason why he can't, with his hands, arm, accuracy and footwork all working well from the premium position. He has a solid approach at the plate, with the ability to work counts, and while there isn't a ton of over-the-fence-power, he can drive the ball from the left side of the plate. If Maton can continue to develop offensively and gets to be a Major League average hitter, he's at least a solid utility type in the big leagues, and he did play a few games at second in 2018. But there's enough upside here to think he could find a way to be a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Solomon established himself as a potential 2017 first-rounder after a strong summer in the Cape Cod League, but control issues relegated him to Notre Dame's bullpen and the fourth round as a junior. He regained his control and advanced to High-A in his first full pro season, only to blow out his elbow in April 2019 and require Tommy John surgery. He returned last year to win Triple-A West pitcher of the year honors and make his big league debut, posting a 1.29 ERA in six relief appearances, but his stuff has regressed in 2022. Solomon regained the 92-96 mph velocity on his four-seam fastball early in 2021, though his heater sat more in the low 90s at the end of last season and has parked at 91 this year. He has fallen in love with his mid-80s cutter even though his low-80s slider with more depth is a better offering. His formerly solid to plus curveball is now merely an average pitch. To remain a starter, Solomon will need to rediscover his previous stuff as well as the feel for his fading low-80s changeup, which wasn't as effective in 2021 as it had been previously. He'll also need to refine his control and command, which are average at best. He may be more suited to be a multi-inning reliever, the role he filled in his introduction to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Solomon ranked as the state of Maryland's top pitching prospect in 2014, when he was coming out of a Mount Saint Joseph High (Baltimore) program that has spawned eight big leaguers (most notably Mark Teixeira), but fell to the Padres in the 21st round because he was strongly committed to Notre Dame. A strong summer in the Cape Cod League after his sophomore season positioned him as a potential first-rounder for 2017, but control issues landed him in the Fighting Irish bullpen and eventually the fourth round. He rediscovered the strike zone and rose to high Class A in his first full pro season, but he blew out his elbow in April 2019 and required Tommy John surgery. Back on the mound last fall in instructional league, Solomon showed he had regained his 92-96 mph four-seam fastball, and he previously had demonstrated the ability to hold that velocity deep into games and over the course of a full season. While his breaking balls lack consistency, his curveball can be a hammer at its best and he flashes a plus slider that he also can turn into a cutter. His changeup is clearly his fourth pitch, yet helps him keep lefties in check and could become an average offering if he uses it more. Placed on Houston's 40-man roster in November, Solomon could be a mid-rotation starter if he stays healthy and throws strikes. He averaged 5.3 walks per nine innings at Notre Dame but slashed that mark to 2.9 in his lone full season as a pro. Like many of Houston's top pitching prospects, he ultimately may fit best as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $100,000 out of the Dominican Republic at the relatively advanced age of 18 in October 2015, Doval has one of the best pure arms in the Giants organization. He averaged 12.9 strikeouts in his first three pro seasons and made a successful jump to full-season ball in 2018. During that time, his fastball gained about 10 mph. Doval has a filthy heater that sits at 93-98 mph and frequently reaches triple digits. His slings the ball from a low-three-quarters arm slot that makes it hard for right-handers to pick up his heater and imparts natural cutting and running action. He relies heavily on his fastball, complementing it with a hard, sweeping slider that has its moments. Strictly a two-pitch guy, Doval could use something to keep left-handers in check. He's deceptive but features a lot of effort in his delivery and has yet to figure out how to throw strikes on a consistent basis. He has a ceiling of a high-leverage reliever but is a long ways from reaching it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-team all-state running back as an Ohio high school junior, Dawson focused on baseball at Ohio State and became the Buckeyes' highest-drafted position player in a decade when he went in the second round in 2016. Signed for $1,056,800, he scuffled in his pro debut, didn't prepare well for his first Spring Training and looked overwhelmed in his introduction to full-season ball early in 2017. After making adjustments and getting in better shape, he looked much better in Double-A and the Arizona Fall League last season. One of the top college power hitters in the 2016 Draft, Dawson offers bat speed and strength from the left side of the plate. He has pop to all fields and could produce 20-25 homers per year if he can drive the ball in the air more consistently. He has improved his timing at the plate as a pro but likely won't hit for a high average unless he can develop more patience. After losing weight, Dawson significantly upgraded his speed to solid in 2018 and showed more upside as a basestealer and defender. Primarily a left fielder in his first two years as a pro, he shifted to center last season. He seems to see the ball better up the middle than he did on a corner, though his reads and routes still require more refinement and his arm remains fringy at best.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted in the fourth round in 2016 after a productive season at Auburn, Palacios carried that success into pro ball, hitting .330 with an .824 OPS in his debut, finishing at Low-A Lansing. Palacios spent a moderately productive 2017 season back with Lansing before advancing to High-A and Double-A in 2018, slashing a combined .290/.355/.416 with eight home runs in 126 games. Back at Double-A in ’19, Palacios’ numbers stayed steady, and the outfielder spent much of 2020 at the alternate training site, eventually earning a spot on the club’s taxi squad. The numbers would suggest that Palacios’ development had plateau’d somewhat, but he took a significant step in 2020 as his athleticism began to translate more into live situations. Palacios has above-average athleticism and defense in the corner outfield spots, where his routes have improved. He’s also been working to see the ball deeper into the zone at the plate with a focus on driving pitches back up the middle. Palacios will need to continue to hit for average, as he has through the Minor Leagues, but there’s still 10-15 home runs in his bat. Palacios earned praise throughout the organization for his second wind of development, and with a spot on the 40-man roster, he earned a first look at the Majors in April. Palacios would have more avenues to similar opportunities if he were a viable option in center, but the rest of his game features very few glaring weaknesses and it’s easy to project seeing the big leagues more down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins went aggressively after high school hitters at the top of the 2016 Draft, with their first four selections being prep position players. Baddoo was the last of the quartet, taken in the Competitive Balance Lottery Round B and starting his pro career that summer in the Gulf Coast League. The toolsy outfielder went back there in 2017 and played his way to the Appalachian League in a big step forward, then after struggling out of the gate during his full-season debut in 2018, played very well down the stretch in the Midwest League. He was trying to get going in the Florida State League in 2019 when an elbow injury required Tommy John surgery in May. More than anything, it seems that Baddoo took a while to adjust to the cold climate in Cedar Rapids at the start of the 2018 season and his bat warmed up as the weather did. He continued to show elite-level walk rates, he finished fourth in the league in free passes last year, and though his strikeout rate also jumped up, he made much more consistent contact in the second half. His extra-base authority continues to show up more and he could approach average power when all is said and done. He also has outstanding speed, which allows him to steal bases, not to mention leg out the league-leading 11 triples he had in '18. His wheels also serve him well in the outfield, where the Twins have more confidence in his ability to play center field long-term. He made strides there and in strengthening his arm, and is now looking more and more like an up-the-middle big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees pulled off a coup when they signed David Robertston as a 17th-rounder in 2006, and they think history may repeat itself with another late-round sophomore from an Alabama college 11 years later. Whitlock signed for $247,500 out of Alabama-Birmingham in 2017, sliding because of back issues and questionable signability. He fashioned a 31-inning scoreless streak early in his first full pro season and logged a 1.86 ERA between three levels, including a brief stint in Double-A, but he succumbed to Tommy John surgery in July 2019. Whitlock's low-three-quarters delivery produces 91-94 mph two-seam fastballs with tremendous sink, leading to a stellar 1.7 groundout/airout ratio in 2018. He'll occasionally reach back and hit 96 mph with a four-seamer, but his No. 2 pitch is low-80 slider with two-plane depth. He uses a decent changeup to keep left-handers in check. Hitters have a tough time picking up Whitlock's pitches because he uses his 6-foot-5 frame to create impressive extension and unusual angle. He has thrown more strikes as a pro than he did in college, enhancing his profile as a starter. He also could be valuable as a multi-inning reliever and his first opportunity in New York could come in that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It didn’t take Perdomo long to establish himself as one of the biggest steals in the 2016-17 international class. Signed by Arizona for $70,000 in July 2016, Perdomo performed well against advanced competition early in his career. After climbing three levels during his 2018 stateside debut, Perdomo continued to move quickly in his first full season, reaching High-A Visalia in 2019. He then opened more eyes in the Arizona Fall League as one of the circuit's youngest regulars and spent the 2020 season at the D-backs' alternate training site. He made his Major League debut early in the 2021 season, though it may have been a bit premature as he struggled in limited action. Perdomo then had a hard time getting on track back in Double-A, though he caught fire late in the year, hitting over .300 in August and September. Perdomo is among the best defensive players in Arizona’s system and a lock to stick as a shortstop. His blend of plus speed and long, quick strides gives him plenty of range in all directions, while his soft hands and plus arm enable him to easily handle the position. In addition to his strong defensive instincts, the 22-year-old has the potential to be an above-average switch-hitter. Perdomo has walked (218) nearly as much as he’s struck out (230) across his first four seasons, indicative of an advanced approach at the plate. However, his 23.5 percent strikeout rate in Double-A last season was the highest of his career. The Jekyll and Hyde 2021 season complicates his overall evaluation, but at his best, he displays advanced barrel control and bat speed while flashing power potential from the left side. Perdomo’s speed helps him impact the game on the bases. He swiped at least 20 bags in back-to-back seasons (2018-19), but there’s still room for growth as he went just 8-for-14 in stolen-base attempts in ‘21. Perdomo's speed and defensive acumen at a premium position bode well for his future, though he’ll have to establish some offensive consistency to reach his overall ceiling. Regardless, it’s easy to envision him as an everyday shortstop in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It hasn’t taken Perdomo long to establish himself as one of the biggest steals from the 2016-17 international period. Signed by Arizona for $70,000 in July 2016, Perdomo made improvements and performed well against advanced competition early in his career. After climbing three levels during his 2018 pro debut, Perdomo continued to move quickly in his first full season, reaching Class A Advanced Visalia. He then opened more eyes after the season in the Arizona Fall League as one of the circuit's youngest regulars and spent the 2020 season at Arizona’s alternate training site. He made his Major League debut early in the 2021 season, though it may have been a bit premature as he struggled in limited action, and then had a hard time getting on track back in Double-A. Perdomo is the best defensive player in Arizona’s system and a lock to stick as a shortstop. His blend of plus speed and long, quick strides gives him range in all directions on the dirt, and he's long received rave reviews for his slick actions, soft hands and plus arm strength. He also earns high marks for having an excellent internal clock and an overall advanced feel for playing the position. Perdomo has the makings of becoming a solid switch-hitter thanks to his bat speed and barrel control, while the fact that he recorded more walks (169) than strikeouts (148) across his first three pro seasons speaks to the Dominican native’s advanced approach -- though he got away from that a bit this season. He will flash some power potential as a left-handed hitter and club officials believe he will develop more pop as he continues to fill out his wiry-athletic and projectable frame. Perdomo’s plus speed gives him impact potential on the bases. He swiped at least 20 bags in back-to-back seasons (2018-19) but will need to become a more efficient basestealer after being cut down in 33 percent of his attempts in 2019. Perdomo's speed and defensive chops at a premium position bode well for his future, though he’ll have to make some offensive adjustments to raise his overall ceiling. Regardless, it’s easy to envision his as an everyday shortstop in the big leagues, and few within the organization would be surprised if he were to ultimately surpass expectations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Campbell displayed arm strength but had little success in three years at Clemson, posting a 7.85 ERA in just 39 innings of work. The Rays saw enough potential to sign him for $50,000 in the 21st round of the 2017 Draft, and he blossomed into a legitimate prospect while reaching Double-A by mid-2019. Tampa Bay didn't have enough room on its crowded 40-man roster for him this offseason, however, and lost him to the Marlins in the big league phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December. Campbell generates high spin rates on his fastball, curveball and slider, each of which is a solid offering. His heater sits at 92-95 mph and plays better than its velocity thanks to its cut action and carry as well as his ability to command it. Scouts debate which of his breaking balls is better, with some preferring his mid-80s slider/cutter and others believing his 78-82 mph curve has more upside. Add in a low-80s changeup that's more effective against same-side hitters than left-handers, and Campbell has a full complement of pitches to start. The Rays helped him locate the strike zone, as he averaged just 2.3 walks per nine innings in his first three pro seasons compared to 4.6 per nine at Clemson. He's durable and efficient but doesn't miss a lot of bats, so there's some thought that he might be best used as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Unheralded as a recruit out of a Northern California high school, Vaughn became the best hitter in college baseball during his three years at California and one of the best in recent memory. He won the Golden Spikes Award as a sophomore in 2018 and batted .374/.495/.688 with 50 homers in 160 games, surpassing Brandon Morrow as the highest drafted player in school history when the White Sox took him at No. 3 overall last June. After signing for $7,221,200, a Draft record for the franchise and for a corner bat, he advanced to high Class A in his pro debut. Vaughn keeps things simple at the plate, allowing his natural hitting ability and natural power to take over rather than trying to do too much. He has a pretty right-handed swing with no holes as well as considerable bat speed and strength. With his all-fields approach and refusal to chase pitches out of the strike zone, he projects as a .300 hitter with 30 homers and 80 walks on an annual basis. Most of Vaughn's value will come from his bat, but his bat will provide plenty of value. Though he worked out at third base for some teams before the Draft, he's limited to first base. He's a below-average runner, but he moves well enough around the bag and has an arm that ran fastballs into the low 90s when he pitched early in his college career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels were excited about Rodriguez's upside and feel for pitching when they went above slot to sign him in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft out of the Miami-area high school ranks. While he pitched well in his debut that summer and did reach full-season ball in '17, it's still mostly about potential for Rodriguez, who missed all of the '18 season with a stress reaction his back. Any hopes for progress in 2019 were dashed when he needed surgery to repair a stress fracture in his back. While all signs had pointed to a successful rehab and Rodriguez gave a lot of focus to conditioning, the recurrence of his back issues is concerning. The hope is that he can get back to refining the four-pitch mix that excited everyone in the organization. He throws both a live four-seam and sinking two-seam fastball, touching the upper-90s with the former at times, and backs it up with a hard slider that flashes plus. His changeup might be as good, if not better and he flips in an average curveball as well. With a relatively clean delivery, he should be a good strike-thrower. Rodriguez has been pinpointed as a breakout candidate ever since he was drafted. If he can get healthy and get a full season's work in, he can finally start living up to those expectations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Rockies took Bowden in the second round of the 2016 Draft, they saw a college reliever from a successful program who might be able to move quickly through the system. When he went straight from Vanderbilt to full-season ball the summer after he got drafted, it was a very good step in the right direction. Then the brakes got hit hard when a bulging disc in his back kept him out for all of 2017. He did return healthy to pitch across both levels of A ball in 2018. While Bowden has the raw stuff to start, and he did get a handful of chances to do so during his junior year at Vandy, his demeanor really fits well in the back end of a bullpen. He'll aggressively go right after hitters with his three-pitch mix with an ability to challenge in all areas of the strike zone. He throws his fastball up to 97 mph downhill with good late life and his tumbling changeup is at least above-average. His breaking ball has been improving and is looking more and more like a tight slider. That breaking ball will be a focus for Bowden and the Rockies think that once it clicks, he has the chance to be a true impact reliever. With his demeanor and ability to miss bats, he could be a valuable left-handed setup man when all is said and done.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a Tennessee high schooler, Sheffield had a chance to go in the first round of the 2013 Draft until he had Tommy John surgery. The older brother of Mariners left-hander Justus Sheffield, Jordan signed for $1,847,500 as a supplemental first-rounder out of Vanderbilt three years later. He had trouble staying healthy and succeeding as a starter, then began to turn a corner as a full-time reliever in the Arizona Fall League last offseason and has built on that momentum in 2019. Sheffield has posted elite swing-and-miss rates with his fastball this year, sitting in the mid-90s and reaching 98 with riding action and improved sink. He has regained the feel for his curveball, which often deserted him earlier in his pro career, and it can be an absolute hammer at times. He also has aptitude for throwing a circle changeup that can flummox left-handed hitters. Though he has three quality pitches, Sheffield's lack of size, the effort in his delivery and his medical history created persistent questions about his durability in a rotation. He also has little track record of providing strikes and may never have better than fringy command, other factors in the decision to move him to the bullpen. He has the weapons to be a late-inning factor if he can do a better job of harnessing them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Isbel reached full-season ball in 2018 -- the summer he was drafted in the third round out of the University of Nevada, Las Vegas -- and while injuries delayed his progress at High-A Wilmington in 2019, he was able to finish the season healthy with a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. In 2021, Isbel stood out enough in big league camp to be the starting right fielder on Opening Day. The 24-year-old struggled in his first stint in the Majors but hit much better in his return from Triple-A Omaha during the final weeks of the season. Isbel has a well-rounded set of tools, and his ability to hit for average and power began to emerge again in Triple-A, where he was hitting line drives to all fields and letting his bat speed and strength fuel his left-handed swing. Isbel holds his own as an above-average defender in center thanks to good jumps and routes, earning high marks from the Royals’ big league coaching staff. He can play all three outfield spots, though, and his arm has improved with better accuracy. Isbel is also a plus runner with speed and good instincts on the basepaths. Isbel hit .286/.362/.524 in 11 games when he returned to Kansas City’s lineup in September last season, a line the Royals believe is much more in tune with Isbel’s skillset. His speed and versatility give him a good chance at making the Royals’ Opening Day roster as a fourth or platoon outfielder, and the club has enough confidence in him to give him a starting job if one opens.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An All-Star performance in the 2017 Cape Cod League improved Isbel’s Draft stock heading into his junior year at UNLV, and he only built on that showing, ranking third in the Mountain West Conference in home runs (14) and fourth in average (.357). The Royals noticed Isbel’s development and selected him in the third round of the 2018 Draft, then watched as he totaled 31 extra-base hits and 24 steals while reaching full-season ball that year. Injuries delayed Isbel’s progress at Class A Advanced Wilmington in 2019, but he was able to finish the season healthy and had a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. He spent 2020 progressing at the Royals’ alternate training site and instructional league at Kauffman Stadium. Isbel’s well-rounded set of tools sets him up well for the future, but it’s his ability to hit for both average and power that gives him a high ceiling. With a natural hitting ability to all fields and bat speed and strength fueling his left-handed swing, Isbel shows solid strike zone awareness. The Royals were pleased with how Isbel fared last summer against their top Minor League pitching, keeping the whiffs and chase trending down, while also instructing him to work on the fundamentals, like baserunning. While he’s not a top-tier runner, Isbel has plus speed and can hold his own as an above-average defender in center field thanks to good jumps on balls. Some see him more as a left fielder, where his average arm strength is a fit and power potential profiles as an everyday player there. The Royals also value his defense more in left field because of the expansive outfield at Kauffman Stadium. If anything, Isbel’s speed and versatility give him a solid floor as a fourth-outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 When the Reds signed Nick Senzel as the No. 2 pick in the 2016 Draft for more than $1.5 million under pick value, it enabled them to land Trammell for $3.2 million at No. 35 overall. The former Georgia high school star impressed at every stop of his development until stumbling a bit at Double-A in 2019. He really stood out on a national stage when he won MVP honors at the Futures Game in '18 after homering and tripling and then returned to the Futures Games again this July before being traded to the Padres later in the month in the three-team deal that sent Trevor Bauer from the Indians to the Reds. A multi-sport athlete in high school who had the chance to play football at Georgia Tech, Trammell's combination of natural ability, feel for the game and makeup have continued to lift him as he progresses through the system. In the Florida State League in 2018, while dealing with a nagging ankle injury, he continued efforts to lower his strikeout rate and draw walks, and he still showed left-handed pop while driving the ball. His ability to get on base will make him a regular stolen base threat that could frustrate defenses. That speed gives Trammell the chance to be a future center fielder. He has a below average arm, something he worked on during his stint in the Arizona Fall League. If he continues to get bigger and stronger and it slows him down, his bat should profile just fine in a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 • 7/22: India promoted to Double-A After a pair of relatively ordinary years at Florida, India enjoyed a huge breakout season as a junior and catapulted into top-10-pick conversations. The Reds selected him at No. 5 overall and signed him for $5,297,500, nearly $600,000 below pick value. Although he appeared to be exhausted following a college season, the College World Series and the Draft process, India still navigated his way through his first pro summer and appeared with three different affiliates. All the while, he still demonstrated why he was a top 5 Draft pick. With an advanced approach at the plate, he has excellent plate discipline and the ability to hit for average that should translate. India also has flashes of above-average power. Despite not being too speedy, he can be deceptively quick and is a solid baserunner with great instincts. A third baseman in college, India played there and at shortstop and could also likely man second base. He has a strong above-average arm with fielding skills and athleticism that would likely enable him to play multiple positions well. Like Nick Senzel, who was also an advanced college hitter from an SEC school, India could move through the Reds' system fairly quickly, and he could potentially be a regular player around the infield until an everyday spot is found.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCormick is one step away from becoming the first Millersville (Pa.) position player to reach the Majors. He batted .373/.441/.524 with a Pennsylvania State Athletic Conference-record 306 hits in four years at the NCAA Division II school before signing for $1,000 as a 21st-rounder in 2017. He set career highs in most categories while reaching Triple-A in 2019 and earned SportsCenter's Top 10 Plays recognition in May when he flipped over the right-field fence to rob a home run. Though McCormick has made consistent contact and controlled the strike zone since turning pro, that's not enough to get a corner outfielder to the big leagues. He has improved his chances by making adjustments to his right-handed swing to drive more balls in the air, allowing him to do a better job of using his solid raw power. An aggressive runner with average to solid speed, he does a nice job of picking spots to steal. McCormick's quick reads and efficient routes allow him to play all three outfield positions. He's a solid defender on the corners and average in center, and his average arm works at all three spots. His grinder makeup allows him to get the most out of his tools and overcome his modest Draft pedigree.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Diamondbacks for $80,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2013, Vargas broke out in 2018 by winning the High-A California League's pitcher of the year award. Arizona added him to its 40-man roster that November but lost him two years later on waivers to the White Sox. After Chicago outrighted him last February, he responded by posting a 2.90 ERA with 99 strikeouts in 84 innings while taking three weeks off to help the Dominican Republic qualify for the Olympics. Vargas lacks sexy stuff but is fearless on his mound, challenging hitters with a low-90s fastball that plays better than its velocity thanks to its carry up in the zone and his ability to spot it on either side of the plate. His best pitch is a low-80s changeup that plummets at the plate and keeps left-handers from teeing off on him. His low-80s slider can be effective but also devolves into a slurve at times. Re-signed as a Minor League free agent last November, Vargas works quickly and relies on throwing strikes and mixing pitches in order to succeed. Without a solid offering or exceptional command, he's a back-of-the-rotation starter at best and perhaps no more than a middle reliever. But he posted better numbers than any of Chicago's starting pitching prospects at the upper levels last year and could contribute to the big league club in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of former Major League pitcher David Weathers, Ryan set a Tennessee high school tournament record with 28 strikeouts as a junior, including 12 in a shutout in the Class A championship game, and turned in two scoreless outings for Team USA as it won the 18-and-under World Cup in September. He followed it up as a senior by going 10-0 with a 0.09 ERA and 148 strikeouts in 76 innings, and the Padres took him with No. 7 overall pick last June, marking the second straight year that the club had selected the Gatorade National Baseball High School Player of the Year, following MacKenzie Gore, the No. 3 pick in 2017. Weathers signed for slot value at $5,226,500, forgoing a Vanderbilt commitment, and finished his pro debut with a taste of the Class A Midwest League. Weathers has three big league-caliber pitches that he mixes well. An uptick in velocity in 2020 now has his fastball topping out at 97 mph and sitting comfortably in the mid-90s. The pitch has a high spin rate that gives it deceptive riding life, and he commands it with pinpoint precision. Weathers’ changeup continues to be his top secondary weapon, and he has made major strides in advancing a relatively new slider -- an above-average, swing-and-miss pitch that he throws at 85-87 mph with hard sweeping action. A good athlete who does the little things well, Weathers was expected to contribute as a two-way player had he honored his commitment to Vandy. He gets his athleticism from both sides of his family, as his mother, Kelli Davis Weathers, was an All-America basketball player at Belmont.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McClanahan spurned the Mets as a 26th-rounder in 2015 and honored his commitment to South Florida, only to have his freshman year wiped out by Tommy John surgery. He emerged as one of more interesting pitching prospects in the 2018 Draft as a junior by ranking second in the nation in strikeouts per nine innings (14.2), though a regression in command cost him some traction late in the spring. He still became a first-round pick in June, going to the Rays with the No. 31 overall pick, and received a slightly above-slot bonus of $2,230,100. McClanahan impressed during his brief pro debut, making four scoreless starts during which he fanned 13 and allowed three hits across seven innings. McClanahan's Draft stock took off early last spring with reports of the left-hander's fastball reaching 100 mph. It set an unfair standard for his future outings, and some teams were turned off when he failed to achieve the same elite velocity in subsequent starts. That being said, McClanahan does throw exceptionally hard, as he'll sit 92-95 mph and reach back for a few extra ticks. McClanahan's slider, though inconsistent, is an above-average pitch and complements his heater nicely, and scouts believe that his upper-80s changeup will be at least average once he develops better feel. McClanahan's high strikeout rate in college came with a high walk rate. That, plus a delivery that features a fairly big recoil, has led some evaluators to project him as a future reliever -- albeit one who could get to the big leagues in a hurry. But with a loose and very athletic frame, McClanahan might be able to get away with those mechanics, and the Rays are committed to developing him as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Kirilloff was one of the better pure hitters in the 2016 Draft class, taken by the Twins in the middle of the first round out of Plum High School outside of Pittsburgh. After a strong summer debut in the Rookie-level Appalachian League, however, the outfielder needed Tommy John surgery and missed all of 2017. There was uncertainty about how he would bounce back after the injury and long layoff, but Kirilloff responded by earning a promotion, going to the Futures Game and leading the Minors in total bases while finishing third in average and seventh in RBIs. If it weren't for Blue Jays phenom Vladimir Guerrero Jr., a strong argument can be made that Kirilloff is the best hitter in the Minor Leagues. He makes consistent, hard contact and can drive the ball to all fields. He has over-the-fence power the other way and also showed he can turn on pitches when needed, while making a seamless transition up to the pitching-friendly Florida State League. He's a sound and consistent right fielder, one who makes all the plays and can stay there long-term with an average arm. He might mix in some first base, where some think he could be a plus defender, to add some positional flexibility. That's more about making sure there's a spot for him when his bat is deemed ready, which might not be too far off in the future. He's already gained a lot of strength; the Twins are excited to see what he can do now that he's completely off of his rehab protocol and doesn't have to rediscover his timing after a year off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Many of Cubs' best pitching prospects missed the entire 2021 season, headlined by Marquez, who tested positive for COVID-19 before Spring Training and then came down with a shoulder impingement when he was ramping up to return to action. That came on the heels of the pandemic shutdown in 2020, when he made his lone appearance and big league debut on the final day of the season, giving up five runs while recording just two outs (one of which was a strikeout of Jose Abreu with a 99-mph fastball). The Dominican received the largest bonus ($600,000) of any left-hander in the 2015 international class but pitched just 257 2/3 innings in his first six years as a pro. As Marquez added strength and refined his delivery, his fastball went from sitting at 91-93 mph in 2017 to 93-96 in 2018 to 96-98 with a peak of 102 in his last full season in 2019. He doesn't always maintain consistent shape on his slider, but it can be a wipeout pitch in the mid-80s when at its best. He also flashes some promising life and deception with his changeup, though it often gets too firm and parks in the low 90s. Marquez still has the best pure stuff in the system, though he also comes with a good deal of reliever risk -- albeit with closer upside if he winds up in the bullpen. He has long limbs and a low three-quarters arm slot and has yet to prove he can repeat his mechanics and throw strikes on a regular basis. He started pounding the zone in his final seven starts back in 2019 but barely has pitched since.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marquez received the largest bonus ($600,000) any left-hander received on the international amateur market in 2015 and continually has added velocity since signing out of the Dominican Republic at age 16. He made his big league debut on the final day of the 2020 season as Chicago toyed with the idea of adding him to its playoff roster until he surrendered five runs while recording just two outs, one on a strikeout of Jose Abreu with a 99-mph fastball. He has yet to pitch in 2021 after coming down with COVID-19 before Spring Training, then a strained shoulder while building up his arm strength afterward. As Marquez has added strength and cleaned up his delivery, his heater has gone from parking at 91-93 mph in 2017 to 93-96 in 2018 to 96-98 in his last full season in 2019, when he peaked at 102. The Cubs have worked with him to maintain consistent shape on his breaking ball, which can be a power mid-80s slider at its best but also devolves into a slurve at times. He has dominated left-handed hitters in the Minors but in order to keep right-handers in check he'll need to continue to improve his changeup, which has promising life but often gets too firm and arrives in the low 90s. With long limbs and a low three-quarters arm slot, Marquez sometimes has difficulty repeating his delivery. He has made progress, however, slashing his walk rate from 5.8 per nine innings in his first 15 starts of 2019 to 1.9 in his final seven. He has the ceiling of a frontline starter but also comes with reliever risk, though he definitely has closer upside if he winds up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davidson hasn’t taken a typical path from the amateur ranks to the big leagues. Drafted by Atlanta in the 19th round of the 2016 Draft out of Midland College, a two-year school, he began his pro career as a reliever, moving into the rotation midway through his first full season. After a rough 2018, things clicked in ’19 as he reached Triple-A and was added to the 40-man roster. He made his big league debut the following year, but then missed nearly all of the 2021 season with a forearm strain, returning to start Game 5 of the World Series. He spent time in the big leagues without much success in 2022, but was pitching relatively well in Triple-A when he was sent to the Angels at the Trade Deadline in the Raisel Iglesias deal. When Davidson was on the mound in 2021, for all 43 regular season innings, he still was showing a four-pitch mix and an idea of what to do with it. His fastball averages right around 93 mph and touches 96 and when he’s fully stretched out and healthy, he’s shown the ability to maintain velocity deep into starts. Davidson entered pro ball with a curve, now in the upper-70s, and a mid-80s changeup, which he didn’t throw much last year, both of which are solid offerings. The addition of a slider in 2020 could be a game-changer, as it gave him a reliable secondary pitch to throw in the zone as opposed to his bigger curve and he’s used it since to miss bats. Davidson’s command has been inconsistent, but has largely trended in the right direction over the last couple of seasons in the Minors. That gives him a chance to start long-term, though the fastball-slider combination from the left side could be really nasty in shorter relief stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A total of four pitchers the Braves took in the 2016 Draft reached the big leagues by the end of the 2020 season. The first three were taken in the top five rounds, led by first-rounder Ian Anderson. The fourth was Davidson, a 19th-round selection out of Midland College, a two-year school in Texas. The left-hander hit the prospect radar with a move to the rotation part of the way through his first full season, scuffled a bit with a promotion in 2018, but then pitched his way from Double- to Triple-A in 2019 to earn a spot on the 40-man roster that offseason. He joined his Class of ’16 alum by making his big league debut with a relief outing near the end of the 2020 season. Davidson entered the 2020 season with a three-pitch mix, starting with a fastball that can touch 97 mph consistently, velocity he can maintain throughout his starts, missing bats up in the zone, but also sinking it down to get weak contact on the ground. He always had shown a feel for adding and subtracting from his curve, but like fellow lefty Kyle Muller, he added a distinct slider during his time at the alternate training site, a pitch that flashes above-average and now gives him four weapons in his arsenal. The lefty was able to cut his walk rate in 2019 and there’s still work to be done command-wise, though no one should read too much into his four-walk big league debut. Consistent strikes would give him the chance to start, though his stuff would tick up should he be needed to come out of the bullpen long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wander Javier was the prize of the 2015-16 international signing period for the Twins, receiving a $4 million bonus to sign on July 2. No one else got more than $10,000, including Colina, who signed as an 18-year-old in September 2015 for just $8,000. Developed mostly as a starter, the right-hander made his United States debut in 2017, his full-season debut in '18 and then pitched across three levels to reach Triple-A in '19. After pitching in relief at the Twins’ alternate training site, he made his big league debut late last September. Short, stocky and armed with power stuff, Colina profiles best as a future reliever. His fastball gets into the upper 90s with ease and has touched triple digits in the past -- he topped out at 99.7 mph in his one big league outing last year -- with a little sink to it. His slider is actually his best pitch, a true out pitch he throws a lot, and he commands it better than the fastball, a hard mid-80s breaking ball with good spin. He’d used a below-average changeup in the past as a starter, but that could be a thing of the past for him. His days as a starter behind him, how well Colina can find the strike zone -- and more precisely, how well he can command his fastball in the zone -- will determine what kind of future role he has. The Twins will continue to stretch him out so he can get reps needed to focus on command, with perhaps a gig as a multi-inning reliever in his immediate future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Doyle spent three years pitching almost exclusively out of the bullpen for the University of Virginia. Acting as the Cavaliers’ closer as a junior, he was among the nation’s best with 14 saves, which led to him being the Rockies’ second-round selection in the 2017 Draft. He’s moved one rung at a time over his first two full seasons of pro ball, pitching well in hitting-friendly environments while racking up 37 saves in 2018-19. The 6-foot-6 Doyle is imposing on the mound and does an excellent job using his size to create good downhill plane. He’s aggressive with his fastball that sits 96 mph and touches 98 at times, filling the strike zone with it. He can miss bats with it while also getting ground-ball outs. He complements his plus heater with a hard slurvy breaking ball that is a wipeout pitch to right-handed hitters and that he can use to back-foot lefties. He doesn’t use his changeup much, but he can be sneaky good with it. Doyle has done a nice job of throwing strikes, especially given his size and power repertoire. All he needs is some upper-level experience and he should be ready to impact a big league bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Oliva was an under-the-radar prospect as an amateur, one who wasn't drafted out of high school or when he was eligible at Arizona as a redshirt sophomore. The son and nephew of professional baseball players, Oliva did put himself on the map as a junior, but still wasn't taken until the Pirates nabbed him in the seventh round of the 2017 Draft. He was sent straight to the Class A Advanced Florida State League for his full season debut and excelled there, putting him on a path to easily surpass expectations. Lean and athletic with wiry strength, Oliva can do a lot of things well on the field. While there was some concern about swing and miss coming from a grooved swing, Oliva managed his strikeout rate well and drew walks while showing the ability to consistently impact the ball. Nine home runs might not sound like a lot, but in the pitching-friendly Florida State League, it's not bad and he has the potential for 12-15 homers a year. His speed is plus, and sometimes grades out as a 70 on the 20-to-80 scouting scale, allowing him to be a basestealing threat (he finished third in the system with 33 steals in 2018) and allowing him to play a solid defensive center field. Oliva has shown steady improvement since joining the organization and could be a steal of his Draft class. He might end up being a fourth outfielder when all is said and done, but don't be shocked if he shoots past that ceiling as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed back in May 2014, close to the end of the 2013-14 signing period, for $70,000, Medina has made a methodical climb up the Phillies’ organizational ladder, playing at one level per year, starting with the Dominican Summer League in the summer of 2014. He was added to the 40-man roster following his 2018 campaign in the Florida State League, moved up to Double-A in 2019 and after pitching at the team’s alternate training site in 2020, made his big league debut in late September and after giving up two runs in the first, put up three zeroes and retired the last eight batters he faced. Medina has always had good stuff, which has made it hard to figure out why he hasn’t dominated Minor League hitters as he advanced through the system. His fastball sits in the low-90s and can tick up to 95-96 and he throws it with a lot of sink, which produces ground-ball outs, including seven of them in his four-inning big league debut.
