His changeup flashes plus, a weapon he uses against lefties and righties, and the pitch that elicits the most swings and misses. His average slider is another weapon used to get weak contact. The right-hander is typically around the zone as he relies on contact early in counts rather than missing bats. The Phillies still love the way he competes and like how he settled down after initially getting touched up in his debut. He still has the ability to be a No. 4 type starter if given the opportunity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crochet rated as Mississippi's best prep pitching prospect in 2017 but wasn't quite ready for pro ball or particularly signable, so he fell to the Brewers in the 34th round. He bounced between Tennessee's rotation and bullpen in his first two college seasons, earning the Volunteers' first NCAA tournament victory since 2005 last June -- just two weeks after a line drive fractured and dislocated his jaw. He was sensational in fall practice, vaulting him into top-10-pick consideration, but missed three weeks as a precaution with soreness in his shoulder and made just one appearance during the truncated 2020 season. After working with a 91-95 mph fastball and topping out at 97 during the spring, Crochet dealt at 96-100 for most of the fall, and his heater already played better than its velocity because it has high spin rates. His 82-85 mph slider features above-average spin rates as well and his long arms create difficult angle on his breaking ball. He flashes a well above-average changeup at times, throwing it around 90 mph with deceptive arm speed. For a 6-foot-6 pitcher, Crochet does a nice job of keeping his long levers in sync and providing strikes. Scouts like his delivery and arm action, though he still needs to refine his command to make the most of his overpowering stuff. His short track record with his improved arsenal is a concern, but he still could surpass R.A. Dickey (18th overall, 1996) as the highest-drafted Volunteers pitcher ever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murphy underwent Tommy John surgery in high school at Hamilton (Ariz.) as a senior, but the Blue Jays believed in his upside and scooped up the right-hander in the third round in 2013. The next few years of his career were also held back by injuries, including thoracic outlet syndrome and ulnar transposition surgery. He finally put it all together in 2018, breaking out to garner Pitcher of the Year honors in the Florida State League before a late promotion to Double-A New Hampshire. Returning to the Eastern League in 2019, Murphy cruised through his first 11 starts (3.69 ERA, 9.2 K/9, 2.3 BB/9) before the Major League Baseball Umpires Association determined in early June that the toe-tap he uses in his delivery before planting his left leg was illegal, per Rule 5.07(a). Murphy made his brief MLB debut in 2020, but injuries popped up again in the offseason, forcing him to start 2021 on the IL with an AC joint injury in his right shoulder. After making eight Major League appearances for Toronto in 2021, Murphy was designated for assignment by the Jays and picked up off waivers by the Nationals in August. His fastball, which has some sink to it, sat in the 96-97 mph range last season, which Murphy pairs with his curveball as a primary secondary pitch. His changeup, which trails behind those pitches, is scarcely used, but there remains a focus on him developing that. Strike-throwing isn't an issue for Murphy, making him a reliable arm when he’s healthy. Given Murphy’s injury history, his career high of 152 2/3 innings from 2018 between Class A Advanced and Double-A is beginning to look like an outlier. His fastball-curveball combination gives him some legitimate upside in a relief role, though, and his ability to handle multiple innings lines him up well with evolving bullpen philosophies. Getting back on the mound will once again be Murphy’s first priority this season, but he should have an opportunity to pitch himself back onto the roster when the time comes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While McKinstry showed some promising contact skills and defensive ability in two seasons at Central Michigan, he didn't hit the ball with much authority or draw a lot of attention as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2016. After the Dodgers took a 33rd-round flier on him and signed him two days before the deadline for $100,000, he reached Double-A during his first full pro season but began 2018 back in low Class A. He finally broke out last year, hitting .300/.366/.516 with 19 homers between Double-A and Triple-A to claim a spot on the 40-man roster. McKinstry has grown into solid raw power since adding strength and some loft to his left-handed stroke. Though he has gotten more aggressive at the plate, he still makes regular contact and draws his share of walks. He has solid speed out of the batter's box but it doesn't translate into basestealing prowess. With his quickness and plus arm strength, McKinstry is a quality defender at second base (his primary position), similar if a bit more erratic at third base and capable at shortstop. He also saw brief action at all three outfield spots last season. His combination of offensive ability and versatility could make him a lefty-hitting version of Chris Taylor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the last 10 Drafts, there have been four high school players taken No. 1 overall. One didn’t sign, another hasn’t made it to the big leagues yet. Carlos Correa, the top pick in 2012, was 20 when he made his big league debut. Moniak, who the Phillies took with the No. 1 pick in the 2016 Draft has been a disappointment to some based on his production in the Minors. But the outfielder still made his big league debut, at age 22, in 2020 after being a late addition to the Phillies’ alternate training site. Perhaps Moniak will never be the elite-level player teams hope to get with the top pick in the Draft, but skeptics should be reminded that he’s both still very young and showing progress, especially in terms of his work at the plate. The left-handed hitter has shown an ability to impact the baseball more as he’s matured, though it came with a free-swinging approach that has led to rough strikeout-to-walk ratios. The Phillies saw a hitter at their alternate site who was making better swing decisions, one who doubled his walk rate there and drew four walks in 18 plate appearances in the big leagues. That should allow him to get to his extra-base pop more consistently. While he’s not a burner, Moniak runs very well underway and is an excellent baserunner. His overall athleticism might be undervalued a bit, as he can play center field and showed an ease with sliding over to left in the big leagues with an accurate arm. He might be a valuable fourth outfielder when all is said and done, but it’s too soon to write him off as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Houck starred during three seasons at Missouri and two summers with the U.S. collegiate national team, though his lower arm slot led some teams to question his long-term future as a starter. The Red Sox have an ace (Chris Sale) who faced the same concerns coming out of college and weren't worried, selecting Houck with the No. 24 overall pick in 2017 and signing him for $2,614,500. Houck tried to reinvent himself during his first full pro season and got shelled for a 6.16 ERA during the first half of 2018, then went back to what worked as an amateur and logged a 2.86 ERA in the second half. Houck is at his best when he pitches off his two-seam fastball and his slider. His 92-96 mph two-seamer has heavy sink and bore, and right-handers have trouble picking it up out of his low-three-quarters crossfire delivery. His low-80s slider has plenty of lateral break and also gives righties fits. At the start of last year, Houck relied more on a four-seamer that can reach 98 mph and a curveball with more depth while working from a higher slot, a combination that cost him command and deception. His biggest need is to improve his changeup so he can handle left-handers more efficiently. The Red Sox are committed to developing him as a starter whose ceiling could land him in the middle of their rotation, though some scouts think he'll become a multi-inning reliever who will beat up on right-handers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A third-round pick by Minnesota in 2015, Blankenhorn didn't progress as quickly as hoped but did make his big league debut last September and doubled in his lone start. He had trouble finding a defensive home with the Twins, who designated him for assignment this May soon after he made a critical error in an extra-innings loss to the Athletics. He made brief stops with the Dodgers and Mariners as part of the waiver-wire merry-go-round before landing with the Mets on June 1. Blankenhorn has a chance to hit for average and power from the left side of the plate, and he set a career high with 19 homers in his last full season in 2019 after he started turning on more pitches. While his bat-to-ball skills allow him to make enough contact, his aggressive approach limits his ability to draw walks and get the most out of his solid raw pop. He has the upside of a .270 hitter with 20 homers per year if he receives regular at-bats. The biggest question is where Blankenhorn fits on the diamond with his fringy speed and hands and average arm strength. The Twins used him primarily at second and third base, but those positions seem to be a stretch at the big league level. They started giving him more time in left field in 2019 and that ultimately may be his best option, though he really profiles best as an offensive-minded utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marchan had just started catching when the Phillies signed him for $200,000 in July 2015 and he’d made incremental progress up the organizational ladder with stops in the Dominican Summer League, Gulf Coast League and New York-Penn League in 2016-18. He made his full-season debut in 2019 and earned a promotion up a level, but wasn’t added to the 40-man roster that offseason because he was so far away. A strong showing in Spring Training put him on the radar with the big league staff, and when there was a need in September, he got called up to fill in behind the plate and picked up his first professional home run of any sort along the way. There’s no question that Marchan’s defensive profile enabled him to get to Philadelphia despite not having played above A ball previously. He’s an outstanding defender with a plus arm that has controlled the running game well in the lower levels of the Minors. An excellent receiver, there’s understandably still work to be done in terms of game-calling at the big league level, but given his high baseball IQ, no one doubts he’ll master that part of his craft as well. Marchan’s offense is also improving. He’s shown an ability to make a ton of contact without striking out, sending line drives to all fields from both sides of the plate. He’s gotten physically stronger, with his exit velocities trending up, meaning he’s impacting the ball more and should run into a few more home runs moving forward. All of this points to a future as a big league starting backstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 The seventh overall pick in the 2016 Draft, Garrett signed for $4,145,900, but blew out his elbow in his fourth pro start and required Tommy John surgery in June 2017. He returned to the mound 22 months later and has spent parts of the past two seasons with the Marlins, logging a 5.18 ERA while winning two of his nine starts. He once had the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter, but his stuff has backed up as he has shuttled between Triple-A and Miami. Scouts rated Garrett's curveball as one of the best in the 2016 high school class, but it wasn't as powerful or sharp as usual in 2021, when it sat around 75-79 mph. He had more success last year with his recently added slider, which operates at 83-85 mph with sweep and drop, and he shows feel for backfooting it against right-handers. He utilizes two- and four-seam fastballs, which usually range from 88-91 mph and feature ordinary life, while his mid-80s changeup has some fade but not enough velocity separation from his heaters. Garrett has a history of throwing strikes but has nibbled around the zone in the Majors, where hitters have teed off on his diminished stuff. The hope is that he can find a better rhythm if he stops bouncing back and forth from Triple-A and reclaim the solid fastball and plus curveball he featured in the past. If not, he's probably looking at a future as a reliever who relies on his breaking pitches to survive.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The third-highest drafted Alabama high schooler ever, Garrett went seventh overall in 2016 and signed for $4,145,900. He blew out his elbow in his fourth pro start and had Tommy John surgery in June 2017, costing him all of the following season. He made a strong return to the mound in 2019 and debuted in the big leagues last September with two brief starts. Garrett has regained what scouts considered one of the best curveballs in the 2016 prep class, a low-80s bender with quality depth that's effective against both lefties and righties. His fastball is more notable for his command and downhill angle than velocity or life, and it parked around 89 mph during his brief stint in the Majors after sitting at 90-93 and topping out at 96 the year before. His fading changeup projects as a solid third offering as he continues to use it more often. Garrett has nice feel for locating his pitches and sequencing them to set up hitters. After big leaguers teed off on his diminished fastball, he'll need to find more consistent velocity in order to reach his ceiling of a mid-rotation starter. The hope is that his heater will bounce back with more regular work in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stiever led the Big Ten Conference with 97 strikeouts in 100 1/3 as an Indiana junior in 2018, but a bad final start and minor physical issues dropped him to the White Sox in the fifth round. He almost immediately emerged as one of Chicago's top pitching prospects but his stuff and control haven't been the same since he had forearm soreness in Spring Training 2020 and lat surgery in August 2021. He didn't pitch last year until making three brief appearances in the final week of the Triple-A season. At his best, Stiever owned a 92-98 mph fastball with run and sink and an unusual ability to locate a plus spike curveball in the upper 70s. During his last extended stretch on the mound in 2021, he showed less life on his fastball and less power and control with his curve. His low-80s slider was his most reliable pitch that season, with a fading low-80s changeup serving as a decent fourth option. An all-state wide receiver and defensive back as a Wisconsin high schooler, Stiever has plenty of athleticism to repeat his delivery and provide solid control. But after his stuff took a downturn, he became less willing to challenge hitters and nibbled around the strike zone. He should be 100 percent physically in 2023, and the White Sox hope he can regain his past form.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stiever topped the Big Ten Conference with 97 strikeouts in 100 1/3 innings as an Indiana junior in 2018, but a bad final start and minor physical concerns enabled the White Sox to grab him in the fifth round. He quickly emerged as one of the organization's best pitching prospects but his stuff and control have taken a downturn since he was bothered by forearm soreness during Spring Training in 2020. He made three appearances with Chicago in 2020-21, surrendering 10 runs in 6 1/3 innings, but hasn't pitched in a game since having lat surgery in August 2021. After his velocity dipped in 2020, Stiever was back working at 92-96 mph and topping out at 98 with his four-seamer last season, but his fastball showed less life and got barreled regularly. His most reliable pitch is now his 81-85 mph slider, while he not only has lost some power with his now-mid-70s spike curveball but also his ability to land it for strikes. His low-80s changeup with fade is a decent fourth option. An all-state wide receiver and defensive back as a Wisconsin high schooler, Stiever has the athleticism to repeat his delivery and provide solid control. But as his stuff has regressed, he has nibbled around the strike zone and been less willing to challenge hitters. He once showed the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter but now looks more like a middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Indiana University's best pitching prospect since Eric Arnett went in 2009's first round, Stiever led the Big Ten Conference in strikeouts (97 in 100 1/3 innings) as a junior in 2018, but a bad final outing and minor physical concerns caused him to slide to the White Sox in the fifth round. His stuff kicked up a notch during his first full pro season, which he finished with a dozen strong starts in high Class A. He was bothered by forearm soreness during the first iteration of 2020 Spring Training and has regressed since then. After sitting at 92-96 mph and topping out at 98 with his fastball in 2019, Stiever has lost a couple of ticks of velocity and hasn't been able to keep his heater off barrels. His only reliable offerings have been his pair of solid breaking balls, a low-80s slider and a mid-70s spike curveball that also has dropped in terms of velocity. He rounds out his arsenal with a decent changeup with fade. An all-star wide receiver and defensive back as a Wisconsin high schooler, Stiever uses his athleticism to repeat his delivery well and throw strikes. He has become less aggressive about challenging hitters as he has gotten hammered in Triple-A and the Majors. He showed the possibility of becoming a mid-rotation starter in 2019 and Chicago hopes he can recapture that form.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Signed out of Mexico in 2016, Kirk appeared in only one game during his professional debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League after he re-aggravated a hand injury that he initially suffered in a car accident. Fully healthy in 2018, Kirk established himself as a legitimate prospect by hitting .354/.443/.558 with 10 home runs and 57 RBIs over 58 games in the Rookie-level Appalachian League. Kirk ranked among the Appy League leaders in a host of categories, as he finished third in average, fourth in OBP (.443) and slugging (.558) and tied for first in RBIs. Employing a direct and impactful swing, Kirk has natural hitting ability and above-average raw power to his pull side. He got to it during games consistently in 2018, though he's expected to be more of a hit-over-power guy as he moves through the Minors. Scouts like Kirk's chances of becoming at least an average hitter, in part because he controls the strike zone so well, as evidenced by the 33/21 BB/K ratio he posted in 2018. Listed at 5-foot-9, 220 pounds, Kirk isn't particularly athletic, nor does he run well. He's a good blocker, though, and earns praise for his solid arm strength and catch-and-throw skills that helped him throw out 43 percent of attempted basestealers in 2018. Kirk will need to make a slew of improvements to stay behind the plate, but there are some scouts who believe he'll do just that, viewing him as a potential bat-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 There are never locks when it comes to the MLB Draft, but Smith, perhaps the best college hitter in his class, sure had the look. As a Virginia junior in 2017, Smith walked three times more than he struck out en route to a .342/.427/.570 line. He also homered more than he struck out and finished sixth all-time on the Cavaliers' career home run list and second on their RBI list. After the D-backs took him with the No. 7 overall pick in June, he posted the Northwest League's third-best average (.318) but didn't show any over-the-fence power. The power wasn't there for Smith in his first full season either, as he finished with 11 homers in 120 games in the hitter-friendly California League. He did, however, swing the bat better as the summer unfolded, hitting .297/.362/.432 over his final 51 contests. At his best, Smith rarely swings and misses and drives the ball to all fields well from the left side of the plate. But he got away from those strengths and become too pull-heavy in 2018, trying to force his power rather than let it happen naturally, as a product of his all-around improvements. Going forward, the D-backs want Smith to focus simply on being a good hitter. But as a below-average runner who is limited to first base defensively, Smith's power will have to start showing up in games for him to profile as anything more than a bench bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-round pick out of an Arizona high school in 2016, Huff broke out in 2019 by slugging 28 homers and winning MVP honors at the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game. He hadn't played above High-A when the Rangers promoted him to the Majors in September 2020 to fill a hole left by injuries, yet he responded with three homers in nine games. He injured his right knee during Spring Training last year, necessitating surgery that cost him the first two months of the season and limited him to first base and DH once he returned. Few players can hit a ball as hard or as far as Huff, who combines bat speed, strength and leverage in a massive 6-foot-5 frame and posts the highest exit velocities among Rangers farmhands since Joey Gallo. The right-handed hitting slugger also has an extreme grip-it-and-rip-it approach at the plate that has resulted in a 31 percent strikeout rate in pro ball and an alarming 39 percent whiff rate in 2021 alone. He probably won't ever hit for average or draw many walks, but he has elite raw power that shows up against both lefties and righties. Huff will return behind the plate this year and is surprisingly agile for his size. He has significantly improved his receiving and framing since turning pro, and his arm earns well above-average grades from some scouts. Only eight players 6-foot-5 or larger have caught as many as 300 games in the Majors, but he has worked hard in an attempt to become the ninth.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The first Arizona high schooler drafted in 2016, Huff signed for $225,000 in the seventh round after leading the state with 14 homers that spring. After spending two years in Rookie ball and a third in low Class A, he broke out in 2019 by slamming 28 homers and winning MVP honors at the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game. Though he hadn't played above High-A, the Rangers promoted him last September when injuries left them shorthanded, and he responded with three homers in nine starts. He missed the first two months of the 2021 season after April surgery on his right knee to repair some minor damage he sustained during Minor League Spring Training, then was limited to first base and DH once he returned. The strength and leverage in Huff's 6-foot-5 frame and his aggressive approach give him more raw pop than any catching prospect in the game and produce the highest exit velocities of any Rangers farmhand since Joey Gallo. His grip-it-and-rip-it approach has resulted in four times as many strikeouts as walks and a 30 percent whiff rate as a pro, so he may never hit for a high average. The right-handed slugger likely will have to make adjustments against more advanced pitching but his power plays against both lefties and righties and to all parts of the ballpark. While just five players 6-foot-5 or larger have caught as many as 300 games in the Majors, Huff has worked diligently to give him a chance to become the sixth. He's surprisingly quick for his size, has significantly improved his receiving since turning pro and scores well in Texas' framing metrics. His pure arm strength earns well above-average grades from some evaluators and he has quickened his release since signing, allowing him to throw out 48 percent of basestealers in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros made a haul early in the 2015 Draft, taking future big leaguers Alex Bregman and Kyle Tucker within the top five picks before selecting Cameron at No. 37 overall and signing him for $4 million. Viewed as someone who might need extra time to develop in the Minors, Cameron was overmatched in his first taste of full-season ball in 2016, and he also struggled at the outset of 2017 before things started to click. He was finishing off a fantastic second half in the Midwest League when the Astros packaged him with Franklin Perez and Jake Rogers to the Tigers for Justin Verlander. He began to put it all together in 2018, ascending from high Class A to Triple-A at age 21 before a standout turn in the Arizona Fall League. The son of former big league center fielder Mike Cameron, Daz has the chance to be an impactful up-the-middle big leaguer as well. Mechanical changes that put him in a better position to hit made a huge difference and contributed directly to his turnaround at the plate. Perhaps more importantly, Cameron has developed a real approach at the plate, showing selective aggressiveness with a hit-to-all fields mentality early in the count. He's started to tap into some power, too, and some scouts believe he'll be a 15-20-homer guy in the big leagues. A plus runner and overall graceful athlete, Cameron can steal a base but will have to learn to be more efficient in the future. That speed to go along with plus defensive instincts will allow him to stay in center for the long haul, and he has the arm strength needed for an outfield corner. Cameron's ceiling is still coming into focus, but all the pieces are there for him to develop into an everyday center fielder at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of high school, Kremer attended San Joaquin Delta (Calif.) JC and became the first Israeli citizen to be selected in the MLB Draft when the Padres took him in the 38th round in 2015. The next year, after a transfer to Nevada-Las Vegas, Kremer became the first to sign with an MLB organization when the Dodgers paid him $147,500 as a 14th-rounder. Kremer struggled as a swingman in the California League in his first full season but returned to the level in 2018 and dominated as a starter. The performance netted Kremer his first Double-A promotion in early July, though he would make only one Texas League start (a seven-inning, 11-strikeout gem) before heading to the Orioles as one of five prospects dealt by the Dodgers to get Manny Machado. He was excellent in eight starts for Double-A Bowie after the trade to finish his breakout campaign with a 2.88 ERA and a Minor League-best 178 strikeouts. His progress delayed by an oblique injury at the outset of 2019, though he made a healthy return to the mound in May. The Dodgers had Kremer focus on throwing his curveball more in 2018, and it quickly became his best weapon. It's a plus pitch with big break that nets him whiffs both inside and out of the zone, one he's comfortable throwing it in any count. Kremer's fastball is lively, as he'll operate at 91-95 mph and touch 96, with late, arm-side run. He fills out his four-pitch mix with a slider that flashes above-average potential and a fringy changeup that requires further development. He throws strikes with his entire arsenal and has the ability to retire hitters on both sides of the plate. Kremer didn't start pitching full-time until he got to junior college and was young for his draft class, so there's reason to believe he has even more room to develop. He looks like a future No. 4 starter given his current profile, though improvements to his slider and changeup could push him higher up the rotational hierarchy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres had high hopes for Campusano’s right-handed bat when they made him the first catcher selected in the 2017 Draft, signing the Georgia high schooler for $1.3 million after taking him in the second round. He broke out at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore in 2019 and earned California League co-MVP honors after he led the circuit in batting (.325) while also ranking second in OPS (.906) and RBI (81). Campusano continued to rake at San Diego’s alternate training site in 2020 and was called up to make his Major League debut that September as a 21-year-old. He announced his arrival by hitting an opposite-field home run in his first Major League game but spent the rest of the regular season on the injured list due to a left wrist strain. He appeared in 11 games with the Padres last season, but spent the bulk of 2021 in Triple-A, where he hit .295 and matched his career high with 15 homers. Campusano’s bat has impressed throughout his time in the Padres organization. A combination of physical strength and explosive bat speed produces impressive exit velocities, and added loft has helped him tap into more power as he’s matured. Campusano possesses an advanced, selectively aggressive approach and has shown the ability to use the entire field. Defensively, Campusano has the athleticism, agility and strong arm needed to stick behind the plate, and he’s made significant gains with his blocking and receiving since signing. Campusano has all the tools to become an everyday catcher in the big leagues, including a combination of hitting ability and power that could make him a middle-of-the-order run producer. He has stalled a bit at Triple-A in 2022, but at just 23 years old, he still has some time to meet that solid ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres had high hopes for Campusano’s right-handed bat when they made him the first catcher to be selected in the 2017 Draft, signing him for $1.3 million after taking the Georgia prep in the second round. He broke out in earnest at Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore in 2019 to earn California League co-MVP honors after he led the circuit in batting (.325) while also ranking second in OPS (.906) and RBI (81). Campusano continued to rake at San Diego’s alternate training site in 2020, so much so that the Padres decided to call up the 21-year-old catcher in early September. He announced his arrival by hitting an opposite-field home run in his first Major League game but spent the rest of the regular season on the injured list due to a left wrist strain. Campusano has demonstrated growth as a hitter in every season. He hits the ball hard using a blend of physical strength and explosive bat speed, while improving the leverage and contact point in his swing has helped him unlock his plus power. Campusano’s plate coverage and bat path through the zone fuel his hit-to-all-fields mindset at the plate, and he already demonstrates an advanced, selectively aggressive approach as well as a penchant for punishing mistakes. Defensively, Campusano has the athleticism, agility and strong arm needed to stick behind the plate, and he’s made significant gains with his blocking and receiving since signing. Campusano has all the components needed to become an everyday catcher in the big leagues, including a combination of hitting ability and power that could make him a middle-of-the-order run producer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Schmidt had Tommy John surgery a month before the 2017 Draft, the Yankees believed in his talent enough to select him 16th overall, allowing them to sign him for a below-slot $2,184,300 bonus and invest more in later picks. He arrived in New York in September 2020 with just 114 innings of pro experience but has battled his command in brief big league trials the last two years. Expected to contend for a rotation spot last spring, he instead strained his elbow and didn't return until late July. Schmidt's velocity was down a bit in 2021, but when at his best he'll range from 92-97 mph with his two- and four-seam fastballs, creating heavy sink on the former and cut and carry on the latter. His secondary pitches did a much better job of dodging bats than his fastball did last season, led by a low-80s curveball with power and depth. He also dusted off an upper-80s slider/cutter that he had shelved for a while, and both it and a tumbling changeup with similar velocity can be plus offerings when they're on. Schmidt has the quality arsenal to help the Yankees as a starter, but he'll have to refine his command to make an impact. He has a history of throwing strikes, but his command has never been as sharp as his control, and he has struggled to keep big leaguers from pounding his fastball. He doesn't have an especially athletic delivery and must prove he can handle a full workload after elbow issues cropped up in 2019 and 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schmidt had Tommy John surgery a month before the 2017 Draft but still went in the first round, signing for a below-slot $2,184,300 as the 16th overall pick. The Yankees didn't really turn him loose until 2019, when he looked better than ever down the stretch while leading Trenton to the Double-A Eastern League championship. He continued to shine in Spring Training, Summer Camp and at New York's alternate training site last year, and he made his big league debut in September with just 114 innings of pro experience. Schmidt employs both two- and four-seam fastballs that range from 92-97 mph with heavy sink on the former and cut and carry on the latter. His curveball took a step forward after he scrapped a promising slider to focus on one breaking ball, and it's now his best pitch, a power bender that sits at 82-85 mph with high spin rates and quality depth. He also has a tumbling changeup that grades as plus at its best. Though Schmidt has a history of throwing strikes, his command isn't as strong as his control and he got knocked around in his brief introduction to the Majors when he fell behind in the count too often. His delivery isn't the smoothest but does provide some deception. His lack of size and his mechanics led to concerns about his durability prior to his Tommy John surgery, and he missed a month in 2019 with minor elbow inflammation before getting sidelined again this spring with an elbow strain.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Twins liked Rooker a bit in 2016 after he turned in a decent redshirt sophomore season at Mississippi State, taking a flier on him in the 38th round. He went back to school rather than sign and had a huge year, catapulting him into first-round consideration. The Twins were ready again, this time getting their man at No. 35 overall and signing him for full pick value. After a huge pro debut in the summer of 2017, Rooker was pushed to Double-A for his first full season, where he hit for power, but saw other parts of his offensive game regress. There is no question that Rooker's best position is batter's box. He's looking more like a power-over-hit type of offensive player, one with legitimate raw pop. He's always had swing and miss to his game, and his strikeout rate spiked with the aggressive move to Double-A. It's offset somewhat by his ability to draw walks and there's some hope that at his peak, he'll be a bit more well-rounded as a hitter than he was in 2018. He should be a good enough hitter for that power to play at any level. The big question surrounding Rooker is where he might play defensively. He saw time at first and left field in 2018, and the plan is to give him a consistent time split at both. He's below-average in both spots, with the hope that he can become adequate enough at one so he's not a DH at a very young age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Weigel bounced around to three different colleges as an amateur and after a solid junior season pitching in relief at the University of Houston, the Braves made him their seventh-round pick in 2015. Given a chance to start, the big right-hander had reached Triple-A and was just about knocking on the big league door when he needed Tommy John surgery. He did return at the very end of the summer in 2018 and participated in instructional league play, then shook off the rust to pitch his way back to Triple-A in 2019 and got called up to Atlanta for the first time in July, though he didn't appear in a game during his first stint in the big leagues. Weigel pitches at 93-94 mph as a starter but showed the ability to get 97-98 mph on occasion, and could pitch there consistently in shorter stints should the Braves ever put him back in the bullpen. He does have two distinct breaking balls, and he'll go back and forth depending on which one he has a better feel for. It might behoove him to focus on one, with the slider the leading candidate, if he returns to relieving. His changeup does give him an option against left-handed hitters. Now healthy, Weigel is once again ready to impact the big league staff. He could serve as a back end starter, but it might be exciting to see how his already-good stuff plays up as a short reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Charlie Hayes spent parts of 14 years in the big leagues as a solid third baseman. His son, Ke'Bryan, the second of two first-round picks of the Pirates in 2015, is just about ready to reach that highest level himself. After a strong season in Double-A that included a trip to the Futures Game and an Eastern League All-Star nod, the younger Hayes has the chance to be a better all-around player than his dad. Hayes continues to improve as a hitter. He's always had a solid approach at the plate, but it's become even more refined, with a walk rate that went up for a third straight season in 2018. So did his ability to drive the ball. While he still largely uses a contact-first approach, Hayes set career highs in extra-base hits and slugging percentage, and there's more over-the-fence power to come as he matures and continues to add strength. That might slow him down a touch, but he's still smart enough on the basepaths to steal bases. There might not be a better defensive third baseman in the Minors, with his agility, hands, arm and instincts all pointing to future Gold Glove awards. Hayes will be 22 years old for all of the 2019 season, with plenty of room for growth from an already-impressive toolset. He has every chance to be an elite-level third baseman at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2015 international class produced a pair of Bahamian shortstops in Lucius Fox and Chisholm. But while Fox was the more touted amateur prospect and signed with the Giants for $6 million, it's been Chisholm who has blossomed into the better pro prospect since signing with the Diamondbacks for $200,000. He led all Minor League shortstops with 25 homers in 2018, starred in the Arizona Fall League after the season and has continued to hit for power in Double-A this year, during which he got traded to the Marlins for Zac Gallen in July. Chisholm posts impressive exit velocities from the left side of the plate with an explosive swing that has natural loft. He showed in 2018 that he not only could tap into his plus raw power, but also apply it across the entire field, as some of his longest home runs were hit to straightaway center. His power does come with swing-and-miss tendencies, so he'll need to refine his aggressive approach as he develops. He's an above-average runner who receives praise for his instincts on the basepaths. There is little question Chisholm can stay at shortstop, with good hands and actions to go along with a strong arm and a knack for making highlight-reel plays on a nightly basis. Those loud tools on both sides of the ball in turn give him an exceptional ceiling as a big league shortstop, but he'll need to tighten up his overall game along the way.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed back in July 2015 out of the Dominican Republic for $50,000, Santos has been moving methodically up the Rockies system, typically earning a promotion halfway through a season, then beginning the following year back at that level. Though he’s had mixed results, that incremental progress got him to Double-A in 2019 as a durable, strike-throwing starter, but he opened some eyes with an impressive performance as a reliever in the Arizona Fall League and earned a spot on the 40-man roster. Santos has perhaps the best control in the system, with a walk rate of 1.7 per nine innings over the course of his career, and has the chance to have a decent three-pitch mix to go along with it. In shorter stints in the AFL, his fastball velocity crept up and he was 94-96 mph and was sitting 95 mph. His secondary stuff, a slider and changeup, aren’t as good as his fastball, but could be average pitches in time. He’ll need them to take a step forward so he can have something resembling an out pitch to complement his firm fastball. Thanks to a simple delivery and arm stroke, Santos consistently fills up the strike zone, though the lack of premium stuff has caused him to be hit at times. If he can refine his secondary pitches, he could be a No. 5 type starter, but the Rockies now know his repertoire ticks up a bit in shorter stints out of the 'pen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Most of the international signings that make a splash involve six or seven figures and a 16-year-old with a ridiculous ceiling. Hernandez has the ceiling right, but he signed at age 19 and received just $15,000 to sign in July 2016 out of Venezuela. His 2017 pro debut in the Appalachian League was up-and-down, but he started showing why the Royals are excited about him with a move to full-season ball in 2018, though his season was delayed by a death in the family early and cut short by some fatigue at the end of the summer. He wasn't able to make much progress in 2019, as a fractured rib suffered in Spring Training kept him off the mound until June. Projectable at 6-foot-4, Hernandez is still growing into his body and his fastball. He easily sits around 94 mph and touches 97 mph regularly, with many feeling he could be sitting in the 96- to 97-mph range at some point in the future. At its best, the right-hander's curve is better than his changeup, though the latter is more consistent. With his long levers, it's hard for him to repeat his mechanics on his breaking ball, but it has the potential to be a plus pitch. He's showing an increasing ability to land all three pitches for strikes. Hernandez's fatigue at the end of the year led to some minor arm issues, but those mostly stemmed from him not being physically prepared for a long season. The hope is to get him through a full season healthy, with a full slate of starts, as he continues to mature both physically and mentally to the rigors of being a starting pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones comes from a long line of gridiron stars. His late father, Andre, starred for the NFL’s Detroit Lions, and his brothers T.J. and Malachi both played professional football. Jones had pedigree with the pigskin, too, but he chose baseball in high school and became a second-round pick of the Angels in 2015, signing an over-slot bonus before climbing their system ranks. Jones made his big league debut with the Angels in 2020 and then was traded to Baltimore in the deal for Alex Cobb in February 2021. He joined the O’s to significant fanfare down the stretch but struggled on both sides of the ball in an underwhelming 26-game cameo. The ups and downs are nothing new for Jones, who changed positions immediately after signing, moved back to second base in 2018, and benefited from strong Arizona Fall League showings in both ’18 and ’19. He’s always been lauded for his makeup and work ethic, which are considered off the charts, and shown a willingness to put in extra work and make adjustments. As a prospect, he’s displayed good bat speed and some raw power from the right side of the plate, solid plate discipline and the ability to string together good at-bats on a consistent basis. While the Angels regularly shuffled Jones back and forth between second base and the outfield, he played mostly second with the Orioles in ’21 and exclusively second in Baltimore. But the early results were not good, either by traditional metrics like errors or advanced stats like Outs Above Average. Jones is expected to get another crack at the starting second base job in 2022 but will need to shore up his glove work, at minimum, to do so. Now 24, he’s still young enough to develop into an everyday second baseman with the floor of a very useful role player off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones comes from a football family. One brother, T.J., is a wide receiver for the Detroit Lions. His other brother, Malachi, was the Arena Football League Receiver of the Year in 2018, and his late father, Andre, won a national title with Notre Dame. Jahmai Jones was a two-sport star but always felt baseball was his passion, signing with the Angels for above pick value in the second round of the 2015 Draft. An outfielder at the outset of his pro career, he shifted to second base in 2018 and reached Double-A. Jones played second base in high school, but the jury had been out in his Draft year whether he would be better suited there or in the outfield. He had played solid defense in the outfield for the Angels, but the organization felt he had a better chance of reaching the big leagues back on the infield. He's still learning the nuances of the position, getting a lot more reps during his strong Arizona Fall League stint, and should be capable enough to stay there. The position switch clearly impacted his offensive output, but he still showed the ability to draw walks, steal bases and drive the ball with sneaky pop, thanks to excellent bat speed. Despite the relatively down year offensively, the Angels are confident Jones will get back to his typical production now that he's more comfortable back on the dirt. His plus makeup and work ethic should aid him in becoming a solid everyday second baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yajure’s professional career started back in March 2015 when he signed with the Yankees for just $30,000. He missed the 2017 season following Tommy John surgery, but came roaring back to reach Double-A and get added to the 40-man roster in 2019. He made his big league debut in the shortened 2020 season, then was traded to the Pirates in the Jameson Taillon deal. He touched the big leagues again with Pittsburgh in 2021, though he missed a large chunk of the season due to a forearm strain. At his best, Yajure is a craftsman who uses at least four pitches to carve up hitters. He’ll throw both a two-seamer with sink and a four-seamer up in the zone, averaging around 91 mph and touching 95, and commanding both extremely well. His changeup elicits a ton of ground balls, and his relatively new cutter has become a bit of a go-to. He also has the ability to fold in an average curveball. It’s a bit of a kitchen sink repertoire, one without a true out pitch, but he can throw all of them for strikes and does a very good job at keeping hitters off-balance. If he can stay healthy, he has the look of a No. 4 or 5 big league starter, one who’s ready to contribute.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees handed out seven seven-figure bonuses during the 2014-15 international signing period, but it’s Yajure, who signed for $30,000, who might end up being the best player from that class, and he’s the first to reach the big leagues. After missing the 2017 season because of Tommy John surgery, he came back with a good feel for pitching in 2018 and his stuff was all the way back in 2019, when he reached Double-A and was added to the 40-man roster following the season. He made his big league debut in 2020 and then was sent to the Pirates in the deal for Jameson Taillon. Yajure is more about that feel for pitching than pure stuff. He can run his four-seam fastball up to 95 mph, commanding the pitch extremely well. His changeup flashes plus and he added a cutter in 2019 to give hitters another look, giving him another above-average secondary offering. He can land his curveball for strikes as well. Because of the lack of a true out pitch, Yajure doesn’t have as much margin for error. His ability to throw all of his pitches for strikes and mix them well has led to a lot of weak contact, and while his ceiling is relatively limited, he’s just about ready to reach his floor as a back-end big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dalbec entered 2016 with Kris Bryant comparisons and a chance to go early in the first round, but he slumped as an Arizona junior and actually performed better on the mound, leading all pitchers with 41 strikeouts during the NCAA Division I tournament. The Red Sox still bought into his power potential and signed him for an over-slot $650,000 bonus in the fourth round. An old hamate injury ruined his first full pro season, but he bounced back in 2018 to rank second in the Minors in extra-base hits (70) and RBIs (109), and fourth in homers (32). Dalbec comes with serious pop and serious swing-and-miss concerns -- as evidenced by his .301 Isolated Power and 32-percent strikeout rate last season. Few prospects anywhere have more raw power, which he creates with an impressive combination of bat speed, strength and launch angle, not to mention an extremely aggressive approach. He shows some patience to draw walks and is at his best when he uses the middle of the field, though he often sells out for home runs, lengthens his right-handed swing and chases pitches out of the zone. While Dalbec has below-average speed, he has worked hard to make himself into a solid defender at third base. His range is ordinary, but he has good hands and a strong arm that delivered low-90s fastballs and effective sliders in college. Because they also have Rafael Devers in Boston and Michael Chavis in Triple-A, the Red Sox began exposing Dalbec to first base in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia advanced rapidly after signing for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2015, reaching Double-A at age 19 three years later and striking out 165 in 111 1/3 innings and getting to Triple-A the following season. He shut out the Mets for six innings in his first big league start in August 2020 and won three of his five starts that September, but he fell apart last year. His stuff and control backed up as he posted a 6.85 ERA in Triple-A and a 6.45 ERA during a brief stint in New York. Garcia displayed one of the best curveballs in the Minors while he was establishing himself as a top prospect, but he dialed back his stuff to throw strikes during his big league debut and regressed when he lowered his arm slot in 2021. His once-hammer curve used to have so much depth that he had trouble keeping it in the zone, but it now sits in the upper 70s with less power and spin and has been equaled by his low-80s slider. His fastball has lost velocity and life, parking at 90-92 mph in 2021 and 92-94 this year, and his low-80s changeup with fade is getting hammered. Because Garcia is just 5-foot-9 and 163 pounds and features effort in his delivery, there always have been concerns about his durability as a starter. Now the question is whether he can fix himself enough to contribute as a reliever. His walk rate ballooned to a career-worst 6.8 per nine innings in Triple-A last summer as hitters stopped chasing his diminished stuff off the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though they were in the international spending penalty box in 2015, the Yankees still found a trio of quality Dominican arms in Garcia ($200,000), Luis Medina ($280,000) and Alexander Vizcaino ($14,000). Garcia advanced to Double-A in 2018 at age 19 and followed up by striking out 13.3 per nine innings the next season, a rate that would have ranked second in the Minors if he weren't two-thirds of an inning shy of qualifying. He shut out the Mets for six innings in his first big league start last August and remained in New York's rotation in September, but his stuff and control have regressed in 2021. Garcia joined the Yankees with a reputation for having one of the best curveballs in the Minors, yet his mid-70s bender was more effective than devastating in his introduction to the Majors, and some scouts thought his low-80s slider showed just as much promise. His four-seam fastball averaged 92 mph and 2,178 rpm after previously touching 97 with higher spin rates. This year, his heater has sat around 91 mph, and he has had difficulty landing his secondary pitches for strikes. Garcia's best pitch in the big leagues thus far has been a low-80s changeup with fade. He was more consistent with his delivery and threw more strikes than ever before in 2020, then posted the worst walk rate of his career this summer. He's just 5-foot-9 and 163 pounds and throws with some effort, so there are some concerns about whether he can maintain his stuff and hold up over 30 starts per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Players taken No. 3 overall have gone on to accomplish great things in baseball, from Hall of Famers Robin Yount and Paul Molitor to All-Star arms like Trevor Bauer and Steve Avery. The Braves took Avery in that spot back in 1988; Anderson was the choice in 2016 and if his progress as a pro, including finishing second in the system in ERA and third in strikeouts in 2018, is any indication, he's not far from joining his predecessors. Anderson has made strides in using his outstanding three-pitch mix more effectively, starting with a fastball he can run up to 96 mph. He throws downhill and has struck out more than 10 batters per nine innings while also generating a good amount of groundball outs. His curve remains an out pitch and his changeup, which he's worked on tirelessly, also is a plus pitch at times. In 2018, he showed an ability to pitch to all quadrants and set up hitters with all three offerings. Anderson's walk rate improved in 2018, but he still needs to refine his overall command. Because of his repeatable delivery and understanding of how to pitch, the Braves are confident he'll have average control, which should allow him to reach his potential as a frontline type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 The cousin of former big leaguer Cody Ross, Rogers showed his potential during a standout turn on the summer showcase circuit but featured less consistency during his senior campaign in the New Mexico prep ranks. The Marlins ultimately nabbed him with the No. 13 overall pick, marking the second straight year the organization had selected a prep lefty in the first round after taking Braxton Garrett seventh overall in 2016. Rogers never took the mound that summer because the Marlins opted to give him additional rest, but he pitched increasingly well as the 2018 season progressed after making his pro debut with Class A Greensboro in May. Rogers features an impressive fastball, one capable of reaching of the mid-90s but typically sits more in the low 90s. His heater plays up because of his long arms, deception and very good command of the pitch. The southpaw's secondary stuff is well behind his fastball, as Rogers will throw a slider and a curveball that tend to bleed together, with the former currently ahead of the latter. He has trouble staying on top of his curve, and some scouts believe he will likely be better off sticking to the slider at the next level. He also throws a changeup that is getting better and approaching average. Already plenty athletic with clean arm action and a repeatable delivery, the Marlins believe Rogers is just scratching the surface of his physical potential. He's been brought along slowly to begin his career, but Rogers has the profile to move relatively quickly as he attempts to achieve his ceiling of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Developing high school catching is a tough exercise. When that catcher comes from a cold-weather area like western New York State, even more patience is needed. The Orioles initially drafted Heim from Amherst High School in the fourth round of the 2013 Draft. He made it to full-season ball in 2015, but missed a large chunk of that year with a foot injury. With his bat not developing, Baltimore sent Heim to Tampa Bay in August 2016 in return for Steve Pearce. He was on the move again after a year with the Rays, coming to the A's to complete the Joey Wendle trade. Things started to click a bit in his first year with Oakland and he reached Double-A for the first time, though he struggled once he arrived. A long-limbed, switch-hitting backstop, Heim stands out more for his work behind the plate than at it. He receives well and has a strong arm that's allowed him to throw out just over 34 percent of potential basestealers heading into 2019. Heim started to swing the bat with a bit more authority over the past two seasons and hit well in the California League before stumbling post-promotion. He has more of a line drive approach now, but he shows some raw power in batting practice and still has room to add strength. While it's more leverage than bat speed, you can dream on some future pop. The A's would love to see Heim play with a little more urgency. A slow heartbeat for a catcher isn't a bad thing, but some added energy could help him reach the big leagues as a backup backstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fleming led the country in ERA (0.67) and WHIP (0.71) as a junior and became the first player ever drafted out of Division III Webster University (St. Louis, Mo.) when the Rays made him their fifth-round pick in 2017. He pitched well at two levels during his first full season and was even better in ‘19, climbing from Double-A Montgomery -- where he ranked among the Southern League leaders in wins (tied for first), ERA (fifth), WHIP (fourth) and innings (sixth) -- up to Triple-A Durham. He made a very strong contribution to the rotation during his big league debut in 2020 and pitched out of the bullpen in the postseason. An athletic left-hander with a clean delivery, Fleming knows how to be effective with each of his three pitches, though nothing he throws is plus. His fastball has a ton of late sink and run, sitting at 90-93 mph and touching 94. He can spot his heater with precision on both sides of the plate or drive it down in the zone to get ground balls, which he did at a 54.4-percent clip in 2019 and a 2.45 GO/AO ratio in the big leagues in '20. Fleming’s average slider and above-average changeup are enhanced by his excellent fastball command, and his changeup missed bats and got weak contact with Tampa Bay last year. Right-handed hitters hit .302/.334/.502 against him in ’19, but he was a bit improved in that area in the big leagues in ’20 (.270/.289/.432). With his blend of stamina, pitchability and command, Fleming looks the part of a future back-end starter. Some evaluators believe he’s better suited for long-relief role due to his struggles against righties (and dominance against lefties), though he’s clearly ready to pitch in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perhaps the most projectable pitcher in the 2015 Draft, McKenzie was a 6-foot-5, 160-pound Florida high schooler who landed the largest bonus ($2,302,500) among prep arms that summer. The Indians have handled him carefully, limiting him to 95 1/3 innings in his first two pro seasons before turning him loose in 2017, when he was the Class A Advanced Carolina League pitcher of the year and finished second in the Minors with 186 strikeouts. Forearm soreness delayed his 2018 debut until June, after which he looked like his usual dominant self, but he missed all of this year after straining his upper back during Spring Training. Though McKenzie's fastball sits around 91-93 mph and tops out at 95, it projects as a plus pitch because he still has room to add more strength and velocity and because of his command, extension, angle and high spin rate. His curveball gives him a second plus offering, with good shape and spin rate to go with upper-70s velocity. His fading changeup helps him keep left-handers in check and grades as solid. McKenzie's advanced feel for pitching stands out even more than his stuff. Even though he's still filling out his extra-long frame, he has no difficulty repeating his delivery and providing quality strikes. If he proves capable of handling a starter's workload, he should fit near the front of Cleveland's rotation of the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crowe looked the part of a future first-rounder during his first season and a half at South Carolina before blowing out his elbow and requiring Tommy John surgery in mid-2015. After sitting out all of 2016 and then turning down Cleveland as a 21st-round pick, Crowe resuscitated his prospect status with the Gamecocks and became Washington's second-round pick in 2017. In his first full season, Crowe garnered Pitcher of the Year honors in the Class A Advanced Carolina League, going 11-0 with a 2.69 ERA in 16 games (15 starts) at Potomac before advancing to Double-A. He was named the organization's co-Pitcher of the Year with Ben Braymer. Crowe's elbow reconstruction has had little impact on his velocity, as he spent 2018 pitching at 91-95 mph with a four-seam fastball that stands out for its high spin rate. His above-average curveball also features an impressive spin rate, which in turn gives it power and depth. His changeup arguably is his best secondary pitch, earning above-average grades from evaluators, and he also has feel for mixing in a slider. Crowe wore down during the second half of his first full season, which prompted the Nationals to shut him down until fall instructional league. Big and physical, he should be able to handle a greater workload once he builds up the necessary strength. Improving his pitch usage and command are the next steps for Crowe, who has the size, stuff and feel to develop into a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves signed Pache for $1.4 million dollars at the start of the 2015-16 international signing period and he jumped on the prospect map almost immediately, coming to the United States for his professional debut in 2016 and performing well across two levels of Rookie ball. Perhaps the best defensive outfielder in the Minor Leagues, Pache moved up the organizational ladder steadily and it looked like his bat was catching up to his glove in 2019. He made his big league debut in 2020, playing regularly in the NLCS in the Braves’ championship season. He began 2021 in the Opening Day lineup, struggled and didn’t really regain any kind of footing until late in the Triple-A season, but the A’s thought the tools were worthy of having him included in the trade that sent Matt Olson to Atlanta. When Pache improved offensively in 2019, his approach led to a lower strikeout rate and higher walk rate, and subsequently greater production. But when he struggled out of the gate in the big leagues, coupled with some injuries, it snowballed and upon his return to Triple-A, his approach regressed and there was way too much swing-and-miss in his game. He did regroup to have a .906 OPS in August and a .296/.349/.438 line from Aug. 1 through the end of the season. If he can continue to fine-tune his discipline and recognition, he can continue to tap into his raw power. While Pache is easily a plus runner, that’s never translated into base-stealing success. It does enable him to cover a lot of ground in center field, where he has a cannon for an arm and the chance to win multiple Gold Gloves. For that, he’ll have to earn the chance to play every day, with the hope he can wipe the slate clean while playing all of 2022 at age 23.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the 2015-16 international signing period might have initially been known for the Dodgers’ spending spree of $37.5 million for three players, it might eventually go down as producing two of the most exciting young players in baseball: Vladimir Guerrero Jr. of the Blue Jays and Pache, who signed with the Braves in July 2015 for $1.4 million. Considered the best defensive player in the Minors, Pache’s bat caught up enough for him make his big league debut in 2020, being placed on the postseason roster and playing regularly in the National League Championship Series. But even though he saw big league time in 2021, his offense regressed, leading some to worry about his hit tool. His combination of tools, however, were enticing enough for the A’s to acquire him as one of the four prospects in the Matt Olson deal. There is absolutely no question Pache is ready to patrol center field in the big leagues right now, a Gold Glove caliber defender who has earned a rare 80 fielding grade, good enough to move Ronald Acuña Jr. to a corner in the NLCS. In addition to nearly top of the scale speed, his instincts and reads are impeccable and he complements it with one of the strongest outfield arms in baseball. Offensively, the right-handed hitter had taken a big step forward approach-wise in 2019 and that continued in 2020 with his work at the Braves’ alternate camp and then in the postseason, when he drew three walks and struck out just four times in 25 plate appearances. He wasn’t able to keep the momentum going in 2021 between Atlanta and Triple-A, but he’s still young enough to right the ship and become a high-level starting center fielder in Oakland.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays signed Sanchez for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2014 and watched him hit .306/.347/.478 in his first four seasons while advancing to Double-A at age 20. He put up the worst numbers of his career and especially struggled in Triple-A while dealing with a sports hernia in 2019, and Tampa Bay traded him and Ryne Stanek to the Marlins that July for Nick Anderson and Trevor Richards. Sanchez went 1-for-25 with 11 strikeouts in his big league debut last year, when he also saw action at Miami's alternate site and in the Dominican Winter League. Sanchez still has the smooth left-handed stroke, quality bat speed and propensity for hard contact to do damage at the plate, but his offensive numbers have declined at each step as he has risen through the Minors, showing his need to make adjustments. More advanced pitchers have been able to exploit his lack of plate discipline, and his tendency to hit the ball on the ground mitigates his plus raw power. If he can become more selective and add some loft to his swing, he could develop into a .280 hitter with 25-homer pop. Primarily a center fielder in his first two pro seasons, Sanchez since has settled into right field. The corners are a better fit for his average speed and his solid arm plays well in right. If they wind up in the same big league outfield, 2019 first-rounder J.J. Bleday likely will push Sanchez to left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Mountcastle was revered by scouts for his potential with the bat as a Florida high schooler before the Orioles nabbed him with the second of their two first-round picks in 2015. That hitting ability has helped him move quickly through the Minors despite concerns about his defense, as Mountcastle raked his way up to Double-A at age 20 in '17. And even though the start of Mountcastle's '18 campaign was delayed due to a fractured right wrist suffered during Spring Training, he still put up strong numbers in the Eastern League and represented the Orioles at the Futures Game in July. Mountcastle just knows how to impact the baseball. He has a quick bat and does an outstanding job of keeping his hands inside the ball to create extension through the zone and generate backspin carry to all fields. It gives him a chance to be at least an above-average hitter with similar power potential, especially if he can further refine his approach. While the move up to Double-A brought a position change from shortstop to third base for Mountcastle, his below-average arm strength and fringy range made him unlikely to stay there long term. Sure enough, the Orioles began working him in at first base during Spring Training before deploying him primarily at the position at the outset of 2019. He's always had good hands on the left side of the infield that should serve him well as a first baseman, and he certainly has the hitting ability and power to profile there at the highest level .

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The move to Double-A can be a challenging one for prospects and how one handles the jump, and the adversity that can often come with it, can be as telling as immediate success. Romero, the junior college standout who went in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft, scuffled with the move to hitter-friendly Reading in 2018, but righted the ship and was pitching very well when an oblique injury ended his season in July. Romero's stuff, and he has a full repertoire of weapons at his disposal, fluctuated at times particularly early in the year. He'll throw both a four- and two-seam fastball and can still get the former up to 95 mph, while he sinks the latter in the low 90s to get groundball outs. The life and deception he uses to throw his fastball allows it to nearly play up to a plus pitch. Both of his breaking balls will flash above-average and he mixes in a cutter to go along with a changeup that is plus at times. At his best, Romero commands his fastball to both sides of the plate and goes right after hitters, something he struggled with in the early going a year ago. Strong and athletic, he shouldn't need too much more time to be ready for a gig as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fletcher began his career at the University of Houston as an effective arm out of the bullpen as a freshman, but he wound up needing Tommy John surgery his sophomore year and took a redshirt. He moved to the rotation in 2018 and drew enough attention from the Nationals to earn a 14th-round Draft selection that season. After making seven starts for the club’s Class A Short Season affiliate, Fletcher moved back into a bullpen role full time in 2019. He pitched his way up three levels to Double-A before being sent to the Mariners in return for Hunter Strickland. And that fall, he was one of the most dominant relievers in the Arizona Fall League. Even at 6 feet tall, Fletcher utilizes an effective cross-fire delivery, hiding the ball well so hitters can’t pick it up which enables his stuff to play up. And he’s got really strong stuff. He was 94-95 mph in the AFL with good life and his above-average slider is a very effective weapon. It has really good action, and particularly in the Fall League, he threw quality strikes with it. The slider works especially well against left-handed hitters, but Fletcher also has a decent changeup that works against righties, though he’ll have to continue to show conviction in throwing it. Fletcher impressed in nine outings at Double-A Arkansas after the trade and further excited Seattle with how good he was in the AFL. Seattle used him as a reinforcement during the shortened 2020 season, but he looked overwhelmed in six relief outings, when he gave up six runs in four innings. Like many impacted by the odd quirks of last year, the Mariners are hoping those were learning experiences more than anything, that he doesn’t get too caught up in those numbers and benefits from reflection and trust in his stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bart signed for $7,025,000 as the No. 2 overall pick in the 2018 Draft, setting a record (since broken) for the largest up-front bonus for a position player. When Buster Posey elected not to play in 2020, Bart wound up in San Francisco ahead of schedule that August and struggled offensively while playing well defensively. After batting .294/.358/.472 in Triple-A last season, he could take over as the Giants' starter following Posey's abrupt retirement. Bart has the bat speed and strength to generate well-above-average raw power, though he doesn't fully exploit it because he tends to hit the ball on the ground too much. He could provide 25-30 homers on an annual basis if he launches balls in the air more regularly and learns to handle high-velocity fastballs. After getting too pull-conscious and aggressive in his big league debut, he displayed a better approach in Triple-A last year but still would benefit by further tightening up his strike zone. There are fewer questions about Bart's defensive game and club officials think he offers Gold Glove upside. He has worked hard to develop solid receiving and blocking skills and he also possesses a strong, accurate arm. He moves well behind the plate for his size and big league pitchers have praised his leadership and game-calling ability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 2 overall pick in the 2018 Draft out of Georgia Tech, Bart set a since-broken record for the largest up-front bonus for a position player ($7,025,000). He joined the Giants last August despite just 130 games of pro experience (including just 22 above high Class A), the product of missing six weeks in 2019 after a pitch broke a bone in his left hand and San Francisco's need for a catcher after Buster Posey elected not to play in 2020. He impressed the club's veteran pitchers so much during Summer Camp that they clamored for him to make the Opening Day roster, and though he struggled at the plate, the Giants won 15 of his 28 starts and just missed the playoffs. Bart's bat speed, strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-2 frame give him well above-average raw pop, more than most catchers possess. The right-handed hitter didn't do much damage in his big league debut, however, as he got too pull-conscious and aggressive and didn't catch up to quality fastballs while posting alarming strikeout (37 percent) and walk (3 percent) rates in 111 plate appearances. He had more success in the Minors when he displayed more patience and let his power, which plays to all fields, come naturally. Bart has progressed from a high schooler with questions as to whether he could stay behind the plate to a potential Gold Glover. He has worked hard on his defense and has become a quality receiver who blocks balls well and displays a strong, accurate arm. He moves well for a big catcher and San Francisco pitchers praised his game-calling ability and leadership.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jeffers hit 26 homers as UNC-Wilmington's catcher during his sophomore and junior seasons, leading the Colonial Athletic Association with 16 in 2018. That led to the Twins taking him in the second round, ahead of where most of the industry had him, thinking those offensive skills would translate. If his pro debut is any indication, the Twins were right as Jeffers dominated the Appalachian League to earn a promotion to full-season Cedar Rapids, where he capped off a successful first summer of pro ball by hitting two postseason homers. A big, strong backstop, Jeffers is definitely a power over hit kind of offensive performer, though his solid approach at the plate allowed him to tap into that power consistently during his debut. If he can continue to manage the strike zone, he could have plus game power when all is said and done. There were questions about Jeffers' ability to stick behind the plate, but the Twins were pleased with his receiving skills and think his blocking will be fine as well, with an arm that plays a tick above average. A physics major at UNC-Wilmington, Jeffers gets high marks for his intelligence and his makeup. He might be a backup when all is said and done, but don't be shocked to see him as a power-hitting leader behind the plate on a daily basis in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Undrafted out of high school, Mize honored his commitment to Auburn and blossomed into one of the top college pitchers in the nation. His combination of stuff and control improved in each of his three years there, and he became the highest drafted player in program history when Detroit made him the No. 1 overall pick and signed him for $7.5 million, a record in the bonus pool era. A lengthy junior campaign during which Mize accrued 114 2/3 innings prompted the Tigers to limit his workload after signing, though it certainly didn't keep the right-hander from having an impressive pro debut that concluded with four abbreviated starts in the Florida State League. He dominated early in his first full season, first in the FSL and then after a promotion to Double-A Erie, though his progress was slowed by a shoulder injury in mid-June. With plus command and the ability to induce whiffs with three different pitches, Mize has the ingredients needed to headline a starting rotation. A plus-plus splitter in the mid-80s that dives at the plate is his best offering, and he's adept at locating the pitch down in the zone or below it. Mize sets it up with a 92-97 mph fastball that he commands exceptionally well despite its running life. His mid-80s slider took a step forward as a junior, consistently grading as a plus offering, and he also has developed the ability to manipulate it into a harder cutter when he desires. Mize has long shown a knack for pounding the zone and attacking hitters. He finished first in NCAA Division I in K/BB ratio (12.1) and fourth in walks per nine innings (1.0) as a sophomore and posted similar numbers as a junior while finishing third among D-I hurlers with 156 strikeouts. That Mize was shut down in 2017 at Auburn and again in the summer with Team USA due to a tired arm and flexor strain in his forearm raises concerns about his durability. However, he did his part by staying healthy throughout his 2018 campaign, and neither his athletic frame nor his clean delivery have a glaring flaw. With his plus stuff and plus command, it should surprise no one to see him move quickly through the Tigers' system.
