mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 A swingman on a 2016 Florida Gators pitching staff that included five future first-round picks and perhaps as many as nine future big league starters, Dunning interested the White Sox as a possible selection with their No. 26 overall pick in that Draft. They opted for Zack Burdi instead and the Nationals signed Dunning for $2 million at No. 29, but Chicago landed him six months later along with Lucas Giolito and Reynaldo Lopez in the Adam Eaton trade. He developed into the Sox's highest-floor pitching prospect before missing the final two months of the 2018 season with a strained elbow and undergoing Tommy John surgery this March. Dunning has three different pitches that grade as plus at their best. He doesn't light up radar guns with a low-90s fastball that peaks at 96 mph, but it's a weapon because its heavy sink makes it hard to lift and he commands it so well to both sides of the plate. Some evaluators believe his curveball has surpassed his slider as his better breaking ball, and both offerings have plenty of depth and enough power. Dunning's changeup gives him a fourth pitch that should be at least solid, though it's not quite as consistent as his others. He repeats his athletic delivery, provides a lot of strikes and has tremendous feel for his craft. Before his elbow gave out, he was on the verge of stepping into Chicago's rotation but now will miss all of 2019 and likely part of 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals did some serious spending on international prospects in 2016, going heavy on Cuban imports and handing out four seven-figure bonuses in the process. Oviedo signed for $1.9 million, the second-highest payday doled out by the organization that year after Jonathan Machado's $2.35 million bonus. The right-hander's United States debut was a bit uneven, and he endured similar struggles early in 2018 at Class A Peoria, posting a 6.47 ERA through his first 10 starts. But Oviedo settled in after that and pitched well the rest of the way, registering a 3.10 ERA and averaging nearly a strikeout per inning over his final 81 1/3 frames. Oviedo's fastball hasn't quite ticked back up to where it was when he was up to 96-97 mph shortly after signing, but there's plenty there, sitting in the 92-94 mph range and touching a bit higher even as he works deep into starts. His curve and changeup are both developing along with his command, which currently is well below-average. The Cardinals think there's an above-average breaking ball in there with further refinement, while his changeup already flashes above-average and could be a near-plus offering at maturity. Club officials were impressed with the adjustments Oviedo made halfway into his first full season, praising him for how he remained focused after a shaky April and May. A huge physical specimen at 6-foot-6, the right-hander will continue to work on getting his frame in sync and repeating his delivery, and the belief is that it will lead to more consistent strike-throwing with his three-pitch mix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Tommy John surgery wiped out much of Skubal's 2016 and his entire 2017 season at Seattle University, but the D-backs still took a shot on him in that June's Draft, selecting him in the 29th round. He chose not to sign and returned to Seattle, where he had an uneven performance, especially with his control. The Tigers saw untapped potential in Skubal for that very same reason, and they went above slot to sign him for $350,000 after taking him in the ninth round. He's quickly proved to be one of the Draft's biggest steals with a dominant first full season that saw him rack up a ton of strikeouts in Florida State League before advancing to Double-A in early July and recording double-digit strikeouts in his first three starts. Skubal pounds the zone with a 92-95 mph fastball that reaches 97 and features late life when he locates up in the zone. His above-average curveball in the low-to-mid-80s is his go-to secondary offering and nets him a ton of whiffs, and he also shows good feel for commanding and misses bats with short, tight slider. Skubal's changeup is a clear fourth pitch for him, though it stands to improve considerably as he learns to better control his arm speed. Staying healthy in the pro ranks hasn't been an issue for Skubal, and he's impressed the organization with his confidence and composure on the mound. He's quickly established himself as one of the top pitchers in the organization, giving the organization a left-handed complement to their rising crop of impressive right-handed starters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $500,000 out of Mexico in July 2015, Paredes was having a solid first full season two years later when the Cubs sent him to the Tigers at the Trade Deadline in a deal for Justin Wilson and Alex Avila. Paredes' advanced bat was on full display during his first season with the Tigers, as he garnered All-Star honors in the Florida State League before a July promotion up to Double-A. He more than held his own in the Eastern League at age 19, slashing .321/.406/.458 over 39 games, then tied a bow on his season with a strong showing in the Mexican Winter League. Paredes' success and overall consistency at the plate reflects just how well he can swing the bat. He has preternatural feel for putting the barrel on the ball and covers the plate well, with an advanced, contact-focused approach that results in low strikeout totals. He projects to have average Major League power, and he hit a career-best 15 homers in 2018, albeit exclusively to his pull-side. Physically mature for his age with a thicker build, Paredes is a fringey runner who could lose a step. Paredes is a reliable defender at shortstop, with good hands and a strong, above-average arm, but also modest range that might require him to move to another position. Second and third base are options, and he saw meaningful time at both in 2018, logging 45 games between the two positions on top of his primary work at shortstop (74 games). Wherever he lands, the Tigers are excited to see how his advanced bat skills play as he moves up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Dodgers for $140,000 out of Venezuela in 2014, Ruiz began to move quickly after hitting .374/.412/.527 in his U.S. debut two years later and spent 2018 in Double-A at age 19. He stalled a bit in two seasons there, however, as Will Smith surpassed him on the organization's depth chart. He spent 2020 at the alternate training site and got only eight official at-bats with the Dodgers, though he did homer off Julio Teheran in his first big league trip to the plate. He showed offensive improvement this season at Triple-A Oklahoma City, where he hit .311/.381/.6131 with 16 homers in 52 games before he was traded to the Nationals at the Trade Deadline as part of the Max Scherzer-Trea Turner blockbuster. One of the premier contact hitters in the Minors, Ruiz has impressive bat control and a disciplined approach that has limited his strikeout rate to 10 percent in his first six pro seasons and just 7 percent in the upper Minors. A switch-hitter, he has much more power from the left side, where he hit 28 of his 30 pro homers entering 2021. He spent last summer at the alternate training site working on unlocking his power, making an adjustment to his lower half that helped him improve the quality of his contact. Ruiz has the tools to be a solid defender but lacks consistency behind the plate. He's agile with soft hands and good framing skills, and his pure arm strength grades as better than average. He can get lackadaisical with his receiving, however, and his transfer and accuracy with his throws still need improvement. Nonetheless, he gives the Nats a legitimate potential position-player star, which the system lacked before his arrival.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 22 by MLB Pipeline on the Top 200 Draft prospects list in 2015, Kaprielian was the type of advanced college starter teams covet because of his feel for pitching and potential to move quickly through a farm system. The Yankees liked that combination enough to take him in the middle of the first round that June, but he's struggled to stay on the mound since. A forearm injury limited him to just 18 innings during his first full season in 2016, though he showed glimpses of who he can be during an Arizona Fall League stint that fall. He needed Tommy John surgery that ended his 2017 season before it began and setbacks kept him from pitching for the A's after they acquired him as part of the Sonny Gray deal at the 2017 Trade Deadline until instructs this past fall. While at UCLA, Kaprielian had a fastball that was largely average velocity-wise, but played up because of his command of the pitch. There was excitement when he experienced a jump in his velocity at the outset of his pro career, going from 88-92 to 93-96 mph while touching 99 mph. He was healthy, finally, at instructs last fall, but wasn't popping the radar gun like that. He does have three secondary offerings that all can be above-average, with a tight slider and a changeup with good fade to it, not to mention a solid curve he mixes in effectively. Kaprielian repeats his delivery well and has always been a strike-thrower. More than anything, the right-hander needs to turn in a healthy season. The A's are sure to proceed cautiously with Kaprielian to give him the best chance of fulfilling his potential as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Hailing from the Elk Grove High School program in northern California that his dad coached, Carlson was one of two first-round picks the Cardinals got at the end of 2016's opening round (Dakota Hudson was the other). Sent aggressively to full-season ball to start the '17 season, Carlson really struggled out of the gate, but righted the ship a bit after that, catching up to the level. Things began to come together for him in 2018, as he showed a mix of power potential and on-base skills at age 19 in the challenging Class A Advanced Florida State League, and he broke out in earnest during his first Double-A campaign in '19, earning a Futures Game selection along the way. Carlson is a switch-hitter who has some serious offensive potential. While his right-handed swing is more impactful and consistent, Carlson has made significant strides as a left-handed hitter in 2019 while regularly tapping into his plus raw power from both sides. His strong knowledge of the strike zone and pitch recognition are major assets, allow him to find more pitches to drive and tap into his power, which could be above-average in his prime. A good athlete and average runner, Carlson has held his own as a center fielder in Double-A but may fit better at a corner-outfield spot long term. Carlson has responded well to challenging assignments at every stage in his career, performing increasingly well against older competition in advanced leagues. With his high baseball IQ, feel for the strike zone and blend of hitting ability and power at the plate, Carlson is on his way toward becoming an everyday big leaguer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed as a high school draftee taken in the 26th round of the 2015 Draft from Maryland, Newsome had largely flown under the radar in the early stages of his pro career as an undersized right-hander with a really good feel for pitching. A slight uptick in his stuff helped him break out a bit in 2019, earning a California League All-Star nod and a promotion to Double-A. Still, the Mariners didn’t protect Newsome from the Rule 5 Draft last December and he wasn’t selected. Newsome can throw four pitches for strikes, and that’s an understatement. His fastball is now in the 90-94 mph range, which is average in terms of velocity, but he can spot it on a dime and it has good riding life. His slider is his best secondary pitch and he manipulates it well, adding shape to it when he wants to. His curve is fringy, but he commands it well and while his changeup isn’t anything special, there is some arm-side run and late bottom to it, and he plays it off of his fastball very well. The strike-throwing for Newsome is exceptional, as he carries a phenomenal 1.1 BB/9 rate for his career into the 2020 season. He’s willing to throw any of his pitches at any point in the count and does a nice job keeping hitters off-balance, so while his ceiling is limited to that of a back-end starter, there’s more confidence that he could get there, or at least fill a swingman role in the big leagues soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After having five right-handers selected in the top five rounds of the past four Drafts, Dallas Baptist produced two more viable candidates for the 2017 Draft in relievers Elledge and Dalton Higgins. The Patriots' career saves leader with 27, Elledge was the first of the pair to be selected, going to the Mariners in the fourth round and then signing for $400,000. After reaching full-season ball in his professional debut, Elledge advanced to Class A Advanced Modesto in '18 and garnered midseason All-Star honors in the California League before getting sent to the Cardinals in return for Sam Tuivailala. Elledge has a strong, durable frame and three pitches. He has a quick arm that consistently produces 93-95 mph fastballs with heavy sink that he can command to either side of the plate. Elledge usually throws his low-80s slider for strikes, and at times it can play like a cutter, with short, glove-slide slice. He shows some feel for a changeup but doesn't need it much in a relief role. Elledge's size and arsenal profile well in a big league bullpen, and he has the potential to get there quickly if he can refine his slider and improve his control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Akin struck out 133 batters as a Western Michigan junior to establish a single-season record, surpassing former big leaguer Pat Misch on the school's all-time list. The Orioles took him in the second round that June, then assigned him directly to Class A Advanced Frederick for his first full season. Akin pitched to mixed results early before settling in during the second half, and he built upon that success during a breakout Double-A campaign in 2018. He was named Baltimore's Minor League pitcher of the year and garnered similar honors in the Eastern League after he led the circuit in wins (14), strikeouts (142), and batting average against (.225), and posted the third-best ERA (3.27). Akin's repeatable delivery and clean arm action allow him to paint both sides of the plate with a fastball that sits at 91-94 mph and touches 95. An above-average slider in the low 80s is Akin's best secondary pitch, and he also demonstrates feel for a changeup that's at least average. He throws each of his three pitches for strikes and is comfortable pitching inside against right-handed hitters with his fastball. While he doesn't generate many ground balls and at times is prone to the long ball, Akin does induce a healthy number of whiffs and induces weak contact by effectively changing speeds. The Orioles changed Akin's heel placement on the rubber back in 2017, and that adjustment has helped him stay on line to the plate and better execute his pitches. He still has gains to make both with his control and command, but all the ingredients are there for Akin to serve as a No. 4 starter, perhaps more, if he continues down his current developmental path.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Lewis-Clark State in Idaho has developed quite a few big leaguers over the years, led by former All-Star closer Keith Foulke and long-time infielder Brendan Ryan, there were few expectations placed upon Brogdon when the Phillies took him in the 10th round of the 2017 Draft out of the NAIA school and gave the senior $5,000 to sign. A starter in college, Brogdon’s move to the bullpen helped him far exceed those expectations as he made his big league debut in the 2020 season, striking out 17 over 11 1/3 innings of work. Brogdon had largely used his 6-foot-6 frame and two above-average pitches to make his way to Philadelphia. He misses bats with a fastball that’s typically been in the 93-95 mph range in the past, but averaged just over 95 mph and touched 98 in the big leagues in 2020. He gets swings and misses at the top of the zone with it and throws it with above-average spin (over 2,400 rpm last year). His go-to secondary pitch is a changeup that flashes plus and produced a 39 percent whiff rate in the big leagues. The right-hander has always thrown a cutter-like slider, with inconsistent results, and really made strides in developing a curve during his time at the Phillies’ alternate site last summer. He’s generally been a strike-thrower, one who has been very tough to hit (.196 BAA in the Minors; .128 in the big leagues in 2020), giving him a chance to establish himself as an effective big league reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fits and starts – some of his own making, some not – have filled Romero’s last half-decade. The 6-foot-3 southpaw showed first-round stuff at the University of Houston, where he fanned 31.1 percent of batters he faced in three seasons, but he was suspended in 2016 and kicked off the team after 10 appearances in 2017 due to off-field issues. The Nationals were willing to roll the dice with the 25 th overall pick. After being sent home during Spring Training in 2018 because of an off-field issue, Romero made seven starts for Class A Hagerstown before eventually needing Tommy John surgery that fall. He returned last year and stood out at Summer Camp and the alternate site, earning a Major League debut. But after three relief appearances, he broke his non-throwing hand when he slipped down some stairs and missed the rest of the 2020 season following yet another procedure. When healthy, Romero averaged 91.7 mph and touched 93 on his fastball. He is capable of recording velocities in the mid-90s in larger samples and is expected to do so as he increases his professional workload. His low-80s changeup is the more consistent of his two off-speed pitches because of its separation off the fastball and Romero’s ability to throw it for strikes and swings-and-misses. The slider has yet to regain its pre-Tommy John form, particularly when it comes to spin action and bite, but the southpaw still used it regularly during his three-game stint in the Majors. His ability to throw strikes drew the attention of manager Dave Martinez and was a primary reason for Romero getting the call last year. Those three pitches have enabled Romero to try to get some starting looks in 2021. But given durability concerns and lack of experience, the safest bet remains that he will settle into relief long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets signed Sanchez for $690,000 out of Venezuela in July 2013 and he already had a reputation as a solid defender. New York hoped the bat would eventually catch up to the defense, and while Sanchez isn’t a huge threat in the batter’s box, he’s developed over time. The catcher hit .265 (88 games) across two levels in 2018, then went on to hit .278 in his first taste of Double-A. Sanchez was promoted to Triple-A Syracuse, but struggled over a small 21-game sample size. The Mets added him to the 40-man roster after the season, and he made his Major League debut, appearing in five games in 2020 before being designated for assignment and traded to the Cardinals for cash considerations in February 2021. Sanchez’s true value is his defensive ability. An excellent receiver, the 6-foot-1, 200-pound backstop moves well behind the plate, is praised for his game-calling and controls the running game with a plus arm. In the batter’s box, Sanchez controls the zone and doesn’t strike out often. While Sanchez currently has below-average power and will never be a slugger, the Cardinals feel there is a bit more pop than what he has shown so far. There’s plenty of value in defensive-minded backups and that’s exactly what Sanchez provides for the Cardinals. St. Louis has other enticing catchers in the system, but Sanchez provides depth and can step in admirably if called upon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever in his first year at Cal Poly, Howard moved into the rotation as a redshirt sophomore and took off, landing in the second round of the 2017 Draft and signing for below pick value. He rode a bit of a roller coaster in his first full season, but finished as strongly as perhaps any pitching prospect in baseball, including a one-walk, complete-game no-hitter in the South Atlantic League playoffs. Howard's stuff and command took a big step forward in the latter stages of 2018, though there is still work to be done in terms of his overall command. Late in the season, he was up to 98 mph with his fastball consistently, sitting very comfortably in the 94-95 mph range, throwing his heater with plus life in the zone. His two breaking balls can be inconsistent and blend into each other at times, but he will show an above-average slider and a distinct curveball, with them occasionally looking like a cutter. His changeup has the chance to be at least average. He misses plenty of bats and has the stuff to be a frontline starter. The only thing that could hold him back is his command and control. If he can build off of his improvements in finding the strike zone as well as consistent mechanics on his breaking stuff, he could reach that ceiling in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Gary Sanchez made Brian McCann redundant in New York, the Yankees traded McCann to the Astros in November 2016 for Abreu and fellow right-handed pitching prospect Jorge Guzman (whom they later spun to the Marlins in a deal for Giancarlo Stanton). Signed for $185,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2013, Abreu has shown frontline-starter upside when healthy. A shoulder strain, appendectomy and elbow inflammation limited him to 126 innings in his first two seasons with his new organization, however. All of Abreu's pitches grade out as plus or better when he commands them, beginning with a 94-98 mph fastball that tops out at 101 with sink and run. His power breaking ball can absolutely wipe out right-handers, combining curveball depth with slider velocity in the mid-80s. His fading changeup can shut down lefties, though it wasn't as effective in 2018 as it was in the past. Abreu has a short-arm delivery that provides deception but sometimes hampers him from locating his pitches. He doesn't dominate as much as he should because he needs more consistency with his secondary pitches and better command of his entire arsenal. If he can't do that and heads to the bullpen, he could fill a high-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Patino may not have come with the type of fanfare like the other players signed by the Padres during their 2016-17 international spending spree, but the Colombian right-hander could end up being the best of the bunch. After finishing his 2017 pro debut as a 17-year-old in the Rookie-level Arizona League, Patino made the jump straight to the Class A Midwest League and dominated against older hitters before hitting his workload limit and being shut down for the season late in August. Patino is both athletic and physically strong for his age, with present feel for throwing and locating four pitches. His quick right arm generates a fastball that's been up to 98 mph and usually sits in the low-to-mid-90s with late life thanks to his extension toward the plate. Patino's power slider in the upper 80s is a swing-and-miss offering, and he also shows aptitude for executing an above-average curveball as well as a changeup that stands to improve as he gains experience. He's consistently around the zone and could have at least above-average command once fully developed. Patino already shows durability and holds his velocity deep into starts. His delivery and arm action require further refinement like so many young, live-armed hurlers, but he has the requisite athleticism and physical tools needed to make the proper adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sharp could have played college basketball but opted to focus on baseball, turning down the Braves as a 30th-rounder out of high school to enroll at Eastern Michigan. He eventually transferred to NCAA Division II Drury (Mo.) and became a Nationals 22nd-rounder in 2016, signing for $40,000. He missed three months last season with an oblique injury but returned to star in the Arizona Fall League, leading Miami to pounce on him in the Rule 5 Draft at the Winter Meetings. He went on to make four appearances out of the Marlins’ bullpen after cracking the team’s Opening Day roster, but was designated for assignment in August and ultimately returned to the Nationals after clearing outright waivers. Sharp has exceptionally low spin rates on his one- and two-seam sinkers, resulting in heavy life and exceptionally high groundball rates, including a 3.2 groundout/airout ratio in 2019. His fastball velocity usually ranges from 89-92 mph and tops out at 94, so he pitches to weak contact more than he misses bats. His changeup sinks as well and gives him a solid second offering, though his slurvy slider needs more work. A pitch-to-contact right-hander, Sharp translates his athleticism into an easy delivery with a high leg kick that provides deception without compromising his control. Sharp’s experience as both a starter and a reliever makes him the type of versatile hurler teams love to have on their roster, though he’s probably best suited for a long-relief role given his combination of durability, excellent ground-ball tendencies and overall solid control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An accounting major at the University of Illinois, Gerber is cerebral and tactical on the mound. A reliever through and through, Gerber pitched three solid seasons out of the bullpen for the Illini and was taken by the Mariners in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft. Gerber utilizes his lower-body strength and shoulders to deliver with an unorthodox, almost side-arm action down the mound, which thwarts hitters’ timing and balance and creates a ton of deception. His delivery has been described as though someone was pitching with his hair on fire. His ability to dial it up to 97 mph really gets on hitters fast. His slider, which sits in the 83- to 86-mph range, could use more depth and polish. The Mariners liked Gerber enough to give him a big league opportunity in the shortened 2020, as well as an invite to big league Spring Training in ’21. He’ll need to continue working on his tempo with his delivery, but the upside with the quirky righty might have a ceiling as a high-leverage arm out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In many ways, Kilome has done as well as, or better than, could have been expected when he signed as a gangly teenager back in 2013. He's gotten bigger and stronger and, after making his full-season debut in 2016, has moved rather quickly, reaching Double-A in '17 while finishing in the top 10 among all Phillies pitching prospects in ERA. He was spending his first full season at the level when he was dealt to the Mets for Asdrubal Cabrera. The Mets won't get a long look at him until 2020, however, as the right-hander underwent Tommy John surgery in October and will miss the 2019 season. Pure stuff-wise, Kilome is as good as just about any pitching prospect in the system, with a fastball that sits in the mid-90s combined with a curve that often flashes plus. His changeup has improved, and it could eventually become an average third pitch, something softer to disrupt hitters' timing. He's generally around the strike zone, though his command has been inconsistent as he is still learning to get all of his 6-foot-6 frame in sync on a regular basis. Kilome doesn't miss as many bats as his stuff suggests he should, though he stands to improve in that department as he learns to sequence pitches and set up hitters more effectively. Kilome gets high marks for his makeup and intelligence, as he learned English quickly so he could better communicate with teammates and coaches. He should continue his development as a starter when he returns in 2020, though there's a non-zero chance that Kilome, with his fastball-curveball combo, will end up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Pacific-12 Conference player of the year as a sophomore in 2017, Madrigal saw his chances of repeating end when he broke his left wrist early in his junior season. He still lived up to his reputation as the best player and hitter in college baseball and became the second-highest-drafted second baseman ever when the White Sox picked him at No. 4 overall (two spots lower than the Brewers took Rickie Weeks in 2003). After helping Oregon State win the College World Series, he signed for $6,411,400 and batted .303 in his pro debut while advancing to Class A Advanced. Madrigal's introduction to pro ball reinforced why scouts considered him the best pure hitter in the 2018 Draft. Unfazed by advanced competition, he used his controlled right-handed swing to spray line drives all over the field while striking out just five times in 173 plate appearances. He's small and doesn't have a lot of raw strength, but his ability to barrel the ball and his plus speed should produce a healthy amount of doubles and maybe 12-15 homers per season. Recruited by Oregon State as a shortstop, Madrigal wound up playing second base for the Beavers in deference to Cadyn Grenier, an Orioles supplemental first-rounder who was rated as the best college defender in the 2018 Draft. Madrigal has the hands and actions to play shortstop, though his average arm makes him a better fit at second base. Chicago planned on trying him at short but he has spent almost all of his pro career at second, where he could develop into a Gold Glover.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The triple-digit velocity and electric stuff that made Pearson a first-round Draft pick arrived in the Major Leagues in 2020, as the Blue Jays summoned the JC of Central Florida product from the alternate training site in late July to make his debut. Pearson pitched well in his first two starts, but he struggled to throw strikes in his next two turns before a right flexor strain forced him to the 10-day injured list. He made a healthy return to pitch out of Toronto’s bullpen late in the regular season, then recorded five strikeouts while hitting 101 mph during a perfect two-inning appearance against the Rays in the American League Wild Card Series. Multiple groin injuries have limited him again in 2021, and he moved exclusively to the bullpen in the second half, though the Jays still hold out hope he could become a starter again in the future. Pearson can be untouchable when he’s firing on all cylinders, operating with an elite fastball-slider pairing and a changeup that continues to improve. His fastball sits 96-100 mph with explosive life as a starter, and he’s shown that he can dial it up even higher in shorter bursts, having famously hit 104 mph in the 2018 Fall Stars Game. His slider is a true swing-and-miss pitch, registering in the upper 80s with two-plane action, and his upper-70s mph changeup can flash plus when he doesn’t throw it too firmly. A 12-to-6 curveball that Pearson throws in the upper 70s rounds out his deep four-pitch mix. The fact that Pearson held big league hitters to a .209 average (.318 xwOBA) in 2020 speaks to the quality of his raw stuff, and he did throw strikes consistently in the Minors (2.3 BB/9) before struggling to do so with Toronto (6.5 BB/9). Some worry about Pearson’s durability because he accrued only 123 1/3 frames in the Minors, but the right-hander has a clean and athletic delivery that he repeats well, along with a frame that bodes well for adding strength. Outside of consistent health, Pearson has the ingredients needed to become a front-of-the-rotation starter, and he’s already shown that he can dominate big league hitters coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 The Reds seem to be getting rewarded for their patience with Stephenson, who endured numerous struggles and injuries after being selected No. 11 overall out of high school in 2015. His first two full pro seasons included a concussion, a right wrist issue and a thumb injury that shut him down in July of 2017. But he was healthy in 2018 and delivered results. There are many reasons to be high on Stephenson, especially because of his defense. Despite being a bigger guy at 6-foot-4, he doesn't look too big when he's set up behind the plate while offering a good target and showing excellent flexibility. One scout felt his hands were the best part of his defense. Stephenson still has length in his throwing mechanics, but has kept working to shorten his throws in order to maximize his plus arm strength, and is making progress calling games. Still learning who he is as a hitter, Stephenson hits for average but has some raw power. He needs to figure out the breaking ball and how to hit it. By staying on the field last season and showing what he can do, it brought optimism that Stephenson can be a quality everyday Major League catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers had not drafted a high school pitcher in the first round since Jacob Turner in 2009 when they made Burrows the No. 22 overall pick in 2015. The Texas native has followed a developmental path most teams hope a prep pitcher will follow since signing for $2,154,000, as he reached Double-A at age 20 in 2017, a month before pitching in the Futures Game. Returning to the Eastern League in 2018, Burrows garnered honors as a midseason All-Star and once again showed he could handle a heavy workload as he logged at least 26 starts and 134 innings for a second straight season. Burrows' four-pitch arsenal is headlined by a plus fastball that sits in the low 90s and consistently touches the mid-90s. He throws the pitch with good life down in the zone, allowing him to miss bats, though it does flatten out when elevated. Burrows' secondary stuff still needs refinement, but he can spin a very good curve, added a slider and has made enough progress in developing his changeup that it's now considered an above-average pitch. Burrows is still learning how to consistently repeat his delivery, and the hope is that with further refinement he'll be able to develop average control. He has the makings of a future No. 4 starter, perhaps more if he can improve his secondaries and miss more bats, and there's little doubt that Burrows' stuff would play up out of the bullpen should he not stick in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Whitley pitched to mixed results as a starter during his first two years at Division II Mount Olive (N.C.) before Tommy John surgery wiped out his junior campaign. He made a healthy return to the mound in 2017, showing well in a relief role that prompted the Cardinals to take him in the 27th round in June. He made easy work of the Class A Midwest League the following year and broke out in earnest during a 2019 season that saw him climb three levels up to Triple-A Memphis, where he recorded a 1.52 ERA over 16 appearances. He improved his prospect stock even more after the season with an impressive Arizona Fall League campaign. A big, physical right-hander, Whitley dominates right-handed hitters with his fastball and slider, both of which grade as at least above average. He consistently beats hitters in the zone with a 94-97 mph fastball that he throws with life and angle, and his slider, a mid-80s offering with downer action, gives Whitley a second swing-and-miss pitch. Whitley turns over his changeup well to impart late fading action that plays well against left-handed hitters. He's consistently around the zone with all three pitches, showing solid command and control. Despite being a fly-ball pitcher, Whitley did not allow a home run last season over 24 innings in the extremely hitter-friendly Triple-A Pacific Coast League. That trait, combined with his natural bat-missing ability gives Whitley a bright future as a Major League reliever, and it might not be long until he's ready for a late-inning bullpen role in St. Louis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Holloway has the potential to be the biggest Draft steal in the organization. A top-five-round talent as a Colorado high schooler in 2014, he dropped to the 20th round amid signability concerns but gave up a commitment to Nebraska-Omaha to sign for well over slot at $400,000. Tommy John surgery in June 2017 sidelined him for most of last year, but he impressed enough during five brief Minor League appearances and instructional league to claim a spot on the 40-man roster. Holloway has the makings of a top-of-the-rotation talent, beginning with a fastball that ranges from 95-99 mph. Though his curveball needs more consistency, it can be an absolute hammer at times. His changeup is more of a work in progress but shows solid potential. While his upside is apparent, Holloway needs to establish health and consistency. He hasn't had much success as a pro because he struggles to command and control his pitches. Though he has scuffled in high Class A this year, the Marlins believe he'll start improving as he gains more experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2016 Western Athletic Conference player of the year, Johnson led the circuit in batting (.382), homers (12) and steals (29) for New Mexico State before the Nationals drafted him in the fifth round. He had a strong first full pro season with 22 homers and as many steals between two Class A levels but slumped in 2018, when he was hampered by a broken hamate in his right hand. The Indians acquired him in November along with infielder Andruw Monasterio and right-hander Jefry Rodriguez when they shipped Yan Gomes to Washington. Johnson is a power-over-hit guy, with his bat speed and strength giving him above-average raw pop from the left side of the plate. He'll need to temper his aggressive approach in order to hit for average, and he has yet to prove he can handle left-handers well enough to be more than a platoon player. He knows how to use his plus speed to steal and take extra bases. Johnson runs well enough to play center field but has spent the majority of his career in right. That's in large part because he has plus-plus arm strength that helped him rack up 11 assists in just 92 games last year. If he can't hit consistently enough to make it as a regular, his tools would make him a dynamic fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best athletes in the 2015 international class, Taveras signed for $2.1 million out of the Dominican Republic. The cousin of former big league stolen-base champ Willy Taveras, he spent the entire 2018 season in Class A Advanced and played in the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game as a 19-year-old. Advanced for his age, Taveras has perennially been one of the youngest regulars in his leagues, but he batted just .253/.315/.351 in his first three pro seasons. A switch-hitter, Taveras has been slightly more effective as a lefty but has a good swing from both sides of the plate. He has advanced bat-to-ball skills but needs to get stronger and more selective so he can make more quality contact. While he won't ever be a slugger, he has the bat speed and projectable frame to develop at least 15-homer power. Taveras' basestealing is also a work in progress, as he's still learning how to use his plus speed on the bases. He's already one of the best outfield defenders in the Minors, a no-doubt center fielder whose solid arm is better than most at the position. His game presently resembles that of Ender Inciarte, though the Rangers believe he'll develop at the plate and reach a higher offensive ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Having MLB bloodlines can be a very good thing. And there's no question that Contreras, the younger brother of Cubs catcher Willson Contreras, has some of the attributes that have made his older brother a big league regular. While Contreras the younger had a very successful first taste of full-season ball as a South Atlantic League All-Star in 2018, there's also been the flip side of that bloodlines coin, where he's fallen into the trap of believing he can do everything his more established sibling can. Contreras has all of the tools to be a very successful all-around catcher at the big league level. While he is a bit of a free swinger and sometimes attacks pitches out of the zone more than he should, he has shown the ability to make hard contact and draw walks while relatively limiting his strikeouts. He's starting to come into a little more power as he learns what he needs to adjust at the plate, and the Braves were pleased that he was making those adjustments in his offseason work. Defensively, he's always had a strong arm and has plenty of agility to be a good blocker and receiver. The biggest thing Contreras needs to learn is that there is a process to becoming a finished product behind the plate, like his brother. As he starts to buy into building the foundation of being able to be a complete receiver, and not think he's already like his older brother, the more he'll be able to develop into the big league starter the Braves envision.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosso entered pro ball initially with the Dodgers, signing for just $62,000 in July 2015. The Dodgers released him a year later without having thrown an official pitch, but he caught on with the Phillies in June 2017, making his pro debut at age 21, pitching his way from the Dominican Summer League up to the short-season New York-Penn League. He pitched well across two levels of A ball in his full-season debut in 2018, then ascended to Triple-A in 2019. He made his big league debut in July of 2020, riding the shuttle a bit between the alternate site and the big leagues, before throwing very well in the Dominican Winter League this past offseason. The big right-hander has good stuff, starting with a fastball that has ticked upward and was up over 97 mph during his time in the big leagues and regularly in the mid-90s. It’s a cutter-like heater that can really ride in on a hitter’s hands. He’s continued to improve his slider, adding sweep and depth to it, giving him a second viable weapon. He’s folded in a curve on occasion and has shown glimpses of a below-average changeup, but he relies on the cutter-slider combination more than anything. Outside of his brief big league debut, Rosso has generally been around the plate, though he needs to improve the consistency of his command. The cutter has a chance to be an elite pitch and should on its own give him a relief role in the future. He looked very good in a starting role in the Dominican, but Rosso will more likely fill a seventh- or eighth-inning role if the velocity gains stick around and the slider keeps improving.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz received the second-highest bonus among corner infielders on the international market in 2013, signing out of the Dominican Republic with the Twins for $1.4 million. He made steady progress before struggling in '18, when he slugged .344 in Class A Advanced before breaking his right thumb, then rebounded to hit 27 homers in '19, when he went to the Marlins as part of the Sergio Romo trade in July. He made his big league debut late last summer, going 6-for-39 (.154), and he made the roster for the Wild Card Series but didn't see any playoff action. Diaz is built to hit for plenty of power from the left side of the plate. He packs loads of strength and leverage in his 6-foot-4 frame, generates good bat speed and looks to drive balls in the air. He does show some feel for hitting and uses the entire field, though he probably won't hit for a high average unless he adopts a more disciplined approach. While he has below-average speed, Diaz has improved his conditioning since entering pro ball and moves surprisingly well for such a large man. He's agile around the bag at first base and has enough arm strength to make all the needed throws there. He stood out with his defense during his introduction to the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Miami traded off most of its veteran players following the franchise's sale in October 2017, Sánchez was the best prospect it received in return. The Phillies had signed him for $35,000 in February 2015, and he became the centerpiece of the J.T. Realmuto trade four years later. He starred in his big league debut in 2020, including six shutout innings against the Cubs in the Wild Card Series, but he hurt his shoulder the following spring and didn't pitch in 2021 or 2022 after having surgeries each year. When healthy, Sánchez had a pair of well-above-average pitches in his fastball and changeup. He could blow hitters away with a 95-97 mph power sinker and a 97-99 four-seamer that hit triple digits with riding action, then make them look silly with an upper-80s changeup that dove at the plate. He also showed signs of developing a mid-80s curveball, though he used it sparingly, and had a promising upper-80s cutter that lacked consistency. Although Sánchez has a short and thick frame, he has a smooth and repeatable delivery and averaged 1.8 walks per nine innings before his shoulder injuries. He hasn't missed as many bats as his high-quality stuff suggests he should, though he has generated plenty of weak ground-ball contact. He had durability questions before missing the last two seasons, losing most of 2019 to elbow inflammation and never topping 114 innings in a calendar year, but the Marlins are hopeful after he dropped a significant amount of weight this offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best prospect the Marlins received when they traded off most of their veteran core following the franchise's sale in October 2017, Sanchez originally signed with the Phillies for $35,000 in February 2015. Part of the J.T. Realmuto trade four years later, he made an impressive big league debut in 2020, permitting just five runs in his first six starts and spinning six shutout innings against the Cubs in the Wild Card Series. He missed all of the 2021 season after hurting his shoulder in March and having surgery to repair a small tear in his posterior capsule in July, and he had yet to return to game action 13 months later. Few pitching prospects can match Sanchez's combination of pure stuff and command. He owns a pair of well-above-average pitches in his fastball -- he throws both a 95-97 mph power sinker and a 97-99 mph four-seamer that reaches triple digits with riding action -- and his upper-80s changeup that dives when it arrives at the plate. He uses his mid-80s curveball sparingly but it shows flashes of becoming a plus offering, and he also has a promising upper-80s cutter that needs more consistency. With a short but strong frame and a fluid, repeatable delivery, Sanchez averaged 1.8 walks per nine innings in his first six pro seasons. He could be a frontline starter if he stays healthy, but in addition to his shoulder woes he also missed most of 2019 with elbow inflammation and never has topped 114 innings in a calendar year. Curiously, he doesn't miss nearly as many bats as his stuff suggests he should, though much of the contact against him comes in the form of weak grounders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins jettisoned many of their best and most expensive players after a group led by Bruce Sherman and Derek Jeter bought the franchise from Jeffrey Loria in October 2017, and the best prospect the franchise received in any of those deals is Sanchez, the centerpiece of the J.T. Realmuto trade with the Phillies in February 2019. Philadelphia initially spotted Sanchez while attending a workout for a Cuban catcher in the Dominican Republic in February 2015 and signed him for $35,000. He made his big league debut at age 22 last August, allowing just five runs in his first six starts and working five scoreless innings against the Cubs in the Wild Card Series, but he will miss all of 2021 after injuring his shoulder at Miami's alternate site in late March and getting diagnosed three months later with a small tear of his posterior capsule that required surgery. He's expected to be ready for Spring Training in 2022. Sanchez utilizes both two- and four-seam fastballs, with the former sitting at 95-97 mph with power sink and the latter parking at 97-99 mph and frequently climbing into triple digits with riding action. His well above-average changeup was his most effective pitch in his first taste of the Majors, arriving in the upper 80s before diving at the plate. He added an upper-80s cutter during alternate camp and will mix in an occasional mid-80s curveball, both of which show flashes of becoming plus offerings. Few pitching prospects can match Sanchez's combination of stuff and command. He's short but has a strong frame and an easy, repeatable delivery that has led to him average 1.8 walks per nine innings in his first six pro seasons. The only knocks on him are that he doesn't miss as many bats as his arsenal suggests he should and that he doesn't have a great track record of health after also missing most of 2018 with elbow inflammation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It has been a long road for Jefferies, a local Cal product who was selected 37th overall by the A’s in the 2016 Draft. Expected to quickly progress through the system, he ran into elbow issues that required Tommy John surgery and kept him out for nearly two seasons. When he returned in 2019, Jefferies again advanced quickly, reaching Double-A and earning a spot on the club’s 40-man roster. Spending most of 2020 at the club’s alternate site, he got a taste of the big leagues with a Major League start in Texas last September. What immediately stands out about Jefferies is his pinpoint command. He posted a ridiculous 93/9 K/BB ratio over 79 innings in 2019 and continued to show that off at the alternate site. The excellent command is key, as it allows his fastball that sits around 91-94 mph to play even better. His changeup is a strong complement as a secondary pitch that has excellent fade and drops off the table at the end. He is still working on the remnants of his breaking ball, which is described as somewhere between a slider and slurve. Figuring out his breaking ball is the final stage of his development. If he can develop a consistent one, Jefferies profiles nicely as a middle-of-the-rotation starter, sort of in the mold of a Kyle Hendricks type with increased velocity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best prospects in the 2014 international crop, Florial was set to receive a seven-figure bonus until MLB banned him from turning pro for one year after learning he had falsified his identity while registering for school in the Dominican Republic. After he produced a Haitian birth certificate with a slightly different birthdate, he signed for $200,000 in March 2015. His loud tools are mitigated by an overly aggressive approach at the plate, and the loss of at-bats to a broken right hamate (2018), a wrist injury (2019) and the pandemic shutdown (2020) have harmed his development. Florial has four tools that grade as plus or better in his raw power, speed, arm and defense, but it remains to be seen if he'll hit enough after he struck out at a 29 percent clip in his first six pro seasons and batted a career-worst .218 with a 31 percent whiff rate in Triple-A last year. He has made some progress with his left-handed stroke in 2022, as it's not as long and uphill as it has been in the past, though he continues to struggle to recognize and do damage against breaking balls and changeups. His bat speed, strength and loft give him 30-homer pop that plays to all fields, but he can't make enough contact to consistently tap into it. Florial has plus speed but still is learning to translate it into stolen bases. His quickness plays better in center field, combining with his instincts to give him tremendous range. His arm earns double-plus grades from some scouts and helps make him an asset anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As one of the best prospects in the 2014 international class, Florial was in line to receive a seven-figure bonus until MLB banned him from turning pro for one year after learning he had assumed the identity of Haniel de Oleo while registering for school in the Dominican Republic. Signed for $200,000 in March 2015 after producing a Haitian birth certificate with a slightly different birthdate, he has loud tools but also an overly aggressive approach at the plate. His development has been slowed by the loss of much-needed at-bats because of injuries to his right hamate (2018) and wrist (2019) before the pandemic shutdown last year. Though Florial's official game action in 2020 was limited to one contest with the Yankees and 18 in the Dominican Winter League, club officials believe he made offensive strides working against advanced pitchers at their alternate site during the summer. His bat speed, strength and the loft in his left-handed swing create well above-average raw power to all fields, but it remains to be seen how much of that pop he'll be able to tap into. He has a tendency to get pull-happy and long with this stroke and has struggled to recognize offspeed pitches, resulting in a career 28 percent strikeout rate in his first six years as a pro. Florial's speed and arm strength earn double-plus grades from some evaluators. If he can refine his plate discipline and his basestealing acumen, he could become a 30-30 threat. His quickness and instincts give him quality range in center field and he's capable of playing all three outfield positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Other teams started asking about Tejeda in trade talks as soon as he made his U.S. debut in 2016. Signed for $100,000 out of the Dominican Republic two years earlier, he immediately demonstrated enticing power potential for a middle infielder. He ranked second in total bases (205) and fifth in homers (19) as a 20-year-old in the Class A Advanced Carolina League last year, though his 2019 season ended in last May when he injured his non-throwing shoulder while sliding into a base. Tejeda stands just 5-foot-11, but his combination of wiry strength, whippy swing and bat speed could develop into plus power. To get all the way there, he'll have to improve as a hitter, because he still gets too aggressive and pull-happy instead of letting his home runs come naturally. A natural left-handed hitter who has scuffled against southpaws in pro ball, he resumed switch-hitting in 2019 after previously batting from both sides as an amateur. Tejeda significantly upgraded his defensive profile last season, erasing any doubts that he could stay at shortstop. Though he's an average runner, he has improved his instincts and range. His plus-plus arm allows him to make throws and plays that many shortstops can't.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite flashing a low-90s fastball as a 16-year-old right-hander in Curacao, Apostel preferred to hit and signed with the Pirates for $200,000 as third baseman in 2015, two years before they inked his younger brother, Shendrik. Sent to the Rangers in the Keone Kela trade in August 2018, Apostel slammed 19 homers at age 20 in his full-season debut the following year. He spent last summer at Texas' alternate site and was an emergency callup when injuries struck the big league club in September, going 2-for-20 with nine strikeouts. Apostel has two well above-average tools in his raw right-handed power and arm strength. Once he added more loft to his swing in 2019, he began to translate the strength and leverage in his still-growing 6-foot-4 frame into home run pop to all fields. He's still learning at the plate because he hasn't faced much advanced pitching yet and his size results in a naturally long stroke. Though there are no plans for Apostel to resume pitching, scouts speculate he might work in the mid-90s if he did. He moves well for his size but is already a below-average runner with subpar range at third base. He has begun seeing more action at first base since the Rangers spent their 2019 first-round choice on Josh Jung, a superior defender at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of North Dakota, Young began his collegiate career at Neosho County Community College before transferring to Indiana State. After two solid seasons there, he signed as a senior with the Cardinals for $3,000 in the 37th round of the 2016 Draft. He went from organizational filler to interesting prospect by hitting 17 homers across two levels of A ball in his first full season, then reaching Double-A in his second and hitting 21 more home runs. After impressing in the Arizona Fall League, he was sent to the D-backs as part of the package received for Paul Goldschmidt. The stocky infielder is mostly all bat, but it's a good one. He's shown the ability to make consistent hard contact from the right side of the plate with at least solid average power. Young hits a ton of fly balls and showed his power by smashing a dozen home runs in Palm Beach in 2018, an extreme pitcher's park. While he doesn't walk a ton, he did cut his strikeout rate down considerably in 2018 and showed a much better overall approach in the AFL. Young has seen time defensively at three infield positions and a little time in the outfield corners. With below-average speed and a fringy arm, his best bet to be a regular will be at second, with a career as an offensive-minded utility type a possibility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners signed Neidert for $1.2 million as their top choice (second round) in the 2015 Draft, then sent him to the Marlins as part of the Dee Strange-Gordon trade two years later. He topped the Double-A Southern League in wins (12) and innings (152 2/3) in his first season in his new organization, but missed time in 2019 (torn meniscus in his right knee) and 2020 (COVID-related reasons). He has bounced on and off the big league roster the last two years, compiling a 4.70 ERA with just 25 strikeouts and as many walks in 44 innings. Neidert's best pitch remains his low-80s changeup, a plus offering with tumble and fade. He sets it up with an 89- to 93-mph four-seam fastball with some armside run that's more notable for his ability to command it than its velocity or movement. He never has shown great feel for spin, but has made some progress with a short mid-80s slider/cutter that works better than his mid-70s curveball. Neidert's repertoire is geared more to induce weak contact than miss bats, and he has been hit hard in the Majors when he has failed to locate his pitches. There's some deception in his delivery but it got out of sync toward the end of 2021, making him more vulnerable when he fell behind in the count. He still might be a back-of-the-rotation starter if he can regain the consistency he showed in the past, though he'll also be 25 this season and may be running out of chances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Mariners for $1.2 million as their top choice (second round) in the 2015 Draft, Neidert came to the Marlins as part of the Dee Strange-Gordon trade in December 2017 and led the Double-A Southern League in wins (12) and innings (152 2/3) in his first season with his new organization. He tore the meniscus in his right knee in early 2019, sidelining him for three months and contributing to a career-worst 5.05 ERA in Triple-A, but rebounded with a strong performance in the Arizona Fall League. He made his big league debut last July, spent six weeks on the injured list for COVID-related reasons, then returned to earn a spot on Miami's postseason roster (though he didn't pitch in the playoffs). More about pitchability than pure stuff, Neidert has one plus offering in his tumbling low-80s changeup. He sets it up with a 90-93 mph fastball that plays better than its velocity because of its sink and his ability to command it to either side of the plate. He's still seeking a reliable breaking ball but is making progess with a mid-80s slider/cutter that's more effective than his slurvy curveball. Neidert has pounded the strike zone throughout his pro career and throws off hitters' timing with deception in his delivery. While he has the arsenal of a back-of-the-rotation starter, his feel for pitching may allow him to be more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peter Lambert went in the second round out of high school en route to making the big leagues, while older brother Jimmy took a different path to get there. Undrafted as a prepster, Lambert pitched his way into 2016's fifth round after three years at Fresno State. He rebounded from Tommy John surgery in 2019 to serve five brief stints in Chicago during the next two seasons and is the best of the organization's big league-ready arms. Lambert's pair of breaking pitches feature some of the best spin rates in the system, creating good depth on a 74-78 mph curveball and an 81-85 mph slider. Both grade as solid offerings, with his slider the better option because it features more power and he commands it better. He can show some good carry on a fastball that sits at 92-95 mph and reaches 97, though his heater is fairly straight and gets pounded if he doesn't locate it well, and also owns a low-80s changeup with some fade. Though Lambert is athletic and repeats his delivery, he hasn't thrown as many strikes against upper-level hitters as he did in the past. He can keep batters off balance by sequencing his pitches well but needs to attack them more. He could fit into the back of a rotation but may be more of a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Unlike his younger brother, Peter, a coveted high school product who made it to the Majors with the Rockies, Lambert went undrafted as a prepster and spent three years at Fresno State. A fifth-round pick in 2016, he quickly blossomed into one of the White Sox best pitching prospects but wound up needing Tommy John surgery in June 2019. He made Chicago's Opening Day roster last summer and pitched in his first two big league games before going on the injured list with a forearm strain. Lambert's fastball and curveball feature some of the highest spin rates in the system and give him a pair of solid offerings to highlight a four-pitch mix. He works up in the zone with a four-seam heater that sits in the low 90s and tops out at 96 mph with riding action, and at the bottom of it with a mid-70s curve with good depth. He also possesses a fading changeup in the low 80s and a lateral-breaking slider with a tick more velocity. Lambert's athleticism allows him to repeat his delivery and throw strikes on a consistent basis. He does a nice job of sequencing his pitches to keep hitters off balance. After some time in Triple-A, he could help the White Sox as a back-of-the-rotation starter or multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Already 19 when the Astros added him as one of the final pieces in their 2015-16 international class, Rodriguez signed for $10,000 out of Venezuela in June 2016. Despite his advanced age and consistent success as soon as he entered pro ball, he didn't reach full-season ball until 2019. He made up for lost time by posting a 2.40 ERA, .183 opponent average and 114 strikeouts in 105 innings between two Class A levels, earning a spot on the 40-man roster in November. Rodriguez has carved up lower-level hitters with one of the best curveballs in the system, a true downer with high spin rates. His fastball often sits at 90-92 mph and tops out at 94, but it has good shape that helps it play better than its velocity. While his changeup is more of a work in progress, he'll flash some with some interesting splitter action. Rodriguez's control slipped a bit when he got to Class A Advanced last May, but he righted the ship and provided strikes like he has for most of his pro career. His curveball is a weapon but it's also his only pitch that grades better than average, leading to questions about his future as a starter. If he moves to the bullpen, he could rely more heavily on his bender and perhaps add some velocity to his fastball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick by the Twins in 2015, Cody agreed to a $1 million bonus that fell through when a post-Draft physical raised concerns about his elbow. He returned to Kentucky for his senior season, signed with the Rangers for $150,000 as a sixth-rounder the following June and swiftly emerged as one of the most advanced pitching prospects in the system. He hurt his elbow last spring and tried to rehab it for two months before undergoing Tommy John surgery in July. When healthy, Cody had a 93-96 mph that topped out at 98, maintaining his velocity into the late innings and using his 6-foot-7 frame to create steep downhill plane. His 82-85 mph slider had added power and bite after he turned pro and did a better job of staying on top of it. Texas had him dial back the use of his slider to work on commanding his fastball and improving his changeup. Cody dominated down the stretch in 2017 and was on course to reach at least Double-A last year before he got hurt. He has a history of throwing strikes and had begun to demonstrate improved command and the possibility of becoming a No. 3 starter. Because has made only five starts above low Class A and will be 25 when he pitches in his next game, the Rangers could shift him to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $7,500 in the middle of the 2014-15 international signing period out of Venezuela, Llovera was an under-the-radar prospect, pitching mostly in relief in his full-season debut in 2017. A strong move to the rotation in the Florida State League in 2018 put him more on the map and though a forearm strain shut him down in July of 2019, he pitched well enough to earn a spot on the 40-man roster that offseason. Llovera spent 2020 at the Phillies’ alternate site, getting called up to make his Major League debut in early September. While Llovera’s fastball has backed up a bit, sitting in the 93-95 mph range, he does a nice job of working east to west with the offering. His changeup is his best pitch, an above-average mid-80s offspeed pitch that misses bats and gets weak contact. While he once worked with two breaking balls, he’s shelved his curve and is focusing on his 83-85 mph slider and has added some sweep to it. Llovera is generally a strike-thrower, albeit without pinpoint command, and he managed to strikeout 10 per nine innings in 2018-19 combined. His big league debut didn’t go well, but it came as a reliever, a role he’s likely going to fill going forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Braymer established a single-season strikeout record in his second season at LSU-Eunice in 2015, punching out 138 batters in just fewer than 95 innings. He transferred from the junior college program to Auburn the following year, pitched well in multiple roles for the Tigers and then became the Nationals' 18th-round pick in June, signing for $100,000. As a pro, Braymer has continued to flex his versatility on the mound while succeeding in a host of roles. The left-hander was particularly impressive in 2018, leading Nats farmhands in ERA (2.28) and finishing third in strikeouts (118) while pitching in 28 games (11 starts) across two levels. In recognition of his season-long success, Braymer was named the Nationals co-pitcher of the year, sharing the honor with Wil Crowe. Braymer showed last season that his stuff would play regardless of his role. The left-hander works with a 92-93 mph fastball and has bumped a few ticks higher in the past, albeit without much in the way of late movement. He complements his heater with an above-average curveball with 12-to-6 action that is lethal on left-handed hitters -- they batted just .174 against Braymer in '18 -- and a changeup gives him a distant third pitch. The Nationals are quick to praise Braymer for having the mental toughness needed to successfully bounce between starting and relieving. As with some of the other pitchers in the system, he'll likely be deployed as a starter in 2019 to refine his secondary pitches and overall command. But given his proven effectiveness against lefties, Braymer is probably ticketed for a bullpen role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres blew past their international bonus pool in 2016 to sign a handful of their top prospects, but none of those signings were bigger than Cubans Adrian Morejon and Oña. Oña received a $7 million bonus, trailing only Morejon’s $11 million. Oña struggled in his first two full seasons, before undergoing shoulder surgery early in 2019. But he returned from that injury stronger than ever, slashing .348/.417/.539 at Double-A Amarillo. That surge prompted the Padres to add him to their 40-man roster in November, protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft. Oña’s time on the 40-man got off to a rough start when he missed the first three months of the 2021 season following surgery to remove a bone spur from his right elbow. Oña was one of the team’s standouts at the alternate site in 2020. He earned a brief big league callup, going 3-for-12 with a mammoth homer and a couple walks in 14 plate appearances. Oña stands out on the field for his muscular physique and huge raw power. At the plate, the right-handed hitter combines strength and bat speed to generate plus power, and he's shown the ability to drive the ball out of the park across the entire field. Oña’s penchant for swinging and missing leads some to question his hit tool. He can play both corner outfield positions but is underwhelming defensively, showing limited range and below-average speed but also a strong arm. Oña’s progression hasn’t always been the steadiest, but the Padres feel the raw tools are there for a big league-caliber slugger.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Burdi has followed the path of his older brother Nick, going from closing games at Louisville to the early rounds of the Draft to Tommy John surgery. Nick (now with the Pirates) was a Twins second-rounder in 2014, while Zack signed for $2,128,500 as a White Sox first-rounder two years later and both needed elbow reconstruction in 2017. The younger Burdi returned at the end of last year to pitch 11 innings between Rookie ball and the Arizona Fall League, then made just 20 appearances in 2019 before needing surgery to repair a ligament tear in his patella. Before Burdi got hurt, he averaged 12.9 strikeouts per nine innings thanks to a fastball that sat at 95-100 mph and peaked at 102 with some armside run and a low-90s slider with impressive depth. Chicago had him control his intensity during his initial return, when his heater parked at 92-96 mph and his slider operated in the mid-80s. A potential closer, he'll be under no restrictions in 2019. Burdi hasn't used it much in pro ball but his tumbling changeup can be a plus pitch at its best, keeping hitters from sitting on his fastball, which can get straight on occasion. Once he's back at full strength, refining his control and command is all he needs to do to earn his first big league callup. He sometimes has trouble keeping his delivery in sync and loses direction to the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals grabbed Barrera in the sixth round of the 2016 Draft after the backstop played 50-plus games in all three of his seasons at Texas. The club moved him methodically through the organization, watching as he picked up All-Star honors in the South Atlantic and Carolina Leagues in 2017 and 2018 respectively. The right-handed hitter performed solidly with a 108 wRC+ at Double-A Harrisburg in 2019, got a Major League callup that September and appeared in two games for the Nats prior to their World Series run. Barrera’s ascent back to the Majors last year was halted when he was suspended 80 games after testing positive for a banned performance-enhancing substance. He made up some of the time with seven games in the Dominican Winter League, but ended that stint early due a family tragedy. Barrera can be a leader from the catching position, showing the glove and arm to both receive and throw well enough to be a Major League defensive asset. The bat is a few ticks behind. Though he hasn’t been a below-average hitter in the Minors, the Nationals felt he was too pull-happy at times and that caused his swing to get loopy. They would rather him focus on being a hitter who puts together more solid contact, rather than one occasionally giving away at-bats with his approach. Given Barrera’s ability to impact the game from behind the plate, he doesn’t need to hit much to find his way into a lineup on a regular basis. He's done just that at every other stop in his career. Right now, he is ticketed to be a backup with the potential for more if a new offensive approach kicks in.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Davis homered off Carlos Rodon on the first pitch he saw in college and took him deep again as a sophomore, positioning himself as a potential top-five-rounds pick as an Appalachian State junior in 2015. But he tore the labrum in his right (throwing) shoulder early that spring, ending his season and dropping him all the way to the 24th round and the Twins, who signed him for $50,000. He didn't make his pro debut until 2016 and didn't break out until 2019, when he slammed 36 homers -- 10 in 27 Triple-A games and his first big league blast after the Giants acquired him as part of the Sam Dyson trade in July. Davis' tool profile and his statistical profile are somewhat at odds. He's very strong and generates at least plus raw power and impressive exit velocities from the right side of the plate, but he doesn't drive the ball in the air consistently and had the fourth-highest ground-ball rate (51 percent) of any Minor Leaguer with 20 or more homers in 2019. He displayed elite sprint speed during his September callup, but he plays closer to average on the bases and in the field, stealing just 34 bases in his first 452 pro games. That dichotomy won't matter if Davis' power continues to play like it did a year ago. To establish himself in the Majors, he'll need to continue to build on the progress he made with his plate discipline last season. He plays all three outfield positions but has spent the vast majority of his time in right field, where his pop and solid arm fit the profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 A strong showing as a Pittsburgh junior in 2016 pushed Zeuch into the first round of the Draft, where the Blue Jays selected the big right-hander with the No. 21 overall pick. A back injury limited Zeuch somewhat during his first full season, but he still jumped on the big league radar by pitching well at Class A Advanced Dunedin and then boosted his stock even more against better competition in the Arizona Fall League. Returning to the Florida State League in 2018, Zeuch made just six starts at Dunedin before moving up to Double-A New Hampshire. He was an Eastern League All-Star at midseason, and continued to pitch well down the stretch while leading the Fisher Cats to an Eastern League title. An imposing presence on the mound at 6-foot-7, Zeuch uses his height to his advantage by creating a steep angle to the plate. The downhill plane only enhances the right-hander's sinker, a plus pitch he throws with heavy late life in the low- to mid-90s. This enables him to generate ground balls at a near-elite rate (57 percent in '18). Zeuch's curveball has become his best secondary offering and plays nicely off his sinker, keeping hitters off-balance with its shape and late bite. His slider wasn't as sharp in 2018 but is still viewed as an average pitch, and he also throws a changeup that's a distant fourth pitch. Despite his size, Zeuch's long levers are consistently in-sync, and he repeats his delivery well. It allows him to pound the zone with his entire arsenal. Zeuch assuaged concerns about his durability last season by accruing more than 156 innings, or more than double the workload from his first full season. The only drawback to Zeuch's profile is that he doesn't miss many bats and therefore doesn't rack up strikeouts. Instead, he mostly pitches to contact, consistently attacking the bottom of the zone early in the count to force weak contact. Altogether, Zeuch has the look of a future backend starter at the highest level, perhaps more if he can improve his breaking balls and start to generate more whiffs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals are still learning about Bolaños, who they acquired with Franchy Cordero from the Padres for Tim Hill in July 2020. San Diego signed Bolaños for $2 million in the 2016-17 international class at age 19 after defecting from Cuba, and it took some time for Bolaños to adjust to professional ball in the United States. He made a serious leap in 2019, posting a 3.66 ERA between Class A Advanced and Double-A, earning a September callup to the Padres’ big league roster. He’s an intriguing prospect for the Royals and was able to flash some stuff for them at the alternate training site and in two abbreviated starts in Kansas City. A right flexor strain has kept him from building on that impact in 2021, though he was on the mend in August. Bolaños has a strong starter’s build at 6-foot-2 and could still grow into his frame. He has a four-pitch mix highlighted by his fastball, which sits around 94-95 mph and has cut, sink or rise to it depending on how he throws it.
