mlb_pipeline.text: After a solid career at Seattle Preparatory School, Franklin hit 23 homers over his first two years at Michigan, becoming more of a power-first type hitter as a sophomore, albeit with a ton of walks. He hit well in the Cape Cod League, but didn’t get to follow that up due to a broken collar bone that wiped out any at-bats in the shortened 2020 season. The Braves had seen enough to take him in the third round of that summer’s Draft and he rewarded their faith by finishing tied for the High-A East lead in home runs and finishing a steal shy of a 20-20 campaign, though he struggled in the Arizona Fall League. He barely got the chance to improve in 2022, playing in just 15 games before being shelved with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. While Franklin’s strikeout rate of around 28 percent in 2021 was too high, it was actually better than league average and was perhaps an acceptable tradeoff for the legitimate power he got to from the left side of the plate. Even with the K rate, his exit velocities and quality of contact were very impressive and he had a .936 OPS after an atrocious May. He still needs to work on his approach, something he was working on in the AFL, leading to a higher walk rate even if it didn’t translate into other positive results. After not being much of a threat in college, Franklin started to use his speed, a tick above-average, to his benefit on the basepaths. He can handle center field if needed, but will continue to be exposed to all three outfield spots as he hits the upper levels. Left field seems to be the best destination for him, with the power profile that works well for an outfield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid high school prospect from the Pacific Northwest, Franklin headed to Michigan rather than sign with the Mariners in the 37th round of the 2017 Draft. He broke out of the gate well as a freshman, hitting .327/.379/.588 for the Wolverines in 2018, then hitting .302 in the Cape Cod League. Selling out for more power as a sophomore did lead to more homers, but worse overall numbers, though he did help Michigan finish as runners-up in the College World Series. Though he broke his collarbone to wipe out even a shortened junior season, the Braves liked his first two years enough to take him in the third round of the 2020 Draft, and he made up for some lost time at the team’s alternate training site and during instructs. While Franklin doesn’t have any one plus tool, he can do a number of things fairly well. The Braves loved the quality of the at-bats he had from the left side of the plate, especially when facing upper-level lefty prospects like Kyle Muller and Tucker Davidson at the alternate site. There is strength and he’s shown a solid approach at the plate overall, with a chance to hit for decent average with some power if he can avoid trying to hit the ball out too much. Franklin is a touch above-average runner, but he’s never really used it to his advantage on the basepaths or in the outfield. He played mostly center field in college, but will likely see time in all three outfield spots as he gets his pro career started, with a fringy arm best suited for left if he were to settle into one spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ziegler was Draft-eligible at 17 years old in 2020, but the pandemic shutdown and shortened Draft hurt his chances. The Ontario native headed south to TNXL Academy in Florida to help his stock, and that paid off when the Mets signed him for $900,000 as a 2021 second-round pick. The 6-foot right-hander’s pro time has been marred by injuries since. Biceps tendinitis limited him to 46 2/3 innings at Single-A St. Lucie in his first full season. Before the 2023 campaign, he underwent surgery to address bone spurs in his right elbow and tore his quad during his rehab. He finally returned to a Florida State League mound on Sept. 9 and struck out all three batters he faced. On a per-pitch basis, there remains a lot to be excited about from the Canadian. Ziegler’s fastball touched 95.7 mph during that brief 2023 outing, and he’s generally been about 92-94 with the pitch in pro ball. The heater plays up too with terrific ride up in the zone. Off that, Ziegler utilizes an 82-85 mph curveball that shows good 12-to-6 drop, giving him a north-south approach. He’s worked with an 83-85 mph splitter that had a healthy whiff rate as well but didn’t use it in his lone 2023 appearance. Ziegler walked 17.6 percent of batters faced in 2022 because of his aggressive delivery. That control was going to be put to the test more in 2024 before injury concerns reared their head again. Ziegler underwent elbow issues early on that required Tommy John surgery, and he’ll miss the rest of the season as a result, wiping out what was looking like a potential breakout season. He’ll still only be in his age-22 campaign in 2025, giving him needed runway to regain his form and health beginning next summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ziegler could have been selected in 2020 when he was 17, but the combination of the pandemic shutdown and shortened Draft that summer did him no favors. To give himself a better showcase the next year, the Ontario native went to TNXL Academy in Ocoee, Fla., and that worked out well when he went in the second round and signed below slot at $900,000. Ziegler’s first full season was limited to 46 2/3 innings at Single-A St. Lucie due to biceps tendinitis and other concerns, but he fanned 70 batters in that span. Before the 2023 season, Ziegler underwent surgery to address bone spurs in his right elbow and later tore his quad during his rehab, keeping him out for much of the season. Standing at just an even 6 feet, the right-hander can good fastball velocity for his size in the 92-94 mph range, and he touched 96.5 mph during his time in the Florida State League. He lost some of that velocity as the season wore on, but the perceived rise of the pitch, stemming from its relatively flat angle, helps it play up. His low-80s curveball generated a ton of whiffs, and FSL hitters batted only .032 against it (per Statcast). His 83-85 mph splitter also kept hitters off guard but is still a low-spin work in progress. Ziegler battled control issues before and after his injured list stints, and his 17.6 percent walk rate won’t cut it at any level. He can be aggressive in his motion on the mound, and that can lead to some of the missed spots. The Canadian hurler will likely to have wait until his age-21 season in 2024 before he can show off how his stuff and control is coming along.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ziegler was technically Draft-eligible as a 17-year-old out of Ontario in 2020, but the pandemic shutdown, combined with the shorter Draft process, kicked his selection down the road by one year. To improve his 2021 stock, the 6-foot right-hander went south to TNXL Academy in Ocoee, Florida, while still occasionally heading home, and that worked out when the Mets selected him in the second round. Ziegler signed for a below-slot $900,000 bonus and still awaits his Minor League debut. Ziegler displays good arm strength for his (or any) size. He typically sits around 93 mph already but has touched as high as 97. His heater works best down in the zone, thanks to its sinking movement. A low-80s curveball has shown good bite and vertical shape in its early days at Single-A St. Lucie, earning the highest whiff percentage of his three pitches. As is typical of high-schoolers entering the pros, Ziegler will focus on developing a mid-80s changeup, though that has kept hitters off-balance at times too. It should be interesting to see how Ziegler’s command develops under the Mets’ watch. He was inconsistent with his location last spring, despite an aggressive approach from the mound. Those woes would point to a bullpen role should they continue, but such a decision is years away for the right-hander, who will be 19 for the entire 2022 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilson burst on the season in his first year at South Alabama, setting a freshman school record with 17 homers in 2019. By 2021, he had become more of a contact-over-power hitter, but his .947 OPS helped him land in the second round of that summer’s Draft. He has yet to find any kind of offensive groove in his two-plus years in the Phillies system, though there were some signs of life power-wise while spending the 2023 season in Double-A Reading. The left-handed-hitting Wilson did find the seats 17 times in 2023, and while the assumption might be it was because Reading's home park is very hitting-friendly, he actually got to his power on the road as well. He’s going to have to find ways to do that more frequently unless he vastly changes what has been an overly aggressive approach as a pro. He’s shown he can make loud contact but chases out of the zone way too much, and his strikeout rate ticked up last year without the benefit of an increased walk rate. A decent athlete who has shown he can run a little, Wilson is limited to corner outfield spots, and he played more left than right for the first time last year with Reading. If he’s ever going to play one spot regularly, it’s likely to be left because of his fringy arm, but he’s going to have to become a much more consistent offensive performer to be an everyday player in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After hitting a South Alabama record 17 freshman home runs in 2019, Wilson opted for contact over power two years later in his Draft season. His .947 OPS helped him climb to the second round of the 2021 Draft with the Phillies, and he made his debut with full-season Clearwater that summer. While he did reach Double-A in his first full season, he struggled to find any kind of offensive consistency in 2022. Some of Wilson’s issues in 2022 stemmed from him being caught between the power and contact-first profiles, but most of it was a result of poor swing decisions. His strikeout rate wasn’t awful, but he swung at just about everything in his first full season and walked at just over a six percent clip. He regularly offered at pitches out of the zone, leading to weak contact and outs. The left-handed hitter didn’t tap into any of the raw power he has as a result. Wilson is a decent athlete, but is definitely limited to an outfield corner long-term. He’s played more right field to date, but his fringy arm might be best suited to left in the future. Still just 23 for the entirety of the 2023 season, there’s time for him to get straightened out, with the hope he can rediscover the swing that made him an offensive force in college.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wilson burst on the scene as a freshman at South Alabama, destroying former All-Star Luis Gonzalez’s freshman home run record by blasting 17 homers to earn Sun Belt Conference player of the year honors in 2019. He eschewed power for more contact in 2021 and his .947 OPS helped land him in the second round of the 2021 Draft, signing for slot value with the Phillies and making his pro debut in Low-A. It remains to be seen what kind of hitter Wilson will be at the professional level. He showed an ability to barrel up the baseball with an advanced approach in 2021, with high contact rates and a willingness to work counts and draw walks. The left-handed hitter sacrificed some pop in the process, but the Phillies believe there is plenty of power to tap into as he learns to find an offensive balance. Wilson is almost certainly limited to playing a corner spot in the outfield, with left the most likely destination because of his fringe-to-average arm. He should be an average defender there, but it does put more pressure on the bat to produce, though it is the offensive potential the Phillies were buying in the first place.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Santos in 2019 out of Acarigua, Venezuela, but his professional debut was delayed by the lost '20 season. Since he got rolling in ‘21, Santos has flashed the ability to miss bats at a high rate. In ‘22, he struck out a whopping 142 batters over 86 innings between Single-A and High-A. The ‘23 season felt like a jumping-off point for him, but an arm injury limited him to 48 1/3 innings with Vancouver. The results were there with a 3.54 ERA, but his strikeout rate dropped and it was another season that pointed to a potential future as a reliever. Santos has finally added weight, which the Blue Jays have been working on for years. He’s never going to be mistaken for a linebacker, but Santos’ weight is closer to 190 pounds now. That doesn’t need to result in a huge velocity bump above his current spot in the low 90s, but if it helps Santos maintain his stuff through a full season, it’s a big win for both him and the organization. Santos is back to using a slightly lower arm angle that comes more naturally to him, and his slider has the potential to be a legitimate out pitch in the big leagues. That’s the biggest reason many point to a relief profile, where Santos' walk rate wouldn’t be as detrimental. Santos dealt with elbow trouble early on in 2024 and didn't make his season debut until mid-June, eventually reaching Double-A a month later. He's worked exclusively as a reliever since, playing right into what some expected his future role to be anyways. He could be a quick mover in '25, assuming the elbow health holds on, and that slider would be a menace at the top level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays signed Santos out of Acarigua, Venezuela, in 2019, but his professional debut was delayed by the lost 2020 season. He eventually debuted in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League and got a taste of Single-A in 2021, posting a combined 5.58 ERA with 58 strikeouts over 40 1/3 innings. Santos’ breakout came in 2022, though, when he split his season between Single-A and High-A with a 4.50 ERA and a whopping 142 strikeouts over 86 innings. That strikeout rate of 14.9 per nine innings is where Santos’ appeal lives. Santos is still working to add more weight, which the Blue Jays hope will bump his fastball velocity up as he moves through his early 20s. It currently sits in the low 90s and touches 94 mph. His slider, which he uses heavily at times as a secondary pitch, can produce plenty of whiffs as a low-80s sweeper. As Santos is tested by more disciplined hitters at higher levels, though, he’ll need to continue to hone that slider and improve his changeup. Santos is now working with a lower arm slot which he adjusted in 2022 and it gives him a more natural, athletic delivery as he slings the ball to the plate. There’s certainly some reliever potential if he shortens up his arsenal to a fastball and a slider to chase strikeouts, but he’ll still get plenty of run as a starter as he tries to develop his secondaries. This is a major year for Santos, especially as he faces older hitters who will be more disciplined against his slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Acarigua, Venezuela, in 2019, Santos had his professional debut delayed by the lost ’20 season, but the right-hander finally debuted in the Florida Complex League in ’21. There, Santos pitched 35 1/3 innings before getting a taste of Single-A at the tail end of the season, where he was hit hard over five innings. Santos ended the season with a combined 5.58 ERA, striking out 58 batters over 40 1/3 innings. He’s been a breakout hurler for Toronto this summer, striking out close to 40 percent of his batters faced back in the Florida State League. Santos spent most of the winter at the club’s complex and added some good weight, though there’s still plenty of room for him to mature physically. Santos’ fastball sat in the low-90s in ’21, but he’s reaching up to 94 mph early in ’22 with the potential for more. He’s leaned heavily on a low-80s slider with two-plane sweep, throwing it 40 percent of the time in some cases, and it’s gotten twice as many whiffs on a per-pitch bases as the heater. His mid-80s changeup can get too firm, and he’s moved away from it some as the season has gone on. Gifted with an electric arm, Santos is still years away, but his raw potential is impressive. He’ll be tested with moves higher up the chain at some point, but the fastball-slider mix has worked wonders in Dunedin in 2022, making him one of the must-follow arms throughout the summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hardman showed off his power by prevailing in the Cape Cod League home run derby and finishing third in the circuit with eight homers in the summer of 2019, then won the Big 12 Conference batting title (.397) at Oklahoma two years later. A fifth-round pick in 2021, he ranked fourth in the High-A South Atlantic League with 22 homers in his first full pro season and then tied for the Arizona Fall League lead with six. He continued to mash in 2023, leading the Double-A Eastern League with 26 blasts despite playing in just 77 games because an errant pitch broke his right hand in late July. Hardman's 6-foot-3, 230-pound frame provides plenty of strength and leverage, which combine with his bat speed to produce high exit velocities and well above-average power that plays to all parts of the ballpark. His right-handed pop comes with plenty of strikeouts, however, because he has a launch-heavy approach and works deep counts looking for pitches to crush. He whiffed in 32 percent of his plate appearances during his first three years as a pro and may not make enough contact to do damage against big league pitching. Athletic for his size despite below-average speed, he's aggressive on the bases and will steal when given the opportunity. After playing almost exclusively at first base for the Sooners, he moved to third base in 2022 and has fared better than expected. He has good reactions and makes most plays, though his fringy range and average arm strength are a bit less than desired and he needs to improve his consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hardman won the home run derby and finished third with eight homers in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2019, then won the Big 12 Conference batting title (.397) at Oklahoma two years later. Signed for a well-under-slot $200,000 as a 2021 fifth-rounder, he topped Yankees farmhands and ranked fourth in the High-A South Atlantic League with 22 homers in his first full pro season. He finished 2022 by tying for the Arizona Fall League home run lead with six and played better defense than scouts expected there. With the strength and leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame to go with his quick right-handed swing, Hardman is built to hit for power. He does pile up strikeouts while working deep counts looking for pitches to punish, but he also shows the willingness to use the opposite field. He hits the ball harder than most players in the system and his pop plays to all fields. Though Hardman has below-average speed, he's fairly athletic for his size and stole 14 bases in 18 attempts last season. Almost exclusively a first baseman for the Sooners, he became a full-time third baseman in 2022 and displayed good reactions and average range. His arm strength is merely average, a bit less than desired at the hot corner, but it doesn't prevent him from making most plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 35th-round pick out of a California high school by the Braves in 2019, Hall improved throughout his three-year college career at Oregon and set a school record with a .640 slugging percentage in 2022. A fourth-rounder that July, he broke the hamate bone in his right hand while popping out in his first pro at-bat and then required a second surgery last January after injuring his wrist. He finally returned to the field in mid-April and hit .246/.353/.403 between two Class A levels. Hall has a quick left-handed swing and produces high exit velocities to all fields. He has enough bat speed and strength to create plus raw power, though he didn't make the most of it in 2023 because he didn't lift the ball in the air consistently. He has a patient approach but struggles against breaking balls from left-handers, so he'll have to make adjustments to be more than platoon player. Hall has average tools across the board, though he's a little quicker than that once he gets going. He played center field in his first two years at Oregon before moving to right field in his third, and he split time between the two positions last year. His range is more suited for a corner and he throws well enough to handle right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two so-so seasons at Oregon, Hall impressed scouts with a strong summer in the Cape Cod League in 2021. He built on that momentum last spring, slashing .333/.402/.640 with 14 homers and setting a Ducks record for slugging percentage. The Yankees were pleased to find him available in the fourth round last July, though his pro debut ended quickly when he broke the hamate in his right hand while popping out in his first pro at-bat. Hall has a quick left-handed swing and regularly makes hard contact from gap to gap. His bat speed and strength add up to plus raw power, and he can drive the ball out of the park from left-center to the right-field foul pole. He's an aggressive hitter who pounds fastballs but will need to make adjustments to handle quality breaking pitches. Hall shows average speed out of the batter's box and is quicker underway, albeit not much of a base-stealing threat. He played center field in his first two years at Oregon before moving to right in 2022. His range fits better on a corner and his average-to-solid arm strength plays well in right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since being selected out of San Jacinto College in the fifth round of the 2021 Draft, Auer has experienced the highs and lows of life in the Minor Leagues. A former two-way player in college and an unquestionably talented athlete, Auer immediately impressed in his full-season debut with his all-out style of play. But he took a frustrating step backward at the plate in Double-A last year, no longer able to hide the deficiencies in his mechanics with his natural ability against tougher competition. There were already questions about how Auer’s contact rate would hold up against higher-level pitching, and he didn’t do much to answer them in Double-A as he slashed .205/.292/.348 with a 36 percent strikeout rate. He often looked lost, struggling to pick up spin or hit anything on the outer third of the plate. He finished better than he started with better underlying numbers over the final six weeks. Auer spent a lot of time with the club’s hitting coordinators, and he didn’t stop hitting all offseason after working his way to a more comfortable setup and swing. Auer does everything else well. He’s in better shape than anyone in the system, with strength that gives him solid power when he manages to make contact. He is the best defensive center fielder in the Rays’ system and arguably the best defensive player, period. He has elite speed, which allowed him to steal 47 bases even in a year he wasn’t on as often as he would’ve liked. He has a true cannon of an arm in the outfield. He works hard and takes care of himself, with a strong focus on his body and his career, so the Rays aren’t worried about him even after an offensive performance he’d like to quickly forget.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays knew they were getting a talented athlete when they selected Auer out of San Jacinto College in the fifth round in the fifth round of the 2021 Draft. He’d hit and pitched for Missouri State in 2020, then did the same as a juco player in Houston and solidified himself as a prospect to watch while playing for Frederick in the MLB Draft League in ’21. The Rays signed him for $312,500, just under slot, only to discover Auer’s impressive tools and all-out style of play were accompanied by much more advanced skills than they expected. In his first full season, the 21-year-old Auer hit .290/.372/.487 with 15 homers, 12 triples and 21 doubles over 115 games between Single-A Charleston and High-A Bowling Green. He shortened his load at the plate, enhancing his ability to make contact and letting his bat speed help him generate some high exit-velocity readings. He still struck out in 20.8 percent of his plate appearances, plus in 23 of his 78 PAs in the Arizona Fall League, which leads to some questions about how his contact rate will hold up against higher-level pitching -- concerns that have held up with his move to Double-A. But Auer has a ton of strength and athleticism -- he's in the best physical shape of any Rays prospect – and his wide-ranging skill-set allows him to create value with more than just his bat. The Rays figured they could expect a strong arm from the 6-foot-1 outfielder/former pitcher, and indeed, he has the best outfield arm in the system, a true plus-plus cannon. But Auer surprised the club with the accuracy of his throws and the relatively clean routes he took to balls in center and right field. He’s a plus runner -- and more advanced than expected there, too, as he swiped 48 bags in 55 attempts while earning the organization’s Baserunner of the Year award. He still has some more polishing that needs to take place, and his other tools will only travel as far as his bat takes him, but he has the look of a future big league outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have looked at creative ways to add young talent under president of baseball operations Scott Harris, and their trade for Dickerson fits the profile. Essentially, they turned $500,000 of international prospect pool money into a domestic prospect. Dickerson ranked 158th on MLB Pipeline’s Draft prospect rankings last summer, but teams shied away from the Virginia Tech commit until the Padres offered him a $500,000 signing bonus. It was a sharp move, but the Padres needed international money. The Tigers, who had scouted Dickerson along with his Team USA teammates Max Clark and Kevin McGonigle, took the opportunity. While Dickerson throws a 91-93 mph fastball, his tall frame provides plenty of projection for a velocity bump as he physically matures and polishes his mechanics. His slider is a swing-and-miss pitch with sharp break. His changeup is a third pitch at this point but has room for improvement. His stretch delivery has little wasted motion and hides the ball well, but his quick release makes it imperative he generates enough rotation to get the ball in on righties or to the outside corner on lefties. The Tigers see him as a starter, but even if he falls into a lefty relief role, it’s worth the cost of acquisition. The Tigers’ pitching development group has turned out good arms over the last year or two, some of which were undervalued by other clubs. Dickerson is an intriguing project, not just for his physical gifts but his aptitude for pitching. He might need time to blossom, but he’s the kind of addition that can deepen an already good farm system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Phillies drafted Sanchez in Round 12 of the 2019 Draft and went over slot to sign him for $300,000, he had some difficulty gaining traction, playing in the Complex League after signing and starting again there in '21 following the lost year because of the pandemic. He had trouble staying healthy in 2022 and then was sent to the Angels with Mickey Moniak in return for Noah Syndergaard at the Trade Deadline. Sanchez stayed relatively healthy last year, playing in over 100 games in a season for the first time and putting up solid numbers overall while finishing things off with an aggressive assignment to the Arizona Fall League. Finally putting in a full season, Sanchez started to unlock some of his raw tools a bit more consistently. He shook off a rough April, when he hit just .209, to hit .304 for the rest of the season. He’s a switch-hitter who’s a little better from the right side, but he showed some ability in both boxes. He’ll draw some walks, rarely strikes out and he started getting to his raw power for the first time. A corner outfielder only, Sanchez has a very strong arm, but unlike many young players with hoses they like to show off, he combines it with very consistent accuracy, which helped him rack up 15 assists from right field in 2023. He may be a fourth outfielder who plays in either corner at best, but he also might just be figuring out how to be a productive hitter, with more projection to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins needed two tries to land Montgomery, drafting him in the 35th round out of a Washington high school in 2019 and then in the 15th round after he spent a season at Boise State and two at Missouri. He batted .365 as a junior and ranked third in the rugged Southeastern Conference with a .374 average in league games before signing for $75,000. He earned Single-A Florida State League all-star accolades in his first full pro season but didn't fare nearly as well in High-A, slashing a combined .288/.413/.402. Like the other top first-base prospects in the system, Montgomery fits an atypical hit-over-power profile for his position, and he has the platoon disadvantage of batting right-handed. Though he's strong, his stroke is geared more for line drives and he doesn't turn on many pitches or drive them in the air. After his OPS plummeted from .968 in Single-A to .587 in High-A, the Marlins began working on him to improve his swing path to add more loft. With below-average speed once he gets going and average arm strength, Montgomery is limited to first base. He's a fringy defender at first who needs to develop more consistency after committing 12 errors in 94 games last season. He'll need to diligently maintain his 6-foot-3, 245-pound frame or risk lapsing into a DH.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cooke pitched two years in relief at Louisiana-Lafayette before finding results (2.03 ERA, 90 strikeouts in 79 2/3 innings) as a starter in 2021. The Blue Jays selected him in the 10th round that July, signed him for around slot at $141,900 and transitioned the right-hander back to relief when he joined High-A Vancouver late in 2022. Cooke took some lumps that year, but broke out in ‘23 with 80 strikeouts over 44 1/3 innings and reached Triple-A. You wouldn’t guess it from a reliever, but Cooke is one of the best athletes in the entire organization. If you need a guy who can touch 98 mph and dunk, Cooke is your man. Whether his fastballs live near 96 mph or begins flirting with triple digits again will determine his ceiling, but it’s already exciting in a short relief role and he should have a fairly short path to the big leagues if this track continues. Cooke’s slider can be devastating with impressive sweep and is already good enough to be an out pitch in MLB. The most important thing for Cooke is setting himself up better in counts, because when he has the advantage, he can be dominant. Spotting that fastball will be key and the Blue Jays trust his natural athleticism will enable him to adjust his delivery on the fly without losing the fundamentals. There is serious upside here in Cooke, who is quietly becoming one of this organization’s better development success stories in recent years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brock dealt with injuries in college, so even though he spent four seasons at Ohio State and took two trips to the Cape Cod League, evaluators were left to stitch together his best flashes over the years. Brock’s biggest NCAA workload was 31 innings as a freshman and he threw just 16 2/3 in his Draft year, but the Blue Jays still loved him as an upside play in the sixth round in 2022. In two seasons since, Brock has flashed an incredible ceiling even though the numbers themselves might not reflect that. Across 65 Minor League innings, he owns a 4.85 ERA but has struck out a whopping 109 batters (15.1 K/9). Brock got off to an excellent start with High-A Vancouver in 2023, but got rocked in Double-A, which the Blue Jays are confident he’ll learn from. Some tutelage from star closer Jordan Romano will be part of that. Brock’s stuff is electric. His fastball lives in the upper-90s and his upper-80s slider, thrown 55 percent of the time in Double-A, is one of the best pitches in the system that could get MLB hitters out tomorrow, but as you can gather from his numbers, Brock needs to put himself in dominant counts more often to attack hitters. The organization has a high level of internal optimism that the numbers will move in the right direction this season, and if they do, Brock could move quickly in his age-24 year. There are clearly some command pieces that still need to come together for Brock, which won’t happen overnight, but his potential in a short relief role is massive.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2016-17 international signing period, the A’s tied for the largest single bonus to one player, giving Lazaro Armenteros $3 million to sign on July 2. While that hasn’t turned out well, they may have struck gold when they signed Diaz about a month later out of Colombia for $275,000. He didn’t make it to full-season ball until 2021, but he showed enough offensive potential with High-A Lansing to get added to the 40-man roster that offseason. He rewarded Oakland's faith by slashing .326/.366/.515 with 19 homers across the two upper levels en route to his big league debut about a month after his 22nd birthday. With excellent bat speed, Diaz has posted elite-level contact rates in his career, and that continued in 2022 with just a 21 percent miss rate across all levels. His 14.4 percent strikeout rate in the Minors was right in line with his career mark (14.7). With that feel for the barrel has come a very aggressive approach that does not include many walks. He’s ditched a leg kick so there’s less movement at the plate, and he’s really starting to tap into his considerable raw power, showing he can hit the ball out to all fields. While big league manager Mark Kotsay really liked Diaz’s right-handed bat during his time up with Oakland, it is a little unclear where Diaz’s long-term defensive home should be. He’s never going to be a great defender, but the A’s felt he played his best defense in the big leagues and he held his own when asked to play second base. He might best be suited for first base or even DH, with the potential offensive profile to fit at either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signing out of Colombia during the 2016-17 international signing period for $275,000, Diaz’s success throughout Short-Season ball transferred over to what was his first season at High-A, where he hit .288 with 13 home runs and 24 doubles in 90 games. The A’s felt he made enough progress to add him to the 40-man roster this offseason. Diaz has shown above average bat speed through the zone, which helps offset his high leg kick during the setup of his swing. He uses the whole field, and now the power the A’s were hoping to see is also starting to show up as he matures and evolves from being more of a gap-to-gap hitter. He already possesses some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the organization. Also showing good plate discipline, Diaz brings quite an advanced approach to the plate, especially for his age. Defense remains a work in progress for Diaz. While it has improved over the last year, the A’s continue to seek a permanent position for him. They tried him out at third base, and while he impressed with his strong arm, lapses in concentration led to him shifting over to first base and even some left field over the past year. Ultimately, Diaz will likely rely on his special abilities with the bat to continue moving up the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz signed out of Colombia for $275,000 during the 2016-17 international signing period. After debuting in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2017, he arrived to the United States that summer. He’s continued to hold his own as one of the younger players in both the Rookie-level Arizona League and Class A Short Season New-York-Penn League. More recently, Diaz performed well in the Caribbean Series this past winter, hitting .368 with three doubles and four RBIs in five games. Considered to have some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the organization, Diaz has displayed good plate discipline as he hits line drives to all fields. His skill set allows him to limit the strikeouts, and although he’s more of a gap-to-gap hitter, the power continues to improve. The big question for Diaz is where he’s going to play. Poor footwork and occasional lapses in concentration have impeded him when playing third base, though he did seem comfortable at first base while playing there during instructional league play last fall. Expected to grow into more power, the A’s will keep moving him through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A college starter with elite stuff, Lacy was the No. 4 overall pick in 2020 out of Texas A&M when the Royals paid him a bonus of $6.67 million. Since then, Lacy’s journey has been extremely bumpy. He was injured in 2021 (shoulder) and ‘22 (back). He pitched just 28 innings in ‘22, and he walked 42 batters. Lacy was able to get back to the mound in the fall, and his offseason revolved around strength and health moving forward. With just his stuff, Lacy has elite starter potential. His fastball is in the upper-90s, his upper-80s slider is plus, and his changeup can be plus with time, diving late away from hitters’ swinging bats. He also has a curveball with depth in his arsenal, although his slider is his preferred breaking pitch. The problem is simply control -- although the fix could be anything but simple. Lacy’s delivery isn’t consistent and falls out of sync quickly. Once he loses the zone, it’s hard for him to find it again. The Royals have their work cut out for them when it comes to developing Lacy. He will be 24 in June and is entering 2023 with just 80 professional innings under his belt. There were times last year when he was pulled out of the starter’s routine and pitched out of the bullpen just to get more reps. But Kansas City will continue to develop Lacy as a starter, depending on health and performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lacy gambled on himself ahead of the 2017 Draft, when he went in the 31st round to Cleveland. It paid off three years later when the Royals took him fourth overall and gave him a $6.67 million signing bonus. His first taste of the pros was bumpy at best. He posted a 5.19 ERA with 79 strikeouts and 41 walks in 52 frames before a barking shoulder ended his regular season in July. He made up for some of the lost time with four abbreviated starts in the Arizona Fall League. Lacy again experienced injury concerns this season at Double-A Northwest -- this time with his back -- and has dealt with serious control woes during the times he has been on the mound. On stuff alone, Lacy shows front-of-the-rotation potential. His fastball can sit in the upper-90s, but the Royals say they may even prefer it when he’s at 92-96 with better command. His best off-speed pitch might depend on the day any evaluator sees him. His upper-80s slider jumped past his curveball to become his preferred breaking pitch during his days as an Aggie, and there were times in the past when he showed promise with a changeup that can dive late away from hitters’ swinging bats. That said, Lacy will be limited if he doesn’t find a way to hit his spots more consistently. As part of his delivery, his head movement can throw his motion out of sync, causing the command to waver. The Royals also believe he tried to prove himself too quickly and overthrew at times to show off what made him such a high pick. Unfortunately in part due to injuries, he hasn’t taken a step forward, especially when it comes to finding the zone, and he may be headed to the bullpen long-term for health and results-based reasons.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lacy showed the talent to go in the first five rounds as a Texas high schooler in 2017, but his $1 million price tag dropped him to the Indians in the 31st round. He opted to attend Texas A&M, where he dominated for three seasons and became the highest pick in school history. The Royals selected him No. 4 overall in June and signed him for $6,670,000, a franchise record for a drafted pitcher. Lacy was limited by an eye issue while at the Royals’ alternate training site but made a healthy return in time for organization’s fall instructional program at Kauffman Stadium. Lacy attacks hitters with a 92-97 mph fastball while using his 6-foot-4 frame to create angle towards the plate. He uses two distinct breaking balls, with his harder, upper-80s slider surpassing his downer curveball during his junior season and becoming a true plus pitch. He can pile up whiffs with both pitches, as well as a fading changeup that is a consistent plus offering and well-above-average at its best. While there are no questions about the quality of Lacy's pitches, he'll need to improve his command and control to reach his ceiling as a frontline starter. There is some effort in his three-quarters delivery and he can't always harness his overpowering stuff -- a problem he's run into a few times with High-A Quad Cities in 2021. Even without precise location, Lacy could still move quickly as a left-hander who can induce swings and misses with four different offerings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The vast majority of players to make it to the big leagues from New Hampshire have been pitchers, though Ryan McKenna has spent time in the Orioles' outfield after being a 2015 fourth-round pick out of high school. Lavigne would like to be the next Granite State prep bat to make it. The Rockies went over slot to sign him for $2 million as a Competitive Balance Round A pick in 2018, then saw him have a tremendous pro debut that summer. It’s taken him a while to find his footing since then, though he started figuring some things out in 2021 and hit his way to Double-A for the first time in 2022, finishing things off with a solid Arizona Fall League showing. Lavigne entered pro ball with a definite hit-over-power profile, but he got into trouble when he started to try to sell out for power too much. He got back to a better overall approach in 2022, drawing more walks and showing the ability to make more consistently hard contact from the left side of the plate. The power is going to come thanks to his natural strength and bat speed and the Rockies were pleased with how he adjusted to the Eastern League after his promotion. It’s possible Lavigne will never be more than a fringy defender at first base, one with a below-average arm, but this part of his game improved as well in 2022. He’s a tireless worker, one who will be at the upper levels of the Rockies' system at age 23 for most of the 2023 season and who still has the potential to develop into a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lavigne was a bit of a pop-up prospect from the New Hampshire high school ranks, not exactly a hotbed for professional talent, as the 2018 Draft approached. He landed in the Competitive Balance Round A and the Rockies went over slot to sign him for $2 million. It seemed like a very shrewd investment based on his pro debut in the Pioneer League (.996 OPS), but he really seemed lost for most of his first full season of pro ball in 2019. A return to Low-A in 2021 was a good move as he righted the ship and earned a bump up a level for the final two months of the season. When he was struggling, Lavigne was getting caught between the hitter he’d always been, one focused on contact with excellent plate discipline, and the one he thought he had to be, a power-hitting first baseman. He sold out for power too much in 2019 and got out of his approach. He’s still learning to catch the ball out front and let his natural strength do its thing. In 2021, he started getting much more comfortable with his swing and was adjusting to velocity more consistently. Lavigne is going to have to hit to keep moving up, as he’s a fringy defender at first base with a below-average arm. He’s grown into more of a leadership role, and the Rockies noticed that after he helped Fresno win a ton of games in Low-A, he led Spokane to the High-A West playoffs as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Right-handed pitcher Chris Carpenter is the highest-drafted high school player ever from New Hampshire, taken No. 15 overall back in 1993. After popping up to land in the Competitive Balance Round A in 2018, Lavigne became just the second prep player since Carpenter (Jeff Locke, 2006) to get taken in the top two rounds from the Granite State. He made a very strong first impression when he posted a .996 OPS in his pro debut, but struggled with the move to full-season ball in 2019, though the Rockies were pleased with his adjustments in instructional league play in 2020. At his best, Lavigne’s strengths as a left-handed hitter are his knowledge of the strike zone and his ability to drive the ball to all fields. While he drew a lot of walks in 2019, he was too passive at the plate and missed too many good pitches to hit. He also got pull-happy and tried to sell out for power, leading to a spike in strikeouts, instead of just letting his natural strength and bat speed do the work. At instructs, he looked more like the 2018 version than the lost ’19 edition, making more hard contact and using the entire field more consistently. It will be Lavigne’s bat that will carry him to the big leagues, as he’s definitely a first baseman only with a below-average arm. The Rockies are optimistic he righted the ship last fall and hope the reps of a full season will fully get him back on track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Groome’s journey through pro ball has been an epic saga, and he hasn’t even reached the Majors yet. Ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 1 prospect in the 2016 Draft, he went 12th overall to the Red Sox due to signability concerns, and then was severely limited by lat and forearm injuries, as well as Tommy John surgery and the lost 2020 pandemic season before finally eclipsing the 60-inning mark in 2021. He moved to Triple-A for the first time in 2022, only to get traded to the Padres at the Trade Deadline in a swap for Eric Hosmer. Forget who Groome was an amateur -- he’s developed into a different pitcher now. His four-seam fastball was around 91-94 mph (touching 96) with some sink in the Pacific Coast League following the trade, making it just an average heater, though he can spot it pretty well. While his upper-70s curveball was considered his best pitch coming out of high school, a low-80s slider has emerged as his better swing-and-miss option, and he likewise upped its usage in his second month with El Paso. A low-80s changeup shows decent sink and separation, and while it isn’t more than average either, it did help him limit righties to a .673 OPS (compared to a .867 OPS from lefties) across all levels in 2022. Groome will have the occasional rough bout with wildness, but he keeps the walks in check enough to stay in a starting role. Without a true plus pitch, it’s tough to say he’s a natural candidate to move into relief, which would otherwise give him a better chance in the Majors; he’s rotation depth for now, with the hope of being a No. 5 someday.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's No. 1-rated prospect in the 2016 Draft, Groome fell the to the Red Sox at No. 12 because of signability and makeup issues and signed for $3.65 million, still a franchise record for a drafted pitcher. He has avoid any off-field trouble but totaled just 66 innings in his first five years as a pro while dealing with lat and forearm injuries, Tommy John surgery and the pandemic shutdown. He stayed healthy, pitched a career high 97 1/3 innings and led the system with 134 strikeouts in 2021, overcoming a slow beginning to the year in High-A to finish with a strong three-start stint in Double-A. He reached Triple-A Worcester in mid-2022 before he was moved to the Padres at the Trade Deadline as the lone prospect return for Eric Hosmer. Groome's fastball velocity isn't what it once was, as he now operates in the low 90s and usually touches 94-95 mph only for an inning or two at a time. His best pitch is a mid-80s slider that he refined at Boston's alternate site in 2020, as it now shows flashes of becoming a plus offering and has surpassed his upper-70s curveball, which scouts considered the best bender in the 2016 Draft. He has developed a low-80s changeup with tumble that helps him handle right-handers, who fared far worse against him (.619 OPS) than same-side hitters (.890) in 2021. Evaluators aren't sure exactly what to make of Groome, who has puffed up to a listed 262 pounds and is less athletic than he was as an amateur. He throws strikes but might find more velocity and consistency if he got into better shape. He’ll try to show San Diego that he can still be a potential No. 5 starter in his second organization, but it might not be long before the Padres give him a look in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLB Pipeline's top-rated prospect in the 2016 Draft, Groome slid to the Red Sox at No. 12 amid huge signability and makeup concerns. He has avoided any off-field issues since signing for $3.65 million, still a franchise record for a drafted pitcher, but he pitched just 66 official innings in his first five years as a pro because of lat and forearm issues, Tommy John surgery in May 2018 and the coronavirus pandemic. He looked better in 2020 at Boston's alternate site than he did in instructional league, where his listed weight was 262 pounds, and he struggled in the first month of the 2021 season before coming on later in the summer. Added to the 40-man roster in November, Groome has worked at 92-95 mph with his fastball for most of 2021 after sitting at 90-92 during instructs. Scouts considered his curveball the best in the 2016 Draft, but it's more of a solid offering now and has been surpassed by his mid-80s slider, which has gained velocity since he added it in 2020. He has developed more confidence in his sinking changeup, which can become an average offering. Known for using his athleticism and clean delivery to pound the strike zone as an amateur, Groome needs to keep his conditioning in check to locate his pitches where he wants. Boston still sees the ingredients of a quality starter and hopes that his finally getting regular innings in 2021 will help him reach that potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci celebrated his 16th birthday in 2018 by signing with the Red Sox for $290,000. He weighed just 140 pounds when he turned pro out of Venezuela, but has added at least 25 pounds of muscle five years into his pro career. In his first extended taste of full-season ball last year, he ranked second in the Single-A Carolina League in walks (89) and on-base percentage (.397) at age 19 and hit all six of his homers in the final six weeks. Though Bonaci has slowed as he has gotten stronger and is now a fringy-to-average runner, he remains one of the best infield defenders and has one of the strongest arms in the system. His instincts and quick first step still give him solid range to both sides at shortstop, though he played more second base last season as a teammate of 2021 No. 4 overall pick Marcelo Mayer. He also saw action at third and even played an inning in right field. A switch-hitter, Bonaci has been a different hitter in 2023 after being too passive and making too much soft contact in the past. Stronger and more aggressive than ever, he's turning on more pitches, hitting the ball with more authority and showing 15-homer potential. If he can keep this up, he'll provide enough offense to profile as an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci had to wait a week into the 2018 international signing period to turn 16 and become eligible to sign, landing a $290,000 bonus on his birthday. The Venezuelan carried just 140 pounds on his 5-foot-10 frame when he turned pro but since has added 25 pounds while still retaining his quick-twitch athleticism. He made his U.S. debut in 2021 and reinforced his reputation as one of the best infield defenders and strongest arms in Boston's system. A switch-hitter, Bonaci displays good bat-to-ball skills and a disciplined approach from both sides. While he won't be a slugger, he has enough hitting ability and bat speed to provide doubles power with 10-15 homers per year as he gets stronger and turns on more pitches. He understands that his focus is getting on base and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. Bonaci has slowed down to more of an average runner as he has started to mature physically, but his instincts help him play quicker than that and he stole 12 bases in as many attempts in 49 games last summer. He still moves well enough to have solid range at shortstop, though he might wind up getting more action at second base if he plays alongside 2021 first-rounder Marcelo Mayer. His double-plus arm strength is his loudest tool and enables him to make any throw needed at any infield position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci signed out of Venezuela for $290,000 on his 16th birthday in 2018, carrying just 140 pounds on his 5-foot-10 frame when he turned pro. While he's still not overly physical, he has added 25 pounds and played well on both sides of the ball during his 2019 pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, eliciting trade inquiries from other teams. While the coronavirus pandemic wiped out plans for his U.S. debut last year, he did come to instructional league and impressed there. A switch-hitter, Bonaci has good bat-to-ball skills and regularly produces line drives from both sides of the plate. He won't ever be a power threat, but he has the hitting ability and enough bat speed to provide some gap power as he gets stronger. He understands his limitations at the plate and focuses on employing a disciplined approach to get on base. Bonaci's loudest tool is a double-plus arm that allows him to make any throw needed at shortstop. He's a solid runner who's aggressive on the bases and covers plenty of ground at short, where he also displays smooth actions and soft hands. Advanced for his age offensively and defensively, he comes with a higher floor but lower ceiling than fellow shortstop and 2019 second-rounder Matthew Lugo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Norge Luis Vera, who won nine gold medals for Cuba (including one at the 2004 Olympics), Norge defected from the Cuban national team while playing in the independent Canadian American Association during the summer of 2019. The top pitching prospect in the 2020-21 international class, he signed with Chicago for $1.5 million in February 2021. He worked just 54 1/3 innings in his first two pro seasons while dealing with mild shoulder soreness (2021) and a lat strain (2022). It's still unclear what exactly the White Sox have in Vera. He displayed a 91-94 mph fastball while working out for teams before he signed, came out blazing at 95-100 while overmatching younger hitters in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2021, but sat at 90-93 in Double-A at the end of last season. His slider is a sharp mid-80s offering at its best but devolved into an upper-70s slurve late in 2022. Vera's changeup is very much a work in progress, featuring modest life and velocity fluctuating from the upper 70s to the mid-80s. He has a loose arm and an easy delivery that could result in average control, but he also struggles to keep his long limbs in sync and often battles the strike zone. On his best days, he can look like a mid-rotation starter, but he needs a lot more consistency to approach that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Norge Luis Vera was a star pitcher in Cuba's Serie Nacional and in international competition, winning nine gold medals, including one at the 2004 Olympics, as well as silvers at the 2000 and 2008 Olympics. His son Norge was starting to follow in his footsteps before defecting from the Cuban national team while playing in the independent Canadian American Association of Professional Baseball during the summer of 2019. The top pitching prospect in the 2020-21 international class, he signed with the White Sox for $1.5 million and overmatched younger hitters in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League during his pro debut, which didn't begin until August because he had mild shoulder soreness. Vera worked with a 91-94 mph fastball while showcasing himself for big league clubs, but he came out firing at 95-98 and touching 100 during his brief debut. His upper-70s curveball shows some flashes of becoming a plus pitch, and he has some aptitude for throwing a mid-80s changeup with fade. He has utilized a low-80s slider and a mid-80s splitter in the past, but Chicago has had him simplify his pitch mix. Vera had trouble finding the strike zone as an 18-year-old in Cuba's top league but issued just five walks in 19 innings last summer. His DSL stint was a small sample size without much in the way of competition, but he displayed a loose arm and easy delivery that should lead to at least average control. The White Sox hope he can become a mid-rotation starter, and they will get a better idea of his future when he makes his U.S. debut in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Norge Luis Vera starred in Cuba and in international play for many years, including winning a gold medal and two silvers in three Olympics appearances. He never pursued pitching in the Majors but his son will chase that dream after signing with the White Sox for $1.5 million in February. He defected while Cuba's national team was playing in the independent Can-Am League during the summer of 2019 and was considered the top pitcher in the 2020-21 international class. Vera's fastball sat at 91-94 mph during showcases for big league teams, and it has reached 96 in the past with the potential for more velocity to come because he has a lot of projection remaining in his 6-foot-4 frame. Scouts generally rate his upper-70s curveball as his best secondary pitch, though his low-80s slider isn't far behind. He used to throw a splitter but now employs a traditional changeup with some fade. Vera is still refining his delivery and doesn't repeat it consistently, though added strength should help in that regard. As an 18-year-old in Cuba's top league in 2018-19, he walked 32 batters in 54 2/3 innings, so he'll have to prove he can throw strikes. He'll need time to develop and is on roughly the same timetable as the high school righties (Jared Kelley, Matthew Thompson, Andrew Dalquist) whom Chicago has collected in the last two Drafts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sequera, a $750,000 signing out of Venezuela in 2019, was one of the surprises of the Tigers' international crop in 2021, when he posted an .823 OPS and 23 extra-base hits in just 46 games to win MVP honors in the Florida Complex League. His promotion to Single-A Lakeland for 2022 left him a bit more exposed, but he still produced 28 doubles and 19 homers in 116 games and had a solid late-season run before fading in the final week. Sequera steps to the plate looking for hard contact to the pull side, an approach that leads to high chase rates and strikeout totals -- though he dropped his strikeout rate 7 percent from 2021 to 2022. He homered on 20 percent of his fly balls in 2021, an unsustainable performance, but answered in 2022 with more line drives and better pitch recognition, if not results. His athleticism has not translated into speed on the basepaths. He moves well at shortstop and has a knack for highlight plays but could eventually shift over to third if he continues to grow. While Sequera has slugged his way alongside Cristian Santana and Roberto Campos to give the Tigers a trio of intriguing international prospects on their way up the system, Sequera is the least heralded of the group. He might never be a high-average hitter, but if he can maintain power numbers, he could work his way into the Tigers’ infield picture. Advanced pitching at High-A West Michigan could temper his aggressiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Roberto Campos was the headline signing of the Tigers’ 2019 international class, Sequera was rather overlooked as a Venezuelan shortstop who received a $750,000 bonus. Despite missing the Dominican Summer League when it was canceled due to the pandemic, Sequera enjoyed an eye-opening pro debut by winning MVP honors in a Rookie-level Florida Complex League well stocked with prospects. He got extra bases on more than half his 42 hits for the season, including 11 home runs, and finished with a flourish, including four long balls, four doubles and 17 RBIs over his final 12 games. Sequera takes an aggressive pull approach at the plate that leads to high strikeout totals but consistently hard contact when he connects. He has enough bat speed to turn on fastballs with authority on different parts of the plate. He shows some pitch recognition, but like many hitters his age looking for power, will also chase breaking balls out of the zone. He moves well at shortstop for his size, especially on balls up the middle, and has worked to improve his range. He could shift to third as his body fills out. The Tigers once had a pipeline of talent coming out of Venezuela, including Avisail Garcia and Eugenio Suarez, but Sequera has the potential to be the best Tigers prospect from the country since those days. He got his first taste of full-season ball with Single-A Lakeland this summer and has shown pop, but little patience at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Initially a 19th-round pick by the Royals in 2017, Howell climbed seven rounds in a year by going back to Kirkwood (Iowa) Community College and signed with the Brewers for $210,000. He showed signs of a breakout with 16 homers and 24 steals in 97 games between High-A and Double-A in 2021, and while he didn’t get added to the 40-man when Rule 5-eligible, he did capture the attention of the Padres, who acquired Howell in an early 2022 trade for Victor Caratini. Howell was off to a solid start at Double-A San Antonio, posting a 124 wRC+ in 48 games before suffering a wrist ligament injury that required surgery. Howell’s loudest tool by far is his plus-plus speed that’s always kept him on a prospect map in some way. While he’s never been overly aggressive on the basepaths, his skillset could take advantage of the new rules across the game geared toward encouraging stolen bases. Those wheels serve him well defensively, and it’s just a matter of finding him a regular spot. Both the Brewers and Padres liked giving him chances up the middle at center, second and short, but a below-average arm also meant he got 2022 looks in left field, where he can still cover lots of space. Offensively, Howell shows fast hands and around average raw power at the plate to go with a patient approach that helped him earn a .390 OBP in San Antonio. But his overall approach is heavy to the pull side, and he can struggle with swing-and-miss on breaking stuff. Even though he’s been passed over twice for 40-man spots, he still has a future as a fast and versatile right-handed-hitting option for San Diego.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howell bet on himself by heading back to Kirkwood Community College in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, instead of signing with the Royals as a 2017 19th-rounder, and the move paid off when he slid up seven rounds a year later. He signed with the Brewers for $210,000. Howell’s breakout came in 2021 when he hit .248/.361/.465 with 12 homers and 20 steals in 69 games at High-A Wisconsin. His numbers dipped at Double-A (.235/.318/.429), and the Brewers chose not to protect the Rule 5-eligible speedster with a 40-man spot following the season. Prior to the 2022 campaign, the Padres acquired Howell and Brett Sullivan in exchange for Victor Caratini and cash. Howell’s plus-plus speed has made him a prospect since his early days. He’s an easy threat to steal 20-25 bags in any season and could exceed that if he gets even more aggressive on the basepaths. His overall athleticism is something the Padres enjoy taking advantage of when putting together a roster and lineup. The wheels absolutely play in center field, and if he had to stick in a position, that’s likely his best bet. But San Diego has liked the concept of keeping him moving around all three spots up the middle. The bat will be the big question. Howell shows fast hands at the plate, can take a walk and has at least average raw power. But his strikeout rate bloomed to as high as 39.6 percent at Double-A in 2021, and it will continue to be a problem. Now in his age-23 season, Howell is trending toward late-game pinch-runner/defensive replacement territory, but there still exists time and room for a larger utility role if he can find a way to make more contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Willis hasn’t been seen a ton in recent years, both at the amateur and pro levels. He underwent ulnar nerve decompression surgery in July 2020, which knocked him out for many showcase events that summer. The Cardinals still liked enough of what they saw to select the Colorado high-school product in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft and sign him away from a Minnesota commitment with a $1 million bonus. Another arm issue limited him to six appearances (four starts) in the Florida Complex League last season. The 6-foot-5 right-hander has plenty of size on the bump, so while he touches the mid-90s but sits more in the 89-92 mph range these days, there’s still hope he can add a few ticks of velo as he continues to age and mature. (He’ll just turn 20 before Opening Day this spring.) His curveball has long been his preferred secondary, and while he’ll flash an occasional good-looking changeup, it’s still lagging behind the other two offerings. One of the promising signs of Willis’ 2022 was that he walked only two of the 46 batters he faced in the FCL, notable for someone with so much missed time. The Cardinals took it easy with Tink Hence out of the gate too, then watched him blossom into a Top 100 prospect. Willis lacks Hence’s premium stuff and ceiling, but like the other right-hander, he has ample time to blossom into a quality starting prospect, especially if his pitches take a step forward the more he throws them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Willis underwent ulnar nerve decompression surgery on his right elbow in the middle of July 2020, knocking him out of many showcase events. Almost exactly one year to the day later, he was a Draft pick in his home state of Colorado. The Regis Jesuit High School product showed enough health and stuff in his senior spring to get the Cardinals to select him in the seventh round, and St. Louis coaxed him out of a Minnesota commitment with a $1 million bonus, well above the $211,500 assigned to the slot. The right-hander, who made one appearance in the Florida Complex League, stands out for his size at 6-foot-5, and with some projection remaining, there is hope that he can add even more velocity. As it stands, he’s around 90-94 mph, occasionally touching a smidge or two higher. His curveball looks like a solid secondary already, and he sells a sinking changeup well with his arm speed, though it remains behind the curve. Willis remains a work in progress with his command, perhaps no surprise for such a young pitcher his size. Interestingly, he was the only high school pitcher selected by the Cardinals over last year’s 20-round Draft, so it’s clear they see enough moldable parts in him as he begins his pro career. It wouldn’t be a shock if St. Louis took a conservative approach with him early on, just as they did with Tink Hence in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was in his fourth year on campus, Love was still technically a sophomore when he finally joined the North Carolina rotation in 2021, posting a 3.71 ERA with 129 strikeouts in 102 innings just in time for the Draft. The Cardinals selected the right-hander in the third round and moved him to High-A Peoria for his first full season with rough results (5.73 ERA, 1.52 WHIP, 151 strikeouts in 125 2/3 innings). His 4.04 FIP and .366 BABIP indicated Love may have been better than his traditional stats would indicate, and his relatively high whiff rate helps that case too. Love shows just average velocity in the 91-95 mph range, but he can ramp it up to touch the high 90s on occasion. A lack of movement can make the heater hittable, so it’s notable that his mid-80s slider has developed into more of an above-average offering, one that can dive down and away from lunging right-handers. Love showed the makings of a plus mid-80s fading changeup in college and still displays it in flashes, but he leaned more on the fastball-slider combo, perhaps a big contributor in why lefties crushed him with a .343 average and .916 OPS over his 26 starts. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has a short arm action, and despite limiting walks, his profile leans more toward control than command, making particularly hittable in the Midwest League. It might be worth seeing how high he could crank the fastball in a move to the bullpen soon, and considering Love is entering his age-24 season in 2023, that transition might not be far off unless his stuff ticks up quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Love was technically a fourth-year sophomore at UNC in 2021, having redshirted in 2018 and then again during the COVID-shortened spring of 2020. It was his first season as part of the Tar Heels rotation and he handled the move well, posting a 3.71 ERA with 129 strikeouts in 102 innings. The Cardinals selected him in the third round and signed him slightly below-slot at $600,000 before sending him to seven appearances in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League and Low-A Southeast. He fanned 13 of the 27 batters he faced in that short Minor League sample. The right-hander earns the biggest raves for a mid-80s changeup that comes with a heavy fade and could be a weapon against batters from either side. He’s typically around 91-95 mph with his fastball, touching as high as 98, but the heater doesn’t come with much movement. An average mid-80s slider/cutter gives him a third pitch, though it’s yet to flash more than average. General command issues have plagued Love in the past, perhaps because of his short arm action, and his fastball and slider can be particularly hittable when they catch too much of the plate. He didn’t show those concerns early in his pro career, but they will be worth watching as he expands that sample. Already 23 before his first full season, the former Diamond Heel may not have as long a runway to prove he can stick as a starter in the pros. This arsenal is a solid start at least, and the fastball, in particular, could play up with more velocity should he eventually move to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While it’s a bit too soon to put a final grade on the Pirates’ efforts during the 2018-19 international signing period, it has netted them a big leaguer already in right-hander Luis Ortiz. Lopez, who signed for $400,000 when the period opened on July 2, has put himself on the prospect map more than anyone other than Ortiz, showing off some raw power in his full-season debut in 2021 and continuing to impact the ball in High-A last year, though a dislocated right knee will sideline him for the 2023 season. Power is the 21-year-old infielder’s calling card and he has as much raw pop as anyone in the system. Greensboro is a good place to hit, and the right-handed-hitting Lopez took advantage, slugging .571 in the friendly confines. He has quick hands at the plate and can go to right-center with authority, but he needs to work on his overall approach to get to better counts after walking in just five percent of his plate appearances in 2022. The Pirates moved Lopez around the infield some to help him maintain his athleticism, but after playing a lot of shortstop early on, he played more third base than anywhere else in 2022. He has the chance to stick there, though given his well-below-average speed, first base might be the best fit for a full-time home. He’s still raw, but the offensive tools are there to profile well at either infield corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners coveted Polcovich enough out of Oklahoma State that they used one of their five picks in the shortened 2020 Draft on him. The immediate transition to pro ball, however, was not seamless, especially after he climbed in the second half of ‘21 to Double-A Arkansas, where he slashed .133/.242/.211 (.453 OPS) and struggled to establish any confidence. But his ‘22 at the affiliate was a big turnaround. He raised his OPS by nearly 300 points and did so with a healthy sample size of 524 plate appearances. He also continued to flash his speed and has drawn praise as one of the best baserunners in the system. He also can play all over the infield and outfield, making him that much more valuable in the eyes of a club that puts a huge premium on defensive versatility all the way up to the Majors. Based on his trajectory, with a few hiccups followed by promise, Polcovich has drawn comparisons to Sam Haggerty. The big thing with him to continue climbing will be showing that his turnaround in ‘22 was legitimate and that he can produce consistently with the bat. The switch-hitter bats more naturally righty, but he’s shown an ability to make enough contact from the left side to continue hitting there. And even with a smaller and stocky build, he’s shown some extra-base potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A promotion to Double-A Arkansas in 2021 was an eye-opening one for the middle infielder, as Polcovich hit .133/.242/.211 (.453 OPS) in 149 plate appearances. The Mariners believe their third-round pick from ‘20 still had a solid process, approach and good pitch recognition, but wasn’t seeing results. As such, it took a mental toll that led him to pressing more. The club has chalked up those Double-A struggles to bad luck. He was much better at High A Everett earlier last season with a .980 OPS. Polcovich has a shorter stature at 5-foot-10, and while his tools aren’t incredibly loud, he profiles with solid on-base potential and he’s a switch-hitter. Though he bats more naturally from the right side, he’s been able to make enough contact from the left to stick with both moving forward. The power profile isn’t exactly strong, but he does have some extra-base potential within the gaps rather than over the wall. He’s also described as a solid runner and smart base runner. Defensively, Polcovich came up as a second baseman at Oklahoma State, but the Mariners have used him all over, including shortstop and center field. He’s dependable with an average arm yet doesn’t necessarily stand out at one spot over the others. The Mariners covet that kind of versatility, which could make him a valued commodity if his bat catches up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of a former 10-year pro ball player, Polcovich spent one year at the University of Kentucky then moved on to Northwest Florida State College for two seasons and Oklahoma State after that. He began to catch scouts’ eyes after hitting .305 in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2019, and he was batting .344/.494/.578 with 19 walks and eight steals in 18 games for the Cowboys last spring before the shutdown, which was enough for the Mariners to nab him in the third round and sign him for a below-slot bonus of $575,000. The switch-hitting Polcovich bats more naturally from the right side, but he’s shown an ability to make enough contact from the left side to continue hitting there. Overall, he has a solid approach, and even with a smaller and stocky build, he’s shown some extra-base potential, though his power is more gap-to-gap than over-the-wall at this point. He runs well and is a smart baserunner. At various stops, Polcovich has played a number of positions defensively, including second and third at OSU and center field on the Cape. He’s dependable at a number of spots with an average arm, but he doesn’t necessarily profile at one defensive home. That could lead to a future similar to his dad’s, albeit with a bit more thump in his bat. He made a strong first impression on the Mariners during his time at the alternate training site last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez didn’t produce much initial hype as a 2017 signing out of Mexico, partly because of his size at 5-foot-8, but he immediately earned some attention in his 2018 debut in the Dominican Summer League. There, Hernandez posted a 2.60 ERA over 55 1/3 innings, striking out 64. That momentum quickly evaporated, though, when Hernandez got rocked in Rookie-level the Gulf Coast League in 2019, posting an 8.02 ERA over 21 1/3 innings. But the up-and-down start to his career continued when he bounced back with Los Mochis in Mexico. That set up Hernandez’s true breakout in ’21. That summer, he climbed from Single-A to Double-A, striking out 108 batters with a 2.74 ERA over 62 1/3 innings. That's when Hernandez’s potentially elite changeup truly began to shine, baffling hitters even when they knew it was coming. He was off to a tremendous start in 2022, with a 1.88 ERA over 24 innings while reaching Triple-A, but his season was slowed by a shoulder issue, and he was hit hard upon his return. The Blue Jays are betting on Hernandez’s upside, though, and after he went untouched in the Rule 5 Draft, he has a chance to make his big league debut as early as 2023. It’s all about the changeup with Hernandez, but can that pitch survive on its own against MLB hitters?
