He expands the zone too much at times, leading to the K issues, and that became even more of a concern last summer when it looked like he was pressing to recreate his Carolina success. The 21-year-old still ended up with a 20-20 season (20 homers, 23 steals) because of his above-average speed on top of the pop, and that speaks to his offensive ceiling if he makes enough contact to reach base. Gray played center primarily and mixed in some right field in 2021. The presence of Sal Frelick, Garrett Mitchell and even Joey Wiemer will likely move him to the corner full-time the closer he gets to American Family Field, and he has enough arm to work there. The Brewers hope a full offseason reset gets Gray back on track and helps him show just enough bat to get the rest of his tools in future Milwaukee lineups.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray emerged as a top prospect for the 2018 Draft as a sophomore, and while he did plateau a bit, there were still few players with better all-around potential in his prep class. After hitting .491 with a .611 OBP and six home runs during his senior year at Hattiesburg (Miss.) High, Gray became the program's first player to be drafted since 2007, going to the Brewers in the second round. He struggled to stay on the field early in his career and move forward with his development as a pro, with pneumonia and a hamstring strain limiting him to just 55 games across his first two seasons, both of which he spent in Rookie ball. Finally able to play regularly in 2021, Gray has taken off, first hitting .289/.407/.632 with 12 homers in 51 games at Low-A prior to a midseason promotion. Gray has two loud tools in his raw power and arm strength. A gifted athlete with a quick right-handed bat, he can hammer balls out of the park to all fields and started to tap into that power more in 2021. The Brewers were most impressed by how he started to make the most of his pop potential and athleticism with an uppercut swing that results in lots of deep fly balls. Though that leads to a good amount of strikeouts, Gray takes his walks as well and now projects as much closer to an average hit tool. Gray’s defense was never in question. His arm strength was among the best among 2018 high-school position players, having been clocked at 98 mph from the outfield at the Perfect Game National Showcase after his junior year. His accuracy sometimes leaves something to be desired, though. He has solid speed and takes good routes in center field, giving him a chance to play there in pro ball. Gray’s advancements in 2021 have made him an even more exciting prospect, and while his profile still comes with risk, his ceiling has jumped to that of a skilled everyday center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best Venezuelan prospect and one of the top all-around talents in the 2019 international class, Rodriguez signed for $2,667,500. The 2020 pandemic shutdown delayed his pro debut until last summer, when he homered four times in his first six games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League before tailing off and finishing with a .216/.326/.367 line and a 31 percent strikeout rate. He spent the offseason working out with J.D. Martinez and Miguel Cabrera, which the Dodgers hope will spark a rebound in 2022. When Rodriguez signed, he projected as a hit-over-power center fielder with a line-drive, all-fields approach. He has gotten stronger and more aggressive since turning pro, looking to crush homers to his pull side with a longer right-handed swing while chasing too many pitches out of the strike zone and giving away too many at-bats. He needs to regain some discipline, get back to barreling balls more consistently and just let his pop come naturally. Rodriguez is starting to slow a bit as he has added muscle, earning average to solid grades for his speed. He didn't stick out on the bases or in center field during his debut despite a reputation for a high baseball IQ that allows him to get the most out of his tools. If he does have to shift to a corner, his solid to plus arm would play in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Los Angeles has landed the best Venezuelan prospect in each of the last three international classes, including signing Rodriguez for $2,667,500 in 2019. He was advanced enough to make his U.S. debut at age 17 last summer, but the coronavirus pandemic cancelled the Minor League season. Instead, he participated in the Dodgers' Dominican instructional league program. More advanced than most teenage hitters, Rodriguez has a mature approach that produces line drives to all fields. He has a definite hit-over-power profile from the right side of the plate, though his bat speed and ability to barrel balls could translate into 20 or more homers per season. He's starting to add strength and show some feel for driving balls in the air. With solid speed and a high baseball IQ, Rodriguez can steal some bases and has a chance to remain in center field. It's possible that he could lose a step as he matures physically, which could push him to an outfield corner. If that happens, his offensive upside and solid to plus arm would fit well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top Venezuelan pitching prospect in the 2019-20 international class, Medina signed with the Padres for $700,000 on July 2, 2019. After the pandemic cancelled the 2020 season, Medina spent some time in San Diego’s fall instructional camp and then made his professional debut in 2021, throwing a combined 33 2/3 innings in the Dominican Summer League and the Arizona Complex League. He’ll continue his professional climb with the Twins, who acquired him as the player to be named later in the deal that sent Taylor Rogers and Brent Rooker to the Padres. Medina is still growing into his 6-foot-1, 180-pound frame but already pitches with good velocity and should be able to add a bit more in the future. His fastball, which features good late life, sits in the mid-90s and touches the upper-90s on occasion. He also throws an above-average slider and shows good feel for a promising changeup. Medina repeats his delivery well and aggressively attacks hitters when he’s on the mound. He shows a good feel for all his pitches, but his consistency will need to improve. The right-hander issued 24 walks over 33 2/3 innings last season and although that’s a small sample size, it’s worth noting. That being said, Medina is still just 19 years old with plenty of ingredients to be high on. If he’s able to make the necessary adjustments to his command, he projects as a starter long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Medina was the top pitching prospect out of Venezuela in the 2019-20 international class, signing with the Padres for $700,000 on July 2. What was supposed to be Medina’s professional debut in 2020 was wiped out by the pandemic, though he did put forth an encouraging showing in San Diego’s fall instructional camp after the season. Medina is the prototypical starting-pitcher package, with a lean, athletic frame that should enable to him to add strength and velocity as he matures. He already features an explosive fastball as a teenager, with the ability to throw in the mid 90s with sink and late movement, and he could ultimately sit in the upper 90s once he’s grown into his projectable body. Medina has the makings of an above-average slider that he throws with power as well as feel for turning over a quality changeup. Medina repeats his delivery better than most teenage hurlers and should continue to improve in that department as he matures physically. He's aggressive on the mound and knows how to attack hitters, showing feel for his entire arsenal as well as an aptitude for making adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for just $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2017, Jimenez has some of the best all-around ability in the Red Sox system. He has batted .306 or better in each of his three pro seasons, including winning the Short-Season New York-Penn League batting title (.359) in his 2019 U.S. debut. But he's still raw in many phases of the game, so Boston declined to protect him on its 40-man roster last November. Jimenez has gained about 50 pounds since signing, giving him solid raw power, while retaining almost all of his speed, which still grades as double-plus. A natural right-handed hitter who began switch-hitting when he turned pro, he's still figuring out his identity at the plate. His strength is more notable than his bat speed, and while he makes a lot of contact with a flat stroke, he lacks selectivity and produces a lot of harmless grounders while showing little feel for pulling or launching pitches in the air. Jimenez also doesn’t make the most of his quickness on the bases, where he's not a prolific or particularly successful thief. His speed plays better in center field, where he has good instincts and plenty of range. His strong arm earns solid to well-above-average grades from evaluators and fits anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A bargain $10,000 signing out of the Dominican Republic in 2017, Jimenez began switch-hitting after turning pro. He won Boston's Latin program player of the year award in his first season and the short-season New York-Penn League batting title (.359) in his second. While the coronavirus pandemic limited his 2020 development to instructional league, he wowed the Red Sox by showing up with significant added muscle while still retaining his game-changing speed. Jimenez uses his plus-plus speed to turn routine grounders into singles and could be a prolific basestealer once he refines his technique. He now has at least solid raw power, though it's still unclear how much he'll be able to tap into it. He had a short, flat swing the last time he was seen in game action and he'll need to become more selective because his hand-eye coordination allows him to make almost too much contact for his own good. In addition to his offensive upside, Jimenez also ranks as the best defender among Boston farmhands. His combination of speed and instincts gives him more range than most center fielders. He also has a strong arm for his position, receiving well above-average grades from some evaluators.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hiraldo was ranked as the No. 17 prospect in the 2017-’18 International class by MLB Pipeline and was considered by some to be the most advanced hitter in the group. Signed for $750,000, Hiraldo debuted in ’18 in the DSL and GCL where he hit a combined .300 over 64 games. He spent most of ’19 in Rookie League Bluefield, again hitting .300, and came out of the lost ’20 season with an assignment to Low-A Dunedin. That ’21 season was a learning experience for Hiraldo, where he hit .249 with a seven homers and a .727 OPS over 105 games, striking out 111 times. With both Orelvis Martinez and Leonardo Jimenez in Low-A in ’21, Hiraldo played second and third base, but could get some reps back at shortstop in ’22. His defense remains a question mark and his throwing accuracy has been inconsistent at times, so finding a defensive home will be important for Hiraldo at this stage. His offensive dip in ’21 was largely due to pitchers making adjustments against him, which he’ll need to counter. That led to some frustrations for Hiraldo, but the raw hitting talent is still in there and his thick build should continue to give him some natural power. At 21, Hiraldo is entering am important season after seeing several prospects around him shoot up these rankings. The main focus will be his approach so that he can get to his natural power, which can still be above-average, but that tool will need some others to support it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hiraldo was ranked by MLB Pipeline as the No. 17 prospect in the 2017-’18 international class, with some evaluators considering him to be the best hitter available. The Blue Jays signed Hiraldo for $750,000 that summer and the early results have matched those reports. Hiraldo hit .313 with an .834 OPS over 54 games in the Dominican Summer League in ’18, earning a late promotion up to the Gulf Coast League. In ’19, the Blue Jays sent Hiraldo to Bluefield, where he hit .300 with an .829 OPS, before bumping him up to High-A Lansing for a one-game taste late in the season. With a frame that was already naturally strong as a 16-year-old, Hiraldo continues to develop physically and that shows in the type of contact he makes. Add in plus bat speed, and Hiraldo profiles as a hitter who will produce high exit velocities and line-drive contact with legitimate home-run potential. Hiraldo’s hand-eye coordination is impressive, but his aggression at the plate can lead to him pulling the ball often. If he’s able to drive the ball to all fields more consistently, that will open up his offensive profile even further. Hiraldo will continue to move around the infield, where his throwing arm is his strongest tool. As his body continues to mature, Hiraldo’s likeliest landing spot could he third, but the Blue Jays believe in his defensive actions enough to continue giving him time in the middle infield as he develops. The 2021 season will be key for Hiraldo’s development path, especially as he begins to face pitchers with more advanced game plans against his pull-heavy approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of La Romana, Dominican Republic, for $1.2 million in the 2018-’19 international signing period, De Castro finally had the opportunity to make his pro debut in ’21 in the Florida Complex League, hitting .238 with a .769 OPS. De Castro mixed in a handful of games at second base but primarily played shortstop, where he profiles as one of the highest-potential defenders in the system. De Castro makes some “wow” defensive plays on the infield, but can balance those out with fundamental errors at times, particularly when it comes to throwing. The club’s optimism lies in those errors smoothing out as he matures, because the upside is significant defensively and enough to carry De Castro to the upper levels of the Minor Leagues on its own. Offensively, there isn’t much power coming given his thin frame, so the focus going forward will be consistent contact and a strong approach. That will be tested well with a full season in ’22. It’s a matter of rounding out De Castro’s game from here, but the twitchy young shortstop still has plenty of development time ahead. In a system that’s been developing some stronger defenders of late, De Castro has the ability to be among the best, so it’s up to his offensive production to decide his long-term ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trained in the Dominican Republic by Angel Perez, a member of MLB's Trainer Partnership Program, De Castro received the top bonus in Toronto’s 2019-2020 international class, signing as a 16-year-old for $1.2 million on July 2. A twitchy defender with one of the better infield gloves in the system, De Castro comes with long-term upside. Scouts viewed De Castro as one of the stronger defenders in that international class, too, due to his natural defensive actions and strong throwing arm. You’ll hear the term “quick-twitch” with De Castro often, which is what makes him such a talented defender, and his baseball instincts and IQ only help the situation. Still listed at 6-foot, 150 pounds, De Castro’s physical development will be one of the most important factors in the coming years. An adjustment to the lower half of his swing has helped him drive the ball more consistently, but adding some muscle to his frame could bump that power tool without slowing him down too much in the field. De Castro is fully expected to stay at shortstop, but his development will require some patience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When he was selected in the third round of the 2017 Draft, Tabor was a skinny, baby-faced kid, but the D-backs saw pitchability and the potential for his stuff to tick up. They signed him for an above-slot $1 million. He overcame a shaky start at Class A Short Season Hillsboro in 2018 to finish the season on a high note, and that success carried over into his age-20 campaign at Class A Kane County, where the right-hander compiled a 2.93 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 101/16 K/BB over 95 1/3 innings spanning 23 starts. Tabor pitched across three levels in 2021, working his way up to Triple-A in the process. His numbers dipped a bit, but the D-backs feel he pitched better than the numbers indicate since pitching in Reno is always tough on the stats. Tabor’s advanced ability and polish are particularly impressive considering his cold-weather background as a Massachusetts prep. A good athlete with a clean delivery, his fastball sits in the low 90s and he can get up to the mid-90s when he needs to. He’s had an advanced changeup since he was drafted and has improved his slider to the point where it can be his best secondary pitch. While he’s capable of missing some bats, Tabor is a command-over-stuff guy and has proved to be an accomplished strike-thrower early in his career. He can pitch to all four quadrants of the zone and features some of the best command in the Arizona system. The D-backs like what they’ve seen from Tabor and believe he has the tools to remain a starter at the highest level. He’s made big leaps over the past four seasons, so as long as Tabor continues on a similar trajectory -- refining his secondary pitches and continuing to gain experience -- it won’t be long until he’s pitching in the back end of a Major League rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When he was selected in the third round in 2017, Tabor was a skinny, baby-faced kid, but the D-backs saw pitchability and the possibility for his stuff to tick up. They selected him in the third round and gave him an above-pick-value $1 million. He overcame a shaky start at Class A Short Season Hillsboro in 2018 to finish the season on a high note, and that success carried over into his age-20 campaign at Class A Kane County, with the right-hander compiling a 2.93 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 101/16 K/BB over 95 1/3 innings and 23 starts. While the numbers dipped a bit in 2021, Tabor did work his way up to Triple-A. Tabor’s advanced pitchability and polish at a young age are particularly impressive considering his cold-weather background as a prep. A good athlete with a clean delivery, he is a good student of the game. His fastball has ticked up to where he sits at 92-93 mph and can pop 94 or occasionally 95. He had a plus-changeup when he was drafted and he has improved his breaking ball to the point where it is his best secondary pitch in some games and in others it's his best. He has proved to be an accomplished strike-thrower early in his career, can pitch to all four quadrants of the strike zone and features some of the best command in the Arizona system. The D-backs liked what they saw from Tabor in Instructional League and believe he has everything needed to eventually be a starter in the big leagues, especially with the recent uptick in stuff. Refining his secondary pitches and gaining experience are the keys now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Doxakis’ numbers didn’t jump off the stat sheet as a freshman at Texas A&M, with a 5.44 ERA and 1.37 WHIP recorded between seven starts and 18 relief outings. But he moved into the Aggies’ rotation as a sophomore and quickly became one of the Southeastern Conference’s best starters the next two springs. His performance was good enough to inspire the Rays to select the lefty in the second round of the 2019 Draft, making him Texas A&M’s highest-drafted player in seven years. He had an excellent professional debut, posting a 1.93 ERA and 0.95 WHIP with nearly a strikeout per inning in the New York-Penn League, and likely would have moved up considerably if there had been a Minor League season in 2020. He’s not going to blow away anyone with his fastball velocity, typically sitting between 88-93 mph, but it plays up due to his command and the pitch’s arm side run. His breaking ball, a low-80s slider from which he can add/subtract velocity, makes him devastating against left-handed hitters and quite tough on right-handers as well because he can back-foot it against them. His changeup is the least reliable of his three offerings, although it’s shown flashes of becoming an average third pitch playing off his fastball if he can command it. He’s a confident pitcher, trusting his above-average control and command and attacking hitters on both sides of the plate. Some scouts look at Doxakis’ delivery and relatively limited arsenal and peg him as a reliever, a projection no doubt bolstered by him hitting 97 mph in that role as a freshman at Texas A&M. That gives him a high floor, even as someone who can turn over a lineup once, but he has the repertoire, control, frame and makeup and recent results to continue starting as he's done for all of 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith already made a name for himself as an amateur as the Most Outstanding Pitcher at the 2016 Area Code Games but had a strong commitment to TCU that caused him to drop to the 38th round in 2017. He made six starts for the Horned Frogs as a freshman but missed all of 2019 due to Tommy John surgery and much of 2020 due to the pandemic. Pitching in his fourth collegiate season last year, he posted a 3.83 ERA with 101 strikeouts and 20 walks in 82 1/3 innings, prompting the Brewers to select him in the second round. Smith signed for below slot at $1 million. The first thing that stands out about the southpaw is his height at 6-foot-7. He puts that to good use by creating good extension and a tough angle on his 89-93 mph fastball. The heater, which can touch 95, also plays up because he commands the pitch well within the zone. His mid-80s changeup gives him another above-average offering because of its tough fade. A low-80s slider rounds out the package and was trending in the right direction before the Draft. Smith’s ability to pitch in the zone and avoid free passes differentiates him from other big hurlers, who typically thrive on throwing hard with little command. The lack of a true plus pitch won’t make him an ace, but the rest of the package makes him a potential back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a sign of what was to come, Holgate followed up a mundane freshman season at Arizona with a circuit-best 13 homers in the Northwoods League in the summer of 2019. He was off to a hot start before the 2020 shutdown, hit .351/.421/.576 with 11 homers as a junior last spring and mixed in a National Baseball Congress World Series win for the Santa Barbara Foresters in between. The Cardinals selected the slugger 70th overall last July and signed him for just under slot at $875,000. Holgate played 30 games with Low-A Palm Beach in his Draft year but managed just a .193/.279/.289 line and 35.7 percent K rate. The left-handed hitter’s power is what originally stood out to St. Louis, and that remained true in those early Minor League looks, where he maxed out with a 109.2 mph exit velocity. His plus raw power shows up more in batting practice, but it should be at least above-average on the pro side too. A longer swing, designed to make the most of that power, led to the swing-and-miss issues with Palm Beach, and it’s a bigger question now than it was on Draft Day if Holgate will be able to hit for a decent average. A career .314 mark in college provides some hope, and further adjustments to increase the contact rate after last year’s humbling could pay dividends. Holgate played his college position of right field in Low-A, but he projects better in left field due to a fringy arm. The former Wildcat will need to hit to be valuable in either corner outfield spot, and that starts with making more contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Elliott starred at Division II Lincoln Memorial University in Tennessee, posting a 2.23 ERA with 134 strikeouts and just 14 walks over 92 2/3 innings during his 2019 senior season. The Padres selected him in the 10th round that summer and inked him to a below-slot $5,000 bonus. The 6-foot-3 lefty posted a 1.77 ERA over 35 2/3 innings in his pro debut then broke out in 2021 as he worked his way up to Double-A. Pitching across two levels last season, Elliott racked up 87 strikeouts and issued just 19 walks over 70 2/3 innings Although Elliott’s velocity has ticked up since college, he remains a command-over-stuff type pitcher. His fastball sits in the low 90s, but plays up because his arm slot creates additional deception. A low-80s changeup, which features good downward action, is currently his best pitch, though there’s a chance his mid-70s slider claims that title in the future. None of Elliott’s pitches will overpower a hitter, but his delivery, coupled with his ability to locate to any corner of the zone helps his stuff play above its velocity. The development of Elliott’s slider may ultimately determine his ceiling. The southpaw has been a consistent performer during his time in pro ball and if the slider comes along, should be able to stick in the back of a rotation. If not, he could profile as an effective longman coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morris enjoyed some success in the 2018 Cape Cod League, where he hit .331, and that hit tool also showed itself in his final season at Virginia, where he handled ACC pitching with a .345 average. The Blue Jays selected Morris in the fifth round of the ’19 Draft, signing him to a slightly above-slot bonus of $397,500. Morris debuted in ’19 in Low-A, hitting .246 with a .730 OPS, but had more success when he returned to Vancouver as Toronto’s High-A affiliate in ’21. That season, Morris hit .285 with seven home runs and a .782 OPS over 103 games, playing across the infield. One of the most cerebral prospects in the system, Morris has an exceptional ability to recall past plate appearances and work through those for development. His hit tool has always been his calling card, but the Blue Jays are now expecting a little more power from Morris, with double-digit home runs the next step. Morris may be a below-average athlete on the field, but he has carved out a valuable resume with time at shortstop, second base and third base, a split that’s expected to continue. As long as he can continue to be reliable in those spots, there’s room for his bat to carry him through the system. Morris’ mental approach has helped him handle more advanced pitching at the upper levels, but he’ll need his offensive production to do most of the work. He’ll have plenty of opportunities in an organization looking to develop some lefty bats, and the utility role should give him plenty of pathways up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guzman signed with the Royals for $1.5 million in the 2015-16 international signing period. While he didn’t hit much early in his career, he impressed defensively and the Royals added him to the 40-man roster in 2019, protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft. He was then non-tendered late in 2020, but re-signed with the Royals on a Minor League deal. His bat started to come around in 2021 as he reached Double-A for the first time. He also played for his native Dominican Republic in the Tokyo Olympics and was the starting shortstop in the bronze medal game victory. He elected free agency after the season and signed a Minor League contract with the D-backs in November. Guzman, who used to switch hit as a kid, just started doing so professionally in 2019. It’s still a work in progress, but he hit well at High-A (.289/.352/.465) prior to his promotion last season, showing signs that hitting from both sides of the plate may stick. He added strength and his .401 slugging percentage last season was a career high, but power still isn’t Guzman’s forte and it’s unlikely he’d hit double-digit homers at the highest level. The 23-year-old is certainly a glove-first shortstop and grades out as a plus defender at the premium position. What’s more, he added to his versatility last season, spending time at both second base and center field. With a plus arm and above-average speed, Guzman has the capabilities to play all over the diamond. It remains to be seen how much he’ll develop as a hitter, but his glove gives him a solid floor and the added versatility could help him reach the Majors as a utility option off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Strotman underwent Tommy John surgery with the Rays back in June 2018 and returned to the mound in July 2019, but the shutdown made it impossible for him to get innings in 2020. Even though the former reliever at St. Mary's College of California earned a spot onto Tampa Bay's 40-man roster that fall and had a strong start to the 2021 season in Triple-A that caught the Twins’ eye enough for them to acquire him along with Joe Ryan in the Nelson Cruz deal, the lack of prior workload may have caught up to the right-hander as he posted a 7.33 ERA in 12 outings following the trade. Typically, Strotman's fastball sits around 95-96 mph and tops out at 99, but the Twins saw a noticeable drop in his velocity and command towards the end of the '21 season, leading them to believe the issues stemmed from the ramp-up in his workload. They're expecting the fastball to be at full strength in ‘22, and though it has good life and is complemented by three solid offspeed pitches, Strotman doesn't miss as many bats as his stuff might suggest. His newer cutter and slider have become more of a singular pitch, with him working to keep adding velocity to the pitch. Strotman has starter-caliber stuff, but he still needs to throw more strikes overall, which the Twins think is feasible considering his lack of extreme control issues in the past. There's a chance that he could maximize his potential more effectively in the bullpen, where the fastball-cutter/slider mix in particular could play up in short stints. Where he falls on that spectrum could depend on his ability to shoulder the workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A reliever for most of his time at St. Mary’s College of California, Strotman moved into the rotation during his junior season and caught the Rays’ attention with his low-mileage arm and untapped upside as a starter. He went in the fourth round of the 2017 Draft, put together an outstanding professional debut and kept pitching well for Class A Bowling Green in 2018 until requiring Tommy John surgery that June. He returned on July 11, 2019, made up for some lost time in the Arizona Fall League then turned heads with a 2020 fall instructional league showing that catapulted him onto the Rays’ 40-man roster. He carried it forward to a successful year in Triple-A when he was sent, along with Joe Ryan, to the Twins in the Nelson Cruz deal. Strotman has a quick arm and plus velocity on his fastball, and that returned last year after coming back inconsistently during his late-2019 performance. He added a cutter while baseball was shut down last summer, and Rays officials believe that pitch is already his best breaking ball and a legitimate weapon for him. He also has an above-average slider, a loopy curveball and a below-average changeup to round out his starter’s arsenal. His fastball-cutter combination alone, especially with his plus command back in place two years after surgery, made him a legitimate risk to be selected in last year’s Rule 5 Draft had he not been protected. In 2017, Strotman posted a 4.67 strikeout-to-walk ratio. In instructs, he showed that level of command again. He has all the traits you’d want out of a starter: plus pitches, a deep repertoire, athleticism, a smooth delivery and plus command. The Rays kept developing him in that role, but the most important thing for the young right-hander in 2021 to keep gaining experience after all the development time he missed due to his surgery and the lost season in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before he missed a month during his 2018 high school season with shoulder tightness, Hankins got mentioned as a possibility to become the first prep right-hander ever to get drafted No. 1 overall. Health and signability concerns allowed the Guardians to grab him at No. 35, where he signed for an over-slot $2,246,022. He hasn't pitched since 2019, however, because of the coronavirus shutdown followed by Tommy John surgery in May 2021. When healthy, Hankins shows off an electric fastball that sits at 92-95 mph and reaches 97 with so much run and sink that he can have trouble commanding it. He has nice feel for a changeup with similar action that plays as a plus pitch when it has enough velocity separation from his heater, though it does get too firm at times. He didn't demonstrate much aptitude for spinning the ball as an amateur but has made some progress as a pro, with his sharper low-80s slider showing more upside than his upper-70s curveball. Though he's 6-foot-6, Hankins does a good job of keeping his delivery in sync and throwing strikes. During his rehabilitation from elbow reconstruction, he has improved his conditioning, which should help expedite his comeback. He may not arrive in Cleveland as early as originally anticipated but still could become a mid-rotation starter, especially if he can upgrade his slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hankins was discussed as potentially the first prep right-hander to get selected No. 1 overall in the Draft until he missed a month during his 2018 senior season with shoulder tightness. Questions about his health and signability allowed the Indians to grab him with their second of two first-rounders that June, and they signed him for an over-slot $2,246,022 as the 35th overall choice. He was healthy in his first three years as a pro, albeit while working just 63 official innings in large part because of the coroanvirus shutdown, but injured his elbow this spring and had Tommy John surgery in May. When healthy, Hankins has an electric fastball that sits at 92-95 mph and peaks at 97 with so much run and sink that it can be difficult to command at times. His best secondary pitch is a changeup with similar action that shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch but can get too firm. The key to his development will be coming up with the reliable breaking ball he lacked as an amateur, and his sharper slider shows more promise than his deeper curveball. With his athleticism and impressive body control for a 6-foot-6 youngster, Hankins should be able to provide plenty of strikes and already shows some feel for locating his fastball to both sides of the plate. Adding more strength will help and could increase his velocity as well. He will vary his tempo to throw off the timing of hitters and even uses a Johnny Cueto shimmy shake on occasion.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene starred at the 2019 Area Code Games and as part of a scout team that faced the U.S. national 18-and-under squad, propelling him to the Mets in the supplemental second round a year later. New York traded him to the Guardians along with Andrés Giménez, Amed Rosario and pitching prospect Josh Wolf for Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco in January 2021, so his pro debut came with his second organization. He has one of the higher ceilings among the system's outfielders but will require time to develop. Greene has some natural feel for hitting and makes consistent line-drive contact from the left side of the plate. He employed an extremely patient approach in his debut, drawing 35 walks in 43 games while repeatedly using the opposite field. He has enough bat speed and projectable strength to deliver 15-20 homers per season if he looks to turn on more pitches and launch them in the air. While Greene has plus speed, he's still learning how to get the most out of it as a basestealer and center fielder. He's smoothing out his reads and routes in center, where his quickness helps him recover from some of his mistakes. His fringy arm strength is playable in center field but precludes him from right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene's athleticism stood out on the prep showcase circuit in 2019, when he starred at the Area Code Games and as part of a scout team that faced the U.S. national 18-and-under squad. The Mets made him a supplemental second-round pick last June and signed him away from a Missouri commitment for $850,000. His only experience with the Mets came in instructional league before they traded him to the Indians along with Andrés Gimenez, Amed Rosario and pitching prospect Josh Wolf for Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco in January. Greene has the hand-eye coordination and line-drive-oriented left-handed stroke to hit for average. Scouts believe he relied more on natural ability than swing mechanics or approach as an amateur, giving him the opportunity to improve quickly as he gets more instruction in pro ball. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to develop 15-20 home run power, especially if he adds some more loft. With speed that earns plus and even some well-above-average grades from some evaluators, Greene is aggressive on the bases. His quickness helps him outrun some of his mistakes, but he needs to improve his reads and routes in center field. If he doesn't, his fringy arm strength will relegate him to left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the Royals scouted Europe in 2017 and ’18, they could not ignore the contact skills of a young player in Honkbal Hoofdklasse, the Netherlands’ top professional level. That hitter was Darryl Collins, and he signed with the Royals at 16 years old for $97,500 on Aug. 26, 2018. A year later, Collins tore up Rookie ball with a .320 average, and his first taste of full-season ball came last season, when he posted a .705 OPS in 86 games for Low-A Columbia. Collins’ advanced bat-to-ball skills are what sticks out for the rare baseball prospect from the Netherlands. His knack for hitting and his hand-eye coordination are what the Royals noticed when they were scouting him and what still stands out now even as he’s added strength and faced tougher pitching in the States. Still filling out his wide-shouldered frame, Collins has shown power potential too, with the ability to pull the ball better now than in ’19 when his swing was more closed off. Collins’ bat has always been ahead of his defense, and his fringy arm strength profiles best in left field. Collins projects to be more of a contact hitter and on-base player with occasional power, but the focus for him is his defense. He makes up for his arm strength with accuracy and good reads, and the Royals hope to get his arm to at least average for him to be able to play in the big league outfield -- because the bat-to-ball skills certainly have a place in the Majors. The good news is that Collins has good makeup and is still young, so time is on his side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Eastlake High School in Southern California, the same program that produced former No. 1 overall pick Adrian Gonzalez, Cavaco played his way into the first round in 2019 with a big senior season. Since being taken No. 13 overall, the infielder has had some trouble gaining much traction offensively, missing a good chunk of his first full season in 2021 with a concussion. A return to Single-A Fort Myers in 2022 resulted in a bit more power, though he also showed there’s plenty of work to be done. The right-handed hitter continues to show glimpses of the raw tools that made him a first-rounder in the first place, and he’s still learning how to tap into them on a more consistent basis. He has plenty of raw power, and he did set a career high in home runs in 2022 as he worked to correct some mechanical issues with his swing -- including a swing path that is too uphill and a tendency to bail in his stride. While he has had a better bat path at times, he still needs to be more selective at the plate and cut down his swing-and-miss after whiffing in 34.8 percent of his plate appearances in 2022. A shortstop in high school who had some skills to stick there, Cavaco made the move to third in 2022, where his plus arm should work just fine. He doesn’t turn 22 until next June, so there’s time for him to figure things out, with more reps needed for him to find a better level of consistency on both sides of the ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Eastlake High School in Southern California has had two first round picks in its history. The first was Adrian Gonzalez, the No. 1 overall selection in 2000. Cavaco became No. 2 when the Twins took him No. 13 overall in the 2019 Draft before he struggled during his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League that summer. While the shutdown kept him from playing in 2020, the Twins were very happy with the work he put in on his own and how he performed during instructional league play last fall. During Cavaco’s brief debut in 2019, the infield struggled to make consistent contact, with a tendency to get too uphill the biggest contributor to all of the swing-and-miss. During his time at instructs, he worked to flatten his swing a little, stay in the zone more and make more contact, showing promising strides in that area. That should allow him to tap into his considerable raw power more consistently moving forward. Cavaco worked on his body and his conditioning during the shutdown, showing up to instructs much leaner and more athletic. That gives the plus runner a better chance to stick at shortstop, with enough arm to stay at the premium position. There is a chance he’ll outgrow the spot and he could easily handle a move to third, where he played for most of his high school career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring at San Jacinto Junior College in 2018, Soularie went on to Tennessee and was one of the best offensive players in the Southeastern Conference the following year. His shortened 2020 season wasn’t as explosive, but the Twins liked his tools enough to take him in the second round. They still haven’t really gotten a great look at him, as ankle and foot injuries limited him to just 34 games total in 2021. Soularie does have some skills from the right side of the plate when he’s healthy. He controls the strike zone very well and showed a propensity for drawing walks even in his brief pro debut last year. He’s capable of making a lot of contact with more of a line drive approach. Power did show up during his time at Tennessee, but he needs to get more physical in order for him to drive the ball with a wood bat in his hands. While Soularie doesn’t have blazing speed, he has good instincts on the basepaths and has shown he isn’t afraid to steal a base. He has pretty solid instincts, both in the outfield and at second base, with many thinking the latter is a better long-term option given his lack of arm strength. He could continue to get reps in both spots, with a full healthy season of reps needed to truly evaluate who he is as a prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Soularie first truly appeared on the Draft map after he hit over .400 at San Jacinto Junior College in 2018. He moved on to Tennessee the following year and was among the Southeastern Conference leaders in average, on-base percentage and slugging. He wasn’t swinging the bat as well before the shutdown in '20, but the Twins had seen enough to take him in the second round, ahead of where projections had him. During his time at San Jac and then at Tennessee, Soularie has shown a very advanced approach at the plate, with a knack for barreling up the baseball. He’s geared more for line drives to all fields than power, though he tapped into his raw power as an amateur, hitting 16 homers in just over 250 at-bats with the Volunteers. His selectivity helps all of it play up, as he walked more than he struck out at Tennessee. Soularie doesn’t possess a lot of speed, but what he has, he uses well, and he likes to be aggressive on the basepaths. Defensively, he played center field at San Jac and mostly left at Tennessee, but while the Twins feel he has a good feel for the outfield, they plan to let him develop as a second baseman, where he worked out some in college. He’s shown good feel, hands and instincts, with the main concern being his below-average arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Michigan recruited Brewer as a wide receiver until he dislocated his shoulder as a high school senior, which led to him playing two years of baseball at Lincoln Trail (Ill.) CC before joining the Wolverines on the diamond in 2019. He led Michigan to within a victory of a national championship, won Big Ten Conference player of the year honors and went in the third round of the Draft. He played just 81 games in his first three years as a pro because of a toe injury he sustained in college and recovery from left knee surgery that also would have cost him the 2020 season had it been played. One of the best all-around athletes in the system, Brewer has the potential for at least solid tools across the board but needs more at-bats against quality competition to refine his offensive game. His bat speed and strength give him plus raw power, but he doesn't have the smoothest right-handed stroke and will have to make better swing decisions. He does show a willingness to take walks and knows how to make the most of his well above-average speed on the bases. Though he definitely has the speed for center field, Brewer's defense also requires more polish. His reads and routes can get better, though his quickness helps him recover. He has the solid arm strength for right field should he move to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brewer drew interest from Michigan as a wide receiver until he dislocated his shoulder as a high school senior, which led him to spend two years playing baseball at Lincoln Trail (Ill.) CC before joining the Wolverines on the diamond in 2019. The Big Ten Conference player of the year that spring, he led Michigan to a stunning runner-up finish at the College World Series and went in the third round of the Draft. A toe injury he sustained in college limited his pro debut to 16 games, and surgery on his left knee last spring prevented him from attending instructional league. The fastest player and one of the best all-around athletes among Astros prospects, Brewer could have solid tools across the board if he can add some polish at the plate. His quick right-handed swing and strength create plus raw power, but his less-than-smooth stroke and aggressive approach lead to swing-and-miss concerns. He was less refined than a typical player coming out of college and injuries severely restricted his development opportunities in his first year and a half as a pro. Brewer's well above-average speed contributes to the possibility that he becomes a 25-25 player and gives him a chance to play in center field. He played mostly right field and first base for the Wolverines because of team needs, but could be an asset in center if he improves his reads and routes. A rare bats-right, throws-left player, he has the solid arm and the offensive upside to profile in right field as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knowles signed with the Angels for $850,000 back in July 2017 out of the Bahamas and it looked like a strong investment when he hit .311 with a .391 on-base percentage in his pro debut across two levels of Rookie ball in 2018. He didn’t perform as well in 2019 and really struggled offensively with a move to full-season ball for the first time in 2021. The fact that Knowles is a super high-energy player is a plus, but it’s also an obstacle. While he’s capable of making hard contact from both sides of the plate, he needs to learn to slow things down and rediscover his approach. Early on, he would draw walks and work counts, but that regressed in 2021, with his strikeout rate ticking up as he chased out of the zone too frequently. There isn’t much power in his profile, so he needs to get back to putting the ball in play and letting his plus speed wreak havoc. On the plus side, the Angels had encouraged Knowles to use that speed more aggressively on the basepaths and he responded by going 31-for-32 in stolen-base attempts last year. He’s a capable defender in center field, but showed that not only can he handle all three outfield spots, but he started getting reps at shortstop as well. If he can get back to more regular contact, he could be an athletic super-utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels handed out bonuses of six figures or more during the 2017-18 international signing period, led, of course, by the signing of Shohei Ohtani. Knowles, a toolsy outfielder from the Bahamas, got the third-highest bonus from the organization that period, $850,000, then made a strong debut in the United States in 2018. His 2019 wasn’t as solid, but he appeared to make some very good strides on both sides of the ball in instructional league play in 2020. While Knowles’ numbers dipped in 2019, he still did show off a good amount of tools to work with. He can make hard contact to all fields from both sides of the plate, and even in 2019, showed an ability to work counts and draw walks. Strong, but not big, he’s not likely ever to have more than fringy power, but should have the ability to drive the ball to the gaps and use his speed to his advantage. The Angels continue to encourage Knowles to use that plus speed more on the basepaths to become a threat to steal, something that improved at instructs. Knowles has the chance to be a very good defensive center fielder, one who could stay there long-term, and he’s shown the ability to play all three outfield spots well. He’s also gotten some time at second base, but it’ll be how much his bat advances that will determine if he can reach his ceiling as an everyday big leaguer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a big senior season at Missouri, where he finished with a .930 OPS, Harris still didn’t get a ton of attention from teams. The Braves took a low-risk chance by drafting him in the 32nd round, signing him for just $10,000. He initially took the opportunity and ran with it, hitting his way to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball and performing well in the Arizona Fall League. The shutdown hurt his momentum and he didn’t replicate his success in a full season in Double-A, posting a .671 OPS in 2021. Harris’ calling card during that first full season was his knack for barreling up the baseball. He employs a simple right-handed swing when he’s in sync that leads to hard, line drive contact to all fields. He has some extra-base authority, with a little home run pop to his pull side, but he’s definitely a hit-over-power kind of guy. An average runner with an average arm, Harris has played both outfield corners as a pro, with left being a better fit. It’s more likely he can carve out a career as a fourth or fifth outfielder if he can get back to the offensive consistency that was his hallmark in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Harris didn’t have much to show for his first three years at Missouri except an uptick in power production as a junior. When he posted a .930 OPS as a senior, the Braves took a flier on him in the 32nd round and gave him $10,000. He hit his way across three levels, reaching Double-A, in his first full season of pro ball, and then performed well in the Arizona Fall League. He wasn’t able to build on that momentum when the 2020 season was shut down and he wasn’t a part of the action at the Braves’ alternate camp. More than anything, Harris’ feel for the barrel is what stands out. He has a simple right-handed swing that allows him to make consistent hard contact and send line drives to all fields. There’s extra-base thump in his bat as well, with home run power more to his pull side, and there could be more raw pop for him to tap into to all fields. Harris is an average runner and is probably best suited to be a left fielder if he’s going to be a regular at one position. He worked on his conditioning and his defense during the shutdown, which should help him maximize opportunities to get his bat into a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a freshman at Arkansas, Martin finished with a .974 OPS and 13 homers. He hit 15 more during his 2019 sophomore season, though saw his strikeout rate tick up, a trend that continued during a rough 2020 that of course was shortened by the pandemic. He had shown first-round caliber tools, but went to the third round as teams were worried about his ability to hit, where the Phillies gave him $1.3 million to keep him from going back to school. The offensive woes continued in his first full season as he posted a .601 OPS while battling an ankle injury for most of the season. With his ankle repaired, the Phillies were hoping to get a real sense of who Martin is as a professional, though he once again struggled with the bat in 2022. At the very least, a return to health will let him use his close to top-of-the-scale speed more consistently, being a legitimate basestealing threat and covering a lot of ground defensively. There’s tremendous raw power from the right side of the plate, but he needs a swing overhaul and to tone down his swing and not sell out for power so he can cut down his tendency to swing and miss and chase pitches out of the zone. While Martin spent time on both sides of second base during his pro debut, the Phillies believe he has the tools to stick at shortstop long-term, with enough range and arm for the position. He’s played third in the past and has the speed to patrol the outfield if need be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A talented yet raw prospect from the Arkansas high school ranks in 2017, Martin jumped on the national stage quickly at the University of Arkansas, hitting 28 homers over his first two seasons with the Razorbacks. A premium athlete, Martin’s slow start in 2020, combined with concern about his hit tool, forced him to slide to the third round, where the Phillies went well over slot to keep him from going back to school in 2021. One of the fastest players in the Class of 2020, Martin got some 80 grades from scouts on the 20-80 scouting scale. He’s still learning to use his speed on the basepaths to be a true threat to steal, but when you combine it with his wiry strength and raw power, it’s easy to dream on a player who could be a 25-25 type threat in the future. To get to his power, he will have to cut down on his swing-and-miss, as he had a tendency to swing for the fences too often and get too uphill. At instructs, he worked on staying in the zone longer and swinging at strikes more consistently. Similarly, Martin can let things speed up a bit on the defensive end. But he has more than enough range and arm strength to play shortstop and the Phillies didn’t see anything that pointed to him needing to move from the premium position, though he played third in college and has the athleticism to handle center field if the need arises.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The injuries have piled up for the 2018 27th overall pick. Biceps tendinitis as a high-school senior. Shoulder surgery in the fall of 2019. Shoulder issues before the 2020 shutdown. Tommy John surgery in the spring of 2021. In the nearly four years since he signed for $3 million, Denaburg has managed only 20 1/3 innings at pro ball, all of which came in the Gulf Coast League in 2019. The good news: he was back to throwing off a mound this spring and is still eyeing a return to play in the summer. If he was healthy and at his best, Denaburg could have been right up there with Cavalli, Henry and Rutledge for the top arms in the system. He could ramp up his fastball to the mid-90s, sitting a little below that, and showed a high-spin hammerlike curveball that also earned above-average grades. His changeup was expected to be the last pitch in his repertoire to come along as he gained experience. Perhaps the Tommy John surgery will be the last procedure needed to get Denaburg into a place of regular health. Even if that’s the case, he’ll need time to regain his stuff and show average control again. The 6-foot-4 right-hander is entering his age-22 season, so he’s far from over the hill as a prospect, but he can’t afford many more lost seasons if he’s going to fulfill his promise as a future Nationals starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Denaburg very much fit the Washington profile when the organization took him 27th overall in the 2018 Draft. At 6-foot-4, he had the size to dream on but slipped some due to biceps tendinitis that limited his high-school senior season. The Nationals signed him for $3 million, going well above the $2,472,700 slot to do so. The injury news hasn’t gotten much better since. Denaburg underwent shoulder surgery in the fall of 2019 after throwing only 20 1/3 innings in the Gulf Coast League and had some other shoulder issues in the spring before the pandemic shutdown. The Florida native worked with pitching and rehab coordinators during the summer and participated in instructional league before struggling with fatigue. Unfortunately, the injury woes continued this spring as Denaburg underwent Tommy John surgery. He will miss the entire 2021 season as a result. When healthy, the right-hander will get his fastball up to the mid-90s, though he’ll typically sit a little below that. The curveball, which comes in in the high-70s, earns points for its high spin rate and its hammer-like manner when it’s on. The changeup continues to need development, and that will only come with experience. Denaburg needed innings in 2021 but will have to wait until 2022 for those to come. There is hope that the Tommy John surgery is what was needed to get him over the healthy hill, and if his stuff returns to its pre-procedure levels, there is still the chance of a Major League starter in his profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals selected Infante with the 71st overall selection in the 2020 Draft, using a compensation pick they acquired after losing Anthony Rendon in free agency, and signed the Miami commit to an above-slot $1 million bonus. While the club was impressed by his early skills coming out of that process, Washington kept Infante in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League for his first season, and it was clear he needed to overcome a learning curve in pro ball. The right-handed slugger hit just .215/.329/.364 with three homers and a 30.1 percent K rate over 37 games in his first taste of the Minors. Technically because of Infante’s lack of experience, everything said about him going into 2021 remains true. With decent bat speed, Infante has the look of a potential average hitter someday, and he projects to add some more power as he matures. But to get to his offensive ceiling, he will need to shorten his swing in hopes of barreling more balls in the zone. He still shows at least average athleticism for an infield prospect, and his move to third base this season at Single-A Fredericksburg had more to do with a deep list of low-level shortstops than it did Infante’s own defensive abilities. Infante was already old for the high-school segment of his Draft class, and he turned 21 in his second Minor League season. He has the power to fit a corner profile but will need to find a batter way to hit for average, if he’s going to meet the higher offensive threshold away from shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals received the 71st overall pick in the 2020 Draft as compensation for losing Anthony Rendon in free agency and grabbed Infante at that spot, signing him to a $1 million bonus (slightly above the $884,600 assigned to the slot). Infante is the sixth-highest pick ever out of Monsignor Edward Pace High School in Miami. Four of the five who went higher made the Majors. The fifth is top Red Sox prospect Jeter Downs. Like Downs, Infante is an infielder, albeit less of a lock to stick at short in the long run. The Nationals are going to give him plenty of opportunity to stay at the six, but with a plus arm and just average speed, a move over to third base could be in the cards down the line. After a brief look at last year’s instructs, Washington came away pleased with Infante’s bat path and average bat speed that is expected to develop well in time. That could lead to average power as he gets more exposure to the pro side. There were some pre-Draft questions about Infante’s hit tool due to contact concerns, but the pieces are there for it to be closer to average. Infante is a classic example of a player who can do many things well, if nothing quite at a plus level. The Nats were impressed by his baseball IQ coming right out of the Draft and think it will help him make the necessary adjustments to find a home on a Major League infield some day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a struggle for Miller to get development time on the field since the Reds took him with the 65th overall pick in the 2020 Draft and signed him away from his Wake Forest commitment for an above-slot bonus of $1.29 million. He’s had hernia surgery and ulcerative colitis, an intestine disorder, and he’s had to deal with COVID, reasons why he managed just seven plate appearances in 2021. The good news is the Reds are excited because he seems fully healthy for the first time since being drafted. If he is 100 percent, Miller has the chance to show off a solid all-around toolset at a premium position. He’s a left-handed hitter with a buggy whip of a swing and a solid approach. There’s strength and raw power to tap into and his line drives to all fields should turn into in-game power as he continues to create more leverage at the plate. Miller is athletic and runs well, especially for a catcher, even if he slows down a tick as he catches more. Miller has the tools to stick behind the plate, too. He has very good hands with good blocking and framing skills, and the Reds like his baseball IQ as well. He has plenty of arm strength with accuracy to come with more reps. There’s still big league regular backstop upside here, with him taking his first real step forward in that direction in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: J.W. Mitchell High School in Florida has had a pair of pitchers make it to the big leagues, Tyler Clippard and Jared Shuster, but before Miller was the Reds pick in Competitive Balance Round B of the 2020 Draft, it had never even had a position player selected. The third prep catcher to be taken in last year’s Draft, Jackson signed for a bit over slot, but wasn’t able to participate in instructional league play because of COVID. A left-handed hitting backstop, Miller could develop into a solid all-around catcher. He’s more of a gap hitter right now, one with a good approach and understanding of the zone who can send line drives to all fields. There is some present strength and he should be able to add more to his athletic frame, pointing to more power as he understands how to create more leverage in his swing. He might slow down with the wear and tear of catching, but he’s an average runner as of now who likes to run the bases. Miller’s athleticism should help him behind the plate, providing the agility for him to improve his blocking and overall receiving. He has an above-average arm as well, giving him every chance to become a big league regular, with an understanding that high school catchers can take a long time to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonnin began his career pitching out of the Arkansas bullpen, but wanted the chance to start, one he got when he transferred to Texas Tech for the 2019 season. He had mixed results in the Red Raiders’ rotation, but showed enough premium stuff for the Reds to take him in the third round of the 2020 Draft. He threw well across two levels of A-ball in his first full season, but managed to amass just 47 innings due to a broken rib suffered as part of his high-effort delivery. Shoulder issues limited him to just 25 IP in 2022. The right-hander has had that rib removed, but now has to get his shoulder healthy so he can go back to using his dominant two-pitch mix to miss bats. He struck out 13.6 per nine in 2021 relying on his fastball-slider combination. The heater touches 97 mph with impressive riding action as a result of that crossfire delivery. His slider is also a plus pitch that cuts across the plate. He does have a distinct curve he’s worked on and he’ll have to show he can use his seldom-used changeup in the future. While there are concerns about Bonnin’s ability to remain a starter because of his delivery, he tends to repeat it well and threw strikes fairly consistently last year. The Reds plan has been to let him continue to start, knowing he’ll have to show he can handle a full workload and command the baseball deep into outings in order to become a No. 4 type starter. If not, that fastball-slider combination could be very nasty in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way standout as a high schooler in Texas, Bonnin began his college career pitching out of Arkansas’ bullpen as a freshman. Seeking a chance to start, he transferred to Texas Tech and was a member of the Red Raiders’ rotation as a sophomore and in his shortened junior season, with mixed results. The Reds saw enough starter qualities to draft him in the third round of the 2020 Draft and signing for just below slot before sending him to get his feet wet in instructional league play. From a pure stuff standpoint, Bonnin does have what’s needed to start. His fastball touches 97 mph with riding action coming from his crossfire delivery. He couples that with a plus slider that cuts across the plate. While he showed a greater feel for that pitch at instructs, he also improved the depth of his curve, making it a more serviceable offering and his changeup can be average as well. Bonnin worked on his command and control at instructs and made strides on that front, focusing on his tendency to overthrow. There is effort in that delivery across his body, but he’s athletic enough to repeat it. It’s definitely control over command, but the Reds think both are projectable enough to be close to average, giving him a chance to start long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thomas was an infielder who only pitched a little bit when he signed with Cleveland for $200,000 out of the Bahamas in the middle of the 2016-17 international signing period. His elite arm strength landed him on the mound after he signed and was what the Pirates were interested in when they acquired him in November 2018 in the Jordan Luplow deal. He took a big step forward in rookie ball in 2019, but the 2020 shutdown seemed to impact him adversely as a move to High-A in 2021 did not go so well. Even though Thomas didn’t throw quite as hard in 2021 as he has previously, there’s still plenty of fastball to work with. He’ll easily sit in the mid-90s and regularly touch the upper-90s and has hit triple digits in the past, with his four-seamer showing very good life up in the zone. He has not made much progress with his secondary stuff. He does show a solid slider that can miss bats, but it can lose its shape, and while he has a changeup, it hasn’t developed much. While he’s an athletic 6-foot-4 presence on the mound, Thomas has struggled to repeat his delivery and his walk rate jumped in 2021. He’s still more thrower than pitcher and was deemed so far away that he wasn’t protected on the 40-man roster last offseason. His best track at this point is probably as a reliever, though the Pirates might let him keep going out as a starter so he can work on his complete repertoire.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: What seemed like a minor trade at the time has provided the Pirates with one of their most exciting pitching prospects. An infielder in the Bahamas who was put on the mound because of his arm strength by the Indians after signing him for $200,000 in December 2016, Thomas spent the summers of 2017 and 2018 in the Dominican Summer League and Rookie-level Arizona Leagues before being sent to the Pirates, along with infielder Erik Gonzalez, in return for Jordan Luplow and Max Moroff. He dominated the Rookie-level Appalachian League in his first year with the Pirates. It’s hard not to like Thomas’ combination of size, arm strength and athleticism on the mound. Thomas has continued to add velocity as he’s filled out his 6-foot-4 frame, and he averaged 96 mph with his fastball in 2019 and reached triple digits, showing good life up in the zone. He will need to rely less on that fastball and trust his slider, which flashes above average and misses bats, but can get slurvy at times, and he will have to commit to throwing his changeup. Thomas took a nice step forward in terms of his command the last time he faced real competition, cutting his walk rate tremendously. He needs more time working on his craft to become a complete pitcher, one who has the chance to be a dynamic starter if his secondary pitches continue to improve.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since signing with the Pirates for $350,000 in the 17th round of the 2017 Draft, Martin has been an on-again, off-again offensive player. He hit 11 homers in 39 games during his debut the summer after he signed, then struggled with a move to full-season ball in 2018. He smashed 35 homers across two levels of A ball in 2019 and the power continued to show up at the alternate site in 2020. There were 22 more long balls in Double-A a year ago, but with a regression in his approach, and the Pirates made the decision not to put him on the 40-man roster in the offseason. Outside of perhaps Oneil Cruz, no one has as much raw power in the organization as Martin does, and he’s shown the ability to get to it, recording tape-measure shots and high exit velocities as he’s moved up the ladder. There have been, and always will be, a lot of strikeouts in his game, but he had offset that in the past by drawing walks. In 2021, however, his walk rate dropped and his strikeout rate climbed to a career-high 34.3 percent. While Martin has worked hard on his defense, his power bat is going to be the thing that gets him to the big leagues. He’s no longer a liability at first, but he’s fringy. Having come from a rural area in Washington state, there should be some patience and the Pirates hope Martin’s desire to get better helps him make adjustments.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few people knew much about Martin when the Pirates gave him $350,000 to sign in the 17th round of the 2017 Draft. The Washington state high schooler gave an early return on the investment and put his name on the prospect map when he hit 11 homers in his 39-game Gulf Coast League debut that summer. A move to the full-season South Atlantic League in 2018 did not go well, but he turned things around in 2019, smashing 35 homers between two levels of A ball, power that continued to show up during his time at the club’s alternate training site in Altoona, Pa., in 2020. There’s no question about Martin’s raw power and whether it will play in any park he’s in. His average exit velocity during his breakout 2019 season was 91.5 mph, among the top averages in the game. There is considerable swing and miss to his game, with a strikeout rate of over 30 percent in his career, something he worked on addressing during his time at the alternate camp last summer. He also worked to put the ball in the air more consistently and cut down on his ground ball rate, and he exhibited the ability to damage any pitch, having added more man strength as he’s matured. Martin has also improved his overall conditioning while working very hard on his defense. He’s committed to not being a one-dimensional player and the Pirates feel he’ll be at least an average defender at first base, with the kind of left-handed swing that could deliver a lot of home runs at PNC Park.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres signed with Cleveland for $150,000 out of Colombia in July 2016 and was traded to St. Louis two years later in a three-player deal that sent Oscar Mercado the other way. A promising hitter in the domestic complex leagues in 2018, the right-handed slugger struggled out of the gate with a jump to Class A Peoria in 2019 and moved back down to Rookie-level Johnson City, where he hit .286/.391/.527 in 33 games to end his age-19 season. Following the canceled 2020 season, Torres was pushed to Peoria (then a High-A club), got off to a solid start and faded down the stretch to finish with a .238/.302/.366 line and six homers in 97 games. Standing in at a listed 6-foot-4, Torres shows the most promise as a potential power bat with good raw pop, bat speed and natural strength out of his large frame. Those same long levers have caused him some issues in trying to sync up an approach at the plate, and he struggled with chasing pitches outside of the zone in 2021, causing even lackluster power numbers. The Cardinals maintain that Torres’ discipline could improve with more exposure to full-season pitching, and the lost pandemic year could have interrupted that necessary experience. Torres has been primarily a right fielder for much of his pro career because of just average speed, and he has the arm to play out there. He picked up six outfield assists from right in 2021 and nine in total across all three spots on the grass. While Torres will still only be 22 for the entire 2022 season, his position as a corner outfielder raises the need for him to start hitting more regularly and turning that raw power into in-game performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres impressed with Colombia’s 15-and-under national team in the Pan-American Championships and signed with the Indians for $150,000 in 2016. However, his prospect stock started to elevate in 2018 with a strong performance in the Rookie-level Arizona League. The Cardinals noticed the impressive stateside debut and acquired Torres and Conner Capel that July in exchange for Oscar Mercado. Torres raked during a short stint in the Gulf Coast League to finish 2018 and was rewarded with an aggressive assignment to begin 2019, though he didn’t fare well initially and was bumped down a level, where he got back on track. Torres got off to a fast start with High-A Peoria in 2021 and showed impressive strides in several areas of his offensive game. Torres, listed at 6-foot-4, has a projectable frame and enticing tools across the board. Bat speed and natural strength help generate power to all fields, though he sometimes has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone. He does show the ability to manage an at-bat and there is confidence that better plate discipline will come with time. While he has played all three outfield positions in his career, he profiles best in right field long term. There’s still plenty of room for growth, but he has the look of a future right fielder. The outfielder has limited experience in full-season ball and will need time to develop on both offense and defense, but the potential is there for Torres to become a regular contributor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vogel was one of the fastest and most athletic high schoolers in the 2020 Draft, he also came with concerns about his physicality (he was the lightest player selected at 165 pounds), swing and strong commitment to UCLA. That enabled the Dodgers to take the local Southern California product with the 100th overall choice and sign him for a well-over-slot $1,622,500. He spent most of his 2021 pro debut in Low-A, where he hit .231/.323/.339 with a 30 percent strikeout rate and 12 steals in 76 games. Vogel's best tool is his plus-plus speed and he ran the fastest 60-yard dash (6.15 seconds) at the 2019 Perfect Game National Showcase. He's a potentially dynamic basestealer and could become a plus defender in center field once he refines his reads and routes. His plus arm is stronger than most in center. Vogel had an awkward load in his right-handed stroke when he turned pro, and Los Angeles is trying to help him smooth it out with some mechanical changes. He has good hand-eye coordination and can display electric bat speed at times, but he must get stronger so he can impact the ball more regularly. He did add 15 pounds this offseason, though he'll also need to develop a more patient approach to get going at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vogel was one of the better athletes in the 2020 Draft, he lasted until the third round because he lacked physicality (he was the lightest player selected at 165 pounds), missed a lot of the summer showcase circuit with a back injury and had a strong commitment to UCLA. The Dodgers pounced on the Southern California prep product with the 100th overall pick and signed him for a well over-slot $1,622,500. He was the youngest player (age 18) at their alternate site during the summer and performed well in instructional league. Vogel ran the fastest 60-yard dash (6.15 seconds) at the 2019 Perfect Game National Showcase and consistently displays plus-plus speed. He uses his quickness to create chaos on the bases and cover a lot of ground in center field, where his instincts could make him a plus defender. He also has a plus arm, stronger than most in center, and can play anywhere in the outfield. Vogel has both offensive upside and work to do at the plate. In addition to his quickness, which should help him get on base, he also can flash some electric bat speed and shows feel for recognizing pitches. He has an awkward load in his right-handed swing that can lead to swings and misses, however, so Los Angeles will try to smooth out his stroke and get him to drive the ball more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
