mlb_pipeline.text: While the Angels have been garnering a reputation of acquiring premium athletes in the early rounds of the Draft, they've also been busy bringing similar players via the international market. At the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, they double-dipped in the Bahamas, signing a pair of outfielders: Trent Deveaux for $1.2 million and Knowles for $850,000. It's been Knowles who broke out of the gate during his pro debut in 2018, earning a promotion from the Arizona to the Pioneer League. Throughout his first summer of pro ball, Knowles showed a solid approach from both sides of the plate, with excellent bat speed. There's emerging power, though it only showed up from the left side during his debut. He's not afraid to draw walks and could be a plus hitter as he continues to refine his approach, perhaps eventually with average big league pop. Knowles has plus speed and loves to use it, though he'll have to learn the nuances of basestealing. The Angels exposed the teenager to all three outfield spots, and he should have the range to play center field and enough arm to man right. Some of that might depend on how he continues to develop as he hopes to join prospects like Jazz Chisholm of the D-backs and the Rays' Lucius Fox in putting Bahamanian baseball more firmly on the map.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prior to the 2018 Draft, the earliest a player from Texas A&M-Corpus Christi had been drafted was the ninth round. Hernandez's path to easily beating that hasn't necessarily been straight. He was academically ineligible as a sophomore, but then came out and showed very good stuff early in the spring. While he wasn't as dominant all year, it was still enough for the Angels to take him in the third round and he went straight to the Class A Advanced California League for his full-season debut. Hernandez was up to 98 mph at times during his junior season, sitting more in the 92-95 mph range, throwing the pitch with good sink and showing he could maintain his velocity through starts. He has good feel for his secondary stuff and can throw a distinct curve and slider, though they sometimes blur together into a power slurve. He can really spin it and his breaking stuff does flash plus and he has solid tumbling changeup. Though he has swing-and-miss stuff, Hernandez didn't dominate in college as much as one would think, as he has trouble commanding his pitches both within and outside the strike zone. With a funky delivery, he might best be suited for the bullpen, but he was given a chance to start at the start of his pro career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery is never thought of as a positive achievement, despite it becoming almost commonplace among young pitchers these days. But there might be a silver lining in having needed the surgery in 2018 for Aquino, the 6-foot-6 right-hander who got $100,000 to sign in Dec. 2016. Yes, he missed development time on the mound by being out for all of 2018, but the strength and conditioning that went along with rehabbing the injury could help him take a big step when he returns to the mound. Before Aquino went down with injury, he had already improved strength-wise enough to add velocity to his fastball. What was a 90-91 mph heater when he first signed was touching 96 mph at instructs in the fall of 2017 with excellent spin and riding life. He's filled out even more now, so dreaming about more velocity once he gets his feet under him isn't unrealistic. He can really spin his breaking ball, giving him the chance for a second plus pitch, and he'll continue to work on what could be a decent changeup. With his size, Aquino will have to work at repeating his delivery. He'll get a chance to do that as he puts his rehab in the rearview mirror and hopefully gets a full season of work in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers selected West Orange High (Winter Garden, Fla.) infielders in consecutive drafts, Kole Enright in the third round in 2016 and Seise in the first round in 2017. While Enright has struggled to get going offensively, Seise has exhibited some of the highest upside in the system since signing for $2 million as the 29th overall pick. But he missed all of 2018 after hurting his throwing shoulder and having rotator-cuff surgery, then played just 21 games this year before injuring his left shoulder sliding into a base and requiring season-ending labrum surgery. With Seise's size, bat speed and developing strength, he has more power than the typical shortstop. To get the most out of his power potential and hit for average, he'll have to improve his plate discipline and guard against his right-handed swing getting too long. He has the plus speed and aggressive mindset to steal bases. Assuming his arm bounces back, Seise has all the tools to remain at shortstop. He's quick, has soft hands and displayed plus arm strength in the past. He also has a good internal clock that helps him make plays, and his athleticism should give him the versatility to play almost anywhere on the diamond if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If there was a candidate for a pitching prospect in the Braves organization who needed a full 2020 season the most, it might’ve been De La Cruz. Signed for just $55,000 in June 2015, De La Cruz’s light really didn’t turn on until 2019, when he pitched his way across three levels of the system, with most of his time spent in Double-A, to earn a spot on the 40-man roster. Though he didn’t get the chance to build off of his breakout, he threw well enough at the Braves’ alternate training site to earn two separate callups to the big leagues in 2020, though he didn’t appear in a game. There’s no question about the right-hander’s pure stuff. De La Cruz will consistently hit 97-98 mph and he’s flirted with triple digits. His slider can be a nasty offering and is consistently an above-average pitch and he does have decent feel for his changeup, giving him an effective three-pitch mix, something that will have to continue to improve if he wants to continue starting, or at least face lefties in high-leverage situations. While his walk rate did improve in 2019, there are questions remaining about whether De La Cruz can harness his big stuff enough and find the strike zone consistently enough to land a spot in a rotation. He’s trending toward a future in the bullpen, where his fastball-slider combination could be downright filthy, though he’ll likely get the chance to pitch multiple innings in the short-term so he can keep working on all of his pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ball’s home run power started showing up during his sophomore season at North Iowa Community College in 2018 and he brought the pop with him when he transferred to Dallas Baptist. His 18 homers last spring made the Braves take a chance in the 24th round and go above pick value to sign him for $197,500. He rewarded the organization’s faith by hitting 17 more homers and finishing with a 1.023 OPS while reaching full-season ball in his pro debut. The Braves think they might have a steal in Ball, who has the chance to hit for average and power. The left-handed hitter has tremendous hand-eye coordination at the plate and a good idea of the strike zone, which helps him tap into his ridiculous raw power. The ball doesn’t typically carry in either Danville or Rome, his home parks during his debut, and he made them seem small. He makes consistent hard contact and generally kept his strikeouts low, though the K rate did go up a bit when he made it to the South Atlantic League. He’s not going to scare anyone on the bases, but he’s more athletic than you might think, given his 6-foot-6 frame, and runs decently underway. Ball is limited to first base and he has work to do there, with some stiff actions defensively. He has good hands and some arm strength, though he’s working to improve his throwing mechanics so he can get to average there. It’s his power bat, though, that has the Braves excited and thinking they have a Day 3 Draft steal on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 After three years pitching out of the University of Alabama bullpen, Burrows left as the school's career leader in saves with 30. Seeing him as a future left-handed big league reliever, the Mariners took him in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft. He spent just one summer with Seattle as he was sent to the Braves in January 2017, along with Luiz Gohara in return for Mallex Smith and Shae Simmons. He reached Double-A in 2018, his second season in the organization, then capped things off in the Arizona Fall League. Burrows' calling card is his breaking ball, and it's a real weapon against left-handed hitters but nasty enough to miss right-handed bats as well. He throws it with deception with late, sharp break, and hitters don't see it. It's the main reason why he carries a 12.2 K/9 ratio into the 2019 season. His fastball sits in the low-90s coming from a low three-quarters slot, allowing it to play up beyond the velocity. Burrows' progress has been slowed a bit by a lack of consistency and command, though it's clear his two-pitch mix is plenty to get big league hitters out. At the very least, he's a left-handed specialist. At the top end, he's a seventh-inning type reliever, with an Eric O'Flaherty career path.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 28 on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects for the 2018-19 signing period, Valdez, with his big body and power potential, was viewed by scouts as one of the more physically advanced players in his class. Targeting exactly that type of prospect, the Mets inked the then-16-year-old Dominican outfielder for $1.45 million on July 2. Listed at 6-foot-3, 212 pounds, Valdez is already a physical specimen and still has plenty of room left to grow into his frame. His bat is his carrying tool, with tremendous raw power that already shows up in games at times. In the past, he's been overly aggressive and pull-happy, leading to some swing-and-miss issues, but scouts were pleased with how he improved his overall approach this past year. He's solid athletically, earning at least average grades as a runner, and the Mets view him as a pure center fielder that should stay up the middle. Earning high praise for his makeup, scouts like the way Valdez competes and his joy for the game. That should help him deal with the long road ahead through the Mets' Minor League system, with enough offensive potential to carry him to Citi Field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cate worked primarily as a starter in all three of his years at UConn, and he left the program as the all-time leader in strikeouts with 270 in 210 2/3 innings, ahead of Major Leaguers Anthony Kay (263) and Matt Barnes (247). Despite his size at 6-foot and past Tommy John surgery from high school, the Nationals liked his breaking stuff enough to take him in the second round in 2018. He rewarded that confidence as the organization’s 2019 Minor League Pitcher of the Year, with a 3.07 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 139 K’s in 143 2/3 innings across two Class A levels. He was an alternate-site participant in 2020. Any discussion of Cate has to start with the curveball. It’s a true plus pitch with a hammer-like drop, and he commands it well for a pitch with that much movement. The velocity on his fastball typically averaged around 89 mph but can touch a few ticks higher, making it an average offering. The changeup developed enough at the alternate site that it’s a good third option at this point. Cate uses that three-pitch mix to get ground balls at an impressive rate – a valuable skill in the age of the launch angle – and he throws plenty of strikes, having walked only 5.5 percent of his batters faced in 2019. Cate’s size and lack of plus velocity do not scream dominant starter who must stick in the rotation, but his stuff is such that he could be able to face batters multiple times in a single outing at the top level. Even if he can’t stick as a back-end starter, a multi-inning reliever role isn’t out of the question.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mendoza was a highly regarded prospect in the 2016 Draft, but a strong commitment to Florida State led to him being taken by the Tigers in the 36th round. Three years later, after batting .298 with 31 homers and 124 RBIs in 160 games with the Seminoles, he became the Nationals’ third-round pick and signed for above slot value. A successful pro debut at Class A Hagerstown came next, with Mendoza flashing his power potential while making a smooth transition as a first baseman. As a 6-foot-5, 230-pound left-handed hitter, it is easy to dream on Mendoza’s potential at the plate. He gets good leverage in his swing and knows how to impact the baseball, showing plus raw power that should improve as he adds strength. He is still figuring out how to get to that power consistently, though, with swing-and-miss issues and a passive approach currently holding him back. Though he does work his share of walks, the Nationals would like to see him be more aggressive early in the count, viewing it as key for unlocking both his hitting ability and power. Mendoza’s defense at the hot corner with the Seminoles drew mixed reviews from scouts, with most of the concerns stemming from his size and actions. The Nationals immediately moved him to first base in pro ball and have been pleased with the early results, noting that his feet and hands both work well there. They may still offer him reps at third base, where his above-average arm fits well, but their hopeful that Mendoza’s bat will flourish now that he no longer has to focus on improving defensively at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dyson was viewed as potential first-round pick going into his junior year at Florida before some early struggles cost him a spot in the Gators’ rotation. His stuff was impressive even when he struggled, though, and he pitched with more velocity while working in shorter bursts in relief. The Nationals saw untapped potential and value in Dyson as a potential starter and went nearly $150,000 over slot value to sign him after selecting him in the fifth round. He rewarded the organization with a strong debut, posting a 1.14 ERA over eight starts at Class A Short Season Auburn. Dyson’s plus fastball carried over into pro ball as the Nationals hoped it would, with the right-hander sitting in the mid-90s and locating it well in the New York-Penn League. Dyson’s heater jumps on hitters due to his clean arm action and easy delivery, though it can be hittable when he misses his spot due to a lack of movement. Dyson’s slider lacks depth but should be an average pitch once developed, and he’ll need to make similar gains with a changeup that currently is below average. Though the Nationals think Dyson can remain a starter and were encouraged by his strong pro, club officials also acknowledge that the 6-foot-3 righty has some major hurdles to clear in his development. If that doesn’t work, Dyson has the type of stuff that could play up in shorter bursts in relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roederer drew Andrew Bentinendi comparisons as a California high school senior in 2018, but also injured his non-throwing shoulder and had a UCLA commitment, so he was available to Chicago at the 77th overall pick. Signed for an over-slot $1.2 million, he endured a rough first full pro season because low Class A pitchers quickly exploited his aggressiveness by throwing him changeups. He made some progress in the final six weeks but has barely played since then, because the coronavirus pandemic cancelled the 2020 Minor League season and he injured his throwing elbow this May, requiring Tommy John surgery. The key for Roederer will be to understand who he is as a hitter. With a smooth left-handed swing, bat speed and the ability to work counts, he could hit .280-.300 with 20-25 homers on an annual basis. He won't reach that potential, however, unless he stops worrying about launching balls to his pull side, develops a gap-to-gap approach and does a better job recognizing offspeed pitches. Roederer is an asset on the bases with solid speed, good instincts and an aggressive nature. The Cubs believe his high baseball IQ gives him the chance to remain in center field, though he'll have to shift to a corner if he loses any quickness as he adds muscle. His arm strength graded as fringy before his elbow reconstruction and is better suited for left field than right.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 One of 15 players signed by the Padres for at least $300,000 during the 2017-18 international period, Santana quickly emerged as San Diego's most promising prospect from the class. A natural shortstop who also projects well at the plate, he garnered Dominican Summer League All-Star honors during his pro debut and then broke out offensively in the 2019 Rookie-level Arizona League, slashing .346/.429/.494 at age 18. The Cubs grabbed him and three other prospects along with Zach Davies in a December trade that cost them Yu Darvish and Victor Caratini. Santana’s selectively aggressive approach is advanced for a player his age, and he has already shown that he can do damage on pitches in the zone. He has a solid foundation for development, possessing a blend of bat speed, patience and feel for the barrel, with remaining physical projection that points toward future power gains. Santana has proven difficult to strike out early in his career, showing a penchant for quality opposite-field contact. Defensively, Santana looks like a future big league shortstop: he’s twitchy and athletic, with smooth actions, plus arm strength and plenty of range, and he already plays the position with confidence. Those qualities all give Santana realistic floor value in the big leagues, and there’s everyday-shortstop upside in the profile should his hitting ability and power both reach fruition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs not only corralled 2019's best high school catching prospect in Ethan Hearn, but also snagged the top international catching prospect in Quintero. A Venezuelan, he signed for $2.9 million, the largest bonus Chicago ever has given an international amateur. The previous record was $2.8 million in 2013 for Eloy Jimenez, one of the game's premier young sluggers (albeit now with the White Sox). Quintero has a lofty offensive ceiling as well. His bat speed and strength give him plus raw power from the left side of the plate, and he already shows some ability to knock the ball out of the park to the opposite field. More than just a slugger, he has good feel for hitting and could offer production similar to that of Willson Contreras if he reaches his potential. Quintero has solid-to-plus arm strength with a quick transfer, and he also exhibits strong leadership skills. In order to remain behind the plate, he'll need to clean up his receiving, but he's also 17 years old and time is on his side. His below-average speed makes him faster than most catchers, though he could slow down as he fills out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top pitcher in Louisville's 2016 recruiting class, McAvene succumbed to Tommy John surgery in April of his freshman year and returned to the mound 12 months later. He became the Cardinals' closer in 2019 and boosted his Draft stock when his velocity surged during the team's postseason run to the College World Series. Though he hadn't started a game since 2017, the Cubs immediately moved him to the rotation after signing him in the third round. After spending most of his junior season operating at 93-96 mph with riding life on his four-seam fastball, McAvene started hitting 98s and 99s in the NCAA tournament and kept doing so in short starts during his pro debut. His breaking ball shows signs of becoming a plus pitch, combining slider velocity with curveball depth. Now that he's a starter, one of his primary focuses will be to develop his nascent changeup. McAvene has a strong, durable 6-foot-3 frame and is throwing more strikes as he puts elbow reconstruction further behind him. Chicago believes he's equipped to stay in the rotation and plans to develop him alongside 2019 fourth-rounder Chris Clarke, another college closer turned starter. Should he return to the bullpen, McAvene could move quickly and eventually claim a high-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts flock to the Excellence Tournament in Puerto Rico every year to get the chance to see the top talent the island has to offer prior to the Draft. Contreras, a middle infielder with some present hitting skills, was the only player to hit homer in this year's event. Big and strong, Contreras has more present strength than some of his fellow Puerto Rican infielders in the class. When he keeps his swing under control, he can drive the ball. He has serious raw power, especially to the pull side, but has the tendency to lose his mechanics and get out of control trying to show off that power. A solid runner when underway, there is some question over whether he has the range to stick at shortstop, though most teams would send him out at the spot and see if he can stick there. He has a plus arm and good enough hands for the position. If Contreras does slow down as he matures, he still has a future on the dirt, perhaps as an offensive second baseman. Some scouts think he'll hit enough to profile at third base, reminding some of an Asdrubal Cabrera type. He'll head to San Jacinto Junior College if the Draft doesn't work out for him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With his selection by the Brewers with the No. 73 overall pick in the 2018 Draft, Bello became the first Hawaiian high school positional player to be taken in the top five rounds since 2013. He signed for $550,000, forgoing his commitment to St. Mary's, then made his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Bello makes consistent contact with a simple swing that enables him to use the whole field and leads scouts to project him as an average hitter. Adding strength should help bring out some of the extra-base potential in Bello's swing, but his game power likely will always be below-average. He has the kind of speed to steal bases and cover a lot of ground in the outfield, with the chance to be an above-average defender eventually, and a plus arm to boot. Bello's bat and above-average speed could one day have him hitting atop a lineup. Being able to stay in center field adds value to his overall profile, as Bello lacks the power potential expected from corner outfielders at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dallas Baptist University has churned out a ton of professional talent over the years, with Ben Zobrist clearly the most successful big league alum in school history, and even had two second-round picks in the 2020 Draft. But only one player, right-hander Vic Black, has been drafted earlier in the June Draft than Hannah, taken No. 50 overall by the A’s in the second round of the 2018 Draft. Since then, the talented outfielder has had to forward his address twice, going to the Reds at the 2019 Trade Deadline in the Tanner Roark deal, then heading to the Rockies along with Robert Stephenson in return for Jeff Hoffman and Case Williams last November. Hannah does have some offensive upside from the left side of the plate. There’s bat speed and the ability to make hard contact, with more gap-to-gap than over-the-fence pop. He’s shown an ability to work counts and take walks, though his approach wasn’t as solid during his first full year. While he’ll record plus run times, Hannah has yet to learn how to use that speed to steal bases. He has shown that his speed plays in the outfield, with a chance to play center field because of how much ground he can cover. He’s seen time at all three outfield spots as a pro, with perhaps a floor as a valuable fourth outfielder. But with a fringy arm, Hannah's best chance at an everyday spot would likely be in center or left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Locey teamed with Jake Fromm to help Houston County High (Warner Robins, Ga.) win the Georgia state 5-A baseball championship as a senior in 2016. Both headed to the University of Georgia, where Fromm starred at quarterback while Locey emerged as a key starter on a Bulldogs team that won a school-record 21 Southeastern Conference games in 2019. While there's debate as to whether he winds up as a starter or reliever in the long run, there's no question that his arm was among the best in college baseball's top conference. That arm was part of the package the Rockies acquired as part of the return for Nolan Arenado in early February. A big right-hander who works from a high-three-quarters slot to create angle to the plate, Locey operates at 94-96 mph and can touch 98 mph with his fastball, He maintains his velocity throughout his starts and figures to hit 100 mph if he works shorter stints out of the bullpen. His low-80s slider can be sharp and a solid pitch when he commands it, and he also shows promising shape on a curveball that's a work in progress. As a power pitcher, Locey didn’t have much need for a changeup in college. Locey is strong and physical, though to remain a starter he'll have to do a better job of repeating his delivery and commanding his pitches. If he does become a reliever, he has late-inning potential and perhaps a chance to become a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As one of the more projectable prep right-handers in the 2019 Draft, Williams intrigued the Dodgers, but the Blue Jays beat them to him in the second round and signed him for an over-slot $1,547,500. Los Angeles got him a year later as the first of two players to be named (outfielder Ryan Noda was the other) in an August deal for Ross Stripling. He logged 16 innings in his 2019 pro debut and spent time at the Dodgers' alternate site and instructional league last year. Williams deals at 91-94 mph and peaks at 96 mph with his fastball while using his 6-foot-6 frame and high three-quarters delivery to create a downhill plane that's tough on hitters. Scouts prefer his upper-70s downer curveball over his harder slider, though he made progress with the latter during instructs. He's also gaining confidence in his changeup, which features some tumble and fade. Williams' velocity was up a bit in instructional league and could continue to grow as he matures physically. He has good body control for a pitcher so young and tall, which should help him repeat his delivery, throw strikes and stay healthy. The Dodgers have been working with him to quicken his tempo and make better use of his athleticism.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lake Travis High (Austin, Texas) had two premium prospects last spring in Brett Baty, the 12th overall pick by the Mets, and Lewis, who went in the second round -- just like his father Jimmy did with the Astros in 1991. The younger Lewis missed the state playoffs with what was believed to be a lat strain but was diagnosed as a partially torn labrum in his shoulder during a pre-signing physical. The Dodgers still signed him for an above-slot $1,097,500 and put his debut on hold. Lewis already demonstrates the ability to carry a low-90s fastball deep into games while topping out at 95 mph, and he should add velocity as he adds strength to his lanky 6-foot-6 frame. He could have a pair of plus pitches if he can develop more consistency with his upper-70s downer curveball. He has some feel for a changeup but didn't have much need for it as an amateur. Lewis's athleticism and strength should help him throw strikes and pile up innings. He has a fairly simple delivery for a tall youngster, using his size and high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill plane. He also intrigued scouts with his hitting ability and power potential, and he might have played both ways had he gone to Louisiana State rather than turning pro.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Largely on the strength of what they considered an advanced bat, the Dodgers gave Estevez a $6 million bonus and paid a matching amount as a penalty for exceeding their international bonus pool in November 2015. They promoted him aggressively, starting the Cuban defector in low Class A at age 18 and promoting him to high Class A at 19, and he showed little consistency at the plate for most of his first three pro seasons. He seemed to turn a corner when he batted .340/.418/.547 in the final six weeks of 2018, finishing the year as the high Class A California League leader in runs (87) and doubles (43). Estevez has an unorthodox batting style in which his lower half tends to leak out while his shoulders remain square to the ball. During his late-season tear, he was more patient and hammered balls from gap to gap instead of trying to pull everything to left field. With his efficient right-handed stroke and advanced pitch-recognition skills, he could become a .275 hitter with 15 or more homers per year if he can maintain a disciplined approach. Estevez's quick hands and internal clock have helped him survive at shortstop, his primary position in two years in high Class A, but it will be a stretch for him to play there regularly in the Majors. His speed and arm are fringy and better suited for second base, where he can be an average defender. His lack of arm strength restricts his utility value, putting pressure on him to hit enough to become a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2009, the Giants used a fifth-round pick on a college first baseman whose hitting ability and plate discipline stood out more than his power, finding a long-term starter in Brandon Belt. They see similar traits in Wyatt, who replaced two-way star Brandon McKay (the No. 4 overall pick in 2017) at first base at Louisville and ranked third in NCAA Division I in walks in each of his two seasons as a starter, including a school-record 72 in 2019. Signed for a well-below-slot $997,500 in the second round last June, he reached low Class A in his pro debut. Wyatt has a sound left-handed swing, good feel for hitting and an extremely patient approach that borders on passive at times. His strength gives him at least solid raw power and 20-homer potential, but he won't tap into it unless he attacks more pitches and drives them in the air more often. After he produced a lot of rolled-over, weak ground-ball contact in his debut, San Francisco is trying to help him become more aggressive while still maintaining his discipline. Wyatt is a better athlete than his well-below-average speed might suggest. He moves well enough at first base, displaying soft hands and decent arm strength. Some evaluators who scouted him as an amateur thought he might be able to handle playing some left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Merryweather pitched at Skyline College for two years before transferring to Oklahoma Baptist, where he dominated as both a junior and senior while leading the program to a third-place finish in the 2014 NAIA World Series. A fifth-round pick by the Indians that June, Merryweather made slow but steady progress early in his career before breaking out in 2016 with an All-Star campaign in the Class A Advanced Carolina League that earned him a second-half promotion to Double-A Akron. He performed well in his return to Akron in 2017, but struggled over 16 starts in his first exposure at the Triple-A level. Impressed with his stuff and progress, Cleveland added Merryweather to its 40-man roster after the season. However, the right-hander will miss all of 2018 following his Tommy John surgery in mid-March. Merryweather pitches with a plus fastball that sits at 93-96 mph and at times touches higher, all while using his height to create downhill plane to the plate and generate ground-ball outs. He throws a pair of breaking balls in a curveball and a slider, though neither is particularly advanced and they bleed together at times. Merryweather's changeup is arguably his best secondary offering, flashing above average at times, but lacking in consistency overall. Though big and physical, Merryweather repeats his delivery well and has a long track record as a strike-thrower. He will, however, need to improve his fastball command as well as the quality of his strikes after International League hitters tagged him for 105 hits (12.5 H/9) and 13 home runs (1.5 HR/9) in 78 innings. Should Merryweather be unable to make the necessary adjustments to remain a starter, the right-hander's power arm could make him an effective late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox rated Bush as a fifth-round talent in the 2018 Draft, but his commitment to Mississippi State clouded his signability and they figured they had filled their quota of pricey prep third basemen when they picked Lency Delgado in the fourth round. When Bush kept sliding, Chicago determined it could close a deal for sixth-round money and signed him for $290,000 in the 33rd round. He opened his pro debut by going 19-for-43 (.442) in the Rookie-level Arizona League and finished it by posting a 1.518 OPS in the Rookie-level Pioneer League playoffs as Great Falls won the championship. Bush already is a physical presence as a teenager and has plenty of strength and bat speed in his right-handed swing. He has a disciplined approach, working counts and using the entire field, but he needs to add some loft to his stroke because too much of his hard contact last summer came in the form of ground balls. If he can make the necessary adjustments, he could become a .280 hitter with 20 or more homers per season. Mostly a shortstop in high school, Bush became a full-time third baseman after turning pro. He has enough arm strength for the hot corner but needs to clean up his footwork and the accuracy of his throws. Some scouts believe he's destined to wind up at an outfield corner, and he runs well enough to possibly develop into an average left or right fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green pitched out of the bullpen during his first three years Southeastern Louisiana before sliding into the starting rotation as a senior in 2018 and showing improved pitchability and control in the new role. The D-backs saw untapped potential in Green as a starter and made him their 14th-round pick in June, signing the right-hander for just $5,000. He impressed during his pro debut that summer, earning All-Star honors as a reliever in the Pioneer League, then opened his first full season as a starter in the Class A Advanced California League. He dominated the hitter-friendly league, going 9-1 with 1 .73 ERA over his first 14 starts to earn a Double-A promotion in July. Green’s calling card is a low- to mid-90s bowling-ball sinker that helps him induce ground balls at an elite rate. After posting a near 68-percent ground-all rate in his pro debut, he led all Minor League hurlers (120 IP min.) in that department in 2019 by inducing grounders at a 67.2-percent clip. Green’s downer curveball is consistently an average or better pitch, and he also throws a slider that has cutter action. A mid-80s changeup gives the right-hander a third usable pitch, though it is behind both of his breaking balls. He issued 1.7 walks-per-nine in 2019, exhibiting above-average control and command. Beyond the effectiveness of his stuff, Green stands out for his stamina and durability. He worked at least five innings in all 22 starts in 2019, averaging better than 5 2/3 innings per turn. Though he did struggle a bit in Double-A (4.28 ERA, .318 BAA) as he attempted to mix his pitches more, the D-backs believe it was a valuable learning experience that will aid him going forward. Green has all the ingredients to become a big league starter, perhaps even a No. 4 if he can trade some of those grounders for a few more strikeouts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green starred at three Knoxville (Tenn.) high schools in four years before the Yankees drafted him in 2018's third round, signing him away from a Vanderbilt commitment with an above-slot $997,500 bonus. His demanding pregame routine often left him worn out during his lackluster pro debut, but he paced himself better and ranked eighth in steals (10) and ninth in extra-base hits (24) in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019. Known for putting on impressive batting-practice displays on the prep showcase circuit, Green generates well-above-average raw power from the right side of the plate with his bat speed and strength. He did a better job of driving the ball in the air during his second pro season after his pull-happy approach led to a slew of rolled-over grounders in his debut. While he has some patience at the plate, he lapses into swinging for the fences and will need to make more consistent contact. Green shows average speed out of the batter's box, is quicker once he gets going and runs the bases aggressively. After spending most of his first pro season in center field, he played much of his second on the corners. He fits best in right field and has the arm for the position, having reached 93 mph with his fastball and backing it up with a hard curveball while pitching in high school.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a Nova Scotia high schooler, Sanford drew no scouting or recruiting interest and his only college offer was to play volleyball at Dalhousie University in his home province. He walked on at McCook (Neb.) CC, where he hit 23 homers in two years with wood bats, then transferred to Western Kentucky in 2019 and won the first regular-season triple crown in Conference USA history. After he went undrafted the previous three years, the Yankees made him a third-round pick. One of the best power prospects in the 2019 Draft, Sanford creates well-above-average raw pop with plenty of bat speed, strength and leverage in his 6-foot-2, 215-pound frame. Some scouts worry about the deep load in his left-handed swing and his tendency to get off balance at the plate, though New York believes his hand-eye coordination and quick stroke can make it work. He struck out in 33 percent of his plate appearances while batting .238/.289/.411 in his pro debut at short-season Staten Island, so he has adjustments to make. In addition to his big power, Sanford features plus speed and can flash even faster running times, though he's not much of a basestealer. A first baseman in junior college, he made a nice transition to right field at Western Kentucky. The Yankees deployed him in center field to see how his quickness played there during his first pro summer, and his fringy arm strength likely will land him in left field if he shifts back to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians rated Sanquintin as one of the five best prospects on the 2018 international market and paid him accordingly, signing him for $1.25 million out of the Dominican Republic. Compared to Cleveland's other top signing from last summer, Venezuelan shortstop Gabriel Rodriguez, he's a little less polished as a hitter but might have a bit more raw power. Sanquintin is stronger and more physical than the typical teenaged middle infielder, and he has impressive bat speed from both sides of the plate. He's aggressive and his power plays to all fields, though he may need to temper his approach somewhat to succeed against pro pitching. An average runner, he won't be a huge factor on the bases. Sanquintin possesses the quickness, hands and arm to play shortstop, though that could change if he loses a step as he matures physically. His bat and defensive tools would profile well at third base, his most likely destination. The Indians also may try him at second base and some scouts project him as a right fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reyes ranked 23rd on MLB Pipeline’s international prospect list, having impressed scouts with his physicality and power potential, before the Tigers signed him in July 2018. He hit .331 with seven homers, 48 RBIs and an .887 OPS in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 before his stateside debut in 2020 was canceled due to the COVID shutdown of the Minor League season. He spent the summer adding strength to his frame and reported to the Tigers’ Florida instructional league in good shape. Reyes moves well at shortstop and on the bases for a relatively big player, though any further growth could bump him over to third. He combines an advanced approach with plus bat speed to barrel pitches in the zone, which should translate to more power as he continues to physically mature. He has reliable hands and a strong arm at short. While he runs well, Reyes is likely to lose a step with physical maturation. Beyond the physical tools, Reyes shows competitiveness and intensity in the field. He opened his 2021 season in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tigers general manager Al Avila and LSU head coach Paul Mainieri worked together three decades ago at St. Thomas University in Miami. When Hess had an up-and-down junior season, bouncing between the rotation and bullpen, Detroit saw him fall down draft boards and selected him in the seventh round of the 2019 MLB Draft, believing he could be a solid reliever. After dominating NY-Penn League hitters, his midsummer jump to Class A West Michigan flashed the potential the Tigers believed they could tap, including 22 strikeouts over 21 innings. The combination of Hess’ 6-foot-6 frame and a projectable power fastball tantalized scouts, even if the statistics didn’t back it up. Though Hess started for most of his collegiate career, he was more effective out of bullpen, including a dominant freshman season. His fastball plays more solidly into the mid-90s in shorter stints, pairing with a slider that works in the low to mid-80s with darting movement. He has a changeup but neither needs nor uses it much in relief stints. While his tall frame creates leverage, command has been a challenge throughout his career, including 11 walks at West Michigan. Like former University of Miami closer Bryan Garcia a few years earlier, the Tigers drafted Hess hoping his college experience would allow him to move quickly through the system and reach Detroit sooner than expected. Garcia moved from West Michigan to Triple-A Toledo in his first full pro season; the Tigers would love to see Hess do the same, giving them a middle relief or setup option in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals took a chance on Haake in the sixth round of the 2018 Draft after the right-hander’s up-and-down college career, which included three different colleges in as many years. Haake responded by being one of biggest surprises of the class when he posted a 2.85 ERA over 18 starts in Class A in 2019. His only 2020 action came during the Royals’ fall instructional program at Kauffman Stadium. Haake dominates with a plus fastball that sits in the mid-90s. It’s a deceptive pitch thanks to his 6-foot-4 frame and features a ton of movement. His changeup plays well off that deception, and the pitch comes in with splitter action. The fastball-changeup combo helps Haake get whiffs from hitters on both sides of the plate and he rounds out his arsenal with an average slider that can flash plus. Haake sometimes struggles with repeating his delivery, and that has led to control issues that he needs to shore up to be successful. Haake missed two months with shoulder issues in 2019 and missed another six weeks with an injury for High-A Quad Cities during the 2021 season. The Royals had hopes he could have made Double-A at least by now, so it’s an open question how much Haake’s health will further hold him back in 2022 and beyond. The stuff, which Kansas City is not concerned about, could work in a relief setting, especially if he squeezes out even more velocity in short spurts. That might be the best role for the right-hander to get him going for good.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rijo was a modest signing by the Yankees, getting $50,000 back in July 2015 to begin his pro career. He's moved incrementally, from the Dominican Summer League in 2016 to two levels of rookie ball in 2017-18. He had made one start in the short-season New York-Penn League in late July when he was included in the package sent to the Twins in return for big league veteran Lance Lynn. A control-over-stuff right-hander, Rijo fills up the strike zone with his three-pitch mix. His fastball typically sits in the 91-92 mph range, but can reach back for 95 mph every once in a while. He throws his average curveball in the mid-70s and mixes in what will be an average changeup. He has a good feel for the pitch, but there isn't enough separation velocity-wise between it and his fastball. Pitching to contact, Rijo is efficient on the mound and can pitch deep into games as a result. Once a bit overweight, Rijo has gotten into better shape and maintains his conditioning well. He gets high marks for his makeup and intangibles, which could help him reach his ceiling as a back-end big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Daniels' loud tools stood out much more than his performance in his first two years in college, when he batted .176 with a 38-percent strikeout rate at Tennessee and .168 with a 44-percent whiff rate in the wood-bat Cape Cod League. He did an about-face to hit .357/.478/.750 with 13 extra-base hits in 17 games as a junior in 2020, though scouts still weren't completely sure what to make of him because the shortened season ended before he could prove himself in Southeastern Conference play. He became one of the highest-ceilinged players in the Houston system after signing for $400,000 as a fourth-rounder. Daniels wowed the Astros during instructional league, where he generated impressive exit velocities and displayed the best speed among position players in camp. The ball makes a different sound coming off his bat and he has well above-average raw power, but he still has to show he can erase a history of swinging through hittable fastballs and struggling against breaking balls and changeups. He spent the fall trying to simplify his right-handed swing, starting his hands higher to shorten his first move and elevate more balls. With speed that draws well above-average grades from some evaluators, Daniels could be at least at 20-20 player if he figures things out at the plate. Though he spent much of his final season in college at DH, he has the quickness to stick in center field as a pro if he improves his reads and routes. He has average arm strength and can play all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers intended to sign Torres for $7,500 out of the Dominican Republic in August 2015 until an age discrepancy killed the deal and landed him on MLB's ineligible list for a year. When he finally turned pro with the Astros for $150,000 in April 2018, he was already 22 years and eight months old, but he made up for lost time by dominating in his U.S. debut in 2019. He also pitched well in the Arizona Fall League that offseason and in Summer Camp and at Houston's alternate site in 2020, though his year ended when he was shut down with a sore elbow in August and he had arthroscopic surgery in July 2021 to remove bone chips from the joint. Torres operates at 94-98 mph and tops out at 100 with high spin rates on his four-seam fastball, showing the ability to keep that velocity for five or six innings per start. If hitters try to sit on his heater, he can make them look bad with a mid-80s slider that peaks at 90 mph. As a contrast to his pair of power pitches, he'll use a changeup that shows some signs of becoming an average third offering. Torres entered his age-25 season with just 135 2/3 innings of pro experience and little track record of throwing strikes. He's not physical and has trouble repeating his delivery, so he may not develop the command required to be a starter. Given his age and lack of finesse, it may be best to just let him try to overpower hitters as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a pitcher in his first two seasons at Gonzaga, Jones didn't become a full-time starter at first base until he was a senior in 2016, when he set a school record and placed second in NCAA Division I with 27 doubles. Signed for $2,500 in the 19th round that June, he didn't start to realize his power potential until he slammed 18 homers in Double-A in 2018. He encored with 22 more last year while enhancing his versatility in Triple-A. Though Jones has plenty of strength and leverage in his 6-foot-7 frame, he only began tapping into his power once he did a better job of staying back on pitches and stopped diving so much at the plate. He's driving the ball in the air more often and to all fields. While his size results in a naturally long right-handed swing, he does a good job of making contact and draws walks with a patient approach. Part of a Washington state 4-A basketball championship team at Kentwood High -- where his baseball teammates included future big leaguers Reese McGuire and Austin Voth -- Jones is athletic for his size. He's a below-average runner but not a baseclogger, and he's a quality defender with a strong arm at first base. He also can provide adequate defense on the outfield corners and looked fine in his initial exposure to third base in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic for $1.8 million last July, Lorenzo received the largest bonus the Astros have given an international amateur position player since they paid since-traded Gilberto Celestino $2.25 million in 2015. Though he had one of the more advanced bats among middle infielders in the 2019 international crop, he'll likely make his debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2020 and come to the United States at age 18 the next summer. A switch-hitter, Lorenzo has a compact swing from both sides that is built for hitting line drives to all fields. While he's a hit-over-power guy, his bat speed and feel for the barrel could produce 12-15 homers per season once he matures physically. He manages the strike zone better than most youngsters. Lorenzo will flash plus speed on occasion but is more of a solid runner who could slow down as he fills out. Scouts aren't completely sold that he'll stay at shortstop, though his instincts and strong, accurate arm give him a good chance. He's capable of playing second and third base, and his bat could profile at both spots if he develops more power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A closer at Cal State Fullerton, Conine had more saves (25) than walks (19) in three college seasons. The Astros made him a tandem starter almost immediately after drafting him in the 11th round in 2018, and they have been pleased with the results. He posted the best K/BB ratio (4.6) and second-best ERA (2.20) in the system last year while advancing to Double-A in his first full pro season. Conine is throwing harder as a pro starter than he did as a college reliever, though his fastball still has average velocity (90-96 mph) with ordinary life. The key to his success has been the development of his changeup as a legitimate weapon with deception, fade and two-plane depth. He also has good feel for spinning two distinct breaking balls, an upper-70s downer curveball and a tighter slider in the low 80s. Conine thrives as a finesse right-hander because he can locate his pitches where he wants. He can't throw his fastball by hitters but can command it to both sides of the plate, and the depth on his offerings creates weak ground-ball contact. Efficient and durable, he could fit toward the back of a rotation or in a multi-inning relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hansen was primarily a reliever at Oklahoma, leading the Sooners with nine saves in 2018 before signing with the Astros as an eighth-rounder. Houston incorporated him into its tandem-starter program during his first full pro season, with impressive results. He fashioned a 33 2/3-inning scoreless streak early in '19 and finished with a 2.11 ERA with a .159 opponents' average and 128 strikeouts in 94 innings between two Class A stops. Despite his relative inexperience as a starter, Hansen has enough pitches for the role. He has a quick arm that produces fastballs that park at 92-95 mph and top out at 97 with some running life. His best secondary offering is a sweeping low-80s slider, and both his upper-70s downer curveball and his changeup show flashes of becoming solid options. While Hansen has improved his fastball velocity and the quality of his secondary pitches since turning pro, he still may be destined for the bullpen. His control and command are shaky and his walk rate has risen as he has climbed through the Minors, increasing to 5.5 per nine innings once he reached high Class A. He lacks physicality and there's some effort in his delivery, so he's probably best served by working shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lopez lacked physicality as a skinny 5-foot-11 right-hander in Venezuela, but the Astros liked his arm speed and polish enough to sign him for $300,000 in 2017. He made an impressive U.S. debut in 2019, compiling a 1.41 ERA, .140 opponent average and 61 strikeouts in 51 innings between Rookie and short-season ball. Other teams already have started asking about him in trade talks. Lopez's most impressive trait is his ability to spin the ball, resulting in a downer curveball in the upper 70s and a tight slider in the low 80s. He already works at 92-95 mph with his four-seam fastball, though he has less projection remaining than a typical teenager. He also shows some feel for a fading changeup. Though he has four pitches and doesn't feature much effort in his delivery, he faces an uphill battle to remain a starter. His size and long arm action make it more likely he winds up in the bullpen. He's still young, so for now Houston will keep feeding him innings so he can work on refining his repertoire and improving his control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fifth-round pick out of a Virginia high school in 2017, Perry spent most of his first two pro seasons in Rookie ball before breaking out in the New York-Penn League in 2019. He finished second in the short-season circuit in homers and won MVP honors at the New York-Penn all-star game, where he went deep in his lone at-bat. He was slated to finally make his full-season debut in 2020 before the coronavirus pandemic wiped out the Minor League season. Perry stands out with his strength and plus raw power, most of which comes to his pull side. He has a short left-handed stroke with natural loft and enjoyed more success once he realized he didn't need to sell out for home runs. He still needs to make more consistent contact, but he's willing to work counts and draw walks. While Perry shared time behind the plate in the New York-Penn League, that was in deference to 2019 first-rounder Korey Lee, and the Astros believe he can stick at catcher. He has improved as a receiver since turning pro and does a nice job of framing pitches, though he can look a bit stiff at times. He has average arm strength, a quick transfer and makes accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 The sixth overall pick in the 2017 Draft by the A’s out of North Davidson High School in North Carolina, Beck positioned himself as a top-10 pick following a strong pre-Draft workout that continued his positive trend that started with an impressive senior season. Progressing nicely through the Minors in 2018, he remained stuck in the Class A Advanced California League in 2019. Beck did not receive an invite to the club’s alternate training site last year. Beck has struggled to live up to the high expectations that were placed on him. His combination of a strikeout rate over 34 percent in 2019 and inconsistent power in games at the pro level has hindered him at the High-A level. But the A’s still believe they have a good player in Beck, it’s just a matter of figuring it all out. He does have premium bat speed and worked hard on calming down in the box with the confidence that if he can make more contact, the power will naturally come. Although it doesn’t necessarily show up in the stolen base numbers, Beck has very good speed. It helps him play strong defense in center field, a spot where he has also shown a solid arm. He’s still young, and there are still some tools he’s working to unlock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former multi-sport star from the Rhode Island high school ranks, Reed showed off his raw tools and athleticism in spurts during three years at the University of Florida. The Padres liked his very high ceiling enough to take him in the second round of the 2016 Draft. Following a rough first full season, Reed broke out in 2018, played in the Futures Game and advanced to Double-A. His struggles there carried over to his 2019 season back in the Texas League and he wasn’t protected from, nor was he selected in, the Rule 5 Draft. He was then sent to the A’s as the player to be named later for Jurickson Profar. The A’s are hoping a change of scenery, some new instructors and new ideas might be just what is needed to unlock Reed’s treasure trove of raw tools more consistently. The switch-hitter can make loud contact and drive the ball from both sides of the plate, though his right-handed swing is a bit better. He had changed his swing path to be shorter to the ball with more extension, leading to his breakout to start 2018, but his strikeout rate soared once he got to Double-A. Reed’s speed is close to top of the scale and he’s a major basestealing threat, swiping 51 bags in 2018. It also helps him cover a ton of ground in the outfield, where he’s a plus defender in center and has an arm that works really well in the corners. He still has 20-20 potential if he can refine his approach enough to make more contact with his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Eierman’s impressive sophomore season at Missouri State, which included 23 home runs and 17 stolen bases, he struggled a bit the following year, which led to him dropping to the second round to the A’s in the 2018 Draft. He flashed some tools at Class A Advanced Stockton with 13 homers and 11 stolen bases, though strikeouts were an issue as he struck out in 32 percent of his plate appearances. Eierman’s power generated from his right-handed swing is often negated by his inconsistency in making contact. He has tinkered with his stance, but his timing sometimes remains off. However, Eierman did show progress in his pitch recognition during the instructional league, something the A’s hope can help him regain some confidence. Oakland believes part of Eierman’s struggles in recent years has been the result of putting too much pressure on himself. He’s worked hard to become a plus defender as a shortstop and should be able to stick at the position. Eierman will look for a bounce-back year in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At nearly 22, Jimenez was ancient by international standards when he signed with the Blue Jays out of the Dominican Republic in 2015. He didn't do much to distinguish himself until the second half of 2019, when he logged a 1.87 ERA with 46 strikeouts in 33 2/3 innings in his first taste of Double-A. When Toronto opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster in November, the Giants nabbed him in the Rule 5 Draft a month later. He was sent back to the Blue Jays last August and was once again left unprotected, leading to the A’s taking him in the 2020 edtion of the Rule 5. Jimenez can overpower hitters with his fastball, which parks at 94-96 mph, peaks at 98 and features above-average spin rates and riding life. He also misses bats with a low-80s slider with two-plane break. He uses a changeup with similar velocity to keep left-handers in check. Jimenez uses his 6-foot-3 frame and high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill angle on his pitches. Though he has three effective pitches and throws strikes, he has been a full-time reliever since 2018 and he should remain in that role. The A’s must keep him on their active big league roster throughout 2021 and can't send him to the Minors without placing him on waivers and offering him back to the Jays for half of his $100,000 draft price.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Romero spent four seasons pitching in Cuba, mostly as a reliever, before he left in the hopes of landing a job in the United States. The A’s signed him for $350,000 in February 2017, and once they could get him to the United States that season, he pitched his way up to the California League. He closed for that Stockton team to start 2019 and earned a bump up to Double-A, then leapt to Triple-A in 2019, where he was considered for a callup to bolster the big league bullpen in September. The A’s opted not to recall Romero because they felt he was lacking in some of the intangibles, like holding runners on and fielding his position, that would get exposed at the highest level. Stuff-wise, there’s no question he’s just about ready to get big league hitters out. He can miss bats with both his fastball and his breaking ball. He’ll throw his heater up to 98 mph and is consistently in the 95-98 mph range. He complements it with a breaking ball he calls a slider, but is a bit more slurvy, thrown 86-89 mph with more tilt than a typical slider. Romero has the right mentality for the back end of a bullpen, going right after hitters without any fear. While he did improve his strike-throwing as 2019 went on, he can get out of whack with his delivery, leading to a spike in his walk rate. He’s worked on the little things that held him back and should contribute to the big league bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels have come to be known as an organization that covets premium athletes. Top prospects in the system like Jo Adell and Jordyn Adams prove that point. Holmes, who was known as William English when the Angels drafted him in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft out of the Detroit high school ranks and signed him for $700,000, belongs in the conversation of best athletes with the Angels. A legitimate two-way player, Holmes did some exciting things both on the mound and at the plate across two levels of rookie ball in his second pro summer in 2019. Holmes continues to add strength to his 6-foot-2 frame and is a physical specimen. As a hitter, he had very competitive at-bats in the Arizona and Pioneer Leagues last year, showing patience at the plate and the ability to make hard contact and drive the ball. On the mound, he was even more impressive. While his control is still below average, the Angels aren’t overly concerned because of his age and lack of experience. He showed he could overpower hitters with a potential three-pitch mix. During the regular season, he averaged 93 mph with his fastball and touched 97. He was up to 98 mph at instructs and his strength gains could mean more consistent velocity is on its way. His changeup took a big step forward and flashed plus and he can mix in a fringe average curve. Holmes is on this list more because of his arm than his bat, but the Angels plan to let him continue to do both in 2020. He’ll develop as a starting pitcher for now and hit between his pitching routines. His development might take a bit longer as a result, but the wait could very well be worth it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Arol Vera and Adrian Placencia received seven-figure bonuses as shortstops at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, Bonilla wasn’t too far behind. The Dominican received $600,000 to sign and was the one of the three to get his professional career officially started, performing well over 20 games in the Dominican Summer League. Bonilla has the chance to really hit. It was a small sample size in the DSL, but he showed off an advanced approach at the plate, limiting strikeouts and drawing walks. There’s extra-base authority for the right-handed hitter now, more to his pull side, and there’s a chance he could eventually be an above average hitter with at least average power. Not known for his speed, Bonilla does have a plus arm and will get the chance to play shortstop for the immediate future. He did get some time at third base during his debut, and given the potential of him being a bit thicker-framed as he matures, the hot corner could end up being his long-term defensive home. That might put more pressure on his bat, but it looks like he might have the tools to profile well at the infield corner spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brady went from his high school in southern New Jersey to East Carolina University, but after not seeing much mound time as a freshman in 2016, he returned to the Garden State and Mercer Community College. A standout season there in 2017 landed him in the seventh round with the Angels. Some arm issues slowed him early on in his career -- he amassed just 144 2/3 innings over his first two-plus seasons, but he’s healthy now and would have been ready to go for a full 2020 season had it transpired. The 6-foot-1 right-hander has a three-pitch mix and an idea of what to do with it, giving him some starting pitcher qualities. His fastball sits in the 92-93 mph range, and he can reach back for 95 mph on occasion. Depending on who sees him and how he’s throwing it, Brady has either a hard curve or a slider, and a decent slurvy breaking ball that he has a good feel to spin while adding to and subtracting from it. He’ll mix in a changeup that flashes average as well. Despite not having wow stuff, Brady has done a nice job of missing bats while filling up the strike zone fairly consistently. The lack of an out pitch or premium velocity kept him off the radar enough to not be selected in the 2020 Rule 5 Draft, even though he was left unprotected. After a solid showing at instructs this fall, the Angels are intrigued to see what Brady can do in a full healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Expectations for a college senior reliever taken in the 23rd round of the Draft are understandably low, so Delaplane flew under the radar after coming out of Eastern Michigan. While he spent his first full season in the Midwest League, his 15.1 K/9 ratio certainly opened some eyes. When he reached and dominated Double-A in 2019, then did the same in the Arizona Fall League, it seemed fairly clear that he had the stuff to be a successful big league reliever. Delaplane goes after hitters with a nasty two-pitch mix. His fastball typically sits in the 94-96 mph range with outstanding life when he's healthy, and he does an excellent job of throwing it by hitters up in the zone. His slider has become an absolutely nasty out pitch, one that had the second highest swing-and-miss rates for a slider of anyone in baseball. It’s a hard, short downer breaking ball that was up to 87 mph in the AFL. The right-handed reliever throws everything from the same arm slot, with hitters clearly never seeing the breaking ball coming out of his hand, which led to his high strikeout rates wherever he’s been, including an astounding 16.9 per nine rate in the AFL. His command has been an issue at times but it improved in Double-A and the Fall League, adding confidence he’ll be able to pitch late in games at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two years at the University of Georgia, Elliott pitched as a reliver and a swingman. He got a chance to be a part of the Bulldogs’ rotation as a junior and had a breakthrough season, establishing himself as the best midweek starter in the nation. The Mariners were hunting college pitching in the 2019 Draft and made Elliott the fifth of five college arms they took to kick things off, signing him for a below-slot $400,000 and sending him out for a solid pro debut in the short-season Northwest League. Elliott was a lean 6-foot-1, 170 pounds when he began his college career, but was up to 200 lbs by the time he began his pro career, allowing his stuff to play up. He throws his fastball in the 89-94 mph range and showed he can maintain that velocity deep into starts. He does a nice job mixing in three secondary offerings. His changeup is the best of the lot, an above-average offspeed pitch, and he makes good use of his average slider and even his fringy curve. Command has been an issue for Elliott at times, though he did much better in the strike-throwing department as a starter during his junior year. If he can continue that, with his repertoire, he has the chance to eventually develop into a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter at California Baptist University, Rinehart pitched well in relief in the Cape Cod League and continued to impress out of the bullpen in his professional debut. After the Mariners grabbed the right-hander in the 16th-round of the 2019 Draft, he pitched his way to full-season ball, where he posted a 3.52 ERA over 10 appearances. Listed at 6-foot-3, 185 pounds, Rinehart showed up to Spring Training in exceptional shape and appeared ready to put together a breakout campaign. Of course, COVID-19 shut down the 2020 Minor League season so Rinehart didn’t get a chance to compete against other organizations, but he did impress at Seattle’s alternate site. The right-hander throws his fastball in the 94-96 mph range and complements it with a trio of secondary offerings. Rinehart has plus control of a changeup that he throws in the upper 70s, a stark separation from his fastball, and also throws both a sweeping slider and a downer curveball that is used as an out pitch early in counts. Rinehart has thrown strikes as a pro, but the improved velocity and usage of the zone has helped him miss more bats. While the Mariners plan to let him start for now, he needs to continue to refine his breaking stuff to remain in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017 Cape Cod League MVP, Jenista's strong summer likely helped his stock avoid falling too much after an uneven junior season at Wichita State, as he landed in the second round with the Braves. He did make it to Double-A and the Arizona Fall League in his first full year of pro ball, but didn’t swing the bat very well and didn’t get any official reps in 2020. The power showed up a bit more in 2021, though he wasn't added to the Braves' 40-man roster in the offseason. There is some juice in Jenista’s left-handed bat, but there are questions as to whether he’ll be able to get to it at the highest level. The power has shown up at times, including hitting 19 homers in a tough hitters' park in 2021. But while he does draw some walks, the swing-and-miss is a real concern, as he has struck out in more than 32 percent of his plate appearances in his first two full seasons of pro ball. Jenista runs well enough for his size and has the athleticism and arm strength needed to play right field well. He saw time at first base in the AFL to close out 2019 and continued to do so in 2021. In the end, though, it will be Jenista’s ability to unlock his offensive potential that will determine his future value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last catcher from the Southern Indiana to make it to the big leagues was Kevin Brown, a Rangers second-round pick who spent parts of seven seasons in the Majors as a backup. His son Logan followed in his footsteps to USI, starting for the Division II school for two years and eventually being taken in the 35th round by the Braves in 2018. The defensive-minded backstop was a South Atlantic League All-Star and earned a promotion up to the Florida State League in his first full season of pro ball. While Brown hit well in Rome, it’s still his defense that stands out. He has excellent catch and throw skills, throwing out 40 percent of potential basestealers in 2019. He also receives very well and gets high marks for his game-calling, working with pitchers and leadership behind the plate. The left-handed hitter makes a ton of contact, though he doesn’t walk a ton, and hasn’t shown much ability to impact the baseball. The Braves think there’s more bat to come, which would help him develop into a very good glove-first backup catcher at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It is somewhat unbelievable to think that Newton is entering only his age-22 season, given the way the clock has already ticked on his professional career. Signed for $50,000 out of the Netherlands in July 2015, Newton spent two seasons playing in the Dominican Summer League before jumping stateside with Rookie Advanced Kingsport in 2018. The switch-hitter truly popped onto the prospect radar at that stop with burgeoning power, a .408 on-base percentage and an .857 OPS. The bat came back down, however, at Class A Columbia where he hit just .209 and struck out in 32.9 percent of his plate appearances. As such, Newton wasn’t added to the 40-man when he was first eligible, and he was left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft last fall as well. He went unselected on both occasions. Any chance to prove his worth in 2021 was ended early when Newton injured his left shoulder while diving for a ball at Low-A St. Lucie in mid-June. He is expected to miss the rest of the season. Despite that inability to crack the roster, Newton retains some prospect stature because of his fielding capabilities on the infield. Even at 6-foot-4, he isn’t too tall for shortstop given that he covers adequate ground and shows good hands. His above-average arm also helps his case at the six, and it helped him move around the infield in 2019 when Ronny Mauricio and Mark Vientos both needed time at short. The bat will be an issue. Newton shows good bat speed, and his power will show up in the cage. But his inability to manage the strike zone and recognize pitches brings down the entire profile. The glove and power give the Mets hope that Newton won’t be lost in the shuffle as he works more into his 20s. A utility infielder role in the Majors is a possibility, but there will have to be more contact from both sides to make even that a likelihood.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gilliam threw to current Reds backstop Tyler Stephenson as his high-school catcher before moving on to Clemson in 2016. He became a full-time reliever as a sophomore and was the Tigers' closer in his junior season, finishing with 11 saves, a 1.41 ERA and 54 strikeouts in 38 1/3 innings. The Mets selected him in the fifth round of the 2018 Draft and signed the right-hander for $550,000, well above the $379,400 assigned to the slot. He climbed three levels in his first full season the following year but saw some a stumble at Triple-A that the Mets chalked up to his quick ascent more than anything. At 5-foot-10, Gilliam doesn’t fit the stereotypical look of a dominant reliever, but the stuff matches the profile. The fastball comes in comfortably at the mid-90s with good spin. The curveball features good sharpness in the upper 70s and is a swing-and-miss power pitch of its own. He started throwing a more horizontal breaking ball in a slider/cutter this past spring. The changeup is little more than a show-me pitch at this stage, and it’s unlikely he’ll need it to be much more, given the other stuff. Control has been an issue for him in both the college and pro ranks. The right-hander has a tendency to speed up and get out of his delivery when he goes too high-effort, leading to walks or just missed command. Gilliam was off to a rough start in 2021 at Double-A Binghamton but showed signs of a turnaround in June and July before things fell off a cliff again. He went on the injured list on July 24 for an elbow issue that required ulnar nerve relocation surgery, the same procedure Jacob deGrom underwent in late 2016. Because it’s not Tommy John, there is hope that Gilliam can return next spring and get back to what has made him such a promising relief prospect. He’ll be entering his age-26 season then, so the clock is ticking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 A high school lefty from Georgia, Lindow’s uptick in velocity as a senior likely helped him go from sure-fire Alabama-Birmingham student to a fifth-round pick in the 2017 Draft, signing for $500,000, a bit over slot. His feel for pitching has been very effective at the lower levels of the Minors, with Lindow winning Phillies Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors after pitching across two levels of Class-A ball in 2019. He didn’t pitch at the alternate training site or instructs in 2020. Lindow’s stuff is largely average, at best, across the board, starting with a fastball that touches 92 mph. The velocity might be a bit below-average, but the spin rate up in the zone allows it to play up. He throws his above-average changeup with good deception and fade and he has a pair of breaking balls, with a curve that hits the mid-70s a touch ahead of his low-80s slider that has cutter action to it. All four of the 6-foot-3 southpaw’s pitches play up because he’s an extreme strike-thrower who really knows how to read swings and hitters’ tendencies. He has a bulldog mentality on the mound and goes right after those hitters’ weaknesses, giving him the chance to pitch in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, the Phillies handed out a $2.5 million bonus to shortstop Luis Garcia. Six months later, and at the other end of the bonus spectrum, they inked Martinez for $10,000.
