Martinez put up pedestrian numbers in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and while he pitched sparingly in his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League in 2019, he created some buzz with his size, stuff and upside potential. The 6-foot-2 left-hander is lanky and loose and has a legitimate three-pitch mix at his disposal. He can throw his fastball in the 91-96 mph range, throwing it with good late life. His slider has the chance to be a true out pitch, and he has surprisingly good feel for his changeup at a young age, selling it well with good arm speed. Martinez has shown the ability to throw strikes with a clean, easy and relatively effortless delivery that also provides some deception, with an idea of how to mix his pitches. It’s been a very small sample size of performance thus far, but scouts are excited to see what he can do with more time on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals landed a pair of promising 16-year-old Dominican outfielders at the outset of the 2018-19 international period, signing Marte and Jeremy De La Rosa for $300,000 apiece -- the maximum amount allowed without incurring a penalty -- on July 2. Though both players flashed a collection of intriguing tools during the pro debuts in the 2019 Dominican Summer League, it was Marte who led the team in home runs (tied, 5), slugging (.448) and total bases (94) at age 17, and he was one of Washington’s most impressive prospects during fall instructional camp in 2020. Marte possesses a blend of athleticism and physicality that has already earned him comparisons to an NFL running back. His projectable frame is ideal for adding more strength, and club officials do not expect those physical gains to detract from the plus speed that also enables Marte to play a quality center field. The Nationals believe he has a chance to remain at the position long-term, but his strong arm would more than suffice if he’s forced to move to an outfield corner. Marte’s development as a hitter will be key in unlocking his overall potential. He can do damage from the right side of the plate, combining strength and bat speed into an explosive swing, and Marte already showcases plus raw power to his pull side that should begin to play to all fields more consistently as he gains experience. Marte’s approach and pitch selection will both require considerable refinement (as is the case with most teenage hitters), but the raw ingredients are all there for him to become an impact talent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schaller flashed a low-90s fastball as an Indiana high schooler in 2016, but he went undrafted because he battled injuries during his senior year and was strongly committed to Vanderbilt. He missed all of his first year with the Commodores following Tommy John surgery and worked just 24 2/3 innings during the regular season in 2018, albeit while hitting 98 mph with his fastball as a rare Draft-eligible redshirt freshman. Intrigued by Schaller’s untapped potential and low-mileage arm, the Nationals made him their third-round pick that June and have developed him as a starter in pro ball. Schaller was sidelined with an oblique injury for most of the first half and didn’t take the mound for Class A Hagerstown until late June. When he finally did, the big-bodied right-hander flashed impressive stuff, sitting 93-95 mph with his fastball and complementing it with a high-spin breaking ball and a changeup that flashed above-average at times. Schaller needs to develop his secondary offerings and refine his control, and the Nationals believe starting offers the best platform for those improvements. He likely will end up in the bullpen as a hard-throwing reliever – a role in which he’s sat 95-98 mph in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star out of the high school ranks in Ohio who played wide receiver at football powerhouse St. Edward outside of Cleveland, Wainwright could have headed to college on the gridiron but committed to Ohio State for baseball. Wainwright wasn’t as strong on the Draft radar because an injury (fractured tibia) had interfered with much of his summer showcase work before his senior year. The team he was supposed to play for at East Coast Pro Showcase was run by Reds scouts, and the relationship they forged with the young outfielder, not to mention a return to health that fall and before the shutdown this spring, gave the Reds confidence to take Wainwright in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft and sign him for full pick value. After signing, Wainwright stood out with his all-around tools and work ethic in his introduction to the club at instructs. He’s strong with an athletic frame, and while it might take some time for his tools to sharpen given his dual-sport focus and living in a cold-weather state, there are some serious skills that show up now. He has excellent bat speed and solid raw power, though he’ll need some reps to learn to catch up to premium velocity and recognize breaking stuff. While he’s not a burner, Wainwright does run well and provides a solid arm to go along with strong defense. He’s a center fielder now and could be given the chance to stay up the middle, though some evaluators feel he’ll outgrow the position and end up in a corner spot, where he could eventually develop into a prototypical athletic run-producing right fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 For the first time since 2016, the Reds were allowed to spend more than $300,000 on a player on the international market. So they were thrilled when they were able to ink Triana out of Cuba for $1.3 million on July 2, 2019, the first day international players could sign with teams. He did not go to an affiliate but the 20-year-old spent the rest of the summer working out at the organization’s complex in the Dominican Republic. A big kid at 6-foot-3 and 230 pounds, Triana has big raw power and a handsy swing. Although still very projectable, he has good hitting tools that scouts can dream on, leaving most to believe he’ll hit enough for that raw pop to show up in games consistently. Considered below average defensively, Triana could develop into a serviceable fielder that won’t be a liability. With his size, first base could wind up being the best fit. But he was taken because he can hit for power and if he does that, the Reds will find a spot for Triana.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Going on four years since he signed to an above-slot bonus of $2,352,000 in 2017 after the Brewers took him with the No. 34 pick, Lutz opened 2021 as an enigma. His baseball card numbers are solid if not eye-opening, including a .742 OPS with 13 homers as a 19-year-old at Low-A in 2018, and 13 more homers en route to a .754 OPS at Class A Advanced in 2019. It’s how Lutz got to those numbers that give the Brewers optimism. He has been traditionally an extreme slow starter who came around after April turned to May, the weather began to warm and Lutz locked in his timing. He took his lumps against older pitchers at the Brewers’ alternate site in 2020, especially early in the summer, and was invited to his first big league Spring Training in 2021. Athletic and strong, Lutz could have four average or better tools when all is said and done -- perhaps five if his bat comes around. His right-handed power is his calling card and he can get to it during games, though he remains pull-heavy. He has some of the biggest power in the entire system, and there is even more to access if Lutz learns to cover the outer half of the plate and cleans up some mechanical issues in his swing. On pitches over the inner half of home plate, he does consistent damage. The Brewers have experimented with moving Lutz around the batter’s box and laud his relatively advanced approach to hitting from a young age. He is also a hard worker who tends to be tough on himself during those moments of struggle. Lutz gets the most out of his average speed, running the bases well and showing better-than-expected range in center field. Most scouts continue to peg him as a future right fielder on account of his strong, accurate arm. He has been challenged at Double-A in 2021, flirting with the Mendoza line for much of the summer, and that has dinged his profile. A fractured hand suffered on a hit-by-pitch didn’t help matters either. At just 22 years old, time remains on Lutz’s side to get back on track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star at Teurlings Catholic High (Lafayette, La.), Cantrelle led his school’s baseball team to the state 4-A championships as a junior and senior and drew college football interest as a quarterback. After turning down the Yankees as a 40th-rounder in 2017, he became an immediate starter at Louisiana-Lafayette and was one of just six NCAA Division I players to total as many as 25 extra-base hits and 25 steals in 2019. That and a strong Cape Cod League performance put him in position to go in the top two rounds, but he batted just .148 during the shortened 2020 season and dropped to the Brewers in the fifth round and signed for $300,000. After picking up summer at-bats in the City of Champions Cup, a pop-up league in Joliet, Ill., Brewers coaches first saw Cantrelle in person during the fall instructional league. He sparked some comparisons to Scooter Gennett, with less power than Gennett at the moment and better defensive skills, with a similar ability to square up the baseball foul line to foul line. Second base is probably Cantrelle’s best position, but he has the quickness, solid arm and baseball IQ to play above-average there. He was primarily at the keystone with High-A Wisconsin in 2021 prior to an August promotion to Double-A Biloxi. Despite his pre-Draft slump, Cantrelle has the potential to hit near the top of a batting order. A switch-hitter who impacts the ball with more authority from the left side, he posted a .315 average with wood bats on the Cape, has a knack for getting on base and possesses plus speed and savvy on the bases. He has some sneaky pop with 15-homer upside, but he's better off when he worries less about power and more about making consistent contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in the 2018-19 international class, Parra was also one of its more physically advanced prospects, showing a promising mix of strength and hitting ability as a Venezuelan amateur. The Brewers signed him for $210,000 on Aug. 30, 2018, Parra’s 16th birthday, and he rewarded the organization by having a successful 2019 pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he was nearly two years younger than the circuit’s average player. Listed at 6-foot-2, 184 pounds, Parra has present strength and plenty of room still to grow into his projectable frame. He has impressive natural hitting ability for a young player, with an impactful right-handed swing that already yields hard contact as well as raw power. Parra’s swing can get long at times, resulting in some and miss, though the Brewers think that will be less of an issue once the teenager adds strength and has more experience under his belt. He split time between second and third base in his pro debut but profiles better at the latter position, where his plus arm and below-average speed are fits. Parra offered an early glimpse of his offensive potential when he went 5-for-5 with two home runs, two doubles and five RBIs in his third game as a professional. He improved as the season unfolded, batting .329/.451/.573 with 19 RBIs in July, and finished the year with 23 extra-base hits and a .770 OPS in 65 games. The Brewers are understandably excited about the 17-year-old’s bat and view him as someone who could one day hit in the middle of a lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dillard led all national high school players with 16 homers as a senior in 2016 -- finishing one ahead of Kyle Muller, who signed with the Braves for $2.5 million as a pitcher -- but went undrafted because he was strongly committed to Mississippi and lacked an obvious position. He continued to hit for power in the Southeastern Conference, and after compiling a .286/.419/.505 line with 31 homers in three years with the Rebels, he became the Brewers’ fifth-round pick in the 2019 Draft. In 2020, Milwaukee pushed Dillard’s defensive development by assigning him to its alternate training site, where he caught a mix of top pitching prospects and more established Major Leaguers. A switch-hitter who earned Kyle Schwarber comparisons for his blend of power and patience at Mississippi, Dillard generates impressive raw pop by combining bat speed and strength with a lofty swing. The Brewers think Dillard also will hit for average because of an advanced feel for the strike zone, with club officials citing the gains he made in his approach and contact rate throughout college as reasons to be optimistic. Though his speed is below average, Dillard is surprisingly aggressive on the bases and picks his spots to steal. The 2020 season was supposed to give the Brewers a gauge on whether Dillard could stick at catcher so as to maximize his offensive value. Dillard saw brief time behind the plate this summer but has played primarily at first base. He did hit enough at High-A to earn a midseason promotion to Double-A, but there will now be even more emphasis on his bat since it looks like he’ll be sticking to the cold corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates spread out their international bonus pool money during the 2018-19 signing period, handing out a total of 17 six-figure bonuses. Mojica’s $390,000 bonus was the fifth-largest of the group, but he made the most noise in his professional debut in the Domincan Summer League, finishing second in the league with an 1.048 OPS while not turning 17 until August. Mojica is strong and big-bodied -- think Vladimir Guerrero Jr. as a physical comparison -- with the chance to hit for both average and power. He has impressive bat-to-ball skills with a ton of impact, regularly registering exit velocities over 100 mph. He also walked more than he struck out and ended up with 23 extra-base hits in 55 games. He earned those because he’s a well below-average runner, one who’s going to have to maintain his conditioning. That’s even more important in terms of his ultimate defensive home. He has decent hands and a plus arm and moves well for his size right now, but he could easily end up having to move across the diamond to first. The Pirates feel the bat has a chance to be special, one that could profile just fine at first if he continues swinging it like he did in his pro debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starting his high school career in New York, Fletcher transferred to Maine and reclassified into the 2019 Draft, where the Cardinals selected him 58th overall. The second-round selection secured Fletcher’s status as the highest position player ever selected out of a Maine high school. (The Tigers’ eighth-round selection of Kurt Hall in 1977 previously held the record.) The Cardinals signed him for an above-slot bonus, which led Fletcher to forgo his Vanderbilt commitment and join the professional ranks, where he hit .244 with four homers over two levels of Rookie ball (43 games) in 2019 and then repeated the level in 2021. Fletcher’s raw tools are exciting, though they don’t always show up in games. He struck out in roughly 44 percent of his plate appearances in his professional debut, prompting the Cardinals to work with Fletcher on eliminating his big leg kick. While he needs to improve his contact rate, Fletcher does hit the ball hard and has plus power when he connects. Fletcher participated in St. Louis’ alternate training site during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic, which provided him with valuable reps against advanced pitchers. There’s 20-20 potential if everything goes well, but the tools haven’t translated to on-field production so far. A good athlete with plus speed, Fletcher has the tools -- including an arm that used to fire 93-mph fastballs from the mound -- to play center field, but needs to improve upon his reads and jumps to stay there long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of six players drafted out of Florida’s IMG Academy in 2019, Romeri went off the board in the 12th round, but signed for an above-slot $200,00, forgoing a commitment to Villanova. The outfielder showed flashes of power in his professional debut, finishing tied for third in the Rookie Gulf Coast League with six homers over 41 games. He also drove in 20 runs and slashed .246/.346/.464. Romeri has a decent all-around game, but the power is his carrying tool. He shows a good feel for the barrel and has consistently posted strong exit velocities as well. With a projectable 6-foot-3, 195-pound frame, the Cardinals believe he will be able to tap into more power as he matures. The power is impressive, but Romeri is still learning his swing and there’s room for improvement in his approach as he can get too pull happy and overly aggressive at times. He’s presently an average runner, but may lose a step as he fills out. A good athlete, Romeri profiles well in either corner outfield spot and takes good routes defensively. His arm, which touched 92 mph with his fastball in high school, is strong enough to handle right field. He could develop into a solid fourth outfielder, or perhaps an everyday player if his hit tools improves. The Cardinals have been pleased with his work ethic and the strides he’s made in the short time he’s been in the organization and view him as someone who has the potential to be a fast riser.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prater was part of a loaded weekend rotation for an Oklahoma squad that also featured 2020 first-round pick Cade Cavalli (Nationals) and fourth-rounder Dane Acker (A’s). However, Prater had the best ERA (3.42) of the bunch and struck out 33 in his 23 2/3 innings before the coronavirus pandemic halted the 2020 season and the Cardinals selected him with the 93rd overall pick (third round) that June. In a more complete sample size, the lefty was named to the 2019 All-Big 12 Second Team and led Sooners’ starters that year with 97 strikeouts and a 3.26 ERA in 80 innings. While there’s still room for growth, Prater did show an ability to miss bats in his professional debut, racking up 83 strikeouts over his first 52 1/3 innings in Low-A. A deceptive, crossfire delivery helps Prater’s stuff play up and makes him hard to hit. He throws his fastball with armside run in the low 90s and sits around 80 mph with his slider. He also throws a changeup around 80 mph that flashes plus, but isn’t always consistent. The development of that pitch, as well as his overall command, will likely go a long way into determining his future role. The Cardinals are giving Prater an opportunity to start as he begins his professional career and he’ll be able to remain there if he’s able to improve upon his control. His delivery features some effort, which may push Prater into a reliever role. He profiles well as a middle reliever and may ultimately wind up in the bullpen, depending on how he develops that third pitch. If he is able to put everything together, his ceiling is likely that of a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing both ways but struggling on the mound as a North Carolina State freshman, Mendoza focused on his bat and his play at third and put together a strong sophomore campaign that he furthered with standout summer in the Cape Cod League. While an inconsistent junior campaign caused him to last until the 11th round of the 2017 Draft, he did rebound to win the New York-Penn League batting title (.370) in his pro debut and then spent most of his first full season in Double-A before reaching Triple-A in the next. Mendoza was a standout at the Cardinals’ alternate training site in 2020. Mendoza has a knack for barreling the baseball from the right side of the plate with a line-drive swing that he controls well. He hits the ball to all fields, showing some extra-base pop but well-below-average over-the-fence power. Mendoza does have some strength, though, and he flashed sneaky power in his first full season. He’s a good athlete and fringy runner who earns high marks for his baserunning. Mendoza is an easy plus defender at third base and has the hands, footwork and arm strength needed to play anywhere on the infield. That includes shortstop, a position the Cardinals deployed him at more consistently with encouraging results in 2020. He also has seen time as a first baseman. Mendoza doesn’t have the power to fit the typical corner-infield offensive profile in the big leagues, but he does hit well enough to serve as a utility infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz received the second-highest bonus the Rockies gave out in the 2017-18 international signing period, behind Ezequiel Tovar, getting $750,000 to sign right when the period opened on July 2. The first Cuban player ever signed by the Rockies, Diaz spent two summers in the Dominican Summer League and one in the rookie-level Pioneer League hitting for average (.317 career average entering 2021) and stealing a lot of bases (104 in 126 games). The right-handed hitting infielder is a gamer who plays hard and at a high speed at all times. Outside of his speed, his tools don’t jump off the page, but he’s the kind of player who helps a team win games. He has a knack for contact and while he has a very aggressive approach, he doesn’t strike out much, though his K rate did go up a bit while his walk rate dropped with his move to the United States in 2019. He has added some strength, but will need more to impact the ball consistently, with a ceiling likely as a gap-to-gap doubles hitter rather than one who clears fences often. If Diaz is going to be a big league regular at one position, it’s likely going to be at second base, though he can handle shortstop as well. He likely profiles best as a super-utility guy who finds ways to help his team win from a number of positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55| Field: 55 | Overall: 40 With baseball bloodlines as the son of former big league infielder Benji Gil, who won the World Series with the Angels in 2002, Mateo Gil endeared himself to scouts with his advanced feel and overall knowledge of the game as an amateur. But a strong commitment to Texas Christian coupled with the fact that Gil lacked prototypical early-round tools led some to question whether he would be drafted high enough to sign. The Cardinals ended up taking Gil in the third round, then lured him away from his college commitment with an above-slot bonus of $900,000. It already looks like money well spent after Gil’s impressive age-18 campaign in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019, but it’ll now be the Rockies who benefit after they acquired him in the package for Nolan Arenado in February. Gil is solid in all facets of the game. He's a natural at shortstop, possessing smooth actions and excellent hands that enable him to make all the plays, as well as a quick first step and advanced instincts that give him range in all directions. The low-to-mid-90s fastball that helped Gil excel as his high school team's closer is also an asset for him as a shortstop, and he earns high marks for his throwing accuracy as well as his strong internal clock. He runs well but will never be much of a threat on the basepaths. The Cardinals saw untapped potential in Gil's right-handed bat when they drafted him, and he's already made significant gains as a hitter early in his career, showing sneaky power potential and a knack for barreling the baseball. And while the progress that Gil makes at the plate going forward will ultimately dictate his role and ceiling, his defense and contact skills give him a solid floor and could one day help him contribute in the big leagues in some capacity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best position player to come out of Loyola Marymount to date has to be Angels infielder David Fletcher, a sixth-round pick back in 2015. Three years later, it was Decolati’s turn to represent the Lions in the sixth round when the Rockies took him. After a very successful debut in 2018, a broken hand kept him out until June '19, and he wasn't able to match his production from the summer prior. Decolati might have been one of the players in the Rockies system to suffer the most from the shutdown as he needs reps to turn his athleticism into consistent performance. He was rusty during instructional league play, though it started to come together by the end of the fall. The right-handed hitter can make loud contact and has plenty of raw power, but his overly aggressive approach was exposed in 2019 and led to a high strikeout rate. With plus speed, Decolati can steal a base and cover a lot of ground in the outfield. He’s shown he can handle center field and his above-average arm works well from right field. He might settle in as a fourth outfielder type, but more than anything, he just needs to go out and play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a sophomore at UConn in 2018, Feole collected the second-most strikeouts in school history. When he followed that up with 11 shutout innings for USA Baseball's Collegiate National Team, he looked poised to be one of the more intriguing college lefties in the 2019 Draft class. But a forearm issue slowed him early as his velocity dipped, hurting his stock considerably, and he underwent Tommy John surgery in July after the Padres took him in the 11th round. After completing his rehab process, Feole appeared physically stronger and operated with better stuff when he returned to mound in San Diego’s fall instructional camp. At his best, Feole leans heavily on his fastball-curve combination. The former will sit in the low 90s and was touching higher during instructional league, while the breaking ball serves as his out pitch, flashing plus at times. Feole has a third-pitch changeup that is below average. An unorthodox delivery that includes a head snap makes it difficult for Feole to find the strike zone consistently and portends a full-time move to the bullpen, where his two-pitch repertoire could play up in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres’ fabled 2016-17 international spending spree is bearing fruit across the system, and they used the entirety of that window to haul in top-tier prospects. Case in point: Osvaldo Hernandez. The Friars inked the then-18-year-old to a $2.5 million contract out of Cuba in March 2017, three months before the window closed. Hernandez pitched at three different levels during his debut season, but his breakout came in ’18 at Class A Fort Wayne where he posted a 1.81 ERA, which would’ve led the Midwest League with a few more innings to qualify. Injuries prevented Hernandez from building upon that performance much in 2019, though he did pitch well in the California League during the second half before losing all of ’20 to the pandemic. Hernandez fits the mold of a crafty and deceptive southpaw, even if he doesn’t boast big-time velocity. His fastball sits in the low 90s but can reach the mid 90s. He’s got a put-away curveball, and he pairs it with a serviceable slider and changeup. What stands out most about Hernandez is his savvy on the mound. He constantly changes speeds and varies his delivery, and he routinely induces weak contact from opposing hitters. Hernandez is athletic, and he boasts an easy, smooth delivery. There’s no one trait that jumps off the page, but his creativity and pitchability could make him a solid middle-to-back-of-the-rotation starter in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivera declined to sign with the Giants as a 32nd-rounder after his freshman season at Wallace State-Hanceville (Ala.) CC, then became the second-highest drafted player in school history (Craig Kimbrel, third round, 2008) when San Francisco landed him in the fourth round for an above-slot $800,000 a year later. With their college connection and his ability to spin a nasty breaking ball that could make him a closer, Rivera has some parallels to Kimbrel. He worked just 94 innings in his first three years as a pro -- he was worn down in his debut, had a lower back strain in 2019 and the cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season restricted him to instructional league -- and missed the first three months of this season with shoulder issues. Rivera's curveball is a legitimate hammer with power in the low 80s, high spin rates and true 12-6 break. His fastball gives him a second plus pitch that touches 97 mph with electric cutting action, though he tends to command it better when he works around 92-93. He also flashes a solid changeup but lacks consistency with his third offering. While he has the upside of a No. 3 starter, Rivera has a long ways to go to get there. He has to prove he can stay healthy, refine his changeup and harness his fastball and curveball to throw more strikes. His stuff could be even nastier if he moves to the bullpen and just airs out his two main weapons in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts had a tough time getting an accurate read on Frechette, who sold out for power too often on the high school showcase circuit before coming down with mononucleosis during his 2019 senior season. He won the Giants over with an impressive pre-Draft workout at Oracle Park, sending multiple balls into McCovey Cove and drilling one off the top of the right-field foul pole. After signing for a well over-slot $797,500 in the fifth round, he batted .290/.364/.366 in Rookie ball. Frechette has the ingredients to hit for both average and power if he doesn't try to do too much at the plate. When he came back from mono, he used a shorter, smoother left-handed stroke and showed the ability to barrel balls consistently. His bat speed combines with the leverage and projectable strength in his 6-foot-3 frame to create considerable raw pop, though he needs to learn to let it come naturally. Frechette displays fringy speed out of the batter's box and is an average runner once he gets going. He moves well around the bag at first base and has decent arm strength. San Francisco plans on trying him in left field, though its outfield depth at the lower levels may make that difficult.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Missouri Valley Conference freshman and defensive player of the year in 2018, Glowenke finished fourth in the league in batting (.328) last spring and then hit .296 in the Cape Cod League. One of the better hitters among this year's college shortstops, he missed the first weekend of his junior year recovering from offseason elbow surgery and didn't play in the field before the season ended. He could go in the first five rounds and is a righty-hitting version of the only Dallas Baptist infielder ever to do so (Ryan Goins, fourth round, 2009), albeit with less arm strength. Glowenke's lone better-than-average tool is his bat, as he makes line-drive contact with ease. He controls the strike zone well and enhances his on-base ability by getting hit by more than his share of pitches. He can provide some doubles and perhaps 10-12 homers per season at the next level, but he didn't drive the ball with wood bats on the Cape. Glowenke's below-average speed almost certainly will push him to second base in pro ball. He's a sure-handed defender at shortstop, but he lacks the range to stay there. His average arm may be enough to get by at third base in a utility role, though neither it nor his power fits the profile to play regularly at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cannon significantly improved from season to season at Arizona and finished second in the Pacific-12 Conference batting race behind No. 1 overall pick Adley Rutschman with a .397/.478/.651 line as a junior in 2019. Boston's top pick (second round) that June, he signed for $1.3 million and hit just .200/.284/.324 in his pro debut. He didn't get a chance to rebound in 2020, when the pandemic limited his development to instructional league. For Cannon to become a big league regular, he'll have to get back to what made him a star with the Wildcats, which was controlling the strike zone with a line-drive, all-fields approach. After walking more than he struck out in college, he whiffed in one-third of his plate appearances in his first month as a pro before making better contact afterward. He doesn't possess more than average raw power, but his hitting ability should allow him to make the most of it and produce 12-15 homers per year. Cannon's bat is his only potential above-average tool. He shows fringy speed out of the batter's box and is a little faster underway, but most scouts don't think he has the quickness or arm strength to play shortstop at the upper levels. He has reliable hands and his average arm is a better fit at second base, where he looked much more comfortable during his first taste of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Politi redshirted in his first year at Seton Hall and went 6-7 with a 5.04 ERA in the next three seasons. Despite his modest success and fastball velocity, the Red Sox liked his pitch data enough to draft him in the 15th round and sign him for $25,000 in 2018. He acquitted himself well as a multi-inning reliever in high Class A during his first full pro season, then posted a 1.27 ERA in five late-season starts that left Boston rethinking his long-term role. Politi has added 2-3 mph to his fastball in pro ball and now deals at 92-95 mph and reaches 97. His four-seamer features some of the highest fastball spin rates in the system, creating armside run that eats up right-handers. His second-best offering is an upper-80s slider, and he also has made progress with a curveball while continuing to try to refine his changeup. While Politi had success in the rotation last summer, his long-term future likely will be in the bullpen. There's a lot going on in his max-effort delivery, making it difficult to repeat and thus to command his pitches. He projects as a long reliever who may not need much more than another year in the Minors before he's ready for an audition in Boston.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he signed for just $35,000 out of Panama, Bailey has provided the most positive early returns from the White Sox 2018-19 international class. He batted .324/.477/.454 in his 2019 pro debut, leading the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in on-base percentage and placing fourth with 52 walks. Beyond those stats, he's a 6-foot-4, 215-pounder with solid raw power and surprising athleticism. Very patient for his age without being too passive, Bailey has a relatively compact right-handed swing for his size and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. Content to make line-drive contact for now, he shows some home run power to his pull side and could have all-fields pop as he gets stronger and drives more balls in the air. As he matures physically, he likely will lose a step and become more of an average runner. Though he's athletic for his size and played all three outfield positions in his debut, Bailey spent most of his time in left field. With average speed and fringy arm strength, that likely will be his long-term position. In addition to his tools, club officials also praise his intelligence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high school outfielder from Mississippi who was the fastest player in the 2019 Draft, Beard inevitably drew comparisons to Billy Hamilton. He had almost no history facing quality pitching, so scouts weren't sure what to make of his bat, but his speed and athleticism landed him in the fourth round with a below-slot $350,000 bonus. His first taste of pro ball was a challenge, as he struck out in 39 percent of his plate appearances in Rookie ball. On the showcase circuit during the summer of 2018, Beard ran a 6.21-second 60-yard dash at a Prospect Development Pipeline event and created havoc on the bases at the East Coast Pro Showcase. He's so fast that he can beat out routine grounders, and once he improves his jumps, he could become a dynamic basestealer. If he gets more aggressive, he could become a plus defender in center, where his fringy arm is playable. Beard needs to gain a better understanding of his right-handed swing, improve his pitch recognition and plate discipline and figure out how pitchers are attacking him. Though he mostly hit soft grounders when he made contact in his debut, he has the bat speed, strong hands and ability to backspin the ball to be more than just a slap hitter. Though he'll require plenty of development time, he has the upside of an average hitter with double-digit homers and league-leading stolen base totals.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs signed Espinal for $200,000 at the beginning of the 2018-19 international period after being impressed with his premium athleticism and raw ability as a Dominican amateur. After he showed advanced baseball skills in the DSL, where he hit .358/.412/.460 over 47 games, the D-backs brought him stateside to finish the season in the Rookie-level Arizona League, where he continued to perform. Espinal began 2021 in Rookie ball once again, but worked his way up Low-A Visalia in July. Espinal’s top-flight athleticism and plus speed are on full display in center field, where he covers a lot of ground and projects as a plus defender. As he continues to develop physically, the D-backs think he will begin hitting for more power. As it is, he shows a really good feel for the strike zone, especially for someone so young. Espinal reminds some D-backs officials of what Geraldo Perdomo looked like at a similar age. It will take a while for Espinal to mature and refine his skills, but given those skills and his tools, there's plenty to dream on.
